## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that have Survived from the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, According to the Most Accurate Editions, Compared with One Another and with Several Manuscripts, and Corrected with the Greatest Diligence; Continuously Enriched with Dissertations, Commentaries, and Variant Readings; Augmented with All Works Discovered after the Extensive Editions Published during the Last Three Centuries; Furnished with Special Analytical Indexes Following Each Volume and Each Author of Any Importance; Adorned with Chapters Properly Arranged within the Text Itself, as well as with Titles Distinguishing the Upper Margin of Each Page and Indicating the Subject Matter Below; Enlarged by Works Both Doubtful and Apocryphal, and by Works Possessing Some Authority with Regard to Ecclesiastical Tradition; Enriched with Two General Indexes: One of Subjects, by Consulting Which Whatever Each Father Has Written on Any Topic May Be Seen at a Glance; the Other of Sacred Scripture, from Which It Is Easy for the Reader to Discover Which Fathers Have Commented on the Texts of the Individual Books of Scripture and in Which Places of Their Works.**

An edition exceptionally accurate and readily preferable to all others when one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes—uniformly similar throughout the entire work—the low price, and above all this collection, which is a single, systematic, and chronological compilation of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; thirteen hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eight hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# Continuation of the Works of Anastasius

[Col. 0009]

## The Eighth Holy General Synod, the Fourth of Constantinople, Interpreted by Anastasius

*(In Labbe, Collection of the Councils, vol. VIII, p. 962.)*

# Preface of Anastasius to the Eighth Synod

[Col. 0009A]

To the holy and co-angelic Father of Fathers, Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, I, your servant Anastasius, sinful abbot and librarian of your supreme apostolic see:

Since divine providence, which so distributes each thing among its proper times that it brings forth its saints, like shining stars, not all together but at distinct intervals for the illumination of its Church, has raised up your apostolate in our times like a certain brilliant star, during whose pontificate and under whose authority the eighth holy, universal, and great synod was celebrated, and sacred doctrine might behold the heaven of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church illumined with the radiance of true light after the darkness of errors had been driven away, I judged it worthwhile—both for the praise of its author and for the eternal remembrance of your apostolate—to commit to writing and briefly explain to your lordship what was the subject of that holy synod’s celebration, and what zeal or authority the Apostolic See exercised in arranging these matters; and also what it treated or defined.

For this reason I also wished to make readers attentive and concerned about why it is called either the Eighth Synod or the Universal Synod, and who interpreted it. I wished to prevent anyone, as time passed, from adding to the synod by presumption something that was not defined in it. In recording these things, I do not report them as though your apostolate were unaware of them; rather, as one who knows them and bears witness to them, I recall them to your memory in historical exposition.

In the time of the emperors Michael and his mother Theodora, after John the Iconoclast had been deposed, Ignatius was elected and consecrated patriarch of Constantinople. He had become a eunuch through the envy of Michael, formerly emperor and his father, when Michael voluntarily abandoned the imperial office out of love for religion. Later, choosing the monastic life, Ignatius shone from his earliest age in a monastery with remarkable splendor of character and virtues. Trained by long exercises and already advanced in age, having been tested in every kind of knowledge and good work, he was chosen and promoted by the unanimous consent of all to the summit of the high priesthood.

A very few bishops resisted his advancement; among them was Gregory of Syracuse. Ignatius had declared, in a canonical and gentle manner, that because certain crimes had been rumored and made public against them, he could not receive them into the priesthood before the judgment brought against them had been reconsidered. Since they did not cleanse themselves by that satisfaction, they were afterward rightly deposed by him and by the synod.

A certain senator serving in a secular administrative office, a secretary named Photius, favored these men. Desiring to rise to the patriarchal dignity, he gathered with them privately and, turning the faithful away from participation in Holy Communion, altogether refused to attend the divine mysteries when they were celebrated by Patriarch Ignatius. He had nothing in the cause of piety with which to reproach his own pontiff, except that he suspected Ignatius of accusing the life of his predecessor, the patriarch Methodius of holy memory. Yet Ignatius not only accused him in no respect whatsoever, but always extolled him with extraordinary praise. Indeed, while celebrating the divine mysteries, he commemorated him among the holy patriarchs and solemnly and unfailingly celebrated the annual observance in his name.

Photius, however, interpreting this and the rest of Ignatius’s actions maliciously, craftily declared to his followers that Ignatius acted with one purpose in his heart but demonstrated another in his deeds.

When Photius, joined to the schismatics whose leader was the aforementioned Gregory of Syracuse, persuaded all those who burned with an apparently pious affection for Methodius—“having zeal for justice, but not according to knowledge”—that Patriarch Ignatius was a detractor of Methodius of holy memory and therefore should be regarded as a kind of parricide, a rumor gained strength that Bardas, domestic of the Schools and brother of the empress Theodora, was polluting his own daughter-in-law by an incestuous relationship. The patriarch rebuked him for this crime and threatened to excommunicate him unless he abandoned so great an outrage.

Unable to endure this rebuke, Bardas joined the schismatics mentioned above and the deposed men, and devised an artful charge against the patriarch. He persuaded the emperor Michael to order the tonsuring of his mother and his sister Thecla, who had shared the imperial scepter with their mother and brother, and to place them in a monastery.

When the patriarch refused, because neither empress had freely chosen this profession—especially since he had sworn to them, according to custom, as he had sworn to other emperors and empresses, that he would never lay a plot against them—Bardas immediately said to the young emperor:

“Ho, emperor! Even now you do not perceive that Ignatius is breathing your death, and that your mother longs to join herself to another, namely, the future emperor, by marriage? This wretch has done these things, sparing not even his own sister, the empress, so that he might both take vengeance on the patriarch and, once both empresses—the mother and the daughter—had been expelled from the empire, either become the companion of the living emperor or, after killing him more easily, be installed as his successor.”

Then the emperor, gullible and enraged by so great a deception, drove his mother and sisters, after they had been tonsured, from the palace. At Bardas’s urging, he expelled Ignatius from the administration of the patriarchate, and Photius—mentioned above—was substituted for him by Bardas’s favor, contrary to the sacred canons and revered laws, which prohibit anyone from being suddenly promoted from lay service to the priesthood.

When Ignatius was being expelled, he placed the church under interdict, so that no one would dare to celebrate the sacred offices in it without him. When Bardas heard this, he inflicted such various tortures upon Ignatius on the island to which he had been banished that he broke his teeth and lacerated him with continual blows, until Ignatius declared that he renounced the administration of his Church—a Church from which he had already been prejudicially stripped and before any investigation completely deprived.

[Col. 0011D]

When these things became known, certain metropolitan bishops, as well as members of the lower clergy and laypeople, sympathizing with the torments of their pontiff and grieving over his deposition, began loudly demanding that their own ruler be restored to them.

Perceiving this, Photius, after persuading the emperor and with Bardas supplying the means, assembled a council of certain bishops who supported him through flattery or fear. He deposed the same Ignatius and struck him with anathema, hoping thereby to separate the people from him as from a condemned man. Nevertheless, up to that time he had permitted him, as though he were still a priest, to celebrate the divine sacrifices.

When this had been done, the piety of the faithful burned more and more intensely, and the whole flock sought its own pastor with greater steadfastness, the more cunningly the cruelty of the wolves raged.

Moreover, seeing that he had been frustrated in this matter, Photius sent to the Apostolic See, then presided over by your great predecessor, Pope Nicholas. He hoped that, once it had approved or decided in his favor, as he expected, the mouths of all who resisted him would immediately be silenced and every avenue of advancement, wherever he wished, would be opened to him.

The fool did not know what is read in blessed Job concerning God: “If he shuts a man in, there is no one who can open” (Job 12).

The aforementioned supreme pontiff received and examined his embassy. Although until then he had been unaware of Photius’s deceptions and deeds, he discovered almost everything that Photius had done through keen discernment. Following the true path of justice, he rejected not Ignatius, as Photius had requested, but Photius himself. He sent legates to Constantinople—namely, Radoald, bishop of Porto, and Zachary, bishop of Anagni—together with letters whose contents can more easily be learned by anyone who reads them. Since the question of the veneration of holy images was also involved, those letters contained certain writings on that matter as well.

When the legates of the Apostolic See reached Constantinople and a council had been assembled, the Greeks received the letters but altered and suppressed everything in them that favored Ignatius or opposed Photius, and would not allow them to be read in the council. The Roman legates understood or noticed nothing of what they were to read or not to read; indeed, they were already on the point of collapsing under force and fear.

What more is needed? Ignatius was brought forward and, already worn out by old age, was placed before the legates of the Apostolic See. He was again subjected to condemnation and even stripped of his priestly insignia, as though his deposition would thereby become more valid because the authority of the Apostolic See had been present through its representatives. Yet in these proceedings the authority of that See had not been involved, nor had those legates been sent in the manner of representatives, as the letters make clear.

When the Apostolic See learned of this, it did not tolerate the abandonment of so great an injustice with impunity. It wrote that such presumption must cease, and by its decree stripped Photius and his accomplices of sacred dignity when they refused obedience. It declared him and all his supporters excommunicated. First, it synodally imposed sentence upon the aforementioned legates, following the examples of Pope Felix of revered memory, who had similarly proceeded against the bishops Vitalis and Misenus when they had transgressed. It made clear to everyone how grievous to it was the deposition of its brother, not sparing even its own sons.

Because Photius did not obey this censure, the sacred company of the faithful was inflamed still more and separated itself in groups from his communion, horrified that he had not consented to be corrected even after being struck by so great a See. Harder than flint, he had shamelessly despised even harsh blows.

Photius bore this most bitterly and became violently enraged. Although Bardas, who had later been made Caesar and whose support had sustained him, was killed by the emperor Michael in a fitting retribution, Photius nevertheless diminished none of his cruelty. Some he condemned by depriving them of honors and dignities; others by confiscating their property; some he banished into prolonged exile and imprisonment; others he afflicted with various tortures.

To summarize everything briefly: no profession, sex, or age escaped him unpunished unless it was found to share his communion. He dragged away some who avoided his communion, except for a few who were shut up because they devoted themselves to contemplation. Others, living an eremitical life on Mount Olympus, he drove away, burning their huts or caves. One man who refused to communicate with him he even buried alive, from the lower part of his body up to the middle.

And—what is more horrible—under the presidency of the emperor Michael he assembled a council, fabricated false men as though they were representatives of the Eastern sees, armed the accusers with bribes, furnished them with lies, and adopted as witnesses those whom he set forward as accusers. Sometimes he admitted judges into the role of accusers; he invented and attributed certain offenses to the aforementioned supreme pontiff and, as he imagined, punished him simultaneously with condemnation and anathema.

Almost everyone present, except a very few who supported this impiety, cried out that it was unjust for a sentence to be pronounced against the supreme and first pontiff by an inferior authority in any manner whatsoever, since no canon permits it and no ecclesiastical custom teaches that it should be done.

But this forger, preparing a mendacious document of false offenses against an innocent man who was absent and undefeated, inserted the false subscriptions of approximately a thousand bishops. Of that great multitude of bishops, not one agreed with or wrote for him, except twenty-one prelates.

Therefore men in the sacred habit increasingly fled from him and avoided him as though he were some kind of filth, calling him another Dioscorus, the forerunner of Antichrist, or rather Antichrist himself—the man of sin and son of perdition whom the Apostle called one who would exalt himself above everything called God or worshiped (2 Thess. 2).

Furthermore, this worshiper of perverse doctrines contrived another device. He persuaded the emperor to order that no one should make a will or distribute alms through anyone’s hands except those of Photius. The inventor of evil devised this for no other reason than that, when he received and distributed the wealth of the rich, he might be thought by the less-discerning to have distributed his own property and thus be loved by all as generous and munificent. At the same time, he intended that everyone might at least in this way be compelled to communicate with him, since they would see that they could not perform even the remedies for their souls except through his hands, at least at the hour of death.

Moreover, weaving another net of his wickedness by which he might ensnare the minds of the simple, he compelled all who came to him for instruction in external discipline to promise in writing that from then on they would believe according to the faith of Photius—as though there were two faiths, one of Christ and another of Photius.

He devised this no less cunningly so that he might entangle everyone in his communion, by whatever means or in whatever manner, and make it impossible ever to tear him out, since it would be clear that he clung to so many firmly fixed roots. For those caught in these bonds were not permitted in any way to hold another faith than the one he himself held.

This caused enormous scandal among mortals, who said:

“So then, if Photius is a heresiarch, must our sons either become deserters from the Catholic faith or violate their oath and their written pledge?”

Some of them were indeed born of the most distinguished families. For several years earlier, Photius himself had declared that every human being consisted of two souls.

When Constantine the Philosopher, a man of great holiness and his most steadfast friend, rebuked him, saying, “Why, by spreading so great an error among the people, have you killed so many souls?” he replied:

“I did not propose such statements with the intention of harming anyone. I intended to test what Patriarch Ignatius would do if, in his time, some heresy arose and became evident through the syllogisms of philosophers—he who had rejected men devoted to secular wisdom. I did not know that, by the tinder of this proposition, I would injure so many souls.”

To this Constantine replied:

“O wisdom of the world, which is made foolish and destroyed! You cast arrows into a great multitude and did not know that one of all those people would be wounded.

“It is certainly clear to everyone that, just as eyes, however large and open they may be, cannot see beyond themselves if the smoke of straw lies between them, so the eyes of your wisdom, however large and wide, are completely blinded by the smoke of greed and envy and cannot see the path of justice. Thus what you say is true: you thought no one would be harmed by your blow, because, with your understanding blinded by the passions mentioned above against the patriarch, you did not foresee what you were releasing.”

Meanwhile Michael was killed, and Basil alone remained in control of the empire. For this reason everyone called him *monocrator*, “sole ruler.”

He began to inquire and investigate what judgment or decree the Apostolic See had issued concerning both the Iconoclasts—who seemed gradually, in a revival of their presumption, to be chattering against the holy images—and concerning Ignatius and Photius.

When he was told that from the eleventh indiction the Apostolic See had established Ignatius in the patriarchal throne of Constantinople, as it had done formerly, while it had judged Photius in no way worthy of any clerical order, and that it had sent various writings to Constantinople and throughout all the regions of the world to make these matters known, he immediately sought out those writings with great curiosity and attention.

When he found them lying buried more deeply by Photius, he placed them before his eyes like mirrors. Taking their reading as his guide, he rapidly brought to completion what had been decreed by that supreme See. That is, he persuaded Photius—who, after his deposition, was irregularly abusing the sacred ministry—to surrender the patriarchal throne of Constantinople, and he urged Ignatius to return to it.

But because Ignatius had resolved not to recover the throne from which he had been unjustly expelled without the renewed authority of the superior See, that is, the first See, and because the emperor desired—shamefully!—to eradicate everywhere the sentence that had been scattered throughout the Church of Christ, it seemed appropriate to both of them that envoys should be sent to Rome and to the three patriarchates of the East.

From Rome they were to request dispensatory decrees, the kinds of penalties to be adjudged according to the distinctions of the offenses and causes, and persons to act as representatives of the Apostolic See; from the Eastern thrones they were likewise to obtain consent and representatives.

It should certainly be noted that the other thrones, situated among the Hagarenes, undertook no labor in this matter. After coming to Constantinople, they reverently accepted what had been prepared and decreed by the Apostolic See, praised it with remarkable acclamations, and determined that nothing at all should be added to or taken away from it.

Accordingly, from the side of Ignatius, John, metropolitan of Sileum, who also presided over the Church of Perge in Pamphylia, was sent to Rome. From the side of Photius came Peter, metropolitan of Sardis, who, together with the aforementioned Gregory, had become the author of the ecclesiastical division against Ignatius.

The ruler also sent a royal *spatharius* named Basil, who was to stand between the two parties before the Apostolic See and faithfully hear and report what that See decreed.

Peter, however, although he sailed in a new ship of his own choosing, suffered both shipwreck and the danger of death. He who had divided Christ’s ship, that is, the Church, not improperly encountered the division of his own ship.

The other legates reached Rome and presented the letters and the profane document containing the proceedings of the council which Photius had falsely fabricated against Pope Nicholas of revered memory. They also presented everything that had been sent to that eminent pontiff, but since he had departed to the better life, they presented it to you, his illustrious successor, Lord Adrian, distinguished prelate of the Apostolic See, who were admirably governing its helm.

You girded your loins like a man, took upon yourself the spirit of the boy Daniel [another reading: “the spirit of the pious zeal of your predecessor,” etc.], and, turning neither to the right nor to the left from the royal road, decreed what he had decreed and established what he had established. As the pious heir, you carried out every command of your provident father and immediately avenged the injuries done to your own See.

For, as soon as a synod had been assembled at blessed Peter’s, you ordered that the profane document be burned. You also rightly commanded that the same be done at Constantinople if any copies of it were found there. This was done. You again condemned its author for so great a presumption and, with a similar censure, removed those who concealed copies of it.

You then sent representatives with apostolic authority and decretal letters, and ordered that a synod be held at Constantinople, for many needs of the Church but especially for those matters briefly recorded above and found in the proceedings of this synod. In that synod Photius was specifically condemned because he had presumed to name Pope Nicholas of holy memory in a sentence of deposition or anathema.

This most holy synod was therefore held in the third year of the reign of Basil, the pious ruler. Since it had all the patriarchal thrones, with prelates preserving their respective places, just as any other synod has had, it is rightly called by everyone “universal.”

It is universal, first, because the Catholic faith and the holy laws—which must be observed and venerated not only by priests but by all Christians—were defended in it with one harmonious voice against their enemies.

Second, because, since Christ has placed in his body, the Church, as many patriarchal sees as he has placed senses in each mortal body, the Church lacks nothing of universality if all those sees are of one will, just as a dead body lacks nothing if all five senses retain their complete and common health.

Among these sees, since the Roman See excels, it is not improperly compared to sight. Sight indeed surpasses all the other senses, being sharper than they and having communion with all of them, as none of the others does.

Third, because, since Photius had stained the whole Church with the disease of so many offenses, a universal cure was applied so that everything that had been wholly stained might be healed.

For the presumption of this ambition spread so widely and abundantly that soon at Jerusalem a certain layman named Solomon was immediately made a cleric and ordained bishop. This had never been done even by James, who was the first bishop there, except after Photius had recently been planted in the clergy and had immediately been heard to have become a bishop.

At Constantinople, moreover, certain men who were then still laymen devoted themselves to virtue only so that they might attain this sacred dignity. But when they were unable to obtain it, they immediately loosened the reins of continence and began to pursue their own pleasures [another reading: “wills”]. They quickly showed that they were not worshipers of holiness but of greed.

Indeed, some of them attempted by various means to obtain from the Roman legates that the rule should not be promulgated which was then issued in this same synod concerning the promotion of laymen suddenly into the priesthood.

Moreover, near Alexandria and Antioch the root of this plague grew so extensively that from the time of the promotion of the frequently mentioned Photius it has not yet been possible to uproot it.

It should not be thought that the synod would rightly have been called universal if it had been celebrated solely for the sake of the faith, since certain matters relating to the faith were defined in it, while in the other universal councils many things were arranged that did not relate to the doctrine of faith.

The acts of the Council of Constantinople show that those who sin against the faith do not sin less than those who violate the law [Note: Something appears to be missing, Col. 0015D]. Yet one sins no less against the holy rules than against the Catholic faith, and the devil remains condemned forever not because of a distortion of faith but because of the perversity of his works.

For just as without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God (Heb. 11), so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself (James 2). Thus those who profess this kind of faith, as it is written, “claim to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1).

Therefore those who profess this kind of faith, defiling the purity of right faith and violating the holy rule of justice, are to be corrected by the equal judgment of all, or certainly punished by a just sentence. Conversely, not only the steadfast guardians of right faith but also the diligent guardians of holy works are to be praised by all and enriched with a worthy share of heavenly rewards.

Now we properly seek the name of this synod. If the names of hydras and hippocentaurs—which do not exist—are nevertheless called names, how much more fittingly should the name of this synod be known, since it certainly exists, lest, lacking a name, it be compared with things placed in the depths of the sea which do exist but, because they have not come to human knowledge, have until now lacked names.

Therefore, if it is called merely “the synod,” it is not properly so called, for it shares that name with numerous other councils. If it is called “the universal synod,” that still does not proclaim what it possesses uniquely, since it shares this name with the seven general synods.

If it is called “the Constantinopolitan synod,” it is not properly named, for there are also other Constantinopolitan synods.

If it is called “the universal Constantinopolitan Eighth Synod,” its name still will not be stated definitively. For it is not the eighth but the fourth of those synods that have been celebrated universally at Constantinople.

It must therefore be called, without any contradiction, **the Eighth Universal Synod**, so that both the designation it shares with the other seven councils may not be concealed and its proper name, which it possesses uniquely, may be indicated.

When this venerable synod was being celebrated, it happened that I, your servant, attended as an envoy sent by the most pious emperor Louis with two other distinguished men. I also bore a legation from the apostolic merits of your adorned episcopate, concerning a marriage alliance that both sides hoped and prepared to bring about between the son of the emperor Basil and the daughter born of the aforementioned Augustus, the worshiper of God.

For in so pious a matter—one that was unquestionably believed to concern the unity of both empires, or rather the freedom of the entire Church of Christ—the assent of your supreme pontificate was sought above all.

By God’s providence it came about that I too rejoiced in the completion of so great a matter with the representatives of the Apostolic See, and that, coming, I bore sheaves of its fruits in gladness, having labored indefatigably for nearly seven years on its behalf and having diligently scattered throughout the whole world, by writing, the seeds of words.

For nearly everything pertaining to the present matter that was delivered from the Apostolic See in the Latin language—whether contained in the record of this synod or in other volumes—I, obeying the supreme pontiffs, explained to your predecessor and to you. Later, when I was staying in Constantinople on the aforementioned account, I provided no small assistance in these matters to your representatives, as they themselves also testify. Considering, moreover, the various turns of human affairs, I proposed to have the proceedings of this synod, which the representatives of the Apostolic See had written out and were carrying with them in one volume, copied into another codex and brought all the way to Rome.

It therefore happened that, when those same representatives fell among brigands and lost the codex itself together with all their belongings, I was recognized as having brought to Rome the codex I had carried. Your Holiness received it graciously and entrusted it to me for translation into Latin. I declared myself unequal to the task, although at the present time I am striving to undertake some effort in translating documents from the archives into the Roman language, and although I am known to have already translated and published certain works for the edification of many, especially at the urging of your predecessor.

Yet the command of so great a pontiff prevailed, since the obedience of a willing servant was not lacking. In translating this holy synod, I extracted it word for word, insofar as the Latin idiom permitted. Sometimes, however, while preserving the meaning, I necessarily changed the Greek construction into a Latin one. I left rare or difficult passages for a more learned translator to elucidate. I also noted in the margins of the codex certain matters as they were known to me—since I had labored diligently in all these affairs both at Rome and at Byzantium—or explained them as seemed appropriate to me.

This too should certainly be noted: I found that certain documents concerning these matters, which had been sent from the Apostolic See to Constantinople, had not been translated entirely correctly into Greek, because interpreters in that city were lacking. I corrected some of them myself, insofar as the short time allowed me to remain there; others, however, I left as I found them, still uncorrected.

Finally, it must plainly be stated, and committed more firmly to the memory of future ages as a precaution, that if in the course of time anything is found in Greek codices as having been added or changed by Constantinopolitan cunning in relation to this holy synod, it should be understood that nothing more or less was defined in this synod except what is found written in the Roman Church in the Greek codex of the acts of that synod, demonstrably translated into Latin with sufficiently faithful wording, and deposited in the archive of that Church; namely, what remains strengthened by the subscriptions of the representatives of all the patriarchal sees, as well as of the emperors themselves and all the bishops, and still bears their seals.

The letters of both the synod and the patriarch and emperors to the Roman pontiff, which are inserted at the end of the codex of the acts of that synod, must likewise be received with reverent respect. For they were decreed and issued with the consent of the entire synod while it was still in session.

Why I have prefaced these matters I shall briefly explain. When the king of the Bulgars, together with his own people, had received the Christian faith through a Roman—namely, a certain presbyter named Paul—he received from the Apostolic See not only the rule of faith but also the discipline of holy law as his instruction and sacred ordinance. This he did, instructed not only by the aforementioned presbyter but also by divine revelation, which so distinguished the circumstances of the times that it restored what came later to its former condition and order.

For all Dardania, Thessaly, Dacia, both Epirus, and the other regions situated along the river Ister had formerly been governed and administered chiefly under the direction of your Apostolic See. But after the emperors of the Romans, who are now called Greeks, became supporters or instigators of various errors and did not fear to tear the holy Church of Christ apart through diverse heresies, God divided their empire. By heavenly judgment they gradually ceased to reign in the western regions, until, having attempted without success to bend the Roman pontiffs to their depravity—and thereby having subjected them to manifold punishments—they completely lost power over Hesperia.

Although they had lost the empire of the West, they nevertheless continued trying to persuade the Roman pontiffs—since they could no longer command them—to accommodate their own injured senses with favor. But because those pontiffs, standing with Peter upon the rock of true confession, can hear such a deadly suggestion but cannot obey it, the Greeks, since they could not otherwise harm them, soon moved the ancestral and ancient boundaries, corrupted the privileges of the Apostolic See, and removed nearly all the rights of administering the dioceses. They bestowed these rights upon their own supporters and followers. With them they also usurped the jurisdiction which the Apostolic See had over the aforementioned regions, because those regions appeared to lie near them, and wickedly attached it to the Constantinopolitan diocese.

The blessed pope Innocent appears to say this in a letter to Alexander of Antioch, writing among other things:

> It therefore did not seem right that the Church of God should be changed according to the shifting needs of worldly affairs, or suffer honors or divisions which the emperor might judge ought to be made for his own purposes.

Yet they themselves did not enjoy these arrangements for long. The aforementioned Bulgar people immediately invaded and occupied everything around the Danube. Thus the Greek rulers in a way restored twofold, and according to the law, what they had taken from the Apostolic See. For, together with the jurisdiction of the usurped diocese, they also lost part of their own power—that is, part of their own empire.

At last, however, almighty God, who formerly rescued the children of Israel from the oppression of their afflicters even after four hundred and thirty years and taught them salutary doctrine, wished to lead these regions and their people also to the right path of faith and the equitable rule of justice. He inspired the aforementioned Bulgar prince, through the merits of Peter—whose intervention he prayed might assist him before God in his straits—to send to Rome and request from the Apostolic See teachings of faith and sound tradition.

The pious prince carried this out without delay. He sent to the Apostolic See, then presided over by your predecessor, Pope Nicholas of outstanding holiness, and requested from it not only the doctrines of orthodox faith but also the discipline of holy life, as well as teachers suitable for both purposes. He received Paul of Populonia and Formosus of Porto, bishops of holy conduct.

When they reached the prince and traveled throughout the entire homeland of the Bulgars, including the regions mentioned above, they did not cease their work. They cut up the soil of human hearts with the plowshare of the tongue, planted Christ in human minds by uprooting the brambles of error, watered them with the streams of holy baptism, laid their hands upon the heads of the faithful, and invoked through the Holy Spirit an increase of perfection upon the temples and altars dedicated to God. This continued while that apostolic pontiff—so to speak, a heavenly man and an earthly angel—remained alive.

Following his example, you, his successor, holy bishop of exalted and supreme greatness, yearned from the depths of your heart that the same things should be carried out energetically, and you did not cease striving to bring them to completion. The prince’s piety had grown so greatly, and his devotion toward blessed Peter had become so abundant, that one day he took hold of his own hair with his hand and, while everyone looked on, surrendered himself to the Roman envoys, saying:

> Let all the primates and all the peoples of the Bulgar lands know that from this day forward, after God, I shall be the servant of blessed Peter and of his vicar.

The Greeks heard this from day to day and grew envious. Eager for so great a glory, they sought various devices by which they might turn him away from the Roman See, sending numerous gifts upon gifts and repeatedly presenting him with sophistical arguments.

But he remained immovable like a pillar, until he was deceived by the fraud of those same Greeks, who wrote to him and said that a canonical dispute had been thoroughly examined between the Roman vicars and the patriarch Ignatius at Constantinople concerning whether that country ought to be subject to the Roman or the Constantinopolitan pontiff. They claimed that the Roman representatives of the Eastern sees, meeting together, had judged that the Bulgar diocese ought to be subject to the city to which it had been subject before the arrival of the Bulgars.

They added that there is one arrangement of jurisdiction in worldly affairs and another in ecclesiastical matters; and that although that region had formerly been subject to the Greeks, they could not legitimately claim any right over it, since they had once lost it by arms and had been unable to recover it through so many years of warfare. Indeed, even before it had been subject to the Greeks, it is evident that the Romans possessed it; nor is it recorded that the Greeks held it, as has been shown above, except while they possessed the Roman scepter.

Even if the Greek rulers had dominated that region in civil matters, they could not thereby prejudice the right of the Church of God. However much they may have struggled with various nations, whether defeated or victorious, the Church knows nothing but charity and peace. Hence one of the Church’s teachers exclaims:

> If anyone seems contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God. (1 Cor. 11)

Nevertheless, there is no reliable evidence that the Eastern representatives actually made this decision.

Although the Roman representatives and the Bulgar envoys had met with the emperor or patriarch and with the representatives of the Eastern sees, when all these persons had been placed in one chamber, no outsider was admitted unless the emperor or patriarch happened to permit it. As a result, whatever the Romans asserted was understood neither by the Eastern representatives nor by the Bulgar envoys; and, conversely, whatever the Easterners said was understood neither by the Roman representatives nor by the Bulgar envoys.

Only one imperial interpreter was present. He dared to render the words of neither the Roman nor the Eastern representatives except in the manner already commanded by the emperor for the subversion of the Bulgars. The Bulgar envoys were, however, given a written document composed in Greek words and letters. It purported to state that the Eastern representatives, acting as arbiters between the Roman representatives and the patriarch Ignatius, had judged that the Bulgar homeland, which lies in Illyricum, should be subject to the Constantinopolitan diocese.

Yet it is clearly established that the Apostolic See had always administered Dardania, Dacia, Thessaly, both Epirus, and the other provinces situated in Illyricum. This is attested by the various letters of the Roman pontiffs sent through those provinces from Pope Damasus onward. The Greek rulers, aided by the Constantinopolitan bishops, subjected these regions to themselves by force, and only for the reason noted above.

The Apostolic See is not found to have lodged any complaint concerning their recovery, because immediately afterward, as has been stated, the often-mentioned Bulgar nation entered these regions and claimed them all for itself by right of power. But when religion returns, the lawful jurisdiction of the diocese is immediately restored to its proper see.

When the Romans and the representatives, observing only the general sense of the Greeks’ words, asserted these and similar points, they pursued the matter further, saying:

> It is clear to everyone that neither we nor the representatives of the Eastern sees were invited to come to Constantinople for the purpose of claiming any dioceses. We were summoned either by the pious emperors or sent by our bishops to settle and define the controversy for which we were appointed. With God as our author, we resolved that controversy and confirmed it by our individual subscriptions.
>
> As for the diocese of Illyricum, which the Apostolic See possesses in peaceful retention by ancient right and by the present restoration of its possessors, and over which it exercises its canonical authority, that principal see was neither summoned nor challenged to send representatives on its behalf. Nor do we assume the role of its advocates or defenders, nor do we know what it would answer to the objections if it were present, since we have received no mandate from it. Consequently, having not been ordered to dispute this matter, we cannot do so.
>
> Nor do we suppose that the representatives of the Eastern sees will assume the role of judges in controversies in which they have not been called or chosen as judges by both parties. The Apostle says: “A mediator of one is not” (Gal. 3:20). The sacred canons teach that the judgment not of just anyone but of chosen judges must by no means be disregarded. And one of the respected Fathers says: “He is not a just mediator who hears one party in such a way that he leaves nothing for the other party.”

We have said these things to make diligent persons vigilant, lest, with the passage of time, anything concerning the subjection of the land of the Bulgars to the Constantinopolitan diocese be thought to have been established or defined by the universal and eighth synod, or lest the Greeks be presumed to have added anything of that sort to the codex of its acts.

This presumption is familiar to them and is in some way a distinctive mark of their ambition. In the second synod, contrary to the decrees of the great Council of Nicaea and the decisions of the holy Roman bishops, they transferred the privileges of the Alexandrian See to the Constantinopolitan pontiff. Certain canonical chapters are also found among them which they say belong to the third synod, although they are not found among the Latin editions, even the most ancient.

In certain codices of the fourth synod they likewise display a chapter concerning the privileges of Constantinople. Yet among the canons of that same synod, venerated by the universal Church, neither Latin nor any other language under the sun is shown to have received it.

Although this chapter may have been secretly produced by Anatolius, the emperor, or their supporters after all the proceedings of the synod and the promulgation of the canons, in the absence of the Roman representatives, it was immediately rejected there by those same representatives. The Apostolic See alone had decreed that the synod should be held and alone possessed the right to receive those whom the synodal decrees had produced. It not only did not admit the chapter but immediately rejected it.

Anatolius or the emperor, since he could not obtain its confirmation from the Apostolic See, then presided over by the great Leo, nevertheless confessed that the matter lay within that See’s authority.

They also display many other highly presumptuous canonical chapters, altogether contrary to ancient tradition, which they falsely claim were promulgated by the sixth synod. But the sixth synod promulgated nothing except the rule of faith. The canons which they claim as belonging to it are known to have been produced privately among them long after the sixth synod.

In the codex of the seventh synod, because bishops are often promoted from among neophytes at Constantinople, and because Tarasius had at that time been ordained patriarch from the laity, they have arranged for the letter of Pope Adrian of blessed memory to be copied in such a way that nothing in it concerning that bishop or against neophytes, which the most holy pontiff had written, is found either written or translated into Greek.

Thus it is clear that the Greeks have frequently acted in this way whenever they have had an opportunity in connection with the universal councils: now diminishing, now adding or changing, now in the absence of their associates, now in a hidden corner, now outside the synod, now after the synod. By their cunning—or rather, by their fraud—they abuse the common decrees and violently bend everything that seems suitable to them to their own desires.

Therefore, whatever is found in the Latin codex of the acts of the eighth synod is free from every taint of falsification. Whatever more is perhaps found in the Greek codex of that same synod, whether concerning the Bulgar diocese or anything else, is entirely infected with the poison of falsehood.

Finally, the dispute which we indicated above had been conducted before the emperor, the representatives, and the Bulgars solely concerning the land of the Bulgars took place after the synod had been completed, after the canons had been issued in twenty-seven chapters and the statement of faith had been produced, after all these matters had been written or compiled in five codices and confirmed by everyone’s subscriptions, and after the codices themselves had been secured with leaden seals and delivered individually to the representatives, to be brought to the patriarchal sees.

Therefore, lest the Greeks’ cunning—or rather their deceit—also operate concerning the present synod, it is enough that I have said these things as a warning.

I know well, moreover, that, according to Proverbs, “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged” (Prov. 1:17). Thus whoever is lifted on the wings of wisdom and prudence to lofty heights will leap over, with lofty contempt, all the traps of ambush which the Greeks may be able to set below.

May the Divinity deem your apostolate worthy to be preserved for many years, most blessed lord pope.

[Note: That is, a brief summary.]

# BRIEF SUMMARY OF THE PROCEEDINGS

Made by the holy and universal eighth synod, in each of its most sacred sessions, for the Catholic Church—that is, for the apostolic and orthodox doctrines—and for its salutary condition.

The first session contains the preface and the sittings of the synod; the synod’s command; the entrance of the patriarchal persons; the bishops who had been mistreated; the exhortation of the Roman representatives ordering them to sit; the imperial document sent for reading; the declaration of the representatives and the princes; the questions of Bahanes, patrician and chief official; the answers of the Roman representatives; Pope Adrian’s letter to Emperor Basil; the synod’s thanksgiving after the letter had been read; the letter of Theodosius, patriarch of Jerusalem, to Ignatius the patriarch; the approval of the commendatory letters; the Roman memorandum; the statement of the aforementioned Bahanes; praise of the memorandum; the definition of Thomas of Antioch and Elias of Jerusalem, the representatives, in chapters; the approval of the definition according to the decrees of Pope Nicholas; the senate’s questions concerning Photius; and the representatives’ answers, together with the approval, thanksgiving, and praise of these matters.

The second session contains the sitting of the synod; the entrance of the bishops who had fallen; their memorandum; the statement of the Roman representatives concerning the writing of the Roman memorandum; the reading and writing of that memorandum; the reception of the bishops; the entrance of the priests, deacons, and subdeacons with a memorandum of repentance; the reception of the Roman memorandum written by them; and a summary and the praise of those who had fallen, together with interpretations of the verses.

The third session contains the sitting of the synod; the petition of Metrophanes and certain of his fellow bishops concerning the reading of the letters of Emperor Basil and Patriarch Ignatius sent to Rome; the demand made of the representatives for the preparation of the Roman memorandum; certain bishops who at first refused to undertake this task but later completed it; the letter of the aforementioned emperor and of Patriarch Ignatius to Pope Nicholas; Pope Adrian’s letter to Patriarch Ignatius, delivered by the bishops Donatus and Stephen and the deacon Marinus; thanksgiving and praise; and verses.

The fourth session contains the sitting of the synod; the report concerning Theophilus and Zacharias, formerly bishops; the statement of the senate, of Metrophanes the metropolitan, and of the Roman representatives; the entrance of Zacharias and Theophilus into the holy synod and their dispute with the Roman representatives; Pope Nicholas’s letter to Emperor Michael, sent through Raduald and Zacharias, then bishops; the statement of the judges; and the same pontiff’s letter to the aforementioned emperor, transmitted through Leo the secretary; the statement of Theophilus, formerly bishop, and of Theodore, metropolitan of Caria; Pope Nicholas’s letter to Photius through Leo the secretary; the presentation of Photius, who was not received by the patriarchal sees; the record of the memoranda made by Zacharias and Theophilus at Rome; and prayers with praises.

The fifth session contains a fuller sitting of the synod; the announcement of Paul the chartophylax, reporting that Zacharias—or Photius—was present; the dispatch of the representatives with an imperial official to him and his conversation with them; the reading of Photius’s speeches and the synod’s statement addressed to him, dictated by Elias the syncellus; the reading of Photius’s response; the synod’s acclamation addressed to Photius; the entrance of Photius; the question of who he was and whether he accepted the decisions of the Fathers; the questioning by the Roman representatives; silence; and finally the speech of Photius and of the Easterners.

The representatives’ reply; the exhortation of the Roman representatives; Photius’s renewed silence; the reading of Pope Nicholas’s letters, which had been read in the fourth session; and, before Photius, the reading of another letter of Pope Nicholas sent to him through Raduald and Zacharias. The address of Elias, the representative of Jerusalem; the address of the Roman representatives; approval of the matters read; the exhortation of the Roman representatives and of Bahanes the patrician to Photius; and his response. Bahanes again admonishes him; Photius remains silent; after being granted a delay, he leaves; and the aforementioned Stephen praises him.

The sixth session records the sitting of the synod; the pronouncement of Metrophanes, metropolitan of Smyrna; the imperial reading-document of the Roman representatives; the admission of the bishops of Photius, before whom the letters of Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael and to Photius, sent through Leo the secretary and contained in the fourth session, were read; the acclamation of Elias the syncellus; the dispute between Emperor Basil and Euchemon and the other bishops of Photius; the declaration of Zacharias, bishop of Photius; and the emperor’s dispute with the bishops of Photius’s party.

The speech of Eulampius and the indignation of the Roman representatives; the emperor’s statement; the questioning of the bishops consecrated by Ignatius, with the Roman representatives speaking to them; the opposition of Metrophanes, metropolitan of Smyrna, to the aforementioned Zacharias; the speech of the Roman representatives; the emperor’s admonition to the schismatics; and likewise the repeated admonition of the Roman representatives and the others to those same persons, together with praises.

The seventh session records the sitting of those assembled; the entrance of Photius leaning on a staff, which Marinus, the Roman representative, ordered to be taken away from him; the Roman representatives’ exhortation to Photius to prepare a memorandum; and their appeal, together with the entire synod, to repentance. He, on the contrary, urged them and his own followers even more strongly to repentance. The speech of the Eastern representatives contradicts him.

Bahanes’s questioning; Photius’s response; the entrance of his bishops; the purpose of the synod and of Photius’s bishops; the emperor’s address to them through Bahanes the chief official; Bahanes’s dispute with them; and the emperor’s declaration. The renewed disagreement of Photius’s bishops with Bahanes; the exhortation of the Roman representatives to read Pope Nicholas’s letter sent to the clergy of Constantinople; and its reading.

Also, Pope Adrian’s letter to Emperor Basil through Theognostus the exarch, and another letter sent to Ignatius; the reading of Pope Adrian’s letters to the emperor and the patriarch, delivered through the representatives Donatus, Stephen, and Marinus, which are written in the third session; and the subscription of the pope, bishops, priests, and deacons to the acts of the council assembled by that same pope in the church of blessed Peter.

The memorandum of the Roman representatives addressed to Photius; the acclamation of Ignatius to the synod; the anathema against Photius and his party; and the proclamations and imprecations of the emperor and synod; together with verses concerning Photius.

The eighth session records the sitting of the synod; the emperor’s address through Bahanes; the Roman representatives’ request that the unjust written declarations be abolished; and the burning of those declarations, together with the acts of the councils held by Photius against Pope Nicholas and Patriarch Ignatius.

The memorandum of Peter the monk; the examination of the false representatives; and a chapter of blessed Pope Martin concerning such matters; the address of Metrophanes; the summoning of Theodore Crithinus the Iconoclast; and the examination of these persons; Pope Nicholas’s chapter concerning images; the conversion of certain Iconoclasts; and the admonitions of the emperor and synod.

The anathema pronounced against the Iconoclasts, Photius, and his party; prayers; and praises.

The ninth session likewise contains, after the sitting of the synod, the senate’s announcement that the representative of the Alexandrian See had arrived. At the synod’s urging, his commendatory letter was read and he himself was received. He approved the proceedings, and his meaning was as follows.

The written examination of the false witnesses who had sworn against Patriarch Ignatius, and their repentance; then the admission and examination of those who, although laymen, put on priestly vestments and appeared to celebrate divine mysteries; the speech of the Roman representatives and another of the Eastern representatives; the repeated examination of the false representatives; thanksgiving; imprecations and praises; and verses concerning Photius.

The tenth session contains the synodal sitting, with the envoys of the emperor of the West and of the Bulgar prince seated there; the canons and the statement of faith set forth by the synod; the emperor’s question and the response of the entire synod approving the canons and statement that had been read; imprecations and praises; and the emperor’s grateful address to the synod.

The same emperor’s speech, in which he promises good things to the bishops and urges them, if anyone wishes to say anything against the synod, to state it without fear. He demonstrates by authoritative reasoning that laymen do not possess the right to govern ecclesiastical affairs. He warns them to avoid schisms, to be vigilant against heresies, to shun quarrels, and to be examples to their subjects.

The emperor’s question whether the synod approved what had been read; the synod’s approval of all these matters and promise to confirm them by subscription; the emperor’s declaration that he wished to subscribe after all the bishops; the order of subscription; the voice of the senate professing its acceptance of the synod; praises; the subscriptions of the representatives, emperors, and bishops; the synod’s encyclical letter; a letter to Adrian, the most holy pope; the emperors’ letter to the patriarchs; and also the letter of Patriarch Ignatius to Adrian, the most holy pope, consulting him concerning the Three Chapters.

Immediately after the synod, at the consultation of that holy council, Emperor Basil’s letter was sent to the same pope, followed by the letter of the same most blessed pope replying to that prince.

Here end the chapters briefly indicating what each session of the synod contains.

# ACTS OF THE HOLY AND UNIVERSAL EIGHTH SYNOD, WHICH WAS ASSEMBLED AT CONSTANTINOPLE

## SESSION ONE

The principal Word of God, who is himself the Truth—namely, Christ, the Savior and Lord of us all—contains within himself the knowledge and comprehension of all ages, and knows all things before they exist. Consulting his holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, he foretold the cunning of evil-doers, saying in the Gospels:

> Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits. (Matt. 7)

By these words he clearly indicated the form of the wickedness and depravity hidden in the inner person: those who display the appearance and form of piety, but perform deeds resembling the worst passions which exist around the soul.

Therefore he immediately added:

> Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but a bad tree produces bad fruits. (Matt. 7)

And showing that it is impossible for things belonging to one kind to be changed into the nature of another, he immediately continued:

> A good tree cannot produce bad fruits, nor can a bad tree produce good fruits. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus you will recognize them by their fruits. (Ibid.)

[Note: That is, false prophets.]

Photius, therefore, is also in our own times a man whose inner person is full of wickedness and evil deeds. Out of ambition and love of glory, and so that he might be called “Rabbi,” he pretended to be good and feigned that he possessed the habit and appearance of piety.

By these means he then deceived and led astray the rulers. Through human contrivance and royal authority and power, he obtained our Church after its lawful and most blessed supreme shepherd, the most holy patriarch Ignatius, had been unjustly deposed and expelled.

But shortly afterward, once the assumed persona had been removed and hypocrisy had been exposed as such, the tree was again revealed by its fruits, even to those very men who were still almost in possession of the empire and had rashly proposed to promote him, only later to repent of it uselessly and fruitlessly.

[Note: He means Bardas Caesar, the supporter of Photius.]

He became someone to be fled and hated by all, and even more so by the pious and industrious people throughout our world. Above all, however, through the most merciful imperial and divine providence, he was made manifest to the holy Roman Church and to the patriarchal thrones situated in the East by the worst and most depraved fruits which he brought forth.

Therefore God, who is jealous and Lord of vengeance, discovering in blessed Pope Nicholas another zealous Elijah, raised him up for the aid of truth. In the Holy Spirit, through what he wrote, he repeatedly tore apart the wolf’s skin, exposed and displayed his inner madness and rage, and, setting against him the word of God—which discerns thoughts—and the sword of the Spirit, immediately cut down the tree by its roots, since it had neither been well planted nor produced good fruits.

He slew the robber, wolf, and ravager of souls like a bandit and thief, and likewise destroyed the priests of confusion who were with him. Indeed, like another Peter, he killed another Ananias, who was secretly taking what belonged to others and lying to the Holy Spirit, by the force of his own words (Acts X), while the friend of Christ, divinely guided and bearing the name of Basil, our most God-loving emperor, served and obeyed the divine will and decree.

[Note: “Bearing the name with him”: that is, his name agrees with his dignity. Indeed, Basil is evidently written with almost the same letters as basileus, that is, emperor.]

Our emperor Basil assembled the universal synod and piously carried out whatever seemed good to the Holy Spirit. He rejected, utterly deposed, and abolished the man who, by an antiphrastic figure, was called Photius.

[Note: Photius means “illuminated.”]

He also deposed those who had been promoted by Photius and consecrated in any ecclesiastical rank. Some of these he deprived only of the entire priestly order, because they had rebuked and rejected their consecrator long before, on account of the things which they saw him carrying out wickedly and irregularly.

Others he deposed and anathematized together with him, because they were discovered to be his followers and to agree with him in all his evil deeds. In addition, the Iconoclasts—those who hold impious and injured opinions against the holy and venerable images—received the same judgment and decree of condemnation as Photius and his followers.

Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople, was lawfully and synodically restored and firmly established in his own see. Thus the divine Scripture’s saying is now fulfilled:

> The integrity of the upright guides them, but the perversity of the faithless captures them. (Prov. 11:3)

# THE SESSION BEGINS.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0029B] Amen.

In the third year of the consulship of our friends of Christ and most devout emperors, Basil and Constantine, perpetual Augusti, in the third indiction, in the month of October, on the fifth day, Wednesday, with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation placed on the right-hand side of the catechumenia [Note: [Col. 0029D] Catechumenia are places where catechumens are instructed.] of the most renowned church of holy and great-named Sophia; with Donatus and Stephanus, bishops beloved of God, and Marinus, venerable deacon, acting in the place of Adrian, most holy and blessed archbishop of senior Rome, and Ignatius, most honorable archbishop of great-named Constantinople, New Rome, and with the most holy legates of the East—namely, Thomas, most holy metropolitan of Tyre, acting in place of the see of Antioch, because [Col. 0029C] that Church was widowed; and Elias, God-fearing priest and syncellus, acting in place of Theodosius, most holy archbishop of the see of Jerusalem.

Then, according to the command of our friends of Christ and most devout, great emperors Basil and Constantine, in the presence and hearing of the most praiseworthy patricians—namely, Theodore, most praiseworthy patrician and praepositus; Himerius, most praiseworthy proconsul and patrician; Theophilus, most praiseworthy proconsul and patrician; Leo, most praiseworthy proconsul and patrician; John, most praiseworthy patrician and logothete of the exodromus [Note: [Col. 0029D] Prodomus means “swift course.”]; Leo, most praiseworthy patrician and commander of the excubitors; Paul, most praiseworthy patrician and prefect of the praetorium; Manuel, most praiseworthy patrician; Theophylact, most praiseworthy [Col. 0029D] patrician; Petronas, most praiseworthy patrician; and Orestes, protospatharius and commander of the ycanatores [kinsmen]—when these had assembled, the most holy legates of senior Rome, and Ignatius, most holy archbishop of Constantinople, and the most honorable legates of the East said:

“Let all the bishops enter, all who have labored and contended for the word of truth, as being in agreement with Ignatius, most holy archbishop of Constantinople.”

When they had entered—namely, Nicephorus, God-loving metropolitan of Amasia; John, God-loving metropolitan of Sile; Nicetas, God-loving metropolitan of Athens; Metrophanes, God-loving metropolitan of Smyrna; Michael, God-loving metropolitan of Rhodes; George, God-loving bishop of Heliopolis; Peter, God-loving bishop of Troad; Nicetas, God-loving bishop of Cephalludium; Anastasius [variant: Athanasius], God-loving bishop of Magnesia; Nicephorus, God-loving bishop of Croton; Antonius, God-loving bishop of Alisa; and Michael, God-loving bishop of Corcyra—the most holy legates of senior Rome and of the East said:

“Let them sit according to their rank, for they are worthy; and we consider them blessed and thrice blessed.”

When they had taken their seats, [Col. 0030B] Bahanes, most renowned patrician and praepositus, standing in the midst, said to the holy synod:

“Our holy emperor has sent an epanagnosticum [Note: [Col. 0029D] An epanagnosticum is a document that is read publicly; for the Greek word ἐπὶ means not only ‘upon’ but also ‘before’ or ‘in the presence of.’ [Col. 0030D]], and if you command and it pleases you, let it be read before the holy synod.”

The most holy legates of senior Rome and of the East said:

“We approve the proposal.”

Theodore, the devout a secretis, took it and read:

“When divine and most benevolent providence had entrusted us with the helm of the universal ship, we applied ourselves wholly, even before our public duties, to dissolving ecclesiastical disputes and transferring into stable tranquility, through a better kind of foresight, the storms which for many years had been spread by the envy of Satan, who hates the good. In this matter, while our divinely fortified empire always bore this desire and judged most carefully that the time was opportune, and while it also judged that, for the aforesaid reason, legates should be brought from the other patriarchal sees, the sole King and Prince of peace, of infinite power, cooperated with the intention of our divinely governed empire. As you see, he has fulfilled our plan and caused us to assemble and converge for the same purpose: from senior Rome, two bishops and one deacon out of the seven prescribed, distinguished by prudence, understanding, and venerable conduct [Note: [Col. 0029D] It was prescribed that there should be only seven deacons in the Church, namely, in the diocese of the first see, Antioch.]; from the East, the protothrone of Antioch, that is, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, full of every reverence; and from the holy Church of God at Jerusalem, namely holy Sion, from which he went forth who was foretold, and the new law, and the Lord’s word, discerner of all nations, the most holy syncellus, an apostolic man [Col. 0030D], filled with every kind of divine and human wisdom.

“Therefore, by the cooperation and grace of Christ, King of all, and of God who holds all things, since we have changed what seemed crooked to all of you into straight paths, and rough places into level roads, through our imperial diligence and zeal, we admonish and exhort all of you, brothers, to come together with great modesty and reverence to this holy and universal synod, as one that is both common and suited to all, [Col. 0031A] and a remedy without envy. Bring no faulty impulse or inclination, and do not look toward a contentious will; rather, know how to be rightly defeated than to win culpably and unjustly. For thus each person who suffers from an inner corruption will receive health and eternal salvation.

“Moreover, we address to you yourselves an acclamation on behalf of our empire, since you have received from God the authority of synodal judgment. Indeed, we have no doubt that, insofar as possible, you are lovers and imitators of truth and divine justice. But, so that it may be clear that our empire, fortified by God and acting according to the measure of authority granted to it, has kept silent about nothing in ecclesiastical matters that ought to be stated and is appropriate, we ask your religious devotion to become, above all now, victorious over every favor and hatred; indeed, to be likened with all your strength, insofar as possible, to the impassible and blessed nature, so that you neither accept the person of the powerful because of rank or friendship, nor pity the poor in judgment. For thus, in accordance with the counsel and will of God and of our most tranquil empire, the churches will receive the most peaceful ordering.

“After the reading, the legates of senior Rome said:

“‘This matter is universal and concerns the benefit of the Church; and it pleases the holy synod and all of us that it be read.’

“Thomas and Elias, the most holy legates of the East, said:

“‘It has likewise pleased us.’

“And the sacred senate said:

“‘It has pleased all of us as well.’”

Bahanes, most renowned patrician and praepositus, then rose again [Col. 0031C] and said:

“The bishops, together with the senate, ask to be assured at this hour of where you come from, what authority you possess, and what sort of letters you bear.”

Donatus and Stephanus, most holy bishops, and Marinus, God-loving deacon and legate of senior Rome, said:

“We have not hitherto found this done in a universal synod: that the legates of senior Rome should be examined by anyone as to whether they possess such standing.”

Bahanes, most renowned patrician and praepositus, said:

“We say this not because we dishonor the apostolic throne, but because your predecessors, Radoaldus and Zacharias, who came as legates, deceived us, having one set of instructions but doing another thing.”

The most holy legates of senior Rome said:

“Therefore, so that we may remove every doubt from your hearts [Col. 0031D], and assure you by both words and deeds that we will act according to what has been entrusted and commanded to us, behold, we also have letters to the emperor and the patriarch; and if you command, let them be read.”

And again the same men said:

“The most devout and Christ-loving emperor and the most holy patriarch of Constantinople, Ignatius, sent their most noble and most faithful envoys, men of their sacred empire and of the Church of God—John, metropolitan of Sile, and Basil, the most distinguished spatharius—to the most blessed pope Nicholas. But since he had departed to the Lord, Adrian, his successor, the most holy pope of senior Rome, received the letter. They asked him to send his envoys to Constantinople, [Col. 0032A] so that error and tares might be uprooted from the Church of Constantinople. And behold, by the grace of God, we came into the presence of the holy emperors and found in that same holy Church of the Constantinopolitans the most holy patriarch Ignatius. We have in our hands the letter which the most holy pope Adrian sent to the emperor; he also gave us authority to arrange, regulate, and confirm matters according to what the most blessed pope Nicholas determined concerning the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans, so that no one might be able to fight against it, and so that we might confirm what the most holy Adrian himself issued. For whoever has received the honor has also received the labor; because of this God placed him in His Church.

“Behold the letter of the most holy pope Adrian; and if you wish, let it be read, as we have said.”

The holy synod said:

“Let it be read.”

Marinus, God-loving deacon of the holy Roman Church, took it and read the letter in Latin in a loud voice for all to hear, while Damianus, most venerable imperial cleric and interpreter, rendered it into Greek.

“Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the God-loving and most devout emperor Basil Augustus, most Christian and most beloved son.

‘The excellent embassy of Your Highness, etc. For the remainder, see among the letters of Pope Adrian II, volume 122 of the Patrologia.’

After the reading of the letter, Ignatius, most holy archbishop of Constantinople, and all the God-loving bishops, together with the most magnificent princes, cried out [Col. 0032C]:

“Blessed be God, who has deemed us worthy to receive complete satisfaction from your holiness.”

After this, the most holy legates of senior Rome and the entire holy synod requested that the commendatory letters of the Eastern legates be read, so that it might be known from where they too had come and what authority they had received from their respective sees.

When this had been done, Elias, most God-revering priest and syncellus and the Jerusalemite legate, stood and said for all to hear:

“Your Christ-loving charity, brothers, does not fail to know—and has not failed to learn from us ourselves and from our rulers, the emperors, who we are, whence we come, and what sort of men we are. Nevertheless, for fuller satisfaction, we now say it again to you.

“For the most holy Thomas, metropolitan of Tyre, [Col. 0032D] as you also know, belongs to the first see, the see of Antioch. Since that patriarchal see is deprived of a patriarch, he himself occupies that see until a patriarch is appointed to it. For this reason he was not required to bring letters sent by someone else, since he himself possessed authority and power in that see. Because he speaks Greek with difficulty, I have now said these things at his request.

“As for me, since I am syncellus of the see of Jerusalem, following the commands of our chief priest Theodosius and having his letters in my hands, I came here; you have also heard them. But if some did not hear them earlier, especially because of the legates of senior Rome, behold, they are at hand and may be read, so that each of you, diligently learning the truth, may be assured.

“We also wish to show your God-loving charity something else: since we have remained here for a long time and have been distressed for an even longer period, we made a supplication to our most devout and holy emperor, asking for a speedy release to return home. He, being compassionate, pitying, and merciful, yielded to our tears and wished immediately to satisfy us and dismiss us more quickly. He ordered us to set down in writing for him our wishes concerning the matters in question, and how we intended to act and judge concerning ecclesiastical cases when the brothers, the legates of senior Rome, arrived.

“But we, with God as our witness [Note: [Col. 0033D] That is, ‘with God as witness.’], who knows the hidden things of human beings and examines hearts and kidneys, approving or judging nothing through favor or partiality, set out our views in writing concerning the matters proposed [Col. 0033B]. These writings, when read by us, will now display those same views and judgments more clearly and plainly. Let what was written by our patriarch be read first; afterward, with God’s help, you will learn our views through the definitions we have set forth.”

The God-loving legates of senior Rome said:

“It pleases us. Let them be read.”

Likewise the holy synod said:

“Let them be read.”

Stephanus, God-loving deacon of the holy Church of Constantinople and devout notary, took the document and read:

“‘To the most holy brother and fellow minister, the lord Ignatius, who guides the helm of the most renowned Constantinople, universal patriarch, Theodosius, servant of Jesus Christ, of Jerusalem.

“‘Having received the honorable and most venerable letter of Your Holiness, glorified by God, we greatly rejoiced in the health and safety divinely granted to you, wishing you to be prosperously preserved from every evil. But the discord in the affairs of your Church caused us grief and filled us with great sorrow, namely, the alternating communion and harmony of its members. For, according to the most ancient saying, among the things belonging to orthodox churches there is one convergence, one concord, and one shared suffering.

“‘But just as among the members of the body some organs have naturally been formed by the Creator for living, and others for living well, and as star differs from star in brightness, [Col. 0033D] so one must also think concerning the churches. For whatever has been placed there in disorder will consequently grieve those who follow and those who are lesser, since it creates a greater division from this point. When the operative cause has been changed for a while from its natural movement, and when what flows and pours forth from the fullest and most capacious places is diverted, the inflow that comes afterward will be greater and will cause distress.

“‘Thus, these events, which occurred as the cause of your confusion, have brought us especially mournful and sorrowful things. But He who placed resin in Gilead and prepared a physician there will Himself restore your Church to pure serenity [Col. 0034A] and peaceful order, and will restore it to universal joy and tranquil repose—the divinity of our common Lord granting long-lasting gentleness and health—so that, through His care for all things and His diligent providence, He may prosper both what belongs to each person and what is common to all, as heavenly assent habitually concurs and cooperates.

“‘Accordingly, because of the individual insults and disruptions you have suffered from those who have exercised power over you with excessive violence and cruelty, we have accommodated both a sorrowful and a grateful feeling: sorrow, because we desire your noble and honorable holiness to remain untouched by every pain and distress in its present exaltation; gratitude, because we clearly know that gold will be more brilliant and radiant if it is subjected to fire, or if, stretched out in a more abundant refining, it is purified from the admixture of inferior material that is in it.
