“‘For sometimes, because of the insolent laziness of our minds, we are partly turned away from the integrity of our souls; thinking that we are arranging and acting well, we are actually led far from what is truly right, turning too carelessly from the path that leads to rectitude, and through the perplexity of what is worse unwisely making what is better turbulent.

“‘Therefore the most wise physician of our souls appropriately broadens the darkness placed upon us in tribulation, gradually cleansing the understanding of our souls, toward the radiant illumination of His kingdom [Col. 0034C] and justice in our hearts. Do not, then, be tortured or anxious by taking the preceding trials to heart. Such a disposition is unprofitable and unfitting for the perfection of virtue and the most pure world of your divine and honorable conduct and discipline. Rather, looking to an honorable and fitting way of life, directed well from infancy to old age, strive to endure all things with long-suffering, modesty, and readiness.

“‘I have not presumed to say these things by way of teaching or admonishing a man radiant with perfection in word and deed. Rather, held by an abundance of charity, I have resolved to use gentle words of consolation. For a river that flows continually in its entirety does not always need a spring; and I say this of your honor, which is full of divine wisdom.

“‘You surely know, most holy one, the reason why we could neither write nor send to you, lest we should perhaps become subject to the power that holds us and expose ourselves to evil judgment or suspicion. For they show us much goodwill and compassion, granting us permission to build our churches and to maintain our customs without prohibition, acting justly and inflicting upon us no injury or violence.

“‘Since, however, we were ordered to send by both the hamera [Note: [Col. 0033D] The Greeks call the prince of the Saracens hamiram; in their language it is interpreted as “governor.” [Col. 0034D]] who is here with us and by letters from the abhominator [Note: [Col. 0034D] Perhaps this should read “from the dominator.”], we have sent, as he requested, our eye and the most distinguished and good cultivator of our apostolic throne, Elias, who occupies our place and person and is able to distinguish and discern rationally the matters under inquiry. With him the prince of the Saracens also sent the most holy Thomas, who holds the episcopate of the city of Tyre, which belongs to the see of Antioch, just as you requested that he be sent by your honorable letters.

“‘You know, most holy ones, that we sent these men with great daring and audacity, precipitately and boldly, as though to rescue certain Saracens who are being held in custody among you. We therefore pray and ask you to speak into the ears of our God-crowned and most devout lord, so that his magnificent dominion may grant us as many Saracens as it wishes, in exchange for our own, [Col. 0035B] and for the restoration of my people—or rather, for our salvation and the security of us all. For if this is not arranged in such a way by both the imperial and your providence, there will be no small fear of our utter destruction when they find the opportunity.

“‘Furthermore, trusting that through your most sacred and diligent affection I may obtain what lies upon my heart, I have sent you the podere and the shoulder-cloth with the miter—the pontifical vestment of the holy apostle and brother of the Lord, James, the first of the archbishops—which my predecessors, the patriarchs, wrapped around themselves and always entered the Holy of Holies while exercising the priesthood; namely, the holy memorial of life and the holy calciare. I too have worn these, and, bearing them, I have sent them to your desirable [Col. 0035C] and honored head out of the abundance of love and affection, so that, as one worthy, you may enjoy the sanctifying sweetness and touch of the holy places.

“‘At the same time I have sent a sacred vessel [Note: [Col. 0035D] A vessel for stored money.] of the cymiliores of the holy Resurrection, a silver chalice with images, to the land of Sylem, with the devout preceptor and syncellus of our apostolic throne, Elias [Note: [Col. 0035D] He says this because of the apostle James.], for the sanctification of our most holy church and as a memorial of our humility.’”

After the reading, the most holy legates of senior Rome said:

“We approve the good exposition.”

After this Bahanes, most renowned patrician and praepositus, rose and spoke on behalf of the entire synod:

“By the form of the letters that have been read, we have become fully certain that those sent from senior Rome to us are truthful, and likewise concerning the two Eastern sees, namely Antioch and Jerusalem.”

Donatus and Stephanus, most holy bishops, and Marinus, honorable deacon acting in place of the most holy pope Adrian, said:

“Let the document presented by the holy Roman Church be read.”

The holy synod said:

“Let us hear it.”

Damianus, most reverend imperial cleric and interpreter, took the document and read the aforesaid document in Latin in a loud voice for all to hear. After the reading of the document, Stephanus, God-loving deacon and devout notary, ascended and read the same document in Greek.

[Col. 0036A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Under the rule of the most devout lords and perpetual Augusti, Basil and Constantine his son, God-crowned, peaceful and great emperors, in the third year, in the month of October, in the third indiction.

“The first salvation is to preserve the rule of right faith; next, to depart in no respect from the ordinances of God and the Fathers. One of these indeed pertains to faith, the other to good works. For just as it is written, ‘Without faith it is impossible to please God’ (Heb. 11), so again we read, ‘Faith without works is dead’ (Jas. 2).

“And because the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be disregarded, when He says, ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ (Matt. 16), these words are proved by the effects of events: for in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been preserved undefiled and holy doctrine celebrated.

“Therefore, desiring in no way to be separated from this faith and doctrine, and following in all things the ordinances of the Fathers, especially those of the holy pontiffs of the apostolic see, we anathematize all heresies, together with the Iconoclasts.

“We also anathematize Photius, who, contrary to the sacred rules and the venerable decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs, was suddenly raised from curial administration and secular military service and, while Ignatius the patriarch was still alive, intruded—indeed, tyrannically—into the Church of Constantinople, being installed by certain schismatics or persons already anathematized and deposed. He persisted in disobedience to the sanctions of the apostolic see, despised its judgment concerning both himself and our patriarch Ignatius, and delayed anathematizing the acts of the conciliabulum which, under his leadership, had been assembled against the reverence due to the apostolic see.

“We follow and embrace the holy synod which Pope Nicholas, of blessed memory, celebrated before the most sacred and distinguished body of the apostles Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0036D] Perhaps “Paul” is superfluous.], and to which you too, most exalted pontiff Adrian, our co-angelic lord, subscribed. We likewise follow the synod which you yourself recently held there, and we shall reverently preserve everything established in these synods, according to the moderation of your decree, receiving those whom they receive and condemning all who were condemned in them—especially the aforesaid Photius and Gregory of Syracuse, patricides, who did not fear to raise their tongue against their spiritual father [Col. 0036D]—as well as their followers who have persisted in schism and those who remained in fellowship with them. We judge them unworthy, together with them, of every grace of communion, unless they obey you.

“For whoever has joined himself to the communion of certain persons has deserved a like sentence in justification or condemnation.

“As for the synagogues of the wicked—or rather, the den of robbers, the gatherings of bloodshed, the fabricators of falsehood, and the inventors of perverse doctrines—which twice conspired factionally against the most blessed patriarch Ignatius under the emperor Michael, and once against the primacy of the apostolic see, we bind them with unbreakable bonds of anathema. We judge those who defend their deeds or conceal their impious actions, instead of burning and anathematizing them when they discover them, to be worthy of the same sentence of anathema, until satisfaction and obedience are given.

“Regarding our most venerable patriarch Ignatius, and those who are on his side, we follow with our whole mind what the authority of your apostolic see has decreed, we venerate it with religious devotion, and according to our knowledge and ability we defend it with pious intention and spiritual struggle.

“For, as we have said, following the apostolic see in all things and observing all its ordinances, we hope that we may be found worthy to belong to the one communion which the apostolic see proclaims to exist, in which lies the complete and true solidity of the Christian religion. We also promise that those who have been separated from communion with the Catholic Church—that is, those who do not agree with the apostolic see—shall not have their names recited among the sacred mysteries.

“I, that certain [Note: [Col. 0037C] ‘That certain one’: from the Greek pronoun ὁ δεῖνα, meaning ‘such-and-such.’ Roman editor.] bishop [Note: [Col. 0037D] ‘Bishop of that holy Church.’ Same editor.], have written this profession with my own hand and presented it to you, our most holy, thrice-blessed, and co-angelic supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0037D] ‘Supreme pontiff.’ Although in Greek he is called ἀκρότατος, ‘highest,’ because this name is unusual among them and appears very foreign to the Greek idiom, the Greek interpreter rendered it as ‘great’ or ‘greatest.’ Nevertheless, those whom the Greeks call ἀρχιερεῖς, ‘chief bishops,’ are found translated by our interpreters as ‘supreme pontiffs,’ ‘supreme priests,’ or ‘chief priests.’ Same editor.], and universal pope Adrian, through your legates, namely Donatus and Stephanus, most holy bishops, and Marinus, deacon of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, in that month [Note: [Col. 0037D] ‘In that month.’ The other chronological details are not supplied here because not all wrote the handwritten copies of this profession at the same time. Each person who sought to be received in his rank, in ecclesiastical communion, or in the synodal assembly inserted in his own handwritten copy the date on which he came and wrote it, and strengthened it by the subscription of witnesses whom he had requested, then handed it to the legates. Same editor.], on that day, in such-and-such an indiction.”

### Subscription

[Note: [Col. 0037D] In the authentic Greek codex, the same document is placed after the Latin document, translated into Greek, although now the Greeks are gradually ceasing to write it in Latin because of their ignorance of Latin letters. It should nevertheless be noted that if some passages of this document appear in the Greek translation differently from the Latin edition, this happened not by choice but by necessity. For in some places the translator followed the peculiarities of Greek expression less closely, and in others he did not clearly understand the Latin language; thus he is recognized to have altered something of the same document. Same editor. [Col. 0038C–D]]

“I, that certain [Note: [Col. 0038D] ‘That certain one.’ Not only bishops of different ranks, but also the remaining priests, clerics, and monks, likewise made such a subscription as well as a handwritten copy. Same editor.], bishop of that holy Church, have subscribed to this document of my profession, drawn up by me under Adrian, most blessed supreme pontiff and universal pope; and I requested witnesses to subscribe.”

### Subscription of the witnesses

“I, that certain Basilicos [Note: [Col. 0038D] ‘Basilicos.’ Here the word is used as a personal name, but it is also a title of rank. In Greek, basilicos means ‘imperial by nature,’ or an imperial exspatharius, prospatharius, or holder of another rank. These were imperial men who, when asked, individually strengthened the handwritten copies with their written testimony and affirmation. Same editor.], here, having been requested by him as a witness, have subscribed to this document drawn up by that man under Adrian, most blessed supreme pontiff and universal pope.”

## Anastasius’s note on the preceding document

From the Roman edition.

It should be noted and committed to memory that Pope Nicholas, of blessed memory, issued the text of this document. But because it was not then accepted by the prevaricators, it was sent again from Pope Adrian, most holy, with the name of the pontiff changed, to Constantinople. According to its confirmations, the archbishops and metropolitans, the other bishops of the diocese of Constantinople, and all the clergy without exception who held either rank or communion, authenticated a document written in Greek for the apostolic see, both by their own handwriting and by the testimony and subscription of witnesses whom they had requested. They marked their names and the date on which each wrote his handwritten copy and presented it to the legates of the apostolic see, so that no bishop or other cleric was admitted into the synodal assembly who had not written a handwritten copy according to the model of this little document and presented it to the envoys of the Church of the apostolic see, the Roman Church.

After all had made their handwritten copies and delivered them strengthened by witnesses, some of them rose and approached the most holy patriarch Ignatius and the pious emperor Basil. Privately they said that it had not been rightly done to permit the Church of Constantinople to be subjected to the Roman Church with so great a submission, so that they had handed it over to her as a servant to a mistress.

Moved by these words, the emperor ordered the leading men assigned to the service of the legates of the apostolic see to send one of their number with his companions to some church. They themselves were to enter the legates’ lodging and secretly remove those handwritten copies, for he entirely refused to cause them public scandal.

Accordingly, when the legates—namely the bishops Donatus and Stephanus and the deacon Marinus—had gone to confer with the patriarch, the guards became thieves, entered the house, and secretly removed a certain portion of the numerous handwritten copies.

When the legates returned and discovered what had happened, they sent the following words, among others, to the emperor:

“We shall indeed not dare to return to Rome because the handwritten copies have been lost; yet you will gain no reward at all for the piety you began on behalf of the condition of the Church.

“We, who were present to bring about a marital agreement between the two emperors, sent him this message:

“‘It is not fitting for imperial power first to do what ought to be destroyed, or to destroy what ought not to be destroyed. Since the handwritten copies were made with your consent, if you consented wrongly, do public penance and destroy what you did—not secretly, but openly. But if you acted rightly in consenting that the bishops should make handwritten copies for future security before the apostolic see, why do you, repenting of a good deed, consent to their removal being concealed?

“‘But if you admit that their removal was not done by your will, we reply: then it will clearly be evident that such a crime was not committed by your will, once you compel those whom you assigned to the legates for their protection to return what was taken. For no one else ought to restore or correct anything the legates have lost or any misfortune they have suffered, except those who, with all their belongings, received us reverently under imperial protection for guarding and preserving us intact.’”

When the emperor heard this, he summoned the legates and returned all the handwritten copies to them, not allowing even one to be missing. He said:

“I approached the apostolic see, as the teacher of ecclesiastical affairs, through my legates, and for this reason I awaited your presence, so that through your decree and diligence our Church might receive remedies for its health and so that we might obey not our own impulses but your judgment.

“Therefore receive the handwritten copies which you have rightly demanded from our priests and from all the clergy, and present them to our spiritual father, the most holy pope. Thus, if any of them should attempt, as is his custom, to walk along the precipices of vices or the byways of perversity, he may in some manner be restrained by these reins and recalled by such bridle-straps to the straight path of justice.”

After this, the legates rejoiced and entrusted to us the documents they had received, so that we might convey them carefully. Before they had begun their journey home, however, we separated, because we traveled by ship from Dyrrhachium to Sipontum, then by land to Beneventum, and afterward to Rome, carrying the same documents. The envoys of the apostolic see, however, likewise boarded a ship at Dyrrhachium and made for Ancona. But encountering Exdavenian pirates, they lost completely everything they appeared to possess, including the book of the acts of the present synod.

But I, who was in charge of the Roman library, took care to bring with me from Constantinople the book of the synod itself. After bringing it, I presented it to the supreme pontiff. Through this it came about that, by God’s agency, the apostolic see received the book of the synod through us and retained the documents sent by us and saved by us. For surely, if the envoys had retained with them the book of the synod and the other writings, they would have lost these documents as well.

[Col. 0039C] And after the libellus had been completed and silence had been made, Bahanes, the most renowned patrician and praepositus, rose and said:

“Our holy emperors seek what is just, and they will fulfill the canon, not according to their own will, but for the benefit of many, and as God is pleased. You, however, have assembled for this purpose: as you see, to establish justice and truth.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said: “Does this libellus please all of you—a libellus that is full of faith, canonically approved, and perfected in every wisdom? It is orthodox, sent by divine grace from the Roman Church.”

The entire holy synod cried out: “The libellus expounded to us has been read justly and appropriately by the holy Roman Church, and therefore [Col. 0039D] it pleases everyone.”

Bahanes, the most renowned patrician and praepositus, speaking on behalf of the sacred senate, said to the vicars of the East: “You also, tell us more plainly what you think about the libellus that has been read. Do you agree with the Romans, or not?”

The most holy vicars of the East said: “We agree. But let the definition that we have set forth here also be read, of which we made mention above, so that you may recognize our agreement.”

The most holy vicars [Col. 0040A] of senior Rome said: “Let it be read.”

And Stephen, the dearest to God, deacon and devout notary, took it and read it [Note: [Col. 0039D] They had already read the decrees of Pope Nicholas. Since they did not think that the vicars should be sent to Rome, they therefore set forth this definition before their arrival; nevertheless, they showed themselves to be following entirely what the aforesaid pope, now remembered among the apostles, had decreed long before.]

## Definition of Thomas, metropolitan of Tyre, first occupant of the see and primate of the see of Theupolis-Antioch [Note: [Col. 0039D] “First occupant of the see.” They call the bishop who is first occupant—that is, the protothronos, or first occupant—the bishop of those bishops who belong to the Theopolitan, that is, Antiochene, Church. EDITION OF ROME.], and of Elias, presbyter and syncellus of the throne of Jerusalem, holding the place and person of Theodosius, the most holy patriarch of Jerusalem, in the holy city of Christ our God, held at Constantinople before the vicars of senior Rome had arrived.

While your ecclesiastical affairs were suffering confusion through the instigation of the demon who hates what is good and sows weeds, the all-provident and all-protecting God raised up for the Roman principate the ruler who is dearest to God and most fervent in his love of truth, namely the most pious Basil, the great emperor, through whom he wished by every means to destroy ecclesiastical scandals and stumbling-blocks, and to bring the whole Christian world into a better and more orderly arrangement. Eager to say and do everything according to the purpose of the divine counsel, he summoned our humility from the eastern sees and dioceses, so that, together with those most holy vicars who were expected to come from senior Rome, we might prudently dissolve the ecclesiastical disputes. For this reason we have continued until now to await their arrival.

But since there has been a great delay, and we suspect that, because of the tyrannical power of the Hagarenes, many calamities and necessities will overtake us on account of so long a delay—indeed [Col. 0040C] that our entire Christian people will be subjected to various trials for this reason—we have judged it by no means right to await those who were expected to come from Rome. Rather, we consider it excessive and entirely unnecessary, especially since we have at hand what was regularly and synodically done at Rome, so that it is evident from this that the most blessed Pope Nicholas is with us through the words of his letters, and also his successor, the most blessed Pope Adrian, through his own letters.

For we appropriately judge and believe that Christ our Lord speaks through the Gospel as through a living voice, and likewise the apostle Paul and all the other apostles, prophets, and teachers. Therefore, since we have with us the most blessed Pope Adrian, we consider it wholly inept and incongruous to despise the wavering Church of Christ our Savior by delaying the disposition that is owed to it.

Accordingly, as if compelled by necessity, we now announce to you God’s justification, and the purpose and judgment of the divine and most merciful providence, insofar as our capacity permits. Therefore, concerning the affairs now in dispute, we have issued and enacted this decree [Col. 0041A]: all people are to comply with and obey in every respect the definitions and decrees of the most blessed Pope Nicholas. We also favor and agree with them, since long before their reading and knowledge we ourselves conceived and judged the same things and proclaimed them [Note: [Col. 0041D] “Judged.” They use “judged” in the sense in which the Apostle says, “I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2). Yet by “judged” they mean “determined,” not “promulgated.” For they did this only after the arrival and definition of the Romans; before that, they merely indicated privately to certain persons that judgment ought to be made in this way. EDITION OF THE SAME.].

### Chapter I

Therefore, let the most holy patriarch Ignatius, by the good pleasure of God the Father, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the operation of the most holy Spirit, remain secure and firmly established on his throne, suffering molestation from no one and not being forced away from his own archierarchical dignity and honor, as he directs the word of truth.

### Chapter II

As for the bishops, presbyters, deacons, and clergy of whatever order who, after the unjust deposition of the most holy and fellow-minister Ignatius, withdrew from Photius and for that reason were removed from their sees and subjected to deposition: let these men receive back their sees and exercise their priesthood without delay, prohibited by no one on any other grounds.

For those who were deprived of what they possessed on account of the truth are worthy not only to share in the things from which they fell, but also in other things whose value may adequately compensate for their earlier afflictions.

### Chapter III

But those bishops, presbyters, deacons, and clergy of whatever order who received the laying-on of hands from the blessed Methodius and the most holy Ignatius, and who endured exercising the priesthood with Photius until the end, but, when Photius was rejected, hastened to the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God and have continued until now to hasten toward the conclusion of the holy synod: these too the mother Church, which loves all Christians as her children, does not turn away. Rather, she will receive them into her bosom, kindled with maternal kindness toward her children and showing an unceasing desire [another reading: “miserably”], adopting them and receiving them peacefully with the appropriate penances of the most holy patriarch Ignatius, whatever he himself may wish [Note: [Col. 0041D] “Penances.” Many interpret this as “reproaches,” but here and in many places it means the penalties that the Church prescribes for each person to observe according to the quality of the offenses—for example, fasts, weeping, abstinence from food, genuflections, and similar practices. EDITION OF THE SAME.].

For the blessed Pope Nicholas gave a definitive condemnation concerning Photius, and concerning only the laying-on of his hands and Gregory of Syracuse. But in the case of the other two consecrations mentioned above, he entrusted authority to the most holy patriarch Ignatius. For it was right that the man who had been tested by many difficulties on behalf of the Church divinely entrusted to him should receive some share of generosity in admitting priests.

### Chapter IV

As for Photius, whom the blessed Nicholas condemned, we consider him in every respect alienated from all priestly dignity, function, and title, and never, by any means or at any time, to receive a place of satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0041D] Perhaps: “nowhere and by anyone.”]. We also consign him to anathema, unless perhaps he obeys the synodical judgment of Pope Nicholas and accepts our sentence.

### Chapter V

Moreover, Gregory of Syracuse, who was previously deposed and previously condemned by us, is likewise judged deposed and condemned. For we have not come as opponents of a just decree, but as equal confirmers and supporters of the canons and enactments handed down by the Fathers.

Those who were led astray and received the laying-on of hands from Photius, as collaborators in and supporters of his evil actions, and as having joined him in making the same decree, are judged unworthy of every priestly office, just as Pope Nicholas synodically proclaimed against them.

### Chapter VI

These things, therefore, have been issued and decreed by us in this manner, and, by God’s will, we say [Note: [Col. 0041D] Perhaps the word “say” is redundant.]; they have also been faithfully prescribed. These things we both declare and proclaim, and commit to you in writing. We also resolve that all who are reckoned among those called by Christ should preserve them.

James, the brother of the Lord and first high priest and prelate of the holy city of Jerusalem, speaks and admonishes with us; and from great Antioch—where Christ’s inheritance received its most celebrated name—Peter, who first exercised the priesthood there [Note: [Col. 0042D] “First in the priesthood.” Note that it does not say “first” as an adverb, but “first” as a noun; for he received the high priesthood first from Christ, and afterward presided as the first bishop of Antioch. EDITION OF THE SAME.], then Ignatius Deifer [Note: [Col. 0042D] “Ignatius Deifer.” The Greeks relate that the little child whom the Lord placed in the midst, saying, “Unless you turn and become like this little child” (Matt. 18), was this Ignatius; and for that reason they call him Deifer. Hence, when he was promoted to the episcopate of the Church, even the apostles did not dare lay hands on him any further, recognizing that he had been praised by the mouth of God and sanctified by his touch. EDITION OF THE SAME.], and his successor—speak and admonish that these things must be preserved and that no transgression of what has been stated must be presumed, lest you be found rejecting the whole right of the Church. For it is no small matter—even though it is almost a small matter. “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2).

Whoever, therefore, knowing the precepts of the most blessed Pope Nicholas and this our judgment, dares to reject any of the things set forth here, or to bring trouble to the ears of powerful persons for the rejection of anyone, or to receive such a person—whoever he may be, whether priest, layman, monk, or cleric of any order—let him be anathema from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, deprived of the glory of God, heir of eternal torment and co-heir with the devil, and alienated from the grace of Christians, as one who mocks the generosity of Christ our true God [Note: [Col. 0043D] “Which he gave to priests.” Note that the holy synod calls the apostles priests on the basis of the words: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16). Therefore Peter, who deserved to hear this especially before all the others, became the first priest. Thus the view of those who thought that James the Lord’s brother was the first priest is disproved. Yet James was the first priest among those who were ordained not by the Lord but by the apostles. He was the first bishop, but among those who held the episcopate at Jerusalem. EDITION OF THE SAME.], which he gave to priests, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16).

For whoever considers Christ’s word truthful, proclaims it, and believes that the things bound on earth are bound in heaven, and that the things loosed on earth are loosed in heaven—how, do you suppose, will he dare to loose what has been bound by priests, or to bind what has been loosed [perhaps: “to bind what has been loosed”]? It is therefore clear that anyone who despises God in this way, mocks divine teaching, and rejects commandments worthy of honor will not escape just punishment.

Along with these things there will follow another very difficult and rapid disturbance [Col. 0043B]. But if he rejects even one of the things written here, which were previously judged by the blessed Pope Nicholas, there will arise a continual fever in your Church and perpetual conflict over ecclesiastical affairs, so that no ecclesiastical order will ever be able to appear in the Church.

For where there is indeed a gathering of the whole patriarchal throne, and the whole sacred catalogue speaks the same thing, if anyone harbors doubt through diabolical counsel, it will certainly be difficult for the ecclesiastical order ever to possess stability or peace.

Therefore let him be anathema who presumes in any respect to reject anything written here, from the Father, as has already been said, and from the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

For the confirmation of the present definition, each one of us signed it with his own hand, as follows.

And after the definition had been read, the whole synod said:

“Behold, we have heard the sentence of the Easterners, which follows and supports the judgment of the most holy Pope Nicholas, and we agree with it.”

The most holy and most honorable vicars of senior Rome said to the vicars of the East:

“You, our brothers, tell us: Is this your definition? And did you give us this document that has been read?”

Thomas, the most honorable metropolitan of Tyre, and Elias, the most worshipful presbyter and syncellus, vicars of the East, said:

“It is ours also, and we wrote it when we were here.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Do you truly hold it as we have heard?”

Thomas and Elias, the most holy vicars of the East, said:

“We hold these resolutions exactly as you have heard them.”

The most honorable vicars of Rome said to the holy synod:

“Does it please you?”

The holy synod cried out:

“It pleases everyone.”

After this, the sacred senate, through Bahanes, the most renowned patrician and praepositus, said to the most honorable Roman vicars:

“We ask you to heal our brokenness. We indeed assent to what your judgment has commanded, but it is fitting that you yourselves order other things which, if we hear them, may assist us. How did you condemn Photius without ever seeing him? How did you pronounce anathema against him when he was found with him [another reading: ‘when he was found before you—how did you pronounce anathema against him’]? Tell us.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Christ our God granted power to the blessed apostle Peter, saying to him: ‘Peter, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers’” (Luke 22).

“Could the most blessed and most holy Pope Nicholas, therefore, have remained in that see for so long without strengthening his brothers and the most holy patriarch Ignatius? For the most holy Pope Nicholas, seeing the letters and epistles of Photius the usurper, and judging him, though absent, as though present, by his letters and representatives [Note: [Col. 0043D] “As though present.” Although the whole world knew that Photius had suddenly been made a bishop from a layman and had invaded the see of a living bishop, nevertheless, since he was absent, Nicholas did not judge him until he had twice learned through representatives and Photius’s letters that he was guilty, and had twice admonished him through his own representatives and letters to correct himself. EDITION OF ROME.], judged him.

The most magnificent princes said:

“And whom did he send?”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“If you order us to listen in due sequence, we will tell you.”

The most magnificent princes said:

“We wish it.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“First Arsabir, the envoy of the emperor Michael, was sent, and four bishops were sent with him [Col. 0044C]—we do not know their names [Note: [Col. 0044D] We do not know their names. Because the continuation of the speech required them to proceed, the names of the bishops could not immediately come to their memory. Their names, however, were Methodius, metropolitan of Gangra; Samuel, bishop of Chonai; Theophilus of Iconium; and Zacharias, pseudo-bishop of Taormina. They brought the legation and letters from Photius to the apostolic see. EDITION OF THE SAME.]—carrying with him a royal letter that indicated that the matter concerned the heresy of the images and, at the end of the letter, also revealed the expulsion [Note: [Col. 0044D] That is, the removal.] of the most holy patriarch Ignatius.

“He requested that Nicholas send his representatives to Constantinople, and Nicholas sent Radoald and Zacharias, formerly bishops. They came here and held a robber council and an assembly of wicked men against the holy man Ignatius the patriarch, and supposedly deposed him.

“Then they returned to Rome with the representative Leo, a secretary of state, who also carried another royal letter, as well as a letter from the usurper and adulterer Photius, and a libellus revealing the assembly of wicked men that had been held against the most holy patriarch Ignatius.

“Then the divine-bearer Pope Nicholas, having learned of this and examined everything, held a synod and summoned [Col. 0045A] all the bishops of the West—archbishops [Note: [Col. 0045D] “Archbishops.” Although he summoned archbishops, none came except the one from Ravenna, because of the difficulties of the time. Yet he, together with several others, rejected Photius and admitted the patriarch Ignatius, relying, of course, on the privilege of the apostolic see, which alone has the authority to loose or bind the bonds of any bishops, since it has the right to judge concerning the whole Church. EDITION OF THE SAME.], metropolitans, and all the clergy of the holy Roman Church, as well as the entire senate of the Roman princes.

“They condemned the libellus and the assembly of wicked men that had been held against the most holy man Ignatius, and deposed the representatives who had come here—namely Radoald and Zacharias—and expelled them from all priestly honor and communion, because they had communicated with, consented to, and appointed Photius, the usurper and adulterer. They repudiated the assembly of wicked men. For this deed, therefore, he condemned and anathematized Photius.”

While these men were silent, Bahanes, the most renowned patrician and praepositus, rose and, speaking on behalf of the sacred senate, asked the vicars of the East:

“You also spent a long time here awaiting the vicars from Rome. How, when you were near Photius, did you not investigate and see the matter and thus condemn him?”

Elias, the most worshipful presbyter and syncellus, rose and, holding the place of Theodosius, the most holy archbishop of Jerusalem, said:

“You all know, friends of Christ and brothers, that the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets, also spoke through the apostles, and that everything accomplished long ago by our Fathers, everything set down in the Law, and everything effected by spiritual grace remains established. For this reason the Holy Spirit placed patriarchal heads throughout the world, so that through them scandals springing up in the Church of God might be eradicated and a peaceful settlement might be introduced and granted within it.

“Therefore, since the presiding and foremost see of senior Rome did not receive Photius, and neither did the three eastern thrones—namely Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—there was no need to summon him for examination or renewed judgment. Such proceedings are customarily carried out concerning those who have been received into the Churches of God and into all the sees. But concerning those who have never been received by senior Rome or by the other sees, no renewed judgment at all ought to be held. Such people carry within themselves an evident condemnation of their own, so that we too acted rightly in not bringing him, who had never been received by senior Rome or the eastern thrones, to a reconsideration of the examination. For he bore with him this most manifest condemnation of himself.

“We therefore neither knew nor received any other patriarch of Constantinople during these times except this holy man, the patriarch Ignatius. From the time when, by the grace of God and ecclesiastical election, he held the throne of Constantinople, we received him in our sees. And if, on coming here, we had not found him in his patriarchate but on the island of his exile, we would not have received another; we would have called this same man the patriarch of Constantinople.

“But since, by the grace of God, we found him on his throne, we communicated and concelebrated with him, and ate and drank with him, as one who had been our communicant and fellow-minister from long ago until the present day.

“We proclaimed these things in a loud voice from the beginning, so that no one might think that we wished to act maliciously, as though we had secretly been drawn away and attached ourselves to this holy man, but rather that, according to the ancient opinion we held concerning him, we continued to hold the same opinion up to the present.

“Although we did not speak face to face with Photius, nevertheless, meeting frequently and in various ways with those who are of one mind with him, agree with him, and protect him, we learned that the things which they produce in his defense are useless and empty.

“As for what they say—that after his unjust deposition the patriarch Ignatius, while he was in exile on the island, made a refutation—we, neither senior Rome nor ourselves, accept such a refutation, because it was made contrary to the ecclesiastical canon.

“If some should say that those who laid hands upon Photius and those who were found with him deserve the same punishment and condemnation as he does, they would not speak truthfully. For, since we are of weak nature, we do not always endure the death threatening us; and therefore, out of fear, we are sometimes compelled against our will to do things we do not wish.

“Finally, these men, who, after the consecration of the blessed Methodius and the most holy Ignatius, were overcome by fear, bent down by royal dread and the tyranny of power, and joined him because of violence, shortly afterward and after a brief interval rejected the things he had presumed to do against the most holy patriarch Ignatius and withdrew from him. They are worthy of pardon—especially those who suffered evil, various tribulations, depositions, imprisonments, and exiles at his hands. We too judge such men blessed, just as before us Nicholas and Adrian, the most holy Roman patriarchs, determined.

“Knowing these things and others like them for the future, and having learned the truth from the beginning, we neither received Photius nor accepted his laying-on of hands. Nothing uncertain has occurred for us during the long time we have remained here.

“We have said these things in summary, demonstrating the reason for which we were summoned and attached ourselves to the most holy patriarch Ignatius, and why we did not summon Photius to examination or renewed judgment.

“For Photius himself also sent someone of imperial rank to the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, asking whether he might at some time be received on the throne of Antioch. He confessed, did not deny it, and acknowledged that we had never received Photius on the throne of Antioch.

“Since, therefore, Photius was received neither at senior Rome, nor on the throne of Jerusalem, nor on the throne of Antioch, how, do you suppose, could he have been worthy of a reconsideration [Note: [Col. 0047B] Perhaps: ‘reconsideration of judgment.’] of judgment among us?

“We now say these things because they are sufficient to demonstrate our will and our answer concerning the matters about which we were questioned.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Behold, you have healed and cured our brokenness, and we all confess that the judgment of God has come from the holy three sees. For Christ says: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’” (Matt. 18).

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“It is the custom of the holy Roman Church to possess canonical diligence and, for the sake of ecclesiastical order, to pursue as a wolf the one who has entered the sheepfold through a window. This holy synod rejoices in your honorable response. Even today you have brought true faith to our ears and displayed it to us; for what you say with your mouth, you desire to complete by your deeds.”

Bahanes, the most renowned patrician and praepositus, said:

“Does your holiness have anything to arrange today?”

The vicars, most dear to God, of the holy Roman Church said:

“We would like to make arrangements concerning the libellus, as far as we can. But since the hour has passed, for this reason we shall do what we ought at another assembly, with God’s favor.”

The sacred senate rose and said:

“Blessed be God, because we have been deemed worthy to see this holy day and our honorable gathering. Behold, all these matters have been concluded according to the rule of truth.”

Then Stephen, the dearest to God, deacon of the holy Church of Constantinople and devout notary, stood in the midst and proclaimed this acclamation:

“Many years to the emperors! Many years to Basil and Constantine, the great princes and emperors! Many years to the orthodox emperors! Many years to the overthrowers of injustice! Many years to the peaceful emperors! Many years to the enemies of falsehood! Many years to the lovers and supporters of truth and justice! Many years to Eudoxia, the most pious Augusta! Threefold memory to Nicholas, the most blessed pope of Rome! Many years to Adrian, the orthodox Roman pope! Many years to Ignatius, the orthodox patriarch of Constantinople! Many years to the orthodox patriarchs of the East! Many years to the orthodox senate! Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!”

# ACT TWO

[Col. 0047]

[Col. 0047B] In the name of the Lord and ruler of all, Jesus Christ, truly God and our Savior.

In the consulship of our protective and most tranquil emperors and lords—of Basil in his third year, and of Constantine, his son, in his second year—perpetual Augusti; in the third indiction; on the Nones of October; with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled and holy Gospels placed before them; and with the holy and universal synod assembled:

Donatus, the most dear to God, bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most dear to God, bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, holding the place of Adrian, the most holy Roman pope; and Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople; and Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, holding the place of the see of Antioch; and Elias, the most worshipful presbyter and syncellus, holding the place of the throne of Jerusalem;

[Col. 0047D] with the sacred senate also present, namely Theodore, the most magnificent proconsul and magister; Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus; Himerius, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Theophilus, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Leo, the most magnificent [Col. 0048B] proconsul and patrician; John, the most magnificent patrician and logothete of the dromos (okeos dromi); Leo, the most magnificent patrician and commander of the guards; [Col. 0048C] Paul, the most magnificent patrician and prefect of the praetorium; Manuel, the most magnificent patrician; Theophylact, the most magnificent patrician; Petronas, the most magnificent patrician; and Orestes, the most praiseworthy protospatharius and commander of the Ycanates;

and with the most holy bishops present, namely Nicephorus, the most dear to God, metropolitan of Amasia; John, the most dear to God, metropolitan of Syleion; Nicetas, the most dear to God, metropolitan of Athens; Metrophanes, the most dear to God, metropolitan of Smyrna; Michael, the most dear to God, metropolitan of Rhodes; George, the most dear to God, bishop of Heliopolis; Peter, the most dear to God, bishop of Troas; Nicetas, the most dear to God, bishop of Cephaloedium; Athanasius, the most dear to God, bishop of Magnesia; Nicephorus, the most dear to God, bishop of Cotron; Antony, the most dear to God, bishop of Alisia; and Michael, the most dear to God, bishop of Corcyra—

when all these had assembled, Paul, the most dear to God, stood in the midst [Note: [Col. 0047D] Paul, the most dear to God. This Paul had once been archbishop, having been consecrated by Photius. But because he was condemned, together with the others who had received the laying-on of hands from Photius, according to the sentence of Pope Nicholas, and because he was useful for consolation in the matter of the condemnation, he was made chartophylax by the patriarch Ignatius. For the Roman pope had written that he should be enriched with whatever other dignity he wished, except the priesthood. EDITION OF ROME.], the chartophylax [Note: [Col. 0047D] “Chartophylax.” This is interpreted as “guardian of documents.” The chartophylax performs in the Constantinopolitan Church the office that the librarian performs among the Romans. He wears the insignia of ecclesiastical ministers and carries out all ecclesiastical services, except those alone that are shown to belong specifically and properly to the priestly office.

Moreover, without him no bishop or cleric coming from outside is admitted into the presence of the patriarch; no one is presented to an ecclesiastical assembly; no letter sent to the patriarch is received, unless perhaps it has been sent by another patriarch; and no one is advanced to the episcopate, to clerical office of another order, or to the superintendence of monasteries unless he approves and commends him, reports about him to the patriarch, and presents him.], and said:

“Those who fell under Photius have come with a libellus. What seems good to you? For they seek to enter this holy and universal synod.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome and of the East, together with the entire holy synod, said:

“Let them enter.”

And the aforesaid bishops entered, carrying the libellus in their hands. They prostrated themselves before the undefiled judgments that had been set forth and fell before the holy synod.

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Who are you, bishops who have entered here, and by whom were you consecrated?”

Theodore, metropolitan of Caria, said:

“By our lord, the most holy patriarch Ignatius, and by the blessed Methodius.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“And how many are you?”

Theodore, the most reverend metropolitan of Caria, said:

“We do not know the number.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“What do you say? What do you have? What do you want?”

The bishops said:

“We have prostrated ourselves before this holy and universal synod, seeking penance.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“What is this that you carry?”

The bishops said:

“A libellus of confession concerning the things in which we sinned against our lord, the most holy patriarch Ignatius.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Do you confess that you sinned in this matter?”

The bishops said:

“We confess it.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Does the libellus state what you are saying with your mouths?”

The bishops said:

“Let the libellus be read, and then you will learn with complete certainty the things concerning us.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said to the God-worshiping vicars of the East:

“Does it seem appropriate to you and to the entire holy synod that the libellus of those confessing their sin be received?”

The most holy vicars of the East and the entire holy synod said:

“If it pleases your holiness, the most honorable patriarch Ignatius, and us, it seems good that it be received and read in the presence of the synod.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Since it pleases everyone, let it be received and read.”

And Stephen, the most dear to God, deacon and notary of the holy Church of Constantinople, took it from the hands of the bishops who had just announced themselves and read it aloud in the hearing of all.

## LIBELLUS
If indeed the dreadful events that took place through the mind of Photius, the opponent of the Church, [Note: [Col. 0049D] The wording of that libellus is directed only to the Roman vicars, up to its conclusion.] were unknown in senior Rome, our humility would have to weave together a very lengthy discourse, strengthening the account of what was continually done against us and of the atrocities—how many and of what kind—to which we were subjected by him. For he was a man who said one thing while thinking another and devoted himself to falsehood. By the skill of the Gentiles he always proposed good things, but came to evil ones; and he was powerful in overcoming and deceiving, such as no human being has been and none will be. Since he was such a man, he supplanted us. Yet we do not wish to make our discourse excessively long, since we have you as witnesses to what is being said.

For surely you know—you who were found worthy to serve the most holy pope Nicholas, the lamp of the Church and the light of the whole world, and who became his fellow ministers—that he was incomparable among priests, shining in life and speech, whom scarcely even a blemish touched. Yet Photius, detained by a most wretched mind, did not hesitate to invent against such a great and noble man—whom he had neither seen nor known—a most extensive, innumerable, and heaped-up collection of blemishes. And not merely in number, but also in magnitude, he prevailed in his vanity. Although they were liars, he led the apocrisarii from the East, from all the patriarchates, as though they were in agreement and most certainly knew what he himself was saying, with great effort, so that he might subject such a man to deposition. Having compliant false witnesses, he sent inventions, lies, and deceived men; and they came to complete what seemed good to him.

And unless God had bound all of them, fettered by the works of their hands, we too would certainly have fallen with such a man—for he appeared to be a wolf in place of a shepherd.

We have said little about Nicholas. But he did not do such things only to him. He also attacked our own most holy priest and shepherd, who, when he was supreme bishop, sanctified us by the laying-on of his holy hands. First, while he was still a secular man, Photius attacked him with many schemes; afterward he breathed hypocrisy against us, denied everything, and persuaded all his accomplices, as well as those who were under him, to profess by terrifying written declarations that they would have him as patriarch of patriarchs and supreme priest of supreme priests. At that time he treated us in this way. On the following day, however, he devised frauds against him and an infinite multitude of lies, presenting them as material for accusations, just as he had acted against the most blessed Nicholas. These things he also wanted to send to all the patriarchates, so that, just as he himself soon afterward carried out deposition and anathema against him—as he had formerly wished—so the other patriarchs might do likewise.

But God did not conceal this fraud of his; he made it manifest to everyone. Those who perpetrated the manifest deceit were subjected to exile, proscription, scourging, and many other afflictions. Yet even then he could not restrain himself. As the impulse of his wretched purpose drove him, he carried out deposition and anathema; and after these things, what evil did he not inflict upon him from that time onward?

Did he not pull out his teeth by the roots, having him struck in the face? Did he not secure his feet in iron fetters? Did he not, together with fugitives and runaway slaves, condemn him to remain for a considerable time amid stench and filth? Did he not strip him of the garments he was wearing, except for his first small tunic, tear his legs, and have him placed in a grave made in the form of a funeral pyre, while pouring out candles that were burning there, so that, when he was thirsty, he could not drink from them for refreshment, since they had water in them? Did they not make him stand upright, take away the staff by which he supported himself while holding it in his hands, and which comforted the weakness of his old age? Did they not make him pass many days without food or drink? Did he not make him an exile in a place where barbarian raids frequently occurred, where the inhabitants of those regions were carried off and their swords became their ruin?

But the things he endured from him are so numerous that it is useless labor to count them; nor will speech suffice to recount them. And whom was he treating so? The son of emperors and the grandson of emperors [Note: [Col. 0051D] Ignatius was the son of the emperor Michael and the grandson of the emperor Nicephorus.], who had embraced an angelic life and clothed himself in the habit of monastic conduct, who appeared pleasing to God, revered by angels, and feared by demons.

From these facts you can gather and know how many severities he inflicted upon our smallness, even if we cannot recount them. For if he acted in such a manner toward such supreme priests as Pope Nicholas and the most holy Patriarch Ignatius, you surely know what he did to us humble men of pure mind.

Many of us were punished in the praetorium together with unbelieving peoples, afflicted by hunger and thirst and other miseries, and condemned to cut marble in place of wood. Others, instead of being struck with wooden rods, were beaten with a sword, while those who struck them did so not as though they were priests, nor as though they were human beings bearing flesh, but as though they were striking inanimate bodies. Moreover, they considered it a light torture to subject them to kicks and to tear out the entrails of those subjected to this punishment. The further torment by which he afflicted them with iron collars and bound them with chains, giving them hay as food only after many days, he considered great humanity.

How many they shut up in darkness and the shadow of death, amid deadly stenches—and did not cover them when they did so! Rather, boasting and laughing loudly, they spoke with savagery and arrogance to those who did not know, while mocking them. When asked to show mercy to such people, they became still more enraged and brought forward worse accusations.

He also caused others to be exiled to the ends of the earth and to the lands of foreign peoples. Subjected to these atrocities, and seeing worse and more savage things committed against our supreme priest and against those who persevered with him, we were afflicted and exhausted—both by seeing such things done to others and by suffering them ourselves. Therefore we were terrified and fell into seduction, error, and the most savage violence; and we did unwillingly what we are ashamed to confess. All these things were done to us by his unceasing compulsion and force, while our will in no way consented to bend. For we were completely filled with tears and groans, both while doing these things and after we had done them.

Yet we have hope of salvation—not from our works, nor from the righteousness that we performed, for we did not perform it. For although we resisted, endured much force, and were subdued by many tortures, nevertheless we did not stand firm to the end amid our miseries. Our hope therefore comes from this: that you are imitators of God, as are those who sent you, and likewise our lord and supreme priest.

For God also set forth the prodigal son as an example: after he had wasted his whole life in evil, when he came to his father he was received—not merely in some ordinary way, but with music and feasting—and, clothed by his own father, he received his former garment and first robe (Luke XVIII). Thus he gave an example of the temperance and moderation to be shown toward us who have fallen back. He justified the humbled publican (Luke VII), received the tears of the prostitute (Luke XXIII), and, accepting the confession of the thief, brought him into paradise that very day (Matthew XX).

He made those who had endured the burden of the whole day in the vineyard, and those who had persevered for only one hour—to pass over those in between—worthy of an equal reward (Luke VII). To the one who owed much and to the one who owed little he gave equally, so that he might draw them toward greater dignity, forgiving those to whom he had forgiven much.

With such hope, in humility of soul and contrition of heart, we approached your holiness and gave you this libellus, not with deceitful lips nor with deception of mind. God himself is witness, and he is also our guarantor. But with sincerity and purity, hoping in the mercy of our God who loves humanity, and in the intercessions of holy and undefiled Mary, the Mother of God, of the holy apostles, of the most blessed and most holy Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0051D; 0052D] Observe that they profess to hope not only in the intercessions of the Mother of God and of the apostles, but also in those of the most holy former Pope Nicholas.], and of our holy father and supreme priest Ignatius, as well as in the prayers of your blessedness and of the most holy vicars of the East, we no longer fear in the same manner, but receive from you a hand that may strengthen us and set us firmly in rectitude. And, as far as our purpose extends, we shall strive to the point of blood in ecclesiastical matters, so that, through this correction, we may receive forgiveness for the faults we have committed, in satisfaction of heart (alternatively: “and with satisfaction of heart”).

We shall no longer agree with Photius, the man wise in his own eyes, or with his accomplices, so long as they remain in their accursed state and disagree with the holy Catholic Church of God; nor shall we taste the turbulent streams of his error and seduction. For behold, having spat out what we drank from him—a bitter, deceitful, and deadly cup—we cast ourselves into this holy synod, professing also that we shall gladly accept from our most holy supreme priest the penance that he has prescribed.

But if, after this restoration, which has been made toward us without deceit or disturbance, we should wish in any way to act deceitfully against the Church of God, may deposition by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit befall us, and may there be no further restoration of us.

Donatus, most holy bishop of Ostia; Stephen, most holy bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, most God-beloved deacon of the holy Roman Church, the Roman vicars, asked the bishops:

“Whose consecration do you possess?”

The bishops said:

“We have said that [our consecration is] that of the blessed Methodius and the most holy Ignatius.”

The most holy Roman vicars said:

“We receive you, according to the command of our most holy pope Adrian, because of your confession in the libellus of your penance.”

The most reverend bishops said:

“And we venerate you, and receive you as judges; and we regard your judgment as being given in the person of the Son of God.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“How many are you in number?”

They replied:

“We have already said that we do not know.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Behold, the holy Roman Church does not close its bowels to any of you, if you offer the libellus with all your heart.”

And again the same most holy vicars of senior Rome said to the bishops:

“We have brought a libellus from the holy Roman Church, from the most holy Pope Adrian, having received a mandate from him to require you to make this libellus and thus to receive you. Do you therefore wish to do what has been commanded by the most holy Pope Adrian?”

The bishops said:

“We do, and it pleases us, and we shall subscribe.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“We wish and command that it be read again in the presence of everyone.”

And Stephen, the most God-beloved deacon and notary, took and read the libellus in Greek, which had been sent from Rome and had also been read in the first session.

After the reading, the most holy vicars of senior Rome said to the bishops:

“Have you heard this libellus? Does it please you? Write it down. Do you accept everything issued by the holy Roman Church?”

The most reverend bishops said:

“It pleases us; we shall write it and accept everything.”

Donatus, the most reverend bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most holy bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, said:

“Write it down as well.”

Theodore of Caria took it and wrote it. Then likewise Euthymius of Catana, Photius of Nacolia, Stephen of Cyprus, the other Stephen of Cyllira, Theodore of Sinope, Eustathius of Acmonia, Xenophon of Milassi, Leo of Daphnusia, and Paul of Meles wrote it. All these men wrote the Roman libellus and gave it to the most holy Roman vicars, together with the signatures of witnesses.

After this, Thomas and Elias, the most holy vicars of the East, said to the most holy Roman vicars:

“Everything that you have arranged pleases us.”

The most holy Roman vicars said:

“Because you love what is good, therefore, our venerable brothers, your decision also pleases us.”

And again the same bishops said to the vicars of the East:

“If it seems good to you, let the libellus of penance of the fallen bishops be presented.”

The patriarchs and most holy vicars of the East said:

“It seems good to us.”

Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople, said:

“Let the libellus be placed upon precious wood and the holy Gospels; then let them receive it and give it to me.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome, together with those of the East, said:

“Let it be placed there.”

The bishops placed the libellus upon the holy Gospels and precious wood; then, taking it up again, they gave it to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople. The patriarch took the shoulder-garments and handed them to them.

First of all, he gave them to Theodore, metropolitan of Caria, and said to him:

“Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin again, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

Theodore, the most reverend metropolitan of Caria, said:

“With our whole soul and a pure mind we flee for refuge to your holiness, delivering with our own hand the libellus of our confession, and professing that throughout our whole life we shall preserve inviolate what is written there.”

Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople, said:

“You have acted well and fittingly, our most beloved sons. Behold, I receive you as a merciful and benevolent father receives his prodigal son when he has returned to repentance; for the holy Roman Church has also been moved by a more gracious disposition toward your reverence, and the Eastern sees have likewise agreed with it.”

After this, Theodore, the most reverend bishop of Sinope, said:

“We are worthy not only of penances but also of punishments; but your mercy is great, O lord.”

Xenophon, the most reverend bishop of Milassi, said:

“Although I am worthy of many punishments, I receive the shoulder-garment.”

After they had received their shoulder-garments, they sat down, each in his proper place.

And again Paul, the most God-beloved chartophylax, standing in the midst, said:

“After the fallen bishops entered this holy synod, behold, the priests are also present, holding the same libellus and asking your holiness to let them enter this holy synod. What therefore seems good to your holiness?”

The holy synod said:

“Whose consecration do they possess?”

Paul, the most God-beloved chartophylax, said:

“That of the most blessed Methodius and the most holy Ignatius.”

The most holy vicars said:

“Let them enter.”

And they entered: Thomas, the first of the presbyters; Cosmas, the second and defender; Pantaleo, presbyter; Joachim, presbyter and defender; Megistus, presbyter; Nicephorus, presbyter; Theodosius, presbyter; Epiphanius, presbyter; Theophylact, presbyter; Sisinnius, presbyter; and Gregory, presbyter. Acting on an equal footing with the bishops, they delivered the libellus of penance. Then they too wrote the Roman libellus and received their oraria from the patriarch, who said to them:

“Know that I am a truthful man and that my word has an end. For behold, you have obtained great compassion and forgiveness from the holy Roman Church and from all of us.”

After the bishops and presbyters had entered, Paul, the most God-beloved chartophylax, again stood in the midst and said:

“Likewise, the fallen deacons, holding the libellus of penance in their hands, beseech the holy synod to let them enter.”

The holy synod said:

“Whose consecration do they possess?”

Paul, the most God-beloved chartophylax, said:

“That of the most blessed Methodius and the most holy Ignatius.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome and of the East, together with the holy and universal synod, said:

“Let them enter.”

And they entered: Constantine the deacon, John the deacon, Stephen the deacon, Michael the deacon, Christopher the deacon, Leo the deacon, Theodosius the deacon, Nicholas the deacon, and Sophronius the deacon.

Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, said to them:

“Surely you made the libellus that you bring deliberately and of your own purpose?”

The most reverend deacons said:

“God knows, lord, that we made it with great eagerness. For he himself knows how our consciences stood toward your holiness when you were suffering tyranny. But what we did for Photius we did under compulsion and unwillingly. Yet we give thanks to God and to your holiness, O lord, because you did not repay us according to our sins and faults; rather, you had compassion on us, showed us mercy, pitied us, and forgave us our sins.”

And, having acted in the same way as the bishops and presbyters, they received the same treatment. The patriarch took their oraria and returned them to them.

After this, Paul, the most God-beloved chartophylax, again stood in the midst and said:

“The fallen subdeacons have also come to this holy synod, holding the same libellus in their hands and asking to enter.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome and of the East said:

“Let them enter; it pleases us.”

And they entered: Thomas the domesticus of the subdeacons [Note: [Col. 0055C] The Greeks call the first of the subdeacons a *domesticus*; the Romans call him an *oblationarius*.], Eustathius, Stephen, Photinus, John, Paul, and Thomas. Having done likewise, they too received the insignia of their proper rank.

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“According to this form, by which today we have received the fallen bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons, we decree that henceforth all who have sinned in the same way and are doing penance shall be received.”

After these things, the most holy patriarch Ignatius said:

“Let the penances imposed upon the fallen bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons by this holy and universal synod be read aloud in the hearing of everyone, so that they may be made known to all.”

And Stephen, the deacon and notary, took the text and read:

“Let it be a remedy bringing salvation to the soul, and a very carefully measured penance for priests who have fallen through long custom and have denied their own written declarations, which were properly and regularly issued for spiritual struggle and the unity of the holy Catholic Church.

“If they eat meat, let them abstain from meat, cheese, and eggs. Those who do not eat meat are to abstain from cheese and eggs, and on Wednesday and Friday (*parasceve*) are to eat legumes and vegetables with oil and a little wine; they are to make fifty genuflections each day; and they are to say *Kyrie eleison* one hundred times, ‘Lord, I have sinned’ one hundred times, and ‘Lord, forgive me, a sinner’ one hundred times. They are also to recite Psalm 6, Psalm 37, and Psalm 50.

“I command you to observe these things until the Nativity of Christ. You shall not have authority to minister or in any way to perform the duties of priests. Then, at the birthday feast of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, you shall receive your priesthood again, and you shall serve with me, ministering to the immortal and eternal God.”

After the reading of the penances had been completed, Stephen himself again led the acclamation:

“Many years to the emperors Basil and Constantine, the great dictators and emperors! Many years to the orthodox emperors! Many years to the peace-making emperors! Many years to the overthrowers of injustice! Many years to the enemies of falsehood! Many years to the lovers and defenders of truth and justice! Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed Roman pope! Many years to Adrian, the orthodox Roman pope! Many years to Ignatius, the orthodox patriarch of Constantinople! Many years to the orthodox senate! Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!” [Note: [Col. 0056C] These are iambic verses among the Greeks.]

“God has overthrown the schemes of Photius, which began in the divine place, and at the same time has overthrown him, as a friend of falsehood and a trampler upon the venerable image.”

## THIRD SESSION

[Col. 0055]

[Col. 0055C] In the name of the Lord and Ruler Jesus Christ, the true God and our Savior. In the consulship of our lords, crowned by God: Basil in his third year, and Constantine, his son, in his second year, the perpetual emperors and Augusti; in the third indiction, on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

The life-giving wood and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation having been placed on the right-hand side of the catechumens in the renowned temple of holy and great Sophia, and Donatus, the most God-beloved bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most God-beloved bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, having assembled—holding the place of Adrian, the most holy and most blessed archbishop of senior Rome, and of Ignatius, the most honored archbishop of the great-named Constantinople, New Rome, together with the most holy vicars of the East: namely Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, holding the place of the see of Antioch, since that Church was widowed; and Elias, the most God-venerable presbyter and syncellus, holding the place of Theodosius, the most holy archbishop of the see of Jerusalem—the reading at this point being uncertain—

Then, by the command of the Christ-loving and God-worshiping great emperors Basil and Constantine, and with the most magnificent princes also present and listening, namely Christopher, the most magnificent magister; Bahane, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus; Paul, the most magnificent patrician and prefect; Leo, the most magnificent patrician and domesticus of the excubitors; John, the most magnificent patrician and logothete of the swift course [read: “rapid course”]; Manuel, the most magnificent patrician; Theophylact, the most magnificent patrician; Petronas, the most magnificent patrician; and Orestes, the most famous protospatharius and domesticus of the Icanates—

And with the God-beloved bishops also seated, namely Nicephorus, the God-beloved metropolitan of Amasia; Nicetas, the God-beloved metropolitan of Athens; Metrophanes, the God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna; Theodore, the God-beloved metropolitan of Caria [Note: [Col. 0055D; 0057D–0058D] Although Theodore, after writing the Roman libellus, had been received through a libellus of penance because of the fault that he had committed against Patriarch Ignatius by withdrawing from him and acting against his own subscription, he was later discovered to have written in the deposition and anathema of Pope Nicholas. For this sole reason he was cast out by the entire synod, with the judgment of blessed Peter alone reserved.]; Euthymius, the God-beloved metropolitan of Catana; Michael, the God-beloved metropolitan of Rhodes; Photius, the God-beloved archbishop of Nacolia; Athanasius, the God-beloved bishop of Anilius in Magnesia; George, the God-beloved bishop of Heliopolis; Stephen, the God-beloved bishop of Cibyra; Nicetas, the God-beloved bishop of Cephaludis; Stephen, the God-beloved archbishop of Cypsalla; Theodore, the God-beloved bishop of Sinope; Basil, the God-beloved bishop of Pyrgius; Gregory, the God-beloved bishop of Messina; Eustathius, the God-beloved bishop of Aemonia; Xenophon, the God-beloved bishop of Milassi; Leo, the God-beloved bishop of Daphnusia; Peter, the God-beloved bishop of Troas; Samuel, the most God-beloved bishop of Antri; Antony, the God-beloved bishop of Aliseos; Nicephorus, the God-beloved bishop of Croton; and Michael, the God-beloved bishop of Corcyra—

When these men had assembled, Metrophanes, the God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna, together with Nicephorus, the God-beloved metropolitan of Amasia, and Nicetas, the metropolitan of Athens, rose and said:

“The great apostle Paul commands and enjoins that everything be done honorably and according to order. It seems honorable to all of us and close to perfect order that this holy and universal synod should now hear the letters of our Christ-loving emperor, which he sent to the most holy Roman pope and to the bishops of the East, and again those of our most holy patriarch, and then of the most blessed Pope Adrian, to our most holy lord. Thus the holy synod, receiving still greater satisfaction, may glorify God, who cooperated with our most pious emperor in councils and excellent endeavors, and may give thanks also to our most holy patriarch and to you, most holy vicars.”

Donatus and Stephen, the most holy bishops, and Marinus, the most reverend deacon, vicars of senior Rome, said:

“We have heard that there are certain men who, though consecrated by the most blessed Methodius and the most holy Ignatius, are in error and do not know the piety, mercy, and judgment of the holy Church of God. For this reason they refuse to write the Roman libellus sent by the most holy Pope Adrian. Above all, therefore, we command your devoutness to go to them and summon them according to canonical authority, saying this:

“‘The holy synod summons you to do what has been decreed and determined by its authority, and to be received by the holy synod. For it does not wish to close its bowels; therefore it invites you to come. According to the satisfaction expressed in the libellus, act as your other brothers have acted, and the holy and universal synod will receive you.’”

Thomas and Elias, the most holy vicars of the Eastern sees, said:

“In accordance with the customary and canonical commands of the apostles and the holy synods, we too, led by the prompting of mercy, are making provision that they may be summoned to this road of salvation, to which their brothers also hastened [alternatively: ‘ran’]. It is therefore fitting that you go to them and invite them to the salvation of their souls. Say to them with benevolence and appropriate brotherly affection:

“‘We summon you. If, therefore, you do what seems good to the holy synod, enter it, and it will receive you.’”

Metrophanes, the God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna; Nicephorus, the God-beloved metropolitan of Amasia; and Nicetas, the God-beloved metropolitan of Athens, departed and delivered the message entrusted to them to Theodulus, the most reverend metropolitan of Ancyra, and Nicephorus, the most reverend metropolitan of Nicaea. They replied as follows:

“Concerning the subscription proposed, we give an account to your holiness: because of the reasonable and unreasonable subscriptions previously made, we have been burdened and have determined, imposing a bond upon ourselves, not to subscribe any further beyond what we have subscribed and professed in the symbol of our faith, which lies in the chartophylacium of the venerable patriarch, from the time of our consecration.

“Therefore we say to you, and ask the holy synod, if it is possible, to forgive us for having decided to preserve this position for as long as we live.”

When the God-beloved metropolitans delivered this response, the most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Let their response be read aloud in the hearing of everyone.”

Thomas, the venerable subdeacon and devout vicar, took it and read it in the hearing of the holy synod.

Again the vicars of senior Rome said:

“Let the letter of our emperor, fortified by God, be read—the letter that he sent to the most holy Pope Nicholas.” [Note: [Col. 0058D] They say that it was sent to Adrian because Adrian received it, although it had in fact been written to Nicholas.]

Theodorus, the devout *a secretis*, took it and read:

“‘In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the one, sole, and true Holy Spirit, Basil, faithful emperor of the Romans, to Nicholas, the most holy Roman pope and also our spiritual father.
