“‘How the will of our mind stands regarding our ecclesiastical affairs, O divine and sacred head, revered like Aaron, we made known in our previous letter. Since we do not know whether it has reached your holiness and those who, like Moses, are most pleasing to God—for many obstacles arise on a long journey—we have judged it necessary first briefly to recall what was contained in that letter and now to supply what was lacking.

“‘That letter indicated in what evils we found our Church lying when, through your divine prayers, we took up the reins of the empire: lying in a bad state, incurably sick, stripped of her legitimate ruler, held by tyranny, subjected to the service of a foreign shepherd, suffering everything like a handmaid rather than doing anything in the manner of a queen.

“‘Some things seemed to us to be our responsibility; others we left entirely to your paternal holiness. Yet we thought that nothing further should be done by us except that Photius should be removed from the see and that we should urge him to remain at rest, since he had stirred up many things against the truth and against your sacred pontificate—for his madness had advanced to such a degree.

“‘But Ignatius, the most holy and our spiritual father, who clearly endured injuries and tyranny, should, according to the judgment and vindication found in your various letters, be restored to his own throne in fair and just truth. Although, through those same letters, we have only now made this clear to everyone—for those who held power before us had buried those letters and shown them to no one—we have left the rest to your spiritual holiness: to bring these matters to an end, indeed to approve them, and to settle what follows from them.

“‘This concerns the priests who sinned on both sides: those previously consecrated by the most holy Patriarch Ignatius who, according to their own written confession, did not remain in the truth; and those who received the laying-on of hands from Photius, the shameless man. It also concerns those supreme priests, priests, and abbots who wrote in different ways. Some were deceived by force or tyranny, others by simplicity or levity, some by seduction and cunning, and others by gifts and honors of various kinds.

“‘Only a few became wholly superior to his snare. [Note: [Col. 0059D–0060D] That is, the stronger or more powerful ones; for a person becomes stronger and more powerful than the snare when he is able to leap out beyond it. Or, he becomes “above the snare” by not being held in it, but escaping as birds fly over it, according to Solomon: “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of the winged.”]

“‘Indeed, it must be said that almost all the consecrated—both those who preceded us and those who came afterward and are under us—have been treated badly and contrary to what was proper.

“‘Concerning them we asked your paternal holiness, in a letter written beforehand, to send us a decree and judgment; and now we ask it again. To this letter we add, on behalf of those who have fallen, a most gracious petition, especially concerning those who seek a place for penance and return to their legitimate supreme priest. We ask that a common shipwreck not overtake the supreme priests and priests of our Church who exist under our entire rule, with nearly all of them tasting the false and undrinkable floods of iniquity.

“‘Concerning these matters, therefore, we ask your most compassionate priesthood to extend a hand of humanity and arrange the salvation of those who acknowledge only their own sin and ask to receive forgiveness from the supreme and most holy priest whom they have troubled wickedly and unjustly. For those who remain in evil and do not wish to return to the path of truth, no method or reasoning will free them from condemnation.

“‘So that your divine and apostolic judgment may also become manifest to those who belong to Photius’s faction, both concerning our most holy father and patriarch Ignatius and concerning the most wretched Photius, apocrisarii have been sent from both sides by our Christ-loving empire to your paternal holiness. From the most holy Patriarch Ignatius, John, metropolitan of Silae; from Photius, Peter, metropolitan of Sardis. With them our empire, fortified by God, has sent Basil the spatharius.

“‘We wish your paternal holiness to receive them and, in the presence of the bishops sent from both sides, to establish whatever your holiness judges concerning the supreme priests and priests according to ecclesiastical laws and canons. Together with them, send us most reverend apocrisarii, so that our most holy Church may be informed more explicitly and purely of what your holiness’s will is regarding both parties.

“‘Therefore, spiritual father and supreme pontiff honored by God, hasten, for the correction and struggle of our Church against injustice and for satisfaction of the truth, to bestow upon us a great store of good things: pure unity, a spiritual structure free from every contention and schism, one Church in Christ, and one flock obedient to one shepherd, whose true minister and sacrificer you are.

“‘I greet through this letter, as though with my lips, the holy and desirable head whom I love. Farewell. It was sent in the month of December, on the eleventh day.’”

After the reading of the aforementioned letter, Stephen, the God-beloved deacon and devout notary, took the letter of Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, which he had sent to Adrian, the most holy pope, and read it:

[Col. 0060C] [Note: [Col. 0060D] This letter was indeed sent to Nicholas, but after his death Adrian received it.]

“To the God-honored and beloved brother and fellow minister, Nicholas, the most holy pope of senior Rome, Ignatius, archbishop of Constantinople by the mercy of God.

[The supplied source ends here.]

Of the wounds and bruises that occur in the limbs of a human being, the art of medicine has produced many physicians: one treating one ailment and another another, cutting away and healing each through experience. But for the wounds that are in the members of Christ and of God the Savior, the head of us all, and of the Catholic and apostolic Bride Church, the one unique, excellent, and most catholic physician—the supreme Prince himself, the mighty Word, organizer, healer, and sole teacher, God of all—has brought forth you, namely, your fraternal holiness and paternal goodness [Col. 0060D]. Therefore he said to the great and supreme apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16). And again: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (ibid.).

For he did not confine and define such blessed words solely according to some particular allotment for the prince of the apostles, but through him he transmitted them to all who were to become, after him and in accordance with him, the supreme shepherds and most divine and sacred pontiffs of senior Rome. Therefore, from ancient times and from the earliest period, many times there have arisen among those who preceded your holiness and supreme fatherhood—successors, namely, of the prince of the apostles and imitators of his zeal for the faith that is according to Christ—eradicators and destroyers of heresies and transgressions, of evil weeds and decayed and utterly incurable members. And now, in our own times, your blessedness has worthily exercised the authority given to you by Christ.

And just as a skilled warrior and an excellent commander, most holy and beloved brother, setting forth as weapons the truth—which is more powerful than all things and conquers all things—as mighty and wholly impregnable arms, you have cast down its enemies, conquered the world with Christ and through Christ, and destroyed the one who stole what was divine, stripped away what belonged to another, entered through the window into the sheepfold like a thief, and plundered the souls of many. Then he raised himself arrogantly and lifted his neck against almighty God, and became so boastfully exalted that he fabricated, against your irreproachable, most divine, and sacred pontificate, an assembly without substance and without person—like the fable of the hippocentaurs and tragelaphs. He even secretly sent this to the emperor.

Thus, this unholy worker, filled with every evil deed—namely, the one called Photius according to the rhetorical figure of antiphrasis—you cut away from the common body of the Church by the work of your pontifical hand and apostolic authority. Equating yourself with the supreme Peter, you killed him, like a new Ananias, by the sentence of your powerful words (Acts 5), and, by anathema, sent him to death, deprived of spiritual life, like another Simon. And us, who had suffered injury, you—as a most just and brother-loving man—justly justified; and the Church that is among us, together with its proper throne, for which you strove and wrote, as the bearer of apostolic and supreme authority, you worthily and reasonably restored. You dispersed the storm that had arisen here and bestowed tranquility upon the Churches.

For our emperor, advanced by God and most beloved by Christ, gentle and most just, formerly favorable to the vote, counsel, decree, and judgment of your holiness and now eagerly obedient to them, has, as your own son and faithful to you both, provided what was fitting. With imperial wisdom he has encouraged and consoled our old age, wearied by much tribulation, as well as all those who have endured many and various tribulations for the justice of God.

For all these things, returning grateful praises and words above all to God and to your blessedness, we have duly sent John, the most blessed and holy metropolitan of Syleion, a worshiper of God and filled with divine understanding, who for nine whole years suffered persecution and other evils together with us for the word of truth; and Peter, the most God-loving bishop of Troas, who likewise suffered these things and struggled together with the imperial person [Note: [Col. 0061D] This alludes to the emperor Louis.]. They will present an account on our behalf and supply and explain orally whatever is lacking from the letter. They will make clear what sort and how great and how abundant is the love and affection that our humility bears toward your fraternal holiness. At the same time, they will also receive decisions and arrangements concerning the remaining ecclesiastical ranks, such as are pleasing to God and appropriate to your understanding, wisdom, and authority.

For the consecration of the priestly catalogue is of two kinds. Some received their consecration from us and voluntarily wrote with their own hand on our behalf; others received it from the unjust and murderous Photius. Many, strengthened by the grace of God, resisted him most firmly in our consecration, refusing in any way to communicate in what they regarded as our dishonor and disgrace and deposition. They endured many and various tribulations, distresses, dreadful exiles, and imprisonments. I know that your blessedness, receiving such men with particular favor, will exalt them with the highest honors as true champions of piety.

But more numerous were those who transgressed their own handwritten declarations, fell away, and, for the sake of the times and their own advantage, became from beginning to end followers, communicants, and collaborators in all Photius’s acts of rashness and wickedness, frequently signing against us, though not willingly, but under force and tyranny. Among them are also some who afterward turned rabidly against the truth and, raging as though by a certain operation of Satan, displayed the most violent madness even against us.

First, therefore, we ask that a disposition be issued concerning such men. Next, we ask about those who received the laying-on of hands from him and themselves likewise acted uselessly and wickedly in every respect according to those things. Further, we ask concerning the presbyters who belonged to our consecration, communicated with him once—or perhaps twice or three times because of severe distress—yet did not sign the document of injustice, withdrew again, and to the present remain voluntarily inactive. We ask also concerning those who, together with communion, gave their signatures but soon afterward embraced idleness. And beyond these, concerning those who received the laying-on of hands from Photius, whether willingly or unwillingly, but, out of reverence, never exercised the priesthood in any way.

Moreover, the most reverend and steadfast Paul, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, received the laying-on of hands from him after the council of vanity that he had previously held against our humility. But at the second synod of the rejected, as the prophet says, he fought most manfully for the truth, triumphed, and publicized their murderous purpose. At no time or in any manner did he sign against our humility; rather, for this very reason he suffered much and endured many kinds of hardship. He will therefore be deemed worthy in your fraternity of a somewhat more favorable treatment.

These, then, are the matters for which we ask that a settlement and regulation be sent in writing to our humility. In addition, we ask for bishops as worthy and reasonable vicars of your blessedness, so that together with them we may properly and suitably regulate the Church that is among us, which, by God’s providence, through the intercession of the supreme Peter and through your urgency and intervention, we have recovered. May these affairs receive a useful and most fitting conclusion, to the glory of God, of your fraternal holiness, and of your most blessed fatherhood, imitator of Christ.

After this letter had been read, Marinus, the most reverend deacon and vicar of senior Rome, took the letter that the most holy Pope Adrian had sent to the most holy Patriarch Ignatius and read it in Latin, in a loud voice for all to hear, while Damian, the most reverend imperial cleric and interpreter, translated and interpreted it into Greek.

“Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow-brother and fellow-minister, Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople.

“Nor can Scripture disclose . . .”

For the remainder, see among the letters of Adrian II, *Patrologia*, volume 122.

After the letter of the most holy vicar of senior Rome had been read, they said: “This letter has been enacted canonically and synodically.” The holy and universal synod said: “The letter of the most holy Pope Adrian that has been read is canonical, duly ordered, and full of justice.”

After this, Metrophanes, the most God-loving metropolitan of Smyrna, rose and said:

“From the letters that have just been read to us, friends of Christ, we have learned more clearly the diligence of our emperor and the zeal he has for bringing peace to the Church of God; the humility of our most holy lord and patriarch Ignatius; and how he fulfills the saying of Scripture: ‘Do everything with counsel.’ We have also learned the prudent speech and reverence of the most holy Roman pope, which he displays in divine matters concerning the preservation and observance of the divine canons, as well as his corresponding mercy and kindness, insofar as possible. Receiving these men magnificently, we all gave thanks to God, who has deemed us worthy to behold such most holy vicars.”

Then Stephen, the most God-loving deacon and devoted notary, stood in the midst and offered this acclamation:

“Many years to the emperors Basil and Constantine! Many years to the great emperors and rulers! Many years to the orthodox emperors! Many years to the peace-making emperors! Many years to those who have deposed injustice! Many years to the enemies of falsehood! Many years to the lovers and supporters of truth and justice! Many years to the most pious Augusta Eudoxia! Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed Roman pope! Many years to Adrian, the orthodox Roman pope! Many years to Ignatius, the orthodox patriarch of Constantinople! Many years to the orthodox patriarchs of the East! Many years to the orthodox senate! Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!”

**Iambic Verses**

The honorable and great chorus of patriarchs

pursues the worst enemy like a wolf,

from the chaste bridal chamber and venerable places;

I mean Photius, the most bitter apostate.

## ACT FOUR

[Col. 0063]

In the name of the Lord and ruler of all, Jesus Christ, true God and our Savior. In the consulship of our God-crowned and most tranquil lords—Basil in his third year, and Constantine, his son, in his second year, perpetual Augusti—in the third indiction, on the third day before the Ides of October, with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation placed on the right-hand side of the catechumenia of the renowned church of Saint Sophia, of the great name; with Donatus, the most God-loving bishop of Ostia, Stephen, the most God-loving bishop of Nepesina, and Marinus, the most God-loving deacon of the holy Roman Church, present as representatives of Adrian, the most holy and most blessed archbishop of senior Rome; and with Ignatius, the most holy archbishop of Constantinople of the great name, New Rome; together with the most holy vicars of the East—namely Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, representing the see of Antioch because that Church was widowed, and Elias, a presbyter and syncellus, a worshiper of God, representing Theodosius, the most holy archbishop of the see of Jerusalem; and thereafter, according to the command of our friends of Christ and most pious great emperors, Basil and Constantine; with the most magnificent princes also present and listening, namely Christopher, most magnificent patrician and master; Bahane, most magnificent patrician and praepositus; Leo, most magnificent patrician and proconsul; Leo, most magnificent patrician and domestic of the Excubitors; John, most magnificent patrician and logothete of the dromos; Manuel, most magnificent patrician; Theophylact, most magnificent patrician; Petronas, most magnificent patrician; Orestes, most magnificent protospatharius and domestic of the Hikanatoi; Sisinnius, most magnificent spatharius; and with the following most God-loving bishops in attendance: Nicephorus, most God-loving metropolitan of Amasia; Nicetas, most God-loving metropolitan of Athens; Metrophanes, most God-loving metropolitan of Smyrna; Theodore, most God-loving metropolitan of Caria; Euthymius, most God-loving metropolitan of Catana; Michael, most God-loving metropolitan of Rhodes; Photius, most God-loving archbishop of Nacolia; Stephen, most God-loving archbishop of Cypsella; Athanasius, most God-loving bishop of Anilius in Magnesia; George, most God-loving bishop of Helios; Stephen, most God-loving bishop of Cibyra; Nicetas, most God-loving bishop of Cephaludium; Theodore, most God-loving bishop of Sinope; Basil, most God-loving bishop of Pyrgi; Gregory, most God-loving bishop of Messina; Eustathius, most God-loving bishop of Aemonia; Xenophon, most God-loving bishop of Milassa; Leo, most God-loving bishop of Daphnusia; Peter, most God-loving bishop of Troas; Samuel, most God-loving bishop of Antrum; Nicetas, most God-loving bishop of Photia; Nicephorus, most God-loving bishop of Corcyra—

when all these had thus assembled, Bahane, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, stood in the midst and said:

“There are two bishops, possessing the consecration of the most blessed Methodius, called Theophilus and Zacharias, who, accepting Photius, proclaim that the Church of the Romans accepted Photius. If it pleases your holiness, let them enter the holy and universal synod and be judged again.”

Donatus, the most God-loving bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most God-loving bishop of Nepesina; and Marinus, the most God-loving deacon of the holy Roman Church, representing Adrian, the most holy Roman pope, said to the most holy vicars of the Eastern sees and to the entire holy synod:

“If you deem it suitable, let some persons be sent to the aforementioned men to ask whose consecration they possess and with whom they communicate.”

The holy and universal synod said: “It is suitable and appropriate.”

Those sent by the vicars of senior Rome—Pancratius, a religious cleric; by the vicars of the East—Ananias, a religious cleric; and by the senate—Gregory, a renowned spatharius and cubicularius—said to them:

“The holy and universal synod has sent us to ask whose consecration you possess and with whom you communicate.”

The former bishops Theophilus and Zacharias said:

“We possess the consecration of Lord Methodius; but we have communicated with Lord Photius, the patriarch.”

When those who had been sent returned, the statement of Theophilus and Zacharias, former bishops, was read by Theodore, a devout secretary, in the midst of the holy and universal synod, for all to hear. The holy synod cried out:

“May the portion of Theophilus and Zacharias be with Photius!”

After this, the most magnificent and glorious princes said through Bahane, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus:

“Our holy emperors have sent their servants, who are called the senate and who, by God’s will, have been honored here in every respect, so that we may be attentive hearers of what is being done. If, therefore, you wish at the end of this holy and universal synod to require from us, according to synodical procedure, our own signatures through me, the unworthy servant of our holy emperors, all my brothers and fellow-countrymen say to our most holy lord patriarch and to the most holy vicars both of senior Rome and of the Eastern sees:

“‘Unless we hear both Photius himself, standing in our presence, and his bishops, as well as those who possess the consecration of the most blessed Methodius and who have become apostates from the most holy Ignatius, so that their mouths may be stopped in our presence by canonical and synodical judgments, our hand will not write a single letter in this synod. Let them hear what was judged by senior Rome in our presence, and if they are unable to contradict anything, the world will be healed by their agreement.

“‘But if this is not done, we know that you have no need of us to write at the end of the proceedings conducted by you. For how shall we subscribe to such a judgment while they cry out and say, “Let us hear our deposition; let us be condemned,” and their words are not heard, as justice requires? In our opinion, this is not just. Therefore, do what seems right to you.

“‘Even before your holiness, preserved by God, came to the city of our holy emperors, we held the same opinion concerning both the judgment of the most blessed Pope Nicholas and the reception of the most holy Pope Adrian, as well as the certification and confirmation of the honorable priest, our most holy lord patriarch. Afterward we saw the vicars of the East, and we also saw and received you as holy apostles.

“‘We ask, therefore, that those who are sick may be healed; that we may correct those who lack certainty of the truth; and that we may raise up those who lie prostrate. Unless all these matters are examined in this way, the consciences of men will not be healed.’”

Metrophanes, the most God-loving metropolitan of Smyrna, rose and said:

“The divine apostle says: ‘Do not despise prophecies; test everything, and hold fast to what is good’ (1 Thessalonians 5). Therefore, receiving the most holy vicars of senior Rome as prophets, we in no way despise them. But, testing the words of the most magnificent princes, we find them just and appropriate. For this reason all the bishops and this holy synod support the request of the most magnificent princes: let those men be examined and questioned as to whether they accept the judges. If they are granted an opportunity to offer satisfaction and are justified, let us all receive them willingly; but if they are found condemned, let everyone acquiesce.

“Let them now be required in writing to acknowledge whether they accept this holy and universal synod and the judgments issued by it, and let them enter lawfully.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“And do the men you speak of know what the holy Roman Church has judged?”

Bahane, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“They do not know. Since they were not present there and did not hear your action face to face, what certainty do you expect them to possess from hearsay concerning their own condemnation? [Note: [Col. 0065D] Perhaps: ‘their.’]”

Donatus and Stephen, most God-loving bishops, and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church and most holy vicar of senior Rome, said:

“We are not permitted to rescind the judgment of the sacred Roman pontiffs, for this is contrary to canonical ordinances. Those who were present there through their own envoys and who stayed in Rome heard and clearly learned the sentence pronounced against them, against Photius, and against his laying-on of hands.

“Nevertheless, in order to make the just judgment of the holy Roman Church clearer to them, let them enter and hear read the synodical definitions and the judgments of the most blessed Pope Nicholas, so that they may become increasingly certain.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“This is good and best. Let them hear the judgment of the most blessed Pope Nicholas in our presence; if they have anything to say in contradiction, let them say it [Note: [Col. 0067D] That is, what they are to say.], or, persuaded, let them acquiesce. But if they have grounds for contradiction [Note: [Col. 0068D] That is, to contradict.], let them accept their own condemnation; if, however, they do not accept it, then what the canons prescribe shall be done.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“They are seeking an excuse. The whole world—the East, the West, and the holy Church of Constantinople—knows that judgment has been issued against them. From the eleventh indiction onward, the most holy Pope Nicholas condemned them synodically, and throughout all this time they have not learned the sentence pronounced against them. This is no excuse; they wish to escape judgment.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“On the contrary, they are not escaping judgment. If they had wished to escape, they ought not to cry out in a loud voice, ‘Let us be judged’; rather, they ought to withdraw privately and take flight. But what the whole community has heard for a long time through clear voices and speeches, they now wish to have confirmed by the deed itself and by the proceedings.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Let them enter and stand down below in the last place, and let them hear the letter that the most holy Pope Nicholas sent to the emperor Michael through Radoald and Zacharias.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“As you command. We ask, however, that they also be summoned, and that at least three or four from the party of Photius be summoned, so that they may hear; or else let these laymen who stand behind us hear. It would be very good for this to happen.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“If those three acknowledge that all those belonging to their side may come, we will allow them to enter here.”

Bahane, the most magnificent praepositus and patrician, said:

“We ask that as many as five be allowed.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Let them enter. We are not summoning them for the sake of contention, but only so that they may hear the letter of the most blessed Pope Nicholas.”

Some attendants were sent to summon them, but did not find them.

The most magnificent and glorious princes said to the vicars of senior Rome and of the Eastern sees:

“Not knowing that they were being sought by the holy and universal synod, they have departed and cannot be found. But those two who were questioned shortly before by your holiness—namely Theophilus and Zacharias—are present and ready, as you command. It appears that the others departed for this reason: they left these two behind and supposed that we had no need of them today. In any event, if it pleases your holiness, let the matter of the two be investigated.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Do those two persons have a petition to present, or do they merely have a speech for the holy synod?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“No. But these are the two who are harming that multitude in every way by assuring them that Pope Nicholas communicated with us. The multitude finds satisfaction in this, for if he accepted these two and communicated with them, then he certainly accepted Photius and communicated with him. If he accepted and communicated with Photius, then he was certainly called patriarch on a single day; and if he was called patriarch on a single day, we have something substantial to say.

“Once these two are convicted of the fact that what they tell their multitude is false, empty, and invalid, great benefit will come to many from this small matter.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Far be it from us that the most blessed Nicholas should ever have accepted Photius as patriarch of Constantinople, even for a day or an hour, into the priestly college of the holy Roman Church.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Blessed be God. Let these men also be made certain, so that they may approach the truth.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Since they say that they communicated with the most holy Pope Nicholas, let them enter, stand in one place, and hear what was decreed concerning them.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Rather, let them be questioned and examined as to how they can say, ‘We communicated with the most blessed Pope Nicholas,’ since they assert this with complete certainty.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Let them enter.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Who is to bring them? They possess the consecration of Methodius. Moreover, the text of your petition expressly grants that those who possess the consecration of the most blessed Methodius and of the most holy patriarch Ignatius, whatever and however great their offenses may have been against him, should receive forgiveness and justification if they wish to repent. Therefore, by summoning such men also, you commit no offense.”

Donatus and Stephen, the most God-loving bishops, and Marinus, the most venerable deacon, the most holy vicars of senior Rome, said:

“Since they were formerly entrusted to those who departed from us, those men said to them: ‘Because we communicate with Photius, we are not summoning them.’”

Bahane, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Many of the bishops sitting here communicated with Photius to the very end.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Nevertheless, these men were received through a petition of satisfaction.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“But those men did not hear the petition. It is not harmful to dispute verbally for a useful purpose. Our Lord Jesus Christ had twelve disciples. But is Thomas, who doubted, condemned as doubtful and faithless? No. His incredulity served to establish the certainty of many. Let these men come as well, so that perhaps through the unbelief of the impious and the refutation of their words, great profit may be gained for many through these two.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Let them enter.”

When Zacharias and Theophilus, former bishops, entered, the most holy vicars of senior Rome said to the sacred synod and the renowned senate:

“These are the men who desired [or: requested] to enter the holy synod. What do they wish to hear? What do they say?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Let them be questioned themselves, and they will state their request.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“What are the names of those who are being summoned?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Zacharias and Theophilus.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Do these men who requested entry into the holy synod accept this petition presented by the most holy Pope Adrian and fulfill everything he prescribed?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Let them be questioned.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Question them.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“In obedience to your word, we question them at your command, not by our own authority; for this authority belongs to you.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Question them whether they are willing to make the petition sent by the holy Roman Church.”

Bahane, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to the aforementioned former bishops:

“Do you wish to hear the petition?”

The former bishops Zacharias and Theophilus said:

“We neither wish to hear the petition nor did we wish to come here. The emperor ordered that we be found in the palace, and there we were found in his presence in this manner—not because of the petition.”

Bahane, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“You said in the palace: ‘We can prove in every respect that we communicated as priests with the most holy Pope Nicholas.’”

The former bishops Zacharias and Theophilus said:

“We said it, and we say it again: we were received by Pope Nicholas as supreme priests, we ministered with him, and we were accepted by him.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Far from it! They are liars and do not speak the truth.”

The former bishops Zacharias and Theophilus said:

“If we are liars, then do not question us.”

Marinus, the most God-loving deacon and Roman vicar, said:

“What do you think? Is everyone who is questioned necessarily questioned as though he were certainly truthful?”

The former bishop Theophilus said to the sacred synod, pointing to Marinus, the most reverend deacon and vicar of senior Rome:

“Question the man who is speaking to me. Was he not in Rome when these things took place?”

Marinus, the most honorable deacon and vicar of senior Rome, said:

“I was a subdeacon of the Roman Church in those days, consecrated by Leo, the most holy Roman pope, and I ministered in the Roman Church from the twelfth year of my life. When these men came to Rome with Arsabir, I was ministering in the Roman church of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, which is called Praesepe.

“There the most holy Pope Nicholas received them after they had presented a petition of satisfaction and taken an oath; but he did not grant them communion in the place of bishops. If they contradict this, let them show that he received them into communion as bishops.”

The former bishop Theophilus said:

“Was I an unknown person? I was sent by the emperor and by the synod.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Did you bring letters when you went up with the vicars Radoald and Zacharias?”

The former bishops Theophilus and Zacharias said:

“We do not know.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“Let every holy and sacred synod know from this that they are liars. They say, ‘We were sent as apocrisiaries with letters,’ and yet, if they brought a letter, they do not know.”

The former bishop Theophilus said:

“I was not investigating the letters; I went to receive the apocrisiaries, not the letter.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said to Theophilus:

“What did the letter that you brought to Rome contain?”

Theophilus said:

“I do not know.”

The most holy vicars of senior Rome said:

“This holy and universal synod believes that the Roman Church never at any time received Photius as patriarch, nor those who possess the laying-on of hands from him.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“How, then, do they say that they were received?”

Donatus and Stephen, the most God-loving bishops, and Marinus, the most venerable deacon of the most holy vicars of senior Rome, said:

“Because they are lying against the holy Roman Church. But so that you may be assured that we are speaking the truth, let the letters of the most blessed Pope Nicholas be read—both those sent to the emperor Michael and to Photius himself, and those sent here at various times through several apocrisiaries.”

Stephen, the most God-loving deacon of the Church of Constantinople and devoted notary, took them and read:

“Nicolaus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Michael, glorious emperor of the Greeks.

‘The primacy of divine authority . . .’”

For the remainder, see among the letters of Pope Nicholas, *Patrologia*, volume 126, column 000.

After the most magnificent and glorious princes had heard the reading, they said:

“We are satisfied by what we have now heard, because you have spoken the truth. The letter refutes those men, and it has become known to us that the most holy Pope Nicholas did not receive Photius or his laying-on of hands. But let another letter also be read, the one sent by the most holy Pope Nicholas to the emperor Michael through Leo, the secretary.”

The same Stephen, deacon of the holy Church of Constantinople and notary, took it and read:

“Nicolaus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most pious, glorious, and beloved son, Michael, great emperor.

‘The glory of your most serene empire . . .’”

For the remainder, see among the letters of Pope Nicholas, *Patrologia*, volume 126, column 000.

While the letter was still being read, the former bishop Theophilus replied and said:

“If Photius is condemned, let those who introduced and consecrated him also be condemned.”

The holy and universal synod said to him:

“Then you too are condemned, as one who accepted and communicated with him.”

The former bishop Theophilus said:

“I am not condemned, because I was not present when he was consecrated; I found him as patriarch and accepted him as such.”

After the letters had been completed, Theodore, the most God-loving metropolitan of Caria, rose and said:

“Until this present hour I held certainty in my mind, and for that reason I rejected the most blessed Pope Nicholas and accused him: believing these men, I thought that he had first received Photius and had finally attempted to destroy him.”

The holy and universal synod said to the former bishop Theophilus:

“Did these letters come from that source, or not?”

The former bishop Theophilus said:

“I do not know whether these are the letters or others.”

Theodore, the God-loving metropolitan of Caria, said:

“How can you show that you ministered with Pope Nicholas?”

Theophilus said:

“Let the emperor give me a written assurance of impunity, and I will demonstrate it to this man here. Before God I say that I communicated with him and ministered with him. Indeed, I say again: we ministered with him and communicated with him.”

After this, the holy synod urged Stephen, the God-loving deacon of the holy Church of Constantinople and devoted notary, to read the letter sent through Leo, the secretary, to Photius. He approached and read:

“Nicolaus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most prudent man Photius.

‘After the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, . . .’”

For the remainder, see the place cited above, column 777.

While the letter was still being read, and an account was being given concerning the reception of Ambrose and Nectarius, Theophilus, formerly bishop, replied:

“I also heard these things from the Romans; nevertheless, at Rome they received Lord Photius.”

Theodore, God-beloved metropolitan of Caria, said:

“How can you say that he was received by the pope, when he writes that he is an adulterer?”

And Theophilus said:

“And how did you receive him?” [Col. 0071D]

Theodore, God-beloved metropolitan of Caria, said:

“Until yesterday I was of one mind with you. But since the most holy Nicholas proclaims with confident voice that we neither rejected Ignatius nor received Photius, I have therefore adhered to the most reverend patriarch Ignatius.”

Theophilus, formerly bishop, said:

“From this learn what sort of man Nicholas is.”

And Theodore said:

“How can you show that the most holy Pope Nicholas received you?”

And Theophilus said:

“I told you that, if today the emperor gives me a written declaration of impunity—that those whom I bring as witnesses will suffer nothing—I shall prove it.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“By no reasonable pretext can Photius demonstrate that he was ever received by the Roman See. Rather, it always counted him among the laity and called him an adulterer and an intruder. Since he did not heed the word of the prelate of the apostolic Roman Church, he was bound, rejected, and condemned, as is contained in the letters that you heard.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said to the representatives of the East:

“We also have something to say to you. We ask your holiness as well: You have certainly heard the judgment of the Roman Church. What does the Church of Antioch say about the aforementioned Photius? Did you receive him? Did you send him letters of reception?”

Thomas, God-beloved metropolitan of Tyre and occupying the place of the See of Antioch, replied:

“We never received Photius in the Church of Antioch; we neither sent him a letter of reception nor received one from him.” [Col. 0072B]

Helias, most holy syncellus and occupying the place of Theodosius, most holy patriarch of Jerusalem, said:

“If our most pious and God-crowned emperor is credulous either toward Photius or toward his communicants, he himself will establish the matter through his own envoys and apocrisiaries—namely, Isaiah and Spyridon, Cypriots—with the letters that he sent to our patriarch. For he extorted me from the hand of Theodosius, most holy patriarch of Jerusalem, when I was syncellus of the apostolic throne of Saint James of Jerusalem.

“Therefore I say, as though before God and his chosen angels, that we never received Photius into the episcopate; we neither accepted letters from him nor sent any to him. But if our God-fearing emperor is incredulous toward them, let him do to them whatever seems good to his most pious and just authority. For what we know with complete certainty, that we also testify.”

Metrophanes, God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna, said:

“We clearly know the divine Scripture to say: ‘All things are manifest to those who understand, and upright to those who find knowledge’ (Proverbs 8). Accordingly, through the grace of Christ, we who understand and possess knowledge of divine and human matters have understood and learned from what has taken place today that Photius was never admitted as bishop into the holy Roman Church, nor into the other patriarchal thrones. Rather, from beginning to end he was rejected, disapproved, and condemned.” [Col. 0072D]

And he said to the remaining bishops:

“What then do you say, brothers—you also?”

Theodore, metropolitan of Caria, said:

“I give thanks to God, because through this holy and universal synod I have been released from those thoughts that troubled my soul every day: whether Photius had been received in the patriarchates or not. Through his apocrisiaries, who at first satisfied me concerning these matters; through the letters that he sent and those that he received; I have been convinced that Photius was never received by them into the dignity of the episcopate.

“Therefore I confess my fault: I followed him in error, and now I have been deemed worthy to be counted among this holy synod.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Do you have anything else to say today? If you wish, we shall question you.

“It is the custom in the Roman Church to require from every visiting person a booklet of faith, and only then to permit him to enter Saint Peter’s. Did these men act according to this custom, or not?”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“They did.”

Zacharias and Theophilus, formerly bishops, said:

“Did we make one booklet or two?”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“You made two booklets.”

[Note: [Col. 0073B] And in fact they made two booklets: one, namely, a profession of faith, before they entered the City; and another concerning obedience to the decrees of the apostolic see, before they were received into communion.]

Zacharias and Theophilus, formerly bishops, said:

“Then they were not there.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes asked the holy representatives what the booklet contained.

The most holy representatives of Rome said:

“That they should hold and defend the truth according to the Catholic Church, and in all things follow the judgment of the holy Roman Church.” [Col. 0073B]

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“They confessed this yesterday also in the secretariat: that they would agree in all things with the Roman Church.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Therefore question the transgressors themselves whether they will make the Roman booklet or not.”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said to Zacharias and Theophilus, formerly bishops:

“Will you make the booklet or not?”

Zacharias and Theophilus, formerly bishops, said:

“We do not even wish to hear it.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Send them outside.”

After they had gone out, Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“We have not investigated Zacharias’s case. Yesterday he confessed that he had been bound by Pope Benedict not to exercise pontifical authority until he came, descended again with those who had separated themselves from the most holy patriarch Ignatius, and submitted to judgment. He did not observe this, nor did he descend there.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“He has a share with those who do not agree with the Church, and he is an accomplice of those who acted against the Church of Constantinople and against the most holy patriarch Ignatius. But since the hour is late, we cannot investigate this today; we shall do so at another examination.”

Then Stephen, God-beloved deacon of the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans and devoted notary, stood in the midst and pronounced the acclamation as follows:

“Many years to the emperors Basil and Constantine! Many years to the great emperors and dictators! Many years to the Orthodox emperors! Many years to the peace-making emperors! Many years to those who depose injustice! Many years to the enemies of falsehood! Many years to the lovers and defenders of truth and justice! Many years to Eudoxia, the most pious Augusta! Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed pope of Rome! Many years to Adrian, the Orthodox pope of Rome! Many years to Ignatius, the Orthodox patriarch of Constantinople! Many years to the Orthodox patriarchs of the East! Many years to the Orthodox senate! Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!”

## FIFTH SESSION

[Col. 0073]

[Col. 0073C] In the name of the Lord and ruler of all, Jesus Christ, our true God and Savior.

In the consulship of our God-redeemed and most tranquil lords, Basil in his third year and Constantine, his son, in his second year, eternal Augusti; in the third indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November; with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled and holy Gospels placed before them; while the holy and universal synod was assembled—Donatus, God-beloved bishop of Ostia; Stephen, God-beloved bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, occupying the place of Adrian, most holy pope of Rome; Ignatius, most holy patriarch of Constantinople; Thomas, most holy metropolitan of Tyre, occupying the place of the See of Antioch; and Helias, most God-revering presbyter and syncellus, occupying the place of the See of Jerusalem—

and while the sacred senate was also present, namely Theodore, most magnificent patrician and praepositus; Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus; Leo, most magnificent patrician and proconsul; Leo, most magnificent patrician and domestic of the excubitors; John, most magnificent patrician and logothete of the imperial road; Petronas, most magnificent patrician; Manuel, most magnificent patrician; another Manuel, most magnificent patrician; and Orestes, most magnificent protospatharius and domestic of the ikanatoi;

with the God-beloved metropolitans also sitting with them, namely Basil, God-beloved archbishop of Ephesus; Barnabas, God-beloved metropolitan of Cyzicus; Nicephorus, God-beloved metropolitan of Amasia; Nicetas, God-beloved metropolitan of Athens; Theodore, God-beloved metropolitan of Caria; Metrophanes, God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna; Michael, God-beloved metropolitan of Rhodes; Photius, God-beloved archbishop of Nacolia; Euthymius, God-beloved archbishop of Catana; and Stephen, God-beloved archbishop of Cypsella;

Athanasius, God-beloved bishop of Magnesia; Theodore, God-beloved bishop of Sinope; Eustathius, God-beloved bishop of Aemonia; Theodore, God-beloved bishop of Lacedaemon; Nicephorus, God-beloved bishop of Zacynthus; Euthymius, God-beloved bishop of the Mosynoi; Basil, God-beloved bishop of Pyrgi; George, God-beloved bishop of Helil; Peter, God-beloved bishop of Troas; Leo, God-beloved bishop of Daphnusia; and Nicetas, God-beloved bishop of Photice.

[Note: [Col. 0073D] Observe that the number of bishops gradually increases in the individual sessions, because, since not all of them had been found in the City at the beginning of the synod, they were admitted to the synodal assembly only when it became clear that each had come from his own Church and had written the Roman booklet in his own hand.]

When these men had assembled, Paul, God-beloved chartophylax, stood in the midst and said:

“According to the preceding session, as your holiness commanded, Zacharias alone is again present here. But our most Christian emperor has also sent Photius to the synod.”

Donatus, God-beloved bishop of Ostia; Stephen, God-beloved bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, occupying the place of Adrian, most holy pope of Rome, said:

“Does Photius wish to come into our presence and before the holy synod?”

Paul, God-beloved chartophylax, said:

“We do not know whether he wishes to or not. But, if you command, we shall find out.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Let him be asked whether he wishes to come to this holy and universal synod.”

Paul, God-beloved chartophylax, said:

“Whom does your holiness command to go and ask him?”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Let laymen go.”

The senate therefore sent to Photius Sisinnius, glorious protospatharius; Eutychianus, first of the mandators of the excubitors; George, first of the mandators of the ikanatoi; Leo, a layman of the representatives of Old Rome; and Cyriacus and Joseph, laymen of the representatives of the East. They instructed them to say:

“The holy and universal synod announces to you: Do you wish to come to the holy synod or not? If he says, ‘I do not wish to,’ ask him why.”

The men who had been sent went and did as they had been instructed. Photius replied to them:

“You never summoned me to the synod before, and now I am astonished that you have done this and summoned me. Nevertheless, I do not come voluntarily. Since you never questioned me about this synod of which you speak, how are you dragging me into it? I said: ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard over my mouth’ (Psalm 38); read the rest yourselves.”

When the aforementioned men had returned, Gregory, the devout notary of the imperial secretariat, was ordered to ascend, and he read Photius’s words aloud for all to hear.

After the reading, the most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“What does the holy synod say to this? We are not summoning him in order to learn something from him, but so that we may now bring to an end, with him present, the labor that the holy Roman Church, together with the Eastern Churches, has endured on his account.”

[Note: [Col. 0075D] They say this as a matter of honor; for before this synod the Eastern sees appear to have undertaken no labor in the controversy. Only the first see is found to have labored on his account, both personally and through its letters and envoys.]

The God-beloved bishops said:

“Let him come.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Does this please you?”

The God-beloved bishops said:

“It does.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Let him come.”

The following was dictated to Photius by the holy synod through Helias the syncellus:

“Since, by a tacit conclusion, you have pronounced this synod, chosen by God, to be made up of sinners—not only the representatives of the most holy thrones and the chief priests, but also the honorable senate of our holy Fathers—by introducing a prophetic saying out of season and inappropriately, it is right to say in response that, because you had works of darkness within yourself, you feared the holy and universal synod assembled in the light of truth, lest you should be exposed and made public through it, just as the holy Gospel declares: ‘Everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed’ (John 3).

“But it is written: ‘Restrain their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you’ (Psalm 31). Therefore, from now on, the authority of the synod, with imperial consent, will fittingly and suitably bring that prophetic saying to its conclusion.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said to the holy synod:

“Does this please you?”

The holy synod said:

“It does.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Let him come.”

When those who had been sent went and the foregoing acclamation had been read to him, Photius said:

“How have you again dragged us here, even against our will? If you still wished to do this, should you not have questioned us about coming together? But from the beginning you resolved to carry it out imperatively and by force of authority.”

When these words had also been read in the synod, the holy and universal synod again acclaimed Photius as follows:

“Following ecclesiastical order, in our first address we awaited your voluntary appearance. But since you are truly a manifest sinner and have most unjustly refused of your own accord to enter the just council, lest you receive a more evident condemnation, for this reason, as we said, we bring you here against your will in our second address.”

After this address had also been read to Photius, Photius was brought in and stood in the midst.

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said to the most magnificent princes:

“Who is that man standing in the last place of this holy synod?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Photius.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Is that Photius on whose account the holy Roman Church endured many labors for seven years and more; who completely overturned the holy Church of Constantinople and disturbed not only these Churches but also the holy Churches of the East, which have continued to suffer labors at his hands up to the present?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“That is he.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Does he accept the constitutions of the holy Fathers?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“Let him be questioned.”

At the princes’ direction, George, most glorious custodian of the palace, and Papias, the doorkeeper, questioned Photius:

“Do you accept the constitutions of the holy Fathers?” [Col. 0077A]

He did not answer.

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Do you accept the constitutions of the holy Roman pontiffs? Do you accept the exposition issued by the most blessed Nicholas, most holy pope of the Romans?”

He did not answer.

“Do you accept what the most holy Adrian, successor to Nicholas as pope of the Roman See, issued anew? Let him speak, let him speak.”

Photius, however, answered nothing.

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“We have heard that he is a rational man”—

[Note: [Col. 0077D] That is, eloquent.]

“and we know that he is a transgressor and an adulterer. Let him speak, let him speak.”

Photius said:

“God hears my voice even when I am silent.”

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“By silence you will not escape a more evident condemnation.”

Photius said:

“Jesus also did not escape condemnation by remaining silent.”

The most holy representatives of the apostolic sees said:

“It is not fitting for us to give you an answer to such a statement, since you have compared what is yours with what belongs to our Lord Jesus Christ. There is no communion of light with darkness, no participation of righteousness with iniquity, no agreement of Christ with Belial, and no accord between the temple of God and idols (2 Corinthians 6).

“But concerning the matters about which you have been questioned by our brothers and fellow ministers, the most holy representatives of Old Rome: answer whether or not you accept the judgments of the holy Roman pontiffs.”

Photius did not answer.

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Let him bow his neck; let him declare his sin by word and in writing; let him anathematize the things that were written and done insultingly, which he twice carried out abruptly against the most holy patriarch Ignatius; let him profess that he will henceforth undertake no plot or disturbance against him; let him receive him, with great shame, as his true pontiff; and let him honorably embrace the judgments promulgated by the apostolic chair, both concerning himself and concerning Patriarch Ignatius.”

While Photius remained silent, the most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Behold the man who stopped his ears, like a deaf viper (Psalm 57), and does not hear the voice that the holy synod addresses to him, but wishes by silence to escape this condemnation that the holy Roman Church promulgated against him many years ago.

“Let the letters sent concerning him by the holy Roman Church be read. Does it therefore please everyone that they be read?”

The holy synod said:

“It does.”

Stephen, God-beloved deacon of the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans and notary, took the letter and read the one sent to the emperor Michael through Rhadoald and Zacharias.

[Note: [Col. 0077D] This letter that was read here is in the fourth session.]

After the first letter had been completed, the most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“What does the holy synod say to this? Is this letter full of canonical exposition or not?”

The holy and universal synod said:

“It fulfills canonical law, as well as synodal command and legislation.” [Col. 0078A]

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Let the other letter sent to Photius himself also be read.”

The God-beloved metropolitans said:

“Let it be read.”

The aforementioned Stephen took it and read it.

[Note: [Col. 0077D] This letter likewise had been read beforehand in the fourth session.]

After the letter had been completed, the most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Why has he stopped his ears and not answered what is being read?”

The most holy metropolitans said to Photius:

“Why do you not answer these things?”

He did not answer.

The most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“Let the letter sent by Leo, the secretary, also be read.”

Stephen, God-beloved deacon and notary of the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans, took the letter sent to the emperor Michael and read it.

[Note: [Col. 0078D] This letter likewise is set out above in the fourth session.]

After that letter had been completed, the most holy representatives of Old Rome again said:

“Let the next and other letter, the one addressed to Photius, be read.”

The same Stephen took it and read it.

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Photius of Constantinople:

“Every benefit and advancement of souls is fortified by the Catholic faith.” . . .

[The remainder may be found among the letters of Pope Nicholas I, in volume 126 of Patrologia, col. 785.]

After the letter had been completed, Thomas and Helias, most holy representatives of the Eastern sees, said to the most magnificent princes: [Col. 0078C]

“We wish to say something to the holy synod. Does this please you?”

The most magnificent and glorious princes said:

“This lies within your authority.”

Helias, most God-revering presbyter and syncellus of the throne of Jerusalem, ascended and addressed all who were listening as follows:

“On the preceding day, when we, friends of Christ, fathers, and brothers, were assembled here, we said a few things to your reverence; now we say the same things again.

“You know that in former times there were emperors who convened synods—

[Note: [Col. 0078D] Universal synods, that is; for emperors are scarcely ever, if ever, known to have convened local synods.]

“and gathered representatives from the whole world to settle matters of this kind. Following their custom, our God-fearing emperor convened this universal synod—not secretly or clandestinely, but openly and manifestly—namely, the college of the most holy representatives of Old Rome and of us.

“For although there are many other things that prove us to be the true representatives of the Eastern sees, this is the greater, most immediate, clearest, and most evident proof: our most pious and Christ-loving emperor, with great diligence and zeal, summoned us and received us from our Churches, although tens of thousands of obstacles and prohibitions stood in the way.

“Let him himself testify from where and by whom we were sent to come to you, and let him provide a sufficient explanation on our behalf. When we arrived and had spent about two years here, he placed his encolpium around our necks—

[Note: [Col. 0079D] An encolpium is something carried on the breast; for *kolpos* (Greek) means ‘bosom’ in Latin. It is customary among the Greeks to wear a cross containing precious wood or the relics of saints suspended before the chest from the neck; this is what they call an encolpium.]

“and said: ‘May God demand the judgment of the Church from your necks on the day of judgment, so that you do nothing through favor, grace, or hatred. For it is fitting that you, having reached such an advanced age, do nothing through partiality or contrary to justice. For it is written: “Do not pity the poor in judgment, and do not show partiality to the powerful” (Proverbs 24).’

“Accordingly, having received judgment from our Christ-loving emperor—

[Note: [Col. 0080D] That is, invoking condemnation upon ourselves if we should deviate from what is right.]

“we have proceeded from that time until now as the requirements of justice demand. For neither, because the most holy patriarch Ignatius presides upon this throne and is powerful by reason of the position he holds, shall we therefore show him partiality; nor, because this man Photius stands here and is consequently thought to be poor, shall we condemn him or irrationally pity him.

“Thus you see the depth of his silence, since he scarcely suffers himself to say anything to the holy synod, clearly rejecting it and in no way accepting it, as he also indicated in his own words.

“But since, by the grace of God, I have been syncellus of the Church of Jerusalem for seven years, I know clearly that we neither received letters from him nor sent any to him at all. You have also often heard what this most holy Thomas, metropolitan of Tyre, has said; and now likewise, affirming the same thing, he says that the See of Antioch neither received letters from Photius nor ever sent any.

“You learned and recognized long ago the decree of the holy Roman Church concerning him, which the most blessed Pope Nicholas promulgated, and subsequently his successor Adrian. We both stated and demonstrated this in our preceding speeches. For this reason I say it now also in his presence and before his face, with his eyes seeing and his ears hearing.

“He is condemned, since he was not received by any of the patriarchal sees, and he has wickedly and unjustly chosen silence today, so that by his silence he might appear to possess some arguments. For he has nothing to offer in his defense.

“We all know both how he assaulted the throne of Constantinople by force and tyranny and what disturbances and tyrannies he has carried out while still occupying that same throne.

“Therefore we now offer him counsel and admonish him to recognize his sin. If he openly and sincerely repents of his injustices and of all the evils with which he has filled the world, let him be received into the Church of Christ our Savior, like any of the faithful, as one who has hope of eternal life; and let him not receive from God the certainty of eternal ruin and condemnation through the anathema that was pronounced against him long ago.”

[Col. 0080A] After this address, Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“We too give this admonition and counsel.”

Then Theodore, the devout secretary, took up and read what had been briefly issued by the most holy representatives of Old Rome. It said:

“You have seen, brothers; you have seen and heard what has long been said and done concerning this case. It has become clear to all of you that the promotion of this man was inadmissible, and that the deposition of the most holy patriarch Ignatius from his see was carried out without justice and without laws.

“Therefore we shall neither judge nor introduce some new or recent judgment, but one judged long ago by the most holy and blessed Pope Nicholas and confirmed by the most holy Pope Adrian. We cannot be transferred or moved away from the definitions and laws of the Fathers, nor turn aside to the right or to the left. For it is written: ‘Hear, my son, the laws of your father, and do not reject the ordinances of your mother’ (Proverbs 1).

“You have also heard from our brothers, the representatives of the East, that they never received him as chief priest. Whom, therefore, neither our apostolic see nor the sees of the East received, who henceforth, if he wishes to be a Christian, will receive?

“Therefore we reject and anathematize such an attempt, lest some other such malicious action ever again be introduced against the Church, and lest a legitimate pontiff be rashly and easily expelled by secular power, with another substituted for him unjustly and illegally.

“What then? Does this judgment please you or not? If it pleases you, these are our views and those of our see. But if they are not acceptable to you, we shall nevertheless ascend the high mountain of the synod and raise our voice with strength, proclaiming to you both the sequence of events and what was done and proclaimed by the mouth of our holy Fathers through the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

After the reading, the most holy representatives of Old Rome said:

“What does the holy synod say to this? Are these things that have been spoken by us in the reading accepted by you?”

The holy and universal synod cried out:

“We accept everything. They are indeed highly discerning, appropriate, and consonant with ecclesiastical rules and laws.”

Donatus, God-beloved bishop of Ostia; Stephen, God-beloved bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, said:

“Then we admonish him to fall before this holy synod and bow his neck before his most holy patriarch Ignatius, to repent of what he has done, to become a member of the holy Church, and to join the holy communion of Christians in the manner [or: as one] of the faithful laity, so that it may result in the salvation of his own soul and of his people, even though some may intend to follow him.”

Bahanes, most famous patrician and praepositus, said: [Col. 0081A]

“Speak, Lord Photius, whatever case you have in your defense. The whole world is here; let the holy and universal synod not close its holy heart. Where will you flee from here? To Rome? Behold, Rome is here. To the East? Behold, those from the East are present here. See that the door is not closed; if these men close it, no one can open it. Speak, man of God: what defense do you have?”

Photius said:

“My defenses are not in this world. If they were in this world, you would see them here.”

Bahanes, most praiseworthy patrician and praepositus, said:

“We maintain that you are overcome by confusion and fear and are speaking irrationally, not knowing what you are saying. Therefore the holy and universal synod grants you time to consider your salvation. Go, and it again commands you to come here.”

Photius said:

“I do not ask for time; but whether I am sent away from you lies within your authority.” [Col. 0081B]

Bahanes, most praiseworthy patrician and praepositus, said:

“It is good to reason with you, to consider what is expedient, and to fall before this holy synod. For the judgment does not show partiality, is divinely inspired, and the holy and universal synod is not composed of one person alone; rather, as we said before, it comes from the ends of the world. Therefore we admonish you to repent, so that the sentence of anathema pronounced against you may be dissolved.

“After the departure of the holy representatives, everything that is established to have been said or done by you will be useless and invalid. We know that you have no power. But if you have any defense, speak; the council is plainly without partiality.”

Although Photius was repeatedly pressed to give an account, he remained completely silent.

Then the holy and universal synod said:

“Let him go and consider what is fitting for him.”

And Photius went out.

Then Stephen, God-beloved deacon of the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans and devoted notary, stood in the midst and pronounced the acclamation as follows:

“Many years to the emperors Basil and Constantine! Many years to the great princes and emperors! Many years to the Orthodox emperors! Many years to the peace-making emperors! Many years to those who depose injustice! [Col. 0082B] Many years to the enemies of falsehood! Many years to the lovers and defenders of truth! Many years to Eudoxia, the most pious Augusta! Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed pope of Rome! Many years to Adrian, the Orthodox pope of Rome! Many years to Ignatius, the Orthodox patriarch of Constantinople! Many years to the Orthodox patriarchs of the East! Many years to the Orthodox senate! Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!”

## SIXTH SESSION

[Col. 0081]

[Col. 0081C] In the name of the Lord and Ruler of all, Jesus Christ, true God and our Savior. In the third year of Basil, crowned by God, and in the second year of Constantine his son, our most tranquil lords and perpetual Augusti, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the third indiction; with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation set forth; with that most pious and Christ-loving emperor presiding, on the right-hand side of the great-named temple of the great church; the holy and universal synod having assembled—namely, Donatus, the most God-beloved bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most God-beloved bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, holding the place of Adrian, the most holy Roman pope; and Ignatius, the most holy [Col. 0081D] patriarch of Constantinople; and Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, holding the place of the see of Antioch; and Elias, the most God-revering presbyter and syncellus, holding the place of Jerusalem; with the sacred senate also present, namely:

Theodorus, the most magnificent patrician and master; Christophorus, the most magnificent patrician and master; Leo, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Hemerius, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Stephen, the most magnificent patrician and treasurer; Leo, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Marinus, the most magnificent [Col. 0082C] proconsul, patrician, and chief secretary; Theophilus, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Tarasius, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Paul, the most magnificent patrician and prefect [Note: [Col. 0081D] That is, prefect.]; Barbatius, the most magnificent patrician; Leo, the most magnificent patrician and commander of the imperial guard; Manuel, the most magnificent patrician; Theophylact, the most magnificent patrician; Petronas, the most magnificent patrician; and Manuel, the most magnificent patrician;

And with these most God-beloved metropolitans seated: Basil, the most God-beloved archbishop of Ephesus; Theophilus, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Ancyra; Barnabas, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Cyzicus; Nicephorus, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Nicaea; Nicephorus, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Amasia; Nicetas, the most God-beloved [Col. 0082D] metropolitan of Athens; Theodorus, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Caria; Metrophanes, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna; Basil, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Gangra; Cyprian, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Claudiopolis; Hilarion, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Corinth; Nicholas, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Synnada; Michael, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Rhodes; Euthymius, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Catana; Photius, the most God-beloved archbishop of Nacolia; Stephen, the most God-beloved archbishop of Cypsela; Basil, the most God-beloved archbishop of Mysia; Theophanes, the most God-beloved archbishop of Selge; Paul, the most God-beloved archbishop of Apamea; John, the most God-beloved bishop of Cius; Athanasius, the most God-beloved bishop of Anhelus in Magnesia; Theodorus, the most God-beloved bishop of Sinope; Eustathius, the most God-beloved bishop of Aemonia; Theodorus, the most God-beloved bishop of Lacedaemon; Nicephorus, the most God-beloved bishop of Zacynthus; Euthymius, bishop of the Mosyni; Basil, the most God-beloved bishop of Pyrgium; George, the most God-beloved bishop of Helium; Peter, the most God-beloved bishop of Troas; Leo, the most God-beloved bishop of Daphnusia; Nicetas, the most God-beloved bishop of Photice; Basil, the most God-beloved bishop of Gratia; Damian, the most God-beloved bishop of Miletopolis; Theophanes, the most God-beloved bishop of Tralles; Leontius, the most God-beloved bishop of Neapolis; Joseph, the most God-beloved bishop of Palaeorum; and George, the most God-beloved bishop of Adrania.

When these had assembled, Metrophanes, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna, rose and, standing in the midst of the holy and universal synod, proclaimed in a loud voice for all to hear:

The sun of justice, which is the great, true, divine, and principal light, and which alone is the infinitely powerful Lord and our God, who said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven for the illumination of the earth,” made two great lights: the greater light for the beginning [Note: [Col. 0083D] That is, for the primacy.] of the day, and the lesser for the beginning of the night, and placed them in the firmament of heaven to rule over day and night (Gen. 1). In like manner, as great lights—namely, the five patriarchal [Col. 0083C] heads—for the illumination of the whole earth, to rule over day and night and to separate light from darkness, that is, between those who perform the works of light, namely, of divine justice, and those who perform the works of darkness, namely, of injustice; so that they may increasingly illuminate the steps of some who live according to God, while reproving others, exposing and proclaiming the hidden works of darkness, that is, of injustice, and presenting and showing forth sons of God and of light.

To such men our God Christ says, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). The great apostle Paul likewise called such men “lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. 3).

Such, therefore, are these great lights, most pious, most Christ-loving, and divinely governed lord: just as in a great house you have gathered and assembled many lamps in your city through great diligence, zeal, and prudence; you have shown yourself more splendid, your conduct more agreeable, and the Church of Christ more radiant. Indeed, most pious lord, through yourself—that is, through your presence—you have shown the lights already mentioned and now present to this holy and universal synod brighter still, like the greatest light of the East.

Let us now briefly represent this present holy synod through other divine utterances. For this is that ancient paradise which God planted toward the east, in whose midst is the tree of life; into it a river flows from intelligible Eden [Note: [Col. 0084D] That is, spiritual Eden.] to water it, as it is written: “A river goes out from Eden to water the garden” (Gen. 2).

Such a river is now plainly present among us: the divine, principal, and most holy Spirit, of whom the divine and principal Word, Christ our Savior, says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this concerning the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive, as the holy evangelist John said (John 7).

For this is the Spirit of whom the prophet David said: “The river’s streams gladden the city of God” (Ps. 47), namely, the holy Church. This river now divides its streams into four sources: namely, the most holy vicars of senior Rome; Ignatius, the God-imitating patriarch of Constantinople; and the most holy vicars who have come from both sees of the East.

This holy and universal synod, therefore, is the ark of salvation, to which all who have been ordained to eternal life flee and will enter. And you, Christ-loving lord, are Noah, found righteous before God in your generation, because you built such an ark. And God blessed you and the offspring of your womb; your fear and trembling, like that of the ancient Noah, shall be upon all the beasts of the field and all the birds of heaven—that is, upon all who love war and are faithless, who are found beneath the whole heaven.

This holy and universal synod is the gracious and good well which you, most God-loving one, Abraham, servant and friend of the Most High God, have dug. The Philistines indeed envy it, but they will not utterly fill it in; rather, they will be overcome by your works and endeavors, just as those ancient friends and blessed patriarchs of Abraham were overcome by his works and endeavors.

Therefore, as he was addressed, so you too, our most God-beloved emperor, are addressed by the counselor and ruler of all, through the voice of your most holy father, our supreme shepherd, and the most God-beloved vicars:

“Unless I bless you, blessing you, and unless I multiply you, multiplying your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore, your seed and your people shall possess by inheritance the cities of their enemies” (Gen. 22).

For he is our God, who blesses those who bless him, who alone is blessed through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

After this proclamation, at the command of our Christ-loving emperor, Leo, the devoted secretary, read the epanagnosticum of the most holy Roman vicars, whose beginning is as follows:
