We believe that this holy and great synod is by no means unaware of how this most pious, most Christian, and God-protected emperor, at the beginning of his reign—when the emperor entrusted him with his monarchy—immediately began to consider the condition and restoration of the holy Church of Constantinople, which had long been held by the invader and tyrant Photius, and how he might expel him from that Church.

Inspired by God, and desiring in every respect to fulfill the commands of the saints and of the Fathers, he cast out from the Church of God the aforementioned adulterer Photius and restored to it the holy, aged, and good cultivator, Ignatius, the most blessed patriarch.

After this, without delay, following the example of his most Christian predecessors, the emperors, he sent his most noble envoys to Rome: namely, John, the most honorable metropolitan of Sylaeum, and Basil, his most faithful spatharius. Through sacred letters he appealed to the holy Roman Church. When they arrived, they found the most holy and honorable Adrian, appointed by God as supreme pontiff, presiding over it. They gave him letters from the great emperor himself and explained verbally, in due order, how great a disturbance and affliction the tyrant and invader Photius had inflicted upon this province preserved by God.

When the most blessed Adrian, Roman pope, learned this, he summoned certain bishops from the Western regions and assembled a synod in the church of the holy apostle Peter—not to overturn the judgment and decrees which his predecessor, Pope Nicholas of blessed memory, had issued concerning the expulsion of the aforementioned invader Photius and the restoration of the most holy patriarch Ignatius, but to strengthen and confirm all the commands of his predecessor.

For this reason he sent us, his servants and servants of the holy Roman Church, here with his letters to the most pious and most Christian emperor and to the holy man Ignatius, patriarch of this holy Church of Constantinople. In those same letters he indicated to what extent we ought to hold and defend his place and authority in this holy synod. With God as our guide, we have arrived safely and in good health in this imperial province.

In the preceding sessions we have also made clear what was defined concerning Photius and the Church of Constantinople by the most holy and praiseworthy men: Nicholas, the Roman pope of blessed memory, and Adrian, his successor by divine grace. We believe it superfluous to say or repeat the same things frequently.

Therefore we ask the most pious and most Christian emperor that the statement which has been brought forward under the protection and advocacy of those who pervert justice and defend calumnies may no longer be delayed.

Nevertheless, just as it is clear to the Roman Church that Photius was never admitted to patriarchal dignity, so we have already been informed by letters and words from the Eastern sees, through their most honorable representatives, that Photius the adulterer and usurper was never received upon the patriarchal throne.

Behold: knowing the unity of the holy Churches of God, why do we await an answer concerning injustice and verbal dispute from wicked and unintelligent men?

After the reading of the epanagnosticum had been completed, Theophilus, the most praiseworthy protospatharius and praepositus, was ordered by our Christ-loving and great emperor to bring into the holy synod those who were called the bishops of Photius. When they were standing in the midst, Stephen, the most God-beloved deacon of the holy Church of Constantinople and devoted notary, was immediately ordered [Col. 0086A] to read the letter which the most holy Pope Nicholas sent through Leo, his secretary, to the emperor Michael, as well as the letter addressed to Photius, which had been written down in the fourth session.

After these had been read, Elias, the most God-revering presbyter and syncellus, holding the place of Theodosius, patriarch of Jerusalem, rose and said:

It is necessary to proclaim and preach the riches of God’s goodness toward us. For he not only makes our lowliness worthy of precious gifts, but also restrains and suppresses the manifold assaults of crimes.

Foreseeing the disturbance that existed in this Christ-loving city, as we now see in the present proceedings, he raised up our most pious and Christ-loving emperor for the stability and restoration of ecclesiastical affairs. May God exalt his horn forever and fulfill him according to his good pleasure, subjecting all barbarian nations to him.

While we were staying here, it became clearly apparent that Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, hastening to uproot and cut away injustice through his pastoral office, was cast from his throne and delivered over to the most extreme exile; in his place another Photius, known among us, was installed upon this throne.

But our most pious emperor, being himself an observer and investigator of the causes and knowing with complete certainty how these things had happened, and also knowing the judgment issued by senior Rome in favor of the most holy Ignatius and against Photius, restored to his own throne the man who had been unjustly and unlawfully cast from it, through a legitimate and just sentence, [Col. 0086C] and assigned the usurper Photius his proper place according to due order.

Because he was just and most pious, and wished the truth to be confirmed more perfectly and clearly, he rightly judged that vicars should be gathered here from all the patriarchates. The Lord God brought his good counsel to completion in what was better and more suitable for ecclesiastical order, namely, with the most holy vicars of senior Rome and our Humility assembling here.

For, investigating all the matters that arose, we learned with greater certainty that, while Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, was in exile—an exile he endured most violently, unjustly, and wrongfully—it was spread abroad that he had rejected the throne of Constantinople. But we say concerning this—and the holy Roman Church proclaimed it to us long ago—that we do not believe any rejection took place. If, however, one did take place, it is not recognized by us, because it was carried out tyrannically, under compulsion, and unwillingly; anyone can readily perceive this.

Thus there is no uncertainty. No one who is in exile and suffering extreme punishments can be considered to have renounced his office according to the true manner of renunciation. For he had utterly despaired of life, awaiting death each day and expecting daily to suffer the loss of his own life. But God’s merciful favor saved him, so that God’s kindness might be revealed and all might recognize more clearly that whoever endures afflictions for the truth and on account of God’s justice will not be consigned to oblivion forever.

Therefore, announcing this to the holy synod in a loud voice, we declare that we have never at any time accepted the deposition of the most holy patriarch Ignatius; we neither received letters from Photius nor sent letters to him. For we were never separated from communion with the most holy patriarch Ignatius.

Accordingly, even if those who say, “We do not consider compelled violence to constitute a renunciation,” are speaking truthfully—and even if those who adhere to Photius should offer this as a reasonable defense, saying that metropolitans and bishops had gathered from every side and presented Photius for promotion, and that therefore, if he was worthy of deposition, they were much more so—we say the following to them:

At the second holy and universal synod, which was assembled in this Christ-loving city under Theodosius the great emperor, a certain Maximus the Cynic and his entire laying-on of hands were rejected; but the man who promoted him to the episcopate was not deprived of his office—namely, Timothy, bishop of the province of Alexandria.

Nor was he alone not rejected: none of Timothy’s bishops, who had likewise been found cooperating in the ordination and advancement of Maximus, was condemned. On the contrary, they earned honors and rewards. Timothy was made president of the aforementioned holy synod as patriarch of Alexandria, and together with the bishops who were with him he advanced Nectarius as patriarch of Constantinople.

Therefore, the bishops who were found to have carried out the consecration of Photius are not to be condemned by us, since they were driven to such an act above all by compulsion from imperial authority and power. They appear all the more justified when compared with Timothy, the aforementioned patriarch of Alexandria: for he had nothing that could have imposed tyranny upon him or compelled him to consecrate Maximus.

But the one who alone had previously been deposed and anathematized, both by Patriarch Ignatius and by the apostolic Roman Church—Gregory of Syracuse—was condemned and deposed.

For we have never judged, nor do we judge, the most blessed and God-bearing patriarch Ignatius to be alienated from his own see, nor have we ever received Photius into the supreme priesthood.

For we believe that the Holy Spirit, who spoke in the holy Roman Church, also spoke in our Churches.

Many of those who belonged to the faction of Photius, knowing these things, therefore fled safely, reverently, and sensibly to the holy synod and received fitting forgiveness. But those who thought they ought to embrace him more contentiously and with greater partiality perhaps have this in mind: that they do not wish to repudiate their own writings, oaths, and crosses which they set up.

But the most holy vicars of senior Rome, and we who are vicars of the other sees, dissolve all these things today by the grace of Jesus Christ, who has given us the authority of the supreme priesthood justly and appropriately to bind and loose, since everything was done violently and under compulsion.

For that Photius, knowing full well that he had not entered through the door of the sheepfold but had climbed in by another way, drew a multitude of bishops to himself through various schemes, supposing that by this means he would make his own episcopate secure and immovable. He thus shaded himself with the fig leaves of documents and oaths which he himself had composed, while also beating the air, fighting in vain, and covering himself with spiders’ webs.

For fig leaves do not seem so much to conceal disgrace as to reveal it, since they are torn or pierced on every side.

Therefore we have made our sentence and judgment manifest before the Christ-loving emperor and the holy synod. We beseech God, the prince of peace, to preserve forever the most tranquil empire of the dominion of our most pious emperor. Amen.

Then Basil, the Christ-loving and great emperor, said to the bishops of Photius after this acclamation:

Behold, you have heard the judgment of the patriarchates—both the Roman and the Jerusalemite and Antiochene. What do you think of this?

The bishops of Photius said:

We shall respond to this.

And Euthymius, who had been made bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia by Photius, said:

Lord emperor, we know that your empire, which is from God, is just, patient, and impartial. We ask that the same be done toward us, your humble and unworthy servants, and that we receive a written word from your God-given authority, so that we may speak without prohibition whatever defense we may have, and that all who wish to speak with us may not be prevented.

We hope in God and in your empire, which is from God, that we shall show these documents and these disputations to have spoken in vain, but [Col. 0088C] in agitation.

Basil, the most pious and Christ-loving emperor, said:

You have spoken in vain, since you dared to call vain the things that were read, because they were spoken by such great and distinguished patriarchal heads, as everyone knows with complete certainty.

You alone, by imperial authority, holding disorderly synods and conducting them individually, without the patriarchal thrones, dared to call them holy; and you are not ashamed to disparage this present synod, which has been celebrated by all the patriarchal thrones through the cooperation and grace of God, who entrusted the empire to us.

You certainly know—and so does everyone beneath the sun—that, under the protection of our true God, the five patriarchates of the world hold right belief, and that there is no injury to the faith. Therefore, whatever they judge, you must necessarily accept.

But, as it appears, you do not believe that the things which have been said come from there. For if you believed it, you would certainly not dare utterly to reject their judgment.

I therefore ask you: Do you distrust, or do you believe, that they come from there?

The bishops of Photius said:

We do not distrust.

Basil, the most pious and most Christian emperor, said:

Then, if you believe it, accept the judgment issued by them. But if you do not believe it, I will also provide what is necessary: go to the patriarchates and ascertain the matter, and let the affairs be laid bare there.

The bishops of Photius said:

Let the matter be laid bare here.

Zacharias, bishop of Chalcedon, appointed by Photius, said:

The canon of Pope Nicholas and of the other patriarchs is the chief canon; when they act according to it, they do nothing outside what it teaches. But when they act outside it—whether Pope Nicholas or anyone else—we shall not comply.

For Julius the Roman received Marcellus of Ancyra, and the Council of Sardica, consisting of three hundred bishops, justified him; yet to the present day he is subjected to anathema as a heretic. And although Apiarius was justified by the Roman bishops, the African synod did not justify him but rejected him, sending him away to put his own affairs in order and not to go beyond his own boundaries. We have ten thousand other examples of this kind.

Now, if these things were done by Nicholas in accordance with the canon, we follow, agree with, and confirm them, and we do not hold opinions contrary to them. But if they were done outside the canon, it is not we who condemn or reject them, but the canon. For, in the two arguments which he employs against the patriarch who consecrated us, I think that no one who has merely been promoted can be condemned.

In saying that this man ought not to have been advanced from the laity, he makes the consecrators cautious, but he does not condemn the one consecrated; and custom has surpassed that canon. For Tarasius was consecrated in this way, as were Nicephorus, Nectarius, Thalassius of Caesarea, Eusebius, Ambrose of Milan, and a thousand others.

Therefore, if those men are liable, so is this man; but if they are innocent, then this man also is certainly innocent.

What is said, namely, that he was promoted by men who had been deposed, we do not initially consider to be true. For they were not deposed on account of crimes, but because they resisted the Church; once united again and rejecting that apostasy, however, they stand ready to be received. But even if Gregory, who consecrated him, was deposed, Photius is not liable; rather, those who promoted him are shown to be liable. Nevertheless, although Gregory was deposed, those who promoted him may also suffer no punishment here. For Flavian deposed Eutyches, and Anatolius received him. The bishops who held the fourth synod had him as a fellow minister, yet they were by no means condemned. Moreover, Peter Mongus [Note: [Col. 0089D] Blesus or Balbus.] was deposed by Proterius because he was a heretic and would not accept the fourth synod. Afterwards he collaborated in the death of that same Proterius, and later became patriarch after Timothy; yet none of those consecrated by him was condemned. Likewise, Acacius of Constantinople was condemned by the Roman pope because he maintained communion with heretics, and he indeed [Col. 0089D] made no statement of condemnation. But after him the patriarchs Phaetas [Flavitas], Euthymius, and Macedonius, receiving him, have been and are regarded as accepted by the Church.

And now we say this: If there is a canon that deposes us, we accept the deposition; but if there is not, then by no means. For the Romans did not receive Flavian, patriarch of Antioch, but no canon at all condemned him.

The most pious and Christ-loving emperor Basil said: “All the cases you mention, which occurred at different times and places, were restored and raised up in the Churches by other patriarchs, and therefore were judged worthy of acceptance, as having been healed by those who were able to cure the wounds of the Church. But none of the ecclesiastical physicians has healed your case and wounds; nor has any of the patriarchal heads permitted or wished to raise you from your downfall. Rather, to the present day you remain in your sin and lie dead in the grave of your wickedness, from which all the supreme shepherds, the patriarchs, unanimously condemn you.

“Yet our empire, fortified by God, is peaceful and benevolent, and it cares for you and advises you, so that you may receive the mercies which the holy and universal synod will determine. For we all know that you are laymen, and we have not brought you here to bark and speak disorderly words; all your statements are lies and deception.”

The bishops of Photius said: “Not even the devil has dared to say this.”

The most pious and Christ-loving emperor Basil [Col. 0090B] said: “If you wished to say that, at the times when God permitted you to exercise the episcopate, he also permitted something more pitiable to happen because of your sins—which you will continually see with your own eyes—and this man here bears witness to it, speaking about Eulampius more fully and clearly: We have other bishops as well. Some are patricians, others hold the rank of protospatharii, some that of spatharii, and others are stable-masters. If you wish, I will produce this before you: Theophilus the protospatharius, wearing the shoulder-cloth as a patriarch, offered incense to your high priest Photius in the presence of this man. To him he also said: ‘Did you not see him?’

“Eulampius said: ‘If I have ever seen him, lord, may the Lord God destroy me, your servant, from the book of life.’

“Nevertheless, good lord, the lord Ignatius rejected him.”

The emperor said: “Who deposed him from the throne?”

Eulampius said: “The emperor deposed him.”

The most pious and Christ-loving emperor Basil said: “And where was he when he made the rejection?”

Eulampius said: “He was outside on his own island, and [lacuna; perhaps: ‘the emperor deposed him’] because of his old age, or because of illness.”

The most pious and Christ-loving emperor Basil said: “Surely he sent someone to inform the emperor, saying, ‘I wish to reject him.’” And he asked him: “Give us the name of the person through whom he informed the emperor.”

Marinus, the most reverend deacon and senior representative of Rome, said: “Who is this man who stands and speaks before the presence of your holy empire?”

The most pious and Christ-loving emperor Basil said: “It is Eulampius.”

Donatus, Stephen, and Marinus, the most holy representatives of the senior see of Rome, said: “This is the man who has been deposed and anathematized by the holy Roman Church. How, then, did he dare to speak such things in the presence of your empire? We do not permit ourselves to speak with one who has been deposed and anathematized. For our spiritual father, Adrian, the Roman pope, has demonstrated to your holy and God-protected empire the law and judgment which the holy Roman Church has established concerning the impious and transgressors; and we do not permit you to converse with them, since it is written: ‘Every wicked man stirs up disputes’ (Prov. VI).

“We wish the document of the holy Roman Church to be read in their hearing, and, if they desire to be converted and repent, so that they may at least deserve to receive communion [Col. 0091A] as Christians. For the holy catholic and apostolic Church does not close its mercies in such disputes to those who sincerely repent. But if they persist, stop their ears and hearts, and refuse to hear what has been set forth by the holy patriarchs, we do nothing else, nor do we overturn or reconsider the judgment of the holy Roman Church issued under the eleventh indiction against Photius the adulterer, tyrant, and usurper, and his followers. If they wish to hear us, we receive all who are worthy through a written statement of satisfaction and assign them a place appropriate to them; but if they do not wish to do so, we anathematize and curse them and separate them from the entire lot of Christians, because we have no other word for them, but we consign them to the pagans and publicans.”

The most pious, Christ-loving, and great emperor Basil said to the most holy representatives of the senior see of Rome: “I have repeatedly and earnestly begged that they not perish, and for this reason I dismissed them to come here. If they do not hasten to the Church, whatever the patriarchs have judged—even if they are unwilling—we confirm. For no one can reject the authority given to them by Christ our God and Savior.”

The most holy representatives of the senior see of Rome said to the bishops of Photius: “Which of you were ordained by the most holy patriarch Ignatius?”

Heracliensis, Cretensis, and Celenderensis stood in the midst and said: “We are of his consecration.”

The most holy representatives of the senior see of Rome said to them: “Are you subject to the just judgment of the catholic synod, and will you act and write according to the document issued by the holy Roman Church, or not?”

They said: “God forbid. But if our holy emperor orders us to hear everything that has been done, we will speak.”

The most holy representatives of the senior see of Rome said: “If you do not wish to obey the holy synod, go to your fathers.”

As these men withdrew to join the others, Metrophanes, the most God-loving metropolitan of Smyrna, said to Zacharias, the Chalcedonian bishop of Photius: “We answer you concerning what you said: Both ecclesiastical and civil laws decree that anyone who chooses a judge must in every respect follow and obey his commands and must in no way reject or repel the decisions and laws issued and pronounced by him. Since, therefore, your party requested and proposed the most blessed pope Nicholas as judge, how did you dare, contrary to the established laws and regulations of Church and state, to challenge and judge him, asserting that he had not acted according to the canon and had not decided according to justice and truth what seemed right to him when he rendered his decision?

“You are therefore found in this matter to reject both ecclesiastical and civil laws, because you now cast aside the one whom you chose and preferred as judge. No one ought ever to judge or condemn in turn the judge whom he himself chose. For no person who has been judged and condemned has ever confirmed the condemnation pronounced against him; and therefore a judgment will never be firm by any time or method.

“Since, however, as though you had not heard at all the explanations read in the letters of the most blessed pope Nicholas concerning the promotion of Nectarius, Ambrose, and Nicephorus, those celebrated hierarchs, you again produce them as an example in defense of your prelate, we say to you that a certain wise man says: ‘Those who are very far apart are plainly distinguished by their differences, but their similarity must also be carefully observed.’ Let us therefore examine very briefly whether your prelate was promoted according to some likeness to the aforementioned high priests, just as each of them was received.

“Thus the blessed Nectarius was both chosen and promoted as archbishop of Constantinople by the universal synod and by various holy patriarchs, with no compulsion from the emperor and with no imperial hand intervening at all in the matter. Nor did the imperial hand tyrannically expel any living person from that see; then Nectarius was advanced.

“Likewise, the memorable Ambrose, after Auxentius the Arian had died, was promoted bishop of the aforesaid city by the synod which had then assembled at Milan concerning orthodox doctrine, with no imperial hand in any way driving the bishops toward his election or promotion.

“In the same way, the blessed Tarasius was promoted by that very new confessor Paul, who, because of the orthodox faith, had been removed from the see of Constantinople and was approved by testimony. Paul declared that Tarasius was worthy of such a throne, as did all the defenders of piety who were then present; because of his zeal and blameless life they were not tyrannically or compulsorily driven to accept him.

“Likewise, after the death of the most blessed Tarasius, the most blessed patriarch Nicephorus was synodically elected and consecrated archbishop of Constantinople, the bishops voluntarily and willingly assembling who issued his decree and performed his consecration.

“But in Photius nothing of this kind is found. He was substituted while the legitimate man of the Church was still alive, and those who promoted and consecrated him were violently, compulsorily, and unwillingly driven and induced by the emperor’s necessity and tyranny to undertake both his promotion and consecration. None of the patriarchal sees permitted him to be received into the priesthood.

“Since, therefore, complete difference is found here, how do you introduce similarity among dissimilar things? Where there is difference in the cause, there must also be difference in judgment and opinion.

“Moreover, because of your biting argument, you said concerning the most blessed pope Nicholas: ‘If he issued his judgment according to the canon, we admit and embrace our condemnation; but if not, then by no means.’ Shortly afterwards you said that when he stated, ‘Photius ought not to have been promoted from among the laity,’ he made those who consecrated him cautious but did not condemn the one consecrated, and that custom overcame that rule. In this you have fallen into an opposing contradiction, since you have confessed and shown that Pope Nicholas resisted canonically and rejected Photius according to the rule, but you have not accepted Nicholas’s canonical judgment as you promised, introducing custom to overturn the canon. Yet you clearly know that things which happen rarely do not overturn established laws, nor do particular cases take precedence over or dominate universal and general principles—especially since there is very great difference between Photius and those previously promoted from the laity, as we have demonstrated in many ways.

“Furthermore, what you said—‘We consider many condemned when the Roman Church justifies them, and again we have those justified whom it condemns’—is false and far from the truth.”

Finally, Julius, the Roman pope, rightly and canonically received Marcellus, who anathematized every heresy, especially the one of which he was said to be a supporter. Likewise, the great Athanasius and Paul the Confessor, towers and pillars of the orthodox faith, saw him acting in the same way, accepted him, and had him as a fellow minister.

But when he finally returned to his own vomit and was discovered to be a heretic, those who were with Silvanus anathematized him. Liberius, who succeeded Julius, also agreed with them in his letters, saying: “Marcellus again teaching impiously.” This was certainly not a rejection of the judgment of Julius or of the Sardican synod because Marcellus had changed his mind.

Likewise, when Apiarius was a priest of the Church of Sicca [Synicensis] in the African province, his own bishop Urban separated him on account of some matter. Afterwards the synod assembled there deposed him completely. Zosimus, the Roman pope, however, justified him when he appealed to him and presented himself as innocent, and, sending him to the African synod with letters, arranged for him to be received again. The synod then gave an account in writing to Boniface, the Roman pope after Zosimus, concerning the deposition which had taken place in the case of Apiarius and his renewed justification, saying: “We now consider him justified, but we judged that he should not exercise the functions of a priest in the Church of Sicca because of the scandals that followed; moreover, having received letters of recommendation from us, he may exercise the priesthood in all other Churches.”

Thus the African synod is found rather to have obeyed the judgment of Zosimus, the Roman pope, and consequently to have rejected its own decision and justified Apiarius—not, as you confessed, to have resisted the wish of the Roman pontiffs.

As for Flavian, patriarch of Antioch, the Roman Church indeed refused to receive him for a time. Meanwhile, out of love for the great Eustathius, they upheld Paulinus, who was the leader of those who resisted, separated themselves, and assembled apart on Eustathius’s account; but they did not maintain this position to the end. For when the most pious emperor Theodosius intervened, they restored him to favor and had him as patriarch of Antioch. Thus in this matter also you have appeared to speak falsely. If they had rejected him to the end, you would indeed have been found to have spoken correctly. [Col. 0094A] But if, while the dispute with Paulinus continued, they resisted on account of the cause I have mentioned, then abandoned such contention and received him, you said in vain that Flavian had been received against the Roman Church.

To say that Peter Mongus of Alexandria was deposed, and also Acacius of Constantinople, but that those who received the imposition of hands from either of them were not deposed, contributes nothing to the justification either of you or of Photius. Ecclesiastical laws judge differently those who return from heresies and those who are promoted by adulterers or without a canon. For they decree that those who submit a written statement and anathematize their own heresy are to be received, just as at that time the bishops of the East, gathering in synod, and Felix, the Roman pope after Simplicius, synodically condemned Peter Mongus and rejected him completely. Likewise, Felix annulled Acacius.

But they issued no sentence against those consecrated by either of them, because of the Church’s evident laws, as I have said; and indeed Peter, and even more so Acacius, were shown to have altered their position concerning the faith.

Those who have been consecrated, however, as Photius and you have been, they do not receive in any way, just as the holy and universal Second Synod acted and decreed concerning Maximus the Cynic and those who had received the imposition of hands from him.

As for Gregory, who consecrated Photius, as you said, the most holy patriarch Ignatius did not depose him as a deserter of the Church, but on account of criminal charges. And you spoke well when you said: “Whether Gregory of Syracuse has been deposed, those who promoted Photius are innocent.”

These men are indeed justified because of the necessity, tyranny, and force involved in the reception of both Photius and Gregory, according to the example given to you of the deposed and impious Eutyches, and of the reception and exercise of priestly office by Anatolius, patriarch of Constantinople, and by the bishops under him, who were considered received and justified by the fourth synod.

But this does not make Photius innocent, since he had previously been a schismatic, had become the author of many scandals, had caused many to withdraw from ecclesiastical communion, and had voluntarily and willingly proposed to be consecrated by Gregory, without being driven to it by any necessity. Indeed, he even received a protest from certain of the bishops who had been elected and were present there.

When Zacharias again attempted to speak, the most holy representatives of the senior see of Rome said to the Christ-loving emperor: “Behold, we have heard many times the contradictions and verbal battles of these men, which profit them nothing because they are at variance with right reason and with synodical and canonical regulations.

“Now, therefore, we say to them again: ‘Stop making excuses in sins, inclining to words of wickedness, and laboring in vain’ (Ps. CXL); fall before this holy synod and be saved from the condemnation of anathema. Otherwise, go to the light of your fire and the flame which you have kindled.

“For every holy and universal synod which by God’s grace has assembled in this church knows that from the eleventh indiction the holy Roman Church, after the Western bishops had gathered in the Church of blessed Peter, where he flourishes in miracles and rests, bound, anathematized, and cast out Photius the usurper together with all his followers, while the most blessed pope Nicholas was still presiding.

“Again, his successor Adrian, divinely appointed pontiff of the Romans, just as that pope had defined and commanded, so this successor defined and promulgated; and he sent us, his unworthy servants, to this city preserved by God, to make manifest and establish the truth and justice of their judgment before your just empire and this holy and great universal synod. Thus they have no voice of retreat or appeal; but just as they have already been judged and cast down, so they shall remain forever.

“And the Churches of the East, by the grace of God, agree with us, uphold the same judgment, condemn, and anathematize in the same way until the consummation of the age.”

After this, Constantinus, the secretary, ascended and read the emperor’s exhortatory address in the hearing of all:

“There are many common sufferings which, in the preceding days, our empire, advanced by God, deemed it right to mourn and grieve as it heard and saw them. But the greater evil, and the citadel of calamities, is the storm of the Church: the malign whirlwind of the devil blowing against her; the expulsion of peace; the dissolution of the ancient order; the audacity of the younger attacking the elder, of the dishonored against the honored; the complete overthrow of ecclesiastical order; injustice acting boldly within the Church, while justice dwells in deliberations among outsiders; love of rule and private affection; the absence of any serious reckoning because of these things; and also rage and madness against the spiritual father.

“These are the things that possessed and troubled my soul, darkened my mind like a dense cloud, and compelled my eyes to pour forth fountains of tears. I invoked the Godhead for help and resolution of the present grief, and this thought was necessary for me: whether I might first of all take care of ecclesiastical unity. This has indeed been done and brought to completion, as all of you know who have assembled in this sacred council.

“Setting aside the other affairs of the empire subject to me, I hastened at the outset to this one matter alone. In accordance with the request of both dissenting parties, and in order to observe the ancient ecclesiastical tradition, I also gathered judges from the remaining patriarchal thrones to examine what had been done in our Church, completing the matter through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. Many rulers before us desired to see this, but by no means all achieved it equally. Everything relating to ecclesiastical unity and order has been diligently carried out by me, without my accomplishing anything, small or great, through imperial hand or power, as some claim.

“For neither was my empire’s work or plan devised so that the most sacred patriarch might return to his own throne. Long before this, the most holy and blessed pope Nicholas, having learned with complete certainty what concerned him, decreed synodically that he should be restored to the right of his own throne, and together with the entire Roman Church pronounced an anathema against those who resisted that decree and judgment.

“We, having long known and feared the judgment of the pronounced anathema, considered it necessary to obey the synodical judgment of the Roman Church, and for this reason restored his own throne to him. Moreover, representatives came not only from the Roman see but also from the sees situated toward the rising sun, through the providence of the better course, prepared thereafter neither to hinder nor oppose anything, but certainly to support our most just empire.

“For this reason he wished no chatter to be found in any synodical judgment, lest anyone say that imperial hands, swords, protectors, and worldly power had adulterated the council. We had only one desire and one request to the aforementioned judges after we saw them: that they not permit anyone to perish, or, if possible, anyone to be cast out from the Church of God. This alone is our crime—if anyone wishes to call it a crime. [Note: [Col. 0095D] As if he were saying: ‘No accusation concerning these matters will be found against me, unless someone should wish to call this work of piety an accusation.’]

“But we entrusted all other matters to the canons and to those to whom the authority of the synod had been committed, earnestly adjuring and condemning them for the present judgment [Note: [Col. 0096D] That is, invoking condemnation.], so that nothing might be decided out of favor or hatred, but that human compassion might rather be shown toward those who had fallen. [Col. 0096C] Today, before everyone’s eyes, we also collectively beg them not merely on their own behalf but for all, to extend a hand to those who need compassion and to complete the festival of those who celebrate one Church.

“Therefore, spiritual fathers and defenders of truth, who are like Aaron in anointing, Phinehas in zeal, and Solomon in judgment: seek the sheep that was lost; turn back the one that wandered; lift the solitary one upon your shoulder; bind the broken one with the bonds of compassion; heal the wounded one with the poultice of condescension; join the one estranged and cast out from the spiritual fold to the ninety-nine according to the manner of a steward’s dispensation. Leave to later generations an everlasting memory of your compassion, for imitation of Christ.

“And you also who need healing and require a remedy, precious members of Christ, although somehow detained by an evil demon and separated from the head: true Vine, who because of your obstinate—or rather unjust—contention have been turned into bitterness (Jer. II); our friends and neighbors, although because of irrational hatred you approach and stand opposite us and look upon vanities, receive the word of admonition—or, I am not ashamed to say, even of entreaty. For the mercy which we have toward you has brought us to this.

“Search the innermost parts of your conscience, and you will find that you have been wrongly separated from the Church. It is the last hour, and the judge is at the door, brothers. Let us not be forestalled by being separated from his Church and cast far from his glory.

“Let us not consider it disgraceful to reveal our suffering, show our wound, seek a place of repentance and medicine, and enter within the court of those who save, lest, by considering obedience a disgrace, we experience eternal disgrace.

“What kind of disgrace is it, brothers, to fall before God and seek forgiveness? For those who fall before the Church and these spiritual fathers fall before God. It is truly disgrace, and the greatest shame—indeed, a battle against God—for each person to refuse to confess his own sin, humble himself for Christ, and gain both himself and many others.

“But if you consider this altogether a disgrace, I, upon whose head the crown of empire has been placed, will become for you an example of this excellent humility. I, who am ignorant and foolish, will be your good beginning, you who are wise and renowned for knowledge. I, who have wallowed in sins, will become the first model for you who are pure and devoted to virtue. I first cast myself upon the pavement, making light of purple and diadem.

“Climb upon my cheeks and walk through my eyes; do not consider it a great thing to tread upon the shoulders of the emperor, nor fear to touch with your feet the head upon which the God-given crown is placed. I am ready to suffer everything, and even more ready to do whatever may seem to you to bring disgrace, but to me glory and the greatest honor.

“For I do not care about my own glory in this matter; I care only to see communion, unity, and one festival of the Church; only that I may not suffer harm to my soul and that the devil, the enemy of all, may not rejoice by taking me captive.

“This alone should be my desire: that the lamp of my hope, through which I hastened to see all illuminated together by joy and gladness, should not unexpectedly be extinguished.

“I do not know what ought to have been attempted and accomplished that I did not attempt or accomplish, nor what exhortatory and entreating speeches ought to have been proposed that I did not propose. You will see the rest. For I am innocent of your destruction.

“But if you defer yourselves to that great and dreadful judgment of the coming day, as though you would give an account on your own behalf, know that I well understand that no word of justice will be available to you either here or there, except insofar as it may be found in this controversy.

“Yet if you wish to question the judgment of your conscience before that judgment, you will learn nothing more than what is being said by our empire.

“Lay aside contention, therefore, brothers, and take up again the love of brotherhood. Flee dissension and embrace unity. Turn away hatred and receive love into your bosom. Stand with those who are approved and be joined to the head. Receive through patience the grace of divine communion, and do not be anxious about worldly matters.

“For our most compassionate empire possesses various means of reception, through which we shall console you and continually provide whatever is useful to you in worldly matters. Again and in many ways we shall strive, beseeching, entreating, and employing every means with our spiritual fathers and patriarchs, so that they may make provision for whatever is in your minds. Only do not act rashly against your salvation, nor embrace your destruction. For there is no time more favorable than the present for repentance and reception; those who today can bind and loose the affairs of the Church are present.

“Cease trying the patience of time and awaiting a change in circumstances, which, even if it should someday occur, will benefit you nothing. For even if time changes other things, it will not be able to move this matter. If the action of one of your men, although wholly mistaken and possessing nothing reasonable, produced such a storm that we have scarcely and with difficulty been able to calm it, tell me: who will be able to dissolve the action and judgment of four patriarchal sees?

“To whom will you flee, seeking release from your bond? To the Roman prelate? But he has condemned you to the end. To the Antiochene? But he has become of one mind and voice with the Roman. To the Jerusalemite or Alexandrian? But they too have agreed with your condemnation.

“And even if time, which eventually destroys everything, should restore to you the Constantinopolitan throne and you should wish to assemble by yourselves, who will follow you? Or how will you be able to open your eyes and look upon anyone, opposed as you are by all the priests and patriarchal sees?

“Therefore, brothers, do not deceive yourselves and lose the time of your salvation. You will never find another such time. Abandon your obstinate contentions and stubbornness, hasten to the common remedy, receive the healing treatment, cling to your spiritual head, and become communicants of the Church of God. Thus you may be stripped of your crime, have God propitious, gladden the Church, cause our empire to rejoice and celebrate the festival spiritually, and fill the entire state with the greatest joy and exultation.

“Let us all together bless the Lord of our glory, the Prince of peace, and the Author who gathers what is scattered and fits it together well, through the intercessions of the holy Lady, Mother of God, of the angels who behold God, and of all the saints. Amen.”

After the reading, Theodorus, the secretary of the representatives of the senior see of Rome, ascended and read:

“Behold how the most holy and Christ-loving emperor, with the empire divinely granted to him, does not wish a single sheep entrusted by Christ to his custody to perish. He turns every exile, every tribulation, and every distress into admonition and prayer—the sufferings which the most holy representatives and faithful of the Church of God endured because of Photius the usurper and tyrant, refusing to receive him.

“Instead, as a true shepherd, he invites you to the fold of rational sheep, so that before the tribunal of Christ he may worthily say: ‘Behold, Father, those whom you gave me; I have not lost any one of them’ (John XVIII). See how much kindness, mercy, and compassion he shows you. For he desires to receive you into the bosom of holy communion.”

Thomas, the most God-loving metropolitan of Tyre, and Elias, the most God-revering priest and syncellus, representatives of the Eastern sees, said:

“The admonitions which our good emperor gives to those men, and thereafter to all who will come after us, are worthy of an imperial and most just mind. We say concerning this: ‘We persuade human beings, but we are manifest to God’ (II Cor. V).

“Let us revere heaven and earth and our gray hairs if we judge or define anything contrary to the divine laws, as our most pious emperor has again reminded us. If we were feeding irrational animals, perhaps we would handle them under compulsion and by force, driving them even where they did not wish to go. But since a human being is a rational creature, he should rather be led by admonitions. You have been sufficiently instructed by the imperial admonitions.

“If, therefore, you want our way and Christ’s way, take it; but if you want your own way, depart.”

The most pious, Christ-loving, and great emperor Basil said:

“Behold how and how often we have admonished you. You have heard and been instructed, yet you have no word of reason. If you wish to submit to the admonitions of all of us, behold, here is the harbor and the medicine. But if not, our empire grants you a delay of seven days, so that, if you take care for your salvation, all will be well and excellent. But if not, on the coming Friday stand altogether before the holy and universal synod, and whatever the holy and universal synod determines concerning you shall be done.”

After this, Stephen, the most God-loving deacon of the Church of Constantinople and notary, ascended and said:

“Many years to the emperors Basil and Constantine!

“Many years to the great emperors and dictators!

“Many years to the orthodox emperors!

“Many years to the overthrowers of injustice!

“Many years to the enemies of falsehood!

“Many years to the lovers and supporters of truth and justice!

“Many years to the most pious Augusta Eudoxia!

“Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed Roman pope!

“Many years to Adrian, the orthodox Roman pope!

“Many years to Ignatius, the orthodox patriarch of Constantinople!

“Many years to the orthodox patriarchs of the East!

“Many years to the orthodox senate!

“Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!”

## SEVENTH SESSION

[Col. 0099]

In the name of the Lord and ruler of all, Jesus [Col. 0099C] Christ, true God and our Savior; in the consulship of our most serene lords, crowned by God, Basil, in his third year, and Constantine, his son, in his second year, perpetual Augusti; in the third indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November; with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation set forth; while the same most pious emperor presided on the right-hand side of the great-named temple of the great church; and while the holy and universal synod assembled—that is, Donatus, beloved of God, bishop of Ostia; Stephen, beloved of God, bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, representing Adrian, most holy pope of Rome; Ignatius, most holy patriarch of Constantinople; Thomas [Col. 0099D], most holy metropolitan of Tyre, representing the see of Antioch; and Elias, most God-revering presbyter and syncellus, representing the see of Jerusalem; while also the sacred senate was present, namely: Theodore, most magnificent patrician and master; Christopher, most magnificent patrician and master; Leo, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Himerius, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Stephen, most magnificent proconsul and treasurer; Leo, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Marinus, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Theophilus, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Tarasius, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Paul, most magnificent proconsul and prefect; Barbatius, most magnificent patrician; Leo, most magnificent patrician and commander of the guards; Manuel, most magnificent patrician; Theophylact [Col. 0100C], most magnificent patrician; Petronas, most magnificent patrician; and Manuel, most magnificent patrician;

while the beloved-of-God metropolitans were also seated, namely: Basil, beloved of God, archbishop of Ephesus; Theodulus, beloved of God, archbishop of Ancyra; Barnabas, beloved of God, metropolitan of Cyzicus; Nicephorus, beloved of God, metropolitan of Nicaea; Nicephorus, beloved of God, metropolitan of Amasia; Nicetas, beloved of God, metropolitan of Athens; Theodore, beloved of God, metropolitan of Caria; Metrophanes, beloved of God, metropolitan of Smyrna; Basil, most beloved metropolitan of Gangra; Cyprian, beloved of God, metropolitan of Claudiopolis; Hilarion, beloved of God, metropolitan of Corinth; Nicholas, beloved of God, metropolitan of Synnada; Michael [Col. 0100D], beloved of God, metropolitan of Rhodes; Euthymius, beloved of God, metropolitan of Catana; Photius, beloved of God, archbishop of Nacolia; Stephen, beloved of God, archbishop of Cypsella; Basil, beloved of God, archbishop of Misthia; Theophanes, beloved of God, archbishop of Selge; Paul, beloved of God, archbishop of Apamea; John, beloved of God, archbishop of Cius; Athanasius, beloved of God, bishop of Magnesia; Theodore, beloved of God, bishop of Sinope; Eustathius, beloved of God, bishop of Aemona; Theocletus, beloved of God, bishop of Lacedaemon; Nicephorus, beloved of God, bishop of Zacynthus; Euthymius, beloved of God, bishop of Mosynus; Basil, beloved of God, bishop of Pyrgus; George, beloved of God, bishop of Helius; Peter, beloved of God, bishop of Troas; Leo, beloved of God, bishop of Daphnusia; Nicetas, beloved of God, bishop of Phote [Col. 0101A]; Basil, beloved of God, bishop of Cratia; Damian, beloved of God, bishop of Miletopolis; Theophanes, beloved of God, bishop of Tralles; Leo, beloved of God, bishop of Neapolis; Joseph, beloved of God, bishop of Palaea; and George, beloved of God, bishop of Adrianopolis.

When these men had assembled, at the command of Basil, most pious and friend of Christ, the great emperor, Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, stood in the midst and said to the most holy legates of senior Rome and of the Eastern sees:

“Now that the period of reprieve granted to Photius has been completed, we have brought him again before this holy and universal synod. If, then, it pleases your holiness, let him be brought in.”

The most holy legates of senior Rome and of the Eastern sees said: “Let him be brought in.”

And Photius was brought in, leaning on a staff, [Col. 0101B] together with Gregory, formerly of Syracuse.

Marinus, beloved of God, deacon of the holy Roman Church and legate, said:

“Take the staff from his hand, for it is a sign of pastoral dignity, which he ought in no way to possess here, because he is a wolf and not a shepherd.”

When it had been taken away, Donatus, beloved of God, bishop of Ostia; Stephen, beloved of God, bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, legates of senior Rome, said:

“In the preceding session this man Photius, a secular and civil official, came before us, and by apostolic authority we admonished him to return to the Church by submitting a libellus, so that we might receive him into communion as a layman. Ask him whether perhaps he has understood what is good and fitting for him, and whether he wishes to submit a libellus.”

Bahanes, most famous patrician and praepositus, went to Photius and said to him:

“The most holy legates of senior Rome and of the Eastern sees command you: Will you submit a libellus to the holy and universal synod, as required?”

Photius said:

“May the Lord preserve our holy emperor for many years; and we, together with Gregory, likewise pray. To our holy emperor we give an account, but to the legates we do not.”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to Photius:

“Do you say anything else in response to this?”

Photius said:

“If they had heard what we said the day before yesterday, they certainly would not have put forward this question. But if they have set forth their own definition in their repentance, let them demonstrate it by their deeds.”

Bahanes [Col. 0101D], most magnificent patrician, said:

“What definition?”

Gregory said:

“That they themselves should do penance for the matters in which they have transgressed.”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to the most holy legates of senior Rome and of the Eastern sees:

“Do you command that a response be made to his statement, or not? Indeed, it is just that you should answer.”

The most holy legates of senior Rome said:

“How?”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“In response to what they said: ‘You yourselves are practicing greater vanities, and you exhort us to repentance.’”

The most holy legates of senior Rome said, with Damian, most reverend imperial cleric, interpreting into Greek:

“We have not come in order to receive rebuke or repentance from them; rather, they ought to receive these things from us. They say this to the confusion of the Church. We ask them nothing else except whether they are willing to submit a libellus of satisfaction; for this reason we questioned them. We seek nothing else from them [Note: [Col. 0101D] That is, we ask for nothing else.]”

And the holy and universal synod said the same together with them:

“We know that they are wounded from the feet to the head by their own injustices, and that there is no soundness in them; therefore we do not answer them.”

After this, Theodore, the devoted secretary, read the following as representing the Eastern sees:

“Thus, at your first entrance, you declared not only us and those who are here with us, but also the emperor’s holy senate, to be sinners, understanding neither what you were saying nor the matters about which you were making assertions. Now you have vomited forth the conclusion of your wicked mind, transferring the imperial admonitions and those of the holy and universal synod—which have cried out for your repentance—to our holy emperor and the holy and universal synod, as though we ourselves were admonishing you and should come to repentance.

“But the fact that the earth appears to move because of vertigo does not mean that it is actually moving. Thus you yourself began this earlier, and now you have brought it to its conclusion. Answer sharply, therefore, the questions put to you by the holy and universal synod [Note: [Col. 0102D] That is, quickly.] If you approach with sound understanding the matters for which you have been summoned, you will do what is beneficial for yourself and for those who are with you. But if you persist in such obstinacy and defiance, you will hear: ‘But those who turn aside to obligations the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity, and peace will be upon Israel’ (Psalm 124).”

Photius said, together with the others:

“This accusation has also become excessive.”

Then Photius was questioned by Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus:

“Do you have anything to say in response to this?”

Photius said:

“We have dealt adequately with what we said; let us add something else: they have surrounded us with accusations, although we have no such thoughts.”

After this, the bishops of Photius entered.

The most holy legates of senior Rome said:

“In the preceding session we admonished them to submit a libellus of satisfaction, so that we might receive them into communion as secular persons, and not let them turn onto the contrary path, like their teacher. Ask them individually whether any one of them will submit a libellus. We do not wish to hear anything else from them; for the most holy legates of the East and we say the same thing.”

Accordingly, Bahanes, most famous patrician and praepositus, went to Photius’s party and said:

“Will any of you submit a libellus?”

The bishops of Photius said:

“Far be it!”

Amphilochius and Zacharias, bishops of Photius, said:

“What kind of libellus are we being required to submit? One concerning our faith?”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, went to the most holy legates of senior Rome and said:

“What sort of libellus do you require from them?”

The most holy legates of senior Rome said:

“The one which we have brought from the holy Roman Church: that they reject Photius and all his acts; anathematize Gregory of Syracuse; receive Ignatius, the most holy patriarch; [Col. 0103A] submit themselves beneath his feet; and carry out in every respect what the holy Roman Church has set forth.”

The most holy legates of the Eastern sees said:

“We think and desire the same.”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, again went to the bishops of Photius and repeated to them, in his own words, the statement of the most holy legates.

John, formerly bishop of Heraclea, answered:

“Let whoever anathematizes this high priest be anathema!”

Zacharias, who had been made bishop of Chalcedon by Photius, said:

“We have neither resolved nor wish to obey things that have been done, enacted, or are to be done contrary to reason [alternative: outside the proper order]. Regarding the matters you demand of us, since we know what has taken place, we accept them in no way whatsoever.”

Euschemon, who had been bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia under Photius, said:

“I do not obey or follow things that have not been done according to reason, or those who do not follow the canons of the holy apostles and of the holy and universal synods—not only if the person is Roman or Jerusalemite, but even if an angel should come from heaven and not agree with a sound word.”

The most holy legates of the Eastern sees said:

“Because they have not known and have not understood, they walk in darkness” (Psalm 81).

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to the most holy legates of senior Rome:

“Our holy emperor wishes to address them through me, his unworthy servant.”

The most holy legates of senior Rome said:

“As his imperial authority commands.”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, [Col. 0103C] said to Photius and his bishops:

“The emperor addresses you in exhortation: ‘Men, tell us, where are you from? Are you from heaven? Are you from the abyss? Or are you from the earth in which we dwell? Show at this hour whether, whenever heresy has been stirred up or schism has arisen in any place, anyone has gone outside the four patriarchates and been saved. I am listening to you.

“‘Today the four patriarchates—or rather five—condemn you with a condemnation. What do you say to this? Is there anyone to help you? Speak.’”

The bishops of Photius said:

“The canons of the holy apostles and of the holy councils.”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, commanded by Basil, friend of Christ and great emperor, said to the bishops of Photius:

“Tell us which canon helps you, and where the Lord placed the canons: in his Churches, or in some other place; and where the Churches are today, and where the Gospel is preached. Is there any other place apart from that occupied by these most holy legates? Speak.”

The bishops of Photius said:

“May God preserve your most holy imperial authority. We asked for a declaration of immunity, so that we might speak about our affairs with confidence, but we have not received it. How, then, are we to speak?”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Our holy emperor says to you with the affection of one who admonishes: ‘Surely God therefore heard my prayer and brought these holy men from all parts of the world, so that nothing might be done according to personal appearance, but the most just judgment might be rendered impartially. You say, “Let us receive a declaration of security”; and whenever anyone has been saddened or injured by me, I wish you to say so. For this reason the most holy legates of all the sees are here, so that you may speak whatever you have in your defense.’”

The bishops of Photius said:

“We know that his most holy imperial authority does not wish anyone to be saddened. What are we to say? If we state our claims, they will not be carried out.”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“For the sake of our holy emperor, nothing is forbidden to you. He commands and wishes it, and he consents that you speak. But the judges, seeing your insults, do not even wish to hear you.”

The bishops of Photius said:

“We do not accept them as judges either.”

Bahanes, most famous patrician and praepositus, said:

“Do they reject the rule of the patriarchates and judge irrationally?”

Amphilochius, bishop of Cyzicus under Photius, said:

“Most irrationally.”

Bahanes, most famous patrician and praepositus, said:

“And do they judge outside the understanding of the rule and of their patriarchs?”

The bishops of Photius said:

“Outside it.”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Then go to the patriarchates and become certain.”

Basil, most pious and friend of Christ, said:

“All of you who say in every respect that these men came from the patriarchates with letters of recommendation, and that you have no doubt about them: accept them and accept what they judge. But all of you who doubt this and do not regard them as just, or as acting according to the word of their patriarchs: go to them, learn from them, and bring them also to us. Indeed, so that the matter may be even more certain, we shall arrange it in this way.”

The bishops of Photius said:

“We do not see the judgment, nor have we heard it pronounced. How, then, are we to follow what we have not seen?”

Bahanes, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, commanded by the emperor, said:

“Our holy emperor says: ‘Do not say, brothers, that I wish to send you there so that one of you may perish. God is my witness that whoever I send there—I say this in the presence of the entire senate and the holy synod—I will bring back here again.’”

The bishops of Photius said:

“Let the matters be examined here.”

Donatus, Stephen, and Marinus, the most holy legates of senior Rome, said:

“Behold, the entire holy and universal synod has heard what the most blessed Pope Nicholas, together with all the Western bishops, judged in the eleventh indiction concerning Photius, the tyrant, adulterer, and invader of the Church of Constantinople, and concerning all his followers, according to apostolic and canonical authority and judgment. This judgment he issued both against Photius himself and against those who were on his side, condemning him because he had invaded the Church of Constantinople and had rejected, dared to depose, and anathematized Ignatius, the most holy patriarch.

“We therefore wish to question him also about this: why, although rejected, bound, anathematized, and a secular person, did he presume to depose and anathematize the high priest of the great and first see, and to compose fabrications and illusions against him? His most holy successor Adrian, vindicating him, sent letters both to the most pious emperor and to the most holy patriarch Ignatius.

“We ask that first the proceedings and acts of the most blessed Pope Nicholas be read, and then what was synodically carried out by the most holy Pope Adrian, both concerning that unspeakable assembly which Photius convened and concerning the repeated judgment pronounced against him by the most holy Pope Adrian and by the holy synod which he summoned.”

After this, Stephen, beloved of God, deacon and secretary, was ordered to ascend, and he read the letter which the most holy Pope Nicholas had sent to the clergy of Constantinople:

> “Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend brothers, the archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops subject to the see of Constantinople, and to all the venerable clergy of the Church of Constantinople [Col. 0105B].
>
> “The events recently carried out at Constantinople …”

For the remainder, see among the letters of Pope Nicholas I, *Patrologia*, volume CXXVI, column 1067.

After the completion of the aforementioned letter, Theodore, the devoted secretary, ascended and read the letter which the most reverend exarch Theognostus had delivered to Basil, most pious emperor, and which had been sent by Adrian, most holy pope of Rome:

> “Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son and most Christian emperor Basil, protected by God, perpetual Augustus.
>
> “Since, most serene emperor …”

For the remainder, see among the letters of Adrian II, *Patrologia* [Col. 0105C], volume CXXII.

Then Nicephorus, the devoted secretary, read the letter which the same most holy Adrian had sent through the aforesaid most reverend exarch to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch:

> “Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most honorable brother and fellow priest, Ignatius, most holy patriarch of Constantinople.
>
> “It was fitting for your holiness …”

For the remainder, see above.

Then a letter was read by Leo, most glorious protospatharius and secretary, which Adrian, the Roman pope, had sent to Basil, most pious and friend of Christ, the emperor, through Donatus, Stephen [Col. 0105D], and Marinus, most honorable legates. (This was written in the first session.)

Then Damian, most reverend imperial cleric and interpreter, ascended and read the letter sent by Adrian, most holy pope, to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, which had been brought by the aforementioned most reverend legates. (This too is set out in the third session.)

After this, Thomas, most reverend subdeacon, read the proceedings of the synod held by Adrian, most holy pope of the Romans.

### Address of Pope Adrian to the council assembled against Photius, read by John, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church

“Since, brothers and most beloved sons, we ought to be diligent and energetic cultivators of the Lord’s field, and ought to use the heavenly precepts as spiritual hoes for its cleansing, whenever we see thorns in it or anything poisonous beginning to grow, let us strive with equal labor and unanimous zeal to uproot these things from the roots. Let us take up the rake of examination and bring forth the sickle of judgment in harmonious contest, lest, I beg you, it be said against us in a reproachful spirit: ‘The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few’ (Matthew 9).

“Let us labor together, then, beloved, and work continually in the Lord’s field, but especially now, when a new presumption and unheard-of rashness has arisen in the Church—which is most clearly called the Lord’s field—under the agency of Photius.

“For this Photius, while he was still a secular official, always carried in his heart a certain innate envy against our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople; and, desiring not to ascend gradually or step by step to the summit of the episcopate, but to leap over it with precipitous strides while Ignatius was still alive, he made himself a stranger to the communion of that most blessed prelate. Through this he made himself entirely an exile from the universal Church, which was in communion with that most blessed patriarch, and, having undoubtedly been placed among the schismatics, he used secular powers against the sacred apostolic canons and finally invaded the Church of Constantinople with tyrannical and adulterous audacity.

“By usurping what did not belong to him, he displayed outwardly what he carried within, desiring what was forbidden in the chamber of his heart and concealing it under a veil of pretense. He gave it clearly to be understood that he had no cause for separating from his patriarch or abandoning communion with the whole Church except the most wicked desire to grasp the pontifical insignia and obtain the reins of a higher dignity and power. Thereafter abusing these things, and suddenly changed not in mind but in appearance, he inflicted so many and such great exiles, various dangers, and even deaths upon the priests of Christ and the other faithful that he seemed in every respect to imitate the savagery of Diocletian.

“On account of these and similar matters, my predecessor of holy memory, Nicholas, bishop of this apostolic see, overcome by brotherly charity, first rightly rebuked him and suitably admonished him, not only through messengers but also by letters; and he made clear in appropriate writings that he could in no way consent to his promotion. Then, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, but that his tyranny was extending ever farther, relying alike upon divine and apostolic authority and following the custom of the pontiffs of the apostolic see over which he presided, having ready, according to the Apostle, the power ‘to avenge every disobedience’ (2 Corinthians 10), he cast him down by a canonical judgment for the restoration of those whom Photius had expelled and for the relief of innumerable afflicted people. Since he could not correct him, as you yourselves know, he deposed him; and by anathematizing him he excluded him from the order which he had obtained in the manner of a robber.

“On account of this, Photius, inflamed, not only did not return to the one striking him—he who, harder than flint, felt no harsh blows—and, imitating the devil, did not cease to be proud even after falling from heaven; rather, frequently gathering assemblies of the wicked, he collected a synagogue of bloodshed, over which he presided as the chief of robbers.

“First, like a most savage parricide, he struck his own father, Ignatius, the most reverend patriarch; and, despairing of reaching the light except through the destruction of his parent, he did not fear to kill him with a cruel bite, like a savage viper.

“After this he set his mouth against heaven, and his tongue crossed over the earth, when, contrary to the divine ordinance established from heaven concerning the primacy of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he opened the throat of a putrid abyss and sharpened his tongue like a serpent against the apostolic see of that keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, and against its foremost and supreme dignity and power.

“He did not fear in the least to attack the life of my predecessor, Pope Nicholas, of blessed memory; nor did he show any restraint toward us, who scarcely deserved to be called his servants, much less his followers. Rather, to the extent of his ability, he thought to assail both him and us with curses and pollute us with blasphemous words, attempting to devise fabrications of falsehood and, by collecting who knows what Pythonic dreams or arguments, to construct his fictions.

“And indeed, all of you who recall the marks of our father’s character and the trophies of his virtues have recognized more fully who and how great he was. You know how, in the dark course of this grim age, he appeared at last like a new star—or rather, how he shone forth like Phoebus in the heavens above all the stars; how neither any form of flattery could break him nor hardship disturb him; and how he did not favor the rulers of the world, namely Michael and Bardas, against justice. Indeed, placing himself like a wall before the house of the Lord, he often rebuked them and frequently resisted them fearlessly when they acted unjustly.

“Therefore, most beloved brothers and sons, consider attentively what ought to be done by us concerning such rashness, what through our ministry should be deliberated concerning that assembly and its profane acts, and what should be defined concerning those who were present or subscribed with their own hands. Discuss these matters carefully, and let each of you freely declare what you think.

“For my part, in defense of the law of God, for the preservation of the ancestral canons, for the veneration of the apostles, for the defense of the privileges of their see, and for the proclamation of the memory of my predecessor Pope Nicholas of holy memory, as well as for the acts that follow and the definitions that are to be celebrated, I am prepared not only to endure various hardships, but, if necessary, to face the danger of death, in the manner of my holy predecessors, the pontiffs.”

### First response of the council, read by Gaudericus, most honorable bishop of the Church of Velletri

“Because we see the heart of your apostolate illuminated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, our mouth has been filled with joy [Col. 0108A] and our tongue with exultation. Therefore we sing innumerable praises and spiritual songs to the Lord, and daily commend your pontificate to the divine majesty, that it may be preserved forever. For, as we see, you are a vigorous executor of the traditions of the fathers, a careful guardian of the privileges of the apostolic see, and a most ardent champion of the decrees of your apostolic predecessor of blessed memory, carrying out every salutary and apostolic decree of his as a pious heir, like the testament of the fathers. You ought to burn with zeal for the piety of the one whose place of dignity you possess.

“That Photius, however, because he was a secular and civil official of the state, immediately crossed into the enclosure of the Church and, like a ravening wolf that spares not the flock, not only rushed like a savage plunderer into the stipends earned by others, but thereafter, sitting in the seat of pestilences [Note: [Col. 0107D] Greek *loimiōn*, ‘of pestilent men’], prepared for bishops and for the sons of the Churches long exiles, dreadful scourges, and—to encompass everything briefly—the utmost dangers in the manner of a robber: being deposed and anathematized, he could not convene a council, and, having been condemned, he could not condemn others.

“Likewise, since he himself has been overcome by the ruin of deposition, he does not possess the right to depose anyone; and, entangled in the nets of multiple obligations, he is plainly shown to have no power to bind anyone in any kind of knot.

“Therefore, since we see fulfilled in this matter what is sung through the Psalmist:

> ‘The unjust man said within himself that he should sin: there is no fear of God before his eyes.
>
> “For he acted deceitfully in his sight, so that his iniquity might be found out unto hatred.
>
> “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he was unwilling to understand, so as to act well.
>
> “He meditated iniquity upon his bed; he stood upon every evil way, but he did not hate wickedness’ (Psalm 35).

“Let your zeal be kindled like fire, most blessed lord pope, and gird your loins like a man; as a just judge, avenge the injury done to the apostolic see.

“For behold, the angel of the Lord—like the angel who once struck Peter’s sides (Acts 12)—warns you to lay aside the sleep of sloth and urges you to rise with Peter for the salvation of the nations.

“Behold another deceitful Ananias (Acts 5), namely Photius; indeed, Photius is shown to be more condemnable than Ananias. Consider, therefore: if that man, having lied once about his own property, incurred the penalty of death, how many deaths is Photius guilty of, since concerning one over whom he had no right he has fabricated not once but repeatedly, not one but many inventions of falsehood?

“Therefore we beg you, lord pope, fellow angel, that, possessing the same spirit of faith and the same zeal for piety as your most fervent fathers and bishops, you cut down with the sickle of your judgment that assembly and its proceedings which was recently convened at Constantinople under the tyrannical rule of Michael against the bosom of the apostolic see, indeed against the truth. Cut it down so completely that no memorial and no trace of it should remain, but that, for its condemnation and execration, it should in every respect be compared with the Council of Rimini or the Robber Synod of Ephesus.

“Those who are known either to have attended or to have subscribed to it, and likewise those who defend the written proceedings of that profane assembly or attempt in any way to conceal them, should again be bound by the chains of anathema. Unless, with their own voice and subscription, they anathematize those things which were spewed forth from their foul throats in that same robbery, they should not in any way be deemed worthy to be received, even among the laity, into communion with the Catholic and apostolic Church.

“For it can rightly be compared with a robbery, since Photius, its supporter, and this Michael, Photius’s supporter—namely, the one called Augustus—were present as its authors and leaders, striving to destroy those who consented in soul but did not consent in body. The Jewish priests are reported to have done precisely this in the temple, buying and selling, when by this twofold kind of death they were scattering the people of the Lord. Therefore the Lord, charging that they had made his house a den of robbers by such a scheme, drove them from the temple with a knotted whip, clearly indicating that they were not his ministers but robbers—those who preside over peoples not in order to save them with every effort, but in order to destroy them entirely either by spiritual or bodily destruction.”

### Second address of the pontiff, read by Marinus, deacon

“What your affection has proposed pleases me greatly, and I too consider that it should be done in this way. But since the book in which the execrations of that wicked assembly have been written—the book which both our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius and the most pious emperor Basil have sent to us through their representatives who are present—has until now remained in our possession, we think it necessary to foresee what reason dictates should be done with it, and what diverse precedents show ought to be done.

“For the moment, however, I recall what the Apostle said: ‘Evil conversations corrupt good morals’ (1 Corinthians 15); and another Scripture says: ‘Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it’ (Ecclesiasticus 13).

“Therefore, since this book differs in practice in no respect from the inventions of heretics’ or schismatics’ perverse teachings—for it was fabricated by the schismatic Photius, who here imitates Dioscorus, and is entirely constructed of lies and perverse doctrines—I decree that it too, like those things, must be subjected to perpetual anathema. In the sight of all, and especially of the Greek envoys, I decree that it be handed over to the fire and reduced to ashes, so that neither the purity of the simple may be polluted by its contagion nor the minds of the faithful in any way be wounded by such filth.
