For, from the sole of its foot, so to speak, to its crown, there is no soundness in it.”

The honorable council cried out through Formosus, bishop of the holy Church of Porto, in these words:

“The pious consideration of the supreme pontiff and the just judgment of the universal Church’s bishop please us all. We all say this; we all desire this; we all request this; we all consent to this with our entire hearts.”

[Col. 0110A] ### Third address of the aforesaid pontiff, read by Peter, deacon and archivist
Intolerable is this presumption, dearly beloved, and, I confess, the ears of our hearts cannot endure it. Who among you, I ask, has ever heard of such a thing, or who has found, even in reading, the enormity of such temerity? For we read that the Roman pontiff has judged all the bishops of the Churches; but we do not read that anyone has judged him. Although Honorius was anathematized by the Easterners after his death, it must nevertheless be understood that he had been accused of heresy, on account of which alone it was permitted for inferiors to resist the movements of their superiors, or freely to reject depraved opinions. Even there, however, it was not lawful for any patriarch or other bishop to pronounce judgment against him unless the authority of the pontiff of that first See had preceded it by its consent. [Col. 0110B]

Meanwhile, we remember what was written when Theodoric, once king of Italy, wished to prosecute Pope Symmachus even to condemnation, and therefore ordered bishops to hasten to Rome for this purpose from Liguria, Aemilia, Valeria, various regions, and the island of Sicily, as many as he could summon. When they had come to him, he told them that many dreadful things concerning the deeds of Pope Symmachus had been brought to his attention, and that the matter would be established by the judgment of a synod if the accusation of his enemies proved true. The venerable bishops, however, declared that the very man who was said to be accused ought to convene the synod, knowing that to his See the first merit, or primacy, of the Apostle Peter had been granted, followed by the authority of venerable councils in accordance with the Lord’s command; that this See had received a unique power in the Churches; and that the bishops of that See had never previously been subjected to the judgment of inferiors in a similar matter, as could easily be demonstrated in a formal statement. [Col. 0110C]  
[Note: [Col. 0109D] Something seems to be missing.]

Finally, when these same venerable bishops saw that they could not raise their hands against the head without endangering themselves, they reserved entirely for God’s judgment whatever had been brought forward concerning the acts of the aforementioned Pope Symmachus. Thus each of them plainly declared this in his subscription, stating [Note: [Col. 0109D] Roman Synod IV under Symmachus.]:

“I, Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, have subscribed to this decree of ours, in which we have committed the entire case to God’s judgment”; and likewise Bishop Peter of the Church of Ravenna, together with the other bishops, subscribed.

But if Photius did not read these things because he perhaps did not find them in Greek, at least he should have wished to recall John, bishop of Antioch, at the Council of Ephesus: he was condemned because he did not fear to condemn Cyril, the bishop of the earlier—namely, the Alexandrian—See. Therefore the aforesaid universal synod, writing to Coelestine, the pontiff of our supreme See, says among other things [Note: [Col. 0110D] In the letter of the Council of Ephesus to Coelestine. It is found in the fifth session of that council.]:

“Let your religious authority therefore be suitably indignant at what has been done. For if permission is granted to those who wish both to inflict injuries upon the greater Sees and to pronounce judgments against them—against Sees over which they have no authority, contrary to the laws and likewise contrary to the canons—then matters will proceed to the utter confusion of the Church.” [Col. 0111A] Since matters stand thus, let the examples of our predecessors be sought, and let judgments be pronounced against those who act presumptuously in accordance with them.

## Petition of the Council to the Supreme Pontiff, read by Benedict, notary and scriniary

Whoever does not consider this presumption worthy of the ultimate condemnation has neither read the Gospel nor truly listened to the Apostle. In the one, the Lord is read to say: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Luke VI); in the other, it is expressly commanded that “all things be done in due order” (I Cor. XIV). How, then, have these presumptuous men not made themselves superior to their teacher, when they are proved to have opened even a mouth vomiting insults against the apostolic See, which is also the teacher of the other Sees? [Col. 0111B] How were all things done in due order, in accordance with Paul’s admonitions, when, in an order turned upside down, those who came later are said to have composed insults rather than judgments against those who came first, and the second against the first?  
[Note: [Col. 0111D] Perhaps one should read: “the second against the first.”]

Moreover, the canonical judgment expressed by the African Council says [Note: [Col. 0111D] African Council, canon 53.]:

“Let each of us acknowledge the order assigned to him by God, and let those who come later show deference to those who came before; nor let them presume to do anything without consulting them.”

The holy Third General Council followed this rule and condemned John of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0111D] Council of Ephesus, in the passage cited above], as your wisdom has long remembered, because, without the consent of the first See, he dared to pronounce judgment against the pontiff of the more eminent See—that is, the Alexandrian See. Then the Fourth Great and Universal Council [Note: [Col. 0112D] Council of Chalcedon, session 3] so execrated this presumption that it condemned Dioscorus of Alexandria without restoration. For he too had presumed to act against the privilege of the first See and against the rule already mentioned: although later in rank, he preferred himself to the one who came before him; and, failing to recognize the order assigned to him by God, he rashly judged the pontiff of the preeminent See, namely Pope Leo the Great. Indeed, he did not even possess the authority to convene a synod, as the vicars of the apostolic See protested in that same council. According to the aforesaid canon, since he was later in rank, he ought not to have presumed to do anything without consulting the one who came before him; how much less, then, to convene a general synod without him, or—what is more detestable—to promulgate any judgment against him? [Col. 0111D]

In accordance with this rule and these commendable examples of the Fathers, all who rashly presumed either to open their mouths or to stretch out their hands against the dignity of the apostolic See in that abominable assembly will in no way be able to escape the punishment of a fitting vengeance, unless the apostolic moderation of your heavenly clemency, divinely inspired, comes to their aid. For no believer has ever broken forth with impunity into an insult against the primacy of blessed Peter. Whoever rises up against it, as Pope Boniface writes, cannot be an inhabitant of the heavenly kingdoms. [Col. 0112A]

“I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI), into which no one will enter without the grace of the doorkeeper. And again: no one has ever boldly laid hands against the apostolic dignity, concerning whose judgment, he says, it is not permitted to appeal; no one has rebelled in this matter except one who wished, as it were, to be judged concerning himself.

Nevertheless, most blessed lord, Pope, supreme apostolic bishop and pontiff, we all pray for these men; we all unanimously beseech you: assist the wretched, raise up those who have fallen, and grant pardon and mercy to those who repent. Apply to them, though they do not deserve it, the medicine of compassion, so that, once the author of the error—namely, Photius—has been cut off, the others may find around themselves the apostolic See’s openly displayed bowels of mercy, as usual. Thus, if the authority of the apostolic See has rightly been moved against them, and if they acknowledge themselves—or if, coming together for complete satisfaction, they condemn by their living voice and present subscription everything wrongly done by them—let mercy toward them not be inflexible, but let the humanity of so great a See show moderation in every respect. [Col. 0112B]

Indeed, although John of Antioch and Dioscorus opened their lips against the pontiffs of the more eminent See and therefore both underwent a sentence of condemnation, one of them—John—was nevertheless received with humane consideration, while the other did not escape the condemnation he had once deserved. Why was this, unless because the one wisely repented, while the other foolishly persisted in folly? The one later chose to be corrected with prudence; the other, remaining uncorrected, obstinately persisted to the end.

Certainly, as Leo, the distinguished pontiff of the apostolic See, recalls [Note: [Col. 0112D] Letter 12, near the end], our true and good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep and came to save, not destroy, human souls, wishes us to imitate his mercy: justice should restrain sinners, but mercy should not reject those who have turned back. For the true faith is defended most fruitfully when the false opinion is condemned even by its own followers. [Col. 0112C]

Therefore your blessed fatherhood will be able to maintain toward these men the just and merciful balance of this holy and blessed pontiff’s teaching: let justice restrain the persistent and obstinate, but let mercy not reject those who repent and obey.

But since your apostleship, occupied with the Church’s daily affairs, has no holidays for rest, let it ultimately decide, if it pleases, whatever it may receive by divine inspiration concerning all these matters, and let it decree this openly in the presence of the Constantinopolitan legates. We shall subsequently show clearly, as is fitting, our agreement with your decision by voice and subscription.

When these proceedings had taken place, the supreme pontiff opened his mouth and continued with a sweet address, saying:

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, the one and true God.

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

## CHAPTER I. On the complete abolition of the profane assembly convened at Constantinople [Col. 0113A]

We decree that the assembly of vanity recently convened at Constantinople by Photius and by his supporter, namely Michael, who was reigning tyrannically, against the reverence and privilege of the apostolic See, as an enemy of truth and filled with every falsehood—indeed, as one that also destroyed the souls of those who consented to it—is to be compared with the Ephesian Robber Council. We decree that its detestable proceedings, wherever they may be preserved in written records, are to be completely abolished by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, the supreme Judge, of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul, and of our own unworthiness, so that they may be handed over to be consumed by fire and struck with perpetual anathema.

Similarly, we absolutely determine that the same is to be done with the other writings issued at various times by the aforementioned men against that same See. [Col. 0113B]

## CHAPTER II. On the similar abolition of the assemblies gathered against Patriarch Ignatius

In like manner, we deliberate concerning the assemblies maliciously gathered twice by the same men—namely, while Michael was reigning, and by Photius, the Constantinopolitan usurper—against our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius. We execrate these assemblies from the depths of our being as parricidal.

## CHAPTER III. On the renewed condemnation of Photius the usurper

We again condemn by the censure of apostolic authority Photius, who, although he was lawfully condemned and anathematized by my predecessor and by us for crimes previously committed, has now, because by more recent excesses he has greatly surpassed his former iniquities, broken forth with renewed temerity, setting his mouth in heaven against the venerable privileges of the apostolic See. For he did not fear to resist the heavenly order established in the primacy of blessed Peter the Apostle; and, sitting not in a chair of health but of pestilence, he gathered bloodstained assemblies, killing the souls of the simpler people who favored him. As an inventor of falsehood and a fabricator of perverse doctrines, he habitually amassed nothing but the tricks of falsehood and inventions of every lie. He did not fear to babble wickedly against my predecessor, Pope Nicholas of holy memory, nor against us, and through him against the apostolic dignity; nor did he fear boldly to stretch out his hands against it, something no one had ever presumed to do. [Col. 0113D]

For these things in particular we bind him with the bonds of anathema, rightly joining him with Dioscorus, whose imitator in this matter he proved to be, and agreeing in every respect with the holy Great Council of Chalcedon in punishing so pernicious a presumptuous man.

Nevertheless, if he promises by his living voice and in his own writing to obey us in everything established both by us and by my predecessor, and, moved to penitential satisfaction, condemns the proceedings of the aforesaid profane assembly, we do not deny him the grace of lay communion.

## CHAPTER IV. On those who consented to the aforesaid assembly, and on the marvelous praises of Emperor Basil [Col. 0114A]

As for those who consented to or subscribed to that impious assembly, if they follow the decrees of my predecessor, return to communion with the reverend Patriarch Ignatius, anathematize that same assembly, and burn whatever records or copies of it they find, let them enjoy communion with the Church; otherwise, let them be judged unworthy of it.

But as for our son Basil, the most merciful and most orthodox emperor, because, as we have learned from the report of himself and of the legates of the most holy Patriarch Ignatius, his name was falsely entered in the proceedings of that profane assembly, and because we have recognized him as in all things a most diligent guardian of the constitutions of the apostolic See, we not only declare him free from every adverse judgment, but now also receive him among the number of the Catholic and pious Augusti; and, if he perseveres thus to the end, we decree that he is to be received there. [Col. 0114B]

## CHAPTER V. On those who do not disclose the writings of that assembly but defend them

Therefore, for as long as anyone, after receiving knowledge of this apostolic sanction, keeps hidden or defends in his possession the records or copies of the proceedings of that detestable assembly, rather than exposing them or handing them over to the fire, let him remain bound by anathema and deprived of the gift of Christ’s communion. Moreover, if he is a cleric and is subsequently convicted of either concealing or defending these things, let him lose the rank he held.

We decree the same concerning one who is believed to conceal these things and, when accused on this account, refuses either to respond or to consent to obey the decrees of the apostolic See in this matter. These decrees we establish by apostolic sanction not only concerning the Constantinopolitans, but also concerning the Alexandrians, Antiochenes, Hierosolymitans, and all the faithful without exception. [Col. 0114C]

## Subscription of Pope Adrian

I, Adrian, bishop, servant, and so forth, of the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed with my own hand to these judgments of ours promulgated by us, as is written above.

I, John, archbishop of Perga in Pamphylia, apocrisiarius of the most holy Patriarch Ignatius of Constantinople, retaining his place and person, and also that of the entire holy synod which is under him, have written out the judgments presented and have subscribed with my own hand.

I, John, bishop of the holy Church of Fano, have agreed to these judgments promulgated by us, as is written above, and have subscribed with my own hand.

I, John, bishop of the holy Church of Forosempronius, have likewise subscribed.

I, Dominicus, bishop of the holy Church of Eugubium, have likewise subscribed.

I, Gerardus, bishop of the holy Church of Lucca, have likewise subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Gavi, have likewise subscribed.

I, John, bishop of the holy Church of Falerii, have likewise subscribed.

I, Sergius, bishop of the holy Church of Sabina, have likewise subscribed.

[Col. 0115A]

I, Boniface, bishop of the holy Church of Blera, have likewise subscribed.

I, Hilderic, bishop of the holy Church of Todi, have likewise subscribed.

I, John, bishop of the holy Church of Ferentino, have likewise subscribed.

I, Stephen, bishop of the holy Church of Nepi, have likewise subscribed.

I, Hildeprand, bishop of the holy Church of Blera? [Berola], have likewise subscribed.

I, Florus, bishop of the holy Church of Manturia, have likewise subscribed.

I, Donatus, bishop of the holy Church of Ostia, have likewise subscribed.

I, Ganderic, bishop of the holy Church of Bletelernum, have likewise subscribed. [Col. 0115B]

I, Formosus, bishop of the holy Church of Porto, have likewise subscribed.

I, Crescentinus, bishop of the holy Church of Cerveteri, have likewise subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Terni [alternative reading: Perugia], have likewise subscribed.

I, Abinus, bishop of the holy Church of Anagni, have likewise subscribed.

I, Adoaldus, bishop of the holy Church of Balneum Regium, have subscribed with my own hand.

I, John, bishop of the holy Church of the Three Taverns, have likewise subscribed.

I, Leo, bishop of the holy Church of Alatri, have likewise subscribed. [Col. 0115C]

I, Stephen, bishop of the holy Church of Gallese, have likewise subscribed.

I, Paul, bishop of the holy Church of Albano, have likewise subscribed.

I, Martin, bishop of the holy Church of Narni, have subscribed with my own hand.

I, John, deacon, retaining the place of the bishop of the Church of Urbino, have likewise subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Senigallia, have likewise subscribed.

I, John, bishop of the holy Church of Segni, have likewise subscribed.

I, Joseph, bishop of the holy Church of Pesaro, have likewise subscribed.

[Col. 0115D]

I, Stephen, bishop of the holy Church of Suana, have likewise subscribed.

I, Georgius, archpresbyter of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Lawrence, called Lucina, have agreed to these judgments promulgated by us, as is written above, and have subscribed with my own hand.

I, Romanus, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saints John and Paul, have likewise subscribed.

I, Maio, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Cyriacus, have likewise subscribed.

I, Peter, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have likewise subscribed.

I, Ursus, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Pudentiana, have likewise subscribed.

[Col. 0116A]

I, Romanus, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Sixtus, have likewise subscribed.

I, John, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Prisca, have likewise subscribed.

I, John, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Eusebius, have likewise subscribed.

I, Leoninus, priest of the holy Roman Church, of the title of the Four Crowned Saints, have likewise subscribed.

I, John, archdeacon of the holy apostolic See, have agreed to these judgments promulgated by us, as is written above, and have subscribed with my own hand.

I, Leontius, deacon of the holy apostolic See, have likewise subscribed.

I, Leo, deacon of the holy apostolic See, have likewise subscribed.

[Col. 0116B]

I, Marinus, deacon of the holy apostolic See, have likewise subscribed.

I, Peter, deacon of the holy apostolic See, have likewise subscribed.

After this, Nicetas, the most devoted archdeacon and notary, came forward and read the admonitory address to Photius and his party, spoken by the voice of the most holy vicars of the elder of Rome:

“It is now manifest, dearly beloved brothers and fellow priests, from the preceding session of this holy and great synod, how Photius, a forensic and curial official and usurper of the Church of Constantinople, was admonished to bow his neck, to declare his sin by word and in writing, and to anathematize the things unjustly done and written by him twice against his own patriarch, Ignatius. He was also admonished to profess that he would make no further plot or disturbance against him, but would receive him with great reverence as his true pontiff and honorably embrace the decrees of the apostolic See issued both concerning himself and concerning Patriarch Ignatius.

“And since in all these matters we see that he does not obey, but stops his ears like a deaf asp, we therefore do not permit the sentence pronounced against him by the most blessed Roman Pope Nicholas in the eleventh indiction to remain unspoken. It has now been pronounced again by his successor, Adrian, bishop of the holy Roman Church, whose place we, his servants, now occupy in this honored synod. This synod has been assembled in this royal city, preserved by God, at the command of the holy and God-protected emperors, Basil and Constantine, not to overturn the judgment made concerning him in the Roman Church, but because we see shut up in his breast the pride of his mind. And because he does not desire to be in communion with the orthodox in the Church of God, we have therefore judged that a sentence of anathema must again be pronounced against him.” [Col. 0116C]

After this, Stephen, the most devoted deacon and notary, came forward and read the acclamatory address of Ignatius, the most holy patriarch.

## Acclamation of Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, to the holy synod

Holy brothers and beloved children, I therefore ask you—your humble pontiff—to consider and behold that the words of Scripture have now been fulfilled most completely, which declare:

“Look to the ancient generations and see: who believed in the Lord and was put to shame? Or who remained in his fear and was despised?” (Psalm XXXIII).

For I think that you who are present with us and stand assembled here for the Lord’s sake are by no means ignorant of what has been done and perpetrated against me; nor is the whole world ignorant. Everyone knows what and how much I suffered from the unjust emperor, truly still a young man, and from Barda, who at that time held power, the domestic of the schools, a most wicked man, together with Photius, then as it were another chief priest, Caiaphas and Annas. For these men had the same purpose: they considered the rank to be made for the person, rather than the person for the rank. [Col. 0117B]

As that man somewhere declares who received his name from theology, they fabricated a recent saint and called him most reverend, although he knew nothing, feared nothing, and brought forward nothing worthy of the rank, except merely his will. But, together with the power of his wicked desire, considering himself wiser than everyone else, he entered through the window into the sheepfold, seized what belonged to another, and, knowing badly how to think or judge, was lifted up by a tyrannical mind.

Therefore David’s melody, composed by the sacred psalmist, was spoken to him:

“Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Psalm LI).

And therefore God destroyed him forever, and forever and ever. [Col. 0117C]

For the merciful and almighty God, having raised up another ruler—a worshiper of God, rightly wise, rightly knowing, desiring justice, seeking divine things, and meditating day and night on the law of his God—expelled, through the piety of the most just emperor, the one who had withdrawn, namely Photius, a certain newly fashioned giant according to the fables, an inconsiderate and disorderly man whom the holy Roman Church now calls a messenger, and removed him from the pontifical See. He took up our humility, which had endured many dreadful tribulations, punishments, and exiles, and recalled us to our proper throne, distributing to both men what was fitting.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] Just as the fables of the pagans tell that the teeth of a dragon were suddenly scattered and giants immediately born, so those who, without preceding labors, suddenly attempt to seize the place and rank of holiness are rebuked.]

Our most wise and God-protected emperor does these things, following the definitions and rules of the most blessed Pope Nicholas, the elder of Rome, which he promulgated synodically and sent to Constantinople in his own letters. [Col. 0117D]

Since our most pious and prudent emperor, caring for universal peace, took great care and trouble to gather the most holy vicars and all the other patriarchal Sees and to celebrate a universal synod, he has brought his plan to a prosperous conclusion, with truth cooperating with him and by the providence of the Almighty, for the sake of complete presentation and satisfaction. And now you see these men present at this holy universal synod, filled with the wisdom and grace of God, adorned and radiant in both deed and word. [Col. 0118A]

Since, therefore, you now see and hear what many kings and princes desired to hear and see but did not see, and since these men—the most holy and wisest vicars who have come from the ends of the earth—are set before your eyes, glorify the benevolent and merciful God, who has prosperously guided our most pious emperor to the fulfillment of such blessings.

Let no one trouble him in any way concerning ecclesiastical affairs, saying wickedly and improperly, “I am of Paul,” “I am of Cephas,” or “I am of Apollo” (I Cor. I). Let no one dare to divide Christ; let him be divided from Christ, fall from his kingdom, and be deprived of eternal life. [Col. 0118B]

But come, all together; stand with us, and, since we belong to one shepherd and one flock, let us concordantly praise and magnify the one God and Lord of three persons, because glory is due to him forever and ever. Amen.

Immediately afterward, Stephen the deacon and notary pronounced the anathema against Photius, his followers, and his accomplices, as follows [Note: [Col. 0118D] Following the example of the anathema previously pronounced synodically in the Roman Church under the most holy Pope Adrian.]:

Anathema to Photius, the curial official and usurper!

Anathema to Photius, the secular and forensic official!

Anathema to Photius, the neophyte and tyrant!

Anathema to Photius, the schismatic and condemned man!

Anathema to Photius, the adulterer and parricide!

Anathema to the fabricator of lies!

Anathema to the inventor of perverse doctrines!

Anathema to Photius, the new Maximus the Cynic!

Anathema to the new Dioscorus!

Anathema to the new Judas!

Anathema to all his followers and supporters!

Anathema to Gregory, formerly bishop of Syracuse!

Anathema to Eulampius, the deposed and schismatic!

After all this, Stephen, deacon of the holy Church of Constantinople and notary, delivered praises as Photius departed:

“Many years to the emperors Basil, Constantine, and Leo!

“Many years to the great rulers and emperors!

“Many years to the orthodox emperors!

“Many years to those who have restored the churches!

“Many years to those who have liberated Christians!

“Because he pierced the adulterers; because he killed the lustful and lying elders; because he cast down false patriarchs synodically: many years to the new Constantine!

“Many years to the new Theodosius!

“Many years to the most pious Augusta Eudoxia!

“Many years to the new Judith!

“Many years to the new Helena!

“Many years to the new Pulcheria!

“Eternal memory of Nicholas, the most blessed Roman pope!

“Eternal memory of the new Phinehas!

“Eternal memory of the new Daniel!

“Eternal memory of the new Martin!

“Many years to Adrian, the most holy Roman pope!

“Many years to the new slayer of Simon!

“Many years to the one who struck down the new lying Ananias!

“Many years to the new Coelestine!

“Many years to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople!

“Many years to the new Athanasius!

“Many years to the new confessor Paul!

“Many years to the new Flavian!

“Many years to the new Anatolius!

“Eternal memory of the most holy and orthodox patriarchs of the East!

“Many years to Donatus, Stephen, and Marinus, the most holy vicars of the elder of Rome!

“Many years to Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre and vicar of Antioch!

“Many years to Elias, the most holy syncellus and vicar of Jerusalem!

“Many years to the Sacred Senate!

“Eternal memory of the holy and universal synod!

“Many years to the emperors—many years!” [Col. 0119A]

## Iambic verses among the Greeks for the acclamation of the council

[Col. 0120A]

Photius, who once foolishly disturbed the unconquerable rock

By wicked deceits,

Is now driven out, like a most savage beast,

From the chaste bridal chamber and venerable temples,

Having been well sent beforehand to Satan,

The worst of beings, and to wretched darkness,

And having deservedly suffered at the hands

Of judges who think rightly and are holy:

Namely, the most blessed Nicholas,

And Adrian, the divine Roman pope,

And Ignatius, who endured martyrdom,

Together with the three remaining Eastern Sees,

Orthodox and exceedingly wise.

## EIGHTH SESSION

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119B]

In the name of the Lord and Ruler of all, Jesus Christ, the true God and our Savior; in the third year of Basil, the emperors crowned by God and our most tranquil lords, and in the second year of Constantine, his son, the perpetual Augusti; in the third indiction, on the Nones of November; with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation placed before us; while the same most pious and Christ-loving Basil presided on the right side of the great-named temple of the great church; and with the holy and universal synod present—namely, Donatus, the God-beloved bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the God-beloved bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, representing Adrian, the most holy Roman pope; Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople; Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, representing the throne of Antioch; and Elias, the God-beloved priest and syncellus, representing the throne of Jerusalem—there was also present the Sacred Senate, namely:

Theodore, the most magnificent patrician and magister; Christopher, the most magnificent patrician and magister; Leo, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Himerius, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Stephen, the most magnificent patrician and sacellarius; Leo, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Marinus, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Theophilus, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Tarasius, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Paul, the most magnificent patrician and eparch; Barbatius, the most magnificent patrician; Leo, the most magnificent patrician and commander of the imperial guards; Manuel, the most magnificent patrician; Theophylact, the most magnificent patrician; Petronas, the most magnificent patrician; and Manuel, the most magnificent patrician. [Col. 0119D]

The God-beloved metropolitans were also seated with them, namely:

Basil, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Ephesus; Theodulus, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Ancyra; Barnabas, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Cyzicus; Nicephorus, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Nicaea; Nicephorus, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Amasia; Nicetas, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Athens; Theodore, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Caria; Metrophanes, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna; Basil, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Antioch; Theophylact, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Iconium; Theodore, the most God-beloved archbishop of Thessalonica; Ignatius, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Hierapolis; Hilarion, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Corinth; Euthymius, the most God-beloved archbishop of Catana; Gregory, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Hypaepa; Photius, the most God-beloved archbishop of Nacolia; Stephen, the most God-beloved archbishop of Cypsella; Basil, the most God-beloved archbishop of Mysia; Theophanes, the most God-beloved archbishop of Selge; Paul, the most God-beloved archbishop of Apamea; John, the most God-beloved archbishop of Poti; Athanasius, the most God-beloved archbishop of Magnesia; Theodore, the most God-beloved bishop of Sinope; Eustathius, the most God-beloved bishop of Aemonia; Theocletus, the most God-beloved bishop of Lacedaemon; Nicephorus, the most God-beloved bishop of Hyacinthus; Euthymius, the most God-beloved bishop of Mosbynum; Basil, the most God-beloved bishop of Pyrgi; George, the most God-beloved bishop of Hylia; Peter, the most God-beloved bishop of Troy; Leo, the most God-beloved bishop of Daphnusia; Nicetas, the most God-beloved bishop of Photice; Basil, the most God-beloved bishop of Cratia; Damian, the most God-beloved bishop of Melitopolis; Theophanes, the most God-beloved bishop of Tralles; Leo, the most God-beloved bishop of Neapolis; Joseph, the most God-beloved bishop of Palaeorum; and George, the most God-beloved bishop of Adrana. [Col. 0120B–D]

When these men had assembled, at the command of Basil, the Christ-loving and great emperor, Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, stood in the midst and said:

“Because of great cunning and wickedness, in former times the priesthood, the Senate, and the entire city subscribed to unjust causes which they did not desire. Today, however, our empire, divinely governed, looks to the mercy of the most benevolent and compassionate God; it wishes these matters to be burned by your hands, and hopes in his compassion and in your holy prayers that every person may be forgiven this ignorance, both by the holy Catholic Church and by the Sacred Senate and our entire city, together with the other regions.”

What, then, seems good to your holiness? Is this pleasing to God and to you?

Donatus, most holy bishop of Ostia, Stephen, most holy bishop of Nepi, and Marinus, most dear to God, deacon and representatives of the most holy elder of Rome, said:

“May God preserve for many years the emperor, dear to Christ, who governs His Church. For God has given him the governance of the whole world, and has heard the voice and supplication of his spiritual father, Pope Adrian, through the letter that he sent; and today [Col. 0121B] he fulfills the desire of the Church, as he announced to him. May God preserve his empire for many years in the governance of the world, because he has broken the bonds of the written documents that were demanded by the enemies of God against the whole Church.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Our holy emperor, beloved of God, commands me to say to you bishops who made the unjust written documents: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak?’ (II Cor. I.) Your sickness and pain are mine; and therefore I give the order that what was wickedly and forcibly done by you be burned and destroyed—not only visibly, but, by God’s providence, also intelligibly.”

The bishops, most dear to God, said:

“Today the saying of divine Scripture is fulfilled under our emperor, protected by God, which says: ‘Dissolve every bond of iniquity, and the obligations of violent contracts, and tear away every unjust document’ (Isa. LV). For these things, may the God of gods grant the emperor, beloved of Christ, a reward for our souls and bodies, and preserve his empire through many years, granting him also the heavenly empire.”

And when Basil, beloved of Christ and the great emperor, had commanded it, a bronze vessel suitable for this purpose was placed in the middle of the synod, full of fire. All the volumes of written documents that Photius had exacted from the entire sacred catalogue and order of the clergy, both of the Great Church and of those outside it, and also from persons of senatorial rank, great and small and all alike, and from all others, both illustrious [Col. 0121D] and obscure, including those who appeared to be engaged in every art, discipline, and various occupation, down to leatherworkers, fish sellers, woodworkers, and needle-makers—were brought in a purse by Theophylact, the most reverend deacon and referendary.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] The patriarch of Constantinople always has a referendary, who announces all his wishes to the emperor. He always has access to the palace in order to report to the emperor whatever things are necessary for the patriarch and the Church, and through him the emperor likewise sends on whatever pleases the patriarch.]

In addition, the books falsely written against the most blessed Pope Nicholas, together with the reports of proceedings and the synods that Photius had held against the most holy patriarch Ignatius, were brought in. Gregory, the most reverend orphanotrophus, took the individual booklets and volumes and handed them to the men of both most holy representatives; they put everything into the [Col. 0122A] fire, and it was burned and reduced to nothing.

Basil, beloved of Christ and the great emperor, said to the most holy representatives of the elder of Rome:

“By our imperial command they have brought in the false representatives whom Photius produced against the most blessed Pope Nicholas. What, then, seems good to your holiness concerning them?”

The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome said:

“Let them enter the holy and universal synod.”

When they had entered, Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, questioned Peter the monk:

“Our holy emperor and the entire holy synod command that you be asked: Who are you, and where do you come from? What do you say, and what is the work that you have done? Were you found in the council that Photius held against the most blessed Pope Nicholas, or did you submit a booklet against him?” [Col. 0122B]

Peter said:

“I was neither found present there, nor do I know this document. Surely I, Peter, am not the only one who came up to this city from Rome? Ten thousand others named Peter came up. Nevertheless, let this booklet of mine, which I am carrying, be read; it will make clear what belongs to me.”

Gregory, the devout notary of the divine secretariat, took it and read:

## The Apologetic Booklet of Peter the Monk

“Because some of you have supposed that I submitted a booklet against the holy Roman Church, on the grounds that my name was contained in the published document, for this reason I have come to render an account before the emperors. I have also often shown myself innocent in the presence of your reverence; and now, being questioned again about the same matter, I offer unchanged the very statement that I offered then: I neither submitted a booklet nor brought trouble before the imperial hearings, nor was I found present at the assembled synod—if indeed it was assembled. Surely those who inserted my name into such writings will acknowledge this.

“This is my candid defense before those who judge me, and I shall offer it with great confidence and a pure conscience whenever I am questioned. But I beg the distinction of your authority at least now to let me, greatly wearied, return to the footprints of the apostles, having offered you my prayers. For by now, I think, it is pleasing to the wise leaders to incline their ear to the supplications of your mother, [Col. 0122D] so that, through the opportunity of returning, I may be drawn into those things [Note: [Col. 0122D] Perhaps: ‘those things which’.] which contribute to my soul’s salvation.”

After the reading, the most holy representatives of the elder of Rome said:

“Behold, through the booklet we have heard what this man has said. But what do the others who are standing there say?”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to Basil, the false representative:

“Our holy emperor, together with the most holy representatives, the sacred senate, and the holy synod, commands that you be questioned. Your name lies in the false book; speak, then. Did you submit a booklet against the Roman Church? Is this how the truth stands?” [Col. 0123A]

Basil said:

“Certainly not.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Then anathematize both the one who submitted it and the one who wrote it.”

Basil said:

“Let the one who submitted the booklet against the Roman Church be anathema.”

Then Basil was questioned again:

“Where are you from?”

Basil said:

“I came from the holy city.”

Basil, beloved of Christ and the great emperor, said to Elias, the most holy representative of Jerusalem:

“Do you recognize him?”

Elias, the most holy synkellos and representative of Jerusalem, said:

“Yes, I recognize him.”

Then, at the command of Basil, the most pious and great emperor, Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to Basil, the false representative:

“Say why you entered Constantinople. For what purpose? And who sent you there?” [Col. 0123B]

Basil said:

“I entered Rome from Tripoli for the sake of prayer. I fell ill on the way, and I entered Venice in order to cross over. I came here under Pope Benedict, and I remained for twenty months; I had no means of arranging my affairs. In the year when the patriarch left his throne, I went down again under Lord Nicholas; I have been here for eight years, and once again I returned here.”

He was questioned again:

“Did you not submit the booklet?”

Basil said:

“God forbid. Was I ever a familiar associate of Nicholas?”

Then, at the command of Basil, beloved of Christ and the great emperor, Leontius, the false representative of Alexandria, was questioned by Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus:

“How were you found occupying the place of representative in the falsely composed book that Photius produced against the most blessed [Col. 0123C] Pope Nicholas?”

Leontius said:

“My author and senior bishop gave me letters to our holy emperors. I am not a representative, and I have no connection with these matters.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to the holy synod, at the command of Basil, the emperor beloved of Christ:

“What do you think about these men? Just as the first speaker made clear his complete ignorance, so has this one. They are businesspeople and know nothing; they did not become representatives. Photius fabricated both the speeches and the persons as he wished.”

The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome said to the false representatives:

“Compose booklets and anathematize those who made those books, so that you may be received into communion.”

Leontius said:

“I neither wrote in this book nor recognize it.” [Col. 0123D]

The holy synod said:

“Anathematize the one who made it and wrote it.”

The false representatives said:

“Let the one who cooperated in this book have the anathema.”

[Note: [Col. 0123D] Perhaps: “Let him have the anathema.”]

The senate said:

“Since you do not wish to anathematize him, it is apparent that you are his accomplices. Therefore either you yourselves must be anathematized, or you must be handed over to the laws.”

The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome said:

“Since they do not permit themselves to anathematize the one who committed this evil, as the most holy Pope Adrian wrote to the most pious emperor, let them be handed over to us, and let them go down with us to Rome.”

Leontius said:

“Anathema to him and to the one who wrote it.”

Basil said:

“Anathema to the one who submitted the booklet against Pope [Col. 0124A] Nicholas.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Our holy emperor, offering admonition and counsel, says to those sitting in this synod, to those standing, and to all the common people:

“‘See how the truth appears, and how the light shines in the darkness, and they do not grasp it. How do lies and deception appear? And how has the truth grown today? Whoever has a scandal in his soul, let him approach the holy Church of God, for he has no excuse of any kind. Thus our holy empire acts, so as to exclude every excuse, so that tomorrow you may have no defense.’”

The holy synod said:

“May God preserve the most pious emperor.”

The metropolitans who had subscribed to that book were questioned about their own subscriptions, which were in the book:

“Are these your subscriptions?”

They all said:

“Certainly not.”

The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome requested Basil, beloved of Christ and the great emperor, that the canon of Saint Martin, Roman pope, which he had issued concerning every false representative, be read. Stephen, most dear to God, deacon and notary, took it and read this canon in the hearing of all.

## Chapter XX of the Lateran Council

“If anyone, following the wicked heretics, unlawfully crosses the boundaries established more firmly by the holy Fathers of the Catholic Church and by the five holy and universal synods—whether by word, time, or place—and rashly devises novelties, [Col. 0124C] expositions of another faith, types, laws, definitions, booklets, reports, letters, subscriptions, false testimonies, synods, records of proceedings, empty ordinations unknown to ecclesiastical rule, or guardians of places, that is, unsuitable representatives without rule, and briefly, if he does anything else customary to the most impious heretics through diabolical operation; if he acts crookedly and cunningly against the pious orthodox teachings of the Catholic Church—that is, against her paternal and synodal proclamations—to destroy [alternative: overturn] the most sincere confession of our Lord and God Jesus Christ, and persists to the end without repentance, let such a person, acting impiously, be condemned forever and ever [Col. 0124D], and let all the people say: ‘Let it be so, let it be so.’”

After the completion of the canon, Metrophanes, the metropolitan of Smyrna, beloved of God, rose and addressed the synod in a loud voice:

“Truth is a thing [Greek: χρῆμα], stronger, mightier, and more powerful than all other things. Truth is an irresistible thing, unavoidable for all human beings. Truth conquers everything, and does so most appropriately. For truth exists; again, truth exists—it is.

“Christ, the Savior and Lord of us all, also approves this most true understanding, calling Himself both by that primary name and by the name ‘Word of God and of the Father.’ In ancient times, when God, speaking to Moses, was setting forth the laws and ordinances of salvation, Moses asked Him carefully what His name was, and He said to him: ‘I am who I am’ (Exod. III). In the latter times, incarnate because of His ineffable mercy and made man like us and for our sake, He says: ‘I am life and truth’ (John XIV).

“Therefore truth is more just than every other thing, unavoidable for all, and alone conquers everything. You too, lord beloved of Christ, having become its lover, appeared today as a triumphator and victor against falsehood. Led by truth itself and relying on its help, you have shown through Christ our God that injustice has been annihilated, and you have prepared the way so that the divine utterances of the prophets might now be shown more clearly and plainly to all people to be true. Scripture says of them: ‘If the unjust man is justified on the balance, and there is a weight of deceit in the purse’ (Prov. II). [Col. 0125B]

“By these things they filled their riches with impiety; and those who inhabit it spoke falsehoods, and their tongue was exalted in their mouth, just as another prophet, namely Hosea, cries out more explicitly:

“‘This is Ahab; in his hand is the balance of injustice; he loved to use force. And Ephraim said: Nevertheless I have become rich; I have found refreshment for myself. No one will find in him any of the pains because of the injustices that he committed’ (Hos. XII).

“Again the same prophet, representing the conduct of people who speak and write vain and empty things, says:

“‘They sowed corruption, and their destruction receives it; a sheaf without strength to make flour; and if it does make it, strangers will eat it’ (Hosea III).

“But today, lord, you have fulfilled the saying of the blessed prophet who says: ‘The remnants of the impious shall be destroyed’ (Ps. XXXVI). For this reason may our God, Emperor and Ruler of all, strengthen you, most pious emperor, as the destroyer of injustice, uprooter of falsehood, planter of piety, and renewer of true doctrines; may He strengthen you in spirit and in body, establish your empire, and always establish you prosperously in all things through the holy prayers of the father equal to the angels and also dwelling in heaven, namely the most holy patriarch Ignatius, and of the other most holy representatives of the elder of Rome and of the Eastern sees. May He subject all barbarian nations to you, and make you worthy of His heavenly kingdom with all who have reigned piously, so that you may glorify Him without ceasing, because glory belongs to Him now and always and forever and ever. Amen.”

After this declamation had been completed, Basil, beloved of Christ and the great emperor, said to the most holy representatives of the elder of Rome and of the Eastern sees:

“Theodore, who is called Crithinus, since he is the author of the Iconomach heresy, has been brought to the holy and universal synod at your piety’s command. What, then, seems good to you concerning him?”

The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome said:

“Most pious lord, let some of the most magnificent princes be sent to him, and let them speak to him as if from us:

“‘The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome say: Through various letters and through the most noble and faithful men who were sent by the holy emperor and prince Basil, beloved of Christ, to his spiritual father, the most holy Pope Adrian, he requested in those letters that he send his representatives to this holy, God-preserved, imperial city and destroy the deception and error that had arisen in the Church of God during his times.

“‘And behold, through the governance of his holy empire, we have been gathered in this holy synod together with the representatives of the East, who share our faith. We have heard that you are erring and deviating from the orthodox faith, and that you refuse with us to honor and venerate the precious icons of our Lord Jesus Christ, of His most holy Mother, and of all His saints. For this reason we admonish you, because now, behold, the harbor of salvation lies before you, opened for you, and the holy Church receives you in her arms through this holy, honorable, and universal synod, upon your defense and the submission of a booklet; and we shall receive you into the communion of the Catholic Church.

“‘But if you refuse to heed us and this holy and universal synod, you shall receive from us, from the entire holy Church of God, and from this universal synod, the sentence of anathema.’”

The representatives of the Eastern sees said:

“We too have been sent by Him from the sacred and holy places of Christ, which the Lord glorified by the manifestation of His glory, for the common salvation both of you and of all. We therefore ask you to obey and not cast yourselves out from the holy Catholic [Col. 0126C] Church, nor bring upon yourselves unending loss in the future. Behold, we admonish you now, at this hour, lest the door be closed to you and you repent without the benefit of repentance.”

Thus, when Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, and Leo, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician, had been sent to the aforesaid man Theodore, who is called Crithinus, by order of Basil, the emperor beloved of Christ, the words of the most holy representatives of the elder of Rome and of the Eastern sees were read.

But when Crithinus gave no answer, Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, gave him a coin bearing the image of Basil, beloved of Christ and the great emperor, and said to him:

“Our holy emperor commands me to ask you: Do you accept the coin bearing my image?”

Theodore, who is called Crithinus, said:

“I am unworthy, but I accept it as worth thousands of gold and silver pieces.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Our holy emperor admonishes you and says: Do you honor the coin bearing my engraving?”

Theodore said:

“I honor it as a royal coin ought to be honored.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“The emperor commands me to ask: Do you dishonor it?”

Theodore said:

“Why would I? I do not dishonor it.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Our holy emperor commands me to say to you:

“‘If you do not wish to dishonor my image, that is, the image of a mortal king, but honorably accepted it from my hand, since I am praepositus, how can you say that you dishonor the human image of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of His most holy Mother, who truly and properly is the Mother of God, and of all the saints? Tell us: Do you dishonor these, or do you honor them?’”

Theodore said:

“All Christian men ought to submit to your holy and just empire, and I more than all others, unworthy as I am, because you have freed me from death, rescued me from unjust exiles, and helped me out of captivity, hunger, and destruction. And because I owe it to your holy empire to pray above all Christians, even if all the hairs of my head and beard became mouths and prayed for your holy empire, they would not be sufficient. Such is your kindness toward me, just emperor and beloved of Christ.

“You sent me a coin of your empire, and I accepted it, knowing that it was yours. You demand that I also accept Christ’s mark and image. If this is Christ’s command and pleasing to Christ, may your holy empire be supplicated to grant delay, grant a period of truce, and grant our weakness some time. After this, when your empire, established by God, commands, if it is shown that this is Christ’s command, I shall do whatever you order.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Our holy emperor did not bring you to this holy and universal synod for disputation, but for admonition.

“For surely you know that Paul, the mouth of Christ, clearly commands every heretic to be avoided after the first and second admonition (I Tim. III). But you, growing old in your wickedness and knowing with complete certainty the darkness in which you are, will walk in the light of your own fire, hearing from the four quarters of the earth, by the just decree of the sacred canons, the condemnation of anathema. Where will you flee? Or where will you go?

“God established His Church in five patriarchates, and defined in His Gospels that they should never utterly fall, because they are the heads of the Church. For this is what is declared by the saying, ‘The gates of hell shall not prevail against it’ (Matt. XVI): when two have fallen, they run to the three; when three have fallen, they run to the two; but if perhaps four have fallen, the one that remains, with Christ our God at the head of all, restores the remaining body of the Church again. Now, however, with the whole world in agreement, you have no means of excuse, as once happened.”

When the most magnificent judges had returned, the words of Theodore, who is called Crithinus, were read aloud in the hearing of the synod.

The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome and of the Eastern sees said:

“Let the chapter of the most holy Pope Nicholas concerning images be read.”

Stephen, beloved of God, deacon and notary, took it and read:

## Chapter VI of Pope Nicholas

“Since we ought to preserve the statutes of our forebears with an unwavering gaze of the mind, and always venerate in all things the doctrines of the holy Fathers, we decree concerning the sacred and venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of His ever-Virgin Mother Mary, and of all the saints who are believed to have pleased God—from righteous Abel onward—which the holy Church spread throughout the world received from ancient times, and which the prelates of the apostolic see decreed and established on their behalf: that they shall remain unimpaired and continue undefiled.

“Therefore, concerning John, formerly bishop of Constantinople, and his followers, who with polluted mouth assert that these images ought to be broken and trampled, we decree that, so long as they do not agree with us concerning these matters and do not think in accordance with the decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs and the ordinances of the other Catholic Fathers, they are anathema from Christ and from the Catholic and apostolic Church.”

After the completion of this reading, Basil, the most pious and great emperor, said to the most holy representatives of the elder of Rome and of the Western sees:

“There are here certain others who agree with Crithinus. If it seems good to your holiness, let them enter into the middle of the synod and be questioned, in case they might wish to repent and profess the orthodox faith.”

Elias, most dear to God, priest, synkellos, and representative of the see of Jerusalem, said:

“Those who serve a long-standing sect are difficult to uproot from the evil opinion by which they are held. For, as though captured by iron fetters through diabolical deceptions, they have their own minds blinded and cannot look up toward the light of truth. For this reason this heretic Theodore, who is called Crithinus, does not accept anything he hears for his improvement and salvation, imitating unfruitful and thorny ground. But as your imperial power, fortified by God, has commanded, if there are others, let them enter.”

When Nicetas the cleric, Theophilus the layman, and Theophanes the notary had entered, the most holy representatives of the elder of Rome said to them:

“Do you anathematize the Iconomach heresy? Do you profess the orthodox faith of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, which was handed down at the ends of the world by Christ, the apostles, and all the most holy teachers of the Church?”

Nicetas the cleric, Theophilus the layman, and Theophanes the notary said:

“We were previously deceived by the malicious words of impious men and held wicked opinions. But now, seeing the harmony and united accord of this holy and universal synod, we despise the heresy of the Iconomachs and anathematize everyone who does not adore the holy and venerable images.”

Each of them then rose individually upon the high tribunal and anathematized the heresy of the Iconomachs, its leaders, and its patriarchs—namely Theodotus, Antony, John, and Theodore called Crithinus.

Then Basil, the most pious and great emperor, summoned each of them, kissed them, and said:

“Now you have been rescued from demonic possession and have become most true Christians. You shall be saved with all the orthodox by Christ our God, and you are made worthy of eternal life. For unless you had anathematized the heresy of the Iconomachs, Christ would have been of no benefit to you.”

Elias, most dear to God, priest and synkellos of the Eastern throne of Jerusalem, said:

“Today the intervention of your holy empire has made them worthy of a great benefit, lord beloved of Christ, and you have made us exceedingly glad—or rather, Christ, who gave you the empire. May He preserve you in zeal for piety now and forever.”

The most holy representatives of the elder of Rome said:

“Christ our God, ineffable Wisdom, truly orders the world, since He has advanced you, most pious lord and emperor, for the correction of all who have erred and for the guardianship and preservation of those who think rightly. The holy Roman Church rejoices in you, seeing such zeal of yours for piety.

“Therefore let this holy and universal synod anathematize him who did not wish to understand so as to act well, nor to repent and depart from his own impiety—namely Theodore, who is called Crithinus—and all those who share his views, both those who still survive and those who died holding the same belief and opinion.”

Stephen, most dear to God, deacon and notary, rose and anathematized as follows:

“Anathema to all heretics!

“Anathema to the council that still rages against the venerable images!

“Anathema to anyone who accepts the impious little arguments of their heresy!

“Anathema to those who take sayings of divine Scripture directed against idols and apply them against the venerable images!

“Anathema to those who do not embrace the holy and venerable images!

“Anathema to those who call the sacred icons idols!

“Anathema to those who say that Christians approached images as they approached gods!

“Anathema to those who knowingly communicate!”

“Anathema to those who abuse and dishonor the venerable icons!

“Anathema to those who say that, apart from Christ our Lord, someone else freed us from idols!

“Anathema to those who dare to say that the Catholic Church ever accepted idols!

“Anathema to Anastasius, Constantine, and Nicetas, who ruled under the Isaurians over the heresies, as unordained and unepiscopal bishops!

“Anathema to Theodore, Antony, and John, who became among themselves instigators of every evil and succeeded one another in impiety!

“Anathema to Paul, who was converted into Saul, and to Theodore who was called Gasta, and to Stephen Molates, and to those like them!

“Anathema to Theodore, who, although he has no reason, pretends to speak rationally, and who is called [Col. 0130A] Crithinus!

“Anathema to those who are still uncertain in mind, but are senseless through their ambiguity; who, possessed by the darkness of their impiety, suppose that they will attain restoration from certain persons!

“Anathema to Laludius, Leo, and everyone here who thinks similarly, whether among bishops, priests, and monks, or among those who are tonsured in whatever manner!”

“Anathema to Photius, the courtier and usurper!

“Anathema to Photius, the layman and forensic advocate!

“Anathema to Photius, the neophyte and tyrant!

“Anathema to Photius, the schismatic and condemned man!

“Anathema to Photius, the adulterer and parricide!

“Anathema to the fabricator of lies!

“Anathema to the inventor of perverse doctrines!

“Anathema to Photius, the new Maximus the Cynic!

“Anathema to the new Dioscorus!

“Anathema to Gregory, formerly bishop of Syracuse!

“Anathema to Eulampius, the deposed man!

“Anathema to all his followers and supporters!

“Many years to the emperors Basil, Constantine, and Leo!

[Note: [Col. 0129C] For while this proceeding was taking place, this Leo, the son, was crowned emperor by the representatives and by the patriarch Ignatius during the Feast of the Theophany.]

“Many years to the great princes and emperors!

“Many years to the orthodox emperors!

“Many years to those who erect churches!

“Many years to those who free Christians!

“Many years to the new Constantine!

“Many years to the new Theodosius!

“Many years to the new Marcian!

“Many years to the most pious Augusta Eudoxia!

“Many years to the new Judith!

“Many years to the new Helena!

“Many years to the new Pulcheria!

“Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed Roman pope!

“Eternal memory to the new Phinehas!

“Many years to the new Daniel!

“Many years to the new slayer of Simon!

“Many years to the new striker of the deceitful Ananias!

“Many years to the new Celestine!

“Eternal memory to the new Martin!

“Many years to Adrian, the most holy Roman pope!

“Many years to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople!

“Many years to the new Athanasius!

“Many years to the new confessor Paul!

“Many years to the new Flavian!

“Many years to the new Anatolius!

“Many years to the most holy and orthodox patriarchs of the East!

“Many years to Donatus, Stephen, and Marinus, the most holy representatives of the elder of Rome; and to Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre and representative of Antioch!

“Many years to Elias, the most holy synkellos and representative of Jerusalem!

“Many years to the sacred senate!

“Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!

“Many years to our emperors, many years!”

## ACT NINE

[Col. 0129]

[Col. 0129D] In the name of the Lord and ruler of all, Jesus Christ, true God and our Savior; in the third year of our divinely crowned and most tranquil lords Basil and Constantine, and in the first year of Leo, the perpetual Augusti; in the third indiction, on the day before the Ides of February; with the precious and life-giving woods, and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation, placed before us [Col. 0130D] on the right-hand side of the famous church of holy and great-named Hagia Sophia; with Donatus, the most beloved of God, bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most beloved of God, bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most beloved of God, deacon of the holy Roman Church, occupying the places of Adrian, the most holy Roman pope, and Ignatius, the most holy archbishop [Col. 0131A] —teeth, who, on some occasion, graciously deigned in his providence to assist our lowliness, so that I might be worthy to address and entreat my lord and ruler, the orthodox emperor.

For this appeared to me a great delight: health, prosperity, and great grace arising from God. For the governor of the regions of Palestine, who holds Tiberias and Tyre and has been entrusted with the administration of those places, sent to us in these days and announced the arrival of the imperial and most noble letters addressed to him. They commanded him to send someone from the Alexandrian see to the imperial court, together with a few lines from us concerning the dissension that had arisen in the royal city on account of the two patriarchs; and because the emperor, advanced by God and most renowned, longs [Col. 0131B] to hear from foreign lips what the truth requires and what certain and firm knowledge exists concerning these matters.

This moved us to do what we had previously desired, and what we hope will be accomplished more quickly because of the man’s justice and because of the love of affection that fears the authority which exercises rule among us: namely, to send one of those who diligently remain with us. We therefore sent him, in reply and on our behalf, requesting a man formerly our own, who for many years had lived under his authority: a venerable monk named Joseph, cultivating the monastic way of life from his earliest years.

With him we also sent this poor little booklet, unworthy and unsuitable for an imperial address. We did this willingly, indeed confidently daring to do so, [Col. 0131C] not because we despise ourselves—far from it—but because we cast ourselves down, truly comparing our lowliness with the exalted and ruling dignity that is higher than every rank. We could not have acted with this intention unless we had clearly recognized in you, emperor most beloved of God, a Christ-imitating and condescending disposition, which once received the widow’s two small coins and preferred them to many gifts.

For one of the poets says:

> “That man is absent …” [Note: [Col. 0131D] “That man is absent.” These verses are found among the Greeks. From the preceding context their meaning appears to be as follows, spoken by the patriarch of Alexandria, who was situated among the Saracens: “Just as,” he says, “a man bound in fetters, leaping somehow or from somewhere and crawling beyond his strength, becomes a horseman, so you, emperor, receive the writings of our humility and tiny knowledge as the widow’s two coins, although, hindered by the fetters of the nations among whom we live, we have scarcely been able to write even these things. Or alternatively: ‘Just as,’ he says, ‘one who has bonds on his feet and is guarded by a powerful man, if he finds a suitable opportunity, can somehow mount a horse and flee, and, according to the poet’s example, escape the power of the angry ruler; so we, although bound by the force of the nations, have nevertheless placed upon the horse of our letter and sent at least with difficulty the word of God, which is not bound. Receive it as though we were free and therefore could have offered you greater things.’ Yet, as I suppose, he writes obscurely for this reason: so that, if the letter should somehow fall into enemy hands, they might not easily understand it. EDIT. ROM.] who, bound in fetters, leaps toward the boundaries like a horseman, and, valuing the highest thing, scarcely casts himself back, leaping boldly.”

Concerning the two patriarchs, lord prince and emperor directed by God, your piety, advanced by God, knows very well that it is impossible, while being removed by bodily distances, to investigate and distinguish so great and serious a matter when it is disliked and has been conducted as though secretly; especially since we know nothing of it—not even its beginnings, [Col. 0132A] middle, later stages, or conclusion.

For one of the wise men who spoke in iambics foretold:

> “For what foreign judge has ever heard anyone alone anywhere, when the accused was not present, or immediately judged him after hearing this?”

If truth considers it wrong and unlawful to hear the case from only one of the adversaries, and rejects this as abominable, how much more should it reject hearing from neither of them? Those who judge what they do not know find a ready refutation in the poems of the most blessed Gregory, and it is plainly said to them that what they utter is darkness.

We know very well that among you, emperor who dictate and are preserved by God, there are supreme pastors, bishops, and abbots, as well as clergy and the *azyges* [Note: [Col. 0132D] That is, “without a yoke,” namely without wives. Monks are meant, because they are free from spouses.], who stand adorned with every wisdom and knowledge, with understanding [Col. 0132B] as well as discernment and prudence. You have been appointed their chief, president, and supreme teacher, holy and orthodox emperor. You know what is fitting concerning all those who are nearer to you, and you know well what is pleasing to God.

For you are the root from which [perhaps: branches] now also comes the intelligible ocean of immortality, from which all springs, every sea, all lakes, and streams flow forth from afar, as the external poet Homer says.

Thus, most just lord emperor, we find in certain ancient histories that two patriarchs once occupied one see at the same time in the holy city of Christ our God, but in the following manner.

The monk Alexander says in his histories that the thirtieth patriarch of Jerusalem after the glorious and celebrated [Col. 0132C] ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven was named Narcissus. Shining with apostolic grace and devoted to quiet, he abandoned the episcopal office and, in the twelfth year of his patriarchate, fled to unknown places. When he was sought by the people, the authorities, and the bishops of the province but was not found, another patriarch was advanced in his place, named Dius. After living eight years, he died in Christ.

After him came Germanus for three years; Gordius succeeded him for four years. Then, behold, Narcissus appeared again as though from hidden places, and he was united with the consecrated Gordius in one understanding and agreement. When Gordius, who had been with him, died, and Narcissus had grown exceedingly old—for he was about one hundred and sixteen years old—they appointed a certain bishop Alexander, who had come from another region for the sake of venerating the holy places, as bishop of Jerusalem by divine revelation, with the aged Narcissus earnestly requesting it. Alexander was later brought to completion by martyrdom.

This [was done] in the holy city of Constantinople, the New Rome, and in the presence of the most holy guardians of the eastern sees: Joseph, the most beloved of God, archdeacon of the Alexandrians of the great city, occupying the place of Michael, the most holy patriarch of Alexandria; Thomas, the most holy metropolitan of Tyre, occupying the place of the see of Antioch, since that Church was widowed; and Elias, the most worshipful priest and syncellus, occupying the throne of Theodosius, archbishop of Jerusalem.

The sacred senate was also present. We mean: Theodore, the most magnificent patrician and magister; Christopher, the most magnificent patrician and magister; Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus; Himerius, the most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Paul, the most magnificent patrician and prefect; Theodore, the most magnificent patrician; Barbatius, the most magnificent patrician; Manuel, the most magnificent patrician; Theophylact, the most magnificent patrician; Petronas, the most magnificent patrician; and Manuel, the most magnificent patrician.

Also seated with them were the bishops most beloved of God: Basil, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Ephesus; Theodulus, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Ancyra; Nicephorus, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Nicaea; Basil, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Chalcedon; Basil, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Gangra; Theodore, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Thessalonica; Nicholas, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Synnada; Theophylact, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Iconium; Ignatius, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Hierapolis; Michael, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of [Hod, perhaps Hadramytus]; Hilarion, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Corinth; Metrophanes, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Smyrna; Michael, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Byzia; Euthymianus, the most beloved of God, metropolitan of Eucharta; John, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Pompeiiopolis; Theophanes, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Selga; Stephen, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Cypsella; John, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Cius; Photius, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Nicolia; Icoo, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Methymna; Basil, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Rhusium; Gregory, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Paros; Paul, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Apamea; Basil, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Pyrgi; and Arsenius, the most beloved of God, archbishop of Aureliopolis.

Also: George, the most beloved of God, bishop of holy Cyriaca; Eustathius, the most beloved of God, bishop of Aemonia; Constantine, the most beloved of God, bishop of Tralles; Germanus, the most beloved of God, bishop of Citri; Constantine, the most beloved of God, bishop of Augustopolis; Nicholas, the most beloved of God, bishop of Documium; Peter, the most beloved of God, bishop of Melitopolis; Joseph, the most beloved of God, bishop of Leria; Tarasius, the most beloved of God, bishop of Cinea; Stephen, the most beloved of God, bishop of Gordoserba; Philip, the most beloved of God, bishop of Tabia; Ignatius, the most beloved of God, bishop of Juliopolis; Constantine, the most beloved of God, bishop of Tius; Sisinnius, the most beloved of God, bishop of Bithynopolis; Xenophon, the most beloved of God, bishop of Mylassa; Leo, the most beloved of God, [Col. 0134A] bishop of Neapolis; Marcian, the most beloved of God, bishop of Nicopolis; Marcian, the most beloved of God, bishop of Thebes; Gregory, the most beloved of God, bishop of Mesina; John, the most beloved of God, bishop of Poleosnomus; Theodore, the most beloved of God, bishop of Eurippus [or Eusippus]; Nicephorus, the most beloved of God, bishop of Croton; Nicholas, the most beloved of God, bishop of Nusa; Constantine, the most beloved of God, bishop of Synai; Gregory, the most beloved of God, bishop of Tripolis; Leo, the most beloved of God, bishop of Daphnusia; Constantine, the most beloved of God, bishop of Onumericus [or Enumericus]; Basil, the most beloved of God, bishop of Adranius [or Eldranius]; Theophanes, the most beloved of God, bishop of Axana; John, the most beloved of God, bishop of Tampsus; Nicephorus, the most beloved of God, bishop of Aspona; [Col. 0134B] Macarius, the most beloved of God, bishop of Elizomenes [or Elysomane]; Michael, the most beloved of God, bishop of Cercyra; Nicephorus, the most beloved of God, bishop of Zacynthus; Joseph, the most beloved of God, bishop of Aventium; Theagnoscus [or Theognostus], the most beloved of God, bishop of Parnassus; Meletius, the most beloved of God, bishop of Heraclea; Asaph, the most beloved of God, bishop of Erythrae; Constantine, the most beloved of God, bishop of Prusias; Cosmas, the most beloved of God, bishop of Adrianople; and Ignatius, the most beloved of God, bishop of Timon.

When these had assembled, Bahanes, the most famous patrician and praepositus, said on behalf of the sacred senate to the vicars of Old Rome and the eastern sees:

“My most holy fathers, you know that in the preceding sessions an ecclesiastical arrangement was made by you, the most holy guardians of the sees of Old Rome and the eastern sees, according to synodical propriety and order. Now, however, a representative of the patriarch of Alexandria has arrived, and this has unquestionably occurred through God’s cooperation and will. What, then, does your holiness think should be done hereafter?”

The most holy vicars of Old Rome said:

“We have indeed seen him, spoken with him, and received satisfaction from his speech. Nevertheless, according to the canonical ordinances, let his letter of commendation be read aloud before everyone in this holy and universal synod, and let him then be numbered among all of us who represent the patriarchal sees.”

The bishops most beloved of God and the entire holy synod said:

“It is good and just, and therefore pleasing to everyone. You have this plainly from the ecclesiastical and synodical order that follows.”

After this, Gregory, the devout notary of the divine secretariats, received and read the letter sent by the patriarch of Alexandria to the most pious emperor.

> To the most pious and magnificent emperor Basil, victor, Augustus, triumphant, and servant pleasing to Christ our God, Michael, an unworthy servant of the children of my Lord, the Alexandrian.

For a long time we have desired to write to your divinely appointed and most illustrious office, excellent emperor, but we recognize that we have been restrained by fear of another tribe. Now, however, having been commanded, we have diligently accomplished both what we desired and what we feared, repaying abundant thank— [text breaks off]. [Col. 0135A] Indeed, we know only historically, and let this be sufficient for us, your humble servants, concerning these matters.
