We beseech you, most benevolent emperor, and we, unworthy servants, entreat you to heap benefits upon those from among us who have been sent to your divinely governed exalted authority—not upon them alone, but upon all who are reckoned under the name of Christ and who, together with them, perform this embassy for the same redemption—in order to remove suspicion from those who have been sent and from us who sent them, so that we may all obtain a favorable hearing before everyone who is with us and may reap the fruit of redeeming the time.

May your principate, which loves God and the world, therefore command and act according to its desire and pleasure, guided by the help of the all-governing God, heaped with continuous and unfailing blessings, and, after a very long life and the passage of many years, enjoy an immortal empire, through the prayers of the undefiled Mother of God Mary, of the wondrous Mark, apostle, evangelist, and martyr, who is also our teacher, and of all the saints who fulfill God’s commandments. Amen.

When the letter of commendation had been read, Donatus, the most beloved of God, bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most beloved of God, bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, said:

“Behold, this most honorable man has brought a letter of commendation, which he received from his patriarch Michael. We have learned who he is and from where he has come, and we receive him as truly the guardian of the see of Alexandria. Let the most holy guardians of the eastern sees, the sacred synod, and the bishops beloved of God also state what they think about this and how they are assured by the letter.”

The holy and universal synod said:

“We have been fully persuaded and all assured by the letter just read before us that he is not a false but a most genuine representative of the throne of Alexandria. Therefore we receive him and glorify the God of all, who supplied what was lacking to the universal synod and has now shown it to be most complete.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said to Joseph, the most reverend deacon and guardian of the see of Alexandria:

“Father, we have something to say to your holiness. Before your holiness arrived here, eight sessions had taken place, concerning both the most holy patriarch [Col. 0135D] and Photius, the transgressor and tyrant, his laying on of hands, and certain other matters. Have you heard anything of what was done in them—how matters were judged or determined? You have learned, surely, about these two necessary matters: namely, the reception of the most holy patriarch Ignatius, how he was established and confirmed, and the charge against Photius, how he has been cast down and expelled, together with all his advancement and laying on of hands.”

Joseph, the most reverend archdeacon and guardian of the see of Alexandria, said:

“I have heard and learned, with much scrutiny and diligence, everything that has been done.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“Then do the judgments of the most holy vicars of Old [Col. 0136A] Rome and the eastern sees please you?”

Joseph, the most reverend archdeacon and vicar of Alexandria, said:

“I approve in every ecclesiastical proceeding and arrangement the decisions of the most holy guardians of the sees of Old Rome and the eastern sees, and whatever they have arranged in holiness and justice. Behold, my opinion is here in writing; if you command, let it be read before this sacred synod. As for what remains, insofar as I learn through the grace of Christ what is just and holy, I shall both say and do it.”

The most holy vicars of Old Rome said:

“Behold, we have heard what you have said, and everything pleases us. Therefore we wish the opinion that you hold to be read in the midst of this holy and universal synod.”

After this, Joseph, the most reverend archdeacon and guardian of the see of Alexandria, rose and placed his written opinion among the precious Wood and the undefiled Gospels. Then Thomas, the most reverend deacon and devout notary, was ordered to stand in the midst of the synod and read it:

> Joseph, monk and archdeacon, and vicar of Michael, the most holy patriarch of Alexandria, says these things to the holy and universal synod:

Now it is fitting to say with the prophet David: “The Lord will do the desire of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer and save them” (Psalm 144).

Because our most gentle and pious emperor Basil established the fear of God as the foundation and base in his soul, and directed all his endeavors according to this principle, the eyes of the Lord consequently look upon him, according to the one who said: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him and upon those who hope in his mercy” (Psalm 32).

Therefore he also resolved to direct his most pious and just will toward the stability of his faith and the adornment of the catholic Church, and he brought it fully toward a prosperous completion. For here he has made easy the things that seemed impossible to human beings, as Scripture says: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (1 Timothy 5).

The Lord wished the true examination of the matters presently at issue to be presented to him through four irreproachable and truthful witnesses, so that perfect satisfaction might always be provided to those who wish to understand. For our emperor, redeemed by God, prospers through God and before God. From the regions of the West he brought representatives of the holy Roman Church; from the places held by hostile nations, which with an inimical purpose oppose the Christian flock, he deigned during the days of his reign to display and raise up cooperators and advocates of the truth.

When our brother Thomas, the most holy bishop of Tyre, the first metropolitan of the Antiochene throne, who also administers its ecclesiastical affairs because there is no patriarch there, came here, together with Elias, the most holy priest and syncellus of the apostolic throne of Jerusalem, he thought that perhaps the universal synod was not yet complete, since two [thrones] had been assembled here.

[Col. 0137A] Therefore God, who is perfect above all and before all, wishing to complete this synod and present it perfect in deed, also drew us from the southern regions as representatives of the apostolic throne of the great Church of the Alexandrians. Arriving here through divine grace and the royal inspiration of the most pious emperor, we carefully investigated everything, so that nothing concerning the proceedings conducted by our brothers before our arrival might remain hidden from us.

Moreover, we examined the causes previously raised here between the most holy patriarch Ignatius and Photius, who, like a robber and adulterer, leapt upon the throne of Constantinople. We also examined the meaning and judgment concerning the venerable and holy images—not superficially or in passing, but thoroughly and sufficiently, as was proper. We were astonished, learning more certainly concerning such matters how manifest is the voice of the Savior, which says: “Nothing is hidden that will not be known and come into manifestation” (Luke 12). And again: “The Spirit blows where it wills” (John 3).

For, truly and inextricably inspired by God and by his divine grace, the most holy vicars of Old Rome and the eastern sees, through God, arranged everything in this assembled synod according to the law of justice and the judgment of truth. They did not shrink from speaking of what was legitimate in matters of ecclesiastical order, as befits saints adorned with the priesthood and embracing the word of truth.

They did not run in vain, nor labor fruitlessly, nor place anything before the reverence and clemency proper to them that could prevent them from being investigators of God’s just judgment. Therefore, having clearly and manifestly recognized this, we consent and agree with what they judged and properly derived, knowing how carefully to preserve the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ, which says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18).

For the three patriarchates beloved of God did not assemble in the name of anyone else, nor for any other reason among those that exist, but for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom they will receive their reward and recompense. For he says: “I live, says the Lord, but those who glorify me I will glorify; and whoever rejects me shall be dishonored” (Proverbs 8).

With them may we also become fellow workers in the same labors, sharing from God in the recompense of the reward to be granted by God, who gives salvation to our emperors Basil, Constantine, and Leo, and through them restores the region and homeland of our parish, which had previously been taken away through the negligence of those who ruled before them, through the prayers and intercessions of our Lady, the Mother of God, and of all the saints. Amen.

And after the reading, the holy universal synod said:

“The letter that has been read has assured us above all that it agrees with the judgment of the holy Roman Church and of the Eastern sees.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“This man has rightly acted as he did, because he followed and agreed with the acts previously decreed by us. Now we all regard him as though he had been our fellow worker and had agreed with us from the first session until today. Therefore we also receive him as the true and most just representative of the See of Alexandria.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said to the most holy representatives of senior Rome and of the Eastern sees:

“This matter has now reached its conclusion, and there is no further discussion of it. We regard him as we regard ourselves. Since this matter has therefore been concluded, what do you advise, or what do you wish to be arranged today?”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Through messengers of certain noblemen, and through reports that have circulated, we have learned that certain men spoke and testified falsely against Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople. If any of the men mentioned are present here, we order them to enter this holy synod, so that we may learn what they said and what they testified.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“Have you heard this?”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“We have both heard it and seen it in writing at Rome, in the book brought by Rhadoald and Zacharias, the bishops who were sent here at that time. And after we entered here, we received further confirmation.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said to the most holy representatives of the Eastern sees:

“You, our holy Fathers, have heard about this matter of which the most holy representatives of senior Rome have spoken. Do you also wish to investigate this matter, or not?”

Joseph, deacon and representative of Alexandria, devoted to God; Thomas, the God-beloved metropolitan of Tyre; the primate of the throne of Antioch; and Elias, the most honored presbyter and syncellus of the throne of Jerusalem, said:

“Since the root of the present evil affairs, together with the malice inherent in it, has now been suitably cleansed, it is fitting that the wicked branches that have sprung up here should also be purged and restored to proper and good cultivation. We too wish this matter to be brought forward.”

Then Stephen, the most reverend deacon and notary of the most holy patriarch Ignatius, standing in the midst of the assembly, said to the holy synod:

“Does it please all of you that this matter be examined?”

The entire holy synod cried out:

“It pleases all.”

After this, by order of the holy synod, the witnesses were brought in—those who had falsely sworn against Ignatius the patriarch before Rhadoald and Zacharias, formerly bishops. As they stood in the midst of the assembly, the most magnificent and most glorious princes said to the most holy representatives:

“What do you think should be done with them? Should you all question them together, or each one separately?”

The most holy representatives said:

“Each one should be questioned.”

Before all the others, Theodore was questioned by the most holy representatives of senior Rome.

“Who are you called?”

He said:

“Theodore.”

The most holy representatives said:

“What rank do you hold?”

Theodore said:

“I am a protospatharius in the service of the emperors.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Did you come to this synod willingly or under compulsion?”

Theodore said:

“I came willingly.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Why did you come?”

Theodore said:

“Because of the oath that we swore concerning the holy apostles.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Concerning whom did you swear the oath?”

Theodore said:

“Concerning Ignatius the patriarch.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Did you swear voluntarily or under duress?”

Theodore said:

“I swore unwillingly. The emperor said to me: ‘Since you were in attendance on the day when the lord patriarch was appointed, and you did not witness his election, enter and swear.’ So I entered and swore. For I had not witnessed his election.”

The most holy representatives said:

“And surely you knew that he had been patriarch for twelve years, and that you had remained in communion with him?”

The protospatharius Theodore said:

“I knew it, certainly. But the emperor said to me: ‘You are not a metropolitan; you are not a bishop.’ So I entered and swore.”

The most holy representatives said:

“How did you swear?”

Theodore said:

“I swore that I had not witnessed his election.”

The most holy representatives said:

“And did you know that you were committing a sin by that oath?”

Theodore said:

“I knew it, but I had no choice.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Did you make confession and receive a penance for that sin, repenting of it?”

Theodore said:

“Yes.”

The most holy representatives said:

“To whom did you confess, and from whom did you receive the penance?”

Theodore said:

“The man who gave me the penance has died.”

The representatives of senior Rome said:

“What was his name?”

Theodore said:

“I do not know. I know only that he was a chartulary, that he had been tonsured, and that he had spent forty years on a pillar.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Was he a priest?”

Theodore said:

“I do not know. He was an abbot, and I had confidence in him, so I reported the matter to him.”

The most holy representatives said:

“And did you observe the penance?”

Theodore said:

“If God wills, I observed it, because I am a Christian.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Did you complete it or not?”

Theodore said:

“Here I am; I am completing it.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Was the lord Ignatius justly restored to his see?”

Theodore said:

“Justly. For if God had not wished him to be restored, He would not have given him life.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Do you therefore receive this holy synod and everything that has been judged by it?”

The protospatharius Theodore said:

“Our holy emperor receives it, as do all Christians; how could I not receive it? I too receive it, because I am Orthodox.”

Then Leo the consul, who had also become a secretary, was questioned by the most holy representatives.

“How did you enter this holy synod?”

Leo said:

“They notified us, and we came.”

The most holy representatives said:

“For what reason?”

Leo said:

“They told us: ‘Come and receive absolution.’”

The most holy representatives said:

“For what sin?”

Leo said:

“For the oath that I swore concerning the holy apostles.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Who led you there?”

Leo said:

“The emperor and Caesar of that time.”

The most holy representatives said:

“By authority and force, or voluntarily?”

Leo said:

“They asked me: ‘Did you witness the election of the patriarch Ignatius?’ And I said: ‘No.’”

The most holy representatives said:

“Did you make the oath willingly or under compulsion?”

Leo said:

“They asked me: ‘Perhaps you were not in this city when the patriarch was elected; enter and swear.’ So I entered and swore.”

The most holy representatives said:

“How many years have passed since Ignatius was consecrated patriarch?”

Leo the consul said:

“I say that it has been twenty-four years.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Before you swore, were you in communion with the patriarch Ignatius?”

Leo said:

“Yes.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Then why, brother, did you most recently turn against him? It appears from this that you ran to kill your father and your shepherd. Do you know that you committed a sin, repented, and received a penance?”

Leo said:

“I did not receive a penance.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Did you neglect to receive a penance? Did you afterwards remain in communion or not?”

Leo said:

“No.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Do you now receive the patriarch Ignatius?”

Leo said:

“Whatever the world and you receive, I also receive.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Are you willing to receive a penance?”

Leo said:

“If you give me one, I will accept it.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Do you receive this holy synod?”

Leo said:

“I receive it.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Do you anathematize Photios and all whom the synod has anathematized?”

Leo said:

“Who am I to anathematize? An anathema is pronounced in a matter of faith; but Photios is Orthodox, so why should I anathematize him?”

The most holy representatives said:

“His deeds are worse than every heresy, for he is a worker of the devil.”

Leo the consul said:

“If you judge that an anathema should be pronounced even apart from heresy, then I too anathematize all whom this holy and universal synod has anathematized.”

After the examination of these two men, Eustathius, the imperial spatharius-candidatus; Constantine, the imperial spatharius; Basil, the imperial mandator; Photios, a spatharius who had become chartulary of the military logothesion; Paul, the imperial secretary; Christopher, the imperial spatharius; the second of the Green faction; Anastasius, formerly a deacon; Marinus [another reading: Marianus], a vestitor who had become an epoptes; Constantine the chartulary; Arsabir, the imperial candidatus; and Constantine, the imperial protospatharius, were questioned.

When all had been thoroughly questioned and examined, they alleged royal violence and fear, deprivation of their money, and exile. With one voice they affirmed that they had been compelled to undertake such an act against their will. Some of them confessed that they had immediately made confession and received appropriate penances; others acknowledged that they had remained until the present without repentance. These received suitable penances from the holy and universal synod, as will be made clear hereafter, when all of them had received the holy and universal synod, anathematized everything that it had anathematized, and likewise willingly accepted everything that it had accepted.

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said, speaking as the representative of the senate to the most holy representatives of senior Rome:

“Not all the men who falsely swore against the most holy patriarch are present here. Some have died, while others are absent from this gathering because of illness or other causes. You have heard the truth.”

The most holy representatives said:

“We wish to hear from those who are absent just as we have heard from those who are present.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to the holy synod:

“What does this holy synod desire? Should these men be judged without the others, or not?”

The most holy representatives said:

“Let us wait for them.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“Another synod cannot be held on their account. Nevertheless, although the others are not present, they must hear the penance that you have to impose. If they hasten to your feet and to those of the most holy patriarch Ignatius, they will receive the penance determined by your holiness. But if they do not come and persist in their wickedness, their penance will be increased as your holiness sees fit.”

Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, said:

“It is impossible that those men should not be examined and that it should not be revealed what sort of men they are and who they are. Many of them are actuaries, stablemen, and veterinary surgeons. Therefore it is just that they come into the presence of this holy synod, be accused, and confess the truth, just as these men have done.”

The most magnificent princes said:

“As we have already said, another synod cannot be held on account of those who have not been found. But, if you order it, they will come before your holiness and all the metropolitans.”

Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, said:

“It pleases me.”

After this, Stephen, the God-beloved deacon and notary, went up and read the penance determined by the most holy representatives and the entire holy synod, as follows:

“Since this holy and universal synod has jointly considered those men who came voluntarily before it and who formerly swore falsely against Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, under the emperor Michael and Bardas the domesticus, having been compelled to do so in the Church of the Holy Apostles before that abominable council, we define and promulgate that those who have not repented, nor made confession, nor received a penance, but have remained in the hardness of their hearts and have not recognized the sin they committed—not only against Ignatius, the most holy patriarch, but also against the most holy Church of God—are to undergo a seven-year penance.

“Because of this manifest sin, they shall spend two years outside the Church; for the next two years they shall remain within the Church and hear the divine Scriptures as far as the catechumens, but shall in no way communicate. They shall abstain from meat and wine for four years, except on Sundays and the feasts of the Lord. During the remaining three years they shall stand with the faithful and shall be worthy to receive divine Communion only on the solemnities of the Lord, together with almsgiving, prayers, and fasting. Thus, on three days of each week—Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—they shall abstain from meat and wine.

“For their sin was not a minor one, but, as has already been said, was committed against the great God, against the first prince of shepherds, and through the pontiff who was anointed by Him. Whoever they may be who have not come today to this holy and universal synod, but hide themselves, unwilling to confess the sin they committed and wishing to escape the judgment of the penance, shall be entirely separated from the Church and bound by the bond of anathema until they are saved through conversion and repentance. Those, however, who first accept the penance and observe it shall, after completing it, become worthy of the holy and divine mysteries.”

After the reading, the most magnificent and most glorious princes said to the most holy representatives:

“It is clear that the condemnation imposed on those who perjured themselves and swore falsely is just, and they are receiving the penance given by the holy synod. But we ask and entreat you to show forgiveness and compassion toward them, because the period assigned for the penance is very long, and because the sin they committed was against our shepherd and pontiff. Let authority also be given to his holiness so that, whenever anyone comes to him with a contrite heart seeking mercy, he may lessen the penance as God directs him.

“For he is an imitator of the one who prayed for those who crucified him. This we ask; this we entreat your holiness; this we implore of you.”

The most holy representatives said:

“We established this definition not only for the present matter or case, but also as a precaution for the future. Nevertheless, we entrust to the shepherd against whom they sinned the present dispensation concerning those who are present in this case.”

And they said to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch:

“The holy synod has unanimously assigned them a penance proportionate to their sin—indeed, one approaching great compassion. Nevertheless, your holiness has the authority, according to the contrition of each person’s heart and the fervor and zeal of his repentance, either to lessen the penance that has been imposed or even to increase it, since they sinned against you and, through you, against God.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“Blessed be God, who in this matter also has shown you to be imitators of His compassion.”

The most honored bishops said:

“This judgment pleases everyone.”

Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said to the most holy representatives:

“This matter has now reached its conclusion. Do you have anything else to arrange, or not? For the hour has passed. If you have nothing else, say so.”

Donatus, the most God-loving bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the most God-loving bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, said:

“We have something else to request today.”

“For after we entered this city preserved by God, we heard that the devil, finding wicked and contemptuous men to be instruments of his malice, had brought about a new and impious practice: laymen and senators were clothed in shoulder garments and, apparently, performed the things belonging to priests.”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“Let your will be done; we too see that this is just.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Let such men enter.”

They entered and stood in the midst of the assembly: Marinus, a spatharius-candidatus; Basil, a spatharius; and George, a spatharius. The most holy representatives questioned them:

“Why did you enter this holy synod, and what cause have you come to report?”

Marinus and those who were with him said:

“Emperor Michael was making a game of it, sending us the pontifical stole—not only to us, but also to many other spatharii.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Did you truly put on the priestly stole?”

Marinus and the others said:

“We truly put it on.”

The most holy representatives said:

“And did they place the holy Gospels upon your heads?”

Marinus and those who were with him said:

“They truly placed them there.”

The most holy representatives said:

“And did anyone recite a prayer over you?”

Marinus and those who were with him said:

“Yes.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Who?”

Marinus and the others said:

“The protospatharius Theophilus.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Is he alive or dead?”

Marinus and Gregory said:

“He is dead, God willing.”

The most holy representatives said:

“He is certainly truly dead and has gone to hell. You knew that this was evil. Why did you do it?”

Marinus and those who were with him said:

“What could we say against the emperor, when we had wives, children, and worldly concerns?”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“If he had offered you an idol, would you have worshiped it?”

Marinus and the others said:

“Far be it from us.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“From your cradles and from the age of infancy, who brought you into the Church of God, or who enlightened you—priests or laymen?”

Marinus and the others said:

“Priests.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Then why, if priests brought you into the Church and into communion, did you profane the divine and fearful mysteries, mock them, and make the priesthood a spectacle?”

Marinus, Basil, and Gregory replied:

“We have said, and we say again: Whatever the emperor did and ordered on that day, we did. If we had spoken out and resisted, we would have died. Nevertheless, some of our own who resisted were beaten.”

The most holy representatives said:

“It would have been good if, having begun well, you had remained steadfast to the end even if you were beaten, and had preserved the truth.”

Marinus and those who were with him said:

“We are weak men and would not have endured death. Nevertheless, we accept a penance, confessing to the most holy lord Ignatius the patriarch. Let him be questioned.”

The most holy representatives said:

“And do you observe the penances?”

Marinus and the others said:

“Yes. God knows that we have observed them.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Who gave them to you?”

Marinus and those who were with him said:

“We spoke to the patriarch, and he said to us: ‘Go individually to wherever you have the means of satisfaction, and receive it.’”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“When you were staging this display, this insult, and this mockery of the priesthood, did Photios see you?”

Marinus and those who were with him said:

“We do not know whether he saw it or did not see it. But God is our witness that the whole world knew of it.”

The most holy representatives said:

“How many of you were there?”

Marinus and the others said:

“There were many of us.”

The most holy representatives said:

“Truly, you were many, to the dishonor and confusion of our one and only true God. Therefore both you who are present and those who are absent must receive a penance from this holy and universal synod for the remission of your impiety.”

After this, Thomas, the most reverend subdeacon and devoted notary, went up and read the following on behalf of the most holy representatives of senior Rome:

“In these latter times a new and highly reprehensible invention has appeared. Laymen, to the disgrace and confusion of Christ our God, His Church, and the priestly dignity, clothed in priestly stoles and episcopal shoulder garments, and receiving a priestly prayer from some layman who assumed a patriarchal form, presumed to exercise the priesthood and to perform what were merely pretended rites, as though they were worthy high priests. They thereby subjected the mysteries of the divine administration to ridicule and reproach, to the disparagement of the God-given honour of the chief priests, and to the detraction of the undefiled faith of Christians.

“When we brought these men before the holy synod and examined them, we learned from others an even fuller account of the impiety that had been committed by these same men. Therefore we have judged it right to subject them also to appropriate and fitting penances, so that hereafter such an abomination may in no way be carried out in the Church of God or among the Christian people in its fullness. We therefore wish to formulate a decree concerning this unlawful undertaking, which, God willing, will be read at another gathering.”

After this reading, Stephen, the God-beloved deacon and notary, went up and read the following on behalf of the Eastern sees:

“Since they were acting under imperial fear and danger—indeed, since the emperor himself appeared to be the one carrying out the act and subsequently compelled them to do it, while they did not possess such an intention or disposition as would have led them to persist even at the cost of receiving capital punishment—their penance shall be determined at another gathering according to their weakness.”

After the reading, the most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“See, this matter has received a fitting conclusion. What, then, does your holiness wish?”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome and of the two Eastern sees said:

“We wish the false representatives whom Photios brought against the most blessed Pope Nicholas, as though they came from other patriarchal sees, to enter here, so that our most reverend brother and fellow minister Joseph, the representative of the patriarch of Alexandria, may also learn the tricks and frauds of Photios.”

Leontius, Gregory, and Sergius entered. As they stood in the midst of the assembly, Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“Which one of you was falsely reported by Photios to be the representative of Alexandria?”

Leontius stepped forward and said:

“I am.”

Joseph, the most God-loving archdeacon and representative of Alexandria, said to Leontius:

“Where are you from, and who are you?”

Leontius said:

“I was a Greek by birth, but I went to Alexandria as a captive.”

Joseph, the representative of Alexandria, said:

“And by whom were you purchased?”

Leontius said:

“By Michael the patriarch.”

Joseph, the representative of Alexandria, said:

“Where is the patriarch’s episcopal residence?”

Leontius said:

“Inside, at the Church of the Holy Mother of God, near the property of Eulogius.”

Joseph, the representative of Alexandria, said:

“How did you come here?”

Leontius said:

“I was a captive, and he made me free. I came here for the blessing.”

Joseph, the most reverend archdeacon and representative of Alexandria, said:

“Did the most holy Michael send you as his representative?”

Leontius said:

“I have often said that he did not send me; I came here on my own for the blessing. But Photios sent me to Rome, so that I might do whatever the metropolitans said. God knows that I went down like a sheep, knowing nothing.”

The most holy representatives and the entire holy synod said:

“He is confessing his sin, and we no longer need witnesses.”

After he had been questioned and examined at length, he said nothing other than what he had said in the eighth session before the holy and universal synod.

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“We have often heard from you before the things you have now said. But you have been brought in here now so that the true representative of the patriarch of Alexandria may see you, since you were a liar and a deceiver, as you yourself have confessed.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Who are those two persons whom we see?”

The most magnificent and most glorious princes said:

“False representatives.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“We have not yet seen them. Let them come to us, so that we may question them.”

As they approached, the most holy representatives asked them:

“Who are you, and where have you come from? Did you come as representatives or as bearers of letters? For what purpose have you come? Tell us.”

George said:

“I came only as a bearer of letters.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“By whom were you sent?”

George said:

“By Constantine, steward of the Church of Antioch. He sent me to Photios and to the emperor Michael for the sake of the blessing.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Did you sign the book against the most holy Pope Nicholas that Photios produced?”

George said:

“Far be it from me.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“And why did you travel down to the city of Rome? What task were you to perform?”

George said:

“Believe me, I do not know why I went there.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“What is your faith?”

George and those who were with him said:

“As the holy Church of God and Christians hold it.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Do you receive this holy synod?”

George and those who were with him said:

“As all Christians receive it, so do we receive it.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Tell us yourselves: how do you receive it?”

George and those who were with him said:

“We have said that we receive it.”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Do you anathematize those whom the holy synod has anathematized?”

George and those who were with him said:

“Who are we to anathematize?”

The most holy representatives said:

“Then why did you travel to Rome with the book of that abominable council?”

George and those who were with him said:

“We were compelled and unwilling. Photios said to us: ‘Reports have appeared in Rome against Pope Nicholas. Go and ascertain whether they are true.’ We replied: ‘We are rustic men; if we reach Rome, what account will we be able to give?’ He said to us: ‘The bishops will teach you what you ought to say.’”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“You were foreigners and newcomers, as you say, bearers of letters. You ought to have received the letters and then returned to your own country. Nevertheless, do you anathematize the council that you carried to Rome?”

George and those who were with him said:

“Anathema to the one who made it, to the one who agreed with it, and to the one who defended it!”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome said:

“Do you receive the most blessed Pope Nicholas and the most holy patriarch Ignatius?”

George and those who were with him said:

“As this holy universal synod receives them, so do we receive them. For who are we to contradict so great a synod, in which all the patriarchs are present through their representatives?”

Donatus, the God-beloved bishop of Ostia; Stephen, the God-beloved bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, the most reverend deacon of the holy Roman Church, said to Joseph, archdeacon and representative of the Alexandrian throne:

“See, most beloved brother, you too have learned through what you have now heard about the evil deeds and tricks of Photios, and that he was deceitful and a liar, and that truth was not in him. Since these men are poor and foreigners, we judge them worthy of pardon because they have confessed that they endured compulsion. But glory be to Christ our God for all things, who said: ‘What is hidden that will not be revealed?’ (Matthew 10). He also deigned to gather this holy and universal synod for the glory of His goodness and for the peaceful ordering of the holy catholic and apostolic Church.”

Elias, the presbyter devoted to God and syncellus of the See of Jerusalem, said:

“Having received great benefits from the true God and our Savior Jesus Christ in the completion of this holy and universal synod, we ought also to offer Him great thanksgiving and hymns of glory, because He has deigned, after so long a time, to unite the patriarchal heads with one another for the glory of His goodness and the salvation of the Church.”

After this, Stephen the deacon and devoted notary went up and pronounced the following acclamations:

“Many years to the emperors Basil, Constantine, and Leo!

“Many years to the great princes and emperors!

“Many years to Eudoxia, the most pious empress!

“Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed Roman pope!

“Many years to Adrian, the most holy Roman pope!

“Many years to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople!

“Many years to the Orthodox patriarchs of the East!

“Many years to the sacred senate!

“Eternal memory to the holy and universal synod!”

## Verses

[Col. 0147A]

Filling the world with schisms,

Impiously holding two faiths,

Saying that mortals have two souls,

Dividing the empire in many ways,

Deposing every patriarch,

Invading another’s throne,

Again branding everyone an adulterer,

Summoning the ignoble populace,

Threatening the unwilling to sign,

[Col. 0148A]

Being a mime’s fellow-patriarch,

Punishing the innocent poor clergy and orphans,

Turning the faith of the faithful into a curse,

Casting away the faith of Nicholas,

Finding Sacacius in the streets,

Gathering his associates from the byways,

Rousing scandal for everyone,

Let us call him the enemy of God, acting impiously.

## Tenth Session

[Col. 0147]

[Col. 0147B] In the name of the Lord and ruler of all, Jesus Christ, true God and our Savior; in the third year of the consulship of our God-crowned and most tranquil lords Basil and Constantine, and in the first year of Leo, the perpetual Augusti; in the third indiction, on the day before the Kalends of March, Tuesday: with the precious and life-giving wood and the undefiled Gospels of our salvation set forth on the right-hand side of the renowned church of holy and great-named Sophia; with our Christ-loving emperors Basil and Constantine presiding; and with Donatus, beloved of God, bishop of Ostia; Stephen, beloved of God, bishop of Nepi; and Marinus, most honored deacon, holding the places of the most holy pope Adrian, the elder, of Rome; and Ignatius, most holy archbishop [Col. 0147C] of the great-named Constantinople, New Rome; and with the most holy locum-tenentes of the Eastern sees, namely Joseph, beloved of God, archdeacon of Alexandria, the great city, holding the place of Michael, most holy patriarch of Alexandria; Thomas, most holy metropolitan of Tyre and locum-tenens of the see of Antioch; and Elias, worshiper of God, presbyter and syncellus, holding the place of Theodosius, patriarch of Jerusalem;

and with the sacred senate also present, namely Theodore, most magnificent patrician and master; Christopher, most magnificent patrician and master; Bahane, most magnificent patrician and praepositus; John, most magnificent patrician and protospatharius; Stephen, most magnificent patrician and sacellarius; Marinus, most magnificent patrician and military logothete; [Col. 0147D] Hemerios, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Theophilus, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Michael, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Leo, most magnificent proconsul and patrician; Palatinus, most magnificent patrician and domestic of the Excubitors; Paul, most magnificent patrician and prefect; Constantine, most magnificent patrician; Theodore, most magnificent patrician; Barbatius, most magnificent patrician; Manuel, most magnificent patrician; Michael, most magnificent patrician; Theophylact, most magnificent patrician; Manuel, most magnificent patrician; and Petronas, most magnificent patrician.

Likewise, on the right-hand [Col. 0148B] side sat the glorious princes and distinguished envoys of Louis, emperor of the Italians and Franks, namely Anastasius, beloved of God, librarian of Rome, subproximus of the conch-bearers, and his wife’s cousin; and Eurardus, praepositus of his table.

Likewise, also, the glorious judges of Michael, the most exalted prince of Bulgaria, sat: Stasiszerco, Borlas, Nesundicus, [the following words are corrupt or otherwise uncertain in the supplied text: *vagantur il vestrannatabare praestit zisunas campsis*], and Alexius Sampsi Hunno.

When these had thus assembled, by command of Basil and Constantine, the great and Christ-loving emperors, Bahane, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, stood in the midst and said to the most holy representatives of elder Rome and of the Eastern sees:

“What seems good to your holiness? What shall we do today?”

The most holy representatives said:

“We consider it necessary above all that the canons which this holy synod must ratify be read first. If this pleases it, let it say so.”

The holy synod cried out:

“It pleases us.”

Then Stephen, most beloved of God, deacon and notary, went up and read aloud, in the hearing of all, the canons written in the upper part of the synod. Likewise Thomas, most reverend deacon and notary, read the same regulations in the lower part of the synod.

# Regulations of the Holy and Universal Eighth Synod Held at Constantinople

## I. On the absolute observance and preservation of the canons previously set forth and handed down to the Church

[Col. 0150B]

Desiring to walk without stumbling along the straight and royal way of divine justice, we must retain the definitions and judgments of the holy Fathers as lamps that are always burning and illuminating our God-directed steps. Therefore, considering and regarding these also as “second utterances,” according to the great and most wise Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0149D] He calls these the “second utterances” of the Fathers, because the divine utterances are first.], let us sing most readily with divine David concerning them:

“ The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Psalm XVIII);

and:

“Your word is a lamp to my feet, and your light to my paths” (Psalm CXVIII);

and with the Preacher let us say:

“Your commandment is bright, and your law is light” (Proverbs VI);

and with a loud voice let us cry out with Isaiah to the Lord God:

“Your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isaiah LX).

For the exhortations and prohibitions of the divine canons are truly likened to light, according as what is better is discerned from what is worse, and what is suitable and beneficial from what is recognized as unsuitable and harmful. Therefore we profess that we shall observe and guard the regulations handed down to the holy catholic and apostolic Church both by the most renowned holy apostles, by the universal councils of the orthodox, and by local councils, as well as by every Father and teacher of the Church who spoke with God. We decree canonically that both our own life and conduct, the entire order of the priesthood, and all who are counted by the Christian name shall be subject to the penalties and condemnations, and conversely to the receptions and justifications, which have been issued and defined through those regulations. For the great apostle Paul clearly admonishes us to hold to the traditions which we have received, whether through speech or through a letter, from the saints who shone forth before us (II Thessalonians II).

## II. On preserving also the definitions issued synodically by the most blessed pope Nicholas and the most holy pope Adrian, Roman patriarchs, for the defense of the Church of the Constantinopolitans and the restoration of Ignatius, most holy patriarch, and for the expulsion and condemnation of the neophyte Photius

[Col. 0150D]

“Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who must give an account” (Hebrews XIII), commands the great apostle Paul. Accordingly, holding the most blessed pope Nicholas as an instrument of the Holy Spirit, and likewise the most holy pope Adrian, his successor, we define and decree that everything which they issued and promulgated synodically at different times shall always be observed and preserved, together with the chapters set forth, unaltered and unharmed—both what was issued for the defense and preservation of the Church of the Constantinopolitans and of its supreme priest, namely Ignatius, most holy patriarch, and what concerned the expulsion [Col. 0151A] and condemnation of Photius, the neophyte and usurper. No bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the order of the clergy shall dare to overturn or reject any of these things.

Whoever, after this definition of ours, is found to despise any of the chapters or decrees issued by them—if he is a priest or cleric, let him fall from his own honor and order; but if he is a monk or layman, whatever his dignity, let him be excluded until, having repented, he professes that he will preserve the aforesaid promulgation.

## III. That the image of our Lord Jesus Christ is to be honored and worshiped equally with the books of the holy Gospels, and likewise the figure of the precious cross, the image of his undefiled mother and God-bearer Mary, and of all the saints and heavenly ministers

[Col. 0151B]

We decree that the sacred image of our Lord Jesus Christ, the liberator and Savior of all, is to be worshiped with equal honor alongside the book of the holy Gospels. For just as through the words expressed in syllables and carried in the book we all attain salvation, so through the pictorial work of colors both the wise and the unlearned alike enjoy its benefit, by means of what is immediately present. What the speech expressed in syllables proclaims and commends, the writing [alternative reading: painting] expressed in colors also proclaims and commends. It is right, in accordance with the fitness of reason and the most ancient tradition, that, because they are referred to the principal originals, derivative icons should also be honored and worshiped equally with the sacred book of the holy Gospels and the type of the precious cross.

Therefore, if anyone does not worship the icon of Christ the Savior, let him not see his form when he comes to be glorified in the glory of the Father and to glorify his saints [Note: Compare this statement with the Apostle, who writes to the Thessalonians: “They will pay the penalty of eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints.”]. Rather, let him be alien from his communion and glory.

Likewise, we honor and worship the image of his undefiled mother and God-bearer, Mary. Moreover, [Col. 0151C] we paint the icons of the holy angels, just as divine Scripture represents them in words; and also those of the most praiseworthy apostles, prophets, martyrs, and holy men, together with all the saints; and we honor and worship them. Let those who do not conduct themselves in this way be anathema from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## IV. That the neophyte Photius never appears to have been a bishop, nor are those whom he consecrated in any priestly rank to be considered what he called them; nor are the honors conferred by him to be left to them, but everything he did to confer priestly rank on others is to be overturned

Cutting out the love of primacy, as a certain evil root of scandals arising in the Church, we condemn by a just decree Photius, who rashly and unlawfully, and irregularly, like a grievous wolf, leapt into Christ’s sheepfold. He filled the world with a thousand tumults [Col. 0151D] and disturbances. We proclaim that he was never previously, nor is he now, a bishop, and that those whom he consecrated or promoted in any priestly rank are not to remain in the rank to which they were advanced. Moreover, we restrain from such protection those who received from him the customary prayers for promotion to a praepositura.

We also decree that the churches which, as is supposed, Photius and those whom he consecrated dedicated—or in which they set up altars that had been moved—are to be dedicated, enthroned, and established again. Everything done by him and through him for the reception or condemnation of priestly ranks is entirely annulled.

For God says through the prophet concerning everyone:

“Because you rejected knowledge, I also will reject you, so that you shall not serve as my priest; and because you forgot the law of your God, I also will forget your children. The more they multiplied, the more they sinned against me; I will change their glory into dishonor. They eat the sins of my people, and they set their souls upon their iniquities” (Hosea IV).

And again he says:

“Because Ephraim multiplied altars for sin, his altars became occasions of guilt; I shall write many things upon them” (Hosea VIII) [Note: By “many” he means “worthless”; for “many” is often used in the sense of “worthless.”].

## V. That no recently tonsured person from senatorial rank or from any lay order should be elected or received as patriarch unless he is found to meet the definition issued by this holy and great synod

Desiring always to ensure that every canonical stability remain in the Churches in Christ, we renew and confirm the boundaries and dispensations [alternative reading: variations] which were formerly established by the holy apostles and blessed Fathers and set down as law in the Church. No one who is a neophyte either in faith or in priestly status should be promoted as a prelate, lest, becoming conceited, he fall into condemnation and into the snare of the devil, as the Apostle says (I Timothy III).

Therefore, agreeing with the earlier canons, we define that no one of senatorial rank or of worldly life who has recently been tonsured, with the intention or expectation of the episcopate or patriarchal honor, and has been made a cleric or monk, may ascend to such a rank, even if he is shown to have spent a considerable time in each of the orders of the divine priesthood. For such a person is found to have been tonsured not on account of religion or love of God, nor because he expected to travel along the way of virtues, but from love of glory and primacy. We restrain such a person all the more if he is compelled to this by imperial authority.

But if someone, without any suspicion of the aforesaid desire or expectation, renouncing the world for the sake of the very good of humility that is found in Christ Jesus, becomes a cleric or monk, passes through every ecclesiastical rank, and is found during the prescribed periods to have lived irreproachably and to have been approved—so that he completes one year in the rank of lector, two as subdeacon, three as deacon, and four as presbyter—it has pleased this holy and universal synod that he be elected and admitted.

For those who have lived religiously in the order of clerics or monks and have been judged worthy of the dignity and honor of the episcopate, we shorten the aforesaid period, according to what the prelates of the bishops in office at the time shall approve.

But if anyone, contrary to this definition of ours, should be advanced to the aforementioned supreme honor, let him be rejected and entirely excluded from every priestly function, since he was promoted outside the sacred canons.

## VI. On the anathema issued against Photius, also because of his invention of false representatives against the blessed pope Nicholas, his fictitious and false written pamphlets against him, and the requirement that all who have done anything similar reject and anathematize it

[Col. 0152D]

Since it has become clear that, after the most just sentence and condemnation issued against him by the most holy pope Nicholas because of his most wicked invasion of the Church of the Constantinopolitans, together with his other evil deeds, Photius also found certain wicked men and flatterers in the streets and alleys, named and presented them as representatives of the three most holy patriarchal sees of the East, and, gathering with them a church of wickedness and a council of vanity, brought forward depositional accusations and charges against the blessed pope Nicholas [Col. 0153A]—and repeatedly proclaimed an anathema insolently and boldly against him and all who communicated with him—we too have seen the books that served as monuments of these acts, stitched together by the wicked man through malicious work and deceitful dictation. These books were also consumed by fire synodically.

For this reason, as a precaution for the ecclesiastical order, we first anathematize the aforesaid Photius also on account of this matter. Then we anathematize anyone who henceforth acts deceitfully through cunning, adulterates the word of truth, pretends to be a false representative, fabricates books of lying dictation, or invents things to secure the favor of his own wishes, just as Martin, the strongest athlete of piety, the most holy Roman pope, synodically expelled such persons.

## VII. That those anathematized by the holy and universal synod should not paint the holy and honored images or teach the disciplines of divine and human wisdom

[Col. 0153B]

What is just, and what must be carried out justly, the divinely speaking Moses clearly promulgates in the law (Deuteronomy XVI). Since a good thing is not good unless it is done according to reason, it is certainly good and highly beneficial to paint the holy and venerable icons, and also to teach one’s neighbors the disciplines of divine and human wisdom. But it is neither good nor at all beneficial for any of these things to be done by the unworthy.

For this reason we define and promulgate that those anathematized by this holy and universal synod may neither work on icons in the sacred churches nor teach in any place, until they turn back from their own deception and wickedness.

Therefore, if after this definition of ours anyone admits them in any way to the painting of holy images in churches or to the activity of teaching, then, if he is a cleric, he shall risk his own rank; but if he is a layman, he shall be separated and deprived of communion in the divine mysteries [Col. 0153C].

## VIII. That no patriarch of the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans should demand written declarations from the priestly order for his own supposed stability and security

“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient; all things are lawful for me, but not all things build up,” says the great apostle Paul somewhere (I Corinthians VI).

Since, therefore, we must do everything for the benefit and perfection of the holy Church of God and absolutely nothing through contentiousness or empty glory; and since a report has reached our ears that not only heretics and those who have obtained the priesthood of the holy Church of the Constantinopolitans, but also orthodox and legitimate patriarchs, demand and compel members of the priestly order to make handwritten declarations for their own protection and favor and supposed stability, it has seemed good to this holy and universal synod that henceforth no one should do this, except for what is demanded according to form and custom for the sake of our sincere faith at the consecration of bishops.

For what is done otherwise is altogether inexpedient and does not contribute to the building up of the Church. Therefore, whoever dares to violate this definition of ours, or demands such declarations, or obeys those who demand them, shall fall from his own honor.

## IX. On overturning and dissolving the bond of the personal written declaration devised and exacted by Photius from all who wished to learn secular wisdom

Photius, the wretched man, practiced varied and diverse wickedness in the Church of Constantinople from ancient times. For we have learned that, long before, he fortified his tyrannical rule with the handwritten signatures of his adherents and dependents, so that they might learn the wisdom which has been made foolish by God, although it was plainly a new invention [Col. 0154A] and entirely alien to our holy Fathers and teachers of the Church.

Therefore, since we command that every bond of iniquity be loosed and that the written declarations of coercive contracts be torn apart, the holy and universal synod has decreed that henceforth no one among all these people shall hold or preserve such a written declaration. Rather, without any offense, all who are capable of either activity may teach and learn with confidence and fearlessness, except those who are found to be enslaved to error and heretical impiety. We most certainly forbid such persons both to teach and to discern.

If anyone is found despising and violating this definition of ours, then, if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman, let him be separated, since he does not believe the Lord’s word, which says:

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew XVI).

## X. That before a distinct examination and synodical judgment no cleric should in any way separate himself from his own bishop, nor any bishop from his own metropolitan, nor any metropolitan from his own patriarch

[Col. 0154B]

Since divine Scripture plainly cries out:

“Do not find fault before examination; first understand, and then rebuke” (Ecclesiasticus XI);

and:

“Does our law judge a man unless it first hears him and learns what he is doing?”—

this holy and universal synod also justly and fittingly defines and establishes that no layman, monk, or anyone from the order of the clergy may, before careful examination and a synodical sentence, separate himself from communion with his own patriarch, even if he claims to know any criminal charge against him. Nor may he refuse to mention his name among the divine mysteries or offices.

Likewise, we command bishops and presbyters who are in the outlying cities and regions to show the same disposition toward their own metropolitans. Metropolitans must do the same toward their patriarch.

But if anyone is found acting against this holy synod, then, if he is a bishop or cleric, let him fall from every priestly function and honor. A monk or layman, however, shall be separated from every ecclesiastical communion and association until, having been converted through repentance, he is received again.

## XI. That everyone who impiously and with impaired understanding believes that a human being has two souls must be anathematized

While the Old and New Testaments teach that a human being possesses one rational and intellectual soul, and all Fathers and teachers of the Church who speak with God affirm the same opinion, certain people, devoting themselves to evil inventions, have descended to such impiety that they shamelessly dogmatize that a human being has two souls and attempt, through certain irrational efforts by means of the wisdom that has been made foolish (I Corinthians I), to confirm their own heresy.

Therefore [Col. 0154D] this holy and universal synod, hastening to uproot the wicked opinion now sprouting like a certain worst kind of darnel—or rather, carrying the winnowing fan in the hand of truth and wishing to consign all chaff to unquenchable fire and present Christ’s threshing floor clean—anathematizes with a loud voice the inventors and perpetrators of such impiety and those who think similarly. It defines and promulgates that no one at all may in any way hold or preserve the statutes of the authors of this impiety.

But if anyone presumes to act contrary to this holy and great synod, let him be anathema and alien from the faith and worship of Christians.

## XII. On not receiving in any way episcopal elections made through the vote and power of a ruler

Since the apostolic and synodical canons entirely prohibit the promotions [Col. 0155A] and consecrations of bishops made through the power [alternative reading: domination] and command of rulers, we agree with them and also issue this sentence: if any bishop has received consecration to such dignity through the trickery or tyranny of rulers, he shall be deposed in every respect, since he wished or consented to possess the house [alternative reading: gift] of God not by the will of God and by ecclesiastical rite and decree, but by the will of carnal understanding, from human beings and through human beings.

## XIII. That in the great church those established in a lower rank should suitably advance to higher honors; but outsiders should not be admitted among them, nor should those who manage or protect estates or secular houses be enrolled or appointed in that same church

Since divine speech says somewhere:

“The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke XI),

for this reason we too decree and promulgate that the clerics of the great church who have remained in the subordinate orders should ascend to higher ranks and, if they prove worthy, deserve to enjoy the better honors, whenever some of those who are in those ranks are summoned through advancement to higher ministries or depart by the common end of nature and fall asleep.

But no one from outside should attach himself to them and receive the dignities or honors due to those who have labored for a long time; and thus the clerics of the church should not be found to advance at all.

Those who have managed the households of rulers or the affairs of suburban estates shall in no way have the power to be gathered into or appointed among the clergy of the great church. [Note: Thus it is found in the Greek copies: “And in truth, no one serving God among them is with impunity entangled in the other affairs of the world.”]

“For no one serving as a soldier for God becomes entangled in worldly affairs” (II Timothy II).

If anyone, contrary to the definition we have now issued, is promoted to any rank of the great church, let him be rejected from every ecclesiastical rank in every respect, as one who has been advanced against the great synod.

## XIV. That those who are called by divine grace to the episcopal office deserve every reverence and honor from those who at various times hold the office of strategos or appear to rule in some other capacity

[Col. 0155C]

We decree that those who are called by divine grace to the episcopal office, as bearing the image and figure of the holy heavenly hierarchs, namely the angels, are to be regarded as worthy of every honor by all rulers and subjects, in accordance plainly with the hierarchical rank and custom.

They are in no way to go out from afar to meet strategoi or any other rulers when they approach their churches. Nor are they to throw themselves from horses or mules at a great distance, or fall down and worship with fear and trembling. Nor are they to enter the dining table with secular rulers at the hour of the meal, showing those rulers the same honors that they show strategoi.

Rather, in accordance with the appropriateness of their spiritual dignity and honor, they should render to everyone what is due: “to whom tax, tax; to whom honor, honor.” But they should be preferred and deserve great veneration and reverence from the rulers of the Christ-loving emperors, as their fellow-seated companions and their equals in honor, so that the bishops may have the confidence to rebuke strategoi many times, as well as other rulers and every worldly dignity, whenever they find them acting unjustly and irrationally, and thereby correct them and make them better.

But if any bishop, after the holy synod’s definition, despises the honor due to him and canonically conferred, and permits anything to be done according to the old, inhuman, and disordered [Col. 0156A] custom beyond what has now been defined, let him be separated for one year, and let that ruler not be worthy to receive communion in the mysteries or sanctifications for two years.

## XV. That church treasures should not be alienated, nor the incomes of churches granted by emphyteusis

Renewing the apostolic and paternal canons, this holy universal synod has defined that no bishop at all may sell or in any way alienate treasures or sacred vessels, except in the case formerly established by the ancient canons, namely when they are taken for the redemption of captives.

Nor may he transfer the incomes of churches under emphyteutic agreements, sell other rural possessions, or thereby injure ecclesiastical revenues, which we decree to exist for proper use and for the support of the poor and strangers. Rather, everyone who has authority over ecclesiastical property must improve it and enlarge the ecclesiastical places as necessary, through which revenues are produced; and, in addition, he may distribute, assign, or entrust the administration of his own property to whomever he wishes and judges suitable, according to his own authority and dominion.

Whoever is found, after this definition of ours, to act contrary to this holy and universal synod shall be deposed as a transgressor of divine laws and precepts. The sale, whether written or unwritten, made by a bishop, or the emphyteutic transfer, or any other alienation of treasures or revenues of these places, shall be entirely annulled.

But whoever has bought or received anything from the aforesaid treasures or revenues and has not restored to the Church what belongs to the Church, or has not surrendered for cancellation the document of sale or emphyteusis, shall be anathema until he has done what has been confirmed by this holy and universal synod.

If a bishop is convicted of having built a monastery from ecclesiastical revenues, he shall hand that monastery over to the same Church. [Col. 0156C] But if he built it from his own property or from some other arrangements, he may possess it according to his own authority and will throughout his life; after the end of his life, he may leave and transfer it to whomever he wishes, provided that it does not become a secular lodging-house.

## XVI. On not using inventions at all to dishonor the holy priesthood; but if an emperor or ruler does such things, he is to be rebuked and separated, and, if he does not repent, also anathematized
A matter worthy of great wailing and many tears has reached our ears from many of the faithful: for they say that there were certain laymen under the emperor who recently ruled, men of senatorial rank, who, according to the various imperial dignities, appeared to wrap and arrange the hair of their heads in a coiled fashion [Note: [Col. 0156D] For they twisted it from the nape of the neck up to the crown, so that they appeared to be tonsured in a circle in clerical fashion], and to assume an almost priestly rank through certain garments and priestly vestments; and, as was believed, to appoint bishops, clothed all around with shoulder-vestments—that is, pallia—and wearing every other pontifical stole. They even appointed as their own patriarch the man who was foremost and chief in inventions that provoked laughter, and they insulted and mocked divine matters: at one time acting and suffering, as though against one another and through one another, in the election, advancement, and consecration of bishops; at another, in sharp accusations, condemnations, and depositions.

Such an action has never at any time been heard of even among the nations, so that it presents and displays those whom we have now exposed as worse and more pitiable than the unbelieving nations [Col. 0157A]. Therefore the holy and universal synod has defined and promulgated that those who rely upon wickedness are to be utterly abominated as criminals, and that henceforth no one among the faithful who is called by the Christian name is to attempt to do anything of this kind, or to admit it, or silently conceal any of those who perpetrate such impiety.

If, however, any emperor, or any of the powerful or eminent, should attempt to mock divine matters in this way, or impiously inflict or permit such a great injury against the divine priesthood, let him first be rebuked by the patriarch of that time and by the bishops who are with him; let him be separated and judged unworthy of the divine mysteries. Thereafter, let him undertake certain other labors under strict discipline and such penalties as seem appropriate. And unless he quickly repent, let him also be anathema from this holy and universal synod, as one who has dishonored the mystery of the sincere and immaculate faith.

But if, when certain persons presume to commit such an outrage, the patriarch of Constantinople and his suffragan bishops, having learned what has occurred, neglect to display the requisite zeal against them, let them be deposed and expelled from their own priesthood and honor.

As for those who have in any way assisted, or are going to assist, such an utterly impious action, and who have not first confessed and received an appropriate *epitimion* [Note: [Col. 0157D] A rebuke, or a penalty imposed for offenses], we have defined that they are to be excluded for three years: for one year they are to stand outside the church weeping; for another year they are to stand within the church as far as the catechumens; and in the third year they are to stand together with the faithful, and thus become worthy of the sanctifications of the mysteries.

### XVII. On the authority of patriarchs, and on metropolitan bishops coming to them

The holy and universal First Synod of Nicaea commands that the ancient custom be observed throughout Egypt and the provinces subject to it, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these matters, saying: [Col. 0157C] “Since such a custom also prevails in the city of the Romans.” For this reason, this great and holy synod likewise decrees that the ancient custom be preserved in all respects both in senior and new Rome, and in the see of Antioch and of Jerusalem, so that the prelates of those sees have authority over all the metropolitans who are promoted by them and who receive the stability of episcopal dignity either through the laying on of hands or through the giving of the pallium: namely, to summon them, when necessity requires, to a synodal assembly, and also to restrain and correct them when report has perhaps accused them of certain offenses.

But since there are certain metropolitans who, in order not to appear in accordance with the summons of the apostolic prelate, falsely claim that they are being detained without justification by the rulers of the world, it has been decided that such an excuse is wholly invalid. For when a ruler frequently holds assemblies for his own affairs, it is impious that they should prevent the chief prelates from celebrating synods for ecclesiastical business, or prohibit certain persons from attending their councils, although we have learned that such obstruction and such fabricated prohibition of metropolitans is brought about in various ways through suggestion.

Metropolitans are accustomed to hold synods twice a year, and therefore, as they say, they are altogether unable to assemble at the patriarchal head. But this holy and universal synod, while not prohibiting the councils held by metropolitans, knows that those convened by the patriarchal see are much more reasonable and useful than the councils of metropolitans, and therefore insists that they be held. For the administration of one province is carried out by a metropolitan, whereas the affairs of an entire diocese are often administered by a patriarch. Thus the common good is provided for; and for this reason a particular advantage ought to be postponed for the sake of the general good whenever a summons concerning these matters has been issued by superiors [Col. 0158A].

Although among certain metropolitans an ancient custom and canonical tradition appear to have been set aside through contempt for their superiors, because they do not hasten to the common advancement, the laws of the Church, condemning them severely and removing every excuse, require them to submit to the summonses of their own patriarch, whether those summonses have been issued generally or individually.

We have also rejected from our ears as something detestable what is said by certain ignorant persons: that a synod cannot be held without the presence of the ruler. For nowhere have the sacred canons prescribed that secular rulers should assemble in councils, but only bishops. Accordingly, we do not find that secular rulers have attended synods except at universal councils. For it is not lawful for secular rulers to become spectators of matters that sometimes occur among the priests of God.

Therefore, whoever among the metropolitans has despised his own patriarch and has not obeyed his summons—whether it has been addressed to one person alone, to several, or to all—unless prevented by the most serious illness or by an invasion of pagans, and has not hastened to come to his own patriarch within two full months after learning of the summons, or has attempted in any way to hide himself or to deny knowledge of the message sent by him, is to be separated. But if within one year he has displayed the same obstinacy and disobedience, let him be deposed in every respect, let him fall from all priestly activity, and let him be expelled from the dignity and honor proper to metropolitans.

Whoever does not obey this definition is also to be anathema.

### XVIII. That the possessions and privileges of churches must not be violated or taken away

It has pleased this holy and great synod that the possessions or privileges belonging to the churches of God by long custom—whether granted in writing or without writing by emperors of blessed memory or by other worshipers of God, and possessed by them for thirty years—must in no way be removed from the authority of their prelate by any secular person through power, or taken away by any device. Rather, everything that is known to have been possessed by the churches within the period of thirty years is to remain in the authority and use of the prelate of the church [Col. 0158C].

Therefore, whoever among secular persons acts against this present definition is to be judged a sacrilegious person; and until he has corrected himself and restored and preserved for the church its own privileges or possessions, let him be anathema.

### XIX. That archbishops or metropolitans must not travel to other churches under the pretext of visitation and afflict or burden their subject bishops through avarice

The great Apostle Paul condemns avarice as a second idolatry, wishing all who are reckoned by the Christian name to abstain from every shameful profit. Much more, then, is it unlawful for those who exercise the priesthood to burden their fellow bishops and suffragans [Col. 0158D] in any way.

For this reason, this holy and universal synod has decreed that no archbishop or metropolitan may leave his own church and approach other churches under the pretext of visitation, abuse his own authority over those beneath him, or consume the revenues found among them, which are intended for ecclesiastical administration and the support of the poor, thereby burdening the consciences of our brothers and fellow ministers in an avaricious manner.

Hospitality is excepted when it may perhaps be required by a necessary journey. But even then, let him graciously accept nothing except what is presently found to have been prepared from available resources, with reverence and fear of God, and let him resume his intended journey as quickly as possible, requesting and demanding absolutely nothing belonging to that church or to its suffragan bishop [Col. 0159A].

For if the sacred canons decree that each bishop must use the possessions of his own church with great frugality, and must in no way spend or consume ecclesiastical revenues importunately and without reason for his own advantage, with what impiety, do you suppose, will he be judged worthy who does not fear to burden or invade churches entrusted to other bishops, and thereby incur the crime of sacrilege?

Therefore, whoever after this definition of ours attempts to do such a thing shall undergo punishment from the patriarch who is in office at the time, according to the measure of his injustice and avarice, and shall be deposed and excluded as a sacrilegious person, and otherwise, having become an idolater, according to the great Apostle.

### XX. That no bishop should receive into his possession places granted to him or through him without the judgment of the one known to preside over that city or region

This holy synod has now also learned that in certain places certain persons, relying on their own authority and without the consent of those to whom such administrations have been entrusted, boldly and tyrannically expel those who have received something by *emphyteusis* from the places they possessed, on the pretext that the agreement concerning the payment of the rent has been broken.

This must not be done in any way unless the person who entered into the *emphyteusis* has first received a formal warning through certain suitable and faithful men: namely, that if he does not pay the assigned census-tax for three years, he is to be expelled from the places he holds.

For after the withholding of the census-tax for three years, it is necessary to approach the rulers of that city or region, accuse before them the person who obtained the *emphyteusis*, and produce evidence of his contempt. Then, by the sentence and judgment of those mentioned above, the church may take possession again.

But no one is to carry out the removal of the aforesaid places by himself or through himself. Such conduct is suspect and indeed constitutes an indication of much shameful profit and avarice [Col. 0159C].
