Therefore, if any bishop or metropolitan, contrary to this definition of ours, takes away any place from anyone, thinking that he is defending his own church, let him be excluded by his own patriarch for a certain period, first restoring what he has taken away or stolen through his authority.

But if anyone persists in contentiousness and does not obey what has seemed good to the holy and universal synod, let him be deposed in every respect.

### XXI. That no one may dishonor the Roman pope or any other patriarch

Believing that the Lord’s saying, which Christ spoke to his holy apostles and disciples—“Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10)—was spoken also concerning all those who, after them and in succession to them, became the chief pontiffs and leaders of the shepherds in the Catholic Church, we define that no worldly potentate may dishonor any of those who preside over patriarchal sees, or attempt to remove them from their own thrones, but must judge them worthy of every reverence and honor.

This applies especially to the most holy pope of senior Rome; thereafter to the patriarch of Constantinople; then to those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem.

Nor may anyone compose and circulate writings against the most holy pope of senior Rome, or weave words together under the pretext of certain alleged crimes—something which Photius recently did, and Dioscorus long before him.

Whoever uses such boasting and audacity as to raise, in writing or without writing, any insults against the see of Peter, prince of the apostles, after the manner of Photius or Dioscorus, shall receive the same and equal condemnation that they received.

But if anyone, enjoying or possessing any secular power, attempts to expel the aforesaid pope of the apostolic chair, or any other patriarch [Col. 0160A], let him be anathema.

Moreover, if a universal synod has been convened and any doubt or controversy concerning the holy Roman Church has arisen, the matter must be respectfully and with due reverence investigated, so that a resolution may be received, or that progress may be made or effected; but no one may boldly pronounce a judgment against the chief pontiffs of senior Rome.

### XXII. On the election and decree concerning the chief priests

In agreement with the earlier councils, this holy and universal synod defines and establishes that the promotions and consecrations of bishops are to be carried out by the election and decree of the college of bishops. It also rightly promulgates that no lay ruler or powerful layman may insert himself into the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and inappropriate confusion or contention arise from this—especially since it is not fitting that any powerful person or other layman should have authority in such matters, but rather that he should remain silent and attend to his own affairs until the election of the future pontiff has been regularly completed by the college of the church [Col. 0160B].

If, however, a layman is invited by the Church to take part in the contest and cooperation, it is permissible for him, with reverence and if he wishes, to obey those who invite him. In this way he may regularly advance a worthy shepherd for the salvation of his Church.

But whoever among secular rulers or powerful persons, or any layman of another rank, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and consents to what the Church has shown that it wishes concerning the election and ordination of its own prelate.

### XXIII. That no bishop should lease the possessions of other churches, nor should any cleric celebrate the sacred mysteries in another church

This too has now reached our ears: that certain bishops, when asked by certain persons, irrationally grant possessions belonging to other churches, and thereby, as far as they can, usurp, at their own discretion, possessions belonging to other bishops.

By this they plainly incur the prophetic curse, which says: “Woe to you who join house to house and field to field, in order to take something away from your neighbor” (Isa. 5); and it makes them guilty of the crime of sacrilege.

For this reason it has pleased this great and universal synod that none of our brothers and fellow bishops, or anyone else, should ask to make such a most wicked lease for himself, or, when asked by another, grant any possession belonging to another or an external church. Nor should he appoint priests or any other cleric in churches that are not subject to him, against the will of the bishop to whom that church has been entrusted.

Nor may any priest or deacon devoted to sacred offices, entering churches of his own accord and by himself, perform anything sacred in churches in which he did not receive his portion from the beginning. For this is unlawful and wholly foreign to canonical commands.

Therefore, whoever after this definition of ours is found doing any of the things now forbidden shall be separated for a specified period, the lease-agreement being torn up and dissolved in every respect—whether it was made in writing or without writing and contrary to the canon.

Likewise, that priest or deacon is to be excluded until he withdraws from the foreign church. But if he also despises his exclusion, let him be deposed in every respect and cast down from all sacred honor.

### XXIV. That metropolitans must not entrust the ecclesiastical ministries of their metropolis to their suffragan bishops

Since divine Scripture says, “Cursed is everyone who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. 48), certain metropolitans, having fallen into extreme negligence and sloth, summon bishops subject to them to themselves by their commands and entrust to them the divine offices, litanies, and all the sacred ministries belonging to themselves in their churches.

Thus they have everything celebrated through those bishops which they ought eagerly to perform themselves, and by this they make those who have deserved episcopal dignity appear in some way as clerics subject to them.

Meanwhile they themselves, contrary to ecclesiastical laws, occupy themselves with secular concerns and administrations, abandoning perseverance in prayers and supplications for their own offenses and the ignorance of the people. Nothing of this kind is found anywhere among others, since it is entirely contrary to canonical commands.

What is more severe is that they are said to order these ministries to be performed for their stipends in rotation during the various months. This is shown in every respect to be foreign to the apostolic institution.

All these things make such men worthy of great, numerous, and most severe condemnations [Col. 0161B]. For by what they do, such men are shown also to suffer from satanic boasting and pride.

Therefore, if any metropolitan after this definition of the holy and universal synod, abusing himself with the same audacity, pride, and contempt, attempts to perform the ministries due in his own city not personally, with fear, eagerness, and a good conscience, but through his suffragan bishops, let him pay the penalty before his own patriarch, and either be corrected or deposed.

### XXV. That those who received consecration in any rank from the most holy patriarchs Methodius and Ignatius, and who consented to Photius the usurper even after the sentence issued synodically at Constantinople, are to remain permanently deposed

The holy synod also duly defined that the bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons of the great church who received consecration from the most holy patriarchs Methodius and Ignatius [Col. 0161C], but, hardened according to that insolent and most obdurate heart of Pharaoh, have until now not at all joined this holy and universal synod, nor wished to agree with us in the word of truth, but instead have unanimously consented to Photius the usurper, are to remain deposed and entirely deprived of priestly activity.

Just as the most blessed pope Nicholas judged not long before, they are in no way to be received into the catalogue of the priesthood, even if they should wish to turn back from this course—except for the reception of the sanctifications [alternative: mysteries], for which we judge them wholly unworthy except through great mercy.

For they are not worthy to find, through repentance, a place for restoration to their former honor, like that hateful Esau, even though he sought it with tears.

### XXVI. That a deposed cleric, or one who has suffered injury from his bishop, has the power to appeal to the greater rulers of the Catholic Church, that is, to the chief pontiffs

[Col. 0161D]

It has also pleased the holy synod that if any priest or deacon has been deposed by his own bishop because of some crime, or if he says that he has suffered any injustice and has not accepted the judgment of his own bishop, claiming that the bishop regards him with suspicion, whether because of enmity held against him or because of favor he wished to show to certain others, and for that reason has done such a thing against him, he shall have the power to go to the metropolitan of that province and report the unjust deposition or other injury that he believes he has suffered.

That metropolitan is to receive such a person willingly, summon the bishop who deposed him or otherwise injured the cleric, and conduct an examination of the case before himself together with other bishops, either confirming the cleric’s deposition without any suspicion or overturning it through a general [variant: “amphora”] synod and the judgment of many bishops [Col. 0162A].

Likewise, we decree that bishops who say they have suffered such things at the hands of their metropolitans may go to the patriarchal head, so that they may receive from the patriarch and the metropolitans subject to him a just and impartial judgment concerning the matter in dispute.

Moreover, no metropolitan or bishop may in any way be judged by neighboring metropolitans or bishops of his province, even if he is said to have committed certain crimes; rather, he is to be judged only by his own patriarch. We decree that the patriarch’s sentence will be reasonable and his judgment just and free from suspicion, because the more honorable persons are gathered before him; and thus whatever has been judged by him is to be entirely valid and firm.

But if anyone does not accept what has been issued by us, let him remain excommunicated.

### XXVII. That one must not wear the pallium except at the defined times and places, and that those who have come from the monastic order must not be deprived of the habit and vesture of monastic life

According to the forms handed down in the individual provinces, regions, and cities, we decree that in ecclesiastical promotions and consecrations those things that are indications and signs of the order belonging to each person are to be retained.

Thus bishops who have been granted the use of the pallium are to put it on at the established times and in the same times and places, and must not abuse such a great and distinctive garment because of pride, empty glory, human approval, or self-love—wearing it foolishly at every celebration of the divine sacrifice and at every other ecclesiastical mystery.

But those who have reverently followed the monastic life and have deserved episcopal honor are to preserve the habit and vesture of monastic clothing, as well as that blessed life. No one at all is to have the power to remove the aforesaid habit because of pride or an arrogant will, lest by this he be found to transgress his own agreements.

For just as the continual wearing of the pallium shows a bishop to be lofty and devoted to his own glory, so the removal and stripping away of the monastic habit likewise subjects to the same crimes the person who is caught doing this [Col. 0162C].

Therefore, if any bishop puts on the pallium outside the times defined for him in writing, or removes the habit of monastic clothing, let him either be corrected or be deposed by his own patriarch.

After the reading of the canons, Bahanes, the most magnificent patrician and *praepositus*, again stood in the midst and, by the command of the Christ-loving emperors, said to the most holy guardians of this place:

“After the reading of the divine and sacred canons, what does your holiness further deliberate should be done?”

The most holy representatives of senior Rome and of the eastern sees said:

“Let the written conclusion follow, in which everything enacted in this holy synod is contained in summary form, and let it be read aloud before everyone, if this is pleasing to the holy synod.”

The holy synod said:

“It is pleasing, for it is just and good.”

After this, Metrophanes, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Smyrna, went up to the upper part of the synod and read the conclusion. Likewise, Cyprian, the most God-beloved metropolitan of Claudiopolis, read the same conclusion aloud to everyone in the lower part of the synod.

## Conclusion of the holy and universal Eighth Synod, held at Constantinople

The holy, great, and universal synod, which was convened by the divine will, grace, and sanction of our Christ-loving and God-confirmed emperors Basil and Constantine in this royal city preserved by God, in the most renowned church of Holy Sophia of great name, defined the matters set out below:

The consubstantial Word of almighty God and Father, who established heaven like a vault, constructed the boundaries of the earth and the order of all other things, brought them into existence from nothing, governs, contains, and saves them—he who says through the voice of the prophet Isaiah: “Look upon heaven, for heaven has been solidified like smoke; but the earth will grow old like a garment, and those who dwell in it will die like this; but my salvation shall be forever, and my righteousness shall not fail” (Isa. 51)—who for our sake became what we are, planted heavenly righteousness upon earth, and said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Luke 21)—who said to all who believed in him: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8).

This Lord and our God, alone of infinite power, formerly and long ago uprooted and destroyed many other men enslaved to falsehood and enemies of truth, who, according to the Gospel’s meaning, sowed evil weeds in his field—that is, in the Church—and tried to cover the pure wheat of divine righteousness (Matt. 13). Like a most wise and almighty farmer, he uprooted and destroyed them and justly reduced them to what absolutely does not exist. Yet he always prepared his salvation for admonition, established his righteousness, and made it more manifest.

Nevertheless, in the present circumstances also, when the sower of weeds, through certain most wicked and impious men, was attempting to render the ecclesiastical field useless, he displayed this field as deserving equal care by the same providence, rescued it from the filth of iniquity, and restored it to its former purity. For he aroused our most pious and tranquil emperor, a lover of divine righteousness and an enemy of injustice, shown to be an incorrupt and knowledgeable disciple who remains in his commandments and preserves the truth, to strengthen injustice.

Through heavenly assistance and the grace of the ecclesiastical tabernacle, he summoned architects from the ends of the earth to this royal city, which God was to build, and convened a universal synod. Guarding the defenses of the Gospel sanctions, the Mosaic and prophetic laws, the apostolic and paternal commandments, and likewise the synodal decrees, this synod renewed the boundaries of piety and proclaimed truth and righteousness in the courts of the Church.

Accordingly, all of us consecrated persons who have assembled here, strengthening the sincere and undefiled faith of Christians and the doctrine of orthodox religion, believe in one God in three consubstantial, divine, and principal persons. That is, just as in three suns [Note: [Col. 0163D] I said “suns,” because I found it so in the Greek, for reasons of necessity.] that are mutually indistinguishable, or in as many radiances, we behold one nature of light: one and singular God according to the account of substance, but three—or three persons—when we proclaim him according to the account of persons.

We confess that he did not receive this existence either from himself, as though he had been made, or in any way from another; rather, he is without beginning, eternal, and always the only one who exists, remaining the same and unchanging, admitting no alteration or transformation, and existing as the maker and creator of all intelligible and sensible things.

Thus also the holy and great Council of Nicaea, expounding the symbol of faith, says: “Light from Light,” plainly proclaiming the true God the Son from the true God the Father, and the rest, as the Catholic Church has received it. Accepting this teaching with one mind, we anathematize the madman and enemy of truth Arius, and all who, with him or after him, concerning the divine and blessed Trinity, suppose with corrupted understanding τὸ ἑτεροούσιον—that is, difference of substance—and dissimilarity.

Likewise, accepting the second holy and universal synod, we anathematize Macedonius, who fought against the Spirit—that is, the Spirit’s opponent—or rather fought against God—that is, God’s opponent. We do not accept, according to the aforesaid heresiarchs, a difference of substance between the persons of the Father, the Son, and the divine and principal Spirit; nor, according to the utterly insane Sabellius, do we confuse the persons within one and the same substance.

Moreover, we confess that the one Word of God was incarnate and became what we are for our sake. For it was not an angel or an envoy, but the Lord himself who came and saved us, and became Emmanuel with us. This one was the true God, the God of Israel, and the Savior of all, according to the divine and prophetic testimonies.

Therefore we confess that the most holy and virgin Mary, who gave birth to him, is properly and truly the Mother of God, just as the universal third synod, formerly assembled at Ephesus, proclaimed. With that synod we also anathematize Nestorius, a worshipper of man, a most boastful man, and one who held a Jewish way of thinking, while teaching one and the same Christ and Lord to be twofold: namely, perfect God and perfect man in one person, with the distinction of each nature, but perpetually preserving the properties of both unaltered and unmixed, just as the holy universal fourth synod also defined.

Accepting that council together with the three already numbered, as the quaternity of the holy Gospels, we anathematize the delirious Eutyches and the senseless Dioscorus. Moreover, proclaiming two natures in the one Christ according to the clearer exposition of the fifth holy and universal synod, we anathematize Severus, Peter, and Zoaras the Syrian; also Origen, who held vain opinions; and Theodore of Mopsuestia; likewise Didymus and Evagrius, who, through the same and differing opinions, were likewise ensnared in the same abyss of perdition.

Accepting the holy and universal sixth synod, which agreed with the aforesaid councils and held the same doctrine, we accept its wise affirmation that, in the two natures of the one Christ, there are consequently two operations and an equal number of wills.

We anathematize Theodore, bishop of Pharan, and Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, impious leaders of the Church of Constantinople, and with them Honorius of Rome, together with Cyrus of Alexandria, as well as Macarius of Antioch and his disciple Stephen. Following the wicked doctrines of the impious heresiarchs Apollinarius, Eutyches, and Severus, they proclaimed, with corrupted understanding and truly without reason, that God's flesh, animated by a rational and intellectual soul, was without operation and without will.

For if one and the same Christ and God existed as perfect God and perfect man, it is entirely certain that no part of the natures belonging to him exists without will or without operation. Rather, according to both substances, by willing and acting he accomplished the great mystery of the dispensation, just as the entire chorus of those who speak of God, from the apostles down to us, knowing this with complete certainty, also raised up an image depicting his human form. They assigned to each part of the one Christ distinct natural properties, through which, undoubtedly, the manifestations and concepts of his divine and human nature are believed to remain unmixed.

Thus also, as we know, the seventh holy and universal synod, celebrated for the second time at Nicaea, defined orthodox doctrine. It confessed one and the same Christ and Lord as invisible and visible, incomprehensible and comprehensible, uncircumscribed and circumscribed, impassible and passible, and both uninscribable [Note: [Col. 0163D] “Uninscribable.” Everything that is uncircumscribed is also uninscribable; for God, being uncircumscribed, is not written. But not everything uninscribable is also uncircumscribed: for the human soul, although uninscribable, is not uncircumscribed. Conversely, everything scriptible is also circumscribed; for whatever is written by means of colors has already been circumscribed by its location. Therefore “circumscribed” does not mean the same as “scriptible,” as must be understood concerning the human soul and similar things. EDIT. ROM.] and scriptible.

In agreement with that synod, this holy and universal synod, with a loud voice, anathematizes Anastasius, Constantine, and Nicetas, who held the irrational episcopate of the name “Stercoralis” [Note: [Col. 0166D] “Stercoralis.” It calls the episcopate of those whom it has named “Stercoralis” because, when they were bishops of Constantinople during the reign of the emperor Constantine, who was called Caballinus, they shamefully lent their support to his heresy. EDIT. ROM.]; or, what is more appropriate to say, the corruption itself. It also anathematizes Theodosius of Ephesus, Sisinnius Pastilas, Basil Tricacabos, and, indeed, Theodore, Antony, and John, former bishops of New Rome, the royal city of Christians—indeed, calumniators of Christ. They proclaimed by deeds and words that the one whom the catalogue of prophets declared had not been able to destroy the statues of idols.

It also anathematizes Theodore, who was called Crithinus, whom this holy and great synod summoned and rebuked, imposing an anathema upon him with a loud voice in his hearing [Col. 0165D].

In the same way we anathematize all their allies and supporters, who said that the statement concerning the divine incarnation had come to exist through phantasy and in appearance only—namely, through the abolition of the image of Christ our Savior, and at the same time of the form accompanying it, his most truly existing and God-bearing flesh.

For everything that is not at all comprehended by an image is understood in two ways: either as existing like us, or as indeed existing but not at all comprehensible, being invisible and hidden. Therefore, if anyone should assert any of these things concerning Christ, the God and Savior of us all, he will plainly be shown to be impious. For the one claim shows that Emmanuel did not truly become man; the other shows that he indeed became man but lacked human properties and laid aside the flesh he had assumed, returning in every respect to divine incomprehensibility. This is alien to all divinely inspired Scriptures, which also affirm that he will come again as judge of all, and that he will likewise be seen just as he was seen by his disciples and apostles when he was taken up into heaven.

That opinion is full of Manichaean error and impiety which senselessly says that the divine utterance of David was pronounced concerning him, namely: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18). This impiety supposes that the passage signifies the rejection and laying aside of the Lord’s divine body.

But the Word of truth, speaking confidently about the true-named Manes [Note: [Col. 0166D] “Manes,” the madness from which the Manichaeans were named; in Greek he is rightly called *pheronymus*, because he bore with himself the name of madness. For *manes* means “madman.”], and about each of those who share his opinions and are the authors of the Iconoclast heresy, as well as about all the other heresiarchs and impious men, says: “They did not know or understand; they walked in darkness. For you who abandon straight paths and walk in the ways of darkness; you who rejoice in evil and exult in wicked overthrow; whose paths are crooked and whose steps are bent, so that they may go far from the straight way and estrange others from a just judgment.”

And again: “They sowed things corrupted by the wind, and destruction received it” (Hos. 8). And again: “He who relies on lies will feed on winds” (Prov. 10).

That same man will pursue flying birds; for he abandons the ways of his vineyard and wanders through the furrows of his field. He walks through a waterless desert and a land stretched out in thirst, and gathers barrenness in his hands.

Therefore, consigning all these men to anathema, and accepting the seven holy and universal synods already enumerated, this eighth universal synod was convened through the grace of almighty Christ our God and through the piety and zeal of our most tranquil and divinely strengthened emperor, to cut off and destroy the offshoots of injustice that had arisen through them, together with their wicked efforts and advances, and to establish peaceful order in the Church and stability throughout the world.

For it is not only deprivation of true doctrines that destroys those who hold evil opinions and causes the Church to be thrown into turmoil and disorder. Transgressions of the divine commandments likewise bring about the same destruction among the negligent, and fill the world that bears the name of Christ with heat and waves.

This also occurred in the present circumstances through the folly, cunning, and wicked activity of the wretched Photius. He entered the sheepfold not through the door but through the window, like a thief and robber, a marauder of souls, as the Lord’s utterance describes him. At every time and with every exertion he attempted to steal, slaughter, and destroy Christ’s rational sheep.

He carried out many persecutions, imprisonments, and confiscations of property, as well as extremely long exiles. In addition, he did not cease contriving accusations, denunciations, false statements, and fabricated writings against all zealous defenders of piety and champions of truth. In particular, he plotted to expel the most just, legitimate, and canonical high priest of the Church of Constantinople, namely the most holy patriarch Ignatius, like another Severus or Dioscorus.

Like an adulterous robber, he invaded Ignatius’s seat and overwhelmed him with a thousand deposition sentences and just as many anathemas, while in many ways and by many means stirring up continual disturbance and turmoil in all the churches of Christ and our Savior.

Nevertheless, the salt of the earth was not made foolish; the eye of the Church was not utterly darkened; nor was the lamp of piety extinguished by the spirits of wickedness. The fire of divine love did not lose its consuming and burning power through sinful and trivial material. Nor was the word of the Lord, sharper than a two-edged sword and discerner of thoughts, found ineffective. Nor did the foundation upon the solid rock collapse, sunk by the assaults or floods of rivers and rains.

Rather, the cornerstone and precious stone set in Sion—that is, in the Church—upon which the foundation of the apostles and prophets was laid for the building of the Church, brought forth in our generation many other rolling stones upon the earth, as the prophet says [Note: [Col. 0167D] The prophet intended here is Zechariah, who mystically says, among other things, according to the old edition: “For the holy stones are rolled upon his land.”], even from every order of the ecclesiastical catalogue in the reigning city, New Rome. These stones shattered and crushed the machinations of those who wished and attempted to devastate truth and divine righteousness.

Rather, and above all, as though preserving as far as possible the imaginal likeness of that cornerstone, he sent Nicholas, the most blessed and true-named pope [Note: [Col. 0167D] “True-named.” A person is called *pheronymus* when he bears a true and fitting name. Therefore Nicholas, who appeared to bear a true and suitable name for his action, is aptly called *pheronymus*. For Nicholas is interpreted as “conquering peoples”; indeed, he rightly conquered not those who held false opinions but those who acted unjustly. EDIT. ROM.], from an elevated and conspicuous place against Photius’s defenses.

Nicholas struck Photius’s princely and powerful supporters with the darts of his letters and words. In a reversal of the ancient history, he pierced Photius—like another Midianite fornicating with the Israelite Church—with the sword of truth, like a second zealous Phinehas. Although Photius consented to receive the remedies of medicinal discipline in order to obtain healing and a scar for the wound of adultery, Nicholas nevertheless destroyed him utterly.

Together with the one joined to him in a kind of priestly dignity, he sent him to death by anathema, like another Peter sending Ananias and Sapphira, who had stolen what belonged to God, to their death (Acts 5).

Relying upon Nicholas’s definitions and decrees, our most pious and Christ-loving emperor, whom the heavenly Emperor and Lord of majesty raised up for the salvation of the world, assigned Photius a fitting place, and restored the most holy patriarch Ignatius to his own throne, for the perfect discernment and distinction of what is acknowledged to be good and expedient.

He also gathered representatives from all the patriarchal thrones, together with the entire catalogue of bishops living under his authority, for this very purpose. They assembled and celebrated this great and universal synod. After much scrutiny, examination, and discussion, we cut out, with the sword of the Spirit, the roots of scandals and weeds together with their shoots, carefully and appropriately, establishing the innocent and most holy patriarch Ignatius firmly upon the hinge of his own throne, and condemning Photius, the invader and adulterer, together with all his followers and supporters of wickedness.

For the God of all says somewhere through the prophet’s voice: “Because of the wickedness of their inventions I will drive them out of my house, and I will no longer continue to love them. Ephraim has mourned; his roots have dried up; he will bear fruit no longer” (Hos. 9).

And again: “Canaan has in his hand an unjust balance; he loved to oppress, and Ephraim said: ‘Nevertheless I have become rich; I have found refreshment for myself.’ All his labors will not be found, because of the injustices that he committed” (Hos. 12).

And again: “The house of Jacob shall inherit those who recover their inheritance, and the house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph a flame; but the house of Esau shall be stubble. They shall burn against them and consume them, and there shall be no one to carry fire to the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken” (Obad. 1:18).

For Photius was truly wretched, like a man who did not set God as his helper but trusted in the multitude of his intrigues and prevailed in the vanity of his wickedness, following that former Ephraim and departing from the divine ordinances.

The prophetic utterance mocks and derides him, saying: “Ephraim has become a cake not turned, and strangers have devoured his strength. He himself did not know; gray hairs also appeared upon him, and he did not know. Israel’s insolence shall be humbled to his face, and in all these things he did not return to the Lord his God.

“Ephraim, a dove, called upon Egypt from the table and went to the Assyrians. When they depart, I will spread my net over them like birds of heaven; I will draw them down and chastise them according to the report of their affliction” (Hos. 7).

For he was lifted up into the utmost arrogance against the most blessed pope Nicholas of senior Rome and vomited forth the poison of his wickedness. He gathered false representatives from what were supposedly three Eastern sees, established what was presented as a synodal council, composed the names of accusers and witnesses, and fashioned persons and words that seemed suitable for each of them as they appeared in the synodal judgment.

As though producing monuments of these things, he fabricated, wrote, and composed false books. He then dared to anathematize the aforementioned most blessed pope Nicholas and all who communicated with him, thereby including under the same anathema all the bishops and priests beneath the heavens—that is, the other patriarchal sees and the entire sacred catalogue living under them.

For they were all most certainly communicants of the eminent pontiff. Concerning him and those who were with him, the prophetic utterance rebukes and denounces them, saying: “They multiplied in order to act impiously; they read the laws outside and invoked confession” (Isa. 59).

And again: “They meditated unjust words in their hearts, they turned judgment backward, and righteousness withdrew far from them, because truth was consumed in their ways. They could not pass along straight paths, and truth was taken away; he turned his mind aside so as not to understand. Whoever turns away from evil is attacked. The Lord saw it, and it displeased him, because there was no judgment” (ibid.).

And again: “Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Judah, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments” (Amos 2).

Therefore this man, who pursued such conduct and disturbed and shook the entire holy Catholic and apostolic Church by so many and such efforts and acts of presumption, and who in no way wished to turn back or repent, nor consented to submit to the decree and judgment of the holy patriarchal sees, was condemned by this holy and universal synod, just as the most blessed pope Nicholas had anathematized him long before, and afterward his successor, the most holy pope Adrian.

The synod pronounced an ever stronger anathema against him, addressing him through the voice of the prophet Isaiah in the name of all and of God: “How will a garment stained with blood be clean?” (Isa. 9). So neither will you be clean, because you have adulterated the Church of Christ and scandalized and destroyed the Lord’s people in many places and in many ways.

But those who are not of this disposition and instead adhere to him and favor him, if they are bishops or clerics, we decree shall be deposed forever. Monks and laymen, however, we anathematize until they turn away from their seduction and wickedness.

**The most pious and most Christ-loving emperor Basil said to the holy synod:**

“Let the holy and universal synod now declare whether this present definition has been produced with all the most holy bishops agreeing and consenting. For divine matters must be proclaimed and confirmed in ecclesiastical assemblies with the agreement and harmony of all.”

The holy synod cried out:

“We all hold this opinion! We all proclaim this! All of us, singing together and agreeing, readily subscribe! This is the judgment of truth! This is the decree of righteousness! This is the exposition of the canons! This is the defense of ecclesiastical order! God, the champion of zeal, has convened this synod! The Lord of retribution himself summoned the most holy representatives of senior Rome and the other three patriarchal sees! God directed our most pious emperor, the lord whom he governs from above!

“We preserve these synodal bonds and apostolic decrees without any annulment! No longer will there be room for the tyranny of those who inflict injury upon the Church! No longer, through fear of worldly powers, shall we be driven violently and compulsorily into unlawful things! This holy and universal synod will henceforth preserve the Church without scandal through the grace of our almighty God Jesus Christ!

“Many years to the emperors Basil, Constantine, and Leo; many years! Many years to Basil, the orthodox emperor! Lord, preserve the lover of truth! Lord, fortify the renewer and guardian of divine righteousness!

“Eternal memory to Basil, the new Constantine! Eternal memory to the new Theodore! Eternal memory to the new Marcian! Eternal memory to the new Justinian!

“Many years to Eudoxia, the most pious Augusta! Eternal memory to Eudoxia, the new Judith! Eternal memory to the new Helena! Eternal memory to the new Pulcheria!

“May God preserve your empire! Through you the universal Church has obtained peace! God, the Prince of peace, grant peace to your empire! May the heavenly King preserve the earthly rulers!

“Anathema to Photius, the invader and adulterer of the Church of Constantinople! Anathema to Gregory of Syracuse and Eulampius of Apamea, deposed men, apostates from and enemies of the truth! They rejected knowledge of the divine ordinances; the Lord rejected them!

“Eternal memory to Adrian, the most blessed Roman pope and founder of the holy and universal seventh synod, celebrated for the second time at Nicaea! Eternal memory to Germanus, Tarasius, Nicephorus, and Methodius, the venerable patriarchs! Eternal memory to Nicholas, the most blessed pope of senior Rome! Eternal memory to the champion of truth!

“Many years to Adrian, the most blessed Roman pope! Many years to Ignatius, the most holy patriarch of Constantinople! Many years to Theodosius, the most holy patriarch of Jerusalem! Many years to Michael, the most holy patriarch of Alexandria! Many years to the most holy representatives of senior Rome and the other patriarchal sees!

“Eternal memory to the holy, great, and universal eighth synod! Anathema to Photius, Gregory, and Eulampius, the threefold cord of wickedness! The life-giving Trinity has deposed the three arrogant men. Anathema to all their allies and followers!

“Many years to the emperors Basil, Constantine, and Leo! Many years to the great emperors and dictators! Many years to Eudoxia, the most pious Augusta! Many years to the orthodox emperors! May God preserve their empire!

“Whoever attempts to resist those tyrants, or, upon discovering those who resist and devise a wicked plot against them, fails to disclose it, let him be anathema from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; from the Church of the firstborn, who are written in heaven; and from the eight holy and universal councils.”

[Col. 0171B]

**The most pious emperor Basil said to the holy and universal synod:**

“Although your holiness has plainly labored, both through the distance of the place and the delay of time, in fortifying our city, which has been preserved by God, Christ our God will repay you with great gifts and riches in worthy return, and through our most tranquil empire, which is to be fortified by God, will grant you whatever you may ask of him for the benefit of your churches and the consolation of your reverence. Thus may you continue always to offer prayers and supplications to the Lord God for the universal condition, continual peace, and salvation of our most tranquil and gentle empire.”

After the reading of the definition, the most pious and Christ-loving emperor Basil said to the holy synod:

“You have certainly heard what has been read. What, then, does your reverence think? Has this definition been properly set forth? Has the exposition of the canons pleased you? Or is there anything in your minds that draws you toward an uncertain opinion? Our empire has delivered a true address to this holy synod; and if you see that it is good, let it be read.”

The holy and universal synod said:

“Let those things that pertain to the benefit of the Church of God be read.”

And Leo, the most renowned imperial *protospatharius* and *a secretis*, ascending, read:

**The most pious and Christ-loving emperor Basil said:**
Your divinely gathered holiness [Col. 0171D] has indeed endured much hardship and labor, as each of you came together from various places to our most fortunate city for the sake of ecclesiastical ordering and establishment. For this reason also you endured a lengthy stay there; many of you disregarded old age, thought little of bodily infirmity, and endured deprivation of the things appropriate to rest [al.: “having become strong in the things that,” etc.]; and you magnanimously bore prolonged separation from your spiritual children.

But behold: you see how sweet the end of your pains and labors is, and how greatly profitable to the Church of God. For the common gathering and the agreement in the Holy Spirit of this great and universal synod have removed every scandal and stumbling block [Col. 0172A] from the midst of the Church, restrained the storms that had long afflicted her, and brought her into clear tranquility. We therefore give thanks to the Lord, venerable Fathers, for all the good things granted to us by God; and we accept your zeal, which is according to God. We pray that the munificence of the great God and King of all may repay you with an abundant reward, recompensing your pains and labors. For these things our tranquility will hasten to refresh and encourage you, and to fulfill every desire of yours.

But we have deemed it right to confess openly before everyone, for the common defense of us all and for the enduring tranquility of the holy Church of God, on account of those who envy the common happiness and are wounded by the serpent’s arrow [Col. 0172B] concerning ecclesiastical order, while they rejoice in its agitation and tumult and consider it a delight if they see it tossed about in a storm. To such persons, therefore, we say plainly today: Whoever has anything to say against this holy and universal synod, or against its canons or its definition, let him stand in the midst and state what he thinks, whether he be a bishop, or someone from the ecclesiastical clergy, or a layman, or one devoted to civil offices. Although, according to the canon, no one but bishops and priests is permitted to say anything at all concerning ecclesiastical matters—for this is their work—nevertheless, wishing all the more to close every unrighteous mouth, we grant permission to everyone, so that whoever has in mind anything doubtful concerning [Col. 0172C] what has been decreed by this holy synod may bring it forward publicly and receive the salutary remedy of satisfaction.

We have fought no small battle and yielded to no labor, as you yourselves know with us, in assembling those who came from the Roman and Eastern patriarchal sees—men whom many before us attempted to bring together but were in no way able to do so. The most God-loving high priests also endured no small hardship and distress, traveling from afar to the deliberations of this holy synod. Therefore, whoever has anything to say, let him say it while these proceedings are being celebrated. For once the holy and universal synod has been dissolved, whoever appears contradicting the Church of God or refusing communion with her—whether he be a bishop, simply a priest, or endowed with some dignity [Col. 0172D] or otherwise conducting himself—will receive no pardon from our empire. He will instead be justly condemned and expelled from our city as a corrupter and pestilential person, a rotten and useless member, and one violating the common body of the Church.

But you, lovers of virtue and most beloved of God, most exalted priests, adorned with the episcopal gift, do not be slow to admonish each one his own flock and lead it to salvation. Show them how great an evil it is, while the Church of God remains in tranquility, to leap away from her, to rage against those who preside over their souls, and to abstain from the divine mysteries on account of irrational or trivial pretexts. As you confirm the flock entrusted to you with words [Col. 0173A] of instruction on each Lord’s Day, direct it toward the perfection of the divine will. Convert those who are held by the error of any heresy, like good shepherds.

For let your perfection, full of virtue, know that if it becomes known to us that any heresy lurking in the province of one of you has not been uprooted completely through your constant teaching, and that all have not been led by the hand to the orthodox faith [al.: “brought back”], such a bishop will be canonically condemned by his own patriarch. Thus your most sacred flock is to be fed through sacred teachings and admonitions in wholesome pastures.

You yourselves, however, be at peace with one another and preserve unbroken the bond of the Church, in which you labored and agreed, and which you confirmed by word and hand in this present holy and universal synod [Col. 0173B]. Do not, through mutual contention and obstinacy, again cause a rupture in the common body of the Church and thereby find no pardon on the day of the most just recompense. Let your friendship and agreement be the strictest rule for the ordering of the entire fold. Let your subjects look to you, as painters do to their models, and let them regulate themselves according to the example of their leaders and according to your life, character, and conduct.

And you who have been appointed to the clergy of the Church of God, preserve this same constitution and mutual harmony, in no respect turning aside or preaching anything other than what has been sanctioned by the Holy Spirit through this great and universal synod. For you too agreed in all things and saw the truth shining more brightly than the sun; you consented to it and appeared in agreement [Col. 0173C].

As for you laymen—both those who live in dignities and those who simply conduct yourselves as laymen—I have nothing further to say except that in no way are you permitted to raise discussion concerning ecclesiastical matters, nor at all to resist the integrity of the Church or oppose the universal synod. To investigate and inquire into these matters belongs to patriarchs, bishops, and priests, who have received the office of governance, who possess the power to sanctify, to bind, and to loose, and who have obtained the ecclesiastical and heavenly keys. It does not belong to us, who must be fed, sanctified, bound, or released from bonds.

However religious or wise a layman may be, even if he possesses every virtue inwardly, so long as he is a layman he will not cease to be called a sheep. Again, however full of irreverence and impiety a bishop may be, and however stripped of every virtue, so long as he is a bishop and rightly preaches the word of truth, he will not suffer the loss of the mention and dignity of a shepherd. What reason, then, have we, who are placed in the order of sheep, to scrutinize shepherds with subtle arguments, or to seek and desire the things that are above us? We ought to approach them with fear and sincere faith, and to revere them in their presence, since they are ministers of the almighty Lord and possess this form of office; and we ought to require nothing beyond [Col. 0174A] what belongs to our own order.

Now, however, we see so many people inflamed by wickedness into madness that, forgetting their own order and scarcely considering that they are feet, they wish to impose a law upon the eyes—not as nature has arranged things, but as they themselves desire. Each is always exceedingly ready to accuse his superiors, but extremely slow to correct anything in the matters of which they accuse and denounce them.

I admonish and exhort all such persons to turn away cursing and mutual hatred, to cease judging those who judge, to attend to themselves, and to strive to conduct themselves according to the divine will. For the heavenly judgment does not rest; rather, divine fury will drip against those who disagree, and will show all people its just vengeance through deeds [Col. 0174B].

Above all, we pray that holy God may make everyone better and cause everyone to shine according to the will that pleases him—not only that they may remain untouched by divine wrath, but that they may obtain eternal goods through the prayers and intercessions of our most holy Lady, the Mother of God, and of all the saints, and through the prayers and supplications of this holy and universal synod. Amen.

After the reading, Basil, friend of Christ and great emperor, said:

“Let whoever wishes among those seated in this holy and universal synod now say in what respect he hesitates or doubts about any of the things that have just been read.”

The holy synod exclaimed:

“Everything that has been read pleases us! We all agree with these very things! Shall we all willingly subscribe?” [Col. 0174C]

The most holy representatives of the elder Rome said:

“Since, by God’s providence, all the affairs of the Church have come to a favorable conclusion, we ought also to confirm these matters in writing with our own hands, according to synodal procedure. Therefore, we wish the Christ-loving emperors to subscribe first, and then this holy synod in due order.”

Basil, most pious and friend of Christ, the emperor, said:

“Our most tranquil empire, following the secure and most just emperors who preceded us—namely, Constantine the Great, Theodosius, Marcian, and the others—wishes to subscribe after the subscription of all the bishops beloved of God. But since your holiness asks that we be placed first, I shall subscribe after the subscription [Col. 0174D] of all the most holy representatives. For we have been taught by Christ our true God to possess humility that exalts.”

After this, Donatus, most holy bishop of Ostia, subscribed in the five books; then Stephen, bishop of Nepi; then Marinus, most reverend deacon; and the most honorable representatives of the elder Rome. Next came Ignatius, most holy patriarch of Constantinople; then Joseph, most reverend archdeacon and representative of the see of Alexandria; then Thomas, most reverend metropolitan of Tyre and occupying the place of the see of Antioch; and thereafter Elias, God-worshiping monk and presbyter, syncellus, and representative of the see of Jerusalem.

After these, the most pious and Christ-loving emperors Basil and Constantine [Col. 0175A] subscribed, placing with their own hands the figure of the precious cross in the five volumes. The great emperor Basil placed it, and Constantine likewise placed the cross for himself and for his brother Leo. He also subscribed the names of the three emperors with his own hand, while Christophorus, protoasecretis and praepositus of the caniculum, subscribed the remainder of the subscription.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] Among the Greeks, the praepositus of the caniculum is the person who takes care of and guards the caniculum, that is, the inkstand [Col. 0176D] from which the emperor writes the crimson letters on documents.]

Then all the bishops subscribed in due order in the five volumes.

After this, when the magistrates and all the patricians were asked what they thought of the holy and universal synod, or how they would subscribe to it, Theodorus, most magnificent proconsul and master, spoke as follows:

“I anathematize everything done by Photius against our most holy patriarch Ignatius and against the most blessed pope Nicholas; and, accepting this holy and universal synod, I accept those whom it accepts and anathematize those whom it anathematizes. But if I should ever accept those whom the synod rejects, may I be anathema from Christ.” [Col. 0175B]

Likewise Christophorus, most magnificent patrician and praepositus, said:

“I anathematize everything done by Photius against our most holy patriarch Ignatius and against the most holy pope Nicholas; and, accepting this holy and universal synod, I accept those whom it accepts and anathematize those whom it anathematizes. But if I should ever accept anyone whom the synod rejects, may I be anathema from Christ.”

Thereafter each of those named above, in the session of the patricians, delivered his own statement in accordance with these words, speaking with his own mouth in a living voice. Swift scribes recorded what each of them said, and these statements were then read aloud before everyone by Leo, the *a secretis*, in a loud voice, in the presence of the holy and universal synod [Col. 0175C].

After this, Stephen, the God-beloved deacon and notary, stood in the midst and offered the following acclamation:

“Many years to the emperors Basil, Constantine, and Leo! Many years to the great rulers and emperors! Many years to Eudoxia, the most pious Augusta! Many years to the emperors!”

## Subscriptions

I, Donatus, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Ostia, occupying the place of my lord Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, have promulgated, presiding over this holy and universal synod, everything written above, according to the will of that eminent bishop, and have subscribed with my own hand.

I, Stephen, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Nepi, occupying the place of my lord Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, have promulgated, presiding over this holy and universal synod, everything written above, according to the will of that eminent bishop, and have subscribed with my own hand.

[Col. 0176A] I, Marinus, deacon of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, occupying the place of my lord Adrian, supreme pontiff and universal pope, have promulgated, presiding over this holy and universal synod, everything written above, according to the will of that eminent bishop, and have subscribed with my own hand.

Ignatius, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, accepting this holy and universal synod, agreeing with and defining all the things judged and written by it, have subscribed with my own hand.

Joseph, by the mercy of God deacon and acting in the place of Michael, most holy patriarch of Alexandria, accepting this holy and universal synod, [Col. 0176B] agreeing with and defining all the things judged and written by it, have subscribed with my own hand.

I, Thomas, by the mercy of God metropolitan of Tyre and acting in the place of the see of Antioch, accepting this holy and universal synod, agreeing with and defining all the things judged and written by it, have subscribed with my own hand.
