Since Photius had exercised tyranny for a long time and had deposed nearly all those consecrated by his pious predecessors, promoting only his own supporters in their places—and none of these has been received in this synod—these alone were found to survive from the consecrations of the earlier patriarchs [Col. 0184D]. Indeed, all the bishops who existed under the supreme pontiffs Nicholas and Adrian agreed with the judgment of this synod, although this small number may be compared, on account of its righteousness, with that little flock to which the Lord says: “Do not be afraid, little flock,” and so forth.]

## Encyclical Letter of the Holy and Universal Eighth Synod
Rejoice in the Lord, our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob, and proclaim the praises of God more eagerly and fully in the gates of the daughter of Zion (Psalm 80).

It is our duty, dearest brothers, to say to your Reverence with the prophet David, and again to address you with the prophet Nahum:

“For behold, swift are the feet of the one who evangelizes and announces peace. Celebrate your festivals, Judah; fulfill your vows to God, because they will no longer continue, so as to pass into old age. It is finished; it has been taken away. He has ascended, breathing upon your face, removing you from tribulation, because the Lord has turned away the insult against Jacob, just as the insult against Israel” (Nahum 1).

[Col. 0183C]

For what else could be more pleasing, or what more particular cause—or reconciliation—of rejoicing could there be than to see the Lord of vengeance acting freely, rendering to the proud a just and fitting recompense, and the zealous Lord avenging his enemies? For this reason the Psalmist also says:

“The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Psalm 57).

He will rejoice, certainly, not because the multitude opposing the faith perishes and the wicked dies in his sin, but because he sees the rod of sinners broken, lest the righteous also stretch out their hands toward iniquities, looking upon injustice as more tranquil than divine justice, and continually seeing falsehood prevail against truth.

[Col. 0183D]

Therefore let them call to mind that passage, and let the prophet Malachi impress his thoughts upon them, saying:

[Col. 0184A]

“Your words have prevailed against me,” says the Lord. “And you said, ‘What have we spoken against you?’ And you said, ‘He is useless who serves the Lord; and what profit is there in our keeping his commandments and walking mournfully before the Lord of hosts?’ Therefore now we call the arrogant blessed: indeed, those who commit impiety have been built up; they have tempted God and have been saved.

“Then those who feared the Lord spoke, each one to his neighbor. And the Lord heard and paid attention, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the Lord and contemplate his name. ‘And they shall be mine,’ says the Lord of hosts, ‘on the day when I act, as my treasured possession. I will spare them as a man spares his son who serves him. And you shall turn and see the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between the one who serves the Lord and the one who does not serve him’” (Malachi 3).

[Col. 0184B]

Let the whole Church of Christ and our Savior therefore rejoice, and, giving thanks to him, sing hymns of glorification, crying out again with the prophet David:

“The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works” (Psalm 145).

For he who said to his holy disciples and apostles, “And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28), and said to Peter, the foremost summit of the apostles, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16), has often closed, crushed, and destroyed the gates of hell, opened against the Church and attempting to devour it—namely, heretical opinions and wicked endeavors—which arose in past generations in their appointed times.

[Col. 0184C]

Nevertheless, even in the present age, when hell has opened and widened its own mouth against the Church of Christ, Christ our God, her protector, has acted in the same and equal manner. He espoused her, and in many forms and by many means closed the mouths of those who spoke wickedness, and delivered her from their injury and pestilence.

For the one who pretended to possess the outward form of piety but denied its power, and who, by the figure of antiphrasis, was called Photius, devised many and various schemes against her from the time of his youth, agreeing and conspiring with foolish and wicked schismatics, separating many from her by persuasive words and drawing them into the snare of perdition.

[Col. 0184D]

Attempting with all his strength to be called “Rabbi” beyond his years, he bound simpler people—and rather, more foolish people—by certain writings and letters of his own, under the pretext, as it were, of learning the discipline of dialectic. He himself would plainly have been foolish and deprived of all understanding, as divine Scripture clearly affirms:

“The Lord said to man: Behold, piety is wisdom; but to depart from evils is instruction” (Psalm 111).

[Col. 0185A]

And again:

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Psalm 111).

For not only did he himself fail to depart from evils or, while still a layman, refrain—contrary to the canonical decrees—from arrogating to himself the title of teacher and separating himself from the Church of Christ; he also hastened, using every device, to estrange from their righteous vow those who wished to worship God, so that the Lord’s saying might be openly fulfilled in him:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you do not enter the kingdom of God, and you prevent those who are entering” (Luke 11).

Moreover, joining sin to sin, he contrived that the legitimate and canonical pontiff of that Church, the supreme pontiff and most holy shepherd, the patriarch Ignatius, should be expelled from the Church. Like a robber and an adulterer, he entered the latter’s seat and stirred up a great storm against him.

[Col. 0185B]

Against those who resisted him, and against the defenders of truth, he scattered everywhere beneath the heavens still more storms and billows, greater turmoil, and the fiercest disorder. Above all, he stretched out his hand against the great shepherd, and afterward against the lesser shepherds, according to the prophetic utterance, striking, scourging, afflicting, and constraining them in various ways: at one time deposing powerful men from their seats; at another delivering them over to prison and custody; sending them to death through prolonged hunger; sometimes banishing them to the longest and cruelest exiles and driving them to the very extremities of the world; sometimes confining them in muddy, foul-smelling, and dark places, which rightly deserve to be called the shadow of death; taking away their various possessions; burning the huts in the mountains of those devoted to virtue and philosophy; and, to put it plainly, inflicting every affliction and tribulation upon the body of Christ and God, who is the head of us all.

[Col. 0185C]

For, having no reverence of any kind arising from beneficence, nor any regard even for his own reception, he thought that he ought to establish himself irrationally through such schemes and acts of recklessness, although he was without any share in goodness and truly ignorant.

For he who “turns the wise backward and makes their knowledge foolish,” as the prophet says (Isaiah 44), turned him, together with all the plans he had prepared as though for his own advantage, toward confusion, disgrace, overthrow, and ruin. For the more he persuaded himself that the things he imagined concerned his own security, the more the all-seeing Eye turned them toward the opposite judgment, showing him day by day like a terebinth stripped of its leaves and like a garden utterly without water.

[Col. 0185D]

But since he often sent letters and envoys to the most blessed Pope Nicholas, the elder of Rome, choosing and proposing him as his judge, and speaking without hindrance, as he himself wished, all that concerned his own justification and the condemnation of the most holy patriarch, as often as he sent, so often he was rejected and condemned by him, and was expressly ordered to relinquish the throne of Constantinople as an outsider—especially while the legitimate ecclesiastical man was still alive.

[Col. 0186A]

In the end, because he did not obey, he received an anathema from Christ and the apostles. Then, raging still more and becoming far removed from his own senses and from every rational mind, he sharpened his tongue even against that same most blessed pope.

Just as fables invent and fashion hippocentaurs and tragelaphs, so he too, gathering from the streets certain dung-workers and swineherds, and [possibly: from the neighborhoods] hiring men and calling them vicars of the other three sees, dared to imagine a synodal judgment composed of accusers, accused persons, witnesses, emperors, magnates, and metropolitans, pretending and fabricating them as though they were suspect.

[Col. 0186B]

He shamelessly deposed and subjected to anathema the most blessed Pope Nicholas and all who communicated with him, sparing neither his supremacy nor, what is more important, the Church which extends from end to end, which undoubtedly communicated with him as one acceptable to God, an imitator of Christ, and a great pontiff.

But the Lord of knowledge, seeing both his manifest wickedness and the works of darkness he had secretly performed—that is, the books full of empty talk which he had falsely written against that most blessed pope—and observing the prophetic saying, “The eyes of the Lord are exalted, open upon all the ways of men, to repay each according to his way and according to the fruits of his devices” (Psalm 66), entrusted the imperial kingdom and principate to our lord Basil Pheronymus [*pheronymos*, “of sacred name”].

[Col. 0186C]

Concerning him we believe that we may plainly address God of all in the words of the blessed King David:

“I have found a man after my own heart, who will do all my desires” (1 Samuel 16).

For this man, placing the meditation of God’s way in his heart, walked according to it and kept his commandments. Having especially experienced the things recently done unjustly and wickedly, he made clear and certain the signs of what had not been apparent.

Seeing the excellent bishops and leaders of the monastic order separated and scattered, and likewise those who, established in the solitary life, sincerely pursued an angelic and heavenly way of life—and, indeed, those endowed with power and authority who held sound opinions—he saw that they detested the invader and adulterer as another kind of abomination of desolation.

[Col. 0186D]

Most worthy and excellent of all, he saw that the elder Rome had cast him out and wounded him with repeated words of reproach, like arrows. He therefore sent him swiftly to the place of disgrace due to him, and, in accordance with the synodal judgment of the most holy Roman Church, restored the proper pontiff to the throne of Constantinople.

For a clearer satisfaction of the truth and also for certainty, he summoned guardians of the place from all the patriarchal sees, and likewise brought together the entire catalogue of bishops who lived under the throne of Constantinople.

[Col. 0187A]

By the grace and cooperation of the Lord Christ our God, and through the decree and care of that same Christ-loving emperor, we celebrated this great and universal synod. After examining with much scrutiny and investigation the things that had been done, we found and recognized that the most holy patriarch Ignatius had been removed from the Church of Constantinople unjustly, irrationally, and contrary to the divine laws and rights; and that Photius had been introduced in his place into it unjustly, irrationally, and contrary to the divine laws and rights.

Conversely, we found that the often-mentioned most holy patriarch Ignatius had received his proper throne reasonably, justly, deliberately—or, rather, canonically—and synodically; and that the often-mentioned most holy patriarch Ignatius had received his proper throne reasonably, justly, deliberately—or, rather, canonically—and synodically; and that Photius had been expelled reasonably, justly, deliberately—or, rather, canonically—and synodically, so that he might fittingly hear the prophetic voice saying:

[Col. 0187B]

“As you have done, so shall your retribution be” (Psalm 30);

“Your recompense shall return upon your own head.”

Therefore this holy and universal synod, repeatedly bringing forward the invader Photius and demanding many and various answers from him, sought to make him openly confess his own [possibly: accounting], humble himself before the glory of God and the greatness of the patriarchal sees—or, if he refused this, speak otherwise and produce words of defense for his own establishment and justification.

It found him in every respect without excuse, speechless, and by his own deeds proving against himself the proverbial saying:

[Col. 0187C]

“His own iniquities ensnare the wicked, and everyone is bound by the chains of his sins” (Proverbs 5).

And again:

“The ways of the wicked are dark; they do not know where they stumble” (Proverbs 4).

For all these reasons, since he was unwilling to understand so as to do what was good, chose neither obedience nor confession of his sin and most wicked episcopate, but was disobedient and resisted this holy and universal synod, we rejected him and anathematized him, and, by the authority given to us in the Holy Spirit by our first and great pontiff, the deliberator and savior of all, made him alien from the entire catholic and apostolic Church.

[Col. 0187D]

As it is written by Moses, the speaker of God:

“And every person who acts with a high hand, whether native-born or a resident alien, that person provokes the Lord. That person shall be utterly cut off from his people, because he has despised the word of the Lord and broken his commandments; that person shall be utterly destroyed, and his sin shall be upon him” (Numbers 15).

The Lord’s saying likewise indicates that one who sins against his neighbor and is in no way corrected, and who also does not obey the Church of God, is to be regarded and treated as a gentile and a tax collector (Matthew 18).

In the same way, we also cut down with the sword of the Spirit those who received the laying-on of hands from him and appeared as even more rotten fruits from a rotten tree, and who, even after the dung, did not wish to become better:

[Col. 0188A]

“Every tree that does not produce good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3),

according to the Lord’s word.

For if the root is holy, so are the branches; and if the leaven is holy, so is the lump, as the great apostle Paul plainly cries out (Romans 11). Conversely, it is evident that if the root is polluted, so are the branches; if the leaven is polluted, so is the lump, for a little leaven leavens the whole lump.

Moreover, Theodorus, the leader of the icon-fighting heresy, who is called Crithinus, was also cast out by this holy and universal synod, together with certain others who shared his views. Some who accepted the word of truth we received and numbered among the choir of the orthodox.

But those who remained in the same mind, impious and depraved together with Pheronymus Crithinus [*pheronymos*, “of sacred name”], we separated even more completely from the Church’s purest grain, like chaff and dung, and anathematized more severely. We also set forth twenty-seven canons for the benefit of the Church, the protection and salvation of Christians, and universal order.

[Col. 0188B]

Knowing all these things, then, dearest brothers and sons of the holy catholic and apostolic Church, whatever your dignity or character may be, praise God worthily—the protector of those who fear him and the deliverer of all who hope in him.

In accordance with the decree and judgment of the holy and universal synod, turn away those who are wicked in disposition; abominate the unjust; hate the iniquitous; and let each of you freely sing psalms with the divine David:

“I have hated the wicked, but I have loved your law” (Psalm 119).

For it is written:

[Col. 0188C]

“He who calls the wicked righteous is accursed among the peoples and hateful among the nations before the Lord” (Proverbs 24).

And again:

“He who calls the righteous unjust and the unjust righteous is unclean and abominable before God” (Proverbs 17).

Therefore let none of those worthy of the Christian name, whether they have received pastoral governance or appear to be governed by another, dare to undertake anything contrary to this holy and universal synod. Otherwise he will be found to contradict God in all things and to despise his counsel and judgment.

For the great apostle Paul says somewhere:

“Therefore, the one who rejects us rejects not man but the living God, who gave his Holy Spirit to us” (2 Thessalonians 4).

And one of our speakers of God says:

“If anyone is severed from the truth, he will not possess the kingdom of God, but will be condemned to Gehenna. And again: If anyone walks in another’s opinion, he is not of Christ. Do not associate with such a one, lest you perish with him.”

[Col. 0188D]

For who does not know that, in the midst of this holy and universal synod, there was Christ and the Lord, incomprehensible and uncircumscribed, who said:

“Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18)?

And that by his will this holy and universal synod, moved by God, both deliberated and acted?

Since the God of all says through the voice of the prophet Isaiah:

[Col. 0189A]

“I will place the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; he shall open, and there shall be no one who closes; he shall close, and there shall be no one who opens” (Isaiah 22),

and the Scripture of Job says:

“If he destroys, who will build? If he closes against a man, who will open?” (Job 12),

it is certain that whoever wishes to open the door which this holy and universal synod has closed, or attempts to close the door which it has opened, will be found and shown to be an enemy and adversary of God, both upon earth and in heaven.

But may it come to pass that all who invoke the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, relying upon his love, keep his fear before their eyes in the equity of truth and be found bringing forth fruits of righteousness, so that all may be guarded and made worthy both to enjoy heavenly providence in the present age and to receive, in the age to come, the heavenly and incorruptible goods laid up for us in promises in that same Christ our God, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

To the most holy, fellow-angelic, greatest high priest and universal pope Adrian, the holy and universal synod assembled at Constantinople in the Lord sends greetings.

[Col. 0189B]

It is fitting that we too should now cry out with the wisest Solomon:

“Wisdom is praised at the exits; in the streets it acts boldly; it is proclaimed upon the tops of the walls; at the gates of the powerful it stands; and at the gates of the city, confidently, it says: ‘For as long as the innocent abound in righteousness, they shall not be put to shame; but fools, being lovers of injuries, having become impious, have hated knowledge’” (Proverbs 1).

This is the proverbial saying.

For Donatus, the beloved-of-God bishop of Ostia, Stephen, the beloved-of-God bishop of Nepi, and Marinus, the most honored deacon of the holy Roman Church, your most holy vicars, being filled with divine wisdom, laying and establishing the house of their own soul upon the pillars of wisdom, and keeping before their eyes the God of all, who founded the earth in wisdom, acted boldly.

[Col. 0189C]

In the streets, certainly, of the divine Scriptures, and upon the lofty, elevated, and strongest walls of God’s truth, they proclaimed the council. At the gates—not only of the powerful, that is, in the hearing of those who possess exercised senses for discerning the better from the worse and a perfected inner person, but also in the hearing of those who are imperfect and small in understanding, living in the city of the living God—they clearly announced the equity of divine justice.

To the former they made manifest, by the divine laws and commandments, the injustice and wickedness that had been accused; while those whom the proverbial saying called innocent—namely, because of their freedom from wickedness—they preserved, through the cooperation and grace of the good God, without shame.

They showed the workers of folly and imitators of wickedness, as being eager for reproaches and having become impious, to be liable to the arguments of truth, just as another proverbial utterance again acknowledges:

[Col. 0189D]

“Examination destroys the wicked.”

For by their deeds the beloved-of-God vicars of your paternal holiness restrained them, in accordance with what the hymn-singing David says:

“The wicked is reduced to nothing in his sight, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord” (Psalm 15).

For what else should these men be thought to have appeared as than derived images—or, rather, indistinguishable representations—of certain good and principal tablets of the most blessed Pope Nicholas, truly the strongest champion of piety, and likewise of your holiness?

[Col. 0190A]

For just as that most blessed and truly God-like man first defined and promulgated these things, and your supreme paternity confirmed and synodically strengthened them, so they too proclaimed and enacted them, making the name and memory of both of you most holy pontiffs, namely, of the elder Rome, praiseworthy in the present age and among all generations that will come afterward.

Thus may what Christ, the Savior of us all, says in the Gospels be fittingly applied to each of them:

“The one who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him” (John 7).

Blessed also is God, who did not hand us over to the teeth of those who hate us, but delivered our soul like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters (Psalm 124).

[Col. 0190B]

Your prayers, constant rebukes, and admonitions—which that *pheronymus* [“sacred-named”] and great high priest of God, the most blessed Pope Nicholas, [the syntax is defective in the source]—for I have continually loved to bear that blessed man’s name on my lips, thereby recalling his memory as well, he who through Christ and with Christ conquered the world—and you, his successor in rank, dignity, and character, zealously exerted for ecclesiastical peace, to drive the wolf from Christ’s sheepfold, as true shepherds of Christ’s rational sheep—indeed, supreme shepherds and leaders of all the Churches.

But concerning wretched Photius and those who were led astray by him and agreed with him, the prophetic saying must be uttered:

“For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous shall walk in them; but the wicked shall grow weak” (Hosea 14),

or even stumble in them. For it was entirely necessary that they delight in their own ways; it was just that fruits and evils should befall them according to the works of their hands, as the eloquent Isaiah says in one place.

But who could convey in articulate words to our Christ-loving and most tranquil emperor the fairness and discipline he has shown in all other matters, and especially in ecclesiastical affairs and toward ecclesiastical persons? He has surpassed all who reigned before him in definitions of piety and the qualities of the virtues, so that we place our confidence more in the direction of his character than in our own virtues.

[Col. 0190C]

May the almighty God and King of all, who through your diligence, intervention, judgment, and synodal exposition was pleased to assemble so great and universal a synod and bring so great a work to a prosperous conclusion, preserve both of you unharmed through many circuits of years. May he also grant your holiness a recompense worthy of your labors, and show you, together with Peter and Paul, the leaders of the apostles, as judges who will judge, in the future age, the impious and unjust among many nations and peoples by their own good works, just as you have now rightly done, receiving from Christ the helm of the ecclesiastical ship.

[Col. 0190D]

Therefore, since your God-imitating holiness gladly, exceedingly gratefully, and in imitation of God receives the agreement and harmony of all our assemblies and of this universal and catholic synod, proclaim it still more, as your own, and confirm it more diligently through your fellow-angelic commands and admonitions, so that through your most wise teaching the word of truth and the decree of justice may resound in and be received by all the other Churches as well.

This letter was sent to all the patriarchal sees.

Basil, Constantine, and Leo, in Christ Jesus, emperors, august rulers of the Romans.

The Apostle plainly cries out that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8). Moreover, the Lord’s voice admonished that the one who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and the doors of hope are opened to the one who knocks (Revelation 3).

[Col. 0191A]

Therefore, guided by these sayings and divinely governed, our empire, loving its giver of the crown as far as it was able, did not cease asking, seeking, and knocking for the discovery of our ecclesiastical order, until, through your prayers acceptable to God, it obtained the fruit of hope.

For the incorruptible pillars of the Churches—namely, the most holy supreme pontiffs of the elder Rome—having undertaken a great labor long beforehand for ecclesiastical order, granted the proper authority to our affairs. Thus the most honored vicars of the holy Roman Church, together with the most reverend guardian of the place of your holiness and those of the other patriarchal sees, more easily, by the grace and cooperation of God, uprooted the tares of wickedness and presented the field completely clean.

They regularly and synodically condemned and rejected, by an irreproachable judgment, those worthy of condemnation and the authors of disorder, together with their acephalous leader. But to the one who had plainly suffered injustice—namely, the legitimate high priest—and to those around him, they decreed and granted triumph.

[Col. 0191B]

The sequence of the proceedings of that synod, set forth above, will explain more fully to your holiness the exact details of what was done.

Therefore, giving thanks to almighty God for the ecclesiastical settlement and the suitable conclusion of the synod, and blessing and receiving the sincere guardianship and preservation of the divine canons conferred upon us by Christ our God through your holiness, because your holiness saves and displays toward us the affection of its goodness in deeds, we present to it the praiseworthy conclusion of this holy and universal synod.

May it offer, together with us, thanksgiving to God the giver, the author of peace and of every most salutary order, while praying for the divine protection of our empire. We wish your most holy paternity good health and our most tranquil empire prosperity before Christ, the wondrous one. Given in the third indiction.

[Col. 0191C]

After this follows another letter, whose beginning is:

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, one and only true God of ours: Basil, Constantine, and Leo, faithful emperors of the Romans in the Lord, to Adrian, most holy Roman pope and our spiritual father.

Keeping the memory of your blessedness unfailing in our mind, and honoring as far as we are able the divine law joined to human nature, which commands sons to render in return to their spiritual fathers, according to the honor of veneration, what is due, we always desire to learn of your safety. Since we cannot embrace our divine and sacred head with bodily lips, let us at least embrace him spiritually through the expression of letters.

We owe this both because of the reasons stated above and because of the love of the one who is among us. He has shown, being steeped in zeal for the truth, how great his piety toward God is, how great his diligence concerning justice, and how great his fervor of fraternal love.

[Col. 0191D]

Since we have also obtained a courier of letters prepared for a journey abroad and magnanimous in enduring hardships, and since he has the same desire to fulfill a vow previously promised to the chief of the apostles, we commend him to your paternal holiness. We also earnestly ask your tranquility concerning this matter.

This is Theognostus, whom you also know well: the beloved-of-God, most praiseworthy hegumen of Peges of the all-praised Mother of God, and guardian of the vessels of the great Church. [Note: Peges, that is, “of the Spring”: a monastery near Constantinople so called.]

Through him, therefore, we have seen that the things we desire may suitably be accomplished. We implore your fellow-angelic holiness first to inform us more quickly by letter about your health, which is according to God, and then also about the prosperous journey of the beloved-of-God apocrisarii and vicars.

[Col. 0192A]

For we have already been waiting for a considerable time, and we do not clearly know the reason for the delay. But even if they should say that they have been absent until now, at least let us learn this late.

Our special father and the patriarch of our great city has also asked us to write to your holiness concerning those readers who were promoted by Photius, of whom there are many and innumerable in various provinces. He has further asked concerning Paul, the most reverend librarian, resplendent in word and life, and concerning Theodore the metropolitan, who himself is exceedingly useful to the Church.

He asks that your holiness grant them a dispensation: for some, toward higher advancement in the sacred orders; for others, toward the recovery of their sees. In making this request, he asks your God-imitating virtue to consider, in the case of the former, their multitude; in the case of the latter, his labors and sweat for the truth; and in the case of the other, the censure of his faults and the fact that he was promoted through canonical laying-on of hands.

[Col. 0192B]

For these reasons our empire also appeals to your piety to dispense something here in a more humane manner.

Farewell, my most loving Father; farewell. Remember our empire in your prayers acceptable to God, which you offer to the Lord. We have read.

We have also sent to your holiness, as a token of remembrance of our empire and of the love we bear toward it, the following garments conveyed by their varieties: three variegated vestments; a yellow checkered *esophorum*, that is, a *chasdium crodium*, having gold ornamentation and a green fleece, that is, a *vilarni pinninum*, for making a chasuble; that is, a red *usin* containing copper, that is, an *usinallum*, that is, a *mulchumat*; and two chestnut-colored *planetilia*.

[Col. 0192C]

The following letter concerns the three chapters, which not all the patriarchal sees, together with the whole synod, dared to define, but whose disposition they customarily humbly requested from the apostolic see through the patriarch Ignatius.

To the most holy and sacred brother and fellow minister, Adrian, most blessed pope of the elder Rome, Ignatius, archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, who has obtained mercy from God, sends greetings in the Lord.

The stone cut from the mountain without hands struck that great image of all the impious kingdoms upon its feet of clay and iron, and scattered it like dust from a summer threshing floor; and it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth with its own magnitude and glory (Dan. II)—namely, Christ, who alone is Lord of infinite power, and our God. In former times, indeed, he made your great city Rome illustrious and renowned through those holy stones that rolled to it from the East—I mean Peter and Paul, the outstanding summit of the apostles’ chiefs. Yet in our own times he has shown it no less, indeed even more, illustrious and renowned through those to whom the pontifical helm of its government has been entrusted in our generation: truly holy and precious stones, namely the most blessed Nicholas and your fraternal holiness.

Just as you, sent down and rolled forth from a certain exalted place against the contrivances of injustice and falsehood, have crushed all the engines and defenses of those opposing the truth through your most wise letters and decrees, sent even to our city, and through the most holy and God-beloved custodians of the place; and now, as you establish a peaceful settlement through the mercies and grace of Christ our God, who is truly the Prince of Peace and the peacemaker, and through your diligence and encouragement, we give thanks to the author of all good things and to the most merciful Lord, our Savior and Redeemer of all. He betrothed the holy catholic and apostolic Church and deigned to call himself its head; and he has shown you and us, the members of his body, joined and agreeing in one Spirit through the working of the Holy Spirit, displaying mutual harmony and concord.

Indeed, we duly commend the gracious words of your blessed holiness, continually entreating God, who is God over all, to repay your holiness with heavenly and fitting rewards worthy of your own labors and struggles; for he alone is the giver and bestower of great rewards suited to you.

Nevertheless, our humility, mindful of your charity and of the loving affection that you bear toward us, and having both the will and the intention of responding to it, found someone to arrange that our intimate son, the most reverend abbot of the Fount, and lord Theognostus, keeper of the sacred vessels of the great church, should be sent on the road to renowned Rome for the sake of prayer. Therefore we were all the more eager to fulfill your desire, and we have sent him with this present letter to visit, greet, and venerate your fraternal holiness. He will also announce the safety granted to us by Christ in this life, which is full of many sufferings and tribulations, as he himself willed and judged who orders all things wisely and suitably.

He will first report the prosperity and victories of our most pious, Christ-loving, God-governed, and divinely protected emperors, and the daily advancement of the affairs of the Roman Empire toward the better, so that you may rejoice with us as we rejoice with you through the mutual affection and compassion of the members of one body. He will then return more quickly, by the good grace and cooperation of God, to our humble station and bring good news to your most beloved life and to our church, so that in this respect also we may rejoice together with you and glorify and magnify him who alone is the unsearchable Lord, the wisest maker of substances, and the continual governor of all things.

May he strengthen your holiness more and more and preserve you on both sides immaculate and unharmed, for the advancement of ecclesiastical affairs and persons, and for the benefit and glory of the all-governing God’s supreme benevolence.

But what, while the most holy representatives of your fatherly holiness are still present, has not been completely accomplished or brought to an end, we now ask to have finished, perfectly arranged, and written out fully for our humility: namely, concerning those readers who were tonsured through the laying-on of Photius’s hands. Since they are an almost innumerable multitude throughout all the regions and cities of the Church, they are compelled by the needs of others to seek advancement to the priesthood. We therefore ask to know with complete certainty and clarity your will and decree concerning this matter: whether they are worthy to be promoted to the higher grades of the priesthood or are not worthy. For they have left us only this one point in doubt.

We also continue to ask concerning our intimate son and most vigorous champion of the truth, Paul the chartophylax: if some dispensation concerning him is possible, may he receive the dignity of the episcopate, as we previously earnestly requested in our letters.

Next, concerning Theodore, whom we consecrated metropolitan of Caria, who labored greatly and was afflicted from the beginning of our unjust and wrongful deposition, but at the end, when he joined the wretched Photius because of the immense torments that Photius inflicted on those who resisted him, gave his consent—and who, even until the latter’s final day, repented, and nevertheless once more sought pardon with a contrite heart and a spirit of humility. For your holiness’s most holy representatives prohibited him from exercising the priesthood in any way, and also because, as they declared, he had subscribed to what had been carried out by the most unhappy Photius, as though it were a deposition of our most blessed and excellent father Nicholas, your holiness’s predecessor.

These are the matters concerning which we ask your holiness, if it is possible, to employ the word of dispensation and mercy, since all the other matters have received an excellent and suitable conclusion and settlement.

For the rest, grant us your holy prayers, prayers that speak with God, most holy brother and imitator of God. May he grant that we remain both unharmed through many cycles of years.

As tokens of our great and dear affection, we have sent to your holiness these things: a Greek-Latin Gospel corrected with the greatest care, a gilded stole, an excellent chasuble, and the most proven theriac.

May God, who created all things, fitted the operation of contrary qualities into one and the same substance, and contains and preserves all things, through your holy prayers bring the holy catholic and apostolic Church into ever greater peace and grant that it may be harmonious and of one opinion from end to end.

> “Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved and spiritual sons Basil, Constantine, and Leo, most pious and tranquil emperors.
>
> “After reading the excellent … of your empire …”

For the remainder, see volume 122 of *Patrologia*, among the letters of Pope Adrian.

[Col. 0195]

# The Holy Seventh General Synod, the Second of Nicaea

Translated by Anastasius the Librarian.

(*In Labbe, Councils*, vol. VIII, p. 29.)

## Preface of Anastasius to the Seventh Synod, addressed to John VIII, Supreme Pontiff

[Col. 0195B]

To the lord John, co-angelic supreme pontiff and universal pope, Anastasius the least.

After recently translating for Pope Adrian of revered memory, the predecessor of your blessedness [Note: Adrian II is meant here], the holy Eighth Universal Synod, I judged it unbecoming and inappropriate that the Seventh Universal Synod [Note: Universal], which was celebrated at the Second Council of Nicaea under the emperors Irene and Constantine, with your predecessor Adrian of blessed memory presiding through his representatives [Note: He speaks of Adrian the First of this name], should not have a Latin version. For the Eighth cannot in any way be called or held to be the Eighth where the Seventh is absent—not because it had never previously been translated, but because its translator, abandoning almost entirely the idiom of either language, followed the word from the word so closely that it can scarcely, or never, be understood what is meant in that version, and it has become so wearisome to readers that almost everyone despises it for this reason. Accordingly, some judge it wholly unworthy even of being read, not to mention copied.

Seeing this, and sparing neither my own weak body, with the Lord’s help I undertook to translate it into Latin, judging it indecent and incongruous that your Roman Church, the teacher of all the churches, should be deprived of this synod, especially when I see that the later one, the Eighth, has been magnificently adorned.

Moreover, since I am by your favor a servant of your sacred library, I am bound to minister from what has been entrusted to me from above—if indeed, following the Apostle’s example, I strive to honor my ministry.

It should certainly be noted that in this synod certain things are found from the canons and judgments of the apostles and of the Sixth Universal Synod which, among us, are neither translated nor accepted. Concerning the canons of the apostles, we know clearly that some did not readily give them their assent. Your predecessor, the most blessed Pope Stephen, synodically declared that no more than fifty of them should be received, although certain decrees of the pontiffs seem to have been taken from those canons.

Therefore, by the decision of your apostolate, the Church receives not only those fifty canons alone [Note: The canons of the apostles], but also all those of them [Note: That is, of the Roman pontiffs], as trumpets of the Holy Spirit, as well as the rules and institutions of all entirely approved Fathers and holy councils—provided only that these neither oppose right faith nor good morals, nor in any slight degree conflict with the decrees of the Roman See, but rather powerfully attack its adversaries, that is, heretics.

Accordingly, the rules that the Greeks claim were issued by the Sixth Synod are accepted by the principal see in this synod in such a way that none of those rules is received which are found to be contrary to earlier canons, to the decrees of the holy pontiffs of this see, or indeed to good morals. Nevertheless, all of them have until now remained wholly unknown to the Latins, since they have neither been translated nor been found in the archives of the other patriarchal sees, although those sees use the Greek language.

The reason is clearly that when they were issued no one from those sees was found either to promulgate them, to consent to them, or even to be present, although the Greeks claim that the same Fathers who were present at the Sixth Synod promulgated them. But they cannot prove this by any certain evidence.

In the matter, moreover, of the Greeks’ frequent and inappropriate calling their patriarch “universal” or “ecumenical” in this synod, may your apostolate pardon what is often done by those who, not without blame, strive to please their superiors.

When I was frequently reproving the Greeks at Constantinople concerning this title and accusing them of pride or arrogance, they maintained that they did not call the patriarch “ecumenical”—which many have interpreted as “universal”—because he held the preeminence over the whole world, but because he presided over a certain part of the world inhabited by Christians.

For what the Greeks call *oikoumene*, the Latins call not only “the world,” from whose totality “universal” is derived, but also “habitation” or “an inhabited place.”

It should also be noted that wherever in the text of this synod I have placed “subsistence,” I wished “person” to be understood. For what is called *hypostasis* in Greek, some have translated as “person,” while others have translated it as “subsistence.” Moreover, many have understood “subsistence” as “person,” while many others have understood it as “substance.”

I followed those who wished “subsistence” to be understood not as “substance” but as “person”—for they are men of great authority—and wherever I found the Greek *hypostasis* in this book, I translated it as “subsistence,” wishing “person” to be understood, as do many others.

Since the holy Church is endowed with such authority, it cannot dissemble: no one can reasonably turn himself away from the adoration of the sacred images. Otherwise your pious teaching ought to instruct him and your apostolic judgment correct him.

Especially since no one is permitted to separate himself from his head, nor in any way to reject what he sees occupying your see, which is the teacher of all. For what the present synod teaches concerning the veneration of venerable images, your apostolic see also held from ancient times, as certain written documents indicate, and the universal Church has always venerated and would continue to venerate—except for certain Gauls, to whom the usefulness of these things has not yet been revealed.

They say, for example, that no work made by human hands ought to be adored, as though the book of the Gospels were not a work of human hands, which they adore daily while kissing it—although they will surely not deny that a dog, though less venerable, is not a work of human hands.

Similarly, they acknowledge everywhere that Christians adore the form of the holy cross. Here it is worth considering that if we adore any golden, silver, or wooden cross—which is certainly not the very cross on which our salvation was accomplished, but its figure and image—why should we not adore the figure and image of him who accomplished that salvation in the midst of the earth?

For the one who accomplished salvation is more venerable than the material in which he accomplished that salvation. Consequently, the image of Christ accomplishing salvation is more worthy of adoration than the image of the cross merely carrying salvation.

Therefore, most blessed pope, ascend a lofty mountain; stand in strength; raise your voice like a trumpet. Behold, by God’s authority, you have risen when your angel, as once the angel of Peter (Acts XII), struck your side; you have girded your loins, lit your lamp, and been consumed with zeal for God.

Only this remains: teach the faith that you believe; show to all the way that you follow. Thus, with God as guide, and with you as leader—the son of those who were shaken out, namely the prophets and apostles—we, all the sheep of Christ entrusted through Peter and in the rock to your diligence, may walk with unhindered steps through trackless places and, when Christ opens the way, deserve happily to enter the pleasant pastures of eternal life. For he has entrusted the keys of the kingdom to you in him and through him.

May heavenly grace preserve your apostolate, most holy lord pope, for the exaltation of his Church and our common salvation, through many years.

# Titles briefly indicating what is contained in this book

[Col. 0197]

[Col. 0197D]

The First Action contains testimonies from various approved Scriptures, by which it is shown that heretics converted from heresy to the orthodox faith may be received. Likewise, it concerns those who have been or are orthodox but have nevertheless received the laying-on of hands from heretics.

The Second Action contains the reading of the letters of Adrian, Roman pope, and, according to their tenor, the profession and promulgation of all the priests who were present at the synod.

The Third Action contains the reception of bishops converted from heresy, the synodical letter of Tarasius the patriarch, the replies of the Eastern priests, and also the subscriptions of the bishops approving the writings of Pope Adrian and the Eastern pontiffs, and declaring that they hold the same view.

The Fourth Action presents testimonies from sacred Scripture and from various holy Fathers on behalf of images.

The Fifth Action contains testimonies showing that the Iconoclasts act or think in matters concerning images in ways equal to those of heretics condemned for various errors.

The Sixth Action sets forth the blasphemies of the heretics and their forceful refutation.

[Col. 0200A]

The Seventh Action presents the decree of this holy synod, the subscriptions of the bishops, the letter sent by the synod to the emperors, and another to the clergy of Constantinople; a laudatory sermon; and the canons promulgated by the same synod.

It also presents the letter of Tarasius, most holy patriarch, to Adrian, supreme pontiff, concerning the synod; another letter of the same to the same concerning the prohibition of purchasing ecclesiastical offices; and another letter of the same to John the presbyter, abbot, and anchorite, concerning the same matter.

# Sacred Imperial Letter of Constantine and Irene, Most August

Addressed to Adrian, most holy and most blessed pope of senior Rome.

[Col. 0199]

[Col. 0199B]

Those who receive from our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, either the dignity of imperial power or the honor of the principal priesthood ought both to consider and to pursue what pleases him, and to rule and govern the peoples entrusted to them according to his will.

Therefore this is owed by us and by you, most holy head: that we think irreproachably about his affairs and occupy ourselves with them, since we receive from him, we the imperial power and you the dignity of the principal priesthood.

We begin our address here. Your fatherly blessedness knows what formerly happened in this imperial city of ours concerning the venerable images: how those who ruled before us destroyed them and subjected them to dishonor and injury. Would that this not be reckoned against them; for it would have been better had they not laid their hands upon the Church.

They also led astray the entire people here, indeed the whole East in the same manner, and drew them back to their own will, until God raised us up to reign over those who truly seek his glory and hold to what was handed down by his apostles and by all his teachers.

Therefore, now with a steadfast heart and true worship, together with all our subjects and these most learned priests, we have spoken about the things that pertain to God, and after deliberation have decreed that a universal council should be held.

We ask your fatherly blessedness—or rather, the Lord God asks, who wills everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II)—to give yourself to this matter, to make no delay, and to come here, firmly and steadfastly, to restore the ancient tradition concerning the venerable images.

This is your duty to do. You know that it is written: “Comfort, comfort my people, you priests, says the Lord” (Isa. XL). And again: “The lips of the priests guard knowledge, and instruction comes from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II).

Again, the divine Apostle and preacher of the truth, who preached the Gospel from Jerusalem and its surroundings as far as Illyricum, gave this command: “Feed the flock of the Lord with discipline, which he acquired with his own blood” (Rom. XV).

As the true chief priest, therefore, and the one who presides in the place and see of the holy and most praiseworthy apostle Peter, let him come, as it is written, and be found together with all the priests who are here, and let the Lord’s will be done: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,” as we have learned from the Gospel (Matt. XVIII).

Let it be confirmed and assured by the great God and King, and by our Lord Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and by us his servants, that when your fatherly and sacred blessedness comes here, we will receive and honor you with every honor and glory and provide whatever is necessary.

And again, when the business has been completed—which we hope will happen by the good pleasure of Christ our God—we will send you back to your own country with honor and magnificence.

But if you cannot come here—which we do not expect to happen, for we know that he is devoted to divine matters—choose honorable men possessing knowledge and send them together with written instructions, so that they may appear here as representatives of your sacred and fatherly blessedness.

Nevertheless, when they have assembled with all the priests who are here, let the ancient tradition of our holy Fathers be confirmed synodically, let every weed badly planted be confounded, and let the word of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ be fulfilled: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI).

Thus there will be no schism or separation in the one holy catholic and apostolic Church, whose head is Christ himself, our true God.

Furthermore, we have brought to us Constantine, the most holy bishop of Leontium [Leontina], of our Christ-loving island of Sicily, whom your fatherly blessedness also knows. We have spoken with him face to face and have sent him to you with this present venerable command of ours.

When he has come to you, release him immediately so that he may return to us, writing to us through him about your arrival: on what days you are to set out from there and travel to us. You must also arrange absolutely that the most holy bishop of Naples come up here with him.

For your journey is to be made through Naples and Sicily. Concerning this, we have ordered the strategos of Sicily to take care of all your rest and honor, so that your fatherly blessedness may come to us. (We have read it.)

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the seventh indiction, from the imperial city.

# Apology to the People, Spoken Briefly by Tarasius, the Secretary

Delivered on the day when the rulers Irene and Constantine announced to the people that he was to become patriarch; he was promoted in the eighth indiction, in the year 6293 from the creation of the world.

[Col. 0201A]

Our faithful emperors, guardians of our undefiled faith—that is, of the Christians—and imitators of those things done for the glory of God, seeking in all things what pleases him and benefits us, namely Christians, and now especially considering ecclesiastical affairs carefully and diligently, so that the supreme priest might be established in this imperial city of theirs, took me into the intention of their piety and commanded me, so that what they had deliberated might be made known to me.

When I declared myself unworthy of this and made no concession—since I could not bear or endure the yoke of this burden—they ordered me to be brought before you, because you too have been made participants in this decision.

And now, men who fear the Lord and always have him in your hearts—I mean you, who are called Christians through the calling of Christ, our true God—hear the account of a brief speech from our lowliness and humility.

Whatever I answered to our most pious and wholly orthodox emperors, I shall answer before you as an apology for my reasoning. I am overcome by fear of consenting to this election, and I fear running before the face of God in such a manner and without due consideration, lest I fall under a terrible condemnation.

For if the divine apostle Paul, who heard the voice of God, had heaven as his reprover [Greek: “school”; another reading: “correction”], became a beholder of paradise, heard ineffable words, and carried the name of God before nations and kings, nevertheless wrote to the Corinthians: “Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. IX)—how can I, who have lived in the world, been counted among the laity, and served in imperial administrations, rashly leap into the greatness of the priesthood without judgment and circumspection?

It is a dreadful undertaking for my smallness and a rash ambition. The cause of my fear and refusal is this: I see and behold the Church, founded upon Christ our God, the rock, now torn and divided; we speak in one way and another, and differently from those Christians in the East who share one faith with us; the Christians of the West agree with them, while we are alienated from all of them and are anathematized by them day after day.

The anathema is a dreadful penalty: it sends one far from God, drives one from the heavenly kingdom, and leads one into the outer darkness. The law or rule of the Church knows neither sect nor contention; but just as it knows one baptism and one faith to confess, so also it knows one harmony in every ecclesiastical matter.

For nothing in God’s sight is so acceptable and pleasing as that we should be one and become one catholic Church, as we confess in the symbol of our sincere faith.

And we ask you, brothers—for I think you also, since I know that you fear God—to request that our most pious and orthodox emperors convoke a universal synod, so that we who belong to one God may become one; we who are worshipers of the Trinity may become united, unanimous, and fellow workers; we who belong to Christ our head may become one body, compact and joined together; and we who belong to the Holy Spirit may become not against one another but for one another.

We who belong to the truth should come to think and say the same thing, and there should be no strife or dissension among us, so that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard us all.

If the defenders of orthodoxy—namely, our emperors—order and agree to grant my just request, I too consent and will fulfill their command. But if not, it is impossible for me to do this, lest I fall under an anathema and be found condemned on the day of our Lord and just Judge, where neither emperor [variant: emperors], nor priest [variant: priests], nor ruler [variant: rulers], nor any multitude of human beings will be able to rescue me.

Whatever seems good to you, brothers, give as your response to my apology—or rather, to my petition.

They all gladly heard what had been said and gave their consent that a synod should be held. A very few of the foolish, however, disagreed.

But the secretary, speaking again to the people, replied that the emperor Leo had overturned the images; and when the synod was held, it found them overturned. The same question therefore arises again: whether they were overturned because of the imperial hand, since the emperors presumed, as it pleased them, to destroy the ancient custom handed down in the Church. But the truth of God is not bound.

After his promotion, he wrote synodical letters to the patriarchs of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, and the Holy City. They are found in the Second and Third Actions, together with their replies.

# Brief Account

[Col. 0203]

Indicating what took place before the synod.

[Col. 0203A]

When Peter and Peter, most beloved priests, came from Rome and brought the aforementioned letters, and from the East the most reverend priests and monks John and Thomas, the patriarchs’ syncelli who were present there, likewise brought the letters mentioned above, the administrators of the empire ordered the bishops to assemble.

When they had arrived in the God-preserved imperial city, the mighty princes delayed in Thrace. But many of the bishops themselves, together with a considerable number of laymen, who had been embroiled in accusing Christians of heresy, disturbed matters. They said that those men should not be admitted to form a synod, but that the deposition and dishonor of the venerable images should be upheld. They also stirred up many factions and murmuring against the patriarch, to such an extent that they formed private gatherings.

While they were deliberating these things, the matter did not escape the patriarch’s ears. While they were still holding their assemblies, he sent word to them that Constantinople has a bishop, and that without his knowledge they had no permission to hold assemblies. For according to the canons they would be subjected to deposition.

When the bishops heard this, they withdrew, overcome by a certain fear.

Then the emperors entered, together with the orders of the people—namely, the scholarians, the excubitors, and the other troops serving in the imperial city—and it was determined that a synod should be held in the venerable church of the holy and praiseworthy apostles.

On the day before the appointed day arrived, at midday, the soldiers were stirred up, burning with rage and breathing madness. They came to the washbasin of the holy catholic Church and shouted one thing and another. But all their voices came to one conclusion: that a synod should not be permitted to take place.

When the patriarch reported the matter to the emperors, he was in no way prevented from allowing the bishops’ assembly to be held in the aforementioned venerable church [Greek addition: “but on the following day the assembly of the bishops took place in the same church”]. After certain addresses had been delivered both by the most holy patriarch and by the God-beloved bishops, and after certain synodical writings had been read which declared that a universal synod ought never to be held without the agreement of the other most holy patriarchs, a disturbance arose among the soldiers.

They made a tumult and shouted before the doors of the venerable church. It was found that they had been moved to this by the instigation of certain bishops who held wicked opinions in the synod.

When these events had taken place, the imperial government ordered the whole synod through a chamberlain to say: “Withdraw for the present, so that we may escape the disorderly assault of the people; afterward the Lord’s will shall be done.”

Thus, when the bishops were leaving the church, certain men who resisted the truth joined with the crowd and composed an impious declaration of the false council. [Note: Words of Anastasius. But the catholic writer calls the gathering of the heretics that took place before this synod, and which they called the Seventh Synod, a *pseudosyllogus*, that is, a false assembly.] They shouted in praise of and gave the name of Seventh Synod to that gathering.

When that wicked assembly had raised its cry, and it was about the sixth hour, they went home already hungry, and thus the agitation of the revolt was quieted.

Then the emperors ordered the soldiers to leave, under the pretext, apparently, of an enemy army, spreading the report that a hostile force of the Hagarenes had gone out. In reality they were driving these men out of the imperial city.

When the soldiers had made their way as far as Malagena, by the emperors’ command they expelled and rejected them all together, lest care should be taken for them [and they dismissed them, saying that they had no need of their services], ordering each one to depart to his own homeland.

After these things had been done, the Church remained quiet for one year, while the patriarch alone preached the word of truth to all.

When the year had passed, the most pious emperors again ordered that a synod should be held in the metropolis of Nicaea. Their command was brought to completion: the bishops were gathered together [variant: “the bishops having been gathered together”], and likewise the patriarch, together with the representatives of the East and West, arrived at the same city. A synod was held by the good pleasure of God, according to the Actions that follow.

# Records of the Synod Held at Nicaea for the Second Time

[Col. 0205]

## First Action

[Col. 0205A]

In the name of the Lord and Master Jesus Christ, our true God, under the rule of our most pious and Christ-loving lords Constantine and his mother Irene, in the eighth year of their consulship, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction.

When the holy and universal synod had assembled—which, by the divine grace and the pious decree of those same emperors confirmed by God, had been convened in the renowned metropolis of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia—there were present:

Peter, most reverend archpresbyter of the most holy Church of Rome, that is, of the Apostle Peter; and Peter, most reverend presbyter, monk, and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sabas situated at Rome, holding the place of the apostolic see’s blessed and most holy senior archbishop of Rome, Adrian;

[Col. 0208C]

Leo, bishop of the Sibyllensians; Manzo, bishop of the Pracanensians; Theodore, bishop of Germanicopolis; Eustachius, bishop of the Cylindereans; Sisinnius, bishop of Sycae; Zachariah, bishop of the Cardabudensians; Sisinnius, bishop of the Musbadensians; Eustathius, bishop of the Lamensians; Theophylact, bishop of Zenupolis; Constantine, bishop of Dalisandus; Anastasius, bishop of the Lauzendensians; Macarius, bishop of Arcandrum.

While they were seated before the most sacred ambo of the temple of the most holy great church called Sophia, in the presence and hearing of the most glorious and magnificent officials—namely, Petronas, the most renowned former consul, patrician, and count of the divinely protected imperial office [Greek: service], and John, the imperial usher and logothete of the imperial [military] logothesion—and of the most reverend archimandrites, abbots, and monks, the holy and undefiled Gospels of God having been placed before them:

The most reverend bishops of the island of Sicily said:

“We consider it worthy, and perceive it to be altogether fitting for this holy and universal synod, that, at the beginning of the investigation of the chapters, the most holy, supreme, and outstanding shepherd and prelate of royal Constantinople, New Rome, should make the prologue, open the door with his word, and loudly proclaim what is appropriate.”

The holy synod said:

“Let it be done according to the request of the most holy bishops.”

Tarasius, most holy and most blessed patriarch of Constantinople, said:

“It is fitting now to speak that prophetic saying which we have often heard proclaimed through the Gospel: ‘The crooked things shall become straight, and the rough ways shall become smooth’ (Luke 3; Isaiah 40). For whenever God does something, ease follows in all that is done, since no one resists his will.

“For although, through the instigation of the ancient enemy, who desires to incite continually and disturb the holy catholic Church, on the Kalends of August of the past year, while we were presiding in the divinely protected imperial city, in the venerable church of the Spirit of the Trumpets—that is, of the holy and most praiseworthy apostles—a crowd of men, filled with fury and bitterness, was stirred up to lay hands upon us, we were rescued from that hand by divine aid. We had with us certain bishops, few enough to be easily counted, whose names we willingly pass over, since they are known to everyone. For a short time they appeared to have prevented speech and to have strengthened the pious word of truth.

“But our most gentle emperors, divinely moved, as defenders of orthodoxy and opponents of the false opinion, did not give sleep to their eyes nor slumber to their eyelids until they restored the tabernacle of God—that is, his Church—to unity and made this dwelling peaceful. Therefore, by God’s counsel and will, they have again gathered us together for the same purpose. For these deeds they will receive good recompense from Christ, the emperor of us all, who is exceedingly powerful to repay them manifold.

“Therefore, sacred men, invoking him as our helper, keeping his fear in our breasts, and holding the future judgment in our minds, let us gird the loins of our minds with truth. Being watchful in all things according to the Apostle, let us judge with balanced judgment, and without any delay let us uproot completely every novelty of words, ambition, and excess, as tares sown over pure wheat, since these oppose the truth and resist the Church.

“For the things handed down in it are not ‘yes and no,’ but ‘yes’ (2 Corinthians 1): they exist in truth and remain incorrupt and unaltered for everlasting ages. For he who promised is without falsehood, saying: ‘The gates of hell shall not prevail against it’ (Matthew 16). And if we are assured [or: have been assured] that this is pleasing in the sight of God, let those who resisted the truth in the past year come forward. If there is among them any statement, objection, or even argument, let them speak. In this way the entire examination will become manifest.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“If it seems good to this holy and universal synod, then, in accordance with what has been said by the most holy and most blessed patriarch Tarasius, let the most holy bishops who have been accused in this matter enter into the presence of this holy and universal synod.”

The holy synod said:

“Let them enter.”

And the bishops mentioned above entered. When they had entered, the most glorious officials said:

“Our gracious lords have commanded that an honorable and venerable sacred letter be delivered to your entire sacred synod. Listen.”

The holy synod said:

“May God strengthen the empire of our good lords!”

And when it had been brought in the hands of the most glorious secretary Leontius, he read the same pious letter.

**Sacred Letter**

“Constantine and Irene, faithful emperors of the Romans, to the most holy bishops who, by the will and grace of God and by the command of our pious empire, have assembled in the synod at Nicaea.

“Wisdom, which by nature is truly God’s and the Father’s—namely, our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God—removing us from the error of idols through his divine and great dispensation in the flesh, assumed our nature and renewed it through the cooperation of his consubstantial Spirit. Having become the first pontiff, he made you worthy of this title, sacred men.

“He himself, therefore, the good shepherd who carried the sheep that had gone astray upon his shoulders, reconciled the fallen human being to his own flock—that is, to his angelic and ministering powers—by associating him with them in himself. Having removed the middle wall of partition, he destroyed enmity in his flesh and granted us peaceful fellowship. Therefore, proclaiming this evangelically to all, he declared: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God’ (Matthew 5).

“Since our pious empire desires to be found within this blessedness, which has granted us the nobility of adoption as children, it hastens to direct our entire Roman commonwealth toward peace and concord. Above all, it wishes to take up the care of good order in the holy Churches of God and continually seeks to secure the unity of the priests of the East, North, West, and South. By God’s will, their prelates are present through their vicars, together with reciprocal replies to the synodical letters sent by the most holy patriarch.

“For this is the ancient synodical law of the catholic Church, which has received the Gospel from end to end of the earth. Therefore, by his good pleasure and command, we have assembled you, his holy priests, who administer his testament over the unbloody sacrifices, so that your judgment may be made like the definitions of the synods that have taught correctly, and so that the splendor of the Spirit may shine upon all. For, according to the Lord’s word, ‘No one who lights a lamp puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house’ (Matthew 5).

“Thus you shall also follow the laws which were once piously handed down to us by our fathers, and the holy Church of God shall remain in peaceful order. We contend so earnestly for the truth, strive so vigorously for piety, and take such care for ecclesiastical order, desiring to confirm the ancient legislation, that although we are occupied with military counsels and engaged in the affairs of the commonwealth, we make the peaceful observance of the catholic Church our first concern. Placing this second, we have not wearied of assembling your most sacred synod, granting each person permission to speak without any restriction whatever may seem right to him, so that a distinct [or: strict] examination may be made, and the truth may be pursued with greater confidence. In this way the dissension of the Churches may be utterly driven away, and the bond of peace may be fitted together among us all.

“And since Paul, the most holy patriarch, when he was about to be released, according to the divine will, from his present bonds, to depart from this life and to go to his dwelling—or rather, to the Lord Christ himself—renounced the episcopate and chose the life of monks, we asked him why he had done this. He replied:

“‘Because if I should be overtaken by death while I am bishop of the divinely protected imperial city, I shall have an anathema from the whole catholic Church, which leads to the outer darkness prepared for the devil and his angels. For they say that a certain synod was held here which overturned the representational paintings [images], which the catholic Church holds, embraces, and receives for the commemoration of the principal persons. This troubles my soul; this brings me to reflect on how I shall escape the judgment of God, because I have associated and been counted with such men.’

“He also spoke these things to certain of our most glorious officials, and so he departed this life. Since our pious empire considered this terrible sentence—and since even before this we had heard from many sources of such a dispute—we deliberated with ourselves concerning what ought to be done.

“We resolved in our council that, once a patriarch had been appointed, the matters that had been spoken would immediately be brought to an end. Therefore, summoning men experienced in ecclesiastical affairs, invoking Christ our God, and taking counsel with them concerning who might be worthy to be advanced to the priestly chair of this divinely protected imperial city, and having become united in one counsel and purpose in all things, we issued the decree in favor of Tarasius, who now presides in pontifical dignity.

“Calling him, we announced to him what had been said and decreed concerning him. He was entirely unwilling to agree or to give his consent to what had been decreed. When we asked him why he refused to obey, he first replied by excusing himself and speaking of the yoke of the priesthood laid upon him. We understood that he was offering an excuse in order not to obey, but we did not withdraw from him; rather, we continued trying to persuade him to accept the dignity of the supreme priesthood.

“Then, seeing our persistence, he announced the reason for his refusal. ‘I see and perceive,’ he said, ‘that the Church founded upon the rock—that is, Christ our God—is now torn and rent apart. I recognize that we speak one way, while those Christians in the East who share one faith with us speak another; that we agree with those who are established in the West, while we ourselves are estranged from all of them and are anathematized by everyone day after day. I also recognize that I demand a universal synod, since vicars are to be found both from the Roman pope and from the priestly rulers of the East.’

“When he had made these things known in the presence of our priests and most glorious officials, and of all our Christ-loving people who were then present, we led the man out. In their presence we repeated everything he had answered us and said to them. All of them, hearing these things, gladly accepted them and requested that our pious empire convene a universal synod.

“Therefore we agreed to this request, God willing to gather you, as we speak the truth, and directing us toward it. Since God has gathered you from the whole world, wishing to establish his counsel, behold, with the holy Gospels set before you and crying out intelligibly, ‘Judge justly’ (John 7), stand firm as defenders of piety. Take care to cut off every novelty of words and every newly appearing sedition, just as Peter, the first leader [or: prince] of the apostolic college, when struck by the madness of servile deception, cut away the sense of Jewish hearing with the sword (John 18).

“Extend the axe of the Spirit, and either transplant every tree producing the fruit of contention, dissension, and introduced novelty by authoritative words, or cut it down with canonical rebukes and send it into the fire of the Gehenna to come. Thus may the peace of the Spirit guard the Church’s body intact, compact, harmonious, and strengthened by the tradition of the fathers; and may the constitution of our entire Roman commonwealth stand tranquil together with the tranquility of the faith.

“We have also received letters sent by Adrian, the most holy senior pope of Rome, through his vicars—namely, Peter the first presbyter, and Peter, beloved of God, presbyter and abbot, who appear to be seated among you. We command that they be read aloud in the hearing of all, according to synodical law. After you have heard them in due silence, together with the documents in two booklets sent by the chief priests and priests of the Eastern diocese through John, the most reverend monk and former syncellus of the patriarchal see of Antioch, and Thomas, presbyter and abbot—who themselves, behold, are also present among you—you will learn from them what the mind of the catholic Church is.”

The holy synod said:

“May God preserve their empire! May God lengthen their years! May he grant them exceedingly great joy!”

[Col. 0212D]

Basil of Ancyra, Theodore of Myra, and Theodosius of Amorium were brought forward. As they stood in the midst of the holy synod, Basil, bishop of Ancyra, said:

“As far as it lay within my power, lords, I sought the cause, and, having received every satisfaction, I, the last of your servants, approached the catholic Church.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Glory to God, who desires all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2).

Basil, bishop of Ancyra, read as follows from his written declaration:

“Ecclesiastical legislation has been canonically handed down from above, from the beginning, both by the holy apostles and by their successors—namely, our holy fathers and teachers—as well as by the six holy and universal synods and by the local councils which were assembled in orthodox fashion. Thus those who have been converted from any heresy to the orthodox confession and tradition of the catholic Church may renounce their heresy in writing and confess the orthodox faith.

“Therefore I, Basil, bishop of the city of Ancyra, proposing to be united with the catholic Church, with Adrian, the most holy pope, and with Tarasius, the most blessed patriarch, and with the most holy and apostolic thrones of Alexandria, Antioch, and the holy city, as well as with all orthodox pontiffs and priests, make this present confession [profession] of mine in writing and offer it to you, who have received authority from the apostolic power.

“In this matter I also ask pardon from your divinely gathered blessedness for my delay. For I ought not to have been deprived of the orthodox confession; but this is the result of my extreme lack of discipline and of my sluggish and negligent mind. Therefore I ask your blessedness all the more earnestly that forgiveness from God may be granted to me [or: that you seek mercy from God and grant forgiveness to me].

“I therefore believe and confess in one God, the Father almighty; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life. The consubstantial and co-enthroned Trinity, to be worshiped and glorified in one deity, power, and authority.

“I also confess everything concerning the dispensation of the one holy Trinity, namely, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, as the six holy and universal synods have handed it down. I reject and anathematize every heretic without exception, in accordance with the anathemas pronounced by those synods themselves.

“I also seek the intercessions of our undefiled lady, holy Mary the Mother of God, and of the holy and heavenly powers and of all the saints without exception. Receiving their holy and precious relics [that is, remains] with all honor, I greet them and reverence them honorably, trusting that I shall become a participant in their holiness.
