“Likewise, I greet and embrace the venerable images of the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, according to which he became human for our salvation, and of our undefiled lady, holy Mary the Mother of God [Greek addition: and of the godlike angels], and of the holy apostles, prophets, martyrs, and all the saints together, and I offer the worship that pertains to honor.

“Nevertheless, with all my soul and all my mind, I reject and anathematize the synod which, assembled through stupidity and madness, was called the seventh synod. By those who think rightly it is legally and regularly called ‘false-syllogistic’ [pseudosyllogos], since it is alien to all truth and piety and has barked boldly and rashly—indeed, godlessly and without God—against the divinely handed-down ecclesiastical legislation, and has assailed the holy and venerable images with insults.

“It also ordered that these images be removed from the holy Churches of God. From that synod came Theodosius, the Ephesian of false name [Greek: over whom it presided]; Sisinnius of Pergé, surnamed Pastillas; and Basil of Pisidia, nicknamed Cacemphatus [‘of ill-omened name’], Tricaccabus [elsewhere, Tricacos, that is, ‘thrice evil’]. The wretched Constantine, who had been patriarch, followed them in his folly.

“Thus I confess and assent to these things, and therefore, in simplicity of heart and uprightness of mind, with God bearing witness for me, I pronounce here the following anathemas:

“Anathema to the slanderers of Christians, that is, to the destroyers of images!

“Anathema to those who apply to venerable icons the words spoken by divine Scripture against idols!

“Anathema to those who do not greet the holy and venerable images!

“Anathema to those who call sacred icons idols!

“Anathema to those who say that Christians approach images just as they approach gods!

“Anathema to those who knowingly communicate with those who insult and dishonor the venerable icons!

“Anathema to those who say that anyone other than Christ our Lord delivered us from idols!

“Anathema to those who despise the teachings of the holy fathers and the tradition of the catholic Church, while citing and adopting the words of Arius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus, and asserting that, unless we have been clearly instructed from the Old and New Testaments, we should follow neither the teachings of the holy fathers nor those of the holy [general] synods nor the tradition of the catholic Church!

“Anathema to those who say that the making of images is an invention of diabolical argument and not the tradition of our holy fathers!

“Anathema to those who presume to say that the catholic Church ever accepted idols!

“These things I confess and to these I assent, and I proclaim them with all my heart, soul, and mind. But if—which God forbid—I should at any time, voluntarily or involuntarily, through submission to the devil, turn away from the things I have now professed, may I be anathema from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and utterly alien from the catholic Church and from the sacred order!

“I shall preserve myself, according to the divine canons both of the holy apostles and of our approved fathers, from every acceptance of gifts and from dishonest gain.”

Tarasius, most holy and most blessed patriarch, said:

“The entire sacred college gives glory and thanksgiving to God for this confession which you have offered to the catholic Church.”

The holy synod said:

“Glory to God, who unites those who are divided from one another!”

Then Theodore, the most reverend bishop of Myra, was brought forward and said:

“I too, a sinner and unworthy, after much consideration and examination, choosing what is better, beg God and your holiness that I, a sinner, may also be united with everyone to the holy catholic Church.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Mercy is pleasing to the Lord Jesus Christ [Greek: ‘It is pleasing to the Lord Jesus Christ also to receive a human being’], and therefore he receives [or: therefore receive] those who repent.”

Theodore, the most reverend bishop of Myra, read a copy of the first written declaration:

“Ecclesiastical legislation is …”

When he had read it, Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Also concerning the most reverend Theodore, bishop of Myra, we give thanks to our God Christ.”

Euthymius, most holy bishop of Sardis, said:

“Blessed is God, who has united him to the catholic Church!”

Then Theodosius, bishop of Amorium, was brought forward and said:

“Most sacred and God-honored lords, and this entire sacred synod: I too am a sinner, miserable and deceived. I have spoken many evil things against the venerable icons. Having recognized the truth, I have acknowledged and reproved myself; I have anathematized, and I now anathematize, the things I wrongly taught and spoke in this world. I beseech and entreat your holy synod to receive me, together with all Christians, as your unworthy servant.”

Tarasius, most holy and most blessed patriarch, said:

“The most reverend Theodosius has shown great contrition of heart and is worthy of reception.”

The holy synod said:

“He is worthy according to the sacred canons.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“If there is no other canonical impediment that prevents him, he is worthy.”

Theodosius, the most reverend bishop, read his own written declaration as follows.

Theodosius, a humble Christian, to the holy and universal synod.

I confess, promise, accept, embrace, and principally venerate the undefiled image of our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, and the image of the Mother of God, who bore him without seed. Each day and night I invoke her help, protection, and intercessions as a sinner, for my assistance, as one who has confidence before Christ our Lord, who was born from her. Likewise, I accept and venerate the images of the holy and most praiseworthy apostles, prophets, martyrs, Fathers, and desert-dwellers, not as gods—far be it—but by displaying even now the affection and love of my soul that I previously held for them. With all my soul I beseech them all to intercede for me with God, so that through their intercessions he may grant me to find mercy with him on the day of judgment.

Similarly, I venerate, honor, and embrace the relics of the saints, as relics of those who contended for Christ and received grace from him to bring about healings, cure illnesses, and cast out demons, just as the Church of the Christians received this practice from the holy apostles and Fathers, down to our own time. I also consent that in the churches the image of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the holy Mother of God be principally painted from various materials—gold and silver and every color—so that his taking of flesh may be made known to all. Likewise, let the conduct of the saints and of the most renowned apostles, prophets, and martyrs be painted, so that their contests and struggles may be made known through a brief inscription, for the encouragement and instruction of the peoples, especially of the simple.

For if, when the laurel-crowned images of kings are sent to cities or regions, the peoples go out to meet them with candles and incense, honoring not the board smeared with wax but the emperor, how much more ought the image of our Savior and God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of his undefiled Mother, and of all the holy and blessed Fathers and devoted men, to be painted in the churches of Christ our Lord?

As Saint Basil also says: “For writers and painters depict the great deeds of wars: the former adorning them with speech, the latter engraving them on panels; and both have stirred many to courage.” And again, the same man: “How much have you labored [variant: would you labor], O man, to find one of the saints entreating the Lord?” And Chrysostom says: “For the grace of the saints is not cut off by death, nor does it grow dull through dying; but after they have departed, they are more powerful than the living,” and many other things, immeasurable in number.

Therefore I beseech you, O saints, and cry out: “I have sinned against heaven and before you; receive me as God received the prodigal, the prostitute, and the thief. Seek me as Christ sought the sheep that was lost, which he carried upon his shoulders” (Luke 15), so that joy may arise before God and his angels over my salvation and repentance, through your intervention, most holy lords.

Anathema to those who do not venerate the venerable images!

Anathema to those who speak blasphemy against the precious and venerable images!

Anathema to those who dare to disparage and blaspheme the venerable images, or to call them idols!

Anathema to those who do not diligently teach the entire Christ-loving people to venerate the holy and venerable images of all the saints who pleased God in this world and are worthy of veneration [Note: [Col. 0215D] Anathema to those who are uncertain and do not confess sincerely that they venerate the holy images]!

Anathema to the slanderers of the Christians—that is, to those who shatter the images!

Sabbas, most reverend hegumen of the monastery of Studium [Note: [Col. 0216D] In the Jol. manuscript, it is explained as “leader, abbot, or superior”], said: “In accordance with the apostolic precepts and the universal synods, he is worthy of reception.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “Those who until recently were slanderers of the orthodox faith have now become advocates of the truth.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “The petition of the most reverend bishop of Amorium drew many tears from us [Cod. Jol., ‘emptied many tears from us’].”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “Does it seem good to you that they should receive their sees?”

The reverend monks said: “Just as the holy and universal synods received those converted from heresy, so do we receive them.”

The holy synod said: “It pleases us all.” And the most reverend Basil, bishop of Ancyra, and Theodore, most reverend bishop of Amorium, were ordered to sit in their rank and seats.

Euthymius, most reverend bishop of Sardis, said: “God has brought in an orthodox man.”

The holy synod said: “An orthodox Father with the Fathers of the holy synod [Orthodox with the synod; a Father with the Fathers].”

After these men, Hypatius, most reverend bishop of Nicaea; Leo, most reverend bishop of Rhodes; Gregory, most reverend bishop of Pessinus; Leo, most reverend bishop of Iconium; George, most reverend bishop of Pisidia; Nicholas, most reverend bishop of Hierapolis; and Leo, most reverend bishop of Carpathus, were brought in [Col. 0217A].

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “As though suddenly rushing forward—from where, shall I say?—you devised a profound plan, and not through the Lord; you made covenants, and not through his Spirit; namely, gathering together secretly and covertly among yourselves in the past year, wishing to drive away the truth. If you did this irrationally, give an account of your ignorance. But if your argument is produced with a kind of false reasoning, let that reasoning itself be brought forward and heard before all of us. With the truth as our helper, this sacred assembly will utterly break apart your constructions and contradictions, and will dissolve them completely, as bonds of falsehood and injustice, having no substance of truth at all.”

Leo, most reverend bishop of Rhodes, said: “We have sinned in the sight of God, in the sight of the whole Church, and in the sight of this holy synod. For through foolishness we fell, and we have no defense to offer on our behalf.”

Gregory, most reverend bishop of the Pessinians, said: “According to the faith handed down by the apostles and Fathers, we confess and hold it.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “If there is any argument among you, let it be brought forward, as has been said to you” [Col. 0217C].

Hypatius and those who were with him said: “We have nothing to say, most sacred lord. Through ignorance and foolishness we spoke.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “What reasoning turned you back to the truth?”

Hypatius and those who were with him said: “The teaching of the holy apostles and Fathers.”

Gregory, most reverend bishop of the Pessinians, said: “At the synod of the holy apostles, which was assembled at Antioch, it is said: ‘So that those who are being saved may no longer err concerning idols, but may instead fashion for themselves an image of our Lord Jesus Christ, the God-man.’ Blessed Isidore of Pelusium also says: ‘There is no temple whose order is complete unless an image crowns it’” [Col. 0217D].

Leo, most reverend bishop of Rhodes, said: “We have examined everything that we learned piously and truthfully, although we are unworthy and sinners. From the legal, prophetic, apostolic, and paternal testimony we have become certain that the truth and piety are such that holy and venerable images should exist in the holy Church, according to the custom handed down from ancient times by the holy apostles; and therefore we obeyed.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “How is it, then, that although you have held the episcopate for as many as eighteen years, you have not obeyed until the present?”

The most reverend bishop Leo said: “Because an evil and wicked teaching had been prolonged for a lengthy period; and when the delay had lasted too long, we were led astray on account of our sins and turned away from the truth. But we hope to be saved by God” [Col. 0218A].

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “Long continuance in sickness is more difficult to cure. So also a soul that is in the darkness of heresy recognizes the light of orthodoxy only with difficulty.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “Since you were bishops together with the other bishops, you ought not to have had any need to learn, but rather to have been teachers of others” [essetis episcopi: “since you were bishops”].

Leo, most reverend bishop of Rhodes, said: “If those who were under the law had not extended [or: ‘had not prolonged’] sin, there would have been no need for grace” [Col. 0218B].

Stauracius, most holy bishop of Chalcedon, said: “But we, brothers, are not under the law but under grace.”

Hypatius and the most reverend bishops who were with him said: “We received evil teachings from evil teachers.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “Since you have said that the teachings of evil teachers are evil, the Church does not consent to admit priests from evil teachers.”

Hypatius, bishop of Nicaea, said: “Custom prevailed in this way.”

Gregory, most reverend bishop of the Pessinians [Pessinusians], said: “Saint John Chrysostom says: ‘I loved a painting smeared with wax, filled with piety’” [Col. 0218C].

Sabbas, most reverend monk and hegumen of the monastery of Studium, said: “Blessed be God, who directed you to the truth!”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “We have now heard their argument and defense.”

The holy synod said: “Yes, lord.”

John, most reverend monk and priest, and vicar of the apostolic throne of Antioch, said: “Many ask, most holy Father, how those who return from the heresies ought to be received. We beseech the holy and sacred synod that the books of the holy Fathers be brought, so that we may see and examine them and obtain from them the true certainty of how such persons ought to be received; for we are uncertain” [Col. 0218D].

Constantine, most reverend bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “We ask your Beatitude, lord, that the books mentioned above be brought, so that, having become certain, we may establish a praiseworthy order.”

Constantine, beloved of God, notary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, said: “In accordance with your Holiness’s command, we are ready, bringing the sacred books that we have taken from those resting in the library of the venerable patriarchate of Constantinople: the canons of the holy apostles, the canons of the holy synods, those of our holy Father Basil, and those of other holy Fathers” [Col. 0219A].

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “Let the book of canonical institutions [constitutions] be read first.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be read.”

Then Constantine, beloved of God, deacon and notary of the venerable patriarchate, took it and read:

From Canon 53 of the holy apostles:

“If any presbyter does not receive one who turns from sin, but rejects him, let him be deposed, because he has made sad Christ, who says that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15) [Col. 0219B].

Sabbas and those who were with him said: “This is clear and accepted by everyone: the Church receives every penitent.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “There is another canon on this matter.”

The same beloved-of-God notary read Canon 8 of the holy Council of Nicaea:

“Concerning those who call themselves Cathars—that is, ‘pure’—if they should at any time come to the catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great council that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy. Above all, they must profess in writing that they accept and follow the doctrines of the catholic and apostolic Church; that is, that they communicate with digamists and with those who fell during the persecution, for whom periods and appointed times have been established, so that in everything they may follow the decisions of the catholic and apostolic Church. Wherever, whether in villages or in cities, they alone are found ordained, those among them who are found in the clergy shall remain in the same rank, and so forth” [Col. 0219C].

Theodore, most reverend bishop of Catana in the province of Sicily, said: “The canon that has been read has nothing to do with this heresy.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “But it also concerns every heresy.”

Epiphanius, deacon of the most holy Church of Catana in the province of Sicily and vicar of the bishop of Sardinia, said: “This canon was spoken at that time about the Cathars—that is, the ‘pure’” [Col. 0219D].

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “How, then, should we receive the heresy that has now arisen in our own time?”

John, beloved of God, vicar of the apostolic throne of the East, said: “Heresy separates every person from the Church.”

The holy synod said: “This is clear.”

The most reverend monks said: “The rule says that those who have received the laying on of hands are to be received.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “How is the laying on of hands to be understood?”

The most reverend monks said: “We beseech you, lord, teach us.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “Perhaps here it speaks only of the laying on of hands in blessing, and not of consecration” [in consecration].

The most glorious rulers said: “If there is nothing else that prohibits it, on account of their repentance they shall be received according to the canons.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “Let us examine other canons concerning the remaining heresies.”

The holy synod said: “We also request that the canons be brought.”

The same beloved-of-God deacon and notary read Canon 3 of the holy and universal Council of Ephesus:

“If any of the clergy in the various cities have been prevented by Nestorius and those who were with him from exercising the priesthood because they held the correct faith, we decree that they recover their proper rank [Col. 0220B]. Those clergy, namely, who think or will think with the universal and orthodox synod, whether now or at any future time, we command in no way to be subjected to bishops who have withdrawn or may withdraw, or who transgress both the holy canons and the orthodox faith” [Greek: “and, in general”].

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “The canon concerning the matter being sought is clearer.”

“But let the remaining canons also be read.”

Stephen, most reverend monk and librarian [keeper of the books] of the venerable patriarchate, said: “We still have at hand letters of our holy Father Basil concerning the matter mentioned above—whether those who turn from heresy are to be received into the priesthood. If you order them to be read, let them be read” [Col. 0220C].

The holy synod said: “Let them be read.”

The monk Stephen read from the first canonical letter of our Father Basil to Amphilochius:

“We must understand the wickedness of the Encratites. In order to be judged unworthy of reception by the Church, they attempted to anticipate us by means of their own baptism. Thus they corrupted their own custom. I therefore think that, since nothing more explicit has been promulgated concerning them, we ought to condemn their baptism. And if anyone has been received by them [Greek: ‘if anyone has received from them’], when he comes to the Church, let us baptize him. Certainly, if this is going to impede the universal dispensation, let us follow the former custom and follow the Fathers who administered each matter according to circumstances [Col. 0220D]. For I fear that, if we wish to make those sluggish people undertake baptism, we may become an impediment to those who were destined to be saved, because of the mystery of prolonged investigation [Greek: ‘because of the severity of the decision’]. But if they preserve our baptism, let this not be demanded from us [alternative: ‘let this in no way move us’]. For we are not debtors to them for granting grace, but are subject to the discipline of the canon.

“Moreover, let the following rule be maintained in every respect: those who are proved to have approached their baptism must first unquestionably be anointed by the faithful, and only then be made worthy of the holy mysteries. I know, however, that we received into the episcopal seat the brothers who were around Izoes and Saturninus, although they belonged to that ordination. Therefore we can no longer separate from the Church those who are associated with their order, since by receiving bishops from them we have established a certain rule concerning communion with us” [Col. 0221A].

The most reverend monks said: “We request that the letter of Saint Athanasius to Rufinianus be brought.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be done according to the request of the most reverend monks.”

Meanwhile Leontius, most glorious secretary, said: “In the meantime, let the remaining letters of Saint Basil be read.”

Stephen, most reverend monk and librarian, read from a letter of our holy Father Basil sent to the Evaisenians:

“Those whom last year they summoned from Galatia, so that through them they might obtain confidence in the episcopate, are such as those who spent even a short time with them know. And a little later:

“If they say that they have repented, let them produce in writing their repentance, their anathematization of the faith of Constantinople, and their separation from the heretics; and let them not deceive the more simple-minded.”

From the same Father’s letter addressed to the Westerners:

“One of those who have caused us much sorrow is Eustathius, namely, the traitor from Sebastia in Lesser Armenia. Formerly taught by Arius, Eustathius of Sebastia in Lesser Armenia was known for composing wicked blasphemies against the Only-Begotten while he was advancing in Alexandria; he followed Arius and was counted among his disciples, together with those who were bound to him by intimate kinship [Col. 0221C]. Finally, coming to his senses [Greek: ‘returning to his own’], he made a profession of sound faith to the blessed bishop Hermogenes of Caesarea, by whom he was being judged concerning his wicked opinion. After receiving consecration from him, however, Eustathius, immediately after Hermogenes’s death, hastened to Eusebius of Constantinople, who likewise proclaimed the impious doctrine of Arius.

“Then, expelled from there for some reason, when he came to his countrymen, he meanwhile excused himself. Concealing his impious belief, he displayed the correctness of certain words; and, having somehow obtained the episcopate, he was soon seen to have written an anathematization of the term ‘consubstantial’ at the assembly that they held at Ancyra. Then, when he reached Seleucia, he wrote together with his associates things that everyone knows [Col. 0221D]. At Constantinople, he again agreed with what the heretics had put forward. Having consequently been expelled from the episcopate because he had earlier been deposed at Melitene, he devised for himself a means of restoration, as though going to you. We do not know what was attempted against him by the blessed bishop Liberius, nor what he himself promised, except that he carried a letter restoring him. When he showed it to the synod assembled at Tyana, he was restored to his position.”

The letter of the same Father to the count Terentius was also read, in which that Father indicated the communion and reception of Eustathius, who had turned from heresy.

Stephen, most reverend deacon and notary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, read:

From the definition of the third holy and universal synod against the impious Messalians, that is, the Euchites:

“It pleased all of us—namely, the beloved-of-God bishops Valerian and Amphilochius, and all the most reverend bishops of the provinces of Pamphylia and Lycaonia—that all the provisions established in the synodal document be observed and in no way violated, while the acts performed at Alexandria likewise remain firm. Therefore, those throughout the entire province who belong to the heresy of the Messalians—that is, the madmen [enthusiasts]—or who are suspected of suffering from such a disease, whether clerics or laymen, when they return and anathematize in writing according to the provisions promulgated in the synodal document already mentioned, shall remain: clerics in the clergy, and laymen in the communion of the Church” [Col. 0222B].

Peter, most reverend reader and notary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, read:

A memorandum of our holy Father Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria, to Maximus, deacon of Antioch.

“I have learned from Paul the monk, dear to me, that even to this day your Piety refuses to embrace communion with the most reverend bishop John, because some in the Church of Antioch either still think wrongly with Nestorius, or have indeed thought so in the past, but perhaps have come to repentance [Col. 0222C]. Let your modesty therefore determine whether those who are said to have gathered together openly and irreverently think with Nestorius and converse with one another, or whether they once had a seared conscience but are now gathering together after having done penance for the matters in which they were ensnared, although perhaps they are ashamed to confess their transgression. For such things sometimes happen among the deceived. And if you see them now hastening toward the correct faith, do not be angry with them over what has passed. For we wish rather to see them as deniers of those men than, with an irreverent mind, as advocates of Nestorius’s wickedness. But, lest we be thought to love contention, let us embrace communion with the most reverend John, showing him indulgence and exercising dispensation, so that the matter may not be handled toward him with excessive precision [Col. 0222D], strictness, or severity; for, as I have said, the affair requires much dispensation.”

From the same Father to Gennadius, priest and archimandrite:

“I did not first recognize today the intention of your Reverence, which you possess concerning divine worship; I have known it from long ago, and I greatly praise your desire to live with such diligent strictness. But the practical administration of affairs sometimes compels certain people to depart slightly from what is owed, so that they may gain something greater. Just as those who sail the sea, when a storm presses upon them and the ship is in danger, throw out certain things in their anxiety so that the remainder may be preserved [Col. 0223A], so we too, when we do not possess complete certainty about preserving every matter, disregard some things lest we suffer the loss of them all.

“I write this knowing that your Piety is distressed with regard to the most holy and God-loving brother and fellow-minister of ours, Proclus the bishop, because he admitted into communion the hegumen [bishop] of Aelia, whom the laws of the Church of Palestine do not recognize as its superior. The love of glory, however, which awakens an unrestrained desire for the matter, has a bitter ending while possessing nothing. Therefore let your Piety not refuse communion with the most holy and God-loving bishop Proclus. For I and his Holiness had one and the same concern; and no wise person has found fault with the manner of this dispensation” [Col. 0223B].

After these things had been read, the monks said: “If it pleases the holy synod, let the letter of Saint Athanasius sent to Rufinianus be brought and read.”

The holy synod said: “Let the request of the most reverend monks be fulfilled.”

The aforementioned monk Stephen, holding the book in his hands, read:

Letter of Saint Athanasius to Rufinianus.

“Athanasius sends greetings in the Lord to his beloved and most loving fellow-minister Rufinianus.

“And after other matters:

“Because of your love of goodness and ecclesiastical order—for this truly befits your Reverence—you asked about those who, having been forcibly taken away by necessity, were not so corrupted in the evil faith; and you wished me to write to you what the synods had judged concerning them, both here and everywhere. Know, my most beloved lord, that at the beginning, when the violence that had occurred ceased, a synod was held, with bishops also present who belonged to the party of those who are outside. A synod was also held among the fellow-ministers who live in Greece, and likewise among those in Spain and Gaul; and what was approved here was approved everywhere.

“Thus, those who fall and preside over impiety are forgiven when they have repented, but are not thereafter given a place in the clergy. As for those who were not authors of impiety, but were carried away through necessity and force, it was decided that pardon should be granted them and that they should retain a place in the clergy, especially when they had offered a persuasive defense [Col. 0223D]. It was decided that this be done as an act of dispensation. For they confirmed that they had not migrated to impiety. But, lest certain most impious men who had been ordained corrupt the churches, they chose rather to yield to violence and bear the burden than to destroy the peoples.

“In pursuing this course, they also seemed to us to speak persuasively, since they excused themselves by saying that Aaron, the brother of Moses, also joined in the people’s transgression in the wilderness, yet had a defense (Exodus 32): namely, that the people should not return to Egypt and remain in idolatry. For the obvious reasoning was that, if they remained in the wilderness, they could cease from idolatry; but if they entered Egypt, they would continue and increase in impiety [Col. 0224A]. Therefore a dispensation was made concerning the clergy, and indulgence was granted to those who had been deceived and had suffered force. These things were also written at Rome and accepted by the Church of the Romans. I report them to your Reverence with confidence that your Piety will accept what has been approved.”

Sabbas and the most reverend monks who were with him said: “This is not merely the voice of Athanasius, but also that of the synods. For the same Father says that both Romans and Greeks accepted it, and he determines that those converted from heresy should indeed be received for repentance, but should not be admitted to the priesthood.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “The same Father does not declare that every heretic who has converted is not to be received; rather, he speaks of the leaders of heresy and of those who, wickedly and deliberately, pretend by their words to profess the truth in the presence of the orthodox, while inwardly they act wickedly. But let the same Father’s letter sent to Rufinianus be read again.”

When the passage was read that says, “Thus, those who fall and preside over impiety are forgiven when they have repented, but are not thereafter given a place in the clergy; but as for those who were not authors of impiety, but were carried away through necessity and force, it was decided that pardon should be granted them and that they should retain a place in the clergy, especially when they had offered a persuasive defense” [Col. 0224B],

the most reverend monks said: “Behold, as we said earlier, this holy Father does not receive into the priesthood those who turn from heresy.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “It is not as you understand it. The Father receives into the priesthood those who were not authors of impiety and who were dragged away and subjected to force; he did not admit into the priesthood those who had led or originated the heresy. In this he spoke well, excellently, and most justly.

“The Church knows the holy Athanasius as a victor five times over. He was repeatedly driven to Rome and expelled by the leaders of the Arian heresy in ignoble flight [that is, shameful expulsion]. When he returned and regained the churches, his enemies clung to him, changing with the times. Whenever they gained confidence during his absence, they returned to their former heresy and stirred up persecution against the pious. Therefore I think that the Father said this concerning such men, so that they would not be received into the priesthood. For both he himself and the other orthodox had suffered the most savage treatment from them” [Col. 0224D].

Sabbas, most reverend monk, said: “The Father was forgetful of injuries.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “This is clear. For he did not repay evil to anyone with evil. But because of his zeal for God and his defense of the Church, he could not possess kindness without discipline; rather, in these matters he placed first those things that belong to the vengeance of God.”

John, most reverend priest, monk, and vicar of the Eastern diocese, said: “That definition is blessed for the safeguarding of its hearers [variant: ‘Well read’; also in the Jol. manuscript].”

The monks, repeating their point, said: “But the Father admits those who were dragged away and subjected to force. Let them therefore say whether they were dragged away and subjected to force, and whether for that reason they departed from the truth” [Col. 0225A].

Hypatius and the bishops who were with him said: “We neither suffered force nor were dragged away; rather, we were born and raised in this heresy of ours, and grew up in it.”

Theodore, beloved of God, bishop of Catana, and the most holy bishops of Sicily who were with him, together with Epiphanius, deacon of the city of Catana, holding the place of Thomas, bishop of Sardinia, said: “Since the canons of the holy Fathers that have been read were spoken concerning both the Novatians and Encratites and the Arians, with whom shall we rank the adherents of this heresy?”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “We also find Manichaeans who do not receive images, and Marcionists, and those who confuse the natures of Christ—among the first [or: ‘one of the first’] being Peter the Fuller and Xenaias of Hierapolis, heretics, as well as Severus” [Col. 0225B].

Epiphanius, deacon of the most holy and great Church of Catana and holder of the place of Thomas, most holy archbishop of Sardinia, said: “Is the present novelty smaller than the earlier heresies, or greater?”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “What is evil is already evil, and especially in ecclesiastical matters. In matters of doctrine, whether one sins in a small matter or a great one, it is the same thing; for in either case the law of God is rejected.”

John, most reverend monk and vicar of the Eastern sees, said: “This heresy is worse than all heresies, the worst of evils, since it overturns the dispensation of the Savior” [Col. 0225C].

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “The statement of our Father Athanasius teaches us that the most reverend bishops should be received, unless some other fault has been committed by them.”

The holy synod said: “Let the remaining testimonies of the canonical authorities also be read.”

Constantine, deacon and notary of the venerable patriarchate, continued reading:

From the acts of the fourth holy and universal synod held at Chalcedon.

The Easterners and the most reverend bishops who were with them cried out: “We have all sinned; we all ask pardon.”

Again Thalassius, Eusebius, and Eustathius, most reverend bishops, said: “We have all sinned; we all ask pardon.”

And after other matters:

The most reverend bishop Juvenal rose and went over with them to the other side, and the Easterners and the most reverend bishops who were with them cried out: “God has brought you in well, O orthodox one; you have come well.”

And after many other things, the most reverend Illyrian bishops said: “We have all transgressed; we all ask pardon [or: ‘deserve pardon’].”

Sabbas, most reverend monk and hegumen of the monastery of Studium, said: “If it pleases the holy synod, let us see whether the ordinations of those who have been received were performed by heretics or not.”

The holy synod said: “Next, inquire also concerning their ordination” [Col. 0226A].

Antonius, most reverend monk, read:

From the Ecclesiastical History of Rufinus, Roman priest.

“Meanwhile Eusebius proceeded to Alexandria, where a council of confessors assembled—a small number, but sound in faith and great in merits. Some thought, burning with the fervor of faith, that no one who had in any way stained himself with the contagion of heretical communion ought ever again to be received into the priesthood.

“But those who, imitating the Apostle, sought not what was useful to themselves but what was useful to the many, or who imitated Christ, who, although he is the life of all, humbled himself and descended into death for the salvation of all, so that life might be found even among the dead, said that it was better to humble themselves somewhat for the sake of those who had been cast down and to bend down for the sake of those who had been crushed, so that they might raise them up again [Col. 0226B]. They should not seek the kingdoms of heaven for themselves alone by the merit of purity; rather, it would be more glorious if they deserved to enter there with many others. Therefore it seemed right to them that, once only the leaders of the perfidy had been cut off, the remaining priests should be given the choice—if they wished, after renouncing the error of their perfidy, to turn to the faith of the Fathers and to the decrees. They should not deny access to those returning, but rather rejoice over their confession.

“For the younger son in the Gospel, who had squandered his father’s property, when he came to himself not only deserved to be received but was also judged worthy of his father’s embraces; he received the ring of faith and was clothed in a robe (Luke 15). What else are these things than the insignia of the priesthood?

“When, therefore, that priestly and apostolic order had approved such opinions, brought forward on the authority of the Gospel, by decree of the council the administration of the East was entrusted to Asterius and the others who were with him, while Eusebius was appointed to the West. In that decree of the council a fuller discussion of the Holy Spirit was also added, so that the Holy Spirit might be believed to possess the same substance and divinity as the Father and the Son, since there were again appearing those who separated that same Holy Spirit from the glorification of the Father and the Son” [Col. 0226C].

Constantine, most reverend deacon and notary, read:

From the Ecclesiastical History of Socrates.

“Photinus, formerly bishop of Sirmium, was a disciple of Marcellus of Ancyra; and he too said that the Lord was merely a man, as did Marcellus” [Col. 0226D].

Again he read from the Ecclesiastical History of Socrates:

“Those who had assembled at Sardica first condemned the madness of these men [or: ‘condemned them without a hearing’]. Confirming the definition of the faith of Nicaea, they rejected and anathematized inequality. They restored their sees to Paul and Athanasius, and also to Marcellus of Ancyra, who gave an account and said that whatever he had expounded in his books had not been understood—especially since he himself had driven away those who said that the Lord was merely a man.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Many canonical books, as well as synodical and patristic writings, have now been reread [Col. 0227A]; and they have taught us to receive those converted from heresy, unless perhaps some malicious fault is found in them.”

The holy synod said: “You have done well, lord, by teaching us through both letters and synodical writings to recognize the reception of heretics.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let what was read from Saint Athanasius be read again.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be read according to the command of our holy Father.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let it be read at the request of the most reverend monks.”

Stephen, most reverend monk and keeper of the books, read the letter of Saint Athanasius to Rufinianus, as it is written.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “As we said beforehand, [Col. 0227B] so is the mind of our Father.”

The most reverend monks said: “We, your unworthy servants, also said earlier that whatever the holy and universal synods receive, we receive—unless there is something that stands in the way.”

Peter, priest beloved of God and occupying the place of Adrian, pope of Rome, said: “This is clear. For in Rome there was Macarius the heretic, sent there by the Sixth Synod; and our Father, Pope Benedict of holy memory, gave him forty days’ time. Each day he sent Boniface, his counselor, to him, and instructed him with admonitory words from divine Scripture. He never wished to be corrected. He did this in order to persuade him and receive him.”

[Col. 0227C] The holy synod said: “If the bishops being examined consent with their whole mind, thanks be to God and to them. But if they harbor deceit, let God judge them, as he judged Arius and Nestorius.”

The bishops who were being examined anathematized themselves, saying: “Because we are not acting deceitfully; but if we do not confess as the catholic Church does, may we have the anathema from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let us proceed with the matters proposed.”

Peter, priest beloved of God and occupying the place of the most holy Roman pope, said: “As the historians relate, Saint Meletius was ordained by the Arians. He went up onto the ambo and preached ‘of one substance’ [homoousion]. His ordination, however, was not rejected.”

[Col. 0227D] Theodore, most holy bishop of Catana, and the bishops who were with him in Sicily, said: “The archpriest of the apostolic see speaks truly.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “We find the holy Fathers differing in nothing; rather, as all possess the same Spirit, they teach and preach the very same thing. But, devising a certain dispensation, Saint Father Athanasius explained it in this way. Therefore he judged that those who were not teachers of heresy should be received into the clergy.”

The most reverend monks said: “Whatever has been judged [Col. 0228A] in the midst of your holy synod, we receive.”

The holy synod said: “We hope that after the synod no one will be led astray, according to what they anathematized themselves in their concessions [Greek: depositions]: ‘For if we return to our former heresy, may we be deposed.’”

Constantine, bishop beloved of God of Constantia in Cyprus, said [Note: [Col. 0227D] Greek adds: “Most sacred lord, if they are bringing petitions, let them present them; otherwise, let them act, and thus the holy synod will judge concerning them.” But they said: “We have petitions prepared, and we shall present them.”]: [lacuna].

“They have their petitions in their hands [Note: [Col. 0228D] The most glorious princes said: “They have their petitions in their hands.”], and are ready to present them.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Meanwhile, let the remaining material concerning the proposed question of the holy canons be read.”

[Col. 0228B] Cosmas, most reverend deacon, notary, and venerable cubicularius of the patriarchate, read.

From the Life of our holy Father Sabbas:

“Origen and Theodore of Mopsuestia were subjected to the common and universal anathema of the holy and venerable Fifth Synod, which was assembled at Constantinople, as were the statements made by Evagrius and Didymus [statements concerning pre-existence and restoration]—namely, their assertion that he existed before the substance, and their confession concerning restoration to the former state—with the agreement and presence of the four patriarchs. When our emperor, whom God preserve, sent to Jerusalem the acts of the synod [Col. 0228C], and all the bishops of Palestine confirmed and strengthened them by hand and word, except Alexander of Abila [of Abila], who for this reason was expelled from the episcopate and buried beneath the earth by an earthquake at Byzantium, certain new Laurites [Neo-Laurites] separated themselves from catholic communion. But Patriarch Eustochius attacked them in various ways and admonished them for eight months. When, despite his prayers, he could not persuade them to commune with the catholic Church, he used imperial orders and, through Anastasius the duke, expelled them from the New Laura and freed the entire province from their contagion.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “You see that the archbishop spent eight months entreating them and acting patiently [Col. 0228D] toward them, although he knew that they had already been anathematized by the synod. Therefore we have now heard the canonical precepts, the synodical declarations, and the judgments of the holy Fathers: all who approached from any heresy were received with one mind.”

The holy synod said: “This is how the truth stands, unless there is another canonical cause that prevents it.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Does this please everyone? [Greek adds: ‘that we should receive them?’; and so also the manuscript of Joly.]”

The holy synod said: “It pleases everyone.”

[Col. 0229A] The most reverend monks said: “It pleases us also.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “And again we say: if there is no other canonical cause that deposes the person approaching, he shall be received. For without doubt the canonical precepts must be preserved.”

The most reverend monks said: “In accordance with the six holy and universal synods, we receive those who are converted from heresy, provided there is no wicked cause in them.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “We too [Greek adds: ‘all of us’] define this way, having been taught by our holy Fathers.”

The most reverend monks said: “If some monks are absent from the holy synod, what is to be done with them?”

[Col. 0229B] Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “We shall persuade them by the canons that have been read beforehand. Nevertheless, why did they not come to this holy synod?”

Sabbas, most reverend monk, said: “I do not know; but they are apart.”

Euthymius, bishop beloved of God of Sardis [Sardeis; Sardis], said: “As we requested, let the books now be brought and read, and let us see whether those ordained by heretics ought to be received.”

Constantine, most reverend deacon and notary, said: “Since you said that examples of those ordained by heretics should be read, we have books at hand; and if you command it, let them be read.”

[Col. 0229C] The holy synod said: “Let them be read.”

Stephen, most reverend monk and keeper of the books, read:

From the Ecclesiastical History of Rufinus:

“This internal persecution, although it was brief, was first made to grow by Macedonius when he advanced into the episcopate. Acacius and Patrophilus, however, expelled Maximus of Jerusalem and appointed Cyril in his place.”

After this Cosmas, most reverend deacon, notary, and venerable cubicularius of the patriarchate, read:

From the fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History of Theodore the Reader:

“For Dioscorus, contrary to what the regulations allow, granting himself the ordination to the episcopate of Constantinople [Col. 0229D], advanced into that episcopate a certain Anatolius, who was carrying out the responses of the Alexandrian Church at Constantinople, while Eutyches was present and assisting him. Anatolius said to him with gratitude [he said it cleverly], not knowing what was to come: ‘Wherever you have walked, you have sanctified.’ These things took place during the consulship of Protogenes and Asterius.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “What do you say about Anatolius? Was he not a leading figure of the holy [Note: [Col. 0229D] Fourth] Synod? And behold, he was ordained by the impious Dioscorus [Greek adds: ‘with Eutyches also present’]. Therefore let us too receive those ordained by heretics, just as [Col. 0230A] Anatolius was received. And again, truly it is the voice of God: ‘Children shall not die for their fathers, but each one shall die for his own sin’ [Ezek. XVIII]; and consecration is from God. But if some perhaps doubt concerning Anatolius, let what concerns him be read.”

Cosmas, deacon and venerable cubicularius of the patriarchate, read:

The Prologue of the holy and universal Council of Chalcedon:

“When the holy and universal council had also assembled, according to the sacred command, in the city of Chalcedon—that is, Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, most religious priest, occupying the place of the most holy [Col. 0230B] archbishop of senior Rome, Leo; and Anatolius, most holy bishop of Constantinople, the great and renowned New Rome—”

The most reverend monks said: “We receive this also.”

Again Constantine, venerable deacon and notary of the patriarchate, read:

From the Life of our holy Father Sabbas:

“Now, when Flavian and Elias, the patriarchs of Sidon, were remaining in place, as has been said, and were using flattering and accommodating letters to the emperor, while abolishing the synod assembled at Sidon against the right faith and returning to their own thrones, those around Soterichus and [Col. 0230C] Philoxenus became greatly enraged and stirred the emperor to immense anger, as though he had been deceived by the patriarchs’ cunning and pretense. Having received whatever authority they desired, together with sufficient gold publicly distributed at Antioch, they afflicted Flavian in many ways and, so to speak, suffocated him, compelling him to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon. Thus they drove him from the episcopate and condemned him to exile.

“When the emperor learned this, he rejoiced and sent Severus, the leader of the Acephali, as bishop of Antioch. Having seized the patriarchate, Severus displayed many atrocities toward those who did not commune with him. He sent his synodical letters to Elias the archbishop; and, when they were not received, he stirred the emperor to anger. Again, in the month of May of the sixth [Col. 0230D] indiction, he sent his own synodical letters to Jerusalem, with certain clerics and imperial force [that is, soldiers]. When our Father Sabbas of holy memory learned this, he went up into the holy city with the other hegoumens of the desert. They pursued from the holy city those who had come with Severus’s synodical letters.

“Gathering a multitude of monks from everywhere, they cried out before the holy Calvary together with the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying: ‘Anathema to Severus and to those who commune with him!’ The magistriani, as well as the officials and soldiers sent by the emperor, were present and heard them.

“For this Severus, held by dreadful arrogance and relying on imperial power, subjected the Council of Chalcedon to ten thousand [Col. 0231A] times ten thousand [or: thousands upon thousands] anathemas. Striving to confirm the foreign opinion of Eutyches, he preached one nature of the Lord Christ, the Son of God, after the incarnation and assumption of humanity from the Virgin—a corrupted nature. Being a friend of disturbance, he devised many innovations against the Church’s correct dogmas and laws.

“For he receives the most impious and most brigand-like Second Council of Ephesus [most brigand-like]; and he says that it is like the council that previously assembled in the same city of Ephesus. He declares equal in teaching Cyril, the God-bearing bishop of the Alexandrians, and Dioscorus, who received the heretic Eutyches into communion as his like-minded associate, while he deposed and killed the most holy and most orthodox Flavian, archbishop of the imperial city. [Col. 0231B]

“Thus advancing in impiety, Severus sharpened his tongue for blasphemy against God and divided in his own words the indivisible divinity of the Trinity. For saying and affirming that essence [Greek: subsistence] is nature and nature is essence [Greek: subsistence], and knowing no difference between these terms, he dared to call the holy, worshipful, and consubstantial Trinity a Trinity of divine essences [Greek: subsistences], natures, divinities, and gods.

“Therefore the emperor Anastasius compelled Elias the archbishop to admit this corrupter and ravager of souls into communion. When Elias absolutely refused to do so, the emperor, boiling with fury, sent a certain Olympius, a Caesarean who held the command [Col. 0231C] of Palestine, and with him also a universal letter [Greek: accommodating letter], written at Sidon, declaring that the Council of Chalcedon was not to be received, so that in every way he might drive Elias from the episcopate.

“When Olympius arrived with imperial power and used many devices and machinations, displaying the aforementioned letter, he expelled Elias from the episcopate and banished him to Aila. But he made John, the son of Marcian, bishop of Jerusalem on the first day [the third, according to the manuscript of Joly] of September, at the beginning of the tenth [another reading: eleventh] indiction. John had promised that he would admit Severus, a communicant, and anathematize the Council of Chalcedon.

“When the sanctified Sabbas and [Col. 0231D] the other Fathers of the desert learned that John had made this promise, they assembled and protested that he should not receive Severus into communion, but should rather risk himself for the Council of Chalcedon, since he would have all of them as his helpers. Thus John violated all that he had promised the duke, out of reverence for the Fathers.

“When the emperor Anastasius learned that John had made his promises ineffectual, and, enraged against Olympius, who had escaped by flight, sent Anastasius Pamphili, who held the command of Palestine, to force John either to receive Severus into communion and anathematize the Council of Chalcedon, or to expel him from the episcopate.

“On arriving at Jerusalem, [Col. 0232A] he suddenly seized the archbishop and sent him into public custody. All the inhabitants of the holy city rejoiced, because he had been the plotter and betrayer of Elias the archbishop.

“A certain Zacharias, who administered the office of governor of the Caesarean city, secretly entered the fortress and gave John this advice: ‘If you wish to act well and not be deprived of the episcopate, let no one persuade you to receive Severus into communion. Instead, make a pretense to the duke and say: “I do not delay doing what is demanded here; but, lest some people say that I am acting under necessity and compulsion, let me be released from here. After two days, when it is Sunday, I shall eagerly do what you command.”’ Trusting these words, the duke restored him to the Church.

“Released [Col. 0232B] during the night, the archbishop summoned the entire monastic community to the holy city, gathering them from everywhere. When certain people had counted the multitude and reported that the assembly numbered ten thousand monks, and since even the whole church could not contain so large a crowd, it seemed best that on the Sundays [on Sunday] they should all assemble in the house of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, since it was sufficient to receive the multitude. At the same time they would hasten to meet Hypatius, the emperor’s cousin, who had then been released from Vitalian’s captivity and was coming to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer.

“When all—monks and citizens alike—had assembled in the aforementioned honored house, Anastasius the duke and Zacharias the consul also arrived. When the consul [Hypatius] had come [Col. 0232C] and entered the temple of the first martyr Stephen with the multitude, and the duke thought that the emperor’s will was about to be accomplished, the archbishop went up onto the ambo, taking with him Theodosius and Sabbas, the chief monks and leaders. For many hours the whole people cried out, saying: ‘Anathematize the heretics and strengthen the synod!’

“Immediately, by common agreement, the three anathematized Nestorius, Eutyches, Severus, and Soterichus of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and everyone who would not receive the Council of Chalcedon.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “We have heard the commands of the Fathers. What, then, is required? Do you receive those ordained by heretics?”

The holy synod said: “Yes, lord, we have heard, [Col. 0232D] and they ought to be received.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Indeed, many of those who sat in the Sixth Holy Synod were ordained by Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter—the teachers, namely, of the heresy that preached one will in Christ. For these men successively occupied the throne of Constantinople. From Peter, the last of them to precede the same throne, until the Sixth Synod, no more than fifteen years passed. Those who were bishops during that period—Thomas, John, and Constantine—were ordained at the indicated time [Greek adds: ‘during the period when those called heretics are known to have existed; [Col. 0233A] and for this reason’] by the aforementioned heretics, and they were not rejected. For the heresy then lasted fifty years. Yet the Fathers of the Sixth Synod anathematized those four, although these men had ordained them.”

The holy synod said: “It is clear.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Cyprus, said: “It has been sufficiently demonstrated, most honorable brothers, that those who approach from the heretics are to be received. But if anyone deliberately goes to a heretic and accepts ordination, let him be without reception.”

The most reverend monks said: “We also have a letter of Saint Basil to the Nicopolitans concerning this, and we beg that it be read.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let it be read.”

[Col. 0233B] Constantine, deacon and notary, read.

From the letter of Saint Basil to the Nicopolitans:

“I do not recognize as a bishop, nor would I number among the priests of Christ, the man who, by profane hands, has been advanced to leadership for the destruction of the faith. This is my judgment. But if you have any share with us, you will undoubtedly think this with us. If, however, you take counsel from us, each person is master of his own judgment. For our part, we are innocent of this blood.

“I have written these things not distrusting you, but strengthening the hesitation of certain persons, by making known my own judgment concerning the refusal to admit certain people into communion, and also those who have received promotion by their hands. [Col. 0233C] Therefore, when peace has been made, consider counting yourselves among the sacred fullness [Greek: ‘and lest, having received the laying-on of their hands, after peace has been made they should later attempt to enroll themselves …’].”

The most reverend monks said: “Behold, the Father rejects ordination by heretics, saying: ‘Nor would I number among the priests of Christ the man who, by profane hands, has been advanced to leadership for the destruction of the faith.’”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “I too reject those who have been ordained for such a reason and for the destruction of the faith—especially if orthodox bishops were present, by whom they could have been consecrated. For this is the Father’s meaning. But if a synodical promulgation and the agreement of the churches have been made for the sake [Col. 0233D] of orthodoxy, whoever presumes to be ordained by profane heretics shall suffer deposition.”

The holy synod said: “This is a just judgment.”

The most reverend monks said: “And how is it that at the end of the letter it is written: ‘Therefore, when peace has been made, [Col. 0234A] consider counting yourselves among the sacred fullness’? For behold, even after peace, those who were ordained are not received.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “The Father did not say that they were not to be received, but that they should beware lest those who wished to unite themselves with the clergy of the orthodox should suffer violence. For in truth this would not happen without necessity and difficulty. Nevertheless, at that time the excellent Father, when there were many orthodox bishops, forbade the sons of the Church to make use of ordination by Arians; for there was no defense available.

“Since this is true, and those who succeeded that Father as leaders of the Church did not misunderstand his intention, they received those who had been appointed by heretics and later improved, as we have learned from what has been read beforehand. Everywhere the Fathers agree [Col. 0234B] with one another; there is no contradiction among them. Rather, they oppose those who have not at all learned their accommodations and intentions.”

The most reverend monks said: “Everything appropriate has been resolved.”

The holy synod said: “Let the bishops present read their own petitions, as those approaching the catholic Church.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let them read them after the matter of the two chapters under inquiry has been carefully examined—namely, both concerning those ordained by heretics and concerning those who approach from heresy to the holy catholic Church.”

Hypatius, bishop of Nicaea, read his petition. [Col. 0234C] It is the same petition that Basil, most reverend bishop of Ancyra, composed.

Leo, bishop of Rhodes; Nicholas of Hierapolis; Gregory of Pessinus; Gregory [George] of Antioch in Pisidia; and Leo of Carpathus read copies of the same petition.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Once their professions have become known through the reading of their petitions, their reception will take place at another gathering, provided there is nothing else in them that forbids it.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be done as you have commanded.”

And at this point the holy synod rose and praised in this manner:

“Many years to the emperors! Many years to Irene and Constantine, the great rulers and emperors! Many years to the orthodox emperors! Strengthen, O Lord, those who depose [Col. 0234D] the utterances of the innovation that has arisen! Grant them a devout life!”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “May the peace of God be with us all. Amen.”

## ACT II

[Col. 0233]

[Col. 0233D] In the name of the Lord and ruler Jesus Christ, our true God, under the rule of our most pious and Christ-loving lords Constantine and Irene, his mother crowned by God, in the eighth year of their consulship, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction.

When the holy and universal synod had assembled—which by [Col. 0235A] divine grace and by the pious decree of those same emperors, confirmed by God, had been convened in the famous metropolis of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia—that is, Peter, most reverend first priest of the most holy Roman Church of the holy apostle Peter, and Peter, most reverend priest, monk, and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sabbas situated at Rome, occupying the place of the apostolic see’s flourishing and blessed archbishop of senior Rome, Adrian; and Tarasius, flourishing and most holy archbishop of the great and renowned Constantinople, New Rome [Greek adds: ‘and the bishops who were with them’]; together with John and Thomas, most reverend priest-monks and vicars of the apostolic sees of the eastern diocese; and while they were seated before the most sacred ambo of the temple of the most holy great church called Sophia [Col. 0235B], with the most glorious and magnificent officials present and listening—namely, Petrona, the famous former consul, patrician, and count of the imperial service preserved by God; John, the imperial doorkeeper and logothete of the military logothesion; and the entire holy synod, according to the order recorded in the first act; with the God-loving archimandrites and hegoumens also present, together with the entire monastic fullness, and the holy and undefiled Gospels of God set before them—

Nicephorus, deacon beloved of God and venerable chartophylax of the patriarchate, said: “A royal messenger is standing before the doors of this venerable temple, bringing with him the bishop of Neocaesarea.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let them enter.”

The illustrious royal messenger entered and said: “I have been sent by our good lords to bring the most reverend bishop of Neocaesarea to your pious and holy synod, and I have presented him.”

The holy synod said: “May God preserve our pious emperors.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said to the bishop of Neocaesarea: “Has the truth remained unknown to you until now? Or did you disregard it as though it were known to you? If it passed you by as unknown, do not be ashamed to learn the correct statement, since you were not ashamed to learn the perverse one.”

Gregory, most reverend bishop of Neocaesarea, said: “Believe me, lord, it was as though it were unknown. But I ask to learn, as the Lord and the holy synod command.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Tell us what you wish to learn.”

Gregory, most reverend bishop of Neocaesarea, said: “Since this entire assembly says and thinks one thing, I have learned and am certain that this is the truth which is now being sought and proclaimed. Therefore I ask pardon for my former wrongs, and I wish, together with everyone, both to be enlightened and to be taught. My offenses and sins are indeed immense. As the Lord moves the holy synod and my most holy lord to compassion, so let it be.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Are you perhaps trying, as though with a veil of cunning, to obscure your own opinion, pretending the truth in words while acting wickedly in your mind?”

Gregory, most reverend bishop of Neocaesarea, said: “Far from it. I confess the truth and do not lie, nor shall I make my statement false.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “You ought to have opened your ears in former years and listened to the divine apostle Paul saying: ‘Hold fast the traditions which you received, whether by word or by our letter’ (1 Thess. II); and again, writing to Timothy and Titus: ‘Avoid profane innovations of words’ (1 Tim. VI; Tit. III). For what is more profane and more an innovation of words than to say that Christians are idolaters?”

[Col. 0236B] Gregory, most reverend bishop of Neocaesarea, said: “It was evil, and we confess that it was evil. But it happened in this way, and we acted in this way; therefore we ask pardon for our offenses. I confess, lord, before the dignity of your holiness and before all the brothers of the holy synod, that we have sinned, committed iniquity, and acted wickedly; and we ask pardon for this.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “We say that, when he comes together again with a petition in the next act, we may recognize what belongs to him.”

The holy synod said: “As your holiness commands, let the bishop who is present come with a petition, and in the next act let action be taken according to what seems good.”

Leontius, illustrious imperial secretary, said: “The most sacred synod, gathered by God, remembers how, at the preceding assembly, the divine writings of our great emperors preserved by God were read. They contained a record of letters sent synodically by the most holy and most blessed pope of senior Rome and by the venerable chief priests of the East, in two quires. Since these have now also been brought, we submit them for whatever may seem good.”

The holy synod said: “Let the petitions of the most holy and most blessed Pope Adrian of senior Rome be read.”

Nicephorus, illustrious imperial secretary, read the translation of the Latin letters of Adrian, Roman pope.

“Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most pious and serene emperors and triumphant rulers, beloved sons in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ, Constantine and Irene, the Augusti.” (See Patrologia, vol. XCVI, col. 1215.)

[Col. 0236D]

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Did you yourselves, after receiving these letters from the pope, bring them to our pious emperors?”

Peter and Peter, priests beloved of God and occupying the place of Adrian, most holy Roman pope, said: “We ourselves received such letters from our apostolic Father and brought them to the pious lords.”

John, most magnificent logothete, said: “The most honorable Sicilians also know this: Theodore, bishop beloved of God of Catana, and the most reverend deacon Epiphanius who is with him, who occupies the place of the archbishop of Sardinia. At the command of our pious emperors, both went to Rome with the most reverend apocrisiarius of our most holy patriarch.”

Theodore, bishop beloved of God of Catana, said: “When the pious imperial power, through its honorable commands, ordered Leo the God-fearing priest, who is with me and is a servant of your holiness, to be sent together with the precious letter of my most sacred lord, the governor [strategos] of the Sicilians—namely, of my province—sent me to Rome with the pious command of our orthodox emperors. When we departed, we proclaimed the faith and [Col. 0237B] orthodoxy of their pious empire.”

And the most blessed pope, hearing this, said: “If this happens during the days of their rule, God will magnify their pious empire above the former kingdoms.” For this reason he also sent the written report that was read to our pious emperors, together with letters to your holiness and with his vicars who are present here and preside.

Cosmas, deacon, notary, and cubicularius, said: “Other letters were also sent by the most holy pope of senior Rome to Tarasius, our most holy and universal patriarch. As your holy assembly commands, action will also be taken concerning these.”

The holy synod said: “Let them be read.”

The aforementioned Cosmas read:

[Col. 0237C] Letter of Adrian, most holy pope of senior Rome, translated from the Latin language into the Greek tongue.

(See Patrol., vol. XCVI, col. 1233.)

Peter and Peter, most reverend priests and vicars of Adrian, the most holy pope of senior Rome, said: “Let Tarasius, most holy patriarch of the imperial city, tell us whether he agrees with the letters of Adrian, the most holy pope of senior Rome, or not.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “The most sacred apostle Paul, enlightened by the light of Christ and having begotten us through the Gospel, wrote to the Romans, approving their zeal for the sincere faith which they had in Christ, the true God, and said: ‘Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world’ [Col. 0237D] (Rom. I). It is necessary to follow this testimony, and he acts foolishly who tries to resist it.

“Therefore Adrian, bishop of senior Rome, since he shared in the company of those who deserved to be strengthened by the testimony just mentioned, wrote explicitly and truthfully to our pious emperors and to our humility, affirming that the ancient tradition of the catholic Church is good and entirely sound. For we too, by examining the Scriptures and proving the matter syllogistically, have investigated it. Thus, what we have confessed, we confess and shall confess; we agree with and confirm it, and we shall remain in the meaning of the letters that have been read, accepting images and representations according to the ancient tradition of our Fathers. We venerate them with affectionate love, as having been made in honor of the name of Christ our God, of the undefiled Lady, the holy Mother of God, of the holy angels, and of all the saints, placing our service [Greek: latria] and our faith most clearly in the one true God alone.”

The holy synod said: “The entire most sacred synod believes this, thinks this, and teaches this as dogma.”

Peter and Peter, priests beloved of God and legates of the apostolic see, said: “Let the holy synod tell us whether it accepts the letters of Adrian, the most holy pope of senior Rome, or not.”

The holy synod said: “We follow them, receive them, and accept them.”

John, priest beloved of God and legate of the eastern diocese, said:

It is also fitting at the present time to sing with the Psalmist: “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have embraced one another” (Ps. 84). We know that our Lord Jesus Christ is Mercy and Truth; and through participation in him the most holy patriarchs and the shepherds of the whole world are both called and truly are so. For mercy and truth have met one another—namely, Adrian, the most holy pope of elder Rome, and Tarasius, the most holy patriarch of reigning Constantinople. Sharing and confessing one and the same belief, they have embraced righteousness and peace.

For Irene, aptly named (Pheronyma) [Const. “sharing and confessing one and the same belief. Righteousness and peace have kissed one another. Phe.”], reigning and governing by God’s decree [Col. 0238C] [having a name consonant and corresponding with the reality of the matter], moved by God and desiring and willing the beauty of the Church, by means of her letter embraced aptly named righteousness—namely, the most holy Roman Church—and moved it to come into their midst, to gladden the holy assembly present, and also to make the orthodox faith manifest. And now great joy has arisen from the reading of the sacred letter of the most holy pope Adrian, sent both to our divinely protected and most tranquil emperors and to the most holy and thrice-blessed patriarch Tarasius; and for this we give great thanks to God, because we have been counted worthy to enjoy so great a joy and gladness.

Blessed is God, who has raised up for us such an empire—one that is always concerned and arouses the peoples to [Col. 0238D] one concerted purpose, unanimity, and preservation of the divine canons and of the traditions of the most holy Church. But may Christ our God, through the most holy Mother of God who bore him, and through all his saints, and through you, his priests, who hold one mind and have no deceit in your hearts but hasten to fulfill what has been written, show your promises to be truthful; preserve our good lords for long life; glorify them and exalt their horn; place their enemies beneath their feet; make them worthy also in the age to come to be numbered among the holy kings; and preserve this most holy synod.

Agapius, the most holy bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, [Col. 0239A] said: It is written in our divine Scriptures that God separated the light from the darkness. Behold, now that the dark heresy of those who hold evil opinions has ceased, the light of orthodoxy has shone forth for all. Following that light, I too receive and salute the sacred and venerable icons, and I submit those who do not hold this view to anathema.

John, the most holy bishop of Ephesus, said: As the honorable letter of the most holy Roman pope contains, so I believe and so I confess, by the grace of Christ our true God.

Constantine, the most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: I agree in every respect with the address that was read and sent by Adrian, the most holy Roman pope, to our good lords; and likewise with the letter directed to the most holy [Col. 0239B] patriarch. Thus I confess, and with this faith I shall depart to the tribunal of Christ our true God.

Basil, the most holy bishop of Ancyra, said: As the letter of the most holy pope Adrian of elder Rome contains, and as the mind of our most holy Father and universal patriarch holds, so I think, so I hold, and so I shall teach; and with this mind of mine I shall also depart into the age to come.

Nicholas, the most holy bishop of Cyzicus, said: According to the letter of the most holy pope Adrian of elder Rome and the exposition of the confession of our most holy patriarch Tarasius, I think and shall think; and with this confession of mine I shall be brought into that world.

Euthymius, the most holy bishop of Sardis, said: [Col. 0239C] I too, sincerely and without hesitation following the letter read aloud of the most holy pope Adrian of elder Rome, promise and confess that I hold this belief both concerning the orthodox faith and concerning the most holy icons—not accepting them as some new dogma, but knowing with complete certainty that there is a tradition concerning them from the holy apostles and the most sacred teachers who established and left this tradition in the holy Church of God. Therefore, with my whole soul I receive such venerable icons, with the honor that is fitting and with reverential veneration. But those who hold or teach otherwise or contrary to this concerning the holy icons, judging them alien to the catholic Church, I reject and denounce as heretics.

Peter, the most holy bishop of Nicomedia, said: According to the letter read aloud of the most holy pope Adrian of elder [Col. 0239D] Rome, and according to the faith of the most holy and universal patriarch Tarasius, I receive and adore the venerable icons, and I shall teach this, as one who will render an account to our judge and God on the day of judgment.

Elias, the most holy bishop of Crete, said: According to the honorable letter of the most holy pope Adrian of elder Rome, so I confess and hold the precious and sacred icons, never at any time to be changed, and not merely adoring them now. But those who do not confess thus I anathematize.

Stauracius, the most holy bishop of Chalcedon, said: According to the letter of Adrian, the most holy pope of elder Rome, which was sent to our most holy patriarch Tarasius, so I too receive, salute, [Col. 0240A] and embrace the sacred icons, since they are like the pledge of my salvation. But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

Nicephorus, bishop of Dyrrachium, said: According to the report sent by Adrian, the most holy pope of elder Rome, to our pious emperors and to the most holy and universal patriarch Tarasius, and also according to the teaching, faith, and confession of that most holy archbishop Tarasius, I think and hold; and with this confession of mine I shall end the brief span of my life and stand before the terrible tribunal of Christ.

Epiphanius, deacon of the Church of Catana and locum tenens of the archbishop of Sardinia, said: [Col. 0240B] The report sent to the pious and Christ-loving emperors by the most blessed pope Adrian of elder Rome, together with his letter sent to Tarasius, the most holy and universal patriarch, has displayed through its reading the clearest boundary of orthodoxy and the tradition of the holy apostles.
