Therefore, agreeing with these things in every respect and following the path of right understanding, I honor, adore, and receive the venerable and sacred icons handed down in the Church from ancient times; but the one who does not agree in these matters I turn away from as a participant in a heretical assembly and consign to anathemas.

Leo, presbyter of the most holy Church of Constantinople and locum tenens of the metropolis of Side, said: According to the synodal letters of the most holy pope of elder Rome that have been read, and the teaching of the most holy patriarch Tarasius, I receive the venerable images according to [Col. 0240C] the ancient custom; and those who do not hold this position I anathematize.

Nicholas, hegumen of Aprus and locum tenens of the metropolis of Tyana, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope, which have been read, I receive the venerable icons according to the ancient tradition; and whoever does not hold this position I anathematize.

Constantine, the most holy bishop of Gangra, said: According to the reports of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I receive the venerable icons according to the ancient tradition. But those who do not hold this view I submit to anathema.

Nicetas, the most holy bishop of Claudiopolis, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I receive the venerable icons [Col. 0240D] according to the ancient custom; and those who do not hold this view I submit to anathema.

Theodore, the most holy bishop of Myra in Lycia, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of Rome, which have been read, I believe and profess, and I adore and embrace the holy and venerable icons; and those who do not hold this view I anathematize and reject.

Theophylact, deacon and exarch, locum tenens of the metropolis of Caria, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I profess; and those who do not hold this view I submit to anathema.

Michael, the most holy bishop of Synada, [Col. 0241A] said: According to the synodal letters sent by Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, I confess and receive, according to the ancient tradition, the sacred and venerable icons; and those who do not receive them thus I submit to anathema.

Eustathius, the most holy bishop of Laodicea, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been recited, I confess and receive the precious and sacred icons according to the ancient tradition; and those who do not hold this view I submit to anathema.

Constantine, bishop of Perga, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I confess and receive the precious and sacred images according to the ancient tradition; and those who do not hold this view I submit to anathema.

[Col. 0241B] Anastasius, the most holy bishop of Old Nicopolis in Epirus, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been reviewed, I confess, receive, and adore the sacred and holy icons according to the ancient tradition. But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

Christopher, the most holy bishop of Phasis, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope, which have been read, I confess and receive and adore the venerable icons according to the ancient custom. But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

Theodore, the most holy bishop of Seleucia, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I confess and receive the sacred and venerable icons according to the ancient tradition. [Col. 0241C] But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

Gregory, presbyter of the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople and locum tenens of the metropolis of Mocissus, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I confess and receive and adore the sacred and venerable icons according to the ancient tradition. But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

Basil, the most holy bishop of Silae [Sylege], said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I confess and receive and adore the venerable and sacred images according to the ancient tradition of the Church. But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

Theodore, the most holy bishop of Catana, said: [Col. 0241D] Through the reading I have recognized the report, full of all orthodoxy, which the most holy pope Adrian of elder Rome sent to our pious and Christ-loving emperors and also to Tarasius, the honored and universal patriarch. Therefore I too agree with these things, and I entirely adore, embrace, and receive the sacred icons. But those who do not hold this view I consign to anathemas as aliens from the catholic Church.

Manuel, the most holy bishop of Adrianople in Thrace, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I confess and receive the holy and venerable icons according to the ancient [Col. 0242A] tradition of the catholic Church. But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

Marianus, the most holy bishop of Pompeiopolis, said: According to the synodal letters of Adrian, the most blessed pope of elder Rome, which have been read, I confess, receive, and adore the sacred and venerable icons according to the ancient tradition of the Church. But those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

John, the most holy bishop of Tauromenium, said: Since the letter sent by Pope Adrian of elder Rome to the pious emperors, and likewise to our universal patriarch Tarasius, is, as it were, the divine boundary of orthodoxy, so I profess, receiving the sacred icons according to the ancient tradition of the catholic Church. Those who do not hold this view I anathematize.

[Col. 0242B] Cyril, speaking on behalf of the most holy bishop of Gothia, promulgated the same declaration.

Theodore, the most holy bishop of Mitra [Greek, from the Joly manuscript: Bizya], promulgated the same declaration.

Gregory, presbyter and locum tenens of the bishop of Smyrna, promulgated the same declaration.

Gaudiosus, bishop of Messina, likewise.

Eustachius [Eustratius], the most holy bishop of Apamea, likewise.

John, deacon and locum tenens of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0241D] “Of the see” is absent in the Joly manuscript, as also in the Greek], likewise.

Peter, bishop of Germia, likewise.

Theodore, the most holy bishop of Palermo, likewise.

[Col. 0242C] John, the most holy bishop of Arcadiopolis, likewise.

Stephen, the most holy bishop of Bubon, likewise.

[gap] vicar of Leontopolis, likewise.

Sisinnius, the most holy bishop of Paros, likewise.

Constantine, the most holy bishop of Leontina, likewise.

Epiphanius, the most holy bishop of Miletus [Mitorum], likewise.

Theodore, the most holy bishop of Tauriana, likewise.

Nicetas, the most holy bishop of Proconnesus, likewise.

Christopher, the most holy bishop of Saint Cyriaca, [Col. 0242D] likewise.

Eustachius [Eustratius], the most holy bishop of Methymna, likewise.

Theotimus, the most holy bishop of Croton, likewise.

Theophilus, the most holy bishop of Chios, likewise.

Leo, the most holy bishop of Cius, likewise.

Basil, the most holy bishop of Nesos, likewise.

John, the most holy bishop of Aprus, likewise.

Ignatius, the most holy bishop of Prina, likewise.

Theophylact, the most holy bishop of Cypsela, likewise.

[Col. 0243A] Theodore, the most holy bishop of Tropaion, likewise.

Stephen, the most holy bishop of Sugda, likewise.

Sergius, the most holy bishop of Nicotera, likewise.

Gregory, presbyter and vicar of Nicopolis, likewise.

Leo, the most holy bishop of Mesembria, likewise.

Theodosius, the most holy bishop of Amorium, likewise.

Cyriacus, the most holy bishop of Drusipara, likewise.

Galata, presbyter, speaking on behalf of the most holy bishop of Rhegium, likewise.

[Col. 0243B] Theodosius, the most holy bishop of Nyssa, likewise.

Georgius, the most holy bishop of Camuliana, likewise.

Soterichus, the most holy bishop of Ciscissus, likewise.

Constantine, the most holy bishop of Mastaura, likewise.

Georgius, the most holy bishop of Briula, likewise.

John, the most holy bishop of Nyssa, likewise.

Theophylact, the most holy bishop of Tralles, likewise.

Basil [Note: [Col. 0243D] “Likewise” is also present in the Joly manuscript], the most holy bishop of Magnesia, likewise.

Sabbas, the most holy bishop of Anes, likewise.

[Col. 0243C] Gregory, the most holy bishop of Palaeaspole, likewise.

Basil, the most holy bishop of Magnesia on the Maeander, likewise.

Theophanius, the most holy bishop of Calpe, likewise.

Leo, the most holy bishop of Algiza, likewise.

Nicodemus, the most holy bishop of Eugaza, likewise.

Lucas [Lycastus], the most holy bishop of Bareta, likewise.

Theophylact, the most holy bishop of Hypaepa, likewise.

Theophanes, the most holy bishop of Lebedus, likewise.

[Col. 0243D] Stratonikos, the most holy bishop of Cyme, likewise.

Cosmas, the most holy bishop of Myrna, likewise.

Olbianus, the most holy bishop of Elaea, likewise.

Pardus, the most holy bishop of Pitane, likewise.

Basil, the most holy bishop of Pergamum, likewise.

Basil, the most holy bishop of Atramyttium, likewise.

Marianus [Marinus], the most holy bishop of Atandrus, likewise.

John, the most holy bishop of Assus, likewise.

John, the most holy bishop of Arcadiopolis, likewise.

[Col. 0244A] Leo, the most holy bishop of Phocaea, likewise.

Nicephorus, deacon and vicar of Gargara, likewise.

Constantine, deacon and vicar of Agae, likewise.

Theognius, [gap], vicar of Sion, likewise.

John, the most holy bishop of Rhaedestus, likewise.

John, the most holy bishop of Panium, likewise.

Melchisedech, the most holy bishop of Callipolis, likewise.

Leo, the most holy bishop of Madytus, likewise.

Theophylact, the most holy bishop of Chariopolis, likewise.

Thomas, the most holy bishop of Daonia, likewise.

Gregory, the most holy bishop of Theodoropolis, likewise.

[Col. 0244B] Sisinnius, the most holy bishop of Chalcis, likewise.

John, the most holy bishop of Brysis, likewise.

Benjamin, the most holy bishop of Lizica, likewise.

## ACT THREE

[Col. 0249]

[Col. 0249C] In the name of the Lord and ruler Jesus Christ, our true God. Under the rule of our most pious and Christ-loving lords Constantine and Irene, his mother redeemed by God, in the eighth year of their consulship, on the third day before the Kalends of October [Greek and Joly manuscript: fourth day], in the eleventh indiction.

The holy and universal synod having assembled—which, through divine grace and the pious decree of those same emperors, divinely confirmed, had been convened in Nicaea, the celebrated metropolitan city of the province of Bithynia—namely, with Peter, the most reverend first presbyter of the holy Roman Church of the holy apostle Peter, and Peter, the most reverend presbyter, monk, and hegumen of the venerable monastery of Saint Sabbas situated in Rome, representing the apostolic see of Adrian, the honored and most holy pope of elder Rome; and with Tarasius, the honored and most holy archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, of great renown, and John and Thomas, the most reverend presbyter-monks and [Col. 0250C] vicars of the apostolic sees of the eastern diocese;

and with them seated before the most holy ambo of the temple of the most holy great Church of God called Sophia; with the most glorious and magnificent judges present and listening—[Col. 0250D] namely, Petrona, the most praiseworthy former consul and patrician, and count of the imperial service preserved by God, and John, the imperial usher and logothete of the military logothesion—and with the entire holy synod according to the order prescribed in the first session; with the God-beloved archimandrites and hegumens also present, together with the whole monastic body; and with the holy and undefiled Gospels set before them:

Demetrius, the God-beloved deacon and sacristan of the holy Church of Constantinople, said:

Since on the preceding day it seemed good to the holy and universal synod, following the paternal and ecclesiastical laws, to receive those who are converted from heresy, and likewise to admit those orthodox persons who had been ordained by heretics, [Col. 0251A] the bishops who have already read their libelli in an orthodox manner are standing at the doors and asking to enter and to be judged according to what seems good to you.

The holy synod said: Let them enter.

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: Let the God-beloved bishop of Neocaesarea, who has recently arrived, render his account in a libellus.

Gregory, the God-beloved bishop of Neocaesarea, said: May God confirm the rule of our good lords; may God gladden them upon their holy throne. May God grant that our most holy lord serve as pontiff for many years, and may God strengthen the holy synod. Pray for my poverty. And, producing his libellus, he read it; it contained copies of the libelli [Col. 0251B] prescribed in the first session.

After the libellus had been read, Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: Do you confess these things with simplicity of heart?

Gregory, the God-beloved bishop of Neocaesarea, said: In the name of God, and through your holy prayer and that of the holy Fathers, with a clean conscience and complete simplicity I confess; and I ask your Beatitude and the entire synod to pray for me.

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: Let us promulgate something concerning these matters. [Greek adds: “The most holy bishops of Sicily said: What was done in the case of the others should also be done in the case of these.”]

The holy synod said: Let it be done.

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: But a certain rumor [Col. 0251C] is making itself heard: that during the time of the persecution some bishops inflicted intolerable persecutions upon pious men. Although these words have been introduced, we do not altogether believe them without confirmation. The entire holy synod knows that the canon of the holy apostles commands that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who strikes faithful persons who have sinned, or unbelievers who are acting unjustly, and who wishes to make himself feared in this way, is to be deposed.

The holy synod said: That is what they declare.

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: And if this is so, what is your judgment?

Theodore, the most holy bishop of Catana, said: According to the sacred regulations of the catholic Church, this holy synod so defines. [Col. 0251D]

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: If a bishop inflicted any blows or tortures upon men who feared the Lord and who were then suffering persecution, he is not worthy of the episcopate.

The holy synod said: He is not worthy.

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said: Since he inflicted slaughter, just as a persecutor did.

Theodorus, most holy bishop of Catana, and the God-beloved bishops of Sicily who were with him, together with Epiphanius, deacon and locum tenens of the bishop of Sardinia, said:

“The Fourth Synod, as soon as it took its seat, cried out at the outset: ‘Send Dioscorus out! Send the murderer out!’—because, at the Robber Synod [Gr. adds: “at the Robber Synod”], he had laid hands upon innocent men.”

John, most reverend presbyter and locum tenens of the eastern diocese, said:

“And the holy synod, inspired by the Holy Spirit, set forth this pledge [constitution].”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“As we said before, we do not believe the words that are being circulated.”

The holy synod said:

“When the proper time comes, whoever has this complaint should bring it before this holy synod or before Your Holiness; and when the truth has been demonstrated, what this holy synod has defined will take effect.”

Gregory, most holy bishop of Neocaesarea, said:

“I will not be accused by anyone of having struck or killed [Gr., felled] anyone.”

The holy synod said:

“In this we too rejoice.”

Gregory, most holy bishop of Neocaesarea, said:

“Neither in the city divinely entrusted to my care nor in my region has anyone suffered vengeance at my hands.”

The holy synod said:

“If this is so, let it be accepted in its proper place.”

Sabbas, most reverend monk and hegumen of the monastery of Studius, said:

“The bishops have acknowledged that he was a leader of the heresy; and we do as you command. For our father Athanasius said to Rufinianus that, for those who were leaders of heresy, it is sufficient if they are admitted to repentance alone.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“But he said that he did not fell anyone, nor did he persecute anyone—”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“Juvenal and those who were around him were the authors [leaders] of the Robber Synod; but they were received at the Fourth Synod.”

John, most magnificent logothete, said:

“It is sufficient for your divinely gathered synod that Gregory of Neocaesarea, who was also an author of the impious synod that has passed away, has been preserved to this day, so that his heresy and teaching might be condemned.”

John, most reverend presbyter and locum tenens of the eastern diocese, said:

“We give thanks to God because men from that badly assembled synod have remained—men who condemn the things wrongly done by them, overturning them and making their own confusion public.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“We all know that Juvenal was patriarch of Jerusalem; and, according to his rank, he was certainly also the leader of the synod. Thus, after his transgression, he was received when he had performed repentance.”

Epiphanius, most reverend deacon of the Church of Catana and locum tenens for Thomas, bishop of Sardinia, said:

“But Juvenal persecuted no one.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“And he replied: ‘I persecuted no one.’”

For Eustathius of Sebaste was also a leader of the heresy of the Macedonians; but our father, Saint Basil, received him together with a written statement.

The most reverend monks said:

“It is true; but because Juvenal remained silent, we therefore replied [Gr. adds: Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: ‘We praise you as imitators of the canonical and evangelical constitutions.’]”

Sabbas, most reverend monk and hegumen of the monastery of Studius, said:

“May God preserve our good lords, by whose gracious favor this has been done and this council assembled for the union and concord of the Church.”

The holy synod said:

“Thanksgiving and praise be to God.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Earlier this holy synod, following our holy fathers, already declared that they ought to be received unless some other cause of this kind expels them from the priestly order [Gr. adds: ‘those coming from heresy’]. We have therefore learned the same thing again.”

The holy synod said:

“We all say the same thing.”

John, most reverend presbyter and monk, locum tenens of the eastern patriarchs, said:

“The good things that are spoken in different ways are holy and useful.”

Peter, God-beloved presbyter and locum tenens for Adrian, most blessed senior pope of Rome, and John and Thomas, God-beloved presbyters and vicars of the East, said:

“Let them receive their sees.”

The holy synod said:

“We say this very thing, and we all agree.”

And the most reverend bishops—namely, those of Nicaea, Neocaesarea, Rhodes, Iconium, Hierapolis, Pisinuntium, and Carpathus—went up to the chairs assigned to them.

The holy synod said:

“God has brought the orthodox safely here.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“Because, in the previous session of this holy and venerable synod, we were deemed worthy to receive through the royal secretary the most pious sacred document of our emperors crowned by God, in which it was stated that letters had been sent by the bishop of senior Rome to their serene imperial majesties, and two quires to the most holy patriarch from the chief priests of the East; and because we heard the letters of the Roman pope and learned what they contained, we therefore ask Your Excellencies, most illustrious patricians, that what was sent from the East be read before this holy and universal synod, so that we may ascertain whether the pope of senior Rome, the most holy patriarch Tarasius—who presides over the imperial city—and the bishops of the East hold and proclaim the same things.”

The most magnificent princes and the holy synod said:

“Let it be done according to your request.”

John and Thomas, God-beloved presbyters and locum tenentes of the eastern patriarchs, said:

“If it pleases this holy and universal synod, we ask that the letters of the most holy patriarch Tarasius, which were sent to the most holy chief priests of the East, be read first, and then their replies.”

The holy synod said:

“Let them be read.”

And Stephen, God-beloved deacon and notary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, read them.

## Copy of the letter sent by Tarasius, most blessed patriarch of Constantinople, to the chief priests and priests of Antioch, Alexandria, and the Holy City

The Lord God, who governs and prolongs the lives of human beings, wisely guiding each person’s progress through life—for without him nothing has been made, since even the hairs of our head are numbered before him—has, by judgments known to himself, raised me, who until now had been numbered among the laity and assigned to imperial service, to the episcopal chair. This occurred through the strong urging of the defenders of truth, namely, our most pious and orthodox emperors, and the most holy bishops and clergy, whose forceful insistence upon me brought this about. Yielding to them, I consented and entrusted to them the reaping of the fruit of my obedience.

I ask you, most sacred fathers, to support me, fainthearted as I am, with the staff of your power—that is, with your paternal instruction—and, like brothers, to help us through your pure prayers, armed with the armor of God, against the devices of the ancient enemy, and to steer me, wavering amid waves rising against one another, so that I may reach the harbor of the will of Christ our God.

For there is truly among us a battle without iron, while words are hurled and hurled back. Yet we possess a triumphant trophy: the truth, which cannot be defeated. Furthermore, when violent storms have arisen and, taking you as our helpers, we have endured a little of their heat, we shall find Christ rebuking these storms, and we shall pass our whole life in tranquility.

Having sufficiently prefaced our letter with these matters, the knowledge of them will be made clear in what follows. Now, however, I proceed to another purpose in speaking. Since an ancient—and, to speak more truly, apostolic—tradition has grown up in all the churches, namely, that those who are advanced to the episcopate should commend themselves to those who preceded them in the same order by explaining what pertains to their faith, it seemed right that I too, following this practice, should bow before you and openly declare my confession: how I was educated from infancy by the trumpets of the Holy Spirit—for their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the earth [Psalm 18]—and by their disciples and followers, namely, our most sacred fathers.

I believe in one God, the Father Almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our God, born from the Father, co-eternal and outside time; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father through the Son, and known and acknowledged to be the same God: a Trinity of one substance, one honor, and one throne, eternal and uncreated, creator of all creatures, one source, one divinity and lordship, one rule, dominion, and power in three subsistences, indivisibly divided and divisibly united—not one perfect thing arising from three imperfect things, but one super-perfect and more-than-perfect thing arising from three perfect things, as the great Dionysius said [Note: [Col. 0255D] The passage is obscure and must be read cautiously.].

Thus, according to the distinct property of the persons, there are three to be worshiped; but according to the common account of nature, there is one God, maker of all visible and invisible things and provider for all.

I confess that, for our salvation, in the last days there took place according to the flesh the birth of one person of the holy Trinity, namely, the Son of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, from the truly holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. He became consubstantial with us in every respect except sin, yet did not cease to be what he was; rather, while the two natures remained without confusion, he remained one with the two wills and operations subsisting in him. He was crucified for us in the flesh, buried, raised again, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

Moreover, I hope for the resurrection of the dead and the requital of each person’s deeds [Gr. adds: “eternal”], namely, good deeds and those contrary to them. I also seek the intercessions of our most holy and undefiled Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and of the holy angels and the holy and most glorious apostles, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and teachers [doctors]. I salute their venerable icons, and I abominate every heretical dispute, together with its leaders and chief men—namely, Simon, Marcion, Manes, Paul of Samosata, and Sabellius the Libyan—and their impious doctrines.

I also receive the six holy and universal synods, together with their divine doctrines and teachings, as having been delivered to us by divine inspiration.

With the First Synod, believing that the Son is homoousios and without beginning together with the Father, I anathematize the impious Arius, Aetius, Eunomius, Eudoxius, and Demophilus; after these, those rightly called Anomoeans and Semi-Arians, together with their entire polluted band.

With the Second Synod, confessing that the Holy Spirit is God and life-giving, I reject Macedonius and all who share his opinion, together with the God-hated Apollinarius, who foolishly raved [Gr., “who held his opinion without a mind”].

With the Third Synod, proclaiming one Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, begotten from the Father, and the same one incarnate in the last days for our salvation from the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, I drive far from my confession the man-worshiper Nestorius, together with the pair associated with him, Diodore and Theodore, who proclaimed their monstrous tale and fashioned a personal duality in Christ.

Furthermore, with the Fourth Synod, understanding that Christ, one of the holy Trinity, our God, came in the flesh from two natures and in two natures, I anathematize Eutyches, Dioscorus, and their entire headless multitude, together with Severus, struck by God’s thunder, and the unspeakable Julian of Halicarnassus, who fabulously asserted that our Lord had received an incorruptible body.

Finally, with the Fifth Synod—which, like the sword of the Spirit, cut away on the surface, as it were, the wicked heresies sailing from earlier times and exposed their inventors, namely Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius—I likewise reject them as monstrous fabrications of heretics.

Moreover, through the Sixth Synod, just as I had formerly learned that Christ exists from two natures, from which he also is, so I have believed that he possesses two natural wills and operations in each nature, namely, the human and the divine. I submit to anathema Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and all their followers. I have hated their dogma as a Sodomite vine, a Gomorrite offspring, and a cluster of bitterness.

I also receive the canons drawn from that holy Sixth Synod, together with all its doctrines, which it promulgated lawfully and by divine authority. Among them it is stated:

“In certain paintings of venerable icons, a lamb is depicted, shown by the finger of the Forerunner; it went before in the figure of grace, demonstrating to us through the Law the true Lamb, namely Christ our Lord. Therefore, honoring the ancient figures and shadows as signs of the truth and as preceding representations handed down to the Church, we prefer grace and truth in honor, accepting them as the fullness of the Law. Thus, so that perfection may also be depicted through the use of colors on everyone’s faces, we define that the figure of the Lamb of God, our Christ, who takes away the sins of the world, should henceforth be painted in icons according to his humanity in place of the former lamb. Through him we contemplate the height of the humility of God the Word, and we are led to remember his way of life in the flesh, as well as his passion and saving death and the redemption thereby brought about for the world.”

As for the superfluous commotions and chatter rashly promulgated afterward, since they have not been received among you and were not spoken by divine grace, we regard them as void. Saying farewell to these things and preparing to make them flee, we gird the loins of our mind in truth, and we rise together with our pious and faithful emperors, the defenders of truth, toward the unity of the holy Church of God. We have requested from them a universal synod in the presence of all their God-beloved people, and they have piously assented to our request.

Therefore, since you have been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, namely Christ Jesus himself, the supreme and cornerstone [Ephesians 2], and since you take as fellow combatants, followers, and helpers those mentioned above, we have such confidence before the Lord—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God [2 Corinthians 3]—that he will cause the disrupted and severed members to grow into one compact and joined body, whose head is Christ, and they will no longer be scattered.

For the rest, we ask Your Holiness to send up to two locum tenentes, together with your God-speaking letter, and to make known to us whatever has been divinely revealed to you concerning this matter. Thus, as is fitting, both the locum tenentes and your letters may be found in all respects synodal, whether for speaking or for reading, so that through this what has been divided may be united.

We have requested the same thing from the bishop of senior Rome. I ask you fraternally, addressing to you an apostolic voice as though God were exhorting through us: search out everything, according to your counsel, and disclose it to us in God. For it is written: “The lips of the priests shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from their mouth” [Malachi 2].

We are certain that you preserve within yourselves the seeds of truth intact. Our pious emperors too pursue the steadfastness of orthodox truth in all things and do not cease to entreat the Lord God, according to Gregory, who received his surname from theology: that we who belong to the one God may become one; that we who are of the Trinity may be united, equal in honor, and found of one mind in all things; that we who are of the Holy Spirit may be not against one another but for one another; that we who are of the truth may be shown thinking and saying the same things; and that there may be no dispute or dissension among us. Just as we have one baptism and one faith, so may we also have one harmony in every ecclesiastical matter.

May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, bring us together, unite what has been divided, heal the long-standing wound, preserve us whole in the soundness of faith, establish all in true confession and concord, unite his holy Church, and restrain the scandals lying upon it—through the intercessions of our undefiled Lady, the Mother of God, and of all the saints. Amen.

Peter and Peter, God-beloved presbyters and locum tenentes for the most blessed pope Adrian, senior of Rome, said:

“The most holy pope received letters of this kind, and for that reason he sent us with the replies that have just been read.”

John, God-beloved presbyter and locum tenens of the chief priests of the East, said:

“These letters and the piety of the empire caused us to come here and to escape the hands of those wicked enemies of the Church.”

The holy synod said:

“God has brought you safely here.”

Constantine, God-beloved deacon and notary, said:

“I have in my hands the aforementioned quires that were sent from the East; and, if you command it, we shall read them.”

## Letter of the chief priests and priests of the East to Tarasius, most holy and most blessed archbishop of Constantinople and universal patriarch, greetings in the Lord

“After the most sacred booklets produced by divine inspiration, written by Your Apostolic and Paternal Holiness, had been read aloud, O most blessed one, we humble men—the last of those who desire to dwell in the desert—were seized at once by trembling and joy.

We trembled because of the fear of those whom, on account of our sins, we have been appointed to serve, who are truly impious and, as it is written, ‘the wicked walk about on every side’ [Psalm 11], seeking almost every day opportunities to hand us over to death and destroy us.

We rejoiced because of the truth of the orthodox faith, which shines in them like the sun’s rays, and because of the most lucid explanation of the apostolic doctrines and those of the fathers.

Appropriately recalling Zachariah, the father of the Word’s voice—that is, the prophet—we cry aloud: ‘The dawn from on high has visited us’ [Luke 1], illuminating with the splendor of theoretical contemplation and divine providence the mind seated in the darkness and shadow of death, namely, the malign error of Arab impiety, in order to guide our intelligible feet into the way and paths of a peace-bearing constitution.

Who can declare the mighty acts of the Lord? Let David, the father of God, sing the psalm with us; or who can make all his praises heard? [Psalm 105] For God has taken pity on his despairing people and gathered what was distant into one harmony of faith. He has raised up for us a horn of salvation [Luke 1] and direction in the house and temple receiving the Lord, the only-begotten Son, namely our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ.

You are the most holy ones [Note: [Col. 0257D] Anastasius explains: ‘Because they hold the first rank among the patriarchs, for the priests possess the first place in the Church.’], together with those who bear the second places in the Church according to the law and order of our Church, namely, our victorious and divinely redeemed—or appointed—princes and lords of the world [Gr.: ‘and those who, according to the law and order, hold the second places in the Church after you are victorious’].

For the priesthood is the sanctification and establishment of the empire, and the empire is the strength and support of the priesthood. Concerning these matters, a certain wise prince, most blessed among the holy kings, said: ‘God has granted humankind the greatest gifts: the priesthood and the empire. The one adorns and governs heavenly things; the other governs earthly things by just laws.’

Now the wall separating the middle has truly been loosed; concord rules over discord; division bows before unity; and dissonance, having fallen into flight, has disappeared. The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, triumphs now with a joyful face and dwells among us confidently.

Now we, who had become a reproach to our neighbors and kinsmen, a mockery and derision to those around us, and who therefore looked down toward the earth in shame, raise our eyes toward heaven with unanimous joy and proclaim in exultation:

‘By this I know that you desired me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me’ [Psalm 40].

You received me, stumbling because of the innocence and simplicity of my error [or: because I was wavering in error]; you saved and raised me, and fixed my faltering feet upon the rock of apostolic faith.

These things, and others in harmony with them, caused us to write after reading your divinely inscribed volumes. Moved by canonical law and guided by the discipline of paternal tradition, you sent them to those who had received the governance of the apostolic sees, through venerable pairs directed by God.

When they arrived and, by God’s will and command, met our God-worshiping brothers, holy men who had given their lives for the correction of the churches, those men recognized them from their former and ancient way of life and rejoiced greatly—especially when they found both living in one place and pursuing a manner of life pleasing to God.

When they made themselves known, they showed them the booklets of your orthodoxy, pleasing to God and worthy of admiration. They reported in due order the thoughts of your holiness, pleasing to God; the pious counsel of our lords, preserved by God; the expectation of the common salvation of all; and the hope in God, free from confusion.

But those men, as though possessing one soul in two bodies, thinking as one, according to the apostle, and moved by the divine Spirit, secretly and intelligently concealing and sheltering their brothers because of fear of the enemies of the cross, which had been arrayed on every side, did not dare, although they were wise, either to believe their vision or to set its cause in motion—especially since the situation was dangerous and required increasingly frequent counsel and careful consideration.

‘Good counsel will guard you,’ he says, ‘and good thought will preserve you’ [Proverbs 2].

And behold, while those who had placed themselves under the protection of their guardianship were unaware, they ran to us. Gathering us together silently, they first bound our humility by a most dreadful adjuration [Gr. and manuscript of Jolius: ‘especially dreadful’] to keep secret and undisclosed what they had to say. Then, emphasizing everything relevant to caution, they revealed to us the entire circumstance of what had happened to them.

Struck with astonishment and compunction of heart, and drenched with hot tears at the miracle [unexpectedness] of such a report and the glory of so great a change in circumstances, we stood in prayer like sinners, with fear and trembling. Giving fitting praise to him who does all things and transfers them toward what is better, we earnestly implored his goodness: that he would become our mediator in small matters, that through the Holy Spirit the light of knowledge would shine into our hearts, and that he would grant the power of good counsel for determining your excellent purpose, together with good thoughts. And he did so, being kind and merciful.

Therefore, most holy ones, recognizing the hostility of the polluted nation against us, we considered retaining those who had been sent and preventing them from approaching those to whom they had been dispatched. We brought them into our midst and strongly admonished them not to introduce disturbance—or, to put it more precisely, destruction—to churches that were at rest and pacified by the grace of God, or to a people miserably afflicted by the yoke of servitude and oppressed by the imposition of unbearable taxes.

But they took this badly and said: ‘We have been sent for this purpose: to deliver our souls to death for the Church and to bring to completion the purpose of the most holy patriarch and the most pious emperors.’

‘But if the danger were confined only to your souls,’ we replied, ‘your statement might perhaps have some force. But since it proceeds against the common body of the Church, what benefit will there be? Rather, what injury will there not be, in building a structure upon decay and depriving it of a firm foundation?’

‘And how,’ they said, ‘with what face shall we return to those who sent us, carrying back none at all of the things they hoped for according to their desire?’

At this point, knowing that our God-beloved brothers John and Thomas were adorned with divine zeal for the orthodox faith, were synkelloi of two holy and great patriarchs, and were also lovers of sanctifying silence, we said to them:

‘Behold, brothers, an acceptable time, a time of salvation, and one more excellent than silence. Go with these men, undertake their defense, and declare aloud what we judge to be beyond our strength to communicate to our lords by letter.

‘For you know how, through a slight accusation, the one who had been chosen to govern the throne of the Lord’s brother, James, was exiled because of two thousand signa [the reading is materially uncertain].

‘When you have completed God’s work and made known to our lords the apostolic tradition maintained in the churches throughout Egypt and Syria, then embrace what is desired of you.’

But they replied:

‘How shall we, although we are uneducated and inexperienced [Gr., unknown], weak and unlearned for so great a matter, presume to undertake a task that exceeds our strength?’

‘But Christ our God,’ we said immediately, ‘who worked through the most humble and uneducated—the holy apostles, I mean—and through them captured the whole world for obedience to the word of his dispensation, is able to give you speech in the opening of your mouths, to supply the intention and understanding of those who could neither receive letters nor dare to write or utter a word about such matters.’

As they were lovers of God and showed themselves sons of obedience, they obeyed our word and accepted our exhortation. After promising them extended prayers and securing no ordinary joy for those who had been sent, we parted from one another in this manner, amid a great outpouring of tears.

But, O most holy and most blessed ones, receive our brothers kindly, as befits your paternal authority, and present them without concealment or fear of men to the lords of the world.

You will have them as clear witnesses to the harmonious and concordant orthodoxy of the three apostolic sees. They proclaim with one voice the six holy and universal synods, admitting no other synod in addition to them—one which some now whisperingly call the seventh—but rejecting it in every way, since it was evidently assembled long ago for the deposition of apostolic and magisterial traditions and for the destruction and abolition of the sacred and venerable images.

But you, most holy ones, enlightened by divine zeal and having as your allies lords preserved by God, who by God’s just decree were foreordained to rule over you, together with a senate protected and fortified by God, prevail and act manfully. Let your heart be strengthened as you apostolically punish every disobedience and bring it into conformity with obedience to Christ.

We consider it necessary to remind Your Pontifical Eminence of this: if, with the consent of all, you wish to celebrate a synod for the good pleasure of the one King, namely Christ our God, and of those who were worthy to reign with him—our God-beloved and victorious lords—do not let the absence of the blessed patriarchs of the three apostolic sees and of the most holy bishops dwelling under them appear burdensome to you. Their absence does not arise from their own decision, but from the dreadful threats and deadly punishments imposed upon them by those who hold them or rule over them.

This must also be considered more carefully in light of the sacred and universal Sixth Synod itself, at which no bishop from these regions during that period was found to have assembled because of the occupation of the impious. Yet this caused no prejudice to that holy synod, nor did any prohibition have the power to prevent it from establishing and making manifest the correct doctrines of piety—especially since the most holy and apostolic Roman pope agreed with it and was present through his apocrisiarii.

And now, most holy ones, let this likewise take place with God’s help. For just as his faith then resounded to the ends of the inhabited world, so the synod now to be assembled by God’s grace through your intervention, and through that of the one who governs the see of the Chief of the Apostles, will be proclaimed in every place beneath the sun—a synod that will raise up what has been tyrannically destroyed and restore it to the ancient and apostolic tradition.

Moreover, to strengthen our humble letter, to satisfy Your Blessedness and Lordship, and for the satisfaction of our victorious and triumphant emperors, we have also examined a copy of the synodical letter of Theodore, of holy memory, our father and patriarch of Jerusalem, to append to what we have written.

This same Theodore, of holy memory, wrote this letter according to the customary rite of the Church to the blessed and illustrious patriarchs, namely Cosmas of Alexandria and Theodore of Antioch, the God-city. It is known that, while he was still alive, he received their reciprocal synodical letters.

May the Lord preserve you unharmed as you pray for us, most holy and divinely honored ones.”

## Copy of the synodical letter of Theodore, most holy patriarch of Jerusalem

“Therefore, most blessed ones, we believe—as we have believed from the beginning—that there is one God the Father, entirely without beginning and eternal, maker of all visible and invisible things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, eternally and impassibly born from that God and Father, acknowledging no other source than the Father and possessing substance from him: light from light, true God from true God.

And in the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, light and God known in himself [and himself known in himself], truly existing, co-eternal with the Father and the Son, homoousios, of the same lot, and of the same essence and nature, and likewise of the same divinity.

We believe in a Trinity homoousios, of one honor and one throne, which is recapitulated and gathered into one divinity and common lordship, without personal or subsistential fusion or division [Gr., contraction].

For we believe in the Trinity in unity and glorify unity in the Trinity: the Trinity in three subsistences, but unity in the singularity of divinity. It neither has the one thing that it possesses as its own confused [perhaps: ‘it does not have one confused thing, etc.’], nor is the threefold reality itself divided throughout; rather, in each, each is preserved [Gr., ‘rather, in the one, the other’].

For it is divided according to the number of the subsistences and numbered according to the diversity of the persons, but united by the identity of substance and nature, and it admits no partition whatsoever.

There is one God, because one divinity is most clearly proclaimed and is recognized in the Trinity of persons. Nor, because he is one God and one divinity, is he to be divided and distributed into three Gods; for that impiety belongs to the Arians.

Nor, because the three are one God and are recognized as such, are three subsistences proclaimed in such a way that the Father, Son, and most Holy Spirit are said to be contracted or compacted, blending themselves into one subsistence; for that wickedness belongs to the Sabellians.

Therefore, it was rightly decreed by the God-speaking fathers that we should understand the Monad in the one and singular divinity, and the Triad in the three unconfused subsistences. We do not acknowledge another one God apart from the three persons, nor do we know the three persons of the one-substance Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—as other than the one God.

Therefore we proclaim the one as three, in whom divinity is; and we announce the three as one, whose divinity it is. Or, to speak more truly, we proclaim that the three both are and are recognized as divinity.”

We believe also in one Lord Jesus Christ, of that same holy consubstantial Trinity: who, although he was in the form of God, did not regard it as robbery, as the Apostle says, to be equal with God; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II). For although he is consubstantial with the Father and co-enthroned with him, in the last times he did not disdain to be born from our holy and undefiled Lady, the Mother of God, taking from her flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul—the firstfruits of our mass—not sown, but fashioned by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0263A].

Thus proceeding as one from two contraries [Note: [Col. 0263D] He calls them contraries because one is visible and mortal, while the other is invisible and immortal, as he explains himself a little below], God the Word, while by nature existing as perfect God, became by nature the same perfect man, without changing his nature or pretending to be carrying out the dispensation; but he was united to the rationally and intellectually [Gr., animated] flesh taken from the holy Virgin, and having received existence in him, was united by subsistence, without confusion and without division. He did not transfer the nature of his divinity into the substance of the flesh, nor again the substance of his flesh into the nature of his divinity.

Two natures, therefore, united to one another without conversion in the one subsistence of God the Word, manifested to us one Son and Lord, visible and invisible, mortal and immortal, the same both circumscribed and uncircumscribed, perfect God and perfect man, to be acknowledged in two natures [Col. 0263B] and worshipped in two free operations and wills. For he could not have acted divinely unless he were by nature God; nor, again, humanly unless by nature he had become man.

We confess that he who is truly God and man was crucified for our salvation, tasted death in the flesh, accepted burial for three days, rose from the dead by the power of his own divinity, despoiled hell, granted freedom to those who had been held captive from of old, ascended into the heavens, sat at the right hand of the Father, and will come, according to the voice conveyed to the apostles by the bodiless beings, at his second coming to judge the living and the dead (Acts I). We also confess the resurrection of the dead on the last day, at the voice of the archangel’s trumpet, and the just recompense by Christ our God for the works we have done well or otherwise [Col. 0263C]; and in the future, eternal and unending life.

We receive, affirm, and eagerly embrace the six holy and universal synods, which, assembled by the Holy Spirit against every heresy in different places and at different times, are proclaimed with a loud voice by all the orthodox Churches under the sun, which are strengthened by their correct and divinely inspired doctrines, receiving those whom they receive and rejecting those whom they reject.

The first was held at Nicaea: the synod of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, for the deposition of Arius, surnamed from his madness, and of his blasphemies that corrupt souls. It anathematized him, as a mad divider and cutter of the unconfused divinity, and as one who, with babbling verbosity, confessed the Son of the Father to be a creature—although through him, of course, all created things were brought forth from nonexistence into existence—together with all who agreed with him, and drove him far from the divine sanctuaries. It proclaimed that our Lord Jesus Christ was born before all ages from the substance and subsistence of the Father, timelessly and without temporal flux, existing consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit; and through the Creed, that is, the confession of right faith, it explicitly taught the whole mystery of Christ’s dispensation.

The second synod was assembled at Constantinople [Col. 0264A], the synod of one hundred and fifty Fathers, against Macedonius, the opponent of the Spirit, and his companions, the God-hated Semi-Arians. This holy synod, having the same Holy Spirit as its guide and teacher, taught that he has his procession from the Father timelessly and eternally, and that he is of one substance with the Father and the Son, to be co-worshipped and co-glorified. But those who blasphemed against the same Paraclete it subjected, without remission, to unspeakable anathemas, together with the foolish Apollinarius, who, being mad, asserted at length that our Savior’s humanity [Gr., our Savior according to humanity] was without intellect.

The third, previously held at Ephesus, was the radiant synod of two hundred holy Fathers, for the destruction and deposition of Nestorius, the worshipper of man [Col. 0264B], and those who agreed with him. Deceived by his own execrable thoughts, he declared with babbling speech that there was one God the Word, who existed before the ages, and another who was incarnate from the Virgin for our salvation, introducing—although unwillingly—a fourth person into the holy and consubstantial Trinity. Not only did he separate the two natures of Christ into two subsistences, but, accursed, he also rejected the title by which she is called Mother of God, wickedly decreeing that she should be called “Mother of Christ” (*Christotocos*). Yet she is truly the Mother of God and, before and after childbirth, a Virgin, exalted above the glory and splendor of every intellectual and sensible nature.

The same holy synod of two hundred Fathers therefore anathematized him [Col. 0264C], together with his soul-damaging ravings, teaching that one Son had shone forth from the Father before the ages, and that the same Son had been born in the last days from the undefiled Virgin and Mother of God, Mary; that he had assumed our nature; and that the same Son of God was perfect God and perfect man. It proclaimed him to be one Son, Christ, and Lord, and absolutely “one incarnate nature of God the Word”—which signifies the union of the two natures accomplished by subsistence. It legitimately established that holy Mary should properly and truly be called Mother of God.

Most opportunely, the synod divinely assembled at Chalcedon then arose: six hundred and thirty holy Fathers, for the deposition of the deceived heresy that asserted Christ’s natures to be confused. The senseless Eutyches first established this through his folly [Col. 0264D], denying that in one Christ there were two natures united without conversion, and monstrously conjecturing that one nature had been made and composed from two. With Dioscorus as his wicked supporter and defender, he was found to be a slanderer of orthodox doctrines and an enemy of the truth.

But the holy synod overthrew both of them and subjected their delirious verbal novelties [Gr., vanities], together with them, to severe anathemas. It proclaimed that the two natures of Christ, our true God, are united without conversion and without change in his one subsistence; and that the same one is perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity [Col. 0265A], to be recognized as existing from two natures and in two natures. Furthermore, it repudiated the wicked division of Nestorius, and Nestorius himself together with those who agreed with him.

Afterward the fifth synod also convened in the city that rules cities, preserving the number of one hundred and sixty-four holy Fathers. Guided by the Holy Spirit himself, it confirmed the four holy synods previously celebrated and, following their correct doctrines, anathematized Nestorius, Eutyches, and Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his blasphemies. It also anathematized Origen, Evagrius, Didymus, and all their fabulous, pagan, and monstrous discourses, as well as the letter called the letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian, and the writings of Theodoret that he composed against the twelve correct chapters of the holy-memory Cyril [Col. 0265B].

After the holy sixth synod shone forth like another sun—the synod of two hundred and eighty-nine holy Fathers, which chose the imperial city as the place of its repose and in which it was celebrated—it anathematized those who deny that our God Christ, in the dispensation of the flesh, possesses two proper wills and operations, and who monstrously assert one will and one operation of our Savior’s divinity and humanity alike. These were Sergius, Pyrrhus, Peter, Cyrus, Honorius, Theodore of Pharan, and the delirious old man Polychronius, together with all who have defined, or will define, or presume to define, one will and one operation in Christ’s two natures.

For if, as a certain wise man said in a certain place, we leave the Lord’s human nature without will and without operation [Col. 0265C], where shall we preserve perfection in his humanity? Thus they lucidly explained the great mystery of the dispensation of salvation by fitting two wills and two operations to Christ’s two natures, corresponding to their natural properties; and they preserved, without slander or doubt, the orthodox faith of all God’s churches for those who think rightly.

We know that these six holy synods alone are universal, admitting no other synod after them. For nothing has been left in the apostolic traditions, or in the paternal or legitimate decrees, that requires correction or any kind of embellishment.

Therefore, with our whole soul and mind, we anathematize all heretics who think wrongly, as disciples of Satan, the sower of weeds, and ministers who corrupt souls, from that evil head, namely Simon Magus, to their detestable tail. In short, we anathematize all the rest without exception, especially those whom the aforementioned six holy and universal synods anathematized, together with Severus, the leader [or author] of the Acephali [that is, of those who confess Christ to be of one nature] [Note: [Col. 0265D] This gloss of Anastasius has been inserted into the text and is also found in the manuscript].

Moreover, I reject Peter, surnamed “the Fuller” (*Cnapheus*), who dared to add an augmentation [the text reads “argument”] to the hymn *Trisagion* and presumed to apply suffering to the impassible divinity, together with all who follow his blasphemy [Col. 0266A].

We do not reject, but strongly affirm and admit, the local holy synods as well, and the canonical corrections drawn from them by divine inspiration, together with their laws that enlighten souls.

We receive and embrace the traditions of the Church handed down by the apostles, through which we are taught to honor and worship the saints and to greet them, venerating them as servants, friends, and children of God. The honor shown to the devout fellow-servants is proof of the good will shown toward their common Lord. For they themselves became God’s storehouses and pure dwelling places, and the most undefiled mirrors of the Holy Spirit (Wis. III).

Their souls are also in the hand of God, as it is written. Since God is life and light, the saints who are in God’s hand plainly abide in life and light. Therefore, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV).

While living, these saints stood before God with confidence. The Lord Christ has left us the saints’ relics as life-giving fountains, watering the sick with benefits of many kinds, emitting an ointment of sweetness, and driving away demons. As the great teacher surnamed “from immortality” says [Note: [Col. 0266D] Anastasius’s words: That is Athanasius; for “immortal” is said in Greek as *athanatos*], the bones of martyrs drive away illnesses, cure the sick, give sight to the blind, cleanse lepers, and dissolve temptations and sorrows—and all this through Christ, who dwelt in them.

The Psalmist rightly sang: “God is wondrous in his saints” (Ps. LXVII). And again: “For the saints who are upon his earth, he has made all his desires wondrous among them” (Ps. XV).

Together with these, we embrace, honoring and worshipping, the holy and venerable images: that is, the image of the Word of God, namely, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who was incarnate for us and took the form of a servant (Phil. II). His image and figure does not bear the character of the divinity, which was immutably united to his undefiled flesh; for the divine nature is invisible, uncircumscribed, and formless. “No one has ever seen God; the Only-Begotten has declared him” (John I). Rather, making an icon in the colors of his humanity, we worship it.

God appeared upon earth, although he was invisible; he was seen and lived among human beings, and he became weary, hungry, and thirsty according to the law of our nature, which he assumed.

We worship Christ’s icon—that is, the image of the person who was seen by human beings—not as divided from his invisible divinity [Col. 0266D]—far from it—but as united to that divinity from the very conception. For although he says to the Jews, “Why do you wish to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?” (John VIII), he was not merely man, but also God. And when he says, “I and the Father are one” (John X), he does not deny our nature; for he asserts this with a human mouth and an organic tongue.

We also honor and worship the undefiled image of his holy Mother, the Mother of God and our immaculate Lady, who ineffably gave birth to him. We likewise honor the images of the holy apostles, prophets, victorious martyrs, confessors, and righteous persons, as friends of God [Col. 0267A]. We do not offer worship to the material or the colors; rather, through these we are led by intellectual perception to the prototype and render it the honor due to it, knowing, according to Basil the Great, that the honor paid to the image passes to the prototype.

Since some contend more obstinately and say that the images of the saints ought not to be worshipped because they are made by human hands, foolishly—or rather impiously—calling them idols, let such people know that the cherubim, the mercy seat, the ark, and the table, which the most holy Moses constructed at God’s command, were made by human hands and were worshipped. Divine Scripture condemns those who worship carved images (Ps. XCVI; Isa. XLII), as well as those who sacrifice to demons.

The sacrifice of the pagans was indeed rejected; but that of the righteous is accepted (Ecclus. XXXV). Since, therefore, the venerable images are material representations, they ought to be honored for the sake of their prototypes.

Having gladly received these synodical statements of ours, most holy men, if anything should be found in them that requires correction, make us participants in your God-filled teaching without envy, and be graciously willing to send back to us what has been corrected. Thus, when agreement has been found between both the faithful—that is, between you and us—may the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be glorified, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

After the reading, Peter and Peter, God-loving presbyters and representatives of the most holy Pope Adrian, the elder of Rome, said:

“We agree, because, according to the faith rightly confessed by Tarasius, most holy and most blessed patriarch of Constantinople, and received by our apostolic pope Adrian together with the venerable holy synod that is with him, he agrees and has embraced communion in the things that Tarasius confessed. Blessed be God, because the most holy high priests of the East have been found in agreement in orthodox faith and in the veneration of the venerable images with Adrian, the most holy Roman pope, and Tarasius, patriarch of New Rome. Let those who do not confess thus be anathema from the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who were previously assembled here.”

The holy synod said: “So be it, so be it, so be it.”

Agapius, most holy bishop of Caesarea, said:

“The most sacred letters sent by the most holy bishops of the East to Tarasius, most holy patriarch, I receive in every respect as a title of orthodoxy; I agree with them and receive communion with them. May I subject those who do not think thus to anathema.”

John, bishop of Ephesus, said:

“We agree with the orthodox letters sent by those high priests who are in the East to Tarasius, the most holy and thrice-blessed patriarch, and we embrace communion with them. But those who confess thus yet neither worship nor receive the holy, sacred, and venerable images, I regard as alien to the apostolic and catholic Church and consign them to anathema.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“Finding no alteration in meaning in the letters now read, which were sent from the East to Tarasius, most holy archbishop and patriarch, and finding them in agreement with the definition of faith that he himself had previously confessed, I, though unworthy, agree with them and become of one mind with them. I honorably receive and embrace the holy and venerable images; but the worship rendered through *latria*, that is, the service owed to God, I offer only to the supersubstantial and life-giving Trinity. Those who do not think and proclaim thus I separate from the holy catholic and apostolic Church, subject them to anathema, and consign them to the portion of those who deny the incarnate and saving dispensation of Christ our true God.”

Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“I agree with and remain faithful to the letters sent by the most holy high priests of the East to the most holy archbishop and patriarch. I receive with all goodwill and willingness what they have confessed. Those who do not think thus I subject to anathema.”

Nicholas, most holy bishop of Cyzicus, said:

“Having read the letters of the most holy and most blessed archbishop and patriarch, and the documents sent in response by the orthodox high priests of the East, I agree concerning the holy and venerable images and receive their communion. Those who do not think thus I consign to anathema.”

Euthymius, most holy bishop of Sardis, said:

“Having pursued the truth in all things and having been educated in the most sacred traditions of the apostles and Fathers [Col. 0268C], I also agree with these writings now read—both those of Tarasius, most holy and most blessed archbishop and patriarch, and those sent to him by the patriarchs of the East. I regard their understanding and my own concerning the sacred doctrines and the holy icons as one and unchangeable. But those who speak and babble vainly against these things, against the holy images, and do not agree with the most holy patriarchs, I recognize as heretics and perverse, and I keep myself far from their communion.”

Peter, most holy bishop of Nicomedia, said:

“According to the letters sent by the high priests of the Eastern diocese to Tarasius, the most holy and thrice-blessed archbishop and patriarch, I receive them as salutary, and I venerate and worship the precious and sacred icons. Those who do not think thus I anathematize.”

Hypatius, most holy bishop of Nicaea, said:

“I agree with the orthodox letters sent from the East—that is, by the high priests who are there—to Tarasius, the most holy and thrice-blessed patriarch, and I receive what they have confessed. I honor, worship, and embrace the holy and venerable images. All who do not follow this confession I regard as alien to the catholic Church and subject to anathema.”

Elias, most holy bishop of Crete, said:

“Following the letters sent from the East, I agree and make common cause with them.”

Stauracius, most holy bishop of Chalcedon, said:

“Having read the letters of the most holy and most blessed archbishop and patriarch, I consider those sent by the high priests of the Eastern diocese to possess such agreement with the letters of the bishop of Constantinople that no difference appears between them, but perfect identity, so that both are one—that is, full of all orthodoxy. Therefore I too confess thus, and I regard as alien those who do not think thus.”

Nicephorus, most holy bishop of Dyrrachium, said:

“I assent and agree with the orthodox letters sent by the high priests of the East to Tarasius, most holy patriarch, and I receive the exposition of what they have confessed. Those who do not think [Col. 0269B] thus I anathematize.”

Epiphanius, God-loving deacon of the Church of Catana and representative of Thomas, most holy bishop of Sardinia, said:

“It is true, because good words are a honeycomb, and their sweetness is health to the soul, as it is written (Prov. XVI). Behold, then, the synodical letters now read, of the most holy archbishop of royal Constantinople, New Rome, which he sent to the most orthodox high priests of the East; and those which they sent back to him, blossoming with the sweet and fragrant honeycomb of the faith of the holy Fathers, have watered the intellectual understanding of us all with sweetness and healed those whose minds were wavering in the faith through the strength of orthodox teaching.

“Therefore, thinking the same as they do, I admit and embrace [Col. 0269C] the venerable images according to ancient custom. But that apostate council, which some improperly and foolishly call the seventh synod, together with those who think the same as it does, I consign to terrible anathemas.”

Leo, most holy provost and representative of the metropolis of Side, said:

“By the grace of Christ our true God, I assent to the letters sent by the high priests of the East to Tarasius, most holy archbishop and patriarch, and I remain faithful. Those who do not think thus I consign to anathema.”

Nicholas, most reverend monk and hegumen of the monastery of Aprus, and representative of the metropolis of Tyana, made the same declaration.

Gregory, most holy bishop of Neocaesarea, said:

“I agree with the letters sent by the high priests in the East to Tarasius, most holy patriarch, and I admit and salute the holy images and venerable icons. Those who do not think thus I subject to anathema.”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Catana, said:

“Those who meditate upon the manner of piety will certainly find the word of orthodoxy shining in these things. Accordingly, after reading the sacred and synodical letters of Tarasius, most holy and most blessed high priest of the Queen of Cities, which he sent to those in the East, and likewise those directed to him by them [Col. 0270A], my brief declaration, fixing the sight of attentive understanding upon them, has recognized through the reading that they agree in every respect with the orthodox faith of the holy Fathers. Therefore, thinking these things with them, I receive and salute the sacred and venerable icons. I consign to anathemas the novelty of words that arose from the synod which is whispered about as the seventh, together with those who think with it.”

Anastasius, most holy bishop of Nicopolis in Old Epirus, said:

“Seeing the agreement between the synodical letters of Tarasius, most holy patriarch, and the replies to them sent by the high priests of the East, I agree with them, confess that I think thus, and intend to remain blameless to the end. I receive and salute the venerable and sacred icons. Those who do not think thus I subject to anathema.”

John, most holy bishop of Tauromenium, said:

“Just as we have come together in one understanding, so we have learned to speak with one voice. Therefore, since the synodical documents of Tarasius, most holy patriarch, which have been read and which he sent to the most holy priests of the East, agree with the replies sent to him by them concerning the holy and orthodox faith of the six universal synods, I too believe accordingly, receiving and worshipping the holy and venerable images. Living in this orthodox faith, I desire to stand with confidence before the tribunal of Christ. Let those who do not think thus be anathema.”

Gregory, most holy bishop of Pisinus, likewise.

Nicetas, most holy bishop of Claudiopolis, likewise.

Basil, most holy bishop of Syleum, likewise.

Michael, most holy bishop of Synnada, likewise.

Theodore, most holy bishop of Myra, likewise.

Leo, most holy bishop of Iconium, likewise.

Leo, most holy bishop of Rhodes, likewise.

George, most holy bishop of Pisidia, likewise.

Eustathius, most holy bishop of Laodicea, likewise.

Constantine, most holy bishop of Perga, likewise.

Theodore, most holy bishop of Seleucia, likewise.

Theophylact, God-loving deacon and representative of the metropolis of Stauropolis, likewise.

Nicholas, most holy bishop of Hierapolis, likewise.

Leo, most holy bishop of Carpathus, likewise.

Theodore, most holy bishop of Amorium, likewise.

Christopher, most holy bishop of Phasis, likewise.

Cyril, monk and representative of Nicetas, bishop of Gothia, likewise.

The remaining most holy bishops [and monastic dignitaries] [Note: [Col. 0271B] These words too are absent from the Joly manuscript] made the same declaration.

The entire synod, which through the grace of Christ our true God and the pious decree of our most tranquil and orthodox emperors, lovers of piety, was assembled, receives, agrees with, salutes, and honorably worships the report made by Adrian, the elder pope of Rome, to our most orthodox emperors; the document of the orthodox definition of Tarasius, most holy and most blessed patriarch, which has now been read; and the letters sent to his Beatitude by the high priests of the East. We dig out and consign to anathema the false council composed against them for their destruction. But may Almighty God preserve our lords and the most holy patriarch [Col. 0271B].

Tarasius, most holy bishop and patriarch, said:

“Contention has fallen silent, and the dividing wall of hostility has been removed. East, West, North, and South, we have been made one under one yoke and in one harmony.”

The holy synod said:

“Glory to you, Lord, who have united us.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Thanks be to Christ, our true God, the peacemaker, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever!”

The holy synod praised him.

“Many years to the emperors! Many years to Constantine and Irene, the great emperors and rulers! Many years to the orthodox emperors! Lord, preserve the guardians of the faith! Lord, preserve the helpers of the Church! Eternal memory to the new Constantine and the new Helena [Col. 0272B]! Lord, grant them a peaceful life! Many years to the patriarchs! Many years to the sacred senate!”

## ACT FOUR

[Col. 0271]

[Col. 0271B] In the name of the Lord and ruler Jesus Christ, our true God. Under the rule of our most pious and Christ-loving lords Constantine and Irene, his God-redeemed mother, in the eighth year of their consulship, on the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction.

[Col. 0271C] The holy and universal synod assembled through the divine grace and pious decree of those same divinely confirmed emperors in Nicaea, the illustrious metropolis of the province of Bithynia: namely, Peter, most reverend archpriest of the most holy Roman Church of the holy apostle Peter, and Peter, most reverend presbyter, monk, and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sabas situated at Rome, representing the apostolic see of Adrian, the venerable and most holy archbishop and elder of Rome; and Tarasius, the venerable and most holy archbishop of the great and renowned Constantinople, New Rome; together with John and Thomas, most reverend presbyters, monks, and representatives of the apostolic sees of the Eastern diocese.

They were seated before the most sacred ambo of the church of the most holy Great Church called Sophia [Col. 0271D], in the presence and hearing of the most glorious and magnificent officials: Petrona, the famous former consul and patrician, count of the God-preserved imperial service; John, imperial usher and logothete of the military logothesion; and the entire holy synod, according to the order recorded in the first act. Also present were the God-loving archimandrites and hegumens, together with the entire monastic multitude. The holy and undefiled Gospels were placed before them.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Through the preceding acts, most attentively [or: recently], our throat has meditated upon the truth, instructed by the breath of the almighty Lord, according to the Preacher, because through the letters that have been read we have been made harmonious—the most holy men of the East and the West.

“But since the prophetic word commands us: ‘Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; proclaim with strength; raise your voice, you who evangelize Jerusalem; proclaim, do not fear’ (Isa. XL), let us follow this prophetic command, priestly men: let us proclaim and raise our voices, announcing peace to the catholic Church, which is the true Zion and the heavenly city of Christ our God and King.

“But how shall this be done? Let the volumes of the glorious holy Fathers be brought here before the hearing of all. Drawing from them, let each of us give drink to the flock entrusted to us. Thus our sound will go forth into all the earth, and the power of our words to the ends of the earth (Ps. XVIII), because we do not move the boundaries established by our fathers, but, instructed by the apostles, hold fast to the traditions we have received.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia [Col. 0272D] in Cyprus, said:

“According to the statement of Tarasius, most holy patriarch, let the books and the testimonies of the blessed Fathers be brought forth and clearly read again before this holy synod.”

Leontius, the most illustrious secretary, said:

“Obeying the beneficial and salutary command of the most holy patriarch and the consent of this universal synod, and striving to bring this matter to an end, we have brought and presented the most sacred books. The first is the divinely chosen and written book, which I shall now read before all the others. Let us all listen with greater attention and prudence, and recognize more certainly the force of what is said, so that we may receive the fruit of complete benefit.”

The same man read:

### From Exodus concerning the children of Israel

[Col. 0273A]

“The Lord spoke to Moses: ‘You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold; its length shall be two and a half cubits, and its width one and a half cubits. You shall also make two golden cherubim, hammered out, on the two sides of the oracle. Let one cherub be on one side and the other on the other. They shall cover both sides of the mercy seat, spreading out their wings and overshadowing the oracle. They shall look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy seat, with which the ark is to be covered, and in which you shall place the testimony that I will give you. From there I shall give commands and speak to you above the mercy seat and from between the two cherubim that will be above the ark of the testimony, concerning everything that I shall command you for the children of Israel’” (Exod. XXV).

### From Numbers

[Col. 0273B]

“These things were offered at the dedication of the altar, when it was anointed. And whenever Moses entered the tabernacle of the covenant to consult the oracle, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was over the ark of the testimony, between the two cherubim; from there also he spoke to him” (Num. VII).

### From Ezekiel

“He brought me into the temple and measured the fronts: six cubits in width on this side and six cubits in width on that side, the width of the tabernacle” (Ezek. XLI).

And afterward:

“And the inner temple, and the vestibules of the court, the thresholds, and the slanting windows, and these roofs around on three sides opposite each threshold, were covered with wood all around. The ground extended up to the windows, and the windows were closed above the doors, and up to the inner house, and on the outside along the whole wall all around, inside and outside, according to measure.
