And cherubim and palm trees were fashioned, with a palm tree between cherub and cherub. Each cherub had two faces: the face of a man beside the palm tree on one side, and the face of a lion beside the palm tree on the other side, represented throughout the whole house all around” (ibid.) [Col. 0273C].

### From the Epistle of Saint Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews

“It had indeed regulations for worship and an earthly sanctuary. For a tabernacle was made, the first one, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place. Behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies [Col. 0273D], having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold. In it was a golden vessel containing manna, and Aaron’s staff that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat” (Heb. IX).

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Let us observe, holy men, that the Old Testament had divine signs: cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat. From this the New Testament also received its pattern.”

The holy synod said:

“Yes, lord; the truth is so.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“If the Old Testament had cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat, let us too have images of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the holy Mother of God [Col. 0274A], and of his saints, overshadowing the altar.”

The most magnificent officials said:

“Truly, it is God’s command.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“As it was read, the cherubim had a human face. And how do some say, ‘Who has seen the face of the cherubim?’ For it says that a carved face was made.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“All the saints who were worthy to see angels saw them in the form of human beings, as we read in various passages of Scripture. Therefore God spoke to Moses concerning the cherubim, saying: ‘See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain’ [Col. 0274B] (Exod. XXV). And from this the servant Moses, having seen particular forms, made forms of the same kind, together with which he also made cherubim.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“But when the people turned toward idolatry, God then said to Moses: ‘You shall not make any likeness for the purpose of serving them.’”

John, most reverend presbyter and vicar of the apostolic sees of the East, said:

“More exalted than these is this, because Jacob too erected a pillar for God. Therefore He blessed him, promising gifts that surpass every word” (Gen. 28). “And elsewhere He wrestled with him in human form and called him Israel, which is interpreted ‘mind seeing God.’ He himself said: ‘I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved’” (Gen. 32). “And behold, **[Col. 0274C]** not only were the intelligible powers seen, but God Himself, who is invisible by nature and incorporeal, when He was manifested in our form.”

Demetrius, most reverend deacon and sacristan of the most holy Great Church of Constantinople, read:

“From the work of our holy Father John Chrysostom, *On the Praise of Meletius*, whose beginning is as follows:

‘Everywhere I turn my eyes over this sacred flock, and as I look upon the whole city present here, I have no one whom I can call blessed.’” And afterward:

“‘And there was a school of reverence which was being formed. For, being continually compelled to remember his name and to keep that holy man before their minds, **[Col. 0274D]** they drove away every passion and irrational thought from themselves by his name. And this became so widespread that everywhere—in the streets, in the marketplace, in the fields, and on the roads—they resounded on every side with that name. But you showed affection not merely for so great a name [Latin *circa tam magni nominis affectum*; Greek-order variant *circa nomen tam magnum affectum*: “with regard to affection for so great a name”]; you did so also with regard to the very form of his body. Therefore, what you did with respect to his name, you also did with respect to his icon. For many inscribed that holy icon everywhere: on the circles of rings, on cups and bowls, on the walls of bedchambers, and everywhere, so that they might not only hear that holy name but also see everywhere the likeness of his body, and enjoy a twofold consolation from his departure.’”

**[Col. 0275A]** Peter, most holy bishop of Nicomedia, said:

“If John of the golden mouth said such things about icons, who would still dare to say anything against them?”

Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“He truly received them; and the pious who lived then had such love for his image that everywhere they fashioned an icon of Saint Meletius. Hence this Father praises them exceedingly.”

The most holy patriarch said:

“And we, receiving the teachings from our fathers, likewise call them venerable icons, holy and sacred.”

Theodosius, most reverend hegumen of the monastery of Saint Andrew of Nesion, brought a book by that same John of the golden mouth, asking that it be reread. Antony the monk took it and read:

**[Col. 0275B]** “A sermon of our holy Father John Chrysostom: *That the Legislator of the Old and New Testaments is one, and on the priestly vestment*, whose beginning is as follows:

‘The prophets formerly proclaimed the Gospel of Christ’s kingdom.’” And afterward:

“‘I too loved a wax-encrusted painting filled with piety. For I saw an angel in an icon driving back the barbarian battalions. I saw the nations of the barbarians trampled down, and David truly saying: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing”’” (Ps. 72).

The most holy patriarch said:

“If he whose mouth was more precious than gold bore witness, saying, ‘I too loved the wax-encrusted painting,’ what shall we say of those who hated them?”

**[Col. 0275C]** Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“When he says, ‘I loved it,’ who dares to utter the contrary?”

John, most reverend presbyter and vicar of the Oriental pontiffs, said:

“Who is this angel, then, if not the one of whom it is written: ‘For the angel of the Lord struck down one hundred and eighty thousand Assyrians who were waging war around Jerusalem in a single night’?” (2 Kings 19).

Nicephorus, most holy bishop of Dyrrachium, said:

“May the Lord be merciful to us for the offenses we have committed [variant *patravimus*: “perpetrated”] against the sacred images.”

Gregory the deacon and notary read:

**[Col. 0275D]** “From a sermon of Saint Gregory of Nyssa, delivered in Constantinople, *On the divinity of the Son and the Spirit, and on Abraham*, whose beginning is as follows:

‘They undergo something like what happens in richly flowering meadows.’” And afterward:

“‘I have often seen in a painting an image of the Passion, and I did not pass by the sight without tears, while the art plainly brought the story before my eyes. Isaac is placed beside the very altar, seated upon the knees, with his hands bound behind him (Gen. 22). The other, climbing behind the boy, leaning upon his knee [Latin *suffragine*; Greek-based reading *suffragini innixus*: “leaning upon his knee”], with his knee joined [variant *vincta*: “bound”], and with his left hand draws the boy’s hair back toward himself; he bends toward the face of the pitiable one looking back toward himself [Greek-based variant *ad ipsum*: “toward him”], and, armed with a sword in his right hand, **[Col. 0276A]** directs it toward the slaughter. Already the sword’s edge touches the body, when suddenly a voice comes to him from God, forbidding the deed.’”

The most glorious princes said:

“See how our Father was grieved by the painting [variant *jucundatus sit*: “rejoiced”].”

Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“Many times the Father had read the story; but perhaps he had never wept. Yet after he saw the painting, he wept.”

John, most reverend presbyter and monk, and vicar of the Oriental pontiffs, said:

“If a painting brought benefit and tears to such a teacher, how much more will it bring compunction and benefit to the unlearned and simple?”

**[Col. 0276B]** The holy synod said:

“In various places we have seen a painting of Abraham, just as the Father says.”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Catana, said:

“If Saint Gregory, awake to divine understanding, wept when he saw the story of Abraham, how much more will the depicted dispensation of Christ our Lord’s incarnation—He who became human for our sake—encourage those who see it toward progress and the shedding of tears?”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“If we saw an icon displaying the Lord crucified, would we not also weep?”

The holy synod said:

“Magnificently stated; for in it the height of God’s humility is clearly contemplated: He who was incarnate for our sake.”

Stephen, most reverend deacon, notary, and referendary, read:

**[Col. 0276C]** “From an epistle of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to Acacius, bishop of Scythopolis, *On the scapegoat* [Latin *apopompaeo*; variant *capro emissario*: “the goat sent away”], whose beginning is as follows:

‘When the messengers sent by Your Holiness arrived, I rejoiced greatly.’” And afterward he said at length:

“‘We say, therefore, that the law was a figure and shadow, and something like a painting set before the sight of those who behold realities. The outlines of art are the initial drawings of those who paint on panels; when blossoms of color are applied over them, then surely the beauty of the painting shines forth.’”

And a little later:

“‘It is therefore written in the book of the creation of the world: “And after these things God tested Abraham, and said to him: Abraham, Abraham.” He answered: “Here I am.” He said to him: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go to the land of Vision, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I will show you.” **[Col. 0276D]** Abraham rose early, saddled his donkey, and took with him two young men and his son Isaac. Having cut the wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place that God had commanded him. On the third day he lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar, and he said to his servants: “Wait here with the donkey; but I and the boy will hurry there, and after we have worshiped, we will return to you.” He also took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it upon his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the sword in his hands’” (Gen. 22).

And afterward:

“‘They came to the place that God had shown him, **[Col. 0277A]** where he built an altar and arranged the wood upon it. When he had bound his son Isaac [Greek-based variant *pedes Isaac filii sui*: “the feet of his son Isaac”], he placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood, stretched out his hand, and seized the sword in order to sacrifice his son’” (ibid.).

“‘Therefore, if one of us wishes to see the history of Abraham painted on a panel—how the painter represented him [Latin *quomodo scilicet eum designaverit pictor*; Greek-order variant *quomodo eum des. pictor*: “how the painter represented him”]—whether he performed the things said of him all together or separately: some depict the same man in different places, now in one form and now in another [Latin *nonnulli in alia atque alia specie diversis eumdem locis depingunt*; Greek-based variant *Siquidem in al. atque al. sp. d. eumd. loc. depinxerit*: “if he has depicted the same man in different places, now in one form and now in another”]. For example, at one time he is seated on the donkey, with the boy taken up and the servants following; at another, with the donkey remaining below with the servants, he is placing the load on Isaac and **[Col. 0277B]** holding before him both sword and fire. Elsewhere they depict the same man again in another form, binding him upon the wood (*compedientem super ligna*) [variant *super ligna adolescentem*: “the young man upon the wood”], and arming his right hand with the sword in order to inflict death. But Abraham was not one man in one place and another in another, appearing differently; rather, he was always the same man wherever the painter’s art represented him according to the requirements of the events. For it was neither fitting nor possible for him to be seen doing in one and the same place everything said of him.’”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“Behold, Saint Cyril too speaks in agreement with Saint Gregory of Nyssa.”

Cosmas, deacon, notary, and cubicularius, read:

**[Col. 0277C]** “From the poems of Saint Gregory the Theologian, from a sermon on virtue, whose beginning is as follows:

‘I invoke first God, the author of all things’ **[Col. 0277D]** [Note: In the Joyan manuscript the translation is also divided into its own verses, as we publish it here].”

And afterward:

“‘Nor will Polemon pass by me in silence.

For he is a marvel among those things greatly deserving proclamation [Greek variant *praedicata*: “among things proclaimed”].

Formerly this man was not among the modest,

but a very foul servant of pleasures.

Yet when he was seized by a desire for the good,

and found an adviser—I must not say whom—

whether some wise man or himself, boldly [Greek variant *subito*: “suddenly”],

he appeared so superior to his passions

that, to mention one of his miracles,

a certain incontinent young man summons a prostitute.

**[Col. 0277D]** When she had come near the gate, as they say,

at which an icon showed Polemon looking out,

when she saw it—for it was worthy of veneration—

she departed immediately, overcome by the sight,

ashamed before Polemon depicted as though alive.’”

Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“And Saint Gregory, the God-speaking Father, recounted the icon of Polemon as a marvel.”

The most holy patriarch said:

“For chastity resulted from it. Had the prostitute not seen the icon of Polemon, she would certainly not have ceased from fornication.”

**[Col. 0278A]** Nicephorus, most holy bishop of Dyrrachium, said:

“Wonderful is the image and worthy of the greatest admiration, since it was able to free the woman from an accursed and shameful act.”

Gregory [variant *Georgius*: “George”], deacon beloved of God and notary of the venerable patriarchate, read:

“From a sermon of Antipater, bishop of Bostra, on the woman who suffered from a flow of blood, whose beginning is as follows:

‘That the calling of the Jews came first, Scripture has taught.’” And afterward:

“‘Having grasped the saving fringe, the woman who suffered from the flow of blood said this, as though holding the Lord, the King of nature, and proclaiming the tyranny of her affliction. **[Col. 0278B]** After receiving the gift, she erected a statue to Christ. Although she had spent her wealth in small amounts, she offered to Christ what remained of her wealth.’”

The most holy patriarch said:

“Therefore, the one who paints an image also offers it to God, just as the woman offered the statue.”

Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“To speak precisely [variant *ut proprie dicam*: “as I should say precisely”], he commands and receives most generously those who make images.”

Thomas, most reverend monk of the monastery of Chenolaccus, said:

“I bring the book of blessed Asterius and offer it to the holy synod, as you command.”

The holy synod said:

“Let it be read.”

Constantine, deacon beloved of God and notary, took it and read:

**[Col. 0278C]** “An account by blessed Asterius, bishop of Amasea, concerning Euphemia the martyr.

‘Some time ago, gentlemen, I had in my hands that excellent Demosthenes, and that passage of Demosthenes in which he assails Aeschines with bitter thoughts [Latin *amaris immittit cogitationibus*; Greek-based variant *impetit*: “attacks”]. Delayed by the discourse and burdened in understanding, I sought rest and a walk [Latin *quietem deprecatus sum, et ambulacrum*; Greek-based variant *quiete egebam et ambulatione*: “I needed rest and walking”], by which the small pain of my soul might be relieved. Leaving my lodging, I went a short distance with some acquaintances to the marketplace, and from there proceeded to God’s temple to pray at the gathering. When I had also accomplished this and was walking in the shade of a portico of the houses, I saw there a certain painting, and the sight carried me to its summit [variant *cepit*: “seized me”], so that you might say the work was the painstaking achievement of Euphranor, **[Col. 0278D]** or of one of those ancient artists who, raising sculpted Junos to a great size although they were small, also produced animated panels [Greek-based variant *qui picturae plurimum dignitatis conciliarum*: “who bestowed great dignity upon painting”] **[Col. 0278D]** [Note: Anastasius seems to have read Ἥραν, “Juno,” instead of ἦραν, “they raised.” In the Joyan manuscript one reads “sculptible Juno”].

‘Come, then, if you wish—for now there is leisure for narration—I shall explain the painting to you. For we, as pupils of the Muses, have remedies [*pharmaka*] no less than painters do. A certain woman, a sacred and undefiled virgin, had vowed her chastity to God; they called her Euphemia. When a tyrant once persecuted those who lived piously, she chose the danger of death with great alacrity. **[Col. 0279A]** Her fellow citizens and those who shared her religion, admiring her as a manly and sacred virgin for which cause she died, built a shrine beside the sanctuary, placed a coffin there, and celebrated honors for her, including an annual festival [variant *communem et publicam celebritatem*: “a common and public celebration”], making this a new and public *commercium* (“communion” or “public observance”).

‘Thus the sacred interpreters of the mysteries of God, the hierophants, always honor her memory in speech as well, carefully teaching those present how she completed the contest of endurance. But the painter, acting piously and representing her whole history on linen, as far as his art was able, placed the image beside the sacred coffin.

‘The lovely work of art is arranged as follows. Seated high upon a throne is an immovable judge, looking angrily and malignantly at the virgin. For art, when it wishes, can make even lifeless materials angry. **[Col. 0279B]** The attendants of the ruler and many soldiers are present. Some of them carry books and tablets, recorders of the proceedings; one of them, with his hand suspended from the wax tablet [Greek adds *iracunde*: “angrily”], looks at the woman being judged, bending his whole face toward her as though ordering her to speak more loudly [variant *clarius*: “more clearly”], lest, troubled by difficulty in hearing, he write something false and blameworthy.

‘The virgin stood in a yellow garment and robe signifying philosophy; and, as it appeared to the painter, with a gracious expression, but, as it seems to me, with a soul adorned by virtues. Two soldiers lead her before the ruler: one dragging her forward, the other pressing her from behind, displaying the virgin’s restrained and steadfast bearing. **[Col. 0279C]** For she indeed inclines her gaze toward the ground, as though ashamed before the faces of men. Yet she stood in no way terrified and suffered nothing fearful [variant *timidum*: “timid”] during the contest.

‘Meanwhile, when I was praising other painters, I looked upon the work of the Colchian woman: she was about to bring the sword upon her children, and mercy and fury divided her face. One of her eyes reveals anger, while the other shows the mother sparing and trembling.

‘Now I have turned my wonder from that conception to this painting, and I greatly admire the artist, because he blended the manner of the colors more skillfully, tempering together reverence and manliness—emotions naturally opposed to one another.

‘As the imitation proceeds farther forward, certain executioners, naked except for short tunics, were already coming to their task [variant *jam aggrediebantur opus*: “were already beginning the work”]. **[Col. 0279D]** One of them, having seized her head and bending it backward, presented to another the virgin’s person prepared for punishment [variant *faciem*: “face”]; another, standing nearby, was gnashing his teeth. A hammer and drill, instruments of torture, are visible.

‘Moreover, I weep at this point, and emotion interrupts my speech. For the painter overlaid drops of blood so vividly that you might say they truly flowed from her lips, and you would leave lamenting.

‘After this comes the scene of the bonds: again the venerable virgin appears in tawny garments, alone stretching out her hands toward heaven and invoking God as her defender amid the atrocities. As she prays, a sign appears above her head—the sign that Christians now worship and trace [or: “set forth”]; and I suppose it was an indication of the passion that awaited her.

‘**[Col. 0280A]** Then, immediately afterward and after a short interval, the painter kindles a powerful fire elsewhere, making the bodily flame shine on either side in red color. He places her in the middle, extending her hands toward heaven and showing no distress at all in her face; on the contrary, she is rejoicing because she is departing for incorporeal and blessed life.

‘Up to this point the painter has stopped his hand, and I have stopped my speech. It is now your task, if you wish, to complete the painting, so that you may examine it closely, unless [variant *si non*: “if not”] we have come much too late after the narration.’”

The most glorious judges said:

“The art of painters is therefore pious, and not as some foolishly denounce it; for the Father himself testified that the painter acts piously.”

**[Col. 0280B]** Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“He also calls that sacred monument sacred. The Theologian calls the image venerable, Chrysostom calls it holy, and the Father whose work was read calls it sacred. What further contradiction can anyone offer to these things?”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Myra, said:

“Hearing the teachings of all our fathers, we have been moved in soul and we mourn the years that have passed. Yet we give thanks to God, because through the teachings of our fathers we have come to the knowledge of the truth.”

**[Col. 0280C]** Theodosius, most holy bishop of Amorium, said:

“Most sacred and God-honored lord, we and the entire holy synod, hearing the teachings of our holy fathers concerning the sacred images, believe, confess, and call them both sacred and holy. Let anyone who does not say this be anathema.”

The holy synod said:

“Let him be anathema!”

Nicephorus, most holy bishop of Dyrrachium, said:

“The good painter always presents things through art, just as the one who depicted the image of the martyr Euphemia did. For this reason the teacher also highly praises the art of painting in these matters.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“Indeed, when he says: ‘At first I praised the things that belonged to the Colchian woman, until I came to the image of the martyr.’”

The holy synod said:

“And after contemplating this, he was struck with awe.”

**[Col. 0280D]** Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“And the Father whose work was read experienced what Saint Gregory [variant *Nyssenus*: “of Nyssa”] experienced; for both of them wept before images.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“The Father commands and gives permission, at the end of the sermon, to anyone who wishes to paint the account of the contests of the martyrs. For he says: ‘It is now your task, if you wish, to complete the painting, so that you may examine it closely, unless [variant *si non*: “if not”] we have come much too late after the narration.’”

John, presbyter beloved of God and holding the place of the apostolic sees of the East, said:

“Therefore the image is greater than speech; and this was accomplished by God’s providence for the sake of simple people.”

**[Col. 0281A]** Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“If sacred images produced such compunction in holy men, how much more in us?”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Myra, said:

“When our fathers say such things, we have nothing to say.”

John, presbyter beloved of God and holding the place of the apostolic sees of the East, said:

“Painters do not oppose the Scriptures; rather, they demonstrate whatever Scripture says, so that they are defenders of the things that have been written.”

Theodosius, most holy bishop of Amorium, said:

“The divine Apostle teaches, saying: ‘Whatever was written was written for our instruction’” (Rom. 15). “**[Col. 0281B]** Therefore those holy and venerable images and paintings—both those made in mosaics and those produced as material representations [Latin *tam quae in musivis, quam quae in materiali scriptione*; Greek-order variant *et materiales efformationes, atque musiva*: “material representations and mosaics”]—exist for our instruction, imitation, and example, and stand as written testimony, so that we too may display the same pattern and contest concerning God, in order that He may make us also worthy of their standing and portion, and coheirs of His kingdom.”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Catana, said:

“Blessed and God-bearing Asterius, like a most brilliant star, has illumined the hearts of us all. Therefore the catholic Church did not receive the sacred and venerable icons without due reason, but appropriately followed the teachings of our holy fathers.”

**[Col. 0281C]** Gregory, deacon beloved of God of the holy Great Church of the Praiseworthy Apostles, read:

“On the martyrdom of Saint Anastasius the Persian martyr, whose beginning is as follows:

‘The Only-Begotten Son and Word of God, through whom all things were made.’” And afterward:

“‘When his desire for illumination had grown strong, he earnestly asked the aforementioned man to make him worthy of the grace of holy baptism. But the other, trembling because of fear of the Persians and lest he be endangered, delayed him. Nevertheless, he went with him to the churches, prayed, and looked at paintings of the holy martyrs, asking him what these were. When he heard from him about the miracles of the saints and the harsh tortures inflicted upon them by tyrants—sufferings beyond human endurance—**[Col. 0281D]** he marveled and was astonished. After remaining for a short time with the aforementioned man beloved of Christ, he conceived an excellent desire in his soul to reach Jerusalem and there to be made worthy of holy baptism.’”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Myra, said:

“It is evident that the tradition of venerable images is solemn [variant *legitima*: “legitimate”].”

Euthymius, most reverend deacon and monk, reading on behalf of the bishop of Gothia beloved of God [Greek-based variant *notarius rever. episcopi Gothiae*: “the most reverend notary of the bishop of Gothia”], read:

“From the miracles of Saint Anastasius the martyr, whose beginning is as follows:

‘I wish to set forth an account of the miracles.’” **[Col. 0282A]** And a little later:

“‘Come now, let us narrate, as far as possible, the things performed by the saint at Caesarea in Palestine. When the blessed corpse drew near the holy city, the news became known throughout the entire city, and all were filled with great joy. Rising and striking the sacred pieces of wood **[Col. 0281D]** [Note: Anastasius’ words: The Easterners strike pieces of wood in place of bells], they gathered in the most venerable temple of the Mother of God called the New Church. Then they went out with crosses and a litany to meet the holy relic, rejoicing and exulting with glorification. As though blooming anew—or rather, revived—in the martyr’s presence from the smallness of faith that was in them and from the mortification caused by their other wickednesses, they received great consolation.

‘**[Col. 0282B]** As they prayed, kissed the relic, rolled themselves around the tomb, and rendered the due recompense to the relic and memory of this saint, a certain woman—who was, so to speak, among the distinguished women of Caesarea, if one should put it so, rather than otherwise, as the facts themselves made clear—named Arete, that is, “virtue,” though entirely contrary to virtue in her conduct, turned to disbelief and said: “I do not worship a relic coming from Persia.”

‘O wretched and senseless soul, who did not hear the most sacred psalmist David rebuking the audacity of the wicked and saying: “Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit!”’ (Ps. 33).

“‘What God, then, who glorifies those who glorify Him, did to her, I shall now relate accordingly. When the holy relic entered the city, the citizens of that city took counsel together and **[Col. 0282C]** began to build a shrine for the saint beside the Tetrapylon, which stood in the middle of the city. They also set up his image there.

‘While the building was still under construction, the martyr appeared to that wretched woman in a dream in the habit of a monk and said to her: “Do your loins hurt?” She answered him: “No, lord; I have no ailment. I am healthy.” At the same time as she spoke, she awoke and felt that a severe pain had fallen upon her. She began to cry out, groan, and suffer continually, so that she could not breathe at all, enduring unbearable agony. While she had leisure to reflect, she considered who he was and for what reason such sudden pain had been inflicted upon her.

‘She spent four days in this condition. **[Col. 0282D]** At daybreak on the fifth day, she saw the saint standing beside her and saying: “Go down to the Tetrapylon and call upon Saint Anastasius, and you will be healed.” She rose, and, remembering the wicked words she had spoken against her own head, summoned her servants and said to them: “Lift me, lift me, so that we may go to the Tetrapylon of Saint Anastasius. For now I know and have learned that I must worship and honor a relic coming even from Persia, and must not treat as common what God has purified—that is, must not declare it common [variant *seu potius, ducere*: “or rather, treat it as common”].”

‘Her servants therefore lifted her in a litter—that is, a carrying chair—and proceeded. When they were approaching the place, she raised her eyes from afar, saw the saint’s image, and began to cry out in a loud voice with an outpouring of tears: “This is truly the one whom I saw in my dream **[Col. 0283A]** proclaiming to me the evils that afflict me.”

‘When she had thrown herself upon the pavement and wept greatly, the saint was appeased, and she rose healed. The woman who shortly before had been carried by others and was in danger at the point of death went home walking on her own feet, joining the others in harmony in praising and glorifying God and magnifying the martyr.’”

Peter and Peter, presbyters beloved of God and vicars of Adrian, the elder pope of Rome, said:

“This image of Saint Anastasius remains to this day in Rome, in his monastery, together with his precious head.”

**[Col. 0283B]** John, most holy bishop of Taormina, said:

“The most honorable vicars spoke truly, for there was also in Sicily a woman suffering from a demon; when she was brought to Rome, she was healed through the aforementioned most sacred image.”

John, presbyter beloved of God, monk, and vicar of the Oriental pontiffs, said:

“From what has been said, and from what has been read, it has been demonstrated that the images of the saints also work miracles and bring about healings.”

Peter, most holy bishop of Nicomedia, said:

“I bring a book of Saint Athanasius and offer it to the holy synod for reading.”

The holy synod said:

“Let it be read.”

Stephen, deacon and notary, took it and read:

**[Col. 0283C]** “A sermon of our holy Father Athanasius, of blessed memory, concerning an image of our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, and the miracle that occurred in the city of Berytus.”

Raise the eyes of your minds and see this new miracle that has now occurred. Gaze upon God’s boundless wonder and give him glory. Contemplate his ineffable mercy and the greatness of his dispensation; and take up lamentation together with joy. Certainly, nothing is foreign to God. For since he is God, he can do all things. But because this has happened in our days and among us, every heart that hears of it will be filled with awe. Truly heaven was struck with terror at what was rashly done. The abysses were disturbed, and the sun was darkened, and the moon and the stars likewise, because of what had been perpetrated. Yet again all the powers of heaven rejoiced at what had been ordained by the Lord.

Listen and marvel at what has occurred in [Col. 0283D] our days. Understanding, understand; incline your ear, extend it outward—indeed, before the external ear, which belongs to the heart—and listen. There is a city called Berytus, situated on the borders of Tyre and Sidon and subject to Antioch. In this city of Berytus there were numerous and populous communities of Jews. Beside their synagogue, which appeared to be very large, a certain Christian rented a small room from someone. Living there, he fixed opposite his couch an honorably painted image of our Lord Jesus Christ [Gr., “on a panel”], depicting our Lord Jesus Christ at full height.

After a short time, the Christian sought a larger dwelling, as he also needed one. [Col. 0284A] This, I believe, was arranged by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II): he shows his miracles to those who worship him and to all who believe in him, for the rebuke of the impious and the strengthening of the faithful. Thus, as I said, the Christian sought a larger house, found one in a certain part of the city, and moved there from the house that stood beside the Jewish synagogue. After removing all his belongings, he inadvertently—but by God’s providential arrangement—left behind the image of the Lord that had been entrusted to him, as I have said.

A certain Jew then rented the house in which the Lord’s image stood. Having brought in all his belongings, he remained in the house, paying no attention to the Lord’s icon standing there. For he did not inspect the place, but entered and [Col. 0284B] remained there.

One day the Jew invited one of his fellow tribesmen to lunch. While they were eating, the invited Jew lifted his eyes, saw the icon of our Lord Jesus Christ, and said to his host: “Since you are a Jew, how do you have an image of this kind?” He also uttered many insults, shameful to repeat, against the Lord. I do not dare write down what the guest said against the Savior—far be it from me.

Then the host, seeing the Lord’s image, gave the invited Jew an explanation, saying: “Until now I had not seen this image.” The guest fell silent. But he went to his chief priests and accused the Jew who lived in the house where the Lord’s image was, saying that [Col. 0284C] “the man has an image of the Nazarene in his house.”

When they heard this, they said: “If you can show us this…” He affirmed: “I will show you in his house.” They, filled with fury, remained silent for the evening. But when morning came, their chief priests and presbyters, taking with them the man who had slandered the Jew, together with a large crowd of their people, went to the Jew’s house in which the Lord’s image stood.

When they reached the place, the chief priests and elders burst in with the informer and saw the Lord’s image standing there. Then, becoming exceedingly angry, they drove the Jew who lived in that house out beyond the synagogue. Taking down our Lord Jesus Christ’s image, they said: “Just as our fathers once mocked him, so let us also mock him.”

Then [Col. 0284D] they began to spit in the face of the Lord’s holy image and to slap it before those who had gathered, striking the Lord’s image in the face from both sides and saying: “Everything that our fathers did to him, let us also do to his image.” And they said: “We have heard that they mocked him; let us do this very thing as well.”

Thus they mocked the Lord’s icon with countless insults—things that we do not even dare to mention. Then they said: “We have heard that they nailed his hands and feet with nails; let us do this to him also.” So they drove nails into the hands and feet of the Lord’s image.

Again, in their fury, they said: “We have heard that they gave him vinegar and gall to drink with a sponge; let us do this to him also.” And they did so, placing a sponge full of vinegar against the mouth of the Lord’s image. [Col. 0285A]

Again they said: “We have learned that our fathers struck his head with a reed; let us do the same.” Taking a reed, they struck the Lord’s head.

Finally they said: “So that we may learn more clearly that they opened his side with a spear, let us omit nothing but add this also.” They had a spear brought and ordered one of their number to take it and strike the Lord’s image in the side.

Immediately a great quantity of blood and water flowed from it.

Christ, glory to you! Incomprehensible one, glory to you! Who is like you, O God? Who besides you does terrible and astonishing things? O miracle of the majesty of our Savior! Truly your heavenly powers were horrified—and now are horrified—at this.

O how great you are, Lord, in humility [Gr., “humanity”]! O how great in forbearance! O how great in mercy! First, for our sake and for our salvation, although you were without flesh, you were made incarnate from the Virgin Mary; you were crucified in that flesh, although in your divinity you yourself were impassible. But now again you have been crucified in an image, Lord, for the rebuke of the impious and of all unbelievers, and for the strengthening of those who truly believe in you.

But glory to you, Lord, who alone can do all things, together with our blessed God and Father and with the Holy Spirit. Amen.

But you, children, hear what else was ordained by that same Lord, for it was his permission. Finally, after the side of that same image of the Lord had been struck with the spear and blood and [Col. 0285C] water had flowed out, as was said above, their chief priests and elders said:

“Since those who worship him whisper that he has performed many healings, let us take this blood and water, carry it to the synagogue, gather all those among the people who are ill, anoint them with it, and see whether what is being said is true.”

Then, bringing a vessel to the side of the Lord’s icon, at the place where the image had been struck by the spear, from which the blood and water had emerged, they filled a flask at the place of the spear-thrust. Carrying it in, they mocked the image, seeking, as they supposed, to insult the Lord of all before everyone.

After gathering all who were ill, they brought forward first a paralytic whom they had known from birth and anointed him. Immediately he leapt up, sprang about, and became completely healthy. [Col. 0285D] Then they brought blind people, who also recovered their sight. Those suffering from demons [Gr. adds: “innumerable”] were immediately cleansed.

A great and boundless disturbance arose throughout the entire city, as everyone flocked there because of the countless miracles. All the Jewish communities were stirred up, for many Jews lived in the city. They ran, bringing those whom they had in their houses—everyone who was sick, paralytic, [Gr. adds: “or lame”], weak, withered, or leprous. They all came running, so that neither their synagogue, though it was large, could contain them, nor could any place accommodate the immense crowd that gathered because of the miracles.

All the chief priests and elders, and the Jewish people—men, children, and women—believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, crying out:

“Glory to you, Christ, whom our fathers crucified, and who have now been crucified by us in your image! Glory to you, Son of God, who have performed such great miracles! We believe in you; be merciful to us and receive us.”

All of them cried this out in mourning; voices were raised, and miracles were accomplished, as the chief priests anointed them and all were healed and restored to life.

After everyone had been healed, the crowds immediately ran to the bishop of the most holy church established there. He had already learned what had happened. They cried out:

“One God, the Father; one God, the Son, and he alone-begotten; one Christ, whom our fathers crucified. [Col. 0286B] We know him as God; in him we believe.”

Thus glorifying God with many praises, showing the image to the archbishop, and announcing what they had done to the Lord’s image—how blood and water had come out from its side—as well as the countless miracles that had occurred, all the crowds begged to be deemed worthy of holy baptism.

The bishop, taking them together with his clergy [Gr. adds: “and initiating them”], baptized them all over many days, and dedicated their synagogue as a church to our Savior Christ. At their request, he also made their other synagogues into martyr-shrines.

And so great joy came to that city—not only because bodies had been healed and restored to life, but also because so many souls had returned from death to eternal life.

Recognizing this, I hastened to report it to you, beloved brothers, for the benefit of your souls: so that, recognizing in this also the power of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ, you may be strengthened still more in faith in him and rejoice over his mighty works, which he has performed even now.

Therefore give him glory with joy, in contrition and lamentation, rejoicing and giving thanks, because by his faith and his knowledge he has made us worthy [in Christ Jesus our Lord], with whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “Behold, the one who has his name from immortality has caused this entire holy synod to feel compunction and weep, because he recognized not only that they are worthy of veneration, [Col. 0286D] but also that they effect the greatest healings.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “But lest someone ask why those icons that are among us perform no miracles, we answer him: Because, as the Apostle says (I Cor. XIV), signs are given to unbelievers, not to believers. For those who approached the image were unbelievers; therefore God performed a sign through the image in order to draw them to our Christian faith. ‘An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it’ (Matt. XII).”

Theodore, God-beloved deacon and notary, read:

[Col. 0287A] From a letter of blessed Nilus to Heliodorus the silentiary.

Through the miracles that occur daily in every place and at different times, the Lord invites those whose faith is small, as well as unbelievers, to steadfastness in faith. He causes the faith of the faithful—and indeed their hope as well—to grow, and demonstrates it to be grave and immovable wisdom [sense].

I wish to tell you one story from the tens of thousands of victories won by our Plato, who is now a martyr. He readily grants grace not only in our homeland but in every city and region, and shows admirable strength to those who seek God through him.

On the mountain called Sinai, where Moses received the law from God, monks—both natives and foreigners—lived. A certain man of Galatian descent lived there together with his own son, embracing the solitary [monastic] life and engaging for a long time in contests of continence in the desert.

And behold, one day, suddenly, certain pagan and detestable barbarians [Gr., “pagans”] invaded the aforesaid mountain. They seized the monks who happened to be at hand and present at that time, together with the son of the old Galatian, and led them into captivity.

After binding their hands behind their backs, they passed through many deserted settlements. They threatened them while they were fasting and naked, entirely without footwear, forcing them by violence and necessity through waterless and most rugged places, places without any comfort, and holding them in immeasurable fear.

But the old man, hidden alone in a certain remote cave, was wasting away in grief, unable to bear the loss of his God-beloved son. He implored the Lord Christ through Plato, the martyr from his own country, to bend toward compassion.

The son likewise, bound in captivity, prayed to God through the same most holy martyr, asking him to have mercy on him and to deign to perform a miracle.

When the prayers of both were heard—the father in the mountain cave and the son in captivity—behold, suddenly our martyr Plato appeared on horseback, leading another suitable [empty] horse. He manifested himself to the wakeful boy, who recognized him because he had often seen the saint’s likeness in images. At once he ordered the boy to rise from among all the others, take the horse, and mount it.

Immediately, like a spider’s web, the bonds were dissolved. He alone was freed through the invocation; rising at God’s command, he mounted the horse and followed the holy martyr who was leading him, steadfast and joyful. In brief and swift fashion [or: “quickly”], both of them—holy Plato and the novice monk—arrived, as if winged, at the dwelling of the old man, who was praying and mourning.

The most victorious martyr restored the son, desired by his grieving father, safe and sound to him, and then disappeared.

Thus, in every place, the glorious and wondrous deeds of the Lord Christ and of the renowned athlete are made memorable: they are able to accomplish all manner of marvelous and glorious things for those who invoke God through them.

I have written these things to you because you are a friend of the martyrs and never grow weary of remembering the blessed martyrs.

[Col. 0288A] The holy synod said: “It has been shown that, through the martyr’s image, which he had previously known, he recognized him as he stood before him when he came to save him.”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Myra, said: “I too have experienced something similar to the story just presented. For when I was suffering injustice at the hands of certain men in authority, my archdeacon, a devout man who feared God, said to me: ‘I saw the patriarch in a vision saying: “Let the metropolitan come up to us, and all his affairs will be arranged as is expedient for him.”’

“I then asked my archdeacon: ‘In what form did the patriarch appear to you?’ He replied: ‘Red-faced, with aged hair.’

“I said to him: ‘The patriarch does not appear in visions in that form; rather, his vestment bears the image of Saint Nicholas. You have described him well: the man you saw is of that form.’” [Col. 0288B]

But he replied to me: “In truth, I also saw a man of just such an appearance, who spoke these words to me.”

From this I learned that Saint Nicholas had appeared to him through the likeness that was in the icon. Immediately, believing the account, I went up to the imperial city, which God preserves; and all my affairs that concerned my episcopate were successfully arranged.

Thomas, most reverend presbyter and representative of the Eastern pontiffs, said: “Some whisper about Saint Nilus that he wrote against the icons. Therefore I have his book at hand; and if you command, let it be read.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be read.”

Cosmas, God-beloved deacon and cubicularius, read:

[Col. 0288C] Of the same holy Father Nilus, to Olympiodorus the prefect.

You write to me asking whether you think it would be appropriate for you, as one who is building a great temple in honor both of the holy martyrs and of Christ, whom they bore witness to through contests, sufferings, and labors, to place images in the sanctuary and to fill the walls on the right and left with various animals and beasts [hunting scenes].

Thus, on the one hand, linen cloths, hares, goats, and other animals would appear to be spread out upon the ground and fleeing; while on the other, those hastening to capture them would eagerly pursue them with hunting dogs. At sea, nets would be cast, every kind of fish would be caught, and carried to dry land by fishermen’s hands. [Col. 0288D] In addition, every form would be modeled in plaster and displayed in the house of God for the pleasure of the eyes. And in the common house, a thousand crosses would be fixed, together with paintings of birds, beasts of burden, reptiles, and various plants.

In response to what you have written, I would say that such things are surely for children; it is suitable for little ones to have their eyes distracted by what has been described. But it is characteristic of a firm and manly mind to form in the sanctuary, toward the east of the divine temple, one single cross.

For through the one saving cross this kind is saved, and hope is preached everywhere to the despairing. But it is appropriate to fill the temple of the saints, here and there, with scenes from the Old and New Testaments, by the hand of an excellent painter, so that those who do not know letters and cannot [Col. 0289A] read the divine Scriptures may, by contemplating the painting, receive a memorial of the brave deeds of those who served God in a proper manner; and so that they may be stirred to emulate glorious and memorable actions, because those people exchanged earth for heaven, preferring things not seen to visible things.

As for the common house, marked with many different small rooms, I consider it sufficient for each little room to have a precious cross fixed in it, and I judge it necessary that superfluities be discarded.

Let it be furnished with prolonged prayers, unwavering faith, almsgiving, humility, continual hope in God, meditation on the divine words, compassion for one’s fellow sufferers, and kindness toward servants. I admonish and entreat you to surround and cover and fortify yourself, your wife, your children, and all your possessions with all the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to adorn them with them. [Col. 0289B]

Theodore, most holy bishop of Myra, said: “When this letter was first read, it was corrupt and ruined and deceived us [Gr.: ‘This letter, which was read, had long ago been corrupted and lost, etc.’]. For we thought it was simple and free of traps.”

The most holy bishops said: “If we had then heard the Father say, ‘Paint the house here and there with old and new narratives,’ we would not have been deceived into believing vanities. Instead of what he said—‘paint here and there’—they substituted ‘whitewash.’ That strongly deceived us.”

Peter and Peter, God-beloved presbyters and representatives of Adrian, the senior pope of Rome, said: “The blessed emperor Constantine the Great once did something similar. For after building the temple of the Savior at Rome, he depicted old and new narratives on the two walls of the temple: on one side, Adam going out from paradise, and on the other, the thief entering paradise; and the rest.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “If the ancient defenders of the Christians who accused them were truthful, why did they not produce Saint Nilus’s own book in their assembly for everyone’s satisfaction? Let the most reverend bishops who took part in the false council—Gregory of Neocaesarea and Theodore of Amorium—say whether they brought the books forward at that council.”

[Col. 0289D] Gregory and Theodore, God-beloved bishops, said: “Not at all, lord. Instead, they showed us scraps of paper in place of books and deceived us through them.”

Euthymius, most holy bishop of Sardis, said: “And how, when you were chief priests, did you not demand complete testimonies from the manuscripts?”

Gregory, most holy bishop of Neocaesarea, said: “Believe me, brother, we did not care, nor did we take any pains about it. Rather, as it is written, ‘our foolish heart was darkened’; and ‘claiming to be wise, we became fools’ (Rom. I).”

Theodore, most holy bishop of Myra, said: “Indeed, those scraps that you produced also led us astray. God knows that this testimony of Saint Nilus, not set out as it had been published, blinded us—especially me. But now, when it has been read in full, it has converted and corrected us and saved us.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “Since another book of the same form is present, let it be read.”

Constantine, deacon and notary of the venerable patriarchate, took it and read another book containing the aforesaid letter of Nilus.

[Col. 0290B] Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “It has been clearly shown that Saint Nilus himself, that excellent Father, accepted the holy icons. Yet he was accused by that false council of having spoken against the icons. Thus those wretched men prove to be not only slanderers of Christians but also slanderers of the saints and murderers of their fathers, falsely accusing the most holy Fathers.”

Euthymius, most holy bishop of Sardis, said: “I have the book of Saint Maximus the Confessor at hand, and I offer it for reading.”

Constantine, deacon and notary of the venerable patriarchate, took it and read:

From the doctrinal proceedings that took place between Maximus of blessed memory and Theodosius, bishop of Caesarea [Col. 0290C] in Bithynia, and the consuls who were with him; the beginning of which is:

“Those matters that were discussed concerning our undefiled Christian faith.”

And later:

“Lords, after it has been decided that this should be done, let the outcome of what is being proclaimed take place [or: ‘of what has been decided’]; and wherever you wish, I will follow you.”

At these words they all rose with joy and tears, made a metanoia [Note: [Col. 0289D] In the Joly manuscript this gloss is added: “Metanoia is interpreted as repentance; in this passage, however, it is used for genuflection. Therefore, when it says ‘they performed the metanoia,’ nothing else is meant except ‘they placed their knees on the ground.’ Since kneeling is especially characteristic of penitents, the Greeks often call genuflection metanoia, that is, repentance.”], and prayer was made. Each of them then saluted the holy Gospels, the precious cross, the icon of our God and Savior Jesus Christ, and that of our Lady who bore him, the most holy Mother of God; they also placed their own hands in confirmation of what had been said.

And shortly afterward:

“Then Abbot Maximus turned to the bishop and said to him with tears: ‘Great lord, we all await the day of judgment. You know what has been inscribed and approved over the holy Gospels, the life-giving cross, and the image of our God and Savior, and of his most holy and ever-virgin mother who bore him.’”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “Here, the Father used ‘saluted’ in the sense of adoration, since he adored the holy Gospel and the life-giving cross; and together with them, the images of the Savior and of his undefiled Mother are also to be honored.”

[Col. 0291A] Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Honorable images are numbered together with the sacred vessels.”

The holy synod said: “It is evident.”

The most holy bishops of the island of Sicily said: “So that holy things may be numbered together with holy things.”

Peter, most holy bishop of Nicomedia, said: “We too have the same book of Saint Maximus; and if you command, let what has been mentioned be read again.”

Cosmas the deacon and cubicularius took it and read the aforesaid testimony of Saint Maximus.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let us observe, brothers, how he said ‘they saluted’; and we too ought to do this out of a disposition of honor. For our *latria*—our worship in the strict sense—is directed to the one God.”

[Col. 0291B] John, most reverend presbyter and representative of the Eastern sees, said: “If images were not necessary, they would never have saluted them as a safeguard, so that honorable images are of equal standing with the Gospel and the precious cross.”

Peter, most holy bishop of Nicomedia, said: “And this was said not by just any man, but by that Maximus, wise in God and like the saints; moreover, a confessor and champion of the truth. He is sufficient for us as an example in saluting the holy images.”

Elias, most reverend presbyter [first presbyter] of the holy church of our Lady the Mother of God, situated in Blachernae, read from a document containing the definitions of the holy and universal Sixth Synod.

[Col. 0291C] Canon eighty-two of the holy and universal Sixth [Note: [Col. 0291D] According to the custom of the Greeks, who attribute the canons of Trullo to the Sixth Synod.] Synod.

“In certain representations among venerable images, the Lamb is depicted as being shown by the finger of the Forerunner. This figure was admitted as a symbol of grace, prefiguring for us through the law the Lamb, Christ our Lord.

“Therefore, embracing the ancient forms and shadows transmitted to the Church as symbols and prefigurations of the truth, and preferring grace and truth, we receive this as the fullness of the law. Accordingly, so that perfection may be represented in the features of all faces and in the work of colors, we decree that the human form of Christ our God, the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, be henceforth depicted in images in place of the former lamb [or: ‘be inscribed as the subject of the image’]. Through him we contemplate the height of the humility [Col. 0291D] of God the Word, and we are led back to the remembrance of his life in the flesh, namely, both his passion and his saving death, and the redemption accomplished through them.”

After reading this, he turned to the holy synod and said:

“Honorable Fathers and saints, no one has chosen persecution against the Church more than I have, because of my sins. But this document has become for me a divine hook: in it the holy Fathers of the Sixth Synod signed their names and drew me toward the faith of orthodoxy. Not only this, but also the most holy patriarch, to whom may God grant a reward on my behalf.”

Sabbas, most reverend monk, said: “Why did he read from a document and not from a codex?”

[Col. 0292A] Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Because it is the principal document, in which the holy Fathers signed their names.”

Peter, most holy bishop of Nicomedia, said: “I also have another codex containing the same rules of the holy Sixth Synod.”

When it had been taken up, Nicetas, most reverend deacon and notary, read the same canon.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Some who are weakened by ignorance take offense at these canons, saying: ‘Are they perhaps the canons of the Sixth Synod?’ Let those who are like this understand that the holy and great Sixth Synod was held under Constantine against those who said that Christ had one operation and one will. At that synod, after the heretics had been anathematized and the orthodox faith had been explained, the Fathers returned home in the fourteenth year of Constantine.

“Then, four or five years later, those same Fathers assembled under Justinian, the son of Constantine, and expounded the aforesaid canons. Let no one doubt them. For those who signed under Constantine also signed the present document under Justinian, as is clearly shown by the unalterable similarity of their own handwriting.

“For those who had presented the universal synod ought also to expound the ecclesiastical canons. And so that we might in some way be led by the hand toward the remembrance of his life in the flesh and of his saving death, they also spoke about the venerable icons. If through them we are led by the hand toward the dispensation of Christ our God, what should we consider those who overthrew the venerable icons to be?” [Col. 0292C]

The holy synod said: “Godless, Jews, and enemies of the truth.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “But the Lord our God is good to receive us all; for ‘he will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous’ (Ps. CXXIV).”

Leo, most holy bishop of Rhodes, said: “It has been shown from the divine Scriptures that our Church was attacked and despoiled for so many years. But we give thanks to Christ our God, who raised up our most holy Lord for its restoration.”

Peter and Peter, God-beloved presbyters and representatives of Adrian, the senior pope of Rome, said: [Col. 0292D] “We have at hand a book of blessed Leontius of Neapolis in Cyprus, and we request that it be read.”

Stephen, most reverend deacon and notary, took it and read:

Of Leontius, bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus, from the fifth discourse in defense of Christians against the Jews, and concerning the images of the saints.

Now, let us proceed to make an apology for the venerably painted images, so that the mouths of those who speak unjustly may be stopped. For this tradition is legal, and hear God saying to Moses: “Make sculptured images of two golden cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat” (Exod. XXV). And again, concerning the temple that God showed Ezekiel, He said: “It had figures [alt., ‘it bore’] of palm trees, lions, and human beings, and cherubim, from its pavement to the ceiling” (Ezek. XLI).

Truly terrifying is the saying that commands Israel not to make any carved image, nor an icon, nor any likeness whatsoever of the things in heaven or of the things upon the earth; yet He Himself commands Moses to make carved figures of living creatures, the cherubim (Exod. XX, XXV), and showed Ezekiel a temple full of images and carved likenesses of lions, palm trees, and human beings. Hence Solomon too, having received the pattern from the law, made the temple full of bronze and carved and cast figures of lions, oxen, palm trees, and human beings (III Kings VI, VII, 7); yet in these things he was not reproved by God.

If, therefore, you wish to reproach me over the images, reproach God, who commanded these things to be made so that they might serve among us as a reminder of Him.

The Jew said: “But those likenesses were not worshiped as gods; they were made only as reminders.”

The Christian said: “You have spoken well, because among us too the representations and icons, or forms, of the saints are not worshiped as gods. For if I worshiped the wood of an image as God, I could certainly worship the other pieces of wood as well. And if I worshiped the wood as God, I would certainly not burn the icon after erasing its representation.

“Again, as long as the two pieces of the cross are joined together, I worship the form because of Christ, who was crucified upon it; but after they have been separated from one another, I throw them away and burn them. And just as one who has received an imperial command salutes the seal does not worship the clay, the paper, or the lead, but offers adoration and honor to the emperor, so we Christians, as children, when we worship the form of the cross, do not worship the nature of the wood, but the sign, ring, and representation of Christ. Looking upon it, through it we salute and worship Him who was crucified upon it.

“And just as the children of a certain father who has gone abroad from them for a time, burning with deep affection for him in their souls, embrace and kiss with tears whatever they see in the house—whether his staff, his seat, or his cloak—not worshiping those things, but longing for and honoring their father, so we too, all the faithful, worship the cross as Christ’s staff; as His seat and couch, His most holy tomb; as His house, the manger, Bethlehem, and His other holy dwelling places; as His friends, His apostles, holy martyrs, and His other saints. We honor His city, Zion; and as His village, we salute Nazareth; and we embrace the Jordan as His divine bath.

“For we honor and worship many things with great and ineffable affection because He ascended, sat, shone, touched, or in some way overshadowed them, as the place of God—not honoring the place, house, region, city, or stones, but Him who dwelt in them, shone through them, became known in the flesh, and delivered us from error: namely, Christ our Lord. Through Christ we portray the Passion and the things that belong to Christ—in churches, houses, streets, images, shrouds, inner chambers, garments, and every place—so that by looking continually upon these things we may be reminded and not forget, as you have forgotten the Lord your God.

“And just as, when you worship the book of the law, you do not worship the nature of the skins or of the ink that is in it, but the words of God contained therein, so when I worship the image of Christ, I do not worship the nature of the wood and colors—far be it from me—but, holding the lifeless representation of Christ, through it I hope [Gr., ‘I seem to myself’] to hold and worship Christ.

“And just as Jacob, having received from his sons Joseph’s multicolored and bloodstained tunic, kissed it with tears and placed it before his own eyes (Gen. XXXVII), and did not do this because he loved or honored the garment, but because through it he reckoned that he was kissing Joseph and holding him in his hands, so all Christians, when we hold or salute an image of Christ, or of the apostles or martyrs, reckon in flesh and soul that we are holding Christ Himself or His martyr.

“Tell me, then, you who suppose that nothing made by hand, or nothing created at all, ought to be worshiped: have you never, many times, kissed the tunic or ornament of your dead wife or children when you saw it in your chamber, and drenched it with tears, and yet were not condemned for this? For you did not worship the garments as God, but showed by the kiss your love for the one who had once been clothed in them.

“We also often salute our children and fathers, though they are created beings and sinners, and we are not condemned for this. We do not salute them as gods, but demonstrate through the kiss the affection of our nature toward them.

“As I have often said, therefore, intention is required in every salutation and every act of worship. If you accuse me because I supposedly worship the wood of the cross as the Lord, why do you not also slander Jacob, who worshiped upon the top of Joseph’s staff (Heb. XI)? It is clear that he worshiped not the wood he saw, but Joseph through the wood of the staff—just as we worship Christ through the cross.

“Abraham also worshiped the impious men who sold him the burial place and bowed his knee upon the ground (Gen. XXIII), but he did not worship them as gods. Again, Jacob blessed Pharaoh, an impious idolater (Gen. XLVII), but he did not bless him as God. And again, Esau fell down and worshiped (Gen. XXXIII), but not as God.

“Do you see how many salutations and acts of worship we have demonstrated to you from Scripture without reproach? Yet you may kiss your wife, perhaps shameless and vicious, every day and are not reproved, although God nowhere commanded you to offer a bodily kiss to a woman. But because you have seen me salute an icon of our Lord Jesus Christ, or of His immaculate Mother, or of some other righteous person, you become indignant, immediately heap abuse upon us, and call us idolaters. Are you not then ashamed? Tell me: are you not horrified? Do you not tremble? Do you not blush when you see me destroying temples of idols throughout the whole world and building temples of martyrs?

“If I worshiped idols, why would we worship [alt., ‘honor’] the martyrs who destroyed idols? If I honor and glorify wood as gods, how do I honor and glorify the martyrs who destroyed wooden images? If I glorify stones as gods, how do I honor and worship the martyrs and apostles who shattered and destroyed wooden signs? How do I honor and praise, build temples for, and celebrate festivals for the three youths who did not worship the golden image in Babylon (Dan. II)?

“Truly great is the hardness of the wicked; truly great is the blindness of the Jews, and great their impiety. Truth suffers injury at their hands; God endures insults from the tongue of ungrateful Jews.

“Through the relics and images of martyrs, demons are often driven away. Yet filthy men who attack these things with insults overturn, mock, and deride them. Tell me how many visitations, outpourings [Gr., ‘overshadowings’], and even frequent streams of blood have proceeded from icons and relics of the martyrs. But those foolish in heart, seeing these things, do not believe; they regard them as fables and delirious ravings. They see impious and lawless men throughout nearly the whole world—worshipers of idols, murderers, fornicators, and thieves—suddenly pierced by Christ and His cross, coming to the knowledge of the truth, renouncing the whole world, and practicing every virtue.

“Tell me, how are we idolaters, when we worship and honor the very bones, ashes, cloths, blood, and tomb of the martyrs because they did not sacrifice to idols?”

The Jew said: “And how does God command throughout all Scripture that no creature whatsoever be worshiped?”

The Christian said: “Tell me, are the earth and the mountains creatures of God?”

He said: “Certainly.”

The Christian said: “How, then, does He teach us, saying: ‘Exalt the Lord our God and worship the footstool of His feet, for it is holy’ (Ps. XCVIII)? And again He Himself said: ‘Heaven is My throne, but the earth is the footstool of My feet’ (Isa. LXVI)?”

The Jew said: “But you do not worship them as gods; through these things you worship Him who made them.”

The Christian said: “Your statement is faithful. Know, therefore, that I too, through heaven, earth, sea, wood, stones, relics, temples, the cross, angels, human beings, and every visible and invisible creature, offer worship and service to the one Creator, Ruler, and Maker of all.

“For creation does not worship its Maker by itself; rather, through me the heavens declare the glory of God, and through me the moon worships God, and through me the stars glorify God; through me the waters, rains, dews, and every creature worship and glorify God (Ps. XVIII).

“And just as all who genuinely attend upon a benevolent king salute and honor the richly wrought and precious crown that he made with his own hands—not honoring the gold and pearl, but honoring the king’s head and his most wise hands, which fashioned the crown—so, O man, all the Christian peoples who salute the figures of the cross and the icons do not offer worship to the wood, stones, gold, corruptible image, ark, or relics themselves, but through them offer glory, salutation, and worship to God, their Creator and the Creator of all.

“For the honor given to His saints returns to Him. Conversely, those who destroy imperial images offend the ruler, not the panel itself. The image of God is the human being, who was made in the image of God, and especially because the Holy Spirit has taken up dwelling in him. Therefore, rightly, whoever honors and worships the image of God’s servants also glorifies the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them,’ He says (Lev. XXVI; II Cor. VI).

“Let the Jews be ashamed, for they have worshiped their own and foreign kings rather than proclaiming Christians to be idolaters. We Christians, throughout every city and region, every day and every hour, arm ourselves against idols, sing psalms against idols, write against idols, and pray against idols and demons.

“And how do the Jews call us idolaters? Where are the sacrifices of sheep, oxen, and children that they now offer to idols? Where are the fragrances, the altars, and the outpourings [alt., ‘pourings’] of blood? We Christians, moreover, know neither altar nor sacrifice—neither what it is nor how it is performed.

“The pagans named temples and idols after adulterous, murderous, and polluted men and deified them; but they did not call the temples or altars of prophets or holy martyrs by those names. For just as the Israelites who were in Babylon had organs, harps, and certain other things, as the Babylonians did, but used some for the glory of God and others for the worship of demons, so let us understand the images of the Gentiles and of Christians: they use theirs in service to the devil, whereas we use ours for the glory and remembrance of God.

“Nevertheless, God also caused many miracles to be wrought through wood, naming one the tree of life and another the tree of knowledge (Gen. II), and naming another shrub Sabec, He made it a means of mercy. Then the rod overwhelmed Pharaoh, divided the sea, made bitter water sweet, lifted up the serpent, split the rock and brought forth water, and the budding wood in Aaron’s tabernacle confirmed the priesthood (Exod. XIV and following). Solomon likewise says: ‘Blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes’ (Wis. XIV).

“Thus Elisha, by throwing wood into the Jordan, brought up the iron as a type of Adam from the underworld (IV Kings VI). Thus he commanded his servant to raise the Shunammite boy with a staff (IV Kings IV).

“God, then, who has worked miracles through so many pieces of wood, cannot, tell me, also work wonders through the precious wood of the holy cross? If it is impious to worship bones, how did they carry Joseph’s bones out of Egypt with every honor (Gen. L; Exod. XIII)? How did a dead man rise when he touched the bones of Elisha (IV Kings XIII)?

“Moreover, if God works miracles through bones, it is evident that He can also work them through images, stones, and many other things. Abraham would not allow Sarah’s body to be buried in another person’s tomb, but in a tomb of its own, for the sake of honor (Gen. XXIII). Jacob honored God through a stone, setting it up and anointing it as a type of Christ, the cornerstone (Gen. XXVIII). He also named the heap of stones at Laban a witness (Gen. XXXI). Joshua set up twelve stones in remembrance of God (Josh. IV).

“If, then, O Jew, you had in your temple those two cherubim sculpted, which overshadowed the mercy seat, and some pagan worshiper of idols entered and, seeing them, accused the Jews of worshiping images themselves, what answer, tell me, would you have to give him concerning the two cast cherubim, the oxen, palm trees, and lions that were sculpted in the temple? You would have no truthful answer to give him except this: ‘We do not have these in the temple as gods, but we have these cherubim in the temple for the remembrance and glory of God.’

“If this is so, how can you accuse me concerning an icon? But you say to me that God commanded Moses to make sculptures in the temple (Exod. XXV). I reply: Solomon, guided by this precedent, constructed even more things in the temple (III Kings VI), things that God had neither commanded him, nor that the tabernacle of testimony possessed, nor that the temple Ezekiel saw from God possessed (Ezek. XL, XLI); yet Solomon was not reproved for this. He constructed such forms for the glory of God, just as we do.

“You too, O Jew, had other things for the remembrance and glory of God: Moses’ staff, the tablets fashioned by God, the unconsumed bush, the dry and water-bearing rock, the urn containing manna, the ark, the altar, the plate bearing God’s name, the ephod manifesting God, and the tabernacle in which God dwelt.

“Would that you had first occupied yourself with worshiping these things and invoking Him who is God over all, and had remembered Him through these little icons and figures, rather than having the calf and flies upon the tablets fashioned by God. Would that you had desired the holy golden altar, and not the cows of Samaria. Would that you had desired the staff that had blossomed, and not Astarte, who laid your city waste. Would that you had saluted the rock that gave rain by divine power, and not Baal your god.

“But you do not worship any of these things, ancient Israel, because you did not love God with your whole heart. Whoever loves a friend, an emperor, and especially a benefactor, when he sees his son, staff, seat, crown, house, or servant, holds, kisses, and honors it, honoring through these things the one who deserved well—how much more so God.

“When, therefore, you see Christians worshiping the cross, know that they offer worship to the crucified Christ, not to the wood. For if they had honored the nature of the wood, they would certainly also have worshiped trees and groves, just as you, Israel, once worshiped these things, saying to the tree and the wood: ‘You are my god, and you gave birth to me’ (Jer. II).

“But we do not say this to the cross, nor to the figures of the saints: ‘You are our gods.’ For they are not our gods, but likenesses and images of Christ and His saints, set up and worshiped for remembrance, honor, and the beauty of the churches.

“For whoever honors a martyr honors God; whoever worships His mother offers honor to Him; and whoever honors an apostle honors the One who sent him.

“Would that you too made images of Moses and of the prophets, and worshiped through them, every day, the Lord and God of those represented, rather than the golden image of Nebuchadnezzar. How can you not be ashamed to rise up against me, to be enraged over images, and to bring accusations against the cross?

“If Abraham worshiped an idolater, Moses Jethro the idolater, Jacob Pharaoh, and Daniel Nebuchadnezzar; if these men, though prophets and righteous, worshiped idolaters upon the earth because of certain benefits, why do you exalt yourself against me for worshiping the cross and the representations of the saints, through whom I receive tens of thousands of benefits from God?

“For whoever fears the king does not dishonor his son. And whoever fears God certainly honors, serves, and worships Christ the Son of God, our Lord, as well as the figure of His cross and the representations of His saints. For to Him is due glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and unto ages of ages. Amen.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “The father whose work has been read here flourished with the greatest sacred distinction in one of the cities of Cyprus, and we possess many encomia and festive sermons of his, among which is also his sermon on the Transfiguration of our Savior. He also wrote the Life of the holy John, archbishop of Alexandria, surnamed Eleemon—that is, ‘the Merciful’—as well as the Life of the holy Symeon the Simple, [Col. 0298C] and certain other works; and in all his sermons he is seen to be orthodox. He flourished during the reign of the emperor Maurice.”

John, beloved of God, presbyter and vicar of the apostolic see of the East, said: “That these things are so, to the glory of the aforesaid Father, is evident. For the vicars of the most holy pope brought his book to the holy synod, especially because he demonstrated at greater length the reception of the sacred images.”

Again John, beloved of God, presbyter and vicar of the apostolic throne of the East, displaying a book to the synod, said: “I found this book, venerable fathers, in the imperial city, in the possession of Procopius the silentiary; and I rejoiced greatly when I found it, because we have in the East a very similar copy.”

[Note: [Col. 0297D] In the Jolyano manuscript: This holy Anastasius of Theoupolis, that is, Antioch, was bishop; to him the holy pope Gregory often wrote affectionately, and among other things he mentions that Anastasius had interpreted his book on Pastoral Rule and offered it to the emperor. [Col. 0298D]]

“He teaches in it, then, blessed Anastasius, about the different kinds of worship; and if the holy synod orders it, let it be read.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be read.”

And Stephen, the most reverend monk, took it and read:

Letter of Saint Anastasius, bishop of Theoupolis, to a certain scholar, in which he answered the difficulty raised by him.
