[Note: [Col. 0298D] From the same manuscript: *inopia* means poverty, confusion, failure, solution, reverence, disturbance, and terror, as the earlier interpreters show.] Its beginning is:

“If wisdom is reckoned wisdom by the one who asks about wisdom.” And after some intervening material:

“And let no one be offended by the meaning of worship. For we worship holy human beings and angels, yet we do not serve them. For Moses says: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone you shall serve’ (Deut. VI; Matt. IV). See how, in what he said, ‘you shall serve,’ he added ‘alone’; but in what he said, ‘you shall worship,’ he did not add it. Therefore worship is permitted, for worship is an indication of honor; but service is not permitted—and therefore neither is prayer.”

For the moment, someone may say this as a first response. A second response, however, is subject to the opinions of many, since the skill of interior reading has not yet been grasped.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Let us see what the Father says about worship.”

The holy synod said: “He demonstrates a distinction in worship. For he said: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone you shall serve.’ In saying ‘you shall serve,’ he added ‘alone’; but in the matter of worship he added nothing. The false syllogist, however, takes this passage as though it were a justification of his own position. Yet it is evident that he has assumed it impiously.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “But observe how the most holy [most wise] Father interprets it. What he placed in the middle leads all of us, and those who contend more stubbornly, toward the reception and worship of images. For worship is an indication of honor. Therefore all who profess to honor sacred images but refuse worship will be convicted by the holy Father of saying this hypocritically. In truth, those who do not accept worship—which is an indication of honor—are shown to do the opposite, namely, to dishonor.”

Leo, most holy bishop of Phocia, said: “It is fitting to say prophetically: ‘You have turned my mourning into joy for me; You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness’ (Ps. XXIX). For the divine Scriptures have turned our understanding away from all impiety and filled us with divine knowledge and instruction.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, handed over the book of Saint Anastasius, bishop of Theoupolis. Stephen the deacon and notary received it and read:

A discourse of our holy father Anastasius to Symeon, bishop of Bostra, on the Sabbath, whose beginning is:

[Col. 0299D] “If, as it has been said, and as you yourself confess, it is necessary to question fathers and likewise elders.” And after a little:

“For just as, while the emperor is loved, his image is worshiped in his place, but when he is already present it is superfluous, after setting aside the original, to worship the image: therefore, because it is not worshiped [Gr., ‘not, however, because’], since the one for whose sake it is worshiped is at hand, it ought to be dishonored.

“And after a little: For just as one who insults the emperor’s image suffers a just penalty, as though he had insulted the emperor himself, although the image is nothing other than wood and colors mixed and prepared with wax, so whoever dishonors a figure directs the insult against the very one whose figure it is.”

John, most reverend monk, presbyter, and vicar of the Eastern chief priests, said: “The Father shows that, while the emperor is absent, his image is honored; otherwise it is dishonored [Gr., ‘yet it is not dishonored when he is present’]. So now, since Jesus Christ, the ruler of all, is sensibly absent from us—for He is invisible to the eyes of our flesh, although as God He is present everywhere—His image is to be honored, just as the Father understood.”

Gregory, most reverend monk and abbot of the monastery of Hormisdas, presented the book of Saint Sophronius. Stephen, the most reverend monk, received it and read:

Praise of Saints Cyrus and John by our holy father Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0300B] “Some honor the saints in one way and others in another, proclaiming their gifts in many forms and praising their benefits in various ways. Some do so by erecting lofty temples, others by adorning them with different marbles, others by arranging gilded mosaics; some by splendid works of painting and gold, others by silver monuments; still others by silk and cotton [bambacine] fabrics. In short, all strive to honor the martyrs as each person’s means and will allow, and they desire to outdo one another in these things, demonstrating and displaying their united [Gr., ‘their own’] affection for the saints, expecting imperishable things in place of corruptible ones and things without end in place of temporal things.

“For such things those excellent men customarily bestow in return upon their lovers.”

From the same writing of the same Father, concerning the miracle of those same saints [thirty-sixth], whose beginning is:

“I hear that Alexandria is the metropolis of Egypt and Libya.” And after other material:

“Thus they came to a certain complete temple, terrifying and splendid in appearance and reaching in height to heaven itself. When we entered it, we saw a great and wondrous image, having in the middle the Lord Christ painted in colors; on the left, Christ’s Mother and our Lady, Mary the Mother of God and Ever-Virgin; and on the right, John the Baptist and forerunner of that same Savior, who proclaimed Him with exultation from the womb (Luke I). For even while he was speaking within, he could not be heard. There was also a portion of the glorious choir of the apostles and prophets and an assembly of martyrs. Among them were Cyrus and John themselves, the martyrs, who stood before the image, fell before the Lord, bent their knees, and brought their heads to the pavement, interceding for the healing of the young man.

“And after other material: Coming to the image a third time, they used the practices and words already mentioned. After they had prayed for many hours and lay prostrate below, crying out only, ‘Command, Lord’ [‘If You command’], Christ, moved with compassion, as He truly is compassionate, nodded; and He said through the image, ‘Give it to him.’ The martyrs rose from the ground and first gave thanks to Christ our God, who had heard their supplication. Then, rejoicing and exulting, they said: ‘Behold, God has granted us grace. Enter Alexandria, and sleep fasting in the Great Tetrapylon; take a little oil from the lamp that burns above before the image of the Savior in a small flask, and, returning to this place fasting, anoint your feet with it; you will receive the gift of healing.’

“And after other material: He himself rose after the lamp had been extinguished, took the oil, and came to the temple of the saints. There, as he had been commanded, he anointed his hands and feet, and immediately laid aside his illness and received health.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “He confesses that all these things are to be received: the works of painters and of the other arts, for the adornment of the sacred buildings.”

[Col. 0301B] Thomas, most reverend monk, presbyter, and vicar of the Eastern chief priests, said: “This image, venerable fathers, still stands in Alexandria, in the Tetrapylon [Note: [Col. 0301D] Anastasius, or someone else, adds in the Jolyano manuscript: ‘It is a building with four sides’; I think the correction should read ‘doors’], and it cures various illnesses.”

The holy synod said: “Glory to God, who also performs miracles through sacred images!”

Eustathius, most reverend monk, presbyter, and abbot of the monastery of Maximinus [Maximus], said: “I too, holy fathers, bring a book by the same Father containing the Lives of many holy men; let it be read as your assembly sees fit.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be read.”

And Stephen the monk took it and read:

[Col. 0301C] From the book *The Meadow* by the same Father Sophronius.

“Abba Theodore the Aeliote said that a certain man was shut up on the Mount of Olives, a great ascetic. The demon of fornication attacked him. One day, when the demon was pressing him very hard, the old man began to lament and say to the demon: ‘How long will you not spare me? Depart from me now; you have grown old with me.’

“The demon appeared to him visibly and said: ‘Swear to me that you will tell no one what I am about to say to you, and I will no longer attack you.’ The old man swore to him by Him who dwells in the highest places: ‘I will tell no one what you say to me.’

“Then the demon said to him: ‘Do not worship this image, and I will not attack you any further.’ The image bore the figure of our holy Lady Mary, Mother of God, carrying our Lord Jesus Christ.

“The recluse said to the demon: ‘Let me discuss this with myself.’ The next day he announced the matter to Abba Theodore the Aeliote, who at that time lived in the laura of Pharos. The abba came, and he told him everything.

“The old man said to the recluse: ‘So, abba, you were deceived into swearing to the demon? Nevertheless, you did well to tell me. It is more profitable for you not to leave in this city a brothel into which you do not enter than to refuse to worship our Lord and God Jesus Christ with His own Mother in the image.’

“After confirming and strengthening him with many words, he went back to his own place.

“The demon appeared again to the recluse and said to him: ‘What is this, wicked old man? Did you not swear to me that you would tell no one? How, then, did you tell everything to the man who came to you? I tell you, wicked old man, you will be judged as a perjurer on the day of judgment.’

“The recluse answered him, saying: ‘I did swear, I did swear; and I know that I committed perjury. Nevertheless, I did not perjure myself against my Lord and Maker; and I do not listen to you.’”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said: “Like golden necklaces, so are our God-bearing Fathers, agreeing in the worship of the sacred images.”

John, most reverend monk, presbyter, and vicar of the Eastern pontiffs, said: “Our father Sophronius’ discourse also signifies this: that it is better for one who has sworn to commit perjury than to keep the oath at all costs to the destruction of the venerable images. We say this because some today excuse themselves on account of an oath.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Because he knew the goodness of God, that He receives those who repent, he determined to violate the impious oath. And now, for those who have sworn in this heresy, if they have committed no other sin, there is a reasonable excuse, and they have nothing else to say. But if they fall into other sins, they must appease God and entreat forgiveness for the unlawful oath.”

Theodorus, most holy bishop of the Subritenses, said: “Peter, the prince of the apostles, denied the Lord, but after doing penance he was received” (Matt. XXVI).

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “Herod did not commit perjury, but he perished. Peter, however, denied with an oath; then he went outside and wept, and was saved. For the good God forgives every sin if a person performs repentance with his whole soul.”

The holy synod said: “Yes, Lord; this is what Holy Scripture teaches us.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “The first prince of theology, the holy John, says: ‘My little children, if we say that we have no sin, we are liars’ (I John I). If, then, we ask God concerning our sins, may He be merciful to us and forgive our transgressions.”

[Col. 0302D] Nicephorus, most holy bishop of Dyrrachium, said: “We are held by great fear, Lord, because we have committed many evils, and we ask for brief repentance and confession.”

Leo, most holy bishop of Phocia, said: “It is written: ‘Do not love a lying oath’ (Zech. VIII). For this reason our lying oath is considered of little account, as having no force.”

John, beloved of God, presbyter and vicar of the Eastern pontiffs, said: “If you command, let those matters concerning the oath now be sought.”

[Col. 0303A] Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said: “The matters pertaining to this have already been stated. If there is anything further, let it be investigated at another examination. For now, let us proceed with what has been placed before us.”

Theodosius, beloved of God, deacon and notary, read:

From the miracles of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

“A certain other very gentle man had a fistula in his thigh and, after using many medicines—even submitting himself to the surgeons’ knives—had been afflicted by this suffering for approximately fifteen years. Overcome by it, his illness grew worse; it became a square-mouthed opening, and he was distressed by the rheum lying above it. Frequently, when drink was introduced into the body, it flowed out from there [Gr., ‘the illness increased, producing a square-mouthed opening and discharging the rheum that was present’]. The physicians said that the illness had so mastered him that no human hand could be found to provide relief for his condition.

“The man therefore despaired of himself, and many advised him to go to the consecrated house of God’s holy servants Cosmas and Damian. When he wished to do this—for necessity gives rise to many plans—he saw the saints in a dream saying to him: ‘Come to us, and you will be healed.’

“Thus, having received confidence through the saints’ encouragement, he came to their glorious house and every day did not cease entreating that he might be delivered from his affliction. But when he had remained there for a year without obtaining any visitation, at last he went out beyond the threshold that had been placed before the saints’ house. Looking at the image of the Savior, which had been set up in the right-hand portico—painted upon it were holy Mary, the Mother of God, as well as the holy servants of Christ, Cosmas and Damian, and one of the great men, named Leontius—he made prolonged prayers and wept bitterly for many hours. After entreating the saints, he went away to his own chamber.

“And during the night he saw the servants of Christ, Cosmas and Damian, coming to him, with the Virgin full of grace in their midst, and saying to him [Gr., ‘saying to them’]: ‘Behold, this is the man; help him quickly.’”

He also read another passage from the same miracles: Concerning the wife of Constantine of Laodicea.

It happened that a certain most faithful man, who served in the army, named Constantine, was a diligent petitioner for the patronage of the glorious saints Cosmas and Damian. He had departed from this beloved royal city of Christ on account of the military service assigned to him. On every expedition he carried, as a means of personal protection, an image of the saints in a small icon. When he reached the city of the Laodiceans, which is called Trimetria [Greek: Trimitaria or Trimitania; elsewhere, Trimetaria], and had remained there for some time because of the duty entrusted to him, he obtained a lawful marriage.

After a few days had passed, the wife whom he had married fell ill in the left side of her jaw, and, as an abscess formed there and she was violently tormented by pain, she caused her husband no small distress. He consoled his wife, having great experience of the saints. But, forgetting that according to his custom he carried them with him, he said to her:

“What can I do for you? I am a stranger here. If I were in my own city, I would take some salve of my lords Cosmas and Damian, and immediately your pains would cease and your illness would be cured.”

Since she was a woman of faith, and had marveled at the saints’ prompt healing [Greek: cure], she prayed that, after her husband’s return, she might be deemed worthy to visit and worship them in their glorious and famous church. For, moved even by hearing alone, because of the love she bore toward the saints, she fell silent; and, overcome by sleep on the following night, she saw these great and fearsome physicians and servants of Christ, Cosmas and Damian, in the form [Col. 0304B] in which they had been painted, standing beside her bed and saying to her:

“What do you have? Why are you struggling? Why are you bringing afflictions upon your husband? We are here with you; let nothing trouble you.”

After saying this to her, they departed. When she awoke, she questioned her husband, wishing to learn from him the appearance of the most glorious saints Cosmas and Damian, how they were depicted, and in what manner they were presented for the treatment of illnesses. When her husband had described their appearance and recounted their images [charisms], she explained to him the forms of the saints and also narrated everything that they had said to her in the vision.

Then the husband, recalling from her account that he had beneath his armpit a small image of the saints, immediately brought it out and showed it to his wife. When she saw it, she worshiped it and recognized that the saints truly dwelt there with her, in accordance with their own words [Greek adds: “and immediately the woman was freed from her illness”].

John, the most reverend presbyter, monk, and representative of the Eastern pontiffs, said:

“It has plainly been shown to us that the saints also appear through images while performing miracles. Through the image they became manifest to the woman and healed her.”

Manzo, the most holy bishop of the Pracanenses, said:

“After I left the royal city last year and came to your servile city, where I reside, I was seized by a most severe illness, so much so that I gathered my relatives to make my testament. While the sickness was weighing me down, I brought the most venerable image of our Savior Jesus Christ and said: ‘Lord, who give grace to your saints, visit me.’ As soon as I placed that image, which was to be worshiped, upon the suffering limb, the illness was immediately driven away, and I was restored to health.”

The most holy bishop Theodore of Seleucia rose and said:

“This has also become known to us, for it is near us.”

Likewise Theodore [Greek: Theodosius], deacon and monk, keeper of the venerable vessels of the patriarchal oratories, read:

## From the same miracles: Concerning a woman suffering from twisting pains

The most wise Paul, the pillar and teacher of the Church, rightly cries out that hope does not disappoint and that the love of God has been poured into our hearts (Romans 5). Possessing this hope, a certain faithful woman, who had been rescued from cruel illnesses in various ways through the glorious saints Cosmas and Damian, remembered them continually and with thanksgiving, frequently coming to their wondrous church and paying them the honor due.

To put it briefly, she had the great and admirable saints Cosmas and Damian constantly in mind and was never satisfied; on every wall of her house she had them painted, insatiable in contemplating them. Thus she acted out of her outstanding love [Greek: “she acted”]. Let no one, O faithful, think this incredible [Greek: “incredible”]. For disbelief concerning the benefit of the soul is everywhere judged worthy of accusation [Greek: “for disbelief concerning the benefit of the soul is worthy of accusation”].

It happened that this woman, afflicted with inward and unceasing pains, was confined in her own house and tossed about upon her bed, suffering continual agony; she had not even a moment’s respite from her torments. While she was in this condition, she happened to be alone for a short time. When she saw herself in danger, she dragged herself down from the bed and approached the place where these most wise saints had been painted on the wall. Using her faith as a staff, she raised herself up, scraped with the nails of her hands some of the ointment [that is, the plaster or coating], put it into water, and drank the mixture.

Immediately she became well, when the pains that had been in her ceased through the saints’ coming. After she had recovered, she came to this great church, giving thanks to the Lord God, who had given such gifts to his saints; and she told everyone of the healing that the saints had granted her in this manner.

Symeon, the most reverend monk and abbot of the district, handed over a book. Nicetas, the God-beloved deacon and notary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, received it and read:

## Sermon of our holy Father John Chrysostom on the washing of Thursday

Everything has been made for the glory of God and for our use: clouds for the service of rain, earth for the abundance of fruits, the sea for the prosperity of merchants. Everything ministers to you—or rather, to the image of God. For when imperial portraits and images are brought into a city, rulers and common people go out to meet them with praise, honoring not the panel nor the painting covered with wax, but the emperor’s likeness. Thus creation venerates not an earthly appearance but a heavenly form.

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said:

“The books that have been read are from the church of the holy Anargyroi [Note: Anastasius, in the Joly codex: ‘Cosmas and Damian are rightly called Anargyroi, that is, those who practice medicine without silver or money.’]. That church is in the divinely protected royal city. The clerics who belong to it brought them to us and adjured us to read them in the holy synod.”

The holy synod said:

“And it was right, Lord, that they should be read. They have been brought for the benefit of all of us.”

Peter, the most reverend lector and notary of the venerable patriarchate, read:

## From the fourth sermon of Saint Athanasius against the Arians, beginning:

“The Arians, as appears, once and for all decided to become transgressors.”

And later:

“This too may be considered more attentively from the example of the emperor’s image. In the emperor’s image there is the emperor’s appearance and form; in the emperor himself there is the same appearance that is in the image. The likeness in the emperor’s image is equal, so that whoever sees the image perceives the emperor in it; and again, whoever sees the emperor recognizes that this is the one who is in the image.

“Concerning the fact that the likeness is not changed, if someone wishing to see the emperor through the image asked it, the image would say: ‘I and the emperor are one. For I am in him and he is in me. What you see in me, you also see in him; and what you have looked upon in him, you see in me.’ Therefore whoever worships the image worships the emperor in it, for the image is his form and appearance.”

Tarasius, the most holy patriarch, said:

“The very nature of things teaches that the honor given to the image is referred to the original, and likewise dishonor. The Father has now taken what was read as an example.”

Epiphanius, the God-beloved deacon of the church of Catana, who was serving in place of Thomas, the most reverend bishop of Sardinia, said:

“Examples are understood in manifest things, just as the eloquent Father spoke of the emperor’s image.”

Nicetas, the most reverend deacon and notary, read:

## From Saint Basil’s work on the Holy Spirit, written in thirty chapters to Amphilochius, chapter seventeen

“Both the king and the king’s image are called ‘king,’ and there are not two kings. For the empire is not divided, nor is the glory divided. Thus our principality, which rules us, and our authority are one; and [Greek adds: ‘so also the praise given by us is one and not many’], because the honor of the image passes over to the prototype.”

John, the most reverend presbyter, serving in place of the chief priests of the East, said:

“We have brought with us from the East the book that we hold before us, and we ask that it be read.”

Constantine, the most reverend deacon and notary, read:

## From Saint Basil’s sermon against the Sabellians, Arians, and Anomoeans—that is, the unlike—beginning:

[Note: This gloss is absent from the Joly codex.]

“Judaism attacks paganism, and both attack Christianity.”

And later:

“But the account of truth rejects both opposing positions. For where there is one principality [Greek: one principle], and one thing that comes from it, and there is one original while there is one image, the account of unity is not corrupted, because the Son, begotten of the Father, exists and naturally depicts the Father in himself.

“As image, he possesses immutability; as offspring, he preserves one substance. For neither does someone who looks at the imperial image in the marketplace and calls the one on the panel ‘the emperor’ confess two emperors—the image and the one whose image it is. Nor, if he points to the painted panel and says, ‘This is the emperor,’ has he deprived the emperor, the original, of that title; rather, through this confession he establishes his honor more firmly.”

John, the most reverend presbyter, monk, and representative of the Eastern pontiffs, said:

“That false syllogism whispered that whoever worships the image divides Christ into two; and that whoever sees images and says or writes upon them, ‘This is Christ,’ divides Christ. This is utterly foolish. For Basil, the God-bearing one, who was a luminary and teacher of the Church of God and was divinely initiated by the Holy Spirit, says that the honor of the image passes to the prototype. Whoever looks at the emperor’s image sees the emperor in it; whoever worships it does not worship or see two emperors, but one emperor.

“The Father clearly said that the emperor is called the emperor’s image, and that there are not two emperors. Therefore whoever worships the image and says, ‘This is Christ, the Son of God,’ does not sin. It is manifest that Christ is the true Son of God, confessed as being with the Father in heaven, together with his own body. But through the image made of colors, his sovereignty is worshiped and glorified, and we are reminded of his presence, in which he lived upon the earth. Thus this Father shows that there are not two acts of worship, but one, both of the image and of the original whose image it is.”

Peter and Peter, God-beloved presbyters and representatives of Adrian, the senior pope of Rome, brought a book. Demetrius, the God-beloved deacon and keeper of the vessels of the most holy great church, received it and read:

## From a letter of our holy Father Basil to Julian the Apostate

“According to the immaculate faith of the Christians, which we have received from God, I confess and promise that I believe in one God, the Father almighty: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit. I worship and glorify one God in three persons. I also confess the incarnation of the Son and holy Mary, the Mother of God, who gave birth to him according to the flesh.

“I receive also the holy apostles, prophets, and martyrs, and I invoke them in supplication before God, so that through them—that is, through their intercession—the merciful God may be favorable to me, and that redemption from my faults may be granted to me. Therefore I honor and worship the representations of their images, especially since this has been handed down by the holy apostles and has not been prohibited; indeed, it is displayed in painted form in all our churches.”

Gregory, the God-beloved deacon of the most holy and most praiseworthy apostles, read:

## From Theodoret, bishop of Cyprus, on the life of Symeon Stylites, beginning:

“Symeon, who was a very great wonder of the world.”

And later:

“For they say that this man became most famous in great Rome, so that they set up small icons of him at the doors of all the workshops, thereby acquiring for themselves a kind of protection and defense.”

Joseph, the most reverend monk and abbot of the monastery of Heraclea, said:

“I too, a sinner, bring a book containing the life of the holy Symeon of the Wondrous Mountain, as you command.”

The holy synod said:

“Let it be read.”

Cosmas, the God-beloved deacon and cubicularius, received it and read:

## From the Life of our holy Father Symeon of the Wondrous Mountain, chapter 118: Concerning a woman who was barren at Rhossopolis and afflicted by a powerful demon, who became healthy and fertile and set up the image of the righteous man in her house, where it performed magnificent miracles

There was a woman in Rhossopolis of Cilicia, named Theotecna, who had lived with her husband for twenty years and had not borne a son. It also happened that she had been tormented by a demon from childhood and would bite her tongue. Her husband, no longer able to endure the distress of her affliction, sent her away from his house and for four years had no woman living with him.

But she, having found a companion, fled to the righteous man. When the demon saw him, it immediately roared and was tormented in his presence, seeing with the woman the spiritual image of Symeon, which spoke with a human voice:

“I shall separate you from her, wicked and unclean spirit, and she will return to her husband and bear him a child in the following year.”

The demon howled, violently disturbed:

“Violence against me! It is not your task to dissolve marriages. Why do you also give them a son, when I have by no means produced a son for them? What evil have I done to you? What have I sinned in your sight, that you separate me from my woman? If you had bought me as a slave, perhaps you would also have given me into human service.”

But Symeon said:

“Since you are a wicked slave, recognize yourself, wicked one, and run to burn in the flame of fire; carry water and gather wood.”

Immediately, like a wind that kindles a fire rapidly and violently, the demon rushed off. Carrying a water jar, he threatened the woman; and after filling it and gathering wood from the forest, he brought them back howling and saying:

“Woe to me, woe to me, an evil slave and inventor of evils! What have I suffered? Holy Symeon is separating me from my woman. What shall I do, unhappy creature? I do not know.”

After saying this before the crowd that had gathered, he completed the service commanded him and cried out in a loud voice. Then, seeing a fiery flash coming toward him, he ran around the woman’s station, suffering immense and painful torment; and immediately he departed in this manner.

Symeon restored the woman to her former condition and sent her away healed, saying to her:

“Go, woman, to your house and live with your husband. For the Lord has inclined his heart to receive you with great joy.”

And so it happened. When she had returned, her husband’s heart was immediately turned to love her. He went in to her, and she conceived at once. When the year was completed, they brought the child to the servant of God, praising and glorifying God.

After they had completed their prayer and returned to their own house, the woman, led by faith, set up an image of the saint in the inner room of her home. It worked miracles, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit who dwelt in the saint. Those tormented by demons were cleansed there, and those weakened by various illnesses were healed.

Among them was a woman who had suffered an unceasing flow of blood for fifteen years. She approached in faith to see the image, and immediately the flow stopped. For she had said within herself:

“If I only see his likeness, I shall be saved.”

[Greek adds: “When she saw that the source of her blood had dried up, she immediately ran to the man of God, worshiped before him, praised and glorified God, and proclaimed the miracle that had occurred in her.”]

## Another miracle of the holy Father Symeon

It happened in those days that a certain townsman of Antioch was held by a dreadful attack of an evil demon and tormented for some time, so that he was strangled by it, his breathing passages being constricted. He went up to the saint, obtained healing through his intercession, and became as though he had suffered no evil at all.

When he returned to his own house, he erected an image of the saint in thanksgiving, in a public and conspicuous place in the city, above the doors of his workshop. Some unbelievers saw it being honored so magnificently with lamps and veils. Filled with zeal, they stirred up their fellows, disorderly men, so that a crowd gathered and shouted tumultuously:

“Take away the life of the man who did this, and let the image be removed!”

By God’s providence, however, the man was not then found in his house. They were attempting to lay hands on him, while different men shouted different things. Their malice was great before God, and their envy immense; [Greek: “incited by furies”] they had gathered to do this, thinking they had found an opportunity to stir up hostility and insult the saint, since he had often reproved the wickedness of their faith and the error of those who lived among them as pagans.

Unable to contain such madness, they ordered one of the soldiers to climb a ladder and throw down the image. He climbed up and stretched out his hands to do what had been commanded, but immediately he was struck down from top to bottom and fell to the ground.

When a great uproar arose among the crowd, they set about placing another man there, in their fury. He too stretched out his hands and in the same way was struck down and fell to the ground.

Fearing what had happened, everyone began to make the sign of the cross over himself. But the unbelievers, becoming even more aggressive, added a third man for this purpose. When he also stretched out his hands to throw down the image, he likewise collapsed upon the ground.

Then great fear came upon all the faithful who were standing around. Shocked by the blindness and audacity of the unbelievers, and not of the holy men, they worshiped the image with prayer and departed.

Constantine, the most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“Honorable Fathers, we have heard and believed these things that have been read. I too, a humble man, shall report similar signs that I know to have occurred.

“A certain Cypriot in the city of Constantia was driving his yoke and going to his work. He entered the church of the Mother of God to pray. While he was praying, he looked up and saw an image of the holy Mother of God made of colors on the wall, and said: ‘What is this doing here?’

“Taking his goad, he gouged out the image’s right eye. When he left the church, he struck the oxen with the goad. When the goad broke, a fragment of it flew back into the man’s right eye and blinded him. I saw this man myself and know that he became one-eyed.

“Another man in the city of Citium, on the feast of the holy Mother of God—that is, on the fifteenth day of August—entered a church to decorate it with veils. Taking a nail, he drove it into the wall directly over the forehead of the image of Saint Peter. When he had tied a rope and spread out the veil, at that very hour an intolerable pain seized his head and forehead. He lay there for the two days of the festival, suffering torment.

“When the bishop of Citium learned of this, he rebuked him and ordered him to go and remove the nail from the image. He went, and as he removed the nail, the pain was relieved.

“Let the bishop also be questioned about this, for he is present.”

The bishop of Citium was therefore questioned, and under oath confirmed before the synod that these things had happened in this way.

“Two years ago, men from Citium sailed in two ships to a city of Syria called Gabala. When they were at Gabala, according to custom they were assessed by the Hagarenes and went down to the coast. Some of them, coming into Gabala, turned aside into a certain church of the city.

“One of the Hagarenes, seeing an image on the wall made of stones or mosaic, asked a Christian who was present: ‘What benefit does this image provide?’

“The Christian replied: ‘It benefits those who honor it, but harms those who dishonor it.’

“The Saracen said: ‘Behold, I shall gouge out its eye and see what harm it does to me.’

“He said this and, stretching out his staff, gouged out the image’s right eye. Immediately his own right eye sprang out onto the ground, and he was seized by a burning fever.

“Those who were with him, seeing that he had fallen seriously ill, carried him away and returned him to his city. These things were reported to us by the men who returned to Cyprus, thirty-two in number.”

The most holy bishop Theodore of Catana handed over a book. Gregory, the God-beloved deacon of the most holy and most praiseworthy apostles, received it and read:

## From Saint Basil’s sermon on the blessed Barlaam, beginning:

“First, the deaths of the saints.”

And later:

“Rise now for me, O most illustrious painters of athletic virtues, and magnify through your arts the abbreviated image of the soldier. Let the one who has been crowned, written by me obscurely, shine forth through the colors of your wisdom. Through you I shall go as one defeated into the victorious martyr’s picture; today I shall rejoice, overcome by such a victory of your strength.

“I shall see hands painted by you more subtly in their contest with fire. I shall see the wrestler depicted more brilliantly in your image. Let the demons weep, now struck down by the martyr’s mighty deeds. Let the hand that was burned and conquered be displayed; and let Christ himself, the director of the contests, also be painted upon the panel, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

Constantine, the God-beloved deacon and notary, read:

[Note: An ancient Vatican codex exists in which many sayings of the Fathers, beyond those found here and recited at this synod, appear to have been inserted. For they correspond neither to the order of the speeches nor are they found in any other codex. Among the inserted materials this account of Photinus appears to be one, since it is not read in all the books of this synod.]

## Of Photinus, the God-beloved presbyter and defender of the most holy great Church of Constantinople

### From the Life of Saint John the Faster, of blessed memory, who was bishop of that city

Let this miracle also not remain hidden, and let us not permit that distinguished Father, who has long been hastening especially to conceal it, to conceal it. It was night, and we were walking very quickly, since we were going to visit the emperor Maurice in a distant land—Maurice, who had formerly been most just and gentle, but was now also a martyr; for the most profound Dragon and the tyrant granted him this, even against his will.

As we hurried along, a woman appeared to me at a distance, very beautiful in clothing, appearance, and soul. She had once been exceedingly rich, though she was not thought so because of the calamity that had befallen her. She was mingled with a crowd of our poor brothers and, although those appointed over them had driven her away [Greek: “rejected by them”], she did not withdraw. With tears, though restrained by modesty according to her nature, she nevertheless shamelessly pressed her plea because necessity compelled her.

When I saw this, I left the place to which I had been assigned, seized the woman, and asked what she wanted.

“I have a husband,” she said, “and he has a demon. This is now the third year since I have brought the wretched man to, so to speak, ten thousand venerable places and religious men, and I have been able to obtain nothing more.

“At last I have now come from the desert. For the very man who, among almost all the saints who perform miracles there, had a reputation for working miracles—[Greek: ‘who himself accomplished nothing toward the healing’]—urged me to seek a cure and said:

“‘Go to John, the great patriarch, and from him you will receive, with the blessing of the high priest of God Almighty, an image of the Virgin, the Mother of God. You will go and carry the image into the house in which you lived in your own land. For from now on you will send your husband away and lodge him in the courtyards of your house; he will not see the great royal city to which you are now traveling. You will raise up and place the likeness, and your house will become sanctified. Everyone who dwells in it will be blessed with blessing. Behold, the spirit will flee away and become alienated, and will no longer approach him, because the Lord is near and his glory is for ever. Amen.’”

After saying this, I brought her to the patriarch on the following day. On Fridays he was accustomed to celebrate in the church of the Mother of God near the entrance [Greek: “while on Friday, according to custom, he was about to enter the neighboring church of the Mother of God”]. I reported the circumstances of the affair, at one moment very youthfully and rhetorically, and at another humbly and sorrowfully. I rejoiced, hoping both to persuade and to be praised because I was presenting such pious proposals.

While I was still speaking to him in my sorrow and explaining that the hermit—[Greek: “while I was still explaining, and speaking freely, that the hermit…”]—had said, moved by God, “My lord, you will rightly drive him out,” he cut off my speech. Burning with anger and raising his voice, he cried:

“Yes, Lord, yes, Lord! The hermit shouted: ‘Yes, so that I, the lord, may drive out the demon; so that I may say, “I tell you, unclean one, come out of the creature and go here and there, and into the invisible.” You command me to babble such things, a filthy and sinful man! If you are workers of wonders, drive out my spirit. You need many prayers, brother Photinus—through the prayers of the saints.’”

Thus dishonored beyond expectation, I withdrew in shame. Silently slipping away, I was carried backward and, as though drunk, stumbled into those coming toward me. With difficulty I grasped the edge of a little chapel.

I was deeply angered—for my sorrow had already turned almost entirely into rage because I had found no favor in the sight of the great high priest of God—and in silence I considered many things within myself [Greek: “I complained”]. I thought that nothing good could be hoped for from this man for any of the sheep, since the shepherd had taken on the nature of a wolf.

While I was hesitating over these matters, a plan came to me. I sent someone from among my attendants to the house and brought the woman an image of the Lady from those that had been placed there, sufficiently beautiful. I adorned it very well, as far as possible, so that it might more plainly appear and be believed that I had received the image from the great Father, as though he had already consented [Greek: “so that I might have the image received from the great Father, as though he had already consented”].

I held it out and gave it to the woman. I ordered her to pray for us, to give many thanks to the patriarch, and to depart joyfully.

She was almost freed and exultant, yet did not know what she should do [Greek: “what might happen”]. Thus there was almost half a joy for each of us. I was thought to have succeeded, but I was not rejoicing. She was both thought to have succeeded and was rejoicing; yet the undertaking and the outcome of the matter had no beginning.

Then, thinking in this way to console the collapse of spirit that had overtaken us, I acquired something else [Greek: “another thing”], considering and weighing whom, when, where, in what manner, and by what means I could leave, having deceived and tricked [Greek: “having deceived and tricked”] the most wretched and pitiable little woman, who had placed such confidence in us.

I was especially distressed because I was separating the woman from the protection of better people and, through another man who thought in such a way, was directing her toward those things [Greek: “toward the services that she needed”] which she feared might be whitewashed.

Again, amid these thoughts and because of such deception, I imagined that the spirit would speak out and revile me; and that I myself, by contrast, had confirmed and established the stability that the demon possessed concerning the man.

I had become for him both material and occasion for just accusations—not yet, I say, against myself alone [Greek: “but”], but against all Christians, and first of all against priests, because, they say, one presbyter had prejudged his wife through one sort of arrogance and another demon, which was the demon of falsehood. This is plainly nothing other than a desire to cast out demons by Beelzebub.

These thoughts and others like them continually entered my soul, cruelly disturbed and infected it, and made me expect great evils both from human beings and from God himself. Nevertheless, I reconsidered matters and offered myself an excuse [simulation], placing upon the present moment a kind of imagined consolation, saying within myself:

“God will take care of the future. During this year, perhaps either the little woman, or the man himself, or someone else will die within the intervening time. I myself shall die many times, and the one who brought me sorrow will cease.”

Thus, thinking that I had then been freed from the troublesome people who surrounded the wretched woman, I thought that I had been freed from the crowd.

About three years later, I think, I was standing beside the sacred gates of the great church. And behold, the woman raised her eyebrows and, speaking and breathing heavily and without pause, looked at me and asked the woman beside her:

“Is that, do you think, the man? Or what?”

Then she said:

“It really is he!”

She moved quickly toward me, fell at my knees, bent down, seized my ankles, and kissed me while embracing me and lying on the pavement.

For my part, I allowed it for the moment and rejoiced. I looked about at the crowds on every side, making myself prominent [text uncertain: “displaying delights”], so that those standing around would see me with the woman lying there and would understand that I too was someone of influence.

But she, after repeatedly addressing me with words belonging to poor women—for she was from that class [Greek adds: “and I worship the Lord”; it has “after speaking repeatedly, for she was there”]—then clung to me very tightly and threw me forcibly onto my back. I fell down, becoming a great object of laughter to those standing around.

With difficulty I rose out of respect, slapped her, summoned the deacons, and ordered them to drag the wicked woman to the deacon’s quarters [decanicum]. For, after looking at her face [Greek: “but afterward looking at her face”], I began to think that she was the woman of former times.

She added this as well:

“May God give you, lord, the reward of my house.”

Then—then indeed—I saw everything. Rejoicing and struggling at the same time, I asked only:

“Have you been healed?” or, “How were you healed?”

Taking me aside in private [Greek: “in leisure”], she related her journey to the region and the carrying of the image to her house; and how it had been raised up high and placed upon the walls of her dwelling, both reverently and most suitably.

She said that, after the spirit had repeatedly railed at the image and torn apart the deceiving creature [Greek: “after insulting it and almost tearing apart the creature, and so forth”], it finally departed. “And we were healed,” she said, “of the condition from which we had formerly truly suffered” [Greek: “which I had suffered”]. For the place—or rather, the figure of the Virgin Mother—heals those who suffer similar things.

This is the end of the matter.

Leo, the most holy bishop of Phocia, said:

“It is written that every word shall be established by two or three witnesses (Matthew 18). Today many sacred books have been presented to us; they have watered our minds and have satisfied us concerning the restoration of the holy images.”

And Peter the lector read:

## From the Life of Blessed Mary of Egypt, beginning:

It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but glorious to proclaim the works of God. And elsewhere:

“Others had the temple open to them, with no one preventing them; but it would not receive me, wretched woman, as though some military multitude had been appointed or commanded for this purpose: to bar my entrance. In this way some bold [Greek: dense, crowded] force prevented me. Again I stood in the courtyards. Having undergone or done this three and four times, I was no longer able to be driven out and driven back, for my body had become utterly exhausted by the force of it. Therefore I stopped and withdrew, and stood in a certain corner of the temple vestibule. At last, with difficulty, I came to understand the reason that prevented me from seeing the life-giving Wood.

“For the saving word touched the eyes of my heart and showed me what a filth my deeds were, the filth that closed the entrance to me. I therefore began to weep and lament, and I beat my breast, drawing groans from the depths of my heart. While I was weeping, from the place where I was standing I saw above me an image of the most holy Mother of God. Looking intently and unwaveringly at it, I said:

“‘Virgin Lady, who according to the flesh gave birth to God the Word: I know, yes, I know that it is neither speakable nor reasonable that I, so filthy and so wanton, should contemplate your image, you who are ever a chaste Virgin, pure and undefiled in body and soul. For it is just that your purity should hate and detest me, a wanton woman. Nevertheless, since—as I have heard—the God whom you bore became man in order to call sinners to repentance (Matt. IX), help me, who am alone and have no one to assist me. Command also that the entrance into the church be granted to me, lest you deprive me of seeing the Wood upon which, according to the flesh, the God whom you bore was affixed and gave his own blood as redemption for me. Command also, O Lady, that the door to the adoration of the most holy Cross be opened to me.

“‘Behold, I give you as surety to God, who was born from you, that I will no longer injure this flesh through any shameful intercourse. Rather, when I see the Wood of the cross of your Son, I will immediately renounce the world and the things that are in the world, and at once I will go wherever you yourself, as the saving surety [Greek: vessel], indicate and lead me.’

“After saying these things, as though I had received a certain assurance, I trusted in the fervor of faith and in the mercy of the Mother of God. I moved myself from the place where I had stood making my supplication, came again, and mingled with those who were entering. There was now no one [Col. 0315B] to push me away or drive me back [Greek: to be driven back], and no one prevented me from approaching the door through which they entered the temple.

“Then horror and ecstasy seized me, and I was altogether tormented and trembling. When I reached the door that until then had been closed against me—as though the power that had previously hindered me had now prepared an entrance for me—I entered without difficulty. Thus I was deemed worthy to enter the Holy of Holies. For I was granted the sight of the life-giving Cross, and I saw the mysteries of God, as well as how ready he is to receive repentance.

“Throwing myself upon the ground and adoring that holy pavement, I ran, intending to ask [variant: having gone out], toward her who had given me her assurance. I came, therefore, to the place where the written pledge had been made; and, kneeling before the most holy Virgin, Mother of God, I spoke these words:

“‘You, Lady who love goodness, have shown your mercy toward me; you have not despised the supplication of one unworthy. I have seen the glory that we wanton people rightly do not see. Glory to God, who through you receives the repentance of sinners. What more do I, a sinner, have to consider or say? It is time, Lady, that the covenants of the pledge to which you gave assurance should now be fulfilled. Now lead me wherever you command. Now be my teacher of salvation, guiding me by the hand along the road that leads to repentance.’

“While I was still saying these things, I heard someone shouting from far away: ‘If you cross the Jordan, you will find a good resting-place.’ Hearing this voice and believing that it had been spoken for my sake, I cried out tearfully and called aloud to the Mother of God:

“‘Mother of God, Lady, do not abandon me!’

“Having said this, I left the courtyard of the temple and walked steadfastly.”

John, most reverend monk, priest, and vicar of the sees of the Eastern pontiffs, said:

“We saw such an image in the holy city of Christ our God, and we greeted it very frequently.”

Stephen, God-beloved deacon, notary, and referendary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat, read:

From the Passion of Saint Procopius the Martyr, which begins:

“In those times the tyrant Diocletian was reigning.” [Col. 0316A] And elsewhere:

“The young man, having received great joy, was strengthened in the faith, as likewise were all who were with him; he returned with the soldiers at that same hour of the night and came to Scythopolis. Having secretly summoned all the craftsmen in gold and silver, he questioned them, saying:

“‘Can you make the vessel that I am describing to you?’

“Fearing the man’s severity, they took counsel and placed before him one who was the foremost among them, a craftsman named Marcus, saying:

“‘This man, Lord, will do your will.’

“And shortly afterward:

“‘Marcus did not obey him. But the young man persuaded him, saying: “I will not disclose the secret to the emperor, even unto death.” Believing him, Marcus worked secretly through the night and made a cross of silver and gold.

“When the cross had been completed and erected, three images appeared upon it. At the top, at the beginning, there was an inscription in Hebrew: Emmanuel; and at the two extremities, Michael and Gabriel. Marcus, therefore, in reverence, wished to erase the images, but he could not. His hand remained as though dried up.

“When the cock crowed, the commander called the young man [Neanias] came to Marcus’s house to take the cross. When he saw it, he adored it and said to Marcus:

“‘What are these faces, and what is this inscription?’

“He answered:

“‘Lord, at the hour when the work was completed, these icons appeared, and I do not know whose they are, nor what the inscription may be.’

“The young man [Neanias], however, recognized that some power was present in it. After adoring the cross, he wrapped it in purple and went on his way rejoicing, giving the craftsman Marcus many payments, and entered his own city with two numeri [units of soldiers].”

Stephen, most reverend monk and custodian of the venerable patriarchal books, read:

From the Life of our holy Father Theodore, archimandrite of the Sicenians, which begins:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Cor. I). And elsewhere:

“When he was about twelve years old, a plague from a bubo broke out in that village, so that he himself became ill, almost unto death. They carried him to the oratory of Saint John the Baptist, which was beside the village, and laid [variant: spread] him at the entrance to the altar. Above that, in the receptacle of the cross, stood an image of our Savior Jesus Christ.

“While he was being tormented by the pain of the bubo, drops of dew suddenly fell upon him from the image; and immediately, by the grace of God, he recovered from the pain, was made well, and went home.”

And shortly afterward:

“Wishing, therefore, to imitate David in God-speaking hymnody, he began to learn the Psalter. Although he had learned it with difficulty and much labor up to the sixteenth psalm, he was unable to commit the approaching seventeenth psalm to memory.

“While meditating in the oratory of the holy martyr Christopher, which was in the neighboring village, and unable to learn it, he prostrated himself upon his face and entreated God to make him teachable for meditation on the psalms.

“But the God who loves humanity, who said, ‘Ask, and it will be given to you’ (Matt. VII), granted his request. Rising from the pavement, therefore, and gazing at the image of the Savior, he felt a sweetness sweeter than honey poured into his mouth. Recognizing God’s grace and receiving the sweetness, he gave thanks to God; and from that hour he committed the Psalter to memory more easily and well [variant: more teachably].”

Cosmas, God-beloved deacon and chamberlain, acted as reader:

Letter of Gregory, most holy pope of Rome, to the most holy Germanus, who had been patriarch of Constantinople.

“What kind of joy, and what delight, knows how to gladden my soul as does the gracious message concerning your name—a name truly worthy of reverence and fittingly worthy of exaltation, O sanctified one and divinely guided one? [Col. 0317B] For when I was evangelized even now by your honorable letter, I rejoiced and was gladdened in spirit by exceeding joy.

“Then I lifted my eyes to heaven and offered thanks to the ruling God of all, who has willed in this way even now to cooperate with you to the end and to bring all your affairs into the light. This is what I must pray for night and day; and, trusting in Christ, I shall declare that this desire must never at any time be abandoned.

“Your remembrance of your goodwill toward me at every hour, O most praiseworthy and God-beloved one, also bears witness to my words. Since I have it dwelling upon my lips and cannot endure the pain of silence, I hastened at once to address you by letter. For it is my duty—and more distinguished than every other duty—to greet and address you as my brother and champion [Col. 0317C] of the Church, and to praise the causes of your struggles.

“Even if someone should say, and say most appropriately: let the precursor of impiety who has now suffered cry out instead, intending to exchange evil action for good action through your blessings. For he thought, after the one who fell from above, that he would rage and prevail against piety. But he is hindered from heaven, deprived of his hope.

“He heard from the Church the things that Pharaoh, the Egyptian tyrant, had previously heard when Moses sang concerning him: ‘The enemy said: I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, I will fill my soul’ (Exod. XV). But he also heard what the devil himself heard when a prophetic curse was announced to him: ‘Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will pluck you up and remove you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living’ (Ps. LI).

“Thus he perished, frustrated beyond hope in the endeavors in which he had placed his hope, defeated by your heavenly struggle and strength. The assault of the apostate against God was weakened, cast down, and almost driven to its final destruction by the ferocity of him who opposes Christ. So the Scripture is truly fulfilled concerning him, which says: ‘The bow of the mighty has been broken, and the weak have been girded with strength’ (I Reg. II). For there is no strength against the weakness of God in the abomination of those who oppose God; and it is written that the world fights on God’s behalf against the senseless.

“How, then, should you not be moved, O most holy one, fighting with God against those who are without God and against God? They find the one who is invisibly opposed—or, more truly, who himself fights alongside you—and turns the enemies to flight. And where did you begin the battle? Where God himself showed you, commanding you to lead in the camps of the kingdom of Christ the glorious and truly distinguished standard, that is, the life-giving Cross, the great trophy of its greatness against death, in which he marked out the fourfold boundaries of the world, distinguishing them with lines.

“Then also the holy image of the Lady of all and true Mother of God, ‘whose face the rich of the people will entreat.’ For she is holy, as the Fathers understand, and, having been piously honored by you in this way, grants corresponding rewards. For the honor paid to the image passes to its prototype, according to Basil the Great.

“There is also great piety in the matter of venerable images, as Chrysostom says: ‘I too loved the painting suffused with wax and filled with piety; for I saw in the image an angel pursuing the ranks of barbarians, and David speaking the truth: “In your city, O Lord, you will reduce their image to nothing”’ (Ps. LXXII).

“The Church did not err at all, although it has been judged to have done so. May God forgive us: the tradition is not, God forbid, in accordance with pagan practice. Rather, the intention of the matter is in some respect approved, and the things that are accomplished are not considered.

“For in the city of Paneas, the woman suffering from a hemorrhage was not piously rejected when, in remembrance of the miracle that had occurred in her case, a plant grew around the feet of the statue that she had erected in the name of the Lord Jesus. It was foreign and unknown in appearance, and had been placed there as a remedy for the illnesses of all, through the condescension and goodness of God and our Savior.

“Indeed, if we may put it so, this kind of erection is lawful in God, although grace and truth are to be preferred to figures and should be expressed more distinctly through figures [Greek: expressed more distinctly through figures]. Therefore, by God’s counsel, the assembly of the saints has handed down this chapter as the greatest cause of salvation [Greek: the Church handed down this chapter]】【：】【“】【: in the faces of all and through the working of colors, let us erect the venerable and holy likeness according to the humanity of him who takes away the sin of the world. Through him, as though led by the hand, we contemplate the exaltation of the humility of God the Word, and remember his life in the flesh—his Passion and saving death, and the redemption thereby accomplished for the world. There is here no dissonance from divine things.

“For if the prophetic declarations did not reach their fulfillment, so that matters not yet accomplished might be written down to display them—that is, if the Lord was not incarnate—then let no holy image of him according to the flesh be formed. If he was not born in Bethlehem from the glorious Virgin Mother of God, then neither did the Magi offer gifts, nor did the angel stand above the shepherds, nor did the multitude of the heavenly host offer a hymn to the one who was born (Matt. XXV; Luke II). If he was not carried as an infant in the arms of his mother, he who carries all things and endured the nourishment of milk, he who gives food to all flesh, then let none of this be depicted.

“If he was not received by the old man who holds the sovereignty of life and death, and through whom the Lord of all was at once recognized, proclaimed, and asked to grant release; if he did not journey into Egypt for the sake of the dispensation, upon a light cloud made radiant with every light—namely, upon his mother, strengthened in holiness—he who sits on high; if he did not return from Egypt and dwell in Nazareth, let none of these things be depicted in colors.

“If he did not raise the dead, raise up paralytics, cleanse lepers, give sight to the blind, make the tongue of the mute articulate, strengthen the feet of the lame, and cast out demons; if he did not open the ears of the deaf, perform all glorious works, and accomplish signs in God, let these things not be painted. And if he did not voluntarily undergo his Passion, plunder hell, rise and ascend into heaven—he who will come to judge the living and the dead—then let neither the writings nor the histories that recount these things be written or depicted, whether by letters [Col. 0319B] or by colors [Greek: neither be written nor depicted].

“But if all these things happened, and the mystery of piety is great, would that it were possible for heaven, earth, and sea, and all living creatures and plants, and whatever else exists, to recount them through voices, letters, and paintings. For the representation of things that do not exist is called idolatrous painting; it also fashioned the poem of pagan fable, foolishly asserting as a creation the making of things that never existed in essence.

“Certainly there is no fellowship between the Church of Christ and idols—far from it. We have not worshiped heifers, nor cast a calf at Horeb, nor judged a creature to be God. Nor, again, have we fallen before a carved image and been initiated into Beelphegor; nor have we been murderers or sacrificers of children, nor celebrated secret mysteries. [Col. 0319C] Nor have we ever sacrificed our sons and daughters to demons, so that what Solomon said to idol-worshipers might be applied to us (III Reg. XI).

“Was the earth polluted by us with blood? Or did we make an image in the temple, with a fourfold idol, and worship it? Did we paint upon the wall the abomination of creeping things and animals? Or did Ezekiel see us mourning Adonis and offering incense to the sun (Ezek. VIII), concerning whom the Apostle says: ‘They served the creature rather than the Creator’ (Rom. I)?

“Do you suppose that we set up and worshiped the images of the two prostitutes in Egypt, Oholah and Oholibah (Ezek. XXXIII)? Or were sacrifices to Bel in Babylon and to Dagon in Palestine offered by us (Dan. XIV)? Or have we fallen before other gods of the nations?

“These things are not so; they are not so. Let no one slander us. For in none of the things that exist and have been made has the people of Christ, down to the present day, honored or served the name that is above every name, apart from the holy, life-giving Trinity—far from it. For the manner of idolatry is manifest.

“But the worshipers of God who are Christians must adore the ruler of all. If someone, moved by the Jewish manner to accusation, should publicize the things once spoken against idol-worshipers and charge our Church with idolatry because of the godly and wondrous guidance of the venerable images toward better things, we think he does nothing more than bark like a dog and, cast far away in a sling, hear this as a Jew:

“‘Would that Israel had also been seen by God as offering worship through visible things, and had remembered the Creator through types, rather than retaining the calf and flies upon the tablets of the covenant. Would that he had desired the holy altar more, and not the calves of Samaria. Would that he had attended to Aaron’s staff, and not to Astarte. It would indeed have been good and just for him to embrace the saving Rock, which gave the divine impress [uncertain reading], and not Baal.

“‘Would that he had looked more attentively upon Moses’ staff, the golden urn, the ark, the mercy seat, the breastplate, the ephod, the table, and the inner and outer tabernacle—all of which were made for the glory of God. Though made by hand, they were nevertheless called holy, the Holy of Holies; and likewise the carved cherubim, concerning which the Apostle says: “Cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat” (Heb. IX). From Scripture we are taught that the divine glory was also borne upon them.

“‘If he had attended to these things, he would certainly not have fallen before idols. For every work done in the name of the Lord is precious and holy.’

“And what need is there to extend the letter at such length—especially to a man pleasing to God, a vessel chosen by God, who has obtained the grace of the Spirit and is able, with God as his guide, to look into the depths of divine doctrines and contemplate the summit of the height of knowledge?

“But let us return from this to the subject: to the magnification of your champion, O most holy one, and of the Lady of all Christians; and let us marvel at how you yourself have been shown to have been guided and saved by her in all things, and strengthened against your enemies. Those who for a long time have raged against her found her resisting them precisely as they found her opposing them.

“This is not surprising. If Bethulia was saved by the hand of Judith, an Israelite woman, whose deed was the killing of Holofernes, and those who lived in Israel at that time proclaimed her the savior of Israel (Jud. XIII), how much more should your most exalted holiness, using such a champion, attack the enemies of the faith, subdue them, and crown them with victory?

“May our God, powerful in battle, strong and long-suffering, through her supplications and those of all the saints—he who led you over Joseph like a sheep—guard you, O most holy one, for many years, working for the good of the whole Christian way of life, teaching and urging everyone to obey the sacred canon, and to preserve the deposit that we received from the Fathers; converting those who have not understood even a little.

“O perpetual joy of ours, common benefit and refreshment, most holy one and beloved by all Christians!”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Imitating the divine Apostle Peter, this blessed Father has sounded the trumpet of truth to us from Rome.”

Theodorus [Greek: Theodosius], most reverend monk and notary, read:

Letter of Germanus, most blessed, who was patriarch of Constantinople, to John, bishop of Synada.

“Tarasius, the most praiseworthy patrician, delivered to us the letter of your God-belovedness, in which there was a report concerning the God-beloved bishop of Nacolia. We therefore inform you that even before we received the letter of your God-belovedness, when that same God-beloved bishop had arrived here, we entered into conversation with him and examined his understanding, to learn what opinion he held concerning the matters we had heard about him.

“He set before us the following account [Greek: reasoning, or defense; the manuscript of Jol has ‘reasoning’]. It is appropriate for us to report everything precisely to your God-belovedness. He said that he had heard the divine Scripture say: ‘You shall not make any likeness for yourself, to worship it, of the things that are above in heaven and upon the earth’ (Exod. XX).

“In response to this [Greek: according to this] I said that it is not right to worship things made by hand, that is, things fashioned by human beings. But we consider the holy martyrs of Christ, the true pearls of the faith, worthy of every honor, and we invoke their intercessions.

“To this we replied: The faith, worship, and adoration of Christians are directed toward one and the only God, as it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deut. VI). Our glorification and service are offered to him alone, both by the saints who are in heaven and by the intelligible and incorporeal powers, and by those who, while they were on earth [variant: are], knew the way of truth.

“Thus also, in the churches of Christ established everywhere, the holy Trinity is praised and glorified under a single sovereignty and deity. Accordingly, one God is proclaimed by us, and there is none besides him who rules in his power through the ages, who brought all things into being from what did not exist, both visible and invisible: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the holy consubstantial and life-giving Trinity.

“In this Trinity we have believed, and in its name we have been baptized—in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. XXVIII)—as the God the Word himself, who became incarnate, our Lord Jesus Christ, handed down. He is one of that holy and incomprehensible divine Trinity.

“We do not worship creatures—far from it—nor do we bend toward fellow servants the worship that is owed to the divine sovereignty. For we are not known to offer to earthly kings or rulers an adoration equal to that which we offer to God.

“It is established, indeed, that the prophet Nathan worshiped David on earth, although David was a human being and a king (III Reg. I). Yet he will not therefore be accused as though he had revered a human being apart from God.

“Nor do we admit the making of images formed through wax and colors as a subversion of the perfection involved in divine worship. For we do not form an image, likeness, shape, or figure of the invisible deity, whom not even the exalted orders of the holy angels are wholly able to contemplate and investigate.

“But since the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, recalled his own creation from the condemnation of death and, by the good pleasure of the Father and the Holy Spirit, deigned to become human, sharing flesh and blood with us—as the great Apostle says (Heb. IV)—and becoming like us in all things except sin, we are compelled to represent the character of his humanity and the image of the human form that he assumed through the flesh, not an image of his incomprehensible and invisible deity.

“Through this means we are impelled [variant: endeavor] to represent the things belonging to the faith, showing that he did not unite our nature to himself merely in fantasy and shadow, as certain ancient heretics, in their error, taught; rather, he was in reality and truth a perfect human being in all things except the one sin that was sown in us by the enemy.

“This is the meaning of the sound faith that we have in him: we form the character of his holy flesh in images, salute it, and judge it worthy of every fitting worship and honor, thereby recalling his divine, life-giving, and ineffable incarnation.

“Likewise, according to the same manner, we depict the likeness of his undefiled mother according to the flesh, the holy Mother of God. We show that, although she was by nature a woman and was not alien to our human mass, she conceived in her womb the invisible God who governs all things, beyond every understanding of humans and angels, and gave birth from herself to him who had become incarnate.

“For we properly and truly honor her as the mother of the true God, magnify her, and consider her superior to every visible and invisible creature.

“We also admire and bless the holy martyrs of Christ, the apostles and prophets—our fellow servants, truly made servants of God, proved by good deeds, the preaching of truth, and endurance in the sufferings that they endured for God himself, and shown to be friends of God, having gained great confidence before him.

“In remembrance of their courage and genuine service to God, we depict their likenesses. We do not proclaim them participants in the divine nature, nor do we render them the honor and adoration due to divine glory and power. Rather, by this we demonstrate our love for them: what we believe to be true through hearing, we establish through imitation in painting for the firmer assurance of our faith.

“For, being joined to them by flesh and blood, and through sight being compelled to recognize with certainty the things capable of satisfying the soul, we strive also through vision to confirm fully the certainty of our soul [Greek: also to confirm through full vision the certainty of our soul].

“For the holy men of God themselves, while preserving the service, glorification, and adoration owed to one and the only God, and calling and teaching everyone to do this, poured out their blood and were crowned with the crown of true confession.

“This is the manner in which images are made. It is not that we transfer to manufactured images, works of human art, or any creatures made by God—whether visible or invisible—the worship in spirit and truth that is fitting for the incomprehensible and inaccessible deity. Rather, by this manner we show the love that we rightly possess for the true servants of our God, and through their honor we refer glorification and worship to the God who was glorified by them and glorified them in the confession of his sovereignty.

“Thus we too may show ourselves imitators of their courage and of their love for God through good works and resistance to vices.

“Let everyone know with complete certainty that, according to this manner, the making of images takes place in the Church of Christ, and that we must expect the things that bring salvation from nowhere else—whether in the visible world or in the age to come—except from the only-begotten Son of God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who bestows divine gifts. For there is no other name given among human beings by which we must be saved (Acts IV).

“And although we salute the images of our Lord and Savior, of his undefiled Mother, who is truly the Mother of God, and of his saints, we do not possess faith in those persons according to the same disposition.

“Rather, we know God [Greek: we know that God] as without beginning and infinite, holding all things in his hand, our maker and the maker of every creature, truly God our Savior, having authority in heaven and on earth and having become incarnate for the human race.

“We receive this handmaid, who is properly his mother, as the most powerful intercessor for our race. We receive him as the ruler and giver of the things that bring about our salvation; her as a mother who asks on our behalf.

“We receive all the saints as our fellow servants and as beings of our own nature, yet pleasing to God, as was said above, having obtained heavenly confidence and blessedness with him and having received from God grace to minister his benefits to us: healings from sufferings and deliverance from dangers, through invocation of our God, when in hymns and songs we recall their blessedness and honor by commemorating them.

“For, as Scripture says, ‘The memory of the righteous is with praises’ (Prov. X).

“We have now explained all these things to the aforementioned God-beloved bishop of Nacolia. He accepted them and professed that he held them in this way before God, the Lord of all, and that he would neither say nor do anything else to scandalize the peoples or cause them disturbance.

“Knowing this, therefore, let your God-belovedness neither trouble the God-beloved synod nor cause it any scandal in this matter. Rather, summon him from now on, read our present letter in his presence, and obtain through it his assent and satisfaction. Let him pray for the long life and victory of our excellent lords and emperors, and let him ask for the Christian people the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV).”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Our holy Father Germanus agrees with the most holy Fathers who preceded him.”

The holy synod said:

“Truly, Lord, he agrees in all things.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“When the man of Nacolia received these letters, he concealed them and did not give them to his metropolitan. For this reason blessed Germanus writes again to the man of Nacolia. The beginning of the heresy came from him.”

Theodorus [Theodos], God-beloved deacon, [Col. 0324A] notary, and custodian of the sacred vessels of the venerable patriarchal oratories, read:

Of the same Father Germanus, of holy memory, to Constantine, bishop of Nacolia.

“John, the God-beloved metropolitan of the Synadans, wrote to us that your God-belovedness did not deliver our letter to him. We were deeply grieved about this, because, as is clear, you had set aside both the love [Greek: fear] of God and the love and honor that are owed mutually to the members of Christ.

“For this reason, through the present letter we command your God-belovedness immediately to deliver that letter of ours personally to the aforementioned God-beloved metropolitan, to show him every honor, and to be subject to him according to the order [Col. 0324B] fitting for priests.

“Just as your God-belovedness accepted our words and professed that you would follow them, so remain in them, not abounding in your own opinion. For, as we suppose, you neither fail to know nor forget that you also asked us for leave to resign your episcopate, alleging that an attack was being contemplated against you concerning matters of which, as you said, you were not conscious.
