“You affirmed that you said or did nothing to injure the Lord or his saints on account of their images, but only followed the teaching of Scripture, since no divine honor is deserved by creatures. We too say that this is so, and we firmly retain and profess it.

“We read to you the things that had been written by us to your aforementioned God-beloved metropolitan; and you professed to remain in them. We gave you copies of such a letter.

“Do not therefore wish to cause scandal to a people that has experienced evils, remembering the end of the Lord’s judgment, which he threatened to inflict even upon those who scandalize one of the little ones (Matt. XVIII; Mark IX; Luke XVII).

“Let him know this: until he has delivered our letter to his most God-beloved metropolitan, by the authority of the holy and consubstantial Trinity he has no power whatsoever to perform the priestly office.

“It is more necessary for us to proceed against him with greater severity than to leave him uncorrected and liable to the condemnation that must be rendered.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“As I said earlier, brothers, the introduction of this innovation that was brought in came from the aforesaid man, that is, the bishop of Nacolia.”

Constantine, God-beloved deacon and notary, read:

Letter of Germanus, bishop of Constantinople, to Thomas, bishop of Claudiopolis.

The most wise Solomon said in one of his sayings: “A brother helped by a brother is like a strong and lofty city; and a kingdom fortified with bars is likewise secure” (Prov. XVIII). But I, not considering myself among those able to help, but rather among those who need assistance, have undertaken to write this present letter to your God-lovingness, unable to bear the distress of my thoughts. For I have heard that she has done certain things which, if indeed—as we may say according to the God-speaking Gregory—are lies borne upon the wind; but if they are true, confusion has seized my mind on every side. Do you suppose, then, that she too, following the negligence of many, has used the sweetness of love only with her lips [Greek: “it becomes unlawful there”], and has not descended into the depth of her mind, imagining that we do not burn with sincere love toward her? Or is this not at all the case, but rather that she rejects our inexperience, sluggishness, and negligence regarding what pleases God, as one who has taken no care to investigate the divine will according to the holy commandment handed down to us through the sacred Scriptures? Or, although neither of these suspicions is appropriate, must we perhaps suppose this: that, having received a better revelation for herself—though I am ashamed to say it, through some kind of exaltation and swollen judgment, for “love thinks no evil,” as the divine Apostle says (I Cor. XIII)—she has arrived at some such conclusion as she must necessarily disclose to us [Greek: “must”].

Indeed, these suspicions have given us no irrational occasion [Greek: “occasion from such suspicions”], because your God-lovingness, having spent and remained for a long time among us, and sometimes proposing questions about the wording of passages and verbal matters [Greek: “not the meanings of Scripture, and questions”], never once raised with us any discussion about images, whether of holy men, or of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself, or of his holy and truly God-bearing mother according to the flesh, nor did she, as one making inquiry and wishing to find certainty—that is, asking what our view of the matter was—ask whether what was being done in these things was reasonable, without imposing any condemnation upon those who did them. Nor, considering such a practice worthy of firm rejection and destruction, did she entrust herself to us for counsel, to learn whether we too held a similar view. Yet, as we have learned, while remaining entirely silent about these matters, she caused the removal of the images in her own city, as though this were a common and unquestionable doctrine. If the truth is indeed so, we shall speak again.

For we are not readily inclined to believe without examination those who are commonly said to slander their neighbors. Considering it necessary [addition from the Greek: “But we also consider it necessary”], in discussion and fraternal examination, to make known the things that are in our minds, we undertake to consider carefully what concerns this matter. First we remind you that we must altogether beware of novelty, especially when disturbance and an occasion of scandal arise among peoples who are in the faith of Christ, and when the custom of a long period has prevailed in the churches. If Scripture commands that wine be drunk with counsel (Prov. XXXI), how much more ought we, after much inquiry, to devote ourselves to matters of greater necessity, lest we become liable to the terrible judgment prepared by God even for those who scandalize one of the least (Matt. XVIII). Otherwise, while we ought to overturn the words or practices gathered by unbelievers to the injury of the Church of Christ, we might instead display even this venerable and divine Church as immovable.

This, then, must first be understood: not only now, but frequently also in the past, Jews have brought such charges against us for reproach, as have those who are truly worshipers of idols, attempting merely to disparage our undefiled and divine faith and pressing the matter without directing their attention to things made by human hands [Greek: “so that attention is not directed”; another reading: “not directing their attention”]. Among them all effort and worship in this regard is brought to completion by placing nothing higher than what is seen and perceived, but variously debasing the divine nature: either enclosing its providence, which observes all things, within some place, or defining it by bodily forms. For this reason certain of our predecessors, not ignobly, drove such people from the sheepfold of Christ as “dumb dogs,” “barking vainly,” as Scripture says. Their activities are not now before us.

Yet the word of truth also restrains them through their own impious inventions. One of them publishes the sacrifices of the pagans, the disgrace and abomination of their myths. Another makes the Jews blush, reproaching them not only because their fathers fell into idolatry, but also because they act against the law which they boast of observing. Although that law determined, at a specified place [Greek: “when it had determined the place”], that the things belonging to typical sacrifices should be offered, they do not shrink from doing this throughout every place on earth, devising, in hereditary succession, the accustomed treachery against the Holy Spirit, and thus sacrificing to demons and not to God.

For true service and worship directed to the true God is most certainly guided by observance of the holy confession concerning him and by keeping the laws and mysteries that have been given by him, either generally or in particular. As for the Saracens, since they too are recognized as advancing some such claim, it is sufficient, for their confusion and shame, to bring forward the acclamation which they still celebrate in the desert to an inanimate stone, whose name is said to be Chobar [Greek: “its invocation, which is called…”], together with the other playful mysteries of their vain tradition and conduct, which they performed [another reading: “perform”] in their solemn festival.

But the distinctive form of all Christians throughout the world, serving God under one yoke—that is, the Gospel, as the prophet says—is faith and confession: belief in one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the uncreated, everlasting, incomprehensible, invisible Trinity, of one substance and one throne; together with confession of the incarnation of the Son of God [Greek: “perfect incarnation”], and the other doctrines according to the power of the most sacred Creed, which the people of Christ offer concordantly to God before the mystical and holy oblation.

There is also that spiritual regeneration celebrated through holy baptism in the name of those same three divine and principal persons of God; and the reception accomplished through divine cooperation [Greek: “the deifying reception”], and participation in the life-giving covenants [Greek: “symbols”] of the bloodless sacrifice. Through these the illumination of truth shines forth, and the darkness of impiety is driven away, while they themselves possess the clearest knowledge of their own error—namely, the superstition of many gods.

These things are opposed to one another, as I may say apostolically, just as in the beginning God divided the light from the darkness. Let blessed John the Evangelist say with us: “This is the victory that has conquered the world, our faith” (I John V). Let us add and say: “This is the rock upon which Christ built his Church, unshaken and incapable of being overturned by the gates of hell”—that is, by the assaults of hostile powers (Matt. XVI).

From this we have received a new name, which, as Isaiah says, shall be blessed. For he said: “They shall bless the true God” (Isa. LXV). We proclaim the incomprehensibility of his ineffable nature, which is beyond knowledge and investigation; we preach with unquestionable certainty that it is invisible, unbounded, and altogether unchangeable; and we contemplate his eternal power and divinity, understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, according to the most sacred Paul (Rom. I).

Thus we have been deemed worthy to serve the living and true God, and have been honored and glorified with the freedom with which Christ freed us, delivered from every idolatrous error and impiety (Gal. IV). The chief expression of this knowledge is to say to a stone, “You begot me,” and to wood, “You made me,” according to the prophet’s word; and not to look up to heaven, as Isaiah cries (Isa. XXIX), so that one may consider who it is who displays all these things, who brings out his world in number and calls it by name, because of his great glory and the multitude of his power, whose hands formed the whole host of heaven, as another of the prophets says.

At the same time, when we observe the whole order of creation in its fitting arrangement, we should likewise consider through it, by the understanding of the soul, the principle of its generation [Greek: “consider its productive Word proportionally”], and through it worship the truly existing God, as blessed Athanasius teaches more clearly in his discourse against idols.

Therefore, just as light has no communion with darkness, nor Christ any agreement with Belial (II Cor. VI), so Christians, who worship the one God in inaccessible brightness and power, have nothing in common with those who fashion a god and are rightly called wretched by the prophet (Isa. XLIV). Their heart is ashes, as it is written. Some of them suppose that the works of an idol made by themselves create for them a new god out of things that do not exist; and when this idol falls for any reason and is destroyed, they firmly hold that they have no god at all unless they fashion something else in the same way.

Divine Scripture clearly teaches us this in what happened in the desert through the work of the calf made by the Israelites. When they raised a rebellion, they said to Aaron: “Make gods for us, who shall go before us” (Exod. XXXII). By this they showed that they considered there to be no god at all—neither a true one nor even one falsely so called—unless an idol were fashioned for them by art, or one specially sought out [Greek: “which they were seeking”]. After their departure from Egypt, they would attribute this to it [Greek: “assign this to it”], thereby displaying the excess of their impiety and madness.

Others, after attacking the confusion of pagan religion and hastening to cover it under the name of the gods worshiped among them, carefully produced structures of images [Greek: “constructions”]—of Jupiter, whom they called both father and consul, that is, the highest of gods and men, as well as of the others, whose names are well known to many. Their purifications [another reading: “venerations”] and honors, performed through the sacrifices they celebrate, included fornications, luxuries, and every kind of impurity; to say nothing of shameful words and blasphemies. Among them murders were deliberately committed in honor of a god, and pomp was bestowed upon shameful deeds, being taken up in honor of those who were worshiped, since they performed such acts and rejoiced in their accomplishment.

The images among Christians, however, of holy men who resisted sin even to the shedding of blood, according to the Apostle’s words (Heb. XII), and who ministered the word of truth—namely, prophets and apostles—or of those who were shown to be truly servants of God through a pious life and the uprightness of their good works, are nothing other than examples of courage, patterns of venerable conduct and virtue, and incitements and awakenings to glorify God, in whom they pleased him during the present life.

For discourse that teaches the deeds of good men benefits its hearers and frequently invites them to the zeal of imitation. The same thing is appropriately accomplished when the purpose of images is considered. What historical narration commends through hearing, silent painting displays through imitation, the great Basil declares, saying that from both of these those who attend to them are raised toward courage. For the brief and summarized narration of deeds, as one might say, becomes for us who look upon it, through the painter’s image [Greek: “through the one depicted”], a representation of the very vision that may be imitated.

Thus, just as the wicked deeds of false gods appear together with their idols, so contemplation of this kind impels one person, who receives through hearing what was accomplished by holy men, to remember it; while it instructs another who is ignorant to inquire carefully, and fervently raises him to love and praise God through learning what was taught by that man [Greek: “having been taught his deeds”]. Consequently, by looking at the good works of the saints through both means, we glorify our Father who is in heaven, according to the Gospel (Matt. V).

Moreover, if through Moses the law commands the people to place a violet thread on the fringes at the upper edges of their garments, for the remembrance and preservation of the commandments (Num. XV), how much more is it fitting, through the likeness of paintings of holy men, to behold the outcome of their manner of life and imitate their faith according to apostolic teaching (Heb. XIII)?

To form an image of the Lord according to the appearance of his flesh is, on the one hand, a refutation of the heretics who wickedly assert that he became man only in appearance and not in truth; and, on the other hand, it is a kind of guidance for those who are not altogether able to ascend to the height of spiritual contemplation, but also need some bodily consideration to strengthen what they have heard—especially since the things heard are more useful and ought to be pursued with greater affection [Greek: “whatever things heard are more useful and ought to be pursued with greater feeling”].

For the mystery which in its majesty covered even the heavens, hidden from ages and generations in God who created all things, possesses faith not only through hearing (“faith comes from hearing,” says the Apostle [Rom. X]), but is also strengthened through vision in the minds of those who see. It proclaims with power that God has been manifested in the flesh and believed on in the world; and it will be found most holy and beneficial to all.

Thus the things written in the Gospel proclamations about his manner of life, by which he lived among human beings on earth according to the flesh, have been recorded in memorials among the peoples so that they would not be erased, and so that the worship of his glory and his goodness toward us might more clearly be proclaimed and worshiped.

For it is not a mixture of wood and colors that is worshiped, but the invisible God, who, being himself in the bosom of the Father, receives worship in spirit and truth, giving us through himself the offering directed to the Father; and he too is to be worshiped together with the Father (John IV).

Jacob, too, is said to have worshiped upon the top of Joseph’s staff—not offering worship to the wood, but displaying honor toward the one who possessed it (Heb. XI). In the same way, therefore, the likeness of the holy and ever-glorious Mother of the Lord is understood and honored by the people of Christ. Thus such things were received by the ancient leaders of the most holy Churches, and they were not subject to any prohibition [Greek: “they were not forbidden by any prohibition”].

Although, after the persecution had passed and the transition to the coming of faith had taken place, these practices were retained everywhere, and universal councils were held even down to our generation—councils which set forth rules concerning images in many chapters [Greek: “Although, when the persecutions had ended and the faith had everywhere prevailed with freedom, general councils had also been held down to our times and had issued canons on many matters of far less importance than the dispute about images”]. It would not be appropriate to abandon these matters without examination and superficially if, according to the opinion of some, the custom anciently maintained among us were to perish together with the forms and abominations of idols contained in the divine Scriptures, or were to be led toward alienation from God [Greek: “has prevailed among us from ancient times, tends toward the same thing, and leads to alienation from God”].

For he who said that he would be with the apostles until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII) made this promise also to those who, after them, are overseers of the Church. He was not going to remain with them bodily until the passing of the present age; indeed, he declared that he would be present with those who were to gather in his name, two or three together (Matt. XVIII). Nor would he abandon such great multitudes gathered through zeal for his piety, divine understanding, and guidance, so that they would not see that they had reached the perfection of endurance of his Church—which we believe he presented to himself without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind—even though this custom had been retained not merely in a few or obscure cities, but, so to speak, in nearly every region and in distinguished and principal Churches.

That it is ancient for the historical narratives of Scripture frequently to be represented in images is proved by a discourse of Gregory of Nyssa, of blessed memory, bearing the superscription “On Abraham.” In it he teaches that the story of Isaac’s sacrifice was taken up in paintings. If this is so in the case of those events, as they say [Greek: “If their deeds are so, much more…”], then surely the miracles and sufferings of the Lord’s dispensation ought much more to receive such approval [Greek: “representation”], as should the triumphs of the contests of the holy martyrs, which lead those who behold them to good zeal.

This is clearly shown also in the contest of the most courageous and wondrous witness of truth, Anastasius. But perhaps someone will say that we must fear [Latin reading: “defend”] the precepts of Holy Scripture. For example: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness whatever that is in heaven above, or on earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not worship them or serve them” (Exod. XX). And again: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (ibid.). And in Deuteronomy: “You shall not act wickedly, and you shall not make for yourselves a carved likeness,” nor anything connected with them (Deut. V).

But all these passages plainly have this meaning: that the divine nature is everlasting [Greek: “without form”] and incomprehensible, and must not be considered like any of the things that are seen. Nor may it be brought, through arguments and human ingenuity, into bodily conceptions [Greek: “so that no one may be led by conjectures and suspicions to corporeal conceptions”].

For Moses, after saying, “Guard your souls carefully, because you saw no likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire,” immediately added: “Do not act wickedly, and do not make for yourselves a carved image” (Deut. IV, V), or anything connected with it. He remembered the making of the calf and urged them to take care lest they too, following the custom of the Egyptians known to them, should fall into such impiety and consider the divinity to be like these things.

The great Apostle also declared this in his speech at Athens: “Since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the divine is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of man” (Acts XVII). He continues in the same sense: “And you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX)—that is, you must not call or consider God what he truly is not, so that he has acquired such an opinion and name in vain.

But for us, says the great Apostle, there is “one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things” (I Cor. VIII). This does not mean a natural alternation introduced through the change of prepositions. Far from it. The three are understood as one God, each with the others, as the wise Gregory teaches.

Therefore, up to this day the people of Christ have applied the name that is above every name [Greek addition: “or worship, or latria”] to no one except the holy and life-giving Trinity. Far from it. For where divine Scripture forbids us to serve such things and commands us by every means to be shown strangers to, and excluded from, such an error [more exactly: “Certainly, by adding that the worship of latria must not be offered to such things, Scripture shows us strangers to and altogether excluded from such error”], the manner of service owed to idols is manifest.

Among us, however, there is one God to be worshiped, one and the same faith in him, and one saving baptism. Likewise there is one service offered by us to him, as it was handed down by the holy apostles and preserved; and a sacrifice of praise, which through Christ must be offered to God and the Father, as the divine Apostle says (Heb. XIII)—that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.

There is also the most divine tradition in the life-giving mysteries, which the prophet Malachi foretold, speaking as though from the person of God: “From the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice” (Mal. I).

Therefore there is no agreement between the temple of God—that is, the Church itself—and idols (II Cor. VI). Far from it. For this is the pillar and foundation of truth, as it is called apostolically (I Tim. III). “The names of idols shall be destroyed from the earth,” the prophet Zechariah cries (Zech. XIII), when every place shall be opened to the house of David—that is, to the Church of Christ, whose house we are—through the reception of his faith.

To these may be added both the things contained in the wisdom called Solomon’s and those that lie in the writings of the eloquent Isaiah. In the former it is said: “The beginning of fornication was the invention of idols, and their invention was the corruption of life. For they did not exist from the beginning, nor shall they exist forever. For through the empty glory of human beings they entered the world, and therefore their end was quickly devised” (Wis. XIV), and so forth.

The prophet says: “Those who fashion a god shall be put to shame” (Isa. XLIV), and those who carve them. All who made them shall wither, and they have been made deaf by human beings, together with the things carried about with them—the invention of a craftsman in wood—and the transformation of pieces of wood, which serve human beings, into the form of a man, together with the publication of the madness of those who worship them. “See, you shall not say, ‘There is a lie in my right hand,’” he says, adding this for the destruction of the impiety described above.

We, therefore, knowing and believing in the Son of God, who is truth and the right hand of the Father, are shown to be strangers to the prophet’s condemnation. Accordingly I shall appropriately speak the prophetic word: “What has straw in common with wheat?” (Jer. XXIII). What fellowship can the unsubstantial lightness, driven about by spirits of wickedness, of those who serve the creature rather than the Creator have with the pupil of the true knowledge of God, found in every [Greek: “with the nourishment found in every”] people of Christ?

Those of whom Isaiah spoke (Isa. LXV) sacrificed upon the tops of mountains and offered sacrifices upon the hills, beneath oak, poplar, and every tree that cast shade, because it gives good cover [Greek: “a good covering”], as another prophet, Isaiah’s contemporary, cries (Hos. IV).

But the people of Christ worships the incorruptible, invisible, only and wise King of the ages, God (I Tim. I), in his holy court, offering worship in spirit and truth, and continually presenting every praise and glorification to the life-giving Trinity.

The short end of idols proclaimed by Wisdom—that is, their destruction, and the fact that they do not remain forever—has occurred through no other cause than the appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. His Church, purchased by his blood from the ends to the ends of the earth, always piously understands, confesses, and glorifies this.

Therefore the true and genuine worshiping people of the Trinity, having images of holy men for the remembrance of their virtue, does not draw upon itself any of the condemnation of idols written against them. Nor does it bring any blame or charge upon blessed Paul the Apostle, who forbade circumcision according to the flesh and rebuked those who wished to be justified according to the law, because he circumcised Timothy according to the law, shaved his head, and was plainly seen to have offered sacrifice in the temple.

For one must not look simply at what is done; rather, in every case the intention of the acts must be approved [Greek: “the intention of those acting must be examined, which either acquits the one acting from accusation or condemns him”]. Unless this is carefully observed, perhaps even God’s own command will be rendered liable to accusation among unbelievers.

Although the law forbade carved images [Greek: “Since, although the law forbade carved or molten images”], we learn not only from Scripture but also from blessed Athanasius, when he interprets the psalm’s words, “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear” (Ps. LXXIX), that the cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat above the ark of the covenant, as the Apostle calls it (Heb. IX), were such crafted structures [another reading: “were”], upon which the divine glory also was contained [another reading: “rested”].

Certainly, the essential nature of those cherubim is altogether unknown to human beings. They are spirit and fire, and are alien to every bodily form and nature. Whatever the prophet says of them in more bodily language has a symbolic and exalted [Greek: “anagogical”] meaning, capable of being understood in a different way [Greek: “not capable of being understood otherwise”] according to venerable reason and in a manner suitable to incorporeal beings.

It is also necessary to say that Christians do not worship, or deem worthy of any honor, by painting the appearance of those related to them according to the flesh, whether acquaintances or relatives. Nor did they devise such things by submitting to the power of imperial decrees. Those, rather, are rightly accused who, while claiming to be wise, became fools and “exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man,” as the Apostle says (Rom. I).

Thus it is clearly demonstrated by this very fact that the accusation contained in Scripture cannot be applied to us [Greek: “the accusation which Scripture brings cannot be applied to us”]. If we were shown to transfer pious opinions about the divinity to bodily forms, and to abandon what belongs to the glory and service owed to God, or to diminish it in any way, then those things which occupy and withdraw us from the worship and diligence we practice toward the one true God would rightly be removed.

But now we see the opposite. When someone looks attentively and with due discipline at an image of one of the saints and says, “Glory to you, O God,” adding the name of whichever saint it is, then in this way too what we say in prayer is fulfilled, so that the most holy name of Christ may be glorified through both invisible and visible things.

Nor do we permit anyone to call one of the holy men “God,” although the one who is properly the only and one God has bestowed such an appellation upon those who pleased him, as is written in the sacred book of the Psalms (Ps. LXXXII).

Nor, again, do we, thinking that we possess sufficient certainty of the knowledge of God, despise such images or scorn the gathering that takes place in the churches of God. Rather, day and night—or, to speak with the Psalm, evening, morning, and noon (Ps. LIV)—we bless God, especially at the time of the divine sacrifice and service.

Indeed, knowing clearly that the hope of salvation comes to us from no other source than the pious faith and confession directed toward the one God worshiped in the Trinity—one of which resides in the heart and the other is expressed by the mouth (“with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Rom. VI])—we always have on our lips praise of the God who made us (Ps. CXLIX), and carry his praises in our throats.

The whole people of Christ is driven by insatiable desire and divinely moved zeal toward receiving his most holy body and blood, through which, according to his own institution, we celebrate the remembrance of his death and resurrection, more intensely than the deer longs for springs of water (Ps. XLI).

Nor should it scandalize some people that before the images of the saints lamps are arranged and sweet-smelling incense is burned. Such things are performed symbolically in honor of those whose rest is with Christ and whose honor returns to him. This is confirmed by the wise Basil (Homily on the Forty Martyrs), because honor shown to the good is an acknowledgment of the goodwill displayed toward their fellow servants for the sake of their common Lord.

The visible lamps are signs of the divine and immaterial light that has been given; the fragrance, moreover, is a sign of the pure and complete inspiration and refreshment [Greek: “fullness”] of the Holy Spirit.

These are the matters we have considered necessary to write, as it were, against the objections and contradictions that arise and are produced as though from the Scriptures. We ask that you pursue by every means what may be done without scandal and disturbance among the people, especially since the Lord commands that not one of the least be despised, and likewise imposes an unbearable and terrible condemnation upon those who cause scandal (Matt. XVIII).

Now all the cities and the multitudes of the peoples [Greek: “the entire cities and multitudes”] are greatly agitated over this matter. Let us take every care so that we may not appear liable to blame in it. Above all, we must provide against what moves my mind: that those who are enemies of our faith and of the cross of Christ may take from this an occasion for exaltation, saying that Christians have been in error until now.

For if they had recognized this as idolatry, they would certainly not now have caused the rejection of things made by human hands. Everyone who confesses will recognize how great an injury and degradation this inflicts upon the faith that is in Christ. Indeed, they will surely say something that appears plausible: that those who have once erred cannot be persuaded at all [Greek: “no ears at all are to be given”], since truth is not found among them.

Why should I say more, when even our most pious and Christ-loving emperors themselves, raising a panel as a true display of their own love of the divinity—that is, an image placed before the imperial regalia—and setting upon it the figures of apostles and prophets, while inscribing upon it their words concerning the Lord, have proclaimed the saving cross to be the glorification of their confidence?

There are also the accounts that say that God has worked various miracles through images [Greek: “the chief point concerning those who say that God worked miracles through various images”]. Many wish to compose extensive histories about them—for example, cures of illnesses, which we ourselves have experienced, and the undoing of deceptions, which we have often seen in dreams through paintings [Greek: “frequent visions in dreams of things depicted”].

Most manifest of all, and admitting no controversy or ambiguity, is the fact that the image of the undefiled Mother of God formerly located at Sozopolis in Pisidia poured forth an emission of ointment from its painted palm. Many are witnesses of this miracle.

Although such a miracle is not now taking place, the earlier ones should not therefore be considered incredible, lest in the same way the things recorded in the Acts of the Apostles at the beginning of the preaching—the various signs and gifts of the Spirit, which are now by no means performed—also be judged incredible.

For God, the lover of humanity, through such condescension perfected those who were weaker in his faith, making them stronger, and likewise displayed his power through them [another reading: “through these things”], just as happened in the time of the apostles. Sometimes their shadow brought healing; at other times handkerchiefs taken from their clothing [Greek: “hanging from their garments”] produced cures.

Thus, in those cases, it was not every bodily shadow that gave healing to the sick, but Peter’s alone; and it was not every garment, but only Paul’s handkerchiefs that healed the infirm. This was for the confirmation of the faith in the one preached by them, who also demonstrated his grace through inanimate things.

In the same way, it has often pleased God that something similar should occur in connection with images—not that this kind of benefit was produced in every image or painting among believers, but only in those of the saints, or even of the Lord himself—so that the healings might not be understood to arise from the image of itself, but solely from the grace of our God.

It is worthy, I think, that we should not omit the account which Eusebius Pamphilius included in his Ecclesiastical History: that in the city of Paneas, which the Gospel calls Caesarea Philippi, there is said to be the house of a woman suffering from an issue of blood [another reading: “of a woman who had suffered”], who was healed by touching the fringe of the Savior, as it is written in the Gospels (Matt. IX).

They say that before the entrance of this house stands a bronze statue bearing the image of the Lord, opposite which stands the figure of a woman who has fallen upon her knees, with hands extended in the likeness of one supplicating. She had carefully arranged this in remembrance of the miracle that had occurred to her.

They also say that at the feet of the statue made in the Lord’s name grows a plant of new and unknown appearance, which is a remedy for various illnesses. Eusebius says that he saw this himself. The Savior was plainly displaying, in response to the woman’s faith, the marks of his own gracious dispensation, confirming what we indicated above: that what is done must not be considered in a simple or superficial manner, but that the intention of the one who performs it must be examined [another reading: “of the one doing it”].

The same Eusebius also says that he saw in paintings images of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of Christ himself, preserved through colors [Greek: “reckoned among, or maintained by, colors”]. But we do not say this in order to—
let us strive to make bronze statues, but so that we may indicate that this too was done according to the custom of the Gentiles—not with the Lord’s refusal, but with his willing consent—so that through it the miracle of his goodness might be displayed for a very long time:

> **[Note: [Col. 0335D]** The Greeks, so that sacred things may not be accessible to everyone, enclose the sacred altar with screens; within these they place images, which at the same time cover the altar and are displayed for the people to venerate. Germanus seems to have alluded to this: statues are less suitably able to serve that purpose, and therefore he called the use of images, as being more convenient and more widely accessible, also in a certain sense more pious. Otherwise, that the use of sacred statues is pious and accepted by the Churches is most clearly evident from certain exchanges among bishops and from the definition of this synod itself. **[Col. 0336D]**]

Let the discourse of our commemoration teach how the custom prevailing among us is more venerable—[Greek: “it is not right to censure the custom that has prevailed among us as somehow more pious. In these matters, therefore, let our com[... be concluded]”]. May the God of truth, who has led us into all truth and drives from our souls every occasion of dissension and cause of disturbance, make us worthy of the supercelestial kingdom as we glorify him unanimously, with one spirit.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“The guardians of the Catholic Church cried out—namely, our holy Fathers, who, ever keeping watch over its rams [intelligible ramparts], repelled every battle and empty word. Preserving it undivided, they pursued the entire phalanx of its adversaries, and, together with the ancient heresies, they pierced with the sword of the Spirit the error of the new depravity of those who attack Christians with slanders. Let us therefore all say with one voice, together with our teacher, the divine apostle Paul: ‘Christ is our peace, who made both one’ (Ephesians 2). To him are due glory, honor, and worship, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.”

The holy synod said:

“The divinely sounding teachings of the Fathers have corrected us! Drawing truth from them, we have drunk our fill! Following them, we have pursued falsehood! Taught by them, we salute the venerable images! The Fathers proclaim; we are sons of obedience, and we rejoice in the presence of the mother, the tradition of the Catholic Church!

“Believing in one God, to be praised in Trinity, we salute the honorable images! Let those who do not hold this view be anathema; let those who do not think thus be driven far from the Church!

“We follow the ancient legislation of the Catholic Church! We preserve the rights of the Fathers! We anathematize those who add anything to, or take anything away from, the Catholic Church! We anathematize the novelty clandestinely introduced by those who accuse Christians!

“We salute the venerable icons! We subject those who do not hold this view to anathema! Let anathema be upon those who accuse Christians—that is, those who shatter images! Let anathema be upon those who apply to the venerable images the sayings of Holy Scripture that are directed against idols! Let anathema be upon those who do not salute the holy and venerable icons! Let anathema be upon those who call sacred images idols! Let anathema be upon those who say that Christians approach icons as though they were gods! Let anathema be upon those who knowingly participate in the insult and dishonor inflicted upon venerable images! Let anathema be upon those who say that, apart from Christ our Lord, someone else has rescued us from idols! Let anathema be upon those who dare to say that the Catholic Church ever accepted idols!”

After the foregoing anathemas had been issued in writing, the holy synod, with Euthymius, bishop of Sardis, reading them, pronounced what follows.

Fulfilling the divine command of our God and Savior Jesus Christ, our holy Fathers did not hide under a bushel the lamp of divine knowledge given to them by him, but placed it upon the lampstand of most useful teaching, so that it might shine for all who are in the house—that is, for those born in the Catholic Church—lest any of those who piously confess the Lord should perhaps strike his foot against the stone of heretical and evil opinion.

For they cast out every error of the heretics, and, if a diseased member has become incurably weak, they cut it off. Holding a winnowing fan, they cleanse the threshing floor: the wheat, that is, the word that nourishes and strengthens the human heart, they gather into the granary of the Catholic Church; but the chaff of heretical and evil opinion they throw outside and burn with unquenchable fire (Matthew 3).

Therefore this holy and universal synod, assembled by the good pleasure of God and at the command of our pious and most faithful emperors—Eirene [Col. 0337A], the new Helena, and the new Constantine, this God-preserved offspring—having been convened for the second time in this illustrious metropolis of Nicaea, and examining through its reading the dogmas of our memorable and blessed Fathers, glorifies God himself, from whom the word was given to them for our instruction and for the perfection of the Catholic and apostolic Church.

But against those who do not think as they did, and who, through their novelty, attempt to obscure the truth that truly is, the psalm sings out: “How greatly have the enemies acted wickedly in your sanctuary, and have exulted, saying, ‘There is no teacher, and he will not know us,’ while deceitfully handling the word of truth” (Psalm 73).

We, however, holding in every respect to the dogmas and commands of those same God-bearing Fathers, proclaim with one mouth and one heart, adding nothing and taking nothing away from what was handed down to us by them; but in these things we are strengthened and confirmed. Thus we confess and teach, just as the six holy and universal synods defined and established.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son and Word, through whom all things were made; and in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, consubstantial and coeternal with the same Father and his Son, who is without beginning together with him.

We worship, with the service due to God [latria], and adore and venerate, the uncreated, undivided, incomprehensible, uncircumscribed Trinity, wholly one and alone: one Godhead, one lordship, one power, one sovereignty and might, divided without division among the persons and joined without separation in substance.

We also confess one Lord Jesus Christ, of the same holy and consubstantial Trinity, true God, incarnate and made human in the latter days for our salvation. Through his saving dispensation, passion, resurrection, and return into the heavens, he saved our race and delivered us from the error of idols. As the prophet says: “It was neither an ambassador nor an angel, but the Lord himself who saved us” (Isaiah 33).

Following him, and making this very utterance our own, we cry out with a loud voice: “It was neither a synod, nor the command of rulers, nor a conspiracy hateful to God that freed the Church from the error of idols, as the Jewish council that raged against the venerable images deliriously asserted; but the incarnate God, the Lord of glory himself, saved us and rescued us from idolatrous deception.”

To him therefore belong glory, thanks, thanksgiving, praise, and magnificence; his is redemption and salvation—he who alone can save perfectly and forever, and not those other human beings who come from the earth. In us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, he brought to completion through his incarnate dispensation the proclamations foretold by his prophets, dwelling in us and walking among us, and wiping the names of idols from the earth, as it is already written.

We also salute the dominical, apostolic, and prophetic utterances through which we have learned to honor and magnify, first, her who is properly and truly the Mother of God, and who is above all the heavenly powers; then the holy and angelic powers, the blessed and most praiseworthy apostles, the prophets and glorious martyrs who contended for Christ, the holy and God-bearing teachers, and all holy men. We seek their intercessions so that they may make us familiar with God, the King of all, as we keep his commandments and strive to live virtuously.

Moreover, we salute the figure of the precious and life-giving cross and the holy relics of the saints. We receive, salute, and embrace the holy and venerable icons, according to the ancient tradition of the holy Catholic Church of God—that is, according to the tradition of our holy Fathers, who received them and established that they should be present in all the churches of God and in every place of his dominion.

As was said above, we honor and salute these precious and venerable icons, and we worship them with honor: namely, the image of the human manifestation of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ; the image of our undefiled Lady, the most holy Mother of God, from whom he willed to become incarnate and to save and deliver us from every impious madness concerning idols; and likewise the images of the holy and incorporeal angels—for they appeared to human beings in visible form—and also the figures and likenesses of the divine and most renowned apostles, the prophets who spoke divine words, the martyrs who contended, and holy men.

Through their painting, these images are able to bring us to remembrance and memory, draw us toward the prototype, and make us participants in a certain sanctification. We have both learned and been strengthened to hold this view by our holy Fathers and by the teaching divinely handed down through them.

And thanks be to God for his ineffable gift, because he did not abandon or forsake us to the end, nor did he leave the rod of sinners over the portion of the righteous, so that the righteous might not stretch out their hands to iniquity—that is, to their active deeds—but dealt well with those who are good and upright in heart, as the hymn-writer David melodiously sang. With him we continue to sing: “For the Lord will lead those who turn aside into crooked ways, together with those who work iniquity; but peace be upon Israel” (Psalm 124).

## Translation of the subscription of the Romans

[Col. 0338D]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I, Peter, by the mercy of God archpresbyter of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, and filling the place of Adrian, most holy and apostolic pope of elder Rome, receiving all who have converted from the impious heresy that rejects the venerable images, according to the teaching and tradition of our holy Fathers, approving and consenting to everything set forth above, have subscribed.

Peter, by the mercy of God presbyter and hegumen of the monastery of Saint Sabbas, and filling the place of Adrian, most holy and apostolic pope of elder Rome, receiving all who have converted from the impious heresy that rejects the venerable images, according to the teaching and tradition of our holy Fathers, approving and consenting to everything set forth above, have subscribed.

Tarasius [Note: [Col. 0339D] In the manuscript Jol., Terasius follows John.], by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, affirming that everything set forth above is true, willingly accepting it, have subscribed to these things.

John, by the mercy of God presbyter and syncellus of the patriarchs, holding the place of the three apostolic sees—Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—I consent to everything presented in this text and, in agreement, have subscribed with my own hand.

Thomas, by the mercy of God presbyter and hegumen of the monastery of our holy Father Arsenius, situated in Egypt, holding the place of the three apostolic sees—Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—I consent to everything presented in this text and, in agreement, have subscribed.

Agapius, unworthy bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

John, bishop of Ephesus, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Constantine, bishop of Constantia on the island of Cyprus, accepting, in accordance with what is set forth above, the orthodox faith that we have confessed, and saluting and worshiping the sacred and venerable icons with honor, have subscribed.

Theophilus, unworthy bishop of Thessalonica, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Basil, unworthy bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Leo, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, likewise.

Nicholas, unworthy bishop of Cyzicus, willingly accepting everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Euthymius, unworthy bishop of Sardis, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Peter, unworthy bishop of Nicomedia, willingly receiving what has been written, have subscribed.

Elias, a sinner, bishop of the island of Crete, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Hypatius, unworthy bishop of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Stauracius, a sinner, bishop of Chalcedon, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Leo, by the grace of God presbyter of the most holy great apostolic Church of God, chief of the monasteries, and defender of the most holy Church of God, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Epiphanius, a sinner, deacon of the most holy Church of Catana in the province of Sicily, and representative of Thomas, most holy archbishop of Sardinia, follow as rational sheep ought to follow the voices of shepherds, as the Lord says: “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10). Therefore I too, following the true voices of the shepherds and intending to walk in their footsteps, have subscribed, agreeing with all the testimonies of theirs that were read.

Nicephorus, unworthy bishop of the province of Dyrrachium, in the region of Illyricum, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Nicholas, monk and hegumen, and representing the see of Tyana, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Daniel, a sinner, bishop of Amasea, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

George, unworthy presbyter, and representing the see of Nazianzus, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Constantine, unworthy bishop of Gangra, likewise receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Nicetas, a sinner, bishop of Claudiopolis, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Gregory, the least of bishops, of Neocaesarea, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Gregory, unworthy bishop of Pessinus, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Theodore, unworthy bishop of Myra in Lycia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Eustathius, unworthy bishop of Laodicea in the province of Phrygia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Michael, unworthy bishop of Synada, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Gregory [George], unworthy bishop of Antioch in Pisidia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Theophylact, unworthy deacon and exarch, and representing the illustrious metropolis of Caria, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Leo, unworthy bishop of Iconium, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Anastasius, unworthy bishop of Nicopolis in Old Epirus, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Constantine, unworthy bishop of Perge, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Gregory, a sinner and presbyter, and representing the see of Trajanopolis in the region of Thrace, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Leo, unworthy bishop of Rhodes, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Christopher, unworthy bishop of Phasis—that is, of the people of Trebizond—willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Manuel, unworthy bishop of Hadrianopolis, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Nicholas, unworthy bishop of Hierapolis in the province of Phrygia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed with my own hand.

Basil, unworthy bishop of the city of Silae, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Galato, the least of presbyters, and representing [Stephen], archbishop of Sicily, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Theophylact, unworthy bishop of Euchaita, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Cyril, monk, and representing John [the monk], bishop of Gothia, nourished by apostolic preaching [Col. 0341B] and the traditions of the Fathers, and receiving what is now prescribed, have subscribed.

Theodore, unworthy bishop of Seleucia, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Stephen, unworthy bishop of the city of the Sugdaeni [Sugdaensians], willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Antonius, unworthy monk, and representing the see of Smyrna, willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

Constantine, bishop of Chios [Greek and manuscript Jol.: Rhegium], willingly receiving everything prescribed above, have subscribed.

John, wretched and sinful, a bad monk [or: sinful monk], acting in the place of Procopius, most reverend bishop, thinking in all things in agreement with the Fathers, have subscribed.

Theodore, unworthy bishop of Catana, considering it right always to follow the lovers of truth and the teaching and footsteps of the holy Fathers, and to adorn oneself with their upright doctrines, hastening to be numbered among them, have subscribed, agreeing with everything they have decreed and with what has been prescribed.

John, unworthy bishop of Tauromenium, following in every respect and in agreement the teachings of the holy Fathers and their testimonies that were brought forward, have subscribed.

Gaudiosus, unworthy bishop of Messina, following in every respect and in agreement the teachings of the holy Fathers and their testimonies, which were brought forward, have subscribed.

Theodore, unworthy bishop of Palermo, following in agreement their teachings and testimonies that have been prescribed, have subscribed.

Constantine, unworthy bishop of Leontini, following in agreement in every respect the teachings of the holy Fathers and their testimonies that were read aloud, have subscribed.

Stephen, unworthy bishop of the Bibonenses, following in agreement in every respect the teachings of the holy Fathers and their testimonies that were presented, have subscribed.

John, unworthy bishop of Treocali, having defined likewise, have subscribed.

Theodoricus [Theodore], unworthy bishop of Tauriana, following in agreement in every respect the teachings of the holy Fathers and their testimonies that were presented, have subscribed.

Christopher, unworthy bishop of Saint Cyriaca, following in agreement in every respect the teachings of the holy Fathers and their testimonies that were presented, have subscribed.

Basil, unworthy bishop of the island of Lipara, agreeing in every respect with the teachings of the holy Fathers set forth above, have subscribed.

Theotimus, unworthy bishop of Croton, agreeing in every respect with the testimonies of the holy Fathers brought forward above, have subscribed.

Constantine, unworthy bishop of Carina, agreeing in every respect with the testimonies of the holy Fathers brought forward above, have subscribed.

Theophanes, bishop of Lilybaeum, likewise.

Theodore, bishop of Tropaeum, likewise.

Sergius, bishop of Nicotera, likewise.

Theodore, bishop of Bizye, likewise.

Maurianus, bishop of Pompeiopolis, likewise.

John, bishop of Salonentia, likewise.

Eustratius, bishop of the province of Bithynia, likewise.

Peter, bishop of Germia, likewise.

John, bishop of Arcadiopolis, likewise.

Constantine, presbyter, and representing the see of Sebastopolis, likewise.

Gregory, presbyter, and representing Nicetas, bishop of Colonia, likewise.

Sisinnius, bishop of Parion, likewise.

Epiphanius, bishop of Miletus, likewise.

Nicetas, bishop of Proconnesus, likewise.

John, presbyter, and representing Nicetas, bishop of Colonia, likewise.

Ursus, bishop of the Church of Avaritianum, likewise.

Eustratius, bishop of Methymna, likewise.

Leo, bishop of Cius, likewise.

John, bishop of Apros, likewise.

## ACT FIVE

[Col. 0351]

[Col. 0351A] In the name of the Lord and Ruler Jesus Christ, our true God. Under the rule of our most pious and Christ-loving lords Constantine and Irene, his mother crowned by God, in the eighth year of their consulship, on the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the eleventh indiction.

[Col. 0351B] The holy and universal synod having assembled—which by the divine grace and pious decree of those same emperors, strengthened by God, had been convened in Nicaea, the illustrious metropolis of the province of Bithynia—namely, Peter, most reverend archpresbyter of the most holy Roman Church of Saint Peter the Apostle, and Peter, most reverend priest, monk, and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sabbas situated at Rome, holding the place of the apostolic see of the most holy and venerable senior archbishop of Rome, Adrian; and Tarasius, most holy and venerable archbishop of the great-named Constantinople, New Rome; together with John and Thomas, most reverend priests, monks, and vicars of the apostolic sees of the Eastern diocese.

[Col. 0351C] Also seated before the most sacred ambo of the church of the most holy Great Church, called Sophia, were the most glorious and magnificent men, present and listening: namely Petronas, most praiseworthy former consul and patrician, and count of the imperial service preserved by God; and John, imperial usher and logothete of the military logothesion; together with the entire holy synod, according to the order previously established in the first session. Also present were the God-beloved archimandrites and abbots, as well as the entire monastic multitude [community], with the holy and undefiled Gospels of God laid before them.

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“God, who through the prophets foretold the manifestation of future events, says through the prophet Jeremiah concerning those who introduce novelty [Col. 0351D] into the catholic Church: ‘For they have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water’ (Jer. 2). For every discourse of the heretics is a cracked cistern, from which the teachers who accuse Christians of heresy have drawn, and have given the simpler people drink in turbulent subversion; against them the prophetic voice pronounces woe (Hab. 2, according to the Septuagint). For they wished to abolish the veneration of the holy images, which has been handed down in the holy catholic Church of God from ancient times, imitating the Hebrews and Saracens, the pagans and Samaritans, and moreover the Manichaeans and the Phantasiasts—that is, those who imitate the Theopaschites—as will be shown in the reading of the books that have been produced.”

[Col. 0352A] Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“Let the books of that convention’s false syllogism, which accuses Christians, be read for its refutation and public exposure.”

Leontius, the devoted imperial secretary, said:

“According to the command of the holy synod, the divine [Col. 0352B] books that ought to be read are present—not only those [the text adds ‘however’], but also the books of the heretics of evil name, who long ago disparaged the honorable images.”

The holy synod said:

“Let them be read.”

Cosmas, deacon [notary] and cubicularius, read:

“Second instruction of Saint Cyril, archbishop of Jerusalem, which begins:

‘Sin is dreadful, and transgression is the most savage disease of the soul.’”

And after other matters:

“What opinion do you hold concerning Nebuchadnezzar? Have you not heard from the Scriptures that he was exceedingly impious, possessing a savage character and a leonine purpose? Have you not heard that he brought out the bones of kings into the light? Have you not learned [Col. 0352C] that he carried away the captive people? Have you not heard that he blinded the king’s eyes, showing him his sons while they were being killed? Have you not heard that he carried away the cherubim? I do not mean those spiritual and heavenly ones, but those constructed in the Temple above the mercy seat of the ark, between which God spoke?”

The most holy patriarch said:

“Let us understand how Nebuchadnezzar was condemned, who overturned the cherubim, and what punishment he suffered.”

The holy synod said:

“A great offense and a great condemnation [Greek: after the fall, and condemnation].”

The most holy patriarch said:

“Therefore, whoever casts a sacred object out of a church and overturns it will suffer the same punishment.”

Petronas, most glorious patrician, said:

“Nebuchadnezzar suffered a great punishment, because he was expelled from the kingdom and remained for seven years in the wilderness, eating grass like an ox (Dan. 4).”

Cosmas, deacon, notary, and cubicularius, read:

“Fifth letter of Saint Symeon Stylites, who lived on the wondrous mountain, to the emperor Justin the Younger.

‘Who will give my eyes, O ever-Augustus and good lord, fountains of tears, so that I may mourn and weep bitterly and unbearably throughout all the days of my wretched life (Jer. 9)? For under the divine zeal of your empire, crowned by God and most Christian, such acts of impiety are presumed to be committed, contrary to all reason, by those who are without God—namely, the Samaritans, who stand polluted and accursed above all uncleanness; [Col. 0353A] they dwell in what are called the Camps beside the city of Porphyreon, in the venerable house which your God-pleasing empire ordered to be built there. Your tranquility, preserved by God, will learn these matters in detail through what has been reported to our humility by Paul, the most holy bishop of that same Porphyreon, and sent to us by the most blessed patriarch of the East, who himself also grieved greatly over this matter. How much more, then, should the most gentle rulers grieve? Especially since even lifeless stones would be able to cry out at such impieties, which the aforesaid most holy bishop saw in person. Indeed, our humility regarded it as worse than death and destruction that such impiety should in any way have reached our ears, an impiety exceeding every blasphemous act committed against the very Word of God, who was incarnate for our sake, against the most holy and glorious Mother of God, against the venerable and precious cross, and also against his saints. Therefore, remembering these things, we bring them to your divine ears: if the laws of your most pious and victorious rule command that anyone who insults an image of the emperor be handed over to the ultimate and most destructive death, what punishment, do you think, do those deserve who, with all unspeakable shamelessness and impiety—and, because of their excessive wickedness, I have no words to express it—have dared to commit such acts against the image of the Son of God and of the most holy and glorious Mother of God, with no [Col. 0353B] mercy shown to them? Therefore we implore your most victorious empire not to show mercy to those who dared to do this, nor to spare them, nor to accept any petition or defense whatsoever on their behalf, lest they be turned to some other purpose, as I have already seen with my own eyes when I informed the most holy and God-honored patriarch in the month of August, indicating meanwhile that this matter should be kept among themselves; for God has not concealed their thoughts from us. Hence I am certain, O ever-Augusti emperors, that your heart, confirmed by God and illumined by his greatness, will not tolerate such brazen dishonor—something we have never yet heard of, and perhaps no other Christian has either. But I adjure you, my lord, by Emmanuel, the Most High God, not to endure even for a short while that the appropriate vengeance should be neglected; rather, order an investigation also into what they did in the well, according to the substance of the letter that was sent to our lowliness. Let not your most gentle rule permit certain persons, should they perhaps think of sowing troublesome arguments, to claim that these matters belong to the power of the Lady Augusta [Greek: that they pertain to the authority of the Lady Augusta], when the God who gave you the empire has been treated with such insults exceeding all impiety. Thus the others may fear them throughout all the days of their accursed and separated life; and their kindred darkness will receive them for condemnation—the worm [ashes] that will consume them, and the fire [Col. 0354A] that will [not] shine. The holy and almighty Spirit of Jesus Christ our Lord, who proceeds from the Father, will anathematize [catathematize] them in the lower regions of the abyss, to destroy them in endless destruction. For by displaying this zeal vigorously on behalf of him who, together with your piety, reigns—the only-begotten God—you, preserved by God and triumphant rulers, will be received above Abraham’s sacrifice by his divinity, which sees all things. Your empire, beloved of Christ, will be all the more blessed by the power of his might and magnified above all preceding kingdoms; for to him be glory forever and ever. Amen.’”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“You know what judgment the Father pronounced?”

[Col. 0354B] Basil, most holy bishop of Ancyra, said:

“He judged them unworthy even of pardon.”

John, most reverend monk and vicar of the Eastern bishops, said:

“It is clear to everyone that the Samaritans are worse than the other heretics; their heresy is exceedingly to be rejected and is perverse, wholly distant from grace. Thus the speech has shown that those who overturn the venerable icons are worse than these people. It is therefore appropriate [Greek: It is sufficient] to call them Samaritans.”

Constantine, most holy bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“I consider the breakers of images so much worse than the Samaritans as the latter acted in ignorance, being strangers to Christianity, whereas these acted knowingly; and therefore they are unworthy of satisfaction [reparation]. For, as it is written: ‘The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it shall be beaten with many blows’ (Luke 12).”

Nicholas, most holy bishop of Cyzicus, said:

“Behold, I, the least servant of your holiness, bring the book of our holy Father John, bishop of Thessalonica, and request that it be read.”

The holy synod said:

“Let it be read.”

Demetrius, most reverend deacon and skeuophylax, took it and read:

“John, bishop of Thessalonica, on the discourse, which begins:

‘Until now the enemy continues tempting our Lord Jesus Christ in the wilderness.’”

And after a little:

“The pagan said: ‘You therefore paint images of your saints in the churches, and worship them? And not only those of the saints, but also those of your God himself? So consider that we too, embracing statues, do not worship them, but the incorporeal powers that are appeased through them.’

“The holy man said: ‘But we make images of human beings, namely of the holy servants of God who bore bodies, in order to remember and honor them; and we do nothing inappropriate by painting them as they were. For we do not act as you do, nor do we represent bodily forms of certain incorporeal beings. Moreover, when we worship, we do not glorify the images, as you yourself have just said, but those who are indicated by the painting. [Col. 0355A] And we do not treat these as gods—far from it—but as God’s own servants and friends, trusting that they intercede for us. We do, however, make images of God, that is, of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, as he appeared upon earth and lived among human beings; we paint him in this way, not as he is understood according to his nature as God. For what likeness or form can there be of the incorporeal and formless Word of the Father? “God is spirit,” as it is written (John 4), that is, the nature of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. But because, by the good pleasure of God the Father, his only-begotten Son and God the Word descended from heaven and was incarnate for our salvation, from the Holy Spirit and the undefiled Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, we paint his humanity, not his incorporeal divinity.’”

[Col. 0355B] The pagan said:

“Granted: God the Word is depicted as incarnate. But what do you assert concerning the angels? You also depict them as human beings and worship them, although they are not human beings but intelligible and incorporeal, both so called and existent. So consider that those honored among us are appeased as gods by statues, without our doing anything inappropriate, just as neither do you act improperly regarding the angels you depict.”

The holy man said:

“Concerning angels and archangels and the holy powers above them, I will add also the souls of our human beings: the catholic and apostolic Church knows them to be intelligible, but not altogether incorporeal and invisible, as you pagans claim. Rather, they are subtle in body, aerial, and fiery [Note: [Col. 0355D] He speaks according to his own opinion; for above, in Session 4, the council affirms in its confession that angels are incorporeal], according to what is written: ‘He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire’ (Ps. 103; Heb. 1). We find that many of our holy Fathers held this view, including that great Basil, Athanasius of holy memory, Methodius, and those associated with them. For, to speak truthfully, only the divinity is incorporeal and uncircumscribed. Intelligible creatures, however, are not altogether incorporeal and invisible as the divinity is; therefore they exist in a place and are circumscribed.

“Furthermore, if anywhere you find angels, demons, or souls called incorporeal, understand that they are so called because they are not gross bodies, like those by which we are surrounded, composed of a mixture of the four material elements. Although, to speak more accurately, they are incorporeal in comparison with us [Greek: invisible], they have nevertheless often been seen perceptibly in the form of their own bodies by many people—seen by those to whom God opened their eyes—and they are shown to be circumscribed in place, since they are not altogether incorporeal like the divine nature. Therefore, when we paint and honor angels not as gods but as spiritual creatures and ministers of God, and not as beings that are properly incorporeal, we do not sin. That we depict them in human form is because they have frequently appeared in that form to those to whom they were sent by God alone.”

[Col. 0356A] Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Let us attend with our ears to what the Father has said. There, as we have learned, the Samaritans overturned images of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of his undefiled mother; here, the pagans did so. The Father has shown that angels too ought to be depicted, because they are circumscribed and have appeared to many in human form.”

The holy synod said:

“Yes, my lord.”

Stephen the monk read:

“On the Dispute between a Jew and a Christian.

“The Jew says: ‘I have believed in everything, and I believe in Jesus Christ, who was crucified, because he is the Son of the living God. But I take offense at you Christians, because you worship images. For Scripture everywhere commands that no one make for himself a graven image or any likeness.’

“The Christian said: ‘The Scriptures command you not to worship a new god, and not to worship every likeness as God. But the images you see are painted as a reminder of the most benevolent salvation accomplished through our Savior Jesus Christ, signifying the person of his incarnation. The images of the saints likewise signify each one’s struggles, which they endured against the devil, as well as their victories and crowns. Christians do not worship them by deifying them, as you understand, but, burning with zeal and faith, they contemplate the images of the saints, preserving the memory of these worshipers of God. And when they worship, they invoke the God of the saints, saying: “Blessed are you, God of this saint and of all the saints, who gave them patience and made them worthy of your kingdom; make us also participants in it, and save us through their prayers.”

“But when we contemplate and worship the icon of the Savior, with spiritual eyes and the vision of our heart we give thanks to God, the Lord of all, who graciously deigned to receive humanity in the form of a servant, to save the world, and to become like us in all things, without any sin. Therefore we do not worship or venerate a wooden or painted image, but glorify Christ the Lord and God of all.

“Nevertheless, brother, I will show you that Moses, who gave you these things in the Law, was also commanded—as it is written (Exod. 7 and 25)—and made two sculpted seraphim, spread out above the tabernacle of testimony on either side. No one was permitted to enter there except the high priest, once a year, and offer incense in the Holy of Holies. Likewise, he made a bronze serpent, fashioning it as a cast work of bronze, and suspended it in the middle of the camp, saying: “Whoever has been bitten by a serpent, let him look at this bronze serpent and believe that this serpent is able to heal him, and he will be healed” (Num. 21). You see how that Moses, who commanded that no likeness be made, himself made a likeness.’”

John, most reverend monk, priest, and vicar of the Eastern bishops, said:

“Behold, most sacred Fathers, those who deny the incarnate dispensation of Christ our God—namely, the Hebrews and Samaritans—plainly say that the holy images must be cast away [Greek: have cast them away]. Therefore those who reject them are like these people.”

The holy synod said:

“They are like them.”

Epiphanius, God-beloved deacon and representing Thomas, bishop of Sardinia, read:

“From the false superscriptions of the itineraries of the holy apostles.

“Thus the painter rested on the first day, after outlining him. On the following day he also blended colors into it and gave the icon to the rejoicing Lycomedes, who placed it in his bedchamber and crowned it. When John later learned of this, he said to him: ‘My dear son, what are you doing, having entered [or: entering] your bedchamber alone from the bath? Do I not pray with you and with the other brothers? Are you hiding us?’ And saying this playfully, he entered the bedchamber with him and saw the icon of the elder crowned, with lamps placed beside it. He summoned and called him, and said: ‘Lycomedes, what is the meaning of this image? Which of your gods is this who has been depicted? For I see that you are still living as a pagan.’

“Lycomedes answered him: ‘God, certainly, is for me that one alone who raised me from death together with my wife. But if those human beings who are our benefactors ought also to be called gods after God, then you are the one depicted in the image, whom I crown, love, and venerate, because you have become a good guide for me.’

“And John, not yet having looked upon his own face, said to him: ‘You mock me, my little son. Am I really of such a form above your lord? How will you persuade me that the image resembles me?’ Lycomedes brought him a mirror. Seeing himself in the mirror and looking at the image, he said: ‘As the Lord Jesus Christ lives, the image resembles me; but you have done wrong in this.’”

He continued reading from the same book, which begins:

“‘Once, wishing to hold Jesus.’”

And after other matters:

“‘They encountered him in a material and gross body [Greek: I laid hands on him]. But at another time, when I again touched him, what was beneath my touch was without matter and incorporeal, as though it did not exist at all. Moreover, whenever he was invited by one of the Pharisees to recline at table, we too went with him; and each of us received one prepared loaf from those who invited him, and he himself received one among them. After blessing his own loaf, he divided it among us, and each of us was filled from the small portion, while our loaves remained whole, so that those who had invited him were astonished.

“Many times I wanted, as I walked with him, to see whether his footprint appeared upon the ground. For I saw him lift himself from the earth, and I never once saw such a footprint.

“I say these things to you still, brothers, as an exhortation and for the sake of faith in him. For since his great and wondrous deeds are ineffable, let them be passed over in silence [Greek: now let them be silent], since perhaps they can neither be spoken nor heard.

“Before he was seized by the impious Jews, who received the Law from the unjust serpent, he gathered us all together and said: “Before I am handed over to them, let us sing a hymn to the Father, and then go out to what is appointed.” When he had commanded us to form a circle, holding one another’s hands, he stood in the middle and said: “Amen. Obey me.” He began to sing the hymn and say:

“‘Glory to you, Father.’ And we, surrounding him, answered: ‘Amen.’

“‘Glory to you, Word; glory to you, Grace.’ Amen.

“‘Glory to you, Spirit; glory to you, Holy One; glory to the glory that is yours.’ Amen.

“‘We praise you, Father; we give you thanks, light in which darkness does not dwell.’ Amen.

“‘As for what we gave thanks in, I say [perhaps: he says]: I wish to be saved, and I wish to save.’ Amen.

“‘I wish to be released, and I wish to release.’ Amen.

“‘I wish to waste away, and I wish to cause to waste away [to make waste].’ [Greek adds: I wish to be wounded, and I wish to wound.] Amen.

“‘I wish to be born, and I wish to beget.’ [Col. 0358B] Amen.

“‘I wish to eat, and I wish to be consumed.’ Amen.

“‘I wish to be heard, and I wish to hear.’ Amen.

“‘I wish to be understood, although I am wholly understood.’ Amen.

“‘I wish to be washed, and I wish to wash.’ Amen.

“‘Grace leads the chorus. I wish to play the flute; all of you, dance.’ Amen.

“‘I wish to lament; all of you, mourn.’ Amen.”

And after other matters:

“‘Having led the chorus with us, the Lord went out. But we, like people who had gone astray—or even fallen asleep—fled here and there. Therefore, when I saw him suffering, I did not even await his passion, but fled to the Mount of Olives, weeping over what had happened.
