And when the cry “Take him!” was raised, he was suspended at the sixth hour of the day, and darkness came over the whole earth.

“‘My Lord stood in the middle of the cave and, illuminating me, said: “John, I am being crucified below by the crowd in Jerusalem; I am being pierced with spears and reeds; I am being given vinegar and gall to drink. But I speak to you; hear what I say. I sent you here to climb this mountain so that you might hear what a disciple ought to learn from his teacher, and a human being from God.”

“‘After saying this, he showed me a cross of light fixed in place, and around the cross a great crowd, not having one single form; and within it there was one form and one similar appearance. I saw the Lord himself above the cross, without any shape, but only having a certain voice. The voice was not the one familiar to us, but a certain distinctive [Greek: pleasant] and sweet voice, truly God’s, saying to me: “John, you must hear one thing from me out of these matters [Greek: you must hear these one things from me]; for I lack one who will hear [Greek: who is about to hear], and you will hear it concerning what is to come.”

“‘That cross of light is sometimes called by me, for your sake, the Word; at another time, Mind; now Christ; now the Door; now the Way; now Bread; now Seed; now Resurrection; now Jesus; now Father; now Spirit; now Life; now Truth; now Faith; now Grace.’”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Let us consider that this entire writing is contrary to the Gospel.”

The holy synod said:

“Yes, my lord, for it speaks of an apparent humanity.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“In these itineraries it is written that he neither ate nor drank nor set foot upon the earth—things resembling the Phantasiasts. But in the Gospel it is written of Christ that he both ate and drank; and the Jews said of him: ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker’ (Matt. 11). And if, as they falsely and fabulously claimed, he did not tread upon the earth, how is it written in the Gospels that Jesus, wearied from his journey, sat beside the well (John 4)?”

Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“This is the book that established that false syllogism.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“These things are worthy of ridicule.”

Theodorus, God-beloved bishop of Catana, said:

“Behold the book that destroyed the beauty of the holy Church of God.”

Euthymius, most holy bishop of Sardis, said:

“[Col. 0359B] It was fitting that that assembly should have this book as evidence.”

Constantine, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus, said:

“O blasphemy, which here says that the apostle John fled into a cave on the Mount of Olives at the time of the crucifixion, whereas the Gospel bears witness that he entered with him into the courtyard of Caiaphas and that he stood beside Christ’s cross with his holy Mother.”

The holy synod said:

“Every heresy hangs upon this book.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Alas, alas! With what sort of heretical books do they establish their heresy!”

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, said:

“This codex deserves every kind of pollution and dishonor. And [Col. 0359C] they produced from it the testimony against the images that was written concerning Lycomedes.”

John, most reverend monk and vicar of the Eastern patriarchs, said:

“It introduces Lycomedes as crowning the image of the apostle, just as pagans crown idols.”

Basil, bishop of Ancyra, said:

“Far be it that holy John the Word-speaker should have spoken against his own Gospel.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Are the passages just read from the Gospel?”

The holy synod said:

“Far be it! We accept neither what has been read nor the final account concerning Lycomedes.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Whoever accepts the second account concerning Lycomedes also accepts the first, just as he accepts that false syllogism.”

The holy synod said:

“Anathema upon it, from the first letter to the last.”

John, most reverend monk and vicar of the Eastern patriarchs, said:

“Behold, blessed Fathers, it has been clearly demonstrated that the bishops who accuse Christians of heresy are truly communicants and participants with Nebuchadnezzar and the Samaritans, and furthermore with the Jews and pagans, or rather even with the God-alienated and accursed Manichaeans, whose testimony they produced. For these are the teachings of those who consider the incarnate dispensation of the Word of God to be a phantom. But let anathema likewise be upon them and upon their writings.”

[Col. 0360A] The holy synod said:

“Anathema!”

Petronas, most magnificent patrician, said:

“If you command, my lord, let us ask the bishops of Amorium and Neocaesarea whether the books were read in that false syllogism.”

Gregory of Neocaesarea and Theodore of Amorium, when questioned, said:

“God forbid! No book appeared there; rather, they deceived us with false scraps of writing.”

Tarasius, most holy patriarch, said:

“Persuaded by their own inclination, they set forth what they wished.”

Petronas, most magnificent patrician, said:

“But they did everything also through imperial support.”

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, said:

“I have often said, my lord, and I say again, that no book or writing of the Fathers appeared among us, except that they brought those false scraps; but that account concerning Lycomedes contaminated our ears.”

John, most reverend monk and vicar of the Eastern bishops, said:

“If it pleases this holy and universal synod, let a ruling be issued that no one henceforth write that filthy book.”

The holy synod said:

“Let no one write it. Not only this, but we judge that it deserves to be handed over to the fire.”

Peter, most reverend reader:

“The book of Saint Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, concerning the false superscriptions of the heretics, which begins:”

We have judged it right to strip bare all their impiety and expose their manifest error, since they also produce certain books bearing superscriptions [Col. 0360C] of the apostles, by means of which they deceive the more simple-minded. [Greek addition. And shortly afterward: For we shall show that these books, which those who have seceded from the Church bring before us, are not acts of the apostles but writings of demons.] And after other matters: The apostle John would certainly never have said this when writing in the Gospel, since the Lord says on the cross, “Behold, your son” (John 19), so that from that day John took Mary into his own home. How, then, does he say that she was not present? But this is nothing strange: for just as the Lord is truth (John 14), so the devil is a liar (John 8). “He is a liar, and the father of it”; and when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own nature. But enough of this concerning the lie.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: Our holy father Amphilochius is a great man, and let us hear what he says about these circuits of false names; for this reason we ought not to submit to their subscription [Greek: inscription, superscription].

The most holy bishop Basil of Ancyra said: Nothing is more contrary to the holy Gospel than this impious writing. Accordingly, he also holds a contrary opinion concerning the images.

The most holy patriarch said: Wisely [Greek: clearly] the Father exposes the confusion and loquacity of this book.

The holy synod said: Indeed, lord.

The most holy bishop Nicephorus of Dyrrachium said: [Col. 0361A] It was necessary, lord, that this should be read for the satisfaction of everyone, and not that other material; for it polluted our ears.

The holy synod said: But it was well done, for the sake of caution, that it was read.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: They brought Eusebius forward as a witness—Eusebius, who chattered against the venerable images—in his letter which he wrote to Constantia, the wife of Licinius. But let us see what sort of doctrine Eusebius held.

The most reverend monk Stephen read:

The eighth book of Eusebius Pamphilus addressed to Euphration, whose beginning is:

“In every respect I confess to my lord.” And after other matters: “For we say that the Son did not coexist with the Father, but that the Father existed before the Son. Therefore, if they coexist, how was the Father Father and the Son Son? Or how is one first and the other second? And one unbegotten, while the other is begotten? For if two beings exist equally and similarly alongside one another and are honored equally, it follows that either both, as I have said, are unbegotten, or both are begotten. But neither of these alternatives is recognized as true; for neither do both exist as unbegotten, nor as begotten. Rather, one is first and greater, and precedes the second in order and honor, being for the second the cause both of existence [Greek: as being, for the second, the cause of existence] and of existence of this kind.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius, questioning certain persons, [Col. 0361C] said: Shall we accept this?

The holy synod said: Far be it, lord. Let him be hated even more than the other.

The most holy bishop Basil of Ancyra said: Far be it that a Christian should say such a thing. And the following was read from the same letter. He teaches that the Father is the same and the only true one by what he says: “That they may know you, the only true God” (John 17)—not as though God were one alone, but as though one true God existed, with the necessary qualification “true.” For the Son himself is indeed God, but not true God: for there is one and only one true God, because he has no one before him. And if the Son himself is also true, he is true only as the image of the true God, and in this sense alone is he God. For “the Word was God,” yet not as the only true God.

[Col. 0361D] The most holy bishop Christophorus of Saint Cyriaca said: Most holy lord, and the entire holy and sacred synod: just as we possess divinely written books of the apostles, prophets, and other saints, so it was fitting that that pseudo-synod should also have such volumes as testimony and authority.

The holy synod said: Anathema both to those books and to those who use them!

Peter and Peter, beloved priests of God and representatives of Adrian, the senior pope of Rome, said: This reading showed that it had the opinion of the Arians. The book of Eusebius that was produced also contained other blasphemies, which the synod could not endure hearing.

[Col. 0362A] The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: We reject his writings.

The holy synod said: We both reject and anathematize them.

The most reverend monk Stephen read:

The first discourse of the Contradictions of Antipater, bishop of Bostra, against Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, in defense of Origen, whose beginning is:

“I considered that I had written sufficiently and had fully satisfied what your Holiness commanded, O most God-beloved and most holy Father John.” And a little later: “Since this man was deeply versed in histories, examining and searching through all the volumes and writings of the ancients, setting out almost every opinion, and leaving behind many writings in the world—[Col. 0362B] some of which are entirely worthy of acceptance—some people, taking advantage of the opinion of such a man, attempt to deceive certain persons, admitting that Eusebius would not have been led to this unless he had known clearly all the opinions of the ancients that showed this to be their wish [Greek: that he would not have wished to undertake this unless...]. But I agree and confess that he was indeed deeply versed in histories and that nothing in the ancient writings escaped his knowledge. For, having the cooperation of the imperial authority, he could easily collect what was scattered everywhere. I do not, however, maintain that he attained precision in doctrine [that is, exact knowledge]. It must therefore be granted that he learned many things; but that he possessed an understanding of doctrine—by no means. We know that he was exceedingly far from precision in these matters. And shortly afterward: Therefore, lest we seem to attack a man concerning matters about which it is not presently our purpose to speak, and lest, by examining more carefully the defense that has been made, we expose both as heretics—the man who is being defended, namely, and the one who set forth the defense on his behalf. And after other matters: Show me anyone among the illustrious teachers of the Church who expressly and indisputably taught as doctrine that souls pre-exist; and do not attempt to produce certain surreptitious passages in proof. For the point you hasten to demonstrate—that some people likewise assert the Son’s subjection to the Father—we need not be surprised at first: such is the opinion of you and those around you. Hence there is no discussion for us at present on this matter, since it was long ago rejected [Greek: subjected to inquiry] and dismissed by universal investigation; nor is obedience rendered to it, nor is it examined, on account of those for whom this material has been proposed. Moreover, concerning the pure title Periarchon, you have never yet heard anyone subtract anything from it, O sharp-witted defender of Origen’s errors.”

The most holy patriarch said: Eusebius’s writings have also been shown, through the voice of the Father, to be alien to the Catholic Church.

The God-beloved deacon Demetrius, keeper of the sacred vessels, read:

From the Ecclesiastical History of Theodore the Lector.

A certain Persian named Xenaias, whom Calendio found adulterating ecclesiastical doctrines and building forts during his episcopate, drove him from the region. I shall recount in part what I have investigated after hearing many things about him from various people. For, fleeing his own master from the land of the Persians, he came to the Romans. And shortly afterward: Peter sent this man as bishop of the Church of Hierapolis in place of Cyrus; but not long afterward the bishops who came from Persia denounced him as a home-born slave and as one excluded from divine baptism. When Peter learned this, without troubling himself about what ought to be done, he said that his episcopal consecration was sufficient as a supplement to the divine sacrament [divine initiation].

The deacon Stephen, notary of the venerable patrimony, read:

From the Ecclesiastical History of John Diacrinomenus [Note: [Col. 0363D] Diacrinomenus, that is, “the separated one.” This was what those who did not accept the Council of Chalcedon were called. From Leontius, On the Sects.]

[Col. 0363B] For Xenaias asserted that it was not lawful, since angels are incorporeal, to represent them as corporeal and to depict them as existing in human forms; nor was it lawful to suppose that one could honor or glorify Christ by producing an image of him through the art of painting [made]. He said that the only worship acceptable to him was worship “in spirit and truth.” And after other matters: He also says that one must recognize this: it is childish thinking to portray the most holy and adorable Spirit in the form of a dove, especially since the Gospel writings by no means say that the Spirit became a dove, but that he once appeared in the form of a dove. Since he appeared once providentially, not substantially, it is not therefore fitting for the devout to make a bodily idol. While Philoxenus taught this, he also put it into practice. For he frequently removed and erased images of angels, while he hid those depicting Christ in secret places.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: Let us hear, consecrated men, concerning those who did not receive the venerable images: the unbaptized, the Manichaeans, and those who proclaim a phantom-like appearance in Christ’s dispensation. From their pollutions the instigators of the heresy that accuses Christians took their kindling.

The most reverend Sabbas, hegumen of the monastery of Studius, said: We give thanks to God and to the good will of our good lords, because the false guardians of that pseudo-synod have been defeated together with the heretics who agreed with them.

The holy synod said: Anathema to them!

[Col. 0363D] Constantine, the most reverend lector of the most holy Church, read:

From the Life of our holy father Sabbas.

When Flavian and Elias, the patriarchs, reached Sidon, as has been said, and used flattering and expedient letters with the emperor, and destroyed the synod that had been convened at Sidon against the true faith [Greek: was being convened], and returned to their own sees, those around Soterichus and Philoxenus, indignant, stirred the emperor to violent anger [Col. 0364A] as though he had been deceived by the cunning and falsehood of the patriarchs. After receiving the authority they desired, distributing much gold to the common people of Antioch, tormenting Flavian in many ways and, so to speak, strangling him, and forcing him to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon, they expelled him from the episcopate in this manner and condemned him to exile. When the emperor learned this, he rejoiced and sent Severus, the leader [prince] of the Acephali, as bishop of Antioch.

The most reverend monk Antonius read:

[Note: [Col. 0364D] It is found in the Constantinopolitan synod under Menas, Act 1, approximately midway through.] From the Supplication submitted to the holy synod assembled in this imperial city against Severus, the heretic and Acephalus, by the clergy and monks of the great city of Antioch, the holy Church of God; whose beginning is:

[Col. 0364B] “Now at last is the time, O most blessed.” And a little later: “But what things he dared to do, O most holy ones, around the springs at Daphne, using magical arts there and appeasing demons with incense, the entire city sings. For he spared neither the holy altars themselves nor the sacred vessels: the former he scraped away as profane [Greek: unhallowed], while the latter he melted down and distributed to those of similar character. Moreover, this too was dared by him, O most blessed. The golden and silver doves suspended above the divine sacraments [sacred fonts] and altars, which represent the Holy Spirit, he also removed along with the other things, saying that the doves ought not to be called the Holy Spirit.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: If the Fathers accepted the doves set above in the name of the Holy Spirit, how much more should they accept the icons of the incarnate Word, who appeared on earth with a body? But believe me, even Anastasius, who presided over the Constantinopolitans, appropriated golden and silver icons for his own use, as Severus did.

The God-beloved deacon, notary, and referendary Stephen read:

The account of John, bishop of the Gabalians, concerning the life and conduct of Severus the leader of the heresy, whose beginning is:

“If only Severus had wished, or if his life had always been…” And a little later: “Nor did he leave the honor of the angels unharmed. Standing in the tribunal, he delivered a lengthy speech and repeatedly attempted to persuade the crowd, in the very sanctuary of the most holy Michael, that purple garments were not appropriate for angels, but white ones were. He did not understand that nothing sensible is appropriate to the holy powers [concern with garments is irrelevant], but he endeavored in the same way to remove even this and to set many people against one another, each behaving in this or that manner.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: Let us consider that, along with the other charges, he was accused on this very point, because he said that it was not fitting for angels to wear purple garments, but white ones.

[Col. 0365A] The God-beloved deacon and keeper of the sacred vessels Theophilus [Demetrius] said: When I was appointed in the great holy Church of Constantinople, I made a brief inventory and found that two books, illuminated with images, were missing. When I searched for them, I learned that those who threw them into the fire had burned them. I also found another book of Constantine the chartophylax, containing material concerning the venerable icons. The leaves on which the words concerning the icons lay had been cut out; and, behold, I have the same codex in my hands and display it to the holy synod.

And Theophilus [Demetrius], opening the codex, showed everyone the cutting-out of the leaves.

Leontius, the devout secretary, said: There is another astonishing feature in this codex, Fathers. As you see, it has silver panels and is decorated on every side with images [Col. 0365B] of all the saints. Yet, leaving aside the actual images, they cut out the writings about the images that were inside. This is the height of madness.

The holy synod said: Anathema to those who cut them out and laid ambushes!

The most holy bishop Leo of Phocis said: This codex has lost its leaves; but in the city where I live they burned more than thirty codices in the fire.

The most reverend monk Sabbas, hegumen and monk of the monastery of Studius, said: It is customary, lords, for those who are blind not to see the light; for this reason those who are blind in soul have been darkened.

[Col. 0365C] The God-beloved deacon and keeper of the sacred vessels Demetrius read:

The work of Constantine the deacon and chartophylax of the most holy great Church of Constantinople, concerning all the holy martyrs, whose beginning is:

“The festivals of Christ.” And after other matters: “Then do you suppose that what those who argue said is true—those who said that we procure salvation from the air [Greek: you, the judges, said that we procure salvation from the air] and stones, and do not look toward some provident and protective virtue from which we obtain good things? And how do painters and stonemasons, they say, build a multitude of idols of martyrs, shaping them in various forms and fastening them to temples, while you celebrate these things with sacrifices, expecting from them the solution of hidden difficulties? [Col. 0365D] And what of your own case? Tyrants persecuted them. For do you not assert that divinity is not engraved in images? How, then, do you speak evil of us, while you are placed in more superstitious practices of the same kind? Therefore, since you also, O judges, produce a painting in your elaborate denunciations of images, come, said the martyrs, and we shall free you from the error and ambiguity of these matters.

“For we do not compare divinity, since it is simple and incomprehensible, with particular forms and figures; nor have we learned to honor with wax and wood the supersubstantial and pre-existent unoriginate essence. Rather, when the first man, having grown old through transgression and laid aside the apostate power that he had rashly exercised, fell, nature feared him who was to raise him up [who had cast him down; when it had become arrogant, nature needed him who would raise it up]. For, lying below, he could neither resist nor reverse his overthrow by his own power [lying below, he could not again resist or recall the encounter], while the enemy was attacking the fallen man. Nor was it fitting, except through a second contest, to wrest victory from the tyrant. The very creator of his own work, who is one of the Trinity, God the Word, just as he did not employ anyone as an assistant in fashioning the ancient [former] nature, so now, in restoring the corrupted image, did not entrust its restoration to another. Rather, using the power of his own activity, he undertook human contests on our behalf. For it was fitting that he himself should engage in the contest that belonged to him [Greek: appropriately corresponding].

“Moreover, since every contestant who struggles in one of three ways overcomes his enemy—by deception, by law, or by tyranny—our leader and champion wholly set aside two of these as useless and not his own, and as unsuitable or profitable even for the two for whose sake the contest exists [Greek: and not even suitable for those for whom the contest exists]. For whether fraud produces a simulated victory by driving away an opponent who resists unjustly, or tyranny prevails by irrational force without making the contest equal, he did not approve the other methods, but proceeded to the struggle that is according to law. He assumed flesh from the mass that had fallen, animated by a rational and intellectual soul; while remaining what he was and not losing what was his, he became everything that a human being is and from which a human being is constituted, without sin, and did not merely appear to have flesh under a pretense.

“And a little later: Therefore we paint on panels the form in which he was manifested and lived among human beings, making a divine likeness as a memorial of the salvation accomplished through him; we do not, as you do, derive or carve various figures according to what is imagined [Greek: according to what may seem right, what is imagined].”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: The pagans condemned the martyrs because of the idols and said to them: “Why do you contend, and reject our likenesses, while you yourselves also have your own icons?” The saints replied: “But we do not make images of demons; we make icons of the incarnate Word of God and of his saints. Yet we do not deify them.”

The God-beloved deacon and cubicularius Cosmas said: We also found this codex, which is of the Old Testament, in the patriarchate, with accompanying scholia. It had a scholion in defense of the images. But the conspirators against the truth erased the scholion; and behold, look at it. It is still faintly visible, however; but look at it, venerable Fathers.

The same most reverend Cosmas opened the codex and showed the erased passage to everyone present at the holy synod.

He then read it; for it was still visible:

“You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness whatsoever of what is in heaven above, [Col. 0367A] or on earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them, nor serve them” (Exodus 20; Deuteronomy 5).

Scholion: “And if we make likenesses of human beings who worship God, we do so not to worship them as gods, but so that, on seeing them, we may be moved to imitate them. But if we make likenesses of Christ, we do not worship the likeness as such, but so that, by seeing it, the mind may fly toward higher things. For we do not worship the corruptible image of a corruptible man; but because God deigned unchangeably to become man, we make his icon as a human being, although we know that he is God by nature. Therefore we do not call the icon itself God; rather, we know God, seeing him depicted in the icon, whose likeness the image possesses. The pagan, however, in error, declares likenesses to be gods, and sacrifices to them.”

Another codex was produced containing an interpretation of Scripture, in which the aforementioned scholion lay written. The God-beloved bishop Gregory of Neocaesarea took it and read it. It had beside it the material that had been erased, and it was reread [Greek: beside which was what had been erased, and it was being reread].

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: These things were done by those called the patriarchs Anastasius, Constantine, and Nicetas, the heretics.

The most holy bishop Theodore of Myra in Lycia said: If this treasure had then been made manifest, no one would have been injured. But may God repay those who concealed it on that day.

The most holy bishop Theodore of Catana said: These men are worthy of anathema, because they adulterated [Col. 0367C] the truth and laid ambushes for the Fathers; and those whom they anathematized are worthy of praise.

The most holy patriarch [Greek: the holy synod] Tarasius said: Woe to their souls, because they concealed the truth!

The most holy bishop Peter of Germia said: “Let their names be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Psalm 68).

The most holy bishop Constantine of Constantia in Cyprus said: Blessed is God, who after so great a burning, cutting, and abolition left these things behind.

The most holy bishop Theodore of Myra in Lycia said: Those who did these things, lord, placed their lamp under a bushel. But blessed is God, who showed the light of salvation in the darkness!

[Col. 0367D] The God-beloved deacon and cubicularius Cosmas said: We also found this codex in the repository of the venerable oratories of the patriarchate. It contains the contests of various martyrs, together with an account of the image not made by human hands of the people of Camuliana. Moreover, they cut out the leaves on which the writings concerning the images had been written; and behold, I display it to everyone.

The most holy bishop Michael of Synada said: Pastillarius used to say, most holy lord, “Anathema to false interpreters and conspirators against divine Scripture.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: But his sorrow has turned back upon his own head.

[Col. 0368A] The God-beloved priest John, monk and representative of the Eastern pontiffs, said: The truth must be spoken: the evil conduct of those who burned books and shattered icons has made the truth shine more brightly.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: They not only erased the holy icons, but also Gospels and certain other sacred things; for thus the truth, having suffered persecution, is known to appear more clearly.

The monk Stephen said: We still have another codex corrupted by the accusers of Christians; and, if you command, I shall show it to you.

The holy synod said: Let it be shown.

It was displayed before the entire synod, with erased material on two pages.

Gregory, a God-worshiping priest and hegumen of the monastery of [Col. 0368B] Herachitius [Greek: Hyacinthus; and the Jol. codex], said: I have, lords, a codex of the same format; and, if you command, let it be read.

The monk Stephen, keeper of the books, took it and read:

From the fourth discourse of Evagrius’s Ecclesiastical History.

When Chosroes had attacked the city and, having launched a thousand assaults, had piled up a great amount of earth so that it exceeded the city walls, and had also constructed other siege engines, he was carrying out an ineffective retreat. I shall describe what happened. Chosroes ordered his officials to collect a great heap of timber for destruction, together with all kinds of material. When these had been collected more quickly than had been ordered, he placed the earth around them and threw it into the middle, advancing toward the front of the city. Gradually building up the wood and dust, and approaching the city, he raised it to such a height above, and exceeded the wall to such an extent, that arrows seemed to be shot from above against those who were about to die on the wall for the city.

Therefore, when those suffering devastation saw the earth, advancing almost like a mountain, drawing close to the city, and their glorious enemies appearing likewise to be about to enter the city on foot, they devised, at daybreak, a countermeasure against the earthwork, which among the Romans is called an agger. Beneath it they dug a trench, excavating earth from this side and that, so that, by setting fire to the wood, they might bring the burning timbers down from the earthwork [Greek: to lead it, and from there send out fire; so that, with the flames]. The work was completed; but when they set fire to the earthwork, their plan was frustrated, because the fire had no way to advance and consume the material after receiving air.

When, therefore, they had reached complete exhaustion, they brought forth an image fashioned by God [made by divine craftsmanship], which human hands had not made. Christ God had sent it to Abgar, because he longed to see him. They brought this most holy image through the excavation they had made and sprinkled it with water; then they spread the water from it against the fire and the wood [Greek: they sprinkled the fire and wood from it]. Immediately the divine power attended the faith of those who acted, and what had previously been impossible for them was accomplished. For at once the wood caught fire, and in a moment it was turned into frost and showered down upon those above, while the fire consumed everything on both sides [Greek: and, sooner than words can say, it was turned into frost and showered down upon those above, while the fire consumed everything].

The most reverend lector Leo of the great imperial Church of Constantinople said: I too, your unworthy servant, when I went down to Syria with the imperial envoys, was in Edessa, and saw the holy image not made by human hands being honored and worshiped equally by the faithful.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: Yesterday the most reverend hegumen Maximinus produced the codex of the most delightful Paradise, the Meadow, and it was read [Col. 0369B]. We too found in the library a copy of the same Meadow with leaves cut out, on which writings concerning the images had lain.

The most holy bishop Christophorus of Saint Cyriaca said: Most holy lord, I, your unworthy servant, presume to speak before the holy, sacred, and universal synod. It is a prophetic saying: “The sinner is caught in the works of his own hands” (Psalm 9). For what those gathered in that pseudo-synod thought to do against us has happened to them. Some passages they cut out, while others they falsified, so that, once the truth was revealed, their impieties might be exposed.

The monk Stephen, keeper of the books, said: The codex given by the hegumen Maximinus contains a discourse [Col. 0369C] that was falsified in another codex concerning the icons [Note: [Col. 0369D] It is also found falsified by other interpreters, and especially in the codex of the Sixth Synod.]

The same monk Stephen, keeper of the books, read:

From the same Meadow.

Some of the elders said that there was a great champion enclosed on the Mount of Olives. The demon of fornication attacked him. One day, when it pressed him fiercely, the elder began to lament and say to the demon: “How long will you not spare me? Go away from me now; you have grown old with me.” The demon then appeared to him visibly and said: “Swear to me that you will tell no one what I am about to say to you, and I shall not attack you again.” The elder swore to him, saying: “By him who dwells on high, I shall not tell anyone what you say to me.” Then the demon said to him: “Do not worship this icon, and I shall not attack you again.”

The image depicted our holy Lady Mary, the Mother of God, carrying our Lord Jesus Christ. The man enclosed by the demon said: “Let me consider the matter.” The next day he reported it to Abba Theodore the Aeliote, who at that time lived in the Lavra of the Pharenites, and recounted everything to him. But the elder said to the recluse: “Abba, you have truly been deceived, because you swore to the demon; nevertheless, you did well to disclose this. It is more expedient for you not to leave in this city a prostitute into whom you would not enter than to refuse to worship our Lord Jesus Christ with his Mother.”

After confirming and strengthening him with many words, he went away to his own place. The demon appeared again to the enclosed man and said to him: “What is this, wicked old man? Did you not swear to me that you would tell no one? And how did you tell everything to the man who came to you? I tell you, wicked old man, you will be judged as a perjurer on the day of judgment.” The enclosed man answered him: “I did swear, certainly I swore; and I know that I perjured myself [committed perjury]. But I perjured my Lord and maker; I shall not, however, obey you.”

From the same Meadow.

The same Fathers also told me this, saying: In these days a woman who loved Christ dug a well in the territory of Apamea. After spending much money, undertaking much labor, and descending to a great depth, she found no water. The woman was greatly discouraged [Col. 0370B], both because of the labor and because of the expense. Then, one time, in a dream she saw someone saying to her: “Send for and bring an image of Abba Theodosius, who is on the rock, and through him God will provide you with water.” The woman sent two of her men and obtained the saint’s icon. When she lowered it into the well, water immediately and without delay came out, so that half the well was filled. They brought us some of that same water, and we drank it and glorified our God.

Another account by the same author.

Dionysius, priest of the Church of Ascalon, told us about Abba John the anchorite, saying: This man was great in the present generation, and he asserted this miracle about him as proof of his state [Greek: as proof of the state pleasing to God].

He said: An elder lived in a cave in the region of Socchus, about twenty miles from Jerusalem. In the cave the elder had an image of our holy, undefiled Lady Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, holding Christ our Lord in her arms. Whenever he wished to go anywhere—to distant deserts, to Jerusalem to worship the holy cross and the holy places, or even to Mount Sinai to pray, or to the martyrs who were many miles from Jerusalem—for the elder was exceedingly devoted to the martyrs—sometimes he went to Saint John at Ephesus, sometimes to Saint Theodore at Euchaita, sometimes to Saint Thecla at Seleucia, or to Saint Sergius at Arapha. He would prepare a lamp and light it, as was his custom, and, standing in prayer that his journey might be directed, he would say to the Lady while looking at her image:

“Holy Lady, Mother of God, since I have a long road to travel, extending over many days, take care of your lamp and keep it unextinguished according to my intention. For I am going with your help as my companion.”

After saying this to the image, he would depart. When he had completed his planned journey, he would return—sometimes after staying a month, sometimes two or three, and sometimes five or six [Col. 0371A]. And he would find the lamp arranged and burning exactly as he had left it when he departed to make the journey. He never saw it extinguished by itself, whether when he rose from sleep or when he returned from the desert to the cave.

The most holy bishop Basil of Ancyra said: It has been demonstrated that the custom of the sacred images is an ancient tradition.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: We have now been satisfied by the testimonies of the Fathers, and we have learned that the erection of venerable images is an ancient tradition. We are therefore followers of the holy Fathers.

The holy synod said: Followers and in agreement.

The most reverend monk Stephen said: We also have as many as fifteen other codices concerning the cause of the sacred images, if you command.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: We are filled and content.

The holy synod said: It is enough.

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: Since it was demonstrated in the preceding reading that the Church was accused on account of the venerable images by Jews, pagans, Samaritans, Manichaeans, and Phantasiasts, and since we have all been convinced, it is right also to hear our brother and beloved lord John, the representative of the apostolic sees of the East; for he has a certain report indicating where the subversion of the images began.

[Col. 0371C] The holy synod said: We also desire, lord, to hear about this.

The most reverend monk John, representative of the Eastern pontiffs, read from a written notice.

I, humble and least of all, wish to demonstrate with complete truth before your present holy and sacred synod how, when, and from where this worst and God-hated heresy—one that accuses Christians and smashes images—had its beginning. I shall endeavor to use only a concise form of discourse; I have judged it good to set down the narrative in writing, so that nothing of the truth may remain hidden from me.

When the tyrant of the godless Arabs had died—namely, the counselor (Seleman was his name)—Umar succeeded him. As soon as he had risen to power, he summoned Masalma, who had been cast out of the pit, and drove him from this land [Greek: “to be thrown out of the pit”], since he was an utterly mad enemy. By the grace of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the most holy Mother of God who bore him, Masalma returned to Syria amid great confusion and the destruction of his own Saracen army, having obtained nothing of what he had hoped for.

After Umar’s death, Ezidus was appointed in his place, a certain frivolous and changeable man. At Tiberias there was a leader of the transgressing Hebrews, a diviner and sorcerer, an instrument of demons that harm souls, surnamed Sarantapechys, an impious enemy of the Church of God. When this utterly wicked Hebrew learned of the fickleness of the reigning Ezidus, he approached him and began to divine and foretell certain things to him. Thus it happened that he became acceptable and pleasing to the tyrant.

“I wish,” he said, “O chief counselor [Note: [Col. 0371D] Anastasius’s words: For this is what the Greeks call the king of the Saracens], as a token of the goodwill with which I burn toward you, to prescribe for you a certain course by which you may more easily and quickly obtain that your life be prolonged and that you remain for thirty years in this principate of yours—provided, however, that you put my words into action.”

But that foolish tyrant, blinded in mind by his craving for longevity—for he was a lover of pleasures and wanton [variant: wanton, or insolent]—replied: “Whatever you prescribe, I shall do most readily; and if I attain what I desire, I shall enrich you by repaying you with the greatest honors.”

The sorcerer and diviner Hebrew then said to him: “Immediately, without any delay or respite, order a circular letter to be written throughout your entire principate, commanding that every image-picture—whether on panels, in mosaic on walls, or on sacred vessels and altar vestments—and all such things found in all the churches of the Christians be eradicated and completely removed [variant: ‘let them eradicate and remove completely’]. Likewise, remove all such images as are displayed in the marketplaces of the cities for ornament and adornment, in whatever form they may be.”

Moreover, moved by Satan’s evil operation, the false diviner added “every likeness,” arguing in this way so as to display the unbearable hatred he had against us [Greek: “cunningly, so that he might give no suspicion of his hatred against us”].

The tyrant, however, caught by deception, yielded to this folly. Sending orders, he removed the holy images and the remaining likenesses from every province that was under him. In this way, sparing nothing, he disfigured the churches of God under his authority through the sorcery of the Hebrew, before the evil reached this land.

Then, when the God-loving Christians fled lest they themselves overthrow the holy images with their own hands, they compelled the Hebrews, hateful to God, and the most contemptible Arabs—who had been sent for this purpose, the Amiraeans—to do the work. Thus they burned the venerable icons and treated the church buildings, sometimes coating them over and sometimes scraping them away.

When the pseudo-bishop of Nacolia and those around him heard this, they imitated the lawless Jews and impious Arabs, inflicting injury upon the churches of God.

It is right to make known to the hearing of your sacred judgment what end that wretched sorcerer Hebrew met. After Ezidus’s counselor had done this, he lived no more than two and a half years before he died and went into eternal fire. The images, however, were restored to their former condition and honor. Then his son, named Ulidus, being enraged, ordered the sorcerer, as the murderer of his father, to be killed by a most disgraceful death, bearing the punishment deserved for his false divination.

The most holy bishop of Messana said: “I too was a little boy in Syria when the counselor of the Saracens overthrew the images.”

The most reverend monk Sabbas, hegumen of the monastery of Studium, said: “Lord, we too, unworthy servants of your holiness, ask that the sacred images be restored to their places according to the former custom, and that the devout Christians celebrate litanies with them.”

The most holy patriarch Tarasius said: “What do you say, venerable brothers?”

The holy synod said: “We all agree.”

Peter, God-beloved archpriest and representative of the most holy senior pope of Rome, read from a written document.

“To Tarasius, most holy patriarch of Constantinople, New Rome, and to this entire holy and universal synod: Peter, archpriest of the most holy Church of the holy and praiseworthy apostle Peter, and Peter, priest and hegumen of the monastery of Saint Sabbas, both representatives of Adrian, senior pope of Rome:

“We judge it right that, according to the pronouncement of us all—or rather, in accordance with the ancient tradition of the catholic Church, as all the holy Fathers teach us—an image to be venerated should come into our midst, and that we should salute it. Let the priests declare what seems good to you concerning this.

“We also propose another matter: that all writings composed against the venerable images be erased with anathema or committed to the fire. We ask that a pronouncement be made on this, as seems good to the holy synod.”

The holy synod said: “Let it come; let it be done!”

Peter, God-beloved archpriest and representative of the most holy senior pope of Rome, said: “If your holy synod commands it, let a venerable image be placed tomorrow, and let us all salute it.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be done, let it be done!”

John, most reverend monk, priest, and representative of the Eastern pontiffs, said:

“Blessed is God, who glorified this city, which loves Christ, Nicaea, in the days of the emperors Constantine and Irene, lovers of Christ. Blessed is God, who made it worthy of a double grace. Here Christ first made the faith more explicitly clear; now, through this holy synod, he has manifested to all the symbols of his dispensation. Here the infamous Arius was deposed; here the heresy of those who hate God and smash images has been eradicated.

“Blessed is God, who says through the holy apostle John: ‘I am Alpha and Omega’ (Rev. 1:22). Blessed is God, who here, both at the beginning and at the end, confirmed the orthodox faith.”

The holy synod exclaimed, pronouncing each verse three times:

“The doctrines of the Fathers, sounding forth divinely, have corrected us! Drawing truth from them, we have drunk our fill!

“Following them, we have pursued falsehood!

“Taught by them, we salute the venerable images!

“Led by them, we offer to them the adoration rendered through honor!

“The Fathers proclaim: we are obedient children, and we rejoice before the face of the mother, the tradition of the catholic Church [Greek: ‘we glory before the face of the mother in the tradition of the catholic Church’]!

“Believing in one God to be praised in the Trinity, we salute the honorable images!

“Those who do not hold this view, let them be anathema!

“Those who do not think thus, let them be driven far from the Church!

“We follow the ancient legislation of the catholic Church!

“We preserve the rights of the Fathers!

“We anathematize those who add to or take away from the catholic Church!

“We salute the venerable icons!

“We anathematize the innovation introduced by those who accuse Christians!

“We subject those who do not hold this view to anathema!

“Anathema to those who accuse Christians, that is, to those who smash images!

“Anathema to those who apply sayings of holy Scripture directed against idols to the venerable images!

“Anathema to those who do not salute the holy and venerable images!

“Anathema to those who call the sacred images idols!

“Anathema to those who say that Christians approach the icons as though they were gods!

“Anathema to those who knowingly share in the injury and dishonor inflicted upon the venerable images!

“Anathema to those who say that, apart from Christ our God, someone else has rescued us from idols!

“Anathema to those who dare to say that the catholic Church ever accepted idols!”

“Many years to the emperors! Many years to Constantine and Irene, the great rulers and emperors! Many years to the peaceful emperors! Strengthen, O Lord, those who have removed the innovation made some time ago! Grant them, O Lord, a pious life!”

## ACTIO SEXTA

[Col. 0373]

[Col. 0373C] In the name of the Lord and ruler Jesus Christ, our true God. Under the rule of our most pious and Christ-loving lords Constantine and Irene, his mother crowned by God, in the eighth year of their consulship, on the third day before the Nones of October [variant: the day before the Nones], in the eleventh indiction.

When the holy and universal synod had assembled—which, by divine grace and by the pious decree of those same emperors, strengthened by God, had been convened in illustrious Nicaea, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia—namely, Peter, most reverend archpriest of the holy Roman Church of the holy apostle Peter, and Peter, most reverend priest, monk, and hegumen of the venerable monastery of Saint Sabbas situated at Rome, holding the place of the apostolic see of Adrian, the blessed and most holy archbishop and senior pope of Rome; Tarasius, the blessed and most holy archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, of great renown; and John and Thomas, most reverend priest-monks and vicars of the apostolic sees of the Eastern diocese;

and when they were seated before the most sacred ambo of the temple of the most holy and great church called Sophia, with the most glorious and magnificent judges present and listening—namely, Petrona, most praiseworthy former consul and patrician, and the count of the imperial service preserved by God—and with the entire holy synod according to the order prescribed in the first session; with the God-loving archimandrites and hegumens also present, together with the entire monastic body; and with the holy and undefiled Gospels of God laid before them:

Leontius [Leo], the illustrious secretary, said:

“The holy and blessed synod knows how, at the preceding assembly, we read various statements of those heretics who must be pursued by God, who accused the holy and immaculate Church of the Christians because of the erection of sacred images [Greek: ‘on account of the erection of sacred images’]. Today, however, we have in our hands their written blasphemy against Christians: namely, an absurd, subversive, and self-refuting definition of a false synod, entirely consonant with the impious opinion of the God-hating heretics. We also have its skillful and most effective refutation, which the Holy Spirit has clearly supplied—for it was necessary that it be published in wise utterances [Greek: ‘contradictions’] and torn apart by powerful refutations. We submit it for whatever disposition may please you.”

The holy synod said: “Let it be read.”

John, God-beloved deacon of the most holy great Church of Constantinople and chancellor, read:

## REFUTATION OF THE DEFINITION THAT WAS PATCHED TOGETHER AND FALSELY CALLED A DEFINITION BY THE ASSEMBLED CROWD OF THOSE WHO ACCUSE CHRISTIANS

### TOMUS PRIMUS

It is always pleasing to the demon who hates humanity both to separate human beings, made in the image of God, from God and to deceive them through manifold seductions. Nothing is more the object of his concern and effort than to resist piety and shake the order of ecclesiastical peace.

He has displayed this also in our times through a certain conventicle, in which those who assembled became the persuaders [Greek: “the authors of the exposition”] of the material set forth below, and proclaimed themselves to be a seventh council. By placing before the simpler-minded, as bait on a hook, that plain and universally recognized hatred of idols, they secretly introduced their own execration in opposition to images [Greek: “and, rejecting their own [execration], they turned it against images”]. They fabricated once again that most ancient and corrupt expression—namely, the worship of idols—by which those who served the devil and his evil powers through demonic images, and served the creature rather than the Creator, were rightly decreed to be called idolaters.

They attempted to compare and equate such people with those who have put on Christ, who by his grace have been freed from idols and saved from their error, and have become a royal priesthood and a holy nation [Greek: “they attempted to brand them as such”]. Would that their words, like those of imperfect, aborted creatures, had perished as soon as they were born, before such contagions had arisen in the Church.

But since, although foolish, they have been nourished by certain people’s milk, even though they have not yet reached maturity, we judge it necessary to destroy them with the sword of the Spirit. In all this, however, let Christ, our true God, be our guide: he who enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1), who alone is the understanding of those who understand piously and of things understood, and the word of those who speak and of things spoken, who is and becomes all things for all people; who gives the tongue of instruction for knowing when it is necessary to speak a word.

“The exposition of his words gives light and grants understanding to the simple” (Ps. 118), so that falsehood may be driven away and truth may enter, shining clearly and brilliantly for all. Those zealous for piety, embracing this truth and remembering the divine Apostle who says, “Woe is me if I do not evangelize” (1 Cor. 9), ought to be its advocates and protectors, refuting falsehood and striking down the false with the sling of the Spirit.

Therefore, both according to the Scriptures and according to the customs of the Fathers, let those who come against foolish talk search out the matter syllogistically and, with the sword of the Spirit, as Phinehas did, strive with one stroke of refutation to strike together those who have banded themselves together in this impiety, and to show all that their tongues are false—since they have been raised up against the knowledge of the only-begotten Son of God and against his Church, and have spoken iniquity against the incarnation of the Son himself.

Then, having finally broken their bonds with the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God (Eph. 6), and having removed the yoke of their indiscipline, let them make the coverings of their cunning manifest to all. For the Lord has laughed at them and mocked them, and will speak to them in his anger, saying: “Depart from me; I do not know you” (Matt. 7).

Concerning them the prophet Jeremiah also foretold: “The prophets prophesy falsely in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them, nor did I speak to them. They prophesy to you a false vision, a fraudulent divination, and the deceit of their heart” (Jer. 14; 23). Therefore they shall be cast out upon the roads of Jerusalem, that is, of the catholic Church, and shall be a trampling-place for all who confess God piously.

“For a strong snare to a man are his own lips, and he is caught by the words of his mouth. The recompense of his lips shall be given him as a rebuke of impiety.” For he says: “I shall rebuke you and set your sins before your face” (Ps. 49).

Let this suffice concerning these matters. But, lest we prolong our discourse through lengthy convolutions, let us continue along the proposed path and speak against them from the very superscription. Their idle and curse-filled foolishness cannot otherwise be exposed unless, with God’s inspiration, we prepare a battle-line against them by refuting them.

We shall thereby gain one safeguard for ourselves: namely, that they do nothing new apart from us in matters known to belong to divine worship [Greek: “gaining one safeguard for us, namely, that nothing be innovated by us in matters known to belong to divine worship”], but rather obey the apostolic and paternal teachings [variant: “we obey”], as well as the ecclesiastical ordinances.

We ask those who come into possession of this writing to read it carefully and not cursorily, so that, clearly and explicitly understanding the subtlety of the objection, they may award the Church of God the crown [variants: “victory”; “victories and praises”].

They used beginnings of this sort.

Gregory, God-beloved bishop of Neocaesarea, read [Note: [Col. 0377D] Whatever is here said to have been spoken or read afterward by this Gregory of Neocaesarea is taken from that synod falsely called the Seventh and is refuted here. Therefore, know that the words expressed here in italic letters, as they are called, are the words of the synod falsely so called; this variation is made not as a mark of honor but for distinction.]:

[Col. 0377B] “Definition of the holy, great, and universal seventh synod.”

John the deacon read:

Beginning with a lie, and using this throughout their entire novelty of rebellious words as an aid, the accusers of Christians ended in a lie. For how could it be holy when it did not even accept in its understanding what holiness is—especially since it was polluted, profane, and accursed?

Those who assembled in it, to speak prophetically, did not distinguish between holy and polluted, nor did they separate clean from unclean, calling the icon of the incarnate Word of God, namely, our Lord Jesus Christ, an idol in the same way as the icon of Satan.

How could it be great and universal, when the hierarchs of the other Churches neither accepted it nor agreed with it, but transmitted it to anathema? It did not have as its supporter the pope of the Romans of that time, nor the priests around him, nor even his vicars, nor an encyclical letter, as the law of councils requires. Nor did it have the patriarchs of the East agreeing with it—namely, those of Alexandria, Antioch, and the holy city—or the fellow ministers and chief priests who are with them.

Truly, their discourse is smoke full of darkness, obscuring the eyes of the foolish, and not a lamp placed upon a lampstand to give light to all who are in the house (Matt. 5), because their words were spoken locally in a hidden place and not upon the mountain of orthodoxy.

“For their sound did not go out into all the earth like that of the apostles, nor their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18), as did those of the six holy and universal synods.

Moreover, how could it be seventh when it did not agree with the preceding six holy and venerable synods? Everything seventh that is properly arranged in a reckoning of preceding things must follow them; but that which shares nothing in the things numbered with it is certainly not numbered with them.

For example, if someone arranged six gold coins in a row and then placed beside them a bronze coin, he would in no way call this one seventh because of the substance of its different material. Gold is a useful metal, abundant and precious, whereas bronze is base and dishonorable. So too, since this synod possesses nothing golden or precious in its doctrines, but is bronze [variant: bronze-plated] and rejected in every respect, full of deadly poison [variant: deadly rust], it did not deserve to be numbered with the six most sacred synods, whose golden words shine forth through the Spirit.

It bears the arrogance of the one who said, “I shall set my throne above the clouds” (Isa. 24), and resounds in this manner.

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, read:

[Col. 0378B] “The holy, great, and universal synod, which was assembled by the grace of God and by the most pious decree of our God-protected and orthodox emperors, Constantine and Leo, in this royal city protected by God, in the venerable temple of our holy and undefiled Lady, the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, which was called Blachernae, defined the following.”

John the deacon read:

If their assembly had been made by divine grace, it would have been adorned with words spoken by the grace of God and would certainly have shone with truth, since grace is joined to truth and they are companions and fellow-dwellers, as John, preeminent in theology, bears witness when he says: “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

They therefore abandoned the truth, in which Solomon glories, saying, “My throat shall meditate on truth” (Prov. 8), and, embracing falsehood, undoubtedly fell away from grace (Col. 4). Hence their discourse is not seasoned with divine salt, so as to give grace to those who hear it.

As for their claim that they assembled in a venerable temple, this is not surprising. They will not thereby be improved by any disguise, just as neither Annas nor Caiaphas, nor their Jewish council that was formed against Christ, was helped by the fact that their unlawful plot against him began in the temple. Rather, they were shown to be more condemnable before God because, in holy places, they made not holy but God-hostile agreements.

Would that they had taken their proem from the paternal voice—namely, from the God-speaking Dionysius—and had preserved his traditions [Greek: “Would that, as a proem from the paternal voice, they had taken Dionysius the God-speaking and his traditions also”], as well as those of all our holy Fathers, without corruption.

But this is not found in them, as the rest of their exposition will make clear, although these people, covered with the false fleece of sheep, make a preface concerning theology and speak as follows:

Gregory read:

[Col. 0378D] “The deity, cause and consummation of all things, which by its goodness brought all things from non-being into being, determined that these things should be moved and governed in a fitting and orderly manner, so that, joined by grace to the safety of what has been granted, they might preserve unharmed the unchanging perpetuity and the inflexible inclination toward either side of the true state.”

Epiphanius the deacon [and cubuclesius, chamberlain] read:

If every creature, created by God, received from what did not exist the power of subsisting, then, now moved and directed by his command, it knows how to keep the Creator’s ordinance, having received providence from him, whether it is inanimate or animate.

But these people presumed to anathematize the tradition given to us by Christ in his holy Church as a memorial of his saving dispensation. They were ignorant that nothing of what exists in it was made without him, and they are shown to be more senseless than inanimate things and more irrational than irrational creatures.

Not only this: thinking that they were proceeding well, they show their tongue to be deceitful in their wicked words and doctrines, claiming that the holy Church of God has been adorned with idols. Placing their hope in falsehood, they address her: “We do not wish to know your ways” (Job 21), nor do we intend to follow the ancient tradition.

They will indeed hear from Christ, who founded the Church: “I do not know you” (Matt. 7; 25). Yet they pretend that the devil triumphs, saying as follows:

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, read:

[Col. 0379C] “Since he who on account of his former splendor was called Lucifer, having his proper order placed near God, extended his thought upward against his Maker, he thereby became darkness together with his apostate power. Falling voluntarily from the most glorious divine sovereignty, which makes light and exists above light, he appeared as the willing maker, inventor, and teacher of every evil, and became darkened.

“Unable to bear seeing the human being created by God brought into the glory in which he himself had been established, he poured out all his malice against him and, through deception, made him alien from divine glory and brightness, urging him to worship the creature rather than the Creator.”

Epiphanius the deacon [and cubuclesius, chamberlain] read:

If their discourse had been directed against the servitude of idols—or against the servitude of creatures, which the holy apostles, clothed with power from on high, and the divine prophets who had previously prophesied, and finally our excellent Fathers who followed them, forbade and condemned—all the Church’s children would certainly agree, and it would be appropriate for this to be committed to writing for them.

But because, abandoning this, they protect falsehood; because, pretending to expose its father, namely the devil, they sharpen their tongue against the immaculate Church; because, like wine merchants, they have mixed wine with water and have not feared to make their neighbor drink it in turbulent confusion, they rightly hear the divine voice spoken against them through David the God-speaking psalmist:

“Why do you recount my ordinances and take up my covenant in your mouth? But you hate discipline and cast my words behind you, assigning your portion with those who adulterate the doctrines of truth” (Ps. 49).

Therefore, pretending to speak the truth, they say:

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, read:

[Col. 0380A] “Therefore, when God the Creator saw the work of his own hands plunged in every way into destruction, he did not endure it, but, after the care that had been accomplished through the Law and the prophets for its salvation, and while it was still unable to return to its former nobility, he deigned to send his Son and Word to earth in the last and predetermined times.

“He, by the Father’s will and through the cooperation of the life-giving and coequal power of the Spirit, dwelling in a virgin’s womb and taking flesh from her holy and immaculate flesh in his own substance [Greek: ‘existence’; ‘subsistence’], joined and formed it for us through a rational and intellectual soul, consubstantial with us. He was born from her beyond every reason, understanding, and thought; he willingly endured the cross and chose death; and, rising from the dead on the third day, he fulfilled the entire saving dispensation.”

Epiphanius the deacon [and cubuclesius, chamberlain] read:

[Col. 0380C] Scripture says that at the creation of the world God said: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Great, therefore, is the dignity, since the earthly creature has been honored with the image of God.

But when humanity fell through deception and did not preserve the dignity of its first formation, the human race slipped into idolatry. God and the Word of the Father, having become human without any change of nature and remaining perfect, recalled it from its fall, removed it from the error of idols, and formed it anew for immortality, granting it a gift without repentance.

This renewed formation becomes more God-like and superior to the former formation, and an eternal gift [Greek: “This re-formation becomes more God-like and superior to the former formation, and an eternal gift”].

Wishing, therefore, to darken the greatness of these gifts, they assert in harsh language that another idolatry is introduced through the making of images, and boastfully claim that a new redemption has been accomplished [Greek: “accomplished by itself”]. Stitching together their opinion with various words, they judge the Church of God as though it were in error, making their words smooth like oil and pronouncing certain writings.

Their words are deceitful, and their tongue is a piercing dart that wounds. They speak peaceful things, but within themselves they harbor hostility. Therefore they add:

Gregory read:

[Col. 0380D] “He removed us from the corruption-producing instruction of demons, that is, from the error and worship of idols alike, and handed over to us the adoration that is ‘in spirit and truth.’”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Against your will, O most excellent men, you are being drawn toward the truth. For the entire sacred assembly of the apostles and the holy company of our Fathers proclaims that the Word and Son of God the Father came to humanity in order to rescue us from the error of idols.

We also have the foretold words spoken through the prophets, crying out as follows: “For behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and their memory shall no longer exist” (Zech. 13).

Thus you are compelled to confess that Christ our God rescued us from the error of idols. And if he rescued us, how did those who believed in him again serve idols? Let your slanderous chatter cease.

God, having become incarnate, redeemed us, and are we again being taken captive? Are we now again overcome by the one who exercised tyranny over us? Hear the divine Scripture saying (Ps. 144; 145): “His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation”; and: “The Lord shall reign forever, your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.”

God is not like earthly emperors, who at one moment overcome and at another are overcome; his victory remains forever. God is not human, to be formed, nor is he a son of man, to be threatened, as it is written.

The Apostle also agrees with these things, saying: “For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance” (Rom. 11).

Yet they utter the same things, thinking that they are adorning themselves. For they continue, attacking themselves:

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, read:

[Col. 0381C] “And finally, with his assumption, he ascended into the heavens, leaving his holy disciples and apostles as teachers of this saving faith. Making our Church beautiful like his bride with various teachings of piety and light, they displayed it as excellent [variant: most beautiful] and most radiant, as though adorned and variegated with certain golden fringes. Our illustrious Fathers and teachers, as well as the six holy and venerable synods, received its appearance and preserved it without diminution.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Having an unlearned and uninstructed understanding, they did not perceive that their tyrannical opinion—born from the novelty of their own words—ought to be rejected, nor did they perceive their own arrogance and haughtiness, as they try by tumultuous whispering to obscure their own meaning under a crafty veil. Through their indolence they suffer something ridiculous: they loudly and grandly praise ecclesiastical legislation, and, although unwillingly, promise [Gr., agree] to preserve it unaltered through the six holy and universal councils. In words they feign piety, but in mind they practice iniquity; with their lips they honor it, but their heart is far from it (Isa. XXIX). They are wholly unwilling to admit the tradition that has been preserved throughout all former time by so many saints.

Would that they had at least respected the multitude of Christians—both those now living and those who have existed from the time the Gospel was proclaimed—by not reproaching and rejecting its account as expressed through the painting of images. For after the holy and universal Sixth Council had taken place, not more than seventy years passed before they themselves assembled against the venerable icons. It is therefore clear to everyone that the paintings of images were by no means introduced during those years, but in the times preceding the Sixth Council; indeed, they came from the preaching of the apostles, as we learn everywhere from the very sight of the holy churches, as the holy Fathers have testified, and as the narrators of histories report; their written records are preserved even to this day.

For in the five hundred and first year after five thousand years had been completed, Christ our God came to humankind and, dwelling with us for thirty-three years and almost five months, accomplished the great and saving mystery of our Redemption. Thus he made his way to the heavens, undoubtedly ascending from where he had descended, and commanded the apostles to teach everything that he himself had taught them.

From those times until the emperor Constantine, who was the first of the Christians to reign, approximately three hundred years passed, while the pagans previously exercised tyranny. At that time, many Christians, fighting the good fight, were leaving this world through martyrdom as they rose up against the idols. When the multitude of Christians was stirred by divine zeal and began building temples, some in the name of Christ, others in honor of the saints, some depicted in colors within them the deeds of Christ our God in his humanity, while others painted accounts of the martyrs’ contests. Others, wishing always to preserve their memory on panels, painted upon them the image of the martyr they desired to remember, or even that of Christ himself.

Images were also painted on sacred vestments and treasures, both by our holy Fathers and by pious men; and in them they celebrated the unbloody sacrifices. All these things have been clearly demonstrated to us and remain forever. Indeed, when heresies arose, full of gall and bitterness against the Church, and when the six universal councils were convened at different times by God’s will for their overthrow, everything handed down in the catholic Church, whether in writing or unwritten, from ancient times onward was strengthened and established together with the evidence of the holy images.

When the holy and universal Sixth Council had promulgated its definition against those who proclaimed one will in Christ our God, and when Constantine, who was then emperor and had convened it by his command in accordance with God’s good pleasure, had shortly afterward departed this life, his son Justinian obtained the empire. The very men who had assembled at that council, gathering together again unanimously by divine prompting after four or five years, issued up to 102 canons for the correction of ecclesiastical affairs.

In these canons they also explained the matter of images in the eighty-second canon [Col. 0383A], as follows:

> In certain venerable paintings, a lamb is depicted, pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner, which was taken beforehand [Gr., assumed] as a figure of grace, showing us in advance through the Law the true Lamb, namely Christ our God. Therefore, honoring the ancient figures and shadows as signs of the truth and as the preliminary forms handed down to the Church, we receive grace with honor and truth, accepting it as the fulfillment of the Law.  
>   
> Therefore, so that what is perfect may also be depicted before everyone’s eyes through the work of colors, we decree that the character of the lamb of Christ our God, who takes away the sins of the world, should henceforth be painted in icons according to his humanity in place of the former lamb. Through it, we contemplate the exaltation of the humility of God the Word; we are led to remember his conduct in the flesh, as well as his passion and saving death; and we are brought to mind the redemption that has thereby been accomplished for the world.

We all therefore see and understand that descriptions of images were handed down in the Church both before and after the holy councils, just as was the Gospel. For through reading, received by the ears, we transmit this hearing to the mind; and, gazing with our eyes upon pictorial forms, we are likewise enlightened intellectually. Through these two things, following one another—reading, I say, and paintings—we receive knowledge of the one reality, arriving at the remembrance of things that have taken place.

Hence this joined operation of the two most universal senses may also be found in the Song of Songs, where it says:

> Show me your face,  
> let your voice sound in my ears;  
> for your voice is sweet,  
> and your face is beautiful (Song II).

In agreement with this, we too say in singing:

> As we have heard, so also have we seen (Ps. XLVII).

These things being so, it is appropriate to say to those who have railed against the holy images:

> Everyone spoke vainly to his neighbor;  
> with deceitful lips and a double heart they spoke evil (Ps. XI).

From them may we be delivered by the grace of Christ, our true God and Savior.

## SECOND VOLUME

Epiphanus the deacon read:

Forgetting the promise of the Lord who does not lie, which he made concerning his Church—that the gates of hell would not prevail against it (Matt. XVI)—they attack it with bare heads and unveiled faces, holding contrary opinions. Stealing the words of the Fathers, they set them forth as their own, saying:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Again, the aforesaid contriver of wickedness, unable to bear seeing her beauty, was not deprived, through the passage of time, of a means by his evil ingenuity to bring the human race under his subjection. Instead, under the guise of Christianity, he gradually introduced [Gr., restored] idolatry, persuading people through his sophistries directed toward this end not to withdraw from the creature, but to worship and venerate it, and to regard a created thing as God, to be called by the name of Christ.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

[Col. 0384A]

Those who assault the spiritual Jerusalem—that is, the catholic Church—are represented by those who assaulted the earthly Jerusalem. They too hasten to use their ancestral language, just as Rabshakeh once spoke against Israel in the Hebrew language (2 Kings XVIII). For these heretics arm their ancestral teaching and ecclesiastical language against the Fathers and against the catholic Church.

But the Lord says, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII). For they are compared to whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people. So too these slanderers of Christians, covered as though with ancestral words, are inwardly full of bones and every impurity (Matt. XXIII)—that is, of dead and stinking doctrines.

Let us now uncover the same tomb and expose all their filth, because they pervert, according to their own desires, what has been set forth in the catholic Church by the holy Fathers. They use the very same words, but cunningly change their meanings. For what they themselves uttered against the Arians, these men now confess against the venerable icons, changing the style of the writing.

What the renowned Father Gregory, bishop of the Church of the Nyssaeans, set forth against the Arians in the funeral sermon that he wrote concerning holy Basil, his brother according to flesh and spirit, these men have appropriated against the images. This may be seen from a passage of the same preface, which runs as follows:

> Certainly no one is unaware of the purpose of the demonstration that took place in the time of our teacher [Gr., why our teacher shone forth at that time]. For when the madness of human beings concerning idols had been extinguished by the preaching of Christ, and when the worship of vain things had everywhere almost been ruined and abolished through the rise of the preaching of piety throughout nearly the whole world, the one who held the leadership of human deception, restrained everywhere and driven from the inhabited world by the name of Christ, nevertheless remained wise in wickedness, the inventor of wickedness. He was not deprived of evil devices by which to subject humankind to himself once again through deception. Rather, under the pretext of Christianity, he gradually introduced [Gr., restored] the worship of idols, persuading people through his sophistries directed toward this end not to withdraw from the creature, but to worship and venerate it, and to regard as God a created thing called by the name of the Son.  
>
