> But if he is from things that do not exist, or is a creature, or is alien by nature from the divine substance, no account need be given of this; instead, let those who have bestowed the name of Christ upon a creature worship it, serve it, place their hope of salvation in it, and await judgment from it [variant: if it is a creature and, according to its own nature, alien from the divine substance, they would care nothing about this; but, bestowing the name of Christ upon a creature, they would worship it, serve it, place their hope of salvation in it, and await judgment from it].  
>   
> And may the apostate, who fell, bestow all his wickedness upon men who are unworthy—namely Arius, Aetius, Eunomius, and Eudoxius, and indeed many others—through whom idolatry, which had already disappeared, was again introduced, as has been said, under the name of Christianity [variant: and when the apostate had found men capable of all his wickedness—Arius, I mean, Aetius, Eunomius, Eudoxius, and many others besides—through them he restored idolatry, etc.].  
>   
> And sickness overcame the people, who served the creature rather than the Creator. Thus, with the assistance of the emperors of that period, the deception was strengthened, and all the leading authorities contended for the same sickness. [Gr., When nearly all people had passed over to the side that prevailed, then, etc.]  
>   
> Then the great Basil was shown forth by God, just as Elijah was under Ahab (1 Kings XVII and following). Coming to the aid of the priesthood, which had in a sense already fallen, he caused the word of faith, like a failing lamp, to shine again through the grace that dwelt in him.

Let us attend to what is true: the whole meaning of this Father is directed against those laboring under the madness of Arius. For he says that holy Basil was manifested in those times when Arius, Eunomius, Eudoxius, Macedonius, and those around them—namely the Anomoeans and Semi-Arians—confessed the Son, the Word of the Father, and our God to be a creature, serving one who was indeed God, but created [Gr., serving that God who had been created].

For this reason they are rightly called worshipers of idols both by him and by the catholic Church, because they confess that the one whom they worship was brought into existence from things that did not exist, just like every creature that has been made.

Thus Christians have neither called the holy images gods, nor served them as gods, nor ever placed their hope of salvation in them, nor awaited future judgment from them. Rather, possessing them for remembrance and memorial, and burning with love for the originals they represent, they embraced them and venerated them honorably. Yet they did not render them the service or worship owed to God—away with the slander!—nor did they render such service to any other things.

The Arians, however, numbering the Son and Word of God among creatures, proclaimed that they had their hope of salvation from him and that through him future judgment would be carried out. For this reason the distinguished Father, reproving them, said:

> To worship this—that is, the creature—to render it service, to place one’s hope of salvation in it, and to await judgment from it.

They are therefore proven to be adulterators of the truth, defenders of this novelty of words, and, according to the prophet (Isa. I), wine merchants who mix wine with water. Not only this, but they have also become falsifiers of the traditions of the Fathers.

For when that same God-bearing Father said that it was called by the name of God [Gr., of the Son], they, wishing to transfer his meaning to the formation of images, falsely said “called by the name of Christ” instead of “called by the name of the Son.”

It is evident that when he said “called by the name of the Son,” he was speaking against the Arians, who blasphemed against the heavenly and uncreated divine generation of the Son. For this reason he also made known the leaders of that heresy, namely Arius, Eunomius, Eudoxius, and Aetius.

They, however, replacing “of the Son” with “of Christ,” attempted to appropriate the blasphemy by changing its meaning and applying it to the formation of the venerable images. Thus in this matter also they are shown to be false speakers and liars, introducing claims that are in no way proved lawful.

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Therefore, just as formerly Jesus, the author and perfecter of our salvation, clothed his wisest disciples with the power of the Holy Spirit and sent them throughout the whole earth for the abolition of such things, so now he has raised up his servants, our faithful emperors, like the apostles, endowed with the wisdom of the same Spirit and made worthy in power, for our perfection and instruction, and for the destruction of the demonic strongholds that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, as well as for the refutation of diabolical argument and error together.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Who has ever spoken such iniquity against the Most High? What could be more cruel than this impiety? O irreverent and wicked blasphemy! O hidden deceit and manifold falsehood! Instructed by the argument of the devil himself, they dare to call demonic strongholds exalting themselves against the knowledge of God, and diabolical argument and error, the vision and appearance that plainly and explicitly lead us, as it were by the hand, to the glory of God, through which we contemplate the exaltation of the humility of God the Word and are drawn to the remembrance of his life among human beings in the flesh—that is, of his passion and saving death.

They have truly bent their bow against a bitter thing, to shoot in secret at the blameless (Ps. LXIII). For if they confessed that the holy disciples, clothed with power from above for the abolition of idols and with the Holy Spirit coming upon them, had been sent, they would certainly not have said that others had been raised up after their tradition and teaching had prevailed for approximately eight hundred years, and after the holy Fathers had confirmed and established it as a secure anchor.

Once and for all delivered from idols throughout the world by Christ, we do not need to complain about idols [Col. 0386D] [Gr., to be reproved concerning idols], unless perhaps they presume to say that a change has taken place in the Church and that other laws and regulations have been handed down, bringing before us irrational and denial-filled pretexts.

This is what those tumultuous men, strong only in rumor, were saying when they declared, “Just as formerly Jesus, the author and perfecter of our salvation…” From this they proceed to say: “Everything that becomes obsolete and grows old is near to destruction” (Heb. VIII); and, because the teaching of the apostles has become obsolete, “we are arranging to raise up a new one.” For Moses and Aaron are likewise shown to have been priests in the same way. But when grace entered, the Apostle said that another priest had arisen.

Therefore now too they ought to have bestowed a certain supreme grace, greater than the grace of the apostles—for this is what they say—for our perfection and instruction. And since they were bishops who had assembled such a council, and possessed the perfection of the apostolic ordinances, they ought to perfect others, not be perfected by others. Instead, they rejected all the more the teaching of the instruction and tradition of the holy apostles and our illustrious Fathers.

Therefore they were in no way shown to be companions or participants in the learning and teaching of those men, since they did not agree with their tradition. The psalmist David invokes a curse upon them, saying:

> May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips  
> and the boastful tongue (Ps. XI).

Let David himself also say truthfully in song, and let us say it together with him:

> The enemies’ swords have failed utterly,  
> and you have destroyed their cities (Ps. IX).

When did the enemies’ swords fail, and when were their cities—that is, their strongholds—destroyed? Was it not at Christ’s becoming human, of whom it is written, “He will divide the spoils of the mighty” (Isa. LIII)?

Or was it written concerning their false council and faction that “the enemies’ swords have failed utterly”? And if the enemies’ swords failed utterly and in every respect, and the cities of impiety were destroyed, how did they dare to chatter that these had again been rebuilt and renewed, so that they might ascribe their destruction to themselves, along with the redemption of the human race that was accomplished through them?

Thus they disparage the great mystery of our salvation and the dispensation of Christ, who is also blessed above all, God forever and ever. Amen.

Then, using flattery toward the emperors, they say:

Gregory the bishop read:

[Col. 0387C]

> “Moved by the divine zeal that is in them, unable to endure seeing the Church of the faithful, which had been seized by the deception of demons…”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

In saying these things, they neither understood the promises that the catholic Church received from Christ, who founded it, nor confess that the human race is saved through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ our Lord. Those whom Christ purchased with his own blood, they sell again to the devil. Those whom he brought to life through his own death, they kill with the poison of their lips and plunge into the snare of hell.

Let them hear the Song of Songs, which openly sings to the Church in the person of Christ:

> You are wholly beautiful, my beloved;  
> you are wholly beautiful,  
> and there is no blemish in you (Song IV).

They have now heard that she is wholly beautiful and beloved of Christ, and free from every blemish. To her he also speaks through Isaiah:

> On my hands I have painted your walls,  
> and you are always before my eyes (Isa. XLIX).

How, then, can she who received these promises be seized by the opposing power of demons? And especially since Christ is her head, according to the divine Apostle (Eph. V), who could seize her as booty? He presented her to himself without spot or wrinkle; how then is she again defiled?

O this accusation [Gr., opinion]! For it is certain that this opinion entails a denial of his dispensation. But they hastened to despise the Church; therefore the Lord will despise them, and they will be rejected and anathematized by all who have been born within her. For she has remained unconquerable and incorruptible [Gr., unshaken] and immovable.

Moreover, filling their mouths with flattery, they proceed boastfully to recount their own deeds.

Gregory the bishop read:

> “They summoned the entire sacred college of God-beloved bishops, so that, having been brought together in one synodal body, it might examine the question of Scripture concerning the deceptive operation of likenesses in colors, which draws the mind away from the highest and God-worthy worship to the humble and material worship of the creature; and, God moving it, might declare what seemed right to it—knowing what is written in the prophets: ‘For the lips of the priests will preserve knowledge, and they will seek the law from their mouths, because they are angels of the Lord Almighty’ (Mal. II).”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Forgetting the birth of God the Word from the Virgin, and this great and saving mystery that he himself, coming in the flesh, bestowed upon us by rescuing us from the error of idols and from their insane superstition, they themselves seize this salvation and wish to heap glory upon themselves. Thus they are proclaimed inglorious by the catholic Church.

Christ our God addresses them openly through the prophet, saying:

> The priests despised the law  
> and profaned my holy things.  
> They did not distinguish between holy and polluted,  
> and they did not distinguish between clean and unclean (Ezek. XXII).

For they did not distinguish the icons of the Lord and of his saints from the icons of demons, calling them likewise idols and slanderously accusing the Church that Christ our God acquired with his own blood. They whisper that the pictorial work is a deceptive exposition of the Gospel, although the faithful call and name it venerable and holy. They certainly do not look at what is seen, but at the things signified in it.

For when they hear with their ears, “Glory to you, Lord,” they proclaim it; and when they see with their eyes, they likewise offer the same act of glorification. For we are brought to the remembrance of his life, by which he lived among human beings. Whatever the written narrative indicates, the painting itself also announces.

Let us examine what they shamelessly and boastfully chattered with their verbose mouths:

> “Which draws the mind away from the highest and God-worthy worship to the humble and material worship of the creature.”

O the madness of those who possess a tongue sharp as a sword and infected with falsehood, and who imagine that the undefiled faith of Christians is being changed into the worship of images! They insultingly declare this to be “the humble and material worship of the creature.”

No Christian among all the people under heaven has rendered an image the worship of service. This is a pagan fable, an invention of demons, and a work of satanic action. It perished at Christ’s coming.

Now there is service in spirit and truth (John IV). The Church has stored up various things that are offered to God for his remembrance and for the remembrance of his saints; among these is the making of images. They themselves, moreover, condemn themselves when they say, “Let it declare what seemed right to it.” They have overlooked what is written from the Lord’s mouth:

> Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory (John VII).

Thus they themselves testify that they speak from themselves and not from the Holy Spirit. Who, then, do you suppose, would listen to them—unless he were one who did not possess the Spirit?

Then, boasting not in the Lord but in their own tongue, they say:

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, read:

[Col. 0389B]

> “And behold, now the sacred council has assembled, numbering, as we complete the number, three hundred and thirty-eight. Following the synodal legislation, embracing it, we receive and proclaim the doctrines or traditions that the councils themselves, by confirming them, decreed that we should securely hold.”

Epiphanius the deacon read.

They boast of having a populous council, glorying in their multitude. Gathering crowds against the Church, they chattered, opening a mouth that had no door, saying what is not lawful; they spoke iniquity against the Most High. They increased like the Hebrew people and became most vile (Exod. VII, according to the Septuagint).

But the Lord was not pleased with them. Why? Because, driving themselves away from the Church, they wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place, lacking the spiritual wine that gladdens human hearts (Ps. CIII).

Again they assert the same things concerning themselves [Gr., concerning these same men], representing in words that they follow the enactments of the synodal laws, but denying this by their deeds. They enumerate the universal councils, saying:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “First, in the first place, the holy and universal and great council celebrated at Nicaea under the emperor Constantine the Great, of holy memory. It deposed the most impious Arius from the priestly dignity because he said that the uncreated Son of God, who is consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit and wholly of one glory and one honor, was a creature. It also brought forth the God-chosen [Gr., divinely dictated] symbol of our saving faith.  
>   
> “Then the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who assembled in this imperial city under the emperor Theodosius the Elder: it condemned Macedonius the Spirit-fighter, as one who blasphemed against the most holy Spirit and impiously dogmatized that he was not of one essence with the Father and the Son. It also expressed more fully the symbol of our saving faith, affirming that the Holy Spirit is God and almighty.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

The impious Nestorius and the heretics who belonged to his party also received these two holy universal councils. Likewise, the council of this factious band, while receiving these councils, introduced another heresy. Those who adhere to it have therefore been called by the holy catholic Church of God slanderers of Christians, differing in no way from senseless men who, seeing the sun above the earth, say to one another: “The stars are hidden by the brightness of the sun; it is day and there is no night.” They deliberate by the clearest and most certain idle reasoning [Gr., they conclude], adding as follows:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “After these, the council of two hundred holy Fathers that first assembled at Ephesus under the younger emperor Theodosius condemned Nestorius, who possessed the mind of the Jews and worshiped a human being, because he preached Christ separately from God the Word and another Christ who was from a woman. Assigning God the Word partly and the human being partly, he dogmatized two subsistences in one Christ and denied the unity that had been effected according to subsistence. According to that unity, one does not worship one together with another as though they were separate, but one understands Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son, who is to be honored with one worship together with his own flesh.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Eutyches, Dioscorus, and those who proclaim the confusion of the two natures in Christ also admitted these things. Yet they remained heretics, introducing another heresy. Therefore these men too will be numbered with them, as introducing into the catholic Church a crafty novelty of words.

And just as children ridiculously recount to one another what their fathers plainly said and did, so these men suppose that they are skillfully setting forth and committing to writing what everyone knows plainly. But they have become an object of laughter to all.

Again, using vain chatter, they say:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Then the great and renowned council at Chalcedon, which assembled under Marcian, the prince beloved of God, and anathematized Dioscorus and the wretched Eutyches, who proclaimed that, after the supreme unity of God the Word—which took place in subsistence, and in which the same one Christ and Lord subsists with the flesh—he did not exist in two natures, but that a union had been made from two natures and had become one mixed and confused nature.  
>   
> “Moreover, the council that assembled at Constantinople, consisting of one hundred and sixty-five holy Fathers under Justinian, of divine memory, anathematized Origen, also called Adamantius, Evagrius, and Didymus, together with their writings composed with pagans; also Theodore of Mopsuestia and Diodore, the teacher of Nestorius; Severus, Peter, and Zoaras, together with their impious doctrines; and the letter attributed [Gr., called] to Ibas, written to Maris the Persian. It piously confirmed the doctrines of the holy and great Fourth Council.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

These holy and universal councils, and those preceding them, were received by Sergius of Constantinople, Cyrus of Alexandria, Honorius of Rome, and those around them who proclaimed one will in Christ. But just as heretics are anathematized by the catholic Church for speaking vainly through their heresy, so these men, although they admit these holy councils, are nevertheless rejected from the catholic Church because of their heresy.

Their speech on this subject is vain and idle and deserves no answer, because when they invoke the holy councils, they contradict and oppose them. If they did this through ignorance, it is madness and full of indiscipline; but if knowingly, it is impiety and every kind of absurd conscience.

Either let them show us a council opposing a council—unless perhaps they mean those councils that have been alienated from the catholic Church and anathematized, as theirs has—or let them follow the approved and holy councils, and accept what those councils left in the Church.

If they receive the venerable icons, they follow the catholic Church, since they were received by the six holy universal councils. But if they do not follow the catholic Church, no one will listen to them when they refuse the God-worthy tradition.

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Likewise, the council that assembled in this city preserved by God during the reign of the pious emperor Constantine, consisting of one hundred and seventy holy Fathers, anathematized and rejected Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Honorius of Rome, Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, who had been bishops here; as well as Macarius of Antioch and his disciple Stephen, because they said that there was one will and one operation in the two natures of our one Christ and God.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

These petty arguments require no refutation, since they have been refuted above. But with profane sophistry they again bring forward the holy councils, saying:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Therefore the six holy and universal councils themselves, piously and in a manner pleasing to God setting forth the doctrines of the undefiled Christian faith and imbued with the divinely delivered Gospels, handed down one subsistence in two natures, wills, and operations in our one Christ, Lord, and God; and they taught that the miracles and sufferings belong to one and the same person.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

O their exaltation and most arrogant understanding! They attempt to teach the Church as though she were ignorant and unacquainted with the divine doctrines, although testimony is given that she is full of all wisdom. The divine Apostle, who imbued her with the mysteries, cried out about her in a loud voice, saying:

> So that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and authorities (Eph. III).

They have therefore judged incorrectly and most dangerously, bringing forward matters that need not be sought. For the catholic Church has received and sealed these doctrines as a secure anchor and has no need of their instruction.

Indeed, together with the divine doctrines, our Fathers also received the venerable images, judged them worthy of a certain worship and honor, and set them up painted in the venerable temples that they built. They also painted them in every suitable place and embraced them.

These men, however, have presumed to surpass the entire divine company of the Fathers and have set their own seat against them, behaving proudly after the father of lies, that is, the devil. They have profaned holy things, treated them with insults, and committed them to fire.

O their argument [deed]! O their audacious madness! May their understanding withdraw, and may the Lord spare his people from their corrupting wickedness. May all who follow the catholic Church receive the evangelical paintings and the representations of the contests of the martyrs, and embrace them, just as the holy Church of God received them from ancient times.

Still continuing their artifices, they curse as follows:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “When we examined and understood these things with great diligence and discussion, and through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, we found in the very doctrine of our salvation—that is, in the dispensation of Christ—an illicit art of painters, blaspheming and overturning those same six holy and universal councils, gathered and inspired by God.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

[Col. 0392C]

And even in evil there were zeal and deliberation, just as he had shown zeal and deliberation with Ahithophel against his father Absalom; so too did these men act against the holy Fathers. And just as Ahab seemed to accept the words of the false prophets as divinely inspired, so this man too was deprived of his hope (2 Kings 15–17). The Preacher says: “There are ways that seem right to a man, but their ends plunge down into the depths of hell” (Prov. 14). Such was the fate of these men also: overcome by their desire to please human beings [Gr., “by their desire to please people”], they uttered words from their own belly, thinking their ways right, yet obedient to themselves they plunge into the snare of hell.

For how, as they claim, is the making of images by a painter, with blasphemous mouth, related to the very [Col. 0392D] mystery of Christ’s dispensation, which is most necessary for our salvation? Or how again does the art of painters despise the six holy universal synods, and how have images been placed in churches contrary to their will, when those same divine Fathers of ours, explaining more explicitly, didactically, and willingly the mystery of our salvation, depicted them in venerable temples, making use of the art of painters—and not in the manner these men confess?

Which of our most holy Fathers declared the art of painters unlawful with respect to that most necessary dogma of our salvation, namely, the dispensation of Christ? For no one permits what he himself accepts to be condemned. They know how to rave, then, but not to demonstrate the things about which they rave. For, as is apparent, they supposed that no one would recognize that they were defrauding the truth of its word.

All manual arts that depart from the counsel of God’s commandments are indeed to be rejected. Those, however, that are not of this kind, but are shown not to be useless for our life, contain nothing indecent; nor have our holy Fathers rejected or cast them aside. But if someone uses the art of painting to depict obscenity, it is to be rejected and is harmful—for example, if someone paints prostitute-like figures, or theatrical spectacles, or unrestrained dances, or scenes from the circus; and whatever else of this sort is produced by the art is a shameful invention [a shameful exercise].

But if we wish to paint the lives of industrious men, accounts of the contests of martyrs, the passions that are to be narrated concerning them, and the mystery of the dispensation of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, then, using the painter’s art, we shall be found to be acting entirely rightly. For the painter forms a cross, and none of those who think soundly rejects a painted cross, nor does he strip the painter of divine grace, even though the painter has produced it with colors.

The same must likewise be understood of books. If someone has depicted shameful narratives in books, they are shameful and must be rejected and excluded from Christian hearing. But if they are divinely inspired words or narratives leading to piety, they are to be praised and admitted, and judged most worthy of the Church. The same must also be thought, as we have said, concerning the icon of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his saints.

For if someone makes a lyre or flutes, the work is shameful; but if he makes something belonging to the sacred vessels, it is acceptable. None of those who think soundly disparages an art if, in matters necessary for this life, it has produced something useful. For one must consider the intention and the manner by which the completion [the work] of the arts is achieved: if it is directed toward piety, it is acceptable; but if toward any kind of disgrace, it is hateful and contemptible.

Moreover, continuing their accusation, they next say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

> “They established Nestorius, who divided into a duality of sons the one who became man for our sake, the one Son and Word of God.” [Alternative: “They established Nestorius, who divides …”]

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

[Col. 0393D]

Again, as we said earlier, they merely make the assertion and do not demonstrate it. How does the one who paints an image of Christ establish Nestorius? Nestorius introduces two sons: one, the Word of the Father; the other, the one who is from the Virgin. True Christians, however, confess one and the same Son, Christ, and Lord. In painting an icon according to the truth that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1)—that is, as perfect man—they act entirely rightly and piously.

For God the Word, having come to us, was circumscribed in the flesh; yet no one has devised a way to paint his divinity. “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4), it says. For he is uncircumscribed, invisible, and incomprehensible. [Col. 0394A] But he is circumscribed according to his humanity [Gr., “but circumscribed according to humanity”]. For we know Christ from two natures, and in two natures indivisibly—that is, divine and human.

Thus, in the one Christ, one uncircumscribed nature and one circumscribed nature are seen. An image is not likened to its original according to substance, but only according to name and according to the arrangement of the limbs represented. For when someone paints the image of a human being, he does not seek the soul in the image—especially since there is an incomparable difference between the human soul and the divine nature. The divine nature is uncreated, creative, and without time; the human soul is created and temporal, and was itself created by the divine nature.

And no one among those who have ever thought rightly, on seeing a human image, has imagined that the human being is separated from his soul by the painter. For the image is deprived not only of the soul, but also of the very substance of the body—namely, flesh, marrow [Gr., muscles], sinews, bones, and bodily elements: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile. It is impossible for the balance of these to be seen in the image. For if we saw these things in the image, we would surely already call it a human being and not an image of a human being.

Therefore, this present empty talk also perishes along with their other arguments [it hastens along with their other arguments]; and what they put forward is moreover worthy of laughter.

**Bishop Gregory read:**

> “And also Arius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, and Severus, who teach the confusion and mixture of the two natures of the one Christ.” [Col. 0394C]

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

O their thoughtless and senile tales, and their concealed fraud! Again, they find it pleasing to linger over the same chatter. Either they do not know the difference between the heretics they have enumerated, or they deliberately contrive to chatter. The heresies of Arius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches are opposed to Nestorius and oppose one another, although they remain equal in impiety.

For Arius, saying that the eternal and uncreated Word of God and the Father came into being from things that did not exist, added another heresy to his impiety: he said that Christ did not have a rational soul, but divinity in place of a soul, and that passion had touched that divinity. Dioscorus and Eutyches, on the other hand, driven in the opposite direction from Nestorius, who asserted two natures and subsistences [Col. 0394D] in Christ, confused the natures and foolishly spoke of one nature. Thus they departed from the royal road, which turns neither to the right nor to the left, and turned backward from apostolic and patristic teaching.

What fellowship or agreement does the catholic holy Church of God have with Arius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches because of the venerable images—unless their words are merely empty, corruptible, and alien to the apostolic commandment, which says: “Let your speech always be in the grace of God, seasoned with salt” (Col. 4)? The much-tried Job, detesting such words, said: “Can bread be eaten without salt? Or is there any taste in empty words?” (Job 6).

It is therefore clear that they slander the Church of God pointlessly and vainly: now saying that it mingles with the impious and divisive Nestorius by painting the Lord’s humanity in icons; now claiming that it confuses the Church with the wicked Eutyches and Dioscorus. For, as was shown above, it is manifest that their views are opposed to one another, although each attacks the Church.

If we grant that the Church follows Nestorius, according to their own statement, then they lie when they say that it thinks with Eutyches and Dioscorus. But if instead we allow—which is contrary to the truth—that it agrees with Eutyches and Dioscorus, then in this too they are shown to be speaking falsely. For, as the preceding discussion demonstrated, Nestorius and Eutyches differ from one another in impiety, and their construction is irrational and superfluous.

## VOLUME THREE

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

[Col. 0395B]

Because they plow among thorns, uttering things alien to the apostolic seeds and bringing forth shoots of heretical tares, the Lord cries out against them through the prophet: “Many shepherds have corrupted my vineyard; they have demolished my portion” (Jer. 12). They say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

> “Therefore we considered it right to show carefully, through our present definition, who create and venerate error. Accordingly, all the God-bearing Fathers and the holy universal synods handed down our pure, undefiled, and God-pleasing faith [Col. 0395C] and confession in such a way that no one might devise any form of division or confusion in that ineffable and unknowable union, which surpasses every sense and thought—namely, the one person demonstrated through the subsistence of two natures.” [Gr., “Accordingly, with all the God-bearing Fathers … handing down the pure and undefiled …”]

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

In truth, those empty-minded men have carefully displayed their error. For all our holy Fathers, who assembled in the six holy universal synods, established and accepted venerable painted images in the holy temples and in other suitable places; yet these men rejected them through certain false little arguments [Col. 0395D], calling them error and substituting another idolatry in place of the demonic one. They did not distinguish from one another two things opposed to each other.

They apply one and the same designation to things done for the glory of Christ our God and for the remembrance of his life in the flesh, and to things done by pagans and by certain Jews who serve demons for the glory and remembrance of demons. They were not ashamed to hand this over in writing, mixing together things that cannot be mixed and offering excuses for sins.

They bring the din of the ravings of division and confusion into the theological teaching of the catholic Church, chattering that no form of division may be devised in the union that took place in the flesh through subsistence of God the Word. And, as is apparent, they have never read the sayings of the Fathers; or, if they have read them, they read them cursorily and not with scrutiny.

The eloquent Gregory destroys their empty construction by saying this (Oration 2, *On the Son*):

> “When natures differ, names too are divided along with concepts” [Gr., “they differ in the consideration of the intellect, and at the same time the names are divided”]; “and all our holy Fathers, refusing confusion, say that the two natures are separated in thought by reason of their difference, not by division.”

Therefore, either they are ignorant even here of the true recognition of the doctrines, or they slander our holy Fathers by claiming that they in no way speak of division in the union of the two natures in Christ’s dispensation.

Nestorius divides the natures in reality, saying that one is the Word of God and the other the one who is from the Virgin—one man in particular and one God in particular. The catholic Church, confessing the union without confusion, divides the natures only in thought and indivisibly, confessing Emmanuel to be one and the same even after the union.

Moreover, breathing insults through their nostrils, they declare:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

> “What kind of senseless understanding belongs to the vain writer [painter], who, for frivolous and shameful profit, applies himself to what cannot be undertaken—that is, to forming with polluted hands what has been believed in the heart and uttered in the confession of the mouth?”

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

[Col. 0396C]

To say or think this is an apoplectic fit. For it is not the mark of a prudent man to blame those who are blameless. What is this invention of their sinister speech, these ravings about things dedicated to the Church? If the one who paints is said, for shameful profit, to imagine our Lord according to the manner in which he became perfect man, and to paint his saints, then they ought also to accuse those who write the divine Gospels, and to call those who draw the cross with colors foolish painters, saying that they do this for shameful profit.

Shall the craftsman who makes a cross therefore be called a craftsman of folly? Shall the stonecutter who cuts and forms the holy table be a stonecutter of folly? And likewise the goldsmith, the silversmith, and the weaver? According to their madness, then, every discipline and art given by God has departed [Col. 0396D]—both that which serves his glory and that which sustains our life.

Since they have reached an excess of ignorance and wickedness, let them hear from divine Scripture and from our holy Fathers that the wisdom given to our nature by the great giver, God who created us, is praised. Job indeed declares concerning God: “Who gave women wisdom in weaving?” (Job 38, according to the Septuagint).

Divine Scripture also testifies that the Lord gave Bezalel wisdom for every craft, saying:

> “I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah; and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every work, to devise whatever may be skillfully made in gold, silver, bronze, marble, gems, [Col. 0397A] and varieties of wood. And I have given him as companion Eliab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And in the heart of every skilled person I have placed wisdom, so that they may make all the things I have commanded you” (Exod. 31).

In agreement with this, Gregory, who is prolific in theology, says (Gregory of Nazianzus, *Funeral Oration on Basil*):

> “The Spirit of the Lord descended and guided them, and the Spirit of discipline filled Bezalel, the chief craftsman of the tabernacle.”

Therefore those who corrupt [Gr., condemn] and criticize the disciplines of God given to human beings are and are called numbered among the heresy divinely rejected, adding, according to what is written, “sin upon sin” (Isa. 31).

These, then, are the genuine and not illegitimate children of the bride of Christ, clothed in robes and having neither stain nor wrinkle—that is, of the catholic Church [Col. 0397B]. Offering rational sacrifices and services to God alone, they behold through visible sense the venerable image of Christ, and properly and truly that of our holy Lady, the Mother of God, and of the holy angels and all the saints. Through remembrance of these they shape their minds, and they believe in the one God with the heart for righteousness, and confess with the mouth for salvation (Rom. 10).

Likewise, when they hear the Gospel, they fill the faculty of hearing with sanctification and grace, and in their hearts they understand the account of the things that have been written. Then, puffed up for no reason, what do they say?

**Bishop Gregory read:**

> “For this man made an image, calling it Christ; and the name ‘Christ’ means God [Col. 0397C] and man. Therefore it is an image of God and man. Thus either, according to what appeared to his vanity, he circumscribed the uncircumscribed divinity by the circumscription of created flesh; or he confused that unconfusable union, incurring the iniquity of confusion. By this he applies two blasphemies to the divinity: circumscription and confusion. The one who venerates it is therefore also subjected to the same blasphemies; and woe alike to both, because they have gone astray with Arius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, and the heresy of the Acephali.”

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

The making of images is not an invention of painters, but an acceptable ordinance and tradition of the catholic Church [Col. 0397D], consistent with antiquity, according to the divine Basil (*On the Holy Spirit to Amphilochius*, ch. 29). Antiquity itself, together with the teaching of our Fathers inspired by the Spirit, bears witness to this: when they saw these images in venerable temples, they gladly received them; and when they themselves dedicated venerable temples, they took pains to have these images painted. In those temples they offered their God-pleasing vows and bloodless sacrifices to the Lord, God of all.

Therefore the conception and tradition belong to them, not to the painter; the painter possesses only the art. The arrangement plainly belongs to the holy Fathers who dedicated the temples. The name by which Christ is called is an indication of his divinity and humanity, namely, the two perfect natures of the Savior. [Col. 0398A]

According to the nature in which he was seen, Christians have been taught to paint his image, not according to the nature in which he was invisible; for that nature is uncircumscribed. “No one has ever seen God,” we have heard from the Gospel (John 1). Thus, when Christ’s human nature is painted, in accordance with what the truth has shown, Christians confess that it shares in the image of what is original only according to name, and not according to substance.

But these men, having become foolish, say that the image and the original are indistinguishable, and judge that the very substance exists in other substances [Gr., “that the same substance exists in different substances”]. Who would not laugh at their lack of discipline—or rather, mourn their impiety? For, having been turned over to a depraved mind, they say what is unfitting, whispering that the Church has the cause [the charge] of confusion through the production of venerable images, and asserting that it applies the form of circumscription to the divinity. Then, adding iniquity to iniquity, they transmit a woe.

But their pain will return upon their own heads. If the one who curses ancient Israel is cursed, and the one who blesses is blessed (Num. 24), how much more is the one who curses the new Israel—who spiritually sees God, that is, the Church of God—filled with a curse?

Who would not curse them when they say, with Arius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches, and with the heresy of the Acephali, that the Church has gone astray—although they themselves have these men as teachers and protectors of the new heresy they have chosen?

For in what follows they cite Eusebius Pamphilus as a witness [Col. 0398C], although the whole catholic Church knows him to be a patron of the heresy of Arius, as is contained in all his writings and expositions. He says that the adorable God the Word is the Father’s minister and holds the second rank of dignity, differing from the majesty of the *homoousios*, and opposing the change [Gr., “opposing the doctrine of consubstantiality,” and “change”] of the Lord’s holy flesh into the nature of divinity. In this way he teaches confusion, and he neither accepts an icon, nor does the entire wicked assembly of the Arians.

For they preach that our Lord became man without a rational soul and possesses divinity in place of a soul, so that they may transfer the passion to it, as the eloquent Gregory testifies (Gregory of Nazianzus, *Letter 2 to Cledonius*). And because they confess that the divinity suffered, they do not accept an image. Severus likewise, who is prone to confusion, by no means accepted the image of Christ our God in the Church, as many historians relate.

How, then, can they claim that the catholic Church followed Arius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches—that is, the heresy of the Acephali—when it accepted pictorial representations? It is astonishing, while they belch forth grandiloquent things and pour certain blasphemous little arguments from their unbridled tongue into the air—and nothing else.

Let them hear the truth, then: as we said, the divine nature is superior to circumscription; or rather, the human nature is circumscribed [Gr., “but the human nature is circumscribed”]. None of those who think rightly, when calling the human nature circumscribed, circumscribes with it the uncircumscribed nature.

For when the Lord, as perfect man, was in Galilee, he was not in Judea; and he himself confirms this by saying: “Let us go again into Judea” (John 11). And when he was speaking to his disciples about Lazarus, he said: “I rejoice for your sake that I was not there” (ibid.). But according to his divinity, he is present in every place of his dominion, remaining in every way uncircumscribed.

How, then, do these empty talkers, clamoring with the vanity of their voice and babbling with an unbridled tongue, say: “The painter circumscribed, according to what appeared to his vanity, the uncircumscribable divinity by the circumscription of created flesh”?

If the divine nature was circumscribed by the human nature of the one reclining and wrapped in swaddling clothes in the manger, then his uncircumscribed divinity was also circumscribed in the painted image of his humanity; likewise, if on the cross the divine nature was circumscribed by the nature of his humanity, then his uncircumscribed divinity was also circumscribed in its painted image. But if it was not so in those cases [Gr., “if these things did not happen”], neither is it so here.

They would surely have recognized the saying of the divine Dionysius in his discourse on the hierarchy, where he says (ch. 2):

> “An exact likeness does not exist between effects and causes” [Gr., “an exact likeness”]; “effects do indeed possess images corresponding to their causes, but the causes themselves surpass their effects and remain established above them, according to the principle of their origin.”

Thus it has been shown even to those capable of understanding very little that their patched-up discourse introduces a certain empty novelty of words against the Church, directing its arguments not against the painter but against the Church.

Moreover, continuing in shamelessness, they rashly say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

> “Those who attempt to paint Christ’s incomprehensible and uncircumscribed divine nature must be condemned by those who think rightly. They will certainly flee to another defense of their wicked scheme, saying that we paint an icon only of that flesh which we saw and touched, and with which we lived; but this is impious and an invention of the worst Nestorian understanding.”

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

[Col. 0399D]

The false defenders of the truth continue their same devices, turning to shameless contradiction. While uttering things that agree with one another, they fall into the snare of blasphemy. Continuing their words of madness—namely, that Christ’s divine nature is incomprehensible and uncircumscribed—they accuse Christians of circumscribing it.

Then, speaking craftily and assuming the role of Christians, they falsely declare that we paint an icon only of that flesh which we saw and touched, and with which we lived, so that they may once again introduce the Church into the blasphemy of Nestorius. Hence they add: “This is impious and an invention of the worst Nestorian understanding.”

Let them hear the truth, then. Knowing one Emmanuel, Christ the Lord, Christians paint him according to the truth that the Word became flesh, and they drive all their manifold chatter far from themselves. With simple hearts they accept everything handed down in the Church, and when they look at the paintings they understand nothing other than what is represented in them.

For when they see in a painting the Virgin giving birth, with angels standing above and shepherds present, they recall that God became human for our salvation. They confess, saying: “The one who was without flesh became flesh; the Word was thickened; the uncreated was created; the intangible was touched.” And they confess one and the same Christ, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man.

Moreover, it was stated earlier concerning the wicked heresy of Nestorius that the representations of images agree with it in no respect; and this has been stated sufficiently. If necessary, it will be said again.

But, supposing that they themselves understand something, they say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

> “This must be discussed: if, according to the orthodox Fathers, the flesh is at once the flesh of God the Word, never receiving any sense of division, but wholly assumed from the whole divine nature and completely deified, how will it be divided or set apart by those who impiously attempt to do this? The same must also be said concerning his soul. For when the divinity of the Son assumed the nature of flesh into its own person, the soul became a mediator between the divinity and the density of the flesh. And just as the flesh is at once the flesh of God the Word, so also the soul is at once the soul of God the Word. Both together—the soul deified, as was the body—remained undivided from the divinity even in the separation of the soul from the body during the voluntary Passion. For where the soul of Christ is, there also is the divinity; and where the body of Christ is, there also is the divinity.”

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

Whenever the subverters of the catholic Church are about to attack someone, they take up arguments that everyone professes, as is the custom of the orthodox. Thus, because a sound meaning appears in these arguments, they may not be judged unworthy of belief [that is, less worthy of faith] in the rest. For after uttering a few things correctly, and in a manner mixing pearls with pebbles, and then returning to their own vomit, [Col. 0400D] they say that the one Christ is divided and set apart by those who accept venerable painted images.

They speak reprehensibly when they say that no sense of division has ever been accepted. It is therefore clear that they are ignorant of the sayings of the Fathers. All the Fathers expressly proclaim the separation of the two natures in thought [Gr., “by reflection”], but not in reality, as was stated above, just as Nestorius blasphemously dared to say.

There is unquestionably no basis for disagreement, separation, or any division, nor again for confusion of essence, as they have repeatedly preached falsely, simply because the Lord is painted according to the manner in which he was perfect man.

For the image is one thing and the original another. None of those who think soundly seeks in the image the properties [Col. 0401A] of the original. In the image, true reason knows nothing other than that it shares, according to name, in the one whose image it is, and not according to substance, as we have repeatedly said, compelled by their own arguments.

Lacking anything to say against the catholic Church, they repeat the same things about the same things, speaking with an empty throat and presenting an exercise in empty talk [Gr., “empty talk”] to their hearers. For this reason they are shown to be objects of ridicule before everyone: sometimes they speak of division, sometimes of confusion, possessing a tongue entirely ready to follow wherever it may lead [Gr., “ready to sin in words”].

Thus they also say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

[Col. 0401B]

> “If, then, in the Passion the divinity remained inseparable from those things, how do these senseless men, filled with every irrationality, divide the flesh that was joined to and deified with the divinity, and attempt to paint it as the image of a mere man? For in this too they fall into another abyss of iniquity, separating the flesh from the divinity, asserting that it possesses a private subsistence, and assigning another person to the flesh, which they also confess they depict [that is, express in images]. By this they show the addition of a fourth person to the Trinity. In addition, they paint as atheotic—that is, not deified—the assumption that was divinely taken up [Gr., “they paint as atheotic, that is, not deified, what was deified through the assumption”].

> “It follows, then, that those who think Christ’s image ought to be painted either regard the divinity as circumscribed and confused with the flesh, or regard Christ’s body as atheotic and divided, assigning a person with private subsistence to the flesh [in the flesh]. In this they become like the attack of the Nestorians against God. Falling into such blasphemy and impiety, let them be confounded and ashamed, and let those who produce, desire, and venerate the image cease from the image that they deceitfully call and declare to be Christ. Let the division of Nestorius and the confusion of Arius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, and Severus likewise cease among us—evils that are immeasurable [Gr., ‘evils diametrically opposed to one another] and equal in impiety.”

**The deacon Epiphanius read:**

[Col. 0401D]

The defenders of the heresy that slanders Christians do not walk by one path, as is customary among the orthodox, who, when discussing divine doctrines, retain only the royal road and in no way deviate from it in either direction. Instead, overturning the Lord’s ways, they gather contradictory opinions among themselves; and, abounding in their own understanding, they are thought to be wise in all things.

But let them hear Isaiah, who speaks boldly: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent before themselves” (Isa. 5).

For they take up things that orthodox Christians have never said, as though they had been preached by them. Weaving deceptive syllogisms, they argue sophistically; and the result is insult [Col. 0402A] and curse, or rather, impiety. Whatever Diodore, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, and Severus adopted against the truth, spewing out their rage, they attribute to the catholic Church. They add evil to evil, asserting that the Church is sprinkled with these impious heretics [“that it thinks with these impious heretics”], possessing words full of stupidity and uselessness. Just as tavern-keepers mix wine with water, so they mix true speech with perversion and temper it with the bitterness of gall.

The heresy of Dioscorus and Eutyches is contrary to Nestorius, as we have already said; and it is impossible for contrary heresies to exist in one opinion and confession. In the same way, it is impossible for white and black, or hot and cold, to be seen in one subject at one and the same time. For no one has ever found heat in snow, or cold in fire.

Let us make the uselessness of their madness still more evident. In their eagerness to slander, they say that the image and the original are the same thing; and for this reason they lead those who depict the Gospel narrative into confusion and division.

The Eutychians—that is, those who preach one nature according to subsistence in Christ’s union, and consequently teach confusion—have no other alteration of the truth than this: they define subsistence and nature as the same thing. The students of the catholic Church know that one is different from the other.

For we call subsistence a substance together with its properties, from the term *hyphestánai* [Gr., *hyphestánai*, that is, “to subsist”]. Nature, however, we confess to be a self-subsisting [Gr., “existing”] reality, not needing anything else for its stability [constitution], from the term *pephykénai*.

In this respect also these men say that Christ’s image and Christ himself differ in no way according to substance. For if they knew the difference, they would never put forward such monstrous novelties of words.

It is evident to everyone that the image is one thing and the prototype another: the latter is animate, while the former is inanimate. And because they have babbled that the divine nature is likewise circumscribed in the image, having departed from right reason they have been handed over to a depraved mind.

Peter and Paul are visibly depicted, but their souls are not present in the images. Indeed, even when Peter’s own body is present, no one sees his soul. Since it is not seen, which of those who follow the truth says that Peter’s flesh is separated from his soul, except in thought alone?

How much more is the uncircumscribed nature of God the Word distinct from the circumscribed flesh assumed by him? For when he was wearied from the journey, asked the Samaritan woman for a drink, and was stoned by the Jews, the divine nature was not wearied or subjected to stones—God forbid such blasphemy.

This manifold mass of arguments was introduced by the empty-mindedness of those who slander Christians with an unrestrained tongue, because it wished to reject pictorial images. It then added other things and heaped iniquity upon iniquities, foolishly speaking of the addition of a fourth person to the holy Trinity.

But we, who have been born in the catholic Church as her own children, accepting everything that belongs to the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and detesting Arius, Nestorius, Apollinarius, and also Eutyches and Dioscorus, his disciples, accept venerable images. We call them images only and nothing else, since they possess merely the name of the original and not its substance.

But proceeding obliquely like crabs, they are led toward another path of blasphemy, saying:

**Bishop Gregory read:**
«Let those rejoice and exult, and let those act confidently who, with the most sincere soul, make and desire the true image of Christ, venerate it, and offer it for the salvation of soul and body: the most holy sacrificer himself and our God, taking from us the whole mass of humanity, handed this over to his ministers, according to the time of his own Passion, as an exceedingly clear type and memorial. For, intending voluntarily to surrender himself to his memorable and life-giving death, he blessed the bread he had taken, gave thanks, broke it, and said as he gave it: “Take and eat, for the remission of sins; this is my body” (Matt. XXVI). Likewise, giving them the cup, he said: “This is my blood; do this in remembrance of me” (Mark XIV; Luke XXII).

“As though no other species beneath heaven, or form [figure], had been chosen by him that could represent his incarnation. See, therefore, how the image of his life-giving body was made precious and honorable [Greek: “Behold, then, the image of the life-giving body, made precious and honorable”]. What did the all-wise God intend by this? Was it not to show and express clearly to us human beings the mystery that he accomplished through his dispensation? For just as that which he assumed from us is merely the matter of a human substance, perfect in every respect, not properly representing a subsisting person, lest an addition of person should be introduced into the divinity, so he also commanded the principal matter of the image—that is, the substance of bread—to be offered, not representing the form of a man, lest idolatry be introduced.

“Therefore, just as Christ’s body, which is holy according to nature, being divinely sanctified [Greek: “being deified”], so it is clear that by adoption—that is, the image itself—is holy, being sanctified [Greek: “deified”] through a certain sanctification of grace. For this also, as we have said, the Lord Jesus deliberately accomplished: just as, through the sanctification proper to its nature, he deified the flesh he assumed by the very union, so likewise he willed the bread of the Eucharist, not as a false image [variant: “so that it would not be a false image”] of natural flesh, to be sanctified through the coming of the Holy Spirit and, through the priest, to become the divine body; for the priest separates the offering from common use and brings it to sanctification.

“Thus Christ’s flesh, by nature animate and endowed with understanding, was anointed with the Holy Spirit into divinity [variant: “endowed with mind, it was anointed with divinity through the Holy Spirit”]. Likewise, the divinely handed-down image of his flesh—the divine bread, namely—is filled with the Holy Spirit together with the cup bearing the life-giving blood of his side. This, then, has been shown to be the true image of the dispensation accomplished in the flesh, namely, of Christ our God, as was said above; and this he himself, the true giver of life and fashioner of nature, handed over to us in his own voice.»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

It is evident how every proposed argument, once it has turned away from the truth, is led by deceptive reasoning into many dangerous perversions—something these teachers of novelty have also suffered. For, having turned away from the truth on account of the making of images, they fell into the opposite extreme, the madness of apoplexy. Indeed, as though they had received these oblique and pernicious doctrines from the Delphic tripod, they uttered them as an oracle [variant: “prophesied them”].

But let them hear the proverbial saying: “A strong snare for a man is his own lips, and he is caught by the words of his own mouth” (Prov. VI). For they have laid down wood, hay, and stubble, whose end is burning. No trumpet of the Spirit—not that of the holy apostles or of our illustrious Fathers—ever called our bloodless sacrifice, which is performed in remembrance of Christ our God and of his entire dispensation, an image of his body. They did not receive from the Lord the instruction to say or confess this; rather, they hear him speaking evangelically: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John IV). And: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid.). And: “Having taken bread and given thanks, he broke it and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’” And, taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Drink from this, all of you: for this is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XXIV; Luke XXII). He did not say, “Take and eat the image of my body.”

The divine apostle Paul, likewise drawing from the Lord’s divine words, says: “I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that on the night in which he was betrayed, he took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after supper, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. XI).

Thus it has been clearly demonstrated that nowhere did the Lord, the apostles, or the Fathers call the bloodless sacrifice offered through the priest an image; rather, they called it the body itself and the blood itself. Before the celebration of sanctification, however, certain holy Fathers piously thought it appropriate to call these things types [Greek: “antitypes at the consummation”]. Among them was Eustathius, champion of the orthodox faith and destroyer of the Arian madness, and Basil, who removed that same wretched superstition and taught the clear foundation of sound doctrines throughout the world.

For, arguing from one and the same Spirit, one of them, interpreting the Solomonic saying found in Proverbs, “Eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Prov. IX), says: “Through bread and wine he proclaims types of Christ’s bodily members.” The other, drawing from the same source—as all who practice the mystical priesthood know—says in the prayer of the divine offering: “With confidence we approach the holy altar, and, setting forth the types of your holy body and blood, we beseech you and entreat you.”

What follows makes this Father’s understanding still clearer: before they have been sanctified, they are called types [Note: Greek Fathers not infrequently call them *antitypes* even after they have been sanctified, as Gregory Nazianzen, *Funeral Oration for His Sister*, and *Apology*; Cyril, *Catechetical Lecture* V, *Mystagogical Lecture*; and others]. After sanctification, however, they are properly called, are, and are believed to be Christ’s body and blood.

But these bold men, wishing to destroy the appearance of the venerable images, introduced another image which is not an image but body and blood. Overcome by fatigue [Greek: “wickedness”] and cunning, and injuring themselves through their perverse sophistry [Greek: “deceiving themselves”], they called this divine offering something that comes to be by adoption [Greek addition: “and just as it is manifest madness to say this, so also to assert that an image is the body,” etc.]. To call it the body and blood of the Lord approaches madness in much the same way and contains an even greater impiety of indiscipline [Greek: “through indiscipline”].

Then, abandoning their falsehood, they touch the truth slightly, saying that it becomes the divine body. Yet, if it is an image of the body, it cannot be this divine body. Thus, driven back and forth, what they have muttered remains altogether powerless. For just as a troubled eye does not see correctly, so they, disturbing and confusing their own understanding through the disorder of their thoughts, suffer what madmen suffer: fantastically mistaking one thing for another [Greek: “judging fantastically”]. At one time they call our sacrifice the intelligible image of Christ’s holy body; at another, they call it the body by designation.

They have suffered this, as we said above, because they wish to eradicate from the Church the appearance of images; and they rejoice over the overturning of ecclesiastical traditions.

## TOME FOUR

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

Again insisting upon the same calumnies, they move their tongues, sharpening them against the holy Church of God; for they say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«The evil of the false designation “images” neither derives from the tradition of Christ, the apostles, or the Fathers, nor does the sacred prayer that sanctifies it transform it from what is common into holiness. Rather, it remains common and dishonored, just as the painter made it.»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

Having a tongue that speaks great things, they magnify the evil without fear of God by their additions. With reckless heart and authority, meditating upon the images made under Christ’s name as falsely designated and evil, they pronounced them such. If they had dared to say this about images of kings, they might perhaps have suffered death as punishment. They will suffer and receive this punishment when recompense is made for words and deeds.

Moreover, together with many things handed down to us without writing, the making of images in the Church has spread from the preaching of the apostles. The history of the woman with the issue of blood also indicates this; it has testimony from various histories, and, according to the account of the holy Gospel, she obtained healing because she erected a statue of the Lord and placed herself touching the fringe of the statue (Matt. IX; Mark V; Luke VIII). Between that statue and the image of Christ a certain plant sprang up, extending toward the statue’s foot, a remedy for every illness.

Many of our holy Fathers have also handed down that these things were practiced by Christians in their writings [Note: Greek: “and Kai”]. Basil the Great, whose teaching resounds throughout all regions, mentions them in various sermons. So does Gregory, his brother in flesh and spirit, bishop of Nyssa, in his sermon on Abraham; and Gregory, surnamed “the Theologian,” in the poems he composed, including the poem entitled *On Virtue*. John, who possesses a mouth more precious than gold, mentions them in his funeral oration for Meletius, bishop of Antioch, and in the sermon whose title is also written above it, “Because the Legislator of the Old and New Testaments Is One.” Cyril, the deposer of Nestorius, mentions them in his letter to Acacius, bishop of Scythopolis [Greek: “in his first letter”]; Sophronius [variant: “Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch”]; Maximus.

But why do we mention these individually, when all our holy Fathers accepted the making of images? These men falsely assert that it is not a tradition of the Fathers—and quite consistently, if the Fathers did not hand down the Gospel to be read, nor images to be depicted. But if they handed down the one, they handed down the other also.

The formation of a title or painting follows the evangelical account, and the evangelical account follows the pictorial narrative; both are good and honorable. For whatever things indicate one another undoubtedly possess, each in the other, their corresponding meanings. If we say that the sun is above the earth, it is certainly day; and if we say that it is day, the sun is certainly above the earth.

Likewise, if we see in an image an angel announcing good news to the Virgin, we certainly recall the coming of the evangelical account: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a Virgin, and entering to her said: ‘Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women’” (Luke I). Thus we heard from the Gospel the event of the mystery enacted through the angel for the Virgin, and we are reminded of it; and, looking at the image, we understand more clearly what happened.

Then, turning again to another path of indiscipline, they say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«Nor does the sacred prayer that sanctifies it transform it from what is common into sanctification; rather, it remains common and dishonored, just as the painter made it.»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

Let them hear what is true. Many things that have been sanctified among us do not receive a sacred prayer, since by their very name they are already full of holiness and grace. Therefore we honor and salute these things as truly venerable. The very type of the life-giving cross, made without a sacred prayer, is venerated among us, and we are content with its figure for receiving sanctification. Through the adoration we offer to it, through the sign impressed upon the forehead, and through the sign made in the air with the finger, we hope to drive away demons [variant: “to pursue them”].

Likewise, through the inscription of the name upon an image, we are led back to the honor of the prototype; and, saluting and honorably venerating it, we receive sanctification. We also have various sacred vessels, and we salute and embrace them, hoping to receive from them a certain holiness.

Therefore, either they will foolishly say that the cross and the sacred vessels are common and dishonored, just as the craftsman, painter, and weaver made them, because they do not possess a sacred prayer sanctifying them; or else they will admit the venerable images as sacred, holy, and honorable. Otherwise, wishing to plant other seeds mixed with tares, they continue to speak as though from a divinatory spirit.

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«But if some of those detained in such error should say: “What we rightly and piously assert concerning the overthrow of the image called Christ’s image is on account of the two inseparable and unconfused natures that came together in one subsistence. Yet we fail in reasoning because, concerning the immaculate and ever-glorious one who is properly the Mother of God, and concerning the prophets, apostles, and martyrs, although they are pure human beings and do not consist of two natures—divinity and humanity—in one subsistence like Christ, we forbid images from being made”—»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

Let no one who has been brought up in the Catholic Church understand or suppose that they judged rightly and piously concerning this novelty. Rather, all the high priests and priests of both East and West, of North and South, delivered to anathema those who held such opinions. They seduced only a small part of these dioceses and cut themselves off from the whole body of the Church, either despising the Lord’s voice, which says: “Whoever causes one of these least ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the sea” (Matt. XVIII), or failing to revere him, since they rage against his image. Nor are they ashamed of his saints; rather, they have stirred their tongues against them also, saying:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«“We fail in reasoning because, concerning the immaculate and ever-glorious one who is properly the Mother of God, and concerning the prophets, apostles, and martyrs, although they are pure human beings and do not consist of two natures, divinity and humanity”—and here one must say to them that, once the first point has been destroyed, there is no need of these either.»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

They did not first destroy the argument evangelically, apostolically, scripturally, patristically, or rationally—and, to speak plainly, they did not do so piously. Rather, speaking from their own belly, they resisted the Catholic Church of God. Nor is their opposition to the proposed images of our undefiled Lady, the Mother of God, or of the saints truthful or pious, as we have already demonstrated, God granting us the word.

For earlier we said, drawing from the holy Fathers, that the honor paid to an image passes to the prototype, and that whoever looks upon the image of a king looks upon the king in it. Therefore, whoever venerates the image venerates the king in it, for the image is his form and appearance [Greek: “in the image”]. And just as one who insults the image of a king rightly suffers punishment, as one who has dishonored the king himself, although the image is nothing other than wood and colors mixed and blended with wax, so also whoever dishonors the figure of anyone directs the insult against the very one whose image it is.

The very nature of things teaches this as well: when the image is dishonored, the prototype is certainly dishonored. All people know this, and they recognize that these men rise up against the Fathers, resist the tradition of the Catholic Church, and do not follow the nature of things.

Again, having a tongue filled with falsehood, they suppose that they can defraud [variant: “offend”] the truth by saying:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«Nevertheless, let us state the points by which they are refuted. Since our Catholic Christian Church, existing midway between Judaism and paganism, possesses the solemn ceremonies of neither, but follows the new path of piety and the mystical sacrifice divinely handed down, it does not admit the bloody sacrifices and holocausts of Judaism, while it abominates, apart from sacrifice, every making of idols and every worship of idols belonging to paganism—the one who became the author and inventor of this detestable art. For, having no hope of resurrection, paganism devised for itself a fitting mockery, presenting what is not present as though it were present, in derision.

“If, therefore, there is nothing foreign in the Church, then this too, as something alien—the invention of men of demonic understanding—should rightly be driven away from the Church of Christ.»

**Deacon Epiphanius [and the chamberlain] read:**

Their writing, produced in full measure by the ravings of an immeasurable and frivolous discourse, is extremely foolish and ridiculous. In their earlier statements they were led by their little arguments into precipices and chasms [Greek: “abysses”]; now they had thrust themselves into the depths of hell by declaring that the Christian Church stands midway between Judaism and paganism.

Then, falling into contradiction with themselves, they say that it possesses the solemn ceremonies of neither. Therefore, either they are lying there or they are not speaking the truth here. To speak more accurately, they are lying to themselves. For falsehood not only contradicts the truth but also contradicts itself, as the sacred psalmist David says: “Iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. XXVI).

Basil, bishop of Caesarea, whose sound has gone out into all the earth, says in the very preface of his sermon written against the Sabellians: “Judaism attacks paganism, and both attack Christianity.” But these men, who think themselves wiser than the Fathers, declared that the Christian faith stands midway between these two adversaries.

Judaism introduced a lack of divinity, while paganism introduced a multitude of gods. Gregory, who is surnamed “the Theologian,” rejecting both, says as follows (*Oration on the Nativity of Christ*): “When I say God, I mean the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—not going beyond these in deity, lest we introduce a common crowd of gods, nor limiting ourselves within these bounds, lest we be judged—or condemned—for a lack of divinity, Judaizing because of monarchy or paganizing because of a multitude of gods. For the evil is similar in both, although it is found in opposites.”

The things of the Old Testament, which the Israelite people observed, were a tradition of God; those of the pagans were traditions of demons. Here, therefore, they have reckoned and mixed together with divinely handed-down commandments what is demonic, declaring the Lord’s image to be an idol, similar to images of demons.

They therefore slander Abel, Noah, Abraham, because of the sacrifices they offered to God through animals, and Moses, Samuel, David, and the other patriarchs, on the ground that they too offered foreign and pagan sacrifices to God, although Scripture bears witness to their sacrifice, saying: “The Lord smelled a sweet savor” (Gen. VIII).

Would that they had understood the truth: those things that are said to be offered to God are acceptable to God. “They sacrificed to the Lord God,” Scripture says. But those things offered to demons are detestable and to be rejected: “They sacrificed to demons and not to God,” says Scripture (Deut. XXXII).

Therefore, the evil and this opposition arise from us and through us, not from the underlying materials. For, as the Apostle says, “What is an idol? And what is an offering sacrificed to an idol, except that what the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God?” (1 Cor. X.)

Yet, greatly erring and fabricating insults and falsehoods, they deliberate and bring forward the following:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«Let every mouth that speaks wickedly and abusively against our God-pleasing decision and judgment be silenced. For the saints who pleased God and were honored by him with the dignity of holiness always live to God, even though they have departed from this life. Whoever seeks to raise them up by means of a dead and hateful art, which never lives but was vainly devised by pagan adversaries, shows himself to be a blasphemer.»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

In what they have now said, they show themselves foreign and alien to the peace of God—the peace our Lord left to those who genuinely and without deceit believe in him, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV).

For how can there be peace if the Catholic Church is raised up, strengthened, and confirmed by its traditions contrary to their decision and judgment? Those who are moved by divine zeal always agree with the Fathers and with the tradition of ecclesiastical laws; but they flee as an enemy anyone who behaves contrary to them.
