Therefore the true worshipers, who serve God in spirit and truth (John IV), who retain pictorial images solely for reference and remembrance, and who embrace and salute them, do not cease to pierce with the dagger of the Spirit, wearing the breastplate of truth, the divinely condemned decision and judgment of those who have cut themselves off from the whole body of the Church.

For the holy Fathers who pleased God from the beginning of the age, leaving us their lives written for our salvation and benefit, also handed down in the Catholic Church the things they accomplished through pictorial narration, for the remembrance of our mind and for the elevation of their manner of life.

Thus Saint Basil, in his sermon on the praise of the forty holy martyrs, says:

“Come, then, bringing them into our midst through remembrance, and let us establish their common benefit for those who are present, displaying to everyone, as in a painting, the brave deeds of these men. For writers of histories and of the praises of wars, as well as painters, often portray such things: some adorning them with words, others engraving them on panels [Greek: “the former with speech, the latter on panels”]. Both have raised many to courage. For what historical discourse presents through hearing, painting, remaining silent, shows through imitation.”

But mixing their praises with their cunning, they say such things:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«How, then, do they dare to paint by the vulgar art of the Gentiles the supremely praiseworthy Mother of the Lord, upon whom the fullness of divinity overshadowed, through whom the inaccessible light shone upon us, who is higher than the heavens and holier than the cherubim?

“Or again, how are they not ashamed to paint by the art of the Gentiles those who will reign together with Christ, sit with him, judge the world, and be conformed to his glory—those of whom, as the sacred words say, the world was not worthy (Heb. XI)?

“For Christians who possess the hope of resurrection, it is unlawful to adopt the customs of the Gentiles who worship demons, and to heap insults upon the saints, who will shine with such and so great a glory, by placing them in dishonor and dead matter. We do not accept proofs of our faith from foreigners. For when demons proclaimed Jesus as God, he rebuked them, disdaining to receive testimony from demons (Mark I; Luke IV).»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**

Beginning with praises, they wish to steal away the simpler-minded into their empty understanding. But those who possess the serpent’s prudence, not its cunning, and the dove’s simplicity know how to honor in words and praises the undefiled and immaculate one who is truly and properly the Mother of God and the saints; how to recall their virtues through historical books; and how, through pictorial inscriptions, to make their struggles and courage known again, magnifying them with the highest honors.

They know that, according to the holy Apostle, the saints have departed and are with Christ (Phil. I), that they intercede for us, and that sincere and supreme faith and service in spirit and truth are to be offered to God alone, not to any creatures beneath heaven.

Why, then, do they take material and wish to disgrace the truth by insults, as though it were something shameful? They ought rather to flee what is worse, pursue what is better, and remember the ancient holy sacrifices praised by Scripture—how the same material was offered at one time to God and at another to demons [Greek: “when they were offered to God, and when to demons; although the same material, being the same”]. Yet, merely looking at the underlying material, they slander the Church as bearing the marks of pagan inventions.

But because material is reproached as useful in different and opposing matters, or shown to be shameful, its usefulness must not therefore be despised. For if they persist in understanding and accepting things in this manner, then, according to their reasoning, everything dedicated to God will be polluted: the sacred vestments and the sacred vessels.

Indeed, those who held pagan beliefs constructed idols from gold and silver, poured libations from wine, and offered cakes of flour to the army of heaven; these were Hebrews who became idolaters. It remains for them, therefore, to accuse the Catholic Church because pagans praised their gods and demons through historical books, and to say that we too must not praise, as the pagans did, either the God who is above all or his saints through historical books, because we receive proofs from what belongs to others.

What an overturning and madness! Since we are plainly sensible human beings, we use sensible things for the knowledge and remembrance of every divine and pious tradition.

Then, as adulterators of the truth, overturning at once the Lord’s ways and his meanings, they say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

«Therefore, after examining and considering this decree [Greek: “dogma”] of ours, let us also provide, from divinely inspired Scripture and from our approved Fathers, clear testimonies agreeing with us and strengthening this pious intention of ours. Let no one who has experience of these matters contradict them; let anyone who does not know them learn and retain them as things belonging to God.

“According to the first argument, then, we appeal to the divinely spoken words from his voice, which say: ‘God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth’ (John IV). And again: ‘No one has ever seen God’ (John I). And: ‘You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form’ (John V); and to the beatitude pronounced upon those who have not seen him and yet have believed.”»

**Deacon Epiphanius and the chamberlain read:**

When some try to pervert doctrines that appear correct to them, no one should be surprised if they use the words of Scripture. For all the heresiarchs gather from divinely inspired Scripture opportunities for their error, adulterating words rightly spoken through the Holy Spirit according to their own wicked interpretations.

The chief trumpet of the apostles foretold this, Peter namely, saying: “The unlearned and unstable distort these things according to their own desires” (2 Pet. III). For it is characteristic of heretics to distort the knowledge of divine and true doctrines according to their own desires.

In general, our holy Fathers, accepting the words “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works” (Prov. VIII) with reference to Christ’s dispensation accomplished according to the flesh, Arius and Eunomius and those associated with them applied them to the heavenly and divine generation, and thereby turned backward from right knowledge.

Apollinarius, again, wrongly understanding the evangelical saying, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John III), turned it toward wickedness. He said that God the Word descended with that flesh which he had in heaven, an eternal flesh consubstantial with himself; and, adducing an apostolic saying, “The second man, the Lord, from heaven” (1 Cor. XIII), he spoke according to what had seemed right to him [Greek: “he was deceived”].

No one should therefore wonder if the followers of this new perversion also bring us opinions from divine Scripture, for they received their opportunities for error from their teachers. They have transferred words spoken concerning the invisible and incomprehensible divinity to the Lord’s dispensation in the flesh, to Jesus Christ our Lord, who is one of the Holy Trinity.

For who among those who think rightly does not know that the statement “No one has ever seen God” was written concerning the divine nature? And if someone understands the statement “You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form” as referring to his humanity, he will overturn the entire Gospel.

Where, then, shall we place the words we confess: “The Lord said to his disciples” (Matt. XXIII)? And: “The Lord said to the Jews who had come to him.” And: “The Lord said: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. V)? Or again, how shall we understand the words, “Opening his mouth, he taught them” (John V)? These clearly refer to his humanity. But the statement “You have neither heard his voice nor seen his form” refers to the divine substance.

For, inasmuch as he became perfect man, the Word of God, as we said earlier, we heard his voice and saw his form even after the resurrection. He was touched, and, appearing to his disciples, he spoke with them about the kingdom.

Next, they also say that Christians, possessing true and sincere faith [variant: “possessing true and sincere faith in themselves”], declare divine service and adoration to resemble affectionate and honorific veneration. These are the two points in which their doctrine is perverse; and for this reason they are and are called slanderers of Christians.

For they say that Christians offer to images the adoration and service due to God, and that they circumscribe the incomprehensible divine nature. O denial and stupidity—and whatever else belongs with them! The statement has no substance; it is full of abuse and slanders.

Christians have not allotted the adoration that is in spirit and truth (John IV) either to images or to the figure of the divine cross. Nor have they ever made an image of the invisible and incomprehensible nature. Rather, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I), they paint and represent in images the things belonging to his human dispensation [variant: “express them through images”].

Knowing that God is spirit and that those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth, they offer to God alone—the one praised above all in the Trinity—the adoration and service that arise through faith. But, burning with desire and affection for the divine type of the cross and the venerable images, we salute them and honorably venerate them according to their relation to the prototypes.

Their vain and empty, or secret [Greek: “weak”], utterly slight words are therefore shown by the truth to be such, just as, understanding the other things alien to piety, they say:

**Bishop Gregory read:**

[Col. 0413D]

«And when the Old Testament says to Moses and to the people: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness whatsoever, whether of what is in heaven above or of what is on the earth below” (Deut. V), because on the mountain, from the midst of the fire, you heard the voice of words, but you saw no likeness—only the voice.»

**Deacon Epiphanius read:**
They draw from this an occasion for impiety, seeking by their sophistries and prodigious frenzy to infect Christian children. For if [Greek: “as though frightening with a mask,” for “for if”] you have Christ or his saints in remembrance through the depiction of images, you lapse into idolatry. And these stalwart men, meditating every kind of injustice, [Col. 0414A] evade in their preliminary statements the wording of the commandment, “You shall not make any likeness.” Possessing the truth in unrighteousness, and wishing to establish their own righteousness, they devote themselves to impiety; and, glorying in the insubstantiality of falsehood, they are estranged from the truth.

For they apply to the consecrated company of Christians the words once given in the Law to the people of Israel who served the calf (Exod. XXXII) and had experienced the abominations of the Egyptians, and they make their pronouncements and speak monstrously [Greek: “and are caught”], their lips scorched by their own mouths. Would that they had understood that, when the Lord was about to lead them into the promised land, because nations inhabited it that worshiped idols and adored demons—also the sun, moon, stars, and other creatures, as well as birds, four-footed animals, [Col. 0414B] and creeping things, and not the living and true God—he gave the commandment: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness whatsoever, whether of what is in heaven above or of what is on the earth below” (Exod. XX). For he immediately adds, drawing them away from idolatry: “You shall not adore them, nor serve them” (ibid.).

When his faithful servant Moses made the tabernacle of testimony according to the Lord’s design, showing that all things served him, he fashioned from gold the sensible cherubim in the likeness of human form, as types of intelligible realities [or: “types of the intelligible”], overshadowing the mercy seat and prefiguring Christ. For he is the propitiation for our sins, as the divine apostle says (I John II). Thus he led them to the knowledge of God by two means: on the one hand, by saying, “You shall adore the Lord your God, and serve him alone” (Matt. IV); on the other, by making golden, cast cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat (Deut. VI)—that is, adoring it. [Col. 0414C] Through sight and hearing he lifted them up to adore the Lord God and serve him alone.

But these men, possessing a mind full of perversity, also bring forward an apostolic saying of this kind:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man; and they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. I). And again: “Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus. [Col. 0414D] For we walk by faith, not by sight” (II Cor. V). And, confirming the same point, he says: “Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Rom. X).

Epiphanius the deacon read:

It must be stated openly that they are comparable to the Gentiles, who exchanged the glory of God and served the creature rather than the Creator, also altering and twisting the apostolic meanings according to their own desires. For it is clear to everyone that the Apostle appears to mock the pagans when he says: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man.” He adds: “and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents” (Rom. I)—although they fraudulently cut off the discussion in its entirety [Col. 0415A], so that, as though this concerned the Church’s images, they might deceive the simpler-minded. The words that follow, however, provide an especially clear explanation.

He mentioned birds, four-footed animals, and serpents, and said that they served the creature rather than the Creator. Those most skilled in historical books know that the Egyptians formerly worshiped oxen and other four-footed animals, various flying creatures, flies, hornets’ nests, and creatures even more contemptible than these; the Persians worshiped the sun and fire. The Greeks, moreover, served every kind of creature; and some of the Hebrews did so as well, as the Book of Kings and the accounts of the prophets relate.

Let them say, then: when did the nations become foolish and their senseless heart become darkened [Col. 0415B]—before they believed in Christ, or after they believed? Clearly, before they believed. For this is evident. If they say that, after the nations believed in Christ, they served creatures and idols, then, according to their own argument, the prophecies concerning the Church of Christ our God will be false—those prophecies that were uttered concerning her: “Jerusalem shall be holy, and foreigners shall no longer pass through her.” And again: “I shall not scatter my mercy from them, nor profane my covenant; and the words that proceed from my lips I shall not annul” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

But if, after making them exiles from the knowledge of God, they were handed over to a debased mind before Christ’s coming, serving the devil, then the accusation now brought by them against Christians is worthless. And Isaiah will confidently say to them, crying out: “Woe to those who write wickedness; for while writing, they write wickedness” (Isa. X, according to the Septuagint). [Col. 0415C]

Thus, maliciously and evasively interpreting the apostolic words and the other words of Holy Scripture, they hasten to overturn the great mystery of our salvation—the dispensation of Christ our God, through whom we were redeemed from the error of idols—and to transfer the glory to themselves. But no Christian believes them. For we all confess that Christ our true God, in his coming by which he came to us according to the flesh, completely drew us away from the error of idols and from every pagan religion.

If they themselves do not in the least confess that this took place, they possess neither his confession nor his calling. Therefore the Apostle says against them: “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV). But if they received it, [Col. 0415D] they ought to have confessed that redemption and accepted the images that have been made visible to our eyes as ecclesiastical adornment, and through which the Gospel narratives are taken into our minds for the remembrance and exposition of the Gospel history, as has been said so often.

Since they also bring forward other apostolic words, saying, “Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (II Cor. V), let us bring forward the interpreters and renowned teachers of these words.

John, then, whose teaching is more radiant than gold and precious stone, interpreting the Apostle’s saying, “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (II Cor. V), says the following (Homily 11 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians): [Col. 0416A]

> “We know none of the faithful according to the flesh. What, then, even if they are in the flesh? That carnal life has perished, and we have been born from above by the Spirit; and we know another citizenship, conduct, life, and constitution, which is in the heavens.”
>
> Again, the same writer demonstrates that Christ is the author of this. Hence he also adds: “Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus.” Tell me: did he lay aside his flesh, and is he now without a body? Far from it; for even now he is in the flesh. “This Jesus, who has been taken up from us into heaven, will come in this same way” (Acts I). In what way? In the flesh, with his body.
>
> How, then, does he say, “Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus”? Because, although we knew Christ as subject to suffering, [Col. 0416B] now we no longer know him so. For our being according to the flesh means being in sins; and our not being according to the flesh means not being in sins. But Christ’s being according to the flesh means being subject to the sufferings of nature—for example, thirsting, hungering, becoming weary, and sleeping. “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII). Hence he also said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII). And again: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV).
>
> Therefore, Christ’s not being according to the flesh means that he has now been freed from these sorrows, not that he is without flesh. For with that same flesh he will come to judge the world, possessing it impassible and incorruptible. Into this state we too shall pass, when our body has been conformed to his body of glory. [Col. 0416C]

Moreover, Cyril of Alexandria, defender of our sincere faith, explaining this same saying, interprets it as follows:

> Since the Only-begotten Word of God became man, and appeared as the second root of the race—not according to the first, which is from Adam, but one to be understood and existing incomparably in better things—we are transformed into life. For we are not under death, but under the Word himself, who gives life to all; and no one is “in the flesh,” that is, in carnal weakness, which is corruption.
>
> Paul does not say that Christ is not in the flesh. For although he says, “We know no one according to the flesh,” this does not mean that Christ is not in the flesh—for how, then, did he die? This is a weakness of the flesh.
>
> What he says, therefore, is this: “The Word became flesh, and died for all; and thus we knew him according to the flesh, yet from that time onward we no longer know him thus.” For although he is now in the flesh—for he rose on the third day and ascended into the heavens—he is understood as being above the flesh. He no longer dies, nor does he endure any other weakness of the flesh, but as God he is superior to all these things. [Col. 0416D]

You see, therefore, adversaries, that you not only pervert the apostolic words but also oppose the holy Fathers. Through the statements quoted above, they show that Christ was freed from sufferings after the resurrection, and they teach us, as those conformed to his body of glory, not to walk according to the flesh—that is, not to pursue carnal pleasures.

But since you cannot bear to follow in the footsteps of these men, and think otherwise than the Fathers, you introduce some empty glory [or: “opinion”]. Walking on an untrodden path, you lead yourselves and your followers into precipices and jaws, plunging yourselves and them into the depths of hell. [Col. 0417A] Yet no one believes you, since you do not follow the teaching of our holy Fathers.

As for the statement, “For we walk by faith, not by sight,” John, interpreting it, says the following (Homily 10 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians):

> “Let no one say: ‘What, then?’ When you say, ‘As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord,’ why do you say this? Are we, then, made alien from him while we are here? He corrected this beforehand, saying: ‘We walk by faith, not by sight.’ Here we know him, but not with complete clarity. [Col. 0417B]
>
> “And elsewhere he says: ‘Now we see in a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face’” (I Cor. XIII).

Both these excellent Fathers said this, since in other sayings also the Apostle clearly indicates the meaning to us, saying: “What does anyone hope for if he sees it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. VIII).

It is therefore evident that we walk by faith and not by sight. For here we do not see God, but we believe in him; and we say by faith that the things he created were made by him, just as the Spirit himself proclaims with a mighty voice, saying: “By faith we understand that the ages were prepared by the word of God, so that visible things came to be from invisible things” (Heb. XI). And, contemplating the ordered movement of the universe, we arrive at the understanding of God, who made all things in wisdom. [Col. 0417C]

This, then, is the meaning of “We walk by faith, and not by sight,” and not what they themselves, through the indiscipline of their tongue, have perverted the apostolic saying into meaning concerning the making of venerable images.

Having therefore heard the teachings of the Fathers, let us follow them and abhor the present innovation, saying: “I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the impious” (Ps. XXV).

# FIFTH TOME

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Since their feet, running toward wickedness, have been entangled in their own snares, behold, it has been shown that none of those who have been nurtured in the Church has exchanged the glory of God for the making of images, or for any other creature whatsoever. [Col. 0417D] Come, then, let us also refute the rest, with the unconquered truth as our helper.

For, wishing to make evil abound through additions, they have also brought forward the holy Fathers, asserting that they spoke against the painting of venerable images, and adding:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Moreover, the disciples and successors of the Apostles, our God-speaking Fathers, teach the same things. Thus Epiphanius of Cyprus, most renowned for working miracles, says: ‘Pay attention to yourselves, and hold fast to the traditions that you have received; do not turn aside to the right or to the left.’ He adds:
>
> “‘And remember this, beloved children: do not bring images into churches or into the cemeteries of the saints; but remember God in your hearts. Nor should you bring them into a common house; for it is not fitting for a Christian to be carried away through the eyes and the wandering of the mind.’
>
> “He also set forth other discourses for the overthrow of the making of images, which those who love learning will find if they seek them.” [Col. 0418A]

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Those who love to investigate ecclesiastical affairs [Greek: “those diligent in investigating ecclesiastical matters”] know that people who think otherwise, wishing to establish their own righteousness and resist divine things, rely on spurious and false writings. They know them to be illegitimate and not genuine sons of the Catholic Church, and they do not receive them as brothers; rather, they repudiate them, saying: “The seed of Canaan, and not of Judah” (Dan. XIII). They know the Evangelist’s saying: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John II). [Col. 0418B]

And again, the most holy Apostle says: “After my departure grievous wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock, to draw the disciples away after themselves. And see that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Acts XX). And again the same Apostle says: “Do not believe every spirit” (I John IV).

It is therefore fitting for every Christian who hears false books to spit them out and in no way admit them. For there is said to be, in certain books, a forged epistle of the divine Apostle to the Laodiceans [Col. 0418C], which the Fathers rejected as foreign to him. The Manichaeans, moreover, introduce a Gospel according to Thomas, which the Catholic Church piously rejects as alien. So too the present testimony is said to exist, but it is not from our holy Father Epiphanius.

For that excellent Father, having composed an edition in eighty chapters, exposed all the heresies—pagan and Jewish, as well as all those that arose after Christianity—omitting none. If he had known the making of images to be foreign to Christ, he would certainly have included it among the heresies. And again, if the Church had accepted these expositions against venerable images, images would not have been painted for the adornment of the venerable temples [Col. 0418D] and for our remembrance. Indeed, the overturning of these writings is found in the very Scriptures that the teachers of innovation produce as testimony.

For Saint Epiphanius lived in the time of Theodosius and Arcadius; thus approximately four hundred years extend from his time to the present heresy. None of the Christians accepted books against images except the advocates of this present false innovation. If they were not received in the Church for so many years, neither should they be received now, since they were never formerly received.

When we took into our hands the letter that some of them produce, falsely superscribed as belonging to the same holy Epiphanius, bishop of the island of Cyprus, and read it carefully rather than cursorily, we found [Col. 0419A] at the end of the letter the following statement:

> “Although I have often spoken with my fellow ministers so that the images might be removed, I was not accepted by them, nor did they even endure to hear my voice for a little while.”

Let us consider, then, who were the illustrious teachers in the Church and the incorruptible defenses of the Church in the time of our aforementioned Father Epiphanius: Basil the Great, great in deed and word; Gregory, surnamed the Theologian; Gregory, bishop of the city of the Nyssans, called by all the Father of Fathers; and John, from whose tongue a voice sweeter than honey flowed, for which he received the surname “Golden Mouth.” In addition, there were Ambrose, Amphilochius, and Cyril of Jerusalem.

If the person who wrote this exposition of sayings against venerable images says that he was not accepted by the holy Fathers who were then still alive, how could we, who have reached the end of the ages and are deficient in knowledge and speech—for we are not even worthy to be called their disciples—receive against the Church false statements that those holy Fathers themselves did not accept? [Col. 0419B]

Far be such a wicked and reckless exposition. Those who attempted this against the Church lacked right speech [or: “right reasoning”]. Let the Apostle’s saying be present among us who love Christ: “Let us hold fast to the traditions that we have received,” and let us avoid profane novelties of speech, knowing these things to be lies (II Thess. II; II Tim. III; III Tim. III).

For the books of our holy Father Epiphanius—whether the work called the *Ancoratus* or his other writings—are famous throughout the entire world; their sound has been widely disseminated and they have been spread through almost [Col. 0419C] the whole Church. But of these little arguments that murmur against venerable images, no more than two or three books are found throughout the world, unless perhaps they have been newly written. If they were known in the Catholic Church, just as the work called the *Ancoratus* of Saint Epiphanius has been spread throughout all the churches, so these too would have been disseminated.

But, as foreign, alien, and falsified writings, they have not yet been received in the Catholic Church, nor have they appeared there. Therefore they should not be received now, so that the peace of God and the ancient tradition may remain in all the churches.

Let not empty talkers utter their tongues in calumny against those who think rightly, claiming that those who receive the ancient legislation of the Catholic Church oppose Saint Epiphanius. This is entirely untrue. We reject the writing, but we recognize the holy Father as a teacher of the Catholic Church.

For the most holy Fathers who assembled at the Fourth Ecumenical Holy Council of Chalcedon anathematized the letter said to be from Ibas, bishop of Edessa, to Maris the Persian, as agreeing with Nestorius; likewise did the Fathers of the Fifth Council. But they did not anathematize Ibas himself. For it did not appear that the letter truly belonged to Ibas. Hence, in the anathemas, they did not subject Ibas to anathema, but the letter that was said to be his; it was called his, although it was not. [Col. 0419D]

So too these writings of false assertion, which are directed against venerable images, are said by some to belong to Saint Epiphanius, but in no way do they belong to him, as has been demonstrated.

Indeed, his disciples dedicated a church on the island of Cyprus, naming it after that same Father; and together with many other titular paintings they placed his image in the church. If he had abhorred the venerable appearance of images in this way, how would his disciples have depicted him in an image?

Judge, all of you who hear, and separate truth from falsehood. These are not the Father’s writings, but certain Manichaean works; let us flee from them as full of the gall of bitterness. For those men themselves, the introducers of confusion, did not accept this representation, since they did not truly dogmatize that the Word of God had become human in the flesh, but rather through fantasy and conjecture. Therefore, having themselves suffered from fantasy and misunderstanding one thing for another, they bring forward the following: [Col. 0420A]

Gregory the bishop read:

[Col. 0420B]

> “Likewise Gregory the God-speaking says in his poems: ‘It is an insult to place faith in colors and not in the heart. For what is in colors is easily dissolved; but what is in the depth of the mind is dear to me.’”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Once again understanding perversely, they bring forward another saying of Gregory the Theologian, which the Father actually expressed as follows:

> “It is an insult to place faith in colors and not in hearts:
>
> “for the colors, being fluid, are washed away; but depth is pleasing to me.”

But these false speakers give it this form:

> “It is an insult to place faith in colors and not in the heart. For what is in colors is easily dissolved; but what is in the depth of the mind is dear to me.” [Col. 0420C]

They have stopped their ears and closed their eyes, and have refused to understand rightly—those who have despised the traditions of the Church. For “hearing, they heard and did not understand; and seeing, they saw and did not know.” Their heart has been blinded, and they have twisted the teachings of the Fathers [Greek addition: “and traditions”] according to their own desires.

For Saint Gregory the God-speaking, in his metrical writings, when composing the very sentiment that they have quoted, introduces a moral discourse shaping our life, so that we withdraw from temporal and worldly affairs and carnal pleasures [Col. 0420D], and pursue the spiritual life that leads to heavenly things. He teaches us not to trust this world or temporal things that do not remain or endure—things that he called “colors”—but rather to cling to spiritual and true realities, which possess firmness in the heart and remain forever.

For our age is fleeting, and the present life is a sojourn. Just as color and ink are quickly washed away, even if they are prepared by a painter [or: “even if it is transformed by a painter”], so in this world, as he himself says, the course of our affairs sometimes proceeds in one way and sometimes in another [Greek: “at one time in one way, at another in another”], within a single day; and sometimes even an hour brings changes. [Col. 0421A]

For everything human is swept away like a shadow, and a bubble formed from rainwater quickly vanishes; so too does every exaltation of human power perish. “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL).

The offering of spiritual works, however, is immovable, and in things that endure it possesses its recompense [or: “its change in return”]. If that saying had been spoken against images, he would certainly have said: “It is an insult to place faith in colors and not in God.” But he said, “and not in hearts”—that is, let us perform firm and stable works for the kingdom of heaven, not for this world, whose things, as fluid and quickly changed, possess no reliability.

Again, allegorizing badly and gathering everything according to their own sense, they bring forward sayings of the great bishops Basil and John as testimony, asserting:

Gregory the bishop read:

[Col. 0421B]

> “John Chrysostom teaches as follows: ‘Through the writings of the saints we enjoy their presence, possessing not their bodies but images of their souls. For the things said by them are images of their souls.’
>
> “Saint Basil says that meditation upon the divinely inspired Scriptures is the greatest means of discovering benefit [Greek: “it hinders”] (Letter 1 to Saint Gregory on the Solitary Life). For in them are found reminders of deeds, and the lives of blessed men are transmitted in writing, like living images of the conduct that is in God, set forth for imitation through works according to God.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

[Col. 0421C]

No one who thinks rightly has understood or will understand these expositions as an overthrow of venerable images. For it is evident to all that, when we hear of the courage of the saints and their perseverance, we bless the steadfastness and strength of their souls; and when we recite the divine Scriptures, reread the Lives of holy men, and gaze upon painted images, we recall their deeds and works according to God.

What speech represents through hearing, a silent painting displays through imitation, as the great Basil says. John Chrysostom also asserts this in his homily (on the Forty Martyrs). He says that the Old and New Testaments have one lawgiver, and, in a discourse on the priestly vestment whose beginning is, “The prophets indeed proclaim the Gospel of Christ’s kingdom,” he says later: [Col. 0421D]

> “I too have loved a painting poured in wax, for the sake of piety. For I saw an angel driving away the ranks of barbarians in an image; I saw the tribes of barbarians trampled underfoot, and David saying the truth: ‘Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing’” (Ps. LXXII).

It has therefore been demonstrated that they, having been made outsiders to the divine choir, have overturned what was rightly set forth by the holy Fathers.

Yet they remain held by wickedness, and they also bring forward, for the overthrow of painted images, the things that our holy Father Athanasius said against idols, saying:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Finally, Athanasius, the light of Alexandria, also says [Col. 0422A] (Saint Athanasius, *Oration Against the Gentiles*): ‘How could we not pity those who worship creatures? For those who see pray to those who do not see, and those who hear to those who do not hear; for a creature will never be saved by a creature.’”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Ah, what madness! Devising a certain empty path of blasphemy, they have been cast away from the truth. Although that excellent Father published these words against idols, they accuse Christians, after the recognition of the truth, sincere confession, and divine regeneration, of serving creatures apart from the one God who is above all, and they declare that Christians practice idolatry.

Spare your people, Lord, and do not allow any of these men to be led astray by blasphemy. For all of us who are called by your name confess that you redeemed us alike from the deception and error of idols. After coming to know you, we who have been deemed worthy of divine regeneration have in no way turned aside to offer your divine worship to any creature beneath heaven. Rather, we sing to you alone, our Redeemer: “Lord, besides you we know no other; we call upon your name.” [Col. 0422B]

You yourself are witness, as are the armies of the holy angels and the most sacred assembly of apostles, prophets, martyrs, and distinguished Fathers. For the remembrance of our whole understanding and for your glory, so that we may be lifted up to your greatness, we possess the figure of the divine cross, the Gospel narrative, painted images, and many other sacred vessels. We salute these because they are made and established in your name.

But, having acquired treasures, they have pursued vanity with a lying tongue [Greek: “those who gathered treasures by means of the tongue”]. Therefore all their chatter proceeds—or perishes [variant: “perishes”]. For just as darkness is driven away when light shines, so, when truth appeared, the falsehood of their tongue was cut down by the sword of the Spirit.

But, retaining certain remnants of what has been cut away, they bring them forward, saying:

Gregory the bishop read:

> “Likewise Amphilochius of Iconium says: ‘For we are not concerned to represent the bodily persons of the saints on panels through colors, since we have no need of these things; rather, we should imitate their way of life through their virtues.’”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

[Col. 0422D]

Therefore it is characteristic of heretics to produce testimonies cut off from their context. For if anyone examines them carefully, he will in no way find the Father’s meaning forbidding the making of venerable images. Rather, praising courage and the steadfastness of the saints’ affection, and setting before us the result of their virtues, the Father spoke these words in order to raise us to imitate their way of life.

For we do not praise or depict them because of carnal affection, but because we wish to possess their virtue by imitation. We describe their lives in books, and we depict them in image-writing, although they have less need of being praised by us historically [Col. 0423A] or of having their features represented in an image; we do this, as was said above, for our own benefit. For it is not only the sufferings of the saints that instruct us toward our salvation, but also the written account of their sufferings when displayed through pictorial representation, as well as their annual commemoration.

The entire structure of the discourse commends this meaning, and what the Father said is in no way directed toward the overthrow of venerable images. Nor does he make any reproach against them. For even when he says, “It is not our concern to represent their bodily persons in panels by means of colors,” he said this with reference to the pursuit of virtue; for he immediately adds, “but to imitate their way of life through virtue.” Indeed, it is our concern to choose the virtues of good men, to imitate their deeds, [Col. 0423B] and to emulate their manner of life.

Moreover, it is not praiseworthy continually to dedicate temples to such persons, or to raise them up in an image, while despising their virtue. No one would plainly praise a person who disregarded the virtues of the saints, yet day after day praised—or, according to another reading, spoke of—their images, or erected many temples, or prepared sacred vessels, while failing to adorn his own temple with godlike virtues.

For God says through the prophet Isaiah to those who behaved in this way: “If you offer me fine flour, it is in vain; incense is an abomination to me. And when you stretch out your hands toward me, I will turn my eyes away from you; and if you multiply your supplication, I will not hear you. But what will you do? Wash, become clean; remove the evils from your souls before my eyes; cease from your evils, [Col. 0423C] learn to do good; seek judgment, rescue the oppressed, judge the orphan, justify the widow” (Isaiah 1, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, when we have corrected these things, then what we offer will also be acceptable to God, whether they are holy temples, sacred vessels, or venerable images. Thus it is fitting, in memory of the saints, not to imitate their virtues insofar as this is possible—or, according to the Greek, “to love and imitate” them. For the praise of martyrs is an exhortation to those assembled toward virtue, as the great Basil says in his moral discourses (On the Forty Martyrs).

Along with these things, as has been said, it is also worthy of praise to erect temples, form images, and offer sacred vessels to God. We must do these things [Col. 0423D] and not omit the others, as the true word teaches us. For no one can acquire virtue unless he becomes accustomed to dwelling in the courts of the Lord, hears the divine words through reading, and is led through sight to an understanding both of the Gospel narratives and teachings and of the accounts and contests of the martyrs.

At every time, in every place, moment, and hour, it is entirely necessary to devote oneself to the virtues, because it is necessary always and continually to live amid the sufferings of Christ and to carry his mortification about in our body. It is beneficial to do this diligently, for it is the reconciliation with the kingdom of heaven.

But to draw many crosses in a single little house while despising Christ’s commandments and the imitation [Col. 0424A] of his sufferings is utter foolishness. For faith without works is dead (James 2). The Lord says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7).

Moreover, continuing with the points already proposed, we shall provide another confirmation of what has been said. It is customary for our holy Fathers, who have explained God’s saving will to us, to teach us at length the words of the commandments and to direct their hearers toward the commandment that is their particular concern, proclaiming it to be exalted and greater, so that, possessing it as a secure anchor, we may not be negligent regarding the other commandments.

Avoiding prolixity, therefore, and passing over many things in silence, let us bring forward Asterius of Amasea. [Col. 0424B] For when composing a discourse on Lazarus and the rich man, explaining at length a certain statement about feeding the poor [a more fully elaborated exposition of a saying about feeding the poor], and speaking against the rich, he admonishes the rich to produce the fruits of almsgiving and not to be splendidly or conspicuously clothed in soft garments. He introduces a certain moral exhortation to some more religious people who sought wealth in the religious life [the wealth of the more religious life], saying:

“Do not paint Christ in garments; rather, distribute the cost of these things to the poor.”

Then, wishing to cut away the desire for wealth, he adds:

“For one humiliation in taking flesh is enough for him”; that is, it does not please Christ our God that the mysteries of his dispensation should be displayed through worldly ostentation and greed. Nor is it pious [Col. 0424C] or acceptable in his sight, under the pretext of commemorating the Gospel, to hoard material wealth in order to devise excuses for sins, while despising the poor who lack bread and are deprived of clothing and coverings. This belongs to greed, not to piety.

For just as there is no communion of light with darkness, nor any participation of righteousness with iniquity, so the desire for wealth and the wearing of soft garments have no connection with the Gospel form and narrative. The latter fully teaches the account of the dispensation and leads to salvation; the former is denounced as wretched and subject to punishment, as James, the Lord’s brother, says: “Weep, you rich, howling over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted, and [Col. 0424D] your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you” (James 5).

Therefore, as has been said, everything done in the world on account of greed will pass away. With modest expenditure we can obtain food, clothing, and coverings, and be content with these. For whatever is acquired not out of necessity but for display bears the accusation of depravity, as the divine Basil says.

Let us therefore be content with what we need, and from what we have let us give sufficiently to the poor and stretch out our hand to them, so that we may hear the Lord’s voice saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5); and: “As long as you did it to one of these, [Col. 0425A] the least of my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25).

And since we have mentioned Asterius, let us use his words to demonstrate that the tradition of venerable images is an ancient ordinance of the Catholic Church. For when he contemplated an image of the passion of the martyr Euphemia, he used the following praises:

“There was a certain woman, a holy virgin, who vowed undefiled chastity to God; they called her Euphemia. When a tyrant once persecuted the pious, she readily chose the peril of death. Her fellow citizens and companions in the religion for which she also died, admiring the holy virgin according to the law of gratitude, dedicated a tomb to her beside the sanctuary, placed a chest there, celebrated honors for her, and annually kept a festive and solemn day.

“Finally, the consecrated defenders of the divine [Col. 0425B] mysteries continually honor her memory in their discourses and carefully instruct the people present concerning the manner in which she completed the contest of perseverance. But the painter, acting piously, also represented by his art, according to his ability, her entire story on a linen cloth and placed an inscription around the tomb [‘a sacred spectacle’].

“The work of art is arranged as follows. A judge is seated high upon a throne, gazing angrily and furiously at the virgin. For art too grows angry, even in inanimate materials, whenever it wishes. Many attendants and soldiers of the ruler are present, some of them recorders of the proceedings, carrying books and tablets [Greek: styluses]. One of them, holding his hand suspended above the wax, looks toward the woman being judged, bending his whole face sharply as though ordered to speak more easily [or: commanding her to speak more clearly], so that, without straining to hear, [Col. 0425C] he might write down what was false and incomplete [or: blameworthy].

“The virgin stands in a yellow-brown [dark] tunic and garment signifying philosophy; and, as it appeared to the painter, with a refined countenance [beautiful face]; but, as it appears to me, adorned with virtues in her soul. Two soldiers lead her to the ruler: one pulls her forward, while the other presses from behind upon the virgin’s restrained manner, marked by modesty and steadfastness. For she looks down at the ground, blushing at the sight of the men’s faces; yet she stands undaunted, suffering nothing, ready for the contest.

“Meanwhile, while I was praising other painters, I saw the work depicting that Colchian woman who, about to bring the sword against her children, divided her face between pity and fury: with one eye she showed anger, while the other [Col. 0425D] revealed the mother sparing them and recoiling in horror. Now I have transferred my wonder from that subject to this painting, and I greatly admire the artist, because he has mingled the colors more skillfully, tempering modesty and courage together—emotions that oppose one another.

“As the representation advanced, certain executioners, naked except for short tunics, were already pressing on with the task. One seized the virgin’s head and bent it backward, presenting to the other her face prepared for punishment; the latter, standing beside her, was gnashing his teeth. A hammer and a drill appear as instruments of punishment. At this I weep, and emotion interrupts my speech. For the painter rendered the drops of blood so vividly that one might say they were truly [Col. 0426A] flowing from her lips, and one would depart overcome by lamentation.

“Next comes the prison [Greek: the prison]. Again the beautiful virgin appears in yellow-brown garments, alone, extending her hands toward heaven and calling upon God as her protector in her sufferings. As she prays, a sign appears above her head, which is the law for Christians to worship and to inscribe. I believe this to be an indication of the passion that awaited her.

“Immediately afterward, and a little farther on, the painter kindles a fierce fire elsewhere, making the flame with red color shining on either side and forming the body. In the midst of the flame he places her with her hands extended toward heaven, yet with no sign of distress appearing on her face. On the contrary, she is cheerful, because she is proceeding to incorporeal and blessed life.

“Up to this point the painter has restrained his hand, and I my speech. But take care, if you wish to complete the same [Col. 0426B] painting, and consider carefully whether we have not come to the narrative much lower down than we ought.”

Such are the words of Asterius.

But when we examine what is said in divine Scripture, we shall find that he read from it the very things he himself had said. For when God instructed his servant Moses concerning the tabernacle, after commanding that various and diverse works be made in it, he said: “You shall make curtains of twisted fine linen, hyacinth, purple, and twisted scarlet; you shall make cherubim on them, the work of a weaver” (Exodus 26).

This arrangement itself teaches us that things dedicated to God are to be made at great expense, but that this is not so in human affairs. For it was said to the people: “You shall not put on a garment woven of two kinds of material” (Deuteronomy 22).

The divine Apostle most clearly commends the meaning of these things when he commands: “Women should adorn themselves in decent [Col. 0426C] [respectable] apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but with what is fitting for women who profess piety through good works” (1 Timothy 2).

Considering these things, we who offer our service to God alone in spirit and truth both salute and embrace everything that has been offered and dedicated, whether it is the divine type of the precious cross, the Gospel, venerable images, or sacred vessels—as though we hoped to receive sanctification from them—and we offer them worship of honor.

“For worship his footstool,” he says, “for it is holy [Greek: holy]” (Psalm 98).

For this reason Gregory the Theologian also says in his discourse [Col. 0426D] on the birth of Christ: “Honor Bethlehem; worship the manger.”

Therefore, whatever belongs to God is holy through his presence and participation, as all Scripture testifies. And honor appropriate to the holiness of the one who is holy is preserved in no other way than through our worship filled with affection.

But those who still breathe out falsehood, stitching together things alien to the Catholic Church, say:

**Gregory the Bishop read:**

> “Theodotus of Ancyra, the companion in struggle of Cyril, likewise teaches in agreement with these things concerning the same matters:
>
> “‘We have not received that the faces of the saints are to be formed in images made from material colors. Rather, we have learned to imitate their [Col. 0427A] virtues through what is indicated about them in writings, as though these were living images, and by this means we are stirred up to a zeal like theirs. For let those who erect such forms say what benefit they suppose they derive from them, or into what spiritual contemplation they are led by their commemoration. But it is evident that this sort of contrivance is vain and an invention of diabolical argumentation.’”

**Epiphanius the Deacon read:**

If Theodotus were still in this life, when blessed Susanna cried out, saying, “Eternal God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to be” (Daniel 13), you would know, she would say, that these men have falsely brought testimony against me—men who imitate the elders [Col. 0427B] of Babylonian confusion and have become the authors of this novelty.

But wishing to present themselves as competent and illustrious, they utter certain empty things from their throat. Their writing-pen is shown to be deceptive, and they are plainly found to be falsifiers of the truth. For many who subsequently investigated and carefully examined the words of Theodotus concerning the statement in question have never found anything of this kind written anywhere.

Nor did he himself say anything of the sort. It has been clearly demonstrated that this is not a testimony of Theodotus. For it is a speech full of bitterness and irritation, the presumption of an undisciplined tongue and unclean lips, to say that venerable figures of images are an invention of diabolical argumentation. It is truly evident that this invention and fabrication [Col. 0427C] belongs to those who accuse Christians, not to Theodotus.

For if, as they claim, they produced the testimony from him, they ought to have stated explicitly from which of his discourses the testimony was taken. But, knowing it to be false, they left the lie in silence.

Accordingly, when his discourses were gathered together—namely, the six books written to Lausus against Nestorius; his interpretation of the creed of the holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea; his discourse on the birth of the Lord; his discourses on the lights, on Elijah and the widow, on Saint Peter and John, on the lame man who sat at the Beautiful Gate, on those who received the talents, and on the man who had been blind in both eyes—we found nowhere the statement they produced.

Nor, when their pseudo-syllogism [Col. 0427D] was assembled, thrown into confusion, and inscribed in their false discourse, was the testimony taken from the Ancyrene codex. Rather, through a certain lying tablet it spread like something pestilential, which simple people accepted. Sensible people, however, and those who submit to the truth, have always judged it to be a lie.

Moreover, they continue to present as an ally of their pestilential heresy the leader of it, as an assistant of Arius and a collaborator of Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea, and Maris of Chalcedon, who presided over those who resisted the holy synod of Nicaea. Thus they claim:

**Gregory the Bishop read:**

> “Likewise Eusebius Pamphili, when the Augusta Constantia [Col. 0428A] requested that an image of Christ be sent to her by him, says the following:
>
> “‘Since you have written concerning a certain image, as though it were Christ, wishing it to be sent to you by us, what image of Christ do you mean, and of what kind is this image that you mention? Is it the true and unchangeable one, bearing the characteristics of his nature? Or is it the one he assumed for our sake, clothed in the form and appearance of a servant?
>
> “‘But as for the form of God, I do not suppose that you are asking even about that, since you have once for all been taught by him that “no one knows the Father except the Son, nor has anyone ever known the Son worthily except the Father alone who begot him.”
>
> “‘And a little later:
>
> “‘But surely you are asking for an image of the form of a servant, and of the little body with which he was clothed for our sake. Yet we have learned that even this was tempered by the glory of divinity and that what was mortal was swallowed up by life.
>
> “‘And shortly afterward:
>
> “‘Who, then, could have traced with dead and lifeless colors [Col. 0428B] and shadowy drawings the flashing and radiant splendors of such dignity and glory? Indeed, even the eminent disciples could not bear to look upon him on the mountain, but fell on their faces (Matthew 17), confessing that what they had seen was unbearable.
>
> “‘Therefore, if his incarnate form at that time acquired such power by being transformed through the divinity dwelling in it, what must we say when, after being stripped of mortality and cleansed of corruption, he changed the appearance of the servant’s form into the glory of the Lord and God—after his victory over death, after his return to the heavens, after his being seated upon the royal throne [Col. 0428C] at the right hand of the Father, after his repose in the ineffable and indescribable boundaries of the Father, into which, as he ascended and was restored, the heavenly powers praised him together, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm 23).’”

**Epiphanius the Deacon read:**
The prophetic utterance applies to these men, for God complains through the prophet Jeremiah against the peoples of the Jews, saying: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. II). For, abandoning the teachings of the approved Fathers, the leaders of deceptive associations—and imitating those who have been cast out from the Lord’s threshing floor, that is, from the Catholic Church, by the winnowing-fan of divine judgment—they bring them forward as a protection for their heresy.

For which of the faithful of the Church, and of those who have received knowledge of the true doctrines, is unaware that Eusebius Pamphili, handed over to a reprobate mind, was of one opinion and understanding with those who followed Arius’s superstition? In all his historical books he calls the Son and Word of God a creature, a minister, and “second in worship.” If, however, certain people defending him say that he subscribed to the synod’s decision, let us grant that it was so. But he honored the truth with his lips, while his heart was far from it, as all his writings and letters demonstrate. Although at different times and for different reasons he is shown to have been sprinkled and changed in different ways [by mixing himself in and changing himself], sometimes praising those who share Arius’s views, and sometimes pretending to the truth, he is shown—according to James, the brother of the Lord (Jas. I)—to be a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways, and one who should not think that he will receive anything from the Lord.

For if he had believed with his heart unto righteousness and confessed with his mouth unto salvation (Rom. X) the true word, he would certainly have asked pardon for his writings, correcting them, and would surely have made a reasoned defense [defense] concerning his letters. But he never did this in any way; for he remained like an Ethiopian, whose skin had not been changed.

Finally, when he was interpreting, “I said to the Lord, You are my God” (Ps. XV), going beyond the truthful sense he says as follows: “By the laws of nature, every father of a son is certainly his lord; and therefore God himself who begot the only-begotten Son of God is at once God, Lord, and Father of him.”

Likewise, in the letter sent to Saint Alexander, the teacher of the great Athanasius, whose beginning is, “With how great solicitude, or with how great care, these letters have come” [“with how great solicitude, or with how great care, I have come to these letters”], he blasphemes more explicitly, saying the following about Arius and his followers:

“Your letters slander them, as though they said that the Son was made from things that did not exist, like one among all things. But they produced the letter that they had written to you, in which, setting out their faith, they confessed these things in the very words: namely, that the God of the Law and the Prophets and of the New Testament begot the only-begotten Son before the eternal ages, through whom he also made all things and the ages; and that he begot him not by conjecture but in truth, and by his own will brought forth into the nature of things the perfect, unchangeable, and immutable creature of God, but not like one among creatures.

“If, then, their letters speak the truth—and these are certainly also with you—in them they confess that the Son of God, before the eternal ages, through whom he made the ages also, is an unchangeable and perfect creature of God, but not like one among creatures.

“Moreover, your letter slanders them as though they said that the Son was made like one among all things, although they did not say this, but clearly defined that he was not like one among creatures. Consider, therefore, whether this does not immediately again give them an opportunity to move as many as they wish to rebuke and defame them.

“Again, you accused them of saying that the one who is begot the one who was not. I wonder whether anyone could say otherwise. For if there is one who is, then surely everything that is, together with him [after him], was made from him. But if he alone is not the one who is, and the Son also was the one who is, how could the one who is beget him who was? For in that case there would certainly be two who existed [two things that exist].”

This is what Eusebius wrote to the memorable Alexander. But other letters of his to the same holy man are also circulated, in which various blasphemies are found, defending those who support Arius.

Likewise, when he sent a letter to Euphrasius, the bishop, he blasphemes more explicitly. The beginning of that letter is: “To my lord I confess thanks in all things”; and elsewhere he says:

“We do not confess that the Son was together with the Father. Nevertheless, the Son of God himself, who knows all things more clearly, knowing himself to be other than the Father and lesser and inferior, teaches us this very day also, saying: ‘The Father who sent me is greater than I’” (John XIV).

And elsewhere: “For the Son himself is indeed God, but not the true God.”

From these writings, therefore, it is shown that he proclaims the doctrines of Arius and his associates. Along with this apostate heresy of his, the inventors of the Arian madness also teach one nature in the union that is according to subsistence, and proclaim that our Lord assumed flesh without a soul in his saving dispensation. They say that the divinity fulfilled the functions and movements of the soul, so that, as Gregory the Theologian says (Ep. 1 to Cledonius), they may ascribe suffering to the divinity. Those who apply suffering to the divinity are plainly Theopaschites; and those who share in this heresy do not admit images, just as neither do the impious Severus, Peter the Fuller, and Philoxenus of Hierapolis, nor the entire many-headed [multicephalous] and headless hydra surrounding them.

Since Eusebius also belonged to this faction, as has been demonstrated both from his letters and from his written histories, he rejects the image of Christ as a Theopaschite [Deopaschite]. For this reason he writes to Constantia, the wife of Licinius, that an image would never be found among his possessions [Note: See Photius, Letter 144, concerning Eusebius and images]. For in the same letter he says that Christ’s incarnate form was changed into the nature of his divinity.

But none of our holy Fathers thought or taught in this way; for the truth is not so. Let us therefore hear what Athanasius, the deposer of the Arian madness, says in his dogmatic letter, which he wrote to Eupsychius, presbyter of Caesarea; and likewise what Cyril says in his first letter to Successus, bishop of Diocaesarea, and in the discourse published against the commixtionists. For both, having a heavenly as well as an earthly way of life and inspired by one Spirit, speak in harmony with one another.

Athanasius, in the aforesaid letter to Eupsychius, whose beginning is, “In those things in which you were accustomed [you thought us accustomed], most reverend sir,” says the following:

“The fleece of sheep is common, and in the summer heat wool is offered for the common use of all. But when dye is taken from the sea, it is called purple and deserves that name. Yet when it is specially reserved for kings alone, it both is wool and is not. In nature it is what it formerly was; but in use it is no longer so, for what was common has withdrawn because of the dignity of the user.

“So also the flesh, assumed from the common nature, because it became the garment of the King, which previously it had not been, deserved the same glory as the one who used it [Greek adds: ‘and as the one who used it’]. Thus he is also called the Lord of glory” [Note: The same words are found in the Joly manuscript: “It deserved the same glory as the one who is recognized to have used it, although by nature it had not previously been made the garment of the King; thus he is called the Lord of glory.”]

Perhaps this is also understood according to the fact that he is human, with human nature admitting suffering and the injury passing over to him who used flesh as a garment. For just as one who tears the purple is punished as though he had plotted against the king himself, because the king transferred the suffering of the purple to himself, although he himself suffered no harm, so the suffering of the flesh is said to have come upon the Word through insult, while the impassibility of God the Word remained.

Therefore Paul teaches that the Lord Christ, according to the fact that he is human, is the Son of God. Before him, the archangel Gabriel, announcing the wondrous birth to Mary, said: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and they will call him Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke I).

Thus Jesus is called the Son of God, not because the flesh was converted into the divine nature, but because, through the union effected with God the Word, it assumed the dignity of sharing the same name [that is, of being called by the same name].

Cyril likewise says in the aforesaid letter to Successus, whose beginning is: “Having read the memorandum sent by your Holiness.” He says the following:

“After the resurrection, the body that suffered no longer had weaknesses in itself. For we do not say that it was any longer capable of hunger, fatigue, or anything of this kind, but that it was now incorruptible; and not only this, but also life-giving, for it is the body of Life, that is, of the Only-Begotten.

“It was glorified with a glory worthy of God, and it is understood to be God’s body. For this reason, even if someone calls it divine, just as what belongs to a human being is called human, he will not depart from appropriate reasoning. Hence I think that the most wise Paul also says: ‘Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer so’ (2 Cor. V).

“For since, as I said, it is God’s own body, it transcends all things that are human. But a body that is from the earth cannot undergo a change into the nature of divinity; for this is impossible. For we do not proclaim the divinity to have been made, nor that it assumed into itself something not proper to its own nature. It is equally perverse to say that the body was changed into the nature of divinity and to say that the Word was changed into the nature of flesh. For just as the latter is impossible—for it is unalterable and immutable—so is the former.

“For no creature can be transferred into the substance, that is, the nature, of divinity; flesh too is a creature. Therefore the body of Christ is indeed divine, because it is God’s body: it is radiant with ineffable glory, incorruptible, holy, and life-giving. But that it was converted into the nature of divinity, none of the holy Fathers either thought or said. Thus we too maintain this.”

Likewise, in the discourse that he published against the commixtionists, whose beginning is: “A blessed discourse on the doctrines of truth has just been prepared for us” [Greek: “has been elaborated”], he says:

“Therefore, if, after his assumed flesh [Greek: ‘changed flesh’], he ceased to be the Son of Man by being changed into the nature of divinity, it will be clear to everyone that we too have abandoned the glory of adoption as sons, as though we no longer had the Firstborn among many brothers, when he was made like us.”

And shortly afterward he says:

“Do you suppose that we have unexpectedly fallen away from the glory granted to us? By no means. For we will not, led astray into a reprobate mind by the profanities and foolish inventions of certain people, think beyond what we ought to think. Rather, receiving the sacred and divinely inspired Scripture as the rule of the right and straight faith, we confess that, having become our Firstborn, the Only-Begotten Word of God did not cease to be and to be called both God and the true Son of Man.

“Nor is he seen to have transformed into the nature of divinity the flesh that he united to himself unchangeably and without confusion. Rather, he is rightly acknowledged to have illumined it with his own glory and fittingly filled it with God-worthy dignities. Thus he will be manifested throughout the ages to those who are upon the whole earth, coming from heaven.

“Therefore, when, with the flesh, after the mystery of the dispensation had been fully accomplished, he returned to heaven, those who witnessed this were immediately terrified. For a cloud received him, according to what is written. Then one of the holy angels called out to those who wondered: ‘Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven’ (Acts I).

“Did those to whom our discourse is addressed therefore see the Word returning to the Father without flesh—that is, stripped of our likeness and no longer existing in a tangible and visible body—or rather as joined to an intangible and invisible nature? In the end, who would dare to say this? But if he will come in the same way as he ascended, how can it not truly be said that he will come again embodied, and that the Word will not come naked and without flesh?”

And shortly afterward he says:

“Understand, therefore, that when he foretold the descent from heaven that would occur in the last times, and what and of what kind it would be, he was transfigured; and the form of the transfiguration also took place, as the distinguished evangelist says (Matt. XVII), not according to the laying aside of his appearance—that is, the abandonment of his human form—but rather according to glory alone. For, he says, ‘his face shone.’ Thus he gave it a brightness resembling the radiance of the sun.”

And shortly afterward:

“The most wise Paul also wrote concerning Christ that he ‘will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory’ (Phil. III).

“What, then, will those who say that his flesh was changed into the nature of the Word assert concerning this? Will the bodies of the saints also be transferred by conversion into the nature of divinity, so that they may be conformed to the body of his glory? And surely how could this assertion not be cold, filled with the utmost lack of discipline? For if the flesh was entirely converted, as they claim, into the nature of divinity, what body will God the Word, being incorporeal, use? For divinity is an incorporeal and truly singular substance; and it is true that ‘no one has ever seen God’ (John I).”

Then, proceeding more explicitly as though addressing Eusebius himself, the same distinguished Father says in the same discourse:

“Another discourse is also brought forward by them, as they say, concerning these matters. For the distinguished Paul is found to have written: ‘Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer so’ (2 Cor. V). Therefore, they say, if he is not known according to the flesh, he must necessarily be said to have changed the flesh into the nature of his Word, so that he might be recognized as God.

“Someone, I think, might answer this as follows. Since he immediately also says concerning us: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; but you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit’ (Rom. VIII), does he know us as naked of flesh and blood? Do you suppose that he addresses incorporeal spirits in this way, while he is not even ashamed to understand or assert this? Thus, in us he calls the flesh the impudent passions that are not without complaint.

“Finally, since Christ our Savior is most chaste and does not know how to sin—for he committed no sin—the phrase ‘according to the flesh’ must clearly be understood in another way. For he is not, nor will he be, any longer in carnal weaknesses.”

We therefore know clearly from the Fathers who speak by divine inspiration that the authors of this contention did not draw from the fountains of Israel, so that it might become for them eternal life, but brought themselves drink from malignant and barren fountains. Following what was alien, they were led into precipices and chasms.

It would have been proper for them, if they were children of the Church, to cite Basil the Great, who says (On the Holy Spirit, to Amphilochius 18): “The honor of the image passes to the prototype”; and Gregory of Nyssa, who declares: “I saw the image of the passion, and I passed by the sight not without sadness, since art more clearly set the history before my eyes”; and John, who says that he loves a painting covered with wax, filled with piety; as well as those who speak and teach together with these.

But they do not yet correct their perverse problems. By their additions they make evil abound, and they continue to assert:

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“Thus, gathering from many sources a few of these scriptural and patristic testimonies, we have set them down in the present definition of ours, so that it might not be extended at length, although there are also many others that we deliberately omit because of their infinite number. Therefore, firmly built upon these divinely inspired and blessed Scriptures and Fathers, and placing our feet upon the rock of divine service, which is in the Spirit, in the name of the holy, supersubstantial, and life-originating Trinity, all of us who are surrounded by the dignity of the priesthood, having become of one mind, define with one voice that every image made from different materials and colors by the evil art of painters is to be rejected, alien, and abominable in the Christian Church.”

**Epiphanius the deacon read.**

These noisy advocates of this novelty, who in no way endured to bow their necks to ecclesiastical tradition, but were blinded in their choice of what was fitting, in their reception of truth, and in their judgment of pious tradition as credible, did not allow themselves to drink from the torrent of pleasure, so that there might be in them “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV). Rather, watered from cracked cisterns, they produced a foul plant bearing the fruit of gall and bitterness. Adding lie upon lie, they brought forward the following:

“There are also many other scriptural testimonies that we have deliberately omitted.”

As has now been shown, therefore, those who seek to establish their own righteousness misunderstood perversely all the testimonies of the approved Fathers that they produced. But none of those belonging to the adversaries is of the divine Spirit. Hence blessed David addresses them in a melody sung in the Spirit:

“Each person has spoken vainly to his neighbor; with deceitful lips and with a deceitful heart they have spoken evil” (Ps. XI).

And again Isaiah speaks boldly, saying:

“The counsel of the wicked counsels iniquity; for they do not know how to understand, because they are darkened from seeing with their eyes” (Isa. XLIV).

For abandoning sound definitions and laws, they feign piety in words and attempt to utter certain pious statements, so that, because of the good sense contained in them, they may not be considered altogether unworthy of belief in the rest, while they say:

“In the name of the holy, supersubstantial, and life-originating Trinity.”

But wishing to act wickedly with regard to the meaning, they pronounce and define from their own understanding, setting forth naked impiety, neither accepting God’s judgment in their minds nor understanding the Lord’s sentence that cries out:

“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be cast into the sea” (Matt. XVIII; Mark IX).

And finally, like certain swine trampling pearls—that is, ecclesiastical traditions—they tumultuously declared that every image made from different materials was to be rejected and abominable in the Christian Church, making a plan that was not through the Lord, and pledges that were not through his Spirit. And like savage wolves they came upon Christ’s flock.

But the clarity of truth and the radiance of light possess immovable confidence. For who does not know that when the image is dishonored, the dishonor is surely referred to the one whose image it is? Truth knows this in this way, and the nature of things teaches it. The divine Fathers also agree with it, especially Saint Basil, who says: “The honor of the image passes to the prototype”; Athanasius, who says: “Whoever worships the image worships the king in it”; and Chrysostom, who says: “Do you not know that when you insult the image of the king, you bring insult upon the dignity of the prototype?”

Those Fathers followed the nature of things; these men, however, rise up both against the Church and against the truth. For their discourse is not only full of blasphemy, but also contains an excess of madness and indiscipline.
