It was therefore proper for them to utter the common voice, in complete agreement with itself, and to strengthen the ancient tradition, carefully acquiring for themselves what the entire multitude of the faithful has held and confessed from the tradition of the Apostles and Fathers, rather than creating a novelty and interrupting the custom that has been piously preserved among us.

For the things handed down in the Catholic Church admit neither addition nor diminution. The greatest punishment overcomes anyone who adds or removes anything: “Cursed is the one who moves the boundaries of his fathers” (Deut. XXVII).

But they had no intention of recognizing the truth. Therefore they will hear those words of Wisdom:

“Whoever gathers treasures with a lying tongue pursues vanity, and will come into the snare of death” (Prov. XXI).

## SIXTH TOME

**Epiphanius the deacon read:**

Would that they had taken to heart the voice that the Lord spoke to the chief of the Apostles, Peter:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI).

But having become alien to this harmony and to this building, they rave in a manner worthy of ridicule while defining the following:

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“No human being is henceforth to dare to pursue such a criminal and impious undertaking. Whoever from now on dares to construct an image, or to worship one, or to set one up in a church or in a private house, or to conceal one—if he is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, let him be deposed; but if he is a monk or layman, let him be anathematized and be liable to the imperial laws, as one opposed to the commandments of God and an enemy of the doctrines of the Fathers.”

**Epiphanius the deacon read:**

Accusing the whole Church, and not at all content with this, nor attaining any satiety of impiety, they continue to define, without law or right, that an image must not be made. But who, I ask, among those who live and think piously would obey them?

The display of venerable images in the churches has been so firmly established that, from the time the Gospel was proclaimed until now, they have remained manifest in the churches; and everything that excels in antiquity is worthy of reverence.

For what else does the divine Apostle command when writing to the Corinthians [Thessalonians]?

“Hold fast the traditions that you received” (2 Thess. II).

And again, when instructing Timothy and Titus to avoid profane novelties of words (1 Tim. VI; 2 Tim. II; Titus III)?

Therefore all Christians, as those born within the holy Catholic Church, hold the traditions that we have received, and are established in them, and avoid novelties of words, following the divine Apostle. Whatever our distinguished Fathers in each generation judged should be built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, we receive; but whatever is otherwise, we curse as hostile and opposed—namely, everything vainly drawn from the worst and most impious heresies. Together with these, we curse and abominate the newly fabricated babbling that accuses Christians, since it is hateful to God.

Moreover, their impiety having become extensive, they not only possessed a sharp tongue for a certain fraud [for sinning through speech], but also taught the hand of rulers to slander and strike, saying:

“Let the one who has not obeyed them be held liable to the imperial laws.”

From this utterance, many and varied evils were poured throughout the world. Cruelty without end became the pursuit of the rulers, their leaders, and alien bishops [Greek: “the leaders and the adversary bishops themselves”].

What tongue could recount these things with tragic lamentation? Where, or how, should I begin to relate the disturbances, fears, persecutions, and imprisonments of monks throughout the cities; their beatings and chains for many years; their feet bound in fetters; the destruction of sacred vessels; the burning of books; the profanation of holy temples; the defiled transfer of venerable monasteries into secular repositories?

Thus the reverend men who inhabited them, after the plundering of their possessions, went to barbarian regions and, in apostolic fashion, chose the better life, preferring to live among foreign peoples rather than to lead an obscene life with their fellow citizens, obeying the divine Apostle who commands us not even to eat with such people (1 Cor. V).

And what is most atrocious of all is that even to the present the impiety of profaning venerable monasteries remains among certain transgressors. In place of sacred hymns and the voice of rejoicing that resound in the tents of the righteous, there are harlot songs and satanic melodies; and in place of frequent genuflections, dancing movements [inflexions].

Along with these came dangers, tumult, upheaval, blows, punishments, the tearing out of eyes, the cutting off of noses, the mutilation of tongues, shameful flights—that is, the exiles of reverend men, since they were scattered throughout the whole world—the burning of holy faces, the fires of barbarians, the wicked and violent marriage of virgins after their covenant had been promised to Christ; and, more savage than all these things, murders.

These are the fruits of those who obstinately contend against the truth. This is manifest madness and not true judgment—things that God saw—and from all these continuous evils he delivered his Church. And glory be to him. Amen.

Despised because of their wicked counsel, they are refuted by the truth while they say as follows:

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“We also define this: no one who presides over the Church of God or over a venerable house may dare, under the pretext of removing such an error of images, to lay his hands upon the holy vessels dedicated to God in order to transfer them to images [Greek: ‘to other uses, because they are painted with images’].”

**Epiphanius the deacon read:**

These are the words vomited forth by mouths that do not fear the Lord. For who among those whose minds are pierced by divine fear would presume, however unlearned and undisciplined he might be, to call the things dedicated to God by the name of idols?

Unless perhaps he had forgotten the great and saving mystery that God the Word, coming in the flesh, accomplished among us, rescuing us from the error of idols. For worshipers of God customarily call the idols of the gentiles “images.”

Truly these words belong to men who draw babblings from the earth and bring forth utterances from their bellies, who, conceiving excremental satieties and emitting the foul vapors of their minds, have become mad and possessed by frenzy.

Hence they also add:

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“Nor may they be transferred into vestments, other veils, or anything else consecrated for sacred ministry, lest uselessness [Greek: ‘something unprofitable’] be produced in them.”

**Epiphanius the deacon read:**

They disparaged and deliberated that the Church wrongly receives pictorial images of the saints, calling them “foul things,” “idols,” and “images.” Now, as though they had forgotten their wicked sentence, they judge that these things should remain in the Church as consecrated to God.

But if they are consecrated to God, how are they foul things and inventions of the devil? Yet it is clear that this is the judgment of Caiaphas (John XI). For he killed Christ out of malice, but in ignorance he spoke the truth, confessing him to be the Savior of the human race.

So these men, having become like him, out of malice call the representation of images an error, idols, foul things, and an invention of diabolical reasoning. But, unwillingly and convicted by the truth, they are forced to confess these things as sacred and dedicated to God, and they fall into the snares of their own contentions.

Therefore, mocking those who follow them, they address them as follows:

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“But if anyone, having received power from God, wishes to transfer the same vessels or hangings, he must not dare to do so without the counsel and knowledge of the most holy and most blessed universal patriarch, and without the command of our most pious and Christ-loving emperors, lest on this pretext the devil humble the Churches of God. Nor may any ruler, or any of those subject to them—that is, anyone of the lay order—on such a pretext lay a hand upon the divine temples and seize these things, as such acts have already been committed by certain people who walked disorderly.”

**Epiphanius the deacon read:**

Who would not ridicule, or rather lament, this legislation? Because of these empty words, many rashly presumed to lay their heavy [Greek: “Briarean”] hands upon the sacred vessels, taking from the very authors their excuses—for malice slips easily.

Foreseeing that the “most blessed” men, as they call them—but, as the truth has it, alien bishops—would plunder the gold and silver of the sacred memorials and the pictures made in mosaics, they themselves acted in this way [Greek: “they themselves also acted in this way”], transferring these things into public houses, baths, and theaters. Thus the sacred things were once polluted according to their judgment, and they boast, saying:

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“Since these things have been well established and strengthened by divine grace, we have judged it right to set forth the capitular definitions in this Catholic and God-pleasing writing of ours. For we too think that we speak apostolically (1 Cor. VII), and we believe that we have the Spirit of Christ. Just as our predecessors who believed in him spoke while defining certain matters synodically, so we too believe in him through whom we speak [and for this reason also speak]. After certain definitions that were commanded, and after the ancestral definitions that will be set forth [Greek: ‘will be prefaced’], we consequently and harmoniously define what seems right to us.”

**Epiphanius the deacon read:**

After raving in many and varied ways above, explicitly declaring their perversity and dividing it into many parts, they attempt to make themselves equal to the teachers of the Church. They arrogantly add their wicked definitions to the sacred utterances of those teachers, wishing to mix falsehood with truth and, in a certain way, sweeten their poisonous draughts with honey.

But those who are led by the Spirit of God distinguish what is better from what is worse. Whatever has previously been defined piously as coming from the holy Fathers, they receive; whatever has been said perversely by these men, they strike down in indignation.

For the false-speaking men confess that they know God, but they swerve from the path leading to the royal road, infecting the words of our sincere faith with the poison of malice and keeping the heresiarchs as their allies in ignorance.

Those men too held many opinions consonant with the Catholic Church; nevertheless, because they transgressed in one or two matters, they incurred the punishment of anathema. Those who speak such things have received a portion with them.

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“If anyone does not confess, according to the apostolic and patristic traditions, one Godhead, nature, and substance, one will and operation, one power and dominion, one kingdom and authority in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in three subsistences—that is, glorified persons—let him be anathema.

“If anyone does not confess one of the Holy Trinity, namely the Son, the Word of God the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, begotten before the ages according to his divinity, but in the last days descending from heaven for our salvation, becoming incarnate from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-Virgin, and born from her beyond all human understanding, let him be anathema!

“If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God—for she bodily gave birth to the Word of God who became flesh—let him be anathema!

“If anyone does not confess that the flesh was united according to subsistence to the Word who is from God the Father, and that Christ is one with his flesh, namely, that he himself is both God and man, let him be anathema!

“If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving and the proper flesh of that same Word who is from the Father, but regards it as belonging to someone other than him, joined to him by dignity—that is, as possessing only divine indwelling, and not rather as also life-giving, as we have said, because it became the proper flesh of the Word who is able to give life to all things—let him be anathema!

“If anyone does not confess in the one Christ, our true God, two natures, two natural wills, and two natural operations, communicably, inseparably, unchangeably, indivisibly, and without confusion, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers, let him be anathema!

“If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, with his assumption—that is, with his animated flesh possessing a rational and intellectual soul—sits with God the Father, and that he will come in his paternal glory to judge the living and the dead, not as mere flesh, yet not incorporeal, but in the God-formed body, by means known to him, [Greek: ‘the divine-form body’] by which he may appear to those who pierced him, while remaining God without material bulk, let him be anathema!”

**Epiphanius the deacon and the cubicularius read:**

Up to this point they think correctly, agreeing with the publications of the holy Fathers—or rather, appropriating their doctrines—and they confer glory upon themselves. But in the remaining matters they vomit forth the doctrines of their bitter, venomous tongue, full of viperous and deadly poison.

**Gregory the bishop read:**

“If anyone undertakes to contemplate the divine image of God the Word according to the incarnation through material colors, and does not worship it with his whole heart, with intelligible eyes, seated above the splendor of the sun at the right hand of God in the heights upon the throne of glory, let him be anathema!”

**Epiphanius the deacon read:**
Certain unexpected allegorists are exposed by this fanciful opinion of theirs. For when the Apostle proclaims the Son to be the Character of God and the Father (Heb. 1), on account of the non-dissimilarity and unchangeability [Col. 0439D] of the substance, they perversely understand that Character as another being—namely, the Character in the flesh assumed by God the Word—and belch forth from senseless notions, putting forward some empty assertion:

“If anyone should attempt to contemplate the divine Character of the Word of God according to the incarnation through material colors…”

For we all know, both from the truth itself and from the holy leaders of the Church—namely, the apostles and our distinguished Fathers—that the flesh which he assumed is of one substance, whereas the nature of the Word of God is of another. Indeed, the divine Apostle Paul, who gazed into the mysteries, wishing, as it is said [Gr.: “it was said”], to proclaim the Son, God the Word, homoousion (“consubstantial”) with God the Father, found nothing proper and fitting except [Col. 0440A] to cry out that the Son is the Character of the Father’s substance. But these men, attempting to turn truth into falsehood, introduce insults and battered expressions, fastening them against the venerable images [Cr.: “having been fastened”] out of hatred. Thus they fall into blasphemous notions and, having been handed over to a reprobate mind, still say:

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone should attempt, because the essence and subsistence of the Word of God became incarnate, to circumscribe that uncircumscribed essence and subsistence through material colors in images in human form, and should not rather proclaim that God remains uncircumscribed even after the incarnation, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

[Col. 0440B]

As though they had been incurably weakened concerning the proper ecclesiastical traditions, and possessed a mind corrupted by a pestilential disease, they assert these things and apply the contagion of deception to upright speech. They are deceived in their minds, confusing the uncircumscribed nature of the divine Word with the circumscribed flesh assumed by him; for this is expressly indicated by what they said: “that he remains uncircumscribed even after the incarnation.”

Where, among the vain, did their wise men ever discover this flimsy assertion? For it is full of blasphemy to assert that our Lord Jesus Christ, the true God, is uncircumscribed after the incarnation, [Col. 0440C] especially when he himself says to his disciples: “Lazarus our friend has fallen asleep; and I rejoice for your sake that I was not there” (John 11). Therefore, “I was not there”—is this not proper to circumscription? Indeed it is, and very much so.

But, leaving aside what the Gospel says about him before the Passion, I shall speak of what took place after the resurrection. When he appeared to the women, he was by no means uncircumscribed. To make himself manifest to two disciples is proper to circumscription. To enter while the doors were shut, and to be touched by Thomas—what is this other than circumscription? Likewise, when the disciples were going to Galilee, he was seen and worshiped by them there; this too is the same thing (Luke 24; John 20). And when the disciples saw him ascend into heaven, while an angel stood beside them [Col. 0440D] and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1)—do you suppose these are not acts of circumscription? Indeed they are, very much so.

For thus all our God-bearing Fathers also teach. It is clear to those who think rightly that, insofar as he is God and the Word of God and the Father, he is invisible, uncircumscribed, incomprehensible, and present in every place of his dominion; but insofar as he assumed human nature, he is visible and circumscribed, just as he himself told his disciples that he was not there; and he is comprehensible, as Thomas made certain for us (John 11, 20).

Thus, through their one blasphemy, they join together many evils—those deluded teachers who accuse Christians. For again, making their accusations, they declare: [Col. 0441A]

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone attempts to paint in an image the inseparable union by subsistence of the nature of the Word of God and the flesh—a union made through the completion [or: accomplishment] that has proceeded from both and is without confusion and without separation—calling him Christ (but the name ‘Christ’ signifies God and man), and thereby monstrously fabricating a confusion of the two natures, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

He knows how to attach the abomination of error to upright speech. For they falsely and wickedly assert that the making [Col. 0441B] of images is opposed to the inseparable and unconfused union that exists in Christ through subsistence, and that it brings about a confusion of the two natures. But the truth of God is not bound.

For “Christ” is the name of two natures, namely, the visible and the invisible. Christ himself was seen by human beings through a veil—that is, his flesh. Although the divine nature was concealed, he made it manifest through signs. Therefore the holy Church of God, as it received from the holy Apostles and Fathers, depicts the very form that was seen by human beings, and does not divide Christ according to their deranged accusation.

An image shares with its prototype according to the name alone, and not according to the definition, as we have often already said. For an image also lacks a soul, which cannot be circumscribed [or: depicted], because it is invisible. And if it is impossible to paint the soul, especially [Col. 0441C] since it is created, how much more would anyone sensibly devise an image of the incomprehensible and unsearchable divinity of the Only-Begotten Son, even though such a thought is utterly beyond sense?

Their pain has therefore turned back upon their own heads. For the anathema which they have incurred [Gr.: “spoken foolishly”] remains upon them forever. Again they say:

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone divides the flesh united to the subsistence of the Word of God, considering it pure in his mind, and for this reason attempts to paint it in an image, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Saint Gregory, surnamed the Theologian, says this (Oration [Col. 0441D] 2, On the Son): “When natures are distinct in one’s understanding, the names too are separated at the same time.” Many of the Fathers also used this expression; for it appears so according to the truth.

But these men, deprived both of this understanding and of the definitions of the Fathers, say: “If anyone divides the flesh united to the subsistence of the Word of God in his understanding.” They are therefore found not to agree even here with the exposition of the holy Fathers. Clearly attacking the truth, they address the same words to themselves [Gr.: “the same things”], and falsely accuse the catholic Church of proclaiming things like Nestorius.

Then, making statements consistent with themselves, they add:

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone divides the one Christ into two subsistences, placing the Son of God separately and the Virgin [Col. 0442A] Mary separately, and does not confess that he is one and the same, but confesses that an affective union was made between them; and therefore paints him in an image as though he possessed a private subsistence from the Virgin, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

They go around pronouncing so many things, always repeating the same matters [variant: “pronouncing so many things about the same matters”], that what they assert through their wicked rumor can scarcely be counted. Having adopted the impious opinion of Nestorius, they apply it to the formation of an image, patching together certain unexpected and absurd notions.

Since we have repeatedly destroyed arguments of this kind, we now judge it necessary to consign them to silence. Yet again they belch forth the following:

Gregory the bishop read:

[Col. 0442B]

“If anyone paints in an image the flesh that has been deified through its union with the divine Word, as though separating it from the divinity that assumed and deified it, and thereby making it without God [Gr.: ‘making it not deified at all’], let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Although the catholic Church paints Christ in human form, it does not separate this form from the divinity united to it. Rather, it believes it to be deified and confesses it to be one with God, in accordance with the great Gregory (Oration 2, On Easter) and with the truth—not as those men, uneducated and uncultivated, barbarously said: that by this means the Lord’s flesh is made without God. [Col. 0442C]

For just as someone who paints a human being does not make a human being without a soul, but the person remains with a soul and his image is called an image because it appears similar to him, so we too, when making an image of the Lord, confess the Lord’s flesh to be deified. We know the image to be nothing other than an image indicating the imitation of the prototype. From this it has also received its name, and it shares with the prototype in this respect alone. Therefore it is venerable and holy.

But if the image is of a wicked man or of a demon, it is polluted and defiled, because its prototype too is profane and defiled. Thus, laboring in vain, they gather barrenness in their hands and receive an anathema from the truth—an anathema from which they will not be free when they say such things:

Gregory the bishop read:

[Col. 0442D]

“If anyone attempts, through material colors, to form the Word of God who is in the form of God, who receives the form of a servant in his own subsistence, and who became in every respect like us except for sin, as though he were a mere human being, and to separate him from the inseparable and unchangeable divinity, thereby introducing a quaternity into the holy and life-giving Trinity, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

O their madness and stupidity! They do not shrink from gathering an anathema. But just as worms, wallowing in dung, are nourished by it, so these men, fastened to this expression, do not allow themselves to receive satiety, attempting to curse the sanctified [Col. 0443A] Church of God, although they themselves are most deserving of a curse. For those who bless her, as Scripture says, shall be blessed [variant: “are blessed”], and those who curse her are accursed (Gen. 27).

But when they imagine the Savior Christ to be a mere human being and separate him from the divinity, thereby introducing a quaternity through painting, who, do you suppose, would not laugh at this? Who would not pour out abundant laughter over their foolishness—or rather, mourn their blasphemy?

For the person who does this does not believe in a quaternity on the grounds that Christ is depicted in an image in human form; rather, he confesses that the Word of God truly became incarnate, and not merely in appearance. In the end, Nestorius, who blasphemously dogmatized in Christ two subsistences as though they were two natures, is recognized as having introduced a quaternity. [Col. 0443B] But the holy Church of God, rightly confessing one subsistence of Christ in two natures, has been divinely instructed to form him in an image for the commemoration of his saving dispensation.

Moreover, wishing to show themselves approved, they also assert something true, saying as follows:

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone does not confess that the holy ever-Virgin Mary is properly and truly the Mother of God, higher than every visible and invisible creature, and does not sincerely and faithfully seek her intercessions, as one who has confidence before our God, who was born from her, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

[Col. 0443C]

Once the catholic Church has been established and confirmed in these matters, she has no need to hear anything from those who think otherwise than her tradition in God teaches. For when the Lord was proclaimed by demons, he drove them away; and the divine Apostle Paul and his companions in their pilgrimage, when they received testimony from them that they were men of the Most High God and were proclaiming the way of salvation, expelled them (Acts 16). So too these men, although they pronounce something true, are nevertheless driven away from the holy Church of God.

Again, like dogs returning to their own vomit and pigs washed only to wallow in the mud (2 Pet. 2), they grunt out such things:

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone attempts to give the figures of all the saints [Col. 0443D] in images that are lifeless and deaf, made from material colors and bringing no benefit—for it is a vain invention and a product of diabolical argument—and does not rather depict their virtues within himself through those things indicated about them in the Scriptures as living images, and is not thereby raised up to a zeal like theirs, as our divine Fathers said, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Our divine Fathers neither taught nor proclaimed anything of the kind; these lying speakers have imposed this name upon themselves. Such are their absurdities, since later they call themselves the seventh synod.

And indeed the Wise Man says: [Col. 0444A]

“Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Prov. 27).

But these men, taught and praised by no one, devise praise for themselves and want to be called Rabbi by human beings, eagerly wishing to be Fathers of the catholic Church.

Yet they accuse this Church of abandoning Christ our God and clinging to idolatry, although he says to her through the prophet Isaiah: “I will make you an eternal exaltation, a joy from generation to generation” (Isa. 60, according to the Septuagint). And through Solomon: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4).

Let us therefore examine their foolishness: the very idolatry of which they accuse the Church, they boast of being its teachers. And if they are fathers of idolaters, let them say: Are they teachers of some party within the [Col. 0444B] Church that practices idolatry, or of the whole Church? If of a party, they themselves ought also to have joined the fullness of the Church, to have remained subject to its authority, and to gather from it the fruits of truth [Gr.: “from her”], just as all our distinguished Fathers did, correcting what was incorrect and fitting together what had been torn apart.

But because the catholic Church is adorned by this tradition, they, having been cut off from her, think [Gr.: “appear”] that they should condemn the whole as erroneous. Certainly it is dreadful to say this, and silence is itself condemnation. For the true confession in Christ goes forth against them [Gr.: “For according to them, the true confession concerning Christ perishes”], and destruction has seized the whole world. But away with such things, as words spoken in vain and without cause.

Thus they will be driven from both sides, because the painting of venerable images has been handed down from former years in the catholic [Col. 0444C] Church and represented in venerable temples—a tradition which the holy Fathers both handed down and received, as did the entire Christian community. These men have not merely been deprived of all these things [variant: “drawn away from them”]; what is more savage and terrible is that the cry of their anathema has been multiplied in a Sodomite and Gomorrite fashion (Gen. 19).

For this reason their sin is exceedingly great. Who could endure the madness of this frenzy and the theatrical faces of these satyric disturbances? If they had recognized the truth, which is manifest to all who wish to understand devoutly, they would certainly know that just as through what is indicated in the Scriptures concerning the saints we become mindful of their sufferings and are raised up to a zeal like theirs, so also, by seeing their sufferings through pictorial representation, we come to the remembrance of their virtue and God-filled life.

Then again they think rightly, saying as follows: [Col. 0444D]

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone does not confess that all the saints who have existed from the beginning until now—those who pleased God before the Law, under the Law, and in the time of grace—are honorable before him in soul and body, or does not ask their prayers, as those who have confidence to intercede for the world, according to ecclesiastical tradition, let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Since they mentioned ecclesiastical tradition, they ought [Col. 0445A] to have proclaimed: “If anyone does not receive pictorial representations, let him be anathema.”

For this tradition is truly ancient in the catholic Church, and it has been rightly recognized by us as a very fitting means of commemorating the prototypes. But shamelessly casting away this mystical knowledge, they address the catholic Church: “We do not want your ways” [Gr.: “We do not want to know them”].

Therefore, after this decree of theirs, they also rejected the offering of intercessions acceptable to God, erasing it from this document of theirs, as everyone knows. For it is characteristic of heretics that, when they have seen [Gr.: “despised”] even one statement of piety, they turn back from the way of truth [variant: “when they have spoken piously in one word and strayed from the way of truth”] and fall into many different errors [variant: “slip into many things”].

Truth is simple, but falsehood is manifold. [Col. 0445B] The Arians, calling the Word of God a creature, deliriously and impiously lied that he became incarnate without a soul. And the unhappy Eutyches, thinking there was one nature in the Lord’s dispensation, blasphemed by saying that he assumed some more divine flesh and not flesh consubstantial with our nature.

Similarly, the bishops of this heresy, imitating these men, were not content with one novelty, nor did they have their fill of evil; instead, they seized upon another novelty adjacent to it. Then, thinking to make their words correspond with those of the holy Fathers, and simulating piety through hypocrisy, they put forward the following:

Gregory the bishop read:

“If anyone does not confess the resurrection of the dead, [Col. 0445C] the judgment, and the fitting recompense to be assigned to each person according to the righteous judgments of God, and does not confess that there will be no end either to punishment or to the heavenly kingdom—that is, to the delights of God (for the kingdom of heaven is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit [Rom. 14], according to the divine Apostle)—let him be anathema!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

This is the distinction [variant: “definition”] of the primacy of our true faith, namely, that of the holy apostles and distinguished Fathers. This belongs to the catholic Church, and not to the confession of heretics. But what follows is peculiar to them, since it is full of indiscipline and lack of learning, as it resounds all around [variant: “circulates all around”].

Gregory the bishop read:

[Col. 0445D]

“If anyone does not receive this holy and universal seventh synod of ours, but in any way detracts from it, and does not wholeheartedly embrace what it defined according to the teaching of divinely inspired Scripture, let him be anathema from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and from the seven universal synods!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Ignorance of the truth is blindness of the senses and of the mind. Their opinion contains more ignorance and madness than impiety. They are wise only in matters of indiscipline.

Calling themselves the seventh synod, [Col. 0446A] as though in addition to the other seven synods that have taken place, they pronounced their anathema, saying: “Let him be anathema from the holy and universal seven synods.” And they are not so much mocked for their lack of learning as mourned with compassion because of their impiety.

For, carrying the truth away [variant: “bringing forward the truth”] but turning away from the good and royal path, they fall into a pit, chasms, and precipices. Of them the proverbial saying declares: “They have wandered in the tracks of their field and gathered barrenness in their hands” (Prov. 9).

Therefore those who love truth and seek righteousness have driven into their hearts the sharp arrows and drawn bows that they shot against the Church. They take up David, singing in the Spirit (Ps. 7):

“The authors of this perversity dug a pit, [Col. 0446B] and dug it out, and fell into the pit that they made; their pain turned back upon their own head, and their injustice descended upon the crown of their head.”

For they call bitter sweet and sweet bitter, and make light darkness and darkness light (Ps. 5), saying as follows:

Gregory the bishop read:

“Having therefore decreed these things among us with all strictness and diligence, we define that no one may put forward another faith—that is, write or compose one, or think or teach otherwise. But if anyone should dare to compose, put forward, teach, or hand down another faith to those who wish to return to the knowledge of the truth from any heresy; or if anyone should introduce a novelty [Col. 0446C] of expressions, that is, an invented wording, for the subversion of the present definitions promulgated by us: if they are bishops, they shall be alienated from the episcopate, and clerics from the clergy; but if they are monks or laypeople, they shall be anathematized.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Deluded through their lack of learning, they extorted these things from our distinguished Fathers and composed them as though they were their own. Therefore their speech is empty and idle, and not worthy even of a reply.

Gregory the bishop read:

“The divine emperors Constantine and Leo said: Let the holy and universal synod say whether the definition now read [Col. 0446D] has been promulgated with the agreement of all the most holy bishops.

“The holy synod exclaimed: We all believe thus; we all think the same; we have all subscribed unanimously and willingly; we all believe orthodoxly; we all worship the intelligible divinity intelligibly! This is the faith of the apostles; this is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the orthodox! Thus all who served God worshiped!

“Many years to the emperors! Lord, preserve the lights of peace; Lord, grant them a devout life! Eternal memory to Leo and Constantine! You are the peace of the world; may your faith preserve you! You honor Christ; he himself will preserve you! You have confirmed orthodoxy! [Col. 0447A] Lord, grant them a devout life! Let envy be far from their empire! May God guard your empire! May God make your empire peaceful! Your life is the life of the orthodox! Heavenly King, preserve those on earth! Through you the universal Church has been brought to peace! You are the lights of orthodoxy! Lord, preserve the lights of the world! Eternal memory to Constantine and Leo! Many years to the new Constantine, most pious of emperors! Lord, preserve the orthodox one by descent; Lord, grant him a devout life; let envy depart from his kingdom! Many years to the most pious Augusta! May God preserve her who is pious and orthodox! Let envy depart from your kingdom! May God guard your empire; may God make your kingdom peaceful!

“You have rightly distinguished the unconfused dispensation in Christ! [Col. 0447B] You have firmly proclaimed the inseparability of the two natures in Christ! You have strengthened the dogmas of the six holy and universal councils! You have exterminated all idolatry! You have exposed the teachers of this error! You have revealed those who think contrary things!”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

While pronouncing the customary acclamations to the emperors, they make the soul blaze with the torches of madness and falsehood, and speak from the devil’s own argument, saying: “You have exterminated all idolatry.”

Would that our ears were deaf, so that they might not hear a voice corrupting souls. “Do not be constantly with a prostitute,” says the proverbial saying (Prov. 5). [Col. 0447C]

For wishing to destroy the account of the saving dispensation, they went to every extreme of blasphemy. And what shall we say in response to this lamentable frenzy, except what was spoken by the Holy Spirit through David the psalmist?

“The poison of asps is under their lips; their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they practiced deceit” (Ps. 13).

Thus they also fell away from their own thoughts, judged by Christ our God, who delivered us from the error of idols. For he himself, deigning to become a perfect human being for our salvation, exterminated all idolatry.

He said through the prophet: “Behold, days are coming, and I will destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and their memory shall no longer exist” (Zech. 13). It is therefore certain that the prophecy refers to him, and not, as they said, to the rule of princes.

For attributing this grace or gift to others is proper to apostasy. Christians cry out, having drunk from the great-voiced Isaiah: [Col. 0447D] “It was not an ambassador, nor an angel, but the Lord himself who saved us” (Isa. 63).

But if, as they themselves confess, a college of bishops or the rule of kings delivered us from the error of idols, the human race has strayed from the truth. To believe this is to say that they did not save us, but that one person exalted another as the great savior, while someone else was saved by him [Gr.: “one saved, and another boasting that the one was saved by him”].

For when Christ our God delivered us from the error and deception of idols, they themselves boast greatly, confessing that they accomplished redemption. O arrogance and madness! Having been deprived of the truth, they have been blinded in mind and senses; deceived by their own conjectures and fantasies, [Col. 0448A] they have been steeped [variant: “immersed”] in flattery.

Refusing to proclaim appropriate and fitting praises to the emperors, they applied to them what is said about Christ our God. Rather, they ought to have proclaimed their victories over enemies, their conquests over barbarians, their subjugation of barbarian peoples—things which many have painted on images and walls as a memorial narrative, drawing those who see them toward love and zeal—the acquisition of subjects [variant: “the preservation of those subject to them”], counsels, trophies, civil conditions, civic arrangements, and the governance of cities.

These are praises worthy to be offered to emperors and good reports, through which everything subject to them might also be prompted to thought [variant: “might be provoked to benevolence”].

Yet, still having sharp tongues and breathing anger and accusation [Col. 0448B], they seem to shoot at the upright in heart at the dark moon [variant: “they are seen shooting”], saying as follows [variant: “these things”]:

Gregory the bishop read:

“You have dissolved the opinion of Germanus, George, and Mansur, men of evil opinion.

“Anathema to Germanus, double-minded and a worshiper of wood.

“Anathema to George, his accomplice and falsifier of the teachings of the Fathers.

“Anathema to Mansur, of wicked name, who thinks like the Saracens.

“Anathema to Mansur, servant of images and writer of falsehood.

“Anathema to Mansur, insulting Christ and plotting against the empire. [Col. 0448C]

“Anathema to Mansur, teacher of impiety and evil interpreter of divine Scripture.

“The Trinity has deposed these three.”

Epiphanius the deacon read:

Let us say to these men the word of the prophet: “The face of a prostitute has become yours; you refuse to be ashamed before anyone” (Jer. 3). For those women, adorned in their own disgrace and shameful pursuits, are accustomed to mock those who live chastely. For the worship of God is an abomination to sinners. Thus these men too, having deceitful lips, have spoken wickedness against the righteous in arrogance and contempt. But the Lord has hidden them in the secret place of his face, sheltered them from their disturbance, and delivered them from the contradiction of their tongues.

For they have shone like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life (Phil. 2:15–16): namely, Germanus, who was nourished in the sacred writings, dedicated to God from childhood like Samuel, and shown to be like the holy Fathers. His written works affirm that it is necessary to follow his disputations, celebrated throughout the whole world. “The exaltations of God are in his throat, and two-edged swords are in his hands” (Ps. 149:6): he hurled them against those who dissented from ecclesiastical tradition.

And Georgius, a Cypriot by birth, who, selling his patrimony in an evangelical manner [variant: establishing his life], and imitating Christ our God, who gave us the pattern of his dispensation, neither contended nor cried out. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten. He turned the other cheek to the one striking him (Matt. 5:39), added another thousand paces to the one compelling him to go one mile (Matt. 5:41), and bore the yoke from his youth (Lam. 3:27), judging it good, according to the prophet, to sit alone and keep silence.

And John, whom they insultingly called Mansur, who, leaving everything and emulating Matthew the evangelist, followed Christ, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure he had left in Arabia [variant: than all the wealth of the Arabs]. He chose rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to possess the temporal pleasure of sin (Heb. 11:25–26). Carrying his own cross and Christ’s and following him, he proclaimed Christ from the East like a trumpet. He considered intolerable the novelty of the words that had been produced in a different manner [Greek: that had been produced in a foreign region], or the treacherous faction and raging madness that had armed itself against the holy catholic Church of God.

By exposing this faction publicly, exhorting and admonishing everyone, he made them cautious, lest they be led away with those who worked iniquity. He sought that the ancient legislation should be maintained in the Churches, together with the peaceful constitution that the Lord gave his disciples when they received the title of his name, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

When such revered and trustworthy men have thus been demonstrated in the catholic Church, what accusation is rising against them, and how dreadful is it—indeed, who could endure it at all? Truly, the wretched men have been ignorant of ignorance, indecently baring their own tongue by calling Germanus, the mystical sacrificer and priest of Christ, “double-minded” and “a servant of wood”; and likewise Georgius and Mansur. Yet no one has ever brought such blasphemy even against a ruler who shared the same faith with him.

Christians have often been accused by Hebrews, Hagarenes, and other unbelievers of such a complaint both concerning the divine sign of the cross and concerning the venerable images and other sacred things dedicated to God. For a Christian has never brought such an accusation against a Christian. But “the righteous man is useless to the unrighteous, as the sun is to bleary eyes.” These men, fleeing from the truth and rejected by ecclesiastical law, have been handed over to falsehoods and curses. They gather nothing else except accusations against Christians and the priests of the Lord, as though they had abandoned the living and true God and devoted themselves to an icon.

They are certain slanderous and afflicted persons, excessively talkative [Greek: revilers, reckless speakers, and babblers], who have become followers of such people; and who among those who fear God and mock them would not pour forth broad laughter—or rather clothe himself in mournful lamentation and spend the deep night grieving over their impiety?

And since, being “inventors of evil” (Rom. 1:30) according to the divine Apostle, they have wearied themselves searching out investigations, we have bidden their chatter farewell; and, by the grace of God, having sufficiently completed [variant: brought the disputation to an end] the complete destruction of the vain thoughts of their falsely named knowledge, and counted the error of their empty perversity among the ancient heresies, we have cut it off with the sword of the Spirit. Come now, let us instruct the minds of those who hear.

All things, therefore, are plain to those who understand and right to those who find knowledge, as the author of Proverbs rightly says (Prov. 8), and as truth itself appears to say. For the holy catholic Church of God draws those born to her from diverse and varied things toward repentance and toward recognition and observance of God’s commandments. She hastens to direct all our senses toward the glory of him who is God over all; and through hearing and sight she brings correction, placing before the faces of those who approach the things that have been done.

When she snatches someone from avarice and the love of money, she shows him in an image Matthew, who became an apostle from among the tax collectors, abandoned the frenzy of avarice, and followed Christ. She also shows Zacchaeus climbing a sycamore tree, desiring to see Christ, and promising him that he would give half of his possessions to the poor and, if he had taken anything from anyone, repay it fourfold (Matt. 9; Mark 2; Luke 5, 19). Thus the continual vision of the images becomes a safeguard of conversion and a perpetual remembrance, lest one return to one’s own vomit.

Again, when she seizes another who is weighed down by lust for a prostitute, she places before him the image of chaste Joseph, who abhorred fornication and overcame it through chastity (Gen. 39), preserving what is said concerning the image; those who have loved this become partakers of it. Elsewhere she presents blessed Susanna, adorned with chastity and, with hands extended, invoking help from on high, together with Daniel sitting as judge and rescuing her from the hands of the wicked elders (Dan. 13). Thus the memory of the inscription in the image serves to preserve a chaste life.

She seizes one who is consuming his substance in luxury, dressed in soft garments that ought to be supplied to the needy and spending his wealth on such clothing while embracing an indulgent life. She shows him Elijah clothed in a sheepskin and content with sufficient food; John dressed in camel’s hair and nourished on wild honey, pointing with his finger to Christ and confessing that he takes away the sin of the world (Matt. 3; Mark 1). Along with these she shows the great Basil and the multitude of ascetics and monks whose bodies had been dried up.

But so that we may not prolong the discourse, mentioning only a few examples, we have left the rest for those who hear to investigate. For we have the whole narrative of the Gospel depicted, leading us to the remembrance of God and filling us with joy. When these faces are placed before us, the heart of those who fear the Lord is gladdened, the face blossoms, and the soul afflicted by weariness is transferred into cheerfulness; and it sings psalms together with David, the father of God: “I remembered God and was glad” (Ps. 76:4).

Through these images, therefore, we always have the remembrance of God. For a reading is sometimes recited less often in the venerable temples, whereas the image, established among them as it were, tells and announces to us the truth of the events in the evening, morning, and midday.

Let us therefore receive the tradition of the Church and honor the legislation. Let us not scrutinize the pious and lawful custom, nor act inquisitively against ancient rights. For everything that is established [variant: spoken] in commemoration of God is acceptable to him. Those who are made outside this tradition, of which all who have genuinely received the adoption of sons in the catholic Church have become participants, are rightly illegitimate children and not sons.

Let us therefore judge it good and most excellent that venerable images be placed in the Church, and that through them we be spiritually recalled to the memory of their prototypes; and that, because of the honor due to those prototypes, we embrace the images and offer them the appropriate veneration.

Whether, then, someone prefers to call this greeting or veneration—for these are the same thing, unless someone means by “veneration” the worship offered according to *latria*, since that is different, as has been shown in many ways—let the one who approaches be worthy of veneration. But if he is not worthy, let him first be purified, and then approach the venerable image.

There must be neither satanic insistence concerning their veneration nor fear providing an occasion for an unjust suspicion: “If I approach this image to greet it, I may be found to be offering to it the *latria* that exists in the spirit.” Away with such suspicion! The enemies of God and empty talkers, imitating the serpent, utter these things with their babbling tongues. For the serpent itself approached the woman and deceitfully whispered: “What, he said, did God say? ‘You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise; but from the tree that is in the middle of paradise you shall not eat’” (Gen. 3:1–3).

So these men seduce effeminate hearts, saying: “Whoever venerates the image of the Lord, or of our undefiled Lady and truly Mother of God, or of the holy angels, or of any saint, offers to it the *latria* that exists in the spirit.” Let us not therefore be deceived by their speech. For this assertion is both an admonition and a perverse statement of the devil.

The theologian Gregory also destroys this fiction, commanding all of us, when he says in his *Oration on the Nativity*: “Honor Bethlehem; venerate the manger.” Along with him we must remember Maximus, whose praise is in all the Churches. When he was disputing with certain men concerning ecclesiastical matters, he ordered the divine and precious sign of the cross, the holy Gospel, and the venerable icon to be brought into the midst, and he greeted these together with them, for confirmation of what had been said.

Athanasius, who received his name from immortality, announces this to us even more explicitly in the letter sent to Marcellinus, which he arranged at the beginning of his book of interpretation of the Psalms, saying:

“When one takes up the book of Psalms, he customarily goes forth, admiring and venerating the prophecies concerning the Savior [Greek: concerning the Savior], as in the other Scriptures, and continues onward [variant: proceeds].”

Do you see how the excellent Father commands us to venerate the prophecies? And if it is pious to venerate these, how much more necessary is it to venerate the fulfillment of the prophetic declarations as seen in an image? For the prophecy says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. 7:14). When we see this prophecy in an image—that is, the Virgin embracing the one whom she bore—how could we endure not venerating and greeting it? What uneducated person would dare delay such a greeting?

Let us make ourselves worthy of veneration, lest, approaching unworthily, we incur the punishment of Uzzah [variant: of Oza] (2 Sam. 6). For he touched the ark and perished at that very hour, approaching it unworthily. Yet the ark itself had been varied in different forms and constructed from wood, just as images are made.

Those who say that images are sufficient merely for remembrance and not also for greeting, accepting one thing while rejecting the other, thereby show themselves to be partly perverse [Greek: partly perverse], partly false, and partly truthful: at one time confessing what is true, and at another corrupting it [that is, condemning it]. O their insensibility! We who once were accusers of orthodoxy and truth should now become advocates of these men and ask pardon for rejecting ecclesiastical traditions.

In all these matters let us keep the commandments through what has been prescribed. Let us walk while hearing the prophetic voice, which says: “If someone announces to you, O man [variant: ‘it has been announced, O man’], what is good, or what the Lord requires from you, except to do justice, love mercy, and be ready to walk with the Lord your God?” (Mic. 6:8).

Beyond this, let us quiet our fury and restrain our tongue, abstaining from lies, shameful speech, and curses. Let us discipline the eye, instruct the belly, devote ourselves to psalmody and prayer, and give thanks to God in everything he has given us. Let us not accustom our mouths to oaths, but hear the Lord’s voice saying: “But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matt. 5:34).

Let us trample glory, which lies below. Let us seize mercy and love, the greatest of all good things, and join them to the fear of God. For without the fear of God, love is rejected. Jehoshaphat was indeed a friend of Ahab, but he heard: “If you join yourself in friendship to a sinner, and if you help one who is hated by the Lord…” (2 Chron. 19:2).

Let us therefore do everything with the fear of God, seeking also the intercession of our undefiled Lady, Mary, ever-Virgin and by nature Mother of God, and of the holy angels and all the saints together. Let us also greet and venerate their relics, so that we may become participants in their holiness.

For thus we shall be perfected for every good work in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom are due glory, dominion, and *latria*, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.

They were seated before the ambo of the most sacred temple of the most holy great Church called [Col. 0457B] Sophia. Also present and listening were the most glorious and magnificent prince, namely Petrona, most praiseworthy former consul and patrician, and count of the service of the imperial household entrusted to God, together with the most reverend archimandrites, abbots, and monks, according to the order previously specified in the first session. The holy and undefiled Gospels of God had also been placed before them.

Theodore, most holy bishop of Tauriana on the island of Sicily, taking the book containing the definition into his hands, read the following:

# DEFINITION OF THE HOLY GREAT AND UNIVERSAL SYNOD ASSEMBLED FOR THE SECOND TIME AT NICAEA

The holy great and universal synod, which by the grace of God and by the decree of the pious and Christian emperors Constantine and Irene his mother was assembled for the second time in Nicaea, the illustrious metropolis of the province of Bithynia, in the holy Church of God called Sophia, following the tradition of the catholic Church, defined the following.

Christ our God, who gave us the light of his knowledge and redeemed us from the darkness and madness of idols, betrothed to himself his holy catholic Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. 5:27), and promised that he would preserve her. He affirmed to his holy disciples, saying: “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). He gave this promise not only to them, but also to us who through them have believed in his name.

Therefore, certain men, failing to consider this gift, became somehow like birds carried about by the crafty enemy and fell away from right reason. Resisting the tradition of the catholic Church, they were deprived of the understanding of truth. As the proverbial saying has it, they wandered in the furrow of their field [variant: of their cultivation], and gathered barrenness with their own hands, because they dared to detract from the sacred monuments and from the ornament pleasing to God. They were called priests, but were not priests. Concerning them God cries out through the prophet: “Many shepherds have corrupted my vineyard; they have defiled my portion” (Jer. 12:10).

Following wicked men and seduced by their own thoughts, they slandered the holy Church of Christ our God, which is betrothed to him, and did not distinguish between the holy and the profane (Ezek. 22:26), calling the image of the Lord and of his saints statues like those of demonic idols.

Therefore the Lord God, unwilling to see his subjects corrupted by such a plague, summoned us, the leaders of the priesthood, from every direction according to his good pleasure, burning with divine zeal [Greek: with divine zeal and command], and brought together by the command of our emperors Constantine and Irene, so that the God-given tradition of the catholic Church might receive stability by common decree.

Accordingly, examining and investigating everything with all diligence, and following the intention of truth, we neither take anything away nor add anything. We preserve without alteration everything that belongs to the catholic Church [Col. 0458B]. Following the holy six universal councils, we follow first the council that assembled in the splendid metropolis of Nicaea, and also the council that was afterward assembled in the divinely protected imperial city.

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages: Light from Light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made. For us human beings and for our salvation he came down from heaven, and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became man. He was also crucified for us under [Col. 0458C] Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; and he will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0457D] Julian, cardinal, in the acts of the Council of Florence, testifies that among the Latins there then existed a very ancient manuscript [Col. 0458D] of the Seventh Synod, in which it read “from the Father and the Son.” In the Jolian manuscript: “who proceeds from the Father,” with “and the Son” omitted], who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets. And in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. I await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

We abominate and anathematize Arius and those who agreed with him and shared his insane opinion; and Macedonius, together with those who, after him, are rightly called Pneumatomachi. We also confess [Col. 0458D] our Lady, the holy Mary, properly and truly to be the Mother of God, because in the flesh she bore one of the Holy Trinity, namely Christ our God, in accordance with what the Council of Ephesus had previously defined: it expelled the weak [impious] Nestorius and his associates from the Church, since he introduced a personal duality.

Together with them we also confess [Col. 0459A] two natures in him who was incarnate for us from the undefiled Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, acknowledging him as perfect God and perfect man, just as the Council of Chalcedon proclaimed, casting Eutyches and Dioscorus, denounced [Gr., blaspheming], out of the divine court. Along with them we likewise condemn Severus, Peter, and their cord, woven into a rope of mutually entangled perplexities and blaspheming in many ways. Together with them we anathematize the fables of Origen, Evagrius, and Didymus, just as the Fifth Council, assembled at Constantinople, is known to have done.

Furthermore, we proclaim two wills and two operations in Christ, according to the particular properties of the natures, just as the Sixth Synod at Constantinople declared, rejecting Sergius, Honorius [Note: [Col. 0459D] Saint Maximus, the Greek doctor and confessor, who wrote during the pontificate of Pope Honorius, strongly defends him [Col. 0460D] in his dialogue with Pyrrhus, as may be seen in Session VI, 13 of the synod], Cyrus, Pyrrhus, Macarius, and those who are without a will in matters of piety, as well as those who think similarly.

To state the matter briefly, we preserve inviolate all the ecclesiastical traditions sanctioned either in writing or without writing. One of these [Col. 0459B] is also the production of images in painting, which accords with the narrative of the evangelical proclamation, for the confirmation of the true—and not merely imaginary—incarnation of God the Word, and which suitably advances to a like benefit for us. For things that mutually indicate one another, without doubt [indubitably], also possess mutually corresponding meanings.

Since these things stand thus, following, as it were, the royal path [or: proceeding by the royal road], and following the divinely inspired teaching of our holy Fathers and the tradition of the catholic Church—for we know this tradition to be that of the Holy Spirit, who indeed dwells within it—we define, with complete certainty and care, that just as the figure of the precious and life-giving cross is to be set forth, so also venerable and holy images are to be displayed: whether formed in colors and tesserae, or made of any other [Col. 0459C] suitable [Gr., suitably constituted] material, in the holy churches of God, on sacred vessels and vestments, on walls and panels, in houses and along roads. These images include the image of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, that of our undefiled Lady, the holy Mother of God, those of the honorable angels, and those of all the saints and holy men.

For the more frequently they are seen through the formation of images, the more eagerly those who contemplate them are raised to the remembrance and desire of their prototypes, and to offering them a kiss and an honorable veneration [Col. 0459D]. Yet not the true worship [Gr., “and a kiss and honorable veneration are offered to them, but not true worship”], which is according to faith and is proper to the divine nature alone. Thus, an offering of incense and lights is to be made to these images, as to the figure of the precious and life-giving cross, the holy Gospels, and the other sacred memorials, in order to honor them, just as was the custom of ancient piety.

For the honor paid to the image passes to the prototype; and whoever venerates the image venerates the person represented in it. Thus the teaching of our holy Fathers possesses its strength—that is, the tradition of the holy catholic Church, which received the Gospel from one end of the earth to the other (I Thess. II). Thus we follow Paul, who spoke in Christ, and the entire divine apostolic assembly, and the holiness of the Fathers [Col. 0460A], holding fast to the traditions that we received.

Thus we prophetically sing hymns in the triumphant Church:

“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem. Rejoice and be glad with all your heart. The Lord has taken away from you the injustices of those who opposed you; he has redeemed you from the hand of your enemies. The Lord the King is in your midst; you shall see evil no more, and peace shall be in you forever” (Zeph. III).

Therefore, if any dare to think or teach otherwise, or, following wicked heretics, despise the traditions of the Church and devise any novelty, or cast away anything belonging to the Church—whether the Gospel, the figure of the cross, an image in painting, or the holy relics of a martyr—or wickedly or cunningly devise anything to overthrow any of the legitimate traditions of the catholic Church; or if they use sacred vessels or venerable monasteries as though they were common property: if they are bishops or clerics, we decree that they be deposed; monks and laypeople are to be separated from communion.

Peter, unworthy first presbyter of the see of the holy apostle Peter, and holding the place of Adrian, the senior pope of Rome, have signed the definition.

Peter, unworthy presbyter and hegumen of the monastery of our holy Father Sabbas, situated at Rome, and holding the place of Adrian, the senior pope of Rome, have signed the definition.

The holy synod exclaimed:

“We all believe thus; we all think the same; all in agreement, we have signed! This is the faith of the apostles [this is the faith [Col. 0469B] of the Fathers]; this is the faith of the orthodox; this faith has established the whole world! Believing in one God, to be praised in Trinity, we kiss the honorable images! Let those who are not thus disposed be anathema! Let those who do not think thus be driven far from the Church!

“We follow the ancient legislation of the catholic Church! We guard the laws of the Fathers! We anathematize those who add anything to or take anything away from the Church! We anathematize the novelty introduced by those who accuse Christians! We receive the venerable images! We subject those who are not thus disposed to anathema!

“To those who apply to venerable images the statements uttered by divine Scripture against idols: anathema! To those who do not salute the holy and venerable images: anathema! To those who call the [Col. 0469C] sacred images idols: anathema! To those who say that Christians approached images as they approached gods: anathema! [To those who knowingly associate with people who inflict injury and insult upon the venerable images: anathema!] To those who say that someone other than Christ delivered us from idols: anathema! To those who dare to say that the catholic Church ever received idols: anathema!

“Many years to the emperors! Many years to Constantine and his mother Irene! Many years to the victorious emperors! Eternal memory to the new Constantine and the new Helena! May the Lord guard their empire! Heavenly King, guard the earthly rulers! Anathema to all heretics! Anathema to the council that rages against the venerable images! Anathema to the one who accepts their impious heretical arguments [Col. 0469D]!

“Anathema to Theodosius, the falsely named bishop of Ephesus! Anathema to Sisinnius, surnamed Pastillas! Anathema to Basil, who by an obscene utterance was called Tricaccabus!”

The Trinity has overthrown the doctrines of these three! Anathema to Anastasius, Constantine, and Nicetas, who successively presided over the Constantinopolitan throne, as new Arius, Nestorius, and Dioscorus!

The Holy Trinity has overthrown the doctrines of these three! [Greek addition: “Moreover, anathema to those who imitated the threefold wickedness of these heresiarch prelates! Anathema to Theodore, Antonius, and John, as supporters of a phantasmal appearance, like Manes, Apollinarius, and Eutyches! Anathema to Theodore of Syracuse [Col. 0470A], surnamed Crithinus, and to those who became apostates together with him!”]

Anathema to John of Nicomedia and Constantine of Nacolea, the heresiarchs! They brought the image of the Lord and of his saints to nothing; the Lord brought them to nothing.

If anyone defends a person who accuses Christians of heresy, or who spends his life in that heresy [who has died in it], let him be anathema!

If anyone does not confess Christ God as circumscribed according to his humanity, let him be anathema!

If anyone does not admit the evangelical narratives made in titles and paintings, let him be anathema!

If anyone does not kiss these images as having been made in the name of the Lord and of his saints, let him be anathema!

[Col. 0470B] If anyone invalidates any ecclesiastical tradition, whether written or unwritten, let him be anathema!

Eternal memory to Germanus the orthodox!

Eternal memory to John and Gregory [Greek and the Jolian manuscript: Georgius]!

Eternal memory to the preachers of truth!

The Trinity glorified these three. May we be worthy to follow their disputations, through the mercies and grace of the first and great High Priest, Christ our God, with the intercession of our undefiled Lady, the holy Mother of God, and of all his saints. May it be so. Amen.

To our most pious and most Christian emperors, Constantine and his mother Irene: Tarasius, unworthy bishop of your divinely preserved royal city [Col. 0470C], New Rome, and the entire holy synod, which, by the good pleasure of God and, in reality, at the command of your God-loving empire, has assembled for the second time in this splendid metropolis of Nicaea.

The Head of the Church, namely Christ our God, is glorified, excellent princes, because your heart, which is guarded in his hand, has brought forth a good word: namely, commanding us to rise up [Gr., to assemble] in his name, so that we may hold most firmly the unshaken, immovable, and divine declaration of ecclesiastical doctrines. For just as your head is crowned with gold and gleaming stones, so your understanding is adorned with evangelical and paternal teachings. Since you were disciples and participants of those whose sound has gone out into all the earth, [Col. 0470D] and guides of the entire people called by Christ’s name toward piety, you have described the word with the stylus of truth and painted the character of orthodoxy and piety. Like brilliant lights, you have shone upon the faithful and extended your hand to churches in peril, confirming sound doctrines and restoring agreement among things that were at variance with one another [which were at variance with one another].

Therefore we may say confidently: “By God’s good will toward piety, correction has been established through you” [Gr., “an eminent work has been established”]. For this reason “our mouth has been filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Ps. 125 [126]); and through our written declaration the works of our tongue speak. What is more delightful than the firm guardianship of ecclesiastical affairs, [Col. 0471A] and what more gratifying to joy?

Since certain men have risen up, indeed possessing the appearance of piety because they are clothed about with the dignity of the priesthood, but denying its power, and taking up the accusation [charge] of the Babylonian priests—men whom prophecy exposes, saying, “Wickedness has gone forth from the priests of Babylon” (Dan. 13)—or rather, establishing a council like that of Caiaphas, they have become begetters of impious doctrines. Possessing a mouth of cursing and bitterness, they considered it glory to prevail in evil. They possessed an infamous tongue and a pen serving it, attacking the words uttered by God himself, and monstrously calling the royal priesthood, the holy nation, those who have put on Christ, and those who by his grace were saved from the error of idols [Col. 0471B] idolaters [Gr., “monstrously called them idolaters,” and so forth].

With a determination toward wicked action, they laid hands upon unlawful things, supposing that they should demolish the depiction of the venerable images. Whatever had been made of mosaic tiles they dug out; whatever had been produced in wax by the application of colors, they erased; and they turned the beauty of the venerable images [Gr., of the temples] into disgrace. Along with these things, they committed to the fire those works on panels that had existed in memory of Christ our God and his saints.

To speak more plainly, they plundered and disturbed our churches. Those who had been leaders of the priesthood became leaders of heresies. Instead of peace they proclaimed contention to the people; instead of wheat they sowed weeds in the ecclesiastical fields; they mixed wine with water and gave their neighbor a drink of turbulent overthrow. Although they were Arabian wolves, they pretended to be clothed in sheep’s wool. Treating truth as a thing of little worth [defrauding it], they seized falsehood; they broke the eggs of asps and, according to the prophet, wove a spider’s web (Isa. 59). Anyone who eats one of them, breaking the egg, will find it heated [rotten], containing a basilisk full of poison and deadly spirit.

Because they arranged these things in this way, and falsehood devoured the truth, you, our most gentle and most powerful emperors, did not permit such a pestilential error, corrupting souls, to remain in your times. Rather, you took care to destroy it by the breath of the divine Spirit who dwells in you, so that the assembly of the Church [Col. 0471D] and the gathering [collection] of all your subjects might remain firm, and your empire might be directed peacefully according to your name.

You did not judge it tolerable or bearable that we should not think as one, come together in the same purpose, or that anyone among us should separate and cut himself off from the chief concern of our life—that is, the peace of the Churches [Gr., “that there should be dissensions among us”]. For Christ is our head, while we are consequently members and one body through the faith of mutual and common agreement.

Therefore you ordered our sacred and populous multitude to assemble in this metropolis of Nicaea, so that, driving away the dissension of the Churches, we might draw what had been separated toward unity; [Col. 0472A] and so that we might strive to tear apart and cut up the shameful and coarse garment which they recently wove from thorny threads—that is, false doctrine—and preserve the untarnished tunic of orthodoxy [Gr., “spread it out”].

Accordingly, following the apostolic and paternal traditions—and we dare to say, being made harmonious by the conspiracy of the most holy Spirit—we all assembled together, possessing as our common agreement the tradition of the Catholic Church. Having become concordant through the harmonies formed by the holy six Ecumenical Councils, we anathematized the madness of Arius, the frenzy of Macedonius, the senseless understanding of Apollinarius, the human construction [construction of a man] of Nestorius, the confusable vanity of Eutyches and Dioscorus, and with them the many-headed Hydra; the foolish tales of Origen, Didymus, [Col. 0472B] and Evagrius; the single, indeed wickedly minded, will of Sergius, Honorius, Cyrus, Pyrrhus, and their followers.

Likewise, the similar vanity that afterward foolishly babbled against the venerable images we, receiving the word harmoniously and unanimously from the Spirit and drawing pure water from him, erased with the sponge of divine doctrines. We drove far from the ecclesiastical vestibules the inventors of evasive and innovative verbal novelty [novel vanity].

Just as hands and feet are moved in harmony by the motions of the soul, so, having received grace and strength from the Spirit, and having obtained at once your participation in piety and assistance, we cried out together and proclaimed the truth: namely, that the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ are to be received in every way, according to the manner in which he became perfect man; and whatever is written historically according to the evangelical narrative; as well as the image of our undefiled Lady, the holy Mother of God, and of the holy angels—for they appeared as human beings to those who were deemed worthy of their appearance—together with all the saints.

We also decreed that the contests of their struggles should be represented on panels and walls, as well as on sacred vessels and vestments, just as the holy Catholic Church of God has received and accepted as law from ancient times, both from the holy and first teachers of our doctrine and from their successors and eminent Fathers.

These images are to be adored, that is, saluted; for the two things are the same [Col. 0472D]. For κυνεῖν in the ancient Greek language means both “to salute” and “to kiss.” The preposition πρὸς signifies a certain increase of love, as in φέρω, “I bear,” and προσφερῶ, “I bring or offer”; κυρῶ, “I meet,” and προσκυρῶ, “I encounter”; κυνῶ, “I kiss,” and προσκυνῶ, “I salute or adore.” The latter indicates a salutation and, by extension, friendship. For what one kisses, one also adores; and what one adores, one certainly also kisses, as human affection, which we show toward our friends, bears witness, as does the reading [Gr., “the encounter with those whom one meets”] that accomplishes both.

We find this written not only among us but also among the ancients in divine Scripture. In the histories of the kingdoms it is written: “David rose, fell upon his face, adored Jonathan three times, and kissed him” (1 Kings 20 [1 Sam. 20]). What does the Lord say again evangelically about the Pharisees? “They love the first couches at banquets and salutations in the marketplace” (Matt. 23). It is certain that here he calls salutation adoration. For the Pharisees, possessing an ostentatious understanding and considering themselves righteous, hastened to be adored by everyone, not to kiss mouth to mouth; for that is rather a sign of humility and not of Pharisaic arrogance.

Again, the divine apostle Paul, as Luke records in the Acts of the Apostles: “When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. On the following day Paul entered with us to James, and all the elders assembled. After he had saluted them, he recounted one by one what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry” (Acts 21).
