Here too the apostolic understanding describes an honoring salutation [Col. 0473B] as the adoration that we offer to one another. Likewise concerning Jacob it says: “He adored the top of his staff” (Heb. 11).

Gregory, surnamed the God-speaker, says in agreement with these things: “Honor Bethlehem and adore the manger” (Sermon on the Nativity of Christ). Who, do you suppose, among those who rightly and sincerely understand what divine Scripture declares, would understand these words as referring to the adoration that takes place in the spirit? Unless perhaps he is senseless, or among those who are inexperienced in all scriptural knowledge and paternal teaching. Did Jacob serve the top of a staff? Or did the theologian Gregory command anyone to serve the manger?

Again, when we salute the life-giving cross, we sing in harmony: “We adore your cross, O Lord,” and “we adore the lance that opened the life-giving side of your goodness” [Col. 0473C]. This is most certainly a salutation, and it is called such, as is shown by the fact that we touch these things with our own lips.

Although adoration is often found in divine Scripture, and our Fathers, speaking courteously, use it for the service that is performed in the spirit—for the word has many meanings—only one of its meanings is found to signify the adoration that is according to latria [one of its meanings is adoration according to latria]. There is also the adoration that is performed through honor, love, and fear, as when we adore your most glorious and gentle empire. There is another that is through fear alone, as when Jacob adored Esau (Gen. 33). There is one through gratitude, as when Abraham adored the sons of Heth for the field that he received from them for the burial of Sarah his wife (Gen. 23). Again, those who expect to receive a benefit from persons of higher rank adore them, as Jacob adored Pharaoh (Gen. 47).

For this reason divine Scripture, instructing us, says: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Luke 4). It uses “adore” absolutely and does not add “alone” [the text places it absolutely and does not add “alone,” as applying to a word with many meanings and an equivocal expression]. Moreover, it says this without restriction, as a word having diverse meanings while remaining homonymous, and does not add “alone.” But it says, “You shall serve him alone,” for we refer our service to God alone.

These points having thus been established, it is truly and indisputably clear that it is acceptable and pleasing before God to adore and kiss the pictorial representations of the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the undefiled Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and of the honorable angels and all the saints.

Whoever does not conduct himself in this way, but disputes or even grows faint regarding the adoration of the venerable images, is anathematized by our holy and universal synod, fortified by the operation of the divine Spirit and by paternal and ecclesiastical traditions. Anathema is nothing other than separation from God.

If there are some who quarrel and do not obey what has been defined, they kick against the goads and injure their own souls, offending Christ and delighting in slanders against his Church, madly attacking piety, as sharers, allies, and fellow members in impiety with the ancient heretics.

We have sent our brothers and fellow ministers, the bishops beloved of God, together with abbots and clerics, so that they may announce and make known to your God-fearing ears everything that has been done among us. Furthermore, as a seal and confirmation of what we have defined, and also as satisfaction for your most pious empire, we have appended paternal testimonies, a few collected from many, illuminating the certainty of the truth with their clarity.

May the Savior of us all, who reigns with you and who through you has willed to grant his peace to the Churches, preserve your empire for many years, together with your senate, princes, most faithful army, and the whole state; and may he grant you [Col. 0474C] victory. For he himself says: “I live, says the Lord, because those who glorify me I will glorify” (1 Kings 2). He is the one who girded you with strength, who will strike all your enemies, and who will grant you all who obey [variant: “he will make the enemies mourn, and the subjects rejoice”].

Rejoice, therefore, city [Gr., “and you, city”]; be glad, new Zion, the world's lookout [watchtower]. For David reigned there, and here Davidic rulers guard you [variant: “pious emperors hold power”]. The Lord is in your midst, and may his name be blessed forever and ever. Amen.

To the priests and clerics beloved of God, both of the most holy Great Church of God and of all the Churches of the God-preserved imperial city, the holy synod assembled for the second time at Nicaea.

Christ our God, who truly is the truth, the paternal light and radiance; who called us from darkness into his wondrous light and rescued us from idolatrous madness; who erased the names of idols from the earth and promised that their memory would no longer exist—he willed to incline our pious, wholly orthodox, and faithful emperors to assemble us in the illustrious metropolis of Nicaea, as you know, so that we might turn the discord of those who were divided into harmony, remove the dividing wall of hostility, and restore to the Catholic Church the firmness of the ancient law.

Therefore, when we had come together in the same purpose through the inspiration and cooperation of the Holy Spirit, we all agreed. East, North, West, and South came together into one unity, and the peaceful order of the holy Churches triumphed [was established] through the truth and faith of reciprocal agreement, which directed the path of our feet. Thus the offshoot of heresy, which had grown from the weeds of the ancient enemy, was uprooted.

And behold, standing upon a high mountain, we proclaim to you the joy of ecclesiastical peace and a public festival. What could be more pleasing than this? Isaiah acted confidently and proclaimed from heaven [variant: “from ancient times”]: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Isa. 52; Rom. 10.)

It was worthy and most fitting, and an example and rejoicing appropriate to your sacred and God-beloved dignity, that all your assembly chosen by God should be found together and contemplate the power of what has been said and done by God’s grace—both the correction [confirmation] of the legitimate traditions of the Catholic Church and the destruction and overthrow of those who raged against the truth, changed the apostolic and paternal traditions of the Catholic Church, or even, according to their own judgment, reduced them to destruction.

But since a watery journey lies in between, and there is again a journey over land, two things were needed: ships for sailing and suitable animals for transport. Lacking both, your most sacred multitude was deprived of our mutual gathering. Nevertheless, in a special and intelligible manner you were present with us, thinking what the fullness of the Catholic Church thinks. Since we are mutually members of Christ God, our head [Christ God, our head], we consider it necessary to send you a brief account of what has been done among us by God’s gift; for tongues speak their matters even through letters and set them forth as though visible.

When we had assembled according to the instruction of the paternal norms, we confirmed as one what we had understood [variant: “we were confirmed, and we thought as one”], not forgetting what Moses taught in his song: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (Deut. 32).

Thus we followed the tradition of the Catholic Church and did nothing either less or more, but, taught by the Apostle, we hold the traditions that we received, accepting and embracing everything that the holy Catholic Church received from ancient times, whether written or unwritten. Among these are also the representations of images in paintings. Conversely, whatever our eminent Fathers rejected, we too reject and consider contrary to the Church.

Among these contrary things is the deliberate [recent] novelty of expressions accusing Christians, like a cancer feeding upon the pastures of our churches. But the Lord God did not overlook it forever. For when the truth was revealed, orthodoxy shone upon all, and falsehood, together with the darkness born with it, was abolished.

If, as they foolishly babbled, the inscription of images is compared with idols, the mystery of our redemption vanishes—the mystery that the Son of God accomplished through his presence, by which he dwelt among us in the flesh without sin. The prophetic promises also become vain, saying: “Let us serve him in holiness and righteousness all the days of our life” (Luke 1). And again: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome with wine. And he struck his enemies on the rear; he gave them everlasting disgrace” (Ps. 77 [78]).

If everlasting disgrace was given to our enemies, namely to the evil powers, through his resurrection, how could Christians again have served idols? O their ignorance and impiety! Would that they had understood that whoever causes one of the least who believe in Christ to stumble incurs unbearable indignation (Matt. 18)—how much more those who make the whole world anxious through dissensions!

But they reduced the word of the Lord to nothing by rejecting ecclesiastical traditions; therefore the Lord reduced them to nothing. He numbered their turbulent factional council together with Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches [Col. 0476B] and Dioscorus, Sergius, Honorius, and their entire wicked sect. Imitating [expressing] the folly of these men, they spoke foolishly, were stoned together with them by the sling of true confession, and their battle line was dissolved.

For the Lord did not leave forever the rod of sinners over the inheritance of the Church, because they devised Jewish vanities and inherited the sequel of that council. This council became a Caiaphan assembly. That one devised vanities against the Lord; this one raged against his image.

For this council ascribed to itself and to others the redemption that was accomplished through Christ. This council devised a deep scheme, and not through the Lord; it made covenants, and not through his Spirit, because the adornment of the venerable temples was demolished.

In this council no human being made in the image of God is found, since they dishonored and smashed the image of the Lord and his saints and committed them to the fire. This council issued a satanic sentence full of fury and senselessness. This council possesses only the name of priesthood, but its knowledge is perverse and profane. This council has a defiant mouth and a spirit steeped in falsehood: it pretended to speak truth but presumed upon deceit [variant: “it openly taught falsehood”].

Our holy synod winnowed this council, as weeds from the Lord’s threshing floor—that is, from the Catholic Church—and cast it away with the winnowing fork of divine judgment. Its fabrications have therefore been removed from and refuted by the Catholic Church.

The true and most upright judgment of the Church allows nothing new to be made in it and permits nothing to be taken away. Following the paternal laws, therefore, and having received grace from the one Spirit, we have guarded intact [without any innovation] and undiminished everything belonging to the Church, as the six holy Ecumenical Councils handed it down. Whatever they left to be honored in the Catholic Church, we receive without hesitation.

Among these things, as has been said, is the making of images, which we honor honorably [Gr., adore] and salute. For the two are the same. Whoever clings to this confession is a true and participating son of the Catholic Church.

Therefore all scandals have withdrawn; everything has been destroyed. Truth flourishes; falsehood has been cast out. The sower of weeds has utterly failed, while the wheat—that is, the people who love Christ—has been brought into one granary of the Church of Christ.

The light of orthodoxy has arisen; the darkness of error has been removed. Mourning has been changed into joy, grief into gladness [Col. 0478A], and lamentation has been turned into joy for us. Everything has been carried over into a better state. Therefore we proclaim to you apostolically: “Rejoice in the Lord; rejoice, and again rejoice” (Phil. 3). For the Trinity has given us triple joy; to it belong honor and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## EIGHTH SESSION

[Note: From the new version. The material that follows, prefaced here by the title of the eighth session, is found only in Greek manuscripts, but is absent from Anastasius and the Vulgate edition, except for the canons, which will be given later. Nevertheless, it seemed appropriate to insert it because it contains what was done after the synod.]

[Col. 0477]

[Col. 0477A] In the name of the Lord and Master Jesus Christ, our true God. Under the rule of our most pious and Christ-loving lords Constantine and Irene, his mother, in the eighth year of their consulship, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction.

As illustrious heralds of truth, guardians of orthodoxy, and its imperial supporters, moved by divine desire, the emperors considered it wholly intolerable not to attend the synod. Accordingly, they issued a written command to the patriarch that he should bring all the bishops beloved of God to their God-preserved imperial city, New Rome. When he received these letters, he carried out the imperial command.

After the discussion of all the matters set out above and the happy conclusion of the affair, he set out on the road with all the bishops beloved of God whom he had taken with him, and they all proceeded to the city preserved by God. When they arrived there, they were graciously received by the emperors.

The most auspicious and illustrious empress, who was guarded by God, then, after adopting a good plan, appointed a fixed day on which she would preside synodically with the bishops. This was done in the palace called Magnaura. The holy Gospels of God having been placed before them, and the empress presiding together with her co-reigning son and the entire synod, the patriarch was ordered to address the synod in suitable words, and he carried out the imperial command.

Then the emperors themselves also addressed the synod in calm and elegant speech, with words received from God, so that all the bishops beloved of God, together with the patriarch, followed them with appropriate acclamations.

When these things had been done, the emperors again addressed the synod in these words: “Let the definition issued by you be read in a clear voice, so that it may be heard by us and by the entire people standing here and loving Christ.” The whole synod assenting, Cosmas, the deacon beloved of God and cubicularius, read the definition that had been delivered to him.

When it had been read, the emperors asked: “Let the holy and Ecumenical Synod declare whether the definition that has been read was issued with the consent of all of you.”

They cried out: “Thus we believe; thus we all think; with one consent we have all subscribed! This is the faith of the Apostles; this is the faith of the Fathers; this is the faith of the orthodox; this faith has established the whole world!

“We believe in one God, praised together in the Trinity, and we salute his honorable images! Let those who do not hold this be anathema! Let those who do not think this way be expelled from the Church! We follow the ancient institution of the Catholic Church! We anathematize those who add anything to or subtract anything from the Catholic Church! We anathematize the adventitious novelty of those who accuse Christians! We receive the venerable images! We subject those who do not think this way to anathema!

“Anathema to those who apply the sayings of sacred Scripture against idols to the venerable images! Anathema to him who does not salute the holy images! Anathema to those who call the sacred images idols! Anathema to those who say that Christians approach the images as though they were gods! Anathema to those who say that we were liberated from idols by anyone other than Christ our God!

“Anathema to those who dare to say that the Catholic Church ever received idols! Anathema to all heretics! Anathema to the council that raged against the venerable images! Anathema to him who receives the impious writings of their heresy! Anathema to Theodosius, the false bishop of Ephesus! Anathema to Sisinnius, surnamed Pastillas! Anathema to Basil of the ill-omened name, Tricaccabus!

“The Trinity has overthrown the three doctrines! Anathema to Anastasius, Constantine, and Nicetas, who successively presided over the see of Constantinople, as a new Arius, Nestorius, and Dioscorus! Anathema to John of Nicomedia and Constantine of Nacoleia, heresiarchs! They despised the image of the Lord and his saints; the Lord despised them.”

If anyone does not confess Christ our God as circumscribed according to his humanity [Col. 0478D], let him be anathema!

If anyone does not accept the evangelical histories expressed in images, let him be anathema!

If anyone does not salute them, since they are in the name of the Lord and his saints, let him be anathema!

If anyone rejects every ecclesiastical tradition, whether written or unwritten, let him be anathema!

After these acclamations, the patriarch offered the emperors the volume containing the written definition and requested, together with the entire synod, that it be authenticated and strengthened by their pious subscriptions. The most religious empress, auspiciously resplendent, received it and subscribed; she then gave it to her co-reigning son so that he too might subscribe. When this had been done, the definition was returned to the patriarch by Stauracius, the most illustrious patrician and logothete of the dromos.

Then, with unanimous consent, all the bishops acclaimed the emperors as follows:

“Many years to the emperors! Many years to Constantine and Irene his mother! Many years to the orthodox emperors! Many years to the victorious emperors! Many years to the peaceful emperors! Eternal memory to the new Constantine and the new Helena! May God preserve their empire! O Lord, grant them a peaceful life! O Lord, may their empire endure! Heavenly King, protect the earthly rulers!”

[Col. 0479B] After the auspicious acclamations, the emperors ordered that the judgments of the Fathers be read from those that had previously been recited in the metropolis of Nicaea and set forth in the fourth session: namely, John Chrysostom’s homily to Meletius, bishop of Antioch; Asterius, bishop of Amaseia, on Euphemia the martyr; John, bishop of Thessalonica, from sermons written by him against the pagans; the letter of Saint Symeon Stylites to the emperor Justin; the letter of the blessed Nilus the Solitary to the prefect Olympiodorus; and chapter eighty-two of the canons of the holy and Ecumenical Sixth Synod.

When these had been read and heard by the emperors themselves, by the most excellent princes, and by the people who loved Christ, all were moved in heart and assented to the truth. Then again the bishops beloved of God acclaimed what was fitting together with the multitude of the people.

For the aforesaid imperial house was filled with a throng of people: the entire city was present, together with the military formations. They rose from their seats, gave glory to God, and, rejoicing, offered thanks to him, since this had been pleasing to him.

## ECCLESIASTICAL CANONS

[Note: From the version of Anastasius the Librarian, which we compared with the Jolyano manuscript.]

PROMULGATED BY THE SAME SYNOD

### I. That the sacred canons must be preserved in every respect

For those who have received the sacred dignity, the forms of the canonical precepts constitute testimonies and directions. Gladly receiving them, we sing with David, the God-speaker, to the Lord God, saying: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches. You commanded justice; your testimonies are forever. Give me understanding, and enliven me [and I shall live]” (Ps. 118 [119]).

If the prophetic voice commands us to preserve God’s testimonies forever and to live in them, they certainly remain unaltered [Gr., “unshaken”] and unmoved. For Moses, the seer of God, said: “Nothing is to be added to them, and nothing is to be taken away from them” (Deut. 4). And the divine Apostle, glorying in them, cries out: “Into which things the angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1). And: “If an angel should preach to you anything beyond what you received, let him be anathema” [Col. 0480A] (Gal. 1).

Since these things stand and bear witness, we rejoice in them like one who has found great spoils. We lovingly store the divine canons in our hearts and hold their entire precept inviolate and immovable: both those issued by the holy trumpets of the Spirit from the blessed and most praiseworthy Apostles, and those promulgated by the six holy and Ecumenical Councils and by the councils assembled locally for the exposition of such decrees, as well as those demonstrably delivered by our holy Fathers.

For, illumined by one and the same Spirit, they defined what is expedient. Those whom they hand over to anathema, we too anathematize; those whom they depose, we too depose; those whom they segregate, we too segregate. Those whom they hand over to an epitimium—that is, to a penalty—we likewise subject to a similar penalty.

“For the conduct of life must be without avarice; be content with present things,” openly cries the divine Apostle Paul, who ascended to the third heaven and heard ineffable words (Heb. 13).

[Note: “Epitimium is a penalty imposed for observance according to the measure of the offense,” says Anastasius in the Jolyano manuscript.]

### II. That a bishop-elect must cautiously promise to observe the canons; otherwise he must not be consecrated

Since, while singing, we promise God: “I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words” (Ps. 118 [119]), it is salutary for all Christians to observe this, but especially for those who have attained hierarchical dignity.

Therefore we define that everyone who is to be advanced to the rank of bishop must know the Psalter in every respect, so that through this every cleric under him may likewise be admonished and instructed. The metropolitan must diligently inquire whether he is prepared to read carefully and not superficially both the sacred canons and the holy Gospel, the book of the divine Apostle, and all divine Scripture, and whether he lives according to God’s commandments and teaches the people entrusted to him.

For the substance of our high priesthood consists in the words delivered by God, that is, in the true discipline of the divine Scriptures, as the great Dionysius declares. If he hesitates [Gr., “if he hesitates and is unwilling to do and teach in this way”; another reading, “if he has not readily promised to do and teach in this way”], he must not be consecrated at all. For God says prophetically: “You have rejected knowledge, and I will reject you, so that you shall not serve as my priest” (Hos. 4).

### III. That rulers must not choose a bishop

Every election of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon made by rulers shall remain invalid, according to the rule that says (Apostolic Canon 30): “If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed; and let all who communicate with him be segregated” [Gr., “let him be segregated, and all who…”].

For it is necessary that the one who is to be advanced to the episcopate be chosen by bishops, just as the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea defined in their rule, which says (Canon 4): “A bishop should most especially be ordained by all the bishops in the province. If this is difficult, either because of urgent necessity or because of the length of the journey, then, in every case, three should assemble for the same purpose, while the others give their consent by letter; and then the consecration should take place. The confirmation of what is done in each province should be assigned to the metropolitan bishop.”

### IV. That bishops must abstain from accepting every kind of gift
The divine Apostle Paul, preacher of the Church, as though laying down a canon for the presbyters of Ephesus—or rather, for the entire consecrated multitude—declared with confidence, saying: “I have coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing. I have shown you everything, because by laboring in this way one ought to support the weak” (Acts 20), considering it more blessed to give. Therefore, instructed by him, we too decree that a bishop must under no circumstances contrive excuses for sins on account of sordid profit, or seek gold, silver, or any other kind of gift from bishops, clergy, or monks subject to him. For the Apostle says: “The unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6); and: “Children ought not to store up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children” (2 Cor. 12).

Therefore, whoever is found, on account of the exaction of gold or any other kind of gift, or on account of his own [corrupt] inclination, restraining someone from ministry or excluding any of the clergy living under him, or closing a venerable church so that God’s services may not be celebrated there, and thus turning his madness upon senseless things, is truly senseless. Accordingly, being subjected to a similar punishment, let his pain return upon his own head, as upon one who transgresses God’s command and the apostolic commandments. For Peter, the chief of the apostles, also commands: “Tend the flock of God that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly, according to God; not for sordid gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Pet. 5).

### V. That those who reproach clergy because they were ordained in the church without gifts are subject to a penalty [epitimion].

[Col. 0481D]

A sin unto death occurs when certain sinners persist without correction. This is still worse if, puffed up with arrogance, they rise up against piety and truth; and, preferring mammon to obedience to God, pay no attention whatsoever to His canonical commands. The Lord God is not in such people unless, once humbled, they perhaps repent of their own transgression. They ought rather to draw near to God, seek forgiveness and pardon for this sin with a contrite heart, and not glory in an illicit gift. For “the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 33).

Therefore, concerning those who boast that they were ordained in the church through the giving of gold, and who place their hope in this wicked custom—which alienates one from God and from every priesthood—and who consequently, with shameless face and uncovered mouth, insult with reproachful words those who, because of the virtue of their life, have been chosen and appointed by the Holy Spirit without giving gold: we decree first that they receive the lowest rank of their order; and if they persist, let them be corrected by a penalty.

But if anyone is found to have done this at any time in connection with a consecration, let what follows be enacted according to the apostolic rule, which says (Canon 30): “If any bishop obtains this dignity through money, or a presbyter or deacon, let both him and the one who consecrated him be deposed, and let him be entirely cut off even from communion, just as Simon Magus was by me, Peter.”

Likewise, according to the second rule of the holy Fathers who assembled at Chalcedon, which says: “If any bishop performs a consecration for money, and reduces to a price the grace that cannot be sold, and ordains for money a bishop, chorepiscopus, presbyters, deacons, or any of those counted among the clergy; or appoints for money an economus, defensor, mansionarius, or absolutely anyone subject to the rule, for the sake of sordid profit: whoever attempts to do this, if convicted, shall incur the peril of his own rank. And the one who has been consecrated shall gain nothing from the consecration or advancement effected through this commerce; rather, let him be excluded from the dignity and [or: the administration] that he obtained through money.

“If, however, anyone appears as an intermediary in such shameful and illicit gifts [profits]: if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be excommunicated.”

### VI. That a local synod is to be held annually

Since there is a rule which says (Council of Nicaea, canon 5): “Twice each year, regular investigations ought to be held in every province through an assembly of bishops.” [Col. 0482D] Because of the weariness involved, and so that those who are to assemble may have suitable opportunities for making the journey [Greek: “because they are burdened by poverty in making the journey”], the holy Fathers of the Sixth Synod decreed (canon 8), with every excuse removed, that such a gathering be held in every possible way once a year and that abuses be corrected.

[Note: Anastasius’s words: “Do not be troubled if we do not possess this definition, since we do not accept into authoritative use some of those that we have among the canons, just as we do not accept certain canons from the councils. Some are observed only among the Greeks, while others are adopted into ecclesiastical observance only in particular provinces. Such are canons 16 and 17 of the Council of Laodicea, which are observed only among the Greeks, as well as canons 6 and 8 of the African councils, which, as is known, no province observes except Africa.”]

We therefore renew this canon also; and if any ruler is found to prohibit it, let him be deprived of communion. But if any metropolitan neglects to carry this out without necessity, compulsion, or some reasonable occasion, let him be subject to canonical penalties.

When the synod is being held [Greek: “When the synod has been completed”] concerning canonical and evangelical matters, the assembled bishops ought to devote themselves to meditation and concern for the observance of the divine and life-giving commandments of the Lord. For there is great reward in keeping them: “The commandment is a lamp; the law is light; and reproof and discipline are the way of life” (Prov. 6); and “the commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18).

Moreover, the metropolitan must not have permission to demand from the things a bishop brings with him either an animal or any other gift. If he is convicted of having done this, let him repay fourfold.

### VII. That newly built churches dedicated without deposited relics of the saints ought to be supplied with them

[Col. 0483B]

The divine Apostle Paul says: “The sins of some are manifest, while those of others follow afterward” (1 Tim. 5). Thus, when sins precede, other sins follow upon them. The impious heresy of those who accuse Christians was followed by other forms of impiety. For just as they removed the faces of the venerable images from the Church, so they also abandoned certain other practices, which ought to be renewed and again maintained according to written and unwritten legislation.

Therefore, concerning all venerable churches that have been consecrated without the holy relics of martyrs, we decree that the deposition of relics, together with the customary prayer, be carried out in them. If, from the present time onward, a bishop is found consecrating a church without relics, let him be deposed, as one who transgresses the traditions of the Church.

### VIII. That Hebrews are not to be received unless they have been converted with a sincere heart

Since those who persist in the superstition of the Hebrews, while pretending to become Christians, imagine that they are mocking Christ God: they deny Him, secretly and covertly keep the Sabbath, and practice other things in the Jewish manner. We decree that such people be received neither into communion, nor into prayer, nor into the church; rather, let them openly be Hebrews according to their religion. Their children are not to be baptized, nor is a slave to be bought or acquired [Greek: “to buy or possess”].

But if any one of them converts with a sincere heart and faith, and confesses wholeheartedly, making public their customs and practices so that others too may be reproved and corrected, we decree that this person be received and baptized, together with his children; indeed, they are also to be kept under watch [made cautious], so that they may withdraw from Jewish inventions. Others, however, are in no way to be admitted.

### IX. On not concealing any book of the heresy that accuses Christians

All the childish mockeries, insane ravings, and written works falsely produced against the venerable images ought to be delivered to the episcopate of Constantinople, so that they may be stored with the books of the other heretics. If anyone is found concealing such things, then, if he is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, let him be deposed; but if he is a monk or layman, let him be anathematized.

### X. That a cleric ought not to leave his parish and transfer to another without the knowledge of his bishop

Since certain clerics, despising the canonical constitution, leave their own parish and rush to other parishes—and especially in this royal city, preserved by God, they place themselves at the disposal of rulers, celebrating Masses in their oratories—it is not permitted to receive them into any house or church without their own bishop and the bishop of Constantinople. If anyone does this and persists in it, let him be deposed.

Moreover, all who do this with the knowledge of the aforementioned priests are not permitted to undertake worldly and secular concerns, especially since the sacred canons prohibit them from doing so. Whoever among those called “elders” is found maintaining such a charge must either cease or be deposed. Rather, let him remain devoted to teaching both children and servants, reading the divine Scriptures to them; for this too is why he attained the priesthood.

### XI. That there ought to be economi in episcopal residences and ministries

Since we are all bound to observe the sacred writings and to preserve inviolate the rule which says that there are to be economi in every church (Council of Chalcedon, canon 26), we must maintain it in every way. If each metropolitan has appointed an economus in his own church, that is good. But if not, the bishop of Constantinople, by his own authority [Greek: “special authority”], has permission to appoint an economus in that church. The same applies to metropolitans if the bishops subject to them have not taken care to appoint economi in their churches. The same rule is also to be observed in monasteries.

### XII. That a bishop or abbot ought not to alienate anything from the suburban properties of the church

If any bishop or abbot is found transferring anything from the revenues [lands or estates] of the episcopate or monastery into the hands of rulers, or granting it to any other person, let what has been given be null, according to [Greek: “let the alienation be void according to”] the canon of the holy apostles, which says (canon 39): “Let the bishop have care of all ecclesiastical property and administer it as one watched by God; but it is not permitted for him to defraud anything from it or give to his own relatives what belongs to God. If they are poor, let him distribute to the poor; but let not the things belonging to the church be defrauded [Greek: “sold”] under their pretext.”

Even if they offer the excuse that the property causes loss and that the land produces no profit, the field or place must not for that reason be transferred to rulers who have the power [the reading is uncertain], but to clergy or cultivators. If a ruler, using cunning, buys a field from a tenant or cleric, the sale is nevertheless null, and the property is to be restored to the episcopate or monastery. The bishop or abbot who does this is likewise to be removed—the bishop from the episcopate and the abbot from the monastery—as one who wickedly scatters what he did not gather.

### XIII. That those who turn monasteries into common dwellings are under great condemnation

Since, on account of the calamity that has occurred in the churches because of our sins, certain venerable houses—both episcopal residences and monasteries—have been seized by certain men and made into common lodgings: if those who hold them wish to return them so that they may be restored according to their former condition [Greek: “to their original state”], that is good and most fitting. Otherwise, if they belong to the sacred order, we command that they be deposed; but if they are monks or laymen, let them be excommunicated, since it is clear that they have been condemned by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Let them be assigned to the place “where the worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished” (Isa. 66; Mark 9), because they oppose the Lord’s command, which says: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce” (John 2).

### XIV. That no one ought to read at the public assembly over the ambo without the laying on of hands

[Col. 0485C]

It is clear to everyone that order must be preserved in the consecrated ministry [Greek: “priesthood”], and that preserving the promotions of the priesthood with diligence is wholly pleasing to God. Since we see certain people receiving the clerical tonsure from childhood without the laying on of hands, and, before receiving the bishop’s laying on of hands, reading irregularly at the public assembly over the ambo, we command that this no longer be done. The same rule is also to be observed among monks.

Each abbot has permission to perform the laying on of hands of a reader only in his own monastery, provided that it is known that the abbot himself has received the laying on of hands from a bishop according to the custom for appointing abbots, and provided that he is a presbyter. Likewise, according to ancient custom, chorepiscopi ought to promote readers by the bishop’s instruction [or: through the bishop’s authorization].

### XV. That a cleric ought not to be enrolled in two churches

From this time onward, a cleric must not be enrolled in two churches. This is a matter of commerce, the characteristic of sordid profit, and is entirely foreign to ecclesiastical custom. For we have heard from the Lord’s own voice: “No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will support the one and despise the other” (Matt. 6).

Therefore, according to the apostolic word (1 Cor. 7), everyone ought to remain in the state in which he was called and be assigned to one church. Whatever is obtained through sordid profit in ecclesiastical matters is alien to God. For the necessities of this life there are various occupations; from these, whoever wishes may acquire what is suitable for the body. The Apostle says: “These hands served for my needs and for those who were with me” (Acts 20).

This rule applies in this city, which is preserved by God. In the villages outside, however, indulgence may be granted because of the scarcity of people.

### XVI. That a consecrated person ought not to wear expensive clothing

All ostentation and bodily adornment are foreign to the consecrated order. Therefore, bishops or clerics who adorn themselves in gleaming and splendid garments ought to be corrected. If they persist in this, let them be subjected to a penalty. The same applies to those who anoint themselves with perfumes.

Since the heresy of those who slander Christians has arisen as a root of bitterness and contamination has occurred in the catholic Church, those who embraced it not only abhorred painted images but also rejected every form of reverence, offending [or: hating] those who live religiously and piously. Thus what is written is fulfilled in them: “The worship of God is an abomination to the sinner.”

Therefore, if they are found mocking those clothed in inexpensive and religious garments, let them be corrected by a penalty. In ancient times every consecrated person lived in a modest and inexpensive garment. For everything acquired not for one’s necessity but for elegance bears the accusation of arrogance [or: the guilt of luxury], as the great Basil says. No one, moreover, used to wear a garment variegated with silk fabrics, nor did anyone add ornaments of different colors to the hems of his garments. They had heard from the divinely inspired tongue that “those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11).

### XVII. That whoever does not possess what is sufficient for completion must not begin to build an oratory

Since certain monks, abandoning their monasteries and longing to preside while refusing to obey, begin to construct oratories without possessing what is necessary for completion, whoever is seen doing this is to be prohibited by the bishop of the place. But if he possesses sufficient funds for completing what he desires, the work may be brought to completion. The same rule is also to be observed with regard to laymen and clerics.

### XVIII. That women ought not to live in episcopal residences or men’s monasteries

The divine Apostle says: “Be without offense both to those within and to those outside” (1 Cor. 10). But for women to dwell in an episcopal residence or monastery is a source of every offense. Therefore, if anyone is found keeping a slavewoman or free woman in an episcopal residence, or in a monastery for the performance of some service, let him be rebuked. If he persists, let him be deposed.

If it happens that there are women on the suburban estates and the bishop or abbot wishes to travel to them [Greek: “there”], then, while the bishop or abbot is present, the woman must in no way perform the monastery’s work at that time. Rather, for the sake of irreproachability, she must remain separately in another place until the bishop or abbot departs.

### XIX. That the admissions [sponsiones] of consecrated men, virgins, monks, and nuns are to be made without gifts

The crime of avarice has become so entrenched among the rulers of churches that even certain men and women called religious, forgetting the Lord’s commandments, are deceived and, through gold, arrange the entrance [reception] of those approaching both the consecrated order and the monastic life. Hence it happens that, as the great Basil says, when the beginning is blameworthy, everything must be cast away. For it is not permitted to serve God through mammon.

If anyone is found doing this—whether he is a bishop, abbot, or anyone from the consecrated college—let him either cease or be deposed, according to the second rule of the holy Council of Chalcedon. Let an abbess be expelled from the monastery and handed over to another monastery for subjection. The same applies to an abbot who has not received the laying on of hands of a presbyter.

But whatever parents give to their children in the manner of a dowry, or whatever is offered from their own possessions by those who declare that they are dedicating it to God [Greek: “dedicated”], we decree that it remain in the monastery according to their promise, whether they persevere or depart, unless the fault lies with the superior.

### XX. That henceforth a double monastery ought not to be established, and concerning existing double monasteries

From this point onward we decree that no double monastery be established, because it becomes a scandal and stumbling block to many. If some wish to renounce the world together with their relatives and pursue the monastic life, the men ought to enter a monastery of men, and the women to enter a monastery of women; for in this way God is appeased.

As for those that have hitherto been double, let them follow the rule of our holy Father Basil and be organized according to his instruction. Monks and nuns must not live in one monastery, for cohabitation gives rise to adultery. A monk must not secretly approach a nun for conversation, nor a nun a monk. A monk must not sleep in a women’s monastery, nor dine alone with a nun. When necessities of life are brought from the men’s side to the community, the abbess of the women’s monastery, accompanied by an elderly nun, must receive them outside the gate.

If a monk wishes to see one of his female relatives, let him converse with her in the presence of the abbess, using only a few and concise words, and let him depart from her shortly afterward.

### XXI. That monks ought not to abandon their own monasteries and transfer to others

[Col. 0488A]

A monk or nun ought not to leave his or her own monastery and depart for another. If this should happen, the person must necessarily be received as a guest; but it is not proper to admit the person without the consent of his or her abbot.

### XXII. That, if it happens, monks may eat with women with thanksgiving, complete restraint, and reverence

To entrust everything to God and not serve one’s own desires is a great matter. For, whether you eat or drink, the divine Apostle says, “do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10).

Therefore Christ our God commanded in His Gospels that the beginnings of sins be cut away. He does not prohibit adultery alone, but also condemns the movement of thought toward the commission of adultery, saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Instructed by this, we ought to cleanse our thoughts. For although everything is lawful, not everything is beneficial, as we are taught by the apostolic word (1 Cor. 6).

It is therefore necessary for every human being to eat in order to live. Among those whose life involves marriage, children, and ordinary lay affection, men and women eating together exposes no one to reproach, provided that they give thanks to the one who supplies the food and do not appear to worship, through certain theatrical pleasures, Satan’s image—through singers, harps, and the contortions of prostitutes.

Upon such people will come the prophetic curse, which says: “Woe to those who drink wine with harp and psaltery, but do not regard the works of the Lord or understand the works of His hands” (Isa. 5). If such people are found anywhere among Christians, let them be corrected. Otherwise, let the rules already promulgated concerning them prevail.

But those whose life is solitary [quiet and solitary] and governed by a single discipline—namely, those who profess to take upon themselves the Lord’s solitary yoke—ought to sit and keep silence. Nor is it permitted in any way for those who have chosen the consecrated life to dine privately with women, except perhaps with certain God-fearing and reverent men or women, so that the meal itself may contribute to spiritual edification and the same may be achieved among relatives.

Again, if on a journey a monk or consecrated person happens not to be carrying what is necessary for food and, because of necessity, turns aside either to a hospice [public lodging] or to someone’s house, he has permission to do so, since necessity compels it.

## A PRAISE SERMON

Pronounced before the holy synod by Epiphanius, deacon of the Church of Catana in the province of Sicily, and locum-tenens of Thomas, archbishop of the island of Sardinia.

Blessed the prophet Isaiah, having received the divine Spirit and foreseeing very well the redemption of the nations accomplished through Christ, and not being unaware of the multitude of those who were to be saved through him, declared somewhere, as from the person of God, to those who in each successive age receive the oversight of the sacred sheepfolds:

“Walk through my gates, and lead my people, and cast the stones out of the way” (Isaiah 62:10).

What are these gates understood to be, unless they are the divinely inspired Scriptures and the words of the holy prophets? These, like certain intellectual gates, rational shepherds open by interpretation; thus they bring them to the broad and true door, namely, our Lord Jesus Christ, who truly became the door to the Father for us, just as he himself says: “I am the door” (John 10:9).

The stones that have been cast out of the way are perhaps the stumbling blocks of the heretical faction. Like stones placed upon the pathway of our faith, they wickedly strive to hinder those who wish to hasten toward Christ, who is the true way, rushing, insofar as they can, to close the road of salvation to them. Again, this way is understood to be our Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself says: “I am the way” (John 14:6).

Therefore, after the most skilled priests, under the guidance of the Spirit, have ingeniously and artfully cleared the scandals of the heretics—as though they were stones—from our way, that is, from the path of faith, they not only hurl them back against the heads of those who cast them, but also in this manner make the path leading to the way [perhaps: to life] easy and well trodden for the subject peoples, so that they can understand and say:

“Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been set free. Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 123:7–8).

Behold, then, the divine assembly of priests, following the Lord’s commandments, has gathered here to order and elucidate, through the teachings of the Fathers, the venerable mystery of Christ’s dispensation. They do not preach this as though they were proclaiming it to the peoples for the first time, since it had been preached throughout the whole world nearly eight hundred years ago. Rather, they have opened with the greatest clarity to the peoples, through interpretations of divine Scripture, that saving counsel which was accomplished through him; and they have judged the heretics, dashed against those very stones, or spirits—or dung [perhaps: “dashed against the Father by the Spirit, or, quite appropriately, regarded as dung”; perhaps: “as dung, or like dung”], to be thoroughly fitting [perhaps: “to be thoroughly fitting as dung”].

For they know the prophetic voice crying out to them, as though also from the person of God:

“Priests, hear and bear witness to the house of Israel” (Amos 6:1), unquestionably the spiritual house.

Joining them as well, since we share their judgment insofar as it lies within us, we congratulate this splendid choir. Moved by the desire of our mind, we stir our pen and strive to contribute whatever it is able to offer; we seek to celebrate the present occasion in words appropriate to the time and to crown this spectacle with flowers of praise. Nothing prevents us: even if, because of poverty and perhaps weakness of understanding, we cannot reach it perfectly, we hasten to contribute what lies within our power. Often a small pebble, placed among great stones, has pretended, insofar as it could, to have contributed firmness to them.

What our discourse is, then, let it be brought into the midst, to be examined with great kindness by the divine money-changers [Note: “From the words of the Lord, which are quoted by the ancient Fathers and are not found among the evangelists: ‘Be good money-changers.’”], and tested by divinely inspired Scripture.

O most sacred assembly, save again for uprightness the human being formed in the image of God, both above and below; and may you merit [or: purchase] for him a return to his original beauty, which was taken away through negligence and restored again through care. For this the observances of the legal commandments, the accounts of people who, in the manner of history, conducted themselves well or badly in the world, the sacred utterances of the Psalms, and the proverbial teachings that recount moral philosophy for us have explained with great diligence.

But it was impossible for our nature, which had easily fallen and been subjected to sin, that ancient nature from which it fell in Adam, readily to recover its dignity. It needed instead another, robust and unconquerable power, a superior power that would heal it from the diseased condition of its swollen wounds and restore it to stronger health with a kind of generous increase.

Knowing this, therefore, the choir of prophets, moved by the divine Spirit, announced such blessings to it in various places and in various ways, each one proclaiming them in his own time. They foretold that the Son and Word of God the Father, coeternal and consubstantial with him, moved by the riches of his goodness toward our extremity, would perfectly assume our nature and reform it into antiquity through the invisible and immaterial fire of his divinity.

One prophet proclaimed the conception without intercourse and the pure, virginal birth; another, universal dominion [perhaps: dominions], the destruction and diminution of the transgression that had prevailed from Adam and had been committed in Adam down to the law, together also with the devil’s offense. Another proclaimed the fatal downfall of Satan himself and of the demons who became apostates with him, from the presence of the appearing God, and the incomparable thanksgiving to be offered by us who have been redeemed to the Redeemer for the exceedingly abundant blessings accomplished in us.

Another proclaimed the voluntary passion of God incarnate, his descent into hell, and his powerful return from hell with the souls that had been held by those inescapable bonds. Another, our glorious return to the Father who is in heaven and our sitting at the Father’s right hand. Another, the advent of the Spirit, descending from heaven and granted to us who believe in him without envy [Greek: ἄφθονον, that is, abundant], and the swift circuit of evangelical preaching among all the nations; and, resulting from this throughout the world, the complete destruction of idols, brought about through a pure return to our one and only true God, together with the uninterrupted and perpetual worship that is intelligibly and spiritually offered to him by us throughout the whole earth.

All these things were brought to completion in their proper times according to the truth, and received a most glorious end. Hear, then, Paul crying out with a loud voice and confirming this truth:

“God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed on in the world, was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16).

O the utterance [perhaps: “the discourse”] of the great teacher! “God,” he says, “was manifested in the flesh”—the cause of every good, unfailing gift, wholly sufficient riches, an everlasting fountain of gifts that cannot be taken away, food for those who hunger without exhaustion, life-giving bread from heaven, an unceasing stream for those who thirst, from which whoever drinks will never thirst forever (John 4:14).

He was manifested in the flesh; but he also says that he was believed on in the world. How was he believed on in the world? Tell us, blessed Paul. Instruct us from those secret words with which you were instructed in the hidden places of paradise. Instruct us now also through the preaching of which you were appointed preacher and apostle to all the nations. Pour into the present Church the word of truth; extinguish the spiritual sight of the heretics, as once happened to Elymas the magician (Acts 13:11); express with confidence the mystery of the dispensation.

For even after death you speak words more excellent, and in the Spirit you accomplish whatever you will. The teacher also says:

“To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given among the nations: to evangelize, namely, the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all, and to teach what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages by God, who created all things” (Ephesians 3:8–9).

Therefore listen. “He was believed on,” he says, “in the world,” reconciling all things to himself and making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven (Colossians 1:20).

O this sublime preaching! O this ineffable mercy! The only-begotten Son of God, reconciling all things to himself, made peace through the blood of his cross.

How, then, do certain people, after such an ineffable reconciliation, assert that we are again becoming enemies of the former rebels? How have they dared to say that Christians worship idols after the recognition of the one and only true God? Especially since the prophet cries out in a manner against the complete destruction of these things and says:

“On that day the Lord will appear and will destroy the gods of the nations of the earth; and each one will worship him from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zechariah 13:2).

Behold, we have heard of the overthrow of idols and of the worship to be offered to God by each person from his own place. How, then, are we who do this accused of idolatry? Who could possibly renew the ancient error of idols upon the earth?

For if the most wicked demons, who are appeased through these things, are able to do this, how will the whole mystery of the dispensation not be destroyed, when holy Scripture openly cries out:

“He struck his enemies on their backsides” (Psalm 78:66)?

By this it indicates that Christ also gave them everlasting disgrace. For whoever is able to accomplish something is unquestionably numbered not among the dead but among the living.

How, moreover, will he speak the truth when he strengthens his own disciples and encourages everyone to undertake manfully whatever difficulties may arise, saying:

“Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33)?

For if those whom he promises here to have conquered were able to take this victory away from him again through rebellion, then such a thing will certainly not be called victory, nor will it be counted among brave deeds. For how will it be victory if the liberator does not win the liberated to the end, but is reduced to struggles like those by which the people previously conquered were overcome—or rather, to stronger ones?

To possess something and then lose it will, in my reckoning, be counted as a greater sign of weakness than never to have acquired and possessed it. Now where, do you suppose, are the statues [or: “the downfall”] of the idols that you who say these things have set up? And if it is in the ancient seats of demonic temples, this will still not be charged as a crime against Christians.

For we see remnants of ancient demonic temples left by former generations in certain places, either, as I think, for the display of those who sacrificed in them, or even as a memorial that we have been redeemed, leading to thanksgiving through visible and feeble representations. From these, they say, abominable forms of Christian worship have been made—forms from which we were rescued through Christ—unless such things were found in our most Christian churches.

O the wickedness that results from this! O the worst blasphemy! For how could this happen where Christ is the head and foundation, according to the wisest Paul (1 Corinthians 3:11)?

We Christians have truly been deprived of our hope; we have also been deceived by the words of the preachers who proclaimed that God came into the world to free us from the superstition of demons.

How, then, could they have said this at all? Let us ask those who think in this way: Was this done with the permission of our head, or perhaps while he wished that it should not happen but was unable to provide assistance? And how, consequently, would this not be the whole of blasphemy?

For if the most sacred Paul is truthful when he calls Christ the Son of God “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), how, I ask, could the unconquerable power and wisdom of the Father—which grants existence to all things—have been surpassed by anything that exists?

It is evident that, if this happened to him, they will not drive away from such accusations even that which is not this. For how can God the almighty, the powerful and mighty Father, still be called such if the things removed by his power have been made subject to enemies? Or how did the Son permit the Church, which he betrothed to himself with his own blood, to serve such savage and merciless spirits again?

Especially since the hymn-writer says:

“For according to the height of heaven above the earth, the Lord has confirmed his mercy over those who fear him” (Psalm 103:11).

For if he became incarnate in order to free us from their hand, according to the prophetic declarations, and if, as they say, we were freed only for a short time, then it was not real but merely supposed. For he became the cause not of the sword [perhaps: “joy”], but of a more abundant and difficult servitude, making our enemies more ferocious in proportion as, in our opinion, we mocked them after being freed.

But where is the continuous mercy that he promised to confirm over us as vast as the height of heaven above the earth, thereby indicating its infinity? Or how is it said that he has removed our iniquities from us as far as the east is from the west—a sign of complete redemption—if we are still entangled in the same errors?

Certainly we see that the most skilled physicians, when through the diligence of their art they have helped someone lying sick in body and restored him to health, do not withdraw the experience of their art as soon as they have freed him from his present illness. Rather, they carefully fortify the course of his life through certain aids, able to bring about vigilance, so that perhaps through inexperience he may not again be overwhelmed by the same troubles.

But again, if it is true—as it has also been demonstrated—that the only-begotten Son of God and the Father assumed our nature, it is clear that he enriched it with his own blessings and filled it with the Spirit of God’s preeminent gifts, so that thereafter it would need no assistance from any other age [saeculi; perhaps: “second” (secundi)], having once received strength from the one who assumed it.

This, I think, is also what the blessed Evangelist indicates when he says that at the time of Christ our Savior’s baptism he saw the Holy Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him (Mark 1:10; John 1:32), signifying that the Word had henceforth enriched the nature without addition [perhaps: “without rejection”].

For he who is in every respect coequal with the Spirit did not need the Spirit’s advent from heaven, insofar as the nature proper to him is concerned. Would he acquire an increase of holiness in himself who bears within himself the Father’s characteristics and is in no way changed in his consubstantiality with the Spirit?

Rather, he prefigured our grace in himself. For by him and in him we have again been enriched with that of which we were deprived in Adam, and the ancient dignity of our nature returned.

Therefore, if the grace of the Spirit is read to have descended upon him and remained—and this certainly must not be rejected [for him]—it appeared that the Word had thereafter preserved the nature; and it follows plainly that such grace passed into the whole human race.

How, then, are we accused of having truly sinned through ignorance and of having offered to idols the honor that ought to be shown to God? For we have been enriched through Christ with such grace.

This must be said to those who presume to speak about everything. But if they confess that we obtained through Christ these blessings beyond expression, yet afterward were again subjected to our former errors, then according to them the grace given through the Spirit was weakened, so that it did not remain sufficient to the end with those who had once received it.

And what could be more impious or more miserable to believe? Or how could he who is altogether just, who provides life-giving power to all, the Spirit of the Father, who observes all things and is almighty, fail in his nature and succumb to measures of weakness?

Or how is this said:

“I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20)?

But can that saving utterance be admitted as true if the reality of his promises is not seen to have proceeded through works to the end? For he gave such a promise to the holy apostles who were then present with him.

How could these men have remained in the flesh until the consummation, when, remaining alive only a short time after his return to heaven, they fulfilled the law of common nature and departed this life through death?

Rather, the gift of the Gospels passes over to us: we have submitted to their preaching, and we possess Christ, who lived with them, as existing with us in the Spirit and throughout our whole life.

It is therefore fitting to lament over the error of the heretics who have despised these things in such a way, who are rebuked by doctrines so manifest, and who impiously render void such promises to the Catholic Church, detracting from them.

For she has in no way been moved from the faith handed down to her. She has remained like a chaste virgin, as it is written (2 Corinthians 11:2), preserving inviolate the pledge of Christ her bridegroom—that is, the grace of the Spirit given within her.

For this reason the divine David, previously proclaiming that the stability of the faith displayed by her would be established among many nations, declared:

“God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved”; and again: “He established the world, and it shall not be moved” (Psalms 46:5; 93:1)—even though she was attacked by the devil’s machinations.

For although some of the ancient or present-day heretics have wished to shake the foundation of evangelical preaching that was given to her, what they devised has nevertheless been reckoned to them as a deed. But immovability alone has been preserved for her forever, according to the promise of him who does not lie:

“Can a woman forget her child, so as not to have compassion on the offspring of her womb? And even if that woman should forget, yet I will not forget you, says the Lord” (Isaiah 49:15).

Having therefore dismissed the distortions of their arguments, which they have employed in these matters, and having said farewell to their chattering speeches from afar, let us delight in the opinions of the holy Fathers’ wisdom [Note: “Perhaps sapidis; the codex Jol. changes nothing, nor was it truly necessary, since saporus is used adjectivally just like sapidus.”].

They have shown that God, who came into the world in human form, freed us from the manifold error of idols. Thus the prophetic declarations proclaimed; thus apostolic grace explained. By this teaching we have been confirmed, not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but—as it is written—in a demonstration of the Spirit.

For it was not the persuasions of speeches that caused us to possess this state; that belongs to the pagans. It was the truth of the very things that have been confirmed [or: “completed”].

Where, then, is the destructive host of demons? Where are the empty and accursed sacrifices of idols? Where are the deceptive divinations of the gods of false name, corruptors of souls? Where are the frenzies of Venus, the sacred rites of Ceres, and the murders of strangers committed in the name of Diana? Where are the mad festivals of Dionysus, with their unlawful madness among men, and the just initiation [or: “proper instruction”] of the one called Mithras?

Where are the murders, committed beneath the earth, above the earth, and in the air, of the so-called gods who took pleasure in such things? Have not all these perished with the coming of the only-begotten Son of God and received the most profane of ends?

Were not their once beautifully dedicated temples later shattered by imperial commands and cast down to the ground? Have not their memories disappeared from the hearts of all Christians? And is not that saying of prophecy seen to have been accomplished in the things themselves:

“The earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the sea” (Isaiah 11:9)?

Let us therefore worship the Lord who appeared and freed us from this most savage error. Let us sing a hymn to his infinite mercy. Let us proclaim to our Church’s most lofty mountain the terrible and ineffable condescension [or: “consent”] of his dispensation.

Let us raise our voices with strength, and let us not spare the incomprehensible magnificence of his majesty as we recount the affection that he showed toward us. Let us say to him, together with the prophet:

“Who is a God like you, taking away iniquities and concealing the sins of the remnant of your inheritance?” (Micah 7:18).

Moreover, let us lead dances together with this present sacred assembly, greeting it and offering it a prize of joy.

Rejoice, then, most sacred college of the divine and consecrated assembly. Rejoice, most holy defenders of the holy Fathers. Rejoice, truthful congregation, in whose midst God walks, as it is written (Psalm 105:3).

Rejoice, council filled with spiritual manifestation, from which the soul illuminated by it will not strike its spiritual feet against the stone of heretical and false speech.

Rejoice, watcher over divine investigations; whoever follows you modestly is rescued from the threatening sword.

Rejoice, ever-flourishing paradise, in whose midst the tree of life has been planted, presiding through the fourfold table of the Gospels.

Rejoice, golden and fiery pillar of the new Israel of God, freeing it from the Egyptian hand—that is, from the error of those who make themselves heretics—through the luminous teachings of doctrine, and leading it to the land of the Fathers’ promise through orthodox belief.

Act boldly and confidently in the manifestation of truth. With unveiled face proclaim the glory of the sacred and Catholic Church. Establish the wavering minds of certain people upon the rock of steadfast conduct through your teachings.

And you especially, O harmonious and most sacred herald of the holy Fathers, leader of our present assembly, who adorn for us the sublime throne through Christ; most diligent mirror of the great and first Shepherd; purest dwelling-place of the Spirit; most exact balance of orthodox doctrines; renowned lamp of the polished rule of conduct lived in Christ, and wholly radiant with the lights of the seven lampstands—

Make the clarity of the most evident words shine upon us as though from the invisible lampstand of the sacred throne. Distribute life-giving bread from divine teaching to the hungry, and nourish the people who have become wanderers in a foreign land through their heretical dwelling.

Become for us a new Joseph, giver of grain, and, explaining the ambiguities of scriptural riddles, nourish us with rich and spiritual interpretations. Lift your eyes and see your sons gathered above you, sons who have been scattered by the assaults of wolves.

This entire most sacred temple of the divine decree is seen to be full for you. By frequent leaps of your mind anticipate the attacks of the beasts, and, forestalling them, exclude them through your wisdom. Always secure tranquility for your sheepfold.

May this reward be increased for you through frequent and well-sounding prayers sent forth to God, according to the promises made to Abraham in the likeness of the number of the stars.

And rejoice also, illustrious city of the Nicenes, most renowned name among the metropolises, most glorious first-fruits of the province of the Bithynians. Formerly you were sanctified by the footsteps of the holy three hundred and eighteen God-bearing Fathers; now you are likewise surrounded by the blessings and graces of their successors, three hundred and fifty in number, together with the venerable monks, whose multitude is almost innumerable.

In you the foundation of orthodoxy [orthodox faith], shaken by a certain satanic overthrow and in danger of collapse [perhaps: “about to collapse”; perhaps something is missing], received a support without disturbance.

In you that savage and pitiless beast, namely Arius, was captured by that divine choir of the Fathers in the sacred nets of the spread-out Scriptures, and struck down by terrible anathemas. From this we have learned to proclaim that the Son of God and of the Father is Lord and consubstantial with his begetter.

For this reason the present sacred gathering, completed by this numerous assembly, was decreed to be convened and strengthened by the harmony of the pious emperors: Irene, the new Helena, with her own son Constantine, the new Constantine. May the grace of the Spirit—which then and now has illumined the holy Fathers—preserve them for very long ages, granting them an undisturbed empire and casting the nations of their enemies beneath their feet, so that the abundance of good things may not fail us.

Rejoice, therefore, in these things, illustrious appearance of the metropolis; for in you both the beginning of good things first arose for us and now their end has dawned: namely, the ancient tradition of the Catholic Church concerning the venerable images has been restored within its proper bounds.

Now heaven rejoices, and the clouds drop righteousness. Now the middle wall of partition has been dissolved through the union granted to dissension, and the four quarters of the world have been gathered into one agreement of assent.

Now the many opinions that were being drawn in different directions have come together, and a harmonious hymn is directed to God from the ends of the earth to the ends of the earth.

Rejoice, then, exulting over these things, you also, Catholic Church spread throughout the entire world. Lead dances in triumph over the assembly of your children. Lay aside the rags of division and clothe yourself in the complete robe of orthodox unity.

You will no longer be made a reproach to your enemies, a mockery and derision to the peoples surrounding you. You will no longer fear the contempt of peoples—namely, the Hebrews and the Hagarenes, who remain without God and without sacred initiation—as though the perfection of faith had not been handed down to you through apostolic teachings.

You will no longer be accused by the mouths of heretics as though, because of the most fitting honor shown toward his friends, you had departed from the one God. You will no longer be considered like the temples of idols because of the erection of the most sacred images within you.

For, as the bride of the Son and Word of the King of the ages, bearing in his flesh the human form of the dispensation, it is fitting for you to carry through painting an anthropomorphic image, so that it may be known that you are the royal bride.

It is fitting for you to bear upon your most sacred walls, in painting and mosaic work [in a painting made from mosaic work], the image of the Mother of God, the Mother of Christ who betrothed you, so that the grace that shone upon you through her may be proclaimed to all peoples together by silent preaching.

For if he had not been incarnate from her, how would you be joined to so beautiful a bridegroom by spiritual union?

It is fitting for you also to bear, in works of painting, the images of all the holy apostles, prophets, confessors, patriarchs, holy Fathers, ascetics [Note: “That is, those living an ascetic and solitary life. In the codex Jol.: ‘that is, confessors.’”], martyrs, and the whole pious assembly, so that by every vision you may display the perfection of the Orient who has shone around you from above.

Some, in a manner, foretold your calling and previously betrothed you to the Bridegroom through their prophecies, as though through dowries. Others ministered the evangelical word to you and gathered for you the rational sheepfolds scattered throughout the whole earth. Others, as though through their own labors and their diligence in doctrine, purchased incorruptibility for your flocks. Still others preserved their sincere affection toward you even unto death through their own blood, and in this way demonstrated the certainty of truth within you.

Bearing a crown with myriads of heavenly angels and proclaiming with the greatest breadth, declare the virtues of him who called you from the darkness of idolatrous error into his marvelous light—that is, into himself and the Father who is without beginning, and into his coeternal and consubstantial Spirit—into the one faith and confession concerning the one nature that is above every principality.

To him be glory and dominion, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

To the most holy and blessed brother and fellow minister, the lord Adrian, senior pope of Rome, Tarasius, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, sends greetings in the Lord.

The saving dispensation of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ would indeed suffice for peace, unanimity, and concord among all Christians. For after his resurrection from the dead, he breathed upon his apostles and said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14). For this reason, that divine apostle Paul, who was caught up into the third heaven and entered paradise and heard secret words, testified to us all and asserted, saying: “Christ is our peace, who made both one; and, dissolving [variant: ‘he dissolved’] the middle wall of partition, the enmity in his flesh” (Ephesians 2). And again, instructing the Thessalonians, he said: “Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you learned, whether by word or by our letter” (2 Thessalonians 2).

But because the enemy, the devil who has been evil from the beginning, has not ceased, at various times, to tear apart and disrupt the Church built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, as seemed good to him—introducing himself through certain wicked men who follow him and sowing weeds in this field, which was cultivated by the trumpets of the Spirit, namely the holy apostles—for they, having received power from on high and having plowed this field with the furrows of divine work, left the food of eternal life for those who believed through them to gather—our holy Fathers, who in each age were its shepherds and guardians, received their God-speaking teaching and rooted out the weeds, that is, heresies and additional [surreptitiously introduced] innovations, from the roots; and they preserved the pure harvest in the field.

Therefore, your fraternal holiness, adorned with the highest priesthood, having in a manner conversed with these through your God-speaking teachings and having received from them the word of truth, hastened, in agreement with the truth of our most faithful and peace-loving emperors, to uproot with the sword of the Spirit the thorny growths that have now sprung up. In accordance with our written petition, you sent to the universal synod men bearing the same name as Peter, the prince of the apostles.

When these men arrived, our pious and most tranquil emperors received them kindly and ordered them to be sent to us; through them we received your letters. After speaking with them about the matters that were appropriate, we also summoned the men who had come from the East, John and Thomas, honored with the priesthood, sharers in word and knowledge, and richly adorned with reverence and modesty. For they too, arriving at the same time, worship here.
