Accordingly, when all the God-loving bishops of this diocese had assembled, by the command and divine zeal of our most faithful and pious emperors, a session of the synod was held. But certain men, moved by senseless impulses and causing disturbance within themselves, made us rise from the assembly; and, being prohibited, we remained silent for one year.

When the year had passed, the God-loving bishops were again ordered by our pious emperors to assemble in Nicaea, the renowned metropolis of the province of Bithynia. We too, taking with us as companions God-loving men and your guardians of the place, as well as those who had come from the East, proceeded to that same metropolis.

When we had all taken our seats, we made Christ the head. For the holy Gospel lay upon the sacred seat, testifying to all of us, the consecrated men who had assembled: “Judge with righteous judgment” (John 7). Judge between the holy Church of God and the innovation that has arisen.

When the letters of your fraternal holiness, previously sent to us, were first read, all of us sat together in a common circle [Greek: “we all sat together in a common circle”], enjoying spiritual nourishment as though at royal banquets, feasting upon what Christ had prepared for those dining through your letters. And, like an eye, you showed the whole body the path of uprightness and truth. Thus the severed members came together into unity; thus true harmony was confirmed; thus the catholic Church received unity.

When the letters sent to us from the Eastern diocese were also read, the complete beauty of the paternal tradition was displayed and the power of truth was strengthened, with many testimonies of the Fathers being set before the reading.

After these things had been accomplished, all of us who had assembled by God’s good pleasure proclaimed the upright and irreproachable confession that had been sent to us by you and, through our report, also to our pious emperors. All the heresiarchs of that wicked heresy, together with those who followed them and ended their lives without turning back, were condemned by an equal deposition [that is, deprivation of ecclesiastical office], along with those who had previously become heretics of the catholic Church [or: “had embraced heresies in the catholic Church”]. Those who were still alive confessed their salvation in written statements of their own [“while they were still surviving”].

Nor did Christ our God—the rock upon which we have been established—allow his tunic, woven throughout from above, that is, his Church, which was built by him and upon him [Greek and Codex Jolyani: “above him”], to remain torn and divided; nor did he allow the members to move in different directions and ways. Rather, together with the ancient heresies, he destroyed by the word of his grace and pierced with the sword of the Spirit the error of the empty [Greek: “new”] wickedness of those who, accusing Christians, bark madly against the venerable images.

And we were satisfied in every respect, and learned by experience that truth prevails over all things and conquers, in accordance with the voice of the one who does not lie. No one among all can resist it [Greek: “nothing at all can resist it”], and it is exceedingly strong, so that it rises up against all its enemies and disperses the legions of those who resist it.

Behold, the lips of those speaking falsehoods have ceased, and the darkness of insolent reproaches has fallen silent; the beauty of the doctrines of truth has shone forth, with heretical disgrace cast away on every side. The Church has received her adornment and has found rest from the pains that oppressed her. For she is immovable and unconquerable; against her faith the gates of hell and of unbelief will not prevail, as we have heard from the Lord’s voice (Matthew 16).

“And our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Psalm 125); and we became rejoicing in the Church over which, according to God’s will, we preside. These things were accomplished by the will of Christ, who is God over all, through our orthodox and most vigorous emperors. For they have erected venerable images everywhere, both in the most celebrated churches and in their royal palaces.

May the Lord God grant them a corresponding reward, exalting the horn of their kingdom both for the peace of his Churches and for the salvation of all Christians. And may his name be blessed forever and ever. Amen.

**To the most holy and blessed brother and fellow minister, Adrian, pope of senior Rome: Tarasius, unworthy bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, sends greetings in the Lord.**

In many ways and by many means—evangelical, apostolic, and paternal—we are taught to maintain conduct free from avarice in the sanctification of the priesthood, and not to exact gold, silver, or anything else in connection with the laying on of hands upon any consecrated person, as we shall demonstrate in the testimonies set out below, drawn both from the declarations of divine Scripture and from the teachings received from the Fathers.

For those who lay on hands are ministers of the Spirit, not sellers of the Spirit. Since they have received the grace of the Spirit freely, they are commanded to give it freely to those who receive it from them, having obtained this freedom [Greek: “generosity”] from the Lord’s word. But if anyone is convicted of having obtained this through money, such persons proclaim that he is to be cast out of the holy order. Even if he bears the name of priesthood, the statement is false in the matter [variant: “in reality”]. “No one can serve God and Mammon,” as we have learned from the Gospel (Matthew 6).

Since we have prophetically heard God crying out, “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, you priests” (Isaiah 40), and again threatening and saying: “If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not guard themselves, and the sword comes and takes a life from among them, I will require their blood at the watchman’s hand” (Ezekiel 33), we declare to all the bishops of the Churches among us, out of fear of condemnation through silence, so that with confidence, according to the divine Apostle, we may say (Acts 20): “We are clean from the blood of those who violate the canons,” and especially from the blood of those who have laid on hands, or lay on hands, for money [Greek: “or who have received the laying on of hands”]. Your fraternal holiness, which has inherited the chair of the divine Apostle Peter, deposes such men as another Simon Magus.

For this reason we do not shrink from announcing the truth, preserving and holding fast what has been canonically promulgated by the holy and most praiseworthy Apostles and by our memorable Fathers; and we abhor those who have despised any of these things.

Therefore your fraternal holiness, adorned with the highest priesthood and rightly ordering the episcopal piety according to God’s will [Greek: “governing the sacred hierarchical order”], possesses the most renowned glory. For Christ our God, the first and great high priest, said through the prophet: “I live, and I will glorify those who glorify me” (1 Kingdoms 2).

You know, O man beloved of the Spirit, that the impious heresy of Macedonius and those around him, who fight against the Spirit, is more tolerable. For while they madly profess the Spirit to be a creature and servant of God the Father, these others make him, as they claim, his own servant. For every master sells whatever he possesses, if he wishes, whether a slave or anything else among his possessions. Likewise, the buyer, wishing to become master of what he has bought, acquires it by the price of money.

Thus those who carry out this wicked act detract from the Holy Spirit, sinning equally with those who blaspheme by saying that Christ casts out demons by Beelzebul (Luke 11). And, to speak more truly, they are compared with Judas the betrayer, who sold Christ to the Jews, the killers of God, for the price of silver.

Since, then, the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with Christ our God, they too will plainly share the same portion as Judas, as has been shown. But if the priesthood is not sold—for it is clear that it cannot be sold in any way—then undoubtedly the grace of the Holy Spirit, that is, the sanctity of the priesthood, is not in them. For they do not possess what they have not received.

Let them therefore remember the holy Peter, who said to the man eager for this: “You have neither part nor share in this matter” (Acts 8). For if the dignity of the priesthood is sold, then upright conduct of life and a way of life in chastity and the other virtues are superfluous among them.

According to them, the divine Apostle Paul is also superfluous when he teaches that a bishop must be blameless, prudent, well ordered, apt to teach, self-controlled, sober, and holding fast the trustworthy word that accords with the teaching, so that he may be able to exhort with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1).

All these things therefore are brought forward against the seller and buyer of the office [variant: “they disappear”; “of the priesthood”]. Moreover, the testimonies of the saints set out below declare that anyone who has given or received anything at any time is entirely alien to the priesthood—whether before the laying on of hands, during the laying on of hands, or after the laying on of hands. For “to receive” means to receive at any time. They also remove all ecclesiastical promotions when money is given.

### Canon 29 of the holy Apostles

If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let both him and the one who ordained him be deposed and entirely cut off from communion, as Simon Magus was by me, Peter.

### From the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 8

When Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying: “Give me this power also, so that whoever I lay my hands upon may receive the Holy Spirit.”

But Peter said to him: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed through money. You have neither part nor share in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.”

### From the Third Book of Kingdoms, chapter 13

Jeroboam did not turn back from his very evil way; instead, he made priests of the high places from the lowest of the people. Whoever wished filled his hand and became a priest of the high places. Because of this, the house of Jeroboam sinned, was overthrown, and was destroyed from the face of the earth.

### From the Fourth Book of Kingdoms, chapter 5, concerning the leprosy of Gehazi

Naaman returned to the man of God with his entire retinue, came, stood before him, and said: “Truly I know that there is no other God in all the earth except in Israel alone. Therefore, I beg you, accept a blessing from your servant.”

But he replied: “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it.” And although Naaman pressed him, he absolutely refused.

A little later: “Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, said: ‘My master has spared this Syrian Naaman by not accepting from him what he brought. As the Lord lives, I will run after him and take something from him.’” And Gehazi followed after Naaman.

A little later: “Naaman said: ‘Take a talent of silver.’ And he compelled him, and bound two talents of silver in two bags, together with two changes of clothing.”

And further on: “Elisha said: ‘Where has Gehazi come from?’ He replied: ‘Your servant went nowhere.’ But he said: ‘Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you? Now therefore you have taken silver and taken clothing, so that you may buy olive groves, vineyards, sheep, oxen, male servants, and female servants. But the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your offspring forever.’ And he went out from him leprous, like snow.”

### From the interpretation of Saint Basil, bishop, on Isaiah  
*(on chapter 8, after the middle)*

He gave the law as an aid, so that they might say: “Not like this, concerning which it is not permitted to give gifts.” This law is not like the word spoken by the ventriloquists. For it was not devised for deception, as theirs was, but is a teacher of truth. Those men indeed divine for silver [variant: “in exchange for silver”]. This is what is mocked, because those who are deceived also give them silver as the reward for their deceit.

But this word, that is, the word of the law, is not such that gifts should be given for it. No one sells the grace of God. “Freely you have received,” he says; “freely give” (Matthew 10).

Do you see how Peter was indignant against Simon, who offered money for the grace of the Holy Spirit? “May your money,” he says, “perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed through money” (Acts 8).

The word of the Gospel, then, is not like the words sold by ventriloquists. For what could anyone give as a worthy exchange for them? Hear David hesitating and saying: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115).

Gifts worthy of this grace, which comes from him, therefore cannot be given. There is one gift that is worthy: namely, the keeping of what has been given. The one who gave you a treasure does not demand the price of what was given, but a worthy guardianship of what was given.

### From the same author’s letter addressed to the bishops under him, that they should not lay on hands for money

They think that they do not sin because they do not receive a gift at the same time as the laying on of hands. But “to receive” means to receive whenever it is received. Therefore I ask you to put aside this offering—or rather, this earthly advantage [variant: “this inducement to Gehenna”]—and not, by contaminating your hands with such receipts, make yourselves unworthy to celebrate the holy mysteries.

### From the Life of Saint John Chrysostom

The man who had been the cause of our long dispute approached all the bishops—namely Eusebius, the accuser of the other six bishops—and requested to be received into communion. Some of the bishops objected that he ought not to be admitted as a slanderer.

Among them he pleaded, saying: “Since the greater part of the lawsuit has been examined for two years, and the matter has been delayed until the witnesses were produced [Greek: ‘since the case has been delayed for witnesses’], I beseech your God-loving assembly that witnesses be granted to me by him today [Greek: ‘that witnesses be granted by me’]. For even if Bishop Antoninus, who promoted men after receiving gold, has died, those who gave and were ordained remain.”

The council then decreed that the matter should be investigated. The case began with the reading of the records of the earlier proceedings.

The witnesses entered; the six who had given money and had been ordained also entered. At first they denied it. But when the witnesses remained—both laymen and presbyters, whom it seemed right to trust confidently [Greek: “who appeared worthy of confident belief”], and even certain women—and when the pledges mentioned, the places, the times, and the amount were specified, they, with their consciences not entirely at ease, confessed voluntarily, without much compulsion:

“Because we gave, we confess it, and we did so believing that the custom was such that we would appear to be freed from public civic obligations. And now we beg that, if it is just for us to remain in the ministry of the Church, we may remain; but if not, at least let us receive back the gold that we gave, for we gave some vessels belonging to our wives.”

John promised the council in response: “As for the public court, I shall free them from it with God’s help by petitioning the emperor. But you order that they receive back what they gave, from the heirs of Antoninus.”

The synod ordered them to receive the gold from the heirs of Antoninus, but to communicate within the altar and to remain deprived of the priesthood, lest, if such men obtained indulgence, a Jewish or Egyptian custom of selling or buying the priesthood should arise.

For they say that the pestilential and deceitful patriarch of the Jews appoints, every year or even more frequently, chief rulers of the synagogue in rotation, for the purpose of collecting money; and likewise his imitator, the patriarch of the Egyptians, so that the prophetic saying might be fulfilled: “Her priests answered with gifts, and her prophets divined for silver” (Micah 3).

### From the canons of the six hundred and thirty holy Fathers assembled at Chalcedon, canon 2

If any bishop performs an ordination for money and reduces to a price the grace that cannot be sold, and ordains through money a bishop, chorepiscopus, presbyter, deacon, or anyone numbered among the clergy; or promotes through money a steward, defender, mansionary, or anyone subject to the rule, for the sake of his own most shameful gain—if he is proved to have attempted this, he shall be subject to the peril of his own rank.

The one who was ordained shall gain nothing from this ordination or promotion, which was carried out through a transaction, but shall be deprived of the dignity and office that he obtained through money.

If anyone acts as mediator in such shameful and abominable gifts, whether given or received, then, if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.

### From the synodical letter of Gennadius, most holy archbishop of Constantinople, and of the synod that was with him

Let him therefore be, and is, cast out, alien and excluded from every priestly dignity and office, and subject to the curse of anathema—both the man who thinks that he can possess this priesthood through money and the one who promises to provide it for money, whether he is cleric or layman, whether he has been convicted or has not been convicted of doing this.

For it is impossible to reconcile incompatible things, or to make Mammon agree with God, or those who serve Mammon to serve God. This too is the Lord’s judgment, which asserts without hesitation that it is impossible to serve God and Mammon (Matthew 6; Luke 16).

### From the canons of the holy Sixth Synod, canon 22

[Note: In the margin of Codex Jolyani, Col. 0503D: “These canons are found not among the Latins, but among certain Greeks, as are some others.”]

We order that those who have been ordained through money—whether bishops or any other clerics—and not according to examination and the choice of life, be deposed; and likewise those who are known to have ordained them.

Let us all hear these things and receive them with our ears—not only high priests, priests, and those numbered among the clergy, but also all of us who inhabit the whole world. For we must pay especially close attention to what we hear, lest we drift away:

“For we were not redeemed from our vain ancestral way of life with perishable silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless and undefiled Lamb” (1 Peter 1).

Thus teach us, most sacred man, to follow divine Scripture and the evangelical, apostolic, canonical, and paternal commandments. For we obey the words of your mouth.

“Climb upon a high mountain; raise your voice with strength” (Isaiah 40). Go out into the open and preach with confidence, so that the laying on of hands performed for money may be removed and abolished, together with everything that follows from it through avarice, injustice, and acquisition for the sake of shameful gain.

When this has been removed, together with the things that belong to it, from the people of possession, who are reckoned by the name of Christ and have freely obtained redemption, every contagion that follows wickedness will be cut off from the roots. Then the priests will flourish like the palm, breathing forth the fragrance of Christ to those who are being saved and singing the Church’s triumphal song: “The Lord has taken away your injustices from you.”

And he will show those who pluck, filling them with sweetness, and multiplying them in the fertile land [variant: “in abundant old age”] [Note, Col. 0505D: Anastasius seems to have read ἐν γῇ or χώρα, “in the land” or “in the country”], making them heirs of that long life—indeed, of life that is incorruptible.

**To the most God-honored fellow minister, Lord John, presbyter and hegumen or anchorite [Greek: “and anchorite,” that is, a despiser of worldly cares]: Tarasius, unworthy bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, sends greetings in the Lord.**
He who, watered by the streams of the divine Spirit and illumined by its inspiration—the David who was both prophet among kings and king among prophets—praising God said: “From the beginning I learned from your testimonies that you founded them forever” (Psalm 118). This hymnody, therefore, is without falsehood for those who possess understanding, and firm for those who sing it. For Moses, the beholder of God, says concerning every utterance of divine Scripture: “Nothing is to be added to them, and nothing is to be taken away from them” (Deuteronomy 12:34).

Those, then, who apply themselves scrupulously rather than superficially to all the sacred Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers, who attend to their reading, fix their minds upon piety and truth, and do not turn these things toward their own will, are wondrously illumined by the everlasting mountains, enlightened by the evangelical and apostolic commandments. For the Psalmist calls these things “mountains” (Psalm 75), because, meditating and walking in them, we pass over to heavenly things; and “everlasting,” because they were foretold not recently or for a temporal purpose, but from the beginning of the world [Gr., “spoken before the foundation of the world”], although they were proclaimed in the last times [Col. 0505C] by the preachers of the evangelical proclamation.

Therefore, man of desires—namely, of the things that belong to the Spirit—we, who have known you from your youth as devoted to God, commend to the encouragement of your mind a few movements and intentions of our heart. Let the greater number be honored with silence.

You have surely heard from us about the synod held by the good pleasure of God in the city of Nicaea. To that synod we came, together with the consecrated men and custodians of the place, from both the senior pope of Rome and the most holy chief priests of the East, as well as with many God-beloved bishops, according to the command of our pious emperors. Likewise there were the revered archimandrites and abbots, and a multitude of monks.

When many matters were discussed among us, what is true and pleasing to God was decreed. In accordance with the ancient legislation of our holy Fathers, the Church received the painting and titles of images, for the elevation of the mind [for “a higher sense,” or “the uplifting of the soul”] and the remembrance of our mind, and for participation in a certain sanctification. For whatever the holy Gospel communicates to us through reading, the images likewise communicate; and whatever the books of the martyrs’ sufferings relate concerning their deeds, the images likewise represent. We salute these images as representations of the originals, and nothing else, believing that the one God is to be praised in the Trinity and serving him alone.

We also seek the intercessions of our undefiled Lady, the holy Mother of God [Col. 0506A], and of the holy angels and all our holy Fathers.

These matters having been settled, the greater part of the revered monks [bishops] brought a complaint before the synod. We too had foreseen this complaint, because many bishops had obtained the priesthood through money. Although we are blinded by our sins [or “entangled in them”] and caught in their nets—may God be merciful to us—we have nevertheless received knowledge of the evangelical commandments and canonical prescriptions. With a pure conscience, a simple heart, a manner of life free from avarice, and an undisturbed disposition toward God, we desire to follow the canonical command in every respect [Gr., “with a conscience joyfully lifting itself toward God, let us follow the canon in every respect”]. We have subdued ourselves [or “submitted ourselves”] and bowed down to serve the evangelical, apostolic, and paternal ordinances, striving that those who have received the priesthood should conduct themselves, live, and behave in this way—and likewise all who are called by the name of Christ.

But if some do not obey these commandments, I do not tolerate being a communicant of such men, who are called priests but are not priests; I am separated from their portion. For me, it is not burdensome to protest these things, while for them it is a safeguard.

The divine canons depose anyone who gives or receives money in the ordination to the priesthood and expel him from priestly dignity. Moses, the beholder of God, as I said, cries out: “Nothing is to be added to them,” he says, “and nothing is to be taken away from them” (Deuteronomy 12:34). Likewise the hymn-writer David sings, and we with him: “From the beginning I learned from your testimonies that you founded them forever” (Psalm 118).

And who is capable of resisting these things, unless he has become foolish in his understanding and wishes to mock divine matters? God’s testimonies have already been founded and rooted in his Church, even if some, disobedient for a time, do not keep them. They therefore remain forever; blessed are those who examine them and obey them, and woe to those who do not obey.

Accordingly, every bishop, presbyter, or deacon convicted of having given or received the laying-on of hands for money falls from the priesthood. Some perhaps say that we repent for the sin and that God forgives it. I say the same: God receives all who repent and forgives through repentance the sins already committed.

I know that David was overcome by adultery and murder (2 Samuel 11), but that, after he had repented, he was received and approved by divine testimony: “I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my desires” (Psalm 88; Acts 13). The holy writings also bear prophetic testimony concerning David. It is therefore clear that he was corrected through repentance [Gr., “it is clear where he was corrected through repentance”].

Yet again I know that he heard this from God: “You shall not build a house for me, because you are a man of blood” (1 Chronicles 17). I know that Manasseh was released from impiety through confession (2 Chronicles 33). I know also that prostitutes and publicans were received through repentance [Col. 0507A] (Matthew 21; Mark 2; Luke 5); but none of them was counted among those holding priestly dignity, unless perhaps he had committed such a deed before baptism.

I know also certain monks who, while they were in the world, had been defiled by every lust, but who, when they lived in solitude, shone like torches throughout the world [“who had been held in fornication, but, having become monks, shone like luminaries in the world through a zealous life”]. Yet none of these was ordained a priest.

If something of this kind has happened once or twice, it does not therefore immediately prescribe a law in the Church. We know that holy Mary [the blessed Mary] [Note: [Col. 0507D] That is, Mary of Egypt] was first a prostitute and afterward became continent [“a fornicator, but afterward chaste”]; yet she was not enrolled among the deaconesses.

Why do I say these things, when I know the word of truth and see the man who was initiated by the divine apostles crying out boldly [“taught by the divine apostles and our holy Fathers, crying out boldly”] (Canon 30): “Whoever has been ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon through money is alien to priestly dignity, for the grace of the divine Spirit is not sold”? This is a Caiaphan endeavor, this is a Simoniac contrivance, and it is foreign to priestly sanctification.

If anyone after baptism is found in fornication or adultery, the divine canons do not admit him to the priesthood. Indeed, if anyone promoted to the priesthood commits such a deed [Gr., “who has been promoted to the priesthood and commits such a deed”], he is immediately expelled.

Every man who persists in repentance therefore obtains, through the goodness and gentleness of God, forgiveness of his sins [Col. 0507C], as we also demonstrated above. But I anathematize Novatian and the adherents of his impious heresy, since he is hostile to repentance and diminishes the gentleness of God.

For this reason I hold the opinion that a bishop ordained through money should be received, provided that he repents. God is good in all things, and his mercies are opened over every repentant person; he also brings that person into his kingdom. But since, according to the divine Apostle (1 Timothy 3), a bishop must be blameless [irreproachable], anyone who ordains another for money, or is himself ordained by others for money, is alien to priestly dignity, as all of us who are members of the Church know.

Good and praiseworthy, therefore, is the repentance that leads to God and frees from sins [Col. 0507D]. I too need mercy, for I know the gentleness of God, who receives everyone who comes to him. Through the prophet he said: “You must first declare your sins, that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43). And: “I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity before the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Psalm 31). And: “For this every holy person shall pray to you at an opportune time” (ibid.). [Gr., added: “I know also that the Corinthian who committed fornication was received by the divine Apostle Paul, but was not raised to the priesthood.”]

For if a father, while his son is away and acting impiously and unjustly, nevertheless receives him when he returns and embraces him with natural affection [Col. 0508A], how much more will God, the Father of us all, receive every repentant person into his arms, since he is uniquely merciful! For he does not seek the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live (Ezekiel 18; 33).

We have also been instructed by the Lord’s own voice in the Gospel, through the parable of the prodigal son and his subsequent repentance (Luke 15), how he was received by the heavenly Father in heaven [Note: [Col. 0508D] “In heaven” is redundant]. For he rejoices over every person who repents.

Repentance is a splendid armor, a great road of salvation, the dispenser [Gr., “conciliator”; Codex Jol., “reconciliation”] of the kingdom of heaven, the guide along the incorruptible way, the equal of martyrial struggles, the one who points out the road to God and makes us be with him; it is the staff of the human race and the raising-up of those who fall and have stumbled.

Blessed are those who embrace and cling to it. Those who practice it lead a life equal to that of the angels, turn away from every evil, and do good. Repentance is the fellow-column and familiar companion [“foster-sister and cohabitant”] of love, almsgiving [Gr. adds: “prayer”], fasting, abstinence, self-control, uprightness, honesty, and gentleness. In short, to speak truly in one word, repentance excels in all these things [Gr., “repentance is all these things”].

But if anyone defiles and despises it, he must be counted not among the saved but among the lost, “whose worm does not die and whose fire is not extinguished.” From these may we be delivered, deemed worthy of the good promises through the mercy and compassions of Christ our God.

These things are proclaimed by us, most holy man, in case there should be some who wish to defame us as well. We know that you are a singular admonition [Gr. and Codex Jol., “a place of refuge”] and a devotee of evangelical, apostolic, and canonical commands. Therefore we write these things to you with still greater boldness, and we ask you to make them known to the monks, ascetics, and all religious men [Gr., “secular religious men”] with whom you have dealings [Gr. adds: “and, if you wish, to display them to them”].

We earnestly ask you also to remember us, who seek heaven, in your prayers, so that at last we may be delivered from the evils surrounding us on every side. Assaults press upon us from within and without; from these we have been delivered by the mercy of God, and we trust that henceforth also we shall escape them.

Therefore, again and again we say: pray, entreat, O friend, man of God and of ours—indeed, rather, our father. For we know that you are disposed toward us with the affection a father has toward his children.

May the God of peace, who summons to himself both those who are far away and those who are near, preserve our life in peace, and save all who worship and admire him and call upon his name, through the intercession and prayers of our Lady, the holy Mother of God, and of all his saints. Amen.

I ask that you greet in our name all the brothers who reach you, so that they too may pray for us with you.

[Col. 0509A] [Note: [Col. 0509D] From the new version.]

## How it is to be understood that the name of God is incommunicable, and concerning every prophetic utterance directed against idols

The divine Apostle Paul, who penetrated into the third heaven and entered paradise, where he heard secret words (2 Corinthians 12), and who preached the Gospel from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum (Romans 15), refuting the impious and empty superstition of the gentiles, says: “They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents; and they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1).

Accordingly, in this sense it is to be understood that they applied the incommunicable name of God to wood and stones. This was done by those who were alienated from every worship of God, and by those among the Hebrews who, in their madness, apostatized from God. For they were mingled among the nations and learned their works.

Having abandoned our invisible, incomprehensible God, the maker of all things, they sacrificed to demons—to Baal, Astarte, Chemosh, Apollo, and Jupiter; to Diana and Venus; to Bacchus and Mercury; and to many others. They called their idols gods, as well as the images of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents.

Therefore the same Apostle says: “God delivered them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are not fitting, filled with every iniquity, wickedness, depravity, and greed; full of envy, murder, strife; whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, arrogant, conceited, inventors of evil” (ibid.).

For this reason God gave the Law through Moses. Then he gave prophets who foretold the coming of the Savior, Christ our God, and who reproved, threatened, admonished, and exhorted the people to return to the knowledge of truth and, having set aside the creature, to serve the living and true God, whose name cannot be shared with creatures and idolatrous images.

For the Apostle says: “What fellowship does light have with darkness? And what agreement does Christ have with Belial?” (2 Corinthians 6). Yet neither the Law nor the prophets were able to convert them, for they remained in their destruction.

The one foretold by the prophets therefore came: the Word of God himself, coeternal with the Father and true God. He assumed flesh from the undefiled Mother of God, the ever-Virgin Mary, and became a man like us except for sin, in order to free us from the error of idols and rescue us from the slavery of the devil.

When all the mysteries of his dispensation had been completed—when he had suffered in the flesh on the cross, been buried, risen again, and ascended into heaven, from which he had descended—he freed us from all that impurity and abomination. He sent his holy apostles and disciples to all the nations, after giving them, as he had promised them, power from on high: the Spirit, the Lord, life-giving and almighty, who proceeds from the Father through the Son.

By his power they became mighty in deed and word, and freed the human race from the empty worship of idols. They taught us to believe in the one God who is praised and glorified in the Trinity. They themselves, and their successors—our most renowned Fathers—also handed down the creeds in the Church [Col. 0510A].

Holding these things, Christians venerate the holy sign of the honored cross, the holy Gospel handed down in writing, venerable images through the representation that expresses the reality, and many other things dedicated to God. Bringing these things near to us, worshiping and saluting them with affection, we become participants in their sanctification.

Christians do not approach these things as gods, however, as the gentiles approached idols. Far be such a crime from them: these are the trifles and empty talk of the Iconoclasts. For this reason they are rightly called the accusers of Christians.

Since they are mad, they have spoken vainly, each one to his neighbor (Psalm 11). “With deceitful lips and with a heart, with a heart, they spoke perversely.” They have wrongly applied to the painted representations of evangelical realities what was pronounced against idols by the divine Law, the prophets, and the apostles, perverting sacred Scripture according to their own desires. They understand nothing other than that we have not been freed or saved through Christ our God from those idols.

O the madness and insanity of these men! They have not distinguished the holy from the profane. For they have called the image of the Lord and of his saints by the same name as the images of demons. Shame upon the wickedness of these men! Woe to them, because they have recoiled from God.

For we Christians, worshiping the one God praised in the Trinity and offering latria to him alone, are led through sensible signs to intelligible realities. Since we are sensible beings, we are raised to intelligible things in no other way than through sensible signs: both through writing, for meditation, and through painting, in which realities are expressed by colors and lines [Col. 0510C].

These signs introduce and elevate us to the remembrance of all the prototypes. One thing we perceive through hearing, another we contemplate with our eyes. These things are so ordered that one conveys knowledge of the other; unquestionably, each also contains the exposition of the other, and both receive the same honors.

For a clearer understanding of the matter, I shall also propose certain further considerations in defense.

It is common to all God’s creatures that they are joined to one another by some participation and affinity. Although some surpass others in dignity and rank, all things are nevertheless joined together by a certain communion. Angels, since they are pure minds, were brought forth from nothing by God, the creator of all things; the human nature likewise. Human nature stands midway between the excellence of heavenly angels and the lowliness of earthly things. Thus creatures correspond to one another.

Angels are pure and incorruptible minds, whereas man is mortal. Yet, because he is capable of mind and discipline, he participates in the angelic nature. Again, human nature participates in the nature of the other animals, since man himself has flesh, eats, sleeps, and shares the common earth—from which we were taken and into which we are dissolved—until our transformation from corruption into incorruption.

In exactly the same way, the four elements are joined together by a common bond: earth, water, air, and fire. Earth is dry and cold; fire is dry and hot; water is cold and moist; air is hot and moist. Earth and fire therefore correspond as dry, while earth and water correspond as cold; in the same way the remaining elements are associated with one another through this commonality.

Hence our bodies also consist, in proportion to these four elements, of four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Blood, being hot and moist, corresponds proportionally to air; yellow bile, being hot and dry, corresponds proportionally to fire; black bile, being dry and cold, corresponds proportionally to earth; and the phlegmatic humor, being moist and cold, corresponds proportionally to water.

I shall add something further for a fuller explanation. The Lord is king and emperor; your empire also shines above all, and you surpass others in dignity together with your lady and mother, the empress. All are obedient and subject to your command. Yet you are human beings and are included within a definition, since every human being is a rational, mortal animal capable of mind and knowledge. Peter, Paul, and all other human beings likewise fall under the same definition. That is, you too possess what is common to human beings, and you share the same common nature with everyone.

God, however, is invisible, incomprehensible, unsearchable, uncircumscribed, impassible, immortal, the one King of kings and Lord of lords. He is joined by no communion whatsoever either with angels, human beings, or any other creature. He is the maker; all other things are created. He governs by providence; all the rest are governed by providence.

God, therefore, is outside every created nature, and for this reason his name is incommunicable. That is why the admirable Moses transmitted special letters for writing the name of God, which they did not use for other words.

If angelic powers and pious people who fear God are participants in God, they possess this through his grace [Col. 0512B], not by nature. May you too become a participant in him through good works. May he himself exalt your empire and raise you up to understand and contemplate those things that lead to his eternal kingdom, through his mercies and the prayers of our holy and immaculate Lady, the Mother of God, and of all his saints. Amen.

[Col. 0511]

# CHRONOLOGY OF SAINT NICEPHORUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE  
Translated by Anastasius the Librarian

*(From the Library of the Ancient Fathers, ninth century.)*

## TO THE READER

[Col. 0511]

With the agreement of all, the author of this Chronology is held to be Saint Nicephorus, bishop of Constantinople. It is reported from the most reliable authorities in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume 9, that he died in the year of the Lord 828. It must therefore necessarily be said that Theodotus Cassiteras, Antonius, John the Syncellus, Methodius, Ignatius the Eunuch, who are listed below in this Chronology as bishops of Constantinople after Nicephorus, were added not by Saint Nicephorus but by Anastasius the Librarian, the translator of this Chronology, who was alive in the time of Ignatius.

[Col. 0511]

In the name of Christ begins the Three-Part Chronology, formerly translated into Latin from blessed Nicephorus of Constantinople by Anastasius, librarian of the apostolic see, and corrected according to an Anastasian exemplar and illustrated with notes by Antonius Contius.

## PART ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

[Note: [Col. 0513A] ON CHAPTER I.—Since Nicephorus had been written and published without any division into chapters, we have divided it into definite chapters for the sake of more convenient instruction, chiefly according to the customary division of the ages of the world: from the beginning to the Flood, from the Flood to Abraham, from Abraham to the Exodus from Egypt, and so forth, with the periods distinguished in succession up to Christ and the subsequent times of the emperors.

It must first of all be kept in mind that the Catholic Church, both Eastern and Western, in a constant and perpetual tradition follows in its computation of times the longer and greater number of years found in the edition of the Septuagint Interpreters, not the greater number found in the Hebrew volumes.

For although, little by little after the time of Jerome, the Western Church began to use the edition of that most holy man, having abandoned the ancient Septuagint edition, which it had always used exclusively, it nevertheless stubbornly retained from that old edition of the Septuagint both the Psalter and the chronology, as Bede, Isidore, the author of the *Fasciculus temporum*, Hugh, and other authors frequently testify.

The tables publicly displayed each year in the cathedral churches of France with the paschal candle also provide the clearest evidence of this matter. I therefore cannot sufficiently marvel at the vanity and desire for innovation of men of our own time, including those who have written chronologies, who reject the authority of the entire Septuagint edition as far as possible and consider correct nothing except what is now read in the Hebrew codices. Relying on this prejudiced opinion, they corrupt everything in editing or translating Greek books, as those themselves have confessed who translated the ecclesiastical history of the other Nicephorus and similar works.

Once this chronology has been explained by us, all these men will be given an opportunity to recover their senses, and they will be compelled to admit with me that this is the certain and customary computation of the entire Greek Church. It agrees exactly with the computation recorded in the Greek *Horologion* and in the Paschal Cycle described there, and it is followed by Cedrenus, Zonaras, Nicetas, the Sixth General Synod, and—in a word—all the Greeks.

Since the Greeks more often compute the periods of the world by the years of the world than by the years of Christ, those who are ignorant of this chronology read them without benefit.

With these matters established, it remains for us to examine the whole of the chronology set out above in relation to the Greek edition of the Septuagint, which today exists enriched in many ways through printing, and to the old Latin edition of the same Septuagint, which no longer exists but is cited throughout the works of Augustine, Jerome, and the ancients.

It must first be understood that it agrees in every respect with both the Greek and the old Latin translation, except for the item concerning Methuselah, whom Nicephorus says, having reached 187 years, fathered Lamech. For Saint Augustine, in Book 15, chapters 10 and 11 of *The City of God*, and Jerome in his *Questions on Genesis*, as well as Isidore, Novatianus Scotus, and Bede, insist that in the edition of the Septuagint Interpreters only 167 years are assigned to him. The Complutensian Greek edition fell short of that computation by two years, assigning him 165 years. But the Aldine Greek edition, from which the German edition subsequently arose, has 187 years and therefore agrees exactly with the computation of Nicephorus.

It is remarkable how greatly the German Greek-Latin edition has been corrupted by carelessness and negligence—not to mention ignorance and barbarism. In its Greek column it agrees with the Aldine edition, but in its Latin column with the Complutensian.

If anyone, amid such diversity and what one might call the sport of copyists, asks which reading I consider more intact, I prefer the Aldine edition alone in this passage. It is probable that the Greek Fathers, having understood the judgment of Augustine, Jerome, and others on this matter—all of whom thought this passage had been corruptly printed among the Septuagint and ought to be corrected according to the Hebrew reading—did not hesitate here to correct 167 to 187. This is testified by the Greek edition of Josephus, by the preface of Epiphanius to the *Panarion*—although it is grievously corrupted in countless places—and by the present edition of Nicephorus.

I therefore judge that nothing here in this passage of Nicephorus should be corrected. In this way the absurdity will be avoided whereby Methuselah would otherwise appear to have died after the Flood, as Saint Jerome discusses at greater length in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.

Once these matters have been settled, however, an irreconcilable conflict arises between the total of that entire computation and the individual numbers. The individual numbers do not agree with the total of 2,242 years collected by Nicephorus; rather, when the individual numbers are added together, the total becomes 2,524 years. Nevertheless, I think the Nicephorian total should also be corrected in this way. It is not unprecedented for the reckoning of the individual numbers to be given priority and the total to be corrected from them, rather than the individual numbers from the total.

The most learned Pythaeus also noted and informed us that he had read this way in a manuscript of this chronology belonging to Anastasius the Librarian, and he suggested other numerical variations as well. But we have thought it best to add only those resting on some plausible basis, lest we keep the reader in uncertainty and delay his judgment amid so much variation.

## On the differing computation according to the Hebrews

The Hebrew codices, which were also published in Latin by Saint Jerome and later by many others—including Saint Pagninus, who translated them from other sources and rendered them completely—count 1,656 years from Adam to the Flood. All who have touched the Hebrew letters, even with the very tip of a finger, now insist that this alone is the true computation. Jerome may perhaps support them, being tenacious of the labor and purpose he undertook when, after so many Greek translators, he himself finally set out to transfer the canonical Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin.

But Augustine does not support them (*The City of God*, Book 15, chapters 10 and 11). He does not consider the Greek edition and translation of the Septuagint faulty merely because it possesses a definite consistency in its variation.

Those who stand by the Jewish and Hebrew text say that the seventy-two translators of the Septuagint were mistaken because in Genesis chapter 5 they always read “two hundred” where they should have read “one hundred.” They also assert that Jerome held this opinion in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.

But neither the Latin nor the Greek Church has ever been able to persuade itself of this. For that reason both Churches continue to follow the Septuagint to this day: the Latin Church considering them simply mistaken, while the Greek Church adopts the emendation of the one passage mentioned above.]

[Col. 0511C]

*(Year of the world 230)* Adam, in the 230th year of his age, fathered Seth, and afterward lived 700 years.

*(435)* Seth, having reached 205 years, fathered Enos.

*(625)* Enos, having reached 190 years, fathered Cainan.

*(795)* Cainan, having reached 170 years, fathered Mahalaleel.

[Col. 0512C] *(960)* Mahalaleel, having reached 165 years, fathered Jared.

*(1122)* Jared, having reached 162 years, fathered Enoch.

*(1287)* Enoch, having reached 165 years, fathered Methuselah.

*(1474)* Methuselah, having reached 187 years, fathered Lamech.

*(1662)* Lamech, having reached 188 years, fathered Noah.

[Col. 0513A] *(2162)* Noah, having reached 500 years, fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

*(2262)* And he lived another 100 years, up to the Flood.

In the 600th year of Noah’s life the Flood occurred.

[Col. 0514A] The total years from Adam to the Flood, according to the Septuagint, are 2,242. This number is confirmed by the testimony of truth and by the traditions of all the ancient Churches.

## CHAPTER TWO

*(Year 2 after the Flood.)*

[Note: [Col. 0515C] ON CHAPTER II.—The preceding computation agrees in every respect with the common Greek edition and with the old Latin translation of the Septuagint used by the ancients. Only the total number of years from the Flood to Abraham, and from Adam to Abraham, does not agree with the individual numbers. But, with the same justification as before, I shall not hesitate to correct the totals so that from Adam to Abraham 3,334 years are read, and from the Flood to Abraham 1,072 years.

In this computation the entire Eastern Greek Church now rests as upon the most certain of all, and this computation appears to agree with the mind of Saint Augustine, as can be understood from Book 15, chapters 10 and 16 of *The City of God*. Since the genealogy of the divine Evangelist Luke, traced backward from Christ to Adam, supports this computation of the Septuagint Interpreters, both the Greek and Latin Churches considered it impious to follow the Hebrew reckoning rather than embrace the one that receives authority from the Gospel.

Let the new pseudo-Christians and those most troublesome Judaizers now go their way—those who, relying on Jewish obstinacy and the bare authority of letters and vowel-points, blaspheme daily against the divine translation of the Septuagint and, together with that translation, against the whole of prophecy and the correction of Hebrew errors.

We shall rest in this Nicephorian chronology. And lest anyone think that we have adopted this merely from despair or weariness of investigating all the authors more carefully, rather than choosing the more certain testimony of truth after nearly infinite reading and a diversity of opinions, I have reduced seven different variations of the years from Adam to Abraham into a brief canon.]

[Col. 0515A]

### Years from Adam to Abraham

1. According to the common edition of Saint Jerome from the Hebrew: **1,948**.

2. According to the Jews, who, in order to complete the forty-ninth jubilee and begin the fiftieth, add two additional years, as Eusebius says: **1,950**.

3. According to the Hebrew edition, with Cainan and his 130 years inserted into it solely from Luke’s Gospel, as Marianus preferred: **2,178**.

4. According to the unadulterated edition of the Septuagint, not corrected in the manner mentioned above: **3,314**.

5. According to the edition of the Septuagint published by Origen under obeli and asterisks, in which Cainan is deleted [Col. 0516D]: **3,184**.

6. According to the personal opinion of Saint Augustine, who adds more than twenty years to Methuselah when he fathered Lamech, but later subtracts six years from Lamech when he fathered Noah: **3,328**.

7. According to the Aldine edition of the Septuagint Interpreters, which Nicephorus here confirms to have been correctly emended, as does the entire Greek Church: **3,334**.]

## CHAPTER THREE
[Note: [Col. 0516D] ON CHAPTER III.—From the individual numbers assigned to each person—which do not differ at this point in either the Hebrew or the Septuagint edition—the total of 505 years is correctly derived. But the separate sums of years assigned to the individuals are not confirmed by the explicit words of Scripture in the manner of those I shall set out below, and which I used in the Chronological Canons appended by me to the Justinian Code. Abraham, at the age of 100, begot Isaac, as is said in Genesis, chapter XXI. Isaac, at the age of 60, begot Jacob, as is also expressly stated in Genesis, chapter XXV. Jacob, at the age of 91, begot Joseph. Although this is not stated expressly in Genesis, it is inferred by necessary subtraction from the facts explicitly established there, as follows. When Joseph explains Pharaoh’s dream to him, he is thirty years old, as is said there in chapter XLI. When that same Joseph summons his father through his brothers, he is thirty-nine years old; for it was then the second year of famine and consequently the ninth year from the interpretation of the dream, Genesis XLV. Moreover, in that same second year of famine, Jacob, having come down to Egypt, tells Pharaoh that he is in his 130th year, Genesis XLVII. Let us therefore subtract Joseph’s thirty-nine years from Jacob’s age; one and ninety years remain, which Jacob had reached when he begot Joseph. Joseph lived 110 years, Genesis, final chapter. After Joseph’s death, the Israelites were oppressed by the Egyptians under harsh servitude for 144 years. This is proved from sacred Scripture not by a direct statement but by subtraction. Exodus XII says that Israel dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan—which the Septuagint translators correctly add by way of supplementation—for 430 years. Subtract, therefore, from this total the 361 years which we have computed from Abraham’s birth to Joseph’s death; the remaining 144 years are consequently the period during which the Israelites served the Egyptians. With these points established in advance, we shall correct the totals, already corrupted by the errors above, as follows: from [Col. 0517D] Adam to the departure from Egypt, 3,839 years; from the Flood to the departure from Egypt, 1,577 years. But Nicephorus’s final words, “According to others, 3,698,” have been judged to read as follows in Anastasius: “3,829 years”—that is, he understands the computation of those who add nothing to the years assigned above to Methuselah. Yet even on that correction they would still fall ten years short of Nicephorus; nevertheless, Nicephorus does not value their computation highly. Now, reluctantly, as I frankly admit, I shall touch upon the recent disagreement of certain theologians, a new disagreement which I do not know whether the ancients ever attempted. Among them is Augustine Steuchus, as well as a certain theologian of this age, exceedingly learned and devout, whom I am greatly astonished could have conceived such an idea. [Col. 0518B] They say, then, that all who today claim to calculate the chronology from the Bible assert that the Israelites remained in Egypt only 210 years. It is probable that they had not read our Chronology, printed at Paris together with the Justinian Code—for I do not think that they despised it, lest I say anything more. For we have written there, as also here, that they remained in Egypt for 144 years. They write and maintain that the Israelites remained in Egypt for 430 years, persuaded by the authority of Genesis XVII, where it is foretold that Abraham’s seed would serve for 400 years—not, as they cite it, “in Egypt,” but “in a land not their own”—and that those who assign a shorter period follow the invention of the rabbis. For my part, I would dare solemnly to affirm that I believe nothing, not even to the slightest extent, on the authority of the rabbis—would that they would make the same assertion about themselves—but that I am also guided by the arguments advanced by Eusebius, Nicephorus, Paul in Galatians III, and Moses in Exodus XII, on the basis of the authority of the Septuagint translators, with all the Greek and Latin Fathers agreeing with them. Certainly their opinion—I say “opinion,” not “judgment”—cannot stand, because there were only three generations in Egypt: namely, Kohath, who lived 133 years, Exodus VI; Amram, who lived there 137 years, Genesis VI; and Moses, who was 80 years old when he led out the people. Hence it is clear that 430 years cannot be made up, and no greater proof is required in so obvious a matter. Let them read Bede, who agrees with us, in his book On the Nature of Things.]

Abraham, being in his seventy-fifth year, was found worthy of a divine oracle, and, after the promise had been made to him, [Note: [Col. 0515D] Jerome translates it thus in the Eusebian Chronicles.]

From that time until the journey out of Egypt, whose leader was Moses, there are 430 years, just as the Apostle also testifies when he says: “The covenant of God, the law which was given after 430 years, does not annul it so as to abolish the promise” (Galatians III). Moses himself agrees in Exodus when he says: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, in which they dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was 430 years” (Exodus XII). These years are reckoned in the following parts.

Abraham, at the age of 100, begot Isaac.

Isaac, at the age of 60, begot Jacob.

Jacob, at the age of 87, begot Levi.

Levi, at the age of 45, begot Kohath.

Kohath, at the age of 63, [Note: [Col. 0516D] Alternatively: Kohath, at the age of 60, but this is erroneous.] begot Amram.

Amram, at the age of 70, begot Moses.

Moses, at the age of 80, led the people out of Egypt.

The total from Abraham’s first year to the journey out of Egypt is 505 years.

From the Flood, however, there are 1,587 years.

From Adam, according to the Septuagint, there are 3,829 years. [Col. 0516C] According to others, 3,698.

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0518C] ON CHAPTER IV.—The whole of the foregoing computation is confirmed by the explicit words of the Book of Judges, whether one follows the Hebrew manuscripts and the translations made from them, or the Greek manuscripts and the translations made from them, with the sole exception of those 27 years [Col. 0518D] assigned here by Nicephorus to Joshua, and the 33 assigned to the elders. Scripture indicates that a considerable period must be assigned to the rule of the elders when it says that after the death of Joshua the elders lived for a long time—those who had seen all the great works of the Lord which he had done for Israel—until the Lord raised up judges to deliver them, Judges II. And what is said in chapter I of the same Book of Judges, that the tribe of Judah conducted the war at God’s command, seems to refer to those elders of the tribe of Judah, such as Caleb and others. In any case, the total of 630 years is correctly derived from the individual totals. Up to this point there is either no disagreement, or not much, with the chronology of the Greeks, the tradition and computation of the Latin Church. But in this calculation of the years from the departure out of Egypt to the first year of Solomon’s reign, he differs very substantially. For he follows the computation of Eusebius, which Augustine, Orosius, Isidore, Bede, and all the Latin Fathers embraced, as did also most of the Greeks. This Eusebian computation is much shorter than the Nicephorian one which we have undertaken to explain. The reasons are these: first, Eusebius assigns no separate period to the rule of the elders; next, he completely removed Ailon with his ten years, because it was absent from the edition of the Septuagint translators—by “edition” I mean the pure edition which existed in the Caesarean library—for it was later added in the Vulgate edition, which, as Jerome shows in many places, [Col. 0519B] is not the pure work of the Septuagint translators. Finally, in the aforementioned Book of Judges he confounds all the years during which the Israelites are said to have served foreigners with the years of the judges who followed, and does not count them separately, preferring in this matter the Jewish tradition, which—as he himself testifies—asserts that those years are included within the years of the subsequent judges and ought not to be counted separately. But it is credible that the Greek Fathers, as time later advanced—for time either reveals everything or provides an opportunity for changing it for the better—preferred to count those years individually and separately, since it would be dangerous to admit against the explicit words of Scripture a Jewish tradition opposed to them; and they also preferred not to remove Ailon, who is found in the Hebrew manuscripts, and not to assign any period to the rule of the elders. How, nevertheless, they precisely derived the 33 years assigned to them, I frankly admit is still unclear to me. Eusebius was moved by the same consideration as the Jews when they imposed their tradition: for at the beginning of III Kings, chapter VI, these words are written: “And it came to pass in the 480th year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the second month, while Solomon was king over Israel, that he built the house of the Lord.” Thus it is found both in the Hebrew and in the Greek of the Complutensian edition, and Eusebius read it that way in both manuscripts. Therefore the Aldine and German editions are wrong to give only 460 years. The authority of this passage in the Book of Kings moved, I say, both the Jews and Eusebius; if it is true, the authority of the Book of Judges will collapse unless we shorten the years individually numbered in it in this way and confuse the years of servitude with the years of the judges. It is not my task to settle so great a controversy. Yet if I had any authority—which I do not claim, but wholly submit myself to the judgment of the Church—I would say that this passage in the Book of Kings might perhaps be understood not of the earlier departure from Egypt but of the later one. For even Psalm CXIII, “When Israel went out of Egypt,” is not understood of the earlier departure, since it says there that the Jordan was turned backward. On behalf of Nicephorus and those who follow the greater number in the Book of Judges, many arguments can also be advanced: specific numbers should not be corrected or conflated on the basis of a single total sum, because many specific and distinctly written figures carry greater weight than one solitary total gathered as a whole, in which copyists could more easily have gone astray. Finally, one should not force the words; yet force seems to be done by that Jewish tradition. Moreover, just as they fight with the authority of III Kings, so we shall defend our position by the tradition of the holy Apostle, who writes in Acts XIII that from the death of Moses until Samuel there were 450 years. Some have wickedly attempted to correct these words; I consider them unworthy of mention. In any case, no one should suppose that Eusebius was so stubbornly determined to follow the smaller number that he rejected the larger altogether. I shall quote his words, by which he seems to permit everyone a free choice between the two. Thus, in the preface to the Chronological Canons, in Jerome’s translation, he says: “From Moses to Solomon and the first building of the Temple there are 479 years according to the lesser number, which the Third Book of Kings contains; but according to the Book of Judges, 600 years are reckoned.” This is what Eusebius says. Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople, therefore follows here the greater number in the Book of Judges, as does Clement Stromateus in the Stromata, and ultimately the whole Greek Church, as well as the Sixth Synod at Trullo, which in canon 3 of its decrees counts the year then in progress as 6199. That number cannot stand unless we follow both the greater number of the Septuagint edition and the longer computation of the Book of Judges. The Greek Horologion, printed at Venice in 1535, follows precisely the same reckoning and computation in the Paschal cycle appended to it. Therefore those who wish to read Greek ecclesiastical affairs, councils, laws, basilicas, and histories with profit and in their proper chronological setting must follow this chronology as their guide. Nevertheless, so that nothing may be lacking from our work, we have also appended that lesser Eusebian computation, which St. Augustine, Orosius, Isidore, Bede, the Fasciculus temporum, the ecclesiastical computation, and ultimately the entire Latin Church—of which we are members—seem to have preferred to the other.]

## CHAPTER V

[Note: [Col. 0521C] ON CHAPTER V.—The foregoing computation of the reigns of each king agrees very well among all the editions, Greek and Hebrew, and with our chronographer, provided that we observe a few points: Azariah and Uzziah are the same person, as is clear from a comparison of the Book of Kings with the Book of Chronicles; Jehoiakim, or Eliakim, reigned eleven years, as is said at the end of IV Kings, chapter XXIII. Amon reigned twelve years, on the authority of the pure edition of the Septuagint translators, as Eusebius reports; in this matter he should be trusted, since he possessed such a pure edition, as we noted above. The Hebrew edition and the Greek Vulgate, however—the edition now printed at Complutum, by Aldus, and elsewhere—assign him only two years. What Nicephorus says about the interregnum indicates the period in which the succession of kingship was altered and disrupted contrary to law and by force by the king of Egypt, and signifies the first captivity, which took place in the time of Jehoahaz, or Jehoiakim, son of Josiah. Theodoret mentions it in his commentary on Daniel, oration 9, where he teaches that there were three captivities. This period must be combined with the following one, not counted separately; otherwise neither the total sum would agree nor would any historian or chronographer say so. If, then, we add these 445 years to the 4,469 years from the beginning of the world to Solomon, the result is 4,914 years from Adam to the Babylonian captivity of the Jews.] [Col. 0519A]

Moreover, if anyone wishes to understand more precisely the parts of this period arranged by the years of the Chaldean or Babylonian rulers, and afterward of the Medes and Persians, let him carefully examine what Theodoret wrote with great learning on Daniel, where he refutes Josephus and teaches that there were three captivities: the first, in the first year of Nebuchadnezzar, in which Daniel was taken away, in the third year of Eliakim, king of Judah, and which ended under Cyrus the Persian; the second, in the ninth year of Nebuchadnezzar, which ended under Darius Hystaspes; the third, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, which ended under Artaxerxes, son of Xerxes. All of them, however, lasted seventy years. But the more recent opinion, which this author also follows here, is that the final deportation and desolation came to an end under Darius, son of Hystaspes.]
