## CHAPTER IX

[Note: [Col. 0523D] ON CHAPTER IX.—There is an error in the totals of the entire computation and in the preceding chapter. Thus, from Alexander’s death to Christ’s birth—that is, to the forty-second year of Augustus—there are 323 years; from Adam to Christ, 5,508 years, if all the individual and total sums previously set out and restored by us are combined into one. The other Nicephorus, in Book I of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 10 and the final chapter, says that Christ was born in the year 5,505 of the world; Cedrenus, in the year 5,506. The former falls short of our figure by three years, the latter by only two. But the figure we have collected is the most exact and has been accepted in practice by the Greek Church, as the third canon of the Sixth Ecumenical Synod at Trullo demonstrates, as does the Greek Horologion printed at Venice in the year of Christ 1535. In the great Paschal Cycle appended there, it makes that year the year 7044 of the world; if you subtract 1536 from that number—that is, the years of Christ—5,508 years remain, namely the years of the world up to Christ’s birth. Even the present year of Christ, 1571, it makes the year 7079 of the world, and it gives its times and principal movable feasts as follows. Greek. [Col. 0525B] I thought it worthwhile to add the Greek, together with a Latin translation, because this matter appears to be known to few Latins and to our own people. “Year 7079, indiction 14, solar cycle 23, lunar cycle 11. The eve of Christ’s birth: Sunday; meat-eating: day 56; the Triodion begins February 4; the legal Passover, April 12; the Christians’ Passover, April 15; the Sunday of All Saints, June 10; the fast of the holy Apostles, day 17.” That is: in the year 7,079 of the world—that is, the seventh thousand and seventy-ninth, the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1571—indiction XIV; solar cycle XXIII (our Latins count only XII); lunar cycle, or cycle of the moon, XI. The vigil, or expectation, of Christ’s birth falls on Sunday; Meat-eating is on day LVI; Apocrea, or the day of abstinence from meat, is February XVIII; the Triodion begins on February 4; the legal Passover is on April 12; the Christians’ Passover is on April 15; the Sunday of All Saints is on June 10; the fast of the holy Apostles is on day XVII. As for the indiction, it is the same as in the Latin tradition. But the solar cycle and the phengarius—[Col. 0525D] φεγγάρη is what the moon is called in the common Greek language today, whereas formerly it was σελήνη—that is, the lunar cycle or golden number and the nineteen-year cycle, do not agree with the Latin ecclesiastical computation. For it reckons twelve years for the solar cycle and fourteen for the lunar. If anyone wishes to know from Greek tradition how to calculate both cycles, lunar and solar, let him see what Balsamon notes on canon 78 of Carthage. The vigil of Christ’s birth falls on Sunday. It should therefore be known that the Greeks, and also the Latin Church, begin the year with the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity—if we believe Nicholas of Cusa, or Cusanus, who distinguishes the ordinary Italian reckoning from the Church’s computation. The ordinary Italian reckoning could not abandon the custom of the pagan Romans, who began the year from the Kalends of January. Since that Sunday is therefore the first Sunday of the entire year, it will be very easy, once this beginning has been established, to arrange all the other feasts of the year. For they do not have, as the Latins do, letters distinguishing their Sundays and weekdays throughout the year. [Col. 0526B] Meat-eating is on day LVI. The Greeks call “Meat-eating” the interval from the Nativity of the Lord to the Monday after the Sunday of Sexagesima, because Greek Christians eat meat only up to that day. Apocrea. This is what they call the Sunday of Sexagesima, because then they begin to abstain from meat. For that Sunday falls on February 18. Triodion. This is what they call the first series of the Sundays and movable feasts of the entire year, which always begins on the Sunday preceding the Sunday of Septuagesima, which they call the Sunday of the Pharisee and the Publican, or Tax Collector. The legal Passover, Φάσχα. Nazianzen says in his Panegyric on Easter that the Hebrew word ought to be written in this way, but that it has generally prevailed for it to be pronounced Pascha, as though derived from the Passion. Yet, to distinguish the Jewish Passover from the Christian Paschal feast, this word is written and pronounced differently. The Sunday of All Saints, June 10. Among the Latins this is Trinity Sunday, which closes all the ancient movable feasts; therefore, after the many feasts of Christ, the Greeks celebrate the feast of All Saints. The fast of the holy Apostles, day 17. I think that the weekdays and feast days between the feast of All Saints and the feast of the holy Apostles are meant; the Greeks celebrate the latter, as is clear from their Menologion, on June 30, that is, on the final day of June. But enough of this. Let us now return to Nicephorus.]

Accordingly, the total from Adam to the beginning of Augustus’s reign, according to the most exact chronographers, is 5,457 years. [Note: [Col. 0524D] Read “eight,” that is, 5,458.] For Augustus, as has been said, held the empire for fifty-six years and six months. In his forty-second year, our Lord Jesus Christ was born according to the flesh from the holy and God-bearing Virgin Mary, the eternal God, in Bethlehem, a town of Judaea, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, which is Choiak [Note: [Col. 0524D] This is the fourth month of the Egyptians, beginning on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, as Bede teaches in On the Nature of Things, chapter 11.] 29, and likewise December 25.

Cyrenaeus, [Note: [Col. 0524D] Anastasius reads “Cyrinus.”] then sent by the Senate, conducted a census of property and inhabitants. Thus the total from Adam to the administration of our Lord Jesus Christ in the flesh—that is, the ἐνσάρκον οἰκονομίαν, “the incarnate economy”—is, by the most exact reckoning, 5,500 years.

## CHAPTER X

[Note: [Col. 0526C] ON CHAPTER X.—He assigns Tiberius twenty-three years, as do Eusebius and Ausonius—or whoever else composed that very familiar verse:

“And Nero Claudius adds two to three times seven.”

Tertullian, in Against the Jews, assigns him twenty-two years and seven months; but Tacitus at the end of Book V, and Sextus Aurelius Victor—not in the printed edition but in a manuscript—assign him twenty-three years. We willingly agree with them. The total number of years of the world up to the Resurrection, to be gathered from the foregoing, is 5,540 years.] [Col. 0525A]

After Augustus, the third Roman emperor was Tiberius, for twenty-three years. In the fifteenth year of his reign, our Lord Jesus Christ began his saving and evangelical teaching.

In the eighteenth year of that same reign, he suffered at Jerusalem for us the saving Passion, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, Phamenoth 29, that is, March 25. [Note: [Col. 0525D] I have restored this from Anastasius; it is the seventh month of the Egyptian calendar, beginning on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.]

Thus from Adam to the saving Passion and Resurrection of our Lord and God, our Savior Jesus Christ, there are 5,533 years.

## CHAPTER XI

[Note: [Col. 0526D] ON CHAPTER XI.—Latin and Greek authors, both pagan and Christian, disagree among themselves concerning years, months, and days. In resolving this disagreement, or in choosing a proper course, I believe there is nothing preferable to joining the consuls and their catalogue, compiled by Cassiodorus and others, to the years of the emperors. We have carried this out as carefully as we could in our chronology, to which I shall gladly refer the curious reader. All agree on Tiberius’s twenty-three years, and this is how it is written in the manuscript of Sextus Aurelius Victor, which I use as my best authority—not, as in the printed books, twenty-four. Therefore, whenever I cite authors as witnesses, readers should know that I use chiefly those copies which I have compared with the best and most numerous manuscripts. In printed books I find almost nothing sound in the notation of periods and years, and in this error the Greek books are always more corrupt than the Latin, because of the similarity and subtlety of the Greek numerals. Verse of Ausonius:

“And Nero Claudius adds two to three times seven.”

Nicephorus assigns the emperor Gaius three years and ten months; but Aurelius Victor, Eusebius, and Harmenopulus in the manuscript Chronology of the Emperors give him four full years. The following little verse, attributed to Ausonius, is well known:]

The third winter flees, thickening Gaius’s seasons.

Here Claudius is assigned 13 years and 1 month; but Eusebius (I always mean the manuscript, for the printed text is wretchedly and most corruptly deformed) assigns him 13 years, 7 months, and 28 days; Harmenopulus, 13 years, 8 months, and 9 days. Nero likewise is here assigned 13 years [Col. 0528D] and 8 months; but Eusebius gives him 13 years, 7 months, and 28 days—not, as the printed text has it, 14 years, 8 months, and 28 days, by which everyone is misled. Aurelius Victor, however, assigns Claudius exactly 14 years and Nero 13. Yet Ausonius’s verse—which in this matter is the most effective kind of proof, since it lies beyond suspicion of scribal error—assigns exactly 14 years to both:

> Claudius completes a double hebdomad, and grim Nero likewise.

Galba too has been omitted here, more probably through a copyist’s error than through Nicephorus’s, although he ruled for 7 months, Otho for 3, and Vitellius for 8. Ausonius compresses them thus:

> Old Galba, wanton Otho, and notorious Vitellius,

> The third summer did not know you reigning over Latium,

> Worthy of deaths hastened by your disgraceful lives. [Col. 0529C]

The same author also assigns Vespasian exactly 10 years, as does Sextus Aurelius Victor:

> Vespasian completes for himself the fated decade.

Titus was shown to the world for the brief span of two years. To these I add the defective verse concerning Domitian:

> Three lustrums destroy him, and due atonements the brother:

But Nicephorus, following Eusebius, adds 15 years and 51 months. The years of the following rulers generally agree with the manuscript chronology of Eusebius. I have no desire either to prove or to refute the brief remarks it sprinkles concerning the manner of death of each emperor. They have nothing to do with the chronology that we are pursuing.

Some writers, among them Harmenopulus, insert Pompeianus, or Pupienus, and Balbinus, with three years; they also insert Aemilianus between Gallus and Valerian, and later Sillianus, Quintilius, and Florianus. But the years assigned to these men belong either to the preceding or to the following rulers. [Col. 0529D] When this author says that Decius perished in the forum, I understand him to mean the Forum Flaminium, in agreement with Eusebius.

As for Diocletian, to whom 20 years are assigned, this is the more common opinion of Eusebius and others, although Victor assigns him 25 years. Between Diocletian and Constantius, Eusebius also inserts Galerius and assigns him two additional years separately. Some complain that he has been omitted here, whether through an error of Nicephorus or of the copyist. I recognize no lacuna here, however, because Cassiodorus, in his list of the consuls, says that the years of Constantius and Galerius are assigned to Constantine, the son of Constantius, and assigns only 20 years of consulships.

He says that in Constantine’s twentieth year the first universal synod, that of Nicaea, was convened. But in the manuscript of Anastasius it is written that this occurred in the tenth year, [Col. 0530B] as also in the Chronology of Harmenopulus. Yet the Greek inscription, or title, of that same synod records that it was held under the consuls Paulinus and Julianus, which appears to be Constantine’s fifteenth year. The same place reckons the year from Alexander as 636.

From Alexander to the forty-second year of Augustus, when Christ was born, there are 323 years. If these are subtracted from 636, 313 years remain; these are the years of Christ in which that synod was held. But Nicephorus here reckons 318 years, as does the Greek Synopsis of the Councils; that was the year of the world 5826. Thus the Greek numeral ε, ω, κ, ς should be read here, and consequently the 285th year from Christ’s resurrection, as has correctly been calculated here.

If we read here that the Council of Nicaea was held in Constantine’s tenth year, and that this was the year 318 of Christ, the total calculation from Adam to Constantine’s death will agree correctly, making 5836 years.

Since authors disagree about the year of Constantine’s reign in which the Council of Nicaea was convened, the reason must be sought. Nicephorus here places it in the twentieth year, as the German printed edition has it, or in the tenth, as the manuscript copy of Anastasius has it. Eusebius, in Book IV of the Life of Constantine, chapter 47, places it in the twentieth year, saying that it occurred when his vicennalia were celebrated. Yet in the Chronicles translated by Jerome, he records it as having been held in Constantine’s thirteenth year. Cassiodorus gives the eighteenth year, and others give other dates.

I therefore think that the reason is that most people count the years of Constantine’s reign in different ways: some from Diocletian’s laying aside of the purple, assigning no time to Constantius, Galerius, or Maxentius; some from Constantius’s death; and some from the defeat of all his imperial colleagues. Because of such great uncertainty, the title of the synod itself does not state in what year of his reign it was held, but only under which consuls and in what year from Alexander’s death, according to the reckoning then used throughout Greece and Egypt.

[Col. 0525B] Julius Caesar, therefore, as has been said, ruled the kingdom he had seized at Rome for four years and seven months. Octavian succeeded him; his reign lasted 56 years and 6 months. [The third emperor was Tiberius, Octavian’s stepson, for 23 years. [Note: [Col. 0525D] The enclosed words are absent from Anastasius, correctly, because they had already been given above.]]

[Col. 0526A] After Tiberius came Gaius, for 3 years and 10 months. [Note: [Col. 0525D] He was killed in the palace.]

Claudius, 13 years and 1 month. He was removed by poison.

Nero, 13 years and 8 months, fled [Note: [Col. 0526D] It should be read this way, as in the Greek κατέφυγεν, “he fled for refuge,” and so forth], and killed himself while still alive. When this Nero first stirred up the persecution, Peter and Paul became martyrs at Rome. James, the brother of the Lord, whom everyone called “the Just,” was also overwhelmed with stones by the Jews at Jerusalem. [Note: [Col. 0526D] Galba has been wrongly omitted here; he ruled for 7 months.]

Otho, 3 months; he killed himself.

Vitellius, 8 months.

Vespasian, 9 years, 11 months, and 22 days; he died in the Sallustian Gardens. In the second year of his reign, Jerusalem was captured by his son Titus, 35 years after Christ’s assumption. [Col. 0526B] [Note: [Col. 0526D] The years stated individually add up to 39, as Eusebius also calculates.]

Titus, 2 years and 2 months; he was killed in the palace.

Domitian, 15 years and 5 months. When he stirred up the persecution, the apostle John was assigned the island of Patmos for residence. After Domitian’s death he returned from there to Ephesus and remained there until Trajan’s reign.

Nerva, 1 year and 4 months.

Trajan, 19 years and 6 months. In his time the god-bearing [Note: [Col. 0527D] Anastasius translates it in this way; others incorrectly have “the divine”] Ignatius became a martyr at Rome, exposed to wild beasts.

Hadrian, 21 years. He died at Baiae, with fluid having accumulated between the skin and the flesh. After Jerusalem had been destroyed, he gave the restored city the name Aelia.

Titus Antoninus, surnamed Pius, together with his sons Aurelius Verus and Lucius, 22 years and 3 months.

Marcus Aurelius, his son, 19 years [Col. 0527B] and 2 months. In his time Justin the philosopher became a martyr. Antonius Verus, 12 years. [Note: [Col. 0527D] It seems that it should be read: “Antonius Verus ruled with him for 11 years”; Eusebius gives 19, but Victor 18.]

Commodus, 13 years.

Aelius Pertinax, 6 months. He was killed in the palace.

Severus, 18 years. During his reign Leonides, the father of Origen, described as κακόφρονος, “evil-minded” [Note: [Col. 0527D] Anastasius translates this as “heretical”], became a martyr. Hippolytus, the Roman historian, also flourished, as did Gregory the Wonder-worker—ταυματουργός, that is, “performer of miracles”—and Clement of Alexandria.

Antonius, the son of Severus, 7 years. He was killed between Carrhae and Edessa.

Macrinus, 1 year. He was killed by the army.

Antonius Gabalus, 4 years. He was killed at Rome.

Alexander, the son of Mamaea, 13 years. He was killed near Mainz. [Col. 0527C]

Maximinus, 3 years. He was killed at Aquileia.

Gordian, 6 years. He ended his life by hanging in Africa.

[Col. 0528A] Philip, 7 years. He was killed in the Tiberian Gardens.

Decius, 1 year and 3 months. He perished in the forum.

In his time Saint Babylas became a martyr at Antioch, along with many others in various provinces, and seven boys at Ephesus.

Gallus and Volusianus, 1 year and 4 months. [Note: [Col. 0527D] Eusebius, Aurelius Victor, and the others assign them 2 years, and in addition 2 months.]

Valerian and Gallienus, 12 years. Valerian was killed in Persia; Gallienus at Milan.

Claudius, 1 year and 9 months. He died at Sirmium.

Aurelian, 5 years and 6 months. He was killed in the New Fortress. [Note: [Col. 0527D] Anastasius has “in prison.” Nicephorus had written ἐν καινῷ φρουρείῳ, “in the new fortress.”]

Tacitus, 6 months. He was killed in Pontus. At that time Saint Charito made his confession.

[Col. 0528B] Probus, 6 years and 4 months. He was killed at Sirmium.

Carus, together with his sons Carinus and Numerianus, 2 years. Carus died in Mesopotamia; Carinus died in the Thracian town of Numeria. [Note: [Col. 0528D] Something seems to be missing here, namely Numerianus and the manner of his death.]

Diocletian and Maximian, 20 years. In their time Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria, became a martyr, along with many others throughout the province. [Note: [Col. 0528D] Galerius, Constantius, and Maxentius seem to be missing here; they reigned between Diocletian and Constantine.]

Constantine the Great, 31 years.

In the twentieth year of his reign, the holy first synod of the 318 Fathers was convened at Nicaea in Bithynia: 318 years after Christ was born in the flesh, but 385 after the venerable Passion and glorious Resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0528D] 351 should be read. Above, Anastasius read 10 instead of 20; Harmenopulus also reports the same.]

[Col. 0528C] Thus, from Adam until the death of Constantine the Great, the total is 5,836 years.

## CHAPTER XII

[Note: [Col. 0530D] ON CHAPTER XII.—What he writes concerning the years of Constantine and his sons agrees with Eusebius, and so does what he writes concerning Julian and Jovian. But there is disagreement concerning Valentinian and those who follow. Here Valentinian and Valens are assigned 10 years and 9 months; Jerome, however, who supplemented Eusebius at this point, gives 14 years. Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius are assigned 16 years. Prosper assigns Gratian, together with his brother Valentinian, 5 years, and Theodosius afterward 11 years; this calculation comes to the same result. Arcadius and Honorius are assigned 13 years. Prosper gives 32 years, but later, where Nicephorus gives Theodosius the Younger 42 years, Prosper gives him only 27; thus Prosper exceeds Nicephorus by four years. Sigebert, to be sure, assigns 13 years, as does Nicephorus; after his death, he assigns 14 years to Honorius, his brother’s son, and after Honorius’s death 3 years to Theodosius alone, then 24 years to the same Theodosius together with Valentinian. All these years add up to 54, a total agreeing with Nicephorus. Martian and Valentinian, 25 years. Sigebert assigns Martian 6 years, Valentinian with him 5 years, and Leo 16 years after Martian’s death; after Valentinian’s death he assigns 2 years to Maximus and Avitus, and 4 years to their successor Majorian; then likewise 4 years to his successor Severus, and likewise 4 years to that man’s successor Anthemius; then 7 months to Olybrius, and assigns the remaining years to Glycerius and Nepos, and to Orestes, Augustulus, and Odoacer, succeeding one another, until the completion of Leo’s sixteenth year of reign. I therefore think that there is an error here in Nicephorus and that 5 or 8 should be read instead of 25; for Harmenopulus assigns them only 7 years, as does Bede. [Col. 0531D] Zeno, 17 years. Sigebert, from the Chronicle of Bishop Idacius, assigns him 19 years; but afterward he assigns Anastasius only 25, while Nicephorus gives him 27. Thus the result is the same. The same Sigebert assigns exactly 10 years to Justin the Elder, whereas Nicephorus and Harmenopulus give 9 years and 3 months. Justinian, 28 years and 7 days. In fact he reigned 28 years and 8 months. For this reason Harmenopulus, Bede, and most others assign him exactly 39 years. Under him the holy Council of Constantinople was held. Some refer this to his twenty-fourth year, including Sigebert and others. In the seventh year of this reign, one cycle of Saint Paschatus, lasting 532 years, was completed from the time when the Lord Jesus Christ had been crucified, in indiction 6. There is very great disagreement between the Latins and Greeks on this matter. Sigebert says that this cycle was completed in the fifth year of Justinian’s reign [ [Col. 0532D] Some, however, note that it occurred in the fifth year, others in the sixth: “Justin­ian did this,” says Sigebert], and calls it the great year of 533 years from Christ’s birth. He also says that Abbot Dionysius began his cycle in that year, a cycle of five nineteen-year cycles. “And because,” he says, “the second year of the work must agree, in the reckoning of the computus, with the first year of Christ’s birth, the thirty-fifth year of Dionysius’s cycle must agree, in the reckoning of the computus, with the thirty-third year of Christ’s birth; that is, the fourteenth day of the moon in April must fall on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, on Thursday; Christ’s Passion on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on Friday; and the Resurrection on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, on Sunday. But since it does not fall thus, but the fourteenth day of the moon in April falls on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, on Sunday, while Easter Sunday falls on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, it is rejected because it conflicts with evangelical truth.” Thus Sigebert.

Bede also writes in On the Nature of Things: “Under Justinian, Dionysius wrote the Paschal cycles, beginning from the year 532 of the Lord’s Incarnation, which is Diocletian’s 248th year, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, in which year the Justinian Code was promulgated to the world. Victor, bishop of Capua, also criticized the errors of Victorius when writing his book on Easter.” Thus Bede.

But all objections of this kind against Dionysius collapse if, as Nicephorus reads here, we reckon those 532 years and those cycles of Dionysius not from Christ’s Incarnation but from his Passion. And from the Greek Horologion, to which the Paschal cycle is attached, it is clear that the Greeks have calculated the date of Easter with complete accuracy and without any error down to the present time. A more careful treatment of this matter, however, is not proper to the present work and would require a greater expenditure of time.] [Col. 0529A]

Constantine died after, as they say, reigning 31 years and having lived 65 years, leaving three sons: Constans, Constantine, and Constantius. Constans ruled old Rome, Constantine the new Rome, and Constantius Antioch. He completed two consulships. [Note: [Col. 0529D] Anastasius correctly reads “ten,” for from the Fasti we know that Constantius entered ten consulships.]

But after Constantine his sons reigned for 24 years.

Julian, 2 years. He was killed in Persia.

Jovian, 9 months.

Valentinian the Great and his brother Valens, 10 years and 9 months. During Valens’s reign Saint Dorotheus became a martyr, exposed to wild beasts in the hunt by the Arians.

[Col. 0529B] Gratian and Valentinian the Younger [Note: [Col. 0529D] Anastasius correctly reads “the Junior”], the sons of Valentinian, and with them—

Theodosius the Great, 16 years; consul for the third time. In the second year of his reign, the second synod was convened at Constantinople, consisting of 150 holy Fathers.

Arcadius and Honorius, his sons, 13 years and 3 months.

[Col. 0530A] Theodosius the Younger, 42 years and 6 months. Under him the third synod was held at Ephesus, consisting of 200 holy Fathers, as well as another, conspiratorial synod [Note: [Col. 0530D] Anastasius correctly calls it “the Robber Synod,” for the Greek has ληστρική], presided over by the impious Dioscorus.

Martian and Valentinian, 25 years. Under them the fourth holy synod was held at Chalcedon, consisting of 630 holy Fathers.

Leo the Great, 16 years.

Leo the Younger died after reigning one year with his father.

Zeno, 17 years, with the tyrant Basiliscus for 2 years.

Anastasius, 27 years and 4 months.

Justin the Thracian, 9 years and 3 months.

Justinian the Great, 38 years and 7 days. Under him the holy Council of Constantinople, the fifth, was held.

Justin, the son of Justinian’s brother, 12 years, 11 months, and 20 days.

In the seventh year of this reign, one cycle of Saint Paschatus, lasting 532 years, was completed from the time when our Lord Jesus Christ had been crucified, in indiction 6, in the year 6065 from the creation of the world.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 0533B] ON CHAPTER XIII.—Because this entire final chapter is miserably corrupted, mutilated, and defective, and because this is also testified by those who first published it, this section must be reexamined somewhat more carefully from other authors. Tiberius, 5 years. Sigebert’s manuscript gives him 6 years; the manuscript Chronicle of Hugo, 7 years; Harmenopulus, in his manuscript List of Emperors, assigns him 4 years. The same author assigns 15 years to Justin, his predecessor, whereas Nicephorus here gives him only 12 and Zonaras 13. Nicephorus Callistus reconciles the matter at the end of Book XVII of his Ecclesiastical History as follows: Justin alone reigned 12 years and 10½ months, and with Tiberius, whom while still alive he adopted as his successor and colleague, 3 years less one month. The same author settles the entire difficulty concerning the years of this Tiberius in Book XVIII of his Ecclesiastical History: Tiberius reigned alone for 4 years and with Justin, his predecessor, for 3 years. Thus Paul the Deacon assigns him 7 years; Evagrius, in Book V, chapter 21, 4 years; Zonaras, 3 years, 10 months, and 8 days; Cedrenus, 4 years. In public monuments he is inscribed in Phoenician letters as TIBERIUS CONSTANTINUS.

Maurice, 20 years and 4 months. In public documents he is written as Mauritius, also called Tiberius; according to Zonaras, the manuscript Chronology of Harmenopulus, and Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History, Book XVIII, he reigned 20 years. Sigebert and Hugo assign him 21 years; Cedrenus, 20 years, 3 months, and 2 days. Phocas, 8 years. Thus Nicephorus Callistus, Book XVIII [Col. 0533D] of his Ecclesiastical History, final chapter, and Zonaras, Cedrenus, Sigebert, and others.

Heraclius, 31 years together with his son. Sigebert gives 30 years; Paul the Deacon, 31, as do Nicephorus, Zonaras, and the manuscript List of Harmenopulus.

Constantius, his son, 28 years. It is thought that the Nicephorian text is extraordinarily corrupt at this point; it must therefore be supplemented from elsewhere as follows: After Heraclius, who died a most shameful death as punishment for incest, Constantius, his son, succeeded him and reigned 15 years. His stepmother and first cousin—ἐξ ἀδελφῆς, “from a sister”—killed him with poison and ruled in his place with her son Heraclona for scarcely a full year, as Zonaras testifies; Hugo assigns two years to both of them. Paul the Deacon, at the end of Book XVIII, gives Constantine, the son of Maurice, 4 months, and Martina and Heraclona 1 year; Sigebert follows him. Cedrenus gives Constantine 4 months and Martina and Heraclona only 6 months, less than a full year for all of them. The Senate, having expelled Martina and Heraclona—and having cut off the nose of the latter—placed Constans, the son of Constantine who had been removed by poison and the grandson of Heraclius, in power. According to Zonaras, Paul the Deacon, and Cedrenus, he ruled 27 years.

Having arranged these matters in this way, I began to notice that the Nicephorian text is not so corrupt here—or rather, is not corrupt at all—if we understand this Constantine, whom Nicephorus makes reign for 28 years, to be the same man whom others call Constans. Sigebert also writes that this Constans was called Constantine. There will be only this error: he called him a son when he should have called him a grandson. Once this error is removed, Nicephorus agrees with the manuscript List of Harmenopulus, which, omitting Constantine, Martina, and Heraclona’s scarcely complete year, assigns a little more than one year to this Constantine—that is, Constans—namely 28 years. That this is the Constantine whom most people call Constans is also strongly demonstrated by the fact that Nicephorus says here that he was killed in Sicily. From Zonaras one may learn that this applies to Constans, as also from Paul the Deacon, Book XIX, who assigns him only 27 years, since he had already assigned one year to Martina and her stepson and son.

Constans, the grandson of Heraclius, 17 years. Constantine should apparently be read here. For it is certain that the subject is Constantine Pogonatus, the son of Constans, an orthodox ruler, under whom the Sixth Synod was held in his thirteenth year, as is noted here. Zonaras likewise assigns him 17 years, as does the Deacon, who says that such a synod was held in his twelfth year; the others and the Greeks give the thirteenth year.

Justin, this man’s son, 10 years. Here too Justinian should apparently be read. The person meant is he who was later called Rhinotmetus, “the Nose-Cut.”

Tiberius, also called Absimarus, 8 years. Cedrenus, the Deacon, Hugo, Zonaras, and Sigebert assign him only 7 years; thus the text should apparently be corrected here.

Justinian, in his second reign, 11 years. Hugo assigns him only 6 years; Sigebert 7, Cedrenus 6, as does the Greek Theophanes; Harmenopulus, however, gives 7. Therefore the reading 11 here is erroneous and should be corrected to 6.

In the second year of this renewed reign, Theophanes, the Greek author cited by the compilers of the latest edition of the Councils, writes that the canons of the Sixth General Synod in Trullo were enacted. Indeed, the preface of that synod expressly indicates that the synod was held under this Justinian, the son of Constantine Pogonatus; it also gives the year in which it was held, calling it, in its canon, the year 6199 from the creation of the world, in indiction 4. I calculate that year as follows: in the seventh year of Justin the Younger, a Paschal cycle of 532 years from Christ’s Passion was completed; therefore it was the year 565 of Christ. Adding the 33 years that he had lived before the Passion, and consequently the year 6073 of the world, I add the remaining 5 years of Justinian, 5 of Tiberius, 20 of Maurice, 8 of Phocas, 31 of Heraclius, 27 of Constans, including Constantine, Martina, and Heraclona, 17 of Constantine Pogonatus, 10 of the first reign of this Justinian, 3 of Leontius, and 7 of Absimarus. The total is 6205, six years more than it should be. But perhaps 4 years must be subtracted from Justin, 3 from Tiberius, and several years from those who follow.

Philippicus, also called Bardanes, 11 years. According to the Deacon, Sigebert, Harmenopulus, and others, 2 should be read. [Col. 0535C] Hugo assigns him 6 years and months.

Leo the Isaurian. He was also called Conon the Syrian and the Iconoclast. He is here assigned 25 years; Harmenopulus gives 24 years, 8 months, and 25 days; the Deacon gives 24 years, 2 months, and 22 days, more correctly than all the others.

Constantine, his son, 34 years, 11 months, and 25 days. He was called Copronymus and was a whelp more cruel than his father Leo, as well as a most wicked iconoclast. Harmenopulus assigns him 34 years and 3 months. He was called Copronymus because, while being baptized by Patriarch Germanus, he defecated in the holy font, giving a great portent that he would become a scandal to the Church of God. Sigebert assigns him 33 years; Zonaras, 34 years and 3 months; the Deacon, 55 years, 2 months, and 26 days.

Leo the Khazar, 5 years. He was the son of Constantine Copronymus by a Khazar woman.

Constantine, his son, together with his mother Irene, 10 years, 2 months, and 2 days. Sigebert published exactly 10 years, as did Harmenopulus. [Col. 0535D] In their second year the Second Council of Nicaea was held. Cedrenus and Paul the Deacon likewise say so. Sigebert says that this synod was begun in their seventh year. Its Greek title records that it was held in the year 6296 of the world, indiction 2. In the *Diegesis* of the councils, published at Paris, the date is given as the year 6293 of the world and 794 of Christ. The reading in the title of the edition of the *Nomocanon* of Hermeti—6696 of the world—is corrupt and should be corrected to 6296.

Constantine alone, 6 years . . . and Irene, his mother, 5 years, and so forth. These facts are certain. Nicephorus gives 8 years and 6 months. Cedrenus assigns him and his son Stauracius 9 years. He was advanced to imperial power with the aid of eunuchs, as often happened among Romans, Greeks, and most barbarians. It would take too long to enumerate how many evils eunuchs have inflicted upon public affairs and empires. The greatest and most significant was that, through the jealousy of one eunuch, Aetius, the marriage arranged between Charlemagne and Irene, empress of Constantinople, was disrupted, and consequently the reconciliation and consolidation of the two empires, East and West, was prevented.

The saying of Chrysaorius, which Cedrenus reports as having been whispered to one of the rulers, is well known:

> If you have a eunuch, kill him; but if you do not have one, buy one and kill him.

Harmenopulus calls this Nicephorus “the Seleucian” and adds ὁ ἀπὸ τυνικῶν ὁ συμπαθής, “the sympathetic one from the [uncertain] *tynika*,” but it should be read ὁ ἀπὸ γενικῶν, “the one from the *genika*.” That is, he was elevated to imperial power from the position of general, or from that of general logothete.

Michael, his son-in-law. This man, surnamed Rangabes, γαμβρός, “son-in-law,” of Nicephorus, reigned for one year according to Harmenopulus, or two according to Sigebert and the Deacon; according to this Nicephorus, 1 year, 9 months, and 11 days. What follows concerning Leo the Armenian and Michael II agrees with the other authors.

Sigebert says that among other gifts Michael II’s ambassadors brought to Louis, emperor and king of the Franks, the books of Dionysius the Areopagite on the Celestial Hierarchy. At Louis’s request they were translated from Greek into Latin and received with joy at Paris on the very feast of the holy martyr, followed immediately by the miraculous healing of nineteen sick persons.

In the eighth year of this Michael, which he places as the year 829 from Christ and 4788 from the creation of the world, he writes that a new great year from the beginning of the world was completed, consisting of 532 years; the arithmetic of the division also demonstrates this.

Theophilus, his son, 12 years and 11 months. Zonaras writes the same, and Cedrenus likewise; Sigebert, however, assigns him 15 years.

Theodora, together with her son Michael, 14 years and 1 month. Sigebert says that Michael and Theodora ruled for 11 years, and afterward Michael alone for 13 years. The total is 24 years. Nicephorus, however, assigns him 14 years with his mother and 11 alone. The total is 25 years. Cedrenus agrees with Nicephorus.

With this Michael, therefore, Nicephorus ends; it may be inferred that he was alive at that time. Cedrenus indeed relates that this man wrote a letter to Michael Balbus, the father of Theophilus, in favor of the restoration of the sacred images.

Basil the Macedonian succeeded this Michael and reigned 19 years, according to Harmenopulus, Cedrenus, and Zonaras; they add that he ruled one additional year jointly with Michael. Sigebert assigns him 17 years. He had resolved to cleanse and revise the Roman laws and statutes. But what he had begun was completed by his son, the emperor Leo, surnamed the Philosopher, who published to the world the sixty books of the *Basilica* and many further Novels. [Col. 0531A]

Tiberius, 5 years.

Maurice [Note: [Col. 0531D] Absent from Anastasius], 20 years and 4 months; he was killed.

Phocas [Note: [Col. 0531D] The Greeks call him a tyrant, as do Zonaras and others], 8 years; he was killed.

Heraclius, 31 years together with his son. In the third year of this reign, the Persian Chosroes occupied many places belonging to the Roman Empire. He plundered Jerusalem and set fire to the holy places, carrying off a great multitude of captives to Persia together with the patriarch Zachariah and the precious wood [Note: [Col. 0531D] Τιμίων ξύλων, “the precious wood”]. In his twelfth year Chosroes the Persian was killed, the captives were recalled, and the life-giving Cross was restored to its own places once they had been rebuilt. Then the Saracens began to lay waste everything, in the year 6126 of the world [al., 6129], indiction 7.

[Col. 0531B] Constantine, his son, 28 years. [Note: [Col. 0531D] He is called Constantine Pogonatus.] He was killed in Sicily; during his time a large part of the empire was devastated by the Saracens.

Constans, the grandson of Heraclius, 17 years. During his reign Byzantium was devastated by the Saracens. [Note: [Col. 0531D] Anastasius has this reading; the German edition has “besieged.”] The Sixth Synod was also held at Constantinople in his thirteenth year. He acted bravely against the Saracens, checking their attack and greatly terrifying them.

Justin [Note: [Col. 0531D] He is called Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine, and is surnamed Rhinotmetus], his son, 10 years.

Leontius [Note: [Col. 0532D] Sigonius calls him Leo], 3 years.

Tiberius, also called Absimarus, 8 years. [Note: [Col. 0532D] This should be corrected to 6 years.]

Philippicus, also called Bardanes, 2 years.

Anastasius, also called Artemius, 2 years.

Theodosius, 1 year. [Note: [Col. 0532D] Paul the Deacon has this reading, but Zonaras gives him two years.]

[Col. 0532B] Leo the Isaurian [Note: [Col. 0532D] He was called the Iconoclast], 25 years, 3 months, and 14 days.

(Constantine, his son, 34 years, [Col. 0533A] 2 months, and 25 days; Leo the Khazar, 5 years.)

Constantine, his son, together with his mother Irene, 10 years, 2 months, and 2 days. In their eighth year the Second Council of Nicaea was held, consisting of 350 holy Fathers of the Church.

Constantine alone, 6 years, 9 months, and 8 days.

The following is added by Anastasius.

## GENEALOGY OF VALENTINIAN THE GREAT

Valentinian fathered Gratian and Valentinian, the emperors, and Galla, the wife of Theodosius the Great. Theodosius the Elder fathered Arcadius and Honorius, the emperors, and Placidia, the wife of Constantius. Arcadius’s children were Theodosius the Younger and Pulcheria, who was the wife of the emperor Martian. From the aforementioned Constantius and Placidia was born Valentinian III. The mother of Theodosius the Younger was that Eudoxia who sent John Chrysostom into exile. The wife of Theodosius himself was called Eudocia.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0536D] ON CHAPTER XIV.—I consider it superfluous to discuss or comment further on this summary collection—which the Greeks call συνοπτικὸν χρονικόν, “synoptic chronicle”—since scarcely anything in the collection is either true, consistent with the preceding detailed calculations, or mutually coherent. I could add many other synoptic chronicles of this sort, including those among the Greeks and that of Suidas. But what value would that have, since Suidas too is equally corrupt and appears to have copied everything word for word from Nicephorus up to Michael, while adding what follows either from himself or from more recent writers? From where, I ask, could they have learned the year of the construction of Nimrod’s tower? It certainly cannot be extracted from the canonical books, whether Hebrew, Greek, or Latin. The rest, too, has been compiled differently from the way it has been shown above that it ought to be calculated.] [Col. 0535A]

The years are calculated in the following manner.

From Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years.

From the Flood to the tower of Nimrod: 525 years.

From the tower to the διχοτομήματα, the “halvings,” of Abraham: 425 years.

From the halvings to the end of Abraham: 76 years.

Total: 3,268 years.

From Abraham to the exodus of the Israelites: 430 years.

From the exodus to the building of the Lord’s Temple: 757 years.

[Col. 0536A] From the building of the Temple to the captivity: 425 years.

Total: 4,880 years.

From the captivity to Alexander: 318 years.

From Alexander to Christ: 303 years.

Total: 5,500 years.

From Christ to Constantine the Great: 318 years.

From Constantine to Theophilus, in indiction 5: 530 years.

Total: 6,350 years.

[Col. 0537A] Thus we began by calculating the first part, and we must add the final part.

From Adam to the birth of Christ: 5,508 years.

[Col. 0538A] From the birth of Christ the Lord to his saving Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven: 33 years.

From Christ’s Ascension to the seventh year of Justin the Younger: 532 years, that is, one great Paschal cycle.

From Justin’s seventh year to the thirteenth year of the reign of the emperor Theophilus, in which there was indiction 5, which Nicephorus names—for Cedrenus says that he began his reign at the beginning of indiction 8—there are 273 years in all; from Christ’s birth, 828 years. [Note: [Col. 0537D] Sigebert gives 843.]

Therefore, from the creation of the world to the final year of Theophilus, the total is 6,336 years. Thus the total of 6,350 years calculated here in the corrupted text of Nicephorus is erroneous.

[Col. 0537B]

Helena, daughter of Constantine the Great, wife of Julian **τοῦ πραβάτου**, “the transgressor.” Karita (or Karito), wife of Jovinian; Severa and Justa [elsewhere, Justina], wives of Valentinian the Great. Dominica, wife of Valens. Galla and Placilla, wives of Theodosius the Great. Eudoxia, wife of Arcadius. Eudoxia, wife of Theodosius the Younger. Pulcheria, wife of Marcian. Verina, wife of Leo the Great. Ariadne, wife of Zeno. The same Ariadne, wife of Anastasius. Euphemia, wife of Justin I. Theodora, wife of Justinian the Great. Sophia, wife of Justin. Anastasia, wife of Tiberius. Constantina, wife of Maurice. Leontia, wife of Phocas. Flavia Eudocia and Martina, wives of Heraclius. Heracleone, wife of Constantine. [Wives of] Justinian, Leo, Absimarus, Philippicus, Theodosius, Justinian, and Artemius. Maria, wife of Leo I the Isaurian. Irene the Khazar, wife of Constantine. Maria Eudocia [Note: From other passages that I have collated, it seems that it should be read “Maria Eudoxia.”], Irene, and Athene, wives of Leo II, who was a Khazar. Maria and Theodore, wives of Constantine. Thebano [elsewhere, Theophanio], wife of Staucatius. Procopia, wife of Michael. Theodosia, wife of Leo. Thecla and Euphrosyne, wives of Michael. Theodora, wife of Theophilus. Eudocia, wife of Michael; Eudocia, wife of Basil [Note: With regard to the foregoing catalogue of the Augustae, which I have cleansed as faithfully as I could, I have judged that nothing should be added by way of annotation, willingly passing this task on to the idle. From Cedrenus, Zonaras, and others, one can learn the wives both of these and of the succeeding emperors. From Suetonius, Spartianus, Capitolinus, Lampridius, and others, one may learn the wives of the earlier Augusti, such as Livia, wife of Augustus; Plotina, wife of Trajan; Sabina, wife of Hadrian; Faustina the Elder, wife of Antoninus Pius; and the other Faustina, wife of Marcus Aurelius.].

## CHAPTER XVI

Kings of the ten tribes of Israel in Samaria, from the time of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, until the deportation of the ten tribes into Assyria under Hezekiah, king of Judah.

1. Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, was anointed by Ahijah [Col. 0537D] the prophet, because his master Solomon had turned aside [Col. 0538B] to foreign wives and to their alien rites.

2. Nabath, his son, for two years.

3. Baasha (he destroyed the house of Jeroboam), for twenty-four years.

4. Elah, his son, under whom was Jehu the prophet, for two years.

5. Zimri, his servant, who killed him, for seven months.

6. Omri, for twelve years.

7. Ahab, his son, under whom Elijah the prophet shut up heaven and killed the priests of Baal, for twenty-two years.

8. Ahaziah, his son, for two years.

9. Jehoram, his brother, whom Jehu killed according to [Col. 0538C] the word of the Lord; under him the prophet Elisha lived, for twelve years.

10. Jehu: anointed by a disciple of Elisha for the destruction of the house of Ahab, according to the prophecy of Elijah, for twenty-eight years.

11. Jehoahaz, whom Hazael, king of Syria, afflicted by laying waste his kingdom, for seventeen years.

12. Joash, under whom Elisha the prophet foretold victory over the Syrians and performed miracles, for sixteen years.

13. Jeroboam, under whom was the prophet Jonah, for fourteen years.

14. Zechariah, in whom the prophecy of Elisha was fulfilled. For God had promised through this Jehu that the Israelite kings descended from him would endure to the fourth generation. His reign lasted six months.

[Col. 0538D] 15. Shallum, slayer of Zechariah, for one month.

[Col. 0539A] 16. Menahem, for ten years.

17. Pekahiah, son of Menahem, for two years.

18. Pekah, son of Remaliah, for twenty years; under him were the prophets Isaiah and Nahum.

19. Hoshea, son of Elah, slayer of Pekah, for nine years. In his time Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, captured all Samaria, its king, and all Israel, except for the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, while Hezekiah was king in Jerusalem. He brought into that land the people called Cuthaeans and settled them in Samaria and in the cities that he had devastated and captured. They worshiped their own gods, and therefore God became angry and sent lions among them, by which they were devoured.

When the king of Assyria learned of this matter and its cause, he sent Israelites to them with priests to teach them the law and the worship of the eternal God. They accepted only the writings of Moses; and while worshiping the eternal God, they did not abandon their idols.

Their descendants are the Samaritans to this day. They preserve only the Pentateuch and avoid Jewish customs.

## NICEPHORUS’S CATALOGUE OF THE BISHOPS OF BYZANTIUM AFTER CHRIST AND THE APOSTLES

1. Andrew the Apostle was the herald of the Gospel at Byzantium. He built a church in which God might be entreated with devout prayers beyond the district of Argyropolis; and he appointed Stachys bishop of that city, whom the Apostle mentions in the Epistle written to the Romans.

2. Stachys, for sixteen years.

[Col. 0544D] 3. Onesimus, for fourteen years.

4. Polycarp, for eighteen years.

5. Plutarch, for sixteen years.

[Col. 0545A] 6. Sedecion, for nine years.

7. Diogenes, for fifteen years.

8. Eleutherius, for seven years.

9. Felix, for five years.

10. Polycarp, for seventeen years.

11. Athenodorus, for four years. He built another church in the district called Olea, and held ecclesiastical assemblies there.

12. Euzoius, for sixteen years.

13. Laurentius, for eleven years and six months.

14. Alypius, for thirteen years and six months.

15. Pertinax, a consular man of the Roman Senate, for nineteen years, ten months, and five days. He built another church in a maritime place called Ficus; he named it Irene.

[Col. 0545B] 16. Olympianus, for eleven years.

17. Mark, for thirteen years.

18. Cyriacus, for sixteen years.

19. Castinus, for seven years. At Byzantium, in a place called Petrium, he built a church for prayer, dedicated to Saint Euphemia, who was later made a martyr.

20. Titus, for thirty-five years and six months.

21. Domitius, brother of the emperor Probus, for twenty-four years and six months.

22. Probus, son of this Domitius, for twelve years. All these were bishops of Byzantium before the emperor Constantine the Great was proclaimed at Byzantium, on account of the war against Licinius, in the time of Bishop Metrophanes.

23. Metrophanes, son of the Domitius mentioned above, brother of Bishop Probus, and son of the emperor Probus’s brother, for ten years. Since, because of his extreme old age, he could not sit in the Council of Nicaea, the presbyter Alexander took his place. See Nicetas, *Treasury*, book 5, chapter 6.

24. Alexander lived ninety-eight years and was bishop for sixty-three years.

25. Paul the Confessor, for three years, expelled by Constantius.

26. Eusebius, declared an Arian, who had previously been bishop of Berytus and then of Nicomedia, for twelve years.

27. Macedonius, presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, opponent of the Holy Spirit, for twelve years. See Nicetas in the *Treasury*, book 5, chapter 6.

28. Eudoxius the Arian, who had previously been bishop of Germanicia and then of Antioch, for ten years.

29. Demophilus the Arian, who had previously been bishop of Beroea in Thrace, for eleven years and five months.

30. Evagrius, appointed by the laying on of hands of Eustathius of Antioch, and immediately expelled by Valens.

31. Gregory presided over the Church of Nazianzus for twelve years and then returned to private life.

32. Nectarius, a man of distinction, was baptized and ordained bishop at the same time by one hundred and fifty fathers; for sixteen years and three months.

33. John, presbyter of Antioch, surnamed [Col. 0546A] Chrysostom, for five years and six months.

34. After John was expelled, Arsacius, a presbyter and brother of Nectarius, for two years.

35. Atticus, presbyter of Constantinople, for twenty years.

36. Sisinnius, presbyter of the same Church, for two years.

37. Nestorius, denier of Christ’s humanity, since he denied that he was God; a presbyter of Antioch, for three years and two months. After this man had been sent into exile,

38. Maximianus, presbyter of Constantinople, for two years and five months.

39. Proclus [Note: Zonaras, *Annals*, vol. III, calls him Proculus and says that he was a disciple of Chrysostom.], made bishop of Cyzicus by Sisinnius. When he was not received there, because the people of Cyzicus had elected another, he devoted himself to private studies. After Maximianus died, he obtained the chief see of the city. He obtained from the emperor Theodosius the Younger permission to transfer the relics of John Chrysostom from Pityus to Constantinople. He served for twelve years and three months.

40. Flavianus, presbyter of Constantinople, for one year and ten months. After Dioscorus deposed him at that treacherous synod at Ephesus,

41. Anatolius, a presbyter and secretary to Dioscorus, was appointed in his place, for eight years and eight months.

42. Gennadius, presbyter of Constantinople, for thirteen years and two months.

43. Acacius, presbyter, administrator responsible for feeding orphans, a heretic, for seventeen years and nine months. He was condemned by Felix, the Supreme Pontiff, because he had composed the Henoticon, in the time of the emperor Zeno.

[Col. 0546C] 44. Phrabitas, presbyter of Saint Thecla at Sycis, three months and seventeen days.

45. Euphemius, presbyter of Constantinople and administrator responsible for feeding the poor in the New City, for six years and six months. After the emperor Anastasius expelled him,

46. Macedonius, presbyter of Constantinople and keeper of the vessels, for six years.

47. Timothy, presbyter of Constantinople and keeper of the vessels, for six years.

48. John the Cappadocian, presbyter and his syncellus, for one year and ten months.

49. Epiphanius, presbyter of Constantinople under Justinian, for sixteen years and three months.

[Col. 0546D] 50. Anthimus, bishop of Trebizond, for ten months. After he was removed, a synod was convened against Severus.

51. Menas, presbyter and superintendent of the hospice of the Sampsians, for sixteen years and six months.

52. Eutychius, presbyter and monk in the monastery at Amaseia, for twelve years and two months. Justinian expelled him in the thirty-eighth year of his reign because he would not accept the emperor’s edict concerning the body of Christ as entirely free from any corruption.

53. John, presbyter of Antioch, from the Scholastic order, for twelve years and seven months.

[Col. 0547A] 54. Eutychius, restored again under Justinian, completed four years and six months.

55. John, deacon of Constantinople, the Faster, in the time of Tiberius, for thirteen years and five months.

56. Cyriacus, presbyter of the same Church and steward, for eleven years.

57. Thomas, deacon of the same Church and treasurer, for three years and five months.

58. Sergius, deacon of the same Church, for eight years, seven months, and twenty-one days.

59. Pyrrhus, presbyter of the same Church, a monk and master of monasteries, and chief of Chrysopolis. When a revolt arose against him, he held office for two years, nine months, and two days.

[Col. 0547B] 60. Paul, presbyter of the same Church and steward, for two years and twenty-six days. Pyrrhus was restored for four months and twenty-three days.

61. Peter, superintendent of receiving guests in the same Church, for twelve years and seven months.

62. Thomas, deacon of the same Church and keeper of the archives, for two years and seven months.

63. John, presbyter and keeper of the vessels of the Great Church, for five years and nine months.

64. Constantine, deacon of the same Church, keeper of the vessels and steward, for one year, eleven months, and seven days.

65. Theodore, presbyter of the same Church, syncellus and keeper of the vessels, for two years and three months.

[Col. 0547C] 66. George, presbyter, syncellus, and keeper of the vessels, for three years and three months. Theodore was restored for one year and ten months.

67. Paul, and a layman from the secretariat.

68. Callinicus, presbyter and keeper of the vessels at Blachernae, for twelve years. He was expelled [Note: Deprived of his eyes.] by Justinian Rhinotmetus.

69. Cyrus, presbyter and monk, from Trogessus of Amastris, for six years. He was expelled by Philippicus.

70. John, deacon and keeper of the archives in the oikonomion, for three years.

71. Germanus, bishop of Cyzicus and confessor, for fifteen years. He was expelled by the impious Leo the Isaurian.

72. Anastasius, presbyter and syncellus, for twenty-four years.

[Col. 0548A] 73. Constantine, monk and bishop of Syllaeum, for twelve years. He was beheaded.

74. Nicetas [Note: He knew nothing except eating and drinking (Glycas, *Annals*, part IV). Once, when one of those standing nearby rebuked him because he had pronounced *Matthaeum* as *Matthaium*, he replied that he intensely hated words that had double and triple sounds (the same author, in the same place).], presbyter of the Holy Apostles and master of monasteries, a eunuch, for thirteen years and four months.

75. Paul the Cypriot, an orthodox deacon and confessor, for five years and six months.

76. Tarasius, from the secretariat, for twenty-one years and two days.

77. Nicephorus, from the secretariat, became a monk and was expelled by the impious Leo the Armenian [Note: He was deported to Proconnesus because he could not be induced to approve the attack on the images. He had foreseen this long before, having dreamed that his hand was joined to thistles and thorns when he first placed the diadem on Leo’s head (see Glycas, *Annals*, part III).], for . . . years.

78. Theodotus Cassiteras, for fifteen years.

79. Antonius, from Syllaeum, for twelve years.

80. John, presbyter and syncellus, who plotted against himself, for nine years.

81. Methodius the Confessor, for four years and three months.

82. Ignatius the eunuch [Note: He was the son of Michael Rangabes, or Balbus, emperor of Constantinople, by Procopia, daughter of the emperor Nicephorus. At first called Nicetas, and elevated by the emperor Leo the Armenian, he assumed another name along with the change in his life (Glycas, *Annals*, part IV). Expelled by Caesar Bardas, he was restored to his see under the emperor Michael the Drunkard, after Photius had been expelled by the emperor Basil the Macedonian (Glycas, in the work cited above).], for eleven years and five months.

83. Photius, after the divine Ignatius had resigned these earthly affairs, was installed a second time in the patriarchal see by the emperor Basil the Macedonian and received that most distinguished throne. In what manner this occurred, see Glycas, *Annals*, part IV. When he had previously been forced to vacate the throne by Samonas, the emperor’s chamberlain, Euthymius, an admirable man, was appointed in his place.

84. After Photius, Stephen, brother of Leo Philippus [Note: Zonaras, *Annals*, vol. III.].

85. After Stephen died, Antonius, surnamed Catuleas, succeeded him.

86. After him Nicholas the Mystic was designated patriarch. He initiated Constantine, son of Leo the Philosopher, in sacred baptism in the year of his pontificate. He was deported by the emperor Leo the Philosopher to the monastery of Galacrenaeum, which he had founded, because he could in no way be persuaded to receive again Samonas the Hagaren, who had defected to his own people, and to exempt him from censure. After the emperor Alexius expelled Euthymius, Nicholas was restored to his own see; and, when Constantine, son of Leo, was administrator of the empire, he was ordained in writing.

87. Euthymius, an admirable man [Note: Euthymius, a holy man, the Syncellus, was designated in place of Nicholas. He resisted by every means the emperor’s confirmation by law of third and fourth marriages. After his dignity had been revoked from the pulpit, he was subjected to many insults by Nicholas’s followers and expelled into exile by the emperor Alexius. Nicholas was restored and held the see for thirteen years. Somewhat later, in the month of July, the metropolitans and clergy who had until then been divided over the cause of Nicholas and Euthymius returned to unity (Cedrenus, under Romanus Lecapenus).].

88. After Nicholas, Stephen, metropolitan of Amasia, occupied the chief see of the city for three years.

89. Trypho, a monk. When the period prescribed by the emperor Romanus Lecapenus during which he was to administer the throne had elapsed, until the emperor’s son Theophylact reached the proper age, he was deceived by Theophanes the Caesarean bishop. After he had signed a blank document, he was removed from office [Note: See Glycas, Zonaras, and Nicetas throughout their accounts of this and the subsequent patriarchs.].

90. Theophylact, son of the emperor Romanus Lecapenus, a eunuch, seized the governance of the Church contrary to the canons in his sixteenth year. An extraordinary lover of horses, he lived an arrogant life. After he had presided for twenty-three years, he was seized with dropsy from riding and brought his life to an end.

91. Polyeuctus, a follower of the solitary life, was appointed in his place. From childhood he had been castrated at his parents’ will; he was altogether venerable, distinguished in eloquence and virtue. He resisted Nicephorus Phocas and John Tzimisces.

92. Polyeuctus was succeeded by Basil, a monk from Scamander. After four years from his appointment, he was removed from office by a council because of certain charges brought against him.

93. Antonius the Studite was appointed patriarch. After he had resigned the priesthood, which he had held for six years, and had died shortly thereafter, and the Church had remained vacant for four and a half years, there was appointed

94. Nicholas Chrysoberges. After he had adorned the pontificate for twelve years and eight months, he died and was succeeded by

95. Sisinnius the Magister, a man who had been devoted to letters from early youth. When he too had governed the Church for three years and died, Sergius was chosen patriarch.

96. Sergius, who presided over the monastery of Manuel and was related by family to Photius. After he had shepherded the Church for twenty years, he died, and in his place was appointed

97. Eustathius, chief of the priests of the palace church. After he had presided over the orthodox Church for eight years, he died shortly before the emperor Basil Porphyrogenitus.

98. Alexius, a solitary, succeeded him. He was transferred from the Studite establishment to the patriarchal throne. Having received ninety pounds of gold, and having given the same amount to the clergy, he confirmed the marriage of the emperor Michael with the empress Zoe, widow of Romanus Argyrus. Through the treachery of John the Orphanotrophus, brother of the emperor Michael the Paphlagonian, he almost lost the patriarchate.

99. After Alexius died, having held that see peacefully for eighteen years, the emperor Monomachus took from Alexius’s monastery twenty-five centenaries of gold that Alexius had deposited in the treasury. He was succeeded by Michael, surnamed Cerularius, a follower of the solitary life. When his dead hand had been arranged in the form of a cross, as it used to be when he announced peace to the people, it remained motionless and unchanged.

[Col. 0550A] 100. Constantine, governor and chief treasurer, surnamed Lichudes, liberal, magnificent, and diligent, after governing the Church for four years and six months, departed into another life.

101. John Xiphilinus, a monk, altogether admirable for eloquence, prudence, learning, and virtue, born at Trebizond, was living on Olympus in religious exercises. Since he was outstanding among the others, he was forcibly drawn to the patriarchate and shepherded the Church for eleven years and seven months.

102. Cosmas, although indeed unlearned, was adorned with virtues of every kind and was therefore also held in the highest esteem by the emperor. He crowned Nicephorus Botaneiates with the insignia of imperial rule. But when he could not approve the mode of governing of his successor, Alexius Comnenus, and despaired of its correction, he said to his attendant: “Take this book of Psalms and follow me.” Having said this, the most holy patriarch departed from the church. In his place was appointed [a successor] who shepherded the faithful people for five years and nine months.

103. Eustratius, a eunuch, a man of simple character and one worthy to hide in a corner. Yet after administering the pontificate for three years, he was unwillingly removed for some unknown reason, and in turn there was elevated to the height of the patriarchal throne

104. Nicholas the Monk, surnamed Grammaticus, who had spent his life in the pursuit of virtue and was not ignorant of letters, although not exceptionally learned. After governing the Church for twenty-seven years, he died at a very advanced age.

105. Leo the Stypiote.

106. Michael, a monk of the monastery of Acuta, renowned for virtue. He anointed the emperor Manuel, by whom he had been anointed, when he entered the sacred church. Surnamed Oxites, he voluntarily relinquished the supreme see and returned to the island of Oxeia, where from childhood he had embraced a life of poverty and simplicity.

107. Cosmas, an Aeginetan by birth, from the diaconate, although extremely learned, more illustrious still in the choir of virtues, cursed the empress’s womb.

108. Theodosius administered and adorned the chief see while Manuel was emperor. Restored to his see, born of an Armenian father, he voluntarily withdrew to the island of Terebinthus.

109. Basil Camaterus, to whom Andronicus transferred—or rather sold—the ecumenical patriarchate by means of a written undertaking that Basil had previously given, promising to do whatever pleased him, was deposed by the emperor Isaac Angelus.

110. Nicetas Mundanus, treasurer of the Great Church, succeeded him. The emperor did not allow him to die of old age in the sacred see; instead, alleging delirium, frivolity, and old age, he expelled him.

111 But a certain monk, Leontius, was appointed shepherd [Col. 0551A]; but before the year had elapsed the emperor also repudiated this “God-bearer” [Note: [Col. 0551D] Nicetas calls him “God-bearer” ironically, because the emperor had contrived to have him designated patriarch, and claimed that the place where he was to reside had been pointed out to him by the Mother of God [Col. 0552D].], etc.

112 Dositheus of Jerusalem was raised to the ecumenical patriarchate. In order to accomplish this, the emperor Isaac deceiv— Balsamon of Antioch—

A short time after these events, when Constantinople had been captured by the Gauls and Venetians and a Venetian patriarch had been elected, the Greeks openly deviated altogether from communion with the Apostolic See. Consequently, in compiling that catalogue of patriarchs, I have not wished to proceed any farther.

# COLLECTANEA

[Col. 0553]

## Preliminary Notice concerning the *Collectanea* of Anastasius the Bibliothecary

*(In Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XIII.)*

[Col. 0553D] The person of Anastasius himself is scarcely relevant to us, since we are concerned only with the character of the writings found in his *Collectanea*. Nevertheless, it is agreeable to say and preface something about him. He was, it seems, a Roman by nationality; certainly he was a presbyter, abbot, and bibliothecary of the Roman Church. He flourished especially from the year 858 to 882, under the popes Nicholas I, Hadrian II, and John VIII. Whether he should be considered identical with Cardinal Anastasius is discussed at greater length by the writers, among whom Cavaeus must especially be consulted. Bibliographers list his writings, among them the more diligent Fabricius [Note: [Col. 0553D] *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. IX, p. 337; *Bibliotheca media*, vol. I, p. 89, Padua edition.]. Above all, our Gallandius—*ὁ πάνυ*, “the very eminent”—has left us an edition of his *Collectanea*. The following monuments of writers circulate in them.

[Col. 0554D]

I. Two letters of Anastasius the Bibliothecary himself: one to John the deacon, the other to Martin, bishop of Narni.

II. An apology of Pope John IV for Pope Honorius.

III. Five letters of Saint Maximus.

IV. Three letters of Pope Theodore.

V. Four letters of Pope Martin.

VI. An account of what Saint Martin suffered at Constantinople.

VII. An account of the proceeding against Saint Maximus, which took place before the imperial officials in the secretariat.

VIII. A letter of Anastasius the monk.

IX. An account of the disputation between Saint Maximus and Theodosius, bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia.

[Col. 0555A] X. A letter of Anastasius the apocrisiarius to Theodosius, presbyter of Gangra.

XI. The *Hypomnesticon* concerning the deeds of Saints Maximus, the two Anastasii, Martin, and others.

These *Collectanea* were first published by Sirmond at Paris in the year 1620. They were also made public by Combefisius and in volume XII of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and were published again in a new recension of Sirmond’s works; from that edition we too transferred them into our collection. But let us now say something about the authors included in the *Collectanea*.

### § I. On Saint Pope John

This was Pope John IV, a Dalmatian by nationality and from the city of Jadera. His father was Venantius Scholasticus. He served as a deacon at Rome and was eventually designated pope, the seventy-fourth from Saint Peter. He held that dignity for one year and nine months [Note: [Col. 0555D] Burius, in the *Notitia*.], until 20 September of the year 642 [Note: [Col. 0555D] Cavaeus, under the year 640.], or until 12 October of the year 641 [Note: [Col. 0555D] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca media*, vol. IV, p. 42, Padua edition.]. Among other things, he wrote to Constantine, the son of the emperor Heraclius, an apology for Pope Honorius on account of the latter’s assertion of one will in Christ. In Eutychius [Note: [Col. 0555D] *Annals*, vol. II, p. 325.] this letter to Constantine is entitled “To the Emperors Heraclius and Constantine, the Brothers.” At the Roman council of the year 640, John condemned the Monothelites.

### § II. On Saint Maximus

Saint Maximus, formerly chief secretary of Heraclius, was abbot of Chrysopolis near Constantinople. The Greeks call him a theologian [Note: [Col. 0555D] In Codex Coislinianus of the Library, cited by Montfaucon, p. 305.], as well as a confessor [Note: [Col. 0555D] Combefisius, on Saint Maximus, vol. I, p. 642; vol. II, pp. 98, 481, 528.], philosopher, and martyr. He was the most vigorous and foremost opponent of the Monothelites. After a thousand persecutions, he was finally deported to Lazica and died in the year of Christ 662, at the age of eighty-two. He held a celebrated disputation with Pyrrhus, patriarch of Constantinople, which Fabricius assigns to the year 645 [Note: [Col. 0555D] *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. VIII, p. 729.]. He took part in the Lateran Council under Martin I.

Anastasius the apocrisiarius [Col. 0555C] wrote the life of his master Maximus, which Allatius praises in *On Purgatory* [Note: [Col. 0555D] P. 730.]; it is found in Combefisius’s first volume of the works of Saint Maximus [Note: [Col. 0556D] Pp. 1–28.]. There are also found there the acts, conferences, and other materials, which we likewise have arranged to publish in Greek and Latin from Anastasius’s translation, as they appear in Sirmond [Note: [Col. 0556D] Works, vol. III.]. Baronius [Note: [Col. 0556D] Vol. VIII, p. 657, no. 31.] and Combefisius should also be consulted in the excellent edition of the works of Saint Maximus.

### § III. On Saint Pope Theodore

Theodore succeeded John IV in the pontificate at the end of the year 642 and held it until the middle of the year 649. He was from Jerusalem. In Latin, some call him Adeodatus, or even Deusdedit. It is said that this pontiff condemned Pyrrhus, the patriarch of Constantinople, who had shamefully fallen back into the Monothelite heresy, in such a manner that, approaching the tomb of Saint Peter, he wrote Pyrrhus’s deposition with a pen dipped in Christ’s blood.

Two of his letters survive, either in Hardouin [Col. 0555D] [Note: [Col. 0556D] *Councils*, vol. II, p. 643.] or in Oldoinus [Note: [Col. 0556D] *Roman Athenaeum*, p. 613.]. Those read in Anastasius’s *Collectanea* are rather fragments or excerpts than complete letters.

### § IV. On Saint Pope Martin

When Theodore died in May, Martin, the first pope of that name, assumed the administration of Peter’s see at the beginning of July. He was from Tuders and was also a martyr, though without the shedding of blood. He was pontiff from the year 649 to 654 or 655. Concerning his period, Sirmond [Note: [Col. 0556D] *Works*, vol. III, p. 465.] and Cointius [Note: [Col. 0556D] *Frankish Annals*, vol. III, p. 456.] should be consulted. His letters are extant in the volumes of the Councils and in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

After convening the Lateran Council of one hundred and five bishops, he condemned the *Typos* of the emperor Constans, together with the leaders of Monothelitism—Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul—as well as Cyrus of Alexandria and Theodore of Pharan. In the year 653, Calliopas, the successor of Olympius in the exarchate, came to Rome with the army of Ravenna, seized the holy pontiff, and placed him on a ship. After a period of three months, he deported him to the island of Naxos. Soon afterward he was taken to Constantinople; yet he could not be induced to approve the *Typos*. For this reason he was deported to Cherson, where he died in exile and was buried in the church of Saint Mary at Blachernae.

Of his letters, the one relevant to us is that addressed to Theodore—or rather, certain fragments excerpted by Anastasius—in which the holy pontiff laments his condition.

### § V. On the Anonymous Author of the Account of the Cruel Deeds Perpetrated against Saint Martin

[Col. 0556B]

The author of this *Commemoration* presents himself as Saint Martin’s companion, since at the very beginning he says: “Learning certain things externally with great diligence, but becoming personally an observer of many others.” And near the end: “I have carefully declared to you what I saw and heard.”

Nevertheless, he does not seem to have been a companion on the voyage. For only six boys were permitted to sail with Saint Martin. It may therefore easily be believed that he was present with the holy pontiff at Constantinople from time to time, since at the very beginning of the *Account of the Proceeding* it is said: “On the day when Lord Maximus and the man who was with him arrived near this royal city.” This sufficiently shows that there were certain people at Constantinople who adhered to the adversaries of the Monothelites.

Whatever the facts may be, he clearly explains to us everything that was cruelly and savagely done against him there until his transportation to Cherson [Col. 0556C]. He also reveals himself as a cleric and monk, both on account of his knowledge of theological matters and because he often calls Saint Martin “our supreme priest,” but Maximus “lord.” He also uses the customary monastic expression: “I, your humble and sinful servant before God, venerable Fathers.”

Whether the author of the proceeding against Saint Maximus is the same person as the author of the account concerning Saint Martin cannot be demonstrated by certain evidence. Nevertheless, the connection between the events narrated, the similarity of style, and the fact that they are joined together in Anastasius’s *Collectanea* suggest this with considerable probability.

### § VI. On Anastasius the Monk

This Anastasius was a disciple and close companion of Saint Maximus the abbot. Cavaeus writes that he was born in the year 618 [Note: [Col. 0556D] Under the year 655, p. 385.], but died in 664. His letter to the monks of Caralis is extant in Anastasius’s *Collectanea*. Perhaps the two preceding accounts also belong to him. He wrote at least in the year of Christ 657 [Col. 0556D], not 655, as Cavaeus seems to think. For he says: “On the ninth day before the Kalends of September, which has now passed, in the fourteenth indiction.” This corresponds to the Greek year 6164, in which both the fourteenth indiction and the year of Christ 657 coincide.

### § VII. On Anastasius the Apocrisiarius

Another disciple of Saint Maximus was this Anastasius, a presbyter and monk and apocrisiarius of the Roman Church [Col. 0557A]. He wrote the life and acts of Saint Maximus, his master [Note: [Col. 0557A] Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. IX, pp. 122 and 340.]. These are contained chiefly in the letter to Theodore, presbyter of Gangra, which Anastasius the Bibliothecary preserved for us in his *Collectanea*.

He wrote in the ninth indiction, and therefore in the year of Christ 666, not 665, as Cavaeus notes. Although the Greek letter itself no longer survives, testimonies of Saint Hippolytus from the codex of Francesco Turriano have been appended from Combefisius.

Saint Anastasius the martyr died on a Sunday, at the third hour, on the fifth day before the Ides of October, while the words “Holy things for the holy” were being said in the sacred assembly, in the tenth indiction. These chronological indications fall in the year of Christ 666: the tenth indiction was running from 1 September, and the fifth day before the Ides—that is, 11 October—was a Sunday, or the first day of the week, as the authors of the *Hypomnesticon* state.

### § VIII. On the Authors of the *Hypomnesticon*

The authors of this little work openly identify themselves [Col. 0558A] as the monk brothers Theodosius and Theodore, as Combefisius notes in his notice, and Cavaeus [Note: [Col. 0558A] Under the year 668.]. They also say that they received the letter of Anastasius the apocrisiarius from Lazica through Gregory, the Bavararuensian abbot, in August, in the eleventh indiction, which has now passed.

It follows that they wrote in the year 668 or 669, reckoning the beginning of the indiction, in the Greek manner, from September. Cavaeus favors the earlier year; Combefisius the later.

In this *Hypomnesticon* we have a concise history of the passion and death of Pope Martin, Maximus, Anastasius the abbot, Anastasius the apocrisiarius, Theodore, and Euprepius, the blood brothers of that same Anastasius the apocrisiarius.

Moreover, James Sirmond, who first published this Anastasian collection and gave it the title *Collectanea*, had received it from the library of the Church of Lyon.

[Col. 0557]

# THE *COLLECTANEA* OF ANASTASIUS THE BIBLIOTHECARY OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, TO JOHN THE DEACON

*(In Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XIII.) Published first by JAMES SIRMOND in the year 1620.*

[Col. 0557C] To his dearest brother John, a worthy Levite of Christ, Anastasius, the least of the servants, sends greetings in the Lord.

I had promised your diligence an ecclesiastical history for the instruction of many, by translating from Greek into Latin certain materials concerning ecclesiastical history. For you had said—and, with Supreme Truth as your teacher, had affirmed—that you could not confidently begin an ecclesiastical history unless a written account in both languages of certain events that had occurred came to your knowledge.

Therefore, although I acknowledge myself to be so ignorant that I am not capable of penetrating the force even of my own language, in which I was born—not to mention a foreign language—and for that reason would never have dared to undertake an attempt at translation by any method, I have hastened, as far as my abilities allow, to satisfy you. I preferred to incur criticism from my teachers by consenting to your request rather than remove you from the history that was to be woven by your labor because of my aforementioned sluggishness [Col. 0557D].

I am entirely confident that you will correct whatever you find distorted in my work and polish whatever you find unpolished. Truly, I confess—and my conscience bears witness—that I would rather have had these and similar things done by others, not so much because I shrink from the labor as because I recognize the ignorance of my knowledge in every respect, if it should be called knowledge at all rather than ignorance. I was not unaware that, with your fraternity’s permission, I might have omitted these things while you pursued your purpose of writing the history [Col. 0558C].

For you shine with so great a light of wisdom that you seem to have proposed testing me—not with something necessary, but with something rash.
