Therefore, since obedience intervenes, let it be enough for me to have gathered what others sowed with a rustic sickle and carried it on a faithful shoulder to the threshing floor of Latin, adding or subtracting nothing.

It will be your task, by adding judgments and extending the work of history—as with a winnowing-fan of discernment—to purify our words, which you decide should be inserted into it, as though they were grains. We have undertaken to translate these and other works in such a way that we may be recognized as having departed neither altogether from the precise circumstances of the words nor, as far as possible, from the truth of the meaning.

I have translated certain brief works concerning recent times because our predecessors—or rather, our greater forebears—who translated the events of earlier times have anticipated us in this kind of work, just as they have far surpassed us in excellence [Col. 0558D].

Accordingly, [Note: [Col. 0557D] After the three-part *Chronography*, excerpted from Nicephorus, George, and Theophanes. We have given it above.] after the three-part *Chronography*, which I translated at your urging, and certain other very brief works that I translated at the request of various Fathers and brothers, an apology of Pope John IV of Rome for Pope Honorius, attacked by his accusers because he had written that our Lord Jesus Christ had only one will, happened to come into my hands [Col. 0559A].

This apology, as I think, makes him sufficiently excusable, although the Sixth Holy Synod pronounced an anathema against him as though he were a heretic and, since he had already been placed under God’s judgment alone, pierced him with the weapon of condemnation. For a heretic is produced not merely by deception through error but by an incorrect choice and contentious obstinacy.

Who, however, will meanwhile tell us whether he himself certainly dictated the letter from which the accusers took the basis for anathematizing him, since something of this kind might have resulted from the writer’s lack of discipline or hatred of the pontiff? Although we do not fail to recognize that, according to Saint Maximus in his letter to the presbyter Marinus, the most holy John the abbot wrote it, let it be so: he himself was the one who dictated it.

Who questioned him about this? Who investigated his intention? Who wished to correct him, and did he resist the person asking questions or attempting to amend the text, or did he answer back in contentious service to his own position? Especially since in that Gospel in which it is said, “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Luke 6:37), and so forth, even the great teachers of the Church seem to command nothing else than that we interpret for the better those acts concerning which it is uncertain with what intention they were done.

There are indeed certain intermediate acts, whose intention we do not know, since they can be done with either a good or an evil purpose. It is rash to judge such acts, especially so as to condemn them. In short, there are two circumstances in which we must beware of rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what intention something was done, or when it is uncertain what sort of person one will become who now appears either bad or good [Col. 0559C].

The Lord plainly indicates how rash judgment must be avoided when he speaks of the Sodomites in our manner, saying: “I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Genesis 18:21). And again through Moses: “You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).

The Apostle gives nearly the same admonition: “Each of us will render an account of himself to God.” Therefore, “let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or a scandal before your brother” (Romans 14:12–13).

Who, however, should be called more deaf or mute than one who, when he lies lifeless and disintegrated in a tomb, has neither an ear open to hear the accusations formally nor a mouth open to refute the accusations rationally [Col. 0559D]?

But concerning such judgments, what the venerable Anastasius, prelate of the Apostolic See, taught in writing to the emperor Anastasius, with the weight of sacred Scripture, is sufficient. Yet, lest we seem to accuse or rashly criticize so holy and revered a synod, we think it permissible to hold concerning it the opinion that we know our holy Fathers held concerning the great Synod of Chalcedon.

One of them, namely Saint Pope Gregory, indicated that it should be accepted only up to the promulgation of the canons. Likewise, blessed Pope Gelasius, in his treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*, intimated through illuminating examples and several divine testimonies how the same synod should be received. There he concludes the matter with this deliberation [Col. 0560A]:

“These and similar examples teach us, and divine testimonies confirm, that we should not indiscriminately accept everything said by anyone or written anywhere, but should retain what is good and reject what causes harm.”

For Greek writings also testify that this holy synod promulgated certain canonical chapters; yet, since the Apostolic See did not approve nearly all of them, the whole of Latin Christianity rejected them.

But why speak only of this synod? The Apostolic See does not admit even the Second Universal Synod, which was first celebrated at Constantinople concerning the primacy of the Churches. Indeed, it decrees that all synods should be received in the manner in which the aforementioned holy Pope Gelasius describes the Synod of Chalcedon as needing to be received: for the communion of faith and Catholic and apostolic truth, on behalf of which the Apostolic See commissioned this synod and confirmed it once it had been held [Col. 0560B].

If we wished to gather everything that can be advanced in defense of Pope Honorius, paper would fail us more readily than speech, and our purpose of translation would certainly be turned into a work of dictation. We shall say only one thing, which we undoubtedly ought not to conceal: Honorius is such as he was said and pronounced to be. If he was not such a person, the sentence imposed upon him will certainly not apply, since, as it is written, “Man sees the face, but God sees the heart.”

But behold: while this preface of ours is being addressed to you at excessive length, we have moved far away from the work of translation [Col. 0560C]. We are eager to show that, as far as the faith is concerned, not even in the time of Honorius was any trace of the serpent—that is, of a venomous sect—ever found on the rock of the Apostolic See.

Take, then, the aforementioned *Apology of Pope John for Honorius*. Take also, for the same man, the *Apology* drawn from the letter of Maximus the Monk—truly a philosopher and martyr of Christ our God—sent to the presbyter Marinus. The most blessed Maximus defends the aforementioned Honorius not only in that letter but also in the one he wrote to the abbot Thalassius; moreover, in his dogmatic letter to Peter the Illustrious, he calls him “great” and “divine.”

From that letter we bring you certain excerpts and translations concerning Pope Honorius himself; Sophronius of Jerusalem, whom we have often mentioned in the writings translated by us; and Pyrrhus, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople. We have also translated from the letter of that same Saint Maximus to the presbyter Marinus a discussion of the procession of the Holy Spirit.

There he indicates that the Greeks accuse us in vain, since we do not say, as they assert, that the Son is the cause or principle of the Holy Spirit. Rather, while acknowledging the unity of substance of the Father and the Son, we confess that just as the Spirit proceeds from the Father, so he proceeds from the Son, understanding “mission” as procession. He piously interprets the matter and teaches those knowledgeable in both languages toward peace, showing that both we and the Greeks teach that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son in one respect and does not proceed from the Son in another [Col. 0561A]. The difficulty lies in expressing the property of one language in the other.

In this way Saint Athanasius once united Easterners and Westerners who differed over the term “subsistence” or “person,” teaching clearly that both groups believed and retained the same thing in their hearts and understanding, although on account of linguistic difference they confessed it orally in different ways and devoted themselves to importunate controversies.

We have also translated certain letters of Pope Theodore, successor to the aforementioned Pope John, written as the order required, to Paul, the successor of Pyrrhus, and to those who consecrated him. The style of the letters of these distinguished prelates of the Apostolic See—John and Theodore—breathes Latin eloquence. From this it is perfectly clear that they were dictated in Latin, not Greek.

Here one should note that Latin Christianity would have lamented that certain works originally published in Latin had been completely buried beneath the weight of oblivion, unless it had drawn them from the later source of Greek books and recovered them with a thirsting heart [Col. 0562A], as with the letter of blessed Pope Felix, which delivers a judgment against Peter of Antioch.

Indeed, this is also the case with Clement, whom Rufinus, writing to Gaudentius, indicates had been rendered into our language, restored, and brought back. He clearly shows that Clement had been written in Latin, lost, and then recovered.

I have also excerpted and now present to you in translation a certain account from the letter of Saint Maximus to the abbot Thalassius: what the Roman legates accomplished at Constantinople, to encourage steadfastness in the cause of the greatest piety, to rebuke the fainthearted, and to acknowledge the authority of the Apostolic See against those who attempt violently to extort something from it.

Moreover, I also offer an account of the exile of holy Pope Martin, which I published at the request of the venerable Martin, bishop of Narni, together with the *Hypomnesticon*, which briefly recounts the deeds of Saint Maximus the Philosopher, both Anastasii, Theodore, Euprepius, and others.

[Col. 0561]

[Note: [Col. 0561D] Concerning this letter, see the testimony in Saint Maximus the Monk’s disputation with Pyrrhus, the patriarch.]

## APOLOGY OF POPE JOHN OF ROME TO CONSTANTINE THE EMPEROR, SON OF HERACLIUS, FOR POPE HONORIUS

Because of the one will in Christ, which his accusers say he mentioned.

[Col. 0561C] The Lord, who said that light should shine out of darkness; who rescued us from the power of darkness into his marvelous light—the light of truth, and the truth of light—in whom it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell, and through whom to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or those on earth (Colossians 1:20); looking upon the face of his Church because of the surpassing greatness of the riches of his goodness, has deigned to call your kindness, foreknown and predestined by him, now to the integrity of the faith, so that, with every deceptive darkness removed far away, he might make the truth victorious through you.

For, as we have learned from the various reports that have come to us in crowds—and indeed also from hearing it directly—all the western regions are disturbed and scandalized because our brother Pyrrhus, the patriarch, is proclaiming in letters sent here and there certain novelties contrary to the rule of faith and is hastening to draw our predecessor, Pope Honorius of holy memory, toward his own interpretation, although that interpretation was utterly alien to the mind of a Catholic Father.

Therefore, so that your kindness may learn the entire matter, I shall recount, with the most exact truth, what happened before the brief interval of time [Col. 0562C].

Sergius, the patriarch of revered memory, informed the aforesaid pope of the city of Rome, of holy memory, that certain persons were saying that there were two contrary wills in our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ. When the aforesaid pope learned this, he wrote back to him that, just as our Savior was one, monadic in manner, so also he had been conceived and born in a most wondrous way, beyond every human mode. From the holy dispensation of his incarnation he further taught that, just as our Redeemer was perfect God, so also he was perfect man, so that what the first man had lost through transgression, he—born without any sin—might renew the noble origin of the first image. [Col. 0562D]

Thus the second Adam was born without any sin, whether in his birth or in his dealings with human beings. Indeed, the Word made flesh assumed everything that was ours in the likeness of sinful flesh, bearing no stain of guilt arising from the transmitted transgression. We therefore understand the likeness to refer not to his flesh, but to sin. [Col. 0563A]

For the Lord truly assumed flesh from the undefiled and blessed Virgin, the Mother of God, and became consubstantial with us. Therefore the holy Apostle calls it “the likeness of sinful flesh”: flesh like ours, which he assumed, without sin, together with a rational soul. For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ graciously possessed one will according to the natural, original formation of Adam’s humanity—not two contrary wills, as we are now recognized to have, since we have been begotten from Adam in sin. For when the first man had become corruptible through transgression and, scorning subjection to his Creator, had experienced the flesh that had previously been subject to him as nevertheless resisting him, he made the entire human race subject to sin, as the Apostle says:

“Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5:14). [Col. 0563B]

Accordingly, we who are born through his transgression and sin are recognized to have two contrary wills. By “two,” I mean the mind and the flesh, mutually struggling against one another, as the same blessed Apostle teaches: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

This is suffered by the entire human race placed under sin, since no one is clean from this sin of transgression—not even an infant, whose life upon the earth, as it is written, is but one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). And as the Holy Spirit says through David: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50:7). For just as all sinned in Adam, according to the Apostle, so all will be justified in Christ (1 Cor. 15:22). And just as through one man many were made sinners, so through one man many will be made righteous (Rom. 5:19).

Therefore the one and only mediator between God and human beings who is without sin is the man Christ Jesus, who was conceived and born free among the dead. In the dispensation of his holy flesh, therefore, he never had two contrary wills, nor did the will of his flesh resist the will of his mind. For he had no sin whatever, having come to forgive the sin of the world, as he himself also said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John 8:46). And elsewhere he said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30).

Therefore, knowing that there was absolutely no sin in him at his birth or during his life, we rightly say and truthfully confess that there was one will in the humanity of his holy dispensation; we do not preach two contrary wills of mind and flesh, as certain heretics are known to rave as though he were merely a human being.

Accordingly, our aforesaid predecessor is known to have written to the aforementioned patriarch Sergius, who had questioned him, in the following manner: two contrary wills—that is, two wills in his members—do not exist at all in our Savior, since he drew no defect from the transgression of the first man.

In us, not in him, the following passage is appropriately understood: “For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18). And again: “I do not do the good that I wish, but I do the evil that I do not wish. But if I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (ibid., 19–20). And afterward: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (ibid., 23). [Col. 0564A]

Thus these two contrary wills of mind and flesh, which the Apostle teaches, were in no way present in our Savior, since this spur of conflict took its beginning from the transgression of the first parent. For our Redeemer assumed nature, not the guilt of sin.

But lest someone who understands less carefully should criticize him for teaching about human nature alone and not also about the divine nature, it must be understood that Christ is recognized, adored, and worshiped as perfect God and man in two natures united in one person. Anyone who doubts this should know that the response was made to the question of the aforementioned patriarch.

Moreover, it is customary that where there is a wound, there medicinal aid should be applied. The blessed Apostle also is known to have done this often, adapting himself to the disposition of his hearers. At one time, when teaching about the supreme nature, he is wholly silent about the human; at another, when discussing the human dispensation, he does not touch upon the mystery of his divinity. [Col. 0564B]

For here he says of the divine nature: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24); elsewhere, however, he speaks of his incarnation in this way: “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (ibid., 25). Wisdom and foolishness, power and weakness, are plainly set forth as contrary to one another.

Does the blessed Apostle therefore teach things contrary to one another? Certainly not. Rather, he wisely adapts himself to his hearers, teaching according to the occasion, like a provident nurse who gives milk to infants but solid food to the mature.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings, and what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings”? This entire passage seems to teach about Christ’s dispensation, not about his heavenly nature. He wishes to show that God, having become man, possessed a human soul and body, which he calls foolish and weak.

Human wisdom, when compared with divine wisdom, is foolishness; the strength of the flesh, when compared with God’s power, is weakness. For human wisdom, however it has been fashioned, is foolishness when compared with the Wisdom who fashioned it.

Accordingly, by joining both aspects together, we confess Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God according to his divinity, and we confess the nature of his divinity. According to the dispensation of his holy flesh, however, we truly preach that which is foolish and weak in God as the nature of his humanity, since this weakness and foolishness are stronger and wiser than all human beings. [Col. 0565A]

For all human beings, as was also said above, are born under the sin of transgression. Our Lord Jesus Christ, however, existing without sin and carrying with him no defect of the old condition, is not only stronger but also wiser than all human beings, although he graciously deigned, out of mercy alone, to assume our weakness and foolishness.

Those who were born from the sin of the first man are called by the teaching of Holy Scripture “children of wrath and darkness.” Christ, however, since he is the true light, graciously deigned to illuminate those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death.

Let us hear what the Apostle teaches when writing to the Ephesians:

“And you,” he says, “when you were dead in your transgressions and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we too once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, as were the others” (Eph. 2:1–3). [Col. 0565B]

These, then, are the two contrary wills—of the mind, namely, and of the flesh—which were in every way absent from our Savior. We are recognized to possess them because of the sin of our forefather Adam, who made both himself and the entire human race subject to sin.

At times the sting of the flesh appears to resist the mind; at other times the will of the mind strives to oppose the will of the flesh. Thus, groaning with the Apostle, we confess: “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.”

Our Lord, however, graciously deigned to assume one natural will of humanity, which, in his own flesh, he carried with authority as Lord of all, since all things serve God. He had and brought with him absolutely no sin arising from transgression, for he alone was born without sin and without the guilt of transgression.

My aforesaid predecessor, therefore, teaching about the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, said that there were not in him, as in us sinners, contrary wills of mind and flesh. Certain persons, turning this to their own meaning, supposed that he had taught Christ’s divinity and humanity to possess one will—something altogether contrary to the truth.

Nevertheless, I wish they would answer the question: according to which nature do they say that Christ God has one will? If according to the divine nature alone, what will they say about his humanity? [Col. 0565D] For he is also perfect man, lest they be condemned together with Manichaeus.

But if they say that this will belonged to Christ’s humanity, and that this will was perfect God, let them take care lest they be judged together with Photinus and Ebion. If, finally, they say that there is one will from both natures, they will confuse not only the natural wills but the natures themselves, so that neither one nor the other—that is, neither the divine nor the human—can be understood.

For just as we do not tolerate, like the impious Nestorius, the two natures being separated in the union of the one Christ, so we do not in any way deny the distinction of the natures, nor do we confuse them. Rather, we confess both natures, in the ineffable harmony of the union of the one person of Christ God.

For when they say that Christ’s divinity and humanity have one will, and likewise one operation, what else are they known to assert than that the one nature of Christ God operates, according to the Eutychian and Severian division? Finally, the orthodox Fathers who have shone throughout the world are shown, by their concordant preaching, to teach both the two natures and the wills and operations of Christ.

We have learned that a certain document was sent out in which priests were compelled to subscribe against the tome of Pope Leo, of blessed memory, and against the Council of Chalcedon. In that document certain things were composed through novelty which are plainly recognized to reject ecclesiastical doctrine.

May divine clemency therefore inspire your most Christian piety; and since you are guardians of our immaculate faith, may it move you to compunction, so that by imperial decrees you may restrain those who are being corrupted by novel inventions, and order that the aforesaid document—which hastens toward the scandal of the faith and has been hung in public places—be taken down and torn apart. [Col. 0566B]

For all who heard of this in the western regions, as well as the peoples of your royal city, were struck to the heart when they learned of the composition of the aforesaid document. Through your authority and apostolic perfection, that document, composed against the Council of Chalcedon, will now and at all times be ineffectual and void of every force.

We pray that the perfection of the faith, which has shone forth until the present, may through you, just as also through Constantine of pious memory, remain firm by divine assistance. [Col. 0566C]

Therefore, most Christian guardians of the faith of Christ, offer this gift at the beginning of your rule to your mother, the Church, whose helpers you are after God, so that the serpentine cunning may not dare to violate the faith of her Bridegroom.

Offer this saving sacrifice to the Lord our God at the beginning of your rule, and disperse from his Church every cloud of novelty by the ray of your piety. Thus may the Lord our God, in return, crush all the nations that rise against you, and those who reject peace and the unconquerable God. And while you care for the things that belong to God, may God in his goodness deign to accomplish the things that belong to you.

For this reason also, with bended knee, the whole Church joins me in supplication that he may deign to remove from the integrity of our immaculate faith—the faith which the holy Apostles handed down to us and the most holy Fathers marked out in their brilliant teachings—the storm of a new confusion.

Thus may our God and Lord, whose immaculate faith is guarded, deservedly and abundantly bestow his mercies upon you. He is almighty and the everlasting Lord. May the Creator of all look kindly upon your empire and prostrate, by his unconquerable power, the nations that trust in their own savagery.

[Col. 0567]

# Extract from a Letter

[Note: In Greek the title is: “The dogmatic tome of Maximus, most holy monk and confessor, to Marinus the presbyter.”]

# The Apology of Saint Maximus to Marinus the Presbyter, in Which, Among Other Matters, He Defends Honorius

*(The Greek text is taken from Combefis’s edition.)*

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0567A]

As for Honorius, the pope of the Romans, I do not think that in the letter written to Sergius he condemned the duality of the natural wills in Christ because he said “one will”; rather, I think that he affirmed it and perhaps even strengthened it.

He did not say this in order to reject the human and natural will of the Savior, but because no will of the flesh or passionate thought preceded his conception without seed or his incorrupt birth. For only the divine and paternal will, through the only-begotten Son himself bringing about his own incarnation, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, accomplished this.

That he follows this meaning is clear from the following. Having said that, because of the ineffable union of the human and divine nature, God is said to suffer, and humanity to have descended from heaven together with the divinity, and having thereby shown the supreme exchange of the things naturally belonging to each nature of the one Christ and Son of God, he adds:

“Hence we also confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

How does he mean this? “Because,” he says, “our nature was plainly assumed from the divinity, not sin”—that is, not from sin—almost speaking in agreement with the great Athanasius, who writes the following against the impious Apollinarius:

“He was born of a woman, raising up for himself the form of man from the first creation, in the manifestation of flesh, without carnal wills and human thoughts, in an image of newness. For the will is solely that of the divinity, since the entire nature is divine.

“For the birth of the Word according to the flesh, undertaken for our sake, was a progression beyond us. For no passionate will or thought of the flesh preceded it, as is seen among us because of the desire that has prevailed in our race through the deception of the first parent.

“Rather, the will of the divinity alone, through the Son who himself brought about his own embodiment, according to the good pleasure of the Father and with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, introduced within himself and through himself in a new way the mode of birth that had been introduced into nature, and accomplished his own conception without seed from the holy Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary.”

Having therefore considered this ineffable account of his birth, the former said that he had in him the will of the divinity alone, while the latter said “one will of the Lord Jesus Christ.” For, he says, our nature was plainly assumed from the divinity, not sin, without carnal wills and human thoughts, as the divine Athanasius says.

Yet he certainly did not mean that, although he was also man while being God by nature, he lacked a human and natural will, just as he had a divine and paternal will.

The same point is also hinted at in what follows, where he says:

“He was conceived without sin from the Holy Spirit and from the holy, immaculate, ever-virgin Mother of God, Mary, and without defilement was born from her according to the flesh.”

He brings forward divine Scripture, both in praise and in blame, when it makes mention of flesh. He does not suggest—God forbid—that the Lord’s flesh is different from ours in nature and substance. He knew that this flesh had been assumed from our substance, that is, from the holy womb of the ever-virgin and God-bearing woman who is of the same stock as we are.

Rather, he means that it is different in being free from sin and in not possessing at all, as we do, the law of transgression resisting the law of the Spirit in its members. [Col. 0569B]

“For,” he says, “the Savior did not assume flesh corrupted by sin, which would resist the law of his mind. For in one whom the law of birth according to sin, through seed, did not precede, that law is altogether absent from his members.

“Instead, the law of divine righteousness is manifested in him as an example for us and completely abolishes the law introduced into nature through transgression. For the sinless one came to seek and save what was lost—that is, the nature of the human race which had sinned.”

“For no other law in his members, nor any different or contrary will, arose in the Father [read: Savior],” he says. By this he shows not that he did not possess a human and natural will—for he does not appear to have said that—but that, as man, he had neither in the body, through his members, any operation contrary to the laws of nature, nor, in the soul, any contrary or irrational movement of the will, as we do, since he was born above the law of human nature.

He makes this still clearer in what follows, demonstrating that his argument was concerned solely with distinguishing in the Savior a will that was corrupted, rather than natural. Although the natural and human will was aligned with the paternal and divine will, it had no difference from it arising from opposition.

He gave himself to us as an example: he voluntarily subjected what was properly his, while commending what belonged to the Father. Thus we too, imitating him, may reject what is ours and fulfill with all zeal what is divine. He says:

“Although it is written: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me’ (John 6:38); and, ‘Not what I will, but what you will, Father’ (Mark 14:36), these are not different wills—that is, contrary and opposed wills—but the assumed human dispensation, compassionately making its own what belongs to us.

“For he said these things on our behalf, giving us an example—the teacher of piety—so that we might follow his footsteps and that each of us might prefer in all things not his own will, but rather the Lord’s.”

Therefore, as I have said, he does not abolish the natural and human will, but the corrupt will and the will that is contrary to nature. In short, he testifies that the God who became incarnate for our sake, according to our condition, is free from every sin. [Col. 0571A]

To put it briefly: by “one will,” I infer that he means to indicate that only the divine will preceded his birth according to the flesh. By saying that there is no difference of wills, he asserts that he has nothing contrary or opposed to it, but something wholly concordant and united.

Thus, when he says that our nature was assumed from the divinity’s will, he mentions one will. But when he introduces the statement, “I have not come to do my own will,” he places it in the middle of his argument while leaving the number unexpressed; he says, “These are not different wills,” that is, contrary and opposed wills. From this it is plainly inferred that there are two wills according to nature in the Savior.

For if he did not have a contrary will, he had a natural will as man. What is not contrary is certainly natural, and no one will dispute this. For nothing in nature, or among the things that are according to nature, is altogether contrary.

It is therefore perilous to assert [read: impose] something that is not properly written in his own words, and for opponents to contrive to make the writings of that man a covering for their own contrary opinion, as though it were not the best, falsely interpreting them in a manner different from his intention. For the argument itself has him as its advocate and drives away every attack of the slanderer.

This, then, is how I understand his meaning, purified from every suspicion. The most holy presbyter, the lord Abba Anastasius, returning from elder Rome, made me more certain of this—an incomparable man, adorned with divine virtue and prudence.

He reported that he had engaged in extensive discussion with the most sacred men of that great Church concerning the letter written by them to Sergius, asking for what reason and in what manner “one will” had been inserted into it. He found them troubled about this and offering an explanation.

Moreover, he found the man who had rendered it into Latin at his command, the lord Abba John, the most holy collaborator, asserting that they had made no mention whatsoever in it, by numerical expression, of “one will,” even though this has now been fabricated by those who translated it into the Greek language. [Note: That is, “collaborator.”] [Col. 0572D]

Nor did he mean any emptying or abolition of the natural will of the Savior according to his humanity, but rather a complete rejection and abolition of the will that is ours and has been made blameworthy—according to which there also arises warfare among things of the same kind.

He wished to show that the flesh assumed was free from every sin, according to the tradition of the most sacred Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers. And these statements appear to harmonize with what has just been explained by my insignificance, as though confirming the defense made on behalf of Honorius.

When he had answered these matters by reasoning, I was greatly astonished at their precision, just as I was also struck with amazement at the cunning of those who, for the sake of one [thing], dare and wish to act impiously in every way, though in vain.

As has long been their custom, both formerly and now, they seek through certain thefts and misinterpretations to draw to themselves those who zealously struggle against them—even contrary to all reason—and to appropriate their meaning, although it does not follow them in the least.

Therefore, having necessarily learned this as well, I have made it known to you, God-honored Father, so that, fortified in every respect, you may know how to shatter the ranks of your opponents: striking them with vigorous argument and overcoming them powerfully through faith, possessing from this point onward the glory of the Only-begotten as your proclamation, and his gracious communion and union as your diadem.

[Col. 0568A]

I do not think that Honorius, the Roman pope, denied the duality of wills according to nature in Christ in the letter he wrote to Sergius because he said “one will.” Rather, I think that he confessed it and perhaps even established it.

For he did not say this in rejection of the human and natural will of the Savior, but because no will of the flesh or passionate thought preceded his conception without seed or his incorrupt birth. For only the divine and paternal will, through the only-begotten Son himself bringing about his own incarnation, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, accomplished this.

That he follows this meaning is clear from the following. Having said that, because of the ineffable union of the human and divine nature, God is said to suffer, and humanity to have descended from heaven together with the divinity, and having in this way shown the supreme exchange of the things naturally belonging to each nature of the one Christ and Son of God, he adds:

“Hence we also confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

How does he mean this? “Because,” he says, “our nature was plainly assumed from the divinity, not guilt”—that is, not from sin—almost speaking in agreement with the great Athanasius, who writes the following against the impious Apollinarius:

“He was born of a woman, raising up for himself the form of man from the first creation, in the manifestation of flesh, without carnal wills and human thoughts, in an image of newness. For the will is solely that of the divinity, since the entire nature is divine.

“For the birth of the Word according to the flesh, undertaken for our sake, was a progression beyond us. For no passionate will or thought of the flesh preceded it, as is seen among us because of the desire that has prevailed in our race through the deception of the first parent.

“Rather, the will of the divinity alone, through the Son who himself brought about his own embodiment, according to the good pleasure of the Father and with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, introduced within himself and through himself in a new way the mode of birth that had been introduced into nature, and accomplished his own conception without seed from the holy Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary.”

Having therefore examined this ineffable manner of his birth, the former said that he had in him the will of the divinity alone, while the latter said “one will of the Lord Jesus Christ.” For, he says, our nature was plainly assumed from the divinity, not guilt, without carnal wills and human thoughts, as the divine Athanasius says.

Yet he did not thereby say that, although he was man and by nature God, he lacked a human and natural will, just as he had a divine and paternal will.

He hints at the same point in what follows, saying:

“He was conceived without sin from the Holy Spirit and from the holy, immaculate, ever-virgin Mother of God, Mary, and without defilement was born from her according to the flesh.”

He cites divine Scripture, whether in praise or blame, when it makes mention of flesh. He does not suggest—God forbid—that the Lord’s flesh is different from ours in nature and substance. He knew that it had been assumed from our substance, that is, from the holy womb of the ever-virgin and Mother of God who is of the same stock as we are.

Rather, he means that it is alien to sin and does not possess, as we do, the law of transgression resisting the law of the Spirit in its members. [Col. 0570B]

“For,” he says, “the Savior did not assume flesh corrupted by sin, which would resist the law of his mind. For in one whom the law of birth according to sin, through seed, did not precede, that law is altogether absent from his members.

“Instead, the law of divine righteousness is manifested in him as an example for us and completely abolishes the law introduced into nature through transgression. For the sinless one came to seek and save what was lost—that is, the nature of the human race which had sinned.”

“No other law in his members, nor a different or contrary will, arose in the Father [read: Savior].” By this he shows not that he did not possess a human and natural will—for he does not appear to have said this—but that, as man, he had neither in the body, through his members, any operation contrary to the laws of nature, nor in the soul any contrary, irrational movement of the will, as we do, since he was born above the law of human nature.

He proves this still more explicitly in what follows: his argument concerned solely distinguishing in the Savior the will that was corrupted, rather than the natural will. Although the natural and human will was aligned with the paternal and divine will, it had no difference from it arising from opposition.

He gave himself as an example to us: he voluntarily subjected what was properly his, while commending what belonged to the Father, so that we too, imitating him, may reject what is ours and fulfill with every effort what is divine. He says:

“Although it is written: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me’ (John 6:38); and, ‘Not what I will, but what you will, Father’ (Mark 14:36), these are not different wills—that is, contrary and opposed wills—but the assumed human dispensation, compassionately making its own what belongs to us.

“For he said these things on our behalf, giving us an example—the teacher of piety—so that we might follow his footsteps and that each of us might prefer in all things not his own will, but rather the Lord’s will.”

Therefore, as I have said, he does not abolish the natural and human will, but the corrupt will and the will that is outside nature. In short, he testifies that the God who became incarnate according to our condition and for our sake is free from every sin. [Col. 0571A]

To put it briefly: by “one will,” I infer that he indicates that only the divine will preceded his birth according to the flesh. By saying that there is no difference of wills, he asserts that he has nothing contrary or opposed to it, but something wholly concordant and united.

Thus, when he says that our nature was assumed from the will of the divinity, he mentions one will. But when he introduces the statement, “I have not come to do my own will,” he places it in the middle of his argument while leaving the number unexpressed; he says, “These are not different wills,” that is, contrary and opposed wills. From this it is plainly inferred that there are two wills according to nature in the Savior. [Col. 0572B]

For if he did not have a contrary will, he had a natural will as man. What is not contrary is certainly natural, and no one will deny this. For nothing in nature, or among the things that are according to nature, is altogether contrary.

It is therefore perilous to assert [read: impose] something that is not properly written in his own words, and for opponents to contrive to make the writings of that man a covering for their own contrary opinion, as though it were not the best, falsely interpreting them in a manner different from his intention. For the argument itself has him as its advocate and drives away every attack of the slanderer.

This, then, is how I understand his meaning, purified from every suspicion. The most holy presbyter, the lord Abba Anastasius, returning from elder Rome, made me more certain of this—a man incomparable, adorned with divine virtue and prudence.

He reported that he had engaged in extensive discussion with the most sacred men of that great Church concerning the letter written by them to Sergius, asking for what reason and in what manner “one will” had been inserted into it. He found them hesitating over this and offering an explanation.

Moreover, he found the man who had rendered it into Latin at his command, the lord Abba John, the most holy collaborator, asserting that they had made no mention whatsoever in it, by numerical expression, of “one will,” even though this has now been fabricated by those who translated it into the Greek language. [Note: That is, “collaborator.”]

Nor did he mean any emptying or abolition of the natural will of the Savior according to his humanity, but rather a complete rejection and abolition of the will that is ours and has been made blameworthy, according to which warfare also arises among things of the same kind.

He wished to show that the flesh assumed was free from every sin, according to the tradition of the most sacred Scriptures and the teachings of the Fathers. And these statements appear to harmonize with what has just been explained by my insignificance, as though confirming the defense made on behalf of Honorius.

When he had answered these matters by reasoning, I was exceedingly astonished at their precision, and in a certain way I was struck with amazement at the cunning of those who, for the sake of one [thing], dare and wish to act impiously in every way, though in vain.

As has long been their custom, both formerly and now, they seek through furtive and false accounts to draw to themselves those who struggle against them with great courage—even contrary to all reason—and to appropriate their meaning, although it does not follow them in the least.

Therefore, having necessarily learned this as well, I have made it known to you, lord and honorable Father, so that, fortified in every respect, you may know how to pursue the ranks of your opponents: hurling vigorous arguments without weariness and overcoming them powerfully through faith, possessing from this point onward the glory of the Only-begotten as your proclamation, and his communion through grace and union as your diadem.

[Col. 0573]

# Extract from a Letter of the Same Saint Maximus to Peter the Illustrious

Where he mentions Pyrrhus, Saint Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, and Pope Honorius, proceeding as follows after some intervening material.

[Col. 0573B] You have deigned to inform your unworthy servant, in your laudable **syllables** [Note: [Col. 0573D] Συλλαβαῖς, “syllables,” instead of litteris, “letters”], concerning the abbot Pyrrhus. And a little later:

And it would certainly have happened that, perhaps for this reason, I should hasten to rebuke him and all who indiscriminately follow that impious innovation, and to preserve your divinely guarded and most famous footprints. Thus all who, according to you, are lovers of piety might know their excessive abundance of impiety, together with their utter ignorance.

But I feared that I might be thought to be doing something outside the sacred laws, acting against the will of the most holy see of the apostolic men, who rightly govern the entire fullness of the Catholic Church and orderly lead it according to the divine law. For by this divine law, heaven and earth are held together, and one must in no way deviate from it; rather, those who have resolved to live piously according to you must do what is divine according to God, so that they may have God as the guardian of their actions and may receive without failure. For, most famous lord, even worse than these things is what I previously mentioned: a new faith and exposition derived even from the ancient heretics.

His predecessor impiously nourished this faith for many years while he remained in the episcopate, so as to reveal his depraved mind—for God often knows how to endure patiently even for the disclosure of wickedness, not in order to make it greater through delay, but so that, once it has become greater, He may punish it more justly. But this man begot it still more impiously. And those who came after them cultivate it in contempt of the divinity. And a little later:

What is still worse than their custom, and as it were the distinctive mark of all perverse heretics, is that they describe as innocent those who are liable to their own impiety. They whisper here and there that Sophronius, who wisely taught and proclaimed the divine doctrines of the Catholic Church, had led himself into error. [Col. 0574B]

And shortly afterward:

For the divine Sophronius, as you yourselves testify, most laudable men, was staying with me and with all the foreign monks in the region of Africa when they were fabricating those perversities against everyone.

And a little later:

There was indeed, by divine concord and unanimity, one house throughout the whole world beneath the sun, peaceful and tranquil, its Churches fortified by faith. But those who envied their harmony and their confession of Christ God, like some dark cloud and a shrieking or heavy wave of the sea and of the barbarians—no one moving them except the devil, the friend of disturbance, who stirred the human race to mutual hostility—suddenly devised a new *Ecthesis* against the true faith of Christians. Then they produced opinions on its behalf and unjust compositions; then acts of synods; then robber synods and gatherings of bishops assembled not by agreement of will but by force, not hastening at the summons of exhortation but departing abroad in flight from the barbarians; then commands and threats sent here and there against the pious. For they reduced the ruler who then held power to servitude by sophistical means and gifts.

And a little later:

They persuaded the man to publish the *Ecthesis* under his own name.

Shortly afterward:

He becomes both their enemy and their defender—or rather, it must be said, their supporter and accuser—by making public the evidence and revealing that he had not been moved at all by himself, but had been compelled by them to produce the most impious *Ecthesis* in writing, saying these things on his own behalf and giving an account to John, of holy memory, formerly the senior pope [Col. 0575A] of Rome.

And shortly afterward:

They convict themselves, for these men, most plainly and forcefully, produced it, and not he at all. Indeed, he had no particular concern for this matter, being occupied with other affairs.

A little later:

Concerning all these matters, the wretched men have not even understood the mind of the apostolic see. And what is laughable—or, to speak more precisely, most deserving of lamentation, as revealing their audacity—is that they did not hesitate recklessly to lie even against the apostolic see itself. But as though they had become the agents of its counsel, and as though they had received from it some decree, in their written acts concerning the impious *Ecthesis* they took the great Honorius along with them, presenting him to others as a witness to their presumption, a man of the greatest eminence in the cause of piety.

Who, then, O most renowned lord, and what kind of Sophronius persuaded these liars to do these things so atrociously and for so long? What Church did not plead with them? What pious and orthodox bishop did not implore them, crying out and earnestly entreating them to cease from their own heresy? Indeed, the holy Arcadius was breathing his last and surrendering his spirit to God, yet he did not cease begging them even until that hour.

And a little later:

But what of the divine Honorius? What of the aged Severinus after him? And finally, what of the holy John who came after him? Moreover, did the most blessed pope who now presides omit anything appropriate to entreaty? Did not the whole East and West alike bring tears, lamentations, supplications, and prayers—through prayers to God and through letters to these men? But God accepted the end of these blessed men and, in return for their suffering, preserved them forever. They, however, despising the Lord’s forbearance, by which He kindly urged them toward conversion, and growing numb amid the earnest supplication of these outstanding men over so long a time, refused in any way to place the heavenly faith before their own interests.

After some intervening material:

The divine and great Sophronius, therefore, coming then to Alexandria, immediately upon the first reading—for Cyrus had also given him those nine chapters of impiety to reconsider—uttered something mournful and immense, pouring forth springs of tears. He fervently entreated, begged, and pleaded with him, prostrated at his feet upon the pavement, that he should proclaim none of these things upon the ambo against the Catholic Church of God, since they were plainly the impious doctrines of Apollinarius.

And a little later:

In this manner, O head whom I revere above all, those men tore one another apart with insults hateful to God and with theatrical mockeries, as it were; and they did not at all console the most sacred Sophronius, who lamented so miserably, mourning the desolation of the Catholic Church like a second Jeremiah and grieving deeply and most compassionately over the downfall of the divine doctrines.

And after some intervening material:

For if the Roman see knows not only the rejected Pyrrhus but also the one who thinks and believes wrongly, it is entirely clear that whoever anathematizes those who rejected Pyrrhus anathematizes the Roman see—that is, the Catholic Church. I omit saying that he also anathematizes himself, if he is such a person and nevertheless remains in communion with the Roman see and the Catholic Church of God.

Therefore I beseech you, my blessed lord, command everyone not to call Pyrrhus most holy or life-giving. For the sacred rule does not permit him to be called anything of the kind. He has fallen from all holiness, since he voluntarily sprang away from the Catholic Church. It is not lawful to know him by any title of praise, since he was long ago condemned and rejected by the apostolic see of the city of Rome because of the character of his foreign opinion, until he is received back by it after converting to it—or rather, to the Lord our God—through a pious confession and orthodox faith, by which he may receive sanctification and the holy name.

Therefore, if the heretic wishes neither to be nor to be heard as a heretic, let him not satisfy this or that person—for that is superfluous and irrational. Just as, when one person is scandalized against him, all are scandalized, so also, when one person is satisfied, undoubtedly all are satisfied. Let him hasten to satisfy the Roman see on behalf of all. For once it has been satisfied, everyone everywhere will together proclaim him pious and orthodox.

He speaks in vain who thinks that people like me must merely be persuaded and won over, while he neither satisfies nor implores the most holy pope of the Roman Church—that is, the apostolic see—which, from the incarnate Word of God Himself and also from all the holy synods, according to the sacred canons and definitions, has received and possesses authority, power, and the jurisdiction of binding and loosing in all things and through all things over all the holy Churches of God throughout the entire world. For when it binds and looses, the Word who rules the heavenly powers also binds and looses in heaven.

If he thinks that others must be satisfied but does not at all implore the most blessed Roman pope, he acts like someone accused of homicide or some other crime who hastens to prove himself innocent not before the one who, according to the laws, has received the right to judge, but merely tries uselessly and fruitlessly to display the purity of his conduct to other private persons, who have no power to release him from his crime.

Therefore, my blessed lord, extend still further the command which is known to have seemed good to you and in accordance with God’s will, so that this man may have no license to speak or contradict anyone concerning doctrine. But learn his will clearly by investigating it more fully, and discover whether he wishes wholly to assent to the truth. If he is eager to do this and hastens toward it reasonably, urge him to make an appropriate petition to the most blessed Roman pope, so that, through his divine command, what concerns him may be regulated canonically and with the greatest propriety, to the glory of God and the praise of your exalted dignity.

[Col. 0577]

## EXCERPT FROM THE LETTER OF SAINT MAXIMUS ON THE PROCESSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

Written to Marinus, the presbyter of Cyprus.

[Col. 0577A] The Constantinopolitans did not criticize this most holy pope in as many chapters of his synodical letter as you wrote, but in only two. One concerns the divine nature: they say that he stated that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. The other concerns the divine incarnation: they say that he wrote that the Lord was without original and actual sin.

In the former matter they brought forward, in agreement, testimonies of the Latin Fathers, as well as of Cyril of Alexandria from his sacred work on the holy evangelist John. From these they did not show that the Son was made the cause of the Holy Spirit. For they know one cause of the Son and of the Spirit, the Father: of the one according to generation, and of the other according to procession; but they indicated that the Spirit proceeds through the Son, and demonstrated this communion and undifferentiation of substance. In the latter matter, however, there is absolutely no need of defense. What controversy is there in this, even if it appears so to slanderers because of their perversity?

Yet they continued, saying that he had neither sin in his mind, in the sense in which Adam is seen to have been corrupted at the beginning, nor an action or operation of evil. Thus these men have made these allegations, although they were not reasonably attacked on these points; but concerning the matters on which they were attacked with complete justice, they have not yet offered any defense, nor have they rejected the innovations introduced by them.

Moreover, in accordance with your command, I asked the Romans to interpret his own statements, in order to avoid the adversaries’ clandestine misrepresentations. Nevertheless, since the custom of doing and sending things in this manner prevails, I do not know whether they will agree. Besides, in another person’s diction and voice they cannot express their meaning with the subtle care with which they can in their own or native speech, just as we cannot express our meaning except in our own language.

[Col. 0577]

## SYNODICAL LETTER OF THE MOST HOLY POPE THEODORE TO PAUL, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE (C)

[Col. 0577C] We inform you that we have received the synodical letter of your fraternity, delivered by the presbyter George and the deacon Peter. As we read through its text, we found it placed between hope and fear, like someone between the safe harbor of two shores, at once confident and tossed about—and not without reason.

For the priesthood is a heavy burden, since concern for the lives of others exhausts one, according to what is written: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. XI, 29). And just as greatly as the priestly mind is shaken by fear lest it be stained through silence or immoderate speech, so greatly—and with the greatest hope—the wing of its own strength is raised to the heights when it rejoices in the progress of those entrusted to it. For it is written: “Where there are very many crops, there is evident strength of oxen” (Prov. XIV, 4).

From this, by contrast, fear strikes back. For it is written: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger. You are ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own speech. Therefore do what I tell you, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hand of your neighbor. Run, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids. Rescue yourself like a doe from the hand and like a bird from the snare of the fowler” (Prov. VI, 1–5).

We have heard, beloved brother, through fear, of our danger; let us hear through hope the promised comfort of consolations. “I am,” says God, “your portion of inheritance” (Num. XVIII, 20). And again: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9).

Fear shakes us when it is said elsewhere: “To whom much has been entrusted, from him much will be demanded” (Luke XII, 48). And again: “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI, 7). Hope, in turn, renews our strength when he says: “The lips of the priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II, 7).

Amid so many storms and tranquil waves, what is it other than the deep being tossed amid tempests in the harbor of the most rugged shore—that is, our mind’s ship being shaken? But because we know that we derive greater confidence from the long-suffering of the God of the Gospels, we rejoice in hope and fear this turmoil in no way.

What, then, are we except stewards of one shepherd? While he feeds, we feed; while he governs, we govern, because under the same shepherd we are all, together with his sheep, sheep of the pasture. For we attribute what we are not to our own strength but to the grace of God. It remains only that, by asking, seeking, and knocking for divine assistance, we may irreproachably display the gift of grace by faith and works, so that, having trampled vices underfoot, we may deserve to receive the promised rewards of virtues.

Let pride, which is the beginning of every sin, be far from the minds of priests. Let avarice, which is the service of idols and the root of every evil, be cut away, destroyed, and removed far from the whirlwind of its dust, since it blinds even the eyes of the wise. Let us therefore hold fast with steadfast faith and certain hope, in unceasing devotion, to love, the mother of all virtues, without which nothing is perfected, and in which all virtues are held together inseparably by the complete bond of peace.

And since human hearts are purified by faith, the written lines of your affection have made clear that you have drawn pure streams of faith from the fountains of the Savior, and that you preach what we preach, believe as we believe, and teach without diminution what we teach.

Since these things are so, and since what Pyrrhus produced against our apostolic faith in order to subvert the synodal decrees has been destroyed both by the doctrinal statement of the apostolic see, set forth by our predecessor, and by the command of our most gentle son, the emperor, why has your fraternity not removed from public places the document that had previously been hung there and canceled? It caused no small scandal to the holy Churches of God. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10).

If, then, your fraternity considers Pyrrhus’s attempt worthy of rejection, why did you not take the aforesaid document down from the wall? No one worships what he abhors. But if—God forbid—your fraternity embraces such a writing, why did it not disclose this to us through its own synodical letter? Neither position can stand harmlessly without the rejection of the other.

For if the right faith, strengthened by so many councils, is corrected by Heraclius and Pyrrhus with some addition and amendment, then the faith carefully examined by the Fathers is understood to have been disturbed, and the dead to have fallen into an empty hope of blessedness—may God avert this from the hearts of the faithful. Those who have died have not perished at all, for “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV, 15). Those who live in this faith have been made pure, and the doctrine of the Fathers, marked out as true and pious by confirmed faith, has been firmly handed down to posterity.

It remains, therefore, that what has been promulgated against the faith be made void and destroyed together with its own author.

We were also astonished that the bishops who consecrated your fraternity called that man “most holy” in their letters. They also stated that he had renounced the Constantinopolitan Church because of popular disturbance and hatred. For this reason, while we were uncertain, we had judged that what your fraternity wrote should be deferred for a short time, until the aforesaid Pyrrhus was expelled from the episcopate of the Church of Constantinople. For popular disturbance and hatred do not know how to remove the rank of the episcopate.

Canonical punishment ought to have been imposed upon him, so that the consecration of your fraternity might stand irreproachable and firm. For it is written: “If her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband. But if her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man” (Rom. VII, 2–3). “The two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery,” says the Apostle; “but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 31–32).

For although we are unworthy, we nevertheless fill his place in the Churches. Since the aforesaid Pyrrhus is alive and has not yet been removed either by nature or by guilt, precautions ought to have been taken lest a schism arise.

Therefore, so that the priestly order of your fraternity may remain stronger, the required assembly of bishops from the neighboring regions must be convened against him. We also command our dearest sons, Sericus the archdeacon and Martin the deacon and apocrisiary, to whom we entrust our place for deliberation on this matter, to ensure that the guilt of the aforesaid Pyrrhus is canonically investigated together with your fraternity.

His presence is not necessary where his offenses and writings contrary to the truth are at hand, so that, when judgment is rendered concerning them, he may by every means be condemned. First, because he extolled Heraclius, who anathematized the inviolable faith of the orthodox Fathers, with various praises; because by subscribing he confirmed Heraclius’s sophistical command, in which he composed something resembling a creed; because through clandestine subterfuges he compelled certain priests individually to strengthen the aforesaid document before him; and because, in an audacious transgression, he presumed to hang it in public places for the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon.

By this he spread no small scandal of dissension among the Churches of God and thought little of being corrected by the admonition of an assembly from our predecessor.

When these and other matters have been investigated in your fraternity’s synod, subject him to canonical execution, so that, once he has been stripped of the priesthood by priestly order, episcopal legislation, and canonical procedure, not only may the faith remain undefiled, but the episcopal rank of your fraternity may also be preserved more securely.

But if, while deliberating, your fraternity carefully observes that the supporters of the aforesaid Pyrrhus are making an uproar, and if you perceive that they repeatedly and insolently impede the matter that must be decided by causing delay, so that they may eventually carry out their own plan, opposing you unless something happens according to their wish; and if on this account they attempt to make your fraternity liable, or even attempt to produce a schism concerning the same person, it is possible for the intention of such crafty men to be cut off even in this matter, and for a command to be obtained from our lord and son, the most Christian emperor.

We have earnestly requested him by our letters to order that the often-mentioned Pyrrhus be sent to this city of Rome, so that, in a synodal assembly convened by us, he may be judged for his presumption.

In this way the episcopal dignity of your fraternity will be able to appear stronger against every future schism of its opponents; the scandal of innovation, driven away from the orthodox faith, will be destroyed; and the Church of God will be granted continual peace.

Scandals must indeed be erased from the Church and uprooted. For many tares of dissension can arise against the advancement of your fraternity unless they are cut off at the root by the canonical sickle before they can grow. For “when one member suffers, all the other members of the body suffer with it” (I Cor. XII).

Therefore, let there be no schisms or dissensions, in accordance with what we have also requested through our letters from our most gentle lord and son, the emperor: that all the scandals recently arisen in connection with the episcopate of your fraternity be cut away, and that we appear to bring the healing of our care as those who grieve like brothers over your inmost being.

Nevertheless, we decree that the aforesaid document, which is shown to have been sophistically set forth against the orthodox faith and the Council of Chalcedon, is entirely void, rejected by the bond of anathema; and we repudiate it as abhorred by us and by all orthodox bishops.

The faith preached by the holy apostles, confirmed by the councils, and sealed by the holy Fathers is sufficient for us. Through it we have been reborn and instructed, and it is what we teach, admitting no addition to the creed established by the synods. Anathema to those who add to the holy *mathema*, that is, the creed; anathema to those who subtract from it—the creed defined at the Council of Nicaea, confirmed at Constantinople, and established at the First Council of Ephesus and at Chalcedon by the holy and orthodox Fathers who flourished in the Catholic faith, through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Let your fraternity proclaim these and similar things with us in harmonious agreement, confessing them in word and deed. Likewise, let us anathematize all heresies and their authors, so that all may say the same thing, as it is written, and so that schisms may in no way sprout in the Churches of God, since they have already been cut away by the spiritual and double-edged sword of judgment.

We commend to your fraternity in every respect the present bearer of this letter, since his character requires that we commend him to you. His venerability and perfection of conduct clearly show that he presents your presence to us.

[Col. 0581]

## COPY OF THE PROPOSITION SENT TO CONSTANTINOPLE BY THE MOST HOLY POPE THEODORE OF ROME

[Col. 0581C] Our Lord and Savior said this to his apostles in the Gospels: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 19). Another Scripture also says: “Do not move the everlasting boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. XXII, 28).

Since these things are so, we bring to the knowledge of your fraternity that Pyrrhus, who once usurped the episcopate of the Church of Constantinople and lurked like a wolf under the guise of a shepherd, raised a warlike horn against the orthodox faith, composed certain inventions of innovation, and compelled certain priests to subscribe to documents dictated by him through clandestine and surreptitious means.

He acted cunningly so that, through the surreptitious subscriptions of others, he might establish the heretical doctrine of his presumption and attempt to compose, as it were, a new *mathema* for veneration in opposition to the creed handed down to us by the holy Fathers.

Since the Council of Chalcedon pronounced anathema on those who add or subtract anything from the faith strengthened by so many Fathers, we have considered it necessary to forewarn your Love, so that, after rejecting what the aforesaid Pyrrhus presumed against the apostolic faith, you may retain that same faith, as we trust—faith which you drank together with us from the very milk of the breasts of the holy Church—destroying every delirium of rash innovation.

For both through other letters and through the decree of this present proposition, we abhor everything introduced against our orthodox and apostolic faith by the new and rash folly of the same Pyrrhus. Together with the document which he proposed and hung in public places, we anathematize it, and we wish all to hold and believe what the holy apostles handed down and what the Fathers who flourished in the orthodox faith, through the holy five councils, firmly established and handed down to posterity.

[Col. 0581]

## OF THE MOST HOLY POPE THEODORE: TO THE BISHOPS WHO CONSECRATED PAUL, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE, ON ACCOUNT OF PYRRHUS, THE FORMER PATRIARCH

[Col. 0581D] We have received the letter of your fraternity, by which you informed us of the promotion of Paul, our brother and fellow bishop, and we have indeed rejoiced over his ordination. But the future grief that will follow this—namely, because of the tares that are expected to arise—has greatly shaken our mind, unless they are uprooted by the most diligent hand and most cautious care before they grow and choke the Lord’s harvest.

Pyrrhus, therefore, who sowed scandal among the holy Churches of God, ought first to have been subjected to canonical punishment, and then our brother Paul should have been consecrated. Otherwise, at some time he might think of bringing a complaint about his expulsion, claiming that he had suffered popular hatred, had surrendered a document under compulsion, and had renounced his Church, just as your fraternity informed us in its letter.

People are easily changed: sometimes they rise from hatred to love, and sometimes they fall from love into hatred. Why, then, do they not look with prudent foresight at what must be anticipated, lest an arising scandal divide the Church of God through various conflicts?

There are grounds on which the aforesaid Pyrrhus can canonically be expelled from the entire priestly order. First, because he extolled in his letters Heraclius, who anathematized the Catholic faith and the orthodox-thinking Fathers; because, through subterfuge and by means of certain priests who had subscribed, he presumed to confirm a sophistical document against the apostolic faith and hastened to hang it in public places, as though raising up a new faith and creed against the holy Council of Chalcedon; because he showed no fear of the punishment of eternal judgment and of the anathema pronounced at that same Council of Chalcedon, by which no one should ever dare to add anything to or subtract anything from the holy *mathema*, that is, the venerable creed.

The aforesaid Pyrrhus did not allow himself to withdraw from his depravity even when summoned and admonished. Therefore, abhorring the document already mentioned and anathematizing everything that the often-mentioned Pyrrhus plotted against the faith, we now anathematize it again and again, embracing only what the holy Fathers handed down to us in the synods, adding nothing to the faith and taking nothing away.

Accordingly, you will recognize what we have decreed concerning the person of the aforesaid Pyrrhus in the letter that we sent to the brother and fellow bishop already mentioned.

Therefore, in order that scandal may not arise in the future, let sacred prudence diligently extinguish it according to the procedure set forth.

The matter itself, however, has provoked us to still greater distress and has made the tares expected to arise appear more probable, because in your letters you called the aforesaid Pyrrhus “most holy.” If we say nothing else, and if he committed absolutely no offense either against religion or against the doctrine of faith, and if no single fault condemned him, why was he removed from his own Church?

Perhaps someone will say that general hatred caused this. But popular tumult cannot remove the right of the priesthood, nor can hatred strip anyone of the sacred order. The canonical causes that can sever priestly rights are manifest.

Unless a bishop dies a natural death, no other person can irreproachably take possession of his Church.

We write these things not in opposition to the ordination of our aforesaid brother Paul, but we open a hidden and concealed wound with a healing hand, lest it creep into the vital organs; we medicinally drain away every impurity of foul corruption and penetrate what can be reached by the careful incision of prudent diligence—not because we desire these things to happen.

For we embrace and cherish our often-mentioned brother in the depths of our mind. But we are shaken by fraternal prudence and the affection of love, lest schisms arise and the laying on of hands by which he received the episcopate be in any way stained.

Finally, once schisms have been destroyed and suffocated, the orthodox faith—which has shone forth through so many spiritual fragrances of the flowers of paradise, cultivated by the farmers of Christ our God, namely the holy apostles—will in no way be wounded by any thorny tares.

[Col. 0583]

## ACCOUNT OF WHAT THE ROMAN LEGATES DID AT CONSTANTINOPLE

From a letter of Saint Maximus written to the abbot Thalassius
[Col. 0583D] Knowing, Father, that you are such in these and similar matters, and recognizing that with every effort you seek above all in our generation to care for the things that belong to him alone, I thought it right to make known to you the importance of what has recently been written to me from the City by certain venerable men who love God with their whole heart, on behalf of the dogmas of his holy Catholic and apostolic Church.

For they reported that, on account of this matter, a considerable and extended agitation had taken place there—that is, in the imperial city—among its consecrated ecclesiastical men; first earlier, but especially at the time when they received the apocrisarii sent there concerning the promotion of the pope, bearing the decrees. For then, after many discussions which they raised with them concerning the consecration, they finally brought forward for its completion and for the fulfillment of that desire a doctrinal document, now set forth by them, asserting:

“We shall not otherwise grant you favor in the matter for which, having crossed so great a stretch of sea, you have come here, unless you first declare that you will persuade the one who is to be consecrated to subscribe to this document and, without delay, to agree to the doctrines contained in it.” [Col. 0584D]

But those men, perceiving the force of what was being demanded of them and recognizing that their opponents had, for this very reason, forced the chief mother and city of the Churches to remain widowed for so long, evidently wishing by such a contrivance to obtain her—since they had judged that their own novelty must irrationally be extended even to her in order to attain what they sought—calmly pursued their argument, as though yielding, and said:

“We have no authority to grant this. A ministry has indeed been entrusted to us, but no command to make a profession. We do, however, assure you that we shall report everything you have demanded, show the document itself to the one who is to be consecrated, and, if he judges that it is sound, ask him to add his own subscription to it. But do not now wish to obstruct us unexpectedly on this account, or to use force by prolonging matters and detaining us here. For no one may use force against anyone, least of all in a matter of faith.

“For in this matter the very weak man stands as exceedingly strong, and the very gentle man is found to be the supreme warrior. Strengthening his soul by the divine word, he is found, even under the greatest attacks, somehow harder to break than to dissolve. How much more so the Church and clergy of the Romans, which from ancient times until now, as the senior of all the Churches under the sun, presides over them all? This it has received and attained canonically from councils and apostles, as well as from their supreme primacy, and has become subject to no writings whatsoever on account of the advancement of its pontificate, nor to the promulgation of synodal documents; just as here also all alike stand subject to it according to sacerdotal right.” [Col. 0585A]
