When these men had thus discussed the matter with the clergy of the imperial city, fearing nothing but standing firm with every sacred and proper confidence—truly ministers of that great, apostolic, firm, and immovable rock, namely the Church that is there—they appeared to have calmed them and wisely brought them to think humbly and moderately, making known to them from the very beginning the sincerity and orthodoxy of their own faith.

Those men, admiring their piety, considered that such conduct deserved a fitting recompense. They therefore abandoned their demand concerning the document and promised that, through their own efforts, they would carry the command into effect concerning the episcopate. When the God-beloved apocrisarii received this assurance, they returned to their own people rejoicing.

A copy of this document, Father honored by God, was also sent to me. In it they had set forth the reason for the natural operations to be performed in Christ God—that is, in his substances, from which and in which he exists and is believed to exist—and that henceforth neither one nor two should in any way be proclaimed in him. They acknowledged only that it must be confessed that, from the one and same incarnate Word of God, things divine and human had proceeded and were to be referred to one and the same person.

[Col. 0585]

**To the most blessed and renowned Martin, bishop of the holy Church of Narni, Anastasius the humble librarian of the apostolic see sends greetings in the Lord.** (C)

[Col. 0585C] Since the dignity of the episcopate, on account of your supreme devotion, has been entrusted by the supreme pontiffs to your holiness together with the superintendence of the monastery of blessed Martin situated near the City, this seemed to urge me to translate into Latin what I had found among the Greeks concerning what happened to blessed Pope Martin on behalf of the faith and correct doctrines. Yet one Martin is the man whose monastery you are seen piously to govern, and another is the man whose experiences you desire fully to know. The former was a bishop of Tours, the latter a Roman bishop.

I therefore obeyed your exhortations, venerable father, not so much from knowledge as from obedience. For I know that Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifice, and to listen than to offer holocausts; for rebellion is as the sin of divination, and refusal to obey is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15:22–23). I therefore preferred ignorance to committing the sin of idolatry.

In fact, I myself did not translate the middle portion of this work, being occupied with other matters; rather, after it had been translated at my request by another, I subsequently corrected certain parts of it. Since, however, I found that some passages from the Acts of blessed Maximus the monk and his disciples were connected and continued with this work, I shall not refuse, if life is granted me, to translate those also, with God as my guide, most holy and reverend father.

Written in the eighth indiction, in the time of Lord John VIII, pope.

The beginning of this work, according to the force of its meaning alone, is as follows:

Only-begotten Son, God, Word of the almighty Father,

Who, willing through mercy alone, are held to have become human,

And by suffering in the flesh have redeemed the human race,

Assist, sheltering us; save and always rescue

Your servants, wherever they are, from the plague of sin,

Through the prayers of the excellent Virgin, your beloved mother,

And of the twelve leaders, together with all the devout,

The glory without end, the way and life of all your own.

[Col. 0586D] From what Theodore Spudeus of Holy Wisdom wrote to the holy brothers Theodore and Euprepius, kinsmen and appointed chief bakers of the king, living in exile at Cherson, concerning the unjust deeds committed by the adversaries against the holy and apostolic Martin, truly a new confessor and martyr of Christ our God, the Roman pope, before he was sent there into exile, when he was violently dragged away from the apostolic see because of the word of truth.

**THEOD.** After he had returned to the watch-post, with the sufferings known to God, I was able to write to him and make known everything that was being spread abroad about him. Along with these matters I added certain others, entreating him not to be overcome in any way by the wicked sect of impious men, but to remain reverent and fearful, keeping before his eyes the shipwreck of Sergius, archbishop of the island of Cyprus.

He replied as follows.

**Martin to Theodore, his brother beloved with sincere affection.**

Since I have understood, as far as I could, what you have reported in writing, I shall explain it in a few words. When I was leaving the church called Constantiniana, in which the army had surrounded me with weapons, in the presence of the exarch and Theodore the chamberlain, as well as the clergy, they said in a loud voice:

“Let whoever says or believes that Martin has changed the faith even by one iota, or will change it, be anathema; and let those who do not remain in their orthodox faith until death be anathema.”

After hearing this, Calliopas began to give an account, saying that there was no faith other than the one we hold and that he believed no differently. But he said this on account of those who were listening, not on account of the faith.

And I want you to know, dearest brother, concerning the faith you mentioned, and also concerning the false accusations which they bring against the truth: with the aid of your prayers and those of all the faithful Christians who are with you, both while living and when dying I shall defend the faith of our salvation. As the blessed apostle Paul teaches, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”

But concerning the false accusations which the heretics have recently brought forward, rejecting the truth of Christ God: how could those who resist God’s truth have spoken any truth at all to human beings?

I therefore give you an account, dearest brother, by him who will judge this world by fire and will repay each according to his work. I have never sent even a letter to the Saracens, nor the document which they say instructs them how they ought to believe, nor have I ever sent them money, except only to certain servants of God who came there for the sake of almsgiving; and we provided them with a small amount, which was not sent to the Saracens.

Moreover, concerning our glorious Lady, the ever-virgin Mary, who gave birth to God and our Lord Jesus Christ, whom all the holy and Catholic Fathers call the Mother of God, since she gave birth to God as man, wicked men have testified falsely against me—indeed, against their own souls. For whoever does not honor and worship the blessed, venerable, and ever-virgin mother of our Lord, exalted above every creature and human nature, except him who was born from her, let him be anathema both in the present age and in the age to come!

But men who seek pretexts bring accusations in order to scandalize many.

[Col. 0588A] **Subscription.** May God keep you safe, most beloved son.

**THEOD.** Having received this, I gave thanks to God, learning the steadfastness of the holy man’s purpose. But I was anxious and wished to learn how he had been removed from his see, and I could not. For everyone whom I questioned about this gave me no true answer, but one account after another. Necessity therefore compelled me to make inquiry about it and to beseech him, so that I might learn the truth from him.

The saint therefore wrote again as follows.

**Martin to Theodore.**

Your dear affection wished to know how I was snatched from the see of the holy apostle Peter, like a solitary sparrow from a building. I marvel that you wished to inquire about this, since our Lord foretold to his disciples concerning these wicked times:

“For in those days there will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh could be saved. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:21–22).

This is said briefly concerning Antichrist. For the holy Paul also, according to the grace given him by the Spirit, foretold these days to his disciple Timothy, saying: “In the last days people will depart from the faith and turn away from hearing the truth, loving themselves, empty” (2 Timothy 3:1–2 and following).

And believe me, my most desired son, no other time should be expected than this, in which the beginnings of sorrows are plainly present, just as the Lord foretold the coming of Antichrist. It also seemed necessary for me to say briefly, before judgment prevails throughout the whole world and I bring my course to its end, what I have judged expedient, so that when others prepare evils for me I may rejoice rather than weep.

Therefore, so that you may know how I was removed and led away from the Roman city, you will hear nothing false concerning what happened. Throughout the entire period I knew in advance everything they were planning. After taking myself and all my clergy, I stayed privately in the church of our Savior Jesus Christ called Constantiniana, the first church constructed and established in the whole world by the emperor Constantine of blessed memory; it is beside the episcopal residence.

There we all remained apart from the day of Saturday, when Calliopas entered the city with the army of Ravenna and Theodore the chamberlain. I therefore sent some of the clergy to meet him. After receiving them in the palace, he thought that I too was with them. When he had searched and did not find me, he said to the senior clergy:

“We wished to pay our respects to him, but tomorrow, which is the Lord’s Day, we shall meet him and greet him; today we have not had enough time.”

On Sunday, after the Masses had been celebrated in the aforementioned holy church of God, suspecting that a large crowd was gathering because of the day, he announced:

“We have been greatly fatigued by the journey and cannot meet him today, but tomorrow we shall certainly meet him and pay our respects to your holiness.”

I myself, however, had been seriously ill from the month of October until that time, namely until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July. [Col. 0588D] Thus, early on Monday, he sent his chartularius and certain members of his retinue, saying:

“You have prepared weapons and have armed men inside, and you have gathered a quantity of stones in order to resist. This is unnecessary, and do not permit anything of the sort to take place.”

When I heard this in person, I considered it more necessary to assure them of the facts than to send them wandering through the entire episcopal residence so that, if they saw weapons or stones, they themselves might bear witness. When they went and found nothing, I told them in words that they had never acted otherwise, but always proceeded against us through collusion [Note: Greek συμπλοκή, “collusion”] and false accusation, although at the arrival of the notorious Olympius, a worthless man, they admitted that I could have repelled him with arms.

I therefore had my bed before the altar of the church, on which I lay. Before half an hour had passed, behold, the army came with them into the church. All were covered with shadow, holding their spears and swords, and also their bows prepared, together with their shields; and things took place there that ought not even to be mentioned.

For just as, in winter, when the wind blows violently, leaves shaken from the trees fall, so the candles of the holy church were struck by the weapons, beaten down, and thrown onto the pavement. A sound was heard in that same church like a dreadful thunderclap, both from the pressure of the weapons and from the multitude of candles broken by them.

As soon as they entered, a command from Calliopas was handed to the presbyters and deacons. It contained the rejection of my humility [Note: Greek ἀποβολή, “ejection”]: that I had unlawfully and illegally usurped the episcopate, that I was not worthy to be established in the apostolic see, but must by all means be sent to this imperial city, with another bishop substituted in my place.

Such a thing had never yet been done, and I hope it will never be done: for in the absence of the pontiff, the archdeacon, archpresbyter, and primicerius represent the pontiff’s place.

While these matters were being set in motion, I had already made known to you what had been done concerning the faith. As for the fact that we were not prepared to resist, I judged it better to die ten times than to have the blood of anyone shed upon the ground. And this was done without danger, though not without the accomplishment of several deeds displeasing to God.

At that same hour I gave myself up to be presented to the emperor and did not resist. When certain members of the clergy called out to me, truthfully speaking, urging me not to do this, I listened to none of them, lest sudden homicides occur. But I said to them:

“Let members of the clergy come with me who are necessary to me—namely bishops, presbyters, and deacons, and, plainly, whomever I deem appropriate.”

Calliopas replied:

“Let as many as wish to come do so willingly. We compel no one.”

I answered:

“The clergy are in my power.”

But certain priests cried out, saying:

“With him we live, and with him we die.”

After this Calliopas himself and those who were with him began to say:

“Come with us to the palace.”

I did not refuse to do this either, but went with them to the palace that same Monday.

On Tuesday all the clergy came to me, and many had prepared themselves to sail with me. They had even already sent their belongings into what were called *levamenta*; and several other clerics and laymen were also preparing themselves and hastening to reach us.

That same night, which dawned into Wednesday, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, at about the sixth hour of the night, they removed me from the palace, having shut in everyone who was with me in the palace, along with the various things that were necessary for me on the journey and here. They led us out of the city with no more than six boys and one cook, and, after placing us in one of the vessels called *levamenta* [Note: These are certain smaller ships used to lighten the loads of larger ships], we reached the harbor at approximately the fourth hour of the day.

At the very hour when we left the city of Rome, as soon as the gates had been locked, they locked them again and kept them so, lest anyone leave the city and come to us at the harbor until we had sailed away. Thus necessity forced us to leave at that harbor all the belongings of those who had sent them into the *levamenta*, and to set out immediately that same day.

We reached Messina on the Kalends of July, where the ship—that is, my prison—was. Not only at Messina, but also in Calabria, and not only in Calabria, which is subject to the great city of the Romans, but also in many islands where our sins detained us for as long as three months, did I receive any compassion—except only on the island of Naxos. Since we spent a year there, I was permitted to wash in two or three baths and to stay in a lodging in the city.

And behold, today is the forty-seventh day since I have deserved neither to pour hot nor cold water over myself. I have wasted away and grown entirely cold, since a discharge of the bowels, both on the ship and on land, has given me no rest at all up to the present hour. Even at the very hour of my necessity, when I am about to taste food, my whole body is shaken, and I have nothing necessary to strengthen my constitution; for what I do have I loathe taking, since it has become utterly repulsive to me.

But I believe in the power of God, who sees all things, because when I have been removed from this present life, those who persecute me will be called to account for all these things, so that at least in this way they may be led to repentance and turn from their wickedness.

**Subscription.** May God keep you safe and unharmed, dearest son!

[Col. 0591]

**ACCOUNT OF THE THINGS THAT WERE SAVAGELY AND WITHOUT REGARD FOR GOD PERFORMED BY THE ADVERSARIES OF THE TRUTH AGAINST THE HOLY AND APOSTOLIC MARTIN, TRULY A NEW CONFESSOR AND MARTYR, POPE OF ROME, IN A LETTER OF A MOST CHRISTIAN MAN ADDRESSED TO THE ORTHODOX FATHERS IN THE WEST, THAT IS, IN ROME AND AFRICA.**

[Col. 0591A] The griefs and tears of affliction, and the common, unceasing, and most sorrowful cry that has arisen from the depths of the heart in the midst of suffering—I think it is also being uttered before God by those who are in Rome, and further by the holy servants of God and faithful peoples dwelling in every place under his dominion—from the time when persecution was made against our most holy Father, blessed by God, the faithful chief of priests, and universal apostolic pope, and through him against the Catholic Church: I think that this same grief still remains among you, and that you are deeply anxious to know how the deed against him was carried out, when he was exiled and driven by persecution from Rome by ship as far as Byzantium.

Keeping these matters in mind, I, your humble and sinful servant, having learned some things externally with great concern and having myself become an unworthy witness of many things, judged that I should recall them in writing, make them known, and set them clearly before you, blessed men, and through you before all the faithful and all who are zealous for divine worship. Thus, recognizing them with sorrow of heart, you may join me in uttering that prophetic saying:

“Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night over the brokenness of the Catholic Church and of all Christians—indeed, over their destruction—because of what has been done against the blessed, God-filled leader and preacher of the truth?”

Nevertheless, glory be to God, who gave him steadfast strength and endurance in the trials that came upon him from opposing powers and men, as he fought and battled manfully for the worship of God, irreproachably and with firm hope laying down his life even unto death, as an imitator of the one who appointed him an athlete—his Lord—so that he might fight for the truth as an example to others. [Col. 0591C]

You yourselves know what was done there in Rome against the blessed and adamantine spiritual father and chief of priests, Lord Martin: the dangers with which he struggled, seeing drawn and sharpened swords crowded together, held by many soldiers ready to stain their blades and take the blessed man’s life, standing around the altar in the entire temple of the Catholic Church of Rome called Constantiniana, in which he was lying sick in the priestly office, at the doorway and on a small bed.

You know also how, broken in spirit, bound in his limbs, driven and expelled, seized and dragged from the apostolic throne, in which place God had established him as an overseer, his apostle, and preacher of orthodox truth, he was treated. [Col. 0591D] But truly this man did not regard his life as more precious than himself; rather, he laid it down unto death, imitating, as has been said, his Lord, who declared: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep”—so that he might save everywhere the wandering and lost people from the heretics rising up in our times.

He was therefore handed over in Rome, from the Catholic Church of Saint John, by the powerful men of this age to ministers and guards worthy of that duty, deposited at the harbor, and cast into a small boat. As they sailed, as you know, and passed by Avidus [Note: Greek Ἀβουδόν], toward the island called Naxos, the guards did not permit that blessed apostolic man even to touch land, although his feet were suffering greatly, while they themselves moved about from place to place and rested altogether.

The priests who were in those places, and the other faithful of that region, sent gifts to the blessed man for his needs, often in no small quantity. But the guards, those beasts, immediately plundered the provisions and quantities sent, in his very presence, heaping upon him many insults and bitter words. Those who had brought the little gifts they dismissed after abusing and beating them, saying:

“Whoever among you loves this man is an enemy of the state.”

Was this alone not enough to inflict incomparable pain upon him, in addition to the illness already grievously pressing upon him?

Then, sending ahead from Avidus certain guards who were holding him, they announced his arrival and capture at Byzantium, bringing many accusations against him: proclaiming him a heretic, a rebel, and an enemy of God, and alleging that he was overturning the whole Roman land.

When that blessed man finally reached Byzantium on the seventeenth day of September, at the harbor near Euphemia, close to Arcadianon [Note: Greek Ἀρκαδιαναί, “the houses of Arcadius in the new district of the city.” Sirmond], the attendants left him lying on the ship’s bed from morning until the tenth hour. He was, as it is written, “a spectacle to angels and human beings.”

Various people came—whom, because of their savage and wolfish behavior, I should call wolves—and, as I infer, they had been appointed to do such things against the holy pope as ought not to be spoken of among Christians. While we remained on the shore, I walked about all day, full of grief and bitterness because I saw such a holy man so degraded. Moreover, when I heard such words spoken against him by certain pagans, I desired nothing else than that my soul might be taken from me.

Then, near sunset, a certain scribe named Sagoleva came with many watchmen. Taking him from the small boat, they placed him on a litter and led him to the watch-house prison called [Col. 0593D] Prandearia [Note: Greek Πρανοδιάρα. See the *Chronicon Paschale*, p. 308, and Ducange, *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book II, section 6, no. 1, p. 138]. He had him shut in under heavy guard, ordering the guards of the watch-house that absolutely no one in the city should know that he was in that same watch-house.

Thus the same holy apostolic man remained confined and entirely without communication with anyone for ninety-three days. On the ninety-third day itself, which was the day of Preparation, they took him from the prison in the morning and ordered that the entire senate assemble the following day in the chamber of the *sacellarius*; and this was done.

They ordered him to be brought in, and he was brought in on a portable chair, for he was extremely ill, especially in those days because of the voyage and the affliction caused by so many days of imprisonment.

The *sacellarius*, who presided, looked at him from a distance with the other officials and ordered him to rise from the litter and stand. When some of the attendants said that he was unable to stand, the *sacellarius*, disturbed by great anger, shouted—and with him certain members of the guard—that he should rise and stand supported from either side; and this was done.

The *sacellarius* then said to him:

“Tell me, wretch, what evil did the emperor inflict upon you? Did he take anything from you? Did he oppress you by force?”

But he remained silent.

Then the *sacellarius* said to him in a commanding voice:

“Will you not answer? Look, your accusers are now entering.”

Immediately many accusers against him were brought in with their speeches. All were sons and disciples of falsehood, like those who killed our Lord Jesus Christ. They contradicted the holy man as they had been instructed, for their statements had been rehearsed and prepared in advance.

Some of them, when questioned shortly beforehand so that they might give testimony, tried—as is customary—to speak the truth. At once those who were staging this contest began to frighten them with severe threats until they persuaded them to utter what suited the death of the blessed and just man.

When the holy pope saw the witnesses entering to testify, he smiled and said:

“These are the witnesses? Is this the procedure?”

The first to enter were men called soldiers, but wolfish and bestial in their character; some of them belonged to Olympius, including Andrew, who had been his notary.

[Col. 0593D] Among the accusers were the wretched Imeritus, Therinus, and the rest—about twenty in number—leading soldiers and others who brought accusations. They swore on the holy Gospels and then gave their testimony.

The chief of all the accusers was Dorotheus, a patrician of Cilicia. Swearing an oath, he said that if Martin had fifty heads, he ought not to live, because he alone had overturned and ruined the entire West, destroyed it, and had truly been of one mind with Olympius; he was an enemy and murderer of the emperor and of the Roman state [Note: Greek πολιτεία, “the state/commonwealth”].

When the just man saw them entering and testifying under oath without restraint, he pitied the destruction of their souls and said to the officials presiding over them:

“I beg you by God, do not prepare them and make them swear an oath; let them say whatever they wish without an oath, and you do whatever you wish. Why should they also destroy their souls by swearing?”

One of the witnesses entered and said that Martin had conspired with Olympius and had prepared soldiers to swear to this. The precious man of God was asked whether these things were true and replied:

“If you wish to hear the truth, I shall tell you what follows.”

And he began to say:

“When the *Typos* was made and sent to Rome by the emperor—”

But when that blessed man had said only this, he was not permitted to say anything further. Immediately, before them all, Troilus began shouting:

“Do not bring faith into this matter! You are now being questioned about the rebellion, since both the Romans and we are Christians and orthodox.”

The same just man replied:

“If only that were so! Nevertheless, you will find me a witness to this also on the day of the fearful judgment.”

Again, among the accusing witnesses, the prefect Troilus said to him:

“What sort of man are you? Seeing and hearing such things against the emperor, who was striving to destroy Olympius, why did you not prevent him, but instead agree with him?”

The blessed apostolic pope immediately replied:

“Tell me, Lord Troilus: when, as you yourselves know and we also heard, George, who had been a monk, entered this city from the army and spoke such words and did such things, where were you and those who are with you? Why did you not resist him? On the contrary, he harangued you, exiled whomever he wished from the Palace, and forbade them entry.

“Again, under Valentinus, when he put on the purple by the emperor’s command and sat beside him, where were you? Were you not here? Why, then, did you not prevent him, saying: ‘Do not touch matters that are not suitable for you’? Did you not all, on the contrary, gather to meet him?

“How could I stand against such a man, especially when he possessed the support of the entire Italian army? Or was I the one who made him exarch?

“Nevertheless, I beg you again by the Lord: whatever you wish and decide to be done to me, complete it quickly. God knows that you have given me the greatest gifts, whatever calamity you use to cut me down.”

The *sacellarius* asked one of the attendants, namely Sagoleva, whether there were any others outside who ought to give testimony. The scribe replied:

“There are many others, my lord.”

But those presiding, being exhausted, and seeing the holy and venerable man standing before them—especially as the Holy Spirit strengthened him—said that the witnesses were sufficient.

Their interpreter was Innocentius, the consul and son of Thomas, who was from Africa. As he interpreted what the blessed man said, he could not endure it, seeing the fiery arrows of the Holy Spirit hurled by the man honored by God against them. The *sacellarius* angrily said to Innocentius:

“Why are you interpreting for us what he says? Do not say what he says.”

The *sacellarius* then rose immediately with many who had been seated with him and went in to report to the emperor whatever he wished.

They led the holy apostolic man from the courtroom—or rather, from the hall of Caiaphas—seated on a portable chair, and placed him in the middle of the courtyard that was before the chamber of the *sacellarius* and the imperial stable, where all the people customarily gathered and waited for the *sacellarius* to enter.

The guards surrounded him, and he was a terrifying spectacle to all the crowds.

After a short time they ordered him to be brought into the upper gallery of the tribunal, so that he might be there while the emperor looked through the grilles of his dining hall at what was to take place. A crowd of people had gathered there in such numbers that they filled the way as far as the hippodrome.

They therefore placed the most reverend man in the middle of the upper gallery of the tribunal, supported on either side by the entire senate.

A considerable throng suddenly formed. The *sacellarius* came out from the emperor, opened the doors of the dining hall onto the gallery, and ordered the whole crowd to disperse.

Going up to the holy and venerable apostolic man Martin, he said to him:

“See how God has led you and delivered you into our hands. You were striving against the emperor—what hope did you have? Behold, you abandoned God, and God abandoned you.”

Then, shouting, the *sacellarius* ordered one of the guards standing nearby, a barber, immediately to remove the *psachnion* [Note: This is a cloak or bag. See Baronius under the year 651, no. 10, who, with others, reads *psachmon*] of the supreme, apostolic, and foremost shepherd of all Christians, who had confirmed the orthodox confession—that is, the faith—of the holy Fathers and councils, and had canonically and synodally anathematized the authors of the new error, namely the new heretics, together with their impious doctrines.

When the guard had cut the *psachnion* of the blessed man and the strap of his *campagia*, the *sacellarius* immediately handed him over to the prefect of the city, saying:

“Take him, Lord Prefect, and cut him to pieces immediately.”

With all this, he ordered those standing there to anathematize him, and they did so. But the souls of twenty men did not respond to such a voice. All who saw this and knew that there is a God in heaven who observes what was being done withdrew with downcast faces, deeply sorrowful and distressed.

The executioners then took him and removed the outer cloak of his priestly vestment. Tearing the sleeves of the tunic that was underneath from top to bottom, they placed iron chains around his holy neck. Dragging him by force, they did not permit him to sit anywhere or restore his strength, but led him publicly and dishonorably from the palace through the middle of the city toward the praetorium, with a sword before him.

The pain of that blessed man was great and indescribable. He was exceedingly exhausted and weak and, amid so many hardships, was about to surrender his life under the pressure of sufferings and the frailty of his body. Nevertheless, strengthened by hope, he rejoiced in the Lord; and the more he was dragged with affliction and violence, the more he was led with tranquil gaze and great steadfastness of soul. The righteous man followed wearing only one garment, torn from the top into two pieces, and without a belt, so that the inner parts of his body were in some measure laid bare. Many of the people, seeing what was happening, groaned continually—and, to tell the truth, wept. A few servants of Satan, however, rejoiced and mocked and, as it is written, shook their heads as they passed by, saying: “Where is his God? Where is his faith? Where is his teaching?”

When he had arrived at the praetorium, dishonored and bound by the executioners with chains, they threw him into one of the prisons with murderers. After about an hour they removed him and transferred him to the place called Diomedes’ guardhouse in the Prefect’s praetorium. With such persistence and force did they drag him, bound in chains, [Col. 0596B] that his legs and the backs of his knees were lacerated, and blood flowed as he climbed the stairs of that guardhouse. For its steps are rocky, extremely rough, and rise steeply upward.

The blessed man himself was already close to being deprived of this present life through its sufferings, his soul failing even before the sword, since he could no longer climb with those who were dragging him. They therefore brought him in, falling repeatedly and rising again as best he could, and placed him on a bench, clothed in iron and chains. At that time, when he had been handed over by Caiaphas to Pilate to be crucified—that is, by the Prefect—when the executioners immediately stripped him, he was severely tormented by the cold, for the winter was intolerable. They placed extremely heavy iron weights upon him, and no one of his own people was present except one young cleric, [Col. 0596C] who remained with him in the guardhouse and, standing over him, lamented for his master like Peter.

The master of the guardhouse was also chained to that blessed man, since it was customary for one who was to suffer death by the sword to be chained to the master of the guardhouse. There were two women, mother and daughter, who held the keys of that prison. When they saw the unbearable suffering of that holy man, who amid all the forms of punishment inflicted upon him was being shaken by the harshest cold, moved by compassion they wished to show him some mercy and cover him, but they did not dare because of the chained executioner who was guarding him. They thought that the sentence for his slaughter would soon arrive.

After several hours, when some persons from below had called the executioner, the master of the watch, to come down from the military ranks, one of the women of those prisons, moved by the compassion of her heart, approached and embraced Christ’s champion, the apostolic father. Carrying him, she laid him upon her own bed, covering and wrapping him suitably. He remained without a word until evening. When evening came, Gregory the Prefect, the eunuch from among the chamberlains, sent to him the chief of his household with a little food. The man refreshed him, saying: “Do not fail in your tribulations. We trust in God; you will not die.” At this the blessed man groaned even more heavily. [Col. 0597A] The iron chains were immediately removed from him.

On the following day the emperor went to the Patriarchium to visit the patriarch Paul, who was near death, and told him what had been done to the most holy man. Paul groaned and, turning toward the wall, said: “Alas for me! This too has been done to increase the account of my judgments.” When the emperor asked him why he had said this, he replied: “My lord, is it not pitiable for bishops to suffer such things?” Then he earnestly entreated the emperor that what the man had suffered should suffice for him and that he should endure nothing further.

When the blessed and apostolic man heard of this, and that he had not received what he was expecting, he did not welcome such a promise, [Col. 0597B] but became utterly sorrowful. For he was eager to complete the good contest and depart to him whom he desired.

Meanwhile Paul died, and Pyrrhus attempted to take his seat, while certain members of the Church opposed and prevented him, publishing his libellus in the palace and asserting that he had also been anathematized by the most blessed Paul. Pyrrhus was rejected from the priesthood because of the libellus he had composed at Rome.

After much disturbance had arisen, eight days after Paul’s death the emperor sent to Diomedes’ guardhouse the magnanimous pope Demosthenes, the rescriptor and associate of the sacellarius, together with Libellifius. Entering, they said to him:

“Our excellent sovereign the emperor has sent us to you, saying: [Col. 0597C] ‘Behold into what glory you formerly stood, and into what condition you have brought yourself! No one did this to you; you did it to yourself.’”

He answered nothing else except this: “Glory and thanksgiving in all things to the immortal King alone.”

The rescriptor Demosthenes said to him: “The sovereign has indicated that you should tell us what subsequently happened concerning Pyrrhus, the former patriarch, here and at Rome. For what reason did he go to Rome: by command or by his own decision?”

The holy pope replied: “By his own decision.”

Demosthenes said: “How did he compose that libellus? Was he compelled by anyone?”

The holy man replied: “By no one, but by his own initiative.”

Demosthenes said: “When Pyrrhus came to Rome, how did the holy man Theodore, your predecessor as pope, receive him—as a bishop?”

The even-tempered pope replied: “How could he have done otherwise? Before Pyrrhus came to Rome, the blessed Theodore openly wrote here—that is, to Paul—regarding him as one who had acted improperly and invaded another’s throne. Then, when that same Pyrrhus came of his own accord to Rome, to the feet of blessed Peter, how could my predecessor not receive and honor him as a bishop?”

Demosthenes replied: “The truth is indeed so. From where did he obtain what was necessary for his bodily use?”

The blessed man said: “Clearly from the Roman Patriarchium.”

The disputant said: “What sort of bread was given to him?”

The venerable man replied: “Do you, my lords, not know the Roman Church? I tell you that whoever comes there, a wretched man seeking lodging, is provided with everything needed for his use; and holy Peter repels none of those who come there, keeping back his gifts from them. The purest bread and various wines are given not only to him but also to those belonging to him. If such things are done for wretched men, when one who is honorable, such as a bishop, comes, what expense is there in receiving him?”

Demosthenes said to him: “We have learned that Pyrrhus composed the libellus at Rome under compulsion, endured wooden fetters, and suffered many painful things.”

That blessed man replied: “None of this happened. Perhaps those who are held by fear cannot speak the truth. There are many here in Constantinople who were then at Rome and know what happened there. Among them there remains Plato the patrician, who was then Exarch and sent his men to Pyrrhus at Rome. Ask him about these things, if I am lying.

“But why should we inquire into many things? Behold, you hold me in your hands, and complete upon me whatever you wish; by God’s permission, I am in your power. Indeed, if you cut my flesh into pieces, as you ordered the Prefect to do when you handed me over, I do not communicate with the Church of Constantinople. Here I am: examine and test me, and by experience you will find the grace of God and of his faithful servants.”

Again Pyrrhus was brought forward, who had so often been anathematized and stripped of divine honor. The rescriptor Demosthenes was astonished and admired, in this utterance, the even-tempered pope’s boldness and steadfastness for Christ in the face of death; indeed, the cup of suffering had been set before him for this. Those who followed him likewise stood amazed. Taking a libellus, they wrote down word for word everything said by the blessed man and withdrew. [Col. 0598C]

The most reverend pope therefore spent eighty-five days in the same prison of Diomedes, in addition to the first ninety-three—that is, one hundred seventy-eight days in all.

Then the scribe Sagoleba came, saying: “I have been ordered to remove you from here, transfer you to my house, and after two days send you wherever the sacellarius commands me.”

When the pope asked where he was to be taken, or to what place, he refused to tell him. The holy man therefore asked to be permitted to remain in the same guardhouse until he was exiled, and then to be removed from the guardhouse at the proper time; but this too was not granted to him.

Around sunset the venerable pope said to those who were in the prison: “Come, brothers; let us say farewell, for behold, the one who will remove me from here is now approaching.” As he said this, each of them drained the cup.

Then he rose with a tranquil face, great steadfastness, and thanksgiving, and said to one of his beloved companions who was there: “Come, my brother, and give me peace.”

As he himself later told me, that brother’s innermost heart was at that hour like—I suppose—the hearts of those disciples who contemplated the Lord upon the cross. Unable, as he said, to restrain himself, when the blessed man called him to the kiss, the brother roared like a lion. All who were present there lamented with him in a terrible lamentation.

The blessed man, distressed by this, begged them all not to act in that way, saying with tranquil gaze. Then, placing his venerable hands upon the brother’s head, he smiled and said: “These things are good, my brother; these things are appropriate. Is it right for you to act in this way? Are these the things of peace? On the contrary, you ought now to rejoice over me.”

Immediately the brother replied with contrition of heart: “God knows, servant of Christ. I rejoice in the glory for which Christ our God has deemed you worthy to suffer all these things for his name; but I lament the destruction of all.”

They all took leave of him and departed. The scribe then came immediately, removed him, and brought him into his house. It was said that he was to be exiled to Cherson; after some days we learned that the most holy apostolic man himself had been secretly transported there by ship. After arriving there some days later, he wrote a letter to Byzantium to a certain man dear to him, one of those who loved him for the Lord’s sake and because of his orthodox faith.

When our most holy Father, mentioned above, was in great tribulation and exile, he repeatedly requested assistance with certain supplies because of his many, frequent, and severe bodily illnesses and because of the region’s every kind of hardship, since nothing was to be found there—especially wheat, which was named there but not actually available.

Therefore he wrote under oath that when a small boat arrived there with a little wheat for exchange for salt, he could scarcely buy one modius of wheat from it for four solidi, and even that only with many prayers. His holy soul wrote that he suffered various hardships there—not only bodily hardship, but also oppression from the evils of those who lived and ruled there—so that he was utterly crushed and might die a worse death, evidently through the persuasion of those ruling in Byzantium.

For this reason, I beg you, venerable Fathers honored by God—I, your humble and sinful servant—that just as I have most diligently explained to you what I saw and heard, namely, the tribulations threatening the most blessed pope because of his true confession in the Lord Christ and because he anathematized the new heretics, although I have written only a small part of many things, yet as much as I could; so you too, who are zealous for the cultivation of God, explain these things, exhort others to imitate him, and hold fast to the traditions of the holy Fathers according to his example, refusing altogether to communicate with those who think otherwise. Pray also for me, the unworthy servant who wrote this, that together with him and with you I may find mercy from Christ our God forever. Amen.

The same most holy, thrice-blessed apostolic pope Martin, a fresh confessor and martyr of Christ our God, died in that same exile at Cherson, in accordance with the petition he had offered with tears to the Lord God when he came down from the ship and set foot upon that land: namely, that he might finish his life there, fighting the good fight, completing the course of martyrdom, and keeping the good faith. [Col. 0600A]

He died in the month of September, on the sixteenth day, on which, according to the annual cycle, the memory is celebrated of the most fortunate martyr Euphemia, who guarded the orthodox faith, most precious and blessed, in the fourteenth indiction.

He was placed in the tombs of the saints outside the walls of the city of the Chersonites, about one stadion away, in the most precious and venerable church of the most holy, more than all the saints to be honored, most chaste, immaculate, greatly blessed, most glorious and excellent of all creatures, full of grace, our Lady who brings and grants joy, by nature and in truth the only Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, who is called Blachernae.

He became an exemplary model for all who choose and desire to live well and contend for the truest truth. Through the intercessions of this Virgin and Confessor, may Christ, true God and our Savior, who ineffably and without seed proceeded from her for the sake of the human race, guard and preserve us and all who faithfully hear this, and the entire people whom he acquired, in sincerity of faith and conduct, in peace, perfect love, and every righteousness to the end.

To him, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong in the one Godhead one substance, equal honor, the same power, an eternal kingdom, beginningless existence, an unfailing scepter, everlasting glory, and like majesty, throughout infinite ages. Amen.

The aforesaid letter of that same most holy and apostolic pope runs as follows.

[Col. 0600C]

“We inform your genuine charity, my lord brother, that after we departed from the place called Ivon at Constantinople, sailing on Holy Thursday of the Lord’s Supper, we passed through the Pharos, traveling through various places. On the Ides of May we reached Cherson.

“The bearer of this letter, who delivers it to you, came to Cherson from the region of Byzantium thirty days after us. We rejoiced at his arrival, supposing that the supplies sent to us from Italy had reached this land and would comfort us when he arrived. But when we questioned him, we learned from him that he had brought nothing here from Italy. I marveled and glorified my God even for this, because, as he knows, he orders our tribulations—especially since there is famine in [Col. 0600D] this land and such need that bread is merely named here, but is not seen at all.

“For unless supplies are sent to us from those regions or from the regions of Pontus, we cannot live here at all. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak, as you yourself know. No means of provision can be found anywhere in this land, not even for the consolation of a small expense.

“If, then, as stated, grain and wine, or oil and certain other things, can in any way be sent from there, hasten to send them to us as you are able. For I do not think that such evils have been displayed by the saints who are there, or by those belonging to that Church, so that they would neglect the Lord’s command to such an extent, [Col. 0601A] especially since the Apostle wrote to the Philippians, thanking them because they had sent supplies to him both once and twice at Thessalonica, where he also adds: ‘I have received everything, and I abound.’

“If holy Peter thus refreshes strangers there—that is, at Rome—what shall we say of ourselves, who are his own servants and served him at least for a moment, and who now remain in such exile and affliction?

“I have also informed your charity of certain supplies that ought to be obtained there. I ask you, as is your custom, to take care of purchasing and sending them to us because of our many necessities and frequent illnesses.”

Copy of another letter.

[Col. 0601B]

“We always desire to console your charity by our letters and relieve you from the anxiety you have concerning us, together with all the saints and our brothers who, for the Lord’s sake, care for us.

“Behold, even now I write to you about the things that constrain us. I speak the truth in the name of Christ our God. Removed from every worldly disturbance and delivered from our sins, behold, we have also been deprived of life itself.

“For all who dwell in this region are gentiles, and those known to live here have adopted gentile customs, possessing no charity at all—the very charity that human nature continually displays, even among barbarians, through frequent compassion toward one another.

“God knows that, except from the small boats that come from the regions of Romania”—as those who are here call them, referring to the regions of the Greeks as the regions of Pontus—[Col. 0601C] “I have not been able even once to purchase grain in this region for as much as one tremissis [Note: It is a tremissis, namely, one-third of a solidus.]. Nor have I been able to purchase any other kind of supply except, as stated, from the boats that rarely come here and depart laden with salt.

“Thus we were able to buy three or four modii for one coin up to the present month of September. Until now, however, we have not been able to buy from the new harvest except four modii for one coin.

“I have marveled, and still marvel, at the lack of discernment and compassion of all who once belonged to me, and of my friends and relatives, because they have so completely forgotten my misfortune and, as I find, do not even wish to know whether I am still upon the earth or not.

“I have marveled still more at those who belong to the most holy Church of the apostle Peter, because they have taken such care regarding their own body and member—that is, concerning our love—in order to leave us without anxiety, at least regarding bodily necessities and daily expense.

“For even if the Church of Saint Peter does not possess gold, by God’s grace it does not lack grain, wine, and other necessities, so that they could have taken care to provide at least a modest contribution.

“What conscience do you think we shall have when we appear before Christ’s tribunal, with all those people then accusing and giving an account—people who are formed from the same clay and substance? What terror has fallen upon human beings, so that they do not carry out God’s commands, or what fear is there where there is no fear? Are evil spirits covering us to such an extent by their withdrawal? Have I appeared so hostile to the Church’s fullness and so adversarial to them?

“Nevertheless, may God, who desires all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, through the intercessions of Saint Peter establish their hearts in the orthodox faith, strengthen them against every heretical and adversarial person opposed to our Church, and keep them immovable—especially the shepherd who is now shown to preside over them—so that, in no respect falling away, deviating, or abandoning even the least of what they have confessed in writing before the Lord and his holy angels, they may, together with my humility, receive from the hand of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ the crown of the righteousness of orthodox faith.

“As for this humble body of mine, the Lord himself will care for it as he pleases to govern it, whether amid unceasing tribulations or in a little relief. The Lord is near, and why should I be anxious? I hope in his mercies that he will not delay in bringing my course to its end, wherever he has commanded.

“Greet all your countrymen for the Lord’s sake, and all who, for the love of God, have had compassion on my chains. May the Most High God protect you with his powerful hand from every temptation and save you into his kingdom.”

Behold, then, what was written by the most blessed apostolic man to his beloved.

Therefore, at least now, when we have been admonished by his holiness, let each of us who love the Lord and are zealous for his saints—those who remained in the catholic faith to the point of death—hasten to refresh him in some measure and have compassion on him, ministering to him from what the Lord has given each of us, so that we too may become sharers in his glory in the Lord.

I do not say this because he was our chief priest, but because he offered to Christ God, in your church, the unbloody sacrifice for the salvation of our souls and so greatly enlightened the people, becoming a confessor and preacher of the truth.

I believe that even irrational animals ought to have understood—and how much more you, rational and discerning people—that everything done against him was done because of his true faith and his rejection of the heretics. This is evident from nothing else than the fact that his adversaries, persisting obstinately, could in no way be bent or converted to the light of truth, but afflicted with still greater hardships and tribulations those around the monk Anastasius, who for a long time has been dragged and tormented from place to place here because of Christ—from guardhouse to guardhouse and from exile to exile. They treated the lord Maximus and his disciple in the same way.

Are these men rebels as well?

Concerning Pyrrhus, it should be known that after they were informed by the thrice-blessed apostolic man and by Plato that he had composed his libellus voluntarily, they installed him on this throne—although God, by his just judgment, immediately erased him from the book of the living.

Likewise, as we have learned, the new bishop called Pyrrhus and his predecessors blessed Fathers and saints. Therefore, beloved, knowing that we have a terrible Judge who will come to judge our thoughts and actions and inquire into his true faith, let us hold fast with much patience to the strong and stable wisdom that we have received in the Lord. Let each of us also refresh our holy Fathers, at least as one of the needy, according to our means, and console their tribulations.

These things, then, have been said concerning the most holy apostolic servant of Christ our God. For the rest, I have thought it necessary also to inform your charity about our Fathers, honored and illumined by God, and his fellow champions.

## Account of the proceedings concerning Saint Maximus

[Col. 0603]

### Explanation of the proceedings that took place between the lord abba Maximus and those with him, and the officials and the Secretariat

[Col. 0603A]

On the day when the lord Maximus and those with him had moored at this imperial city, two officers, accompanied by ten members of the excubitors, came around sunset. They lifted them from the ship naked and barefoot. Separating them from one another, they guarded them in different excubita. After some days they brought them into the palace and led the old man into the place where the senate and a large crowd had assembled. They made him stand in the midst of the seated officials.

The sacellarius said to him with great anger and madness: “Are you a Christian?”

He replied: “By the grace of Christ, the God of all, I am a Christian.”

The other said: “That is not true.”

The servant of God replied: “You say that I am not; but God says that I am and remain a Christian.”

“And how,” he said, “if you are a Christian, do you hate the emperor?”

The servant of God answered: “And from what is that evident? Hatred is a hidden disposition of the soul, just as love is.”

He said to him: “From what you have done, it has become manifest to everyone that you hate the emperor and his government. For you alone handed Egypt, Alexandria, Pentapolis, Tripoli, and Africa over to the Saracens.”

“And what proof of these things is there?” he asked.

They brought forward John, formerly the sacellarius of Peter, who had been commander of Numidia in Africa, saying that twenty-two years earlier the grandfather of the sovereign had ordered the blessed Peter to take an army and go to Egypt against the Saracens. He had written to you as one speaking to a servant of God, having confidence in you as a holy man, asking whether you advised him to go.

You replied in writing, saying that he should do nothing of the sort, since God did not approve that, under the reign of Heraclius and his dynasty, the Roman state should cooperate.

The servant of God said: “If he is telling the truth, surely he possesses both Peter’s letter to me and my letter to him. Let them be produced, and I will submit to the penalties prescribed by the law.”

He said: “I do not have a letter, nor do I know whether he wrote to you at all. But everyone in the army was saying these things about him at that time.”

The servant of God said to him: “If the entire army was saying this, how can you alone accuse me concerning it? Have you ever seen me, or I you?”

He replied: “Never.”

Then the servant of God turned toward the senate and said: “Judge whether it is just to bring forward such men as accusers or witnesses: ‘With whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you,’ says the God of all.” [Col. 0604D]

[Col. 0605A]

After him they brought forward Sergius Magoudas, who said:

“Nine years ago the blessed abba Thomas, having come from Rome, told me that Pope Theodore had sent him to the patrician Gregory to tell him not to fear anyone. For the servant of God, abba Maximus, had seen a dream: in the heavens, toward east and west, there were companies of angels. Those toward the east cried: ‘Constantine Augustus, may you conquer!’ Those toward the west shouted: ‘Gregory Augustus, may you conquer!’ The voice of those toward the west prevailed over the voice of those toward the east.”

Then the sacellarius cried out: “God sent you to be burned in this city!”

The servant of God said: “I give thanks to God, who purifies me of voluntary evils through involuntary punishment. ‘But woe to the world because of scandals! For scandals must come, but woe to the one through whom the scandal comes.’”

“Surely such things ought not to have been spoken in the presence of Christians, nor should those who do such things to please human beings—who exist today and tomorrow do not—remain unpunished. While Gregory was alive, this man ought to have said these things and made known to the emperor his good will toward him. It is just, if it seems so to you also, that the former slanderer be compelled to come forward: the patrician Peter, this abba Thomas, and that blessed Pope Theodore.”

Then, in the presence of everyone, I would say to the patrician Peter: “Tell me, my lord patrician: did you ever write to me about what your sacellarius has said, or did I write to you?” And, when he testified, I would submit to punishment.

Likewise I would say to the blessed pope: “Tell me, my lord: did I ever recount a dream to you?” And, if he exposed me, the fault would be his, not mine, who had seen it. A dream is an involuntary matter; the law punishes only voluntary acts, if indeed they oppose it.”

Then Troilus said to him: “You are joking, abba; do you not know where you are?”

He replied: “I am not joking, but mourning over my life, preserved until now so that I might experience such phantoms.”

The patrician Epiphanius said: “God knows that he is right to treat these things as a joke, if they are not true.”

At this the sacellarius again said to him angrily: “Are all of them simply lying, and you alone telling the truth?”

The servant of God replied, with tears accompanying his words: “You have authority, with God’s permission, both to give life and to put to death. But if these men speak the truth, then Satan too is God by nature. If he is not—as indeed he is not—then neither have these men spoken the truth.” [Col. 0605D]

“May I never be deemed worthy, together with Christians, to behold the manifestation of the transcendent God, maker, creator, providential governor, judge, and Savior of all, if I ever recounted such a dream or heard another recount it, unless I do so now before the lord Sergius, the one favorable to the empire.”

Next they brought forward a third slanderer, Theodore, son of John called the candidatus, nicknamed Chilas, now the son-in-law of the lord Plato the patrician. He said that, when a conversation had taken place between us at Rome concerning the emperor, he had reported what was being said, making “buckets and little boats” [the exact sense of these colloquial terms is uncertain].

The servant of God said to him: “I never spoke with you except once, in the presence of the most reverend elder, the lord Theoc haristus, brother of the Exarch, when I had been prompted by written instructions concerning the primicerius. If I am found to be lying, let me suffer the consequences.” [Col. 0607A]

After him they brought a fourth man, Gregory, son of Photinus, who said:

“I went to the cell of abba Maximus in Rome, and when I said that the emperor was also a priest, the abba’s disciple Anastasius said: ‘May he not be deemed worthy to be a priest.’”

Immediately the servant of God said to him: “Fear God, lord Gregory. My fellow servant said absolutely nothing in the discussion concerning these matters.”

He threw himself upon the ground, saying to the senate: “Bear with your servant, and I will tell everything as it was said; he will convict me if I lie.”

“My lord Gregory, having come to Rome, deemed it worthy to come to the cell of your servant. When I saw him, as is my custom, I threw myself upon the ground, bowed before him, and greeted him. After he had sat down, I said to him: ‘What is the reason for my lord’s desired visit?’

“He said: ‘Our good and God-supported sovereign, caring for the peace of the holy churches of God, has issued an order to the God-honored pope, sending an offering also to Saint Peter and urging him to unite with the president of Constantinople. His pious authority has deemed it fitting that these things be sent through my humility.’

“I said: ‘Glory to God, who has made you worthy of such a ministry. But tell me again, if you know: in what manner has his God-crowned Serenity commanded that the union be effected?’ You said: ‘By the Typos.’

“I said: ‘This seems impossible. For the Romans do not tolerate that the light-bearing words of the holy Fathers be destroyed together with the words of impure heretics, or that truth be extinguished together with falsehood, or light disappear together with darkness. For nothing that we worship will remain if the God-taught words are abolished.’

“You said: ‘The Typos does not abolish the sacred words, but commands silence, so that we may arrange peace.’

“I said: ‘In divine Scripture there is both silence and abolition. For God said through David: “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard.” Therefore, if the words concerning God are neither spoken nor heard, according to Scripture they do not exist at all.’

“You said: ‘Do not drag me into arguments; I am content with the holy Creed.’

“I said: ‘How can you be content with the holy Creed while accepting the Typos?’

“You said: ‘What harm is there in accepting the Typos and reciting the Creed?’

“I said: ‘I say that the Typos plainly abolishes the Creed.’

“You said: ‘For the Lord’s sake, how?’

“I said: ‘Tell me the Creed, and learn how it is abolished by the Typos.’

“You began to say: ‘I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.’

“I said: ‘Wait a little and learn how the faith of Nicaea is denied. God could not be Creator if he were deprived of natural will and activity, since he made heaven and earth by willing, not by compulsion, if David speaks truth in the Spirit: “All that the Lord willed, he made in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the abysses.”’ [Col. 0609A]

“But if, for the sake of an arrangement, the saving faith is abolished together with unbelief, such an arrangement is complete separation from God, not union with God.

“For tomorrow the ill-named Jews too might say: ‘Let us arrange peace with one another and be united. Let us remove circumcision, and you remove baptism, and let us no longer fight one another.’ The Arians once proposed this in writing under the great Constantine, saying: ‘Let us remove homoousion and heteroousion, and let the churches be united.’ Our God-bearing Fathers did not accept this. Rather, they chose to be persecuted and to die than to silence the word that expresses the one transcendent Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—even though the great Constantine joined in censuring those who proposed such things, as many have recorded who carefully wrote what happened then. [Col. 0609B]

“No emperor was able by ambiguous words to persuade the God-bearing Fathers to compromise with the heretics. Instead, they used clear, authoritative, and appropriate expressions concerning the doctrine at issue, saying plainly that it belongs to priests to inquire into and define the saving doctrines of the catholic Church.”

“You said: ‘What then? Is not every emperor a Christian and a priest?’

“I said: ‘He is not. For he does not stand before the altar and, after the consecration of the bread, lift it up saying, “The holy things for the holy.” He neither baptizes nor performs the rite of chrism, nor lays on hands and appoints bishops, priests, and deacons, nor consecrates churches. Nor does he wear the symbols of priesthood—the omophorion and the Gospel—as he wears the symbols of kingship, the crown and the purple robe.’ [Col. 0609C]

“You said: ‘How then does Scripture say that Melchizedek was king and priest?’

“I said: ‘Since the one who is by nature King, the God of all, became by nature, for our salvation, high priest, Melchizedek was a single type of him.’

“If you say that, according to the order of Melchizedek, there is another who is king and priest, dare to say the rest also: ‘Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life.’ And consider the evil that follows from this. Another God will be found, one who became human according to the order of Melchizedek, but not according to the order of Aaron, by which he performs our salvation.”

“But why should we proceed at length? In the holy anaphora at the holy table, after the high priests, priests, deacons, and every priestly order, the emperors are commemorated together with the laity, when the deacon says: ‘And for the laity who have fallen asleep in the faith, Constantine, Constans, and the rest.’ In the same way, the living emperors are commemorated after all those ordained.” [Col. 0609D]

While he was saying these things, Menas cried out: “By saying this you have divided the Church!”

He said to him: “If the one who speaks the things of the holy Scriptures and the holy Fathers divides the Church, what will be shown to the Church by the one who abolishes the doctrines of the saints, without which it is impossible even for this to be called a Church?”

Then the sacellarius turned and shouted to the men of the Exarch: “Tell the Exarch: ought you to have allowed such a man to live where you rule?”

They took him outside and brought in the disciple. When they demanded that he accuse his superior as one who had afflicted Pyrrhus, he replied calmly with the words of truth: “No one honored Pyrrhus as my superior honored him.” [Note: The text has additionally, “my superior”; immediately afterward: “Command him.”]

When he refused to be deprived of the reverent speech proper to monks, the order was given that he be beaten by those standing nearby. They struck him with their fists and left him half dead.

After releasing them to their quarters, Menas approached the old man in the presence of the officials and said: “God cast you down and brought you here so that you might receive what you did to others, deceiving everyone with the doctrines of Origen.”

The servant of God said in the presence of all: “Anathema to Origen, to his doctrines, and to every associate of his.”

The patrician Epiphanius said: “The accusation you brought against him, lord abba Menas, has been dissolved. Even if he had been an Origenist, by anathematizing him he has freed himself from such a charge. I no longer accept anything of this kind being said about him.”

Each of them was then taken back to the place where he was being guarded.

On the same day, at about the same lighting of the lamp, the patrician Troilus and Sergius the temperate, who was in charge of the imperial table, came to the servant of God, the old man. They sat down, ordered him also to sit, and said to him:

“Tell us, lord abba, the dispute that took place between you and Pyrrhus in Africa and Rome concerning the doctrines, and by what arguments you persuaded him to anathematize his own doctrine and agree with yours.”

He recounted to them everything in order, as much as memory restored, and said this:

“I have no doctrine of my own, but the common doctrine of the catholic Church. For I did not utter any word so that it might be called my own doctrine.”

After the account they said to him: “Do you not communicate with the throne of Constantinople?”

He said: “I do not communicate.”

“Why do you not communicate?” they asked.

He replied: “Because they expelled the four holy councils through the nine chapters produced at Alexandria, through the Ekthesis produced in this city by Sergius, and, consequently, through the Typos issued recently in the sixth indiction. What they defined through the chapters, they condemned through the Ekthesis; what they defined through the Ekthesis, they invalidated through the Typos; and so many times they condemned themselves. Those who have thus been condemned by themselves, by the Romans, and deposed by the council subsequently held in the eighth indiction—what holy rite can they perform? What Spirit descends upon what is performed by such men?” [Col. 0611D]

They said to him: “Are you alone being saved, and are all the others perishing?”

He said: “The Three Children did not condemn anyone when they refused to worship the image, though all other human beings were worshiping it. They did not consider what others were doing, but considered how they themselves might not fall away from true piety. So too Daniel, when he was thrown into the lions’ den, did not condemn any of those who failed to pray to God according to Darius’s decree; he considered his own conduct. [Col. 0613A] He chose to die rather than offend God and be scourged by his own conscience for violating what is lawful by nature. May God likewise not permit me to condemn anyone or say that I alone am saved. I choose rather to die than to have an agitated conscience because I have in any way gone astray concerning faith in God.”

They said to him: “What will you do if the Romans unite with the Byzantines? For yesterday the Roman representatives arrived, and tomorrow, on Sunday, they will communicate with the patriarch; it will become clear to everyone that you have led the Romans astray. Indeed, as soon as you were removed from there, they agreed with those here.”

He said to them: “Those who have come with whatever preliminary authorization from the throne of Rome—even if they communicate—do not do so unless they have brought a letter to the patriarch. And I certainly do not believe that the Romans will unite with those here unless they confess that our Lord and God is, according to each of the natures from which he is, and in which and as which he exists, naturally endowed with will and activity for our salvation.”

They said: “But if the Romans compromise with those here, what will you do?”

He said: “The Holy Spirit, through the Apostle, anathematizes angels who establish anything contrary to the proclamation.”

They said: “Is it absolutely necessary that wills and activities be spoken of with respect to Christ?”

He replied: “It is absolutely necessary, if we wish to be truly pious. For nothing that exists subsists without natural activity. The holy Fathers plainly say that no nature whatsoever exists or can be known apart from its own essential activity. If a nature neither exists nor is known without the activity that essentially characterizes it, how can it be possible for Christ to exist or to be known truly as God by nature and as human being, without divine and human activity? For, according to the Fathers, when a lion has lost its roaring it is no longer a lion, and a dog without barking is no longer a dog; likewise, anything that has lost whatever constitutes it naturally is no longer what it was.”

They said to him: “We know that this is indeed so. But do not grieve the emperor, who made the Typos solely for the sake of peace, not to abolish anything understood concerning Christ, but to arrange silence concerning the words that produce division.”

The servant of God threw himself upon the ground with tears and said: “The good and pious sovereign ought not to be grieved by my humiliation. I cannot grieve God by remaining silent about what he himself commanded to be spoken and confessed. For if, according to the divine Apostle, he is the one who established in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, it is clear that he himself spoke through them. Throughout all holy Scripture, both the Old and the New Testament, and through the holy teachers and councils, we are taught that the incarnate God possesses will and activity in both divinity and humanity. For he is not lacking, apart from sin, in anything by which he is known as God or in anything by which he is recognized by nature as human. If he is perfect in both respects, lacking nothing in either, then plainly the whole mystery concerning him is falsified by anyone who does not confess him to be what he is, together with all the natural properties belonging to him in each respect, in and as what he is.” [Col. 0615A]

After remaining silent for a little while and signaling to one another, they said: “From where can you show that the thrones of Constantinople expel the councils?”

He said to them: “This has already been shown in part through what I said at Rome to the lord Gregory, the asēkrētis. And now, if it seems good to the sovereign that this be demonstrated, let him order permission to be given to your unworthy servant, and I will produce the books and make it known that mine were removed, making this plain to everyone without any crookedness of words.”

After many other matters had been discussed, they turned to scriptural, natural, and technical exercises and investigations. Pleased by these, they became more cheerful and began to say: “The Lord knows that we have benefited, and from now on we have no further reason to trouble you.”

The lord Sergius said to him: “I often came to your cell at Bebbas and listened to your teaching, and Christ will help you; do not be anxious. But you grieve everyone in one respect: you cause many to separate themselves from communion with the Church here.”

“Is there anyone,” said the servant of God, [Col. 0615C] “who says that I have said: ‘Do not communicate with the Church of the Byzantines’?”

The lord Sergius replied: “Your very refusal to communicate is a great statement to everyone that they should not communicate.”

The servant of God said: “Nothing is more forceful than an accusing conscience, and nothing more outspoken than a conscience that does not support the accusation.”

When the lord Troilus heard that the Typos was anathematized throughout the West, he said to the servant of God: “Is it a good thing that the reputation of our pious sovereign is insulted?”

The servant of God replied: “May God forgive those who compelled the sovereign to make the Typos and those who consented to it.”

He said: “Who are those who compelled him, and who are those who consented?”

He replied: “Those who drove it out from the Church, and the officials who consented.”

“Behold,” he continued, “the filth has been shaken from those responsible onto the innocent man, pure of every heresy. But advise him to do what his pious grandfather did when he was alive. For when he learned that certain people in the West were pouring reproach upon him, he freed himself by an official declaration from the charge against the Church, writing:

“‘The Ekthesis is not mine; I neither dictated it nor ordered that it be made. Rather, the patriarch Sergius composed it five years before I came up from the East and, while I was in the most blessed city, asked me to place it under my name with my subscription. I accepted his request. But now, learning that certain people are disputing over it, I make it clear to all that it is not mine.’

“He issued this order to the blessed Pope John, condemning the Ekthesis in the documents then written to Pyrrhus. From that time Sergius has everywhere been represented as the author of the Ekthesis.

“Our present pious emperor should do the same, and his reputation will remain entirely unstained by every accusation.”

Then they shook their heads and fell silent, saying only this: “Everything is difficult and impossible.”

After many other matters of various kinds had been discussed, they exchanged bows and withdrew in complete good humor.

On the following Saturday they brought them again into the palace. They first brought in the old man’s disciple, while the two patriarchs also assembled. They brought Constantine and Menas as accusers of the old man and demanded that the disciple agree with what was being said against them.

With complete frankness the disciple said fearlessly to the senate:

“Are you bringing Constantine into the secretariat of the palace? He is neither a presbyter nor a monk, but a theatrical tribune. He became known to Africans and Romans for the woman whom he was keeping when he came there. Everyone learned his schemes, which he practiced in order to remain hidden: sometimes saying that they were his sisters, and sometimes saying that, because they did not communicate with the Church of Constantinople, he had taken them up so that they would not be defiled by heretical communion. But whenever he lacks money and finds a place that does not know him, he does the same things, for the sake of shameful gain and filthy pleasure. It is a great disgrace even to meet him for those who wish to live decently.”

After this, when he was asked whether he had anathematized the Typos, he said fearlessly: “I not only anathematized it, but also composed a libellus.”

The officials said to him: “Then do you not admit that you acted wrongly?”

He said: “May God forbid that I should say that what I did rightly, according to ecclesiastical ordinance, was done wrongly.”

After being asked many other questions and answering as God granted him, he was taken out of the secretariat.

Then they brought in the old man, and the lord Troilus said to him:

“Speak, abba. Look to it; tell the truth, and the sovereign will have mercy on you. If we proceed according to the legal account and find even one of the charges brought against you to be true, the law will put you to death.”

He said: “I have already said, and I say again, that if only one of these things is said to be true, then Satan is God. But if he is not God, but an apostate—as indeed he is not God—then the charges brought against me are false and without substance. Nevertheless, if you command anything to be done, do it. Since I fear God, I am not wronged.”

He said to him: “Did you not anathematize the Typos?”

He replied: “I have often said that I anathematized it.”

He said to him: “You anathematized the Typos? You anathematized the emperor.”

The servant of God replied: “I did not anathematize the emperor, but a document foreign to the orthodox and ecclesiastical faith.”

He said to him: “Where was it anathematized by the council of Rome?”

He replied: “In the Church of the Savior and in the Church of the Mother of God.”

Then the prefect said to him: “Do you communicate with the Church here, or do you not communicate?”

He replied: “I do not communicate.”

“Why?” he asked.

He replied: “Because it cast out the councils.”
