He said: “If it cast out the councils, how are they mentioned in the diptychs?”

He said: “What benefit is there in names when the doctrines have been expelled?”

He said: “Can you demonstrate this?”

He replied: “If I receive permission and you command it, I can demonstrate it very easily.”

When they fell silent, the sacellarius said to him: “Why do you love the Romans and hate the Greeks?”

The servant of God replied: “We have been commanded not to hate anyone. I love the Romans as people of the same faith, and the Greeks as people of the same language.”

Again the sacellarius said to him: “How many years do you say you have lived?”

He replied: “Ninety.”

He said to him: “How many years has your disciple been with you?”

He replied: “Thirty-seven.”

Then one of the clerics cried out: “The Lord has repaid you for everything you did to the blessed Pyrrhus.”

He gave him no answer at all.

[Col. 0619B]

After so much had been said in the secretariat, none of the patriarchs uttered a word. When the discussion turned to the council of Rome, Demosthenes cried out:

“The council has not been ratified, since the one who convened it has been deposed.”

The servant of God said: “He was not deposed, but persecuted. What conciliar and canonical act, securely establishing his deposition, was ever issued concerning what was done? But even if he was canonically deposed, that does not invalidate the matters ratified in orthodox fashion according to the divine canons, with which the writings of the holy Pope Theodore also agree.”

When he heard this, the patrician Troilus said: “You do not know what you are saying, abba. What has happened has happened.”

[Col. 0619C]

These are the matters that memory preserves, the things that were discussed and said. The proceedings against them reached this conclusion: they released the holy old man from the secretariat into custody.

On the following day, which was Sunday, the members of the Church held a council and persuaded the emperor to condemn them to this bitter and inhuman exile, separating them from one another: the holy old man to the fortress of Bizya in Thrace, and his disciple to Perberis, beyond which the Roman empire has no farther place for a foot to stand. They were left without provision, naked, unfed, deprived of every means of sustaining life, and kept away from the sea so that they would not receive visits from those who might show them mercy.

Thus they are naked and unfed, possessing only hope in God, and exhorting all Christians, crying out:

“Pray for the Lord’s sake that God may complete his mercy together with our humiliation and teach us.”

For those sailing with him undergo an experience of a storm-tossed sea: the vessel is shaken by winds and waves, yet remains unshaken. He permits them to be tested by a great disturbance, testing their disposition toward him, so that they may cry out with a loud voice: “Lord, save us; we are perishing!” and learn to ascribe to him alone everything concerning their salvation.

And when they no longer trust in themselves, they obtain a great calm, the wind and the waves having been quieted. He sends them into the midst of wolves and commands them to enter through the narrow gate and travel along the constricted path. He sets before them hunger and thirst, nakedness, bonds, prisons, deportations, scourges, the cross, nails, vinegar, gall, spitting, blows, buffeting, mockery, suffering, and deaths of many kinds.

Their end is the all-radiant resurrection, bringing peace to those persecuted for his sake, joy to those afflicted for his sake, ascent into the heavens, approach to the princely and transcendent throne, and a portion above every principality, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, whether in this age or in the age to come.

May we all attain it through the prayers and intercessions of the all-praised, all-revered, and supremely glorious one who is truly by nature the Mother of God and ever-virgin, Mary, and of the holy apostles, prophets, and martyrs. Amen.

### Account of the proceedings that took place between the lord Maximus the monk and his companion, before the officials in the secretariat

[Col. 0604A]

On the day when the lord Maximus and the one who was with him arrived by ship near this imperial city, around sunset two officers came with ten excubitors. They took them from the ship naked and barefoot, separated them from one another, and guarded them in different excubita. After some days they brought them into the palace and introduced the old man into the place where the senate and a large crowd had assembled. They presented him in the midst of the seated officials.

The sacellarius said to him with great anger and fury: “Are you a Christian?”

He said: “By the grace of Christ, the God of all, I am a Christian.”

The other said: “That is not true.”

The servant of God replied: “You say that I am not, but God knows that I am a Christian.”

“And how,” he said, “if you are a Christian, do you hate the emperor?”

The servant of God replied: “And from what is this evident? Hatred is a hidden disposition of the mind, just as love is.”

He said to him: “From what you have done it has become manifest to everyone that you hate the emperor and his government. For you alone handed Egypt, Alexandria, Pentapolis, and Africa over to the Saracens.”

“And what proof of these things is there?” he asked.

They falsely brought forward John, who had been the sacellarius of Peter, formerly governor of the province of Numidia in Africa, saying that twenty-two years earlier the grandfather of the sovereign had ordered the blessed Peter to take an army and go to Egypt against the Saracens. He had written to you as one speaking to a servant of God, having confidence in you as a holy man, asking whether you advised him to go.

You replied in writing, saying that he should do nothing of the sort, since God did not approve that, under the reign of Heraclius and his dynasty, the Roman state should cooperate.

The servant of God said: “If he is speaking the truth, surely he has both Peter’s letter to me and my letter to him. Let them be produced, and I will submit to the penalties prescribed by the laws.”

He said: “I do not have a letter, nor do I know whether he wrote to you at all. But everyone in the army was saying these things about him at that time.”

The servant of God said to him: “If the entire army was saying this, how can you alone accuse me concerning it? Have you ever seen me, or I you?”

He replied: “Never.”

Then the servant of God turned toward the senate and said: “Judge whether it is just to bring forward such men as accusers or witnesses: ‘With whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you,’ says the Lord of all.” (Matthew 7.)

[Col. 0606A] After this they bring forward Sergius Magudas, saying:

“Nine years ago the blessed abba Thomas came to me at Rome and said: ‘Pope Theodore sent me to Gregory the patrician, to tell him that no one should be afraid. For the servant of God, abba Maximus, saw a vision: in heaven, toward the east and the west, there were choirs of angels.’ [Note: [Col. 0605] In Greek: ‘Those toward the east were crying out: “Constantine Augustus, may you conquer.” But those ...’ SIRM.] Those who were in the west were raising their voices, saying: ‘Gregory Augustus, may you conquer,’ and the voice of those in the west sounded louder than the voices of those in the east.”

Then the treasurer shouted: “God sent you so that you might be burned in this city.”

The servant of God said: “I give thanks to God, who cleanses me from voluntary evils through involuntary punishment. Nevertheless, woe to the world because of scandals. For it is necessary that scandals come; but woe to the one through whom the scandal comes” (Matthew 18:7).

“Truly, such things ought not to have been said in the presence of Christians, nor should those who invent such things to please men who exist today and are gone tomorrow remain unpunished. While Gregory was still alive, this man ought to have said these things; Gregory ought also to have made known to him his own devotion toward him. It would be just, if it seems so to you also, that the accuser who preceded this man should be compelled to depart, bringing the patrician Peter; this man, abba Thomas; and the latter, the blessed Pope Theodore. Then, in the presence of all, he should say to the patrician Peter: ‘Tell us, lord patrician: Did you ever write to me concerning what your treasurer said, or did I write to you?’ And when he had been convicted, I should submit to punishment. Likewise to the blessed pope: ‘Tell me, lord: Did I ever relate such a dream to you?’ And when he had convicted me, the crime would be his, not mine, since I had seen it. A dream is not a voluntary matter. Moreover, the law punishes only voluntary acts, provided that they have been directed against it.”

Then Troilus said to him: “You are joking, abba. Do you not know where you are?”

He replied: “I am not joking, but grieving that I have been preserved alive until now in order to undergo an experience of this kind of deception.”

Lord Epiphanius said: “God knows that he is doing well by deceiving them, if these things are not true.”

After this, the treasurer again said to him angrily: “Are all the others lying outright, and are you alone telling the truth?”

When the servant of God heard this, he replied with tears: “You have authority, with God’s permission, both to give life and to put to death. Nevertheless, if these men are telling the truth, then Satan is God by nature. But if he is not—as indeed he is not—then neither have these men spoken the truth. In short, may I not deserve to see with the Christians the coming of the superessential God—the maker, founder, creator, providential governor, judge, and savior of all—if I ever saw such a dream or heard it from anyone else, apart from this hour, from Lord Sergius, beloved of the empire.”

Then they put forward a third accuser, Theodore, son of John, formerly a candidate, surnamed Chila, who is now the son-in-law of Lord Plato the patrician. He said that, when a conversation had taken place between us at Rome concerning the empire, he had disparaged what was being said, muttering and making mocking gestures.

The servant of God said to him: [Col. 0608A] “I never disputed with you, except once, in the presence of the most holy presbyter Lord Theocharistus, brother of the exarch, because of the primicerius, having been ordered by letter to do so. If I am found to be lying, I shall accept the penalty.”

After him they bring forward a fourth, Gregory, son of Photinus, who says:

“I went to Rome, to the cell of abba Maximus, and when I said that the emperor was also a priest, abba Anastasius, his disciple, said: ‘He is not worthy to be a priest.’”

Immediately the servant of God said to him: “Fear God, Lord Gregory. My fellow servant did not say anything of this kind in such a discussion.”

When he had thrown himself upon the ground, he said to the senate: “Support your servant, and I will tell you everything exactly as it was said. Let him convict me if I have lied.” [Col. 0608B]

“This Lord Gregory of mine, when he came to Rome, deigned to come to the cell of your servant. When I saw him, as is my custom I threw myself upon the ground, worshiped him, kissed him, and after we had sat down said to him: ‘What is the reason for my lord’s welcome visit?’

“He replied: ‘Our good ruler, strengthened by God and concerned for the peace of the holy Churches of God, issued an order to the divinely honored pope. He also sent an offering to Saint Peter and urged him to unite himself with the bishop of Constantinople. His pious imperial power has deigned to send this through my humble agency.’

“I said: ‘Glory to God, who has deemed you worthy of such a ministry. Nevertheless, if you know, under what terms did his tranquility, crowned by God, order the union to be made?’

“You said: ‘Under the Typos.’

“I said: ‘In my opinion, this is impossible. For the Romans will not tolerate the removal, together with the impure voices of heretics, of the radiant voices of the holy Fathers; nor will they tolerate truth being extinguished together with falsehood, or light being dispersed together with darkness. If the removal of the words divinely proclaimed has taken place, we will have nothing left to worship.’

“You said: ‘The Typos does not produce the removal of the sacred words, but silence, so that we may arrange peace.’

“I said: ‘In divine Scripture, silence is also a removal. For God said through David: “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard” (Psalm 18:3). Therefore, unless the words concerning God are spoken and heard, they do not exist at all according to Scripture.’

“You said: ‘Do not send me into the woods; I am content with the holy Creed.’

“I said: ‘How can you be content with the holy Creed while accepting the Typos?’

“You asserted: ‘What harm is there in accepting the Typos and reciting the Creed?’

“I replied: ‘Because the Typos clearly cuts the Creed to pieces.’

“You said: ‘How so, on account of the Lord?’

“I said: ‘Let us recite the Creed, and you will understand how it is mutilated by the Typos.’

“You began to say: ‘I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.’

“I said: ‘Pay attention for a little while and learn how the faith of those who assembled at Nicaea is denied. For the Maker would not be God, deprived of natural will and operation, if he made heaven and earth willingly and not under compulsion, if David speaks the truth in the Spirit, saying: “The Lord has made all things whatsoever he willed, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps” (Psalm 134). But if, under the pretext of an arrangement, the faith of salvation is removed together with the confession, God is wholly divided. Yet such a form of what is called arrangement is not unity.

“For tomorrow the impious Jews could say: ‘Let us arrange peace with one another; let us unite and cut ourselves off from one another’s practices: let us remove circumcision, and you remove baptism, and let us no longer attack one another.’ The Arians once made the same proposal in writings under Constantine the Great, saying: ‘Let us remove the expression “of one substance” and the expression “of another substance,” and let the Churches be united.’

“But our God-bearing Fathers did not accept this. Instead, they chose to suffer persecution and die rather than silence the voice affirming the one superessential deity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Constantine the Great restrained those who were making these proposals, as is reported by many who carefully recorded what happened at that time. None of the emperors was able, by equivocal expressions, to persuade the God-speaking Fathers to agree with what those men were pursuing. Rather, they used explicit and proper expressions appropriate to the doctrine in question, clearly saying that it belongs to priests to investigate and define the saving doctrines of the catholic Church.’

“You said: ‘Then is not every Christian emperor also a priest?’

“I said: ‘He is not. For he does not stand at the altar, nor, after the sanctification of the bread, lift it up and say: “Holy things for the holy.” He does not baptize, perform the preparation of chrism, make bishops, presbyters, or deacons, anoint churches, or bear the insignia of priesthood—namely, the vestment and the Gospel—as he bears the imperial crown and purple.’

“You said: ‘Then how does Scripture say that Melchizedek was both king and priest?’

“I said: ‘Melchizedek was a single type of the King of all, God, who by nature also became high priest for our salvation. But if, according to the order of Melchizedek, you say that another is king and priest, then go on and say the rest as well: “without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life” (Hebrews 7).

“Observe what evil may arise from this. Another such one will be found, God incarnate according to the order of Melchizedek, accomplishing our salvation not according to the order of Aaron.’”

Nevertheless, why should we go through many examples? [Col. 0610D] In the sacred offerings upon the holy table, after the bishops, priests, deacons, and the entire consecrated order, emperors are commemorated together with the laity, when the deacon says: “And those of the laity who have fallen asleep in the faith: Constantine, Constans, and the others.” Likewise, the living emperors are commemorated after all the consecrated persons.

As he said this, Mennas shouted: “By saying these things you have divided the Church.”

He said to him: “If the one who says what belongs to the holy Scriptures and the holy Fathers divides the Church, what will be shown to be done to the Church by the one who removes the doctrines of the saints, without which it is not even possible to call it the Church?”

The treasurer turned and shouted to the exarch’s men: “Tell the exarch: You ought to have allowed such a man to live where he presides.”

After they had led him outside, they brought in the disciple. They demanded that he speak against his master, saying that he had troubled Pyrrhus. He replied in a calm voice with what was true: “No one honored Pyrrhus as my master honored him, and you order me to shout?”

Because he did not tolerate departing from the reverent voice proper to monks, he was ordered to be beaten by those standing nearby. They struck him with their fists and left him half-dead.

After these men had been taken away to the prisons, he came to the old man Mennas and said in the presence of the rulers: “God sent you and brought you here so that you might receive whatever you did to others when you led everyone astray into the doctrines of Origen.”

In the presence of all, the servant of God said to him: “Anathema to Origen, to his doctrines, and to every associate of his!”

The patrician Epiphanius said: “Lord abba Menna, the complaint brought by you against him has been destroyed. Even if he were an Origenist, by anathematizing Origen he has freed himself from such a charge. Therefore I will not admit such a statement against him any further.”

Each of them was then led into the place where he was being held.

On the same day, around the lighting of the lamp [Note: [Col. 0612D] that is, its kindling], the patrician Troilus and Sergius Eucratas, who was in charge of the imperial table, came to the elderly servant of God. They sat down and ordered him also to sit, and said to him:

“Tell us, Lord abba, the development of the doctrines discussed between you and Pyrrhus at Rome and in Africa, and by what words you persuaded him to anathematize his own doctrine and make an agreement with yours.”

He related to them in order everything that his memory was able to retain. He added this:

“I do not have a doctrine of my own, but the common doctrine of the catholic Church. For I have not uttered any word so that it might be called my own doctrine.”

After the whole account, they said to him: “Do you not communicate with the see of Constantinople?”

He said: “I do not communicate.”

“Why do you not communicate?” they asked.

He replied: “Because the four holy councils have cast it out through the Nine Chapters composed at Alexandria, through the Ecthesis produced in this city by Sergius, and through the Typos recently published—that is, in the sixth indiction. For what they defined through the Nine Chapters they condemned through the Ecthesis, and what they defined through the Ecthesis they declared invalid through the Typos; thus they have deposed themselves so many times. Those, therefore, who have been condemned by themselves and deposed and stripped of priesthood by the Romans and by the synod held afterward in the eighth indiction—what mysteries, I ask, do they celebrate? Or what kind of spirit comes to what is celebrated by such men?”

They said to him: “So you alone will be saved, and everyone else will perish?”

He said: “The three youths, by not worshiping the image, did not condemn anyone, though all people worshiped it. They did not concern themselves with what belonged to others, but with not falling away themselves from true piety. Likewise Daniel, when he was cast into the lions’ den, did not condemn any of those who did not worship God according to Darius’s decree; he concerned himself with what was his own, and chose to die rather than fall away from God and have his conscience scourged by transgressing what is lawful by nature.

“May God not grant me to condemn anyone or to say that I alone will be saved! As far as I am able, I choose to die rather than have the terror in my conscience that I have in any way erred in the faith that is directed toward God.”

They said to him: “What will you do when the Romans have become united with the Byzantines? For yesterday the Roman apocrisiarii arrived, and tomorrow, on the Lord’s Day, they will communicate with the patriarch. Thus it becomes clear to everyone that you are subverting the Romans. Indeed, once you had been removed from there, they immediately agreed with those here.”

He said to them: [Col. 0614B] “Those who came do not in any way prejudice the Roman see, even if they communicate, since they have not brought a letter to the patriarch. And I do not believe that the Romans will ever unite with these men unless they confess that our Lord and God is what he is according to both of that from which he is and that which he is, and that he possesses a naturally voluntary and operative capacity for our salvation.”

They said: “But if the Romans are joined to these men, what will you do?”

He said: “The Holy Spirit anathematizes even angels when they innovate beyond what has been proclaimed.”

They said: “Then is it indeed necessary to speak of wills and operations in Christ?”

He replied: “It is wholly necessary, if we truly wish to think piously. For nothing that exists subsists without natural operation. The holy Fathers plainly say that nothing exists or can be known without a substantial operation [Note: [Col. 0613D] The translator omitted the following; supply: ‘any nature whatsoever.’ ‘But if nature neither exists nor is known without an operation that substantially characterizes it ...’ SIRM.], which substantially characterizes it. How, then, is it possible for Christ to exist, or for God by nature and man to be truly recognized? For, according to the holy Fathers, once the quality of roaring has been removed, a lion is no longer a lion; and once the quality of barking has been removed, a dog is no longer a dog. When anything whatsoever that naturally establishes it has been removed, it is no longer what it was.”

They said to him: “We truly know that this is so. Nevertheless, do not grieve the emperor, who made the Typos solely for the sake of peace—not to remove anything understood to be in Christ, but, as an arrangement, to impose silence upon the expressions that were causing dissension, for the sake of peace.”

The servant of God threw himself upon the ground with tears and said: [Col. 0614D] “The benevolent and pious lord ought not to be grieved by my humility. For I cannot grieve God by remaining silent about what he himself commanded us to speak and confess. If, according to the most sacred Apostle, he is the one who first placed apostles in the Church, second prophets, and third teachers, it is clear that he is the one who spoke through them.

“Throughout the whole of holy Scripture, both the Old and the New Testament, and through the holy teachers and councils, we are taught that God incarnate possesses will and operation both in divinity and in humanity. [Col. 0616A] He is imperfect in none of the things by which he is known as God or of those by which his nature is recognized as man, except sin alone. If he is perfect in both, just as he is diminished in nothing belonging to either, then the one who does not confess him to be what he is plainly corrupts his entire mystery, since all his natural properties exist together with him—those from which, in which, and which he is shown to be.”

After they had been silent for a little while and had signaled to one another, they said: “How can you show that those who occupy the see of Constantinople reject the holy councils?”

He said to them: “This has already been shown in part by what I said at Rome to Lord Gregory the a secretis. Now, if it pleases the ruler that this be demonstrated, let him order that permission be given to your unworthy servant, and I will identify the books, since mine have been taken away. I will make this clear to everyone without any verbal distortion.”

After many other things had been said, they turned to exercises and discussions in the Scriptures, in nature, and in the arts. They were pleased and became more cheerful, and began to say: “The Lord knows, we have made progress, and from now on we will not trouble you.”

Lord Sergius said to him: “I have often come to your cell at Bellas and heard your teaching. God will help you; do not be anxious. But there is one thing alone by which you distress everyone: namely, that you cause many to separate themselves from communion with this Church.”

“Is there anyone,” said the servant of God, “who claims that I said: ‘Do not communicate with the Church of the Byzantines’?”

Lord Sergius replied: “This very fact—that you yourself do not communicate—is unquestionably, for everyone, a loud declaration that one should not communicate.”

The servant of God said: “Nothing is more certain than a conscience that accuses, and nothing gives greater confidence than the testimony it bears.”

When Lord Troilus heard that the Typos was being anathematized throughout the entire West, he said to the servant of God: “Is it good that the reputation of our pious ruler is being torn apart by insults?”

The servant of God replied: “May God forgive those who persuaded the ruler to make the Typos, and those who permitted it.”

He said: “Who are those who persuaded him, and who are those who permitted it?”

He replied: “Those who belonged to the Church persuaded him, and the rulers permitted it.” [Col. 0616D]

“And behold, the filth of the guilty has been shaken off onto an innocent man who is free from every heresy. But give him this advice: let him do what his grandfather of blessed memory once did. For when he learned that certain men in the West were speaking abusively against him, he freed himself from the Church’s complaint by a letter, writing:

“‘The Ecthesis,’ he said, ‘is not mine; for I neither composed it nor ordered that it be made. But when Sergius the patriarch had composed it five years earlier, before I returned from the East, he begged me, when I reached this blessed city, to have it published in my name with a subscription. I accepted his request. But now, having learned that some are disputing about it, I make it clear to everyone [Col. 0618A] that it is not mine.’”

He issued this order to the blessed Pope John, condemning the Ecthesis in what he then wrote to Pyrrhus. From that time onward, the Ecthesis has everywhere been said to belong to Sergius. Let the ruler who now governs us piously do the same, and his reputation will remain entirely untouched by every reproach.

Then they shook their heads and fell silent, saying only: “Everything is difficult and perplexing.”

After these and various other edicts, having been honored and honoring others, they departed in complete good humor.

Again, on another Saturday, they brought them into the palace and first brought in the old man’s disciple; at that time the two patriarchs were also present. They brought in Constantine and Menna, the old man’s accusers, and demanded that the disciple agree to what was said by them.

But the disciple boldly and fearlessly said to the senate: “Are you bringing Constantine into the palace secretariat? He is neither a presbyter nor a monk, but a theatrical tribune. It has become known to Africans and Romans what sort of women he supports and with what sort of character he came from there. Everyone has learned his tricks, which he practiced in order to remain hidden: now saying that they were his sisters, now asserting that he had removed them so that they might not communicate with the Church of Constantinople, lest they be polluted by heretical communion. But even if his meals should again run out and he should find a place that does not recognize him, he does the same thing for the sake of shameful gain and sordid pleasure. It is a great disgrace even to speak with him for those who wish to live religiously.”

Then, when asked whether he had anathematized the Typos, he fearlessly said: “I not only anathematized it, but also composed a written statement.”

The rulers said to him: “So you admit that you acted wrongly?”

He replied: “May God not grant that I should say that what I did well and according to the custom of the Church was not done well.”

After he had answered many questions according to what God had granted him, he was led out of the secretariat.

They brought in the old man, and Lord Troilus said to him: “Speak, abba; look, speak the truth, and the ruler will have mercy on you. For if we proceed to a legal inquiry and find even one true charge among those of which you are accused, the law will kill you.”

He said: “I have already spoken, and I say again: if even one of the things you say is true, then Satan is God. But if he is not God, rather an apostate, then the charges against me are false and have no foundation. Nevertheless, whatever you order me to do, do it. As one who worships God, I suffer no injustice.”

He said to him: “Did you not anathematize the Typos?”

He replied: “I have said many times that I anathematized it.”

He said to him: “You anathematized the Typos; you anathematized the emperor.”

The servant of God replied: “I did not anathematize the emperor, but a document alien to the faith of the Church.”

He said to him: “Where was he anathematized by the Roman synod?”

He replied: “In the church of the Savior and in that of the Mother of God.”

Then the prefect said to him: “Do you communicate with this Church, or do you not communicate?”

He replied: “I do not communicate.”

He said to him: “Why?”

He replied: “Because it has cast out the councils.”

He said: [Col. 0620A] “If it has cast out the councils, how are they recited in the diptychs?”

He replied: “What benefit is there from the recital of names when the doctrines have been cast out?”

He said: “Can you demonstrate this?”

He replied: “If I receive permission and you order it, this can be demonstrated very easily.”

While everyone was silent, the treasurer said to him: “Why do you love the Romans and hate the Greeks?”

The servant of God replied: “We have been commanded to hate no one. I love the Romans because they share the same faith with me; I love the Greeks because they speak the same language as I do.”

Again the treasurer said to him: “How many years do you say that you are?”

He replied: “Seventy-five.”

He said to him: “How many years has your disciple been with you?”

He replied: “Thirty-seven.”

Then one of the clerics cried out: “May God repay you for everything you did to the blessed Pyrrhus.”

He made no reply whatsoever.

Although so much had been said in the secretariat, none of the patriarchs uttered a word. When discussion arose concerning the Roman synod, Demosthenes shouted: “The synod is not valid, since the one who held it has been deposed.”

To this the servant of God replied: “He was not deposed, but expelled. For what action, carried out synodally and canonically in the sequence of the proceedings, contains a careful account of his deposition? Nevertheless, even if he had been canonically deposed, this would not prejudice what has been firmly established in accordance with the orthodox faith and the sacred rules. The things written by Pope Theodore of blessed memory also agree with these.”

After hearing this, Lord Troilus said: [Col. 0620C] “You do not know what you are saying, abba. What has happened has happened.”

These are, as far as memory retains them, the matters that were raised and spoken, and the proceedings against those men ended with such a conclusion. The holy old man was also dismissed from the secretariat to prison.

On the following day, which was the Lord’s Day, a council was held. Those who belonged to the Church persuaded the most pious emperor to condemn both men to a bitter and inhuman exile and to separate them from one another: the holy old man was to be held near Bysohe, a fortress in the province of Thrace; his disciple at Perberis, beyond which the Roman power does not extend even the length of a foot. They were to be naked, without provision, without cause, and deprived of every means of sustaining life; they were not to approach the sea, lest they receive visits from compassionate people. [Col. 0620D]

Thus they remain naked and without food, having only hope in God. They ask and proclaim this to all Christians:

“Pray for the Lord’s sake that God may complete his mercy through our humility and teach us.”

For those who sail with him also undergo the experience of the sea: the small boat is shaken by winds and waves, yet remains wholly stable. He allows them to be tested by great storms, proving their disposition toward him, so that they may cry out in a loud voice: “Lord, save us; we are perishing!” They learn to ascribe to him alone everything recognized as belonging to their salvation. He prevents them from trusting in themselves, and then grants them great calm when the winds and waves have subsided.

He commands them to be given over among wolves, to enter through the narrow gate and walk along the constricted path. He sets before them hunger and thirst, nakedness, chains, prisons, abductions, beatings, the cross, nails, vinegar, gall, spitting, slaps, blows, mockery, suffering, and deaths of many kinds. Their end is the most splendid resurrection, bringing peace to those who have suffered persecution for his sake, ascent into heaven, ascent to the paternal and consubstantial throne, and the portion that is above every principality, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, whether in this age or in the age to come.

May we all become sharers in this through the prayers and intercessions of the supremely praiseworthy, more venerable than all, glorious, truly and by nature Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and of the holy apostles, prophets, and martyrs. Amen.

## [Account of the discussion with the monk Anastasius]

[Col. 0621]

### Of the holy abba Maximus to Anastasius the monk

[Note: [Col. 0621] The Latin and Greek versions of the following section are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0621B]

Yesterday, on the eighteenth day of the month, which was the holy Pentecost, the patriarch declared to me:

“Of which Church are you: Constantinople, Rome, Antioch, Alexandria, or Jerusalem? Behold, all of them, together with the provinces subject to them, have been united. If, then, you belong to the catholic Church, unite yourself, lest by introducing an unfamiliar way into your life you suffer what you do not expect.”

I replied to them:

“God, who is God of all, declared the catholic Church to be the straight and saving confession of faith in him, when he blessed Peter for confessing him rightly. Nevertheless, let me learn the confession upon which the union of all the Churches has taken place, and I will not estrange myself from what has been rightly done.”

They said:

“Although we have no command concerning this, we say it so that you may become entirely without excuse. We confess two operations because of difference, and one because of union.”

I said: “Do you say that the two have become one because of the union, or, in addition to these, another?”

They replied: “No, but that the two are one because of the union.”

I said:

“We have been deprived of reality, fabricating for ourselves a faith without subsistence and a God without existence. For if we confuse the two into one because of the union, and again divide the one into two because of difference, there will be neither oneness nor twoness, since the operations are continually cancelling one another and making what they belong to inoperative and entirely without substance.

“For that which has no movement naturally incapable of being removed, altered, or brought to an end by any principle of change is, according to the Fathers, deprived of every substance, since it has no operation substantially characterizing it.

“I cannot say this. Nor have I been taught by the holy Fathers to confess it. Do what seems good to you, since you possess authority.”

“Then listen,” they said. “The ruler and the patriarch have decided, by order of the pope of Rome, that you should be anathematized if you do not obey, and that you should undergo the death they have decreed.”

I answered them, hearing this:

“May what was determined for me by God before every age reach its fulfillment, bringing him the glory known to him before every age.”

And so that you may know and add prayer and supplication to God, I have made clear to you what was announced to me, asking you to make these things known to Lord Theios and to our holy Fathers who are there with him, for the sake of the same matter.

### Anastasius

[Col. 0623]

[Col. 0623A] “He ordered me to transcribe this for you and make it known to you, most holy Fathers, so that, having learned from it the course of the discussion, you may all offer prayer to the Lord for our common mother, namely the catholic Church, and for us, your unworthy servants, to strengthen all of us—and us also, who persevere there with you—according to the orthodox faith piously proclaimed in her by the holy Fathers.

“For a great fear exists throughout the world, since she is suffering this persecution with unanimous opposition from all, unless he who always gives help in his accustomed manner grants assistance through his grace, leaving at least a seed of piety in elder Rome and confirming his promise to us—a promise that does not deceive us and that was made to the one who is regarded as prince of the apostles.”

### Of the same holy Anastasius the monk, disciple of the holy abba Maximus, to the common community of monks residing at Caralis

[Col. 0623B]

“Time prevented us from writing much, even beyond our intention. We make everything known to you, most holy Fathers, in a single statement.

“Those who belong to the opposing party, though they ought to establish the paternal teaching as an immovable definition, as it is, and especially as their own profession, prefer this less and are driven by the opinions of another party, which I now consider too laborious to enumerate. They have now been transferred from non-existence to inconsistency: that is, from saying neither one nor two, they have been brought to proclaiming two and one—that is, three wills and operations in one and the same Christ. Neither the paternal, nor the synodical, nor the natural doctrine has determined this; nor did the frenzy of the ancient and later heretics ever devise it to this point, knowing that the same opinion was empty and corrupted by its own defect.

“For if natural properties characterize what is composed from different substances, while the distinction of the natures is in no way removed because of the union, but rather the property of each nature remains intact as they converge into one person and one subsistence, as the holy Council of Chalcedon says—and if that same one is recognized as God from God the Father and man from the ever-virgin mother, born according to nature, although immaterially and without a cause from the Father, but bodily and for a cause from her, namely for our salvation—how is it possible for one and the same person, that is, one and the same Christ our Lord and God, to be naturally characterized, in addition to two, by yet another property, according to their view, so as to establish the reality of that from which, in which, and which he is?

“For if they believe that the same things are manifested in him through another—that is, a third—will and operation, besides the two that are naturally his, it is necessary that, from the identity of the manifestation, the dissimilarity of existence be recognized, and that the same thing be one in relation to two—that is, three in relation to one another—whether natural or substantial.

“Yet they do not call them natural, but, according to their position, substantial, and on this account they combine against him either three substances or as many subsistences, with properties of equal number: namely, the uncreated, the created, and the neither—that is, the nonexistent. For that which participates by nature in neither is nonexistent. Thus, by the identity that belongs to this third, according to them both the two natures and his natural wills and operations are nonexistent.

“But if they say that the third is not the same, but another, apart from those from which he must be believed to exist, they again bring forward the same second inexistence, as though it were something intermediate between neither of the two: between the uncreated, which is such by nature, and the created substance and power. For they either wish this to be subsistential, or composite, or deiviril [God-man], or unitive because of the union.

“Not only, as has been said, do they introduce this as nonexistent, since nothing belonging to what constitutes him characterizes him according to nature; they also make him external to the natural kinship he has with God the Father. Indeed, this is the lesser charge: they even represent him as alien from the innate property he has toward his undefiled and virgin mother, as though according to neither of these he possessed a proper composite, subsistential, deiviril, or unitive will and operation.

“Yet from the Father he has the uncomposite, beginningless, substantial, and divine nature; from his mother, the nature created and human.”

Then they also introduce the divided natures from which he exists, as though their unity were made known through operation and not through hypostasis [Col. 0625A], if they dogmatize one operation on account of unity. Those who have been corrupted by division fabulously invent this as a passible operation. Thus, allowing room for confusion, they misinterpret Severus’s “theandric” (deivirile) operation, insisting that it signifies one nature, rather than two natures, in the divine and human union; and they insinuate that this “God-man” is a certain nature, not a man who has become God—especially since Dionysius, the true revealer of God, foreseeing this [Note: [Col. 0625B] Epistle to Caius], did not call it “one,” but said that he lived among us through some new, deivirile operation.

He showed that neither nature was separated from the other, but that both were naturally united through each other, so that certainty might be brought forward concerning the things from which, in which, and which he was [Col. 0625B]; and, to speak in the manner or words of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0625B] “Paternally”: in the manner or words of the Fathers], with the participation of the one in the other, both of these things belong to each. [Note: [Col. 0626B] Pope Leo, Epistle to Flavian.] Thus the astonishing passions and the compassion-bearing miracles are undoubtedly recognized through the complete fitting together of the things naturally accomplished by him.

All things are twofold, all are true, and all are united in him who is twofold in nature: so proclaim the things that are according to nature, the heralds of God and our Fathers. Since those men were unwilling to correct their own speech, they even compelled the representatives of senior Rome to agree with their own sect: to preach in the same Lord Jesus Christ one will and operation above two—that is, three wills and operations—mixing together a taste like that of the tree of knowledge [Col. 0626A], just as those men put forward a faith from good and evil for those who desire it. Therefore, by deceiving them with such letters, they sent them to the one who had dispatched them.

Since almost the whole Catholic and apostolic Church of God has consequently been placed in great danger on this account, we beseech and implore you, most holy men, not to disregard her in peril, but to aid her laboring amid storms. Know that, in a time of tribulation, the love that is in the Holy Spirit is born. If possible, hasten to pass over, as though for another reason, to the devout men of senior Rome, firm as a rock—who are always, together with you, our guardians and most ardent defenders of the truth—and entreat them with supplicatory voices and tears on behalf of all Christians, so that they may receive their reward from the Lord [Col. 0626B]. Likewise, for everyone and for yourselves, without introducing anything novel, recently accepting or approving anything more or less concerning these matters beyond what has been defined by the holy Fathers and synods, pursue this great work directly, with God’s help, in emulation of their good zeal. Then, whether now or on the day of judgment, may they have the Lord as their debtor, whom in such matters they had as creditor—not anything other than himself, but the whole of him, giving himself through you and through them as eternal delight and refreshment.

Pray that we too may have him against the Arians who remain here, blessed men and guides of our journey to God, since we are needy, poor, and unworthy servants of yours.

# A Tome Concerning the Doctrines, between Saint Maximus and Theodosius

[Col. 0625C]

## Tome II of Our Holy Father and Confessor Maximus, concerning what occurred during his first exile, that is, at Bizya: the matters discussed between Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, and himself

[Note: [Col. 0625] The Latin and Greek versions of the following section are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0625C]

I have judged it necessary to make clear to all of you who remain in orthodoxy what was discussed concerning the undefiled faith of us Christians and concerning the contrary innovation introduced between Abba Maximus and Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea, so that, having come to know these matters more accurately, you may glorify still more the God who loves humanity, who gives speech at the opening of the mouths of those who fear him. Perhaps the enemies of truth, as is their custom, by proclaiming things contrary to it, may throw your hearts into confusion.

[Col. 0625D] Accordingly, on the twenty-fourth day of August, in the fourteenth indiction just past, the aforesaid Bishop Theodosius went out to him in the exile in which he was being guarded—that is, to the fortress of Bizya—as he said, having been sent in the person of Peter, the president of Constantinople; and Paul and Theodosius, the consuls, as they themselves said, having likewise been sent in the person of the emperor.

When they had gone up to the aforementioned monk Maximus, in the place where he was confined [Col. 0627A], they sat down and permitted him also to sit, while the bishop of Bizya was with them. The bishop Theodosius said to him:

**THEODOSIUS:** How are you, lord abba?

**MAXIMUS:** As God predetermined before all the ages the providential dispensation concerning me, so I am.

**THEODOSIUS:** What, then, did God determine concerning each of us before every age?

**MAXIMUS:** If he foreknew it, he certainly also predetermined it.

**THEODOSIUS:** What is this that you say, “he foreknew” and “he predetermined”?

**MAXIMUS:** Foreknowledge concerns the thoughts and deeds that depend upon us; predestination concerns what happens to us without depending upon us.

**THEODOSIUS:** What things depend upon us, and what things do not depend upon us?

**MAXIMUS:** It seems that my lord, knowing everything, is questioning his servant for the sake of examination.

**THEODOSIUS:** By the truth of God [Col. 0627B], I asked in ignorance, wishing to learn the difference between what depends upon us and what does not, and how some things fall under God’s foreknowledge while others fall under predestination.

**MAXIMUS:** Everything voluntary depends upon us—that is, virtues and vices. What does not depend upon us is the imposition of punitive circumstances that befall us, or their opposites. For neither illness, which causes suffering, nor health, which brings joy, depends upon us, although the causes that produce them do depend upon us. For example, disorder is the cause of illness, just as good order is the cause of health; and the cause of the kingdom of heaven is observance of the commandments, just as transgression of them is the cause of eternal fire.

**THEODOSIUS:** Are you therefore suffering in this exile because you have done things worthy of this suffering?

**MAXIMUS:** I pray that God, through this suffering, may limit the punishments that I deserved for having sinned against him by transgressing his justifying commandments [Col. 0627C].

**THEODOSIUS:** Is suffering not also imposed upon many for the sake of testing?

**MAXIMUS:** The testing of the saints occurs so that, through suffering, their dispositions toward what is naturally good may be manifested to human life, revealing through themselves the virtues unknown to all, as in the case of Job and Joseph. One was tested for the manifestation of hidden courage; the other was tested for the proclamation of sanctifying chastity.

Every saint who is unwillingly afflicted in this age is afflicted under such providential arrangements, so that, through the weakness permitted to burden him, they may trample upon the proud and apostate dragon—that is, the devil. For endurance is the work of testing in each of the saints.

**THEODOSIUS:** By the truth of God, you have spoken well; I acknowledge the benefit, and I have always desired to converse with you about such things. But since I and my lords, the future patricians, have come to you for another matter, and have traveled such great distances, we ask you to accept what is proposed by us and to make the whole inhabited world rejoice.

**MAXIMUS:** What are these things, my lord? And who am I, and where do I come from, that my agreement to what is proposed to me should make the whole inhabited world rejoice?

**THEODOSIUS:** By the truth of our Lord Jesus Christ, what I and my lords, the future patricians, are telling you, we heard from the mouth of our lord the patriarch and the pious lord of the inhabited world.

**MAXIMUS:** Command my lords to say what you wish and what you have heard.

[Col. 0629A]

**THEODOSIUS:** The emperor and the patriarch ask through us to learn from you for what reason you do not communicate with the throne of Constantinople.

**MAXIMUS:** Do you have written authorization concerning this from the most pious emperor or from the patriarch?

**THEODOSIUS:** You ought not, my lord, to distrust us. Although I am insignificant, I am called a bishop; and my lords are members of the senate. We have not come to test you—God forbid.

**MAXIMUS:** Whatever manner brought you to your servant, I shall state without reserve the reason why I do not communicate with the throne of Constantinople. Even if it were proper for others to ask me for what reason, it is not proper for you, who know the reason more certainly than I do [Col. 0629B].

You know the innovations that arose from the sixth indiction of the preceding cycle, beginning in Alexandria through the nine Chapters issued by Cyrus, who—I do not know how—was made president there, and which were confirmed by the throne of Constantinople. You also know the other alterations, additions, and subtractions made synodally by those who presided over the Church of Byzantium—Sergius, I mean, and Pyrrhus and Paul. The whole inhabited world knows these innovations.

For this reason I, your servant, do not communicate with the Church of Constantinople. Let the stumbling-blocks placed by the aforesaid men be removed, together with those very men who placed them, as God said: “And throw the stones out of the way” [Col. 0629C]. Then, when the level and well-worn road of the Gospel has been found free from every thorny wickedness of heresy, I shall walk upon it without any human urging.

But as long as the presidents of Constantinople take pride in the stumbling-blocks that have been placed and in those who placed them, no argument or method can persuade me to communicate with them.

**THEODOSIUS:** What evil do we confess, then, that you should separate yourself from our communion on this account?

**MAXIMUS:** You confuse the account of theology and of the dispensation by teaching one operation of the divinity and humanity of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. If we must believe the holy Fathers, who say that those whose operation is one also have one essence, you make the holy Trinity a quaternity [Col. 0629D], as though his flesh had become consubstantial with the Word and had departed from the natural identity that he has with us and with her who gave him birth.

Again, by abolishing the operations and affirming one will of his divinity and humanity, you deprive him of the distribution of good things. For if, according to those who enacted this, he has no operation, it is clear that, even if he wishes to have mercy, he cannot, since the operation of good things has been removed from him. Without a good operation, nothing that exists is naturally able to act or do anything.

Moreover, you make the flesh, by will, co-creator with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit of all the ages and of the things in them, while by nature it is created—or, to speak more accurately, beginningless with respect to will, since the divine will is beginningless, as belonging to a divinity that is without beginning, but recent with respect to nature [Col. 0631A]. This exceeds not only every lack of understanding but also every impiety.

For you do not simply say “one will,” but “one divine will.” No one can conceive a temporal beginning or an end for the divine will, any more than for the divine nature, of which the will is substantial.

Again, introducing another innovation, you altogether remove all that marks and constitutes the divinity and humanity of Christ, legislating and prescribing that neither one nor two wills or operations may be spoken of in him. This is a thing without reality.

Nothing that exists, if it is intellectual, is deprived of the power and operation of willing; if it is sensory, of sensory operation; if it is vegetative, of the operation of growth and nourishment; and if it is entirely inanimate and shares no life at all, it is nevertheless not without what is customarily called habitual operation and aptitude.

All such things reveal themselves by becoming perceptible to the senses. The operation of such things is to fall under sight through their own appearance, under hearing through sound, under smell through a suitable vapor, under taste through certain juices, and under touch through resistance. Just as we call seeing the operation of sight, so we call being seen the operation of visible things; and we understand all the rest to occur in the same way.

If, then, nothing that exists is entirely deprived of natural operation, while our Lord and God—have mercy, Lord!—has no natural will or operation according to either of the natures from which, in which, and which he is [Col. 0631C], how can we be or be called worshipers of God if we say that the one whom you worship as God exists in no way as willing or operative?

The holy Fathers clearly teach us this when they say: “That which has no power neither exists, nor is anything, nor has any position at all.”

**THEODOSIUS:** Do not take what was done for the sake of the dispensation as an authoritative dogma.

**MAXIMUS:** If the dogma of those who accept this is not authoritative, and if the Type—the decree and law—prescribes that no will or operation of the Lord is to be spoken of, although their removal indicates the nonexistence of the one deprived of them, for what reason did you hand me over without honor to barbarous and godless nations [Col. 0631D]? For what reason was I condemned to live at Bizya, while one of my fellow servants was sent to Perberis and the other to Mesembria?

**THEODOSIUS:** By God, who is to judge me! When it was made, I said, and I say the same now: the Type was wrongly made and to the injury of many. The occasion for issuing it was the quarrel among the orthodox concerning wills and operations. In order that all might make peace with one another, some judged that such expressions should be silenced.

**MAXIMUS:** What faithful person accepts a dispensation that silences expressions which the God of all arranged to be spoken through apostles, prophets, and teachers? Let us examine, my great lord, to what evil this matter leads.

If God appointed in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, and third teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, saying in the Gospel to the apostles, and through them to those who came after them, “What I say to you I say to all” [Mark 13:37], and again, “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” [Matthew 10:40; Luke 10:16], it is clear and evident that whoever does not receive the apostles, prophets, and teachers, but rejects their words, rejects Christ himself.

Let us consider another matter. God chose and raised up apostles, prophets, and teachers for the perfecting of the saints. The devil, however, chose and raised up false apostles, false prophets, and false teachers against piety, so that both the ancient law and the Gospel might be attacked. By false apostles, false prophets, and false teachers I understand only the heretics, whose words and thoughts are perverted.

Therefore, just as the one who receives the true apostles, prophets, and teachers receives God, so the one who receives the false apostles, prophets, and teachers receives the devil. Thus whoever expels the saints together with the wicked and unclean heretics—receive me as one speaking the truth—has plainly condemned God together with the devil.

If, then, by examining the innovations made in our times, we find that they have reached this extreme evil [Col. 0633C], see to it that, while pretending to make peace, we are not found to be sick with and proclaiming the apostasy that the divine Apostle said would precede the coming of Antichrist.

I have told you these things without reserve, my lords, so that you may spare yourselves and us. Do you command me, carrying these things written in the book of my heart, to come and communicate in the Church in which they are proclaimed, and to become a participant with those who truly expel God but falsely claim to expel the devil together with God?

May this never happen to me through God, who for my sake became what I am, without sin. And, bowing in repentance, he said: “Whatever you command me to do to your servant, do it. But I shall never communicate with those who accept these things.”

[Col. 0633D] Stunned by what had been said, they lowered their heads and remained silent for a considerable time. Then Bishop Theodosius raised his head, looked directly at Abba Maximus, and said:

**THEODOSIUS:** We assure you, on behalf of our lord the emperor, that if you communicate, he will abolish the Type.

**MAXIMUS:** We are still far from one another. What shall we do about the synodically confirmed statement of one will, with the removal of every operation, by Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul?

**THEODOSIUS:** That document has been taken down and discarded.

**MAXIMUS:** It has been taken down from the stone walls, but not from rational souls. Let them accept the condemnation of these things issued synodically at Rome through pious doctrines and canons; then the dividing wall is broken down, and we shall need no urging.

**THEODOSIUS:** The synod held at Rome is not valid, since it took place without the emperor’s command.

[Col. 0635A]

**MAXIMUS:** If the commands of emperors validate the synods that have been held, but not pious faith, then let them also accept the synods held against the homoousion, since they took place by command of emperors: the synod at Tyre, the one at Antioch, the one at Seleucia, the one at Constantinople under Eudoxius the Arian, the one at Nicaea in Thrace, and the one at Sirmium; and, many years later, the second synod at Ephesus, presided over by Dioscorus. An imperial command assembled all these, yet all were condemned because of the impiety of the wicked doctrines they ratified.

Why, then, do you not reject the synod that deposed Paul of Samosata, held under the holy and blessed Fathers Dionysius, pope of Rome, Dionysius of Alexandria, and Gregory the Wonderworker, who presided over that same synod, since it did not take place by an imperial command?

What canon decrees that only those synods are to be approved which were assembled by an emperor’s command, or that all synods must be assembled by an emperor’s command? The pious canon of the Church recognizes as holy and approved those synods that the correctness of their doctrines has judged to be such.

Moreover, as my lord knows and teaches others, the canon decreed that a synod should be held a second time in every province each year, without making any mention of imperial command, for the security of our saving faith and for the correction of all matters that do not agree with the divine law of the Church [“not agreeing,” supplied in the text].

[Col. 0635C]

**THEODOSIUS:** It is as you say: the correctness of doctrines approves the synods. Yet you do not accept the libellus of Menas, in which he dogmatized one will and one operation of Christ?

**MAXIMUS:** May the Lord God forbid! You do not accept them; rather, you expel all the teachers who, after the holy Council of Chalcedon, fought against the pollution of Severus. And am I to accept the libellus of Menas, composed after the council, through which he plainly sides with Severus, Apollinarius, Macedonius, Arius, and every heresy, and accuses the council—or rather completely rejects it through what he dogmatized?

**THEODOSIUS:** What then? Do you not accept one operation at all?

**MAXIMUS:** And which of the approved teachers of the Church says there is one operation?

The same Bishop Theodosius produced and read testimonies falsely circulating under the names of Julius of Rome, Gregory the Wonderworker, and Athanasius.

**MAXIMUS:** Let us now fear God and not wish to provoke him by producing testimonies of heretics. No one is unaware that these are the words of the impious Apollinarius. If you have others, show them. By producing these, you persuade everyone all the more that you have truly revived the wicked opinion of the impious Apollinarius and of those who think with him.

The same Bishop Theodosius then produced two testimonies in the name of Chrysostom. After reading them, Abba Maximus said:

**MAXIMUS:** These are Nestorius’s, who madly dogmatized a personal duality in Christ [Col. 0637A].

The bishop, immediately burning with anger, said:

**THEODOSIUS:** Lord monk, Satan has spoken through your unbridled mouth.

**MAXIMUS:** May my lord not be angered against his servant.

He immediately took the passages and showed him that the same words belonged to Nestorius and in which of his writings they occurred.

**THEODOSIUS:** God knows, brother, the patriarch gave me these testimonies. But look: you have said that some belong to Apollinarius and others to Nestorius.

He then produced a testimony of Saint Cyril which said: “Showing one and cognate operation through both,” and said:

**THEODOSIUS:** What do you say to this?

**MAXIMUS:** Some have demonstrated that this phrase was truly inserted as an addition in the interpretation of the Gospel made by Timothy the Cat, from this holy Father. But let it be his, according to you. Let us therefore examine the meaning of the paternal words, and we shall know the truth.

**THEODOSIUS:** I do not permit this to be done. You must accept the words as simple. [Note: [Col. 0637D] Sirmond translated this from Anastasius’s version into Greek, apparently; in Anastasius, however, the Latin should read “the difference … of simple words.”]

**MAXIMUS:** Tell me, I beg you, the difference between simple words and varied words.

**THEODOSIUS:** So that you may accept the word as it is and not investigate its meaning.

**MAXIMUS:** You are plainly introducing new and foreign rules of the Church even concerning words. If, according to you, one must not investigate the words of Scripture and the Fathers, then let us cast out the whole of the Old and New Scripture.

For we have heard David say: “Blessed are those who examine his testimonies; with their whole heart they will seek him,” as though no one can seek God without investigation. Again: “Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law and keep it with my whole heart,” as though investigation leads to knowledge of the law, and knowledge persuades the worthy through desire to keep in their hearts what is contained in it, through fulfillment of its holy commandments.

Again: “Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul searched them out.” Why does the proverbial word wish us to investigate parables, riddles, and obscure sayings? Why does the Lord, speaking in parables, wish the disciples to understand, teaching them the meaning of the parables? Why does he command, “Search the Scriptures,” since they testify about him? What does Peter, chief of the apostles, wish to teach when he says, “The prophets sought and searched concerning the salvation” [Col. 0637C]? What does the divine Apostle Paul mean when he says, “If the Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, whose minds the god of this age has blinded, so that the illumination of the knowledge of Christ may not shine upon them”?

It seems that you wish us to become like the Jews, who, as you say, by fixing their mind upon simple words—that is, upon the letter alone, as though upon a covering—fell away from the truth, having the veil over their hearts so as not to understand the Lord’s Spirit hidden in the letter, concerning which he says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

Let my lord be assured that I cannot accept a word without its meaning, which is contained in it, lest I plainly become a Jew.

[Col. 0639A]

Having heard this, Theodosius said:

**THEODOSIUS:** We ought to speak of one hypostatic operation of Christ.

**MAXIMUS:** Let us examine the evil produced by this, and flee this strange expression. It belongs only to heretics who multiply gods. If we call Christ’s one operation hypostatic, but the Son does not coincide in hypostasis with the Father and the Spirit, it is clear that he does not coincide with them in hypostatic operation either. We are then compelled to assign hypostatic operations to the Father and the Spirit as well as to the Son.

According to you, therefore, blessed divinity will have four operations: three distinguishing the persons in whom it exists, and one common operation signifying the natural commonality of the three hypostases. And if we accept the teaching of the Fathers, we shall fall into the sickness of quaternity. For they declare that every operation is natural, not hypostatic.

If this is true—as indeed it is—we shall be shown to speak of four natures and four gods, differing from one another in hypostasis and in nature.

Moreover, who has ever seen or contemplated an operation peculiar to any of those included under a species and naturally classified under the common definition of that species? The natural common element never becomes the property of one individual alone. For hypostatic marks—such as hookedness, snubness, grayness, thinness, and the like—are distinguishing accidents of individuals differing from one another numerically.

Every human being naturally acts as something that has the nature, not as someone who has an individual hypostasis, according to the most particular and the common categorical account, both conceived and spoken: for example, animal, rational, mortal—what belongs to the generic account concerning us [Col. 0639C].

We all participate in the same life, the same rationality, and the same flow and withdrawal; in sitting, standing, speaking, being silent, seeing, hearing, and touching. These belong to the common account conceived concerning us.

Therefore we must not introduce expressions that possess no scriptural, patristic, or natural force, but are foreign and invented by human distortions. Show me this expression located in any Father; then we shall again seek the mind of the one who used it.

[Col. 0639D]

**THEODOSIUS:** What then? Must we not speak of one operation in Christ at all?

**MAXIMUS:** According to holy Scripture and the holy Fathers, we have received no such statement. Rather, just as we believe and confess Christ to possess two natures, from which he exists, so also we have been permitted to believe and confess that he possesses, correspondingly, his natural wills and operations, since he is at once God and man by nature.

**THEODOSIUS:** Truly, my lord, we too confess the natures and the different operations—that is, divine and human—and his divinity as willing and his humanity as willing, since his soul was not without will. But we do not say “two,” lest we introduce him as fighting against himself.

**MAXIMUS:** What then? When you speak of two natures, do you introduce them as fighting because of the number?

**THEODOSIUS:** No.

**MAXIMUS:** Why, then, does number, when applied to natures, not divide them, but when spoken of wills and operations possess the power of division?

**THEODOSIUS:** Certainly. The Fathers did not speak of wills and operations in that way because they avoided division. They said “another and another,” “divine and human,” “double and twofold.” I speak as they spoke, and as they have said.

**MAXIMUS:** For the Lord’s sake, if someone says to you “another and another,” how many do you understand? If he says “divine and human,” how many do you understand? If he says “double and twofold,” how many do you understand?

**THEODOSIUS:** I know how I understand them, but I do not say “two.”

Then Abba Maximus turned to the officials and said:

**MAXIMUS:** For the Lord’s sake, if you hear “one and one,” or “another and another,” or “twice two,” or “twice five,” what do you understand and answer that the speakers mean?

They replied:

**OFFICIALS:** Since you have put us under oath, by “one and one” we understand two; by “another and another,” two; by “twice two,” four; and likewise by “twice five,” ten.

Theodosius, ashamed of their answer, said:

**THEODOSIUS:** I do not say what the Fathers did not say.

Abba Maximus immediately took the book of the acts of the holy apostolic synod and showed that the holy Fathers explicitly spoke of the two wills and operations of our Savior and God Jesus Christ. The consul Theodosius took the book of the acts and also read all the Fathers’ testimonies.

Then Bishop Theodosius replied:

**THEODOSIUS:** God knows, if this synod had not imposed the anathemas personally, I would have accepted it more than any other human being. But, so that we do not waste time here, whatever the Fathers said, I say; and I shall immediately put it in writing: two natures, two wills, and two operations. Come in with us to communicate, and let there be union [Col. 0641C].

**MAXIMUS:** My lord, I, being merely a monk, do not dare accept from you a written agreement concerning such a matter. But if God has moved you to accept the words of the holy Fathers, as the canon requires, send a written communication about this to the pope of Rome—that is, the emperor, the patriarch, and the synod under him.

For even if these things occur, I shall not communicate while those who were anathematized are commemorated at the holy offering. I fear the condemnation of the anathema.

**THEODOSIUS:** God knows, I do not condemn you for fearing it, nor does anyone else. But give us advice, for the Lord’s sake, if this can be done.

**MAXIMUS:** What advice can I give you about it? Go, investigate whether anything of this kind has ever happened, and whether, after someone’s death, anyone has been released from an accusation concerning the faith and from the condemnation pronounced against him.

Let the emperor and the patriarch agree to imitate God’s condescension. Let the emperor issue a supplicatory command and the patriarch a synodal petition to the pope of Rome. If an ecclesiastical means is found that permits this for the sake of the orthodox confession of the faith, I shall certainly be reconciled with you in this matter.

[Col. 0643A]

**THEODOSIUS:** This will certainly be done. But give me your word that, if they send me, you will come with me.

**MAXIMUS:** My lord, it is more advantageous for you to take with you my fellow servant who is in Mesembria than me. He knows the language, and they rightly respect him, since he has been punished for so many years both for God’s sake and for the orthodox faith maintained in their throne.

**THEODOSIUS:** We have various disagreements with one another, and I am not pleased to depart with him.

**MAXIMUS:** My lord, when it has been decided that this should happen and the outcome of what has been agreed upon has been determined, wherever you wish, I shall follow you.

At this, they all rose with joy and tears, bowed in repentance, and prayed. Each kissed the holy Gospels, the precious cross, the image of God and our Savior Jesus Christ, and the image of our Lady, the all-holy Mother of God who bore him [Col. 0643B], placing their own hands upon them as confirmation of what had been said.

After they had spoken briefly with one another about life according to God and the observance of the divine commandments, Bishop Theodosius turned to Abba Maximus and said:

**THEODOSIUS:** Behold, all the scandals have been dissolved; peace has come through God, and it shall be established. But, for the Lord’s sake, do not conceal anything from me: do you in any way say one will and one operation concerning Christ?

**MAXIMUS:** I cannot ever say this, and I shall explain why. It is foreign to the holy Fathers to say that two natures have one will and one operation. Moreover, whoever says this in any way immediately encounters the absurdity.

If I say “natural,” I fear confusion. If I say “hypostatic,” I divide the Son from the Father and the Spirit, and will appear to introduce three wills that do not coincide with one another, just as the hypostases do not coincide.

If I say that he has one will and operation as one individual, I am compelled, even against my will, to say that the Father and the Spirit likewise have a will and operation as one individual; and the argument will be found to fall into polytheism.

If I say “relative,” I introduce the personal division of Nestorius. If I say “contrary to nature,” I destroy the existence of the one who wills; for what is contrary to nature is corruption of nature, as the Fathers have said.

[Col. 0643D]

**THEODOSIUS:** We must in every way say that our Savior has one will because of the union, as Sergius and Pyrrhus, as I think, rightly understood and wrote.

**MAXIMUS:** If you command me, my lord, accept two arguments from me concerning this. If, as Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul have written, one will came to exist in God and our Savior because of the union, then, according to them, the Son will have a will different from the Father because of nature, but not because of the union, since he has one will according to the Son, if union and nature are not the same.

If one will came to exist in our Savior because of the union, it will necessarily have the union as its cause, not either of the natures from which he exists; and, according to them, the will will plainly be of relationship, not of nature. For the account of truth knows the union as a relationship, not as a nature.

If one will of our Savior came to exist because of the union, by what will do they say that the union itself came to exist? Surely those who care for truth and avoid absurdity would not say that it came to exist by the will that came to exist through it.

If one will of our Savior came to exist because of the union, it is clear that before the union he was either possessed of many wills or entirely without will. If he possessed many wills, he endured the reduction of many to one will and plainly suffered change, since the many wills naturally belonging to him were diminished.

But if he was entirely without will, the union from which he obtained a will was shown to be superior to nature, since nature lacked what the union supplied. Again, he was shown to be changeable, since he acquired through relationship what did not belong to him by nature.

If one will of our Savior came to exist according to one of the natures from which he is, then God became recent in will while remaining eternal in nature through the union; and man became without beginning in will while remaining recent in nature. This is impossible, not to say impious.

If one will of the natures came to exist because of the union, why, for the same reason, did one nature of the natures not come to exist?

At this point Bishop Theodosius interrupted the flow of the argument and said:

**THEODOSIUS:** What, then, came to exist because of the union, if none of these things came to exist through it?

**MAXIMUS:** It truly showed the bodiless one to have become embodied. It plainly manifested that the one who is God by nature and Creator of all had become man by nature—not through a change of nature or a diminution of anything belonging to nature, but through the true assumption of an intellectually ensouled body, that is, a complete humanity, naturally pure from every ancestral fault.

In the language of distinction, it manifested the truly wondrous and astonishing fact that the same one is wholly God among human things, remaining wholly and completely within his own properties, and wholly man among divine things, remaining wholly and completely without falling away from his own properties.

For, according to the teaching of our theological Fathers, there has been an interpenetration of the natures and of the natural things belonging to them into one another, not a transfer or diminution because of the union. Transfer and diminution belong to those who wickedly make the union a confusion and consequently mix it in many ways with innovations, and who, through lack of firmness in their argument, persecute the pious.

Having heard this, Bishop Theodosius, with the others who had come with him, decided to accept what had been said.

Again the same bishop said to Abba Maximus:

**THEODOSIUS:** Do me a kindness. What is this that you said to us: that no one acts as someone according to his hypostasis, but as something according to his nature? Explain what you said to me.

**MAXIMUS:** No one acts as someone according to his hypostasis, but as something according to his nature. Peter and Paul act, for example, but not in a Petrine or Pauline manner; rather, in a human manner. Both are human beings naturally, according to the common and defining account of nature, but not hypostatically, according to what is individually particular.

Likewise Michael and Gabriel act, but not in a Michaelic or Gabrielic manner; rather, angelically, for both are angels.
