Thus, in every nature predicated of many individuals numerically, we contemplate a common operation, but not one that is solitary. Whoever, therefore, speaks of a hypostatic operation introduces the one nature as having become infinite in operations and differing from itself according to the multitude of the individuals brought under it [Col. 0647B]. If this is thought to be correct, we destroy together with every nature the account of how it exists.

After these things had been said, as they were greeting one another, the consul Theodosius said:

**THEODOSIUS:** Behold, everything has turned out well. Will the emperor therefore consent to issue a supplicatory command?

**MAXIMUS:** Certainly, if he wishes to be an imitator of God and humble himself with him for the common salvation of us all. Let him consider that, if God, who saves by nature, did not save until he willingly humbled himself, how will man, who is saved by nature, be saved without humbling himself?

The consul Theodosius said:

**THEODOSIUS:** Since I hope that God will preserve the memory of this for me, I shall say this very argument to him, and he will be persuaded.

Having kissed one another, they departed in peace. The bishop gave Abba Maximus a small amount of money that had been sent to him, together with a tunic and a cloak. The bishop of Bizya immediately gave the tunic away at that very hour; at Regium, not only the money given to him but also anything else he possessed through charity was taken from him, together with the remainder of his wretched belongings and clothing.

After the aforesaid men had departed on the eighth day of September of the fifteenth indiction, Paul the consul again went out at Bizya to Abba Maximus, carrying an order which read as follows:

“We command your illustriousness to go to Bizya and bring the monk Maximus with great honor and flattery, both because of his old age and weakness and because he is our ancestral relative and has become dear to them; and to place him in the venerable monastery of Saint Theodore, situated near Regium; then come and report to us. We send two patricians in our name, who are to discuss with him the matters before us, since they love us from the soul and are loved by us, and to come and announce his presence to us.”

The same consul therefore brought him and placed him in the aforementioned monastery, then went to report.

The next day the patricians Epiphanius and Troilus came to him with great pomp and display, together with Bishop Theodosius. They went up to him in the catechumenium of the church of the same monastery. After the customary greeting, they sat down, compelling him also to sit. Troilus began speaking to him:

**TROILUS:** Our lord commanded us to come to you and tell you what has been decided by his God-supported policy. But first tell us: will you obey the emperor’s command or not?

Maximus said:

**MAXIMUS:** My lord, I shall hear what his pious authority has commanded and then answer appropriately. What answer can I give concerning something unknown?

**TROILUS:** It is impossible for us to say anything unless you first tell us whether you will obey the emperor’s command.

When he saw them resisting, looking more bitterly at his delay, and answering more harshly, together with all those accompanying them and adorned with the honors of their offices, Abba Maximus replied:

**MAXIMUS:** Since you are unwilling to tell your servant what has been presented to our lord and emperor, behold, I say—while God, the holy angels, and all of you hear—that whatever he commands me concerning any matter belonging to this age, which is destined to end and decay, I shall willingly do.

Troilus immediately rose and said:

**TROILUS:** Pray for me; I am leaving. This man does nothing.

After a great commotion and much disturbance and confusion, Bishop Theodosius said to them:

**THEODOSIUS:** Tell him the answer and learn what he says. It is not reasonable to leave in this manner without saying anything or hearing anything.

Then the patrician Epiphanius said:

**EPIPHANIUS:** Through us the emperor makes this clear to you: “Since the whole West and those in the East who are being led astray look to you, and all are in rebellion because of you, unwilling to be reconciled with us concerning the faith, may God move you to communicate with us according to the Type issued by us. We ourselves shall proceed to the Chalkē, greet you, offer you our hand, and bring you into the Great Church with every honor and glory. We shall have you stand beside us where emperors customarily stand, celebrate the gathering together, and communicate together in the immaculate and life-giving mysteries of the life-giving body and blood of Christ.

“We shall proclaim you our father, and there will be joy not only in our Christ-loving imperial city but throughout the whole inhabited world. We know assuredly that, if you communicate with the holy one on the throne here, all those who have separated from our communion because of you and your teaching will be united with us.”

The Abba Maximus turned to the bishop and, with tears, said:

**MAXIMUS:** My great lord, we all await the day of judgment. You know what was sworn and affirmed over the holy Gospels, the life-giving cross, the image of our God and Savior, and the image of the all-holy ever-virgin Mother who bore him.

The bishop lowered his face and said to him in a subdued voice:

**THEODOSIUS:** What can I do if something else is presented to the most pious emperor?

**MAXIMUS:** Why, then, did you touch the holy Gospels, you and those with you, when the fulfillment of what was said did not depend upon you [Col. 0651A]? Truly, the whole power of heaven could not persuade me to do this. For what defense shall I make—not to God only, but to my own conscience—that, for human glory, which according to its own account has no existence, I have sworn away the faith that saves those who cherish it?

At these words they rose, anger directing them all, and they disabled him with blows, pushes, and kicks, drenching him from head to toe with spittle. The stench remained until the garments upon which it had been cast were washed.

The bishop rose and said:

**THEODOSIUS:** This should not have happened. They should merely have heard his answer and entered to report it to our gracious lord. Canonical matters are administered in another way.

With difficulty the bishop persuaded them to be quiet. They sat down again, and after insulting him with countless abuses and unimaginable curses, Epiphanius said with anger and harshness:

**EPIPHANIUS:** Speak, you evil and gluttonous wretch! Why, treating us as heretics, and our city and emperor as heretics, did you speak these words? In truth, we are more Christian and orthodox than you. We confess that our Lord and God has both a divine will and a human will, and an intellectual soul; and that every intellectual nature necessarily has willing by nature and operation, since motion belongs to life and will belongs to mind. We know him to be willing not only in divinity but also in humanity. Nor do we deny his two wills and operations.

**MAXIMUS:** If you believe in this way, as do the intellectual natures and the Church of God, why do you compel me to communicate according to the Type, which contains only the abolition of these things?

**EPIPHANIUS:** This was done for the sake of a dispensation, so that the people would not be harmed by such subtle expressions.

**MAXIMUS:** On the contrary, every person is sanctified through an exact confession of the faith, not through the abolition contained in the Type.

**TROILUS:** I told you in the palace that it did not abolish them, but commanded that they be silenced, so that we might all live in peace.

**MAXIMUS:** The silence of words is the abolition of words. For through the Prophet the Holy Spirit says: “There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard.” Therefore a word that is not spoken is not a word.

**TROILUS:** Keep it in your heart as you wish; no one prevents you.

**MAXIMUS:** But God did not confine salvation entirely to the heart when he said: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I shall confess him before my Father who is in heaven.” The divine Apostle also teaches, saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation.”

If God and God’s prophets and apostles command the great, fearful mystery—the salvation of the whole world—to be confessed through the words of the saints, then the voice proclaiming it must not be silenced in any way, lest the salvation of those who remain silent be diminished.

Epiphanius replied in the harshest terms:

**EPIPHANIUS:** Did you sign the libellus?

**MAXIMUS:** Yes, I signed it.

**EPIPHANIUS:** How did you dare to sign it and anathematize those who confess and believe as do the intellectual natures and the Catholic Church? Indeed, by my judgment we shall bring you into the city, bind you, and set you in the forum. We shall bring actors, actresses, prostitutes who preside over them, and the whole people, so that every man and woman may strike you and spit in your face.

**MAXIMUS:** Let it happen as you have said, if we anathematized those who confess two natures from which the Lord exists and the two natural wills and operations corresponding to him, since he is truly God by nature and man. Read the acts, my lord, and the libellus; if you find that we anathematized these things as you have said, do what you wish.

For I and all my fellow servants who signed anathematized those who, following Arius and Apollinarius, say there is one will and operation, and who do not confess our Lord and God as intellectual by nature according to another of the things from which, in which, and which he is; and for this reason as willing and operative according to both natures for our salvation.

They said: “If we are delayed by this, we shall neither eat nor drink. Let us rise, dine, enter, and tell them what we heard. This man has delivered himself to Satan.”

They rose and dined. Then they entered in anger on the vigil of the Exaltation of the precious and life-giving Cross.

[Col. 0653C]

The next morning the consul Theodosius went out to the aforementioned Abba Maximus and took away everything he possessed, saying to him in the emperor’s name:

“Because you did not want honor, it shall be taken far from you. Go wherever you have judged yourself worthy to be, bearing the judgment of your disciples, the one in Mesembria and the one in Perberis, who became notary to our blessed grandmother.”

The patricians, Troilus and Epiphanius, were also present and had said:

“We shall certainly bring both disciples—the one in Mesembria and the one in Perberis—and examine them also, and see what outcome awaits them.

“But so that you may see, lord abba, that if we obtain even a little respite from the turmoil of the nations, by the Holy Trinity we shall have power to deal with you, the pope now being removed, all who speak there, the rest of your companions, and all of you; we shall melt each one down in his proper place, as Martin was melted.”

The aforesaid consul Theodosius took him and handed him over to soldiers, who brought him as far as Salembria.

They remained there for two days, until one of the soldiers went to the army and told the whole army that the monk who blasphemed the Mother of God was coming there, so that they might stir up the army against the aforesaid Abba Maximus as one who blasphemed the Mother of God.

After two days the soldier returned and took him to the camp. God moved the general—or rather the general’s deputy—and he sent to him the senior officers of the units, priests, deacons, and reverent signal-keepers. When the aforesaid Abba Maximus saw them arrive, he rose and bowed in repentance. They returned his bow, sat down, and ordered him to sit also.

A very old and honorable man said to him with great reverence:

“Father, since some have scandalized us concerning your holiness, saying that you do not call our Lady, the all-holy Virgin, Mother of God, I adjure you by the holy, consubstantial, and life-giving Trinity to tell us the truth and remove this scandal from our hearts, so that we may not be unjustly harmed by being scandalized.”

[Col. 0655B]

He bowed in repentance, rose, stretched his hands toward heaven, and said with tears:

“Whoever does not call our Lady, the most praised, all-holy, undefiled one, revered by every intellectual nature, who truly became by nature the mother of God who made heaven, earth, and the sea and all that is in them—let him be anathema and condemned, from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the consubstantial and worshiped Trinity, and from every heavenly power, and from the choir of the holy apostles and prophets, and from the innumerable assembly of martyrs, and from every spirit made perfect in righteousness, now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.”

They wept and prayed for him, saying:

“God will strengthen you, Father, and deem you worthy to complete this course without stumbling.”

After these things had been said, many soldiers gathered, listening to many excellent arguments that had been stirred up. One of the general’s domestics saw that a large army was gathering, forming up, and condemning what was being done to him. God knows what he intended; he allowed Maximus to be carried off and thrown two miles from the camp until the gathering should be completed and those who were to take him to Perberis should arrive.

But the clergy, overcome by divine love, harnessed themselves to the two-mile journey, came, greeted him, and prayed for him. Carrying him with their own hands, they placed him upon the animal and returned peacefully to their own places; he himself was taken to Perberis, where the guard assigned to him continued.

[Col. 0655D]

It should also be known that, when they were at Regium, Troilus said to Abba Maximus:

“The consular John wrote to him concerning an agreement proposed to them, and the fact that this had not yet occurred was, I think, prevented by the disorder of your disciples.”

But I think that the aforesaid consular John did not write to Troilus, but to Menas the monk, and that Menas told the men of the palace.

After this they brought them to Constantinople [Col. 0657A] and proceeded against them. After anathematizing and degrading Maximus, the holy man, his blessed disciple Anastasius, the most holy pope Martin, Saint Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, and all the orthodox and those who thought with them, they also brought the other blessed Anastasius. Having used the same anathemas and insults against him, they handed him over to the officials, saying:

“You, then, Anastasius, having put on the dark garment of the universal curse of anathemas, depart from the canonical hearing, to which you have chosen the stance of Gehenna, being led away, while the illustrious, honorable, and holy senate—which has shared all our deliberations—is with us and will immediately undertake the judgment concerning you and carry out upon you what the civil laws decree, as they themselves judge, because of such great blasphemies and tyrannies.

“For the vote of the present synod, enacted canonically with the cooperation of Christ almighty, our true God, has decreed what is fitting against you, Maximus, Anastasius, and Anastasius. It remained that you should be subjected to the severe penalties of the laws for the impious things you said and did,” even if a penalty worthy of such offenses and blasphemies should not be imposed, we leave you to the just Judge for the greater matter. Yet, in the present life, to avoid emptying the strictness of the laws and to allow you to live, we decree that the present most renowned prefect shall immediately receive you into his many-commanded praetorium and, striking your backs with thongs [Maximus, Anastasius, and Anastasius—the instrument of the wantonness of your Maximus, Anastasius, and Anastasius], shall have your blasphemous tongue, the instrument of your impious reasoning, cut out.

“Then he shall cut with iron the most wicked right hand that served your blasphemous reasoning. At the same time, after you have been deprived of these detestable members, you shall be led around the twelve districts of this imperial city. Thereafter we deliver you to perpetual exile and imprisonment, so that afterward and throughout all the remaining time of your lives you may lament your own blasphemous errors, the curse devised against us having turned back upon our head.”

The prefect took them and punished them. He cut off their members, led them around the whole city, and then exiled them to Lazica.

# Tome Containing the Report Concerning the Doctrines Discussed between Saint Maximus and Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, or the Consuls Who Were with Him

[Note: [Col. 0625D] “The second tome of our holy Father Maximus the Confessor: what was done during his first exile, that is, at Bizya: namely, what was discussed between Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, and himself.” Sirmond.]

[Col. 0626C]

What was discussed concerning the undefiled faith of us Christians and the contrary innovation introduced between Abba Maximus and Theodosius, Bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, I judged it necessary to make manifest to all of you who remain in orthodoxy, so that, when you have appeared to learn these things more certainly, you may glorify more and more the God who loves humanity, who gives speech at the opening of the mouths of those who fear him—lest perhaps the enemies of truth, as is their custom, by proclaiming things contrary to it, disturb your hearts.

[Col. 0626D]

Accordingly, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September—that is, on the twenty-fourth of August—in the fourteenth indiction just past, the aforesaid Bishop Theodosius went out to him in the exile in which he was being kept, that is, to the fortress of Bizya, having been sent, as he said, in the person of Peter, president of Constantinople, and likewise Paul and Theodosius, the consuls, as they themselves acknowledged, having been sent in the person of the emperor.

When they had gone up to the aforementioned monk Maximus in the place where he was confined, they sat down [Col. 0628A] and ordered him also to sit. The bishop of Bizya was with them. Bishop Theodosius said to him:

**THEODOSIUS:** How are you, abba?

**MAXIMUS:** As God predetermined before all the ages that the providential dispensation concerning me should be, so I am.

**THEODOSIUS:** Did God therefore predetermine before every age the things concerning each individual?

**MAXIMUS:** If he foreknew them, he certainly also predetermined them.

**THEODOSIUS:** What is this that you assert, “he foreknew” and “he predetermined”?

**MAXIMUS:** Foreknowledge concerns the thoughts, words, and deeds that proceed from us; predestination concerns what does not happen from us.

**THEODOSIUS:** What are the things that proceed from us, and what are those that do not proceed from us?

**MAXIMUS:** As is evident, my lord, knowing everything, questions his servant to test him [Col. 0628B].

**THEODOSIUS:** By the truth of God, I asked in ignorance and wishing to learn the difference between the things that proceed from us and those that do not, and how some things exist under God’s foreknowledge while others exist under predestination.

**MAXIMUS:** Everything voluntary proceeds from us—that is, virtues and vices. What does not proceed from us is the imposition of punitive circumstances that befall us, or their opposites. For neither harmful illness nor joy-giving health proceeds from us, although the causes producing them do proceed from us: for example, intemperance is the cause of illness, just as temperance is the cause of health. The cause of the heavenly kingdom is observance of the commandments, just as transgression of them is the cause of eternal fire.

**THEODOSIUS:** Are you therefore suffering in this exile because you have done things worthy of this suffering?

**MAXIMUS:** I ask that God, through this suffering, measure my excesses, by which I sinned against him in transgressing his justifying commandments [Col. 0628C].

**THEODOSIUS:** Is suffering not also imposed upon many for the sake of testing?

**MAXIMUS:** The testing of the saints is so that their dispositions toward what is naturally good may be revealed through the sufferings of human life, making their virtues, unknown to all, known through themselves, as in Job and Joseph. One was tested for the manifestation of hidden courage; the other was tested for the disclosure of sanctifying chastity.

Every saint who is unwillingly afflicted in this age is afflicted under some such providence, so that, through the weakness permitted to trouble him [Col. 0628D], he may trample upon the proud and apostate dragon, that is, the devil. For patience is the work of testing in each of the saints.

**THEODOSIUS:** By the truth of God, you have spoken well, and I acknowledge the benefit. I have always desired to converse with you about such things. But since I and my lords, the future patricians, have come to you for another matter, and have traveled such great distances, we ask you to accept what is proposed by us and to make the whole inhabited world rejoice.

**MAXIMUS:** What are these things, my lord? Who am I, and from where do I come, that my agreement to what is proposed to me should make the whole inhabited world rejoice?

**THEODOSIUS:** By the truth of our Lord Jesus Christ, what I and my lords, the future patricians, tell you, we heard from the mouth of our lord the patriarch and the pious lord of the inhabited world [Col. 0630A].

**MAXIMUS:** Command, my lords, that they say what you wish and what you heard.

**THEODOSIUS:** The emperor and the patriarch ask through us to learn from you for what reason you do not communicate with the throne of Constantinople.

**MAXIMUS:** Do you have written authorization concerning this from the most pious emperor or from the patriarch?

**THEODOSIUS:** You should not, my lord, distrust us. Although I am insignificant, I am called a bishop, and these lords are members of the senate. We have not come to test you—far be it from us.

**MAXIMUS:** Whatever way brought you to your servant, I shall state without reserve the reason why I do not communicate with the throne of Constantinople. Even if it were proper for others to ask me for what reason, it is not proper for you, who know the reason more certainly than I do [Col. 0630B].

You know the innovations that arose from the sixth indiction of the previous cycle, beginning in Alexandria through the nine Chapters issued by Cyrus, who—I do not know how—was made president there, and which were confirmed by the throne of Constantinople. You know also the other alterations, additions, and subtractions made in council by Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, who presided over the Church of Byzantium. The whole inhabited world recognizes these as new inventions.

For this reason I, your servant, do not communicate with the Church of Constantinople. Let the stumbling-blocks placed by the aforesaid men be removed, together with those who placed them, as God said: “Throw the stones out of the way” [Jeremiah 50:26]. Then, when I find the level and well-worn road of the Gospel free from every thorny wickedness of heresy [Col. 0630C], I shall walk upon it without any human urging.

But while the presidents of Constantinople glory in the stumbling-blocks that have been placed and in those who placed them, no word or method can persuade me to communicate with them.

**THEODOSIUS:** Do we confess any evil, then, that you should separate yourself from our communion on this account?

**MAXIMUS:** You confuse the account of theology and of the dispensation by teaching one operation of the divinity and humanity of God and our Savior Jesus Christ. If we must believe the Fathers, who assert that those whose operation is one also possess one substance, you make the holy Trinity a quaternity [Col. 0630D], as though the flesh of the Word had become co-natural with him and lacked the natural kinship that it has with us and with her who gave him birth.

Again, by abolishing the operations and asserting one will of his divinity and humanity, you deprive him of the distribution of good things. If, according to those who decreed this, he has no operation, it is clear that, even if he wishes to have mercy, he cannot, since his operation of good things has been cut away. Apart from natural operation, nothing that exists can operate or act.

Moreover, you make the flesh, by will, co-creator with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit of all the ages and of the things in them; but by nature created—or, to speak more truly, without beginning in will, since the divine will is without beginning, as belonging to a divinity existing without beginning, while by nature it is recent [Col. 0632A]. This exceeds not only all understanding but also all impiety.

For you do not say simply that there is one will, but that it is divine. No one can conceive a temporal beginning or end of the divine will, any more than of the divine nature, whose substantial will it is.

Again, introducing another innovation, you altogether remove everything that signifies and establishes the divinity and humanity of Christ, decreeing by laws and types that neither one nor two wills or operations may be spoken of in him. This is an entity without essence.

Nothing that exists, if it is intellectual, is deprived of the power and operation of will; if sensory, of sensory operation; if vegetative, of the operation of growth and nourishment; and if entirely inanimate and without life in the customary sense, it is not without operation and aptitude.

All such things make themselves known by becoming available to the senses. Their operation is to present themselves to sight through appearance, to hearing through sound, to smell through some suitable odor, to taste through certain juices, and to touch through reciprocal impression. Just as we call seeing the operation of sight, so we call being seen the operation of visible things; and we observe all the rest to occur in the same way.

If, then, nothing that exists is entirely deprived of operation, while our Lord and God—be merciful, Lord!—has no natural will or operation in either of the natures from which, in which, and which he is [Col. 0632C], how can we be or be called worshipers of God if we say that the one worshiped by you as God exists in no way with will or operation?

The holy Fathers clearly teach us this when they say: [Note: [Col. 0631D] Dionysius, *On the Divine Names*.] “That which has no power neither exists, nor is anything, nor has any position whatsoever.”

**THEODOSIUS:** Do not take what was done for the sake of the dispensation as an established dogma.

**MAXIMUS:** If the dogma of those who accept this is not established, and if the Type that decrees and legislates that no will or operation of the Lord is to be spoken of—although their removal indicates the nonexistence of the one deprived of them—why did you hand me over without honor to barbarous and godless nations [Col. 0632D]? Why was I condemned to live at Bizya, while one of my fellow servants was sent to Perberis and the other to Mesembria?

**THEODOSIUS:** By God, who will judge me! When it was made I said, and I say the same now, that the Type was wrongly made and to the injury of many. The occasion for its publication was the mutual quarrel of the orthodox concerning wills and operations. In order that all might be at peace with one another, some judged that such expressions should be suppressed.

**MAXIMUS:** What faithful person accepts a dispensation that causes the expressions to be silenced which the God of all arranged to be spoken through apostles, prophets, and teachers? Let us examine, my great lord, to what evil this matter leads.

If God placed in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, and third teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, saying in the Gospel to the apostles and through them to those who came after them, “What I say to you I say to all” [Mark 13:37], and again, “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” [Matthew 10:40; Luke 10:16], it is manifest that whoever does not receive the apostles, prophets, and teachers, but rejects their words, rejects Christ himself.

Let us consider another matter. God chose and raised up apostles, prophets, and teachers for the perfecting of the saints. But the devil chose and raised up false apostles, false prophets, and false teachers against piety, so that both the ancient law and the Gospel might be attacked [Col. 0634B]. By false apostles, false prophets, and false teachers I understand only the heretics, whose words and thoughts are perverse.

Therefore, just as the one who receives the true apostles, prophets, and teachers receives God, so the one who receives the false apostles, prophets, and teachers receives the devil. Thus whoever expels the saints together with the wicked and unclean heretics—receive me as one speaking the truth—has plainly condemned God together with the devil.

If, then, by examining the innovations made in our times, we find that they have reached this supreme evil, see to it that, while pretending to make peace, we are not found to be suffering from and proclaiming the apostasy which the most holy Apostle said would precede the coming of Antichrist.

I have told you these things without reserve, my lords, so that you may spare yourselves and us. Do you command me, carrying these matters written in the book of my heart, to enter and communicate in the Church in which they are proclaimed, and to become a participant with those who truly expel God but falsely claim to expel the devil together with God?

May this never happen to me through God, who for my sake became what I am without sin. And, kneeling, he said: “Whatever you command me to do to your servant, do it. I shall never communicate with those who accept these things.”

[Col. 0634D]

As though chilled by what had been said, they bowed their heads and remained silent for a long time. Then Theodosius looked at Abba Maximus and said:

**THEODOSIUS:** We assure you on behalf of our lord the emperor that, if you communicate, he will abolish the Type.

**MAXIMUS:** We are still very far from one another. What shall we do about the statement of one will, confirmed synodically by Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, with the exclusion of every operation?

**THEODOSIUS:** That document has been laid aside and thrown away.

**MAXIMUS:** It has been laid aside from the stone walls, but not from intellectual souls. Let them accept the condemnation of these things issued synodically at Rome through pious doctrines and canons; then the dividing wall is dissolved, and we shall need no exhortation.

Bishop Theodosius said:

**THEODOSIUS:** The synod held at Rome is not confirmed, since it was held without the emperor’s command [Col. 0636A].

**MAXIMUS:** If imperial commands confirm the synods that are held, and not pious faith, then accept the synods held against the homoousion, since they were carried out by command of rulers: the first at Tyre, the second at Antioch, the third at Seleucia, the fourth at Constantinople under Eudoxius the Arian, the fifth at Nicaea in Thrace, the sixth at Sirmium, and after these, much later, the seventh, the second at Ephesus, presided over by Dioscorus. An imperial command assembled all these, yet all were condemned because of the impiety of the unbelieving doctrines they confirmed.

Why, then, do you not reject the synod that deposed Paul of Samosata, held under the holy and blessed Fathers Dionysius, pope of Rome, Dionysius of Alexandria, and Gregory the Wonderworker, who presided over that synod, since it was not held by an emperor’s command?

What canon decrees that only those synods are to be approved which were assembled by an emperor’s command? [Note: [Col. 0635D] The Greek reads here: “or that all synods should be assembled by an emperor’s command?”] The pious canon of the Church recognizes as holy and approved those synods which the correctness of their doctrines has approved.

Moreover, even if you assemble synods entirely by imperial command, the canon knows as holy and approved those which the correctness of doctrine has judged such. It also decrees, as my lord knows and teaches others, that synods be held twice each year in every province, without mentioning imperial command, for the protection of our saving faith and the correction of all matters that do not agree with the divine law of the Church.

[Col. 0636C]

Bishop Theodosius said:

**THEODOSIUS:** It is as you say: the correctness of doctrines strengthens the synods. Yet you do not accept the libellus of Menas, in which he dogmatized one will and one operation of Christ?

**MAXIMUS:** May the Lord God forbid! You do not accept them; rather, you expel all the teachers who, after the holy Council of Chalcedon, fought against the detestable heresy of Severus. And am I to accept the libellus of Menas, which was composed after the council and through which he is plainly perceived to side with Severus, Apollinarius, Macedonius, Arius, and every heresy, and to accuse the council—or rather completely reject it through what he dogmatized?

**THEODOSIUS:** What then? Do you utterly reject one operation?

**MAXIMUS:** And which of the approved teachers of the Church says there is one operation?

[Col. 0636D] And Theodosius produced writings which they falsely claimed to be by the saints Julius of Rome and Gregory the miracle-worker, together with testimonies of Athanasius, and read them aloud.

MAXIMUS said: “Let us now fear God, and let us not wish to provoke him by producing testimonies of heretics. No one is unaware that these statements belong to the impious Apollinarius. Therefore, if you have anything else, produce it. For by producing these you persuade everyone to believe all the more that you have revived the opinion of the impious Apollinarius and of those who shared his wicked views.”

The same bishop, THEODOSIUS, produced two testimonies under the name of Chrysostom. Recognizing them, Abba MAXIMUS said: “These are Nestorius’s, the man who madly taught a duality of persons in Christ.”

Immediately THEODOSIUS, burning with anger, said: “Lord monk, Satan has spoken through your unbridled mouth.”

MAXIMUS said: “May my lord not be angered against his servant.”

Then he at once took the texts and showed him that these were indeed Nestorius’s words, and identified the works in which they occurred.

THEODOSIUS said: “God knows, brother, the patriarch gave me these testimonies. But look: you have said that some of them belong to Apollinarius and others to Nestorius.”

When he had produced a testimony of Saint Cyril, which says, “Demonstrating one operation, kindred through both,” he said: “What do you say to this?”

MAXIMUS said: “Some people show that the phrase ‘proper to both’ was inserted into the interpretation of the Gospel made from this holy Father by Timothy the Cat. Nevertheless, let it be as you say. Let us examine, therefore, the meaning of the Fathers’ words and learn the truth.”

THEODOSIUS said: “I do not permit this to be done. You must accept the simple words as they stand.”

MAXIMUS said: “Please tell me the difference between the various expressions.”

THEODOSIUS said: “You must accept the expression exactly as it stands, and must not examine its meaning.”

MAXIMUS said: “Clearly, then, you are introducing new and foreign laws into the Church even concerning words. If, according to you, it is not proper to examine the words of Scripture and of the Fathers, we must cast away all Scripture, both the Old and the New. For I have heard David say: ‘Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart’ (Psalm XVIII, 2), especially since no one can seek God without examination. And again: ‘Give me understanding, and I shall examine your law and keep it with my whole heart’ (ibid., 34). He urges those worthy of it, with desire, to keep it wholeheartedly through the fulfilment of the holy commandments contained in it, as though examination leads to knowledge of the law and of understanding. And again: ‘Wonderful are your testimonies; therefore my soul has examined them’ (ibid., 129).

“What, moreover, does the proverbial saying wish us to understand by commanding us to examine parables, riddles, and obscure sayings? What does the Lord wish his disciples to understand when he speaks in parables and teaches them the meaning of the parables? What also does he mean when he commands: ‘Examine the Scriptures’ (John V, 39), since they bear witness concerning him? What does the chief of the apostles, Peter, wish to teach when he says that ‘the prophets sought and examined’ the salvation (I Peter I, 10)? And what does the divine apostle Paul mean when he says: ‘If the Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, among whom the god of this age has blinded the eyes of their minds, so that the illumination of the knowledge of Christ does not shine upon them’ (II Corinthians III, 6)?

“It appears that you wish us to be like the Jews, who, clinging to simple words—as you call them—that is, to the letter alone, as though crushing the mind beneath a massive weight, were torn away from the truth while having a veil over their hearts, so that they would not understand the spirit which truly exists and is concealed in the letter. Hence he also says: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life’ (II Corinthians III, 6). Let my lord be certain that I will in no way agree to accept a word without the meaning contained in it, lest I become an evident Jew.”

[Col. 0640A] When THEODOSIUS heard this, he said: “We must speak of one subsistential operation of Christ.”

MAXIMUS said: “Let us consider the evil that will arise from this, and let us flee this foreign expression. It belongs only to heretics who worship a multitude of gods. For if we call Christ’s operation subsistential, since the Son is never subsistentially adapted to the Father and the Spirit, there can be no doubt that neither will his operation be subsistentially adapted to them. We shall be compelled to attribute subsistential operations to the Father and the Spirit as well as to the Son. According to you, therefore, the blessed divinity will have four operations: three distinguishing the persons in whom it exists, and one common operation signifying the communion that belongs by nature to the three subsistences. And, according to the Fathers—if we accept their teaching only in this respect—we shall become afflicted with a divided fourfold deity.

“For they determine that every operation is natural, not subsistential. And if this is true, as it truly is, we shall appear to be asserting four natures and four gods, differing from one another in subsistence and in nature. Yet who has ever said, or conceived, that any one of those things gathered under a certain form and defined by nature under a common definition of the species possesses an operation separately? For what is common to a nature can never become the property of one individual alone.

“Subsistential characteristics—for example, the length or shortness of the nose, the whiteness of the eyes, baldness, and whatever else is similar—are accidents that distinguish individuals numerically from one another. [Col. 0640C] Every human being, insofar as he exists as something according to nature, but not insofar as he is a particular person, is recognized as operating according to the categorical account, which is understood and spoken both individually and commonly. For example, ‘rational animal’ is a general definition according to our understanding.

“We all possess the same life, the same rationality, bending and straightening, sitting and standing, speaking and keeping silent, seeing and hearing, touching—activities belonging to reason, which are understood commonly in us. Therefore we must not introduce new expressions that possess no authority from either holy Scripture or the Fathers, nor anything natural, but are foreign inventions devised by human cunning. Nevertheless, show me this expression in any Father, and then let us examine the meaning of the one who used it.”

THEODOSIUS said: “What then? Is it not altogether necessary to say that Christ has one operation?”

MAXIMUS said: “According to holy Scripture and the holy Fathers, we have not undertaken to say anything of the kind. Rather, just as we have been commanded to believe and confess that Christ has two natures, from which he exists and which he is, so also we must confess his natural wills and operations, appropriate to him, since he is by nature God and at the same time the same person is man.”

THEODOSIUS said: “Truly, lord, we too confess both the natures and the distinct operations—that is, the divine and the human—and the deity with its will, as well as the humanity with its will, since his soul in no way existed without a will. But we do not say ‘two,’ lest we introduce him as fighting against himself.”

MAXIMUS said: “So, when you say that there are two natures, do you introduce them as opposed to one another because of the number?”

THEODOSIUS said: “No.”

MAXIMUS said: “So, when number is assigned to the natures, does it not divide them, but when it is spoken of with respect to wills and operations, does it possess the power of division?”

THEODOSIUS said: “Certainly, in those matters it entails division. The Fathers did not speak of number with respect to wills and operations, avoiding division; but they said ‘one and another,’ and ‘divine and human,’ ‘twofold’ and ‘double.’ What they said, I say; what they acknowledged, I acknowledge.”

MAXIMUS said: “For the Lord’s sake! If someone says to you ‘one and another,’ how many do you understand? Or, if he says ‘twofold’ or ‘double,’ how many do you understand?”

THEODOSIUS said: “I know how I understand it; but I do not say ‘two.’”

Then Abba MAXIMUS turned to the officials and said: “For the Lord’s sake! If you heard someone say ‘one and one,’ or ‘one and another,’ or ‘twice two,’ or ‘twice five,’ what would you understand and answer those who said this?”

They replied: “Since you have adjured us, we understand ‘one and one’ as two; ‘one and another’ as two; ‘twice two’ as four; and likewise ‘twice five’ as ten.”

THEODOSIUS, somewhat abashed by their answer, said: “What was not said by the Fathers, I do not say.”

Abba MAXIMUS immediately took the book containing the acts of the holy and apostolic Roman synod and showed that the holy Fathers explicitly spoke of two wills and operations of our Saviour and God Jesus Christ. The consul Theodosius took the book from him and read it, together with all the testimonies of the holy Fathers.

Then THEODOSIUS the bishop replied: “God knows: if this synod had not imposed anathemas on persons, I would have accepted it more than any man. But let us not delay here. Whatever the Fathers said, I say, and I shall immediately put in writing two natures, two wills, and two operations. Come in, share communion with us, and let unity be established.”

MAXIMUS said: “Lord, I do not dare to accept from you a written agreement on such a matter, since I am merely a monk. But since God has stirred you to repentance, [Note: [Col. 0641D] Insert from the Greek: ‘so that you might receive the words of the holy Fathers, as the rule of the Church requires, write concerning this matter to the bishop of Rome,’ etc. SIRM.] send it in writing—that is, the emperor, the patriarch, and their synod must do so. For even after these things have been done, I do not communicate while the anathematized are recited during the holy offering; I fear the condemnation of the anathema.”

THEODOSIUS said: “God knows, I do not blame you for being afraid, nor does anyone else. But, for the Lord’s sake, give us advice as to whether this can be done.”

MAXIMUS said: “What advice can I give you about this? Go and investigate whether anything of this kind has ever been done: whether, after his death, anyone was released from a charge incurred in a matter of faith, and from the accusation or condemnation brought against him. Let the emperor and the patriarch agree to imitate God’s condescension. Let the emperor send a supplicatory imperial order, and let the patriarch send a synodical petition to the pope of Rome. And certainly, if a practice is found that is undoubtedly ecclesiastical and prescribes this, he will agree with you on the matter because of your correct confession.”

[Col. 0644A] THEODOSIUS said: “This is indeed done. But give me your word that, if they send me, you will come with me.”

MAXIMUS said: “Lord, it is more expedient for you to take with you my fellow servant who is in Mesembria rather than me. He knows the language, and they will respect him more honorably because he has been tortured for so many years for God’s sake and for the true faith maintained in their see.”

THEODOSIUS said: “We have just had various quarrels with one another, and for that reason I am not pleased to proceed with him.”

MAXIMUS said: “Lord, since it has now seemed right that this should be done, let the outcome be what has been anticipated, and I shall follow wherever you command.”

At this, they all rose with joy and tears. They knelt upon the ground, and prayer was offered. Each of them venerated the holy Gospels, the precious cross, the image of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ, [Col. 0644B] and that of our Lady who gave him birth, the most holy Mother of God. They also laid their hands upon them as confirmation of what had been done.

After they had spoken together for a little while about the life lived according to God and the observance of the divine commandments, THEODOSIUS the bishop turned to Abbot Maximus and said: “Look, all scandals have been removed, peace has been made through God, and it will continue. But, for the Lord’s sake, do not conceal this from me: do you not in any way say that Christ has one will and one operation?”

MAXIMUS said: “It is not possible for me ever to say this. I give the reason: it is foreign to the holy Fathers to say that the two distinct natures have one will and operation. Moreover, in every possible way, whoever says this will rightly encounter error.

“First, if I call it natural, I fear confusion. Second, if I call it subsistential, I separate him from the Father and the Holy Spirit, and I shall appear to introduce three wills corresponding to one another, just as there are three subsistences. Third, if I say that, as though belonging to one, there is one will and operation, I am compelled also to say that the Father’s will and operation and, as though belonging to one, the Spirit’s will and operation exist—even if I do not wish to do so—and the statement will be found to have fallen into a plurality of gods. Fourth, if I call it affectual, I introduce the personal division of Nestorius. Fifth, if I call it beyond nature, I corrupt the existence of the will. For what is beyond nature is a corruption of nature, as the Fathers have said.”

THEODOSIUS said: “We must in every respect say that our Saviour has one will because of the union, as Sergius and Pyrrhus—and, as I think, correctly understanding the matter—have written.”

MAXIMUS said: “If you command, lord, accept two arguments from me on this subject.

“First, if, because of the union, one will of our God and Saviour was produced, as Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul have written, then according to them the Son will have a will different from the Father because of nature, but not because of the union, since the Son possesses a will—unless union and nature are the same thing.

“Second, if, according to them, one will of our Saviour was produced because of the union, then it will certainly have the union itself as its cause, and not another of the natures from which he exists. According to them, therefore, the will will plainly belong to affect, not to nature; but reason grounded in truth recognizes nature, not affect.

“Third, if, as they have acknowledged, one will of our Saviour was produced because of the union, by what will do they say that the union itself was produced? For surely they will not admit that it was produced by that will which was produced through it, if they devote themselves to the truth and flee what is irrational.

“Fourth, if one will of our Saviour was produced because of the union, it is plainly evident that before the union he either existed with many wills or entirely without a will. If he possessed many wills, he suffered a diminution of those many wills, having been contracted into one will, and underwent an evident changeability through the diminution of the many wills naturally belonging to him. But if he was altogether without a will, the union has shown itself to be better than nature, since through it he acquired a will which nature lacked. [Note: [Col. 0645D] The Greek reads: ‘and again he showed himself changeable, acquiring by habit what was not naturally present in him.’]

“And again he plainly demonstrated that what was not naturally present in him was acquired through affect. Fifth, if one will of our Saviour, according to both elements from which he exists, was produced because of the union, then God, while remaining by nature eternal, became newly made by will through the union; and man, while remaining without beginning by will, became newly made by nature. This is impossible, not to call it impious.

“Sixth, if one will of the natures was produced because of the union, [Note: [Col. 0646D] Read from the Greek: ‘Why, for the same reason, was not one nature of the natures made?’ SIRM.] was anything at all made one nature of the natures for the same reason?”

[Col. 0646C] At this point THEODOSIUS the bishop interrupted the force of the discussion that had been taking place and said: “What, then, does ‘because of the union’ mean, if none of these things was done because of it?”

MAXIMUS said: “It showed, without falsehood, that the one who had been without flesh had become incarnate, and clearly demonstrated that the one who is by nature God and creator of all had by nature become man—not through a change of nature or a diminution of anything belonging to nature, but through the true assumption of intellectually ensouled flesh, that is, of an undiminished humanity, free from every ancestral sin according to nature.

“And what is truly wondrous according to the account of salvation, and to be held in great amazement by all, is this: God wholly in human beings, while remaining complete within his own properties; and man wholly in divine things, while remaining the same man in full, not falling away from his own properties. For, according to the teaching of our God-speaking Fathers, the mutual reception of the natures and of the natural properties belonging to them was brought about because of the union—not a transference or a fall. Those who wickedly produce confusion call this ‘oneness,’ and therefore introduce confusion in many ways through their innovations; because of their abandonment of consistency in their own reasoning, they persecute the godly.”

When he heard this, THEODOSIUS the bishop appeared, together with the others who had come with him, to have accepted what had been said.

Again the same bishop said to Abbot Maximus: “Do me the kindness of explaining what you said to us: that no one operates as a particular person, but as a nature. For what was said is unclear to me.”

MAXIMUS said: “No one operates as a particular person, but as a nature. For example, Peter and Paul operate, but not ‘Petrine’ and ‘Pauline’; rather, they operate humanly, since both are naturally human according to the common and defining account of nature, but not subsistentially, according to what each does in his own particularity.

“Likewise, Michael and Gabriel operate, but not ‘Michaelically’ or ‘Gabrielically’; rather, they operate angelically, since both are angels. And so, in every nature that includes many individuals numerically, we observe a common operation, though not one that has been annihilated. Therefore, whoever says ‘subsistential operation’ introduces the nature itself, although it is one, as having been made infinite in its operations and differentiated according to the multitude of individuals brought under it. If we admit this as sound, we destroy within every nature the account of how it exists.”

After these words, while they were kissing one another, THEODOSIUS the consul said: “Look, everything has been set right. Do you think the emperor will agree to issue a supplicatory order?”

Abba MAXIMUS said: “Certainly, if he wishes to imitate God and humble himself with him for the common salvation of us all, considering that if God, who saves by nature, did not save until he willingly humbled himself, how will a man, who must be saved by nature, either be saved or save others without humbling himself?”

THEODOSIUS the consul said: “I hope that, if God saves me and grants me remembrance, I shall say this very argument to him, and he will agree.”

After they had exchanged greetings, they departed in peace. The bishop gave Abbot Maximus a certain amount of money, a tunic, and a cloak, which had been sent to him. The bishop of Bizye immediately took away the tunic, at that very hour. But in Regium they took from him not only the amount of money given to him, but also whatever else he appeared to possess through the generosity of certain people, together with the rest of his poor belongings and clothing.

After the aforementioned men had departed on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the present fifteenth indiction, the consul Paul again went out to Bizye, bringing an order for Abbot Maximus in the following form:

“ We command Your Glory to go to Bizye and bring the monk Maximus with great honour and courtesy, both because of his old age and infirmity and because he belonged to our ancestors and was honoured by them. Place him in the venerable monastery of Saint Theodore, which lies near Regium. Then come and report to us. We shall send to him, on our behalf, two patricians who are to declare to him what pleases us—men who love us sincerely and are loved by us. Then come and announce his arrival to us.”

Accordingly, when the same consul had brought him and placed him in the monastery already named, he returned to make his report.

On the following day the patricians Epiphanius and Troilus came to him with much pomp and display, together with Bishop Theodosius. They went up to him in the catechumenium of the church of that monastery. After making the customary greeting, they sat down and compelled him also to sit. TROILUS began the speech addressed to him and said:

“The lord of the world has commanded us to come to you and tell you what has seemed good to his divinely strengthened empire. But first tell us whether you will carry out the emperor’s command or not.”

MAXIMUS said: “Lord, I shall hear what his pious authority has commanded and shall necessarily answer. For what answer can I give to something unknown to me?”

TROILUS persisted, insisting: “It is impossible for us to say anything unless you first tell us whether you will carry out the emperor’s command or not.”

When Abba MAXIMUS saw that they were pressing him more and more to give his answer, looking at him more bitterly and replying more harshly, together with all who were with them, while even their secular dignities had made them haughty, he answered:

“Since you do not allow your servant to hear what pleases our lord and emperor, I say, with God, the holy angels, and all of you listening, that whatever he commands me concerning any matter connected with the destruction and corruption of this world, I will readily do.”

Immediately TROILUS rose and said: “Pray for me; I am leaving. This man does nothing.”

After a great and violent tumult, with much disturbance and confusion, Bishop THEODOSIUS said to them: “Give him the answers and learn what he professes. For it is not reasonable to return in this way, saying nothing and hearing nothing.”

Then the patrician EPIPHANIUS said: “The emperor conveys this message to you through us. He says: ‘Since the entire West, and those in the East who are causing disturbances, look to you, and since all are stirring up disputes because of you, refusing to agree with us in the matter of faith, may God bring you to repentance, so that you may share communion with us in the Type which we have issued. We shall go out ourselves to Chalcedon, kiss you, place our hand beneath yours, and bring you into the Great Church with all honour and glory. We shall stand together with you where emperors customarily stand, celebrate the synaxis together, and partake of the undefiled and life-giving mysteries of the life-giving body and blood of Christ. We shall again proclaim you our father, and there will be joy not only in our Christ-loving imperial city, but throughout the whole world. For we know with complete certainty that, once you communicate with this holy throne, all who have separated themselves from our communion because of you and your teaching will be united with us.’”

Abba MAXIMUS turned to the bishop and said with tears: “Great lord, we all await the day of judgment. You know what has been ordered and defined over the holy Gospels, the life-giving cross, the image of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ, and that of the most holy ever-virgin Mother who gave him birth.”

The bishop lowered his face and said to him in a gentler voice: “What am I to do, now that something else has seemed preferable?”

MAXIMUS said to him: “Why did you touch the holy Gospels, and why did those who were with you do so, when there is no fulfilment among you of what was said?”

Indeed, not even the whole power of heaven could have persuaded me to do this. What account would I have to render—to God, not to mention to my own conscience—if, for the sake of human glory, which according to its own nature possesses no substance capable of saving, I were to deny the faith that sustains it?”

At these words all of them rose, rendered unstable by anger, and weakened him with tearing, pushing, and dragging, competing with one another to drench him in spittle from head to toe. Until the garments in which he was clothed had been washed, a stench from them spread far around.

The bishop rose and said: “This should not have happened. They should merely have heard his answer, entered, and reported it to our good lord. Canonical matters are arranged in another way.”

When the bishop had barely persuaded them to be quiet, they sat down again. After disgracing him with ten thousand insults and unimaginable curses, EPIPHANIUS said in great fury and harshness:

“Speak, ultimate scoundrel, devourer of citizens! Do you regard us, our city, and even the emperor as heretics, that you have uttered these words? In truth, we are more Christian and orthodox than you, and we confess that our Lord and God possesses both a divine will and a human will, and an intellectual soul. Every intellectual nature naturally possesses willing and acting, since motion is proper to life and will is proper to intellect. We recognize the capacity of his will not only according to his divinity, [Col. 0652C] but also according to his humanity. Indeed, we do not deny that he has two wills and two operations.”

Abba MAXIMUS replied: “If you believe in this way, as do the intellectual natures and the Church of God, why do you compel me to communicate in the Type, which contains only the division of those things that you yourselves profess?”

EPIPHANIUS said: “This was done for the sake of the dispensation, so that people of this kind would not be harmed by more precise expressions.”

Abba MAXIMUS replied: “On the contrary, every person is sanctified through a strict confession of the faith, not through the division placed in the Type.”

TROILUS said: “I told you in the Palace that it did not abolish them, but ordered them to be silent, so that we might all enjoy peace.”

Abba MAXIMUS replied: “Silence concerning words is the abolition of words. For through the Prophet the Holy Spirit says: ‘There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard’ (Psalm XVIII, 3). Therefore a statement that is not proclaimed in speech does not exist at all.”

TROILUS said: “Keep it in your heart as you wish; no one prevents you.”

Abba MAXIMUS said: “But God did not confine the whole of salvation to the heart when he said: ‘Whoever does not confess me before men, neither will I confess him before my Father who is in heaven’ (Matthew X, 33). And the holy Apostle teaches, saying: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ (Romans X, 10). If God, and God’s prophets and apostles, command the mystery of the saints to be confessed in words—a mystery that is great, dreadful, and saving for the whole world—then the voice that proclaims it must not in any way be silenced, lest the salvation of those who remain silent be diminished.”

EPIPHANIUS replied with an even harsher word: “Did you sign the libellus?”

Abba MAXIMUS said: “Yes, I signed it.”

EPIPHANIUS said: “And how did you dare to sign and anathematize those who confess and believe as do the intellectual natures and the Catholic Church? In truth, in my judgment we shall bring you into the city, set you bound in the marketplace, and bring actors, actresses, prostitutes, harlots, and the whole populace, so that each man and woman may strike you in the face and spit upon you.”

Abba MAXIMUS replied: “Let it be as you have said, if we have anathematized those who confess two natures, wills, and operations in him who is by nature truly God and at the same time man. Read, lord, the record of the proceedings and the libellus; if you find that it is as you have said, do whatever you wish. For I, my fellow servants, and all who signed anathematized those who, following Arius and Apollinarius, say that there is one will and one operation, not those who confess our Lord and God as intellectual in both and from both, and who confess that, according to each nature, he possesses the will and operation proper to our salvation.”

They said: “If we discuss this with him, we shall neither eat nor drink. Let us rise, dine, enter, and report what we have heard. This man has sold himself to Satan.”

When they had risen, they dined. Then they entered in anger during the vigil of the Exaltation of the precious and life-giving cross.

On the following day, at dawn, the consul Theodosius went out to the aforementioned Abbot Maximus and took away everything he possessed, saying to him in the emperor’s name:

“Because you did not wish for honour, it has been withdrawn from you. Go wherever you have judged yourself worthy to be, also bearing the judgment of your disciples—both the one who is in Mesembria and the one who is in Perberis, who was the notary of our grandmother of blessed memory.”

The patricians, Troilus and Epiphanius, had also said: “By every means we shall bring both your disciples as well—the one in Mesembria and the one in Perberis—and we shall test them too and see their outcome.”

“Nevertheless, so that you may know, Lord Abba, if we have even a little respite from the confusion of the nations, we shall be joined to you through the Holy Trinity. We shall remove the present pope, and all who speak there, as well as the rest of your disciples and all of you; we shall melt down all of you, each one in the place suited to him, just as Martin was melted down.”

The aforementioned consul Theodosius then took him and handed him over to soldiers, who led him as far as Salembria.

They remained there for two days, until one of the soldiers went to the camp and told the entire army that the monk who blasphemed the Mother of God had arrived there. They did this to stir up the army against the aforementioned Abbot Maximus, as though he had blasphemed the Mother of God.

[Col. 0656A] After two days the soldier returned, took him into the camp, and the praetor—or rather the praetor’s locum tenens—was moved by God. He sent to him the commanders of the bands, [Note: [Col. 0655D] That is, the standard-bearers. Hence *bandera*, or standard.] together with priests, deacons, and venerable guardians of the standards.

When the aforementioned Abba Maximus saw that they had arrived, he rose and made a *metanoia*. [Note: [Col. 0655D] He made a *metanoia*—Greek: μετάνοιαν ἔβαλε—that is, he knelt and prostrated himself.] They likewise returned the gesture, and they sat down, ordering him also to sit.

A certain very old and honourable man said to him reverently:

“Father, since certain people have scandalized us concerning your holiness, saying that you do not call our Lady, the most holy Virgin, the Mother of God, I adjure you by the holy and consubstantial Trinity: tell us the truth and remove this scandal from our hearts, lest we be unjustly harmed by having been scandalized.”

He made another *metanoia*, then rose and, stretching his hands toward heaven, said with tears:

“Let the one who does not call our Lady, most praiseworthy, most holy, undefiled, and worthy of veneration by every intellectual nature, truly the natural mother of God who made heaven, earth, and the sea and all that is in them, be anathema and accursed by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the consubstantial and supersubstantial Trinity; by every heavenly power; by the choir of the holy apostles and prophets; by the innumerable multitude of the holy martyrs; and by every spirit perfected in righteousness, now and always and unto the ages of ages. Amen.”

They all prayed for him with tears, saying: “May God strengthen you, Father, and make you worthy to complete this course without offence.”

[Col. 0656C] After these words, many soldiers gathered to hear the many good words that were being spoken. When one of the praetor’s household saw that a large crowd was assembling and that the army was gathering, and reproved what was happening—God knows what he suspected—he ordered him to be seized and sent outside the camp, two miles away, until those who were to lead him to Perberis had assembled and arrived.

But the clerics, moved by divine love, went on foot those two miles, came to him, greeted him, and prayed for him. Carrying him in their arms, they placed him upon a beast, then returned peacefully to their own stations. He himself was brought to Perberis, to the custody in which he was continually subjected to vexations.

[Col. 0656D] It must also be known that in Regium Troilus maintained to Abbot Maximus that the councillor John had written to him about certain events, advising him concerning them and approving them, although the disorder of your disciples had meanwhile prevented this from being done. I think, however, that the aforementioned councillor John did not write to Troilus, but to the monk Menna, and that Menna subsequently reported it to the members of the Palace.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Anastasius did not give this passage, nor does it belong to the *Collation*. Nevertheless, because it is joined to the work, we append it from Combefis’s edition of the *Works of Saint Maximus*. SIRM.]

After they had brought those men to Constantinople, instituted proceedings against them, and made them anathematize and curse Saint Maximus and his disciple, the blessed Anastasius, as well as the most holy pope Martin, Saint Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, and all the orthodox—indeed, all who held the same opinion as they did—they also brought forward the other blessed Anastasius. Having used against him the same curses and insults, they handed him over to the judges, saying:

“Therefore, Anastasius, clothed in the garment of the curses and imprecations of the whole people, released from canonical hearing and expelled from it, may you be conveyed to the station and seat of Gehenna that you have chosen. The most noble and sacred senate, which is with us and governs everything by common counsel, will immediately take up the judgment, and will inflict upon you, as it sees fit, the punishment prescribed by the civil laws, in just retribution for those great blasphemies of yours and the machinations of your rebellious spirit.

“For the present synod has rendered this sentence against you. Since, by the help of omnipotent Christ, our true God, it has sanctioned against you, Maximus, Anastasius, and Anastasius, the decree that was appropriate, and since what remains is that you be subjected to the harsher penalties of the laws for the impious things you have said and done—although, because no such penalty exists as could appear proportionate to your crimes and blasphemies, we entrust you to the just judge who will impose something greater—in this present age, as though some gain were being granted you, we allow you the use of life, and, by this leniency, temporarily leave vacant the exacting discipline and severity of the laws.

“We decree, therefore, that, immediately taking with us the most illustrious prefect who is present, he shall bring Maximus and both Anastasii to the praetorium of his most exalted authority, beat their backs with rods, and cut out from the root the organ of your insolence—namely, the blasphemous tongue of Maximus and of both Anastasii—which served your blasphemous reasoning and mind. Then let him also cut off with a sword the right hand that ministered to your blasphemous thought. After he has thus led you about, mutilated in those accursed limbs, and traversed all twelve districts of the august city, let him consign you to perpetual exile and unceasing custody, so that thereafter, and for as long as life remains to you, you may mourn your errors full of blasphemy, the curses and imprecations you devised against us having been turned back upon your own heads.”

The prefect accordingly took them and, after subjecting them to other tortures, amputated their limbs. Then he dragged them shamefully through the whole city and banished them to Lazica.

[Note: [Col. 0657] Anastasius either added this himself or translated it from the Greek of another. SIRM.]

Glory to you, only-begotten God, Word of the Father, and one of the consubstantial Trinity, who strengthen and make wise in the Holy Spirit those who, for your sake, are driven out and suffer with you in word and deed. But those who are your enemies—and truly and properly the enemies of your ever-virgin mother—and slanderers of the truth, you always put to shame.

Glory to you, holy Trinity, uncreated, eternal, without beginning, infinite, unchangeable, [Col. 0658D] supersubstantial, and indivisible, our God. Glory to you, glory to you, glory to you, the same and only Trinity, hope and salvation of all who worship you in orthodox faith and serve you in truth unto the end.

Only undefiled and most holy one, truly by nature and without falsehood the Mother of God, and after giving birth again truly a chaste Virgin, help us.

[Col. 0659]

# Letter of Anastasius the Presbyter and Apocrisarius of Rome to Theodosius, Presbyter of Gangra

[Col. 0659A] A copy of the autograph letter of our holy Father and teacher Anastasius, presbyter and apocrisarius of Rome, a senior of great renown, a new confessor—or, what must more truly be acknowledged, a great combatant and martyr for the truth—written, together with the sacred testimonies and syllogisms appended below, by his holy right hand after it had been cut off, through altogether admirable ingenuity—or rather by divine power and grace—after he himself and the Fathers who were with him had suffered in wretched Byzantium solely for the word of truth, because they had refused—or, more accurately, had been unable—to communicate with them in their openly displayed perfidy and manifest impiety. This accords with the holy and great Gregory in theology [Note: [Col. 0659D] *Oration* 25], who, in the sermon that he delivered against himself, addresses the Arians:

“Some beasts we released upon the bodies of the saints, because certain men made their inhumanity public, making against them only one charge: that they would not yield to impiety or defile themselves by communion with it. They fled from that communion as from the serpent’s poison, which does not injure the body but darkens the deepest parts of the soul.”

It was sent from the third exile, namely Lazica, to Theodosius, presbyter of Gangra and monk established in the holy city of our Christ.

## Address

To my lord, in every respect most holy, God-honored spiritual father and teacher, Theodosius the presbyter: Anastasius, a humble presbyter and monk by the mercy of God, servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 0659C] Proverbs, inspired by God, commands us to make the memory of the righteous with praises. I, then, a humble man, wishing at the present time to commemorate those righteous men in my speech, and especially Maximus, truly *megistos*—for this is what the name Maximus signifies—and being wholly unable worthily to praise his virtue and knowledge, as well as his martyrdom accomplished for Christ our God, have considered it sufficient to signify by this letter to Your God-honored Reverences what you yourselves, as I have learned, have especially desired to know: namely, when those blessed men fell asleep in the Lord.

I therefore make known to you, passing over in silence many of the evils inflicted upon us here—because of their number, the weariness of speaking about them, and the inopportune time—that when we came to the region of the friends of Christ, the Lazicans, on the sixth day before the Ides of June of the fifth indiction, they immediately separated us from one another by order of the man who at that time had perhaps deserved to preside over those who were there. They plundered everything, down to a single needle and thread, whatever we had acquired for necessary use from you and from other friends of Christ.

As for that most sacred man, my lord Maximus the abbot, because he was unable to sit either on a pack saddle or in a vehicle, since he was ill, they wove rods together into something resembling a litter, carried him on it, and shut him up in a fortress called Schemari, near the people known as the Alans. They placed Lord Anastasius the abbot and me, a sinner, on horses and led us away. They confined him in the fortress called Scotori, in Apsilia, which lies near Abasgia; but they confined me in another fortress named Buculus, in the region called Mesimiana, on the borders of the aforementioned Alans. That fortress is known to be presently held by those same Alans after they captured it.

Then, after a few days, they removed both me and the blessed Anastasius from the fortresses just mentioned. They sent him to a fortress called Suania, when he was already half-dead, both from the multitude of tortures and beatings that we had endured in Byzantium and from the hardships and distresses inflicted upon us here. Accordingly, he died in the middle of the journey, as some say; according to others, he died as soon as he had been shut up in the fortress of Suania to which he had been assigned.

I therefore infer that he fell asleep in the Lord around the eleventh or ninth day before the Kalends of August. For on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August we were both led, by order of the ruler at that time, to a place called Mucurisin, to be presented in the midst of the army of the friends of Christ. By then he was already, as I said, half-dead, and from that moment I never saw him again. They immediately sent him, as stated, to the fortress of Suania, while they sent me to the fortress called Thacyria, near Iberia. Hence I conclude that he fell asleep in the Lord around the eleventh or ninth day before the Kalends of August of the fifth indiction, as I have said.

Moreover, the martyr of Christ our God, namely Lord Maximus the abbot, while he was confined in the fortress mentioned above, received a divine vision. He summoned certain people who were in the fortress and said to them:

“On the thirteenth day of this coming month of August, of the fifteenth [Note: [Col. 0661D] *Fifth*, as Combefis corrects it.] indiction, on the seventh day of the week, the Lord will take me.”

And so it happened. On the thirteenth day of the aforesaid month of August of the past fifth indiction, on the seventh day of the week, in accordance with his divine prophecy, he left behind those who were present and departed to the Lord.

There is also another miracle divinely accomplished at his holy tomb. Those who inhabit that fortress and the surrounding region see and proclaim it to the present day, and it has even reached certain rulers and dignitaries. It is worthy that it be made known by letter to Your Most Holy Reverences and through you to all the holy men who are there, for the glory and praise of God, who works wonders in his saints and glorifies the memory of those who glorify him in orthodox and sincere faith.

The matter is this: three lamps that give light illuminate the tomb of that holy martyr Maximus on each successive night.

I have briefly recorded these things concerning this memorable man and the blessed Anastasius for Your God-honored Reverences, and through you for the whole holy Church of God that dwells there in right faith, so that, having learned them, you too may glorify God, who is wondrous in his saints.

In the meantime, I shall likewise make known in very few words what happened to me, a sinner and humble man, afterward, and the condition in which I now am. After I had spent two months in the aforementioned fortress of Thacyria, lying ill and having obtained a little rest, the ruler at that time again sent me to the regions of Apsilia and Mesimiana, to be confined in the fortress of Phustas.

To speak plainly, for seven months he led me about and dragged me through all the regions mentioned above, naked, barefoot, on foot, and oppressed by cold, hunger, and thirst, evidently wishing to remove me also from this life. But God, who brings all things to fulfillment by his saving providence, foresaw—I do not know what—concerning me, a humble man, and preserved me until now in this life of many tribulations and misery.

After some days the aforementioned ruler was driven from there. Another succeeded him and appeared to show compassion. During this period he took me from the fortress of Phustas and lodged me near his own house. After a year, however, moved by diabolical action, he sent me to the fortress mentioned above.

Meanwhile, as they were leading me to the fortress just named, it happened that he was again expelled and became a fugitive in the place where he had been the first time. God stirred up his spirit in a man zealous for good, who possessed within himself both fear and love of God and, truly *pheronymously* [Note: [Col. 0661D] Greek *pheronymōs*, “appropriately named,” corresponding to the name Gregory, which means “watchful”], possessed a mind watchful according to God. He now presides over the region with God.

Moved by a God-imitating condescension, or compassion, he brought me back from the road to the frequently mentioned fortress of Schemari and settled me about five [Note: [Col. 0662D] *milliaria*, “miles.”] markers away from his house, which is divinely guarded, in a place truly suitable for monks, providing most generously the necessities of bodily life.
