For all these things, may Christ, the true God, through the intercessions of Mary, the Mother of God and ever-virgin, who gave him birth according to the flesh, and of all the saints, protect him together with his beloved children and their honorable and altogether praiseworthy mother from every troop of the malicious and from the multitude of those who work iniquity. May he grant them refreshment in good things, so that, always possessing complete sufficiency, they may abound in every good work; may he make them worthy of the station that will be on the right, and grant them to hear that divine and wondrous voice which will say:

“Come, you blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, for I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25:34–35),

and the rest. Amen.

I entreat Your Most Holy Reverences to ask for the same things for them in your holy prayers, especially when you pray in holy and venerable places. For they are worthy of receiving these things from you. They are the natural sons of the holy Anastasia of Christ our God.

Finally, when Stephen, who is among the holy ones—the son of the blessed John the presbyter, who had been treasurer of that most holy Church—came to this region, as I have said, to seek out my humility, they received and honored him with every zeal and joy and provided every assistance at my request [Note: [Col. 0662D] Combefis reads “assistance” (*subventionem*).], as they would certainly have done for a man of the holy Anastasia of Christ our God. Thus, with their assistance, that holy Stephen found me. May the Lord God show mercy to him on that day, when he is the just judge, and also to those who sent him, since he truly performed the work of an evangelist.

For just as a spiritual horse, carrying its rider—God himself—according to the Scripture that says, “You mounted your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Habakkuk 3:8), traversed all Lazica, Apsilia, and Abasgia without fear, proclaiming both the things of truth and the innovations that had been introduced, so his presence became a cause of usefulness and salvation for many, as well as of my own rest and consolation. It also destroyed the wicked name that the true apostates had imposed upon us, and made the truth evident to many.

After correcting these matters by his personal arrival, that noble man fell asleep in the Lord on the Kalends of January of the eighth indiction, which has just passed, at the home of the friend of Christ, the ruler of Abasgia. All who knew him desired for him rest as for a saint.

Therefore some of the lovers of God among your people, who possess zeal for God according to knowledge, ought to come here and testify to the things of truth and for the sake of truth, so that orthodoxy might grow stronger and the innovation that has been introduced might be more fully refuted. I too would receive consolation and refreshment, while those who came would receive from Christ our God, for whose sake this matter exists, a good reward—especially since, as I have learned, they come from there as far as Iberia—why, then, do they not come here as well?

I therefore entreat Your Most Holy Reverences, if it is possible, to send me through some faithful man, among those who come to Iberia, a copy of the canonical acts of the holy and apostolic synod celebrated in elder Rome by the sacred order of Saint Martin, martyr and apostolic supreme pope. In this way the sacred doctrines of the holy Fathers, and the abominations of the heretics that arose both formerly and now, may be made much clearer here.

For this is the only good thing that those who unjustly persecute God and us accomplish, even against their will and unwillingly: they drive us exiles into different places and regions, so that the orthodoxy of the holy Fathers, which we too proclaim, may be made more manifest, and their own false doctrine may be publicly exposed and refuted in every place and region. This accords with the saying of Saint Dionysius [Note: [Col. 0663D] *On the Divine Names*], bishop of Athens and martyr, who said:

“God knows evil or good—that is, for the sake of good; and with him the causes of evils are virtues that accomplish good.”

For it is truly good to make known and confirm, as I said, the orthodoxy of the Fathers, and to publish and refute heretical false doctrine, when exile and other tribulations bring this about. Thus, from the beginning, the word of truth was spread abroad, while impiety was diminished and disappeared, through the persecution and exile—or other terrible sufferings—endured by the holy prophets, apostles, and other teachers.

Therefore, if, as I requested, you send the sacred book, moved by God, and if those who are to carry it are willing to come here, let them go voluntarily to the most renowned patrician, guarded by God, and to Gregory, the teacher who is with God. They should present to him openly a letter from the honorable patrician and prefect of Iberia. But if they should perhaps be unwilling to come this far, let them give it to the aforesaid honorable prefect of Iberia, who should send it to the aforementioned lord, our most exalted patrician and teacher with God, Gregory. By doing this, may you receive from Christ our God a good reward, you and all who benefit from it.

Moreover, with this letter I have now sent Your God-honored Reverences, and through you the most holy and orthodox Church of God that is there, a scroll containing testimonies from the sayings of Saint Hippolytus, bishop of Roman Portus and martyr of Christ our God. Through these testimonies you may learn how harmoniously, together with all the other holy Fathers, he proclaims two natures and operations of our Savior Jesus Christ, and refutes those who dogmatize one operation and one nature of his divinity and humanity, announcing at once the convertibility, commingling, confusion, and division of his two natures.

Seek diligently this sacred book of that Father, according to the superscription placed above the testimonies. If you find it, you will be able to read many necessary testimonies from it concerning these same natures and operations of our Savior. This book was brought to us in Byzantium before we suffered there. We wished to transcribe it in full, but suddenly our adversaries, as was their custom, attacked us and seized it like thieves. We were unable to extract from it more than these eight testimonies.

I shall not hesitate to say what escaped me amid the things already mentioned. It is this: when the blessed Lord Stephen announced the unity and concord that had been established there among everyone, through orthodox confession, with one another and with God, I was filled with spiritual joy, as I say before God. Though a sinner, I offered grateful hymns to the merciful God for so great and excellent a good, and I shall not cease offering them. I ask that this unity be preserved immovable unto the end, for the glory of his most gracious mercy and for our salvation.

I greet Your God-honored Reverences and all the saints who are with you, and through you the whole holy catholic and apostolic Church of God that is there. I ask that remembrance be made of me, a sinner and prisoner, in your holy prayers directed to God, in holy and venerable places. Strengthen me with your precious and much-desired words, console me, the least of men, and pray that I may be made worthy to see your faces—although it is presumptuous to say so—before I myself depart from this wretched life of many tribulations.

## Scholion

That holy Father of ours and martyr Anastasius, who wrote this letter, also died on Sunday, at the third hour, on the fifth day before the Ides of October, while he was saying in the holy assembly, “Holy things for the holy,” in the tenth indiction.

[Col. 0665]

# Prologue to the Sacred Testimonies That Follow

[Col. 0665A] Sacred and divinely inspired testimonies through which we learn more clearly that, through an unconfused and undivided union, just as there are two natures, so also there are two wills and two operations, suited and corresponding to the natures—namely, a divine and a human one, the one without beginning and the other having a beginning—of our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ. These are to be believed with the heart for righteousness and confessed with the mouth for salvation.

But the illegitimate ones, who now teach and disturb the illegitimate Churches, dogmatize in the same person one will and not one, neither two and again one, and two wills and two operations. This doctrine, besides the instability and absurdity of the thinking of those who expound such teachings, is altogether impious and alien to our Christians’ immaculate faith.

For our renowned founders and teachers reject and detest those who dogmatize one will and operation, or even one nature, of his divinity and humanity. Such a doctrine belongs to heretics who wander in confusion, fantasy, and division.

Therefore, do not those who now dogmatize only one of the two wills and operations, together with those heretics and according to their teaching, overthrow and deny the mystery of the supersubstantial theology and of the dispensation accomplished in the flesh? They assert a quaternity of persons instead of the Trinity, while subscribing that the one and same person—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, the true God—according to the manner in which he became man among us, is at once soulless, irrational, and without intellect. They introduce conjecture, fantasy, confusion, and division of his two natures.

But those who refuse to confess either a will or an operation in him proclaim him to be without essence and without existence according to both his natures. By their own doctrines they show themselves to be even more impious than the heretics just mentioned.

Furthermore, those who dogmatize one and two wills and operations in his incarnate dispensation, beyond the novelty and fiction of such a doctrine, wish not only to proclaim a heretical opinion mixed into the orthodox and paternal confession like water into wine, according to the saying, but also to introduce him as possessing three wills and three operations, and necessarily as many natures—that is, essences—since it is impossible for a nature to exist without operation, or operation without nature.

Let the testimonies mentioned above be set forth as follows: [lacuna]

[Col. 0665]

# On Theology and Incarnation

## Of Saint Hippolytus

[Note: [Col. 0665] The Latin and Greek versions of the following section are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Bishop of Portus—that is, of the harbor of Rome—and martyr of the truth, from the work *Against Beron and Hēlikos, the Heretics [Note: [Col. 0665D] “Hēlikiōnos” in the royal manuscript of Nicephorus and in the Colbert manuscript.], on Theology and Incarnation*, arranged according to the letters of the text. Its beginning is: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth,” whom the seraphim glorify, crying out to God with an unceasing voice.

### 1

For by the will of God, whose power is infinite, all things came into being, and what has come into being is preserved, each thing being maintained without confusion according to its own proper principles, by him who is by nature the God of infinite power and maker of all things. His divine will, which made and moves all things, remains unmoved, while each thing is brought forth according to its own natural laws.

For what is infinite does not in any way or by any principle admit motion, since it has no place toward which, or around which, it could move. Motion is a change of that which by nature is infinite and is not naturally subject to motion.

Therefore the Word of God, having truly become man like us without sin, and having acted and suffered humanly whatever belongs to nature without sin, and having accepted for our sake the circumscription of natural flesh, did not undergo any change at all through the self-emptying [Note: [Col. 0667D] The manuscript of Nicephorus reads “union” (*henōsin*).]. He did not become identical with the flesh in any respect, just as he is identical with the Father.

Rather, just as he was without flesh, he remained beyond every circumscription; and, acting divinely through the flesh, he performed whatever belongs to divinity. He showed himself to be both through the things by which he acted in both ways—divinely, that is, and humanly—according to the truly true and natural existence itself: existing and being understood as God, infinite, and simultaneously as circumscribed man; possessing the perfect perfection of each, together with its corresponding operation, that is, its natural property.

From these things we know that their difference remains always according to nature, without change. Yet not, as some say, by comparison, lest we say that the same person is, in relation to himself and in the same respect, greater and lesser than he ought to be.

Comparisons belong to things of the same nature, not to things of different natures. The created is not compared with God, the creator of all; the finite is not compared with the infinite, nor the end with infinity, according to any principle. They differ from one another always and in every respect naturally, not comparatively, even though an ineffable and indissoluble union of both has taken place in one subsistence, wholly surpassing the knowledge of every created thing.

For the divinity, as it was before the incarnation, is also after the incarnation, infinite by nature, unrelated, impassible, incomparable, unchangeable, immutable, self-sufficient, and, to say everything at once, substantially subsisting—the one good of infinite power.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 2

[Col. 0667C] Thus, truly and according to the Scriptures, without being changed, the God of all became a man without sin, as he alone knows, since he is by nature the craftsman of things beyond understanding. In the saving incarnation itself he joined the operation of his divinity to the flesh, an operation not circumscribed by the flesh because of the self-emptying, nor naturally arising from the flesh in the same way as from his divinity, but manifested through the flesh in whatever things he performed divinely after becoming incarnate.

For the flesh did not become divinity by nature through a change of nature, becoming flesh according to the nature of divinity. Rather, it remained what it was, and, though united with the divinity, retained its nature and operation, as the Savior said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41).

In that flesh, by acting and suffering whatever belongs to flesh without sin, he demonstrated the self-emptying of divinity on our behalf, confirmed naturally by miracles and by the sufferings of the flesh. For this reason the God of all became man: so that, suffering in passible flesh, he might redeem our entire race, which had been sold to death; and, working wonders through passible flesh by his impassible divinity, might restore it to his incorrupt and blessed life.

He also established the holy orders of the intellectual substances in heaven in immutability through the mystery of his embodiment, whose work is the recapitulation of all things in him.

Thus, even after becoming incarnate, he remained God, infinite by nature, possessing an operation cognate and appropriate to himself—arising substantially from the divinity, but manifested dispensationally through his most holy flesh in the miracles—so that he might be believed to be God, himself accomplishing the salvation of the universe through flesh weak by nature.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 3

For I too, in order to make clear by an example what has been said concerning the Savior, possess a natural word that is cognate and appropriate to me, since I am a rational and intellectual soul. The soul’s natural operation and first power is self-moving and perpetually in motion, and the word naturally flows from it.

Having articulated this word and carefully inscribed it in lines, I produce it organically through the tongue when necessary, and artistically through letters, showing it as heard through dissimilar means without itself being changed. For my natural word does not belong to the tongue or to the letters, although through them I make its utterance.

Rather, it belongs to me, who speak by nature and pronounce it through both as my own: it is always naturally issuing from my intellectual soul, and, through my bodily tongue, is produced organically, as I said, when necessary.

Just as in our case—so far as we can estimate what is altogether beyond estimation—the rational power of the soul, which exists by nature, is unchangeably expressed through our bodily tongue, so also in the transcendent embodiment of God.

Through his most holy flesh, in whatever things he acted divinely, the almighty and creative operation of the whole divinity was manifested without change. It remained outside every natural circumscription, even though it shone through flesh circumscribed by nature.

For what is uncreated by nature is not naturally circumscribed by created nature, even though it is joined to it in conception, which circumscribes every intellect. Nor do nature and natural operation ever become identical with one another, so long as each remains within its own natural immutability.

For only among things of the same nature is there an operation producing the same result, revealing the substance whose natural power it is. A substance of another nature cannot, in any way, possess or become the property of that operation without change.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 4

The mystery of the divine incarnation is recognized by the apostles, prophets, and teachers as possessing a twofold and diverse natural contemplation in all things: it is a demonstration of perfect divinity and a full manifestation of humanity.

Unless one Word is recognized according to substance as belonging to one operation, the movement of neither of the two will ever be recognized in any respect. For God, who always exists according to nature and, by his power beyond infinity, became man without sin as he willed, is what he was and is, with all that by which he is understood as God.

And what he became, he is, with all that by which a human being is understood and is naturally capable of being known. Always remaining without fall in each of the two, he preserves himself naturally unchangeable according to the perfection proper to each, in the things through which he acted at once divinely and humanly.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 5

For recently Beron, together with certain others, abandoned Valentinus’s fantasy but became entangled in a worse error, saying:

“The flesh assumed by the Word became co-acting with the divinity through the assumption, while the divinity became co-passible with the flesh through the self-emptying. They dogmatize at once change, nature, commingling, and the mutual transformation of both into one another.””

For if the assumed flesh became co-acting with the divinity, plainly it also became God by nature, with all those properties by which God is naturally understood.

And if the divinity, having been emptied, became co-passible with the flesh, plainly it also became flesh by nature, with all those properties by which flesh is naturally known.

For things that work together with one another, perform the same work, and are of the same nature must also be co-passible and admit no distinction of nature.

If their natures are confused with one another, Christ will be a dyad; and if their persons are divided, he will become a tetrad. This is something to be avoided above all.

And how, according to them, will Christ be one and the same, both God by nature and man? What existence will he possess, according to them, having become man through a change of divinity and God through a transformation of flesh?

For the transition of these things into one another is the complete abolition of both. Let us therefore examine the argument again in another way.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 6

[Col. 0671C] A pious doctrine has been established among Christians: according to nature itself, operation itself, and every other property belonging to him, God is equal to himself and identical with himself, possessing nothing in himself that is altogether unequal or inappropriate to himself.

Therefore, if, according to Beron, the flesh assumed by him became possessed of the same natural operation as he, plainly it also became possessed of the same nature as he, with all the things by which the theological Word sees the nature of divinity to be characterized in its superiority: beginninglessness, unbegottenness, infinity, eternity, incomprehensibility, and all the rest.

And both things have undergone change, since neither retains any longer the essential principle of its own nature.

For one who attributes co-action to things of different natures at once introduces a natural commingling and a personal division of them; and, through the alteration of their properties, their natural existence becomes wholly indistinguishable.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 7

But if the flesh did not become of the same nature as he, it will never become possessed of the same natural operation as he, lest he be shown to possess an operation unequal and inappropriate to his nature, and to have fallen outside the equality and identity of his natural condition in all respects. That would be impious.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 8

[Col. 0673A] They were led into this error because they were wrongly persuaded that the divine operation manifested through the flesh in the miracles became the flesh’s own operation, by which Christ gives substance to the whole and holds it together insofar as he is understood as God.

They did not understand that it is impossible for the operation of a divine nature to become the property of a substance of a different nature without change. Nor did they grasp that what is manifested through the flesh but does not naturally arise from the flesh is not at all necessarily the property of the flesh, although the demonstration is clear and evident to them.

For when I speak with my tongue and write with my hand, I manifest through both one and the same thought of my intellectual soul, which is its natural operation. I do not thereby show in any way that this thought naturally arises from the tongue or the hand. Nor has the thought become theirs, or come to be called the thought of the tongue or the hand, because it is manifested through both.

No reasonable person knows of an intellectual tongue or hand. In the same way, no one should say that the most holy flesh of God became creator by nature because it was assumed and because the divine operation was manifested through it.

Rather, the believer piously confesses that, for our salvation and to bind the whole immutably together, the creator of all things, from the ever-virgin Mary, through a pure conception, without change, made an intellectual soul with a sensory body his own in essence and became man by nature, the same Word of God, foreign to wickedness.

In his divinity he performed divine things through his most holy flesh, though they were not by nature properties of the flesh; and in his humanity he suffered human things, though they were not by nature properties of the divinity, the divinity enduring them by condescension. He performed no divine act without the body, nor did the same person perform any human act without participation in divinity.

In whatever manner he acted in both ways, he preserved in himself the natural immutability of both, in order to confirm his perfect becoming human, truly genuine and possessing no defect.

Beron, then, holding the view I have described, confused the divinity and humanity of Christ in a single operation, while at once dividing them naturally and personally, and thus destroys the true account of life, because he did not know that co-action signifies only the identity of persons of the same nature who are naturally the same.

# Saint Hippolytus, Bishop of Roman Portus and Martyr of the Truth

From the discourse arranged according to the letters of the text, *On Theology and Incarnation*, against the heretics Beron and Helicon, whose beginning is: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth,” whom the seraphim glorify, crying out with an unceasing voice.

[Col. 0666C]

## 1

For by the will of God, whose power is immeasurable, all things came into being, and what has come into being is saved, each thing being suitably preserved according to its own proper principles, by him who is by nature the immeasurably powerful God and maker of all things. His divine will, which made and moves all things, remains unmoved, while each thing is brought forth according to its own natural laws.

For what is immeasurable does not receive motion by any reason or manner, since it has no destination toward which, or around which, it might move. Change is the motion of that which by nature is without motion and is not naturally subject to movement.

Therefore the Word of God, having truly become man like us without sin, and having acted and suffered humanly whatever belongs to nature without sin, and having endured for our sake the circumscription of natural flesh, underwent no change at all because of the self-emptying. [Note: [Col. 0665D] Anastasius’s translation is mutilated here. It seems that it should be translated: “In no respect whatsoever did the Word, who is identical with the Father, become identical with the flesh because of the union.” SIRM.]

But just as he was, without flesh, he remained beyond every circumscription; and, acting divinely through the flesh, he performed whatever belongs to divinity. He showed himself to be both through the things by which he acted in both ways—divinely, that is, and humanly—according to the same truly true and natural substance: existing and being understood as God, immeasurable, and at the same time as a circumscribed man; possessing the perfect perfection of each, together with the same operation, that is, natural property.

From these things we know that their difference remains forever according to nature, without change. Yet not, as some say, by comparison, lest we say that the same person is, in the same respect, greater and lesser than himself contrary to what is fitting.

Comparisons belong to things of the same nature, not to those of different natures. The creator, God of all, is not compared with the created; the finite is not compared with the infinite, nor the end with infinity, according to any principle. They differ from one another naturally in every respect, always, but not comparatively.

Even though an ineffable and indissoluble union of both has taken place in one subsistence, it wholly surpasses the knowledge of every created thing.

For the divinity, as it was before the incarnation, is also after the incarnation, infinite according to nature, incomprehensible, impassible, incomparable, unchangeable, immutable, self-powerful, and, to say everything at once, substantially subsisting—the one good possessing infinite power.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 2

[Col. 0668C] Thus, truly and according to the Scriptures, without being changed, the God of all became a man without sin, as he alone knows, since he is by nature the craftsman of things beyond understanding. In the saving incarnation itself he joined the operation of his divinity to the flesh, an operation not circumscribed by the flesh because of the self-emptying, nor naturally arising from the flesh in the same manner as from his divinity, but manifested through it in whatever things he performed divinely after becoming incarnate.

For the flesh did not become divinity by nature through a change of nature, becoming flesh according to the nature of divinity. Rather, it remained what it was, joined to the divinity: flesh weak and passible in nature and operation, as the Savior said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41).

In that flesh, by acting and suffering whatever belongs to flesh without sin, he demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0668D] “Proved” or “persuaded.”] the self-emptying of divinity on our behalf, confirmed naturally by miracles and by the sufferings of the flesh.

For this reason the God of all became man: so that, suffering in passible flesh, he might redeem our entire race, which had been sold to death; and, working wonders through the flesh by his impassible divinity, might restore it to that immortal and blessed life from which it had fallen by obeying the devil.

He also established the holy orders of the intellectual substances in heaven in immutability through the mystery of his embodiment, whose work is the recapitulation of all things in him.

Thus, even after becoming incarnate, he remained God, infinite beyond measure according to nature, possessing an operation cognate and appropriate to himself—arising substantially from the divinity, but manifested dispensationally through his most holy flesh in the miracles—so that he might be believed to be God, himself accomplishing the salvation of the universe through flesh weak by nature.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 3

For I too, in order to express by an example what has been said concerning the Savior, possess a natural word that is cognate and appropriate to me, since I am a rational and intellectual soul. The soul’s natural operation and first power is self-moving and always in motion, and the word naturally flows from it.

Having articulated this word and carefully written it in lines, I produce it organically through the tongue when necessary, and artistically through letters, showing it as heard through dissimilar means without its being changed. For my natural word does not belong to the tongue or to the letters, although I make its pronunciation through them.

Rather, it belongs to me, who speak according to nature and utter it through both as my own. It continually flows naturally from my intellectual soul, while through my bodily tongue it is produced organically, as I said, whenever necessary.

Just as in our case—so far as we can estimate what is altogether beyond estimation—the rational power of the soul, which exists according to nature, is produced unchangeably through our bodily tongue, so also in the glorious embodiment of God.

Through his most holy flesh, in whatever things he acted divinely, the almighty and creative operation of the whole divinity was manifested without change. It remained naturally beyond every circumscription, even though it shone through flesh circumscribed by nature.

For a created nature cannot naturally circumscribe what is uncreated according to nature, even though it is joined to it in conception, which circumscribes every intellect. Nor do nature and natural operation ever become identical with one another, so long as each remains within its own natural immutability.

For only among things of the same nature is there a self-producing motion, manifesting the substance whose natural power it is. A substance belonging to a different nature cannot in any way possess or become that property without change.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 4

The mystery of the divine incarnation is recognized by apostles, prophets, and teachers as possessing a twofold and diverse natural contemplation in all things, being a demonstration of perfect divinity and a full manifestation of humanity.

Unless one Word is recognized according to substance as belonging to one operation, the movement of neither of the two will ever be recognized in any respect. For God, who always exists according to nature and, by power beyond measure, became man without sin as he willed, is what he was and is, with all that by which he is understood as God.

And what he became, he is, with all that by which a human being is understood and is naturally capable of being known. Always remaining without fall in each of the two, he preserves himself naturally unchangeable according to the perfection proper to each, in the things through which he acted at once divinely and humanly.

## Of the same, from the same discourse 5
But a certain Bero recently, and certain others as well, abandoning Valentinus’s phantasy, have become entangled in a worse perversity, saying that the flesh assumed by the Word performed the very same operations as the divinity. They dogmatically assert that the divinity became passible together with the flesh through its self-emptying, and likewise assert convertibility and commixture—or confusion—and the mutual transformation of both. For if the assumed flesh became a co-worker with the divinity, it is evident that it also became God by nature, since whatever it is understood to be, it is God. And if the divinity, having been emptied, became passible together with the flesh, it is evident that it also became flesh by nature, since whatever it is naturally understood to be, it is flesh. For things that mutually cooperate, perform the same operations, and have the same origin are certainly also mutually passible and do not admit a distinction of nature. And if the natures are confused with one another, Christ will be a duality; and if the persons are separated, there will be a quaternity—which must be avoided above all. And how, according to them, will this one and the same person be God and man by nature at once, Christ? What essence will he have, having become man through the transformation of the divinity and God through the transference of the flesh? For the falling of one into the other is the complete destruction of both. Let us therefore examine the matter in another way.

### The Same Author, from the Same Sermon 6

[Col. 0672C]

The pious dogma established for Christians who believe that, according to the same nature and operation, and everything else corresponding to it, God is equal to himself and the very same, possessing nothing at all unequal or incongruous with what belongs to him, is this. If, therefore, according to Bero, the flesh assumed by him became of the same operation, there is no doubt that it also became of the same nature as he, since whatever belongs to nature—that is, principiality, uncreatedness, infinity, eternity, incomprehensibility, and whatever else theological reasoning contemplates most fully in the divinity according to its greatness—would belong to it; and both would have undergone mutual alteration, with neither retaining any longer the substantial account of its own nature. For whoever attributes the same operation to things belonging to different natures introduces at once a natural confusion and a personal division of them, their natural existence being rendered completely unknown through the exchange of properties.

### The Same Author, from the Same Sermon 7

But if it was not of the same nature as he, neither will it ever become of the same natural operation as he, lest he appear to possess an operation unequal and incongruous according to nature, and to have become in every respect a stranger to the natural equality and identity of all that belongs to him—which is utterly impious.

### The Same Author, from the Same Sermon 8

[Col. 0674A]

Those who believe wrongly have been led into this error by making the divine operation that was manifested through the flesh in miracles a property of the flesh, an operation by which Christ, substantiating the whole universe insofar as he is understood as God, holds it in being. For they did not understand that it is impossible for the operation of the divine nature to become a property of the substance of another nature without convertibility. Nor did they understand that what was indeed manifested through the flesh is not thereby proper to the flesh, since it did not arise naturally from it—especially since this is a clear and manifest proof.

For I, speaking with my tongue and writing with my hand, express through both one and the same thought of my intellectual soul: its operation is natural, but in no way do I show that it arose naturally from my tongue or hand, nor that the thought was produced or spoken by them merely because of its manifestation through both. No one who understands matters wisely calls the tongue or the hand “thought-bearing”; likewise, one should not call the most holy flesh of God, because it was assumed and through it the divine operation was clearly manifested, a creator according to nature. Rather, the believer piously confesses that, for our salvation and in order to bind the universe to inconversibility, the Creator of all things, through an inviolable conception from the ever-holy Virgin Mary, became man—without convertibility, substantiating for himself an intellectual soul together with a body endowed with sensation—alien to malice: wholly God himself, wholly the same man; wholly God and, likewise by nature, wholly the same man. According to his divinity, he operated divinely through his own most holy flesh, without the nature of the flesh itself being divine; according to his humanity, he operated humanly, without the nature of the divinity being human [Note: [Col. 0673C] In the Greek there is added: “the divinity suffering by suspension.”].

He performs nothing divine apart from the body, nor does this same person do anything human deprived of divinity. He preserves for himself, in both respects, an immutable mode, by which he operated in both ways fittingly, for the proof of the perfection and truth of his incarnation, which contains no depravity. Thus Bero, holding the position I have described, by confusing naturally and simultaneously the divinity and humanity of Christ through the unity of operation, and dividing them personally, dissolves life, failing to understand that the same operation signifies only the natural identity of persons that are connatural.

[Col. 0673]

## SYLLOGISMS OF THE SAME ANASTASIUS

Concerning testimonies divinely wise in their subjects, and others.

[Col. 0673D] Behold now this most sacred and great teacher, and faithful witness of the truth, in agreement with all the other holy founders of the Catholic and Apostolic Church of God, confesses and proclaims in a loud voice—and commands us to confess without deviation—that, just as there are two natures according to an unconfused and indivisible union, so likewise there are two wills and two operations, corresponding and fitting to the natures: divine and human, uncreated and created, without beginning and begun, belonging to one and the same Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, who is both God and man. He defines it to be exceedingly difficult and altogether impossible for those who wish to live piously to confess one will and one operation, or one nature of his divinity and humanity. Therefore, he rejects and condemns as impious and alien to our immaculate Christian faith those who dogmatize such a thing in him, and declares that we must do the same.

Concerning the two natures and operations of our Savior Christ, I shall briefly extract a few things from his sacred words. He states this clearly:

“Showing both, according to the two ways in which he operated—namely, divinely and humanly—that, according to the same substance, which is truly true and natural, he is understood and exists as immense God and circumscribed man, possessing the perfect perfection of both substances together with their operation, that is, their natural property.”

And again:

“For the nature of the divinity did not become transformed into the nature of the flesh, nor did the nature of the divinity become flesh; rather, what it was, it remained flesh, fitted also to the divinity: weak and passible in nature and operation, as the Savior says: ‘The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’” (Matt. 26:41).

And again:

“Through which, by operating and suffering what belonged to the flesh without sin, he showed the self-emptying of the divinity on our behalf, naturally confirmed by miracles and by the sufferings of the flesh.”

And again:

“The mystery of the divine incarnation is recognized by the apostles, prophets, and teachers as possessing in every respect a twofold and different natural contemplation, existing as a demonstration of undiminished divinity and complete humanity.”

And again:

“Through which he operated both divinely and humanly, preserving for himself, through the whole account of both, a perfection naturally immutable.”

And again:

“He operated nothing divine apart from the body, nor did this same person perform anything human deprived of divinity; preserving for himself in both respects an immutable mode, through which he operated in both ways fittingly, for the demonstration of the perfection of his incarnation, which is true and contains no depravity.”

But concerning those who dogmatize one operation of his divinity and humanity and one nature, he says:

“For a created nature does not circumscribe that which was not made according to nature, even though it arose together with it through a conception that circumscribes every sense; nor does nature and natural operation ever become differentiated from itself in the same thing, so long as both remain within their own natural inconversibility.”

And again:

“For motion that operates in the same way belongs only to things that are connatural, revealing the substance whose natural power it is established to be; the property of the substance of another nature cannot in any way exist or come to be without convertibility.”

Again:

“For things that mutually cooperate, perform the same operations, and have the same origin are certainly also mutually passible and do not admit a distinction of nature. If the natures are confused with one another, Christ will be a duality; and if the persons are separated, there will be a quaternity—which must be avoided above all.”

And again:

“If, therefore, according to Bero, the flesh assumed by him became of the same operation, there is no doubt that it also became of the same nature as he, since whatever belongs to nature—that is, principiality, uncreatedness, infinity, eternity, incomprehensibility, and whatever else theological reasoning contemplates most fully in the divinity according to its greatness—would belong to it; and both would have undergone mutual alteration, with neither retaining any longer the substantial account of its own nature.”

And again:

“For whoever attributes the same operation to things belonging to different natures introduces at once a natural confusion and a personal division of them, their natural essence having become completely unknown through the exchange of properties.”

Again:

“But if it was not of the same nature as he, neither will it become of the same natural operation as he.”

And again:

“They have been led into the same error, wrongly believing that the divine operation manifested through the flesh in miracles became a property of the flesh—an operation by which Christ, substantiating the whole universe insofar as he is understood as God, holds it in being.”

And again:

“For they did not understand that it is impossible for the property of the divine operation to become a property of another nature without convertibility.”

And again:

“Until the Word, one in substance, is recognized as belonging to one operation, the motion, which belongs to both, will never at any time be recognized.”

And again:

“Thus Bero, holding the position I have described, by confusing naturally and simultaneously the divinity and humanity of Christ through the unity of operation, and dividing them personally, dissolves life, failing to understand that the same operation signifies only the natural identity of persons that are connatural.”

Since these things have thus been stated even more clearly by this most sacred and great teacher and martyr of the truth—for it is the same thing if we say that they were stated by the most holy Spirit speaking in him—let those who wish, and especially those who associate with those who have now introduced innovations, pay careful attention. Let them know with complete certainty that those who deny and reject the two natural wills and operations of our Savior Christ, and call this most sacred and orthodox confession of Christian doctrine impious and alien, while dogmatizing one will and operation of his divinity and humanity and anathematizing those who do not confess in agreement with them, plainly anathematize the holy prophets, apostles, and teachers—or, to speak more truly, the most holy Spirit who spoke, and indeed still speaks, through them. They deny and reject the sacred and orthodox confession transmitted to us by that Spirit through them, and assert that it is impious and alien to Christian doctrine.

They are like the aforementioned heretic—or rather, like all the profane heretics who have been deceived by confusion, phantasy, and division. They do not merely deny and overturn the mystery of the supersubstantial theology and the incarnate dispensation, while confessing the holy Trinity as a quaternity of persons; rather, they introduce one of these persons, our Lord Jesus Christ, as lifeless, unintelligent, and irrational insofar as he became man for us. They pronounce convertibility, commixture, mutability, confusion, phantasy, and division of his two natures, and write that the holy ever-Virgin and Mother of God is merely the mother of a man or of some prodigy.

Then, rejecting the one will and one operation that they have dogmatized in him, and refusing to confess in him either one or two—that is, a divine and a human—will or operation, or any will or operation whatsoever, they show themselves by their own words and dogmas not only unstable and evasive, but even more impious than the heretics who have erred through confusion, phantasy, and division. For the latter at least wish him to have one will or operation; these others do not wish him to have even one will or operation. Thus they proclaim him insubstantial and without essence; for it is less to say that he is without will, and they declare him impotent according to both natures.

For according to the sacred definitions and accounts, corruption—that is, destruction and nonexistence of nature—consists in the weakness and deficiency of natural dispositions, operations, and powers. Whatever is deprived of natural will and substantial operation neither exists, nor is anything, nor possesses any essence whatsoever. And they establish not only him but also the Father and the Holy Spirit as without substance and nonexistent. For the Savior exists with the same substance—that is, divinity—and with the same will and operation as those two, insofar as he is and is called God by nature. Consequently, they do not describe our truly most holy Lady, to be revered and praised above all the saints, as properly and truly the Mother of God, the true Mother of God and ever-Virgin, but as the mother, according to their own account, of one who in no way exists. Such people are exposed through their own dogmas as captives of such and so great impieties.

But those who, together with the two wills and operations that are piously affirmed in our Savior Christ by the holy founders of the Catholic Church, wish to confess another single will and operation, invented I know not from where, and anathematize those who do not confess in agreement with them one and two—that is, three wills and operations in him, likewise anathematize the holy prophets, apostles, and teachers, and, above them, the most holy Spirit who spoke in them and now speaks through them. By adulterating through new inventions the holy and immaculate faith transmitted to us through them by that Spirit, they deny it and invent in the Savior Christ another nature besides the divine and human, a certain extraneous nature alien to everything that exists [Note: [Col. 0677D] “Alien to all things that exist”: a. fingunt. COMBEF]. They want the one will and operation they have fabricated in him to belong to this nature, since every natural and substantial will and operation is certainly a property of a willing and operative nature.

Every natural operation indicates the substance from which it proceeds and in which it exists [Note: [Col. 0677D] “In which it exists”: cui inest. ID.]. The operation that indicates each nature both is and is known to be natural. Every nature is known through the substantial account of its proper operation, and every nature has an operation that corresponds to it and signifies it, distinguishing it from others. True reasoning recognizes the natural definitions of substances through their operations. In short, it is established neither that nature exists without an operation that substantially characterizes it, nor that will or operation exists without some substance—that is, without something possible [Note: [Col. 0677D] “To exist without some substance is possible”: constare sine quadam substantia, est possibile. ID.], as the divine utterances proclaim and the nature of things itself declares.

Therefore, by inventing one will and operation besides the two in Christ the Savior, and by necessity fashioning and applying to him another nature besides the divine and human—a certain extraneous nature alien to all that exists [Note: [Col. 0678D] “From necessity”: ex necessitate. ID.]—they make the previously mentioned single will, which they claim as their own, belong to it [Note: [Col. 0678D] “Which they claim it to be”: cujus velint esse. ID.]. That will is an empty fabrication of a fictitious thought, a product that differs in no way from idolatry.

For the Savior, existing as God and man at once, has only two natures, wills, and operations corresponding to him—namely, the divine and the human—as our renowned teachers and instructors affirm. He does not have one and two, that is, three, as the adversaries dogmatize. By this they plainly enact what was once said by God through the prophet Isaiah as an accusation: “Your wine merchants mix wine with water” (Isa. 1:22).

For, as is evident, these people adulterate the word of truth in the manner of wine merchants. By mixing the natural duality of the wills and operations of our Savior Christ with the one will and operation impiously dogmatized in him by the heretics deceived through confusion, division, or phantasy, they compel both sects to be confessed, as though mixing wine with water. This is truly impious and alien to our Christians’ immaculate faith. In precisely the same way as their predecessors, they too fall from the truth.

For it is an equally and precisely similar evil both to cast away and reject the paternal orthodoxy in favor of heretical opinion, and conversely to confess and approve both that opinion and the orthodox faith together. “What participation is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship between light and darkness? Or what agreement between Christ and Belial? Or what portion does the believer share with the unbeliever? And what agreement is there between the temple of God and idols?” says the divine Apostle (2 Cor. 6:14–16). I myself also say: What participation, communion, agreement, portion, or accord can paternal orthodoxy have with the wicked opinion of the heretics, so that one may be proclaimed or rejected together with the other?

Let them also pay close attention to this: if, as the great one called “from immortality”—or rather, the entire chorus of the saints—asserts, faith in our Savior scarcely admits this, since according to its own account it is something unstable, then, if it undergoes this, it will undoubtedly also endure what is contrary to it: an addition. And how will faith thereafter remain unchanged amid defects and advances? Let those who create faith anew each day—or rather, fashion different gods for themselves—tell us, since what is believed is changed and multiplied by such people together with the word of faith.

Therefore, the adversaries, establishing different faiths for themselves, plainly change and multiply what is believed according to the quality, quantity, and alteration of their dogmas. They are shown to have fashioned as many as five Christs: one having one operation; another having not even one operation; another having one will; another having not even one will; and a fifth having one and two—that is, three operations and three wills, as they say.

Let those who expound such dogmas and those who associate with them say, if they wish, in which of these many Christs fabricated by them those who believe in them were or are baptized. Or whose body and blood do they receive and distribute? Is it the body and blood of the one who has one operation, or of the one who has not even one operation? Of the one who has one will, or of the one who has one and two—that is, three operations and three wills—and therefore necessarily already has three natures?

“But there was no voice, and there was no hearing” (1 Kings 18:29), as the great prophet Elijah said when rebuking the wicked priests and false prophets of confusion. For whatever they say, their speech will carry away from there, together with its impiety, its own refutation, since they do not believe in or baptize into the true and truly existing Christ, nor do they receive and distribute his body and blood.

Our renowned teachers and instructors, knowing that he is the true Christ, God and man at once, confess in him two—and only two—natures, and likewise two wills and an equal number of operations corresponding to them: the divine, as has already been stated and demonstrated, and the human; the uncreated, without beginning, and the created [Col. 0680A]. They command us to confess the same. They do not confess him, as these innovators now do, as having one, or neither one nor two, or again one and two—that is, three wills and operations.

In addition to everything that has been said, let them know with complete certainty this as well: those who dogmatize one, neither one nor two, and again one and two wills and operations, all together with anathemas, depositions, and excommunications, are plainly proved to contradict both themselves and one another. They overturn and destroy their own and one another’s words and dogmas; they anathematize themselves, one another, and those who associate with them; and they expel and depose themselves and one another from every sacred dignity and ministry [Col. 0680B]. They also exclude them from receiving the undefiled communion of the life-giving body and blood of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

Therefore, since we wish to be and to be called Christians in truth, let us clearly and without any obstructing veil preserve ourselves from their impiety and communion—not only because of the manifold error, but also because of the instability, absurdity, and mutual contradiction of such men and dogmas. For it is alien to Christians both to accept impiety together with orthodoxy, and to confess the orthodox faith while associating with those who deny and adulterate it through new inventions.

Therefore the divine and apostolic law commands us together to turn away from and anathematize those who attempt to teach and introduce anything other than what we received from the Christ-bearing men—not only if they are human beings, but even if, perhaps, they should be angels descending from heaven. If we do this, fulfill the divine command without deviation, and possess and confess the sacred and orthodox faith without adulteration or innovation, we shall be saved unto eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. With him, to God the Father, together with the most holy, good, and life-giving Spirit, be glory, honor, dominion, and worship, now and always, and throughout the ages of ages that shall never end. Amen.

[Col. 0679]

## LATER TESTIMONIES OF SAINT HIPPOLYTUS

*(From Combefis’s edition of the Works of Saint Maximus.)*

[Col. 0679D] [lacuna] He states this clearly:

“Showing both, because he operated in two ways—namely, divinely and humanly—that, according to the same substance, which is truly true and natural, he exists and is understood as immense God and circumscribed man, possessing the perfect perfection of both essences together with the operation of each, that is, its natural property.

And again: The flesh did not become, by nature, the divinity, with its nature transferred; that is, the flesh did not become divinity according to nature. Rather, what it was, fitted also to the divinity, remained what it was—namely, flesh, weak and passible in nature and operation, as the Savior says: ‘The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’” (Matt. 26:41).

And again: By operating and suffering what belonged to the flesh, which was free from every sin, he demonstrated the self-emptying of the divinity on our behalf, confirmed naturally by miracles and by the sufferings of the flesh.

And again: The mystery of the divine incarnation has been found by the apostles, prophets, and teachers to possess in every respect a twofold and different natural contemplation, since it has the power of revealing perfect divinity and complete humanity.

And again: Through these he operated both divinely and humanly, preserving the account of both aspects of himself perfectly and naturally immutable.

And again: He operated nothing divine apart from the body, nor did this same person perform anything human that was without divinity. By this new and fitting manner he operated in both ways, preserving himself free from alteration according to the account of both, in order to establish the faith of his perfect humanity, which is plainly true and admits neither fault nor stain.”

But concerning those who dogmatize one operation and one nature of his divinity and humanity, he says:

“For nature that has been generated cannot circumscribe what is ungenerated according to nature, even though it has coalesced with it through conception, which circumscribes the whole power of the mind. Nor do they ever become converted into the same nature and natural power or operation, so long as both remain within their own natural inconversibility.

And again: The motion of things that are of the same nature alone belongs to the same power and efficacy, signifying the substance whose natural power it is; for the substance of a property belonging to a different nature cannot in any way exist or come to be without convertibility.

Again: Things that are of the same power and operation toward one another, and of exactly the same origin and the same passions, do not admit a distinction of nature. If the natures are confused with one another, Christ will be a duality; and if the persons are divided, there will be a quaternity—which must be avoided above all.

And again: If, then, as Bero asserts, the flesh assumed by him became of the same power or operation as he, it plainly also became of the same nature as he, since whatever is included in nature is included in it: that which is without beginning, ungenerated, infinite, eternal, incomprehensible, and whatever else theological discourse contemplates supremely in the divinity according to its excellence. Both underwent mutual alteration, with neither preserving the substantial account of its nature intact.

And again: Whoever attributes the same operation to things of different natures introduces at once their natural confusion and their natural division, their natural substance and existence being wholly unknown and obscured through the exchange of properties.

Again: But if it did not become of the same nature as he, neither will it ever become of the same operation as he.

And again: They fell into this error, wrongly believing that the divine operation manifested through the flesh in miracles became a property of the flesh—an operation by which Christ, insofar as he is understood as God, holds and preserves what has been created in this whole universe.

And again: They did not understand that it is impossible for the operation of the divine nature to become the property of another and different substance without convertibility.

And again: As long as the Word, one according to essence, is not recognized as belonging to one operation, it can never in any way happen that the motion of both is recognized.

And again: Thus Bero, holding the position I was describing, by confusing naturally and simultaneously the divinity and humanity of Christ through one operation, and dividing them personally, dissolves life; for he does not know that the same operation signifies only the identity of persons that are of the same nature.”

[Col. 0681]

## SCHOLION, OR MEMORIAL NOTE

Briefly declaring for those who wish, with divine desire and zeal, to read it, what few have learned [perhaps *suffered*], namely: amid athletic contests, how many exiles they endured, in what places and at what times they suffered martyrdom, and the day on which our holy and God-bearing Fathers and teachers—truly new confessors and great martyrs—departed in faith to God and appeared before him. This concerns especially him who wrote with the finger of God the letter set down here: for he indicated, as stated above, the day of the death of those who had died before him, namely Maximus and his disciple Anastasius; but of himself and his own blood-brothers, Theodore and Euprepius, no one did so. It also concerns Martin, the most holy and supreme apostolic pope and martyr, who surpasses every sacerdotal dignity under the sun; and certain others whom the present letter, nor, I think, any other document or person, mentions.

[Col. 0681D] Those who read these copies of that present sacred letter must, in obedience to God, who searches hearts and reins, believe most firmly that they have been transcribed in it, God the witness of truth, from the very letter written in his own hand—or rather, to speak more truly because of the remarkable miracle, with the finger of God—by our holy father and teacher, Lord Abbot Anastasius, presbyter and apocrisiarius of the elder and most renowned city of Rome, a strenuous combatant and truly great new martyr of the truth. He wrote it after he had suffered, as has been said, at Byzantium together with his fellow-combatant and true philosopher—or rather, one greatly wise in God—Maximus, his fellow martyr for Christ, the true God and our Savior: that is, after their precious, sacred, and truly divinely mobile tongues and hands had been cut off from within, amid most bitter beatings and tortures, by which they suffered a flow and spectacle of blood throughout the whole city, such as no one truly living an evil life had ever endured.

[Col. 0683A] Had God alone, who brought all things from nothing into being and raises the dead, not preserved them through such cruelty and such great loss of blood—no cautery having been allowed them, nor any compress applied to the cuttings of their hands and tongues, as is customary, to stop the bleeding—they would then have surrendered to the God whom they desired their own truly holy and undoubtedly blessed souls, to the shame of their adversaries. These utterly profane and wretched apostates from the truth did all this to them for no other reason than the truly wicked and sole envy which the ancient enemy, the devil, had sown in them, as in the Jews like them: because they could not resist, even a little, the wisdom rightly given them by God—for the sake of the true truth, and solely because those men would not share in their so manifest and godless impiety.

With that holy right hand which had been cut off, and of which only the stump remained, without palm and fingers, he unexpectedly, after fastening together two very small thin pieces of wood, spoke readily, altogether without hindrance, by divine and invisible power and grace—or rather, as is truer to say—although his tongue had been cut away from its very root. Lebarnicius, patrician of Lazica, recounted this to us with dreadful oaths, having himself, by God's dispensation, become an eyewitness of this very thing, although he had doubted this glorious and great miracle. Theodore, protosecretary of the praetorian prefect of Constantinople, had also told me this earlier, likewise with terrible oaths, since he knew of their holy sufferings, as a master and instructor in such matters, glorifying and praising God and giving thanks to him for so great a miracle and for their confident power. For, like a dog or a stag exhausted by much running, thirst, or heat, they loosened and gave up their tongues as also their hands, although holy Maximus was very short of stature and weak in body, as is manifest to all.

[Col. 0683C] Therefore the adversaries, their minds wounded still more by such great and such cheerful courage in the saints, being inwardly most wicked and truly inhuman, cut them off like wild beasts. Not only was this letter written by him in this manner, but also many other books and volumes of his studies. By divine providence we ourselves became not only their inspectors, but were also deemed worthy, by God's grace and at his command, partly to receive them as our lot; and they too were written by the same wondrous means and hand—or rather, more truly, by the finger of God—as is recorded to have happened in the time of the great Moses.

This occurred by the providence and cooperation of the one almighty God, who, being a lover of goodness and of humankind, works great wonders in his saints and truly glorifies those who glorify him by unwavering deed, word, and truth. While he was still living in his last, that is, third, exile in Lazica, in the fortress called Thusumes, situated above the village of Mochoes, at the boundary of the district of Apsilla, east of the Pontic Sea, at the very foot of the Caucasian mountains, near the country of the friends of Christ, the Abasgians, and the people of the Alans—about five signs from Zichachorium, that is, from the first house of Gregory, the true friend of Christ, patrician and magister of the same land of the Alans—the same Anastasius, whose excellent memory this kind of letter rightly makes, had been removed there by force and by the command of the wretched rulers who governed before and up to his time.

[Col. 0684A] In that third exile, after seven removals, in harder places and amid much affliction, he fell asleep in the Lord in the aforementioned fortress of Thusumes, having himself fought the good contest, truly kept the orthodox faith, and completed the course of martyrdom, on the eleventh day of October, the first day of the week, at the third hour, while during the holy offices the words “Holy things for the holy” were being said, in the tenth indiction. Three months earlier, he had himself foretold the day of his holy death to some who were with him.

And also through many other miracles wrought by the cooperation of the most holy and all-effecting Spirit, both there and during his two exiles, namely at Trebizond and Mesembria, and through very many who were converted and enlightened unto the truth.

When they had lived and persevered in this holy and most blessed struggle of many labors—that is, in a confession and testimony bearing a crown—the aforesaid holy Anastasius, presbyter and Roman apocrisiarius, from the sixth indiction of the preceding cycle until the tenth indiction, throughout all three of his aforesaid exiles, subjected to various transfers, tribulations, necessities, and no ordinary or moderate hardships, remained for twenty years.

His disciples, however, Theodore and Euprepius, brothers by birth and holy brethren, sons of Plutinus, the most blessed imperial baker—that is, the one who stands above all the public bakers, namely those who distribute the grain allowances of all the scholae, which is called *Tetransiton*—were adorned with precious wealth, various dignities, divine virtues, and virginity, which is greater than all these. Through this, as I believe, they also deserved to be honored with holy struggles and crowns for Christ, as the pure and clean of heart, for they shall see God.

After the first exile of their master and ours at Trebizond, once many alms and offerings had been made, they wished to flee at once to Rome; but in that same persecution they too were arrested near Abydos, for the same and sole reason, and because they did not wish to defile themselves with them through such manifest impiety in the profane and wholly godless imperial *Typos*, which had been produced through the submission of those who belonged to the Church of Constantinople. They were publicly stripped—that is, deprived of all the property they possessed and of the dignities they held—and, after receiving deadly scourging from the prefect, were sent into exile at Cherson. There they were repeatedly separated from one another by force and assigned to military camps among the neighboring peoples.

The younger brother, who, truly in all things a bearer of a fitting name, was called Euprepius, having completed such a contest as a friend of God, departed to the Lord in the ninth year, in the month of October, on the twenty-sixth day, in the fourteenth indiction.

[Col. 0685A] The other, the elder brother, who was deservedly called by the Lord “God’s gift,” has persevered from that same sixth indiction until the aforesaid tenth indiction of the present cycle—that is, until the holy repose in the Lord of the most holy Father and master of them and of us, Anastasius the presbyter. He is truly most wretched, and orphaned because of the rarity and lack of the word of truth and of every spiritual food, so that even now what the Lord says concerning the evils of the last times has been fulfilled: that he would send not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. The aforementioned brother Theodore is still persevering, now in his twentieth year, in athletic labors and struggles in that same exile at Cherson.

This was the aforementioned brother Theodore, who with his own hand was graciously pleased to present us with many little works of the saints. We had gone there to visit and venerate him, and Martin, of precious memory, the supreme and truly universal pope and great martyr of the truth. Theodore also recounted to us the abundant miracles that had occurred there, together with those unbearable sufferings; and he gave us a fragment of the holy *orarium*, that is, the face-cloth, which Martin had left to him, as well as one of his *campagi*, that is, shoes—none of which any other among men wears except the holy Roman pope.

For Martin too had been banished into exile there after enduring every terrible thing, when he was led away from the city of Rome. He had surrendered himself, eagerly and with the greatest desire, to undergo martyrdom for Christ, as imitator and successor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, both during the voyage and in Byzantium itself, so that he was openly struck on the face by the enemies of God.

[Col. 0685C] In carrying out against him a deed worthy of their father the devil, they stripped him of his clothing, and placed upon his holy neck and his precious remaining limbs the burdens of iron bonds and chains. Then, displaying him in those same iron fetters, they dragged him through the entire street from the palace to the prefect’s praetorium, bound to the master of the watch, that is, the chief of the executioners. Someone preceded him with a sword, intending to cut him limb from limb, at the deliberation and command of the detestable *sacellarius* Bucoleon, fittingly surnamed “the beast that devours blood,” as one who possessed works filled with bestial fury, and with the knowledge and counsel of the emperor Constantine, who had also composed the aforesaid obscene and wicked *Typos*, and of Gregory the eunuch, prefect of that miserable city.

This would certainly already have been done, so far as his rash eagerness and purpose were concerned, had not the protection of the most merciful and benevolent God restrained them, and had the enemies not been ashamed before this man’s most robust strength. For even fierce and inhuman tyrants frequently know how to suffer this, although they are exceedingly pitiless and cruel, in accordance with the one who works in them, Satan: perhaps they begrudged him his martyrdom, like that apostate resembling them, Julian, famous and truly learned in evil and devoted to the madness of idols.

Or else God, in some better manner known to himself alone—who plainly orders all things for the sake of their usefulness—preserved him through immense and ineffable providence. He spent one hundred and eighty days in two prisons, namely in the watch-house and under the prefect’s guard, amid great tribulation and the gravest illness. His entire struggle of tribulation lasted three years and more, as we have been able to learn from what was written about him by Roman soldiers and by his own men, who endured exile with him in various places while being subjected to many tortures.

He too fell asleep in the Lord, after he had enlightened by synodal teaching the one holy, catholic, apostolic, and glorious Church of our God with its most sacred and true doctrines, and had strengthened the sacred and most devout doctrines both of the five holy and universal synods—namely, the Nicene, the Constantinopolitan, the first Ephesian, the Chalcedonian, and again the Constantinopolitan under the emperor Justinian—and of all our holy, divinely wise, approved Fathers and true teachers.

Those who wish to read with pious love will find this in the sacred acts of the holy, apostolic, and most devout synod held by him at Rome, since they have been sent to every place and every region. He had also boldly manifested and preached the truth, and brought to light and exposed more clearly the crimes of its enemies, contending in a good and greatly beloved struggle. He departed in abundant joy to the desired Lord, for whom, so far as it lay within him, he had also poured out his own blood, in the month of September, on the sixteenth day, in the fourteenth indiction—the day on which every year the honored memory of Euphemia, who guarded piety, contended abundantly, and was a chaste virgin and martyr, is celebrated.

He was laid among the tombs of the saints in the church of the most holy, undefiled, ever-praised, gracious, and truly ever-glorious Lady, our sovereign, who by nature, truly and without falsehood, is the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. This church is called Blachernae and lies one stadion outside the walls of the henceforth blessed city of Cherson. In this holy church the aforementioned Saint Euprepius also rests beside that most richly adorned and truly masterful man, who fulfilled in deed the evangelical saying: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 11:11).

Moreover, the holy, memorable, excellent, altogether wise—indeed, divinely wise—great defender of the truth and fellow martyr of these men, Megistus, who is also Maximus—for, as we indicated earlier, the Latin expression signifies the name *Maximus*—has had a lamp burning at his holy tomb every night from the day on which he is known to have fallen asleep, shining upon everyone to the present and forever and revealing the confidence he possesses before God, as the preceding letter commends.

We ourselves became hearers in person of this from many leaders and inhabitants of that place, who confidently proclaimed with oaths that such a truly marvelous miracle had occurred. One of those who had seen it with his own eyes was Mistrianus, the count of the same fortress of Chemareos. Keeping watch with the soldiers, he observed it not once or twice but many times, and he was the first openly to proclaim all these things to us, since we were unable to go there because of the difficulty of climbing that mountain—the summit of the Caucasus, higher than which there is no mountain on earth—as well as because of the winter season and the turmoil among the peoples that occurs in those regions.

Likewise, his disciple Anastasius, after the eleventh indiction of the preceding cycle, passed through three exiles—Bizye, Perberci in the Thracian region, and the aforesaid Lazica—amid many afflictions, unbearable necessities, and athletic struggles of this kind. After completing ten years, they departed to the heavenly kingdom.

Saint Maximus, as has been said, departed in the month of August, on the thirteenth day, in the fifth indiction, having foretold through divine revelation, fifteen days beforehand, that his falling asleep in the Lord would occur, as was already stated; and, many years earlier, he had foretold his holy martyrdom in Christ our God for the truth.

His disciple Anastasius departed in the month of July, on the twenty-fourth day, in the same indiction.

Accordingly, this most sacred letter, written by his own hand—or rather, divinely inscribed—was sent to us, together with the testimonies and arguments placed beneath it and uttered by God. It came from the same exile of theirs, namely Lazica, and we possess and preserve it, along with the divinely given object entrusted to him with which he wrote, namely the two aforementioned little rods of exile, and with his other blessings and gifts, sacred and venerable, as well as with all his goods after God—namely his studies in books and compositions written by his own hand—as truly holy praises and relics.

It was given to us, the very least, Theodore—brothers by birth, humble and sinful monks— through Gregory, a monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist in the region of the Albanians, called Bavararu, on the twentieth day of August, in the eleventh indiction that had passed, as we were returning from the aforesaid region of the Lazoi.

We had gone there, although we were very weak, poor, and unworthy, according to our custom, to visit them—not only because of the written burden entrusted to us, namely the command of the aforementioned holy and supreme apostolic Roman pope Martin, when we personally came to him in that city of great renown and received and heard from the pope himself, and from another of those who were present with him, confirmation in his own hand concerning the matters that had been synodically confirmed by him, but also because he himself had commanded us with his own mouth concerning this matter.

This was after they had suffered these things, while they were still in Byzantium under guard in the prefect’s praetorium, which is called Diomedes. From there we had previously sent them grieving into their aforementioned third exile in Lazica. During their remaining exiles and imprisonments, their labors, anxieties, and no ordinary hardships, we ministered to them as far as it was possible for us, through the prayers they offered to God and which were accepted, while he himself cooperated with us—he who repeatedly rescued us from the unjust hands of the ungodly, from dangers at sea, and from various storms.

We ministered from the small means that were ours through our parents’ blessing in the Lord—or, to speak more truly, through God’s gift—and not from the possessions of others; and we ministered no less to their other fellow-strugglers and fellow-martyrs. We did this also so that we might become eyewitnesses of the scars and sufferings that they endured for Christ, our true God.
