Indeed, having ourselves become hearers, we were also made participants in their divinely wise and saving teaching, might enjoy their prayers, persuasive before God and well received by him, and might receive from them and carry away certain garments that had been torn from their bodies by their own hands during their passion, together with sanctified cloths reddened by precious blood. These had been wrapped around their holy hands after those hands had been cut off, in order medicinally to restrain the blood.

We have judged it not without reflection, I think, to embrace and commemorate both of them, because they are recognized as having become one and the same in the struggle of the truly holy and orthodox faith and in the bond of peace and charity.

Furthermore, an innumerable multitude of those who, in the aforesaid unbearable and intolerable persecution, were openly and secretly subjected to martyrdom by various blows and tribulations, were assailed by that cunning and crafty scheme in different ways, as though not for the faith but under the pretext of other charges and penalties. Thus these matters remained unknown to the simpler people, who are easily deceived, and were known only to God, the knower of hidden things, and to those more diligent persons who knew without doubt who these sufferers were and why they had suffered.

For all these matters, we entreat and implore all of you who read about the truths that truly are truths—as though present and prostrate before you, bowing the knees of our hearts together with our bodily knees, and with the feeling of our hearts together with tears, and lying prostrate before the feet of you all—that you first grant pardon in all things to our smallness and lack of discipline. As truly faithful men, we have faithfully undertaken such matters for the sake of certainty and satisfaction.

We also ask that forgetfulness not conceal such great and such holy struggles, since very few and rare people learn of them with diligence. We, as has been said, had become aware of these things through our own eyes to the greatest extent, by God’s will, and had feared the danger that arises from negligence. For no other reason, as I say before God, than this, we dared somehow to write these things and were scarcely able to set forth their life or praises, because of our unpolished and rustic compilation and our utter lack of discipline, through which we possess a poverty of speech greater than all others.

We think it sufficient for the deeds and praises of such a great life if those who wish to read out of love for truth and learning should read their divine writings and the very many labors and writings which they undertook truly and without weariness against impiety and for piety. We have written these, with all care and diligence, together with the material drawn from the detestable writings of their adversaries, although we are humble and truly worthless above all in every respect.

According to the ability within us, we have written these things in various books and volumes and handed them over to lovers of the truth, for the glory, unceasing praise, and thanksgiving of almighty God, who is truly marvelous in his saints; for the zeal and eagerness of those who wish to contend for piety; for the confusion and unavoidable disgrace of the enemies of the truth and of God himself; and for the exposure and refutation of the false accusations brought against them, and of their empty and unstable decrees, as well as, absolutely, of all their most sacred and pious struggles and labors, which were carried out in various ways by those who opposed them.

These opponents were the newly introduced and heretical invention that accepts everything, namely Heraclianus, Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, the Petrites, and the involuntary Inoperatists—or, to speak more accurately, the new Epicureans, that is, those utterly without God—as the writings of the events themselves and of the opposing parties demonstrate to those who know how to discern such matters.

Thus those who come after us, if they are diligent and powerful in speech, may take from these discoveries an occasion to render due thanksgiving to God and his saints. “Give an opportunity to the wise man, and he will become wiser,” it says (Prov. 9:9).

[Note: Heraclianus, Cyrus, Sergius, etc. The name seems to be compounded from several names: Heraclianus–Cyrus–Sergius–Pyrrhus–Paulus–Petritae; likewise Inoperativus–Inoperatistae, that is, those who take away from Christ will and operation—namely, human will and operation.]

Second, by unceasing prayers and supplications, together with good works and tears, let us appease God, benevolent and merciful by nature, so that he may have compassion on our weaknesses and put an end to the deceitful, crafty, utterly contrived, and exceedingly grievous persecution that still presses upon us, surpassing all the preceding pagan and heretical persecutions.

For he knows the frailty of our dust and our easy fall because of the excessive fraud and wickedness of these men. May the uprising come to an end, and may there be a limit to this most atrocious evil, in which they shed precious blood, just as happened under the impious and godless Arians with regard to the rose-red blood of Saint Peter, patriarch and martyr of Alexandria.

For this reason also our aforementioned holy Fathers and true teachers of piety, especially our apostolic and preeminent pope Martin, likewise delivered himself as a sacrifice for the faithful people, imitating Christ our God, the director of the contest in all things, and Peter, the chief of the apostles, following him in everything, and truly becoming his worthy successor.

May he grant his holy Churches firm peace and indissoluble unity everywhere, and may he no longer permit any heresy to arise until the end, both because of the multitude of his mercies and because of the weakness and instability of our nature, which has increased beyond that of all preceding generations.

Third, may we be preserved immovable to the end—not only we, but all the devout—in the one truly holy, orthodox, immaculate, catholic, and true faith of us Christians; and may we receive forgiveness of sins and salvation, we who are truly sinners and servants of all, who are truly orthodox and proper worshipers of Christ, our true God and Savior, who truly glorifies those who glorify him in truth.

To him belong all glory, honor, dominion, majesty, in heaven and on earth, worship and thanksgiving, in the understanding of the heart and in truth itself, with fear and trembling as well as exultation, according to the prophetic utterance, together with the immortal Father, lover of mercies, most compassionate and most merciful beyond nature, and with the most holy, consubstantial, life-giving, and almighty divine Spirit, now and always, and throughout all infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0689]

# THE AUTHENTIC ACTS OF SAINT PETER, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA AND MARTYR

Translated by Anastasius the Librarian.

(In Maius, *Spicilegium*, volume III, p. 671.)

## MAIUS’S NOTICE

[Col. 0689D] Anastasius the Librarian translated from Greek the Passion of Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria. Anastasius himself first affirms this in his prologue to the Passion of the 1,480 martyrs, which Mabillon published in *Museum Italicum*, volume I, part II, p. 80:

“After I had translated, at the request of your Holiness”—he is speaking to Peter, bishop of Gubbio—“the Passion of the preeminent teacher and martyr Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria.”

Then the anonymous biographer of Pope John VIII, in Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, volume III, part I, p. 269, confirms the same thing:

“Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church, also translated from Greek into Latin the Passion of Saint Peter, archbishop of Alexandria.”

Nevertheless, from the various Passions of Saint Peter that exist, it must be determined by conjecture which one Anastasius translated. For Surius, under 26 November, recounts a somewhat shorter set of Acts and believed it to be by Anastasius because he had read in manuscripts the prologue to the Passion of the 1,480 martyrs mentioned above. Accordingly, Surius uses the same words as Anastasius in that prologue, namely: “of the preeminent teacher and martyr Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria” (or “patriarch,” as Surius and Vatican manuscript Regina Suecorum 542, folio 72 verso, have it).

Baronius, however, did not accept the opinion of Surius, which rests on no certain argument, in his annotations to the Martyrology under that day. For he says:

“We have another, fuller set of Acts of the same Peter in an old manuscript. Since these are known to have been written more carefully, they seem, in my opinion, rather to be attributed to Anastasius. Their beginning is: ‘If all my senses…’”

(Baronius’s memory fails him here; he should have written: “If all the joints of my body,” as it is read in our text.)

Baronius had previously preferred the same opinion concerning these Acts in the *Annals* under the year 310, and he also made diligent use of them in composing Peter’s history. Therefore, relying on Baronius’s authority, and furthermore captivated by the excellence of these Acts, which I found in a very ancient Vatican manuscript, number 602, I present this Passion of the celebrated bishop and martyr of the city of Alexandria.

Besides these authentic and Anastasian Acts, of which I have so far spoken, I was reading another Latin version in Vatican manuscript 622, almost equally ancient. These, however, are precisely the Acts that Combefis published in Greek in his *Lectis Triumphis martyrum*, pp. 189 ff., and furnished with a new Latin translation, because he did not know the older text of the Vatican manuscript.

There are therefore three sets of Acts of Saint Peter of Alexandria, the martyr:

1. Our authentic and best Acts, according to Baronius;
2. The shorter Latin Acts printed by Surius;
3. The Greek Acts of Combefis, which are the same in Latin in manuscript Vatican 622, as we have said.

We shall recite the first, which is excellent and unpublished.

# HERE BEGIN THE ACTS

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691B] If all the limbs of my body were changed into tongues, and all the articulated structures of my limbs uttered voices, I would still be wholly unable to express what kind of man, how great, and of what stature our most blessed Father Peter, archbishop of the Alexandrian see, was.

Above all, we consider it utterly inappropriate to commit to papyrus all the dangers he endured from tyrants and all the conflicts he underwent with pagans and heretics, lest we appear rather to be offering a panegyric in his praise than an account of his sufferings, when by his glorious exertion he ran manfully to save the people acquired for God.

Nevertheless, since reason falters in recounting the praises of his intimate life and wondrous deeds, and speech is wholly unable to suffice, we therefore consider it appropriate to describe only those matters by which it may be shown that he ascended to the summit of the episcopate and, after Arius had been cut off from catholic unity, was crowned with the laurels of martyrdom.

I believe that this glorious end and mirror of magnificent struggle will suffice for those who attend to our devotion and do not doubt that our narrative is truthful, without the stain of falsehood. Thus, as we begin the episcopal account of this most holy man, let us seek his prayer, so that we may rejoice to have it cooperating with us through our style.

Alexandria, then, is a city of great size, which holds authority not only over the Egyptians but also, not far from Egypt, over the Thebans and Libyans. The cycle of 285 years of the saving Incarnation of Jesus Christ our Lord was turning when the venerable Theonas, pope of that same city, ascended by an airy flight to the heavenly realms.

[Note: In Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, in both my Milanese and Roman editions, the beginning of Theonas’s episcopate, not his death, is assigned approximately to this year.]

The aforementioned Peter succeeded him in administering the government of the Church and was ordained pontiff by all the clergy and Christian people, being the sixteenth from Mark the Evangelist, who was also archbishop of that city.

He rose like the morning star among the stars, shining with the rays of holy virtues, and most magnificently governed the citadel of faith. In the divine Scriptures he was inferior to none of his predecessors, and he devoted himself nobly to the benefit and instruction of the Church. He was also singular in prudence and perfect in all things, truly a priest and a sacrifice of God, laboring vigilantly day and night in every concern of the priesthood.

But because virtue is always struck by envy and lightning strikes the highest mountains, he endured on every side many conflicts with his rivals. What more need be said? He spent almost the whole time of his life in persecution.

Meanwhile he ordained fifty-five bishops. Finally, Meletius, blackest in name and mind, became a schismatic bishop in the city of Lycopolis. He did many things against the rule of the canons and surpassed even the ferocity of the bloodstained soldiers who, during the Lord’s Passion, feared to tear the Lord’s tunic.

He was so carried away by the loosened reins of madness that, while rending the catholic Church, he appointed his own followers as bishops not only throughout the cities of Egypt but also throughout its villages. He cared nothing for Peter, nor indeed for Christ, who was in Peter.

The aforementioned Arius, still a layman and not yet marked by clerical tonsure, adhered to him and was exceedingly dear to him and to his household; and not without reason, for, as Scripture says, every creature loves what is like itself.

When the man of God learned these things, he was overcome with grief and said that this persecution was worse than the former one. Although he was hidden in certain retreats, he nevertheless sent exhortatory letters everywhere as far as he could, preaching the unity of the Church, and strengthened the people against Meletius’s ignorance and impious audacity. Thus it happened that quite a few, encouraged by his saving admonitions, withdrew from Meletian impiety.

At about the same time Arius, armed with viperous cunning, as though abandoning the Meletians, fled to Peter. When the bishops asked for it, Peter raised him to the dignity of the diaconate, not knowing the extent of his hypocrisy. He was like a serpent swollen with deadly poison.

For this laying on of hands could not be counted as a crime against this holy man, any more than the simulated magic of Simon can be attributed to Philip.

Meanwhile the detestable wickedness of the Meletians increased beyond measure. The most blessed Peter feared lest the plague of heresy invade the entire flock entrusted to him, and he also knew that “there is no fellowship between light and darkness, and no concord between Christ and Belial.” Through letters he therefore separated the Meletians from the Church.

And because an evil intention cannot remain hidden for long, the most wicked Arius immediately groaned, given over to grief because he saw his supporters separated from the dignity of the Church. This did not escape the notice of the most holy man.

When Arius’s hypocrisy had been exposed, Peter immediately used the evangelical sword—“If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you”—and expelled Arius from the structure of the Church, cutting off the rotten member, and commanded that he remain an exile from the communion of the faithful.

After these things had occurred, the storm of persecution suddenly abated greatly, and peace, though slight, shone forth. Then the most elegant pontiff of the Lord appeared openly and shone before the people. The faithful began to run in crowds to the memorials of the martyrs and to gather assemblies for the praise of Christ. The bishop of the divine law gave them life, raised them up, and strengthened them by divine utterance, and the multitude of believers in the Church continually increased.

But the ancient enemy of human salvation, seeing these things with hostile eyes, did not remain quiet for long. Suddenly the storm of paganism thundered from the opposite quarter and, like a winter rainstorm, struck the Church’s serenity and drove it far away.

To make this more clearly understood, we must turn to the cruelty of the most impious and God-defying Diocletian, and likewise to that of Maximian Galerius, who at that time, with his son Maximinus, oppressed the eastern regions by tyrannical rule.

In their time the fire of the Christian persecution burned so fiercely that the storm of impiety thundered not only in one climate of the world but throughout the whole earth, by land and sea. Imperial edicts and most cruel decrees were sent here and there, and the worshipers of Christ were slaughtered, now openly and now by clandestine ambushes. No day and no night passed free from the shedding of Christian blood.

Nor was the manner of execution simple or uniform. Some were killed by various and most severe punishments; others were transferred to different places, so that they would lack both the humanity of their parents and burial in their homeland, and were driven toward the goal of martyrdom by new devices of punishment unheard of in the age.

Alas for the impiety! Their wickedness was so great that they even destroyed the sanctuaries of divine worship from their foundations and burned the holy books in the fire.

When Diocletian, of execrable memory, had died, Constantine the Great was chosen to govern the kingdom and began to direct the reins of his rule in the western regions.

In those days certain people reported to Maximinus concerning the aforesaid archbishop, namely, that he was the leader and standard-bearer of Christianity.

[Note: Our author most correctly places Peter’s Passion under Maximinus, not under Diocletian, as does that Greek biographer published by Combefis. At this point the learned editor, on p. 222, exposes the error.]

Inflamed by his customary wickedness, Maximinus immediately ordered Peter to be arrested and thrown into prison. For this reason he sent five tribunes, accompanied by troops of soldiers, to Alexandria. When they arrived, they carried out what had been commanded them: they suddenly seized the bishop of Christ and consigned him to the custody of the prison.

What marvelous devotion of the faithful! When it became known that so great a man had been confined in prison, an incredible multitude rushed there in extraordinary numbers, especially a chorus of monks and virgins. Not with material weapons but with streams of tears and the affection of a pious mind, they surrounded the prison. Like good children toward a good father—or rather, like Christian members clinging with all the compassion of their hearts to a most Christian head—they formed a wall around him, watching so that no pagan might have an opportunity to enter.

The prayers of all were one, their voice harmonious, and their compassion the same: they preferred to die rather than see anything evil happen to the holy man.

[Note: Thus the devout people of Milan kept watch around Ambrose, their bishop, when the fury of Justina, the Arian empress, threatened him, as Augustine, an eyewitness, testifies in *Confessions* IX.7.]

When the man of God had been confined in the same prison for a few days, the tribunes made a report about him to the king. The king, according to the custom of his ferocity, issued the sentence that the most blessed patriarch should be punished with capital execution.

When this news spread through the ears of the Christians, they all began with one accord to guard the entrance of the prison with mourning and lamentation, resisting and allowing none of the pagans to enter him.

But since the tribunes could by no means gain entrance to kill him, they took counsel and decided that all the soldiers, with drawn swords, should break into the crowd, and in this way drag him outside solely to be beheaded; and that if anyone attempted to resist, he should immediately perish by the sword.

[Col. 0694D] Meanwhile Arius, still adorned only with the Levitical dignity—

[Note: This is rightly stated, unlike the Greek Acts of Combefis and Vatican manuscript 622, in which Arius is falsely called a presbyter under Peter.]

—fearing that after the departure of so great a Father he would be unable to obtain reconciliation, approached those who were more distinguished among the clergy. As a dissembler, with mournful entreaty and flattering speech, he tried to persuade the holy archbishop to show him mercy and release him from such an obligation.

But what is more deceitful than a hypocritical heart? What is simpler than holy integrity? Without delay, those who had been asked entered to see the bishop of Christ. After the customary prayer, they fell prostrate with groans and tears, kissed his sacred hands, and pleaded with him, saying:

“Most blessed Father, the Lord has called you, in accordance with the dignity of your faith, to the crown of martyrdom, which we do not doubt you will receive very soon. Therefore we consider it just that, in accordance with your customary piety, you forgive Arius and grant pardon to his tears.”

When the man of God heard this, he drove them away in indignation and, raising his hands upward, cried out:

“Do you dare petition me on behalf of Arius? Arius, both in this age and in the age to come, shall always be separated from the glory of the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, and shall always remain an outcast.”

[Note: [Col. 0695D] The Acts of Combefis add here that Arius had separated the Son of God from the Father’s glory and substance. This is incorrect, because Arius had not yet revealed his heresy, but had been excluded merely on account of the Meletian schism and his suspect conduct. Nor does the other manuscript, Vat. 622, recognize this addition.]

While he was making this declaration, all who were present were struck with fear and, as though mute, kept silent. [Col. 0695B] Moreover, they suspected that he had pronounced such a sentence against Arius not without divine prompting. When the most merciful Father saw them silent and sorrowful in contrition of heart, he did not wish to remain stern or, as though despising them, leave them without satisfaction. Instead, taking Achillas and Alexander, who appeared to be the senior and holiest among the priests—one at his right hand and the other at his left—he led them a little apart from the others and said to them privately:

“Do not regard me, brothers, as inhuman and harsh. Indeed, I too am a human being living under the law of sin. But believe my words. Arius’s hidden deceit surpasses every iniquity and exceeds every impiety. And I assert this not on my own authority: it was [Col. 0695C] this very night that I decreed his exclusion.

“For while I was solemnly pouring out prayers to God, a boy appeared before me, apparently about twelve years old. I could not endure the brightness of his face, for this entire cell in which we stand was radiant with immense light. He was dressed in a linen colobium, split into two parts from the neck to the feet; holding the two openings of the colobium in both hands, he pressed them against his chest so as to cover his nakedness.

“At this vision I was astonished and overwhelmed. As soon as I was granted the confidence to speak, I cried out: ‘Lord, who tore this garment of yours?’ And he replied: ‘Arius tore me; but take every precaution not to receive him into communion. For behold, tomorrow those who will come to petition you on his behalf. See, therefore, that you do not yield when persuaded by them.’ [Col. 0695D] Rather, command the priests Achillas and Alexander, who after your departure will govern my Church, not to receive him in any way. You, however, are destined to complete the lot of martyrdom swiftly.’

“This was the whole cause of the vision. Behold, I have satisfied you and have announced exactly what I was commanded. As for what you will do about these things, that is for you to decide.”

Such was what he said concerning Arius.

[Col. 0696A] “Furthermore, dearest brothers, you know—and know well—how I have lived among you until now, and what great struggles I have endured from the idolatrous pagans who, ignorant of the Lord and Savior, foolishly do not cease proclaiming a multitude of gods who do not exist. You certainly know how, avoiding the fury of the persecutors, I wandered as a fugitive from place to place. I spent a very long time hiding in Mesopotamia; likewise, I lay concealed in Phoenician Syria; in both Palestines I endured a lengthy exile; and from there, so to speak, I remained for no little time in another element, namely, on the islands.

“Living amid all these hardships, I did not cease, day and night, to write to the Lord’s flock entrusted to my insignificance, strengthening them in the unity of Christ. [Col. 0696B] Their anxious care continually stirred my heart and did not permit me to rest. I considered myself relieved only when I commended them to the power above.

“But now, because of the fortunate bishops—I mean Phileus, Hesychius, [Note: [Col. 0696D] The Acts of Combefis and Vat. 622 add Pachomius.] and Theodore—who were rightly called by divine grace, how grievously was I shaken by tribulation! As you yourselves know, they were being tortured with various punishments, together with the other confessors, for the faith of Christ. And because in such a contest they were leaders and teachers not only of the clergy but also of the laity, I greatly feared that they might fail under prolonged tortures, and that their failure—which is grievous to say—might become an obstacle causing many to deny the faith. For they numbered more than six hundred and sixty, and they were confined with them in prison-workshops. [Col. 0696C]

“Therefore, with great labor and striving and with great sweat, I did not cease writing to all of them from the places mentioned above, exhorting them to the palm of martyrdom by the teaching of divine speech. When I heard of the magnificent perseverance of them all and of their glorious end in suffering, I fell to the ground and worshiped the majesty of Christ, who had deigned to number them among the ranks of the martyrs.

“What, moreover, should I tell you about Meletius of Lycopolis [Note: [Col. 0696D] Our author is entirely correct: Meletius was bishop of Lycopolis in the Thebaid. The Acts of Combefis are entirely wrong in placing him in Lycaonia. The affairs of Meletius are discussed at length by the early historians and by Baronius under the year 306, no. 45 and following.]? I have no doubt that you know perfectly well how many persecutions and how many plots he hurled against me. Shame upon him! He did not fear to divide the most holy Church, which the Son of God redeemed with his precious blood and for whose liberation from the tyranny of the devil he did not hesitate to lay down his life.

“This most wicked Meletius, as I began to say, divided her and also continued to attack and afflict in prison custody the holy bishops who, shortly before, had entered heaven through martyrdom. Therefore beware of his snares.

“For my part, as you yourselves see, bound by divine love, I am departing, placing God’s will before everything. I know indeed that the tribunes, trembling at my death, mutter among themselves, but I shall not on this account delay them with any speech; for I shall not make my life more precious than myself. Rather, I am ready to complete the course which my Lord Jesus Christ has deigned to promise me and faithfully to hand back to him the ministry I received from him.

“Pray for me, brothers. You shall no longer see me living with you in this life. Therefore I testify before God and your brotherhood that I have kept my conscience clear toward all of you. I have not avoided announcing to you what was enjoined upon me by the Lord, nor have I refused to disclose what would thereafter be necessary.

“Therefore watch over yourselves and over the whole flock among whom the Holy Spirit has successively appointed you bishops: you, Achillas, first, and Alexander, second. Behold, I declare to you in a living voice that after my departure certain men will rise from within the Church, speaking perverse things, and will again divide it, like Meletius, dragging the people after their madness. Behold, I have foretold this to you.

“But I implore you, my inmost selves: keep watch, for you must undergo many tribulations. We are not better than our fathers. Do you not know how much my father, the most holy bishop Theonas, who raised me and whose episcopal chair I undertook to govern, suffered at the hands of the pagans? Would that I might also have his character! And what shall I say of the great Dionysius, his predecessor, who, driven from place to place, endured many hardships from the madman Sabellius?

“Nor will I pass over you [Note: [Col. 0697D] Again our author rightly avoids the error of Combefis’s Greek biographer, who expressly states that Heraclas and Demetrius [Col. 0698D] came after Sabellius and Dionysius.], most holy Fathers and stewards of the divine law, Heraclas and Demetrius, whom Origen, the fabricator of perverse doctrine, subjected to manifold temptations. He cast into the Church a detestable schism which still confounds it today. But I believe that the grace of God, which then protected them, will protect you also.

“But why do I delay you any longer, dearest brothers, with a lengthy speech? It remains for me to accompany you with the apostle’s final prayer, praying thus: ‘And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to govern both you and his flock.’”

When he had said this, he knelt and prayed with them. After the prayer was completed, Achillas and Alexander kissed his hands and feet and, overcome with bitter sobbing, broke into tears, especially because they had heard him say that from that moment onward they would no longer see his life in this world.

Then the sweetest teacher went to the rest of the clergy who, as has been stated, had entered on behalf of Arius. He spoke to them his final and consoling words and whatever else was necessary; then, having poured out prayers to God and bid them farewell, he dismissed them all in peace.

When these things had been done, it was widely proclaimed everywhere that Arius had not been cut off from Catholic unity without divine prompting. But that craftsman of deceit and sower of every wickedness continued to conceal a viper’s poison in the labyrinth of his breast, hoping that he would be reconciled by Achillas or Alexander.

This is that Arius, arch-heretic, divider of the consubstantial and undivided Trinity. This is the man who, with reckless mouth, did not fear to blaspheme the Lord and Savior above all heretics—the Lord, I say, and Savior who, in pity for human error and grieving that the world was perishing in the destruction of deadly condemnation, deigned to suffer in the flesh for us all. For the divinity, which is certainly impassible, must not be believed to have undergone suffering. But since the theological Fathers have taken care, in a better style, to remove such blasphemies far from Catholic ears, and another matter now presses upon us, let us return to our subject.

The exceedingly shrewd bishop, therefore, perceiving the tribunes’ bloodstained stratagem—that in order to accomplish his death they wished to kill with the sword the entire multitude of Christians who were then present—did not wish them to undergo the bitterness of death together with him. [Col. 0698B] Rather, imitating the Lord and Savior, his faithful servant, who said and did, “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep,” he summoned, as an act of piety, one of the elders among those who were attending upon his instructions there and said to him:

“Go to the tribunes who seek to kill me and tell them: ‘Let all anxiety cease. Behold, I am ready to place myself voluntarily in their hands. Let them come tonight behind this prison house, and at the place where they hear a signal made from within on the wall, let them dig through and receive me, and complete what has been commanded them.’”

The elder, obeying the commands of the most holy man—for he could not contradict so great a Father—went to the tribunes and reported what had been enjoined upon him. When they heard this, they were very glad, and taking stonecutters, they came without soldiers at about dawn to the place that had been shown to them.

The man of God had spent the whole night awake in prayer and vigil. When he learned of their arrival, while all who were with him were resting in sleep, he entered the inner part of the prison at a slow pace and, according to the agreed arrangement, made a sound against the wall. Hearing it from outside, they made an opening and received the athlete of Christ, who was fortified on every side not with a bronze cuirass but with the power of the Lord’s cross, and ready to fulfill the divine saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.”

A remarkable thing! A storm of rain and collisions of winds roared so violently through that same night that none of those guarding the prison doors could hear the sound of the digging. But the steadfast martyr urged on those murderers, saying: “Do what you are going to do before those who were guarding me become aware of it.”

They took him and led him to the place called Bucolia, where Saint Mark also received martyrdom for Christ.

What an astonishing virtue in the saints! As they led him and saw such steadfastness before the prospect of death and such strength of spirit, dreadful fear and timid trembling suddenly seized them, [Col. 0699A] so that none of them dared look directly at his face.

The blessed martyr also begged them to allow him to go to the memorial of Saint Mark the Evangelist, for he desired to commend himself to his patronage. But they, looking down at the ground in shame and confusion, said: “Do what you wish, only do it quickly.”

Approaching, therefore, he embraced the most sacred cemetery of the Evangelist and, as though speaking to him alive and listening, prayed in this manner:

“Most honorable Father, you, the evangelist of the only-begotten Savior; you, witness of his sufferings; you, whom Christ, the liberator of all, chose as the first bishop and foundation of his chair; to you he entrusted the proclamation of the faith, so that it might resound throughout all Egypt and its surrounding territories.

“You, I say, diligently fulfilled the ministry of human salvation entrusted to you. For this labor you deserved to receive the palm of martyrdom. Therefore you are rightly proclaimed both evangelist and bishop.

“Your successor was Anianus, and the others [Note: [Col. 0699D] Our author rightly avoids the confusion of names found in the Acts of Combefis and in Vat. 622.] in continuous succession down to the most blessed Theonas, who deigned to strike my childhood with blows and nurture my character. I, a sinner and unworthy, also became his successor by hereditary succession, beyond my merit.

“And what is most important: behold, the generosity of the Lord’s mercy has granted me to become a martyr of the precious cross and the festive resurrection, bestowing upon my devotion the sweet fragrance of his passion, so that I too may be made worthy to pour out to him the offering of my blood.

“And because the moment of this libation presses upon me, pray for me, that by divine assistance I may deserve to complete the course of this contest [Col. 0699C] with a strong heart and most ready faith.

“I also commend to your glorious fatherhood the Christ-loving flock entrusted to me for pastoral governance. To you, I say, I humbly commend it—the one who is shown to be the author and protector of all who preceded and followed you on this episcopal throne, and who, holding primacy in it, are successor not of a man but of God and of the man Jesus Christ.”

Having said this, and moving only a short distance from the sacred tomb, he raised his hands to heaven and prayed aloud:

“Only-begotten Word of the eternal Father, Jesus Christ, hear me as I appeal to your mercy. I beg you, calm the storm of your Church; by the shedding of my blood, your servant, bring the persecution of your people to an end.”

Then a consecrated virgin who had a small ascetic dwelling adjoining this Evangelist’s cemetery, and who was spending the night in prayer, heard a voice from heaven saying:

“Peter, the beginning of the apostles; Peter, the end of the martyr-bishops of Alexandria.”

When his prayer was completed, he kissed the tomb of the blessed Evangelist and of the other bishops buried there, and went out to the tribunes. When they saw his face like the face of an angel, they were struck with terror and hesitated to speak to him of the ordeal that awaited him.

Nevertheless, because God does not abandon those who hope in him, he did not wish to leave his martyr without consolation at the moment of such danger. Behold, an old man and an aged woman were hurrying from the villages into the city. One of them was carrying four hides for sale, and the other two linen sheets.

When the blessed bishop saw them, he recognized the divine providence concerning him. Immediately he asked them: “Are you Christians?” They replied: “Yes.” And he said: “Where are you going?” They answered: “To the city market, to sell what we are carrying.”

The most merciful Father then added: “My faithful children, God has sent you here. Remain with me.”

At once recognizing him, they said: “As you command, lord.”

Turning to the tribunes, he said: “Come, do what you are going to do, fulfilling the imperial command, for day is already beginning to dawn.”

They, as though suffering violence because of the ruler’s wicked decrees, carried him from opposite the Evangelist’s sanctuary to a valley near the tombs. And the saint said: “Spread out the hides you have brought, old men, and you too, old woman, spread out the linen sheets.”

When they had spread them out, the most powerful martyr climbed upon them, extended both palms upward, fixed his knees upon the ground, and, with his mind directed toward heaven, offered thanksgiving to the almighty champion of the contest. Then, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, he said: “Amen.”

Next, loosening his omophorion from his neck, he extended his throat and said: “What you have been ordered to do, decide to do without delay.”

Meanwhile the hands of the tribunes stiffened, and they urged one another to undertake the deed; but all of them, seized by fear, stood dumbfounded. At last they agreed to set aside a common purse as the reward for the killing, so that whoever dared to commit such a crime would receive the proceeds of the homicide. Immediately each of them produced five solidi.

But, as the pagan poet says, “What do you not force mortal hearts to do, accursed hunger for gold!” One of them, following the manner of Judas the betrayer and made bold by greed for money, drew his sword and cut off the head of Christ’s bishop on the seventh day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 0699D] Vat. 622 gives the twenty-ninth day of the month Athyr. The Acts of Combefis give “the twenty-fifth day of the month of November” (πέμπτην ἐπὶ εἰκάδα τοῦ Νοεμβρίου μηνός).], when he had been in the episcopate for twelve years—three before the persecution and the remaining nine amid various kinds of persecution.

Then, after taking the price of blood from the executioner, the evil purchasers—or rather, bloodstained murderers—departed as quickly as possible, for they feared the multitude of the people, since, as has been stated, they were without military protection.

The body of the most blessed martyr, as the Fathers who first came there affirmed, remained standing as though engaged in prayer, until many people came running and found it standing in the same manner. What he had often done while alive, his lifeless flesh itself bore witness to.

They also found the old man and the aged woman keeping watch with mourning and groaning over the Church’s most precious jewel. [Note: [Col. 0700D] Let us note the vocabulary. Above also, col. 699, line 32, read *Christicolum*, as it stands in the manuscript, not *Christicolam*. The former ending also has another example in the additions of the distinguished Furlanetti.]

They accordingly arranged the triumphal funeral and, placing the sacred head against the neck, covered him with linen sheets. They reverently gathered with a small brush the holy blood that had flowed beside him. [Note: [Col. 0701D] Here is new testimony concerning the devoted care of ancient Christians in preserving the blood of martyrs; Boldetti discusses this matter at length in *On the Cemeteries of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 27 and following.]

Meanwhile an innumerable crowd of both sexes hastened from the populous city. Weeping and wailing, they asked one another what had happened, for from the least to the greatest all were drenched in the fiercest grief.

When the city’s leading men saw the commendable persistence of the multitude, who were trying to tear apart his sacred remains as relics, they wrapped him in hides and linen sheets and bound him more securely. For the most holy minister of God had always worn white priestly garments, namely, a tunic, a colobium, and an omophorion.

After this, a considerable dispute arose among them. Some were trying to carry the most sacred limbs to the church he himself had built, where he now rests; others attempted to take them to the Evangelist’s sanctuary, where he had completed the course of his martyrdom. Since neither side would yield to the other, they began to turn the service of religion into a quarrel of combat.

Meanwhile, a bold company of certain senators, among those called *cursus* [Note: [Col. 0701D] Understand this as the public transport service, by land or by boat.], seeing what had happened—for they were near the sea, prepared a boat. Suddenly seizing the sacred relics, they placed them in the vessel and, sailing behind the Pharos, came by way of the place called Leucado to the church of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, which, as we began to say, he himself had built for the cemeteries of the martyrs [Col. 0701C] in a certain suburb [Note: [Col. 0702D] A Greek expression, used for “suburb.”] on the western side.

Then the crowds of people, as though a heavenly treasure had been snatched away from them, followed in swift procession, some along the roads and others by every possible shortcut. When they finally arrived, they no longer disputed where he should be placed; instead, by common and commendable agreement, they first decided to place him on his own episcopal chair and only then consign him to burial.

And, most discerning reader, do not regard this as idle nonsense, for if you learn the reason for this innovation, you will marvel at and approve the people’s praiseworthy zeal and action.

When this blessed bishop celebrated the sacraments of the divine mystery, he did not sit, as ecclesiastical custom requires, on the episcopal throne, but on the footstool beneath it. [Col. 0701D] When the people saw this, they were displeased and complained, crying out: “Father, you ought to sit on your chair.” When they repeatedly said the same thing, the Lord’s minister would rise and quiet such complaints in a calm voice, then sit again on the same footstool. To everyone it appeared that he did this out of humility.

On a certain great feast day, however, while he was celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass and was about to do the same thing, not only the people but also the clergy cried out with one voice: “Sit on your seat, O bishop.”

But he, aware of a certain mystery, pretended not to hear this. Giving a sign that they should be silent—for no one dared obstinately oppose him—he made everyone keep quiet and nevertheless sat down on the footstool of that same chair. After celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass according to custom, each of the faithful returned home.

The man of God then summoned the clergy and, perfectly calm in inward serenity, reproved them for their boldness: “Why were you not ashamed to join your voices to those of the laity in reproving me?”

“Nevertheless, because this reproof did not flow from the muddy stream of boasting but from the pure fountain of love, I shall reveal to you the secret of this mystery. Often, when I wish to approach that throne, I see a certain power sitting upon it, radiant with an exceedingly brilliant light. [Note: [Col. 0702D] Understand this as either God himself or an angel.] Immediately, suspended between joy and fear, I recognize that I am entirely unworthy of such a seat; and if I had not feared introducing a seed of scandal among the people, there is no doubt that I would not even have dared to sit upon the footstool.

“That is why, dearest sons, I seem to you to exceed the episcopal rule in this matter. Nevertheless, whenever I see it vacant, as you yourselves are witnesses, I do not refuse to sit upon it in the customary manner. Therefore, now that you know this secret and have learned by experience that, if it is permitted to me, I shall sit upon it—not disregarding the dignity of the office—cease any longer to encourage the acclamations of the crowd.”

The most holy Father explained this to the sacred clergy while he was still alive, compelled to do so.

Remembering these things, therefore, the faithful of Christ in pious devotion took his most sacred body and made it sit upon the episcopal throne. Finally, such joy and exultation were bestowed upon the people from heaven that they seemed to behold him alive and breathing.

Then they embalmed him with fragrant spices and dressed him in silk garments; for each person considered whatever he could contribute by carrying it to be the greatest gain for himself. Carrying palms as signs of victory, with blazing candles, resounding hymns, and burning incense, they celebrated the triumph of heavenly victory, laid down the sacred relics, and buried them in the cemetery that had long before been built by him. [Col. 0702D] From that time until the present day, the powers of miracles have never ceased to occur there. Pious vows rejoice in their happy fulfillment; the sick are restored to health; and the expulsion of unclean spirits testifies to the martyr’s merit.

These gifts are yours, Lord Jesus, whose custom it is to magnify your martyrs more gloriously after the end of death. You live and reign with the Father and the consubstantial Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0702D] What follows concerning Arius, unhappily admitted to the priesthood by Peter’s successor Achillas, is entirely absent from the Acts of Combefis and from Vat. 622.]

[Col. 0703A] After this, we shall briefly explain how the crafty wolf, Arius, covered in sheep’s clothing, entered to tear apart the Lord’s fold, and by what means he was able to usurp the dignity of the priesthood.

We do not say this to disparage those who dared to restore to the threshing floor of the Lord’s harvest the tares of apostate contagion that had been cast out of the Church by the heavenly winnowing fan. They are undoubtedly distinguished for holiness, but, thinking too little of believing so great a man, they transgressed the prohibitions of the divine command.

What then? Do we condemn them? Not at all. As long as this corruptible body burdens us and an earthly dwelling weighs down the perception of our weakness, many people are deceived while thinking, more easily than not, supposing that what is unjust is just and what is incestuous is chaste.

The Gibeonites, threatened with complete destruction by a heavenly decree, had one thing in their intention but presented another in their speech and appearance; nevertheless, they were able to deceive Joshua, the most just divider of the promised land, with great speed.

David too, filled with prophetic inspiration, when he heard the words of the lying young man [Note: [Col. 0703B] I think either Absalom or Ziba, II Samuel 14:33; 16:3.], although acting under the inscrutable and just judgment of God, nevertheless did something quite different from what the facts warranted.

What could be greater than the apostles, who seemed to separate themselves from our weakness? For one of them declares: “In many things we all offend.” Another likewise says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

But when we repent of such things, we more easily obtain pardon, since we sinned not by intention but through ignorance or weakness. And certainly this kind of offense proceeded not from a desire for transgression but from merciful indulgence.

As for these matters, we leave it to others to compose a defense. [Note: [Col. 0703B] A fine defense indeed; from it I also infer that the Greek biographer of Peter lived close to Peter’s own time, since he so zealously defends Peter’s successor as though his memory were still recent.] We shall attend to what lies before us.

After, therefore, the magnificent champion Peter, worthy of his name, through the triumph of martyrdom . . .

The remainder is wanting.

## Maius’s Notice to the Following Prologue

*(Roman Spicilegium, vol. IV, p. 226.)*

[Col. 0703C] After publishing in the preceding volume the extensive history by Saint Sophronius of the holy martyrs Cyrus and John and their miracles, it seemed to me a sacrilege to omit two other histories written in the same manuscript, and indeed placed first in it. The author of both—or certainly of one of them—was the same Sophronius, as will become clear below.

The first begins, “The divine and sovereign Word” (Ὁ θεαρχικὸς ἡμῖν λόγος); the second is acephalous in the manuscript. In both, brief discourses of Saint Cyril concerning the same martyrs are mentioned—previously unknown and unpublished—which in fact are inserted in the manuscript between the two histories.

All these materials are found in a very ancient Greek manuscript that was once in the monastery of Crypta Ferrata and is now preserved in the Vatican Library under number 1607. In the Latin Vatican manuscript 5410, however, the first history is not read because the manuscript is acephalous, nor was it taken from the Greek manuscript mentioned above, as the different order and quantity of the material demonstrate. The second is found there, but it lacks its beginning and ends with Cyril’s brief discourses.

Both histories are unpublished in Greek. In Latin, Otho Zylius published the first, which he had himself worked over, but with enormous variation, in Bollandus; as we shall say below. No one had published the second even in Latin, for the one which Surius recites under January 31 is entirely different.

It happened conveniently that John Mabillon, in his *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, part II, pp. 83–84 of the preface, published a certain fragment belonging to the work of Sophronius as a whole, which he judged, not without reason, to be by Anastasius the Librarian. To this fragment of the preface he appended the beginning of the history that starts, “The divine and sovereign Word,” in Anastasius’s Latin translation. This work of Anastasius, scarcely indicated by Mabillon, is not found in the Vatican manuscripts.

For the rest, we have taken the other little history, together with Cyril’s accompanying discourses, from the Vatican manuscript. That it too proceeds from the translator Anastasius is demonstrated by the distich added at the place of the concluding inscription, in which Anastasius names himself.

Thus Mabillon writes in the work cited, p. 84:

“After the preceding prefaces of Anastasius”—which Mabillon presents in the same work—“it seemed appropriate to append this one as well, although mutilated, from the very ancient manuscript of our library of Saint Peter at Chartres. Bollandus published the history of this passion, translated into Latin from the Greek by Otho Zylius of the Society of Jesus, under January 31, since he had not seen Anastasius’s version. But the uncertain author whom he supposed it to have is Saint Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, as is clear from this preface. We restored the name of Anastasius by conjecture, since it had been obliterated in a defective and dislocated exemplar, and because the date and style agree with Anastasius.”

## Mutilated Prologue of Anastasius the Librarian to the Translation of the Passion of Saints Cyrus and John

[Col. 0703D] You have wished to compel my lowliness . . . to translate the passion of the saints Cyrus and John from Greek [Col. 0704D] into the Roman language; and I considered with myself for what reason you had pressed me with such insistence to undertake this while I was occupied with many other matters. But nothing else occurs to me at all, except that you are held by fraternal affection and are eager, evidently, to refresh your neighbors who approach—not only in Greek but also in Latin—with the salutary nourishment of the word, and to kindle them toward pious examples and toward the courageous struggles of these men for Christ.

This is especially so since the church in which you are occupied with divine worship and service near Rome [Note: [Col. 0705B] Understand this as the church of Saints Cyrus and John, still surviving near the city of Rome.] shines with the memory, indeed with the miracles, of these most victorious martyrs, and the feast day of their annual celebration is drawing near.

Therefore, as best I could, I have satisfied your charity; and, setting aside for a little while the work I had in hand, I preferred, even in weakness, to comply with your wishes.

Certainly, the passion of these men has two editions [lacuna]. Its author was Saint Sophronius, who later became renowned as bishop of Jerusalem. His celebrated memory is found in many writings of our ancestors and also in the holy sixth ecumenical council [Note: [Col. 0705B] Namely, Sophronius’s synodical letter was read at that council, and it still survives.], especially since he published several little works for the instruction of many and proclaimed sound doctrines of orthodox faith.

He also wrote not only the passion of these distinguished martyrs but also seventy chapters of their miracles, the number seventy being sacred among us [Note: [Col. 0706B] Sophronius himself discusses this number at length in his praise of the saints.]. Indeed, he opposed the rulers of the world—not only of the Christian religion but also of pagan religion—with an impenetrable wall of truth on behalf of the house of the Lord, and with strong steadfastness reproached their attacks.

Of these miracles, Boniface, a counselor, at the request of Theodore the *primicerius*, defender of the Roman Church, once translated twelve chapters with a preface.

As for the rest, if life by God’s favor should accompany me, our . . . to pray to God . . . most . . . priest of priests.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the eighth indiction, in the year of our lord Pope John VIII.

[Col. 0706B]

“Receive at last, O priest, rejoicing, the struggles of the saints,

Which were composed in Greek, but are now, by art, in Latin.”

## The Text of the Passion Begins

[Col. 0705]

[Col. 0705C] The divine Word, who is truly the Truth, namely Christ our God, proclaims in a resounding voice in the Gospels, saying: “All things are possible for one who believes.” Blessed Paul also . . . [lacuna].

Mabillon continues by saying:

“Anastasius’s translation adheres more closely to the letter than the Bollandian one, in which the name of the place in Arabia where Cyrus and John professed the monastic life has been omitted. Anastasius renders it as follows: ‘He came to the Arabia that lies along the Egyptian coast and lived in the fortress called Cetzo; and together with his dwelling he also changed his habit.’”

He likewise calls the workshop of the medical art an *ergasterium*, which we call a laboratory.

You see, therefore, that there were two editions of the work on Saints Cyrus and John, such as they actually are in our codex; Anastasius translated both of them, as Mabillon shows with regard to the first, while the distich of the Vatican codex attests the second. We, however, do not possess the translation of the former in the Vatican codex; for that reason we have supplied only its beginning from Mabillon. Nevertheless, we find the greater part of the latter in the Vatican codex. In any case, we neither give the Zylian translation of the former, since it differs very substantially, nor supplement in Latin the defect of the second, which is acephalous both in Greek and in Latin. Indeed, the Vatican Latin codex was not taken from the Greek codex of Grottaferrata, which begins somewhat earlier, but from the old Latin codex of the Canons of Saint Mary in Via Lata, which is now nowhere to be found, as I have said elsewhere.

[Col. 0705]

# ACEPHALOUS HISTORY OF THE HOLY MARTYRS CYRUS AND JOHN. TRANSLATED BY ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN

[Col. 0705D] 3. [lacuna] since he had been altogether unable to accomplish [it], he made an agreement, saying that he desired to dedicate a church to the three youths and wished this young man to be placed in charge of the pious work; once it had been completed, he again promised that he would obtain his request.

Accordingly, since he had a gerocomium at Doryzin, as the place is called, and had purchased a hall adjoining the gerocomium, in the middle of whose hall there was a sanctuary of the saints, that is, a medical establishment, he demolished the hall and laid it out in the form of a church [Col. 0706D]; he dedicated the medical establishment as a marvelous apse. Moreover, so that we may not pass over in silence the account of the benefit thereby accomplished, at the young man’s urging the work was completed by divine cooperation, and a very large temple was built. For, as the most wise Paul says, we hear that all things work together for good for those who love the Lord.

Having established both a gerocomium and a nosocomium, the high priest summoned a distinguished man—indeed, I am certain, one highly commendable and pleasing to God—and, giving him a letter addressed to the three holy youths, sent him to Babylon. The letter was a petition to those same saints, earnestly asking them through this man to send him relics to be placed in the temple that he had erected for them with great desire.

This venerable and honored man, neglecting none of the religious instruction, reached Babylon and delivered an excellent letter to the saints, addressing them as follows: “Holy ones, the good and supreme priest of God and your servant has sent you this petitionary letter. Having received it, give a reply.”

When he had said this, one of them sat up, stretched out his hand, drew the letter toward himself, and then reclined again, sending the man away without an answer. When the abbot had spent an entire week in supplication without receiving any response [Col. 0707B], he returned ineffectually to the one who had sent him and recounted what had happened to him.

## 4

But that most loving and supreme priest of God, with unshaken faith and a good conscience, sent them the same man a second time, saying: “Go again, and ask the saints on my behalf. At least now they will hear my petition. Take with you the letter you received, which I shall accept for the relics as though it had already been accepted and sanctified by them.”

Obeying the Father, obedient in every way to Christ both in action and in contemplation, he went again to Babylon and once more addressed the saints in supplication: “O thrice-blessed martyrs, the supreme priest of God has sent me to you again. Do not dishonor him, therefore, since he has dedicated such a temple to you—large and splendid—moved by the love that burns within him for you.”

When the saints were still sending him away without a reply, he began to carry out the high priest’s command, moved by a certain divine impulse. Placing his hand upon his breast—for there he had the letter—the saint held it in his hand, and blessedly drew it piously toward himself once he had accepted it. The most holy hand that held it followed along. Embracing it with profound reverence, he reached the city of Alexandria with this undefiled and worshipful treasure as well, by carrying out the most sacred command conveyed to him, displaying the hope he held in God as unconfounded.

## 5

When the great and supreme priest of God received it, rejoicing and exulting alike, he urged his brother’s son to prepare for the wedding. After he had proclaimed the dedication of the temple to the people [Col. 0707D] and had been filled with divine joy, on the following day, together with the entire clergy, he placed in a repository that precious and venerable hand of the saint, along with the petitionary letter held by it, just as it had indicated should be done. After the church had been consecrated, he ordained his brother’s son deacon, saying to him: “Behold your wife”—saying this of the church—and he added: “Care for her as is fitting.”

This deed brought the young man great progress in God, according to his hope. Finally, it made him a lover of chastity, displayed the operation of divine virtues, and God, hearing the will of the high priest who feared him, brought it about.

[Col. 0708A] ## 6

The saint whom we mentioned shortly before was a physician. Although he wore secular clothing, not a secular spirit, he practiced medicine; for he did not heal only the bodies of the suffering, but also their souls, bringing the worthy out of the unworthy and instructing the faithful from among those alien to the faith. He consoled the sick in their visitations not from the writings of Galen and Hippocrates and other such authors, but by prophetic, apostolic, and evangelical admonitions, leading them toward the life that is true health, numbering them among Christ’s flock, and showing them to be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

## 7

When the devil, who hates good, saw that he was offering many people to Christ, he informed the city’s ruler through wicked men, saying: “A certain Galilean physician has led astray the entire population of the city by his teaching, removed them from the worship of the gods, made them worship Jesus, whom the Jews crucified, as God, and is utterly abolishing the service that ought to be rendered to our gods.”

The wretched man, inflamed beyond measure by these words and by criminal fury, immediately ordered the saint to be seized. When the blessed man learned of this, he fled; he came to Arabia, which is on the coast of Egypt, and lived in a fortress called Cetzo. With his dwelling he also changed his clothing: for, shaving his head, he put on monastic dress.

Passing beyond a life that imitated earthly and temporal things and rising to higher matters, he became altogether exalted in both action and contemplation. He no longer healed illnesses with various medicines or with the aid of herbs, but by prayer alone [Col. 0708C] and devout teaching he freed souls from sorrows and bodies from sickness.

## 8

At that time, therefore, while Diocletian was impiously governing the scepters of the Romans and stirring up persecution everywhere against the churches of God, the most blessed John learned of these things. By birth he was an Edessene according to the flesh, but as a believer he was recognized as a citizen of heaven. Since he possessed military rank, he set out for Jerusalem; and, after fulfilling his vow in a manner pleasing to God, he came to Egypt, drawn by the fame of Saint Cyrus. He lived with blessed Cyrus as though they shared one faith, and, seeing healings advancing toward virtue, he was encouraged still further toward them.

When the persecution was raging with greater violence, while Cassian the pagan was exercising the priesthood of vanity at Canopus, three virgins living in that place and betrothed to Christ were seized by those who had been assigned to capture them and were brought, together with their mother Athanasia, before the city’s ruler. When Saint Cyrus heard of them, he was weighed down by fear as Christ’s friend, lest they, being young girls and afraid of the tortures, should renounce Christ and deny the faith. For they were indeed very young: Theoctiste, the eldest of them, was fifteen years old; Theodote, the second, was thirteen; and Eudoxia, the youngest, was eleven.

Their mother was rightly called Athanasia, “Immortality,” for she truly became, together with her beloved daughters, an heir of immortality. In speaking of these matters we have reached this point [Note: [Col. 0707D] More precisely, “concerning whom, as we said above.”]. Fearing, Saint Cyrus, together with John, entered the city and, soothing the virgins previously mentioned, raised them above nature. He strongly persuaded them to undergo the tortures fearlessly, out of their great love for Christ their bridegroom, assigning to them crowns of chastity and joy without end.

## 9

But the wretched enemy, again through his savage ministers, exposed these saints to the ruler. They darkened his mind and suggested that two men—a monk and a soldier—were misleading the virgins brought before them and preventing them from rendering the service owed to the gods, while persuading them to rebel against Caesar, refusing altogether to obey his commands and proclaiming Jesus to be the eternal king.

Syrianus, the governor destined to be struck by divine lightning, gnashed his teeth at what had been reported and ordered the two men themselves to be brought before the tribunal. He said to them: “O wretched men, enemies of the blessed gods and most deserving of death, why do you not allow the virgins to obey the decrees of Caesar? Or have you decided that they should rebel, as you yourselves, manifestly tyrants against the Roman emperor, fight on behalf of the utterly detestable religion of the Christians?

“Repent, therefore, and make our greatest lords favorable to you; then you will receive from the emperor honors of no ordinary kind.”

They replied to him: “Syrianus, we do not accept dishonorable honors. The things that are seen are temporal, and we do not offer worship to the images of demons, since worship belongs to God alone [Col. 0709C]. Nor will we deny him who made all things. Since we possess him as the eternal king, we hold the better gifts promised by him—gifts without end, full of immortal crowns and delights.”

## 10

Syrianus groaned at them and gnashed his teeth. Gazing at them with fiery eyes, he said: “You ought, by yielding to mercy, to gain salvation according to the law. But because you are held fast by arrogance, I shall persuade you by blows to obey the emperor’s commands.”

After saying this, he made the virgins stand by to witness what was being done, and inflicted every kind of torture upon the saints. He had them beaten with whips, pierced with nails, and burned with fire; he poured brine over the inflamed limbs and ordered them rubbed with haircloths. He filled their feet with boiling pitch [Col. 0709D] and, having employed every kind of torture, as has been said, watched the martyrs grow stronger. As though they themselves were suffering in alien bodies, they resisted all the more vigorously, drawing many to imitation and bringing them to the faith by their steadfast perseverance.

From such endurance of blows and from the cheerful, untroubled joy of the martyrs, many formed an image of the rewards of the incorruptible life to come. Therefore, when he had ordered the martyrs to be removed, he had the virgins beaten, together with their God-loving mother. But, as though kicking against the goads, he was overcome even by these women, for they had been strengthened by the martyrs. At last the wretched man pronounced sentence and ordered the heads of Christ’s brides, together with their mother, to be cut off.

[Col. 0710A] ## 11

He subjected the martyrs Cyrus and John to tortures again, and again he was repulsed, like waves dashed against rocks. When he had been unable to bend the saints by flatteries, prayers, admonitions, the offer of what he considered the greatest honors, scourges, boiling pitch, boiling water, fire, or instruments that twisted their limbs, he grew weary and pronounced sentence against them as well, saying:

“We subject Cyrus, the patron of the Galileans, and his associate John to capital punishment, because they do not obey the decrees of the emperors and in no way intend to worship the greatest gods.”

By this decree they put on the crown of incorruption on the day before the Kalends of February, when, preserving the faith, they completed the good course of the saints: namely, the three virgins, brides of Christ, Theoctiste, Theodote, and Eudoxia; Athanasia, who bore and piously nurtured them; and Cyrus the abbot, beloved of God, together with John the soldier, who shared with him one faith and equal honor.

They placed the three holy virgins on the eastern side of the church of Saint Mark, dedicating to them a beautiful church. But Cyrus the sweet-speaking one and John, Cyrus’s fellow martyr, they buried together in one reliquary in the church of the apostle and evangelist Mark.

## 12

After a considerable time had passed, when the pagan tyranny had been overthrown and Christians held the scepters of Roman rule, Theodosius the Great gained the empire. He adorned faith with works and adorned works with faith, as the books of ecclesiastical historians also testify [Col. 0710C], and as the events themselves loudly proclaim.

We shall also present a remembrance of one of his virtues, to demonstrate what has been said. They say that a war arose against him from the western regions, through a certain coalition of peoples and mixed nations, advancing and mingling together, flowing into one another like torrents and forming a sea by the multitude of their waters, or resembling locusts and numberless grains of sand.

But amid these circumstances the pious Theodosius did not seek the protection of other nations, send an embassy, or promise treaties of the sort that the weak like to make amid the turmoil of wars. Rather, as was his custom, he ran to God and seized the faith that brings aid [Col. 0710D].

## 13

When he learned that in Scete—the desert adjoining Egypt so called—there lived a man Egyptian by birth but adorned with every virtue pleasing to God, who had obtained divine grace and was a worker of the greatest miracles, he immediately wrote to Theophilus. At that time Theophilus was recognized as governing Christ’s sheepfolds. Theodosius asked that the remarkable man mentioned above be sent to him, requesting that he aid him with supplications poured out to God, since he rightly believed in the battle [Note: [Col. 0709D] So the codex reads; it refers to Theophilus.].

The bishop hastened to him, explained the situation, went up to him, and earnestly implored him. But Senuphius—for that was the blessed man’s name—begged the supreme priest earnestly to excuse him, declaring himself a sinner and calling himself an unprofitable servant of the Lord.

Since he was unable to obtain permission to leave him, he stood facing east. Taking the cloak that he wore over his shoulders, together with his staff, and extending his hands toward heaven, he cried out to God:

“Lord Jesus Christ, our God, grant to this staff and to this cloak the strength that you have given to me, your sinful servant.”

Having handed these things to the high priest, he said to him:

“Send these to the emperor, and write that, placing the cloak around his head and holding the staff in his right hand, he should go out before the whole army, taking precedence over the enemy line. For if Christ our God has appointed me as his servant, he will also hear my prayer, and through the faith that burns within him toward God he will obtain victory” [Col. 0711B].

## 14

When the things described above had been sent, Theodosius, crowned by God, was adorned with the cloak as a helmet of the hope of salvation. Having received the staff in his right hand, he advanced to battle and led the faithful army. When the barbarians saw him, they immediately turned to flight and slaughtered one another in mutual carnage, without receiving any arrow or blow at all from the army.

The pious and God-loving emperor was adorned with this helmet of salvation, as with every diadem, until the end. In Alexandria they celebrate a public festival of this event every year, calling it the “Iconium.” For they possess an icon of the pious emperor himself, with his head covered by the cloak and holding the staff in his right hand [Col. 0711C]; during their annual solemnity it continually proclaims the miracle to everyone.

## 15

By divine grace and through the cooperation of the faithful and pious ruler Theodosius, Theophilus, the bishop of the Church, the most watchful shepherd of the flocks in Alexandria, and a man filled with divine zeal, removed, so to speak, all the practices of the pagans. He adorned the entire city with houses of prayer and erected at the place called Canopus a very large and magnificent church dedicated to the apostles.

This place lies outside the city, twelve milestones distant from it, and was, as they say, especially revered by the pagan children. For they believed that an assembly of gods was located there. Thus the entire road leading there from the city was paved with stone slabs and lined with estates and baths. Twenty-four baths are recorded as standing here and there along it [Col. 0711D]. Many who know the place say that they had not yet been excavated. It was also thought that as far as the place called Canopus there extended the shrine and entire marketplace of the city. Two milestones from it stood a fortress containing an idol called Menuthis, in which the most wicked spirits openly operated.

In that fortress, then, the holy Theophilus again built a church dedicated to the evangelists.

## 16

After Theophilus’s death, when Cyril had assumed the government of the Church—Cyril, I mean, that great lover of piety and overthrower of those who violate the faith—he took special care to destroy the phantoms of Menuthis. He also removed certain simpler Christians who were rushing there of their own accord to receive healing.

After making many petitions concerning this matter to the most merciful God, he saw an angel of God, the God of all, announcing that his petition had been accepted and commanding him to take the body of Cyrus, the great martyr, from the church of Saint Mark and to place it in the Church of the Evangelists at Menuthis [collocaret: “to place,” rather than the transmitted “to behead”].

For this reason they also called the fortress by that name, out of reverence and love for the demon. In using a single name, the angel had referred to both martyrs, as will also be shown from the sermons of blessed Cyril.

The loving high priest neglected nothing. He did what had been commanded him, transferring the martyrs’ relics on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and delivering brief sermons to the people on this matter. We shall insert them for the readers’ belief and benefit alike, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with the Father and the Spirit, are glory, honor, and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

Hail, holy one, beloved of God, hail without boundary [Note: [Col. 0711D] So the codex reads, that is, “without end.”].

And remember your brother Anastasius.

# ACCLAMATION OF BLESSED CYRIL TO THE TABENISIOTAN MONKS WHO ARE IN CANOPUS, CALLED THE PLACE OF REPENTANCE, CONCERNING THE HOLY MARTYRS CYRUS AND JOHN

## Second Epiph, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of August

Strength and good endurance, and the visible duality of virtues, befit the saints above all. Blessed David cries out to them: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.” The Savior’s disciple says: “You have need of endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise.”

For we ought to begin with good things but seek their completion, so that we may inherit the kingdom of heaven, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power. Amen.

# OF THE SAME, THE SEVENTH EPIPH, THAT IS, THE DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF AUGUST: TWO ACCOUNTS CONCERNING THE HOLY MARTYRS ABBAS CYRUS AND JOHN, WHO REST HERE

Through these accounts this father makes known their honorable passion and the deposition of their holy relics. The present first narrative was delivered in the Metanoea, which is interpreted as “Repentance,” or in the Church of the Holy Apostles.

We have not been idle concerning our customary discourse, but, as the Savior said, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” We believe that, through your holy prayers and by God’s mercy, our affliction will be diminished.

Since we had both considered and undertaken what was useful, we judged it necessary to tell you again. These regions needed physicians who heal by God. Therefore, wishing to help all the places, and especially those adjoining the church of the holy evangelists [Col. 0713A], we investigated the matter, since people who had no oracle were going to other places and, although they were Christians, were wandering astray.

We therefore necessarily sought the relics of the holy martyrs. We discovered and carefully learned that at the time when the holy virgins suffered martyrdom—we have their fountain at the church of Saint Mark—two men were present, one a temperate monk and the other a soldier. They encouraged the same virgins and prepared them for the contest, so that they might endure danger with manly courage for our Savior.

These men also rest with them in the oratory. They entered courageously, suffered martyrdom for Christ, and laid down their lives for him. The bodies of the holy martyrs were lying together in one place. Since their relics were indistinguishable—for it was not clearly discernible which was this one and which that one—we necessarily took both and transferred and reburied them in the Church of the Evangelists, commemorating them as is customary for martyrs.

Let us therefore meet tomorrow, God willing, honoring both the holy evangelists and the blessed martyrs called Cyrus and John.

# OF THE SAME, THE EIGHTH EPIPH, THAT IS, THE KALENDS OF AUGUST, AT THE CHURCH OF THE EVANGELISTS, WHERE HE PLACED THE RELICS OF THE HOLY CYRUS AND JOHN IN A TOMB, TWO MILES EAST OF CANOPUS, BESIDE MENUTHIS

[Col. 0713C] “Large crowds were traveling with him. He turned and said to them: ‘Whoever comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, children, wife, brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not carry his cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.’”

These words urge us to be fervent in reverence for the Savior and persuade those who wish to love him to consider nothing more precious: neither bodily affection, nor love of fathers, nor reverence for mothers and sisters. For he knows that those who despise these things will find a great and splendid reward.

And what more need I say about this? They will learn how great a love he has for us, since he does not even make the things concerning himself better than our affairs [Note: [Col. 0713] Rather say: “He did not value his own concerns more highly than ours.”]; he did not place what concerned himself before the life and salvation of all.
