Although he is God, he became human for us and endured the cross, despising its shame. But those who suffer with him will also reign with him; those who were dishonored together with him will in every respect also be glorified with him.

We believe that the holy martyrs Cyrus and John also advanced in this way. Devoted to God, they entered the contest for piety. The worst beast, death, sprang upon them; but they remembered their Lord, who said: “Whoever does not bear his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.” They fulfilled the commandment; they too bore the cross and followed their Lord.

At that time they were led to the contests not alone, but with a chorus of holy virgins, who were women but pure in mind. Thus this excellent equality of the two athletes was completed with them also, and they obtained the reward of the charity that is in Christ: the power to trample Satan and drive out evil demons.

Let those who once wandered astray come, then; let them come to the true medicine from above, which cannot be bought. No one among us fabricates dreams, nor does anyone say to those who arrive, “The lady said, Do this or that.” A lady can indeed also be a god and wishes to be worshiped. Among demons there is neither male nor female. Observe what sort of purpose they have, that they even wish to be called by women’s names.

Trampling underfoot these old wives’ tales [Col. 0714C] and the deceptive riddles of diviners, let them come to the true physicians from above, to whom almighty God granted power to heal, saying: “Heal the sick; you received freely, give freely.”

Having received every healing that was bestowed by the Savior, let us praise our Lord together, so that we may also deserve the heavenly kingdom, in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom glory, honor, and power belong to God the Father with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

# LIFE OF JOHN THE ALMSGIVER, BY LEONTIUS, BISHOP OF NEAPOLIS IN CYPRUS, TRANSLATED BY ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN

(See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXIII, col. 337 and following.)

# BEGINNING [Note: [Col. 0715C] Vincent mentions this Life in *Speculum historiale*, book XII, chapter 150. It was written by Anastasius in the year 876, since it was dedicated at that time to Charles the Bald, emperor. It was written at the urging of John, a deacon of the Holy Roman Church, for whose benefit Anastasius likewise translated the Greek *Collectanea* into Latin, published by Sirmond, so that they might assist John in his study of ecclesiastical history. This is the Anastasius whom Hincmar calls his most faithful brother and religious abbot in a letter addressed to him. This Anastasius was the nephew of Arsenius, bishop of Orte, legate and counselor of Pope Nicholas, as Anastasius himself states in the encyclical letter concerning the death of Pope Nicholas I; in published copies that letter is addressed to Ado, archbishop of Vienne. Moreover, Surius, under 8 October, contains a little book on the Passion of Saint Demetrius the martyr, published by Metaphrastes; but the work of Anastasius surpasses it both in authority and in its commemoration of individual events.] PASSION OF SAINT DEMETRIUS THE MARTYR, BY ANASTASIUS THE LIBRARIAN

(At Mabillon, *Veterum Analectorum*, p. 172.)

[Col. 0715]

[Col. 0715A] To the most pious emperor Charles, forever Augustus, Anastasius the lowly [offers] a crown and a kingdom with Christ.

At the urging of the brethren, and especially of the highly learned man John the deacon, well known for the purity of your faith and the brilliance of your knowledge, I recently translated from Greek into Latin the Passion and miracles of the blessed Demetrius of Thessalonica. The aforesaid John had in his own house an oratory of remarkable antiquity and beauty dedicated to this martyr, yet he did not know what sort of martyr of Christ he was.

I, however, as I learned at Thessalonica, where his precious body lies buried, exhaling its fragrance, and shines with the splendor of miracles, made the matter known to him in due order. But because I know that your empire should not be deprived of knowledge of so great an athlete [Col. 0715B], I took care to send the same account to you at a suitable time, so that your greatness might obtain grace with God through the intercessions of the saints and friends of God, and through the prayer of this saint as well, and might deserve to enjoy everlasting glory.

May the King of kings and Lord of lords protect your kingdom with his right hand and transfer you from a temporal kingdom to an eternal one.

When the emperor Maximian was residing in the city of the Thessalonians, he, a superstitious man, persecuted those who listened to the pious religion, and they were put to death by him. Among them was the blessed Demetrius, who openly displayed himself without any fear. From his youth he had performed good works and taught others.

For he taught how divine Wisdom had descended from heaven to earth [Col. 0715C] in order to give life to the human being who had died through sin by his own blood. While he was preaching these and many other things, certain ministers of the emperor, who had been assigned to seize Christians, apprehended Saint Demetrius and brought him before Maximian.

The emperor had happened to go to the city stadium because of those who were about to engage in single combat. There a circle enclosed by certain boards had been prepared, where he was to watch those who fought against one another face-to-face in the arena [Col. 0716A], because he took pleasure in watching the shedding of human blood. Nevertheless, what he saw as pleasurable was not without care and anxiety for him.

He was burning with desire concerning a certain man named Lyaeus, a single combatant who had already killed many, abusing his strength and bodily mass, and who possessed, through practice and habit, the experience of killing. Because everyone feared him and no one seemed capable of resisting him, Maximian kept him among the foremost, cherished him, and gladly looked upon him. He praised and admired him and, as though over a great matter, took pride in the man’s arrogance.

When he had come near the stadium, those who had seized the blessed Demetrius brought him to the emperor [Col. 0716B]. On hearing that he was a Christian, the emperor—who had devoted himself entirely to the spectacle—ordered blessed Demetrius to remain there beside the stadium and to be guarded near the public bath.

The emperor himself took his seat. After Lyaeus had been brought in, he asked who wished to enter single combat with him, promising and offering gifts. Then a certain youth named Nestor leapt down from the upper seats and stood opposite Lyaeus, wishing to undertake single combat.

Maximian was astonished and summoned Nestor, who had leapt down for this purpose, and gave him advice, saying: “I know that poverty has raised you to such a height of madness that either, by conquering, you will acquire sudden wealth, or, deprived of your hope, you will lose your life while still suffering from poverty [Col. 0716C]. But out of compassion for the age that adorns you, I shall give you suitable and sufficient gifts merely for your bold attempt. Go, and possess gifts together with your life. Do not oppose Lyaeus, for he has defeated many stronger men than you.”

After hearing this, Nestor neither accepted the emperor’s advice nor feared Lyaeus’s strength. He replied to the emperor: “I have not come to this contest for money, as you said, but to prove myself better than Lyaeus.”

Immediately both the emperor and those around him, who favored Lyaeus, rose in anger at Nestor’s words, unable to tolerate his boastfulness. The emperor encouraged Lyaeus and made him confident. But Lyaeus hastened to show himself worthy of the emperor’s judgment.

When the combat began, Lyaeus received a mortal blow and died at once, bringing extreme disgrace upon the emperor. Therefore the emperor did not compensate Nestor with any of the agreed or promised money, but immediately leapt back onto his throne and returned sadly to the palace.

When certain people informed him about Demetrius, he was immediately stirred to anger and ordered him to be pierced with spears in the very place where he had been detained. Thus blessed Demetrius completed the martyrdom of a good confession.

His body was treated with contempt by the executioners [Col. 0717B]. But certain devout men secretly came at night, took it from the very dust into which it had been thrown and, carrying away the earth with it, concealed it as best they could, lest it suffer injury from any of the savage and bloodstained beasts.

After this, no one took care to transfer the saint’s little body, and it remained beneath a marker. Although it was celebrated only modestly, many notable acts of power and healings took place in the same place for those who invoked him in faith.

When the martyr’s merit had already become widely known, Leontius, beloved of God, a man who adorned the throne of the Illyrian prefecture, found the house containing the most holy martyr’s body extremely humble, buried on every side and hemmed in by the porticoes of the public bath and stadium [Col. 0717C]. He cleansed and purged everything harmful, enlarged it with more extensive grounds, and erected there an oratory in honor of the holy martyr Demetrius, to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom are glory, honor, and dominion to the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

A certain Marianus, one of the senators, was ordered by the emperors to govern the peoples who were in Illyricum, according to the manner of prefects. When he came to Thessalonica, he governed the prefecture’s reins piously and was acceptable to God and to human beings.

Then the devil, envying his prosperity, sought him out for testing, as he had sought Job. At first he began to test him with the seven vices. But Marianus, supported by God’s grace, overcame all his schemes. When the devil still made no progress, he took away from him all the riches of this world [Col. 0717D]; even then he could not conquer him, for aid from above was with him.

Therefore, finally, with God’s permission, the devil struck him with so grave an illness that he had control over none of his limbs except his tongue, with which he continually praised God. After he had endured this illness patiently for a long time, the devil came into the city in human form, carrying a certain parchment in his hands, and said to one of Marianus’s servants: “If your master lays this upon himself, he will be freed from his illness.”

The servant entered before his master and said to him: “What is your patience worth? Listen to me, then, and you will be healed. There is an unknown man in the city who has a certain parchment and says that, if you are willing to place it upon yourself, you will be freed from your illness.” He replied: “What is written upon it?” “I do not know,” the servant said, “but it mentions the names of gods and angels.” Marianus said: “God, without whose will nothing happens, can make me well without a written charm. Let him keep what belongs to him; let God’s will be done in me.”

After saying this, he was immediately overcome by sleep because of his pain and sorrow. While he slept, blessed Demetrius appeared to him and said: “Rise, and order your servants to carry you to Demetrius’s house; there, with God’s help, you will recover your health.”

When he awoke and asked those standing around him for the house of Demetrius the martyr, someone said: “It is a most wretched house near the stadium, where they say that Demetrius lies—the man who was formerly killed with spears by order of the emperor Maximian.” Then Marianus said: “Carry me there, because in a vision I was told that I could recover my health there.”

The servants then carried their master to the place where they had been ordered to take him, and he commanded them to lay him down only on the pavement. While he lay there, he was suddenly seized by sleep, and behold, blessed Demetrius appeared to him again, saying: “You can be healed through me, but I fear that after your recovery you may entangle yourself in the cares of this world.” Marianus replied: “You know, Lord, that I have never done this, nor do I desire to do so.” And he said: “Christ heals you, he who raises up the fallen.”

When Marianus awoke, he began to recount the vision. When he came to the point at which the martyr had said, “Christ heals you, he who raises up the fallen,” he rose healed, giving thanks to God together with all who were present there—God who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

There was also a certain prefect of the city of Thessalonica who suffered from a flow of blood. Like the woman who was healed by touching the fringe of the Lord’s garment, he had spent nearly all his resources on physicians, yet no one could heal him. At last, inspired by divine mercy, one day he said to his servants: “Carry me to the house of the protector of our city.”

They replied to him fearfully: “To whose protector’s house do you order us to take you?” He said to them: “Of the First [Protector].” They said: “Whose ‘First’? Tell us his name, lord.” But he looked at them and said: “Alas! I, lying here half alive, know him, and you, though you are healthy, do not know him? Do you not know that this city has many protectors, but one surpasses them all, who always fights for it eagerly? The whole region has deserved to possess him as an impregnable wall, not only the city. Carry me, therefore, to his house. Either, when he visits me, he will take pity on me; or certainly, when I die there, he will receive my soul and, interceding for me in the future presence of Christ’s dread tribunal, will rescue me from eternal punishment.”

When they heard this, they understood that he was speaking of the holy Demetrius, who frequently restored health to the sick, and they quickly lifted him up and carried him there. What tongue, dearest brothers, can honor this martyr with praises worthy of him? He performed such a great miracle that, in a moment of a single hour, he restored to health the man whom many and various physicians had been unable to heal. For as soon as he entered the doors of the martyr’s church, he obtained not only bodily health but also the health of his soul through the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0718A]

We have heard a friend of truth—namely, the chief priest—recount what happened concerning the martyr Demetrius; with God’s help, we shall strive to relate it in what follows.

He said that one night the ciborium in the holy temple of Demetrius, which was entirely splendid silver, caught fire, so that it was completely melted. The most holy bishop therefore endeavored to make the aforementioned ciborium, but he could not find the full weight of silver that had been melted for the completion of so great a work. He was considering within himself dismantling the silver throne that was in the same venerable temple and using it to finish the work.

When he had decided this within himself, with no one else knowing his plan, Christ’s martyr Demetrius appeared in a dream to a certain presbyter, a man of excellent life named Demetrius, and said: “Go and tell the bishop of the city: Do not dare to destroy the throne of my house.”

When the presbyter reported this to the bishop, the prelate was first astonished that his private thought had been revealed. Then he supposed that the man—who was the administrator of the temple of the venerable martyr—had fabricated the story out of some suspicion. The bishop said to him: “You never heard this from me, brother.”

After many days, however, when he had again examined the matter and found no other plan by which the ciborium could be completed, he confirmed his original decision to make the ciborium from the throne. When he ordered the silversmith to be summoned so that he might instruct him to remove the throne, someone announced to him: “The presbyter Demetrius asks to enter before Your Holiness.”

When he had entered, he said to him: “The martyr Demetrius, who previously appeared to me, a sinner, appeared to me again in a vision, with a somewhat sorrowful face, and commanded me to announce these words to Your Beatitude: ‘For the sake of charity, do not grieve me by destroying the throne.’”

When the bishop heard this, he became angry with the presbyter, for he thought that the man was inventing such things. He dismissed him from his presence rather harshly and made his own intention clear, saying: “You judge that enough should be given, although the weight of silver is insufficient. Do not make rash judgments while philosophizing over the tribulations of others.”

Then the presbyter went out in confusion. For the saint had not yet told him what should be done, but only: “Do not destroy my throne.”

That very night, Saint Demetrius appeared to the presbyter Demetrius and said to him: “Go and tell the archbishop: Do not concern yourself about my ciborium, for I myself will complete it.”

The presbyter carried out the martyr’s command and told these things to the bishop. When the prelate heard them, he gave praise to God and to the holy martyr Demetrius.

While they were still speaking about these matters with one another, behold, the doorkeeper arrived, saying: “Holy prelate, the wealthy Menas is standing before your door and wishes to speak with you.” He said: “Let him come.”

The aforementioned Menas came and offered seventy-five pounds of silver toward the ciborium. Then John arrived—“the sweetness of the poor”—and offered him a weight of forty pounds of silver. The citizens who came also offered what they could, so that the ciborium might be rebuilt.

Thus the often-mentioned work was rebuilt through the merits of the holy martyr, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0720A]

Nor do we think that we should omit what we heard from the most holy archbishop. He related the story of a custodian of the temple of the martyr Demetrius named Onesiphorus.

“One day, as I was going to the church of the aforementioned martyr, I found the aforesaid custodian Onesiphorus lying half alive before the door of the holy martyr. When, disturbed, I lamented my friend’s illness, Onesiphorus recovered consciousness and, seeing me weeping, said: ‘Why are you grieving on my account, lord Eusebius? If you love me, do not be troubled, but order my tomb to be prepared, and bury me alive in it.’

“Troubled and sorrowful, I said to him: ‘For what reason, brother?’ He replied: ‘Because by my sin I provoked the holy martyr to anger. The holy martyr appeared to me, a sinner, in a dream and spoke to me in a gentle voice: “Brother Onesiphorus, I am not pleased with what you are doing. The salvation of souls pleases me more than thousands of weights of gold. Do you not know that a candle offered for sins, the more brightly it appears to burn, the longer it remains before the saints on behalf of sinners, to intercede for them? Therefore allow the larger and smaller candles to burn, because my house must be entirely illumined by candles.”

“‘“But I, wretched man, when I awoke, thought that I had seen a phantasm and said to myself: ‘A saint does not appear to sinners.’ Twice and then a third time I received the same admonitions in dreams, and I wished to observe them and desire to preserve them to the end.

“‘“But on this very night a devout man came to the church carrying large candles to offer. After his prayer he left the church. I considered extinguishing them, having forgotten the holy martyr’s command. When I rushed to extinguish the candles, Saint Demetrius shouted at me from his silver resting place in a loud and terrible voice: ‘Greedy one!’ and again, ‘Greedy one!’ I, most wretched and exceedingly terrified, was struck to the ground and thrown outside the monastery gates. That is where you found me lying, almost dead.”’

“Our father the archbishop often recounted these things. We, however, must obey what the saints command us by divine authority. May their kindness always protect us and make us steadfast in Christ’s commandments. Amen.”

[Col. 0720D]

It happened to the inhabitants of the city of Thessalonica, evidently because of their sins, that a barbarian people ravaged their land: they burned their houses, uprooted their vineyards, and carried their sons and daughters, horses and asses, sheep and cattle into captivity. They laid waste the grain, wine, and oil during the siege of the city. A severe famine followed the persecution throughout that entire region.

Therefore the leading men of the city sent envoys to the emperor, asking him to free the city from the barbarians’ siege and from the famine that threatened. Meanwhile, the most glorious martyr Demetrius, just as he is painted in images, appeared in part of the island of Chios to a certain shipmaster named Stephen, who was carrying a cargo of two hundred *modii* of grain to the imperial city, and said to him: “Listen to me, and sail quickly to Thessalonica.”

As though transported out of his mind because of the martyr’s vision, and scarcely able to speak, Stephen said: “Lord, we have heard that it is to be captured by the barbarians.” The saint replied: “Sail there, then, and tell the ships you meet that Thessalonica has been saved through God’s mercy.”

After saying this, the saint began to go before Stephen, walking across the sea. As Stephen sailed toward Thessalonica, he recounted the martyr’s vision to everyone he met. He arrived before the envoys whom the citizens had sent to the emperor, together with many merchants, turning the city’s mourning into joy and also explaining how the martyr had appeared to him. For, terrified by divine fear, the enemies had withdrawn from the siege shortly beforehand.

[Col. 0721B]

You all know of the famine that occurred some time ago, not only in this city of Thessalonica but almost everywhere, to such an extent that it even seized the queen of cities, and affected not only grain but other necessities as well.

When the city was being oppressed by so great an affliction of famine, that holy martyr Demetrius, by divine providence, sent them ships from many different regions, full of various crops—both liquid and dry—and laden with every kind of good human food. Thus their hope was immediately released from their necessities, as you shall now hear.

There was a man appointed by his master over the island of Chios to purchase the grain brought by the ships there. When he could find no ships and was held by deep sorrow, he heard a voice saying to him: “Why are you anxious? Know that Demetrius has made the first payments in order to send grain to Thessalonica.”

He arose and went to the church of Saints Victor and Isidore, wishing to learn from the country people who this Demetrius was. When he asked this and could find no indication, he suspected that a man named Demetrius had been sent by the prefect of the city of Thessalonica. He immediately sent a letter to his master, explaining how the grain was being purchased from Demetrius.

The master reported these same things to the emperor. When he investigated the matter, he found that no one had been sent by the prefect of Thessalonica and that there was not even a man named Demetrius. Both the emperor and the people therefore understood that no one else had appeared to the aforementioned man except the martyr Demetrius. Everyone who heard this glorified God, who through the merits of the martyr had freed the city of Thessalonica from the danger of famine.

[Col. 0721D]

A certain prefect was in charge of the cities of Illyricum. There is no need to state his name, because it remains for everlasting disgrace. Inflated with pride, he summoned certain men who governed the city of Thessalonica and demanded that they carry out a particular arrangement.

They fell at his knees and said that they could not obey his commands. But he said that they were pretending. Then they said: “If you do not believe us, we shall swear before the tomb of Saint Demetrius that we cannot accomplish this.”

But he broke into blasphemy against the martyr, telling his fellow citizens some sort of deception about the glorious martyr. Unable to endure the blasphemy, they stopped their ears and went out.

After two days, the prefect’s body was seized by such an illness from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head that the disease could not even be diagnosed by physicians. He remained in this illness for eight months. In the eighth month, the wretched man came to such misery that half of his body became paralyzed: although he could see all his limbs, he had no power to move them. Wondrous is the power of God, who performs such things through his servants!

[Col. 0722A]

Eusebius, archbishop of the city of Thessalonica, saw a vision which I wish to relate to you.

Before the barbarian storms descended upon the city of Thessalonica, the aforementioned bishop saw himself in a dream sitting in the city’s theater with a great crowd of servants. While he wondered why he was sitting in such a shameful place and wished to rise and leave, he saw an actor standing on the stage where plays are performed, saying to him: “Wait, because I have you and your daughter to lament.”

He said to him: “Do not trouble yourself. I have neither a daughter nor anything in me that calls for lamentation.” But the actor replied: “Indeed you have a daughter, and you are the mother of many children; and you must lament her.”

Then the bishop understood that he was calling the city his daughter and said: “I adjure you by God not to lament either me or her.” When the actor wished to repeat the lamentation for a third time, but the bishop prevented him, the bishop awoke from sleep and understood that the tragedy had no good meaning.

After a few days had passed, an innumerable multitude of barbarians surrounded Thessalonica, and the bishop recognized that the vision he had seen was true.

When, as we have related above, the barbarian people were ravaging the Thessalonian countryside, the inhabitants of the surrounding areas were oppressed by famine because of their persecution. At last, when the inhabitants had been nearly destroyed by both sword and famine, the barbarians took counsel and suddenly attacked the city, thinking that it was empty of human defenders—as was in fact the case—and desolated by famine. We were few, while they exceeded the number of locusts.

They then constructed embankments, engines, iron battering rams, catapults, and enormous covered sheds, covering everything with ox and camel hides so that the citizens could not destroy them by setting fire to them. They pressed upon the citizens so severely that no one had any hope of life.

They besieged the city until all provisions suitable for both human beings and animals had been exhausted. Having resolved to attack the city unanimously at first light on the following day, they surrounded it on every side with their instruments of war.

When the city was now about to be captured, they saw what seemed to be a swarm of bees—a multitude of armed men—emerging from the city. A certain red-haired young man of exceedingly beautiful appearance led them, carrying the sign of the cross in his hands and riding a white horse. He charged upon them.

Shaken with terror, they abandoned the city and seized the protection of flight. A few, however, who were unable to flee, remained there half alive. The citizens captured them and asked why such a multitude was fleeing without any apparent cause.

The barbarians then said: “A multitude of men whom you had concealed, together with a most powerful leader, drove our troops away.” The citizens understood that their leader was the martyr Demetrius, who had driven away the enemies with an army of angels.

They gathered the spoils of the enemy and assembled at the church of blessed Demetrius, giving immense thanks to God, who through his intercession had freed their city from its enemies.

While several people were saying various things about the barbarians’ flight, one of our brothers rose and said to us:

“One night during this week, after Matins, I remained in the temple of Saint Demetrius the martyr and prayed before his holy tomb. A heavy sleep overcame me, so that I was neither entirely asleep nor fully awake.

“And behold, two men of terrifying appearance appeared and said to the temple’s custodian: ‘Where is the lord of this temple?’ He replied: ‘He dwells beneath that ciborium.’ They said: ‘Go and tell him that we have been sent to him.’

“The custodian went, and they followed him. He called the saint, saying: ‘Holy Demetrius, two soldiers sent to you by their lord are here.’

“Immediately the most holy martyr of Christ appeared from within and stood beside the doors; he also appeared to me, unworthy as I am. I fell face down, unable to endure looking upon his angelic face. His appearance was not like the form depicted in his older images; rather, his face emitted rays like the sun.

“Although I lay prostrate, I listened carefully to what they said to one another. I heard the men greet the saint kindly. He said to them: ‘The grace of God be with you. Why have you been sent to me?’

“The men said: ‘Our lord sent us to Your Holiness to announce this to you: Come out quickly and come to me, for the city will be handed over to its enemies.’

“When I heard this, I was troubled by the painful message. I raised myself on my hands and, looking upward for a while, saw the exceedingly sorrowful face of the most merciful martyr. After an hour had passed, I saw tears flowing from his eyes down his cheeks.

“Then the temple’s custodian said to the two young men whom he had brought in: ‘Why have you troubled my lord? If I had truly known your purpose, I would not have led you to him.’

“Then the saint of God said to his servant: ‘These are my servants, and what was commanded to them they have also announced to me.’

“Afterward the holy martyr said in a loud voice:

“‘O Lord Jesus Christ, you said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live”; and again: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” Although you are Lord of all the angels, you gave your soul for the redemption of sinful human beings.

“‘Lord, you entrusted this city and its fellow citizens to me, so that I might dwell with them forever and guard them. How, then, can I abandon them in such great distress? Or with what face shall I behold the destruction of my homeland? What life shall I have if my fellow citizens are destroyed?

“‘Just as I was spiritually with them while they feasted, so I shall not abandon them while they are in danger. Whatever they are worthy to suffer, I too would rather suffer with them.

“‘But you, almighty and merciful God, who heard Jonah from the belly of the whale, the three youths from the furnace of blazing fire, and Susanna from the false accusation, hear your people and free them from destruction by the barbarians.’

“Immediately a voice sent by the Lord was heard: ‘Let it be done for them according to your will.’

“Then, with great joy, he greeted the two young men who had been sent to him, giving thanks to God because he had heard him.

“Know without doubt that through this saint you have received life and victory, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.”

[Col. 0724A]

I wish to insert among the other miracles this miracle which the holy martyr Demetrius performed in our own times.

There was a certain bishop from the region of the Africans named Cyprianus, who was diligently devoted to the true priesthood and led a life most worthy of God. He undertook a journey to the queen of cities, Byzantium, compelled by a necessary matter.

When they had sailed for many days and were already approaching the regions of Greece, he was captured, together with all his companions, by the fiercest Slavs. After they had divided the captives among themselves, they also divided the aforementioned bishop among them for servitude.

When these things had occurred and they were returning to their own places, each barbarian imposed upon his captive whatever burden of service he wished. Bishop Cyprianus guarded his master’s basket and wisely distributed his food by providence, while nobly strengthening his own life through prayers, vigils, and fasts.

Considering that the people entrusted to him were absent, he entreated the Lord, the chief shepherd, to preserve them under his governance. He said to the Lord:

“When I had no merit, you appointed me shepherd of your flock. How have I now been reduced so that I have been transferred from such an office to the service of barbarians? Yet I remember that this has happened to me because of my sins, and therefore I am held entangled in this tribulation. Who will tell my sheep that their shepherd has been captured by barbarian beasts?”

As he wept over these and similar matters, a handsome and beautiful young man appeared before him, bearing the appearance and clothing of a soldier, and said to him: “If you wish to be freed from the slavery in which you are held and rescued from the barbarians, rise and follow me.

“But observe this: as we travel, do not speak to me at all. Let us both devote ourselves to silence and proceed on our journey, praying to God inwardly.”

Then the bishop replied: “Who are you, and from where have you come here?” He said to him: “I am called Demetrius, and I am a soldier of the great emperor. My house stands in the middle of the city of Thessalonica. If you follow me there, I shall bring you without loss.”

He rose and followed him, and the two proceeded in silence. They traveled by night and rested during the day. Demetrius would leave the bishop in the morning and return again as evening approached, bringing with him fruit from various trees and vegetables and herbs, with which he fed his companion. After taking food, they resumed their journey.

After eight days, when they had approached the walls of the aforementioned city, Demetrius halted Cyprianus before the city gates and disappeared.

When the bishop sought his faithful guide and good companion but could not find him, he entered the city. He asked everyone he met and addressed where the house of the soldier Demetrius was.

Although many admitted that there were several Demetriuses in the city and that they served in the military order, he kept saying: “The house of the man I seek is in the middle of the city.”

As everyone wondered along with him, the man he sought was found nowhere. The inhabitants of the city led the bishop to the martyr’s church.

When he entered, he immediately devoted himself to prayer and offered grateful praises to God the Savior. Then, rising with his hands extended upward and his eyes looking up, he saw an image of the martyr Demetrius wearing the clothing of his companion and guide.

He cried out before everyone, affirming without doubt that this was Demetrius, who had led him and saved him, and that this was the martyr’s house, which, when he appeared to me at the beginning, he himself had revealed.

The presence of the man was then announced to the bishop of the city, and what had happened to him became known. The bishop immediately received him as a fellow minister into his episcopal residence and treated him kindly.

But Cyprianus would not endure being separated from the holy martyr’s church even for an hour. Throughout the entire time he remained in the city, he stayed in that same church.

After he had wintered there and awaited the season for sailing, as soon as the time arrived he boarded a ship, taking with him an image of the martyr Demetrius. He sailed safely to the city of Constantinople. Having properly arranged his business, and with the assistance of the victorious martyr Demetrius, he returned to his own region and flock, promising the martyr abundant worship because of what had happened.

Then, considering how he might repay the kindness and striving to show gratitude for his liberation, he began to dedicate a temple in his own city to his companion and martyr Demetrius. He wished to construct a similar ciborium and a similar ambo, which he had seen, with marble columns, in honor of Saint Demetrius the martyr.

He was greatly troubled because he had no idea at all how or from where he could obtain the materials for these things. Finally, one night, when the bishop was exhausted by the excessive rush of his thoughts, sleep overcame him and he immediately fell asleep.

And behold, the holy martyr Demetrius stood before him and said:

“Why are you troubled, brother? Have you not heard the Lord Jesus say to his disciples: ‘Amen, I say to you, if anyone says to this mountain, “Be taken up and thrown into the sea,” and does not doubt in his heart but believes that whatever he says will happen, it will be done for him’? Where is your faith?

“O man, do not be anxious about the columns or the ambo. For a ship is today descending from the sea, carrying everything that you appear to need for the preparation of the temple.

“There is a bishop in the regions of Gaul, in the city of Massilia, preserving the people entrusted to him. He is building a temple in honor of the holy martyr Victor, our companion or brother, and wishes to build for him an ambo and a ciborium, just as you have in my house.

“For this reason he sent a ship with his servants to the porphyry mountain, to purchase for him columns and sufficiently large porphyry slabs for completing the work of the holy martyr Victor. But, through the intercession of the holy martyr Victor, the aforementioned bishop has already found within the city columns and porphyry slabs, wonderfully decorated, which had long before been laid upon the ground.

“The ship, with the columns and porphyry slabs purchased by his representatives, the martyr of Christ sends to us, so that from them you may make the work that you wish to make for me.”

Then the bishop arose from his bed and recounted the vision in order to his clerics. For this reason he sent them to the seaport.

When they found the ship and had spoken with the shipmaster, they asked him to accept a suitable price for the columns and marble slabs and to fulfill the bishop’s desire. But the shipmaster and those who were with him denied that they possessed anything whatsoever of the things being sought.

The clerics who had been sent reported these matters to their bishop, making him sad, and he went about grieving because his plan had come to nothing.

Again the holy martyr Demetrius appeared to him in a vision and said:

“Go yourself to the aforementioned shipmaster and say to him: ‘Do not be a liar. In your own ship you have a stowed ambo and the remaining marble, hidden away.” Do not hesitate to give these things to me, because of the bishop who sent you to seek them. My brother has found in the city of Massilia the means by which the work of his own oratory will be completed.’”

The bishop went, said these things to the shipmaster, and recounted the marvelous visions. He persuaded him to accept from him the price for the marble. And so it was done.

The bishop therefore dedicated the temple that he had built for the holy martyr Demetrius, with an ambo and ciborium, to the praise of Christ and the glory of the aforementioned martyr.

Through his prayers, if any sick person comes devoutly to that temple and is anointed with the oil of his lamp, he will immediately be healed through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## Acts of Saint Crispina, Virgin and Martyr, by Anastasius the Librarian

*(In Mabillon, Ancient Analecta, from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Theodoric near Rheims.) (C)*

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727A]

In the consulship of Diocletian II and Maximian Augustus, on the day of the Nones of December, at the Colony of Thebeste, in the records office, while the proconsul Anulinus was seated on the tribunal, the clerk’s office said:

“Crispina of Thagora, who has despised the law of our lords and rulers, is to be heard, if you order it.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Let her be brought in.”

When blessed Crispina had been brought in, the proconsul Anulinus said: “Have you now learned the sentence of the sacred command?”

Blessed Crispina replied: “I do not know what has been commanded.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “That you sacrifice to all our gods for the safety of the rulers, according to the law given by our lords Diocletian and Maximian, the pious Augusti, and by Constantius, the most noble Caesar.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “I have never sacrificed, nor do I sacrifice, except to the one God and our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, who was born and suffered.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Cut away your superstition and bow your head to the sacred rites of our gods.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “Every day I worship my God, beside whom I know no other.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “You are obstinate and contemptuous, and you will begin to endure the force of the laws against your will.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “Whatever may arise on behalf of the faith that I hold, I shall gladly suffer.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Your mind is vain, since, without abandoning your superstition, you continue to venerate sacred names.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “Every day I worship, but my Lord, beside whom I know no other.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “I shall present you with a sacred command for you to observe.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “I observe the command, but that of my Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 0727C]

The proconsul Anulinus said: “You will lose your head if you do not obey the commands of our lords the emperors, whom you are compelled to serve after being subdued; and all Africa has done so. You cannot doubt this.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “May it never go well with them if they make me sacrifice to demons. I sacrifice instead to the Lord, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Then these gods are not accepted by you, although you are known [manuscript: ‘are compelled’] to render them service, so that you may arrive safely at the act of devotion.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “There is no devotion that compels unwilling people to submit.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Would that you followed the devout path, so that with bowed head in the sacred temples you might offer incense to the gods of the Romans.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “I have never done this since I was born, nor have I known it, nor shall I do it for as long as I live.”

[Col. 0727D]

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Do it, if you wish to escape unharmed from the severity of the laws.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “I do not fear what you say; it is nothing. But if I should despise the God who is in heaven, I would be sacrilegious, and he would destroy me once and for all, so that I would not be found on that coming day.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “You will not be sacrilegious if you obey the sacred commands.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “What do you want? That I should be sacrilegious before God but not before the emperors? Far from it. God is great, who made the sea, the green herbs, and the dry land. But human beings, made by him, what can they provide for me?”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Worship the Roman religion, which our invincible lords the Caesars and we ourselves observe.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “I know only God. Those things are stones and creations made by the hands of human beings.”

[Col. 0728A]

The proconsul Anulinus said: “You are speaking blasphemy, for you do not pursue what is suitable for your salvation.”

The proconsul Anulinus added and said to the clerk’s office:

“After being reduced to every kind of disfigurement, let her be shaved bald by the razor, so that her face may first be brought forth for public spectacle.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “Let the gods themselves speak, and I shall believe. If I were not seeking salvation to be heard, I would not be standing before your tribunal.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Do you desire to live for a long time, or to die in punishments, as did your other companions Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda?”

Blessed Crispina replied: “If I wished to die, to surrender my soul to destruction and to eternal fire, I would give my will to your demons.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “I shall cut off your head if you disdain to adore the venerable gods.”

[Col. 0728C]

Blessed Crispina replied: “I give thanks to my God if I shall have attained this. I lose my head once; but if I were to offer incense to idols…”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Do you persist entirely in this foolish frame of mind?”

Blessed Crispina replied: “My God, who is and who was, commanded me to be born. He himself gave me salvation through the water of baptism. He himself is with me, so that my soul may not commit sacrilege, as you wish.”

The proconsul Anulinus said: “Why do we tolerate the impious Crispina any longer?”

The acts containing what was said were read back. When they had been reread, the proconsul Anulinus read the sentence from the written document:

“Crispina, persisting in unworthy superstition and refusing to sacrifice to our gods, according to the commands of the Augustan law, [lacunose and uncertain text], has been ordered to be punished by the sword.”

Blessed Crispina replied: “I give praise to Christ; I bless the Lord, who has deemed me worthy to free me in this way from your hands.”

[Col. 0729A]

Blessed Crispina suffered at Thebeste, on the day of the Nones of December, while Anulinus was proconsul and our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning in the unity of the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon of Saint Theodore the Studite on Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, translated by Anastasius the Librarian

*(In Acher, volume II of the Spicilegium.)*

[Col. 0729]

## Anastasius’s dedicatory letter

[Col. 0729B]

To the holy and venerable Aion, bishop of Beneventum, Anastasius, librarian of the holy apostolic see: greetings in the Lord.

Your fervent devotion toward the apostle Bartholomew, moved by an affection of great love, recently urged me—since his celebrated memory was already held among you—to send you anything found in his praise, at least in Greek, that might be translated into Latin or Greek. Although many things are indeed found in his praise that have been written either in Latin or in Greek, there is nevertheless one sermon recently published for which no evidence has yet shown whether it exists in Latin. I therefore resolved to translate it and send it to your fatherly care.

But if you ask who is the author of so great a sermon, I shall gladly disclose it. [Col. 0729C] It was a certain Theodore, a priest who lived in the city of Constantinople in the times of the Roman pontiffs Hadrian and Leo, a man of extraordinary distinction, endowed not only with steadfastness of faith but also with the grace of knowledge and the power of miracles. He was appointed abbot of two celebrated imperial monasteries, namely Studium and Saccudium.

Always remaining in communion with the apostolic see, he restrained the ravings of heretics and the madness of emperors by the steadfastness of his faith, even when subjected to torments; and, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he composed a number of works, among them this sufficiently useful sermon on Blessed Bartholomew, [Col. 0730B] which he published in Greek, in obscure diction—as you wished me to translate it. In Greek it is called an *enkōmion* (Ἐγκώμιον), a term expressed in Latin as “panegyric” or “praise.”

Faithfully translated into Latin, it should consequently be read, so that it may remove every scruple from wavering hearts, silence the wicked tongues of the envious and slanderers, and instruct the ignorant. Indeed, since Solomon says, “The memory of the just is with praises,” I know that some who do not know either language will disparage my translation and make me suffer what that former cultivator of the heavenly library endured from his rivals.

But whoever he was, instructed by his salutary admonitions, let him not thrust himself forward to slander like a wicked man, but approach to correct like an upright one; nor let him gnaw at his brother’s flesh behind his back with the tooth of envy, but, if he can, let him openly correct what departs from the truth with an affection of charity. I do not begrudge anyone who has attained greater favor; rather, I give thanks to the Author, who, even if not through me, nevertheless through whatever Latins there may be, fills them day by day with gifts of which the Greeks would boast greatly that they had been enriched.

You, however, I beg: if this small translation pleases you, deliver it to the Church to be read, and command whoever reads it to say at least once, on my behalf, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”). Hail, bishop beloved by God. “Without end” [Note: [Col. 0729C] That is, “without end.”], hail, and remember your brother Anastasius.

## Prefatory Note

[Col. 0729]

[Col. 0729D] In what manner the venerable body of the blessed apostle Bartholomew, worthy to be raised up in a solemn panegyric of every kind of praise, was brought from Armenia, a province of the Indians, after the death of King and Pontiff Polimius, when some years had passed, through the treachery of the wicked and unbelieving—or rather, by the prompting of divine providence—miraculously to the island of Lippari, where today’s solemnity is celebrated, has been disclosed by the truthful account of a certain most reverend priest, Theodore. For his narration runs as follows.

## Sermon of Saint Theodore

[Col. 0729]

[Col. 0729D] It is indeed a great labor, and, let me add, a glory, to weave together the praises of the saints and proclaim their virtues; [Col. 0730D] yet every martyr ought to be raised up with greater devotion, since no discourse is sufficient for his beatification. But to praise an apostle irreproachably—how great, do you suppose, might even the industry of distinguished teachers be required for this, especially one whom the Spirit raised to contemplation through praises and melodious voices?

Since his sound has gone out into all the earth, so that by the power of his words he might establish the boundaries of the world, surely his praise must likewise be understood in equal measure and faithfully proclaimed. And for this, who is so suitable, so competent, so strong? Because divine Bartholomew was neither Peter nor John, is he therefore to be proclaimed in fewer words and, as though he were not worthy of abundant praise, extolled less?

You hear that he is wholly Christ’s apostle, and yet you do not fear the one who sent him? You grasp in him a witness of the truth, and do not marvel at him who is worthy to be sung? Indeed, even if he was one among many, he is nevertheless comparable to none of God’s servants in lesser praise.

Or is it because he occupies the middle place in the divine number twelve? For he too is a half of twelve, six being the middle, just as in the harmony of a lyre it gives a corresponding sound and, from both sides, an equal likeness of divine speech. But if you wish the number to be distributed equally and in every respect usefully within the apostolic order—as in the annual cycle of any month—while each person has his own distinction according to quantity and quality, then the one being praised will plainly appear not small to us but exceedingly exalted through the power of the Spirit, possessing in the very reckoning a mystical pattern of God’s words according to the art of arithmetic.

For six alone is a perfect number, completed by its parts from the first unit: from those same parts it fulfills its own half, which is three; its third, which is two; and its sixth, which is one. In this number, if we count according to the Gospel’s catalogue, this apostle is found to be sixth. Moreover, if we count according to the catalogue in the Acts of the Apostles, we shall place Bartholomew seventh; and thus he will again be the beginning and summit of the second group of six.

From this we may argue that he bears comparison with Peter: in the first group of six Peter is reckoned as the beginning, while in the second, because Bartholomew is the summit of those who come after Peter, he is counted as their beginning.

Mark this, my dearest: Peter teaches the nations, but Bartholomew likewise accomplishes comparable deeds. Peter’s beautiful feet belong to him who proclaims the good news, but Bartholomew’s are equally welcome as he speaks sublime things about God. Peter performs great wonders, but Bartholomew also works powerful miracles. Peter is crucified head downward, whereas Bartholomew, enduring sufferings for Christ, is executed after being flayed alive.

Whatever Peter does, Bartholomew does equally. Whatever mysteries Peter is capable of grasping, Bartholomew is equally sufficient to penetrate. He carries out the account of the divine word equally, founds the Church equally, and possessed, on an equal scale, the other divine gifts.

Come, then, appeased and rich in speech, blessed one; unseal [Col. 0732A] my mute tongue; grant me material for recounting the praises of your greatness—not so that you yourself may advance in any way, since you possess within yourself the fullness of blessedness, but so that, in whatever manner, the love divinely predestined toward you may be declared, and so that I, your poorest servant, may by your fatherly prayers share in the praise of your solemn festival.

For no one who approaches the splendor of the sun’s ray or raises his pupils toward it can remain without sharing in its illumination.

One apostle, then, received one portion of the world for proclaiming the knowledge of God, and another apostle another portion; and, distributing the whole among themselves, they were appointed preachers of Christ, the King of kings. “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44:17), Scripture declares.

To him who is now celebrated with renowned praise fell the lot and portion of Armenia, the region extending from Evilath to Gabaoth and distributed among many nations and cities. When he was sent, therefore, mystically to announce the word of God, he heard these things divinely from the Lord:

“Go, disciple, to preach; go forth to battle; be capable of dangers. Care for my creation, for which I have taken pity and become man, and for which I chose the shame of death. I have completed the work of the Father; I have become the first witness of the truth. You must complete what is necessary, and supply, in my likeness, what the world lacks after my words of preaching.

“Imitate your Master; emulate your Lord. Pour out your blood for me in an equal passion, and surrender your flesh to torments. Endure whatever I endured for you. Display in yourself the manifest works of my character. Let kindness in your labors, gentleness among those who curse, and patience toward those who will kill you be your weapons. Become a sheep in the midst of wolves; armed with virtues, sharpen yourself for battle.”

The apostle did not recoil. He did not say, “How can one lamb encounter ten thousand wolves? How can a stranger command the city’s leading citizens, an exile command rulers, or one who possesses a single tunic command kings?” But, as a faithful servant, obeying the Lord’s command, he went forth joyfully, carrying nothing with him except the precious name of Christ in place of every weapon.

As he therefore approached the province allotted to him with the word of preaching, the following sermon will portray how much he accomplished there and how much he endured in undergoing hardship. Some of these events rest on the tradition of an ancient account; others are presented according to the reasoning of evangelical teachings. For if he is the light of the world, as the Truth said to the disciples, “You are the light of the world,” then surely he performed the works of light among those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death.

And if he is the salt of the earth, it is clear that by seasoning irrational nations with the reason of truth he cleansed them. And if he was called an evangelical laborer, then he consequently completed spiritual cultivation; for what the Teacher, the Truth, says collectively to all must be understood rationally of each individual.

See him, then, allegorically: sometimes not plowing the earth with oxen dragging iron, but furrowing rational fields with the plow of his tongue, by the yoke [Col. 0733A] of contemplation and action; not sowing anything that falls away and is corruptible, but concealing the word of faith in the depth of the heart. At other times he plants the gardens and vineyards of the Lord—those who, having already received the word, have grown toward better things and, from the beginning of their life, have produced abundant fruits in every season. At still other times he provides medicinal remedies for the sufferings of each person.

But you should know him as one who illuminates blind eyes, cleanses lepers, drives away fevers, enables the lame to walk, gives the deaf hearing, and, by driving out the many forms of the remaining illnesses, restores those weakened by disease to the twofold health of their nature.

You should also know him as one who assumes the pastoral way of life and, with God bringing it to completion, leads along paths, bringing back, fighting, and driving away the beasts of heresy and the battalions of demons; watering what is imperfect, raising those who are growing into the age of Christ, pulling up intelligible thorns, cutting down dense forests, setting doctrinal hedges around them, and readily foreseeing whatever among the things suitable for pursuit might be found lacking.

He is himself the builder and architect of a structure and workmanship not made by hands—namely, the temples of the Lord, which are built and perfected through Spirit and truth into a people acceptable to God, zealous for good works.

Look with me, human being, at the cities and dwellings that once belonged to a people deceived by unbelief, wickedly setting up a tower against the knowledge of God, and easily abandoning the ambushes of their adversaries; at flowering fields, vineyards sprouting in dense growth, fragrant gardens, and those sick with every disease and every infirmity restored to their former health. Such things are, so to speak, the first spoils and trophies.

The labors of so great a contest were endured in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in insults and reproaches, in prisons and chains, in persecutions and transfers from place to place, from city to city, from theater to theater, in torments and scourges, and finally in slaughter and by the sword.

For these things, instead of rewarding their Master, Savior, and Physician with good things, they inflicted atrocities upon them: they reviled, slandered, struck, tortured, and gnawed at them. What did they not learn? What did they not do? What did they not devise? What did they not invent among the things they thought would contribute to sharper affliction and an increase of tribulation? Alas, what cruelty! O savage madness! What sort of rewards did they offer their Creator—those who had received sight and hearing? In place of honor, dishonor; in place of blessing, cursing; in place of a life of rest, the bitterest death!

It is also read in the older and more carefully corrected accounts of his deeds that he preached the word of life in Lycaonia. Then, evangelizing in India, he finally came to Greater Armenia, which belongs to the same province. In Albanus, a city of that Armenia, after undergoing many intolerable torments, he was flayed by the impious like a leaf and beheaded; thus, at last, he was buried there by the faithful.

This glorious patron of the faithful appeared, even after his death, as a great preacher of God. After departing from this world, he did not neglect his killers; rather, like a good shepherd, for as long as it was possible, he invited the lost by miracles and admitted the estranged through wonders.

But there was nothing that could restrain or turn back their bestial mind and inhuman heart until they fell into the depths of evil. What, then, did they do afterward? They raged against that sacred body; they were furious against the chest containing the sacred body, which continually granted various healings. The sick rejected their remedy; the blind, the hand that led them; those without sight, the giver of light; the shipwrecked, the helmsman; those stricken by death, the giver of life.

And how did they do this? They cast into the sea the stone chest that enclosed the sacred [Col. 0734B] body, so that, sunk utterly into the depths, it might no longer appear—as though so great an apostle had bestowed no benefits upon them. For such is the vice of the envious: in their voluntary destruction they do not allow salvation to come even to others.

But he who had long before cried out through David, “In the sea was your way, and your paths in many waters; and your footsteps shall not be known” (Psalm 76:20), provided here a swollen sea that could be traversed and crossed by the stone chest. Peter the Great is known to have walked upon the sea when Christ called to him. Divine Bartholomew likewise displayed the same thing, walking against the waves while carrying his body in the chest.

O divine miracle! O magnificent deed! The chest itself was moved with force from the region of Armenia, together with the chests of four other martyrs, which had likewise been thrown into the sea with it while working signs. After traveling through so great an expanse of sea, with the four chests walking and preceding it, and in a manner rendering service to the apostle, they came to the farther regions of Sicily, to an island called Lipparis, following a revelation made to the most holy Agatho, who was bishop of Hostia there.

Who has heard of so great a wonder? Who has learned of so magnificent a deed? O miracle within a miracle! Lipparis, that is, “fat” or “rich,” was in a way an island bearing for itself the name of its future abundance. Perhaps it was itself crying out in inexpressible words:

“Come to me, poor little one, richest treasure of the Holy Spirit. Come to me, dishonored one, most precious pearl. Come to me, suppliant one, you who were most wickedly cast away by the faithless; dwell in me, and I shall be inhabited in many ways. Save me, and I shall become populous; I shall bear your name and resound everywhere.

“If others despised and rejected you, the great light of heaven, I, though hitherto sad and mournful, desire your splendor. If others have enjoyed the table of your living eloquence, I desire, like a little dog, to gather crumbs from your relics.”

After this, leaving behind certain ministers of his—one martyr here and another there—the apostle departed again. He left Papinus in a Sicilian city called Mylas; he sent Lucian to Messina; and he directed the remaining two to the land of Calabria: Gregory to the city called Columna, and Acacius to the city called Cale. Thus each of them might be a protecting inhabitant of the people in his respective city; and even to this day they shine through their intercessions.

He himself, like a king who had obtained rest in his own household, went forth to the city to which he was called from heaven. He was received with great honor, with many lights, perfumes, and hymns, while all who were there came out joyfully to meet him.

When they had reached the city, however, the chest did not move forward. Some were exerting all their strength to pull it, but it remained motionless. And while the people were in great bewilderment, joy finally replaced their sorrow, because he had obtained what he had asked from the Lord; “for the Lord is near to all who call upon him” (Psalm 144:18).

The chest was therefore placed upon two pure heifers and set down where his sacred temple was immediately established, with a further and extraordinary miracle completing the event. Finally, since the mountain called Vulcan was almost contiguous with the island and was harmful to those who lived all around it, it was moved by an invisible retreat and suspended as if seven stadia away around the sea, so that even today it appears to those who look upon it like the outline of a course of fleeing fire.

How many and how great things he subsequently performed miraculously, or continues even now to perform among those who flee to him in faith, bound by various diseases and infirmities, need not be recounted because of the length of the treatise; nor will they seem incredible to one who hears them, since from this single pledge he possesses demonstrations of other wondrous deeds.

But hail, blessed one of the blessed, thrice and four times blessed Bartholomew. Hail, lover and imitator of God, the good Master. Hail, light of divine illumination, splendor of the holy Church. Hail, well-sounding instrument of spiritual melody. Hail, skillful rhetorician of true wisdom. Hail, fisherman skilled in the catch of rational fish. Hail, branch bearing many clusters and sweet fruit, of Christ’s living vine and the cultivation of the Father. Hail, servant of the Lord of all, worthy in your merits. Hail, rightly desirable friend of the heavenly Bridegroom. Hail, flowing stream of wisdom, abundant drink, and light of the spiritual paradise. Hail, one who by divine power wounds the devil, who wounds the world by his robbery. Hail, you who appear to the world in many ways as Lucifer, the bearer of the knowledge of God.

Rejoice, illuminated by God and fiery pillar of orthodoxy. Rejoice, sun of the earthly world, illuminating all things. Rejoice, mouth of God’s wisdom, possessing a tongue made fiery. Rejoice, ever-flowing fountain of healings. Rejoice, terrifying pursuer of demons. Rejoice, beauty of Armenia, desirable in many ways. Rejoice, you who gloriously walked upon the sea from east to west. Rejoice, salutary and in many ways venerable glory of Lipparis. Rejoice, you who sanctified the sea with traversing steps. Rejoice, you who made the earth purple with the redness of your most holy blood. Rejoice, you who filled the air with the fragrances of sweetness, through the sacred breath of your divine words. Rejoice, you who have gone up to the heavens and shine there, midway among the choir of your divine host, [Col. 0736A] in the inaccessible splendor of glory and the unquenchable joy of exultation.

From there, most gracious one, look upon us; from there bless those who bless you; from there glorify those who glorify you; from there reconcile the peaceful world. Let priests be clothed in justice and holiness; let kings be armed with good works in orthodoxy against the barbarians; let those who hold the monastic life preserve a manner of life equal to that of angels and free from deceit.

Let husbands and wives preserve the law appropriate to one another; fathers with children, superiors with subjects, masters with servants, lenders with debtors, sellers with buyers—let all the rest likewise be protected by the effect of your benevolence for the benefit of the commonwealth. Protect everything that ought to be directed according to the good pleasure of God through your patronage, [Col. 0736B] and especially the inhabitants of adorned Lipparis, as well as the shepherd and the flock who built your sacred temple, and the one who, although briefly, presumes to praise you from himself, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom, with the almighty Father and the most holy and life-giving Spirit, belongs all glory, honor, and worship, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

These things concerning the praises of Bartholomew and his body, miraculously brought to Lipparis, Theodore—distinguished by the reputation of his sanctity and the dignity of his priesthood—set forth in a trustworthy account. By what occasion and in what sequence it was later transported from that island of Lipparis, while the body of that blessed apostle rested there until the year 808 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, must now be related.

The Saracens arrived, therefore, plundered, and laid waste the island mentioned above. Breaking open the apostle’s tomb, they scattered his bones in different places. Soon after they had departed, the same apostle of God appeared in a vision to a certain Greek monk who had been custodian of that church and said to him:

“Rise and gather my bones, which have been scattered.”

He replied: “Why should we gather your bones or render you any honor, since you allowed us and this people to be destroyed by the pagans and gave us no assistance at all?”

The apostle said: “Through long cycles of years I prayed to the Lord for this people, and by my prayers the almighty God granted them the security in which they have remained until now. But because their evils multiplied and their iniquity grew exceedingly, I could no longer obtain that they should remain safe; therefore they perished. You, however, rise and gather my bones, as I told you, and carefully store them away as I shall instruct you.”

The monk said to him: “And how shall I be able to find them, when I do not know where they have been scattered?”

The apostle said: “Go at night to gather them, and whatever you see shining like fire, pick it up, for those are truly my bones.”

He immediately rose and went to the place. He found them as the apostle had said, gathered them without hesitation, carefully concealed them in a small chest, and departed, leaving his companion there.

While Longobard ships were going there to seek out the Saracens, by God’s will they found the monk and the body of the holy apostle there, took them aboard, and departed. The Saracens then came upon them and surrounded the ship carrying the holy apostle’s body, so that there was no hope at all of escape.

Suddenly, however, extremely dense darkness arose before the Saracen ships, so that they did not know where to go. Thus that ship was delivered. While they were still traveling across the sea, divine mercy, through that apostle’s intercession, saved one of the ship’s sailors from a serious illness.

They came ashore and, with great honor, brought the holy apostle’s body to Benevento [Col. 0738A] and placed it in an altar, in the year 809 from the incarnation of the Lord, namely on the twenty-fifth day of October.

The first translation of his body from the region of the Indians to the island of Lipparis is celebrated on the thirteenth day of June; his festival of dormition is celebrated, as stated above, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. Thus the most sacred solemnity is fittingly celebrated three times a year, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0737]

# Three Letters of Anastasius the Librarian

## First Letter: To the Emperor Charles the Bald

Against the false opinions of certain persons who assert that the blessed Dionysius, first bishop of Paris, was not the Areopagite.

(*In Surius, Lives of the Saints, for 8 October*)

[Col. 0737B]

To the most devout and most serene Lord Charles, Emperor, true worshiper of God, ever Augustus, Anastasius, unworthy librarian of the apostolic see: eternal dominion with Christ in the Lord.

Behold, most diligent and most Christian of emperors, you who dig out and search for wisdom as for treasure, and toward whom nothing is left-handed, since you use both hands as though they were right hands. For you so govern the reins of the human commonwealth entrusted to you according to the law of God that you do not abandon divine things but place them first.

The Passion of the holy hieromartyr Dionysius, formerly the Areopagite and afterward bishop of Athens, which I read at Rome when I was a boy and which I heard from the envoys of Constantinople, after it had long been sought at your command and was finally found in the largest of the monasteries located at Rome, I translated into Latin while suffering from various illnesses. I undertook the contest of translating it and, with God’s help, rendered it into Latin speech as far as I could, drawing out the meaning completely, even if not everywhere word for word.

Let the opinion of certain persons cease, then—those who assert that the Dionysius whose body and virtues flourish near Paris was not the Areopagite. For the style of the Greeks, agreeing with the Latin language, both bears witness to and proclaims this; he was plainly born in that language and is proved to have composed his lofty writings in it.

This is especially clear since we know that the foremost interpreters of the Church who wrote in Latin, whenever they found something doubtful in Holy Scripture, immediately hastened to Greek copies and, by reference to their meaning, at once removed every cloud of ambiguity from themselves.

Nor is it surprising if one of the learned, occupied with many matters and not having examined the writings of the Greeks, has thought otherwise, since the apostle Peter himself judged that certain matters should be held in such a way that his fellow apostle Paul rightly considered him blameworthy.

The blessed teacher and martyr Cyprian also made a definition concerning rebaptism that the whole Church rejected. What shall we say of Saint Augustine, who, when composing his books of *Retractions*, criticized certain things that he had formerly thought he had understood correctly?

For almighty God sometimes acts providentially: although he reveals much to one person, he leaves something concealed, and what he closes to one he opens to another. Yet he does not leave without the gift of reward what he knows proceeds from the root of charity; for since he searches the heart, he accepts not so much the statement as the effect of the intention.

I could say many things on this subject, God teaching me, if I had intended to write an apology rather than a preface. Receive, then, most devout emperor, Dionysius, coming again from Greece on a second flight; and since you rejoice to possess him in Latin speech, rejoice also that he has been given to you from Greek speech.

Since some recall that the blessed Dionysius was called by the Greeks *pterygion tou ouranou* (πτερύγιον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ), it should be noted that blessed John Chrysostom, in the last of his sermons, describes him as *peteinon tou ouranou* (πετεινὸν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ), that is, “the bird of heaven.”

The books of the sacred Gospels and Psalms written in Greek demonstrate the difference between these two names. In the one passage, the Greek has *pterygion*, and the Latin codex shows that it is to be translated not as “wing” but as “pinnacle.” In the other, *peteinon*, frequently translated into Roman speech, signifies “bird.”

The text of this Passion was published by the blessed Methodius, who was sent by the apostolic see as a priest to Constantinople, held the bishopric of that city, and from that time has rightly been venerated and honored by all among the saints because of his confession and his struggle. He excerpted a few passages from many earlier writings.

May the God of peace swiftly crush Satan beneath your feet; and may he who granted you a broad empire on earth bestow upon you in heaven the richest reward of the kingdom.

Written in the month of June, in the ninth indiction, in the fourth year of the pontificate of our most blessed lord, Pope John VIII, and in the first year of the reign of our most merciful lord Charles, ever Augustus.

## Second Letter: To the Same

Concerning the Areopagitic writings and John Scotus, their translator.

(*In Usserius, Collection of Ancient Irish Letters*)

Among the other studies to which both your most praiseworthy action and your most salutary admonition—and even the fragrant opinion that flies abroad concerning the greatness of your virtues and character—rouse the minds of mortals, urging them to dig out wisdom as though it were treasure, there is also this matter, which is not merely but extraordinarily worthy of admiration: you do not cease examining not only the Latin Fathers but also the Greeks, and you make those skilled in Roman speech not ignorant of Greek matters.

You do this because you awaken and encourage others to do the same. For we too are often said to have built a great house—not with our hands, but with our words.

The blessed Areopagite Dionysius, bishop of Athens, whose translation into Roman speech, among your other achievements, was brought about by your efforts, is, as you yourself know more clearly, as difficult to understand as he is lofty in language. Indeed, the more difficult to understand and the higher in mysteries are the things he investigated and learned through the revelation of heavenly grace, the more deeply he entered the sanctuary of God, under the guidance of the divine hand, and penetrated the secrets of theology after the veil had been removed.

It is therefore remarkable that your piety has not left such matters unexamined. Although you walk upon the earth, you move about as one dwelling in heaven, so that you seem, as it were—if we may put it so—to enter the Holy of Holies through contemplation like some angel or heavenly man, and to have approached, as far as is possible for mortals, the hidden recesses and innermost sanctuaries of divine ineffability with the keen vision of spiritual eyes.

It is also remarkable how that barbarian man—situated at the ends of the earth, and, as far as human association is concerned, as distant from men as he might be thought to be in the language he spoke—was able to grasp such things intellectually and transfer them into another language.

I mean John Scotus, a man whom I have learned by report to be holy in every respect. But it was that craftsman, the Spirit, who made him both ardent and eloquent. For unless he had been set aflame by the fire of charity through the Spirit’s grace, he would certainly never have received the gift of speaking in tongues. The teacher Charity taught him what he accomplished for the instruction and edification of many.

Although the Spirit was given to him according to a measure, he nevertheless, imbued with the teachings of the Fathers, did as much as he could and attempted to benefit his neighbors beyond his strength. Yet, apart from those things that are known to have escaped him, he deprived the works of much usefulness by striving with such zeal to extract word from word—as you certainly know from your diligent experience—that distinguished translators avoid this kind of translation, although I myself often follow it.

I think he did this for no other reason than that, being humble in spirit, he did not dare depart from the exactness of the word, lest he should in any way fall away from the truth of the meaning. Consequently, a man so great—who, because he had resolved to examine the innermost and most difficult recesses of both kinds of philosophy, already seemed perplexing to our understanding—became entangled within the difficulties of a kind of labyrinth and was placed, in a certain sense, still deeper in invisible caverns. The man whom he had undertaken to translate he made yet more in need of translation.

For this reason, anxious with good cause, I began diligently to seek whether some teacher or some writing might perhaps be found that, by explaining him, would make so great a Father shine more clearly for us.
