Since he had already been handed over into our language through the translator’s industry, I hoped that he might also be rendered more perfectly intelligible to our open understanding.

Then suddenly parentheses, or scholia, on him—which I had seen while staying in Constantinople—came into my hands. When I had translated them as best I could, he shone somewhat more clearly for me. In the margins of the translated copy of his work, as I found them in the Greek, I, a sufficiently inexperienced translator, inserted my own tentative translations opposite the corresponding marks, until they could be translated better by a learned person. I rightly judged that these should be sent chiefly to your glorious wisdom, so that she who had been the promoter and helper of another translation might also be the recipient and approver of our own, whatever its quality.

Those scholia or parentheses that bear at their end the sign of the life-giving cross are said to have been discovered by the blessed Maximus the Confessor and monk; the rest are reported to belong to Saint John, bishop of Scythopolis.

Wherever I saw that the scholia disagreed with the translator’s words, so that the reader might easily recognize both what the translator understood by the appended wording and what the scholion suggested, I inserted the translator’s words into the scholion and indicated how the composer of the scholion had set them forth.

And wherever I thought it useful, I also interposed a very few remarks of my own—since it could not otherwise be done—which an intelligent reader could recognize more easily.

Moreover, it should be noted that, although this holy Dionysius was a man of such great glory and learning—or antiquity—nevertheless, so far as I know, he never published any small works before the Roman pontiffs—namely, Gregory, Martin, and Agatho—mentioned his statements in their own writings and, judging them credible on that account, accepted them: Gregory, specifically, in his homily on the Gospel passage concerning the hundred sheep and the ten drachmas; Martin in his synod, which he held at Rome against the heretics; and Agatho in the letter that he sent to the Sixth Synod. Hence I infer that the opinion of the Greeks is true: they say that his books were concealed by earlier heretics until, after a long period, the single codex that is now extant was found at Rome from among his works and, since the others had not yet been discovered, was carried off to Greece. For he published other books, as he himself implies, which neither any Greek nor, to this day, any Latin has been able to find.

Indeed, Luke in the Acts of the Apostles (17:34), as well as Eusebius Pamphili and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, report certain admirable things about him; but what he wrote they do not report at all, unless forgetfulness deceives me. The following consideration also urges us to believe this: none of the credible commentators, who customarily excerpt the statements of earlier writers and insert them into their own works, makes use of his writings or recalls anything from them.

Finally, the great man and teacher of the apostolic see [variant: life], the philosopher Constantine, who came to Rome under Pope Hadrian the Younger, of venerable memory, and restored the body of Saint Clement to his see [Note: Concerning him, see the preface of our Anastasius to the Eighth Synod above], had read the entire codex of the aforesaid and memorable Father, and commended to his hearers the marrow of usefulness that it contained. He was accustomed to say:

> If the saints—namely, our earlier teachers, who scarcely, and only in a manner of speaking, beheaded the heretics with a club—had happened to possess Dionysius, they would unquestionably have slaughtered them with a sharp sword.

By this saying he clearly implied that those whose mouths the saints had closed with greater labor and, perhaps, more slowly, they would have forced into silence more easily, more sharply, or more swiftly—for *ὀξύ* signifies both “sharp” and “swift.” But after the time of the holy prelates, bishops of the apostolic see, both the holy Seventh and Eighth Synods, and Latin and Greek teachers not only indicate that this venerable Father wrote, but frequently draw testimonies from his writings, so that they might render their own interpretations and statements pregnant with the weight of so great a man’s authority and, at the same time, worthy of approval and imitation by all mortals.

May almighty God at some time transfer your glory from earthly things to the heavenly kingdom.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction.

## LETTER III. TO ADHO, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE

He announces the death of Pope Nicholas and the election of Hadrian II in his place.

*(In Labbe, Councils, vol. VIII.)*

To the holy Lord Father Adho, my venerable and greatly beloved archbishop, I, Anastasius, librarian of the holy Roman Church, offer the fullest greetings.

Alas, I send you news that is very sad, with profound sadness and mourning. Our Father and pope Nicholas, of venerable memory, was taken from this wretched life on the Ides of November to heavenly blessedness, as we believe, leaving us wretched and utterly desolate. For after his departure ravenous wolves enter, sparing not the Lord’s flock. I beseech you, and adjure you before God, to resist courageously; and I also ask you to direct earnest prayers to the Lord on his behalf.

Alas, how late the Church obtained such a man, and how quickly he left it. I truly confess that it would have been preferable for the sun to conceal its rays rather than for death to close his mouth or his eyes—the very eyes that, until the moment of his death, he kept open for divine service and always directed toward the advancement of the Church.

But now the whole faction of those whom he rebuked, either for various forms of adultery or for other crimes, has been inflamed to such a degree that they do not fear planning to destroy all his works and erase all his writings. Their attempt is believed likely to succeed for this reason: it is said—falsely, as we believe—that the emperor’s hand is with them. Announce these things, then, to all the brethren, and take care to labor wherever you trust that you can be of help for the house of God. For if the acts of so great a pontiff are annulled, where, I ask, will your own acts remain?

Yet I know that although he left few supporters among us, the Lord has nevertheless left him among you many who have not bent the knee before Baal. We now have a bishop named Hadrian, a man in every respect—so far as good morals are concerned—very vigorous and industrious. As for him, we do not yet know whether he wishes to attend to all ecclesiastical affairs or only a part of them. His mind, however, hangs upon that of my uncle—your Arsenius. Although he endured many hostilities from the departing bishop and, because he favors the emperor, had on that account cooled somewhat in his zeal for ecclesiastical correction, I beg you quickly to bend him back again by your holy admonitions, lest, in his days, while he has influence with his emperor and the supreme pontiff, the Church of Christ [Note: Something is missing], and especially the first Church. In this way may I always deserve to rejoice in your prosperity.

### APPENDIX

I adjure you to inform all the metropolitans of Gaul that, if a council is held here, they must not behave as though they had recovered their former status and rush forward in contempt of the deceased bishop. This is especially important because no one will now rebuke them, and no one remains who might answer the charges, although he neither [lacuna] held public office nor, as they pretend, ever assented to heresy, but acted out of zeal for God [lacuna]. Therefore I also write to you and adjure you before God: do not consent to or approve what is being attempted against Pope Nicholas; rather, resist it, because the authority of this Church is immediately dissolved if the bishop is [lacuna] handed over.

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF ANASTASIUS, LIBRARIAN OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, ON THE PASSION OF THE ONE THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED AND EIGHTY MARTYRS

*(In Bollandus, 22 June.)*

To Peter, distinguished bishop of the holy Church of Gavinum, Anastasius, librarian of the supreme and apostolic Church, sends apostolic greetings.

After I had translated, at the request of Your Holiness, the passion of the eminent teacher and martyr Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria, you wished to command me to render into Latin speech the passion of the one thousand four hundred and eighty saints who suffered among the Greeks. Considering the inadequacy of my limited learning, I did not initially presume to undertake this task. Then, unwilling to appear disobedient to your fatherhood, I obeyed and, aided from heaven, completed what you commanded. I preferred to be criticized by learned men for ignorance rather than to be judged guilty of disobedience in the presence of your fatherhood.

This was especially so because Your Holiness, burning with love for the martyrs, attends not to the rusticity—which the Apostles themselves plainly did not lack before their calling—but to their triumphs, which can be known through that same less-polished learning, and desires to have them clarified for the veneration of many. May your fatherhood, enjoying long-lasting health in the Lord, deign to pray for us.

Take, gentle Father, the deeds of many godly men. Rustic is the speech, and the pen that translates what was written in Greek.

**In the year of the Lord 890. Erchembert, Cassinese monk.**

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ERCHEMBERT

*(In Pertz, Monuments of German History.)*

Erchembert was a Lombard by nation. As Leo of Ostia reports [Note: Book I, 47], he was born, apparently, of Adelgarius, at the castle of Pilanum in the county of Teano [Note: Chapter 44]. On the tenth day before the Kalends of September in the year 881, he was captured there by Pandonulf and his fellow Neapolitans, stripped of all the goods he had acquired from childhood, and, as he himself writes, driven into exile on foot before the heads of horses all the way to the city of Capua.

Afterward, while living at Capua and professing the Rule of Saint Benedict [Note: Chapter 61], he was captured again on the road from Monte Cassino to Capua by the Greeks [Note: Chapter 69], and was badly treated along with his companions, among whom he mentions his teacher. He then returned to Capua through Naples and was placed in charge of a cell of Saint Benedict.

The following year, when Atenulf ordered the possessions of Saint Benedict situated within the city of Capua to be taken from the exiled brothers, he was sent by Angelarius, abbot of Cassino, and by the bishop to Rome, to Pope Stephen V. From him he brought the brothers a blessing, the privilege of their monastery, and letters of exhortation to Atenulf. By these means he secured the restoration of the monastery’s possessions, but incurred Atenulf’s anger and was forcibly deprived of the cell that the abbot had entrusted to him [Note: Book I, 22].

Although he did not approve Atenulf’s other actions either, and recoiled from his desire to rule and possess and from his harsh authority over the sons of Saint Benedict, Erchembert was nevertheless held by such a great love of his homeland and people that he undertook to celebrate the victory that Atenulf won over the Greeks at Saint Cartius, by which the dominion of the Bards was established.

Accordingly, when his friends insistently asked him to compose a history of the Lombards living in the duchy of Benevento, beginning with their origin and especially from the time of Prince Adelgis, he undertook the work. He describes not only, as he modestly states in his preface [Note: Compare chapters 21 and 31 and the second part of the history], imitating the evangelists Mark and Luke, what he learned by hearsay rather than what he himself saw, but also his own time [Note: Chapter 1]. He did this as an example for posterity, so that from the work itself it might recognize a just and pious man, deeply devoted to his homeland, mourning from his inmost heart the miseries caused by the discord of its princes, and wholly zealous for its glory, peace, and security [Note: Chapter 74]. His history stops in the year 889, perhaps because death overtook him, since at the end of the work he had promised to add the affairs of Wido and Berengar [Note: Chapter 82].

The book, which several writers of the tenth, eleventh, and early twelfth centuries used as a source, has survived to our own time in only one codex, written at Salerno around the year 1300. It is preserved in the Vatican Library, where it is marked number 5001 [Note: The sentence continues at Col. 0744C], and is recognized as the true source both of all the more recent manuscripts preserved at Rome and in Lower Italy and of the editions.

Before it was brought to Rome, it was copied in the year 1560 by Marino Freccia, whose exemplar several learned men subsequently transcribed [Note: See Peregrini’s preface to Erchembert]. It is a parchment quarto, written in Lombard script, but so disfigured by erasures and corrections—apparently in Freccia’s hand, certainly in the sixteenth century—that it sometimes presented me with great difficulty in reading and distinguishing the text.

For that reason, it was especially necessary to distinguish the copyist’s hand [Note: The codex often writes *Rachis* for *Ratchis*, *gencium*, *conticuum* for *contiguum*, *corructum* for *corruptum*, *dissencio* for *dissensio*, *scitus* for *situs*, *abscente* for *absente*, *procintu* for *procinctu*, *selus* for *scelus*, *silicet*, *defunto*, *cunti*. It sometimes omits the letter *h* in *aut* for *haud*, *yems*, *ystoria*, *ausi* for *hausi*, *alitus*, *exalaverat*, *veatur* for *vehatur*, *traens* for *trahens*, *scribit in harena*, *hac* for *ac*, *habiit*, *habeuntibus*, *hedificare*, *his* for *is*, *hovile*, *honestatus*; these forms we too have preserved. Moreover, *b* and *v* are interchanged in *valbus* for *balbus*, *Vari* for *Bari*, *velvis* for *beluis*, *improvitas*, *praevito*, *bassis* for *vassis*, *fribolum*; *b* and *g* in *Liguria* for *Liburia*; *b* and *s* in *assumitur* for *absumitur*; *d* is omitted in *animavertat*, *aiuvandum*, *quemamodum*; *s* and *x* are interchanged in *estremitas*, *iusta*, *iuxit* for *iussit*, *exitare* for *haesitare*; *ph* (*f*) and *v* in *Vari* for *Phari*; *o* and *a* in *Longobardi*; *i* and *e* in *declevis* and *congemescit*; *i* and *g* in *agebat* for *aiebat*, *gurgium*; *u* and *o* in *commutio*; *u* is omitted in *Agustus*. *Frebis* is also written once for *febris*. But all these features are inconsistent] from the corrector’s hand, especially since the latter has passed into all the earlier editions.

Yet even the first hand departs so far, both in the spelling of words and in the text itself, from the true reading—as it can be inferred from the earlier chapters and passages drawn from Erchembert—that it was necessary to use additional aids. We therefore consulted:

1. The *Salernitan Chronicle*, which exists in the same codex but is corrupted in the same way.
2. Book I of Leo of Ostia, whose chapters 9–47 contain copies of our chapters 2, 3, 9, 11, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 23, 29, 33, 35, 37, 39, 44, 46–48, 61, 65, 66, and 69.
3. The *Chronicle of John of Saint Vincent at the Volturno*, from which the ancient reading of chapters 4, 20, 29, 32–36, 38, and 39 can quite often be recognized.

After comparing these materials, I saw that the spelling system we encountered in the Vatican codex of the late thirteenth century departed from the language of the older Cassinese chronicles, especially in its use of the letter *c*, which is sometimes written in place of *t*, *g*, *p*, or *s*, and sometimes added or omitted altogether. I therefore judged that the authority of the codex should be abandoned in this matter, while preserving the other features as faithfully as possible.

The earlier editions, prepared with the aid of copies of the Vatican codex, were as follows:

A. Carracciolo’s edition, included among the four ancient Neapolitan chroniclers, Naples, 1626, and reproduced by Muratori, *SS. V.*, p. 15.

B. Camillo Peregrini’s edition, corrected with the aid of several readings from the Vatican codex supplied by Holstenius, in *History of the Lombard Princes*, Naples, 1643, vol. I. From this edition it was reproduced by Burmann in *Thesaurus* IX, part I; by Eckhard, *SS.* I.49; by Muratori, *SS.* II.237; and by Pratillo I.46ff.; and excerpts were included in Bouquet’s *Gallic Historical Writers*, vols. V, 324; VI, 205; and VII, 155.

We judged that only a few of the annotations of the earlier editors, especially those of Pratillo, should be retained. The excerpts from the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* concerning the kings Liutprand, Hilprand, Ratchis, Aistulf, and Desiderius, which were wrongly invoked on the authority of chapter 1 of Erchembert and attributed to him by some editors, we have determined should be placed under Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*.

## ERCHEMBERT’S HISTORY OF THE LOMBARDS

### 1

The succession of the Lombards, the departure and situation of their kingdom—that is, their origin, how they departed from the island of Scandinavia for Pannonia, and then migrated from Pannonia to Italy and assumed a kingdom—Paul, a very learned man, set forth in a concise but prudent account. Nevertheless, extending the history from Gammara and her two children almost to the reign of Ratchis, he was not without reason prevented by old age from continuing the narrative [Note: That is, old age prevented Paul, not without cause, from bringing the history to completion]. For with them the kingdom of the Lombards ended. It is the custom of a learned historian, especially one discussing his own people, to unfold only those matters that are known to contribute to the accumulation of praise.

At last, compelled by many, I, Erchembert, as though [Note: The following passage has troubled interpreters. Peregrini and Pratillo understand Erchembert to have written the history at the urging of a Lombard named “Algelgis,” whom they believe to have been perhaps the same man encountered in chapter 68; but I do not see what the words “as though from the origin” would then mean. The passage must therefore be explained differently. Erchembert says that he was compelled by many to write a history of the Lombards living in the duchy of Benevento, beginning with the origin of the principate and especially with Prince Adelgis. The work itself indicates that this is correct: it begins with Duke Arichis and proceeds in fuller narrative from Adelgis onward] from their origin, and especially from Adelgis [Note: *Algelgis* in the codex], an outstanding and perceptive man, I undertake to compose a little history of the Lombards living at Benevento.

Since nothing worthy or praiseworthy is found concerning them in these days that can be committed to a truthful style, I shall therefore describe—not their kingdom, but its destruction; not their prosperity, but their misery; not their triumph, but their ruin; not how they advanced, but how they declined; not how they overcame others, but how they were overcome and defeated by others. Drawing deep sighs from my inmost heart, and doing so as an example for posterity, I shall pursue the account with a pen that is concise, though inept [Note: *calomo* in the codex].

Overcome by this insistence, I confess that I shall relate not only what I drank in through my eyes, but even more what I drank in through my ears [Note: The corrected reading is *auribus*, “through my ears”; the codex has *aribus*], imitating, at least in part, the proclamations of the evangelists Mark and Luke, who described their Gospels from what they heard rather than what they saw.

### 2

[Note: The codex does not recognize the division into chapters before chapter 44.]

After Italy had been captured and subjected by Charles (774), he established his son Pippin there as king and, accompanied by an innumerable host of armies, frequently went with him to attack Benevento (781).

At that time Arichis, son-in-law of the aforementioned Desiderius, a most Christian and highly illustrious man, and exceptionally vigorous in military affairs, ruled the duchy of Benevento. When he heard that they were advancing against him, he ceded peace to the Neapolitans, who had long been wearied by oppression from the Lombards. He distributed to them, in place of a merciful concession, the daily payments [Note: Taxes] established by the inhabitants in Liburia [Note: The codex has *Illiguria*, though it consistently writes *Liguria*] [Note: Leburia, the land of Terra di Lavoro] and Cimiterium [Note: The Nolan territory], hesitating—as can be conjectured—lest through their cunning the Franks find an entrance into Benevento.

When the Gallic army arrived above Benevento (787), the aforesaid Arichis at first resisted vigorously with all the strength he possessed. But at last, when all were fighting fiercely and gnawing everything down to the roots like locusts, he considered the safety of his citizens more important than his affection for his children and handed over his two offspring as pledges to the aforesaid Caesar—namely, Grimoald and Adelchisa—and at the same time his entire treasure.

Of these, Adelchisa was restored to her own father after much pleading; Grimoald, however, Charles carried back with him to Aachen [Note: The codex has *a quo*], peace having been granted to Arichis under the terms of a tribute.

### 3

Having thus found this opportunity and, so to speak, terrified by fear of the Franks [Note: The codex has *met*], that same Arichis built, between Lucania [Note: Paestum] and Nuceria [Note: Nocera], a very strongly fortified and lofty city in the manner of a most secure camp, by marvelous construction [Note: Arichis had fortified Salerno before Charles’s arrival. Compare *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *SS.* 1, 118, 168, 169].

Because of the adjacent sea, which is called *salum*, and because of the stream called the Lirinus [Note: West of Salerno], it was given the name Salernum, formed from the two corrupted names [Note: The codex has *corructum*, “corrupt”] [Note: The first hand may have read *appellatum*; the same prince fortified that city in this way, according to the second hand]. It was destined to be a defense for the princes whenever an army arrived against Benevento.

[The passage from “Here Arichis first ordered himself to be called prince of Benevento” through “he ordered it to be written at the end” is absent from the codex. It was taken from a fourth manuscript, which quotes it from Erchembert.]

Here Arichis first ordered himself to be called prince of Benevento, whereas those who had ruled Benevento up to that time had been called dukes. He also had himself anointed by bishops, placed a crown upon his head, and ordered the following words to be written in his charters: “Written in our most sacred palace”; and he ordered them to be written at the end.

Within the walls of Benevento he founded for the Lord a most wealthy and splendid temple, which he called by the Greek name *Agia Sophia*, that is, “Holy Wisdom.” Endowing it with extensive estates and various resources, he established a convent of nuns and handed it over in perpetuity to remain under the jurisdiction of blessed Benedict.

In the territory of Alife [Note: This appears to require restoration; the codex has *preditto alfano*, and another manuscript *aliphano*] he likewise built, for a man beloved by God, a church in honor of the Lord the Savior, established a monastery for girls, and placed it under the authority of Saint Vincent the martyr.

### 4

After Arichis had died, the magnates of Benevento, having taken counsel, sent envoys to Charles, repeatedly entreating him to deign to permit the aforementioned Grimoald—whom he had earlier received from his father as a hostage—to rule over them.

The king granted their petition and immediately sent the aforesaid man there, at the same time granting him the right to govern the principate. But first he bound him by an oath of this kind: he was to have the Lombards’ chins shaved, and was always to order charters and coins to be inscribed with the marks of his own name [Note: An alternate reading says: “he was to destroy the walls of Salerno, Acherentia, and Conza down to their foundations.” This is accepted by the editors from another manuscript].

After receiving permission to return, he was welcomed with great joy by the citizens of Benevento. For a while he allowed gold coins to be struck with his name and likewise ordered documents to be written for some time; but he considered the remaining requirements not worth observing. Soon he began the quarrel of rebellion.

### 5

At this time the same Grimoald took as his wife Wantia, the niece of the Augustus of the Greeks [Note: The codex has *acivorum*]. But it is unknown why the marriage did not reach consummation. For their first eager love broke out into such hatred that, taking the opportunity provided by the Franks who were resisting him on every side, he voluntarily separated her from himself in the Hebrew manner. He gave her a writ of repudiation and forcibly carried her away to her own home.

Although he acted cunningly in this matter, he could not at all calm the ferocity of the barbarian peoples mentioned above. For at that time the territories of the people of Teano and the cities were taken from the lord of the Beneventans [Note: The reading may be *dominis*], and they remain so to the present. The city of Nuceria was also captured at that time, but was quickly recovered by the aforesaid Grimoald (802), who seized within it Guinichis, duke of the Spoleto men, together with all the warriors found there.

### 6

Charles frequently attacked Benevento to fight, accompanied by all the sons whom he had already made kings and by an immense army of warriors. But because God fought on our behalf, under whose rule we were still being nurtured, countless numbers of his men perished by pestilence, and he sometimes returned ingloriously with only a few.

As a result, while Pippin ruled at Ticinum and Grimoald governed at Benevento, extremely frequent warfare harassed the Beneventans, so that peace did not exist among them even for a moment during their lifetimes. Both were in the vigor of youth and inclined toward disturbances and wars [Note: That is, “inclined”].

Pippin, supported by the protection of his warriors, continually harassed him with unbroken warfare. But Grimoald, surrounded both by fortified cities and by a great number of leading men, regarded his persecution as insignificant and contemptible and yielded to him in nothing.

Accordingly Pippin said through his envoys:

> I indeed wish, and I strive to arrange matters with such power, that just as his father Arichis was once subject to Desiderius, king of Italy [Note: One manuscript has *regis*, “of the king”], so Grimoald may be subject to me!

Grimoald, on the other hand, declared:

> Free and noble I was born of both my parents;  
> I shall always be free, I trust in God’s protection!

### 7

When Grimoald had been taken from this life (807), another Grimoald assumed responsibility for defending the rights of Benevento. He was the treasurer [Note: The codex has *thesarius*] of the former Grimoald, of blessed memory, and was also a sufficiently gentle and exceedingly gracious man. He made a treaty of peace not only with the Gauls but also with all the peoples settled round about, and granted favor and peace to the Neapolitans mentioned above (808).

But because the ancient enemy always envies peaceful and pious men and attempts to sow in them the seeds of wars and discord, he inflamed a certain Dauferius, a notable man, with the malice of his own craft and induced him, together with certain sons of Belial, to enter upon a dreadful plot against the aforesaid prince.

They laid the ambush in this way: while the prince was traveling across a bridge of the ancient city [Note: Vietri, near Salerno] and hastening toward the aforesaid city of Salerno, he was to be pushed by Satan’s minions into the depths, submerged in the waves of the sea [Note: The codex has *fructibus*, “fruits,” instead of *fluctibus*], and offered as food to the beasts.

But when God, the knower of hidden things, revealed this to him, he summoned his men to him and crossed the bridge safely. He seized those who had been enemies of his safety and put them in chains.

Dauferius, however, was not there at the time. When he learned what had happened, he took flight and was received by the Neapolitans (816).

### 8

When Grimoald learned this, he did not act sluggishly. He immediately set out for Naples and ordered the army to hasten after him.

When he arrived near the aforementioned city [Note: That is, he came around and reached it on every side] [Note: One manuscript reads “the city immediately”; another, “a great multitude”], the young men of that city, armed and mounted, boldly came out to meet him in battle from a distance.

When he realized this, he immediately attempted first to entangle their routes of retreat, and only then wished to rise against them. In the battle that followed he caused such a slaughter of the enemy by land and sea that the adjacent strait could scarcely be cleansed of the blood of the slain for seven days and more. On land, burial mounds of the dead can still be seen. From the inhabitants themselves, who reported it to me, I learned that nearly five thousand men fell in that battle.

Dauferius and the master of the soldiers who then ruled there alone escaped. Fleeing, they eventually entered the walls of that city, but even there they found no rest. The wives of the slain men came out with swords and pursued them, saying:

> Give back to us, you doomed traitors [Note: That is, “traitors”; the codex has *ppitori*], those whom you wickedly killed! Why, they said, did you attempt to rise against the man whom you know with certainty to be invincible?

Grimoald pursued them more fiercely as far as the gate called Capuana, striking it with his own spear; and there was no one who could resist him. Only when the doors had been closed and barred did those who remained within the walls protect themselves.

Grimoald therefore returned safely to the camp with his army. On the following day, in payment for his exhaustion and for his slain kinsmen, the aforesaid fugitive duke gave the aforementioned prince eight thousand gold pieces as a gift and restored the aforesaid Dauferius to favor.

Immediately, in his customary mercy, Grimoald confirmed by charter a grant of the man’s own possessions and did not deny him his former favor and intimacy.

Meanwhile, Count Badechis of Conza and Sico, the castellan of Agerentia, whom Grimoald had formerly received as a newcomer [Note: That is, an outsider or newcomer] and honored with many distinctions, rose against him by treachery and killed him with a sword when he was already drawing his final breath (817).

### 9

After he had been killed unjustly, the aforesaid Radechis appointed Sico prince in his place.

Not long afterward, renouncing all worldly things with manly resolve through fear of Gehenna, Sico betook himself to the aid of blessed Benedict. Bound with a chain up to his neck, he entered his monastery to serve Christ as a soldier, loudly proclaiming himself guilty and impious, crying out that he had acted wickedly and cruelly.

Thus, taking on the monastic habit [Note: The codex has *sema*], he confined himself in that same monastery with such severity of body and soul, before the eyes of his inward judges, that no doubt remains that he deserved to obtain forgiveness for all his crimes.

The devil often went around, circling the enclosure of the sacred monastery, and with a clear voice, in the hearing of many, he cried:

> Alas, Benedict, woe is me! Why do you gnaw at me from every side? Unjustly  
> you first drive me from here, and now you win my members!

### 10

When Sico had assumed the principate (818), he renewed the treaty with the Franks, pursued the Beneventans with bestial ferocity, and, while he was still alive, made his son Sicard heir to the principate—a very slippery, restless, and insolent man [Note: The codex has *petulante*], swollen with pride of spirit.

At the same time, war was repeatedly stirred up against the Neapolitans whom I mentioned earlier (821). The city was vigorously besieged by land and sea and fiercely attacked with arrows and scorpions; it would nearly have been captured if ingenuity had not intervened.

For after the wall beside the seashore had been completely shattered by battering rams and engines [Note: The codex has *muros*, plural], and the people were already striving to enter the city in crowds, the duke of that city, having immediately given his mother and two of his own children as hostages, sent messengers to him with an earnest request, employing a clever stratagem, as follows:

> The city is yours, together with everything it contains. Therefore may it please your mercy not to give it over to plunder. Tomorrow, enter in the greatest glory with the trophy of victory, and take possession of us and all that is ours!

Trusting these suggestions, he waited for the appointed day.

During the following night, however, the breached city was strengthened with a very solid wall [Note: The codex has *solida*, “solid”], and at dawn, when the duke had promised to surrender himself and his city, he took up weapons of war and rose against him in a great struggle.

The citizens of that city, having been harshly oppressed by father and son for sixteen continuous years, and having now reached the greatest extremity, sought the protection of the Franks.

At that time Caesar Lodoguicus, surnamed Almus, son of the earlier Augustus Charles, ruled over them. When he had associated his son Lothar with himself as a partner in the kingdom, he was captured by him together with his wife and consigned to custody; but he was rescued by his nobles and restored to his former glory. Through their efforts the siege was relieved for a time (831).

### 11

Around this time, the people of the Hagarenes came out in a powerful force from Babylonia and Africa like a swarm of bees and hastened to Sicily (832), laying waste everything around them. At last they captured the distinguished city called Palermo and remain there to this day. They have demolished many cities and fortified places on that island, which now, almost in its entirety, groans beneath the dominion of those peoples.

Meanwhile Lodoguicus died. He had exercised the imperial authority in Gaul as its second Augustus. The aforementioned Lothar became heir to that kingdom (840), and from this point the kingdom of the Franks was divided: Lothar ruled the realm of Aachen and Italy; Lodoguicus ruled Bavaria; and Charles, born of another mother, ruled the realm of Aquitaine.

### 12. (833)

But, to return to the earlier part of my narrative: after Sico’s death, Sicard alone obtained the monarchy. [Col. 0751D] He had already ruled successfully for several years together with his often-mentioned father; but then, through fickleness of mind, he began to pursue the people entrusted to him with beastly voracity and cruelly to tear them apart.

Meanwhile, just as Ahasuerus preferred Haman above the others, so this man preferred a certain Rofridus, son of Dauferius, surnamed “the Prophet,” above all the rest. Under the pretext of his counsel he committed many sacrilegious and blasphemous acts. [Col. 0752A] This man was prudent in worldly affairs, excessively crafty, and cunning beyond belief. Indeed, he so ensnared the aforesaid man with his deceitful tricks that, while he was absent and opposed, Sicard dared never undertake anything—not even for a moment.

Thus he was deceived and trapped by him, so that he gratuitously condemned his own brother, named Siconolfus, to perpetual exile (834), and consigned all the nobles of the Beneventan people either to imprisonment or to death. The plotter’s aim was plainly that Sicard, left without the nobles’ support, might be killed with the greatest ease, without the shedding of the plotter’s own blood or that of his followers.

For this reason he ordered his kinsman Maion to be tonsured and shut away in a monastery. Finally, he had Alfanus—the abbot, a distinguished man [Col. 0752B] and exceptionally strong in bodily power, than whom no one at that time was more faithful—hanged by the neck. Then a great perjury occurred at Benevento, from which it may be inferred that God’s anger was first provoked toward the destruction of the land.

### 13

While he was occupied with such matters, divine providence brought it about that, as he sought to destroy another man unjustly, he himself was overtaken by a sickness that came upon him first and, struck from heaven in spirit and body alike, he died.

Before he died, however, so that the accumulation of his ruin might be increased more justly, for love of money he deposed from the pastoral charge of the monks’ monastery and committed to custody a man worthy of God, conspicuous for holiness, named Deusdedit, vicar of the most blessed Benedict. He did so through secular power rather than by proper reason. His ashes, in the place where he [Col. 0752C] lies buried, are known even to this day to cure, very frequently, some who are fever-stricken or oppressed by various illnesses, when they ask in faith.

What need I say about this man’s wickedness, when, after selling the estates of churches and monasteries and violently taking away the property of nobles and commoners, he gathered extremely wealthy estates—“curtes,” that is, manors—equal in number to the days of an intercalary year? (839.)

When this wretched man had died in this way, shortly afterward the aforementioned prince, Sicard, was killed by the sword by … a son, or Adelferius by name [the printed *a filii vel Adelferio … nomine* is grammatically damaged; the relationship is uncertain]. God was justly repaying him: he often returns a father’s iniquity upon his sons, striking only the flesh and thus taking vengeance. Since Sico, his father, had unjustly killed Grimoaldus, his elder, God avenged it by having his son killed by his subjects.

When this man had thus departed, his slayer [Col. 0752D] did not rejoice for long. For shortly afterward the aforesaid murderer was killed by Sico the bastard [the source adds an unattached “4” here], surnamed Albus, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s word, the one who had pierced his neighbour’s body with a sword might, by a very just judgment, experience upon himself the law of retaliation—that is, a similar vengeance.

### 14

When Sicard had thus departed from this bodily life, [Col. 0753A] Radelgisus assumed the rule of the principate. He had been treasurer of the aforesaid man, and in his election the whole province of Benevento, so to speak, gave its consent. He was a gracious man and outstanding in good morals.

(840.) But when he had attained the primacy, Siconolfus, whom I previously mentioned as an exile, escaped from prison and began to flee to a hiding place. For some time he remained concealed by Ursus, count of Conza and his kinsman.

At that time the sons of Dauferius Balbus—namely Romoalt, Arichis, and Grimoalt—as well as Guaiferius, left the walls of Benevento and seized Salerno. They found Siconolfus where he maintained his hiding place and unanimously made him their elder. A division then arose such as had never existed in Benevento since the Lombards entered it.

[Col. 0753B] Before Siconolfus’s arrival at Salerno, Radelgisus, the aforesaid prince, sent Adelmarius to convert the sons of Dauferius to his allegiance. He went there, but by deceitful cunning abandoned the prince and joined them, inciting them still more fiercely.

### 15

At the same time Landolfus was already gastald (district governor) of Capua, a man exceedingly ready for war and a vigorous fighter. Because he maintained an ancient enmity with certain men of the family of the Seductors—men cruel in mind and lineage like vipers—he had seven of their leading men killed, and the hands of one of them cut off. The survivors, taking refuge in flight, went to Benevento to Radelgisus, their relative by marriage.

Landolfus entered Sicopolis, withdrew from Radelgisus’s rule, joined Siconolfus, and [Col. 0753C] first made a peace treaty with the Neapolitans. Relying on the help of Landolfus and his sons, Siconolfus brought all Calabria and most of Apulia under his service. Then he strove to rise against Benevento in battle, taking many cities and some fortified towns from its rule and subjecting them to his own authority. Since he was an exceptionally warlike man, almost the whole surrounding population followed him, partly out of fear.

Before Siconolfus obtained Salerno, Radelgisus had been invited by the aforesaid Adelmarius, and, deceived by the counsel of his own attendants, he approached Salerno as though he were going to capture it. When he arrived, he decided to encamp with great boldness. But suddenly that man came out of the city with the aforesaid sons of Dauferius, like a crowd [the printed *velud turbae civitate* is irregular], and they slaughtered them in an unheard-of massacre. They plundered all their possessions [Col. 0753D] and enriched themselves. Radelgisus escaped dishonourably, scarcely managing to flee with a few men, and thereafter never dared to set foot within the boundaries of Salerno.

### 16. (848)

In those days a certain Pando ruled Bari. Obeying Radelgisus’s orders, he stationed phalanxes of Saracens, who had been summoned for assistance, beside the city wall and along the seashore, where they were to remain.

But they, being naturally crafty and [Col. 0754A] more clever than others in doing evil, carefully examined the fortifications of the place. In the dead of night, while the Christian people were sleeping, they entered the city through hidden places. They slaughtered the innocent population, some with swords, and handed others over into captivity.

They tormented the aforesaid traitor to his people and fatherland with various and many punishments and finally, as he truly deserved, strangled him in the sea’s depths.

When Radelgisus learned this, because he was entirely unable to drive them from the city, he nevertheless began to honour them as though they were familiar friends and gradually to summon them to his assistance. First he sent them, together with his son Ursus, to attack the fortress of Canne.

As soon as this was reported to Siconolfus, he set aside all delay and hurried to defeat them. Attacking them boldly, [Col. 0754B] he struck down with weapons all who could not flee, and was raised to such a trophy of victory that scarcely a few escaped from the innumerable pagan army, to explain to those remaining in the city the disaster of those who had perished.

Their king, named Calfo, alone fled in disgrace. After losing his horse on the road when it was already exhausted, he finally entered the city very weary, on his own feet.

### 17

Meanwhile Siconolfus was grievously afflicting Benevento with repeated battles. As the saying goes, “a bad tree—now a bad wedge must be driven in”: Siconolfus summoned Libyan Ishmaelites, Spaniards, against the Agarenes of Radelgisus.

While these peoples fought among themselves in internal and external war, the overseas regions were filled with captives of our people, of different sexes and ages.

(843.) One day both armies met at the Caudine Forks, [Col. 0754C] and battle was joined. At the first attack, Radelgisus’s side appeared victorious and put the whole army of Siconolfus to flight.

Siconolfus, however, then stationed in a very secure place, soon attacked the Beneventans who were triumphing and pursuing his men, together with a few of his own, with manly courage. He struck down a considerable number of them; after winning the battle, he killed many with swords, captured some, and forced the rest to flee.

Trusting in his many victories, he took all the cities and castles from Radelgisus, except Siponto, and surrounded Benevento to besiege it. When the city was being severely pressed by weapons and the plague of hunger, a message was immediately sent to Guido to hasten to the city.

Guido was duke of the Spolitans and a kinsman of Siconolfus. Yet, out of greed for money—[Col. 0754D] the vice to which the Frankish race is especially subject—he set aside the bond of kinship and immediately went to Radelgisus’s aid. Through messengers he suggested to Siconolfus, while he was besieging the city, that he should abandon the siege and return home, adding among other things: “Let me speak with Radelgisus, because I shall favour your side more.”

Siconolfus therefore withdrew from that place. Guido meanwhile arrived, and, having received from Radelgisus one saddle [Col. 0755A] for seventy thousand gold coins, broke everything he had promised his kinsman. Alienated from him, he returned by the road on which he had come.

### 18

After this the aforesaid Guido persuaded Siconolfus: “Give fifty thousand gold coins for the unification of the province of Benevento, and I shall make you possess it on both sides—just as though you were measuring it out with your palm!”

Siconolfus then accepted this advice, went to Rome, paid the gold, gave oaths, and received an oath. Having accomplished nothing, he departed empty-handed.

There was still very frequent fighting between Siconolfus and Radelgisus, and daily sedition through disputes. Consequently, those from either side who disliked the way of justice alternately fled from one to the other. Frequent acts of plunder and incestuous fornications took place [the printed *par* is uncertain; see the note].

[Col. 0755B] All were wandering and eager for evil, like beasts straying without a shepherd into the forest. Since they continually tore one another apart in civil war, and since everyone was being destroyed—indeed, as I may say, there was utter ruin of soul and heart—the Saracens who lived at Benevento, whose king was Massari, devastated everything completely, inside and outside the city. They even treated its nobles as worthless and flogged them harshly with leather thongs like useless little slaves.

### 19. (855)

In these days, after the aforementioned Lutharius had died, the Frankish kingdom was divided into five parts. For his brothers Lodoguicus and Karlus ruled Bavaria and Aquitaine; his first-born son, named Lodoguicus, governed Italy; the second, Lutharius, ruled Aachen; and the third, Carlictus, held Provence.

[Col. 0755C] A humble petition was therefore brought to this emperor Lodoguicus through Lando, count of Capua, son of the aforementioned Landolfus, and through the aforesaid Ademarius. [The petition’s fuller wording in Leo is quoted in the source note below.]

Although he was very young, nevertheless, out of zeal for God, he listened to their humble petitions and gave his consent. Coming swiftly, he had all the enemies belonging to the profane people forcibly driven from the city and killed with the sword (849). In the presence of all the Lombards, he divided the whole province of Benevento by an equitable settlement under oath between the two men mentioned above.

After this had been done, Siconolfus did not live long. Paying the debt owed to death, he left his still nursing son as heir to his office. Radelgisus survived him only a short time. When Radelgisus had died, his son Radelgarius [Col. 0755D] was elected to the principate in his place—a man plainly strong in bodily power and pious in spirit, and pleasing to everyone in appearance.

### 20

At the same time the Agarenes living at Bari began to devastate and plunder all Apulia and Calabria from their roots, and gradually began to lay waste Salerno [Col. 0756A] and Benevento (852).

A lamentable petition was therefore once again conveyed to the often-mentioned most pious emperor through Bassacius, the venerable man and vicar of blessed Benedict, and through Jacobus, abbot of Saint Vincent. They asked him to hasten as soon as possible and by his arrival rescue those whom he had previously redeemed in mercy.

“And let us,” they said, “be his most faithful servants, and let him appoint us to be subject to the least of his servants!”

He came without delay, and with an immense multitude proceeded to Bari. But the Capuans, having entirely forgotten their voluntary pledge, hid themselves in the cities and sent there in their place only Landulfus, their bishop.

When the aforesaid emperor saw both their deceit and that he was accomplishing nothing, he departed without benefit. He granted [Col. 0756B] the principate of Salerno to Ademarius, a very brave and distinguished man, and made Siconolfus’s son an exile.

(854.) Meanwhile Radelgarius died at Benevento. His brother Adelchis succeeded him, an exceedingly gentle man and beloved by all, so mild that he was loved even by foreigners. But, what was worse, the province, divided in many ways, was led day by day by its rulers toward destruction rather than salvation.

### 21

When Count Landolfus of Capua had been removed from this life (843), let me return to what happened earlier. He left four sons: namely Lando, the man already mentioned; Pando; Landonolfus; and Landolfus, later a bishop. They were men of singular prudence and virtue, very capable in effectiveness.

Of these, Lando ruled Capua; Pando held the marepahissate (the office of marepahis); Landonolfus ruled Teano; [Col. 0756C] while Landolfus, still a young man, served in the palace duties.

This last-named man, as later became publicly clear, was still in his mother’s womb when, one day, she lay down to sleep beside her husband’s back and dreamed that she had given birth to a fiery torch. When the torch fell to the ground, it grew into a huge globe of fire and appeared to burn the entire territory around Benevento. Thus both sleep and vision passed away together.

She was greatly terrified and soon sorrowfully took care to report it to her husband. When the father heard the conclusion of the vision, he summed up the future man’s dreadful deeds in a few words, saying:

> Alas, my sweet beloved, what fates will then pursue us?  
> [Col. 0756D] Your dreadful vision shows a savage omen!  
> Here is concealed your offspring, shut within the womb;  
> He will love no one and will reject those dear by blood;  
> At last he will devour his fellow citizens with a viper’s mouth,  
> And, like consuming fire, burn the hearts of rulers.

[Col. 0757A] Although he foretold this while in a state of mental ecstasy, we too have seen it with our own eyes: we witnessed innumerable innocent men, through his deeds, fall by swords in place of fire.

That fire therefore signified, in a kind of image, the human blood which later was to be shed through his agency. To prevent anyone from thinking that this is unbelievable or perhaps imaginatively fabricated, I have as many witnesses as there are nearly people living in the city. His conduct and its final outcome will be disclosed in what follows.

### 22

When their father was already approaching the final day of his life, as I heard from those who reported it, he summoned his sons and gave them this injunction: they were never, insofar as it depended on them, to allow Benevento to make peace with Salerno.

“For it will not be [Col. 0757B] beneficial to you,” he said.

His sons heard this warning and carried it out in action. They also left it as a perpetual right to their heirs, just as they had received it from their father. They left their descendants a great, sound, hereditary … [the printed sentence lacks a clear noun; the editor queries “counsel,” while the edition has “truly hereditary crime”; see the notes], acting against the divine command which Jesus gave to his disciples: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14).

Having received the right to rule, they now obeyed Siconolfus, but made light of his commands. But above all Landonolfus was always hostile and ungrateful toward him, to such an extent that, compelled by necessity, he even betrothed his daughter to Siconolfus’s son.

At this time Paulinus, a man worthy of and dear to God, bishop of Capua, was removed from the dross of this fleshly life. Through the vigorous efforts of the aforesaid Lando, his brother Landolfus was ordained bishop [the Latin uses an irregular active construction]. [Col. 0757C] Yet after the father’s death Landolfus repaid his sons unworthily, punishing them like the harshest enemies with various and perpetual exile.

### 23. (851)

When Siconolfus had died, the people appointed his son, who was not yet a year old, in his place, so that each man might act as he thought fit.

Then the aforesaid brothers, driven partly by ambition and partly by fear, began to pursue their fellow citizens with bestial greed and commit them to custody. For this reason they took Suessula from their kinsman Pandulfus by a trick and attached it to their own ambition. They made him and his sons exiles. Thereafter they killed one of them with the sword and another by fire, while condemning the two survivors to constant and perpetual exile.

Later Landulfus, son of Lando, captured Suessula [Col. 0757D] with the support of Sergius the master of soldiers, who was his father-in-law, and he still retains it.

### 24. (856)

At this time, whether it happened by chance or by heavenly judgment, the entire city of Sicopolis was burned by fire, so that not a single house remained unburned except the episcopal palace.

Taking advantage of this opportunity, Bishop Landulfus and his brother Landonolfus [Col. 0758A] agreed that they should abandon their dwelling in the narrow mountain and descend to live on the broad and splendid plains.

“We are not,” they said, “a fold of goats, to shelter in caves of rock! Let us at last descend to the lowlands, so that we may appear lofty and unbowed to those who look upon us!”

Lando, however, would not at all consent to this. It was madness and folly, amid so many storms, to abandon a very strongly fortified city in order to settle in swine’s filth.

### 25

While they were arguing among themselves in this way, the two men mentioned above began to build a wall above the bridge commonly called Casilinum. When Lando saw their work, he began to build a city and completed it magnificently.

When it had been fortified and people had begun to inhabit it, Guido arrived with all the Tuscans, [Col. 0758B] besieged it on every side, and severely distressed it (858). They did not wish to submit to Ademarius, the man already mentioned, because of the wickedness of Bishop Landolfus and Landonolfus. Ademarius favoured the former above the others with fraternal affection, despising the others as though they were foreigners.

While those inside were being severely afflicted by daily fighting and the crops outside were being destroyed, they were finally conquered by strength and violence and submitted their necks to servitude—except Landonolfus.

Therefore Sura and all the neighbouring fortified towns were taken from Landonolfus their lord and handed over to Guido, as had been promised. After this, the aforesaid man fell into such deep sadness of spirit that he breathed out his life soon afterward.

### 26

At the same time, wishing to avenge an old enmity, Ademarius deceitfully captured the son of Marinus of Amalfi, the kinsman of Pando, and handed him over as an exile [Col. 0758C] to Sergius the master of soldiers, with whom he had made a treaty. For this reason Marinus too was captured by Sergius through treachery.

From this arose an eternal quarrel between Ademarius and Pando. Consequently, without Lando’s knowledge, Bishop Landulfus and Pando advised Guaiferius, son of Dauferius Balbus, and arranged for Ademarius the prince to be seized. They voluntarily chose Guaiferius as their elder and swore to him with a solemn oath.

(861.) But, quickly slipping back into their customary vices, immediately after Lando’s death—he was Guaiferius’s father-in-law—they broke faith with him.

### 27

Finally, after Landonolfus had died (859), not long afterward Lando was struck by a grievous paralysis. Weakened, he was confined to his bed for an entire year.

When Sergius the master of soldiers learned this, enticed by Ademarius’s military support—[Col. 0758D] to repeat what happened earlier—he broke the oath that had been made with Lando and raised war against his son.

On the eighth day before the Ides of May (8 May), the day on which we solemnly celebrate the feast of blessed Michael the archangel—and on which, as we read, in ancient times the people of Benevento courageously defeated the Neapolitans—on that day, [Col. 0759A] giving no honour to God, he sent his two sons, Gregory the master of soldiers and Caesarius, together with his son-in-law Landulfus of Suessula. With them he sent an army of Neapolitans and Amalfitans, both infantry and cavalry, numbering nearly seven thousand men, ordering them to besiege Capua.

The younger Lando boldly met them like a fiery lion. He found them having crossed the Theodemund Bridge, fiercely attacking his men. With all his forces he charged them, split their formation, and scattered them with swords. He captured Caesarius and nearly eight hundred others, put the rest to flight, and returned in triumph.

Pando, his uncle, fearing Ademarius’s arrival, meanwhile kept watch at the monument of the late Trasaricius. [Col. 0759B] After this Pando freed Marinus from his chains and restored Caesarius, together with all the others, to liberty.

### 28. (860)

In these days the elder Lando, as his illness increased, was brought to his final hour. He summoned his two brothers, Pando and Bishop Landolfus, and earnestly tried to commend his son Lando to them. He placed him in their hands, saying:

> With God and his holy Church as witnesses, I commend him to you, so that you may be judged at the same judgment by which you will have abused him in this present life!

Thus, having fulfilled his human duty, he died.

After he had departed, his brother did not long remain faithful to his oath. Out of a desire for the castaldate (the office of gastald), they treacherously expelled Lando and his other brothers from the city and withdrew from Guaiferius, to whom they had recently sworn oaths. Above all, Landolfus had sworn to him more than once [Col. 0759C] by the Gospels, the solemnities of the Mass, and his own consecrated hands.

After this Lando entered Caiazzo, capturing there Aioaldus, who had been sent by the aforesaid men to guard it.

At the same time Landolfus, Lando’s brother, captured Casa Irta. But Pando arrived, captured him together with forty leading men, and, after they had been surrendered, recovered the castle of Caiazzo. Lando’s sons, in turn, were received at Suessula by Guaiferius and their brother Landolfus [the printed construction is elliptical].

After these men had been expelled, their rage did not cease. They began constantly to pursue them, even attacking the territory of Suessula.

Guaiferius the prince actively helped them, and often yielded the place to them, unwilling [Col. 0759D] to shed Christian blood needlessly. But Bishop Landolfus attributed this not to religious devotion but to weakness, and by force compelled his brother to fight against Christ’s anointed.

Relying on the three sons—Maio, Maienolfus, and Radelgisus, son of Adelgisus, prince of Benevento [the printed construction is compressed]—[Col. 0760A] he sent him against his aforesaid prince. But by God’s just judgment, from whom all power and authority proceed, he himself was the first to fall. Some of them were captured, while the rest were put to flight.

### 29. (862)

Meanwhile Saugdan, the most wicked and criminal king of the Ishmaelites, was cruelly devastating the whole land of Benevento with fire, swords, and captivity, so that not a breath of life remained in it.

For this reason the army of the Franks frequently arrived to suppress their savagery. But, accomplishing nothing, it returned by the road on which it had come.

Consequently Adelgisus, prince of Benevento, was compelled by the payment of a tribute and by hostages to make peace with him.

At that time Maielpotus of Telesia and Guandelepertus of Boiano, both gastalds, persuaded [Col. 0760B] Lambertus, duke of the Spolitans, and Garardus, count, with much entreaty to come. When Saugdan was returning from the devastation of Capua, they met him and attacked him in the territory of Arvium.

But the aforesaid man rose up and hurled himself fiercely against the Beneventans and Franks. He broke their formations, killed many of them, captured some, and cruelly put them to death. Count Garardus, Maielpotus, and Guandelepertus, the men mentioned above, fell in that same battle.

From that day he gained still greater boldness. He utterly destroyed Benevento and its territory, so that no place except the principal cities escaped his savagery.

In those days he also captured the castle of Benefranum, plundered the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr, and received [Col. 0760C] three thousand gold coins in return for sparing the buildings from burning. After this, he received the same number of coins from the vicar of blessed Benedict.

### 30. (862)

Finally, after Pando’s death, Bishop Landolfus remained alone. He appointed his nephew Pandonolfus count of Capua in place of his father Pando. Pandonolfus had escaped half-alive after being wounded in the battle in which his father had fallen.

He had among his companions Dauferius, the kinsman of Maion. Fearing Dauferius’s cunning, Bishop Landolfus advised Pandonolfus to provide him with assistance and send him elsewhere to live. But Pandonolfus refused to follow this advice. The three brothers secretly left the city of Potenza with Dauferius and seized castles.

Pandonolfus entered Suessula; Landulfus entered Casa Irta; and Landonulfus entered Caiazzo, [Col. 0760D] entering the old castle, which had long before been damaged by his father. They began to plunder everything in the surrounding area.

Landolfus deceived them by cunning. He also deceived the princes Guaiferius and Adelgisus, and, by trickery, summoned the sons of Lando, his nephews, whom he had previously made [Col. 0761A] exiles from their own land. He caused them to plunder and burn the territories of his brothers.

As the ruin of Capua increased daily, the same man urged the sons of Pando, together with the sons of Lando, to enter the city and live there under a treaty binding both sides.

But they came together from opposite directions and joined themselves by oath. They approached the city, but the aforesaid man immediately deceived them by his own art and made them perjure themselves. After dividing them, he broke faith with them.

For this reason Pandonolfus also sent to the imperial majesty. After letters and commands had been obtained, he did not enter the city mentioned above until the most pious emperor Lodoguicus came, having been invited by many people over various periods of time.

### 31

This same Landolfus was, [Col. 0761B] as I promised to set down [chapter 21], prudent by nature, but crafty by habit—exceedingly slippery and insolent, more ambitious than any man, and lifted up beyond belief. He was also an enemy and plunderer of monks. Sitting swollen with pride on his tribunal, he used to say to those standing around:

> Whenever I see a monk with my eyes, the coming day always provides me with gloomy omens.

By a very just judgment of God he suffered hardships at the hands of those whom he cursed and persecuted as utterly impious enemies, and by whom he was also destined to be tormented in the future.

He was also a mocker of his prince and a perjurer, and hated his nephews. He loved no one except the incitements of his own flesh, and he never embraced peace—not even on the day of his death.

Thus, whenever he perceived that people had formed an alliance, he threw himself into the midst of it energetically and [Col. 0761C] sowed the seeds of weeds. If this seems incredible to anyone, let him consider how many times he deceived Guaiferius, to whom he swore three times and whom he himself had established as his prince.

For he much more willingly desired innocent people to be taken captive than to have Guaiferius as his equal, let alone his elder. In this he acted contrary to the Apostle’s command, which says: “Be subject,” he says, “to every authority, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Peter 2); and elsewhere: “There is no authority except from God; therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Romans 13).

Setting aside ecclesiastical doctrine and episcopal rights, he loved only half-men, preferring them above all others. Thus he nevertheless fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah, who says (chapter 3): “The effeminate shall rule over them.”

If I wished to [Col. 0761D] recount in detail this man’s deeds, I think that time would more easily be exhausted than the account brought to an end. Yet if anyone desires to know him thoroughly, let him seek the verses composed by me.

Before the day of his death he divided Capua among the sons of his three brothers in such a way that the sword of strife would never, at any time, [Col. 0762A] be absent from among them. If anyone does not perceive this in his heart, let him see it with his eyes.

#### Source notes (chapters 12–31)

Witness labels and abbreviated readings are retained as printed. The notes below follow source order and identify the relevant Latin lemma.

1. Chapter 12. [Col. 0751] *blasima*: 1 reads *blasmia*, 2 *blasma*, variant forms for “blasphemous things.”

2. Chapter 12. [Col. 0751] *supradictum*: c reads *supraditum*, “aforesaid,” as spelled.

3. Chapter 12. [Col. 0751] *unquam*, “ever”: 2 reads *inquam*, “I say.”

4. Chapter 12. [Col. 0751] *momentum*, “moment”: 1 reads *monimentum*, “memorial/monument.”

5. Chapter 12. [Col. 0751] *auderet*, “he dared”: 2 reads *afferre auderet*, “he dared to bring forward.”

6. Chapter 12. [Col. 0751D] Alfanus: “Abbot.”

7. Chapter 13. [Col. 0751D] The vicar of Benedict: “That is, the abbot of Monte Cassino.”

8. Chapter 13. [Col. 0751] *a pastorali*, “from the pastoral [charge]”: c reads *apostorali*, a fused or corrupt form.

9. Chapter 13. [Col. 0751] *seculari*, “by secular [power]”: 1 reads *secularis*, “secular/of a secular [person],” a different inflection.

10. Chapter 13. [Col. 0751] *cujusque … cineres*, “whose ashes”: c reads *quos*, “whom/which,” masculine plural accusative.

11. Chapter 13. [Col. 0752D] “An intercalary year exceeding 380 days.”

12. Chapter 13. [Col. 0752D] *curtis*: “That is, *curtes*,” estates/manors.

13. Chapter 13. [Col. 0751] *Adelferio*: c reads *adelferio nomine nomine*, “Adelferius by name by name,” with the repetition retained.

14. Chapter 13. [Col. 0751] *ultionem*: c reads *ulcicionem*, “vengeance,” as spelled.

15. Chapter 14. [Col. 0753] *thesaurarius*: c reads *thesausararius*, “treasurer,” as spelled.

16. Chapter 14. [Col. 0753] *Balbi*, “of Balbus”: c reads *batui*, an uncertain form of the name.

17. Chapter 14. [Col. 0753] *principem*, “the prince”: c reads *principe*, a different case.

18. Chapter 14. [Col. 0753] *illis sociavit*: c reads *illisociavit*, “joined [himself] to them,” run together.

19. Chapter 15. [Col. 0753] *juri*, “to [his] authority/right”: c reads *juris*, “of authority/right.”

20. Chapter 15. [Col. 0753] *Adelmario*: c reads *aldemario*, “Aldemarius”; compare chapter 14.

21. Chapter 16. [Col. 0753] *quidam*, “a certain”: c has *quidem*, “indeed,” corrected to *quidam*.

22. Chapter 16. [Col. 0753] *oram*, “the shore”: c reads *ora*, a different case.

23. Chapter 16. [Col. 0753] *captivitati*, “to captivity”: c has *captu*, “capture/captivity,” with the remaining letters erased (*caeteris crasis*, as printed).

24. Chapter 16. [Col. 0753] In the margin a hand of the fifteenth or sixteenth century has written: “It was a city, but it is now destroyed, near Barletta, and today the place is called Prior at Canne.”

25. Chapter 16. [Col. 0753] *innumerabili*, “innumerable”: c reads *numerabili*, “countable.”

26. Chapter 16. [Col. 0753] *urbe residuis casum*, “to those remaining in the city, the disaster”: e reads *urbem r. casu*, “city … disaster,” with altered cases; *r.* abbreviates the intervening word.

27. Chapter 17. [Col. 0753] *diversi*, “of different [sex and age]”: c reads *diversis*, a different inflection.

28. Chapter 17. [Col. 0753] *Furculas Caudinas*: c reads *ferculas caudina*, variant forms of the Caudine Forks.

29. Chapter 17. [Col. 0753] *suos*, “his own men”: c reads *suo*, singular oblique form.

30. Chapter 17. [Col. 0753] *extinxit*: c reads *extincxit*, “killed/extinguished,” as spelled.

31. Chapter 17. [Col. 0753] *obsessione*: c reads *obssessione*, “siege,” as spelled.

32. Chapter 17. [Col. 0753] *Permitte*: c reads *permicte*, “allow,” as spelled.

33. Chapter 18. [Col. 0755] *consenciens*: c reads *concencient*, a malformed variant of “agreeing.”

34. Chapter 18. [Col. 0755] At the uncertain *par*, the editor queries *pariter*, “likewise/together.”

35. Chapter 18. [Col. 0755] At *devastavit*, “he devastated,” the editor queries *devastaverunt*, “they devastated.”

36. Chapter 18. [Col. 0755] *flagellarent*: c reads *flagarent*, apparently a defective form of “they flogged.”

37. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] *pentifarie*, “in five parts”: so 4 (I.29); c reads *pentifari*.

38. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] At *Landonem*, “Lando,” c has *est. pandonem*, “was … Pando”; compare chapter 21. The opening *est.* is retained as printed.

39. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] *filium*, “son”: c reads *filii*, “of the son/sons.”

40. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] Leo I.29 continues: “the man, and also through the venerable abbot Bassacius, asking him to come to these regions, rescue them from the devastation of the impious Saracens, and deign to put an end to such calamities.”

41. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] At *parvuli*, “of a little one/little ones,” the editor queries *parvulus*, “a little one,” here “very young.”

42. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] *consensum*: c reads *consensensum*, “consent,” with repeated syllables.

43. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] *hostes*, “enemies”: c reads *hoste*, “enemy,” singular oblique form.

44. Chapter 19. [Col. 0755] *distrahi ac*, “to be dragged away and”: c reads *distrai hac*, “to be dragged away … this way,” a defective spelling and altered division.

45. Chapter 20. [Col. 0755] *pedetentim*: c reads *pededentim*, “step by step,” as spelled.

46. Chapter 20. [Col. 0755] *initiarunt*, “they began”: 5 reads *intrarunt*, “they entered.”

47. Chapter 20. [Col. 0755] *Bassacium*: c reads *bassicium*, “Bassicius,” a form of the name.

48. Chapter 20. [Col. 0755] *pro*, “for/in place of”: 5 reads *prae*, “before/in comparison with”; with *omnibus*, “above all.”

49. Chapter 20. [Col. 0755] *sponsionem*: c reads *sposionem*, “pledge,” as spelled.

50. Chapter 20. [Col. 0755] *emolumento*, “benefit”: the note records this same form in 1.

51. Chapter 20. [Col. 0755] 5 reads: “Adelgis, deformed in respect of every virtue; but, what is worse,” etc. The printed *deformis* reverses the favourable description of the main text; it has not been silently changed to “adorned.”

52. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *post tergum*: c reads *postergum*, “backward,” written together.

53. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *virtutisque*, “and of virtue”: c reads *viros tutisque*, “men and …,” a defective word division with no secure complete sense.

54. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *compotes*, “capable/possessed of,” plural: c reads *compotens*, a singular form.

55. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *marepahissatum*, the office of marepahis: c reads *mare pahissatum*; the edition reads *marepahis Suram*, “as marepahis, Sura.”

56. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *juvenis*, “young man”: “So I have emended”; c reads *indolis*, “of character/disposition”; the edition reads *tenerae indolis*, “of tender character/age.”

57. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *palatinis*, “palatial/of the palace”: c reads *palatis*, “palates” or a defective form in this context.

58. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *ut*, “as”: c reads *et*, “and.”

59. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *visio*, “vision”: c reads *viso*, an altered inflection, “having seen/what was seen.”

60. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *indicare*, “to report”: c reads *indagare*, “to investigate.”

61. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *in paucis*, “in few [words]”: “So I correct”; 1 reads *in pacis*, “in … peace,” grammatically irregular; 2 *in facis*, “in … torch,” likewise irregular; the edition *infatis*, an uncertain fused form.

62. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *fata*: c reads *fatta*, “fates,” as spelled.

63. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *ortus*, “offspring/birth”: c reads *orcus*, “Orcus/the underworld.”

64. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *haut ullum*, “no one”: “So I read with the editions”; c reads *aut illum*, “or him.”

65. Chapter 21. [Col. 0755] *devoret*, “may he devour”: 1 reads *duret*, “may he endure”; 2 *devoret*.

66. Chapter 21. [Col. 0757D] “Compare the final verse.”

67. Chapter 21. [Col. 0757] *humani*, “of human [kind]”: c reads *humanum*, a different inflection.

68. Chapter 22. [Col. 0757] *pertineret*, “it concerned”: c reads *pertinerent*, “they concerned.”

69. Chapter 22. [Col. 0757] *profuturum*: c reads *profurum*, defective spelling of “beneficial/going to benefit.”

70. Chapter 22. [Col. 0757] At *sanum*, “sound,” the editor queries *consilium*, “counsel/plan.”

71. Chapter 22. [Col. 0757] The edition reads *M. sane hereditarium scelus s.*, “A great, truly hereditary crime … [for their] offspring”; *M.* and *s.* are abbreviated as printed.

72. Chapter 22. [Col. 0757] *modo*, “now”: the edition reads *nullo modo*, “in no way.”

73. Chapter 23. [Col. 0757] *carentem*, “lacking [a year]”: c reads *carente*, a different case.

74. Chapter 23. [Col. 0757] *subrogarunt*, “they appointed in his place”: c reads *subrogarent*, “they might appoint in his place.”

75. Chapter 23. [Col. 0757] *gladio*, “with the sword”: 1 reads *gladium*, accusative “sword.”

76. Chapter 23. [Col. 0757D] “In what year Landolfus died is unknown.”

77. Chapter 25. [Col. 0758D] “Namely, the newer Capua.”

78. Chapter 26. [Col. 0757] *filium*, “son,” accusative: c reads *filius*, nominative “son.”

79. Chapter 26. [Col. 0757] *sponte*, “willingly”: c reads *spontem*, an altered form.

80. Chapter 27. [Col. 0757] *Lando*: c reads *landonem*, the accusative form of Lando.

81. Chapter 27. [Col. 0759] *libertati*, “to liberty”: 1 reads *libertatis*, “of liberty.”

82. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759] *antistite*: c reads *antiste*, defective form of “bishop/prelate.”

83. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759] *Landolfus*: c reads *landonlfus*, a variant spelling of the name.

84. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759D] Casa Irta: “Caserta.”

85. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759] c reads *casam irtam*, “Casa Irta,” agreeing with the printed text.

86. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759D] Suessula: “Castello di Sessola.”

87. Chapter 28. [Col. 0760D] *exterminatis*: “That is, expelled.”

88. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759] c reads *ex tminatis*, a defective form of *exterminatis*, “expelled.”

89. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759] *segniter*, “sluggishly”: c reads *signiter*, an altered spelling.

90. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759] *frustra*: c reads *fustra*, “in vain/needlessly,” as spelled.

91. Chapter 28. [Col. 0759] *nonnulli*, “some”: c reads *nonnullis*, a different case.

92. Chapter 29. [Col. 0759] *Saugdan*: c reads *Saugolan*, but compare chapter 29; 5 reads *Saogdam*. These are forms of the king’s name.

93. Chapter 29. [Col. 0759] *halitus*, “breath”: c reads *alitus*, a spelling variant; 5 *habitus*, “condition/appearance.”

94. Chapter 29. [Col. 0759] At *adveniens*, “arriving,” 5 reads *a. ob e.*, “arriving for the purpose of …”; the abbreviations are retained, with the remaining expansion uncertain.

95. Chapter 29. [Col. 0759] At *pacem eo firmaret*, “he made peace with him,” 5 reads *p. cum eo f.*, “made peace with him,” with explicit *cum*, “with,” and abbreviated surrounding words.

100. Chapter 29. [Col. 0759] *efferitati*, “savagery,” dative: 5 reads *feritatem*, “savagery,” accusative.

101. Chapter 29. [Col. 0759] 5 reads: “In those days [*d.*, abbreviated], he captured Telesia, Alife, Sepino, Boiano and Isernia, and also the castle of Benefranum, and utterly destroyed them. But the monastery,” etc. The note stops there; it does not say that the monastery was likewise destroyed.

102. Chapter 29. [Col. 0759] *Benefranum*: c reads *bñfranum*, an abbreviated form of the name.

107. Chapter 30. [Col. 0761] *Landonis*, “of Lando”: so B; c reads *Pandonis*, “of Pando.”

108. Chapter 30. [Col. 0761] *illi*, “they”: c reads *ille*, “he.”

109. Chapter 30. [Col. 0761] *quos statim*, “whom immediately”: c reads *quo statim*, “where/to whom immediately,” with a different relative form.

110. Chapter 31. [Col. 0761] *praedator*: 1 reads *predor*, a defective form of “plunderer.”

111. Chapter 31. [Col. 0761] *tristia*, “gloomy [omens]”: c reads *tristicia*, “sadness,” or an altered form in this construction.

114. Chapter 31. [Col. 0761] *absumitur*, “is exhausted”: c reads *assumitur*, “is taken up.”
