### 32. (866) [Cols. 0761–0762B]

Thus Emperor Louis, invited—as I said—by all the Beneventans, Capuans, and inhabitants of the neighboring districts to defend their ruined homeland—but Graifer did not do this, because he abhorred the capture of Ademari—entered Beneventan territory through Sora and first came to the monastery of blessed Benedict. There legates came to him from various cities; among them came the aforementioned Landulf and his nephews, each from a different direction.

Accordingly, when the august emperor and his wife had been received with the greatest courtesy by Bertharius, the venerable abbot, Landulf, reverting to his customary deceit, forced the Capuans whom he had presented to the emperor to flee. He alone remained with him, as though assuring him that he had done nothing blameworthy against him. The aforesaid emperor, therefore, then regarding Landulf as worthless, went to Capua and, after besieging it on every side for three months—a period absent from one manuscript but restored from other witnesses—utterly destroyed it. When its citizens refused to accept whatever settlement he proposed, they surrendered themselves to Lambert, its count; thinking that they were acting more rightly, they fell into the worst possible ruin. Thereafter, being regarded as worthless, they were handed over almost every month as plunder to different judges.

When this too had been accomplished, Guaifer was first received at Salerno without any prior pledge, and only then at Benevento by Adelchis.

*Apparatus:* The source has *praedixi* (“I said beforehand”), with one witness reading *predixit* (“he said beforehand”). It has *Ademari*, with one witness *Ademario*. The form *Landulfum* is marked as variant in one witness. One witness omits “three months,” restored from two others. The source reads *funditus* (“utterly”), with one witness *fundi*. The source has *ita peracto* (“this having been accomplished”), with one witness *ita pacto* (“this having been agreed”). “Without any prior pledge” translates *sine sponsione*.

### 33. (867) [Cols. 0762C–0762D]

In the following year, supported by many auxiliaries, he went to Bari and engaged in battle with the army of the aforementioned Saugdan. He was defeated by them and fled, having lost no small part of his fighting men. Then, burning all their crops round about, he went to Matera, which he captured and set on fire without delay. He then came to Venosa; having encamped there, he began to rebuild it, and, attacking Bari heavily from both sides, demolished it. Having stationed a garrison of warriors at Canosa, he in turn harassed them from the flanks.

Struck with terror by this, many fled to the emperor’s mercy and asked that right hands—that is, assurances of protection—be given them; at that time he did not deny them his customary clemency. After this they went to the city of Oria—also recorded as Uria and Orea—and then returned likewise to Benevento. With the aid of the heavenly right hand, when the Saracens had already reached the utmost extremity, he sent an army and captured Bari, taking there the savage king Saugdan together with several of his retainers. Then, in February 871, he ordered Taranto to be besieged.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *Saugdagne* for *Saugdane*. Another reads *proculsi* (“driven away”) rather than *perculsi* (“struck with terror”). One manuscript omits *non* (“not”) in “he did not deny them,” but another restores *non negavit*. The place-name is variously written *Uria* and *Orea*.

### 34 [Cols. 0762D–0763B]

When these things had been accomplished, so that I may bring forward what was promised above, the devil, seeing his own followers expelled and everything restored to Christ, recalling his beginnings and grieving over the losses of hell, incited the Franks (*Galli*) to persecute the Beneventans severely and harass them cruelly.

For this reason Prince Adelgisus too rose up against Emperor Louis. While the emperor was living within the walls of Benevento with his men and resting securely, Adelgisus, by deceitful cunning, seized the most holy man—namely, the savior of the Beneventan province—and committed him to confinement. He plundered his goods and enriched himself, stripped all the military men, and forced them to flee; he was loaded down with their spoils. Thus the Lord’s saying, taken from prophecy, was fulfilled: “Strike the shepherd,” he said, “and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 12).

While the emperor remained in custody, God stirred up the spirit of the Ishmaelites and immediately brought them from Africa, so that they might avenge the emperor’s disgrace, just as Vespasian and Titus avenged the passion of the Son of God. But the Lord’s defense was delayed for forty-two years, in accordance with the prophecy of Elisha, who gave the forty-two boys by whom he had been mocked to two bears to be devoured. Yet He did not defer punishment for contempt of this man even forty days; from this it may be understood what sort and how great a man he was, since he was defended so quickly.

*Apparatus:* The source has *astū doloso* (“by deceitful cunning”); one witness reads *actu* (“by an act”), and other witnesses have different readings at this point. The form *exuviis* (“spoils”) is supported by one witness, while another has an uncertain reading. *Sumptus* (“taken”) is printed, with one witness *suptus*. Another witness has *restauri* (“restored”) rather than *restaurari*. One reading has *dilatata* (“delayed”) instead of *dilata*.

### 35 [Cols. 0763B–0763D]

When the innocent emperor was released at the Lord’s command, nearly thirty thousand Saracens immediately arrived at Salerno. They besieged it fiercely and, on every side, utterly destroyed everything outside it, killing innumerable inhabitants. They also ravaged parts of Naples, Benevento, and Capua.

At that time both counts Lambert, fearing the emperor’s anger, withdrew to Benevento and were honorably received by Adelgisus. Relying on their aid, he attacked the Saracen force and struck it down bravely, killing nearly three thousand of them. During those same days they killed a thousand of them near Capua, beside Suessula.

In 872, when the year was nearly over during this siege, the aforementioned emperor, having sent an army at the suggestion of Bishop Landulf—for this was the only memorable good deed he performed from the day of his birth—destroyed nearly nine thousand pagans in Capua.

In 873, after this, he deigned to come to Capua in person. When the Saracens learned of his arrival, they abandoned Salerno and went to Calabria. Finding it divided among its inhabitants, they utterly ravaged it, so that it became deserted as though in a flood.

Before that wicked people took flight, God showed many a sign of this kind from heaven: a very large fiery torch, moving with swift speed, fell among the ships. A storm immediately followed it and shattered all the vessels into pieces.

Guaifer, because he was under siege, first sent his kinsman Peter and his son Guaimarius as legates to the aforesaid emperor. On Landulf’s advice, however, the emperor detained them and condemned them to exile. Later he also took two sons of Guaifer as hostages and sent them to Lombardy.

*Apparatus:* The source has *forinsecus* (“outside”), with an uncertain reading in one witness; *stirpitus* (“utterly”) is printed against *stirpatus* in another; and *deleverunt* (“they destroyed”) against *delauerunt*. The source reads *scaram*, “force” or “battle line,” while one witness has *sacram* (“sacred”). The fiery torch is described as moving *praepete cursu*, “with swift flight”; one witness has an unclear form.

### 36 [Cols. 0763D–0764B]

At the same time, the aforesaid emperor took Landulf into his intimacy and appointed him third in his kingdom. Attracted by this appointment, Landulf sought with all eagerness to obtain the archbishopric of all Benevento and to make Capua a metropolis; but, since the Lord did not permit it, he achieved no success.

Louis, wishing to acquire Benevento but unable to do so, returned to his own lands, leaving his wife and daughter at Capua. Taking advantage of this opportunity, the same Landulf had Prince Guaifer, to whom he had recently sworn allegiance, arrested and thrown into custody.

In 874, since what they had expected did not happen, Guaifer was released and gave Lando’s sons—namely Lando and Landonulf, his own kinsmen—as hostages in his place. Returning with them, the empress carried them away and left them in exile at Ravenna. The offspring of that empress remained at Capua; after she departed, her father, Louis of blessed memory, soon afterward closed his final day, in 875. Thus the sons of Guaifer and Lando were released.

When they had returned to their native soil, they found the sons of Pando exiles outside their own city and joined them. When Landulf learned of this alliance, he was distressed and immediately summoned Prince Guaifer to his aid. Guaifer came without delay and subjected both brothers to his service.

*Apparatus:* The source has *asciscens* (“taking into his intimacy”), with variants *ascicens*, *alcicens*, and *alliciens*. One witness reads *innectus* (“entangled”) rather than *illectus* (“attracted”). *Retrudi* (“to be thrust back”) appears in one witness instead of *detrudi* (“to be thrust into custody”). One witness has *Landolfum* rather than *Landonulfum*. Another reads *nescione* or *noxionem* for *nexionem* (“alliance”).

### 37 [Cols. 0764B–0764D]

But why, with the Lord permitting it, the Beneventans were able to inflict the aforesaid disgrace upon the aforementioned emperor, I shall mention two reasons among many.

First, at one time he came to Rome to restore two condemned bishops to their former dignity. When Pope Nicholas, a man full of God, refused to consent to him, he came out to meet him in the ancient manner with a white-clad priestly procession. But Louis, scorning the fear of God, ordered the clergy to be beaten with sticks and ordered the crosses and all the sacred vessels to be trampled underfoot. He plundered Rome for nearly a mile around and wished to deprive the vicar of blessed Peter, as though he were a worthless slave, of the office of his ministry, had the Lord not resisted him.

Second, after Bari and Saugdan—the most criminal of all men—had been captured, he did not immediately, as was fitting, have him cruelly put to death according to the Lord’s will. He had forgotten what Samuel did before Saul to Agag, the very fat king of the Amalekites, and how he had him cut to pieces (1 Samuel 15); and also what a certain prophet said to the king of Samaria concerning a wicked man: “Because you have released a man deserving of death,” he said, “your life shall be for his life” (1 Kings 20).

*Apparatus:* One witness has *consentiret* (“would consent”) rather than *consentire*. Another reads *depraedata* (“having been plundered”) rather than *depraedatus* (“having plundered”).

### 38 [Cols. 0764D–0765A]

When Adelgisus had let Emperor Louis go, he retained the entire treasure, as well as Saugdan, Annosus, and Abadelbach.

When they had recovered their strength, the Saracens in Taranto—whom the emperor had left almost captured—began gradually to plunder Bari and the territory of Canosa. Adelgisus met them three times in the districts of Apulia. Unable to prevail against them, he departed unconquered and without triumph.

At that time, in 876, Utmagnus—possibly Othman or Osman—since Saugdan had been exiled, came from Africa with Annosus and entered Taranto, where he was made king. Departing from there, he heavily ravaged Benevento, Telesia, and Alife. He achieved such a victory that he recovered the aforementioned Saugdan’s authority from Adelgisus; for he had already sent Annosus and Abadelbach as envoys.

When those who were staying at Bari heard this, they summoned Gregory, the imperial *bajulus* of the Greeks, who was then living at Otranto, together with many armies, and brought him into Bari out of fear of the Saracens. He immediately seized the gastald and the leading men of that place and sent them to Constantinople, despite the fidelity that had been given them by oath.

*Apparatus:* The name appears as *Ut magnus*, *Atmanus*, and *Athmannus*; an editorial note asks whether it may be Othman or Osman. The place-name is written *Odrontum*, *Idrontum*, or *Ydrontum*, with an editorial identification of Otranto. One witness reads *triumphator* (“triumphant”) rather than *intriumphator* (“without triumph”). The note *ante apocrisarios* is transmitted with a variant *antea pocrisarios*.

### 39 [Cols. 0765B–0765D]

Meanwhile the Greeks repeatedly sent envoys with documents to Benevento, Salerno, and Capua, asking them for assistance against the Saracens; but these men, united in spirit, rejected their requests.

At that time Salerno, Naples, Gaeta, and Amalfi, being at peace with the Saracens, were severely harassing Rome by naval ravages.

But when Charles, son of Judith, had assumed the distinguished scepter at Rome in 875, he gave Duke Lambert and Guido, Lambert’s brother, to Pope John as auxiliaries. With them Pope John himself went to Capua and Naples in 876. Guaifer obeyed in everything, broke the treaty, and killed many of them—that is, of the Saracens.

Sergius, however, the *magister militum*, deceived by the counsel of Adelgisus and Lambert, refused to separate himself from them. He was immediately anathematized and began to wage war against Guaifer in 877. It therefore happened that on the eighth day after his excommunication he had twenty-two Neapolitan soldiers who had been captured beheaded; for so the pope had ordered.

Sergius, likewise punished by this excommunication, was not long afterward captured by his own brother and sent to Rome with his eyes put out. There he miserably ended his life. His brother, however, appointed himself prince in his place.

When Adelgisus captured the castle of Trebentum in 878 after besieging it, he was killed on his return to his own city by his sons-in-law, nephews, and friends. He was killed in the middle of the twenty-fifth year of his principate. In his place Gaideris, son of Radelgar and grandson of the deceased, was appointed. Cailo and Dauferius, his sons-in-law, were expelled—though one witness reads “elected”—and Gaideris wished to rule in his own right, driven by the desire that had led him to kill his father-in-law. He too was received by Athanasius, bishop and *magister militum*.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *sedis* (“seats”) rather than *scidis* (“documents”). The source’s difficult sentence is supported by Leo of Ostia: “being at peace with the Saracens, they severely harassed Rome by naval ravaging.” One witness reads *papae optemperans* (“obeying the pope”) rather than *in cunctis optemperans* (“obeying in everything”). The source explicitly identifies “them” as the Saracens. The castle is *Trebentensem*, with one witness *Trivensem*; a marginal note identifies it with Triventum and continues incompletely. The note explains that Adelgisus was killed by relatives and friends on the road, not far from the city, in the twenty-fifth year of his principate. One witness has *electus* (“elected”) instead of *ejectus* (“expelled”). The name *Radelgari* is uncertain in one witness.

### 40. (879) [Cols. 0766A–0766B]

During these days the aforementioned Bishop Landulf was struck down and died. On the day of his correction—that is, his death—he was expecting horses from all the priests of Saint Benedict, so that he might fall into the abyss not without horses.

When his nephews saw his downfall, they gathered together and divided Capua among themselves under oath, in equal portions. Pandonulf received the city of Teano and Casa Hirta; Lando received Berelais—this is the region of Old Capua—and Suessa; the other Lando received Calino and Caiazzo; Atenulf began to build a castle at Calvo. As for the young Landulf, son of Lando, some appointed him bishop by oath, while others did so by common consent.

But, detained by the sluggishness of his own father, which naturally makes him inert, he was not consecrated at once. The brothers’ oath did not remain unbroken for long: it lasted scarcely from the fourth Ides of March to the seventh Ides of May.

Driven by greed, Pando’s sons captured their cousins, the brothers Landenulf and Atenulf, sons of Landonulf, by deceit and placed them in custody, having seized from them the castle of Caiazzo, which they themselves had voluntarily assigned to them by oath as their portion.

*Apparatus:* “Berelais” is identified in a marginal note as the region of Old Capua. One witness has *unamiter* for *unanimiter* (“unanimously”). A marginal note identifies the captured men as cousins or brothers’ sons.

### 41 [Cols. 0766B–0766C]

But, to pursue briefly what was begun, the sons of Landonulf joined the sons of Lando and went to the aid of Prince Guaifer, by whom they were sometimes protected.

Pandonulf likewise sent envoys with various documents to the same Guaifer, but he was not received by him, since Guaifer favored the brothers mentioned above. Seeing that he was entirely abandoned, the aforesaid man invited Prince Gaideris and Gregory, the imperial *bajulus*, who at that time had met with the said Guaifer at Nola for a conference and were proceeding together toward Benevento, sending them a message that whichever of them arrived first should come to his aid, and that he would be subject to him.

When they came from different directions without delay through Caiazzo and Sicopolis, they took up position to the west near the city of Capua. Guaifer, coming from the east, from the direction of the rising sun, arrived with his men at Berelais—that is, the amphitheater—and the city was surrounded by enemies.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *legatos invitabant* (“they invited legates”) instead of *legatis invitabat* (“he invited them by messengers”). The source has *perapplicuit* (“arrived at”) with a variant *peramplicuit*. One witness reads *supradict’* for *supradictos*.

### 42 [Cols. 0766D–0767A]

Meanwhile Pandonulf refused to submit to Gaideris, as he had promised, strongly resisting especially Lando, son of Landonulf and kinsman of Gaideris. For this reason both the aforesaid *bajulus* and Gaideris became alienated from him.

Soon some men crossed through the city of Capua, while others crossed the river by boat to the opposite side and joined Guaifer. After Landonulf and his brother Atenulf had been brought back and joined to them, they wished to subject Pandonulf to Guaifer. They could not do so, however, because Pandonulf did not wish to receive his cousins within the city; for that reason Guaifer was rejected.

When the aforesaid men recognized Pandonulf’s cunning, they returned to their own places. Guaifer, however, remained then in the city of Capua.

At that time nearly all the distinguished Capuans and the entire common people, with their wives, children, and all their household goods, left the city. Some attached themselves to the sons of Lando, while others joined the sons of Landonulf. A violent conflict and terrible devastation arose among them. For Guaifer, stationed in a hostile manner beside the city wall, besieged it; across the river he placed Lando with the Franks of Count Lambert.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *luntris* (“boats”) for *lintris* and *fluvii* (“of the river”) for *fluvium*. Another reads *parte* (“part”) rather than *partem*. One witness has *omnique cum omni* (“with everything”) instead of *omnique cum supellectili* (“with all their household goods”). Other witnesses read *filii* (“sons”) where the syntax requires *filiis* (“to the sons”).

### 43. (880) [Cols. 0767B–0767C]

In the following year the aforementioned Prince Guaifer came with the Amalfitans at harvest time and besieged the aforesaid city on every side. Peace was made among the brothers under oath, but only on this condition: neither of them was to gather grain from the fields into his cities before an anathema had been sent against them by apostolic authority, so that, once they had entered the aforesaid city, none of them would dare rise up against the others.

When Guaifer had returned to his own territory, Pandonulf immediately forgot the oath and became a perjurer. For he did not send the envoys to Rome as he had promised, and, acting against his own soul, gathered all the grain. Divine vengeance immediately followed him: fire was sent from heaven and utterly consumed nearly half of the aforesaid city.

*Apparatus:* One witness has the masculine *dictum* (“the aforesaid [city]”) rather than *dictam*. Another reads *media* (“the middle part”) rather than *mediam* (“half”).

### 44 [Cols. 0767C–0768A]

At the same time Athanasius was bishop of Naples and *magister militum*. As we have stated above, after exiling his own brother, he made peace with the Saracens, first stationing them within the harbor and beside the city wall. They ravaged the entire land of Benevento, together with the Roman territory and part of Spoleto; they plundered all the monasteries, all the churches, every city and town, villages, mountains, hills, and islands.

The splendid monasteries of most holy Benedict, venerated throughout the world, and the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr were also burned by them, along with countless others. Suessula alone was excepted, though in truth it was pitifully undermined through the treachery of Christians.

Pandonulf joined himself to Athanasius. Relying on his assistance, he began to persecute his cousins more fiercely; at the outset he ravaged and took away their possessions on every side. Joined by the Neapolitans, Gaetans, and Saracens, he made a two-day assault upon the castle of Pilanum; having achieved nothing, he departed empty-handed.

In the following year, 881, he made a general expedition with his men, the Neapolitans, and the Saracens. He took up position against the Colossus—that is, the amphitheater of Old Capua—where the sons of Lando lived. First, however, he imposed a monetary payment on those who were staying in the baths near the arena and sent them back to Capua. To the others, namely the sons of Lando, who were surrounded in the amphitheater, he offered peace, receiving Liburia from them under oath.

On that same occasion the aforementioned Pandonulf again made a sudden attack with the Neapolitans on the castle of Pilanum and captured it by treachery, after those inside handed it over. I too was captured there and stripped of all the goods I had acquired from childhood. I was carried into exile on foot, ahead of the horses’ heads, as far as the city of Capua, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September in the year of the Lord 881.

*Apparatus:* The source reads *Suessula*, with a marginal note identifying the “Colossus” as the amphitheater of Old Capua. Another marginal note places Pilanum in the county of Teano, not far from the castle of Conca, on Monte Piano. One witness has *filii* rather than *filiis*. The printed text has *acquisitis* (“acquired”), while the manuscript variant is *exquisitis*.

### 45 [Cols. 0768B–0768C]

Pandonulf immediately marched with an army against Calvo, accompanied by a troop of Neapolitans, and remained there while building a fortification. But the sons of Landonulf resisted them bravely with their men, and Pandonulf suddenly withdrew from there, after Suessa had previously been taken from the sons of Lando, though it had once been granted to them by oath.

But now let me turn my pen back to earlier events. When Atenulf had been captured by the aforesaid man, his brother Lando did not act sluggishly. He immediately began to build, with his men, the castle of Calvo, on account of which Atenulf himself had been captured.

Part of the nobles was ready for battle, while part of the common people constructed a rampart and walls, and so the work was completed. After the castle had been consumed by fire nearly two years later, the same Lando repaired it. He then went there with all his men, providing each inhabitant of the town with houses from his own resources, as well as wine vessels, provisions, and wine; laboring with every vigilance, he restored the town to its former condition.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *ablatam* (“taken away”) rather than *ablata*. The source’s *haedificare* is an orthographic form of *aedificare*, “to build.”

### 46 [Cols. 0768C–0768D]

Nor should this be omitted from the earlier account: at the beginning of the quarrel, when the same Pandonulf was persecuting his cousins with beastly savagery, he expelled Landulf, the elected son of Lando, whom we mentioned above in chapter 40, from the episcopal cloister. Although he himself had assigned him the episcopal seat of Saint Stephen under oath, he installed him in a lowly place, namely a service-cell, and ordered an episcopal lodging to be provided for himself in a little dwelling (*zetula*). This was done.

When the aforesaid elect of God saw this, he feared that man’s deceit and left the city, hastening to the episcopal seat of his own blessed protomartyr, so that he might lead a quiet life.

Meanwhile, finding an opportunity, Pandonulf installed his own married brother Landonulf as a cleric and, sending him to Rome, requested of Pope John that he be made bishop. In this request he was heard.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *caustro* (“cloister”) rather than *claustro*. One has *humilico* for *humili loco*. The marginal note identifies Pandonulf as the subject of the action.

### 47 [Cols. 0768D–0769B]

Because of this madness and fraternal and civil warfare, Bertar, the most discerning abbot of the aforementioned monastery of most holy Benedict, and Leo, the venerable bishop of Teano, were urgently entreated. They went to the City and approached the aforesaid pontiff, earnestly beseeching him not to commit so grave a sacrilege, from which the ruin of the land and the shedding of blood would undoubtedly follow.

The said abbot also told him explicitly: “Certainly, if your authority carries this out, you will kindle such a fire there that it will reach even you.”

Nevertheless, the pontiff’s will prevailed, and he ordained Landonulf bishop. This was done because Pandonulf had previously submitted himself to the said pope, in whose name charters were drawn up and coins were minted.

In accordance with the foresight of the said abbot, such a fire then arose that the entire land of Benevento, and Rome itself, were utterly ravaged by the Saracens.

For this reason the said pope came to Capua twice. On the first occasion, while he was staying near the city in a place called Antenianus, all the Lombards approached him as enemies. On one side were Bishop Athanasius and Pandonulf; on the other, the two groups of cousins had arrived with Princes Gaideris and Guaimarius, bringing Greeks with them. Every day, in the pope’s presence, both armies rushed forward in battle formation.

With what purpose he honored him is uncertain: the surviving text reads, “Laudonulf [lacuna], previously elected, he consecrated bishop in the church of blessed Peter at Capua.” He ordered the entire bishopric to be divided equally between the two. [The apparatus proposes, editorially, that Landonulf was appointed to preside over the church of Capua and that Landulf was the previously elected man; cf. Leo of Ostia I.42.]

The church in which the consecration had been celebrated was shortly afterward half burned by the Saracens summoned by Pandonulf and sent by Athanasius.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *carte* for *certe* (“certainly”). The source has *exercuerit* (“carries this out”). The defective clause following *Landonulfum* is preserved in the apparatus; the proposed reconstruction is editorial, not a continuous surviving reading.

### 48 [Cols. 0769C–0770A]

Around this time Prince Guaifer became a monk. Weakened by a serious illness, he died. Since his body could not be carried to the monastery of Father Benedict because of the incursions of the Ishmaelites, he was buried in the church of his castle at Teano, until, after rest had been granted from heaven, he might be carried to the holy place.

At the same time Isernia and Suessula were captured and burned within one month; the castle of Bovianum was likewise captured and burned in that same year.

At that time Gaideris, having been induced to estrange himself from his kinsman Lando, joined Pandonulf and gave Pandonulf’s daughter to his own son. But soon afterward he was captured by the kinsmen of the said Lando and committed to custody. In his place Radelgis, son of Adelgisus, was appointed prince in 882.

After ruling for scarcely three years, Radelgis was expelled by the Beneventans, and Aio, his brother, was substituted in his place in 885.

Gaideris, handed over to the Franks in custody, escaped and reached the city of Bari, where the Greeks were staying. They sent him to the imperial city to Basil, the pious emperor. Basil honored him and enriched him with imperial gifts, and gave him the city of Oria to live in.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *teanensis* for *Teanensi*. One reads *Pandonolfus* for *Pandonolfo*. Another has *constitus* for *constitutus* (“appointed”). One marginal note identifies Oria as a city in the principality of Salerno.

### 49. (883) [Cols. 0770A–0770B]

At this time Athanasius, unable to endure Pandonulf’s excesses, abandoned him and joined the sons of Landonulf and Lando in alliance.

During those days the same bishop sent envoys to Sicily and requested King Suchaym for the Saracens who were staying at the foot of Mount Vesuvius; when Suchaym came, Athanasius appointed him over them.

But by God’s just judgment, Suchaym first rose up against Athanasius himself. He began to afflict Naples severely, devouring everything outside it and forcibly demanding girls, horses, and weapons.

Driven by this upheaval, and wishing to expel from himself and his city the apostolic anathema with which he was bound, Athanasius summoned Prince Guaimarius, all the Capuans from the cities and towns, and all the coastal inhabitants to his aid. With their help he violently drove the Saracens from that place.

They departed and encamped at Agropoli.

Not long afterward, the aforesaid bishop, together with the sons of Lando and the sons of Landonulf, came against Capua to capture Pandonulf. Besieging the city on both sides, he afflicted it. Compelled by this necessity, Pandonulf invited Prince Radelgis, his kinsman, to his aid.

Radelgis, setting aside sluggishness, immediately summoned his brother Aio and boldly entered Capua, which had been captured, in his company.

Afterward Aio went out with the Beneventans and Capuans and engaged in battle with the Amalfitans who were supporting the sons of Landonulf. They fought for some time near the city gate. Since neither side yielded to the other, both armies returned to their own positions.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *missi* (“sent”) instead of *missis*. The mountain is transmitted as *Vesuvit*, with a variant *Vesubii*. One witness has *devora* for *devorare*. Another reads *Aione* for *Ajonem*. The source has *expugnatam* (“captured”), with a variant *expugnatam* in a different inflectional form. One witness reads *ne ultra* (“no further”) for *neutra* (“neither”).

### 50 [Cols. 0770C–0770D]

When Radelgis had returned to his own territory, Athanasius returned to his customary weapons and pretended that all the cousins had agreed to terms. He urged them to enter the city together and live there jointly after giving one another an oath.

Pandonulf, however, received from the same bishop an oath that he would plot no ambushes against him. Then all the brothers gathered together and went to Capua. First, they handed the amphitheater over to Athanasius, and he handed it over to Guaifer for permanent habitation, to the continual quarrel of the Capuans.

When all had arrived, as we have said, they all swore that they would enter and live there peacefully and without any molestation. Pandonulf received them in triumph, with clergy clothed in white garments.

But as soon as they had entered, they seized Pandonulf and his brother Landonulf, whom we described above as bishop, together with all their supporters, followers, and partisans. These two were sent to Naples; afterward their wives, sons, and daughters were also sent there.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *ulla* (“any”) for *ullas*. Another has *Athanasius* spelled *Athasius*. The source’s *et ut* is transmitted with a variant *et*. The amphitheater was given to Athanasius and then to Guaifer.

### 51 [Cols. 0771A–0771B]

Meanwhile the Saracens were cruelly tearing apart the entire land mentioned above, so that the land, deprived of cultivators and filled with thorns and brambles, was left desolate.

Guaifer, residing at the Colossus, persuaded by Athanasius—or rather, Athanasius compelled by him—began to wage war against the aforesaid brothers. Together with the Saracens he afflicted and pursued them with excessive severity.

Then, by the will of God, from whom every good thing proceeds, he summoned from Africa a certain Agarene, described in the compressed source as “born of the royal stock of his son-in-law,” and sent him from Agropoli to Garigliano, where the Ishmaelite forces were staying. The syntax does not identify the relationship more securely. By his exhortations he inflamed the minds of all of them. All the Saracens gathered jointly from both Garigliano and Agropoli and hastened to Calabria, where the Greek army was stationed against the Saracens dwelling at Santa Severina.

There all the Greeks were slain by the sword. After this the castle of Amantea was captured. Then the town of blessed Santa Severina was also seized, in 881.

*Apparatus:* The source has *suentibus* in one manuscript, corrected to *sentibus* (“thorns”); another witness reads “thorns and brambles.” The marginal note identifies Amantea as being in Calabria.

### 52 [Col. 0771B]

In these days the most serene Emperor Basil died, in 886. Two of his sons were elected to the imperial office: Leo, the firstborn, and Alexander, who followed him.

The third, named Stephen, assumed the governance of the archbishopric of that same city. Photius had been expelled—he had formerly been punished by Nicholas, pontiff of the first see, with perpetual anathema for invading the episcopate while Ignatius was still alive, and had been restored to his former rank by Pope John, so to speak in ignorance.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *ide* for *id est* (“that is”). Another reads *electo* (“elected”) rather than *ejecto* (“expelled”).

### 53. (884) [Cols. 0771C–0772A]

Meanwhile Athanasius, desiring by his customary deceit to separate the aforesaid brothers from one another, gave his own niece, still nursing, in marriage to the elder Lando, namely the son of the singular and most excellent Lando. He did this so that the daughter of women might ensnare him.

After bringing Lando into his confidence, he warned him with a serpent’s tongue to capture his cousins or, what he desired more, to kill them—namely, so that, by quarreling among themselves, they might either perish altogether or grow weak, and he himself might seize Capua.

Although Lando naturally enjoyed the torpor of sluggishness, he remained immovable and steadfast in the matter he had begun. When Athanasius noticed this, he was distressed and immediately found a counsel most suitable for himself, though ruinous in the long term.

With fitting haste during these events, he summoned Atenulf and said to him privately:

“From the whole people of the Lombards I have chosen Capua as suitable for me, and from Capua and from all your brothers I have preferred you alone, an energetic man, agreeing with me and obeying me in everything. Therefore, if you lend your ears to my words, you will prosper in everything.”

Atenulf replied that he would carry out everything commanded of him. Athanasius said to him:

“Seize the sons of Lando, and be the sole ruler of Capua, just as your grandfather is known to have ruled it alone.”

Atenulf, however, deferred this through the counsel of his brothers. When he returned, he revealed to his brothers the poisonous proposal that had been planted in him.

They were astonished and fortified themselves with the sign of Christ’s cross, saying:

“Let us die or go into exile before we ever rise up, justly or unjustly, against our brothers. For as long as there is breath in our nostrils, we shall not plot against our own blood.”

The sons of Landonulf then joined together and secretly bound themselves with the sons of Lando by a terrible and almost unheard-of oath, under the severe prohibition of anathema.

Atenulf immediately departed and reported to Athanasius that the will of his brothers would remain firm toward their cousins and would not be moved in the least. Athanasius took this very badly and became estranged from them—literally, “became an outsider,” that is, an enemy.

*Apparatus:* One witness has *longibardorum* for *Langobardorum*. Another reads *opt emrantem* for *opt emperantem* (“obeying”). One has *sicontuus tuus* for the phrase concerning the grandfather’s solitary rule. The source reads *fratrum* (“of the brothers”) where the sense requires *fratrem* (“brother”). One witness has *inscitam* (“unlearned”) instead of *insitam* (“planted”). A marginal note explains that “as long as it is in our nostrils” means “as long as there is breath.” The form *juncti* (“joined”) has an orthographic variant. A marginal note explains *extus* as “alien, hostile,” as in the printed editions.

### 54 [Col. 0772B]

At the same time, Guaimarius, the aforementioned prince, was being grievously afflicted by Bishop Athanasius together with the Saracens. His land had been entirely ravaged, so that it could have been captured had divine mercy not intervened. He therefore sought the assistance of the Greeks, by whom he was nobly helped.

He was aided with gold and grain and supported by auxiliaries who guarded his city and its people. This arrangement remains in force to the present, as has been said.

Aio, Prince of Benevento, had been partly weak and partly strong both before and after his accession to the principate.

*Apparatus:* The source has *roboreus* (“strong”), with one witness repeating the same form. The supplied text ends here.

## Ordered source-form apparatus register

This register follows the notes in their exact source order. It supplements the translated chapter apparatus with every printed form, witness siglum, marginal identification, and surviving fragment; spelling-only readings retain the source form and are identified as such.
