132. [Col. 0771D], at “as long as it is in our nostrils”: “Namely, breath.”
133. [Col. 0771], at *juncti* (“joined”): c has *jucti*, a spelling form.
134. At *fratruelibus* (“to the cousins”): c has *fratulibus*, a spelling/damaged form.
135. [Col. 0772D], at *extus* (“outside”): “that is, alien; hostile, as in the printed editions.”

### Chapter 54

136. [Col. 0771], at *roboreus* (“strong”): witness 3 supports the editor’s *ita* statement, while c also reads *roboreus*.

### 55

But, to return to what happened earlier: when the Saracens held Calabria and were perishing there, Decivilis, duke of Gaeta, retained nearly one hundred and fifty of them with him, so that he would not remain without priestly service—after the manner, it is said, of the Jewish kings who, when the kingdom had been divided between them into two parts, gathered the Levites for the most part at Jerusalem, where there was a temple authentic throughout the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0771] *illicque* (“and there”) in witness 2.]

Of this number, nearly one hundred and twenty of the aforesaid Saracens boldly approached the city of Teano, just as they had previously been seen to do, when they had numbered almost two thousand five hundred. But Lando, like a lion, boldly rushing upon them with his men, crushed them to utter destruction, so that of so great a number no more than five escaped; the rest being killed—if I am not mistaken, one hundred and fifteen. [Note: [Col. 0771] *quinquagita* in manuscript c.] [Note: [Col. 0771] That is, “aforesaid”; manuscript c. has *facti*.] [Note: [Col. 0771] Witness 3 has *ita*; manuscript c. has *infectis*.]

### 56

But Athanasius, seeing that he had been deceived by the replies of both brothers, became more sorrowful than usual, yet quickly found a plan suited to himself. Accordingly, he sent envoys and summoned three hundred Greeks to his aid, with Chasan leading them. [Note: [Col. 0771] Witness 1 has *chasanos*.]

Then, having craftily made peace with the Capuans, at the time when the grape harvest is gathered, when Capua was severely afflicted and its countryside laid waste, all went out eagerly to gather the grapes, both the leading men and the common people. But he, chiefly at the suggestion of Guaifer of Collese, sent the Greeks from Naples out of hiding, together with the theatrical troops [Note: [Col. 0773] Or something of that sort.], and plundered all Capua, capturing in it many men of rank and considerable possessions.

From that time, therefore, devastating everything around him, he claimed Liburia for himself. For he secretly summoned the Agropolitans—Saracens who had recently killed nearly two hundred men from his magnates beside the stream of Lanius [Note: [Col. 0773] A recent hand has written in the margin: “From this it is called the land of Lania.”], not far from Suessula [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *Assuessula*.], at the place where he had perpetrated that unspeakable crime—and sent them to Capua. There the Capuans, coming out against them, resisted them vigorously; and for this reason they returned to the camp without booty. At that time the elder Lando died, struck by apoplexy.

### 57. (885)

The man mentioned above, therefore, rose up against the Capuans with new and unheard-of devices, just as he had conceived in his mind. Thus, during Lent, when all Christian people were mourning the evils that had passed and asking God not to allow them to commit such things to be mourned in the future, on the Sunday festival that followed, at twilight, after gathering the Greeks from Matera, the Egyptians, and the Neapolitans, with Duke Guaifer informed of the plan [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *consio*.], and with Chasan leading them, he attempted to invade the city of Capua. [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *commictat*, “commit.”] [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *mediante festo*, “with the festival intervening.”]

Having scaled the wall with nearly three hundred armed men equipped with various kinds of weapons, they were, with the Lord’s help, all overcome: some leapt down of their own accord, some were thrown down to the depths as far as their necks, and others fell by the sword. Of our men, only one, named Onericus, was killed—and, so it is said, by his own men.

For the Judge and Arbiter waged this battle on the wall, as it has been related, not through fighting and heavily armed men, but marvelously through four boys, to the praise of his name. [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c omits each occurrence of “through”; witness 3 retains it.]

Although his forces had been shattered, he did not abandon what he had conceived. For he had often attempted to capture Salerno, first through the Saracens and afterward through the Greeks, but the Lord did not permit it.

### 58

At the same time, Guido, son of the elder Guido, attacking the Saracens who were encamped at the Garigliano [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *gariliano*.], stormed and plundered their camp and killed some of them with swords. The rest poured through the dark places of the mountain like water.

As he approached Capua [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *approprians*.], he crossed beyond it and encamped at the bridge called Teudemund’s. He remained there for some time, and, after grain and other provisions had been taken from Liburia, the Capuans were refreshed. They had not entered into an alliance with this duke; but when he turned back and passed through the city, they were compelled by fear to submit to him.

When he had returned to his own territory, the aforesaid Athanasius rose manfully against them and, aided by Greek forces, took from them all the crops planted in the countryside, together with whatever they appeared to possess on the side of Capua and also farther above; these things were then gathered up. After the return of the duke mentioned above, many operations were carried out through Chasan, which I have briefly related.

[Note: [Col. 0773] *castrametatus*, “having encamped”; manuscript c. has *castrametus*.] [Note: [Col. 0773] *dirrupta*, “broken open”; manuscript c. has *dirructa*.]

### 59. (886)

After this, it was suggested to the same duke that he should come as quickly as possible and rescue those who trusted in him; otherwise, they would be entirely ruined. [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *confidentes ipse sin*, “those trusting in him—otherwise.”]

He therefore came at once to Capua and captured Aio, prince of Benevento, who was coming to him on the advice of the Capuans. He had him taken under guard to Benevento and, entering the city, arranged its affairs. [Note: [Col. 0773] Three witnesses read *quam*, “which,” instead of *in qua*, “in which.”]

Departing from there [Note: [Col. 0773] Three witnesses read *proficiens*, “advancing,” instead of *proficiscens*, “departing.”], he entered Sepontum and left Aio outside in the camp. When the people of Sepontum learned that their elder Aio had been captured, they unanimously attacked the aforesaid duke, shut him up in a certain temple, and captured his leading men.

Messengers were then sent here and there [Note: [Col. 0773] Three witnesses have *missus*, “a messenger was sent.”], and Aio was brought in, released, and restored to his own men. [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *reditusque*, “and restored.”] On the following day, after an oath had been given, he scarcely escaped, and only with disgrace. [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *est a suis*, “was restored by his own men.”]

### 60

Thereafter, when Chasan departed for Constantinople, a certain imperial *strategos* sent John the Candidate—whom they call Janniccio in the Pelasgian language [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *pelastica*.]—to Bishop Athanasius with three hundred fighting men. With John, Athanasius plundered Capua on both sides. With the aid of these troops, he rescued Pandonolf from prison and restored him to freedom; Pandonolf was received by Magipert at Suessa. [Note: [Col. 0773] I have corrected the reading; manuscript c. has *perfidiam*, “treachery.”]

Pandonolf joined the Greeks, and all the livestock of Capua was carried away. For this reason Lando, son of Landonolf, and Bishop Landolf went to the aforesaid duke at Spoleto, asking him for help. Bishop Landolf returned from Spoleto, while Lando came with the same duke through Sepontum to Capua.

The duke remained for several days at Atella and filled Capua with grain. On receiving news, he suddenly set out for Rome, leaving the Capuans in the hands of the said bishop. The bishop immediately sent Greeks and Neapolitans against the monastery of Saint Hermes. After besieging it for a long time, he captured those who were staying in the heights [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *sullimibus*, “in the higher places.”], and afterward gravely afflicted Capua from both sides, so that it seemed almost besieged.

For the Greeks and Neapolitans, together with Pandonolf, were staying near Sicopolis and devouring everything around them root and branch. Hence it happened that eighty of them, coming to Calinulus [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *adventes*, “coming.”], secretly attacked Teano. Lando with the people of Teano and Atenolfus with some of the Capuans met them from the opposite direction near Saint Scholastica, close to the fortress of Teano; and they were defeated by them. [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *glaviter*, “gravely,” for *graviter*.] [Note: [Col. 0773] Manuscript c. has *stripitus* for *stirpitus*, “root and branch.”]

### 61. (886)

At that time the monastery of blessed Benedict, previously destroyed by the Saracens in the year of the Lord 884 [Note: [Col. 0773] One witness gives the date as *DCCCLXXXXIIII*—894.], began to be rebuilt by the venerable abbot Angelarius in the year 886, in the month of August, by order. [Note: [Col. 0773D] That is, *ginso*, below.] [Note: [Col. 0773] Three witnesses read *de jusso*, “by order.”]

As we were returning from there to Capua, I and seven other brothers, traveling from Teano to Capua near Anglena, were captured, stripped, and violently mistreated by the Greeks. [Note: [Col. 0775] “Herchempertus, together with seven other brothers, traveling from Teano toward Capua, were all stripped and robbed by the Greeks near Anglena.”] After all the horses, possessions, and servants had been taken, the men were ransomed for silver; we recovered the horses. [Note: [Col. 0775] Another witness has *exequietati*.]

I alone remained on foot with my teacher. The Capuans brought us into the city; from there we went on to Naples, but accomplished nothing, and returned to Capua without result. [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *infrutuosi*, “without fruit.”] Afterward, three wagons loaded with provisions and many valuable goods were seized and plundered near Anglena, where we had previously been captured.

### 62

After these cruel events had taken place, Atenolfus went to Spoleto and, by paying a price to Suabilus, gastald of the Marsi, brought back with him, together with other companions and vassals [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *bassis*, apparently “lower-ranking men.”], nearly three hundred armed men. With them he also made an agreement that they should secure the gastaldate of Capua for him.

But when they entered Capua and were unable to accomplish this, the Franks mentioned above, Landolfus his brother especially resisting and opposing them—for Atenolfus himself had previously appointed Landolfus gastald, together with the other brothers, over the matters belonging to them [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *hisque*, “over those matters.”]—were released by Atenolfus and returned by the road on which they had come.

Then the aforesaid Atenolfus, after taking counsel with his men, secretly sent his kinsman Sadi to the often-mentioned Athanasius, asking him for assistance so that he might be helped to become count of Capua in his own right. When Athanasius heard this, he rejoiced and promised that he would assist him in everything. [Note: [Col. 0775] Three witnesses read *illi*, “assist him.”] When this had been reported many times, and especially three or four times, to Lando, he, held by his customary sluggishness and torpor, made light of it and regarded such a message as nothing.

### 63

Afterward, the aforementioned Lando, inflamed with the heat of fever [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *frebis*; even today the Neapolitans call it *la frebbe*.], went to Teano to be cured of the illness by which he was afflicted. Meanwhile, Atenolfus did not move either his step or his intention from the enterprise he had begun [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *arepta*, “from the thing seized.”], but, being ready and ardent, set about bringing to birth what he had long conceived in his heart. For this reason he hastened to go to Naples.

When this came to Lando’s ears, he immediately sent Alcisus and Adelfridus to Capua, so that by their urging they might divert the man mentioned above from the journey he had begun. He added: “But I, after I have heard the news and finished my meal, will follow you.”

They went away, but when they found the aforesaid man, they could not persuade him to remain; for it was Sunday. Then Lando set out and did not find him at all, for he had already departed. After this [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *facto*.], Lando awaited his return. When he returned, Lando and the other brothers said to him: “What did you do there, where you went?”

He answered them with good and consoling words, full of deceit. Having heard these words, they were exceedingly credulous and believed him, accepting what he said.

Thereafter, Lando perceived his brother’s deceit, but, overcome by sleep and weighed down by negligence, he did not understand the weapon that was being hurled against him until it pierced the fiber of his liver. He returned to Teano to recover. His brother Landonolfus came to visit him there, and Landonolfus alone was left in the city.

### 64

When Atenolfus saw this and perceived that a suitable opportunity had come to him, he first pretended that he was leaving the city with his wife and children and going to Calvi as though he intended to live there. [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *et* for *e*, “from.”] [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *habitarus*, “to inhabit.”]

Meanwhile, he made agreements with ambitious young men and, after giving an oath and promising many gifts, broke the oath that he had sworn three times with the sons of Lando. When the time for sleep came, on the Saturday after Epiphany [Note: [Col. 0775] Three witnesses read “on the Saturday before Epiphany.”], that is, on the seventh day before the Ides of January, he summoned his companions [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *solalibus*.] and attacked the sons of Lando in order to fight them (887).

The sons of Lando did not prepare themselves negligently against such an attempt, but when those on whom they had placed their trust fled, they were badly shaken. They were especially disturbed because they thought that Lando, with all his brothers, was present in this conflict.

When they saw that they had been abandoned by everyone, they yielded to Atenolfus and left the city by night, reaching Teano: Landonolfus, Pando, and their nephew Guaiferius. From the city, people shouted after them: “Do not go to Teano, for you will certainly be captured!”

But as they approached Teano [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *apropriantes*.], they began to hesitate, fearing that they might be held captive by Lando [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *exitare*, apparently “to hesitate.”]. When their arrival was announced, however, they were received with the greatest courtesy.

### 65

Atenolfus, taking sole possession of the gastaldate of Capua, immediately ordered himself to be called count. He then sent his son as a hostage to Athanasius, as he had promised under oath [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *si cosacramento*, “under oath.”], and under that oath granted him Liburia and Capua.

Athanasius kept his son until the aforesaid Atenolfus received the agreement that Duke Guido had promised him. When Atenolfus had accepted the Frankish treaty, Athanasius returned his son to him, and peace was maintained between the two for one year and three months.

At the same time, Atenolfus sent envoys to Rome—Majone, the venerable abbot, and Dauferius the deacon—to submit himself to Pope Stephen and become his personal servant. He also promised to return the Gaetans whom he had previously captured by deceit and to aid him against the Saracens residing at the Garigliano. But afterward he forgot all these things and fulfilled none of what he had promised.

### 66

In those days Theophylactus, the *stratigos* of Bari, came hostilely to Teano in winter, attempting to attack the Saracens. Accomplishing nothing, he departed without result. On his way to Naples, he captured Marinus, the gastald of the fortress [Note: [Col. 0775] Manuscript c. has *castris*, “of the fortresses.”] of Saint Agatha [Note: [Col. 0775] A recent hand has written in the margin: “This is a noble fortress in the Capitanata, near Asculum.”], who was rebellious against Aio. [Note: [Col. 0775] Three witnesses read *praecepit*, “he ordered,” instead of *percepit*, “he captured.”] Returning to Apulia, he seized by force some of Aio’s fortifications.

Taking this as an opportunity, Aio began a quarrel of rebellion against the imperial administration, which will be related in its proper place. [Note: [Col. 0777] Three witnesses read *inferetur*, “will be inserted,” instead of *inseretur*, “will be inserted in its proper place.”]

### 67

Before this, Guaimarius, the prince, had gone with confidence to Constantinople, to the feet of the emperors. He was kindly received by them, made a patrician, and sent back home with honor.

While he was still staying there, Athanasius, allowing the pain he had conceived to burst into action [Note: [Col. 0777] Witness 3 has *dolore conceptus*, “having been seized by sorrow.”], moved the Greeks, the Neapolitans, and generally all the Capuans, and sent them against the fortress of Abellinum [Note: [Col. 0777D] Avellino.], over which Landolfus of Suessula was then in command.

As soon as the army arrived there, the fortress was captured through the treachery of those who were inside [Note: [Col. 0777] Three witnesses read “who had gone inside.”] Landolfus, his younger son, and his daughter-in-law were seized in it—the wife, namely, of Lando [Note: [Col. 0777] A witness has *uxorem*, the accusative form, for *uxore*.], who had gone away with Guaimarius. [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *prophectus*, “who had departed.”]

### 68

After these events had passed, Lando, urged by Algegisius [Note: [Col. 0778D] That is, Adelgisius.] and other Capuans, was brought in together with Guaiferius, concealed in a cart carrying a certain load [Note: [Col. 0777] One witness reads *vehementem*, “carrying a heavy load.”], and entered the city of Capua. He went to the episcopal palace, where a few of his men gathered [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *paucis ex ui*, apparently “a few of his men.”], while Atenolfus hurried there.

A battle then began. When the illustrious man Valane was killed, the courage of those who were on Lando’s side collapsed, and they began to abandon him and join Atenolfus.

Then, although only deceptively, the brothers offered one another the kiss of peace, which they did not at all retain in the ark of their hearts. After this, Lando and Guaiferius returned home, while the rest of their fellow supporters were captured and bound in chains. Among them Bishop Landolfus was also captured and thrown into custody. After not much time had passed, all of them were released one by one.

### 69

In those days, when Atenolfus had obtained the rights of governing the gastaldate, he ordered that everything Benedict possessed within the city of Capua be taken away from the exiled brothers.

For this reason, sent by the venerable abbot Angelarius, I myself went to the supreme pontiff Stephen, to the apostles’ shrines [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. punctuates the phrase in this way.], to plead for our abbot’s property. From him I brought back a blessing for the brothers, the privilege of our monastery, and letters of exhortation for the aforesaid man. [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *licteras*, “letters.”]

The property of the Church that had been taken away was restored; but my own property was entirely removed. [Note: [Col. 0777] I correct the reading to “mine”; manuscript c. has *me*, “me.”] Soon afterward, in his anger, he forcibly took from me a cell that had been assigned to me by the abbot.

### 70

Meanwhile, after the aforesaid Atenolfus had captured the Capuans, Athanasius, observing that Capua had been severely shaken, began to seek an opportunity against Atenolfus and to renew with him both the hostage arrangement and the peace.

As messengers passed between the two sides [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *missis maio*, apparently “with Maio sent.”], the aforesaid abbot Maio and Ausencius went to Naples. Athanasius ordered them to go to the amphitheater and also wanted Atenolfus to be there, so that, after a treaty had been secured with Guaiferius the consul, he might send his son, together with some men from Capua, as a hostage.

While doing this, however, he secretly laid an ambush with the Greeks and his own men to capture them. [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *suos*, “his own men.”] But because, as may be conjectured, the wickedness that was soon to be punished by divine judgment had not yet reached its fullness, a short delay occurred. He shut his own son inside the city and sent the men mentioned above to the arena.

The Greek force immediately went out, seized the men mentioned above together with others, and gravely plundered all Capua. Then, without delay, he sent the entire cavalry and infantry and caused all the crops of Capua to be cut down and utterly destroyed.

### 71. (888)

God, foreseeing the wickedness of the man mentioned above and wishing to show mercy to the Capuans amid such cruel and impious persecution, permitted that Athanasius should burst into such arrogance that he even caused the territory of Benevento to be plundered two or three times.

At that time Aio, staying at Bari, was attacking the Greeks who were attacking him. When he heard this, he immediately laid aside his sluggishness and secretly came with nearly three thousand warriors to the fortress at Abellinum.

When he learned that the Greeks were staying with the Neapolitans above Capua and devastating it utterly, he immediately tried to march straight against them boldly. But a certain natural sower of weeds, Dauferius, father of our Dauferius, went out deceitfully from the city of Benevento as if to follow the prince, hurried in the opposite direction to Capua [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *cursum*, “he hurried.”], and announced Aio’s arrival to the army in question.

They therefore abandoned Capua and fled headlong back to Naples [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *precipientes*, “hastening.”] Aio, however, completed the journey he had begun, and, not finding them, entered Liburia. Atenolfus also departed with him.

After almost all Liburia had been burned and plundered, its people and animals carried away, and its wells blocked with stone, he proceeded to the amphitheater. Remaining there for several days, he fiercely attacked it with siege engines and various weapons. [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. has *illi*, “him,” instead of “it.”]

From there he went and settled above the fortress of Saint Agatha. He received Marinus, the gastald who had rebelled against him, when Marinus returned to his allegiance, and then departed. After staying for some time at Benevento, he returned to Bari through Sepontum.

### 72

Atenolfus, however, submitted himself to Aio under oath and received from him nearly one hundred and twenty fighting men to assist him. With them he heavily plundered all Liburia.

But because despair sometimes gives rise to danger, the people of Matera, having risen as one, came from Calvi [Note: [Col. 0777] Manuscript c. writes *ecalvo*, “from Calvi,” as one word.], and some Capuans joined the Apulians mentioned above. They went around Liburia, plundered Suessula, and began to return.

The army of the Greeks and Neapolitans met them near the stream of Lanius. When the two sides had joined battle, Atenolfus’s party was overpowering the Greek side. [Note: [Col. 0777] The manuscript has *supervale valebat*.] But the theatrical squadron came upon them from behind and in the middle, and they were surrounded and defeated: some were captured, and some were killed by the sword.

For this reason Athanasius took courage and began to seek battle. Atenolfus, therefore, no longer inactive, immediately went with his men to Atella; but, finding no battle, he returned to his own territory.

### 73

Not long afterward, at the instigation of the enemy of the human race, Athanasius gathered a large army composed of Greeks, Neapolitans, and Ishmaelites, both cavalry and infantry, and sent them to fight against Capua.

Atenolfus met them beyond the stream of Lanius near Saint Carcius [Note: [Col. 0779D] San Carzio in the district of Aversa.], having in his company auxiliaries sent by Aio as well as Saracens. The Saracens stood joined on both sides, offering assistance to neither.

Seeing this, Atenolfus rose more fiercely against his enemies and, overcoming them with powerful strength at the first assault, crushed them to utter ruin. He killed many of them and captured many others, forcing the rest to flee in haste. Victorious and triumphant, he returned to the camp with all his men, laden with spoils and rejoicing.

Of his own men he lost only one, named Aldericus, and he too, it is said, was killed by his own men. From that day Atenolfus began to be, as it were, powerful, while Athanasius became powerless.

From then on he began to plunder all the crops of those who lived in Collese [Note: [Col. 0779] Witness 2 has *colosso*, “in Collese.”], and to have all their goods carried to the city in various vehicles.

### 74

Let all ears hear this also that I relate, just as the Lord often said parabolically to his followers: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 13), so that every person may tremble, be astonished, and return to God, even if late. [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *fero*, apparently “late.”] Otherwise, if he remains obstinate in mind, what happened to the proud Dathan and Abiram may happen to him, as it is known to have happened also to Korah with his supporters. [Note: [Col. 0779] A word is missing in witness c.]

For Guaiferius, prefect of the arena, who himself perpetrated through his own deeds, and caused others to perpetrate, nearly all the evils committed in his days, by whose trickery the Roman land was devastated and the Beneventan region utterly desolated—he received both the beginning and the end of these things from that same source. [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *finis*, “end,” for *finem*.] Therefore, by God’s judgment, he brought his criminal wickedness to such an end. [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *selus*, apparently for *scelus*, “crime.”]

For suddenly, by the inspiration of heavenly grace, from which every good proceeds, those whom he had thought would save him were stirred up against him. Changing their minds, they rose against him, seized him, plundered his possessions, and bound him. [Note: [Col. 0779] The place is erased.] Nevertheless, they returned to the very ground from which they had never been severed by the devil, and sent him, the contemptible proconsul, back to Capua, agreeing with Atenolfus [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *consenciente*, “with Atenolfus agreeing”], there to suffer the bread of affliction and the water of distress.

When this had been done, all those who had once been arrogantly exiled from their native seat returned obediently to their own homes. Great joy, peace, and security came about. Those who had been accustomed to be subject began to rule, and those who had ruled by law for three hundred years and more [Note: [Col. 0779] One witness has *anno imperaverat*, “he had ruled for years.”] began to rule over those who had prevailed with the Saracens for some days.

Then the Bardic cohort [Note: [Col. 0780D] That is, the Lombard cohort.] began to reign triumphantly over those whom they had always subdued by arms.

### 75

Meanwhile, Athanasius, seeing that he had been defeated in everything, sought a treaty out of shame at the peace that had been offered. [Note: [Col. 0779] Witness 1 has *objecte*; witness 2 has *objecto*.] He obtained it, and after an oath had been given [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *praevito*, “after an oath had been advanced”; witness 3 has *praevinto*, “after an oath had been exacted”], they made an agreement with one another.

The first oath, however, had stood firm for perhaps a month or a year; this one did not last even twelve days. Finally, the Ishmaelites ran about here and there, invited by everyone, devouring everything and consuming all things, and unanimously rose up against Naples. [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *invitantantur*.]

By an equal judgment, he who had hurled himself against the heavenly throne would unquestionably be struck down by those with whom he had nearly destroyed the whole Christian people, just as John says in the Apocalypse—or rather, the Lord through John—concerning Babylon: “As much as she has ministered to you, minister to her; in the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double” (Revelation 18).

When you hear these things, do not set your hearts upon the thought that God has done this because of the merits of some prelate. Rather, he acted in his mercy, finding an occasion in human misery, as he himself says through the Psalmist: “Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.” For he says to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” and so on, until he says: “You did these things, and I was silent; you thought that I was like you. In what, then, shall I be like you?” (Psalm 49).

Yet I am troubled by one matter: when the Apostle says, “Will not the one who plunders himself also be plundered?” (Isaiah 33). What, then, will become of those who plunder their neighbors, both men and women, and hand them over to a brothel [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *prosribulo*, apparently “to the brothel”]? Will they themselves then be plundered?

Just as the Neapolitans are devastated—those who devastated others—so perhaps we too shall be devoured, who are now devouring. Blessed, therefore, are those who, under the Lord’s protection, remain free from this storm of the world, in which every evil and no good without the Lord reigns, and who are counted among eternal life, in which every happiness and enduring blessedness flourishes forever and ever. Amen.

### 76

Finally, Aio departed from Benevento through Sepontum toward Bari. There he found Constantine, courtier and patrician of the emperors [Note: [Col. 0779] Manuscript c. has *aulicet*, “courtier”; witness 3 has *vaiulus*, “vicar.”], occupying the city and manfully fighting against the rebels of the emperors.

Against him the aforesaid Aio, supported by the help of the Ishmaelites and surrounded by a column of Apulian infantry, boldly rose up. At the first assault he proved victorious and killed many of the enemy.

Then [Note: [Col. 0779] Witnesses 1 and 3 read *ita* (“thus”); witness 2 has *deinde* (“then”).] Aio was severely defeated, while Constantine stood in a secure place with three thousand horsemen [Note: [Col. 0779] Witness 2 has *a Constantino*; witness 3 has *Constantino locum*.], and scarcely managed to enter the city of Bari with a few men. The remainder were either put to the sword or handed over into captivity.

He himself, surrounded by a Greek rampart, remained hidden within the city [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *occulatur*, “was hidden”], awaiting the assistance of Atenolfus, whom he had previously protected, but he did not find it. For although he repeatedly invited both the Franks and the Hagarenes together with promises of gold [Note: [Col. 0781] Witnesses 2 and 3 have a corrupt reading.], he could not obtain it.

### 77

Atenolfus therefore maintained peace with Athanasius for nearly twelve days. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *bis bonis*, “nearly twelve good days”; I have corrected it; see chapter 75 above.] When the treaty was broken, both sides rushed out to plunder.

But the Capuans, having become much stronger, devastated and ravaged Naples and its surroundings with great violence, both on their own and together with the Saracens, consuming everything like fire, by an equal judgment of God. For the one who handed countless Christians over to the Saracens for slaughter and captivity and enriched himself with their possessions was deservedly scourged, gnawed, and plundered by them, as Solomon says: “Who will heal the enchanter who has once been bitten by a serpent?” (Ecclesiasticus 12).

### 78

Meanwhile, after the capture of the bishop and after the entire clergy had been bound by oath [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *reuictum*, apparently “rebound.”], Atenolfus turned to new and recent legal regulations.

He compelled the monks of blessed Benedict to swear concerning the property that had been lost, although all earlier princes and all the Gallic emperors had granted them that privilege: that they should give an oath by themselves to no man except through *scariones* [Note: [Col. 0781D] The same as *scariti*, soldiers.]. In this matter he displayed himself as wiser and superior to his predecessors. [Note: [Col. 0782D] Said ironically.]

### 79

When Lambert, son of the elder Guido, died, he left Spoleto to his son. When the son also died, Guido the Younger, taking possession of Spoleto and Camerinum, made peace with the Saracens encamped at Sepino, hostages being given and received. During his time, all the monasteries, cities, and towns mentioned above were captured and burned by the Saracens.

While sending an embassy to the royal city, he acted against the law and accepted money. For this reason he was captured by the emperor Charles III, and, unless he had taken flight, he would have been punished by decapitation.

I shall relate one deed of his, not at all unlike what happened at the Garigliano (883). [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *aut* (“or”) for *haut* (“not at all”).] Finally, when the same duke was traveling from Sepontum to Capua with Atenolfus accompanying him, at a place called Caudi he killed Arranes the Ishmaelite, a most cruel tyrant, together with nearly three hundred of his followers (887).

When Guido learned that the emperor Charles was lying half-dead, overcome by the desire to reign and deceived by his kinsmen, he abandoned the Beneventan province that he had subjected to himself [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *subacta*, feminine, “subjected”] and the duchy of Spoleto and went to Gaul to reign.

The land of Benevento was captured by the Greeks, Spoleto was plundered by the Hagarenes, while he himself remained unseen and unheard. When he appears and is heard, I shall relate in due order what he said or did, for those who wish to know. [Note: [Col. 0781] Witness B has *erit*, “will be,” instead of *dixerit*, “what he said.”]

### 80. (888)

Meanwhile, while Aio was being besieged within the city of Bari by the Greeks and was demanding help from the Franks and his own people, Atenolfus, wavering before Athanasius’s threats, sent his envoys to the patrician Constantine, who was stationed above the city in question.

By establishing a peace treaty with him, Atenolfus craftily diverted the forces that might have resisted Aio. [Note: [Col. 0781] Witness 1 has *utuerit*; witness 2 has *advertit*.] Seeing himself deceived by these and similar devices, Aio grieved. At last, pressed by necessity, he made peace with the aforesaid patrician, returned the city, and went back home, threatening Atenolfus and Abbot Maio—the man who had carried out the aforesaid embassy [Note: [Col. 0781] Witness 1 has *supra facta*; manuscript c. has *funtus*, for *fata ... functus*.]—not without cause. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *aut*, “or,” instead of *haut*, “not.”]

At the same time, Atenolfus was properly arranging for Dauferius [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *Dauferius*.], our deacon, to go to Taranto and from there to send him to the royal city. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *transmicteret*, “to transmit.”] Dauferius complained against him about his poverty. A dispute arose between them, and they were separated from each other; Atenolfus remained at Capua, while Dauferius hastened to Teano to stay there.

Shortly afterward, when an agreement had been arranged, he returned to the man from whom he had separated.

### 81

At that time, the Greeks came by sea from Constantinople toward the territory of Rhegium, while the Ishmaelites hurried from Africa and Sicily in the opposite direction. The two forces joined between Messana, a city of Sicily, and Rhegium.

After fighting each other for a short time [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *confringentes*, “after crushing one another.”], the Greeks were defeated. The remaining Achaeans were so terrified by such fear that men, women, and children alike abandoned both cities, together with everything in them, and found safety; no one continued the war. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *contrahens*, “engaging in war.”]

But I shall briefly relate why divine justice permitted such things to happen to that bestial people. The Achaeans, just as they are alike in bodily appearance, are equal to beasts in spirit—Christians in name, but in conduct more wretched than the Hagarenes.

These men plundered all the faithful on their own account, bought them from the Saracens, and of these captives filled the shores of the ocean with some for sale, while reserving others as male and female servants. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *famulis*, “as servants.”]

Seeing these and similar things, God handed them over to disgrace and destruction, so that they might perish and reconsider and understand that by their dreadful deeds they had hurled themselves against God.

These events took place in the narrow stretch of sea that separates Rhegium [Note: [Col. 0781] Witnesses A and B have *regnum*, “kingdom.”] from Sicily. In former times that place was land, but in modern times it has been occupied by the sea of the Pharos. [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *avari*, “of the greedy one.”]

These events therefore took place in the year of the Lord 888 [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript c. has *DCCCLXXX*, “880.”], in the month of October.

### 82

In this same year Guido returned to Italy, where he desired to rule but could not prevail. In Italy, near the city of Brescia, he fought with Berengarius and with the duke himself. [Note: [Col. 0782D] I have corrected the reading; manuscript c. has *conflictis*, “having been fought.”] In that conflict the forces of both sides were cruelly slaughtered.

The spoils of the slain were collected by Berengarius. Nevertheless, they made an agreement with one another lasting until Epiphany, which is celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides of January (889). [Note: [Col. 0781] Manuscript 2 has *celebratur*, “is celebrated.”]

When the two join together either for an agreement or for battle, I shall insert in this little work what they do afterward.

## In the Year of the Lord 890

### Angilbert, Abbot of Corbie

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783]

## Historical Notice Concerning Angilbert

*(From Fabricius, Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis.)*

Angilbert, or Engilbert, was abbot of Corbie around the year of Christ 880. He prefixed certain elegiac verses and added others in hexameters to Saint Augustine’s book *On Christian Doctrine*, which he presented to King Louis of the Franks, the brother of Carloman. Mabillon published both sets in volume II of the *Analecta*, pages 657ff., and in the new folio edition, page 425.

[Col. 0783]

# Verses of Angilbert, Abbot of Corbie, to Louis, King of the Franks, Brother of Carloman

[Note: [Col. 0783B] The first of these verses appears at the beginning, and the later ones at the end, of the books of St. Augustine *On Christian Doctrine* in the Corbie codex, which Angilbert—or Engilbert—the abbot of that place, had copied for the benefit of Louis, king of the Franks, in the year 880 or the following year. Whether Angilbert did this at the prince’s request or without his knowledge, it certainly shows that Louis was rightly devoted to sacred literature, since Angilbert judged that no gift would be more pleasing to him than these books of St. Augustine. It is appropriate here to observe that sacred reading was at times familiar to the ancient kings of the Franks. Hence Adalbero, bishop of Laon, urges King Robert to read the books of Augustine, Dionysius called the Areopagite, and Gregory the Great.]

Sent as a gift to that same king, in a book of St. Augustine *On Christian Doctrine*.

(Apud Mabillon, *Analecta vetera*, p. 425.)

[Col. 0783A]

Here shine Augustine’s devout teachings,  
which he published concerning life-giving doctrine.

These many things teach you, reader, what you honorably seek,  
if you desire to review the sacred writings of the book.

For this small volume, whose body you see here,  
contains within it four books.

The first relates the keeping of Christ’s commandments,  
which the gracious God has ordered to be observed throughout the world:

it aptly teaches how to use the present things of this age  
and how rightly to enjoy eternal things.

The second also teaches through various signs and matters  
how, or in what manner, we may recognize signs.

The third shines forth from these same signs and words;  
it explains what they are, what they signify, and what things it sings must be avoided.

Then the fourth brings forth the teachings of the preceding books:  
what things, what signs, and what devout words teach.

It resounds in mighty speech, explaining  
how all that has been understood may be expressed—

quietly, equally, moderately, and grandly.

Reader, when you have read it through, say: “Have mercy, O God.”

This little book was ordered to be made by the humble abbot,  
Angilbert, indeed, lowly and insignificant,

[Col. 0784A]

so that he might give it, supported by the gracious heavenly power,  
to King Louis, who is devout and humble,

who strives to examine the secrets of holy wisdom,  
noble in understanding, alike by night and by day;

and who is also a glorious lover of the Lord and of his brother,  
remaining constant in devout speech of great power.

May almighty God glorify him, preserve him, love him,  
adorn him, and cherish him through many prosperous years.

## And at the end

When you, devout reader, have read through this teaching of the pious patron,  
pour forth devoted and unceasing generous praises,

first to the Lord, who created the whole world,  
who founded the sea and created heaven and earth,

who enclosed all things by number, measure, and weight.

[Col. 0784B]

Through whom all things remain, or through whom all things will remain—  
the things that are, that were, that will be, and all things yet to come—

to that same Lord pour forth great thanks again  
for such a great, chaste, and learned teacher,

who, in worthy order, wrote such things for us.

[Col. 0785]

Kindly remember King Chlodovic in your prayers,  
a man worthy of his divine name and supported by divine favor,

shining with life-giving praises and with great majesty.

May almighty God, for many prosperous years,

[Col. 0786]

graciously grant him to hold prosperous kingdoms.

With him may the Ruler of heaven deign to govern  
his marriage, his offspring, and all the faithful from heaven’s height,

and after this course may he ascend to the heavenly kingdoms, and so forth.

# In the Year of the Lord 891. Stephen V, Roman Pontiff

# Letters, Decrees, and Privileges of Pope Stephen V

(From Mansi, Bouquet, and certain more recent collectors.)

## I. [Note: [Col. 0785A] These letters of the emperor Basil, which he himself had written to Adrian—full of blasphemies and insults on account of Photius, who had been excommunicated by Marinus and Adrian—were received and read by Stephen, Adrian’s successor, after Adrian’s death. Persevering, after the example of his predecessors, in hatred and detestation of that same Photius, he wrote a letter back to the emperor, rebuking him for insulting Pope Marinus and the entire Roman Church while defending Photius, a thoroughly layman excommunicated for a just cause, so vehemently. The letter was delivered, after Basil’s death, to his son and successor Leo. When Leo received it, he removed Photius from the throne and confined him to the monastery of the Armenians all the more willingly and promptly because Photius, together with Santabarenus, had adopted an even worse plan in choosing his relative as emperor; and he arranged that his own brother Stephen should be substituted for him. Since Stephen, who was to be substituted for Photius, had been ordained by Photius, the bishop Stylianus of Neocaesarea, together with the emperor Leo, asked Pope Stephen by letter not to disdain to dispense, by apostolic authority, with the impediment in this matter involving the designated patriarch of Constantinople, Stephen, the successor of Photius. That this favor was obtained from the Apostolic See after careful examination of the case seems to be attested clearly enough by the communion between the two sees, which was thereafter practiced and frequented. Photius, expelled and exiled under this pontificate, died when and in what manner, the deceit of the schismatics and followers of Photius has left obscure. For, knowing that their master was severely reproached by all the records left to posterity in favor of Ignatius against Photius, and being ashamed to follow such an author of schism, they not only thought that everything transacted between Ignatius and Photius ought to be buried in silence, but also actually condemned it with a sentence of anathema, as appears in session 6 of the Council of Florence. SEV. BIN.]**

## Letter to the Emperor Basil

(Year 88.)

[Col. 0785A]

He rebukes him for defending Photius and refutes the insults directed against Pope Marinus.

We have received the letters of Your Serenity sent to our predecessor Adrian, and we have been astonished at your magnificence: how could you write such things, when you are the balance of justice? Above all, your pious power ought rightly to know that our priestly and apostolic dignity is not subject to royal authority. Although you bear on earth the likeness of Christ the Emperor, you must nevertheless concern yourself only with worldly and civil affairs—which we also pray you may continue to do for many years.

Since God has granted you authority over earthly matters, in the same way God has placed us, through the prince Peter, in charge of spiritual matters. Please receive with a kindly face what follows.

You have been given charge to cut down the impiety and savagery of tyrants with the sword of your power; to administer justice to your subjects; to enact laws; and to deploy military forces on land and sea. This is the chief concern of your power and principate. The care of the flock, however, has been entrusted to us, and is so much more excellent as the things on earth are distant from heaven.

Hear the Lord saying to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew XVIII). But what does he say concerning your authority and empire? “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew X). And again, concerning the ministry entrusted to us, he says: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVI), and what follows.

I therefore beg your piety to adhere to the decrees of the princes of the apostles and to honor their name and dignity. The institution and priesthood of all the Churches throughout the world received their origin from the prince Peter, through whom we also admonish and teach everyone with the most sincere and pure doctrine.

Let your kingdom not raise itself from arguments concerning trivial matters to investigate matters of greater importance, but let it consider by what authority it undertakes these things. The man who stained your sacred ears with insults against the most holy Marinus undoubtedly did not hesitate to utter blasphemies against our Lord Jesus Christ, who rules the whole world with his own hand.

Who, I ask, was the man who dared to say such things against his spotless spouse and priest, and against the mother of all the Churches? Whoever thinks that the disciple is above his teacher and the servant above his lord is surely deceived (Matthew XIX).

We are truly astounded to see your perfect and enlightened prudence led astray, so that it conceived such things against that holy man. What kind of man he was, though we pass it over in silence, these stones will cry out: “Let deceitful lips which speak iniquity against God, or against the just man, be silenced” (Psalm XXX). If you are a sheep of God—as we pray that you are—do not transgress the bounds of the princes of the apostles.

Tell us, please: who deceived you, that you should assail the universal pontiff with comic taunts and attack the holy Church of the Romans with curses, though you ought to be subject to it with every reverence? Do you not know that it is the foremost of all Churches? Who made you judge of pontiffs, by whose sacred teachings you ought to be guided, and by whom prayers for you are offered to God? You know that sacred saying: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not malign my prophets” (Psalm CIV). These words were spoken concerning all priests. You make yourself equal to God, who dare to judge his angels. For the prophet says: “The lips of the priest shall speak judgment, and they shall seek the law from his mouth: for he is the angel of the Lord Almighty” (Malachi II). How will you judge priests, who are subject to the judgment of God alone and who alone have the power of binding and loosing? See into what depth you have hurled yourself headlong. I hear, most magnificent emperor, that in you the meekness and patience of Job are praised; therefore I cannot sufficiently wonder how you have fallen so disgracefully.

You wrote that he was not a bishop. How do you know this? But if you do not know it, how did you pass judgment against him so rashly? Great indeed is the power of pontiffs. You cannot be unaware of the affairs of blessed Ambrose, or of what he himself did against the emperor Theodosius.

Let those who say that Marinus was previously a bishop, and therefore could not be transferred to another see, prove this clearly. Know, beloved emperor, worthy of every honor, that the alleged canon does not exist, although the multitude, authority, and judgment of the holy Fathers could establish him in the highest rank. Divine providence, foreseeing the benefit of the Church of God, placed him in the see of Peter, the prince of the apostles.

And what of that great Gregory, surnamed the Theologian? Was he not transferred from Nazianzus? And Meletius from Sebaste to Antioch; Dositheus from Seleucia to Tarsus in Cilicia; Reverentius from Phoenice to Tyre; John Gordolia to Proconnesus; Theodore from Apamea to Selymbria; Alexander from Cappadocia to Hierapolis? And many others were transferred in different places from their own sees to those of others.

Let Your Highness say by which accusers and by which witnesses, affirming that blessed Marinus had done what you say, you condemned him. Are you unaware that at the first Council of Nicaea blessed Pope Sylvester proclaimed through his legates, in the presence there of the holy Constantine: “Let the first see be judged by no one”?

What did the holy Roman Church do to deserve that this seducer should induce you to brandish and stir up your tongue against it? Did it not, according to ancient custom, send you letters concerning the synod to be held at Constantinople? Did it not take responsibility for that same synod? I ask you: To whom was the Roman Church to write—

[Col. 0788D]

to the layman Photius, of course? For if you had a patriarch, our Church would visit him more frequently by letter.

But alas for me: that glorious city of Constantinople, guarded by God, has been deprived of the comfort of a shepherd and is illuminated only by your royal power. And unless the love with which we cherish you had restrained us from avenging the injury inflicted upon our Church, we would have been compelled to inflict upon the transgressor Photius, who vomited impure words against us, more severe penalties than our predecessors did.

We do not say this to insult you. We proclaim you beloved of God throughout the whole world. We say it only in our own defense and for the greater glory of Marinus, who thought and understood the same things as our predecessor and teacher, the most holy Pope Nicholas.

While he wished to fulfill what had earlier been determined by that predecessor, that divine Marinus came into the greatest contempt and derision among you [another version: “Marinus, the most ardent defender of the Eighth Synod”]. Because he refused to be led together with those who held foreign opinions, and because he would not dissolve, annul, and render void the things that he himself had done synodically in the presence of Your Majesty, he was detained in prison for thirty days. He counted this rather as glory than as insult, because he suffered for the truth.

But, O younger Constantine, why did you not imitate the great Constantine, who, when he received the writings of priests, threw them into the fire, declaring that he was unworthy to judge priests?

We therefore admonish you, our spiritual son, not to rise up against the holy Roman Church. When we heard that you had dedicated a son born of your seed to the priesthood, we were filled with great joy on this account.

We also ask you to fortify the *chelandion* and provide everything necessary in it from the month of April through the month of September. Furthermore, send men to guard our walls against the incursions of the Hagarenes.

We pass over the rest in silence, since we do not even have oil for the lamps of the church according to the honor due to God.

To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

# Note of Severinus Binius

[Col. 0789C]

In the Greek codex, the following is appended after this letter of Pope Stephen:

> “This letter was sent to the emperor Basil, but it was received by his son Leo after his father had already died. When Leo understood the force of the letter and learned all the crimes of Photius, he immediately recalled all the priests of the truth who, after Photius had been condemned by anathema, had suffered severe persecutions. After expelling the tyrant and usurper Photius, he introduced his own brother, summoning also Stylianus, metropolitan of Neocaesarea, surnamed Mapa, together with his fellow soldiers in the persecution and the other bishops, superiors, priests, deacons, and other followers of piety. He said to them:
>
> “‘Our empire, received from God, having weighed the truth, has expelled that wicked man Photius from the patriarchal see and has brought your persecution to an end. I will in no way compel any of you to communicate unwillingly with him. Rather, I ask your piety to communicate with my brother, so that there may be one flock.
>
> “‘But if, without consulting the Romans who condemned Photius, you are unwilling to meet with my brother because he was ordained a deacon by Photius, come: let us write and send together to Rome, to the pontiff, asking him to dispense from the anathema those who were ordained by Photius.’
>
> “Therefore the emperor wrote a letter to the pontiff; Mapa, the metropolitan of Caesarea, and his companions did likewise. The metropolitan’s letter reads as follows.”

# Letter of Stylianus to Pope Stephen V

To the most holy and most blessed Stephen, lord and universal pope: Stylianus, bishop of Neocaesarea in the province of Euphratesia, servant of the servants of God; and the bishops who are with me; and all the bishops, priests, and deacons of the most holy Church of Constantinople; and all superiors established throughout East and West; and the priest-monks leading a quiet life.

The catholic and apostolic Church of God always prevails against those who stir up war against it. For it is written that the Lord makes its enemies weak. Whoever wages war against the Church makes himself an enemy of God.

The enemy of the human race therefore employs many forms of deceit, O sacred and venerable head, at different times withdrawing people from the straight path into crooked ways by different methods. He is especially accustomed to do this in the Church of God, where right action is worthy of praise, while departing from what is right is dreadful.

When he had found many vessels of iniquity in the Church of God, he attempted to remove from ecclesiastical discipline the veneration shown to the holy images of Christ, of his most pure mother, and of his servants. But, by the favor of divine grace and through the assistance of our pious emperors, our Church has now recovered its beauty and cast far away that abominable error of the heresy concerning images.

What then did the demon, the enemy of good works, do? He stirred up a new storm. For he again raised up Gregory, surnamed Asbestas—that is, “inextinguishable”—together with Eulampius, Peter, and their companions. Through them he did not hesitate to tear apart the members of Christ from one another and to alienate them from the most holy patriarch Ignatius.

The patriarch repeatedly summoned these men synodically and treated them with the humanity that was fitting, hoping in every way to prevent them from being separated from the Church of God and becoming the devil’s prey. But he could not accomplish this. Therefore he finally condemned them by deprivation and anathema.

They sent letters and envoys to the most holy pontiff of that time, the blessed Leo, asking to be vindicated by him as though they had suffered injustice. The pontiff wrote to the patriarch Ignatius, asking him to send someone in his name to Rome, so that through him he might learn how the matter concerning those schismatics stood.

Patriarch Ignatius did not delay in doing this. He sent Lazarus, a monk and confessor, together with letters. Lazarus knew the whole matter concerning Gregory and instructed the pontiff concerning every detail. Therefore the pontiff himself likewise condemned those whom Ignatius had condemned, as schismatics.

But after blessed Pope Leo had died, they again brought trouble upon his successor, Pope Benedict. Benedict, the most holy man, carefully reexamined the matter and confirmed their condemnation together with that of Ignatius.

Afterward, they adhered to a certain schismatic named Photius, who had been placed in a position of dignity by the Church of Constantinople. With his favor, and through Barda, the prince and uncle of the emperor Michael—who himself had been accused by Patriarch Ignatius of shameful incest—they violently expelled Ignatius from the patriarchal see, fabricating many accusations against him. They so deceived the emperor that he placed Photius in the patriarchal see in place of Ignatius, Photius having been elected by the schismatics and ordained on that same day by the condemned Gregory.

When the pontiffs themselves, the more distinguished among the priests, and all who held higher rank in the Church were separated because of the unlawful intrusion of the schismatic Photius, I too was among them, the least of all.

Afterward Photius drew many people to himself: some he terrified, others he mistreated, and others he deceived with gifts. He also wrote with his own hand a written pledge that he would never attempt anything harmful against Ignatius or against those ordained by him.

Yet not much time passed before, with no regard for his own written pledge, Photius himself—the adulterer and fornicator—assembled a cabal in the famous church of the Holy Apostles and condemned Patriarch Ignatius by deposition and anathema.

Then, wishing further to confirm his iniquity, he sent bishops with letters to your city of Rome and to Pope Nicholas, who was pontiff at that time. He asked that legates be sent to the Church of Constantinople to examine what he had done against Ignatius.

This was done. Rhadoaldus and Zacharias were sent with letters of recommendation to the emperor Michael and to Photius. When the legates arrived at Constantinople, a synod was assembled. Photius bribed the legates with gifts, while the emperor coerced them by threats. They did none of what had been entrusted to them; rather, they condemned Ignatius and, contrary to the pontiff’s command, confirmed Photius in the patriarchal see. Thus they returned to the Apostolic See with letters from the emperor and Photius.

At that time the monk Theognostus, who was also an archimandrite, was moved by a certain zeal. He secretly traveled to Rome himself, disguised in the clothing of a layman, and informed the most holy Pope Nicholas of everything that had been done against Ignatius.

Therefore the pontiff assembled a synod and condemned his own legates, Rhadoaldus and Zacharias, because they had done things contrary to what had been entrusted to them. He then assembled another synod and condemned Photius the fornicator and usurper by anathema. He declared Ignatius to be patriarch of Constantinople, and openly informed both the emperor Michael and Photius of everything that had been done.

When, after Michael, the imperial scepter passed to Basil, Basil, moved by divine zeal, confirmed the proceedings carried out in Rome by Pope Nicholas concerning the expulsion of Photius and the restoration of Ignatius. He recalled Ignatius from exile, expelled Photius from the patriarchal see, and sent envoys from both sides—Ignatius and Photius—to the Apostolic See, together with his own letters. He also sent that fabrication of Photius’s false synod against Pope Nicholas, who was found by the legates to have died.

When Adrian succeeded Nicholas, the materials that had been sent were shown to him. Pope Adrian therefore again assembled a local synod and decreed against Photius the same things that blessed Pope Nicholas had decreed.

After choosing pious men, he sent them to Constantinople. When an ecumenical synod had been assembled, with the legates of the Eastern sees also present, sentence was again pronounced against Photius, because he had invaded the Church of Constantinople as a fornicator and adulterer. He was therefore deposed and condemned by anathema, and Ignatius was restored.

Photius nevertheless found no peace. He gathered wicked men, sorcerers, and deceivers, and did not cease fabricating false accusations until he brought it about that the most blessed Ignatius miserably departed this life.

Nor was this all. Even while Ignatius was seated in his own see, Photius—condemned and anathematized by the ecumenical synod—carried out various ordinations in the diocese of Constantinople.

Indeed, he once more attacked the holy Church of God with military force, like that impious Macedonius of old, while we, his fellow ministers, were celebrating the sacred liturgy in the famous church of Hagia Sophia. When we saw Photius entering God’s tabernacle so shamelessly, we fled, leaving the sacred rite unfinished. Photius, however, seized the Lord’s priests and our fellow ministers with great force and many blows, even against their will, and dragged them over to his side.

But I, and the bishops, priests, and deacons who were with me, together with all the superiors of monks and those leading a quiet life throughout East and West—an innumerable multitude—remained unshaken by divine grace, although neither before nor afterward did we communicate with Photius.

Since he had invaded the Church unlawfully, as has been said, he caused many to doubt. They said that we would not accept this Photius unless the Apostolic See at Rome confirmed him.

When Photius learned this, he deceived the simpler people in the following manner. Pope John had sent the bishops Paul and Eugenius to Patriarch Ignatius to discuss matters concerning the province of Bulgaria. When they discovered that blessed Ignatius had already died, Photius deceived them with gifts and compelled them by the emperor’s threats to say before all the clergy, bishops, and the rest of the people that they had been sent by Pope John against Ignatius, in order to condemn him by anathema and proclaim Photius patriarch.

For this reason many of our fellow ministers were deceived.

Photius also wished to deceive your Apostolic See by fraud. He composed letters in the name of Patriarch Ignatius and his fellow ministers, in which they asked the blessed Apostolic See to receive Photius; and these letters were sent to us.

Therefore, when the priest Peter came from you to the royal city together with Paul and Eugenius, they proclaimed that Photius had been received by the Apostolic See.

Taking this opportunity, Photius also assumed political responsibilities and attempted in this way to usurp royal power. He joined to himself in familiar association a certain low-born abbot, humble and wicked, whose father was called Santabarenus. He belonged to the Manichaean sect and practiced sorcery. When he was recognized and feared capture, he fled to the Bulgarians, who were still suffering from the disease of impiety, and there he renounced the Christian faith.

This man’s son, the aforementioned little abbot, while still a young man at Constantinople, was entrusted by Barda Caesar to the monastery of the Studites and was raised there.

When he reached maturity and had learned every form of iniquity, he attached himself to his like, Photius, who ordained him a priest during his earlier intrusion into the patriarchal dignity.

After Photius had been expelled from the patriarchal see following the promulgation of the ecumenical synod, the aforementioned little abbot, Santabarenus’s son, suggested to Photius that he find one of the emperor’s household. He claimed that through such a man he could restore Photius.

They found Nicetas, surnamed “the Weeping.” He was deceived by many gifts. Santabarenus the sorcerer prepared magical drinks and foods, and Nicetas served them to the emperor. As a result, the hated Photius came to seem a friend.

While the most holy Ignatius still held the patriarchal see, Nicetas recalled Photius to the palace from the place called Augustus. He kept Photius as a companion in the palace, so that Photius might be more truly patriarch than Ignatius himself, although Ignatius was actually seated in the patriarchal see.

For this reason, as we have said, he carried out ordinations. He so incited the emperor against Ignatius that the emperor wickedly deprived him of life.

When Ignatius had died so wretchedly, Photius immediately seized his see. He kept with him that Santabarenus whom he had made most intimate with the emperor, and appointed him bishop of Euchaita.

He also took away distinguished monasteries established in other dioceses and subject to other bishops, handed them over to Santabarenus, and arranged for them to be incorporated into the Church of Euchaita. Santabarenus then ordained bishops in those monasteries.

This Santabarenus, together with Photius, also devised an evil plan against our most pious emperor Leo, who now rules, and incited his father Basil against him, claiming that Leo was plotting against and opposing his father’s will.

When Basil was suffering from an incurable illness and already near death, they thought that, if he wished it and his son were already far away, they could easily obtain the empire and administer it either themselves or through someone of their choosing.

But God’s providence did not permit their iniquity to be fulfilled. Although Leo, Basil’s son, was treated by his father as a private person and was even held under guard in prison, after his father’s death he was raised to the imperial throne.

He immediately expelled Photius as the author of many iniquities. We, who did not obey Photius and who had also suffered many evils, were freed by the emperor Leo from those miseries.

Since we know that we ought to be corrected by your Apostolic See and rebuked according to the canons, for this reason we ask your venerability through these humble letters to deal mercifully with us, and with the people who accepted Photius’s ordination not without reasonable cause.

May those who received the legates of the Apostolic See, Rhadoaldus and Zacharias, who at the beginning confirmed Photius in the see of Constantinople, and afterward Eugenius and Paul, who communicated with Photius a second time, not be condemned to destruction together with Photius; and may another innumerable multitude not be expelled from the Church. For this is what the Church has customarily done.

The Fourth Ecumenical Synod condemned Dioscorus, the chief and agent of iniquity, the murderer of Flavian—the blessed patriarch of Constantinople—as a murderer and a heretic, because he had dared to impose excommunication upon the most holy Pope Leo. But those ordained by Dioscorus, or those who had fallen, provided that they had been followers of piety, it received through repentance.

The Seventh Council of Nicaea likewise condemned the authors of the Iconoclast heresy, but admitted their followers through repentance.

Therefore it is fitting that your singular virtue should expel Photius as one who was a schismatic from the beginning, unlawfully ordained by schismatics, and responsible for many other evil deeds. But we ask that you deal mercifully with those whom he deceived, so that peace and tranquility may be restored to the Church of Constantinople, and so that the Church’s single body may not be divided, with some saying, “I belong to Apollo,” others, “I belong to Cephas,” and others, “I belong to Paul” (1 Corinthians I).

Rather, let all be of one mind, having Christ, our God and Savior, as one head, and let us all together offer him praises and proclaim his commandments alike. Let not so great a number perish on account of one sinful man.

As we have said, we came to Constantinople at the command of the emperors beloved of Christ. Many pressed us to communion and affirmed under oath that they had obtained a dispensation from the Apostolic See allowing them to exercise priestly dignity without hindrance. Nevertheless, we in no way believed them, but awaited something firm and certain from your holiness.

I dare to affirm this, O venerable head, calling God as witness: none of those who communicated with Photius did so of their own will, but rather under the violence of the rulers.

We therefore ask your blessedness to receive mercifully a people who are almost in despair. Peter asks you—the one whose see you administer—Peter who was taught by the Lord of all to forgive even those who had knowingly sinned seventy times seven (Matthew XVIII).

Hear us, so that you too may obtain kindness from God above and may govern the Apostolic Church for a long time, through the prayers of the most holy Mother of God, the heavenly powers, the apostles, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and all the saints. Amen.

## II. To Count Guido

(Year 886.)

[Apud Gratian, *Decretum* I, distinction 63, chapter 18.)

[Col. 0793D]

### Stephen to Count Guido

Having read the documents of your sagacity, in which you reported that, after the death of the bishop of the Church of Rieti, the clergy and people of that Church had chosen for themselves a future bishop and had sent him to us through your efforts for consecration, so that the Church itself might not remain long without its own shepherd, we—while grieving over the death of the former bishop—have not, as you instructed, hastened to ordain the man now elected by unanimous and canonical election of that Church. The reason is that he did not bring us the imperial letter of authorization, as is customary.

For this reason the matter is uncertain to us. We have therefore delayed complying with your wishes, lest the imperial mind should receive this in the harshest possible way, whatever the circumstances.

But because we know that the Church of God ought not to remain long without its own shepherd, we instruct Your Glory that, once your skill has obtained imperial permission, as ancient custom dictates, and an imperial letter has been sent to us—as we believe you know we require—we shall then comply with your wishes in this matter and, with the Lord’s help, consecrate the same elected man.

Do not, dearest son, in any way take this amiss.

## III. Decree for the Monastery of Corbie

(Year 887.)

[Apud Schaten, *Annales Paderbornenses*.)

[Col. 0794B]

Stephen (V), servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Wicbert, bishop of the holy Church called Hildesheim, dedicated under the patronage of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, and to Bovo, abbot of the venerable monastery called New Corbie, dedicated under the title and name of the blessed protomartyr of Christ, Saint Stephen, where the blessed martyr of Christ Vitus rests with his body intact, forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance, through devout religion, to come to the aid of those who possess power through pious compassion, and to grant the minds of those who make requests assent out of devotion to gain. For from this we earn from the Lord, the Creator of all, the reward of the greatest gain, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have unquestionably been brought into a better condition [Col. 0794C].

Therefore we wish all the faithful and devoted of the holy Church of God, both present and future, to know that both of the churches named above, with all their families or congregations and with their immovable properties justly belonging to them everywhere—the one of which is called a see under the patronage of the holy and exalted Mother of God, our Lady, while the other was established as a community of monks and dedicated in honor of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, where the blessed martyr Vitus also rests bodily—are, under the protection of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and under the special defense of the apostolic see, through this privilege of our apostolic confirmation, in every respect subjected to it and to remain under its perpetual right.

For this reason we have decreed, and by the prerogative and authority of almighty God [Col. 0794D] and of that same prince of the apostles, to whom the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth has been given, and whose office we perform by divine gift, we command that no human being inflict upon the property or possessions of those churches, in any manner whatsoever, force, oppression, harassment, opposition, or seizure; nor may anyone usurp or tyrannically plunder their possessions or the tithes granted to them from churches everywhere. Rather, everything shall remain under the discretion and authority of the bishop or abbot of each church, subject to the most diligent scrutiny of canonical discipline.

More than this, both churches, of either order, together with all their possessions, are by the privilege of this apostolic statute to be held and observed unimpaired and inviolate by all who are reckoned by the Christian name, under the protection of the holy apostolic see, for the praise of almighty God, for reverence toward the apostolic see, and for the stable strengthening and advancement of the Church’s condition. But if anyone—which we do not desire—should presume, through reckless audacity, to act against this privilege of our authority and apostolic confirmation, piously granted by us, and should attempt to transgress it in whole or in part, and should fail to observe all due reverence toward the holy apostolic see, let him know that he has been excommunicated by God the almighty Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and, unless he repents, condemned to perpetual anathema. But may whoever proves to be its guardian and observer deserve to obtain blessing and grace from God and [Col. 0795B] our Lord.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the fifth indiction. Farewell. Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Leo, treasurer of the holy apostolic see, in the sixth year of the reign of the most pious lord, Prince Charles Augustus, crowned great emperor, and in the sixth year after his consulship, in the fifth indiction.

## IV. Letter to the Eastern Bishops. (Year 888)

When they requested a dispensation concerning the ordination of Stephen as patriarch of Constantinople, on the ground that he had been ordained deacon by Photius, he replies and requests further information.

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops and the remaining clergy, etc.**

The Catholic Church of Christ and of our God, founded upon the firm rock—namely, the confession of the apostle Peter—although it is shaken by many storms and waves, is nevertheless strengthened and increased. Nor is it surprising that the enemy of the human race undertakes to tempt the members of the Church, since he did not hesitate to tempt the very head, our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0796A].

It is therefore not surprising that you expelled Photius, sufficiently hated and condemned by the Church, since he so mocked the life-giving cross of the Lord, through which, namely, all the gifts of priestly ministry are accomplished and the laver of holy baptism is sanctified. Thus, if the aforesaid Photius, a layman, had walked along the royal road and adhered to the decrees of the holy Fathers, he would never have reached such madness.

Therefore those who despise Christ’s humility, namely the venerable cross, have been struck down like the firstborn of Egypt. For then the firstborn of the Israelites, once marked, were saved and protected (Exod. 12). What, indeed, was that blood of the lamb on the Israelites’ threshold except the cross of Christ’s passion, which is impressed upon the foreheads [Col. 0796B] of the faithful? Whoever, therefore, thinks little of the saving cross is slain by the evangelical sword.

But concerning Photius you wrote to us in one way; when we read the emperor’s letters, however, we found them to be far from what you had written. For they stated that Photius had chosen a quiet life. We are therefore in doubt. There is a great difference between renouncing and being expelled. We therefore cannot issue any kind of judgment without careful investigation. For this reason we have now deferred our decision. It is necessary that the most religious bishops of both parties be sent, so that, after weighing every doubt and establishing the truth, we may be able to state clearly what God wills on both sides.

For the Roman Church is established as a mirror and model for the other Churches. Whatever it defines remains incorrupt forever; and for this reason judgments ought to be issued only after very careful investigation [Col. 0796C].

## V.
