[Note: [Col. 0795C] In reviewing the contents of this letter, Flodoard, book IV of the *History of Rheims*, writes the following: “Pope Stephen writes to Fulco, archbishop of Rheims, on behalf of Teutbold, bishop of Langres, indicating that a complaint from this Church of Langres had reached him: when Bishop Isaac died [ [Col. 0795C] Around the year 880.], Aurelian of Lyon had ordained as bishop a certain monk, Egilo [ [Col. 0795C] Robert, the Sammarthani, our Vignier, and others call him Geilo or Gerlo; he is said to be named in the *Chartulary* 3 of Stephen of Dijon, in the fourth year of Carloman, on Monday, the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the year 889; and in the year 884 he is said to have attended the Council of Chalon on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January and to have obtained confirmation of the right to mint coin among the people of Langres [Col. 0796C] and Dombes.]—a man recently come from the world—without consulting the clergy and people, and had imposed him upon them by force against their will. When he departed this life by divine calling [ [Col. 0796C] Toward the end of the year 888.], lest they fall into the same situation, the clergy and people, by unanimous vote, chose Teutbold, a deacon of that Church, and asked the pope to consecrate him as their bishop. But the pope, wishing to preserve inviolate the privilege of each Church, delayed doing so and sent him to the aforesaid Aurelian, writing to him that, if the votes of the clergy and people were in agreement concerning him and the sacred canons did not oppose it, he should not delay laying hands upon him. If reason prohibited this, he was nevertheless to write back to the pope; meanwhile, he was in no way to presume to ordain another there without consulting him [Col. 0796C]. At the same time he sent Oirannus [ [Col. 0796C] Otrannus.] bishop of Senones from his side as executor. Aurelian, mocking him, sent him ahead to the city of Langres, promising that he would follow immediately. Although he was awaited there for a long time, he neither arrived himself nor saw fit to make known or report to the pope the reason for his delay. Therefore the clergy and people again sent the aforesaid elected man to Rome, with a decree strengthened by the hands of all, earnestly requesting that he be consecrated for them. But even then the pope did not agree to do so, wishing the privilege conferred upon the Church of Lyon to remain unaltered. Accordingly, he wrote again to the aforementioned Aurelian, ordering him that, since the clergy and people with one accord desired the aforesaid deacon, he should either consecrate him or hasten to write what he judged reprehensible in him. But Aurelian, adding the obstinacy of his former disobedience, not only scorned either to consecrate the man offered to him or to write what he judged reprehensible in him, but also, contrary to the prohibitions and statutes of the sacred canons, presumed to impose upon them a certain outsider, unknown to that Church, ordained in some obscure corner [ [Col. 0796C] This was undoubtedly Algrimus or Argrimus, whom Vignier says in the *Chronicle of Langres* gave the monks of Bèze a privilege in April of the year 889.] [Col. 0797D]. But they, preferring to endure hardship rather than submit to an unknown man, returned to their own people, imploring that the rights of the Church not be permitted to be violated.” —SEV. BIN.]

### To Fulco, Archbishop of Rheims, on behalf of Teutbold, Bishop of Langres. Fragment. (Year 889)

But we, who have undertaken the care of all the Churches in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0797A], knowing that no one is to be regarded among the bishops who has been neither elected by the clergy nor desired by the people, moved by the lamentable petitions of the Church of Langres, have consecrated the often-mentioned venerable deacon Teutbold as its bishop, after imposing an appropriate sentence upon the transgressors, although they had also been hindered by other transgressors.

Therefore we enjoin upon your holiness that, once you have received these apostolic letters of ours, setting aside delay, you go to the Church of Langres and there reinvest the same Teutbold, solemnly consecrated by us, as bishop. You are also to make known to all archbishops and bishops that, as punishment for such great contumacy, we have undertaken special care of that Church, in response to the affliction of such great labor [Col. 0797B] and the exposure of the oppression inflicted upon it.

Whatever the same venerable Bishop Teutbold reports to you on our behalf, believe, and do not hesitate in any way to put it into effect; for we believe that your reverence remains devoted toward us.

## VI. To Leutbert, Bishop of Mainz. Fragment. (Year 889)

[Note: [Col. 0797D] *You consulted*, 2, question 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0798D] The printed editions incorrectly have *Humbert*. Ivo, letter 74.]

You consulted us concerning infants who are found dead in one bed while sleeping with their parents, asking whether the parents must purify themselves by red-hot iron, boiling water, or some other ordeal, to prove that they had not suffocated them. Parents must be admonished and warned not to place such very young children in the same bed with themselves, lest, through some negligence, they be suffocated or crushed, and the parents thereby be found guilty of homicide [Col. 0797C].

[Note: [Col. 0798D] See Alexander III, letter 19 of the first appendix, in Labbe, volume XIII, p. 132.]

For the sacred canons do not approve of extorting a confession from anyone by the ordeal of red-hot iron or boiling water. What has not been sanctioned by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be presumed upon through superstitious invention. It is our responsibility to judge offenses committed and publicly disclosed through spontaneous confession or the testimony of witnesses, with the fear of God before our eyes; but hidden and unknown matters must be left to him who alone knows the hearts of human beings.

Those who are proved or confess themselves guilty of such an offense should be punished by your moderation. For if the person who destroys what has been conceived in the womb by abortion is a murderer, how much more can one who has killed an infant of even a single day not excuse himself from being a murderer? [Col. 0797D]

## VII. To Luythobius [Luitbertus], Bishop of Mainz. Fragment. (Year 889)

[According to Ivo, book IV, chapter 232.]

**STEPHEN to Luythobius, bishop of Mainz.**

We do not doubt that the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, on the testimony of Athanasius, were written as seventy, in the form of the seventy disciples [Col. 0798A]. Of these, only twenty are found in the holy Roman Church; it is uncertain through what neglect the remainder are lacking. For many suppose that they were inserted into the Council of Antioch.

## VIII. To Paul, Bishop of Piacenza. Fragment. (Year 889)

[Note: [Col. 0798D] Chapter *Our place*, 35, question 9.]

Consideration of our position reminds us that, by the authority of reason, we should strengthen what was usefully decided by our predecessors and promptly punish what has been rashly attempted. Let the accused know that he stands before the sight of the divine Judge if he strives to rescind decisions usefully concluded or to violate, through any act of audacity, what has been confirmed [Col. 0798B].

For the order of ecclesiastical authority is thrown into confusion if either unlawful acts are rashly attempted or unauthorized things are retained with impunity. Therefore, if we negligently overlook what has been wrongly usurped, we undoubtedly open the way of excess to others.

## IX. To Romanus, Archbishop of Ravenna. Fragment. (Year 889)

[According to Gratian, *Decretum*, I, distinction 63, chapter 12.]

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROMANUS, archbishop of Ravenna.**

We wish your fraternity to know that it has reached our ears that the bishop of Imola has departed from this life [Col. 0798C], and that, in the election of his successor, division among the people has arisen. Since this often tends to happen—when individuals seek what is their own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ—we are not greatly surprised.

Nevertheless, in this matter you must exercise the greatest care, so that, once the clergy and people have been summoned, a person may be elected there by God’s mercy against whom the sacred canons do not object. The election belongs to the priests, and the agreement of the faithful people must be added, because the people are to be taught, not followed.

## X. To Dominicus, Archbishop of Ravenna. Fragment. (Year 890)

He states that he has consecrated a bishop for the people of Piacenza, but that he does not wish in any way to injure the right of the metropolitan of Ravenna.

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother DOMINICUS, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna.**

The divine majesty, [lacuna] the pastoral ministry to us . . . as we bear concern with watchful care, to extend our apostolic assistance. Therefore let the knowledge of all the faithful of the holy Church of God recognize that, when the Church of Ravenna had been left without a shepherd through the death of Romanus, formerly archbishop of that Church, suddenly the holy Church of Piacenza, its suffragan, was also left bereft of its former shepherd, Bishop Paul [Col. 0799A].

Therefore, while the storms of the Italian kingdom were surging in various directions, because the same holy Church of Ravenna, deprived of its own shepherd, could not provide the holy Church of Piacenza with the means of obtaining a remedy through its own bishop, they appeared to flee for refuge to the apostolic see and to our apostolic authority, as to the head and mother of all Churches. [Lacuna.] They offered us their own elected candidate, named Bernard, serving in the office of deacon, and, presenting with him the decree made by them concerning him, they suggested that we consecrate him as their bishop, lest that Church be destroyed by remaining long without a shepherd and lest they, having elected and requested him, should go about acephalous [Col. 0799B] and wandering.

But, as we have said, since their own metropolitan was absent, and after they had earnestly petitioned us, we judged it appropriate to consecrate the aforesaid Bernard bishop in that Church of Piacenza. We expressly ordered and commanded him that he should observe, in complete submission and fidelity, the authority of the holy Church of Ravenna, because this was our pleasure: namely, that he should devoutly strive to fulfill in the holy Church of Ravenna all the obedience, devotion, custom, and practice which his predecessors are proved to have rendered.

Therefore we wish and decree from this present eighth indiction that the same holy Church of Ravenna should henceforth suffer no [lacunose] on account of the consecration granted by us [Col. 0799C]. Rather, it should be [lacunose] in every respect by us and by our successors, the pontiffs. Indeed, the aforesaid holy Church of Piacenza shall at all times remain under the jurisdiction, consecration, and due obedience of the same frequently mentioned holy Church of Ravenna, as it is remembered to have been in ancient times. We wish the right and privilege of each Church to remain unimpaired and to be guarded inviolably.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary and scrivener of the holy apostolic see, in the month of March, in the eighth indiction written above. Farewell. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Zacharias, by the mercy of God primicerius of the holy apostolic see, in the fifth year, God being favorable, of the pontificate of the lord Stephen, supreme pontiff and universal pope, for the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the aforesaid eighth indiction.

## XI. To the Clergy and People of Piacenza. Fragment. (Year 890)

[Col. 0799D]

He grants them Bishop Bernard and commends submission to the metropolitan of Ravenna.

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the priests and judges, clergy and people, and to the entire community residing at Piacenza, greeting.**

We know that you are fully aware how the holy Church of Ravenna, deprived of its own shepherd, remained widowed through the death of your bishop. But, for the support and relief of your Church, we appeared to provide our apostolic assistance, so that through our consecration we might appoint Bernard the deacon as your shepherd [Col. 0800A].

Therefore we enjoin upon the fidelity of all of you, and decree and sanction, that both Bernard himself and all his successors forever vigorously observe complete obedience and total fidelity under the pontificate of the Church of Ravenna. In the manner of his predecessors, both he and his successors are to be most devoted, observing in all things the obedience, custom, and practice owed to the holy Church of Ravenna and to its archbishops, without any contradiction or harassment, as he has irrevocably promised.

For if he himself, or any of his successors, or any one of you, whether from the priestly order or from the lay assembly [Col. 0800B], should appear contemptuous or transgressive through disobedience, the priest who is involved shall, by the authority of almighty God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and our apostolic authority, remain suspended from his own ministry until he has received the grace of release from the archbishop of Ravenna.

But the layman who appears as an opponent shall remain suspended from wine and cooked food until he attains the aforesaid grace of release. Moreover, let him know that he must pay five pounds of refined gold to our Lateran palace and remain bound forever by the chain of anathema.

We decree that the holy Church of Ravenna shall possess this letter of ours as a sacred testimony.

## XII. Letter to the Bishops of the Province of Cologne. (Year 890)

[According to Lappenberg, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*, p. 777.]

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother HERIMANN, archbishop of Cologne in Agrippina, and to the venerable bishops FRANCO of Tongeren, ODIBALD of Utrecht, WOLFGELM of Mimigernaford, DRUOGO of Minden, and EGILMAR of Osnabrück, etc.**

Furthermore, you wrote that the see of the Church of Bremen, subject to Cologne in Agrippina, had existed in the office of ecclesiastical discipline, and you indicated that its boundaries touched barbarian peoples. For this reason, when we read that you had written that the former Guntarius deserved to obtain the use of the pallium from the apostolic see so that he might preach the word of God with greater honor and obey his archbishop, we laughed, astonished that your prudence should suppose that the use of the pallium could be granted at will to anyone, not for the honor of the most sacred ministry but for secular dignity.

Certainly, if he lacks a province and suffragans over whom he presides, it is doubtful how he deserved the use of the pallium. Nevertheless, to remove ambiguity and weigh correctness by a just examination, we summon the disputants of both parties to come into our presence, so that, once the truth is known, apostolic judgment may more freely decide what reason dictates. For we have written to him in the same way.

No reason, therefore, permits a dispute between two parties to be brought to an end by the voice of one alone [lacunose].

## XIII. To Zuentopolk, King

[From Wilhelm Wattenbach, *Contributions to the History of the Christian Church*.]

[Col. 0801A]

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ZUENTOPOLK, king of the Slavs.**

Because you have devoted yourself with complete devotion, through zeal for the faith, to the holy apostle Peter, namely, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, and have chosen his vicar as your principal patron above all the rulers of this fluctuating age, and have entrusted yourself, together with your nobles and the rest of the people of your land, likewise to his protection, we continually implore God, the giver of all good things, that you may be fortified by the aid of him in whose hand are all the rights of kingdoms, so that, surrounded by his help [Col. 0801B] and by the intercession of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, you may be protected from diabolical snares and rejoice in bodily health. Thus, safe in soul and body, adorned with good works before the eternal Judge, may you be granted everlasting happiness.

We also, who perform his vicariate, caring for you with due solicitude, promise that in whatever matter you may have need, in all things pertaining to your salvation, you will find us, with God’s help, a protector. Because of the dignity of your faith, we embrace you and all your faithful with spiritual arms as though present, in love, without any intervening distance of lands, as a spiritual son.

Therefore, because we have heard that you eagerly pursue the orthodox faith, and recognize this from the sure indication that you wished to have recourse to your mother, namely the holy Roman Church, which is the head of all the Churches through the privilege conferred upon it in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the true Shepherd entrusted his sheep, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it”—calling the gates of hell the mouths of those who blaspheme the orthodox faith—which, with Christ as its author, destroyed all heresies and established all who wavered in the faith of their Creator, strengthened by his help, when our Lord Jesus Christ said: “Simon, behold, Satan has sought you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.”

Who, I ask, unless foolish, would dare to plunge so deeply into the abyss of blasphemy as to defame Peter’s faith? For whose sake the Word of God, existing in two natures—[the following clause is textually corrupt: “what the nature of a servant, however, bestowed by the nature of divinity”].

We embrace your devotion, since you wish to learn, so that we may raise your prudence with worthy praise: it has chosen not to wander elsewhere but to consult the very Church that is the head, from which all the Churches also received their origin.

Nevertheless, the foundation of the faith upon which Christ established his Church is this: the three subsisting persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are co-eternal and co-equal with one another; and the nature of these three persons is one deity, one substance, one divinity, and one majesty. In these persons there is distinction, not confusion; differentiation, not separation.

I speak of distinction because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For the Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father; and the Holy Spirit is from both, of the one and same substance of which the Father and the Son are.

This holy Trinity is one and true God. It neither begins with a beginning nor is enclosed by an end; it is not contained by place nor altered by time. The Father alone is not from another, and therefore alone is called unbegotten. The Son is the eternal Son from the Father and is therefore called begotten. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son without any interval; no times involving a before or after are to be conceived here. Therefore he is called neither unbegotten nor begotten but proceeding. Let there be believed neither two fathers nor two sons.

That the Spirit is the Son’s, the apostle and the Evangelist testify: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his.” The apostle Paul testifies that he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.” And again, he most clearly distinguishes that he is the Spirit of the Father, saying: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will give life also to your mortal bodies.”

That he is the Spirit of the Son, the same Paul testifies: “Because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”

That he proceeds from the Father, Truth itself says: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father—he has glorified me.” That he proceeds from the Son, the same Truth testifies: “He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine.”

Far be it from us to believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father into the Son and from the Son toward the sanctification of creation as though by certain steps; rather, just as he proceeds from the Father, so also he proceeds simultaneously from the Son [Col. 0802C].

For who will deny that the Holy Spirit is life? And, just as the Father is life, so is the Son life. Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself.

Let what I have said to you from among many things suffice: you ought to confess these things without ambiguity with your tongue and believe them in your heart, but not examine them beyond your powers. If the gaze of the eyes is blunted by the ray of the bodily sun, how much more is the earthly mind blunted by the radiance of the ineffable divinity?

The holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church holds this faith, founded by the Lord in the apostles and by the apostles. We admonish, implore, and charge you to hold it firmly.

In that Church we have found the venerable bishop and most beloved brother Wiching, instructed in ecclesiastical doctrine. Therefore we have sent him back to you [Col. 0802D] to govern the Church entrusted to him by God, because we have recognized him as most faithful to you and in every respect sufficiently concerned for you.

Receive, retain, and embrace him as a spiritual father and your own shepherd, with due honor, proper reverence, and sincere heart, because in the honor shown to him you confer honor upon Christ, who says: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

Let him therefore take care of all ecclesiastical affairs and offices, and, keeping the fear of God before his eyes, administer them, since he himself will have to render an account before the strict Judge both for these matters and for the souls of the people entrusted to him.

Concerning fasting, know that it has been approved by the Law, the prophets, and the Lord himself in the Gospel. Moses fasted for forty days and nights in order to receive the Law. Elijah, who by prayer closed heaven so that it did not rain for three years and six months, and again by prayer opened it, so that heaven gave rain and the earth yielded its fruit, fasted for forty days and nights. Jesus Christ our Lord himself, the author of the Law, fasted for forty days and nights [Col. 0803A].

If anyone rejects fasting, let him also reject prayer and blasphemously declare that it is evil to cast out demons, since the Lord says: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.”

It is commanded to fast, but on which days one should fast and on which one should eat has not been defined by an explicit command of the Lord or the apostles; rather, the Church observes it according to the ancient custom of the Fathers, since the institutions of earlier generations and the custom of our ancestors are to be held as law.

One must fast on Wednesday, because, according to the Gospel, on the fourth day of the week the Jews took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. Friday is rightly devoted to fasting because of reverence for the Lord’s passion. One must likewise fast on Saturday, in order to renew the memory of what happened, since the disciples, understanding the Lord in a human way, grieved on that day while he rested in the tomb.

Some have considered Thursday to be free from fasting because on that day penitents are reconciled, on that day the holy chrism is prepared, on that day the Redeemer dined with his disciples and handed over to them the sacrament of his body and blood, and on that day he ascended into heaven in the sight of his disciples.

Sunday, certainly, has been consecrated to joy because of the glory of the resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0803C]. Let us leave the two remaining days to the discretion of each person, while observing this principle: let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats, so that whatever we do, we may do it for the glory of God.

The fast called that of the Four Times the ancient Fathers rightly decreed to be celebrated, as the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times,” so that at each season of the year we may humble our soul through fasting. The Lord commanded the fast of the first month in Exodus, and through the prophet Zechariah the fasts of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, so that at all times we may rely upon mercy through repentance [Col. 0803D].

Let what I have said to you briefly concerning fasting suffice, although much could be said about its mystery, which there is not now time to explain. Believe, however, that the fast acceptable to God above all others is this: “Undo the bonds of wickedness, loosen the bundles that oppress, set free those who are broken, and break every burden.” It must be adorned with these jewels: “Break your bread for the hungry and bring the poor and homeless into your house.”

Know that these are the lamps acceptable to God with which fasting must be adorned daily, so that it may please God.

We were greatly astonished to hear that Methodius was devoted to superstition rather than edification and to contention rather than peace; and, if what we have heard is true, we utterly reject his superstition. The anathema which he pronounced for contempt of the Catholic faith will fall back upon his own head.

But you and your people will be innocent before the judgment of the Holy Spirit, provided that you inviolably hold the faith preached by the Roman Church.

As for the divine offices, sacred mysteries, and solemn celebrations of Mass which the same Methodius presumed to celebrate in the language of the Slavs—although he had sworn over the most sacred body of blessed Peter that he would not do so again—we shrink from the guilt of his perjury and in no way permit anyone henceforth to presume upon this.

By the authority of God and our apostolic authority, we prohibit it under the bond of anathema, except insofar as it concerns the edification of the simple and those who do not understand: if an exposition of the Gospel or of the apostle is proclaimed in that same language by learned persons, we both grant and encourage it, and admonish that it be done very frequently, so that every tongue may praise God and confess him [Col. 0804B].

But we decree that the obstinate and disobedient, who persist in contention and scandal, are to be expelled from the bosom of the Church as sowers of weeds if, after a first and second admonition, they do not correct themselves. And lest one diseased sheep contaminate the entire flock, we command them to be restrained by our authority and excluded far from your borders.

## XIV. To Amelius, Bishop of Uzès. (Year 891)

[According to D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, volume IX.]

[Col. 0804C] He declares that Girbert, bishop of Nîmes, will be excommunicated unless he repents.

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Bishop AMELIUS.**

Know that we have heard what you reported and have established matters as you suggested and requested. Behold, we have written letters both to Archbishop Teudard and to Count Richard and to his viscount Alberic. We command and inform them that Bishop Girbert will be excommunicated unless he repents and withdraws from his invasion of our abbey, and so that you may securely retain it under our protection, in order to govern and preserve it, and yearly send the customary census to the blessed apostle Peter.

You, however, must always be solicitous concerning our fidelity, by which we wish to favor you more greatly in all things, and you must not fail to send the census. We wish you well in Christ [Col. 0804D].

## XV. To Girbert, Bishop of Nîmes. (Year 891)

[According to D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, volume IX.]

He warns him not to inflict any force upon the monastery of Saint-Gilles.

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bishop GIRBERT.**

It has been reported to our apostolate that, concerning the property of our abbey of Saint-Gilles—which was granted by our predecessors or by us to Amelius, bishop of Uzès [Col. 0805A], for its governance and preservation—you do not cease to cause various inconveniences and many injuries, postponing obedience to apostolic commands and refusing equally to observe apostolic letters.

You ought to have been sufficiently rebuked for this, but the moderation of apostolic kindness has been awaited in your case until now. Therefore we admonish you and command by apostolic authority that, returning to your senses, you inflict no force or oppression of any kind upon any of the property of that abbey, nor consent to anyone who does so. Rather, let the same venerable Bishop Amelius be permitted to enjoy peace, send the census securely to the blessed apostle Peter, and govern that place in safety.

But if you remain in the same obstinacy through reckless audacity, know that you are excommunicated until, coming to Rome with the same Bishop Amelius, you acknowledge before me that you have made satisfaction, since we shall in no way overlook such great recklessness [Col. 0805B].

## XVI. To Walbert, Patriarch. Fragment. (Year 891)

[Note: [Col. 0805D] He cites Aquileia, 130, letter 86.]

We are astonished at your prudence for denying a shepherd to the Church of Como, when you know that you were urged to this by apostolic exhortation. Now we write to you again, unwilling to infringe the privilege of any Church, although by apostolic prerogative it is permitted to ordain a cleric for any Church, etc.

## XVII. To Rotbert, Bishop of Metz. (Year 891)

[Col. 0805C]

He replies concerning the manner in which a cleric whose finger has been amputated is to be promoted to the ecclesiastical orders.

**STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROTBERT, bishop of Metz.**
[Note: [Col. 0805D] Gratian, Distinction 55, canon “Lator.”]

The bearer of this letter, Flavinus, namely a cleric who has come to the apostolic see, brought us a letter sent to us by you, in which you sought to investigate whether, after he had recently been captured by the Normans, he had the finger of his left hand cut off, asking whether for this reason he could be promoted to ecclesiastical orders or not. When we examined the matter and found that your diligence was all the more concerned about it and was demanding instruction from the apostolic see, since you desire always to follow the rule of justice, we rightly commend the zeal of your holiness. We wish your Reverence to know that, if it is true that he had that finger cut off by the Normans, it will in no way hinder his promotion, provided that otherwise he is worthy. For we do not believe that it is unknown to your Charity what the sacred canons decree concerning those who, at the hands of masters, physicians, or pagans, suffer such a thing unwillingly; nor do we find that this ought in the least to stand in his way, if the matter is as stated [Col. 0806A]. We therefore admonish your Religiousness to act toward him in such a way that you may thereby incur a great reward and, with canonical authority not obstructing him in other respects, complete his desire with God’s help.

### XVIII. TO SIGEBERT, BISHOP OF CORSICA. Fragment. — (Year 891.)

[Note: [Col. 0805D] Canon “Quia te,” 38, Distinction 50.]

You rightly judge yourself liable, because, after being captured by the Saracens, you appear to have killed men. But since it is recognized that you did this not of your own will, you are in no way to be judged canonically on that account.

### XIX. TO LEO, BISHOP OF SCIANUM. [Note: [Col. 0805D] This same fragment, with a few changes, is read in canon “De manifesta,” Question 2.1, and is quoted from a letter of Pope Stephen V to Leo, bishop of Theanum. [Col. 0806D] The correctors of the Roman canon note, however, that this letter exists in full in a certain Vatican collection of canons compiled by an anonymous author.] Fragment. — (Year 891.)

[According to Mansi, in the same place.]

[Col. 0806B]

In a case that is manifest and known to many, witnesses need not be sought, as Saint Ambrose says in his Letter to the Corinthians, explaining the Apostle’s judgment concerning fornication:

“‘It is not,’ I say, ‘the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser; for the Lord did not reject Judas, although he had been a thief, because he had not been accused. But when this deed became known, He judged that he ought to be expelled from the fellowship of the brothers. For everyone knew his crime and did not rebuke him. He publicly kept his stepmother in the place of a wife. In this matter there was no need either of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.’” [Col. 0806C]

And shortly afterward:

“Although absent in bodily presence, yet present by the authority of the Spirit, who is absent nowhere, I have already judged—as though present—that the man who committed this deed is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.”

### XX. TO LEO, BISHOP OF THEANUM. Fragment. — (Year 891.)

Your deacon truly confessed that he was free from the crime charged against him. Nevertheless, if suspicion concerning the offense [f. *piaculum*, “sin” or “crime”] exists, and suitable accusers are found, together with witnesses of the kind sanctioned by the sacred canons, then, once the matter has been proved by lawful witnesses, let him be struck by canonical judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0806D] Canon “De crimine,” 15, Question 5; Ivo, Letter 77, which nevertheless reads *Tianensi* for *Theanensi*.]

But if he neither confesses voluntarily, nor lawful accusers or witnesses are found, and evil report grows, let him clear himself not by public examination but before you and before the most reverend priests and deacons, by a secret oath. Thereafter proclaim him a man of good reputation, restrain him, and admonish the sons of your Church not to presume to defame God’s priest any further, remembering that Ham was cursed because he mocked his father’s nakedness.

### XXI. TO STILIANUS [Note: [Col. 0807D] The reading “Stilianus” is supplied from the Vatican manuscript by the Roman Correctors. Chapter “Nunquid,” On Consecration, Distinction 5.] (Year 891.)

[Col. 0807A]

Are not all the anointings of the priestly mystery performed by means of the figure of the cross? Are not the sins of baptism forgiven by water unless it has been sanctified by the cross? And, to pass over the rest, does anyone ascend the rank of priesthood without the sign of the cross?

### XXII. TO GIRARD, BISHOP OF LIÈGE. Fragment. — (Year 891.)

[According to Gratian, Decretum, Part II, Part 3, Question 3, canon 3.]

Things violently taken away before the joinder of issue are to be restored.

[Col. 0807B]

You must first ensure that restitution is made both of the cities, monasteries, and estates that have been seized and, generally, of the remaining property; for we must neither contend naked nor oppose ourselves unarmed to our enemies.

### XXIII. TO THEODOSIUS, BISHOP. Fragment. — (Year 891.)

[According to Ivo, Decree VIII, chapter 59.]

That no one may have two lawful wives.

STEPHEN to Theodosius, bishop.

Are you instructing a barbarian people to marry two brides at the same time? Have you not read the Apostle, who explains the sacrament of the Church: “The two shall be one flesh”? Or do your books perhaps falsely assert that three are one flesh? Cease now to waste away in such sloth, and learn to obey the rules of the Fathers, lest you be found to be transgressing the boundaries established by the Fathers, or, through ambition, transferring from a greater Church to a greater still; the sacred canons deprive one who attempts this even of lay communion.

### XXIV. TO LAMBERT, BISHOP OF LE MANS. Fragment. — (Year 891.)

[According to Ivo, Decree, Part X, chapter 186.]

STEPHEN (IV [Note: [Col. 0808D] For Stephen IV, I believe “Stephen VI” should be read. Jaffé.]) to Lambert, bishop of Le Mans.

[Col. 0807D]

Having read the letter sent to us by your Holiness, which stated that this woman, Hildegard by name, had killed her children and had performed a seven-year penance, we were deeply grieved. Therefore, since you instructed us to show her the compassion of our heart, we both desire and mercifully command that she must receive the sacred Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ on the solemn feasts, namely the revered Nativity, holy Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Apostles, and that throughout the days of her life she must remain enclosed in a monastery and live a monastic life according to the rule.

### XXV. COMPLAINT OF EGILMAR, BISHOP OF OSNABRÜCK, TO POPE STEPHEN. (Year 891.)

[According to Erhard, *Regesta* I, *Codex Diplomaticus*, p. 357.]

[Col. 0808A]

To the most holy lord and pre-eminent in the summit of holiness, Pope STEPHEN, EGILMAR, the insignificant servant of the servants of Christ, bishop of Osnabrück, together with the whole company of the congregation subject to him, implores the crown of true happiness.

While we grieve that the orthodox Church of Christ, founded by apostolic institution and most firmly strengthened by the holy Fathers, has been torn apart by the rage of persecutors and the deceit of the wicked, and therefore lament that she is rather lukewarm and less fervent in divine worship, we earnestly ask for the rights of your piety, which are manifest before God, so that you may deign to support and assist us, to whom the care of the Lord’s sheep has been entrusted, in order that we may lead them back from wandering error to the way of truth and from darkness to light. This is rightly accomplished when wickedness is converted into uprightness. It has long been sprouting among us through various negligences because, for many past years, no holy synod has been assembled to cut it away.

Therefore may your most holy diligence deign to hear the judgment of reason concerning the controversy by which our faintheartedness is shaken. First, we speak of the tithes from which we ought to feed the company of our subjects, which have been unjustly and contrary to canonical law and ecclesiastical right forcibly taken from us. We shall explain why they were taken and how it came about that, of the tithes by which the bishoprics in Saxony alone were established, only a fourth part should serve the Church of Osnabrück, consecrated in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, whose servants we also are. The remaining and larger portions, both in amount and number, which by right belong to the same see, have been divided between the monks of Huxili, where they call their establishment New Corbie, and the women of Herford. In addition, certain estates belonging to them from that bishopric have been placed under their authority, as well as baptismal churches N. that were formerly attached and subject to the bishopric. We do not now demand these, but at least we urgently request that the tithes properly belonging to us, which have been taken away, be returned to us. This is the truthful account.

[Col. 0808D]

Long ago, I say, when the great and admirable prince Charles, with God’s assistance, converted the Saxon people to the faith of Christianity through strenuous campaigns of war, he established, with the advice of synodal and canonical jurists, each bishopric of that province from the revenues of tithes, since the pastors and bishops there lacked other endowments from which Christianity could gradually be strengthened. After his death, his son, Louis of blessed memory, continued for a long time as a vigorous propagator of the holy Church.

It happened, however, that his three sons, following wicked counsel, sent him into custody. The bishop of the aforementioned see of ours, dedicated in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle, a man named Goswinus, agreed by common conspiracy to this counsel and offered assistance, even to the point of violently stripping the sword from him himself. When, by God’s will and through the help of his son, his namesake Louis, he had returned honorably from that custody to the kingdom, the aforementioned bishop, conscious of his treachery and disloyalty, fled to the monastery of Fulda, assumed the monastic habit, and used to visit the place of that bishopric secretly once a year. Thus the episcopal care remained at that time without a bishop and ruler.

Meanwhile it was invaded, seized, scattered, and dissipated by many persons, until, after the death of the aforesaid most gentle prince Louis, when a serious and dangerous dispute over the kingdom was impending between his three sons, and the division of this bishopric fell by lot to one of them, namely to his namesake, a certain very wealthy faithful count named Cobbo obtained the power to do whatever he wished with the aforesaid bishopric. While his brother Werin was then abbot in the monastery of Huxili and his sister was abbess in the women’s monastery of Herford, Cobbo caused as much as he wished of the tithes belonging to that bishopric to be handed over to those monasteries, which were situated in another parish and another diocese, without the synod or the knowledge of the bishops.

Meanwhile Bishop Gozbert, who was of the Swedish people—among whom he had been ordained—was driven out by persecution. Compelled by necessity, he approached the aforementioned Cobbo, and through Cobbo’s request, with the king’s permission, he gladly received the same bishopric, largely emptied of the tithes from which alone it had been established. With Cobbo’s support, and fearing lest what he had not been ordained for should be taken away from him, he allowed matters to remain in this condition throughout his tenure without any opposition.

My predecessor and fellow bishop Egilbert, however, repeatedly appealed to the archbishops Guntharius and Willibert concerning this matter. Because of various occupations, which prevented a holy synod from being assembled for a long period, the case was never brought to a conclusion.

But when the care of that bishopric had been imposed upon me, and I had found, amid various negligences that would take too long to explain, many churches unconsecrated and some even polluted by murders committed there, and not cleansed of various impurities and crimes [Col. 0809D], priests unknown to us, arriving from the western region and subject to the aforesaid monasteries, were celebrating the offices there—priests whose ordination we doubt—I prohibited and forbade divine mysteries from being celebrated there by them until I could consult you, venerable Fathers and teachers, about the matter.

For this reason the aforementioned monks and women immediately brought an accusation against me before Prince Arnulf, contrary to the canonical decrees. They produced, as they claim, a document established by King Louis and Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, the bishop of another diocese. But it was not supported by reliable testimony suitable for establishing its credibility, since it is said to have been fraudulently fabricated by them so that they might possess [Col. 0810A] the tithes of the aforesaid bishopric without our authority or any opposition, contrary to canonical law. We do not understand how what was first established at the foundation of that Church by the aforesaid great Charles, by the fellow bishops, and by canonical decree—namely, that it should remain valid—could in this strange and detestable manner be rendered void by the bishop of Mainz, who belongs to another diocese.

Therefore, most blessed lord Father, judge whether what appears contrary to canonical authority, or what was previously established according to rule concerning the tithes, ought to be restored and strengthened. Meanwhile the aforementioned accusers, who accused me of disloyalty to the king—not, however, in my presence—asserting that I wished to destroy what earlier emperors or kings had decreed, compelled me to appear for judgment. Before Prince Arnulf and nine bishops, whose names are these—Willibert, archbishop of Cologne (Colonia Agrippina); Arn of Würzburg; Odilbald of Trier; Drogo of Minden; Godethanc of Speyer; Wicbert of Hildesheim; Wibert of Verden; Evulf of Halberstadt; and Biso of Paderborn—I laid this case before them.

With earnest prayers, in honor of the supreme Shepherd and Pontiff Jesus Christ, whom they are believed to represent, and of Saint Peter the Apostle and all the saints, I asked them to decide the matter correctly, in accordance with the written document that I had caused to be read before them and that we possess, and in accordance with just judgments and canonical decrees. But they knew the will of the prince and of certain counts, and, fearing to offend him, did not dare to respond concerning the case brought before them [Col. 0810C]. Instead, justice, which I had requested in the love of God, was wholly denied me together with a canonical answer.

Thus, by flattering the prince, I was ordered by him—if I wished to retain his favor and not resist his authority—to allow everything concerning the tithes and other matters of this kind to remain as I had found it. My appeal was thereby forcibly annulled. I could not even obtain that the accusers be brought into my presence and that the case be properly examined.

And, most kindly Fathers, unless you extend the right hand of justice over this dispute and complaint, we can neither exercise the episcopal ministry for the observance of Christianity, nor repair the monastery buildings—which, because of poverty and the seizure of the tithes, I found there were none and which we have only recently begun to construct [Col. 0810D]—nor feed and clothe the clergy for God’s service. Instead, we shall grieve to see them compelled by various hardships to scatter and unable to be gathered together again.

Behold, distinguished Fathers: after so many years, during the time of my predecessors, the churches of the aforementioned Church have remained unconsecrated up to the present. Against our will, because this is forbidden by the canons and commanded by divine law, the offices of the Mass are celebrated there by men whose ordination is doubted. The tithes are taken from us, and our smallness is treated with no little contempt in every matter that deserves correction, because the enemy has found there an opening through which to enter; and, by striking the sheepfolds, he will bring enemies against the sheep.

Therefore we invoke you, the authority of the highest apostolic see, as the head of all Christianity. We who lie prostrate on the pavement before the altars and implore the patronage of the saints, pray that the prosperity of your salvation and holiness may be prolonged and that your glory and your horn may be enlarged forever. Prostrate in spirit at the feet of your piety, we ask you to determine what we ought to do in this matter: whether we should trample these things under the bond of silence and suppress them quietly in order to avoid scandals, or whether we should hope to recover the tithes; and whether we ought to proceed so as to demand that justice be done to us concerning this judgment. May your most blessed Fatherhood deign to explain this fully to us and make it certain, and may the ineffable and eternal mercy preserve you.

### XXVI. RESPONSE OF POPE STEPHEN

[Col. 0811B]

STEPHEN, bishop of the holy apostolic and universal Roman Church, sends greetings in the Lord to EGILMAR, venerable bishop of the Church of Osnabrück.

There can be no doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual pursuits. Therefore your writings have made me rejoice because of the good purpose and integrity of your faith and devotion, but they have also caused me to grieve greatly because of your affliction, about which you have complained and concerning which the speech of those who come to us has repeatedly been reported.

You ought not, we believe, to have suffered so many and such great oppressions, innocent as you are, at the hands of those by whom you should have been supported, borne, and honored. For you informed us that your Holiness was being harassed and torn apart by various calamities by Godescalc, abbot of New Corbie, and the abbess of Herford, together with their supporters, and was being excessively defamed before our son Arnulf by repeated accusations, while your Church was being stripped of its endowments and the offerings of the faithful.

Therefore, brother, do not be surprised if a wicked and impious member persecutes you, since they persecuted Christ himself, our head, just as the Truth says: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household” (Matthew 10:25). Do not be greatly troubled; do not be shaken, but take courage in the Lord and in the power of his strength.

For our part, to provide assistance, we have summoned more than fifty of our brothers and fellow bishops. With them, after regular deliberation, we have decided what answers we should send to you and to those who are in litigation with you, since we received their letters concerning these same matters together with yours on the very same day.

When these letters had been read aloud in the hearing of everyone, yours contained, as you know, many complaints and accounts of oppression concerning their presumption; but their lamentation against you was no less. Therefore we considered it necessary, after removing evasions, to provide you with the support of an investigation into the truth and to obtain assistance for you from the apostolic see, lest this shameless intention proceed to the disturbance of the entire Church and lest matters that had long ago been prohibited by our holy predecessors revive again.

To the abbot, however, we sent a letter in reply, in these words: . . . . .

### XXVII. PRIVILEGE FOR THE CHURCH OF PIACENZA. (Year 891.)

[According to Campi, *History of Piacenza*, vol. I, p. 472.]

[Col. 0812A]

STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy BERNARD, bishop of the holy Church of Piacenza, and through you to that same venerable bishopric forever.

If we grant assent to the pious supplications of our fellow priests and brothers, we both make God favorable to us and, with his favor, make them more vigilant against the snares of the devil, lest the Lord’s flock be harmed. For the condition and honor of the Churches of God, over which they appear by divine appointment to preside, is the common advancement [Col. 0812B] of all, and certainly their common salvation and glory.

And therefore, because your special devotion, clinging to the things that belong to God, asks us to receive the holy Church of Piacenza under our apostolic protection and to establish it by our privilege, yielding to petitions worthy of God, from the present ninth indiction we confirm and establish in that same holy Church of Piacenza all privileges and due services, and the consecrations of all monasteries, both of men and of women, which are known to have been established in the parish of that Church. Likewise, we confirm all written commands and instruments, rights and transfers, whatever that Church was justly able to obtain from our predecessor pontiffs, from the most Christian emperors, from kings or queens, or from Catholic people.

Let it possess these things by peaceful right, so that no tyrant, count, judge, or collector of any public authority, driven by anyone’s impulse, or by anyone’s unhappy presumption, or even by anyone’s favor or goodwill, may presume to trouble it contrary to the right anciently handed down to it and preserved until now, or inflict prejudice upon it, or in any way attempt to dishonor it without consulting us.

And if anyone should perhaps—which we utterly abhor—wish to transfer the consecrations of monasteries or convents of nuns situated in the parish of that Church to another see; or if, which may it not happen, tithes are not handed over by certain persons who appear powerful in the world, we have decreed that they are to be expelled from the thresholds of the Church, unless, after being admonished, they repent, until they have corrected everything canonically. Thus due honor and ecclesiastical vigor may be provided to it as is fitting, and canonical order may remain unimpaired forever by this apostolic command.

And if anything disordered is recognized in the aforesaid Church, let it be put in order by your foresight and diligence, under the full authority that we have conferred, since everyone will be able to understand this. But if thereafter anyone, setting aside the rule of the Fathers and disregarding this present prohibition, acts against this our pontifical decree, let him know that he will be punished with the utmost severity.

Whoever, however, proves to be the guardian and observer of this our apostolic privilege, may deserve to obtain the grace of blessing and mercy from our Lord Jesus Christ.

But if anyone, which may it not happen, whether great or small, should attempt to violate this our apostolic sanction in whole or in part and does not observe it in every respect, let him know that he is to be bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and burned, unless he rejects his offense and offers full satisfaction.

Written by the hand of Anastasius, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of February, in the aforementioned ninth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, by the hand of Zachariah, first secretary of the holy apostolic see; while our most pious lord Augustus Vuido, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the first year, and after the first year, in the ninth indiction.

### XXVIII. PRIVILEGE GRANTED TO ABBOT HUOGGI. (Year 891.)

[According to Dronke, *Codex Diplomaticus Fuldensis*, no. 292.]

[Col. 0813B]

STEPHEN, servant of the servants of the Lord, to HUOGGI, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through him to his successors and the abbots of that same venerable monastery forever.

Taking the greatest care of all venerable places, insofar as possibility is granted through divine assistance, we strive to care for their stability. For by this concern divine clemency is appeased and praise for the Church of Christ is advanced. Indeed, with greater confidence we dare to implore eternal mercy for the obtaining of pardon for our sins.

Therefore your Reverence requested from us that the aforesaid venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, constructed by Saint Boniface the archbishop at a place called Boconia, beside the bank of the river Fulda, should be adorned with the protection of an apostolic-see privilege, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it should no longer be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church.

Favoring your pious desires in this matter, by this our apostolic authority we commit to effect what has been requested, in accordance with the text of the privilege which you have taken care to show us as having been perpetually established there by our predecessor, Marinus of blessed memory, bishop of this life-giving see.

Therefore we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any dominion or authority in the aforesaid venerable monastery, except the apostolic see and the bishop in whose diocese that venerable monastery is known to have been constructed. To the latter we grant permission only when the occasion for consecrating an altar arises. No one is to presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery.

Thus, in accordance with what has been established under the apostolic see by the firmness of the privilege, it may remain endowed without disturbance. Its lands and possessions, both those that it now holds or possesses and those that divine mercy may in future increase within the right of that monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful, are likewise to enjoy perpetual security without contradiction from any person [Col. 0814A].

Furthermore, after deliberation, we establish that at suitable times it be reported to our ecclesiastical care how the monastic life is directed in the regular habit and committed to harmonious agreement through appropriate ecclesiastical discipline. This is so that, under the pretext of this privilege—which may it not happen—the mind and conduct of your Rectitude may in any way be diverted from the rule of justice.

Nor shall it be lawful for a king, any bishop, count, or any other person, great or small, to inflict any force upon the property or dependents of the aforesaid venerable monastery, or to raise any dispute concerning them.

By apostolic censure we establish and decree through this page of our decree that whoever—whether a bishop of any Church or any person endowed with whatever dignity—presumes to violate the authority of this our privilege, which we confirm by the prerogative of the prince of the apostles, and does not quickly repent, shall be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, he shall be excluded from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain forever inviolate and strengthened by apostolic authority.

Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian shall obtain blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of Gregory, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the eighth indiction. Farewell. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Stephen, assistant secretary of the holy apostolic see, in the year—by God’s favor—the sixty-ninth year of the pontificate of our lord Stephen, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most holy see of blessed Peter the Apostle, in the eighth indiction.

### XXIX. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT LIUDGER. (Year 891.)

[Eccard, p. 39.]

[Col. 0814C]

STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HEMBIL, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Liudger, and through you to that same venerable monastery forever.

Whenever we are asked to grant things that are suitable for pious and venerable places, it is fitting that we grant them willingly and favor the wishes of religious persons by apostolic sanction.

Therefore your Religiousness has represented to our apostolate that we should fortify by apostolic authority the aforesaid venerable monastery, with all that canonically and legally belongs or is adjacent to it, just as it is known to have been fortified and strengthened by the pious emperors, namely the religious Augusti Louis, Charles, and Arnulf, through their imperial commands.

For this reason, judging your request to be appropriate, we have decided to incline our ears to your prayers, since we are known, with the support of divine grace, to have undertaken universal care of the rule.

Accordingly, by the sanction of this present privilege, we fortify that sacred monastery as we have stated above. From the present ninth indiction we decree that no power, nor any person, great or small, endowed with whatever dignity, may in any way invade it or lend it to another. No one may presume to claim for himself or give to another anything belonging to its dependents, estates, male or female servants, free or unfree persons, or anything of the movable or immovable property, cultivated or uncultivated, of the aforesaid monastery.

Rather, with all its property, possessions, offerings, and revenues that have been canonically and lawfully given, bestowed, or donated there, and that will thereafter be given, we confirm perpetually under your authority, to be governed and regularly administered for the right and benefit of the frequently mentioned monastery and for the uses of those serving God there.

Indeed, we decree that no member of the faithful may exercise any dominion over the people of that monastery or compel or constrain them to any unreasonable exactions [Col. 0815B]. But just as these things have been granted and confirmed by the aforesaid emperors and God-fearing men, so we command that all the provisions contained in those imperial commands be observed inviolably by all the faithful of the holy Church of God, confirmed by apostolic authority.

We establish and decree that whoever, with rash presumption—which may it not happen—dares to go or act against this our apostolic privilege, or attempts to violate in whole or in part—which we absolutely forbid—what we have established, touched by divine love, for the praise of almighty God, the stability of that monastery, the support of the monks, and the increase of our reward, shall know that he is to be excommunicated; and, unless he obeys, struck with anathema.

Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian and observer shall obtain blessing and grace.

Written by the hand of Gregory, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the ninth indiction.

+ Farewell. +

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, by the hand of Stephen, assistant secretary of the holy apostolic see, in the year—by God’s favor—of the pontificate of our lord Stephen, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most holy see of blessed Peter the Apostle, the sixth, in the eighth indiction. Amen.

### XXX. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF HERTI. (Year 891.)

[Eccard, in the same place, p. 38.]

[Col. 0815D]

[lacuna] which is situated in a place [lacuna] Hersi [lacuna] and through you to that venerable monastery forever.

The more solicitous we are to promote the condition of pious and venerable places, and the more continuously we devote ourselves to advancing their interests through pastoral vigilance, the greater rewards of eternal recompense do we obtain from the one who grants them, who said: “Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching.”

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people that the most reverend Biso, bishop of Paderborn, represented to our apostolate that we should fortify by the privilege of this authority the aforesaid venerable monastery, over which you are known to preside, situated in the territory of his diocese, together with all its lawful belongings and dependencies.

Desiring especially to favor his request, since the care of all the Churches has been entrusted to us, we have decreed that this our apostolic privilege be drawn up. By it we both strengthen that same venerable monastery and, by apostolic authority, confirm there for the support of the handmaids of God all the properties that have been lawfully exchanged with that monastery from the right of the aforesaid bishop, as well as those that have been granted there by the faithful and by people who fear God for the use and benefit of those same holy women. We also decree that the tithes which ought to be given and paid annually to that monastery from the appointed estates are to be paid to it by both episcopal and synodal decree.

Moreover, it has been established, with consultation and consideration, and ordered canonically, that, if the matter stands thus, it must not be violated, lest synodal and canonical vigor [lacuna] in the aforesaid holy Church of Paderborn, just as we have found it established, since we find that care of the same venerable monastery belongs to it.

By apostolic censure we establish and decree that no member of the faithful may in any way act against the text of this privilege of our confirmation, which we have promulgated piously and mercifully, nor, with rash presumption, diminish or take away anything from all that has been lawfully handed over or granted to that monastery and its congregation, or that is henceforth to be handed over or conferred upon it by legitimate right. No one may seize anything for himself; rather, these things are to remain with firm authority for the benefit of those serving the Lord there [Col. 0816C], together with the good things that are now held or that are justly acquired [lacuna].

For whoever is found, setting aside the fear of God, to oppose this privilege of our confirmation in whole or in part, and delays to observe it completely, shall, unless he quickly repents after being admonished [lacuna], be struck by the apostolic sword [lacuna]. Whoever, however, proves to be its guardian and observer shall obtain mercy from the just Judge, our Lord God.

Written by the hand of Gregory, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the ninth indiction.

+ Farewell. +

### XXXI. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF ALEXANDER. (Year 891.)

[According to Eccard, *History of the Princes of Saxony*, p. 217.]

[Col. 0816D]

STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both of the present and of future times.

Since the care of all the Churches rests upon our apostolic office, we ought to provide every possible consent and assistance for the accomplishment of the wishes of those who have labored to enlarge the service of God. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the Church, present and future, that a certain venerable Walbert built a community in honor of the holy martyr Alexander in the district of [Col. 0817A] Lerigau, at a place called Wildeshausen. The intention behind this foundation, and the manner in which he assigned to that community a portion of his possessions, was reported to us after his death by his son, the venerable man and venerable bishop Wihibert of the Church of Verden. He sent us a document in which his father’s wish was fully set out, together with the signatures of all his relatives in confirmation of that same wish.

And because the same venerable bishop asked us to confirm the institution of the aforesaid community as set out in that charter, we decree and by this authority of ours, under the solemn appeal of the divine judgment, command that neither a bishop nor anyone of his family, nor any person, whether great or small, dare violate it. If anyone—something we do not wish—should attempt to act against this decree of ours, let him know that he will be struck down by the sword of anathema on the day of judgment and condemned by the devil’s lot as liable to everlasting punishment. We wish you well in Christ.

Given on the Kalends of June, in the ninth indiction.

## XXXII. TO HERIMANN, BISHOP OF COLOGNE (Year 891)

*[In Lappenberg, Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch, p. 78.]*

**STEPHANUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother, HERIMANN, archbishop of Agrippina-Cologne.**

[Col. 0817C] We foresee that we must answer briefly the letters of yours, which wander on at such great length, because, since questions from various provinces continually converge without interruption upon the apostolic see, and since it is not proper to resolve them without an answer, unless a concise note were to respond, the notaries themselves would be turned to nausea.

You complain that the Church of Bremen was subject to the see of Agrippina-Cologne, and that the bishop of that Church, recently sending to us and now coming in person, has complained that you or your predecessor are attempting to violate the privileges of his Church. Concerning the privilege of Churches, therefore—a matter obscured by the distance of the lands and not made clear by the authority of the Fathers of earlier times—we do not think that anyone should judge rashly according to his own pleasure. For it is written: “The cause that I did not know, I investigated most diligently” (Job XIX, 10).

Accordingly, this discussion must not be entrusted to ink and parchment, but must be weighed through an exchange of conversation, with caution and careful examination. Therefore it is necessary that both of you come into our presence and that we bring the matter to an end by a synodical decision, lest some renewed dispute, arising from hatred, obscure brotherly charity. For it is wicked if those who have been placed upon the watchtower, and who ought to kindle others by the light of their example, offering guidance in love and leading them toward justice, tear one another apart with wolfish bites.

But because, when Adalgarius, the venerable [Col. 0818A] bishop, arrived, you delayed coming, and, as those whom you sent themselves admitted, did not fully entrust them with your representation, we did not wish to put an end to so great a dispute, lest we should appear to have decreed something too hastily.

But so that the truth of the matter may break forth into clearer light, we have written to Folko, venerable archbishop of Reims, that in our place he should summon a synod at Vangion in the month of August, on the future feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, in the tenth indiction, God willing. We instruct your Reverence to attend it, together with the venerable archbishop Sunderold, both your suffragans, and the assembly of the other most holy bishops who are connected with you. We have also ordered that the same Adalgarius, our most reverend bishop, be present, so that the examination carried out there may show what is owed to each party, though it must impose no final settlement.

Afterward, if possible, we order both of you to come before our presence; otherwise, send representatives instructed by both of you, entrusting them with your full authority, so that they may have freedom to discuss and deliberate. For this reason we have also appointed the most reverend Folko to preside there, so that through the truthful testimony of a vigorous man of episcopal rank we may learn the truth of the matter, all ambiguity having been set aside, and so, with God’s favor, deliberate in such a way that in no future time will it be necessary to reopen this question.

## APPENDIX. LETTER TO SELVA, ERMEMIR, AND FRODOIN, Attributed to Stephen V

[Col. 0818C] It is entitled in the *VV. CC.*: **PRIVILEGE CONCERNING THE ARCHBISHOPRIC OF TARRAGONA**, although it should rather be called some sort of declamation or a judgment composed in favor of the archbishop of Narbonne and directed against the archbishop of Tarragona and the other Spanish prelates.

*[In Mansi, *Conciliorum*, volume VIII.]*

**STEPHANUS, servant of the servants of God, to SELVA, ERMEMIR, and FRODOIN of Barcelona.**

Know—yes, know, brother Selva, if you may rightly be called by the name of brother—that, at the command of the most glorious and Catholic emperor Odo [Note: [Col. 0817D] What has the Council of Troyes to do with Odo, and what has an emperor to do with it? All this is highly suspect.], I recently came to Troyes to celebrate there a council concerning many and various matters, together with fifty-two fellow bishops and fellow priests distinguished by pontifical insignia, who attended that council with us.

When certain ecclesiastical cases were being carefully discussed and the manner in which they ought to be handled was being properly arranged, among the other matters which we decreed and established by a just judgment, we came to the most indecent disgrace of your most insolent and excessively presumptuous arrogance. With the stomach of your pride swollen, you presumed to rebel against—or rather, to resist—the perpetual disposition of almighty God, wishing to tear down and wholly abolish his ordinances and those of his holy apostles, especially those of the blessed apostle Peter.

Finally, to explain the cause of this matter carefully to you: long ago the universal Church was entrusted to Peter by our Lord Jesus Christ, not merely generally, as to the others, but also specially, above all his fellow apostles, and was committed to his see, as you have written: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI). And again, when he was asked by him after his resurrection whether he loved him, the same Lord charged him three times to feed his sheep (John XXI). Strengthened by this authority, he and his successors after him have always arranged and determined ecclesiastical affairs.

But you, still persisting in your wickedness and filled with madness, acting not as a wise man but as one bereft of understanding, suppose that you can overturn the constitution of the eternal God, who, as it is written, “changes times and seasons, removes kings and establishes them,” while you attempt to tear away from its proper right the archbishopric of the Church of Tarragona and from the right of your own Church. By the Lord’s disposition, it has passed into the jurisdiction of the Church of Narbonne—not by stealth or any violence, but by will and election, and with the surrender of all the inhabitants of that land, both noble and ignoble, especially the bishops, counts, and even the kings of the Franks, to whom the high sovereignty of that land especially belongs.

Indeed, the right of the Church of Tarragona passes into the service and jurisdiction of the Church of Narbonne under such a condition that it can never withdraw from its subjection by any agreement or for any reason, even if the metropolitan Church of the province of Tarragona should be restored to its former condition. For the Church of Narbonne has always stood in the place of a guardian to the aforesaid Churches of that diocese, which could scarcely escape the devastation of the pagans.

Moreover, even if the aforesaid metropolitan Church should return to its former state, and all the Churches of that diocese which had previously obeyed it should return to its service according to the decision of the Catholic Fathers, the metropolitan Church itself must nevertheless, according to the institutions of the pontiffs of the Roman Church and the apostolic privileges, remain perpetually subject to the jurisdiction and service of the Church of Narbonne. Thus whoever obtains the dignity of its pontificate must not be ordained, or [cor., consecrated.] appointed in any manner, by the election of the entire Church, clergy, and people, until the pontiff of the aforesaid Church of Narbonne comes and consecrates the one elected to the honor of archbishop.

If, compelled by some difficulty, he cannot come to consecrate the bishop of the aforesaid metropolitan see, he must send one of his suffragan bishops in his place, who shall diligently carry out the matter and solemnly strive to seat and enthrone him upon the pontifical throne. Therefore the one who has been consecrated must always yield in all things to the Church of Narbonne the obedience that is owed, provided only that he receives the pallium from the Roman pontiff together with the authority of the privilege.

For the pontiff of Tarragona, as well as all the clergy and people, if the matter should take effect, must always remember that the Churches of those parishes which had been nourished under the power and jurisdiction of Narbonne, where they had long been raised as by a nursing mother, after they have passed into the maternal embrace—if the matter should ever attain that effect—must repay the grace of that nurture with abundant acts of thanksgiving and, moreover, because of the aforesaid education, must offer submission and honor as though paying a mother her due.

If we return to the ancient institutions established by the primates of the holy Church, doubtless by Peter and Paul, it is clear that not only the metropolitan Church of Tarragona but all Spain, insofar as ecclesiastical right is concerned, ought always to be subject to the precedence of Narbonne and to its protection, as though nourished by a mother’s milk. For it first received the documents of the holy see from that Church, and, illumined by the light of faith, as though awakened from the sleep of perpetual death, it awoke to the splendor of eternal life, as the records preserved to this day in the archive of blessed Peter carefully testify.

The same is true of the things that are said to have been accomplished shortly afterward by Sergius, a disciple of the apostles Peter and Paul—things which, as you can see, you entirely ignore. For if you truly knew them, I think that, stirred by such swollen madness of pride, you would never dare even to sigh in protest.

Now, because these matters have remained hidden from you until this time, they must be made known to you by us, in a brief and concise but truthful discourse, so that you may not presume to act in this way again. To show clearly how the matter stands: when the blessed apostle and teacher of the nations Paul departed from Rome for Spain for the sake of preaching, as he had previously indicated in his Epistle to the Romans who had believed, he took with him Trophimus of Ephesus and the most prudent man Sergius Paulus, whom he had already won for Christ, as well as Torquatus, Secundus, Endalatius [in Cardinal de Aguirre’s edition, Endelvius], and certain others.

After reaching the Cisalpine Church, he went as quickly as possible to Arles, which is the metropolitan city of the province. While he remained for some time in that city, preaching and proclaiming the kingdom of God, and many were converted to Christ through his teaching, he left there Trophimus, a bishop previously ordained by the apostle Peter, to strengthen the souls and minds of those who had believed.

He himself, proceeding with the others as far as Narbonne, immediately sent the aforesaid Torquatus and six other companions and fellow disciples of his into Galicia to preach, in accordance with the command of the apostle Peter. Then, after many people not only from that same city but also from several cities had streamed to him from every direction, he diligently evangelized them with the aforesaid Sergius and taught them, converting them splendidly to Christ.

When he recognized that those whom he had taught were already strong and completely immovable in faith, he sent some of them to preach the Lord Jesus Christ through the various regions of Gaul. After this, he departed from there with Sergius Paulus, and together they reached as far as the farther parts of Spain, preaching in each city, as we said, the glory of the future kingdom of God.

After spending a considerable time in preaching, they charged those who had believed to preserve faithfully the faith they had received and to strive earnestly to distribute it to others to whom it had not yet been preached. Then the aforesaid apostle resolved to return to Rome and again promised that, for the consolation and strengthening of the believers, he would send himself among them together with Sergius Paulus, his fellow evangelist. He instructed them to offer him service in all things and in every respect, and to obey his admonitions most willingly.

As the apostle encouraged the brothers who had believed in each city with these and similar words, commending them to the Lord and bidding them farewell, he earnestly hastened to return to Rome.
