On his return, when he came again to Narbonne, after arranging everything that needed to be done, Paul likewise left his colleague there, instructing him to nourish with the milk of consolation those whom they had already brought forth in various regions of Spain through the grace of faith, as women in labor, until they could know with certainty that they were able to eat the solid food of perfect belief.

Therefore, with the Lord cooperating, he entrusted that entire region to him for the office of the apostolate. He entrusted the peoples of Gaul to him for preaching because blessed Peter had sent him for this very task, had in his stead and for this purpose consecrated a church [read: “a bishop,” as in Cardinal de Aguirre’s edition], and had also specially entrusted to him the distinguished metropolitan city of Narbonne in Gaul, so that he might teach and evangelize its peoples.

After all the things had been completed which the common purpose of the two excellent preachers required, they parted from one another with affection [add, “in affection,” from the same edition], striving to commend one another to the Lord with mutual exhortations and embraces. After kissing and weeping, they separated from one another: the apostle departed for Rome, while Sergius remained at Narbonne.

For [read: “each of them,” from the same edition] exercised the office of preaching entrusted to him so vigorously that he would not abandon it because of any terrors or punishments, until by martyrdom each fearlessly approached Christ, who was calling him to himself, so that he might offer the talent entrusted to him multiplied fivefold and receive from him the recompense of an eternal reward multiplied a hundredfold.

If you wish to know what Sergius Paulus did for the Lord after the apostle’s departure, when the flock entrusted to him had been acquired for Christ together with the apostle, let it be known to you and to all the inhabitants of Spain, of both sexes, that, both personally and through his disciples—whom he had already nurtured and taught in the faith of Christ—he traversed all the regions of Spain and continually taught their inhabitants. He raised some of them so high in the summit and practice of the Christian faith that neither they nor certain of their successors needed anyone besides him for sound doctrine.

Read, therefore, the books of the blessed Leander, of Isidore, and also of Braulio, likewise of Julian, and of the ancient Catholic teachers of that province; then perhaps you will acknowledge that I speak the truth. If you do not believe that this has sufficiently satisfied you, examine with the greatest care the volumes of his deeds, comprised in three books by three disciples of that same Paul. Then you will openly recognize what previously, unless I am mistaken, you entirely ignored, with regard to this same matter.

But if you do not wish even then to admit that this course is appropriate, and if, always persisting in perverse obstinacy and filled with madness, you consider contemptible the judgment of the Roman pontiffs—by whose decree, established by divine authority, the entire Church of Christ throughout the world is always ruled and ordered—to such an extent that you refuse in any way to withdraw from the injury which you inflict upon the aforesaid archbishop Theodard with shameless boldness and unrestrained rapacity [cor., “rapacity”], let it be known to you and to all who offer you any support or assistance in these matters for which we rightly prosecute you, that you will be perpetually bound and indissolubly fettered by the bonds of anathema.

Accordingly, so that we may not appear to do you an injustice, I and the fifty-two bishops who are with me have established a period for you to satisfy the one whom you wrong—the pontiff of the Church of Narbonne—which extends until the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel.

If, by the approaching solemnity of that archangel, you have not satisfied him by restoring completely and without any reservation or withholding to him personally and to his Church everything that you have taken from the right and jurisdiction of that pontiff, then, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the pontiffs of the Roman Church, as well as by my authority and that of all the bishops attending this synod of Troyes, we excommunicate you by excommunicating you, curse you by cursing you, and bind you indissolubly with the perpetual bond of anathema: you, your accursed Ermemir, Frodoin the perjurer and apostate anti-bishop, and all who offer you any assistance against so unjust a presumption, so that from the time established or fixed by us you may always be regarded as exiles and outcasts from every Christian assembly.

## In the Year of the Lord 896. Pope Formosus

[Col. 0821]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Mansi, *Conciliorum amplissima Collectio*.)*

[Col. 0821C] Formosus, highly praised for his religion, integrity of morals, and learning, was made pontiff in the year of the Lord 791 through a tumultuous election, with the deacon Sergius rising against him. He was truly an excellent man, as is evident from Liutprand.

All the ancient writers of the Roman pontiffs, apart from Liutprand and Flodoard in book four, chapter one, assert that he was immediately substituted for Stephen V; all the ancient monuments of the Greeks also say the same. For in the Greek Codex Colonnensis, cited above several times, where the Photian pseudo-synod is refuted and the succession of Nicholas’s and Hadrian’s successors among the Roman pontiffs is set out, we read:

“After this Hadrian, John; after John, Marinus; after Marinus, Hadrian; then another Stephen V, then Formosus; after him four others, namely Boniface, Stephen, Romanus, and Theodore; and after these John, who wrote this.”

Therefore, what Leo of Ostia states in book one, chapter forty-eight of his *Cassinese History*—that Formosus followed Hadrian and preceded Stephen V—is erroneous, unless perhaps, with intervening figures omitted, he intends to refer to Stephen VII, commonly called the sixth.

Marianus and Sigebert, however, and the more recent historians who imitate them, seem to have devised in a dream the notion that Agapetus and Basil—two imaginary pontiffs whom no one ever saw or heard of—preceded Stephen and his successors.

[Col. 0822C] Anastasius calls him, in his account of Nicholas, a bishop of great holiness. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, according to Flodoard, book three of the *History of Reims*, chapter 20, wrote to him, praising the reputation for holiness and learning that he had heard about him, seeking his friendship, asking him to deign to pray for him, promising to return the favor, and sending him certain gifts so that he might remember him in his prayers.

For a long time he administered the bishopric of Porto piously and holily, to such an extent that, in the judgment of the most holy pope Nicholas I, he was considered worthy to be sent as an apostle to the Bulgarians to imbue them with the orthodox faith. After he had spent many years there and converted that people to the faith of Christ, he acquired still greater glory for himself.

Pope John VIII, who appears to have opposed, to his great disgrace, the well-arranged actions of his predecessors—for Nicholas and Hadrian, John’s predecessors, had repeatedly condemned Photios of Constantinople and Zacharias, bishop of Anagni, and had justly determined that they should scarcely be received even to penance or lay communion, whereas John not only restored them but also made Zacharias of Anagni, whom he had honored with the office of librarian of the apostolic see, his own counsellor and entrusted him with several legations—removed Formosus from the bishopric, degraded him, reduced him to the status of a layman, and banished him from the city [Col. 0823A], forcing him to swear that he would never reclaim his bishopric but would thereafter remain quiet, content with lay communion.

For what reason John proceeded against him in this manner is not known, unless perhaps, because Formosus had rebuked and admonished him for his evil actions, he judged that Formosus, as a rebel, ought to be erased from the register of bishops.

Marinus, John’s successor, raised up, as was fitting, the man distinguished by the merits mentioned above, who had been adorned with the honor of the apostolate but overwhelmed by this disgrace. Having raised him up, he undoubtedly absolved him from the oath extorted by force and fear and restored him to his former dignity. Obeying the pontiff’s judgment and command, Formosus resumed his bishopric.

At this time in particular, when the Roman Church was being grievously afflicted by the invasion of the worst tyrants, and Formosus, bishop of Porto, was regarded and venerated throughout the world as at once most holy and most learned—as we have shown above from Flodoard and Liutprand—he was transferred, for the good of the whole Catholic Church, as had often happened before, from the bishopric of Porto to govern the reins of the entire Catholic world, becoming bishop and pontiff of the Roman Church.

At the beginning of his pontificate he received the letter which Stylian had sent to Stephen V before the latter died, before it could be brought to Rome, and he issued the letter found below in response.

He was very anxious to establish Charles the Simple, son of Louis the Stammerer, as the legitimate heir of the kingdom of Gaul, as may be seen from the letters concerning this matter in Fulco. He legitimately created, anointed, and crowned as emperors of the West Wido, who had usurped the imperial name fifteen years earlier—as Baronius shows from an ancient diploma—in the second year of his pontificate, and Wido’s son Lambert in the following year.

Therefore it could have happened only through some act of deceit, as the Acts of the Roman Council under John IX testify, that the same Pope Formosus, in the sixth and final year of his pontificate, summoned Arnulf and placed upon him the crown of the Western Empire.

The common error of the chroniclers must therefore be corrected. Contrary to the prescription of the sacred canons and the authority of the apostolic see, they enumerate Arnulf in the succession of Western emperors after Charles the Bald, omitting Wido and Lambert. Arnulf, who was never lawfully elected or crowned, ought never to have been honored with the title of emperor.

Through the elections and coronations described above, Formosus incurred the greatest envy and hatred of the Roman citizens, and, both while alive and after his death, suffered the gravest injuries, insults, and sacrileges from them. What he endured from the Roman citizens during his lifetime is recounted by Liutprand, book I, chapter 8, in these words:

“At this time Pope Formosus, a religious man, was being severely harassed by the Romans, at whose urging King Arnulf had come to Rome. To avenge the pope’s injury, upon his entry he ordered many Roman nobles who were hastening to meet him to be beheaded.”

What injuries and insults his successors Stephen VI and Sergius III inflicted upon that pontiff, whether through ignorance of the facts or through the height of sacrilege; how he was exhumed and mutilated by three fingers; and how the orders of those whom Formosus had ordained were repeated and repeated—I shall relate below, in the section on Stephen VI.

Regino, Liutprand, and Adam of Bremen testify that in the year of the Lord 896 he died, having been highly commended by the writers of that period and having held the pontifical see for six years. Therefore the more recent writers are mistaken when they say that he departed this life in the year 895, in the fifth year of his pontificate. *(Baronius, volume X of the Annals.)*

[Col. 0823]

## INVECTIVE AGAINST ROME ON BEHALF OF POPE FORMOSUS

*(Blanchini, *Prolegomena ad Librum Pontificalem*, Roman-Vatican edition.)*

[Col. 0823C] “. . . of this prophecy, God will remove his part from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things [Note: [Col. 0823D] The codex, incorrectly: “you should remove.”] that are written in this book” [Note: [Col. 0823D] Revelation, chapter XXII, verse 19.].

Therefore, because we have learned that something new and previously unknown and unheard of has recently happened in the holy Roman Church—which is the mother of all the Churches and has neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind—we consent to it more by weeping than by disputing, and we waste away under excessive terror.

Crushed, saddened, and seized by profound astonishment, we would prefer to remain silent rather than speak. But who could restrain the speech that has been conceived [Note: [Col. 0823D] Job, chapter IV, verse 2.]?

That twisted and, alas, most savage serpent which by the cunning deception of fraud expelled our first parents from the joys of the delightsome paradise now raises its neck, hissing, and does not cease to disturb the Roman Church with the poison of its [Col. 0823D] li . . . o . . . [Note: [Col. 0824D] Read “envy.”].

But the divine right hand of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will crush the Lernaean serpent, lurking in the marshes of Arcadia, to which, when one head had been cut off, three grew back in its place. He who caused blessed Peter to walk with dry feet upon the waters will bring his Church, tossed on every side by the immense waves of the sea, into the harbor of salvation. After crossing the Jordan and overthrowing Jericho, he will permit her happily to enter the eternal joys of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Yet it is a mystery, and a very astonishing one, that while all the Churches, both those on this side of the sea and those overseas, remain in their proper condition, the Roman Church alone, like a ship tossed by stormy waves, overflows with those near death [Note: [Col. 0824D] In the first correction, “overflow”; a solecism.].

Let us return, then, to the matter at hand, and enumerate, lamenting rather than expressing in words, the scandals by which, with Rome as their instigator, small and great alike are scandalized.

For worldly and canonical laws, and barbarian statutes as well, decree and determine in every respect that violators of tombs are to be counted among the infamous, so that clerics are subjected to the canonical rules, while laymen are to be counted among the reprobate according to the saying made famous in verse: “what the wolf deserved to see first” [Note: [Col. 0824D] That is, a quotation from Publius Vergilius Maro.].

[Col. 0825A] [Note: [Col. 0825D] Corrupt reading; it must be restored from Virgil, *Eclogue* IX, verse 54, where he expresses the meaning as follows:

“. . . The voice itself has also fled from Moeris;

the wolves saw Moeris first.”

The saying has the appearance of a proverb. According to popular belief, the sight of wolves deprives for a time of speech the person whom they see first. See Pliny, *Natural History*, book VIII, chapter 32, and Theocritus, *Idyll* 14.]

—and assigned to three years of penance. Alas! Alas! Alas!

“How does the city sit alone, full of people? She has become like a widow, the mistress of nations; the princess of the provinces has become tributary” [Note: [Col. 0825D] Lamentations, chapter I, verse 1.].

O Rome, your founders Romulus and Remus, whom one womb bore, were not received by your walls so that they might reign together. But, weakened by fratricide [Note: [Col. 0825D] The codex incorrectly has “weakened by fratricide” in the plural.], you handed one over to death, while the other, turning [Note: [Col. 0825D] The codex has *imperiendo*, likewise incorrectly, instead of *impertiendo*.] with the Quirinal sword and imposing deadly laws upon you, rolled . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . indeed, to the people of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0825D] The codex has “to all.”], as masters, Peter and Paul, apostolic princes indeed [Note: [Col. 0825D] If one wishes, read “truly apostolic princes”]. You crucified one and beheaded the other with the sword among murderers. For, as a certain wise man said:

> For unless the merit of Peter and Paul were cherishing you,
[Col. 0825B] For so long a time, Rome, you would have been wretched. Is this the repayment that we have heard from you? No one ever could have been called agreeable to anyone, either in appearance or in speech. Recently, therefore, we heard from the brothers and learned from what was discussed in the synod [Note: [Col. 0825D] Read *collocatum* (“set forth”) for *collatum*.] that your patron, Pope Formosus, raised in your bosom from his very cradle, elected by the bishops, clergy, and people to receive the height of apostolic dignity, and enthroned by pontiffs of this official rank in the sacred see, was not permitted, after the end of this life, to have rest in an underground cavern when dead [Note: [Col. 0826D] The codex has *clem. τ*; read *culmen* (“height”).] [Note: [Col. 0826D] The codex has *examinatum* (“examined”) for *exanimatum* (“dead”).].

For you dragged his corpse—already buried for nine months—from the tomb by the feet; and, as Saul recalled Samuel from the dead, you consulted him and made him sit in the synod. We believe that, if he had spoken as Samuel’s spirit, he might perhaps have said to you: “Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.” But although he did not speak, you and your sons will nevertheless descend to the underworld; while he, received by the angels, departed long ago to the regions above.

O unheard-of deed! O abhorrent crime! O unprecedented sacrilege! Him whom you had nourished from infancy with milk, fed with solid food, instructed in letters, and whom, advanced through the ecclesiastical ranks to the pontifical summit because his worthy conduct deserved it, you had revered [Note: [Col. 0826D] The codex’s second corrections read *secundis curis, elegisti* (“you chose”).]; whom you sent to preach to a most pagan people, received with joy when he returned, and, once received, cast far from his fatherland into exile—to your own harm, though you ought not to have done so [Note: [Col. 0826D] The first corrections in the codex read *patre* (“father”) incorrectly.]. But, received for a time and restored to the rank from which he had been removed—whether through zeal or through fault, we do not know—he fulfilled the service of Christ that he owed.

[Col. 0825D] When Pope Stephen also, son of Hadrian, whom the same Formosus had consecrated, entered upon “the way of all the earth” [Note: [Col. 0826D] 1 Kings 2:2], your bishops and nobles assembled, as did the clergy and people, and the whole multitude of the common folk. They came to the Portuense see, situated within the City and presided over by Formosus, acclaiming him as pope and supreme pontiff.

When he refused and protested, and, clinging to the altar [Note: [Col. 0826D] The first corrections read “from the altar.”], they dragged him away by force together with the cloth with which the altar was covered; then, after dragging him away, they enthroned him amid praises and choirs in the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Once placed in the apostolic see, he bestowed many benefits upon you: he rebuilt, constructed, built, adorned, and decorated churches; he performed consecrations; he consecrated deacons, priests, and bishops, from whom afterward the supreme holy apostolic see was adorned with the episcopal insignia [Col. 0826B]; he governed your clergy and people with remarkable moderation; and he crowned Emperor Lambert with the imperial diadem [Note: [Col. 0826D] The codex reads “and Lambert,” or *Landebertum*.].

Did you, Rome, consent to the election of Formosus? Say yes or no. But you cannot deny it. The whole world is witness to this deed. You sent to the Portuense see—which is the second apostolic see within your walls—asking Formosus to move from it and preside over you. When he resisted and in no way yielded to your invitation, you dragged him by force from the step of the altar, as has already been said, tore him away, and enthroned him with banners, songs, hymns, proclamations, and praises in the loftiest stronghold of the apostolic see. You cherished [Note: [Col. 0826D] Read *fovisti*, “you cherished,” rather than *favisti*.] him, adored him, swore allegiance to him; and whoever he blessed, you blessed, while whoever he cursed, you cursed.

[Col. 0826C] And, Rome, what more will you add? When the term of this life had passed, he was gathered to his fathers [Note: [Col. 0826D] 1 Maccabees 2:69]; flesh was joined to earth and dust to dust [Note: [Col. 0826D] Read *sociatus*, “joined,” rather than *sociata*.], and his spirit, as we believe, was borne away [Note: [Col. 0826D] The codex has *dictus est*; we have corrected it to *ductus*, “was led,” and so forth] and carried to the stars.

But you, Rome, attempting to forestall the future and dreadful day of judgment [Note: [Col. 0826D] The second corrections read *tremendi*; read *tremendum*.], assembled a horrible synod; after nine months you dragged from the tomb the corpse, putrefied and almost reduced to dust, and judged him dead whom once alive you had feared.

If no one judges a Roman pontiff while he is alive, will anyone judge him when he is dead? If he were questioned, what would he answer? If he answered, that whole horrible assembly, terrified by fear, would separate from one another, leave the place, and go out one after another; and the Lord would say to him: “Formosus, who condemned you?” And he would answer: “No one, Lord.” And the Lord would say to him: “Neither will I condemn you.”

[Col. 0827A] If that wondrous king, mighty in hand and psalmist David, had been present, he would have played the harp and said:

“Will you work wonders for the dead?  
Or will physicians raise them up,  
and will they confess to you?  
Will anyone in the tomb recount your mercy,  
or your truth in the place of destruction?  
Will your wonders be known in darkness,  
or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?”  
[Note: [Col. 0827D] Psalm 87:11.]

And perhaps, while he played the harp, the spirit of Formosus would approach [Note: [Col. 0827D] The codex reads *Formosus*. If that reading is retained, the preceding word must be read *spiritu*, “by the spirit,” rather than *spiritus*.].

Nevertheless, as we see, having set aside the reverence due to all the Scriptures and the ancient Fathers, you disinterred him, [lacuna] the ground … to lay down … [lacuna] … cut off his hand, and threw it into the Tiber.

Let us therefore cry out with the prophet Joel [Note: [Col. 0827D] Supply “and”]: “Hear this, elders, and give ear [Note: [Col. 0827D] The codex has *prohibite*, incorrectly.], all inhabitants of the land: has such a thing happened in your days or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children about it; and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation” [Note: [Col. 0827D] Joel 1:2–3].

And again:

“Gird yourselves and lament—lament, priests; howl, ministers of the altar; enter and lie down in *caseis* [uncertain: “sacks”], ministers of my God, because sacrifice and offering have perished from your house” [Note: [Col. 0827D] Joel 1:13].

Perhaps someone will say: “Formosus lived excommunicated; he was a despoiler [Note: [Col. 0827D] The codex reads “he says: excommunicated, despoiled.” We have corrected it as in the text.], a usurper, and an invader; the consecrations he performed are invalid, and he possessed nothing and gave nothing.”

And we answer this: “As I live,” says the Lord, “this proverb shall no longer be used in Israel” [Note: [Col. 0827D] Ezekiel 18:3].

Did the king and his nobles [Note: [Col. 0827D] Supply “and.”] bring Formosus to Rome with military array, and without the consent of the bishops, the senate [Col. 0827C], and the Roman people, establish him, adorned with the episcopal insignia, upon the tribunal [Note: [Col. 0827D] Supply “upon”]? Far from it. Your princes, phalanxes, and satraps, your common people and schools, from the greatest to the least, elected him, acclaimed him, praised him, and adored him; and the bishops enthroned him with the sacred Lateran order.

The whole world remembered his celebrated name. The priestly order set forth his name, throughout the whole world, in the festive and daily solemnities of Mass, in the catalogue of the secret *Eulogium* [Note: [Col. 0827D] The codex has *secraetalis*], and in public praises [Note: [Col. 0827D] Read *universum*, “the whole,” rather than *universarum*, “of all.”].

How, then, do you wish to extinguish the name of Formosus, which was proclaimed through the three parts of the world [Note: [Col. 0828D] Perhaps read *tripartita et recoluit*, “remembered it through the three parts [of the world]”], and which resounded for all from the rising of the sun to the boundary of the earth?

Does the name of Peter, prince of the apostles, stand? Let the name of his vicar Formosus stand also. Does the name of the apostolic men [Note: [Col. 0828D] The codex has *apostolorum*, “of the apostles,” incorrectly; the context requires “the apostolic men” or “apostolic pontiffs.”] who held the place of blessed Peter remain? Let the name of Formosus remain also. Just as the name of Nicholas, Hadrian, Marinus, [Col. 0828A] John, Stephen, and the rest flourishes, so let the name of Formosus flourish.

Someone also says: “It was not permitted to him to minister after his deposition [Note: [Col. 0828D] That is, “after his being deposed.”]; and if he ministered, he was not permitted to move from city to city.”

Let us therefore examine each point, and scrutinize most carefully those things that appear just, possible, useful, honorable, and approved by the benefit of the holy Fathers.

For those who have been injured [Note: [Col. 0828D] Perhaps read “heretics” rather than “the injured.”] and condemned it is written in the Psalms: “Does the one who falls not rise again?” [Note: [Col. 0828D] The Vulgate reads “the one who sleeps.” The codex has *addiet*; we have corrected it to *adjiciet*, “will add.”] [Note: [Col. 0828D] Psalm 40:9.]

But concerning those who change their see and move from one city to another, the Lord says in the Gospel: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” [Note: [Col. 0828D] Matthew 10:23].

There is indeed a distinction between the cause of necessity and that of usefulness, and between the ambition of avarice and presumption, personal will, and invasion. There is likewise a similar difference between one who is condemned by canonical laws through the stain of spite and envy, and one convicted of some crime and stained with heretical defilement.

For the sake of usefulness, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, moved from Antioch and was transferred to Rome. Eusebius Pamphili, therefore, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: [Col. 0828D] Chapter 11, page 212 of Valesius’s edition], reports that Alexander, bishop of one city of Cappadocia, when he had come to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, was detained by its citizens and appointed in place of Bishop Narcissus [Note: [Col. 0828D] Read *Narcissi* rather than *Necersi*]; thereafter he presided over that Church for the rest of his life.

If, then, among the ancients a bishop was transferred without distinction from one city to another when usefulness called him, this rule must also be joined to the present case, so that it may be shown that those who prohibited Proclus from being enthroned were liars.

Let it suffice for the present that we have mentioned these men; for, by way of example, we would recall more [Note: [Col. 0828D] Read “we would recall” rather than “we shall recall.”]. Meanwhile, let us return to our address to the city of Rome, so that through it we may address its citizens.

And since the case of Pope Formosus is at issue [Note: [Col. 0828D] The codex has *ratio*, “reasoning,” rather than *ratione*, “case.”], let us bring forward the examples of the holy Fathers; for the whole burden of this argument rests upon the case of Formosus. And because the dead are not to be judged by the living, let us demonstrate it to all, clearer than daylight, throughout the ages.

At the very beginning, let us set forth the judgment of a certain bishop of Ticinum, named Ennodius, a most holy man:

“God,” he says, “willed that the cases of other men be determined through a human being; but he reserved the prelate of the Roman see, without question, to his own judgment and decision. For he willed that the successors of blessed Peter should possess the privilege of such great dignity that the Roman pontiff may be judged by no one.”

Perhaps you will say: “Such will be the whole order of things in the future dispensation.”

No. To one alone it was said [Note: [Col. 0829D] Read “it was spoken” rather than “it was given”]: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind shall remain … [Note: [Col. 0829D] The word *usque* (“until”) is an editorial reminder that the address is to be continued. The complete words of Jesus Christ, drawn from the Gospel, are in Matthew 16:18.] loosed in heaven.”

For concerning this Church the prophet seems to have said to me: “If it is humbled, to whose help will you flee? Or where will you leave your glory?”

This concerns the living. Concerning the dead, however, Pope Anastasius gives this warning:

“Warned by the most blessed Apostle, lest there be any stumbling block in the Church, we try to judge those who have already departed, although we cannot do so. … For he says concerning those who presume to judge matters belonging to God alone: … ‘Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. For to this end Christ rose again, so that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. But who are you that you judge your brother? … Therefore let us no longer judge one another; but judge this rather, that you do not place a stumbling block or scandal before your brother’” [Note: [Col. 0829D] Romans 14:11–13. We have supplied “so that,” as above and below.].

The Apostle therefore warns us not to presume to pass judgment upon these matters, concerning which no one can judge more truly or better than God. In this matter someone rashly claims for himself a daring authority; and for this reason the peace and unity of the Church are destroyed [Note: [Col. 0829D] Anastasius II, in his letter to Anastasius Augustus, chapter 1, in Binius, *Councils*, vol. II, col. 270. The edition differs in many respects from our codex. We have added punctuation where the antiquarian transmits an incomplete authority.].”

It therefore appears that no one who has already departed from the world has been held for judgment by human judgment. If no subordinate, stripped of the flesh, is to be judged, what shall we say of the supreme pontiff, who was not to be reproved even while alive, and who, resting in the sleep of death under the protection of the tomb, was dragged from the grave and thought worthy of anathematization?

For although Pope Marcellinus had sacrificed to the gods, he was nevertheless judged by no one, because it is unlawful for anyone to judge the supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0829D] Read “the supreme pontiff” rather than “a supreme pontiff.”]. No one can be condemned by human examination—as has been written above [Note: [Col. 0829D] Supply “as”—whom God has reserved for his own judgment.

This principle had such force [Note: [Col. 0829D] The codex has *voluit*, “willed,” incorrectly; read *valuit*, “had force.”] that such men are not only not judged, but are even seized amid bitter and public sedition [Note: [Col. 0829D] It is uncertain whether *non*, “not,” should be added.].

Let us now come to the ordination of Pope Formosus, from whom the discussion must begin, since some people, as is read in the decrees of Pope Hilary [Note: [Col. 0829D] The codex incorrectly has *Ilarii* for *Hilari*], think that the episcopate is not a divine gift but a shortcut to inheritance [Note: [Col. 0830D] The codex has *putatur*, “is thought,” rather than *putant*, “they think.”].

For this reason the restraint of moderation is betrayed, charity is neglected, that tunic woven throughout from above is torn apart and, badly apportioned, violently rent; and the shepherd who was thought to be one is turned into a wolf.

Pope Formosus did not do this. He did not hold the holy Roman Church by hereditary right, nor, as is alleged, did he invade it out of ambition. For it seems impossible that he could have invaded a Church of such eminence. By what crowd, by what violence, could the head of the whole world have been invaded by a poor, lowly, and simple little man, unless he had been supported by imperial, royal, patrician, or tyrannical power [Note: [Col. 0830D] The codex has *ni enim imperatori*.]? Could he otherwise have seized the summit of such authority [Note: [Col. 0830D] Supply *non*, “not,” or place a question mark after “could he have seized”?]

Where, then, O Rome, is your great nobility and your ancient, unconquered power? If, as is alleged, he seized the apostolic see, then the entire counsel of your princes, together with the courage and wisdom of your nobles, must have fallen completely asleep.

What, then? Did he bind them? Or did he demand by force that the bishops consecrate him [Note: [Col. 0830D] The codex has *exigit*, “demands,” in the present tense rather than *exegit*, “demanded”]?

For it is known that he was consecrated by those very bishops by whom his predecessors had been consecrated and to whom the right of consecrating belonged. How, then, can it be said: “He possessed nothing; he gave nothing”?

Behold: although it is said that he possessed nothing, it is clear how it is shown that he received something [Note: [Col. 0830D] This passage appears corrupt. Perhaps read *declaretur*, “it may be declared,” and below, “what he received.”]; and what he received he was able to distribute. He did not dare to ascend the apostolic see or seize the summit of such power except through the laying on of their hands and their consecration—and indeed it was impossible otherwise [Note: [Col. 0830D] The codex reads *culpnem eripere*, corruptly, for “to seize the summit.”].

Did Pope Marinus give what he did not possess? He certainly possessed it, and he gave it. For who can give what he does not have?

The bishop of Caere [Note: [Col. 0830D] Read *Caerensis* rather than *Cerensis*.] was one of the Seven, like Formosus, but one of the *Forenses*; nevertheless, this was for reasons of usefulness and necessity. Not through pride [Note: [Col. 0830D] The codex has *superbe*, “proudly,” rather than *superbia*, “pride”], but through the advocacy and election [Note: [Col. 0830D] The codex has *electione*.] of the Roman people, he was enthroned in the holy and apostolic see, just as Formosus was.

What, then, O Rome, do you assert concerning Marinus? Do you wish to say of him: “He possessed nothing; he gave nothing”? In truth, he possessed much and gave much. In accordance with the word of Truth: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” [Note: [Col. 0830D] Matthew 25:29].

Perhaps you object and say: “Was Marinus not a bishop?” Did not Pope John ordain him? He traveled through Italy, Germany, and Gaul; he corrected, raised up, and directed whatever was crooked, impassable, and rough; and he established and crowned both Charleses—the Gallic and the German—with imperial crowns [Note: [Col. 0830D] The codex has a corrupt reading, *cosett*.].

If you invalidate the ordination and consecration of John, through which, if I am not mistaken, he shone in the most sacred see of blessed Peter for years … [lacuna] … adorned with the episcopal cap [Col. 0830D], and shone in the sacred orders through apostolic favor [Col. 0831A], your princes will be like Dathan and Abiram and their accomplices, who rebelled against Moses and Aaron in the camp, against the holy ones of the Lord. Therefore the earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram [Note: [Col. 0831D] Psalm 105:16–17]; indeed, they descended alive into the underworld.

For just as those men murmured against the Lord and against the leaders whom he had appointed over them, so you murmur against the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one and true God, and against his apostles, to whom authority was granted by him to bind and loose in heaven and on earth.

“Through you,” says the Lord through the prophet, “my name is blasphemed among the nations” [Note: [Col. 0831D] Isaiah 52:5].

From this it is understood that, before the supreme Judge, it would have been better and more fitting for the presumption of Formosus, as it is called, to be corrected by being silently overlooked than, by breaking the bond of charity, to bring scandal upon the whole world.

O Rome, you are perplexed and apostatize, and are swept into madness and frenzy [Note: [Col. 0831D] The codex reads “you will be able to fall into madness and frenzy”; the text has been emended]: turn to God, and you will be saved. For he himself says through the prophet: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved” [Note: [Col. 0831D] Isaiah 45:22].

Stand and contend with me. I will question you, and answer me; and you question me, and I will reply to you.

You say, then, as has often been said, that the aforesaid pontiff Formosus did not possess anything that he could give [Note: [Col. 0831D] The codex has *dari*, “to be given,” rather than *dare*, “to give.”]. He certainly possessed it—he possessed it—from Marinus, first a bishop and afterward supreme pope and universal pontiff. By him Formosus was absolved, kindly received, and worthily and canonically recalled to his former honor, from which he had been removed because of the stain of envy [Note: [Col. 0831D] In place of *depositus*, “removed,” the text is corrupt; a more fortunate editor may correct it.]; not as a schismatic or heretic, but as a holy, just, and catholic man, separated from sinners and made higher than the heavens.

How, then, did he give what he had not received?

Nicholas consecrated Formosus as a bishop [Note: [Col. 0831D] *Ad episcopum* seems superfluous; perhaps read *episcopatum*, “to the episcopate,” unless the author is using a vulgarism of that period, which I have no doubt was current], knowing him to be an outstanding teacher; and for that reason he sent him to Bulgaria to preach. There, vigorously teaching a once most cruel and pagan people the way of truth, the rule of faith, and the doctrine of the Christian religion, he returned to your walls with the cross and in triumph [Note: [Col. 0831D] *Et* is superfluous.].

Later, expelled from your city in the ocean of envy [Note: [Col. 0832D] Perhaps read *veneno*, “poison,” or *coeno*, “filth,” rather than *oceno*], he was then, as has been said, received and restored by Pope Marinus; and finally, through the acclamation of the people because of the increase of his good conduct, he was favorably advanced to the summit of the pontificate.

But if Formosus possessed nothing and gave nothing—which is an utterly absurd and most profane thing to say, and the claim of minds actually bereft of reason [Note: [Col. 0832D] Read, if desired, “and of minds actually seized by madness”]—then John, who consecrated Marinus, possessed nothing and gave nothing.

Pope Marinus also, whose consecration remains unimpaired, possessed nothing and gave nothing to Stephen the deacon, son of Hadrian, whom he himself consecrated and who afterward became pope and was consecrated as an apostolic pontiff by the aforesaid Formosus in due succession.

If Pope Formosus possessed nothing and gave nothing, why do your nobles, with brazen foreheads, adamantine minds, and satanic thoughts, say: “Therefore the consecration of Marinus, whom Pope John consecrated as bishop, is invalid; the consecration of Stephen, son of Hadrian, whom Marinus advanced to the diaconate and whom Formosus afterward consecrated in the holy apostolic see by the election of the entire people, is invalid”?

Do you perhaps wish to say, O Rome, adding iniquity to iniquity, that Marinus was not a bishop? Then the consecration of Pope John [Note: [Col. 0832D] The word *Joannis* is incorrectly repeated in the codex. In the same place read *Caerensi*, “of Caere.”], which he imposed upon Marinus of Caere, bishop—worthily or unworthily, as you say—is invalid.

If John our apostolic pontiff acted unworthily—which it is sacrilegious even to say—then Marinus was not a bishop. But if he acted worthily, as the whole upright world has judged, then Lord John is an apostolic pontiff and Marinus a bishop; and thereafter, for reasons of usefulness and necessity and with the advocacy of the whole people, he remained enthroned in the holy Roman and apostolic Church.

If you now profess that Marinus was not a bishop, you accuse Pope John—God forbid—who consecrated him, of having violated the canons and transgressed all sacred laws. Either say that Marinus, who was consecrated by John, was a bishop, thereby proving that John truly was what he was—a pope [Col. 0832C]; or, if you deny it, you will declare, by staining all Christendom, that John was an invader [Note: [Col. 0832D] The codex has the corrupt *irriptorem*; we have restored *irruptorem*, “invader,” that is, “violator”] and destroyer of the Nicene Council and of all councils.

Moreover, the consecration of Stephen and of Sergius, whom Stephen consecrated to the diaconate, will be invalid. And, to speak more freely, if we trace the succession of Roman consecration, we shall see, as you assert, the entire series of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0832D] Read *sacerdotii*, “of the priesthood”; or supply “of the order or dignity”] rendered invalid and void from the time of John himself, who died thirty years ago [Note: [Col. 0832D] Pope John VIII died in 882. Since the author wrote this work thirty years after his death, the apology must therefore have been composed in 912.].

For if John, who consecrated Marinus as bishop, was rejected, Marinus will be rejected; and if Marinus was not a bishop, why did he carry out ordinations, consecrations, baptisms, and confirmations of the people at the see of Caere?

Therefore, if Marinus was not a bishop, Stephen, son of Hadrian, who afterward became an apostolic pontiff, was not a deacon; for once Marinus was not a bishop, and had usurped and performed the sacred ministry of episcopal jurisdiction [Note: [Col. 0833D] Read here and shortly below *ministerium*, “ministry,” rather than *mysterium*, “mystery”], he would undoubtedly have been subject to the punishment of Uzzah, who presumptuously dared to touch the ark of the Lord.

Likewise, Stephen was neither a deacon nor could he become an apostolic pontiff, because, if your claim is true, he unworthily touched the sacred ministry of the diaconate.

If you condemn Marinus, condemn John; condemn also Stephen, Formosus, Sergius, and all who, beginning with John, the predecessor of Marinus, held a seat in the holy apostolic see with supreme pontifical authority.

Let the whole world, and all who inhabit it in the Christian faith, cry out against you: “You have deceived everyone, and you yourself have been deceived.”

For Constantinople, Sicily, all Italy, Gaul, and Germany—in whose territories metropolitan bishops appear to dwell, claiming episcopal suffragan communities for their own consecration—bring charges and complaints against you, because no metropolitan can perform a consecration unless he receives the pallium from the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0833D] The codex has *palleum*, here and below, for *pallium*.].

From whom, then, do Byzantium, which is called Constantinople, Ravenna, Forum Julii, Milan, Ebredunum, Arles, Lyons, the city of Reims [Note: [Col. 0833D] The codex incorrectly has *Remororum*], Cologne, Mainz [Note: [Col. 0833D] The codex has *Magontia*], and the other metropolitan cities receive the pallium, unless they receive it from apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0833D] Read “unless they receive it,” rather than “unless they should receive it.” The writer falsely closes the sentence from here to the words “would loose or bind.”]?

If matters are as you proclaim, almost the entire world has been placed in ruin for thirty years—not only to the condemnation of bodies but, what is worse, to the destruction of souls [Note: [Col. 0833D] This too, if it is indeed to be understood as referring to the metropolitans who received the pallium from Pope Formosus and to their ordinations, involves a major error on the part of our apologist; for the pallium, even when received from an illegitimate pope, does not invalidate the ordinations of metropolitans.].

The one who can count the stars of heaven and the sand on the seashore will be able to count the souls and bodies of those who, without baptism and the anointing of sacred chrism, have been plunged into Tartarus through so many years.

Even the solemn celebrations of Mass have scarcely been performed except by the most ancient men. For who would bless the sacred fonts and prepare the holy chrism, or who would loose or bind penitents, when the entire ecclesiastical order had fallen so low that, as you impiously slander with reckless mouth, it possessed nothing and gave nothing?

It is therefore now time to return to the discourse we promised to take up, and, since we have shown that Pope Formosus was not an invader, to make equally clear, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, that one who was deposed—justly or unjustly—could be restored, and that it was valid to move from one Church to another.

For we have learned, from the salutary examples of the holy Fathers, that very many bishops moved from one city to another for reasons of necessity and usefulness, as well as through invitation and advocacy [Col. 0834A]. The first of these was, as we have related, the most blessed prince of the apostles and holder of the keys of the heavenly kingdom; and Alexander, as the book of *Ecclesiastical History* reports, bishop of one city of Cappadocia, acted nobly in view of usefulness and necessity [Note: [Col. 0833D] It is uncertain whether *mobiliter*, “readily,” should be read].

Let us follow the others.

Perigenes was ordained bishop at Petras [Note: [Col. 0833D] Perhaps Patras, as in Auxilius cited below; the codex incorrectly has *Petrus*.] [Note: [Col. 0834D] Auxilius, booklet I, ch. 3, and book II, ch. 22, on ordinations performed by Formosus, lists these names of bishops transferred to another see almost word for word, as here. Consult Morinus, *On Sacred Ordinations*, part II, pp. 349 and 371, to whom we also refer the reader for several variant readings.]; but because the citizens of his city refused to receive him, the bishop of Rome ordered him to be enthroned in Corinth, the metropolis, after its bishop had died, and he presided over that Church for as long as he lived.

Alexander, bishop of Antioch, transferred Dositheus, bishop of Seleucia [Note: [Col. 0834D] The codex has *Seleuticae*], to Tarsus in Cilicia.

Reverentius was transferred from Arca in Phoenicia [Note: [Col. 0834D] The codex has *Archis*] to Tyre.

John was transferred from Gardila [Col. 0834B] to Proconnesus. Palladius was transferred from Helenopolis to Aspona. Alexander was transferred from another Helenopolis to Adrianople.

Gregory of Nazianzus was first bishop of a city of Cappadocia called Sasima; afterward, with the consent of blessed Basil and the other bishops, he became bishop of Nazianzus.

Meletius first presided over the Church of Sebastia and afterward was appointed bishop of Antioch.

Theosebius was transferred from Apamia in Asia to Eudoxiopolis, formerly called Salambria.

Polycarp was transferred from the city … [lacuna] … [Note: [Col. 0834D] Supply “Antapristena,” or “Antepristena,” in Mysia, from Auxilius.] to Nicopolis in Thrace.

Hierophilus was transferred from Trapezopolis in Phrygia to Antioch in Pisidia [Note: [Col. 0834D] The sentence may also require: “Obtimus was transferred from Agardamia in Phrygia to Antioch in Pisidia,” according to the same manuscript; the codex has *Pasidiae* for *Pisidiae*.].

Silvanus was transferred from Philippopolis in Thrace to Troas.

Eusebius too was transferred from some small city to Alexandria by apostolic authority [Col. 0834C].

Likewise Felix was transferred to Ephesus from the city in which he had been ordained, by the election of its citizens and by the common counsel of the bishops, the other priests, and the people [Note: [Col. 0834D] The codex has *Apli*. We have interpreted it as *ac populi*, “and of the people.”], because of his learning and the good life that he led.

For one does not move from city to city when one does so according to personal inclination or ambition, but when one is transferred through some usefulness or necessity and at the urging and counsel of other peoples [Note: [Col. 0834D] The codex is corrupt: *aliorum ortatur, ex concilio pociorum*.].

Nor is one transferred from a smaller city to a larger one when one does not do so from ambition or personal will, but has either been driven by force from one’s own see, compelled by necessity, transferred because of the usefulness of the place or the people, and enthroned by others—not proudly but humbly.

“For man sees what is before his eyes, but God sees the heart.” Therefore one does not change one’s see who does not change one’s mind.

Let what has now been said about the change and transfer of sees suffice. I shall now clearly discuss the reconciliation of pontiffs who have been condemned justly or unjustly, as authority teaches [Note: [Col. 0835C] From here through the words “Pope John,” compare Auxilius, book II, chapter 21, who reports the same cases.].

John Chrysostom was judged by two synods of the orthodox, but was restored again to his Church.

Likewise, Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, was deposed; but afterward he recovered his own episcopate.

Asclepius [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex has *Asclipius*], likewise judged by a synod, afterward recovered his Church.

Lucian, bishop of Adrianople [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex has *Adrianopolitis*], was condemned by Pope Julius, but afterward recovered the Church of his episcopate.

Likewise, Cyril [Note: [Col. 0835C] Read *Cyrillus* rather than *Quirinillus*], bishop of Jerusalem, was deposed; afterward he was reconciled to his Church.

In the same way, Pope Sixtus [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex has *Sextus*] condemned Polychronius [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex has *Palichronium*], pontiff of that same Church of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0835C] Read *ejusdem* (“of that same”) for *eidem* (“to that same”); *suae* is superfluous]; and afterward he himself reconciled him [Note: [Col. 0835C] Auxilius, book II, chapter 21, identifies Sixtus as the one who reconciled him.].

Pope Innocent likewise condemned the bishop Photius [Note: [Col. 0835C] Read *Photium*, “Photius,” rather than *Fotinum*]; but afterward he himself restored him to the proper status of his Church.

Likewise, when Bishop Misenus had been condemned by Pope Felix, Pope Gelasius, his successor [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex reads “Gelasius, the successor of Pope,” rather than “the successor of that man”], entered into communion with him and restored him to his Church.

Leontius, while he was a presbyter, was deposed; but afterward he became patriarch of Antioch.

Pope Gregory IV of Rome consecrated Theodosius, whom his predecessor Eugenius had deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate, as bishop of the holy Church of Signia [Note: [Col. 0835C] Auxilius, book II, chapter 21, in Morinus, reads *Seguinae*.].

Bishop Ibas was judged, but the holy synod canonically restored his Church to him.

Pope Nicholas rightly condemned Bishop Zacharias [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex incorrectly has *episcopus*, “bishop,” and below “suddenly made a cleric from a layman and advanced …”], because, after being sent to Constantinople, he approved Photius the invader, suddenly made a cleric from a layman and advanced without proper procedure through the ecclesiastical orders to the patriarchate of Constantinople, while rejecting Ignatius, a holy and just patriarch. But Pope Adrian—

[The supplied source ends here.]

He restored him to the former state of his own Church. He reconciled Rothad, bishop of the holy Church of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex, incorrectly, has *Rochadum sanctae Sessionis*.], who had been condemned by a synod [Note: [Col. 0835C] Supply *a*: “by.”] attended by King Charles, and restored him to his own Church. Pope John condemned Anspert, archbishop of Milan, because he refused to receive legates of the supreme holy Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0835C] Supply *et*: “and”] and disdainfully refused to appear when summoned to the synod; but afterward he restored him to that same Church [Note: [Col. 0835C] The codex has *ejusdem*: “of the same.”].

Why say more? If we attempt to bring forward [Col. 0836A] all the restorations and transfers of pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0836C] The codex has *retemptavimus*.], the day will end before—or so we think—our speech does. To whom, then, shall we compare you, or to whom shall we liken you, O Rome? For great is your devastation [lacuna], like the sea [Note: [Col. 0836C] Supply *est velut*: “is like.”]. Who will heal you? Your prophets saw falsehoods and follies; nor did they expose your iniquity in order to turn you [Note: [Col. 0836C] The Vulgate has *ad poenitentiam provocarent*: “to summon you to repentance”] and heal you. All who passed along the road lamented over you; they hissed and shook their heads, saying: “Is this the city of perfect beauty and the joy of the whole earth?” [Note: [Col. 0836C] Lamentations 2:16ff.] Examine your ways, therefore, and turn to the Lord, and you will be saved.

What, then, will you say to these things? For it is commonly said that it is foolish to restrain others when one is unable to place a bridle upon oneself. By what right, then, do you wish to rebuke others when you have no power to correct yourself [Note: [Col. 0836C] The codex has *temetipsum*: “yourself” (masculine).]? Through intrigues and seditions, by waging war [Col. 0836B]—by waging war [Note: [Col. 0836C] *Belligerando* is mistakenly repeated.]—your princes strive to ascend to the summit of the highest eminence; and, still persisting [Note: [Col. 0836C] Supply *in*: “in.”] in their iniquity, each attempts to accomplish in action what he has conceived in his mind.

For this reason [Note: [Col. 0836C] The codex has *res*, an incorrect solecism.] the Flood came upon the whole world, and all flesh was destroyed [Note: [Col. 0836C] The codex incorrectly has *delectaque*.] from the face of the earth, except for the eight persons saved in the ark. Thus the holy Scripture says in the preceding passage: “When the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all those whom they had chosen” [Note: [Col. 0836C] Genesis 6:2.].

And, to restrain the rashness of your persistent activity, Truth itself says: “For you have had five husbands, O Rome, and this man whom you have is not your husband” [Note: [Col. 0836C] The Vulgate has *nunc*: “now.”] [Note: [Col. 0836C] John 4:18.]. For Formosus, whom you dragged from the tomb in the most savage presumption and who, while alive, sat in the supreme, holy, and apostolic [Col. 0836C] See [Note: [Col. 0836C] For *et*, read *in*: “in.”], consecrated John [Note: [Col. 0836C] Namely, Pope John IX.] to the priesthood. He afterward ascended, in accordance with Roman custom and consecration, to the summit of the apostolate, and consecrated Kailo, archbishop of Ravenna; afterward, in a holy synod assembled in that same city, which Emperor Landebertus attended [Note: [Col. 0836C] Read *Lambertus*: “Lambertus.”], he took his seat courageously with apostolic favor.

Kailo, however, consecrated Peter, bishop of Bologna. Peter, bishop of Bologna and suffragan of Archbishop Kailo [Note: [Col. 0836C] The codex has *Kalionis*: “of Kalio.”], consecrated John [Note: [Col. 0836C] Namely, John X, the antipope.]—who unlawfully presides over your see [Note: [Col. 0836C] Perhaps one should read *legentium*, “of those reading”: “who, abusively, presides over your see,” and so forth.]—as deacon through the successive stages of the sacred orders.

After Peter’s death, this same John, while Kailo [Note: [Col. 0836C] The codex has *Kalone*.] was still archbishop [Col. 0837A], presumed to invade the Bolognese Church [Note: [Col. 0836C] The codex has *Bonihensem*, incorrectly.] in defiance of all canonical authority. Once consecrated, he also unworthily performed the solemn rites of the Mass by pontifical right and exacted illicit consecrations. After abandoning that Church, he seized the holy Roman and Apostolic Church through nefarious acts.

And now [Note: [Col. 0837A] Read *nunc*, “now,” or *tamen*, “nevertheless.” The passage also makes it clear that our author wrote this *Colloquium* at Rome under the antipope John X.] he wishes, according to his own pleasure, to loose and bind; and, like that Lucifer who wished to establish his seat in the north and, exalting himself on high, boasted that he would be like God, he wishes to excommunicate the Catholic and universal Church and seeks to anathematize those who are more just and holier than himself. For who will believe him after this?

(Let neither the one distinguished nor the one girded boast in the same way.) For God is not like man. If he did not spare angels who exalted themselves [Col. 0838A], how much more must human beings beware lest they become exalted [Note: [Col. 0837A] The codex has *extollatur*: “he becomes exalted.”]. For it is written: “Do not be wiser than one ought to be wise; lest perhaps, while he wishes to be more than he is, he be less than he is.”

Moreover, although we unworthily exercise Christ’s embassy and priesthood [Note: [Col. 0838A] The author of this defense here reveals himself to be a bishop, or at least a priest.], as the Apostle teaches, we ask for peace, we seek unanimity, and we earnestly beg you, O Rome, who are the head of us all, to be healed [lacuna] and, so that you may not afterward be scandalized so lightly [Note: [Col. 0838A] The codex has *scandalizari*: “to be scandalized.”], we entreat you by every means; with the help of him to whom praise, honor, power, and glory belong with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

# Letters and Privileges of Pope Formosus

*(From Mansi and more recent collections.)*

## I. To the Monks of Saint Theuderius (892)

[Col. 0837B]

He grants immunity and a firm and stable right to their possessions.

Formosus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable congregation of the monks of the venerable monastery of Saint Theuderius, confessor of Christ, situated in the territory of Vienne, forever.

The more diligently we administer the affairs of pious places, according to what has been divinely entrusted to us, the greater abundance of reward we acquire for ourselves, and their condition will flourish under a better administration. Therefore true devotion, through Barnoinus, the most reverend archbishop of Vienne, brought it to our apostolate’s attention that we should fortify that venerable monastery, together with you, by apostolic authority.

Accordingly, since we are concerned for all, and especially since we have heard that you escaped from the monastery of Dervo in the county of Trecassinus from the presence of the pagans, and that you were mercifully received by the same venerable archbishop, we have yielded to your prayers. By this privilege of our apostolic authority we confirm that you shall serve God there firmly and peacefully, diligently laboring day and night at whatever appears necessary for the place and monastery, and obeying the canons, indeed the rule of blessed Benedict, both in restoring the church and wherever else this is required.

This is on the condition that neither the same venerable archbishop nor any of his successors shall be permitted to impose harsh service upon them, require departure on an extremely long journey, or impose burdensome lodging obligations, or any tax beyond what has been established: namely, one pound of silver at the feast of the aforesaid Saint Theuderius at the end of the year.

Moreover, we decree, ordain, establish, and solemnly declare that, when the abbot of the aforesaid congregation dies, as human beings must, neither the present bishop named above nor any of his successors shall presume, at any time or in any manner, through any display of pride or arrogance, avarice or greed, or anger, to impose another abbot upon that congregation, except one whom the monks themselves, by free election and devotion, shall have chosen for themselves according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

Nor shall anything be taken away or diminished in any way from all the movable and immovable possessions which they presently hold, or which they may thereafter justly acquire from their elders or in any other manner; nor shall anything be exchanged except by the will of the monks.

Furthermore, if anyone attempts to act against this authority, access to our presence and that of our successors shall in no way be denied or prohibited to their abbot and monks, nor shall anyone lie in wait to obstruct their ability to do so.

In order to obtain the assistance of almighty God, the intercession of Saint Peter, and the aid of our charity, their abbot, Adalricus by name, hastened to the threshold of Saint Peter with the most reverend archbishop Barnoinus.

Moved by this affection and by the authority of our apostolate, we ask and beseech, and by God and through God, by the merit of Saint Peter and the reverence due to our ministry, we adjure and solemnly declare that no noble or powerful person, whether neighboring, arriving from elsewhere, or dwelling in the surrounding area, shall presume in any way to inflict harm upon them, disturb them without legal cause, or usurp their movable and immovable property.

Nor shall anyone attempt to destroy their servants. From now on, we wish them to remain secure and peaceful, protected and defended by apostolic protection, together with all the immovable and movable possessions belonging to that venerable monastery.

If anyone, which we do not wish, should presume by rash endeavor to act wholly or partly against this provision of our privilege—which we have decreed for the praise of almighty God and the stability of that pious place—and should not observe it in all respects, let him know that he is to be bound by the chains of anathema by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter and by ours, and, unless he repents, excluded from the kingdom of God. But whoever proves to be a true guardian and observer of it may deserve to obtain blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of Anastasius, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of November, in the tenth indiction. Farewell.

[Col. 0839B] Issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of December by the hand of Sergius, first secretary and defender of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious lord Pope Augustus Wido, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in his first year, and in the first year after his consulship, in the tenth indiction.

## II. To Stylianus, Bishop of Neocaesarea in the Province of Euphrasia (892)

He replies to the letters sent by Stylianus to Pope Stephen V, which we transcribed above.

“Your letters, sent to the apostolic see, etc.” Thus abbreviated in the manuscript; after much has been omitted for the sake of brevity, the following continues:

You ask for mercy, but you do not explain how it is to be shown, or to whom—whether to a layman or to a priest. If you say that he was a layman, he will be worthy of pardon, as one who obtained his dignity from a layman. But if you call him a priest, you do not attend to the fact that one who did not possess dignity could not confer dignity.

Photius could do nothing except inflict the condemnation which he himself had received through the laying on of a crooked hand, and he conferred condemnation. How could one who became a partner of a condemned man receive dignity?

Since you ask that mercy be obtained for the ordained man, observe that you are rather favoring the ordainer, in accordance with the Lord’s sacred saying: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad. Can a fig tree produce grapes, or a vine figs?” (Matthew XXII).

That Church, therefore, in which such deeds are found ought to have suffered the gravest penalties, so that by such penalties your Church might be cleansed. But kindness and love of the brethren restrain us; they persuade us to tolerate certain other things.

Accordingly, we have sent from our side the most religious bishops Landulfus of Capua and Romanus, and with them we urge Your Holiness to meet, together with Theophylactus, metropolitan of Ancyra, and our faithful Peter. Thus, first of all, the sentence synodically pronounced by our predecessors, the universal pontiffs, against Photius, the transgressor and overthrower of the laws, and confirmed by our humility, shall remain immutable forever.

As for those who were ordained by Photius, we shall deal mercifully with them. We decree that, after presenting written statements, they shall confess that they have sinned and beg pardon through penance, promising that they will never again commit such an act.

When this has been done, Your Holiness, together with the men named above, shall carry out everything that follows and that is set down in our letters, adding, removing, or changing nothing. When they have thus been received by us and by Your Reverence into the communion of the faithful as laymen, the scandal will be erased.

But if, after these things have been completed, any one of them refuses communion, let him know that he will be separated from our communion. Farewell in the Lord.

## III. To Herimannus, Archbishop of Cologne (892)

*[Lappenberg, Harburgisches Urkundenbuch.]*

[Col. 0840B]

Formosus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Herimannus, archbishop of Agrippina Cologne.

We caused your letters, addressed to our apostolate, to be read in our presence. They stated that Pope Leo, our predecessor of blessed memory, during the time of the emperor Charlemagne, had confirmed by his own authority, through a written charter, all the parishes, monasteries, churches, families, and possessions belonging to Agrippina Cologne, and that from that time the see of Bremen had been subject to that Church until the time of Guntharius.

We have indeed heard this and believe that it was so. But we have learned from the report of certain persons that it lies at the farthest borders, where the pagans are its neighbors. It is asserted, however, that during the time of Guntharius, the former king Louis, with pious zeal, on the advice of the most reverend archbishops and nobles and leading men, and with apostolic consent, decreed that a prelate should be established there who, with the favor of Christ’s grace, would sow the word of faith among peoples who had no knowledge of it.

After sending Solomon, the most reverend bishop of Constance, he requested from the lord Nicholas of holy memory, our predecessor, that this holy and God-worthy decree be confirmed, so that the peoples who were ignorant of God might be awakened to holy work by the teaching of the Church of Bremen—which, although situated nearby, had at times languished through neglect—and, casting off sloth, might gird itself for the cultivation of the Lord and Savior; and so that, when the thorns of idolatry had been uprooted, a seedbed might be scattered from which abundant fruit could reach the divine granaries.

Last year, however, when a dispute arose between the envoys of the Church entrusted to you and the bishop of Bremen, since the matter was uncertain, it ought not to have been rashly decided.

For this reason it was decreed that an assembly of the most holy bishops should be held at a suitable place, presided over by the archbishop of Mainz, fortified by apostolic authority. There both your complaint and that of the aforesaid bishop were to be investigated with the greatest care, and only then were you, with envoys from their college or with whichever bishop either of you chose, to come to the apostolic deliberation to receive a decision.

You were instructed to hear and investigate, not to decide. Therefore we await and command that this be done at the appointed time, namely in August of the present tenth indiction.

Indeed, at that time the matter will be more freely decided, because, after the question has been more carefully examined, it will emerge into the clearer light of truth, following the example of blessed Job, who says: “The cause which I did not know I investigated most diligently” (Job XXIX, 16).

Such a dispute must certainly be decided not according to anyone’s pleasure, but in a manner pleasing to God. We wish Your Reverence’s holiness good health in Christ.

## IV. [Note]

[Col. 0841D] A papyrus charter of Formosus, Roman pontiff, addressed to Servo-Deus, bishop of Gerunda, is preserved in the church of Gerunda. Martenius recently published this charter in the *Collectione amplissima Anedoct.*, volume I, page 239.

I received a copy of it from the Gerundan original in 1736, compared it with the published text, and found that Martenius’s copy ends at the words “we establish in perpetuity,” with the remainder missing. The pontifical dating is also absent from the original; nevertheless, the text contains the tenth indiction, from which it is inferred that this charter was issued in the year of Christ 892.

Petrus de Marca, in the appendix to *Marca Hispanica*, page 384, produces from the chartulary of the church of Gerunda a charter of the Roman supreme pontiff to Servo-Deus, bishop of Gerunda, composed in almost the same words as that of Formosus, except for a few details. He also presents another charter by the same Roman pontiff for the church of Elne. In book III of *Marca Hispanica*, page 370, he discusses the dates of these charters; Pagius examines them at the year 897, no. 6.

Meanwhile, we judge that Formosus’s charter for the church of Gerunda should here be printed according to the authority of the original.

Dominicus Georgius Rodiginus.

### Bull for the Church of Gerunda (892)

[Col. 0841B]

Formosus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Servo-Deus, bishop of the holy Church of Gerunda, and through you to that venerable Church forever.

Just as, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, the evangelical power of binding and loosing was given by the Lord himself to the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, as the subsequent reading says among other things: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI), and so forth; so the apostolic see, supported by canonical and legal authority, is required by the order both of divine and human law to provide assistance and the just support of petitions to all the Churches of God spread throughout the world.

Therefore, venerable bishop Servo-Deus, you came to the threshold of the same most holy blessed apostles for the sake of prayer and submitted to us that, by the privilege of our apostolic confirmation, we ought to confirm all the movable possessions of the same Church of Gerunda, in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, our Lady, where the blessed Felix, martyr of Christ, rests bodily.

These possessions are houses, *pleves* (communities), cells, churches, estates, and islands—namely Majorca and Minorca—courts, parishes, lands, vineyards, meadows, and forests, together with dependants of both sexes and all their appurtenances, which pious emperors, kings, or other God-fearing persons have bestowed upon the same Church of Gerunda, just as you now appear to hold them according to lawful order.

Therefore, yielding to your salutary petitions, from this present tenth indiction, by this our apostolic privilege we strengthen, confirm, and establish in perpetuity, for the use and benefit of the same Church of Gerunda over which you preside, all the houses, cells, churches, estates, courts, parishes, lands, vineyards, meadows, and forests, together with the male and female servants, and all other possessions which emperors, kings, and other God-fearing persons have bestowed or shall hereafter bestow upon the same Church.

Together with the *raficum*, that is, pastureland [uncertain], we confirm all these things in every respect under your authority and power and that of your successors.

We establish, under apostolic censure, or the declaration of divine judgment, and under the prohibition of anathema, that no person, great or small, shall ever be permitted to exercise any force or oppression against any of its possessions, to claim any authority over them, to impose any exaction, or [lacuna] to presume to summon them wherever they may be for any cause whatsoever. Instead, their case shall be heard by the foresight of their bishop and settled canonically.

If anyone, which we do not wish, should presume by rash endeavor to act against this privilege established by us, let him know that he is bound by the chains of anathema, and, unless he withdraws himself from the matter [lacuna]. The remainder is missing.

## V. To Adalgar, Archbishop of Hamburg (892)

He decrees that the Church of Hamburg shall have the Church of Bremen as a source of support until it is able to establish suffragan bishoprics.

Formosus, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Adalgar, archbishop of Hamburg.

We suppose that Your Holiness, as had been commanded, was hastening to the apostolic see so that the dispute being conducted between you and Herimannus, the most reverend archbishop of Agrippina Cologne, concerning the Church of Bremen, might reach an end.

But since he has persisted through his representatives and has multiplied his complaint that you did not present yourself, at least through a deputy defender, we are not a little surprised. This gives the strongest grounds for suspecting that one who tries to evade the fairness of judgment does not hate contention.

This is especially so since the most holy archbishop of Mainz, who had been instructed to investigate the truth of this matter through neighboring bishops and fellow bishops, wrote to us that, when the most reverend bishops came to Frankfurt, the matter had been investigated with the greatest care. All the diocesan bishops of the same bishop of Cologne—namely Francho of Tongeren, Vodelbaldus of Utrecht, Wofelmus of Minden, Druogo of Mimidom, and Egilmarus of Osnabrück—testified that, up to your time, no bishop of the Church of Bremen had scorned the manner of subjection to the bishop of Cologne, but that your predecessors, who had governed that Church of Bremen from the time of its conversion to Christianity, had always been subject to the see of Cologne.

Since it is not fitting that the testimony of so many men should be disregarded, and since you delayed either hastening to the appointed time for coming or delegating a deputy, it seemed inhuman to treat so lightly a complaint of such duration and the steadfast insistence of the envoys.

Therefore, constrained on the one hand lest the Church of Cologne lose its right, and on the other lest the Church of Hamburg—which had been established for the calling of the nations—fail for lack of support, we have judged, by way of dispensation, that the Church of Hamburg shall have the aforesaid Church of Bremen as a source of support until, with divine grace assisting, the Church of Hamburg has expanded so greatly that it can establish a bishopric.

Whenever major and especially necessary canonical matters require it, the archbishop of Hamburg, who governs the same Church of Bremen, shall come, either personally or through a deputy acting in his place, when invited to assist the archbishop of Cologne—not under any form of subjection, but out of fraternal charity.

When the Church of Hamburg has expanded, with the giver of all good things providing assistance, and bishoprics have been founded, the often-mentioned see of Cologne shall receive back the Church of Bremen.

For if it is inhuman for secular persons to invade one another’s rights, how much more is it wrong for the most holy bishops to transgress the boundaries established by the Fathers and to litigate with one another, when they ought to offer examples of peace to those subject to them?

This dispensation has been decreed so that peace may flourish, contention cease, and the strength of justice be tempered by compassionate mercy, since we know that without the good of peace no gift is acceptable to God.

## VI. To Herimannus, Archbishop of Cologne (892)

*[Lappenberg, Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch.]*

[Col. 0843D]

Formosus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy brother in Christ, Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne.

Dearest brother, we rejoiced at your visit when we received the venerable priests sent by you. But while we were diligently questioning them in order about your health, we learned from their inquiries that you were suffering from bodily illness, and we felt very great sorrow.

Nevertheless, we are consoled by knowing that it is written in Scripture: “The Lord chastens the one whom he loves, and scourges everyone whom he receives” (Hebrews XII, 6; Proverbs III, 12). We therefore pray that, by Christ’s gift, this illness may prove beneficial to your salvation and that you may quickly recover your health.

We had indeed expected Your Holiness to come to the threshold of the apostles, as we had commanded, so that we might discuss with you in person the general salvation of that barbarian people. But since matters turned out otherwise than we had wished, we attribute this to your illness and cease bringing any accusation on that account.

The dispute that has been conducted between you and Adalgar, the most reverend archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, concerning the Church of Bremen—a matter about which last year we had decided to write to the venerable archbishop of Mainz, so that through his efforts the truth might be investigated and, the uncertainty removed, emerge into clearer light—now appears, as we have learned from his letter, to concern a church belonging to your diocese. The most holy bishops who assembled at Frankfurt testified to this.

Therefore it was necessary to determine the matter by way of dispensation, in such an order that the Church of Cologne would not be deprived of its resources, while the Church of Hamburg, devoted to its pious labor, would not suffer want, thereby being forced to cease a work acceptable to God.

Accordingly, we establish that, until, with the dispenser of all things granting his favor, the Church of Hamburg is able to expand within the borders of the pagans, where bishoprics can be founded, it shall hold the Church of Bremen as a source of support.

For this reason, out of fraternal charity and not under any form of subjection, whenever sound judgment requires that major ecclesiastical matters be weighed, you should not hesitate to come personally, when invited, to assist the Church of Cologne.
