Or, if you are unable to come in person because you are occupied with the work of preaching, you should at least delegate a deputy who will represent you and take part as an assistant in the canonical deliberation.

When, with divine authority assisting, the Church of Hamburg has been enlarged as we have stated, the Church of Cologne shall receive back its own, because among secular affairs it is not fitting for anyone to invade the rights of another; how much less is this fitting for religious bishops, who ought by their leadership to lead the people entrusted to them along the way of justice to the heavenly kingdom.

Our apostolate has not seen fit to deliberate otherwise, lest the aforesaid Church of Hamburg, established for the conversion of the nations, should be destroyed when deprived of support, and lest, compelled by poverty and want, it should cease from a work worthy of God.

This is especially so since our predecessor Nicholas, of revered memory, confirmed the Church of Bremen by his privilege to Ansgar, archbishop of Hamburg, when Louis, the glorious king, intervened through Solomon, the most reverend bishop of Constance.

But since we judged it unworthy for any priest to invade the rights of another while transgressing his own boundaries, we have therefore established this arrangement by way of dispensation, taking account of the circumstances: so that justice may retain its proper force, mercy may show compassion, contention may cease, and charity may remain inviolate.

We have also renewed the privilege of your Church, as you requested, and have sent it to Your Reverence through the priests presently here. We admonish you to love peace in all things and above all, and always to insist upon it. Peace is the special pledge of all the faithful, without which no gift is acceptable to God.

May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your heart and your understanding in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## VII. To Berno, Abbot of Gigniacus

Concerning the privileges of the same monastery.

Formosus, servant of the servants of God, to Berno, the religious and venerable abbot of the community of monks situated in the territory of Lyon, which is known to have been built in honor of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in a place called Gigniacus, and to that venerable monastery forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid, with benevolent compassion, of those distinguished by pious religion, and to grant the minds of those who ask with eager devotion the consent they seek. By this we earn from the Lord, the creator of all things, the greatest reward of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, are undoubtedly brought to a better condition.

Therefore, venerable abbot Berno, hastening to the threshold of the blessed apostles and approaching our apostolic presence, you reported to us that the aforesaid monastery had been built and dedicated solely from your own possessions and those of your cousin Laifinus, in honor of Saint Peter.

So that it might be preserved unaltered by everyone, you offered it through a testamentary document, which you entrusted to us for safekeeping, to the blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, and to us, by God’s grace his vicar, so that it might be granted to you as an everlasting remedy.

You therefore submitted to our apostolate that we should fortify it with the sanction of our apostolic privilege.

Accordingly, accepting with devotion what you have established and judging your petition worthy of assent, we yield to your prayers. Through the present decree, by apostolic authority, we confirm and fortify the aforesaid venerable monastery in perpetuity, together with its cells or dwellings, lands, vineyards, farmsteads, estates, meadows, and forests, together with male and female tenants, as well as the cell called Balma with its appurtenances, and everything in every respect that has been given or granted there by glorious kings or by other God-fearing persons, or that thereafter, with the Lord’s help, shall be given.

In this present thirteenth indiction we confirm and establish all these possessions under the right, jurisdiction, and power of the blessed apostle Peter and ourselves.

No person, whatever dignity he may possess, shall be permitted to inflict any force or oppression there, or to take away in any manner the donated possessions or those that shall henceforth be devoutly donated—not even any of the donors themselves.

Rather, it shall be preserved firm and unaltered by everyone, under the right and protection of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

If, as is human, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery should die, the congregation of that monastery shall always have the right to choose from among themselves, according to God and the rule of blessed Benedict, whomever they judge suitable, by unanimous vote, and to appoint him abbot according to custom.

You have also complained concerning tithes, because it is sought that they be paid by you from your own possessions. If this is indeed the situation, we forbid this, especially since it is written that priests should not be compelled to give tithes.

Whoever, which we do not wish, whether one of the donors or someone else, should presume by rash endeavor to take anything from the donated possessions or those to be donated, or should attempt to bring any accusation against the same monastery or its monks, and should not fear to act against this apostolic privilege of ours, let him know that he is to be bound by the chains of anathema and, unless he repents, excluded from the kingdom of God.

But whoever proves to be a true guardian and observer of this pious statute of ours may deserve to obtain blessing and grace from the Lord our God.

Written by the hand of Sergius, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of November, in the aforesaid indiction, by the hand of Stephen, chancellor of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious lord Augustus Arnulf, crowned by God, was reigning. Farewell.

## Admonition Concerning the Following Letter

The following letter of Pope Formosus has provided the subject of a dispute among scholars, whose definitive resolution is still awaited. Since the distinguished Wilkins wished to present his conjecture on this matter in the latest great collection of the councils of Britain and Scotland, I thought that it should be transferred here, both because the matter itself called for it and because it would not be unwelcome to readers.

Therefore, so that the subject of the controversy might be held more clearly before the eyes, I have decided to present both the letter itself and the dissertation of that most learned Englishman.

## VIII. To the Bishops of England

[Note: [Col. 0845D] This letter appears to have been written after the English synod had been held, although its date is not entirely certain. Concerning this synod, William of Malmesbury writes:

“But to return to our Edward: I think it pleasant to recall what was ordered in his time by Pope Formosus concerning the renewal of the bishoprics. I shall therefore insert it in the very words in which I found it written.

‘In the year 904 after the birth of the Lord, Pope Formosus sent letters to England, by which he pronounced excommunication and a curse upon King Edward and all his subjects, in place of the blessing which blessed Gregory had given to the English people from the see of Saint Peter.

For seven full years the whole region of the Gewisse, that is, the West Saxons, had been deprived of bishops. When he heard this, King Edward assembled a synod of the leading men of the English people. Pleigmund, archbishop of Canterbury, presided over it and strictly interpreted the words of the apostolic legation.

Then the king and the bishops chose a salutary plan for themselves and their people. In accordance with the Lord’s saying, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matthew IX), they chose and appointed individual bishops for the individual provinces of the Gewisse; and what had formerly been held by two, they divided among five.

After the council had been concluded, the archbishop went to Rome with honorable gifts, placated the pope with great humility, and recited the king’s decree, which especially pleased the apostolic pontiff.

On returning to his homeland, in the city of Canterbury, he ordained seven bishops for seven Churches in a single day: Fridestan [alternative reading: Frethelsthanus] for Winchester, Adelstan for Cornwall, Werstan for Sherborne, Athelelm for Wells, and Eidulf for Crediton in Devon.

He also appointed two bishops for other provinces: Bernegus, a suitable man, for the South Saxons; and Cenulph for the Mercians, at the city of Dorchester in Oxfordshire. The pope also confirmed all this, so that whoever weakened this decree would be condemned forever.

He also sent letters to Britain, a copy of which follows.’]

To all the bishops of England, brothers and sons in Christ, Formosus.

[Col. 0847A]

Having heard that the impious rites of the pagans have begun to sprout again in your regions [manuscript: “having heard that the impious rites of the pagans have sprouted again”], and that you have kept silent like dogs unable to bark, we had resolved to strike you with the sword of separation from the body of God’s Church [manuscript: “from the body of the Church”].

But since, as our beloved brother Plemundus has informed us [manuscript: Plegemundus here and below], you have at last awakened and begun to renew the seeds of the word of God once reverently sown in the land of the English, we draw back the sword of devouring [manuscript: “of devotion”] and send you the blessing of almighty God and of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, praying that you may persevere in the good work you have begun.

For you are the brothers of whom the Lord says, among other things: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted?” (Matthew V). And again: “You are the light of the world” (ibid.).

By this he wished to signify that, through the wisdom of the word, the minds of human beings ought to be seasoned by you; and that in your conduct and your life the zeal of good action should appear like the light of faith. Through this light, those who walk toward life may see how carefully they should walk, so that they may reach the promise of eternal blessedness without stumbling.

Now gird yourselves, therefore, and watch against the lion who prowls around [manuscript: “goes around”], seeking someone to devour. Do not allow the Christian faith [manuscript: “religion”] to be violated any longer in your region through a shortage of pastors, nor the flock of God to wander, be scattered, or be dispersed.

When one dies, let another suitable person be canonically substituted immediately. For, according to the law, priests were appointed in greater number because they were prevented by death from remaining. David, considering this [manuscript adds: “and foreseeing in the spirit of Christ that the future Church would remain until the end of the age”], says: “Instead of your fathers, sons shall be born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” [the words “over all the earth” are absent from the manuscript] (Psalm XLIV).

Therefore there should be no delay in substituting another when any priest departs this life. As soon as the death of a brother has been announced to the one who holds the primacy of the first see and is recognized as presiding over the other bishops among you, another should be chosen canonically and consecrated to succeed him.

Who among you ought to hold the primacy, and which episcopal see should excel the others and possess primacy, has been well known since ancient times [manuscript: “from long ago”]. For, as we know from the writings of blessed Gregory and his successors, it is established that in the city of Dorobernia there is the metropolitan see and first episcopal see of the kingdom of the English, over which our venerable brother Plemundus is now recognized to preside.

We do not permit the honor of his dignity to be diminished in any way, but command him to exercise the apostolic vicariate in all things.

And just as blessed Pope Gregory established that all the bishops of the English people should be subject to Augustine, the first bishop of your people, so we confirm that same dignity to the aforesaid brother, the archbishop of Dorobernia or Canterbury [manuscript: Cantuburiae], and to his legitimate successors.

We command, both by the authority of God and by the precept of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that everyone obey his canonical decrees, and that no one prove to be a violator of anything granted to him and to his successors by apostolic authority.

If any person should at any time attempt to resist or diminish these provisions, let him know that he will undoubtedly be punished with a grave anathema and, unless he repents, separated forever from the body of the holy Church which he attempts to disturb.

### Note of David Wilkins
[Col. 0848B] “Here there is an inextricable error. Baronius detected it and, as he thought, remedied it; but meanwhile he introduces no lesser error. ‘In the year,’ says William of Malmesbury, ‘in which nine hundred and four years had passed from the birth of the Lord, Pope Formosus sent letters to England by which he pronounced excommunication and an interdict against King Edward, etc.’ To this Baronius replies: ‘Thus writes William of Malmesbury; but I think that, through the copyist’s error, what happened in the year eight hundred and ninety-four was written as having happened in the year nine hundred and four. It is certain that Formosus could not have lived until that time, but had died long before.’ This is correct with regard to Pope Formosus, but no less erroneous with regard to King Edward. For just as Formosus died nine years before the year 904, so Edward was not acclaimed king in 904, nor for six years thereafter, if our historians have not lost their sight. If, then, it is true that Formosus promulgated this interdict, it must necessarily have occurred in the time of Alfred the Great, who, although he enjoyed the title of king, had nevertheless been driven from his dominion by the Danes and had not fully recovered it when Formosus almost entered upon the pontificate. Malmesbury, or some copyist, therefore seems to have erred, either by subjecting the king to the interdict, or perhaps by writing Edward instead of Alfred. But this does not remove the error either: for those seven whom he says were made bishops on one day were not elected before the year 904 of the Lord, nor subsequently consecrated until Archbishop Plegmund had made the journey to Rome and had brought back the letter from the pope to the bishops which we have given here, together with the absolution—that is, in the year 905 or thereabouts. That letter is also addressed solely to the bishops of England, and contains not a word about the king; so that it is doubtful whether the king was placed under an interdict at all. Certainly, if with Malmesbury we accept Pope Formosus as the author of this interdict and letter, there is a huge error in our histories, one not even to be disentangled by Oedipus. But if I suppose that Formosus has crept in in place of Pope Leo V, I do not see why everything should not be set right.” Thus Spelman.

[Col. 0848D] Gabriel Cossart added the following strictures to Spelman’s notes in the edition of the Councils, volume IX, page 431:

“Malmesbury assigns the English synod not to the year 904, as Baronius says, but to 905: ‘In the year,’ he says, ‘in which 904 years had passed from the Nativity.’ Who could deny that this is the nine-hundred-and-fifth year? And, as you see, the acts of the Church of Canterbury agree. But here a knot presents itself, deserving of a defender: how could this council have been held in the year 905 under Pope Formosus, who had died ten years earlier? How could Formosus have sent papal letters to Edward the Elder [Col. 0849A], when he was not pope during Edward’s reign? Formosus died in 896, whereas Edward began to reign in 901?

“Spelman offers a rather unhappy conjecture for repairing this lapse. ‘If,’ he says, ‘I suppose that Formosus has crept in in place of Pope Leo V, I do not see why everything should not be set right.’ Yet matters will be no less certainly hopeless. First, Leo V was made pope only in 906, and some postpone him to 907. Thus, if there were any room for Spelman’s divination, the error would lie not only in the name of Formosus but also in the date itself [Note: [Col. 0849D] But the more accurate calculation of Pagi and others places the beginning of Leo V with the year 993. MANSI.]. Moreover, Leo V held the pontificate for only forty days. No one will persuade Spelman that in so short a time Leo sent letters to the English, that after reading them a council was compelled to meet in England, that Plegmund, as the council’s legate, reached Rome, appeased the pope, and brought back a letter from him.

“Therefore, if the name of Formosus must be removed, John IX would much more conveniently be substituted in his place [Col. 0849B], since he presided over the Church in the year 905, while Edward was reigning in England. Indeed, Polydore Vergil, in the sixth book of his History, relates that the whole affair occurred under that pope—whether he himself corrected Malmesbury’s error, or learned the matter from other records. Although John X is incorrectly written instead of John IX in Polydore’s book, the same is true in the English History of André Duchesne, who followed Polydore, perhaps with excessive confidence. For I can scarcely persuade myself that he had examined and discussed this difficulty, since in his History of the Roman Pontiffs, even in its second edition, he says that all these events took place in 904, in the time of Pope Formosus and King Edward.

“Baronius attributes the whole error to a copyist who wrote the year 905 instead of 895. But it should have been observed that although Formosus was pope in that year, Edward was certainly not reigning in England [Col. 0849C].

“If to this Baronian correction another is added, and Alfred, Edward’s father—also called Alvred and Aelfred—is written instead of King Edward, no difficulty will remain, except that those seven bishops mentioned here were not created until the year 905. But this is a minor matter, since those who wrote the account followed Malmesbury and must therefore be corrected in the same way as Malmesbury.

“There may be some whom this conjecture does not displease; others may prefer the alternative that substitutes the name of John. We leave the matter undecided.” Thus Cossart.

I freely confess that I do not possess the talent or strength to declare war upon so many vigorous defenders of history, who have fought with considerable distinction in the chronological arena of the Roman pontiffs, or to engage them openly in battle. Since none of those athletes has dared to claim the palm for himself, however, may I—without offending the peace of so many distinguished names in the republic of letters—if not cross hands with them, at least explain my own opinion with an open countenance?

If we believe Platina, Onuphrius Panvinius, Laertius Cherubinus, and the other celebrated men who followed them, Pope Formosus was created on 27 May 991 and died on 14 December 995, while Aelfred was reigning in England. Sergius III, meanwhile, was raised to the Roman see on 25 December 903, while Edward the Elder was reigning, after the papal schism between Leo V, Christopher I, and Sergius himself—three popes of the same year—had been ended. Sergius was the antipope of Formosus III and John IX; he sat in schism against the former in the year 991 and against the latter in 897. Yet, compelled by supporters of both, he abdicated and was driven into exile.

Since, then, at the beginning of the tenth century the face of the Roman Church had been disfigured by so many antipopes and torn apart by so many dissensions [Col. 0850A], what wonder if a false or corrupted name of a pope was reported to Malmesbury from such distant regions, or came to his notice through the account of others who hated Sergius? What wonder if the Canterbury monks heard the name Formosus from Malmesbury’s mouth instead of Sergius? What wonder if Roman scribes, deceived by this opinion, wrongly read the initial word of the letter, which expressed the pope’s name, and entered what they had read into their commentaries, despite the contradiction of all modern chronologies of the popes? Therefore, above all, I think the name of Formosus should be removed from Malmesbury, the first author of this error—through whose negligence many others began to be negligent—and Sergius III substituted in its place. In this way the history and chronology of the pope, King Edward, Archbishop Plegmund of Canterbury, and the seven bishops will all stand according to a correct calculation. All the other authors, however great their names—those who assign this letter to Leo V, John IX or X, King Aelfred, or the year 895—have strayed far from the target and wholly contradict the chronology and history accepted both today and in former times. If, therefore, the error is to be attributed to a copyist with Baronius, it must lie not in the year [Col. 0850B] but in the identification of the pope’s name.

OBSERVATION OF FATHER ANTONIO PAGI ON THE YEAR OF CHRIST 894, NO. 9 AND FOLLOWING

Wartonus, in part I of *Anglia Sacra*, pages 554 and following, discusses this synod—the English one—under the bishops of Bath and Wells, and says that he encountered certain excerpts from a history written by some monk of Abingdon before the end of the tenth century. They contain the following:

“In the year 904, when all Wessex had been completely without bishops for seven years, and the provinces of the South Saxons and South Mercians likewise, the king, together with Archbishop Plegmund, decreed that one bishop should be ordained for each province of the Gewissae, distributing the see among five parishes [Col. 0850C], whereas previously two men had held them. Accordingly, seven were ordained on one day: Frithestan for Winchester; Aethelstan, the first, for Cornwall; Werstan for Sherborne; Aethelhelm, the first, for Wells; Eadulf, the first, for Crediton; Beornoc for the South Saxons; and Cenulf for the South Mercians at our Dorchester.”

No older document concerning this synod survives, since Malmesbury belongs approximately to the middle of the twelfth century, while these events were committed to writing by that monk at the end of the tenth.

There is, however, considerable controversy about the date of this council. Baronius’s opinion, which places the synod in 894, is rejected by everyone; but some connect it with 904, others—with Alford in the *Annals of Britain* and Cossart—with 905, and Wartonus, following Ralph de Diceto, with 909. To me it seems almost certain that the council was assembled in 904 and that the seven bishops were consecrated at Canterbury by Plegmund in 905, according to the decree of that same council [Col. 0850D]. Alford correctly saw that these events occurred in different years, but he wrongly postponed the ordination to 906.

“But,” says Cossart, “Malmesbury explicitly indicated the year when he wrote: ‘In the year in which 904 years had passed from the Nativity.’ Who could deny that this year was 905?” But elsewhere I have already established as a certain rule of chronology that historians often call the current year, or a year only just begun, a year that has passed; and that among the same writers the same year is often called both the year after the fourth and the fourth year, and similarly in other cases. The learned man also relies upon a narrative of this synod taken from the archives of the Church of Canterbury, which begins with these words: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 905, Pope Formosus sent into the land of the English to King Edward, etc.” But this anonymous writer is referring to the ordination [Col. 0851A] of the seven bishops, which he later reports as having taken place after Plegmund had returned from Rome following the council. On his return, he says, Plegmund ordained seven bishops for seven churches in one day in the city of Dorobernia. Certainly Malmesbury, whom he follows, sufficiently indicates that this ordination occurred in 905, as is clear to the reader.

Wartonus, both in the place cited and on pages 209 and following, says that he believes not only the letter of Formosus but also the entire story told by Malmesbury and the *Florilegus* concerning Plegmund’s consecration of the seven bishops and the seven-year vacancy of the bishoprics to be fictitious. Yet not only Malmesbury and Worcester, but also Ingulf, Gervase of Canterbury, Westminster, and the more important historians of England report it. Nor is it surprising if they have erred in some circumstance, since this has happened not only to them, on this point and on many others, but also not rarely to historians with exceptionally keen vision. The very learned man first derives an argument for his supposition from Asser, bishop of Sherborne, whom he says was appointed bishop of Sherborne by King Aelfred, was still in office in 903, and lived until 969 [Col. 0851B]. But from what we brought forward for the year 884, and from what will shortly be said, it is clear that the Asser whom King Aelfred appointed bishop of Sherborne died in 883 and was entirely different from Asser, the writer of this king’s Life. King Edward appointed the latter bishop of Sherborne after the death of Werstan, who obtained that bishopric only in 904; thus both Werstan and Asser II governed that Church for a short time. This is confirmed by the Westminster account under the year 899, where, speaking of Ethelwald, the successor of Asser I and Sighelm, it says:

“In that same year, when Ethelwald, bishop of Sherborne, had died, the province of the West Saxons remained without bishops and pastoral care for seven years, because the Danes were ravaging that province by sea and land.”

[Col. 0851C] Wartonus and others therefore committed a grave error by conflating the two bishops of Sherborne named Asser into one.

Secondly, Wartonus says that Deneulf, bishop of Winchester, was created, according to certain historians of British affairs, in 879 and died in 909. From this he infers that before 904 or 905 the see of Winchester had not been vacant for seven years, and therefore that the English council in question was either fictitious or was assembled in another year. I reply that it cannot be denied that the death of Deneulf, bishop of Winchester, is connected with the year 909 in both Saxon chronologies. But the only conclusion is that both authors erred in recording it, just as they did when they assigned the ordination of his successor Frithestan to 910. Both chronologists therefore erred both in the year of Deneulf’s death and in the year of the consecration of Saint Frithestan, since writers much older than either of those chronologists, and far more numerous and authoritative, testify that Frithestan was elected bishop of Winchester together with six other bishops promoted to other churches, after the Church of Winchester and the others had been vacant for seven years.

[Col. 0851D] Thirdly, Wartonus says that the see of Winchester was occupied in 900 and the following years, and that Deneulf took part in public affairs throughout that seven-year period. He proves this from charters issued at that time for the new monastery at Winchester and from the register commonly called the Hyde Register, where these documents are recited. Wartonus does not produce them, but they are found in Alford, who under the year 901, no. 1 and following, reports a donation made by King Edward to the new monastery at Winchester, to which, among other bishops, Bishop Asser and Bishop Deneulf subscribe. But Alford correctly replies that, since all Wessex had been without a bishop, Asser and Deneulf must be erased from the list of bishops subscribing in that year. Nor can it be doubted that those subscriptions were added later, and perhaps that the whole charter is fictitious, since Asser I, bishop of Sherborne, and even his successor Sighelm had already died in that year, while Asser II succeeded Werstan only in 904, when he is called bishop of Sherborne [Col. 0852A]. Wartonus also cites a donation made by King Edward to the same monastery in 904, to which, among others, Bishop Deneulf and Bishop Asser subscribe. Alford gives it in full under that year, no. 6 and following, and aptly replies that it is exceedingly ignorant to imagine that Deneulf of Winchester and Asser of Sherborne—the first of that name, whom alone Wartonus acknowledges—were still alive and subscribed in 904.

It is established not only that Sherborne and Winchester had been deprived of pastors before 904, but also Dorchester, over which Bishop Cenulf was placed in that year. In both Saxon chronologies, Bishop Ealhard of Dorchester is said to have died in 897. Cenulf, or Kenulf, therefore cannot have been raised to the see of Dorchester until after a seven-year vacancy. There remains a fourth see that had been vacant for seven years before this council; the other three had been taken from Winchester and Sherborne. This was Selsey, commonly called Selsey, which was then a peninsula but has now been swallowed by the sea, and whose see was transferred to Chichester around the year 1070. Among the South Saxons, among whom Selsey was situated, Beornoc was designated bishop in 904. But since the succession of the bishops of Selsey—or, as we now say, Chichester—is obscure for this period, it is easy to understand from the time during which the other three sees were without bishops that Selsey too had been without a bishop before 904. Consequently, this English council cannot be removed from that year of Christ.

Wartonus observes that English historians consistently affirm the tradition of a seven-year vacancy of the aforementioned bishoprics. He concludes that he does not wish to reject its credibility, but, as I have already noted, he postpones Plegmund’s ordination of the seven bishops on one day to 909. [Col. 0852C] By doing so, however, he himself overturns what he had previously established, since he had earlier asserted that Deneulf of Winchester and Asser of Sherborne—the first of that name, whom alone he acknowledges, like Alford and others—survived until 909. In that case, the sees of Winchester and Sherborne would not have been vacant for seven years before 909. It must therefore remain certain that Plegmund appointed seven bishops on one day at the council held in 904, after there had been no bishops in the kingdom of the West Saxons for seven years.

Nor should anyone be troubled by Wartonus’s assertion that the year 905 was unsuitable for founding the new bishoprics and distributing the parishes, because the Danes had then occupied Northumbria and East Anglia; because the Mercians were not yet subject to King Edward’s authority; and because Edward conquered both peoples in frequent battles during that very year, taking them into his dominion after peace had been made in the following year. For Edward [Col. 0852D], who had resolved to subject all those territories to himself, wished to establish bishops in advance, much as Gelasius II gave a bishop in 1118 to Zaragoza, which was still under Saracen control. There are other examples of the same practice.

The date of this council, entangled in so many controversies, ought now at last to be beyond doubt, once all the arguments that can be brought against it have been resolved.

Cossartius reports the aforementioned synod and the letter of Pope Formosus to the bishops of England in a single continuous account, as though the letter—concerning the proper ordering of the English Church—had been part of that council. In reality, it was issued by Pope Formosus and therefore must not be moved away from the year 894, although the year in which it was written is unknown. In it Formosus says: “Having heard that wicked pagan rites have again arisen in your regions and that you have kept silence, etc.” Therefore this letter was issued by Pope Formosus after 891, when he was ordained Roman pontiff [Col. 0853A], and after Fulco, archbishop of Reims, had written the two letters mentioned shortly below, which Flodoard records as having been sent to King Alfred and to Plegmund, archbishop of Canterbury. In those letters he speaks of a most perverse sect arising from pagan errors and mentions the incestuous incentives of lust, as Alford observes in the passage cited. He adds that Eadmer, a Canterbury monk, an accurate author older than Malmesbury, prefixed the name of Formosus to these letters in Book V of the *New History*.

Hence Parker, a man of the Protestant sect, wrote not inaccurately in *British Antiquities*, when speaking of Plegmund: “Warner declares in his *Fasciculus temporum* that this was an effeminate age. ‘Faith,’ he says, ‘then began greatly [Col. 0854A] to fail, and clerics were devoted to sorcery, while sects arose. For some priests engaged in relations with women and abused them; and, when admonished by the bishops, obstinately continued to defend themselves.’”

Moreover, this letter to the English bishops is not quoted by Malmesbury in the Books of the Kings, as the aforementioned synod is, but in Book I of *On the Deeds of the Pontiffs*, page 211, where he discusses the primacy of the archbishop of Canterbury. It could therefore have been issued during the time of Pope Formosus, but there is no connection between it and the English synod. For after the death of Formosus, while wars threw everything in England into confusion, the kingdom of the West Saxons remained without a bishop for seven years, and after that seven-year period the English council was convened.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 897. STEPHEN VI, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Col. 0853]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON STEPHEN VI

(From Mansi, *Collection of the Councils*)

[Col. 0853B] Stephen VI succeeded Formosus. Boniface, who seized the apostolic see and held it for fifteen days, should not be counted among the pontiffs, since, as a wicked man who had already been deposed twice, first from the diaconate and then from the priesthood, he had been condemned in a Roman synod under Pope John IX. Although both men obtained the see by force, fear, and tyranny, so that one intruder expelled another intruder, Stephen is nevertheless counted in the number and succession of the pontiffs by common agreement, because, to avert the danger of schism, the whole clergy approved him, although he was an extremely wicked man, and the entire Catholic Church recognized him as Christ’s vicar and Peter’s successor.

For when Fulco, archbishop of Reims, learned that he had been substituted for Formosus, he honored him with the services and attentions customarily offered to newly created pontiffs and, as Flodoard testifies, wrote letters to him. He did not fail to understand that he would also be venerating Peter and Christ in unworthy successors if he rendered them the worship and obedience due to them [Col. 0853C]; conversely, he would despise them in those same men if he did not show them the reverence he owed.

He began his pontificate with that sacrilege in which he had the body of Formosus exhumed, clothed in priestly vestments, mutilated by the cutting off of three fingers, and thrown into the Tiber. He also ordered all those ordained by Formosus to be consecrated and ordained again. I am astonished that Onuphrius, in his notes on Platina, rejects the whole history of this event as entirely fictitious, since, apart from ancient records and synodal acts, which will be discussed below under John IX, Liutprand clearly describes and condemns it in these words in Book I, chapter 8:

“After Formosus had died and Arnulf had returned to his own country, the man who had been appointed after the death of Pope Formosus”—namely Boniface, mentioned above—“was expelled, and Pope Sergius”—Liutprand had evidently suffered a lapse of memory in the name—“was appointed through Adalbert. Once established, this man, being impious and ignorant of sacred teachings, ordered Formosus to be dragged from his grave and placed in the papal chair clothed in priestly vestments. He then said to him: ‘When you were bishop of Porto, why did you usurp the universal Roman see through the spirit of ambition?’ When this was finished, he ordered him to be stripped of the sacred vestments, his three fingers [Col. 0854B] to be cut off, and his body to be thrown into the Tiber; and he ordained again all whom Formosus had ordained, after deposing them from their proper rank.

“How wickedly he acted in this, most holy Father, you will be able to observe: even those who had received apostolic greeting or blessing from Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, before the betrayal, were not deprived of it after the betrayal and the hanging of his own body, except those whom perhaps shameful crimes had defiled. For the blessing bestowed upon Christ’s ministers is not poured through the priest who is seen; for neither is he who waters anything, nor he who plants, but God who gives the growth.”

[Col. 0854C] We may gather from the following how great was Pope Formosus’s authority and religious standing: when fishermen later found him and carried him to the church of the blessed prince of the apostles, certain images of the saints reverently greeted him while he lay in the coffin. I often heard this from the most religious men of the city of Rome.

Pope Stephen added guilt to guilt when he convened a synod and approved that abominable, impious, and detestable crime. The very stones, abhorring such a monstrosity, cried out then with a voice produced by their mutual collision that they would rather willingly suffer ruin than allow the Roman Church to remain crushed beneath so great a scandal. At that time the most sacred Lateran basilica, the principal see of the pontiff, collapsed from the altar to the doors, driven by an evil angel. Its walls could not possibly stand when the first cornerstone of the Church’s foundation had been shaken by the earthquake of such a crime.

The heretical innovators of our own time rightly rebuke and detest with you the sacrilegious deed of the pontiff, by which he unjustly exacted punishment from the dead and, contrary to Christ’s institution and God’s command, repeated orders lawfully conferred. But they wrongly rise up against the promises made by Christ to Peter and to the Church on account of that impious act, and, boasting prematurely of victory, celebrate a triumph. For everything that Stephen said or did against Formosus was done by a man inflamed with fury, fulfilling whatever raging madness suggested.

[Col. 0854D] But, in the legitimate exercise of papal authority, he defined nothing contrary to the faith or to good morals. The bishops and presbyters who were summoned to the synod for this reason were no different from Stephen: they pursued Formosus with the same hatred and therefore pronounced the same judgment, knowing that it would please a man driven mad by fury [Col. 0855A]. Accordingly, in this matter we acknowledge violent tyranny in the deed itself, but we firmly deny that any error in faith was defined or approved by Stephen while he was legitimately exercising papal authority. Nothing would prejudice the apostolic see, moreover, if we were to say that an invader who had not been lawfully elected, but was an intruded pseudo-pontiff, had erred in asserting articles of faith.

During his time, after King Arnulf of Germany had died of a disease caused by lice [Col. 0856A], Emperor Wido also died, as Liutprand testifies in Book I, chapter 9. Stephen, the invader of the apostolic see, was overcome by the faction of the nobles that prevailed against Adalbert, prince of Tuscany, and was thrown into prison in the year of Christ 900. After he had held the apostolic see for six years, he was strangled in that same prison and, with God taking vengeance, ended his life by an infamous death.

These things concerning Stephen are taken from ancient records and charters by Baronius, volume X of the *Annals*.

[Col. 0855]

LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE STEPHEN VI

(From the Councils of Mansi and Acheri’s *Spicilegium*)

LETTER I. TO ARNOUST, ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE

[Col. 0855B]

Privilege of the archbishopric of Narbonne

STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow-brother ARNOUST, archbishop of the first see of the holy Church of Narbonne, and through you to that venerable Church forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this we earn from the Lord, the creator of all things, the richest reward, when venerable places, properly ordered, are undoubtedly brought to a better condition.

Therefore your Fraternity’s reverence requested that, by the privilege of this apostolic authority of ours, we should confirm all the immovable property of the same holy first see of the Church of Narbonne, built in honor of the saints Justus and Pastor, where the blessed Paul, confessor of Christ, rests in body. This includes all houses, cells, churches, estates, farms, parishes, lands, vineyards, meadows, forests, and half of the saltworks, tolls, or *raficanum* [Rafiam], and shipwreck dues, together with the monastery of Saint Lawrence and its cells, all their adjacent properties and appurtenances, their servants of both sexes, and everything else that pious emperors and kings, and other God-fearing people, have bestowed upon and established in the same holy Church of Narbonne [Col. 0855D], both in the county of Narbonne itself and in the counties of Redès, Minervois, Ausona, Béziers, and Nîmes.

Therefore, yielding to your wholesome petitions, we have decreed that from this present day, in the fourteenth indiction, by this privilege of our apostolic confirmation, we strengthen, establish, and confirm forever by our apostolic authority, for the use and support of the same holy first Church of Narbonne over which you are known to preside, all houses, cells, churches, estates, farms, parishes, lands, vineyards [Col. 0856B], meadows, forests, and half of the saltworks, tolls or *raficanum*, and shipwreck dues, together with the monastery of Saint Lawrence and its cells, all their adjacent properties and appurtenances, their families of both sexes, and everything else that pious emperors and kings, or other God-fearing people, have bestowed upon or shall bestow upon that same church, both in the county of Narbonne itself and in the counties of Redès, Minervois, Ausona, Béziers, and Nîmes.

We wish all these possessions to be held and governed by you and your successors under the firmest legal title, just as they were formerly possessed by your predecessor, Bishop Daniel of blessed memory, and by the reverend Sigebod, bishop of that same first see of Narbonne. We likewise confirm them in every respect under your authority, power, and benefit, and under those of your successors [Col. 0856C].

We establish by apostolic censure, under the invocation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no person, great or small, shall ever be permitted to inflict any force or oppression upon any of these possessions, to exercise any authority over them, to distrain anyone, to exact any kind of toll from them, or to summon them to court anywhere for any cause, except that their case be heard and regularly settled [or: confirmed] in the presence of the archbishop.

We also wished to add, by our authority and according to canonical sanction, that if, by divine calling, you or your successors should depart this life, then, so long as someone worthy of exercising the office of bishop of that Church of Narbonne is found within it [Col. 0856D], no one may enter it from another place or, relying upon any dignity or royal authority, usurp for himself the aforementioned see. Rather, the assembly of neighboring fellow-bishops who are willing [or: able] to attend shall proceed without the prohibition of any power, and he shall receive the dignity of the blessing of the clergy or people.

If it should happen that one of the suffragan fellow-bishops dies, the metropolitan bishop shall seek the election of that people and take care to visit it, since it is a widowed Church. But if no one should be found there capable of bearing the priestly burden [Col. 0857A], then, by canonical authority and with our apostolic permission, it shall be lawful for him, without any reconsideration, to enthrone from his own Church someone who is worthy and able to preside as pastor over that suffragan Church.

If anyone—which we do not desire—should presume to act with reckless boldness against this apostolic privilege of ours, piously established by us, let him know that he is bound by the chains of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God. But whoever proves to be its true guardian and observer shall obtain blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of Nicholas, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of August, in the fourteenth indiction. Farewell. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, by the hand of Stephen, bishop of the holy Church of Nepi, treasurer [or: in the treasury] of the holy Church of the apostolic see, while the most pious lord Augustus Arnulf, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning in his first year.

LETTER II. TO ARIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE

Complaint that the Jews have been granted the power to possess allodial property

Pope STEPHEN to ARIBERT, archbishop of Narbonne, and to all the rulers of Septimania and Spain, greeting.

It is fitting for us, who have received the key of the heavenly granary in apostolic succession, to offer the medicine of faith for every plague of the divine flock. If we cannot provide a measure of wheat, let us at least be able to contribute a sextarius [or: a small measure].

Therefore we were touched with grief and troubled even unto death when we learned from you yourself that the Jewish people, always rebellious against God and disparaging our ceremonies, possess, within the boundaries and territories of Christians, hereditary allodial estates in villages and suburbs, as though they were inhabitants of Christian communities, by virtue of certain commands of the Frankish kings. For those enemies of the Lord have dangerously purchased for him things which [lacuna] are, and Christian men cultivate their vineyards and fields. Within the cities and outside them, Christian men and women who live with these transgressors are defiled day and night by words of blasphemy [Col. 0857D], and the wretched men and women continually render to those aforementioned dogs every service that can be named or imagined.

This is especially grievous since possessions of this kind were promised to the fathers of the Hebrews by Moses, their chosen lawgiver, and by his successor Joshua, and were enclosed and delimited by these boundaries, sworn and handed over by the Lord himself to those unbelievers and their wicked fathers; yet, deservedly, they have been taken away from them as vengeance for the crucifixion of the Savior.

And indeed the teacher of the Church declares to orthodox flocks, saying: “What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what partnership has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Corinthians 6). And the supreme counselor of the Word admonishes us, saying: “If anyone says to him, ‘Hail’” (2 John 11), etc.

The rest is missing.

LETTER III, or

[Col. 0858A]

Privilege for the monastery of Vézelay

STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to EUDO, venerable abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and to the entire congregation of that monastery, forever.

Whenever those things are requested from us which plainly accord with reason, we ought willingly to grant them and provide appropriate assistance for the desires of those who ask. And therefore, because you requested that we should issue an apostolic-see privilege for the monastery of Vézelay, over which you are known to preside—a monastery evidently built long ago by Gerard, a most noble and Christian man, and by his wife Berta, in honor of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, mother of that same Lord of ours Jesus Christ—in the kingdom, namely, of Burgundy, in the county of Aval, and which was granted by the aforesaid founders, with pious devotion and by the instrument of their testament, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: moved by your prayers, we have willingly decreed that this should be done.

By this apostolic privilege, therefore, we confirm and establish that no king, no bishop, no count, and no other person whatsoever shall be permitted to disturb that monastery, or to diminish, remove, or apply to his own uses—under any pretext or occasion whatsoever—those things which have been offered there by the founders just mentioned or by other faithful people, or which may happen to be offered in the future. Rather, we wish and command that they be possessed without disturbance for the support of that monastery and for the uses of the abbots and monks serving God there under the rule of the holy Father Benedict.

This is on the express condition that none of our successors, the pontiffs of this holy see in which, by God’s authority, we serve, shall ever or anywhere in future permit any of these possessions to be granted as a benefice to anyone, exchanged, or conceded under any form of rent. Instead, our successors, receiving only the rent assigned in the founders’ deed of donation—namely, one pound of silver each year—from the founders who made this holy Roman Church heir of that monastery, shall diligently strive, through fatherly support and pastoral vigilance, to bestow their care upon that monastery against all who attack it.

We also establish that, when the abbot of the aforesaid monastery dies, no other person shall be appointed there through any device of concealment, except one whom the consent of the monks, in accordance with the fear of God and the institution of the Rule of Saint Benedict, has chosen, and whom the pontiff of this apostolic see has judged should be appointed, or whose appointment he has approved at the monks’ suggestion.

To this present chapter we also append the following provision, so that we may exclude avarice: no king, no bishop or priest, nor any of the faithful, either personally or through an assumed intermediary, shall dare to receive anything in any form as a gift in connection with the appointment of that abbot or of clerics or priests, or with the giving of chrism, the consecration of the basilica, or any matters pertaining to that monastery; nor shall the abbot himself presume to give anything for his appointment, lest on this account the things offered by the faithful to a pious place be consumed.

Nor shall the bishop of that city or diocese celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of that monastery; nor shall he announce stations in that same monastery, lest the peace of God’s servants be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering; nor shall he presume to demand provisions or lodging dues from it.

As for receiving the faithful and religious men, and showing the charity which the Apostle commands to be offered to all according to the capacity of the place and its resources, we not only do not refuse this to be done there, but also recommend it. Yet the number of the community must be preserved in such a way that neither an excessive number should bring poverty nor too few inhabitants cause the place to be abandoned.

We also confirm by our authority the privilege granted to that monastery by our predecessor, Pope Nicholas of pious memory, except only that he assigned it under the name of the handmaids of God who, because of the frequent disturbances of the world, are now unable to remain there in an orderly manner. We, however, for the sake of more suitable usefulness, decree appropriately that they should be under the habit of monks.

If, however, any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person should attempt to act against this charter of our institution, struck by apostolic anathema, let him lose the dignity of his power or honor, recognize himself guilty before the divine judgment, and—unless he mourns the things he has done wrongly—be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the strict vengeance of eternal judgment.

But upon all who rightly observe the provisions made for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

[Col. 0858B–D]

Written by the hand of Samuel, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Samuel, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, while our lord Landebert, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, was reigning as great emperor, in indiction 15.

**In the year of the Lord 897. Pope Romanus.**

[Col. 0859]

## Historical Notice

*(From Mansi, The Most Extensive Collection of the Councils.)*

Romanus, a native of Galesia, born to a father named Constantine, became pope in the year of the Lord 900. He sat for four months and twenty days. He thoroughly disapproved of the acts of Stephen held against Formosus, and crowned Louis IV, the son of Boso, emperor after Berengar had been driven out. *(From Liutprand.)*

[Col. 0859]

## Letters of Pope Romanus

*(Mansi, in the work cited above.)*

### First Letter: To Riculfus, Bishop of Elne

[Col. 0859C]

Romanus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Riculfus, bishop of the holy Church of Roussillon, and through you to that same venerable Church, forever.

Whenever those things are requested from us which accord with the interests of the holy Churches, it is fitting that we grant them willingly and provide appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. And therefore, most holy Bishop Riculfus, when you came for the sake of prayer to the most holy thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, you represented to our apostolate that we should confirm and fortify by a privilege of our apostolate the same holy Church of Roussillon, over which you are known to preside, together with the cell of Saint Felix and the estate called Torrente, as well as the estate called Alamannis and Spedulia; and, for the suitable benefit of your Church, the property from Tetrafita above its cloister, together with the cell of Saint Julian, with its waters, mills, and lands from the mountain called Auriol, along with everything generally belonging to them; and whatever Miro, who is called count, granted to that same Church of yours; as well as the estate called Nogaretum; and all the other possessions which pious emperors and kings, or other God-fearing men, have bestowed or will bestow upon that Church, both in that county itself and in other places.

Therefore, we, to whom the care of all the Churches of God has been entrusted, favoring your salutary petition and moved by your prayers, because we desire that ecclesiastical property be preserved unimpaired through its legal authority, fortify by this our apostolic privilege the aforesaid holy Church of Roussillon, with all the possessions mentioned above, by the apostolic authority granted to us in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and confirm that they are to remain perpetually unharmed.

This is together with the Church of Saint Mary, built by a certain woman named Anastasia, who was also called Mater, and which remains subject to your Church, to pay annually to your aforesaid Church one solidus. We also confirm there, justly and canonically, half of the toll and traffic—that is, the market dues—together with the pasture dues, and half of the saltworks; and all the churches belonging to that same Church of Roussillon, from the confluences of the port of Jardon as far as the sea, and from the boundary of Narbonne as far as Basillun; and whatever, as was stated above, the same aforementioned count Miro granted there; as well as the estate itself called Nogaretum; and the other possessions which the pious emperors and kings and the rest of Christ’s faithful have granted there by their charters, or will grant anywhere in the future.

We establish these things justly and canonically, provided that you have requested them from us justly and reasonably and that they are not being unlawfully held by other men.

It is likewise our will that no person be permitted to create any accusation or any kind of opposition concerning all these things against you or your successors in the episcopate, because we wish the privilege of every Church to remain undisturbed. Concerning the monasteries canonically belonging to your Church, we establish in the same way that they are to remain subject to it, as is just for one who makes a rightful request.

If, however, any count, public judge, or any other person should at any time—which we do not wish—presume to act or contend against this our apostolic privilege, or should attempt in any way to violate the provisions we have made for the love of divine worship, let him know that he is bound by the chains of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God. But whoever proves to be its true guardian and observer may deserve to obtain blessing and grace from the Lord our God.

Farewell.

Written by the hand of Gregory, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the first indiction, on the Ides of October, by the hand of Stephen, called Calator, of the holy apostolic see, while our lord Lambert, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, was reigning as great emperor [read: emperor], in the sixth year, and in the sixth year of his pontificate [read: consulship], in the first indiction.

### Second Letter: To the Servant-of-God, Bishop of Girona

[Col. 0862A]

Romanus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend Servant-of-God, bishop of the holy Church of Girona, and through you to that same venerable Church, forever.

Just as, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, the power of binding and loosing was given by the Lord himself to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, as the Gospel reading confirms when it says among other things, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” and so forth, so the apostolic see, supported by canonical and royal authority, is required by both divine and human law to provide assistance and the rightful support of petitions to all the Churches of God spread throughout the world.

Therefore, venerable Bishop Servant-of-God, you came to the apostolic see and, after the Church of Girona had been received justly and canonically, with Hermomirus expelled, deposed, and excommunicated, you represented to us that by this privilege of our apostolic confirmation we ought to confirm all the immovable property of that holy Church of God of Girona, dedicated in honor of the holy ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and our Lady, where the blessed martyr Felix rests bodily: namely, houses, parishes, cells, churches, estates, and islands—Majorca, namely, and Minorca—as well as courts, parishes, lands, vineyards, meadows, and woods, together with households of both sexes and all their appurtenances and dependencies, which pious emperors, religious men, or other God-fearing persons have granted to that Church of Girona, just as you appear to hold them until now in lawful order.

Therefore, moved by your salutary petitions, we decree and, from this first indiction onward, by this our apostolic privilege strengthen and confirm them, and establish them forever for the use and benefit of that Church of Girona over which you are known to preside. These are: all houses, cells, churches, estates, courts, parishes, lands, vineyards, meadows, and woods, together with their households, and all the other possessions which emperors, religious men, or other God-fearing persons have granted or will grant to that Church, both in those counties themselves and in other places, together with the traffic dues or pasture dues.

We confirm all these things in every respect under your dominion and power and under that of your successors, establishing by apostolic censure, under the solemn appeal of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no person, great or small, shall ever be permitted to exercise any force or oppression concerning any of its possessions, to claim any authority over them, to distrain anyone, or in any way to exact toll from them, or presume to summon them to a court anywhere for any cause whatsoever, unless their case is heard and canonically settled under the oversight of their bishop.

If anyone, however—which we do not wish—should presume with reckless boldness to act against this privilege, piously established by us, let him know that he is bound by the chains of anathema and, unless he repents, is excluded from the kingdom of God. But whoever proves to be its guardian and observer may obtain blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of Sergius, archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the first indiction. Farewell.

**In the year of the Lord 898. Saint Tutilo, monk of Saint Gall.**

[Col. 0863]

## Historical Notice concerning Saint Tutilo

*(In Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin.)*

Tutilo, a monk of Saint Gall, was called *Itinerarius* (“the Traveller”) toward the end of the ninth century because he was accustomed frequently to go abroad from the monastery; after his death he was reckoned among the blessed. He was an outstanding poet, painter, and musician. Some of his poems, among them several tropes or chants, were published by Canisius, *Antiquae Lectiones*, vol. II, part III, p. 212. More concerning him is found in Jodocus Metzler, *On the Illustrious Men of Saint Gall*, I.24. See also *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 671.

**In the year of the Lord 898. Wolfhard, priest of Hasenriet.**

[Col. 0865]

## Life of Saint Walpurgis, Abbess of Heidenheim in Germany, by Wolfhard, Priest of Hasenriet

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict.)*

## Preliminary Observations

[Col. 0865A] 1. Saint Walpurgis, or Walpurga—called by others Walburgis or Galburgis—abbess of Heidenheim, must be distinguished both from Walpurga, the Westphalian virgin of the monastery of Heres, or Nienheers, mentioned in the *Acts of Saint Rembert, Archbishop of Bremen*; and from Saint Werburga, daughter of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, and of Saint Ermenild, whom some call Walpurga. She of whom we here undertake to treat had several writers, who devoted their efforts to describing and elucidating her deeds, besides the authors who wrote about her brothers Saints Willibald and Wunebald.

2. The first author encountered is not Saint Willibald, her brother, as designated by the Centuriators—although no work by him on Saint Walpurga is found—but Wolfhard, priest of the monastery of Hasenriet or Haser, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Eichstätt. This monastery, founded by Charlemagne, was later transferred by Emperor Arnulf to secular canons. Wolfhard dedicated his composition to Erchanbald, bishop of Eichstätt from the year (as they say) 884 to 802 [sic]. To this composition he later added three books of Miracles, and moreover promised a Dialogue on Saint Walpurga in the preface to Book IV; whether he composed it is uncertain. The second author was Adelbold, ordained bishop of Utrecht in 1008, according to William Heda in his book *On the Bishops of Utrecht*. The third was Medibardus or Medingaudus, a poet of obscure name and date, who celebrated Saint Walpurgis’s deeds in rhythm; these are his verses in his preface:

> Wolfhard made prose; Medibardus made rhythm.

The fourth, Aldebert, abbot of Heidenheim, briefly treated the same matters in his *Historical Account*. The fifth was Philip, formerly abbot of Barisis of the Cistercian Order, made bishop of Eichstätt in 1306. After these authors come the nuns of the monastery of Saint Walpurgis within the walls of Eichstätt, who caused an epitome to be made from the works of others, “by the art of printing, but in style, order, and form from the most ancient original book of their monastery; wishing not for novelties, but to recall ancient things to the memory of very many people, since at the monastery of Saint Walpurga of the order of the gracious father Saint Benedict, in which the body of the same virgin Saint Walpurga rests, her Legend and Life are very frequently requested without number.” Peter Stevartius, doctor of Liège and director of the Academy of Eichstätt, printed and illustrated this Life together with the four books of miracles written by Wolfhard in 1594. Godfrey Henschen, in the Bollandist February, revised it together with other texts published by Canisius and Gretser and explained it with learned commentaries; he added readings customarily read concerning Saint Walpurga in certain churches. Here we present Wolfhard alone, omitting certain miracles here and there; of this we have warned the reader in the appropriate places. Whoever wishes for further material should consult Bollandus for 25 February, where he will find the other authors, apart from Aldebert’s *Account*, published in Gretser, book II of the *Observations on the Life of Willibald*. Let him also read Stevartius, and John Spagnoli, doctor of theology and lately archpriest of the monastery of Saint Remigius near Rheims, who published Saint Walpurgis’s Life in French.

3. The renown of Saint Walpurgis was great in the ninth century, as is evident both from her relics distributed in various places and from the oratories dedicated to her—of which we shall speak in the Appendix to Wolfhard—and finally from her miracles at Eichstätt, Mowenheim, and Tiel in the duchy of Guelders. Evidence for this is supplied by Wolfhard and by the two letters of the custodian of Tiel to Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht from 1008 to 1027. In these letters, published by Bollandus, various miracles of Saint Walpurgis performed at Tiel are recorded.

4. What is lacking in the history of Saint Walpurgis must be supplied from the *Acts* of Saint Wunebald for the year 771 and of Willibald for the year 781.

## Wolfhard’s Preface to Bishop Erchanbald

[Col. 0867]

[Col. 0867A]

To the most blessed lord and pontiff truly most worthy of God, ERCHANBALD, his priest WOLFHARD asks that, in Him who is the way, the truth, and the life, he may find the way, the truth, and the life.

You require of me, Father to be remembered through the ages and prelate renowned throughout the world, that I should diligently strive to record, to the praise and name of the life-giving Trinity and for the stirring of the minds of the Lord’s people, the signs and wonders which divine mercy has performed in our times through Walpurga, Christ’s virgin now most renowned in the world, after painstaking inquiry, insofar as the generous and divine Trinity itself has bestowed them. For a heavy burden is imposed on me by you, one heavily weighed down by the grave burden of sins, since for one liable to sin it is dreadful to handle sacred matters and to mingle what belongs to others with what is not one’s own.

Yet, most glorious pontiff, because I have learned that you are a man of desires, and see that, like the prophet Daniel, you are ever more curiously investigating new things from hidden places, I am greatly constrained and surrounded on every side by immense difficulties. Entirely ignorant of what I should choose, I first steel the face of my mind, shut up with shame, because I do not doubt that I am unworthy. Then, considering the rule of obedience, the first form of humility, I fear that if I disdain with a proud ear the words of him who commands, I shall incur the law of transgression. Turning the point back upon myself, I languish in the weakness of inexperience; then, against my weakness—indeed, against my scrupulosity—I set forces not my own but Olympian.

Again, if I attempt the undertaking, though trembling, I am terrified lest the reader brand me with the reproach of being *philocompic* [Note: [Col. 0867D] That is, pompous. Greek *kómpos* (*κόμπος*) means “pomp,” and *philókompos* (*φιλόκομπος*), “pompous.” Read Fridegod’s poem *On the Deeds of Saint Wilfrid* for the year 709.], when, passing over philosophical men and men of distinguished talent, who in prophecies are designated by the name of the pen, I, who do not deserve even to be styled by the name of a green rush, begin so arduous a work in an unpolished style. And I fear that the untamed pride of many worldly people, who insolently trample underfoot the ways and Lives of the saints and, if they hear any of their wonders, receive them with a louse-infested ear, may, hearing me set forth publicly unheard-of yet wholly true miracles, begin to gnaw at them with canine tooth and prefer falsehoods to the truest things.

Beset by these and countless other difficulties, because I am full of contagions as a hedgehog is of spines, to speak in Solomonic words, the frequent meditation of my mind is an affliction of the flesh (Ecclus. XII.12). Therefore, fleeing to the citadel, I shall cry to the Lord in these words: “Lord, thou shalt open my lips, and my mouth shall declare thy praise,” so that, with his help—though I am of frail flesh—the requirement of your command may be discharged. I commend myself, therefore, again and again to the merits of the virgin and to your, Father, unwearied prayers, that they may obtain for me a path on which to go and lead me by a happy journey to the end.

## [Book I]

## The Chapters Begin

[Col. 0867C]

I. On the origin of the virgin Saint Walpurgis. II. How Blessed Walpurgis became abbess after the death of her brothers. III. On the occasion when a heavenly light shone in the lodging of the virgins. IV. On the occasion when Christ’s virgin restored a dying girl to life. V. The occasion when Walpurgis departed from the world. VI. The occasion when she appeared to Bishop Occarius. VII. The occasion when she came to the borders of Eichstätt. VIII. The occasion when the virgin’s mausoleum was opened. IX. On the occasion when an epileptic encountered the virgin’s relics and was cured. X. On another epileptic cured. XI. On Abbess Liubila, afflicted with gout. XII. On a certain man crippled from birth. XIII. On a candle illuminated from heaven. XIV. On a mother and daughter cured. XV. On a paralytic woman cured. XVI. On a certain lame man cured. XVII. On a woman whose leg was broken. XVIII. On six signs performed in one woman. XIX. On a bent woman made upright. XX. On a certain squeamish man cured.

## The Life Begins. Chapter I

[Col. 0867D]

Accordingly, after the blessed people of the English, through the apostolate of the memorable Pope Gregory—who, even if he did not deserve to be and be called the apostle of other nations, did deserve to be and be called the apostle of this people—had been rescued from the darkness of unbelief and had begun to embrace Christ’s holy name and Christianity, it put forth an offshoot like the root of a fruitful tree planted beside the moisture of cold marble; and, as if from the shoot of its first and original youth in faith, it grew into a great tree, the stream of evangelical teaching supplying it with verdure. Many branches drawn from it grew so greatly that, crossing the Ocean, they put forth wondrous shoots and became taller than the woods of our land.

A blessed branch of this towering tree was Boniface, the orthodox bishop. Because his merit in faith was worthy of imitation by all, setting aside the boundaries of his native land and its sweet fields, while he made his way as an exile along an unknown path, he received the mitre of the highest pontificate at Mainz and began to regard our foreign soil as though it were his own.

Two blessed confessors of Christ, Willibald and Wunebald, with their most chaste sister, Walpurga, Christ’s virgin, were branches of that same flourishing and leafy British tree extended as far as us. Likewise desiring to journey abroad for love of their heavenly homeland, they followed the king who “went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and return,” their loins girded with the covering of chastity and carrying in their hands the lamps of good works.

The former, after much emaciation of his frail body, with which he had afflicted himself throughout many regions, attained the summit of the episcopate when, in obedience to the rule laid upon him, he was ordained by the aforementioned bishop Boniface of pious memory. He obtained the flock as faithful pastor of the Church of Eichstätt; and there, leading among men a heavenly and angelic life, when the hour of the Lord’s call came, he entrusted to the saving Lord, the supreme shepherd, the sheep he had ruled, and flew away to receive his reward in a most blessed end.

The other, wholly devoting himself to Christ’s service, rejected with a wholly pure heart all worldly things, chose as his dwelling-place the place called Heidenheim, and there fortified himself by prayer, strengthened himself by hope, armed himself by faith, stoutly bore the monastic life which he had undertaken with his brother, and led many onward to the rule of good living. Then, when the time of heavenly recompense arrived, he entered the gates of heaven in assurance and left the mass of his outward man to be buried in the aforesaid place of Heidenheim, to receive it, and no other, with the other saints on the last day of the Lord’s judgment.

Then the one whom he left surviving in this life—namely, the outstanding bishop Willibald, whom, because of the sacred summit of his episcopate, we placed before his brother in the order of writing—although he lived some years after his brother’s most blessed end, took most diligent care to bury the lifeless body of his own brother and, as was fitting for so great a man, buried with hymns and songs one now a pilgrim from the world and a citizen of the angels.

## Chapter II

Thus far we have briefly passed over the memory of the blessed brothers, Willibald and Wunebald, so that the people devoted to Christ might know that men of heavenly soldiery and angelic life, of one and the same merit, had a sister: Walpurga, namely, Christ’s bride and virgin. Now, since, with her aid, I strive to turn my pen to that same woman, let it suffice that enough has been said of these matters.

Therefore, after the departure of blessed Wunebald, a man of wonderful holiness, the virgin Walpurgis, admirable to those living piously, gathering together all the nuns who could truly be devoted to Christ, began most earnestly in the aforesaid place of Heidenheim to adhere to the Lord’s commandments, having abandoned and trampled down all worldly things and the many and innumerable transitory pomps of this world. Persisting night and day in prayer, ever applying herself to vigils and fasts, and preserving the chaste body she had kept from the first freshness of her birth, she commended her whole self more intently to the Lord, so that he might preserve in chastity of body the woman whom he had fortified by faith. Thus she always had the Lord as protector and guide in all her works, and obtained whatever she asked.

## Chapter III

[Col. 0870B]

It happened that, while she dwelt in Christ’s diligent service in the monastery of Heidenheim founded by her brother, after the evening office had been completed and she was returning from church to her customary lodging, the blind darkness threatened the approaching night. A certain custodian of that church, named Goumeradus, foolishly refused her the guiding light she requested. But she, as is the custom of holy minds, bore the injury done to her with a patient spirit. When the nuns, as the time properly required, went to table for supper, she sought her bed without having eaten.

Then, in wondrous fashion, so great a light shone in the common dormitory of those nuns until the sounding of the morning office that, because of the excess of its brilliance, it seemed to penetrate the innermost parts of the earth. Therefore all those consecrated to God who saw these things were astonished, and all exulted with joy; they came devoutly to Mother Walpurga and reported the terrifying vision of light.

But she, turning herself wholly to the Lord and shedding tears, broke out in these words: “To thee, Lord, whom I, thy humble handmaid, determined to serve from my cradle, I render thanks for the gift bestowed: thou hast deigned, to stir the minds of thy handmaids who cling to me, to visit me, unworthy as I am, with the comfort of thy light and to dispel the dense darkness of grim horror by the rays of thy mercy. And this cannot be attributed to my merits, but to the mercy of thy freely bestowed generosity and to the prayers of my brother, thy servant and mine, devoted to thee.”

## Chapter IV

[Col. 0870D]

Moreover, Walpurgis, the virgin so often mentioned and ever to be held in remembrance, bearing heavily in her heart the death of her brother Wunebald, as is customary for women of her sex, happened one evening—while no one in the monastery perceived it in the slightest—to go out and arrive at the house of a certain rich man, where she stood alone before the doors like some unknown pilgrim.

When the master of the house, or the household within, busy in the duties of service, noticed her standing there but did not know who she was, the householder, anxious together with all his household lest the rabid boldness of his dogs should tear to pieces by biting a person of whatever condition she might be, ordered her quickly to state who she was.

Then she said: “By no means will your dogs, as you fear, be able to touch me with their mad tooth, nor will they be able to bite Walpurga—for that is my name. He who led me safe to your house will bring me back sound to the place from which I came; and he who brought me, unknown to you, to your threshold will bestow on your house the gift of healing, if with all your strength you believe him to be the physician of physicians.”

On hearing this, the distinguished man immediately sprang up from the place where he sat and, dismayed in mind, asked why so noble a person and handmaid of the Almighty had stood at his door. She declared that she had not come without cause. Then the aforesaid man received her in his house with every reverence and rendered every service of due attendance.

When the hours of night were to be moderated by the silence of sleep, he tremblingly led the holy virgin, who did not wish to rest elsewhere, into the chamber of his ailing daughter. For the illness was already penetrating the fibres of her heart, and, as the vital breath was cut off, she was struggling with gasping breaths to reach the gates of her gaping mouth by the swift path of death.

Then the father of the girl, moaning over her quivering lips, wailed and prepared the funeral rites for his most beloved daughter with bitter tears.
