Her mother, almost dead already in the inmost recess of her heart, waited in grief, in a faltering voice, for the departure of her dying daughter, for whom the mourning household had already prepared a pyre.

But the most merciful compassion of the Lord, who kills and makes alive, strikes and heals, recalled the sick girl from threatening death; and while the holy virgin prayed throughout the entire night, the girl rose healthy on the following day. When her parents saw this miracle, they gave praise to almighty God.

Then, still trembling, they offered her many gifts and commended themselves wholly to her holy prayers. But she, recognizing Christ as the worker of wonders, rejected the money and returned to the monastery from which she had come; and the more she saw divine mercy active in herself, the more she advanced herself to the degrees of a stricter life.

## Chapter V

I judged it fitting to insert in this little work only these two outstanding miracles which the blessed virgin performed in life and which have reached our memory, lest, by passing faithfully to the other prodigies of signs which the Lord has hitherto worked through her and works daily, through the Lord’s own generosity, I should be blamed for having omitted them. For it seems foolish to begin by narrating the truth of a matter from its end and so reach the heading of its beginning.

Therefore I first described her earlier deeds in a running style, so that what follows might also be recorded through the virgin’s intercessions. Thus, when the holy virgin Walpurgis had wholly established herself in the love of God and overcome the world with its concupiscence—full of faith, distinguished in conduct, abounding in charity, adorned with wisdom, gemmed with chastity, crowned with mercy, supported by humility, and adorned with every virtue—she went to meet the Lord who called her, accepting the swift course of death in order to receive the reward of recompense, and departed by a happy end from this tearful abyss of the world [Note: [Col. 0871D] That is, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, namely the day after Saint Matthias the apostle, says Philip, bishop of Eichstätt, both in her Life and in chapter 31 of the *Acts of Saint Willibald*; and indeed before Saint Willibald, by whom she is said to have been committed to ecclesiastical burial beside Saint Wunebald; thus about the year 780. See the Appendix below.].

In the same monastery in which she had served Christ in her holy purpose, amid the greatest lamenting and cries of grief, she received the rite of mortal burial. There, resting for some time after the body’s dissolution, she gave help by her blessed intercessions to those whom she left surviving in the world and, as a mother, brought up her children.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 0872B]

After a short interval, while the greedy earth still held the ashes of the holy virgin in that same place, it happened that, when the former pastors of that church had died, the venerable man Otkarius [Note: Otkarius, or Otgarius, or Orgerus, the sixth bishop of Eichstätt, is said in the catalogues of the bishops of Eichstätt by Democharis, Bruschus, and Gretserus to have enrolled Saint Walpurgis among the heavenly host with the consent and command of Pope Adrian; concerning this matter, see below in Appendix 1. Otkarius presided over the Church of Eichstätt in the middle of the ninth century. Henschenius, in his preliminary commentary on this Life, no. 24, argues against Democharis, Bruschus, and Gretserus, who place Otkarius’s episcopate from 858 to 881, because Otgarius had already attended the Council of Mainz as bishop in 848. Thus, if he governed the Church of Eichstätt for only twenty-three years, he can scarcely have reached the year 870.] was deemed worthy of the Eichstätt episcopal see.

Since he cultivated the same monastery, which covered the bones of the blessed holy woman, less carefully than propriety required, it is related that one night, while he was sleeping in bodily repose and dreadful darkness provided him with silence, the virgin addressed him in these words:

“Why, Ockarius, who have deserved to be called and to be a bishop, have you until now wished to treat dishonorably the house of God in which I rest in the sleep of my body, and the tomb in which, with my flesh laid away, I await the final day of judgment? For every day I am trampled here beneath the muddy feet of the servants who gather, and I am pressed by indecent footprints. Know for certain, therefore, that I shall disclose some sign by which you may discover that you have acted improperly toward me and the house of God. But if you recognize that you are guilty, you may deserve pardon.”

The outcome proved the matter after a short time had passed. For immediately afterward, when the projecting walls of that structure had been raised and the broad framework of beams was to be placed upon the open walls on the following day, suddenly, after the silence of night had already fallen, the northern wall, rolling itself down to the ground, collapsed in a terrible fall and inflicted a terror unheard-of not only upon the household concerned but upon all who lived around it.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0872D]

When, at daybreak, everyone had assembled in fear to witness such a spectacle, the custodian who was then present there, Reinfridus, announced it by a direct route to the aforementioned bishop with trembling lips. Understanding that the vision he had previously seen in sleep had been fulfilled, he went there with his people and, together with almost all the inhabitants of the surrounding region, restored the church, which he also dedicated with sacred chrism.

After some days had passed, the aforementioned bishop regularly sent there the archpriests Wlto and Adalungus, and he ordered Ommo also to go with them, together with the holy woman Liubila from the monastery of Mowenheim [Note: Mowenhim or Mouhim, now a small town under the authority of the Count Palatine of Neuburg, not far from Wendinga in Bavaria and Pappenheim; Leubila was in charge of this monastery, according to Philip of Neuburg.], so that with the greatest care they might raise the holy ashes of the virgin and transport them with hymns and the harmony of psalmody to the monastery at Eichstätt.

They fulfilled these fortunate commands on a prosperous journey. While the melodies of the bells resounded toward heaven and harmonious spiritual songs rang out everywhere, they weeping for joy lifted the pious remains from the field in which they had been lodged and carried them to the aforesaid monastery [Note: Into the church of the Holy Cross, which was afterward called Saint Walpurgis, as we shall see in the Appendix.]. This was done on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. After they had been brought there with due honor, three days later the same bishop ordered the holy body of the distinguished confessor Wunibald to be carried back to the place from which he had taken the ashes of his sister—that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

## CHAPTER VIII

After blessed Walpurgis had deigned to visit the Eichstätt region in person, and, revisiting her brother’s lands, had been joyfully received by everyone, it happened, as time passed, that the aforementioned holy woman Liubila was so harassed by her relatives and connections, as well as by others living nearby, that they nearly expelled her from her maternal inheritance by force or cunning.

But while she resisted with all her strength, a salutary thought was divinely suggested to her mind: although anxious, she should ask the venerable bishop Erchanbold, who still wore the episcopal insignia of the see of Eichstätt, for the holy relics of the Virgin. If, by God’s granting, she should deserve to be enriched with the sacred ashes, she would consign to God and the virgin the rights belonging to her own property and hand over the gift perpetually into the bishop’s keeping.

Because this undertaking took its beginning from God, it deserved to receive its completion and increase from him. Although at first, when attempted, it seemed extremely difficult, the fortunate and desirable vow nevertheless achieved a fortunate fulfillment. Moreover, after taking the advice of the king and the royal men concerning this matter, the same bishop promised that he would give her the virgin’s patronage [Note: Medieval authors commonly use this word for the relics of saints.]. He later did so at the appropriate time.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0873D]

In the year 893 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the third indiction, while the most serene king Arnulf was reigning with fortunate prosperity, the mausoleum of the blessed virgin Walpurgis was opened in the basilica in which it had been placed in the time of Bishop Otkarius.

The most prudent and sagacious Bishop Erchanbold, outstanding in all affairs, sent religious archpriests with other men of good repute and ordered them to search out the bones consecrated to the holy virgin, to handle those they found carefully, and to divide and deposit them with the greatest reverence, so that the relics long desired might be given to Liubila and the treasure of that body might be preserved through the ages in her church.

Those to whom the bishop’s command came hastened to carry it out, although they trembled with simple-hearted uncertainty. Entrusting themselves entirely to the Lord’s mercy and persisting without interruption in psalms and hymns, they dug and found the ashes of our blessed mother Walpurgis moist as though with a thin fluid, so that drops of dew could seemingly be wrung from them drop by drop [Note: This “dripping,” as it is called, or oil of Saint Walpurgis, is said to have continued to flow from her sacred relics down to the present day; see Appendix 3 below.].

Although they were filled with such moisture, not even a speck of dust was able in any way to adhere to the hands of those touching them. At last, after the portion most eagerly desired had been removed according to the incomparable value of the treasure, they restored the remainder to its place.

What grief, what sorrow of anguish would have invaded the citizens of Eichstätt when such pledges were divided, as they thought that Lady Walpurgis had been wholly taken away from them—let the one who recognizes the truth as truth demands confess it truly! But to those who do not know, as the uninformed townspeople also seem to be, I offer words of consolation, while I affirm on sound grounds that only relics were removed.

The man who took part in this dreadful affair while it was being carried out and deposited the relics that were given into a small reliquary himself narrated these events to me, who desired to write them down.

## CHAPTER X

Meanwhile, while the long-desired gift of patronage was being carried with great rejoicing glory to the aforementioned place, the nunnery of Mowenheim, when they had reached the village of Saint Boniface called Mulinheim, a certain boy afflicted with falling sickness met the bier bearing the sacred burden. When he was placed beneath it, he received the very health he had sought.

Then suddenly, as those who travel there still confess today, such a force of fragrance spread through that place that the noses of those carrying, preceding, and following the bier could scarcely endure it.

On that same day, before the church to which the virgin’s relics were being carried had been entered, a certain little boy named Rudolf, who still rejoices with his life restored, was brought there by his mother. He had been afflicted with the same illness mentioned above. When he touched the bier, he recovered the health of all his limbs and joyfully ran back to the house from which he had come.

## CHAPTER XI

After the holy gifts of that same virgin had been placed upon the altar, with the full praise of the people, in the basilica situated in honor of the Maker and Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Yet Saint Walpurgis at some time ceased to perform miracles for this reason, as Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, testifies in Book II of the Conferences, chapter 28; see Appendix 5 below. Read the preface placed before this century.], on the following night the aforementioned holy woman Liubila—who was then and still is abbess in this monastery—had given her limbs over to sleep with other women consecrated to God in a stranger’s house in that town. She was staying there for three nights because of the hereditary transfer she had made to blessed Willibald of the same monastery, as the law of Sualafeld [Note: Sualafeld is the district or territory in which the monastery of Heidenheim lies; it now belongs to the county of Württemberg.] prescribes, and she was being tormented by a severe attack of gout.

A cleric of venerable gray hair appeared beside her and addressed her thus:

“Liubila, why are you sleeping? Why do you not rise and go to the church?”

She replied to him, as she still maintains, like one sleeping:

“Why must one go to the church now, when the morning signals have not yet been sounded? I myself cannot go there on foot unless I am carried by the hands of others.”

He said:

“Go quickly; do not delay, because blessed Willibald is approaching the church with a great company, wishing carefully to inquire from you how you are keeping his holy sister, who has been laid to rest.”

Immediately she rose, as though she had suffered no trouble, and leaped from place to place. She entered the basilica to which she had been going in perfect health and gave thanks at once to God and to the virgin for the health she had received.

## CHAPTER XII

There was a poor man named Leibolfus who had been born from his mother’s womb so contracted and bent that everyone regarded him as some kind of monster. While he sought both food and the comfort of healing in the same monastery among the many who flocked there for the virgin’s patronage, blessed Walpurgis appeared to him in a vision one night while he was sleeping beneath his bedding and commanded him to go to the church.

When he replied that he dreaded the hoar-frost of the cold and feared the icy assaults, and therefore did not even dare to rise from his resting place, she said to him in gentle words:

“Go, go, poor man, quickly. I shall remove from you the cold beneath which you now suffer and restore the ardent structure of your limbs. In return for this favor, you will have to give me the stools [Note: She calls them tripods below. Adrevaldus also mentions stools or little benches in his book On the Miracles of Saint Benedict, chapter 36, in the second century.] on which you still make use of your bent limbs.”

Although sluggishly, he entered the church and, after remaining there a little while, returned anxiously to the lodging from which he had come. When the desired dawn arose, he went again to the basilica and approached the virgin’s bier in order to receive the benefit.

About the third hour he suddenly began to writhe and roll about, palpitating, and to bend himself upon the pavement. Then, behold, the three-legged stools he had used throughout his life were, as if torn from his hands by divine power, thrown down before the altar.

Thus, with all his limbs made firm and upright, he stood and walked—he who had formerly crawled miserably on his buttocks and completed the painful course of his former life. Now healthy and strong, he continues to serve in that church’s ministry down to the present day, so that it may be clearly demonstrated to all what kind of saint this virgin is, and of what merit before God, since she deserves to obtain such things and similar favors.

## CHAPTER XIII

After this miracle had been performed, the illustrious count Adelbert of Alamannia, devoted to the virgin, came there, brought a sizable candle, and humbly placed it upon the altar. He prayed to the Lord and the virgin for himself and his people, and then, having obtained the blessing, returned to his own home.

Liubila received the same candle, since she was especially familiar with and dear to the aforementioned count, set it upon a candlestick, and happened at that time to leave it unlit. On the fourth day, however, it received a heavenly light. The flame remained in it for three days and nights, and on the fourth day it was extinguished without anyone snuffing it.

At the hour when divine power [Note: Perhaps the reading is “Divinity.” Philip has it thus: “At the hour when divine power wiped away the locks of the radiant fire,” and so forth.] had wiped away the locks of the radiant fire—that is, at the ninth hour—the doors of the church closed of their own accord, so that no one was able to keep them open and passable for nearly two hours. Then Christ, who had closed them, appeared and made them open to those wishing to enter.

## CHAPTER XIV

Two women, a mother and daughter, came there seeking the virgin’s aid. Both had an unsightly curvature of the hands, and they came from the village called Wemedinga [Note: Wendingen, a not unattractive town on the borders of Bavaria, according to Stevartius.].

As they raised the eyes of their hearts toward heaven and with humble devotion sought help from him who made heaven and earth, and as they attended the solemn rites of the Mass, divine power, through the merits of the virgin, came to their aid. At the beginning of the festive singing of the Mass, the mother obtained health and praised God and the virgin.

Then the daughter, carrying uncertain thoughts in her trembling heart and standing with a wavering mind, expressed indescribable joy to her mother over the health restored to her, but mourned over her own twisted contraction. She now saw her mother, whom nature had given her, blessing the Creator of heaven with outstretched hands, yet still saw the wretched curvature reigning in herself.

While she repeatedly reflected on this with an uncertain mind, and remained standing, after the singing of that Mass had ended she too deserved to obtain health from him who wished to reveal himself as the beginning and the end.

Then the same mother and daughter, the nuns with Mother Liubila, and the entire assembled household of both sexes, with rejoicing hearts, gave praises to the Lord in heaven with hymns and songs—he who grants release to the fettered and raises up the fallen.

## CHAPTER XV

A certain woman named Reginswindis was brought to the same monastery. She was a neighbor of that church and so completely deprived of the use of all her limbs that she could not have reached the place by any means except in a vehicle, carried by two people, with her arms inserted and supported on either side.

Her own people carefully laid her before the altar containing the virgin’s bier. Through Walpurgis’s intervention she immediately obtained health from the Lord, and all who were present heard her give thanks to the giver of salvation.

## CHAPTER XVI

There was a man from a village called Megenshaim, named Wolfgerus [Note: Others have Magericchesheim. Stevartius conjectures that the reading should be Merashem, a village near Monheim in the diocese of Eichstätt.]. He had one foot so fastened over the other that, for a sorrowful period of seven years, he had never been able to take a morsel of food while sitting in a circle.

For, in a remarkable fashion, one foot had adhered to and become joined with the neighboring foot, and the raging illness denied the lame man the repose of sitting. Coming to the aforementioned sanctuary of the holy virgin at the appropriate time, and traveling not by walking on his feet but by miserably hopping as though with a staff, he traversed the broad intervening countryside, entrusted himself entirely to her merciful compassion, and immediately recovered the health to walk.

## CHAPTER XVII

There is a village in Franconia called Bergila by its inhabitants, where there was a woman named Engilswindis.

When she wished to hurry from place to place on horseback for the sake of some nearby business, she fell in a swift and dreadful fall from the horse on which she was sitting and was about to fall. The shinbone of her frightened body was broken in this kind of plunge, and the support of all her limbs was miserably shattered [variant: altered]. Although she attempted to use the steps of others, as two years gradually passed she did not deserve to use her own.

At last, the merciful and compassionate Lord, who in his accustomed goodness pitied the wretched woman’s injuries, wished, through the merits of the virgin’s aid, to bring an end to her tearful suffering.

While the most dreadful chaos of the night fleeing the light had troubled the grace of day, and she was arranging her languishing limbs upon the same sob-filled bed, and had tasted at least a little of the grace of rest beneath trembling eyelids, Lady Walpurgis appeared beside her. She has been granted to us by the Lord as an intercessor, promising generously to grant pardon if the woman, removing her doubt, would reveal the faith of her heart.

“Go,” she said, “little woman ignorant of the grace of salvation, and take care to seek out the chief physician for your operation. When you find him willing to perform this service, after the bones have been extracted from within your cut shin, you will afterward obtain from Christ the grace of health.”

When she heard the means of her recovery, she gave thanks to the Almighty with all her strength and hurried to seek the physician’s assistance. Finally fulfilling the salutary commands of the vision, and after the small bones had been extracted, she obtained the grace of her former health.

When she saw that the aid of divine mercy had come to her, she went joyfully, praising the virgin, on her own feet to the monastery. She openly recounted the whole sequence of what had happened, placed the offerings she had brought upon the altar, and also displayed part of the broken shin as proof of her truthful declaration. Leaving there the part of her body that had served as her support, she took the other part back to her homeland.

Liubila, the servant of Christ, took that part, ordered it to be fashioned in silver, and suspended it in the same basilica, so that if anyone heard this and persisted in unbelief, he might come there and open the eyes of his blindness; and when he saw a fashioned part of a woman’s body hanging upon the wall, he might at least depart confounded and, asking pardon for his stupidity, blush.

The rest has been omitted.

# BOOK TWO

Containing several miracles performed in the women’s monastery of Mowenheim in the year 894

[Col. 0877]

[Col. 0877D] I considered it worthwhile, since Christ daily performs and has performed marvelous things through his most famous virgin, to begin long ago collecting them on a small sheet of paper, so that I might seek out what ought to be investigated and, applying careful vigilance, briefly record what I have investigated, insofar as my strength permits.

This is not because, as I think, anyone could fully explain such and so many prodigies as have been performed hitherto in the aforesaid monastery through the merits of the virgin’s intercession and are performed on almost every day. Their number is so great that they can scarcely be brought forth in the speech of the tongue. Rather, I wish the humble pledge to obey the command of the Father who orders it, and gradually to make his way along the path of the undertaking, so that the assistance of the creative Trinity may direct him wherever he is heading.

As I begin the second little book, I nevertheless advise the curious reader to regard lightly the ugly heap of barbarisms in this booklet, to lend the ear of faith to the truth expressed in popular speech, to read simply what he finds here, and to search for a pearl as though in a dung heap. Thus it happens that he may faithfully take away what is his and leave ours uncontaminated.

For wax-bearing bees, although they pour Hyblaean honey from hidden vessels, do not refuse to settle upon foul sewers.

## THE CHAPTER HEADINGS BEGIN

[Note: The chapter headings marked with asterisks are absent from the text.]

I. Concerning the woman who found the lost hairpin.  
II. Concerning the illumination of the woman blind from birth.  
III. * Concerning the place where a little pouch containing blessed tokens was found.  
IV. * Concerning the place where a lost sword was found.  
V. * Concerning the healing of one afflicted with falling sickness.  
VI. * Concerning the place where a pilgrim was killed and proved to be dead.  
VII. * Concerning the place where a girl received a vision.  
VIII. Concerning the illumination of a blind man.  
IX. * Concerning the boy born blind who received his sight.  
X. * Concerning a blind woman.  
XI. Concerning two stolen horses, found at the morning hours.  
XII. * Concerning the place where a lame boy was healed.

## CHAPTER ONE

In the year 894 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the third indiction [Note: Read “the thirteenth,” which indiction began on 24 September in the year 894], while Arnulf held dominion over the fourfold kingdom [Note: Namely, Bavaria with Pannonia, Bohemia, and Moravia, which had belonged to his father Carloman; East Francia with Thuringia, Saxony, and Frisia, which had belonged to his uncle Louis; Alamannia, which had likewise belonged to his uncle Charles the Fat; and Lotharingia. Arnulf was placed over these kingdoms after Charles the Fat abdicated in 897, as Henschenius observed.], in the eighth year of his rule, while the famous bishop Erchanbold governed the see of Eichstätt, a woman, fulfilling certain vows she had desired, went with the husband whom the marriage bond had given her to the monastery already known to almost everyone, the monastery of our mother and of many faithful people, to entreat the Lord, who is near to almost all who call upon him in truth.

There, while she beat her breast with her fists for all the crimes she had committed from the beginning of her maidenhood, and repeatedly sought the pious intercession of the virgin, she asked for the aid of a vehicle, having received the customary blessing.

She then traveled joyfully along the road by which she had come, turning many things she had heard and seen over in her mind. At the first stopping-place on her return, she accidentally lost the risile [Note: Risile, or perhaps rasile, seems to be a rather long pin of the kind women of Rheims still use today for scratching the head and parting the hair; it was customarily fastened into the orah, that is, the head covering.], which she had fastened above her ear to her head covering, without knowing at all how she had lost it.

When she secretly confessed the loss to her husband, he immediately attributed it to the thoughtless carelessness of his beloved wife, who was joined to him in body, and gently reproved her in measured speech, asking why, like frivolous boys, she had carelessly lost the object she had taken with her.

Then she returned to the aid of the mother whom she had previously sought and said:

“If you deign to have pity on your servant, Lady Walpurgis, and are willing to hear the voice of one unworthy, restore to me the loss of the object that has now been taken from me.”

When she had finished speaking, the risile lay openly before them as they sat together. It was not another one, nor changed, but the very same one that had previously provided her with aid, and so forth.

## CHAPTER TWO

Since above we dealt first with the memory of the blind porter, it is fitting that we should tell how he deserved to receive the grace of sight.

While this same man—he is still living and is called Ratfridus—was formerly oppressed by blind darkness and suffered from the evil white films in both eyes that the common people call pearls, he possessed no light of vision whatsoever in his head by which he could see even a tiny spark of light. He came to the monastery and completed two full weeks there.

Meanwhile, it happened that one day he entered the church to pray for himself, the wretched man, to the Lord and the virgin. When the sacred solemnities of the Mass had continued up to the harmonious singing of the Lord’s Gospel, the aforementioned blind man applied his raised right hand to his eye and carried away for the nuns who were attending the singing of the Mass, rejoicing to see it, the cloudy film that had fallen into his hand by divine power. He recovered sight in one eye and, in that same place, rendered the service owed for the gift he had received [Note: Five miracles are omitted here.].

## CHAPTER VIII

A certain poor man of the famous Count Adalbert, named Frideradus, whom I saw with my bodily eyes possessing sight and to whom I offered a portion of bread from the table of my poverty, had been darkened by the foulness of blindness from the very beginning when his mother brought him forth from her womb.

Now, when he had borne the former darkness into old age, oppressed by dreadful blindness in mature years, and his sister provided him with guidance, he approached the threshold of blessed Walpurgis.

When, exhausted by the journey, he had arrived there, he asked to be led before the virgin’s altar, so that by placing upon it the modest gifts he had brought with him he might deserve to obtain pardon for his sins.

He was therefore led to the altar beside which the virgin’s mausoleum stood. When all his limbs immediately grew weary, he prayed as best he could that he might quickly be led away from the altar and that a seat suitable for him might be sought.

When this was promptly done, he rested for a little while with trembling body. Then suddenly he slipped to the ground and began to roll his pale limbs over the stony earth, repeatedly bending himself upon the pavement as though about to close his final day.

When those standing nearby were already discussing his funeral rather than the dignity of the sight he had sought, his little eyes, which had never seen anything, began to drip blood drop by drop, moist with blood, and to stain the pavement abundantly.

When the hour that was then present had passed, he deserved to receive the sight that had long been denied him. Both he himself and all who were present gave thanks to the Most High [Note: Two passages are omitted here as well.].

## CHAPTER XI

When the widely celebrated reputation of the famous virgin had spread far and wide through almost the entire world, the once royal and renowned city of Regensburg also sent its citizens to the same monastery, bringing blessed offerings pleasing to the Most High according to the measure of their previously considered devotion and their acknowledged means.

Having obtained their desirable vow, they entered the basilica with great rejoicing. There, opening the chests of their hearts and bodies, they offered some gifts upon the altar, which had been displayed for them and for all who entered, and sent other offerings from the altar of their most limpid hearts toward heaven.

Having experienced with eyes and ears the reason for which they had come, and having received the blessing they had sought, they camped near the monastery because the hour had grown late, intending to return home on the following day.

But when the silence of dark night arrived and sleep gently approached the doors of their lights, now nearly at rest, thieves—whose ancient etymology derives from *furvus*, that is, “black”—saw that the limbs of the Regensburg men, wearied by the journey, were weighed down by excessive sleep. No watchman was awake, and across the broad extent of the field the animals were scattered.

Two men, whose hearts had already been possessed by a dark desire made more blind than the night, one secretly seized a halter and the other grasped a girth strap, and they carried off the empty capture of two horses belonging to a certain Alamannus named Ratharius.

After the same ineffective robbers had seized their prey and mounted the animals they had taken with brazen audacity, they joyfully set out on the road home.

But he who shows himself glorious and praiseworthy to all in his saints turned the joy of presumptuous greed into shame and sorrow, so that the world’s foolish contentiousness might openly recognize what the omnipotence of Christ in heaven and on earth can do.

For the robbers, carried on another man’s vehicle and skilled in riding, exercised their riding ability through vain vigils in the thick darkness around the monastery beloved of God. They undoubtedly thought that with all their effort and exertion they were treading their ancestral fields, wishing, as though agile, to approach their own homes in cheerful conversation with one another.

When the rosy light of morning appeared, they were found by themselves in a nearby field belonging to the holy virgin’s estate.

It is difficult to consider in the mind, express in words, and record on a page hastening toward other matters what terror seized them and what shame wholly possessed them.

At last, returning to their senses as best they could, the greedy men recognized that a miracle had been performed through the intercession of the holy virgin. Punished beyond words by shame and trembling, they who had previously attempted to enjoy another’s stolen vehicles returned to their own homes on their own feet, leaving behind the horses in which they had earlier rejoiced.

By this sign of the Lord’s manifestation, all who saw or heard it marveled, but most of all those who by divine command deserved to recover the lost animals.

The citizens of Regensburg who had come gave most grateful praises to the one Trinity and returned home, faithfully recounting everything that had happened on the journey, both the blessing they had acquired and sought from the church and the gift of the wonderful sign [Note: The healing of a lame man is omitted here.].

# BOOK THREE

Containing miracles performed there in the year 895

[Col. 0881]

[Col. 0881C] As the sorrowful sequence of the times still advances, the many varying qualities of human minds also change together. From this it is evident that a person cannot always do what he happens to wish. Rather, when the external world slips, the inner spirit also inclines, pierced by various blows, so that it more frequently falls away from the disposition it had previously conceived, in which it had long stood with fixed step.

Thus it happens that, when the body receives what it does not desire, it suffers harm, while the ready inclination of the spirit receives its reward.

At the demand of your command, venerable bishop, I briefly treated, according to the capacity of my very slender intellect, two little books of the miracles of Mother Walpurgis, who must always be retained in mind and mouth. But, pressed by the many-parted labyrinths of secular occupations, with almost two weeks of revolving time having passed, I could neither reach nor deserve to arrive at the beginning of the third.

Now, however, since the end of the second already demands the beginning of the third, may I deserve to have as guide and most kindly director of my little heart him who by his wisdom opened the mouth of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent!

## THE CHAPTER HEADINGS BEGIN

[Note: The chapter headings marked with asterisks are absent from the text.]

I. Concerning the place where a blind woman was given sight.  
II. * Concerning the woman’s bread, lost from her bosom and later found.  
III. * Concerning the small pillow lost at home and found on the road.  
IV. Concerning the place where a certain man lost his *wantos* (gloves).  
V. Concerning the place where a vessel was found on the journey.  
VI. Concerning the place where five miracles occurred in one and the same woman.  
VII. * Concerning a lame woman who was healed.  
VIII. Concerning three blind people who were given sight.  
IX. Concerning a fish miraculously found on the road.  
X. Concerning the place where a mute woman was healed.  
XI. * Concerning four oxen found on the road.  
XII. * Concerning the place where a pig was snatched away by a wolf.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0881D]

In the year 895 from the memorable Incarnation of the Lord, a girl from the household of the blessed martyrs Gordianus and Epimachus—namely, a maiden of the monastery of Kempten—was blind from birth. Her name was Guntrada. When she heard of the famous grace of the Lord being manifested in that celebrated place, she too began with all the longing of her heart to yearn that she might be found worthy to come to the shrine of the most blessed virgin.

While her limbs were enjoying a brief taste of the sleep of most blessed repose, at the very moment of her falling asleep there appeared someone who addressed her as follows:

“Why, wretched woman, deprived of the twin lights of your eyes, do you lie sunk in such murky darkness? Why do you not rather seek, by turning over with yourself in the gentle vigil of your household, the matter essential to your salvation? For although, as is customary, the morning and daytime light joyfully welcomes you, it nevertheless receives a blind woman from the darkness [Canisius: perhaps *haustis*, “having been drawn in”] and sends her back bereft into the darkness.

“But if you strive to drive away the foul chaos from yourself, and desire to see the clouds spread across the heavens, as well as to contemplate the green earth, cast off the sluggishness of untimely sleep, restrain the idle weakness of your accustomed rest, and hasten to the monastery of Monheim. When you have reached it with a happy step, first place upon the altar, as an offering, cakes or loaves [the reading *actas* is uncertain] that have been properly prepared and finely baked and pressed into a small box, and thus entrust your whole self to the Maker of all things and to the virgin.”

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Fortunatus likewise testifies of Saint Radegund in her Life, century I, no. 16: “Making offerings with her own hands, she distributed them unceasingly to venerable places.” See the preface prefixed to the first volume of this century, where oblations are discussed.]

“When you have placed these little offerings upon the altar, two hens coming from nearby will devour them with greedy teeth; and, nourished by such food, they will keep watch over the altar.”

After these words, and after the speech had withdrawn together with the saving vision, the girl spent the remainder of the night joyfully. When the terror of night had ended, and the waters of the vast Ocean were already sending the bright locks of Titan back over the fields, she sprang cheerfully from the bed in which she had surrendered her limbs to sleep. She procured the expenses of the journey, took a girl as companion and guide, and, unfamiliar with the roads, set out upon the fortunate journey.

Thus, passing through pathless fields, she was found worthy to draw near to the monastery which she was seeking with uncertain steps. But before she reached its boundaries, remembering the most salutary vision announced from heaven, she properly baked the offerings, placed them in a small box, and began to continue her way.

When at last she came to the long-desired entrance of the basilica, as the celebrated day of Palm Sunday was drawing to its close, she entered the oratory with an inward groaning of the heart. Prostrating herself upon the ground and pouring streams of salty tears from the dark caverns of her eyes, as the command of the vision had more expressly ordered, she commended herself entirely to the one Lord and to the saving virgin.

After she had prolonged her sighs for a long time in prayer, she finally rose from the floor upon which she had lain humbly, approached the altar, and with trembling little fingers placed upon it the offerings she had brought. Then she withdrew a short distance to rest. And behold, the two hens which she had seen in the vision—namely, two nuns [read *sanctimoniales*, nominative plural]—standing beside the altar, carried away the offerings that had been placed there, carefully seeking the reason for which the blind woman had come.

She explained to them the whole sequence of events and brought it to its conclusion. When her speech had ended, help immediately came from the virgin. For the Almighty, who always looks down from heaven upon the children of men “to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God,” immediately looked down from heaven upon the believing woman and supplied the rays of the sun to her eyes, which had been deprived of light.

She was therefore terrified by the light, because she saw what she had not seen before. She gave thanks, together with the others standing there, to Christ her illuminator and to the virgin who had interceded for her, and departed healed.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Three items are omitted here.]

## CHAPTER V

In a similar manner, when the noble matron Gisila, wife of Burchard, son of Count Walacho [Note: [Col. 0883D] Here Henschenius corrects the anonymous author of Erfurt concerning the landgraves of Hesse. That anonymous writer says that Burchard’s father was Ludwig, and his grandfather another Ludwig, whom he says was appointed landgrave of Thuringia by Charles the Fat in 885. Henschenius proves from the Annals of Fulda, Regino, and others that Poppo was then in charge. Burchard is discussed below, chapter 10.], who had previously been married to Count Megingaudus [Note: [Col. 0884D] Count Megingaudus, grandson of King Odo, was treacherously killed by Alberic and his associates in the monastery of Saint Sixtus called Rotila on the fifth day before the Kalends of September in the year 892, according to the Annals of Metz.], had visited the virgin’s cell for the sake of prayer, as was her custom, she first prayed to the Lord for herself and all her people. Then she rose, fortified herself with the Lord’s sign, and offered the *eulogiae*—blessed gifts—which she had brought with her.

When the time came to distribute alms among Christ’s poor, and suitable portions of food had been given, she was also diligently serving cups. The vessel called a *hanap* [Note: [Col. 0884D] The French call a drinking vessel with a handle *un hanap*; in German, *hennapi*.]—the vessel in which the mixed drink was being prepared—was so emptied and removed from the hands of those serving drinks that none of those present could in any way know how it seemed to have been lost.

The woman serving knew in her own conscience that it had not slipped away by some accidental circumstance, that it had not been snatched from the hand of the dispenser, and that it had not been removed by any deception. Yet inwardly she was distressed, because she had never seen anything like it and had never heard of anything similar. She was astonished: what she had previously carried before her eyes in her hands was now gone, although no one had stolen or carried it away.

Why say more? As the hours of the day passed, the hope of recovering the strangely vanished vessel likewise disappeared. Therefore, having completed the purposes for which they had come, they arranged their journey and tried to return home.

While, as is customary among travelers, they were talking and inquiring among themselves about many things, the lost vessel was repeatedly mentioned. Then suddenly one of them, looking into the distance, saw that very vessel lying exposed and unchanged in the middle of the road.

They picked it up and brought it to the aforementioned lady with great astonishment; together with her, they joyfully gave thanks. From that place they immediately sent it back to the monastery, so that it might be wonderfully preserved there, where Christ performs wonders through the virgin.

## CHAPTER VI

There is a village in the Bavarian region, in the district of Chelesgowe, commonly called Adaloltestoch, well known to many people—and also most fully known to me, who faithfully write these things. In it there is still living a little woman named Asnia, in whom heavenly mercy, with the assistance of the merits of our mother, deigned to perform five most evident signs.

Her whole body was weak and trembling, entirely fallen and infirm; moreover, because of the obstruction of an inflexible tongue, she was miserably mute. She was brought to the monastery known to everyone, so that there she might find a remedy, where many had found the help they sought.

When she poured out tearful prayers to the Lord there, the voice of one supplicating was heard on high, and bodily health was joined to her tears. The woman returned home unharmed.

But the foolish minds of many peasants and worldly people, when they receive undeserved gifts and rewards from the Lord, do not prepare themselves for praise or for fitting acts of thanksgiving. Rather, they think that they have received the heavenly gift because of their own merits—or certainly without any preceding merits, but solely through the help of divine mercy. Thus they fail in good works and are by no means found steadfast in faith.

The accidental course of this little woman’s experience proves this, as the hearing of what happened will show. When she came home completely restored to health, she offered, as I suppose, no fitting thanks to the Most High for nearly ten weeks. Rather, weighed down by the carelessness of temporal sluggishness, she turned her unstable mind back toward passing things and forgot the health that she ought never to have forgotten.

Therefore, after the aforesaid period had passed, almighty God, wishing by a salutary chastisement to admonish his servant so that she would not appear ungrateful for the most blessed gift of so great a benefit, came to her one night in a vision and said:

“Why, little woman, now already pleasing to the Lord, have you wished until now to remain ungrateful to heavenly grace for such great benefits received? Return, therefore, to your right mind, banishing all doubt, and, after clearing away the cloudiness of your heart, consider what divine power has worked in you. Examine with the most careful inquiry of your mind from where health came to you, unworthy as you are.

“When you have diligently investigated the darkness of your ignorance without hesitation, rise quickly and go to the monastery of Monheim. There, after completing a suitable prayer, receive from Deithilda, the sacristan of the church, some work to perform with your own hands, so that you may know that thereafter you owe service to your mistress, from whom you were found worthy to receive the exchange of unexpected health.

“If you do not do this, know without a doubt that you will encounter some affliction in your body, so that the very suffering may bring understanding to your hearing, which gentle admonition did not govern,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] One item is omitted here.]

## CHAPTER VIII

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, three unknown men who had been blind from birth arrived. Driven by poverty, they were beggars, seeking the comfort of bodily health and sight, and asking for it with tearful and sobbing voices.

When the mistress of the household, Liubila, had received them kindly with her devoted servants of God and had mercifully supplied them with food, it seemed good to them to implore the virgin’s assistance more earnestly, so that through her merits and prayers they might be found worthy to obtain sight, which they had never experienced from the beginning of their lives.

They therefore entered the church as best they could and, after making their votive prayer, asked that their blind eyes be touched with the virgin’s *cambuta* [Note: [Col. 0885D] The staff or rod of Saint Walpurgis, enclosed in silk, is said to be preserved in Cologne on Saint Walpurgis Mount, where the church of the Society of Jesus’ Fathers stands.].

When this had been done, unfamiliar sight gradually came into their eyeballs, and their eyes, illumined by the rays of the radiant light, grew in joy. All who saw and heard it were astonished, and they offered abundant thanks to him who alone performs great wonders.

## CHAPTER IX

One day, when I had come to that same monastery wishing to hear something new and desirable, and was seeking with a faithful mind whether there might be anything worthy of hearing that could be brought to my notice, two of the virgin’s servants, Diethildis and Ruathildis, appeared and satisfied my wish. While I sat with writing materials and a sheet of paper, they carefully related to me, among other things, the following miracle.

“It happened,” they said, “as often happens among those who seek the Lord and the intercession of his saints, that certain people came to the same oratory for the sake of prayer. Entering the church, they adored him who lives forever and, with bowed faces, also sought the assistance of the most blessed Walpurgis.

“When they had completed the vow for which they had come, and had received a blessing to accompany their souls on their journey, the mistress of the household also gave them a *eulogia* for their bodily journey. It was a time when abstinence from meat was required; therefore they devotedly carried with them what the generous hand had provided: bread, cheese, and beer.

“Since they sought fish but could not obtain it because the circumstances of the season forbade it, they began their return journey, loaded with the provisions described above. As they walked along, talking about many things in the manner of traveling companions, they came to a place where pleasant green grass suitable for the season was available for the animals.

“There they unloaded the animals’ burden and, intending to partake of God’s gifts and provisions and of the virgin’s blessings, lay down upon the green hay. Then the man who was accustomed to put his hand most familiarly among their baggage opened the *sistarcia* [Note: [Col. 0886D] In Greek, σιταρκία signifies provisions or food supplies. In Latin, *sitarcia*, corruptly *sistarcia*, is used for a chest, basket, or pack in which food is carried; see 1 Kings, chapter 9, verse 7.] clearly and, in a most astonishing manner, saw and lifted out a fish that had previously been unseen and untouched,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER X

Two soldiers of Count Burchard from the region of Thuringia, Deitharius and Heio, sought the protection of the holy virgin. They brought with them a certain woman who lacked the faculty of human speech, so that, by the Lord’s mercy, she might be found worthy to receive grace there, where many had obtained manifold forgiveness.

When they had come there with joyful hearts by a prosperous road, having attained their earlier desire, they asked forgiveness for their offenses, pouring forth prayers from the depth of their hearts. Then, placing the little gifts they had brought upon the altar, they commended the mute woman whom they had brought from her homeland to the lavish mercy of the Almighty and to the virgin’s munificent kindness, with devout minds and believing hearts.

She too, since her tongue could not speak, asked forgiveness with the contrition of a humbled spirit.

Having completed the purposes for which they had come, they tried to return home, taking the same mute woman back with them to her homeland. As they went back sadly toward home because her carefully sought healing had not been found, one night, when they had all surrendered their weary bodies to rest and she too was resting in a sleep-filled little bed, a girl of elegant appearance and extraordinary beauty appeared to her. She breathed upon her ears with a very gentle breath.

The woman immediately awoke and, pondering the happy vision with careful meditation, found that the bond of her tongue had been loosed. She began to exercise the forms of ready speech, offering due praises to the giver of gifts, who had granted that the many saints dwelling with him in heaven should be powerful on earth.

Therefore her companions and all who heard her were astonished, and with joyful steps they returned to their own lands. But, wisely considering that so evident a miracle ought not to be kept silent, they took care to make it known through their own people to the monastery of the holy virgin, so that the servants of God and all who faithfully heard it might learn what had been divinely manifested in the same woman.

[Note: [Col. 0887A] Two items have likewise been cut out here.]

# BOOK FOUR

Containing other miracles performed there

[Col. 0887]

I had intended to bring this little work to its end with a brief conclusion. But the desirable novelty of the miracles and signs that continually arise drives and urges me again and again to write, and frequently invites me to carry the work through to its completion.

For the courage of an armed soldier engaged in battle is not proclaimed at the beginning; rather, at the end, the strength of effective victory is made known with approval by those who report it. It is fitting that praise be proclaimed at the end and that the end be adorned with praise, since the Lord says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13).

Therefore, with Christ’s favor, I shall begin the fourth little book, so that, having passed with a running pen through the glorious miracles of the holy virgin, I may come to the promised dialogue and, with the modest measure of my talent, contend in it after expending my labor.

If the reader finds anything unseen or unheard-of in this little work, let him read it with devout intention of mind and recognize the Lord alone as the one who performs wonders. These things would not have been written on parchment if they had not been wonders. For we read that signs were given not to believers but to unbelievers (1 Corinthians 14:22).

Therefore we believe that in the last and perilous times Christ wishes to perform many unheard-of wonders through his beloved virgin, so that the innumerable bestial minds of men in the world, which disdain to be converted by the words of preachers, may at least be inclined by signs that have not been heard before.

Whoever, then, desires to read and hear, let him remove the rust from his heart. When he has learned by experience that I write the truth, let him believe and know that I am not a fabricator of signs, but a most faithful excerptor, so that for this labor I may deserve to be freed from sins through the prayers and intercessions of the virgin.

## CONTENTS

[Note: [Col. 0887D] The chapter headings marked with asterisks are absent from the text.]

I. * Concerning a certain lame man who was healed.  
II. * Likewise, concerning another lame man who was healed.  
III. * Where another lame man was restored to health.  
IV. Concerning a woman whose feet were restored.  
V. Where another person weak in the feet was likewise healed.  
VI. Concerning a mute and a lame person who were healed.  
VII. * Concerning a woman possessed by a demon who was healed.  
VIII. * Concerning a blind woman who received her sight.  
IX. * Where a certain blind man was given sight.  
X. Concerning another blind man who was given sight.  
XI. Concerning the illumination of another blind man.  
XII. * Concerning a woman who for a long time was unable to take ordinary food and drink as nourishment.

## CHAPTER IV

If I wished to weave an account of all the lame people who there received the use of their feet, the day would fail before I could recount the manifest evidence of the many signs. Nevertheless, I do not think that the things which come to mind ought to be silenced, since, as we read, the works of God—whose judgments are unsearchable—are to be recounted.

Therefore let us hasten to bring a certain woman named Manswinda back to mind, so that we may also narrate how she was healed. Coming from a village called Truthinga and seeking the healing of body and soul in the monastery—for she was deformed and disfigured by weakness of the feet—she sent up to heaven the voices of prayer from her mournful breast for a long time, and begged at length that the Almighty might deign to have mercy upon her.

Divine power and mercy immediately came to her aid and restored completely the step that she had lost.

## CHAPTER V

In the very village where the celebrated monastery is situated, there was a boy named Beretgisus, in whom the life-giving Trinity deigned to perform one and the same sign. For three years he had been deprived of the ability to walk, so that he seemed incapable of undertaking any useful work.

His mother, Ratila by name, took him, overcome by immense grief, to the healing basilica and set him before the eyes of the divine majesty. With tears and groans she begged for its ineffable mercy.

The Lord, seeing the woman’s faith from the lofty dwelling of heaven, healed the child and, through the mother’s prayers, made him walk. When this became known, the lady gave the child to that church to possess by perpetual right, so that for as long as he lived he might render the obligations of service there, where he had been found worthy to receive strength for serving.

Similarly, a certain Roman arrived and lay miserably in the northern portico in the cart on which he had been carried. On the following day he was found worthy to receive the ability to walk.

## CHAPTER VI

It also happened at a certain time that the lady Hildegard [Note: [Col. 0889D] Accused before Arnulfus and deprived of her royal possessions, she lived in exile in the monastery of Chemissen. Having been restored to favor, she recovered most of her property, says Regino under the year 894.], daughter of the peaceful King Ludwig, came to the aforementioned monastery for the sake of prayer with the most renowned Count Luitpoldus.

She was not forgetful of the benefits of the holy virgin, especially since she knew and believed that many miracles had been performed there and were almost daily being performed. She brought with her in her retinue a man who had been mute from birth, so that, if by heavenly disposition he were found worthy to receive the most welcome gift of articulate speech, he might believe more openly what he heard, while what he saw gave faith to what he heard.

Luitpoldus too, as I suspect, moved by a similar desire, brought with him a lame man.

While they were resting that same night, all hastened into the church when the morning assembly approached. When the women serving God there began to sing the divine chants, with those who had brought the aforesaid afflicted men also standing present, the mute man, with the fetter of his tongue loosed, began to utter clear words in a fluent voice and to praise God, wondrous in his saints, with rejoicing of heart.

And not only he: all who were present at the morning service also praised almighty God. Seeing that the outcome of the matter had been fulfilled as he had desired, he was filled with great delight and exultation of heart, raised his hands to heaven, and gave thanks to almighty God.

Then, at the following moment of that same blessed hour, the staff-bearing lame man brought by the aforementioned Count Luitpoldus began to leap joyfully and to bless his Savior fittingly. When the venerable count learned that the lame man he had brought was leaping and praising God, he too, exulting in the joy of his heart, blessed the wondrous Lord.

And so, in order that the joy of the two rejoicing men might be increased still further, a third evident and open miracle strengthened the first two. For the mother of a certain lame child, when she had seen that the two preceding signs had plainly been manifested, brought forward for healing her own son, whom she had presented with lamentable cries.

After the two who had preceded him had been healed, the third was healed in the presence of everyone. Having witnessed these three miracles, two men who especially desired such signs returned home, recounting them to many others.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] Three items are omitted here.]

## CHAPTER X

It happened at a certain time that, in order to admonish the servants of God and strengthen them in the fear of God, the good and devout bishop Erchanboldus visited the monastery itself, as was frequently his custom, and sowed in them, with honeyed lips, the seed of holy preaching entrusted to him.

While he was still staying in the same cell and laboring diligently to win souls for Christ, a poor man blind from birth arrived from the regions of France with a company of clerics and poor people carrying banners and singing *Kyrie eleison* in melodious voices. He entered the basilica with his companions by whatever efforts he could make.

When, kneeling in prayer, he also raised the fiber of his heart, the merciful Lord graciously inclined his kindly ear and heard the poor man’s prayer poured forth. He granted by his wondrous power the light that nature had denied him.

When the bishop and all who were present saw this, they returned praises in the highest to God.

## CHAPTER XI

It does not seem inappropriate if the following miracle is made equal to the preceding one, since that blind man, as we said, plainly received light there, and this man too was deprived of sight, of whom the account now proceeds, and who likewise became worthy to see the day in the same church.

When the festive solemnity of Easter had passed and the following week, clothed in white, arrived, a count named Adalbertus came from the countryside of the illustrious Franks to the monastery.

While he was standing in the basilica with his people and listening to the divine office, an unknown blind man was brought in and stood among the others. Without delay, after he had offered a most humble prayer to God, the light drove night from his eyes, while everyone present saw and marveled.

When he recognized such power in himself, he gave praise to his Creator and Restorer. Returning healthy and unharmed to his homeland, he spread abroad wherever he could what divine kindness had accomplished in him.

The remaining material is omitted.

# APPENDIX

Concerning the canonization of Saint Walpurgis, feast days, oil, relics, and sacred places

[Col. 0891]

## 1. Canonization

The nuns of Eistetten say in the Life of Saint Walpurgis that her canonization was “obtained from the Apostolic See through Erchanboldus, bishop of Eistetten.” They add:

“This canonization took place, they say, on the very day of the apostles Philip and James, on which her feast of canonization is celebrated to this day. For this reason, every year on that same day, a solemn procession is made from the cathedral church by the bishop and canons to the parish church of Saint Walpurgis, and there the divine office is performed with the greatest solemnity by the canons. To them are also served for drinking the relics, or the distillation—that is, the oil—of the same holy virgin.”

But Bruschius, and Gretserus after him, write in the catalogue of the bishops of Eistetten that Saint Walpurgis was enrolled among the heavenly citizens by the nod and command of Pope Adrian through Bishop Otkarius.

Certainly, Otkarius arranged for the body of Saint Walpurgis to be lifted from the earth. At that time canonization of the saints was celebrated by this rite. Nevertheless, the elevation of Saint Walpurgis took place on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, not on the Kalends of May, or the feast of the apostles Philip and James.

Nevertheless, “the feast of her canonization and translation is commonly celebrated” on that day, says Bishop Philip in her Life. Whatever the truth may be, Wolfhardus does not state that the consent of the Roman pontiff intervened in the elevation of Saint Walpurgis carried out by Otkarius; certainly it was not the consent of Adrian, who was placed upon the Roman see in the year 884, after Otkarius’s death.

## 2. Feast days

Saint Walpurgis is honored on several feast days. Philip and the nuns of Eistetten record her nativity on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, and the Church of Eistetten celebrates it on that day.

Although her elevation took place on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, some celebrate it on the fourth day before the Ides of October, and another translation on the Kalends of May.

But since “the relics of Saint Walpurgis are dispersed throughout the whole world,” as the nuns of Eistetten write—that is, “throughout various provinces of the entire kingdom of the Franks,” as stated in the Utrecht Lectionary—it has happened that each church established a celebration in her honor on the day when it received the relics.

## 3. Oil

Philip speaks of the oil flowing from the relics of Saint Walpurgis in these words:

“As a final conclusion, we have decided to record that the sacred body of the glorious virgin Walpurgis was carefully and reverently placed by the aforementioned bishop Erbertus”—in fact, Otkarius—“in the public altar of the same monastery, which will be discussed below. There miracles continue happily to multiply even to the present day.

“For from her virgin limbs, especially from the region of the breast, sacred oil flows. By the grace of God and through the intercession of Blessed Walpurgis the virgin, it gives sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and walking to the lame; and it mercifully grants the desired result to all the infirm who devoutly ask for it.

“We ourselves have experienced this healing grace. For, suffering from a grave illness, we had come near to death. Remembering the grace which Blessed Walpurgis continually displays to those who love her, we ordered that a greater quantity of the oil of her most holy effusion be brought to us, and we drank a full flask in a desired draught, praying in these words,” and so forth.

“On that same day we experienced a crisis”—that is, we emitted the sweat that indicates recovery—“and shortly afterward we were restored completely to health.

“This too should be known: at the hour when Masses are celebrated, when the sacrament of the body and blood of Jesus Christ is consecrated upon the altar in which she is buried, oil more frequently and more abundantly drips from her sacred body. Therefore that hour is observed with the greatest care for receiving the oil.

“If the flasks in which the sacred oil is to be received are not placed directly or perpendicularly beneath the dripping, drops of the same oil hang together, suspended like a cluster of grapes or a honeycomb, and do not fall elsewhere. But once the negligence is corrected and the vessels in which the sacred oil is to be cleanly received are properly placed beneath the dripping, it flows into them without any human assistance.

“By this it is plainly shown that it ought to be received into clean vessels, because it entirely avoids unclean places or vessels. It has also often been discovered that, even when received in a clean vessel, if it is kept uncleanly or irreverently, or is carried to a place where sinful pleasures are customarily practiced, it completely vanishes; or else the oil does not emerge from the mouth of the vessel to produce healing.

“We also gather from written accounts and have learned through the reliable testimony of trustworthy people that at one time the city of Eistetten, together with its entire diocese, had been placed under an ecclesiastical interdict because of certain damaging injuries which the bishop then in office had suffered from the barons and inhabitants of the land.

“From that time onward the liquid of the sacred effusion ceased to drip, until the day on which the church had been restored to its former condition. Then that venerable bishop, together with the whole city, proclaimed a fast and went barefoot and without linen garments up to the monastery of Blessed Walpurgis. With the whole people, he devoutly and humbly begged that the city should no longer be deprived of the affection of such great kindness as the effusion of the sacred liquid.

“The bishop then approached the altar and, with the people standing present, devoutly celebrated the solemn Mass. During the consecration and reception of the sacrament, the most sacred liquid—which for the space of an entire year had not dripped or shown itself in any way—burst forth so abundantly that it filled a flask with a capacity of half a pint or one *seria* [the source first prints *serici*; the note suggests *seria*, a long earthen wine vessel].”

Philip adds that the same sacred oil is of such purity and unmixed clarity that, after being preserved for two hundred years without any corruption or foul sediment of defilement, it is found to possess the same purity as that which on the present day has been collected from the dripping of the same sacred effusion.

The nuns of Eistetten testify to much the same things.

Gretserus published a special Treatise on this oil at Ingolstadt in 1610. In it, chapter 1 contains the following words:

“The relics of Blessed Walpurgis the virgin were placed at Eistetten in the hard, solid, hollowed-out stone of the high altar, which is closed above, in the very place where the sacrificing priest offers the body and blood of the Lord. It is therefore probable that this tomb serves as a sepulcher, such as is seen in all consecrated altars according to the rite and prescription of consecration.

“Beneath the aforesaid stone there is a cavity or square opening into which the distillation drips from the upper stone that holds the sacred bones of the virgin. You may see drops, sometimes larger and sometimes smaller, the size of a pea or hazelnut, hanging from the upper stone; all of them are received by a broad silver basin.”

Gretserus reports various miracles, and Bollandus after him; we shall pass them over. Wolfhardus mentions this oil in Book I, chapter 9.

## 4. Relics in the Eistetten Parthenon, Monheim, and elsewhere

A large part of the relics of Saint Walpurgis is preserved in the Parthenon of Benedictine nuns in the higher part of the city of Eistetten. Formerly the church of the Holy Cross stood there; after the holy relics had been transferred there, it received the name of Saint Walpurgis.

The first founder of this monastery was Otkarius VI, bishop of the Church of Eistetten, whom we have read above to have been the originator of the translation. Bishop Heribertus XV restored and enlarged it, and Leodegarius, or Leutgarius, assisted him with his generosity. He was the restorer of the nuns in that place, as Gretserus reports from Philip and others in *Observations*, Book I, chapter 19.

The nuns of Monheim also obtained a portion of the holy relics, according to Book I, chapter 9 of Wolfhardus. Numerous miracles are reported to have been performed among them in the three books that follow.

Fragments of the same relics are also found at Furnes, Antwerp, Cologne, and other places, as Henschenius explains at length in the Preliminary Commentary, sections 6 and 7, where he also discusses various churches consecrated to Saint Walpurgis.

In a certain manuscript History of the Franks, the following is read under the second year of King Rudolf of the Franks, A.D. 824:

“In that year the body of Saint Remigius and the bodies of certain other saints were carried from their monasteries into the walls of the city of Rheims by their own people, because of fear of the Huns. Among them were also placed the relics of Saint Galburgis, at which miracles often take place.”

### 5. Basilicas and Oratories

Among the churches dedicated to Saint Walburga, the most famous is the Eistett Parthenon, mentioned above. At Chester, on the island of Britain, there was a monastery of Saint Wilburga, built by Hugh the consul—that is, the count of Chester—as Orderic Vitalis testifies in *History*, Book VIII, p. 671. At Tiel, in the duchy of Guelders, beside the River Waal, there was a Walburgian basilica, with a college of canons established in it; in the year 1315 it was transferred to Arnhem, a town on the Rhine. There are two other churches at Zutphen in Guelders, and at Groningen, the principal city of West Frisia.

Nor should we omit here what Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, records concerning an oratory of Saint Walburga in Book II, chapter 28, of his *Collations*:

> “There is,” he says, “a church of Blessed Walburga in this neighboring region of ours, in which miracles take place. It happened, as the abbot Lord Berno relates, that the relics of this same Saint Walburga remained for several days upon the altar. But immediately the miracles ceased. At length the virgin herself appeared to one of the sick and said: ‘For this reason you are not being healed: because my relics are upon the altar of the Lord, where only the majesty of the divine mystery ought to be celebrated.’ When he reported this to the custodians, they removed the reliquary, and immediately miracles began to occur.”

At the palace of Attigny, beside the Aisne, Charles the Bald built an oratory of Saint Walburga, which, together with the palace itself, was destroyed by the Northmen. After peace and tranquillity had been restored to Gaul, another church was built for the same virgin. Hugh, count of Champagne, received it as a dowry from Philip, king of the Franks, on account of his marriage to Philip’s daughter Constance; afterward, in the year 1102, he donated it to the monastery of Molesme, to which it has remained subject under the title of a priory, as we learn from the French *Life of Saint Walburga* published by Spagnolius. This church and the village called Saint Walburga—commonly Saint-Waubourg—are one mile from Attigny, formerly a royal town. Finally, in the diocese of Strasbourg, Count Theodoric of Montbéliard built a monastery of Benedictine monks in honor of Saint Walburga, which the emperor Frederick I later enlarged.

[Col. 0893]

## PREFACES OF WOLFHARD, A PRIEST, TO HIS TWELVE BOOKS ON THE ACTS OF THE SAINTS, ADDRESSED TO ERCHANPOLD, BISHOP OF EICHSTÄTT

(From Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, from the Tegernsee manuscript.)

### Preface to Book I, or the Month of January

[Col. 0893C]

As we celebrate with worthy and devout veneration the sufferings of the blessed martyrs who, having despised the pleasures of this present life with its pressing hardships, entered the starry kingdoms, it is pleasing to select many things from among the many accounts of the blessed virgin Martina and of the other martyrs, confessors, and virgins—accounts marked by a wondrous course, glorious struggle, most courageous triumph, and brilliant deed—so that their actions and sufferings may be made known to those who hear them in a brief commentary, and the length of this volume may be avoided, while the mind is refreshed inwardly by concise reading and the body is not burdened outwardly by excessive labor.

Although I do not doubt that I am unworthy of so great a task, nevertheless, because this pious labor proceeds on a fortunate course, with the Lord’s help and his generous granting of ability, and supported by your prayers, Father Erchanpold, I undertake the work entrusted to me.

[Col. 0894C] Here begins Book I, the Kalends of January. Blessed Martina, then, although she was noble by birth, etc.

### Preface to Book II, or the Month of February

(I cannot provide this one now, since the Tegernsee manuscript is not at hand, nor is this month any longer found in the Melk manuscripts, from which I shall henceforth present the remaining prefaces for the individual months.)

### Preface to Book III, or the Month of March

With the two little books of the work begun, covering two months, now completed by God’s favor, and with the most holy name of Jesus the Good invoked, the third book seeks the beginning of the third course, so that, with him supplying the measures of speech and displaying the effectiveness of the work, and with the consoling aid of the prayers of the saints whose memory is commended here, it may be worthy to reach the end, and may please him who revealed both beginning and end to the faithful.

### Preface to Book IV, or April

[Col. 0895A]

Thus far, excellent Father and supreme pontiff, as we have traversed the little works of the holy Fathers, gathering together in brief form the three preceding books, it remains, with the saints of whom we speak interceding for us and your merits assisting us, that we come to the beginning of the fourth.

Therefore we humbly implore the reader that, when he has searched through everything by plowing it, he retain what is Catholic and approved, but cut away and scrape off what is less suitable, knowing that we have invented no foolish trifles from our own judgment; rather, we have taken extracts from the books of the Fathers and joined them to our little page. If this should happen, let him act watchfully, lest, by rashly mangling the writings of the saints, he pass carelessly over our own.

### Preface to Book V, or May

[Col. 0895B]

We have heard from sacred instructions of the divine works of the archangel Raphael, sent from heaven to blessed Tobias, which he was to announce to all: he wonderfully brought relief to the saints, and, returning to heaven after the blessing accomplished by his household, bestowed words of salvation.

Therefore we too, according to the measure of our health, praise Christ in his saints, although guilty through the sins of the matter, because we believe that the saints stand firm in Christ. For he was their victory in the struggle; he was their strong protection, lest they fail; he was their crown after triumph; he enriched them with the promised glory.

Let us therefore offer in the house of the Lord not gold, not silver, not costly garments, but only goats’ hair, and let us ask [Col. 0895C] that the portion of the saints granted to us by merit may be ours in the land of the living. For we read that the poor widow offered two small coins to the treasury.

### Preface to Book VI, or June

Having completed the compendia of the five preceding books of this little work, in which, searching the writings of the Fathers, we touched briefly upon many matters by writing only a few things, now, with Christ propitious, both the natural order demands that we come to the beginning of the sixth and your exhortation, most sacred bishop, compels us—your exhortation which always urges us to write.

We devote labor, indeed, but we cannot bring the labor to its result unless he grants it who gives a reward at the end to those who labor for him. Hence we ask his help, [Col. 0895D] and set the stylus to the page.

### Preface to Book VII, or July

After an interval of many days, during which, weighed down by secular burdens and harassed by worldly cares pressing upon us, we were quite unable to drag the little work long ago begun onward to its conclusion, we have left you suspended, jewel among bishops, though unprofitably.

For the strength of summer, while it burns the highest brow of the rough countryside with its fiery crest and often grazes with a lion’s jaws the innermost streams of its veins, has prevailed. But as the wheel of time turns and winter’s hoariness approaches, it violently summons the waters almost previously swallowed back to their proper channels.

So too, Father, until now the channel of our pipe has dried up completely and [Col. 0896A] has found nothing at all. As winter therefore approaches, we seek the spring again. And since we have no jar, and the well is deep, and we have no means at all by which we may draw for ourselves, let us ask from him who said, “Let whoever thirsts come to me and drink,” a delightful draught, and we shall find the means of drawing.

And since it is not ours to drink from the depths with only a reed lowered by a bent neck, let us, with his favor, strive to draw the cup by sucking, and let us take our beginning from January with the sixth book of the sixth month.

### Preface to Book VIII, or August

We read that the name *August* received its designation from *increasing*.
