Therefore we implore the mercy of the author of all things, that he who established the saints as the temple of his dwelling and chose them to be his lodging-place may pour upon us, through their most pious assistance, the gift of blessing; grant us to walk along the path we have begun; graciously provide the nourishment of the word; moisten the dry stylus with the dew of his kindness; grant the gifts of writing to us who are beginning August; increase them powerfully by accumulation; and, since the work is his, may his power also be magnified.

### Preface to Book IX, or September

Since, with God’s help, we have crossed the feverish fields of August and drawn in, by sucking, whatever we could from the paternal spring, it remains that we seek more diligently, though with labor, the shadows of mild September.

For September is suitably named from rain, according to the definition of its sound, because it is the seventh. Therefore we implore the mercy of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, that he may pour the work begun with the rain of his flowing kindness and bring it happily to its end, so that the power of the work may be a reward for our labor, even for us sinners.

### Preface to Book X, or October

Obeying your commands, truly blessed pontiff and memorable throughout the ages, we have briefly treated, with as much commendation as we could, the calendar days of nine months in an equal number of volumes, and, flowering in very rich meadows, we have passed through sweet honey, content only with its pleasant brilliance and burdened, according to our strength, with the scantiness of the grasses.

Now the command of your dignity also compels the tenth book to follow the ninth, and the obligation of our earlier promise demands it, while you more insistently order us to set the stylus to work. May, therefore, our Father Remigius—through whom the book takes its beginning—assist both his own people and all peoples of the faithful.

### Preface to Book XI, or November

As, with Christ favoring us, we now undertake the month of November, may the intercession of all the saints assist us, whose most sacred solemnity is venerated under one celebration on the very day of the Kalends.

For if, according to the Apostle James, the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful, how much more powerful is the united and pious intercession of all the saints! We are indeed unworthy of this work and of the most gracious intercession of the saints. Yet he who justifies sinners and hears them, who generously grants the word according to the manner of one who desires it, who rains most abundantly upon the just and the unjust, is powerful from on high to send down a drop and mercifully to moisten a dry tongue.

### Preface to Book XII, or December

Reason itself establishes that the number twelve is perfect, showing that it is sacred in the catalogue of the saints, prophets, and apostles. For we read that Moses found twelve symbolic springs with the people in the wilderness, and that Jesus took twice six stones from the Jordan river.

Our Jesus likewise chose twelve apostles as firm and clear stones, so that, joined together with the cornerstone, they might build the wall of the Church. Since one of these was broken away and fell from the order, lest perfection suffer loss, the Truth itself, who had consecrated him, restored the number.

The wheel of the year also turns through the course of twelve months. During them the deeds and struggles of the saints lift up the ears of the faithful, nourish their minds with spiritual food, and draw them toward love of heavenly blessedness.

Since we too, having brought the sequence of this little work to completion in the eleventh book, have, as it were, accumulated and contributed it thus far, let us, with Christ propitious, begin the twelfth, lest imperfection be blamed for failing to attain perfection. When it reaches the end on a fortunate course, may he himself be praised who grants eloquence of speech to his own through his gifts, who established all things in number, measure, and weight, and who consecrated what he established by blessing.

[Col. 0897]

## POEM ON SAINT WALBURGA, BY WOLFHARD

(From Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. II.)

[Col. 0897B]

She was the daughter of a king, but made herself poor,

So that she might reign forever in Christ, always in him;

How dear she is to God, miracles frequently show;

[Col. 0898B]

Which he who was born of a virgin grants through her merits;

From her tomb flows the sacred stream of her breast;

That light shone forth for the handmaid of God . . . .

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 899. ANAMODUS, SUBDEACON OF THE CHURCH OF REGENSBURG.

[Col. 0897]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK

(From Piz, *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. I, part III, p. 192.)

[Col. 0897C]

“The *Book of Traditions*,” says the most learned Mabillon in the *German Journey* prefixed to volume IV of the *Analecta*, “is a distinguished manuscript, written by Anamodus and dedicated to Bishop Ambricho—or, as it seems to us, to Bishop Aspert of Regensburg, who, according to some, succeeded Ambricho or Ambricon in that see in the year 886, while Charles the Fat was still emperor. Certainly the initial A. of the bishop to whom Anamodus dedicated this illustrious monument admits either identification.”

This Anamodus was a subdeacon of the Church of Regensburg, as we learn from Book II, chapter 29, where there is a transfer between Bishop Ambricho and Anamodus. In it, a certain ruddy cleric named Anamodus, namely a devout subdeacon, was pleased to bring certain properties of his own into his possession for his benefit.

Thus, says Anamodus himself, “such property as the same Anamodus received into his possession through the donation of the most pious King Arnulf, in the district called Westermannomarcha, near Prointala, at the place called Reitinpuoch, in the county of Count Engildeo, he handed over and bound, together with seven dependents, to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and the holy martyr Emmeram, [Col. 0897D] into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocates Gerbert and Gundbert, etc. It was enacted at Menzinpah.”

This is the same Anamodus who, as he says in the little preface to Bishop A., gathered very many sheets of traditions, transfers, and boundary records, and brought and enclosed them in the single body of this little collection, so that, once error had been removed, they might more easily be found and recognized by the previously noted chapters whenever necessary.

The manuscript from which we have published this monument—one which Bavaria perhaps possesses nothing superior to—is without doubt an autograph and authentic copy, written on quarto parchment. In it no charter later than the ninth century is found. Through its aid not only Bavarian matters but also Austrian matters are remarkably illuminated, as could be demonstrated in many places if leisure permitted.

In any case, these three diplomatic manuscripts should surely suffice for those who have so vehemently demanded an edition of the *Diplomatic Code* collected by Ulrich of Babenberg, even after the repeated writings of a certain opponent directed against us. For here they have the more readable part of Ulrich’s code, which concerns German charters, much more accurately emended and more complete; and all the remaining material not yet published—including even those things which he most undeservedly resented being brought into public view—they will have in another of our *Diplomatic-Historical-Epistolary Codes*, almost ready for the press.

We therefore suppress a complete edition of Ulrich’s code—not at all because of the reasons brought forward by our adversary, which could not prevent learned and scholarly men from urging us, both publicly and privately, with the greatest enthusiasm to carry out our original plans, [Col. 0900A] but rather so that we may not be compelled to publish twice, once in full and complete form the monuments of better quality that we have produced from these three Emmeram manuscripts, and again in mutilated, truncated, and therefore useless form, as they appear in Ulrich’s code.

If this policy of ours should please certain learned men less, nothing else is needed than that they publicly demonstrate their own wishes to us.

[Col. 0899]

## THE TWO BOOKS OF THE TRADITIONS OF ANAMODUS, SUBDEACON OF REGENSBURG, CONCERNING SAINT EMMERAM

Containing the charters of donations, transfers, boundary agreements, exchanges, and settlements pertaining to the imperial monastery of Saint Emmeram, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and established in the ninth century of Christ.

(First brought to light from the autograph manuscript preserved in that celebrated monastery, through the study and work of Father Bernard Pez, Benedictine and librarian of Melk.)

## VERSES OF ANAMODUS

[Col. 0899]

Behold here the beautiful form of the venerable bishop,

Who often favors us through his sacred merit.

His honor shines broadly throughout the world,

His love is sweetly present to all peoples.

He is humble and gentle, yet finally becomes strong against the wicked;

He feeds everyone, always nourishing his own.

And therefore I believe that his praise will be in heaven,

For what is the voice of the people is also the voice of the Lord.

With his heart indeed, and also with his whole body,

He readily serves Christ by night and by day.

May almighty God, who establishes the kingdoms of the world,

Return to him full rewards for his good deeds.

And may he receive in heaven the special gifts

Of this little book, where true hope is revealed.

## LITTLE PREFACE OF ANAMODUS

[Col. 0899]

[Col. 0899] To the most excellent lord Bishop A., Anamodus, his most humble servant.

Since I knew that your mind was always devoted to every study of books and to every service of divine worship, I undertook, of my own free will, to present this little work to the most beautiful hands of your holiness.

For, gathering very many sheets of traditions, transfers, and boundary records, I brought them together and enclosed them in the single body of this little collection, so that, once error had been removed, they might more easily be found and recognized by the previously noted chapters whenever necessary.

# BOOK ONE OF THE TRADITIONS OF SAINT EMMERAM

[Col. 0901]

## CHAPTER I — Concerning the Transfer by King Louis of Certain Clerics

[Col. 0901A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Let the matter become clear to all the faithful whose eyes this charter is presented for inspection: how the most pious King Louis, namely the father of Carloman, exchanged a certain cleric named Gundpert from the church of Saint Peter the Apostle with one of his own clerics.

Therefore, by his clemency, he took the aforesaid Gundpert for himself, so that, for the remedy of his soul, he might make him free and secure from servile labor by the authority of his command; and this he mercifully carried out.

In return, he gave his own cleric, named Elefant, into the hands of the holy church of God mentioned above and of the venerable Bishop Ambricho. Moreover, because Gundpert was more useful and more gifted in writing and also in reading, the most prudent king added what I shall relate below.

For by his donation he gave into the hands of the aforesaid holy church of God and of its administrator the newly cleared lands that lie opposite the monastery at Uderida and opposite the central forest, which is situated there before it. Whatever had recently been cleared there of fields or meadows, he transferred there in its entirety, and afterward attached to it the neighboring land on the eastern side in exchange.

At that time Wuito was the king’s ministerial, chief over all the forest districts. His subordinate, named Wichad, was also dispatched to carry this out and to effect the investiture.

## CHAPTER II — The Donation of Count Ekkibert

[Col. 0901C]

In the name of God.

I, Ekkibert, count by the mercy of God, for the remedy of my soul and the remission of my sins, so that I may deserve to obtain eternal pardon in the future, have handed over and invested my vassal Deotpert, who appears to dwell in the district called Folcfeld, with whatever property of mine I appeared to possess in the district called Rangewi, within that wilderness, whatever was handed over to me in that place where the two rivers called Piparodi converge.

I did this so that the aforesaid messenger of mine, Deotpert, might hand over and reinvest the same property, with everything intact, to the monastery of the holy Savior [Note: [Col. 0901D] See below, chapter 45.] which is built beside the waters of the Rehtratanze, where, in God’s name, Bishop or Abbot Adalwin appears to preside, [Col. 0901D] for the remedy of my soul, and so that he might reinvest Bishop Adalwin with the same property.

Then Deotpert, vassal and messenger of Count Ekkibert, came to the same monastery, which Bishop Adalwin appeared to govern, in the district called Swalavelda, and handed over the same property. His associate Fridabert then stood surety for him according to their law, in the presence of the following men, whose names are:

Erchanloh, Muniholf, Herimot, Reginfrid, Leidrat, Adalpreht, Gisalfrid, Pereger, Wolfhart, Herirat, Wico, Altuni, Irminfrid, Halpdurinc, Amalger, Einhart, Egispreht, Rihpold, Otfrid, Adalram, Gisalpreht, Meginhart, Meginfrid, Deotolf, Sigihart, and Engilhart.

These men saw and heard this donation being made, as well as the same investiture to Bishop Adalwin.

Afterward Bishop Adalwin came to the same place called Piparodi, together with his witnesses; Deotpert summoned Rodfrid to reinvest him according to the command of Count Ekkibert. Rodfrid immediately did so, and Deotpert himself reinvested Bishop Adalwin and his advocate Erchanloh with the same property, in the presence of the witnesses whose names are inserted below, together with all buildings, houses or barns, lands, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, and a mill—everything that he appeared to possess as his own property in that place.

As for the boundary district, it extended on the eastern side as far as the boundary district of Abbot Deotkar, and on the southern side as far as the boundary district of Gundpert, where they made their mark. They then proceeded to the boundary district of Gundpert, and Gundpert objected to Bishop Adalwin and Deotpert concerning a certain portion between the two rivers called Piparodi.

Afterward Gundpert, Hurih, and Gozmar examined the matter, and they donated to the Savior, for the remedy of their souls, the portion to which they had objected. It measured three miles on the southern side and two miles on the northern side.

After the investiture had been made, Odilwart came with his two sons, Peziro and Reginwart, and with others whose names are Reginhoh, Arphert, and Adalolf.

These are the names of the witnesses who saw this investiture made:

Napuhhi, Hunrih, Gundperht, Gozmar, Fridaperht, Otrih, Heriwic, Rantwic, Rodfrid, Petto, Peronzan, Frohnolf, Kipiho, and Eccho.

It was done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 810, in the place called Piparodi.

## CHAPTER III — Concerning the Boundary District at Chamba

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 819, in the sixth year of the reign of Louis Augustus and the third year of Bishop Baturic, Bishop Baturic came to Chamba, where the cell itself had been built upon the river called the Regen, between two waters—that is, between the Gewinaha and the Marclaha.

He had with him Rodold the huntsman, as well as Betto the deputy, and also Hatto’s messenger, named Hiltiroch, whom Hatto had assigned to the same place at Chamba, so that he might hear what claim the bishop himself had with those neighbors who had unjustly usurped for themselves the boundary district of Saint Peter the Apostle and the blessed martyr Emmeram.

Those men also came who had unjustly cleared the same boundary district beyond what they were entitled to, contrary to law. They were Ratpreht, Scurz, Engilmunt, Tago, Rihhart, Liupger, and Meio.

Bishop Baturic then began to investigate the entire boundary district in every respect, in the manner in which Duke Tassilo, renewing an earlier donation, had restored it to the blessed Emmeram for the sake of his own soul and those of his parents.

And while many things were being said on both sides—both by those who had unjustly possessed and claimed the same land and by those who desired that its lawful right should once again belong to blessed Peter and Saint Emmeram according to the law of the Bavarians—Bishop Baturic rose and, together with Rodold, Betto, and Hiltiroch, first came westward to the stand of trees which Gewinahar had unjustly and unlawfully usurped, as far as the stream itself, the Gewinaha.

There Rodold and Betto said that the boundary district of Bishop Baturic ought to belong to that house of God. Southward it ran upward beside the stream as far as the place where the stream rises. From there Rodold and Betto led Bishop Baturic eastward as far as the Marclaha.

They said that the boundary district of Bishop Baturic ought to run through the middle of the stream—that is, through the Marclaha. From there they led the same bishop to the place where that stream rises on the same mountain.

Rodold and Betto said: “This boundary district ought to run through the middle of this Mount Bosun: from the place where the Marclaha falls into the River Regen to the place already mentioned, toward the south; and then through the middle of the mountain eastward as far as the place where the Gewinaha rises; and from there along the eastern side of that water as far as the River Regen, where the Gewinaha enters the Regen.”

Then Rodold and Betto said: “We dare to say and affirm this, even if it should be before the Lord Emperor: that this entire boundary district, just as we have marked it while leading this same Bishop Baturic around it, ought, with all its rights, to belong to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram by virtue of the donations of the dukes who possessed this land.”

These are the names of those who heard this declaration, surveyed that boundary district on horseback, and were present at this boundary inspection on Wednesday, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January:

Bishop Baturic; Welo, priest and monk; David, priest and monk; Folrat, priest; Couperht, priest and monk; Hunrih, monk; also Rodold, Betto, Hiltiroch, Immo, Baldram, Pillinc, Meiol, Fridaperht, Welagrim, Cotaperht, and Avo; also Cotaperht, Amalperht, Radholf, Irminolf, Baldrih, Irminperht, Mauri, Waltrih, Unlaz, Cunzo, Folchuni, Ogast, Betto’s son, Willibato, and many others.

Ellinhard wrote this.

## CHAPTER IV — The Transfer between Bishop Ambricho and Egilolf

[Col. 0904A]

A very fruitful and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among men: namely, to exchange certain properties for the advantage of both parties. In our own times this is carried out ever more frequently by the permission of the most pious kings, and it very often occurs between the possessions of nobles and portions of ecclesiastical property.

Therefore a certain nobleman named Egilolf handed over to Saint Peter the Apostle and the holy martyr of God Emmeram, into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Helfric, such property as he possessed beside the waters of the Labara and beside the place called Perc.

That is: four homesteads, two orchards, 160 acres of arable land, 50 acres of meadows, 82 acres of productive woodland, and one millstone; leaving nothing outside, he transferred everything there in its entirety, including roads, pastures, waters, and watercourses.

In return, Helfric and Ogo, with the consent of their lord the bishop, handed over to the same nobleman from the property of the aforesaid saints, namely at Talachirichun: one homestead, 320 acres of arable land, 50 acres of meadows, six acres of productive woodland, one mill site, and a road six feet wide leading into that church.

They excluded, however, that church itself, one small plot, thirty acres of territory, and extraneous claims—whatever had previously been seized. All the rest they transferred to the aforesaid Egilolf, to possess as his own by perpetual right.

The names of the witnesses are these:

Patho, Ogo, Papo, Sigipold, Nanzo, Fastmot, Machelm, Wicram, Lantperht, Rihker, Amalperht, Ato, Engilperht, Rodhart, Engilscalh, Lantfrid, Swidker, Adalhoh, Rihheri, Egilhelm, Elindeo, Rodmunt, Anthat, Heriwic, Walto, Wegalanzo, Immo, Peregher, Otperth, and Gernando.

Lantpert, brother of the same Egilolf, and Adalhun, the bishop’s vassal, served as sureties and agents of the investiture.

## CHAPTER V — The Settlement between Bishop Ambricho and Arndeo

Let the quality of this present exchange become known to certain faithful men. It was carried out in the following manner, according to the ancient custom that had formerly arisen among men.

A certain nobleman named Arndeo therefore handed over to Saint Peter the Apostle and the martyr of God Emmeram, specifically into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his deputy Ogo, such property as he possessed with his wife in the village called Hartinga:

A house with a court, thirty acres of arable land, ten cartloads of meadows, and sixteen dependents.

In return, the aforesaid bishop and his deputy Ogo handed over to the same nobleman and to his wife, named Tota, that benefice at Tanna, namely a house with a court, a church, and everything contained in it; three hides of arable land, thirteen cartloads of meadows, and thirty-six dependents.

They were to possess it until their death. Afterward it was to revert by perpetual right to the original property of the saints.

## CHAPTER VI — The Transfer between Bishop Ambricho and Bishop Otkarius

A very fruitful custom had long since arisen among men—not only honorable but also exceedingly useful—of exchanging certain properties for the benefit of both parties.

Accordingly, a certain exchange was agreed between Ambricho, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, and Otkarius, bishop of the Church of Eichstätt.

Otkarius and his advocate Wicpot therefore handed over such property as he had obtained from the king at Zullingon, Mammingon, and Ustarlingon, together with twenty dependents, whose names are these:

Ratmunt, Rihholf, Adalmot, Otmar, Adalperht, Otmunt, Rodilo, Alprat, Liupcundo, Wolfliup, Arnhilt, Gozpire, Wasa, Swanahilt, Perhetger, Rihni, Alpwiz, Altrat, Eparhart, and Cundperht, to Saint Peter.

In return, the aforesaid Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Ratold, with the consent of the servants of God serving there, handed over to the aforesaid Bishop Otkarius such inheritance as a certain nobleman named Teuit had donated to Saint Peter for the remedy of his soul at Perga and Egiwila, namely to be held as property, together with another twenty dependents, whose names are these:

Wolfolt, Ilina, Gundigart, Ruodilo, Wolfolt, Rihholf, Rodflat, Popo, Purcman, Adalgoz, Nendilo, Alphilt, Ata, Reginhart, Frowihilt, Isanhart, Machelm, Adalswind, Heimo, and Odalperht.

And, so that this exchange and the advantage of both parties might remain unshaken, it was decided to summon witnesses, whose names are recorded here:

Fritilo, Papo, likewise Papo, Wolfdregi, again Wolfdregi, Erchanperht, Chuniperht, Reginpold, Irminolt, Reginolf, Otachar, Adalger, Masso, Patager, Odalperht, Arfrid, Machelm, Otperht, Hartrih, Mahalfrid, Irminolt, Otachar, and Heimperht.

It was enacted in the city of Regensburg beside the altar of Saint Peter, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 863.

## CHAPTER VII — King Louis’s Donation of Maninsea

This record contains how Abbot Lantpert petitioned King Louis, with Ernost and Adaipert interceding, to donate as his alms to the monastery of Saint Michael, which was established at Maninsea, a certain lake called Aparinessea, together with all the surrounding forest, for the benefit of the servants of God who strive to serve the Lord in that monastery.

The king himself, for the benefit of his soul, did so, and donated the aforesaid lake and forest to Saint Michael, so that from that day onward no one would dare to cause any opposition concerning these properties. He also sent his messenger to invest the aforesaid abbot and the servants of God in them.

Then that messenger, fulfilling the king’s command, carried out the investiture. On the west, it extended from the stream called Zinchinpah, where it flows into Aparinessea; on the east, from the place where Tinnilipah flows into the same lake, as far as the place where Iscula falls into the Truna, so that it should stand there without anyone’s objection.

On the other side it had a boundary extending as far as Wizinpah, where that stream also enters Atarsea, and to another Wizinpah, as far as the point where it flows into the Truna.

This was established so that no outsider would dare to fish in this lake or hunt in the places mentioned above, but that everything should belong fully to the aforesaid archangel.

This donation was made at Rantesdorf in the year of the Lord 829.

## CHAPTER VIII — The Transfer between Bishop Ambricho and Amalpert

A very fruitful and exceedingly reasonable custom had formerly begun to grow among men: namely, exchanging certain properties for the benefit of both parties.

The greatness of kings also, since people in different regions of the earth employed the same practice, decreed that this should be done especially in ecclesiastical matters, and permitted it to stand with the addition of five hides.

Therefore a certain nobleman named Amalpert handed over to the holy martyr of God Emmeram his properties, which he appeared to possess at Perga, Hasalpah, and Gamminchova.

In the homesteads and houses, together with all their buildings—but excepting the servants’ dwellings—he transferred and handed over everything else to the aforesaid saint: cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, omitting nothing, but transferring everything to the aforesaid saint into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho [Col. 0906C] and his advocate Antarboto.

In return, the same advocate, with the consent of the bishop, handed over to the aforementioned Amalpert from the property of Saint Emmeram, at Drudpah, one church and three homesteads with all their appurtenances—territories, meadows, pastures, waters, and woods—together with the entire boundary district belonging there.

This was enacted in the presence of the bishop, with Egilpert, Deotpert, Faramund, priests and monks, assisting him. Among the canons were Erempert, Ermanold, and Germund, priests.

The witnesses, who were led by the ears, are also:

Harahad, Gerperht, Poso, Adalhun, Folcpold, Reginperht, Foleger, Richolt, likewise Rihholt, Ato, Gammo, Egilolf, Helfrih, Faramunt, Waldger, Liutprant, Liuthart, Rihmunt, [Col. 0906D] Perehtrih, Freso, Reginhoh, Rasfolt, Nordheri, Gregorius, and others.

## CHAPTER IX — The Transfer between Bishop Ambricho and Count Engilpert
All faithful readers should know, and let the knowledge of this charter’s declaration be made manifest to everyone, how the present exchange was carried out for the benefit of both parties; its meaning is also made entirely clear by the order of the following words.

Thus Count Engilpertus, exalted by great dignity, transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram, into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Wicrammus, 130 jugera of his woodland property in the place called Atinga. In return, the distinguished prelate and his aforementioned advocate transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, in the same place, to the aforesaid Count Engilpertus, 24 jugera of meadowland, to be held as his own in perpetuity.

These are the witnesses who saw and heard this: Framrih, Wichad, Pernbart, Perehtgoz, Nanzo, Egilpreht, Engilhelm, Helmrih, Hartnand, Gatahelm, Plidker, Gotascalch, and others.

## Chapter X — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the Priest Alawih

A very fruitful, honorable, and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties. In accordance with this practice and arrangement, an exchange was agreed between Ambricho, venerable bishop of the Church of Regensburg, and a certain noble priest, Alawih, the chancellor of the revered Count Rodoldus.

The aforesaid priest, together with his advocate, transferred into the hands of the bishop and his advocate Immo such property as he possessed at Ottarpah, leaving nothing out, but transferring the whole of it in its entirety into the power of Saint Emmeram. At Hacinhofa he also transferred one plot and two jugera.

In return, the aforementioned Immo, together with the bishop already named, transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram such property as Poppo once transferred to Saint Emmeram, in the place called Holzhusa, to Alawih, to be possessed as his property by perpetual right. Leaving nothing out, he transferred the whole of it in its entirety—woodlands, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and the revenues from roads—with the strongest legal force.

Those who performed the investiture were Ratoldus, Berehtricus, and Immo. And so that this exchange might remain more firmly and undisturbed forever, it was agreed to bring forward witnesses, whose names are: Count Albrat, Polo, Count Cundpold, Herrant, Perehtrih, Ratolt, Snelhart, Garaheri, Reginperht, Fridaperht, Kepahart, Somperht, Hunrih, Hisso, Helmger, Hiltrih, Grimuni, Gomerih, Sigiwunds, Count Cotascalch, and Odalhart.

It was enacted in the city of Regensburg in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 871, indiction 4.

## Chapter XI — Agreement between Bishop Ambricho and the Deacon Baldric

Among created beings, no living creature is granted the capacity to foresee an eternal reward or to know what share it will have in everlasting blessedness for good deeds, except the creature endowed with rational understanding—that is, the human being.

The ecclesiastical man named Baldric therefore did not forget this understanding, but thought very profitably in advance about the future recompense of his soul, considering the divine saying: “Give earthly things so that you may acquire eternal ones.”

Moved here by this exhortation, the aforementioned venerable man transferred part of his money to Saint Emmeram, into the hands of the most reverend prelate Ambricho and his advocate, named Walah, on the condition that the property which his paternal uncle Otachar had transferred to the aforesaid saint of God, in the place called Rorpah, should be returned to him for the rest of his life; and that after his death the same property should remain perpetually in the possession of Saint Emmeram, together with the money he donated.

That is: one silver chalice with paten; two lectionaries; two missals; one book of homilies; two graduals; two nocturnals; one book of canons; one psalter; two passionaries; one office book; one collectary; one penitential; one male slave and one female slave, namely Adalhoh and Imma; six horses; and the offspring born from them after the donation was made. All these, together with everything else in that property, were to belong securely and firmly to the often-mentioned holy martyr of God.

So that this agreement might be made more secure, the following witnesses were led forward by the ears: Heriperht, Avo, Helfrih, Jacob, Erchanfrid, another Jacob, Salmon, Sigiperht, Erchanperht, Rupo, Cundachar, Erchanpold, Oto, and Nidhart.

## Chapter XII — Exchange between Bishop Baturicus and Abbot Sigimodus

After Baturicus, a man orthodox in faith and of holy memory, bishop, and Abbot Sigimund had made a mutual agreement, they carried out the following exchange: the venerable prelate granted the abbot, as the benefit of an exchange, the slaves whom he possessed at Perindorf; and the abbot, in return, gave what he possessed beside the banks of the Labara.

On Sigismund’s side it happened that the slaves whom the bishop had given in exchange suffered injury and often complained to the aforesaid pontiff. Although the gentle bishop listened to this, he nevertheless wished to avoid dissension and asked to speak with the abbot, so that the slaves whom he had received in exchange might not suffer unjust abuse from him.

The abbot, however, was unwilling in any way to correct the matter. While things remained thus, Bishop Baturicus, unable in good conscience to endure the cause of the injuries suffered by his slaves, came with his friends and men to the aforementioned village to meet the abbot.

When they had sat down and silence had been made, Bishop Baturicus, with due agreement, returned to the abbot the exchange he had received from him, together with his staff; and the abbot, in the same manner, returned to the bishop, with his own staff, the exchange he had conducted with him.

Thus they agreed that their settlement should henceforth stand in this form: if at any time either wished to raise a claim between them concerning those matters, they would then establish it at the outset.

Present there were Oto, Kamanolf, Rodolt, Swarzloh, Pillunc, Uzant, Cundheri, Pern, Erchanpold, Jacob, Marcho, and others.

It was enacted in the village mentioned above in the year of the Lord 829.

## Chapter XIII — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Gundpert

A fruitful association and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange not only the resources of various possessions because of the convenience of their locations, but perhaps—and this seems to me the more important reason—through the peaceful valuation of the thing exchanged.

Accordingly, royal authority ordained that this should henceforth be done in its own possessions, especially ecclesiastical ones, and allowed it to be valid up to the amount of five hobs. Once that number had been exceeded, if any exchange was to be carried out, it could be confirmed only by a royal precept and ring.

Accordingly, a certain noble man named Cundbert decided to carry out an exchange of some of his property. He transferred to Saint Peter the apostle and to God’s holy martyr Emmeram, into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Ogo, such property as he possessed at Purcpah. This consisted of a house with a courtyard, a church, and within it one silver reliquary; one silver-prepared altar; two other altars; two silver-prepared altar stones; one silver chalice with paten; one silver cross; one missal; one lectionary; one alb; one scarlet chasuble; one stole; one bronze censer; one bell; two bronze bells; one orchard; one vineyard; one mill; one fishpond; thirteen hobs of arable land and meadow; 110 jugera of woodland; and eleven slaves, namely Ratkis, Motuni and his daughter, Perehtwar with his son and daughter, Ciliga and his two sons, Deotpurc, and Nordpold.

At Hapuhpah, one hob; at Sulzpah, one hob and one mill. These too belong to the upper holding. Leaving nothing out, therefore, he transferred and conveyed everything to the aforesaid saints: streams and watercourses, pastures, and woodlands.

This was done on the condition that, if the benefice which he held at Filesa should be granted to him as his own by royal command, namely a house with a courtyard, a church, and within it one altar, one small altar cloth, five hobs of arable land, forty wagonloads of meadow, thirty jugera of woodland, and one mill, then the following would also belong to the same holding:

Nearby, in the same boundary, one hob which Advocate Jacob had acquired from Megilo and his brother Hungar, with eight jugera of meadow; and at Hasalpah, which also belongs there, a house with a courtyard, two hobs of arable land, eight wagonloads of meadow, and five jugera of woodland.

At the same place, at Filesa, with the following appurtenances, there were eleven slaves, namely Wolfpero, Ratpoto, Heimpreht, Liutfrid, Otfrid, Anthad, Kisalolf, Somni, Helmdrud, Mahtlind, and Chunipreht.

These are the witnesses, led by the ears, to the transfer of the aforementioned Gundbert: Ogo, Avo, Adalhun, Karaheri, Rodheri, Hittipero, Hitto, Erchanperht, Marcho, Lantperht, Liutperht, Folcrih, Ascrih, and others.

It was enacted at Rockinga beneath the oak opposite the church, in the first year of the reign of Emperor Charles over the Bavarians and Franks.

## Chapter XIV — Agreement between Bishop Erchanfrid and David

Oh, how transient and fragile is the human race, which is undoubtedly always subject to miserable death; and how joyful is the heavenly life, where the saints will have happiness without end!

I, David, weighing these matters with the utmost attentiveness of mind, transfer certain possessions of mine in the places called Perge and Egiwila—whatever I possess in those places, together with twenty-five slaves—to Saint Peter, where the venerable Bishop Erchanfrid is known to govern God’s Church.

This is done on the condition and arrangement that he should possess the chapel at Alarespurc, and, if he outlived his father-in-law Werinpert, that he should possess the benefice at Biucheim until the end of his life; and that afterward everything, with all improvements, should remain with Saint Peter without opposition from him.

And so that this arrangement might stand firmer and more securely for those who come after, it was agreed to bring forward witnesses: Count Babo, Meginhart, Ratolt, Masso, Elit, Epo, Sigimot, Odalperth, Walah, Avo, Jacob, Albrih, and another Jacob. Testimonial witnesses: Waldker, Ogo, another Ogo, and others.

## Chapter XV — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Adalpert

A very fruitful and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

In accordance with this practice and arrangement, Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and a certain noble man named Adalbert agreed to exchange certain properties.

The bishop’s advocate Puolo, with the consent and command of the aforesaid bishop and of all the monks of Saint Emmeram, transferred such property as Wolfheri had transferred to the aforesaid saint at Frumdorf, to be possessed by perpetual right.

In return, Adalpert transferred at Reitinpoh such a contiguous holding, and the property he possessed in that contiguous holding, as was suitable for the affairs of the aforesaid Saint Emmeram, so that it might belong perpetually to the saint of God without anyone’s opposition.

This exchange was made in the year of the Lord 866, indiction 13, in the place called Pereharteshusa, in the presence of the aforementioned bishop and Count Rodolt.

## Chapter XVI — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Chresting

Let the attention of many faithful people, both present and future, learn through the account of my most humble abridger how the reverend worshiper of God, Ambricho, carried out a suitable exchange with a certain noble champion named Chresting.

This strong and free man transferred to Saint Emmeram, martyr of God, in the place called Cheleheim, twenty-one jugera of arable land and a sufficiently fine portion of woodland. As most people judge, that woodland consists of twenty jugera or more.

In return, the venerable bishop of the holy see, Ambricho, together with his advocate Cundbert, gave back to the same aforementioned noble man from the possessions of God’s saint an equal number of jugera of arable land and an equal portion of woodland, in the place called Arnhelmashova. Each of them thus sought the utility or advantage of the locations for himself, as they indeed did.

So that this agreement might be firmer and more readily believed by posterity, it was agreed that two charters written in the customary manner should be produced concerning it and that the names of the witnesses should be recorded. They are: Ascrih, Adalhun, Cotaperht and his brother Irimperht, Helfrih, Paldrih, Cundhart, Arperht, Strupo, Hiltiprant, Rafolt, Engilpero, Odalscalch, Odalhart, Reginger, Cundperht, and his brother Rihho.

## Chapter XVII — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ogo

[Col. 0911A]

Thanks be to God that a very useful and exceedingly fruitful custom had formerly arisen among people, and is still carefully and properly practiced by many nobles: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

Then the faithful men of Bishop Ambricho decided to urge him to make an exchange with his faithful man Ogo, who possessed good property acquired as his own and belonging suitably to the aforesaid bishop’s estates.

Ogo then declared that he had done so on the condition that he be properly compensated. Immediately the bishop consulted the monks and canons to determine whether this was their will. They said that it would be proper, provided that he first sent his own faithful men to investigate which portion was better.

The bishop then ordered Egilpert the provost, Avo the advocate, Wolfhoh the cleric, and Deotfrid the deputy to go, investigate, and measure everything carefully with a measuring rod.

They agreed and reported to the bishop what they had found concerning Ogo’s property: 179 jugera of arable land and woodland. What the bishop was required to give in return amounted to 133 jugera.

Then the bishop said that it would be better if he asked his lord the king what his will was. The king then said that it should be done according to the permission he had given, so that an exchange might be made up to five hobs. This statement was made by the king on the Ides of June.

Afterward Lord Bishop Ambricho summoned his monks, canons, and other faithful men, and they carried out that exchange.

The aforesaid Ogo therefore transferred to Saint Emmeram, in the presence of the servants of God and of the advocate of that church, named Avo, in the place called Puohhusa, a house with a courtyard, seventy jugera of arable land, ten jugera of woodland; at Punninchova, ten jugera of arable land and thirty-nine jugera of woodland; and at Munolfinga, a house with a courtyard, thirty jugera of arable land and twenty jugera of woodland.

In return, Avo, the advocate of the aforesaid bishop, transferred to the aforementioned Ogo, from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, in the place called Matinga, a house with a courtyard and 133 jugera of arable land.

These monks were present at the time: Egilperht, Faraman, Deotperht, Reginfrid, Adalgoz, and almost all the rest. Among the canons were Sandrat, Ermanolt, Erchanperht, Wolfhoh, Rodult, Rihholf, and others.

Afterward the bishop and his faithful men ordered Advocate Avo and Ogo to proceed to the assembly of counts at Eitaraha, where witnesses were to be led forward by the ears. This took place in the presence of Count Chunipert, Count Cundopold, and Count Rumold.

These witnesses were led forward there: Reginhoh, Pazrih, Nidhart, Rodmunt, Liudhart, Eparhoh, Wihmunt, Arhart, Perahthelm, Pern, Erchanpold, Rodmar, Erchanfrid, and the rest.

## Chapter XVIII — Exchange between Berehtgunda and Grimharius

Let the attention of all faithful people recognize how the venerable matron Berehtcund and Grimheri made a suitable exchange.

The aforementioned noble man Grimharius therefore transferred to Saint Emmeram thirty jugera of arable land and fourteen wagonloads of meadow in the place called Stinpah, into the hands of Perehtgunda and her advocate, named Lantbertus.

In return, Perehtgund herself and her advocate Lantbertus, with the permission of the honorable Bishop Ambricho, transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram to the same noble Grimharius, at Imminpere, thirty jugera of arable land and twelve wagonloads of meadow.

These are the witnesses to this transaction, led forward by the ears: Strachol, Hunolt, Deotolt, Sigimunt, Meiol, Hunger, Amalger, Otperht, Reginhart, Deotcoz, Ermenperht, Ruodolf, Petilo, Hamadeo, Engilwart, and Reginolt.

It was enacted at Stinpah in the first year of the most serene King Karlmann.

## Chapter XIX — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Winicho

A very fruitful, honorable, and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange for the benefit of both parties.

Accordingly, a certain noble man named Winicho transferred to Saint Emmeram his property at Puocha and Stupinga, leaving nothing out.

In return, with the permission of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and the consent of the brethren, the bishop’s advocate Isan transferred to the aforesaid Winicho, from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, in the place called Buohloh, a house with a courtyard and buildings, fifty-three jugera of arable land, and twelve wagonloads of meadow, to be possessed as his property.

Whatever either party had transferred to the other from that point onward, they were to have free power in every respect, without the hindrance of anyone’s opposition.

And so that this exchange might more firmly be believed by posterity, it was agreed to bring forward witnesses, whose names are: Folcrat, Masso, Immo, Luitprant, Wicpold, Waninc, Jacob, Adalscalh, Pazrih, Albrih, Altmar, Truogilo, Adalunc, Rafolt, Gotafort, Swapilo, Meginhart, and Teorotnand.

## Chapter XX — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ellinpold

A very fruitful, honorable, and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

Accordingly, this exchange was agreed between the venerable Bishop Ambricho and a certain noble man named Ellinpold.

The aforementioned Ellinpold therefore transferred to Saint Emmeram, into the hands of the aforesaid bishop and his advocate Appo, from his own property at Perga, one plot and one meadow for establishing a mill.

In return, the aforementioned advocate, with the bishop’s permission, transferred to Ellinpold from the possessions of Saint Emmeram a portion of a plot at Hedinpah: twelve measuring rods in length and two in width.

And so that this exchange might be firmer and more readily believed by posterity, it was agreed that two charters written in one form should be produced concerning it and that witnesses should be brought forward, whose names are: Erchanperht, Grimperht, Amalperht, Petilo, Otmar, Erchanhart, Amalrih, and others.

## Chapter XXI — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Reginpert

[Col. 0913A]

A very fruitful and exceedingly useful custom had long arisen among people: namely, to exchange their possessions for the benefit of both parties and to take on either side what was contiguous to them.

With this arrangement in mind, the noble Reginpert, a vassal of the venerable Bishop Ambricho, transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram certain possessions that had come to him by inheritance through the marital union with his wife, named Wicbirga, in the province of the Bavarians, in the district of Tonocgewa, in the settlement of Tuncilinga.

These consisted of an abandoned building site, forty-eight jugera of arable land, fifteen wagonloads of meadow, one hundred jugera of woodland, roads, waters, and whatever he was visibly seen to possess in that place. The aforesaid bishop and his advocate Cundpert accepted the transfer.

In return, from the possessions of the aforementioned holy martyr, he received from the same transferors a certain place called Puoh, near the court commonly called “Tan Monachorum,” that is, “the Church”: a courtyard with an orchard, forty-eight jugera of arable land—equal to what he had given—fifteen wagonloads of meadow, three jugera of woodland, and whatever he had previously been seen to have received as a benefice in that place.

This was done on the condition that he and his descendants, or anyone to whom he wished to give it, should possess it perpetually by hereditary right.

Finally, so that this transfer might be more indissoluble, it was agreed that witnesses from both sides should affirm it, being led forward by the ears according to Noric custom. We also considered it fitting to record their names, lest any error should later affect posterity:

Cundpert, advocate of Bishop Ambricho, who, as stated above, both received and made this transfer together with the bishop. Witnesses: Helfric, Durinchard, Waltung, Askaric, Rodharius, Deotmar, Rihpald, Rihpert, and Cundhart.

And so that there might be no impediment whatsoever from either side, it was agreed that two charters should be assigned: one was to be deposited in the library of the holy martyr, while the other was to be retained by the aforementioned Reginpert.

It was enacted in the presence of the bishop mentioned so often and of many others, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 879, indiction 12, while the sons of the most illustrious King Louis—Karlmann, Louis, and Charles—were reigning, in the fourth year.

## Chapter XXII — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ekkihard

[Col. 0913D]

A very fruitful, honorable, and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

Accordingly, this exchange was agreed between the venerable Bishop Ambricho and a certain noble man named Eckihard.

The aforementioned Eckihard therefore transferred to Saint Emmeram, into the hands of the aforesaid bishop and his advocate Adalric, his property which he appeared to possess in the place called Stargina, together with one slave.

In return, the aforementioned advocate, with the bishop’s permission, transferred to the aforesaid Eckihard, at Ewistun, from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, an equal measure of arable land and three wagonloads of meadow.

And so that this exchange might be firmer and more readily believed by posterity, it was agreed that two charters written in one form should be produced concerning it and that witnesses should be brought forward, whose names are: Rihhart, Sigiperht, Helmperht, Engilperht, Marcholt, Eparhart, Kepahart, Erchanpold, and many others.

## Chapter XXIII — Agreement between Bishop Ambricho and the Deacon Gundbato

Let the attention of everyone faithful learn—or rather, let it learn very clearly—through this charter how the following transfer and agreement was made manifest.

A certain venerable deacon named Cundbato reflected for the salvation of his soul. He hoped—and this is entirely to be believed—that if he enriched God’s holy churches with earthly possessions, his bodily care and eternal salvation of soul would thereby be increased.

Therefore, moved by divine thought, he transferred to Saint Emmeram, martyr of God, his property which he possessed at Quartinaha near Bilisaseo, with the permission of his lord Arnolf, the royal son, from whom he had received it as a possession.

The aforesaid property was transferred by the same venerable Cundbato for his lord Arnolf and for himself to the altar of Saint Emmeram, into the hands of the most reverend prelate Ambricho and his advocate Gundbert.

It consisted of the church of Saint John the Evangelist with all its appurtenances and dependencies, with its courtyard and parish, and with everything granted to it: slaves, cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, pastures, woodlands, tithes, waters and watercourses, and the places transferred with them—namely, at the river Sala, what Froperht formerly held as a benefice, and at Velih—as well as all other movable and immovable property.

In return, the aforesaid advocate Gundpert, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned venerable deacon Gundbato what Duke Chezil once donated to the aforesaid saint for the salvation of his soul, beside the river called Raba.

This was done on the condition that Gundbato should firmly and usefully possess both properties until his death. Afterward, everything in its entirety was to return and be restored to the often-mentioned saint of God.

And so that the authority of this transfer might be held more firmly, the following witnesses were led forward by the ears: Polo, Jacob, Reginhoh, Solomon, Eckirih, Adamar, Avo, Fastmot, Gotaperht, Irmperht, Heripold, Unlaz, Pernhart, Herrant, Engilscalh, Erchanperht, Reginhart, Strupo, Hungis, Ambricho, Liutperht, Sigihart, Vicker, and Patto.

Also Avo, Switker, Gammo, Adalrih, and Salacho.

Moreover, beside the altar of the aforesaid saint, the bishop granted the same Gundbato permission to search for and seize the slaves of Saint Emmeram who had fled beyond the Raba, and to establish them in those same ecclesiastical properties, so that after his death, as we have said above, everything, with all improvements, might return to Saint Emmeram, martyr of God.

## Chapter XXIV — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ernustus

[Col. 0915A]

An exchange between Bishop Ambricho and a certain venerable man named Ernustus.

Bishop Ambricho gave twenty-six jugera from the possessions of the holy Church in the place called Gundpatinga. In return, Ernustus gave twenty-eight jugera from his own property in the place called Preitprunnin.

This was done on the condition that, if any successor of the aforementioned bishop should attempt to alter this exchange, Ernustus would then have the power to transfer his own possessions wherever he wished.

These are the names of those standing by and hearing the matter: Erchenmar, Willihelm, Wichart, Anthelm, Eigil, Reginhart, Herilung, Anzo, Gundpold, Gerolt, Drudolt, Hartnid, Helfrih, Eckirih, Weladeo, Ato, Ermanolt, Rodcog, Merimuz, and others.

## Chapter XXV — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Richelmus

A very fruitful, honorable, and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

Accordingly, this exchange was agreed between the venerable Bishop Ambricho and a certain dominical slave named Rihhelmus.

The aforementioned Rihhelmus therefore transferred into the hands of the aforesaid bishop and his advocate Hahard, from the property of his wife, one meadow measuring twelve jugera and eight jugera of arable land, situated beside the small estate called Dehtapeta.

In return, the aforementioned advocate, with the bishop’s permission, transferred to the often-mentioned Rihhelmus from the possessions of Saint Peter twenty jugera of arable land situated near the village called Winzara.

And so that this exchange might be firmer and more readily believed by posterity, it was agreed that two charters written in one form should be produced concerning it and that witnesses should be brought forward, whose names are: Kaganhart, Ciliman, Pezo, another Ciliman, Odalperht, Engici, Eiorih, Plidker, Salacho, Alpgoz, Amalheri, Sono, and others.

## Chapter XXVI — The Transfer of Avaluna

In the name of God, Avaluna transferred to Saint Emmeram ten slaves, whose names are: Leva, Kerhart, Paldrih, Folcrat, Willirih, Deotperht, Willipurc, Reginpold, Cotaperht, and Kisalfrid.

In return, Immo the advocate and Ogo transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram five slaves to the aforementioned Avaluna as her property, namely: Unroh, Helidolf, Snelhart, Hitto, and Egilwih.

These are the witnesses: Ogo, Masso, Epucho, another Epucho, Wago, Isanpero, Adalperht, and Rodolt.

It was enacted at Potinreinna.

## Chapter XXVII — The Transfer of a Certain Roman, Ratharius

In the name of the Most High God, let it be known to all people of the Christian faith who wish to know this matter: I, Ratheri, reflecting on the reward to come and mindful of the service pleasing to me, transferred to the altar of God, which is known to have been dedicated in honor of Saint Emmeram, martyr, my own female slave, Ellinpurg, acquired through my own labors; and after my death I dedicated her to that place.

This was done on the condition that she should hope thereby for protection and defense, pay no more than four denarii each year, and dispose of the remaining time of this life according to her own judgment.

Finally, I left my three sons, whom the aforementioned woman bore to me—Alawinus, John, and Bernhard—free and secure from every bond of human servitude.

My brothers were also present, named Allino and Alawino, and they willingly consented to both matters, that is, concerning the woman and the sons.

This was enacted before the citizens of the royal city of Regensburg, whose names appear below: Lantolt, deputy-vicar of the city; Adalpero, collector of the toll; Odalman, Egilolf, Ratker, Wolffrid, Ratcoz, Huntolf, Otwin, Welo, Wachilo, Adalrat, and Enci.

## Chapter XXVIII — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Rihcowo

A very fruitful and exceedingly useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

A certain noble man named Rihcowo did not neglect this custom, but transferred to Saint Emmeram his property in that boundary at Menzinpah, into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Garaheri.

In return, the same advocate, with the bishop’s permission, transferred to the aforementioned Rihcowo from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, at Talamazinga, nine jugera of arable land and one small wood.

These are the witnesses to this exchange: Unlaz, Erchanfrid, Askarih, Deotmar, Helfrih, Sigifrid, Tinto, and others.

## Chapter XXIX — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Engilmar and His Brothers

Let the attention of certain faithful people learn, whoever’s ears may receive the knowledge contained in this charter, how the most reverend prelate Ambricho and a certain noble man named Engilmar, together with his brothers Mezi and Vitalis, carried out the present exchange for the benefit of both parties.

The aforementioned young man Engilmar, with the consent of his brothers, transferred to Saint Peter and to God’s holy martyr Emmeram such property as he possessed at Menzinpah, leaving nothing out except the right to take three cartloads of wood and to pasture forty pigs.

He transferred all the rest, without any opposition, to the aforesaid saints, into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Gundbert. This consisted of a house with a courtyard, a good tract of woodland, forty-four jugera of arable land, thirty wagonloads of meadow, and one slave named Othelm.

In return, the aforementioned bishop, a man of great merit, and his advocate Gundbert transferred to the same noble men from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, at Sallahopit, a house with a courtyard, a church, and everything that was in it; forty-five jugera of arable land; thirty wagonloads of meadow; two woodland groves; and one slave named Egilwolf.

These are the witnesses to this exchange, led forward by the ears: Ogo, Adolf, Avo, Strupo, Sinzo, Helfrih, Hartwic, Truhthad, Hawart, Unlaz, Cheftinc, and Engilperht.

It was enacted before Count Engildeo and Abbot Engilmar, while Emperor Charles was reigning.

## Chapter XXX — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Salamannus

A very fruitful and wonderfully useful custom had formerly arisen among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the convenience of both parties.

The noble man Salamannus likewise decided to imitate this practice, faithfully considering his own advantage.

The noble man named above transferred to Saint Emmeram, martyr of God, with the consent of his wife Adalburna, his wife’s property which he appeared to possess at Menzpah by hereditary right, into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Helfric.

That is, he transferred to the aforesaid saint everything he possessed there in its entirety: cultivated and uncultivated territory, its woodland and boundary, meadows, waters and their watercourses, and all the rest.

In return, the prelate and the aforementioned advocate transferred to the same noble man, from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, the territory at Reitinpoh which Otmar once transferred to the often-mentioned saint.

The witnesses to this exchange are: Avo, Strupo, Rupo, Ogo, Hahart, Polo, Unlaz, Hiltipero, Hatto, and others.

## Chapter XXXI — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Rathard and His Brother

A very fruitful and exceedingly useful custom began long ago to arise among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties. This is now practiced more and more, especially among nobles.

Two noble men, uterine brothers named Cundhart and Rathart, did not wish to neglect this for their own advantage.

The aforementioned men therefore transferred to Saint Emmeram, martyr, into the hands of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate named Gundbert, in the place called Atinga, two courtyards with an equal number of houses, seventy jugera of arable land and ten jugera of newly cleared land, twenty-five wagonloads of meadow, twenty jugera of well-maintained woodland, and one mill.

In return, the aforementioned venerable worshiper and his advocate transferred to those noble men, from the possessions of Blessed Emmeram, martyr of God, at Totinaccharon:

To Cundhart, a house with a courtyard, fifty-two jugera of arable land, and one wagonload of meadow;

and to Rathart, a house with a courtyard, forty-two jugera of territory, twelve wagonloads of meadow, and three jugera of woodland, in the place called Vekkinga.

And so that this might remain stable in the future and be more readily believed by posterity, it was agreed that two charters should be written in identical form.

## Chapter XXXII — Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the Deacon Altoltus
Some faithful people may learn—so that this charter’s notice may be inserted into the ears of anyone—that a certain venerable deacon named Altoltus transferred to the holy martyr of God Emmerammus such property as he possessed at Atinga, namely, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Wicrammus: thirty acres of arable land and meadows, and fifteen or more acres of scrubland to be cleared. Conversely, the aforesaid advocate, named Wicrammus, transferred from the property of Saint Emmerammus, with the permission of the lord bishop, to that venerable deacon thirty acres of arable land, six acres of woodland, four cartloads of meadow, and one building plot. This lies beside the lake called Munituna, so that the aforesaid saint and the steward of his property might possess the former at Atinga, while that deacon of peaceful distinction might hold the latter securely at Munituna. And so that this exchange might remain equally firm, it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced, together with the witnesses named below: Polo, Adolf, Avo, Strupo, Karaheri, Cotaperht, Helfrih, Liuthart, Waltunc, Erchanperht, Hungis, and Adalhun. It was enacted at Rockinga, in the presence of the abbots Engilmar and Hitto, and of the archpresbyter Sandrat and the deacon Regino.

### CHAPTER XXXIII—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Lantpertus

Let the diligence of the faithful learn how the reverend worshipper of God Ambricho carried out an exchange with a certain freedman named Lantpertus. For the man just mentioned transferred to Saint Peter and the holy martyr of God Emmerammus 150 acres of his own property, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Helfricus. This lies beside the fortress called Erilinga. Conversely, the aforesaid advocate, with the bishop’s consent, transferred from the property of the saints named above to the same Lantpertus 133 acres of arable land at the place called Eidrateshusa. And so that this exchange might be held more securely, it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced.

### CHAPTER XXXIV—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Adolf

Through the brief account of this charter I shall attempt to disclose the purpose of an exchange to every willing listener. A certain nobleman named Adolf therefore transferred to Saint Peter and the holy martyr of God Emmerammus, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocates Helfricus and Gundbertus, his property at Husun: namely, sixty-three acres of arable land, a house with an enclosure, a granary, an orchard, nine cartloads of meadow, and twenty-five acres of woodland. He also transferred and conveyed to the aforesaid saints everything belonging to him that was attached to that place.

Conversely, Helfricus and Gundbertus, with the bishop’s consent, transferred from the property of the saints to the aforesaid nobleman Adolf, at the place called Altaha, a house with an enclosure, a granary, an orchard, sixty acres of arable land and meadow, and an extensive tract of woodland. The witnesses to this transfer are Polo, Avo, Strupo, Heidfolc, Gataperht, Irmperht, Perehtrih, Isanperht, Sindperht, Adalliun, Hiltiprant, Patarih, and Ilpunc.

### CHAPTER XXXV—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Polo

Let the diligence of many faithful people recognize how certain servants, with their lords and masters not objecting, carried out an exchange of various possessions. Polo, the king’s representative, therefore gave half a hide belonging to Cotabald, son of Kaganhar, at Chuningesdorf, together with one building plot and one orchard, to Rinco, a servant of Saint Peter, into the hand of the venerable bishop Ambricho and of his advocate Helfricus.

Conversely, the aforesaid advocate, in the bishop’s presence, gave to Cotabald, the king’s dependent, one hide and one building plot belonging to Rinco, the servant of Saint Peter, into Polo’s hand, in the village called Tanhusa. This exchange was therefore made with Bishop Ambricho’s permission, by Polo, in the bishop’s house built between Erilapah and Menzinpah.

### CHAPTER XXXVI—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Poso

In former times a useful and fruitful custom began to grow among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the advantage of both parties. Even people of the present day, for their part, generally strive to do this, exchanging more and more frequently in imitation of the conduct of their forefathers. A certain nobleman named Poso did not wish to neglect this either, but for his own benefit took care to transfer a certain part of his property to the holy martyr of God Emmerammus, and he carried this out. It consisted of 118 acres at Perga and Hasalpah, among cultivated and uncultivated fields and the boundaries of meadows, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable worshipper of God and bishop, and of his advocate Adalhun.

Conversely, the same venerable bishop and his advocate transferred from the property of Saint Emmerammus to the aforesaid nobleman an equal portion of fields and meadows at Hedinpah and Tecchinpah. And so that it might remain more firmly in the future, they called witnesses, whose names are: Ogo, Adolf, Sindperht, Tevit, Grimperht, Embricho, Engilmar, Otachar, Rihker, Helfrih, Albrih, Gammo, Petilo, Unlaz, Cotahelm, and another Embricho.

### CHAPTER XXXVII—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Hahard

Let the diligence of certain faithful people, into whose ears the execution of this charter is entrusted, learn how usefully and honorably the following exchange was carried out. The emperor Charles therefore granted a certain nobleman named Hahard permission to conduct an exchange involving his benefice, and sent prudent envoys to carry it out with great care: namely, Willihelm, Sindbert, and also Hadamarus.

At that time the aforesaid nobleman, with the consent of his lord the Caesar, transferred to Saint Emmerammus, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his representative Ogo, 170 acres of arable land and meadow beside the streams of the Fattara, at the place called Bozilinga.

Conversely, the venerable bishop and his representative gave the same nobleman, from the property of Saint Emmerammus, seventy acres of arable land and sixty acres of woodland at the place called Hitinchova, beside the river Isura. And so that this exchange might be held firm and unshaken, it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be retained by both parties.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII—The transfer of Hiltigart at Mencinpah

Let the understanding of many faithful people learn through the notice of this charter how Hiltigart, moved by divine inspiration for the remedy of herself and her parents, acted by transferring her property. Thus Hiltigart transferred to Saint Emmerammus, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate named Helfricus, such property as she possessed at Menzinpah: namely, arable and non-arable land, meadows, waters and watercourses, a tract of woodland, and everything that she possessed there. She transferred all this to the aforesaid saint, omitting nothing except the cutting of wood sufficient for one cart from the boundary of that woodland.

This is attested by Berehtcoz, Ogo, Avo, Strupo, Rodmunt, Liutperht, Erchanperht, Rupo, Avo, Hiltipero, Ambricho, Adalpold, Walah, Gammo, and Eparhart.

### CHAPTER XXXIX—The transfer of the deacons Engilpertus and Gundpertus

A record of the transfer of the deacons Engilpertus and Cundpertus, his nephew. Engilpertus and Cundpertus, his nephew, therefore transferred to the monastery of Maninseo, to the holy archangel of God Michael, in the district of Rotacgewa, in the village called Skefowa, whatever they appeared to possess there in that village: a house with an enclosure and the remaining buildings, lands, meadows, an orchard, fishponds, pastures, woodlands, and six dependent persons, whose names are Rodker, Lantker, Paldmunt, Reginpurc, Rihdrud, and Rihger.

All the things stated above, in their entirety and by a firm legal act, with no one objecting, were transferred by the aforesaid Engilpertus and Cundpertus; on the condition, however, that they should possess by their own right, for as long as both lived, this benefice in the village called Ezinpah and also the aforesaid transfer at Skefowa.

These are the witnesses who were physically summoned: Count Kerolt; Kerolt, his son; Ratolf, the representative; Antrib, the representative; Pazrih; Cundperht; another Antrih; Isanperht; Meginpold; Gerhart; Hotto; Kerhoh; Ato; Adalhoh; Erchanfrid; Lantperht; Ratolt; Saxo; Wlfrih; Avo; Samuel; Nothart; Cundhart; Wirunt; Otachar; Reginperht; Isanger; Cuniperht; Rato; Engilscalh; Otker; Cozolt; Otperht; Gisalmunt; Mahtheri; Cundpold; and others. The sureties are Pazrih and Cundperht, one from each side.

Bishop Erchanfridus and his advocate Cundpertus received that transfer and, with the consent of the monks, granted the aforesaid benefice to the deacons Engilpertus and Cundpertus. Enacted at Rota, in the church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 852.

### CHAPTER XL—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Morenzo

A very fruitful and honorable custom had long prevailed among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties. For this reason Morenzo, with the permission of the venerable Bishop Ambricho, transferred seven acres from the property of Saint Emmerammus at Otmuntingon to a certain nobleman named Wolframmus as his property.

Conversely, the aforesaid Wolframmus transferred seven acres of his own property to Saint Emmerammus at Scussinchofun. And so that this exchange might be firmer and more readily believed by posterity, it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be prepared: one for the holy saint of God and the other for the aforesaid man.

### CHAPTER XLI—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ekkiricus

The very fruitful custom of exchanging possessions for the benefit of both parties began long ago to prevail among the ancients. For this reason, in more recent times the authority of kings also decreed that this should be done very frequently with ecclesiastical properties, and permitted it to extend up to the number of five hides.

Following this example, a certain nobleman named Ekkiricus transferred to the holy martyr of God Emmerammus his property at Homeres, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Reginhoh: namely, a house with an enclosure, forty-six acres of arable land, twenty-six cartloads of meadow, abundant woodland, one mill, waters and watercourses, together with everything belonging to that place. He transferred and conveyed all this to the aforesaid saint.

Conversely, the advocate mentioned above, with the bishop’s consent, transferred to Ekkiricus from the property of Saint Emmerammus, at Espilipah, a house with an enclosure and an equal number of acres of fields and meadows, to be held forever together with everything belonging there.

The witnesses physically summoned for this exchange are Ogo, Willihelm, Oto, Helfrih, Adalperht, Sigiperht, Helinger, Gammo, Erchanpold, Pern, Gemmunt, Rafolt, Nidhart, and others.

### CHAPTER XLII—The transfer of the presbyter Engilmarus

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, that a certain presbyter named Engilmarus transferred seven dependent persons to Saint Peter. Their names are Zeiza, Sigipirc, Wolfo, Asflat, Toto, Nordker, and Rodmunt. He arranged that Zeiza should merely sweep Saint Peter’s church and serve it as she was able; but that Asflat should serve Wolfo, the cleric and her brother, for the days of his life, and after his death should remain with the same endowment.

Salomon, the vassal of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, received this transfer. These are the witnesses physically summoned: Durinchart, Hiltipero, Perehtcoz, Pillunc, Folrat, Reginhoh, Ekkirih, Arperht, Egilfrid, Erchanfrid, Adalger, Wippo, Adalperht, Otili, Anthelm, and Strupo. It was done in Saint Peter’s church.

### CHAPTER XLIII—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Otmar

A very useful and highly convenient custom had long prevailed among people: they began to exchange their possessions with one another according to the suitability of places. For the same benefit it was agreed between Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and a certain nobleman named Otmar that they should make an exchange of some of their possessions, and they did so.

The aforesaid Otmar therefore transferred to Saint Emmerammus, from his own property, one building plot and nine acres of arable land at the place called Ipah. Conversely, the aforesaid venerable bishop gave Otmar, to hold as his property, from the property of Saint Emmerammus at the same place Ipah, ten acres of arable land.

The witnesses to both transfers are Ogo, Pirihtilo, Walah, Terpiton, Jacob, Erchanfrid, Willihelm, Willipold, Parto, Meiol, Ekkirih, Adalger, Ludo, Wago, Isanpero, Reginhart, and Amalker. In the year of the Lord 865.

### CHAPTER XLIV—The transfer of Otbert the castald

A brief memorandum concerning the property of Otbert the castald from Lombardy, which he gave to Saint Emmerammus and which is at Statuaras. First, two houses with their entrance, and a garden; ten olive trees; three portions of meadow; two measuring-rods of vineyard; and six measuring-rods of arable land.

He was invested with these possessions in the presence of Plagivertus, Ratbertus, Batruinus of Banilo, Gunduinius, Gumarius of that place, and others. Also present from Romania were Florinus, Manulfus, and Valerius. Liutpold the presbyter and Heimo the layman of Ergoltespach received these possessions for the soul of Otbert the castald in the house of Saint Emmerammus.

### CHAPTER XLV—The transfer of the presbyter Einhardus and Erhardus

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

We, Einhardus the presbyter and Erhardus, have reflected deeply upon the future blessedness and the reward of those who have been worthy to possess eternal life. Therefore we transferred our own possessions, which we appeared to possess in the settlement called Wolfmuntingas, to the monastery of Bishop Adalwinus, situated beside the streams called Rehtratanze, to the holy Savior, for the remedy of our souls and of the souls of our parents: a church with buildings, lands, woodlands, fields, meadows, mills, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, houses or sheds. We wish these things to be secured forever.

Afterward Bishop Adalwinus came with many noblemen to the settlement called Wolfmuntingas. Then, in their presence, Einhardus, Erhardus, and his wife Willipurc made the transfer before them, together with the church, buildings, lands, woodlands, fields, meadows, mills, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, houses or sheds; they transferred all the buildings and coverings to the holy Savior, as written above.

They also made investiture to Bishop Adalwinus of all the things mentioned here, except the places called Turunfeld and Altstat. Willipurc transferred four dependent persons. We agreed that Pernhardus, the son of Erhardus, should have pasture there for his livestock and use of the woodland for his own purposes, on the condition that these things should remain in their power for as long as they lived.

After their death, however, everything should return, as stated above in the transfer, to the monastery of the holy Savior, which Bishop Adalwinus is known to govern, for the benefit of the servants of God who are known to serve God in that place.

If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, someone among our heirs, or any opposing person—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to challenge this charter of transfer, may he not prevail in his claim. Rather, from the present day forward, this charter, supported by a formal stipulation, shall remain firm and inviolate forever.

This transfer was made in the presence of Bishop Adalwinus and the other noblemen, whose names are Hadager, Wicterb, Sigihart, Adalperht, Wicco, Grimuni, Meiol, Waldperht, Erchanloh, Huswart, and others.

### CHAPTER XLVI—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Arnmodus

Let the diligence of many people learn how Ambricho, the venerable worshipper of God and bishop, and a certain nobleman named Arnmodus exchanged their possessions with one another for the benefit of both parties.

The aforesaid nobleman therefore transferred one part of his property to the holy martyr of God Emmerammus: namely, twelve acres of arable land at the place called Lipolfinga, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Ato.

Conversely, the aforesaid bishop, with his advocate, transferred to the same nobleman from the property of Saint Emmerammus an equal number of acres of cultivated land at the same place. And so that this might remain unshaken, it was also decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced.

### CHAPTER XLVII—The formal settlement made by Thevit and his wife Erhilt

A memorandum renewing the transfer that a certain nobleman named Thevit and his wife Erhilt had previously made to Saint Emmerammus.

Ambricho, the venerable bishop, came to the church of Saint Emmerammus, together with Pernhardus and many other noblemen of the same province. Then the aforesaid Thevit approached the altar of Saint Emmerammus and renewed his former transfer, namely by transferring such property as he appeared to possess at Hornpah, together with four dependent persons, whose names are Hucimor, Gamanhilt, Deotfrid, and Walahilt. He omitted nothing of all that he appeared to possess in this place, Hornpah.

The condition was that he should possess all his benefices as property until the end of his life, and that Erhilt, if she lived longer, should possess them as property. After the death of both, all the aforesaid things, improved and together with their acquisitions, should belong to the holy saint of God by perpetual right, without anyone’s objection.
