The aforesaid venerable bishop and his advocate Helfricus received this renewal and investiture. Erlapoldus was surety and witness. There were also many other witnesses: Pernhart, Ogo, Reginperht, Isanperht, Terpaton, Walto, Saxo, Uzant, Rihholf, Durinchart, Hiltrih, Erchanfrid, Pazrih, Sigivuns, Salomon, Sigihart, Folcrat, Dancholf, Liutperht, and Lantperht. These acts were performed in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 868.

### CHAPTER XLVIII—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Gerpertus

A very attractive and highly useful custom had long prevailed among people: that they should exchange their possessions through reconciliation. Therefore it was agreed between the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his vassal Gerpertus that they too should exchange their possessions for the benefit of both parties.

The aforesaid Gerpertus therefore transferred whatever property he appeared to possess in the village called Sempinchova and in the village called Altaha: namely, two servants, whose names are Frumolt and Walger, together with the land, meadows, and everything, as written above, that he appeared to possess in these two places. He transferred all this to Saint Emmerammus into the hands of the bishop and of his advocate Wicrammus, including twenty acres of arable land and thirty cartloads of meadow. Gerpertus gave more than he received.

Conversely, the bishop and his advocate Wicrammus transferred to Gerpertus, as his property by perpetual right, whatever Saint Emmerammus appeared to possess in the village called Pilinga, together with two servants, Lupus and Winimarus.

The witnesses to both transfers are Lantpero, Uzant, Engilscalc, Adalperht, Lantperht, Liuthart, Fastmot, Otker, Horscmot, and Helfant.

### CHAPTER XLIX—Exchange between Ambricho and Witold

Let the account of this charter inform the diligence of many faithful people how an exchange of various possessions was carried out for the benefit of both parties.

A certain nobleman named Witold therefore transferred four acres to Saint Emmerammus, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Rodkarius, beside the Filsea, at the place called Niwinhusa.

Conversely, in the same territory, with the permission of the most pious king Karlomannus, the aforesaid advocate, with the bishop’s consent, transferred to the same nobleman three acres from the property of the holy martyr of God Emmerammus.

This was enacted at the place called Chirichun, in the presence of Counts Geio and Rumold, with the leading men of that district standing by. The witnesses who attest this by physical summons are Milo, Perehtheri, Perehtcoz, Offo, Rodolf, Lantperht, Egilpern, Hadager, and Pero. It was also decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced concerning this matter, so that it might be more readily believed.

### CHAPTER L—The transfer of Count Chozilo

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

We therefore wish it to be made known to all faithful and unfaithful Christians, present and absent, and also to those of the future, that I, Chozil, the humblest count, transferred from my inheritance to Saint Emmerammus, as property at Stromogin, whatever Gundpoldus possessed as property and as a benefice in the village called Reginwartesdorf and in Rosdorf, together with land, plowed fields, vineyards, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, and all boundaries.

In the name of the Lord. Amen.

The witnesses are Count Ratpot, Count Gundram, Count Gundpold, Huogo, Hunolf, Engildeo, Gundpold, Puoso, and Cotahelm.

### CHAPTER LI—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the presbyter Alawih

A fruitful, honorable, and highly useful custom had already long prevailed among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

Following this custom, a certain nobleman and presbyter named Alawih was likewise moved to transfer, together with his advocate Gundalpertus, to Saint Emmerammus, into the hand of Ambricho, the most reverend bishop, and of his advocate Adalricus, such property as he possessed at Ottarpah, which the most pious king Hludowicus had graciously granted him by a written command of his authority for perpetual possession.

Conversely, Adalricus, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmerammus to the same Alawih, for secure possession as his own, the church at Holzhusa with its attached territory, which the presbyter Popo had once held as a benefice.

The witnesses to this matter are Polo, Ogo, Deotpold, Jacob, Wago, Reginhoh, Odalperht, Gozperht, Unlaz, Eparhart, Sigifrid, Adalperht, Gammo, Job, Ambricho, and Albrih. The persons making the investiture were Adalricus, the bishop’s advocate, and Gundalbertus, the advocate of the presbyter Alawih.

### CHAPTER LII—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Rodolt

In the name of the highest and eternal God.

It was agreed between the venerable man Ambricho, bishop, and a certain man named Rodolt concerning the exchange of certain possessions, and they carried it out accordingly.

The aforesaid Rodolt transferred to Saint Emmerammus, martyr of Christ, one servant named Arndeon, and fifteen acres of arable land at the place called Prunnon.

Conversely, the aforesaid Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and his advocate named Rodker, with the consent of the monks and of the entire household, transferred to Rodolt, as his property, one female servant named Anstrat and fifteen acres of arable land at the same place called Prunnon, and confirmed it with perpetual stability.

### CHAPTER LIII—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Truhthard

A useful and highly fruitful custom had long prevailed among people, and it is still frequently practiced carefully and prudently among certain noblemen: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

Accordingly, the exchange described below was carried out between Bishop Ambricho and a certain nobleman named Truhthard. Truhthard therefore transferred to Saint Emmerammus, into the hand of Bishop Ambricho and of his advocate Avo, three fields at the place called Sallohopit.

Conversely, Avo, the advocate of the aforesaid bishop, transferred at the same place one field from the property of Saint Emmerammus to the aforesaid Truhthard.

### CHAPTER LIV—Exchange between the same parties

A record of how Lord Ambricho, bishop, and Truhthad, the advocate of Waltrata, made an exchange for the benefit of both.

The aforesaid bishop gave a female servant named Deotmot as property to Waltrata. Conversely, his advocate transferred into the hand of the bishop and of his advocate Helfricus another female servant named Deotpurc, without the children of either woman.

The witnesses physically summoned for this are Avo, Rihger, Alawih, Alprih, Atto, and Ermenhart.

### CHAPTER LV—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Count Heinric

A very fruitful and highly useful custom had long prevailed among people: namely, to exchange certain possessions for the benefit of both parties.

For this reason Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and Count Heinric made an exchange for the benefit of certain dependent persons. Count Heinric therefore transferred two dependent persons to Saint Emmerammus, Cirnin and Razo, into the hand of the aforesaid bishop and of his advocate Helfricus.

Conversely, the same bishop, together with that advocate, transferred to Heinric, into the hand of his advocate Rodhardus, Hadaricus Sciurra. So that this exchange might be held firm, it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced.

### CHAPTER LVI—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the deacon Altoltus

Let it be known to all the faithful that a certain deacon named Altoltus, born of a noble lineage, transferred one field of his property at Munolfingon to the holy Emmerammus of God, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Oto. The aforesaid bishop and Count Rumold were also present.

In recompense, the aforesaid bishop and his advocate transferred from the property of Saint Emmerammus one field at the same place to the same noble cleric. The witnesses physically summoned are Kerperht, Ekkirih, Gotaperht, Wicram, Reginperht, Reginwart, Rihpold, Rodperht, Willihelm, and Askarih.

### CHAPTER LVII—Exchange between Ambricho and Folcrih

Let the diligence of certain faithful people learn that a certain nobleman named Folcrih transferred to Saint Emmerammus, at the place called Pisinga, twenty-five acres lying among arable land, meadows, and woodland, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Gundbertus.

Conversely, the same advocate, with the bishop’s permission, transferred to the aforesaid nobleman twenty-three acres from the property of Saint Emmerammus, to be held as his own forever. And so that this exchange might be held more firmly and more readily believed by posterity, it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced.

### CHAPTER LVIII—Exchange between Engilscalchus and Engilbertus

Let it be known to all the faithful that a certain nobleman named Engilscalch transferred one field of his property beside the village of Aespilipah to Saint Emmerammus, into the hand of Engilbertus, who held this benefice at the aforesaid place.

Conversely, the same Engilbertus transferred from the property of Saint Emmerammus to the aforesaid Engilscalch, with the consent of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, one meadow beside the watercourse called Alaha.

### CHAPTER LIX—The transfer of a certain woman called Sicca

Let the diligence of many people learn how Sicca and her advocate Richo ceased to claim a portion of one church and of the rural property attached to it at Erininga. They renounced that portion and thus released it to Saint Emmerammus, declaring that they no longer wished ever to claim it.

To confirm this, the witnesses are Avo, Strupo, Gundperht, Erchanperht, Woladeo, Rihger, Arperht, Hiltigoz, Gammo, Embricho, Amalperht, Rihperht, Petilo, Wallah, and Adalger.

### CHAPTER LX—Exchange between Bishop Erchanfrid and Perehthard

A very fruitful and highly useful custom had long prevailed among people: namely, to exchange portions of any possessions for the convenience of both parties.

Therefore a certain nobleman named Perehthard transferred to Saint Peter the apostle and the holy martyr of God Emmerammus one mill at Atinga, into the hand of Erchanfrid, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Odalpertus.

Conversely, the same advocate, with the bishop’s consent, transferred three acres to the same nobleman beside the aforesaid village, to be held as his own. For this reason it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced, so that this exchange might be held more firmly and more readily believed by posterity.

The witnesses are Pernhart, Dultinc, Anthelm, and many others.

### CHAPTER LXI—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Richo

In ancient times the fathers who lived in former generations sometimes, considering their necessary commercial and earthly interests, mutually granted consent to sell or purchase possessions of every kind, to transfer them, or even to transform one thing into another.

Therefore their modern successors, imitating their institutions, commonly do the same, joining acres of fields and meadows, houses, and properties to their possessions more suitably through harmonious exchange.

This was not neglected by Ambricho, the elect bishop of God, and certain noblemen, Richo and his son Freso. With their consent, the following exchange was appropriately carried out.

The aforesaid noblemen transferred to Saint Emmerammus, the holy one of God, into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate Helfricus, at the place called Atinga, a house with an enclosure and twenty-seven acres, on the condition that, if anyone wished to dissolve this arrangement, Saint Emmerammus should retain his property and those noblemen should receive theirs back.

Conversely, the frequently mentioned bishop and his advocate Helfrih transferred from the property of Saint Emmerammus, at the place called Mezinga, to the same men named above a house with its estate and twenty-seven acres.

The following were physically summoned to testify for both parties: Helfrih, Lantpero, Erchanpold, Sindiho, Reginolt, and Froperht.

### CHAPTER LXII—Exchange between Ambricho and Gisala

Gisala gave Bishop Ambricho a servant named Ratpertus. Conversely, the bishop gave Gisala Petonus.

They also carried out this exchange with a pledge, through Wolfger, Gisala’s representative, and Helfrih, the bishop’s advocate, in the presence of the same bishop, Abbot Hitto, and others named Adolf, Ogo, Wicram, Odalperht, Sindperht, Westargowo, and Gerperht.

This was enacted on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the meadow at Mozinga.

### CHAPTER LXIII—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Tatto

In the name of the highest God.

An agreement and settlement was made between Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and a certain faithful man of his named Tatto, a nobleman, that they should exchange certain possessions with one another for their common benefit and advantage.

The aforesaid Tatto therefore gave to Saint Emmerammus, from the property of his wife, 150 acres consisting of arable land and woodland to be cleared, and, separately, one woodland at the village of Perge. In return, the aforesaid Ambricho, the venerable bishop, was to acquire as property from the king by a royal precept whatever he had previously appeared to hold as a benefice from that same holy and aforesaid church of God at Fatiragimundi: namely, a church, seventy-five acres of arable land, eight cartloads of meadow, and two acres of woodland.

Those physically summoned are Arnmot, Folcrat, Dultinc, Tevit, Cotaperht, Vulvilo, Wichram, Ogo, Oto, Waltunc, Otachar, Fastmot, Perchart, Gemmunt, Hunrih, who was also surety for the investiture; Waldperht likewise; Gerwih likewise; Gernod, likewise a witness; Pazrih, Irinc, Abrih, Liutperht, Engilhelm, Odalperht, Salagrim, Folrat, Rodmunt, Otker, Wisunt, Hiltimot, Lantrat, Salomon, Durinchart, Pillinc, Samuel, Ratpero the monk, Wolfram the monk, Adalger the monk; and Wichart the presbyter examined and approved the exchange.

### CHAPTER LXIV—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the deacon Altoltus

A very useful and highly fruitful custom had long begun to grow among people: namely, to exchange any possessions, whether inheritances, benefices, or attached properties, for the benefit of both parties.

For this reason a certain ecclesiastical deacon, Altoltus, decided to transfer three acres of arable land to the holy martyr of God Emmerammus. They lie on the plain of the fields beside the village called Atinga. He transferred them into the hand of Ambricho, the venerable bishop, and of his advocate named Wicrammus.

Conversely, the advocate himself, with the permission of the aforesaid bishop, transferred two acres from the property of Saint Emmerammus to the same noble Altoltus.

The names of the witnesses who will attest this follow: Hiltimar, Gerperht, Deotmar, Irinc, Nanzo, Engilhelm, Cozperht, and Adalhoh.

### CHAPTER LXV—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ellanpurc

In the name of the highest and eternal God.

It was agreed between the venerable man Ambricho, bishop, and a certain woman named Ellanpurc concerning the exchange of certain possessions, and they carried it out accordingly.

The aforesaid Ellanpurc and her advocate named Folcrat transferred to Saint Emmerammus two acres of arable land at the place called Murcilashaha.

Conversely, Rodker, the advocate of Saint Emmerammus, with the consent of the venerable bishop, the monks, and the entire household, transferred one acre to Ellanpurc and her advocate from the property of Saint Emmerammus, at the same aforesaid place at Murcilashaha, and confirmed it with witnesses.

They again made an exchange in a public assembly, in the presence of Othelm, Wago, Pirihtilo, Isanspero, Hadager, Willihelm, Snellolf, Isandeo, Ellandeo, Ogo, Paldram, Francho, Ermperht, Isanperht, Gozperht, Willipold, Engilperht, Chuniperht, Chuntilo, Rupo, and many others.

### CHAPTER LXVI—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Paldricus
A fruitful and exceedingly useful custom long ago began to take root among rational men: namely, exchanging certain properties for the benefit of both parties. Indeed, that custom of the ancients is practiced increasingly often among the younger generation.

[Col. 0929C]

Accordingly, a certain nobleman named Baldricus transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram, from his property, one meadow with a mill situated at the right bank of the water called the Filisa, near Opirinhusa, into the hands of the venerable bishop Ambricho and his advocate Rodkarius. The length of this meadow is fifty perches, and its width twelve. In return, the aforesaid venerable man of God and his advocate Rodkarius transferred to the same nobleman, on the left bank of the same stream, another meadow of equal measurement from the property of the aforesaid holy man of God.

And, so that this might be made more secure, it was decided that two charters written in identical terms should be produced and witnesses summoned. These are: Othelm, Wago, Heriperht, Paldrih, Einhart, Arnamar, Isangrim, Heimger, Gerhart.

### CHAPTER LXVII — The Transfer of Abbot Rihpald [Cols. 0929D–0930D]

Since in ancient times a certain nobleman, Abbot Rihpald by name, and his aunt, named Deotlind, transferred to God and Saint Emmeram, for the salvation of their souls, whatever property they possessed at Phetarah, or at Yvpinpah, or at Ahu, Rihpald himself later wished to grant it as a benefice to his nephews Engilmon and Isandeo, but did not complete this. They unjustly seized it away from the authority of Saint Emmeram; and Bishop Baturicus and his advocate Immo demanded it from them in the public court at Phetarah, before Count Cotafrid and many others present there. Compelled by law, they returned the whole of it to Bishop Baturicus and his advocate Immo, and Immo received investiture of it from them.

Afterward, however, they and other good men requested that this same property be granted to them again as a benefice. Bishop Baturicus’ kindness did not wish to deny them this, but granted it to them as a benefice for the duration of their lives, in return for a suitable rent, with the consent of the congregation of Saint Emmeram. Having received the benefice from Bishop Baturicus and his advocate Immo, they gave security that they would pay a rent of four solidi every year on the feast of Saint Emmeram, and that they would show no negligence regarding it and would in no way cause any further dispute with the pastors of Saint Emmeram or with his household.

If they should do so, let them make full compensation according to the law, and let them in no way have the power to alienate this property from that house of God, but rather to improve it as far as they are able. Therefore the aforesaid bishop decreed that two charters written in identical terms should be made for security and for the memory of posterity.

Those present there who saw and heard this were: Odalperht, Salahho, Immo, Rihhart, Pillinc, Cundalperht, Marcho, Otger, Mauri, Adalger, Puoso, Aopi, Ritant, Wichart, Cundfrid, Engilpald, Adalperht, Appo, Antrih, Winiho, Atto, Cotaperht, Sigiperht, Ratperht, Truhthad, Ratolt, Ratolf, Amalrih, Wolfbero, Ratpald, Nidhart, Egino, Berehttold, Waldger, Rahholf.

This was enacted at Reganaspurc in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 822, in the eighth year of Hludowic’s reign, at the Mass of Saint Martin, in the first indiction, on Tuesday; and I, Dignus by name, wrote this charter at the command of Bishop Baturicus for confirmation.

A brief account, concluded in concise form, of the inheritance of Abbot Rihpald, which he transferred to Saint Emmeram in these places: at Ahu, at Yvpinpah, and at Pheterah. Later Engilmon and Isandeo, its unjust usurpers, returned it to Immo, advocate of Saint Emmeram, according to the settlement they had made, paying every year as rent, before Count Cotafrid, four solidi.

This was enacted before all these men: Gamanolf, Salaho, Sahso, Adalrih, Reginhart, Wichart, Kerrih, Erchanpald, Rihlant, Frehholf, Gisalfrid, Engilpald, Odalscalc, Herigoz, Staracholf, Rodicho, Wolfrid, Adalo, Heimo, Cundbertus, Cozzol, Frumolt.

Three of our men were sent to these places to receive investiture of this property: Cundperht at Ahu, Stephanus the cleric at Jupinpah, and Cadenchilo, who took possession of this investiture at Phetarah. Thus these legal proceedings were concluded and restored to concord.

### CHAPTER LXVIII — The Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Count Rodolt [Col. 0931A]

[The manuscript here consistently has *comis* for *comes* (“count”).]

A record of how Ambricho, bishop of Regensburg, and Count Rodolt reached a settlement between themselves.

The aforesaid bishop therefore gave the aforementioned count, at a place called Umpalasdorf, eighty-three jugera of arable land. In return, Count Rodolt gave Bishop Ambricho, into the hands of his advocate Perahtricus, forty jugera at the place called Stupinga, and an equal amount at the place called Pirihhinwanc.

This was done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 874, in the seventh indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

### CHAPTER LXIX — Concerning the March at the River Brama [Col. 0931B]

This account or record concerns our estate at the place called Braama, which belonged to Sconinowe and to the monastery of Saint Martin. It had long been unjustly taken from us, but was finally restored by Anawanus and his brother Rihwassus.

It extends from the river called Braama to the place called Tiufbah, between cultivated and uncultivated land, amounting to 120 jugera. This was done before Wichelmus, envoy of Count Gerold, in our estate, before all these men, whose names are as follows. Ellenricus was our advocate on behalf of the monastery of Saint Martin: Erchanpertus, Eigil, Paturih, Cundperht, Cuniperht, Rodperht, Anthelm, Reginhart, Regino, Engilperht, Tevit, Rodperht, Hetin, Helmuni, Engilpero, Friccho, Rodolt, Egilmunt, Willihelm, Etilo, Reginperht.

Enacted on the eighth day before the Ides of March, Tuesday, during Lent, at the place mentioned above. I, Ellinhard the deacon, wrote this at the command of my lord Bishop Baturicus.

### CHAPTER LXX — The Transfer by Abbot Rihpald at Sezpah [Cols. 0931C–0932C]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, in God’s name, I, Abbot Rihpald, transferred the inheritance that I possessed at Sezpah and at Niwinhusun into the hands of Abbo, Engilmon, Isandeo, Paldricus, Ratolf, and Ano. If I should die on this journey while going to the palace, then those men were to transfer all these things for the sake of my soul to Saint Emmeram. I ask Bishop Adalwin, or his successors, that these two places—namely Sezpah and Niwinhusun—always serve Saint Emmeram, that they not be given to anyone as a benefice, and that the inhabitants themselves not be moved, but remain in their places, together with the dependents.

After Abbot Rihpald’s death, Abbo came together with Paldrih and Ratolf, and likewise Ano, to Saint Emmeram, and they transferred to Saint Emmeram, for the eternal reward of Abbot Rihpald’s soul, the same property that Abbot Rihpald had placed in their hands. They invested the house of Saint Emmeram with everything they had transferred: namely, fourteen resident households at Sezpah, four at Niwinhusun, together with dependents and houses, as well as estates, lands, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters, movable and immovable property—everything cultivated and uncultivated, everything.

Rihpald omitted nothing except three hides, which he exchanged with Abbot Meginhard; this alone he omitted. For this reason I, Rihpald, placed this property in the hands of so many men—namely, six men—so that whichever of them wished, whether one, two, three, or all together, would have full power to transfer everything to Saint Emmeram.

After this Abbo and Paldrih came, together with Ratolf and Ano, and invested Immo, advocate of Bishop Adalwin, and Wicrammus, the priest and provost, with these two places, namely Sezpah and Niwinhusun; and these places were granted. At Sezpah Ratolf the monk resided with the servants of Bishop Adalwin; at Niwinhusun, Wicrammus the provost.

Abbot Rihpald also requested Bishop Adalwin that a church should be built in that estate, namely at Sezpah, and that a priest should be installed there who would sing the liturgy there and serve Saint Emmeram in all things.

The names of those present who saw this were: Erchanperht the deacon, Reginperht the deacon, Welto the cleric, Heriperht the cleric, Pillinc, Frumolt, Cunthart, Paldmot.

This was done at the tomb of Saint Emmeram. These are those who saw that Rihpald transferred his inheritance, as stated above, into the hands of Abbo and the others: Gerhart, Liutperht, Engilperht, Pillunc, Ogast.

These are the names of the witnesses who were taken by the ears: Chuniperht, Ambricho, Pillunc, Immo, Crimuni, Fridaperht, Erchanperht, Hadamar, Gerpald, Toto, Sipihho, Wolfpero, Adalrih, Unolz, Huno, Altiperht, Hegilo, Wiclant.

This transfer was made at Cundareshuson in the year 814 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the second year of the reign of the lord Emperor Hludowic, in the seventh indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, on Sunday. The investiture at Saint Emmeram was made on Monday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the church of Saint Emmeram itself. I, Ellinhart the deacon, commanded by my lord Bishop Adalwin, wrote this transfer.

### CHAPTER LXXI — The Transfer of Count Willihelm [Cols. 0932C–0933A]

It is clear to all mortals that this life is exceedingly short, but the future life is long. Therefore Count Willihelm, considering that these things are so, for the attainment [sic; manuscript: *pro adipiscendi*] of eternal joys and for the salvation of his soul, transferred to Saint Emmeram the property that he appeared to possess at the place called Bersnicha: namely, a church and a house with an estate, together with the other buildings, the dependents within the house, resident servants, lands, meadows, pastures, half a forest, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, cultivated and uncultivated land—everything that can be said or named, together with all the profit that now appears to be in those properties or that may hereafter accrue to them, leaving nothing outside.

These properties were to remain in his power for as long as he lived, and in the power of his wife Engilrada for as long as she lived and preserved the marital bed. In every respect they were to remain firm if no heir were born to him.

Moreover, he reached an agreement with the venerable bishop Baturicus that at Eskituna and Wesin they should possess for the duration of their lives everything that the aforesaid bishop might grant to them there as a benefice. After their deaths, the aforesaid properties transferred by him, as well as those received by him as a benefice, improved in every respect, were to remain firmly with the aforesaid saint of God, without anyone’s contradiction.

Bishop Baturicus received this transfer together with his advocate Erinpertus.

The witnesses to this transfer, taken by the ears, were: Hilpung, Fezzilo, Madalhelm, who were also guarantors of the investiture, Pazrih, Arnmot, Mahalfrid, Alaman, Adalwart, Poso, Reginwart, Eckeo, Ermperht, Kerhart, Eccho, Odalhart, Erchanpald, Kerhoh, Wldar, Willihelm, Trostmar, Eigil, Pillunc, Erinperht, Cotaperht, likewise Madalhelm, Engildeo, Odalhart, Wolfhart, Reginhart, Gewibald, Erchanperht, Ellenperht, Sigibald, Albrat, Adalperht.

This was enacted at the monastery of Sconinowa, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 834.

### CHAPTER LXXII — The Transfer of Count Willihelm [Cols. 0933B–C]

Whoever in this life, which is uncertain for all mortals, carefully regards himself with complete devotion of mind will undoubtedly reach that life happily, where those who here prudently kept the commands of their Lord reign with Christ.

Moved by this caution, a certain count named Willihelm, in order to acquire refreshment for his soul and the glory of everlasting blessedness, transferred to Saint Emmeram, God’s martyr, everything he possessed in the places written below. He left outside none of his property that he did not transfer in these villages: Sconheringa, Cheminatum, and Purcheim.

The arrangement was this: after his death, if he had no heir, the property transferred was to belong firmly to that holy man of God; nevertheless, his wife was to retain those properties under her authority for as long as she preserved the marital bed. If, however, as may happen according to human custom, she did not preserve the marital bed, the transfer was immediately to return to its proper place. But if he should have a surviving heir, he himself was to possess his inheritance with full authority, without anyone’s contradiction.

The witnesses to this transfer were: Count Ratpot, Cundpald, Cuniperht, Count Orendil, Heriperht, Crimuni, Madalhelm, Rodolf, Poso, Cundperht, Outo the vicar, Mezzi, Vitalis, Sahso, Rihpald, Rubo, Isangrim, Cotafrid, Ougast, Scroth, Reginhart, Egilolf, Hadager, Willihelm, Mahalfrid, Hessi, Urolt, Trogo, Graman, Cundwin.

Bishop Baturicus, together with his advocate Pazricus, received the transfer. This was done at Reganesburg in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 833.

### CHAPTER LXXIII — The Transfer of Count Ratpod [Cols. 0933D–0934A]

After Ratpod the count had transferred to the holy man Emmeram, as is found written in the charter of transfer, whatever property he appeared to possess at Tullina, he came into the presence of King Ludovic at Reganesburg. He transferred to the aforesaid holy man of God everything he appeared to possess at Tullina, leaving nothing outside, with this arrangement: if no heir were born to him, after his death this transfer would immediately and firmly belong to the place of the holy man of God.

But if an heir were born to him, the property included in the transfer could be redeemed for two hundred solidi. As stated above, this transfer was made in the presence of the king, his nobles, and all who stood beside him. We make known the names of some of them: Count Ernost, Werinheri, Timo, Ermfrid, Ratperht, Uto, Waning, Willihelm, Rihheri, Wolfdrigil, Poso, Eginolf, Perehttolt, Count Rihho, Adalo, Ratolt, Popili, Rodolt, Fritilo, Reginperht, Adalhoh, Managolt, Papo, Albker.

This transfer was made at the place mentioned above in the year of the Lord 837.

### CHAPTER LXXIV — The Exchange between Bishop Erchanfrid and Eparhoh [Col. 0934B]

In the name of the holy and only Trinity.

It was agreed between the venerable bishop Erchanfrid and the nobleman Eparhoh that an exchange should be made for the benefit of both parties. And so they did.

Wicrammus, the bishop’s advocate, with the command and permission of our lord King Hludowic, transferred to the aforesaid layman the conveyance which the cleric Pernger had made to Saint Emmeram, martyr of Christ, at the place called Tahhinga.

In return, the aforesaid Eparhoh transferred such an inheritance as he possessed at Atingun, in its entirety, leaving nothing out, but transferring everything with the strongest legal security.

These witnesses were therefore taken by the ears: Unolz, Erchanperht, Otperht, Ratolf, Herigoz, Wicram, Alo, Swidker, Odalger, Rodker, Freso, Wlfilo, Ratolt, Vulfrih, Rihho, Richolf, Sigo, Deotpato.

And, so that this exchange might remain more secure and posterity might know it with greater certainty, it was agreed that two charters should be written in identical terms, so that each party would have one and it would remain perpetual without any contradiction.

### CHAPTER LXXV — The Settlement between Bishop Ambricho and Adalfrid [Cols. 0934C–D]

Let the discernment of the many faithful learn how a certain vassal of the king, also a venerable man named Adalfrid, transferred portions of his inheritance to Saint Emmeram, thereby arranging a certain benefice.

Accordingly, the nobleman mentioned above transferred to the aforesaid holy martyr of God his properties at Gimundin and at Adinhard, with their enclosures and houses, territories, pastures, waters and watercourses, and eight dependents: Ditolf, Hiltipirc, Rihhilt and her two sons, Liutto, Gerhoh, and Perehtman.

He transferred all of it in its entirety into the hands of the most reverend bishop Ambricho and his advocate Gundbert. The arrangement was that he should firmly possess as his own the benefice at Utilinga until the end of his life. After his death it was to be released in its entirety into its former authority.

This was done with the consent of the aforesaid administrator of the holy Church of God, with the permission of the vigorous King Karlomannus, already in the second year of his reign in the region of the Bavarians and in the first year among the Lombards.

These are those who, taken by the ears, testify to this: Reginolf, Albrih, Perehtolt, Pillunc, Arperht, Unlaz, Gammo, Amalperht, Liutperht, Machelm, Wolfmunt, Freso, Ogo, and the rest.

### CHAPTER LXXVI — The Exchange between Bishops Erchanfrid and Hartwig [Cols. 0935A–D]

In God’s name.

It was agreed and settled between the venerable Erchanfrid, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, and the venerable Hartwig, bishop of the Church of Passau, that they should exchange certain properties among themselves for their common benefit and advantage. And so they did.

The aforementioned Bishop Erchanfrid and his advocate Nordher gave to the aforesaid bishop, for perpetual possession on behalf of his monastery of Saint Quirinus, from their own property at the place called Hunolzenghova: one hide, one house, thirty-nine jugera of arable land, thirty wagonloads of hay from the meadows, and twenty-four jugera of productive woodland.

In return, the aforesaid Bishop Hartwig and his advocate Liuthard gave to Bishop Erchanfrid, for his own possession, from the property of his monastery of Saint Quirinus, with the consent and agreement of the monks living in that monastery and also by permission of the lord Hludowic, the most glorious king, at the place called Bodolunghova: one house and two hides of land, twenty wagonloads of hay from the meadows, or whatever Heitfoleus had transferred from his own property at that place to the monastery of Saint Quirinus.

Therefore they asked that two exchanges written in identical terms be made and confirmed between them, so that each might hold and possess what he had received from the other and do with it whatever he wished.

They further agreed to insert the following provision: if, after this day, any one of them, or any opposing, appointed, or substituted person, should attempt to act against this exchange, for which two charters appear to have been written in identical terms, or should try to violate it by any device, he shall pay to the party against whom he has brought the suit, under compulsion of the fisc, two pounds of gold and five weights of silver; and his claim shall have no effect. The present exchange shall remain firm and stable at all times, supported by a stipulation.

Enacted in the city of Regensburg.

The sign of Bishop Hartwig, who requested that this exchange be made and confirmed.

These are the witnesses, taken by the ears, who saw and heard when this exchange was made in the presence of our lord Hludowic, the most glorious king: Eginolf the hunter, Engilscaldh, Uzzant, Bernhart, Patager, Engildeo, Rumolt, Batto, Odalrih, Engilbold, Isanperht, Gamanolf, Waning, Eccho, David, Rihmar, Wicbold.

### CHAPTER LXXVII — The Exchange between Bishop Baturicus and Erchanpert [Cols. 0935D–0936C]

In God’s name.

It was agreed and settled between the venerable Baturicus, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, and a certain man named Erchanpert, that they should exchange certain properties for their common benefit and advantage. And so they did.

The aforesaid venerable Bishop Baturicus therefore gave, from the resources of the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, with the consent and agreement of the canons and monks living there, and also by permission of the lord Hludowic, the glorious king, to Erchanpert for his own possession, in the district called Feldun, at the place called Jazaha: one church with three hides, namely one hundred jugera of land and fifteen wagonloads of hay from the meadows.

In return, the aforesaid Erchanpert gave from his own property to the venerable Bishop Baturicus, for the portion of his bishopric, in the district called Tonahgewi, at the place called Hahalinga: three hides, namely one hundred jugera of land, fifty wagonloads of hay from the meadows, and 120 jugera of woodland.

Therefore they asked that two exchanges written in identical terms be made and confirmed between them: the bishop was to retain one on behalf of his church, and Erchanpert himself was to retain the other, so that in the future each party would have, hold, and possess whatever one side had received from the other, and do with it whatever it deemed advantageous.

They agreed to insert this provision: if, after this day, any one of them, or any opposing or appointed person, should attempt to act against this exchange, for which two charters appear to have been written in identical terms, or should try in any way to violate it, he shall pay to the party against whom he has brought the suit, under compulsion of the fisc, a fine of two pounds of gold; and his claim shall have no effect. The present exchange shall remain firm at all times, supported by a stipulation.

Enacted in the city of Regensburg on the fourth day before the Nones of September.

These are the witnesses, taken by the ears, who saw and heard this: Rodhoh, Cozzilo, Macho, Cundolf, Altram, Sigihart, Kisalolt, Erchanmar, Immo, Willibato, Cundperht, Heririh, Petilo, Oto, Isanpero, Immo, Wicbald, Rodolt, Helmrih, Sahso, Warmunt, Albker, Adalperht, Eparswind.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII — The Exchange between Abbot Apollonius and the Deacon Erchanfrid [Cols. 0936C–0937B]

In God’s name.

It was agreed and settled between the venerable Abbot Apollonius and the deacon Erchanfrid that they should exchange certain properties for their common benefit and advantage. And so they did.

Abbot Apollonius therefore gave, from the resources of his monastery of Perga, with the consent and agreement of the monks living in that monastery, and also by permission of the lord King Hludowic, to the aforementioned deacon Erchanfrid for his own possession, in the district called Tonahgewi, at the place called Ginginchova: cultivated and uncultivated land, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, appurtenances, access roads, rights of exit and return, whether already acquired or still to be acquired, or whatever the aforesaid Abbot Apollonius appeared to possess there at that place from his benefice.

In return, the aforesaid deacon Erchanfrid gave from his own property, in the same district of Tonahgewi, at the place called Scampah, to the same Abbot Apollonius, for perpetual possession on behalf of his monastery: the same kinds of cultivated and uncultivated land, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, appurtenances, access roads, rights of exit and return, whether already acquired or still to be acquired, or whatever he appeared legally to possess there from his own property.

Therefore they asked that two exchanges written in identical terms and strengthened by the hands of good men be made and confirmed between them, so that each might henceforth hold and possess what he had received from the other and do with it whatever he wished.

They agreed to insert this provision: if, after this day, any one of them, or any opposing, appointed, or substituted person, should attempt to act against this exchange, for which two charters appear to have been written in identical terms, or should try to violate it by any device, he shall pay to the party against whom he has brought the suit, under compulsion of the fisc, two pounds of gold and five weights of silver; and his claim shall have no effect. The present exchange shall remain firm and stable at all times, supported by a stipulation.

Enacted in the city of Regensburg on the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

Uzzand, Deotrih, Strupo, Egilolf, Werilo, Hartwig, Hiltiroh, Rodhart, Unolz, Erchanperht, Haguno, Ishad, Waltunc, Trogo, Eckibart, Hartmot, Florenti, Folcpold, Isanhart, Avo, Walto, Deothart.

### CHAPTER LXXIX — The Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Eckilind [Cols. 0937C–0938A]

In God’s name.

It was agreed and settled between the venerable Bishop Ambricho and a certain noble widow named Ekkilind that they should confirm certain properties for their common benefit. And so they did.

The widow Ekkilind therefore transferred from her property to Saint Emmeram, together with her advocate Bernhard, whatever she appeared to possess in the village called Ucchinpiunt, with seven dependents, whose names are: Helfrih, Ellanrih, Maganrih, Rodimar, Willipirc, Regindrud, Reginswind; also one hide in the village called Talamazinga and one wood near the village called Tuzilinga. All these properties are in the district called Tonahgewi.

The aforesaid Bishop Ambricho received this transfer, together with his advocate Helfrih; Helmoni and Waltunc were guarantors.

In return, the advocate Helfrih transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram, with the consent and will of the aforesaid bishop and of the servants of God living in that see, whatever Billunc, the father of the aforesaid widow, possessed as a benefice in the village called Talamazinga, with nineteen dependents, whose names are: Cundram, Mahhelm, Cristan, Salvan, Gerlinto, Folcmar, Paldhilt, Ratpirn, Wolfpirc, Waldcund, Frohilt, Sonpirc, Peinhart, Lantswinto, Merigis, Rodni, Mahtheri, Magolf, Ceizperht.

In addition, he transferred seventeen jugera of arable land and nine wagonloads of hay from the meadows adjoining the village called Leichilinga, so that the aforesaid Ekkilind, or her mother if she should live longer, might hold this as her property.

This agreement was made on the condition that, if any successor of Bishop Ambricho should attempt to dissolve this settlement, then the aforesaid widow Ekkilind would have the power either to retain the properties written above or to transfer them to whomever she wished.

These are the witnesses from both parties, taken by the ears: Engilpero, Cuniperht, Helmuni, Avo, Ogo, Perehtrih, Salomon, Erchanfrid, Strupo, Sanuel, Amalperht, Fridaperht, Appo, Lantrih, Gomarih, Adalperht, Rodmunt, Odolung, Terpiton, Cotaperht, Ato, Fastmot, Amalperht, Erchanfrid, Walto, Anthelm, Waltunc, Adalhun, Alo, Petilo, Rihholt, Hiltimot, Engilmar, Hardperht, Irmperht, Parto, Perehtgoz, Ellinpald, Trogo, Reginhart, Pigo, Harpold, Patirih, Rodmunt, Erchanpoldt.

This was enacted in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 866, at the place now called Letinchoua.

### CHAPTER LXXX — The Exchange between Bishop Baturicus and Uccian [Cols. 0938B–D]

In God’s name.

It was agreed and settled between the venerable Baturicus, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, and the illustrious man Uccian, that they should exchange certain properties for their common benefit and advantage. And so they did.

The aforesaid venerable Bishop Baturicus therefore gave, from the resources of his churches of Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, with the consent and agreement of the brothers living there and also by permission of the lord Hludowic, the glorious king, to the aforesaid Uccian for his own possession, at the place called Mahalgozzinhovon: three hides with the church built there, together with the other buildings placed upon it, lands, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and everything that was seen to be held at the aforesaid place.

In return, the aforementioned Uccian gave from his own property to the aforesaid venerable Bishop Baturicus, for the portion of his church, at the place called Atinhard: six hides with houses, other buildings, and estate buildings, together with lands, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, as much as he appeared to have possessed at that place.

Therefore they asked that two exchanges written in identical terms be made and confirmed between them, so that each, from this day and time onward, might hold and possess what he had received from the other, and might have full power to do or decide whatever he wished [sic; manuscript: *facere sui*] with it for his own benefit or advantage.

They agreed as follows: if, after this day, any one of them, or any opposing or appointed person, should attempt to act against this exchange, for which two charters appear to have been written in identical terms, or should wish to violate it, he shall pay the party against whom he has brought the suit a fine of two pounds of gold; and his claim shall have no effect. The present exchange shall remain firm at all times, supported by a stipulation.

Enacted in the city of Regensburg on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the fourth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of the lord King Hludowic in East Francia, in the fifteenth indiction, happily, in God’s name.

The sign of Uccian, who requested that this exchange be made and confirmed. The sign of Meilo. The sign of Alberat. The sign of Swarzaloh. The sign of Odalfrid. The sign of Hugolf. The sign of Herard. The sign of Billung. The sign of Berehttold. The sign of Alberic. The sign of Randulf. The sign of Adalpert. The sign of Wolfhar. The sign of Grimo. The sign of Egilolf. The sign of Rodpert. The sign of Ogast. The sign of Wicco. The sign of Unlaz. The sign of Albun. The sign of Hildric.

I, Dominicus the cleric, commanded to do so, wrote this.

### CHAPTER LXXXI — The Transfer of Archpriest Andarbod [Cols. 0939A–0940B]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

I, Baturicus, bishop by the grace of Christ the Redeemer, ordered this document to be written so that all might know, both those present and those to come, how the venerable man Antarbod, archpriest, while going to Rome to seek the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul for the salvation of his soul, gave all his property into my power, in this manner: if death should overtake him on that journey—as, alas, it did—I was to distribute everything for the salvation of his spirit among holy places wherever I should judge that it would be of the greatest benefit to him.

His brother Ternod is therefore a witness to this willing affection, also praising in every way that it was good and that he himself approved of it.

Finally, when the aforesaid illustrious man had departed from this light on that same journey, as the debt of death compelled him, and the news had reached us, I suddenly came to Ergeltesbah and sent for Bernhard, another brother of Antarbod, and for his son Engilhard, as well as for his other relatives, asking them to come so that I might know what they themselves wished and would say about the matter—namely, whether they would contradict the authority that had already been placed in my hands, or whether they would willingly permit it to be made firm in this way.

This was done. They came to me, and Bernhard himself willingly consented, as did his other relatives, saying that, according to the authority I had received from the aforesaid man of blessed memory, I should do with his property whatever I wished on his behalf.

This was enacted at the place written above, in the presence of those whose names are as follows: first Job, vicar and vassal of Cotafrid; also Cundalpert, son of Helmoni; Immo, our advocate; and Biltunc; Mezzi, nephew of Count Walto; Hunger, Ato, Erchanpreht, Antarbot, Isangrim, Suidger.

When this agreement between us had been completed, Bernhard came to a public court at the place called Rodhoheskirihha on the Lapara, where Count Walto was seated with his entire ministerium. With him were Machelm, son of Otleip; a great crowd of noblemen was also present, and Bishop Baturicus was likewise there.

Bernhard brought Bishop Baturicus and his advocate Immo before the court concerning the case of Antarbod, contrary to the lawful settlement already established before the men mentioned above.

Then Immo arose and gave Count Walto his security, because Bernhard had presumptuously disturbed a settled case contrary to law. He had his witnesses present and brought them forward: Billunc, Mezzi, Nidhart, Hunolt, Erchanperht, and Hunger.

But Bernhard was unwilling to give security in this manner and said: “If you find for me such witnesses as can testify that Antarbod acted in this way, I will consent and do what the law commands.”

Then, immediately, a free man of Ternod named Herini came to that court, sent by Ternod himself to Bishop Baturicus and Count Walto, and in the hearing of all reported what had been commanded to him: namely, that Ternod had sent word that he neither wished nor was able to contradict anything of all that his brother had entrusted into the hands of Bishop Baturicus, but would rather consent in every respect, wherever Bishop Baturicus wished to give it.

Then at last Bernhard was convicted by that security and testimony. He did not trust himself, and gave security according to law and the judgment of the people, for himself and his son Engilhard, that they would cause no further disturbance concerning this matter. Nidhart and Erchanpert therefore became his guarantors, and the matter was concluded in this way.

Those present at this settlement were: Bishop Baturicus, Count Walto, Machelm, Immo, Eckirih, Billunc, Jacob, Tevit, Rodgoz, Meginhelm, Hunolt, Heribald, Freso, Rihhart, Nidhart, Hegilo, Mezzi, Rihperht, Ratolt, Adalrih, Reginhart, and others.

Enacted in the year of the Lord 822.

### CHAPTER LXXXII — The Transfer of Haward
Happy is this active life; but far happier the contemplative life. Striving toward this, therefore, a certain nobleman named Hawart transferred to Saint Emmeram, into the hand of Arnimar, his kinsman, such a portion of his property as he possessed at Tegarindorf, with no one objecting; so that Arnimar himself might transfer that same portion of the property, together with the dependents, to the aforesaid saint on behalf of the aforementioned Haward, Odalhard, and Meginhard. These are the witnesses of the same transfer: Pillunc, Gozpold, Wanninc, Immo, Liupoton, Perethtuni, Salamari, Chuniperht, Alpuni, Heriperht, Ellingrim, Liuthart, Adalperht, [Col. 0940C] Horscolf, Gisalmar, Eginolf.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Swidkarius

An agreement was reached between the venerable Bishop Erchanfrid and a certain man named Swidker concerning an exchange of certain properties, and this is what they did. The aforementioned venerable bishop, for the benefit of both parties, with the permission of King Louis the Venerable and of all the monks residing at the monastery of Saint Emmeram, gave the aforementioned Swidker, at the place called Wolamotasaha, whatever Otram held there as a benefice. Conversely, Swidker himself transferred his hereditary property to Saint Emmeram, near the river called Apansa, whatever he had acquired from the sons of [Col. 0940D] Sigihelm through a purchase. The suitable witnesses are these: Fritilo, Reginperht, Einhart, Friccho, Albato, Count Alprat, Isanger, Ambricho, Dultinc, Piligrim, Horscrat, Alpuni, Hunolf, Lantperht, Wolfdrigil, Walto, and others.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Atto

Let the diligence of many of the faithful know how certain men exchanged property among themselves. Thus a certain nobleman named Atto transferred to Saint Emmeram two yokes of arable land at the place called Wolfhareshusa, into the authority of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Berchtric. Conversely, a certain servant named Rodheri, with the bishop’s permission, transferred [Col. 0941A] to the same nobleman an equal number of yokes from the property of Saint Emmeram at the same place. These are the witnesses: Atto, Herrant, Egilolf, Kaganhart, Etti, Engilrih, Eparachar, Folrat, Alpolt, Reginperht, Willipold, Odalperht, Purchoh, Ratolt, Albuni, Egino, Bernhart, Rihho, Analo, Amalperht, Nidhart, and others.

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Count Engilpert

Let the diligence of certain men, into whose ears knowledge of this charter has been entrusted, learn how the most reverend prelate Ambricho and an honorable man of distinguished rank, namely Count Engilbert, completed the present exchange for the benefit of both parties. The aforementioned Count Engilbert transferred to Saint Peter the Apostle and to God’s holy martyr Emmeram [Col. 0941B] fifty-nine yokes of arable land at the place called Swindpah, leaving nothing outside it: whatever he appeared to possess at that place in lands, meadows, and woods, he transferred in its entirety to the aforesaid saints, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Oto. Conversely, that same Oto, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of the aforementioned saints, at the place called Eholtinga, forty-nine yokes of arable land to the same venerable Count Engilbert, to possess as his own in perpetuity. The witnesses of this transfer are Reginhoh, Cotaperht, Ogo, Hadamar, Willihelm, Askarih, Nidhart, Rodmunt, Irinc, Odalperht, Pern, Erchanperht, Folcpold, and Arnimar.

### Another exchange

[Col. 0941C]

Count Engilbert transferred two dependents to Saint Emmeram, namely Liupuni and Irminhilt. Conversely, Oto, with the consent of Bishop Ambricho, transferred Wilcozum. These are the witnesses: Hadamar, Ogo, Erchanperht, Reginhoh, Cataperht, Willihelm; likewise Cotaperht, Patarih, Warmunt; likewise Ogo.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Liupato

Let it therefore be known to all the faithful, present and future, that a certain nobleman named Liupato transferred a woodland which his sister’s son Hartbert possessed to God’s holy martyr Emmeram, at the place called Waltinhova beside the river [Col. 0941D] called Napa. Liuthard, together with his father Liupato, carried out the same transfer into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Gundbert. Conversely, the same advocate Gundbert, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram another woodland at the aforesaid place to the same nobleman Liupato and his son Liuthard, to possess as their own in perpetuity. These are the witnesses: Count Geio, Hunolf, Jacob, Strupo, Erchanfrid, Adalperht, Rafolt, Arnamar, Paldrih, and others.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the Deacon Gundpalto

Let the diligence of certain of the faithful know that [Col. 0942A] Gundpato, the venerable deacon, confirmed a second time the transfer written in chapter 23, adding also the other properties. Therefore, in the presence of Duke Arnulf, the aforementioned Gundpato, together with his advocate Starchand, transferred to Saint Emmeram such property as he possessed at Quartinaha, Sala, and Weligam, into the hand of Hitto the abbot and Ekkirih, the envoys of the aforesaid holy and venerable Bishop Ambricho. These are the witnesses: Count Gundram and his son Megingoz, Sigihart, Droant, Willihelm, Hoholt, Lantperht, Rihger, Drudolt, Sigiperht, Eparachar, Witger, Otachar, Einhart, Einhart Pero, Framrih, Karentanus, Glaz, Mirei, Kasiz, Necliuchim, and others.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Baldric

[Col. 0942B]

Let the diligence of the faithful know that a certain nobleman named Baldric transferred twelve yokes of his property to God’s holy martyr Emmeram, at the place called Hiltrateschiricha, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his deputy Ogo. Conversely, that same Ogo, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram twelve yokes to the aforementioned nobleman, beside the mountain called Paninperc. These are the witnesses of the same transfer: Askrih, Adalo, Liufo, Plidgoz, Hagano, Erchanperht, Alprih, Oto, Charaf, Hucperht, Eccho, and others. It was enacted at Rispah at the assembly of all the Bavarians.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Altmann

[Col. 0942C]

A record of how the venerable bishop and a certain nobleman named Altmann reached an agreement, completing an exchange between themselves. Accordingly, that same nobleman transferred to Saint Emmeram twelve yokes of arable land at the place called Rorpah, adding also one yoke and two yokes of meadow, into the hand of the venerable prelate Ambricho and his advocate named Reginhoh, in order to complete the exchange. Conversely, the aforementioned advocate, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram twelve yokes of arable land to the aforementioned Altmann at the place called Ratinpah. And so that this exchange might be held more firmly, it was agreed that two charters written in the same form should contain the agreement on both sides, and that the witnesses should be recorded. Their names are: Ogo, [Col. 0942D] Wago, Isanpero, Wasagrim, Askarih, Ekkirih, Gundheri, Arbo, Chuntilo.

## CHAPTER XC.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Pernuvin

Let the diligence of all the faithful know that a certain nobleman named Pernuvin transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram such property as he possessed at Tuncilingon, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Avo: namely, forty-eight yokes of arable land, fifteen yokes of meadow, and one hundred yokes of woodland, leaving nothing outside it—roads, waters, pastures, approaches, and exits—but transferring everything there. Conversely, the aforementioned advocate, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the same Pernuvin [Col. 0943A] forty-three yokes of arable land, thirty-five yokes of woodland, and fifteen yokes of meadow at the place called Nisindorf. These are also the witnesses of the same exchange: Polo, Engilperht, Reginolf, Fridarih, Erchanperht; likewise Reginolf, Rihheri, Helfrih, Arnimar; likewise Erchanperht, Adalperht, Hiltiperht, and others.

## CHAPTER XCI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Witagovo

Let it be known to all the faithful that a certain nobleman named Witagovo transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram three parts of a meadow and one stream for a mill at the place called Sempinchova, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Garahari. Conversely, that same advocate, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram [Col. 0943B] at the same place, one enclosure to the aforementioned nobleman, to possess forever. These are the witnesses: Ogo, Avo, Helfrih, and the others.

## CHAPTER XCII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Swidgarius

Let the diligence of all the faithful learn how the following exchange was carried out. A certain nobleman named Swidger transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram forty-five yokes of arable land, three cartloads of meadow, and forty yokes of brushland to be cleared, near the place called Puopinga, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Reginhoh. Conversely, that same advocate, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned nobleman, as his own, forty-five yokes of arable land, [Col. 0943C] three cartloads of meadow, and three yokes for uprooting brush at the place called Beninga. These too are the witnesses: Wicram, Ogo, Engilhelm, Cozperht, Giso, Gerhoh, Deotolt, Machelm. The transferors and retransferrers were the aforementioned Swidger and Wicram.

## CHAPTER XCIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Reginhoh

A record of how the most reverend prelate Ambricho and a certain nobleman named Reginhoh reached an agreement with one another to carry out an exchange. Accordingly, the aforementioned nobleman transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram such property as he appeared to possess at Ellinuvolfesdorf: namely, a church, a house with a courtyard, four hides of arable land, [Col. 0943D] meadow, and woodland, lacking only two yokes, and whatever else he possessed at the same place; he transferred it all to the aforesaid saint, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate, also named Reginhoh. Conversely, that same advocate, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned nobleman named Reginhoh a church and a house with a courtyard, together with arable land, meadows, and woodland, an equal number of hides, to be possessed by perpetual right at the place called Heikkinga. These are the witnesses who were led by the ears: Isanpero, Wago, Wasagrim, Ekkirih, Eparachar, Sigipreth, Cauzo, Rihpold, Nidhart, Rodmunt, Warmunt, Tato, Arbo, Gundheri, Adalpold, Ogo, Rafolt, Gemmunt, Oto, Liuthart.

## CHAPTER XCIV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Hatto

[Col. 0944A]

Let the diligence of all the faithful know how the present exchange was carried out. The advocate Elfric of the venerable Bishop Ambricho transferred to a certain man named Hatto, with the bishop’s consent, one part of an enclosure from the property of Saint Emmeram at the place called Iniringa. Conversely, that same Hatto transferred to God’s holy martyr Emmeram, into the hand of Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Elfric, two parts of arable land at the same place.

### Another exchange on the same day: Wolfhoh

Accordingly, Wolfhoh, together with his advocate Helfric, transferred one part of an enclosure at the aforementioned place to Saint Emmeram. Conversely, a certain nobleman named Hiltipero [Col. 0944B] transferred to the same Wolfhoh, from his benefice which he held at Iniringa, with Bishop Ambricho’s permission, two parts of arable land. These are the witnesses: Helfrih, Avo, Waltunc, Strupo, Fastmot, Unlaz, Wetti, Wirot, Meginhoh, and the others.

## CHAPTER XCV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Waldgarius

Let it be known to all the faithful that a certain nobleman named Waldgarius transferred one yoke to Saint Emmeram at the place called Mezinga, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Oto. Conversely, that same advocate, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned Waldgarius one-third of an enclosure at the same place. These are the witnesses led by the ears: Lantfrid, Wicram, Hadamar, [Col. 0944C] Engilhelm, and others.

## CHAPTER XCVI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the Deacon Altold

Since among mortals the highly useful and exceedingly fruitful custom of exchanging certain things for the benefit of both parties had long since become established, the most excellent clemency of kings decreed that the same could lawfully be done among ecclesiastical properties, and that it should remain valid up to the supplement of five hides, with charters and witnesses. Accordingly, a certain noble and venerable deacon named Altolt transferred to Saint Peter the Apostle and God’s holy martyr Emmeram such property as he possessed at Gartheringon, Haninchova, and Atinga: houses, courtyards, barns, orchards, lands, [Col. 0944D] meadows, woods, pastures, waters, and watercourses, leaving nothing outside it but transferring the whole to the aforesaid saints, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocates Gundbert and Ogo, the deputy. Conversely, the aforementioned advocate Gundbert, together with his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram to the same venerable deacon Altolt, to possess as his own in perpetuity, whatever he appeared to possess at Munolfinga: buildings, lands, meadows, woods, pastures, waters, and watercourses. These are the witnesses led by the ears: Herrant, Askarih, Ambricho, Albrih, Pernhart, Epoho, Engilperht, Avo, Strupo, Karaheri, Hungis, Salomon, Cotaperht, Irmperht, Gerperht, and others. The transferor [Col. 0945A] was Albricus. It was enacted before Count Engildeo at Reganespure.

## CHAPTER XCVII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ehamarus and Helmpert

Let it be evident to all the faithful that a certain nobleman, namely Ehamarus, and his brother Helmpert transferred to Saint Emmeram whatever property they possessed at Atinga, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Wicram, on this condition: that each of them should possess his wife and children, who are dependents of Saint Emmeram—namely Herosta, Chuonrat, Wasa, Cotahilt, Deotfrit, and Gozlind—together with the property, until his death. Afterward, everything shall return to the aforementioned saint. These are the witnesses: Adalhun, Nanzo, Hiltigoz, Gozpreht, [Col. 0945B] Helfrih, Engilhelm, Eparachar, Ellinpoto.

## CHAPTER XCVIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Count Engildeo

Let the diligence of all the faithful learn the proper terms of the exchange which the venerable Bishop Ambricho and Count Engildeo completed with one another. Whatever the aforementioned Count Engildeo appeared to possess at Stupinga, belonging to his county, namely enclosures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, and woods, his advocate Atto transferred entirely to Saint Emmeram, at the count’s command, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Herrand. Conversely, that same Herrand, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred to the aforementioned count from the property of Saint Emmeram whatever Bishop Ambricho had assigned at Elisindorf: namely, three dependents and a house with a courtyard, together with all its appurtenances. It was enacted at Reganespunc in the presence of the aforementioned bishop and count. Atto was also the transferor; the retransferrers were Owart the priest and Gundhart.

## CHAPTER XCIX.—Transfer of Polo

Polo transferred to the venerable Bishop Ambricho a certain servant named Adalfrid, to possess as his own. These are the witnesses: Albrih, Pald, Sigifrid, Raffolt, Sonperht, Ratolt, Lantpero.

## CHAPTER C.—Exchange between Ambricho and Hartwig

Let it be known to all the faithful that a certain nobleman named Hartwig transferred to Saint Emmeram one enclosure and one field at Illinchova. Conversely, the advocate Strupo, at the command of his lord Bishop Ambricho, transferred to the aforementioned nobleman two fields of arable land at the same place. These are the witnesses: Suindperht, Pernhart, Hartuvic, Avo, Gozperht, Rodmunt, Arnhelm, Hiltiprant, Heriperht, and others.

## CHAPTER CI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Engilhard

Let it be known to all the faithful that a certain nobleman named Engilhart transferred to Saint Emmeram one field of arable land and two cartloads of meadow at the place called Sempinchova. Conversely, the advocate Strupo, at the command of his lord Bishop Ambricho, transferred to the aforementioned nobleman one enclosure at the same place. These [Col. 0946A] are the witnesses: Sindperht, Pernhart, Hartuvic, Avo, Gozperht, Wicram, and the others.

## CHAPTER CII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Helfric

Since the custom of exchanging certain things for the advantage of both parties had long ago become very useful and exceedingly fruitful among men, a certain nobleman named Helfrih and his wife Hiltisnot, remembering this, transferred to Saint Emmeram such property as she possessed at Chaparussa. They immediately abandoned it to the aforesaid saint; and Avo was guarantor and transferor. Conversely, the venerable Bishop Ambricho and the aforementioned Avo, his advocate, who received this transfer, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the same Helfric and his wife a benefice such as Helfrih himself possessed at Sempinchova, on this condition: if one of them should die, the other should possess it until his or her death; afterward, it should be restored to its former place. The witnesses led by the ears are Count Egilperht, Odalperht, Bernhart, Egilperht, Askarih, Erchanperht, Hungis, and Irmperht.

## CHAPTER CIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ogo

Since the authority of royal enactments permitted suitable exchanges to be made concerning ecclesiastical properties, a certain nobleman named Ogo did not delay in practicing the same custom frequently. Accordingly, the aforementioned nobleman Ogo transferred to Saint Peter and God’s holy martyr Emmeram such property [Col. 0946C] as he appeared to possess at Samotinga: namely, one hundred forty yokes of woodland; at Haholstat, thirty yokes of woodland; and at Sempinchova, ten yokes of arable land and seven dependents, namely Perehtuni, Dechila, Perehtuni, Perehtsuvinto, Germunt, Rodmunt, and Wolfpurc, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocates Gundpert and Herrand. Conversely, Gundpert and Herrand transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram, with Bishop Ambricho’s consent, to the aforementioned Ogo, at Eskinhart, two enclosures and everything belonging to them—lands, meadows, woods, waters, watercourses, and all other things—and seven dependents, namely Ellinpurc, Wolfpirc, Pazrih, Weidherii, Reginolt, Walttrut, and Hiltrud. Leaving nothing outside it, they transferred the whole to the same Ogo [Col. 0946D] for perpetual possession. These are the witnesses: Folrat, Waltrih, Albrih, Perehtolt, Rodker, Salacho, Wolfmunt, Ambricho, Rodperht; Trogo, Perehtolt, Otperht, Perehtrih, Durinc, Teor, Avo, Strupo, Heripold, Lantfrid, Oto, Amalperht, Marcho, Gundhart, Adalrih, Erchanperht.

## CHAPTER CIV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Engilscalh

Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church that a certain nobleman named Engilscalh transferred to Saint Emmeram five yokes of arable land at Popinga, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Wicram. Conversely, that same Wicram, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned nobleman Engilscalh four and a half yokes of arable land at Pilinga, to possess as his own in perpetuity. And so that this exchange might be held more firmly and believed more readily by posterity, it was agreed that two charters written in the same form should be produced.

## CHAPTER CV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Count Chunipert

This exchange was made between Bishop Ambricho and Count Chunipert. For Count Chunipert gave Saint Emmeram six yokes of arable land from the property of his benefice at Atinga. His envoys sent to complete this were Engilscalh, Hiltimar, and Willihelm. Conversely, the venerable Bishop Ambricho gave Count Chunipert an equal number of yokes of arable land at the same place; his envoys were the priest Lio, Wicram, and Deotfrid, sent to complete this. So that it might be believed more truly and firmly, it was agreed that two charters written in the same form should be produced.

## CHAPTER CVI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Wicpert

Let it be known to all the faithful in Christ that a certain nobleman named Wicperht transferred to Saint Emmeram at Mulihusun five yokes of meadow with brush to be uprooted, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Heripold. Conversely, that same Heripold, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned Wicpert an equal number of yokes of meadow at the same place, to be held in perpetuity. And so that this exchange might be held more firmly [Col. 0947C] and believed more readily by posterity, it was agreed that two written charters and witnesses should be provided. Their names are: Liutperht, Wolf, Schilpunc, Engilperht, Eckihart, Ratpot, Nidhart, Otperht, Lantperht, Isanparto, Perehart.

## CHAPTER CVII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the Priest Otgis

By divine grace, a certain noble and venerable priest named Otkis transferred to Saint Peter and holy Emmeram [Col. 0948A] his property such as he possessed at Illinchovum, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Strupo, leaving nothing outside it but transferring and releasing the whole there. Conversely, the aforementioned Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Strupo transferred from the property of the aforesaid saints, at the same place, the house situated on the southern side, namely Herimarinchova, with lands, meadows, woodland, and everything belonging there, to the priest Otkis as his own until his death; afterward it shall be restored to its former place. These are the witnesses: Gozpold, Herrant, Heripold, Gundperht, Albrih, Rupo, Witker, Ascrih.

## CHAPTER CVIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Helmpert

[Col. 0948B]

Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church that a certain nobleman named Helmperht transferred to Saint Emmeram whatever he possessed at Dorniginpah, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Antarpot. Conversely, that same Antarpot, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned nobleman Helmpert, at Wolfratinchofun, whatever he possessed there, to possess as his own in perpetuity. These are the witnesses: Adalrih, Avo, Strupo, Reginolt, Eparhart, Ascrih, Rupo, Folchrat, Erchanperht.

## CHAPTER CIX.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Adalric

Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church [Col. 0948C] that a certain man named Adalrih transferred to Saint Peter and God’s holy martyr Emmeram, at Fetarah, one hundred yokes of cultivated and uncultivated land. Conversely, Antarpot, with the permission of Bishop Ambricho, transferred from the property of Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram thirty yokes near Niwinhusun to the aforementioned Adalrih. These are the witnesses: Avo, Strupo, Gundperht, Reginolf, Rupo, Erchanperht, Eparhart.

The First Book ends.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0947]

## CHAPTER I.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Unlaz

[Col. 0947D]

Let the diligence of all the faithful, present and future, learn that a certain nobleman named Unlaz transferred to Saint Emmeram such property as he possessed at Erilingun: namely, five enclosures, five houses, five barns, and seven hides of fields and meadows, leaving nothing outside it but transferring the whole to the aforesaid saint, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Askarih. Conversely, that same Askarih, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned nobleman Unlaz, at Wilhsin, one church, a house with a courtyard, one barn, four hides, [Col. 0948D] and five dependents, to possess as his own. The witnesses, whose names are: Nordpold, Adalfrid, Zeizilo, Rattrud, Deotflat.

## CHAPTER II.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the Priest Oward

Let the diligence of many learn how a certain venerable priest named Oward carried out a suitable exchange. For the aforementioned priest transferred to Saint Peter and the holy martyr Emmeram such property as he appeared to possess at Stupinga: namely, three hides and twenty yokes of arable land, woodland, and meadow, a house with a courtyard, a barn and an orchard, leaving nothing outside it—lands, meadows, pastures, waters, watercourses, [Col. 0949A] exits, and entrances—but transferring the whole there, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocates Herrand and Gundbert. Conversely, Herrand and Gundbert, with the consent of their lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned Oward, to possess as his own in perpetuity, at Tagaratinga, one church, a house with a courtyard, a barn, an orchard, and three hides with all their appurtenances. These are the witnesses: Hadamar, Plidger, Leopanto, Lantfrid, Chreftinc, Waltrih, Albrih, Perehtolt, Schilpunc, Durinc, Isanperht, Reiginperht, Ruodhart, Heimo, Eparolf, Strupo. The transferors and retransferrers are Herrand, Gundbert, and Epatolf. It was enacted at Reganaspurc before Count Engildeo. In the year of the Lord 888.

## CHAPTER III.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Rafolt and Truhmann

[Col. 0949B]

Let it be known to all the faithful that two noblemen, namely Rafolt and Truhman, brothers by the same mother, transferred to Saint Peter and God’s holy martyr Emmeram such properties as they possessed at Stupinga, leaving nothing outside it—buildings, lands, meadows, pastures, woods, waters, and roads—but transferring everything to the aforesaid saints, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Gundbert. Conversely, that same advocate, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned noblemen, at Punninhart, a house with a courtyard, a barn, and one hide; and, in addition, [Col. 0949C] to Truhmann one part of an enclosure, three yokes of arable land, and one cartload of meadow, for perpetual possession. These are the witnesses: Avo, Strupo, Durinchart, Machelm, Askarih, Folrat, Riphold, Adalrih, Waltrih, and others.

## CHAPTER IV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Liutbert

Let it be known to all the faithful of God’s holy Church that a certain nobleman named Liutperht transferred to Saint Emmeram seventy yokes of woodland at the place called Tucilinga, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Gundbert. Conversely, Gundbert, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred to the same Liutperht, at the same place, fifty yokes of woodland, to possess as his own [Col. 0949D] in perpetuity. These are the witnesses: Durinchrat, Eparhart, Gammo, Pirihtilo, Ratolt, Pald, Lantepero.

## CHAPTER V.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Fries

Let all the faithful learn that a certain nobleman named Fries transferred to Saint Emmeram, at Geilunaspah, three yokes of meadow, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Eparhard. Conversely, that same Eparhard, with the bishop’s permission, transferred to the aforementioned nobleman two yokes of meadow at Guttinga, to possess as his own. These are the witnesses: Helfrih, Rafolt, Adalhun, Hiltipero.

## CHAPTER VI.—Exchange between Ambricho and Wolfpert

[Col. 0950A]

Let it be evident to all the faithful that a certain nobleman named Wolfperht transferred to Saint Emmeram his own servant Anthelm and ten yokes of arable land at Snudinga, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Adalbert. Conversely, that same Adalbert, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the property of Saint Emmeram to the aforementioned nobleman Wolfpert, likewise at Snudinga, one servant named Gebarad and ten yokes of arable land. These are the witnesses: Pernhart, Antarpot, Avo, Herrant, Gundpert, Erchanperht.

## CHAPTER VII.—Agreement between Bishop Ambricho and Abbot Hitto

[Col. 0950B]

Through this charter, which is to be plainly and truthfully placed in the ears of certain faithful, let it be known how this agreement was carried out.
