For the honorable abbot Hitto transferred to Saint Peter and God’s holy martyr Emmeram six hides of his property, with buildings and fifteen dependents—Meginheri, Adalger, Milo, Meginheri, Willihelm, Liupuni, Liupkis, Ratkis, Wolfheri, Hiltipirc, Deotpurc, Adalswind, and Liupdrud with her two sons—at the place called Sulzpah, into the hand of the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocates Gundbert and Herrand. Conversely, Gundbert and Herrand, with the permission of their lord the bishop and with the consent of the entire household, transferred to the aforementioned Hitto, from the property of the aforesaid saints, three places with all their appurtenances, namely: [Col. 0950C] Chuningesfeld, Vuaso, and Purcpah; so that he might securely hold and possess them until the end of his life, and afterward everything should return and be retransferred to the aforesaid saints. These are the witnesses of the same transaction: Ogo, Strupo, Erlapold, Chadal, Hartperht, Hiltipero, Righer, and others.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the King

These dependents are under the authority of Bishop Ambricho: Emhilt, Appa, Rihholf, Rato, Engilhilt and her daughter Rihhilt, Rihmot, Engilmar, and Hiltisnot. Conversely, the following are under the king’s authority at Ergoltinga: Gerni, Dultin, Gundhelm, Engilpero, Machelm, Regindrud, [Col. 0950D] Elisa, Emhilt, Gerni, Ermpold, Ellinhilt, Liupila, Rihhilt, Rahhila, Reginolf, Perehtgunto, Reginhilt, Pecchilt.

## CHAPTER IX.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Count Engilpert

Let it be known to all the faithful that Count Engilpert transferred to Saint Emmeram three dependents, namely Alblind and her two sons, into the hand of Ambricho and his advocate Polo, on this condition: that he should possess Erfo, a servant of Saint Emmeram, as his own until his death and that of his wife. These are the witnesses: Engilscalch, Pernhart, Erchanperht, Rafolt, Heripold, and others.

## CHAPTER X.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Reginharius

[Col. 0951A]

Let the diligence of all the faithful learn that Reginheri transferred to Saint Emmeram two parts of one yoke into the hand of Adalpold at Cholinpah. Conversely, that same Adalpold, with the permission of his lord Bishop Ambricho, transferred from his benefice one-third of a yoke to the aforementioned Reginharius at the same place. These are the witnesses: Reginhoh, Albrih, Rihpold, Folcrat, Gerhelm, and others.

## CHAPTER XI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Patarih

Let the diligence of all the faithful know that a certain nobleman named Patarih transferred to Saint Emmeram one enclosure, two rods in width and [Col. 0951B] ten rods in length, at the place called Mezinga. Conversely, the venerable Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Oto transferred arable land two rods in width and twenty rods in length at the same place. These are the witnesses: Erchanperht, Waltrih, Patarih, Gammo, Perehtolt, Sigifrid, Hitto, Oto, Adamar, Hitto, Chazo, Liutfrid, and others.

## CHAPTER XII.—The transfer of Rodheri and the agreement, as it were, of Stomachus between Bishop Ambricho and Rodheri

Let every blessed order of God’s Church know how a certain nobleman named Rodheri, looking ahead to an eternal reward for himself and attending to his present need, transferred to Saint Emmeram the whole property he appeared to possess in the village called Samutinga, including dependents whose names are these: Tiso, Albuvar, Sigifrit and his sons; buildings; cultivated and uncultivated lands; water; woods; roads and pathless places, except only three dependents and one poor woodland acquired elsewhere. The venerable Bishop Ambricho received this transfer, through his advocate Gundbert, on this condition: that conversely Rodheri should receive three hides from the property of the aforesaid saint, together with the revenues, and, for every year while he lived in this fragile life, one downward-woven garment [the text abbreviates “cam.”], sixteen cubits long, as well as one shirt and one tunic; one cartload of wine, namely thirty buckets; ten measures of flour; two [“pracials,” an uncertain term in the text]; four [“Frisking,” uncertain]: two [vervecinas, “wethers”], the other two pigs, each valued at one tremissis; and that, together with the inheritance transferred, all these things serving his use and passing into his right, he should firmly possess for as long as he lived.

And if any bishop, or any member of their household, should attempt to withdraw or violate any of these things and should carry it out, that Rodheri should have free power to dispose of his property wherever he wished. The names of the witnesses, also led by the ears according to Noric custom, may be seen here: Hadamar, Wago, Unlaz, Avo, Strupo, Ambricho, Rupo, Durinchart, Eparhart, Ilpunc, Wetti, Strupo, Rihhad, Herirat, Rodhart, Lantpero. This is the second transfer. These are the witnesses: Herrant, Strupo, Rihpold, Karaheri, Eparahchar, Petilo, Adalhun, Unolz, Deotperht.

[Col. 0952A]

It was enacted in the second year of King Arnulf, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, at the place called Menzinpah, in the presence of very many monks and canons, namely: Rodolt, provost of the monastic community of the holy martyr Emmeram; Deotpert, sacristan and monk; Tuto, monk and deacon; Erimpert, priest and provost of the canons; Regino, deacon; Erminold, priest; Perideo, priest; Enolt, priest; Wihgozo, deacon; Wolfhelm, deacon; Mahtharius, subdeacon; Harpert, subdeacon; Deotmunt, subdeacon; Wolfolt, deacon; Atto, subdeacon; and Wolfrat, subdeacon.

## CHAPTER XIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Pervum

Let the diligence of all faithful persons, both present [Col. 0952B] in the holy Church and future, know how this present exchange was carried out. A certain nobleman, named Pervum, transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, at the places called Hittinchoba and Dentichoba, 194 acres of his own and his wife’s property, consisting of arable land, meadows, and woodland, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Gundbert. In return, the aforesaid bishop and Gundbert, with the consent of the monks and canons, transferred from the possessions of the aforesaid saints to the same Pervum and his wife, at Puningon, a house with its court, also a church with all its appurtenances, and 183 acres of arable land, meadows, and woodland, to be held as their own property in perpetuity.

And so that this exchange might be held more firmly, it was decided that two documents written with identical wording should be produced and that witnesses should be drawn by the ears. These are Erchanperht, Ambricho, Sigifrid, Ratolt, Hitto, Salacho, Eparhart, and others. Albrih was the conveyor and reconveyor.

## CHAPTER XIV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Oto

A certain nobleman, Oto, transferred to Saint Emmeram such property as he possessed at Swindpah, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Reginhoh, in exchange for 60 solidi. These are the witnesses: Engilscalch, Westargowo, Gerperht, Ocgo, Cundachar, Nidhart, Rihpold, Eparachar, Azo, Pero, Perideo, Chuniperht, Helfrih, Erchanperht, Albrih, Ambricho, [Col. 0952D] Racholf, Willihelm, Rodolf, Strupo, and Adalperht.

## CHAPTER XV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Hardpert

Let the diligence of many faithful persons know how the following arrangement of a transfer was completed. A certain freedman, a free man named Hartbert, namely a subdeacon, transferred his property to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, which he appeared to possess at Folinchova—lands, meadows, pastures, roads and trackless places—and at Rogkinga seven acres of woodland, leaving nothing outside it: whatever he possessed in these places he transferred wholly to the aforesaid saints, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable [Col. 0953A] bishop, and his advocate Gundbert.

In return, the same advocate, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred to the aforesaid Hartbert the benefice at Eigilstat with all its appurtenances, on this condition: that Hartbert himself and one of his nearest relatives after him should firmly possess that benefice as their own property until his death; thereafter it should belong to the saints named above.

These are the witnesses: Hadamar, Plidker, Reginpold, Albrih, Reccho, Motmunt, Isanperht, Perehtolt, and very many others. This was enacted at Weltinpurc, with the consent of the canons: the priest Ermpert, the priest Germund, the deacon Regino, Rodolf the priest and monk, Deotpert the priest and monk, Tutone the deacon and monk, and all the others.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Exchange between Hiltigarda and the priest Richolf

[Col. 0953B]

Let it be known to all faithful persons that Witagowo, advocate of Hiltigarda, transferred one plot of land from the possessions of the lower monastery of Saint Mary, at the place called Pah, to the priest Rihholf, with the consent of Lady Hiltigarda. In return, the same priest Rihholf and his advocate Sindpert, with the permission of Ambricho, venerable bishop, transferred to Witagowo two parts of the arable land at the same place.

These are the witnesses: Adolf, Penhart, Helfrih, Cundfrid, Ardwit, Sindperht, Hunrih, Geilolf, Willipato, Hiltiperht, Ekkihart, and others.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Engilscalch

[Col. 0953C]

Let the intelligence of all faithful persons know that a certain nobleman named Engilscalch transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, a house with its court and 83 acres of arable land and meadows at the place called Purringa, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Reginhoh.

In return, Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Wicram transferred from the possessions of the aforesaid saints to the same nobleman, at Talachirchon, a church and 30 acres of arable land.

These are the witnesses: Count Engilperht, Erchanperht, Helmrih, Reginhoh, Rihpold, Westargowo, Helfrih, Racholf, Hitto, Egilpold, Rodmunt, Mezzi, Strupo, and others.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Hiltipero

[Col. 0953D]

Let it be known that a certain nobleman named Hiltipero transferred to Saint Emmeram one acre at Rodrantinchova. In return, the advocate Helfric, with the consent of his lord, Bishop Ambricho, transferred to the aforesaid nobleman, at the same place, one acre to be held as his own property.

These are the witnesses: Waltunc, Avo, Strupo, Wetti, again Strupo, and Lantperht.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Lantfrid

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that a certain nobleman named Lantfrid transferred to Saint Emmeram whatever he possessed at Capurisso, into the hands of Ambricho, bishop, and his [Col. 0954A] advocate Wicram.

In return, the same Wicram, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram to the aforesaid nobleman Lantfrid, at Sunichingon, 34 acres consisting of arable land and meadows, and 6 acres of woodland.

These are the witnesses: Ogo, Erchanperht, Helfrih, Engilpold, Folrat, Derpheri, Strupo, Sindperht, Adalperht, Hadamar, Tato, Gerhoh, Hitto, and others.

## CHAPTER XX.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Ato

Let it therefore be clear to all faithful persons that a certain nobleman named Ato transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram 11 acres of arable land at the place called Samutinga, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Hadamar.

In return, the same advocate, by order and with the consent of the aforesaid bishop, transferred to the aforementioned nobleman Ato, from the possessions of the saints named above, 10 acres of arable land at Zeizinchova, to possess as his own property by perpetual right.

And so that this exchange might be held more firmly and believed more securely, it was decided that two documents written with identical wording should be produced and witnesses brought forward. Their names are: Pernhart, Strupo, Erchanperht, Helfrih, Ambricho, Sigifrid, Hitto, Folcrat, Wetti, again Strupo, Ratolt, Mezzi, and others.

## CHAPTER XXI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Eigil

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that a certain nobleman named Eigil transferred to Saint Peter and Saint [Col. 0954C] Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, such property as he possessed at Chaparussa, with buildings, lands, roads and trackless places, leaving nothing outside it but transferring the whole into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Adalric.

In return, the same Adalric, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the possessions of the aforesaid saints to the same Eigil, to be held as his own property, whatever Hahicho had formerly possessed as a benefice at Feterah.

These are the witnesses: Hadamar, Antarpot, Otachar, Machelm, Hungis, Amalperht, Rihpold, Rihperht, Ternod, Strupo, Reginperht, Sigifrid, and Adalp.

## CHAPTER XXII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Sigipert

[Col. 0954D]

Let it be known to all faithful persons that a certain nobleman named Sigipert transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, whatever he possessed at Chaparussa, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Adalric.

In return, the same Adalric, with the consent of the bishop, transferred to the same Sigipert an equal measure at Engilmonaschirichon.

The witnesses of the preceding exchange are also witnesses of this one.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—Arrangement of the Archpriest Sandrat

The venerable archpriest Sandrat transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, such property as he appeared to possess at Gliumin [Col. 0955A], and ten slaves, whose names are: Dancrat, Purgund, Isanpero, Guodliud, Purat, Frecholf, Alazeiz, Folcrat, Ratolf, and Egilmar. He left nothing outside it except one plot and three acres, but transferred the whole to the aforementioned saints, on this condition: that he should retain as his own property the benefice at Erininga until his death.

And Anzo, son of Adalric, should possess the same property together with the benefice until the end of his life. Thereafter, everything should belong to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram.

These are the witnesses: Count Cundpold, Count Orendil, Ascrih, Adalperht, Oto, Engilpold, Chuniperht, Engilscalch, Eicco, Herimar, Adalrih, Oto, and others.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—Arrangement between Bishop Ambricho and Aspert the Chancellor

[Col. 0955B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let the diligence of many faithful persons know how the following arrangement was carried out.

Aspert, venerable deacon and chancellor of King Arnulf, with the king himself granting permission, transferred to Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, his property: namely, the chapel at Feldun, the one at the place called Cella, the place called Gepantespah, Gisalpah, and whatever belonged to those places—buildings, slaves, lands, meadows, and woods—leaving nothing outside it except the little benefices held by Oto and Gundperht, but transferring and handing over the whole to the aforementioned saints, into the hands of Ambricho, [Col. 0955C] venerable bishop, and his advocate Gundbert.

In return, the same Gundbert, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the possessions of the saints mentioned above to the same Aspert, venerable deacon, these places: Oparinhusa, Niwinhusa, and Lorcin, and whatever appeared to belong to those places, on this condition: that Aspert himself and one of his nearest relatives, to whom he might wish to transfer them after himself, should firmly possess all the places named above until his death. Thereafter, everything should belong to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, except those two little benefices.

This was enacted at Reganasburc, with the testimony and affirmation of the monks, canons, and laymen.

These are the witnesses: Herrant, Gundperht, Ogo, Erchanperht, Strupo, Ambricho, Sigifrid, [Col. 0955D] Albrih, Pald, Wicker, Gundpold, Eparhart, Hitto, Folcrat, again Strupo, Wetti, Lantperht, Werinheri, and others.

## CHAPTER XXV.—Exchange between Helfric and Patto

Let it be known that Patto transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram two female slaves of the same name, both named Wolfhild, into the hands of the advocate Helfric.

In return, Helfric transferred to the same Patto, from the benefice of Gotapert, one female slave named Waltfrida, to be held as his own property.

These are the witnesses: Ogo, Ambricho, Gotaperht, Patarih, Durinchart, Rodmunt, and others.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Liutgar

[Col. 0956A]

Let it be clear to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that a certain nobleman named Liutger transferred to Saint Emmeram, at Homeres, five acres, into the hands of Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Reginhoh.

In return, Reginhoh, by order of his lord the bishop, transferred to the same Liutger, at Zeizinchofa, five acres to be held as his own property.

These are the witnesses: Askarih, Ambricho, Pald, Irimperht, Erchanperht, Trago, Ino, Adalo, Gunzo, and Adalpero.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Waltung

Let the diligence of all faithful persons know that a certain nobleman named Waltunc transferred all his property, which he possessed at Teningon, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Gerpert, to Saint Peter and Saint [Col. 0956B] Emmeram, the holy martyr of God.

In return, the same Gerpert, together with the bishop, transferred to the same Waltung, in its entirety, the benefice at Otperchtinchofa, to be held as his own property.

These are the witnesses: Askarih, Helfrih, Eparhart, Rupo, Strupo, Erchanpold, Gundalperht, Gozperht, Isanhart, and others.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Perahtger

Let it be clear to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that a certain nobleman named Perahtger transferred to Saint Emmeram, at Gundinhart, one plot, ten acres of arable land, and six acres of woodland, into the hands of Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Marcho.

In return, Marcho, by order of his lord the bishop, transferred to the same Perahtger, at Hedinpah, one plot, ten acres of arable land, and six acres of woodland, to be held as his own property.

These are the witnesses: Cotaperht, Reginhoh, again Reginhoh, Salomon, Ambricho, Sigifrin, Askarih, and Kermunt.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Anamodus

[Note: [Col. 0955D] The author Anamodus is speaking of himself.]

Since the diligence of innumerable men has striven to seek out and investigate opportunities concerning their property, it also pleased a certain red-haired cleric named Anamodus, a religious subdeacon, to bring certain possessions of his own into his use and join them to it.

Accordingly, such property as the same Anamodus had received into his possession through the gift of the most pious King Arnulf, in the district called Westarmannomarcha, near Prointala, at the place Reitinpuoh, in the county of Count Engildeo, he transferred and bound to Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr, together with seven slaves, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocates Gerpert and Gundbert. [Col. 0956D]

In return, Ambricho, venerable bishop, together with his advocates Gerpert and Gundbert, laying their hands upon it, transferred from the possessions of the aforementioned saints to the same Anamodus whatever he possessed as a benefice at Beningon, together with seven slaves; and at Pondorf, 22 acres of arable land, together with the estate which his parents had there; and at Nordgewe, the little benefice at Niufara; and whatever—buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, pastures, waters, and all other goods—appeared justly and lawfully to pertain to those places.

They transferred and handed all this over to the already three-times-mentioned Anamodus, to be possessed perpetually as his own property, with no one contradicting.

These are also the witnesses: Adolf, Pernhart, Patto, Avo, Strupo, Herrant, again Strupo, Eparhart, Rupo, Sigifrid, Gozpold, Gundpato, Waltrih, Oto, Hadamar, Perehtolt, Rafolt, and others. Gerpert and Gundpert were the conveyors and reconveyors. Enacted at Menzinpah.

## CHAPTER XXX.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Epa

Let it be known to all faithful persons that Peren transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram one plot at Weipilingun to a certain woman named Epa.

In return, the same Epa transferred to the aforementioned saint, at the same place, two measures of arable land.

These are the witnesses: Reginhoh, Gouzo, Altman, Cundheri, Cundalperht, and Othelm.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—Exchange between Cundram and Avo

Let it be known to all faithful persons that Cundram transferred three slaves into the power of Saint Emmeram, named Adala, Wolfmunt, and Pazhilt, into the hands of the advocate Avo.

In return, Avo transferred to the same Cundram, from the benefice of Mahtarius, three slaves to be held as his own property, named Helmgart, Perahthero, and Ratuni. [Col. 0957C]

These are the witnesses: Odulman, Sigifrid, Adalhoh, Otperht, Willihelm, and Engilhart.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—Exchange between Adalhun the Elder and Meginhard

Let it be known that Adalhun the mayor, with the permission of Bishop Ambricho, transferred to Meginhard one part of an estate at Chaparussa.

In return, the same Meginhard transferred to Saint Emmeram two parts of one field at the same place.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and the priest Ermpert

Because of the prosperity [perhaps: “falsehood”] of the wavering faith of many, and because, when rulers succeed one another through the chance mutability of affairs, the long labor of earlier service is either consigned to oblivion or perhaps cast behind one’s back, some people, as though wiser than others, began to devise more profoundly how they might bind the benefits of the present life more tightly to themselves for their comfort, and how they might reserve properties—if it should happen that anyone possessed them—with more cautious judgment, for the relief of present necessity and the hope of future recompense. [Col. 0957D]

Armed with this same thought, a certain religious priest and provost of the canons of the bishopric of Regensburg, named Ermpert, transferred to Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and to Saint Emmeram, martyr and bishop, his property in the county of Count Engildeo, at the place called Scornashova, such as he had been able to acquire with money from a certain nobleman named Arnimar and his coheirs, together with a court and buildings and ten slaves, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocates Avo and Gundpert. [Col. 0958A]

The same advocates—namely Avo and Gundpert—acting by order of Bishop Ambricho, transferred to Ermpert as his property whatever he appeared to possess as a benefice, together with buildings and courts, slaves, and all utensils, on this condition: that, in both what he gave and what he received, he should enjoy a similar right of property for as long as he lived in this fragile life, with no one disturbing or contradicting him.

After his death, all these things, preserved and undefiled, should without delay pass into the service of the saints mentioned above.

These are the witnesses: Hadamar, Rodker, Strupo, Ermperht, Erchanperht, and Herirat.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—Exchange between the priest Ermpert and Sigifrid

[Col. 0958B]

Let it be known to all faithful persons that Ermpert, with the permission of Bishop Ambricho, transferred to Sigifrid, from the possessions of his benefice, two parts of one acre at Espilapah, to be held as his own property.

In return, the aforesaid Sigifrid transferred one acre of his own property at the same place to the aforementioned Ermpert.

These are the witnesses: Albric, Folcrih, Hitto, and others.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho, Attimar, and Cundram

Let it be known to all faithful persons that Wicram, advocate of Bishop Ambricho, with the permission of the aforesaid venerable bishop, transferred to Attimar and Cundram five acres of arable land at the place called Atinga. [Col. 0958C]

In return, Attimar and Cundram gave seven acres of woodland to Saint Emmeram. Afterwards, Attimar also transferred four acres of arable land to the saint mentioned above.

In return, Wicram transferred the same number of acres to Attimar, to be held as his own property.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—Transfer of the Archpriest Adalung

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that Adalunc, archpriest, transferred his property—whatever he possessed at Sulactala—to Amalung and Adalung, to be possessed by them until their death.

After their death it was to pass to Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, into the hands of Ambricho, venerable bishop, and his advocate Reginhoh.

He also transferred the slaves whom he had there, whose names are: Ekko, Hiltipold, Ratheri, Paldker, [Col. 0958D] Ratperht, Liubhilt, Hiltisnolt, Rihhilt, and Ratfrit.

These are the witnesses to this transfer: Ogo, Egilscalch, Wago, Gerperht, Rihpold, Perehtheri, Eparahchar, Hitto, Adalperht, Helfrih, Oapi, and also Adalperht, son of Engilscalch.

This was done at Pilistingon, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—Exchange between the advocate Gerbert and Otnia

Let it be known to all faithful persons that Oto transferred to Saint Emmeram a small wood at Reinna.

In return, Gerbert the advocate, by order of his lord Bishop Aspert, transferred to the same Otnia a girl named Ermanhilt.

These are the witnesses: Gundperht, Odalperht, Deotrih, Engilrih, Wicker, Deotpato, [Col. 0959A] Hitto, Lantpero, Hartperht, Patarih, and Sindperht.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—Arrangement between Bishop Aspert and Mahtarius

Let it be known to all faithful persons that a certain freedman, the religious subdeacon Mahtarius, transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram such property as King Arnulf had granted to him as his own property at Stupingon, into the hands of Aspert, venerable bishop, and his advocates Herrant and Gundbert.

This was on the condition that Mahtarius should possess his benefice at Owanashovon, with all its appurtenances, as his own property until his death; afterwards, everything should be restored and secured to the saints mentioned above.

These are the witnesses: Askarih, Waltrih, Durinchart, Hardperht, [Col. 0959B] Garaheri, Hitto, Alboni, Mezzi, Eparhart, Albric, Perehtolt, and Deotrih.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—Exchange between Bishop Aspert and the deacon Wikkern

Let the entire most blessed order of the Church know how a certain noble deacon named Wikkern, looking ahead to eternal recompense for himself and providing for his present necessity, transferred to Saint Michael, the holy archangel of God, such property as he possessed at Rossidorf, with all its appurtenances and four slaves, whose names are Kerperht, Ratmot, and his two sons.

Aspert, venerable bishop, received this transfer, together with his advocate Jacob, on this condition: that in return Wikkern should possess his benefice, which he appeared to hold at Chessindorf and Grammanesdorf [Col. 0959C], with all its appurtenances and slaves; that he should possess all these things together without dispute until the end of his life; and that after his death all improvements should be restored to the aforesaid holy archangel of God.

He also arranged that, if at any time he wished to adopt the monastic life, he should have his seat in the same monastery of the aforesaid archangel Michael.

The names of the witnesses, also drawn by the ears according to Noric custom, may be seen here: Gernod, Albrat, Ratmunt, Ascrih, Deotrih, Tevit, Deotpato, Waltilo, Strupo, Ekkiperht, Nordheri, Waltrih, and Rodhoh.

This was enacted on the fifth day before the Ides of April, at the place called Maninseo, in the presence of all the monks who were then present at that place, young and old. [Col. 0959D]

## CHAPTER XL.—Exchange between Bishop Aspert and Amalpert, Pernhard, and Richo

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God that Amalperht, Pernhart, and Rihho, certain noblemen, transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, 40 acres of arable land and 22 acres of woodland at the place called Punninhard, into the hands of Aspert, venerable bishop, and his advocate Herrant.

In return, the same Herrant, with the permission of his lord the bishop, transferred from the possessions of Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram to the aforesaid noblemen, at the same place, an equal number of acres of arable land and woodland, to be held as their own property in perpetuity.

These are the witnesses: Wicker, [Col. 0960A] Sigifrid, Helfrih, Ermperht, Hitto, Gammo, Albrih, Gundpold, and Reginpold.

## CHAPTER XLI.—Exchange between Bishop Ambricho and Herrant

Let it be known to all faithful persons that Herrant transferred to Saint Emmeram two male slaves named Poson and Pumann.

In return, Bishop Ambricho and his advocate Gundpert transferred to the same Herrant an equal number of slaves, named Liutfrid and Grimold, to be held as his own property in perpetuity.

These are the witnesses: Erchanperht, Albric, Perehtolt, and others.

## CHAPTER XLII.—Arrangement between Bishop Aspert, Hadamar, and Sahlind

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, let the diligence of many faithful persons know how the following arrangement was fully completed. [Col. 0960B]

A venerable matron named Sahlind, together with her advocate Hadamar, transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, into the hands of Aspert, most reverend bishop, and his advocate Gundpert, such property as she appeared to possess through royal gift at Hardheim, excepting three slaves—Christan, Deotwih, and Albswind—in order that they might remain free—and 30 acres of arable land and 6 acres of meadows, so that Altman might possess all these things as his own property until his death, after which they should return to the saints mentioned above.

All the remaining property, both buildings and slaves, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, waters and watercourses, meadows, pastures, together with all the appurtenances of the same place, was donated and assigned in its entirety to the saints already named, on this condition: that Hadamar and his wife Sahlind should securely hold and possess, until the end of their lives, the estate at Haholstat belonging to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, as well as the same property at Hardheim.

Afterwards, the aforesaid saints and their steward should receive both places into their power without any contradiction.

The witnesses to this transfer are also: Count Engildeo, Count Orendil, Pernhart, Avo, Folrat, Durinchart, Reginpald, Lantpero, Askarih, Deotker, Rodolf, Amalperht, Strupo, Engilperht, Albrih, Perchtolt, Rupo, Gozpold, Herimar, Ringolf, Geio, and others.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—Exchange between Bishop Aspert and Reginhoh

Let it be known to all faithful persons that a certain nobleman named Reginhoh transferred to Saint Emmeram, at Pilistingon, one acre of arable land.

In return, Rihpold the advocate, by order of his lord Bishop Aspert, transferred to the aforesaid nobleman, at the same place, half of one acre.

These are the witnesses drawn by the ears: Reginhoh, Sigifrid, Pald, and again Sigifrid.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—Exchange between Bishop Aspert and Sigifrid the Widow

In the name of God, an agreement and meeting took place between Aspert, venerable bishop, and a certain noble widow, Sigifrit, so that they might confirm certain possessions between themselves for their common benefit; and so they did.

Accordingly, the aforementioned widow Sigifrit, together with her advocate named Ratolt, transferred to Saint Peter and Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, such property as she appeared to possess at Milizreod: one plot, 26 acres of arable land, and eight cartloads of meadow, into the hands of Bishop Aspert and his advocate Herrant.

In return, the same Herrant, with the consent of his lord the bishop, transferred from the possessions of Saint Emmeram, at Pezcinmos, to the aforesaid widow, one plot and 30 acres of arable land, to be held in perpetual possession.

These are the witnesses: Garaheri, Chuniperht, Sindperht, Rodger, [Col. 0962A] Gundpald, Folcrih, Hitto, Wetti, Ambricho, and Asperht.

## CHAPTER XLV.—Exchange between Bishop Aspert and Ratfrid

Let the diligence of all faithful persons know how the following exchange was completed. A certain nobleman named Ratfrid transferred to Saint Emmeram, the holy martyr of God, into the hands of Aspert, venerable bishop, and his advocate Garaheri, at the place called Samutinga, a house with its court, arable land . . . . . . . . . .

The following few lines are missing because the final leaf was cut from the codex.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 900. EUTROPIUS THE LOMBARD, PRIEST

[Col. 0961]

## AROUND THE YEAR OF THE LORD 900. ON THE RIGHTS AND PRIVILEGES OF THE EMPERORS IN THE ROMAN EMPIRE

*(In Goldast, Scriptores Rerum Alamannicarum)*

[Col. 0961B]

In ancient times imperial dignity flourished at Rome, under whose domination various kingdoms existed and to which all peoples submitted their necks. It therefore established consuls, who, through the daily practice of government, arranged the reins of the kingdom by their counsel. Offices were distributed among senators and magistrates, according to the work appropriate to each person’s function. Imperial dignity, however, was exalted by all through praises and honors alone.

After the coming of the only-begotten Son of God and the glory of his Ascension, the Roman Empire transferred itself to Byzantium, which was called Constantinople after Constantine the Great Caesar. Since it gloried in the Roman Empire, it was called New Rome, though ancient Rome was still preferred as glorious above the others.

When the apostles and their successors went to preach the Gospel throughout the whole world, in accordance with the divine command, the Caesars returned to Rome, inflicting various tortures upon the saints in order to please their gods. Consequently, blessed Peter, who had been placed above the others by Jesus Christ our Lord, came to Rome for the sake of preaching. Rome was proclaimed mistress of all nations; and just as it had previously been deceived by many images of idols, so it was converted, together with the others, through the many preachings of the apostles and the exhortations of other martyrs.

There also blessed Peter and Paul, teacher of the nations, were crowned with martyrdom. Thus, just as Rome, through its ancient walls, had been the head of many peoples in the division created by images, so it was called the head and mistress of all Christians in the unity of true faith and unconfused divinity, possessing primacy over all Christianity [Col. 0961D] by the privilege received from Jesus, where he says: “You shall be called Cephas”; and elsewhere: “I shall pray for you, that your faith may not fail.” [Col. 0962B]

When the Roman Empire was divided, because the imperial seat, which had formerly been established at ancient Rome, had been transferred to Constantinople, the peoples of many nations had rebelled against the City. Hence great and numerous wars arose against it, as Orosius bears witness.

At that time Rome was ruled by patricians. It was subject only to its emperor, so that if an emperor was ever found cruel after the manner of the pagans, he would, through his legates, crown the most holy bishops and other Christians with martyrdom by various punishments.

As the Christian religion grew, such fervor of faith blazed forth from the fathers, until the Lombards entered Italy. When they approached the Po, it was reported at Rome—Pope Silverius then presiding over the Roman Church—to the patrician Narses, whose wife was called Polyxiana. It was reported to them that the aforesaid pontiff had sent to the Lombards, inviting them to Rome, so that Greek power might be abolished and the rights of the Church raised under the power of the pontiff.

The pope’s necessity was so great that he had care for nothing except the churches and clergy. His daily provisions were customarily supplied from the palace, and annual gifts were given for the restoration of churches and, from the Caesar, as alms in honor. This was solely out of reverence for the apostles Peter and Paul.

Whenever an imperial legate was sent by the ruler ordering the Roman pontiff to travel to Constantinople [Col. 0962D] to the emperor, he went, neglecting every other consideration, [Col. 0963A] even if he knew for certain that he would be sent into exile.

On one occasion a messenger was sent by the patrician Narses to Pope Silverius. When he went to the pope’s house, where Silverius lay ill, Narses’s wife said to him: “Lord pope, why are you sinning against us, since you wished to bring the Lombards upon us?”

After saying this, she had him seized and tonsured, clothed in a monastic habit, and led, seated on a donkey, to the monastery of Saint Sabas. When he had gone outside, seated upon the donkey, one of those standing nearby said: “Alas! The lord pope is dead.”

Moreover, when the Lombards flooded into Italy, the Greeks, converted to the faith of Christ, were driven out, and imperial rule ceased from the city of Rome as far as the Franks. [Col. 0963B]

The Lombards were ruled by kings. After the boundaries of Italy had been divided, the duke of Spoleto was established at Rome in place of the king, on the agreement that whenever the pope departed, the aforesaid duke would take part in the election of the future pontiff, receiving very many gifts as the royal share.

If disputes arose among the Romans, a legate from the king’s leading men would come with the same duke to deliberate the cases and judicial proceedings. Those who were found guilty of a crime were punished by royal power or sent into exile, even without consulting the pope.

This continued until Zacharias was governor. He deceitfully, as though out of a certain familiarity, made a proposal to Charles, king of the Franks: since Charles had the daughter of Desiderius, king of Italy, as his wife, he invited that same Charles into Italy, sowing discord among the kings, praising him, and holding out imperial scepters to him. He received from Charles an assurance regarding the time when he should enter Italy; and after they had sworn to one another, he returned.

When Charles passed through the borders of Desiderius’s kingdom, he detached some of his men from him, giving great gifts to some and promising others that similar gifts would be given to them.

After Charles took possession of this kingdom, he went to Rome and gave many gifts there, which to this day retain Roman dominion over the borders of this kingdom. He made an agreement with the Romans and their pontiff concerning the appointment of the pontiff: a legate should be present, and he himself should decide contentious disputes.

They established annual gifts to be brought to the palace at Pavia: ten pounds of gold, one hundred of silver, and ten excellent cloaks, apart from private gifts.

Whenever the emperor, or his legate, came to Rome, judges were sent from the palace each year. Throughout all the Roman territories they administered legal judgments, compelling the inhabitants of those places to come to court, while their judges declared the proper law in the presence of the imperial judges.

If inhabitants of another nation were found there, they were judged by royal judgment.

There were, moreover, monasteries in the Sabine territory: that of the Lord Savior and that of holy Mary, Mother of God, as well as the monastery of blessed Andrew the apostle near Mount Soracte, and other fiscal estates within the Roman boundaries for imperial use.

The monks traveled not only through the Italian kingdom but also into Francia [Col. 0964A], carrying tribute, wine, and other gifts according to their ability.

While the Romans were rejoicing in their security, their hearts were lifted up according to their custom, and they wished to claim imperial power for themselves. When Pope Leo resisted, they seized him and wished to tear out his eyes. They tore out one, but could not tear out the other, because divine mercy delivered him; and they expelled him from the City, as though both his eyes had been destroyed.

Fleeing to Francia, he reached Charles. Consequently Charles came to avenge the pope, seized the Romans, and in a single day had three hundred of their leading men beheaded in the Lateran field.

Therefore it was established that all the leading men of Rome should be imperial—both bishops and laymen—and that the entire populace likewise should swear fidelity to the emperor with them; and that his envoy should remain in Rome at all times to adjudicate contentious disputes. He lived in the palace of Saint Peter; and it had been determined how great and what kind of daily allowances were to be given him from the palace, while whatever remained was supplied abundantly from the monasteries or estates mentioned above.

Indeed, imperial authority was then so powerful that if, in a legal proceeding, the case of a lesser or ignorant person was postponed, and that person, on someone’s advice, grasped the feet of the emperor’s legate and begged him for justice, and the envoy adjured the leading men of Rome, saying, “By the fidelity that you owe the Lord Emperor, render this man justice,” no one dared to turn aside either to the right or to the left—even if it was certain that the injury had been caused by relatives of the pontiff. Very often they did not settle cases before the apostolic ruler, but in the judicial place at the Lateran, where there is a certain place called “at the She-Wolf,” which was called the mother of the Romans; there they brought the judicial process to an end. The compositions that had customarily been exacted from wrongdoers were likewise divided equally between the emperor’s envoy and the apostolic ruler. But if the offense was of such a kind that the criminal matter was to be subjected to the public treasury, it did not pass under ecclesiastical jurisdiction unless by an imperial grant.

For if anyone incurred the emperor’s anger—whether a bishop or a Roman judge—and it was possible for Caesar to come to Rome, he came; otherwise the duke of Spoleto was sent, the offender was arrested, and he was led into exile. His house, however, was sealed with the king’s ring until the emperor’s decision, so that, if he should ever be restored to favor, he might find his property preserved; otherwise his possessions were distributed among the soldiers by imperial commands. If anyone was referred to the authority of a judge and appealed to Caesar’s clemency, an imperial legate was sent for that matter to examine the truth of the case carefully; and if the person proceeded against was himself at fault, he endured the injury.

The Romans followed this custom until the emperor Louis the Great—also called the Second—the son of Lothair. Since he preferred to reside in Italy, he became nearer to Rome; there he exercised a certain greater authority, having with him vigorous men of that city who knew the ancient custom of the emperors and reported it to Caesar. They urged him to restore the ancient imperial practice. And unless he had relinquished it out of reverence for the blessed apostles, he would certainly have done so.

This prince also entered the territory of Benevento and all Calabria for two reasons. First, because the province was part of Italy, he wished to claim the boundaries of the whole kingdom under his authority. Second, because the most savage nation of the Hagarenes was already touching those borders: they had captured a certain city called Bari, fortified it, filled it with many revenues, and kept it as a refuge. For this reason he was kindly received by the inhabitants of that land.

The aforesaid Caesar therefore proceeded with a multitude of people to receive those peoples. And, so as not to burden those who had been plundered by the Hagarenes, he sought assistance from Ravenna; but he also sought assistance from nearby Venice, so that, supported by naval aid, he might bring abundant supplies to Apulia. At that time John, archbishop of Ravenna, presided over the Ravennate Church and was especially close to the emperor because he served him. Moved by jealousy, therefore, the Roman pontiff, named Nicholas, burst into anger against him. He craftily summoned him to Rome, so that he might condemn him as though by an ecclesiastical judgment and install another in his place.

When the archbishop heard this, he fled to Queen Engelberga. She sent her legates to the apostolic ruler, asking him to restore his favor to the archbishop. When she could not obtain this, she humbly informed her lord, asking him to intervene with his protection on behalf of the archbishop and forbidding the apostolic ruler to cause him any disturbance. Because the apostolic ruler, without having heard the prince, pronounced excommunications against him, a serious enmity arose between them.

At last the royal dignity was raised against the apostolic dignity, bringing forward the ancient statutes of the Fathers: that a prelate was not permitted to excommunicate a bishop without consulting a synodal council; and that a synod ought to be summoned not by the pope but by the emperor. Very many acts of hostility were inflicted upon the Roman pontiff on this account. In the Pentapolis he distributed benefices among his own men, ordering that no administration be provided to Rome except assistance by the transport of ships. He also caused certain estates in the regions of Campania to be seized for royal use and for that of his faithful men. Daily services were likewise demanded from the monasteries mentioned above for the king’s table, through various arrangements.

Finally, with the advice of the Roman leaders, he established in the city of Rome a certain bishop named Arsenius, adorned with holiness and learning, and papal representative of the Roman See. He gave him as an assistant John the deacon and archchancellor, his own secretary, who afterward became bishop of Rieti, to which office he had already been elected.

At the appropriate time the emperor came to Rome and was honorably received by everyone, both great and small. The aforementioned archbishop of Ravenna came with him, fearing none of the pontiff’s threats. Hence a greater discord arose between the pope and the emperor. The emperor was in the palace of the holy apostle Peter, while the pope was at the Church of the Holy Apostles. Since all the pope’s plots against the royal dignity were regarded as nothing, he appointed monks and virgins consecrated to Christ from the monasteries of Rome to celebrate daily litanies around the circuit of the walls, as though under the pretext of religion, and to sing Masses against the princes who were acting wickedly.

When the king’s chief men heard this, they approached the pope humbly and asked him privately to prohibit such actions. Since they could obtain nothing from the emperor, they returned sorrowfully. One day, however, when certain soldiers of the aforesaid prince were going to Saint Paul’s and were returning, they came upon the litanies. Stirred by the ancient enemy, they were driven into anger and took vengeance upon those men for the fidelity they owed their lord, striking and severely beating them with the clubs they carried in their hands. In their flight the men threw down the crosses and images that they were carrying, as is the custom of the Greeks; some of these were trampled, others broken.

The emperor was therefore greatly moved to anger, and for this reason the apostolic ruler became more moderate. Finally the same pontiff went to Saint Peter’s and pleaded with the emperor on behalf of those who had committed such acts; he could scarcely obtain his pardon. They thus became intimate with one another. Nevertheless, royal authority remained in Rome and its surrounding regions until the end of the emperor’s life, as was stated above.

When he fell ill and approached his final hour, since he had no son, he wished Charles the Great—also written elsewhere as Carolomannus—to succeed him and take up the imperial scepters. While these events were taking place, the Roman pontiffs continually sent letters through envoys to Charles, king of the Franks, inviting him secretly. And because he was, so to speak, a philosopher in his letters, they asked him to come to blessed Peter and lead his Church from the yoke of servitude back to its own liberty, as though it had been oppressed by someone through force.

After these schemes had unfolded, Louis died. John, who was then in charge, immediately sent a legate from the pope, summoned for this purpose, to Charles. A papal legate, summoned by John, who was then in charge, was immediately sent to the same Charles. Charles made no delay in coming, entered Italy, and sought Rome. Another envoy was then sent to Charles the Great by the emperor’s wife Engelberga, or by her chief men, revealing to him the wishes of the deceased. Since he was farther away, he did not wish to come so quickly that he could prevent the journey of Charles the Bald.

When Charles the Bald came to Rome, he renewed the pact with the Romans, remitting to them the rights and customs of the kingdom, and granting them revenues from the three monasteries mentioned above: the monastery of the Lord Savior, that of blessed Mary Ever-Virgin in the Sabine territory, and that of Saint Andrew near Mount Soracte, as well as from very many other monasteries and fiscal estates. He also granted them the districts of Samnium and Calabria, together with all the cities of Benevento; and, further, to the disgrace of the kingdom, the entire duchy of Spoleto, together with the two cities of Tuscany that the duke himself had customarily held, namely Arezzo and Chiusi, so that the man who had previously governed in the king’s stead might afterward appear subject to the Romans.

He also removed from them the royal legations and the regular attendance or presence at the apostolic election. What more is there to say? He granted them everything they wanted, just as things are given which are neither rightly acquired nor expected to be possessed. After this Charles had fled through fear of the other Charles, who was coming, he fell ill before he could leave the Italian kingdom. Having scarcely departed, he died.

From that day no emperor and no king acquired the honorable customs of royal dignity, because either strength was lacking or knowledge, amid the many disputes of the kingdom and its continual divisions. Hence there were many battles, accusations, and plunderings throughout the kingdom.

# Supplement to the Letters and Diplomas

## Supplement to the Letters and Diplomas of the Roman Pontiffs Who Flourished During the Ninth Century

### I. Leo III

#### I. Privilege of Leo III for the Monastery of Saint-Denis (Year 798)

[Doublet, *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 452.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Fulrad, beloved of God, priest and abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Dionysius, martyr of Christ, and to all his successors forever.

Since you requested that the privilege which our predecessor, Pope Stephen, of good and holy memory, formerly confirmed from the monasteries founded by him should be renewed by the apostolic See, and that we should again renew and confirm it by our authority for you and all your successors in the abbacy, so that they might in every way remain and endure forever under the jurisdiction of the holy See of the Roman Church, namely according to this order: whatever, through the donation of our most excellent son, King Charles, or of other kings, good men, and your relatives, and from your own property and exchanges, you are now seen to possess and rule, or you and your successors may hereafter acquire—whether in monasteries to be built, or in estates, or in slaves established in whatever counties, places, and fields—shall remain forever established and valid.

In the aforesaid monasteries, moreover, no bishop or priest shall have permission to celebrate Mass without the consent of our most eminent son, King Charles, or of you, except by your summons. But since you have your own bishop, and your own tablets and chrism to be consecrated, as well as the other sacred orders, just as is more fully contained in the privilege of the lord Pope Stephen, we grant authority and permission in all matters, and, supporting this declaration by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we proclaim that you and all your successors in the abbacy shall have permission to bring all your causes and necessities, and those of your monastery of the most holy martyr Dionysius and of the other monasteries subject to it, before the apostolic See.

The properties and estates, whether monasteries founded and arranged by you or those which, according to your testament, have been given and confirmed to the monastery of Saint Dionysius, martyr of Christ, and to its monks, shall continue to remain so in the future. By this series of writings we establish and prohibit that anyone, whatever his dignity or rank, from the greatest to the least, who attempts or dares to violate this privilege shall be bound under the ban of anathema by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our authority. The universal Church shall know this, unless he performs penance before God and his saints with worthy satisfaction. Farewell.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the third year at the most sacred see of blessed Peter, and in the twenty-fifth year of our lord Charles, the most excellent king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, by whom Italy was conquered; indiction six.

#### II. Letter of Leo III to Fortunatus, Patriarch of Grado (Year 803)

[In Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol. V, p. 194.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Fortunatus, patriarch of the Church of Grado.

If we consider the office of the priesthood that you have undertaken with inward vigilance, it is more a burden than an honor, since no one is sufficient to care for his own affairs unless he also administers those of others in a wholesome manner. For this reason a man undertakes the care of pastoral government: to assume, through pious foresight, responsibility for others and to place himself watchfully in their guardianship, so that the lurking wolf may find no opportunity to break in upon him or inflict harm upon the sheep.

Thus we who have taken up the care of souls must maintain constant concern, so that we may close every entrance against the crafty ancient enemy of the human race and resist his voracity with all our strength. Otherwise, through our negligence, he might—God forbid—swallow someone in his rabid jaws, and the destruction of one committed to us, whom we neglect to guard with solicitous care and due caution, might justly be charged to our punishment.

Let us therefore demonstrate what we say, and let us hasten to benefit as much as we can those whom divine providence has allowed us to govern, so that when the creditor comes to settle accounts with us, he may find that we have made a profit and may gladden us with his promised reward.

Consider this, therefore, dearest brother, and recognize that you have undertaken the position you obtained not for rest but for labor. Strengthen the hearts of the faithful by exhortation; convert the unbelieving with the utmost effort. In order that you may more easily attain this, let your life commend your preaching. Let it itself be their instruction and their teacher. Let them, taught by your example, sigh for the desire of eternal life while living according to it; let them reach it, despising temporal things and scorning what passes away, and let them pant in desire for those things that endure forever and are enclosed by no end.

Apply your efforts to these matters; persist in them with complete devotion of mind, so that when they have attained these things through your preaching and imitation, you may receive so much greater things from our God, the more diligently you have not ceased to exercise the duty of your office in winning those souls.

Moreover, according to ancient custom, we have given your fraternity the pallium. Remember to use it in the manner in which our predecessors granted it to your predecessors, with the integrity of their privileges preserved. Although in the letter you sent us you ought to have explained the faith of your fraternity with greater precision, nevertheless we rejoice in the Lord because we have learned from your solemn synodal confession that it is correct. We pray almighty God to surround you with his protection and grant you to fulfill by your works the office of the priesthood that you have undertaken.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March, indiction fourteen. Farewell.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Eustachius, first secretary of the holy Apostolic See, while our lord Charles, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor, was reigning in his third year; indiction eleven.

#### III. Letter of Leo III to Bishop Alim of Sabiona and to the Other Bishops of the Province of the Bavarians (Year 8)

[In Hansiz, *Sacred Germany*, vol. II, p. 109.]

Leo, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved Alim, bishop of the Church of Sabiona—now Brixen—to Atto, bishop of the Church of Freising and likewise of the Church of Regensburg, and to Waltricus, bishop of the Church of Passau, and Simbert, bishop of the Church of Neuburg, bishops of the province of the Bavarians.

We received with willing spirit the words of your petition which you sent us. In them it was stated that we should ordain an archbishop in your province of the Bavarians, so that the province itself, through our son, the lord Charles, most excellent king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, might be completely and properly organized in every respect.

It was therefore fitting that we ourselves should organize the province of the Bavarians through ecclesiastical governance, faithfully and spiritually according to canonical judgment and in the sacred order. And because, with God’s favor, we found a gracious man, most learned in the divine Scriptures, most merciful in all things, and approved in spiritual conduct, we ordained him for you, with the consent and will of the aforesaid son of ours, the lord Charles, the most eminent king, as archbishop according to the sanctions of the Fathers—namely Arno, of the Church of Juvavia, which is also called Petrine, and which has been reverently consecrated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

There the body of the holy bishop Rupert rests, together with his venerable companions, namely Chunald and Gisil, whose bodies are honored there by the faithful. He was formerly our co-bishop, but now is our brother and co-bishop, and your archbishop. Since you possess his venerable metropolitan see, we have granted the use of the pallium to Saint Arno, your archbishop, and have instructed him that, according to the canonical constitutions, he should be able to provide canonical assistance to all the Churches named above in the dioceses subject to him, so that at the future judgment before the tribunal of Christ he may freely hear:

“Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

Farewell. In the third year, and in the twenty-fifth year of the lord Charles, the most excellent king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, by whom he began the conquest of Italy; indiction six.

#### IV. Letter of Leo III to All the Faithful (Year 816)

[In Coquelines, *Expanded Collection of Letters and Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 161.]

He declares divine and human vengeance against those who usurp the property and rights of the monastery of Saint Paul in Rome.

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, makes known to all Christians this declaration.

Whoever presumes to remove the gifts or offerings of the most sacred altar of the glorious apostle Paul and of his entire church from the use and benefit of those who serve the Lord here; or whoever, contrary to the statutes of the Fathers and our command, appoints a rector in this place through money or any evil device; or whoever dares, by destroying the inheritance of this place, to sell or purchase it—let him have the curse of almighty God upon his body and his possessions. Let whatever he has presumed to do be nullified; let him be regarded by all as infamous and sacrilegious; let his testimony be accepted in no legal proceeding; and let whatever he possesses be transferred to the public treasury. If he does not repent, let him be condemned to hell by the authority of the princes of heaven. So be it, so be it, so be it.

#### V. Letter of Leo III to Wolferius, Archbishop of Vienne (Year 80)

[In Bosco, *Florilegium of the Royal Library*, p. 477.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wolferius, archbishop of Vienne, and to all the bishops established throughout the province of Vienne.

At the request of the illustrious and triumphant son, Charles, Augustus and most just emperor, we have confirmed the rights of the bishops of Gaul, according to the custom of our predecessors. For this reason you also sent your priest to us, so that we might strengthen your ancient privileges.

Know that we do not wish to depart from their ordinances, and that we wish to preserve unshaken what they granted to your Church. Although the bishop of Tarentaise may appear to be a bishop over certain towns, nevertheless the province of the Graian Alps, subjected to the jurisdiction of the Church of Vienne, shall remain so, just as our predecessors confirmed.

Nor ought the bishop of the aforesaid province to disdain the path of humility in subjection to the greater authority, since it is evident that he excels certain prelates by the grace of his office. We do not doubt that you know how much we have suffered from the impious. Therefore, for the sake of blessed Peter, we ask and admonish you with apostolic reverence that you and your people favor us, so that the wickedness of evil men may not prevail.

Given on the fifteenth day of the month of July, while the most pious Augustus, Charles the Great, emperor crowned by God, was reigning.

#### VI. Diploma of Leo III for the Church of Saint Martin of Tours (Year 803)

[In Mousmier, *On the Status of Saint Martin of Tours*, p. 1367.]

Leo, servant of the servants of God, to all our most beloved brothers, the bishops residing in the regions of Gaul.

Although the usefulness of ecclesiastical teaching is struck by the stormy violence of tempests, nevertheless through the vigorous diligence of pontiffs it receives the desirable remedy of salvation; thus the increase of peace is nourished and the splendor of justice flourishes.

In the sixth year of the most pious emperor Charles, when a holy council of bishops was being held unanimously by command of the great orthodox emperor Charles, among various matters conducive to canonical progress and especially suitable for spiritual profit, it happened that Gulfardus, the devout abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, in which the body of that saint rests honorably buried, entreated in a humble voice that we should grant him a privilege. He declared that the place over which he now presided was being torn apart by the savage bites of wolves, and that it was in danger of being shipwrecked through the storm of violent tempests. He asked that it be protected by the pastoral sword, supported by the staff, and raised up by assistance.

Therefore, having examined the decree of royal munificence, and likewise assenting to the wishes and prayers of the faithful, we confirm by the decree of this holy Apostolic See, in the form of a privilege, that—as the text of the aforesaid command contains, and as we have examined the institutions of our holy apostolic predecessors, namely Gregory and Adeodatus, and the subscriptions appended below of the other bishops established throughout the Gallic province who gave their consent to this matter, and as these same most reverend brothers and prelates provided—we too grant permission to confirm it with a similar judgment, supported by apostolic authority.

Thus the devout abbot and the canons residing there shall suffer no burdens from any bishop under the pretext of investigation. Nor shall any bishop ever have permission to give or sell the altars of their churches, wherever they may be established, in any province, without the advice of the clerics who devoutly serve blessed Martin there.

No public official or administrator of the commonwealth, of either higher or lower rank, shall presume to enter their churches, estates, residences, or territories, in whatever provinces or counties they may be situated, to hear cases; nor shall he distrain their free or enslaved people, take sureties, or exact tolls or shipping dues. The tithes and ninths from all their property shall be rendered in full, without contradiction from any bishops or princes, for the hospitality of their nobles and poor.

Moreover, whatever useful rights their other privileges from apostolic rulers and prelates, and the commands of emperors and kings, preserve for them, the dean, priests, and clergy of that monastery shall continue to possess fully and perpetually, under the aforesaid law, all that has been granted to them by the generosity of kings or by the gifts of other Christian faithful, and whatever shall hereafter be granted, together with all their appurtenances. As we have stated above, no authority shall presume to remove anything from their lordship or possession which the dignity of the merciful kings has determined to bestow as a benefit upon the brothers dwelling in the same monastery of blessed Martin.

The most reverend bishop in whose parish the aforesaid venerable monastery, or its properties and possessions, is situated shall have only the permission to ordain and promote priests and deacons and to prepare chrism. The administration of the venerable place and the examination of the canons’ way of life shall belong to the devout abbot, his dean, and whichever men are most approved in that monastery. This too, the aforesaid prelates having defined by unanimous judgment, we decree. They shall not, under the pretext of canonical discipline, inflict upon them any injuries by prying into or enforcing whatever matters; rather, we establish that they shall have a salutary freedom in all things.

Whoever attempts to violate the ordinance of this constitution, or to overthrow it by any presumption or pretext, or to remove from their authority the tithes that have been subject to it for the lawful years, shall know that he will bear the burden of perpetual condemnation with the transgressors of the holy law, unless he corrects the matter through worthy satisfaction.

Therefore, trusting in the power granted by the Lord to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to bind and loose—since he said, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16)—we, relying on the confidence of this power, close the entrance to heaven with the barrier of anathema against the malice of their greed for anyone who consents to or cooperates in this most necessary benefit being withdrawn, together with the things and honors granted, unless, as we have stated, relying upon divine assistance, he repents through the gift of correction, restores what he has seized, and makes satisfaction for what he has neglected.

We ask all the faithful to observe inviolably the judgment of this definition and apostolic determination. So that it may be believed more certainly and observed without dispute, we have taken care to record it with our own signature and have established that it shall endure forever.

Written by the hand of Boniface, chief archivist of the Roman Church, in the month of April, indiction seven. Farewell.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Leo III, in the sixth year of Charles reigning as the great emperor.

### II. Stephen IV

#### Bull of Stephen IV for the Monastery of Farfa (Year 817)

[In Muratori, *Writers on the Affairs of Italy*, II, II, p. 366.]

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord, Ingoaldus, devout priest and monk, and abbot of the venerable monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God, which is situated at Farfa, in the place called Acutianus, and to his successors forever.

With great concern, the care of watching over all the Churches of God and the holy places presses upon us, lest they suffer any loss through necessity, but rather obtain the revenues of their own benefit. Therefore it is fitting that, with the whole eagerness of our pastoral mind, we should safeguard the fullest stability of these venerable places [Col. 0973D] and diligently bring aid there for their advantage, so that what it is certain that we have bestowed upon their venerable places for the honor of his holy name and for the praise and glory of his divine majesty may be acceptable to our almighty God, and that from his richest mercy we may receive a worthy reward for such a pious work in the heavenly mansions.

Therefore, because you asked us to grant, from our generosity and gift, to your religious community and your monastery confirmation of all the possessions which it now has and will possess forever, we confirm to you and to your successors the estate of Acutianus, where that venerable monastery has been built, with all its boundaries and appurtenances in their entirety; the estate of Calistianus, in which is the church of Saint Laurence; the estate of Pompeianus; the estate of Pinianus; the estate of Cervinaria; the estate of Marianus, in which is the church of Saint Paternianus; the estate of Arturianus; the estate of Ordeolus; the estate of Mutella, where is the church of Saint Angelus, just as it has been possessed by that venerable monastery from the time of Pope Hadrian; the estate of Urbanus, also called Vicus-auro, where is the church of Saint Vitus, with meadows, woods, watermills, and everything belonging to it in its entirety; three unciae from the estate of Adrianus, in which is the church of Saint Valentine; the estate of Medianus; the estate of Casalmontis; one uncia from the estate of Arverrianus; six unciae from the estate of Ternianus; nine unciae from the estate of Antianus, where is the church [Col. 0974D] of Saint Felix; the estate of Agella; the estate of Cicilianus, in which is the church of Saint Donatus; the estate of Paternionus; the estate of Gignianus; four unciae from the estate of Scandilianus; the estate of Cryptula; four unciae of the estate of Marcianellus; the estate of Apicianus, in which is the church of Saint Gordinarius; the estate of Scaplianus; the estate of Testa; the estate of Ceritus; the estate of Alianus; the estate of Turris, where is the church of Saint Laurence; two unciae from the estate of Pendigianus; the estate of Caesarianus; the estate of Ventilianus; the estate of Fornicata, with its crossing-place, or Gualdus, and everything belonging to them in their entirety; nine unciae from the estate of Germanicianus, where is the church of Saint Peter; the estate of Musileus; the estate of Cassianus; six unciae from the estate of Averrianus; the estate of Casula; the estate of Lavanianus; the estate of Marcilianus; the estate of Monatianus; the estate of [Col. 0975A] Fisinianus; the estate of Canianus; the estate of Lurignianus; the estate of Balburianus; three unciae from the estate of Classicella, where is the church of Saint Peter; six unciae from the estate of Fulinianus; six unciae from the estate of Rigianus; six unciae from the estate of Pontianolus; the estate of Perticatula; six unciae from the estate of Aurifex; the estate of Pacilianus; six unciae from the estate of Casianus, in which is the church of Saint Justa; the estate of Mellianus, in which is the church of Saint Eugenia; three unciae from the estate of Fignianus; eight unciae from the estate of Cisternula; seven and a half unciae from the estate of Occianus; the estate of Olivola; the estate of Pontianellus; nine unciae and three scruples from the estate of Ursulus; likewise one uncia from the estate of Bussulus; six unciae from the estate of Macerula; three unciae from the estate of Rufianus, in which is the church of Saint Stephen; four unciae from the estate of Macerula; [Col. 0975B] one uncia from the estate of Cassianus; one and a half unciae from the estate of Rapicianus; two unciae from the estate of Medianus; two and a half unciae from the estate of Marcianus, where is the church of Saint Victorinus; three unciae from the estate of Prata; four unciae from the estate of Argasianus; two unciae from the estate of Catonianus, in which is the church of Saint Sabina; four unciae from the estate of Arsura; two unciae from the estate of Agellarius; two unciae from the estate of Latinianus; two unciae from the estate of Altariolus; three parts of an uncia from the estate of Argasianus; two unciae from the estate of Petinianus; four unciae from the estate of Paptianus; four unciae from the estate of Domitianus, in which is the church of Saint Stephen; three unciae from the estate of Cispinianus; nine unciae from the estate of Cisinianus, in which are the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Silvester; one uncia from the estate of Lacanianus, where is the church of Saint Peter; two unciae [Col. 0975C] from the estate of Begianus; one uncia from the estate of Ciprianus, where is the church of Saint Calistratus; one and a half unciae from the estate of Belgianus; the estate of Catilianus; the estate of Cryptula; the estate of Montanianus; the estate of Retianus, in which is the church of Saint Abundius; three unciae from the estate of Lamnianus; the estate of Turianus, in which is the church of Saint Mary; the estate of Morianula; the estate of Follianus, in which is the church of Saint Sabinus; three unciae from the estate of the Monument of Cupus; the estate of Tervilianus; three unciae from the estate of Praetoriolus; three unciae from the estate of Servilianus, where is the church of Saint Anthimus; two unciae from the estate of Gabinianus; [lacuna] and a half uncia from the estate of Lavarianus, where is the church of Saint Getulius; four unciae from the estate of Leugianellus; the estate of Aurianus, in which is the church of Saint Laurence; three unciae from the estate of Tullianus [Col. 0975D], where is the church of Saint Valentine; three unciae from the estate of Muccianus; the estate of Paternus, in which is the church of Saint Valentine; six unciae from the estate of Vassianus, in which is the church of Saint Victorinus; six unciae from the estate of Cassianus, in which is the church of Saint Cesigius; six unciae from the estate of Oricignanus, in which is the church of Saint Peter; three unciae from the estate of Silignanus, where is the church of Saint Angelus; one uncia from the estate of Granianus; the estate of Nignianus, in which is the church of Saint Helena; the estate of Mallianus, in which is the church of Saint Juvenal; three unciae from the estate of Atianus, where is the church of Saint Peter; six unciae from the estate of Robe; six unciae from the estate of Praetoriolus, where is the church of Saint Sebastian; six unciae from the estate of Usianus, also called Hilianus, in which is the church of Saint Anatolia [Col. 0976A]; six unciae from the estate of Feclinula, where is the church of Saint Victoria; six unciae from the estate of Paternus, where is the church of Saint Victorinus; three unciae from the estate of Sallianus, where is the church of Saint Martin; three unciae from the estate of Curilianus; the estate of Forianus, in which is the church of Saint Ptolemy; three unciae from the estate of Jusianus; half an uncia from the estate of Acilianus.

Also half of the Gualdus called Laurus; half of the portion of Probatus the castald; one and a half unciae from the estate of Paternus; half an uncia from the estate of Valerianus, in which is the church of Saint Martin; six unciae from the estate of Corvianus, where is the church of Saint Pancratius; six modii of land from the estate of Bagianus; one and a half unciae from the estate of Vorrianus; one and a half unciae from the estate of Lavigianus; three unciae from the estate of the Vicar; [Col. 0976B] eight unciae from the estate of Acutianus, in which is the church of Saint Gregory.

The estate of Montianus, in which is the church of Saint Angelus; the estate of Farianus; the estate of Paternus, situated at Varianus and at Tullianus; the entire estate of Jussianus. Nine unciae from the estate of Agellus; the estate of Sensianus, in which is the church of Saint Anthymus; the estate of Privatus; the estate of Albucianus with its appurtenances. The entire Gualdus of Tancies, in the designated places, just as it was first possessed by that monastery.

Two unciae of the estate of Findilianus; six unciae from the estate of Passianus; six unciae from the estate of Antarianus; two unciae from the estate of Casa-Surda; six unciae from the estate of Tervilianus; six unciae from the estate of Casa-Candida; six unciae from the estate of Pollianus; six unciae from the estate of Baianus; six unciae from the estate of Betusianus; [Col. 0976C] four unciae from the estate of Servilianus; seven unciae from the estate of Mussinus; three unciae from the estate of Seriola; six unciae from the estate of Marianus; one small portion from the estate of Servilianus; seven unciae from the estate of Sisianus; one uncia from the estate of Catinianus; half an uncia from the estate of Gaius; eleven unciae from the estate of Turrianus; eleven unciae from the estate of Barianus; one uncia from the estate of Salisianus; from the estate of Bastanus, where is the church of Saint Mary.

The estate of Corbonianus; the estate of Luccianus, where there is a cultivated dwelling, in its entirety. Two unciae from the estate of Arianus; one and a half unciae from the estate of Septinianus. Likewise seven unciae from the estate of Septinianus.

Among these, the farm of Pipinianus, with houses and vineyards, as well as olive groves and tenant farmers; likewise the farm of Scandilianus, measuring eight unciae, and also the small farm called Antiquus. Six unciae from the farm of Antianus, and the olive grove at Proporaria, [Col. 0976D] in exchange for which our holy Church received, in the time of Pope Hadrian, from your aforesaid venerable monastery, by way of exchange, two and a half unciae in the farm of Flavianus.

Likewise the entire farm of Canonus, with houses, vineyards, olive groves, and tenant farmers. Four unciae in the farm of Ortisanus; three unciae in the farm of Argasianus; six unciae in the farm of Caesarianus; one uncia in the farm of Fabricianus; two unciae in the farm of Valerianus; six unciae in the farm of Secundilianus.
