Both farms, however, with houses, vineyards, olive groves, and tenant farmers only, which were given and likewise received from our predecessor, Pope Hadrian.

Now, the aforesaid estates, or the unciae of the aforesaid estates, together with the churches, houses, vineyards, [Col. 0977A] meadows, woods, willow groves, streams, waters, and watermills, as well as the olive groves with vineyards, their appurtenances and tenant farmers, and all households generally belonging to them in their entirety, just as they were confirmed to that same venerable monastery by the authority of the privileges of our predecessors, the Fathers, and of blessed memory, Pope Hadrian, and just as they were first and are now possessed by that venerable monastery, we grant from this present tenth indiction onward to your religious community and to your successors, the abbots of the holy monastery, to hold perpetually.

On this condition, namely, that throughout all the days of your lives, while that venerable monastery continues to exist, every day, when you complete the chant in that same holy monastery, you shall strive to cry out one hundred Kyrie eleison for the remission [Col. 0977B] of our sins.

All these aforesaid estates, or the unciae belonging to them, being part of the body of our Sabine patrimony, belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, you shall hold in such a way that, from you and your successors, the abbots, ten gold solidi shall be paid at each indiction as rent to the ecclesiastical *rationibus* [Note: Perhaps rather *rationalibus* (“accounting officials”) or *actionariis* (“agents”), as below], without any difficulty; and you shall certainly take effective care to protect and improve the aforesaid places impartially. Moreover, let no delay on your part arise in paying the annual rent; rather, let it be paid at the proper time to the actionarii of our holy Church.

We decree by apostolic censure, under threat of anathema and by adjurations of the divine judgment, that no one at any time—whether one of our successor Fathers or any other person, great or small—may wholly remove from those places, estates, and farms which were given by the aforesaid Pope Hadrian and confirmed by us, as is written above, anything belonging to the use and benefit of the holy monastery, or alienate anything from those same venerable places by right. Nor may anyone presume to inflict any violence or loss there. Rather, we confirm through the page of this privilege and by the authority of our lord, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that all these things set forth above shall perpetually remain under the right and control of that monastery, subject to the annual rent payable to our holy Church, as well as the hundred Kyrie eleison to be cried out for our crimes.

This is for the praise of our Redeemer, the Lord, and for the support of the monks who serve there the mercy of his mother, our lady, so that these servants of God, having obtained this benefit, may remember us in their frequent prayers, entreating God with a hundred Kyrie eleison.

All these things confirmed by us we decree to remain forever unaltered. But if anyone—which we do not wish—should become a violator of what has been confirmed by us in pious consideration, let him know that, by the authority of our lord, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the chain of anathema and, with the devil and all his most dreadful pomp, as well as with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, bound in eternal unquenchable fire. But whoever proves himself the guardian and observer of this apostolic institution of ours, granted by us to that venerable monastery, may deserve to receive from our most merciful God, before all the saints, the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Written by the hand of Christopher, scriniarius, in the month of January, in the tenth indiction. Farewell.

[Col. 0978C] Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, by the hand of Theodore, nomenclator of the holy apostolic see, while our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the third year of his reign and the third year of his patriciate, in the tenth indiction.

## III. PASCHAL I

### I. Bull of Paschal I for the Farfa Monastery (Year 817)

[In Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* II, II, p. 317.]

[Col. 0977D]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Ingoald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, situated at Farfa, in the place called Acutianus, and to your successors forever.

With great concern, the care of watching over all the Churches of God and the holy places presses upon us, lest they suffer any loss through necessity, but rather obtain the revenues of their own benefit. Therefore it is fitting that, with the whole eagerness of our pastoral mind, we should safeguard the fullest stability of these venerable places [Col. 0978D] and diligently bring aid there for their advantage, so that what it is certain that we have bestowed upon their venerable places for the love of his holy name and for the praise and glory of his divine majesty may be acceptable to our almighty God, and that from his richest mercy a worthy reward for such a pious work may be conferred upon us in the heavenly mansions.

Therefore, because you asked us to grant, from our generosity and gift, to your religious community confirmation of your monastery and of the possessions which it now has and will possess forever, we confirm to you and to your successors castles and villages, fields and woods, meadows and waters, vineyards and olive groves, and watermills, with all their appurtenances and everything generally belonging to them in their entirety, just as they were first and are now possessed by that venerable monastery, in the counties of Sabina, Narnia, Reate, Furconium, Asculum, Firmum, Aprutium, Pinnum, Balbium, Teate, Rome, and Tuscany, together with all the adjacent lands and appurtenances of those monasteries, in their entirety, to be held both as regards what you now possess by right and what you and your successors may hereafter acquire by the Lord’s generosity, just as they were confirmed to that venerable monastery by the privileges of Pope Hadrian of holy memory.

We also confirm perpetually to you and your successors the offerings and tithes, and the offerings of the dead, to be collected under your authority, to be received from all and prohibited by none.

No bishop, however, shall dare to summon to a synod or excommunicate any monk or cleric of that monastery. We grant them to the aforesaid abbot and his successors to admonish and restrain, and from this present tenth indiction we grant them perpetually to your religious community and to your successors in your monastery to hold.

We decree by apostolic censure, on the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, under divine adjurations and prohibitions of anathema, that no one at any time—whether any of our successor pontiffs or any other person, great or small—may in any way remove or alienate from your power and control, or from that of your successors and your monastery, the aforesaid places, or those acquired thereafter with God’s help and established as above.

But if any person, great or small, should presume by rash audacity to act against this privilege of ours, let that person know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to eternal fire and punishment.

But whoever, moved by pious regard, proves himself the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours, may deserve to obtain the grace, mercy, and eternal life of our most merciful Lord, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0979D] Written by the hand of Christopher, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of February, in the aforesaid tenth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the Kalends of February, by the hand of Theodore, nomenclator of the holy apostolic see, while our lord Louis, most pious perpetual Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the third year of his reign, in the tenth indiction.

### II. Letter of Paschal I to Barnard, Abbot of Ambroniacum (Year 817)

Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, fourth century, part II, p. 562.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in the Lord to the venerable abbot of Ambroniacum.

[Col. 0980A] Since you have laid aside military service and secular dignity, we are greatly astonished that you flee from serving or ruling for God. For he will not appear before the divine presence without guilt who, neglecting the salvation of many, seeks to be useful only to himself.

Accordingly, we admonish your fraternity, and in admonishing you we adjure you not to strive to rebel against the divine ordinance. For, according to the Apostle, no one takes the honor upon himself except the one who is called by God, as Aaron was.

Since, therefore, the Church of Vienne has chosen you, though called, as its shepherd, we command you, in the apostolic capacity which, though unworthy, we hold, to undertake this good work, because before Christ’s tribunal those who will be saved through you will testify concerning your glory. But if you refuse, we judge to be valid and confirmed whatever sentence our son Gregory the notary, whom we have sent from our side, has pronounced concerning your disobedience.

### III. Bull of Paschal I for the Monastery of Saint Vincent at the Volturno (Year 819)

[In Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, I, II, p. 384.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable man Josue, abbot, and to the monastery of Christ’s martyr Vincent, situated at the source of the river Volturnus, in the region of Samnium, in the territory of Beneventum, and through you to that venerable monastery and to all your successors who are regularly to be appointed, forever.

Knowing that by the divine commands we ought diligently to serve in the worship of the sanctuary for the governance of souls—for this is the greatest work of piety—we have resolved and confirmed, for the peace of the monks, to remove the burdens imposed upon them and to restrain the tyranny of laymen, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessors.

Therefore we decree and confirm that the aforesaid monastery of Christ’s martyr Vincent, with all that belongs to it by right—cells and lands, villages, castles, and other revenues—shall be perpetually secured under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, so that it may be subject to the jurisdiction of no other church.

In the first place, the monastery of blessed Peter the apostle, situated beside the river Sabbatus in the territory of Beneventum; the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at the place called Sano, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary at Due Basiliche beside the river Sangro; and another church of Saint Mary at Due Basiliche in the territory of Teate; the church of Saint Mary at Quinquemillia; the church of Saint Mary at Canneto; the church of Saint Mary at Palena; the church of Saint Mary beside the river Trinius; the church of Saint Mary at Musanum; the church of Saint Mary at Arola; the church of Saint Mary at Planisi; and the church of Saint Mary at Casale Plano.

Likewise, the monastery of blessed Peter the apostle at Trite, with all its appurtenances; the cell of Saint Peter at Vipera; the cell of Saint Peter at Vairano; and the cell of Saint Peter at Tontole.

Likewise, the monastery of the Lord Savior at Alife; the cell of Saint John at Lisine; the cell of Saint Focas; the cell of Saint John and Saint Martin at Luceria; the cell of Saint Vincent at Canusium; the cell of Saint Vincent at Trani; the cell of Saint Vincent at Sipontum; the cell of Saint Vincent and Saint Angelus at Telesia; the cell of Saint Vincent at Toccu; the cell of Saint Vincent at Caieta; the cell of Saint Vincent at Cumae; the cell of Saint Vincent at Tremojola; the cell of Saint Vincent at the river Tuscanus; the cell of Saint Vincent at the river Tersa; the cell of Saint Vincent at Pettorianum; and the cell of Saint Vincent and Saint Angelus at Isernia.

Likewise, the monastery of Saint George within the city of Salernum; the monastery of Saint Martin at Monte Marsico; the monastery of Saint Columba at Sera; the cell of Saint Donatus at Canunum and of Saint Julian; the church of Saint Maurus at Anglone and of Saint Valentine; the cell of the Holy Cross at Monte Marsico; the cell of Saint Hilary at Calinola; the cell of Saint Vincent at Suessa; the cell of Saint Agatha at Tercinum; and the church of Saint Gregory at Matese; the cell of Saint Sossius at Liburia, with the illustrious Gualdus.

Concerning all these and the other things belonging to it by right, we command, forbid, and protest that no one presume, on any pretext, to introduce fraud or any encroachment. We also grant to you and to your successors, the abbots, by this present authority, permission from our apostolic see to invite to the aforesaid venerable monastery whatever bishop you may wish, whenever Christians in need require any ecclesiastical ministry; likewise for the consecration of churches and for ordinations of clerics or priests as occasion demands.

You shall obtain chrism and confirmation from whatever bishop is agreeable to you. We also declare that no bishop from that place may summon a subdeacon to his synod unless it is the subdeacon’s own will; nor may he in any way judge or excommunicate the abbot or a monk; nor do we permit any priest of any church to exercise any authority in the aforesaid venerable monastery, except the apostolic see. Thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one shall presume to celebrate solemn Mass there.

We desire and enjoin by apostolic authority upon you and your successors, the abbots who in due time shall be appointed there, that if priests or clerics from any church should come to live in the community of the brothers or to receive the monastic habit, they shall immediately be received.

Moreover, decreeing by apostolic censure, under adjuration of the divine judgment and under the force of the most severe prohibitions of anathema, we declare that no one, whatever authority or dignity he possesses, may ever presume to interfere in that venerable monastery or in its affairs, or in any way remove or alienate its property, possessions, or subject churches, or anything that appears to belong to them; nor may anyone in any way inflict there any harm or loss. For we have decreed that the aforesaid monastery shall remain perpetually, as has been said, firmly secured under the jurisdiction and protection of our holy Church.

We also promulgate, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and his terrible future judgment, through the page of this apostolic privilege and constitution, we decree and establish that the various possessions of the place which have been granted and offered by kings, dukes, castalds, and other Christians, or which may hereafter be granted there, shall belong by firm right to the aforesaid monastery and remain so forever.

Nor, as has been said, may anyone inflict harm upon any of its possessions or upon anything belonging to that monastery, or remove what has been given to it. All these things, as is evident from the apostolic constitutions and privileges established for those venerable places, shall remain unshaken.

The monks shall always be permitted to choose an abbot from their own community. The abbot shall be permitted to judge his monks, and not only the men’s monastery but also the women’s monastery subject to it.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with wicked audacity to oppose or in any way violate what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid venerable monastery, unless he corrects himself through fitting repentance, let him be bound by the chain of anathema and assigned to be burned in eternal fire with the devil, with his most dreadful companions, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, moved by pious regard, proves himself an observer in all things, guarding our apostolic constitution directed toward the worship of God, may obtain the grace of blessing in abundance from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life. Farewell.

Written by the hand of Theodoric, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of July, in the twelfth indiction, in the most sacred basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, in the fourth year of the pontificate of our lord Paschal, first pope.

### IV. Letter of Paschal I to All Christians in the Northern Regions

Commending Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, and Halitgar, sent to propagate the faith of Christ. (Year 822.)

[In Lappenberg, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*, p. 9.]

[Col. 0982D]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the most holy brothers, fellow bishops, priests and the other ecclesiastical orders, most glorious princes, dukes, magnificent counts, and all the Christian faithful of God.

Since it is well established that we must exercise the most religious care and concern for the Lord’s flock, which by divine dispensation we have undertaken to govern and to supply with heavenly nourishment through salutary instruction—especially for those who persist at crossroads and in villages under the cunning persuasion of the prince of darkness, and who, ignorant of the way of life, wander astray and foolishly seek not the things above [Col. 0983A] but those below—we have learned that in the northern regions there are certain peoples who do not yet possess knowledge of God and have not been reborn through the sacred water of baptism. They remain under the shadow of death and, with sluggish minds, serve the creature rather than the Creator.

For this reason, with the agreement of God’s faithful, we have judged it necessary to send to those regions our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Ebo, archbishop of the holy Church of Rheims, for the illumination of the truth. Having instructed him in our fraternal capacity by the authority of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, before the body and confession of that prince of the apostles, we have granted him by public authority full freedom in every respect to evangelize [Col. 0983B], so that he may everywhere provide the word of life and the way of salvation, confirm the rule of faith through heavenly instruction, and strengthen by living speech the teaching of the apostolic institution, driving away every diabolical error.

And if anything doubtful should arise concerning this divine office, let him always have recourse to the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church of God and draw waters from its purest fountain, so that, with divine grace intervening, he may cleanse harmful errors from the hearts of mortals.

Finally, providing him with a colleague for this divine administration and adding the religious minister Halitgar, we have appointed him so that, at a suitable time, he may more easily report to the apostolic see concerning the business entrusted to him, with the Lord’s assistance, and that he may never neglect in any region the ministry committed to him by our authority. We solemnly prescribe that he will undoubtedly have to render an account of this before the strict Judge and receive eternal punishment for an abandoned ministry.

Therefore, exhorting and admonishing you all unanimously, for the love of almighty God and of our Lord Jesus Christ and for veneration of his apostles, we ask that in all the needs of this mission you strive with all your strength to assist them, and that you receive them in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40); and “whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). And again: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 9:41).

Therefore we admonish you more and more to provide, with prudent devotion, generous charity, a pure mind, and sincere intention, whatever is necessary for this journey, and not to refuse to assist them piously and according to your means. Thus, for certain, you may receive from the Lord the reward merited by this work of piety, and in the heavenly register you may be counted among the saints as compensation for such a service.

If anyone, however, should give consent or assistance to this service of God, sent by the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church with pious ecclesiastical purpose for the illumination of the nations, may he, through the intercession of the blessed apostles, the martyrs, and all the saints, deserve to be enrolled according to his merits among the heavenly joys.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should persist as an opposing adversary of this divine worship, or should attempt in any way to hinder it, and should prove a violator toward them or their fellow workers in carrying out this ministry, let him, by divine command and apostolic authority, be punished with the chain of anathema and condemned by the devil’s lot as guilty of perpetual condemnation.

### V. Letter of Paschal I to Stephen, Bishop of Cahors (Year 822)

[ *Gallia Christiana* I, I, Instruments, p. 43.]

The monastery of Figeac, situated in your diocese, which our predecessors wished to keep under their own governance and protection because of a certain excellence of holiness, and which they specially exalted by privileges [Col. 0984B], we now know to have been destroyed and burned by the pagans, with its monks scattered everywhere.

For this reason, sharing in the desolation with grief for that most holy church, which is known to have been dedicated by Christ—as the decretal letters of Pope Stephen II, of glorious memory, shown to us testify—we have taken care, as far as circumstances permit, to promote its restoration.

Accordingly, entrusting this undertaking and labor to our venerable Aymar, we command him, for the absolution of his sins, to restore that place to its former condition and gather monks there. For this reason he was made a monk and blessed as abbot by us: so that he might remove from that church the domination which clerics had arrogated to themselves by rash audacity, and restore the monks there as they had formerly been.

We admonish your blessedness also to take care to assist him in everything, and we command that the treasures, books, and holy relics, as well as all the things which are known to have been carried to the castle of Capdenac because of fear of the pagans, be returned to him without delay.

We also command that the same castle be restored to the monastery, just as it was formerly given at Innanti by King Clovis. We admonish our dearest sons, the soldiers William and Girbert, who are lords of that castle, to be helpers of Abbot Aymar in prayers, and to recognize his right and that of his monastery both in themselves and in the castle, and in the property or honor which they ought to hold from the altar of Figeac [Col. 0984D].

Moreover, we decree that all the honor, monasteries, and churches granted to that monastery by King Pippin or by other kings or good men, as well as those which had first been given to the place at Innanti by the aforesaid Clovis, shall, as the authority of the charters affirms, be possessed in perpetuity by Aymar and his successors.

We therefore grant the monastery called Conques under his governance and that of the abbot of Figeac, as it formerly was, and we admonish him to restore it to its dignity as a priory, since it has been destroyed.

We endow the aforesaid monastery with the same liberty with which it was endowed by our predecessor Stephen, of blessed memory: namely, that it shall be subject to the excommunication of no bishop or other person, except the Roman pontiff alone; that it shall be placed under the dominion of no church except the Roman Church alone; that burial there shall be freer; and that all the other provisions written in the decree of that same predecessor and deposited in that church shall be preserved unshaken.

But if anyone should oppose this grant of ours or of that predecessor, and should trouble Abbot Aymar or the inhabitants of that church, and should refuse to correct himself, he shall suffer the loss of his own rank and remain anathema, like a profane and incorrigible person.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Gregory, deacon and notary of the Sacred Palace of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, the second feria after the octave of Easter, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 822 from the Lord’s incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of our lord Paschal, pope, who is counted as the hundredth among the pontiffs.

[Col. 0985]

## IV. Pope Eugenius II

### I. Fragment of a Privilege of Eugenius II for the Church of Saint Peter of Rouen (Year 827)

[ *Neustria pia*, p. 20.]

[Col. 0985B]

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

Since our most beloved son, [the church] of Saints Dionysius, Medardus, and Germanus, at the request of our dearest [son], the Emperor Louis, brought this before us: namely, that we should confirm by our authority a privilege of this kind for the church of Saint Peter, which had been built by Clothar in the regions of Neustria and where the most holy Audoenus rests bodily: that is, that we should perpetually confirm for possession all the lands and customary dues of the lands granted to this place by the kings who preceded us—Clothar, Theuderic, another Clothar, Dagobert, Clovis, another Theuderic, Charlemagne, and his most pious son, the Emperor Louis [Col. 0985C]—and so forth.

Accordingly, all these things that have been stated above, namely, those granted by our predecessors, we confirm, with the consent of Rainoard, archbishop of that city, and of the emperor, under such an anathema, and so forth. Hilduin died in the year of Christ 842.

## II. [Note: On the various kinds of ordeals]

Many writers have written much about the various kinds of proof. I include the ordeal by cold water here because it is said to have been instituted by Pope Eugenius and is mentioned in very ancient Remigian manuscripts written in the ninth century, from which I have taken the material above. An old collection of canons preserved in the monastery of Saint Marien at Auxerre supports this evidence; in it the procedure of judgment by cold water is recorded under this title:

“This judgment and examination the apostolic lord sent into France, so that the holy altars of the saints might not be violated, but that through this adjuration and judgment by cold water the truth might be revealed.”

The adjuration is then appended in these words:

“I adjure you, man, by the Father, [Col. 0986D] and the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, Louis Augustus, in the capitulary issued at Aachen in the year 828, § 7, chapter 12, decreed that “the examination by cold water, which they have hitherto been conducting, is to be prohibited by our envoys, so that it may no longer take place.” Louis issued this decree after Eugenius’s constitution, namely, in the year following the death of Pope Eugenius II.

This rite of purification was not, however, entirely abolished by Louis’s decree. For Hincmar, bishop of Reims, when asked about the matter by Hildegarius, bishop of Meaux, approved the judgment by cold water with many arguments. An old codex of Utica (Uticensis) shows us that Mass used to be celebrated at the point of the ordeal.

### RITE OF THE ORDEAL BY COLD WATER, INSTITUTED BY POPE EUGENIUS II

[Mabillon, *Veterum Analectorum*.]

When you intend to send men to the ordeal, you must proceed as follows. Take those whom you intend to send into the water, lead them into the church, and in the presence of everyone let the priest sing Mass and have them offer at that Mass. When they have come to Communion, before they communicate, let the priest question them under adjuration, saying:

“I adjure you, men, by the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by your Christianity which you have received, and by the only-begotten Son of God, and by the Holy Trinity, and by the holy Gospel, and by these relics which are in this church, that you do not presume to receive Communion in that manner or approach the altar if you have done this, or consented to it, or know who has done it.”

But if all remain silent and no one discloses this, let the priest approach the altar and give them Communion. Afterwards let him say to those whom he communicates:

“May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ be for you today a test.”

When Mass has been completed, let him prepare blessed water, and let the priest take that water and go to the place where the men will be tested. When they have arrived at that place, let him give each of them some of the blessed water to drink, saying to each:

“May this water be for you a test.”

Afterwards let him adjure the water into which he is putting them. After the adjuration of the water, let him strip them of their clothing and have each of them kiss the holy Gospel and the cross of Christ. Then let him sprinkle each one with blessed water and throw them individually into the water.

You must do all these things while fasting; nor should those who send them into the water eat beforehand. [Col. 0986D]

### Adjuration of the man

[Col. 0987A]

“I adjure you, man N., by the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the judgment of cold water. I adjure you by the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the inseparable Trinity, and by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by all angels and archangels, and by the day of the dreadful judgment, and by the four evangelists Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, and by the twelve apostles, and by the twelve prophets, and by all the saints of God, and by the Principalities and Powers, by the Dominions and Virtues, and by the Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim, and by the three boys Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and by the one hundred and forty-four thousand who suffered for Christ’s name, and by that [Col. 0987B] baptism by which the priest regenerated you: if you knew of this theft, or saw it, or carried it, or received it into your house, or were consenting to it or an accomplice in it, or if you have a hardened or thickened heart, may your heart vanish and may the water not receive you, and may no sorcery prevail against this; rather, may it be revealed.

“For this reason we earnestly beseech you, Lord Jesus Christ: perform such a sign that, if this man is guilty, he may in no way be received by the water. Do this, Lord Jesus Christ, for the praise and glory of the invocation of your name, so that all may know that you are our Lord, who live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.”

### Prayer over the blessed water

[Col. 0987C]

“We humbly beseech you, Lord Jesus Christ, deign to perform immediately such a sign that, if this man is in any respect guilty of what is charged against him, this water may not receive him, but may he himself vanish and in no way now enter it. Do this, Lord Jesus Christ, for the praise and glory, at the invocation of your name, + so that all may know that you are the true God and that there is no other besides you, who live and reign with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.”

This judgment was created by almighty God, and it is true, and it was devised by the apostolic lord Eugenius, so that all bishops, abbots, counts, and all Christians throughout the world might strive to observe it, because it has been tested by many and found to be true. For this reason it was devised and instituted by them, so that no one might be permitted to place his hand upon a holy altar, or swear over relics or the bodies of the saints.

## III. LETTER OF EUGENIUS II IN FAVOR OF THE MONASTERY OF AGAUNUM (827)

[Gallia Christiana, vol. XII, instruments, p. 425.]

Because our Lord entrusted to blessed Peter the feeding of his own sheep, which he acquired with his holy and precious blood, it is plainly evident that all worshipers of God are subject to the protection of him whose patronage we do not doubt protects us everywhere. Therefore it is entirely fitting that all Christians should hasten to the holy mother Church and the apostolic see in such a way that both the devotion of the founder may suitably attain its purpose and assistance may by no means be denied to the pious foundation when privileges are granted.

Accordingly, because Louis, called the Pious, the most excellent king of the Franks, requested of us that the monastery of Agaunum in the kingdom of Burgundy, on the Rhône River, which King Sigismund of blessed memory is known to have built in honor of blessed Maurice and the other martyrs, and in which Aedalongus, bishop of Sion, appears to govern the canonical rule under the title of abbot, should be adorned with the insignia of an apostolic-see privilege, and that, having been constituted under the holy Church over which, by God’s authority, we preside, we should confirm anew, with episcopal honor, the order established by the glorious King Sigismund and by the other kings after his statutes and privileges, so that they may never thereafter be violated in any way;

and that, just as our predecessors had done for the monks of that place, so we should, by the authority of the apostolic see, adorn the canons whom the most glorious king had appointed in that same place after expelling the monks, polluted by an unspeakable and miserable defilement;

and that no superior should be placed over them without their common counsel or election; that nothing should be undertaken from the common goods of the Church contrary to their disposition; and that no violence by an aggressive superior should be used to seize their own property [Col. 0988C], but that everything should be arranged and subjected to their decrees by the authority of the privilege;

and that, when a brother is anticipated by death, his own goods or goods due to him should be distributed, by the disposition of his fellow brothers or relatives, according to the wish of the person still living, lest through worldly perversity the rust of ecclesiastical plunder thereby [lacuna] corrode, or the voice of joy be darkened by any cloud of disturbance: we bind all this under the bond of anathema.

In the regions of Burgundy we also grant to the brothers of the church a certain estate, namely one called Arcus, situated in the territory of Langres, with its churches and tithes, woods, waters, pastures, and all its appurtenances.

Furthermore, accommodating the pious wishes of the king of the Franks, by the authority of this decree we commit to effect what we have been asked on behalf of the congregation of the same monastery, which adheres to God’s commandments and observes the rule of the apostolic see.

Therefore we forbid every priest of whatever church from exercising in the aforesaid monastery, or in the churches situated on its estates and built and endowed from its alms, any episcopal authority belonging to his own see, except the apostolic see. We likewise forbid the one who now holds, or may in the future acquire, the city of Sion from extending any jurisdiction or power there, except through the apostolic see.

Thus, unless invited by the person then presiding over the church or by the brothers, no one may presume to come in order to celebrate the solemn rites performed there, or begin to exercise his domination in that place, or put forward any assemblies, or demand for himself any share of the alms which the faithful have contributed to the holy monastery, or attempt to take away the tithes granted there by the aforementioned Saint Sigismund, since these remain secure under the subjection of the apostolic privilege.

For by the page of this decree we establish and prohibit all bishops of whatever church, and persons distinguished by whatever dignity, under the bond of anathema, from presuming to violate this page of our institution, or the gifts, honors of liberty, and sanctions established by the aforesaid King Louis and by the other kings and granted to the aforesaid monastery under privileges.

[Col. 0989B]

I, Eugenius, by God’s authority, have reread and subscribed this text of the privilege, made by me for the love of God and in honor of the holy martyrs, and I have ordered the bishops of our episcopate to sign below.

I, Crescentius, a sinner, subscribed at the command of the lord pope.

I, Boniface, a sinner, subscribed at the command of the lord pope.

I, Jerome, a sinner, subscribed at the command of the lord pope.

I, Peter, a sinner, subscribed at the command of the lord pope.

## IV. PRIVILEGE OF EUGENIUS II FOR THE MONASTERY OF LAURIACUM

[In Lunig, *Spicilegium Ecclesiasticum*, continuation, vol. I, p. 678.]

When we heard of your most Christian way of life and of the progress of your holy faith and good works, we were filled with the greatest joy and gladness, because, as the Apostle says, through the divine clemency working in you, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5), and because the holy Church of God in our times receives daily increase through your election. The most reverend Yrolfus, archbishop of the holy church of Lauriacum and our most holy brother, but your spiritual father, was the herald of this desirable report; through his holy preaching he has begotten you as adopted sons for God.

Accordingly, when he came to the threshold of the apostles for the sake of prayer, he earnestly commended to us a new church to be shaped by our apostolic blessings, since, with the Lord’s help, he had undertaken to govern it according to Catholic faith in your regions.

In those regions, as is established by reading, his predecessors had once held, under metropolitan right, a diocese divided into seven episcopal parishes, even in the time of the Romans and the Gepids. By this justice and law, the aforesaid archbishop, most worthy of God, is bound by duty: he is the evangelical farmer who must scatter the heavenly seeds of life over that land, formerly Christian and entrusted to the care of his ancient predecessors, but which you now possess, as though by hereditary right, through the hidden judgment of almighty God; and he must nourish from you a renewed harvest for Christ by winning souls.

Recognizing him as a most learned minister of the divine word and, in every respect, necessary to your salvation, we rightly preserve toward that region the apostolic sentence which says: “How will they believe without a preacher, or how will they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10). Therefore, from this holy Roman mother Church we have sent him among you as your ruler, and in the aforementioned regions of Hania, also called Avaria, as well as in Moravia and in the provinces of Pannonia and Moesia, we canonically entrust to him and to his successors our apostolic vicariate, the exercise of the diocese and ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and the usage and authority of his predecessors, namely, the archbishops of the holy church of Lauriacum. We strengthen the decree of this constitution by the subscription of a privilege.

Furthermore, according to ancient custom, we have given his holiness the pallium, granting it to him in the same manner in which our predecessors granted it to their predecessors, with the integrity of their privileges preserved.

Although we would have permitted this to his affection as a matter of duty, at the repeated insistence of your petition on this subject we have added, for his honor, our apostolic vicariate and authority—something never granted to his predecessors—so that you, brothers and fellow bishops, may henceforth know to show him greater reverence; so that you may obey him, as wise sons, in sound doctrine and heavenly instruction for your edification; and so that you, lay leaders and common people, may humbly obey his salutary commands, not as those of a man but as those of God, and remain strong in the Catholic faith which you have obtained through the Lord Jesus Christ.

For the devil, the contriver of every deceit, whose dominion you renounce in baptism, grieves bitterly over the loss and damage of your saving conversion. By sowing the weeds of unbelief through various opportunities, he rages as though committing a great injury and continually strives to make one of you turn his back on the holy profession.

Therefore give a kindly ear to the instructions of the oft-mentioned archbishop, your shepherd appointed by God. He teaches you to beware of Satan’s cunning and to escape his eternal torments, and on the day of judgment he himself will present you to the Lord of the ages as people who are to be rewarded with everlasting glory for your good works.

For the complete hearing and necessary salvation of your instruction, as we have learned, the few bishops who have now been established among you are not sufficient, because many are still held there in the error of paganism, and, owing to the lack of heralds of the divine word, knowledge of Christ has not yet reached them.

Therefore, so that the company of the faithful may increase, let your diligence, for the sake of reward and the remission of your sins, provide assistance and support to the most reverend Archbishop Yrolfus, so that the number of bishops long ago established there may be completed. Properly appointed, they will be able to benefit you and your descendants if, for the restoration of the churches, you contribute from your possessions—possessions which, as the report spreads, you know once to have been their revenues and endowments—thereby securing eternal sufficiency for yourselves, and entrust them to suitable men chosen for this ministry.

Let bishops be ordained especially in those places where opportunity and usefulness recommend it, where the remains of churches and buildings show that episcopal sees formerly existed. Otherwise, we leave it to the judgment and deliberation of that man to determine where bishops are to be appointed, since we have entrusted our vicariate among you for the whole of ecclesiastical government to him.

## V. LETTER OF EUGENIUS II TO *** (Date uncertain)

[In Goldast, *Collection of Imperial Decrees Concerning the Worship of Images*, p. 725.]

…But throughout the whole world I pray and entreat—for I shall use the words of my blessed predecessor, Pope Gregory—my brothers and lords: insofar as I am a sinner, my brothers; insofar as I am righteous, my lords. Insofar as it depends on me, I humbly ask; but insofar as it depends upon so great an authority, I solemnly admonish you: let no one despise me here on my own account. For although I appear wholly unworthy of imitation, nevertheless the power of charity, peace, and unity is great; and in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the place of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, I presume by high authority to invite you to this.

Since Saint Paul says with truthful voice: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one shall see God,” what could be happier than to desire to see God in this world and to enjoy seeing him in the next? What, conversely, could be more wretched than not to deserve to see God either by happily desiring him in this world or by happily enjoying him in the next?

And although there are throughout the world so many testimonies to this assertion and truth that no tongue in the present age can unfold them all, nor can any mortal know when the decline or end of any one person—or, what is greater, of the whole world—will occur, a great necessity presses me, as is known in all things, so that I must render what I owe and dare not postpone it any longer, lest, perhaps, by withholding so great a debt of charity, I should appear guilty on behalf of you all before the sight of the eternal Judge.

For this reason I pray and admonish you: Michael and Theophilus, my first sons of the Church of the most high God, glorious emperors of the Romans, exalted by God on high, together with the whole Catholic and most noble senate and people entrusted to you by God for governance—I ask that you patiently hear what we have judged necessary to admonish, exhort, and explain to you for your salvation, on the authority of blessed Peter, to whom our Lord and God Jesus Christ deigned to entrust the keys of the kingdom of heaven, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Strive to prepare your minds, pleasing to God, not to despise but to obey and preserve these things.

We exhort you to obey us because everything we are going to say to you concerning this matter we are prepared both to arrange and to confirm principally under three headings: reason, authority, and counsel.

First, we will establish the reason; then, insofar as that reason is rational, discerning, honorable, and useful, we will confirm it by authority; and we will beneficially understand that authority according to the truth and rectitude of the Catholic faith. Finally, we will give a counsel pleasing to God concerning what must be observed in these matters for the salvation of the universal Church, and we will confirm that counsel.

Although divine authority rightly surpasses all else, we nevertheless first wish, by reasoning, to satisfy everyone, in order to calm and unite minds tending in different directions, so that they may more easily receive divine authority in accordance with the sound understanding of the Catholic faith, and afterwards embrace our certain counsel more readily and preserve what they have embraced in the future.

[Col. 0991]

## V. GREGORY IV

### I. PRIVILEGE GRANTED BY POPE GREGORY IV TO ABBOT RABANUS (828)

[In Drouke, *Codex Diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 209.]

[Col. 0991D]

GREGORY, pope, servant of the servants of God, to RABANUS, religious abbot of the monastery of the Lord Saviour, and through you to the abbots, your successors in the same venerable monastery, forever.

Since those things that accord with reasonable desires ought always to be granted, it is fitting that the authority of a pious foundation should by no means deny, in granting privileges, what is due to the devotion of the founder. Accordingly, because you have requested of us that the monastery of the Saviour, built by Saint Boniface, archbishop, in the place called Boconia, on the bank of the river Uulda, be adorned with the support of a privilege of the apostolic see, so that, being established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s ordering we serve, it may not be subjected to the jurisdictions of any other church: favouring these pious desires, by this our authority we bring what is requested into effect.

Therefore we prohibit every priest of whatever church, except the apostolic see and the bishop in whose diocese the venerable monastery appears to have been built, from having any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery. We grant that bishop permission only when there is occasion to consecrate an altar. Thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one may in any way presume to celebrate there the solemnity of Masses; so that, indeed, just as it stands subject to the apostolic see by the firmness of this privilege, it may remain securely endowed, and may enjoy in perpetual security, without the objection of any person, both the places and property which it now holds or possesses and whatever divine mercy may in future increase within the right of that monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful.

We also establish by this page of our decree that whoever, whether a person of any church or a person endowed with any dignity, attempts to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the princes of the apostles, shall be anathema; incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the fellowship of the saints. Nevertheless, may the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Farewell in Christ, mindful of your religious profession.

Given on the Kalends of April, in the sixth indiction.

### II. BULL OF GREGORY IV FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT JUSTINA AT PADUA. It confirms all its goods and privileges. (828)

[In Muratori, *Italian Writers*.]

[Col. 0993C] + GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, bishop, to MILO, most reverend abbot of the monastery of Saint Justina, virgin and martyr of Christ, and of Saint Prosdocimus, confessor of Christ, situated outside the city of Padua, in which the bodies of these saints and of very many others rest, and to your successors forever.

Since your humility has justly and reasonably humbly petitioned our apostolic office that, for the love of God and the remedy of our soul, both by the authority of this present privilege of ours and by the authority of our most beloved spiritual son in Christ, Lord Lothair, Augustus and emperor, we should grant and confirm all the property and estates of the aforesaid monastery, whose church Opilius, patrician of the Romans, founded, and whose little body rests there in peace in the courtyard of that church above two columns—he also bestowed many gifts upon that monastery—we therefore by this present privilege confirm and strengthen the monastery itself with all its appurtenances.

These are: those situated both within and outside the city of Padua; four mills on the river Rodolone; the church of Saint Angelus with its estate, tithes, and fourth-parts; the church of Saint Daniel the martyr; the church of Saint Juliana, virgin and martyr of Christ; the church of Saint Matthew the apostle; and the estate called Macerata, entire, with male and female slaves, tithes, and fourth-parts; the estate called Runco with all its appurtenances, tithes, and fourth-parts; the cell of Saint Martin at Monselice with its court; the church of Saint Saviour; the church of Saint Thomas the apostle with all its property; Tribianum and Pernumium; Monte Gutuli; Saccum; Lignarium, with its church built in honour of Saint Blaise, tithes, and fourth-parts; the church dedicated in honour of Saint Michael; and another church likewise built in honour of Saint Michael in the estate called Bruzolo.

Also, the church of Saint Nicholas built in the estate called Flumisello; and in the territory of Vicenza, the castle of Saint Gall with the churches of Saint Blaise and Saint Gall, with the tithes and fourth-parts of that castle; the whole tithe and fourth-part; the estate called Maxone; the whole tithe and fourth-part of the estate called Rovolone; the church of Saint George at Rovolone; and all other property, with male and female slaves and with tithes, wherever these are situated. Likewise, the church built in honour of Saint Justina, virgin and martyr of Christ, in the estate called Corriza.

And in the territory of Bologna, both within and outside the city, and in the wood called Plano: whatever Opilius, patrician of the Romans, alienated to that monastery; whatever he held from the right of the aforesaid monastery under the name of rent; and whatever Flavius Ildebrandus, most excellent king, likewise held from the right of that monastery under the name of rent, or appeared to hold by whatever means in the territory of Bologna. One monastery dedicated in honour of Saint Justina, situated within the city of Bologna, with its plot and with all its cultivated holdings, both in that city and outside it, with cottages, houses, buildings, and all its appurtenances in their entirety.

Likewise the estates Trecenta, Sadrianum, Nuncianum, Pulianum, Silbamunda, Valle de Lambris, Veterana, Fraxenito, Memoriola, the other New Memoriola, Uncianum, Vicoarucias, Carpenetulo, Soldenicus, and Judicosus with their appurtenances; the estate Cassinium; the other Musianus; six ounces in the place Paretes; Saxorias, Mauriano, Casiliello, and Vallefrigida; in the estate Rutilianis, cultivated land and scrubland together, thirty *iugera*; in the hamlet Socioria, ten *iugera* of land; in the estate Veterana, the hamlet called Granariolo; the estate Sitilianum; Centumpaulinis; in the estate Trimano, the deserted Quinquagintula, Praxeletudo, Pissiano [lacuna], Gavinho, Barbiano, Filiolis, Gabiano called Vicocecorum, the estate Columbiano, Granariolo, and Villamagna, with cottages, farmsteads, and all their appurtenances; the estates Quingentula and Sacioso; Julianus or Omicarini, which is above Naves; the hamlet called Laurentiacus; and the hamlet named Numianus—that is, Silisis, between Misianum and Columbianum.

Likewise, in another place the estate Socioso; the other estate Micauri, which is above the bank of Barbiano and Gabiano, between Claudia and Strata; the plot in the village Romanulo; the whole garden estate; the estate Sitiriano; Monticlo; Vindemiolo or Marcio; Arucias, with the hamlet Paulinis; Rotarioro or Saturioro; and the village Fraxenito. All the aforesaid property, with male and female slaves, woods and mills, watercourses, usages and rights, and all appurtenances and dependencies, wherever situated, in their entirety.

We therefore command that no duke, count, or any other person may enter upon the aforesaid property of the said monastery of Saint Justina, whether under the pretext of hospitality or in any manner whatever, nor presume to commit any violence; rather, under the protection of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, both those serving and residing there, together with the property itself, shall remain safe and unharmed, all dispute by any person being removed.

For if anyone is found to be a violator contrary to the authority of this our privilege, let him know that he will fall under the wrath of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all our predecessors, and under the most grievous displeasure of our aforesaid most beloved son, Lord Lothair, Augustus and emperor, and of ourselves; and that he will be condemned under the bond of anathema. Moreover, unless he comes to his senses and turns from evil, let him know that he shall pay a fine of two thousand mancuses of the finest gold, one half to our sacred palace and one half to the aforesaid monastery. But whoever, out of pious regard, proves a guardian and observer in all matters, may he deserve to possess, without end, the grace of blessing and eternal life with all the saints, for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0995C] Written by the hand of Gregory, protoscriniarius of the Lateran patriarchate.

Given at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the first year of the same see and the second of Lord Lothair, in the eighth indiction.

Fare well.

### III. LETTER TO THE BISHOPS AND OTHER FAITHFUL OF GOD ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT GAUL, CONCERNING THE DIGNITY AND PRIVILEGES OF THE MONASTERY OF FLEURY (834)

[Baluz, *Sacred Miscellanies*, vol. III.]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops and other faithful of God established throughout Gaul.

[Col. 0995D] Since, by apostolic succession, we ought to devote care to all the Churches, we desire to provide for the common need in such a way that we may also examine the individual cases of anyone whatsoever without reluctance. Accordingly, when, because of the many concerns of the Church of God, we had gone to the region of Gaul and had come to the most glorious emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0995D] See Thegan, chapter 42], among other matters that most serene Augustus brought to our attention was the following: the venerable abbot of your region, from the monastery called Floriacum in the district of Orléans, had reported that this monastery had been built by a certain devout abbot named Leodebodus for monks, in honor of God and of holy Mary, Mother [of God], and also of blessed [Col. 0996A] Peter, prince of the apostles; and that, by divine revelation, the body of Saint Benedict had been brought there by monks of that place from the province of Capua and reverently buried there, as the very clear history records.

For the strengthening of monastic religion, the emperor Charles, his father, of pious memory, had bestowed many things upon that place by a decree of his authority and had confirmed by testament what had been bestowed by others. Therefore that beloved prince of God requested that a privilege of our authority be granted to the same monastery, as the aforementioned abbot had asked, in order to restrain the greed of certain persons.

Accordingly, with the counsel of all the bishops who are present, we establish that the possessions and property of the same monastery, whether movable or immovable, which have now been given [Col. 0996B] or which in the future shall be given by devout persons, shall be held and possessed perpetually without any disturbance. Henceforth no bishop, duke, count, viscount, vicar, toll-collector, judicial officer, or person of great or small rank shall dare to disturb that monastery or the property belonging to it, to constrain its people without the abbot’s consent, or in any way to seize in advance anything that the fisc might have been able to demand.

We add also that, because the venerable father Benedict, legislator and lord of monks, is the leader of monastic religion, whoever presides over that monastery shall likewise be first among the abbots of Gaul. Nor shall anyone from the priestly order—namely, an archbishop, bishop, or cleric—dare to disturb it, come to that monastery without the abbot’s consent, perform any ordination, [Col. 0996C] or celebrate Masses there, so that at all times the monks may serve God in that monastery in peace and security, free from every annoyance and controversy.

The abbot who is to be appointed there shall be chosen with the consent of the brothers because of the merit of his life and the uprightness of his conduct, and not because of shameful profits or through payment of money. He shall be blessed by whichever bishop he prefers, without any accusation being brought against him. With regard to priests or deacons to be ordained, the provision prescribed in the Rule shall be observed [Note: [Col. 0996D] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 62], so that no bishop may require submission from those whom he has ordained, nor ever delay ordaining those worthy of ecclesiastical office.

Finally, if it should happen that the abbot is accused of criminal offenses, the sentence shall not be determined by the judgment of a single bishop, but the decision of a provincial council shall be awaited. Or, if he should prefer to appeal to the Apostolic See, the matter shall be deferred to the hearing of the Roman pontiff. Whenever necessity presses, he shall be permitted by every means to come to Rome. He shall possess the power of binding and loosing over the men and women of his order.

But if an abbot or monk from that monastery should be promoted to the clerical order, he shall no longer have authority to remain there or to do anything there. Since, moreover, monks from that monastery, when guilt requires it, are deprived of communion and go to various places in that diocese, where they receive communion without any reservation, it is necessary to forbid the priests more strictly [Col. 0997A] to presume to do this in the future, because by it the regular order is dissolved and an occasion of destruction is provided.

If, however, because of the sins of the inhabitants of the land, an anathema should reach them, we have granted the same monastery the privilege that the brothers of that congregation may perform the divine office in every respect free from restriction.

It has also seemed good to us to grant the same permission, namely, that if brothers in certain monasteries are distressed because they cannot live according to the rule, they may, if they wish, go to that leader of monks in the desire to improve their life. They shall be permitted to remain in that monastery for as long as they are content to follow the monastic custom, until the regular order is seen to be restored in their own monasteries. We also permit that, if the conduct of any one of those brothers should become burdensome, he himself should depart at his own loss rather than contaminate the others.

All these provisions, therefore, which the document of this decree and command of ours contains, we decree shall be observed perpetually both by the same abbot and by all who shall succeed him in the office and place that he now holds, as well as by anyone whose interest may be involved. If any king, priest, judge, or secular person, recognizing this document of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he will stand guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity he has committed. Unless he restores what he has wrongly taken away or mourns his unlawful actions with worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of the Lord God, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, under the prohibition of anathema, [Col. 0997C] and let him be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, [Col. 0998A] so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Theodore, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in indiction 7 [12].

## IV. LETTER OF GREGORY IV TO OTGAR, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ (834)

[In Mabillon, *Veterum Analectorum*, p. 570.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Otgar, archbishop.

That you love us with such affection and goodwill is due more to your holiness than to our merits, [Col. 0998B] although we have recognized this especially through the gifts you sent, for which we give you our greatest thanks, since you take care to offer everything fitting to the prelate of the Apostolic See. With God’s will, we strive to repay this to your holiness.

Regarding the holy body which your prudent devotion humbly asked us to send, we had none to dispatch, since our predecessors had brought all the bodies of the saints together with them, and we had placed each one with the greatest reverence in newly dedicated churches. Therefore we ask your goodwill to grant us time to search more diligently, so that we may be able to find a holy body with which to fulfill your request. If one is found, let your diligence trust us: we shall immediately accomplish what you have asked. For the present, however, we have not sent it because, although we searched, we were entirely unable to find one.

[Col. 0997]

## VI. SERGIUS II

### I. LETTER OF SERGIUS II TO ANSCHAR, BISHOP OF HAMBURG (846)

[In Lappenberg, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*.]

[Col. 0997D]

Sergius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anskar, archbishop of the holy Church of Hamburg, grace from God forever.

Since it belongs to the dignity of the Apostolic See not only to found churches but also to raise up those founded by other spiritual architects of the churches, we have judged it fitting, dearest brother, duly to incline the ears of our benevolence to the devout wish of your petition. We therefore grant you, as it was granted by our predecessor, blessed Gregory, that the peoples of the Wimodians, Norblingians, Danes, Norwegians, Swedes, [Col. 0998D] and whatever northern nations you bring under the yoke of faith through your preaching, you may possess under spiritual authority as belonging to the see of Hamburg, and may leave them to all your successors to possess perpetually by that same see.

We also decree that you and all your successors shall have the use of the pallium at the feasts and times designated for you by our predecessor: namely, at Easter, Pentecost, the Nativity of the Lord, the Assumption, the Nativity, and the Purification of Saint Mary; on the feast days of the apostles and on Sundays; and on all the principal feasts celebrated in your diocese. You may also adorn your head with the mitre and carry a cross before you.

Go, therefore, most blessed brother, and carry out the good work that you have begun. Do not cease until you have advanced it. Found churches in suitable places, consecrate priests, and establish bishops within defined boundaries, of all of whom you shall be archbishop. All the bishops who will henceforth be appointed for the aforementioned peoples, together with the congregations subject to them, shall remain subject to you and to all your successors at the see of Hamburg in perpetual submission and obedience.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm to you, to the holy Church of Hamburg, and to all your successors whatever has already been given to your Church by Christians or shall henceforth be assigned to it in parishes, estates, and all movable or immovable property, including slaves of both sexes, so that the said church may possess these things forever with inviolable authority.

But if anyone should attempt to act against the privilege of this authority of ours, and in any way try to break it in whole or in part, whatever his power or dignity, let him perish through eternal excommunication with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, unless he repents and makes satisfaction to the Church of Hamburg.

But let the observer of this admonition and command have the blessing of almighty God, of the blessed apostles, and of us, who exercise their vicarious office. May the Holy Trinity deign to preserve your brotherhood unharmed at all times and, after the bitterness of this age, lead you to everlasting blessedness.

Given by the hand of Leo, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in indiction nine.

[Col. 0999]

## VII. LEO IV

### I. LETTER OF LEO IV TO ANSCAR, ARCHBISHOP OF HAMBURG (849)

[In Lappenberg, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*.]

[Col. 0999B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most blessed Anskar, archbishop of the holy Church of Hamburg, the blessedness of eternal life, etc., up to “make satisfaction to the Church of Hamburg”; as above in the bull of Pope Sergius II concerning the same matter.

Given by the hand of Stephen, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in indiction twelve.

### II. PRIVILEGE OF POPE LEO IV FOR THE MONASTERY OF THE SAVIOR AT FULDA (850)

[Drouke, *Codex Diplomaticus Fuldensis*.]

[Col. 0999C]

In the name of the Lord, Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hatto, devout abbot of the venerable monastery of our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior and Redeemer of all, and to all the succeeding abbots of that monastery, perpetual salvation and apostolic blessing.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires ought always to be granted, the authority of pious construction should in no way be denied to the devotion of a founder when privileges are being granted. Therefore, since you asked us that the monastery of the Savior, constructed by Saint Boniface [Col. 0999D] the archbishop, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river Fulda, in which that most glorious martyr of Christ, Boniface, physically rests, should be adorned with the supports of a privilege of the Apostolic See, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authorization we serve, it might be subject to the jurisdiction of no other church, for this reason, favoring your devout desires, we bring into effect by this authority of ours what you have requested.

And therefore we prohibit every priest of any church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery of the church of Fulda, except the Apostolic See and the bishop in whose diocese that venerable monastery appears to have been constructed; to the latter we grant permission only when the occasion arises for consecrating an altar. Thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one shall presume at all to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there, so that, in accordance with the fact that it stands firmly subject to the Apostolic See, it may remain undisturbed [Col. 1000C] in its endowments, places, and properties—both those which it now holds or possesses and those which divine piety may in future wish to increase within the legal ownership of the monastery through the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful—and may enjoy perpetual security without contradiction from anyone.

Therefore we command, under the testimony of Christ and his Church, and confirm by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, that no one presume to take away or receive as a benefice any of the property and revenues, or of the households, belonging to the support of the brothers, to the hospital of the poor, or to the guesthouse. Rather, just as the most blessed martyr of Christ Boniface, who happily rests in that monastery, established, let everything be regularly ordered.

May these things also, by God’s favor, remain undisturbed, [Col. 1000D] both those which that monastery received in ownership in his time and those which it has received in our time or shall receive in the future from the tithes and offerings of the faithful.

We also establish by this document of our decree that whoever, whether a prelate of any church or a person endowed with any dignity, should attempt to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be anathema. Incurring the wrath of almighty God, let him be excluded from the assembly of all the saints; nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of Benedict, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of May, ten days before the Kalends of June, in indiction thirteen.

### III. LETTER OF LEO IV TO THE AUGUSTI LOTHAR AND LOUIS (850)

[In Ivo, *Decretum*, Part I, distinction 63, chapter 16.]

[Col. 1001B] The pope asks the Augusti to deign to grant the Church of Rieti to a certain elected man. Chapter 16.

The Church of Rieti, which has remained deprived of pastoral care for so long, ought to be raised up by the arm of your greatness and protected under the shelter of governance. Therefore, after conveying our greeting, we beseech your gentleness to deign to grant that same church to the humble deacon Colonus to govern, so that, once your permission has been received, we may, with God’s help, consecrate him there as bishop. But if you do not wish a bishop to be placed over the aforesaid Church, may your serenity deign to grant him the Church of Tusculum, which is now without a bishop, so that, consecrated by us in our episcopal office, he may give thanks to almighty God and to your empire.

### IV. LETTER OF LEO IV TO RITA, COUNTESS (850)

By royal command, Colonus is ordained bishop of the Church of Rieti by the Apostolic See.

[In Ivo, as above, chapter 17.]

[Col. 1002B]

The lord emperor and empress told us through their letters that we ought to make Colonus bishop of the Church of Rieti, which had apparently long been deprived of the office of a pastor, just as we did.

[Col. 1001]

## VIII. POPE BENEDICT III

### I. CONFIRMATION OF THE PRIVILEGES OF CORBIE (855)

[In d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, from the chartularies of Corbie.]

[Col. 1001C]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Gaul.

Since it is clear that the pontiff of the Roman See is the head and prince of all the Churches of Christ, acting as the representative of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom Christ entrusted the primacy of the whole Church, saying, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18), no hesitation is left to any of the faithful that we ought to extend our care to all the Churches and provide for the salvation, peace, and tranquility of all who believe in Christ, so that what is wrong may be corrected, what is established may be strengthened, what is corrupted may be restored, and what is whole may be preserved.

Although we must guard this care for the body of the universal Church, spread throughout the breadth of the whole world, nevertheless, after the Roman and Italian Churches, it is especially appropriate for us to maintain it toward the Churches of Gaul, as it is evident that our predecessors did. The present condition of the commonwealth itself testifies that this ought now to be done all the more suitably, since the scepter of one empire does not divide the two provinces, and the dignity of the Roman Church, together with earthly sovereignty, governs the realm of both provinces by common [Col. 1002C] right. Thus the rulers of earthly affairs fortify their decrees with the sanctions of the Roman Church, and ecclesiastical rights are supported by the statutes of the rulers. The governors of the earthly commonwealth judge that they rule happily when apostolic authority is joined to their sanctions; and when they receive and venerate that authority in us, they rejoice that they are receiving him who says to his disciples, “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40). Conversely, concerning those who despise them, he says, “Whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16).

Accordingly, since, as has been said, the administration of the universal Church has been entrusted to apostolic care, and since it is fitting that we keep perpetual watch in our concern for the condition of all the faithful, we must nevertheless exercise the greatest diligence in caring for those Churches whose special supervision reason teaches us to undertake by virtue of the office we have received. Thus not only must those things which have remained unimpaired in their established condition be preserved, but those which have fallen must also be restored to the dignity of their former state.

Therefore let the reverend brotherhood of all the bishops dwelling throughout Gaul know that the venerable man Odo, abbot of the monastery of Corbie in the province of Gaul, constructed in the district of Amiens above the river Somme, approached us through the venerable abbot Amrelmus, asking that we grant the monastery of Corbie a privilege of our authority concerning the status of its own election and the free possession and administration of its property.

He also showed us privileges issued by bishops: one by the bishop of Amiens [Note: [Col. 1003D] “Of Amiens”: namely, Bertefridus. You will find that privilege in volume I of the Gallican Councils edited by Sirmond, p. 502, [Col. 1004D] and the other in volume III of the same Councils, p. 60], made and confirmed in ancient times by that bishop and his fellow bishops, since the place belongs to his diocese; and another, written a few years ago by Hincmar, archbishop of the Church of Reims, and by the universal council of the bishops of Gaul, and strengthened by their own subscriptions. They requested that, wherever these documents should reach, whether to bishops or abbots, those receiving them should not hesitate to subscribe.

In these privileges it was decreed that the monastery of Corbie should possess free dominion over its property and should always have the power to elect an abbot for itself from among its own members; but that those who contradicted or resisted this sanction should be condemned by perpetual anathema.

In addition to this came the mandate and petition of the magnificent emperors Lothar, Louis, and Charles, who likewise requested that the privileges of the bishops be confirmed by our authority.

Since we saw that this petition was religious and that what holy pontiffs had piously established for the tranquility of the servants of God was not to be neglected by apostolic care; since the magnificent princes were devoutly asking for it and the abbot of that congregation was necessarily requesting it, we judged it appropriate to grant what we had been asked to grant and what our pastoral care ought of its own accord to provide.

We also learned, from the report of the venerable abbot Amrelmus, that the monastery of which we speak had been nobly built by the most excellent Frankish queen Balthild [Col. 1003C] [Note: [Col. 1004D] “Built”: see volume I of the Gallican Councils, p. 500], and that from the beginning of its foundation it had always flourished both through the nobility of holy men and the observance of monastic religion, and also through the special favor and protective patronage of the Frankish rulers.

For this reason it came about that everyone granted it both immunities for its property and the privilege of electing an abbot, decreeing that this grant should remain in force forever, and placing the documents of their transfers in the monastery’s archives to be preserved for the memory of future generations.

Having learned all this, we judged it wrong not to follow the devotion of religious rulers and the examples of holy prelates by granting the monastery of Corbie the authority of our own grant. Otherwise, although we ought to be found first in the ordering of ecclesiastical affairs because of the primacy of the Apostolic See, we might ourselves be found later; and although, by the Lord’s words, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14), we are commanded by our example to provide the light of authority to others for securing the tranquility of the servants of God, through the tepidity of negligence we would fail to offer others the radiance of good works.

Therefore let the whole Church of Gaul and the entire assembly of bishops presiding over that Church know that we confirm by this present decree of our authority the privileges of the holy prelates, whether those enacted for the monastery of Corbie in ancient days or in our own time. The monastery is constructed in the district of Amiens above the Somme in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr.

This means that the monastery’s property, and whatever the faithful have offered to God and to the congregation of brothers serving Christ there, shall remain under the administration of the abbot and the brothers. Neither the bishop of Amiens, to whose diocese that monastery belongs, nor any bishop in whose parishes the monastery is known to possess property or basilicas, shall presume to take anything from it. Nor shall any bishop, steward, archpriest, archdeacon, or any of his ministers or officials do so in the fields, villages, estates, or cells, or in any of the things belonging to their jurisdiction and dominion; they shall not hold banquets, claim anything for themselves by right of power, or demand anything that may be demanded.

Let all bishops whose parishes are known to contain property belonging to the monastery of Corbie know that they are bound by this condition. Let no one claim that what we decree is new or unprecedented, since it is clear that this was long ago granted to this monastery, and we see that it remains granted today to many others—not only to monasteries of monks but also to those of canons—not merely in Gaul or Italy but throughout the entire world. Each Church ought to remain content with its own privileges, and no Church should be invaded or usurped by another in matters that are evidently the right of the other.
