Since it is clear that the Churches of Gaul are exceedingly enriched by the offerings of the faithful, so that scarcely any bishop exists whose Church’s revenues are not fully and more than sufficiently adequate, let them not presume, under the pretext of necessity, to divert to their own expenses what has been contributed for the use of the servants of Christ.

For the sharing of clerics who abound in their own revenues is prohibited with what is contributed to the Church, lest, while those who are well supplied from their own resources receive it, the poverty of those who possess nothing should not be relieved. With what conscience, then, would a bishop whose own Church supplies his expenses sufficiently presume to touch what has been contributed for the use of God’s servants? Does he not fear what the Lord reproaches the priests through the prophet, saying: “The plunder of the poor is in your houses” (Isaiah 3:14)?

Who does not know that those are Christ’s poor who, scorning the wealth of the world and following the footsteps of our Savior—who, although he was rich, became poor for our sake—regard the title of holy perfection as their riches?

Therefore, whoever presumes to take any of what has been contributed for their needs and applies it to his own advantage gathers into his house the plunder of the poor from their substance. Everything offered or assigned to churches is known to be destined for the needs of the poor, orphans, and widows. Therefore, whoever demands any of it for his own use holds in his house a store of the poor’s plunder. The Apostle also says: “The greedy shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10).

Accordingly, from everything belonging to the monastery of Corbie, whether offered to it or possessed by any lawful right—money, fields, estates, houses, cells, or churches—neither the bishop nor any of his ministers shall presume to take anything for himself, lest, acting against our authority and that of our predecessors, and despising the decrees established by kings for the tranquility of the servants of Christ, he make himself liable to the judgment of the holy council and to perpetual condemnation.

And since monks ought to have peaceful tranquility and the leisure of security, so that, devoting themselves to God, they may observe the rule of their profession, neither the bishop nor his archdeacon shall approach the aforesaid monastery or presume to disturb the peace of God’s servants, unless perhaps the abbot or the brothers should wish to summon him for some useful purpose.

Otherwise, he shall possess no power over the abbot or any of the brothers, nor shall he be permitted to do anything to them through episcopal arrogance. Rather, the abbot shall have free authority over his monastery according to the Rule of Saint Benedict (chapter 65), and the monks shall look only to his governance, as to that of their shepherd. Nor shall episcopal ministry exercise any jurisdiction over them.

Since the abbot is believed to exercise Christ’s office in the monastery, he is recognized as holding the shepherd’s office over the sheep entrusted to him. In order that he may worthily carry out the ministry of his administration, he ought not to be disturbed by the authority of anyone to whom he is subject; instead, freed from every episcopal domination, he should recognize Christ alone as his judge, to whom he will render an account of the sheep entrusted to him.

Therefore we establish in every way that the bishop’s arrival and presence must not disturb the tranquility of the monastery, that he must not presume to do anything there by episcopal authority, and that he must not inflict any annoyance or disturbance upon the brothers or the abbot. If he should presume to violate this, let him know that he is exercising not the office of a shepherd but the tyranny of one who overturns and disturbs the Lord’s flock. Consequently, he is not to be received as a shepherd but removed from Christ’s sheepfold like a wolf, and, struck by the sword of anathema, let him suffer the punishments of his condemnation.

But, if requested by the abbot in Christ’s name, he shall consecrate and bless the altars or basilicas in the monastery. He shall also provide chrism, or oil of sanctification, each year. If the abbot should ask him to consecrate one of the monks or one of his canons to an ecclesiastical rank, he shall in no way refuse, unless the person requested should be shown by reliable testimony to be unworthy of such an honor. For just as it is not right to bestow the sacrament of divine blessing upon an unworthy person either for gifts or out of favor, so it ought to be freely bestowed upon the worthy, as the Savior says: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:8).

We decree that the brothers of that monastery shall have the privilege of election: namely, that they shall have the power, in accordance with the authority of the Rule, to elect from among themselves anyone who is a professed monk and yet worthy of pastoral leadership, whoever they may wish to choose.

And, moreover, we admonish and beseech our glorious sons, the Augusti Lothar, Louis, and Charles [Note: [Col. 1005D] “Charles Augustus”: the expression has been placed in the wrong position; it should read “Lothar Augustus, Louis, Charles,” as in volume III], that just as their father and grandfather, and the Frankish kings before them, granted that same monastery the right to elect an abbot from among its own members, and they themselves established this by their decrees, so they too may deign, for the love of Christ, to preserve it during their reigns and establish by laws of perpetual validity that it be preserved forever.

Thus, by granting the servants of Christ freedom of election and striving to preserve what has been granted, may they deserve to receive from the Lord both the kingdom of the present life and the glory of eternal blessedness. Whatever has been offered to that monastery, to God and to his servants, either by royal gift or by the devotion of the faithful, let them neither take away themselves nor permit others to take away.

For it is plainly just and religious that those who have deserved to receive from the Lord the honor of kingship should preserve for God what has been bestowed upon him by the devout faith of believers; and that those who have been raised above others by royal magnificence should not take away from Christ’s servants the freedom to choose their own shepherd.

For who does not know that what has been bestowed upon God through the hands of the faithful is entrusted to the divinity for possession, transferred from human right into divine right, and cannot be registered under human dominion, since it is clear that it has once been surrendered into the possession of the divinity?

Therefore, whoever attempts to add such things to the dominion of his own right is certainly an invader of the right of another—that is, of God. For if anyone tries by force to usurp the possession of another human being, he becomes liable under public law and, as a robber and invader of another’s inheritance, is subject to punishment by legal judgment. Much more, then, whoever transfers things consecrated to God into his own possession is held guilty not only under human but also under divine law, and, condemned not merely for the crime of robbery or invasion but also branded with sacrilege, will be punished by heavenly judgment.

[Col. 1006D] Therefore let the magnificent princes consider how great a crime they bind themselves to before the sight of the divine majesty when they do not fear to invade things entrusted to God and convert them from ecclesiastical uses to their own advantage.

If they unjustly invade and violently take away the possessions even of private persons, although freeborn, they are called and regarded not as kings—that is, just and moderate men—but as tyrants, that is, cruel and unjust men. By what name and with what honor, then, should those be judged who unjustly invade and violently take away the divine inheritance, namely, the possession of the Church of Christ?

Therefore, considering these things, let our most religious sons, the princes, guard the property of the monastery of Corbie inviolate and undefiled, as belonging to the sacred divinity. Let them neither take it away themselves nor permit it to be taken away by others, so that before the sight of the heavenly King they may rightly be judged kings in reality, as they are called in name; and so that, while they preserve for God what belongs to him, God may preserve for them both the sovereignty of their earthly kingdom and grant them the crown of eternal blessedness.

Accordingly, we admonish and exhort them to preserve undisturbed both their own grants and those of the earlier princes, never violating the decrees of the bishops or of us, and to maintain for the said monastery the privilege of election in their own times and in those to come, establishing by perpetual sanction that it be preserved.

For we are taught by the voice of Truth that if anyone enters the sheepfold of Christ not through the door but climbs in by another way, he is a thief and a robber; and such a person seeks not the salvation of the Lord’s flock but his own profits—not in order to save but in order to destroy.

No prudent person doubts that the holy community of monks is Christ’s sheepfold. Someone enters this sheepfold through the door when, according to the order of election and the constitution of the Rule, he obtains pastoral ministry. But whoever, supported by the power of royal domination and not by the grace of election, seizes primacy over the Lord’s flock is known to be not a shepherd—that is, Christ’s vicar—but a thief and a robber. He is found to enter not to guard the Lord’s flock but to destroy and scatter it.

Therefore, whoever grants him this domination of power will be judged guilty on the day of judgment for the death of so many souls, to the extent that he was the cause of their destruction through examples of wickedness.

For this reason, most glorious princes, grant this monastery the prerogative of election. Do not, by royal power, appoint over it any person—whether lay or canonical, which is contrary to the whole ecclesiastical order—or even a monk from another monastery, or one not elected according to the Rule, lest the house of God, which ought to be a house of prayer, be made by you a den of thieves. For you are not unaware that such prelates, and the authors of such prelacy, are to be driven out by divine judgment from the house of eternity and carried away to the punishments of perpetual vengeance. What sentence of condemnation, then, is to be exercised by us against such men except that which the Holy Spirit uttered through the prophetic mouth, saying:

> “All their princes who said: ‘Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’ My God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind; like a fire that burns the forest, and like a flame burning up the mountains, so pursue them in your tempest, and in your wrath trouble them” (Psalm 82:11).

For who are those said to possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance, except those who seek to obtain, through the domination of secular power and not through the grace of election, the things dedicated to God and bestowed for the uses of the poor and of his servants? Their princes, moreover, are those who, by lending support to their desires or handing over ecclesiastical property to them, give their consent. With what vengeance, divinely inflicted, both parties are struck is contained in the sentence stated above. It shows that they will be cast out from the stability of the heavenly homeland; that, fallen from temporal nobility, they will be whirled about like a turning wheel; and that, after the end of the present life, they will be snatched away by the tumult of divine punishment, like stubble exceedingly light in its dry vanity. Their fruitlessness and pride will be burned up like the barrenness of a forest and the swollen arrogance of the earth rising up against God, consumed by fire and flame.

Therefore, so that they may not undergo this severity of divine vengeance, let the most Christian princes strive to preserve the rights of election for the churches of Christ, and let them not take away from the monastery of Corbie what is owed to the universal Church. If, out of honor for God, they grant it the right of election and preserve the monastery’s possessions undefiled, so that they do not serve the ambitions of violent men, they themselves will obtain a share in the heavenly kingdom with Christ.

Nor should they ever permit it to fall into the hands of secular persons or under canonical domination; this would mean the utter destruction of its inhabitants and the utter condemnation of both giver and receiver. For what else is it than to establish the abomination of desolation in the temple of God to place a secular person before the Church of God in the role of pastor? Whoever does this is found to resemble Pilate, who set up Caesar’s images in the Lord’s temple to be venerated.

And when the Apostle speaks to the faithful, saying, “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind” [Col. 1008C] (Romans 12:2), whoever places a secular person over monks drives them, insofar as it lies within him [Note: [Col. 1007D] The printed reading is *quantum in saeculo* (“insofar as in the age”); read *quantum in se est*, “insofar as it lies within him.”], from the form of the spirit toward the form of the age, and from the image of Christ toward the image of the earthly king, since everyone under an elevated superior ought to imitate him by following his image.

Therefore let no one think himself involved in a minor crime who places such men over the Church, in whose character the servants of Christ will always contemplate and learn not the humility of Christ but the pride of the world, not desire for the heavenly homeland but the lust of this age.

Because you see this, most excellent princes, to be utterly wicked, always drive this impious sacrilege away from the monastery of Corbie. Nor should you ever place over it a person of canonical rank, or permit such a person to be placed there. Remember that Nadab and Abihu, because they offered strange fire to the Lord as incense, were consumed by divine fire. Indeed, whoever advances someone serving under a canonical profession over monastic religion so that he may take the place of a pastor offers strange fire to the Lord as incense.

Since such men are struck by vengeance, their destruction signifies what their imitators deserve: consumed immediately by the punishment of the present life, they marked out for later generations, by the example of their own condemnation, what fate awaits those who imitate them.

All those also—even if they profess the monastic life—who are not established by regular election as superiors of the same monastery of which we speak, and who are known to have been admitted in such a manner, that is, either through money, [Col. 1009A] favor, or service, are condemned by us, by the authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, together with Simon, whose imitators they are, by anathema.

And so that religious princes may remain free from this sentence of condemnation, let them strive in every way always to preserve inviolate around the aforesaid monastery the privilege of election. For, in accordance with the promulgation defined long ago by the holy Fathers, we anathematize the person who assumes the prelacy of the Church of Corbie—not through the legitimate election of the monks serving Christ in that same monastery, but contrary to regular and canonical authority—as well as the person who gives and the person who receives it, excluding them from the kingdom of Christ and from the fellowship of the saints. Nor will those be able to share in the heavenly Jerusalem who attempt to divide her while she journeys on earth.

All who do not hesitate to set over her not pastors but thieves, not vicars of Christ but followers of Antichrist, are certainly doing this, so that the house of God may exist not as a house of prayer but as a den of thieves, and so that not the form of Christ but the abomination of desolation may stand out within it.

But if the rulers of the state, contemptuous of the divine commandments and of the bishops, and also disregarding our authority, which has issued a decree on this matter, place over that congregation not the man whom regular election has chosen but whoever their domination desires, let the monks of that place beseech the bishop to whose diocese the monastery belongs to report the matter, either by himself or together with them, to the archbishop of Rheims [Col. 1009C]. Let them also approach the prince together and warn him of the danger arising from his transgression.

But if the bishop of that diocese, whether through fear or favor toward the prince, through imprudence, or through negligence of pastoral care, is unwilling or refuses to offer assistance, let the brothers themselves approach the aforesaid archbishop and the neighboring bishops, disclose to them the cause of their distress, and beg them to bring them aid.

Let the archbishop, either alone or together with the other bishops of his diocese, approach the king and warn him about the violated election. Let them not cease urging him with words and entreating him with prayers to correct the matter. But if he refuses to listen to them and is unwilling to correct the fault of his sin, let him receive the sentence of apostolic excommunication and be condemned by it.

If, however, the bishop whose parish it is, or the archbishop, or the other suffragan bishops are negligent in this matter, or disregard it, or consider it of no account, they know that they are liable to the condemnation of that sentence. For the prophet says: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:20). Therefore let them know that they will be bound by the same anathema if they neglect to exercise pastoral concern for the Lord’s flock.

Written by the hand of Theodoric, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the fourth indiction. Farewell.

## II. PRIVILEGE OF POPE BENEDICT III FOR THE MONASTERY OF THE SAVIOR AT FULDA (Year 857)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*]

[Col. 1010A]

Benedict, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theoto, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through you to your successors, the abbots of that same venerable monastery, forever. Amen.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires should always be granted, the authority of pious construction ought not to be denied to the devotion of the founder when privileges are being granted. Therefore, because you asked us that the monastery of the Savior, constructed by Saint Boniface, archbishop, in the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Uoldaha, should be adorned with the supports of an apostolic-see privilege, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church, we, favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours commit to effect what has been requested.

And therefore we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see and the bishop in whose diocese that venerable monastery appears to have been constructed. To that bishop we grant permission only when the opportunity arises to consecrate an altar. No one, unless invited by the monastery’s abbot, is in any way to presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there.

Thus, in accordance with what has been established as subject to the apostolic see by the firmness of this privilege, it shall remain securely endowed in its places and possessions, both those which it presently holds or possesses and those which divine goodness may in future increase in the right of that monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful. It shall enjoy perpetual security without contradiction from any person.

We also establish by this document of our decree that if any prelate of any Church, or any person endowed with whatever dignity, should attempt to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, let him be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the company of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of Zacharias, notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the sixth indiction. Enacted on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Theotfolctus, secundicerius of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious lord prince Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the ninth year, in the sixth indiction. Amen.

## III. PRIVILEGE FOR THE CITY OF INTERAMNA (Year 858)

[In Ughelli, *Italia sacra*]

[Col. 1011A]

In the name of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in the year 857 from the Incarnation of the same Lord Jesus Christ, in the month of May, in the sixth indiction.

It appears to be a highly honorable and necessary undertaking … to obtain services in return for the remuneration of their labor. From our possessions and from public resources we grant and bestow these upon them. For the divine command is that the vows of the faithful should be fulfilled, together with the fruit and reward of their labors. By the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, and of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, [Col. 1011B] of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and of all the saints together, I, Benedict III, pope and governor of the holy and apostolic see and of the whole Church throughout the world, from this present day, by the grace granted by the Lord and under the auspices of his divine mercy, and also prompted by gratuitous piety, give and grant, by the authority of the Lord Savior, to you, the inhabitants of the city of Teramo, both older and younger, and to your heirs and successors forever, namely, the whole aforesaid city, with its walls, buildings, watercourses, channels, banks, and their confluences, and with all its appurtenances, including valleys, hills, mountains, plains, [boundaries?], and place-names situated all around.

Moreover, we grant you other properties within these boundaries, as they appear to run along the road called Domnita and to go out through the gate called Roman; then, by the old bridge, they rise onto the hill called Altilianum; from that hill they descend into the ditch commonly called Cuda; then they proceed to the lagia, and by the courses of the aforesaid lagia descend to the fork called Petra de Confinio; from there they rise over the mountain where the place is called Aquae Vivae; then they ascend the mountain called Matum; and across the mountain valleys they appear to pass over the mountain toward the field called Rusclum. From there they descend along the road that leads to the marble quarries; then they descend along the mountain’s bank into the river channel at the place where the aforesaid water called Marmora appears to plunge; and by the course of the aforesaid river they flow into the aforesaid city of Teramo.

Within these boundaries and under these names we grant to you, and to your heirs and successors forever, fortresses, walls, and other buildings; lands, vineyards, fruit trees, and other trees, both fruitful and barren; mountains with valleys, cultivated and uncultivated land; waters and their courses, with their entrances and exits; and everything, in every respect, which appears to be contained above or below them, or which in future may be found to be contained there, for the honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, and Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, but for your benefit and that of your successors … [Col. 1012B]

With sound reason and fitting agreement we grant the aforesaid properties to you and to your heirs and successors forever, because you have always been obedient to us in all things, have been ready for our benefit and service, and voluntarily promise to fulfill these obligations in the future. At the holy and supreme apostolic see I confirm that you may have and possess these things, you and your heirs and successors forever, with the Lord’s blessing; and I further bind and confirm them for you and your successors.

If, however, anyone, rashly wishing by any device to molest, disturb, or litigate against you in any matter, or to act in opposition to this charter of our grant, should do so, let him be anathema, and let him be anathematized in addition. Let him pay at the supreme and apostolic see one hundred pounds of the finest gold. Once the penalty has been paid, this charter shall nevertheless remain stable forever.

John, the pope’s nephew; Gualterius, likewise his nephew; witnesses. Sanxo, Count Raynerius of Joseph, Adam of Alberto, witnesses.

I, Peter, scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed this document with my own hand by order of Benedict III, pope.

[Col. 1011]

## IX. NICHOLAS I

### I. PRIVILEGE OF POPE NICHOLAS FOR THE MONASTERY OF THE SAVIOR AT FULDA (Year 859)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*]

[Col. 1011D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theoton., religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord [Col. 1012D] Savior, and through you to your successors, the abbots of that same venerable monastery, forever.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires should always be granted, the authority of pious construction ought not to be denied to the devotion of the founder when privileges are being granted. Therefore, because you asked us that the monastery of the Savior, constructed by Saint Boniface, archbishop, in the place called Boconia beside the bank of the river Fuldaha, should be adorned with the supports of an apostolic-see privilege, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church, we, favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours commit to effect what has been requested.

And therefore we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any jurisdiction or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see and the bishop in whose diocese that venerable monastery appears to have been constructed. To that bishop we have granted permission only when the opportunity arises to consecrate an altar. No one, unless invited by the monastery’s abbot, is to presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there.

Thus, in accordance with what has been established as subject to the apostolic see by the firmness of this privilege, it shall remain securely endowed in its places and possessions, both those which it presently holds or possesses and those which divine goodness may in future increase in the right of that monastery from the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful. It shall enjoy perpetual security without contradiction from any person.

Moreover, after deliberation, we decree that at suitable times it be reported to our ecclesiastical solicitude how the monastic community is being directed in regular habit and entrusted to ecclesiastical observance in fitting harmony, lest, God forbid, under the pretext of this privilege, your mind and steps of uprightness should in any way be turned aside from the norm of justice.

[Col. 1013C] We also establish by this document of our decree that if any prelate of any Church, or any person endowed with whatever dignity, should attempt to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, let him be anathema. Incurring the wrath of God, let him be excluded from the company of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us, shall remain perpetually inviolate, supported by apostolic authority.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the seventh indiction. Farewell.

Given on the second day before the Ides of June, by the hand of Tiberius, primicerius of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious lord prince Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, was reigning, in the tenth year; and in the tenth year of his patriciate, in the seventh indiction. Amen.

### II. (Spurious) BULL OF POPE NICHOLAS I CONFIRMING THE DIPLOMA OF CHARLEMAGNE FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-DENIS

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Apart from the unusual style of this papal bull, its greatest indication of forgery is the fact that Emperor Charles IV transcribed it in his diploma in the year 1348 and called it a confirmation of the preceding document. It is said that Pope Nicholas issued this bull at the request of Charlemagne. But no Nicholas presided over the Roman see in that age; and everyone even minimally acquainted with the history knows that Nicholas I was elected pope only in the year 858, under the emperor Louis, son of Lothair. Leo III was Roman pontiff in the year 803, when the spurious diploma attributed to Charlemagne is said to have been issued.]

[In Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, greeting.

[Col. 1014A] In accordance with the written petition of our son, the most excellent King Charles, by the present document we perpetually grant, concede, and confirm, with the unanimous consent of the sacred council, our privilege of authority to the beloved sons of the monastery of Christ’s martyr Dionysius, living a religious life under the Rule of Saint Benedict in the small abbey of Lebrac.

Just as our most glorious son Charles, led by divine love, established and confirmed by a document of his authority the arrangements made in the time of his father of pious memory, Pippin, concerning the villages and possessions, or stipends, specially preserved, improved, or increased for the adornment of the aforesaid brothers, the hospitality of their church, and the uses of the poor, so, exactly as is contained in those same documents and donations, may all these things remain forever undisturbed.

Again, by the authority of blessed Peter, we establish that no one, whatever his condition, may under any pretext or appearance of a legal claim presume to diminish, remove, pledge, alienate, obstruct, seize, sell, buy, or apply to his own uses anything that has been granted in the documents of that son of ours, Charles, or of other kings, to the prejudice of the donation; nor may he transfer it to others under the guise of pious causes as an excuse for his own greed. Rather, everything that has been offered, or may be offered, for the aforesaid uses of the monks shall remain forever untouched and undisturbed, beneficial to them without any disturbance.

Therefore, wishing to oppose human wickedness, we annul documents made to the prejudice and detriment of the aforesaid persons, and instruments issued contrary to our decree; we declare them to be of no validity.

Nor shall any archbishop or bishop appointed by those same judges be permitted to pronounce against the monks themselves, or against anyone who owes them tithes or other revenues, a sentence of excommunication or interdict to their prejudice, nor to compel them against their will to appear before him for judgment, provided that they are willing to obey the command of their abbot as their ordinary.

And because we desire to assent to the petition of that son of ours, Charles, we appoint our beloved sons, the archbishops of Mainz and Trier and their suffragans, together with those who in due order and place succeed them, as protectors of all that is contained in this kind of document, in our decree, and in his charter. We command each of them, jointly and severally, when called upon, not to permit the monastery of Lebraha to be harassed or disturbed in its rights, goods, or privileges, as set out above and granted to it.

But if anyone, whether a great or insignificant person, should presume with rash boldness to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and wholly alienated from the kingdom of God, condemned together with all the impious to the fire of eternity.

But whoever proves to be an observer of this decree may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most benevolent Lord Jesus Christ.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Humbert, chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the Lateran basilica, in the third year of our pontificate.

### III. BULL OF POPE NICHOLAS I FOR THE MONASTERY OF SUBIACO (Years 858–867)

[Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, vol. V]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved son Azzon, religious abbot and presbyter, and to the monks of the venerable monastery of the most holy Father Benedict and of the holy virgin Scholastica, situated at Subiaco, and to their successors serving and entering there in the service of God, forever.

Since the pious desire of the will, etc., we hand over and confirm to your religious care the governance and abbacy of the monastery; we confirm everything which our predecessors—the pontiffs, emperors, and kings, etc.—[concerning] Mount Cervaria for the construction of a fortress, the estate of Marano, the estate of Conticuli, the estate of Rubiano, Mount Arsula, etc.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the first indiction. We have read it. Given in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in the year—God being favorable—of the pontificate of the lord Nicholas, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and in the reign of the lord Louis, most pious emperor Augustus, crowned by God, great emperor, in the tenth year, by his command, on 20 August, in the first indiction.

### IV. LETTER OF NICHOLAS I TO ADO, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE (Years 858–867)

[Bosco, *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, p. 53]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother Ado, archbishop.

The perpetual decree of the Church of Vienne, which your Holiness reverently requested from the apostolic see and humbly sought, asking us to renew for the sacred see of Vienne the ancient privilege granted by our fathers and predecessors: the authority of this holy see, because a worthy matter was requested, did not refuse.

Therefore, just as it was granted by our predecessors—namely, blessed Leo and nearly all the others down to our own time—to your predecessors by apostolic generosity, so that seven provinces should belong to the privilege of the Church of Vienne, within which its bishop, acting in our place, should convoke synodal assemblies and define ecclesiastical rights justly and according to the canons; and just as seven towns or cities—namely Grenoble, Valence, Die, Alba, Viviers, Geneva, and Tarentaise—should remain perpetually subject to the right of the Church of Vienne, so also we establish by the present decree that Maurienne, now part of our jurisdiction, shall remain firm and undisturbed in future times. We have determined that it shall belong inviolably to the power and jurisdiction of the metropolitan Church of Vienne.

Nevertheless, by this arrangement the bishop of the Church of Tarentaise does not lose the right conferred upon him. For the archbishop of Vienne, its primate, did not request from our authority that the bishop of Tarentaise should be forbidden to ordain in any towns entrusted to him or to summon them to himself whenever he sees fit. Rather, the bishop of Tarentaise should always know himself to be placed under the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Vienne, so that he may do all these things by that archbishop’s direction; when summoned to his synod, he should attend together with those entrusted to him; and, insofar as general observance is concerned, he should not presume to define anything without the authority of the bishop of Vienne.

Let him be humbly subject, as our predecessors salutarily established, so that the Church of Vienne may thereafter more freely possess and retain the dignity granted to it by us. Otherwise, if he acts or presumes otherwise, he will not only lose what was granted but, because of his disobedience, will be more severely condemned and humbled in the future.

[Col. 1015]

## X. ADRIAN II

### I. BULL OF ADRIAN II GRANTED TO JOHN, BISHOP OF AREZZO, FOR THE FOUNDATION OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY AT BAGNO IN EMILIA (Year 871, Ides of November)

[In Mittarelli, *Camaldolese Annals*, III, appendix 1]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son John, most reverend bishop of the holy Church of Arezzo, for the days of his life only, and after his death to the abbots of the venerable monastery of the holy Mother of God Mary, situated at Bagno in Massa, forever.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires should always be granted, the devotion of the founder ought not to be denied the authority of pious construction when privileges are being granted. Therefore, because you asked us that the baptismal church constructed in honor of God’s Mother and ever-Virgin Mary at Massa, which is called Bagno, belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, should be granted to you for the construction, governance, and administration of a monastery with the fear of God, after the fonts had been transferred by document of command to the church of the Lord Savior constructed in the middle of the aforesaid Massa, where the gathering of the people appears to be easier, we, inclined by your prayers, readily grant our assent.

In this way we may obtain the chief reward of profit from God, the Creator of all, if the venerable places suitably ordered by you are brought to a better condition.

Therefore, by this document of command, we grant to you, from the present sixth indiction, for the complete construction of a monastery and for as long as you live by God’s help, the church of God’s Mother mentioned above, with the adjoining buildings and with as much land and vineyard surrounding it as the aforesaid church of the Lord Savior is known to possess, so that whatever remains belongs to the aforesaid church of the Lord Savior.

We likewise grant you, for the days of your life, the forest in the territory of Arezzo belonging to your property, which you yourself transferred to blessed Peter the apostle by a deed of donation and which, through your efforts, you have partly brought under cultivation, together with the houses constructed there and those to be constructed, God willing; with lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, streams, and springs, cultivated or uncultivated, within the stated boundaries. These are: on one side, from the artificial stone to the Great Ridge; from there to Castellione; then again from the summit of Montione to Thetolitium; and from there to the Stilus of Filiolus. Leaving the Stilus on the right hand, the boundary proceeds by the road through Pontecellum; on the other side lie the territory and Massa called Bagno, belonging to the holy Roman Church.

After your departure from this life, we confirm this same forest perpetually to the monastery, with this condition only: that the abbot elected and ordained there in due course from that same community shall foster and govern the servants of God, the monks whom he is able to gather in that monastery, in chastity, regular modesty, and the monastic discipline of the Rule—namely, that of Saint Benedict—as a father of the household who keeps the fear of God before his eyes.

We also decree by this present statute that the monastery, once established, shall not be subjected to the jurisdiction or authority of any other Church except our holy Church, which, by God’s authority, we preside over. Therefore we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any jurisdiction, apart from the apostolic see. No one is to presume to celebrate solemn Masses there unless invited by the monastery’s abbot.

We do not, however, deny the bishop of the holy Church of Ficocle, in whose diocese it appears to lie, permission—when invited by the monastery’s abbot—to sing Masses there, consecrate altars, and promote worthy men to the priestly ministry.

Nor may any of our successors, the pontiffs, grant the monastery by beneficiary right to any person. By the protection of the apostolic see we decree that it shall prosper under the governance of its own abbot alone [Col. 1018A]. When the abbot departs from this light, a successor worthy of that office is to be elected from his own community by the common consent of all. Coming into our presence or that of our successors, he shall receive the gift of consecration without delay. From him no greater offering than one pound of silver is then to be demanded. Thus, from him and from his successors, twenty Lucanian gold solidi are to be paid without difficulty in each indiction, as a pension and according to ecclesiastical accounts.

All the possessions which the aforesaid monastery now appears to have, or which the Lord may deign to confer upon it, including the aforesaid properties belonging by fiscal and colonate right to this holy Roman Church, whether movable or immovable, the abbot of that monastery is to care for, govern, and administer diligently with the fear of God. He must not, seeking private gain, presume to accumulate them elsewhere, appropriate them to himself, or take them away from the brothers.

Nor should he attempt to give, sell, pledge, or alienate the immovable properties in any manner. Rather, everything is to remain forever intact and undiminished for the use of its own monastery and under its fiscal right, for the support of the monks serving God there, the provision of lamps, and the reception of guests and the poor.

Therefore, whoever presumes to disregard or violate in any way the sanction of this apostolic privilege, or maliciously attempts to handle, plunder, or remove the monastery’s property or household, or harasses the monks because of the alteration of the baptismal fonts, or attempts by secular power or force to choose as abbot of the aforesaid monastery an outsider cleric of any order instead of the person chosen by the entire monastic community, shall, together with the man who attempts to usurp the name of abbot for himself, remain excluded from participation in the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until he repents.

If anyone, forgetful of God’s judgments, should at any time attempt to act against this apostolic command of ours and fail to preserve it in every respect, let him remain bound forever by the chain of anathema. But whoever proves to be its guardian and protector may, through the bounty of Christ the Lord, deserve to obtain the grace of heavenly blessing.

[Col. 1018D] Farewell. Written by the hand of Paul, scriniarius and secundicerius of the holy apostolic see, on the Ides of November, in the sixth indiction, while the most pious lord Louis, crowned by God, was reigning, in the twenty-third year of his reign, in the year 887 from the incarnation of the Lord.

### II. BULL OF ADRIAN II FOR THE MONASTERY OF CORBIE (Years 867–872)

Corbie is received into apostolic protection, and the donations made to it are confirmed.

[In Schaten, *Paderborn Annals*, I, 171]

Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Adalgar [Col. 1019A], religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy martyrs Stephen and Vitus, which is called New Corbie, and through you to that same venerable monastery, forever.

It is fitting for those endowed with apostolic authority, moved by devout religion, to come to the aid of petitioners with benevolent compassion and to grant the requests of those who ask with eager devotion. For from such acts we chiefly earn a reward of profit from the Lord, the Creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better or more secure condition.

And therefore, since it is clear that your Religiousness has humbly submitted to our pontifical concern that we should deign to receive the aforesaid monastery under the perpetual protection of the holy apostolic see—over which we are recognized as presiding, though unworthy—we decree and establish by apostolic authority in every way that the same monastery may flourish to the end in the dignity of our privilege, and that the monks who serve the Lord there with daily praises may have the power, after your departure, to appoint from the fellowship of their own community the person whom, with the highest divine approval, they shall all unanimously choose.

And because you affirm—and request and suggest—that the monastery itself was enriched by the generosity of princes with landed possessions, you ask that we should likewise confirm by a formal decree both what it now possesses and whatever the faithful may perhaps have offered or granted to it. Concerning these matters we have not only rejoiced in the Lord, but, because we have seen them to be devout, we have resolved, as is customary for the apostolic see, to favor your wishes, moved by the love of God, and to provide these benefits for you.

Therefore, from the present sixth indiction, we have received the said monastery into the protection of apostolic authority, indeed into perpetual guardianship. We have confirmed all its estates, both those granted and bestowed there by glorious princes or by other Christian faithful, and those which thereafter, by the Lord’s favor, may be granted or bestowed there, whether movable or immovable. By apostolic authority we publish, command, and decree that none of them may be usurped, invaded, or seized by anyone. Likewise, for the increase of our reward, we inviolably establish by apostolic censure that the monks of the same monastery shall have every right and full license to choose from among themselves as abbot such a man as the votes of all may unanimously request and whom, with one mind and with the grace of the Holy Spirit assisting, they may wish to be placed over them in the service of the Lord there. No one, however, shall presume ever to appoint or introduce there an abbot who is alien or an outsider.

Rather, as we have said, when you have been called from this life and departed to the Lord, or thereafter, let men from that very community be chosen by the unanimity of all to preside regularly over the monastery—men who maintain the life and the entire monastic order and who make every effort to administer all things with the fear of God and reverence for regular discipline.

We establish by apostolic censure, under the testimony of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no person, great or small, of whatever dignity or order, may ever infringe, despise, or violate in any way, wholly or in part, this sanction of our authority, which we have promulgated with pious regard. If anyone—which we do not believe—should at any time, now or thereafter, presume by rash audacity to transgress, despise, violate, or infringe this our decree, and should not observe it in every respect, let him know that he is to be bound by the chains of anathema and utterly separated from the kingdom of God.

But whoever proves to be a true guardian and diligent observer of this apostolic decree, may he deserve to obtain from the Lord our God blessing, mercy, and eternal life.

Written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the sacred chamber of the Roman Church, during the reign of our lord, most pious, perpetual Augustus, Louis, crowned by God, great emperor, in the eighteenth year, and in the twenty-fourth year after his consulship, in the month of October, in the sixth indiction. Farewell in the Lord. Given on the Ides of October by the hands of Sergius, first of the defenders of the holy apostolic see.

## III. LETTER OF POPE ADRIAN II TO SALOMON, KING OF THE BRETONS

*[Note: This letter appears in Argentré’s History of Brittany and is of highly doubtful authenticity. In the definitive judgment of this case, Innocent III declared it false and spurious in the section dealing with the pallium, and fabricated by a certain P., a cleric of Dol. The people of Dol, when summoned to produce the original of that letter, replied: “We have not yet been able to find Adrian’s register, nor do we have the bull here.” These words are prefixed to the letter in the Tours parchment; nevertheless, the letter appears in the Roton cartulary, which is of excellent quality, but without the aforementioned conclusion.]*

*(Years 867–872.) He sends him the arm of Pope Leo III and the pallium for the bishop of Dol.

*[In Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, vol. III.]*

### [Col. 1020C]

To our most beloved son and dearest Salomon, duke of Brittany, with all his faithful people, Adrian, by God’s will pope, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Let Your Highness understand that we truly asked God, during an interval of seven days, for an answer worthy of your petition. After the seven days had passed, while we and all the Romans persevered in prayer and fasting, it seemed to me and to three of my cardinals, through a revelation of the Holy Spirit, that we should send you something from the body of blessed Pope Leo, because it is a great gift.

Therefore, dearest son, let it be known to you and to all the Christians dwelling there that, with the authority of our people, we are sending charitably to illuminate, assist, and defend your region the arm of the aforementioned Pope Leo. For we have certainly proved through him that the Lord performed many miracles.

And so that your faith in him may increase more and more, he is that most holy Leo who, through the envy of the Romans, was deprived of his eyes and tongue, but by the working of God’s grace was wondrously restored, so that with those same eyes he saw more clearly sevenfold, and with that same tongue preached the word of God more eloquently.

Therefore, the Roman authority presumes so much concerning God in his case that all from the river Loire whom age, sex, or personal condition does not prevent visit his relics three times a year; and by our permission and authority they fulfill the vow that they made to go to Rome.

We also send to your charity the pallium, with its privilege, which you requested for our brother and fellow bishop Festinian.

Farewell in Christ, faithful inhabitants of Brittany.

## [Col. 1021]

# XI. STEPHEN V

## LETTER OF STEPHEN V TO ADALGAR, ARCHBISHOP OF HAMBURG

*(Year 891.)*

*[Lappenberg, Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch.]*

### [Col. 1021B]

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Adalgar, archbishop of the holy Church of Hamburg and our brother, and, after you, to his successors in the same Church, forever.

Since the desire of a pious will and the purpose of praiseworthy devotion must always be aided by apostolic efforts, diligent care must be taken that things legally done and conforming to the rule of equity may not be disturbed by any opposition, but, by God’s authority, may remain by irrefragable right. For this reason, once apostolic sanctions have been promulgated, justice demands that each person’s possessions, insofar as reason supports them, be confirmed as rightfully held.

And since you requested that we make a privilege for your Church and strengthen it by apostolic protection, we grant that it may remain in its former condition. By apostolic right we confirm for you, for your holy Church of Hamburg, and for your successors, that dignity and those proper boundaries, together with all estates, parishes, and all movable or immovable property, including persons of both sexes, which Gregory of blessed memory, our predecessor, granted to Ansgar, your predecessor, whom he ordained archbishop in your Church, established by fixed right and with all the boundaries which Louis, the emperor of blessed memory, and Louis his son wished your Church to possess and defined by imperial authority.

We decree also that you shall have the power to ordain bishops within your parish and diocese, provided nevertheless that they remain under the authority of you and your Church, without prejudice to its dignity.

If anyone should attempt to oppose this privilege of our authority, or in any way strive to break it, wholly or in part, let him be excommunicated from the body and life-giving blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and separated from access to and fellowship with the holy Church of God.

But let whoever observes this our admonition and command have the blessing of almighty God, of the blessed apostles, and of us, who exercise their vicariate.

Written by the hand of John, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the eleventh indiction.

# SUPPLEMENT TO THE ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS OF THE NINTH CENTURY WHOSE YEAR IS GIVEN

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 900

### PREFACE OF SMARAGDUS, MONK OF SAINT MAXIMINUS, TO HIS EXPOSITION OF THE PSALMS

*He explains how useful meditation on the Psalms is.*

*[In Martène, Amplissima Collectio, vol. I, p. 63.]*

The preface of Smaragdus the presbyter begins.

*[Note: Since this Smaragdus assumes only the title of presbyter for himself, we do not think that he is the man who was abbot of Saint Michael on the Moselle and wrote the Diadem of Monks, but rather Smaragdus, a monk of Saint Maximinus of Trier, whom Trithemius mentions—especially since this work is found at Saint Maximinus.]*

We have collected this exposition of the Psalms in brief from the sayings of many fathers, so that its abridgment may remove harmful weariness and sharpen and open the mind’s profitable understanding, allowing what lies hidden under the covering of the letters in the Psalms to become visible to it more quickly.

A short reading is read more eagerly, understood more quickly, more easily entrusted to memory, and more firmly retained. It is therefore necessary that this spiritual exposition of the Psalms be frequently read by the faithful, and that the Psalms themselves be recited wisely, constantly, and humbly, because in them one always finds care of the mind, health of the heart, and medicine for the soul.

In them there is great consolation for mourners, blessed hope for the righteous, health for the sick, strength and refuge for those in danger, and, for those who feast spiritually, a most delightful nourishment. Through continual meditation on the Psalms, the penitent’s heart is pierced, and a fruitful rain of tears pours forth from him.

In the Psalms the promise of eternal life is read, and hope of the heavenly kingdom is firmly established in the mind. Forgiveness of sins is promised in them, and for those who labor, refreshment with perpetual glory is happily prepared.

In them there is a treasure of wisdom and knowledge, hidden beneath the covering of the letters, which, once revealed, gives eternal life to the faithful. It is a locked garden, watered with such waters and crowded with aromatic flowers. It is a sealed fountain full of a heavenly drink, always suitable for the faithful to drink from, and, for those who draw from it without ceasing, sweet as honey.

It is the Lord’s banquet, filled with spiritual delights and supplied with every life-giving nourishment. Through the melodious sweetness of the Psalms, the divine offices are performed in the Church by alternating choirs. Through them the night praise of the Lord begins to be sung with an eager mind; and when the silence of night has been dismissed, the mouths of the faithful burst forth into honey-sweet song.

Through them the meditation of daily praise is performed at the appointed hours, and through their most sacred words the memory of the Lord is brought back to the heart, so that unwearied praise may continually be sung to him with thanksgiving. Through them hymnic songs are sweetly composed, honey-sweet melody is sung in jubilation, and, to put it briefly, through the sweetest singing of the Psalms, with praises, hymns, and spiritual songs, the whole adornment of the Church is begun, carried out, and completed.

There is also something else wondrously composed and stored up by the Holy Spirit in the treasure of the Psalms: whoever sings or recites the words of the Psalms, whether in prayers for the cleansing of past sins, in supplications for acquiring virtues, or in thanksgivings for blessings already received, sings and recites them not as another’s prophecy but as his own and personal words.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 837

### SERMON OF AUTPERT, ABBOT OF CASSINO, ON SAINT MATTHIAS

*[In the Bollandists, Acta Sanctorum, February, vol. III, p. 487. (G)*]*

## CHAPTER I — Saint Matthias’s election as Christ’s disciple and then as an apostle

### [Col. 1023C]

**1.** *[Note: This prologue occurs in our manuscript and in Mombritius, and is read in the ancient Breviaries; Baronius does not mention it. It is taken from Isidore.]*

Matthias is Hebrew; in Latin he is called “Given,” with “in place of Judas Iscariot” understood.

*[Note: Isidore, Book VII of the Etymologies, chapter 9: “Matthias, who alone among the apostles is found without a surname, is interpreted as ‘Given,’ so that ‘in place of Judas’ is understood,” and so forth.]*

For he was elected as the twelfth apostle in Judas’s place when the lot was cast between two men. He alone is found without a surname, and to him the preaching of the Gospel in Judea is entrusted. His feast is celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of March. He was also one of the seventy disciples.

*[Note: Isidore adds this, whereas by others he is regarded as Zacchaeus or Barnabas, as stated above.]*

*[Note: Baronius cites this opening in his Notes on the Martyrology.]*

**2.** We ought to venerate and glorify the renowned and glorious feast of blessed Matthias, apostle of our Lord Jesus Christ, with as much devotion as we recognize that, by the dispensation of divine grace, he was elected to apostolic dignity. But how and in what order this was accomplished through the holy apostles, and what the holy Fathers wonderfully said in his praise, we shall endeavor to set forth through the sequence of sacred Scripture.

For our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, Creator and Redeemer of the human race, when in his profounder and hidden counsel he had determined most mercifully to visit the sick world and wondrously rescue his creature from the power of the devil’s deceit—which had possessed it for five thousand years and more—although he was King of kings and Lord of lords, deigned humbly to be born under the authority of a human king, namely Octavian Augustus.

*[Note: This is absent from Mombritius. It is found in the manuscript and in the Breviaries.]*

And he who was the Creator of heaven and earth did not disdain to assume the frailty of our flesh. Then, growing through the stages of life, in order to show the reality of his incarnation—for he was indeed the true day, which shone for twelve hours—he determined to choose twelve apostles. Then, corresponding to the seventy-two languages, he took seventy-two disciples and sent them out in pairs to preach.

Among them, blessed Matthias, undertaking the ministry of holy preaching, so entirely subjected himself humbly to the divine commandments that by faithful preaching he strove to bring the pagan people into the bosom of holy Mother Church. Thus he became especially acceptable and devoted to Christ. When that traitor Judas betrayed God the Christ, became his own murderer, and lost the apostolate, this man of God was appointed the twelfth apostle in his place by the lot and prayer of the holy apostles. To him was entrusted the preaching of the holy Gospel in Judea, just as it was entrusted to the holy apostles in their respective regions.

**3.** Nevertheless, if it is fitting that the feasts of all the saints be celebrated throughout the lands of Christ’s worshippers, how much more those of the blessed apostles? They adhered especially to Christ, conversed with him, ate and drank with him, and drank in all his power with thirsty hearts. They also deserved to be called brothers and friends by the Lord himself, when he said: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15).

And elsewhere: “These are my brothers” (Matthew 12:49). Moreover, bestowing great reciprocity upon them, he said: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

Since this was fitting with his approval, because of their excellence it was proper that their solemnities be celebrated in one feast, just as they had shared a common life and fellowship with the Lord. Blessed Jerome also asserts this in the Martyrology which he composed for the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus. He judged that they should be commemorated together, saying:

“Certainly, in the first part of my little book we most suitably wrote the feasts of all the apostles, so that those whom one apostolic dignity made exalted in heavenly glory might not appear to be divided by different days.”

*[Note: The commonly published text reads: “so that they might not appear to be divided by different days.” Mombritius reads: “so that we might not appear to divide them on different days.”]*

*[Note: Mombritius reads: “Intus sancta secunda Ecclesia” (“Within, the holy second Church” [sense uncertain]).]*

But since it soon prevailed in the holy Church that the feast of each apostle should be celebrated individually on the day when he was born into heaven and crowned, we ought to honor today the birthday of blessed Matthias, the twelfth apostle, with as much veneration as we understand that he was wondrously elected among the apostles, as has been said.

But how this was accomplished through the praise of blessed Peter the apostle—or rather through the grace of the Holy Spirit—is a sacrament of great authority and excellence, narrated by blessed Luke the evangelist. It is fitting to recount it more suitably to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the glory of that holy and glorious apostle. For the evangelist says:

**4.** “Then Peter, rising in the midst of the brothers, said”—there were about one hundred and twenty persons gathered together—“Men and brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became the guide of those who arrested Jesus. He was numbered among us and obtained a share in this ministry. He indeed acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness; and, having been hanged, he burst open in the middle, and all his inward parts were poured out. This became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

*[Note: Luke adds: “So that in their language that field was called Haceldama, that is, the Field of Blood.”]*

“For it is written in the book of Psalms (Psalm 68:26): ‘Let their dwelling be deserted, and let there be no one dwelling in it, and let another receive his episcopate.’ Therefore, from these men who have accompanied us throughout the whole time during which the Lord Jesus entered and went out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us, one of these must become with us a witness of his resurrection.”

And they appointed two: Joseph, who was called Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias. And praying, they said: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of men, show which one of these two you have chosen to receive the place of this ministry and apostleship from which Judas transgressed, so that he might go to his own place.” And they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles (Acts 1:15 and following).

*[Note: Joseph is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 20 July.]*

**5.** In this election of the most holy apostle, therefore, the dispensation of divine power and human glory must be considered and admired, since, as divine Scripture declares, God does not foresee as man sees (Job 10:4).

Joseph, who was called Barsabbas and surnamed Justus, was chosen by human beings. But Matthias, whose name means “little one of God” or “given,” was made great by the election of the Holy Spirit.

*[Note: Arator below, Bede in his commentary on Acts, and others interpret the name as “little one of God”; Cornelius a Lapide discusses its Hebrew etymology in his commentary on the same passage of Acts.]*

O truly little one! O truly great one! He was not great because he was exalted, but great because he became humble, following the footsteps of his Lord, who said: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28).

And that other saying which he gave when compelling the sons of Zebedee to holy humility: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14).

*[Note: Rather, he spoke the preceding sentence about the monastery; the following sentence he spoke frequently on another occasion.]*

The same Matthias is also called “Given.” By whom, and why? By the Lord Jesus Christ himself, certainly. For when he had foreknown him before the foundation of the world and before his holy incarnation—so that, when the fullness of time should one day come, when he should take flesh from the holy Virgin, when he should be born, and when he should be betrayed by one of his disciples, the Given might be exalted and glorified by the Lord himself among the twelve and the number twelve might be found complete—there is nothing strange or incredible in this. Nothing is impossible to God’s wisdom, and nothing is believed to be unknown to it.

For everything whatever he willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses. O how far human merits differ from heavenly and divine judgments! O how far human wisdom differs from that wisdom of which the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!”

We find this wisdom perfectly fulfilled in the election of blessed Matthias. The wisdom of God had kept him hidden in its treasure, humble and little; yet it willed to reveal him in the world as great and glorious, namely when it exalted him to the twelfth throne.

Let us therefore receive him as one given by God, as one foreordained by him; let us venerate him as one greatly glorified by him among the disciples. For the aforementioned Barsabbas must not be considered to be that Barnabas, companion of blessed Paul the apostle. The one is interpreted as “son of consolation,” whereas this one is interpreted as “son of rest.”

## CHAPTER II — The election of Saint Matthias by lot; the gift of tongues bestowed at Pentecost; the privilege of judging the world with Christ

### [Col. 1027C]

*[Note: This passage to the end of the section is copied from Bede, with some omissions and a few additions concerning Saint Stephen. Saint Dionysius has some remarks on the casting of lots for Saint Matthias in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, ch. V, §5. Consult the commentators on Acts of the Apostles.]*

**6.** “And they cast lots,” says Luke the evangelist, “and the lot fell upon Matthias.”

Nor should we believe indiscriminately in lots because of this example, or because the prophet Jonah was discovered by lot. The privileges of individuals cannot by any means establish a common law.

*[Note: Bede inserts: “as Jerome says.”]*

In the lot concerning the prophet Jonah, the Gentiles, driven by the storm, sought by lot the author of the danger. Here, blessed Matthias, beloved of God, was chosen by lot so that his election would not appear to differ from the law of the Old Testament, where the high priest was ordered to be selected by lot. Thus it is said concerning Zechariah: “According to the custom of the priesthood, he went out by lot to burn incense” (Luke 1:9).

But this figure was permitted to be practiced until the truth was fulfilled through Jesus, whose sacrifice, offered at the time of Passover, was truly consumed on the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit appeared in fire.

*[Note: Bede reads: “was truly consumed.” It was an ancient custom that victims accepted by God should be consumed by heavenly fire.]*

Hence blessed Matthias was appointed by lot before Pentecost. The seven deacons, however—including the most blessed first martyr Stephen himself, who, by glorifying Jesus Christ, was granted to behold him standing at the right hand of God—were afterward appointed not by the casting of lots but solely by the election of the disciples, and the apostles’ prayer and laying on of hands.

Those who wish to maintain this rule after the example of the apostles must take care and observe that the blessed apostles did this only after the assembly of the brothers had gathered and prayers had been poured out to the Lord.

**7.** Who could adequately recount the perfection of this mercy of God, or who could prevail to describe the grace of his dispensation? He himself deigned to confirm the election of his apostle through the fire of the Holy Spirit, just as he wondrously consummated through the fire of the Holy Spirit, on the day of Pentecost, the sacrifice of his body which he offered for us.

*[Note: The manuscript reads “confirmed.”]*

For the order of sacred Scripture announces this through the blessed evangelist, saying:

“When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in the same place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:1 and following).

That sacrifice was acceptable to God under the Law which was consumed by heavenly fire, as we read that this was divinely done in the holocaust of the righteous Abel, of Manoah, the father of the exceptionally strong Samson, and of Elijah and the other prophets.

For where we read, “God looked upon the gifts of Abel” (Genesis 4:4), the Greek text says “he set fire to” or “kindled.”

*[Note: Thus Saint Jerome follows Theodotion: “And the Lord kindled a fire upon Abel and upon his sacrifice; but upon Cain and upon his sacrifice he did not kindle one.” In Greek, Theodotion has ἐνεφύρισεν, “he kindled”; the Septuagint translators have ἐπεῖδεν, “he looked upon.”]*

Therefore the sacrifice of the election of the apostle Matthias possesses the greatest sanction and the most holy firmness by the testimony of sacred Scripture. Whence, and from what source? Because the Lord confirms and approves it from heaven, giving the fire of the Holy Spirit to all the apostles, and therefore also to blessed Matthias, so that they might speak perpetually in the languages of all nations.

**8.** But perhaps someone may say: The Holy Spirit was given to the apostles and to blessed Matthias only at that time and in that place, and afterward was taken away, just as it was taken away from all the prophets and from blessed Elisha, who is said to have spoken to the woman deprived of children concerning the boy: “Leave her, for her soul is bitter; the Lord has hidden it from me and has not revealed it to me” (2 Kings 4:27).

Away with such a thought, I say; away with it from Catholic truth. For if the Holy Spirit was once given and taken away from blessed Elisha and the other prophets, this was by no means so with the holy apostles and blessed Matthias.

For although it was given and taken away from those prophets for a time, this was expedient and appropriate, since they were proclaiming the truth. But when Christ, the Truth, came, the Holy Spirit was given and confirmed perpetually to the holy apostles, together with the grace of all languages.

And rightly so. Is there not a great difference before the Lord between apostles and prophets? The prophets, as servants, proclaimed the Lord’s coming and believed, but did not see him incarnate. The holy apostles, however, both saw and believed his incarnation; they ate and drank with him and, as has been said, deserved to be called his friends. Moreover, they poured out their blood for love of him.

The Lord Christ himself approves this when he says: “Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24).

Those who wish perversely to reject this must take great care lest they resist the truth and depart from the truth, which is Christ. For he himself confirms this judgment when he says to the apostles: “If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever” (John 14:15).

One must observe what it means to remain forever. What does “to remain forever” mean? It means what never ends, what never departs, having neither end nor decline. And indeed he did not say “today or tomorrow,” or “for so many days or years,” but “forever.”

Blessed Jerome, understanding this, affirms it in two questions, saying without hesitation:

“I boldly and with complete freedom declare that from the time when the apostles believed in the Lord, they always possessed the Holy Spirit and could not perform signs without the grace of the Spirit of God.”

And below, concerning the grace of all languages:

“It was more necessary for the apostles to speak the variety of the languages of all nations, so that, when they announced Christ, they would need no interpreter. Hence in Lycaonia, when the inhabitants heard Paul and Barnabas speaking in their own languages, they thought that gods had become human beings. The same Apostle, approving this in his Epistle, says: ‘I give thanks to God that I speak in the languages of all nations’” (1 Corinthians 14:18).

We have brought this forward to indicate the matter, so that we may understand to what perfection of grace blessed Matthias was elected. He deserved to ascend among the twelve apostles to the summit of the twelfth apostolate; and therefore, when the Lord comes to judgment, he will appear seated in glory with him.

*[Note: The manuscript reads: “He will shine forth.”]*

Concerning the wondrous election of this apostle Matthias and the rejection of the traitor Judas, Arator, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, following the text of blessed Luke the evangelist—which blessed Peter the apostle expounded in prose—set it forth in heroic verse, saying:

*[Note: Mombritius reads “his own.”]*

*[Note: He dedicated this accompanying elegy to Pope Vigilius, elected in 540 and deceased in 555. Under him, Ughellus places Arator among the cardinals, after others, in his Additions to Ciacconius.]*

### [Col. 1029D]

**9.**

First among the apostolic band, called from a little boat,  
Was Peter, whom the scaly multitude of fish  
Was accustomed to catch as a fisherman; suddenly, seen from the shore,

*[Note: Ten intervening verses are omitted in Arator.]*

He rises, and, explaining the divine matters, reverently says before them:

“You know that the mad traitor paid himself  
The reward of his crime, the penalty due for his guilt,”

*[Note: Four verses are again omitted.]*

He shuddered, himself choking the voice in his throat.

*[lacuna]*

That he might set before the common enemy in midair  
The punishment he deserved. Hated by heaven and earth,  
He perished between the two; his ruptured entrails,  
Fit for burial in no tomb, fell, and, escaping into the thin air,

*[Note: Ten other verses are omitted.]*

*[lacuna]*

Now what the prophetic words proclaim requires our prayers:  
Who may be permitted to supply the vacant place? Then, having prayed earnestly,  
They appointed two, Joseph, surnamed Justus,  
And Matthias—the name, they say, means “little one of God”  
In the Hebrew language; by calling him humble,  
It confirms the meaning. O how far human beings differ  
From heavenly judgments! By the merit of the little one, he is surpassed—  
he whom human praise had called just. The twelvefold signs  
Of the choir shine forth, and Olympus hurls its radiance upon the earth.

**10.** Nevertheless, if certain ignorant men, less competent in the testimony of the holy Scriptures, should wish to object to the election of this most holy apostle, saying: If blessed Matthias fulfilled the apostolate of the number twelve and will sit as the twelfth with the Lord in judgment, then blessed Paul the apostle will be excluded from that session—let them know that the number twelve in this matter, as in other scriptural expressions, is taken according to the figure called synecdoche, in which a part is understood for the whole. By this reasoning, beyond doubt, blessed Paul the apostle and the other saints will also sit with the Lord in judgment.

Blessed Augustine most truthfully confirms this in his exposition of the Gospel concerning the steward (Luke 16), saying:

“We see that the Apostle Paul, the Lord’s apostle, said without any ambiguity: ‘Do you not know that we shall judge angels?’ (1 Corinthians 6:3). Which angels, unless the wicked ones, and their prince himself, did he place under judgment? (Matthew 19:28.) Therefore that apostle himself will sit on one of the twelve seats of which the Lord says: ‘You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.’ But he was not among the twelve apostles. Therefore I suggest that you understand what the twelve seats mean.

“For we know that first the traitor Judas fell away from the twelve chosen by the Lord, and blessed Matthias was substituted in his place.”

*[Note: Mombritius reads: “and who fell away from them, and who was substituted in his place was blessed Matthias.”]*

“If each one will sit on an individual seat, the number has already been completed. Where, then, will the apostle Paul sit? Or did he perhaps usurp a seat not owed to him when he said: ‘Do you not know that we shall judge angels?’ The twelve seats, therefore, are all the seats on which the apostles and the other saints will sit with the Lord in judgment.”

## CHAPTER III — The remaining deeds of Saint Matthias; his death
11. With these matters thus established, let us briefly return with the utmost devotion to the praise of blessed Matthias the apostle. Let us glorify and venerate him, and proclaim him with triumphal praise in everlasting encomia. Meanwhile, imitating his holy humility, which is the mother of all holy virtues, let us beware of pride, which is the root of all evils. By following pride, he who was first cast out and became the prince of all evils was hurled into eternal damnation. Therefore our merciful and almighty God, not allowing the ruin to remain in the heavenly homeland [Note: Mombritius: “damnation”], deigned to create new angels and to fashion man, a new creature, in his own image and likeness; from his offspring he determined to raise there, with the restoration, that is, of the tenth order, as many as are believed to have remained there as holy angels, as the holy prophet teaches: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.”
