To rescue his disciples from this ruin of pride, the Lord Christ, when they said to him, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us,” replied: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:17–18). As though he were saying: “Strive to live humbly in all things, and do not glory in miracles, lest you fall in the same way as the one who loved such things.” Accordingly, blessed Matthias, the apostle of God, embracing and retaining this command of the Lord, established upon the foundation of charity and firmly bound in humility [F.: “closely bound”], strove to live so humbly that, chosen by divine grace from among the seventy-two disciples, he was deemed worthy to ascend to the glory of the apostolate.

12. Therefore the glorious apostle of the Lord possesses—indeed, unquestionably possesses—the prerogative and excellence of apostolic dignity, not above all, but together with all; not more excellent than everyone, but equal to everyone. Why is this? Because when the Lord Christ gave blessed Peter the apostle authority to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, he did not confer that privilege upon him alone, but upon all the apostles and upon all who have been placed in priestly dignity.

Thus, just as Ananias and Sapphira, rebuked by blessed Peter the apostle, died bodily rather than spiritually, as the rule of blessed Benedict the abbot attests [Note: St. Benedict, chapter 57: “Let them remember Ananias and Sapphira, lest perhaps they suffer in the soul the death which those men endured in the body—both they and all who commit any fraud concerning the monastery’s possessions.” [Col. 1032D] As for what the Fathers thought concerning their damnation, Haftenus discusses it in book IX of the *Disquisitiones monasticae*, treatise III, disputation 4; so do Cornelius a Lapide and other interpreters in Acts, chapter 5.], so, through the rebuke of blessed Paul the apostle, a certain magician, Bar-Jesus, called Elymas, was deprived of his sight (Acts 13). The same apostle also handed over the man who had committed incest with his stepmother to the devil by the mere sending of a letter (1 Corinthians 5:1), and afterward, when he wished, restored him, saying: “Confirm your love toward him, lest perhaps such a one be swallowed up by excessive sorrow” (2 Corinthians 2:7). Likewise, together with his fellow apostle Peter, he miraculously cast down that magician Simon from the heights of the air.

Then, when Christ instructed them, saying, “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John 14:12)—which, as we read later in Luke’s account in the Acts of the Apostles, was accomplished through handkerchiefs and even Peter’s shadow (Acts 19:12; 5:15)—he did not prefer one above the others, but granted that power equally to all.

13. If it is asked whether so great an apostle of the Lord became especially distinguished by miraculous powers, it must be understood in every respect that he performed many astonishing wonders together with his fellow apostles and apostolic men. For he was certainly among those to whom Christ granted power, saying: “The signs that I perform, you also will perform” (John 14:12); and elsewhere: “If you say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ it will move from its place” (Matthew 17:19). Likewise: “You have power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke 10:19).

If, with Christ bearing witness—Christ who is truly the Truth—we must hold that this man of God performed miraculous works among the other apostles, how many miraculous powers do we believe he exercised in the province of Judea, which fell to him as his allotted field of preaching? For he would not have sought to convert an unbelieving people to the faith of Christ without performing miracles, just as we read of the holy apostles: “Through the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done” (Acts 5:12). Concerning blessed Stephen it is written: “Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people” (Acts 6:8).

But since the miracles of Saint Matthias have not been written down, they should not be argued against as unbelievable, but accepted as true, since it is written of the Lord and Savior himself: “Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book” (John 20:30). And, to bring forward matters of greater importance, it must certainly be understood that he raised as many dead as he rescued from eternal death through his life-giving preaching. This is judged to be in every respect more excellent and glorious: to restore to Christ a soul dead through sin than to give life to a body destined to die.

For what is more glorious and excellent than to live eternally with Christ, rejoice with Christ, and possess the heavenly kingdom with the angels and with all the saints? How much better and more fitting it is to see blessed Paul raised from the death of the soul than Lazarus raised from bodily death.

14. Nor should this be omitted from the glory of this apostle: although all the apostles are believed to have been chosen by the Lord before the ages, as the Apostle teaches when he says, “He chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight” (Ephesians 1:4), nevertheless Christ the Lord made mention not of just anyone, but of this holy apostle, when he said in the Gospel: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John 11:9.) By the twelve hours he signified the holy apostles, including Judas among them.

If they were hours, then, as Saint Augustine teaches, they shone. If they shone, how could Judas have handed over Christ, the day, to death? Therefore in this passage he did not mean Judas the betrayer, but blessed Matthias, his successor and preacher. He foresaw and indicated this man, whom he later miraculously appointed in the place of the other.

For he himself, already reigning in heaven, established as an apostle the man who, while placed on earth, chose the other apostles. For at that time he reigned in heaven with the Father, and on earth governed them as sons, as he promised when he said: “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). From this it is understood that, just as he restored the tenth order to heavenly glory from the human race, so he restored the number twelve through the worthy election of blessed Matthias.

15. If his passion is sought, as in the case of the other apostles, it is most clearly evident that he inflicted passion upon himself: by carrying his cross, he followed Christ, saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

Since it is clear that there are two kinds of passion—one hidden and the other manifest—it is plainly evident that the world had been crucified to him because he hated it and regarded it as dead. Likewise, he had been crucified to the world because the world could not draw him toward its own pleasures.

For what wise person does not know that it is a harder punishment to stand every day in spiritual battle and resist the devil’s deceit than to bring life to an end in a single moment by a tyrant’s sword? Blessed Peter the apostle, recognizing this, took care to admonish us, saying: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5:8).

Blessed Paul likewise says: “Stand, having girded your loins with truth, so that you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:14, 16–17).

Was not the great James slain by Herod’s sword, while John the Evangelist, greatly beloved by Christ and his brother, was called and crowned by Christ in the peace of the holy Church?

[Col. 1034A]

16. Therefore, most blessed apostle of Christ, Matthias, rejoice and glory in the Lord Jesus Christ. Rejoice now, joyful with everlasting joy, and rightly so: called by a name foretelling your destiny and given by Christ, you are now no longer small but great; no longer lowly in the world but glorious and powerful in heaven.

Why and how did this happen? By what grace? Because, when you were humble in your heart and desired neither human praise nor fear, neither gold nor gems nor the fleeting kingdoms of the world, you gained the heavenly homeland in place of an earthly kingdom, and the delights of paradise in place of perishable joys.

For, in a wondrous manner, he called you peacefully from heaven, as he did the apostle Paul. First depriving Paul gloriously of his sight, he sent him from heaven to the bosom of the holy Church; and through the holy assembly, by the action of the Holy Spirit, he caused you also to ascend the lofty and apostolic throne.

He surely chose you from the flock of disciples—the one who chose Peter and Andrew, James and John from the shore of the Gentiles. Therefore rejoice exceedingly; rejoice in every respect, blessed one: now joined to the angelic assemblies, now filled with Christ’s nectar, exalted among the apostolic seats in that great judgment, when he will judge the world in righteousness, exalted together with Christ the Lord.

But because all this was given to you by Christ’s grace, we humbly and suppliantly ask that you deign to intercede with him for us, so that he may mercifully hear us when we pray and graciously reward us in our struggle.

After [Note: This word is absent both from Mombritius and from the manuscript, but I have supplied it from the old Morin Breviary.] blessed Matthias had left Judea, the homeland he had received as his allotted field of preaching, and had converted many Gentiles to the Catholic faith, he departed to our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: The word *dies* is absent from Mombritius; it is found in the manuscript and in the Morin Breviary.], on the sixth day before the Kalends of March [February 24]. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, throughout infinite ages of ages.

[Col. 1033]

## In the Year of Our Lord 849: Verses of Haldoinus, Abbot, for the Tomb of Saint Remigius

(*In Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 423.*)

[Col. 1033D] Haldoinus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Altivillar [Note: The monastery of Altivillare, in the territory of Rheims, was especially renowned for the confinement of the monk Gottschalk, who was entrusted by Hincmar to Haldoin, abbot of that place and author of the foregoing verses. Hincmar did not attach these verses to the tomb of Saint Remigius, but others composed by himself.], set forth this memorial—namely, twelve verses—which, if Bishop Hincmar had wished, would have been placed around the shrine where Saint Remigius was to be transferred. They concerned the transfer of the precious body of Remigius by King Charles and the aforesaid Bishop Hincmar to the place where it remained until the year 881, when, because of the pagan incursions, it was secretly removed from there by God’s judgment and, after an unsuccessful attempt, carried beyond the Marne as far as the monastery of Orbais. He began with a hymn:

The first teacher of the Franks and shepherd of Rheims,  
Remigius rests in this sacred tomb.

The temple’s threshold once held him buried,  
while he guarded the Lord’s enclosure and his flock.

As soon as the people, already filled with his teaching,  
grew together, this house likewise grew.

He transferred the saint and placed him in an exalted seat,  
so that he might behold the people, and the people, in faith, their Father.

King Charles, noble son of the Emperor Louis,  
and Bishop Hincmar indeed together enlarged and adorned

the sacred buildings and laid in the tomb  
the great pontifical glory of the Franks.

In the year from the Nativity of the Lord 852, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June; in the twelfth year of King Charles’s reign, in the thirteenth year of Hincmar’s episcopal ordination, and in the fifteenth indiction.

[Col. 1035]

## In the Year of Our Lord 855: Hebernus, Archbishop of Tours — Miracles of Blessed Martin

Performed after the return of his body, or its deposition; edited by Hebernus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Marmoutier and afterward archbishop of the city of Tours.

(*In Baluze, *Miscellanea sacra*, vol. II, p. 300.*)

[Col. 1035B] The outer shrine in which the body of blessed Martin was contained, which they had also brought from Auxerre, was cast from gold and silver—what is called electrum—two fingers thick. By means of engraved letters and verses it identified blessed Perpetuus as the maker of the work [lacuna]. It had neither crack, hole, window, nor door.

Blessed Perpetuus had made it when he raised Martin’s body from the ground. The body had first been wrapped in red-purple cloth and carefully sewn up, and he then placed it in this outer shrine. He also made a square altar and a crown of dressed stones, covering it with a large slab and cementing it together with the other parts.

Inside he made another shrine of cast electrum, copper, and tin, a palm in thickness, with a cast door, hinges, and bolts; it was secured with four keys. Finally, he made above it a *freda* [an uncertain term] of the finest gold and precious stones, worthy of so great a priest.

At last that same consul, together with the venerable bishops Adalaud of Tours, Saint Lupus of Angers, Mainoldus of Le Mans, and Raimon of Orléans, earned the privilege of placing the body of the often-mentioned confessor Martin within the altar enclosure, in another shrine. They sealed the door together with the shrine, so that no access or entrance was open.

With the unanimous counsel of all, they granted Count Ingelger the benefice of Saint Martin, to be possessed by him and his heirs in perpetuity. Because the church of that saint at the time lacked both a treasurer and a sacristan, they enthroned Ingelger the consul, appointed him treasurer, made him defender of the church, and assigned him as guardian of all its possessions, wherever they might be.

He held the office of treasurer and its houses with their revenues for as long as he lived. All who were with Count Ingelger and had been summoned to restore the body of blessed Martin—especially the barons of the district of Tours—entered into an association and bestowed a benefice upon the church.

It happened in that same month, while Ingelger was consul at Tours, that Adalaud, worn out by old age, entered upon the way of all flesh. Ingelger the consul, with God’s help, through the intercession of blessed Martin, with the assistance of the clergy and the agreement of the citizens of Tours, enthroned and elevated to the episcopal seat Hebernus, an old man, abbot and minister of the greater monastery of blessed Martin.

After blessed Martin’s return from Auxerre, or after the deposition of his body, the Lord graciously deigned to perform at his tomb very numerous miracles, so that his merits might be proclaimed far and wide. We have often heard of many such wonders. Of the many, however, we have decided to relate some miracles that we ourselves witnessed.

### I

Hildricus, bishop of Liège, a man praiseworthy for the integrity of his conduct, was miserably—or rather wondrously—afflicted, by God’s hidden judgment, with a disease commonly called lupus. He suffered in the buttocks. It was a pitiable sight.

The force of the illness advanced so severely that, in a remarkable manner, it consumed, gnawed, and devoured the man’s flesh in the manner of a wolf. His only relief—not hope of escaping the illness, but merely a postponement of death—was that each morning two plucked and eviscerated chickens, and two more in the evening, were consumed in place of the man’s flesh by the disease, as though they were being offered to the wolf’s ravenousness. Yet even this did not stop the consumption of his flesh.

For the disease, lodged in his inward parts, though at times fed from outside, consumed his inner substance all the more intimately. What more is there to say? With the physicians despairing and everyone’s care being uselessly and fruitlessly exhausted, the bishop, as though already dying, was utterly abandoned by human remedies.

But, as the Lord says, “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Luke 18:27).

When the same bishop heard that, after blessed Martin’s return from Auxerre, or after the deposition of his body, the Lord graciously performed many miracles at his venerable tomb so that Martin’s merits might be proclaimed far and wide, the bishop, sensing this through an inward prompting, conceived hope in Martin’s intercession, as it were against hope. He turned wholly and with all his heart toward Martin, trusting that through him what human skill could not accomplish might be done.

He therefore bound himself by a vow to visit Martin’s tomb and faithfully to seek from him the healing which, after God, he expected to receive from Martin alone. There was no delay: pious intention carried out the pious vow.

Taking with him highly honorable companions and abundantly preparing what was necessary, he set out, taking the greatest care to arrive for the approaching feast of the supreme pontiff. And so it happened. Neither the dignity of the sick man nor the illness of so dignified a person could remain hidden. The more eminent a person is, the farther his misfortunes are spread abroad. For fame accompanies fortune: the one whom fortune casts down, fame exposes.

Thus the dying bishop attended the festivities celebrating Bishop Martin with their lively praises. But, as the saying goes, music is an unwelcome story to one who is in mourning. Nevertheless, by his devotion he overcame his sadness and never allowed himself to be absent from the nightly vigils. The canons showed him great compassion and extraordinary goodwill.

He himself spent the night sleepless and prostrate before the holy tomb, since, owing to the severity of his condition, he could stand only when bent forward. For seven successive days the clergy and people rejoiced according to customary solemn practice. He, however, ceased neither day nor night from tears and prayer.

At last, on the seventh night, exhausted by continuous prayer and by the severity of his pain, he fell into a brief sleep while lying prostrate before the most holy tomb. Then the wonder-working Martin appeared to stand before him, adorned with a bishop’s mitre. Saint Briccius followed him as a son follows his father and as a disciple follows his teacher; Briccius too was wearing episcopal insignia.

Martin then said to him: “What do you think, brother Briccius? Does it seem right to you that this sick man should receive the healing he desires, since he has come to our tomb from such distant regions with such devotion and has sought our help with such humility and perseverance?”

Briccius replied: “Lord, if it pleases your mercy, it is right that this man should recover his former health—especially since he belongs to our order and his life does not dishonor it.”

Then Martin turned toward the sick man and, uttering with his sacred mouth the sign of the cross familiar to him, traced that same cross over him, saying: “Hildricus, the Lord Jesus Christ heals you. Rise up healed, and call my clerics and inform them that you have obtained your health through my prayers. Tell them also, by my command, that they are to make you a canon of this church of mine.

“As a testimony to the glory of Christ and to your healing, I command you to sing the greater Mass today, so that the entire people who knew of your incurable illness, seeing you healthy at the celebration of Mass, may glorify God and place greater confidence in our intercession.”

After saying this, he seemed to touch the place of the illness with the point of his pastoral staff. At that touch both the vision disappeared and sleep departed. The bishop awoke and, to test what had happened, placed his hand on the site of the wound. But his attendants, who had been keeping watch nearby, fearing that his touch would aggravate the itching, tried to stop him.

“Do not be afraid,” he said. “Lord Martin has restored me to health.”

They roused him, lest perhaps he were speaking in his sleep. He said: “Light the lamps. Come and see the place where the disease had been.”

They followed him at once, for desire cannot endure delay, lighting the lamps as they went, and stopped in the chapter house of the church. There they untied the bandages with which he had been bound according to custom. They found the chickens which had been placed before the disease, like an insatiable beast, untouched. They found that new flesh had grown; the remaining flesh was in no way lower than the rest, nor did it differ from it except that a certain reddish line divided one side of the scar from the other.

Why delay? The cry of those who marveled and rejoiced together rose to the heavens. The canons, who were singing the matins hymns according to solemn custom, were roused by the voices and hurried in. After confirming with their own eyes an event worthy of so great a miracle, they declared that none of the saints could be compared with Martin in the efficacy of holy signs.

The bells were therefore rung, and the *Te Deum laudamus* was sung with joy. When morning came, the assembly of canons was summoned to the chapter house. In obedience to Martin’s command, they made the healed bishop a canon. On that same day, as the saint had ordered him, he celebrated the Sunday Mass in the presence of the clergy and people.

When all this had been duly completed, he returned home joyful and in good health. Yet he was not ungrateful either for the saint’s benefaction or for the service of his canons. He sent the saint precious silk vestments and golden and silver vessels, with which the Lord and the saint are still served there today, and he sent individual gifts to each of the canons.

Even this did not seem sufficient to him. In the course of time he built a church in his diocese in honor of blessed Martin and endowed it with such abundant revenues that fifty canons serving God and Saint Martin there could be maintained at the greatest expense.

### II

Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, had made it his devout custom to visit the most holy tomb of blessed Martin every year on the saint’s feast day. Neither the length and difficulty of the journey, nor the ambushes of enemies lying between, nor frequent warfare, nor any other business could prevent him from hastening to obtain the saint’s intercession. So firmly was this purpose established in the faithful man.

On one occasion he had come according to custom when, suddenly, while he was engaged in prayer, a very dangerous concern struck his memory. In his homeland he had borrowed sixty thousand solidi from a certain man of Bourges, under the pledge of his own good faith, with many guarantors also interposed; and the agreed day for repaying the money was now approaching.

What could he do? Even if he could fly away on swift wings like a bird, he could not arrive by the appointed day. He therefore turned wholly to seeking Martin’s intercession, entreating him with vows and imploring him with groans to help him in such great need. He begged that the one who, out of devotion to Martin, had forgotten himself and his affairs might not himself be forgotten by Martin; that Martin would not allow the faith of the guarantors and his own faith to be put at risk, but would divinely make possible, as was his custom, “what is impossible with human beings” (Mark 10:27).

Exhausted for a long time by this supplication, which pressing necessity forced upon him, he finally fell asleep. Then that wonder-working Martin, who was always overflowing with the deepest compassion, appeared to him in a vision, wearing episcopal mitre and accompanied by two bishops.

The man saw those two bishops supplicating Martin on his behalf. The saint, graciously and generously granting their prayers, bade him have faith and promised assistance. There was no delay: the vision and sleep ended together.

The man awoke and began to rejoice over the vision. Martin’s promise, however, immediately became reality. For suddenly the illustrious man found near him two golden vessels containing the sum of money about which he had anxiously petitioned Martin.

As soon as he saw them, with no one attending them, he wondered to himself and looked around in every direction, fearing that someone might have placed so much money there to test him. He remained astonished.

His servants, who had been waiting at a distance to see the outcome of his prayer, noticed his concern and came closer. They declared that, while they were keeping watch, no one had been present to deposit the vessels. They were affected no less by the miracle than by joy.

Then the marquis said: “I believe that the wonder-working Martin has sent me from the heavenly treasures the sum of money by which I am bound as a debtor in these days. If only he would also produce the creditor, lest his visitation become an occasion for me to break faith.”

After saying this, he ordered the money to be gathered and carried to the lodging. Then, behold, at the entrance of the very church there appeared unexpectedly the man to whom he was indebted.

The marquis cried out for joy, explained the miracle, exalted Martin, called upon Martin, and caused Martin’s wonders to be proclaimed. At last he returned the money to the creditor.

The urban and rural population gathered. With the clergy proclaiming it, and with the marquis present and testifying, the miracle was related. The glory of Christ and the compassion of Martin were praised by all.

The illustrious man, adorned both by nobility and generosity, and further encouraged toward what was better by Martin’s extraordinary kindness, returned home and did not prove ungrateful for the saint’s benefits.

He founded a church in honor of Lord Martin on his own hereditary estate and enlarged it through his munificence with revenues from his own possessions. He established it permanently as an abbey by gathering a community of monks there and placing an abbot over them. To this day religious life flourishes there in honor of God and praise of Saint Martin, and generous service to Christ is performed daily.

It is believed that he, though inferior to the illustrious marquis in nobility of blood, proved himself noble in character, especially in his honor toward Martin. He too built at his own expense a church in Martin’s honor and acquired so much revenue for it that it could have supplied the fullest support for the community of monks serving God and blessed Martin there.

Both churches still flourish today, near the district of Susa, accessible to us as we enter Italy.

### III

In those days, the possessed were brought from every part of the country to the most holy tomb of the blessed man. In a wondrous manner, the power of the dead worked salvation among the living, and no one was disappointed of the health he desired except one whose faith in Martin’s power faltered.

At that time there was a certain demoniac, a young man of military lineage named Gimo, from the castle of Prierato. His parents had him brought to the saint’s basilica, bound in chains and accompanied by servants.

The demon who had invaded him and held him as a harsh master abused him as its own instrument, to the confusion of many. Whoever came into his presence burdened by guilt of a capital crime, the demon immediately and shamelessly exposed before everyone, through the man’s mouth, the time, place, person, and manner of the offense.

The demon had such knowledge of crimes that a certain cleric of the saint, Frederick by name, rich in possessions, of distinguished birth, and holding some rank in the church—for he was subdeacon—heard of it and was deeply troubled. He was troubled that God had permitted the devil such power to expose people, especially Christians, to disgrace.

At last he came into the demoniac’s presence with this complaint. The devil directed the eyes of the possessed man toward him and spoke through his mouth: “And you reproach us from a sound head, though last night you committed such a crime with such a person in such a place.”

The cleric blushed. Turning away from the demoniac, he summoned a priest and withdrew privately. He condemned with a contrite spirit the crime the demon had charged him with, together with any other matters that weighed upon his conscience; he confessed them in a humble voice, submitted himself to the priest’s judgment, and gladly accepted the penance imposed upon him.

Thus, strengthened by the power of faith, he returned at last to the demoniac’s presence and said: “And what do you say about me?”

The demon fixed its fierce eyes upon him, as was its custom, and, after looking at him for a long time, said: “Depart from me, for I find nothing of ours in you.”

When the cleric heard this, placing the glory of Christ and the power of holy confession above his own shame, he cried out and said: “Hear, faithful people; attend, O peoples, to the power of our faith, and how wondrous and effective is the unspeakable sacrament of confession.

“You who were present heard how many shameful things the demon who possesses this man charged me with—and they were true. But now, after confession and the true renunciation of sins from the heart, behold, it recognized nothing belonging to itself in me.

“Therefore let us all together faithfully beseech God to free this man from the demon that possesses him.”

Then the demon spoke through the possessed man: “I fear none of you, nor will I release my wrestler because of you. Martin alone can do this—and even then only after a Mass has been celebrated in his honor.”

When the clerics heard this, they took counsel among themselves and said: “Although the devil is a liar, it is certainly sometimes compelled to speak the truth. Therefore we do not take our faith from him, but from the one to whom, against its will, it bears witness. Let us celebrate the Mass of Lord Martin in this matter, believing in the one who makes good use even of evil things.”

There was no delay. The next day a solemn Mass was celebrated in honor of the saint. After the sacred Communion, while Martin was joyfully received into Abraham’s bosom and the clergy were singing, the devil, unable to bear such great praise of Martin, uttered a dreadful cry and left behind a dreadful odor. It departed from the possessed man and, unwillingly, left him healed.

When the cleric saw this, it did not seem enough to him merely to serve Saint Martin within the common clerical life. He professed Martin’s approved way of life, received the monastic habit and monastic discipline at the greater monastery, and, having become a monk, devoted himself to monastic observances. Later, because of the holiness of his life and his guardianship of religious discipline, he was appointed keeper of the order in that monastery.

O Martin, scarcely inferior in merit to any of the saints, second to none in power, and surpassed by none in the depths of charity! He wondrously healed the demoniac and mercifully granted that the man’s healing should become, for his own cleric, the cause of true salvation.

The healing of the possessed praises Martin. The wonder and devotion of the people magnify Martin. The cleric’s complete conversion to the Lord glorifies Martin. Everywhere Martin is considered so much more wondrous as the faith of those who ask and their devotion toward the Lord and toward Martin prove worthy of his favor.

### IV

At the same time, a certain Sanubertus, afflicted by a long illness for which no remedies had been effective, was brought on a bed to the tomb of blessed Martin. First, around his knees, where he suffered the more severe pain, he began to become wet with a considerable sweat. Then, as his veins warmed and his sinews were restored, he stretched out his feet as though they had come alive again.

Not long afterward, as the people watched, he rose up healed and returned to his own home on his own feet—he who had been carried there on the hands of others.

### V

Likewise, a certain woman named Roscelina had been possessed by an evil spirit for five years. She had been deprived of the use of all her limbs and had long been prevented even from entering the church.

After she entered the basilica of the holy bishop, she was immediately freed from the demon and, to the amazement of many, regained the agility of her entire body in an instant.

As she afterward returned home to prepare a candle, which she intended to bring and offer with the other faithful, she had no money at all with which to buy one. A certain monk, distinguished by angelic white hair, met her at the church door. He gave her a coin of the purest brightness and then suddenly disappeared.

The woman took the coin, showed it to the moneychangers, and borrowed three obols. With these she bought a candle and returned to offer it at the saint’s tomb. The woman herself made this event known to all the citizens of Tours.

### VI

At the same time, another woman named Agnes, from the town of Faye, had been deprived of the use of her hands and feet for two years. After long exertions she was able to reach the tomb of the blessed bishop. She received her health as quickly as she had asked for it.

### VII

When, in response to such great and manifest miracles, the clerics were ringing the bells and singing the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* in joyful voices, a certain cleric from the church of Saint Peter of the Maidens was afflicted by a cancerous ulcer on his foot.

Hearing the voice of those who were singing, he made his way as best he could, supported by the help of his companions, wishing to see the miracles being performed there. He entered the basilica of blessed Martin and immediately—wondrous to relate—was deemed worthy to obtain, that very hour, the health he had not asked for.

### VIII

A girl named Osanna had lost the use of her hands for work because of long-standing swelling in both hands. Having devoutly invoked the aid of the holy man, she was restored to her former health through the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

### IX

On that same day, a boy named Gaufridus had supported his unfortunate limbs with a staff for three years because his knees were contracted. Renewed by the power of blessed Martin, he deposited in the basilica of the holy confessor, suspended from a beam as a memorial for posterity, the staff he had used in place of a foot. Then, rejoicing and in good health, he returned home while the people watched.

[Col. 1042C] **X.** Nor must another similar miracle be left unmentioned. A certain woman named Maria had had the tendons of her legs severed with an iron instrument by her husband, at the devil’s instigation. Having lost the ability to walk, she had languished at home for three years. When she heard of the power of so many signs, she did not delay in approaching the tomb of the holy man, supporting herself with a staff and exerting herself as best she could. There she remained for a long while at prayer, in tears. A wondrous event followed. For when her prayer was completed, with many people watching, her tendons were rejoined and her knees restored, and suddenly the woman stood upright. Soon afterward she came home at a brisk pace; then, returning that same hour, she joyfully brought a curtain that she had at home and offered it with joy and devotion in memory of the holy man.

[Col. 1042D] **XI.** Moreover, a certain fisherman named Hedigunnis, whose two hands had long been bent and swollen and had prevented him from fishing, as soon as he touched the tomb of the holy bishop with firm faith, obtained the health he had asked for with a pure heart. Before the surrounding crowd, the swelling of both palms subsided and the pain departed. With his right hand restored, while the whole people acclaimed the praises of God and wept for joy, he made the sign of the cross.

**XII.** I believe that a no less glorious miracle should be added to these. As the proclamation of so many and such great signs spread everywhere, among the other afflicted people flocking from all sides to the memorial of the holy bishop there also came a wretched girl named Theophenia, [Col. 1043A] known to many because of the wasting—indeed, the near death—of her body. An incurable disease, which physicians call a fistula, had consumed all her flesh; scabies continually flowed through numerous openings, leaving her bloodless and emaciated. Thus, deprived of every hope of ever recovering her health, she received in an instant the soundness of all her limbs, the disease having been driven away through the merits of blessed Martin.

**XIII.** At the same time a young girl named Petronilla was fettered by such a grievous weakness that the soles of her feet, bent back toward her knees, were useless for their proper function. Carrying her paralysed limbs with two pieces of wood that she used in place of feet, she approached the mausoleum of blessed Martin with firm faith. Embracing it devoutly and kissing it in tears, [Col. 1043B] she invoked the name of the holy confessor and in that same hour was deemed worthy to obtain the complete health she had long desired.

**XIV.** Nor was a certain matron named Galliciana any less so. Born of no humble family and known to many, she was loved for her honourable conduct, but, worn out by a long illness of her entire body, she led a wretched life close to death. For, with her throat closed and the passages of her gullet obstructed, she had entirely lost both the ability and the desire to eat. At last, having received salutary advice, she was carried on horseback and led by the service of her attendants; then she prostrated herself at the tomb of Saint Martin. Not long afterward, when her prayer had been poured out, her whole body was renewed through the merits of blessed Martin. Giving thanks, she was raised from the pavement and, rejoicing and in good health, returned home after several days.

**XV.** On that same day a girl named Prima, saddened by the disability of contracted knees and the misfortune of a withered right hand, had led an unhappy life for eighteen years. Finally Christ restored her steps and renewed her right hand, and, to manifest the merits of his servant for the glory and praise of his name, sent her back home safe and joyful.

**XVI.** At that time there was also Alexandra, a woman known to many because of the affliction of a withered foot. She had miserably carried the dead foot for three years, attached to the framework of her living body, not as an instrument but as a burden, whereas it ought rather to have been carried by others. Strengthened by faith, she approached the tomb of the glorious confessor, where many sick people are healed every day, and prostrated herself on the pavement with tears and prayers. Without delay—for it was the Lord’s Day—she obtained complete health from the Lord before the watching crowd, and the next day she returned home rejoicing.

[Col. 1043D] **XVII.** On that same day another paralysed woman, deprived for a long time of the function of all her limbs, was carried by the faithful on a pallet to the tomb of the holy man. Through the merits of the holy man, Christ drove away all her illness and graciously granted her the gift of living another day.

**XVIII.** Likewise, on that same day a girl beautiful in face, but whose name we do not know, was freed from the same affliction through the merits of glorious blessed Martin, to the praise of Christ, with many standing by and weeping for joy.

[Col. 1044A] **XIX.** About the same time a young girl named Guiburgis, deprived of the light of her eyes from her mother’s breasts, heard of the miracles of the holy confessor and earnestly begged to be led to his tomb. When she had been brought there, all blindness was dispelled and she received without delay the light she had long desired. Rejoicing and giving thanks, she returned home the following day.

**XX.** A boy named Orientius, who had long been afflicted by paralytic disease, touched the mausoleum of the blessed man with a pure heart and unfeigned faith. To make the merits of his servant increasingly manifest, Christ drove away all his weakness and restored him completely to health. He returned that same day, having previously been carried by the services of his mother.

[Col. 1044B] **XXI.** At the same time Gonerannus Burellus—for that was the sick man’s name—received a remedy of divine power through Saint Martin. For seven years he had been deprived of the use of his broken and withered arm. Full of faith, he came with other believers to spend the night at the vigil of Saint Martin the Confessor. As he prayed with intense weeping and groaning that Christ might be appeased toward him and restore his former health, he suddenly discovered that his arm, which had long been bent, was being divinely extended. Once he had been healed that same hour, blood flowed most abundantly from it, providing the watching people with a glorious and extraordinary spectacle. How many praises the multitude of believers then sang to the Lord, and with how many acclamations they extolled the confessor, we leave the reader to judge.

[Col. 1044C] **XXII.** Among the other events that have occurred here, there is one—not greater than those I have already described, but so clear and illustrious a miracle that, I believe, no one throughout the whole territory of Tours failed either to see it or to learn of it by hearing, and no one could or should in any way have forgotten it. An elderly peasant named Herbetus, from a village called Noviacus, was cleaning wheat in the threshing-floor at midday during the summer when he was seized by a demon. Foaming and vomiting, burning with fever and raging, he lost the use of his tongue after three days. Since for six days he took no food by himself at all, his family led him to the tomb of blessed Martin. When it was touched, Christ performed three miracles there at once and in an instant: the evil spirit was driven out, the bonds of his tongue were loosened, and the man was freed from every illness. Finally, when he was being led to the shrine of the holy confessor in thanksgiving, he begged all those around him, laymen and priests alike, not to allow his enemy—namely, the demon—to follow him. This sign, which we have briefly touched upon in accordance with the truth, became known throughout the entire city of Tours, the man himself recounting it.

[Col. 1044D] **XXIII.** On the feast of the protomartyr Stephen, which is celebrated in summer, while the clerics were singing the nocturnal office, a certain paralytic from a village called Puteolus, deprived for many years of the use of all his limbs, kept vigil at the saint’s tomb with many others and was restored to the health he had long desired. How many tears his master, Alermus of Carenciacum, a nobleman, and many others with him, of both sexes and various ages, shed there for joy, and how many thanks they gave you, good Jesus, it is beyond our power to say.

[Col. 1045A] **XXIV.** We also saw a certain boy named Peter, born to respectable and honourable parents in the territory of the city of Orléans. Illness, not nature, had bent him for two years and would not permit him to raise his eyes toward heaven. We saw him walking briskly with his whole body upright and, by displaying his restored health, making known the power of the holy confessor to the peoples arriving from every direction.

[Col. 1045B] **XXV.** No less was another boy, brought from the city of Le Mans, whom Count Ingelger of Anjou had carefully raised and adopted as a son. As soon as he touched the saint’s mausoleum, he was healed of the same affliction.

**XXVI.** At the same time another boy named Guffierus, crippled by a long-standing weakness of his limbs, was being brought by his mother on a beast of burden to the saint’s memorial. While he was still far away—that is, four miles from this city—he felt the remedy of divine power being granted to him. He immediately descended from the animal on which he was riding and came to the confessor’s shrine at a brisk pace, completely well. Before the assembled faithful he described both the old illness he had endured and the new health that Christ had bestowed upon him through the merits of blessed Martin.

**XXVII.** A woman from Barbivium named Ermengardis was hurrying to the memorial of the man of God when, while she was still far away on the road, the Orient from on high visited her (Luke 1:78). For, as we learned from her own account, when she had left her house to hurry to the vigil of the saint, she recovered on the road the sight of her eyes, which she had lost long before, to the amazement of those accompanying her. No longer requiring anyone to guide her, she reached the place she had desired; there, after pouring out her prayer and solemnly presenting her offering, she returned home the following day rejoicing and in good health, giving thanks.

[Col. 1045D] **XXVIII.** About the same time two most wretched women, whose names have escaped my memory, had long suffered from the affliction of a fistula. For a full week they filled our entire basilica with their cries and disturbed our hearts with their sorrowful lamentations. At last the Father of mercy, granting health equally to them and to us, brought their misery to an end.

**XXIX.** At that time another girl, known throughout our entire city because of her long-standing blindness, spent several days keeping vigil at the tomb of the servant of God with tears and prayers. The old darkness was driven away, and in an instant she received an unfamiliar light.

[Col. 1046A] **XXX.** I do not think this should be omitted, for I rejoice that I learned it from the account of venerable persons. Theophania, a servant of Christ and abbess of the monastery of blessed Mary the perpetual Virgin, called Bellusmons, wished to honour the holy servant of God with religious gifts. She had prepared candles to offer him, but, being occupied with ecclesiastical business as usual, delayed in bringing them. Then blessed Martin appeared by night in a vision to one of her servants named Bosogonus, a man of good reputation. Addressing him kindly and stroking his head with a gentle hand, he said: “Come, brother, rise and go to your lady, and tell her from me not to delay any longer in rendering the little gifts that she had vowed to give me.” When Bosogonus awoke, although he was entirely unaware of what his mistress had promised the holy confessor, he ran quickly to her and revealed what the saint had said to him. When the religious woman heard his words, she immediately remembered her promise and reproached herself for her negligence. In order at last to fulfil her vows, she came hastily and solemnly and devoutly presented to the confessor the candles that she had promised him long before.

[Col. 1046C] **XXXI.** A certain young man named Herveus, from the territory of Poitiers, had for about ten years carried his withered arm to many shrines of the saints in the hope of obtaining health, but had as yet received no reward for his labour. On the vigil of Saint Lawrence, which was observed as the Lord’s Day, he came with other believers, with devout faith and a pious mind, to the tomb of the most gracious Father. When this had been done, through the merits of the holy confessor he received in that same hour the health he had long desired, while all the people acclaimed the praises of Christ.

**XXXII.** On another day two young men, both deaf and mute—one called Draco, from a village called Launacum, and the other, whose name is omitted in the text [lacuna], from a village called Cameliacum—eagerly kissed the mausoleum of the most merciful confessor with beautiful faith. In one and the same hour they were deemed worthy, through the merits of the holy man, to receive the use of both tongue and ears, which nature had denied them.

**XXXIII.** Likewise, on that very day a woman named Hildegardis, from a village called Novus Burgus, condemned to the same misfortune as the young men mentioned above, obtained from Christ an equal grace.

[Col. 1046D] **XXXIV.** Later, on the solemnity of blessed Lawrence, when a boy named Andreas from Oratorium, who had spent seven years in the darkness of blindness, was dragged by his mother to the confessor’s shrine, he immediately deserved, before the surrounding crowd, suddenly to see the unknown daylight amid the arms of his mother.

**XXXV.** On that same day a woman named Aiga, from the castle called Cormanacum, had been sorrowfully afflicted for five years by weakness of contracted joints. Through the merits of the most merciful Father she was restored to her former health.

**XXXVI.** On that same day Christ also deigned to free a girl from Asiacum named Hildegardis from the same calamity, to the honour of his servant.

[Col. 1047A] **XXXVII.** Likewise, on that very day a boy named Fulco, from the village of Saint Clement, had long carried a weakened foot with the aid of a staff. As soon as he touched the saint’s tomb, he was free of all pain. Another boy, who had lost the use of his hands, departed with him, restored to health.

**XXXVIII.** After this, a boy named John from Semblenciacum was so afflicted by an annual fistula in his arm that, after the flesh had been consumed by putrefaction, even the bones, eaten away by worms, fell out from within. Keeping vigil for several days at the tomb of the holy bishop and begging the Lord Jesus with repeated groans to have mercy on him, he had the deadly disease driven away. Having completely recovered his former health through the merits of blessed Martin, he provided great joy to the people, greater joy to us, and the greatest joy to his own family.

[Col. 1047B] **XXXIX.** The merits of the holy confessor were also remarkable and should be proclaimed everywhere for this reason: he was accustomed, through the grace of Christ, to heal absent and distant sick people no less than those who were present—that is, attending his tomb—provided that they had firm hope and faith. Let not one or two but several examples be brought forward. Garinus, a boy from Faia, was afflicted by dizziness of the head and distress throughout his body. At the same time a girl named Ermengardis, from a village called Bucseias, suffered the injury of contracted hands, because of her angry mother’s curse—or rather, by the inscrutable judgment of God. When their parents and relatives, full of faith, made a vow on their behalf and brought them to the saint’s shrine, they were still far away on the road, yet rejoiced that through blessed Martin they had received from Christ the health they had long desired.

[Col. 1047C] **XL.** At that time there lived near the castle of Saumur a wealthy woman known to many, but whose name has escaped my memory. She had suffered the misfortune of contracted palms. Having heard the fame of the signs Christ performed through his servant, she retired to bed one night so that the following day, if life permitted, she might hasten with a worthy offering to the vigil of the holy confessor. She fell asleep and immediately awoke; then she opened her renewed hands with such ease as though she had never before suffered any illness in them. When morning came, she went to the saint’s shrine to fulfil her vows. There, after pouring out her prayer with tears and solemnly presenting her offering, she returned home joyful and in good health.

[Col. 1047D] **XLI.** There was likewise an Osanna in the territory of the castle of Chinon who suffered from a long-standing illness of her entire body. Having heard of the power of such great miracles, she was unable to walk on her own feet to the saint’s memorial in order to recover her health, and therefore had a vehicle prepared for herself. When she wished to climb into it, she felt in that same hour that the remedy of divine power had come to her. Finally, abandoning the vehicle, she did not delay in coming joyfully and with offerings to the tomb of blessed Martin at a brisk pace, and in due order recounted to the surrounding people the health divinely granted to her through the merits of the holy bishop.

[Col. 1048A] **XLII.** A boy named Gaufridus from the village called Blarenciacum was also freed from the same calamity, at the same time and through the intervention of the holy confessor, in an instant.

**XLIII.** At the same time a woman named Ermengardis from the castle of Montaureum, condemned for five years by the misfortune of a broken and withered arm, provided the material for a miracle of the saint. For, after spending the nights of an entire month keeping vigil at his mausoleum with much weeping and groaning, she was finally visited by divine power. Her arm came back to life at the end of the month: the bone was restored, the veins filled, and the tendons renewed. Thereafter it served her body for necessary tasks no less actively than the other arm.

[Col. 1048B] **XLIV.** Likewise, at the same time a certain boy from a village called Senterius, afflicted by the same illness, obtained a similar grace from God.

**XLV.** But a girl named Menoldis from the village called Montricardum was resting one summer night with the harvesters on the threshing-floor when she suddenly saw most terrifying spirits in the form of armed soldiers running about above her and oppressing her violently. Terrified by this horrible vision and rendered almost insane, she lost the use of speech in that same hour. When, after three weeks, her family had brought her to the saint’s tomb, she soon opened her mouth in praise of Christ and his servant Martin—the mouth that the terrifying apparition of the demons had, by divine permission, closed. We believe this happened so that the works of God might be manifested in her through blessed Martin.

[Col. 1048C] **XLVI.** Two girls also—one named Legardis, from a village called Espeniacum, and the other from the castle called Vilencastrum—were both deaf and mute. He who has done all things well caused them, on one and the same day, to hear and speak, to the honour of his servant (Mark 7:37). Therefore no mortal could recount or express how many people gathered there from different regions at the memorial of the holy confessor offered praise to the Creator.

[Col. 1048D] **XLVII.** Likewise, on that day the Lord mercifully deigned to visit a boy named William from the castle called Prulliacum. A deforming hump, growing along his spine, weighed upon his entire back. Since he had been completely bent from his mother’s womb, the hump was removed, and through blessed Martin he was renewed and straightened. Thus he received in an instant the beauty of form that nature had denied him, while the people wept for joy and gave thanks.

**XLVIII.** The following day a girl named Joanna from a village called Crevanturus had for two years been condemned by the weakness of a contracted body. Forced to use the functions of her palms and knees as though they were feet, she entered the church of blessed Martin with a pure heart and an unfeigned mind. Immediately, in the midst of the surrounding crowd, she was gladdened through blessed Martin by the gift of the health she had long desired.

**XLIX.** Likewise, on that day a boy named Bernardus from the castle of Montesaurus, afflicted for ten years, rejoiced that he had received an equal grace of divine favour.

[Col. 1049A] **L.** I do not think this should be omitted, since I do not doubt that it is known to many believers. A small child had developed stones because his bladder was diseased. His mother carried him to the tomb of the holy man in the hope of obtaining health. After spending the whole night sleepless, gripped by excessive pains, he awaited only the arrival of death. At last, when morning came, the urge to urinate came upon him. When his mother perceived this, she immediately placed her hand beneath the child’s little penis. Seeing a stone like a bean expelled with the urine, she turned her lamentation into joy and her tears into praises, and returned home that same hour with her restored child.

[Col. 1049B] **LI.** After a few days had passed, a girl named Vinargandis from a certain town in the district of Bourges called Paludellum, deprived of the light of her eyes from the very cradle, was deemed worthy to kiss the tomb of the holy confessor. The old darkness was driven away, and, before everyone present, with God’s favour, she received in an instant the clearest sight.

**LII.** As time went on, two boys—one named Peter, from the town called Castellio, and the other named William, from a village called Luciacum in the territory of Bourges—were both horribly tormented by the attacks of unclean spirits. They gnashed their teeth violently and tore themselves and everyone who came near them with bites. For this reason they were bound with ropes and, having completely lost their senses, were brought with great difficulty to the place where the body of the holy man is honoured. After remaining there for several days, through the mercy of the Lord and the intercession of blessed Martin they were freed from the rage of the evil spirits. Their senses restored, they returned home unharmed.

[Col. 1049C] **LIII.** About the same time two smiths—one named Robert from the castle of Busenciacum, the other named Gaufridus from Argeium—had long suffered from withered arms and contracted hands, and were subject to prolonged idleness, not voluntary [lacuna], but they were subject to it. After keeping vigil for several nights at the tomb of the man of God with prayers and vows, they were both restored in the same hour to the health they had desired for two years.

[Col. 1049D] **LIV.** Nor do I think this should be left unmentioned, for I know that it happened in the presence of many. The daughter of a certain woman in the city of Tours was afflicted with the burning fever of fevers. The heat consuming her body had so wasted the little girl’s marrow and body that no hope of life remained in her; she was already being mourned as lost. What more need be said? The physicians’ remedies failed, and only grief remained for the mother. Turning all her hope toward the holy man, she lifted up the body that, as we have said, was already almost lifeless. Although many urged her to prepare a burial for the extinguished corpse, she carried the nearly dead limbs of her child, full of faith, to the tomb of the man of God, hastening there with weeping and wailing. After prayer and an offering had been presented, the girl immediately rejoiced that, with every pain driven away, she had in an instant recovered the health of her entire body through the mediation of blessed Martin.

[Col. 1050A] **LV.** Likewise, I must not be silent about a similar miracle. On that same day another woman at Pont de Cher was mourning a little child already given up to the danger of death. While the infant awaited only death and the mother was already thinking about his burial, believers advised her to make a vow on behalf of the child and bring him to the memorial of the holy man. When she had done so, the little boy recovered his health, and the mother returned home joyfully with her child.

[Col. 1050B] **LVI.** We omit many miracles that we saw and heard, lest we seem to bore the reader. But what we write we testify before God: at the venerable memorial of this saint of whom we speak, the illnesses of many weak people are frequently healed. Sight is restored to the blind; indeed, the world itself is either given anew to them or returned after being lost. The dull ears of the deaf, their insensibility driven away, are granted the use of their proper sense. Hands and feet weakened by disease are restored to their desired functions. The paralysed are repaired, the withered renewed, and those possessed by demons are freed. But why delay over individual cases? Let anyone who has time enumerate the healings, as he may enumerate the illnesses. To conclude everything briefly: whoever, afflicted by any ailment, approached his tomb full of faith obtained from God the healing assistance that he rightly and faithfully sought.

[Col. 1050C] But let us now return to the grace of miracles. Vodium is the name of the estate where a sick man named Hugo lay. For many days he had been weakened throughout his entire body, and his relatives repeatedly urged him to implore the help of blessed Martin with a pure heart and commit himself to him with complete devotion. Finally, already near death, he yielded to their advice. As soon as he devoted himself to the holy man with firm faith, the illness gradually receded, and he began to recover; leaving his bed, he walked about. The next day he set out, attempting to come to the saint’s memorial, and on the road he received such health from God that it was as though he had never before suffered any illness.

**LVII.** It is worthwhile to entrust to the treasury of memory a glorious event concerning three sufferers from dropsy. They lived in different places but were afflicted by the same disease; all their limbs had been swollen by dropsy, and they had abandoned hope of ever recovering their health. The first was from the district of Le Mans, from a town called Malicorna. The second was from the province of Anjou, from a village called Burgulium. The third was from the territory of Poitiers, from a borough called Estubiliacum. These three, continually entreating the Saviour’s mercy in the same place, that he might grant them health through the merits of blessed Martin, though they lived in the different provinces mentioned above, obtained the grace of the same spiritual medicine.

[Col. 1051A] **LVIII.** On that same day a certain woman named Maria was freed from the same affliction as the three men mentioned above.

**LIX.** About the same time another woman named Nia, from the castle of Loca, was mute, deaf, and blind. Through the saint’s mediation, in a single instant she received from God sight, hearing, and the use of her tongue.

[Col. 1052A] **LX.** A little boy named William, from the town called Montaureum, was already surrendered to death and near it, since his illness was growing stronger. His mother, with complete devotion, entrusted her dying son to the merits of blessed Martin. When she had done so, the child, already held in the jaws of death, was immediately given life.

## In the Year of Our Lord 889. Luidbert, Archbishop of Mainz

[Col. 1051]

## Historical Notice

*(Gallia Christiana vetus, vol. I, under the archbishops of Mainz.)*

[Col. 1051B] Luidbert, successor of Charles, is recorded under the year 863 in the *Annals of Fulda*. He is mentioned in the Third Council of Soissons in 866, whose bishops, in a synodal letter written to Pope Nicholas, congratulated him that, through the pope’s favour, he had been granted the pallium of a bishop, and, out of reverence for his holiness and the greatness of his wisdom, requested—through the intervention of King Charles the Bald—that he be added to that synod. He attended the assembly at Metz in 868, held at Saint Arnulf’s, and the meetings held at Aachen in 870 with Kings Louis and Charles, as the capitularies of Charles the Bald relate. He was also present at the dedication of the metropolitan church of Cologne in 873.

During his pontificate the Third Council of Mainz was convened on the occasion of King Arnulf, both to reform ecclesiastical discipline and because of the incursions of the Normans. In the city he founded the collegiate church of Saint Maurice. There survives a letter of the monk Otfrid addressed to him, which is read at the end of Hincmar’s little works, as well as a letter of Pope John VIII preserved in Ivo, chapter 51. Finally, he departed this life in 889 and was buried at Saint Alban. Regino, Otto of Freising, Trithemius in the *Chronicon Hirsaugiense*, Aventinus in book IV of the *Annals of Bavaria*, Serarius, and the author of the *Annals of the Franks of Fulda* mention further details about him; the latter calls him a noble archbishop, distinguished for uprightness of character and learned.

[Col. 1051]

## Letter of Luidbert to King Louis

*(Bibliotheca Patrum Maxima, vol. XVI.)*

[Col. 1051]

[Col. 1051C] To the most devout, most beloved, and most flourishing in the Catholic faith, King Louis, Luidbert, archbishop and servant of the holy Church of God, sends present and perpetual salvation in the Lord.

I have no time for silence or deliberation. The matter does not permit me to remain silent; if I abandon it, I shall be without excuse before our Lord Jesus Christ, whose concern it is, and I shall be convicted of having rashly violated the loyalty I promised you. I have been placed on a watchtower, where I see the danger threatening you; if I conceal it through sluggish or faithless silence, and neglect the Church of God, whose pastoral care and solicitude I, unworthy though I am, have undertaken, I shall appear to be a hireling rather than a shepherd.

For its primacy and dignity are being gravely shaken and dishonoured in the see of Saint Peter, by a persecution of a kind unheard of and hidden—not from unbelievers and those who do not know the Lord, but from those who, which is grievous and lamentable, ought to be the leaders and rulers of God’s people. They assail it with injuries, attempting to place human things before divine things. The pain that exists in the head must necessarily spread little by little through the limbs unless a health-giving and swift remedy comes to its aid. [Col. 1051D]

Therefore, although I know that your prudence has no need of human admonitions—for it has drawn the most sincere teaching from the grace of the Holy Spirit—it is nevertheless my duty both to disclose what has happened and to point out what must be done. You know the danger that terribly threatens God’s people, and it cannot be hidden from you, since it has been heard everywhere. Even the elements themselves, so to speak, tremble: rulers who ought to labour for the salvation of the weak have abandoned the path of salvation, rush headlong, and open before those who follow them a pit of perdition.

[Col. 1052C] Therefore I exhort your prudence, which loves truth and justice, to deliberate, in accordance with the wisdom divinely granted to you, with those who know the law of God and love his justice, [Col. 1052D] how, once the scandals of dissension that the Sower of tares tries by cunning plots to scatter have been removed, the desired peace and unity may be restored to the Churches, and how vigilant progress may quickly be made, lest careless security provide an opportunity for wounds.

For the whole body of the Church has not yet been injured, although, with its head struck by insults, some of its limbs may appear weakened. Therefore, if those who are found to be sound can be induced to accept medicine, they must come to the aid of the weakened; otherwise, according to the command of our true physician, they will be held accountable, lest the whole body fall into destruction (Matthew 5). [Col. 1053A]

For this reason it seems necessary and useful to me [Col. 1054A] that the devout prince Charles, your brother, be promptly consulted on this matter by envoys and letters sent by you, so that both he himself and the priests of his kingdom, who have thus far remained free from such filth, may join you and your bishops and share the same care and concern with you. Then, after you have successfully and peacefully returned, with God’s help, from the journey on which you intend to depart, may you, by common agreement and united effort, restore peace and harmony to the holy Catholic and apostolic Church through orthodox doctrines, with the Lord’s help.

## Authors of the Ninth Century, Year Uncertain

## Auxilius the Frank, Priest

[Col. 1053]

[Col. 1053]

## Historical Notice

*(In Fabricius, Bibliotheca of Medieval and Late Latin.)*

[Col. 1053B] Auxilius the Frank, a priest ordained by Formosus around the year 894, wrote two books on the ordinations performed by Formosus, against Stephen VII and Sergius [Note: See Baronius under the year 908.], and against the internal discord of the Roman Church; or, as Sigebert says in chapter 112, concerning the person of the Accuser and the Defender, on the ordinations, deordinations, and superordinations of the Roman pontiffs, and on the deordinations and superordinations of those ordained by them.

John Morinus published the work at the end of his distinguished treatise on sacred ordinations, p. 348 of the Paris edition of 1655, and pp. 285–294 of the Antwerp edition of 1694. From there it was reprinted in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyon, vol. XVII, at the very beginning, and in more recent editions, in volume XII of Baronius. His *Dialogue on the Cause and Affair of Pope Formosus* appears in Mabillon, [Col. 1054B] volume IV of the *Analecta*, pp. 610–624, and in the new edition, pp. 28, 32, and 39.

Whether Auxilius was a Frank or an Italian is uncertain, since he reveals nothing about the matter himself. Although he seems to affirm that he was ordained by Pope Formosus, I would not readily accept his assertion, for elsewhere he writes that he sat with the other bishops at a synod held in Rome by Pope Nicholas I, whereas it is entirely certain that Nicholas preceded Formosus. Therefore, when he says in the dialogue that he was ordained by Formosus, he is speaking not in his own person but in the person of the clerics who, having received orders from Formosus, defended the validity of their ordination. I wrote this in my notes on Pagi under the year 897.

[Col. 1053]

## Two Books of Auxilius on the Ordinations Performed by Pope Formosus

### Preface by John Morinus, Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory

This preface explains from whom the books were obtained and who Auxilius was; that much can be extracted from them to illuminate the history of certain pontiffs; that his arguments do not always reach their intended point; that the action of Stephen VII, the pontiff, against Formosus is ambiguous; that Formosus himself gave him ample occasion for it; and, finally, that certain passages are noted which must be read with caution.

[Col. 1055A] When, in the year of salvation 1641, Toulouse happened to lie on the route I was then traveling, I remained there for eight days. In the meantime, while I was examining the library of the most illustrious prelate, Lord de Montchal, archbishop of Toulouse—a library rich in many manuscript codices—these little books of Auxilius fell into my hands, written in an ancient script, if I remember correctly, and one approaching the author’s own period. I copied out much of what I foresaw would be useful to me.

Later, when I had spoken with our reverend Father Viguier, a priest of our congregation, a most learned man and a most diligent and penetrating investigator of antiquity, both sacred and profane, he told me that he possessed little books of Auxilius copied in his own hand from an ancient codex which he had perhaps happened upon by chance [Col. 1055B] in a monastery of Lorraine. He indicated the monastery, but I do not remember it. He later compared his copy with another ancient codex belonging to the reverend Father Jacques Sirmond, known to every learned man. At my request, he willingly granted me the use of his copy for editing and publication.

Thus, reader, I obtained the little books that I now publicly present to you. Papyrius Masson formerly sent the titles of the later book to Cardinal Baronius at Rome. Baronius valued them so highly that, lest they perish, he appended them to the final volume of his *Annals*. The cardinal calls this book the *Acts of Pope Formosus*. In the same place he transcribes in full Auxilius’s letter to Leo, bishop of Nola, just as the final chapters of the little book—chapters 29 and 39, but chapter 32 in our codex—also present them to us, [Col. 1055C] whereas the earlier book was wholly unknown to Baronius and Papyrius.

Who Auxilius was is unclear. He was not an Italian, as he himself testifies in Book II, chapter 31. For he objects to himself in these words:

> “Moreover, since you are a man of a foreign people and, among us, require the necessities of human life, what concern is it of yours to resist our disputes?”

And shortly afterward:

> “If you are newcomers and foreigners, are you permitted to accuse, judge, or prejudge the rulers of the Church?” etc.

He does not deny this; indeed, he assumes it in his reply. He says only that he belongs to the group whom the apostle Peter calls “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Peter II). He maintains that this is sufficient to prevent him from being excluded from giving testimony in this matter, as you may read more fully at that point. But whose subject he was is difficult to say, since he does not indicate it in his little books.

That he was a Frank can scarcely be doubted. But in that period the name “Franks” was understood to include Germans no less than Gauls. Which of the two he was is unclear, nor is there much reason to investigate the matter. At the end of the same chapter, however, he appears to deny that he was a foreigner, although he had admitted this at the beginning.

He was a presbyter and had been ordained by Pope Formosus, as may be inferred from the beginning of chapter 31. This also seems to be shown by the fact that bishops consulted him about the canons and their observance. But the final chapter of the first book makes both points explicit: that he was at least a presbyter and that he had been ordained by Formosus.

Many things may be drawn from these little books that shed light on several events of the greatest importance in the history of the pontiffs—Formosus, Stephen VII, John IX, and Sergius III—which have been handed down to us very obscurely, partly through the negligence and partly through the scarcity of historians of that age. From them it becomes clear that the pontiffs Stephen and Sergius were not so wicked, nor Formosus so holy, as many have persuaded themselves; and that Stephen and Sergius had plausible, indeed apparently serious, reasons for invalidating Formosus’s ordinations.

For Formosus had been deposed and degraded by Pope John VIII on account of various crimes, reduced to lay communion, and expelled from the bishopric of Porto. The sentence of Pope John against him is published in volume III of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 432. He was accused, together with certain others, of conspiring against the life of Pope John; of plotting the ruin of Emperor Charles the Bald and the kingdom of France; of wishing to betray Rome to the Saracens so as to involve the pope in its destruction; and of committing many other crimes, which are recounted in the sentence of John VIII.

Because of such atrocious crimes, the pontiff deposed the fugitive and contumacious man from every priestly and clerical ministry and pronounced an anathema against him. Nor was he content to pronounce this at Rome: he sent his sentence and the record of the proceedings through his legates to all the bishops of Gaul and Germany assembled at Pontigon, urging them to ensure that his sentence was published throughout their dioceses, as may also be seen in volume III of the *Councils*, part I, chapter 5, of the Council of Pontigon.

When Formosus and his fellow criminals persisted in their crimes and contumacy, John VIII came to Troyes in Gaul two years later. There, having assembled a synod of the bishops of Gaul and Belgium, he renewed the excommunication of Formosus and, with all the bishops consenting and subscribing, once again pronounced it himself. This may be read in Aimo, Book V, chapter 37, and in volume III of the *Councils of Gaul*, at the Council of Troyes XI, chapter 4. The same pontiff also wrote to various nobles of the provinces, urging them carefully to avoid “association with the anathematized Formosus,” as may be seen in letter 305 of that pontiff.

[Col. 1056D] The supporters of Formosus did indeed oppose to this the fact that Pope Marinus, the successor of John VIII, had absolved Formosus from the anathema and restored him to his orders and bishopric. But whatever may be said about this absolution, the adversaries of Formosus further replied that he had unjustly and contrary to the canons arranged to be transferred from the see of Porto to the Roman see, something that had never previously been done in that see. For all pontiffs elected before Formosus had been chosen from among the Roman deacons and presbyters.

That crime of episcopal translation, entirely foreign to Roman custom, was aggravated by Formosus’s oath, by which he had solemnly promised Pope John that he would never return to Rome. Yet he had not only returned; he had also sought and obtained the pontificate.

Nor did they repeat Formosus’s ordinations without precedent. They claimed to be following the example of Stephen IV, who, after summoning a great council of Italian, Frankish, and German bishops, declared, with everyone’s consent, the ordination of Pope Constantine invalid and void because, while still a layman, he had been elected to the pontificate and had received all the orders within a few days, with scarcely any intervals observed.

Nor were they content with Constantine’s degradation. They also declared that all who had been ordained by him had acquired nothing through that ordination and therefore had to be ordained again, if the Churches to which they had been assigned [Col. 1057B] urgently requested them. By these and similar arguments and examples those pontiffs defended their bold action. Perhaps they relied on other reasons which Auxilius passes over, since he was an adversary of those pontiffs.

Nor should those reordinations and superordinations be judged as they would be judged today. The matter had not yet become legally settled, nor had it yet passed into the axiom of the Catholic faith that any ordination celebrated according to the rite of the Church by a bishop ordained according to that same rite is valid and may under no circumstances be repeated.

There were various and contradictory traditions on this subject, various practices, and various and contradictory answers from learned men. These little books teach this variety most evidently, indeed more clearly than daylight. They show that the dispute between the parties concerned not merely the exercise of orders but, first and principally, the very substance of orders.

So far as may be gathered from their proceedings, all parties commonly acknowledged that ordinations performed by Catholic bishops according to the prescriptions of the canons and ritual books were never to be repeated. But on many questions that commonly arise in this matter, opinions differed. These questions were not universally settled either in that century or in the two following centuries, and consequently various practices concerning them are recorded.

For example: whether an ordination undertaken contrary to the canons was nevertheless an ordination; and whether a bishop who had been deposed, degraded, and condemned to lay communion could ordain. There were other doubts, but these two particularly troubled the pontiffs of that time and stirred up immense disturbances.

Many of the testimonies Auxilius adduces in support of his position do not reach the point at issue.
