He confuses many things whose reasoning is different, as though they expressed the same view, and he does not always examine with sufficient accuracy whether the arguments he employs actually touch the matter at hand. We leave these points, however, to the judgment of the reader.

He attacks at great length the action of Pope Stephen, who summoned the dead Pope Formosus to judgment, ordered him exhumed, stripped the condemned man of his pontifical vestments, and, after having three fingers cut off, thrown him into the Tiber. Nor is he alone in this: most later writers also exaggerate this deed tragically and therefore load that pontiff with insults and reproaches and [Col. 1058A] tear him to pieces.

This action is ambiguous and, viewed from different perspectives, assumes different and opposing appearances. Viewed from one perspective, it certainly seems cruel, inhuman, and barbarous. Almost all historians who have so far written about this action have viewed it unfavorably and have therefore assailed Pope Stephen with innumerable insults, showing no respect for so great a dignity.

But if someone considers it from another perspective, and a more favorable one, it will appear to be a just and rigorous observance of the laws, and a zeal for ecclesiastical discipline worthy of respect—just as those are praised who spared neither princes, relatives, nor even guilty sons, but punished their crimes according to the laws.

Let us leave this matter undecided, however, prejudging neither side. Let each person in this case have his own preference and perspective. I ask the reader to note only this: the whole dispute among those pontiffs had nothing whatsoever to do with the faith. It concerned only two matters subject to human opinion.

The first was a particular question: whether the promotion of Formosus to the papacy had been canonical. One side affirmed this; the other denied it. The second was a universal question, but one not yet decided or confirmed by a peremptory decree: whether a bishop who had been deposed and degraded could validly confer orders.

The reader should also be warned that certain things in this author are evidently remote from the truth. It is enough to mark them; to compose a lengthy argument refuting them would lead us very far from our purpose.

In Book I, chapter 11, he accuses Hosius [Col. 1058C] of Novatianism and attacks him in the following four chapters, as well as in Book II, chapter 23. His reason is that Hosius is reported to have said in canons 1 and 2 of the Council of Sardica that no lay communion should be granted to a bishop who had changed his see through fraud and bribery, even if he offered as an excuse that the people had sought him.

Yet the entire Council of Sardica, which is regarded as universal and as one with the Council of Nicaea, approves and confirms Hosius’s position. Nor are those two canons considered to be Hosius’s, but the council’s. “Does this please everyone?” All the bishops said: “It pleases us.”

Moreover, the manner in which the Fathers impose that penalty directly contradicts the heresy of the Novatians. For it shows that the imposition or remission of that penalty lay within their power, whereas denial of this truth constituted Novatianism.

In the preface to Book II and in his reply, he writes that an order received through pure coercion is valid, and proves and illustrates this by a similarly absurd argument. He repeats the same point in the final chapter of the book:

> “If someone,” he says, “is unwilling to believe in Christ but is baptized by force, and afterward consents to believe in Christ, should he be baptized again? Certainly not.”

But baptism of this sort—and likewise ordination—does not imprint a character, as all the doctors teach, and as is stated most explicitly in the *Extravagantes*, chapter *Majores Ecclesiae*, section “Item quaeritur,” *On Baptism and Its Effect*. The baptism of infants is irrelevant here, because just as they sin without their own will, so they are baptized and cleansed in baptism without their own will.

In Book II, chapters 12–15, he seems to me to speak with insufficient care about the obedience owed to the supreme pontiff when he gives a command. Although what he writes may perhaps be true under the hypothesis he is treating, stated generally it is false and dangerous. This should have been explained and expressed more cautiously.

The same applies to the distinction he makes in Book II, chapter 18, between the apostolic see and those who preside over it. It should have been explained more carefully. Under the pretext of preserving the honor owed to the apostolic throne, the reins are loosened for those who insult pontiffs, and consequently the insults are necessarily and plainly turned back upon the see itself.

[Col. 1059B] I also think that in Book II, chapter 4, he rashly condemns the decree of Pope Stephen. For Stephen decided nothing concerning Constantine and his ordinations except with the approval and praise of a large council of bishops whom he had summoned for this purpose from Italy, Gaul, and Germany.

All the bishops of the Roman council, in body and spirit, followed the position of Stephen and the Roman clergy. John XII, approximately fifty years after Auxilius, judged very differently concerning the sentence of Stephen VI against the false pope Constantine. Following Stephen’s example and citing his action as a precedent, John pronounced an entirely similar sentence against the false pope Leo and those ordained by him, with the unanimous consent of the entire council.

After deposing Leo from every episcopal ministry, he defined the following concerning those whom Leo had ordained:

> “But those whom Leo himself, a neophyte and invader of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, promoted to any ecclesiastical order, we restore, by apostolic and canonical authority and by synodal decree, to their former rank, because their ordainer possessed nothing for himself and gave nothing to them. Just as formerly our predecessor, Pope Stephen of blessed memory, pronounced sentence concerning those who had been ordained by a certain Constantine, a neophyte and invader of the holy apostolic see, and afterward consecrated some of them as presbyters or deacons acceptable to him.”

The council’s first sentence concerning those ordained by Leo the schismatic—or Leo VIII—had declared that Pope John “ordered them to enter the council wearing their garments and stoles, and made each of them write the following words on a document: ‘My father possessed nothing for himself; he gave me nothing.’” Thus he stripped them and deprived them of the honor that the invader and neophyte, a courtier, had given them, and restored them to their former rank.

Besides the council’s acts, Sigebert expressly reports this under the year 963. But Auxilius, pressed by the arguments of his opponents, who opposed to him the decrees of Hosius at the Council of Sardica and of Pope Stephen at another council, brought himself into these difficulties. He failed to consider carefully enough, as he should have done, that by condemning Hosius and Pope Stephen he was also condemning great and numerous councils of bishops.

What he says in Book I, chapters 15 and 27, and Book II, chapter 4—that Pope Liberius was a heretic and an apostate—may perhaps be excused more easily. For in this belief he has excellent authorities leading the way: namely, Saints Athanasius, Hilary, and Jerome, and the ancient author of the book containing the *Lives of the Pontiffs*, from whom Auxilius drew what he reports about Liberius.

These distinguished men formed their opinion about Liberius because, overcome by weariness from exile and by the cruelty of the persecutions inflicted by the Arians, Liberius eventually subscribed to the condemnation of Athanasius, although he never professed the Arian heresy.

Liberius had committed three offenses which, as Cardinal Baronius says under the year 357, no. 42, gave occasion for the report of his heresy:

> “That, overcome, he weakened priestly constancy by subscribing unjustly against Saint Athanasius; that he entered into communion, as he himself admits, with those whose communion he had previously detested; and also that he subscribed to that profession which, although it might appear Catholic, nevertheless lacked the Nicene term ‘consubstantial,’ which all our predecessors had always defended against the Arians with the greatest glory.”

The spread of this infamy was greatly increased by the opposition that the Roman clergy, led by Damasus, and almost all the Catholic citizens of Rome offered to Pope Liberius when he returned from exile. For when what had happened to him through human weakness became known, they refused to maintain communion with him and instead adhered to Felix II, separating themselves from Liberius. Hence many killings, exiles, and martyrdoms occurred, as the prefects of the Arian Emperor Constantius raged against those unwilling to embrace communion with Liberius.

Anyone who wishes to learn these matters in detail should read Cardinal Baronius’s *Annals* under the year of Christ 357, no. 32 and following; and Cardinal Bellarmine, *Controversies*, volume I, Book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 9.

Since Auxilius therefore has such distinguished authorities for his position, he may easily be excused, as may the many serious authors who, both before and after him, fell into the same opinion. Among them were Saint Peter Damian and Cardinal Hostiensis, both highly renowned in the Church for learning, piety, and dignity.

# AUXILIUS ON THE ORDINATIONS PERFORMED BY POPE FORMOSUS

[Col. 1059]

## PREFATORY NOTE

[Col. 1059D]

Prudent reader, we have culled a few points from the abundance of the Scriptures and the teachings of the holy Fathers, namely: that if a bishop has been driven from his own see, he may, when a definite necessity or advantage requires it, be enthroned in another Church that lacks a bishop, though not without the authority of the Roman pontiff; and that the ordination performed by Pope Formosus may reasonably be shown to be valid and legitimate, even if Formosus himself, as some claim, was not rightly ordained.

Therefore, for anyone who has little time to read extensively, there is no doubt that this brief compilation, if read attentively, may be abundantly sufficient to convey the meaning.

## CHAPTER I.—An Extract from the Decretal Letter of Pope Anterus

He does not pass from one city to another, or from a smaller city to a larger, who does not do so at his own whim, through ambition, or by his own will, but is transferred either by force, driven from his own see, compelled by necessity, or for the advantage of the place or people—not arrogantly, but humbly.

Thus he does not migrate from city to city who does not abandon his own see out of greed or voluntarily, but, as has been said, is transferred and enthroned in another city because he has been driven from his see, compelled by necessity, or moved by the election or exhortation of priests and peoples.

This is why Eusebius was transferred by apostolic authority from a certain small city to Alexandria. Felix, too, was transferred from the city in which he had been ordained to Ephesus, at the election of its citizens, because of the learning and good life he possessed, and by the common counsel of the bishops, the other priests, and the peoples. This is Anterus.

## CHAPTER II.—On Saint Gregory

[Col. 1061C]

But if anyone should attempt to object that this same Anterus lived before the Council of Nicaea, let him finally learn without shame that the most holy Father and wonderful teacher—I mean Gregory, truly the theologian—migrated from one city to another for the benefit of the Church, not a few years after the Council of Nicaea.

For after he had first been bishop of a city in Cappadocia called Sasima, he was appointed to Nazianzus at the exhortation and with the consent of blessed Basil and the other bishops. Then he moved to Constantinople.

Nor should we listen to those who assert that he was expelled from the see of Constantinople by synodal judgment. It is true that the bishops assembled, but not against him; rather, they acted against those who had enthroned him, because they had dared to enthrone him without the consent of their own people.

The most holy Father himself bears witness to this, and his testimony is certainly true: he had rightly received that see and had properly presided over it. Indeed, he had been pressed by entreaties not to abandon it. But because of his constant bodily pains, his other illnesses, and his bent old age, he refused to yield to such requests. He returned to the quiet and philosophical life that he had always loved, in which he brought forth many rich and beneficial fruits, and there he rested in the Lord.

These matters are found partly in the accounts written about his life [Col. 1062A] and partly in his own discourse called the *Syntacterius*. They are stated even more clearly in the homily he delivered about himself at Constantinople against those who said that he had desired that see.

[Note: [Col. 1061] Compare this chapter and the following chapters with Book VII, chapter 35, of Socrates’ *Ecclesiastical History*.]

## CHAPTER III.—The Names of Bishops Who Transferred to Another See

Nevertheless, since we have mentioned the transfer of bishops, it remains for us to recall others who were enthroned because of advantage or necessity.

Perigenes was ordained bishop at Petrae. But because the citizens of that city refused to receive him, the bishop of Rome ordered him to be enthroned in Corinth, its metropolitan city, after the death of its bishop; and he governed that Church for as long as he lived.

Alexander, bishop of Antioch, transferred Dositheus, bishop of Seleucia, to Tarsus in Cilicia. Reverentius was transferred from a fortress of Phoenicia to Tyre. John was transferred from Gordylis to Proconnesus and presided over that Church. Palladius was transferred from Helenopolis to Asponia. Alexander was transferred from another Helenopolis to Hadrianopolis.

Meletius first presided over the Church of Sebaste and was afterward appointed bishop of Antioch. Theosebius was transferred from Apamea in Asia to Eudoxiopolis, formerly called Salambria. Polycarpus was transferred from the city of Antapristena in Mysia to Nicopolis in Thrace. Hierophilus was transferred from Trapezopolis in Phrygia to Antioch. Optimus migrated from Agardamia in Phrygia to Antioch in Pisidia. Silvanus was transferred from Philippopolis in Thrace to Troas.

Thus Eusebius Pamphilus, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, reports that Alexander, bishop of a city in Cappadocia, came to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, was detained by its citizens, and was appointed in place of Bishop Narcissus; thereafter he presided over that Church for the rest of his life.

## CHAPTER IV.—The Same Matter Is Also Recorded in the Greek Chronicles

In the second year of the reign of Artemius, also called Anastasius, emperor of the Romans, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eleventh day of the month of August, Germanus, archbishop of Cyzicus, was transferred from the metropolitan see to Constantinople, in the presence of Michael, the most reverend presbyter and apocrisiary of the holy Roman and apostolic see, with the consent of the bishops and of all the presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and the entire clergy or senate.

The same presbyter addressed all of them as follows:

> “For divine grace, whose constant work is to raise up the weak and complete what is incomplete, has transferred and appointed the present most holy archbishop Germanus to the most sacred see of the city of Constantinople, which is preserved by God.”

We have mentioned these matters, however, not to suggest that it is lawful for any bishop to transfer himself from one see to another, except when a definite necessity or advantage is impending.

## CHAPTER V.—That the Blessed Gregory and Basil Were Not Ignorant of the Council of Nicaea

Having recalled these matters briefly, let us return to what I began to say above about the blessed Gregory the theologian.

If anyone, inflamed by rashness, should presume to object that blessed Basil and that most illustrious teacher, Gregory, were ignorant of the Council of Nicaea and departed from the holy Roman Church in an action of this kind, would he not also provoke the laughter of those who understand the matter?

But it must be observed that, in this affair, those same holy Fathers understood the Nicene canons in the same way in which the Council of Chalcedon, as well as the most holy Pope Leo and Gelasius, are known to have understood them. This will appear more clearly in what follows.

## CHAPTER VI.—On Avoiding the Transfer of Bishops from See to See, from the Council of Nicaea

Because of the great disturbances and seditions that arise, it has seemed good that the custom which appears to have been admitted contrary to the rule in certain regions should be abolished in all respects [*omnibus*; variant *omnimodis*: “in every way”], so that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may be transferred from one city to another.

If anyone should attempt to do such a thing after the definition of the holy and great council, and should involve himself in such an undertaking, let the act be considered entirely void, and let him be restored to the Church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

## CHAPTER VII.—How the Council of Chalcedon Understands the Same Nicene Decree

Clerics ministering in a Church, as we have already established, ought not to be appointed to the church of another city, but should remain content with the ministry in which they were deemed worthy to serve from the beginning. The exception is those who, having lost their own provinces, have transferred to another Church out of necessity.

If anyone, after this definition, receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, it has been decreed that both the one received and the one receiving him are to be deprived of communion until the migrated cleric (*clerus* [variant *clericus*]) has returned to his own Church.

## CHAPTER VIII.—That the Council of Chalcedon Was Established by the Authority of Pope Leo

The Council of Chalcedon was therefore established and strengthened by the authority and legates of blessed Pope Leo, as is recorded in his letters. Consequently, that pope should not be considered to have differed from it.

## CHAPTER IX.—Saint Pope Leo

[Col. 1063D]

If any bishop, despising the smallness of his own city, should seek the administration of a more distinguished place and transfer himself by any means to a larger people, he will indeed be expelled from the foreign chair, but he will also lose his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he coveted through greed nor over those whom he despised through pride.

Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries, and let no one desire to be enlarged beyond the measure of his jurisdiction.

## CHAPTER X.—Pope Gelasius

Whoever, abandoning his own Church without any existing cause, thinks he ought to transfer to another, and is rashly received there, will not escape the regulations that the sacred canons established for such presumptuous persons—whether he himself, or the one who receives and promotes him—because he has acted insolently against the reverend canons.

You have heard, judges of equity, how the Council of Chalcedon—which in no way departs from the Council of Nicaea—decreed that no one should migrate to the Church of another city without losing his province.

You have also heard that the most blessed Pope Leo judged that a bishop, despising the modesty of his own city, ought not to seek the administration of a more distinguished place or transfer himself through greed to a larger people.

Pope Gelasius also appears to have defined the same thing, as was shown above. But if anyone should presume to set against these statements a chapter of an earlier pontiff, let him know that the Council of Chalcedon, as well as the apostolic prelates whose testimonies we have cited—I mean Leo and Gelasius—considered and treated all the institutions of the preceding Fathers that had been canonically established more carefully than the people of our own time. Therefore no one should be preferred to them.

## CHAPTER XI.—A Passage of Hosius

Some people oppose, as though it were an exceedingly strong wall, the statement of Hosius:

> “If any bishop changes his see through greed or ambition, and in order to exercise domination, let him not even have lay communion.”

Then, in the following chapter:

> “Even if such a person should have contrived frauds and corrupted certain people by reward and payment, offering as an excuse that he might appear to have been sought by the people, let him not receive lay communion at the end.”

## CHAPTER XII.—That Hosius Did Not Speak Catholically

> “Let him not receive lay communion at the end.”

Pay attention, I ask, lovers of truth, to what we are about to say. What Hosius says—“If any bishop changes his see through greed or ambition, and in order to exercise domination”—we gladly accept.

But what he adds—“Let him not receive lay communion at the end”—we cannot hear with equanimous ears. Where did Hosius learn this, especially since nothing of the sort is found in the Nicene synod, which holds primacy among all councils and in which he himself sat with the holy Fathers?

On the contrary, as was indicated above, they made a more humane ruling, saying:

> “Let this act be considered entirely void, and let him be restored to the Church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.”

Therefore the statement “Let him not receive lay communion at the end” is not Catholic but sounds like the teaching of the Cathari. In Greek, *Cathari* means “the pure,” although they are altogether impure.

These are the heretical Novatians, who dogmatize that no one can do penance after sin. Against them the Lord cries through the prophet:

> “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel XXXIII).

There are also very many other passages showing that a sinner, even if he seeks penance at the end of his life, should neither be rejected nor abandoned to despair.

## CHAPTER XIII.—Saint Augustine on This Very Matter

For this reason blessed Augustine, whose authority shines throughout the whole Church like the sun, explaining to the people what blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is, says:

> “We must not understand as every blasphemy, or every word spoken against the Holy Spirit, that which is not forgiven in this age or in the age to come, but a certain blasphemy and a certain word—namely, an impenitent heart against the Holy Spirit, through whom sins are forgiven in the Church.

> “A person speaks a very evil and exceedingly impious word, whether in thought or with his tongue, when God’s patience leads him to repentance, yet he, according to the hardness and impenitent state of his heart, stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s righteous judgment (Romans II).

> “This impenitence has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come, because repentance obtains forgiveness in this age, a forgiveness that is effective in the age to come.

> “But as long as anyone lives in this flesh, judgment cannot be passed concerning him. For no one is to be despaired of as long as the patience of God leads him to repentance.

> “Today he is a pagan; what if tomorrow he becomes a Christian? Today he is an unbelieving Jew; what if tomorrow he believes in Christ? He is a heretic; what if tomorrow he follows Catholic truth? Today he is a schismatic; what if tomorrow he embraces Catholic truth [or unity]?”

## CHAPTER XIV.—An Inquiry Concerning the Definition of Hosius: “Let Him Not Receive Lay Communion at the End”; and Which Canons Possess Authority

I think that this point also must not be passed over. For, according to blessed Pope Gelasius in his letter to the Emperor Anastasius, no canons possess authority except those that the apostolic see has strengthened by its judgment.

Therefore, let them show, if they can, which of the apostolic Fathers confirmed what Hosius said:

> “Let him not receive lay communion at the end.”

Since they cannot show anything of the kind, it remains that such a definition sounds not Catholic but, as has been said, Catharist.

## CHAPTER XV.—To What Conclusion Hosius Carried His Opinion

Moreover, what must still be said about Hosius we can express, since we are human beings, only with a heavy sigh.

This was Hosius, bishop of the Church of Córdoba, who had once been apocrisiary of the apostolic see and, together with the presbyters Vincent and Victor, had attended the holy and great Council of Nicaea. Later, it is reported that he held the Council of Sardica with a very large number of bishops, where the chapters attributed to him were established.

He remained alive until the time of the Emperor Constantius. Constantius was a participant in the perfidy of Arianism. When a dispute arose against that heresy, an episcopal delegation was sent to Hosius, who was living in Spain, and said to him:

> “You who were present at the Nicene synod, tell us, please: did the three hundred and eighteen Fathers decree that we should rightly confess *Omousion*—that is, the Son as having one substance with the Father—as we Catholics confess? Or did they decree, as the Arians chatter, *Omoiousion*—that is, the Son as having a substance similar to the Father?”

He is said to have replied—whether because, weakened by old age, he had lost his understanding, or certainly in order to flatter the ruler—that both sides were correct, whether they confessed *homoousion* or *homoiousion*.

His opinion, expressed with such folly, was ridiculed and rejected with one voice not only by Catholics but also by Arians. Finally, in the city of Córdoba, where he held the episcopate, after this response his name was not recited among the Catholic bishops who preceded him or among those who succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Here Follow Distinguished Testimonies Showing That the Ordination of Pope Formosus Was Valid and Legitimate: From Saint Pope Leo, That Pseudo-Bishops Are to Be Rejected but Their Ordination May Remain Valid
No consideration permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the metropolitan’s judgment. Therefore, when a dispute about an improperly assumed dignity frequently arises, who could doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred must by no means be attributed to such men? [Col. 1066B] If, however, any clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches belonging to their own bishops, and their ordination was carried out according to the customary judgment of the presiding authorities, it may be held valid, so that they may remain in those churches. Otherwise, the appointment must be regarded as void, since it is founded neither upon the proper place nor secured by authority.

## CHAPTER XVII

From Saint Pope Gregory: just as no one can be baptized a second time, so no one can be consecrated a second time to the same order; addressed to John, bishop of the Church of Ravenna.

But what you say—that the man who has been ordained should be ordained again—is extremely ridiculous and foreign to the exercise of your understanding, unless perhaps this is the example being brought forward, concerning which the man who is said to have done such a thing was also judged. [Col. 1066C] Far be it from your fraternity to think in this way. Just as someone who has been baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one who has been consecrated once cannot be consecrated again in the same order.

## CHAPTER XVIII

As stated above in the canons of the apostles.

If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon receives a second laying-on of hands from anyone, let both him and the one who attempts to ordain him be deposed. For it is impossible that those who have been baptized, or even ordained, by persons of this sort should be either faithful Christians or clerics.

## CHAPTER XIX

From Pope Anastasius: those whom Acacius baptized or ordained after his condemnation are touched by no share of injury; addressed to the emperor Anastasius.

For, according to the custom of the Catholic Church, let your most sacred and serene heart recognize that none of those whom Acacius baptized, or whom he ordained as priests or Levites according to the canons, is touched by any share of injury on account of Acacius’ name—an injury by which the grace of the sacrament, perhaps unlawfully conferred, might seem less secure. [Col. 1066D] For even baptism administered far from the Church, whether by an adulterer or by a brother, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift, because that voice which sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution; it declares and says: “This is the one who baptizes in the Spirit and in fire” (Matthew 3; Mark 1; John 1). [Col. 1067A]

For if the rays of this visible sun, when they pass through the most foul places, are not stained by the defilement of any contact, how much more is the power of the one who made this visible sun untouched by any unworthiness of the minister. Judas, too, although sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he did among the apostles by virtue of the office entrusted to him: the benefits given through an unworthy man suffered no loss on that account. The Lord himself made this clear in the plainest voice: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat: whatever they say, do; but whatever they do, do not do, for they say and do not do” (Matthew 23).

Whatever, therefore, anyone in the Church appears to perform for the advancement of human beings by virtue of his office, the effect of divinity completes and fulfills all of it. [Col. 1067B] Thus Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3). God does not ask who or what sort of person preaches, but whom he preaches, so that he confirms that even the envious preach Christ well. By this very evil the devil himself was cast down.

## CHAPTER XX

From the same author: when evil men administer good things, they harm only themselves and do not defile the sacraments of the Church.

Therefore this Acacius also, whose name we say ought to be passed over in silence, harmed only himself by badly administering good things. For the inviolable sacrament given through him obtained for others the perfection of its power, but proved harmful to him. [Col. 1067C] The curious suspicion of certain people has extended so far that, after Pope Felix had approved the judgment, it imagines that Acacius later acted ineffectively in the sacraments that he usurped; and consequently they fear those who received the mysteries conveyed either in consecrations or in baptism. But pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others.

## CHAPTER XXI

As stated above: Saint Augustine against the Donatist Parmenianus.

What is read in the Book of Wisdom—“The holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom 1)—is to be understood in this way: the Spirit is absent from that person’s salvation, yet does not abandon the ministry through which he works the salvation of others. [Col. 1067D] Hence the apostle says: “For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Corinthians 9). It is as though he said: “It benefits those to whom I administer this, not me, who am deceitful.”

## CHAPTER XXII

That the Bonosiac clerics are received with their honors; from Pope Innocent.

It is certain that the Bonosiac heretics are to be compared with the Jews, because they deny that Christ is God, from the substance of the Father before the ages, just as the Jews denied and deny his divinity. It follows, therefore, that they share the condemnation of those whose error they imitated. And further: The principal deliberation of our former brother Anysius and the other priests was this: those whom Bonosus had ordained should be received as ordained, so that they would not remain with him and a considerable scandal arise. [Col. 1068A]

## CHAPTER XXIII

The Council of Nicaea orders that clerics called Cathari be received in this manner.

Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, “the pure,” if they ever come to the Catholic Church, the holy and great council decreed that, after receiving the laying-on of hands, they should remain in the clerical order.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Concerning Anatolius: although improperly ordained, he was nevertheless not expelled.

When Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, was sent into exile on account of the Catholic faith, Anatolius was ordained in his place while Flavian was still alive. [Col. 1068B] Saint Pope Leo addressed him as follows:

“Since your predecessor, Flavian of blessed memory, was expelled for defending Catholic truth, it was not unreasonably believed that your ordainers appeared, contrary to the provisions of the holy canons, to have consecrated one like themselves. But God’s mercy was present, loving and strengthening you in this respect, so that you might make good use of your evil beginnings and show that you had been advanced not by human judgment but by God’s kindness. This must truly be accepted in that way, provided that you do not lose the grace of this divine gift through another offense.”

Having read these chapters again, lovers of justice, you have heard more clearly that ordination performed by pseudo-bishops can stand as valid. You have also heard that, just as no one ought to be baptized again, so no one can be consecrated again in the same order. Nevertheless, you have heard that those whom Acacius ordained after his condemnation were touched by no share of injury, since evil men, by administering good things, harm only themselves and cannot defile the ministry, which the Holy Spirit himself presides over as its author. [Col. 1068C]

Hence, surely, the Bonosiacs who wished to return to the Catholic Church were received with their honors. Hence also the Novatians are received by the laying-on of hands, just as they had been ordained. Anatolius, too, as has been said, was ordained more as a sacrilegious usurper than as a bishop; yet he was not condemned by Saint Pope Leo, but rather admonished not to lose his priestly kindness through another offense.

And who are these people—and of what learning or authority—who strive to overthrow, not in a Catholic but in an apostolic manner, a sacred ordination administered by a Catholic man, who for many years faithfully served God and ministered ecclesiastical offices to the Christian people? [Col. 1068D]

## CHAPTER XXV

Concerning Liberius.

Who does not know that Liberius—alas, alas!—subscribed to the Arian heresy, and that through his transgression unspeakably wicked crimes were committed? A multitude of priests and clerics was killed and crowned with martyrdom; the remaining Catholics were prohibited not only from the churches but even from the baths. Liberius, however, became an apostate and lived for six years; nevertheless, the ordinations he performed remained secure. [Col. 1069A] Nor is this surprising. Indeed, although Judas was a thief and sacrilegious, no one dared to condemn what he beneficially did among the apostles.

## CHAPTER XXVI

That no one dared to annul the ordinations performed by Vigilius.

This is why no one dared to disturb the ordinations of Vigilius. You should know that this is the Vigilius who first plotted against Pope Boniface, so that, while Boniface was still alive, he might sacrilegiously obtain the apostolic dignity. But, because the senate resisted, he was unable to do such a thing. Later, by his customary intrigues, he attempted to strip Pope Silverius of the apostolic dignity. [Col. 1069B]

When Silverius noticed this, he summoned the bishops and, by the authority of the Holy Spirit and apostolic power, bound Vigilius with the bonds of anathema as a simoniac and usurper. But Vigilius, as he had conceived in his mind, wickedly condemned that same apostolic father through imperial power and false witnesses, clothed him in monastic garments, and sent him into exile at Pontia, sustaining him with the bread of affliction and the water of distress. There he died and was buried and became a confessor; the sick were healed at his body.

Vigilius, however, deservedly entangled in the bonds of anathema and moreover publicly branded by the charge of murder, sacrilegiously made himself pope. O ineffable mercy of God! Vigilius, who had already been despaired of, was preserved for repentance. He had promised to reconcile Anthimus, the heretical patriarch, but refused to reconcile him; worn down by prolonged exile and prolonged affliction, he received what was worthy of his deeds, and at last, dying far from his homeland, he came to rest in the Lord. [Col. 1069C]

Nevertheless, his ordinations, as has been said, remained secure. These matters that we have related concerning Silverius and Vigilius are found partly in the synodal decree of that same Silverius and partly in the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Apart from Liberius’ sacrilege, which was the worst, Vigilius is recognized to have committed worse deeds than Formosus.

Having briefly set these matters out, it is worth asking which of them committed the worse offenses. Formosus, they say, was transferred from an episcopal see to the apostolic throne because of ambition. If they object that he had been deposed and afterward reconciled, let them know that many priests were deposed and afterward reconciled—reconciled, I say, but not consecrated again to the same office. For reconciliation is one thing, and consecration another. One who has been consecrated once cannot be consecrated again to the same office; nevertheless, he can be reconciled through worthy satisfaction. [Col. 1069D]

Is it not sufficiently established in authentic documents that many priests were reconciled after deposition? This is clearer to those who read them. Once these matters have been arranged, if human beings are silent about the unspeakable crimes of Vigilius, the stones themselves will cry out. No one has dared, or will dare, to imitate his detestable crime, except one who has become a partner of him who says: “I will set my seat in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14). [Col. 1070A]

Moreover, we read in decretal letters that bishops may, when necessity or usefulness requires it, be transferred from one see to another or from one city to another; and there is no doubt that many priests, even saints, did such a thing. Among them stands blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, as we related above.

Prudent reader, we have not set these matters out beforehand in order to say that any priest is freely permitted to move from one see to another or from one city to another, but in order to prove by testimonies that the laying-on of hands administered even by pseudo-bishops is valid and lawful.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

That whoever argues that Pope Formosus’ sacred ordination is or was nothing is an enemy of the Christian religion.

[Col. 1070B] Those who fabricate the claim that the aforementioned ordination is false and void, and who therefore assert that priests and Levites must be consecrated, are they saying anything other than that the regions of Italy, far and wide, have now for approximately twenty years been living without the Christian religion?

Accordingly, what else remains except that the churches dedicated throughout Italy by bishops of this kind, the altars consecrated, and the chrism solemnly instituted have altogether perished? Likewise, that the fonts sanctified by bishops and other priests for the remission of sins, and the solemn Masses celebrated on Sundays and on other feast days, were celebrated in vain, as these blasphemers claim? That the offerings made both for the living and for the dead—an unspeakable assertion—have perished as mere trifles? [Col. 1070C] That the morning, evening, and other Hours’ prayers were not heard, as though they were worthless? That the offices of Levites and subdeacons were administered in vain?

The entire Church that gave synodal assent to this ordination would likewise be endangered, since not only those who commit wrongful acts but also those who consent to those committing them receive an equal punishment.

O incomparable sacrilege! Who among those who fear God could hear this with an impartial ear without immediately being scandalized by Christian zeal? Would it not have been better for that tongue entangled in such blasphemies to be given piece by piece to the birds than to burst into such madness?

We know that, in cases of necessity, even a layperson may baptize. [Col. 1070D] But it is one thing for a layperson to be able to give baptism when the danger of death is pressing, and something incomparably different for fonts sanctified for the remission of sins by priests’ prayers and blessings, by the mingling of chrism, and by the votive responses of clergy and people to have possessed no sanctification at all, as these men maintain.

Who but a heretic would dare to teach such a doctrine? And who speaks such things through such a mouth except one of whom the Lord says: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and the father of it” (John 8)?

## CHAPTER XXIX

If Pope Formosus displeases those opponents, they ought to blame not outsiders and foreigners but the Roman people.

[Col. 1071A]

If Pope Formosus appears to displease those opponents on the grounds that he was not properly ordained, whom ought they to blame for this except the Roman people who elected him? To whom should this be attributed except the clergy and the leading men of the city of Rome, who willingly sought to receive from him the sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood for as long as he lived, communicated with him in the customary manner at all solemn celebrations and stations, and shared in everything with him?

Moreover, anyone of sound mind says that he has absolutely nothing concerning Formosus to charge against those who came from distant parts of the earth, trembling through a thousand dangers, so to speak, to the apostolic see, and received sacred ordination, as is customary, more from the apostle Peter than from his vicar—or rather from the Holy Spirit, as Pope Anastasius teaches, a point already mentioned above. [Col. 1071B]

## CHAPTER XXX

Whether the man who bound himself by oath to overthrow that ordination is truly a priest, Levite, or subdeacon.

Since, under the pressure of necessity, a dispute has arisen concerning sacred ordinations, it is appropriate to ask what should be thought of a man who has no consecration at all in the sacred ordination now under discussion, yet not only declares before witnesses that this ordination is nothing and was nothing, but also promises to overthrow it by oath. [Col. 1071C]

Should such a promisor be counted among the sacrilegious and among those who have wickedly sworn together, who bind themselves by oaths to perpetrate a crime? Indeed, secular law punishes such men most strictly; and if they are clerics, ecclesiastical judgment removes them from their honors. The canonical provision reads as follows.

## CHAPTER XXXI

From the Council of Chalcedon concerning oath-bound conspiracy and plotting.

The crime of conspiracy or collusion is altogether prohibited by secular laws; it is much more fitting to warn that such a thing must not occur in the Church of God. Therefore, if any clerics or monks are found conspiring or plotting, or laying snares for bishops or clerics, let them be completely removed from their proper rank. [Col. 1071D]

Once these testimonies have been presented, it is clearer than daylight that a priest, Levite, or subdeacon of this sort must be counted among the sacrilegious and wicked conspirators, and must likewise be rejected by canonical judgment.

## CHAPTER XXXII

That no one should ever obey in order to commit iniquity.

Moreover, certain people preface their defense in this way, saying: “Why do you decide that the overthrow of this ordination should be imputed to us at this time? Do you not know that he commands it who must be obeyed absolutely in all things?” [Col. 1072A]

Far be it from me—far be it—to say that God has commanded anyone to obey in order to commit iniquity. The psalmist sings to him: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity. You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5). And the Lord himself says to Jeremiah: “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you will be like my mouth” (Jeremiah 15).

David also testifies about himself, saying: “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and with those who act wickedly I will not enter. I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the impious” (Psalm 25).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

That the Gospel saying, “Observe and do everything they tell you,” must be understood only in a good sense.

The Gospel says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Observe and do everything whatever they tell you” (Matthew 23). [Col. 1072B] Everything of this sort in that passage must be understood only in a good sense. Otherwise, the Jews who crucified the Lord at the counsel and urging of the scribes and Pharisees ought to have been free from such a great crime.

But Scripture testifies how gravely both those who spoke and those who acted sinned, and this is extended in their descendants until the end of the world. That “all” does not always refer to the whole but often to the greater part is demonstrated not only by the divine writings, which must be believed above all, but also by the authority of pagan books.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

That no excommunication should be obeyed when it requires the commission of crimes.

“But,” they say, “whether the pastor binds the flock justly or unjustly, the flock must fear lest, through the arrogance of swollen reproach, a fault that did not exist should be created.” [Col. 1072C]

This is indeed a true statement, but it must not be understood in such a way that the word “unjustly” means that one must obey any pastor in matters that are clearly shown to be hostile to God. For example, if by excommunicating you he compelled you to perjury, false testimony, sacrilege, or murder, is it decreed that the pastor’s excommunication must in such matters or similar matters be feared or carried out? Certainly not.

For not only those who do such things—these are the apostle’s words—but also those who consent to those who do them are made worthy of eternal death (Romans 1).

That we ought not to consent to pastors in matters hostile to God is testified by the Savior himself. When the disciples said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were scandalized when they heard this saying?” [Col. 1072D] he replied: “Leave them; they are blind, leaders of the blind. If the blind lead the blind, will not both fall into a pit?” (Matthew 15).

Therefore both the one who leads and the one who follows into wrongdoing are blind, and rightly both fall into the pit of condemnation.

“But in what way,” they say, “does the apostle say: ‘Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance? For there is no authority except from God’ (Romans 13)?”

Let them hear this: in matters that Christian law abhors and prohibits, we must never obey or consent to any authority—that is, not by carnal means or deceitful schemes, but by a rational reply and the most humble deliberation.

What more need be said? Turn your attention from pastors to the apostle, who says: [Col. 1073A] “He is God’s minister for your good” (ibid.). Why does he add “for your good” except because God’s minister is not for your harm?

## CHAPTER XXXV

Concerning observing excommunication, and the distinction between pontifical sees and those who preside over them.

Moreover, if the pastors of the churches wish to bind us because of our offenses, justly or unjustly—justly, if our guilt preceded it; unjustly, if we have no guilt—such a binding is rightly to be feared and most carefully observed until we deserve to be absolved through the forgiveness of the one who bound us.

For pontifical sees are one thing, and those who preside over them another. Accordingly, the honor and dignity of each see must be observed according to the rule. [Col. 1073B] But if those who preside deviate, they must not be followed in their deviation; that is, if they begin to act against the faith or Catholic religion, we must by no means follow them in such matters.

In what they rightly say, however, even if they do not do what they say, we ought willingly to obey them. Hence we must pluck the grapes and avoid the thorns.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

Concerning the unjust binding imposed by a pastor.

Blessed Jerome, explaining the Gospel passage, “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18), says: [Col. 1073C]

“Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, take to themselves something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or imagine that they can absolve the guilty, when before God it is not the priests’ sentence but the life of the accused that is sought.”

Thus speaks Saint Jerome.

The prophet also says: “They were putting to death souls that do not die, and bringing to life souls that do not live” (Ezekiel 13). As Saint Gregory teaches, the one who condemns the just puts to death someone who does not die; and the one who attempts to absolve the guilty from punishment tries to bring to life someone who will not live. [Col. 1074A]

## CHAPTER XXXVII

As stated above, in Solomon.

“As a bird flying in the opposite direction, and as any sparrow passing by, so a curse uttered without cause will come upon the one who sent it” (Proverbs 26).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

Likewise, in the same place.

“The soul that blesses will be made prosperous; but whoever curses without cause will himself be under a curse” (Proverbs 11).

## CHAPTER XXXIX

As stated above, from Saint Pope Gregory.

In everything that is said about us from without, we ought to return to the secrets of the mind; and even if everyone condemns him, the person whom conscience does not accuse is free. [Col. 1074B] And even if everyone praises him, he cannot be free if conscience accuses him.

## CHAPTER XL

Concerning awaiting a universal council.

This collection of scriptural testimonies may therefore seem superfluous to some, because at present there is no one who can pronounce a judgment of equity. For we cannot obtain the palm of justice among those who are themselves our opponents, judges, witnesses, and advocates all at once.

Nevertheless, in accordance with blessed Jerome’s judgment, we sing this for ourselves and our people: let us be of good courage, and let us believe—not in ourselves but in the holy Fathers—that we have a good cause, observing what is written: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes 10). [Col. 1074C] And also: “Hold fast what you have, so that no one else may take your crown” (Revelation 3).

Therefore, remaining in the sacred order in which we were consecrated, we await the most equitable examination of a universal council, under the guidance of him to whom we cry: “Arise, Lord, and judge your cause” (Psalm 73). To him be honor and glory through infinite ages of ages.

[Col. 1073]

# A TREATISE OF THE SAME AUXILIUS ON THE SAME QUESTION, CALLED “THE ASSAILANT AND THE DEFENDER”

## Preface

In the form of question and answer.

[Col. 1073D] **Question concerning those who were first consecrated by force and afterward voluntarily in the same order.**

I would like to know what should be decided after proper deliberation concerning those who, as they say, were first consecrated by force and afterward voluntarily in the same order.

Suppose [Col. 1074D] that they initially received a violent laying-on of hands and therefore did not wish to exercise the priesthood; afterward, however, they willingly consented to minister in the priesthood. Should they have been consecrated again [Col. 1075A] in the same order in which they had previously been consecrated by force?

According to the definition of the holy Fathers, must not a second laying-on of hands be avoided in precisely the same way as a second baptism?

But they say: “That first consecration, although performed by a Catholic bishop, was nevertheless forced, and therefore must be considered as nothing.”

Tell me, please: if someone were perhaps baptized by force, unwilling to believe in Christ, but afterward voluntarily professed belief in him, should he therefore be baptized again?

Blessed Alexander the patriarch did not think so when Saint Athanasius, still a small boy but already baptized, baptized some other little boys by the seashore, acting as a priest, although merely in play.

What more need be said? As I have stated, I would like to reach certainty concerning a judgment of this kind. Therefore, whoever knows the proposed question should graciously clarify it fully in our presence, for he will receive a crown among those of whom it is said to Daniel through the angel: “Those who are learned will shine like the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel 12). [Col. 1075B]

### Answer

A clear line of reasoning resolves the difficulties of this question.

You ask whether, if someone unwilling to believe in Christ were baptized by force and afterward consented to believe in Christ, he should be baptized again. Certainly not.

Take the example of little children who are carried in other people’s arms and, insofar as they can, struggle with all their strength so as not to be plunged into the baptismal font. [Col. 1075C] But when they attain rational understanding (*pertinxerint*; alternatively *pervenerint*, “arrive at”), even if they cannot remember when they were baptized, they nevertheless believe without hesitation those who tell them, and they begin to practice the Christian religion without repeating baptism.

Hence blessed Pope Leo says: “If there are no indications among relatives and family members, nor among clerics and neighbors, by which it may be shown that those about whom inquiry is being made were baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they perish manifestly, because reason does not permit what is not shown to have been done to be regarded as repeated.”

But concerning those who come from Africa or Mauretania and do not know in which sect they were baptized: they do not fail to know that they were baptized; rather, they profess that they do not know of what faith those who baptized them were. [Col. 1076A] Therefore, since they received the form of baptism in some manner, they are not to be baptized, but are to be joined to the Catholics through the laying-on of hands and by the power of the Holy Spirit, whom they could not receive from heretics.

Do you not see that the holy Father orders even those baptized by unknown heretics not to be baptized again, but to be received through the laying-on of hands?

It should also be recalled that Saint Genesius, bishop of Arles, when he was an actor, was baptized in jest and while pretending. But after learning the truth, which is Christ, he adhered sincerely to the Christian faith that he had deceitfully promised to believe, without repeating baptism.

But you say: “Baptized children, if they die at an early age, undoubtedly receive at least some share in the joys of paradise. But if the person who was baptized by force as an adult is taken from this life before he voluntarily believes in Christ, should prayer be offered for him as for a faithful Christian? Especially since the apostle John says: ‘There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it’ (1 John 5).” [Col. 1076B]

As Augustine says, the sin unto death is abandoning the faith that works through love until death.

The knot of this question is resolved as follows. Children are not charged with the fact that they are baptized while resisting and unwilling, because they cannot yet use reason and are not yet able to know the difference between good and evil. But if those who have reached a lawful age are baptized by force and die before voluntarily believing in Christ, baptism cannot benefit them, nor should prayer be offered for them, because they were capable of reason and could distinguish between truth and falsehood. [Col. 1076C]

From these matters, briefly set out, it is evident that one who was baptized by force, if afterward he wishes to believe in Christ, must not be baptized again; rather, he should be exhorted to preserve, through love and works to the end, what he received unwillingly.

Thus, by this formula, it is understood that one who received the sacred order unwillingly, if afterward he wishes to minister, must not be consecrated again in that order, but should instead be admonished to strive to minister reverently, through love, what he was compelled to receive by force.

*The preface ends.*

# Preliminary Letter

To Leo, bishop of Nola.

[Col. 1075]

[Col. 1075D] To the most reverend lord Leo, bishop of the holy Church of Nola, Auxilius sends greetings in the Lord.

You state, through the legation that has been sent, that you are suffering violent oppression, so that you may invalidate the episcopal priesthood which you once received from Pope Formosus, as though it were nothing. For this reason, you admit that you consulted men of remarkable skill among the Franks, as well as experts from the city of Beneventum, and that you retain their opinions in rescripts (*rescripta*, “written replies”; alternatively *te scripta*, “written to you”), which clearly prohibit you from committing such a transgression. [Col. 1076D]

Nevertheless, you compel me to respond briefly in a dialogue to the objections that certain people raise against that same Pope Formosus and his ordinations. I have already sent what I set out in a little work concerning such a dispute. [Col. 1077A] Yet, because different forms are made from a single quantity of gold, pleasing the differing tastes of human beings, supported by your prayers I shall do what you urge, provided only that in each objection the word “Assailant” is placed at the beginning, and in the response “Defender.”

Let no strict syllogistic conclusion be sought here, nor any Perihermeneutic subtlety, since we are disciples of the fisherman—that is, the apostle Peter. [Col. 1078A] And although we sit in his little boat, we suffer the storm, calling upon the Ruler of all to command the winds and the sea, so that a great calm may arise.

# Here begins the text

[Col. 1077]

## CHAPTER I

That the ordination performed by Pope Formosus can reasonably be shown to be valid and legitimate, even if Formosus himself, as they say, was not properly ordained.

[Col. 1077B]

INFENSOR. Formosus, abandoning his own wife, took another—that is, abandoning the episcopate, he took away the apostolic see from those who were rightly to be ordained—and for that reason is recognized as rejected and counterfeit.

DEFENSOR. I am not concerned with what Formosus was, but that the ordination he performed plainly appears beyond doubt to be valid and legitimate.

INF. Formosus was not pope; therefore the ordination he performed must be regarded as nothing.

DEF. It was proclaimed not only throughout the Roman realm but also far away in barbarian nations that Formosus had been apostolic pontiff for many years. [Col. 1077C] And therefore clerics hastening from distant regions of the earth to the threshold of the apostles sought to receive sacred ordination from him, as is customary.

INF. He did indeed hold the apostolic dignity, but he was counterfeit, rejected, and not lawfully ordained.

DEF. It does not concern me whether he was rightly ordained; what concerns me is that the ordination he performed be shown more clearly to be valid and legitimate.

INF. If Formosus was counterfeit and rejected, by what reasoning can the ordination he performed stand?

DEF. By the very reasoning with which the most holy Pope Leo judged that pseudo-bishops should be deposed while their ordination could nevertheless remain valid; and also by the reasoning with which Pope Anastasius confirmed that the ordinations performed by the heretic Acacius—even after Acacius had been condemned—should remain in force. The ordinations of Liberius likewise remained unimpaired, as did those of Vigilius, who was not only a Simonian usurper but also, deservedly entangled in the bonds of anathema, was ordained contrary to canonical law. This is known to nearly all who read. For when the holy Flavian had been sent into exile on account of the Catholic faith, Anatolius was ordained by the heretics in his place; yet he was not condemned by holy Pope Leo but admonished.

INF. The Council of Nicaea expressly decreed that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon should be transferred from one city to another. If anyone should attempt such a thing and commit himself to such an undertaking, the act was to be considered wholly null, and he was to be restored to the Church in which he had been ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon. Certainly, when it says, “Let this act be wholly null,” both points must be understood: namely, that a bishop must not be transferred from one city to another, and that, if after being transferred he performed an ordination, the ordination itself must be considered wholly null. [Col. 1078B]

DEF. This knot need not be sought in a reed. Who cannot see that this decree contains no obscurity and can mean nothing other than that the transfer from one city to another must be considered wholly null? It says nothing at all about the ordination he performed, as the following article makes clearer when it says, “And let him be restored to the Church in which he had been ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.” If, therefore, he is restored to the Church in which he had been ordained bishop, how can the ordination he performed at that time be invalid?

INF. Formosus, as I said, was counterfeit and rejected and did not possess the sacred order there. How, according to Pope Innocent, could he bestow it upon others? [Col. 1078C]

DEF. Pope Innocent said this about heretics; yet it must not be understood of all heretics, in accordance with the fact that he consented to receive the clerics of the Bonosians, whom Bonosus had ordained before he was condemned, together with their ecclesiastical ranks.

INF. I am amazed that you can argue that, although Formosus was rejected, his ordination can stand, when members cannot exist in any way without a head. And, to add something further, to whom, then, should it be attributed that Formosus was deceitful and rejected, if his ordination remains unimpaired?

DEF. It should be attributed, of course, to the Roman clergy and people who elected him and, throughout his lifetime, shared in everything with him. But as for me, who have journeyed from distant regions of the earth to the threshold of the apostles and, as is customary, received sacred ordination more from the apostle Peter than from his Vicar—indeed, from the Holy Spirit, as blessed Pope Anastasius teaches—it is determined that nothing should be ascribed to those who are sound in mind. [Col. 1078D]

INF. I do not want verbal evasions. If you can, show by concrete matters how a just and suitable ordination could come from a counterfeit and rejected ordainer.

DEF. If a judge of equity were present, he would already have shown you to be defeated. Have you forgotten the testimonies that I briefly brought forward concerning holy Pope Leo, Anastasius, Liberius, Vigilius, and also Anatolius?

INF. Acacius was rightly ordained, and therefore his ordinations remained unimpaired.

DEF. The decretal text itself shows more clearly that Pope Anastasius was speaking of those whom the heretic Acacius baptized and ordained after he had been condemned by Pope Felix. The same, moreover, must be understood of Liberius, who subscribed to the Arian heresy. But what should be said of Vigilius, who was not only a Simonian usurper but also guilty of homicide, and who had moreover been justly anathematized by Pope Silverius, the same apostolic Father whom Vigilius sent into exile? Although he established a sacrilegious pope, no one nevertheless dared to remove the ordinations he performed.

## CHAPTER II  
### Testimonies brought forward by Pope Anastasius in defense of the ordinations performed by the heretic Acacius

INF. Since, as I have said, members cannot exist without a head, I cannot sufficiently wonder how counterfeit ordainers can produce valid ordinations.

DEF. The aforesaid pontiff Anastasius establishes how this can happen by credible proofs. For among other things he says:

“According to the custom of the Catholic Church, none of those whom Acacius baptized, nor any of those whom he ordained as priests or deacons according to the canons, should suffer any portion of harm on account of Acacius’s name. Hence baptism, even when administered far from the Church or by an adulterer or a thief, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift. For that voice which sounded through the Dove excludes every stain of human pollution, when it declares and says: ‘This is he who baptizes in the Spirit and in fire’ (Matt. III; Mark I; John I). [Col. 1079C]

“For if the rays of this visible sun, when they pass through the most foul-smelling places, are not stained by contamination from any contact, much more is the power of him who made this visible sun untouched by any unworthiness of the minister. Judas too, although he was sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he did among the apostles by virtue of the office entrusted to him caused the benefits given through an unworthy man to suffer no loss on that account.

“Thus Paul, through whom Christ speaks, affirms: ‘I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth’ (1 Cor. III). [Col. 1079D] God does not ask who or what kind of person preaches, but whom he preaches; hence he confirms that even the envious may preach Christ well, just as the devil himself was cast down.

“Therefore this man too, whose name we say ought to be withheld, harmed only himself by administering good things wickedly. For the inviolable sacrament given through him obtained the perfection of its power for others, but brought harm to him. The curious suspicion of certain people extends so far that, once Pope Felix had issued his judgment, they imagine Acacius acted ineffectively thereafter in the sacraments he usurped, and consequently fear those who received the ministries imparted either in consecrations or in baptism.”

## CHAPTER III  
### How the Holy Spirit avoids a counterfeit minister of discipline but does not abandon his ministry

INF. How, then, is it written in the Book of Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the counterfeit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. I)?

DEF. Blessed Augustine explains this against the Donatist Parmenianus as follows:

“What is written—‘The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the counterfeit’—must be understood to mean that he is absent from that person’s salvation; yet he does not abandon the ministry through which he works the salvation of others by means of that person. Hence the Apostle says: ‘For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship’ (1 Cor. IX). It is as though he were saying: it benefits those to whom I administer this, not me, who am counterfeit.”

INF. Since the Holy Spirit does not abandon the ministry of a counterfeit priest, give me another testimony.

DEF. The same Augustine argues at greater length and with greater clarity on this point in his exposition of John, where the Lord was baptized. Thus, for those who understand rightly, it has been sufficiently established that the ordination performed by blessed Formosus is valid and legitimate. [Col. 1080B] Now tell me by what proofs or authority you strive to overturn the aforesaid ordination and, what is worse, do not fear consecrating someone a second time in the same rank.

INF. Everything judged to be false must be destroyed; therefore that ordination must be destroyed because it is false. We endeavor to bestow upon each person the ordination that is true, as reason requires.

DEF. I see that, in a childish contest, you shamelessly return to matters already examined and confirmed by testimonies. You act as though secure because the censor of justice is absent. Yet Isaiah’s prophecy is present: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. V).

## CHAPTER IV  
### That the ordination of the neophyte Constantine was deposed contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers

INF. You should not find it surprising if a counterfeit is ordained, cast out, and his ordination rejected. For Constantine, as is read in the *Pontifical Book*, suddenly became a neophyte from a layman and, armed with force, wickedly invaded the apostolic see. He was deposed and condemned so that even his eyes were removed; and those whom he ordained were reduced to their former ranks. For the bishops were consecrated again by Pope Stephen. Concerning the presbyters and deacons, it was decreed that, if the choice of their fellow citizens so desired, they should be consecrated again by Pope Stephen to the same ranks from which they had been deposed, provided only that they promised under oath that they would never thereafter be promoted to a higher dignity, lest such an error grow through injury. They also decreed that all the ecclesiastical sacraments performed by Constantine should be repeated, except baptism and chrism.

DEF. An example must never be taken from wicked men. Of what is read in books, only those things that are shown to be good should be imitated or performed; evil things, however, must be utterly detested and entirely avoided. Thus Abel the righteous is praised, while Cain the murderer [fratricide] is condemned. Thus, I say, Sixtus is crowned with martyrdom, while Liberius is stained by Arian pollution.

Therefore Constantine, who, as a neophyte and surrounded by weapons, usurped the apostolic chair for himself, was rightly condemned [Col. 1081A] and deposed. But the fact that they deprived him of his eyes was apostolic in no sense; it was apostatic. They also reduced his ordination to the former ranks, not out of concern for rectitude but through the zeal of envy against the decrees of the holy Fathers, adding an oath and binding them by it so that none of the presbyters or deacons would be promoted to higher ranks. What else can this decision be understood to signify except fear of retaliation—namely, lest those who had later been advanced to the height of apostolic dignity should avenge the wrong done to them?

INF. They decided to inflict this sort of punishment in order to cut ambition completely out of the sacred order.

DEF. Just as one disease cannot drive out another disease, so one vice cannot exclude another vice. It was good—indeed, good—that they cast the neophyte out from the apostolic eminence; but they plainly sinned against those who had been ordained according to the canons, and did not fear deposing them and, with wicked audacity, decreeing that they should be consecrated again in the same ordination.

Otherwise, holy Pope Leo judged in vain that pseudo-bishops should be deposed while their ordination could remain valid. Pope Anastasius likewise decreed in vain that no portion of harm should touch those ordained by Acacius. The ordinations of Liberius and the consecrations of Vigilius would also have remained unimpaired in vain. Was anyone after the apostles greater in the Church than the most blessed Pope Leo, at whose—as I might say—heavenly roar various and numerous heretics were terrified and driven away? Nor is Pope Anastasius to be despised, for he strengthened his decretal pronouncements with evangelical and apostolic testimonies alike. Nor is the most holy Pope Gregory to be regarded lightly, for he wrote that just as baptism must not be repeated, so consecration must not be repeated.

Therefore, if the statutes of these Fathers are not to be observed, where is what is written: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. XXII)? And the Apostle’s words: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached, let him be anathema” (Gal. I)?

INF. That the ordination of the same neophyte was deposed contrary to the statutes of the Fathers is by no means explicitly stated in the *Pontifical Book*. But many remember that Pope Stephen deposed Formosus after his death and permitted none of those whom Formosus had ordained to vest with him in the Church. [Col. 1081D]

DEF. In the same *Pontifical Book* it is written that Liberius subscribed to the Arian heresy, but it is not added there that he did wrong. Nor is it added concerning Vigilius that he acted wrongly when he sent his own pontiff Silverius into exile and established himself as apostolic pontiff. Yet no one doubts that they acted against the prohibitions of Scripture.

Therefore the same must be understood concerning the ordination of the aforesaid Constantine: that it was wickedly deposed. Moreover, the fact that Stephen deposed Formosus after his death can in no way prejudice the ordination he performed, as has already been carefully emphasized above. For those whom Stephen prohibited from vesting with him in the Church were ordered by Pope Theodore—who certainly had no connection with the ordination of Formosus—to vest and perform their office; and Theodore brought back Formosus’s little body, which had been obstinately cast out, with rejoicing to the apostolic tomb.

## CHAPTER V  
### That repeated consecration is the same transgression as repeated baptism

INF. Is there anything contrary to the Catholic rule if someone is consecrated a second time in the same order?

DEF. Repeated consecration is unquestionably the same transgression as repeated baptism.

INF. Who says this?

DEF. Holy Pope Gregory wrote to John, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, saying:

“What you say—that one who has been ordained should be ordained again—is exceedingly ridiculous and foreign to the consideration of your intelligence, unless perhaps the example that is brought forward concerns the man who is said to have done such a thing and who was judged for it. Let such a way of thinking be far from your fraternity. Just as one who has been baptized once must not be baptized again, so one who has been consecrated once cannot be consecrated again in the same order.”

This is attested not only by blessed Gregory but also by the canons of the apostles. For holy Isidore confirms in the preface to the canonical collection that the canons of the apostles are to be received. If anyone dislikes this, whether he wishes it or not, Gregory—whose authority shines throughout the entire Church like the sun—is not to be rejected.

INF. The authority of councils is greater than that of one Pope Gregory.

DEF. Nowhere is it read that a Catholic consecration can be given a second time in the same order. Moreover, blessed Gregory is recognized to have considered and understood the decrees of the councils incomparably better than the people of our time; therefore no one is to be preferred to him.

## CHAPTER VI  
### That repeated consecration is the same transgression as that of the heretics who dare to rebaptize Catholics

INF. Repeated consecration in the same rank: of what transgression do you consider it to be?

DEF. I know with certainty, not merely by supposition, that repeated consecration is the same transgression as that of all the heretics who dare to rebaptize Catholics. Have you forgotten that, just as one who has been baptized once must not be baptized again, so one who has once been consecrated cannot now be consecrated again in the same order?

INF. Does heresy arise from lesser offenses?

DEF. Does it seem a small matter to you to invalidate the most sacred ministry through which faith in the divine Trinity is received and the Christian religion is continually celebrated—and, as though that were not enough, not to fear adding a repeated laying-on of hands?

## CHAPTER VII  
### That a lesser fault than repeated consecration is found included among the designations of heresies

INF. It seems unbelievable to me that errors which are not altogether harmful can be counted among the designations of heresies.

DEF. Saint Augustine recalls the matter in his book *On Heresies* as follows:

“The heretics called Coluthians took their name from a certain Coluthus, who said that God does not make evils, contrary to what is written: ‘I am God, creating evils’ (Isa. XLV). The Florinians likewise took their name from Florinus, who said the opposite, namely, that God created evils, contrary to what is said: ‘God made all things, and behold, they were very good’ (Gen. I). Thus, although they said things contrary to one another, both resisted the divine utterances. God creates evils by inflicting most just punishments, which Coluthus did not see; but he does not create evil natures and substances insofar as they are natures and substances, as Florinus erroneously held.”

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Against those who excuse themselves by saying, “We were unwillingly consecrated again to the same rank”

INF. If the repetition of sacred ordination is weighed on an even balance, it should be attributed not to me but to the one who compelled me to deny the first consecration and accept the second.

DEF. O Lord, Teacher of all, what do you say to this? “‘Let them alone; they are blind, leaders of the blind. If the blind lead the blind, will not both fall into a pit?’” (Matt. XV.) Therefore, according to this saying of the Lord, in doing evil both the one who leads and the one who follows are blind, and deservedly both fall into the pit of condemnation.

But you, vessel of election, through whom Christ speaks, what do you say? “Not only those who do evil, but also those who consent to those who do it, are deserving of eternal death” (Rom. I).

INF. What, then, should be done against those whom we are entirely unable to resist?

DEF. What the Savior says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X).

## CHAPTER IX  
### Against those who say, “God will not destroy such a multitude of sinners”

INF. Are all those who professed that the consecration of Formosus was nothing and who were consecrated again in the same order to be hurled into hell? Surely God will not destroy so great a multitude of bishops, presbyters, and deacons?
