DEF. Does God look to the multitude or number of just anyone, rather than to those of whom he himself says: “To whom shall I look except to the humble and quiet one who fears my words?” (Isa. LXVI.) And in the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII).

What more is needed? That God does not spare a multitude of transgressors unless they repent, hear the Apostle Peter saying: “For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but, casting them into the chains of hell, committed them to Tartarus to be kept for punishment at the judgment; and if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, the eighth person, a herald of righteousness, when he brought the flood upon the world of the ungodly, making them an example of those who would act ungodly” (2 Pet. II). [Col. 1083D]

Likewise, if God looked to the multitude of the wicked, he would not have struck down so many thousands of men in the desert of Sinai—and would that he had struck down only their bodies and not their souls! Hence it is read in the Epistle of Jude: “Jesus, having saved the people of Israel from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude V).

Moreover, transgressors against righteousness are not to be imitated, in accordance with what Mattathias says: “Even if all consent to King Antiochus, I and my father’s house will not consent” (1 Macc. II). The Prophet likewise says: “Do not envy those who act wickedly, nor emulate those who practice iniquity” (Ps. XXXVI).

In the time, therefore, of the most holy Father Athanasius, nearly the whole world turned to the Arian heresy; nevertheless, the very few who persevered in the Catholic faith won the palm of victory.

## CHAPTER X  
### That one who has been consecrated once and again in the same order must be excluded from the sacred ministry

INF. By what reasoning have you dared to assert that one who has been consecrated once and again in the same order must be excluded from the sacred ministry?

DEF. I have asserted no such thing on my own authority, but, as was reported above, on that of blessed Gregory and also of the canons of the apostles.

INF. Then is one who has been baptized again to be expelled from Christianity?

DEF. Certainly not. One thing is baptism, another consecration. Everyone who has been consecrated can administer baptism; yet not everyone who is baptized can either possess consecration for himself or confer it upon others. Hence baptized bigamists, if necessity arises, may baptize, but they cannot canonically receive sacred orders.

Do you see that baptism belongs to faith, whereas consecration belongs to the ministry through which that faith is received and the Christian religion celebrated? Therefore one who incurs such sacrilege must be removed from the sacred ministry. [Col. 1084C]

Add also that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven without baptism; therefore it would be impious to exclude someone baptized twice from Christianity.

INF. Priests who denied the faith during persecution were not stripped of their honors. How, then, are these men to be excluded from the priesthood because of a repeated laying-on of hands?

DEF. The cases are different. Among priests who denied the faith during persecution, there is a considerable distinction between those who denied it without danger and those who denied it under violent coercion. The Ancyran canon is witness to this, saying:

“Presbyters who sacrificed and then again entered the struggle, if they did so not through some pretense but in truth, neither standing before their parents nor seeking or persuading others, so that they might indeed be considered suited to suffer torture but nevertheless submitted to these things only in appearance and outward conduct—it has pleased us that these retain the honor of their own seat, but that they may not offer, address the people, or perform any priestly functions at all” (canon 1).

Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, concerning those who denied the faith during persecutions and were afterward promoted within the clergy:

“Whoever among the lapsed was promoted to the clerical order through ignorance or through the dissimulation of those who ordained them does not prejudice the ecclesiastical rule; once they are known, let them be deposed.”

With these matters set forth, we are reminded that Pope Innocent did not wish Rusticus, who had become a presbyter through repeated ordination, to be retained in the Church. For he wrote to Marcianus, bishop of Naissus, saying (Epistle 21):

“When I was established in the city of Ravenna, because of the frequent needs of the Roman people, Germanius, who asserts that he is a presbyter, and Lupentius, who says that he is a deacon, having undertaken the embassy of many such men and poured forth their prayers, eagerly expressed their own grievances. They asserted that they retained the churches situated in the parishes entrusted to your affection, but that they had been unable to obtain your communion, for the following reason: a certain man named Rusticius had received the presbyterate through repeated ordination. And this causes no small difficulty, whether because they grieve that such a man is retained in the Church, or because he thinks that another ought to sin in the same way in which he recognizes that he himself has sinned.” [Col. 1085A]

Likewise, this too must be recalled: Pope Gregory, writing to John, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, says:

“What you say—that one who has been ordained should be ordained again—is exceedingly ridiculous and foreign to the consideration of your intelligence, unless perhaps the example that is brought forward concerns the man who is said to have done such a thing and who was judged for it.”

Do you not see that transgressors of this kind have already been judged by the Fathers of old?

## CHAPTER XI  
### That an oath pertaining to the commission of a crime must not be observed

INF. Since everyone must obey the supreme pontiff in all things, you say, on the contrary, that anyone from the clergy who binds himself to him by an oath to assist in overturning the ordination must be punished by canonical judgment.

DEF. No one should ever obey any authority in committing crimes, because “the Lord hates all who work iniquity, and will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. V). And the Apostle says: “Not only those who do evil, but also those who consent to those who do it, are deserving of eternal death” (Rom. I).

INF. Would any believer dare lawfully to invalidate an oath that he has once sworn?

DEF. An oath that is free from sin must not be violated. But an oath that pertains to the commission of a crime must not be observed. To omit other examples, David, moved by Abigail’s entreaties, chose to incur perjury rather than commit murder. Herod, however, because he neglected to exercise discretion in his oath, fell into the abyss of homicide.

Consider, I say, what Isidore judges on this matter. He says:

“An oath that is promised wickedly and imprudently must not be kept. For example, if someone should promise an adulteress perpetual fidelity to remain with her, it is more tolerable not to fulfill the oath than to persist in the disgrace of fornication.”

INF. These testimonies do not sufficiently show that someone should be removed from the sacred order because of such an oath.

DEF. After the Council of Nicaea, the Synod of Chalcedon retains the palm of authority. It certainly decreed as follows:

“The crime of conspiracy or collusion is altogether prohibited even by secular laws; much more must care be taken that it not occur in the Church of God. Therefore, if any clerics or monks are found conspiring, colluding, or laying ambushes for bishops or clerics, let them be deposed from their proper rank.”

Do you see with what sublime authority the clerics about whom the discussion has arisen are to be counted among sacrilegious conspirators and condemned by canonical judgment?

## CHAPTER XII  
### That one must not attend a synod that manifestly acts contrary to Catholic rectitude

INF. The apostolic pontiff summoned you to a synod, but you, despising his command, refused to attend.

DEF. If a sheep has ever run at the voice of a wolf, then I too ought to have attended that synod. This is what the Savior says: “The sheep follow the shepherd because they know his voice; but they do not follow a stranger; rather, they flee from him because they do not know the voice of strangers” (John X).

Are they not wolves, are they not strangers, those who, overturning the aforesaid ordination, blaspheme that nearly all Italy has lived for many years as though pagan and without the religion of Christ? For the Lord said and did this: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (ibid.). You, on the contrary, are not ashamed to tear the Lord’s sheep apart with wolflike teeth, not only in body but, what is more wretched, also in soul.

This is what blessed Gregory says in grief: “Consider what happens to the flocks when wolves become shepherds, against whom they ought to have guarded God’s flocks.”

He despised hastening to the council—but to what council? To one where I would be baptized with a second baptism and thus become not purified but polluted. Therefore I wisely chose, with David, to sing in word and deed:

“I did not sit in the council of vanity, nor will I enter with those who act wickedly. I hated the assemblies of the evil, and I will not sit with the impious” (Ps. XXV).

## CHAPTER XIII  
### That the faults of superiors are neither all to be concealed nor all to be exposed

INF. Following the respect shown by the sons of Noah, the faults of superiors are not to be exposed by their subjects but rather concealed.

DEF. We ought to imitate the example of Shem and Japheth, who covered their father’s nakedness (Gen. IX), with discernment added, so that we appear to incline neither to the right nor to the left. For this reason, not all faults of superiors are to be concealed, nor are all to be exposed.

To omit other matters, that fault which harms the Catholic religion must unquestionably be exposed if it cannot be corrected by another means, lest ignorant or simple souls perish through it. Certain faults of superiors, as the *Pontifical Book* bears witness, are so excessive that they are committed to writing—not for imitation, but so that posterity may avoid them.

For it is well known that the evil action of superiors generally harms their subjects, and that the sins of a king spill over into his kingdom. But now the discussion is specifically about that fault which undermines the fearful or simple in the Catholic religion. In this matter the fault was not exposed by subjects but rather aggravated by its own authors.

We, however, dare not offer such wrongdoing either favor or assent; we must distance ourselves far from it. Finally, the Apostle Paul, who cries, “Be imitators of me” (Phil. III), opposed the apostle Peter, the leader of the apostles, to his face because he was blameworthy—because he was compelling Gentiles in certain respects to practice Judaism (Gal. II). The keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven accepted this so willingly that he in no way contradicted him and, moreover, praised his teaching in his own Epistle.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### That an excommunication which pertains to the commission of a crime must not be observed

INF. How, despising an apostolic excommunication, did you dare to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass?

DEF. That excommunication which pertains to the commission of sacrilege must be regarded as nothing and in no way observed. For under such a pretext you compel me to deny the priesthood which, as you see, has governed the Church of the Lord Savior throughout Ausonia for nearly twenty years and has never ceased, as is customary, to perform ecclesiastical offices both for the living and for the dead. And, what is worse, you do not fear consecrating again in the same rank those who consent to you. Is such an excommunication to be observed?

## CHAPTER XV  
### Concerning what is written: “Whether justly or unjustly the shepherd binds, the flock must fear”

**ACCUSER.** Whether justly or unjustly, as Saint Gregory says, if the shepherd binds, the flock must fear, lest through the arrogance of swollen criticism a fault that did not exist should be created.

**DEFENDER.** If excommunication has been pronounced because of our negligences and our offenses, it must certainly be feared and observed without fail until worthy satisfaction or pardon has been obtained. But in matters that are plainly shown by reason to be hostile to God, no one’s excommunication is to be feared or observed. For example, if someone were to drive me, by excommunicating me, into perjury, false testimony, sacrilege, or murder, surely in such matters or their like is the shepherd’s excommunication to be feared or carried out? Especially since the Apostle says: “Not only those who do evil things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are made worthy of everlasting death” (Rom. I).

**ACCUSER.** Behold, you have not hesitated to bring this statement of the Apostle against me twice already.

**DEFENDER.** Whenever necessity demands it, I shall confidently oppose the same testimony to sinister arguments—not merely twice or three times, but even a hundred times, and not without reason. For an athlete uses one shield against the various weapons of his enemies.

**ACCUSER.** Answer me: how is it that until now no one has presumed to make such a distinction concerning the excommunications of pontiffs?

**DEFENDER.** Have you then forgotten the testimonies by which it was declared somewhat earlier that one must not obey unjust commands or consent to wicked actions? Thus we read in those same testimonies: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity. You hate, Lord, all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. V); and this: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. V); and this: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. XV); and this: “He is God’s minister for your good” (Rom. XIII).

Meanwhile, this too must be recalled: the one who says, “Whether justly or unjustly the shepherd binds, the flock must fear,” says in the same passage: “With great moderation let the shepherds of the Church strive either to loose or to bind. It often happens that one occupies the place of judge who is in no way suited to the character of that office; and it frequently occurs that he condemns the innocent, or, himself bound, releases others.” And below: “Those who follow either their own hatred or their own favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects rightly.” Hence it is rightly said through the Prophet: “They were putting to death souls that do not die, and making alive souls that do not live” (Ezek. XIII).

Finally, this too must not be consigned to oblivion: the Teacher of the Gentiles, rebuking them, says: “Therefore, you who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abominate idols, do you commit sacrilege?” (Rom. II.) And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV).

### CHAPTER XVI.—On the statement: “Observe and do everything that they tell you.”

**ACCUSER.** Where, then, is that Gospel passage: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat; observe and do everything that they tell you”? (Matt. XXIII.)

**DEFENDER.** In this passage, “everything” must be understood only in the good sense. Otherwise the Jews who crucified the Lord at the counsel and urging of the scribes and Pharisees ought to have been free from so great a crime. But Scripture testifies how gravely both those who spoke and those who acted sinned, and this guilt has been extended in their descendants to the end of the world. Thus, that “all” does not always refer to the whole, but often to the greater part, is attested by Jerome, where he discusses with Damasus the frugal and extravagant son.

### CHAPTER XVII.—That no one is to obey any authority when obedience would lead to sin

**ACCUSER.** Since one must not resist other authorities, because “there is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII), one must certainly not resist apostolic authority—which unquestionably surpasses all human authorities—in anything that it commands.

**DEFENDER.** We must be subject to every human authority, and especially to apostolic authority. But certainly not in those matters that Christian law abhors and forbids, and that are shown to be hostile to God, of whom the Prophet says: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity.” “You hate,” Lord, “all who work iniquity; you will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. V). And the Lord himself says to Jeremiah: “If you separate,” he says, “the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. XV).

### CHAPTER XVIII.—That pontifical sees are one thing and their occupants another, and that occupants who deviate are not to be followed in their deviations

**ACCUSER.** The holy Roman Church holds primacy over the Churches; therefore it judges all, and is judged by no one. Who, then, are you to speak against it?

**DEFENDER.** Far be it that I, the least of men—or rather, a worm—should speak against it; rather, as God grants, I speak for it. Please attend carefully to what I am about to say, for it is altogether beyond comparison. Pontifical sees are one thing; those who preside over them are another. Therefore the honor and dignity of each see must be reverently observed. But if those who preside deviate, they are not to be followed in their deviations—that is, if they begin to act against the faith or the Catholic religion, we must by no means follow them in such matters. This often happened in the case of the sees of Constantinople and Alexandria. In matters that they rightly declare, even if they do not practice them, we must willingly obey them.

This is why we are commanded to gather grapes and avoid thorns. What more need be said? Turn your attention from shepherds back to the people, to whom it is said: “He is God’s minister for your good” (Rom. XIII). For this reason he added “for your good,” because God’s minister is not for your harm.

### CHAPTER XIX.—On the statement: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven” (Matt. XVIII)

**ACCUSER.** The power of binding and loosing has been bestowed from heaven upon all bishops, but especially upon the vicar of the apostles, who holds the place of the Apostle Peter and the keys of the kingdom from heaven. Therefore, however he binds, the matter will be bound.

**DEFENDER.** Jerome, interpreter of the divine law, does not understand it in this way. Explaining the Gospel passage, “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven,” he says:

“Understanding this passage in this way, bishops and presbyters assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or imagine that they can release the guilty, whereas before God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the accused that is examined.”

Nor must we omit what is said through the Prophet: “They were putting to death souls that do not die, and making alive souls that do not live” (Ezek. XIII). For, as Saint Gregory teaches, the one who condemns the just puts to death one who is not dying; and the one who attempts to absolve the guilty from punishment tries to make alive one who will not live.

Likewise Solomon says: “As a bird flying into the opposite direction and a sparrow going wherever it will” (Prov. XXVI), so a curse uttered without cause will come upon the one who sent it. It is also said there: “The soul that blesses will be made rich” (Prov. XI); but the one who curses without cause will himself be under the curse.

Likewise, Saint Gregory the pope says: “In everything that is said about us outside ourselves, we must return to the secret judgment of the mind; and even if everyone condemns a person, he is nevertheless free whom conscience does not accuse. For although everyone praises him, he cannot be free if conscience accuses him.”

### CHAPTER XX.—How Formosus, after his deposition, was reconciled by apostolic authority

**ACCUSER.** Now, as we draw near to the shore of our begun discourse, we lower our sails; and Formosus, who was not afraid to stir up storms, has remained as though immune from so great a danger.

**DEFENDER.** He neither ought nor can be judged by human examination who has already been placed before the judgment of him who is judge of the living and the dead; who does not judge according to the hearing of the ears or the sight of the eyes, but according to that which God, searching hearts and reins, [judges] (Ps. VII).

**ACCUSER.** Do not hesitate to acknowledge how, through him, a seedbed of scandal arose in the holy Church, where supreme concord ought to exist.

**DEFENDER.** Formosus, as I said, does not pertain to me—that is, to the ordination which he performed—but to those who elected him, ordained him, communicated with him as long as he lived, and were participants with him in all things. Nevertheless, do as seems right to you.

**ACCUSER.** After his deposition, Formosus could not be a bishop; how much less could he be pope?

**DEFENDER.** Just as it is true that he was deposed by apostolic authority, so it is true that he was reconciled by apostolic authority.

**ACCUSER.** When he was deposed, he confirmed by oath, with the holy Gospels as witnesses, that he would never enter the city of Rome and would in no way resume his episcopate; therefore he could not be reconciled.

**DEFENDER.** Such an oath is judged not only among Christians but even among pagans to be bloody and impious. In truth, nothing else is found in it except that he should never worship at the thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul, never approach reconciliation, and never resume his episcopate. What an outrage! The cruelty of such an oath is found nowhere even among pagans. Woe to those who extorted such a pledge from him by force. Blessed and merciful was that apostolic Father who decided to reconcile him.

**ACCUSER.** Was the apostolic pontiff truly obliged to reconcile a man who had condemned himself with his own mouth before the bishops and had therefore been deposed?

**DEFENDER.** I could answer that when he condemned himself with his own mouth, he did not satisfy his interrogator by a truthful profession, but, terrified by great fear, did so under compulsion, although not entirely without fault. But it is enough that afterward he was reconciled by apostolic authority.

Hear also what Pope Alexander decrees synodally on this matter. He says:

“This too has been brought to this holy see—a matter shameful to mention and hostile not only to the priestly name but to every Christian name: namely, that certain bishops or priests are compelled by fear, extorted by force, or deceived by fraud to make writings concerning their confession for some other purpose that they ought not to serve—whether at the demand of their own affairs or, what is worse, in adherence to another’s error—and to authenticate them with their own hands and recite and confess them before the people. They say that some are shut up in workhouses and prisons, so that, terrified by such snares, they may deceive the priests of the Lord and make them subject to their own will.

“Considering these impieties and avoiding dangers to souls, together with all the priests who have gathered with you in this holy city, and with all the members of this body, as we have received from the blessed apostles and the other holy Fathers and their successors, we establish and decree that all who persecute the holy Fathers, or are shown to remove or tear them apart, are to be infamous and made strangers to the thresholds of the Church until they have given satisfaction.”

From the same letter [*Supplement to the letter*]:

“Likewise, if any writings have in any way been extorted from such persons through fear, fraud, or force, or if anything has been written or authenticated by them by any means so that they might free themselves, we decree that no prejudice or harm shall result to them from this, nor shall we ever, with the Lord and the holy apostles and their successors as guarantors, permit them to suffer any infamy, accusation, or separation from their possessions.”

### CHAPTER XXI.—That many priests were deposed and afterward reconciled

**ACCUSER.** If this applies to the reconciliation of those who have fallen, confirm it by examples.

**DEFENDER.** Very many priests were deposed and afterward reconciled—reconciled, I say, not consecrated again to the same office, since reconciliation is one thing and consecration another. For the one who is reconciled is restored to his former rank; the one who is consecrated receives what he does not possess.

But, as I began to say, John Chrysostom was judged by two synods of orthodox bishops, yet was restored again to his own Church. Likewise Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, was deposed but afterward regained his own episcopate. Asclepius, likewise judged by a synod, afterward regained his Church. Lucian, bishop of Adrianople, condemned by Pope Julius, regained the Church of his episcopate. Likewise Cyril of Jerusalem was deposed and afterward reconciled to his Church.

In the same way Pope Xystus condemned Polychronius, pontiff of that same Church of Jerusalem, and then himself reconciled him. Pope Innocent likewise condemned Photinus the bishop, but afterward restored him himself to his proper place in his Church. Likewise, when Bishop Misenus had been condemned by Pope Felix, Pope Gelasius, his successor, both admitted him to communion and restored him to his Church.

Leontius, although he had been deposed while a presbyter, afterward became patriarch of Antioch. Pope Gregory IV consecrated Theodosius bishop of the holy Church of Siguina, after his predecessor Eugenius had deprived him of the honor of the presbyterate. Ibas, indeed, was judged, but the holy synod canonically restored his Church to him. Pope Nicholas reconciled with us Rothad, bishop of the holy Church of Soissons, who had been condemned by the synod attended by King Charles, and Soffrenius, bishop of Piacenza, who had been rightly rejected.

### CHAPTER XXII.—That what is uncertain must be left to God’s judgment alone; and concerning bishops transferred from one see to another

**ACCUSER.** Suppose that Formosus was reconciled, but afterward, desiring human praise, abandoned his own wife and took another’s—that is, having abandoned his episcopate, he seized the apostolic see from those who were to be ordained.

**DEFENDER.** Whether he ascended the apostolic throne out of desire for human praise is uncertain and therefore must be left to God’s judgment alone. Nevertheless, the whole city of Rome and all the surrounding regions testify that he was a man of outstanding holiness, except for a very few who are not ashamed to defame him. Nor is this surprising, since it is also written concerning the Savior: “Some were saying, ‘He is good’; others, ‘No, but he is misleading the crowds’” (John VII).

But that in such a transfer he did not take another’s wife can be made clear by credible examples. I pass over those who were transferred from one see to another before the Council of Nicaea. Was Gregory of Nazianzus, a most holy and learned man, ignorant of that council? Or does anyone understand it better than he is known to have understood it? He had been bishop of a city called Sasima, but by the counsel and urging of the blessed Basil and other bishops he was appointed to the town of Nazianzus and afterward transferred to Constantinople.

Alexander, bishop of Antioch, transferred Dositheus, bishop of Seleucia, to Tarsus in Cilicia. Reverentius moved from Arcis in Phoenicia to Tyre. John was transferred from Gordo in Lydia to Proconnesus and presided over that Church. Palladius was transferred from Helenopolis to Aspama. Alexander was transferred from another Helenopolis to Adrianople. Meletius first presided over the Church of Sebaste and afterward was appointed overseer of Antioch. Theosebius was transferred from Apamea in Asia to Eudoxiopolis, formerly called Salambria. Polycarp was transferred from the city of Antepristena in Mysia to Nicopolis in Thrace. Hierophilus moved from Trapezopolis in Phrygia to Antioch. Optimus moved from Agardamia in Phrygia to Antioch in Pisidia. Sylvanus was transferred from Philippopolis in Thrace to Troas.

Perigenes was ordained bishop in Petras, but because the citizens of that city refused to receive him, the [bishop] of the Roman city ordered him to be enthroned at Corinth, the metropolis, after its bishop had died; and he presided over that Church as long as he lived.

Eusebius Pamphili, in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, reports that Alexander was bishop of a city in Cappadocia. When he had come to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer, he was detained by its citizens, appointed in the place of Bishop Narcissus, and thereafter presided over that Church for the rest of his life.

Germanus, archbishop of Cyzicus, was transferred from that metropolis to Constantinople. In connection with this transfer, Michael, a presbyter of the holy Roman Church and an apocrisiarius by title, delivered the following address:

“For divine grace, which deigns to choose the weak and complete what is incomplete, has transferred and appointed the most holy archbishop Germanus, now present, to the most sacred see of the city of Constantinople, preserved by God.”

Aitardus also was enthroned from the episcopate of Tarragona in the archiepiscopate of Tours, by the grant of the emperor Charles II and with the consent of Pope Adrian II.

### CHAPTER XXIII.—That Hosius did not speak catholically:

“And let him not receive lay communion at the end.”

**ACCUSER.** Hosius says: “If any bishop changes his see through avarice or ambition, or in order to exercise domination, let him not have lay communion.” Then, in the following chapter: “Even if he should be such a person that, through frauds and by corrupting certain people with gifts and payment, he offers an excuse so that the people may seem to request him, let him not receive lay communion at the end.”

**DEFENDER.** I gladly accept what Hosius prohibited—avarice and ambition, domination and fraud. But what he added, “Let him not receive lay communion at the end,” I do not accept, since it sounds not Catholic but Catharist. Especially since the Lord cries out through the Prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII). And in the Gospel he says: “There is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need repentance.” But concerning the end with which Hosius concluded his own position, I would rather weep than express it in words.

### CHAPTER XXIV.—Concerning one who has once been a lector in any Church

**ACCUSER.** The African council decreed that whoever has once read in a Church may not be admitted to the clergy by another Church. And if this was decreed concerning lectors, how could Formosus have been transferred from an episcopal see to the apostolic throne?

**DEFENDER.** What you have raised concerning the lector is not to be understood as though one who had once been a lector in any Church could thereafter in no way be admitted to the clergy in another Church. Rather, the African council more clearly decreed—when Epigonius complained on behalf of his disciple and fosterling—that no bishop should seize another Church’s cleric for himself against the will of the bishop to whom he belonged.

**ACCUSER.** Pope Celestine issued the following decree concerning clerical election:

“The consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought. Then another person may be sought and chosen from another Church if, among the clergy of the city in which the bishop is to be ordained, no worthy person can be found—which we do not believe can happen. For those clergy must first be rejected before someone from another Church is rightly preferred. Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has spent his life through all the offices. Let no one intrude upon another’s stipend, nor dare one person claim for himself the reward owed to another.”

**DEFENDER.** No one doubts that this decree of Pope Celestine is praiseworthy and just. But sometimes it happens that, when a definite necessity is imminent or definite reasons exist, a bishop may lawfully be transferred from one see to another, as has already been explained at greater length above. Likewise, one may pass from another Church to the clerical office. This is so true that even Pope Siricius decreed that religious monks should ascend through the canonical ranks to episcopal eminence.

Hence Saint Pope Gregory writes to Marianus, concerning the ordering of other monasteries, that monks should be taken from a monastery for the clerical office with the consent of the abbot. But if the abbot has a sufficient number of monks and refuses to give one, the bishop in whose diocese the monastery is located should diligently take one of those mentioned above.

### CHAPTER XXV.—That, without necessity or definite reasons, a bishop should not pass from one see to another

**ACCUSER.** What, then, can you raise against these statements? The Nicene synod defined as follows:

“Because of the great disturbances and seductions that occur, it has seemed good that the custom which appears to have been admitted contrary to the rule in certain regions be abolished entirely, so that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may be transferred from one city to another. If this should happen, let it be regarded as altogether invalid, and let him be restored to the Church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.”

**DEFENDER.** It is not proper for my insignificance to expound the judgment of so great a council. Nevertheless, I boldly say that no one has ever been able to consider and understand the Nicene canons more correctly or subtly than Gregory of Nazianzus, whom we mentioned above, as well as the Council of Chalcedon, the blessed Pope Leo, and Gelasius.

**ACCUSER.** You have already raised the fact that Gregory of Nazianzus passed from one see to another. What remains now is for you to present the rest.

**DEFENDER.** As I began to say, the Council of Chalcedon and the most holy Pope Leo and Gelasius appear to understand the aforementioned rule of the Council of Nicaea as follows.

**From the Council of Chalcedon**

“Clerics serving in a Church, as we have already decreed, ought not to be appointed to the Church of another city, but should be content with the Church in which they were initially worthy to serve, except for those who, having lost their own provinces, have transferred themselves by necessity to another Church. If any bishop, after this definition, receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, it has been decided that both the one received and the one receiving him shall be deprived of communion until the cleric who migrated has returned to his own Church.”

**From Pope Leo**

“If any bishop, despising the modesty of his own city, should seek the administration of a more celebrated place and transfer himself by any means to a larger people, let him indeed be expelled from the foreign chair, but let him also lose his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he coveted through avarice nor over those whom he despised through pride. Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries, and let no one desire to enlarge his authority beyond the measure of his lawful jurisdiction.”

**From Pope Gelasius**  
[Note: [Col. 1093D] See Pope Gelasius, Letter 9, chapter 25.]

“Whoever, abandoning his own Church, thinks he should pass to another when no reasons exist, and is rashly received and promoted in his insolence, whether he himself or the one who received and promoted him will not escape the penalties that the sacred canons have established for such presumptuous persons.”

**ACCUSER.** These chapters serve my objections. I see that the Council of Chalcedon established that, without the loss of one’s province and without necessity, one should not move into the Church of another city; and that Pope Leo judged that a bishop, despising the modesty of his own city, ought not to seek the administration of a superior place or transfer himself through avarice to a larger people. Gelasius likewise says that, when no reasons exist, no one should dare abandon his own Church. For what necessity, or for what reasons, was Formosus ordered to abandon his own Church and ascend the apostolic throne?

**DEFENDER.** What reasons existed, or what necessity caused Formosus to become pope, is for the clergy and nobles of the city of Rome to know. They were compelled neither by the siege or pressure of the Franks nor by that of any other people, but decided of their own accord to elect and enthrone him. They say that they elected him for no other reason than the benefit of the Church. He himself gave his consent to being enthroned, as many bishops are recorded to have done, as was explained somewhat earlier.

**ACCUSER.** It is known to almost everyone that the authority of many pontiffs is greater than that of a few. Therefore, in this question the Council of Nicaea must be observed more carefully, since it abolished altogether and without qualification the custom of transferring from one see to another.

**DEFENDER.** You appear not to have understood what the Council of Nicaea says: “It has seemed good that the custom which appears to have been admitted contrary to the rule in certain regions be abolished entirely.” What custom, I ask, did it decide to abolish? Clearly, the one that appears to have been admitted in certain regions contrary to the rule—that is, without rectitude.

Does not the Council of Chalcedon itself, applying discernment, which is the mother of all virtues, appear to assert the same thing when it says that clerics ought not to be appointed in the Church of another city, except those who, having lost their own provinces, transferred themselves by necessity to another Church?

Nor is what the blessed Pope Leo judged dissimilar: that a bishop, despising the modesty of his city, ought not to seek the administration of a more celebrated place. Gelasius likewise says that no one who has abandoned his own Church should pass to another when no reasons exist.

In this way Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, neither ignorant of nor contemptuous of the Council of Nicaea, was transferred from one see to another. But whoever, with no necessity compelling him and with no reasons existing, is transferred to another see solely through avarice or ambition is unquestionably a transgressor of rectitude, and is therefore convicted of having undertaken such an act contrary to the rule.

**ACCUSER.** Then is Formosus, who changed his chair solely through avarice and ambition, to be punished more severely?

**DEFENDER.** It has already been answered above that an ambiguous crime must be left to God’s judgment alone.

**ACCUSER.** I see that under the guise of a certain defense you are asserting as doctrine that an episcopal transfer from one see to another may lawfully take place.

**DEFENDER.** Far be it that such a statement should proceed from my mouth: that any bishop may lawfully do such a thing except when a definite necessity is imminent or definite reasons exist.

### CHAPTER XXVI.—That when Formosus was enthroned he did not receive again what he already possessed as a bishop, but received an increase of apostolic dignity, which he did not possess

[Col. 1096A]

**ACCUSER.** Until now, by applying various scriptural poultices from one side and the other, you have treated a sick head. But now we have come to an incurable wound, for which no remedy can provide relief. When Formosus came to be made pope, he ordered that the laying on of hands be performed upon him as though he were not a bishop. Thus he not only failed to acquire apostolic dignity, but also lost what he had as a bishop.

**DEFENDER.** Is this the incurable wound that no remedy can heal? Does not the person whose eye, according to the Gospel saying, is “single” (Matt. VI), perceive in the laying on of hands not a wound but an increase of dignity, not a loss but an enrichment of the sacred order?

To make this clearer, hear the evidence. That a presbyter is the same as a bishop is attested by blessed Jerome in Letter 85, where he says:

“I hear that someone has erupted into such madness that he places deacons before presbyters, that is, before bishops. For although the Apostle plainly teaches that presbyters are the same as bishops, what is happening to the minister of tables and widows, that he should presumptuously exalt himself above those at whose prayers the body and blood of Christ are made?”

Hear the testimony: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons” (Philipp. I). And in the Acts of the Apostles Paul speaks thus to the priests of one Church: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the Church of the Lord, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts XX).

And lest anyone contend stubbornly that there were several bishops in one Church, hear another testimony in which it is plainly proved that a bishop and a presbyter are the same: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking and appoint presbyters in each city, as I commanded you: if anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having believing children who are not accused of dissipation or disobedience. For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus I).

And to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate” (1 Tim. IV). Peter likewise says in his First Letter: “I exhort the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter and a witness of the sufferings of Christ and of the glory that is to be revealed” (1 Pet. V).

But afterward one was chosen to be placed above the others as a remedy for schism, lest each person, drawing Christ’s Church to himself, should rend it apart. Thus far Jerome.

But let us return to what we began. It has been made clear by credible evidence that a presbyter is the same as a bishop. Therefore, when a presbyter receives the laying on of hands so that he may be placed above the others and specifically called a bishop, is he consecrated again in what he already is as a presbyter? Or does he rather receive, through that same laying on of hands, an increase of the episcopal ministry [or: mystery] that he does not possess?

Thus Formosus, in that laying on of hands, did not lose what he had as a bishop; rather, he received an increase of apostolic dignity, which he did not possess. Let this suffice as my response to what you yourself had raised concerning the laying on of hands.

Moreover, we questioned those who were present when Formosus was enthroned. They said: “It is unquestionably false that Formosus received the laying on of hands during that transfer. Rather, just as travelers on a journey entreat God with poured-out prayers, so we too, entreating the ruler of all, led him to the apostolic see and there enthroned him, offering the appropriate prayer.”

### CHAPTER XXVII.—That those who have hostilities and lawsuits among themselves cannot give testimony against one another

**ACCUSER.** There are still competent witnesses who testify that Formosus was not properly enthroned, but caused the laying on of hands to be performed upon him again in the same order that he had held.

**DEFENDER.** This accusation is plainly absurd. Otherwise, according to your view, those who enthroned him were not bishops but rather brute animals. I and many others with me know with absolute certainty that no one reports these things about Formosus except those who had quarrels and enmities with him.

Indeed, not only divine law but also human law commands that those who are known to have quarrels and lawsuits with one another may in no way give testimony against each other. Hence Pope Anacletus says:

“Those who were enemies yesterday or the day before yesterday cannot be accusers and witnesses, lest, being angry, they should desire to cause harm, or, having been injured, should wish to take revenge.”

For this reason Pope Sixtus also wrote: “One must not believe suspected accusers or those who come from the household of enemies.” Pope Telesphorus likewise says: “Those who remain enemies or are considered suspect must not be admitted, because their rivalry tears the innocent apart.”

### CHAPTER XXVIII.—That human judgment is most justly established by four persons

[Col. 1097D]

**ACCUSER.** Perhaps you wish to plead Formosus’s case before judges. The accusers are present; come forward, so that the truth of this dispute may become clear through a manifest examination.

**DEFENDER.** We cannot obtain the palm of justice before those who are simultaneously the witnesses, judges, and accusers. For every judgment is most justly completed by four persons: the accused, the accuser, the witnesses, and the judges. This is not a matter concerning trivial cases. Therefore, with God as its author, a universal council must be assembled, and, after the example of the great Constantine, the king’s presence must be included. Then this kind of scandal will be brought to an end and peace will be restored to the Church.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—On the council held in the city of Ravenna concerning Formosus and his ordination

[Col. 1098A]

**ACCUSER.** But in the city of Ravenna a synod was assembled and decreed that both Formosus and his ordination should remain established in their full force. Since this was instituted not through sincere concord but through an abundance of gold, it must therefore be considered worthless.

**DEFENDER.** As I think, what the Psalm says has happened to you: “They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it” (Ps. LVI). You will certainly be unable to prove that such a decision was established in that synod through gifts that had been brought. We, however, and many others with us know with the clarity of daylight that not only the prelates of the city of Rome but almost all the prelates of Italy attended the aforementioned council. Therefore, if, with God’s favor, royal authority should convene a universal council, what judgment will be passed upon you, who have not feared to invalidate the decrees of so many bishops?

### CHAPTER XXX.—On the crime perpetrated against the corpse of Pope Formosus
INF. Stephen, who became pope third after Formosus, judged that same Formosus to be so utterly reprobate that he had his corpse dragged from the tomb and hauled into the council. There they stripped him of his former garments, clothed him in a layman’s robe, cut off two fingers of his right hand with a sword, and buried him in a certain pilgrims’ tomb; not long afterward they threw him into the river Tiber.

DEF. Just as beasts, forgetful of humanity, understood the matter, so they acted. Wretched men—where did they learn this, especially [Col. 1098C] when the Lord did not say, “Whatever you bind beneath the earth or beneath the river,” but said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 18)? Of such people the Apostle says that some have “zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10). Shame upon the crime! At least they ought to have heeded the poetic saying:

> Spare, spare your pious hands from profaning; now spare the buried man!

Yet if such a transfer from one see to another had in some manner been unlawful, ought they not to have borne it with ecclesiastical charity rather than magnify it by unheard-of cruelties? Then, after summoning a universal synod, they should finally have decreed generally that the city of Rome must not dare to commit such an act again.

## CHAPTER XXXI — That no person of any nation should be forbidden to testify to what is right

[Col. 1098D]

INF. At last I shall return to you. Since you are a man of a foreign nation and depend upon us for the necessities of human life, what concern is it of yours to resist our debates?

DEF. Know that I belong to the race which the apostle Peter extols with these praises: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” (1 Peter 2). And because this people worships and honors Christ throughout the whole world, I must be received among them and nowhere excluded from bearing witness to the truth. For who does not know that the apostles were Hebrews, who made the holy Gospel shine throughout the whole world by their preaching? To conclude briefly: if the Apostle to the Gentiles confirms that even the envious preach Christ well, who can forbid me, when out of priestly compassion I testify to what is right?

INF. If newcomers and foreigners are permitted to accuse, judge, or prejudice the leaders of the Church, or to compose any writing against them, then it is pointless that this should be so expressly set forth in pontifical letters.

Anacletus: “Subjects who criticize the conduct and life of their rulers or teachers, even when those rulers are wicked, are worse than those who seize the property and estates of others and are therefore justly infamous and deservedly expelled from the Church. Teachers, or anyone who occupies the place of a shepherd in the Church, if he has strayed from the faith, must be corrected by the faithful; but because of reprehensible conduct he is to be tolerated rather than judged.

Telesphorus: “Let no sheep be received as an accuser against its shepherd; rather, we decree that all who take up arms against him who occupies the place of a shepherd are infamous.”

Pius: “Let sheep not reproach their shepherd; let the people not accuse their bishop, even if they have acted otherwise, for God has chosen to reserve their judgment to himself.”

Callistus. [Note: [Col. 1099D] This does not occur in the letter of Callistus.] “Let no one receive accusations, conspiracies, or whisperings against a teacher or anyone who occupies a superior position, because children ought not to reproach their fathers, nor servants to tear apart their masters. Those who slander or reproach their superiors do not live well. Teachers are to be borne, not reproached, unless they have strayed from the right faith. Let no doctor be accused through a written document, nor should anyone who leads a reprehensible life respond to an accuser, since it is unworthy for an unlearned person to answer a teacher, or a sheep to answer its shepherd.

“Again, just as a layman who has been lawfully convicted is not to be admitted as an accuser, so a priest cannot accuse or testify without a title, for a stained and infamous man is not permitted to accuse; and not only such men, but also those who consent with them, must be rejected.”

Thus far Callistus.

Likewise, the Council of Nicaea: “By a general decree we prohibit judgments by foreigners. How is it fitting that one should be judged by outsiders who ought to have provincial judges—judges chosen by and from among his own people?”

You have heard, defender, what the authority of the pontiffs decrees concerning accusations of this kind. There are many other passages belonging to the same subject, but I have considered it tedious to repeat them.

DEF. You cannot truthfully oppose any judgment of a pontiff to the principle that the truth of the Scriptures must not be recounted and explained to those who ask. These chapters are plainly shown to apply to those who do not hesitate to accuse any leaders of the Church, asserting that their crimes—whether committed or fabricated—are such as murder, robbery, adultery, or something of that sort. They do not apply to a decree that the truth contained in the sacred books must not be brought forward for those who ask, or, when necessary, be briefly incorporated into letters.

As for the statement that no one should write against any bishop and that no teacher should be accused in writing, I am astonished that you wish to understand it in such a way that, when people question us, we dare not briefly take down on tablets the things that ought to be answered from the divine books and satisfy them. For it is one thing to compose deceitful letters against someone in order to injure him in some way, and another to gather testimonies from Scripture into one place so that ignorance—which is the mother of errors—may not harm those seeking the truth. The former belongs to fraud and deception; the latter to the knowledge of truth.

How, then, do you claim that I resist the decrees of the Fathers, when I do not presume to charge any bishop with a crime or vice, but consider it a sin to conceal in silence from those who ask the truth that I have learned in the sacred books—especially since the Psalmist says to God: “I have not hidden your truth in my heart” (Psalm 39). Jesus, son of Sirach, likewise says: “Fight for your life in righteousness, and contend for righteousness even unto death” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

For Saint Isidore says: “A false witness and one who keeps back the truth are the same; nevertheless, the false witness who causes harm is worse than the one who refuses to testify to the truth. The former is malicious, the latter useless.”

Therefore, as I began to say, I strive neither to accuse anyone nor to drag anyone before judgment. Rather, I shall endeavor to repeat, to those who are present, by the living voice, and to those who are absent, by writing, the truth that I have been able to read in the Scriptures, lest the talent entrusted to my littleness be buried and I be punished more severely by the one who entrusts talents. Otherwise the holy teachers labored in vain to produce so many books if they are not to be recited and their truth defended, especially when people ask. Who, even if foolish, would dare to teach such a thing?

Moreover, as for what you wished to object from the same chapters—that the shepherd of the Church must not be reproved by the faithful unless he has erred in the faith—who does not see that you are killing yourself with your own sword? I seek to reprove no one, but if someone should wish to baptize me again, would he not be erring in the faith? It is clear that he would err, and consequently would without doubt be erring against the Holy Spirit, through whom all the sacraments of the Church are sanctified and believers are purified by baptism, and through whom they are established in the sacred orders by which the faith itself is received.

And truly, “whoever blasphemes against him, unless he corrects himself through repentance, will not be forgiven, neither in this age [Col. 1100D] nor in the age to come” (Matthew 12; Mark 3; Luke 12). In this matter, as Saint Augustine teaches, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—which will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come—is an impenitent heart, namely, the heart of one who dies in his sins without repentance. Therefore, whoever has erred in the sacred orders, as was explained above, will undoubtedly not be forgiven in this age or in the age to come unless he withdraws from such error through repentance.

Behold, when those who ask about priestly consecration seek the truth that is found everywhere in the sacred writings, I have taken care, to the best of my ability, to gather it together, although I am a foreigner and newcomer, as you shamelessly pretend without cause. For the rest, what remains now except that, invoking the Lord of all, we say with the Prophet: “Arise, O Lord; judge your own cause” (Psalm 73)?

## CHAPTER XXXII — That an oath given even under compulsion, if it does not concern the commission of sin, must be observed irrevocably

INF. You trample upon reverence and, like a slanderer, assert that I incur perjury in the matter of what I promised under oath: that, according to my ability, I would overturn the ordination performed by Formosus. I admit that I swore under violent pressure, and that, according to my knowledge and ability, I would defend the aforesaid ordination. But since there is one authority among the apostolic pontiffs, just as Pope Marinus was able to release Formosus from the oath he had given unwillingly, so the Apostolic Father released me from the bond of that oath and bound me by the promise of an oath to reduce that same ordination to nothing according to my strength.

DEF. It was established above, through testimonies of Scripture and the teaching of the Fathers, that no one should be bound by an oath to do evil; and if this has in some way occurred, the oath must not be observed but rather submitted to repentance.

For Formosus did not swear in order to inflict injury on anyone, but, wickedly hard pressed, he promised under oath that he would never enter the city of Rome, never seek the restoration of his honor, and never reclaim his episcopate. Is it lawful for such an oath to be imposed upon any Christian? Is it not plainly contrary to sacred religion?

It was contrary to sacred religion that he unwillingly swore never to enter the city of Rome—that is, never to worship the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul. But what he added, that he would never seek the restoration of his honor and never reclaim his episcopate, was likewise contrary to it. Therefore they rightly resolved, out of compassion, to release Formosus from such an oath, in accordance with what the Lord says: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than a burnt offering.”

But open the eyes of your heart and see how, in these very oaths of yours, you are a transgressor in two ways. You swore—although, as you yourself admit, unwillingly—that according to your knowledge and ability you would defend that ordination against its opponents; and this plainly concerned no one’s ruin but rather the common good. Later, no longer unwillingly but wishing to please certain persons, you swore that according to your ability you would overturn that same ordination, and this undoubtedly concerns the doing of evil.

Finally, who doubts that there is one authority among the apostolic pontiffs? But that authority exists for binding those who deserve to be bound and releasing those who deserve to be released. Otherwise blessed Gregory speaks in vain when he says: “Those who seek either their own hatred or their own favor in their subjects cannot judge their subjects.” Hence the prophet rightly says: “They put to death souls that should not die and gave life to souls that should not live” (Ezekiel 13). Whoever condemns the just kills one who should not die; whoever endeavors to acquit the guilty from punishment tries to give life to one who will not live.

And Jerome, discussing the Gospel passage “Whatever you bind on earth” (Matthew 18), says: “Bishops and priests who do not understand this passage assume something of the Pharisees’ haughtiness, so that they either condemn the innocent or imagine that they can release the guilty, whereas before God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the accused that is examined.”

It is therefore plainly understood that no one could release you from the bond of that oath which you had given for the doing of good. But the oath you gave for the doing of evil must certainly not be observed; rather, it must be submitted to repentance.

[Col. 1101]

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF A CERTAIN QUESTIONER AND RESPONDER, OR THE LITTLE BOOK OF AUXILIUS, CONCERNING THE CAUSE AND AFFAIR OF POPE FORMOSUS

*(From Mabillon’s Analecta.)*

## NOTICE TO THE READER

There was once a famous controversy concerning the case of Pope Formosus, which consisted chiefly of two questions. The first was whether his promotion to the Roman see was canonical; the second, whether the ordinations performed by him at that time should be regarded as valid. The second question depended upon the first, whose uncertainty was based on three grounds: first, that Formosus, formerly bishop of Porto, had been deprived of office by Pope John VIII and reduced to lay communion; second, that, as an exile, he had sworn never to return to Rome; third, that he had been transferred from the see of Porto to the Roman see. This transfer was contrary to ecclesiastical rules and Roman custom.

Nevertheless, there were those who then undertook Formosus’s defense. Among them was a certain Auxilius, a Frank—whether that was his true name or an invention—but living in Italy and ordained by Formosus. He wrote two books in his defense. The first comprises forty chapters, the second thirty-two, together with a preceding letter to Leo, bishop of Nola, at whose request he had undertaken the work. The illustrious Cardinal Baronius inserted this letter, together with the table of the thirty chapters of the first book, in the Appendix to volume 12. Joannes Morinus published both books in full in part 2 of *De sacris Ordinationibus*, beginning on page 348.

The second book survives in a Fiscamnian manuscript, before which, in place of the first book published by Morinus, the dialogue edited here is placed. I have no doubt that it is by the same Auxilius. Our Julian Bellasius sent me a transcription of this dialogue from that manuscript, and it seemed worthwhile to bring it into public view if it might contribute something toward illuminating the controversy of that extremely obscure period.

Frodoard agrees with Auxilius in praising Pope Formosus, both in his history and in his metrical book on the Roman pontiffs. A large part of that book has been printed in part 2 of the third century of the Benedictines, where the following, among other things, is read concerning Formosus:

> This distinguished bishop Formosus is raised  
> On high by lofty praises: chaste, sparing toward himself, generous to the needy;  
> He scattered the seeds of faith among the Bulgarian people,  
> Destroyed their shrines, and armed the people with heavenly weapons;  
> He instructed them, enduring many dangers, ever ready,  
> Giving the example that adversity must be borne  
> And that no brief troubles should be feared by the living.

Morinus, however, maintains that Formosus was not so free from fault that Stephen VI lacked a plausible reason for acting savagely against him after his death. Let others judge concerning this.

[Col. 1103A]

You ask me to answer you concerning the Formosian disaster, as though you were ignorant of the truth. I do not find what I should answer, for the entire answer is already given. It is a fault to make a vain clamor with an abundance of words, especially when the Apostle answered in a brief sentence, saying: “If anyone should preach another gospel, even if an angel coming from heaven should preach it, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8).

I am now ashamed of such foolishness. What, then, is the benefit of filling so many parchment sheets and transferring chapter after chapter every day from complete exemplars into volumes, when there is no audience? Worse still, a serpent lies sunk in deep sleep and pressed down by a heavy lethargy, so deeply that it cannot be awakened by any sound.

Let those to whom the helm of teaching has been entrusted undertake this task; they ought to listen so as to resist even unto blood. I, however, a worthless and stupid sheep, must listen to the one who says: “In your patience you shall possess your soul” (Luke 21:19). And again: “The worship of justice is silence” (Isaiah 32:17).

Paul, therefore, although he was a chosen vessel and teacher of the Church, chosen for the apostolate not by man but by God himself, did not consider himself competent to command the flying Magus, but said: “It is yours, Peter, to command; mine, however, to pray.” Thus, indeed, thus it is ours to pray that Jesus, sleeping in the boat, may rise and judge his own cause.

Nevertheless, overcome by your favor, accusing no one and reproving no one, touching no particular person, I shall distribute to you, with you as presiding officer and judge, beneath a rhetorical apparition, the active voices of the cases. By their assertion and refutation you may watchfully discern who gains the palm of variation.

But first, before entering the audience chamber, the power of the art must briefly be disclosed at the doors, so that the status of the cases and the limits of the constitutions may more easily be inspected. This will be brief, for in truth every orator delights in brevity: brevity in words, fewness in propositions, and completeness in each point.

Let the principal statuses therefore be said to be three: whether something exists, what it is, and of what kind it is. “Whether it exists” belongs to the question being asked. Formosus is at issue, and the question concerns him. “What it is,” however, belongs to the case: what did he do? From this arises the question. “Of what kind it is” relates to conjecture.

From this arise the four constitutions of controversy. What distinction there is among them must now be explained. The question is conjecture; conjecture, however, is an ambiguous interpretation: whether something exists or does not exist, or whether it could have happened—for example, whether Formosus was able to perform ordination after excommunication.

The case concerns whether he acted justly. From the question arises the case, from the case the constitution, and from this the question whether the case may be examined.

Questions are either determinate or indeterminate. A determinate question is whether something was done lawfully; it arises from a definite act and indicates the person being discussed, which is called the hypothesis. Every matter is therefore confirmed by argument. Every matter that rests upon a hypothesis is called a case, and the definition of a case is: “a dispute involving a definite person.” Every such matter draws its arguments from seven places. Two of these—who and what—contain everything.

The hypothesis therefore contains the dispute. A dispute has two voices, that of the accuser and that of the refuter, which operate through the *hypophora* and *antipophora*. But enough of this.

We have stated these things so that it may be more clearly understood by what argument one voice may hurl a weapon at the other. Let Formosus’s definite person now be placed in the middle; let the advocates [the text has *causidicus*], alternating their civil voices as one side and the other, test the truth or falsity through the demonstrative third genre of cases.

Dialectic contributes nothing to either side here, because there is controversy between them and a definite person is displayed, in a situation where it is impossible for either party not to be defeated. Come, then: let the defender argue for the case, and let the accuser argue against it. Behold, Formosus stands present.

THE ACCUSER says: This Formosus was an excommunicated bishop.

THE ADVOCATE: He was indeed, but he was absolved.

ACCUSER: Not at all.

ADVOCATE: He was absolved.

ACCUSER: It was not possible.

ADVOCATE: If it was possible for him to be justly bound, it was also possible for him to be justly released.

ACCUSER: He was not absolved, therefore, because he had confirmed it by writing and by an oath.

ADVOCATE: It is permissible to erase evil deeds by good deeds. This man, however, was first excommunicated and afterward absolved.

ACCUSER: How do you know that he was absolved?

ADVOCATE: By the same means by which you know that he was excommunicated. A true report is heard just as a false report is. For here are present the bishops in whose presence he was absolved.

ACCUSER: He was excommunicated, not absolved, I say.

ADVOCATE: From what was he excommunicated? And since the prefix *ex-* signifies separation, while *communicare* is polysemous and has an ambiguous sound, how can you assert that he was excommunicated, especially since there are six modes of division? One is genus into species; another, whole into parts; another, a word according to its proper meanings; another, subject into accidents; another, accidents into subject; another, accidents into accidents. Clarify this ambiguous and amphibological expression. Since you have committed a fault in speaking, supply what you left unsaid.

ACCUSER: I say that this Formosus was excommunicated—that is, rejected from communion with the order of bishops.

ADVOCATE: It is a greater thing to exclude someone from the fellowship of Christians than to remove him from the office of bishops. And yet from the greater matter one returns to one’s former pardon. If what is more serious and much greater can be restored, what is less could be recovered much more easily. And since it could be recovered, undoubtedly it was. He was therefore absolved.

Behold the multitude of witnesses to the truth, who say that they saw it, took part in it, and that it truly happened so. But obstinacy could say that heaven and earth do not exist, if it wished. Hence comes the saying that “the fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13:1).

The mass of falsehood is therefore destroyed here by its three forms. It is unbelievable that Rome, the wisdom of the whole world, would have made an excommunicated man its head. It was likewise impossible that the vigorous power of the senates could have been attacked by some worthless little man. On the contrary, it follows that he could have ascended only after being absolved and reconciled with everyone, by the equal will of all.

ACCUSER: Was he absolved, I ask?

ADVOCATE: He was absolved.

ACCUSER: You mean, justly?

ADVOCATE: Whether justly or unjustly, I prove that he was absolved.

ACCUSER: Was he then absolved so that, having left his own things behind and forfeited his own [see—the wording is defective], he might ascend to the primacy? To prevent this, he had perpetuated the prohibition by writing and oath. Was this lawful?

ADVOCATE: No indeed.

ACCUSER: How, then, was he absolved?

ADVOCATE: He ascended.

ACCUSER: Do you say justly?

ADVOCATE: No.

ACCUSER: Why?

ADVOCATE: Because he had confirmed it forever.

ACCUSER: Although you assert that he had confirmed this forever, and that he entered upon it unlawfully, why did he then undertake it?

ADVOCATE: For the common good, obviously. And he did it because it was beneficial; he did it lawfully.

ACCUSER: Above you conceded that it was done unlawfully, and now you maintain that it was lawful. “Unlawfully” and “lawfully” are contraries of the first mode and admit no middle. If it was unlawful, it could not have been lawful. If it was done lawfully, it was not unlawful. Therefore what you maintain sounds contradictory.

ADVOCATE: It is a greater evil to destroy many than to save one. Whatever is done is done in two ways: by deeds and by words. A deed stands still; a word travels. Every conjecture therefore possesses three modes: from the cause, from the person, and from the deed.

In this case, the will of this person must be considered, so that we may see whether, out of love for liberating his country, he exceeded the words of his oath. At that time he was more distinguished than his fellow countrymen in nobility, good conduct, and every more serious virtue. When he saw his people and homeland humbled and suffering degradation, he chose, moved by zeal, to die rather than see the state utterly overthrown and dishonorably defiled.

And because he acted at the urging of everyone, it was unlawful to abandon the cause—still more unlawful not to come to his homeland’s aid by placing himself in its defense, rather than, by concealing himself, observe an unlawful oath and perish together with his homeland and the whole people. Happy indeed is the fault by which the whole homeland is redeemed. Whoever can help one who is perishing and does not offer assistance is undoubtedly the author of his death.

ACCUSER: The law declares that it is unlawful to swear and to commit perjury.

ADVOCATE: The law, on the contrary, commands the defense of one’s homeland and orders punishment for the person who has not brought assistance. There are many contradictions among laws. In the same matter, the law both forbids and commands. The public advantage separates such provisions.

Nevertheless, the law that forbids is greater than the one that commands, because when it forbids, it restrains what is unjustly, rashly, or unexpectedly commanded. If, therefore, the person who destroyed his homeland deserves punishment, much more does the person who defended it deserve the greatest rewards and praises.

If he was a son of the Church, then, seeing it torn apart and shaken, he ought to have resisted with all his strength. Otherwise, in a time of war, what is it to avoid every right and every unlawful act except to destroy one’s homeland and inflict death? The laws are silent amid arms.

ACCUSER: It was unlawful to swear and not observe the oath.

ADVOCATE: The law declares it unlawful for a foreigner to climb the wall of a city; if he does so, he is to be punished. Again the law says: “Whoever sees an enemy attempting to climb the wall and does not oppose him shall be punished.”

This man saw, climbed, defeated, and repelled him. Is he to be *obmallatus*—[interlinear gloss: “given over to death”]? Likewise, there was a law that no male should enter the temple of Vesta; anyone who entered was to be punished. Conversely, there was a law that whoever saw a mother being assaulted and did not bring assistance should be punished.

A certain man was passing by and, seeing a mother being beaten, entered and brought assistance. Is he to be *obmallatus*? Therefore all laws, all rights, words, and oaths of promises must be referred to the advantage of the state. Our ancestors possessed such virtue and wisdom.

Therefore, in this judgment too, stop weighing the literal words of the law and what is unlawful. Consider what was more beneficial: that one man preserve his oath and the head of the world collapse, or that one man exceed his words and save the people and the homeland.

If all laws must be referred to the advantage of the state, the lesser evil is preferable to the worst. Good, therefore, is the evil that drives out the worst evil. A particular evil by which a general evil is expelled must be embraced.

Indeed, it is a remarkable spectacle, and must be called lawful rather than unlawful—indeed, praiseworthy and venerable—when a finite and simple evil overcomes a double and boundless one.

The time had to be regulated. Every virtue is useful, and moderation is a virtue; therefore moderation is useful. The time consequently had to be regulated according to the circumstances.

Moreover, if you argue from the law, let it be enough to say that one law is broken by another, through the honor and usefulness of the state. Finally, the statement that the same act was both lawful and in accordance with right is resolved by the division of accidents into accidents: what was unlawful for him became lawful and right for the state.

ACCUSER: I certainly agree with you, because you conceded above that it was unlawful, since he had confirmed it forever; and you partly cleared this by reference to the advantage of the state, satisfying me by saying that both the commanding and the prohibiting law must be obeyed.

If you conceded that the first act was unlawful with respect to him, though only in part, what do you assert concerning the deeds that followed from that deed?

ADVOCATE: I say that the act of ascending to the see was in part lawful and in part—I say—in part unlawful, since one and the same man consists of an interior and an exterior aspect. But let no one suppose that his subsequent deeds were invalid!

ACCUSER: Why, then, do you say “the deed” and not “the deeds”? If that one was valid, why not these? And if these were not valid, why was that one?

ADVOCATE: One thing is a deed, another is the act resulting from a deed, and again another is a later deed that follows a deed. Of the three kinds of deeds, only the first is at issue here. The question is not about the two later deeds, but about the act underlying the deeds.

ACCUSER: I say that the subsequent deeds are not valid if the first was not valid but void.

ADVOCATE: Not so. Even if we grant that his ascent was transgressive, what he did afterward was not thereby transgressive.

ACCUSER: What good thing did he do that was not transgressive?

ADVOCATE: That which he preached and ordained.

ACCUSER: No, I say that he could not ordain.

ADVOCATE: Then he could not preach either.

ACCUSER: He could, but only after being restored to his own see.

ADVOCATE: If you concede that he was able to do so in his own see, you must also concede that he was able to do so in another’s, even if, as has been argued, it was unjust in part.

Therefore let the first act be called void in part, but not the second, because what is within one’s power is undoubtedly possible according to one’s will. For what is said to be possible, if it is possible, is called possible both in lawful and in unlawful matters.

But if you deny that the Holy Spirit can be invoked in an unlawful situation, it follows that you must deny that God can send a soul into an unlawful union. By “unlawful” I mean the case of one who, having been consecrated for a time on any pretext and separated from the altar, performs his office during the very fervor of his separation.

For although an act is for a time separated from its form, its power is not thereby separated. Power cannot in any way be detached from form. It would be ridiculous to say that what is possible—living, sleeping, and the other things belonging to the form—are always in actuality, since they are in potentiality.

If a baptized person does not lose baptism even when expelled from the Church, how could a consecrated person, even if excommunicated, lose the power of the sacrament of his ordination? He may for a time obey the earlier ruling, so that when absolved shortly afterward he may again exercise the office, just as a baptized person may again enter the Church. The power therefore exists, but not in actuality.

ACCUSER: I do not agree with what you say.

ADVOCATE: Then say why you condemn his deeds, since his deeds, unlike the first deed, were not bound by writing and oath.

ACCUSER: Because what he did not possess he could not give.

ADVOCATE: He plainly could, because he possessed it. He possessed it because he received the imposition of hands from bishops. He received it, possessed it, and gave it, because he was able to do so.

ACCUSER: What he did not possess, I say, he could not give.

ADVOCATE: Are you speaking of not possessing the power, or not possessing the act, or of both?

ACCUSER: Of both. Neither exists without the other. If he lost the office, he does not possess the office. If he does not possess it, he can no longer give it. He lost the office when he lost both the power and the act.

ADVOCATE: I shudder greatly at your blind hostility, by which, having set aside the truth, you strive to establish falsehood. It is natural that what is unknown should become known through what is familiar. An argument has two forms: one implicit and one explicit.
