Baptism occurs through the power of the Holy Spirit, and remission is given, and this happens once. Likewise, the ordination of the sacred orders occurs through the power of the Holy Spirit, and this too happens once.

If harm should occur and someone should therefore be excommunicated, are we to say that, because he was excommunicated, he is no longer a Christian, although he had received the gift through the grace of the Holy Spirit? If one gift given through the same Holy Spirit cannot in any way be abolished, how can you say that another similar gift can be expelled?

Acknowledge this, lest you suspect that the Holy Spirit who cooperates in all things is not one, since “there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5), and one priesthood.

If baptism cannot be taken away, then undoubtedly neither can priesthood. It can indeed be separated from its exercise by divine authority; but that a priest should cease to be a priest in perpetuity, just as a baptized person remains baptized, is altogether impossible.

And just as there is one beginning, so there is a similar possession and a similar end. Hence it is evident that just as one who has been baptized cannot be rebaptized, so one who has been ordained cannot in any way be reordained. Whoever contradicts this falls into the heresy of the Donatists.

Therefore, since it is through one Holy Spirit, it is one thing and not different things. Otherwise, if the Spirit is conferred in baptism but not in priesthood, it is no longer one thing but rather something different.

Baptism and priesthood are not accidents that come and go through excommunication, as any ordinary accident does—for example, wisdom, which departs from the mind that possesses it when that mind becomes foolish or forgets. Nor are they lost through separation from the exercise of their power; nor do they in any way suffer a stain of pollution in themselves; nor are they changed so that they cease to be holy. Nor are they torn out in such a way that, whether for evil or for good, they are no longer judged according to the order originally received.

You must therefore concede that priesthood is inseparable from what has been received, just as baptism is. If not, then the gift of baptism is one thing and the gift of priesthood another. To say this is impious.

ACCUSER: Innocent says that what a man did not possess he could not give.

ADVOCATE: He said this, but not concerning this Catholic man Formosus. Even if Innocent had said it concerning anyone at all—even if he said it concerning certain heretics—Leo and Anastasius spoke otherwise earlier.

In human laws, the greater number prevails, since “every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18:6). It is less serious for one person to have gone beyond the mark than for many. Therefore, neither in giving an example nor in the matter itself is one person or one witness sufficient.

Nor is someone baptized by a heretic rebaptized by any Catholic. Observe that not even a heretic loses the right of a pontiff, nor the right of his consecration. If this is granted concerning heretics, why should it not be granted concerning Formosus, a Catholic and orthodox man?

He was certainly the man who throughout his entire life was an example of such great gravity that he did not drink wine and knew nothing of the taste of meat. Free from sexual intercourse, at eighty years of age he laid aside his human body, still virgin, and entrusted it to the earth.

By preaching a life of holiness, he also confirmed the faith among those peoples of the Bulgarians and led them to the faith as a true apostolic man. When, through such integrity, he had been praised throughout the world and shone like another Lucifer, he was subjected to violence in his tomb: the tombs were destroyed, his bones were shattered, and, like some Memphite thing [*memphiticum*, sense uncertain], he was cast out in public.

For such a man, tested like gold, even the schools crying out, “O spare the buried man! There is no contest with the dead,” could do nothing to help. Yet in his case what was desired was declared lawful. For even the apostles themselves were not granted the right to prejudge the dead.

ACCUSER: What, then? Is something given that is not possessed?

ADVOCATE: Indeed, it is given.

[Col. 1109C]

ACCUSER: Let us suppose that a certain priest baptized someone yesterday and was himself a criminal. When he baptized, did he remit original sin?

ADVOCATE: I approve that point by yielding to you, as though I were favoring your assertions and standing with your side—not, of course, from that part of the truth of which I am the defender. Therefore repeat what you have said.

ACCUSER: I say this: “The priest will remit, because no one remits except God” (Luke 5:21).

ADVOCATE: I concede that this is so. Nevertheless, God does not remit without the testimony of the Church, which says: “Unless a priest has baptized.” When a human being approaches a human being, and God approaches the mind, a third receives remission from the two. Namely, when the priest baptizes, remission is effected, and what he does not possess from himself he offers by virtue of his office.

Behold how he gives what he does not possess.

**INS.** “No one, I say, forgives sins except God alone (ibid.).”

**ACTOR:** It is true; I agree. But consider God made from God—namely, the accidental from the essential—who, when made, honored him in such a way that he gave him power to become even sons of God (John 1:12), and gave him power to forgive and retain, to loose and to bind (Matthew 16:19).

**INS.** But not Formosus.

**ACTOR:** If you had hated him with perfect hatred, you would have done less. Hence the hatred of antiquity cannot be sweetened by a small trickle of words amid the gall of bitterness. For if it is incredible that the Holy Spirit is given through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, how was the life of the soul handed down by the Fathers? It is not rightly said that one person cannot lawfully be believed to possess something when it is said that all possess it equally. Either all will equally be able to possess it, or all equally will not be able to possess it. Indeed, it is credible that the Holy Spirit is received through the laying on of the bishops’ hands.

Since Formosus, like the other apostolic bishops, also received the laying on of hands from the bishops themselves, he was certainly not without that power. He received it, therefore he could also give it. For if he did not possess it, either he did not receive a similar laying on of hands; or, if the laying on was similar, then, since it could not be changed, he could likewise give, under the same condition, what he had received, just as did the others who received it. If that was the case, this was also the case; and if this was not the case, then in no way was that the case either. But that was the case; therefore this was also the case.

If, then, you maintain that anyone is not lawfully able to use the sacrament, while another is lawfully able to confer it, you unquestionably admit that the sacrament exists in an altered form. Therefore I ask you whether it is lawful to say that the sacrament has been altered. By “altered sacrament,” I mean whatever is celebrated divinely through the hands of ministers—for example, baptism, the laying on of hands, and the other heavenly rites.

**INS.** Nor do I expect it.

**ACTOR:** Why?

**INS.** Because it is not different. Since “different” is constituted in three ways—by matter, by operation, or by both—and since the sacrament is none of these, it has not been altered.

**ACTOR:** I am grateful for what you assert. In this matter, indeed, you obey the truth and speak against yourself on my behalf. For if the sacrament is neither another thing nor altered, since there is in it neither a genus nor a species distinct from another species, nor an accident in the same subject; and since it possesses neither quantity nor quality, and can neither be increased, diminished, nor changed; and therefore you admit that it is not different, but rather the same thing, one in the same thing—how, then, do you say that Formosus could not use the power he had received, as the others did among the others, when you confess that the sacrament and Formosus, in their respective species, even if they are altered, are nevertheless not other things—especially since everything “other” is “altered,” but not everything “altered” is “other”?

For Paul is other than Peter, yet he is not another kind of thing. A man is not greater than a man today, nor will he be tomorrow; nor is a horse greater than a horse. So, likewise—yes, likewise—even if the sacrament may be called altered because of its efficient cause, it is nevertheless not altered in the same subject, since one sacrament is neither greater than another sacrament today in the same subject, nor will it be tomorrow.

**INS.** I confess that in this matter I yield to the truth. But because he was an invader, he could not have been an apostolic bishop.

**ACTOR:** Three things, it is said, are attributed to a lie: that it is incredible, impossible, and contrary to fact. If, then, I concede that he was an invader, I will seem to be bringing disgrace upon the commonwealth, since it also appears incredible and impossible that so great a sublimity, so great a majesty, the head of the world, could have been subjected to and invaded by one such insignificant little man. But if you defend that this did happen, without doubt you show him to have been more prudent, wiser, and more useful than all the others; and by this you openly declare him worthy of ascending alone to the summit, since one man was able to do what all could not do against one.

But if I concede that he was an invader, I shall prove that there were many accomplices in that crime. If, I say, you should claim that it is unlawful for a bishop to ascend to the papacy, one must fear that you are declaring Marinus and his action invalid. Therefore know and consider this: to conquer is indeed good, but to conquer too completely is exceedingly liable to provoke envy.

Moreover, what follows is now necessary, and reason demands that the conclusion of what has been said be closed by a recapitulation. The proposition was that Formosus, an excommunicated man, was a bishop; but it was proved that he had been absolved. It was said that, although absolved, he could in no way transfer to another see. It was conceded that the first act had taken place; and even if that act were invalid, the subsequent acts nevertheless could in no way be invalidated. Innocent was brought forward in opposition; while Anastasius, Leo, and Gregory, crying out on the other side, establish that even the ordination of heretics is in no way invalid.

It was asserted that he could not give what he had not received. The contrary was proved: just as baptism is not taken away even from sinners, so the gift of the Holy Spirit, once given through the laying on of hands, cannot be taken away from sinners with respect to their power, even though it may be absent in actual exercise. Come, then, see how one who had been absolved could furthermore have possessed, through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, the power to ordain, to give, and to perform the entire pontifical office.

I make one final appeal to you, a matter that moves me most vehemently: you spare in no way those ordained by your men, nor those ordained by men whom they ordained. Why, then, do you show indulgence toward those baptized by them? And if you cannot allow that, how can you allow this, when there is one sacrament and one gift of the Holy Spirit? But enough of this.

Turn back now at last, my soul; flee and hide yourself in the chamber of your mind. And if there are few good things in what you have said, and some matters in which you have gone astray, pray to be taught and ask to be forgiven. At last, enter your room; and, fleeing the joy of the frenzied, mourn your dead man. Say also to your own people—indeed, to everyone: “But you, Lord, have mercy on us.”

### Syllogism from antecedents

If there is one power in all bishops, it is also in one bishop. But there is one power in all. Therefore it is also in one.

### Syllogism from consequents

[Col. 1112B]

If there is not one power in all bishops, neither is there one in a single bishop. But there is one power in all. Therefore it is also in one.

### Syllogism from incompatibles

There is not one power in all, and there is not one in a single bishop. But there is one power in all. Therefore it is also in one.

### Syllogism from disjunctives

Either unity or diversity exists in the ordination of bishops. But there is unity. Therefore there is no diversity.

### Fifth mode

Either unity or diversity exists in the ordination of bishops. Unity does not exist. Therefore diversity exists.

[Col. 1111]

# Chronicle of Sebastian, Bishop of Salamanca

Published under the name of Alfonso III.

## Notice

*(In Flórez, España Sagrada, vol. XIII.)*

[Col. 1111C] Most people attribute this Chronicle to Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca, and its sufficiently ancient preface confirms that opinion. Others dissent; and so does the heading of this Chronicle’s preface itself, in which King Adefonsus—namely, the one surnamed the Great—dedicates the work to Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca, an attribution confirmed by the evidence of a sufficiently ancient Gothic codex, specifically the Sorian one. The author himself says that, in the era 749, he populated—that is, restored—the city of Viseo in Lusitania and its suburbs. I do not know whether this could suit the bishop of Salamanca, given the poverty of ecclesiastical revenues. It is likely that the work was composed by Sebastian and published under the name and title of King Adefonsus, as though the king himself had written it. I see that the same thing happened with other kings in Spain, particularly with Adefonsus X, king of Castile, surnamed the Wise; hence the variety of opinions may have arisen.

The work certainly begins with the era 710 and ends with the death of Ordoño, whom Adefonsus himself, surnamed the Great—namely, the son—succeeded in the kingdom in the era 904—that is, in the year of Christ 866. Through the fault of copyists and the very crudeness of the age, some passages are so confused that they can scarcely be understood. Otherwise, the work is not merely useful but necessary for understanding the history of that period.

## In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the Chronicle of the Visigoths, compiled from the time of King Wamba up to the present time of the glorious King Garsean, son of Adefonsus.

[Note: [Col. 1111C] Mariana of blessed memory added this here.]

[Col. 1111]

[Col. 1111C] **1. King Adefonsus sends greetings to our Sebastian.**

[Note: [Col. 1111C] The royal-library codex of Madrid also reads: “to Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca.”]

Know that, concerning the history of the Goths, about which you informed us through the presbyter Dulcidius, the ancients did not wish, through laziness, to write the old history,

[Note: [Col. 1111C] Mariana, Pérez, and Ferreras read *notuerunt pigritiaque* (“they did not make known, and through laziness…”). Berganza reads *notuit pigritiaeque*.]

but concealed it in silence.

[Note: [Col. 1112C] Mariana and the royal-library codex of Madrid read this way. Others read *noluerint* (“they may have been unwilling”).]

And because Isidore, bishop of the see of Seville, fully instructed us in the Chronicle of the Goths up to the times of the glorious King Wamba,

[Note: [Col. 1113A] The author is mistaken.]

we shall briefly communicate to you certain things from that time onward, as we have heard them from the ancients and our predecessors and have recognized them as true.

## WAMBA

**2.** King Recceswinth, therefore, departing from the city of Toledo, came to his own estate, whose name was Gerticos,

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Situated in the territory of Salamanca. From Don Julius in *Vamba*. Flórez, additions in manuscript.]

which is now recognized as being on Mount Caura.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Mariana reads *Cauro*.]

There he died of a natural illness. When the king had ended his life and had been buried in that same place, Wamba was chosen by everyone for the kingdom in the era 710. But although he refused and did not wish to acquire the kingdom, he nevertheless unwillingly accepted what the army demanded. He was immediately conveyed to Toledo and anointed king in the metropolitan church of Saint Mary.

At that hour, in the presence of everyone, a bee was seen to fly out from his head and soar toward heaven. This sign was made by the Lord to announce future victories, as the outcome later proved. He repeatedly subdued the Asturians and Basques who rebelled, and subjected them to his rule. The citizens of the provinces of Gaul, having formed a conspiracy, separated themselves from the Gothic kingdom and submitted themselves to the kingdom of the Franks.

To restore and subdue these provinces, Duke Paul was sent by Wamba with an army. He not only failed to carry out the task entrusted to him but, acting against his country, became the leader of wicked tyrants. But if you wish to know more fully how many killings, how many burnings of cities, how many massacres, how many troops of Franks or Gauls were slain by Wamba, how many famous victories he achieved, and what destruction resulted from Paul’s tyranny, read the blessed Julian, metropolitan bishop, who composed the history of this period with complete clarity.

**3.** In his time, 270 Saracen ships attacked the coast of Spain. There all their troops were destroyed by the sword, and their fleets were burned by fire. And so that we might make the cause of the Saracens’ entry into Spain fully known to you, we explain the origin of King Ervigius.

In the time of King Chindaswinth, a certain Ardabastus, expelled by the emperor, came from Greece as an exile to Spain. Chindaswinth received him honorably and gave him his female cousin in marriage; Ervigius was born from her. Ervigius, having been raised in palace training

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Mariana and the royal-library codex read this way. Ferreras and Berganza read “educated.”]

and elevated to the rank of count, plotted proudly and cunningly against the king.

[Col. 1114A]

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The royal-library codex adds “Wamba” here.]

He mixed into the king’s drink a herb called *spartum*, and immediately the king lost his memory. When the city’s bishop—or the palace nobles who were loyal to the king, but entirely unaware of the cause of the potion—saw the king lying without memory, moved by compassion and fearing that the king might depart this life without due preparation, they immediately imposed upon him the order of confession and penance.

When the king recovered from the potion and learned of the order imposed upon him, he sought the monastery of Pampliga

[Note: [Col. 1113D] *Pampligiae* is absent in Mariana and in the royal-library codex.]

and remained in religious life there for as long as he lived. He reigned nine years, one month, and fourteen days,

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The fourteen days are likewise absent there.]

and lived in the monastery seven years and three months. He died a natural death in peace in the era 719.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The royal-library codex adds this era. Since the golden booklet of the Chronicle of the Visigoths establishes that he reigned eight years, one month, and fourteen days, he lived only one year in the monastery. The era 719, in which he is said here to have died, also supports this; for in the preceding era, 718, he received penance.]

## ERVIGIUS

**4.** After Wamba, Ervigius obtained the kingdom, which he cunningly invaded. He corrupted the laws instituted by Wamba and issued others in his own name. He is said to have been moderate toward his subjects. He gave his daughter Cixilo in marriage to the distinguished man Egica, Wamba’s cousin.

Ervigius himself died a natural death at Toledo in the era 725.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Mariana: “He reigned six years, three months.” The royal codex reads “three months.” But the Chronicle of the Visigoths gives seven years and twenty-five days, which should be followed.]

## EGICA

**5.** After Ervigius died, the aforementioned Egica was chosen as king. He was very wise and patient. He frequently convened synods, as the canonical statutes clearly demonstrate. He subdued the peoples rising within the kingdom. Against the Franks invading Gaul, he fought three times but won no triumph.

He made his son Witiza his associate in the kingdom and ordered him to reside in the city of Tui, in the province of Gallaecia, so that the father might hold the kingdom of the Goths and the son that of the Suevi. Before the election of his son, he reigned ten years; with his son, five years. He died a natural death at Toledo and was buried there in the era 739.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Mariana and the royal codex read this way. Ferreras and Berganza read “he died in the era 738,” omitting the remaining words.]

## WITIZA

**6.** After Egica’s death, Witiza returned to Toledo, to his father’s throne. He was disgraceful and depraved in his conduct. Like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding, he defiled himself with many wives and concubines. And, lest ecclesiastical censure rise against him, he dissolved councils, violated the canons,

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The words in brackets are absent from Berganza.]

and corrupted the entire order of religion. He ordered bishops, presbyters, and deacons to have wives.

This crime was indeed the cause of Spain’s destruction. Because the kings and priests abandoned the law of the Lord, all the Gothic forces perished by the sword of the Saracens. Witiza died a natural death at Toledo after ten years of reign and was buried there in the era 759.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Mariana adds: “and was buried there in the era 749.” All of this is absent from Berganza, although Ferreras has “era 749.”]

## RUDERICUS

[Col. 1115A]

**7.** After Witiza’s death, Rudericus was chosen king by the Goths. He followed Witiza in sins and, armed not only with zeal for justice, failed to put an end to this crime but rather increased it.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Berganza reads: “into the king. But he …,” etc.]

Witiza’s sons, driven by envy because Rudericus had received their father’s kingdom, plotted cunningly, sent messengers to Africa, and requested the aid of the Saracens. They brought them by ship and admitted them into Spain. But those who had brought destruction upon their homeland perished by the sword together with the Saracen people.

When Rudericus learned of their entry, he went out with the entire Gothic army to fight them. But, as Scripture says, “In vain does he run whom iniquity precedes,”

[Note: [Col. 1115D] In Berganza’s text this is corrupt: “But the priests…”]

either crushed by the weight of the priests—or of their own sins—or exposed through the treachery of Witiza’s sons, they and the entire Gothic army were put to flight and destroyed by the sword.

As for King Rudericus, no known account of his death remains. When, in our own times, we had populated—that is, restored—the city of Viseo and its suburbs, a monument was found in a certain basilica. Above it an epitaph was carved that said:

“Here rests Rudericus, king of the Goths.”

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Thus the royal codex. Others add “the last,” but incongruously.]

## PELAGIUS

**8.** With their homeland and kingdom crushed, the Arabs served as governors for many years, paying tribute to the Babylonian king, until they chose a king for themselves and established a kingdom for themselves in the patrician city of Córdoba. The Goths perished, some by the sword and others by hunger.

But some of those who remained of royal stock went to Francia. The greater part entered this land of the Asturians

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Berganza and Ferreras read “Asturian land.”]

and chose Pelagius as their prince,

[Note: [Col. 1115D] The royal codex reads “then Pelagius.” Sandoval’s edition, which begins here, likewise omits everything reported above.]

the son of the former Duke Fafila and descended from royal stock. When the Saracens learned what had happened, they immediately sent against him into Asturias, with an innumerable army, Duke Alqama—who himself had earlier invaded Spain with Tariq—and Oppa, metropolitan bishop of the see of Seville and son of King Witiza, through whose treachery the Goths had perished.

**9.** When Pelagius learned of their entry, he withdrew to Mount Anseva, into a cave called the Cave of Saint Mary. Immediately the army surrounded him.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Thus Mariana and the royal codex. Others read “surrounded her.”]

Bishop Oppa approached him and addressed him as follows:

“I know, brother, that it is not hidden from you how all Spain was formerly established under one Gothic rule,

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Perhaps read *dum* (“when”); a little below Mariana’s codex adds “and when all …”.]

and how, when the entire army of Spain had been gathered together as one, it was unable to withstand the assault of the Ishmaelites. How much more will you be able to defend yourself in this hole? Rather, listen to my advice and turn your mind away from this purpose, so that you may enjoy many benefits and peacefully make use of everything that was yours under the Arabs.”

Pelagius replied:

“I shall neither join myself to the friendship of the Arabs nor submit myself to their rule. But you do not know

[Note: [Col. 1116D] *Non* (“not”) is absent in Berganza.]

that the Church of the Lord is compared to the moon, which suffers an eclipse and then, in due course, returns to its former fullness. For we trust in the Lord’s mercy that from this little mountain which you see there will come the salvation of Spain and the restoration of the army of the Gothic people, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled in us:

‘I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not take my mercy away from them.’

“Therefore, even if we receive the sentence of severity according to our deserts,

[Note: [Col. 1116D] The royal codex reads *etsi* (“even if”); the others read *ut* (“so that”), which is much less appropriate.]

we await his mercy, which will come in the recovery of the Church, the people, and the kingdom. Therefore we despise this multitude of pagans and are not at all afraid of them.”

**10.** Then the unspeakable bishop turned to the army and said:

“Hurry and fight, for unless by the vengeance of the sword, you will have no treaty of peace with him.”

Immediately they took up their arms and joined battle. Sling-machines were raised, slings were prepared, swords flashed, spears bristled, and arrows were shot without cease. But in this matter the mighty works of the Lord were not lacking. When stones had been launched from the sling-machines and had reached the house of the ever-virgin Saint Mary, they returned upon those who had thrown them and fiercely slaughtered the Chaldeans.

And because the Lord does not count the spears but gives the palm to whomever he wishes, when the faithful had gone out from the Cave to battle,

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Thus Mariana; others read “and when the faithful had gone out.”]

the Chaldeans immediately turned in flight and divided into two bands. There Bishop Oppa was immediately captured and Alqama was killed. In that same place 124,000 Chaldeans were killed. The remaining 63,000 climbed to the summit of Mount Auseva and descended headlong through the mountain’s precipice, commonly called Amosa, into the territory of the Lebanienses.

But they too did not escape the Lord’s vengeance.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] *Ipsi* (“they themselves”) is absent in Berganza.]

For when they were passing over the summit of the mountain situated above the bank of the Deva River, near the estate called Casegadia, the judgment of the Lord was so manifestly carried out that a portion of the mountain, tearing itself from its foundations, astonishingly threw the 63,000 Chaldeans into the river and overwhelmed them all.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Thus the royal codex. Others, less suitably, read *stupentes* (“astonished”).]

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Berganza reads: “threw … and overwhelmed.”]

Even to the present day, when the river fills its bed in winter and breaks through its banks, it displays very clearly the signs of their weapons and bones.

[Col. 1117A]

Do not think this miracle empty or fabulous. Remember that the one who drowned the Egyptians pursuing Israel in the Red Sea himself crushed these Arabs, who were pursuing the Church of the Lord, beneath the immense mass of the mountain.

**11.** At that same time, in this region of the Asturians, the Chaldeans had a governor in the city of Gijón named Munuza. Munuza was one of the four commanders who had previously oppressed the Spains.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] *Prius* (“previously”) is absent in Berganza.]

When he learned of the destruction of his people’s army, he abandoned the city and fled. The Asturians pursued him and found him at the place of Olalía; together with his army, they destroyed him by the sword, so that not one Chaldean remained within the passes of the Pyrenees.

[Col. 1117B]

Then the armies of the faithful were gathered, the homelands were repopulated, and the churches were restored. Then everyone together gave thanks, saying:

“Blessed be the name of the Lord, who strengthens those who believe in him and brings wicked nations to nothing.”

After completing the nineteenth year of his reign, Pelagius died a natural death. He was buried with his wife, Queen Gaudiosa, in the territory of Cangas, in the church of Saint Eulalia of Velapnio, in the era 775 (A.D. 737).

## FAFILA

**12.** His son Fafila succeeded him in the kingdom. Because of the brevity of his reign, he accomplished nothing worthy of history. On one occasion, through an act of rashness, he was killed by a bear in the second year of his reign. He was buried with his wife, Queen Froleba,

[Col. 1117C]

[Note: [Col. 1117D] “His queen” is absent in the same royal codex.]

in the territory of Cangas, in the church of the Holy Cross, which he himself had built, in the era 777.

## ADEFONSUS I (the Catholic)

**13.** After Fafila’s death, Adefonsus

[Note: [Col. 1117D] Berganza: “Adefonsus, who is called the Catholic”; Ferreras: “who is called the Great.” Nothing of this appears in Mariana or Pérez.]

succeeded to the kingdom: a man of great virtue, son of Duke Peter, descended from the stock of the kings Leovigild and Reccared,

[Note: [Col. 1117D] He was military commander in the time of King Egica and was Adefonsus’s father, not his son, as is clear from their ages. It should therefore be read as follows: “descended [from Peter, who was military commander in the time of Kings Egica and Witiza], with divine favor…” Flórez, additions in manuscript.]

He was military commander in the time of Kings Egica and Witiza, and with divine favor received the scepter of the kingdom. He often curbed the boldness of the Arabs.

How great he was in grace, virtue, and authority is shown by the deeds that follow. Together with his brother Froila, he fought many battles against the Saracens and captured many cities formerly oppressed by them: Lugo, Tui, Porto, Braga, the Metropolitan City, Viseo, Flavia,

[Note: [Col. 1117D] Thus Mariana and the royal codex. Others read “Flavia.”]

Agatha, Ledesma, Salamanca, Zamora, Ávila, Segovia,

[Col. 1118A]

[Note: [Col. 1117D] Thus the aforementioned codices and Ferreras and Berganza. Others read “Abula.”]

Astorga, León, Sayago, Mabe, Amaya, Septimanca, Oca, Velegia, Álava, Miranda,

[Note: [Col. 1117D] Berganza reads “Alanense.”]

Rebende, Carbonaria, Abeica, Briones,

[Note: [Col. 1117D] Thus Mariana and the royal codex. Others read “Abtica, Abeica.”]

Cinisaria, Alesanco—Cenicero and Alesanco in Rioja—Osma, Clunia, Argantia, Septem Publica, except for the castles,

[Note: [Col. 1117D] Berganza reads “excepting all the castles.” Ferreras reads “excepting from all the castles.”]

together with their villages and hamlets. He killed all the Arabs occupying the cities mentioned above and led the Christians with him back to their homeland.

**14.** At that time Primorias, Liébana, Trasmiera, Sopuerta, Carranza, Bardulia,

[Note: [Col. 1118D] Mariana, Berganza, and Ferreras read “Bardulies.”]

which is now called Castile, and the maritime part of Gallaecia, Burgos, were repopulated. Álava—namely Vizcaya, Alaone, and Urdunia—were always found to be possessed by their own inhabitants, as were Pamplona, Degius, and Berroza.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] Sandoval reads “it was said.”]

The aforementioned Adefonsus was therefore exceedingly magnanimous. Without offense toward God or the Church, he led a life deservedly inimitable.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] Mariana and the royal codex read this way. Berganza reads: “he led a glorious life, truly worthy of imitation.”]

He built and restored many basilicas. He reigned eighteen years. He ended his life happily in peace and was buried with his wife, Queen Ermesinda, in the territory of Cangas, in the monastery of Saint Mary.

**15.** Nor should this astonishing miracle be omitted, which certainly occurred at the hour of his departure.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] Berganza reads *decessionis* (“departure”).]

For when he had breathed out his spirit in the silence of the dead of night, and the palace guards were carefully watching over his body, suddenly a voice of angels singing was heard in the air by all the guards:

“See how the just man is taken away, and no one considers it; and righteous men are taken away, and no one perceives it in his heart. The just man has been taken away from the face of iniquity; his burial will be in peace.”

Know with complete certainty that this is true, and do not think the saying fabulous. Otherwise I would have preferred to remain silent rather than willingly utter falsehoods. Era 795 (A.D. 757).

## FROILA

**16.** After Adefonsus’s death, his son Froila succeeded to the kingdom. He was a man exceedingly fierce in mind and in arms. He won many victories against the enemy from Córdoba. In a place called Pontumio,

[Note: [Col. 1118D] Pérez reads “Pontrivio.”]

in the province of Gallaecia, he fought them and, after defeating them, killed 54,000 Chaldeans. Their young commander, named Hammar, son of Abderrahman Ibn Hisham, was captured in the same place and killed by the sword.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] *Gladio* (“by the sword”) is absent in Berganza.]

[Note: [Col. 1118D] Pelagius of Oviedo inserted his own fanciful additions here: “This king,” he says, “transferred the bishopric to Oviedo from the city of Lugo, which is in Asturias and was built by the Vandals,” as we read in Sandoval and Berganza. But this is absent from the Gothic codex of Soria, which Mariana used, as well as from the royal-library codex and the copies of the distinguished Juan Bautista Pérez.]

He overcame and subdued the rebelling Basques. He ordered a certain young woman named Munia, taken as booty from the Basques, to be kept for him; afterward he married her in a royal marriage, and by her he fathered a son, Adefonsus.

He devastated the peoples of Gallaecia who rebelled against him, together with their homeland. Finally, he killed his brother, named Vímara, with his own hands. Not long afterward, he justly received retaliation and was killed by his own men. He reigned eleven years and three months and was buried with his wife Munia at Oviedo, in the era 806 (A.D. 768).

## AURELIUS

**17.** After Froila’s death, his first-degree cousin Aurelius, son of Froila, the brother of Adefonsus, succeeded to the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] “First-degree” is absent in Mariana.]

During his time, the freedmen took up arms against their own masters and rose tyrannically. But, overcome by the prince’s diligence, they were all reduced to their former slavery. He fought no battles because he maintained peace with the Arabs. He reigned six years; in the seventh year he rested in peace and was buried in the church of Saint Martin the Bishop in Valle Lagneyo, in the era 812 (A.D. 774).

## SILO

**18.** After Aurelius’s death, Silo succeeded to the kingdom because he had taken Adosinda, daughter of Prince Adefonsus, as his wife. He maintained peace with the Ishmaelites. He defeated the peoples of Gallaecia who rebelled against him in battle on Mount Cuperius and subjected them to his rule.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] Here again Sandoval and Berganza published the following passage from the codex of Pelagius of Oviedo, which we do not find in the others:

“Then he gathered a very large army of soldiers and foot-soldiers and went to the city called Mérida. He took out the most blessed virgin Eulalia, who had been killed there by the prefect Calpurnius and buried by Christians, from the tomb in which she lay buried, and placed her in a silver casket that he had ordered to be made. There he found a fourth part of the virgin’s cradle, which he brought with the body of the blessed virgin Eulalia with him to Asturias, to the territory of Pravia, and placed her in the church of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist and of the holy apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, which he himself founded.”]

He reigned nine years and ended his life in the tenth. He was buried with his wife, Queen Adosinda, in the church of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist at Pravia, in the era 821 (A.D. 783).

[Note: [Col. 1119D] Berganza reads: “in the aforementioned monastery of Saint John at Pravia,” etc.]

## MAURECATUS

[Col. 1119C]

**19.** After Silo died, Queen Adosinda, together with the entire palace establishment, placed Adefonsus, son of her brother Froila the king, on his father’s throne. But Maurecatus, his uncle, the son of the elder Adefonsus, though born from a slave woman, forestalled him by treachery and expelled him from the kingdom. Adefonsus then lived among his mother’s relatives in Álava.

Maurecatus, however, claimed for six years the kingdom he had cunningly invaded. He died a natural death and was buried in the church of Saint John the Apostle at Pravia, in the era 826.

[Note: [Col. 1120D] Thus Mariana, the royal codex, and Ferreras. Berganza gives twenty-five years; Sandoval gives twenty-seven. The authority of twenty-six codices, as well as the chronology of the preceding and following kings, supports the reading given here.]

(A.D. 788)

## VEREMUNDUS

**20.** After Maurecatus died, Veremundus, cousin of the elder Adefonsus, namely the son of his brother Froila, was chosen king. Veremundus was a magnanimous man. He reigned three years, then voluntarily relinquished the kingdom, remembering the order imposed upon him as a deacon. He made his cousin Adefonsus—whom Maurecatus had expelled from the kingdom—his successor in the kingdom.

[The small sons Ranimirus and Garcia having been set aside.]

[Note: [Col. 1120D] These words are absent in Mariana and Pérez.]

This was in the era 829 (A.D. 791). He lived with him for many years in the greatest affection. He ended his life in peace.

[Note: [Col. 1120D] Berganza, following Sandoval, adds: “He was buried at Oviedo.”]

## ADEFONSUS II (the Chaste)

**21.** In the third year of this reign, an Arab army entered Asturias with a certain commander named Mokehit.

[Note: [Col. 1120D] Also Makehit, Moet, and Mugaiz.]

They were intercepted by King Adefonsus at a place called Lutos

[Note: [Col. 1120D] Others read “hurled headlong.”]

and, together with the aforementioned commander, nearly 70,000 were killed by sword and mire.

This king was the first to establish firmly the royal throne at Oviedo.

He also built, with marvelous workmanship, a basilica in the name of our Redeemer and Savior, Jesus Christ,

[Col. 1120B]

[and had it consecrated by seven bishops.]

[Note: [Col. 1120D] These words are absent from the Sorian codex used by Mariana.]

For this reason it is specifically called the church of Saint Saviour. On the principal altar he added, on either side, twice six titles containing relics of all the apostles.

He also built a church in honor of Saint Mary ever-virgin, adjoining the aforementioned church on the northern side. Outside the principal altar, he erected on the right-hand side a title in memory of Saint Stephen and on the left a title in memory of Saint Julian.

On the western side of this venerable house he also constructed a building for storing the bodies of kings. He further founded a third basilica in memory of Saint Thyrsus. The beauty of its workmanship can be admired more by the present observer than praised by an educated scribe.

[Note: [Col. 1120D] Others read *pulchritudo* (“beauty”) rather than *pulchritudinem* (“the beauty”).]

[Col. 1120C]

He also built, to the northwest, about one stade distant from the palace,

[Note: [Col. 1120D] Berganza reads “one stade.”]

a church in memory of Saint Julian the Martyr, with twin altars placed on either side in a marvelous arrangement of adornment.

He also built beautiful royal palaces, baths, dining halls, and covered buildings, as well as courts, and made all the furnishings of the kingdom extremely splendid.

## 22

In the thirtieth year of his reign, a double army of the Chaldaeans marched against Gallaecia. One of them was called Alhabbez and the other Melih; both belonged to the Alcorexis. They therefore entered boldly—and were destroyed even more boldly. For at the same time one perished at a place called Naharon, and the other in the river Anceus.

Thereafter, during this king’s reign, a certain man named Mahzmuth arrived, a fugitive from the presence of the king of Córdoba, Abderrahman [Note: Mar. and Perez: “Spaniensis.”], against whom he had fomented a long rebellion. Formerly a citizen of Mérida, he was received with royal clemency in Gallaecia, where he remained for seven years. In the eighth year, however, having gathered a band of Saracens, he plundered the neighboring districts and withdrew for protection into a certain fortress called Santa Christina.

When this deed was reported to the royal ears, [Adefonsus] advanced an army, besieged the fortress in which Mahzmuth was staying, drew up his battle line, and surrounded the fortress with warriors. Soon, in the first clash of the battle, that most famous warrior Mahzmuth was killed. His head was presented to the king’s gaze, and the fortress itself was stormed. Within it, fifty thousand Saracens who had gathered from Spain to aid him were beheaded. Adefonsus then returned victoriously and in peace to Oviedo.

Thus, after governing the kingdom for fifty-two years in chastity, sobriety, purity, piety, and glory, beloved by God and human beings, he sent his glorious spirit to heaven. His body, buried with every funeral honor in the stone tomb of the church of Saint Mary founded by him, rests there in peace, in the era 880 (A.D. 842).

## RANIMIRUS I

### 23

After the death of Adefonsus, Ranimirus, son of Prince Veremundus, was elected to the kingship. At that time, however, he was absent in the province of Bardulia to receive his wife. Because of his absence, Nepotianus, count of the palace, seized the kingdom tyrannically for himself.

When Ranimirus therefore learned that his cousin Adefonsus had departed from this world and that Nepotianus had invaded the kingdom, he entered the city of Lugo in Gallaecia and gathered for himself an army from the entire province. After a short time, he made an incursion into Asturias. Nepotianus met him at the bridge of the river Narcea with a gathered force of Asturians and Basques. Soon, abandoned by his own men, he was put to flight and captured by two counts, namely Scipio and Somnanus, in the territory of Pravia [Note: Perez and Mar., “Premoria.” Sand. and Berg., “Pravia.”]. Thus receiving what his deeds deserved, he was blinded and assigned to a monastery.

After this, a fleet of Northmen arrived across the northern Ocean at the shore of the city of Gijón, and from there proceeded to a place called the Lighthouse of Brigantium. When Ranimirus, already made king, learned this, he sent an army against them with dukes and counts, killed a great number of them, and burned their ships with fire. Those who survived attacked the Spanish city of Seville and, taking booty from it, killed many of the Chaldaeans with sword and fire.

### 24

Meanwhile, Prince Ranimirus was often driven into civil wars. For Count Aldoroitus of the palace, plotting against the king, was blinded by royal command. Piniolus, who afterward became count of the palace, also rose against the king in open tyranny and was killed by him together with his seven sons.

Meanwhile, the aforesaid king founded a church in honor of Saint Mary on the slope of Mount Naranco, two miles distant from Oviedo, of marvelous beauty and perfect elegance. To say nothing of its other adornments, it is vaulted with numerous barrel vaults and constructed solely of lime and stone [Note: So Perez and Mar. Others: “constructed of stone without lime.”]. If anyone wished to make a building like it, he would not find its equal in Spain.

Not far from the aforesaid church he built many palaces, as well as beautiful and elegant baths. He fought twice against the Saracens and emerged victorious. Having completed the seventh year of his reign, he died in peace at Oviedo with his wife, Lady Paterna, in the era 888 (A.D. 850).

## ORDONIUS I

### 25

After Ranimirus died, his son Ordonius succeeded him in the kingship. He was a man of great power and moderation [Note: Here Berg. adds from Sand.: “He also had a wife, Muniadona, by whom he fathered the following sons: Adefonsus, Veremundus, Nunnius, Odoarius, Froilanus, and also Aragon, a daughter”—which is a fabrication of Pelagius of Oviedo.].

He repopulated the deserted cities from which Adefonsus the Elder had driven out the Chaldaeans: namely, Tui, Astorga, León, and Amaya Patricia. He fought against the Chaldaeans very frequently and triumphed at the beginning of his reign.

When he moved an army against the rebellious Basques and had subjected their homeland to his authority, as he was returning to his own territory a messenger arrived saying: “Behold, an Arab enemy is approaching from the opposite direction.” Immediately the king turned his weapons and battle line against them. Without delay he put their troops to flight and, brandishing his sword, cut them down.

Nor will I be silent about an event that I know to have truly occurred. A Goth named Muza [Note: “Goth,” or “Gotus,” is found in three manuscripts. The editions read “Gaetulus.” The monk of Silos clearly indicates that he was Gothic by origin when he says: “A Goth by nation, but since some are ensnared by various errors of demons, Muza, deceived by Abderraman together with his entire household through the superstitious sect of Muhammad, received the name Muza, having abandoned the Christian sect,” etc.], but deceived according to the rite of Muhammad with the entire multitude of his people [Note: So Mar. and Perez: “with the entire multitude of his people.” Others: “with his people.”], whom the Chaldaeans call the Banu Qasi, rebelled against the king of Córdoba. He seized many cities from him, partly by the sword and partly by deception: first Zaragoza, then Tudela and Huesca, and finally Toledo, where he appointed his son, named Lupus, as governor.

Afterward he turned his arms against the Franks and Gauls. There he inflicted many slaughters and carried off much booty. He also captured by treachery two great Frankish leaders, one named Sancho and the other Eplon [Note: So the manuscript codices. Ber., “Eylon.”], and sent them bound into prison.

Of the Chaldaeans, two great tyrants were captured in battle: one of the family of the Alcorexis, named Ibenamaz, and the other a soldier named Alporz, together with his son Azeth. Muza the father and Lupus the son took them partly by fighting. Because of such a victory, he swelled with such pride that he ordered his own people to call him the third king in Spain [Note: Mar., “because of such a victory”; others, “because of the deed”; Codex Regius, “because of such a great…”].

### 26

Against him King Ordonius moved an army toward the city that Muza had recently fortified with marvelous workmanship and named Albailda. The king came to it with his army and surrounded it with fortifications. Muza himself arrived with an innumerable multitude and pitched his tents on a mountain called Laturzo.

King Ordonius divided his army into two bodies: one to besiege the city, and the other to fight against Muza. Battle was immediately joined, and Muza with his army was put to flight. Such slaughter was made among them that more than ten thousand Magnates [Note: Sandoval, in the margin: “Perhaps Moors.”], together with their people, whose name was Garseane, were killed at once, apart from the common people.

Muza himself, pierced three times by the sword, escaped half alive. He lost there a great quantity of military equipment and also the gifts that King Charles of the Franks had sent him, and afterward he never achieved the effect of victory again.

King Ordonius then brought his entire army against the city and stormed it on the seventh day. He killed all the warrior men with the sword [Note: So the manuscripts. Berg., “gladiators.”], utterly destroyed the city to its foundations, and returned home with a great victory.

Lupus, the son of that same Muza, who governed Toledo as consul, heard that his father had been defeated and submitted himself with all his men to King Ordonius. As long as he lived this life, he remained subject to him; afterward he fought many battles with him against the Chaldaeans.

The aforesaid King Ordonius also captured many other cities by fighting: namely, the city of Coria with its king, named Zeth, and another city like it. He captured the city of Talamanca [Note: I would prefer Salamanca, from the resemblance suggested by the phrase “another like it.” Florez: [Col. 1124B] “The manuscripts of Sand. and others add Talamanca, as do the Chronicle of Albelda, Ferreras, and Ber.; Salamanca.”] with its king, named Mozeror [Note: So the Chronicle of Albelda, Ferreras, and Ber., “Muzerot.” Perez, “Mozror.”], and his wife. He killed all their warriors and sold the remaining populace, together with their wives and children, under the crown.

Again, at this time Northman pirates reached our shores. Then they proceeded into Spain and devastated its entire coast by plundering with sword and fire. Afterward, crossing the sea, they attacked the city of Nachor in Mauretania and killed a multitude of Chaldaeans there with the sword. Finally, attacking the islands of Majorca, Formentera, and Minorca, they laid them waste with the sword. Later they sailed to Greece and, after three years, returned to their own country.

After the aforesaid King Ordonius had completed the sixteenth year of his reign, he was seized by gout and died at Oviedo (A.D. 866). He was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary with the earlier kings.

He passed happy times in the kingdom; happy he stands in heaven. He who was greatly loved by the peoples here now rejoices with the holy angels in the heavenly kingdoms, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified in the unity of the Godhead throughout the ages of ages that never end. Amen.

[Col. 1123]

# THE CHRONICLE OF ALBELDA

Perhaps by Dulcidius, bishop of Salamanca, continued by Vigila, monk of Albelda.

## NOTICE

*(In Florez, España Sagrada.)*

The Chronicle of Albelda, issued by an unknown author in the era 921 and supplemented by Vigila, a monk of Albelda, in the era 1014, exists in the Gothic Book of Councils, which belonged to the monastery of Saint Martin of Albelda and has now been transferred to the library of the Royal Monastery of Saint Lawrence.

This chronicle was written in the eighteenth year of Adefonsus the Great, king of Oviedo, in the era 921 (that is, A.D. 883), in the thirty-second year of Muhammad of Córdoba, the Saracen.

It was perhaps written by Dulcidius, bishop of Salamanca, who took part in the consecration of Compostela in the era 917 and appears, from the letter of Adefonsus III to Sebastian, to have been a diligent investigator of chronicles. He was therefore able to continue the history of his predecessor Sebastian of Salamanca.

Vigila, a monk of the monastery of Albelda (now Albelda near Logroño), added to this Chronicle, which ended in the era 921, the eighteenth year of Adefonsus the Great and the thirty-second year of Muhammad [Col. 1124C] of Córdoba, continuing it to the era 1014, especially with matters concerning the kings of Pamplona, and a catalogue of the kings of Oviedo up to Ranimirus III.

Thus Vigila’s addition ends in the era 1014—that is, A.D. 976—in the sixth year of Sancho, king of Pamplona, son of Garsea, and the tenth year of Ranimirus III, king of Oviedo.

Accordingly, on the fourth folio of this book of Albelda it is said that the era was then 1014, the year from the Incarnation 976, and the sixth year of King Sancho. The same ending is copied here from the Albelda codex in the book of the councils of Saint Emilianus, folio 4.

This Chronicle was also found in the Emilianus codex at folio 394, but it has been torn out from there, leaving only one final folio.

# PRELIMINARY MATERIAL OF THE CHRONICLE

[Col. 1125]

## An Account of the Whole World

### I

The whole world was surveyed by the wisest men, namely Nicodorus, Didymus, Theodotus, and Polyclitus, in the time of Julius Caesar. The East was measured over twenty-one years, two months, and eight days. The West over twenty-six years, three months, and seventeen days. The North over twenty-nine years, two months, and three days. The South over twenty-two years, one month, and thirty days.

[Note: From here to “the South” is missing in Berganza and Saz. It is supplied from Pellicer. Aethicus, however, in the Cosmography of the Groningen edition, Leiden 1693, relates the matter as follows:

“Therefore, beginning with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony as consuls, the measurement of the world began—that is, from the consulship of the aforesaid men to the third consulship of Augustus and Crassus, twenty-one years, five months, and nine days. Zenodoxus measured the whole East, as is shown below. Likewise, from the consulship of Julius Caesar and Mark Antony to the tenth consulship of Augustus, twenty-nine years, eight months, and ten days, Theodotus measured the northern part, as is clearly demonstrated. Similarly, from the consulship of Julius Caesar to the consulship of Saturninus and Cinna, Polyclitus measured the southern part, over thirty-two years, one month, and ten days, as the calculation shows. Thus the whole circuit of the earth was traversed by the surveyors within thirty-two years, and an account of all its extent was conveyed to the senate.”

Here you will look in vain for the measurement of the West, which must be attributed to our Didymus, or Didymicus, and was completed in twenty-six years.]

### II

The East contains eight seas, eight islands, seven mountains, seven provinces, seventy-five towns, seventeen rivers, and forty-five peoples.

The West contains eight seas, nineteen islands, fifteen mountains, twenty-seven provinces, seventy-five towns, sixteen rivers, and twenty-five peoples [Note: This entire description of the West is absent from Pellicer, as are the words below beginning “In the time of Julius Augustus”; these should be corrected to “in the time of Julius Caesar.”].

The North contains twelve seas, twenty-five islands, thirteen mountains, fifty-eight towns, eighteen rivers, twenty-nine peoples, and seventeen provinces.

The South contains two seas, seventeen islands, six mountains, thirteen provinces, sixty-two towns, six rivers, and twenty-four peoples.

In the time of Julius Augustus, throughout the whole world there were thirty seas, sixty-nine islands, forty-one mountains, sixty-four provinces, two hundred seventy towns, fifty-seven rivers, and one hundred thirty-three peoples [Note: This summation of the numbers is excellent; therefore we have omitted, as an appendix, the contrary readings of others.].

## Also, a Description of Spain

### III

Spain was first called Iberia from the river Iberus, and afterward Spain from Hispalis. It is also Hesperia, named from Hesperus, the evening star. It lies between Africa and Gaul, closed on the north by the Pyrenees, and enclosed on all the other sides by the sea. It is fertile in every kind of crop and exceedingly rich in supplies of gems and metals.

### Another Account

It has six provinces with episcopal sees.

The first is Carthage, which is Carpetania.

The metropolitan see of Toledo has under it: Oretum, Baeza, Urci, Bigastrum, Elche, Játiva, Dianium, Castalona, Valencia, Valeria, Segobriga, Arcabrica, Complutum, Sigüenza, Osma, Segovia, and Palencia—seventeen.

The second province is Baetica.

Its metropolitan see is Seville. Under it are Italica, Assidonia, Arepla, [Col. 1125C] Atigi, Córdoba, Egabrum, Málaga, Iliberis, and Acci—nine.

The third province is Lusitania.

Its metropolitan see is Mérida. Under it are Pace, Lisbon, Exonoba, Agitaunia, Coimbra, Veseo, Lamego, Caliabria, Talamantica, Ávila, Talavera, Elbora, and Coria—thirteen.

The fourth province is Gallaecia.

Its metropolitan see is Braga. Under it are Dumium, Porto, Tui, Ourense, Iria, Lugo, Vittania, and Astorga—eight.

The fifth province is Tarraconensis.

Its metropolitan see is Tarragona. Under it are Barcelona, Egara, Gerona, Ampurias, Ausona, Urgell, Lérida, Tortosa, Zaragoza, Huesca, Pamplona, Auca, Calahorra, and Tarazona—fourteen.

The sixth province is Tingitana, across the sea.

Gaul is not one of the provinces of Spain, but it was under Gothic rule, as follows:

Narbonne, Béziers, Agde, Maguelonne, Nîmes, Lodève, Carcassonne, Elne, and Toulouse.

### The Rivers of Spain

There are four.

The Baetis runs 410 miles. The Tagus [Note: Saz, “Taccus.” The Durius is absent, as also in Aethicus.] runs 602 miles. The Miño runs 313 miles. The Ebro runs 304 miles.

## The Seven Wonders of the World

### IV

1. The Capitol at Rome.  
2. The Pharos of Alexandria.  
3. The Bellerophontic monument of Smyrna.  
4. The theater of Heraclea.  
5. The Colossus of Rhodes.  
6. The temple of Quiricus.  
7. The Tetrapylon of Emesa, which is better than the church of Saint Sophia at Constantinople [Note: Others list different wonders.].

## Also, the Characteristics of the Peoples

### V

1. The wisdom of the Greeks.  
2. The strength of the Goths.  
3. The counsels of the Chaldaeans.  
4. The pride of the Romans.  
5. The ferocity of the Franks.  
6. The anger of the Britons.  
7. The lust of the Scots.  
8. The hardness of the Saxons.  
9. The greed of the Persians.  
10. The envy of the Jews.  
11. The peace of the Ethiopians.  
12. The commerce of the Gauls.

## Also, Famous Products of Spain

### VI

Polla from Narbonne; wine from Vilasz; figs from Baeza; wheat from the Gothic Fields; a mule from Seville; a horse from the Moors; oysters from Mancario; lamprey from Thatther; a lance from Gaul; scanda from Asturias; honey from Gallaecia; discipline and learning from Toledo. These were the chief products in the time of the Goths.

## On Letters

### VII

The letters are vowels—A, E, I, O, U—because they are emitted through a direct opening of the throat without any collision and fill the voice.

The semivowels are F, N, L, N, S, R, because they begin with the vowel E and end in an insatiable sound.

[Col. 1126C] The mutes are B, C, D, T, P, Q, G, because they do not burst forth without the vowels placed beneath them. A letter is used for aspiration, which is a raised sound only for the Kalends. This concludes the work.

# A Briefly Collected Order of the Years

### VIII

From Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years.

From the Flood to Abraham: 942 years.

From Abraham to Moses: 505 years.

From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt to their entry into the Promised Land: 40 years.

From their entry until Saul, the first king of Israel, there were judges for 356 years [Note: In the Aemilianus codex of the Book of Councils, 366 years, according to Joannes Vazquez del Mármol. Nevertheless, from the calculation made in the following section under the third age, 356 must be assumed here.].

[Col. 1127A] Saul reigned forty years.

From David to the beginning of the building of the Temple: 43 years.

From the first building of the Temple to the migration into Babylon, there were kings for 443 years.

The captivity of the people and the desolation of the Temple lasted seventy years, and it was restored by Zerubbabel [Note: Pellicer’s edition adds, “four years.”].

From the restoration of the Temple to the Incarnation of Christ: 540 years.

The entire time from Adam to Christ amounts to 5,199 years.

From the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ to the first year of the reign of Prince Wamba: 672 years.

From the time of Wamba until now, which is the era 921, there are 211 years.

Now the whole time from the beginning of the world to the present era, 921, and the eighteenth year of the reign of Prince Adefonsus, glorious son of King Ordonius, totals altogether 6,082 years [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent in Berganza but present in two other editions.] and from the Incarnation of the Lord until now 883 years.]

## Also, the Six Ages of the World

### IX

The first age, from Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years.

The second age, from the Flood to Abraham: 942 years.

The third age, from Abraham to David: 941 years.

The fourth age, from David to the migration into Babylon: 486 years.

The fifth age, from the migration to Christ and the emperor Octavian, in whose time Christ was born of the Virgin Mary and the Holy Spirit [Note: The numbers are absent but must be supplied from the preceding section.].

The sixth age, which began with Christ, now has 883 years in the era 921. How far it will extend further is known to God alone; for us it remains uncertain, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is not for you to know the times or the moments which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7).

## Also, an Account of the Distances between Cities

### X

From Cádiz to Córdoba: 200 miles.

From Córdoba to Toledo: 220 miles [Note: So Pellicer. Berganza, 300.].

From Toledo to Zaragoza: 300 miles.

From Zaragoza to Huesca: 60 miles.

From Huesca to Lérida [Note: Berganza corrects to “Ilerda.” Pellicer, “Eldra,” 70.] 80 miles.

From Lérida to Gerona: 50 miles.

From Gerona to Girona: 130 miles.

From Girona to the Cluses: 40 miles.

From the Cluses to Roussillon: 20 miles [Note: Pellicer, 30.].

From Roussillon to Narbonne: 40 miles.

From Narbonne to Béziers: 15 miles.

From Béziers to Nîmes: 75 miles.

From Nîmes to Avignon: 25 miles.

From Avignon to Valencia: 102 miles [Note: The same source, 192.].

From Valencia to Tours: 250 miles.

From Tours to Milan: 170 miles.

From Milan to Rome: 316 miles.

From Rome to Thessalonica: 842 miles [Note: The same source, 815.].

From Thessalonica to Heraclea: 316 miles.

From Heraclea to Constantinople: 130 miles.

The total is 3,281 miles [Note: This is not the sum obtained from the preceding figures.].

## Also, a List of the Bishops with Their Sees

### XI

Hermenegildus holds the royal see [Note: That is, Oviedo.] (A.D. 881; see no. 25).

Flaianus of Braga; Reccaredus, bishop in Lugo [Note: Pellicer, “Laianus.”] [Note: So Pellicer. In Berg. and Saz., “Asce” instead of “arce,” and Reccaredus is absent.].

Tudemirus, residing at Dumium and Mendunieto [Note: Pellicer, “Monduneto.”] [Note: Pellicer, “Rudezindus”; Saz, “Tuderindus”; Berg., “Tudemirus.”].

Sisnandus, powerful at holy James of Iria.

Nausticus holds the see of Coimbra [Note: Pellicer, “Austusque.” Sampirus, “Naustus.”].

Brandericus also holds the Lamego see [Note: Pellicer, “Candericus.”].

Sebastianus indeed holds the see of Ourense.

Justus likewise holds that of Porto.

Alvarus of Velegia [Note: Yepes, vol. IV, writing 20, “Albar, Bishop of Velegia,” p. 437, p. 443. See Pellicer on Dulcidius. Florez, additions from the manuscript.] and Felmirus of Osma [Note: Pellicer, “Vellemirus of Osma.” Saz, “Felemirus.”].

Maurus at León, Ranulfus at Astorga.

The aforesaid prelates shine conspicuously among the people of the Church through the king’s wisdom.

The king also, made renowned throughout the whole world,

the aforesaid Adefonsus by name,

placed at the summit of the kingdom, suited to the title of war,

renowned among the Asturians, strong among the Basques,

[Col. 1128C] avenging the Arabs and protecting the citizens.

To this prince may sacred victory be granted,

helped by Christ the leader, ever glorified.

May he prevail victorious in the world, shine in heaven itself:

devoted to triumph here, endowed with a kingdom there.

Amen.

# THE CHRONICLE OF ALBELDA

[Col. 1127]

# The Order of the Roman Kings Begins

[Col. 1127C]

### 1

In Rome Romulus first reigned for thirty-eight years. He built Rome [Note: Written in the margin of the Gothic codex of Albelda:

“Also concerning Romulus and Remus. Numitor, the leading nobleman and eldest son of the former king, was expelled from the kingdom by his brother Amulius and lived in his own field. His daughter was chosen as a Vestal virgin so that her childbearing might be prevented. When, in the seventh year of her uncle’s rule, she gave birth to twins, she was buried alive in the earth according to the law. The infants, exposed near the bank of the Tiber, were carried by Faustulus, the royal shepherd of the herd, to his wife Acca Laurentia. Because of her beauty and her greed for money through the sale of her body, she was called ‘the She-Wolf’ by her neighbors. Hence, even to our own memory, the cells of prostitutes are called ‘lupanaria.’ When the boys had grown up, they gathered a band of shepherds and robbers and, after killing Amulius at Alba, restored their grandfather Numitor to the kingdom. After Numitor’s death, Romulus, his grandson, founded Rome and reigned.”]

Titus Tatius, king of the Sabines, for five years.

Numa Pompilius reigned thirty-two years. He first organized the year into twelve months.

[Col. 1129A] Tullus Hostilius, thirty-three years. He was the first to wear purple.

Ancus Marcius [Note: The word “Philippus” intruded into the text; it is absent from the codices of the monastery of Saint Emilianus.] reigned twenty-nine years [Note: In the archetype: “Ancus Marcus and Philippus reigned twenty-eight years.”].

Tarquinius Priscus reigned thirty-eight years. He built the Capitol.

Servius Tullius reigned thirty-eight years. He was the first to conduct a census.

Tarquinius Superbus reigned twenty-five years. He was expelled from the kingdom for his conduct.

There were consuls for 376 years.

The decemvirs, one year.

There were kings for two years.

Therefore, from Romulus and the founding of Rome to Gaius Julius Caesar: 666 years.

Gaius Julius Caesar was therefore the first to rule, for four years. He fought with Pompey for the empire.

From this point the next age begins.

### 2

Octavian reigned fifty-six years. In his twelfth year (42), Christ was born. He alone ruled the whole world.

[Col. 1129B] Tiberius, son of Gaius [Note: Perhaps “his son” or “of Augustus,” as in the Aemilianus codex], reigned eighteen years. In the eighteenth year of his reign, the Lord Christ was crucified. Because, out of greed, he would not send back the kings who came to him, many peoples withdrew from the Roman Empire.

Gaius Caligula reigned four years. He was greedy, cruel, and enslaved to luxury. He fished with golden nets. At this time the apostle Matthew first wrote the Gospel in Judaea.

Claudius reigned fourteen years. At that time the apostle Peter came to Rome, and the evangelist Mark wrote in Alexandria [Note: In the archetype, “the Gospel.”].

Nero reigned fourteen years. He was cruel and devoted to luxury. He fished with golden nets. In his time Peter and Paul were killed, one on a cross and the other by the sword.

Vespasian reigned eight years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. He was forgetful of offenses. In his second year Titus captured Jerusalem, where 1,100,000 Jews perished from hunger and the sword, and 100,000 were publicly sold.

Titus [Note: In the archetype, “Titus the king reigned.”] reigned two years. He was eloquent and pious, and also dear to human beings.

Domitian, the brother of Titus, reigned sixteen years. Abominably proud, he ordered himself to be called a god and launched a persecution against the Christians; he killed senators. Under him the apostle John was also banished into exile on Patmos for four months.

Nerva reigned one year. He was a man moderate in the exercise of power. In his time the apostle John returned to Ephesus; and when requested by the bishops of Asia, he was the last to publish the Gospel [Note: In the archetype, “he gave it.”].

### 3

Trajan reigned nineteen years and seven months. In his time the apostle John came to rest.

[Col. 1130A] Hadrian reigned twenty-one years. He restored Jerusalem and called it Aelia after his own name.

Antoninus [Note: “Antoninus.” Both here and under the other emperors of this name, the codex of Vigila writes “Antoninus.”] Pius reigned twenty-two years. He was very merciful. He was called “Father of his Country.” Galen the physician, born at Pergamum, is regarded as famous at Rome.

Antoninus the Younger reigned seventeen years. He was victorious.

Commodus reigned thirteen years.

Helvius [Note: In the archetype, “Helius.”] Pertinax reigned unwillingly for one year. He did not wish his wife to be called Augusta [Note: Mariana adds “to be called” in his manuscript.].

Severus Pertinax reigned eighteen years. In his time Origen was educated at Alexandria.

Antoninus Caracalla, son of Severus, reigned seven years. He was lustful. He took his stepmother [Note: Thus it is written there: “stepmother.”] as his wife.

Macrinus reigned one year. He accomplished nothing memorable.

Aurelius Antoninus reigned three years. He was killed in a military uprising because of his conduct.

Alexander reigned thirteen years. In his time Origen of Alexandria flourished.

Maximianus [Note: “Maximinus” should be read.] reigned three years. He persecuted the Christians.

### 4

Gordian reigned seven years. He perished through the treachery of his own men.

Philip reigned seven years. He was the first Christian emperor and believed in Christ, in the thousandth year of the City.

Decius reigned one year. He was a persecutor of the Christians. In his time Saint Antony the monk was renowned in Egypt; the first monasteries were founded by him.

Gallus and his son Volusian reigned two years.

Valerian with Gallienus [Note: “Gallienus.”] reigned fifteen years [Note: The following should be placed here, although it is wrongly attributed below to Aurelian: “He persecutes the Christians, is captured by the king of the Persians, and there grows old and dies in disgrace.”].

In his time Saint Cyprian, bishop, was crowned with martyrdom.

Claudius reigned two years. He overcame the Goths, who were devastating Illyricum and Macedonia.

Aurelian reigned six years. [He persecuted the Christians, was captured by the king of the Persians, and there grew old and died in disgrace [Note: This passage has been moved from its place, as we have just noted.].]

Tacitus reigned one year.

[Col. 1130C] Probus reigned six years. He was vigorous in military affairs and renowned for victories.

Carus reigned two years. He perished by a stroke of lightning.

Diocletian and Maximian reigned twenty years. Diocletian persecuted the Christians. He was the first to order gems to be set into clothing and footwear, whereas formerly the emperors used only purple. But both, having abandoned imperial rule, lived as private citizens.

Galerius reigned two years.

### 5

Constantine reigned thirty years. Having become a Christian, he granted permission to the Christians [Note: In the Albelda codex this is written in the margin: “Era 380: the Arian impiety arose.” But an error entered the number, since that plague began to spread around the era 353—that is, A.D. 315.]. At the same time the Lord’s cross was discovered by Helena, the mother of Constantine.

He ordered the Council of Nicaea to be held, as on another folio [Note: Thus in the autograph of Mármol. After “he ordered” Mariana has: “Here he held at Constantinople a synod of 318 bishops. At the end of his life he became an Arian.” In the archetype, as in Mariana, Berganza, and Saz: “He ordered the Council of Nicaea to be held. At the end of his life he became an Arian. A council of 318 bishops…” It is quite clear that the reading should be: “He ordered the Council of Nicaea to be held, of 318 bishops.” Evidently the words “At the end of his life he became an Arian,” perhaps written by someone in the margin, were rashly inserted by another into the thread of an incomplete sentence.].

[Col. 1131A] Constantine and Constans reigned thirty-three years. Constans, cruel in character and having become an Arian, persecuted the Christians.

Arius, his friend, poured out his entrails together with his life at Constantinople.

Hilary was regarded as renowned for his learning [Note: The manuscript, “Clarius.”].

Donatus, who was distinguished at Rome for the art of grammar [Note: Berganza and Saz: “Donatus was distinguished at Rome by his skill in grammar.” Antonius, etc., entirely omit what follows: “At the same time he suffered”; if this is to be retained, it would be better arranged as in Ferreras: “Donatus was distinguished at Rome by his skill in grammar. At the same time he suffered … Antonius, etc.” That is, with a lacuna marked, so that it may be clear that something is missing by which the grammatical sense is completed.], suffered at the same time.

Antony the monk died at that time.

The bones of the apostles Andrew and Luke were transferred to Constantinople.

### 6

Julian, two years. Having been an emperor from the clerical state and having become a pagan, he worshiped idols. He inflicted martyrdoms on Christians. Out of hatred for Christ, he ordered the Temple at Jerusalem to be restored to the Jews, but the Lord did not permit it. Julian, however, died among the Persians after being struck by a spear.

Jovian reigned one year. A Christian, he did not wish to accept the empire; but, because the entire army had become Christian out of love for him, he finally yielded. Immediately he granted privileges to the Christians and ordered the temples of the idols to be closed.

Valentinian and his brother Valens reigned fourteen years. The Goths were divided into two groups under Athanaric and Fritigern. Alaric overcame Fritigern with the assistance of Valens, the Arian emperor [Note: The manuscript has it incorrectly, “of the empire of Arius”; and immediately afterward, “he himself the king, together with all…”]. Consequently, through the emperor Valens, that king himself became an Arian together with the entire Gothic people. Their bishop Ulfilas invented letters for them.

Gratian, with his brother Valentinian, reigned six years. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, flourished [Note: The archetype adds, “in learning.”], and Martin, bishop of the Gallic city of Tours [Note: In the archetype, “of the city of the Turunenses.”], shone forth through signs of miracles.

### 7

Valentinian with Theodosius reigned seven years. The Council of Constantinople of 150 bishops was assembled [Note: In the archetype, “The 150 Fathers were assembled at Constantinople,” etc.]. Jerome the presbyter was regarded as renowned throughout the whole world at Bethlehem.

The head of John the Baptist was brought to Constantinople and buried at the seventh milestone of the city.

[Col. 1131C] The temple of the idols was overturned by Theodosius [Note: Better in Berg. and Saz: “The temples … were overturned.”].

Theodosius with Arcadius reigned three years.

At that time John the anchorite was renowned for miracles.

Arcadius with his brother Honorius reigned thirteen years. At this time Augustine the bishop was renowned for his knowledge of doctrine.

At that time Donatus, bishop of Epirus, was regarded as distinguished for his virtues. He killed an enormous dragon by spitting into its mouth; eight yokes of oxen could scarcely drag it to the fire.

At that time the bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed through divine revelation.

Theophilus flourished.

The Goths attacked Italy, while the Vandals and Alans attacked Gaul.

### 8

Honorius with Theodosius the Younger, his brother’s son, reigned fifteen years. Under their rule the Goths captured Rome. The Vandals and Alans, together with the Suebi, occupied Spain.

[Col. 1131D] The Council of Carthage of 214 bishops was held.

Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, is held in high distinction.

Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, reigned 27 years.

The Vandals crossed from Spain into Africa and there overturned the Catholic faith through Arian impiety.

[Col. 1132A] The synod of Ephesus was held against Nestorius, the bishop.

At this time also the devil, appearing to the Jews in Crete in the form of Moses, promised to lead them across the sea on dry ground to the promised land. After many had been killed, the survivors became Christians.

### 9. Martianus reigned six years.

At the beginning of his reign the Council of Chalcedon was held.

Rudericus [Note: [Col. 1132D] Read *Theudericus*.], king of the Goths, entered Spain with a huge army.

Leo the Elder, together with Leo the Younger, reigned 16 years.

Zeno reigned 17 years. At this time the body of the apostle Barnabas, and the Gospel of Matthew, were discovered through his own revelation.

Anastasius reigned 27 years. At that time Fulgentius, the bishop, was renowned for his knowledge of doctrine. Many heresies arose.

Justin the Elder reigned eight years. As a supporter of the Council of Chalcedon, he rejected the heresy of the Acephali [Note: [Col. 1132D] Manuscript: *Acevalorum*.].

[Col. 1132B] ### 10. Justinian reigned 39 years.

Accepting the heresy of the Acephali, he condemned the bishops who supported the Council of Chalcedon.

In Africa the Vandals were destroyed by Belisarius, the Roman patrician.

In Italy also Attila was defeated by Narses, the Roman patrician.

In Spain Atanagildus tyrannized over the imperial power [Note: [Col. 1132D] The manuscript lacks *imperium*; it is found in the copy used by Ferreras.].

At this time the body of Saint Antony the monk, discovered through divine revelation, was brought to Alexandria and buried in the church of Saint John.

Justin the Younger reigned 11 years. He destroyed what had been promulgated against the Council of Chalcedon and ordered the people to sing the Creed of the 150 Fathers during the sacrifice.

At that time the Armenians first accepted the faith of Christ.

At this time also Martin of Braga, the bishop, was held in Galicia in high repute for his wisdom concerning the Catholic faith [Col. 1132C], during the time of the Suevi.

### 11. Tiberius reigned seven years.

The Lombards, driven from Rome, went to Italy.

The Goths, divided into two factions through Hermenegild, son of King Liuvigild, were devastated by mutual slaughter.

Mauritius reigned 21 years. The Suevi, conquered by Liuvigild, king of the Goths, were subjected to the Goths.

At the same time the Goths were converted to the Catholic faith by King Reccared, a most religious ruler.

At this time Leander, bishop of Seville, was renowned throughout Spain for his teaching of the faith and of the sciences in the conversion of the Gothic people.
