Phocas reigned eight years. Having become emperor through a military revolt, he killed the emperor Maurice and many nobles.

Extremely serious wars were also stirred up by the Persians against the Empire; the Romans were soundly defeated by them.

### 12. Heraclius reigned 27 years.

The Slavs took Greece from the Romans [Col. 1132D], and the Persians took Syria and Egypt.

In Spain also Sisebut, king of the Goths, captured certain cities belonging to the same Roman military force and converted the Jews subject to his kingdom to the faith of Christ.

He also magnificently founded the church of Saint Leocadia at Toledo.

[Col. 1133A] After him, the ruler Suintila completed the recovery of the kingdom from the Romans and, through swift victory, obtained dominion over all Spain.

The kings of the Goths from Suintila up to Chintila also ruled during his reign.

Constantine reigned nine years. At that time Tulga and Chindaswinth ruled in Spain, one after the other, for nine years.

### 13. Constans reigned 20 years.

At that time Recceswinth ruled in Spain for 20 years and survived three years longer.

Constantine the Younger reigned 16 years.

The aforementioned Recceswinth ruled three years.

Wamba reigned nine years.

Ervigius reigned five years and survived for two years and 15 days.

Justinian reigned 11 years.

The aforementioned Ervigius ruled two years.

Egica reigned nine years and survived six years.

Leo [Note: [Col. 1133D] Manuscript: *Neon*.] reigned seven years.

Egica ruled in Spain for six years. After him his son Wittiza ruled for one year.

Under the emperor Tiberius, Wittiza ruled for eight years.

Rudericus reigned three years. [Then the Saracens occupied Spain [Col. 1133B] and the Gothic kingdom was destroyed, in the era 852.] [Note: [Col. 1133D] In my manuscript these events are in the wrong order. For here it reads “Rudericus reigned three years,” which in other copies is written before the arrival of the Saracens in Spain. In the archetype these words occur at the margin, enclosed in parentheses, and *exterminated* is lacking.]

## Likewise, the succession of the Gothic people.

### 14. Athanaric was the first among the Goths; he reigned 13 years.

He was the first, together with the entire Gothic people, to enter the Arian heresy through the emperor Valens. Under him the Goths began to have laws and letters. During the reign of this same king, the Goths were expelled from their own land by the Huns [Note: [Col. 1133D] Manuscript: *Agnis*.]. The king also ended his life at Constantinople under the emperor Theodosius.

### 15. Alaric reigned 18 years [Note: [Col. 1133D] It should be read as 28, and immediately afterward “this same” should be supplied.].

Then, in vengeance for the Goths—the 200,000 and Radagaisus the Scythian—whom the Romans had killed, he moved his army and captured Rome. There he plundered Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius, together with great riches. Later he died in Italy under the emperors Honorius and Arcadius.

### 16. Ataulf reigned six years.

He took the aforementioned Placidia as his wife. In the fifth year of his reign he went from Italy to Gaul; and when he wished to proceed to Spain, [Col. 1133C] he was killed by his own men at Barcelona under the emperors Honorius and Arcadius.

### 17. Sigeric reigned one year.

When he wished to make peace with the Romans, he was immediately killed by his own men under the aforesaid imperial rule.

### 18. Wallia reigned three years [Note: [Col. 1133D] *Wallia*.].

He was a warrior. He made peace with the emperor Honorius and returned his sister Placidia to him. Entering Spain, he destroyed the Vandals and Silings in battle in Baetica and reduced the Alans to nothing. He intended to cross by fleet to Africa, but the Strait of Cádiz did not allow him to do so. He returned to Gaul and there ended his life under the emperor Honorius.

### 19. Theuderic reigned 33 years.

He killed Litorius, the Roman commander, together with many thousands of Romans [Note: [Col. 1133D] Manuscript: “with many thousands.”]. He killed 200,000 of the Huns [Note: [Col. 1133D] Manuscript: *Agnis*; 200 should be followed by “thousand.” See Hydatius in the Chronicle.]. He himself was killed there in battle under the emperor Theodosius the Younger.

### 20. Turismund, his son, reigned one year.

Because he was savage and harmful, he was killed by his brothers Theuderic and Frigdarius [Note: [Col. 1134D] Hydatius has *Fredericus* in the same passage.] under the emperor Marcian.

### 21. Theuderic reigned 13 years.

He gave the Goths assistance in taking up the imperial power of Avitus [Note: [Col. 1134D] Read “the empire,” or understand *imperio* as “by imperial authority.”]. For this reason, with the permission of that same emperor Avitus, he entered Spain with a huge army and, twelve miles from Asturica, near the river Urbicus, defeated Ricciarius, king of the Suevi, in battle. Pursuing him, he captured him at Porto [and killed him. He captured Braga.] [Note: [Col. 1134D] The words in parentheses are missing in Berganza; Ferreras also omitted “he captured Braga.”]

Thus he returned from there through Lusitania toward Gaul. There he was killed by his brother Euric under the emperor Leo.

### 22. Euric reigned 26 years.

He plundered Lusitania. He captured Pamplona and Zaragoza. He was the first to give laws to the Goths. He died at Arles under the emperor Zeno.

### 23. Alaric, his son, reigned 23 years.

Huduildus, king of the Franks, killed him in battle near Poitiers. To avenge him, his father-in-law Theuderic, king of Italy, crushed the Franks and restored the Gothic kingdom intact under the emperor Anastasius.

### 24. Gesalec, son of Alaric, reigned three years.

Defeated at Narbonne by Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, he fled to Barcelona. From there he went to Africa to seek aid from the Vandals, but did not obtain it. Returning from there, he was killed near Barcelona by the commander of Theuderic, king of Italy, under the emperor Anastasius.

[Col. 1134B] ### 25. The aforementioned Theuderic, after killing Gesalec, held the Gothic kingdom for 15 years and left it to his grandson Athalaric, who survived him.

He himself returned to Italy and there ended his life under the emperor Justinian.

### 26. Amalaric reigned five years.

Defeated by Vildebert, king of the Franks, he was killed at Narbonne under the emperor Justinian.

### 27. Theudis reigned 17 years [Note: [Col. 1134D] *Theudis*.].

Although a heretic, he granted peace to the Church and gave the bishops permission to hold councils in the city of Toledo. He defeated the Frankish kings far inside Spain, advancing an excessive distance [Note: [Col. 1134D] Mariana: “who had advanced very far.”]. Someone killed him in the palace while pretending to be insane [Note: [Col. 1134D] In the archetype, “someone.”] under the emperor Justinian.

### 28. Theudisclus reigned one year.

Because he had stained the beds of many men and for this reason contrived the deaths of many, he was immediately stabbed with a sword at Seville during a banquet under the emperor Justinian.

### 29. Agila reigned five years.

While he was fighting against the city of Córdoba, and had polluted, through some dreadful act, the tomb of the holy martyr Acisclus in contempt of Christ, his son was killed there together with a great number of men, and he lost the entire royal treasury. He fled to Mérida, where his own men killed him under the emperor Justinian.

### 30. Atanagild reigned 14 years.

He fought for a long time against the troops of the emperor Justinian, which he had requested as his aid against Agila, and destroyed them. He died a natural death at Toledo under the emperor Justinian.

### 31. Liuva reigned three years at Narbonne.

He gave the administration of Spain to his brother Leuvigild; he himself governed Gaul [Note: [Col. 1134D] In the archetype, *praefugiit*.].

### 32. Leuvigild, having acquired Gaul and Spain, reigned 18 years.

He was deeply devoted to the Arian heresy, persecuted the Catholics, and removed the privileges of the churches. [He confined Masona, bishop of Mérida [Note: [Col. 1134D] The words in parentheses occur in the archetype.].] He was destructive to his own people; through greed he condemned the powerful. He defeated the Suevi and added the kingdom of Galicia to the Goths [Note: [Col. 1134D] So Mariana and Marmol; the manuscript has “mixed it in.”]. He was the first to sit upon a throne clothed in royal garments. He founded a city in Celtiberia and called it Recopolis. He first revised the laws of the Goths. He died a natural death at Toledo under the emperor Maurice.

### 33. Reccared, his son, reigned 15 years.

At the beginning of his reign he embraced the Catholic faith and recalled the entire Gothic people to the worship of the true faith. Through a synod of the bishops of Gaul and Spain he confirmed the Catholic faith. He struck down 60,000 Frankish enemies in battle in Spain and adorned the years of his reign with every form of goodness. He died peacefully at Toledo while Maurice was emperor.

### 34. Liuva, his son, reigned two years.

Vitericus cut off his right hand and, although he was harmless, killed him; he then took the kingdom for himself under the emperor Maurice.

### 35. Vitericus reigned seven years.

He was indeed a vigorous man skilled in warfare, but without victory. He received what he had done: during a banquet he was killed by his own men under the rule of Phocas.

### 36. Gundemar reigned two years.

In a single campaign he devastated the Basques. He died a natural death at Toledo under the emperor Heraclius.

### 37. Sisebut reigned eight years.

By his authority he brought the Jews to the faith of Christ. He magnificently founded the church of Saint Leocadia [Note: [Col. 1135D] The archetype adds: “at Toledo.”]. He subdued the Asturians and Basques rebelling in the mountains and was gracious to his own people in every respect [Col. 1135B]. Some say that he was killed by a disease of his own; others, by an excessive draught of drink, under the emperor Heraclius.

At that time the impious Muhammad preached the wickedness of his law to foolish peoples in Africa.

### 38. Suintila reigned ten years.

He was great in victory and counsel. He defeated the Basques and captured two Roman patricians. He governed all Spain and Gaul vigorously and, because of his merit, deserved to be called the father of the poor. He died a natural death at Toledo under the emperor Heraclius.

### 39. Sisinand reigned four years.

He held a synod of bishops. He was patient and proved orthodox in accordance with the Catholic rules. He ended his life at Toledo under the emperor Heraclius.

### 40. Chintila reigned three years.

He held many synods at Toledo with the bishops and strengthened the subject kingdom in the faith. He died at Toledo under the emperor Heraclius.

### 41. Tulga reigned three years.

He was gentle in all things.

### 42. Chindaswinth reigned alone six years, and with his son Recceswinth four years.

During his time Spain was at peace, and the Church was instructed through synods. He died at Toledo under the emperor Constantine the Younger.

### 43. Wamba reigned nine years.

In the first year of his reign, when Paul, his duke, rebelled against him with part of Spain, or with the entire province of Gaul, this king first subdued the fierce Basques [Note: [Col. 1135D] *Fascones*, that is, Basques; the Mozarabs often used *f* for *v* or *b*.] on the borders of Cantabria with the army of Spain. Then, proceeding onward, after capturing all the cities of Gothic Spain and Gaul, he finally defeated Paul himself in the city of Nîmes and subjected him to himself in a celebrated triumph.

Later he was deprived of the kingdom by Ervigius under the emperor Constantine the Younger.

### 44. Ervigius reigned six years.

He held many synods at Toledo with the bishops. He gave his daughter as a wife to Egica. He died at Toledo under the emperor Justinian.

### 45. Egica reigned 15 years.

When he received the kingdom, he subjected Ervigius’s daughter to himself by the oath of Wamba [Note: [Col. 1135D] “He rejected her through Wamba’s conspiracy.” Rudericus of Toledo, in Flórez, *Additions*, manuscript.]. He placed his son Wittiza in charge of the kingdom with himself. He died at Toledo under the rule of Leo.

[Col. 1135D] Wittiza reigned ten years [Note: [Col. 1135D] The Aemilian manuscript reads as follows in Saz: “During his father’s lifetime he resided in the city of Tui in Galicia. There, on some occasion, he struck Fafila, duke and father of Pelagius, whom King Egica had sent there, on the head with a staff, and as a result Fafila later died. When that same Wittiza received his father’s kingdom, he expelled Pelagius, son of Fafila, who later rebelled against the Saracens together with the Asturians, from the royal city because of the cause of his father that we have mentioned. Wittiza ended his life at Toledo under the emperor Tiberius.” The Tudense likewise places this under Egica.]. He ended his life at Toledo under the rule of Tiberius.

[Col. 1136A] ### 46. Rudericus reigned three years.

In his time, in the era 752, the Saracens, summoned by Farmalio [Note: [Col. 1135D] See below, no. 77.], occupied Spain and captured the Gothic kingdom, which they still stubbornly possess in part. Christians wage wars against them day and night and engage them daily, while divine predestination has decreed that they shall thereafter be cruelly expelled. Amen.

## Likewise, the names of the Catholic kings of León.

### 47. Pelagius [Note: [Col. 1136D] Some material is missing. See Saz, p. 37.], son of Veremundus and grandson of Rudericus, king of Toledo.

He was the first to enter the mountains of Asturias, beneath a crag, into the cave of Auseva.

Then his son Fabila. Then Adefonsus, son-in-law of Pelagius. After him his brother Froila. Then Aurelius [Note: [Col. 1136D] After Aurelius, Silo, Maurecatus, and Veremundus are missing; after this preliminary general mention, the author immediately discusses them individually.]. After him Adefonsus the Chaste, who founded Oviedo. Then Nepotianus, kinsman of King Adefonsus. After Nepotianus, Ranimirus. After him his son Ordonius, who struck down Albailda.

[Col. 1136B] Then his son Adefonsus, who struck down Ebrellos.

### 48. After him his son [Note: [Col. 1136D] Up to this point the first author of the work wrote; he testified that he was writing in the era 921, that is, in the year 883. The remainder through no. 50 exclusive was added in 976.] Garsea.

Then Ordonius. Then his brother Froila. [Note: [Col. 1136D] These two lines are redundant.] After him his son Adefonsus. Then Sancius, son of Ordonius. Then Adefonsus, who gave away his kingdom and turned to God. After him his brother Ranemirus. Then his son Ordonius. [After him his brother Sancius [Note: [Col. 1136D] The words in parentheses occur in the archetype.].] Then Ranemirus, son of Sancius.

Joannes Vazquez del Marmol says that a space of about eight or nine lines is blank here.

## Likewise, the names of the kings of Pamplona.

Joannes Vazquez again notes that a space is blank here, and at the margin of the manuscript is written: “Here I do not know what sort of men the kings mentioned above were.”

[Col. 1136C] ### 49. Sancius, son of King Garsea, reigned 20 years.

[Here it is noted in the margin: “The era 914 began.”]

Garsea, son of King Sancius, reigned ten years (and more). Sancius.

## Likewise, the succession of the Gothic kings of Oviedo.

[Note: [Col. 1136D] In the manuscript at Marmol, *Obetensium* and *Obeto* are almost always written with *b*.]

### 50. Pelagius was the first to reign in Asturias; he reigned at Cangas for 19 years.

Expelled from Toledo by King Wittiza, he entered Asturias after Spain had been occupied by the Saracens. He was the first to rebel against them in Asturias, while Joseph was reigning at Córdoba and Munuza was administering, by order of the Saracens, the city of León over the Asturians. Thus the Ismaelite army was killed by him together with Alahor, and Bishop Oppa was captured. Finally Munuza was killed, and from that time the Christian people recovered their freedom.

At that time those who had survived the sword from that Saracen host [Note: [Col. 1136D] That is, the army or battle-line, using the archaic Spanish word *hueste*, here written *hoste*.] were crushed at Libamina [Note: [Col. 1136D] Other authors have *Libana*; today it is Liébana.] when the mountain collapsed by God’s judgment [Col. 1136D]. Thus the kingdom of the Asturians arose through divine providence.

The aforementioned Pelagius died at Cangas in the era 775.

### 51. Fabila, his son, reigned two years.

Led on by recklessness, he was killed by a bear.

### 52. Adefonsus, son-in-law of Pelagius, reigned 18 years.

He was the son of Peter, duke of Cantabria. When he came to Asturias, he took Ermesinda [Note: [Col. 1137D] Pellicer has *Ermisendam*.], daughter of Pelagius, at Pelagius’s command. When he received the kingdom, he waged battles enough with God’s help [Note: [Col. 1137D] Mariana adds the word *multa*, “many.”].

He victoriously invaded the cities of León and Astorga, which were held by the enemies. He laid waste to the fields called Gothic as far as the river Douro and extended the Christian kingdom. He proved pleasing to God and to men. He died a natural death.

### 53. Froila, his son, reigned 11 years.

He won victories, but was harsh in character [Note: [Col. 1137D] In the archetype: “he acted or was harsh in character,” and so forth.]. Through envy of the kingdom he killed his brother, named Vimarane. Later, because of the savagery of his mind, he was killed at Cangas in the era 806.

### 54. Aurelius reigned seven years.

During his reign, slaves who opposed their masters were captured through his efforts and restored to their former servitude [Col. 1137B]. During his time Silo, who would later become king, took Adosinda [Note: [Col. 1137D] Eterius and Beatus mention Adosinda in their letter to Elipandus.], sister of King Froila, as his wife. With her he later obtained the kingdom.

Aurelius died a natural death.

### 55. Silo reigned nine years.

When he received the kingdom, he established his throne at Pravia. He maintained peace with Spain on account of his mother. He died a natural death and left no offspring.

### 56. Maurecatus reigned five years.

[Note: [Col. 1137D] The manuscript of Saint Emiliano adds “having seized the kingdom tyrannically.” Berganza and Saz have the same. So also Pellicer.]

### 57. Veremundus reigned three years.

For three years he was present as a merciful [Note: [Col. 1137D] So the manuscript of Saint Emiliano. The Albeldensis instead has “he was for three years and more.” So Joannes Vazquez del Marmol.] and pious ruler. During his reign a battle was fought at Burbia [Note: [Col. 1137D] Ferrer has “at Burebia.” Berganza: “a battle was fought under the era 830.” Pellicer: “a battle was fought at Burobia, under the era …” without the numerals.].

Afterward he voluntarily relinquished the kingdom.

### 58. Adefonsus the Great reigned 51 years.

In the second year of his reign he was expelled from the kingdom by tyranny and confined in the monastery of Abelania. From there he was brought back by a certain Theudanus or by other faithful men and restored to the summit of the kingdom at Oviedo.

At Oviedo he magnificently built the temple of the Holy Savior with the twelve apostles, of stone and mortar. [Col. 1137C] He also built the hall of Saint Mary with three altars. He likewise laid the foundations of the basilica of Saint Tirso, a marvelous structure with many angles.

He carefully adorned all these houses of the Lord with vaults and marble columns, with gold and silver; at the same time he decorated them with various paintings together with the royal palaces. He established the entire Gothic order at Oviedo, both in the church and in the palace, just as it had been at Toledo.

He won many victories over the Ishmaelites. He defeated the armies of the Getulians [Note: [Col. 1137D] That is, armies; in Spanish, *huestes*.] in battle: one in Asturias at the place called Eutis, and another in the province of Galicia at the place called Anceo.

During his time a certain man from Spain named Mahamut, driven out by the king of Córdoba, was received by this ruler in Asturias together with all his men. Later, when he had perverted the rebels in Galicia in the fortress of Saint Christina [Note: [Col. 1137D] So the manuscript of Saint Emiliano. Ferrer has “to the rebellion.” Marmol has neither. In the archetype: “Afterward, in Galicia, to the rebels in the fortress,” and so forth.], this king killed him there in battle and captured the fortress itself with all its possessions.

He lived a most chaste life without a wife. Thus he passed from the kingdom of earth to the kingdom of heaven. He accomplished everything in peace and rested in peace. He lies buried here beneath the twelve holy altars that he founded and established [Note: [Col. 1138D] Pellicer has “founded”; others have “founded” in the plural.].

[Col. 1138A] ### 59. Ranemirus reigned seven years.

He was a rod of justice. He punished robbers by putting out their eyes. He brought magic to an end by fire and overthrew and destroyed tyrants with marvelous speed.

First he defeated Nepotianus at the bridge of Narcea, and thus took the kingdom. At that time the Northmen [Note: [Col. 1138D] Understand “Northerners.”] first came to Asturias.

Afterward, together with a certain tyrant Aldoitro, he gouged out their eyes from their foreheads and, victorious, killed the arrogant Puniolus.

At the place called Ligno he wonderfully constructed a church and palaces with vaulted workmanship [Note: [Col. 1138D] So Mariana. *Dicto* is absent from the archetype and from other copies.]. There he departed from this age, and he rests in a tomb at Oviedo on the day before the Kalends of February, 888 (that is, 850).

### 60. Ordonius, his son, reigned 17 years.

With God’s help he enlarged the kingdom of the Christians. He populated León and Astorga, together with Tui and Amaya, and fortified many other castles. He was often victorious over the Saracens.

He captured the city of Talamanca [Note: [Col. 1138D] Berganza has *Taramanca*; Ferreras, *Salamanca*.] in battle. After capturing its king, Mozeror, he voluntarily allowed him, together with his wife Balkaiz, to depart with their children to the sacred rock [Col. 1138B].

He likewise entered Albailda, a very strongly fortified city, by fighting; its extremely powerful king, named Muz, was found in ambush on Mount Laturcio. His army was cut down by the sword, and Muz himself [Note: [Col. 1138D] The archetype has *ipsum*, “him.”], wounded by a spear, is known to have been saved by a former friend from among our people and carried by that friend [Note: [Col. 1138D] Berganza has *amici*, “of a friend.”] on a horse to safer places.

During his time the Northmen came again to the coastal regions of Galicia and were killed by Count Peter. The Moors, arriving in ships, were defeated in the Gallican strait [Note: [Col. 1138D] Ferreras and Joannes Baptista Perez have “the strait of Cádiz” in the Cádiz manuscript.].

This ruler possessed such kindness of spirit and such usefulness in mercy, and proved so pious toward everyone, that he deserved to be called the Father of the Nations. He died peacefully at Oviedo on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the era 804 (that is, 866).

### 61. Adefonsus, his son, completed the eighteenth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 1138D] The year in which this was written was the eighteenth year of Adefonsus III, that is, A.D. 883, as is stated below at no. 74; this is also clear from the era in which his reign began, 904.].

In the first bloom of adolescence, in the first year of his reign, and in the eighteenth year of his life, he was deprived of the kingdom by the apostate Froila, count of Galicia, through tyranny. The king withdrew to Castile. Not long afterward, when the tyrant and unfortunate king Froila had been killed at Oviedo by the faithful men of our ruler, that glorious boy returned from Castile and, reigning happily from his ancestral throne, rejoiced.

From the beginning of his reign he continually enjoyed the favor of victories against his enemies. Twice he crushed and subdued the fierceness of the Basques with his army.

During his time, after a long interval, the Ishmaelite army came to León under its commander Abulmundar, son of King Abderrahman and brother of Muhammad, king of Córdoba. But when it came, it obstructed itself; for after losing many thousands, the rest of the army escaped by flight.

In those same days another army entered Vergidum and was destroyed almost to the last man; he gained many of the enemies’ strongholds. He captured the fortress of Deza. He acquired Antezana through peace. He laid waste Conimbriga, held by the enemies [Note: [Col. 1138D] Others write *Conimbriga*.], and afterward populated it with Galicians; he also subjected many other castles to himself.

### 62. During his time the Church grew and the kingdom expanded.

[Col. 1139A] The cities of Braga, Porto, Ourense [Note: [Col. 1139D] Flórez reads *Auriensis*.], Mérida, Viseu, and Lamego were also populated by Christians.

By his victory he laid waste and destroyed the Caurese, Egitanian, and other territories of Lusitania [Note: [Col. 1139D] The lesson is *caeterae* or *caeteri*.], consumed by sword and famine, as far as Mérida and the sea-straits.

After a short interval [Note: [Col. 1139D] Joannes Vazquez has “after the preceding interval.”], in the era 915, Abuhalit, the counselor of Muhammad, king of Spain, was captured in battle on the borders of Galicia and brought to our king at Oviedo. When he later ransomed himself, he gave two of his brothers, his son, and his nephew as hostages until he had paid the king 100,000 gold solidi.

### 63. In those same days, under the era 916, Almundar, son of King Muhammad, came from Córdoba with the commander Ibn Ghanim and a Saracen army to Astorga [Note: [Col. 1139D] Others write *Asturias*.] and León.

But the opposing army followed that army, consisting of men from Toledo, Talamanca, Vathlelhara [Note: [Col. 1139D] Concerning Vathlelhara, Joannes Vazquez del Marmol says: “I suspect from the letters that it is Guadalajara.”], and other castles. Thirteen thousand in all were killed by our ruler at the place called Polvoraria, near the river Urbicus [Note: [Col. 1139D] Mariana has “another army.”].

When Almundar wished to proceed to the fortress of Sublantia, he learned what had happened at Polvoraria. He also discovered that our king was already in the fortress of Sublantia with his entire army, prepared to fight him. He waited, but in fear turned back in flight before daylight.

Then, while Abuhalit was in command, there was peace between the two kings for three years.

### 64. Afterward our king, bringing war against the Saracens, moved his army and entered Spain in the era 918.

Proceeding through the province of Lusitania and plundering the castles of Nepza, he advanced, having already crossed the river Tagus [Note: [Col. 1139D] Read “the river Tagus.”] [Note: [Col. 1139D] The archetype adds *aûm*.], to the borders of Mérida. Proceeding to within ten miles of Mérida, he crossed the river Anas [Note: [Col. 1139D] The archetype writes *unum* instead of *Anam*.] and reached Mount Oxiferium, which no ruler before him had attempted to approach.

In this glorious event he also triumphed over the enemy. For more than fifteen heads are known to have been killed on that same mountain [Note: [Col. 1139D] Pellicer: “five thousand heads”; Saz: “15,000 heads.”].

Thus our ruler returned in victory to the royal seat.

[Col. 1139C] ### 65. Through this ruler all the temples of the Lord were restored.

The city at Oviedo was built together with the royal halls. He stood renowned for knowledge, gentle in face, dress, and stature.

May the Lord always incline his mind so that he may rule the people piously, so that after a long reign he may pass from the kingdom of earth to the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1139D] Up to this point is the edition of Doctor Ferreras, who passes over the entire lacuna that follows through no. 77. Here Pellicer inserts: “Likewise, the list of bishops,” the lines that appear above in the Preface, no. 11, concerning which see no. 25.].

### 66. (Continuation, year 882.)

While this aforementioned ruler was reigning, in the era 920, the aforementioned Almundar, son of King Muhammad, sent by his father with the commander Abuhalit and an army of 80,000 men, advanced from Córdoba toward Zaragoza. There Zmael Ibn Muza was stationed, hostile to the men of Córdoba.

The army surrounded Zaragoza and fought there for 25 days, but achieved no victory. From there it departed and attacked the fortress of Tudela, which Fortunio Ibn Muza held [Note: [Col. 1139D] Pellicer has *Fortun Ibn Muza*.], but accomplished nothing there.

### 67. Then Ababdella—the same man who was Muhammad Ibn Lupi [Note: [Col. 1139D] Pellicer: “Ababdella, who was Muhammad Ibn-Lupi.” Marmol: “Ababdella himself, who was Muhammad Ibn-iuph.” [Col. 1140D] Saz: *Iben Lup*. The reading *ipse qui* is more suitable than *ipseque*, as in no. 71, where Ababdella is called the son of Lupi, that is, Ibn Lub. (*Iben* is Arabic for “son” in Latin.) Ababdella therefore was the same man as Muhammad Ibn Lup. The event narrated is likewise the same in both places. In the archetype, *Luph*.], who had always been our friend, as had his father—

Out of jealousy concerning his uncles [Note: [Col. 1140D] Pellicer, Berganza, and Saz have “his uncles”; Marmol and Mariana, as in the text. The Greek *theios* means the same as Spanish *tío* and Latin *patruus*.], to whom the king had given his son Ordonius to raise, he made peace with the men of Córdoba and sent his own forces against their enemies [Note: [Col. 1140D] Saz has *fortiaque*. Without hesitation I read *fortiam* with the others; it is a word of late Latin meaning “forces” or “army.”].

Thus, when the enemies of the Chaldeans entered the borders of our kingdom, they first fought at the fortress of Cellorigo and accomplished nothing, but lost many of their men there.

### 68. Vigila Scemeniz was then count in Álava.

That same army, coming to the farthest parts of Castile, fought for three days against the fortress called Pontecurvo. It achieved no victory but lost many of its men to the avenging sword.

### 69. Didacus, son of Rudericus, was count in Castile.

Because of the arrival of the Saracens, Munio, son of Nunnius, abandoned the fortress of Sigeric as a wilderness, since it was not yet strongly fortified [Col. 1140B].

### 70. Our king was awaiting that army in the city of León, strongly protected by a military force, so that he might fight them lawfully at the city’s suburb.

But when that army learned that our king daily, with eager spirit, wished to chastise it as it approached the city, it went beyond the river Esla at the urging of Abuhalit, who had already seen the royal men fifteen miles from the city [Note: [Col. 1140D] Pellicer has: “desired to correct him as he approached from the city.” From the combined readings one should read: “desired to correct him as he approached the city.”].

It burned fortified castles and sent messengers from the field of Alcoba to the river Urbicus to our king, asking him to receive his son Abulcazem, whom the king was still holding.

He likewise sent to our king Abohalit the son of Zmael Ibn Muza, whom they had brought from Córdoba to his father for the sake of peace, and also Furtun Ibn Alazela, whom they had captured in the fortress of Tudela [Note: [Col. 1140D] Others have “the fortress of Tudela.”].

Thus, by asking for many gifts, he recovered his son [Note: [Col. 1140D] Manuscript: “he had recovered”; Pellicer: “he recovered”; I read “he recovers.”], and made a road over the river Urbicus as far as Zela [Note: [Col. 1140D] See *Zeia* below, no. 75]. Thus he then returned to Córdoba.

They returned to Córdoba in September, from which they had departed in March. Afterward our king gave the men of Benikazi, whom he had received from Abuhalit in exchange for his son, to his own friends without payment.

### 71. The aforementioned Ababdella, son of Jub [Note: [Col. 1140D] Marmol has *Iuph*; in the archetype, *Luph*.], because of his friendship with the men of Córdoba, turned against his own uncles and cousins in hatred, and a dispute arose between them in which they fought.

That winter, because of the defiance of that same Ababdella, his uncle Zmael and his cousin, that same Zmael Ibn Furtun, moved an army of about 7,000 men against him, wishing to engage Ababdella in battle.

Ababdella also awaited or expected them in rugged terrain. Thus, when the two Zmaels came, led by recklessness [Note: [Col. 1140D] Pellicer has “recklessness”; others have “gentleness.”], they climbed the very rugged mountain where they had learned that he was, with only a few men and servants [Col. 1140D] [Note: [Col. 1140D] Mariana and Pellicer have “servants”; others have “torch-bearers.”].

Ababdella, rushing upon them at a headlong pace [Col. 1141A], caused them to flee [Note: [Col. 1141D] In the archetype: “they took flight,” and so forth.]. There Zmael Ibn Furtun fell from his horse and was immediately captured.

Likewise Zmael Ibn Muza, when he wished to rescue his nephew, was captured there. Many of the leading men of Benikazi were also captured there.

The rest of the army, remaining on the plain, escaped by flight.

### 72.

After achieving victory, Ababdella sent those whom he had captured to his own fortress of Beccaria, bound in chains. He himself then advanced and came to Zaragoza, which he captured without a sword, under the pretext of peace, and subjected to his own authority. Immediately he sent messengers to Córdoba, as though he had done all this for the king’s favor and had thereby shown himself faithful in everything. But when the king of Córdoba demanded the city itself and the men whom Ababdella had captured, and Ababdella in no way consented, the people of Córdoba were soon stirred to anger; and these men were thereby brought into agreement with one another. Then Ababdella released a relative [the reading *tium* is corrupt or incomplete], and received from him the fortress of Valterra in return; likewise he released his cousin and, in exchange, received from him Tudela and the fortress of San Esteban; and Zaragoza, just as he had captured it, he both held and continues to hold.

### 73.

In those same days Ababdella endured many attacks and battles from the counts of Castile and Álava, Diego and Vigila. When he saw that he was being very severely oppressed by them, he immediately sent envoys to our king seeking peace, and he sends them repeatedly; but up to the present he has by no means received a firm peace from the prince [Note: In the archetype, *firmen* (“they may make firm”).]. Nevertheless, he persists in our friendship and would wish to persist in it [Note: In the archetype, *velit si rex* (“if only the king would wish it”).]; but our king still does not agree to this.

### 74.

Afterward, in the year 921 of the era, which is the present year, the aforementioned Almundar, son of King Mahomat, was sent by his father, together with the commander Abohalit and the entire army of Spain, toward Zaragoza. When he arrived there, he found Ababdella inside. He fought there for only two days; he plundered the fields and orchards, and did likewise not only around Zaragoza but throughout the whole land of the Banu Qasi. He entered part of Deio [Note: See Moret, *Invest.*, p. 532, and below, n. 87. Deio or Degio is today Monjardín, formerly San Esteban de Deyo. See Moret, cited work.] and plundered it; but he captured neither cities nor fortresses, but had already ravaged it [Note: Mariana: *sed ea* (“but that one”); Moret, *Invest.*, p. 532: *sed eam populavit* (“but he ravaged it”). See below, n. 87. Flórez adds this from a manuscript.].

Afterward that same army entered the borders of our kingdom and first fought against the fortress of Cellorigo, leaving many of its own men dead there. Count Vigila was defending the fortress.

### 75.

Then he reached the borders of Castile at the bridge of Castro Curbo, and there began to fight at his own initiative; but on the third day he was thoroughly defeated and withdrew from there. Count Diego was in command. Next he found the castle of Sigeric fortified, but accomplished nothing there, and in August approached the borders of León.

When he heard that our king was in that same city, and learned that it had already been decided to fight them at the fortress of Sublantio, he moved away by night from the river Cea [Note: In the archetype, *Zeiae*; Berganza has *Ceia*, while Juan Vázquez writes *Zeiam* below.]. At daybreak he reached that fortress before our army had proceeded there; but he found nothing in the fortress except empty houses.

On the following day, however, our king hoped that they would eagerly come to the city to fight. Yet the enemy not only failed to come to León, but did not take the route of the preceding year at all, nor did they cross the river Esla. Instead, they returned again through the fortress of Coyanza toward the Cea, and demolished the church of Saints Facundus and Primitivus down to its foundations. Thus, turning back, they entered Spain through the pass called Balatcomalti.

While Abuhalit was in the territory of León, he sent many messages concerning peace to our king. For this reason our king also sent an envoy named Dulcidius [Note: Pellicer and Berganza print *Dulcidium*; the Oviedo Breviary, in its account of the translation of the body of Saint Eulogius, likewise names him *Dulcidium*. In the archetype: *Dulcium*.], a presbyter of the city of Toledo, with letters to the king of Córdoba in September. He has still not returned, although November is now passing.

### 76.

The aforementioned Ababdella likewise does not cease sending envoys, repeatedly seeking peace and the favor of our king; but as yet it will be fulfilled [Note: Perhaps, “for this reason.”] according to what pleases the Lord [Note: Thus the Albeldensis manuscript, Mariana, and Berganza. Others read *est* (“it is”). Nicolás Antonio, book VI, no. 254, emends the passage to *sed adhuc non perfectum est* (“but it has not yet been completed”), which does not fit well with the supplicatory words that follow concerning what may please the Lord.].

## Thus is the entry of the Saracens into Spain.

### 77.

As we have already related above: while Roderic was reigning and the Goths were in Spain, a division arose among the Goths through the sons of King Witiza, so that one party of them desired to see the kingdom destroyed. With their support and agreement, the Saracens entered Spain in the third year of Roderic’s reign, on the third day before the Ides of November, in the era 752 [Note: The archetype has *aera 752* written in the margin.], while in Africa Ulit, son of Abdelmelic, was ruling as Commander of the Believers, in the one hundredth year of the Arabs [Note: Berganza and others read: “in the one hundredth year of the Arabs he entered”; the archetype likewise. Ferreras reads as in the text, from which the true reading may be sought: namely, “he entered in the ninety-first year of the Arabs,” for that ninety-first year accords with Arabic chronology.]. Abzuhura [Note: The Pacensis manuscript has *Abuzara*.] first entered Spain under the command of Muza, who was residing in Africa [Note: Ferreras has *commorante* (“dwelling”).] and subduing the homelands of the Moors [Note: Berganza has *de faecente*, perhaps for *defendente* (“defending”).].

### 78.

In the following year Tarik entered. In the third year, while that same Tarik was already fighting Roderic, Muza ibn Nusayr entered, and the kingdom of the Goths perished; and then all the glory of the Gothic people perished through fear or the sword.

Concerning that same King Roderic, the cause of his death remains known to no one to the present day.

These are the Arab commanders who reigned in Spain [Note: Juan Vázquez copied this in the margin. It is absent from Berganza and Saz. It is found in Ferreras.].

### 79.

The aforementioned Muza ibn Nusayr entered Spain and reigned one year and three months.

Abdelaziz ibn Muza reigned two years and six months.  
Ayyub reigned one month.  
Al-Hurr reigned two years and ten months.  
Zama reigned three years.  
Abd al-Rahman reigned one year.  
Hodera reigned one year.  
Yahya reigned one year and six months.  
Hodifa reigned six months.  
Autuman reigned four months.  
Geleitam reigned ten months.  
Abdelmelic reigned two years.  
Aucuba reigned four years and five months.  
Abdelmelic, a second time, reigned one year and one month.  
Abulhatar ibn Dimar reigned two years.  
Tauba reigned one year and two months [Note: The archetype has “twelve.”].

In all, twenty-seven years and twelve months [Note: Berganza: twenty-three years and twelve months. Saz: twenty-seven years; read “within one year,” as below. Yet from the calculation of the individual years and months only a total of twenty-five years and four months results. From Isidore of Beja, however, more than thirty-four years are obtained.].

These commanders held their authority for a short time [Note: The manuscript has “a short timespan.”], because one succeeded another, according to what had been appointed by the Commander of the Believers. Some, however, were brought to an end by death, until the Banu Umayya came to Spain.

These, then, are the kings of Córdoba descended from the house of the Umayyads.

### 80.

Yusuf reigned eleven years.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Muawiya reigned thirty-three years.

Hisham reigned seven years and six months.

Al-Hakam reigned twenty-six years and six months.

Abd al-Rahman reigned thirty-two years and six months. During his reign Ordoño, prince of the Christians in Spain, won many victories.

Mahomat is completing the thirty-second year of his reign [Note: Since Mahomat began in 852, the author, writing in 883, correctly counts the thirty-second year of his reign.]. In his time Abuhalit, commander of his army, as we have already stated above in the sequence of our kings, was captured in the borders of Galicia and brought before our lord King Alfonso of Oviedo. Many victories were won by the Christians in Spain [Note: In the archetype, *finiunt* (“end”).].

In total, the years of the Arabs in Spain amount to 179 [Note: The count begins with the year 714, corresponding to era 752, stated above in section 77.], and on the third day before the Ides of November they begin their 170th year; from the preaching of the most wicked Mahomet in Africa there are 270 years [Note: It would be better to say 161, namely, counting from the year 622, when the persecution began against that most wicked man.], in the era now running, 921.

### 81.

Added in the margin: From the time when the Saracens entered Spain until the present era, 1014, there are 262 years. From the time of the most wicked prophet Mahomet until the present era, 1014, there are 363 years.

## Likewise, the origin of the Saracens, as they themselves believe.

### 82.

The perverse Saracens think that they are descended from Sarah; more correctly, they are Hagarenes, from Hagar, and Ishmaelites, from Ishmael.

Abraham begot Ishmael by Hagar. Ishmael begot Kaldar; Kaldar begot Nepti; Nepti begot Alhumesca; Alhumesca begot Eldano; Eldano begot Muncher; Muncher begot Excib; Excib begot Jaman; Jaman begot Autith; Autith begot Atinan; Atinan begot Mahat; Mahat begot Nizar; Nizar begot Muldar; Muldar begot Hindaf; Hindaf begot Mutirik; Mutirik begot Humeia; Humeia begot Kinana; Kinana begot Melik; Melik begot Fehir; Fehir begot Galib; Galib begot Juhei; Juhei begot Murra; Murra begot Kelib; Kelib begot Cutzei; Cutzei begot Abdilmelef; Abdilmelef begot two sons, Escim and Abdiscemiz.

Abdiscemiz and Escim were brothers. Escim begot Abdelmutalib; Abdelmutalib begot Abdella; Abdella begot Mahomat, whom his own people believe to be a prophet.

Abdiscemiz, the brother of Escim, begot Humeia; Humeia begot Abilaz; Abilaz begot Accam. Accam begot Maroan; Maroan begot Abdelmelic; Abdelmelic begot Iscem; Iscem begot Mavia; Mavia begot Abderrhaman; Abderrhaman begot Iscem; Iscem begot Haccam; Haccam begot Abderrhaman; Abderrhaman begot Mahomat; Mahomat begot Almundar.

### 83.

This Mahomat reigned in the aforementioned era 901 [Note: In the archetype, 821.] and fought against the king of Oviedo, named Alfonso. Thereafter, may divine clemency, without distinction [Note: “Without distinction,” that is, “without delay.”], expel the aforesaid Ishmaelites across the sea from our provinces, omitting and never again adding their names; and may it grant their kingdom forever to be possessed by the faithful of Christ. Amen.

## Likewise, an explanation of the Gothic people.

### 84.

The Gothic people descend from Gog. Just as, for the whole race of the Ishmaelites, only Ishmael is written below when the prophet says, “Set your face against Ishmael,” so Gog is named for the whole Gothic people, from whose origin they come. From this they also derived their name.

And because the Gothic people came from Magog, the *Chronicle of the Goths* of the blessed Isidore confirms this when it says: “They are the most ancient people of the Goths, whose origin descends from Magog, the son of Japheth; hence they are also named from the likeness of the final syllable, that is, Gog,” drawing this conclusion especially from the prophet Ezekiel.

The Book of Genealogies likewise affirms that the Goths come from Magog, the son of Japheth, and that Gothia and Scia [Note: Probably *Scythia*.] were named after Magog.

### 85.

Likewise, that the Saracens were destined to possess the land of the Goths, we find stated in the book of the prophecy [Note: Probably *vaticinii*, “prophecy.”] of the prophet Ezekiel:

“You, son of man, set your face against Ishmael and speak to them, saying: ‘I have given you as the strongest among the nations; I have multiplied you, strengthened you, and placed a sword in your right hand and arrows in your left, so that you may crush the nations and they may be laid low before your face, like straw before the face of fire. You shall enter the land of Gog with level foot; you shall cut down Gog with your sword, set your foot upon his neck, and make his people tributary servants.’” [Note: In the archetype: “and in his left hand,” and so forth.]

### 86.

We recognize that this has now been fulfilled. The land of Gog signifies Spain under the rule of the Goths; into it the Ishmaelites entered because of the sins of the Gothic people, cut them down with the sword, and made them tributary to themselves, as is evident at the present time.

But when that same prophet again says to Ishmael: “Because you abandoned the Lord, I too shall abandon you and deliver you into the hand of Gog, and he shall repay you after you have afflicted them. They will do to you for 270 periods what you did to him,” our hope is in Christ: when the 270 years have been completed—the period since they entered Spain—may the enemies be reduced to nothing and may the peace of Christ be restored to the holy Church, since “periods” are used for “years.”

May almighty God bring this about, so that, as the courage of the enemies repeatedly fails, the Church of the Catholics may always grow for the better. Amen.

[Note: Without a title, though with an intervening blank space, the following appears in the Albeldensis codex: “In the era 943,” and so forth.]

## Addition concerning the kings of Pamplona

### 87.

In the era 913, a king named Sancho Garcés arose in Pamplona. He was inseparably devoted and most reverent toward the faith of Christ, kind toward all the faithful, and merciful toward oppressed Catholics. What more need be said? In all his works he remained outstanding.

He was a warrior against the peoples of the Ishmaelites and inflicted many kinds of slaughter upon the lands [Note: The archetype lacks “lands.”] of the Saracens. Through Cantabria he captured all the fortresses from the city of Nájera to Tudela. He possessed the whole land of Deio, together with its towns [Note: See n. 74.]. He subjected Arba [Note: Perhaps “the city.”] of Pamplona to his authority; likewise, together with its fortresses, he captured the whole territory of Aragon.

After expelling all the Banu Qasi, he departed this life in the twentieth year of his reign. Buried in the portico of Saint Stephen, he reigns with Christ in heaven.

Likewise, his son García was king and reigned ten years. He was benevolent and won many battles against the Saracens, and thus died. He was buried in the fortress of Saint Stephen.

His sons remain in their father’s homeland, namely Sancho and his brother Ramiro. May the Almighty preserve them through many courses of years. Amen.

## In the present era, 1014.

# SIGLOARD, CANON OF RHEIMS: RHYTHM ON THE DEATH OF FULCO, BISHOP OF RHEIMS

(From Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, from the Igny codex, which contains Flodoard’s *Breviary* in two books. After Fulco’s epitaph, book IV, chapter 8.)

O Fulco, excellent bishop,

O most beloved by all,

A pontiff in office and in name!

A man, yet greater than man,

A noble man by lineage,

And of such wisdom

As no one possesses today.

Beautiful in your whole body,

And of great eloquence,

At your funeral weeping,

We can scarcely restrain ourselves.

May Christ grant you rest

And an everlasting crown.

But we shall mourn you

By days and by nights:

For you loved us truly

And treated us gently,

Adorned the Church,

Governed your household

Through the highest grace of God,

And ruled your homeland well.

But a slippery serpent,

Not a father but a stepfather,

Laying ambushes for you,

Increased our injuries.

May he, accursed by the Lord,

Be punished in the abyss.

With sword and clubs,

And armed soldiers,

Guinemar attacked you,

Sweet to no one, but bitter,

Although you had taken nothing from him,

And had committed no wrong against him.

On the day when he betrayed you,

He destroyed both you and himself.

As soon as the clergy heard

Of such an evil, they trembled.

The people and the clergy alike groaned;

They rushed there and carried away

The body with them,

And shed many tears

While celebrating the funeral rites.

Having been carried into the church,

He stood upright before the altars.

The abbots and bishops,

Clothed in their vestments,

Supported him.

They put the mitre on him,

And the pallium and tunic;

The stole was placed around his neck,

And a candle was lit.

Nor was the staff absent there;

It was placed in his hands.

Then the dean of the bishops

Commands and begs the people

That all should pray to the Lord

For the soul of the pontiff,

So that he may not be plunged into the underworld,

But may rejoice among those above,

And that they should offer God a sacrifice

To cleanse his soul.

Then all beseech God

And pray with tears.

Each bishop and presbyter

Holds a candle.

They excommunicate the tyrant,

And inflict death upon him while he lives,

And upon the whole company of soldiers

Who gave him assistance.

After this they carry out the dead man

And bury him honorably.

Before his tomb

They commend his spirit to God.

May his soul be at rest

Now and through all ages.

Amen, amen; may it be so:

Let the whole Church say it.

# GOSBERT’S ACROSTIC POEM TO WILLIAM, COUNT OF BLOIS

(*Ansberti Familia rediviva*, by M. Antonius Dominici; Paris, 1648.)

## To William, Count of Blois

Gosbert played in verse for Count William.

May the Saviour crown you, William, through the virtue of the Cross,

He who gave you an excellent family line,

And a blossoming appearance of countenance, lovable to behold,

A firm natural ability for the government of equitable rule,

The strength of a ruler, a power remarkable in form.

So many gifts shine upon you through the grace of the fathers

That no one can attempt to conceal your achievements,

You whom the first-born of Trojan lineage applaud as prince,

And whom the fathers of the Church rightly honour with these distinctions.

The learned, with pious heart, tread upon these things here

With very sweet matters in which trust must be placed,

Whenever they are struck by blows;

They truly regard it as a living gain to weep more in prayer,

To be pierced by holy tears, rather than to be counted there

Among the games of the devil in the mourning of Stygian death.

Thus, thus you add yourself to the simple,

Thus to the prudent.

Among monks also there are sacred duties of praise belonging to you,

So that the whole crowd together may sing and sound forth your praise.

May the Saviour crown you, William, through the virtue of the Cross.

Come, prince of your heart, open your inner being to yourself:

The wealth of kingdoms is certainly shown to surpass it.

For the glory of the mind, loving Gog, also weighs Magog,

As the outstanding Paul teaches—an excellent thing to say.

Indeed, the pious Lord Jesus teaches us from here to seek joys,

Brighter than usual light, as the almighty Sun admonishes.

The fruit of joy, and the unique treasure of exalted wealth,

Is enduring life, the highest blessedness of life.

This light, I say, shines before you, O good consul,

May the power of the death-bringing one flee the proud and ever-hostile enemy,

And stand high beside your virtues.

When, however, having completed your age, you depart from here,

May the excellently composed *doxa* inscribe [you] in the white [book],

O King whose banners you carry bravely in battle,

Now glorified by him through the duties of your works.

Now the people of life, now, now your venerable name—

Let us sing this clearly with rejoicing from the heart:

May the Saviour crown you, William, through the virtue of the Cross.

For William, of the French, first from forefathers and ancestors of lofty descent,

Dinami and Sophia, adorned with lineage,

Gosbert—*tapeinos*, *mikros*, *apodēmos*—humble, small, and an exile.

# PSEUDO-LIUTPRAND’S BOOK ON THE LIVES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS

## PREFACE

(From the Mainz edition of 1602.)

This year, 1602, at the spring fair, there appeared from the Mainz press a history of the lives of 109 Roman pontiffs by the very ancient writer Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church; it was illustrated with various readings from manuscript codices. Now, since through the kindness of certain distinguished men we have obtained another work on the same subject, equally ancient and hitherto never printed, we thought we would perform a worthwhile service by adding it to the work of Anastasius.

We have inscribed it to Liutprand of Pavia, a deacon who flourished around the year of the Lord 950, according to John Trithemius—not because the manuscript codex from which we transcribed it identifies its author (for we found no name written in it), nor because firm and solid grounds support this attribution, but because not a few people have consistently attributed it to Liutprand as its genuine author. Let them determine for themselves what weight of argument led them to do so.

For our part, we strongly suspect, first, that the earliest historians used no manuscript copy other than this very parchment codex from which we transcribed the present history. Second, we suspect that they were persuaded to name Liutprand by no other argument than the undeniable fact that the final life in this history, that of the Roman pontiff Formosus, is wholly contained in Liutprand’s own words, preserved in chapter eight of the first book of his history of events in Europe, of which Liutprand of Pavia is acknowledged to be the author.

This argument, however, seems to weaken rather than establish their opinion. Since it is clear that the whole narrative concerning Formosus was copied word for word from the book of Liutprand just mentioned, including the words “Most holy Father,” which plainly reveal theft and deception, there can be no doubt that, after the words “Formosus, bishop of Porto, sat for five years and six months,” some ignorant person stitched on the rest of the narrative.

Liutprand used the words “Most holy Father” in that history of events in Europe because he had written it for Regimundus, bishop of the Church of Lérida in Spain. It is clear, however, that this history of the pontiffs was not inscribed or dedicated to any bishop or to any other most holy father.

Furthermore, neither Sigebert, nor Trithemius, nor Gesner attributes any book of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs to Liutprand. Moreover, Trithemius writes that Liutprand—although he calls him Eutrand—flourished around the year of the Lord 950, under the emperor Otto I. And rightly so, since he brought his European history down to Otto.

But Formosus, with whom our history ends, died in the year 895. From that year until the aforementioned 950, about twenty Roman pontiffs are counted, yet the present history of the pontiffs contains not a word about them.

In addition, certain particulars are mentioned in the final lives of this little work, which seem to have come only from someone who flourished in the time of Formosus and his predecessors—or rather, from someone who lived in Westphalia or Saxony, perhaps in the monasteries of Corvey, Hersfeld, or Fulda, which at that time were flourishing.

For, in the life of Hadrian I, it relates that Charlemagne vowed to God in the basilica of Saint Peter at Rome that he would establish a bishopric at Osnabrück in the province of Westphalia, which he had recently converted to the faith of Christ; and he did so, as Albert Krantz records in book I of the *Metropolis*, chapter 11, and book II of the *Saxonia*, chapter 11.

Then, in the life of Hadrian II, it says that the emperor Louis—namely Louis II, son of the emperor Lothair—gave to the churches of Corvey and Herford certain tithe-paying churches, together with their tithes, established in the parish of Osnabrück, with the consent of the bishop and the entire clergy.

It also says that Charles, emperor of the Romans, gave certain tithes in Frisonevelt and Hassega, adjacent to the diocese of Halberstadt, to the church of Hersfeld, honoured by the emperor and destined to be honoured by God. Pope Stephen IV, called III, confirmed these tithes in the basilica of Saint Peter on Holy Easter Day, by his own authority, with the emperor’s subscription and in the presence of Hildegrin, bishop of Halberstadt.

Furthermore, in the life of Stephen VI it states that Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, and Hadalgar, archbishop of Hamburg, disputing over the Church of Bremen, were ordered by the supreme pontiff to come to Worms, and there the pope entrusted Fulco, bishop of Rheims, with acting on his behalf in examining their case. Krantz treats this matter carefully in book II of the *Metropolis*, chapters 19, 20, and 24; Albert of Stade mentions it in his *Chronicle* under the year 896, as does Trithemius in his *Hirsau Chronicle*.

Finally, in the lives of the later pontiffs, especially Paschal, Benedict III, Nicholas I, Hadrian II, and John VIII, it quotes at length many of their decrees that do not appear in the volumes of the Councils, although nearly all those attributed here to the earlier pontiffs do appear there.

In the life of Leo IV, it transcribes forty-two chapters from a Roman synod convened with the counsel of the emperors Lothair and Louis; these too receive no mention in the said volumes.

From this one may make the quite evident conjecture that the author of this little work flourished especially in the time of the later pontiffs, that is, around the year of the Lord 860, and not around 950, the time of Liutprand; and that the author was not Italian but German, living in the monastery of Corvey—some men from which were raised to the bishopric of Osnabrück in that century—or in the monastery of Hersfeld.

What if the author was Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corvey, whom Trithemius asserts flourished in the time of Charles the Fat? For Charles the Fat ruled under John VIII, Marinus, Hadrian III, and Stephen VI, with whom this history concludes.

Finally, as for the work we have undertaken in editing this little book, we have nothing else to tell you, dear reader, except that we carefully compared the decrees of the supreme pontiffs cited throughout these lives of the pontiffs with their source—that is, with the decrees preserved in the volumes of the Councils—and that we have noted both variant readings in the margin whenever they occurred and the chapters of Gratian’s *Decretum*.

We have no doubt that this work of ours will be very pleasing to all students of theology. Farewell.

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK

## I. SAINT PETER THE APOSTLE  
*(In the year of Christ 45.)*

Blessed Peter the apostle, prince of the apostles, an Antiochene, son of John, from the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of Andrew, first sat in the episcopal chair at Antioch for seven years.

Afterward, in order to overthrow Simon Magus, as Jerome says (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Peter”), he entered Rome in the second year of Claudius and sat in the episcopal chair for twenty-five years, two months, and three days.

At one and the same time and on the same day—namely, after the Lord’s Passion in the year 38, but in the final year of Nero III, on the Kalends of July—he completed his martyrdom together with Paul.

He wrote two Epistles, which are called Catholic. In the first of them he initially instructs the Church in general, explaining the benefits by which divine goodness calls us to salvation, or the gifts by which it once deigned to honour the Jews but now honours us.

Afterward he earnestly exhorts the various classes of the faithful not to make themselves unworthy, by living according to the flesh, of so great a grace of the Spirit; and not to degenerate through the wickedness of their vices from the glory of the nobility granted or promised to them, since they have been marked with the royal and priestly title.

First he addresses free persons and slaves, then women and men in particular; and after a general exchange of exhortation, he shows how elders and young men ought to conduct themselves.

In the second Epistle, which he wrote to the same people as the first, he pities them and, as though they were now more perfect, repeatedly admonishes and exhorts them to greater and more perfect things.

He is also said to have composed the Gospel of Mark, because Mark was his assistant and his son through baptism.

He ordained three bishops—Linus, Cletus, and Clement—and ten presbyters and seven deacons.

## II. SAINT LINUS  
*(In the year of Christ 69.)*

Linus, an Italian by nationality, from the region of Tuscany, son of Herculanus, sat for eleven years, three months, and twelve days.

He lived during the time of Nero, from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio until that of Capito and Rufus. Under these consuls he was crowned with martyrdom on the ninth day before the Kalends of October.

At the command of blessed Peter, he established that women should enter the church with veiled heads.

He ordained fifteen bishops and eighteen presbyters.

## III. SAINT CLETUS  
*(In the year of Christ 81.)*

Cletus, a Roman by nationality, from the district of the Patrician Village, son of Aemilianus, sat for twelve years, one month, and eleven days.

He lived during the time of Vespasian and Titus, from the seventh consulship of Vespasian and the fifth of Domitian until the ninth consulship of Domitian and that of Rufus. Under these consuls he was crowned with martyrdom on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

At the command of blessed Peter he ordained twenty-five presbyters in Rome.

Note that these two men, Linus and Cletus, did nothing pontifical except at the command of blessed Peter; hence it is clear that they were his assistants, not his successors.

## IV. SAINT CLEMENT  
*(In the year of Christ 93.)*

Clement, a Roman by nationality, from the district of the Caelian Hill, son of Faustinus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days.

He lived during the time of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Tragalis and Italicus until the ninth consulship of Vespasian and that of Titus [Note: Baronius, volume I, year 69, responds to this.].

Although he appears third in the order of the catalogue after blessed Peter, in reality, as he himself wrote in his letter to James, bishop of Jerusalem, he unquestionably held the governance of the Roman see immediately after blessed Peter, with no one intervening. Linus and Cletus, however, are counted as Peter’s successors because he made them his assistants during his lifetime, so that he himself might devote himself more fully to prayer.

Pope John III clearly confirms this understanding of the truth in a letter he wrote to bishops established in the provinces of Germany and Gaul, saying among other things:

“If Peter, prince of the apostles, took Linus and Cletus as his assistants, he did not nevertheless hand over to them the power of the pontificate or the rule of binding and loosing. Rather, he handed these to his successor Clement, who deserved to hold the apostolic see after him, together with pontifical power, because blessed Peter entrusted it to him. Linus and Cletus administered external affairs; but Peter, prince of the apostles, devoted himself to the word and to prayer.”

Likewise, a little farther below in the same letter, Pope John adds concerning these men:

“For Linus and Cletus are nowhere read to have exercised anything from the pontifical ministry with authority; they did only what blessed Peter commanded them.”

While writing many books out of zeal for the Christian religion, Clement was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan, in the third year of his reign, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.

He carefully and diligently ordered that the deeds of the martyrs be investigated and written down.

He wrote two Epistles to James, bishop of Jerusalem, which are called Catholic. He wrote the first of them to him at the command of blessed Peter. In it, at Peter’s instruction, he tells James how the prince of the apostles, sensing that the end of his life was approaching, ordained Clement as pontiff in the assembly of the Roman see, appointed him as his successor, and handed over to him the power of binding and loosing that had been entrusted to Peter by the Lord.

Thus, whatever he should decree on earth concerning these matters would also be decreed in heaven.

He immediately added why he had given him such great power:

“For he will bind what ought to be bound and loose what should be loosed, as one who knows the rule of the Church with complete clarity.”

In this, I do not doubt that the following must be noted: if any bishop ignorant of ecclesiastical rule, or driven by any agitation of anger or desire, binds or looses on earth otherwise than he ought, his action will be void in heaven.

He also relates in the same Epistle that the prince of the apostles admonished him before everyone concerning how he ought to preserve the order of ecclesiastical administration, both in himself and in the others subject to him.

He was to live irreproachably and not be found entangled in the occupation of worldly business, because no bishop is appointed as judge or examiner of secular affairs, lest, stifled by the cares of the present world, he be unable to devote himself to the word of God and to distinguish the good from the evil according to the rule of truth.

For a little farther below the same prince of the apostles says to all bishops in the person of Clement:

“If you are occupied with worldly cares, you will deceive both yourself and those who listen to you. You will not be able to distinguish fully for each person the things that pertain to salvation. As a result, you will be deposed as though you had not taught those things that pertain to human salvation, and the disciples will perish through ignorance.”

Likewise, he reports that the same prince of the apostles taught the following concerning bishops:

“He who presides over others ought to act in the place of a physician and not be moved by the rage of a wild beast.”

In the same way he instructed the same Clement:

“If many of the brethren hate you because of the strictness of justice, you will not be harmed by this; rather, through such hatred the love of God is won for you. Therefore strive all the more and avoid being praised by the wicked or loved by those who act most wickedly. Instead, because of your administration of justice and the most equitable rule of discipline, may you deserve to be praised by Christ.”

But he instructed that priests should conduct themselves as follows (32, q. 7, c. *Quid in omnibus*): above all, they should strive to preserve chastity both in themselves and in their subjects, and should beware and forestall any hidden fire of adultery from growing within them. For he says that among all sins nothing is more serious than adultery [Note: [Col. 1153] “Among sins directed against one’s neighbor generally, none is more serious.” D. THOMAS, *Summa theologiae* II–II, q. 73, art. 3. AUGUSTIN BARBOSA, *Collectanea* on the same chapter, *Quid in omnibus*.]. He testifies that it occupies second place among punishments, since first place belongs to those who stray from God, even if they have lived soberly. He calls the first form of adultery this: that a man is not content with his own wife, and that a woman does not preserve herself exclusively for her own husband.

He also commands that, if they have business dealings with one another, they should not be judged before secular authorities, but that whatever dispute exists between them should be settled before priests. He taught that it is the duty of deacons diligently to investigate all the activities of the Church and to consider them carefully, so that, if they see anyone approaching a precipice and near to sin, they may report him to the bishop, in order that the person who is about to fall into the precipice may be warned and recalled by him, so that he does not fall into sin (Dist. 93, c. *Diaconi*). Likewise, they should admonish and encourage the negligent and sluggish to attend the bishop’s instruction concerning the word of God. Similarly, they should carefully seek out those who are sick in body and report them to the people, so that the people themselves may visit them and provide what is necessary for them. He established that the deacons should be responsible for all such matters as pertain to the worship and discipline of the Church.

He established that the laity should render the following service to bishops: by faithfully attending to matters concerning the ordinary conduct of common life, they should all work together to relieve the bishop of everything from which he ought to be free. He also said that all who live under the care of bishops must exercise the necessary vigilance: they should withdraw themselves from the friendship, conversation, and every form of association of all those whom they see to be hostile to the bishop on account of their actions, and they should not wait for the bishop to tell them this. For if anyone is a friend of those with whom the bishop does not speak, he is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God; and he is a more wicked enemy than those who are outside and openly hostile, because through the appearance of friendships he carries on what is hostile, and he disperses and devastates the Church.

Likewise, in the same epistle he informs James (6, q. 1, c. *B. Petr.*) how the prince of the apostles, passing through each city, instructed all the faithful in the word of God. Among other things, he relates that Peter forbade murderers, adulterers, and all who were bound by the chains of crimes, as well as those who were not their equals, to harass or accuse bishops. He also asserted that superiors could in no way be accused or judged by inferiors. He further commanded that no priest should do anything in the parish of any bishop without that bishop’s permission, but that all priests should obey their own bishops in everything without delay.

The same prince of the apostles also commanded in his sermon that all rulers of the earth and all human beings should obey bishops, bow their heads before them, and submit themselves to them. If the bishops themselves should act otherwise—God forbid—than they ought, they are not to be reproved or rebuked by their subjects, but borne with, unless they have erred in the faith (2, q. 7, c. *Sacerdotes*). He showed that all who contradict bishops are infamous and commanded that, unless they repented, they should be excluded from the thresholds of the Church [Col. 1155A] (11, q. 3, c. *Si autem*).

But so that bishops would not become proud on this account, they should consider what he says about them. He taught that the life of all priests must be superior, holier, and distinct from that of secular and lay persons; that spiritual persons must always be placed above carnal persons, and priests above the laity. He prohibited carnal persons from resisting spiritual persons. He strictly prohibited drunkenness, because he proclaimed that drunkards are dead in body and soul.

He said that there are three kinds of murderers (On Penance, Dist. 1), and taught that their punishment would be equal. Thus he clearly showed that those who slander their brothers and those who hate them are murderers, just as are those who kill them: for the one who kills, the one who hates his brother, and the one who slanders are shown alike to be murderers (1 John 3).

[Col. 1155B] In the second epistle, which he wrote to the aforementioned James, bishop of Jerusalem, he instructs him in order concerning the sacraments celebrated among holy things, as he had been taught by the prince of the apostles. For he says that the sacraments of the divine mysteries have been entrusted to three ranks: the priest, the deacon, and the subdeacon (On Consecration, Dist. 2, c. *Tribus*). He indicates that these men must guard the remnants of the Lord’s body with fear and trembling.

On the altar, he commands that as many offerings be made as seem sufficient for the people. If anything remains from them, it must not be kept until the next day, but must be consumed with fear and trembling through the diligence of the clergy. Those who consume what remains of the Lord’s body and blood must not immediately approach ordinary food. If they received it in the morning, they should fast until the sixth hour; and if they received it at the third or fourth hour, they should fast until evening.

The altar cloths (On Consecration, Dist. 1, c. *Altaris palla*), the veil, and the other things kept in the sanctuary, if worn out by age, must be given to the fire; their ashes, however, must be deposited in such a way that they are not polluted by the feet of those entering.

He instructs that ministers of the altar should be chosen who have left their wives before ordination. If, however, after ordination a minister enters his wife’s bed, he is to lose the office of minister (17, q. 4, c. *Si forte*). Likewise, if a priest or deacon steals and sells, out of greed, the linen cloths of the sacristy or the veil, he must know that he will suffer the punishment of Judas the betrayer.

[Col. 1155D] Clerics are strictly forbidden (Dist. 23, c. *Tales*) to approach a woman’s dwelling alone, to converse privately with a woman who is alone, or to live with a stranger woman. Otherwise, if this is discovered concerning anyone, he is to be deposed. He commands that such clerics be chosen for ministry as are able to handle the Lord’s sacraments worthily. For it is better for the Lord’s priest to have a few ministers who can worthily perform the work of God than many useless ones who impose a heavy burden upon the one who ordains them.

Likewise, in the same epistle he commands both clergy and laity always to pray to the Lord with their whole heart, to ask from him what is fitting, and to give him thanks. They must also do true penance for their past deeds and, if possible, assist their penance somewhat through acts of mercy toward the poor [Col. 1156A]. Through these things forgiveness will be granted more readily, and mercy will be shown more quickly.

Likewise, he commands (16, q. 7, c. *Ecclesias*) that churches be built in suitable and useful places, consecrated through divine prayers, and provided with priests whom everyone ought to honor and no one ought to burden.

Likewise, in the third epistle, which he wrote generally to all bishops and the other clergy, to all rulers, and to all their subjects, he says that those who enjoy the Lord’s priesthood and have been placed as watchmen must know more than the others, so that they may fully teach the peoples subject to them and provide them guidance toward the kingdom of heaven. It is their duty to teach the peoples; it is the duty of the peoples to obey those bishops.

If all of them, clergy as well as laity, do not obey them, they will be not only infamous but exiles from the kingdom of God and excluded from the thresholds of God’s holy Church, because the tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 7).

In the same epistle he teaches how each person must obey, adding the following (16, q. 1, c. *Cunctis*): “Therefore all the faithful, and above all priests and deacons and the remaining clergy, must take care that they do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No priest may celebrate Mass in his parish without his command, baptize, or do anything without his permission. Likewise, all the other people, both great and small, must do whatever is to be done with the permission of the bishop, and they must not depart from their parish without his permission, nor presume to remain there when they arrive.”

A little farther below in the same epistle he says (On Consecration, Dist. 1, c. *Hic ergo*): “It is not permitted to sacrifice or celebrate Mass in other places except those in which one’s own bishop, or a bishop regularly ordained—namely, one who holds a city—has consecrated the place.”

In the same epistle he says: “One who remains in evil and is a servant of evil cannot become part of the good so long as he remains in evil. For from the beginning God established two kingdoms, and it was determined by him that one person cannot be a servant of both kingdoms. He will belong to that kingdom to which he has submitted himself in obedience.”

In the fourth epistle, which the same most blessed Pope Clement and martyr wrote to Julius and Julian and his other fellow members, he taught that bishops, who have been established for the salvation of souls and consecrated for winning souls, ought to be solicitous for all and bring back those who err to the way of truth and the harbor of salvation.

In that same epistle he showed the way of returning to the harbor of salvation in a most fully salutary discourse, saying that it is necessary for everyone to become angry with and indignant at himself, in a certain sense, for the useless and shameful things he has done; then, without delay, to hasten to be reborn to God through the water of baptism; and finally to be signed by the bishop—that is, to receive the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Otherwise no one can in any way be a perfect Christian or have a place among the perfect, if he has remained there not from necessity but through negligence or by his own will.
