He affirms that he received this teaching from blessed Peter and that the other apostles taught it in the same way.

After a person has been baptized and confirmed, he must recognize that he ought to honor the Lord. His honor consists in living as he wills. God wills each person to live in such a way that he knows no murder or adultery, avoids hatred and greed, rejects and abhors anger, pride, and boasting, and keeps envy and all things like them entirely far from himself.

The aforementioned blessed Pope Clement and martyr wrote a fifth epistle to his fellow disciples living in Jerusalem with James, the brother of the Lord. In it he earnestly exhorts them to lead a common life, as they had learned from the apostles. He says that this is necessary for everyone, and especially for those who wish to serve irreproachably and to imitate the life of the apostles and their disciples.

In the same epistle he also warns that, because certain people were interpreting Holy Scripture not according to Peter’s tradition but according to their own judgment, contrary to sound doctrines, the understanding of Scripture must be received from the person who preserves it as it was handed down to him by his elders according to the truth, so that he himself may competently defend what he rightly receives.

For once someone has received from the divine Scriptures a complete and firm rule of truth, it will not be absurd for him also to contribute to the defense of true doctrine something from common learning and the liberal studies that he may have encountered in childhood—provided that, once he has learned what is true, he avoids what is false and fabricated.

He ordained fifteen bishops, ten priests, and five deacons.

## V.—SAINT ANACLETUS. (A.D. 103)

Anacletus, a Greek by nationality, from Athens, son of Antiochus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days. He lived during the times of Domitian, from the consulship of Domitian for the tenth time and Sabinus until Domitian’s fourteenth consulship and the consulship of Clement. He built a memorial to blessed Peter after having been ordained priest by him. He ordained six bishops, five priests, and three deacons. On the third day before the Ides of July he was released from the prison of the body.

In the epistle that he wrote generally to all bishops (Epistle 1), and to all the other faithful who shared with him an equal faith, he offers fatherly consolation to those to whom he wrote—especially to bishops—and earnestly exhorts them to patience in tribulations.

Concerning the slander and accusation of bishops, he inserts the following in the same epistle (Epistle to James, 3, q. 4, c. *Beatus*): “Our blessed predecessor Clement, an apostolic man filled with God’s Holy Spirit, together with his other holy colleagues, established the following decree: Let permission to accuse or testify be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, the norm of their own law or profession, or the prohibitions established by rule. Those who voluntarily transgress their law and violate it are called apostates.

“Every apostate must be rejected before his return, and must not be received as an accuser or witness against those who act rightly, because a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.”

A little farther below he adds: “Therefore the judges and primates of the Church must not be shaken by various slanders and accusations, but must rather be instructed and strengthened by the rules of the apostles and teachers. Hence it is just that all teachers of the law throughout the Roman world should rightly understand and practice the things of the law, and should not confuse the rules of the nascent Church or defile the faith or teaching of the apostles with various doctrines.”

Further below in the same epistle: “Therefore no one should prejudice another, nor do what he does not wish done to himself. Let no one find a statement concerning someone that he does not recognize in that person’s actions.”

Again in the same epistle: “I do not wish, through my error, to defend the faults of others, so that I may be convicted of having committed what I deplore.”

Likewise, in the same epistle, because of the slander directed against good bishops, he gives the following command (On Consecration, Dist. 1, c. *Episcopus*): “A bishop who sacrifices to God must have witnesses with him, and more witnesses than another priest. For just as he holds a position of greater honor, so he requires a greater increase of testimony.

“On more solemn days he must have with him either seven, five, or three deacons, who are called his eyes, together with subdeacons and the other ministers. Clothed in sacred vestments, they must stand before and behind him, while the priests stand opposite him on the right and left, with contrite hearts, humbled spirits, and bowed faces. They must guard him against malicious people and give their assent to the sacrifice.

“After the consecration has been completed, all who do not wish to be deprived of the thresholds of the Church should communicate. For thus the apostles established it, and the holy Roman Church maintains it.”

Likewise, in the same epistle he says (12, q. 1, c. *Qui abstulerit*): “He who spreads malice among human beings and he who slanders his brother is a murderer. He who takes anything from his father or mother, saying that this is not a sin, is a participant in murder.

“Our father is undoubtedly God, who created us; our mother is the Church, which regenerated us in spiritual baptism. Therefore whoever steals, takes away, or defrauds the money of Christ [c. *Qui Christi*] and of the Church is a murderer, and will be reckoned a murderer before the sight of the just Judge.

“Whoever steals his neighbor’s money (12, q. 4, c. *Qui rapit*) commits iniquity; but whoever takes away money or property belonging to the Church commits sacrilege. For the privileges of churches and priests (25, q. 2, c. *Privilegia*) the holy apostles, by command of the Savior, decreed should remain undefiled and inviolate for all time.

“We too confirm the laws of the Church by apostolic authority and remove foreign judgments. Each province (3, q. 6, c. *Unaquaeque*) ought to have its own just, not unjust, judges, according both to ecclesiastical law and to the law of the world, and not outsiders, as the authority of this apostolic see has decreed.

“If the matter is ecclesiastical, let it be brought before bishops, with the primate intervening if it is a greater case, and before the metropolitan if it is a lesser one. If it is secular, let it be brought before men of the same order, but under the judgment of bishops, since the apostle wished the cases of private Christians to be brought rather to the churches and settled there by priestly judgment (1 Corinthians 6).

“Therefore every oppressed person (2, q. 6, c. *Omnis oppressus*) may freely appeal, if he wishes, to the judgment of priests. No one may prohibit him; rather, he must be supported and delivered by them.

“If difficult cases or greater matters arise, let them be brought to a higher see. If they cannot there be easily discerned or justly settled, let them be judged justly and in a manner pleasing to God wherever the assembly of the highest authorities has gathered—a gathering that is accustomed and required to occur twice or three times each year—before the patriarch or ecclesiastical primate, and before the patrician; secular matters [or, before the secular patrician] are to be judged in common.

“If more difficult questions arise, or questions of times [or, of bishops], or judgments of greater authorities, or greater cases, let them be referred to the apostolic see if an appeal has been made, since the apostles established by command of the Savior that greater and more difficult questions must always be referred to the apostolic see.”

The same blessed Anacletus wrote another epistle to the bishops established in Italy. In it, responding to their questions concerning the ordination and accusation of bishops, he instructs them as follows (Dist. 64, c. *Ordinationes*): “The ordinations of bishops, by apostolic authority, are to be celebrated by all the bishops who are in the same province. Coming together, they must conduct a careful examination, celebrate a fast with all accompanied by prayers, and, laying their hands upon them with the holy Gospels that they are to preach, anoint them with sacred oil while praying on the Lord’s Day at the third hour.

“If all cannot assemble together, they must nevertheless give their assent through their prayers, so that in spirit they are not absent from the ordination itself. For James, the Just, who was called the brother of our Lord, was ordained by the apostles Peter, James, and John. A form was thereby given to his successors, namely, that no bishop should be ordained by fewer than three bishops, with the consent of the others.

“The remaining priests (Dist. 67, c. *Reliqui*) are to be ordained by their own bishop, with the assent of the citizens and the other priests, and the ordination is to be celebrated while they fast. Deacons are to be ordained in the same way.

“For the distribution of the remaining ranks, the testimony of three truthful witnesses, together with the bishop’s examination, may suffice.

“The accusation of them, about which you wished to consult us (2, q. 7, c. *Accusatio*), must be made only by suitable and thoroughly proven men who are free from both suspicion and crimes. And it must be made by them in the manner that the aforementioned pope teaches below, saying:

“‘If anyone approaches them out of charitable concern, so that, after being admonished in familiar conversation, they may heal what must be healed and charitably correct what they recognize must justly be corrected, this is proper. But if anyone presumes to tear them apart, accuse them, or harass them before doing these things, let him be excommunicated and not absolved until he has made satisfaction and performed worthy penance.’”

Likewise, the same holy and most blessed Pope Anacletus writes an epistle to all bishops (Dist. 80, c. *Episcopi*) and the other priests of Christ, in which he proves by the authority of the apostles that the order of priests is divided into two ranks: bishops and priests. No one ought to disturb this order, which was established by the Lord.

Bishops, however, should not be established in castles or small towns. Only priests are to be placed by a bishop over whatever place or church has been established there, and they are to remain in it throughout the days of their lives.

He says that there are no more than these two orders of priests. For although some are called primates or patriarchs and others metropolitans, the order is nevertheless one. The distinction of names indicates a distinction among superiors in the judgment of precedence, not in the power of the pontificate.

He calls the Roman Church the first see because blessed Peter and Paul, through their martyrdom, placed it before all the others. He says that the second see is at Alexandria because it was consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. The third see is at Antioch because blessed Peter lived there before coming to Rome, established Ignatius as bishop there, and there the first name of the new people, “Christians,” arose.

He says that accusers and witnesses (3, q. 5, c. *Accusatores*) cannot be those who were enemies even yesterday or the day before yesterday, lest, being angry, they desire to cause harm or, having been injured, wish to take revenge.

He also says that, according to the merits of the people, the shepherds of the Church are often corrupted, so that those who follow may fall more easily; when the head is weakened, the remaining members of the body are more easily infected.

He also says: “If a teacher or pastor of the Church deviates from the faith, he must be corrected by the faithful. But for blameworthy conduct he is to be tolerated rather than disciplined, because the rulers of the Church are to be judged by God.”

## VI.—SAINT EVARISTUS. (A.D. 112)

Evaristus, a Greek by nationality, son of a Jew named Juda, from the city of Bethlehem, sat for nine years, ten months, and two days. He lived during the times of Domitian and Nerva, from the consulship of Valens and Vetus until the consulship of Gallus and Braduas [Braduas]. Under them he suffered martyrdom on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. He ordained five bishops, six priests, and two deacons.

In his decrees he commanded that seven deacons be established in each city to guard the bishop, so that he would not be harassed by plotters while preaching, nor the word of truth be polluted by any kind of slander.

He also sent a written communication to all the bishops of the African region (Epistle 1, to the African bishops), stating that a legitimate marriage must be recognized in every church. He says as follows (3, q. 5, c. *Aliter*):

“Otherwise a marriage is not made legitimate, as we received from the Fathers and found handed down by the holy apostles and their successors, unless the woman is requested from those who appear to exercise authority over her and by whom she is guarded; unless she is betrothed by her parents or relatives, endowed according to the laws, and at the proper time blessed by a priest in priestly fashion, as is customary, with prayers and offerings; and unless, as custom teaches, she is guarded and preserved [or joined] by her relatives, requested at the proper time according to the laws, and given [or endowed] and solemnly received.

“Let them devote two or three days to prayers and preserve chastity. Otherwise, arrangements made presumptuously are not marriages but, without doubt, adulteries, or concubinages [or unions], or illicit sexual relations, or fornications rather than legitimate marriages, unless free consent has given its support and lawful recognition has intervened [or, lawful vows have intervened].”

In another epistle, which he wrote to all the bishops living throughout Egypt (Epistle 2), he speaks of the bishop and the Church as follows:

“The Church is joined spiritually to the bishop, just as a bride is joined bodily to her husband. And just as a man must not neglect his wife but love her, guard her chastely, and govern her wisely, so the bishop must do this for his Church, and the Church must obey in all things just as a wife ought to obey her husband.

“And just as a man may not dismiss his wife, so a bishop may not dismiss his Church, except because of unavoidable necessity or an apostolic or canonical transfer, so that he may join himself to another for the sake of ambition. And just as a wife may not dismiss her husband, even if he has committed fornication (1 Corinthians 7), in order to marry another while he is alive, so the Church cannot bring in another bishop while her bishop is alive.

“Concerning bishops who have been disgraced and driven from their sees, he commanded in the same epistle that they be recalled and fully restored, and that those who have been imposed in their place be expelled as adulterers. Once this has been done, if anyone has a complaint against them, it must be investigated and settled by the authority of the Roman see.

“They are not to be reproved or accused by the people or by common men, even if they are disorderly, because God orders the life of teachers according to the merits of their subjects.”

Further below he says (2, q. 7, c. *Si qui*): “If there are any revilers or accusers of bishops or of the other priests, they ought not to be heard by the judges of the Church before the suspicion or reputation concerning their character has been examined: with what intention, with what faith, with what rashness, with what manner of life, with what conscience, and with what merit they have presumed to do this—whether for God, for empty glory, because of enmities or hatred, or out of greed. All these matters must be searched out and carefully considered.

“For God, wishing to restrain us from pronouncing a hasty judgment, although all things are naked and open to his eyes (Hebrews 4), nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely on hearsay, before he had clearly ascertained what was being said (Genesis 18).”

He also established a decree against insulting or tearing apart bishops.

## VII.—SAINT ALEXANDER. (A.D. 122)

Alexander, a Roman by nationality, son of Alexander, from the district of Caput Tauri, sat for ten years, seven months, and two days. He lived during the times of Trajan until the consulship of Helianus and Vetus. He was crowned with martyrdom on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

He commanded that priests not be harassed and that writings not be extorted from them by force, fear, or any kind of fraud. In an epistle that he wrote to all orthodox bishops living in various provinces he says (3, q. 4, c. *Hi qui*):

“We close the mouth of those who accuse bishops or testify against them, since we know that they are dead—not through human actions, but through divine ones.”

Further below: “We read that our predecessors prohibited anyone from constraining teachers or accepting an accusation against them.”

A little farther below: “We establish and decree that all who persecute the holy Fathers or strive to remove or tear them apart are manifestly infamous and are to be made strangers to the boundaries of the Church until they make satisfaction.”

Further below in the same epistle he says (15, q. 6, c. *Si quandoque*):

“Likewise, if any writings have in any way been extorted from such persons through fear, fraud, or force, or if writings have been drawn up or contrived [or confirmed] by them through whatever device so that they might free themselves, we decree that these writings bring them no prejudice or harm. Nor do we permit them, by the Lord’s authority and that of his apostles and their successors, ever to suffer infamy, calumny, or sequestration of their property on this account, because in such matters confession must be voluntary, not compelled.

“For it is exceedingly wrong to judge anyone on the basis of suspicion or a confession that has been elicited.”

In the same epistle he also commanded (On Consecration, Dist. 2, c. *In sacramentorum*, and c. *Aquam*) that, in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood, his Passion should be commemorated; that water mixed with salt should be blessed and sprinkled in the houses of the faithful; and he instructed us in writing concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity as he had received it from the Fathers.

He ordained five bishops, six priests, and two deacons.

## VIII.—SAINT SIXTUS. (A.D. 132)

[Col. 1162C]

Sixtus, a Roman by nationality, son of Pastor, from the district of Via Lata, sat for ten years, two months, and one day. He lived during the times of Hadrian until the consulship of Verus and Annic(u)lus. Under them he was also crowned with martyrdom on the third day before the Nones of April.

In his decrees he admonished and commanded that the right faith, handed down by the apostles, be preserved without compromise. He instructed us in it by writing (Epistle 1, to all bishops).

He also commanded (Epistle 2, to all bishops; On Consecration, Dist. 15, *In sancta*; 2, q. 6, c. *Si quis vestrum*) that sacred vessels be touched only by men consecrated by God for this service.

He established that any bishop afflicted by adversity might lawfully appeal to the Roman and apostolic see and, when summoned there, should not refuse to come. Nor should he return from there to his own see without apostolic letters, so that his neighbors might thereby understand how he had settled his own case and those of others there.

He also established that no one should strip a bishop of his property or presume to excommunicate or judge him after he had been expelled from his own see.

He ordained four bishops, eleven priests, and three deacons.

## IX.—SAINT TELESPHORUS. (A.D. 142)

Telesphorus, a Greek by nationality, from Anachoreta, sat for eleven years, three months, and twenty-two days. He lived during the times of Antoninus and Marcus. He was crowned with martyrdom on the fourth day before the Nones of January.

In his decrees [Col. 1163A] (Epistle 1, to all bishops) he firmly established that all clerics called to the Lord’s portion should fast from meat for the full seven weeks before Easter. He also decreed that clerics should in no way accept laymen in a summons or accusation against them (c. *Statuimus*, Dist. 4), just as the laity themselves, according to secular law, do not wish to accept clerics in matters of their own defamation.

He also established that Mass should be celebrated on the holy night of the Nativity of our Lord and Savior (On Consecration, Dist. 1, c. *Nocte sancta*) and that the angelic hymn—namely, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be solemnly sung.

At other times he prohibited Mass from being celebrated before the third hour of the day, because it is recorded that the Lord was crucified at that hour and that the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles.

He also commanded that all accusations (3, q. 5, c. *Accus.*) which the laws of the world do not admit should not be admitted as ecclesiastical accusations.

He ordained thirteen bishops, eleven priests, and eight deacons.

## X.—SAINT HYGINUS. (A.D. 154)

Hyginus, a Greek by nationality, formerly a philosopher from Athens, whose genealogy I have not found, sat for four years, three months, and eight days. He lived during the times of Verus [Severus] and Marcus, from the consulship of Magnus and Camerinus until that of Orfitus and Priscus. He went to the Lord on the third day before the Ides of January.

He organized the clergy and distributed its ranks. He instructed us in the faith of Christ through many firm testimonies of divine Scripture, showing that the Father did not precede the Son so as to be greater than the Son, nor was the Son born later so as to be inferior in divinity to the Father (Epistle 1, to all the faithful).

He also established that no metropolitan should hear the cases of bishops without the presence of the other provincial bishops, since proceedings conducted otherwise would be invalid. He also established that accusations against elders should not be brought by others but by those who themselves bring the charges (2, q. 7, c. *Criminationes*). He likewise prohibited foreign judgments.

He ordained six bishops, fifteen priests, and five deacons.

## XI.—SAINT PIUS. (A.D. 158)

Pius, an Italian by nationality, son of Rufinus and brother of Pastor, from the city of Aquileia, sat for ten years, four months, and three days. He lived during the times of Antoninus, from the consulship of Clarus and Severus. He was removed from this life on the fifth day before the Ides of July.

In his decrees he firmly established (Epistle 2, to the Italians) that anyone who presumed to take from God estates devoted to divine purposes and apply them to his own uses should be regarded and unquestionably judged as a sacrilegious person (12, q. 2, c. *Praedia*). He likewise confirmed that anyone who persecutes God’s priests is sacrilegious (17, q. 4, c. *Sicut*) and must be judged as sacrilegious, because every sin committed against God is more serious than one committed against a human being.

He also established (Epistle 1, to all the faithful; On Consecration, Dist. 3, c. *Nosse vos*) that, since an angel appearing in the garb of a shepherd commanded Hermas, the teacher of faith and Scripture, Easter should always be celebrated by all Christians on the Lord’s Day.

He ordained twelve bishops, nineteen priests, and twenty-two deacons.

## XII.—SAINT ANICETUS. (A.D. 148)

Anicetus, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, from the village of Umisa, sat for nine years, three months, and three days. He lived during the times of Verus and Marcus, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus until that of Praesens and Rufinus. He died a martyr on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

By his own authority he commanded (Epistle to the bishops of Gaul, 66, Dist., c. *Archiepisc.*), and confirmed by the authority of Anacletus’s decrees, that no bishop should be consecrated by fewer than three bishops. A metropolitan bishop must be chosen and consecrated by all the suffragan bishops of the metropolitan see assembled at that see [Col. 1164B]. There is no doubt that anything done otherwise lacks force, because whatever is presumed against the statutes of the Fathers will undoubtedly be invalid before God, even if not before human beings.

He also established (ibid., c. 3; 9, q. 3, c. *Si autem*; Dist. 23, c. *Prohibete*) that no metropolitan should undertake anything concerning the cases of suffragan bishops without their presence and common counsel.

He also commanded that clerics should not be permitted to grow their hair long.

He ordained nine bishops, seventeen priests, and four deacons.

## XIII.—SAINT SOTER. (A.D. 175)

Soter, a Campanian by nationality, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi [Col. 1164C], held the see for nine years, six months, and eleven days. He lived during the reign of Severus, from the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus until that of Cethegus and Clarus. He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. He decreed (Epistle 2, to the bishops of Italy) that no consecrated woman or nun should touch sacred vessels or consecrated cloths, nor carry incense around the altar. He ordained eleven bishops, eighteen priests, and nine deacons.

### XIV.—St. ELEUTHERIUS (A.D. 179)

Eleutherius, a Greek by nationality, son of Abundius, from the town of Nicopolis, held the see for fifteen years, three months, and two days. He lived during the reigns of Antoninus and Commodus, until the consulships of Paternus and Bradua. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June. [Col. 1164D]

He received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, requesting that he be made a Christian through his command. In his own decree (Letter to the provinces of Gaul, ch. 1), he confirmed that no common food which appeared reasonable and suitable to human nature should be rejected by Christians; and that the definitive judgment of all bishops should be concluded only at the Roman see (ibid., ch. 2), whereas the cases of other clerics could lawfully be settled by the bishops of their own province.

The same aforementioned pope says the following, among other things, concerning accusations against bishops (ibid.): “Let nothing be done without a legitimate and suitable accuser. For our Lord Jesus Christ knew that Judas was a thief; but because he was not accused, he was not expelled, and whatever he did among the apostles remained valid by reason of the dignity of the mystery” (ibid., ch. 3). Concerning accusations against fellow provincials, it is likewise recorded as having been decreed: “If anyone believes that any cleric should be brought to trial for any crimes, let him pursue his action in the province in which the person being accused resides, and let him not suppose that the man may be dragged elsewhere to judgment. Let neither the slander nor the voice of a traitor be heard.”

He ordained fifteen bishops, twelve priests, and eight deacons.

### XV.—St. VICTOR (A.D. 194)

Victor, an African by nationality, son of Felix, held the see for ten years, two months, and ten days. He lived during the reign of Caesar Augustus Antoninus, also called Verus [Col. 1165B], from the fifth consulship of Commodus and the consulship of Glabrio until those of Lateranus and Rufinus. He was crowned with martyrdom on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.

He decreed (Letter 1, to Theophilus of Alexandria—On Consecration, distinction 3, ch. “Celebritatem”) that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, as had previously been done. He also decreed that, if necessity required it under the threat of death, anyone might lawfully be baptized at any time and in any place—whether at sea, in a river, or in springs—provided that it was done in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

He further decreed that uncertain matters, even if true, should in no way be judged unless they were first established by clear indications, or proved by manifest judgment, or made public through judicial procedure. Nor might the case of any bishop be decided without consulting the Roman pontiff (ibid.). [Col. 1165C]

He ordained twelve bishops, three priests, and seven deacons.

### XVI.—St. ZEPHERINUS (A.D. 203)

Zepherinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Abundius, held the see for eighteen years, seven months, and ten days. He lived during the reigns of Antoninus and Severus, from the consulship of Saturninus and Gallicanus until the consulships of Praesens and Strigatus. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

He also decreed (Letter 1, to the bishops of Sicily) that a bishop’s case should not be concluded without the command of the Roman pontiff; nor should a bishop be judged unless either he confessed himself guilty or was convicted by suitable witnesses, of whom there must be no fewer than seventy-two.

He also decreed (2, q. 1, ch. “Primates”) [Col. 1165D] that no one of the highest rank should be attacked by accusations from his inferiors; that in a doubtful matter a definite sentence should not be pronounced; that no judgment should be upheld unless it had been conducted in due order; that no one should be judged in his absence; that no one should be harmed by a sentence except one pronounced by his own judge; and that an accused bishop should choose twelve bishops as judges, if necessary (3, q. 4, ch. “Detractores”; 3, q. 9, ch. “Absens”). He further decreed that the accused should not be heard, excommunicated, or judged until those judges had themselves been chosen; and that, once regularly summoned before the assembly of his own bishops, his case should again be heard by them [fairly heard] and examined reasonably. For one must not rashly judge what is hidden in another’s heart, all must avoid unjust judgments, and bishops must be borne with by the people and clergy. [Col. 1166A]

He also decreed (Letter 2, to the bishops of Egypt—distinction 83, ch. “Ordinationes”) that the ordinations of priests and Levites should take place at the proper time and in the presence of many faithful standing by.

He ordained thirteen bishops, fourteen priests, and seven deacons.

### XVII.—St. CALIXTUS (A.D. 221)

Calixtus, a Roman by nationality, son of Domitius, from the district of the Urberavennans, held the see for five years, two months, and ten days. He lived during the reigns of Macrinus and Heliogabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Alexander. Alexander the emperor brought him to martyrdom on the day before the Ides of October. [Col. 1166B]

He decreed (Letter 1, to Bishop Benedict) that the fasts of the Four Ember Seasons should be observed by all Christians. By his decrees he confirmed that no unjust judgment or unjust decision (11, q. 3, ch. “Injustum”), arranged or carried out by judges through fear of a king, by command, or at the order of any powerful person, should have validity: for no emperor, nor anyone who guards piety, is permitted to presume anything against the divine commandments.

He decreed (in the same letter) that no one should undertake an accusation against a teacher, and that an accusation made in writing should not be received (Letter 2, to the bishops of Gaul); nor should testimony about an accused person be given in his absence. Nor should anyone give testimony concerning other cases or matters except those known to have been conducted in his presence.

Neither accusers (2, q. 8, ch. “Accusatorum”; 11, q. 2, ch. “Excommunicatus”; 9, q. 2, ch. “Nullus alterius”; 9, q. 3, ch. “Nullus primas”) nor suspect witnesses or those stained by infamy should be admitted. No one should receive excommunicated persons from priests, or communicate with them in any way, before a just examination of both parties. No one should usurp another’s boundaries, nor presume to judge or excommunicate another’s parishioner, because anything presumed in this way would be invalid.

Nor should a metropolitan presume to excommunicate or judge the church or parishioner of a diocesan bishop, or to undertake anything concerning his parish, without that bishop’s counsel and judgment; for whatever he did would be invalid, and he himself would be exposed to danger concerning his rank.

He also decreed that no bishop should be transferred to another city on account of ambition; but if a transfer had to be made, it should occur at the invitation of the other brethren, with the authority of the Roman Church and for the benefit of the church to which he was to be transferred. [Col. 1166D]

He further commanded (3, q. 4, ch. “Consanguineorum”) that unions between blood relatives be entirely prohibited, because such persons possess no weight as witnesses.

He also confirmed (at the end of Letter 2), and demonstrated by the most salutary examples of divine Scripture, that both the priests of the Lord and the other faithful can, after making worthy satisfaction, be restored to their former honors.

He ordained eight bishops, fifteen priests, and four deacons.

### XVIII.—St. URBANUS (A.D. 226)

Urbanus, a Roman by nationality, son of Pontianus, held the see for nine years, ten months, and twelve days. [Col. 1167A] He lived during the consulship of Antoninus and Alexander. He died as a confessor during the reign of Diocletian, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

In his decrees he confirms (Letter 1, to all the faithful) that estates and every kind of property given by the faithful to the church of God must always remain under the authority and disposition of the bishops in whose parishes those churches are situated. The bishops themselves must provide from these goods everything necessary for all who wish to live a common life, and must not convert any of them to uses other than ecclesiastical ones, because they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor.

Whatever they convert to uses other than those mentioned necessarily makes them guilty of sacrilege; and even if they do not die bodily, they nevertheless fall dead in soul. The seats of bishops are therefore established in elevated places within churches (ibid.), so that from this it may be understood that bishops possess the authority and power of binding and loosing. All the faithful must also receive the Holy Spirit after baptism through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, so that they may be found to be fully Christian. [Col. 1167B]

He converted Valerian, the husband of Caecilia, and many others to faith in Christ, and led them to the palm of martyrdom.

He ordained eight bishops, nineteen priests, and seven deacons.

### XIX.—St. PONTIANUS (A.D. 233)

Pontianus, a Roman by nationality, son of Calpurnius, held the see for nine years, five months, and two days. He lived during the reign of Alexander, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Pelinianus [Pelagianus]. At that time [Col. 1167C] the aforementioned pontiff was deported with the priest Hippolytus by Alexander into exile in Sardinia, on the island of Bucina, during the consulship of Severus and Quintianus. Having been afflicted and beaten with clubs on that same island, he died on the third day before the Kalends of November.

He also commanded in his decrees (Letter 1, to Felix) that priests were not to be accused by enemies, criminals, or people belonging to another sect or religion. If they happened to sin, he ordered that they be admonished by other priests and restrained by the highest pontiffs, so that in no way should they be reproved or barred by secular persons or men of evil life.

He ordained seven bishops, six priests, and five deacons.

### XX.—St. ANTHERUS (A.D. 237)

[Col. 1167D]

Antherus, a Greek by nationality, son of Romulus, held the see for twelve years, one month, and twelve days. He lived during the reigns of Maximinus and Africanus, the consuls. He carefully sought out the records of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church. He was crowned with martyrdom on the third day before the Nones of January.

He ordained one bishop (Letter to the bishops of Baetica). When consulted concerning the transfer of bishops (7, q. 1, ch. “Mutationes”), he replied in his decrees that this could be done—not, however, at anyone’s whim or through domination, but for the common good or out of necessity. Thus Peter, the prince of the apostles, was transferred from Antioch to Rome for the sake of usefulness, so that he might accomplish more there.

Eusebius, too, was transferred by apostolic authority from a certain small city to Alexandria. Likewise Felix was transferred from the city in which he had been ordained to Ephesus, by the choice of the citizens, on account of the learning and good life he possessed, with the common counsel of the bishops, the other priests, and the people.

For just as bishops have the power regularly to ordain bishops and other priests, so, whenever usefulness or necessity requires it, they have the power, in the manner stated above, both to transfer and to enthrone them. A person is not transferred from a smaller to a larger city when he is transferred and enthroned not through ambition or his own will, but because he was driven from his own see by force, compelled by necessity, or transferred for the benefit of the place and people—not arrogantly, but humbly—by others. [Col. 1168A]

In the same decrees [Col. 1168B] he also sanctioned (in the same letter) that anyone who was disobedient should be cut off by spiritual punishment and, expelled from the church, torn apart by the swift jaws of demons. Thus, in the old law, whoever failed to obey the priests was either placed outside the camp and stoned by the people, or, with his neck exposed to the sword, expiated his contempt in blood (Deut. 17).

### XXI.—St. FABIANUS (A.D. 238)

Fabianus, a Roman by nationality, son of Fabius, held the see for thirteen years, one month, and eleven days. He lived during the reigns of Maximinus and Africanus, until the second consulship of Decius and that of Quadratus. He was crowned with martyrdom on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February.

He ordained eleven bishops, twenty-two priests, and seven deacons. [Col. 1168C] He divided the seven deacons in the city of Rome among the city’s seven regions, so that they might always be found ready to perform the duties appropriate to them. He also ordained seven subdeacons, who were assigned to the seven notaries and were to collect the records of the martyrs accurately and completely.

During his time the heretic Novatus came from Africa. He separated Novatian and certain other confessors of Christ from the Church of Christ and converted them to a perverse doctrine.

He gave a fatherly warning and, by a salutary decree binding on all Christians, sanctioned (Letter 1, to fellow ministers—6, q. 1, ch. “Omnes”) that all those with whom the Apostle forbids us to eat (1 Cor. 5) should be completely excluded from the fellowship of Christians and should in no way be admitted to accuse any of the faithful, until satisfaction, provided there was no doubt that they had come worthily. [Col. 1168D]

He also commanded in the decrees sent to the bishops of the East (Letter 2) that the following be observed inviolably: every year new chrism was to be made, and the old chrism burned in the holy churches. For just as the solemnity of that day is celebrated every year, so the making of the holy chrism must be performed every year, renewed from year to year, and given to the faithful, because it is a new sacrament. The apostles taught this; their successors maintained it; and they firmly commanded that it always be maintained.

In the same decrees he established [Col. 1169A] (3, q. 5, ch. “Suspectos”), and adduces that the apostles and their successors had established, that in every accusation—that is, in the ecclesiastical accusation of any Christian—suspect persons and all enemies should be rejected, as should those who did not lead a good life, whose conduct was blameworthy, whose orthodoxy was doubtful, whose faith, life, and freedom were known, who were stained by the blemish of infamy, or entangled in crimes.

Concerning the accusation of priests, he says that no one should or could be admitted who could not become a priest or who was not one of their own—that is, a member of the priestly order (2, q. 7, ch. “Sicut”). For just as priests and other clerics are excluded from accusations by secular laymen, so laymen are to be excluded and kept apart from accusing them. [Col. 1169B] If each person’s right and proper order is preserved in secular matters, much more must right and order be preserved in ecclesiastical arrangements; no confusion should be introduced.

He likewise commanded in the same decrees that no one should ever presume to be at once accuser, judge, and witness. For in every judgment—namely, a synodal judgment—four persons must always be present: chosen judges, accusers, defenders, and witnesses.

He also established that the sheep should not dare to rebuke their shepherd unless he had erred in the faith. If he had erred in the faith, he was first to be corrected privately by his subjects; but if he appeared incorrigible, he was then to be accused before his own primates or before the apostolic see. For his other actions, however, he should be tolerated by his subjects rather than publicly disparaged or accused. [Col. 1169C]

In another decretal letter (Letter 3), which the aforementioned pope sent to Bishop Hilary, he established the same rule concerning accusations against priests and persons of higher rank as he had established in the letter sent to the Eastern bishops.

Moreover, while preserving the apostolic authority in every respect, he prohibited foreign judgments by a general sanction. He decreed that accusations against bishops should proceed in due order, so that any bishop accused of specific crimes should have chosen provincial bishops as judges, and should be heard by all of them within that province. For the accused ought to be heard nowhere but in his own forum; and if there he found the judge hostile to him—namely, the metropolitan or primate—he should freely have the opportunity to appeal and defend himself, without any affliction or humiliating detention. [Col. 1169D]

He also established (3, q. 6, ch. “Si quis episcopus”) that anyone who had not been brought before his own judge might, if he wished, remain silent, and that the accused should be granted delays whenever they appealed.

In addition, he decreed (1, q. 6, ch. “Si quis judicem”) that any crime rashly charged against anyone in anger should not be considered an accusation. He also decreed (3, q. 6, ch. “Pulsatus”) that whoever admitted that he would prove an accusation in writing should suffer the penalty he had imposed if he did not prove what he had alleged.

The proof and the case should always be conducted where the crime was committed (3, q. 6, ch. “Qui crimen”), unless the bishop had appealed to the apostolic see. [Col. 1170A] In that event, whatever the pontiff of that see decided was to be established.

### XXII.—St. CORNELIUS (A.D. 254)

Cornelius, a Roman by nationality, son of Castinus, held the see for two years, two months, and three days. Because he had received a letter from Blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, he was beheaded by order of Decius on the third day before the Nones of March.

He ordained seven bishops, four priests, and four deacons. At the request of a certain matron named Lucina, he secretly removed by night the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul from the catacombs. First, the body of Blessed Paul was quietly removed and placed on the estate of the aforementioned matron on the Ostian Way, beside the place where he had been beheaded.

Afterward he took the body of Peter [Col. 1170B] and reverently placed it near the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount in the Vatican, at Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

The same aforementioned pope and martyr, in a letter sent to his fellow bishop Rufus in response to a consultation (Letter 2), following the Lord’s command in the Gospel, that of the apostle James in his letter, and the commands of all the apostles and his predecessors, and confirming the law, completely forbade priests to administer rash oaths, because before his time oaths had not been demanded or given by the highest priests or by other priests except as testimony to the true faith.

In the same letter (2, q. 4, ch. “Nos sanctorum,” and ch. “Nos sacramentum”), as his other predecessors had done, he affirmed that care must be taken [Col. 1170C] lest the sheep presume to rebuke or accuse their shepherd unless he had departed from the faith. For such accusations have no force and cannot harm shepherds.

He also prohibited any priest from entrusting his case to the judgment of another; rather, he should always have judges from his own province who were known to him, unless he feared the violence of a reckless crowd there or had hostile or suspect judges. For these reasons he was permitted to appeal and go to judges of greater authority and to other provinces.

In the same letter he affirms (3, q. 6, ch. “Omnia”) that everything done or judged against absent persons in any matter or place is entirely void, because no one can condemn an absent person [assign an absent person to judgment], and no law condemns him.

### XXIII.—St. LUCIUS (A.D. 255)

[Col. 1170D]

Lucius, a Roman by nationality, son of Porphyrius, held the see for three years, three months, and three days. He lived during the reigns of Gallus and Volusian, until the third consulship of Valerian and that of Gallicanus.

He was first sent into exile, then returned unharmed to the church; finally he was beheaded by Valerian on the Nones of March.

He ordained seven bishops, four priests, and four deacons. Because of malicious persons and the persecutions of priests, he decreed that two priests and three deacons should remain with the bishop in every place, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, a good reputation might be preserved even among those outside (1 Tim. 3). He urged that this be observed among them in the letter he sent to all the bishops of Gaul and Spain (On Consecration, distinction 2, ch. “Jubemus”). [Col. 1171A]

In the same letter he established (2, q. 7, ch. “Criminationes”) that accusations against persons of higher rank should not be made through intermediaries, but only by those who bring the charges; and that such persons must be worthy and appear irreproachable, demonstrating through public records that they were free from every suspicion and enmity, and showing that they led a blameless life and conduct.

Because he observed that this was sometimes difficult before just any judges, he decreed that a petitioner should not be denied a hearing before other ecclesiastical judges where greater authority existed.

In the same letter, following the decree of the holy apostles and their successors, he established by command [Col. 1171B] that if any metropolitan bishop attempted to do anything outside what belonged solely to his own parish without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he would endanger his rank, and whatever he had done would be held invalid and void.

He decreed that a metropolitan bishop could act and make arrangements concerning their cases, churches, clerics, secular needs, or any common matters that required action only with the consent and counsel of all the provincial pontiffs (9, q. 3, ch. “Nullus”).

He likewise established concerning the provincial bishops themselves that they could do nothing separately or jointly without the metropolitan, except what pertained to their own parishes.

Similarly, by apostolic authority [Col. 1171C] he commanded that no metropolitan bishop should hear the cases of any of his suffragans without the presence of all the suffragans; otherwise the proceedings would be invalid, and he himself would bear responsibility for what had been done.

He further commanded that throughout each province bishops observe the following: later bishops should not set themselves above their predecessors, nor should they do anything without consulting them except what pertained to their own parish. Rather, concerning their common cases they should issue and determine a concordant judgment; for proceedings conducted otherwise would have no force and would not be regarded as ecclesiastical.

In the same letter, when consulted about the stripping of churches of their endowments and offerings, he first demonstrated through many arguments and on the authority of many persons that this kind of seizure and robbery was sacrilege (17, q. 4, ch. “Qui rapit” and ch. “Omnes Ecclesiae” [Col. 1171D “raptores”]). Then, on the authority and by the decree of the prophets, the apostles, their successors, and all the Catholic Fathers, he anathematized and condemned such presumptuous persons, robbers of the church, and alienators of its resources, excluding them from the threshold of Holy Mother Church, and judged them to be sacrilegious. He condemned not only them but also all who consented to them, because not only those who act but also those who consent to those acting are guilty and are judged guilty (Rom. 1). The same punishment will encompass both the perpetrators and those who consent.

### XXIV.—St. STEPHANUS (A.D. 257)

Stephanus, a Roman by nationality, son of Lobius, [Col. 1172A] held the see for seven years, five months, and two days. He lived during the reigns of Valerian, Gallicanus, and Maximus, until the third consulship of Valerian and the second of Gallicanus.

He was sent to prison with two bishops, eight priests, and three deacons; ultimately, by order of Valerian, each was punished with capital execution. Stephanus was executed on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

He ordained three bishops, seven priests, and five deacons. In a letter sent to Bishop Hilary (Letter 1), he prohibited infamous persons from being promoted to sacred orders or admitted to make accusations.

He described as infamous persons (6, q. 1, ch. “Infames”) those marked with infamy for any fault—that is, all who rejected the standard of Christian law and despised ecclesiastical statutes. Likewise included were thieves, [Col. 1172B] sacrilegious persons, and all entangled in capital crimes; violators of tombs; those who willingly violated the religious statutes of the apostles, their successors, and the other holy Fathers; all who took up arms against the Fathers; incestuous persons, murderers, perjurers, robbers, practitioners of magic and poisoners, adulterers, deserters from wars; those who sought to occupy places unworthy of them or unjustly seized the church’s resources; those who slandered or accused their brothers without proving the charge; those who provoked the anger of princes against the innocent; all who had been anathematized or expelled from the church for their crimes; and all whom ecclesiastical or secular laws pronounced infamous.

He described all these as infamous and forbade them to be promoted to sacred orders [Col. 1172C] or admitted as accusers. He also prohibited repentant slaves from being promoted before they had obtained lawful freedom; likewise, bigamists, those who serve in public office, those who were physically impaired, those who lacked a sound mind or understanding, and those who were disobedient to the decrees of the saints.

He asserted that none of these persons—nor freedmen, suspects, those without sound faith or worthy conduct—could accuse the highest priests (On Consecration, distinction 1, ch. “Vestimenta”).

In the same letter the aforementioned pope established that priests and Levites should not use ecclesiastical vestments for purposes other than ecclesiastical services.

The same pontiff, in another letter (Letter 2), which he sent [Col. 1172D] to all the bishops in the various provinces, removed from accusations against priests the other persons whom we listed above. He also declared beyond doubt that whatever was unjustly done concerning things consecrated to God, and concerning bishops, who are sacred [because they are sacred], was to be regarded as sacrilege; such things must not be violated by anyone.

In his decree he further asserted (2, q. 2, ch. “Nullus”) that no bishop, while deprived of his property or driven from his own see for any reason, should be accused; nor could any charge first be brought against him until he had been completely restored. Everything taken from him by whatever means was to be restored to him in full, without deceit or fraud, according to the law, because not only ecclesiastical but also secular laws prohibit this from being done.

He also decreed [Col. 1173A] (3, q. 5, ch. “Accusatores”) that anyone who believed himself injured by a bishop or by the bishop’s ministers, or who wished to correct them for some error, should not presume to accuse them before first approaching them charitably once or three times, so that he might receive from them either a friendly correction or a just explanation. If he presumed to do so, he ordered that the person be expelled from the threshold of the church until he had made worthy satisfaction.

He also established that no anathema expressed in writing should be accepted; rather, it must be pronounced in the accuser’s own voice, provided that the accuser was a legitimate and suitable person, and in the presence of the person whom he wished to accuse, since no absent person can be accused or accuse another.

He established that no bishop should first be accused or required to answer his accusers until he had been regularly summoned by his own primate [Col. 1173B] and given an opportunity to defend himself and clear the charges.

He further established that no bishop should be accused or heard except in the presence of all the provincials and by all the bishops of his province; for in their absence he neither ought nor can be heard or judged.

He decreed that the permission to accuse should not extend beyond the boundaries of the province (3, q. 6, ch. “Ultra”; 3, q. 11, ch. “Neganda”).

He established that an accuser should not first be permitted to charge anyone with a crime until he had freed himself by purging the crime weighing upon him. For one must not believe the confession of persons entangled in crimes against others unless they had first proved themselves innocent.

He also stated (2, q. 7, ch. “Quaerendum”) that he had nowhere read that laymen, even religious laymen, had been granted authority to dispose of ecclesiastical property.

He also commanded [Col. 1173C] concerning the persons of accusers (2, q. 8, ch. “Accusatorum”) that their faith, life, and conduct should first be carefully investigated, and only afterward should the matters alleged be faithfully examined. For nothing should be done before the faith, life, and conduct of the persons mentioned above had been carefully scrutinized, lest anyone be harassed by another’s envy, enmity, or evil intention.

### XXV.—St. SIXTUS II (A.D. 260)

Sixtus, a Greek by nationality, formerly a philosopher, held the see for one year, ten months, and twenty-three days. He lived during the reigns of Valerian and Decius, at a time of the greatest persecution.

At that time he was arrested by Valerian and led away to sacrifice to demons. Because he despised Valerian’s commands, he was beheaded, together with six deacons, on the eighth day before the Ides of August. Three days after his passion, Blessed Lawrence, his archdeacon, also suffered martyrdom, on the fourth day before the Ides of August.

He ordained two bishops, four priests, and seven deacons.

In a letter sent to Bishop Gratus in response to his consultation (Letter 1), he asserted and proved beyond refutation, by arguments and the authority of many persons, that the Son of God was not born in time or after time, but was ineffably begotten from the Father’s womb before all times.

In the same letter he showed that he had strengthened, for the assistance of all bishops, what many of his predecessors had established (2, q. 6, ch. “Omnes”): namely, that all bishops [Col. 1174A] who were brought to trial or accused in certain more serious cases should, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the apostolic see and flee to it as to a mother.

If any bishop, even after being judged by the bishops of his province, came to the bishop of the Roman see, it should be in that bishop’s power, either personally or through his vicars, to reopen the case. While the matter was being handled and completed before the Roman pontiff himself, no other person was to be placed or ordained in that bishop’s position. For although the bishops of the province were permitted to investigate the case of an accused bishop, they were not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff (3, q. 6, ch. “Accusatus”).

In another letter, sent to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Spain (Letter 2), he likewise established, as his predecessors had done (2, q. 7, ch. “Si quis”), that no one should presume to accuse a bishop or any prelate of the Church before confronting him; whoever acted otherwise was to be deprived of communion.

He likewise established that no pontiff should presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop who had been stripped of his possessions or expelled from his see, because there is no privilege by which one who has already been stripped can be stripped again.

He also decreed that no bishop should presume to retain, ordain, or judge another’s parishioner. For just as his ordination would be invalid, so would his judgment; no one can be held except by the sentence of his own judge, since the person who could not ordain him cannot in any way judge him.

He likewise established that uncertain matters should not be judged. For although they may be true, they are not to be believed unless they are confirmed by certain indications, proved by manifest judgment, or made public through judicial procedure. [Col. 1174C]

By the authority and words of the Apostle he confirms (Exod. 23) that a charge against a priest should not be received without two or three suitable witnesses (1 Tim. 5).

He recalls that his predecessors had often established that no one should take up an anathema in an accusation against bishops; likewise, those who refuse to receive them in their own complaint or accusation should not be admitted.

### XXVI.—St. DIONYSIUS (A.D. 261)

Dionysius, formerly a monk, whose parentage we were unable to discover, held the see for six years, two months, [Col. 1174D] and four days. He lived during the reign of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus.

He assigned parishes and churches in Rome to priests (13, q. 1, ch. “Ecclesias”), one to each. He left [divided] among them those parishes and cemeteries and established that each should have his own jurisdiction, so that no one might invade the boundaries or jurisdiction of another’s parish, but each should remain content with his own.

In a letter sent to Severus, bishop of the province of Corduba (Letter 2), he commanded Severus himself and the other bishops to observe and follow what he had established on this matter.

In the same letter, as his predecessors had done (15, q. 3, ch. “Nemini”), [Col. 1175A] he established that crimes could not be brought against bishops through intermediaries, but only by those who brought the charges; and that such persons must have the qualifications which, as we have often shown above, his predecessors had determined.

He ordained eight bishops, twelve priests, and six deacons.

### XXVII.—St. FELIX (A.D. 272)

Felix, a Roman by nation, son of Constantius, held the see for four years, three months, and twenty-five days. He was crowned with martyrdom on the third day before the Kalends of June. He ordained five bishops, nine priests, and five deacons. In a letter that he wrote to Paternius [Paternus], bishop (Letter 1), he ordered that detractors and supporters of enemies be excluded from episcopal accusation. Likewise, following his predecessors, he confirmed [Col. 1175B] (3, q. 4, c. *Detractors*; 2, q. 7, c. *Of the greater*) that no one of the highest rank should be attacked or destroyed by accusations brought by inferiors, that no definite judgment should be rendered in a doubtful matter, and that no judgment should be upheld unless it had been conducted in due order. Likewise, if anyone should believe that a cleric ought to be charged with any crimes (3, q. 6, c. *If anyone*), he should bring his proceedings [exercise his actions] in the province in which the person charged resides, and should not suppose that the accused ought to be summoned elsewhere or brought over a greater distance for judgment. If the person charged should regard the judges as suspect, he should be permitted to appeal to the primates.

Moreover, when the primates examine an accused bishop (2, q. 1, c. *The primates*), they should not pronounce a sentence of condemnation before, relying upon apostolic authority, either the accused himself confesses, [Col. 1175C] or he is regularly convicted by innocent witnesses who have been canonically examined, and so forth. In the same letter he added provisions concerning the unjust condemnation of bishops (11, q. 3, c. *Void*), the absence of the accused, and the slander of an informer—matters which, as we have shown above, his predecessors repeatedly prescribed in their decrees.

This pontiff, after hearing the complaints of all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Gaul, and having shown them fatherly compassion in their oppressions, summoned more than fifty [seventy] bishops. Because of the plots of wicked men who indiscriminately raged against the Church and ecclesiastical persons, he established by synodal decree the following rule concerning accusation: if the accuser is suitable, he should not first bring the case of any bishop before the primates [Col. 1175D] until he has approached him charitably. Only when he understands that the bishop is unwilling to correct the matter should the case finally be referred canonically to the supreme primates.

These primates, at a suitable time—that is, in autumn or summer—and in a suitable place, or within the province, must regularly summon a council of all the bishops of the province. The bishop himself, having been regularly summoned, must attend, unless illness or some other serious necessity prevents him. For if he has been stripped of his own possessions or of the ecclesiastical goods entrusted to him, or has been separated from his flock by some form of detention, he cannot be canonically summoned or judged until he has been restored to his former dignity with all its privileges and all his possessions have been legally restored [Col. 1176A] (3, q. 2, c. *If a bishop*). After his restoration and the restitution of his possessions, he should then be summoned regularly within four, five, or seven months, as circumstances permit, and should come to a lawful and suitable council. If it appears just, he should answer the allegations of his accusers.

For it is sacrilege to deprive a bishop of his episcopate before the outcome of his case has become evident, and the author of such an act is sacrilegious. If the bishop is ill (5, q. 3, c. *If he is ill*), or some necessity prevents him from attending, he should send a representative to the synod on his behalf, lest he be suspended from communion on the charge brought against him—unless, having been summoned by letter on the appointed day by the chosen judges to present his case, he entirely fails to appear [Col. 1176B].

But if both parties have come to present their case, since one should not be heard without the other, the court must inquire into the character, faith, and possible suspicion of the accusers, and into the intention with which they are acting. They should not be admitted for this purpose unless they are of good conduct, sound faith, and entirely free from suspicion. If the persons of the accusers appear culpable in the judgment of the bishops (3, q. 10, c. *If the accusers*), they should not be admitted to bring the charge.

When the opposing party is absent, the accuser should not be heard (3, q. 9, c. *When the opposing party is absent*), nor should a sentence pronounced by a judge in the absence of the other party have any force. An absent person may neither accuse nor be accused through another person, and a related witness should not be admitted. He likewise removed foreign judgments by a general enactment (3, q. 6, c. *Foreign judgments*) [Col. 1176C]. In the same synod he established that Masses should be celebrated over the memorials of martyrs, so that their memory could not be extinguished by evil persons or their veneration prohibited.

### XXVIII.—SAINT EUTYCHIANUS (Year of Christ 275)

Eutychianus, a Tuscan by nation, son of Marinus, from the city of Luna, held the see for eight years, one month, and one day. He lived during the time of Aurelian, from the third consulship of Aurelian and that of Marcellinus. He ordained nine bishops, fourteen priests, and five deacons. He was crowned with martyrdom on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

In a letter that he sent to John, bishop, and to the other bishops established throughout the province of Baetica (Letter 1), he decreed that beans and grapes, and the other things that the apostles had established, should be offered at the altar, while other kinds of produce should be taken to the priests’ house; after being blessed with a simple blessing, they should then be received by the people (Canon, chapter 4) [Col. 1176D].

This same pontiff, in another letter that he sent to all the bishops established throughout Sicily (Letter 2), set out the procedure for accusation, which he established and defined together with all the bishops and with the faithful of both orders of the holy Roman Church, saying:

“It is not to be conducted in ecclesiastical matters as it is in secular matters (2, q. 6, c. *Not so*). For in secular matters, once someone has appeared after being summoned according to the laws and has begun to plead in court, he may not withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical matters, however, once the case has been stated, it is permissible to withdraw if necessary, or if one sees that one is being overburdened.

“We declare and order that the procedure of accusation is to be as follows. If one of the clergy is charged with a crime, he should not immediately be regarded as guilty merely because he could be accused, lest we make innocence suspect [subject]. But whoever brings the charge must come into court, state the name of the accused, take up the bonds of a written indictment, and submit to a form of custody [guard it], while nevertheless being treated [enjoying treatment] in accordance with the dignity of his rank. Otherwise, he might regard the license to lie as permitted, since the likeness of the punishment demands vengeance upon those who bring false accusations.

“He entirely excluded from the privilege both of accusing and of testifying heretics, persons under suspicion, the excommunicated, murderers, sorcerers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, those who have given false testimony, [Col. 1177B] and all who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, the norm of their own law or profession, or prohibitions established by rule.

“Likewise, he prohibited ecclesiastical judges from hearing cases that are not contained in the laws or that are known to be prohibited, because not only ecclesiastical laws but also the laws of the world command that these things be observed. He also affirms that those who are excluded from the kingdom of God are, beyond doubt, denied by the Church.”

### XXIX.—SAINT CAIUS (Year of Christ 283)

Caius, a Dalmatian by nation, of the family of the emperor Diocletian, son of Caius, held the see for eleven years, four months, and twelve days. He lived during the time of Diocletian [Col. 1177C]. Fleeing his persecution, he lived for nine years in crypts; at length he deserved to become a martyr on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

In a letter that he wrote to Felix, bishop, having been asked to instruct him concerning many matters held in his own time by the authority of the apostolic see according to Catholic discipline, he took care to say:

“First, you should know that pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians (2, q. 7, c. *Pagans*), or bring a voice of defamation against them. Furthermore, no one should ever presume to accuse a bishop before secular judges, or to accuse other clerics. If a bishop, priest, deacon, or any cleric is accused before bishops—for elsewhere an accusation should not be received from any person who is not properly admissible—whoever undertakes this kind of blameworthy intention, whether he is a man of high honor or of some other rank, should know that he must present the evidence that ought to be taught and display the documents [should know that he must bring forward the proof and documents].

“Therefore, if anyone brings an unprovable charge against such persons, let him understand, by the authority of this enactment, that he will suffer the loss of his reputation.

“As for the manner in which one should come to a council (3, q. 1, c. *To the bishops*), and other matters, and concerning annual postponements, he says that he did not include them in the same letter because he believes that sufficient treatment of such matters has already been given by the apostles, their successors, and his own predecessors.

“Concerning the ecclesiastical orders, he wrote in the same letter and commanded all to observe the following sequence: if anyone is worthy to be a bishop, he should first be a doorkeeper, then a lector, afterward an exorcist, then be ordained an acolyte, then a subdeacon, then a deacon, and afterward a priest. Thereafter, if he deserves it, he should be ordained bishop. He also ordered that the districts of large cities be divided among the deacons, and that all difficult questions that arise should always be referred to the apostolic see.”

### XXX.—SAINT MARCELLINUS (Year of Christ 296)

Marcellinus, a Roman by nation, son of Projectus, held the see for nine years, four months, and twenty-five days. He lived during the time of Diocletian and Maximian. At that time the persecution of Christians was so great that within thirty days seventeen thousand men and women of every kind throughout the various provinces were crowned with martyrdom.

At that time Marcellinus himself was compelled to sacrifice to demons [Col. 1178B]. But after a few days, when a synod had been assembled in a city of Campania before one hundred and eighty bishops, he duly repented. Therefore Diocletian, enraged because he had not been able to compel him to sacrifice, ordered him to be beheaded with three others on the sixth day before the Kalends of May. He was buried thirty days later by Marcellus the priest. His episcopate then remained vacant for seven years, six months, and twenty-five days because of the excessive persecution of Christians.

He ordained five bishops, four priests, and two deacons. In a letter that he sent to Solomon, bishop (Letter 1), he proved by many arguments and confirmed by the irrefragable authority of many persons that the Father is not greater than the Son except according to the nature of humanity. He did this because certain heretics had arisen at that time [Col. 1178C] and were striving to prove the contrary.

In another letter, which he sent to all the bishops established throughout the Eastern provinces (Letter 2), he urged and commanded everyone to cease persecuting and litigating against the brethren, and ordered that whatever disputes arose among Christians should be brought to the Church and settled by ecclesiastical persons. He also decreed that a superior could not be judged by an inferior, and that no bishop could prejudice the pontiff by whom he was proved to have been consecrated. If anyone presumed to do so, the act was to be void and was not to be counted among ecclesiastical statutes.

Likewise, in the same letter he decreed (11, q. 1, c. *Cleric*) that no cleric, whatever his order, should presume to drag anyone before a secular court without the permission of his pontiff [Col. 1178D], nor should a layperson be permitted to accuse him [nor should a layperson be permitted to accuse a cleric].

Like Pope Calixtus, he confirmed by his decree (2, q. 7, c. *To a layperson*) that neither an emperor nor anyone who observes piety may presume to do anything against the commands of God, or to act in any way contrary to the rules of the Gospel, the prophets, and the apostles. Thus he concluded:

“An unjust judgment, therefore, and an unjust decision of a king, arranged by judges through force or command, has no validity. Nor shall anything stand that has been done contrary to the constitutional teaching of the Gospel, the prophets, or the apostles, without the consent of the holy Fathers. Whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics shall be entirely abolished.”

### XXXI.—SAINT MARCELLUS (Year of Christ 304)

[Col. 1179A]

Marcellus, a Roman by nation, son of Benedictus, from the district of Via Lata, held the see for five years, seven months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the time of Maxentius and Maximian. Maxentius arrested him and handed him over to the animals in the *catabulum* to serve them, because he refused to sacrifice to demons. After spending a long time there clothed in sackcloth and weakened by hunger, he ended his life in Christ on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

He ordained twenty-one bishops, twenty-five priests, and two deacons. In a letter that he sent to all the bishops subject to the Church of Antioch (Letter 1), he wrote that the holy Fathers, under the inspiration of the Lord, had established that no synod could legitimately be summoned without the authority of the Roman see [Col. 1179B], in which a bishop charged with any crimes ought to be heard or judged. All the affairs of bishops, all major cases, and every doubtful matter must be conducted and concluded by the authority of the apostolic see, and all provincial affairs must be reconsidered by the authority of that same see.

He commanded that these same provisions be observed with the greatest care in another letter that he wrote to Maxentius, bishop (Letter 2). He included many other matters concerning the affairs of bishops in that letter, which we have not recorded here because we have already prescribed the same things repeatedly by repeating them in the decrees of his predecessors.

### XXXII.—SAINT EUSEBIUS (Year of Christ 309)

[Col. 1179C]

Eusebius, a Greek by nation, a physician, held the see for six years, one month, and three days. He lived during the time of Constans [Constantine]. On the sixth day before the Nones of October he departed to the Lord.

He ordained four bishops, thirteen priests, and three deacons. He composed three decretal letters. In the one that he wrote to all the bishops established throughout Campania and Tuscany (Letter 3), he solemnly ordered that the feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross be celebrated; the cross had been found in his time on the fifth day before the Nones of May (On Consecration, distinction 3, c. *Of the Cross*).

Likewise, in the same letter he ordered (On Consecration, distinction 5, c. *Hands*) that all heretics who came to conversion, if they had been baptized in the faith of the Holy Trinity, were to be reconciled by the laying on of hands. He said that this sacrament, namely the laying on of hands, neither should nor could be administered by anyone other than bishops, and that anything presumed otherwise was to be regarded as void and empty and not counted among ecclesiastical rights [Col. 1179D].

In the letter that he sent to the Gallican bishops (Letter 2), he likewise commanded that the same rule be observed concerning the reception of heretics. He also excluded from accusations against clerics and bishops the infamous and the others whom his predecessors had often prescribed should be removed. He himself likewise removed them, saying: “Those who do not wish to imitate their chastity and gravity cannot attack them.”

In the letter that he addressed to the bishops established throughout Alexandria and Egypt (Letter 1), he prohibited sheep from reproaching or accusing their shepherd in any way, unless he had departed from the true faith (2, q. 2, c. *In the Scriptures*) [Col. 1180A]. For although the deeds of shepherds may appear rightly subject to reproach, they are not, nevertheless, to be struck by the sword of their subjects.

Concerning those who had been expelled or stripped of their possessions, he added the following in the same letter:

“You should know that they cannot be summoned either to a provincial synod or to a general one, nor can they be judged in any matter, until all that has been taken from them has been legally restored to their authority. Afterward, they should not be summoned within a short period of time; rather, they should be granted as much time as they appear to have spent in being stripped or expelled before they are summoned to the synod” (3, q. 2, c. *First*).

Each person should also be heard by all the bishops of his province. For one who has been stripped of his possessions or expelled can neither be summoned to answer a case nor judged, since there is no privilege by which one who has already been stripped can be stripped again [Col. 1180B].

For this reason it was also decreed in ancient times that all possessions, everything taken from him, and all fruits received before the joinder of issue should be restored by the primate to the original possessor. Elsewhere it is written (2, q. 2, c. *No one*): “The one who has suffered violence should receive everything in the condition in which it had been, and should securely retain what he possesses.”

Elsewhere, in the synodal decrees of the Fathers and in the edicts of kings, it is established (3, q. 1, c. *Restoration*):

“All things are to be restored to bishops who have been stripped or expelled, immediately by the ordinance of the pontiffs, and they are to be completely recalled to the authority from which they departed. Whatever things they are known to have lost—whether ecclesiastical or personal property, or their possessions—through any condition of time, fraud, captivity, the force of the wicked [the power of their superiors], or any unjust causes, before their accusation or regular summons to a synod, must be restored to them” [Col. 1180C], and so forth.

He adds many further provisions in the same letter to prove the same point.

### XXXIII.—SAINT MELCHIADES (Year of Christ 311)

Melchiades, an African by nation, held the see for four years, seven months, and eight days. He lived during the consulships of Maxentius, Volusianus, and Rufinus. He ordained eleven bishops, seven priests, and five deacons, and on the fourth day before the Ides of December he departed to the Lord.
