In a letter that he sent to the bishops of Spain, he instructed them by asking and earnestly exhorting them always first to investigate everything carefully and to decide with justice and charity; to condemn no one before a true and just judgment; to judge no one by the arbitrariness of suspicion; but first to prove the matter and afterward pronounce a sentence charitably; and not to inflict upon another what they do not wish to have inflicted upon themselves (Tobit IV). He also instructed them not to judge or condemn bishops without the authority of the Roman see. If they did so, the act would be void and those who did it would be condemned.

For it had been established that this privilege should be preserved for the Roman see from the time of the apostles. Although the election of all the apostles was equal, it was nevertheless granted to blessed Peter to take precedence over the others and prudently to dispose of cases and inquiries brought forward as complaints.

The same pontiff, in the same letter, instructed those who were seeking clarification that the sacrament of the bishops’ laying on of hands is greater than baptism, because it is administered by greater persons—that is, by the supreme pontiffs—and cannot be completed by lesser persons. Therefore it must be venerated and preserved with greater reverence. Nevertheless, these two sacraments are so joined that they cannot in any way be separated from each other except by death intervening, and one cannot properly be completed without the other. One can be received without the other when death intervenes; the other cannot.

We should not, however, doubt that, when we receive fullness from the font, the Holy Spirit who descended upon the waters of saving baptism grants fullness in the font for innocence and provides an increase of grace in confirmation. In baptism we are regenerated for life; after baptism we are confirmed [Col. 1181B] for battle. If the benefits of regeneration are sufficient for those who will immediately pass away, the aids of confirmation are nevertheless necessary for those who will continue to live.

Regeneration by itself saves those who are soon to be received into the peace of the blessed age; confirmation arms and trains those who are reserved for the struggles and battles of this world.

In the same letter the pope forbade anyone to observe a fast on the Lord’s Day or on Thursday, so that there might be a true, not a false, distinction between the fast of Christians and that of pagans, and between the faithful and the unfaithful.

### XXXIV.—SAINT SILVESTER (Year of Christ 314)

Silvester, a Roman by nation, son of Rufinus, held the see for twenty-three years, ten months, and eleven days. He lived during the consulships of Constantine and Volusianus [Col. 1181C]. At different times he ordained sixty-five bishops, forty-two priests, and twenty-six deacons.

Fleeing persecution, he hid for a long time on Mount Soracte. Later, returning with glory, he baptized Constantine, whom Christ cleansed from the uncleanness of leprosy in the very baptism. Having received the power to serve God freely, he established regulations for the whole Church.

In his time also, at his command, a synod was held at Nicaea in Bithynia. Three hundred and eighteen Catholic bishops assembled there; they set forth the complete, Catholic, and immaculate faith and condemned Arius, Photinus, Sabellius, and their followers.

At the same time, the pope just mentioned, with the counsel of the aforesaid Augustus Constantine and by canonical summons, gathered two hundred and seventy-seven bishops in the city of Rome [Col. 1181D]. He again condemned both Callixtus and Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius. He decreed that no priest should receive a repentant Arian unless the bishop of that place reconciled him and confirmed him with sacred chrism.

In that synod it was also established, by the agreement and subscription of all, that no layperson should dare to bring a charge against a cleric (2, q. 7, c. *No one*; 2, q. 7, c. *A cleric*); that priests should not bring an accusation against a bishop, nor deacons against priests, nor anyone of a lower grade against anyone holding a higher grade [Col. 1182A]; and that no prelate should be condemned except by seventy-two witnesses. No supreme prelate should be judged by anyone. A cardinal priest should not be condemned without forty-four witnesses; a cardinal deacon should not be condemned without twenty-six witnesses; and a subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, lector, or doorkeeper should not be condemned except, as it is written, by six witnesses.

The witnesses and accusers must be free from every form of infamy. No one should accept the testimony of a layperson against a cleric (11, q. 1, c. *Testimony*). No one should presume to examine any cleric publicly except in a church. No cleric, deacon, or priest should enter a court for any cause, or presume to plead his case there before a judge. If any cleric, accusing another cleric, enters a court, he should receive anathema [Col. 1182B].

In the aforesaid synod he decreed (On Consecration, distinction 1, c. *Deliberately*) that no one should presume to celebrate the sacrifice of the altar in silk or dyed cloth, but only in pure linen consecrated by a bishop—that is, linen produced and woven from earthly flax.

If anyone wishes to serve or advance in the Church, he must first be a doorkeeper, then a lector, and afterward an exorcist, for the periods established by the bishop. He must then serve as an acolyte for five years, as a subdeacon for the same number of years, and as guardian of the martyrs; likewise as a deacon for five years, and as a priest for two [three] years. He must be tested in every respect, so that he may even have a good testimony from those outside, and be “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy III), who must nevertheless have been blessed by a priest [Col. 1182C].

After being so tested, if he is worthy and the votes of the clergy and people support him, he should be canonically consecrated bishop. Neither clergy nor people should afterward disturb a person of such a life who advances, as stated above.

He also established in the aforementioned synod (On Consecration, distinction 1, c. *No one*) that no priest should presume to celebrate Mass except in places consecrated by a bishop who wishes thereafter to share in his priesthood.

He also decreed that a priest should anoint with chrism anyone baptized and washed with water because of the danger of sudden death. He established that deacons should use dalmatics in the church and wear cloaks on the left side. On the day before the Kalends of January, this Catholic confessor of Christ [Col. 1182D] departed to the Lord.

### XXXV.—SAINT MARK (Year of Christ 336)

Mark, a Roman by nation, son of Priscus, held the see for eight months and twenty days. He lived during the time of Constantine, Nepotianus, and Secundus.

He decreed that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the bishop of the city of Rome, should wear the pallium. He sent a letter to Athanasius and to all the bishops of Egypt. In it he consoled them in a fatherly manner, in many ways, concerning their complaint of affliction, and said that, as a consolation and aid in their defense, he was sending them the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, which through the violence of wicked men were no longer available among them.

He ordained twenty-seven bishops [Col. 1183A], twenty-five priests, and six deacons. He died as a confessor on the Nones of October.

### XXXVI.—SAINT JULIUS (Year of Christ 336)

Julius, a Roman by nation, son of Rusticus, held the see for fifteen years, two months, and six days. He lived during the time of Constantius, the heretical son of Constantine, beginning with the consulship of Felicianus and Maximinus.

He spent ten months in exile and suffered many tribulations. After the death of the aforesaid Constantius, he returned to his see. While the Augusti Constantius and Constans were ruling, he held a synod at Rome with one hundred and sixteen bishops. In it he confirmed and set forth the faith strengthened at the Council of Nicaea by three hundred and eighteen orthodox bishops, and anathematized by the decree of all those who held any opinion against it [Col. 1183B].

In his first letter, which he sent to all the Eastern bishops, he attempted in many ways and with sound reasoning to draw them away from accusations against the brethren by means of documentary evidence. He presented to them many passages from the chapters of the Council of Nicaea and himself confirmed the same things from the decrees of his predecessors, together with all those subject to apostolic rule.

In the letter that he wrote to the same Eastern bishops, who were heretics, he reproved them openly and freely for the arrogance they had shown against the Roman Church. By many chapters, supported by the authority of many persons and inserted into the letter, he convicted them of having unjustly expelled Athanasius and the other Catholic bishops from their sees [Col. 1183C]. He showed that they were culpable for this reason: although summoned so many times, they had delayed coming. He said:

“It is plainly evident that those who, though summoned so many times, delay coming without an unavoidable cause, and do not make use of the opportunity to clear themselves, confess their own crime.”

He also decreed that no cleric should plead any case in public except in a church. He ordained nine bishops, eighteen priests, and four deacons. He died as a confessor on the day before the Ides of April.

### XXXVII.—SAINT LIBERIUS (Year of Christ 352)

Liberius, a Roman by nation, son of Augustus, held the see for fifteen years, seven months, and three days. He lived during the time of Constantine until Constantius Augustus, the heretic, who afflicted the aforesaid pope in exile for three years because he refused to consent to the Arian heresy [Col. 1183D].

Then the priests assembled and ordained Felix the priest as bishop in Liberius’s place. After holding a council of forty-seven [forty-eight] bishops, Felix separated Ursacius and Valens, priests who consented to the Arian heresy, from communion with himself and with those who believed rightly.

Therefore, inflamed by the zeal of fury, they formed a plan and, by the authority of Constantius, sent for Liberius and recalled him from exile, on the following condition: that he would participate with them only in the communion of those to be rebaptized. He consented to the rebaptizing, was brought back from exile, and lived [Col. 1184A] in the cemetery of Saint Agnes.

Then, when the Arians held a council, Felix, a Catholic man, was deposed and expelled from the city; he lived on his small estate on the Via Portuensis. Liberius, however, having consented to Constantius the heretic, was restored to his see. He himself was not rebaptized, but he gave his consent to the rebaptizing. He afterward held the Roman see for seven years, and there was great persecution in Rome, both among the clergy and among the people.

He ordained nineteen bishops, eighteen priests, and five deacons. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

Before he became a transgressor by sharing communion with the Arians, he sent a decretal letter to Athanasius and the other orthodox Eastern bishops (Letter 1). In it he commended the faith of the Council of Nicaea with the greatest care. Showing the reward and punishment connected with preserving that faith, he earnestly urged each person to strive for it [Col. 1184B].

Likewise, before he consented to the Arian heresy, he wrote a letter to all the bishops collectively (Letter 2), in which he urged and admonished them that no bishop should abandon his own church because of any disturbances, so long as he could endure them, nor choose the quiet of a monastery rather than strive to labor for the people entrusted to him. Among other things he said:

“Let us strive to reject the foolish plots of men, to follow the Fathers, and not to transgress the boundaries of the Fathers, insofar as the Lord has granted. That is, let us not hasten to abandon our churches while we are able to resist evil, nor neglect the peoples entrusted to us, nor choose rest [Col. 1184C] rather than labor for them, for whom we must even lay down our lives.”

Later in the same letter he says (7, q. 1, c. *The report*):

“For it has been reported to us that, because of past labors and persecutions, some of you abandon the peoples assigned and entrusted to you by God; and that more brothers [in the future, more] wish to abandon the churches that they ought to protect and neglect to labor for the sheep entrusted to them. They hasten to devote themselves to the quiet of monasteries and choose release from the labors of the episcopate, preferring to live in silence and leisure rather than remain in the matters entrusted to them. Yet the Lord says: ‘Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end’ (Matthew X, XXIV), and so forth.

“Therefore, dearest brothers, do not let the bitterness of afflictions constrain you to withdraw from the godly purpose of your minds. Pay attention, then, to yourselves and to the entire flock in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood (Acts XX). Let no one deceive or mislead you by the subtlety [sublimity] of speech, so that you abandon the peoples entrusted to you and surrender yourselves somewhere to rest because of the reproach of wicked men—so that you alone may save yourselves and leave your children orphans.”

Likewise, in the same letter he admonishes them concerning the observance of the canons, saying:

“Do not permit the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated in anything, so that both the institutions of the Nicene canons and the provisions wisely and beneficially decreed by us or by our predecessors [Col. 1185A] may remain undefiled.”

### XXXVIII.—SAINT FELIX II (Year of Christ 355)

Felix, a Roman by nation, son of Anastasius, held the see for one year, three months, and two days. He declared Constantius, the son of Constantine, to be a heretic and to have been rebaptized a second time by Eusebius of Nicomedia. Because he made this declaration, he was later beheaded by order of the aforesaid Constantius in the city of Coranna, on the third day before the Ides of November.

He consecrated nineteen bishops, twenty-one priests, and five deacons.

In a letter that he sent to Athanasius and to all the bishops of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya (Letter 2), he inserted certain chapters established by the holy Fathers both in the Council of Nicaea and in the holy Roman see, by which the aforesaid bishops might better escape the plots of their enemies. It does not seem useless for us to insert them into this work as well. It begins as follows:

1. It has been decreed by synodical regulations that no one may accuse a bishop before secular judges, but only before the highest primates.

2. If anyone has a case against a bishop, he must not approach other bishops to accuse him before first making his complaint known to him privately and receiving from him either a just correction or a reasonable explanation, as the Truth itself instructs us: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone; if he does not listen to you, take with you two or three witnesses; and if he does not listen to you, tell it to the Church [Col. 1185C]” (Matthew XVIII)—that is, only then accuse him publicly, and not before—and so forth.

3. If anyone thereafter chooses to accuse a bishop, he must state his case to the highest primates of the bishops, and not to secular judges, who should recall them more to peace than to judgment, so that charity may be preserved in all things and by all. If the primates (5, q. 2, c. *Si primates*) or the accusers of the bishops are altogether unable to reconcile with them privately, then, at the proper time, they shall summon them canonically to a synod duly convened—not within excessively short periods—and first inform them in writing [“what is” (*quaw est*)] of what they accuse them, so that they may come prepared to answer.

4. For if they have been expelled by force or fear, or stripped of their possessions, and therefore cannot be canonically summoned to the synod, they must answer their adversaries before they are canonically [Col. 1185D] restored and all their property is legally returned to them. The bishop must first be restored; afterward, not immediately but only after a long interval, during which he has arranged his affairs at his own authority and prepared what is necessary for himself, he shall come at the appointed time to the case; and, if it seems just, he shall answer his accusers.

5. No infamous or sacrilegious person may give testimony against a religious Christian in any matter, even if that Christian is of humble and servile status; nor may he bring a Christian to trial concerning any matter, action, or formal charge.

6. If a bishop has been lawfully accused and, according to the order stated above, has been canonically summoned to the council, he must go without any hesitation; and, if he is unable to do so himself, he must send an envoy to the synod on his behalf.

7. Ecclesiastical judges must hear no cases that are not contained in the laws or that are known to be prohibited [Col. 1186A].

8. If anyone will not be satisfied in any other way than by accusing a bishop, he must proceed according to the procedure laid down above, since an accusation cannot otherwise be considered valid. First, therefore, the accuser must canonically bring the case of the accused before the primates. The accused must not be barred from communion unless, after being canonically summoned to the judgment of the elect, he has delayed coming to give an account of himself for three, six, or more months; but if he has been unable to come, this shall do him no harm.

The man who has been driven from his see by force [or fear], or stripped of his possessions, must not be summoned to the synod until everything has been restored to him according to law; and he must remain peacefully and with full authority in his own see, arranging all things, for as long as he is seen to be deprived of his property because he was expelled or despoiled (3, q. 2, c. *Tandiu*) [Col. 1186B]. When he comes to the judgment, if he wishes and it is necessary, any postponement requested by him must be granted without hindrance by the brothers [fathers], and judges chosen by him must be assigned in the place from which the accused comes. Or, if he fears the force of some reckless crowd elsewhere, he may choose a suitable place where, without fear, he can have his own witnesses, should necessity demand it, and bring his canonical case to an end without hindrance, since many things commonly occur through underhanded dealing.

9. Permission to testify must be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, the rule of the law, the norm of their own profession, or matters prohibited by ecclesiastical rule.

10. Defamation becomes especially powerful when the defamer is believed. Therefore one must not weaken a primate through various slanders [*detractionibus* / *detrectationibus*] [Col. 1186C] and accusations; rather, he should be strengthened by the rules of the Fathers, so that he does not presume to receive accusations readily or indiscriminately, the Lord saying: “You shall not accept a false report” (Exodus XXIII [the text reads XXIV]). He must first establish the suspicion, the case, and the motive with which the accuser acts, and only afterward receive the accusation, because proximity [*propinquitas* / *propinquitas*], enmity, fear, love, hatred, and desire commonly obstruct the profession of truth and cause injury to the brethren.

11. The persons of the accusers must be such that their faith, conduct, and life are approved and without reproach, and that they are free from every suspicion. For, as you know well, even at the present time, these matters and many others were brought forward [*delata*; the text also reads *deleta*, “deleted”] in the Council of Nicaea because of the plots of wicked men. [Col. 1186D] Those alone should be called primates who were appointed in the aforementioned synod, and no others.

12. The others who hold metropolitan sees should be called archbishops, and not primates, while in all things preserving the dignity of the Apostolic See, which was granted to it by the Lord himself (Matthew XVI) and afterward confirmed by the holy Fathers.

13. In every accusation of a bishop, the person, life, and conduct of the accusers must always first be investigated in detail; afterward, the matters alleged must be examined faithfully. Nothing should be done otherwise unless the faith, person, life, and conduct of the aforementioned complainants [*impetitorum*] have been scrutinized, since the destruction wrought by wicked or treacherous men must not tear apart the lives of the innocent. Indeed, the good are very often persecuted by the wicked, who do not cease [Col. 1187A] to defame others through their own misfortunes. Therefore this must be guarded against with the greatest care.

14. No slave, no free person, no unbeliever, no one entangled in crimes, no slanderer, no one devoted to enmities, no one who willingly [frequently] engages in litigation and is readily inclined to accuse or defame, no infamous person, and no person whom the public laws do not admit to accuse others of public crimes, may presume to accuse bishops. For I cannot discover why the sacerdotal order should receive accusers and accusations that the laws of the world do not admit, since these things were also prohibited in the Council of Nicaea, and such persons ought rather to be judged by these men than these men by them. The Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (1 Corinthians II).

15. Heretics [Col. 1187B], by whom we are grievously oppressed, excommunicated persons, homicides, sorcerers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, those who have given false testimony, and those who have resorted to diviners and magicians must in no way be admitted either to bring accusations or to give testimony.

16. Ecclesiastical cases must not be conducted in the same way as secular cases. In secular matters, once someone has been summoned according to the laws and has begun to contest the case in court, he may not withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical matters, however, once the case has been stated, he may withdraw if necessity requires it or if he sees that he is being overburdened.

17. Whenever a bishop is accused of specific crimes, if the accusers are such as ought to be admitted justly and canonically, then, when the lawful synod has been assembled at the proper time, he must be heard canonically by all the bishops in the province [Col. 1187C]. But if the accusers are not legitimate, the bishop must not be wearied, since priests ought to be summoned to offer sacrifice [*vacare*, “to be free for service”], not to litigate; nor should those who are called the thrones of God be disturbed by the plots of wicked men, but should serve Christ the Lord freely.

18. Although the bishops of a province, together with their metropolitan, may deal with the cases of the bishops of their province charitably and harmoniously, nevertheless, as was established in the aforementioned synod, they may not issue a definitive judgment without the authority of the Roman pontiff. If certain persons presume to act otherwise, those who have done so must bear the penalty of their presumption; and those whom they have wrongly excommunicated or condemned must, by the authority of this holy see and by the power of blessed Peter, our teacher [Col. 1187D] and key-bearer, be released and restored. For the Lord himself says: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI).

19. Whenever bishops believe that they are being overburdened by their fellow-provincial bishops or by their metropolitan, or whenever they regard them as suspect, they must immediately appeal to the Roman See, and they must be allowed to go freely, without any detention or confiscation of their possessions. Once they have appealed to the aforementioned Roman Church or have requested to be heard by it, no one may presume to excommunicate them, seize their sees, take away their property, or inflict anything upon them before the case of both parties has been confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiff. If anyone presumes to act otherwise, it will do them no harm [“there will be nothing” (*nihil erit*)], and there is no doubt that such an act will lack force [Col. 1188A].

20. Concerning postponements for bishops, about which you consulted us, we find different rules established by the Fathers. Some (3, q. 3, c. *De induciis*) ordered that a year and [or] six months be granted in order to repel the devices of their accusers, prepare their responses, secure their witnesses, and seek the counsel of their bishops [*episcoporum*; the text reads *eorum*] and friends. Others ordered a year, with which many agree. I have found no period shorter than six months, since these concessions have also been granted to laymen; how much more, then, to the priests of the Lord?

The aforementioned pope wrote another letter to all his spiritual brothers and to the others consecrated to the Lord in the priestly college (Letter 2), in which he earnestly exhorts them to endure persecutions and tribulations patiently, so that they may prove to be sons of the one whom they daily invoke as Father, God in heaven; and so that they may not answer their detractors with detraction, but may perform everything in a spirit of humility and, with patient perseverance, teach what must be taught.

### XXXIX.—Saint Damasus (A.D. 367)

Damasus, a Spaniard by nationality, the son of Antoninus, held the see for eighteen years, three months, and eleven days. Ursinus was ordained at the same time amid a dispute; but after a council of priests had been held, Damasus was appointed, because he was the stronger party and had the larger multitude. Ursinus, however, was expelled from the City, and was appointed bishop of Naples. Damasus was afterward maliciously accused of adultery; and when a synod was held on the matter, he was cleared by forty-eight [forty-four] bishops. His accusers, the deacons Concordius and Callistus, were condemned by the council and expelled from the Church. He ordained seventy-two bishops, thirty-one presbyters, and eleven deacons. He died on the second day before the Ides of December.

In a letter that he sent to Stephen, archbishop of Mauritania, and to all the bishops of the African province (Letter 3), he instructs them how metropolitan bishops and the highest ecclesiastical matters may be examined: namely, in such a way that none of them is absent and all agree concerning each person’s cases. He adds other matters in the same letter that his predecessors had also established: namely, concerning those bishops whom it is not permissible to condemn, and the fact that a canonical synod may not be summoned without the authority of the Roman See; concerning canonical summonses to a synod; concerning postponements, which he orders to be granted for six months in criminal cases involving bishops; concerning the sort of persons accusers and witnesses ought to be; concerning the formal charge of a slanderer, which must always be made first; and concerning the fact that the examination of crimes must be conducted where the crimes themselves were committed. We have already clearly noted the remaining matters above in the decrees of his predecessors.

The aforementioned pope also wrote a decretal letter to Prosper, bishop of the first see of Numidia, and to the other orthodox bishops residing throughout the world (Letter 4), concerning chorepiscopi [*coepiscopi*]. [Col. 1189A] Among other things he says:

“Their institution is already excessively reprehensible and exceedingly perverse. For, if these men presume to claim something from the highest ministry of the priesthood, their action lacks every authority, appears contrary to the sacred canons, and whatever they have done in the ministry of the aforementioned high priesthood is empty and void. For we know that there are no more than two orders among the Lord’s disciples (Distinction 68, c. *Chorepiscopi*). From where this third order proceeded, we utterly do not know; and what lacks reason must be eradicated.

“For since they are not bishops—those who have been ordained by fewer than three bishops, or by one or two, are not called bishops—if they do not possess the name, how can they possess the office? Therefore the blessing that the aforementioned co-bishops [chorepiscopi] used to give by the laying on of hands before their prohibition seems to us to inflict a wound rather than bring salvation. For those who did not possess the apex of the episcopate—how could they give what they did not possess? There was nothing in the giver that the recipient could receive; and therefore they wounded more than they gave by any blessing those heads upon which they laid their hands, since they were unable to confer what had not been granted to them.

“Where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied; and once applied, the stain must be healed. That is, what was not legitimately done or conferred must be repeated if it is to be regarded as complete. For I cannot see how one could retain an honor received from another who had no legitimate power to give it, since one who did not possess episcopal honor cannot confer episcopal rights. Nor could they claim for themselves what they were not capable of receiving, because of the impediment that stood in their way.”

The aforementioned pope wrote another letter to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy (Letter 6), in which he prohibited the accusation of brothers by written documents. Among other things he says:

“‘The laws of the world require accusers to be present, not absent and represented by writings. Therefore the canonical decrees of the Fathers cry out, not once but very often, that neither accusations nor testimony can be presented in writing, and that no one may give testimony concerning other matters except those known to have been conducted in his presence (5, q. 2, c. *Relatum*). Likewise, whoever chooses to accuse another (3, q. 9, c. *Qui accusare*) must accuse him in person while present, and not through another [Col. 1189D], with a formal charge having first been made. No one must ever be judged before he has legitimate accusers present and has been given an opportunity to defend himself and clear the crimes.’”

He confirmed the judgment of the presbyter Jerome concerning the celebration of Mass: namely, that on Sunday no one should presume to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass after the third hour of the day. He ordered that psalms be sung in the church day and night.

### XL.—Saint Siricius (A.D. 385)

Siricius, a Roman by nationality, the son of Tiburtius, held the see for fifteen years, eleven months, and twenty-five days. He ordained thirty-two bishops, thirty-one presbyters, and sixteen deacons [Col. 1190A]. He departed from this world on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.

In a letter that he wrote to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona (Letter 1), he prohibited the rebaptism of those baptized by the Arians if they hastened to the Catholic faith, because the Apostle prohibits it (Ephesians IV), the canons contradict it, and the decrees of Pope Liberius sent to the provinces after the annulment of the Council of Rimini prohibit it. He asserts that they are to be joined to the Catholic assembly solely by the laying on of the hand of a bishop.

In the same letter he also affirms that at no time of year may anyone be baptized except on the Lord’s Day of Easter or Pentecost, unless the person is threatened by the danger of imminent death. Again, he orders that those who pass over to apostasy and are polluted by the worship of idols and the contamination of sacrifices [Col. 1190B] be cut off from the body and blood of Christ; but he commands that those who repent and turn to lamentation must perform penance during their lifetime, and that at the very end they must be granted the grace of reconciliation.

He also prohibits anyone from taking as wife a girl betrothed to another (27, q. 2, c. *De conjugali*), because the blessing that the priest bestows upon a woman who is to marry, if violated by transgression, is regarded among the faithful as something like sacrilege.

Concerning those who, after performing penance, return like dogs and pigs to their former vomit and wallowing, reclaim the military belt, and live incontinent lives (33, q. 2, c. *De his vero*), he decrees that, since they no longer have a refuge for repentance, they are to be joined to the faithful in prayer only within the church, but separated from the banquet of the Lord’s table [Col. 1190C]. Yet when they pass from this life, he orders that they be assisted with the provision of viaticum.

Concerning monks or nuns who first secretly polluted themselves through illicit intercourse and afterward, driven into the depths of despair by conscience, openly fathered children from their illicit unions, he ordered that they be expelled from the company of monasteries and the assemblies of churches. They were to be confined in their own workhouses, where they might be consumed in the purifying [*purgatorio* / *purificatorio*] fire of repentance, so that, at least at death, indulgence might come to their aid through the grace of communion, solely out of mercy.

Concerning priests and Levites (82, Distinction, c. *Plurimos*) who, after many years of their consecration, fathered offspring either from their own marriages or from shameful intercourse [Col. 1190D], and defended their crime on the grounds that in the Old Testament the ability to beget children had been granted to priestly ministers—for no one was admitted to God’s ministry except from the tribe of Levi—he ordered that mercy not be denied to those who confessed that they had fallen through ignorance, on this condition: that they remain in the office in which they were discovered, without any increase of honor, for as long as they live, provided that thereafter they strive to show themselves continent.

But those who attempted to defend themselves by an illicit appeal to privilege he deprived entirely, by apostolic authority, of every ecclesiastical honor, while forbidding them hope of attaining it in the future. And because men of untested character, including some who had had numerous marriages, were freely and without restraint aspiring to the aforementioned dignities, each according to his own inclination, he decreed by a general pronouncement what all the churches should follow and what they should avoid.

Namely, a man who had lived commendably from childhood until his thirtieth year, content with one wife—and she a virgin, and blessed by a priest with him—could be promoted through the several grades after the prescribed intervals, provided that he had lived irreproachably in each. But the cleric who had married either a widow or a second wife (Distinction 84, c. *Quisquis*) was immediately to be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical dignity, with only lay communion granted to him. He could retain that only if he possessed nothing else [afterward] on account of which he would lose it.

He excluded women from all clerics (Distinction 81, c. *Feminas*), except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted them to have living with them solely because of family necessities. He permitted monks (16, q. 1, c. *Monachos*) whom the seriousness of their conduct and the holy discipline of their life and faith commended to be added to the offices of the clergy, at the appointed times and with the individual grades duly observed.

He also decreed (Distinction 50, c. *Illud*) that, just as it is not permissible for any cleric to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no one may ever attain the clerical honor. For although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, they ought not to receive any instruments for administering the sacraments if they had been vessels of vices [Col. 1191C].

But because in such cases (Distinction 50, c. *Quicunque*), when they are reproved, the sole excuse usually offered is ignorance, he grants pardon, on this condition concerning penance, to any bigamist and to a husband of a widow who has been improperly promoted to any grade: deprived of all hope of promotion, he must remain permanently in the order in which he is found.

The aforementioned pope sent a decretal letter to the African bishops because of the many presumptuous acts that had arisen in his time (Letter 4). In it he ordered that no one should dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the Apostolic See—that is, the primate—because he says that a judgment is sound when it is reached by the opinion of many (Distinction 64, c. *Extra*). Likewise, no single bishop should presume to ordain another bishop, lest the benefit appear to have been conferred secretly, since it is clear that this was also defined in the Council of Nicaea (canon 4).

He also ruled that if anyone, after the remission of sins, had worn the belt of secular military service, he was not to be admitted to the clergy. Likewise, he ordered that a cleric must not marry a widow. Again, he ordered that a layman who had married a widow must not be admitted to the clergy.

He further ordered that no one should usurp the right to ordain a cleric from another church or receive one who had been expelled from his church; and that those coming from the Novatians and Montenses should be received by the laying on of hands, since they had been rebaptized. Moreover, in the same letter he warned and urged that priests and Levites should not have intercourse with their wives, because ministers engaged in the ministry are occupied with daily [Col. 1192A] necessities, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

The same pope of holy memory wrote another decretal letter to the orthodox living throughout the various provinces (Letter 4). Since many things contrary to ecclesiastical canon were being presumed, he ordered and warned that no unworthy and insufficiently examined person should be made a bishop, and that the priesthood should not be given to those whose faith, baptism, and life were unknown. Nor should neophytes or laymen be carelessly ordained deacons or presbyters, since the Apostle says: “Lay hands suddenly on no one” (1 Timothy V).

The aforementioned pope also wrote another letter to the Italian bishops (Letter 2), in which he informed them that he had condemned Jovinian, Epicurus, and their associates [Col. 1192B], who were abolishing the reward of virginity and condemning fasts.

### XLI.—Saint Anastasius (A.D. 398)

Anastasius, a Roman by nationality, the son of Maximus, held the see for three years and ten days. He ordained eleven bishops, nine presbyters, and five deacons.

He wrote a letter to the bishops of the regions of Germany and Burgundy, in which he gave a reasoned answer to their consultations. Namely, by apostolic authority he ordered and prohibited (On Consecration, Distinction 2, c. *Apostolica*) that, when the Gospels are being read in the holy church, priests and the others should presume to sit; instead, they should listen attentively to the Lord’s words with reverent bows and worship them faithfully.

Likewise, he prohibited a foreigner [Col. 1192C] from being admitted to clerical honor (Distinction 98, c. *Transmarinos*) unless he had been designated by the written attestations of five or more bishops, since many things commonly occur through underhanded dealing and therefore these matters must be guarded against with the utmost care.

He also ordered that the Manichaeans who existed at that time were not to be received and that no association with them was permitted until they had converted to the true faith. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.

### XLII.—Saint Innocent (A.D. 402)

Innocent, an Albanian by nationality, the son of Innocent, held the see for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days.

He wrote a decretal letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio (Letter 1), in which he instructed him in Catholic doctrine concerning many matters about which Decentius had consulted him. It begins as follows [Col. 1192D]:

“If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed Apostles, there would be no difference or variation in these orders and consecrations. But while each person considers that what he himself has thought proper to hold—not what was handed down—is to be maintained, the result is that different things appear to be held or celebrated in different places or churches, and scandal arises among the peoples. Since they do not know that the ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, they think either that these traditions do not suit them or their churches, or that a contradiction has been introduced by the Apostles or apostolic men. For this reason all must follow what the Roman Church observes, since there is no doubt that they received their beginning from it.”

He then explains what they should do in each of the matters about which Decentius had consulted him [Col. 1193A].

1. He orders, namely, that peace be given after the sacred mysteries have been completed (On Consecration, Distinction 2, c. *Pacem*), so that by this it may be evident that the people have given their assent to everything performed in the mysteries.

2. He also orders that the offerings first be commended in the Mass, and afterward the names of those whose offerings they are be recited.

3. Concerning the signing of infants, he says that it is clear that this may be done by no one other than a bishop, because, although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the apex of the episcopate (On Consecration, Distinction 4, c. *Presbyteros*).

4. He demonstrates with clear reasoning that one must fast on Saturday (On Consecration, Distinction 3, c. *Sabbato*). For if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we must not pass over Saturday [Col. 1193B], since it appears to lie between the sorrow of the Passion and the joy of the Resurrection. It is established that the Apostles were in mourning during these two days, and there is no doubt that they fasted so extensively during the two days mentioned that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments are not celebrated at all during them.

This practice must certainly be observed every week, because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated. If it is thought that one must fast only once, on a single Saturday, then surely Sunday and Thursday would likewise be celebrated only once during Easter.

5. Concerning the fermented bread that was prepared by the pope at Rome and sent through the acolytes to the titular churches on the Lord’s Day—since on that day the presbyters could not meet with him because of the people entrusted to them—he says that the day must not be made elsewhere among the parishes, because the sacraments must not be carried over a great distance [Col. 1193C].

6. Concerning those who have been baptized and afterward are seized by a demon, some illness, or an intervening sin, he says that they neither ought nor are able to be signed by a presbyter or deacon unless the bishop has ordered it. Hands must not be laid upon them unless the bishop has given authority for this to be done, especially because someone who is far away can often be brought to the bishop only with difficulty.

7. Concerning penitents (On Consecration, Distinction 3, c. *De poenitentibus*) who are performing penance for either serious or lesser offenses, he shows that, according to the custom of the Roman Church, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter, provided that no illness intervenes. If, however, someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair [Col. 1193D], his penance must be relaxed before the time of Easter, so that he does not depart from this world without communion.

8. Concerning the passage in the Letter of James, “Is anyone among you sick?” (James V), and so forth, he says that there is no doubt that it must be understood of the faithful who are sick, who may be anointed with holy oil. This oil, consecrated by the bishop, may be used not only by priests but by all Christians in their own need and that of their families; and what is unquestionably permitted to presbyters is certainly permitted to bishops (Distinction 95, c. *Illud*).

It was mentioned in connection with presbyters for this reason: bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot go to all the sick. But they may freely go to and anoint those whom they choose [Col. 1194A]. Yet this oil cannot be poured upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For if the other sacraments are denied to them, how can they be thought capable of receiving one kind of sacrament?

The aforementioned pope also wrote another letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen (Letter 2), because certain persons at that time, through ignorance or negligence, were not observing ecclesiastical discipline and were presuming many things that ought not to be presumed. In it he orders and commands:

1. No one may dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop (Distinction 64, c. *Extra*). For a judgment is sound when it is confirmed by the opinions of many. Nor may one bishop presume to ordain another bishop, lest the benefit appear to have been conferred secretly. This was also established and defined by the Council of Nicaea [Col. 1194B].

2. If anyone, after the remission of sins, has worn the belt of secular military service, he is prohibited from being admitted to the clergy.

3. He also ordered that, if cases or disputes should arise among clerics, whether of a higher or lower order (11, q. 1, c. *Si quae causae*), the quarrel should be settled according to the Council of Nicaea by assembling the bishops of that province. No one may, to the prejudice of the Roman Church, abandon the priests who by God’s will govern the Church in that province and rush to other provinces.

If anyone should presume to do so, he ordered that the man be removed from clerical office and judged by all to be liable for the injury. But if greater cases should arise, he ordered that, after episcopal judgment, they be referred to the Apostolic See, as the synod established [Col. 1194C].

4. He also decreed in the same letter, as Siricius had done, that a cleric must not marry a widow, lest, hindered by this impediment, he be unable to attain the priesthood.

5. He likewise ordered that a layman who had married a widow, whether before baptism or afterward, must not subsequently be admitted to the clergy, because he appears to be excluded by the same fault (Distinction 34, c. *Si quis*). For in baptism sins are forgiven, but the union with a wife already taken is not dissolved.

6. Likewise, he ordered that one who marries a second wife must not become a cleric, because it is written: “The husband of one wife” (1 Timothy III); and again: “Let my priests marry only once.”

7. He also ordered that no one should usurp the right to ordain a cleric from another church unless that cleric’s bishop, having been entreated, grants permission (Distinction 34, c. *Si quis*) [Col. 1194D]. The Council of Nicaea also established this (canons 16 and 17): that one church must not receive a cleric rejected by another.

8. He ordered that those coming from the Novatians or Montenses should be received by the laying on of hands, because, although baptized by heretics, they were nevertheless baptized in the name of Christ—except those who, after passing from us to them, were baptized by them. If these persons return to us in repentance, they are to be admitted after a prolonged satisfaction of penance.

9. He commands that it be observed altogether that priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives (Distinction 31, c. *Tenere*). For if a priest, whose constant duty is to pray and offer sacrifice, has been polluted by carnal desire [Col. 1195A], with what modesty will he presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience and merit will he believe that he can be heard, since it has been said: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus I)?

10. Concerning monks who have attained the clerical order (16, q. 1, c. *De Monachis*), he orders that they must not depart from their former way of life. Since they lived in a monastery, they must not now lose what they preserved for a long time merely because they have been placed in a better rank.

11. He also orders that men from the curial class—that is, those occupied with certain public functions and legally subject to recall to the curia—must not be admitted to the clergy (Distinction 51, c. *Frequenter*).

12. Concerning veiled virgins who afterward marry publicly or are secretly corrupted, he ordered that they must not be admitted to perform penance unless those to whom they had joined themselves have withdrawn from the world (27, q. 1, c. *Quae Christo*), because this rule is already observed concerning lay adulteresses. This judgment is extremely severe and greatly to be feared; in our time it had to be considerably mitigated because of the cases of many people. Otherwise, many, deprived of the salutary comfort of penance, would end their lives with unrepentant hearts.

13. But concerning virgins who have not yet been veiled (27, q. 1, c. *Ne vero*), although they have pretended to remain committed to virginity, he says that if they should happen to marry, they must perform penance for some period of time. For their promise was held by the Lord. If widows who depart from their commitment to widowhood have condemnation according to the Apostle (1 Timothy V), because they have made their first faith void, how much more do virgins deserve condemnation when they have tried to break faith with their earlier promise [Col. 1195C]?

1. The aforementioned pope also wrote another letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse (Letter 3—Distinction 82, c. *Proposuisti*). In it he replies that those deacons or presbyters whom the children they have fathered reveal to be incontinent must be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor, as Pope Siricius had also done; nor are they to be admitted to any ministry of this kind, which ought to be fulfilled only through continence.

2. But to those who have devoted themselves throughout their lives to the pleasures of incontinence and, only at the end of life, simultaneously request penance and restoration to communion—although according to the earlier custom penance was granted but communion denied—he ordered that communion be granted together with penance, so that, at least in their final hour, by the permission of our Savior, they might be rescued from eternal destruction [Col. 1195D].

3. But concerning those who either inflict torture alone or also pronounce capital sentences, he replies (23, q. 4, c. *Quaestitum est*) that nothing had been defined by the earlier authorities. This was because they remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that God’s minister had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. Thus he maintained the practice preserved down to his own time, lest he either overturn discipline or appear to act against the authority of the Lord (Rom. XIII).

He says that men do not associate with adulterous wives (32, q. 5, c. *Christiana*), just as wives themselves do the same with their husbands if the husbands commit adultery, for no other reason than that hidden sins do not receive punishment. Women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery as husbands accuse their wives. Therefore, when a husband’s offense remains hidden, no one is readily removed on the basis of suspicions; but he will be removed if his crime is discovered. Yet although the cause is equal, when proof is lacking the exercise of punishment sometimes comes to a halt.

4. But concerning the man who dictates petitions and asks rulers, on account of guilt, for someone’s death or blood, he says (23, q. 4, c. *Illud*) that the man is exempt from guilt, because rulers never grant such requests without investigation. Rather, they always refer the matters or crimes committed to judges, so that, once the case has been examined, they may punish. When the matter has been delegated to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case; and while the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the petitioner remains free from guilt.

6. But those who, after a repudiation, have joined themselves in marriage to another, he declares without doubt to be adulterers on both sides. For although the marriage may appear abandoned or dissolved, those cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers who hastened to another union while their wife was alive (Matt. XIX). Indeed, even the persons joined to such people appear to have committed adultery.

The aforementioned pope also wrote another decretal letter to Felix, bishop of Nuceria (epist. 4). In it, when Felix complained of the scarcity of clergy and said that he had some *murcos* [mutilos] and some digamists, the pope replied:

1. A man who has deliberately cut off part of his finger cannot, according to the canons, be admitted to the clergy; but one to whom this happened by some accident can become a cleric and cannot be expelled after having been found suitable (dist. 55, c. *Qui partem*). In the former, the will is judged; in the latter, accident has merited pardon.

2. He ordered that digamists, as was written above, must be entirely expelled.

3. He did not forbid the admission to the clerical order of those laymen (dist. 51, c. *Designata*) who, after baptism, had conducted themselves in such a way that their reputation was in no respect unstable; who had attached themselves to clerics and monks; who had known no concubine or mistress; and who had been vigilant in good works. But he prohibited the admission of those who had served in the army, had been occupied with secular lawsuits, or had administered secular affairs.

The same aforesaid pope, in the letter that he sent to the bishops Maximus and Severus (epist. 5), ordered that those priests who were said to have fathered children while in the priesthood should be placed before the tribunal. After the charges brought against those priests had been investigated, if they could be convicted, they were to be removed from priestly office, because those who are not holy cannot handle holy things (dist. 81, c. *Maximilianus*). In the same letter he also praised the layman who would not allow the Church to be polluted by such men.

The same often-mentioned pontiff, in the letter that he wrote to the bishops of Apulia, namely Macedonius and Marinus (epist. 6), commanded that, if it were established that a cleric had done penance for his crimes, he was to be removed from every clerical office (Col. 1197A)—that is, if after penance he attempted to advance to a higher rank. In the same letter he rebuked bishops who, while trying to show favor either to friends or to those who served them, violated religion and corrupted the orders. Thus it came about that unworthy men received ecclesiastical honors and were admitted to the clergy, although they did not deserve even an honorable place among the laity.

Likewise, in the letter that he wrote to the bishops established throughout Macedonia (epist. 7), he says:

“It ought not to seem burdensome” (35, q. 9, c. *Grave*) “to reconsider anyone’s judgment, because truth, more often disturbed, shines more brightly in the light; and evil, recalled for judgment, is condemned more severely by repentance [more gravely and without repentance]. It is a divine benefit that justice be reviewed repeatedly.”

Likewise, in the letter that he sent to Florentinus, bishop of Tibur (epist. 8), he ordered that the boundaries established by the Fathers ought not to be crossed, because it is wicked if one person invades what another has always possessed. He recalled that the aforesaid bishop had done this, because he had invaded another’s parish.

Likewise, in the letter addressed to Bishop Probus (epist. 9), he ordered that a woman who had returned from captivity be restored to her husband, who had already entered another marriage. For, with the support of the Catholic faith, he determined that the marriage established originally by divine grace was the true marriage, and that the union with a second woman, while the first wife was still alive and had not been expelled by divorce, could in no way be legitimate (34, q. 1, c. *Cum in*).

Likewise, in the letter that he wrote to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage (epist. 12), he says that he cannot express how deeply he grieves when he reads and hears that the Church, and especially bishops, are treated with such indignity and distress: when hands are laid on people too readily; when the chief priest is elected carelessly; and when clerics trained and honored according to the rule of ecclesiastical doctrine are rejected among Christ’s altars, as though it were wicked to reach the primacy through the proper order. For when laymen and monks are suddenly taken from anywhere and admitted to the fellowship of so great a priesthood, those from whom the choice ought to have been made appear to be despised, while those who force their way in contrary to order appear to be wrongly admitted rather than properly chosen.

Likewise, the same aforesaid pope wrote to Alexander, bishop of Antioch (epist. 1, or 20), and ordered that, if one province were determined by imperial judgment, the metropolitan bishops should nevertheless be counted only according to the former custom of the provinces. In the same letter he commanded him not to receive clerics of the Arians with any dignity of priesthood or ministry. For although their baptism is permitted to be regarded as valid, we do not believe that they possess the Holy Spirit through that baptism [unworthily received] and those mysteries; nor can they impart its fullness [*ex opere operantis*], which operates especially in ordinations.

By letter (epist. 21) he ordered Bishop Marcianus to receive into communion those clerics whom Bonosus is known to have ordained before he was condemned.

Likewise, he wrote to all the bishops assembled at the synod of Toledo (epist. 24), saying that something ought to be decreed, according to the tradition of the earlier authorities, concerning ordinations illicitly performed by the bishops of Spain—unless he took into account that very great disturbances would thereby be stirred up in the churches. After listing the acts that he knew had been performed unlawfully, he added:

“If we order each of these matters to be examined separately, we shall introduce no small disturbances or scandals into the Spanish provinces, which we wish to heal, under the pretext of zeal for correction. For this reason we think that these matters should rather be set aside.” But he ordered that care be taken so that such things would not be committed thereafter.

## XLIII—SAINT ZOSIMUS  
*(A.D. 417)*

Zosimus, a Greek by nationality, son of Abramius, was seated for one year, three months, and eleven days. He ordained eight bishops, ten priests, and three deacons. He was released from the prison of the body on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

He wrote a letter to Hesitius [Hesychius], bishop of Salona (epist. 1), in which, concerning monks whose solitude is greater than any crowd, and concerning laymen hastening to become bishops, he ordered that no one who had not been instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines according to the order established by the Fathers (dist. 36, c. *Qui ecclesiasticis*), and who had not been trained over a period of time in divine service, should dare in any way to aspire to the supreme priesthood of the Church. Not only was such ambition to be regarded as ineffective, but those who ordained him were also to be deprived of the order that they had presumed to confer contrary to the precepts of the Fathers (dist. 59, c. *Qui ecclesiasticis*).

## XLIV—SAINT BONIFACE  
*(A.D. 419)*

Boniface, a Roman by nationality, son of the priest Jucundus, was seated for three years, eight months, and seven days. During a dispute, he was ordained on the same day as Eulalius. This dissension lasted seven months and fifteen days among the clergy. Eulalius was ordained in the Constantinian basilica, Boniface in the basilica of Julius.

When the Augusta Placidia, residing at Ravenna with her son, the Augustus Valentinian, heard what had happened at Rome, she informed the Augustus Honorius, who was residing at Milan. Consequently, by imperial authority, both men were ordered to be expelled from the City. Later, however, Eulalius was entirely expelled and sent to Campania, because on Holy Saturday he presumed to perform the pontifical office contrary to the emperors’ edict, since he had been ordained in the Constantinian basilica. Boniface, however, with the consent and command of the emperors, was recalled to the City and firmly established in the see.

He ordained thirty-six bishops, thirteen priests, and three deacons. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

He sent a letter to the Gallican bishops (epist. 2), in which he ordered (3, q. 9, c. *Decernimus*) that a synod should be assembled within the province concerning Bishop Maximus, who, having been accused by the clergy of the city of Valence, had repeatedly evaded judgment. If he wished to appear in person, he was to answer the charges, trusting in his case; but if he neglected to appear, he was not to gain a postponement of the sentence through his absence. For it is evident that a man confesses his crime when, despite a postponement and repeated assignment of the judgment, he does not make use of his opportunity to clear himself.

During the time of the aforesaid pope, with his consent and approval, the Augustus Honorius established the following by a constitution concerning the Roman pontiff, so that the election might take place without ambition. He said (in the rescript to Boniface’s epistle 1):

“Finally, since your Blessedness has proclaimed this, we wish it to reach the knowledge of all the clergy: if anything should happen to your Holiness—as we do not wish—through the lot of human affairs, let everyone know that ambition must cease. And if two men should be ordained through rashness and contrary to law, neither of them will ever become a priest; only the one chosen by divine judgment and by the consent of all, from among the clergy through a new ordination, shall remain in the apostolic see.”

He also established that no woman or nun should touch or wash the consecrated *palla* (sacred cloth), or carry incense through the church, except ministers. He also prohibited a slave or a man bound to the municipal curia from becoming a cleric.

## XLV—SAINT CELESTINE  
*(A.D. 423)*

Celestine, a Roman by nationality, son of Priscus, was seated for eight years, ten months, and seventeen days. He ordained forty-six bishops, thirty-two priests, and twelve deacons. He passed to Christ on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

He sent a letter to the Gallican bishops (epist. 4), in which he admonished them to rebuke those priests who brought undisciplined questions before the public, preached things contrary to the truth, and cultivated dissension in the churches. They were not to allow such men freedom to speak according to their own will, because a disciple ought not to claim doctrine for himself as an insult to his teachers. He likewise says that bishops must not permit the aforementioned priests to utter such things, because in such cases silence is not free from suspicion: the truth would come forward if falsehood were displeasing. “For,” he says, “the matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence.”

Likewise, he sent another letter to the bishops established in the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne (epist. 2), in which he ordered them no longer to tolerate the following practice: namely, that those who believed they were to complete the faith of Holy Scripture not through the Spirit but through the letter should stand in church clothed in a pallium and girded around the loins, like burning lamps, holding a staff in their hands. The untrained minds of the faithful ought not to be led into such practices.

Likewise, in the same letter he ordered that penance not be denied to anyone who requested it at the end of life (26, q. 6, c. *Agnovimus*), because true conversion to the Lord must be judged more by the mind of those at the end of life than by the amount of time, as the prophet declares: “When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII).

He also prohibited anyone who had not been initiated into the ecclesiastical ranks in due order (dist. 59, c. *Ordinatos*) from reaching the office of bishop, as well as anyone said to have been polluted by incest with virgins. Whoever ordained such a man would not obtain the dignity of the episcopate, just as the man ordained would not obtain it.

He also ordered that each province should be content with its own metropolitan, and that each man, content with the boundaries granted to him, should presume nothing in another province. Nor should strangers and outsiders be preferred over those who had earned distinction in their own churches, to the exclusion of those who had earned a good reputation through the testimony of their fellow citizens (dist. 61, c. *Ne emeritis*).

He also ordered that no bishop be imposed on unwilling people (c. *Nullus*) unless the agreement and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order had first been sought. Only then should someone be chosen from another church if no worthy man could be found among the clergy of the city in which the bishop was to be ordained—a situation that, he said, they did not believe would occur. Those men must first be rejected, so that outsiders might rightly be preferred; and each man should receive the fruit of his service in the church in which he had spent his whole life through every office.

Clerics were to have the freedom to resist if they saw themselves being overburdened; and if they recognized that men were being forced upon them from elsewhere, they were not to fear rejecting them.

In the same letter he also ordered that illicit ordinations be avoided, saying:

“No layman, no digamist, and no man who is or has been the husband of a widow shall be ordained, but only one who is irreproachable and such as the apostle chose” (I Tim. III).

Further on he says:

“And if any illicit ordinations have been carried out, let them be removed, since they cannot stand and cannot evade our investigation.”

Likewise, the aforesaid pope sent a letter to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria (epist. 3). In it he ordered that no priest be permitted to be ignorant of his canons (dist. 38, c. *Nulli*), or to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers.

He also ordered that no one admit a layman to the clerical order.

He further taught that the people are to be instructed (dist. 62, c. *Docendus*), not followed; and that, if they do not know what is permitted and what is not, we must admonish them and must not give them our consent:

“Whoever attempts to try what is forbidden will feel that the discipline of the apostolic see will by no means be absent. For the man whom we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone must necessarily be punished with severity appropriate to the rules.”

## XLVI—SAINT SIXTUS III  
*(A.D. 432)*

Sixtus III, a Roman by nationality, son of Sixtus, was seated for eight years, eight months, and nineteen days. He ordained fifty-two bishops, eighteen priests, and twelve deacons.

A certain nobleman named Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 1199D] See volume I of the Councils, p. 703], whom Bassus, a former consul, was attempting to deprive of his free status and his own estates, was so strongly assisted by Sixtus before the Augustus Valentinian that, protected by the emperor’s written warrant, he retained both.

The aforesaid pontiff was accused before the Augustus Valentinian by the aforementioned Bassus and by Marinianus, to whom the pontiff had denied an estate that Crescentius had given to the Roman Church in Sicily. He was accused of having violated a consecrated woman named Chrysogona. The Augustus and his mother were so inflamed by this that they suspended communion with the aforesaid pontiff, and a large part of the people joined them.

Therefore the Augustus Valentinian ordered a synod to be assembled by the authority of the aforesaid pontiff. Although he could have escaped by another course, Sixtus wished to remove suspicion and cleared himself before fifty-six bishops. He did not do this merely for his own vindication, but in order thereby to provide a pattern and example for others who might be unwilling to do so. For it is clear from the written record and the order of the synod that the accuser must prove the crime, and that anyone who brings forward charges that cannot be proved must understand that he will suffer loss.

Bassus, however, was condemned by the aforesaid synod and proscribed by the Augustus Valentinian.

Sixtus sent a letter to the Eastern bishops (epist. 1), in which he wrote back to them concerning by whom and in what manner the aforementioned quarrel against him had been stirred up, and by what means and with what outcome it had been concluded. In the same letter he added many provisions by which bishops, thereafter protected, might safely reject unjust opposition and the accusations of malicious men. We do not insert them here because we remember that the same matters have often been recorded above.

During the time of the aforesaid pope there was in Jerusalem a certain bishop named Polychronius [Note: [Col. 1201D] See volume I of the Councils, p. 705]. Led by the folly of old age into pride, he claimed to be the universal pontiff. He recklessly, and not without payment, ordained as Levites and priests clerics who came to him from whatever province. He consecrated no bishop without a worthy gift. If he was asked to consecrate a church in that region, he did not grant the authorization of his authority unless he had received ten pounds of gold as compensation.

Therefore Pope Sixtus assembled a synod of eight bishops at Rome and brought forward Bishop Euphemius, who had accused Polychronius of these matters, so that Euphemius might confess the same things before everyone.

After this had been done, they sent three bishops, an equal number of priests, and two deacons to Jerusalem. Once the bishops of that region had been assembled [seventy-six], and forty witnesses had been brought forward who, in accordance with Euphemius’s accusation, proved all these things concerning Polychronius to be true, they condemned Polychronius and also Euphemius. The reason was that Euphemius had accused his own pontiff, who had consecrated him.

Later, however, because of the compassion and almsgiving that Polychronius had shown to his besieged fellow citizens, Sixtus recalled him and restored him to his former see.

## XLVII—SAINT LEO I  
*(A.D. 440)*

Leo, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Quintianus, was seated for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. He ordained one hundred and ninety-five [one hundred and eighty-five] bishops and eighty-one priests. He died peacefully on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

He sent a letter to all the bishops throughout Campania and to those established in all the provinces (epist. 1), in which he prohibited many things that, as we have often noted above, his predecessors had also prohibited.

Specifically, he ordered that men who had not been able to obtain freedom from their masters, and those bound to some hereditary status, should not be advanced to the height of the priesthood (dist. 54, c. *Admittuntur*), unless perhaps the request or consent of those who claimed some authority over them had been obtained.

2. He also ordered, by the authority of the apostolic see, that anyone who had been admitted from among the husbands of widows or those who had contracted numerous marriages should be barred from ecclesiastical offices and from the title of priest.

3. He decreed that severe punishment should be inflicted on clerics who practiced usury and sought to grow rich through lending at interest (14, q. 4, c. *Nec hoc*). He also warned that, just as no cleric may practice usury in his own name, so no one should attempt to do so in another’s name, because it is an indecent crime to devote one’s wrongdoing to another person’s advantage (dist. 46, c. *Sicut*).

Likewise, in another letter that he wrote to all the bishops of Italy (epist. 2), he ordered them to diligently investigate the Manichaeans everywhere and separate them from the peoples entrusted to them.

He also wrote a letter to all the bishops established throughout Sicily (epist. 4), in which he rebuked those who differed from the custom of the Roman Church in that sacrament which, among the other sacraments of the Church, is primary in order of execution [*ordine exsecutionis*], namely baptism. They celebrated the sacrament of baptism more frequently on the day of the Epiphany than during the season of Easter, believing that there was no difference between the day on which Christ was worshiped by the Magi and the day on which he rose from the dead.

Yet it was specifically through the death of the Crucified One and the resurrection of the dead One that the power of baptism created a new creature from the old, so that in those who are reborn both the death of Christ and his life might operate (de Cons. d. 4, c. *Proprie*; and c. *Si quis*). For the threefold immersion imitates Christ’s three-day burial, and the raising from the waters resembles his rising from the tomb.

The very nature of the rite therefore teaches that the proper day for the general celebration of grace is the day on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose. To this observance is also rightly added the sacred solemnity of Pentecost, arising from the coming of the Holy Spirit and depending upon the central event of the Easter festival (de Cons. d. 4, c. *Duo tempora*). He prohibited the mixing of other days into this observance.

The same aforesaid pope wrote a letter to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia (epist. 3), in which he admonished him not to receive into Catholic communion priests, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order who sought to return to the Catholic faith that they had lost long before (2, q. 7, c. *Saluberrimum*; 1, q. 1, c. *Omnis*) before they openly confessed, without any ambiguity, that they condemned both their errors and the authors of those errors.

For the faults of lower orders must be attributed to no one more than to negligent and careless rulers, who often nourish great pestilence while they pretend not to apply the necessary medicine.

Likewise, in response to the questions of Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, he wrote a letter (epist. 95), advising him to apply spiritual medicine to the sick. Citing Scripture, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccles. VII), he urged him to deal more gently with those who seemed to have exceeded the proper measure of punishment through zeal for chastity, lest the devil, who deceives adulterers, rejoice over those who avenge adultery.

Because the aforesaid bishop, troubled by excessive opposition, greatly desired release from the burdens of the episcopate and said that he preferred to spend his life in silence and leisure rather than remain in the duties entrusted to him, the aforesaid pope admonished him to remain in the work committed to him and in the labor assigned to him, to hold justice steadfastly, and to extend clemency generously.

Sins are to be hated, not people (dist. 86, c. *Odio*). The arrogant must be corrected, the weak tolerated; and what must be punished more severely in sinners should not be inflicted with a savage spirit, but with the spirit of a physician.

Likewise, in the same letter:

1. “No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor established [consecrated] by the provincial bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan” (dist. 62, c. *Nulla*). Since disputes often arise concerning an improperly received honor, who could doubt that what is not shown to have been given should in no way be granted to these men?

If, however, some clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination took place with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, it may be considered valid, so that they may remain in those churches. Otherwise, the consecration must be regarded as void, since it was founded neither in the proper place nor supported by authority.

2. He also says that it is contrary to ecclesiastical custom (dist. 50, c. *Alienum*) that those consecrated to the dignity of the presbyterate or the rank of the diaconate should receive, for some crime of their own, a remedy of penance through the laying on of hands.

3. He likewise says that the same law of continence applies to the ministers of the altar as to bishops and priests.

He also says (dist. 31, c. *Lex*) that not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir.

4. He says that marriage contracts among freeborn people and among equals are legitimate (32, q. 2, c. *Non omnis*). Since the society of marriage was established from the beginning (27, q. 2, c. *Cum societas*) in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church (Eph. V), there is no doubt that a woman in whom the nuptial mystery is shown not to have existed does not belong to a marriage.

Therefore, if someone gives his daughter in marriage to any man who has a concubine, this is not to be understood as giving her to a married man—unless perhaps the first woman appears to have been made free, provided with a lawful dowry, and honored by a public marriage.

Likewise, women joined to men by paternal decision are free from guilt if the women previously kept by those men had not been wives in marriage (Col. 1204A), because one thing is a married woman and another is a concubine.

5. To cast a slave woman away from one’s bed (32, q. 3, c. *Ancillam*) and take a wife of established free status is not a duplication of marriage but an advancement in honor.

6. Concerning those who receive penance during illness (de Poenit. d. 7, c. *Nemo*) but, once they recover, refuse to perform it, he says that their negligence must certainly be blamed but not entirely despaired of. They should be stirred by frequent exhortations to carry out faithfully what they necessarily sought.

7. Concerning those who receive penance when already failing and die before communion, he says:
