“The case of these people must be reserved for the judgment of God, in whose hand it lay that the death of such persons was not postponed until the remedy of communion” (24, q. 2, c. *De communione*). “But we, who did not give them communion while they were alive, cannot give it to them when they are dead.”

8. Concerning those who, pressed by excessive pain, ask that penance be given to them (de Poenit. d. 1, c. *Poenitentia*), but, when the priest arrives to give what they requested, excuse themselves if the pain has ceased and refuse to accept what is offered, he says:

“This pretense may arise not from contempt for the remedy but from fear of committing a more serious offense. Therefore, when penance is earnestly requested, it must not be denied.”

9. Concerning those who have professed penance but have begun to litigate in court, he says:

“It is one thing to demand what is justly owed” (de Poenit. dist. 1, c. *Aliud*), “and another to despise it out of love for perfection. But one who asks forgiveness for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from many lawful things. Therefore, if a penitent has a case that he perhaps ought not to neglect, he should seek ecclesiastical judgment rather than a secular court.”

10. Concerning those who engage in business during penance or afterward (de Poenit. dist. 5, c. *Qualitas*), he adds:

“The nature of the profit either excuses or condemns the merchant, because there is both honorable gain and shameful gain. Nevertheless, it is more useful for a penitent to suffer losses than to bind himself to the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the transaction between seller and buyer.”

11. “For it is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules when Paul says: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular business’ (II Tim. II)” (c. *Contrarium*). Therefore, the man who wishes to entangle himself in worldly service is not free from the snares of the devil.

12. Concerning those who performed penance in adolescence, or through fear of death or the danger of captivity, he says that they did something pardonable [Note: [Col. 1203D] In withdrawing from the more perfect continence] if afterward, through fear of falling into sexual incontinence, they chose union with a wife. Yet he says that he is not establishing a rule in this matter, but judging what is more tolerable, because nothing is more fitting for one who has performed penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body.

13. Likewise, a monk’s commitment, undertaken by his own decision and will (20, q. 3, c. *Propositum*), cannot be abandoned without sin, because what one has vowed to God one must also repay (Ps. XLIX). Therefore, if after abandoning the profession of solitude he has fallen into military service or marriage, he must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance. Even if military service is innocent and the marriage can be honorable, abandoning the choice of better things is a defection.

14. Likewise, girls who, not compelled by the authority of their parents (20, q. 1, c. *Puellae*) but by their own free judgment, have undertaken the commitment and habit of virginity, if they later choose marriage, are transgressors, even if the grace of consecration has not yet been conferred.

15. Concerning those who have already been consecrated, if they later marry, there can be no doubt that a great crime has been committed, since both the commitment has been abandoned and the consecration violated.

16. Concerning children left behind by Christian parents, if no indications exist by which they may be understood to have been baptized (de Cons. d. 4, c. *Si nulla*), action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they perish openly. For reason does not allow something to be regarded as repeated when it is not shown to have been done.

Likewise, if children have been captured by enemies and, when they return, both they and the others are uncertain about their baptism, it seems that what is not known to have been conferred should be conferred upon them. For there is no rash presumption where there is diligent piety.

17. But concerning those who come from elsewhere and know that they have been baptized (de Cons. d. 4, c. *Hi de quibus*), but confess that they do not know to what faith those who baptized them belonged, he says that they should not be baptized, but joined to the Catholics by the laying on of hands.

18. Those who were baptized as children and were captured by pagans, if they return and seek communion, may be cleansed by the laying on of hands alone if they merely participated in the meals of the pagans and ate sacrificial foods. But if they worshiped idols, or were polluted by homicide or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

The aforesaid pope also wrote another letter to Anastasius, primate of Thessalonica (epist. 82). In it he first rebuked him because he had unjustly afflicted Atticus, metropolitan of Egypt, and deprived him of ecclesiastical office. The reason was that Atticus had delayed appearing when summoned, offering only an excuse of illness; and Anastasius had incited the prefect of Illyricum against Atticus to increase his misery, although the Roman see had not entrusted him with the power to depose a bishop. The aforesaid pope testified as follows:

“We entrusted our authority to your charity in such a way that you were called to share the burden of concern, not the fullness of power.”

2. Because Anastasius had exceeded the measure of his office, the pope prudently instructed him point by point about what he ought to preserve after cutting away every excess of usurpation. He said:

“Therefore” (25, q. 2, c. *Igitur*), “according to the holy canons, we decree that metropolitan bishops are to retain inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor through presumption.”

3. Concerning the appointment of bishops, he ordered the following rule to be observed (dist. 32, c. *Omnium*): no layman, no neophyte, no husband of a second wife, and no man who has or has had a widow as wife is to be ordained bishop. When the election of a bishop is being considered, the man who has been requested unanimously by the agreement of the clergy and the people is to be preferred to all others.

4. If the votes of the parties should happen to be divided among different persons (dist. 63, c. *Si forte*), the metropolitan’s judgment is to prefer the one supported by greater influence and merits. Yet no one is to be ordained against the will of the people and those who have not requested him, lest a city either despise or hate a bishop whom it did not desire, and become less religious than it ought because it was not permitted to have the man it wanted.

5. When a metropolitan has died (dist. 63, c. *Metropolitano*) and another has been substituted in his place, the provincial bishops must come together in the metropolitan city. After the will of all the clergy and citizens has been examined, the best man from among the priests or deacons of that church is to be chosen.

He ordered the provincials to report the name of the metropolitan, and the metropolitan likewise to report the person of any bishop to be consecrated, to the knowledge of the primate, so that the ordination, which ought to be properly celebrated, might be confirmed by his authority.

6. Concerning councils of bishops (dist. 18, c. *De conciliis*), he ordered that, as the holy Fathers beneficially established, they should be celebrated twice each year.

7. He also ordered that a bishop who, despising the modesty of his own city, aspired to a greater one (7, q. 1, c. *Si quis*) and transferred himself there should be expelled from the foreign chair, and should lose his own as well.

He further ordered that, for the preservation of perfect continence, even subdeacons should not be permitted a carnal marriage.

8. He also prohibited anyone from receiving another’s cleric against the will of that cleric’s bishop (19, q. 2, c. *Alienum*), and prohibited anyone from soliciting such a cleric unless an agreement had been reached between the giver and the receiver.

[Col. 1206C] Likewise, the blessed and most discerning pope sent a letter to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, at his request (Letter 77), in which, after applying a prudent remedy in view of temporal necessities, he decreed as follows:

1. Women who, after their own husbands had been captured and carried away into captivity, had meanwhile married other men (34, q. 1 and 2, c. *Cum per*) must be restored to their former husbands when those husbands return from captivity, because it is written that a woman is joined to a man by God (Prov. XIX), and, “What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. XIX). Nevertheless, the man who took the place of her husband, who was already thought no longer to be alive, is not to be judged culpable or regarded as an invader of another’s rights.

2. But if some women were so captivated by love for their later husbands that they preferred to remain with them rather than return to their lawful marriage, he said that they deservedly ought to be censured, so that they might even be deprived of ecclesiastical communion; for from an excusable circumstance they chose the contamination of a crime, showing that, through their lack of self-restraint, they had approved for themselves what a just remission could have expiated.

3. Concerning those who were compelled by fear or led astray by error into repeating baptism, and who are known to have acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith (26, q. 7, c. *Tempora*), he determined that they should be treated with such moderation that, through the remedy of repentance and the imposition of the bishop’s hand, they might recover the unity of communion.

When many illicit acts were being committed in the ordinations of priests in the territory of the bishop of Caesarea and in that province, the aforementioned pope wrote to all the bishops of the same province (Letter 85), reproving them (dist. 61, c. *Miramur*) because the presumption of those who sought office and popular tumult had such power among them that the pastoral dignity and governance of the Church were entrusted to any unworthy persons. He said that this was not to provide for the peoples but to harm them; nor was it to confer a kingdom [governance], but to increase danger, because the integrity of those who preside is the safety of their subjects, and where obedience is secure, there the form of doctrine is sound.

But a principate (1, q. 1, c. *Principatus*) that either sedition has extorted and conferred, or ambition has seized—even if it gives offense in character rather than in actions—is nevertheless dangerous because of the example of its very beginning; and it is difficult for those things to reach a good outcome that were begun with an evil beginning. Therefore, what is contained in general regulations must not be permitted in anyone’s case; nor is that honor to be considered legitimate which has been conferred contrary to the commands of divine law.

Likewise, below: “All ecclesiastical discipline is dissolved and every order is disturbed when, in the Church, those who have undertaken no ministry obtain, through the perverse judgment of the electors, an undue principate.”

Likewise, farther below in the same letter: “If any bishops should consecrate such a priest as it is not permissible for him to be (1, q. 1 and 25, q. 2, c. *Si qui*), even if they somehow escape damage to their own honor, they shall nevertheless have no further right of ordination, nor shall they ever participate in that sacrament which, having neglected divine judgment, they unworthily bestowed.”

[Col. 1207C] Likewise, he wrote another letter to Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii (Letter 89), in which he instructed him concerning those who request penance at the point of death, as follows:

“It ought to have been the order of your concern that you first confer with your metropolitan concerning the matter that seemed to require inquiry. Nevertheless, so that the uncertainty of the person seeking advice may in some way be instructed concerning what the ecclesiastical rule holds about the state of penance, I will not remain silent” (dist. 1, *On Penance*, c. *Multiplex*).

“The Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, entrusted authority to the leaders of the Church, so that they might both grant the practice of penance to those who request it [confess it], and admit those same persons, cleansed by salutary satisfaction, to communion in the sacraments through the door of reconciliation.

“But if any one of those for whom we implore the Lord, having been prevented by whatever obstacle [Col. 1207D] from receiving the gift of present indulgence, should fall away from it, and should end his temporal life according to human condition before reaching the remedies that have been established, he cannot obtain, after being stripped of the flesh, what he did not receive while remaining in the body.”

And farther below: “But for those who, in a time of necessity and pressing danger, urgently seek the aid of penance and immediately implore reconciliation (26, q. 6, c. *His qui*), neither satisfaction should be forbidden nor reconciliation denied; for we can impose neither measures nor times upon the mercy of God, with whom true conversion suffers no delays in pardon, as the Prophet says: ‘When he has turned’ (Ezek. XXXIII),” and so forth.

“If, even after losing the power of speech, they make their request through unimpaired signs of understanding, the practice of penance and the grace of communion must not be denied them. And if they have been so weakened by the force of illness that they cannot, in the presence of a priest, indicate by signs what they had requested shortly before, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them, so that they may obtain together both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation. Nevertheless, the rule of the fathers’ canons must be preserved concerning those who have sinned against God by abandoning the faith.”

The same pope, in a letter addressed to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia (Letter 84), says: “If anyone refuses to satisfy salutary precepts, whether he is a cleric or a layperson, let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church.”

Likewise, in a letter sent to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria (Letter 79), he ordered that on solemn occasions, whenever the basilica to which the people were going had been filled by the presence of a new congregation, the sacrifice should be offered as often as that occurred.

Likewise, in a letter sent to all the bishops of Campania (Letter 78), he forbade that those requesting penance be required to recite their profession publicly (*On Penance*, dist. 1, c. *Quamvis*), because it is sufficient for them to disclose the sins of their consciences to priests alone in private confession. For that confession is sufficient which is first offered to the Lord and then also to the priest, who approaches the sins of penitents as an intercessor.

Likewise, in the letter that he wrote to the bishops of the region of Gaul (Letter 86), he affirms that chorepiscopi possess no authority different from that of presbyters. For *chore* means “village”; hence chorepiscopi are understood as village presbyters [Col. 1208C], who can neither sign foreheads nor reconcile any penitent during Mass.

## XLVIII.—SAINT HILARY  
*(A.D. 461)*

Hilary, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Crispinus, sat for six years, three months, and ten days. He ordained twenty-two bishops, twenty-five presbyters, and six deacons. In Rome he assembled a synod of many bishops (Roman Synod, chapters 2, 3, 4), in which, with the approval of all, he confirmed that no one who had a non-virgin wife, or who had married a second time, or who was ignorant of letters, or who had suffered the loss of any bodily member, or who was among the penitents, should dare aspire to sacred orders.

Likewise, he decreed that whatever illicit act anyone had committed, or had found committed by his predecessors, he should condemn if he wished to avoid his own danger. Likewise, he generally forbade anyone ever to presume to appoint a successor for himself.

Likewise, in another letter that he sent to Bishop Ascanus (Letter 3), he permitted those bishops who had been consecrated without the consent of the metropolitan to remain in office, saying:

“Although those who were ordained priests without the knowledge and consent of Your Affection ought to have been removed together with those responsible for them, nevertheless, so that we may not decree anything harsh in so great a necessity, we wish those who have become bishops to remain in this way, provided that they are not found liable under the apostolic commands and the statutes of the holy Fathers, and provided that henceforth nothing contrary to ecclesiastical discipline is perpetrated, as has happened up to now.”

[Col. 1209A]

## XLIX.—SAINT SIMPLICIUS  
*(A.D. 467)*

Simplicius, a Tiburtine by nationality and son of Castinus, sat for fifteen years, one month, and eighteen days. He ordained thirty-six bishops, fifty-eight presbyters, and eleven deacons. He died on the sixth day before the Nones of March. He established that presbyters should remain at Saint Peter’s, Saint Paul’s, and Saint Lawrence’s because of baptism.

He wrote a letter to John, bishop of Ravenna (Letter 2), in which he reproved him for having forcibly consecrated Gregory as bishop, saying that the person who abuses the authority entrusted to him deserves to lose the privilege granted to him (11, q. [Col. 1209B] 3, c. *Privilegium*). And farther below in the same letter:

“We declare that, if hereafter you presume anything of this kind and should perhaps think of making anyone, whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon, against his will, you should know that the ordinations of the Church of Ravenna and of Emilia will be taken away from you.”

Likewise, he wrote another letter (Letter 3) to the bishops Florentinus [Florentius], Equitius, and Severus, in which he ordered that the entire power of ordaining be taken away from Gaudentius, priest of the Church of Aufinum, because he had carried out illicit ordinations contrary to the statutes of the canons and to his own commands; and he instructed Severus to perform in the aforesaid church the office of which Gaudentius had been convicted of abusing himself.

Likewise, he ordered that the Church ministries which had been alienated by the aforesaid Gaudentius [Col. 1209C] should, at the insistence of the aforementioned brother, namely Severus, be recovered by compulsion from the usurper (12, q. 2, c. *De redditibus*).

## L.—SAINT FELIX III  
*(A.D. 483)*

Felix, a Roman by nationality, son of Felix the presbyter, of the title of Fasciola, sat for eight years, eleven months, and eighteen days. He ordained thirty-one bishops, twenty-seven presbyters, and five deacons. He lived until the time of King Theodoric.

In a letter that he sent to all the bishops established throughout the various provinces (Letter 1), he ordered that bishops, presbyters, and deacons who had been rebaptized, whether voluntarily or under compulsion, should, if they repented, remain in penance until the day of their death, so that they should not even attend the prayer of the catechumens, and that lay communion should be restored to them only at death.

But concerning the others (On Consecration, dist. 4, c. *Eos quos*), namely clerics, monks, nuns, or laypersons of either sex, who were shown to have undergone a repetition of baptism because they had been compelled by violence and danger, or who by some contrivance claimed that they were not held by the stain of such a crime, he decreed that they should remain in penance for three years and be received into the fellowship of the sacrament through the imposition of hands. In all things this condition was to be observed: none of them was to be permitted to enter the ecclesiastical service.

He also established that it must be especially guarded against that any bishop or presbyter should receive, in another’s city, someone subject to another priest, or someone claiming to have been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or presbyter; or that a presbyter be received in a parish or a bishop in a city.

In the time of the aforementioned pope, the emperor Glycerius [Note: [Col. 1209D] On Glycerius, see Baronius under the year of the Lord 474], because at that time the episcopate was for the most part obtained more by money than by merit, established an edict, saying:

“We have enacted this as a law to endure forever: whoever reaches the episcopate with the support of powerful persons and possesses secularly what he acquired secularly shall know that, when the limits of one year have been completed, he is to be deprived of the episcopate. Those who consecrate such a man shall likewise be expelled from the priesthood and shall pay the corresponding penalties for their reckless consecration.

“Let the citizens of each city also know that they will be expelled from residence in the country to which they give such evil counsel, and stripped of their property and handed over to our treasury—those whom the acclamations of ambitious persons have stirred up, not the dignity of the person that ought to be sought, but the venality that ought to be punished.”

[Col. 1210B]

## LI.—GELASIUS  
*(A.D. 492)*

Gelasius, an African by nationality and son of Valerius, sat for four years, eight months, and eighteen days. He lived during the times of King Theodoric and the Augustus Zeno. He ordained sixty-seven bishops, thirty-two presbyters, and two deacons. He departed to Christ on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

He sent a general decree to all the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily (Letter 1), concerning the moderate regulation of ecclesiastical institutions according to the character of the times (dist. 55, c. *Priscis*). He ordered that these institutions be regularly observed whenever no necessity arising from circumstances or times pressed upon them.

But because, in his time, war and famine had consumed the clerical offices in many parts of Italy, so that everywhere the service of ministers was failing, he balanced the decrees of the ancient canons in such a way that he permitted any cleric to be promoted from the first to the last rank within the space of one year (dist. 77, c. *Si quis*). A layperson, however, could be promoted within one year and six months, provided that none of the matters prohibited by the judgment of the canons stood in the way.

He established that these regulations, which the necessity of the times required to be enacted, were the ancient form of the fathers’ canons, because a new law is not proposed against the decisions of the elders when provision is made for remedying an accidental deficiency.

Likewise, he prohibited the exaction of any payment for baptizing and signing the faithful (1, q. 1, c. *Baptizandis*), and ordered that anyone discovered to have committed such an act should face the danger of losing his own honor.

Likewise, he ordered presbyters to observe their proper measure (dist. 95, c. *Presbyteros*): namely, that they should not make chrism, should not perform the signing, and, in the presence of any bishop, should not presume either to pray or to sit unless ordered to do so by the bishop; nor should they make acolytes or subdeacons.

He also ordered deacons (dist. 93, c. *Diaconos*) to observe their proper measure: namely, that they should not dare to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless extreme necessity compelled them to do so when these were situated far away—a practice that is also often permitted to Christian laypeople.

Likewise, he prohibited them from sitting in the presbytery or from having the right to exercise, in the sight of a bishop or presbyter, the privilege of distributing the sacred Body, even when those persons were absent.

He says that it is unworthy for anyone, whether a pontiff or one of the succeeding orders, to reject the observance that the apostolic see strives to maintain with pious and devout purpose (On Consecration, dist. 1, c. *Basilicas*).

Likewise, he ordered that the ordinations of presbyters and deacons take place only on prescribed days (dist. 75, c. *fin.*): namely, during the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months. He also decreed that they should be celebrated around evening on the Saturday at the beginning of Lent and on the middle Saturday of Lent.

He prohibited virgins (20, q. 1, c. *Devotis*) from receiving the veil except on Epiphany, during the white garments of Easter, or on the feasts of the apostles, unless, having been seized by illness, they themselves should plead that they not leave this world without receiving that gift.

He also prohibited what neither divine authority has chosen nor the form of the canons has prescribed, and ordered that ecclesiastical assistance be brought to them in such a way that nothing illicit be committed.

Likewise, he ordered (dist. 54, c. *Generalis*) that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor any of those known to preside over monasteries, should retain a slave or an agricultural tenant against the will of the owners, or attach such a person to ecclesiastical service or religious congregations, unless the owners’ consent had first released them under written testimony. Otherwise, they should have no doubt that they would incur the danger of losing their own honor.

[Col. 1211C]

Likewise, concerning clerics who devote themselves to commerce (14, q. 4, c. *Clerici*), he says:

“Accordingly, let such men know that they must henceforth abstain from shameful profits of this kind, and cease from every device and desire of any sort of commerce; or, whatever rank they occupy, they must immediately be compelled to withdraw from clerical offices.”

Likewise, he says that those who are entangled in demons and other afflictions may not handle the sacred mysteries (dist. 35, c. *Usque adeo*).

But those who rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after a commitment dedicated to God, mingle incestuous and sacrilegious unions, he orders to be immediately expelled from sacred communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance. Yet if such persons should depart from this world after repenting, he permitted the Viaticum to be given to them.

He does not deny second marriages to laypeople, but entirely forbids those same persons to enter the clerical college.

Likewise, he says:

“Whoever, abandoning his own Church, thinks that he should transfer to another without any existing cause, and is rashly received and promoted, shall not escape the established provisions of the revered canons and precepts concerning such presumptuous persons—whether he himself or the person who receives him.”

Likewise, farther below he says:

“Those who are shown to have purchased sacred dignity with money, though unworthy by their merits, must be excluded when convicted. They do not perpetrate such a crime without danger, because the condemnation of Simon, which sacred reading attests, involves both the giver and the receiver” (Acts VIII).

He also reproved those who presumed to consecrate new basilicas in the name of the dead without the command of the apostolic see (On Consecration, dist. 1, c. *De locorum*). He did this because at that time many were even building structures in the names of deceased unbelievers and boldly establishing them with sacred processions.

He also strongly reproved and harshly censured, declaring that they incurred the loss of their own honor, those priests who caused or permitted women to minister at sacred altars and to undertake all the services assigned exclusively to the ministry of men, though such service does not belong to their sex.

Likewise, he ordered that four portions be made both of income and of the offerings of the faithful (12, q. 2, c. *Quatuor*): one for the pontiff, another for the clerics, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the buildings. He taught that the restoration of the holy places clearly demonstrates that this fourth portion has truly been assigned to that work, because it is wicked for a prelate, when sacred buildings are left destitute, to turn to his own profit the expenses designated for them.

Moreover, although the portion assigned to the poor may appear to have been distributed by him for divine purposes, it must nevertheless be proclaimed by present testimony and not be silenced by the praises of a good reputation.

And, lest the matters he had previously stated be neglected, he adds:

“Let no cleric (2, q. 2, c. *Quapropter*) believe that he will be free from this offense if, having seen a bishop, presbyter, or deacon transgress in these matters that we have set forth as salutarily to be followed, he does not immediately take care to report it to our ears, provided that appropriate proofs are duly supplied, so that punishment may be inflicted on the transgressor and the others may be prohibited from offending.”

[Col. 1212C]

Likewise, in a letter sent to the bishops of Sicily (Letter 2), he says:

“The authority of our predecessors has issued this ruling (16, q. 3, c. *Praesulum*): bishops have power over the resources of the Church for its governance, but in such a way that they must distribute stipends to widows, orphans, and the poor, as well as to clerics.”

Likewise, farther below:

“If the resources of the Church, and likewise the dioceses possessed by certain bishops, are claimed by right, the claim is limited to what the thirty-year law has settled; for the authority of the emperors has issued this provision, that after thirty years no one may appeal concerning what the time fixed by the laws has excluded.”

The same pope briefly noted what the Catholic Church accepts from the divine Scriptures and what it ought to avoid.

Of the Old Testament he lists: one book of Genesis; one book of Exodus; one book of Leviticus; one book of Numbers; one book of Deuteronomy; one book of Joshua son of Nave; one book of Judges; one book of Ruth; four books of Kings; two books of Chronicles; one book of Psalms; three books of Solomon; one book of Proverbs; one book of Ecclesiastes; one book of the Song of Songs; one book of Wisdom; one book of Ecclesiasticus; one book of Isaiah; one book of Jeremiah; one book of Ezekiel; one book of Daniel; one book of Hosea; one book of Amos; one book of Micah; one book of Joel; one book of Obadiah; one book of Jonah; one book of Nahum; one book of Habakkuk; one book of Zephaniah; one book of Haggai; one book of Zechariah; and one book of Malachi.

Among the ancient histories: one book of Job; one book of Tobit; two books of Ezra; one book of Esther; one book of Judith; and two books of Maccabees.

Of the Scriptures of the New Testament he receives four books of the Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; likewise one book of the Acts of the Apostles; fourteen Epistles of Paul; one book of the Apocalypse of John; and seven Catholic Epistles: two of the apostle Peter, one of James, three of John, and one of Jude, the apostle called Zelotes.

Likewise, the holy Roman Church does not prohibit the acceptance of the holy Council of Nicaea, in which Arius was condemned; the holy Council of Constantinople, in which Macedonius was likewise condemned; the Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was condemned; and the Council of Chalcedon, [Col. 1213B] in which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices, were condemned. It also preserves and accepts any councils instituted by the holy Fathers after the authority of these four.

The following works of the holy Fathers are also received in the Church: the works of Caecilius; Cyprian, martyr and bishop; Gregory of Nazianzus; Basil, bishop of Cappadocia; Athanasius of Alexandria; John of Constantinople; Theophilus of Alexandria; Cyril of Alexandria; Hilary of Poitiers; Ambrose of Milan; Augustine of Hippo; Jerome the presbyter; Prosper; and the letter of Pope Leo to Flavian, bishop [Note: [Col. 1213] On this letter of Blessed Leo, see Covarrubias, Book IV of the *Variarum*, chapter 16, no. 6]. If anyone has disputed against its text down to a single iota and has not reverently accepted it, let him be anathema.

Likewise, he decreed that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who have deviated in no respect from the holy Roman Church should be read.

Likewise, the decretal letters written by the Roman pontiffs, and the acts of the holy martyrs. Some of these are rejected by the Roman Church because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown.

Likewise, the Lives of the Fathers Paul and Antony and of all the hermits, which the most blessed Jerome nevertheless composed.

Likewise, the Acts of Pope Sylvester, although the writer’s name is unknown.

Likewise, the writing concerning the Discovery of the Holy Cross and the other writing concerning the Discovery of the Head of John the Baptist are to be received and read with caution.

Concerning Rufinus and Origen we hold the same opinion that Jerome held and recorded concerning them.

The Church does not entirely reject the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea and his books of Ecclesiastical History because of their exceptional information.

Likewise, he praises the history of Orosius and the works of Sedulius and Juvencus.

But he says that the following works are apocryphal and must be entirely rejected:

First, the Council of Rimini; likewise, the Itinerary of the Apostle Peter, which is attributed to Clement; the Acts of the Apostle Andrew, the Apostle Thomas, the Apostle Peter, and the Apostle Philip; the Gospel of the Apostle Thaddeus; and those of James the Less, Barnabas, Thomas, Bartholomew, and Andrew; and the Gospels falsified by Lucian and those falsified by Hesychius [Ysithius].

[Col. 1214A]

Likewise, the book concerning the infancy of the Savior; the book concerning his birth and concerning Mary and the midwife; the book called *The Shepherd*; the books composed by Leucius; the book called *The Foundation*; the book called *The Treasure*; the book concerning the daughters of Adam; the Acts of Thecla and the Apostle Paul; the book called *The Book of Nepos*; the Book of Proverbs bearing the name of Sixtus; the Revelation called that of the Apostle Paul; the one called that of Thomas; and the one called that of Stephen.

Likewise, the book called *The Passing*, that is, the Assumption of Saint Mary; the book concerning the Penance of Adam; the book concerning Og, the giant; the book called *The Testament of Job*; the book called *The Penance of Jamne and Mambre*; the book called that of the Apostle Jude; the book called *The Canons of the Apostles*; the book called *The Lots of the Apostles*; and the book called *The Physiologus*, written by heretics and marked with the name of Blessed Ambrose.

Likewise, the History of Eusebius Pamphilus; the works of Tertullian, Lactantius, Africanus, Postumianus, Gallus, Montanus, Priscilla, Maximilla, Faustus the Manichaean, Commodianus, another Clement of Alexandria, Cyprian of Tharsus, Arnobius, Thonius, Cassian the presbyter of Gaul, Victorinus, bishop of Poitiers, Faustus of Riez in Gaul, and the blind Frumentinus; *Contende* [perhaps *Commentary on*] *Christ*; the letter of Jesus to Abgar and of Abgar to Jesus; the passion of Quiricus, Julitta, and George; the writing called *Solomon’s Contradiction*; and all phylacteries written not with the names of angels but with those of demons.

These works, and others like them, were taught by Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Bonosus, and those who fell away through similar error; also Montanus with his most obscene followers; Apollinaris, Valentinus or Manichaeus, Faustus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabatius, Callistus, Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinianus [Jubianus], Pelagius, Julian of Eclanum, Caelestius, Maximianus, Priscillianus, Nestorius of Constantinople, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter, and another Peter, one of whom stained Alexandria and the other Antioch; Acacius [Acatius] of Constantinople with his associates; and all the heresies that they or their disciples, or schismatics, taught or wrote, whose names are not retained at all.

The aforementioned Pope Gelasius professes that these were not merely rejected but also expelled from the entire Catholic Roman Church and condemned, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, under the unbreakable bond of anathema.

The aforementioned Pope Gelasius, in the treatise *On the Bond of Anathema*, sets forth many reasonable arguments against those who say that a person bound by the bond of anathema can already be released, because the bond of anathema is an unbreakable and perpetual bond. Among other things, he says:

“Those who are in error are bound by the judgment of error; and as long as they remain in it, they are in no way absolved, just as the error itself in which they are cannot be absolved. For error itself never merits pardon, but the person who has truly been without it and withdraws from participation in it does.

“Therefore, as long as error is in them, they retain their condemnation and are never absolved, because error always deserves punishment. Those who participate in it either always share its punishment, if they do not cease to persist in the same error, or, if they have withdrawn from it, they will consequently be as far removed from its punishment as they have become alien to the error and separated from participation in it.

“For the same punishment is assigned to the person who errs: as long as he remains one who errs, he is constrained by the same punishment, because one who errs cannot exist without punishment. This punishment is perpetual for the person who errs and is never to be released for as long as he persists in being one who errs.

“But if he ceases to be one who errs, the punishment assigned to the erring person is not perpetual for one who no longer errs, that is, for one who has become different from the person to whom it was assigned. It can not only fail to be perpetual; it can no longer even be punishment, for the person to whom it was assigned is no longer there. It was assigned to the erring person, not to one who does not err.

“What was assigned to the erring person is perpetual and perpetually constrains the erring person; it can no longer hold one who does not err.”

Likewise, farther below:

“What ought reasonably to be considered in the judgment concerning Acacius is this: if it was said, ‘You shall never be released,’ it was nevertheless not added, ‘even if you repent, even if you withdraw from this error, even if you cease to be a transgressor.’ Therefore it is clear that the words ‘never to be released’ were spoken of one who remains such as he is when bound, not of one who has become different from the person who was bound.

“Just as he would have been free from the obligation if he had been free from the cause of the obligation, so he would certainly exist as absolved, insofar as he would no longer appear unable to be released by necessity of the sentence pronounced. Having become different and free from the obligation, he would be absolved; and the sentence fixed concerning such persons would in no way be made unbreakable.

“But because he neither sought this himself nor, when seeking it, was cast aside, he himself made the sentence unbreakable in his own case, by choosing to remain such as he truly could not be absolved while he remained, and by willing to become such a person as could not be permitted to remain in that state.”

Likewise, farther below in the same work he says:

“For an inferior see cannot absolve a superior one. Therefore only the superior can fittingly absolve the inferior.”

Likewise, in the memorandum of Faustus, the master serving in the office of envoy, he says:

“They propose that pardon be granted to them. Let it be shown (22, q. 2, c. *Legatur*) whether, from the beginning of the Christian religion, pardon was ever granted except to those who corrected themselves; or at least let an example be given from any pontiffs in the Church of God, from the apostles themselves, or finally from the Savior himself.” But nowhere is it read or said under this sky that the words of such persons were, ‘Grant us pardon, while we nevertheless remain in error.’”

Likewise, farther below:

“We read that Christ raised the dead (Matt. IX; Mark V; John XI), but we do not read that he absolved the dead in error. And to the blessed Peter the apostle, the one who alone certainly possessed the power to do this, he principally commanded: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. XVI). ‘On earth,’ he says; for in this commission he never said that a dead person was to be absolved. Therefore, what has never been done we fear even to conceive in our minds, knowing that it cannot be entirely excused in divine judgment.”

Likewise, farther below:

“It is not lawful for us to enter into a contest with people of another communion, since divine Scripture warns us: ‘Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition’ (Titus III), knowing that such a person is perverse and condemned by his own judgment.”

Likewise, farther below:

“Guilt from the past can be remitted, with correction unquestionably following. For if a perversity that is to remain thereafter is allowed [or: pretended], the announcement is not the kindness of the one who remits but the assent of the one who consents.”

[Col. 1216B]

Likewise, the aforementioned pope, in the letter he sent to the emperor Anastasius, says (dist. 95, c. 2):

“There are, Emperor Augustus, two things by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. The burden of the priests is so much heavier in these matters because they must render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.

“They may be assailed by human prescriptions, though they have been established by divine judgment; but they cannot be overcome by the power of anyone.”

Likewise, you have read: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVII).

## LII.—SAINT ANASTASIUS II  
*(A.D. 497)*
Anastasius, a Roman by nationality, son of Peter, held the see for one year, eleven months, and twenty-two days [Col. 1216C]. He lived during the reign of King Theodoric. He ordained sixteen bishops and twelve priests. He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December. In a letter that he sent to the emperor Anastasius, among other things he proves that those whom Acacius baptized or ordained even after his condemnation were in no way touched by any share in the injury, saying:

“For, according to the custom of the Catholic Church (Dist. 19, chap. *Secundum*), let the breast of Your Serenity recognize that none of these persons—whether those whom Acacius baptized or those whom, according to the canons, he ordained as priests or levites—is touched by any share in injury on account of the name of Acacius, so that perhaps the grace of the sacrament, handed down through an iniquitous person, might appear less secure. For even baptism, although it is far removed from the Church, whether it has been administered by an adulterer or by a thief, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift: because that voice by which it is declared and said, ‘This is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire’ (Matt. III), excludes every stain of human pollution” [Col. 1216D].

To prove the same point he adds:

“Judas, too, although he was sacrilegious and a thief, whatever he did among the apostles caused no detriment to the benefits entrusted to them according to their dignity, though those benefits had been given through an unworthy man.”

Again, below, on the same subject:

“Whatever any minister in the Church appears to perform in the exercise of his office for the advancement of human beings—all of this is sustained by the effect of divinity as it brings it to completion; and so it is with the one through whom Christ speaks. Paul affirms: ‘I planted, but the Lord gave the growth’ (1 Cor. III). And this man, whose name we say ought to be withheld, by administering good things badly harmed only himself. For the inviolable sacrament that was given through him obtained for others the perfection of its power” [Col. 1217A].

But if the curious suspicion of some extends so far that they imagine that, after the judgment pronounced by Pope Felix, the sacraments that Acacius usurped were subsequently ineffective, and consequently fear for those who received the mysteries conveyed either in consecrations or in baptism, lest the divine benefits should appear void, let them remember that the foregoing treatment prevails similarly in this matter also. For he did this only after he had been condemned under the usurped title of priesthood; and, while the mysteries retain their power, the guilty person did not thereby harm others. For this too applied to him, concerning whom the Davidic trumpet sings:

“Nevertheless God will crush the heads of his enemies” (Ps. LXXXVII), etc. [Col. 1217B].

For pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others. Therefore, since he had usurped the name of priest while condemned, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head; for it was not the people, who knew [or: thirsted for] his gift in the mysteries [ministries], who were excluded, but only the soul that had sinned, which by a just judgment would be liable to punishment for its own offense. The abundant authority of Scripture everywhere bears witness to this [or: this instruction].

From the communion of the aforesaid pope, as is read in the *Acts of the Roman Pontiffs*, many of the clergy of the city of Rome withdrew. This was because he had entered into communion, without their counsel, with Photinus, a deacon of Thessalonica, who belonged to the communion of Acacius; and because he secretly wished to restore Acacius, but, struck by divine will [Col. 1217C], was unable to bring this about.

## LIII.—SAINT SYMMACHUS (A.D. 498)

Symmachus, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Fortunatus, held the see for fifteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days. He ordained one hundred and eighteen bishops, ninety priests, and sixteen deacons. He lived during the reign of King Theodoric and the time of Emperor Anastasius.

Symmachus and Laurentius were ordained in a dispute on the same day: Symmachus at the Lateran, Laurentius in the church of the Blessed Mary. Since the revolt arising from this disagreement could not be settled among the parties themselves, both were sent to Ravenna for royal judgment. Symmachus, however, was restored to and confirmed in the see by the judgment of King Theodoric, because the larger and more worthy part of his clergy and people had consented to his election [Col. 1217D]. Laurentius was later appointed bishop of Nuceria by Symmachus, out of consideration for mercy.

But a year and four days after the day of his ordination, certain men, moved by jealous hostility, denounced him to the king on charges of adultery and many other offenses. To support this accusation they suborned false witnesses, recalled Laurentius, and caused him to consecrate the chrism. The clergy and people were again divided: some adhered to Symmachus, others to Laurentius. Then, as though to suppress the force of the aforementioned dissension, certain Romans brought this about, and Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum, was sent by the king to Rome as visitor of the apostolic see [Col. 1218A].

Meanwhile massacres and murders were being committed everywhere. For whichever clergy or laypeople, even virgins, who were communicating with Symmachus fell publicly or secretly into the hands of their persecutors were killed or afflicted with wounds and beatings. Only Faustus, the former consul, resisted on the side of Symmachus and the Church.

Compelled by this necessity of danger, Symmachus, with the king’s consent, convened a synod (the Roman Synod), at which one hundred and fifteen bishops were present. With the king’s agreement and as ecclesiastical law required, since the accusers had been unable to prove anything against Symmachus from the charges brought against him, they unanimously judged him free and acquitted of the charges. They likewise condemned Laurentius of Nuceria and Peter of Altinum as men who had invaded the Roman see while the pope was still alive [Col. 1218B]. This confessor of Christ departed this life on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

In order to extinguish for future times the exceedingly harmful presumption arising from frequent canvassing for office, the stripping of the Church, and the clashes among the people—which the greed of those improperly desiring the episcopate had very often produced—this pope established in a synod [Note: [Col. 1217] Roman Synod II. See vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 329]:

“If any priest (Dist. 79, chap. *Si quis*), deacon, or cleric, while the pope is alive and without consulting him, attempts either to lend his signature or to take an oath beforehand concerning the Roman pontificate, or promises something in return for a definite support, or deliberates and decides on this matter in private meetings [Col. 1218C], let him be deprived of the dignity of his position or of communion.

“But if, God forbid, the pope’s unexpected death should occur (Dist. 79, chap. *Si transitus*), so that he was unable beforehand to decide concerning the election of his successor, then, if the election of the entire ecclesiastical order has inclined toward one person, let the elected bishop be consecrated. But if, as usually happens, different factions should arise among those concerning whom the dispute has emerged, let the judgment of the majority prevail. Nevertheless, let the one who, having been caught by a promise, has made his decision concerning the election without sound judgment be deprived of the priesthood.”

In a letter that the aforesaid pope wrote to Bishop Caesarius, he answered many of the latter’s questions, saying:

1. “We do not permit possessions that each person has given or left to the disposal of a particular church (16, q. 1, chap. *Possessiones*) to be alienated under any title, through any sale, or by any argument whatsoever, unless perhaps necessity should persuade us to give them to clerics because of their worthy services, to monasteries for the sake of religion, or certainly to pilgrims; and even then, so that they may enjoy these things not perpetually but temporarily.

2. “In the same letter he warns that those who strive to approach the priesthood by means of the promised possession of ecclesiastical property should be deprived of the fulfillment of such desires.

3. “He vehemently condemns abductors of widows or virgins (36, q. 2, chap. *Raptores*), pursuing with especially severe hostility those who attempt, willingly or unwillingly, to unite consecrated virgins to themselves in marriage [Col. 1219A]; he orders that such men be suspended from communion.

4. “He forbids widows (27, q. 1, chap. *Neque*) who have remained in a religious vocation through daily observance to pass over to marriage. The same applies to virgins who have spent many years living in monasteries.

5. “He also decrees that no one is to be permitted to approach the honor of the episcopate through canvassing (1, q. 1, chap. *Nullus*), and that he is not to employ powerful persons as supporters, nor compel clerics or citizens, by fear of any kind, to subscribe to a decree made on his behalf, nor encourage them with any rewards (1, q. 6, chap. *Si quis*). No decree is to be drawn up without the presence of the witness [or: visitor], whose testimony may be confirmed by the unanimity of the clergy and citizens.”

In another synod (the Fifth Roman Synod), the same pope composed decretal commands concerning the offerings of the faithful [Col. 1219B] and many other matters, saying:

“It is altogether fitting that everyone carefully observe that no one presume to seize offerings of the faithful, or attempt to possess or retain them without the consent and will of the bishop in whose parish they are known to be. For many, mindful of themselves, have given from their resources, for the remission of their sins and in exchange for eternal life, certain movable and immovable goods to churches by written instruments, and have given them to God their creator to be held perpetually.

“These things, and others like them, are held by various people who fear God less with such deadly cunning that another person’s offering becomes their ruin; nor can they perceive in their hearts the day of judgment while they delight in the heat of excessive greed. Therefore let such a judgment be made concerning them that either they be regarded as manifest heretics, because they divide the Church of God, and as anathematized and banished from the Church of God; or that, through satisfaction to the Church, they be admitted to penance and thereafter, according to ecclesiastical rules, to reconciliation, and, if found worthy, to communion [Col. 1219C].

“Again: Whoever, without the order of his own bishop, presumes thereafter to possess and retain in any place property entrusted to the Church and offered to the Lord, and, once the truth has been discovered, conceals it or refuses to restore it, is first to be barred by the bishop of that place from the thresholds of the same [church—perhaps: ‘from the threshold of the church by the bishop of that place’]. Provision must nevertheless be made that a clear admonition precede vengeance, and that the one who has unjustly taken away the usurped property, or unjustly retains what was taken away, restore it with equity supported by the laws. But if he neglects this, and necessity compels it, then at last duly exercised priestly discipline is to strike the robber [Col. 1219D].

“Again, below: It is exceedingly unjust and a great sacrilege that whatever anyone has bestowed upon or left to a venerable church, either for the remedy of sins or for the salvation or repose of their souls, should be transferred or converted to another purpose by those to whom it is especially fitting to preserve these things—that is, by Christians and people who fear God, and above all by rulers and the principal men of the regions.

“Therefore whoever has failed to foresee these matters and has sought, accepted, possessed, unjustly defended, or retained estates handed over to churches contrary to what is written, unless he quickly corrects himself, is to be struck with anathema by which God in his anger strikes souls; and let anathema rest upon the one who receives, the one who gives, and the one who possesses [Col. 1220A].

“Again, generally (16, q. 1, chap. *Generaliter*): Whoever presumes to confiscate, claim, or seize the property of the Church by dangerous aggression or his own assault, unless he corrects himself immediately through satisfaction to the Church concerned, is to be struck with perpetual anathema. Likewise, those who have retained the property of the Church by the order or gift of rulers or certain powerful persons, or through some invasion or tyrannical power, and have left it as an inheritance to their sons or heirs, unless, after being admonished by the bishop and recognizing the truth, they quickly return God’s property, are to be struck with perpetual anathema. For wounds that do not respond to remedies must be cut away with the sword (16, q. 1, chap. *Ferro*).

“Again, below: The Catholic Church defends everything that is irreprehensible. Therefore it is not lawful for an emperor (Dist. 10, chap. *Non licet*) or for anyone who guards piety to presume to do anything against the divine commandments, or to undertake anything that conflicts with evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic rules. For an unjust judgment (11, q. 3, chap. *Injustum*) and an unjust decree arranged by judges through fear of or command from the ruler have no force; nor will anything stand that has been done against evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching or constitution, or against that of the holy Fathers. Whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics will be completely annulled” [Col. 1220B].

## LIV.—SAINT HORMISDAS (A.D. 514)

Hormisdas, a Campanian by nationality, son of Justus, held the see for nine years and fourteen days. He lived during the reign of King Theodoric and the time of Emperor Anastasius, from the consulship of Senator to the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius [Col. 1220C]. He ordained fifty-five bishops and twenty-one priests. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of August as a defender of the Catholic faith.

With the consent and advice of King Theodoric, he sent his legates to Greece, giving them instructions to absolve, under the condition of satisfaction, the Greeks who, because they had shared communion with Peter of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople, were bound by the bond of anathema. They accomplished nothing, because Emperor Anastasius refused to agree to the statement of the true faith, since he himself was also an Eutychian. Wishing, therefore, to incline the Roman legates toward his error in faith, he attempted to corrupt them by offering gifts. But they rejected the gifts and insisted that satisfaction for communion with heretics had to be made to the Roman see [Col. 1220D].

The emperor, inflamed with fury, expelled them through a small door, put them aboard a dangerous ship, and sent them back, ordering that they enter no city, lest they should at least be able, while passing through, to show the letters concerning the faith to Catholics. But when he later learned from his associates that they had displayed the letters throughout all the cities, he was angered and is said to have written to the Roman pontiff, saying among other things:

“We wish to command, not to be commanded.”

But at that very time he was struck by a thunderbolt from heaven and died. After him, the orthodox Justin assumed the empire. With his assistance, the Greeks later repented of the error of Acacius and returned to communion with the apostolic see [Col. 1221A]. Hormisdas organized the clergy and instructed them in the psalms.

In a letter that he sent to all the bishops of Spain (Letter 4), he clearly showed that care must be taken in ordaining bishops, saying:

“It is fitting that those who must preside over people requiring correction should be irreprehensible, and that nothing be lacking in the person in whom resides the highest point and substance of religious discipline. Let each person consider the price of the Lord’s flock, so that he may know what merit the shepherd who is to be appointed ought to possess.

“The one to whom the governance of the Church is entrusted ought to demonstrate his life by a long period of probation.

“He who must pray for the people ought to be more corrected than the people.”

He also forbids a benefice to be purchased with money through the laying on of hands, which is believed to belong to the Lord [or: to be divine], because it ought to be kept before one’s eyes how Simon Magus, wishing to buy the Holy Spirit with money, was struck by the apostles’ condemnation (Acts VIII).

Concerning the one who does not sell but consents to the seller, he adds:

“What does it profit him not to be polluted by his own error, if he gives his consent to one who is in error? Without doubt, both the one who has his own sin and the one who follows another’s sin act against the commandments. The greedy mind resists desire in vain if it does not also resist fear” [Col. 1221B].

In another letter, which he sent to the priests, deacons, and archimandrites of Coelesyria, he says concerning clerics caught in adultery:

“Behold [Col. 1221C], it is most clearly established that, according both to the titles of the ancient Fathers transmitted by Pope Saint John and to the judgment of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, and also, as the Gallican canons appear to contain, clerics caught in adultery, whether they have confessed themselves or have been convicted by others, cannot return to the rank of honor. If there are any who are not at all pleased by the severity of the holy Fathers stated above, let them know that they are criticizing or condemning their judgments. For this is not mercy in them; rather, such kindness is hostile to justice—namely, to caress criminals and leave their wounds untreated until the day of judgment.

“But if we see them performing the most severe penance for many years, we ought both to consult their salvation and to preserve the statutes of the canons. When, however, neither contrition nor humility nor earnestness in praying or weeping appears in some of them, we can recognize how great their negligence and their security hostile to the soul would be if they returned to their former honor [Col. 1221D]: believing that God dismissed them without a worthy performance of penance in the same way that priests appear to have indulged them.

“I truly say that those very people whom we see being indulged through dangerous and false mercy, when they come before the tribunal of Christ to be condemned for such great sins, will bring charges against us ourselves, saying that, because we feared the harshness of their words or gladly accepted their false blandishments and dangerous flatteries, we allowed them to remain in their sins by uselessly indulging them, or even allowed the sins themselves to increase. We did not remember what is written in the Old Testament: ‘When one person sins, the anger of God rages against all’ (Num. XVI, 22) [Col. 1222A].

“Concerning such people, Blessed Cyprian the martyr says: ‘He who caresses the sinner with flattering words supplies fuel for sinning; he does not restrain offenses but fosters them.’”

Again, the same pope says below:

“I altogether dare not place myself in this danger, because my merits are not such that I should presume to take the sins of others upon myself, nor do I possess such eloquence that I could plead before the tribunal of Christ against so many and such priests who established the canons.”

Again, the same pope adds:

“If clerics who return to their own wives are suspended from office, and bigamists are not ordained, but, if they have been ordained, are deposed, how will one who has committed adultery be able to return again to the rank of honor?

“Nevertheless, he does not say that he denies the mercy that says, ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner’ (Ezek. XXXIII, 11) [Col. 1222B], and other passages of this kind. Rather, he most firmly believes that whoever performs penance until the end of his life will not only receive pardon but will also attain eternal life” [Col. 1222A].

Concerning clerics who return to their wives, Saint Faustus says in his letter:

“A consecrated man who still wishes to perform the office of a husband has lost grace.”

Again, the aforesaid pope says below:

“I greatly fear and tremble before the condemnation that Eli the priest deserved to receive because of his foolish indulgence. Because he lightly chastised his sons and was unwilling either to beat or to excommunicate them, both the sons were killed on a single day, thirty thousand of the people were slain, the Ark of the Testament was carried into captivity, and he himself, falling backward and breaking his neck, died [Col. 1222C], and his name was erased from the book of life.

“By contrast, Phinehas, moved by zeal for God, killed two adulterers together and freed the entire people of God from God’s anger. He does not say this so that those resembling the men mentioned above ought to deserve bodily death, but so that they may beware lest, after bodily death, they come to punishment.”

## LV.—SAINT JOHN (A.D. 523)

John, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Constantine, held the see for two years, eight months, and sixteen days. He lived during the reign of King Theodoric and the time of the Catholic Emperor Justin. He ordained fifteen bishops.

For the Catholic religion and on Theodoric’s behalf in a matter of state, he came to Constantinople. There, with Emperor Justin’s support, he consecrated the churches of the Arians as Catholic [Col. 1222D]. When Theodoric heard this—for he too was a heretic—he was inflamed with fury and burned to destroy all Italy by sword and fire because of the Arian churches, of which there were many in Italy, and which Pope John had ordered to be consecrated as Catholic everywhere. Before the pope’s return, he detained and killed two exiled Catholic men, Symmachus and Boethius.

He detained the pontiff himself, after his return, in custody at Ravenna. There, harshly afflicted, he eventually died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January. But on the ninety-eighth day after the death of the aforesaid pope, the heretical king himself was struck by a thunderbolt of divine power and, dying suddenly, freed Italy.

John sent a letter to Bishop Zacharias in which, having been consulted about certain matters, he instructed him, saying among other things:

“It is unjust to judge rashly about the hidden heart of another, and it is sinful to accuse on suspicion one whose works appear to be nothing but good.”

In the same letter he adds what has often been said: namely, that sheep ought not to accuse their shepherd except on account of the faith; and that the bishop himself can neither be summoned nor judged before what has been taken away has been restored to him by law. We therefore consider this matter to be passed over here.

## LVI.—SAINT FELIX IV (A.D. 526)

Felix, a Samnite by nationality, son of Castorius, held the see for four years, two months, and twelve days. He was ordained by order of King Theodoric and without opposition [Col. 1223B]. He ordained twenty-nine bishops, fifty-five priests, and four deacons. He died on the Ides of October, while Athalaric was reigning.

He wrote back to many bishops established throughout various provinces, answering them concerning the consecration of churches and the celebration of Masses, as follows (On Consecration, distinction 1, chap. *Sicut non*):

“It is clear to all who know the precepts of the New and Old Testament that [Masses] ought not to be celebrated anywhere except in places consecrated to the Lord, unless there is great necessity.”

He sets out those precepts and, having set them out, says:

“If the Jews did this, much more ought we to build, adorn, and consecrate temples, and celebrate Masses nowhere except in places consecrated by bishops to God, nor offer sacrifices to the Lord unless the greatest necessity demands it. It is better not to sing or hear Mass than for it to take place in places where it ought not to take place” [Col. 1223C].

He affirmed that the solemnities of the dedications of churches and of priests should be celebrated every year. In the same letter he says that the Lord himself gave examples, since he came to the feast of the dedication of the temple (John X), and that the books of Kings show that the *encaenia*—the dedication festivities—are to be celebrated for eight days after the dedication of the temple had been completed (3 Kings VIII).

Concerning the consecration of churches, he commanded:

“Whenever there is doubt, and neither a certain document nor reliable witnesses exist by whom the consecration is known, know without any doubt that the churches are to be consecrated. Nor should such hesitation cause deterioration [or: be made a deterioration] through repetition, since what is not known to have been done is not shown to have been repeated.”

## LVII.—BONIFACE II (A.D. 530)

[Col. 1223D]

Boniface, a Roman by nationality, son of Dehabentinus [Sigibuldus], held the see for two years and twenty-two days. He lived during the reign of the heretical King Athalaric and the time of Emperor Justin.

After dissension had arisen among the clergy and senate, he was ordained in a disputed election together with Dioscorus. Dioscorus, however, died not long afterward. Boniface, having thus obtained the see peacefully, as though condemning Dioscorus, refused to receive into communion the clergy who had favored Dioscorus unless they first made satisfaction through penance for the bond of anathema.

Afterward, having convened a synod, he issued a decree that his successor should be elected by him, and he ordered that the decree be secured by writing and oath [Col. 1224A]. Since this had been established contrary to the canons, it was annulled for legal reasons by the assembly in another synod of bishops; and the written document drawn up for that purpose was consumed by fire.

He wrote a letter to Eulalius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, in which he indicated that the Carthaginian Church had returned to communion with the Roman Church, from which it had separated since the time of Aurelius. For Aurelius, formerly bishop of the aforementioned church, began, with his colleagues and at the devil’s instigation, to grow proud against the Roman Church during the times of our predecessors Boniface and Celestine. Boniface died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

## LVIII.—JOHN II (A.D. 531)

[Col. 1224B]

John, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus, held the see for two years, four months, and six days. He lived during the reign of King Athalaric and the time of Emperor Justinian. He ordained twenty-one bishops and fifteen priests. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

He sent a letter to Bishop Valerius in which, by reasoning and by the authority of many, he demonstrated and proved that the Son is indeed less than the Father in the form of the humanity assumed, but equal to the Father in the substance of the divine nature. He did this because there were certain people among them who denied that the Son was equal to the Father.

## LIX.—SAINT AGAPETUS (A.D. 535)

Agapetus, a Roman by nationality, son of the priest Gordianus [Col. 1224C], held the see for eleven months and nineteen days. He ordained eleven bishops and four deacons.

He committed to the flames the document of anathema against Dioscorus, to which Boniface, driven by the spur of envy, had compelled priests and even bishops to subscribe.

Justinian had become angry with King Theodahad because he himself had killed Amalasuntha, the daughter of King Theodoric, who had been entrusted to him. Therefore the aforesaid king, fearing the emperor’s anger, sent the aforementioned pope to Constantinople to the emperor. Justinian received him honorably. After a long dispute, Agapetus convicted Anthimus, bishop of that city, who denied that there were two natures in Christ, and suspended him from communion with Christians. After Anthimus had been deported into exile, he consecrated another bishop, a Catholic man named Mennas, in his place [Col. 1224D].

Later, having been seized by illness, he died there in Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. Before he came to Greece, the same pope sent Anthimus a letter in which he wisely admonished him and urged him to return from his error to the truth of the Catholic faith.

## LX.—SAINT SILVERIUS (A.D. 536)

Silverius, a Campanian by nationality, son of Ormisdas, bishop of Rome, held the see for one year, five months, and forty days. He ordained eighteen bishops and fourteen priests.

He was appointed without deliberation or decree by the tyrant Theodahad [Col. 1225A]. The tyrant, corrupted by money, induced such fear in the clergy that anyone who did not consent to his ordination would undoubtedly be punished by the sword. Thus, after Silverius had been ordained under compulsion and fear, the priests finally subscribed to his confirmation according to custom.

After two months, the aforementioned tyrant was destroyed by divine will. The Augusta Theodora, grieving at that time that Anthimus the patriarch had been deposed by Blessed Agapetus and Mennas had been installed in his place, consulted with the deacon Vigilius and begged Silverius by letter either to come to her quickly or to restore Anthimus to his former position.

Although, after reading the letter, he feared that this request might bring about the end of his life, he nevertheless trusted in the Lord and wrote back to the Augusta that he would never consent to restore an heretical man who had been justly condemned in his wickedness [Col. 1225B].

The Augusta, therefore, angered, ordered the patrician Belisarius to depose Silverius on any pretext he could find and to substitute the archdeacon Vigilius, who had promised to restore Anthimus, in his place.

At length, finding an opportunity on the pretext that Silverius wished to hand the city of Rome over to the Goths, he summoned him to himself. While the clergy and people were detained at the first and second curtains, he ordered Silverius’s stole and alb to be taken from him and commanded that he be clothed in a monk’s garment.

When those who had come with him heard of this impious deed, they fled. The archdeacon Vigilius, as though receiving him into his own allegiance, banished him into exile in Pontus. Sustained there by the bread of tribulation and the water of distress, he finally wasted away and died in that same place on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July as a confessor [Col. 1225C]. Many sick people are healed there.

Silverius wrote a reply to Bishop Amator, in which he briefly recounted, in response to the bishop’s request, what had been done to him. He indicated that he had not therefore abandoned his office, but that, having gathered whatever bishops he could, he had bound those who had deposed him with the bond of anathema. He also declared that the others who thereafter deceived any bishop in such a way were to be anathema *maranatha*.

He also sent a letter to Vigilius, who had by then been established as pope, for his condemnation, saying among other things (23, q. 4, chap. *Belisarius*):

“Therefore, together with those who consent to you, accept the sentence of condemnation; recognize that your name and the office of priestly ministry have been taken from you, and that you have been condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority from us. For thus the faith of the holy Fathers ought to be preserved in the Catholic Church: that the one who has assumed through reprehensible rashness what he had not received should lose what he possessed” (25, q. 2, chap. *Sic decet*) [Col. 1225D].

## LXI.—VIGILIUS (A.D. 540)

Vigilius, a Roman by nationality, son of the consul John, held the see for seventeen years, six months, and twenty-five days. He ordained eighty-one bishops, forty-six priests, and sixteen deacons.

When the Augusta Theodora learned that Vigilius had been established in the apostolic see, as she herself had ordered, she wrote to him, asking him to come to her and fulfill what he had promised concerning Anthimus of his own good will.

Although Vigilius had previously made this promise foolishly [Col. 1226A], he replied that he would never consent to restore an heretical man who had been condemned by the most holy Agapetus and Silverius.

At that time the Romans, grieving that Silverius had been deposed through Vigilius’s advice, seeing an opportunity, accused Vigilius before the Augusta of having murdered two men. When the Augusta heard this, she sent Scribo to Rome. He seized Vigilius, placed him on a ship, and took him to Constantinople.

The emperor initially received him honorably as the vicar of Blessed Peter. But after two years had passed, the emperor and empress, showing him the written undertaking of their own hand, persisted in begging and arguing that Anthimus be restored.

Vigilius, however, steadfast in his willingness to suffer anything, did not yield in the least to their request. At last, after being slapped, because he had said that he had found not the most pious Justinian and Theodora but Diocletian and Luteria [Eleutheria], he answered each demand:

“Do as you wish; for I receive what is worthy of my deeds.”

Wishing somehow to escape the outcome of this misery, he fled into the church of Saint Euphemia and clung tightly to a column of the altar. But he was seized there and led outside the church. A rope was tied around his neck, and he was dragged all around the city until evening. He was then held in custody, while the clerics who had come with him were dispersed and banished into exile.

Later, at the request of the Roman clergy and senate, Vigilius was returned and restored. But on the very journey of his return, in the city of Syracuse, he died from the pain of kidney stones.

He sent a reply to Bishop Eutherius [Eucherius], in which he instructed him what he ought to maintain concerning those [Col. 1226C] who simulate abstinence to such an extent that they believe anyone is polluted by eating meat. After many preliminary remarks, he added:

“Therefore we neither condemn abstinence that is pleasing to God nor receive into our fellowship those who curse the Lord’s creation.”

Concerning those who, at the end of the psalms, omit one connecting syllable and say, “Glory to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” and by saying this attempt to diminish the designation of the perfect Trinity, he adds:

“If they persist in error, they cannot be our companions.”

Concerning those who have been rebaptized by Arians, he says how they are to be received:

“Their reconciliation does not take place through that laying on of hands which is performed through invocation of the Holy Spirit, but through that by which the fruit of penance is acquired and restoration to communion [holy communion] is completed” [Col. 1226D].

Again:

“Concerning the restoration of any church building, if it has been destroyed (On Consecration, distinction 1, chap. *De fabrica*), and whether the solemnity of consecration ought to be repeated when there are no sanctuaries, we have judged that it causes no difficulty if exorcized water is not sprinkled over it, because we know that the consecration of any church in which no altar is placed for the Holy Spirit consists only in the celebration of Masses. Therefore, if any basilica of the saints has even been renewed from its foundations, without any doubt, when the solemnity of Masses has been celebrated in it, the sanctification of the entire consecration will have been completed. But if the sanctuaries that it possessed have been removed, it will again receive the reverence of sanctification through their replacement and the solemnity of Masses” [Col. 1227A].

Again:

“We are never to have a different order of prayers in the celebration of Masses, at any time or on any feast, but are always to consecrate the offerings made to God in the same order.”

Again:

“If anyone does not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, let him be cast out of the Church.”

## LXII.—PELAGIUS (A.D. 555)

Pelagius, a Roman by nationality, son of John the Vicar, held the see for eleven years, ten months, and nineteen days. Since there were no bishops present who ought to ordain him, he was ordained by John of Perugia and Bono of Ferentino, bishops, and by Andrew, priest of Ostia. Many religious men of both orders withdrew from communion with him, charging that he had involved himself in the death of Vigilius, who had been afflicted with such great punishments.
