Therefore Pelagius took up the Book of the Gospels and, taking up the cross, assembled the clergy and people in the church of Blessed Peter; by oath he gave satisfaction concerning the aforementioned crime and confirmed, with the assent of all the Romans, that no cleric should be promoted to holy orders for any price or promise.

He sent a letter to the bishop Virgilius [Vigilius], in which he fully teaches and prudently instructs him how he ought to answer and refute those heretics who chatter that the Father and the Son cannot be one God. He ordained forty-nine bishops, twenty-six priests, and nine deacons. He died on the sixth day before the Nones of March.

## LXIII.—JOHN III. (In the year of Christ 559)

John, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius, held the see for twelve years, eleven months, and twenty-six days. He loved and restored the cemeteries of the holy martyrs, and decreed that offerings and lights should be provided there every Sunday from the Lateran. During his time, Narses, accused by the Romans before Justinian and the empress Sophia, summoned the Lombards to occupy and possess Italy; not long afterward he died at Rome.

He sent a decretal letter to all the bishops of Germany and Gaul, in which, with the clearest reasoning and the firmest authority of many writers, he proves that chorepiscopi are not bishops and ought to exercise none of the privileges of the episcopate. To prove this, he introduces Linus and Cletus: although they had been Peter’s assistants, they had no episcopal authority but had administered only external matters. Since we have noted the very judgment and words themselves when, at the beginning of this little work, we wrote about Clement’s order and activity, we consider it not inappropriate to pass on to the matters that follow.

He ordained fifty-nine bishops, twenty-eight priests, and twelve deacons. He died on the second day before the Ides of July.

## LXIV.—BENEDICT. (In the year of Christ 573)

[Col. 1228A]

Benedict, a Roman by nationality, son of Boniface, held the see for four years, one month, and twenty-eight days. He wrote to Bishop David and ordered that those who said that no one could truly prove the Trinity to be unity—since no one could establish either that three are one or that one is in three—should be brought back to the right faith or expelled from the Church. He proved in many ways, and confirmed by the authority of many writers, that there is unity of substance in the Trinity of persons, and a Trinity of persons in the unity of substance.

During his time the Roman people were afflicted by a severe famine. He ordained twenty-one bishops, fifteen priests, and four deacons. He died on the second day before the Kalends of August.

## LXV.—PELAGIUS II. (In the year of Christ 576)

Pelagius, a Roman by nationality, son of Vinigildus, held the see for ten years, two months, and ten days. He was ordained without the emperor’s command, because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome. At that time there were such great rains that everyone said the waters of the Flood were overflowing, and there was such a disaster as no one in the ages remembered having occurred.

He wrote (Letter 1) to all the Eastern bishops whom John, bishop of Constantinople, had presumptuously summoned to a synod, and instructed them that, if they did not wish to be condemned along with the aforesaid John by consenting to him, they should withdraw from their proud presumption and strive to do penance, since those things known to have been done contrary to order and authority must necessarily be annulled. For John was writing that he was the universal bishop, and on the basis of this presumption was convening a general synod, although the authority to convene a general synod had been entrusted to the Apostolic See by the singular privilege of Blessed Peter.

Likewise, when those same men were uncertain what should be called a definite province, he informed and instructed them, saying:

> Know (Decretum, 6, q. 3, c. “Scitote”) that a definite province is one that has ten or eleven cities and one king, with an equal number of lesser cities [or powers] subject to it, and one bishop, together with ten or eleven other suffragan [or supporting] bishops as judges. All cases concerning bishops and the remaining priests and cities are to be referred to their judgment, so that all these matters may be justly decided by them with one harmonious voice.

Likewise, he sent a letter (Letter 2) to Archbishop Benignus, who had consulted him about the transfer of bishops. In it he instructed him fully concerning how such transfers could or could not be made according to the rule. We have already noted these matters above.

In the same letter, while exhorting the aforesaid archbishop to pursue justice, he says:

> The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked [Note: [Col. 1227D] Immediately, toward glory.], nor does he regard the offerings of the wicked [Note: [Col. 1227D] By approving, toward glory.], nor will he be appeased for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices [Note: [Col. 1228D] As arising from deserved merit.] (Sirach 34:23).

> Whoever offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor slaughters a son, as though in the presence of his father (ibid., 24).

> Whoever is baptized by one who is dead and again touches a dead person—what benefit does his washing provide? So also a person who fasts in his sins and then commits the same sins again—what benefit does he gain by humbling himself? Who will hear his prayer? (ibid., 30–31).

> In every gift make your face cheerful, and sanctify your tithes with rejoicing (Sirach 35:11).

Likewise, he wrote (Letter 3) to all the bishops, and especially to the bishops of Campania and Italy. At their request he fully set out the admonitions concerning bishops, accusers, and other matters that had often been established by his predecessors and noted above. Among other things, concerning monks he says:

> Let no monk (Decretum, 2, q. 7, c. “Nullus”) at all undertake such matters, nor presume to disturb secular or ecclesiastical business, since their voice in such matters is dead.

Likewise, when the bishops of the regions of Germany and Gaul asked to be instructed about the order of prefaces observed by the Roman Church, he replied (Letter 4), saying:

> Carefully rereading the sacred Roman order (De consecratione, distinction 1, c. “Invenimus”) and the sacred constitutions of our predecessors, we find that only these nine prefaces are to be received into the sacred catalogue—the prefaces that the long antiquity of the Roman Church has preserved until now: one for the Paschal season, another for the Ascension of the Lord, a third for Pentecost, a fourth for the Nativity of the Lord, a fifth for the Epiphany of the Lord, a sixth for the Apostles, a seventh for the holy Trinity, an eighth for the Cross, and a ninth for the Lenten fast [we command you to retain these]. If anyone removes or adds anything to those listed above, let him be anathema.

He ordained forty-eight bishops, twenty-eight priests, and eight deacons. He died on the seventh day before the Ides of February.

## LXVI.—SAINT GREGORY. (In the year of Christ 590)

Gregory, a Roman by nationality, son of Gordianus, held the see for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. He composed forty homilies and expounded Job and Ezekiel; he composed the *Dialogue* and the *Pastoral Care*. He also wrote numerous decretals. Since these are very numerous, with God’s help and if life permits, we shall excerpt them briefly and separately, each in its proper place. Now, however, since in the course of the present undertaking we have reached matters that must be noted concerning the order and activity of the aforementioned pope, we think that at least a few should be included.

In a synod he decreed (Roman Synod, ch. 2) that lay boys should not be assigned to the private chamber-services of the Roman pontiff, but clerics or monks should be assigned instead, so that the man who occupies the place of governance might have witnesses, and so that such men might observe his private conduct and, from their attentive observation, take an example of progress.

He also decreed (ch. 4) that the bier on which the body of the Roman pontiff is carried for burial should not be covered with any covering or veil. He did this because, when the bodies of pontiffs were carried to be buried in the ground, they were covered with dalmatics; people would cut these up out of reverence for their sanctity and distribute them.

He also decreed (ch. 5), and prohibited under threat of anathema, that nothing should be received in connection with ordinations, the granting of the pallium, or the delivery of documents. But if the man who has been ordained, after receiving the documents or pallium, should wish to offer something, he does not deny that it may be accepted solely as a token of gratitude, since his offering brings no stain of guilt when it does not proceed from the recipient’s solicitation.

He replied point by point to Augustine, bishop of the English, who had consulted him about many matters [Note: [Col. 1229D] Councils, volume II, p. 764.], adapting his answers to the barbarism of the people and the novelty of their conversion. He said:

> Indeed, as long as they recognize themselves to be related by kinship, they ought not to enter into the marriage bond. But among so barbarous a people, regard for moderation is more pleasing than strict severity. It should be permitted that they marry after the fourth generation.

Regarding the question what the spouse should do if a woman were held by illness and could not discharge the marital obligation to her husband, he replied that it would indeed be good if he remained in that condition and devoted himself to abstinence; but since this belongs to the spiritually strong, the man who cannot contain himself should rather marry, although he must not withdraw the help of support from the woman whom illness prevents, and whom no detestable fault excludes.

Concerning a priest accused by the people, he says:

> If there are no reliable witnesses who establish the truth of the charge brought against him, an oath shall be introduced; and let him produce as witness of his innocence the one to whom all things are naked and open. In this way let him remain in his own rank.

He also ordered that those whom their father or mother had entrusted, during childhood, to regular discipline within the precincts of a monastery should not be allowed to leave after they had reached the years of puberty.

He prohibits the rebaptism of those who had been baptized without deceitful questioning by adulterous priests.

He permits Christian lepers to receive the body and blood of the Lord, but forbids them to celebrate banquets with the healthy.

He also judges it extremely foolish, if disease or an epidemic has entered any place, for those whom it has not yet touched to flee from the city, since no one can escape the hand of God.

Concerning priests entangled in many vices, whose lives stain the priesthood within themselves, he ordered that they be rebuked and admonished with apostolic authority and brought to ecclesiastical purity. If they obey, they will save their souls, and he himself will receive a reward. Nevertheless, do not refuse to converse and share a common table with them. It often happens that those whom disciplinary correction has made slow to receive the rule of truth are led onto the path of justice by the diligent nourishment of table fellowship and gentle admonition. You must observe the same practice with the leading men who provide you assistance.

He added to the canon: “And dispose our days in peace,” and so forth.

During his time the English were converted to the Lord. He ordered that Mass be celebrated over the body of Blessed Peter, and he did the same in the church of Blessed Paul. He ordained sixty-two bishops, thirty-nine priests, and eight deacons. He departed to Christ on the fourth day before the Ides of March.

## LXVII.—SABINIAN. (In the year of Christ 604)

[Col. 1231A]

Sabinian, a Tuscan by nationality, from the city of Blera, son of Bono, held the see for one year, five months, and eight days. He added lamps in the church of Blessed Peter. He ordained twenty-six bishops. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.

## LXVIII.—BONIFACE III. (In the year of Christ 606)

Boniface, a Roman by nationality, son of John, held the see for eight months and twenty-two days. He obtained from the emperor Phocas that, just as the Roman Church is the head of all Churches, so it should also be the head of the Constantinopolitan Church, which arrogantly claimed to be first among all Churches.

He decreed that no one should discuss a bishop’s successor while the bishop was alive, but that on the third day after his deposition, once the clergy and people had assembled, an election should be held. He ordained twenty-two bishops.

## LXIX.—SAINT BONIFACE IV. (In the year of Christ 607)

Boniface, a Marsian by nationality, from the city of Valeria, son of John the physician, held the see for six years, eight months, and twelve days. During his time there was a severe famine and very serious floods. He requested from the emperor Phocas the temple called the Pantheon, and consecrated it in honor of Saint Mary the Virgin and all the martyrs. He ordained thirty-six bishops and eight deacons. He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

## LXX.—SAINT DEUSDEDIT. (In the year of Christ 614)

[Col. 1231C]

Deusdedit, a Roman by nationality, son of Stephen the subdeacon, held the see for three years and thirty days. He greatly loved the clergy and recalled priests and the other clerics to their former places.

During his time, in the month of August, there was a great earthquake, followed by disaster and a severe outbreak of scabies, so that no one could recognize his own dead. Gordianus, bishop of the Church of Spain, consulted the aforementioned pope by letter concerning men and women who, without knowing it, because of the great influx of people, had received children from the baptismal font on Holy Saturday: should they now return to their proper use?

He says that such things had formerly occurred in the Church of Isauria, in Jerusalem, and in many other churches, and asserts that his predecessors Julius, Innocent, and Celestine, together with an assembly of many bishops, had issued regulations forbidding such unions. Thus men and women who, by any means, had received children as sponsors were in no way to take one another in marriage; instead, they were to separate, lest, with the devil’s persuasion, such a vice of sin grow throughout the world and universal error increase.

He added, saying:

> You know that just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism, beginning with the first nourishment of consecrated salt and entry into the holy Church and continuing until the confirmation of the Holy Spirit through chrism. Therefore, from this first gift of the Holy Spirit up to the seventh, no Christian ought to take his baptismal co-mother [godmother] in marriage. Whoever presumes to do so shall be bound forever by the bond of anathema, unless he performs worthy penance.

But when women have been separated from their own husbands on account of this illicit union, we order that they receive the entire dowry that they received on the wedding day, and after a year has been completed they may receive another husband, if they wish. The same applies to the husband with respect to his wife.

## LXXI.—BONIFACE V. (In the year of Christ 617)

Boniface, a Campanian by nationality, from the city of Naples, held the see for five years and ten months. He decreed that a will should be valid in accordance with the emperor’s command. He also decreed that no one should be forcibly removed from a church, and that no one except a priest should presume to remove the relics of the holy martyrs from a church.

He was a very gentle man and loved the clergy. He ordained twenty-nine bishops, twenty-six priests, and four deacons. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

## LXXII.—HONORIUS. (In the year of Christ 626)

Honorius, a Campanian by nationality, son of Petronius the consul, held the see for twelve years, eleven months, and eighteen days. He educated the clergy.

Concerning the matter that the ordination of bishops should not be delayed, he says [Note: [Col. 1231D] Gratian, Distinction 100, chapter “Quoniam,” attributes this to Pelagius.]:

> It has been decided that, if any metropolitan, after three months from his consecration, has not sent to the Apostolic See for the exposition of his faith and the reception of the pallium, he shall lose the dignity entrusted to him. Other metropolitans are to have permission, after a second and third warning, to assist churches left vacant by ordaining a bishop, with the counsel of the Roman pontiff. But if the negligence of those responsible for consecrating a bishop causes a church to remain vacant for more than three months, let the negligent party be deprived of communion until he either resigns his office or no longer delays providing one to be consecrated. If he retains the vacant church through his negligence for more than five months, let him receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere; rather, let him yield to the judgment of his metropolitan.

Likewise:

> If any metropolitan presumes to use the pallium in the streets or in litanies, and not only on the principal feasts and at the times appointed by the Apostolic See for the solemn celebration of Mass, let him be deprived of the dignity whose permitted use he abuses. For he rightly deserves to lose the privilege who audaciously usurps what is unlawful.

Likewise:

> If anyone presumes to strike bishops, mutilate them, defame them contrary to canonical authority, strip them of their property without legal judgment, or drive them from the churches entrusted to them by pursuing them, let him be deprived of communion. If, after being summoned two or three times, he does not make satisfaction by correcting the offense against the one whom he is known to have wronged, let him be bound by the bonds of anathema.

Likewise:

> If anyone violates the house of God and removes anything from it without the permission of the person to whom its care is known to have been entrusted, or inflicts an injury upon ecclesiastical persons, let him know that he is deprived of communion until, having been summoned and lawfully admonished, he makes satisfaction.

> If, after being summoned a second and third time before the bishop, he refuses to make satisfaction, let him be held by all as liable to the danger of sacrilege.

> Whoever carries off a nun or any woman into marriage or concubinage shall know that he is excommunicated, together with all his supporters, until he restores her before the bishop of the city to her parents or fellow citizens. If, after a second and third summons, he does not return the woman he has carried off with suitable satisfaction, let him be driven from all Christian fellowship as one under anathema.

> We rightly call them “carried off” who, without the consent of their parents or the bishop of the city, either flee away of their own accord or are taken away by others against their will.

> If anyone commits murder, mutilates limbs, burns houses, orders such acts to be committed, or consents to the one committing them, let him know that he is deprived of the Church until he has made legal or amicable reparation for these matters before the bishop of the city and the other citizens.

> If, after a second and third summons, he has not corrected everything of which he is accused, let him be separated from the entire Christian community as a heathen and a publican.

> Concerning those who have committed depredations, ordered them to be committed, or consented to the one committing them, we establish that, if they do not repent after being admonished by the bishop of the city, they shall be content with bread and water for forty days and be entirely deprived of all other food and drink.

> If they are suspected of having violated this excommunication, let them satisfy the bishop that they did not violate it. If they are finally convicted of having violated it, they must not only make amends for whatever each is accused of having done; but, if after being warned twice or three times they do not reform, they shall be deprived of all communion. If, after the second and third warning, they have not completely corrected everything of which they are accused, let them know that they are bound by the sentence of anathema.

Likewise:

> Those who attempt to receive communion before a hearing must not be restored to communion in any way until, through penance, they mourn their guilt, except in the urgent danger of death.

> Whoever knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person, even if he merely prays together with him in the same house, and provides hiding places for his defense so that he may not be brought face-to-face to make satisfaction, shall know that he is deprived of communion of the body and blood of the Lord until he receives penance from the one who imposed the excommunication.

> Whoever, within the space of a year, does not humbly or publicly plead his case before those who excommunicated him may be considered to have closed the way to a hearing for himself. If they die with obstinate hearts without communion, we reserve their case for divine judgment according to the sentence of our predecessor Blessed Leo. Those with whom we did not communicate while they were alive, we cannot communicate with after their death.

Likewise:

> All bishops must take care to announce the names of the excommunicated fully both to neighboring bishops and to their own parishioners, and, having placed the names in a public location by the doors of the church, proclaim them to all who assemble. In this way, through both forms of diligence, access to the churches will everywhere be denied to the excommunicated, and every excuse will be removed.

> If any venerable bishop or priest does not watch over this matter with the greatest strictness, or in any respect restrains the enforcement of ecclesiastical severity against delinquent persons, let him know that he is suspended from communion until satisfaction has been made before a provincial synod. If, after a third summons, he remains in his negligence, he shall be subject to canonical judgment.

> Those who, fearing to be lawfully summoned on account of their various offenses, flee to another jurisdiction and there commit worse acts than before are not to be received by anyone until they have made satisfaction, under the discipline of their former lord, to all those whom they have wronged. If they have already been received, both they and the one who received them shall be deprived of communion.

> Concerning those who, wishing to evade the pronouncement of a sentence, withdraw from the mother churches or baptismal churches, he decreed that those who, while remaining within the region, voluntarily absent themselves for more than three Sundays from the public assemblies of the churches in order to evade the sentence shall be deprived of communion until they demonstrate, with suitable satisfaction, that they have been corrected.

Likewise:

> The administrators of secular dignities, whom we know to have been appointed for the protection of churches, the defense of orphans and widows, and the restraint of the rapacious, whenever they have been summoned by bishops and ecclesiastical men, must faithfully hear their complaints and, as necessity requires, examine and remedy them without negligence and with diligent effort.

> If they are found, after a second and third warning, to have neglected these matters without keeping the fear of God before their eyes, let them know that they are deprived of all communion until they have made fitting satisfaction.

Likewise:

> Whoever considers it necessary to ordain a priest should assign him to a church in which he may continually persevere in the service of the Lord.

He ordained seventy-one bishops, thirteen priests, and eleven deacons. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

## LXXIII.—SEVERINUS. (In the year of Christ 638)

Severinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Abienus, held the see for two months and four days. He ordained four bishops. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

## LXXIV.—JOHN IV. (In the year of Christ 639)

[Col. 1234D]

John, a Dalmatian by nationality, son of Venantius the scholastic, held the see for one year, nine months, and eighteen days. He sent a great deal of money through Dalmatia and Istria for the redemption of captives. He ordained four bishops. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

## LXXV.—THEODORE. (In the year of Christ 642)

Theodore, a Greek by nationality, son of Theodore the bishop, from the city of Jerusalem, held the see for six years, five months, and fourteen days. He ordained fifty-six bishops, twenty-one priests, and four deacons. He died on the day before the Ides of May.

## LXXVI.—SAINT MARTIN. (In the year of Christ 649)

Martin, from the city of Tuder in the province of Tuscia, held the see for six years, one month, and twenty-six days. He assembled one hundred and five bishops in the city of Rome. With them he condemned a certain Theodore, bishop of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, and Sergius of Constantinople, together with his successors Pyrrhus and Paul, who had presumed to introduce innovations against the immaculate faith.

Because the aforesaid pope refused to consent to the heretics, he was taken into exile, where he ended his life in Christ on the fourth day before the Ides of November. He ordained thirty-four bishops, eleven priests, and five deacons.

## LXXVII.—SAINT EUGENIUS. (In the year of Christ 652)

Eugenius, a Roman by nationality, son of Rufinianus, held the see for two years, nine months, and twenty-three days. He ordained twenty-one bishops. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of June.

## LXXVIII.—SAINT VITALIAN. (In the year of Christ 655)

Vitalian, from Signia in the province of Campania, son of Anastasius, held the see for fourteen years and six months. He preserved the ecclesiastical rule and discipline in every respect, as was customary. He ordained ninety-seven bishops, twenty-two priests, and one deacon.

During his time Constantine Augustus came to Rome. There he ordered everything that had been hung up for the adornment of the city to be taken down. He stripped the church of Saint Mary ad Martyres, which had been roofed with bronze tiles, and sent those tiles, together with various other objects he had ordered removed, to the royal city.

He wrote a letter to Paul, archbishop of Crete, in which he rebuked him because he had ordered John, bishop of the city of Lampe, to be taken into custody. Moreover, contrary to the commands of the canons and the provisions of the laws, while he was in custody John was compelled to provide sureties. Therefore he decreed that everything the archbishop had done against the aforementioned bishop in the synod was invalid, and, by letter, ordered that his church be restored to him in accordance with the judgment of the synod. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of February.

## LXXIX.—ADEODATUS. (In the year of Christ 669)

Adeodatus, a Roman by nationality and formerly a monk, son of Jovinianus, held the see for four years, two months, and five days. He ordained seven bishops, fourteen priests, and two deacons. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of June.

After his death there were rains and thunder so great that no one then living had heard that such things had occurred before. Consequently, people and animals perished from the excessive force of the lightning.

## LXXX.—DONUS. (In the year of Christ 676)

Donus, a Roman by nationality, son of Mauritius, held the see for one year, five months, and ten days. He ordained six bishops and five deacons.

After his election, in the month of August, an exceedingly bright star appeared in the East. It rose continually at cockcrow and remained visible until morning; but after a period of three months, it hid the rays of its beauty and was never seen again. This was followed in that same eastern region by the death of an innumerable multitude of people.

During his time, the Church of Ravenna, which had previously raised an acephalous head against the Roman Church, once again broke the neck of its pride and submitted humbly to the Apostolic See. He died on the third day before the Ides of April.

## LXXXI.—SAINT AGATHO. (In the year of Christ 678)

[Col. 1236B]

Agatho, a Sicilian by nationality, held the see for two years, five months, and four days. He ordained eighteen bishops, ten priests, and four deacons.

Legates sent to Constantinople from this pope’s side deposed Macarius, patriarch of Antioch, in a synod because he denied that there were two natures and two wills in Christ.

The aforementioned pope obtained from the emperors—namely Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius—that the amount customarily paid for the ordination of the Roman pontiff should be remitted, according to his request. Nevertheless, if after his death or election an ordination should take place, the elected man was not to be ordained unless a general decree had first been carried to the royal city according to ancient custom, and unless the ordination took place with the knowledge and command of those emperors.

He died on the fourth day before the Ides of January.

## LXXXII.—SAINT LEO II. (In the year of Christ 683)

Leo, a Sicilian by nationality, son of Paul, held the see for ten months and seventeen days. He was highly eloquent and learned in the Greek and Latin languages.

He issued a decree that an archbishop who had been ordained should not be required, under any custom, to make payment for the use of the pallium or for various ecclesiastical offices. He ordained twenty-one bishops, fourteen priests, and three deacons. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

## LXXXIII.—BENEDICT II. (In the year of Christ 684)

[Col. 1236D]

Benedict, a Roman by nationality, son of John, held the see for ten months and twelve days. He received an edict issued by Constantine Augustus to the clergy, the people, and the Roman army, by which it was granted that, whenever anyone was elected to govern the Roman See, he should immediately and without delay be consecrated pontiff. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of May.

## LXXXIV.—JOHN V. (In the year of Christ 685)

John, a Syrian by nationality, from the province of Antioch, son of Cyriacus, held the see for one year and nine days. He was a very vigorous man, endowed with knowledge, and thoroughly moderate.

He was consecrated by three bishops—the bishops of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri—just as his predecessor Leo had been. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

## LXXXV.—CONON. (In the year of Christ 686)

Conon, born to a Thracian father and brought up in Sicily, held the see for eleven months. At his election there was a considerable dispute, because the clergy were striving to elect the archdeacon, while the army was striving to elect Theodore the priest. After this dispute had continued for some time, the clergy and people finally chose him unanimously, calling him by name. A few days later, when the army saw the agreement of the clergy and people, it too subscribed to the decree of the aforesaid election. He ordained sixteen bishops. He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.

## LXXXVI.—SERGIUS. (In the year of Christ 687)

[Col. 1237B]

Sergius, a Syrian by nationality, from the region of Antioch, son of Tiberius, held the see for thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-three days.

Before his election, the Roman people were divided, as commonly happens: one party elected Theodore the archpresbyter, while another elected Paschal the archdeacon. When these two elected men contended, and neither wished to yield to the other, the greater part of the clergy, together with the leading judges and the army of the Roman military, deliberated at length about how the dispute between the two rivals might be settled. After reaching an agreement, they finally elected the aforementioned Sergius unanimously; suppressing the tumult of the rivals, they established him harmoniously in the see.

In the sacristy of Blessed Peter the Apostle, God revealing it to him, he discovered a silver chest lying in a dark corner. Because of the blackness caused by its extreme age, it no longer even appeared to be silver. After praying, breaking the seal, and opening the chest, he found in it a cross richly adorned with various precious stones. In the opened chest he also found deposited an inexpressible portion, of wondrous size, of the saving wood of the life-giving Cross. From that day onward, for the salvation of the human race, it has been venerated by all the Christian people in the church of the Savior on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

He decreed that, during the fraction of the body and blood of the Lord, the clergy and people should sing “Lamb of God.” He ordained twenty-seven bishops, eighteen priests, and four deacons. He died on the Ides of September.

## LXXXVII.—JOHN VI. (In the year of Christ 701)

John, a Greek by nationality, held the see for three years, two months, and twelve days. He redeemed with his own gifts the captives whom Gisolphus, duke of the Lombard people, had captured in Campania. He ordained fifteen bishops, nine priests, and two deacons.

## LXXXVIII.—JOHN VII. (In the year of Christ 705)

John, a Greek by nationality, son of Plato, held the see for two years, six months, and seventeen days. He ordained nineteen bishops. He was buried on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November.

## LXXXIX.—SISINNIUS. (In the year of Christ 708)

[Col. 1238A]

Sisinnius, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, held the see for twenty days. He ordained one bishop. He died a sudden death.

## XC.—CONSTANTINE. (In the year of Christ 708)

Constantine, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, held the see for seven years and fifteen days. He ordained Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, who, held back by the pride of arrogance, refused to write according to the custom of his predecessors. Later, because of the arrogance of his pride, he was ordered by Justinian Augustus to be captured, was deprived of his eyes, and was sent into exile in Pontus. After the emperor’s death, he returned to his own see; thus humbled, he sought pardon from the Apostolic See and obtained absolution.

During the time of the aforementioned pope, Benedict, archbishop of Milan, came to Rome and contended on behalf of the church of Ticinum. But he was convicted, because from the aforementioned times the consecration of the bishop of the church of Ticinum had belonged to the pontiff of the Apostolic See.

He ordained sixty-four bishops, ten priests, and two deacons. He died on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

## XCI.—SAINT GREGORY II. (In the year of Christ 714)

Gregory, a Roman by nationality, son of Marcellus, sat for sixteen years, nine months, and eleven days. In Germany, through the bishop Boniface, he preached the word of salvation and converted to Christ that people sitting in darkness [Col. 1238C] by the teaching of light. During his pontificate, the Saracens attempted to occupy France; but, by God’s judgment, three hundred and sixty-five thousand of them fell to the Franks in a single day, as a letter sent to the pope by the Frankish leader reported. He established that during Lent, namely on Thursday, a fast should be observed and Mass celebrated, which previously had not been done.

During his pontificate, the emperor Leo advanced to worse things and compelled all the inhabitants of Constantinople to remove the images of the saints and consume them by fire. Because the patriarch Germanus did not consent to this error, he was driven from his see, and Anastasius the presbyter was ordained in his place. At a general synod, confirming the judgment of all the presiding bishops, Gregory said (C. Romanum, [Col. 1238D], vol. III of the Councils, chapters 1–12):

> If anyone takes as his wife a presbyteress [*presbyteram*], a deaconess, a nun, a daughter-in-law, a female cousin, a woman from his own kinship, or one whom his kinsman had had as a wife, let him be anathema.  
>   
> Likewise: If anyone abducts a widow to make her his wife, or a virgin unless he has betrothed her, let him be anathema.  
>   
> Likewise: If anyone observes augurs, diviners, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema.

He ordained one hundred and fifty bishops, twenty-five presbyters, and four deacons. He died on the third day before the Ides of February.

## XCII.—SAINT GREGORY III. (In the year of Christ 731)

Gregory, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, sat [Col. 1239A] for ten years, eight months, and twenty days. He was a very gentle man, well instructed in the sacred writings, and thoroughly learned in both the Greek and Latin languages. While presiding at a synod, he bound with the bond of anathema all those who, opposing the ancient ecclesiastical custom, scorned to venerate the images of the saints. He ordained eighty bishops, twenty-four presbyters, and three deacons.

## XCIII.—SAINT ZACHARY. (In the year of Christ 742)

Zachary, a Greek by nationality, son of Polychronius, sat for ten years, three months, and fourteen days. During his pontificate, Karlomannus, son of Karlomannus [Charles Martel], king of the Franks, abandoned the glory and power of the present life and received the yoke of the clerical state [Col. 1239B] at Rome from that very pope. Then he reached Monte Cassino; there, after making his profession according to custom, he devoutly assumed the habit of his profession.

During the time of the same pope, King Ratchis of the Lombards abandoned his royal dignity, was tonsured by the aforesaid pope, and, together with his wife and sons, was clothed in the monastic habit. Zachary ordained thirty-five bishops, twenty-three presbyters, and six deacons.

At a synod he decreed that bishops should not live with women at all, and that presbyters or deacons should in no way dare to keep women living under their roof with them, except their mother and those who avoid suspicion; otherwise they were to be deprived of the honor of their rank.

He likewise decreed that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should not use secular clothing, except, as is fitting, a priestly tunic [Col. 1239C]. Nor, when walking in the city, on the road, or through the streets, should they presume to walk without clothing, unless they were traveling on a long journey; for a priest walking without suitable covering disgraces his priesthood. If he presumes to do so, let him be deprived of communion until he hastens to fulfill what has been established.

Likewise, presbyters and deacons are not to take a nun or even a spiritual co-mother [*spiritualis commater*]. Whoever commits such an act should know that he is bound by the bond of anathema, condemned by God’s judgment, and excluded from the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, by decree of apostolic discipline. Any priest who presumes to associate with such persons shall, being condemned along with them, be deprived of the honor of his priesthood [Col. 1239D]. If those who have been convicted, after being admonished, withdraw and separate themselves from adultery, they are to be subjected to penance, as the local priest shall determine.

Likewise, presbyters, deacons, or clerics who have a dispute among themselves are in no way to presume to make an appeal to public authorities, except to their own bishop. If the bishop himself should have a dispute, they are to have recourse to a neighboring bishop, in accordance with the statutes of the canons. If they cannot settle the dispute among themselves, let them come to the apostolic see. If anyone presumes to act contrary to these statutes, let him be deprived of the honor of his rank and expelled from the Church until the case has reached its conclusion.

Likewise, when a bishop or presbyter has entered [Col. 1240A] to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, he must in no way dare to leave after the prayer has been offered so that another bishop or presbyter may complete the solemn rites of Mass; rather, the one who began must complete it to the end. If anyone presumes to act otherwise, let him be suspended from the Lord’s body and blood.

The aforesaid pope sent a letter to all the bishops, and also to all the dukes, counts, and all those who fear God established throughout Gaul and the provinces of the Franks. In it he admonished them all to expel from their territories false and schismatic priests, murderers, and fornicators.

## XCIV.—STEPHANUS III. (In the year of Christ 752)

Stephen, a Roman by nationality, son of Constantine, sat for five years and twenty-three days. After [Col. 1240B] the death of Pope Zachary, a certain presbyter named Stephen was elected by the entire people and enthroned in the patriarchium. After two days he suddenly became deranged, lost his speech, and died the following day.

After this, all unanimously chose this man and introduced him into the patriarchium according to custom; for he was a lover of churches and preserved ecclesiastical tradition with firm constancy. During his pontificate, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, seized the goods of the Church, inflicted many evils upon the Romans, and threatened still more. Therefore the aforesaid pope, compelled by necessity, went to Pippin, king of France, to request assistance. Karlomannus, the king’s brother, came against him, although he was a monk, having nevertheless been deceived by Aistulf’s wicked persuasions so that he might frustrate the pope’s request. But, through God’s action, his undertaking proved ineffective; and there in France, having been placed by his brother in a monastery, he ended his life. The pontiff, however, obtained from the king the fulfillment of his request.

He ordained fifteen bishops, two presbyters, and two deacons. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

In a certain letter concerning his deliverance from illness, the aforesaid pontiff says, among other things:

> When the physicians had already despaired, I was, as if in prayer, in the church of the blessed martyr Dionysius beneath the bells. I saw before the altar the lord Peter and the lord Paul, and with a discerning mind I recognized them; and, third, the blessed Dionysius, on the right of the blessed Peter, slender and taller.  
>   
> The lord Peter said: “This brother of ours is asking for health.” And the blessed Paul said: “He will now be healed.” [Col. 1240D] Approaching, he amicably placed his hand upon the breast of the lord Dionysius and looked toward the lord Peter. The lord Peter said cheerfully to Dionysius: “His health is by your grace.”  
>   
> Dionysius came to me and said: “Peace be with you, brother. You will not die until you have safely returned to your own see. Rise, and dedicate this altar in honor of God and in veneration of the apostles Peter and Paul.” Immediately restored to health, I fulfilled what had been commanded.

## XCV.—SAINT PAUL. (In the year of Christ 757)

Paul, a Roman by nationality, son of Constantine, sat for ten years and one month. At his election the Roman people were divided. Some wanted the archdeacon Theophylactus, while others wanted this man as pontiff; but the party that was larger and stronger eventually elected him. Thus, when the others had dispersed, he obtained the see. He consecrated twenty bishops, twelve presbyters, and two deacons.

## XCVI.—STEPHANUS IV. (In the year of Christ 768)

Stephen, a Sicilian by nationality, son of Olivius, sat for three years, five months, and twenty-seven days. When Pope Paul had departed this life, a certain layman named Constantine was immediately brought by force into the patriarchium by his blood brothers and by those whom they were able by any means to draw to their side. There he was suddenly made a cleric on one day, and on the next day a subdeacon and deacon, and was consecrated by George, bishop of Praeneste [Col. 1241B]. On the following Sunday, hastening with a multitude of armed men to the church of the blessed Peter, he was ordained pontiff by the aforesaid George and two other bishops, namely the bishops of Albano and Porto. He held the Roman Church by this usurpation for the space of one year and one month, and during that time ordained eight bishops, as many presbyters, and four deacons.

But not long afterward the aforesaid bishop of Praeneste was seized by divine vengeance. His right hand withered and contracted, so that he could not raise it to his mouth; and, suffering in this condition, he ended his life.

After the year and month had elapsed, Constantine was suddenly attacked by Romans and Lombards and captured, one of his brothers having been killed. Then he was presented to the already elected Pope Stephen, and there, by the judgment of those present, he was deposed. Afterward the aforesaid elect was ordained pontiff.

Meanwhile, the bishop Theodore, Constantine’s *vicedominus*, was seized by the mob, deprived of his eyes, and had his tongue cut out; Passivus, Constantine’s brother, was blinded; and Constantine himself was eventually captured, deprived of his sight, and miserably left lying in the street.

Then, after a synod had been assembled in the city of Rome because of the presumption of this impious invasion, first the entire written record of his actions was committed to the fire. It was then decreed that everything Constantine had performed in the ecclesiastical sacraments or in divine worship was to be repeated, except holy baptism and sacred chrism.

Concerning the obstinate and disobedient, and those who persisted in contention and scandal, Stephen commanded that, if they did not correct themselves after a first and second admonition, they should be cast out from the bosom of the Church as sowers of weeds.

He established seven cardinal bishops, who were to celebrate by turns for weekly periods in the church of the blessed apostle Peter and sing the angelic hymn during the solemn rites of Mass. He ordained ten bishops, five presbyters, and four deacons.

## XCVII.—SAINT ADRIAN. (In the year of Christ 772)

Adrian, a Roman by nationality, son of Theodore, from the district of the Via Lata, sat for twenty-three years, ten months, and seven days. He was a very noble man and a most vigorous defender of the orthodox faith, his country, and the people entrusted to him. To suppress the slanders and devastations that Desiderius, king of the Lombards, had inflicted upon the possessions of Saint Peter, he summoned Charles the Great, king of the Franks, to Rome.

When Charles came there in the fifth year of his reign, among the many splendid deeds he performed there, he also offered to God as a sacrifice, on the second day of Easter in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter, a portion of Saxony in the province of Westphalia, which he had converted to the Christian faith—as the aforesaid pope had commanded and taught—along with the other gifts he was offering to the pope. He vowed, if he returned safe and sound, to establish a bishopric at the place called Osnabrück and endow it with the tithes of those newly converted to the faith, as the pope directed and confirmed by his privileges.

He ordained one hundred and eighty-six bishops, twenty-four presbyters, and six deacons. He died on the Kalends of January. He sent a letter to the bishops of the Spains, in which, by many arguments and the authority of many writers, he proved that Christ is the true and not putative [the printed *putavium* is apparently corrupt], proper and not adoptive Son of the Father.

## XCVIII.—LEO III. (In the year of Christ 795)

Leo, a Roman by nationality, son of Azuppius, sat for twenty years, five months, and sixteen days. He was elected on the feast of the nativity of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and ordained on the following day.

When he was proceeding, according to custom, prepared for the greater litany [Col. 1242C], he was seized by wicked Romans, deprived of his eyes, had his tongue cut out, and was confined in strict custody. But, with God’s cooperation and the assistance of the blessed Peter, he recovered his sight, his tongue was restored to him for speaking, and, freed from that confinement by God’s aid, he went to King Charles, the patrician of the Romans. Charles received him with the greatest devotion.

When the most impious Romans heard this, they tried to impose false charges upon him so as to make him hateful to the king and to everyone. But the aforesaid pontiff returned to his see and, shortly afterward, in the presence of the aforementioned king and with all the clergy and people also present, cleared himself by oath of the charges brought against him—not under compulsion, but voluntarily.

After this, on the day of the Nativity of our Savior, the aforesaid king was proclaimed by everyone Roman emperor Augustus, crowned by the named pope, and thus in his time the Roman Empire first passed to the Franks.

He established that litanies should be celebrated for the three days preceding the Lord’s Ascension. He ordained one hundred and thirty-six bishops, thirty presbyters, and eleven deacons. He was buried on the second day before the Ides of June.

## XCIX.—STEPHANUS V. (In the year of Christ 816)

Stephen, a Roman by nationality, son of Marinus, sat for seven months. He ordained five bishops, nine presbyters, and four deacons.

## C.—PASCHAL. (In the year of Christ 816)

[Col. 1243A]

Paschal, a Roman by nationality, son of Bonosus, sat for seven years, five months, and thirteen days. He ordained bishops, presbyters, and deacons in various places.

When asked about those who claimed that, because of a cold nature, they were unable to unite with one another in the works of the flesh, he replied:

> If they cannot, let them have a wife as a sister. But if they wish to sever the marital bond, let them remain unmarried. For if he could not naturally agree with this woman, how will he agree with another?

Therefore, if a man wishes to take another wife, the obvious explanation is apparent: persuaded by the devil, he held her hateful through the fuel of hatred, and therefore seeks to dismiss her through the false pretext of a lie. But if [Col. 1243B] the woman brings forward the plea and says, “I want to be a mother and bear children,” let three close relatives be chosen from each side, who shall swear, touching the most holy Gospels, that these two were never joined by intercourse of the flesh and made one flesh. Then the woman appears able to contract a second marriage.

I speak humanly, because of the weakness of their flesh. The man, however, who is of a cold nature, must remain unmarried. But if he seeks another union with someone suitable to him, then those who swore the oath are perjurers and are held liable for the crime. Their fraud is clearly exposed by this: both are seeking other marriages.

He wrote a letter to the Church of Milan concerning the heresy of simony, which begins as follows:

> Anyone who can defend a brother from death but does not do so incurs the guilt of his brother’s death. We, however, who have heard of the supreme danger threatening Your Eminence, incur the penalty of the gravest guilt if we remain silent, since the Lord threatens through the prophet: surely he sheds blood who, by remaining silent, conceals the wickedness of the impious.  
>   
> For we have heard something that greatly astonishes us: that the sacred orders among you are sold for money, although all who attempt anything of this kind are proved to be altogether heretics, as the Holy Spirit thundered through Gregory: “Whoever is ordained through money is promoted for the purpose of becoming a heretic.” And whoever does not burn with zeal against the Simoniac heresy, according to the office entrusted to him, should not doubt that he shares in the portion of the one who first committed this abominable crime.  
>   
> Augustine and Fulgentius show that this crime deserves eternal death, saying: “Hold this most firmly and have no doubt whatsoever: every heretic and schismatic, even if he gives many alms or even sheds his own blood, is destined with the devil and his angels for the fires of eternal punishment, unless before the end of this life he has been incorporated into and restored to the Catholic Church.”  
>   
> It is exceedingly shameful that the Church, now established in full strength, should yield to so savage an enemy, over whom it triumphed with such power at the beginning of its infancy.  
>   
> If anyone objects that it is not consecrations but the things arising from consecration that are sold, he seems to say something, but in fact understands nothing at all. For since a bishop, abbot, or anyone else of the corporeal Church can accomplish nothing without corporeal and external possessions, just as the soul does not live temporally without the body, whoever sells one of two things without which the other cannot be possessed has left neither unsold.  
>   
> The sacred canon utterly eliminates this objection when it forbids the procurator, defender, or subject of a church or rule to be appointed through money, to such an extent that it also cuts down those who intervene in so great a crime with the sword of anathema.  
>   
> Likewise, a little farther below in the same letter: If we do not avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics, but listen to their Masses or pray with them, we undergo excommunication with them. To believe that such men are even priests is altogether an error.

## CI.—EUGENIUS II. (In the year of Christ 824)

[Col. 1244B]

Eugene, a Roman by nationality, sat for four years, seven months, and twenty-three days. In his time the Roman judges who were being held captive in France returned.

## CII.—VALENTINUS. (In the year of Christ 827)

Valentinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Leontius, sat for one month and ten days.

## CIII.—GREGORY IV. (In the year of Christ 827)

Gregory, a Roman by nationality, son of John, sat for sixteen years. He ordained bishops, presbyters, and deacons in various places, one hundred and eighty-five in number.

He rebuilt from its foundations the city of Ostia, which had been ruined by age, so that the Agareni, who were then roaming about, could not harm the Christians living there; and he ordered that the city be called Gregoriopolis.

## CIV.—SERGIUS II. (In the year of Christ 844)

Sergius, a Roman by nationality, son of Sergius of the fourth district, sat for three years. He was ordained without the command of the emperor Lothair. When news of his consecration reached the ears of the aforesaid emperor, he was angered by this presumption and sent his son Louis and Drogon, bishop of Metz, to Rome with a large army.

After inflicting many injuries upon the Romans, they compelled the Romans to swear fidelity to the emperor and, after many disputes, finally confirmed the aforesaid Sergius in the see [Col. 1244D]. He, in turn, anointed the emperor’s aforesaid son king of the Lombards.

This pontiff had a brother named Benedict, a brutish and extremely foolish man. Because of the pontiff’s weakness, Benedict usurped ecclesiastical and public authority; moreover, by means of enormous gifts, he acquired from the emperor the primacy and lordship of Rome. Finally, he did not hesitate to usurp the bishopric of Albano, and by his greed and vanity devastated everything inside and outside Rome.

During the time of this pontiff and his brother, the Simoniac heresy flourished to such an extent that even bishoprics were sold: whoever gave the most received the bishopric. Nor was there any bishop or ecclesiastical man who, moved by zeal for God, would approach the emperor or king to prevent this wickedness.

Since there was no Christian through whom this evil might be corrected, divine power sent the scourge of the pagans to avenge the sins of Christians. The Saracens came upon them and killed countless people; after capturing many strongholds and cities, they set them on fire once they had taken the booty. Finally, after defeating and putting the king to flight, they returned laden with immense plunder of people and all kinds of goods, after capturing and killing many.

He ordained twenty-five bishops, eight presbyters, and three deacons.

## CV.—LEO IV. (In the year of Christ 847)

Leo, a Roman by nationality, sat for eight years, six months, and three days. All the Romans unanimously elected him [Col. 1245B]. While they were rejoicing greatly at his election, they soon began again to grieve considerably because they did not dare to consecrate a pontiff without imperial authority, and they were especially afraid of danger to the city of Rome, lest it again, as formerly, be besieged by other enemies.

Terrified by fear of this future disaster, they immediately consecrated him pontiff without awaiting the prince’s decision.

Following the ancient custom and by canonical authority, he established that, while the sacred solemn rites of Mass were being celebrated in a church, no layman should presume to stand, sit, or enter in the presbytery, except those who appeared to have been appointed for this ministry of sacred service.

During his pontificate, a basilisk arose in certain caves at Rome. By its breath and its gaze [Col. 1245C] it killed and consigned to death everyone who approached. The aforesaid pontiff came to the very opening and drove it away by his prayer; afterward no sign of harm from it appeared.

He was the first to celebrate with the greatest devotion the octave of the Assumption of the holy Mother of God, Mary, and by firm institution commanded that it always be celebrated.

With the counsel and assistance of the emperor Lothair, he completed in full the city he had begun around the church of the blessed Peter. He surrounded it with a litany, sprinkled it with exorcised water, sanctified it, and afterward called it Leoniana after his own name.

Seeing that many things were being done in his time shamelessly against God and the salvation of souls, he held a synod at Rome, with the counsel of the emperors Lothair and Louis, [Col. 1245D] together with sixty-seven bishops. With them he issued forty-two chapters necessary for the salvation of Christians and commanded that they be firmly upheld.

1. In the first chapter he established that a bishop should be consecrated irreproachable and desirable in good works, according to Paul’s discernment and admonition (1 Tim. 3).

2. Second, every priest must beware lest he obtain consecration through rewards, lest, following the example of Simon, he fall into the devil’s snare (Acts 8).

3. Third, a bishop must be a man of good works and carefully consider how he ought to instruct the people by the word of preaching.

4. Fourth, if a bishop is found to be unlearned, he is to be admonished by the metropolitan; presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons are likewise to be admonished by their bishop so that they may be taught. Meanwhile, such presbyters and clerics are to be suspended from celebrating the divine mysteries and offices, so that, once instructed, they may attain the ministry proper to them.

5. Fifth, he confirmed what Celestine and Leo the Great had established concerning bishops: namely, that a bishop should not be consecrated unless he has been requested by the clergy and people, since no reason permits those consecrated otherwise to be counted among the bishops. If no worthy man is found in that church, another church is to be chosen first; and even if necessity arises, no one is to be consecrated through envy.

6. Sixth, in accordance with the Council of Sardica, he commanded that bishops should not remain away from their own churches for more than three weeks, unless necessity should arise through the command of the metropolitan or the ruler; for the absence of a bishop often becomes a calamity for the people.

7. Seventh, he commanded that the following be necessarily observed: cloisters should be established beside the church, in which clerics may be instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines, and there should be one refectory and dormitory for all, together with the other workshops necessary for the use of clerics. After the bishop, such ministers should be chosen whose life and teaching adorn rather than disgrace them.

8. Eighth, bishops must diligently care for the baptismal congregations; and when the need to ordain presbyters among them arises, it should be reverently observed that this should not be done without the consent of those living there [Col. 1246C].

9. Ninth, when clerics are gathered, no more are to be admitted than the resources canonically assigned to them can adequately support.

10. Tenth, priests should not be appointed unless they are assigned to churches or to a particular monastery, lest the necessity arise for them to live in secular houses. Otherwise, by their own bishops, they are to be established for residence and conduct either in the episcopal residence or in monasteries, for the exercise of their office, where women have no opportunity to associate with them.

11. Eleventh, priests must diligently study the divine utterances, admonish the people, and take no pleasure in having games performed before them. Those who transgress are to cease after the bishop’s admonition; otherwise they are to be judged canonically.

12. Twelfth, priests, who ought indiscriminately to be present in the churches for the proper and opportune offices, must not be occupied with usury, hunting, bird-catching, or the service of peasants. Nor should they appear outside their homes without priestly dress. They are to observe only what has been established by the Fathers. Those found acting otherwise must either cease or submit to canonical discipline.

13. Thirteenth, priests should not be summoned in secular affairs as witnesses or for drawing up documents, since it is not fitting for them to be involved in such matters. If by chance they see or hear something concerning a case where no suitable secular persons can be found, the bishop must take care that, lest the truth be concealed and the evil man be considered good, they raise this truth honorably before him and the competent judges [Col. 1247A].

14. Fourteenth, if a priest or anyone else advanced in the ecclesiastical order is found guilty of a crime for which he should be expelled, he is to be deposed and, through the bishop’s care, placed in a suitable location where he may mourn his sins and commit them no longer.

15. Fifteenth, if a bishop (Distinction 81, chapter “If Anyone”), presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon is suspected of the crime of fornication with any woman and, after a first, second, and third admonition by the metropolitan, another bishop, or the person to whom he appears subject, is found conversing with her or associating with her in any way, he is to be judged canonically. For one who is not permitted to have a wife of his own must abstain from every woman.

16. Sixteenth, no bishop may take immovable property from subject congregations or other pious places, lest the poor be found to suffer from such an act. Anyone acting contrary is to be restrained by canonical authority.

17. Seventeenth, presbyters are to receive the offerings of all who come to them in any sacred place for the solemn rites of Mass, because, as mediators between God and human beings in the fulfillment of vows and the remission of sins, they ought to offer the most generous prayer.

18. Eighteenth, a bishop must not issue dimissory letters to a priest subject to him or to any other cleric unless he has been requested to do so by another. And, lest false letters be believed true or true ones suspected of being false, they ought to be authenticated by the seal of the universal pontiff, the emperor, or the metropolitan.

19. Nineteenth, because bishops and all priests are appointed solely for the praise of God and the performance of good works, they ought, for both ecclesiastical and their own affairs—except in a public crime—to have an advocate who is not suspected of a bad reputation, but is of good standing and known for praiseworthy skill, lest, while they pursue human profits, they lose eternal rewards.

20. Twentieth, if any priest is found unable to produce an advocate in court, his own bishop must examine that priest before his own people, determining whether he lives a good or bad life and for what reason he cannot properly have an advocate. If he is found blameworthy, the bishop must arrange for him to be corrected according to the nature of his fault and the rule of the canon.

21. Twenty-first, a monastery or oratory canonically constructed may not be taken away from its founder’s authority against his will. He may entrust it to whichever presbyter he wishes for the sacred office of that diocese, provided that the presbyter is of good standing and holds dimissory letters with the bishop’s consent, lest he prove unsuitable. The priest must obediently have recourse to that bishop for the agreed and proper reverence; otherwise he is to be subjected to canonical penalties.

[Col. 1248A]

22. Twenty-second, he decreed that if anyone proved to be an invader says that he acted on behalf of the Church concerning private property belonging to him, the penalty for the invasion is to be paid by him and his heir. A priest found poor through such guilt is to be judged canonically by his own bishop; a bishop is to be judged by the metropolitan, so that the Church entrusted to him does not suffer loss through the invasion.

23. Twenty-third, concerning monasteries of monks or nuns, and all other establishments founded for almsgiving to meet various needs, he commanded that, through the diligence of the bishops in whose dioceses they exist, they be administered for the very purposes for which they were established.

24. Twenty-fourth, concerning churches in various regions that, deprived of priests and left desolate, give voice to no duly performed office [Col. 1248B], he decreed that if they are subject to the church’s own jurisdiction, the bishop must establish a presbyter there without interruption. If they are held under the jurisdiction of secular men, the bishop is to admonish them; and if, after being admonished, they neglect to establish presbyters there within three months, without disregard for the ruler, the bishop must press for the matter to be corrected by his decision.

25. Twenty-fifth, every church that has been destroyed is to be restored at its own expense; if that is insufficient, it is to be assisted by the people of the congregation.

26. Twenty-sixth, no bishop may demand from a priest subject to him or from any other cleric, in connection with pious places, donations beyond what the Fathers have established, or impose additional burdens [*superposita*, apparently corrected from *superimposita*] through forced labor.

[Col. 1248C]

27. Twenty-seventh, abbots are to be appointed who can unquestionably fulfill before God the ministry signified by their title. They must be so learned that they can fully recognize and correct any negligence occurring among the brothers.

28. Twenty-eighth, the bishop must diligently investigate in his diocese those who possess only the habit of monks and compel them to return to their own monastery, or send them to another with suitable provision, so that they may observe the regular life.

29. Twenty-ninth, women who have assumed a religious habit or a veil under the pretext of religion are not thereafter to be permitted to join themselves to a man. Those who transgress are to be compelled to do penance.

30. Thirtieth, on Sunday no one may presume to conduct business, except in foodstuffs, or to perform any rural labor. Otherwise the transgressor is to be brought to penance.

31. Thirty-first, on Sunday a person suspected and disgraced by guilt is either to be released upon the fullest satisfaction or placed in custody so that he may be judged on lawful days; for according to the laws, a judgment delivered on Sunday is invalid.

32. Thirty-second, no layman may stand in the place where the presbyters and other clerics are located, which is called the presbytery, when Mass is being celebrated. For just as each place in the church appears to have been assigned its purpose, so the men and women ought each to remain within their respective parts.

[Col. 1249A]

33. Thirty-third, he decreed that, just as those who have chosen monasteries are not permitted to leave them, so those who have been brought into monasteries against their will, without the guilt of a legitimate offense, are not to be held there unless they wish it; for they do not observe what they have not sought.

34. Thirty-fourth, teachers and instructors are to be appointed in each place where necessity arises, so that they may teach the liberal arts diligently. If such teachers cannot be found, there must nevertheless be no lack of teachers of divine Scripture and instructors in ecclesiastical office.

35. Thirty-fifth, priests must admonish the men and women who gather at church on feast days not to hold and lead dances while singing shameful words, behaving like pagans [Col. 1249B]. For if such people come to church with lesser sins, they return with greater ones. If they do not cease after being admonished, they are to be suspended from communion by every means.

36. Thirty-sixth, no one may leave his wife and join himself to another, except on account of fornication. Otherwise the transgressor ought to be compelled to reunite with his first marriage. If husband and wife agree to separate from one another solely for a religious life, this must in no way be done without the knowledge of the bishop, so that he may place each separately in a location provided for the purpose. If the wife or either one of them is unwilling, the marriage is not to be dissolved even for such a reason.

37. Thirty-seventh, no one may have a wife and a concubine at the same time; for when there is no gain at home, the soul suffers loss [Col. 1249C]. Otherwise he is to be regarded as unworthy of ecclesiastical communion; and if he persists, he is to be completely cut off from the Church.

38. Thirty-eighth, no one may dare to marry a woman from his own kinship or one whom his kinsman had had as a wife. If anyone does so and persists, he should know that he is bound by the chains of anathema.

39. Thirty-ninth, no presbyter is to be ordained absolutely—that is, without an assigned title or provision—and clerics are to be ordained in accordance with the resources, offerings, or revenue of the church.

40. Fortieth, urban, suburban, and all rural presbyters are to come without exception to the bishop’s council, or submit to the corrections of the canons.

Forty-first: that a layman who, on his own authority and without the consent of his own bishop, appoints a priest in any church [Col. 1249D] is to be separated from the communion of the faithful. If priests, after being admonished three times by the bishop or his legate to withdraw from another’s church, refuse to obey, they are to lose the rank of their own office.

In the final chapter he immutably decreed that no abbot, nor anyone else, should presume to appoint priests in churches, except those who are lawfully able to confer the priestly rank and canonically to rebuke priests for neglect. Rather, priests are to be respectfully requested from the bishops for the ministry of divine service—those to whom the dioceses in question uniquely belong, who canonically ought to provide for those churches and order what has been provided.

The aforesaid pontiff deposed Anastasius, a priest residing in another diocese, who had been summoned repeatedly and finally excommunicated, yet refused to return to his own parish; he deprived him entirely of priestly honor. Likewise, at the same synod he admonished and, by apostolic authority, ordered that each bishop, throughout his dioceses and parishes, personally and through his priests, should admonish the people subject to him to pay their first fruits and tithes without delay. Those unwilling to pay them were to be suspended from food and drink until they made up what was owed. If they did not take care to make it up even under this suspension, they were to be deprived of holy communion. Likewise, at the same synod he established, with irrefragable affirmation, that no bishop or priest should presume to seize or alienate property belonging to his own title; whoever did so was unquestionably to undergo canonical punishment. He ordained forty-three bishops, nineteen priests, and seven deacons. He fell asleep in the Lord on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

## CVI.—BENEDICT III (In the year of Christ 855)

Benedict, a Roman by nationality, the son of Peter, occupied the see for two years, six months, and ten days. He lived in the time of Emperor Louis, son of Lothair, son of Emperor Louis. After the clergy and people had elected him, despite his resistance, and had led him, according to custom, to the patriarchium, they drew up a decree and confirmed it with their own hands, as ancient practice required, and sent it to the most invincible Augusti, Lothair and Louis.

But the legates carrying the decree were bribed on the way by Anastasius, the priest deposed by Leo. Wishing to place him in office, they turned aside and, by crafty deception, brought it about with the aforesaid princes that, consenting to their will, they should send legates to Rome to enthrone Anastasius. When these arrived there, they forcibly introduced the deposed man into the patriarchium; they ordered Benedict, expelled and stripped of his pontifical vestments, to be held in close custody.

At last, however, after all had observed a three-day fast with prayer and vigils, and even those who had earlier favored the excommunicated priest had joined them, all unanimously, by divine prompting, rallied to Benedict. In the presence and with the consent of the imperial legates, he was consecrated pontiff.

[Col. 1250D] To Bishop Ratold concerning a parricide he wrote as follows:

“We wish him to be placed under the burden of penance for twelve years, so that every day he may fast until evening and take food without meat, wine, or fish, except on feast days and Sundays and from Easter to Pentecost. For five years he is not to presume to enter the church or to receive communion; he is to remain only before the doors of the church while the sacred offices are celebrated. When the course of five years has been completed, he is to enter the church and stand among the hearers with all fear and obedience. When he reaches the tenth year, he is to share in holy communion and remain among the company of the faithful. If the end of his life should come before the appointed time, the viaticum is not to be denied him, according to the traditions of the canons.”

## CVII.—NICHOLAS I (In the year of Christ 858)

Nicholas, a Roman by nationality, the son of Theodore the regionary, occupied the see for nine years, seven months, and nineteen days. Elected unanimously by the Roman clergy and people, he was consecrated in the presence and at the command of Caesar Louis.

He deprived John, bishop of Ravenna, of communion because he had presumed many things contrary to canonical institutions and had scorned to come when summoned three times by letter to the synod. Later, moved by mercy, he restored communion to him when he humbly sought pardon. Among other instructions, he ordered him not to consecrate bishops in Emilia unless, after the election of the duke, clergy, and people, he had received through a letter of the apostolic see permission to consecrate those prelates.

The same pontiff ordered that a certain deacon, who had appealed to the apostolic see after being maliciously deposed by his bishop, be restored to his office. Since the deacon had been judged without a fixed number of bishops, indeed without proof of the charge and without a confession from his own mouth, he annulled the entire judgment and, through apostolic compassion, brought the case back to the path of justice.

During the time of this pontiff, King Lothair dismissed his lawful wife, named Thietberga, and took his concubine Waldrada in marriage. The authors and defenders of this crime were Theotgaud, archbishop of Trier and primate of the province of Belgica, and Guntarius, archbishop of Cologne. Accordingly, the aforesaid bishops were summoned to Rome and came confidently. They presented the supreme pontiff with a document containing a defense of the incestuous marriage, saying that they had done neither more nor less than what was contained in that document.

But it contained many things for which a sentence of deposition was later rightly pronounced against the aforesaid archbishops, as the supreme pontiff says in the letter he sent to the archbishop of Reims and the other bishops living in the kingdom of King Charles, and in another letter written to all the bishops who were in the kingdom of Louis. For he says that they were deposed:

First, because they were disobedient to the commands he had issued concerning Ingeltrude, Thietberga, and Waldrada.

Second, because they presumed to receive and absolve Ingeltrude, who had been bound by the bond of anathema, although those rejected by one person are not to be received by others.

Third, because by removing and adding to apostolic writings, they plainly proved themselves guilty of falsification.

Fourth, because they consented to adulterers and attempted to defend so great a crime, according to the passage: “And with adulterers was your portion” (Psalm 49).

Fifth, because they rashly presumed to judge and decide, without apostolic authority, a matter concerning which an appeal had been made to the Roman see—something wholly impermissible.

Sixth, because they carried this out in the person’s absence, contrary to the passage: “You shall not curse the deaf” (Leviticus 19). For someone who is placed in absence is, in a certain sense, deaf, since he does not hear what is alleged against him; such was Thietberga, to whom the king refused to grant suitable security for coming.

Seventh, because they subscribed to profane proceedings, compelled others to subscribe, and were held responsible for as many souls as, being in positions of authority, they drove into the precipice of transgression by word or deed.

The same supreme pontiff established by decree in another letter, which he wrote to the archbishop of the Church of Vienne, that bishops afflicted by some illness were not to be deposed, nor others consecrated in their place, unless they had been taken from this life. Priests were to carry out on their behalf those aspects of their ministry that were lawful; in matters that were not lawful for them, the assistance of neighboring bishops was to be supplied instead.

Likewise, in the same letter he ordered that bishops who had undertaken the care of the Lord’s flock were not to withdraw from their ministry. Likewise, clerics who were known to have been oppressed by demons in adolescence were not to be permitted to rise to a higher rank.
