Likewise (Distinction 50, chapter “Those Who”), if a falling tree happened to kill a man, those who had cut it down were to be innocent if the homicide had been committed neither by their will nor by their desire. But if it was recognized that the danger to the dying man had arisen through some fault or negligence of theirs, they were to be removed from their rank and under no circumstances received into holy orders.

He also granted that men who appeared to be doing penance for illicit acts, if they could not remain continent, might, after completing their penance, take wives because of the danger of fornication.

In a letter which the same pontiff sent to Charles, bishop of Mainz, he forbade a bishop to bind the people entrusted to him by oaths. Likewise, he decreed that no Christian might take a wife from his own blood relationship or kinship for as long as the relationship was known or remembered.

Likewise, concerning priests (Distinction 50, chapter “Priests,” and chapter “Let Him Strive”): if they had fallen into the snare of fornication and the act of the crime had been made manifest or exposed, they could not canonically retain the honor of the priesthood. But if they had been accused of the crime of fornication and that crime had not been proved, or they themselves had not disclosed it, they were permitted, if they wished, to clear themselves by oath. The same applied to deacons if they had been accused.

Likewise, women consecrated under a veil, if they had committed fornication, were nevertheless not to remove the veil; rather, submitting themselves to the yoke of penance, they were to strive to attain the grace of remission.

Likewise, he ordered parricides and fratricides to remain outside the church during the first year and to be admitted into the church during the second, but not to receive communion. In the third year he ordered that they be given communion of the body and blood of the Lord. They were to abstain from meat and wine, except on feast days; fast until the ninth hour; and not presume to take wine and broth except three days a week. They were not to carry weapons except against pagans, nor were they to be transported in any vehicle; they were to travel on foot wherever they ought to go.

The bishop was to have discretion to shorten the period of this penance according to their conduct. If they had wives, they were not to be separated from them; but if they had none and were unable to remain continent, they were to take wives lawfully. If anyone had committed fornication with two sisters, or with women whom Sacred Scripture forbids, he might, if he performed worthy penance, take a wife. The same was permitted to a woman who had fallen into such a crime.

When asked whether, under secular law, a husband might kill an adulterous wife, he replied: “The holy Church of God is never bound by secular laws. It has no sword except the spiritual one, which does not kill but gives life.”

He also ordered that homicides might enter the church after the passage of one year. Likewise, concerning a veiled widow who had professed to remain in the same habit, he ordered that she should not presume [the object is absent from the supplied text].

In another letter, which the same pontiff sent to Archbishop Luitbert, he ordered that one who had killed a pagan, not in war but out of hatred or through greed, should do penance as a homicide.

Likewise, according to the custom of the Roman Church, he ordered that even laymen should abstain from meat from Quinquagesima until Easter.

Concerning a man who killed another on his spear, he ordered as follows: “If it was done by the will of the one who held the spear, he is held guilty of homicide; but if it was committed without his knowledge, he appears to be innocent.”

He ordered a man who, while shooting an arrow to test its cord, unintentionally killed his own son to do penance for an involuntary homicide. Concerning one who killed someone while insane, he says: “If he should return to sound mind, he ought to do lighter penance than one who did this while of sound mind.”

The same pontiff wrote a letter to Solomon, bishop of Constance (30, question 1, chapter “To Solomon”), in which he forbade one man to take two spiritual co-mothers (*commatres*), one after the other. Since husband and wife become one flesh through marriage, it necessarily follows that he is constituted a spiritual co-father (*compater*) to the woman of whom the wife he has taken in marriage was spiritual co-mother (*commater*). Therefore, he says, a man cannot be joined in intercourse to the woman who was the spiritual co-mother of the woman with whom he had become one flesh.

Likewise, he ordered that a woman who had lifted her husband’s son, born of another woman, from the sacred font should not be separated from her husband on that account. According to the sacred canons, a spouse ought not to dismiss the other except by the consent of both and for the sake of religion. Nevertheless, the woman who, out of hatred for her husband, commits impiety under the pretext of piety has a grave sin.

Likewise, concerning a priest (15, question 5, chapter “The Priest”) or deacon whom Bishop Solomon asserted did not wish to confess his crimes publicly but wished to defend himself by oath, while nevertheless saying that it was known to the bishop that the man’s crime had been committed, he replied that the crime was not lawfully manifest to the bishop if the priest or deacon had not perhaps been convicted by the testimony of witnesses, or had not voluntarily confessed the crime himself.

Therefore, before either of these things occurred, he ought not to be deprived of his office. For only voluntary confession, or the canonical number and quality of witnesses, when the bishops are deciding and the accuser proves what he has alleged, deprives a cleric of his own rank.

Likewise, he says that a monk who has once vowed himself to God and accepted the rule of the holy Fathers can no longer turn back from his purpose.

The aforesaid pontiff deposed Photius of Constantinople because, having been a layman, he was consecrated by an excommunicated bishop and suddenly made bishop while Ignatius, the patriarch, was still alive; and because he had presumed to share communion with excommunicated persons before a hearing.

The same pontiff restored Rothad, bishop of Soissons, who had been deposed by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, to his see, because an appeal to the Roman see had been unable to obtain a period of delay from the aforesaid archbishop.

He ordained sixty-five bishops, seven priests, and four deacons. [Col. 1254B] He departed to the Lord on the Ides of November.

## CVIII.—ADRIAN II (In the year of Christ 867)

Adrian, a Roman by nationality, the son of Thalarus, occupied the episcopate for four years, eleven months, and ten days. He was unanimously elected by all the Romans. When Emperor Louis heard of their unanimity and desire, and also learned how they had confirmed the decree with their subscriptions, he rejoiced greatly and immediately wrote an imperial letter in which he commended the election of the chosen prelate.

During his time, Louis gave the Churches of Corbie and Hereford certain tithe-paying churches, together with their tithes, in the parish of Osnabrück, with the consent of the bishop and all the clergy.

Charles, emperor and patrician of the Romans, gave to the honored Church—and one to be honored by God—of Hersfeld certain tithes in Frisonevelt and Hassega, adjoining the diocese of Halberstadt. Pope Stephen confirmed them in the basilica of Blessed Peter on the holy day of Easter by his authority and by the emperor’s subscription, with Hildegrin, bishop of Halberstadt, present. [Note: [Col. 1253] On Hildegrin, see Albert Krantz, *Metropolis*, book I, ch. 2.]

For Charles had assigned all tithes established in Saxony to royal service, and the king could give them to whomever he wished.

By apostolic authority he confirmed that henceforth, if anyone should attempt to kill, flog, or even strike a bishop, he was to be anathema from God and all his saints.

He decreed that those who contracted illicit and incestuous unions, if they did not dissolve them after being admonished a second or third time and did not perform worthy penance, were to be expelled from the thresholds of the church together with their followers.

Likewise, he ordered that abductors of virgins, who were known to have acquired them by legitimate matrimonial right, or according to custom, law, or peace, were to be struck by the same sentence. Finally, unless they withdrew from their wicked intention, he judged that they were to be subjected to anathema in every way.

Likewise, he said that homicides and mutilators of men, if they did not make amends according to the law and perform penance, and likewise invaders, arsonists, and abductors, were to be struck by the same sentence.

Likewise, he decreed that no one except the bishop, to whose ordination and authority the diocese of every church belonged by right according to the ancient constitution, each within his own parish, might assign a cleric to a church.

## CIX.—JOHN VIII (In the year of Christ 872)

John occupied the see for ten years and two days. By his decree he established that no duke might bring any bishop into the presence of the Roman prelate, or demand from him a census for public expenses or any gifts; nor did he permit a bishop to be brought before laymen.

He decreed that clerics and nuns, orphans and widows, were to be under the protection of the bishops, and absolutely forbade them to be dragged before secular courts. He decreed that any duke or other person acting against these provisions was to be excommunicated; if he persisted, he was to be bound by the bond of anathema.

Among other things, he issued the following instruction concerning tithes to be given to priests:

“We have decreed that each of the faithful should give these tithes to the priest in whose parish he is, as is beyond doubt, established to remain under the authority of his own bishop, since he has been appointed by his bishop to receive them. Therefore no priest or levite of another diocese is insolently to entertain, or rashly to seek or receive, such dues owed to another by a *novum* [perhaps *canonum*, ‘of the canons’] right; the text then reads *damnationem* [perhaps *tantum*, ‘only,’ or *donationem*, ‘a gift’] *vel donationem*, ‘or a gift.’ [Note: [Col. 1255D] The passage is corrupt.] But whoever presumes to give or receive otherwise, we judge is to remain deprived of ecclesiastical communion until he undertakes to act according to this chapter of our apostolic authority.”

During his time, Emperor Louis, compelled by fear for his life by Adalgis, duke of Benevento, confirmed by oath that he would never again enter the territory of Benevento and would never exact vengeance for the danger of the injury then inflicted upon him.

Later, the aforesaid pope absolved him from this oath at Rome by the authority of God and Saint Peter, affirming that what he had been compelled to do in order to escape the danger of death could not harm him, and that an oath should not be called an oath when it had been uttered, even with many curses, against the welfare of the state.

## CX.—MARINUS (In the year of Christ 882)

[Col. 1255D] Marinus occupied the see for one year and five months.

## CXI.—ADRIAN III (In the year of Christ 884)

Adrian occupied the see for one year and four months.

## CXII.—STEPHEN VI (In the year of Christ 884)

Stephen occupied the see for six years. He ordered Heriman [Hermann; Note: [Col. 1255D] See Arantzius, *Metropolis*, book II, chs. 19 and 24; Albert of Stade, *Chronicle*, under the year 896; Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*], archbishop of Cologne, and Adalgar, archbishop of Hamburg, who were disputing over the Church of Bremen, to come to the synod at Worms. [Col. 1256A] There he entrusted the examination of their case to Fulco, bishop of Reims, acting in his place.

## CXIII.—FORMOSUS

Formosus, bishop of Porto, occupied the see for five years and six months. [Note: [Col. 1256D] The remaining words are from Liutprand, *De rebus per Europam gestis*, book I, chapter 8.]

This Formosus, a man of great religious devotion, was grievously persecuted by the Romans; and it was at his urging that King Arnulf had come to Rome. When Arnulf entered, he ordered many Roman leaders who were hastening to meet him to be beheaded in vengeance for the injury done to the pope.

The cause of the conflict between Pope Formosus and the Romans was as follows. After Formosus’s predecessor had died, a certain Sergius, a deacon of the Roman Church, was chosen pope by one faction of the Romans. But another faction, not the least distinguished in age, eagerly desired Formosus, bishop of the city of Porto [the name “Formosus” is supplied in the source], to become pope because of his true religion and knowledge of divine teachings.

For when Sergius was about to be ordained vicar of the apostles, the faction supporting Formosus, amid considerable tumult and injury, expelled Sergius from the altar and made Formosus pope. Sergius then went down into Tuscany so that he might be aided by the powerful margrave Adalbert; and this was done.

For after Formosus had died and Arnulf had returned to his homeland and died there [or: had returned], the man who was made pope after Formosus’s death was expelled, and Sergius was made pope by Adalbert. Once established, this impious man, ignorant of divine teachings, ordered Formosus to be dragged from his tomb and placed on the papal throne dressed in priestly vestments. He then said to him:

“When you were bishop of Porto, why did you usurp the universal Roman see through the spirit of ambition?”

When these proceedings were completed, he ordered Formosus to be stripped of his sacred vestments, to have three fingers cut off, and to be thrown into the Tiber. He also ordained again all those whom Formosus himself had ordained after they had been deposed from their proper rank.

How badly he acted in this, most holy Father, you will be able to observe, since even those who received a greeting or apostolic blessing from Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, before the betrayal were not deprived of it after the betrayal and the hanging of his own body—unless perhaps they had been defiled by disgraceful crimes.

For the blessing bestowed upon the ministers of Christ is not poured out through the one who appears to be the priest. “Neither is he who waters anything, nor he who plants, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

We may also gather from this how great was the authority and religious devotion of Pope Formosus: when he was later found by fishermen and carried to the Church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, certain images of the saints reverently greeted him while he lay in the coffin. I often heard this from the most religious men of the city of Rome.

# ANONYMOUS AUTHORS OF THE NINTH CENTURY

## LETTER OF THE PILGRIM MONKS LIVING ON THE MOUNT OF OLIVES TO LEO III, ROMAN PONTIFF

*(In Baluze, Sacred Miscellany, volume II, page 84.)*

To the most holy and most reverend lord in Christ, Father Leo, supreme pontiff and universal pope of the holy apostolic see of the city of Rome: the congregation of the Mount of Olives.

Lord Father, the Lord has deigned to exalt you above all priests, and your holy see has been exalted above all the sees of Christians. Christ deigned to say to it with his own mouth: “You are Peter” (Matthew 16:18), and so forth.

Most gracious Father, we who are pilgrims here in the holy city of Jerusalem love no person on earth more than you. As far as we are able, in these holy places we pour out prayers to the Lord for you day and night, all your servants prostrate on the ground with tears.

Therefore, we make known to you our tribulation, which we suffer here. John, who was from the monastery of Saint Sabas, whom Theodulus, your servant and *iguminus* [abbot], knows, has set himself over us, saying that the Franks who are on the Mount of Olives are heretics. He told us, “All you Franks are heretics,” and rejects our faith, saying that there is no greater heresy.

We said to him: “Brother, be silent. If you call us heretics, you are calling the holy apostolic see heretical.”

He disturbed us to such an extent that on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, in holy Bethlehem, at the holy manger where our Lord, the redeemer of the human race, deigned to be born for the salvation of the world, he sent laymen who wanted to throw us out, saying, “You are heretics, and the books you possess are heretical.”

But through your holy prayer and faith the Lord strengthened us. They were not able to throw us out. We all said: “Here we wish to die. You will not throw us out.”

Therefore, all of us, your servants, raised our voice together, saying to the priests who are in the holy city: “See, fathers and brothers, what this man says against us and against the holy Roman faith. We have never heard such words from our people.”

After this, on the holy Lord’s Day, the priests gathered with the clergy and people opposite the holy sepulchre of the Lord and between the holy place of Calvary. The priests questioned us about our faith and how we believed the creed.

We said that we believe as the holy Roman Church believes. We also said, and we say, in our language what you do not say in Greek: in the *Gloria Patri* you do not say “as it was in the beginning”; in the *Gloria in excelsis* you do not say “You alone are the Most High”; and you say the *Our Father* differently. In the creed we say more than you do: “who proceeds from the Father and the Son.” Because of this statement, John, the enemy of his own soul, says that we are heretics.

We entreated the people of Jerusalem, saying: “Do not listen to this man, nor call us heretics. If you call us heretics, you are calling the throne of blessed Peter heretical. If you say this, you bring sin upon yourselves.”

The priests wrote us a document concerning our faith, which we were permitted to believe, saying to us: “Do you believe as the holy Resurrection of the Lord?”

We replied that we believe as the holy Resurrection of the Lord and the holy Roman apostolic see. [The elliptical wording is that of the supplied text.]

After this, the archdeacon himself went up with us into the gallery of Saint Constantine and read that document aloud before the people. We, your servants, anathematized every heresy and all who should call the holy Roman apostolic see heretical.

And now, most gracious Lord Father, deign to think of us, your servants. Although we are far away, we are your sheep, and the whole world has been entrusted to you, as your holiness knows, just as the Lord said to Peter: “If you love me, Peter, feed my sheep” (John 21:16).

Most gracious Father, when I, Leo, your servant, was at your holy feet and at the pious feet of Lord Charles, the most pious emperor and your son, we heard it said in his chapel in the creed of the faith: “who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

We also heard it in the homily of Saint Gregory which your son, Lord Charles the emperor, gave us, in the explanation of the octave of Easter, where he said: “But his sending is itself his procession, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

And in the rule of Saint Benedict which your son, Lord Charles, gave us, containing the written faith concerning the holy and inseparable Trinity, it says: “I believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

It says the same in the dialogue which your holiness deigned to give us. The faith of Saint Athanasius says the same.

Thus, through this John, great confusion has arisen for us in the holy city, since he says that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father and the Son. He has spread great error concerning this through all the monasteries, and has demanded to examine our faith and our books. He says that the books of Lord Gregory are not to be accepted.

Therefore, again and again, holy Father, prostrate on the ground with tears, we ask and beseech you, by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is called the inseparable Trinity, to deign to inquire, both in Greek and in Latin, of the holy Fathers who composed the creed about this statement, where it says “proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

In Greek they do not say as we do, but say “who proceeds from the Father,” and they regard as serious the statement which we make in Latin.

And may you deign to command Lord Charles, your son and emperor, that we heard this statement in his chapel: “who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

May you deign to assure us, your servants, that no form of this sacrament appears so dear to us as your holy face, your holy prayer, and your intercession or remembrance.

Therefore, most gracious Father, we ask your most holy piety to deign kindly to receive these servants of yours—John the priest, when, with God’s guidance, they reach your most sacred presence—and to send us, your servants, a sure command.

We commend ourselves—Dominicus, Theodore, Arimundus, Gregory, John, Leo, and the entire congregation of the holy Mount of Olives, your humble servants—to your sacred and God-worthy prayers.

May God and our Lord, most holy Father, deign to guide and protect you with all that belongs to you, for the exaltation of his holy Church, the salvation of your soul, and our joy, and in his merciful compassion guard you in all things and through all things—he who is called blessed forever.

## Pope Leo III to Charles Augustus

To the most pious, most serene, victorious, and triumphant son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Charles Augustus: Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

It is necessary for us to report to your imperial power everything that happens to us in each region. In the present year, the monks who dwell on the holy Mount of Olives sent us a letter containing the dispute over the faith which they had among themselves.

We sent them the creed of the orthodox faith, so that all of them might hold the faith of our holy Catholic and apostolic Church as right and inviolate. We have sent that letter to your imperial power for rereading.

Meanwhile, your faithful servants who have now returned—namely Agamus and Roculphus—brought us from Jerusalem a letter from Thomas, patriarch of Jerusalem. On rereading it, we found that they asked us to commend them to your piety by our letter of entreaty.

Therefore, we ask your imperial power that, just as you are accustomed to extend assistance to all your faithful, so you may order mercy to be shown to them.

We have sent to your serenity the very letter which the aforesaid faithful servants brought us.

Having prefaced these matters, may almighty God guard you by his protection, defend your kingdom from all treacherous people by the extension of his arm, and lead you, after a long course of years, to eternal joys.

May heavenly grace preserve the most pious rule of Lord Charles and bow the necks of all nations beneath him.

## Here begins the Creed of Pope Leo concerning the Orthodox Faith
LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the Eastern Churches.

We send you this creed of orthodox faith, so that both you and the whole world may hold, according to the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic Church, the right and uncorrupted faith. We believe in the holy Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one almighty God, of one substance, one essence, and one power; Creator of all creatures, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are.

The Father is from himself, not from another. The Son is begotten from the Father, true God from true God, true light from true light—not, however, two lights, but one light. The Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son. The Father is wholly God in himself; the Son is wholly God, begotten from the Father; the Holy Spirit is wholly God, proceeding from the Father and the Son.

Yet we do not speak of three gods, but of one almighty, eternal, invisible, unchangeable God, who is wholly present everywhere, not divided into parts, but wholly in all things—not locally, but personally. Without changing himself, he created mutable things and governs what he created, always remaining what he is. Nothing accidental can befall him, because nothing can be added to or subtracted from the simple nature of divinity. He is always what he is; for him, what he is is always first and eternal, and for him being, living, and understanding are the same.

These three are one God. These three are the same God and Lord: a true and eternal Trinity in persons, and a true and eternal unity in substance, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one substance. This holy Trinity, when the three persons are named together, is no more than any one person named once, since each person is wholly substance in himself. Yet there are not three substances, but one God, one substance, one essence, one eternity, one greatness, and one goodness: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The Father in nature is not other than the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor are the Son and the Holy Spirit in nature other than the Father, since they have one nature. But the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person. In the Father there is eternity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the connection of eternity and equality. All three are one in substance, essence, omnipotence, and divinity.

For just as the same holy Trinity is inseparable in substance, so it is inseparable in works, although the works of God are specially attributed to certain persons. Thus the voice that sounded from heaven over Christ at his baptism belongs to the Father, and the assumption of humanity belongs only to the person of the Son, while the dove belongs properly to the person of the Holy Spirit, since in the form of that dove the same Holy Spirit descended upon the same Son when he was baptized according to his humanity. Nevertheless, without any doubt, the whole holy Trinity worked both that voice and that dove into Christ’s humanity, for its works are inseparable.

We believe that the same Son of God, the Word, was eternally born from the Father, consubstantial with the Father in all things, and was born in time from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. He has two births: one eternal, from the Father, and the other temporal, from his mother. He, the Son of God, was conceived through the conception of his flesh and born through the birth of his flesh. We confess that true God was conceived and true God was born: the same true God and true human being, one Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, [the preceding phrase is corrupt in the source], perfect in two natures within the singularity of one person, impassible and passible, mortal and immortal, crucified in our weakness, yet always living in his own power.

He died by the death of his flesh and was buried; then, returning from the dead after the condemnation and despoiling of the prince of all wickedness, he rose on the third day. With a triumph of glory, in the sight of his disciples, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, in the majesty of his divinity. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. The wicked will see him judging in the form in which he was crucified, not in the humiliation in which he was unjustly judged, but in the glory in which he will justly judge the world. The vision of this majesty is the eternal blessedness of all the saints.

Whoever does not believe rightly according to this faith is condemned by the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, which was founded by Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

## HOMILY ON TITHES AND FASTING

By an uncertain author, but one who lived in the age of Charlemagne.

*(In Baluze, Capitularia, vol. II.)*

**[Col. 1261C]** You ought to love and do good to all people, beloved brothers. But you ought to do more good to those who serve God more fully and live in good faith.

You ought to offer the firstfruits of your crops and labors at the altar—that is, fresh ears of grain, grapes, and beans. You ought to bring other firstfruits from every crop to the priest’s house, and the priest should bless them. Thus eat them with the Lord’s blessing. Pray to the Lord that in his grace and mercy he may grant you to gather the other crops in peace, to persevere in his holy service, and to do from them what pleases him.

You must not withhold your tithes, give them late, or give them [for an uncertain reason: the text reads *peimi*]. Nor should you wait for priests or other clerics to ask you for your tithes; rather, of your own good will, without being admonished, you should give them and carry them to the priest’s house.

You ought to distribute other alms among guests and the poor. But you are not permitted to give tithes to anyone other than a priest. He distributes them with fear and reverence for God for the roofs of the Church, for lamps, for receiving guests and the poor, and for his own uses and needs.

You ought to observe the Four Ember Fasts in the year. In March, during the first week, when March begins, you must fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. In June, during the second week after June begins, you must fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. In September, during the third week after September begins, fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. In December, during the fourth week, fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday.

On those days you ought to come to church, each one hear Mass, offer sacrifices to God, and give lamps, incense, and alms. No Christian should relax these fasts, unless he is such an infant that he cannot fast, or such an old person or sick person that he cannot do so. Whoever relaxes or neglects these fasts incurs great sin.

You ought to observe these fasts: on the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent, and on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. You ought to fast throughout Lent, except that you must not fast on Sunday. Whoever fasts on Sunday without some necessity incurs sin.

Fast on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, on the vigil of Easter, and on the vigil of Pentecost. Fast on the vigils of Saint Peter, Saint Andrew, and Saint John the Baptist, and pray that they may pray for you to the Lord. Fast also on the three days before the Lord’s Ascension.

Follow the crosses and relics, not in play or on horseback, but celebrate these Rogation days with humility and contrition of heart. Abstain from all meat and hear Masses. Whoever fasts at another time or on other days receives a reward for it. Nevertheless, no one should omit the fasts we have mentioned; rather, with good will, he should observe them and pray for himself and his friends, so that through these fasts, through other good works, and through almsgiving we may have the merciful Lord favorable and propitious to us—through him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## NARRATIVE CONCERNING A MONK OF LE MANS CONVERTED TO THE CANONICAL LIFE AND HABIT

*(In Baluze, as above.)*

**[Col. 1263A]** Just as the holy Church strives every day, through various summonses, to draw to the lot of the elect and the attainment of the blessedness of everlasting life not only those who despise the world, but also—and this is the greater thing—those whom worldly activity causes to flourish, so that here the diversity of good works may multiply them and there the difference of varied rewards may adorn them, so conversely the ancient enemy never ceases to steal away the devout. Those whom he cannot have as companions in glory, he at least desires to recognize as partners with him in punishment.

For although in the three orders—that is, of laymen, canons, and monks—there are some who from the beginning have attempted, after searching out nobler actions with an understanding mind granted by God, to undertake them, the enemy especially strives to ambush those whom he has seen grow in youth and voluntarily devote themselves to the Lord’s commandments. Thus he may joyfully cast them more deeply into the depths, the more he grieves that they once escaped from his bloody jaws.

How damnable their deviation from a holy purpose is, the evangelical and apostolic teachings make clear; and they strengthen such persons with their remedies so that they may be restored once again, showing how they have been wounded by the serpent’s poisons. Since a mode of correction appropriate to the seriousness of the contagion is suitable for each person, and since this has been sanctioned by the teachers of the Church under the authority granted by the high-thundering Judge—so that hidden things may be exposed in one way and open things erased in another—it has also been decreed that greater vigilance and care must be applied to those who, after a nobler devotion, fall back again into secular dress and become apostates.

This worst kind of transgression is found beyond measure in both sexes in our own times. It has entangled many wavering people in its turning paths and, with their vision obscured, struck them away from the straight path toward ruin. But since this avoidable kind of thing appears to stand openly before us, and since for this reason among the assembly of good and bad Catholics some are engaged in rebuke and others in defending the evil—so that those whom they find crushed by such a crime, whom they cannot make wholly innocent, they nevertheless try to present as innocent by their deceptive arguments, either through denial, concealment of the deed, or some pretext—and since the fall of many is now more serious than that of one person, it remains to bring something concerning this very controversy, which has recently grown in our regions, into the open. Thus, once the truth is known, the judgment of truthful people may be observed, and falsehood may vanish in confusion.

There was a certain priest named Urso, a man of great nobility in the city of Le Mans, who wished one of his nephews to survive him. When he sought counsel concerning this matter from the bishop of that city, the venerable Rotbert, the bishop not only assented to his request but also encouraged him in every way to carry it out. He considered that in the boy the Church would gain a benefit from his distinguished lineage, and that by living more sweetly and serving the institutions of the Church he would receive the immortality of his soul.

The priest mentioned above, therefore, hastening to accomplish this undertaking, took with him his brother named Wanilo and presented the aforementioned nephew, named Rigrannus, to the lord bishop and his Church, so that he might deserve to receive from him and his congregation the honor of the clerical state.

When this had been nobly done during the days of holy Easter, the lord bishop again commended the boy to the aforementioned uncle, who had received him in place of a spiritual son, so that he might become guardian and keeper of his body and soul and provide him with nourishment, in order that after his education he might return him fit for divine and human service.

The uncle willingly obeyed the command of his superior and took the boy. Recognizing that he himself did not have sufficient learning, he sent him to a certain monastery belonging to that bishop, where the monastic order flourished, so that he might there be instructed in the sacred Scriptures and educated.

Thus the boy was received into the monastery and handed over to a teacher. After devoting many days to scholarly disciplines, he began at a certain time to be afflicted by a severe bodily illness. As he was very frequently tormented by such attacks, and a dreadful pain in his intestines and internal organs troubled him without remedy, with no medical art providing relief, the teacher began to be astonished at what was causing and provoking such a great illness in the young man. He asked him why he was suffering so many dreadful things.

Although he was questioned for a long time, he gave no definite answer. Then one day, suffering sharper torments and lying almost lifeless, with scarcely a weak breath escaping him, he finally confessed that in earlier years he had been dedicated to God by his father in a monastery called Cormaricus, because, after a vow, the Lord had restored him to his father when he was already as good as dead from the outcome of an overwhelming illness; for that reason he expected to suffer such grave things.

When he heard this, the teacher remained silent and considered within himself that, once the boy had recovered his strength and the time for inquiry had come, he should determine whether what he had heard from him during his illness had been madness. But the boy affirmed that it was true and explained the sequence of events. He also said that he wished to be a monk, so that both his own soul and his father’s might be freed from the danger of the vow.

For his father, mentioned above, namely Rohtbertus, had already departed from human affairs. He had fallen into the hands of the Northmen and, worn down by their torments, had died.

Thus the young man was gradually instructed to submit his neck to the light yoke of Christ and fulfill his father’s purpose. But the teacher denied that this could be done, saying:

“By no means did you come here to become a monk; nor did you receive the tonsure for that purpose. Your parents will not agree to these words.”

While the young man persisted in affirming and defending the request that was not to be carried out, it happened that his uncle Urso, who had received him with paternal affection, came to the monastery for a visit.

As preparations were being made for a meal and they were conversing with one another, among other things the young man began to explain to his uncle his desire for the monastic purpose, the struggle he was enduring, and his father’s vow.

When he heard this, the priest was deeply troubled. He did not dare at all to contradict what he did not wish to encourage. Nevertheless, unwillingly, he consented to the young man’s persistent request that he should do what he was asking.

Immediately, after changing his clothing, the young man put on the cowl and fell at his uncle’s feet and kissed them. From that day forward, both the teacher who had denied the request and those who had mocked the speaker’s words were converted to encouragement and consolation.

Meanwhile, during those days the bishop had withdrawn some distance from the city, carrying out the work of preaching and confirmation throughout the province in places where it was necessary. When he was returning and was not far from the city, he summoned the teacher of the young man mentioned above, who was also abbot of the monastery, so that he might learn what was being done concerning the monks and the monastery.

After he had learned everything, he finally asked about the disciple. The abbot answered his questions and related everything that had happened.

When the lord bishop heard this, he was astonished. Hurrying on his journey, he reached the city, wishing to learn what appearance this matter—heard but incredible—actually had. He ordered the abbot, the novice, and some of the brothers to be summoned.

When they stood before him, while a whole crowd of clerics and laypeople stood around—for it was the hour for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, since the feast of the Purification of holy Mary was approaching—he said in astonishment to the novice mentioned above:

“Recently, brother Rigrannus, I left you a canon, and now I see you wearing the cowl. Tell us, therefore, why you did this, and who compelled you or gave you the advice.”

He replied:

“No one advised or urged me; I did this solely by the will and promise of my own mind.”

He then recounted before all who were listening everything related above. He added that he had seen a remarkable dream, whose interpretation was that he should leave the world and maintain the monastic life.

Since the bishop still did not believe him, and the others were not paying attention, he solemnly adjured him by the authority of his office to declare whether these things were true. The young man affirmed under oath that he had said nothing false.

For this reason the venerable bishop and his whole congregation were saddened and grieved, as though the support and assistance of their Church had been taken away and handed over. They also asked one another in astonishment what such prudence could have appeared in the young man, especially since he had already reached a more dangerous age. For he was thought to be eighteen years old.

Again the venerable bishop asked whether he had determined to persevere in the monastic order throughout all his days. When the young man affirmed and attested this before everyone, the lord bishop gave him his blessing and granted him the place and monastic order that he requested.

When these matters had been completed, the aforementioned uncle Urso heard what had been done by the bishop—for he had not been present at the time, since he was lying ill in a certain place. He and the other relatives were deeply distressed that their nephew had been lost to the world and gained for God.

He sent for him. When the young man stood before him, Urso addressed him in great anger and madness of mind:

“What have you done, wretched boy? Why did you wish to be a monk? Why did you choose one small loaf instead of a hundredfold quantity, and a little wine instead of drinking from cups until you were satisfied? Why did you wish to make the life of pigs among vegetables and a garden sufficient for yourself? Where will be the delights of the meats you have abandoned, the sweetness of drinks, the pleasure of dogs and hawks, and the voluptuous touch of women?”

When he saw that the young man’s mind resisted these things firmly and that his replies showed not youthful weakness but the strength of an old man, he added much more criminal arguments. He even sent pimps to provoke him. He also stirred up the other uncles, namely Lethardus, Wanilo, and many other relatives, who said to him:

“Why did you wish to make us degenerate? The work of our lineage was not with the poor and beggars. The world flourished for us; among us there was abundance of gold, silver, and precious stones. Shining weapons glittered for us, and horses with gilded mouths and curved necks delighted us. And you have despised all these things?”

So spoke the wicked men, who ought to have stirred him toward better things. They preferred to live more pompously and to be submerged in Lethean waters rather than to be washed with the life-giving fountain and, after the labor of forgiveness, sing in praise of the most merciful Liberator, saying:

“We passed through fire and water,  
and you brought us out into refreshment.”

*(Psalm 65:12)*

But the young man’s spirit remained unconquered, eager to observe what he had begun. For five years they could not recall him; he maintained his order and regular devotions in the monastery with the others.

Meanwhile, while they harassed the teacher mentioned above with every kind of outburst, blaming him and demanding the disciple, the hurried teacher did not fail to return the one entrusted to him. The relatives received the nephew and kept him among them, still retaining the appearance of a monk.

After keeping him for eight days and more, they again sent him back to the monastery, at the disciple’s earnest entreaty and with their consent.

When the time for receiving the first ecclesiastical orders had passed, the venerable bishop, having heard of the unworthy conduct of the uncles, sent to the aforementioned priest that he should now consent—as we have said he had previously granted permission, but afterward had withdrawn from that consent—so that the young man might receive the ecclesiastical orders while remaining under the same monastic habit.

After the priest had long delayed, he finally instructed the lord bishop to do what reason and authority recommended. This was done, and the young man received the blessings of the five orders, living and persevering voluntarily in holy conduct.

Two years later, the unexpected day of Urso’s death suddenly arrived. As he was being pressed toward death, he summoned the monk mentioned above, his nephew. When the monk stood before him, Urso sought to admonish him about the glory of the world that he was leaving. He did not abandon the intention he had always held that the monk should return to the canonical life. He gave him advice and especially offered him all the property he had been able to possess, in order to stir his mind toward greed and empty glory.

Thus he died. In death he fulfilled what he had been unable to accomplish in life.

From that day the subdeacon began to be alienated from his former purpose, joined in conduct and mind to his uncles, namely Lethardus and Amarricus, by whose counsel and cunning he is said to have been driven headlong into ruin. They themselves became priests contrary to law, seizing the bishop’s ministry.

For they shut him up in a certain upper room, where, without the judgment of the venerable bishop and priests, they stripped him of his monastic clothing and dressed him in white garments. Thus he returned to secular conduct.

They heaped every accusation upon the teacher and the lord bishop in return for their good deeds. Empty cunning, darkening their eyes, led them grievously into the snare of ruin. For seven years they had feared to commit this violence, so that, even if the deed were evil, it might become all the more damnable by being prolonged and carried out later.

For the longer some good thing endures, the more deeply it falls if it should collapse. Likewise, the more an evil grows, the more severe a punishment it will undergo.

Those who pursue such things, neglecting the fruit of repentance, desire to have empty companions [the text is corrupt: *inanes socius*; probably “empty companions”], and hell longs to receive them.

The entire order of that Church is a witness to this matter; each person, according to his ministry, can testify that it happened in this way.

## LETTER OF THE CLERGY OF RAVENNA TO CHARLES THE YOUNGER

*(From the Great Library of the Fathers.)*

**[Col. 1267C]** To the lord King Charles, glorious through the gift of divine generosity, resplendent in wisdom and power: may the holy Church of Ravenna always see his celebrated triumphs endure with happy success.

Although, because of the height of your wisdom and the honor of your sovereignty—which is regarded as supreme among mortals—almost everything concerning the rule of ecclesiastical life and teaching may seem known to your exalted majesty, and although there may be nothing in the sacred readings that your royal prudence would consider insufficiently understood, nevertheless we have heard that your sacred mind has at some time been troubled by difficulty and scruple concerning the habit of certain men who come to sacred dignity from different disciplines of conduct and rule.

Therefore, having gathered certain examples of the ancient Fathers concerning this matter—what those who came before us happened to think about it and what they ordered by their authoritative decisions—and preserving the custom of our Church in such matters, we have judged it appropriate both to demonstrate the practice of our Church and to calm your ardent diligence in these affairs.

The authority of the Roman pontiffs, to whom the Lord Jesus Christ entrusted in blessed Peter the care and solicitude of feeding the flock of the Church, clearly teaches, with the pure light of faith, by what matters and rules the life of Christians ought to be ordered in each person’s profession, and what discipline is maintained in the churches of the city of Rome.

The blessed Celestine, discussing this matter, says among other things:

> “For we say that the priests of the Lord serve a superstitious observance rather than purity of mind or faith. Nor is it surprising, he says, if those who did not grow up in the Church act contrary to ecclesiastical custom; coming by another path, they have brought into the Church with them the things they had in another manner of life. Wearing a cloak, like Greek monks, and girding their loins, they believe that they embrace the faith of sacred Scripture not through the spirit but through the letter. For if these commandments were given so that they might be observed in this manner, why are the things that follow not likewise done, so that burning lamps are held together with a staff? These things have their own mystery, and to those who understand they are so clear that they are observed with more significance than is fitting. For the girding of the loins signifies chastity, the staff pastoral rule, and the burning lamps the splendor of good works.”

**[Col. 1268D]** Perhaps such men have this form of observance because they follow custom rather than reason; they live in more remote places and dwell far from others. Why, then, should this habit be introduced into the Gallican Churches, so that the custom of so many years and so many pontiffs should be changed into another habit?

We are to be distinguished from the common people and from others by teaching, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by outward adornment. The people are to be taught rather than entertained; commandments are not to be imposed upon their eyes, but infused into their minds.

For Leo, bishop of the holy Roman See, says:

> “The purpose of a monk, undertaken by his own judgment or will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what a person has vowed to God, he ought to repay. Therefore, one who has abandoned the profession of solitude and fallen into military service or marriage must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance.”

By “abandoning the profession of solitude,” we understand not the scapular, which is said to be worn for work, but the matter described in the example above. Nor is the point that someone has risen to the dignity of the priesthood; rather, if he has fallen into military service or marriage, he is considered in need of cleansing through the satisfaction of public penance.

Although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, nevertheless to have abandoned the better choice—which cannot exist within the priestly office—is a transgression.

In this passage, understanding the monk’s purpose as devotion to holy conduct, not the observance of clothing—for monastic dress is multiple and varied according to the diversity of places and kingdoms, as is found among Greek and Latin monks—we are entirely confident, to the best of our understanding, that those who are consecrated to ecclesiastical governance in canonical order and episcopal dignity, if they serve the churches to which they have been advanced in priestly dress and custom, do not violate the rules of the ancient Fathers.

Rather, relying upon ecclesiastical and apostolic rules, we judge that the harmony preserved by the Roman Church in the dress of priests must be followed in every way. We consider it far better that, through the uniform equality of priestly clothing, they should share the common ministry of serving the Church than that, wearing the distinctive cloak of episcopal honor, they should differ in life and conduct from either order—that is, from the profession of solitude or from the episcopal profession.

Nor do we say that we grant authority to bind the dress of all churches by this law.

We know that each person may abound in his own understanding. But we, and the bishops of our churches—whom we rejoice to have come to sacred dignity from different disciplines of conduct and rule—judge, on the basis of the institutions of the ancient Fathers, that if they minister to the churches in priestly dress, no prejudice should be held against them and that we need not fear that they should be struck by canonical censure on account of the quality of their dress.

Moreover, we judge that the custom and practice of our Church must be retained harmoniously: the stole should be laid over the other garments according to the dignity of the priesthood, by which they preside over the people. The following phrase concerning a pontiff’s garment of penance and labor is textually uncertain. Yet no one of this order, on account of the quality and style of his clothing, is subject to the rules or institutions of the decrees of the Fathers, provided his life, in whatever profession, is not found defiled by any grave crime.

That is, provided he is not bound by a union with a second wife, is not notorious for public penance, is not physically impaired in any part of his body, is in no way subject to servile or hereditary status, and is proved free from the bonds of public office.

Rather, the ancient custom of that Church must be observed in every way without violation.

For, in order to preserve the whole profession of solitude—which the priestly office in the form of ecclesiastical life scarcely permits—we do not, in the judgment of all authorities, consider the mere monastic cloak sufficient if the other practices prescribed by the authority of that rule are neglected: eating, silence, observance of the hours, and the performance of all regular acts.

Instead, we judge that those who differ entirely in life from their distinctive habit, while participating in the common life, must be reproved more severely.

Nor do we say that, when men of this religious order reach sacred dignity, they should all generally change their clothing, abandoning the custom of the Church or of the religious order in which they were advanced. Rather, in either form of priests’ dress, we judge that the custom and order of the churches in which they were advanced should be followed irreproachably, without being subject to any prejudice from the Fathers.

Therefore, good king, in order to explain the reason for this custom of ours, insofar as our accountability requires it, we wish humbly to reassure your majesty by authoritative testimony concerning your God-pleasing solicitude. We have learned from the report of many that you devote yourself with the most fervent zeal of mind to the state of the holy Church of God and to all its interests.

At the same time, we offer immense thanks to your royal greatness, which has deigned, through its sacred letters, to admonish and correct us in the persons of our sons—that is, your faithful envoys—and has also shown us, in its devotional admonition, how fervently you are concerned for holy religion, lest we appear blameworthy.

Therefore, lest we seem before you always to be transgressors of the established canons in this custom of ours, we have gladly taken care to show your royal greatness, in this letter of explanation, on what rules we rely in preserving the practice and order of our Church in this matter.

If your devoted and royal prudence should discover something better, or something more consonant with pious rules and canonical writing, we agree in every respect with your admonitions.

May God preserve all your wholesome rule, for governing and defending his holy Church. Amen.

## FRAGMENT FROM THE HISTORY OF THE CONVERSION OF THE BAVARIANS AND CARANTANIANS TO THE CHRISTIAN FAITH

Written around the year 858.

*(In Duchesne, Scriptores rerum Francicarum, vol. II, p. 220.) (C)*

**[Col. 1269D]** Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 716, the Emperor Charles sent Count Eric, together with a vast multitude, to exterminate the Huns. Since they offered very little resistance, they surrendered themselves through the aforementioned count to the Emperor Charles.

In that same year Charles sent his son Pippin into Hunnia with a large army. When Pippin reached their celebrated place called Rinch, all their leaders again surrendered themselves there to Pippin.

Returning from there, he designated to Arno, bishop of the Juvavian Church, as far as he had authority, the part of Pannonia around the place called Lower Pelessa, beyond the river called Rapa, and from there as far as the Dranus [or Dravus] River, and as far as the place where the Dranus flows into the Danube, so that he might govern by teaching and ecclesiastical ministry the people who remained in those regions from among the Huns and Slavs, until the presence of his father, the Emperor Charles.

Later, in the year 803, the Emperor Charles entered Bavaria. In the month of October, when he was at Salzburg and saw the aforementioned grant of his son, he confirmed it with authority in the presence of many of his faithful and permitted it to be made irrevocable.

Again, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 798, it happened that Arno, already a bishop and having received the pallium from Pope Leo, returned from Rome and came beyond the Po. There he encountered a messenger of Charles with a letter from him, instructing Arno to go by that route into the regions of the Slavs, inquire into the will of that people, and preach the word of God there.

But because he could not do this before bringing back a reply to his mission, he hurried to the emperor and reported to him everything that Pope Leo had commanded through him.

After the mission had been completed, the emperor ordered Archbishop Arno to proceed into the regions of the Slavs, inspect the whole region, cultivate ecclesiastical worship according to episcopal custom, and strengthen the people in faith and Christianity by preaching.

He did as he had been ordered. Coming there, he consecrated churches, ordained priests, and taught the people by preaching. On his return he announced to the emperor that great benefit could be achieved there if someone undertook the task.

Then, at the emperor’s command, Theodoric was ordained bishop by Arno, bishop of the Juvavian Church. Arno himself and Count Gerold led him into Slavonia and handed him over to the leaders. They entrusted to that bishop the region of the Carantanians and their neighbors on the western side of the Dranus River, as far as the Dranus flows into the Danube, so that with authority he might govern the people by his preaching and teach them through evangelical doctrine to serve God.

After Emperor Charles had expelled the Huns, he entrusted the dignity of the episcopate to the rector of the Church of Juvavum—namely, Archbishop Arno—and granted it perpetually to him and his successors, to hold and govern. Then peoples, whether Slavs or Bavarians, began to inhabit and multiply in the land from which the Huns had been expelled. At that time the emperor first appointed Gonterannus as count of the frontier; second, Werenharius; third, Albricus; fourth, Gotefridus; fifth, Geroldus.

Meanwhile, while the aforesaid counts administered the eastern region, certain dukes lived in those districts belonging to the aforementioned see. They were subject to the aforesaid counts for the emperor’s service. Their names were Prinnihlawga, Ceincias, Hroymar, and Etgar. After them, the Bavarian dukes began to hold the aforesaid land as a county, with royal grant: Hebriwinus, Albgarius, and Palio.

When these matters had been completed, Ratbod undertook the defense of the frontier. During his period of office, a certain Prinnina, exiled by Moymar, duke of the Moravians above the Danube, came to Ratbod. Ratbod immediately presented him to our lord King Louis; by the king’s command, after receiving instruction in the faith, he was baptized in the church of Saint Martin, at a place called Treisma, which had formerly belonged to the see of Juvavum. He was afterward entrusted to Ratbod and remained with him for some time.

Not long afterward, Hecilo came from the Bulgarians into the territory of Duke Ratimar [Col. 1272C]. At that time King Louis of the Bavarians sent Ratbod with a large army to destroy Duke Ratimar. Ratimar, despairing of being able to defend himself, fled with his men, who escaped the slaughter; but the aforementioned Prinninas remained with his own men, crossed the river Sava, and was there received and reconciled with Ratbod by Count Salacho. Later, when another opportunity arose and the king’s aforesaid faithful men made a request, the king granted Prinnina a portion of Lower Pannonia as a benefice, around the river called the Sava.

[Col. 1271]

## EXCERPT FROM THE LITTLE BOOK ON THE CONVERSION OF THE CARANTANIANS

(From Wilhelm Wattenbach, *Contributions to the History of the Christian Church*, from Cod. Bibl. Caes. 423, thirteenth century)

[Col. 1271D] Modestus, a bishop sent and consecrated by Saint Virgilius under Pippin, king of the Franks, first preached to the Carantanians. After him, Theodoricus was sent and consecrated bishop in the presence of Emperor Charles by Archbishop Arno. After him, Bishop Otto was consecrated by Archbishop Adelrammus. After him came Bishop Hosbaldus under the archbishops Liuprammus and Adelwinus. Pope Nicholas wrote Hosbaldus two canons, which are found in the body of the decretals.

After him, some time having intervened, a certain Slav named Methodius came from the regions of Istria and Dalmatia. He devised Slavic letters and celebrated the divine office in Slavic, causing Latin to fall into disrepute. At last, driven out of the Carantanian regions, he entered Moravia, where he now rests.

In the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, the duke Samo ruled the Carantanians; after him came Boruth, after him Carastus, after him Cheitmarus, and after him Waltunc. Likewise, under Charles and his successors: Priwizlauga, Cemicas, Ztoimar, and Etgar.

[Col. 1274A] In the eastern part of Bavaria also, after the Huns had been expelled, these counts were appointed by Emperor Charles and his successors: Goterammus; second, Werenharius; third, Albricus; fourth, Gotfridus; fifth, Geroldus. After these came the dukes Helmwinus, Albgarius, and Pabo; and the dukes of the Carantanians mentioned above were subject to these counts and dukes.

[Col. 1273]

# ANONYMOUS BOOK ON COMPUTUS

(From Muratori, *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 108)

## NOTICE

[Col. 1273B] *Computus*, or *compotus*, among writers of the less cultivated centuries meant nothing other than knowledge of the course of the moon and of the Kalends, or the science of determining time according to the progress of the sun and moon, as Durandus says in book VIII, chapter 1 of the *Rationale*. The name is derived from *computare*, “to calculate,” because it is necessary to calculate the course of the sun and moon, years, months, and days, so that the nineteen-year cycles, epacts, leap day, lunar saltus, Kalends, Ides, and especially the date of Easter, as well as other matters of that kind, may be learned. All these things are now more commonly signified by the term “calendar.”

In former times the science of computus was entrusted with great diligence both to priests and to clerics; it was even provided by law that no one should be exempted from learning it, as Ducange demonstrates in his *Latin Glossary* from many documents. On this subject we have published some books by ancient authors; the more distinguished libraries still preserve others in manuscript. In explaining computus, Bede excelled especially, and more than one short work on the subject is found among his writings. Baluzius published Rabanus Maurus’s *Book on Computus* in volume I of the *Miscellanea*, p. 1. We have also learned from Usserius that in the Cotton Library there is a manuscript book on computus by the monk Gildas, consisting of ninety-nine chapters. I pass over Maximus the monk, Isaacus Argyrus, Durandus, and many others much more ancient, both Greek and Latin, who dealt with paschal cycles or computus in various letters and treatises.

In the centuries immediately preceding our own, when letters began to be cultivated with such prosperous success that we ought now rather to envy the ancients than the ancients us, the science of the calendar was treated with exceptional care and learning, and produced very famous writers whom every age must admire. Even in our own time we have Cassini, Blanchini, Bonjour, Manfred, Quartinoni, and other outstanding men, in whose writings the controversy over the Gregorian reform has been renewed and debated. I think I shall do a service not unwelcome to learned men and other students of the calendar if I publish this book as well, since the learning of the ancients—although sometimes sterile and sometimes mixed with fables and errors—can and often does contribute considerably to assisting and perfecting the learning of later scholars, especially in this subject.

Here, then, is the *Book on Computus*, which, since it had not yet been published, I transcribed from manuscript 70, shelfmark S, of the Ambrosian Library. The characters of the manuscript are extremely ancient, but I would not dare to assert that they belong to the period in which the author of the book lived. There are countless errors there, to the point of tedium, both in grammar and in orthography. Some of them, because they were too conspicuous, I removed; the rest I left, to be pardoned as belonging either to those times or to the weakness or usage of scribes.

It is not easy to determine when the author lived, for he gathered here the works of other writers belonging to various periods. Nevertheless, he seems to have flourished around the year of Christ 810, or at most a few years afterward; this may be conjectured from chapter 153 and from other passages. I do not doubt that, besides the many passages repeated from the books of Bede, Rabanus, and others, this work contains other material that one would seek in vain elsewhere, although it is not always separable from falsehoods and fables.

I omitted the letters of Proterius, Dionysius, and others, since they had already been published by Bucherius and partly also by the celebrated Petavius. I nevertheless retained the book’s prologue, namely the letter of Saint Cyril of Alexandria, although Petavius published it in an appendix to his books *On the Doctrine of Time*, so that scholars may compare the two exemplars, both of them teeming with errors, and attempt to discover Cyril’s true meaning.

With the aforementioned prologue or letter, the Ambrosian manuscript joins another fragment under this title: “Likewise, the explanation of the sun, or the course of the moon, and of the leap day.” This is not read in Petavius and certainly cannot be attributed to Cyril, or to a Greek author, although everything is connected in the same continuous style in the Ambrosian manuscript. But I do not wish to detain the reader any longer.

[Col. 1275]

# BOOK ON COMPUTUS

## The prologue of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, on the calculation of Easter, begins. (C)

[Col. 1275A] The holy mystery of Easter, and its sacred solemnity, as it was handed down by our Savior to the apostles, would have remained undefiled had not the perversity of certain persons violated it, along with the other sacraments of the faith. Even those who attempted to answer their perversity, and established an eighty-four-year cycle, would have maintained the cycles of a complete reckoning had they been able in their calculation of months or years to follow human or divine tradition.

Hence they became so entangled in the darkness of ignorance that they fell into the danger of paschal ignorance on both sides. Thus they are frequently taught to have erred by celebrating Easter on the evening of Saturday, and before the month of new things, when the moon was actually the fourteenth—which the common people regard as the sixteenth—although the circle of its course had not yet completed its ninth [day/portion]. Others perceived and criticized this, and, as though wishing to correct it, added worse errors to those of the former group. Since they were not enlightened by divine revelation but exalted by the presumption of human knowledge, they attempted, just as the former group had done with six sets of four decades, to describe different and inextricable cycles through seven sets of sixteen, marking doubled or multiplied numbers and monograms, and certain little measures.

Through the narrow difficulties and endless controversies arising from these matters, some became so embittered by their mutual attacks that, abandoning all the observances, they irrationally celebrated not the Lord’s Easter—which occurs on the day of the solemnity of the Resurrection, under the moon’s fullness of light, in fellowship with the eternal Sun—but merely the birthday of the world, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, regardless of whatever moon or weekday happened to fall then.

Human ingenuity and a polished tongue are extended in vain unless the one who makes the wisdom of this world foolish directs a person’s understanding toward true wisdom. Since, therefore, the paschal rule was disturbed throughout the entire world by these and similar disagreements, the holy synod of the whole world decreed, after consultation, that since a Church had been found at Alexandria that excelled in this science—namely, on which day of the Kalends or Ides, and under which moon, Easter ought to be celebrated—it should notify the Roman Church in writing each year, so that by apostolic authority the universal Church throughout the world might know the appointed day of Easter without dispute.

Although this was partly observed for many centuries, no one supposed that any writing existed in which no question was left unresolved. Sometimes it happened that, when the moon was the twentieth on Saturday—which they considered the twenty-third—they feared to celebrate Easter from the twelfth day before the Kalends of May to the eighth day before those same Kalends, as though Easter were being celebrated in the second month. Thus there was great confusion in every church, court, and palace. The most devout Theodosius, who always sought to please God not only in human but also in divine laws, summoned in a letter Saint Theophilus, bishop of the whole city of Alexandria, and asked him to explain the mystery of Easter with the clearest possible reasoning and to be willing to send the explanation to him.

Obeying his most holy instructions, Theophilus established a paschal cycle of 428 years. Calculating from the first year of Theodosius’s consulship through the hundredth year, he sent him in writing an account of on which day of the Kalends or Ides, and under which moon, Easter ought to be celebrated. He faithfully and briefly set out the manifest truth in a little book, in which, with the Lord revealing it to him, he disclosed the order of a perfect calculation and defeated and dissolved, with light clearer than day, all errors and superfluous questions.

Since the various cycles had already been disseminated throughout the world and had already taken unshakable possession of the minds of our people, this fifth [cycle/decree?] could scarcely reach a few. When I perceived that almost everyone’s understanding was unable to penetrate its excessive depth, I asked for the Lord’s revelation. I ventured to draw in the little book from the very source what I had been privileged to draw, since I recognized that even those among whom I had seen the cycle itself had not understood it.

And lest the enormous accumulation of 428 years bring some people either distaste for learning or laziness in copying, I shortened the same cycle to ninety-five years; I learned that these years turn without any difference through all the years of the cycle. I warned that in certain years one single unit—because of the calculation of the leap day, which could not occur until that final year of the cycle which returns to the beginning—must be added, or rather omitted.

Affirming that holy Easter is to be celebrated from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April through the eighth day before the Kalends of May, a period of thirty-five days making five weeks, he added the remaining five days of that week, so that, because of Sunday, it might extend from the fourteenth to the twenty-first moon, as prescribed. This moon becomes the fourteenth from the twelfth day before the Kalends of May; it is recognized and completed at the limits of the first month, according to the reckoning of the Hebrews, from whom the calculation of Easter was received by Christ.

When an intercalary year occurs—one that has thirteen lunar months and, as was divinely revealed to holy Moses, the same 384 days—it is clear that these five added days of the month of new things belong not to the second month but to the first. For even if they belonged to the second month, they would rightly seem to have been added on account of the Lord’s resurrection for the fullness of the Church. Those who lived farther away, or who were unclean in soul, were commanded to celebrate Easter in the second month; this is understood as a type of the holy Church, which, having fornicated with all the demons, seemed unclean in soul, but after being cleansed by saving confusion appeared, according to its birth, to pass as if into the second month.

Before the month of new things is the final month of the old things, in which Easter is absolutely forbidden to occur. But, to state briefly what is different in their dispute: the moon which they improperly call the third, sixteenth, or twenty-third, Saint Theophilus confirms to be the first, fourteenth, or twenty-first, as heaven demonstrates. As for Easter, which they fear to celebrate beyond the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, Saint Theophilus does not hesitate to postpone it until the eighth day before those Kalends.

In their sequence of years, some added one lunar day from the lunar increments in the fourteenth year, others in the sixteenth. Saint Theophilus added it in the nineteenth year. Hence their calculation, because it is inappropriate and inconsistent, is defective. His calculation, however, because it rests upon truth, prevails and endures forever.

For Theophilus wishes the fourteenth moon to be seen in the heavens, in the full circle of its course, rising at the very moment when the sun sets; and, after that same night has passed, the moon to set and the sun to rise. It is therefore plainly evident that the moon which they fear to observe as the twenty-third during the vigil of Easter, he, assigning it as the twenty-first, judges without hesitation that holy Easter should be celebrated; and the moon which they, measuring it on the preceding Saturday as the fifteenth, anticipate, he displays as the sixteenth, maintains that they do not celebrate it rightly, and does not hesitate to defer the celebration until the twenty-first.

It is clear that the moon has twenty-nine and a half days; doubled, these make fifty-nine, to which one day is added beyond the two half-days, so that they appear to complete sixty. This produces the legitimate lunar saltus, so that if the moon was verbally said to be five on one day, it is not called six but seven.

No one is unaware that the moon has half of a thirtieth day in its waning and half in its waxing; this is counted as the thirtieth, and also as the first. Thus the twenty-ninth should be understood as the day preceding the first. The thirtieth moon cannot be seen at all, because at the very end it is consumed in the middle of the thirtieth day and is joined to the sun; at that same moment it is reborn, gradually withdrawing from the sun and increasing through the remaining thirtieth part of that day until the next day, which is called the first. After sunset it is seen just as, as I said above, the twenty-ninth was held at dawn on the preceding day.

What blindness or madness of mind, therefore, is it to say that the thirtieth can be seen when it is already waning, and sometimes to call it the first and even the second—as though they were lying throughout the entire sequence? For just as they call the second instead of the thirtieth and the third instead of the first, so they are compelled to say the sixteenth instead of the fourteenth and the twenty-third instead of the twenty-first. It is as though the devil, by means of this deception, were hunting Christian souls among the very sacraments of the faith.

He places this also as a supreme and unconquerable example: our Savior celebrated Easter with his disciples under the fourteenth moon, on the fifth day of the week, and commanded that it always be done on this basis. Even today it is celebrated as it was handed down; the holy chrism is consecrated, and the Lord’s Supper is completed in its annual solemnity. This is the perfect and greatest sacrament of Easter, as the holy Apostle relates that it was handed down to him and boasts that he handed it down to the Corinthians. The fourteenth is handed down, he suffered on the fifteenth, and he rose on the seventeenth—under that moon which, without any intervening darkness, is joined at dawn to the light of the sun, even according to the common reckoning.

This is the sign of true salvation: that, leaving behind the darkness of all wickedness, they may enjoy the light of the sun through that eternal Sun.

If, therefore, you remove this superfluous two-day span of the moon, understand those five days added according to the calculation of the month of new things, and also add in the nineteenth year that day from the lunar increments which they added in the fourteenth or sixteenth year, you will recognize the whole force and calculation of the truth of this mystery.

The moon which they call the third is also called the first today by the Jews and Greeks, and rightly appears in the evening, since it already has half of the thirtieth and is likewise the first.

## Likewise, the explanation of the sun, or the course of the moon, and of the leap day

A year has 365 days, twelve months, and four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. In the four seasons there are two equinoxes and two solstices. One equinox occurs on the ninth day before the Kalends of April; one solstice occurs on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, on the nativity of Saint John; and the other solstice occurs on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The sun shines for 365 days in the year, while the quarter shines for 354 days; the remaining eleven days are those by which the sun appears to shine above this number. They are eleven because they are added each year to the course of the moon. To make the calculation clearer: there are twelve months in a year, and seven of these months have more than thirty days each: January, March, May, July, August, October, and December. Therefore remove one day each from December and January and add them to February, which has twenty-eight days; it will then have thirty.

Remove the remaining days which lie above the number thirty in the five months at the beginning, and all the months become equal, so that they have thirty days. A lunar month shines for twenty-nine and a half days, as we have already stated in the letter above, because it does not complete the thirtieth day. Therefore there are twelve lunar months in a year.

For each lunar month the moon shines one half-day less. Thus remove twelve half-days from the twelve lunar months and combine them into one; they produce six days. Add to these the five days from the five months, and together they produce eleven days, which they seem to add to the lunar course, because in the lunar year the moon shines eleven days less than the sun.

The quarter, which produces the leap day by which the 365 days increase after four years, has three ounces.
