In one year three grow; in another year three; in the third year four; in the fourth year likewise three. Together they make twelve hours, producing one day, which is called the leap day. Just as the other days which make up the year are counted and then omitted, so, when the leap day arrives after four years, the day that occurs in sequence to carry that year—for example, Wednesday—is omitted, and Thursday is counted. Thus the leap day is transmitted according to the tradition of our elders.

The prologue of Saint Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, ends.

# [BOOK ON COMPUTUS]

[Col. 1279D] If you wish to know on which weekday any date occurred, calculate how many days of that month you have, and subtract the day of the Kalends. Remember, reader, which weekday you had on the Kalends; add that weekday to the days mentioned above, divide by seven, and whatever remains will be the weekday. If nothing remains, it will be the seventh weekday.

If you wish to know under which moon any date falls, calculate how many days of that month you have. Subtract the day of the Kalends. Remember, reader, which moon you had on the Kalends; add that moon to the days mentioned above, and divide by thirty. Whatever remains will be the moon of the day; if nothing remains, the moon will be thirty. Similarly, if you have the twenty-ninth moon, divide by twenty-nine. Whatever remains will be the moon of the day. If nothing remains, it will be the twenty-ninth moon.

To find the weekday in February, from the thirty-second day before the Kalends to the end.

[Col. 1280D]

If you wish to know which weekday this or that day is, count the days from the Kalends of January up to the day about which you are asking. When you know them, add the weekday that occurred on the Kalends of January and, if it is a leap year, also the leap day. Divide everything by seven; add the days that remain to the week, and wherever you are seeking, it will display [the weekday]. The figure 350 is shown: 50 multiplied by seven makes 350, through to the end.

## On the moon at the Kalends of January

If you wish to know which moon this or that day has, count the days from the Kalends of January up to the day about which you are asking. When you know them, add the age of the moon that was at the Kalends of January. Divide everything by fifty-eight. If more than thirty remain, subtract thirty; what remains is the moon of the day you seek. At the end add six; seek this through to the end: A, B, C, D.

## On the moon at the Kalends of January

If you wish to know this, take the cycle of the current year. Multiply it by eleven and add the regular epact. Divide by thirty. What remains is the age of the moon at the Kalends of January. But remember only that in cycles 17, 18, and 19 you should not add one but add two regular units.

If you wish to know which moon belongs to any year you choose, take its cycle and add one. Take the same six times, or [the reading is uncertain: “with thirty placed”]; if one remained, you will find the whole moon. Afterward add sixteen to two.

## The computus of the Greeks or Latins begins: how we ought to calculate in every year

[Col. 1281C]

### I

January, August, and December have the fourth day before the Nones, the nineteenth day after the Ides, and thirty-one days.

March, May, July, and October have the sixth day before the Nones, the seventeenth day after the Ides, and thirty-one days.

April, June, September, and November have the fourth day before the Nones, the eighteenth day after the Ides, and thirty days.

The month of February has the fourth day before the Nones, the sixteenth day after the Ides, and twenty-eight days.

All the months have the eighth day before the Ides.

## Likewise, another matter

II. In January, August, and December, the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the eighteenth day before the Kalends, the eleventh day before the Kalends, and the fourth day before the Kalends each contain one day.

In March, May, July, and October, the Kalends, the eighth day before the Ides, the Ides, the eleventh day before the Kalends, and the fourth day before the Kalends each contain one day.

In April, June, September, and November, the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the seventeenth day before the Kalends, the tenth day before the Kalends, and the third day before the Kalends each contain one day.

In February, however, the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the fifteenth day before the Kalends, and the eighth day before the Kalends each contain one day.

The month that has the fourth day before the Nones makes the Nones fall on day 5 and the Ides on day 13; the month that has the sixth day before the Nones makes the Nones fall on day 7 and the Ides on day 15.

## Here you will find the days of the year

March: at the Kalends, 60; at the Nones, 66; at the Ides, 74.

April: at the Kalends, 91; at the Nones, 95; at the Ides, 103.

May: at the Kalends, 121; at the Nones, 127; at the Ides, 135.

July: at the Kalends, 182; at the Nones, 188; at the Ides, 196.

August: at the Kalends, 213; at the Nones, 217; at the Ides, 225.

The Kalends of May: the day before the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of June: the sixth day before the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of July: the fourth day before the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of August: the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of September: the fifth day before the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of October: the third day before the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of November: the Kalends of March.  
The Kalends of December: the fifth day before the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of January: the day before the Nones of March.  
The Kalends of February: the sixth day before the Nones of March.

If you wish to know on what day the Kalends of the months begin, this calculation will make it known for any desired year.

June: 6.

September: 7.  
October: 2.

## On common and intercalary years

Common, common, intercalary; common, common, intercalary; common, intercalary, eighth; common, common, intercalary; common, common, intercalary; common, common, intercalary; common, intercalary. End.

Add these regular [numbers], which are placed before the four limits, to the concurrent days of the year in question; then divide by seven. If seven remain, those limits will fall on the seventh weekday. If more than seven remain—1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7—those will be the complete weekdays of the limits.

## On common and intercalary years
## IV. The First Common Year

The first common year begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. The second begins on the Nones of April. The third, an embolismic year, begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. [Col. 1283D] The solar year has 365 days. The common year has 354 days. The embolismic year has 384 days. It is called “common” because it corresponds to the ordinary number of days. “Embolismic,” however, is Greek, and is rendered in Latin as *augmentum*, “increase,” or “a greater year.”

## On the Letters of the Greeks

### V.

We read in the letters of the Greeks that, after the passion of the apostles, Saint Pachomius, abbot in Egypt, prayed to the Lord with his monks that He might show them how they ought to celebrate Easter. The Lord sent his angel, who wrote to the aforementioned Saint Pachomius a nineteen-year cycle in the following manner: “The Nones of April,” and so on to the end.

## How You Ought to Find the Paschal Computations Correctly, According to the Latins or the Greeks

[Col. 1284A]

### VI.

The Latins, accordingly, judged that the period from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April—namely, twenty-nine days—should be observed above all, so that, on whichever of those days the moon was born, that day would constitute the beginning of the first month. If its fourteenth day fell on a Friday, you will celebrate the Paschal feast without ambiguity on the following Sunday, that is, on the sixteenth day of the moon [the final printed “14” is unexplained]. Moreover, the moon of that same month is to be observed from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, with regard to the weekday.

### The More Accurate Account

### VII.

The holy synod of 318 bishops who assembled at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, with the Holy Spirit illuminating them, firmly decreed that from the eighth day before the Ides of March to the day of the Nones of April—twenty-nine days—the beginning of the first month should be reckoned, regardless of what day the moon was born. [Col. 1284B]

### Again, How the Day of the Month and the Last Paschal Moon Are to Be Celebrated

### VIII.

We find it established in the council of the Romans that Easter should occur neither before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April nor after the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

### Again, Among the Greeks

### IX.

The bishop Theophilus of Alexandria, of holy memory, in letters sent to the emperor Theodosius, announced that from the eighth day before the Ides of March to the day of the Nones of April—namely, twenty-nine days—the beginning of the first month was to be reckoned at any point within the interval, regardless of what day the moon was born. The fourteenth day of the moon was to be carefully sought from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May; even if it fell on a Saturday, he wrote that Easter was to be celebrated on the following Sunday, that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon. If the fourteenth day of the moon of that same month, that is, of the first month, fell on a Sunday, he wrote that Easter was unquestionably to be celebrated on the following Sunday, after that week had passed. [Col. 1284C]

### Again, Among the Latins

### X.

There is another example concerning the beginning of the first month: whatever lunar day it is on the Kalends of January, you will count that many days at the end of March, and you will undoubtedly find the moon. The beginning of the first month can have only three lunar ages, namely 25, 28, or 26.

### Again, Concerning the Birth of the Moon

### XI.

The fourteenth day of the moon is to be sought from the eighth day before the Ides of March to the Nones of April; this period indicates the beginning of the new moons of the first month. From the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, on whichever day the fourteenth moon occurs, that day leads you to the celebration of holy Easter. [Col. 1284D]

But if the fourteenth moon occurs before the twelfth day before the Kalends—whether on the thirteenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day before the Kalends of April—know that it is not the Paschal moon. Instead, when you have brought that same moon to the thirtieth day, and another moon has been born on a different day, you will celebrate holy Easter on that latter moon. Likewise, take care that the fourteenth moon does not pass beyond the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, so as to fall on the thirteenth or twelfth day before the Kalends of May. Otherwise, you will begin to be led into great error.

### Another Account

### XII.

The Easter of Christians is celebrated from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on whichever Sunday the lunar rule indicates the moon has occurred. [Col. 1285A] But if the moon occurs before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, or after the seventh day before the Kalends of May, Easter is not celebrated at all.

## On the Common and Embolismic Years

### XIII.

The rule of the common and embolismic years is this: they must proceed according to the eight-year and eleven-year cycles. There are eight-year cycles and eleven-year cycles.

The eight-year cycle is:

> Common, common, embolismic, common, common, embolismic, common, embolismic.

The eleven-year cycle is:

> Common, common, embolismic, common, embolismic, common, common, common, embolismic, common, embolismic.

For example, the fourteenth day of the Paschal moon in the preceding year is to be found. That fourteenth moon was on the day before the Ides of April. In the present year, if the date extends forward by nineteen days, the year will be embolismic; if it is found eleven days earlier, the year will be common. [Col. 1285B]

### Again, Concerning Common and Embolismic Years

### XIV.

If you wish to know when Easter should be celebrated in a common year and when in an embolismic year, follow this calculation. The nineteen-year cycle, called in Greek *enneakaidekaetērís*, continually revolves through the eight-year and eleven-year cycles—that is, through eight and eleven years, which together make nineteen.

The eight-year cycle therefore begins with year 1 of the nineteen-year cycle and closes with year 8. Its years 1 and 2 are common, year 3 embolismic, years 4 and 5 common, year 6 embolismic, year 7 common, and year 8 embolismic. Thus the eight-year cycle is completed with five common and three embolismic years.

The eleven-year cycle begins with year 9 of the nineteen-year cycle and ends with year 19. It proceeds as follows: years 1 and 2 are common, year 3 embolismic, years 4 and 5 common, year 6 embolismic, years 7 and 8 common, year 9 embolismic, year 10 common, and year 11 embolismic. [Col. 1285C]

Thus it is called an eleven-year cycle because the lesser years—which are completed with twelve lunar months and 354 days according to the course of the moon—are joined together in Paschal observance. In relation to the course of the sun, eleven days are lacking from them. The Egyptians call these days *epacts*, that is, “additions.” When they are added to the days written above, they complete the number of the solar year, namely 365 days. This is also investigated in the calculation of the embolismic years, whose character is such that, by their length, they compensate for the deficiencies of the common years.

For *embolismic* is Greek and is called in Latin *superaugmentum*, “super-increase,” because this year is completed with thirteen lunar months and 384 days, exceeding the solar year by nineteen days. [Col. 1285D]

The following is the established calculation of common and embolismic years. If from the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the fourteenth of the following year there were 354 days, it will be a common year. But if there were 384 days, it will be an embolismic year. For greater clarity, the following table, extending from the first year of the nineteen-year cycle to its last year, will teach you the order.

In year 1 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 17. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding Paschal feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May to the Nones of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 2 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 18. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the day before the Nones of April to the eighth day before the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year. [Col. 1286A]

In year 3 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 19. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the seventh day before the Kalends of April to the Ides of April—there are 384 days, because it is an embolismic year.

In year 4 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 1. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the day before the Ides of April to the fourth day before the Nones of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 5 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 2. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the third day before the Nones of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 6 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 3. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the tenth day before the Kalends of April to the third day before the Ides of April—there are 384 days, because it is an embolismic year. [Col. 1286B]

In year 7 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 4. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the fifth day before the Ides of April to the third day before the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 8 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 5. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—there are 384 days, because it is an embolismic year.

**Eight-year cycle.**

In year 9 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 6. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to the seventh day before the Ides of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year. [Col. 1286C]

In year 10 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 7. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the eighth day before the Ides of April to the sixth day before the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 11 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 8. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the fifth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May—there are 384 days, because it is an embolismic year.

In year 12 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 9. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May to the day before the Nones of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 13 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 10. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the third day before the Nones of April to the ninth day before the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year. [Col. 1286D]

In year 14 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 11. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April to the day before the Ides of April—there are 384 days, because it is an embolismic year.

In year 15 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 12. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the Ides of April to the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 16 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 13. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the day before the Kalends of April to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year. [Col. 1287A]

In year 17 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 14. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the fifth day before the Ides of April—there are 384 days, because it is an embolismic year.

In year 18 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 15. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the sixth day before the Ides of April to the fourth day before the Kalends of April—there are 354 days, because it is a common year.

In year 19 of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 16. From the fifteenth moon of the preceding feast to the following fourteenth—that is, from the third day before the Kalends of April to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—there are 384 days, because it is an embolismic year.

You will always proceed in this way for all the years, except in the first year, in which you will count the last twenty-four days up to the first fourteen from the Paschal solemnity. In this way you will properly and without any error discover whether Easter is to be celebrated in a common or an embolismic year. [Col. 1287B]

## On the Four Differences among the Moons

### XV.

There are four differences among the moons. According to Victorinus, the lunar month has 30 days; according to Onatilius and another *Laterculus*, 30 days; according to another authority, 29 days; among the Hebrews, 29 and a half; among the Egyptians, 29.

The Egyptians make twelve months in every year. Each month has thirty days, and in one month there are five additional days. The common year has 354 days. Add eleven, and the total is 365 days. Add nineteen beyond this, and it becomes embolismic. This year has 384 days.

## On the Celebration of Holy Easter

### XVI.

On which day ought we to celebrate Easter? The calculation is the same whether it is 30 or 31; as I said, this occurs in the nineteenth year of the cycle because of the agreement of the epacts. [Col. 1287C]

These thirty days increase beyond the 354 days of the common year until they reach the 384 days of the embolismic year, because Easter may not be celebrated in a common year at 354 days. It may be celebrated only beyond that number. In an embolismic year, however, Easter should not be celebrated before 384, or 5 [the text is uncertain]. Beyond that it may be celebrated. This number of days, therefore, is to be observed in common and embolismic years when celebrating Easter.

## On the Greater Embolism

### XVII.

The account of the greater embolisms begins here. The greater embolisms are shown to exist because they supply what the common years lack, so that the solar period may follow the lunar course. [Col. 1287D]

Why does an embolism occur, how does it occur, and what would happen if it did not exist? This is how it works. A common year and another common year make two solar years, and twenty-two days remain from the two solar years. A third year occurs, and twenty-three solar days remain. A lunar embolism occurs in the third year, and it removes thirty days; three remain. Then two common years occur in the same way, with three days belonging individually to the third lunar year; the embolism removes thirty days. Three remain—that is, six days from the sixth common year. Thus eleven days remain in the solar year.

For if the year were otherwise common, twenty-two days would remain from the sun between the second year and the preceding six. Therefore it is necessary that an embolism occur in another year. The embolism not only completes nineteen days, but two lunar days remain.

## On the Increase of the Moon

[Col. 1288A]

### XVIII.

The account of the increase of the moon begins here. Why does the increase of the moon occur, how does it occur, and what would happen if it did not?

The reason is that there is a slowness in the nature of the moon. Its ascent is, by its nature, earlier than might be supposed; its slowness adds to it until there is no difference between what it adds at the beginning of the nineteenth night and what it would add through the nineteen [days] by fifteen, when the ascent of the moon might be thought to be at its fullness, although it would be detected earlier. [The passage is materially uncertain.]

## On the Kalends of the Months

### XIX.

“Kalends” is a Greek expression, but is said to relate to *colere*, “to observe”; in Latin it is called *vocatio*, “calling.” Among the Greeks, *Kalendae* comes from *calo*; among the Latins, *vocationes* comes from *voco*, “I call.”

*Nones* is a Greek expression, from which *Nonae* comes. Among the Greeks, *Nonae* derives from *nundinae*. Among the Latins, they are called *mercatus*, “market,” or *mercimonia*, “trade.”

*Ides* is a Greek expression. In Latin it is said to mean “the heart of the months,” or “the middle of the months.” [Col. 1288B]

### Again, Concerning the Kalends of the Months

### XX.

What are the Kalends said to be? *Kalends*, *Nones*, and *Ides* are Greek expressions. The Romans instituted them on account of feast days, or on account of the duties of magistrates; for on those days they assembled in the cities.

Some thought that *Kalends* was derived from *colere*, “to cultivate or honor,” or from *calo*, that is, “I call.” For the astrologer would call the people so that they might see the kindling of the moon, that is, the beginning of the first moon, or the course of the stars, which run ahead or behind. Among the ancients, the beginnings of all the months were honored.

Why are they called *Nones*? *Nones* were called from *nundinae*. For *nundinae* are public gatherings—that is, gatherings for business—and the solemnity of the market, whether from trade or commerce, is called *nundinae*. [Col. 1288C]

Why did the ancients divide the Nones as the fourth or sixth day before the Nones? They did not divide them in this way in order that robbers should not know when their market was to be held. The robbers hid themselves in various hiding places, in secret spots beside the road; when people came to the market, they killed and robbed them.

For what reason are the Ides called “the heart of the months,” or “the middle of the months”? Most Latins think that the Ides are called from *edere*, “to eat,” because in ancient times these days were occasions for banquets, or because they were regarded as a form of the following month, or because they are in the middle of the month—since *iduvare* in Greek means “middle.”

## On Showing the Weekday on the Kalends of the Twelve Months

[Col. 1288D]

### XXI.

If you wish to know the weekday—that is, the seventh day—on the Kalends of the twelve months, know how many regular numbers each month has, beginning with March. For on that day the world was made, and that month was the beginning of the year among the ancient Romans in the time of Romulus. In that month the solar epacts proceed, that is, the seven concurrent days, and the ninth day before the Kalends of April in the twenty-eight-year cycle.

March therefore has the regular number 5; April, 1; May, 3; June, 6; July, 1; August, 4; September, 7; October, 2; November, 5; December, 7; January, 3; February, 6.

Add these regular numbers to the concurrents of the particular year, throughout the twenty-eight years, for then the solar cycle returns entirely upon itself. Divide the resulting sum by seven; whatever number remains will be the weekday on the Kalends of the twelve months.

If you divide the entire number by seven, the Kalends of the month whose weekday you are seeking will fall on Saturday. But if that total of the regular numbers and concurrents does not reach seven, whatever number it is will be the weekday on the Kalends of each month throughout the year. [Col. 1289A]

## On the Epacts on the Kalends of the Twelve Months

### XXII.

If you wish to know the epacts on the Kalends of the twelve months, determine how many regular numbers each month has, beginning with September, because September is the beginning of the year and the beginning of the months among the Egyptians. At the beginning of September the Egyptians change the epacts.

Those first epacts that the Egyptians have at the beginning of the cycle are what we call regular numbers on the Kalends of the twelve months. For example: September, 5; October, 5. Thus, after adding the regular numbers, whatever epacts there may be on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, you will find the epacts on the Kalends of the twelve months in any year. [Col. 1289B]

## For Finding the Weekday in Each Month

### XXIII.

If you wish to know which weekday falls on any given day throughout the year, take the days from the beginning of the month in question to the Paschal limit, which in the present year is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

The days of the month are 17. Add the days of the week that preceded the Kalends of that month, namely 6; combine them with 17, making 23. Divide this by seven; set aside 21, which is three times seven, and 2 remain. The second weekday is the Paschal limit of the present year.

In this way the weekday of every day of all the months is shown: gather all the days from the Kalends of that month to the present day that you wish to calculate. Add the days of the week that preceded the Kalends of that month, whatever they were. But if the Kalends fell on the first weekday, that is, on Sunday, add nothing except the days of the month. Divide by seven; whatever number remains will be the present weekday. But if you divide the entire number by seven, that weekday which you seek will be Saturday. [Col. 1289C]

### Again, Concerning the Weekday, or the Paschal Limit

### XXIV.

If you wish to know which weekday it is, on whatever day you wish to calculate, take the regular number of the current month and add the concurrents of whatever year you choose; combine them into one. If they reach seven, it is the seventh weekday. If they are less than seven, that will be the weekday. If they exceed seven, subtract seven, and whatever remains will be the entire weekday.

This has been stated concerning the Kalends. Similarly, if you wish to know the age of the moon on any day, determine what lunar day was found on the Kalends of that month through the epacts and regular numbers, and retain the number stated above. Also add the elapsed days of the month, as we explained above concerning the weekday, and always subtract one. Combine the total. [Col. 1289D]

If it reaches 30, it is the thirtieth moon. If it is less than 30, the moon is correspondingly that number. But if it exceeds 30, subtract 30, and however many remain constitute the moon.

Remember this: always subtract the present day; and if it is the thirtieth lunation, subtract 30. If it is 29, then subtract 29. For from the beginning of January to the Kalends of December, one lunation is 30 days and another is 29. When it is a leap year, the day is disregarded in relation to the moon. For example, if today is counted as the sixth, tomorrow is also the sixth.

*[Note: Chapter 25, on the concurrents, is missing; nevertheless, it exists in the summary of chapters.]*

## On the Epacts on the Eleventh Day Before the Kalends of April

[Col. 1290A]

### XXVI.

If you wish to know the epacts on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, determine what lunar day it was on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; you will have that epact at all times.

For the Greeks place the epacts on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April because the moon holds the primacy of the night at the Lord’s command. Scripture says:

> “And God made the two great lights and placed them in the firmament of heaven: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.”

Therefore the three days that antiquity calls dark days, which were made before the lights were created by the Lord and are described in Genesis in their respective parts, claim their own place. To this end, as has been said, they establish the beginning of the year, which prevailed. [Col. 1290B]

## On the Seasons of the Months

### XXVII.

How many are the seasons of the months? Four: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

Spring begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, lasts 91 days, and consists of moisture and fire. Summer begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, lasts 91 days, and consists of fire and dryness. Autumn begins on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, lasts 92 days, and consists of dryness and moisture. Winter begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, lasts 91 days, and consists of cold and moisture. Thus the revolving year consists of 365 days.

### Again, Concerning the Seasons of the Months

### XXVIII.

There are four seasons of the months: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. They are called seasons because their temperaments are mutually combined, moderating one another through moisture, dryness, heat, and cold. They are also called courses, because they do not stand still but run. [Col. 1290C]

After the world was made, the seasons were divided according to the qualities produced by the course of the sun into three months each. The ancients distinguish these seasons in the following way: the first month of spring is called new, the second mature, and the third declining. The same applies to summer: new, mature, and declining; likewise to autumn: new, mature, and declining, or final.

Hence the line:

> “The final [season] beneath the approach of winter.”

Spring is so called because it becomes green; for then, after winter, the earth is clothed with grasses, and all things burst into flower. Summer is called from *aestus*, “heat,” and *aestas* is as though it meant *usta*, “burned” or “parched.” For heat is dry.

Autumn is named from the stormy season, when the leaves of the trees fall and everything ripens. The explanation of winter’s name is derived from *hyems feri* [uncertain], that is, from its being called by this name, because at that time the sun revolves through a shorter circle. [Col. 1290D]

Hence this season is also called *bruma*, as though from *brachys*, “short,” or from food, because the appetite for eating is then greater. For gluttony is called *bruma* in Greek; hence those who have an aversion to food are called *inbrumati*.

*Hibernus* means “between winter and spring,” although *hibernus* often signifies the whole of winter by reference to one part.

These seasons are also assigned to the individual regions of the sky. Spring is assigned to the east, because at that time everything rises from the earth. Summer belongs to the south, because that region is more fiercely burned by heat. Winter belongs to the north, because it is numb with cold and perpetual frost. Autumn belongs to the west, because it brings severe illnesses; hence at that time all the leaves of the trees fall. [Col. 1291A]

Thus autumn abounds in illnesses, but it brings to an end both cold and heat, as opposing forces fight within one another.

## On the Solstices and Equinoxes

### XXIX.

There are two solstices. The first is the winter solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when the sun stands still and the days grow longer. On that very day is the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, at Bethlehem.

The other is the summer solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when the sun stands still and the nights grow longer. On that day, in a city in the province of Palestine, is the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; and at Ephesus, that of Saint John the Evangelist.

Opposed to these are two equinoxes. One is the spring equinox, according to the Latins on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and according to the Greeks on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. From that point the days grow longer. On that day our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified at Jerusalem, and it is the Conception of Saint Mary, Mother of God, when she was greeted by the angel. [Col. 1291B]

The other is the autumnal equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, from which point the days grow shorter. At Machaerus castle occurred the Conception of Saint John the Baptist.

### Again, Concerning the Solstices and Equinoxes

### XXX.

A solstice is so called as though it meant “the station of the sun,” because when the sun stands still at that time, the days or nights grow.

There are two solstices. One is the winter solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, at which time the sun begins to seek higher circles. Each day it ascends two moments and a half, and a sixth part of a moment.

The other is the summer solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, at which time the sun begins to return to lower circles. Each day it descends two moments and a half, and a sixth part of a moment. Hence at the winter solstice the shortest day is found, just as at the summer solstice the longest day is found.

There are likewise two equinoxes, one spring and the other autumnal, which the Greeks call *εὑκομενίας* [as printed; apparently a Greek term for “equinox,” though the form is uncertain]. The equinox is so called because at that time day and night consist of equal intervals of hours.

The equinoxes occur on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and, for the autumnal equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, because formerly the year was divided into only two parts, namely winter and summer.

The solstice is divided into two hemispheres—that is, into two [the text is corrupt]. [Col. 1291C]

## On the Solstices

### XXXI.

If you wish to understand how the two solstices proceed through the twelve signs, and how day and night increase by moments and hours, there are two solstices: the winter solstice on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and the summer solstice on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, at which the sun ascends and descends.

If you wish to know this, investigate it as follows. From the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, the day begins to increase each day by two moments and a half, and a sixth part of a moment—that is, two-thirds of a moment. [Col. 1291D]

In the first sign, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, there are 80 moments. Those moments make two hours, and there are 30 days.

In the second sign, from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February to the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, there are 80 moments. Those moments make two hours, over 30 days.

In the third sign, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of March to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, there are 80 moments. Those moments make two hours, over 31 days.

In these three signs there are 30 days in each sign, with one additional day, making 91 days in all; there are 210 moments, and those moments make six hours from the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. Then the spring equinox stands with equal days, nights, moments, and hours. [Col. 1292A]

In the fourth sign, from the tenth day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, there are 80 moments. Those moments make two hours, over 30 days.

In the fifth sign, from the tenth day before the Kalends of May to the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, there are 80 moments. Those moments make two hours, over 31 days.

In the sixth sign, from the tenth day before the Kalends of June to the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, there are 80 moments and two hours, over 30 days.

Thus in these three signs, from the spring equinox to the summer solstice—that is, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of July—there are 91 days, 240 moments, and six hours. Across the six signs, the total increase is 380 moments and twelve hours.

The summer solstice begins at night; thereafter the night grows and the day diminishes. Each night increases by two moments and a half, and a sixth part of a moment—that is, two-thirds of a moment. [Col. 1292B]

In the seventh sign, from the tenth day before the Kalends of July to the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, there are 80 moments and two hours, over 31 days.

In the eighth sign, from the tenth day before the Kalends of August to the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, there are 80 moments and two hours, over 30 days.

In the ninth sign, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of September to the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, there are 80 moments and two hours, over 30 days.

Thus, in these three signs, from the summer solstice to the autumnal equinox, there are 30 days in each sign, with one additional day, making 91 days. There are 240 moments and six hours from the tenth day before the Kalends of July to the twelfth day before the Kalends of October. Then the autumnal equinox stands with equal days, nights, moments, and hours.

In the tenth sign, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of October to the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, there are 80 moments and two hours, over 30 days. [Col. 1292C]

In the eleventh sign, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of November to the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, there are 80 moments and two hours, over 30 days.

In the twelfth sign, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of December to the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, there are 80 moments and two hours, over 30 days.

In these three signs there are 30 days in each sign, with one additional day, making 91 days, 240 moments, and six hours from the eleventh day before the Kalends of July to the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

The nights increase by 480 moments, or twelve hours. In the entire year there are 365 days, 960 moments, and 24 hours.

## Again, Concerning the Seasons of the Months

### XXXII.

Saint Augustine, bishop, speaks concerning the years. From the fifth day before the Ides of February to the fifth day before the Ides of May is the spring season, consisting of 91 days. From the fifth day before the Ides of May to the fifth day before the Ides of August is the summer season, consisting of 91 days. From the fifth day before the Ides of August to the fifth day before the Ides of November is the autumn season, consisting of 92 days. From the fifth day before the Ides of November to the fifth day before the Ides of February is the winter season, consisting of 91 days. [Col. 1292D]

December, January, and February are winter; March, April, and May are spring; June, July, and August are summer; September, October, and November are autumn.

## On the Moment

### XXXIII.

“Moment” is Greek. The Greek bishop Anatolius said: During the fifteen days in which the sun ascends, through individual moments—that is, four in one day—from the eleventh day before the Kalends of January to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the hour diminishes, and a half [hour diminishes].

One point makes ten moments. Two points make twenty moments. Three points make thirty moments. Four points make forty moments. [Col. 1293A] These forty moments make one hour. Six hours make one quarter-day. Four quarter-days, over four years, make one day and night.

### Again, Concerning Moments

### XXXIV.

A moment is named from speed, as though from “the movement of the mind.” For we have nothing more rapid than the movement of the mind; from these two words the name *moment* was derived.

A minute is so called as though it were something diminished. The verb *minuo*, “I diminish,” is found as an active verb of the third, contracted conjugation; from it are derived the participles *minutus*, *minuta*, *minutum*. It is taken as a noun referring to smallness, as its etymology shows.

A point derives its name etymologically from pricking, because one says *pungor*, “I am pricked,” and from this come *punctus*, *puncta*, *punctum*. [Col. 1293B]

This term is defined by the Greeks. A point is therefore the beginning of an interval and, by nature, indivisible; the Greeks call it an *atom*, that is, something so diminished and so exceedingly small that no equal can be found to it. One [the text is uncertain: perhaps “not from the number”] is called a point.

Finally, one must ask how many moments, minutes, or points are found in each hour. There are 40 moments and 10 minutes, as well as 4 points, in each hour, because in four moments, in one minute, two and a half minutes are also contained in a point.

In the 24 hours of day and night, there are said to be 960 moments, 240 minutes, and 96 points. In a week there are believed to be 6,720 moments, 1,680 minutes, and 671 points.

Take the aspiration, as though some say it comes from *milite*, “soldier,” because these are the boundaries of day and night. A lunar [term missing] from noon to noon is called a day; that day is pleasant. Or, by dividing light and darkness, the solar day extends from sunrise to sunrise.

The word “number” derives its name from counting, or from the goddess Numeria. It is a collection of units, as Augustine says: when there are two individual units, and four more, this constitutes the definition of number; and number adheres to ninety thousand *myriads* [the syntax is corrupt]. The beginning of the lunar year is from the beginning of the first month among the Hebrews, and so according to the rule of the Church. [Col. 1293C]

The Greeks, however, count the year from the fifteenth to the fourteenth, apart from the year of the nineteen-year cycle, which begins with the fourteenth because of the change of the moon.

### Again, Concerning Moments in Relation to the Leap Year

### XXXV.

“Moment” is Greek; in Latin it is called *minimum*, “the smallest,” and *angustissimum tempus*, “the narrowest interval of time,” named from the movement of the stars. It is the extremity of an hour in brief intervals, when one thing yields to and succeeds another. [Col. 1293D]

Anatolius, the Greek bishop of Alexandria and of the city of Laodicea, said: Through the middle sign—that is, through fifteen parts—fifteen days are produced as the sun ascends by moments. Each day, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, it ascends two parts of a moment.

In the first sign there are 20 moments, making half an hour, over 30 days. In the second sign there are 20 moments. In the third sign there are 20 moments.

In these three signs, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, there are 60 moments. Those moments make one and a half hours, over 90 days. From the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the hour diminishes, and a half-hour of darkness grows into light.

Likewise, in the three signs from the tenth day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, there are 60 moments, one and a half hours, and 91 days. [Col. 1294A]

Again, in the three signs from the tenth day before the Kalends of July to the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, there are 60 moments, one and a half hours, and 91 days.

Likewise, in the three signs from the eleventh day before the Kalends of October to the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, there are 60 moments, one and a half hours, and 92 days.

Thus there are twelve signs, 355 days, and 240 moments in the year. Those moments make six hours, and those hours make one quarter-day. Four quarter-days, multiplied over four years, make 24 hours, which is one natural day. The Latins call this the leap day, which is added on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

## To Find the Leap Day through the Twelve Signs

### XXXVI.

If you wish to know how the leap day increases each year, month, and day through the sun’s course across the twelve signs, there is half an hour in each sign, consisting of two points; that half hour makes 20 moments.

Assign to each day of the 30 days two parts of a moment.

On the second day: 1 moment and a third part of a moment.  
On the third day: 2 moments.  
On the fourth day: 2 moments and a second part of a moment.  
On the fifth day: 3 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the sixth day: 4 moments.  
On the seventh day: 4 moments and two parts of a moment.  
On the eighth day: 5 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the ninth day: 6 moments.  
On the tenth day: 6 moments and two parts of a moment.  
On the eleventh day: 7 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the twelfth day: 8 moments.  
On the thirteenth day: 8 moments and a second part of a moment.  
On the fourteenth day: 9 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the fifteenth day: 10 moments.  
On the sixteenth day: 10 moments and two parts of a moment.  
On the seventeenth day: 11 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the eighteenth day: 12 moments.  
On the nineteenth day: 12 moments and a second part of a moment.  
On the twentieth day: 13 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the twenty-first day: 14 moments.  
On the twenty-second day: 14 moments and a second part of a moment.  
On the twenty-third day: 15 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the twenty-fourth day: 16 moments.  
On the twenty-fifth day: 16 moments and a second part of a moment.  
On the twenty-sixth day: 17 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the twenty-seventh day: 18 moments.  
On the twenty-eighth day: 18 moments and a second part of a moment.  
On the twenty-ninth day: 19 moments and a third part of a moment.  
On the thirtieth day: 20 moments. [Col. 1294B–C]

In each sign the total is therefore 20 moments; those moments make half an hour, over 30 days.

In the second sign there are 20 moments from the half-hour, over 30 days. In the third sign there are 20 moments from the half-hour, over 30 days, and so with each sign.

These twelve signs make 860 moments. Those moments—240 of them—make six hours, and those hours make one quarter-day in one year. Multiplied forty times over four years, they make 24 hours, which is one natural day; the Latins call this the leap day. [Col. 1294D]

## To Find the Five Intercalary Days through the Twelve Signs
XXXVII. If you wish to know how the five intercalary days increase through the individual months and days in one solar year during the Sun’s course through the twelve signs, ten hours increase in each sign. I multiply ten by ten, making one hundred, because one hour consists of ten minutes. Multiply ten by ten: one hundred minutes. Assign to each day of the thirty days three minutes and one third of a minute, because each day, out of the thirty days, adds three minutes and one third of a minute.

In the first year, [illegible] the bissextile begins when the first hour of the night enters Aries in the first sign; on each of the thirty days, three minutes and one third of a minute are added. On the second day, six moments and one half of a minute; on the third, ten minutes; on the fourth, thirteen minutes and one third; on the fifth, sixteen minutes and one half; on the sixth, twenty minutes; on the seventh, twenty-three minutes and one third; on the eighth, twenty-six minutes and two thirds; on the ninth, thirty minutes; on the tenth, thirty-three minutes and one third; on the eleventh, thirty-six minutes and two thirds; on the twelfth, forty minutes; on the thirteenth, forty-three minutes and one third; on the fourteenth, forty-six minutes and two thirds; on the fifteenth, fifty minutes; on the sixteenth, fifty-three minutes and one third; on the seventeenth, fifty-six minutes and two thirds; on the eighteenth, sixty minutes; on the nineteenth, sixty-three minutes and one third; on the twentieth, sixty-six minutes and two thirds; on the twenty-first, seventy minutes; on the twenty-second, seventy-three minutes and two thirds; on the twenty-third, seventy-six minutes and two thirds; on the twenty-fourth, eighty minutes; on the twenty-fifth, eighty-three minutes and one third; on the twenty-sixth, eighty-six minutes and two thirds; on the twenty-seventh, ninety minutes; on the twenty-eighth, ninety-three minutes and one third; on the twenty-ninth, ninety-six minutes and two thirds; on the thirtieth day, one hundred minutes.

This makes one complete sign, and the total is 190 minutes. These minutes make ten hours and thirty days. The same number applies to the twelve signs: in each sign there are one hundred minutes, and these minutes make ten hours and thirty days. The twelve signs make 360 days and 120 hours. These hours make 1,200 minutes. Divide 120 hours by 24: five times 24 result, namely the five days called intercalary days; thus the whole year has 365 days.

### On points

XXXVIII. One point is a quarter of an hour. Four points make one hour. One point makes ten moments. Four points make forty moments, and these forty moments make one hour. Six hours in one year make one quarter, and four quarters in four years make a day and a night; these four quarters—that is, six multiplied by four—make twenty-four hours, namely one day of twenty-four hours, which is called bissextile because the sixth day before the Kalends of March is read twice.

One point makes two minutes and one half. Two points make five minutes. Four points make ten minutes. These minutes make one hour. Forty points make ten hours, and these hours make 100 minutes. These minutes, multiplied four times, make 1,500 minutes, because one minute multiplied four times makes four minutes. In twelve months, multiplied three times and four times, they make 1,200 minutes. These minutes, multiplied four times, make 4,800 moments out of the 360 days in one year.

### On the days of the year

XXXIX. One year has 365 days, and between days and nights 8,760 hours. Take seven portions of one thousand from this; 1,760 remain. Take seven portions of two hundred from these; 360 remain. Take seven portions of fifty; ten remain. From these take seven portions of one; three hours remain. These make one day in four years, which is added on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

### On the calculation of the bissextile day

XL. A year has twelve months, fifty-two weeks, and one day; when a bissextile occurs, it has two days. The year has 1[8]770 hours, 1,035 points, and in addition forty hours. Divide these hours into seven portions: the seventh portion of these hours is 1,260 hours; three hours remain outside the portion of hours, and these three hours make the bissextile day.

### Again concerning the bissextile day

XLI. In twelve months, twelve points accumulate in one year; these make three hours. In another year, three hours; in the third year, three hours; in the fourth year, three hours. These hours together make twelve hours. The sixth day before the Kalends of March makes one day, and February receives that day when the bissextile occurs.

### Again concerning the bissextile day

XLII. One should not believe that the bissextile is made because of that day on which, as some suppose, Joshua prayed for the Sun to stand still, since that day existed and passed away. Rather, it is called bissextile because one point is added in each month. One point, however, is a quarter of an hour; four points make one hour; twelve points complete three hours. Therefore, in four years, four sets of three hours—that is, twelve hours—make one day, which is added to February. When the sixth day before the Kalends of March has occurred, it continues to be the sixth day before the Kalends of March on the following day as well.

For example, if today is the sixth day before the Kalends of March, that day which has been completed in the fourth year is added, so that the following day is also the sixth day before the Kalends of March. Therefore it is called bissextile, because the sixth day before the Kalends of March is read twice.

### Again concerning the bissextile day

XLIII. God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Therefore, so that the computation may be understood more fully, see how many hours a year has and divide them into seven portions, whatever remains thereafter.

First calculate 300 days: ten times one hundred makes 1,000; twice three hundred makes 600; in 300 days there are 1,600. Again, calculate ten times sixty: 120; this makes 720 hours. Again, calculate five times ten: fifty; and twice five: ten. Thus you will have 365 days. Together, days and nights in the whole year make 8,760 hours.

Divide these into seven portions. First take seven times one thousand; 1,760 remain. Again take seven times two hundred: 1,400. Again take seven times fifty: 350; ten remain. Again take seven times one: three remain. These three hours make one day in four years.

An eight-year period has 70,080 hours. An eleven-year period has 95,360 hours. Together the eight-year and eleven-year periods make 165,900 [165,440 hours].

### Again concerning the bissextile day

XLIV. Why is the bissextile made, how is it made, and what would happen if it did not exist? It is made because the solar year does not contain exactly 365 days unless there were a quarter-day. The quarter accumulates throughout the year, the month, and the day.

In the first year the quarter begins at sunrise and continues to midnight. In the second year the quarter begins at midnight and continues to sunrise. In the third year the quarter continues until the sixth hour. In the fourth year the quarter extends from the sixth hour until sunset. The order of times would be disturbed if the quarter did not exist.

A quarter is so called because it is the fourth part of a natural day or of anything else. It is therefore the fourth part of the day, because the day, together with its night, is completed in twenty-four hours; for this reason we customarily call six hours a quarter.

Why is the bissextile day intercalated on the sixth day before the Kalends of March? The answer is that the Romans decided to intercalate the bissextile day in February because this was the shortest and last month of the year. Yet they did not complete it in the manner in which the Egyptians and Greeks wished to do so, after the cycle of the whole year had elapsed; nor did they entirely sever, according to their ancient law, the beginning of March from the end of February. For this reason, they did not [alter it] from the sixth day before the Kalends of March, the boundary on which those observing the Terminalia had once established the sacred rites of that month on its twenty-third day and did not dare to change any other day at all. But these [words uncertain], while duly celebrating the rites, inserted one quarter-day.

### On the solstice and equinox

XLV. There are two solstices. The first is the winter solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when the Sun stands still and the days begin to grow longer; this is the day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh.

The other is the summer solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when the Sun stands still and the nights begin to grow longer; in the province of Palestine this is the birthday of Saint John the Baptist.

Opposed to these are the two equinoxes. One is the spring equinox, according to the Latins on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and according to the Greeks beginning on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, because the holy synod does not permit those three days—namely, the fifth day of the week, on which the Lord was seized by the Jews; the sixth, on which he was crucified; and the seventh, when he lay in the tomb—to be excluded beyond the limit.

At that time the days begin to grow longer. On that day our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified, and it is also the Conception of the holy Mother of God, Mary, when she was greeted by the angel.

The other is the autumnal equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, from which the days grow shorter; at the fortress of Machaerus the conception of Saint John the Baptist and martyr takes place. In these four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—the entire order of the years runs its course, through which the conceptions and births of our Lord and Savior, as well as of Saint John the Forerunner, are most fully recognized.

### On the lunar leap

XLVI. They place the lunar leap in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle because, in that year, the last year of the nineteen-year cycle, retaining the lunar epact of the nineteen-year cycle, accommodates not eleven days, as is customary in the other years, but twelve days.

Because the cycles turn at the completion of thirty days, no epacts are placed at its beginning; in the second year, however, it receives epacts. From where they take their beginning must now be explained. Take the solar year, which has 365 days, and the common year, which has 354 days, in this way: first subtract 300; 65 remain. Then take away 50; 15 remain. Again subtract 4; 11 remain. From this they take their beginning, and from this the remaining epacts are multiplied.

The lunar leap is extended over nineteen years because, just as a day is added to the Sun’s course through points, moments, and quarters—and these make the bissextile in four years—so through the Moon’s course a night decreases over nineteen years, producing the lunar leap. The Moon has a slower course than the Sun, because the Sun, owing to the speed of its course, lengthens the interval from it.

### On the course of the Moon

XLVII. All lunar cycles, according to the reckoning of the Hebrews and Egyptians, can follow the natural course in each month: twenty-nine and a half days, half an hour, and nearly ten moments.

For every day, in the reckoning of the Moon, does not begin and end at the same number with the morning and evening. The day which [illegible] in the morning in the Moon [illegible] until the sixth, and half an hour is counted as the fourteenth hour. The same [illegible] is found at evening [at the hour] 14. It plainly seems to say that the lunar course ends in twenty-nine and a half days—that is, six hours—and half an hour, that is, twenty moments—though nearly ten moments are added, as was said above; then the first day of the other Moon begins.

“Kalends” is derived from *calare*, “to call,” or from *calo*, that is, “I call.” The astrologer called the people together so that they might see the rising of the Moon—that is, the beginning of the first Moon—or the course of the stars, those which moved ahead and those which moved behind.

The Nones—namely, the market-days—were associated with business and commerce. They divided the period between the fourth or sixth day before the Nones so that robbers would not know when their market was to be held. For the robbers concealed themselves in forests and secret places beside the road, and when people came to the market they killed or plundered them.

The Ides are said to derive from *edere*, “to eat,” or they are a form of the following month.

Over eight years, at the Council of Nicaea, they reckoned fourteen lunar days; and again in the eighteenth year they reckoned without the quarter. They did not return to the same point unless they had added a year [illegible], nor did the course of the Sun agree with the course of the Moon. Therefore they divided the nineteen-year cycle into an eight-year period and an eleven-year period.

The indiction was named according to the Roman census, not according to the five intercalary days of the Egyptians. The indictions begin on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, at the beginning of the years [illegible] five. They always returned to Rome with *sensu* (“understanding” or “calculation”; the sense is uncertain in context); at the beginning of the fifteenth they returned to the first order. If the image of Caesar was made of gold, they gave gold; if of silver, silver; if of bronze, it was bronze.

### On the interrogation of the nineteen-year cycle

XLVIII. First, therefore, one ought to ask about the nineteen-year cycle; second, how the Moon is reckoned through the Kalends of the months; third, how the Moon has its number in its own month; fourth, on what day and under what Moon the solemnity of Easter falls; fifth, how Easter is to be calculated from memory; sixth, concerning the Moon’s rising and the Sun’s setting; seventh, an answer for those who disagree about the Easter computation.

Although everything that concerns compunction of heart and the salvation of the soul ought to be meditated upon by every person, anyone who wishes to know the computation must carefully consider how holy men, inquiring into the proper order for celebrating the festive Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection at Easter, arrived at it. It is therefore not useless to know how they wrote that cycle and arrived at that understanding.

### On the months

XLIX. In what four ways are the months named—as objects of worship, after things, after kings, and by numbers?

How is January named? In two ways: after an object of worship and after a thing. It is named after an object of worship because it received its name from the pagan Janus, who was two-faced. It is named after a thing because, just as a person enters a house through a doorway, so the years enter through the doorway of January.

In what ways is February named? In two ways, after an object of worship and after a thing. As an object of worship, it was associated with the generation called the Luperci or Lurcones, because all the impurities that occurred throughout the year were washed from their bodies only in this February, and so they performed the February purification in cold water. It is named after a thing because all God’s creatures are joined together in it.

March received its name from an object of worship, from the pagan Mars, as did the day of Mars.

April is named after a thing and from *aperire*, “to open,” because it opens the world and the world blossoms in it.

May received its name from Maia, the mother of Mercury, or from the wisdom of the Roman ancestors.

June received its name from the wisdom of the younger Romans.

Julius Caesar and Augustus received the names of July and August as honors.

September, October, November, and December received their names from numbers: September because it is the seventh from March; October because it is the eighth; November because it is the ninth; and December because it is the tenth, and because rain is a winter storm.

### On the paschal Moon

L. At Easter the Moon cannot be less than fifteen or more than twenty-one. In Lent it cannot be less than three or more than nine, unless a bissextile occurs. At the Rogation days it cannot be less than twenty-two or more than twenty-eight. At Pentecost it cannot be less than five or more than eleven.

If the Moon at Easter is fifteen, it will be three in Lent, twenty-two at the Rogations, and five at Pentecost. By as many days as it has increased at Easter, it increases likewise in Lent, at the Rogations, and at Pentecost.

### Rule for finding the beginning of Lent

LI. By as many days as Easter falls before the day preceding the Kalends of March, you will have Lent in February; and by as many days as Easter falls after the day preceding the Ides of April, you will have Lent after the Kalends of March. If Easter falls on the day preceding the Ides of April, you will have Lent on the Kalends of March.

### Likewise, for finding the Rogation days

LII. By as many days as Easter falls before the Kalends of April, the Rogation days will fall before the Nones of May. By as many days as Easter falls on the day preceding the Kalends of April, the Rogation days will fall on the day preceding the Nones of May. If Easter falls on the Kalends of April, the Rogation days will fall on the Nones of May.

### Likewise, for finding Pentecost

LIII. By as many days as Easter falls before the Kalends of April, Pentecost will fall before the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June. By as many days as Easter falls on the day preceding the Kalends of April, Pentecost will fall after the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June. If Easter falls on the Kalends of April, Pentecost will fall on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### On the reckonings

LIV. The reckoning of Eusebius and Jerome: from Adam to the Flood, 2,252 years. From the Flood to Abraham, 942 years. From Abraham to Moses, 505 years. From Moses to Solomon and the first construction of the Temple, 488 years. In [illegible], according to the shorter reckoning contained in the Third Book of Kings, already according to the calculation, 650 years. From Solomon to the restoration of the Temple, which took place under King Darius, 512 years are gathered. From Darius to the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, the first [illegible] completes 548 years.

Thus, from Adam to the preaching of Christ and the fifteenth year of Tiberius, the total is 5,228 [5,897] years.

An age is properly spoken of in two ways: either of human beings, as infancy, youth, and old age; or of the world. The first age is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity of Judah; the fifth from then to the coming of the Savior; the sixth, which is now taking place, continues until this world comes to an end.

If you wish to know the years from the beginning of the world, multiply fifteen times 400, then 15, then 10, then 15, then 9. Add the indiction of that same year and divide by fifteen.

### On the paschal term

LV. If you wish to find quickly what the paschal term is, and the term falls in March, take the regular number for March, 36. Subtract the lunar epact of that year. Gather into groups the number of days remaining after the epact has been subtracted from that number; on whichever date the result falls, you will have the term.

If the term falls in April, take the regular number for April, 35, and proceed from those regular 35 in the same way as we stated above. If, after the epact has been deducted in March, only 30 remain, you will have the term on the thirtieth day before the Kalends of March, that is, on the third day before the Kalends of April.

When the first year of the nineteen-year cycle begins in April, you have no epact at all by which you would withdraw from the regular 35. Withdraw 30 from April; 5 remain. On the fifth day of April, that is, on the Nones of April, you will have the term, and so in all the years.

### On the week

LVI. Among the Greeks and Romans, the week proceeds in a course of seven days. Among the Hebrews, however, there are seven years. Daniel makes this clear in his account of the weeks.

The week consists of weekdays. *Feria* is derived from *fari*, “to speak,” because at the creation of the world God said on each day, “Let there be.” Since the Sabbath day has been regarded as a day of rest from the beginning, the day of the Sun is therefore called the first weekday, because it is the first after the day of rest. Likewise, the Moon is the second weekday, because it is the second after the day of rest, that is, after the Sabbath, which is a day of rest. The remaining days likewise took their names from their number.

Among the Romans, however, these days received their names from the planets, that is, the wandering stars. The first day was called after the Sun, which is chief among all the heavenly bodies, just as that day is the head of all the days. The second was named after the Moon, which is nearest to the Sun in brightness and size and receives its light from it. The third was named after the star of Mars, which is called Vesper. The fourth was named after the star of Mercury, which some call the white circle. The fifth was named after the star of Jupiter, which they call Phaethon. The sixth was named after the star of Venus, which they call Lucifer and which has more light than the other stars. The seventh was named after the star of Saturn, which is placed in the [illegible] sixth heaven and is said to complete its course in thirty [illegible] years.

Accordingly, the pagans gave the days their names from these seven stars because they thought that through them something was accomplished for them, saying that they received spirit from the Sun; body from the Moon; speech and wisdom from Mercury; pleasure from Venus; heat from Mars; moderation from Jupiter; and slowness from Saturn. Such was the folly of the pagans, who invented for themselves such ridiculous fictions.

### Again concerning the week

LVII. “Week” is derived from the Greek designation, as though *hebdomas*, from the number seven days. For among the Greeks, the ancients said that seven [words uncertain] days are present. Hence it is called a week, and the remaining weeks likewise.

Among the Greeks and Latins the week proceeds in a course of seven days; among the Hebrews they said it consisted of seven years. Daniel speaks of this in the seventy weeks: from the issuing of the word and the release of the captivity from Babylon under Ezra, Nehemiah, and Zerubbabel, the seventy weeks—that is, seventy times seven years—amount to 490 years. This was the period from the return from the Babylonian captivity to the Nativity of Christ.

The week is completed in seven days because God worked the whole of creation in six days and rested on the seventh. On the first day he created light; on the second, the firmament; on the third, the sea and the lands; on the fourth, the heavenly bodies, that is, the Sun and Moon; on the fifth, birds and reptiles; on the sixth, humankind in his own image and likeness; on the seventh day he rested from all his works.

According to the Hebrews, the names of the days of the week are expressed in two ways, namely by order and by rest, as follows: first of the Sabbath, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth of the Sabbath, Sabbath.

According to the Greeks, they are named by wording and order as follows: first weekday, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh weekday.

According to the Latins, they are named after the gods of the pagans and the others. They had two heavenly gods and five earthly ones: Mars, the father of Romulus; Mercury, lord of eloquence and intelligence; Jupiter, [lord] of virtue and [illegible], his idol; Venus, inventor of lust, desire, and every disgrace; and Saturn, father of Jupiter and ruler of crops and winds.

Ancient paganism, deceived by these errors, imposed the names of its gods on the days of the world because those names were frequently used. But Christians did not change these names on account of their widespread use, so that whenever they are named with the individual days, both the gods themselves and their worshipers may be despised at every hour.

### Again concerning the months

LVIII. The month received its name from a certain measure, because every month is measured according to the course of the Moon as twenty-nine and a half days. Months were first discovered in the lunar course, and this observance was first taken up from the Hebrews; among them the Kalends and the new moons were first so called. For *menes* among the Hebrews means “Moon” or “new moon.” Hence they celebrate new moons by observing the new Moon.

Later, solar months were discovered among the Latins. The Arcadians reckoned their year in three months, counting 121 days by name [or “in all”]. The Archanenses reckoned six months, counting each month as sixty-two days. The other Greeks reckoned their proper year as 354 days. It began in March and was reckoned in eleven months.

The Romans, under Romulus, reckoned their year in ten months. They began with the month of March, and it was completed in December, in 301 days. Symphronius added one month called February, which is still called February, and they reckoned the year as 322 days.

Aurelius Clepa added a month of thirty days, which the Greeks call Aphroditus and which we call April; the year was then reckoned as 364 days.

Numa Pompilius added one day in honor of the even number, established the year as twelve months, and distinguished its four seasons by dividing the two solstices and two equinoxes in the reckoning.

According to the Egyptians, the names of the months are as follows: Dius, Apollonius, Dyneus, Philisteus, Distreus, Artemisius, Pharemeneus, Laus, Scurpeus, and Iperventius.

### Again concerning the months

LIX. A month is the circuit and renewal of the Moon’s light, from new moon to new moon. In its figure, the course of this life is often understood: it proceeds by its increases as a month and, at the same [uncertain word], is bounded among its nations by most certain limits.

The ancients defined a month as the time during which the Moon traverses the zodiacal circle.

The ancient pagans gave the months various names: some from their gods, some from their causes, and some from numbers. They began with March because they preserved from it the order of the year’s rising.

They called this month March in honor of Romulus, because they believed him to be the son of Mars. They called April not by the name of any of their gods but from the thing itself, as if “opening,” because at that time the buds first open into flowers.

They then named May after Maia, the mother of Mercury, whom they considered a goddess, or because of the ancestors. They named June after Juno, whom they assert was the sister or wife of Jupiter. Others said that June was named for the younger people, just as May was named for the elders.

They said that July was named after Julius Caesar and August after Augustus Caesar Octavian. Previously July was called Quintilis and August Sextilis, but their names were changed after the Caesars Julius and Augustus.

September was so called because it is the seventh from March, which is the beginning of spring; likewise October, November, and December received their names from numbers, rain, and the weather.

They called January after Janus, but it is specifically called January because it is the doorway and beginning of the year. They called February after the February rites of the Luperci.

Among the ancient Latins, therefore, the course of the year was reckoned in ten months. The Romans added January, while Numa Pompilius added February and divided the year into twelve months.

Many assert that Cymin, king of the Sabines, first divided the year into months and established the Ides, Kalends, and intercalary days. The books of the holy Scriptures, however, show that there were twelve months in the year even before the Flood. For it is written there: “The waters were diminishing until the eleventh month. In the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, the summits of the mountains appeared.” Thus they then counted the months—not as now: the Kalends and Ides closed these months, whereas the completion of the Moon closed those months.

The Kalends are named from *colere*, “to observe,” because among the ancients the beginnings of the months were always celebrated. The Ides were also named from “days,” and the Nones from the market-days.

Among the Latins, the months take their beginning from the Kalends; among the Hebrews, from the return of the newborn Moon. Among the Egyptians, the beginnings of the months are announced as two or three days before the Kalends.

Some think that “year” (*annus*) is derived from a certain ring (*anus*), that is, a cycle; hence *anuli*, “little rings,” are derived from it.

Some consider the beginning of the year to be from Rome, like the Roman people; others from the spring equinox, like the Hebrews; others from the solstice, like the Greeks; and others from autumn, like the Egyptians.

The era begins to increase from the day of the Kalends of January. The bissextile is proposed according to the lunar course from the sixth day before the Nones of March until the day of the Kalends of June.

The Egyptian year without bissextile has its beginning on the seventh day before the Kalends of September; when a bissextile occurs, the year [begins] on [illegible] Kalends, as above in the Scriptures.

The solstice is so called as though it were the Sun’s station. The equinox is so called because at that time day and night return to an equality of twelve hours, their intervals having been made equal.

The summer solstice is therefore called a lamp, because from it the Sun’s lamp pours forth the day, receives greater brightness, and brings the new heat of the approaching summer.

### Again concerning the months
