LX. The Chinese, as also these [uncertain words]—Egyptians, Easterners, Moors, Greeks, Macedonians, Alexandrians, Asians, Persians, Medes, and Chaldaeans—do not count the days of their months by Kalends, Nones, and Ides; the Romans, however, take precedence over them in this matter.

All the Greeks and those mentioned above have twelve months, and in their months they all agree on thirty days, except the Egyptians. In the same month, twice, and in the Sun [and] Moon [cycle—text uncertain], except among the Egyptians, who make thirteen months: when the thirteenth month has been completed from the five remaining days, August has [illegible] years without a bissextile; and in the third year, when the bissextile enters, six days still remain from August because of the bissextile. Thus this thirteenth month consists of six days. The Egyptians call these days *epagomenae*, that is, in Latin, “concurrent” days.

### Again concerning the months and the length of the Moon

LXI. The lunar months, according to the Latins, differ in length: six are long and six short throughout every [illegible]. In a common year, together with the embolismic Moon in an embolismic year, the lunar month and the bissextile day coincide in the same year.

For example, if the Moon is thirty on the Kalends of January, the Moon of January is thirty, and the Moon of February, because of the bissextile, will be reckoned as thirty. The Moon of March is always thirty according to the Latins.

But when we say that lunar months differ in length according to number, not according to nature, all lunar months are equal. Thus among the Hebrews all months always have twenty-nine and a half days.

For example, if the Moon is lit at midday, and four weeks of that same month have been completed, the next Moon is lit at midday after twenty-nine days and then remains for half a day until midnight. Among the Hebrews the Moon is lit once at midday and another time at midnight.

The Romans differ little from the Hebrews. It does not make much difference whether you add a whole day to one Moon or divide two months and distribute equal portions to each. When the Moon is lit at midday, the place of its illumination is said to be in the middle of the south. When it is illuminated at midnight, it is in the middle of the north; but it is said to be illuminated in the fiery region of the sky.

Among the Hebrews the Moon is lit within two hours—that is, half an hour after the sixth hour—and among the Romans, at midnight. It seems that one Moon is thirty and the other twenty-nine, and it is lit after the seventh hour. For among them it is easier, in order to maintain the reckoning, to assign one day, which makes thirty.

Therefore the northern peoples do not observe this rule, because among them it follows that a month has thirty-one days and a Moon thirty; a month has thirty days and a Moon twenty-nine.

But if we say this because of the preparation for the bissextile, or because the illumination of the Sun varies, so that in the entire circuit of the sky through which the Moon travels we consider no place empty of its illumination, then there is a long Moon of thirty days, a short Moon of twenty-nine, a January Moon of thirty, and a February Moon of twenty-nine, and likewise with all the months.

But assigning the Moons to the months has been handed down more by the tradition of teachers, especially the Latins, than disseminated in written texts. A text concerning the Egyptians reports that they assign individual Moons to individual months.

The reader must know, however, to whichever month he assigns a given Moon, whether it is illuminated in that month or in the month in which it disappears. For if Moons always used to wane on the Kalends of the months, and the first Moons always supplied the computations on the Kalends of the months, and the Moon of one month did not wander into another, the question would certainly be solvable, and they would define as belonging to a given month the Moon which disappeared and was illuminated in that same month.

But because on the Kalends of the months and on the other days at the beginning of the month Moons wane and are illuminated, it is fixed by an unchanging rule that any Moon which wanes and does not shine in a given month is the Moon of that same month for only one day, except for the embolismic Moon. The embolismic Moon is not assigned to thirteen months without a month or Moon, while it is being made into a month, in which two [periods] of disappearance occur and a month without a disappearance is found.

### On the month and the questioning of the Moon

LXII. State how many days the Moon has in each month and how the solar months are counted. We have said that in each month the Moon has twenty-nine and a half days, and therefore in one lunation twenty-nine. On the following day the first day is already counted; in the next lunation, together with the other half that had been left over, the Moon is counted as thirty, and on the following day as one. Thus throughout the year, in one month the Moon is counted to twenty-nine and in another month to thirty.

Consequently, at the beginning of the solar year the Moon is said to have eleven fewer days—that is, the days mentioned above—and five days are added to the solar month beyond the thirty days.

When, in the thirteenth lunar month, the eleven days needed to complete the solar years have been added, nineteen lunar days remain from that same month. From this the reckoning of embolismic years is shown to arise, because it supplies the apparent deficiencies of common years until, when the nineteen-year cycle has been completed, they coincide in one.

This also must not be accepted: that in the solar year in which the Moon begins to be illuminated, if it has thirty-one days, the Moon is then called thirty; but in one that has fewer than thirty-one, it is called twenty-nine and then one, except when it is twenty-nine on the Kalends of August, which, with the other reckonings interrupted by a day, is known to add or subtract.

The number itself clearly shows in which months there are said to be thirty-one days: January, March, May, July, and October; all the others have the fourth day before the Nones and all the eighth days before the Ides.

### Again, how many hours the months have by day and by night

[Col. 1305B]

LXIII. April and September have twelve hours at night and twelve by day. May and August have eleven hours at night and thirteen by day. June and July have nine hours at night and fifteen by day. October and March have thirteen hours at night and eleven by day. November and February have fourteen hours at night and ten by day. December and January have fifteen hours at night and nine by day.

### Again concerning the months

LXIV. January: the fourth day before the Nones, nineteen; 31 days; Moon 30.

February: the fourth day before the Nones, sixteen; 28 days; Moon 29.

March: the sixth day before the Nones, seventeen; 31 days; Moon 30.

April: the fourth day before the Nones, eighteen; 30 days; Moon 29.

May: the sixth day before the Nones, seventeen; 31 days; Moon 30.

June: the fourth day before the Nones, eighteen; 30 days; Moon 29.

July: the sixth day before the Nones, seventeen; 31 days; Moon 30.

August: the fourth day before the Nones, nineteen; 31 days; Moon 29.

September: the fourth day before the Nones, nineteen; 30 days; Moon 30.

October: the sixth day before the Nones, seventeen; 31 days; Moon 29.

November: the fourth day before the Nones, eighteen; 30 days; Moon 30.

December: the fourth day before the Nones, nineteen; [31] days; Moon 29.

### On the points of the Moon

LXV. On the first day of the Moon, it shines for four points, that is, forty moments. On the second day, one hour and three points. On the third, two hours and two points. On the fourth, three hours and one point. On the fifth, it shines for four hours. On the sixth, four hours and four points. On the seventh, five hours and three points. On the eighth, six hours and two points. On the ninth, seven hours and one point. On the tenth, it shines for eight hours. On the eleventh, eight hours and four points. On the twelfth, nine hours and three points. On the thirteenth, ten hours and two points. On the fourteenth, eleven hours and one point. On the fifteenth, sixty points, that is, twelve hours. On the sixteenth, eleven hours and one point. On the seventeenth, ten hours and two points. On the eighteenth, nine hours and two points. On the nineteenth, eight hours and four points. On the twentieth, it shines for eight hours. On the twenty-first, seven hours and one point. On the twenty-second, six hours and two points. On the twenty-third, five hours and three points. On the twenty-fourth, four hours and four points. On the twenty-fifth, it shines for four hours. On the twenty-sixth, three hours and one point. On the twenty-seventh, two hours and two points. On the twenty-eighth, one hour and three points. On the twenty-ninth, the Moon has four points. On the thirtieth, it increases by two points and decreases by two.

Tell me how many hours the Moon shines, or how many points the Moon has, and by what divisions this can be determined. Why do you multiply the Moon by a quarter? Because the Sun and Moon were made on the fourth day. Why do you divide by a fifth? Because five points complete one hour.

### On numbers

[Col. 1306A]

### LXVI. The Number

Among the Hebrews, Chaldaeans, and Syrians, number is called *mina*; among the Greeks it was called *arithmos*; among the Egyptians, *laterculus* (“little tablet”); among the Macedonians, *calculus*; among the Latins, *compotus* (“calculation”). *Ema* among the Hebrews, *emera* among the Greeks, and *dies* among the Latins mean “day.” *Libia* in Hebrew, *nicta* in Greek, and *nox* among the Latins mean “night.” Among the Gentiles, the first day is named after the sun, the second after the moon, the third after Mars, the fourth after Mercury, the fifth after Jupiter, the sixth after Venus, and the seventh after Saturn.

### On natural years and great, or solstitial, years

### LXVII

A natural year is when the moon places itself beneath the sun, so that, lying between the sun’s sphere and our eyes, it produces darkness throughout the whole world; this is called an eclipse.

[Col. 1306B] A great year is said to occur when all the stars, at fixed times and after completing their appointed numbers, return to their proper place or order. The ancients said that this year was brought to an end or completed.

A solstitial year occurs when the sun, having completed its circuit through all the signs, returns to the point from which it began its course. This is the solar, or civil, year, which is completed in 365 days.

### On the moon’s burning

### LXVIII

The moons are kindled in 225 calculated minutes, that is, almost 10 minutes in each hour, comprising 10 moments apiece. Thus day and night are gradually diminished until, at the end of the year, they amount to 14 [such units]. In this way the moon’s change is understood over nineteen years.

### On the day of the rising sun

[Col. 1306C]

### LXIX

Day is the presence of the rising sun, until it reaches sunset. Day is customarily said to be named in two ways: properly, from sunrise until it rises again; improperly, from sunrise until it reaches sunset, a span of twelve hours.

The day has three customary divisions: morning, midday, and the last part. Some think that the day begins at sunrise, others at sunset, and others at midnight. For the Chaldaeans make the beginning of the day at sunrise, calling the whole of that interval “day.” The Egyptians, however, derive the beginning of the day from the beginning of the following night. The Romans wish the day to begin at midnight and to end at midnight.

The *fasti* are days on which one may speak, that is, on which one may transact business; the *nefasti* are those on which one may not. Holiday days are those on which a religious rite is performed and on which people ought to abstain from lawsuits. Working days are the opposite of feast days, that is, days without religious observance. Black days are also called common days.

Sideral days are those in which the stars are in motion and people are excluded from navigation; these last continuously thirty [days]. Battle days are those on which it is permitted to challenge an enemy to war.

Intercalary days are five, which, according to the Egyptians, remain after the twelve months. They begin on the ninth day before the Kalends of September and end on the fifth day before those Kalends.

The days of the *epacts* are eleven; they are added each year to the lunar course. For in a year the twelve moons have 354 days, leaving eleven days in relation to the solar year’s course. The Egyptians called these days *epacts*, because they are added throughout the year in order to determine the moon.

Solstitial days are those on which the sun stands still, [Col. 1307A] while the length of the days or nights increases. Equinoctial days are those on which day and night correspond, or unfold, in equal spans of hours.

Night is the absence of the sun, for as long as it returns from sunset to sunrise. We believe that night is the earth’s shadow, given as a time for the body’s rest, not for the performance of any task. It is called *nox* (“night”) from *nocere* (“to harm”), because it harms the eyes.

### On the day

### LXX

Day is the first of created things, the manifestation of realities, and the companion of the sun. Day is also the presence of the sun until it reaches sunrise.

Isidore says: “Day is customarily called in two ways: properly, from the rising of the sun until it rises again; improperly, from sunrise until it reaches sunset. It was therefore called day from *dividere* (‘to divide’), because it divides [Col. 1307B] light from darkness.”

Phragonus likewise says: “The sun above the earth is day; the sun beneath the earth is night.”

According to the Hebrews, there are four beginnings of days: from sunrise, the day; “In the beginning of the works of the Lord,” and so forth. According to the Chaldaeans, from midday. According to the Greeks and Egyptians, from the rising of the stars. According to the Romans, from midnight.

The Hebrews reckon from sunrise because of the physical understanding of things, since the nature of created beings took its beginning from light. For on the first day, according to Moses’ testimony, God created light: “Let there be light,” and light was made.

The Chaldaeans therefore begin from midday because they observe the course of the moon, which is regularly kindled and extinguished around midday. The Egyptians, because they are astrologers and observe the circle of the stars, begin from evening and from the rising of the stars, whose courses [Col. 1307C] and periods they observe.

The Romans begin from midnight, following what is written: “At midnight the world was made, and at midnight it will again be destroyed.” And in the Gospel: “At midnight a cry was made,” and so forth. Again: “As a thief in the night, so he will come.”

There are three parts of the day: morning, midday, and the last part.

*Morning* (*mane*) is said to derive from the *Manes*, gods of the underworld, who distill things for rejoicing crops, and with whom the moon [the text is uncertain at *conversata*] is associated with the earth. Or *mane* derives from the Manes, the gods whom ancient paganism worshipped at sunrise. Or *mane* is said to derive from *Manus*, which the ancient Latins used to mean “good,” as Isidore recalls: “*Mane* from *Manus*,” and so forth.

*Midday* (*meridies*), as though *medies*, means “middle of the day.” For then the light shines more purely, when the sun glows in mid-heaven and illuminates the whole world with equal brightness. [Col. 1307D] Or *meridies* is as though *meridios*, because at that time the ether shines more purely; *merum* means “pure.”

The *last part* (*suprema*) is so called because it is the final portion of the day, since it remains last. Then the day is suppressed toward evening, when it is overshadowed by the darkness of the cloudy night.

Morning is said to extend from sunrise to the fourth hour, as an artificial quarter. Midday appears to occupy the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth hours. The last part appears to occupy the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth hours.

### On the night

### LXXI

Night is the world’s darkness, a hiding place, and the rest of the living. It is called *nox* from *nocere* (“to harm”), because it harms human sight, or because thieves and wild animals do harm in it. Or because it seems to harm or impede human business and labor. Or because it took its name from a Greek etymology: [Col. 1308A] the Greeks called it *nictus*, while the Latins called it *nox*, as it is written in the Psalms: “In *merasce nictus*,” that is, “by day and night.”

There are six parts of the night: evening, twilight, the time of silence, the untimely hour, cockcrow, and morning.

*Evening* (*vesper*) is so called from the western star called Vesper; that star itself took its name from the region of Hesperia, with *v* changed for *h*, and is called *vesper*. Hesperia was called so because it lay near Spain, after Hesperus, the son of the region [the text is uncertain], who subdued that land by his military prowess.

Sailors observed this star while sailing from Gallograecia, so that they would not lose their way in nighttime navigation. Some report that for one year it precedes the sun, shining with Lucifer, the morning light, in equal rays, and that for two years afterward it remains at sunset. [Col. 1308B] When its name is changed, it is called *vesper*; with Lucifer, however, it is called *Lucifer*.

*Twilight* is so called from *creperum*, that is, from the mingling of darkness and light. The Greeks call it *diafodi*, that is, uncertainty between the passing of day and the entrance of night, or between the end of night and the entrance of day. It is uncertain because, if someone is awakened from the heaviness of sleep at this time, he considers it unclear whether, after the night has passed, he has reached the brightness of day, or whether, after the day has ended, he has been brought to the beginning of night.

*The time of silence* (*conticinium*) means silence. For *conticescere* means “to be silent,” because at this time everyone is quiet and silent, and they are weighed down by the onset of their first sleep.

*The untimely hour* (*intempestivum*) is the middle and inactive interval of the night, the time when nothing can be done and everything is quiet in sleep. [Col. 1308C]

*Cockcrow* (*gallicinium*) is named from the crowing of birds, as though *gallicanium*, on account of the roosters, heralds of the light. This time is also called *antelucinium*, because roosters are called “before-light” birds, since by nature, through their proclamation and the clapping of their wings, they announce the coming of the light.

*Morning* (*matutinum*) is the period of night named from the approach of the light and the coming day, as dawn withdraws.

*Dawn* (*aurora*) is as though *Eurora*, named from the east wind, because at that hour the breath of the east wind is sent forth from the south to awaken the crops.

There is this distinction among *vesperum*, *vespera*, and *vesper*: *vesperum* belongs to the day; *vespera* is the sun’s inclination toward sunset; and *vesper* is the completion of any thing, which is called *vespere*. These are the six intervals of the night, and each occupies two hours.

### On the paschal fourteenth moon

[Col. 1308D]

### LXXII

If you wish to know in which years of the nineteen-year cycle the paschal fourteenth moon falls in the month of March, it is in years 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, and 18. You will find these seven years in March; you will calculate the remaining twelve without doubt in April according to the rule appended below.

### Again, on which weekday the paschal fourteenth moon falls

### LXXIII

[Col. 1309A]

The calculation begins by which it can be determined on what weekday the paschal fourteenth moon falls in each year, that is, in the first nineteen-year cycle.

In the first year, because it has no lunar epacts—since the 18 epacts of the preceding nineteenth year and its own 11 epacts [the text is uncertain] are added by the Egyptians, making 30, that is, one complete lunar month, with nothing remaining from the epacts—and because the paschal fourteenth moon falls in April that year, always take 35 regular units in that month. Subtract 30, that is, the complete moon, and 5 remain. On the fifth day from the Kalends of April, that is, on the Nones of April, the paschal fourteenth moon occurs. Take the foregoing 5, add the concurrents of that year, 5: they make 10. Add also the regular units always assigned to April, 7: they make 17. Divide these by 7—twice seven makes 14—and 3 remain. The paschal fourteenth moon falls on the third weekday, and the Sunday of the paschal feast falls on lunar day 19.

In year 2 of the aforesaid cycle, from which the epact of 11 takes its beginning, the paschal fourteenth moon falls in March. Always take 36 regular units in that month; subtract the 11 epacts, and 25 remain. [Col. 1309B] On the twenty-fifth day of March from the Kalends, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the paschal fourteenth moon occurs. Take the aforesaid 25, add the concurrents of that year, 5: they make 30. Always add the regular units at the end of this month, March, 4: they make 34. Divide these by 7—four sevens make 28—and 6 remain. If nothing remained, it would be Saturday; the paschal fourteenth moon will be on the seventh weekday, and the Sunday of the paschal feast will fall on lunar day 15.

Again, in April of year 3 of the aforesaid cycle, always take 35 regular units at the beginning; subtract the epacts of that year, 22, and 13 remain. On the thirteenth day of the month, that is, the Ides of April, the paschal fourteenth moon occurs. Take these 13, add the concurrents of that year, 6: they make 19. Add the regular units always assigned below in April, 7: they make 26. Divide these by 7—seven times five make 21 [as printed, despite the arithmetical inconsistency]—and 5 remain. [Col. 1309C] The paschal fourteenth moon will fall on the sixth weekday, and the Sunday of the paschal feast on lunar day 15.

Thus you will calculate for each year from the first year through year 95. Whenever the paschal fourteenth moon falls in March, take 36 regular units at the beginning. From these subtract the epacts of whatever year you wish, add the concurrents, and always increase the total at the end by 4 regular units.

In April, however, take 35 at the beginning. From these subtract the epacts written above, add the concurrents of that year, and increase the total at the end by 7 regular units. In this way you will calculate all the paschal computations more fully and briefly.

The reader should nevertheless know this: whenever, in either of the aforementioned months, the first rule yields more than 30 after the epacts have been subtracted, 30 must be omitted. If 1, 3, or more remain, that many days of the month from the Kalends mark the paschal fourteenth moon. When, after the epacts have been subtracted, less than 30 remains—for example, 20 or more, or less—the same number of days of the month from the Kalends marks the paschal fourteenth moon. For if exactly 30 remains after the epacts have been subtracted, which plainly occurs once in nineteen years, the paschal fourteenth moon will be on the thirtieth day from the Kalends.

[Col. 1309D]

### Again, on the lunar date of Easter

### LXXIV

If you wish to know on which lunar day the paschal feast occurs, and Easter is celebrated in March, count the months from September: they make 6. Always add 2 regular units: they make 8. Add also the epacts, that is, the lunar additions, of whatever year you wish—for example, [Col. 1310A] in indiction 3, epacts 12, which make 20—and add the day of the month on which Easter is celebrated, that is, the thirty-first day of March. Together these make 51 days. Subtract 30; 21 remain. The moon is therefore at lunar day 21 on the Lord’s day of Resurrection.

If Easter is celebrated in April, count the months from September through March: they make 7. Always add 2 regular units: they make 9. Add also the lunar epacts of whatever year you wish—for example, in indiction 4, epacts 23, which make 31—and add the day of April on which Easter is celebrated, that is, April 13. Together these make 45. Subtract 30; 15 remain. The moon is at lunar day 15 on the day of the Resurrection.

### On determining the weekday

### LXXV

If you wish to know which weekday a day is, count the days from January through the month you wish—for example, through March 31; they make 90 days. Always add 1: they make 91. Always add the concurrents of whatever year you wish—for example, in the present year, indiction 3, with concurrent 1; together they make 92. Divide these by 7: ten sevens make 70; again, three sevens make 21; 1 remains. In this way you will find which weekday any day from the Kalends of January through December 31 falls on, provided that you take together the regular 1 and the concurrents of that year, which always begin with the month of January.

If you wish to determine which weekday today is, on whatever day you wish to calculate, treat all the months as having 29 days. Whatever remains from them, extend 29 on your hand for the purpose of calculation, [Col. 1310C] and add the number of days that have elapsed in the month in which you are when you make the calculation, together with the solar additions of the year you wish and the indiction of the year you are investigating. Divide by sevens, and remove from the total the number of complete sevens; whatever remains is the weekday.

For example, in indiction 1, in the year in which we celebrated Easter on the seventh day before the Ides of April, the sun has 4 additions. Add the indiction’s 1. To these add the 1 of the Kalends of January, 3; and subtract from 9, 2, and from 10, 3, [and] 8; therefore 6 also—what are they except 14? If nothing remains, the Kalends of January in that year will be Saturday, the sixth weekday. If 1 remains, Sunday; if 2, Monday. The same rule must be observed for the remaining weekdays.

If you wish to know on which weekday the Kalends of January begin in each year, take the years from the Incarnation of our Lord [Col. 1310D] Jesus Christ, 808. Divide them by 7; add the fourth part, which you have divided, to 909. Together they make 1,011. Divide these by 7; 3 remain. The Kalends of January will be Tuesday. If 4 remain, Wednesday; if nothing, Saturday; if 1, Sunday.

If you wish to know on which day the Kalends of the months begin, this can be learned by the following calculation as the years turn. October has 1 as its letter; November, 4; December, 6; January, 2; February, 5; March, 5; April, 1; May, 3; June, 6; July, 1; August, 4; September, 7. Always add to these the solar epact of any year, and then divide by 7—one seven, or two sevens—and in this way you will discover the sequence of the calculation without error, except in a leap year. In these five months there is a gap—that is, October, November, [Col. 1311A] December, January, and February—and thereafter it falls in the number given above.

If you wish to recognize which weekday any day of a month is, calculate as follows. October has 3, November 2, December 3: for months having 31 days, take 3 from that month; for those having 30 days, always take 2 from that month; then add the day of the month you are seeking. Divide by 7, and whatever remains in your hand, with the solar additions occurring in that year, is the weekday for that year. Omit February, because it has an incomplete number, except for the days of that month themselves, from its beginning to its end.

### On the moon at the Kalends of January and the eleventh day before the Kalends of April

### LXXVI

[Col. 1311B]

If you wish to determine the lunar day at the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, take the years of the Lord that have elapsed in the same year, as many as you wish to calculate. Divide them by 19, and whatever remains, multiply again by 11. Then divide by 30, and whatever remains from the same calculation gives the full lunar day at the eleventh day before the Kalends of April in that year.

If you wish to calculate from September through December, add 3 regular units for these four months. In a leap year alone, always count 2 regular units in the month, and take 32 instead of 30 days in each year, adding the month at the end.

If you wish to know what lunar day it was in whatever month you choose—for example, in the year in which we celebrate Easter on the third day before the Ides of April—suppose it was nine months after that Easter and calculate the moon as follows. Subtract 1 from September; that is, [Col. 1311C] for that 1 place 1 from October. Add 2 regular units; together they make 4. Add the days of the month that have elapsed in the month you are calculating—for example, today, when I made this calculation, 23, or whatever number has occurred. Add also the lunar addition, 22, and add 7; together they make 52 days. Subtract 30; 22 remain. Today, when I made this calculation, the moon was lunar day 22 of the month of November. By this procedure you can easily find the age of the moon on every day of the months, if you always calculate in this way.

If you wish to know the lunar day at the Kalends of January, determine which lunar cycle it is. For example, cycle 15. Keep 1 for yourself—that is, the Kalends of January themselves—and add fifteen times five: they make 75, which you add to 1, making 76. Again, sixteen times fifteen makes 90, which you add to 76, making a total of 166. Dividing this by 30 leaves 16. The moon will therefore be at lunar day 16 on the Kalends of January, with 16 points. [Col. 1311D]

In this way, throughout the nineteen-year cycle, you will always find the lunar calculation and determine without error which lunar day falls on the Kalends of January. When you reach lunar cycle 17 and say “seventeen times five” above the Kalends of January, which makes 85, if you divide by sixty and add 1 to 85, they make 86. Then sixteen times seventeen makes 102, which you add to 87 [the text earlier gives 86], making 189. There 9 remain after the thirtieth [division]. The moon is at lunar day 9 on the Kalends of January, with 27 points. You will do the same for cycles 18 and 19. But from the first lunar cycle through cycle 16, do not divide by 60, lest you fall into error.

[Col. 1312A]

Here is another brief method recently discovered. Know which lunar cycle it is—for example, in the present year, 3. Multiply this by 11: eleven times 3 makes 33. Divide by 30; 3 remain. Add the first day of the Kalends of January; they make 4. The moon will be at lunar day 4 on the Kalends of January in the present year. In this way, throughout the nineteen-year lunar cycle, you can easily discover which lunar cycle it is, without dividing by 19 and then multiplying again by 11. Divide again by 30, add whatever remains, and also add 1 for the Kalends of January; the full lunar day will be found at the Kalends of January.

Remember this most firmly: whenever you reach lunar cycle 9, thereafter take another 1 up to the first cycle, and without hesitation you will find which lunar day falls on the Kalends of January.

[Col. 1312B]

For this reason, according to the Egyptians’ reliable methods, they are shown to have used the following abbreviated calculation. First they set down the epacts, that is, the lunar additions, which in indiction 4 are 23. To these they add 4, that is, half of the number 8, the months from September through April; they make 27. Above these they add the day of the month on which Easter falls, that is, the nineteenth day from the Kalends of May. Since the Egyptians are known to precede us by 5 days, together they make 24, and thus the entire sum is gathered as 51. From these they subtract 30; 21 remain. This is the number of the paschal moon.

These are the true explanations of the calculations. Thanks be to God. Amen.

### On the years from the beginning of the world

### LXXVII

From the beginning of the world to the Flood there were 2,245 years. Likewise, from the Flood to the birth of Abraham there were 942 years. Abraham was born in the 43rd year, [Col. 1312C] while Ninus was already reigning, as the same records testify. From Ninus’s time, public writers of historical events among the barbarians also began to exist. They report that 3,688 years had been completed on the fifth weekday, the ninth day before the Kalends of April, with lunar day 13 beginning at evening. On the following day, that is, as the year 3,690 was advancing, in the first month, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, at lunar day 14 and the beginning of night, it became clear that the Hebrews had performed the sacrifice of the lamb.

Our Lord Jesus Christ suffered after [the text is uncertain: *peractis*] 2,228 years from the world’s origin. This occurred at the beginning of year 2,229; there can be no doubt that he was crucified and buried on the sixth weekday, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of April. On the third day, that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of April, Sunday, he rose from the dead.

There are 430 years with consuls, and thereafter 102 future years without consuls, so that the entire sum consists of 532 years.

### Again, on the years from the beginning of the world

[Col. 1312D]

### LXXVIII

From the beginning of the world to the Flood there were 2,245 years. From the Flood to Abraham there were 942 years. From Abraham to the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt and to the building of Solomon’s Temple there were 481 years. From the building of the Temple to its destruction and the deportation to Babylon there were 390 years. From the Babylonian deportation to the Passion of the Lord there were 659 years. From the Passion to the death of Saint Martin there were 412 years. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of King Chlodovaeus there were 141 years. From the death of Chlodovaeus to the death of Theodobert there were 30 years. From the death of Theodobert to the death of Sigibert [Col. 1313A] there were 29 years. From the beginning of the world to the reign of Theodoric there were 5,660 years.

### On the number of years from the origin of the world to the coming of the Lord

### LXXIX

The years from the origin of the world to the Nativity of Christ are therefore, as it is read in Orosius, 5,199. He himself says that from the founding of the world to the founding of the City there were 4,484 years. From the founding of the City to the Nativity of Christ there were 715 years. Thus the years from the origin of the world to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ total 5,199.

### On the years from the origin of the world, or from the Incarnation

### LXXX

From the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ to the present year there are, as in all correctly written cycles and as is shown by [Col. 1313B] the calculations, 784 years. Yet according to the moon, year 99 began on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. Altogether, from the origin of the world to the present year, there are 5,989 years.

It is read in the chronicles that from the origin of the world to the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, which took place in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and to the Lord’s baptism, there were 5,228 years.

Orosius likewise says that from Adam, the first man, to the great Ninus, whom they call the first king of the Persians, when Abraham was born, there were 3,184 years; these years have either been omitted or ignored by all historians. From Ninus or Abraham to Caesar Augustus—that is, to the Nativity of Christ, which occurred in the forty-second year of Caesar’s reign, when the wars throughout the world ceased—there are reckoned [Col. 1313C] 2,015 years. Together they make 5,199.

It is likewise read in the chronicles, according to Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, that from Adam to the Flood there were 2,242 years. From Abraham to Moses and the departure of Israel from Egypt, 505 years are reckoned. From Moses to Solomon and the first building of the Temple, there were 479 years. From Solomon to the restoration of the Temple, which took place under Darius, king of the Persians, there are reckoned 512 years. From Darius to the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, ruler of the Romans, 547 years are completed. All the years to the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ therefore total 5,235.

[Col. 1313D]

Isidore says: “When the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews had ceased, our Lord Jesus Christ was born of the Virgin in the forty-second year of the reign of Caesar Augustus, with fifteen years of his reign still remaining.” He reigned for 56 years. After him, Tiberius Caesar reigned for 23 years; in the fifteenth year of Tiberius’s reign, the Lord was crucified, after 5,228 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world. Victorius confirms this same number, saying: “Our Lord Jesus Christ therefore suffered,” and so forth.

### Here begins [the account] of the beginning of the world

### LXXXI

How the world was made, at the beginning of God’s creation, and so forth. The remainder is omitted, because the same material is found below in chapter 148.

### Again, on the beginning of the world

### LXXXII

A question concerning the beginning of the world: how was it made, at the beginning of God’s creation? On what day? [Col. 1314A] And on which day of the week? In which year? At what time? We ask whether it was on a day of the year, at night, and at what hour.

It was created at the equinox, on Sunday, in an ordinary second year, in the ogdoad, and at the first hour; and everything was created simultaneously by God in the blink of an eye.

The Latins wish to place the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, but the holy synod by no means allowed this, on account of those three days: the fifth weekday, when our Lord Jesus Christ was arrested; the sixth weekday, when he was crucified; and the seventh weekday, when he rested in the tomb. The synod judged that these days should not be excluded so far beyond the boundary. Therefore it was established in that holy council that the equinox should be calculated from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

### On the years from the incarnation of the world

[Col. 1314B]

### LXXXIII

If you wish to know which year it is from the incarnation of the world, calculate 391 by 15: they make 5,865. Always add 33 regular units: they make 5,903. These are the years from the beginning of the world, namely, 703 years from the Incarnation of the Lord. Remember to observe the aforesaid rule in the fifteenth indiction.

If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years from the beginning of the world—for example, 5,903. Always add 7 regular units: they make 5,911. Divide by 15: fifteen times 300 makes 4,500; 1,311 remain. Fifteen times 60 makes 900; 511 remain. Fifteen times 30 makes 450; 61 remain. Fifteen times 3 [the text reads “4”] makes 60; 1 remains: the first indiction. If nothing remained, it would be the fifteenth indiction.

If you wish to know which year of the solar cycle it is, and how many times the cycle has revolved within itself, take the years from the beginning of the world, for example, 5,903. Divide them by 28. Twenty-eight times 210 makes 5,880; 34 remain. Year 24 is the year of the solar cycle.

[Col. 1314C]

If you wish to know the weekday concurrents, retain the aforesaid number 24. Always subtract 1; 23 remain. Add the fourth part: it makes 28, and divide by 7—that is, four sevens—which makes 28. Nothing remains: it is Saturday on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. Whatever remains above 7 will be the complete weekday.

### On displaying the first moon of the first month

### LXXXIV

If you wish to know how the beginning of the first month, that is, the first moon, is found, determine in the same year how many epacts there are at the Kalends of June and what lunar day it was. Subtract that many days backward from the end of March, and wherever you arrive, there you will find the beginning [Col. 1314D] of the first month, except in the three embolismic years: the last embolism of the ogdoad, the first of the endecad, and the last one.

In the last embolism of the ogdoad, the beginning of the first month is found on the Nones of April. In the first embolism of the endecad, the first moon of the first month is found on the fourth day before the Nones of April. In the final embolism of the endecad, the beginning of the first month is found on the third day before the Nones of April.

### On displaying the leap year through the solar cycle

### LXXXV

If you wish to know about the leap year, take whatever year of the solar cycle the present year may be—for example, the fourteenth year of the solar cycle. Always omit 1; 13 remain. Divide by 4; omit 12. Four times four leaves 1: it is the first year [Col. 1315A] of preparation for the leap year. If nothing remains, it will be a leap year.

### Again, calculations for displaying the concurrents

### LXXXVI

If you wish to know the solar additions, that is, the weekday concurrents on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, take whatever years have elapsed from the Incarnation of the Lord—for example, 810. Divide these by four, and always add the fourth part of the years elapsed; the leap day is always found in every fourth year. [Here he adds.] In 400 years, therefore, there are 100 leap days. In 200, 50 leap days. Likewise, in 160 years—that is, in two periods of eighty—there are 40 days; in 28 years there are 7 leap days. In 810 years altogether there are 204 leap days.

What Dionysius adds to the years of the Lord is shown by the same account of the chronicles: 5,228 years had elapsed from the world’s origin. [Col. 1315B] It is likewise read in the chronicles: all the years from the origin of the world to the preaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, which took place in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and to the Lord’s baptism, total 5,228; to the present year, 6,038.

### For the preparation of the leap year from the beginning of the world

### LXXXVII

If you wish to know again whether the year is a leap year or a year of preparation for a leap year, take the years from the beginning of the world to the present year—for example, 5,989. Divide them by 4. Set aside 4,000, which make four equal parts, and then set aside 1,600, because 400 occurs four times. 389 remain. Set aside 320, because there are four eighties; 69 remain. Set aside 40, because there are four tens; 39 remain. Set aside 28, because there are four sevens; 1 remains. The first year [Col. 1315C] is the year of preparation for the leap year.

If 2 remain, it is the second year of preparation for the leap year; if 3, the third. But if you divide the entire number of years from the beginning of the world into four equal parts, it will be a leap year.

### On displaying the concurrents through the years from the beginning of the world

### LXXXVIII

If you wish to know how many concurrents there are in the present year, take the years from the beginning of the world—for example, 5,989. Divide them by four: that is, 1,497 four times. Put the fourth part you have divided, namely 1,497, above 5,989. Together they make 7,486.

Divide these by seven, because you are seeking the weekday. Set aside 7,000, since these are seven equal parts, namely 1,000 sevens; [Col. 1315D] 486 remain. Set aside seven twenties; 56 remain. Set aside 63, because there are nine sevens; 3 remain. There are therefore 3 concurrents in the present year.

In this way you will find the concurrents for other years: gather the entire number of years from the beginning of the world to the present year, add the fourth part to it, and divide by 7. Whatever number remains will be the number of concurrents in the present year. But if you divide the whole number by 7, there will be 7 concurrents in that year, and the ninth day before the Kalends of April will be Saturday in that year.

### On the divisions of time

### LXXXIX

There are 16 divisions of time: the atom, moment, minute, point, hour, quarter, [Col. 1316A] day, week, month, season, year, cycle, threefold succession, age, lifetime, and world.

*Atom* is a Greek word interpreted as “indivisible.” For among the Greeks *atomon* means “undivided” or “indivisible.” Everything in the world, whether corporeal or incorporeal, that cannot be divided or partitioned is an atom.

As Isidore says: “Philosophers call atoms certain smallest particles in the world, so minute that they are not visible and do not admit division. They are carried here and there like the tiniest grains of dust, which, scattered through darkness, are seen in the rays of the sun.”

There are five kinds of atoms: an atom in a thing, an atom in a body, an atom in speech, an atom in number, and an atom in time.

An atom in a thing is like the particles of dust mentioned above. An atom in a body is as when you divide any part of a stone [Col. 1316B] into 1,000 particles: the thousandth part, which cannot be partitioned or divided, is called an atom in a body, that is, indivisible.

An atom in speech is as follows: just as speech is divided into verses, verses into parts, and parts into syllables, so a syllable is divided into letters; but a letter cannot be divided or dissolved, and therefore it is called an atom by Latin philosophers.

An atom in number is as follows: a thousand is divided into 1,000, 1,000 into 100, 100 into 20, 20 into 10, 10 into 5, 5 into 2, and 2 into 1; but 1 cannot be divided or dissolved, and therefore it is called an atom in number.

An atom in time is as follows: a century is divided into ages, an age into years, a year into months, a month into weeks, a week into days, a day into quarters, a quarter into hours, an hour into points, a point into minutes, a minute into moments, and a moment into [Col. 1316C] 16 atoms. The sixteenth part, which cannot be divided, is called an atom, that is, indivisible. But concerning this, philosophers say that the world was made.

### Again, on atoms in the first moment

### XC

If you wish to know how many atoms there are in one moment, divide one moment into 12 parts, and each part into 47, because one forty-seventh of the 12 parts of a moment is an atom in time. Forty-seven multiplied by twelve makes 564: there are therefore 564 atoms in one moment. There are 480 moments in one day.

If you wish to know how many atoms there are in one hour, multiply 564 by forty: they make 22,564 [22,560]. Likewise, if you wish to know how many atoms there are in one natural day, which has 24 hours, multiply the aforesaid number of atoms in one hour, namely 22,564. Multiply it by 24 [the text says “twenty-four times”]; together they make 541,540 [541,536]. There are therefore this many atoms in one day. [Col. 1316D]

Reader, forgive us, because these are matters of calculation and [the text is uncertain at *litteriolo doxibus*].

### On how many hours there are in a year

### XCI

If you wish to know how many hours there are in a year, multiply 365 by 24. Three hundred twenty multiplied by 24 makes 7,680. Likewise, 60 multiplied by 24 makes 1,440. Together with the preceding number they make 8,640. Likewise, 5 multiplied by 24, or 24 multiplied by 5, makes 120. Add these to the preceding number; together they make 8,760. There are therefore this many hours in a year.

We said that 365 should be multiplied by 24 because there are 24 hours in one natural day, that is, between [Col. 1317A] day and night. Thus, by this number of hours in one natural day—24—all the days of the year, which are 365, multiplied by 24, or 24 times 365, produce 8,760 hours. In a leap year there are 8,780 hours.

### Again, on how many hours and moments there are in the first year
## On the Hours and Moments in the First Year

**XCII.** The first year is divided into 7 parts, and 7 parts make 52 days and nights; and 7 times 52 days and nights make 288 hours. Another 12 days and nights likewise make 288 hours. Add the two: the total is 576 hours—52, 52, 52. Add another 20 days and nights: they make 1,152, in addition to 4, 52, 52, 52; days and nights make 60, 56. And so, in this first part, you will find 1,000 in CIL, 53; likewise in the second, and in the third the same number; in the fourth, 360 equally; and in the fifth likewise equally; in the sixth, not an odd number; and in the seventh you will also count the same number in five days, with one day and night remaining; and a quarter has 27 hours. The entire number of hours in the days and nights of the year, counted seven times, is 8,760 hours.

The number of moments in the days and nights of the year begins as follows. An hour has 40 moments; 4 hours have 160. Add them: the total is 480 moments. The night likewise has 12 hours and makes the same number, 480. Add day and night: 960. Twenty-five days and nights make 24,000 moments. Another 25 days and nights make 24,000 moments. Let no one doubt it. The total for 50 days and nights is 48,000. The two days and nights that remain make 2,000.

If two hours are added—that is, 80 moments—to those two days out of the 53-day period, 380 moments remain from that same day mentioned above. The second part, that is, 52 days and nights, amounts to 50,000; two hours are added from that same day mentioned above, and 300 moments remain in that day. The third part likewise amounts to 50,000; two hours are added from the aforementioned day, and 220 moments remain. The fourth likewise amounts to 50,000; two hours are added from the same day, and 140 moments remain. The fifth part likewise amounts to 50,000; two hours are added from that day, and 60 moments remain. The sixth likewise amounts to 50,000; two hours are added from that day, and 480 remain. The seventh part likewise amounts to 50,000 moments; two hours are added from that same day to each part, as above, and 400 moments remain. A quarter is then counted, that is, 3 hours, making 120 moments. To put it briefly, the year of 365 days and a quarter has 8,753 hours. It has 350,040 moments.

## On the Points in a Year

**XCIII.** If you wish to know how many points there are in a year, multiply by 4 the number of hours we stated, namely 8,760. Thus, 8,000 multiplied by 4 makes 32,000. Seven hundred multiplied by 4 makes 2,800. Together they make 34,800. Again, 60 multiplied by 4 makes 240. Add this to the preceding number: the total is 35,040. That many points there are in a year.

We said that the number of hours in the whole year, namely 8,760, should be multiplied by 4 because 4 points complete one hour in the sun. In a leap year, however, there are 35,136 points.

## On the Minutes in a Year

**XCIV.** If you wish to know how many minutes there are in a year, multiply the preceding number of points, namely 35,040, by 2; this makes 70,080. Add half of the preceding number of points, namely 17,540; together they make 87,620. That many minutes there are in a year. In a leap year, however, there are 87,680 minutes.

We said that the whole number of points should be multiplied by 2 and that half should be added because 2 minutes and a half make 1 point. [The final clause is incomplete in the supplied text.]

## On the Moments in a Year

**XCV.** If you wish to know how many moments there are in a year, multiply the preceding number of minutes, namely 87,620, by 4; multiplied by 4, this number makes 352,480. That many moments there are in a year. In a leap year there are 352,540 moments.

We said that the number of moments should be multiplied four times because 4 moments make 1 minute. [The supplied text reads *munitum*, apparently an OCR error for *minutum* or a related form.]

## Again on Moments

**XCVI.** A moment is a minute and an exceedingly brief period of time, named from the movement of the heavenly bodies. For it is the extremity of an hour in brief intervals, when the sun yields something of its position and succeeds to another. A moment is also, as it were, *motus mentis*, “a movement of the mind”; for our mind knows that the creature has been changed. At that time the mind is changed through knowledge of the changed creature.

There are 6 kinds of moments.

In the sun, a moment is that interval during which the sun displays something of the upper part of its circuit, until it has placed the lower part there in turn. That is, while it moves through its entire course, the delay of time during which it appears to be there, the fixed course of the sun is in heaven. [The source is corrupt here; the marked words are incomplete.]

In the mind, we call it a moment when, through some obstacle or any kind of loss, the human mind is changed. For after our first-created ancestor, having committed the offense, saw that all the elements had changed their force through the power of sin, then suddenly, because of the loss suffered by creation, his mind was changed from the lofty summit of blessedness and the path of incorruptible joy into mortal sorrow. Hence arose the first moment of days, namely the movement of the mind.

In time, a moment is said to occur when time changes from serenity into cloudiness, from calm into storm.

A moment in heaven occurs when the upper sphere of heaven turns or changes from setting to rising.

A moment is said to occur in a flying creature when any bird, after flying for however long a period during a time of rest, changes the time being spent there by beating its wings; or when a rooster, with the clapping of its wings, gives a sign of daylight, until by the sound of its voice it has prolonged the interval of time placed between them.

A moment in a human being is said to occur when someone fixes his gaze without moving his eyelids. A moment in the eye is also spoken of, concerning which the philosophers say that all things were made “in a moment,” or “in the blink of an eye.”

In a wheel, [the source is corrupt: *rota … commutatur de cantu*]. In song, a moment is said to be one step.

There is also a great moment, which is the movement of heaven from setting to the meridian.

A bad moment is the movement of the upper sphere from setting toward the east; this is the interval of 12 hours.

The greatest moment of heaven is the natural movement through the two hemispheres from east to east, or from west to west; it occupies the interval of 24 hours, and is called by others a great moment.

The prophet Zephaniah says that a minute is named from the minute elements, whose sight and touch are sharpened.

Again: a minute is like a lesser moment, because they count as smaller what fills a greater measure.

A point is named from *pungere*, “to prick,” the sharpness of the eyes. For after winter and the darkness of winter’s cold, when 10 moments have been added and the sharpness of the sun has passed over eyes closed to the grace of its light through the mists of the cold, human sight seems as though it were pricked or made to shine by the solar ray. Hence that interval of time is called a point.

Isidore says otherwise: a point is the work of those who make sundials, for at the end of 12 lunar periods they placed [a point]; from this hour is the end of time. Thus there are “hours” as the boundaries of seas, rivers, and garments. The hour of boundaries is to be written with *o*, whereas the hour of days is to be written with *h*.

The word *hora* is also said to be derived from *hora*, because it regulates the divisions of the day. We speak of the hour of the sea and of the hours of garments. This is a Greek word which in Latin means “appearance” or “beauty”; for Homer calls the daughters of Jupiter “10 hours,” that is, 10 beauties.

## On the Quarter

**XCVII.** A quarter is so called because it weighs a fourth part of an ounce. Among geometers, the fourth part of anything was called a quarter. The fourth part of a day is called a quarter.

In the divine Scriptures also, the fourth part of a human action is called a quarter; for a human act is understood to consist in four ways, whether in good or in evil: deed, consent, and thought. [The supplied enumeration appears incomplete.]

As we read in the Gospel: “He will not come out from there until he has paid the last quarter,” that is, the final thought of guilt.

A quarter of time is also called the fourth part of a year, as it is read that the Antichrist will deceive the world for three years and two quarters, and will mock the nations for three years and six months.

Theophilus also says: “A quarter is so called from a square figure, which consists in its own solidity.” For when a fourth part of anything has been removed, a threefold figure remains. He explains this more clearly: “A quarter is so called because it suspends the fourth part of a day; the Hebrews call it a quarter, the Greeks a *dodrant*, and the Latins a quarter.”

*Quadrans* ought to be written without *n*, just as *gigas*, not *gigant*, and therefore *quadras*, not *quadrans*. For the rule of writing is that [a word] should grow in letters or syllables from the nominative [the supplied text is corrupt].

Jerome says: “Not, as the unlearned write, *gigans gigantis*, but as *gigaphi* … *gigantes*; so also *quadras*, *quadrantis*.” [The source is materially corrupt in the forms cited.]

## On the Weeks in the Whole Cycle of the Year

**XCVIII.** If you wish to know how many weeks there are in a year, multiply 12 by 4: the result is 48. That many weeks there are in 12 months, namely 4 weeks for each month. The remaining days, however, which are left over—that is, from the four months of 30 days and the 22 days from the months having 31 days—together make 29, that is, 4 weeks and 1 day. Whenever there is a leap year, the year has 52 weeks and 2 days.

## On the Solar Concurrent Days Throughout the Year

**XCIX.** If you wish to know, for a date throughout the year—for example, the ninth day before the Kalends of April—on which weekday it will fall in the hundredth year, where the solar concurrent days run, you must investigate as follows.

Whatever weekday the ninth day before the Kalends of April falls on in the present year, count the next 6 weekdays after that weekday. Know that the sixth day you encounter will be the weekday on which that same date will fall in the hundredth year.

For example, in the present year the ninth day before the Kalends of April fell on the third weekday. Take the next 6 days: the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, first, and second weekdays. The second weekday occurs 6 days after the third; on that second weekday the ninth day before the Kalends of April will fall in the hundredth year.

For whatever weekday any date falls on in the present year, as we stated above concerning the ninth day before the Kalends of April—3 concurrent days, because it fell on the third weekday in the present year—it will likewise fall after 28 years: the third weekday will be the eighth day before the Kalends of April, that is, 3 concurrent days. But after 56 years, when the seventh year begins, the third weekday will fall on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. Similarly, after 84 years, when the fifth year begins, it will fall on the third weekday, with 3 concurrent days—that is, one year of preparation for the leap year.

You have 16 years remaining out of the 100. Proceed through the order of the recurring numbers: 4, 5, 6, with two; 1, 2, 3, 5, with two; 6, 7, 1, 2, with two; 4, 5, 6, 1, with two; 2. The hundredth year will therefore fall on the second weekday. In that year the eighth day before the Kalends of April will have 2 concurrent days.

In the same way you must investigate any other date throughout the year, to determine on which weekday it will fall up to the hundredth year. Whatever weekday is present for you on that date, the preceding weekday—that is, yesterday—for example, as the sixth day of the week that follows, will have the same weekday. On that same date it will occur in the hundredth year. Whatever the sequence of concurrent days is in that year—whether with two, or with one, two, or three years after the leap year—the weekday, or the concurrent days, will follow that same sequence in the hundredth year. [The source is corrupt at the end of the paragraph.]

## On the Lunar Epacts on the Eleventh Day before the Kalends of April

**C.** If you wish to know the lunar divisions from any present day up to the hundredth year, you must observe the following.

Whatever the epact is on the present date throughout the year—for example, if the epact on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April is 20 in the present year—add 11 epacts for the following 5 years, which make 55. If there is a saltus, they will make 56. Add also the epact of the present year, namely 20; together they make 75. Remove 60: 15 remain.

The epact 15 will occur in the fifth year after the present year. This epact will also occur in the hundredth year, because whatever epact occurs in the present year—for example, as we said, 20 on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April—the same will occur in year 20; that is, epact 20. Likewise, in year 38 there will be 20, and in year 76 there will be 20, and in year 95 there will be 20.

You have 5 years remaining out of the 100. Proceed through the order of the epacts: 1, 12, 23, 4, 15. Thus in the hundredth year the epact will be 15, as we also stated. In the fifth future year there will be 15; this is the fourth [epact].

Together they make 986. To this add 3 regulars, because in the year of the Incarnation of Christ they made the fourth weekday on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Thus, with 4 added to the preceding number, the total is 990.

Divide these by 7. Remove 700; there are one hundred sevens. 290 remain. Remove 214; there are twenty [sevens], that is, twice seven twenties, which has 47. Ten remain. Remove sevens; 3 remain.

There are therefore 3 concurrent days in the present year on the ninth day before the Kalends of April; it fell on the third weekday. By this argument it is also shown what weekday falls on the Kalends of January in each present year, after removing only 1 regular, as the good holy Primicerius demonstrated.

## On Showing the Concurrent Days

**CI.** If you wish to know the concurrent weekday on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, you will know which year of the solar cycle it is. For example, take 14 and always add a fourth part, namely 3; together they make 17. Divide by 7. Remove 14, since there are twice 7; 3 remain. There were therefore 3 concurrent days on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, that is, the third weekday in the present year.

Proceed in the same way for the other years, whatever they may be: divide by four parts and add the fourth part. For example, in the fifth year of the cycle, after 4 add 1; in the ninth year, after 8 add 2; in year 13, after 12 add 3; after 16 add 4; after 20 add 5; after 24 add 6; after 27 add 7. In this way you will find the concurrent days of any present year.

This solar cycle contains 28 years, that is, 4 weeks, or four groups of seven, because it cannot be completed before the leap year—which customarily returns every fourth year—has passed through all the weekdays and touched them: Sunday, the sixth weekday, the fourth weekday, the second weekday, the seventh weekday, the fifth weekday, and the third weekday. For they revolve and run through all the weekdays in this order.

Each year therefore has its own concurrent days. These concurrent days are affixed to the ninth day before the Kalends of April, so that they may reveal the proper Paschal festivals, on what weekday the fourteenth lunar day falls, and the day of the epacts; and by this means they make clear the method for finding the day of Easter.

Dionysius says concerning the concurrent days: “The reckoning of the concurrent weeks, which comes from the course of the sun, is completed by a continuous circuit of a cycle of seven years taken four times. In it, for each year—that is, 3—you will take care to add one and [reckon] the concurrent days of the preceding year. Only in that year, namely the fourth, in which there is a leap year, shall you add two.”

The authorities place these solar epacts—that is, the concurrent weekdays—on the ninth day before the Kalends of April because, according to the tradition of divine authority or of the holy Council of Nicaea, they assign the heavenly bodies—the sun and the moon—which the Lord created on that dated day and placed in heaven, to the service of the human race.

## Again on the Concurrent Days

**CII.** If you wish to know immediately how many concurrent days there are in the same year, proceed by the weekday. Find on which weekday the Kalends of April fall; and wherever you find the Kalends, immediately count backward to find the ninth day before the Kalends of April. On whatever weekday you find that date—for example, on the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh weekday, since they do not increase beyond that—you will have that number as the concurrent day.

For the Greeks place the solar epact—that is, the concurrent weekdays arising from the course of the sun—on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. According to the tradition of divine authority or of the holy Council of Nicaea, they assign the heavenly bodies, namely the sun, the moon, and the stars, which the Lord created on that dated day or placed in heaven, to the service of the human race.

## On Showing the Weekday on the Kalends of January

**CIII.** If you wish to know on which weekday the day of the Kalends of January falls in each year, take the years from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ—for example, now 810. Always subtract 1: 809 remain. Divide these into four parts, and add the fourth part that you have divided out; this is 202. Together they make 1,011.

Divide these by 7. Remove 700, which is seven hundred; 311 remain. Remove 280, which is seven times 40; 31 remain. Remove 28, which is four times seven; 3 remain. The Kalends of January in the present year therefore fell on the third weekday.

## Demonstrating the Solar and Lunar Cycles with the Fingers

**CIV.** Some people, to abbreviate the calculation of the order of both cycles, namely the solar and lunar cycles, transfer them to the joints of the fingers. Since the human hand has 19 joints, counting the nails as belonging to the joints, and since they fit one year of the lunar course to each joint and nail over 19 years, they begin on the inner base of the thumb of the left hand and complete the same lunar cycle on the nail of the little finger, that is, the inner side of the little finger.

Since the two hands have 18 joints internally, excluding the nails, they assign one year to each of these joints. [The text is corrupt here: *in quantas … a minimo digito*.] Beginning with the little finger of the left hand—that is, the uppermost joint of the little finger, as though with the first weekday together with the leap year—and ending at the left thumb, namely from the uppermost joint, they complete and terminate the solar cycle on the sixth weekday.

They do not proceed through the fingers by counting each beginning as in the lunar cycle, but, because of the reckoning of the quarter, they mark every four-year period by moving across the fingers, so that they assign the seven leap years to the two sets of three joints of the little fingers—that is, 6 joints—for the corresponding years.

Likewise, the two sets of three joints of the fingers next to the little fingers, immediately before these, amount to 6 [joints and] show the first year of preparation for the leap year on both hands. Similarly, the second fingers from the little fingers, on both hands, show 2 six-year periods of preparation for the leap year through 6 joints. The third fingers from the little fingers on either hand show 3 years and 6 [years?] of preparation for the leap year through the 6 joints of each finger. [The source is corrupt in this enumeration.]

Moreover, the seventh leap year, together with the three years following it, occupies two pairs of joints on the two thumbs.

Following this order, the calculator finds the 7 leap years by running through 28 years. He begins the leap year on the first weekday at the little finger, on the uppermost joint, and says: “The first weekday with the leap year.” On the second joint of the little finger: “The sixth weekday with the leap year.” On the third joint: “The fourth weekday with the leap year.”

Then, on the right hand, at the uppermost joint of the little finger, he says: “The second weekday with the leap year.” On the second joint: “The seventh weekday with the leap year.” On the third joint, that is, at the base of the little finger: “The fifth weekday with the leap year.”

Then, at the base of the right thumb, he says: “The third weekday with the leap year.”

Thus far concerning the concurrent days.

## On the Beginnings of the Four Seasons

**CV.** If you wish to know on which weekday the four seasons begin—that is, spring, summer, autumn, and winter—take your starting point from the Kalends of May. Whatever weekday the Kalends of May falls on, the next weekday is the beginning of autumn at the Kalends of August; on the third day before the Kalends begins winter; and on the fourth day begins spring, that is, at the Kalends of February. Nor does a leap year alter this reckoning.

## Sesebutus Also Speaks about Eclipses of the Sun and Moon

**CVI.** Sesebutus says:

Why, when the Moon is weary, does its circle grow faint in its orb?

Why does its purple radiance, at snowy hours, fade away?

Why does its lowest part, newly discolored by neighboring shadows,

Care for its brother, and, bloodless, fail in the empty hour?

The earth will remain inviolate, but with its vast body,

While it occupies the middle, or rather the pole, its summits

Abandon their brothers during shadow-bearing nights;

While, with the star withdrawn, the earth’s shadow grows pale,

Until it crosses the axis of the wheel,

The swift one acting with its heap and rosy mirror,

So that it may restore its brotherly flames freely through heaven.

But why is the Moon alone stripped of its light?

There is nothing surprising: since it lacks its own light,

Alien light nourishes it; but when the part nearest the boundary

Looks upon it with envy, the ray awaits its brothers, darkly.

The remaining [body] is not touched by shadows at the choir of the southern winds.

[Note: [Col. 1323D] Perhaps read: “But the chorus of the stars …”]

Its own radiance belongs to all of them, and they do not redden like the Sun,

But onward, beyond the Sun, it is carried with the summit of heaven.

Now why does it not always grow pale in its monthly orb?

The winding courses immediately provide an explanation along their bent path.

For when, wandering in a measured error, it is twisted off course,

Then the Sun reaches the boundary from afar,

And twists the veil of night and shines upon its sister.

The same explanation applies when the august Sun’s red radiance,

Needy of light, is suddenly broken by shadows,

When, between the earth and the Sun, the wheel of the white body

Was the Moon, accusing its brother with straight lines. [The final lines are corrupt.]

## An Argument concerning the Solar Epacts at the Kalends of the Twelve Months

**CVII.** If you wish to know the weekday of the Kalends of each month through one week, you will find it as follows, using those 7 days.

The first [day of] March up to the Nones of March: whatever weekday the Kalends of March falls on, the Kalends of November falls on that same weekday. Whatever weekday the sixth day before the Nones of March falls on, the Kalends of June and the Kalends of February fall on that same day. Whatever weekday the sixth day before the Nones of March falls on, the Kalends of February and of December likewise fall on it. Whatever weekday the fourth day before the Nones of March falls on, the Kalends of April and the Kalends of July fall on that weekday.

Likewise, the third day before the Nones of March corresponds to the Kalends of October; the day before the Nones of March to the Kalends of May; the Nones of March to the Kalends of January; and the Kalends of August falls on that same weekday.

## On the Twelve Signs of Heaven, which Move through the Zodiacal Circle Called the Sign-Bearing Circle, that Is, the Course of the Stars

**CVIII.** The zodiacal course, that is, the stellar or sidereal course, is also called sign-bearing because it appears to carry 12 signs. For everywhere, around the most perfectly rounded circuit of heaven, along the line of the zodiacal circle, distinct rows of 12 jewels touching one another, like the figure of an immense sphere, surround and bind it from east to west.

This zone, therefore, which is called zodiacal and sidereal, and *Mazaroth*, and whose [source reading *cobus* is uncertain], surrounds heaven, marked out with 12 stars, through which the sun and moon travel. They are of such magnitude that each sign can rise, set, or move from its position in no less than two hours. The zodiac completes so great a circuit in 365 days and 6 hours. The moon, however, flies through the same 12 signs in 26 days and 8 hours; through each individual sign it travels in 2 days and 6 hours and two-thirds of an hour.

These 12 signs through which the sun and moon run are called: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces.

In each of these signs the sun remains 30 days, 10 hours, and half an hour. The moon travels through each sign in 2 days and 11 hours. These 12 signs move with the firmament along an oblique line, in a bright circle, from east to west and from west to east once in a day and night, over 24 hours.

The sun, the moon, and the stars Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury move against the firmament; but the force of the firmament’s movement draws them backward with it, and hence they appear to move backward. This is the cause of the unequal length and brevity of days and nights: the obliquity of the sign-bearing circle through which the sun and moon travel, although an equal portion of the world is made above and below the earth at every moment.

Hence Isidore says: “For the sun proceeds along an oblique line toward the north, and thus returns toward the east.”

## The Causes from Which the Twelve Signs Received Their Names

**CIX.** The 12 signs received their names either from annual causes or from the myths of the Gentiles.

They assign the Ram to the month of March because of Ammonian Jupiter. According to the myth, in that month Jupiter appeared in the form of a ram to Liber Pater and his army in the sandy regions of India, where they had no water and were suffering from thirst, and showed them a spring. For this reason they fashioned horns on the image of the ram.

Eusebius likewise says in the *Chronicle*: “Phrixus, fleeing with his sister Helle from the plots of his stepmother, was seen to be carried through the air by a ram with a golden fleece.” A ship had been prepared for him as he fled, and its emblem was a ram.

They assign the Bull to April because of the same Jupiter, since, as the myths tell, he was changed into a bull.

The Twins, that is, Castor and Pollux, are assigned to May because of their outstanding virtues.

They assign the Crab to June because the sun turns back toward the lower regions in that month, just as a crab, when driven, customarily directs its course backward.

The Lion, which Hercules killed, is assigned to July because of the force of the heat.

The Virgin is assigned to August because then the earth, scorched by the heat, produces nothing.

The Balance belongs to September because of the equality of day and night.

They take Scorpio and Sagittarius, formed with horses’ legs, for October and November because of the thunderbolts of those months.

December receives Capricorn because of Jupiter’s nurse, the she-goat, whose lower parts are depicted as resembling a fish, since the final portions of that month are rainy.

Aquarius belongs to January and February. Pisces is assigned to those rainy months.

Each of these 12 signs always begins from the middle day of its month, that is, on the twenty-fifth day before the Kalends of June [for the relevant month], except for January and February: the sun enters Aquarius on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, and enters Pisces on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.

In the other 10 signs the sun enters the beginning of each sign on the fifteenth day before the Kalends. The first sign, Aries, begins to rise in the middle of March, that is, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April. The second, Taurus, begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. The third, Gemini, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June. The fourth, Cancer, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July. The fifth, Leo, begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. The sixth sign, Virgo, begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September. The seventh sign, Libra, begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October. The eighth sign, Scorpio, begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends [of November]. The ninth sign, Sagittarius, begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. The tenth sign, Capricorn, begins on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January. The eleventh sign, Aquarius, begins on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February. The twelfth sign, Pisces, begins on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.

The ten and a half hours that exceed the individual signs are disregarded in calculation, but nevertheless ought to be calculated and remembered. For the sun remains in each sign for 30 days, 10 hours, and a half—that is, 20 moments. Thirty parts are assigned to each sign, in three decades; and each sign has 10 points, that is, 2 hours. Five *Emm.* points in the moon make 1 hour. [The abbreviation *Emm.* is retained as printed.]

Thus each month has its own sign: April has Aries, May Taurus, June Gemini, July Cancer, August Leo, September Virgo, October Libra, November Scorpio, December Sagittarius, January Capricorn, February Aquarius, and March Pisces, as one of the ancients also explained in verse.

## On the Course of the Sun and Moon, That Is, in Which Sign the Sun Runs and in Which Sign the Moon Runs

**CX.** If you wish to know in which sign the moon is, and how many signs and parts lie between the sun and the moon on each day, take whichever moon you wish—for example, the first. Multiply 1 by 4: the result is 4. Therefore the first moon is always 4 points distant from the sun. Multiply 4 by 3: the result is 12. Thus the first moon is always 12 parts—that is, 12 days—away from the sun.

Whatever moon it is is multiplied by 4 because the moon’s brightness always increases by 4 points as it moves away from the sun, and after the full moon its brightness always decreases by 4 points each day as it approaches the sun, until its rising; and the waxing moon moves away from the sun by 4 points each day until the full moon. Likewise, the waning moon approaches the sun by 4 points each day. Therefore, as we said, whatever moon it is is multiplied by 4.
