Afterward that number, whatever the fourfold product is, is multiplied by 3 because there are 3 parts in each point; thus 4 points multiplied by 3 make 12 parts. Or it may be more, namely 13 parts. Since the moon travels through the space of heaven and time represented by 4 points each day, the sun cannot travel in less than 12 or 13 parts, that is, days.

For the second moon, multiply 2 by 4: the result is 8. There are therefore 8 points between the sun and the moon, that is, 1 hour and 3 points. When it is the second moon, multiply 8 by 3: the result is 24. That many parts lie between the sun and the moon when it is the second moon.

For the third moon, multiply 3 by 4: the result is 12. Multiply by 3: the result is 36. The third moon is therefore 1 sign and 6 parts away from the sun.

For the fourth moon, multiply 4: the result is 16. Multiply by 3: the result is 48. The fourth moon is 1 sign and 18 parts away from the sun.

For the fifth moon, multiply 5 by 4: the result is 20. That many points lie between the sun and the moon when it is the fifth moon, namely 2 complete signs; for 10 points in the moon, that is, 2 hours, make 1 sign, while 20 points complete 2 signs. If you multiply by 3, the result is 60, that is, twice 30, which make 2 signs, since 30 parts make 1 sign.

For the sixth moon, if you wish to know how far it is from the sun, multiply 6 by 4: the result is 24. Divide these by tens: twice ten, that is, 2 signs, remain 4. Multiply by 3: the result is 12. The sixth moon is therefore always 2 signs and 12 parts from the sun.

For the seventh moon, multiply 7 by 4: the result is 28. Multiply by 3: the result is 84. The seventh moon is 2 signs and 24 parts of the third sign away from the sun. [The source is corrupt at this point.]

For the eighth moon, multiply 8 by 4: the result is 32. Multiplied by 3, these make 96: the eighth moon is 3 signs and 6 parts away from the sun.

If you wish to know how far the ninth moon is from the sun, multiply 9 by 4: the result is 36. Multiply by 3: the result is 108. The ninth moon is 3 signs and 17 parts away from the sun.

For the tenth moon, multiply 10 by 4: the result is 40 points, that is, 8 hours. The tenth moon is therefore 40 points from the sun. Ten points, that is, 2 hours, make 1 sign; 40 points, that is, [the source reads “14,” apparently corrupt], complete 4 signs, and thus the tenth moon is always 4 signs from the sun.

If you wish to know how far the fifteenth moon is from the sun, and how many signs lie between them at the full moon, multiply 15 by 4: the result is 60. There are therefore 60 points in the fifteenth moon, and it shines with that many points, that is, for 12 hours; and with that many points and hours the fifteenth moon is distant from the sun, namely 6 signs. For if 60 is divided by ten—that is, by complete signs, since 10 points always make 1 sign—there are six tens, that is, 6 signs.

Likewise, 60 multiplied by 3 makes three sixties, that is, 6 thirties, which complete 6 signs. The fifteenth moon is therefore always separated from the sun by 6 signs, that is, half the celestial sphere.

Finally, when the moon’s orb is completely full, you see it opposite the sun: the sun is high and the moon low, or the moon high and the sun low. When the sun occupies the summer circle, that is, the boundaries of the summer solstice, the full moon occupies the winter circle, that is, the boundaries of the winter solstice. When the sun declines and inclines toward the winter circle, the full moon’s ascent into the solstitial circle reveals the longest night. When the sun occupies one equinox, the moon at the full moon preserves the other equinox.

When the sun has passed beyond the length of the equinox, the moon at the full moon surpasses the length of the night: throughout the night it shines in the equinox and after the equinox; that is, it illuminates the whole space that the sun, traveling by day, illuminated, just as the moon illuminates the whole night by traversing it.

Thus far we have spoken of the waxing moon: by how many points, hours, parts, and signs it moves away from the sun up to the full moon. Let us now see how the waning moon approaches the sun each day: by an equal number of points, hours, parts, and signs until its conjunction on the thirtieth day.

Therefore, just as the waxing moon moves away from the sun by 4 points each day, so the waning moon approaches the sun by 4 points each day. By as much as the fifteenth moon is distant from the sun while moving away—that is, 5 signs and 18 parts—by that same interval the sixteenth moon is distant from the sun while approaching it, namely 5 signs and 18 parts.

And by as much as the thirteenth moon moves away from the sun—that is, 5 signs and 6 intervening parts—so the eighteenth moon approaches the sun. And just as the twelfth moon moves away from the sun by 4 months and 24 parts, so, with this number interposed, the eighteenth moon approaches the sun. And so with each moon up to the thirtieth.

## Arguments concerning the Course of the Sun through the Twelve Signs

**CXI.** If you wish to know in which sign, or in which part of a sign, the moon is, and how many parts or months lie between the sun and the moon, on any day take the present moon, whichever you wish, and multiply it by 12, because the moon moves away from the sun by 12 parts each day. Whatever number results from that multiplication represents the number of parts—that is, days—or signs between the sun and the moon.

But if you multiply any moon by 13, whatever number results will represent the number of parts or months between the place where the moon was kindled and the part of heaven where the moon is presently running.

Thus, for example, the part of heaven that the first moon traverses in a complete day and night will be reached by the sun after 24 days wherever the second moon is running. The same method must be followed for the others.

## On the Seven Wandering Stars
## On the Seven Wandering Luminaries

**CXII.** Between heaven and earth hang seven luminaries, separated by fixed intervals: the sun, the moon, the star of Saturn, the star of Jupiter, the star of Mars, the star of Venus, and the star of Mercury. These seven luminaries are called “wandering” because they pursue a course contrary to the [usual order of the] world: that which is on the left is always perceived on the right, although through their continual movement they are raised from it in the course of a month in accordance with their speed and are carried toward setting. Nevertheless, because of their oblique motion, each is observed to move now lower, now higher, along its own path. They wander through the zodiac; but, hindered by the sun’s rays, they become anomalous, retrograde, or stationary.

The highest of the planets, that is, of the wandering luminaries, is Saturn, cold by nature. Hence Augustine said: “The star of Saturn completes its circuit in the space of thirty years; because of its proximity to the waters it is said to be cold.” In thirty years it traverses the zodiac. This star is therefore said to be placed in the seventh heaven, for there are said to be seven heavens. Hence Isidore says: “The philosophers introduced seven heavens of spheres, with harmonious motion.”

In the sixth heaven is said to be the star of Jupiter, which is otherwise called the star of Phaethon. It is temperate by nature and completes its course in twelve years.

In the fifth circle the star of Mars is said to run; it is called Vesper, is fiery by nature, and appears to complete its course in two years, but traverses the whole zodiacal circle in fifteen years.

In the fourth heaven the sun, midway among the planets, runs its course in 365 days and a quarter; nevertheless, after twenty-eight years have been completed, it returns to the same circle.

In the third heaven runs the star of Venus, below the sun; it is called Lucifer and completes its course in 348 days [text uncertain]. It is said to complete the whole circle in nine years.

In the second heaven the star of Mercury is said to run its course in 340 days, in a more rapid circuit, shining sometimes before sunrise and sometimes after sunset.

In the first circle the moon is said to traverse its course in 28 days and 12 hours; others, however, say that it flies through the zodiac in 27 days and a third of a day, that is, 8 hours. After nineteen complete years it returns to the same circle.

[Col. 1328A]

## On the Speed of the Moon’s Course

**CXIII.** The moon is nearer to the earth than the sun, and therefore completes its course more rapidly in a shorter orbit. For the journey which the sun completes in 365 days and a quarter, the moon traverses in thirty days. Hence the ancients assigned their months to the moon’s course, not to the sun’s course.

When waxing, the moon turns its horns toward the east; when waning, toward the west—and rightly so, because it is about to fall and lose its light.

## On the Sun’s Ascent and Descent Throughout the Year: How It Increases or Decreases Each Day

[Col. 1328B]

**CXIV.** How many days are there in the sun’s ascent and descent, so that there may be an equal division between light and darkness, that is, between the sun’s ascent and descent? If you wish to know this, it must be investigated as follows.

From the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, the day begins to grow until the eleventh day before the Kalends of July—that is, through two periods of ninety days and two additional days, or six months containing 182 days. During these six months and half a natural day, that is, twelve hours, light and day increase, while night and darkness decrease each day by two moments, a half, and a sixth of a moment—that is, by two-thirds of a moment. Thus, in fifteen days and a little more, one hour increases.

In thirty days two hours increase; yet those two hours are not complete until one reaches the eighth hour of the day in the following month. In two months four hours increase in the sun, as the day grows; yet those four hours are not complete until the sixteenth hour of the day in the third month.

Thus, in three months of thirty days each, with one additional day—that is, over 91 days—six hours increase. There are as many days from the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April: twelve hours in the day and twelve in the night. There is therefore an equal number of hours and moments, namely 480, in the day and in the night. In the six hours of increase there are 211 moments.

Likewise, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the twelfth day before the Kalends of July there are three months, containing 91 days. Thus the sun increases each day by two moments and two-thirds of a moment. In fifteen days one hour increases, though slightly more, since that hour is not complete until the fourth hour of the fifteenth day. Thus, in one month of thirty days, two hours increase.

[Col. 1328C]

In two months, four hours; and so in three months—that is, from the spring equinox to the summer solstice, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of July—over 91 days, another six hours increase. Thus Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of the city of Laodicea, demonstrates it [text uncertain]:

“For fifteen days, as the sun ascends by two moments, a half, and a sixth of a moment, one hour is diminished from darkness, that is, from night, and increases in light, that is, in day. Thus twelve hours, that is, 480 moments, increase from the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the eleventh day before the Kalends of July. Then there are eighteen hours in the summer solstitial day, that is, three parts of the natural day, which contains twenty-four hours; and a fourth part of that natural day occurs in the solstitial night, namely six hours.”

[Col. 1329A]

In the same way, and over the same number of days—namely, 182—through six months and half a natural day, that is, twelve hours—the light decreases by two moments and two-thirds of a moment each day, while darkness increases. From the eleventh day before the Kalends of July to the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, until the winter solstice, night increases and light decreases by a similar number of hours, moments, and days.

Thus, just as light decreases, darkness increases: one hour in fifteen days, two hours in thirty days, four in two months, and six in forty days [text corrupt]. Over three months, that is, from the summer solstice—the eleventh day before the Kalends of July—to the winter solstice and the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, according to the Greeks, twelve hours increase in darkness and two decrease over 182 days, that is, over 480 moments.

[Col. 1329B]

Then, in that winter solstitial night, there are eighteen hours, that is, three parts of the natural day, and a fourth part in that solstitial day, namely six hours. Let this suffice concerning the sun’s ascent and descent, leaving greater matters to the wiser.

## On Lunar and Solar Eclipses: Pliny and Jerome

**CXV.** Pliny the Elder described it thus in his magnificent work, the *Natural History*:

“It is certain that a solar eclipse occurs only at the last or first moon, which they call conjunction. The moon, however, suffers an eclipse only when full. Eclipses of both luminaries occur each year below the earth, though when they occur above they cannot everywhere be seen—sometimes because of clouds, more often because the globe of the earth and the convexities of the world stand in the way.”

Jerome likewise says:

“A failure of the sun, that is, an eclipse, tends to occur in the seasons of spring and summer; it never occurs except at the rising of the moon.”

The Milky Circle is a white path visible in the sphere. It is named from its whiteness, because it is white. Some say that it is a road because the sun circles through it by the passage of its own splendor; likewise [text uncertain] the lunar [path].

Although the sun is fiery, it grows hotter because of the excessive speed of its revolution. The philosophers say that its fire is nourished by water and, conversely, that it receives from the opposing element the power of light and heat.

## On the Various Names of the Sun in Various Languages

**CXVI.** [The moon?] is called *simplicia* in Hebrew [text corrupt]. *Aelios* in Greek, *Phanath* among philosophers, *Tithan* among the Chaldeans, and *sun* among the Latins, from the solidity of its light, or because it alone appears when the other luminaries are darkened by its powerful rays.

[Col. 1329D]

## Rules Concerning the Beginning of Lent, the End of Easter, the Rogations, and Pentecost

**CXVII.** If you wish to know what lunar day marks the beginning of Lent in the Rogations, know what lunar day Easter has in each year. From the current epact at Easter subtract 12; that will be the moon of the beginning of Lent.

Likewise, add 7 to the lunar age that you have at the current Easter; that will be the moon at the Rogations.

Know also this: whatever the moon is at the end of Easter in a given year, such will it be at the Rogations. For when the moon is 15 at Easter, the moon is 22 at the end of Easter; likewise it will be 22 at the Rogations. Thus, through seven lunar ages, the moon at the end of Easter and at the Rogations runs from 22 to 28.

[Col. 1330A]

Likewise, when the moon is 15 at Easter, it will be 25 at the Ascension of the Lord; and when the moon is found to be 21 at Easter, the first moon will be at the Ascension of the Lord, from lunar day 25 through 31.

Whenever the moon is 15 at Easter, it will be 5 at Pentecost; and when it is 21 at Easter, it will be 11 at Pentecost. These are the seven lunar ages to be observed at Pentecost, from lunar day 5 through 11.

When the moon is 15 at Easter, it is 8 on Palm Sunday; and when the moon is 21 on that Palm Sunday before Easter, these are the seven lunar ages of that day, namely from lunar day 8 through 11 [text as supplied].

## Rules Concerning the Great Nineteen-Year Cycle, the Lunar Cycle, and the Great Cycle Computed by Years from the Beginning of the World

[Col. 1330B]

**CXVIII.** If you wish to know which year of the solar cycle it is—the cycle that returns into itself after twenty-eight years, with the twenty-ninth year beginning—and if you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, or even which year of the great cycle, which returns into itself when the 533rd year begins, or how many years have passed from the beginning of the world, and how many solar and nineteen-year cycles, leap-days, and great cycles there are, calculate eleven times 533.

Thus 500 years multiplied eleven times make 5,000. Likewise, 30 multiplied eleven times makes 330; together with the preceding number, 5,830. Likewise, 3 multiplied eleven times makes 33; added to the preceding number, the total is 5,863.

Thus in eleven great cycles there are 5,863 years; 126 remain. Concerning the number of years from the beginning of the world: the 126th year is now being completed in the twelfth great cycle.

Divide all these years by the solar and nineteen-year cycles, so that we may know how many solar and nineteen-year cycles there have been from the beginning of the world, and which year of the solar and nineteen-year cycles the present year is.

In one great cycle, which they say returns into itself when the 533rd year begins, there are 19 solar cycles and 28 nineteen-year cycles. For if you multiply 28 by 19, or 19 by 28, they produce 532.

In eleven great cycles there are 209 solar cycles: 10 multiplied eleven times make 110, and 9 multiplied eleven times, or 11 times 9, make 99; together, 209.

Likewise, in eleven great cycles there are 308 nineteen-year cycles: 20 multiplied eleven times make 220, and 8 multiplied eleven times, or 11 times 8, make 88; together, 308,

[Col. 1330D]

within which are 5,863 years.

In the remaining 126 years there are four solar cycles: 20 multiplied four times make 80, and 8 multiplied four times make 32; together, 112. Add these four solar cycles to the 209 mentioned above: the total is 213.

Thus there are 213 complete solar cycles from the beginning of the world, containing 5,575 years; 14 remain. The fourteenth year is the year of the solar cycle.

Likewise, in the remaining 126 years, divided by 19, there are six nineteen-year cycles beyond the eleven great cycles. For if you subtract 6 from 120, you have made six nineteen-year cycles; the six that you subtracted, together with the other six that remained beyond 120, make 12 [text supplied as “62”]. It is the twelfth year of the nineteen-year cycle.

This common year begins on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May and runs to the day before the Nones of April, containing 354 days.

Add the six nineteen-year cycles that you made from 120 to the 308 mentioned above: the total is 314. Thus there are 314 complete nineteen-year cycles from the beginning of the world, containing 5,977 years; 12 remain. The twelfth year of the nineteen-year cycle is therefore current, as we have said.

## The Number of Cycles, Leap-Days, and Saltus from the Beginning of the World

**CXIX.** How many nineteen-year cycles are there from the beginning of the world? There are 314; therefore there are 314 *saltus*, that is, 314.

There are 1,497 leap-days, containing four years and 37 days.

## The Nineteen-Year Cycle Begins, Which the Greeks Call the *Enneacaidecaeteris*

**CXX.** Established by the holy Fathers, in this cycle you will always find the fourteenth Paschal [moon] without any error, provided that you remember each year which lunar cycle and which nineteen-year cycle is current.

At present, in the consulship of the younger Probus, it is the third Indiction, the thirteenth nineteen-year cycle, and the tenth lunar [cycle]; it ends.

This cycle of Dionysius consists of five nineteen-year cycles, that is, 95 years. It begins with the thirty-second year of the Lord’s Incarnation and ends in the year 526. We have therefore passed over this cycle, because it has entirely elapsed.

## The Preface of Saint Felix, Abbot of Cyrillitana

**CXXI.** In the middle of the 194th Olympiad, that is, in the 42nd year of the reign of Octavian Augustus, our Lord Jesus Christ was born in the flesh.

From the Lord’s nativity to the 45th Olympiad, and from that point to the first year of Diocletian, there are 284 years. From the first year of Diocletian to the first cycle of Dionysius there are 248 years, making 532 years in all.

From this point Dionysius counts 532 years in his first cycle from the Lord’s Incarnation. For this cycle of Saint Cyril ended in the year 247. Add 1, which Dionysius begins, and you find 248 years, as stated above. It ends.

## The Prologue of Saint Chyllitanus Begins

Again, the discourse of Felix begins concerning Dionysius and concerning himself, in the name of Christ.

**CXXII.** Dionysius, once the most holy abbot of the City of Rome, learned in both languages, Greek and Latin, and endowed with elegant learning, previously composed, with ingenious skill, five nineteen-year cycles of Paschal computations. He took his beginning from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and, continuing the sequence of the aforesaid cycles, carried it from the tenth Indiction in the year 532 to the fourteenth Indiction in the year 626 of the Incarnation.

And since the fifth cycle of that distinguished man is now being completed, with ten years still remaining for its completion, our smallness has undertaken to compose five further nineteen-year cycles, following the pattern of the preceding cycles and arranged by rational calculation. We have established a fixed boundary, beginning with the fifteenth Indiction in the year 627 of the Incarnation and extending to the fourth Indiction in the year 721 of the Incarnation.

Therefore we have admonished the reader that, when the fifth cycle of the aforesaid venerable Dionysius has been completed, he should pass, as we have said, to our five subsequent cycles; and without any obscuring error he will be able, by reliable calculation, to find the Paschal days and moons in their proper order.

The five nineteen-year cycles of Chyllitanus are here completed, having been passed over because they have all elapsed.

The reason why the seventeenth moon begins in the year of the computation on the very day on which the preceding year ends, and not on the following day as in the case of the others, is that, because of the lunar *saltus* which they call [such], one might otherwise think that ten days belonged to the same year. Dionysius, while traversing and explaining this nineteen-year cycle, called it of this kind because the age of the first moon begins on the same day on which the age of the last year is brought to completion.

A lunar month has 29 and a half days, that is, twelve hours. But the computists join that half-day to the other month and make one day; therefore one month in the moon is said to have 29 days and another 30.

## On the Agreement of the Months

**CXXIII.** January agrees with December in the measure of hours. February completes an equal span with November. March corresponds with October. April equals September. May answers to August. June is equal to July.

## The Cycle of the Book of the Romans Begins, Which Was Found among the Romans Thirty Years before Christ’s Nativity

**CXXIV.** Within the fifth cycle, the lunar cycle is included, beginning in the fourth year of this cycle and ending in its third year.

This cycle properly belongs to the Romans and pertains to the month of January. For just as the year of the nineteen-year cycle, because of the legal observance of the Hebrews, begins with the Paschal month and ends there, so this cycle, by Roman institution, begins with the moon of the month of January and ends there.

As that cycle does, so this one has its first and second years common, its third embolismic, its fourth and fifth common, its sixth embolismic, its seventh common, and its eighth embolismic. Thus far there is an *Ogdoas*.

The *Endecas*, likewise, following the pattern of the nineteen-year lunar cycle, has seven common years and four embolismic years. A common year has twelve lunar months, that is, 354 days. An embolismic year has thirteen months, namely 384 days, except for the seventeenth year of this cycle, which is the first of the nineteen-year cycle, in which one of the days arising from the lunar *saltus* is omitted.

To make this clearer, let us examine the order and course of the individual years, and what Dionysius arranged in the Paschal month, let us arrange in January.

A solar year begins on the Kalends of January and has 365 days. A common year has 354 days. An embolismic year has 384 days and 13 months.

How many months have 31 days? Seven: January, March, May, July, August, October, and December. Likewise, there are four months with 30 days: April, June, September, and November. February has 28.

Equalize all the months so that each has 30 days; five intercalary days remain. Add these wherever necessary. Know this, however: if there is one day too many or too few, there is an obvious error.

## Concerning the Moon’s Age, for Those Unable to Calculate It

**CXXV.** If someone is so idle or dull that, without any labor of calculation, he wishes to know the moon’s course, let him rely on the Alphabets distributed in this annual booklet according to the lunar course. Three Alphabets contain two circuits of the moon, that is, 59 days.

Whatever letter the moon has once at a particular age, it continues to have that same letter, marked in the same way, throughout the year at that age—unless, perhaps, which nevertheless rarely happens, the calculation of the embolisms changes this.

For example, in the third year of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon, which will have 30 days, always begins at the letter A, is second at B, and third at C, likewise at the marked points, that is, with no point [text uncertain]. Thus, according to the order of its letter, it preserves each lunar age.

Likewise, the moon that will have the same 30 days, beginning from the letter marked I, is always second at M and third at N, with a similar figure; and so, recurring in order, it restores its age to each of its letters.

For the sake of descending [through the sequence], antiquity provided that the first of the three Alphabets should be marked with points and letters on both sides, the second beneath it, and the third should always be marked as the terminus [text uncertain].

## Likewise, Concerning the Moon’s Course, for Anyone Who Is Ignorant of It

**CXXVI.** If someone, still less capable of calculation, is nevertheless curious about the lunar circuit, we offer him this aid suited to his modest understanding, so that he may find everything.

We have divided the entire sequence of the annual circuit, which is contained in twelve months, by means of Alphabets, with the following arrangement: the first and second orders contain 27 days each, while the third contains one additional day, namely the day that increases from the eight surplus hours repeated in the third [order]. So that the letter would suffice to mark the day we intended, we did not add these [letters] to every individual day; therefore it was not necessary to use beyond the letter O.

We placed at the beginning of this work a regulating page that could contain nineteen such Alphabets, beginning from different letters, corresponding to the same number of years in the nineteen-year cycle, together with the names of the individual months and the twelve signs, arranged in the following order.

According to the number of days in which the moon completes the zodiac, it has 27 lines in length, with the names of the individual signs written above and the names of the months written below, so that someone unfamiliar with the signs may nevertheless find what he seeks from knowledge of the months.

It has nineteen lines in width, which, in the order of the nineteen-year cycle, display the year by the number written above.

When, in any year, you wish to know on what day the moon is in what sign or in what part of a month, first determine what letter is assigned to that day. Then return to the regulating page, where the mass of letters is arranged. Having immediately found the same year from the heading at the top, find the letter you were seeking for that day; then, beginning above and below, note which sign and which month are written opposite it.

Let us provide an example by which the reader may gain strength for the rest. You ask where the moon is—for example, on the Kalends of April in the sixth year of the nineteen-year cycle. Open the codex and look for the day of the Kalends just mentioned; you will find the letter E written above it.

Return to the regulating page. You will see the sixth year; examining its Alphabet, you will find the letter E. Turn your eyes to the sides: on one side you will discover the end of Gemini, and on the other the beginning of the month of June marked there. Whether you are a learned or a simple reader, you will rejoice to see openly that you have investigated what you desired. In that year mentioned above, on whatever days you see the letter E, whether the moon is waxing or waning, you will know that it is moving through these same regions of the sky.

## The Epistle on the Calculation of the Moon in the First Embolismic Year of the *Ogdoas* Begins

**CXXVII.** In the first embolismic year, that is, in the third [year] of the *ogdoas* [text uncertain], the epacts are 22. Therefore the moon is 27 on the Kalends of September and October, and 29 on the Kalends of November and December.

The moon that is 29 on the Kalends of December ends there; that is its own moon. But the second moon, which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of December and ends at 30 on the second day before the Kalends of January, belongs to the embolism.

The moon that is on the Kalends of January is the first moon and belongs to that month; you must likewise bring it to an end at 30. Thus you have found the first moon on the Kalends of January in the first embolismic year.

## Likewise, Concerning the Second Embolismic Year of the *Ogdoas*

**CXXVIII.** In the second embolismic year, that is, the sixth of the *ogdoas*, the epacts are 25. The moon on the Kalends of September is 30 and ends there, because it is the moon belonging to that month.

The moon that begins first on the fourth day before the Nones of September and ends at 30 on the Kalends of October is embolismic. The moon that begins first on the sixth day before the Nones of October and ends at 29 on the third day before the Kalends of November belongs to October.

On the Kalends of November and December the moon becomes 2; on the Kalends of January it becomes 4, as the order requires.

## Likewise, Concerning the Third Embolismic Year of the *Ogdoas*

**CXXIX.** In the third embolismic year, which is the final embolismic year of the *ogdoas*, the epacts are 17.

The moon is 22 on the Kalends of September and October; 24 on the Kalends of November and December; 26 on the Kalends of March; 27 on the Kalends of April and May; 29 on the Kalends of June and July; 1 on the Kalends of August; and 3 on the Kalends of September.

Why do we make one lunar age on the Kalends of April and on the Kalends of May, when this is nowhere otherwise required in the calculation? The reason is that the moon which is 27 on the Kalends of April is 28 on the fourth day before the Nones of April, 29 on the third day before the Nones of April, and 30 on the day before the Nones of April; it is embolismic and ends there.

The moon that begins on the Nones of April is the Paschal moon. It occurs at 14 on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May and ends at 29 on the fifth day before the Nones of May; this is the April moon.

The moon that begins at 1 on the fourth day before the Nones of May and ends at 30 on the fourth day before the Nones of June is the May moon. The moon that begins at 1 on the third day before the Nones of June and ends at 29 on the Kalends of July is the June moon. The moon that begins on the sixth day before the Nones of July and ends at 30 on the day before the Kalends of August is the July moon.

Afterward the moon becomes 1 on the Kalends of August and 3 on the Kalends of September, as the order requires.

For if you had not made one lunar age on the Kalends of April and on the Kalends of May, and if the embolismic moon that ends at 30 in April had ended at 29, then in that year at the Paschal limit, which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, you would have had not 14 but 15; and there would have been an error in Easter or in the lunar ages.

## Likewise, Concerning the First Embolismic Year of the *Endecas*

**CXXX.** In the first embolismic year of the *endecas* the epacts are 20. Therefore the moon is 25 on the Kalends of September and October, 27 on the Kalends of November and December, 29 on the Kalends of January, 1 on the Kalends of February, and 29 on the Kalends of March.

On the sixth day before the Nones of March it is 30, the March moon. The moon that begins on the fifth day before the Nones of March and ends at 30 on the Kalends of April is embolismic.

The moon that begins at 1 on the fourth day before the Nones of April belongs to April and ends at 29 on the day before the Kalends of May. The moon that occurs at 1 on the Kalends of May belongs to May. The remaining moons follow their order.

## Likewise, Concerning the Second Embolismic Year of the *Endecas*

**CXXXI.** In that year the epacts are 23. The moon is 28 on the Kalends of September and October, and 30 on the Kalends of November and December.

The moon that ends at 30 on the Kalends of November is the moon of November. The one that ends at 30 on the Kalends of December is embolismic.

The moon that begins at 1 on the fourth day before the Nones of December and ends at 29 on the third day before the Kalends of January belongs to December. On the Kalends of January it is 2, and on the Kalends of February 3. The remaining moons follow their order.

## Likewise, Concerning the Third Embolismic Year of the *Endecas*

**CXXXII.** The epacts in that year are 26. Nevertheless, you will not find the embolismic moon through these epacts unless you return to the epacts of the preceding common year. For in the preceding common year the epacts were 15.

Therefore the moon is 29 on the Kalends of August and ends there, because it is the moon belonging to that month. The moon that begins on the fourth day before the Nones of August and ends at 30 on the day before the Kalends of September is embolismic.

Thus on the Kalends of September and October, by the epact 26, the moon becomes 1. The remaining moons follow their order thereafter.

## Likewise, Concerning the Fourth Embolismic Year of the *Endecas*

**CXXXIII.** In the final embolismic year of the *endecas* the epacts are 18.

The moon is 23 on the Kalends of September and October; 25 on the Kalends of November and December; 27 on the Kalends of January; 28 on the Kalends of February; 27 on the Kalends of March; 28 on the Kalends of April and May; 30 on the Kalends of June; 1 on the Kalends of July; 2 on the Kalends of August; and 5 on the Kalends of September.

We therefore make one lunar age on the Kalends of April and on the Kalends of May, because the moon that is 28 on the Kalends of April is 29 on the fourth day before the Nones of April and 30 on the third day before the Nones of April; it is embolismic.

The moon that begins at 1 on the day before the Nones of April and extends to the sixth day before the Nones of May is the April moon, 29 in age. It is the Paschal moon and occurs at 14 on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Unless you had done this, the Paschal limit would have produced moon 15, and there would have been an error in Easter or in the lunar ages.

The moon that begins at 1 on the fifth day before the Nones of May and ends at 30 on the Kalends of June is the May moon. The moon that is 1 on the Kalends of July ends on the third day before the Kalends of August; it is the July moon, 30 in age.

The moon that is 2 on the Kalends of August now follows its proper order; it ends at 29 on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

Therefore the moon is 1 on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, 2 on the third day before the Kalends of September, and 3 on the day before the Kalends of September. But on the Kalends of September, according to the computation, it is not 4 but 5 because of the *saltus*.
