## On the course of the sun through the twelve signs

### CXXXV

The gifts of four days, in a certain manner, seemed to designate the primordial creation of the four days. Since light was created on the first day, on the first day it showed me the material of light. On the second day the Creator extended the beauty of the firmament between the waters and the waters. On the second day, among the gifts, I recognized that priestly garments demonstrated divisions between the bodies of the priests and of the people. On the third day the earth appeared with its ornaments. On the third day the most excellent kind of gold, which is extracted from the earth’s bosom, was brought before me. [Col. 1343B] On the fourth day the sun, the honor of the world, together with the stars, was set in the heavens. On the fourth day a bright and rounded object, resembling the sun, was brought to honor the table. It had twenty-seven semicircles, which, if doubled, would make fifty-four, corresponding to the hours of the lunar course through which the moon ordinarily travels through each sign. It had a round circle in the middle, because of the sun’s perpetual roundness, just as ten and a half hours ordinarily increase each month.

Therefore, in the first year after the leap year, the sun enters Aries at the beginning of the first hour of the night. After thirty days and ten and a half hours it leaves Aries—that is, at the eleventh hour of the night of the thirty-first day—and at the second point and the third point of the eleventh hour of that same night it enters Taurus. It remains there thirty days and ten and a half hours; [Col. 1343C] it leaves Taurus at the full ninth hour of the day. There you have one hour from four points in the two signs, making for the two signs sixty days and twenty-one hours.

At the tenth hour of the day it enters Gemini. It leaves Gemini at the full seventh hour of the night, and at two points of the eighth hour of the night; at the third point it enters Cancer. It leaves Cancer at the full sixth hour of the day. There you have the second hour and five points of the two signs. Thus Gemini and Cancer contain sixty days and twenty-one hours, and in these four signs you have forty-two hours and 120 days.

It enters Leo at the seventh hour of the day and leaves Leo at the fourth hour of the night, with two points of the tenth hour and the third point. At the fifth hour of the night it enters Virgo and leaves Virgo at the full third hour of the day. It has one hour from the four points of Leo and Virgo, and these two signs contain sixty [Col. 1343D] days and twenty-one hours.

Thus the six signs contain 182 days and sixty-three hours: that is, as I said, 182 days, and *tertius dies dimidius ex duodecim horis* [a damaged expression apparently counting two full days and a twelve-hour half-day], with three hours beyond the quarter-days.

The sun enters Libra at the fourth hour of the day and leaves Libra at the first hour of the day. At the second point of the second hour of the night it leaves Scorpio, at the full twelfth hour of the night. You have one hour from four points, and these two signs contain sixty days and twenty-one hours.

The sun enters Sagittarius at the first hour of the day and leaves Sagittarius at the full tenth hour of the day and two points. At the tenth hour it enters Capricorn at the third point of the eleventh hour of the day, and leaves Capricorn at the full ninth hour of the night. These two signs contain sixty days and twenty-one hours.

Add these to the signs written above [Col. 1344A], and you have 300 days and 105 hours.

The sun enters Aquarius at the tenth hour of the night and leaves Aquarius at the seventh hour of the day and the second point of the eighth hour. At the third point of the eighth hour of the day it enters Pisces and leaves Pisces at the full sixth hour of the night. These are the six hours that increase from the points of the individual signs, and these two signs contain sixty days and twenty-one hours.

Add these to the days and hours written above: the twelve signs total 360 days and 126 hours. Divide 120 hours by twenty-four, and there are five times twenty-four, that is, five days. Thus the whole year has 365 days and six hours, since you previously had 126 hours.

These six hours, accumulated over four years, make twenty-four hours, which is one day. The Latins call this a bis-sextile, or leap day. **[Col. 1344B]** If this day were not added in February in the fourth year, `*` the sun would enter Aries at the first hour of the night on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April. After 120 years, when it ought to have entered Aries, it would instead enter Taurus, unless thirty days were added to its course through leap years in those 120 years.

These and similar calculations are so pleasing in contemplation to those who understand them as the other philosophical arts are to one who speaks of and understands them. The philosophers were not the creators of these arts, but their discoverers. The Creator of all things established them in nature as he wished. Those who were wiser in the world were discoverers of these arts within the natures of things, as can easily be understood concerning the sun, moon, and stars.

For what else do we contemplate and admire in the sun, moon, and stars [Col. 1344C] except the wisdom of the Creator? Their natural course is maintained. Thus the patriarch Abraham understood and worshiped God the Creator through the principles of astrology, and for this reason he was called God’s friend; when tested in faith, he was found already strong.

For the Hebrews say that he came out of Ur of the Chaldeans—that is, from the fire of the Chaldeans—for the Chaldeans worshiped fire as a god. My teacher often used to say to me: “The wisest of human beings were those who discovered the arts within the natures of things.”

It is a great disgrace if we allow them to perish in our own days. But now the faint-heartedness of many does not care about the principles of things that the Creator established in nature. You know very well how sweet it is to engage in the principles of arithmetic, how necessary they are for understanding the divine Scriptures, and **[Col. 1344D]** how delightful is knowledge of the heavenly stars and their courses. Yet there are few who care to know such things. Worse still, they criticize those who study this knowledge, so that `*` their ignorance of the nature of things might have been blameless to them `*`, if they had devoted themselves to the divine Scriptures and labored in them, in which the knowledge of eternal life is contemplated. In this way they could have defended the Catholic faith truthfully and stood confidently against the enemies of Christ, through whom the devil’s cunning seeks in many ways to attack the Catholic faith.

These are the times of which blessed Paul foretold: “The Spirit clearly says that in the last times some will indeed depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience branded” [Col. 1345A].

### Another passage

If you wish to know how the solar course increases by ten and a half hours in each year’s months, multiply ten by ten: the result is 100, because one hour contains ten minutes. Ten times ten minutes makes 100 minutes. Assign three minutes to each of the thirty days: they make ninety minutes, leaving ten minutes. Add the five minutes that come from half an hour, and there are fifteen minutes. Divide these by thirty: thirty times half a minute makes fifteen minutes. Thus each day, over thirty days, increases by three minutes and half a minute.

### Another passage

**[Col. 1345B]** If you wish to know how much increases daily toward the leap day, divide five minutes by thirty: there are six times five; one-sixth of a minute increases each day, so that half an hour is completed in one month. Multiply this half hour by twelve, and the result is six hours. Multiply these by four: four times six makes twenty-four, the number of hours in one day. Over four years this increase makes a leap day, and the fourth year has 366 days.

The number six is highly significant in the circle of the year. For 360 makes six times sixty. The number sixty, if it is `*` perfect through ten, just as six is perfect through one—for one, two, and three make six, and six is a perfect number in its parts. Likewise sixty has a certain perfection when divided by the number ten. One ten, two tens, and three tens make sixty. For the value that the number six has in **[Col. 1345C]** the first series of numbers, so as to reach ten, the number sixty has in the second series, so as to reach 100.

Each of the days remaining beyond the 360 days in the individual months is one-sixth of each month. The six hours from which, in the fourth year, the sixth day increases have their perfection in the division of the number six, as we said shortly before. Likewise, the most just Creator made all the works of the primordial world in six days, so that it might be signified that in the perfection of the number six he made all things perfect in their natures. That same great, wondrous, perfect Creator is perfect in his own nature, and it pleased him to perfect all things in the perfection of the number six.

Therefore, on the sixth day the human being was created perfect in soul [Col. 1345D] and body, for whose sake all things were created, which are read to have been established in six days. Hence God himself, the Son of God, who is the power and wisdom of God, came into the world in the sixth age to save the human being whom he created on the sixth day.

Thus the number six has great significance both in the establishment of the primordial creatures and in the succession of the ages of the world, which proceeded in six ages; and in the fact that, in the sixth age, the Son of God came to restore the human race to the former dignity of its creation.

### Another passage

If almighty God arranged all things in weight, measure, and number, so that he even encompassed the multitude of the stars by their names and number, [Col. 1346A] how much more gloriously ordered is the course of that chief and greatest star, which surpasses all the stars alike in splendor and power?

Although much has been said and can be said subtly and magnificently about its subtle and magnificent course, scarcely anything is found that requires more labor in calculation when it is examined than what is distinguished concerning the leap day and the quarter-day. Although many distinguished men have already said and published many important things about this leap day, nevertheless, for the convenience of readers, or of those wishing to know its increases, I have decided to note briefly certain matters according to the small talent freely given to me by almighty God. I ask that readers receive them with the affection they show toward our humility.

[Col. 1346B] If, through Christ’s generosity, anyone finds something useful, let thanks be given with me to the giver of all good things. If anything is inept, let no one disdain to correct or amend it in the spirit of charity.

Although some things are ordinarily counted from greater to lesser and others from lesser to greater, as can be shown by many examples, nevertheless, since the aforesaid leap-day increments `*` proceed by growing from lesser to greater rather than from greater to lesser, and since we intend to examine their increase as subtly as our weakness can comprehend by reasoning, let us begin from the smallest, so that, with the Lord leading, we may reach the greater.

This, however, must not be passed over: in certain places the calculation can be conducted by equal divisions or collections, **[Col. 1346C]** either from lesser to greater or from greater to lesser, because no division can be made on account of the indivisible or imperceptible size of an atom.

It should also be recalled that, in certain names or numbers among those mentioned above, we follow authority, while in others we follow customary usage in this work, until someone grants us greater authority or demonstrates a better usage.

Thus, as some hold, 376 atoms make one ostentum. One ostentum and a half produce one momentum containing 564 atoms. Two momenta and two parts of one momentum produce one part containing 4 ostenta and 1,504 atoms.

One part and a half produce one minutum [Col. 1346D] containing 4 momenta, 6 ostenta, and 2,256 atoms.

Two minuta produce one punctum containing 4 parts, 8 momenta, 12 ostenta, and 4,512 atoms.

Five puncta complete one hour, consisting of 10 minuta, 15 parts, 40 momenta, 60 ostenta, and 22,560 atoms.

Twenty-four hours produce one day containing 120 puncta, 240 minuta, 360 parts, 960 momenta, 1,440 ostenta, and 541,440 atoms.

Thirty days produce one sign containing 720 [hours, implied by the numerical sequence], 3,600 puncta, 7,200 minuta, 10,800 parts, 28,800 momenta, 43,200 ostenta, and 16,243,200 atoms.

Twelve signs produce 360 days, 8,640 hours, 43,200 puncta, 86,400 minuta, 129,600 parts, 345,600 momenta, 518,400 ostenta, and 194,918,400 atoms.

**[Col. 1347A]** Five and a quarter days remain for the completion of the solar year. They contain 126 hours, 630 puncta, 1,260 minuta, 1,890 parts, 5,040 momenta, 7,560 ostenta, and 2,842,560 atoms.

If these individual numbers are considered with careful attention, they yield, as stated, five and a quarter days. The sum of these days and the quarter, in turn, arises because of the sun’s slowness through the signs.

### Another passage

You may ask how the first spiritual day can be said to be a creature, and how it had evening and morning.

The answer is that all knowledge of a creature, considered in itself, was evening; in God it was morning, because the creature itself is seen more fully in God than it is seen in itself. **[Col. 1347B]** A creature is seen more fully in the art by which it was made. Therefore the Evangelist John says: “What was made in him is life.”

Everything that was made, and has life in the Word of God, is life in him, but is not life in itself. Heaven, earth, and a stone do not have life, yet in God they are life. Therefore all the principles of creatures live in God without beginning and immutably. Accordingly, they are seen more fully in the holy angels in the Word of God, where they are life, than in themselves.

Thus [the first day signifies] knowledge of the firmament; the second, knowledge of the distinction between earth and sea; the third, knowledge of the sun, moon, and stars; the fourth, knowledge of reptiles; the fifth, knowledge of beasts of burden and wild animals; and the sixth, knowledge of the human being. The transmitted punctuation is defective at the transition to the sixth day.

These are not to be understood as solar days [Col. 1347C], but as the one day that we understand to be the spiritual creature—that is, the Gospel creature—whose knowledge was made six times. He made six days because of the perfection of the number six.

If you wish me to gather something for you from the Scriptures, attend willingly and prepare your whole self to listen.

One cannot be divided in numbers, for every number rises from one. Therefore two can be divided, and one is its part. Thus the division of two is into one. What does this number show here except the Trinity, which is God? Although there are three persons, they are believed in the unity of one nature.

The number four has two parts: its fourth is one, and its middle is two. One and two are three. Behold, its parts neither increase beyond it nor complete it; therefore it is an imperfect number.

**[Col. 1347D]** Five has only one part, namely its fifth, which is one.

The number six is perfect because it is completed by its parts. It has one, which is its sixth; two, which is its third; and three, which is its half. One, two, and three therefore make six.

For this reason God worked all creation in six days, according to the perfection of this number. These three parts of the number six demonstrate to us that the Trinity made the whole creation in number, measure, and weight.

We frequently find the primary importance of the perfection of the number six in the Holy Scriptures, especially in the Lord’s death, which is single. The death of our Lord Jesus Christ was not in the soul, but in the flesh alone. Our death, however, is not only in the flesh but also in the soul: in the soul because of sin, and **[Col. 1348A]** in the flesh because of the punishment of sin.

Since he had no sin in his soul, he died only in the flesh, and this because of the likeness of sinful flesh that he had drawn from Adam. The source then survives in a damaged sequence: “Therefore his single death benefited *de* `*` *plebe nostrae* [literally, ‘of/from our people,’ syntax corrupt], and his single resurrection benefited *duple nostra* [‘our double …,’ syntax corrupt]; the death of his flesh, and his resurrection; the death of our soul, and its resurrection; our two deaths and our two resurrections. Two and two are four; add the Lord’s one death and his one resurrection to our four, and they make six.”

Thus the Lord’s single element and our double element make three, and the number six has three parts, as we said above. The thirty-six hours during which the Lord was in the underworld also correspond to this single and double division of twelve. **[Col. 1348B]** Therefore twelve hours were daylight and twenty-four were night. Those twenty-four nocturnal hours correspond to our double death, while the twelve hours correspond to the Lord’s single death.

In truth, his nature has the number six. The Jews asserted in the Gospel that the temple had been built in forty-six years, and this is understood of the Lord’s body. The forty-six years are set in place of days: they say that an infant is formed in the womb in forty-six days and thereafter grows until the day of birth. For forty-six times six makes 276, which makes nine months and six days.

Count, then, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the Lord suffered and when he is also believed to have been conceived, up to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and you will find 276 days, a number established through six.

What else does the woman in the Gospel whom **[Col. 1348C]** Satan had bent over for eighteen years signify, whom the Lord healed, except that those years also possess the number six? Three times six, ten, and eight make eighteen.

That woman signifies the human race, which the Lord liberated from the captivity of the devil in the sixth age.

The first age is from Adam to Noah.  
The second age is from Noah to Abraham.  
The third age is from Abraham to David.  
The fourth age is from David to the Babylonian captivity.  
The fifth age is from the captivity to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.  
The sixth age, which is now taking place, continues until the Most High comes for judgment.

Thus in the sixth age of the world the human race is restored to the image of God.

The eighteen years clearly signify not only the six ages but also three periods: one before the Law, **[Col. 1348D]** another under the Law, and a third under grace.

Thus the year itself is contained in the number six. It has 365 days; six times sixty makes 360, leaving five and a quarter. Five days are a sixth of a month, but if you count the quarter also as a day, the whole makes six.

Behold, as far as God helps me, I have given an account of the perfection of the number six—not as much as I wished, but as much as I was able.

## On the moon through the twelve signs

### CXXXVI

The moon passes through each sign in two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour, according to its swifter course. Each sign has thirty parts.

If you wish to know how many hours the moon takes to traverse half a sign—that is, fifteen parts of any sign—**[Col. 1349A]** divide fifty-four and two-thirds hours, which are the hours of each sign, into two halves. You will have twenty-seven hours and one-third—one-third of an hour—for traversing half a sign, fifteen parts.

If you wish to know the interval in which it passes through one part of a sign, take away twenty-two hours from that amount. Assign fifteen hours, one hour to each part; twelve hours remain. Divide these twelve by the individual points, according to the damaged rule that “an hour from the moon `*` has five points”. Thus, if twelve is multiplied by five, it makes sixty points. Divide by fifteen: four times fifteen is sixty.

Assign four points to each part, and you will see that the moon passes through one part of a sign in the space of one hour and four points, with one-third of an hour remaining. This equals twenty ostenta, **[Col. 1349B]** since a full hour has sixty ostenta. Assign one ostentum to each part, and you will see that the moon traverses one part of a sign—which is one-thirtieth of a sign—in the space of one hour, four points, and one ostentum, which is one-third.

## On the moon’s leap over nineteen years, and how the night diminishes

### CXXXVII

If you wish to understand how day and night diminish over nineteen years, when the moon makes its leap, through momenta and atoms in each year and month, each year produces fifty momenta and a half—**[Col. 1349D]** [Note: Another hand has added this: “and a nineteenth part of half a momentum.”]

That half momentum consists of 282 atoms. **[Col. 1349C]** In each month there are four momenta and one-sixth of a momentum, namely twenty-four atoms. In the second month, four momenta and one-sixth of a momentum, twenty-four atoms. In the third month, four momenta and one-sixth of a momentum, twenty-four atoms. And likewise in each month.

Thus the twelve months leading to the moon’s leap amount in one year to fifty and a half momenta. From this momentum we make 282 atoms.

The fifty momenta themselves make one hour and a quarter of an hour, together with half a momentum, in the same number over nineteen years. For the moon’s leap, there are 960 momenta in nineteen years. These momenta make twenty-four hours, by which day and night are diminished over the nineteen years in which the moon makes its leap.

## On the bending of the fingers

### CXXXVIII

The bends of the fingers are made as follows.

**[Col. 1349D]** Begin with the first of the three fingers on the left, from the outermost. Bend it toward the middle joint of the palm; this signifies 1, 2, and 3. When you say 4, raise the outer finger.

When you say 5, raise in the same way the second finger from the outside. When you say 6, raise the finger slightly toward the middle of the palm, with the outer and middle fingers raised.

When you reach 7, place only the little finger, with the others raised, on the root of the palm. For 8, place the finger beside it toward the middle.

For 9, place the “shameless” finger opposite it. For 10, fix the nail of the index finger on the middle joint of the thumb. For 20, place the tip of the thumb at the middle joint between the index finger and the “shameless” finger. For 30, `*` [text uncertain: *in inmollis*] encircle the tip of the thumb and index finger. For 40, place the tip of the thumb beside the joint, in the middle of the side, `*` [text uncertain] from the back of the index finger. For 50, bend the thumb into the palm while the other fingers remain erect. **[Col. 1350A]** For 60, bend the thumb at the outer joint between that same joint and the nail of the index finger; `*` [text uncertain] rub around the middle joint of the index finger. For 70, encircle the front of the thumb, situated between the joint and the nail. For 80, with the thumb joint bent, circle around the root of the thumb across the middle joint of the index finger `*` [text uncertain]. For 90, extend the thumb lengthwise toward the tip of the index finger and encircle the nail of the index finger with it; raise the nail at the root of the thumb.

One hundred is made on the right hand as ten is on the left. Two hundred on the right as twenty on the left. Three hundred on the right as thirty on the left. Four hundred on the right as forty on the left. Five hundred on the right as fifty on the left. Six hundred on the right as sixty on the left. Seven hundred on the right as seventy on the left. Eight hundred on the right as eighty on the left. Nine hundred on the right as ninety on the left.

**[Col. 1350B]** In the same way the reckoning proceeds on the right from 1,000 up to 7,000, as the units proceed on the left from 1 through 9.

For 10,000, place the left palm above the head, turned backward. For 20,000, place it in the same position, palm downward, over the neck. For 30,000, in the same position, palm downward, on the middle of the chest. For 40,000, in the same position, palm downward, on the right side. For 50,000, place the thumb at the navel. For 60,000, place the left palm supine beneath the navel. For 70,000, in the same position, palm downward, at the groin. For 80,000, in the same position, on the left thigh. For 90,000, in the same position, palm downward, but outward.

The same is done with the right hand when you say 100,000.

When you say 1,000,000, place the two open palms toward the face, opposite one another and before the ears, with the fingers turned backward.

The three fingers of the left hand—the little finger, middle finger, and “shameless” finger—contain 1 through 9: 1, 2, 3, and so forth.

**[Col. 1350C]** The two fingers of the left hand—the index finger and thumb—contain up to 90: 10, 20, 30, and so forth.

Two fingers of the right hand always contain up to 900: the thumb and index finger—100, 200, 300, and so forth.

Three fingers of the right hand contain up to 9,000: the little finger, “shameless” finger, and middle finger—1,000, 2,000, 3,000, and so forth.

The left hand contains, by its parts, up to 90,000: 10,000, 20,000, 30,000, and so forth.

The right hand contains, by its joints, up to 900,000: 100,000, 200,000, 300,000, and so forth.

In the name of God begins the Paschal reckoning, and [that] of the other 318 bishops who [wrote] concerning the reckoning of the Paschal feast, and of the other wise men who pronounced authority. [The transmitted syntax is fragmentary.]

CXXXIX. When all the Apostles had departed from this world, various fasts were observed throughout the whole world, in each province of the churches. For all the Gauls, on whatever day the eighth day before the Kalends of April occurred, always celebrated Easter, saying: “What have we to do with calculating Easter with the Jews from the fourteenth day of the moon?” But just as the Lord’s birth is celebrated on whatever day the eighth day before the Kalends of January falls, so also on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when Christ’s Resurrection is handed down, we ought to keep Easter.

[Note: [Col. 1349D] Compare this with what Bede, Baronius under the year 198, and Labbe, volume I of the Councils, page 596, have concerning this council [Col. 1350D].]

The Easterners, however, as the statements of Eusebius of Caesarea relate, celebrated Easter on whatever day of March the fourteenth day of the moon was found. In Italy, some fasted for forty days, others for twenty, others for seven days, during which the whole world is contained; they considered it sufficient to fast for that period. Others fasted because the Lord had fasted for forty days, and others for forty hours.

When such a variety of observance existed in each province, and hence there was error among the priests—for those who held one correct faith differed among themselves in their fasts—then Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, chose to send an authoritative directive. For at that time the metropolitan see from which the regulation of Easter was to proceed was called not Jerusalem but Caesarea, so that Easter might be celebrated by all the catholic churches, according to right law, in the place where the Lord and Savior of the world had dwelt in the flesh.

Accordingly, after receiving the authority, Theophilus summoned to a council not only all the bishops of his own province but also bishops and learned men from various regions. When that multitude of priests and learned men, instructed in all the Scriptures, had been gathered together, the aforesaid bishop produced the authority sent to him by Pope Victor and showed what task had been assigned to him.

Then all the bishops said together: “We must first inquire how the world was made in the beginning; and when this has been investigated more carefully, the regulation of Easter may suitably be derived from it.”

Therefore the bishops said: “On what day do we believe the world was first made, if not on the Lord’s Day?”

Others said: “How, then, can you prove that the first day was the Lord’s Day?”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.”

The bishops replied: “According to the authority of Scripture, ‘There was evening and there was morning, one day,’ and the second, and the third, and the fourth, and the fifth, and the seventh. On this seventh day he rested from all his works, and he called that seventh day the Sabbath. Since the last day is therefore the Sabbath, what can the first day be except the Lord’s Day?”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Behold, it has been proved concerning the Lord’s Day that it is the first day. What do you think about the season? Four seasons of the world occur in the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Which season, then, do you believe was first made in the world?”

The bishops said: “Spring.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.”

They replied: “It is written: ‘Let the earth bring forth the herbage of grass according to its kind, and a fruit-bearing tree bearing fruit.’ We see these things taking place in spring.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Where do you believe the beginning of the world occurred: at the beginning of time, in the middle of time, or at the end?”

The bishops said: “At the equinox, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you say.”

They replied: “Scripture says that God made the light, and God called the light day; and God made the darkness, and he called the darkness night; and he divided the light and the darkness into equal parts.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Behold, you have proved the matter concerning the day and the season. What do you think about the moon? Was it created by the Lord waxing, full, or waning?”

The bishops replied: “Full.”

He said: “Prove what you say.”

The bishops replied: “Divine Scripture says: ‘God made two great lights and placed them in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light at the beginning of the night.’ It could not have been [otherwise] except full.” [The text is corrupt.]

We have now investigated how the world was made in the beginning: namely, on the Lord’s Day, in spring, at the equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, with the moon full. At that very time alone the days and the elements rise again.

Bishop Theophilus said: “Now, therefore, we must consider the regulation: how ought we to keep Easter?”

The bishops said: “Can the Lord’s Day be passed over, and Easter be celebrated on another day, when that day has been sanctified by so many and such great blessings?”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Speak more plainly, then: by what and by how many blessings do you assert that it was sanctified, so that we may write them down?”

The bishops replied: “Its first blessing is that on it the darkness was removed and the light appeared. Its second blessing is that the Israelite people were liberated from the land of Egypt, as from darkness, through the Red Sea, as through the fountain of baptism, from harsh servitude. Its third blessing is that on the same day heavenly food, manna, was given to human beings. Its fourth blessing is that Moses commanded the people: ‘Let the first day and the last day be observed for you.’

“Its fifth blessing is stated in Psalm 117, which is sung entirely concerning the Passion and Resurrection. Concerning the Passion it says: ‘Surrounding me, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them. They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns.’ And after intervening verses: ‘The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.’

“Concerning the Resurrection it says: ‘This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.’ And again, after intervening verses: ‘Establish the feast day with the multitudes, even to the horn of the altar.’

“Its sixth blessing is that on it the Lord rose again. We therefore see that he commanded the Lord’s Day to be kept specially for Easter.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Concerning the season, God commanded Moses: ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; celebrate Easter in it.’ He did not say ‘on the first day of the months,’ or ‘on the tenth,’ or on any other particular day, but sanctified the entire thirty-day period for Easter.”

The bishops replied: “Which are those thirty days?”

“We have already answered above that the beginning of the world was at the equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; and from the eighth day before the Kalends of April until the eighth day before the Kalends of May, we read that the days are to be consecrated.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Is it not impious that those three days of the Lord’s Passion should be excluded from outside the boundary of so great a sacramental mystery? For the Lord suffered from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the fifth feria, which we call the Lord’s Supper, because on that night he was handed over by the Jews, when he also reclined at table with the disciples and foretold to Judas that he would be betrayed by him. This is also known to have been fulfilled, and he rose again on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. How, then, can these three days be excluded beyond the boundary?”

The bishops said: “By no means should so great a sacramental mystery be excluded beyond the boundary; rather, these three days must be introduced into the Easter period.”

It was therefore established in that synod that Easter should be observed neither before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April nor after the seventh day before the Kalends of May, and that no one should have the freedom to cross the boundary established either before or afterward.

Likewise, the divine command concerning the moon must be observed: Moses commanded that it be observed from the fourteenth day of the moon through the twenty-first. These seven lunar days are therefore clearly consecrated. But because the Jews keep Easter from the fourteenth day of the moon, we must celebrate Easter from the fifteenth through the twenty-first.

Whenever, therefore, within that established boundary—from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the seventh day before the Kalends of May—the Lord’s Day occurs and one of those seven sanctified lunar days falls upon it, we are commanded to celebrate Easter.

Here begins the letter of Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

CXL. In ancient times the Church celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, whichever day it happened to fall on. But the holy Fathers prohibited this practice at the Council of Nicaea, establishing that it was necessary to determine not only the Paschal moon and month but also to observe the day of the Lord’s Resurrection. For this reason they extended Easter from the fifteenth day of the moon through the twenty-first, so that the Lord’s Day would not be omitted.

The word “Easter” is not Greek but Hebrew; nor is it derived from the Passion, which in Greek we call πάσχειν (*paschein*, “to suffer”), but from the Hebrew word *Pascha*, meaning “passing over,” because at that time God’s people passed out of Egypt. Hence in the Gospel it says: “When Jesus saw that the hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father.”

That night is therefore spent in vigil because of the coming of our King and God, so that the time of his Resurrection may find us not sleeping but keeping watch. There are two explanations of this night: either because in it he then received life when he suffered, or because afterward, at the hour when he rose again, he will come to judge.

We celebrate Easter in such a way that we recall not only Christ’s death and Resurrection but also consider the other things testified concerning him in relation to the meaning of the sacraments. For the beginning of new life, and because of the new man whom we are commanded to put on and the old man whom we are commanded to put off, we cleanse out the old leaven, so that we may be a new dough, because “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.”

Therefore, because of this newness of life, the first month of the new months was mystically assigned among the months of the year for the celebration of Easter.

That Easter is celebrated in the third week—that is, on whichever day occurs from the fifteenth through the twenty-first—signifies that, throughout the entire period of the world, which is governed by the number seven, this is now the third age in which this sacrament has appeared. The first age is before the law, the second under the law, and the third under grace. Here the sacrament, formerly hidden in enigmatic prophecy, is now manifest.

For this reason also, because of these three ages of the world, the Lord’s Resurrection lasts three days. But the fact that the Paschal day is sought during seven days, from the fifteenth day of the moon through the twenty-first, is because of the number seven in its universality. Hence the Apostle John writes in the Apocalypse to seven churches.

The Church, while still established in the mortality of the flesh, is signified in Scripture by the name of the moon, because of its mutability.

Various observances of opinion concerning the Paschal feast sometimes generate error. For the Latins seek the moon of the first month from the third day before the Nones of March through the third day before the Nones of April; and if the fifteenth day of the moon falls on the Lord’s Day, they defer Easter to another day.

The Greeks observe the moon of the first month from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the day of the Nones of April; and if the fifteenth day of the moon coincides with the Lord’s Day, they celebrate holy Easter.

Such disagreement therefore disturbs the Paschal rule between the two groups.

A common year is called one that has only twelve lunar months, that is, 354 days. It is called “common” because often two such years proceed in succession, joined to one another, and follow one another in the Paschal observance.

An embolismic year, however, always stands alone. An embolismic year is one that is shown to have thirteen lunar months, that is, 384 days. This is the year divinely revealed to holy Moses, in which those who lived farther away were commanded to celebrate Easter in the second month.

“Embolism” is a Greek word which is translated into Latin as *superaugmentum*, “additional increase,” because it completes the number of common years, which are observed to lack eleven lunar days.

Embolismic and common years are found as follows. If there are 384 days from the fifteenth day of the moon of the preceding Easter to the fourteenth day of the following moon, it is an embolismic year. If there are 354, it is a common year.

A bissextile year is one day added every four years. For each year a fourth part of the unit increases; when it has completed a full unit in the fourth year, it makes a bissextile year. It is called *bissextus* because twice six multiplied makes a full unit, which is one day; likewise, a quarter is so called because it is multiplied four times, producing the bissextile addition, which the sun makes above the ordinary course of days in the year.

From the seventh day before the Nones of March until the day before the Kalends of January, it is added twice in the course of the moon, and from that point it is subtracted.

Intercalary days are so called because they are inserted, so that the reckoning of the moon and sun may agree. *Calare* means “to place”; *intercalare*, “to insert.”

The Greeks call them *epacts*; the Latins call them annual lunar additions. They revolve within themselves from the number eleven up to thirty. The Egyptians add them for the reason that the reckoning of the lunar month may be made equal to that of the sun.

The moon is known to shine, according to its course, for twenty-nine and a half days. There are 354 lunar days in the year; eleven days remain in relation to the course of the solar year, and the Egyptians add these. Hence they are also called additions.

Without these additions you will not determine what day of the moon it is in any year, month, or day. These epacts are always found on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in whatever lunar phase occurs on that day.

They are contained within a nineteen-year cycle. But when they have reached nineteen, which is the nineteen-year cycle, in the following year you must no longer add eleven to twenty-nine so as to announce ten after the thirty have been removed; rather, return from there and announce eleven.

Here ends the letter of Saint Cyril.

CXLI. Letter of Bishop Paschasinus to the most blessed Pope Leo concerning the investigation of the Paschal reckoning. (Published by Bucherius and others.)

Concerning the names of the stars and the reasons why they received their names.

CXLII. The sun is called *Sol* because it alone appears, its radiance obscuring all the other stars.

The moon is called *Luna*, as though *Lucina*, with the middle syllable removed. Virgil says: “Chaste Lucina, favor me.” It received its name by derivation from the light of the sun, because it receives light from it and returns what it has received.

The stars are called *stellae* from *stare*, “to stand,” because they always stand fixed in heaven and do not fall. For the stars that we see sliding from heaven are not stars but little fires fallen through the air. They arise when the wind, seeking higher regions, draws the ethereal fire along with it; by its movement it imitates falling stars. Stars cannot fall, but, as stated above, are immovable and are carried fixed together with the heavens.

They are called *sidera* because sailors, observing them, direct their course by them, lest deceptive waves or winds carry them elsewhere.

Some stars are called signs because sailors observe them in guiding their oars, contemplating their arrangement and radiance; from these things the future condition of the sky is revealed. All people also attend to them in order to foresee the qualities of the air through summer and winter and the temperate season of spring. By their rising or setting, at fixed stations, they indicate the qualities of the seasons.

The first of the signs is the Bear, *Arcton*, which, fixed at the northern pole, revolves around itself. The name is Greek; in Latin it is called the Bear. Because it turns in the form of a wagon, our people called it the *Septentrion*. For *triones* properly means plow-oxen, from *terere*, “to wear away,” as though *teriones*. The proximity of the pole causes the *Septentriones* not to set, because they are located there.

*Arctophylax* is so called because it follows the same course as *Arcton*. They called it *Bootes* because it clings to the wagon; it is a sign worthy of observation because of its many stars. Among these is Arcturus.

Arcturus is a star placed behind the tail of the Great Bear in the sign of Bootes. Hence it is called Arcturus, ἄρκτου οὐρά, “the tail of the Bear,” because it is placed near the breast of Bootes. It rises in the autumn season.

Orion shines toward the south before the tracks of Taurus. He is called *Urion*, from *urina*, “urine,” that is, from the flooding of waters; for when he rises in winter, he disturbs the sea and lands with waters and storms.

The Latins call him *Jugula*, because he is armed like a sword and is terrible and exceedingly bright by the light of his stars. When he shines, all serenity is removed and darkened, and a storm is seen to threaten.

The Hyades are named from *Hyan*, that is, from sap and rains, for rains are called ὑετοί (*hyetoi*). By their rising they produce rains; hence the Latins also called them *Suculae*, “little sows,” because when they rise, signs of rain arise. Virgil says of them: “Arcturus and the rainy Hyades.” They are seven in the forehead of Taurus and rise in spring.

The Pleiades are named from their plurality, because the Greeks call plurality *to tylicton* [the text is corrupt]. They are seven stars before the gate of Taurus, of which six are visible, while one is hidden.

The Latins, and Virgil as well, name them from their indication of the season, which is spring, when they rise. For by their setting they show winter, and by their rising summer, as well as the season of the first navigation.

The Dog-Star is a summer star, also called Sirius. During the summer months it is in the middle of the center of heaven; and when the sun rises toward it, joined with the sun, its heat is doubled, bodies are dissolved, and they are vaporized. Hence those days are called the Dog-Days, when purgations are also troublesome.

It is called the Dog because it afflicts bodies with disease, or because of the whiteness of its flame, which is such that it appears to shine more brightly than the others. Therefore, so that they might recognize it more clearly, they called it *Syrion*.

A comet is called a star because it pours forth from itself a mane of light. When this kind of star appears, it signifies either pestilence, wars, or famine. In Latin a comet is called *crinitus*, “long-haired,” because it scatters flames in the form of hair. The Stoics say that there are more than thirty kinds, whose names and effects certain astrologers have written down.

Lucifer is so called because among all the stars it bears more light. It is one of the planets. Properly it is also called *jubar*, because it displays manes of light. The radiance of the sun, moon, and stars is likewise called *jubar*, because their rays extend in the form of a mane.

Vesperus is the western star, which they report was named after Vesper, king of Spain. It too is one of the five planetary stars, leading the night and following the sun. It is said that this star makes Lucifer in the east and Vesper in the west. Statius speaks of it: “And one hangs in alternating rising.”

The planets are stars fixed in heaven like the others, but they are carried through the air. They are called planets from the Greek ἀπό τοῦ πλάνου, *apo tou planou*, “from wandering”; for sometimes they move toward the south, sometimes toward the north, often against the world, and sometimes with the world.

Their names are Greek: Phaethon, Phaethonta, Phyrion, the harsh one, and Stilbon. The Romans consecrated them under the names of their gods, namely Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Venus, and Mercury. Deceived, and wishing to deceive others through flattery of those who had shown them something according to their desire, they observed the stars in heaven, saying: “That star belongs to Jupiter, and that one to Mercury.” Thus an opinion of vanity was conceived. The Devil confirmed this erroneous opinion; Christ overturned it.

Those signs which the pagans themselves call signs, in which the image of living creatures is formed from the stars—such as the Bear, Aries, Taurus, Libra, and other similar figures—were devised by those who observed the stars, moved by superstitious vanity, assigning them a bodily form and number of stars. They confirmed the names of the images from various stories concerning their gods.

They called Aries the first sign, to which, as to Libra, they assign the line of the world, because of Ammon-Jupiter [the passage is corrupt]. Those who make images of him fashion the horns of a ram on his head. The pagans placed this sign among the signs because they say that in the month of March, which is the beginning of the year, the sun makes its course through it.

They also place Taurus among the stars, likewise in honor of Jupiter, because, according to the fable, he was changed into a bull when he carried Europa across the sea.

They placed Castor and Pollux among the final signs after their death; this sign they call the Twins.

They also called it Cancer because, when the sun comes to that sign in June, it moves backward in the manner of a crab and makes the days shorter. This animal has an uncertain first part and directs its movement toward both sides, so that the front part becomes the rear and the rear the front.

In Greece, Hercules killed an enormous lion, and on account of his valor they placed it among the stars and the twelve signs. When the sun touches this sign, it gives excessive heat to the world and produces the annual winds, namely the Etesian winds.

They placed the sign of the Virgin among the stars because, during the same days in which the sun travels through it, the earth, exhausted by the sun’s heat, produces nothing. For this is the season of the Dog-Days.

They called Libra by that name because of the equality of the month itself, since on the eighth day before the Kalends of October the sun, traveling through that sign, produces the equinox. Hence Lucan says: “At the weight of the just balance.”

They also named Scorpio and Sagittarius from the flashes of the month itself. Sagittarius is a man deformed with horse’s legs, to whom they attach an arrow and bow, so that the lightning of that month may be indicated by it; hence he is called Sagittarius.

Here begins the letter of Dionysius Exiguus.

CXLIII. Dionysius Exiguus to his lords, most greatly to be revered, Boniface, First Secretary of the Notaries, and Bono, Second Secretary, etc. (Published by Bucherius in the Appendix.)

Here begins the letter of Saint Cyril, dated the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

CXLIV. To the venerable lords, holy brother bishops Aurelius and Valentinus, and also to the entire Holy Congregation, and so forth. (Published by Bucherius, page 72. In our codex it has this conclusion.)

“And I have presented all the authentic writings of the Council of Nicaea to the presbyter Innocent, so that he may bring them to you. Peace be with your spirit and mine in Christ Jesus. It is finished. Amen.”

Here begins the letter of Saint Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to the most blessed Pope Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, concerning the Paschal reckoning.

CXLV. “To my most beloved lord, brother, and fellow priest Leo, Proterius,” and so forth. (Published by Bucherius, p. 82.)

Here begins the letter of Morianus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the origin of Easter, on which others held differing views.

CXLVI. Concerning what is written, “After two days Easter will take place”: it was incongruous for the Easter of the Jews to occur at the equinox, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

At the equinox there was the final renewal of the world and redemption through Christ’s Cross, because at the equinox the world was constructed, and in its composition the two parts had been unequal to one another [the text is corrupt]. Then Adam’s length was made, and by the power of God, after three days had been made, the sun increased the course of the days when it shone upon the world on the fourth day; conversely, it diminished the course of the nights [the text is corrupt]. For Adam’s reverence and honor of the final equinox and of Christ’s Easter were signified, and the first construction of the world took place at the first equinox.

At the equinox likewise occurred the release and redemption of Israel from the servitude of the Jews. In the same equinox, after the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, he commanded the children of Israel to celebrate Easter, which in every respect is a type of Christ’s future Easter, from the beginning to the end.

For the lamb is a type of Christ: it was killed, and the Lamb is eaten daily by seven men, that is, by the seven grades of the Church.

Know only this ministry of God: [the text is corrupt] if the equinox should come to judgment, namely the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the sixth feria, with the moon fourteen days old, and the Resurrection with the moon sixteen days old after the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

This is the spring equinox, that is, the beginning of the solar year. Before this beginning Easter is not celebrated among the Hebrews, Greeks, or Latins except in error, because the Lord’s Day, on which light was made, did not occur before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, which is on the night of the second feria, according to the number of the Cross.

The twelfth day before the Kalends of April was the third feria, and the tenth day before the Kalends of April was the fourth feria, on which it was said: “After two days Easter will take place.”

Let it therefore be understood that “after two days Easter” means after the completion and integrity of the two Testaments, and the passage into the kingdom of God, corresponding to the sixth feria at the equinox, with the moon fourteen days old, and to the solemnity of the Resurrection on the Lord’s Day.

This is also the Easter of the whole human race, from which race the shoot went forth from the root of Jesse, which redeemed Israel from Egypt and was changed into a serpent, so that the Israelites might be delivered from Egypt.

What the serpent persuaded upon the human being—that is, death—the Devil did. If, therefore, death came from the serpent, then the rod became a serpent, and Christ became death. The serpent was lifted up in the wilderness in the air, so that it might heal bodily wounds for one looking upon the bronze [serpent; the text is corrupt].

As it loosed the servitude of the Israelites serving in Egypt, so also all [the text is corrupt] of Moses, from serpents and poisons, by looking upon the serpent—the great sacrament, namely to be healed by looking upon the serpent—[are healed]; unless I believe in the dead Christ, [I cannot] be healed from the death of sins.

And just as the people were delivered from Egypt by the rod changed into a serpent and by the lamb killed at Easter—that is, by Christ delivered into death—so the entire human race is delivered at the Easter of Christ’s Passion. He is the true serpent that kills the serpent, that is, the Devil, and devours the rods of the magicians, that is, of philosophers and servants of the Devil.

When Moses saw this, he was afraid and fled; so too, when Christ was put to death, the disciples were afraid and fled. “Take hold of the tail,” grasping the rear part, as in the saying: “You shall see my back parts.”

First the serpent was made, but when its tail was held, it was seen by Cephas, and afterward by the eleven [the text is corrupt]. There is also in the serpent’s tail the end of the world, because the mortality of the human race proceeds through the death inflicted by the Devil. But at the end of the world, just as we return from the tail to the hand of God, so we become the established kingdom of God.

After all this I shall say briefly that among the Hebrews Easter never occurs before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, because the moon is born on the eighth day before the Ides of March, is fourteen days old on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [the text is corrupt].

Observe, therefore, the lunar course according to the rule of the Greeks and the custom of the Egyptians, and not according to the epacts, that is, the lunar additions; for in the former one reaches from the fourth lunar day through the sixteenth, but in the latter to the fifteenth, according to the computation of Eusebius, who first wrote the nineteen-year cycle, of Athanasius, Theophilus, Cyril, and Dionysius Exiguus, until Victorius wrote to Hilary, pope and bishop of the city of Rome.

Then Alexandrian and Antiochene disputants began to describe cycles after the others.

These letters end in the name of God. Amen.

Here begins the preface to Bishop Patronius.

CXLVII. To the most blessed and greatly desired father, Bishop Patronius, Dionysius Exiguus, and so forth. (Published by Bucherius, page 485. Here, however, the following is read.)

“Since Saint Cyril began the first cycle from the 152nd year of Diocletian and ended the last in the forty-seventh year, we begin from the 248th year of the same [Diocletian],” and so forth.

In the name of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, concerning the beginning of the world.

CXLVIII. How was the world made at the beginning of God’s creation? On what day? During which days of the month? During which days of the week? In what year? In what season? Was it by day or by night, and at what hour? We ask.

It was created at the equinox, on the Lord’s Day, in a common year, in the Ogdoad, and at the first hour. Everything was made simultaneously by God in the twinkling of an eye, according to the Apostle, who says these words: “As he said, all things were made together.” Likewise, by the living God, at the Day of Judgment all things will be destroyed together and renewed into a better state.

Accordingly, by the proper sequence of the days which we mentioned above, their beginning and end are reckoned as follows. First, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April begins at the beginning of the Lord’s Day, as though half of that day had previously fallen on the Sabbath; it ends at the sixth hour of the Lord’s Day, but shortly afterward the tenth day before the Kalends of April followed.

Likewise, the second feria was completed at the sixth hour. From the tenth day before the Kalends of April until half of the third feria, beginning at the sixth hour of the second feria, it passed over. From the ninth day before the Kalends of April until half of the fourth feria it appeared, beginning before the sixth hour of the fifth feria; and on this day the sun shone.

At its beginning, and from the eighth day before the Kalends of April until half of the fifth feria, it remained, beginning earlier, from the sixth hour of the fourth feria. On the eighth day before the Kalends of April the moon was shown in the sky at the end of that day, at the age of fourteen days.

It should be understood why the sun’s dawn was made greater at the beginning of the world than it remains in these times: because before Adam’s sin the sun was more splendid, with the seven lamps that it possessed, and now only one part of those seven lamps remains because of Adam’s sin.

But no one could have endured it because of its heat, unless God had protected us with three heavens on its account.

To those who wish to know how the Hebrews say that the year has twelve months, we reply in this way: the Jews do not count according to the sun but according to the course of the moon.

They announce only that those who use twenty-nine and a half days count the age of the moon, with each year beginning from the fifteenth day of the moon of the first month through the fourteenth day of the moon of Easter, except, evidently, the first year, which we take care to count from the fifteenth day of the moon through the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month.

The beginnings of the months among the Egyptians are these: the fourth day before the Kalends of September, the fourth day before the Kalends of October, the fifth day before the Kalends of November, the fifth day before the Kalends of December, the fifth day before the Kalends of January, the seventh day before the Kalends of February, the fifth day before the Kalends of March, the sixth day before the Kalends of April, the sixth day before the Kalends of May, the seventh day before the Kalends of June, the seventh day before the Kalends of July, and the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

These are the intercalary days: the ninth day before the Kalends of September, the eighth day before the Kalends of September, the seventh day before the Kalends of September, the sixth day before the Kalends of September, and the fifth day before the Kalends of September. Among the Egyptians the intercalary days are gathered into one, because they do not have the [uncertain corrupt numerical reading: “300* … trecentesim 12 menses”] of one month according to the Sun. The Egyptians mentioned above complete the whole year, beginning with the fourth day before the Kalends of September and ending with the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

We should know how many divisions a month has, and how many there were among the Romans. The first matter is explained in this way. They are shown to have had four divisions: three months, and fourteen, and the tenth. Nevertheless, beginning with the months of March, April, and May, they completed their entire year in three months; and sometimes in four months, when June was joined to those three months mentioned above. Then, in the ten months, five were added to them—namely July, August, September, October, November, and December—and afterward, in the twelve months, January and February were added to all those we have just mentioned. Thus the solar year is completed through these twelve months.

But the wise men of the pagan peoples added January and February to the end of the year. Therefore, when we ask who these men were who first established the months among the Romans, the matter is explained as follows: Numa Pompilius and Zyngus, remarkable leaders, arranged the months among the Romans. Their individual names are found in the numbers of those months, because Numa Pompilius [uncertain reading: “added only July and August”], while Zyngus composed all the other months so that, through these months mentioned above, they might serve the commemoration of their idols. Therefore they were all made by the power of the Lord.

By what methods did the months receive their names among the Romans? They are said to have received them in four ways: from idols, from kings, and from numbers, as follows.

January received its name from the idol Janus, because in that month he taught the Romans to fulfill all his words, saying:

“Burn smoking wood, and oil stained for the devouring of my body; and with all your enemies lying behind you, because you see me dying, all of you, my friends, kindle it. And after I am about to die, build a temple in my name, to pray in it, and make my image with two kinds of faces, the face of a man and of a woman, so that men and women may worship me in this temple. Fit many doors into that temple, so that they may be opened against those who persecute you, and so that they may be unable to wage war against you on account of this.”

This is Janus with two faces, from whom January received its name. Alternatively, January received its name from *janua*, “door,” because it is the door of the year.

The month of February was named from washing, because *febrium* is interpreted as “bath,” since the bodies of the Luperci or Lupercal priests washed themselves from the uncleanness of winter; or because it is [named] from fever. Next, February is named on account of the coldness of that season.

March received its name from the idol Mars, because he had died in that month, and on account of this the month was worshiped among the pagans.

April is so called from “opening,” because the world opens its flowers in it, or because the sky, which had previously been covered with clouds, is opened to the eyes.

May was named either from the Romans’ *maiores*, “elders,” in wisdom, or from Maia, the mother of Mercury. Alternatively, it was named from the idol-god Majo, who is called Opiter because of the greatness of his power.

June was named from the Romans’ *iuniores*, “younger men,” in wisdom. Alternatively, it was named from Juno, who was the sister of Jupiter and daughter of Saturn.

July is named from Julius, king of the Romans, in honor of the king. His name was placed upon that month because he was the first to give a kingdom to the Romans. Numa Pompilius added these two months, July and August. Julius Caesar did so when the people yielded, because he seized the kingdom by force.

August was named from Augustus Octavian, the king. Augustus, interpreted as “standing solemnly,” [received the name] because he found the kingdom through peace.

September is so called because it is the seventh rain-month after March, which is the beginning of spring. In a similar order, October, November, and December received their names from the number of the rains and from spring.

The Kalends were so called from *kalendo*, or *colendo*, because they are the beginnings of the months among the pagans. Alternatively, they are so called from “calling,” which comes from the Greek verb *kalo*, interpreted as “I call.” Therefore the Kalends are named from calling, because on that day all the pagans were called to the great town to sacrifice, and it was announced to them who ought to make the offering.

The Kalends of the moon were initially called by this lunar name; that is, the first moon of the first month is called the Kalends of the months in the days.

The Nones are named from *nundinae*, “market days,” because markets were held on that day. Alternatively, they are so called because it is the ninth day before the Ides.

The Ides were initially named from “day,” in the middle of the month, so that its midpoint might be recognized. *Id* is derived from *day* by changing one letter, and *u* is changed to *e*, producing the name. Alternatively, it is Greek and is interpreted as “the heart of the months.” Its genitive is found in the name, as follows: *idus*, *iduum*, *idibus*.

It must be asked why a month is said to have four Nones, and six Nones, and why not ten days after the Ides, or seventeen, eighteen, or sixteen. This was done by the Roman emperors, lest other plotters should commit deceit on a single day [uncertain passage concerning] the day of an agreement, so that there might be uncertainty about the day of the agreement, without doubt as to when [uncertain] it would be given in the month. Thirty [days] is called the third [month?], [uncertain reading: “malioniensem aurem”].

In a month of thirty days, one day is called the fourth [uncertain passage]. The thirty-day months are separated by one day; the thirty-day months are said to be separated by two days, beginning with the day before the Kalends of January. April begins without doubt, apart from the bissextile year; but on the same day they begin if it is a bissextile year. On the fourth day February and March begin, counting from the day on which January begins. On the day from which the Kalends of January begin, May begins second, August third, and November fourth. These are the observations concerning the Kalends of the months.

## Here begins the letter of Pope Leo to the Emperor Marcian, through Darianus

### CXLIX

“Your faith, Most Pious Majesty, has become known throughout all the churches of Christ,” etc. (It was published by Bucherius, p. 78.)

## Concerning Easter

### CL

As though I were going to speak somewhat more fully about the greatest sacrament of our salvation, although it is not appropriate to discuss everything at this time, I first wish to show by what and how many arguments the Lord’s Passover is commanded to be observed.

In the first month, on the tenth day of the month, an unblemished year-old lamb is commanded to be set apart and kept until the nineteenth, and on the nineteenth day, toward evening, to be killed by the entire assembly of the children of Israel through Moses. When the true Lamb, the Lord himself, proceeds to the true Passover, wishing something of this to remain, he preserves certain things and, because he does not wish others to remain, changes them. For when he deigned to be sacrificed in the first month according to the command of the Law, he in no way permitted himself to reach the fourteenth day at the time of his Passion.

Nevertheless, the Gospel relates that he did certain things contrary to the figure. For when he was handed over by Judas to the Jews, he was not presented on the tenth day of the month; and when he deigned, while still alive, to give his disciples the sacraments of his body and blood, he is shown to have done this contrary to the figure.

That lamb, which in the Passover is commanded to be killed as a type of Christ, was roasted in fire with its head, feet, and entrails, and after its slaughter was to be consumed and eaten by the people. The Lord is understood to have done this for two reasonable causes, as it seems to me.

When he ate the Passover with his disciples, unless he had afterward changed the sacrifice, saying, “This is my body,” it would have been believed that it ought also afterward to be observed in that manner.

The other reason, as I think, was that when they saw the Lord’s body whole and containing his own blood within it before the Passion, they might believe that they were spiritually nourished by this body, and that even now we should believe the same.

We must also observe that the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, Christ who is our Passover, was not sacrificed on the fourteenth day toward evening, as the Law commands, but on the fifteenth day. Here it is evident that the Jewish feast, together with its sacrifice, was brought to an end by the Lord.

But what should we understand by the fact that the figurative lamb’s flesh was eaten first, and afterward he nourished his apostles with the food of his body, and that after the Jews’ typological Passover Christ was sacrificed as our Passover? This, as I think, signifies that reality should not precede the figure, but the figure reality: not first what is spiritual, but what is natural, and afterward what is spiritual.

Thus the beloved Bride, the universal Church of Christ the Bridegroom, elegantly anathematizes those who determine that the Paschal feast should be celebrated with the Jews on the fourteenth moon, and so forth.

Of this kind of shadowy observance he also deigned to observe only this much: that the Lord judged without any ambiguity that, in the first month after the fourteenth day, the Paschal feast should be celebrated on the day following one of the Sabbaths, although disagreement arose in the Church on this matter. Some believed it sufficient that they should not celebrate Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth moon. Others, however, firmly and cautiously observe this, so that they do not dare to celebrate the immolation of the true Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, before the fourteenth moon.

According to them, the legal command—which the Lord also, when coming to his Passion, in no way disregarded—says: “You shall keep him until the fourteenth,” which the Church now chiefly observes by following the authority of the Apostolic See.

But leaving these matters also, since it is not appropriate at this time to go through them individually, let us turn our minds to the spiritual understanding. We are commanded spiritually, on the fourteenth day of the first month of new things, to eat the Paschal flesh, so that, when the fruits of good works are born within you, and the words of the Decalogue have been completed by us in the perfection of the Gospel, standing four times in groups of three [uncertain passage concerning] our lamb in the evening of the world, when the end of the ages has arrived, we may eat [uncertain passage] with the Holy Spirit illuminating our night, not [with] hearts darkened. Finished.
