## Concerning the regular [reckoning of the] Year of the Lord and concerning the Indiction

### CLII

For the years of the Lord from the Incarnation, we add twelve regulars because, when our Lord Jesus Christ was born, three years of the Indiction then current had already passed and twelve remained. Therefore the authors established twelve regulars from these, in order to complete the number.

For the Indiction, we add three regulars because the three years that had passed in that Indiction established three regulars.

For the bissextile year, seek one, because when the Lord was born, the first year was after the bissextile year.

For the nineteen-year cycle, we add one regular, because when the Lord was born, one year of the nineteen-year cycle had preceded.

From the years of the Lord, we subtract two for the lunar cycle, because when the Lord was born, two years of that lunar cycle remained.

For the concurrent days, we add four regulars, because the solar cycle runs through four sevens, that is, twenty-eight years.

For the epact, we multiply by forty, because eleven remained from the solar year, and by those eleven we multiply the remaining epacts.

Here begin, in Christ’s name, the computations of the Greeks concerning the Egyptian Paschal cycles. Dionysius, the most holy abbot of the city of Rome, endowed with elegant knowledge of both languages, namely Greek and Latin, investigated and composed them. He wrote concerning the number of years from the beginning of the world or from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, explaining how one ought to find it, together with the other matters appended below.

[Col. 1363D]

[Col. 1364A]

### CLIII

If you wish to know the years from the beginning of the world, multiply fifteen by four hundred; the result is six thousand. Again multiply fifteen by twenty-one; the result is three hundred fifteen. Add the Indiction of the same year in which you are calculating—for example, that of the present year, which is three—and the total is 6,318. These are the years from the beginning of the world.

Remember this alone, diligent reader: as the years succeed one another, whenever you reach the fifteenth Indiction, multiply twenty-one by fifteen; then multiply twenty-two by fifteen; and after the fifteenth Indiction has been completed, always add one.

## Concerning the Indiction

[Col. 1364B]

If you wish to determine the Indiction from the years since the beginning of the world, take the years from the beginning of the world—for example, 6,318. Divide these into groups of fifteen, because the Indiction runs through fifteen years, as follows.

First subtract 15,400; the result is 6,000. Three hundred eighteen remain. Again, twenty times fifteen makes 300. Likewise, fifteen once makes fifteen; three remain. The total Indiction is [three]. If nothing remains, it is the fifteenth.

## Concerning the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ

If you wish to know which year it is from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, calculate fifteen times fifty-four; the result is 810. Always add twelve regulars to this. The authors added twelve regulars to the years of the Lord because, when the Incarnation took place, twelve years of that Indiction remained.

They are called regulars because they appear to regulate the number of the years of the Lord. Therefore, after twelve have been added to the number stated above, the result is 521 [uncertain numerical reading]. Add the Indiction of whatever year you wish—for example, six—and the total is 827. These are the years of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Remember this alone, diligent reader: as the years succeed one another, whenever you reach the fifteenth Indiction, if you multiply fifty-four by fifteen, and then multiply fifty-five by fifteen, after the fifteenth Indiction has been completed always add one. When these have been added to the twelve regulars written above, you will complete the number of the years of the Lord. Nothing remains that can be added by twelve, as remains in the other Indictions: in the first Indiction, one; in the second, two; in the third, three; and so up to fourteen—however great the Indiction is, that much remains from the calculation written above.

But in the fifteenth Indiction, if you multiply the higher total, namely fifty-four or fifty-five, by fifteen, always add one. By this computation you will arrive at the years of the Lord.

## Another method concerning the years of the Lord

If you wish to find the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, multiply fifteen by forty; the result is 600, and fifteen by thirteen; the result is 795. Always add twelve regulars to the number stated above, and add the Indiction of the same year, three; the total is 810. These are the years of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Remember this alone, diligent reader: as the years succeed one another, whenever you reach the fifteenth Indiction, if you multiply thirteen by fifteen, and then multiply fourteen by fifteen, after the fifteenth Indiction always add one.

## Concerning the Indiction

[Col. 1365A]

If you wish to know which Indiction the present year has, take the years of the Lord, whatever they may be—for example, 810. Always add three regulars to these. The authors placed three regulars for the Indiction because it was the third Indiction when the Incarnation took place.

After three have therefore been added to the number stated above, the years of the Lord become 813. Divide these into groups of fifteen, because the cycle of the Indictions runs through fifteen years. Thus fifty groups of fifteen make 750. Again, four groups of fifteen make 60; three remain. The third Indiction is that of the present year. If nothing remains, it is the fifteenth Indiction.

## Concerning the nineteen-year cycle

### CLIV

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years of the Lord, whatever they may be—for example, 810—and always add one regular, because when the Incarnation took place, one year of the nineteen-year cycle had preceded.

After one has therefore been added to the years of the Lord, the result is 811. Divide these into groups of nineteen, because the nineteen-year cycle runs through nineteen years. Forty groups of nineteen make 760. Again, twice nineteen makes 38; thirteen remain. The thirteenth cycle is the nineteen-year cycle of the present year. If nothing remains, it is the nineteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle.

## Concerning the lunar epacts

### CLV

If you wish to know how many epacts there are—that is, lunar additions—take the years of the Lord, whatever they may be—for example, 810—and divide them into groups of nineteen, because the lunar cycle runs through nineteen years.

Forty groups of nineteen make 760. Again, twice nineteen makes 38; twelve remain. Multiply these by eleven; the result is 132. Divide these again into groups of thirty. Four groups of thirty make 120; twelve remain. The twelfth epact is the lunar addition.

## Concerning the lunar cycle

If you wish to know which lunar cycle is contained within the nineteen-year cycle, hold the years of the Lord in your hand, whatever they may be—for example, 810. Always subtract two from these, because when the Incarnation took place, two years of that lunar cycle remained.

After two have therefore been subtracted, 808 remain. Divide these into groups of nineteen, because the lunar cycle returns to itself after nineteen years. Forty groups of nineteen make 760. Again, twice nineteen makes 38; ten remain. The text then says: “the ninth [year] of the moon is [that] of the nineteen-year cycle” [an apparent inconsistency in the supplied calculation]. Whenever nothing remains, it is the nineteenth.

## Concerning the concurrent days

If you wish to know the solar additions—that is, the concurrent days of the week—take the years of the Lord, whatever they may be—for example, 810—and always add a fourth of the years of the Lord. This is 202, making 1,012 in all.

Always add four regulars to these. The entire total is 1,016. Divide this by seven, because the solar cycle runs through twenty-eight years. Seven times one hundred makes 700. Again, seven times forty makes 280. Likewise, seven times five makes 35; one remains. Such are the concurrent days of the week, which arise from the course of the Sun.

## Concerning the bissextile year

If you wish to know whether a year is bissextile or the year of preparation for the bissextile year, take the years of the Lord, whatever they may be—for example, 810. Divide these into quarters.

If four alone remain, it is a bissextile year, because it occurs after four years have been completed. One hundred groups of four make 400. Again, ninety groups of four make 360. Again, ten groups of four make 40. Again, two groups of four make 8; two remain. It is the second year of preparation for the bissextile year.

If three remain, it will be the third year of preparation for the bissextile year. If nothing remains—that is, if the entire number is divisible evenly into groups of four—it will be a bissextile year.

So that perhaps no obscurity of error may arise for you throughout the entire calculation that you perform, if nothing remains above, you will know that the divisor itself is the result: for example, if you divide by nineteen and nothing remains, you will know that it is nineteen; if you divide by fifteen, fifteen; if by seven, seven; if by four, four.

## Another account of the bissextile year

If you wish to know about the bissextile year, take the years of the solar cycle, whatever they may be in the present year. For example, it is the fourteenth year of the solar cycle. Always omit one; thirteen remain. Divide by four. Omit twelve, because four times three is twelve; one remains. It is the first year of preparation for the bissextile year. If nothing remains, it will be bissextile.

The nineteen-year cycles of Cyril and Dionysius follow, beginning in the year 798 and ending in 987.

## Concerning the Paschal cycle

### CLVI

The Paschal cycle was established by Bishop Hippolytus in the time of the Emperor Alexander, etc. (It was published by Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 17.)

## Here begins the treatise of Saint Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, concerning the calculation of Easter

“This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year for you,” etc.

(I formerly sent this little work to the distinguished Bernard de Montfaucon, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, who also published it in volume II, p. 741, of the works of Saint Athanasius edited by him; for this reason I have thought it should be omitted here.)

Here begins the eighty-four-year cycle, which is calculated from the day of the Kalends of January, during the consulship of Festus and Gallus (that is, the year 298), is completed under the consuls Siagrius and Antoninus (that is, the year 382), and returns to its beginning under the consuls Merobaldus and Saturninus (that is, the year 383); and for the third time returns to its beginning under the consuls Posaeus and John, men of consular rank (that is, the year 467).

[Note: [Col. 1365D] The distinguished reader should consult the excellent *Dissertation on the Paschal Cycle of the Latins*, published by the late Henry Noris, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, who elucidated these matters at greater length.]

It returns again to its beginning. Finished.

[Col. 1369A]

Let no one, certainly, be disturbed because the fifth year of the cycle has the designated day of Easter, namely the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, on a Sunday with the sixteenth moon. This is to be done only once in eighty-four years, for the following reason: the violence of the moon, or the law of Easter, forbids anyone presumptuously to judge that Easter should be celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, on which day the moon will be twenty-three and more than a half.

Especially since the law has taken care that no one exceed the established measure of the moon and incur serious offense, it is preferable that Easter be celebrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, where there is a light reproach, rather than under the mark of a crime, as is also contained in the old table.

It was also necessary that there be some years in which a double Easter occurs, or two [Easters] come together as one. Since only one is to be observed, it will be at the discretion of the supreme Priest, in consultation with the presbyters, to determine which day ought to be chosen, provided that we all, unanimously meeting together, celebrate that day as Easter.

The treatise concerning the calculation of Easter, that is, concerning the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, is finished.

Among Victorinus’s commentaries we also find the following, among many other writings. We found in the parchment manuscripts of Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, that he copied with his own hand from exemplars of the Apostles the following:

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, under the consuls Sulpicius and Camerinus. He was baptized on the eighth day before the Ides of January, under the consuls Valerianus and Asiaticus. He suffered on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, under the third consulship of Nero and the consulship of Valerius Messala. He rose again on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, under the consuls written above. He ascended into heaven on the fifth day before the Nones of May, after forty days, under the consuls written above.

John the Baptist was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of July and was circumcised on the Kalends of July. The angel spoke to Mary on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, saying that Elizabeth was already in the sixth month of her conception [uncertain reading]. From this it is calculated that the Lord was conceived on the same day on which he also rose again. Amen.

## Isidore to the Lord and his son Sisebutus

“While you are outstanding in talent and eloquence,” etc. (This little work was published among the works of Saint Isidore of Seville under the title *On the Nature of Things*.)

## Here begin the verses

The solar year is contained

In four seasons,

And afterward is completed

By twelve months.

It runs through fifty

And two weeks,

With one day added,

And six equal hours.

With three hundred sixty

And five days,

[Col. 1370A]

Thus it traverses the circuit of the Zodiac

By its movements,

Except for the fourth part

Of night and day,

Which is seen to remain

The calculators decreed

That it should be gathered as the bissextile year.

Such honor was given to it

From the royal height,

That it was so named

From Julius Caesar.

It was to be placed at the end of the year,

When Gaius [uncertain passage]

Had determined [uncertain]

By repeating five days,

How short February is.

Hence the years of the moon

Differ in length,

Of which the embolismic years

Certain ones become common;

For the short year, which is called

Common in lunar reckoning,

Is always completed

In twelve months,

With three hundred fifty

And twice two days.

This year runs through

Eleven movements of the Sun;

[Col. 1370C]

The long embolismic year,

It is gathered from

This long lunar year,

In its number of days,

Eighty-four.

With nine embolisms

And likewise ten days,

It is seen to surpass

The solar year in its courses.

The whole year of the shorter [uncertain]

Is completed in cycles

Of three hundred fifty

[Col. 1370D]

And four days.

[Col. 1371A]

For this cycle, as calculation

Thus, at a moment multiplied fourfold,

[Col. 1371B]

The course [uncertain] always monthly,

And a fraction of the twelfth hour

The individual cycles

By a number of two hundred,

Together with their total.

The leap of the moon grows beyond this

By its most subtle course,

In the two-hundred-fifth month,

When these are multiplied fourfold,

They produce a total

[Col. 1371C]

Of nine hundred forty

Moments altogether.

By these all the points are made:

Six times nineteen,

Of nine hundred

And ten moments,

Have an equal weight of divisions.

Dionysius, attentive,

[Col. 1372A]

Handed down the cycle to us,

# HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF THE BODY OF SAINT CORNELIUS, POPE, AT COMPIÈGNE

(Lebeuf, *Collection of Various Writings Serving to Clarify the History of France; Historical Monuments Concerning Charlemagne and Charles the Bald.*)

## NOTICE

[Col. 1371C]

I was not among the last to express contempt for du Saussay’s Gallican Martyrology. Many years ago I learned from the late M. Chastelain, canon of Paris, what regard ought to be paid to it. It is unnecessary to recall here the judgment others had formed of it before him. André du Saussay indiscriminately wrote down whatever came to him, good or bad, and always without citing his authorities or making known the sources from which he drew what he said. This manner of writing prejudiced readers against him, and with sufficient reason. Nevertheless, I would not on that account bring a suit against him concerning every article of his work in general.

Here is one concerning which he must have had some records, and which proves that even in the least accurate books one may find something useful. It concerns Saint Cornelius, patron of the abbey of Compiègne. Baillet, who can scarcely bring himself to pardon du Saussay, observes that this hagiologist marks the translation of the body of this holy pope to Compiègne on 4 March, and says that it was transported directly from Rome and placed beside Saint Cyprian by the Emperor Charles the Bald. The same Baillet, after attributing all this to du Saussay, immediately adds: “Although there is no proof of it.”

It is unfortunate that these proofs, which are not entirely lost, were not known to Father Mabillon. He had every reason to mention them in the third volume of the annals of his order, had he known of them. He contents himself with citing Helinand and Alberic concerning a translation of this saint made in 1073, without saying where it was made.

He also tells us that in the library of Steinwchius, volume II, one reads that the *R. Cives apostolorum* was composed on the occasion of the reception of the bodies of Saint Cornelius and Saint Cyprian at Compiègne. Far from clarifying the matter, all these circumstances seem to me to confuse it further. For the translation of Saint Cornelius’s body certainly belongs to the ninth century, not the eleventh; and his body was received alone, not together with that of Saint Cyprian.

It is true that I have seen a chronicle composed in the fourteenth century in which I read nearly the same things as in Steinwchius. It attributes this circumstance to Charles the Bald:

“Here he placed the relics of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian; and at their arrival he composed the responsory which the Church sings: *Citizens of the apostles*.”

But I do not believe this event authentic enough to deserve consideration. And in the collection of the deeds of Charlemagne by the monk of Saint Gall, I find another origin for this responsory.

[Note: [Col. 1373D] He says that this chant was composed by the Romans when Pepin, after defeating the Lombards, went to Rome out of devotion, and that it was sung at his arrival. M. Servin reports the matter in this way in his pleading against the bishop of Angers concerning the Angevin Breviary (in quarto, p. 25).]

To support the view held at Compiègne that they possess the body of Saint Cornelius through the generosity of Charles the Bald, I shall not cite an author who was entirely contemporary, but shall produce a writer who had known people who witnessed its reception. I draw from his own words the proof that he lived shortly afterward.

“And, as it is recognized to have been reported by the mouths of certain of our own people then present, namely of the bishops themselves who were carrying [it], it seemed to them that they bore a most light burden, as though the casket in which the bones of the blessed pope were carried remained wholly empty.”

The writer is speaking here of the ease with which the bishops carried the shrine. He tells us that Charles the Bald brought these holy relics from Rome when he returned from there with the title of emperor; that people went as far as three thousand paces to meet the body; that it was there that the bishops began to carry it; that three blind men recovered their sight, three deaf men their hearing, three mute men the use of their tongues, and many paralytics their healing, at a place where, in memory of this, a great cross had been erected.

[Note: [Col. 1374D] Could this be the place now called the Cross of Saint-Ouen?]

He also tells us that on this occasion the emperor founded clergy under the title of Saint Cornelius, making them equal to those of Notre-Dame, which was the former title he had given to the church of Compiègne built through his care; that he filled this church with gifts, such as vessels and other furnishings; and that the French officers imitated him.

Although the author was very close in time to this event, he nevertheless says that since that famous ceremony the church had been burned twice. He also records that the holy body had been deposited in the crypts of this church.

The most singular feature of this writer’s style is that, although he writes in prose, his style is filled with rhymes occurring at every division of the periods, which often makes it unintelligible.

[Note: [Col. 1374D] The end of the Life of Saint Chaffre, Theofridus, in Father Mabillon is in the same style. *Sac. III. Bened.*, vol. I, p. 481.]

Since in his time the prosodic meter was greatly valued as a way of transmitting events to posterity, he suddenly undertakes, after his prose narrative, to celebrate his saint in a kind of verse that seems to come from another hand. As a supplement to the narrative, he adds that twenty thousand people were present at the ceremony; that the church was adorned with silk carpets and crowns of gold and silver; that the relics were deposited in a tomb; and that countless miracles took place there.

He says a word about barbarians numbering ten thousand—apparently Normans—who set fire to the church with the intention of burning it, and who actually burned the king’s palace and the clergy’s cloister. He adds that they were afterward killed in great numbers by the Christians, none of whom perished because of the saint’s assistance.

Neither the historian nor the poet says a single word about the relics of Saint Cyprian. This shows that his body was not brought together with that of Saint Cornelius, and that one should not be surprised to see, at the Council of Reims in the year 1049, a shrine bearing only the name of this holy pope, without any mention of Saint Cyprian.

[Col. 1374C] M. Baillet was not wrong to ask for evidence concerning traditions such as these; but it does not always follow that no such evidence existed merely because that historian did not know it. M. Baillet was not a scrutinizer of manuscripts. I found the manuscript from which I have just made this extract among those belonging to M. Loisel of Beauvais, which later came into the possession of M. Joly, cantor of the church of Paris, and which he bequeathed to that church. I am surprised that this learned man, who communicated so many others to Dom Mabillon, did not also inform him of this one. I do not publish it in its entirety, because several passages have been damaged by the passage of time and are illegible, while others contain only rather useless moral reflections. Nevertheless, I shall try to give it as accurately as possible, because it concerns an important event in the life of Charles the Bald, and nothing concerning the history [Col. 1374D] of our kings of the second dynasty—still full of obscurities and difficulties—should be neglected. The city of Compiègne may well be grateful to me for bringing from darkness a monument that sheds light on the beginnings of the celebrated church of Saint-Corneille. It is always honorable to contribute to the distinction of a city which our glorious monarch so often honors with his presence and which he takes such pleasure in embellishing in every way.

# History of the Translation of the Body of Saint Cornelius the Pope to Compiègne

[Col. 1375]

[Col. 1375A] It is worthwhile and sufficiently beneficial for all who trust in the merits of the blessed pope Cornelius not to be ignorant of the circumstances of his glorious translation, so that, knowing the place of that archimandrite where his holy bones rest, and abandoning every labyrinthine error, they may be able to seek his intercession more swiftly in body and soul.

Let the Christian brotherhood spread throughout the world therefore know how the lord Charles, son of Louis, called the third Charles by that magnanimous Charles, and the fifth in descent, who at that time rejoiced in the government both of Rome and of France, having, with Christ as his leader, cut to pieces the banners of his enemies, began diligently to search through every region of the Frankish realm, examining its places one after another, so that he might fittingly build and found, in honor of Christ’s name, a basilica as a result of the victory that divine mercy had granted him over the enemy. His excellent and good-hearted desire was mercifully disclosed and suggested by that illustrious Eye which, looking down from on high, could not, cannot, and never could be deceived, so that he might complete whatever pertained to the service of God according to his wish.

For while the aforesaid emperor, like another Solomon, inflamed by the fire of heavenly love, was traveling with his entire army through the open and wooded regions of various parts of France in order to lay the foundations of the divine temple, it happened—not by chance but at the prompting of heavenly providence—that he swiftly entered a certain forest. If, brother, you ask the name of that forest, know that, according to the ancient account of our fathers, it was called [Note: [Col. 1375D] Here the copyist omitted the proper name of the forest, perhaps because the author himself intended to paint it in vermilion and later forgot to do so.]. [lacuna]

[Col. 1375C] The emperor, seeing the lodging-place of the aforesaid forest—like a second paradise, wonderfully planted with trees of various kinds, suitable both for fishing and for healthfully restraining the burning plague of fire, and abundantly watered by streams—immediately perceived, under the inspiration of heavenly mercy, that Christ wished a dwelling to be built for him there. When he had discovered that the place was divinely suitable for the construction of a tabernacle to God, and the entire army of the Franks had been gathered together in one imperial formation at his command, Charles began to ask his men for advice about establishing a church in that place, being inwardly stripped of spiritual vices in mind and outwardly shorn of bodily hair on his forehead [Note: [Col. 1375D] The shaving of the forehead should be noted in this circumstance.]. Strengthened by the assent and good-will of them all in this salutary decision, the emperor ordered that, after all sharp thorn-bushes and forest shoots had been removed and uprooted, a wholesome asylum should be built under the praise of Christ’s name—that is, a healing refuge for all believers.

For it was rightly and carefully arranged [Col. 1376A] that, after the burdocks, hawthorns, and thistles had been removed, the walls of a church should be erected in such a place that from that time forward, for those who sought it with devout hearts and knocked at Christ’s ears with sound minds, the sharpest force of material thorns would be broken, while the stains of human sins would be blotted out by heavenly mercy.

There was much that we could say about the construction of this church, built with wonderful stonework; but because we are not deprived of its presence, reason forbids us to divide our account of it into many parts. Yet it would be most unworthy to conceal how the devout father Charles, who shone conspicuously in the world like a heavenly star, [Col. 1376B] after the royal hall had been raised on shining golden vaults to the summit of the highest height, richly adorned with a hundred clerics and endowed with the gifts of many different possessions, began to be anxious and concerned, not knowing with what relics of the saints he could more attentively adorn this, so to speak, heavenly Jerusalem.

While these and similar thoughts were turning over in the emperor’s mind, divine mercy recalled to him that, by the grace of God, he possessed authority over almost the whole world. Therefore he need not become excessively troubled in his innermost mind by pondering such matters, since from whatever part of the world he wished, without any human opposition, he would be able to take what he could use to adorn and enrich the basilica already mentioned. Refreshed by this secret and divine counsel [Col. 1376C], he assembled the entire Frankish army once more and said that, with a desire more ardent than usual, he wished to go to Rome [Note: [Col. 1376D] The Bertinian Annals state that Charles was invited by the supreme pontiff, that he arrived there on 15 December, and that he was crowned there.].

Without delay, every distinguished soldier of the Frankish armies, daring in no respect to oppose the imperial commands, hastened as best he could to acquire the equipment for so great an expedition, so that when the emperor Charles ordered the camp to move, no delay would hinder the royal wagons as they hurried eagerly toward Italy. And so it happened: the emperor hastened to Rome with loosened reins, and, with Christ’s help, fulfilled the holy desire that he had long cherished in his mind, bringing from there the body of the most blessed pope Cornelius and joyfully conveying it, rejoicing in body and soul, into the victorious regions of the Franks.

[Col. 1376D] Here the author turns his discourse to the city of Rome, and afterward to Saint Cornelius; then he continues by addressing that same saint:

I cannot recount what took place there (he is speaking of Compiègne and the neighboring places). I shall at least communicate to fraternal ears one thing that I learned from the truthful account of the Fathers and committed to writing, though to my frail memory, speaking of Christ and rejecting frivolity, as I heard it.

For it is said that, while your most holy body was being carried on episcopal shoulders through the darkness of the aforesaid forest, it happened on the road, almost at its midpoint, by divine will, that the burden became so heavy that the bishops carrying it could no longer bear the supports on their shoulders. They immediately removed their golden garments, set down on the ground the burden of such weight, and ordered forgiveness of sins to be proclaimed, so that people might hasten to be present at this spectacle [lacuna].

For without doubt the emperor Charles, sound in mind, [lacuna] wishes to glory in you as the guest of this palace after the Virgin of blessed memory and, as was fitting, as lord of the entire domain and basilica. Once this had been divinely understood, he did not willingly delay, but with bent knees according to the custom of the place promptly fulfilled with devoted mind whatever he could perceive that you wished, to the extent of imperial power.

Afterward he enacted such an imperial privilege that between your servants and those of holy Mary there would henceforth be no distinction and no quarrelsome dissension, but that they might equally carry out your service and be supported by an equal share of prebends. So that they might perform this securely, free from all worldly want and without any interval of hindrance, he arranged, from his own furnishings and together with a considerable body of Franks who appeared there, under the illustrious honor of your name, to enlarge the entire endowment of this royal palace with imperial gifts doubled [Col. 1377C]. Indeed, no Frankish soldier was then seen who was unwilling, according to his ability, to bestow a benefaction upon this church.

For what mortal could have been present there with so obstinate a heart that, after seeing so many signs of miracles in that solitude, he would not, in response to the triple power of eternal deeds accomplished there, provide this blessed pope—whose merit demanded such service—with a gift of substance from which those who served him might be fed? Three blind men received sight, three deaf men hearing, and three mute men release from the bonds of their tongues; moreover, very many paralytics recovered, before the blessed pope’s door, the remedy of their former health [Col. 1377D]. The sign of the cross, fixed on a lofty pillar in that same place, still bears witness to this with the greatest truth.

From that time this place grew so greatly in honor that, even if it had been found ruined on so many occasions, no place in France would have presumed in any way to compare with it in ornament. But wherever consuming fire is recognized as having occurred because of the mass of the people’s sins, it ordinarily produces grievous and inextricable destruction and loss of earthly things. Let no one among those present therefore be surprised to find the place now stripped of its abundance of gold and silver, because, after the invasion of flames had twice brought devastation, [lacuna] it was not restored by those who withdrew; rather, ceasing to marvel at such things, let him strive humbly to pour out prayers to Christ [Col. 1378A], asking him mercifully, through the prayers of the blessed pope Cornelius, to preserve this place, so that it may no longer need restoration for such a reason.

O supreme and ineffable power of the eternal God, who never ceases in such wondrous ways to bestow honor upon his witnesses! As soon as he had looked down effectively from the height of Olympus and seen the desire of the martyr of whom we speak fulfilled, he again allowed his little body to become so light that, if I may put it thus, had it wished to travel through the vast emptiness, once every barrier had been removed it could have flown like a bird, beating its wings beyond the clouds whenever it wished.

The certain outcome of the event itself proves this: what shortly before could not be moved by two thousand human hands was now seen to be carried [Col. 1378B] on the shoulders of two bishops from the court of this flock to the atrium. And, as some of our people who were present at that time are known to have said with their own mouths, the bearers found the burden so light that it seemed to them as though the case carrying the bones of the blessed pope remained entirely empty.

Therefore, blessed pope, without hesitation I believe that, obeying the divine will, you wished to rest beneath the shadow of the crypts of the basilica standing there, as a fortress beneficial to all the inhabitants of France. How greatly this place has flourished from that time under your blessed name—speaking to you, brother [Note: [Col. 1377] Some error seems to have entered the manuscript here . . . Perhaps *ill.* occupies the place of a proper name.]—grew in his mind, holy pope; thus he then began in verse:

That blessed place,

Most holy Cornelius,

Where, after struggles and crowns,

You rest in body,

Which, blessed by your triumph,

Glories in its mighty power.

Once Rome, enjoying you,

Flourished in its deeds;

Now France, supported by your power,

Rejoices,

Noble in prosperity and changed circumstances

By so great a gift.

In the church which the devout king built,

Charles transferred you there,

And its enormous weight

Rises in its prominent structure,

Which excels greatly

In precious gifts.

In that place, amid much triumph,

With the king and princes,

With the favor of the clergy

And the following soldiers,

And with the uproar of the clamoring crowd,

You were received beneath the burden.

So great a [lacuna] glory, triumphing there,

Came to meet you,

That Phoebus’s companion-lamp

Seemed to be present,

So brightly did it shine

Along three miles of road.

Some carried golden crosses,

Others candlesticks;

Incense smoked on either side,

Others gleamed in scarlet:

All prayed suppliantly,

And walked with bare feet.

The bishops’ necks

And those of the illustrious king

Carried the sweet burden

To the sanctuary of the church,

While the suppliant people streamed together,

Rejoicing to touch the supports.

A great crowd of clergy

In white went ahead;

A crowd of common people followed,

As many as twenty thousand,

Singing with a loud voice

Thanks to the Most High.

No voice and no speech

Can adequately express

How great was the joyful service

Of that day

When, O patron, you were received

Into the king’s palace.

Some sing, others resound

Clear songs of praise;

A mighty blast of trumpets arises,

And organs thunder;

[Col. 1379C] Moreover, very many

Weep for joy.

The church gleamed

With silken hangings,

With gold and silver,

And splendid crowns,

With the greatest adornment

Of lamps and perfumes.

What joy of heart was yours then, O king,

When you saw great crowds

Restored to health,

And saw many others

Rise up for salvation.

O blessed Charles Caesar!

[Col. 1379D] O blessed France,

Which, supported by so great a patron,

Deserves such joys!

You will not fear the ruin

And dangers of that place.

Then this king endowed the one received there

With many gifts;

For he doubled

The sacred order of clerics,

And by bestowing many possessions

Made it rich.

He added much silver,

A great weight of gold,

And piled up many

Precious garments;

At the same time he most generously offered

Shining gems.

You have nevertheless been placed in the church,

Among golden seats,

Alive, in which you are glorious

And manifold in miracles;

Here the Franks surround you as patron

With their mouths and prayers.

Glorious miracles of healing

Take place here;

Whoever asks receives health,

And no one entreats in vain;

Hence the blessed place triumphs,

And the region flourishes.

[Col. 1380B] Here demons, fearing you,

Confess their crimes,

And the shapeshifting robber

Leaves the bodies he has seized,

Then flees miserably and suddenly

With a dreadful roar.

Words are given to the mute,

And light to the blind;

The sluggish bonds of ears and feet

Are severed:

All sickness rests here,

And disease is driven away.

Often, indeed, the weak

From a distant part of the kingdom,

When they seek your tomb

For the sake of healing,

Are restored on the road

To their former health.

There is also this very wondrous thing

Reported in those regions:

When the sick send their vows

To your presence,

And, as though sleep were withdrawing,

So healing comes to their aid.

Here no robber will raise his spear

With impunity,

As the great destruction

Of the barbarians proved;

Five thousand wished

To burn the church with fire.

[Col. 1380D] While they fought with arrows,

Another five thousand likewise,

They made the war-machine bristle

With flying iron,

Drawn up in ranks

Like dreadful demons.

And as though part of hell

Were vomiting forth sulfur,

A mingled fire surged,

Striking the lofty stars;

The barbarians raged all around,

Kindling such fires.

Indeed, such wondrous spectacles of fire

Were then present,

When it devoured the clergy’s cloister

And the nearby royal palace,

And licked the church with flame

But could not burn it.

Thus you raised up your little servants,

Supported by your favor,

So that they might lay low here and there

Many bodies of barbarians,

And none of these should perish,

Although they were very few.

Horrors for the wicked in war,

Victory for outsiders;

Thus says the one who called you,

The enemy in battle,

As is clearly proved to have been done

By your servants [Col. 1381B]

With the gift of salvation.

May that power remain with you,

Stronger still,

The power with which once, as a warrior against schisms,

You bore in your breast.

[Col. 1382A] For this reason you now triumph

And trample down the barbarians.

Wonderful are the things we recount;

We pass over many;

Yet they have been spoken

With measured judgment, not frivolously.

Let us now restrain the account,

Lest salvation grow weary.

Ask, O holy one, the Thunderer

For your dependents,

That we may be cleansed

From every affliction

And strengthened in blessedness

By the assembly of angels.

Gathered together with your translator,

Charles,

May we deserve to behold

The form of the supreme God,

Who, ordering all things,

Rules throughout the ages of ages.

[Col. 1381]

# On Ancient Promotions of Bishops, with Various Related and Formal Examples

(Apud Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XVI, Appendix, p. 879.)

## Preface of Jacques Sirmond, S.J.

[Col. 1381C]

### The manner and rite formerly followed in the promotion of bishops, both in the Church generally and especially in Gaul

In ancient times it was the custom of the whole Church for bishops to be chosen by the suffrages of the clergy and people over whom they were to preside. Thus, not to go further back, Cornelius is said to have been made bishop of Rome by the suffrage of the clergy and people. Cyprian, in his forty-first and fifty-second letters, attests that Cornelius was made bishop at Rome by the votes of clergy and people; Pontius the deacon, in his *Life*, that Cyprian was elected at Carthage to the priestly office and episcopal rank by the judgment of God and the favor of the people; and Gregory of Nyssa that Alexander was designated bishop of the Church of Comana by Gregory of Neocaesarea, after those whom the citizens had recommended by their votes had been rejected.

Although a practice later became established in the East whereby the people’s suffrages were not sought in episcopal elections—namely, after the Council of Nicaea, which in canons 4 and 6 orders bishops to be chosen and ordained by the bishops of the province, without mentioning either clergy or people, and after the Council of Laodicea, whose thirteenth canon forbids the election of priests to be entrusted to crowds, that is, to the people—the authors of their Lives relate that Epiphanius was elected bishop of Salamis in Cyprus by the bishops of the island, and Basil bishop of Caesarea by the bishops who had assembled for that purpose. Basil himself, with this in view, writes to the Nicopolitans in his 194th letter that it is the bishops’ role to give a bishop to the people, and the people’s role to receive the one given.

In the Western Churches, however, the people’s right of suffrage in proclaiming bishops continued even after the Council of Nicaea. This is shown both by the decrees of the Roman pontiffs Siricius, Celestine, and Leo, which establish that bishops are to be elected with the consent of clergy and people, and by the countless examples of Damasus, Ambrose, Augustine, Fulgentius, and others who are known to have been appointed in this manner.

It is equally clear that this custom prevailed in our Gaul for as long as it remained under Roman rule. Fortunatus relates that Hilary was made priest at Poitiers with the harmonious support of the people; Severus says that Martin was made bishop at Tours by the united votes of the multitude that had come to cast its suffrages; and Gregory of Tours reports that the people likewise elected Illidius as priest of the Church of Auvergne and appointed him its pastor.

Constantius the priest further records that Germanus was sought at Auxerre by the decision of the clergy, the nobility, and the urban and rural people; and Hincmarus testifies that Remigius at Reims was carried to the height of the episcopate by the unanimous votes of all, rather than elected. Sidonius mentions the judgment and will of the people and townsmen in the election of Simplicius, bishop of Bourges, and John, bishop of Chalon. Finally, concerning Caesarius of Arles, the deacon Cyprian relates that Aeonius, when near death, addressed the clergy and citizens so that after his death they would substitute Caesarius for him.

From these and similar examples it appears that, in Gaul, as long as it obeyed the Roman Empire, the free suffrages of clergy and people prevailed in the election of bishops. But after kings arose in Gaul and among other peoples once the Romans had been driven out, the exceptional dignity of bishops caused rulers to consider it their own concern that bishops should not be appointed except at their discretion and by their will.

Although our bishops frequently protested against this and attempted in their councils to preserve intact the ancient freedom of elections—as at the Third Council of Orléans, canon 3; the Council of Auvergne, canon 2; the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 11; the Third Council of Paris, canon 8; the Fifth Council of Paris, canon 1; the Council of Reims, canon 25; and the Council of Chalon, canon 10—the authority of the kings nevertheless prevailed. It was established that no bishops should be recognized except those whom the kings themselves commanded to be appointed or whom they approved and accepted after they had been sought by the clergy and citizens.

Thus Gregory of Tours teaches that Nicetius was summoned to the episcopate at Trier by order of King Theodoric and, with the consent of the people and the king’s decree, was ordained. Likewise, Quintianus and, after his death, Gallus were given as bishops to Auvergne by the same King Theodoric. Thus, to mention a few among many, Gregory himself and Fortunatus record that Germanus of Paris obtained his see by order of Childebert; Ommatius of Tours by order of Clodomir; Medard of Vermand; and Euphronius, again of Tours, and Domnolus of Le Mans by order or consent of King Clotaire.

In the same manner, thereafter under Chilperic and his brothers, then under Clotaire II, Dagobert, Clovis the Younger, and the other kings of the Merovingian family, bishoprics were conferred or granted. This is shown both by the histories and by the old forms then in use, preserved by Marculf and others. Some contain petitions from the people to the king, asking that this or that man be made their bishop; others contain the king’s order concerning a bishopric that has been conferred; others are letters to the metropolitan and bishops for the ordination of the new bishop.

The same arrangement continued under the first kings of the second dynasty, Pepin and Charles. This is shown both by examples of those to whom they entrusted bishoprics and by the councils held during their reigns. Although these councils prescribe many things concerning the office and discipline of bishops, nowhere do they mention episcopal elections.

Louis the Pious was the first to recall the ancient custom. In the third year, I believe, of his reign, he restored to the Church the power to elect bishops by issuing a law found in book one of the *Capitularies*, chapter 84, in these words:

“Concerning the election of bishops. Not ignorant of the sacred canons, and wishing that the holy Church might possess her honor more freely in the name of God, we have given our assent to the ecclesiastical order, namely, that bishops should be elected by the election of clergy and people, according to the decrees of the canons, from their own diocese, without acceptance based on persons or gifts, but on account of merit of life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may be able to benefit in every way those subject to them by example and word.”

Nevertheless, the churches used the benefit of this law and the right of election thereafter in such a way that, whenever a bishop died, each church first asked the king, through the metropolitan, for permission to elect a new bishop, together with a visitor who would preside over the election. The decree of the election that had been held was then reported to the metropolitan, so that, once it had been approved by the king and the elected candidate had been examined before the provincial bishops, he might finally be ordained and receive from the ordaining bishops instructions on how he ought to conduct himself in the episcopal office according to the provisions of the canons.

Since Hincmar of Reims often explains each of these matters in various places, they are all briefly expressed in the book against Hincmar the nephew, where he treats the metropolitan’s dignity and pre-eminence over the other bishops in these words:

“In the province of Reims,” he says, “if a bishop should die, I, and not you, shall appoint a visitor for the church that has been widowed, and I shall order the election to be held with a canonical decree. And if the votes of those electing should be divided, it will be mine, and not yours, to choose the man who is supported by greater zeal and merits for ordination; and it is mine to examine the man to be ordained, not yours. It is yours, however, to ordain the bishop with the others together with me, and, after me, to sign in your place the canonical letters which the ordained man is ordered to receive from his ordainers.”

So that it might be more clearly and fully known and understood how each of these procedures was ordinarily carried out, we have thought it worthwhile to append here the various forms of letters and other acts relating to the matter that have come into our hands, prefacing them with the older forms mentioned above, which were used before elections were restored.

# Ancient Forms Concerning the Episcopate

Formerly used under the first kings. **Index**

[Col. 1384A]

1. Petition of the clergy and people of a widowed city to the king for the appointment of a bishop.  
2. The king’s command concerning the bishopric, addressed to the designated bishop.  
3. The king’s letter to the metropolitan, ordering him to ordain the designated bishop with his fellow provincials.  
4. Another letter to the bishop concerning the same ordination of the designated bishop.  
(See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXVII.)

# Various Forms

Used in the promotion of bishops after the freedom of elections had been restored.

[Col. 1384B]

1. Hincmar’s letter to the king, asking him to grant an election and a visitor to the Church of Senlis.  
2. Hincmar’s letter to Gedenulfus, asking him to act as visitor in the Church of Cambrai.  
3. Hincmar’s letter to the clergy and people of Cambrai, asking them to hold an election.  
4. Hincmar’s letter to the people of Beauvais concerning the form and manner of conducting the election.  
5. The excuse of the people of Reims, who were said to have held an election before the visitor’s arrival.  
6. The visitor’s address to the electors.  
7. Decree of the election of Hedenulfus, bishop of Laon.  
8. Another decree of the election of Aeneas, bishop of Paris.  
9. Third decree of the election of Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens.  
10. Letter of the Church of Sens to Hilduin, archchaplain, in defense of the election they had held.  
11. Examination of Willebertus, the bishop to be ordained at Châlons.  
12. Profession of Adalbertus, future bishop of Thérouanne.  
13. Another profession of the future archbishop.  
14. Letter of Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, since he was unable to attend the election of Aeneas.  
15. Document concerning the ordination of Electrannus, bishop of Rennes.  
16. Canonical letters given by the ordainers to Hedenulfus, bishop of Laon.  
(See the work cited above.)

# Formal Letter

**In the name of the Father (ΠΑΤΡΗΣ) and of the Son (ΦΙΛΙΗ).**

[Col. 1384D] And of the Holy Spirit (ϹΡϹ ϹΚΗ). To the most holy and most venerable lord, N., bishop of N. province, our brother in Christ the Lord, designated by us with the greatest affection.

I, N., bishop, servant of Christ, humble bishop of the holy Church of N., your fellow brother and devoted petitioner, offer you peaceable health in the Lord, for this transitory life and the life to come.

Let your holiness know that this cleric, our tonsured man named N., has requested from our humility a letter of dismissal, or formal letter, so that he may be promoted by you to sacred orders. Therefore, yielding to his requests, we send this letter of dismissal—or, as we have said, formal letter—to your fraternity and holiness, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, so that you may not hesitate to consecrate him to the burden of the priesthood and send him back to us.

And so that you may believe and recognize this as true, we have ordered it to be authenticated below with Greek letters and their numerical value, in accordance with the aforesaid council.

Fare well in the Lord, most beloved and dearest brother.

ΠΟϹΑ  LXXX LXX CCI  
ΠΔΜΟΛΛΩ

## Another Formal Letter of M., Bishop of Teano

[Note: [Col. 1385D] In this second formal letter, which is extremely corrupt and full of errors, we have omitted certain words marked by dots, since they yielded no sense. We have also corrected a few things ourselves, such as *M. speculator* for what is written as *inspeculator*. The bishop’s name, which is represented here, begins with the letter M, as is stated at the end of the formal letter; and through the easy carelessness of copyists, *in* is sometimes written in place of *m*. Ughellus’s catalogue of the bishops of the Church of Teano is incomplete and does not suggest the name of this bishop beginning with M. Since an empress is mentioned as being in the region of Benevento, and the fifteenth indiction is noted, the reference seems to be either to Adelaide, wife of Otto I, or to Theophanu, wife of Otto II, both of whom were present in those regions on several occasions. Although Angilberga, wife of Louis II, was also there, the fifteenth indiction does not suit her. This Theatine bishop M., therefore, lived under the rule of Otto I or Otto II and should be added to the catalogue of the bishops of the Church of Theate. (Ballerini.)]

2. Φ, Υ, Α. To the most celebrated poet [perhaps *celeberrimo*, “most celebrated”], most holy and ready brother, to be honored with wisdom and every distinction and adorned in all things, faithful in the Lord and most learned, or adorned among all the orthodox with manifold knowledge [lacuna], beloved in Christ, John: M., bishop and overseer (*speculator*) of the holy see and Church of Theate [lacuna].

We, N., bishop of the holy see and Church of N., wish you great health and honor in Jesus Christ our Lord, here and forever. Because of the difficulty of the journey, since I have been summoned to the regions of Benevento, as the lady empress made known in her letters, so that we might bring to her service those things by which we are already continually wearied for a long time by bodily distress, we consider ourselves unable to raise the clerics of our diocese to the sacred orders.

Therefore, by these letters of our mediocrity, we ask that this cleric of ours, Lupus, who is here present, be promoted to the rank of a Levite, that is, deacon, and we send him especially to your fraternity. And so that this may be believed with greater certainty and credibility, we order that Greek letters be inserted into this page according to the statutes of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, namely, “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

The first letters ΠΟϹΑ signify the numbers LXXX, LXX, CC, and one. The first letter of Peter, prince of the apostles, Π, signifies LXXX. The first letter of our mediocrity is Μ; the second of your sublimity is Ο; the third of the one who receives is Π; the fourth of our city is [lacuna]; and the indiction of this present year is XV. His name is Lupus, a cleric who will become a deacon. We have also added XCVIIII q Θ, which are represented by these Greek letters.

ΑΜΗΝ.

# Formal Letter of Burchard, Bishop of Worms

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

To Walter, bishop of Speyer.

I, Burchard, devoted servant of Christ’s flock and of the holy Church of Worms, wish you in God the blessedness of true and supreme happiness.

Since the holy Catholic Church is ready to follow the evangelical teachings that say, “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person,” and so forth (Matthew 10:41), and since the Apostle commands us to pursue hospitality and to share with the needs of holy men (Romans 12), nevertheless, because of those who have a seared conscience, saying that they are simple when they are filled with diabolical cunning, and who claim that they are traveling from place to place for the work of piety when in fact they are fugitives because of their own wickedness, and who say that they have been admitted to the sacred ministry when they have not, the holy Fathers have decreed that no bishop may receive or enthrone an alien and unknown cleric in his church unless he has from his own bishop a letter which the canons call a *formal letter*.

Therefore we make known to your fatherhood that this brother of ours, the bearer of these letters, named Ecmannus, was not expelled by us for any wickedness of his own. Rather, because our brothers requested it, and because he belonged to our household and was baptized by us, we granted him freedom canonically by the horn of the altar and ordained him to the priesthood. We have also prepared these letters of dismissal or commendation for him and send him to your beloved fraternity, so that he may be able to remain in your parish under your sacred governance and protection.

I, Burchard, humble bishop, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and in the unity of the holy Church, in which the power of binding and loosing was given to Peter, absolve Ecmannus, priest of the city of Worms, in the tenth indiction, and I grant you permission to enthrone him in whichever church of your parish you wish.

We have therefore decided to strengthen this letter with Greek letters on every side; the following words concerning the church of the Firmacrenses are corrupt and uncertain: “and by no one of our church of the Firmacrenses.”

May Christ preserve your fraternity safe and sound for us.

Π. Υ. Δ. Π. Β. Θ. V. W. d.)-(. H. Z.

Given at Worms on the Ides of March, in the year 1012 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the tenth indiction.

# Oaths of Bishops Given to the See of Arles
I, Pontius, now to be ordained bishop of the see of Sainte-Marie of Aix, promise that I shall perpetually render to the Holy See of the Church of Arles and to its rulers the due submission, reverence, and obedience established by the holy Fathers according to the precepts of the canons, in the presence of the lord Archbishop Raimbald; and with my own hand I confirm this upon the holy altar.

I, Brother Rostagnus, to be ordained bishop of the Church of Aix, [Col. 1386D] promise the due submission, etc., as above.

I, Stephanus, called bishop of the Church of Vence, promise before God and his saints every submission, canonical obedience, and fidelity to the Church of Saint Stephen of the see of Arles, where the body of the blessed confessor Trophimus rests, and to Anno, [Col. 1387A] the present archbishop, and to his successors, if I outlive him.

I, Arnulphus, called bishop of the Church of Vence, etc., as in the preceding oath. Only, instead of Anno, the present archbishop, he has Pontius, the present archbishop.

I, Bertrandus, now to be ordained bishop of the Church of the holy see of Fréjus, etc., as above in the oath of Pontius of Aix.

I, Bertrandus, called bishop of the Church of Riez, profess that henceforth I shall remain under the authority of the metropolitan of Arles and obey his commands.

I, Agelricus, now to be ordained bishop of the holy Church of Riez, etc., as in the oath of Pontius [Col. 1387B] of Aix.

I, Adilricus, called bishop of the Church of Orange, etc., as in the oath of Stephanus of Vence.

I, Adilricus, called bishop of Orange and Tricastin, etc., as in the oath of the same Stephanus. Only, instead of Anno, he has Raimbald.

I, Petrus, called bishop of the Church of Avignon, profess that I shall, etc., as in the oath of Bertrand of Riez.

I, Benedictus, called bishop of the Church of Avignon, swear before God and his saints every submission, canonical obedience, and fidelity to the Church of Saint Stephen of the see of Arles, where the body of the holy apostle Trophimus rests, and to Raimbald, the present archbishop, and to his successors, [Col. 1387C] if I outlive him.

# ELEVEN EXAMPLES OF ANCIENT FORMS OF CANONICAL LETTERS

After the forms used for the promotion of bishops, it is not out of place to append examples of the canonical letters called *formatae*. Their use was extremely common among bishops, especially on behalf of clerics when they migrated elsewhere, since it was not permitted to receive them into communion or ordain them in another church without such letters. Their Greek origin is shown by the Greek letters, whose numerical values they observed even in Latin names. While some commonly report that these letters were instituted on the authority of the Fathers of Nicaea, this is also taught by the ancient formula for composing *formatae* that circulates under the title of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople. We shall place it first.

## On the method of composing canonical letters, which the Council of Nicaea established that bishops should observe when writing letters to one another

[Col. 1387D]

No one who has even slight knowledge of the Greek language is unaware that the Greek characters also express numbers. Therefore, so that no fraudulent falsification might rashly be attempted in composing the canonical letters which Latin usage calls *formatae*, the Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, numbering 318, both wisely discovered and established the following rule of calculation or reckoning for *formatae*: namely, that the first Greek characters of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit should be included in the reckoning—Π, Υ, Α—which signify respectively the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one; likewise the first letter of the apostle Peter, Π, which signifies eighty.

There should also be included the first letter of the bishop who writes; the second letter of the person to whom he writes; the third of the recipient; the fourth of the city from which he writes; and the number of the Indiction current at the time. All these Greek letters, which, as we have said, express numbers, are then added together, and the resulting total is to be written in the letter. The recipient must expressly seek it with every precaution. In addition, the number ninety-nine, which in Greek characters is signified by ΑΜΗΝ (*Amen*), should be added separately in the letter.

*(From the foregoing it is clear that, among the numbers observed in all* formatae, *some are always the same in every formata, while others differ in each one: the former are therefore common to all, the latter proper to individual letters. The common numbers are those formed from the first letters of the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, and Peter—namely, from the letters Π, Υ, Α, Π, whose corresponding numbers are 80, 400, 1, and 80—and from all the letters of ΑΜΗΝ, whose numbers are 1, 40, 8, and 50; that is, ϟθʹ, 99. Their total is therefore 660. This same number is common to all* formatae *and is the same in every one. The proper number, however, is derived from the first letter of the writer, the second of the person to whom he writes, the third of the recipient, the fourth of the city from which he writes, and the sign of the Indiction. These hardly ever coincide in different* formatae. *Thus the proper number is different in each, and consequently the total of the two numbers is different in different letters. This will become clear from the following examples of* formatae, *once we have first shown which numbers the Greek letters signify.)*

## The numbers signified by the individual Greek characters

Α α — 1  
Β β — 2  
Γ γ — 3  
Δ δ — 4  
Ε ε — 5  
ϛʹ — 6  
Ζ ζ — 7  
Η η — 8  
Θ θ — 9  
Ι ι — 10  
Κ κ — 20  
Λ λ — 30  
Μ μ — 40  
Ν ν — 50  
Ξ ξ — 60  
Ο ο — 70  
Π π — 80  
Ϟ ϟ — 90  
Ρ ρ — 100  
Σ σ — 200  
Τ τ — 300  
Υ υ — 400  
Φ φ — 500  
Χ χ — 600  
Ψ ψ — 700  
Ω ω — 800  
Ϡ ϡ — 900

# INDEX OF THE FOLLOWING *FORMATAE*

I. Ebroinus, archbishop of Bourges, to Magnon, bishop of Sens.  
II. Wolfeo, bishop of Constance, to Bernaltus, bishop of Strasbourg. [Col. 1388D]  
III. Teutgaudus, bishop of Trier, to King Charles, the bishops, etc.  
IV. John, bishop of Cambrai, to all the bishops.  
V. Liutadius, bishop of Vienne, to Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen.  
VI. Aeneas, bishop of Paris, to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.  
VII. Hedilo, bishop of Noyon, to Dido, bishop of Laon.  
VIII. Hedilo, the same bishop, to Radulfus, bishop of Laon.  
IX. Rathbodus, archbishop of Trier, to Rotbertus, bishop of Metz.  
X. Dado, bishop of Verdun, to Rattbodus, archbishop of Trier.  
XI. Durandus, bishop of Arles, to Radulfus, archbishop of Tours.

## I [Col. 1389A] Ebroinus of Bourges to Magnon, archbishop of Sens, on behalf of the presbyter Dodobertus, so that he may remain in his parish with Hercambaldus

To the holy and God-beloved Magnon, archbishop by the gift of God from the city of Sens, I, Ebroinus, archbishop by the gift of God from the city of Bourges, wish perpetual salvation in the Lord Jesus.

Furthermore, we make known to your holiness that we ordered this present presbyter, named Dodobertus, our parishioner, born in our diocese and instructed in the sacred writings, to be promoted to the sacred order. Afterwards, however, he asked us for permission to remain in your parish with a certain man named Hercambaldus. We did not deny his request, [Col. 1389B] but granted him permission, because we know that he was born of legitimately free parents.

Therefore we have sent your holiness this letter of recommendation, composed according to ecclesiastical custom, so that your God-worthy charity may know that he has neither fled nor been expelled by us because of his own wickedness, but has been sent with our consent. And so that you may believe this more certainly, we first appended the Greek characters expressing the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one: Π. We also asked that the first letter of Peter’s name be written in the middle. Nevertheless, we added the first letter of our humble name, Ε; the second letter of your greatness, Α; the third letter of the name of this brother, Α; the fourth letter of our city, Υ; and the fourth Indiction. [Col. 1389C]

We added the number ninety-nine: that is, ϟʹ and Θʹ. Thereafter we confirmed the letter below with the impression of our seal. We strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it to be strengthened by our clerics. Done in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Charles and the forty-third year of his kingdom; in the name of God, successfully. Amen.

*(The fourth Indiction and the years of Charles the Great’s reign and imperial rule indicate the year of Christ 810. The total of all the numbers contained in the* formata *is 1,074; for the proper number, 414, formed from the letters Ε, Α, Δ, Υ and Indiction IV, must be added to the common number of all* formatae, *660.)*

## II. Wolfeo, bishop of Constance, to Bernaltus, bishop of Strasbourg, [Col. 1389D] on behalf of the cleric Anno, so that he may remain in the parish and be promoted to the sacred orders

Π, Υ, Α, Π—to the most holy brother in Christ, embraced with the greatest sweetness, Bernaltus, bishop of the city of Strasbourg—I, Wolfeo, prelate of the Church of Constance, wish perpetual blessedness and salvation in Christ. Υ, Ε, Ν, Σ.

Furthermore, let your holy fraternity know that this cleric, named Anno, instructed and tonsured in our parish, asked our lowliness that we write him letters of recommendation by which, commended to your eminence, he might live under the protection of your government.

Agreeing to his wish, we gave him letters of release according to canonical authority, [Col. 1390A] by which we also grant him permission, while devoting himself to divine service under your instruction, to serve his own proper good; and we grant you permission, if you judge him worthy, to promote him to the sacred orders.

Receive him, therefore, as commended to your care, and, released from our jurisdiction, guard him among the number of your sheep. So that these letters may be received by you without doubt as confirmed by the force of truth, we have taken pains to confirm them with Greek letters, as canonical authority teaches. May the Holy Trinity grant your blessedness perpetual well-being for the governance of its holy Church. Π. Indiction X. This *formata* contains the total number 1,325.

*(Indiction X and Wolfeo’s episcopate indicate the year [Col. 1390B] 817. The total number written at the end of the* formata *is composed of the common number, 660, and the proper number, 665, which arises from the letters Υ, Ε, Ν, Σ and Indiction X; joined together, they produce 1,325.)*

## III. General letter of Teutgaudus, archbishop of Trier, to King Charles the Bald, the bishops, and all others, on behalf of the presbyter Hegilo, who was journeying to the holy places

To the most glorious and God-crowned great and peaceful King Charles, and to all most blessed prelates, to all others ordained in ecclesiastical orders, to all administering secular office in his kingdom, and to all the faithful who love the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, Teutgaudus, [Col. 1390C] the most humble archbishop of Trier, implores full peace and the desirable salvation of everlasting joy.

It often happens that great men, conspicuous by the highest stronghold of religion, exceedingly powerful in the strength of their virtues, girded with the weapons of justice, distinguished by the brightness of chastity, and resplendent with the beauty of wisdom, conceive a desire to depart from their own places, so that on such an occasion they may escape human praise and be esteemed by strangers as men of lesser merit, although we had honored them greatly.

There are indeed very many exhortations of the Old and New Testaments and exceedingly clear examples before our eyes concerning such an occasion. Since we do not doubt that these are sufficiently known to you, we pass over them as more fitting.

Moved, therefore, by this most happy custom [Col. 1390D] and salutary teaching, a certain brother most dear to us and to all who love goodness, named Hegilo, since he was our diocesan—brought up and tonsured in our diocese, fully instructed in the sacred teaching of the Holy Scriptures, and conducted most honorably—having been promoted in the Church entrusted to us to the dignity of the priesthood, asked us for permission, so that, having received canonical release and the blessing bestowed upon him, he might visit the holy places more safely and securely and approach your presence more freely and familiarly, wherever the variety of his journey might lead him among you.

Accordingly, granting assent to his request and agreeing to his reverence, we consented [Col. 1391A] by consenting to what he appeared to desire according to God. Therefore we humbly beg and earnestly request your humanity that, having received him honorably as the temple of God and dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, as the habitation of the Holy Trinity, and as a most precious member of Christ, enriched by the gift and generosity of God’s sevenfold grace, wherever he may arrive—whether he is to remain among you for a short time or for a longer period—you treat him kindly and show him humaneness. Thus, receiving Christ in him as we ask, you may faithfully acquire eternal merit from your generosity toward him.

Finally, when, because of the memorable excellence of his righteousness, we decided to present these peaceful letters to you, we thought it worthwhile [Col. 1391B] also to insert the Greek characters from the name of the Father, Π; of the Son, Υ; and of the Holy Spirit, Α; likewise the first letter from the name of the blessed apostle Peter, Π; II; and ΑΜΗΝ at the end. We also included the total of those letters, expressed by Greek characters, ΦΞΑ, so that by this means the honor due to him whom we commend might shine more clearly for you.

We prefixed the characters of the Holy Trinity, so that the Holy Trinity might everywhere preserve, strengthen, and defend him, through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter. We also took care to place ΑΜΗΝ at the end, desiring that his journey might be directed toward health, become acceptable to the eyes of the divine majesty, receivable by the saints, and memorable forever, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

For this reason we placed Greek characters in this letter, not in order to compose a canonical *formata*, [Col. 1391C] but so that, through those characters, we might pray for prosperity also for Hegilo, to whom this had been made known. Farewell. May the right hand of God the Father, through whom the ages were made, protect your religious devotion and fulfill your good will according to your desire—together with all the faithful and all the most blessed brothers, and with King Charles, who is to be crowned forever by the King of all kings according to his greater merits. Amen.

*(The episcopate of Teutgaudus corresponds with the times of Charles the Bald, but there is no Indiction here from which the year of Christ can be established. As for the numbers, since some are common to all, as stated above, and others proper to each* formata, *I expressed only the total of the common numbers, omitting the proper ones, and not even that total in full, was expressed in the Greek letters ΦΞΑ, that is, 561; for the 99 contained in ΑΜΗΝ had to be added in order to make [Col. 1391D] the complete total, 660.)*

## IV. General letter of John, bishop of Cambrai, to all the bishops, on behalf of the presbyter Ursio, so that he may be received in any of their parishes

In the name of Π, Υ, Α, Π, Ι, Π, Σ, Α; Indiction XIII; ΑΜΗΝ. To all the pastors of Holy Mother Church who, with devout solicitude, care for her children: John, the least of the bishops of Holy Mother Church of Cambrai, sends the dance of unfailing prosperity.

Overburdened by the enormous weight of crimes, we are worn down by the frequent attacks not only of pagans but also of pseudo-Christians. Therefore [Col. 1392A] pastoral vigilance cannot govern within the enclosure of its own fold the flock entrusted to our divine solicitude.

Among them, this present priest, named Ursio, canonically promoted through every rank in our mother Church by our predecessor of blessed memory, Theuderic, and having conducted himself religiously as long as he was able, earnestly begged for letters strengthened by the unfailing Greek characters of the decrees of the most holy Council of Nicaea. He asked that our pastoral indulgence grant him letters by which, released with their protection, he might be canonically received wherever he found a suitable place and carry out the ministry divinely entrusted to him.

We therefore received this kind of request, sympathizing both with our own misery and with his, and recognizing him as entirely free from deceit. We most generously granted him permission to migrate, earnestly asking your eminence, wherever he may arrive, to receive him into the most holy bosom of your fatherhood and allow him to exercise his ministerial office within your diocese.

So that these letters of our lowliness may be believed more truly, we have inserted the Greek number-characters with their calculations: namely, the first letter of the Father, Π; the first of the Son, Υ; and of the Holy Spirit, Α; likewise the first of Peter, prince of the apostles, Π. We have also inserted the first letter of our own name, I. Since we do not know which bishop’s diocese he must specifically approach, in place of the particular letter of the bishop’s name—which should here be second—we have placed the second letter of the general name, namely II, which likewise signifies eighty. [Col. 1392C]

In addition, we have appended the third letter of this brother’s name, Σ; the fourth letter of our city, Α; and the Indiction of the current year, XIII, together with ΑΜΗΝ.

These things have been appended so that the pure simplicity of your blessedness, which is in Christ, might not be clouded by any approach of fraud; and so that you may certainly know that this brother has neither fled nor been stained by any blemish of crime, but was unwillingly driven out by the imminent ferocity of the Northmen.

May your holiness, protected by the heavenly assistance of Christ’s mercy, prosper. The total of the numbers in the letter is 964.

*(Indiction XIII and the episcopate of John of Cambrai indicate the year 865. The total of the numbers added at the end and also expressed by its own letters at the beginning is composed of the common number, 660, and the proper number of this* formata, *304, which is formed from the Greek letters [Col. 1392D] Ι, Π, Σ, Α and Indiction XIII.)*

## V. Liutadius, bishop of Vienne, to Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen, concerning the deacon Wlfadus, whom he had formerly received from Ebbo of Reims and now entrusts to him

Π. Σ. Α. To the most reverend and holy father Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen, Liutadius, bishop of Vienne, eternal salvation in the Lord.

I would greatly wish, if the distances of the lands allowed it, to have a fraternal and most friendly conversation with you and to discuss our common concerns. But since the length of the journey appears to prevent this, I humbly ask your holiness to deign to remember me before the holy altar and to commend me to your Church, since we have already received your charity into the bosom of our Church and daily entreat God for you.

Furthermore, let your holiness know that a certain brother of ours and son of our Church, named Wlfadus, a subdeacon, was entrusted to me at my request by letters which ecclesiastical custom calls *formatae*, from the venerable Ebbo, formerly archbishop of Reims. Since, after he had been entrusted to me, certain matters arose and he remained in his own Church, the same Ebbo, at my suggestion, ordained him to the grade of deacon.

Now, because you know that he must remain in your region on account of necessary business, I entrust him to you, just as he had been commended to me, [Col. 1393B] and delegate him to your custody and care; I humbly ask that you advance him to the higher grades. For we believe that both his wisdom and his conduct show him worthy of this.

We therefore commend to your blessedness and to your Church our aforesaid brother Wlfadus, and we ask you to rejoice forever in his progress.

As is ecclesiastical custom, and as was discovered and established by the 318 bishops at the Council of Nicaea, when composing a *formata* we have taken into the reckoning, so that our work of granting and releasing this beloved brother might be strengthened in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity and become more fruitful and useful, the first Greek characters of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, Π, Υ, Α, which [Col. 1393C] signify eighty, four hundred, and one.

We have also attached the first letter of our own name, Α; the second letter of your blessedness’s name, Υ; the third letter of the receiving brother’s name, Α; the fourth letter of our city, from which the letter is written, Σ; and, following canonical order, Indiction I.
