We have caused the numbers of the Greek letters to be collected into one total and made the letter contain them: namely, 80, 400, 1, 30, 400, 30, 200, 1, so that the authority of our letter of release might proceed fully valid and legitimate.

Separately, to close the letter, we also marked the number ninety-nine with Greek characters and confirmed it completely: ϟθ.

*(Indiction I and Wenilo’s episcopate correspond to the year of Christ 868. The proper number of the* formata *is 661, formed by the letters Λ, Υ, Δ, Σ and Indiction Ι. The common number is not 660, as in the others, but 580, with the letter Π omitted, since it was the first letter of Peter’s name. The total of both numbers is therefore 1,241.)*

## VI. Aeneas, bishop of Paris, to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, so that he may retain and ordain the acolyte Berno in his parish

To the venerable father in Christ, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, Aeneas, bishop of the holy Church of Paris, greetings in the Lord.

The brothers from the monastery of Saint-Denis, with the permission of the lord abbot Ludovicus, entrusted to me for education and instruction a certain youth named Berno, whom your fraternity [Col. 1394A] ordained as an acolyte. Therefore, since we do not wish him to remain for a long time in our church without your permission, we ask your affection to provide us with canonical letters concerning him, so that we may regularly ordain him in our Church.

Hincmar, unworthily bishop of Reims and servant of God’s people, sends greetings to his beloved brother and venerable bishop Aeneas.

Canonical and ecclesiastical authority decrees that no bishop may presume to retain or ordain in his own parish anyone ordained in another Church without the consent or letters of release of the bishop by whom he was ordained. Holding this institution of the holy Fathers most fully, you asked us [Col. 1394B] about a certain son of our Church, recently ordained an acolyte by us, named Berno, who had once been sent to your region for study and education, etc. The rest is missing.

## VII. Hedilo, bishop of Noyon, to Dido, bishop of Laon, on behalf of the presbyter Arnegisus, so that he may migrate to his parish and submit to him

In the name of the Father, Π; and of the Son, Υ; and of the Holy Spirit, Α. Hedilo, bishop of Noyon, sends eternal happiness in the Lord to Dido, illustrious and venerable fellow bishop.

Let your affection know that Arnegisus, presbyter, our brother and son, asked that, through my permission and through a *formata* letter issued by me according to canonical authority, as ought to take place between the giver and the recipient, he might be placed under your authority.

We have therefore sent you this letter, composed according to canonical institution, so that you may know that he received from me a just and canonical permission. The three Greek characters inserted at the beginning contain the numbers eighty, four hundred, and one. Likewise, the first letter of the name of the apostle Peter, Π, expresses eighty, as before.

From the name of our lowliness, likewise, the first letter, Ε, corresponds to the number five. The second letter of the name of your holiness, Ι, undoubtedly forms the number ten. The third letter of the aforesaid presbyter’s name, Ν, displays the number fifty. Finally, the fourth letter of our city’s name, Ι, expresses ten, as above. The fifth letter of the name of your city, Υ, also establishes the number four hundred.

The Indiction is now XI. We have additionally included the number ninety-nine, which in Greek characters signifies ΑΜΗΝ. The total of all the numbers added together is 1,146. All these things must be carefully sought and examined with every precaution. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of October.

*(Indiction XI and the episcopates of Heidilo and Dido indicate the year of Christ 892. The total of the numbers written at the end, 1,146, is derived from the common number, 660, and the proper number, 486, which is formed from the letters Ε, Ι, Ε, Ι, Υ, with Indiction XI added. A special feature of this* formata *is therefore that it also observes the fifth letter of the city of the bishop to whom he writes.)*

## VIII. Hedilo, the same bishop of Noyon, to Rodulfus, bishop of Laon, on behalf of the deacon Rotgerus, who had asked to be transferred to his parish

In the name of the Father, Π; and of the Son, Υ; and of the Holy Spirit, Α. Hedilo, humble bishop of Noyon, by the gracious favor of that same Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, wishes double peace and glory in Christ to the holy, venerable, and most dear to us Rodulfus, bishop of the holy Church of Laon.

Let the experience of your greatness observe that this present cleric, named Rotgerus, is to be promoted by us through each grade of ecclesiastical honor to the burden of the diaconate. This same brother, for the sake of his own advantageous circumstances, very properly and justly sought from our moderation permission to go to you, remain in your parish, and depart from ours entirely.

We therefore willingly assented to his request, which we recognized as not deceitful but genuine, and did not deny him its just and appropriate fulfillment. Therefore, earnestly striving with all our strength, we humbly beseech your eminence that your paternal solicitude deign to receive him and accept him in the bosom of your affection as a pious and prudent pastor and father.

You should know that thus far, in life and conduct among our people, he has been upright and praiseworthy. He is also capable of the ministry entrusted to him and, as we judge, is recognized as knowing how to perform his office. [Col. 1395C]

According to canonical custom, we have granted him this *formata* letter, marked with Greek characters in accordance with the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, to be delivered to you. Through it we entrust him to your protection and separate him completely from our parish.

In it, after the Aeolic characters above had been taken into the reckoning for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, we also logically added the first character of Peter, Π, so that, holding the faith of the Holy Trinity in our hearts, we might confess it with our mouths for salvation through the teaching of that prince of the apostles.

And so that no fraud of falsification might prevail in it, we added the first letter of the name of us who write, Η; the second of the person to whom we write, Ο; the third of you who receive, Δ; [Col. 1395D] and, in addition, the fourth of our city, Ι; together with Indiction V.

We therefore took pains to record the total of this calculation, all together, as follows: Π, 80; Υ, 400; Α, 1; Π, 80; Η, 8; Ο, 70; Δ, 4; Ι, 10.

We further added the number ninety-nine, which in Greek characters signifies the most sacred oath of our Lord Jesus Christ: XC, Θʹ. We wish your happiness health here and forever.

*(Indiction V, compared with the years of the episcopates of Heidilo and Rodulfus, indicates the year of Christ 902. The sum of the numbers formed from the proper signs of the* formata *is 97; added to the common number, 660, this produces a total of 757.)*

## IX. [Col. 1396A] Rathbodus, archbishop of Trier, to Rotbertus, bishop of Metz, on behalf of the presbyter Gislemarus, so that he may henceforth remain in his parish

In the name of Π, the Father; and Υ, the Son; and Α, the Holy Spirit. Rathbodus, humble servant of the holy Church of Trier and of its people, sends to Rotbertus, reverend bishop of the holy Church of Metz, glory in Christ, the chief shepherd, with enduring joy, prosperity, and perpetuity.

Faithfully observing the salutary decrees of the 318 holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, we approach your God-worthy and devout fraternity canonically, and respectfully come before your holiness under the title of a *formata* letter. We make known to you [Col. 1396B] that we have given these letters of release to this present presbyter of ours, named Gislemarus, whom we educated ecclesiastically in our diocese and advanced from the clerical order to the grade of the priesthood.

Thus, fortified by these canonical letters, he may, with our permission, dwell in your parish under the protection and governance of your dear affection. We entrust him to you to be canonically cherished and governed in the bosom of holy Mother Church.

We have therefore decided to strengthen this letter with Greek characters on every side and have judged it appropriate to seal it with the ring of our Church. May Christ, chief of shepherds, through the intercession of the blessed Peter, to whom the Lord’s sheepfold was specially entrusted, preserve your fraternity safe for us for a long time in the guardianship of his flock. ΑΜΗΝ.

The total of these is 1,439. [Col. 1396C] Π, Υ, Α, Ρ, Ο, Σ, Θ. ΑΜΗΝ.

Given at Trier on the Ides of October, in the year of the incarnation of the Lord 906, Indiction IX.

*(Indiction IX on the Ides of October and Rathbodus’s episcopate correspond to the year of Christ 905. The total of the numbers written at the end is obtained from the common number, 660, and the proper number, 779, which is formed from the letters Π, Ο, Σ, [lacuna], and Indiction IX. The sum of both numbers is therefore 1,439.)*

## X. Dado, bishop of Verdun, to Rathbodus, archbishop of Trier, on behalf of the presbyter Adruinus, so that he may henceforth remain and be counted in his parish

To the most reverend and holy Rathbodus, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, Dado, devoted servant of Christ’s flock from the Church of Verdun, [Col. 1396D] wishes in the Lord the blessedness of supreme happiness.

Since the holy Catholic Church is ready to follow the evangelical teaching which says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man,” and so forth; and since the Apostle commands us to pursue hospitality and to share in the needs of holy men: nevertheless, because of those who have a seared conscience, claiming to be simple while filled with diabolical cunning, and who say that they move from place to place for the sake of piety when in fact they are fugitives because of their own wickedness, and who say that they have been admitted to the sacred ministry when they have not, the holy Fathers decreed that no bishop should receive an alien and unknown cleric or enthrone him in his Church unless he possesses from his own bishop a letter which in the canons is called a *formata*.

Therefore we make known to your fatherhood that this brother of ours who is present here, the bearer of this letter, named Adruinus, was not expelled by us on account of his wickedness. Rather, at the request of our brothers, since he had belonged to our household, we granted him the freedom canonically received from the horn of the altar, and ordained him to the rank of presbyter. We have also made for him this letter of dismissal, or letter of recommendation, and send him to your beloved fraternity, so that he may be able to remain in your parish under your sacred governance and protection.

I, then, in the name of Π, the Father, and of Υ, the Son, and of Α, the Holy Spirit, and in the unity of the holy Church, in which the right of binding and loosing was given to Peter, I, Dado, humble bishop, release the presbyter Adruinus from the city of Verdun, in the ninth indiction, and I grant you, Ratbod, venerable archbishop, permission to enthrone him in whatever church of your parish you wish. May almighty God deign to preserve your beloved fatherhood, distinguished by the flowers of virtue.

**AMEN. DCCLXXVIII. Π. Υ. Δ. Π. Δ. Δ. Δ. Θ. . Τ.**

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 906, in the ninth indiction.

*[Note: The ninth indiction in the month of May, and the episcopate of Dado, correspond to the year of Christ 906. The sum of the numbers expressed at the end and represented by Greek letters is formed from the common number DCLX and the proper number CXVIII, which the letters Δ, Α, Ρ, Δ produce, together with the ninth indiction. The total sum of all of them is therefore DCCLXXVIII.]*

### XI. Π, Υ, Α, Π, Δ, Α, Θ, Η, Μ Χ. Bishop Durandus of Clermont to Radulf of Tours, concerning a certain subdeacon whom he entrusts to his care.

Durandus, bishop of Clermont by the grace of God, to Rodulfus, most excellent archbishop of Tours: on earth may things go well for you, and in heaven may they go better and more blessedly.

May your belovedness learn that this subdeacon who is present here, whom we consecrated with our own hand, mercifully requested from us a properly formed letter and every canonical authorization, as ought to be made between the giver and the recipient, so that, secure by this authorization, he might be able by right to submit himself to your jurisdiction.

Granting his requests, we send to your nobility this letter formed according to canonical institution, so that him whom we now commend by our request to the custody of your holiness, you may, by our free permission, promote to whatever office or rank seems appropriate, and may lawfully exercise over him all the authority which until now we were permitted to exercise. And so that no scruple of hesitation may remain in your mind, we have written at the beginning and at the end the signs which the holy Fathers established at the Council of Nicaea should be written in letters of this kind.

**AMEN.**

*[Note: The letters prefixed to the beginning do not appear sufficiently complete, and the fact that the subdeacon’s name is not given makes the matter obscure. From the date of the *formata*, however, it may be conjectured that it belongs to the period of Durandus’s death, which is known to have occurred in the year 1095, near the beginning of Urban II’s Council of Clermont. Thus far there have been eleven examples of formularies, identified by the names of their authors. To these may be added, at the end, another general form, which is read as number 12 among the old formularies published after Marculf. It is as follows:]*

### General form of a letter of authorization

In the most holy name of God, to that most reverend brother, Bishop So-and-so: Bishop So-and-so of the city of So-and-so sends everlasting salvation in the Lord.

Let your fraternity, or charity, know that this presbyter who is present here, named So-and-so, was educated in sacred letters in our parish and in our church, and from childhood was with us or with our predecessors, having a good reputation, maintaining good self-restraint, and leading an innocent life.

Therefore it has now pleased him to transfer to another Church, wishing to seek for himself an elder who may assist him in temporal matters, and to whom he may render service according to the ministry entrusted to him. Accordingly, we make known to your fraternity that, whoever may wish to receive him, may do so without any ambiguity, knowing that he is a man of good reputation and that he has received from us permission to depart from the Church which has been entrusted to us to govern.

And so that this letter may possess firmer authority and be more readily believed, we have confirmed it below with our own hand.

---

## THE BLESSING OF GOD

That is, a little commentary on how God is especially to be blessed and praised through the Psalms. Compiled for the most part from Cassiodorus and Isidore by an anonymous writer, apparently a monk of Regensburg, for Bathuric, bishop of Regensburg, who held that see in the year 814 of the Redeemer. First published through the efforts of Petrus Stevartius of Liège, doctor and professor of sacred theology, and so forth.

*(Library of the Ancient Fathers, Lyons, vol. XXVII, Supplement.)*

The following little work, good reader, which deserves the first place among the anonymous writings, is placed here last through the negligence of the typesetters.

### PETRUS STEVARTIUS OF LIÈGE SENDS GREETINGS TO THE READER

This little commentary, compiled several hundred years ago from the words of the ancient Fathers, seemed worth adding to the others, since after thirty-two years during which I publicly lectured on Holy Scripture at the Academy of Ingolstadt, I have begun this very year to undertake an explanation of the Psalms of David. This booklet contains no small number of things that can greatly contribute to the commendation and understanding of the Psalms discussed.

The compiler of this little work—whoever he was—followed the established practice of certain men who, whenever they wrote something, always preferred to speak in the words of the ancients rather than in their own. The same practice may also be seen in some of the commentaries of the venerable Bede.

You, friendly reader, enjoy this little book, now published for the first time, and put into practice what it teaches. Yet it teaches nothing other than what that angel taught who gave this admonition to Tobit and his family: “Bless the God of heaven and confess before all the living that he has shown his mercy toward you” (Tobit 12:6).

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

### To Bathuric, bishop of Regensburg

To the lord Bathuric, ever to be venerated in Christ, bishop.

Burning with love for your desire, mindful of your kindness and charity and of the conversations we have often held together concerning the duties of divine service—namely, with what reverence and honor they ought to be celebrated—I searched, according to the limitations of my understanding, the writings of the holy and venerable teachers. From them I gathered, with whatever brevity I could, certain little flowers and offered them to you for rereading, so that, through your study, the great sweetness received from them might be offered before the divine presence.

These excerpts are drawn chiefly from explanations of the Psalms, which by a certain privilege of the Godhead are consecrated to praise. Our holy Fathers and doctors of the Church explained them: Jerome, Augustine, and Cassiodorus, that great and eloquent man. I have also included material from Isidore concerning antiphons, responsories, and other matters, as well as admonitions from Bede, that outstanding teacher, so that what you meanwhile reverently perform, having observed the authority of the Fathers, may kindle in your Church an even more fervent desire, stirred by divine grace, to carry these things out with greater devotion.

As I traveled through many places, I happened to hear the divine offices celebrated disorderly and without any pleasure for those who heard them. There are some who enter the church merely out of shame before men, lest they perhaps be judged lazy by them; without antiphons, hurriedly and with every possible speed, so that they may leave sooner to attend to the care of the flesh, they negligently assist at the divine praises, although they are considered diligent in worldly activities.

They do not know that the holy teachers and instructors of the Church, filled with the Holy Spirit and the grace of God, established a most proper melody in the repetition of antiphons or responsories, so that, through this sweetness, the minds of those listening might be delighted and stirred more ardently to the praises of God and to love of the heavenly homeland. Such people not only fail to stir others to praise God, but do not stir themselves either. For if they could do so without shame, they would abandon the practice altogether.

Others—who, shameful as it is to say, include even bishops—devote the entire day to banquets and drinking, and almost until the middle of the night, or until cockcrow, or even longer, take pains to satisfy their appetite with various drinks. To them applies what the Holy Spirit said through Solomon: “For whom is woe? For whom is sorrow? For whom are quarrels? For whom are pits? For whom are wounds without cause? For whom are bloodshot eyes? Is it not for those who linger over wine and devote themselves to drinking cups?” (Proverbs 23:29–30.)

And likewise the prophet’s words: “The harp and lyre and tambourine, and flute and wine are in your feasts; but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands” (Isaiah 5:12).

Such men, more concerned to please human beings than God, before going to sleep lazily perform the night watches, then immediately lie down on their beds until the time for eating and drinking returns. When they rise, as they put on their clothing, they perform the daytime offices, thinking it sufficient if they chant them somehow or other; unaware that hours have been established in the holy Church at which the offices of divine service are to be performed by day and by night: matins, prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, and compline.

Of these the Prophet said: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118:164). Concerning the nocturnal watches he said: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (ibid., 62). And elsewhere concerning the morning offices: “In the mornings I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper” (Psalm 62:7).

At these hours we must return praises with the utmost devotion to our Creator. The remaining hours have been granted for our own uses. If we neglect them, we oppose the institutions of the holy Fathers, and it is dangerous to oppose them. Those who strive to attack the institutions of the holy Church—not in words, perhaps, but in deeds—cannot possess communion with it. For they do not celebrate what is most important in the holy Church, namely, the melodious psalmody of divine praise and the solemnities of the Mass, either at the proper times or with religious devotion.

I do not wish, by mentioning such things, to accuse you; rather, with the greatest humility and submission, I presume to warn you not to become participants in them. For this reason I have offered a few sayings of the holy Fathers which follow, so that, avoiding the error of these men and following their example, you may perform without reproach before God and human beings the works of God, worthy of the divine presence, with vigor in your Church. Thus, just as you are distinguished in other admirable and praiseworthy works, so may you also shine in this, so that by your example the laziness of those mentioned above may be corrected.

These few things, lord Father, I have gathered from many sources solely at the prompting of charity and love. Although your discernment may be able to find better things, as they exist in the sayings of the holy Fathers, receive them with the greatest gratitude, so that my labor may be completed through your devotion. I always wish you good health in the Lord, remembering you kindly.

## ON THE PRAISE OF THE PSALMS AND THE PSALTER

From Cassiodorus’s preface to the Psalms.

After I had at last set aside in the city of Ravenna the cares of office and the worldly concerns seasoned with harmful flavor, and had tasted the heavenly honey of souls contained in the Psalter, I eagerly undertook the task of an investigator, as those who desire something customarily do, so that after the bitterest activities I might sweetly absorb saving words.

But a familiar obscurity confronts beginners, woven through various persons and veiled in parables. This obscurity is passed over in the life-giving writings through a harmful concealment, although one often encounters something ambiguous that bears the secret of a great mystery.

Then I turned to the celebrated reading of Augustine, that most eloquent Father, in which such an abundance of statements had been amassed that what has been thoroughly explained can scarcely be retained after rereading. I believe that, when he wished to fill the hungry peoples with ecclesiastical food, the streams of so great a preaching necessarily flowed forth.

Therefore, mindful of my weakness, with the mercy of God bestowing the gift, I have led the sea poured forth from the springs of certain of his Psalms into shallow streams, in a concise abridgment, encompassing in one book what he wonderfully explained in fifteen decades.

Yet, as someone says concerning Homer, “To steal something from his meaning is like taking Hercules’ club from his hand.” For he is an outstanding teacher of all literature and, what is rare in such abundance, an extremely cautious disputant. He flows like a purest spring, polluted by no dregs, persevering in the integrity of faith. He does not know how to give heretics anything with which they might defend themselves in debate. He is entirely Catholic, entirely orthodox; and, shining in the Church of the Lord with most gentle brilliance, he radiates with the splendor of heavenly light.

After so remarkable a teacher, I have added certain newly discovered material, presuming only upon the Lord, who grants confidence to little ones, sight to the blind, speech to the mute, and hearing to the deaf.

I have divided this book, together with its prefaces, into three sections of fifty Psalms each, so that the clarity of the text might reveal itself more beautifully to sounder eyes and so that, for the desire of the reading brothers, the numerous parts of the book might be available. Thus one copy has been left for the protection of the library, while for the benefit of the community it has perhaps been most conveniently divided.

Therefore, trusting in the Lord’s command, let us knock at the gates of the heavenly mystery, so that he may open to our understanding the flower-bearing dwellings, and so that, introduced safely into that heavenly paradise, we may pluck spiritual fruits without any transgression like that of the first man.

A truly shining book, a word made luminous [*sermo lampabilis*; note: thus in the manuscript and also in the printed text. Cassiodorus derives the expression from *lampas*, “lamp,” as though meaning “a lucid word that gives light”]; the care of the wounded heart, the inner honeycomb of the human being, a tablet of spiritual persons, the hidden language of virtues. It bends the proud to humility and subjects kings to the poor; through its graciousness it nourishes little ones.

What beauty of meaning and what medicine of dripping words are found there, so that Solomon’s statement in the Song of Songs may rightly be applied to it: “A garden enclosed and a sealed fountain, a paradise full of every kind of fruit” (Song of Songs 4).

At one moment, formed by the saving instruction of the Psalms, people turn troubled and stormy spirits toward a clear and utterly tranquil life. At another, they promise that God will become visibly human for the salvation of believers and will come to judge the world. At another, they admonish us to wash away sins with tears and heal offenses through almsgiving. At another, they are reverently awestruck by sacred prayers; at another, profound through the power of the Hebrew alphabet; at another, they proclaim saving things about the Lord’s passion and resurrection; at another, they are most compassionate in the lamentation of mourners; at another, they disclose certain mysteries to us through the repetition of verses; at another, they are marvelous in the ascent of the Songs of Degrees; finally, they joyfully cling to heavenly praises.

They are blessed in abundance, an inexplicable desire, an astonishing depth. The faithful mind that has begun to be nourished from them cannot be filled to satiety.

The Psalms, finally, are what make our vigils welcome, when in the silent night, as choirs sing psalms, the human voice breaks forth into music; and, through words skillfully modulated, makes us return to him from whom divine speech came for the salvation of the human race.

The song delights the ears and instructs souls; it becomes one voice among those singing psalms, and with the angels of God, whom we cannot hear, we mingle words of praise—through him, that is, who came from the seed of David, the Lord Christ, as he himself says in the Apocalypse: “I am the root and origin of David” (Revelation 22:16). From him we have received saving religion and have come to know the revealed mysteries of the Holy Trinity.

Therefore one glory is rightly joined to them—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that their praises may be recognized as perfect. They bring the coming day through morning rejoicing; they dedicate the first hour of the day to us; they consecrate the third hour to us; they gladden the sixth hour with the breaking of bread; they release our fasts at the ninth hour; they conclude the final part of the day; and, at the coming of night, they prevent our mind from being darkened, as they themselves say: “Night is my illumination in my delights, for darkness will not be darkened by you, O Lord” (Psalm 138:11–12). Thus anyone who does not enjoy the delight of this gift may rightly consider himself estranged from true life.

To summarize their powers briefly, divine speech will say in Psalm 70: “But I will confess your truth to you in the vessels of the Psalms.” Truly, they are vessels of truth, containing so many virtues, filled with so many divine fragrances, and heaped with so many heavenly treasures.

They are jars receiving heavenly wine and always preserving its purity in freshness. They are a marvelous sweetness that does not turn sour through the corruptions of the world, but, remaining in its own dignity, is continually increased by the grace of the purest sweetness. They are a very well-stocked storeroom: although such great peoples of the earth drink from it, its abundance never runs out.

How marvelous a sweetness flows from them! They imitate a sweet-sounding organ through human voices. They return the sound of trumpets in grandiloquent cries. They construct a vocal lyre through the mingling of living strings. Whatever once seemed to be performed through musical instruments is now shown to be accomplished through rational beings.

Nevertheless, we must not sing merely like parrots and blackbirds, which, while trying to imitate our words, are utterly unaware of what they sing. A pleasing melody delights the mind, but does not compel it to fruitful tears. It caresses the ears but does not raise those who hear it to heavenly things.

We are pierced in the heart, however, if we are able to notice what we say with our mouth, as it is written in the Psalter: “Blessed is the people who understand the joyful shout” (Psalm 85:16); and again: “For God is King of all the earth; sing psalms with wisdom” (Psalm 46:8).

When the apostle Philip learned that the eunuch of Queen Candace was reading Isaiah, he suitably explained the holy Scriptures to him. After he understood what he was reading, he immediately sought the grace of baptism, and soon received the gifts of salvation perfectly (Acts 8:27, 39).

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart” (Matthew 13:19). From this it is rightly understood that such things cannot happen to those who deserve to attend to the holy Scriptures with a pure heart.

The Father Jerome beautifully says of this: “Divine Scripture is a certain pearl, and it can be pierced from many sides. Therefore, apostolic Father, you who by God’s favor have rendered heavenly writings through holy morals, prompted by your example I shall enter the divine abysses—you who mercifully correct errors and do not harshly reckon against one what you amend.”

But before I reach the spiritual storehouses, I think that certain matters should be tasted in advance in separate chapters, seventeen in number, so that when the place of those matters presents itself, the drink of great nectar may be drawn with the sweetest delights.

1. Something must also be said about the various kinds of prophecy, so that we may be taught more distinctly what this Davidic prophecy is.

2. Why different names, as though names of authors, are found in the titles of the Psalms.

3. What “for the end,” which is frequently found in the titles, signifies.

4. What the Psalter is, or why the Psalms are so called.

5. What a Psalm is.

6. What a song is.

7. What a psalm-song is.

8. What a song-psalm is.

9. Concerning the fivefold division.

10. Concerning the single inscription of the titles.

11. What the *diapsalma* is.

12. Whether the sequence of the Psalms should be divided into five books, or whether they should be called one book.

13. How Christ the Lord should be understood in the Psalms.

14. How the exposition of the Psalms has been arranged.

15. Concerning the eloquence of the whole divine law.

16. Concerning the particular eloquence of the Psalter.

17. Praise of the Church.

Now, with the Lord’s help, let us proceed according to the order set out above.

## I. Concerning prophecy

Prophecy is a divine breathing-in which announces events with immovable truth, either through deeds or through the words of certain people. Someone aptly said of it: “Prophecy is a sweet utterance of heavenly teaching, composing honeycombs and the sweet honeys of divine speech.”

Therefore David himself says in Psalm 118: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.”

The gifts of this grace were bestowed in many ways. To include a few among the many, it was expressed through human actions, as in Noah’s ark, Abraham’s sacrifice, and the crossing of the Red Sea. It was also expressed through the births of the twins Esau and Jacob, who bore the mysteries of future events; through angels, as when they spoke to Abraham, Lot, Zechariah, and Mary; through visions, as to Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the other saints; through dreams, as to Solomon and Daniel; and through a cloud and a voice from heaven, as to Moses.

It is therefore clear that, in David’s case, prophecy was fulfilled not through human actions, not through the birth of twins, not through angels, not through visions, not through dreams, not through a cloud and a voice from heaven, nor through any other method, but through heavenly inspiration, as we read of him in the First Book of Kings: “And the Spirit of the Lord was directed into David from that day and thereafter.”

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “If David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how can you say that he is his son?” (Matthew 22:45). By this statement we recognize clearly that the Psalms were prophesied through the Holy Spirit.

It should certainly be known that every prophecy either speaks or does something concerning past, present, or future time.

It should also be noted that the Holy Spirit was attributed to the most holy prophets in such a way that, for a time, because of the weakness of the flesh and the opposition of sin, he might depart from them when offended, and, once appeased, return at the appropriate time.

Thus Saint Jerome, explaining the Evangelist Mark at the passage where he says concerning John, “He saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him” (Matthew 3:16), treated the matter with such evident reasoning that no one should presume to oppose his judgment.

In Psalm 50 also, the Prophet asks as a prophet: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” For if, as blessed Jerome says, divine speech were always present in the prophets and had a perpetual dwelling in their hearts, Ezekiel would never so often write: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying” (Ezekiel 6:1; 7:1).

Moreover, in the Book of Kings, the prophet Elisha says concerning the woman whose son had died: “Let her alone, for she is in bitterness; and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not told me” (4 Kings 4:27).

The Apostle also says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Corinthians 7:25). Likewise he says: “This I command—not the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:10; Vulgate: “not I, but the Lord”). And elsewhere he says: “What I speak according to God” (2 Corinthians 11:17; Vulgate: “what I do not speak according to God”).

Similarly, then, to the other prophets the Lord spoke some things and not the prophet, while the prophets spoke some things and not the Lord.

John the Baptist would not have said this specifically concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: “The one who sent me to baptize said to me: Upon whoever you see the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). For the words “remaining upon him” would never be peculiar to the Lord Christ if they did not show that the Spirit sometimes departed from others.

In Christ he remained because Christ had no sin. From others he rightly departed because they had received the stain of pollution. The Holy Spirit cannot have communion with sins, for it is written in the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon: “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom 1:5).

Prophecy is a most exalted and truthful mode of speaking, not composed by human will but poured forth by divine inspiration, as the Apostle Peter says: “For prophecy was not brought forth at any time by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

The Apostle Paul also says: “Whoever prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation” (1 Corinthians 14:4). And shortly afterward: “Whoever prophesies edifies the Church” (1 Corinthians 14:4).

He plainly edifies when, through the benefit of foretelling, he makes unknown and exceedingly necessary matters thoroughly known. Those who have been given the ability to understand or interpret the divine Scriptures also do not seem excluded from the gift of prophecy, as the Apostle says in his First Epistle to the Corinthians: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.”

But since we have perhaps adequately learned what is read concerning the gifts of prophecy, let us now carefully examine what remains.

## II. Why different names, as though names of authors, are found in the titles of the Psalms

In the First Book of Chronicles we read that, when the prophet David had grown old in devoted service to the Lord, he selected four thousand young men from the people of Israel to sing with great joy in heavenly grace the Psalms which he himself had produced by the Lord’s inspiration—on organs, lyres, *nabli*, tambourines, cymbals, trumpets, and with their own voices.

This sweet union was divided into three parts. The rational part belonged to the human voice; the irrational part to the musical instruments. The common part was fitted from both, so that the human voice might be produced in definite melodies and the melody of the instruments might be joined to it in harmonious proximity.

Thus that sweet and joyful music prophetically signified the Catholic Church, which, from diverse languages and varied harmonies, was destined, by the Lord’s favor, to believe in one concord of faith.

From this number of singers we frequently find names inserted in the titles, such as Idithun, Asaph, the sons of Korah, and similar names. This is not because they were, as some wish, the authors of the Psalms, but because, like overseers placed over craftsmen, they proved to be trustworthy administrators of those matters. They deserved honor through such mention because they served the sacred office with devoted minds, especially since their names are also understood to indicate meanings appropriate to the matters involved.

For we do not read that the men mentioned above were chosen to compose the Psalms; we read only that they were gathered to sing. No history testifies that they were psalm-writers. To assert otherwise is presumptuous, since it cannot be confirmed by any authority.

That the Psalms belong solely to the prophet David is declared by sure indications. Finally, in the Apocalypse, wishing this work to be understood, the Lord mentions David alone, saying: “Thus says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” (Revelation 3:7).

In the Gospel, too, the Lord himself says to the Pharisees: “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: The Lord said to my Lord, etc.?” (Matthew 22:43–44).

Thus it is proved that all the Psalms belong not to many people but only to him whom we know was named by the Lord. The practice of the Catholic Church, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, holds generally and immovably that whenever one of those Psalms which are marked with various names is to be sung, the reader must proclaim nothing other than the Psalms of David.

If they belonged individually to Idithun, the sons of Korah, Asaph, or Moses, their names would certainly be proclaimed, just as in the Gospels they are identified by the names of Mark, Luke, or John. Following this view, Father Augustine also appropriately says that all the Psalms are Davidic.

## III. What “for the end,” frequently found in the titles, signifies

We use the word “end” in two ways.

The first is the ordinary and mortal sense, when something has been brought to its conclusion and can proceed no farther, having reached the limit of its movement. Thus we speak of food as finished when it has been consumed by careful eating, of money as finished when it has been spent, and of other things which are said in this way.

The second is the perfect and perpetual end, which we are now seeking. This end begins to extend and expand for us when the devout mind reaches it.

The end, therefore, and fullness of the Law is our Lord Christ, as the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). When we reach him, we will seek nothing further; content with the end of blessedness in him, we will enjoy the fullest delight.

His love advances in proportion as our understanding, by the Lord’s favor, grows brighter. Therefore, whenever you find “end” in the titles of the Psalms, direct your gaze toward the Lord the Savior, who is the end without end and the completing perfection of all good things.

## IV. What the Psalter is, or why the Psalms are so called

The Psalter, as Jerome says, is a resonant hollow of wood shaped like the letter Δ, having a broad belly in its upper part. The strings are fastened there and, struck methodically with a plectrum, are said to produce a most pleasing song.

Its position appears contrary to that of the lyre: what the Psalter contains below, the lyre, in the reverse arrangement, bears at its top.

This kind of sonorous and distinctive instrument is suited to the body of the Lord the Savior. For just as the Psalter sounds from above, so that body celebrates from on high the glory of its divine institution, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth; but whoever comes from heaven testifies to what he has seen and heard” (John 3:31–32; the supplied citation reads “Joan. XXXIII, 32”).

For this reason some have determined that this Davidic work is called the Psalms because it is known to resound from the heavenly summit. Understand, however, that only the Psalms contained in this volume are called Psalms in accordance with their excellence.

That the Psalter is a type of musical instrument is also testified by the prophet Daniel, who says: “The sound of the trumpet, pipe, *sambuca*, lyre, psalter, and symphony, and every kind of musical instrument.”

The Second Book of Chronicles also explains this when it says that steps were made in the house of the Lord and in the royal house from thyine wood, commonly called *evelina* [Greek: πεύκινα, “of pine”], and that lyres and psalteries were provided for the singers (2 Chronicles 9:31; the supplied citation reads II Par. IX, 31). Among the Hebrews this is called the *nablum*, a term that is nevertheless frequently used in the book mentioned above.

The word *psalm* itself is plainly Greek. Some wish it to be derived from ἀπὸ τοῦ ψάλλειν (*apo tou psallein*), that is, “from touching.” We also call those who play the psalteries *citharoedi*, because with a trained thumb they produce musical melodies.

## V. What a Psalm is

A Psalm is a sweet and melodious modulation poured forth from the musical instrument alone—that is, from the Psalter.

## VI. What a song is

A song is what is sung to the honor of God when someone uses the freedom of his own voice and is not joined to any talkative musical instrument by a harmonious melody. This is what is now performed in the praises of the Godhead.

## VII. What a psalm-song is

A psalm-song existed when, with a musical instrument leading, a singing choir acclaimed with joined voices, obeying only the divine words.

## VIII. What a song-psalm is

A song-psalm existed when, with the choir leading, the art of the musical instrument was graciously fitted into one harmony, and the words of the divine hymn resounded in a sweet union.

## IX. Concerning the fivefold division
This fivefold division that we have described I shall point out, as each category can appropriately correspond to the titles of the Psalms, in the most suitable places, where they convey by mystical interpretation a certain significance to the matters that follow. But since there are also other numerous superscriptions, which I do not think should be passed over, I judge that they should be briefly gathered into a single conclusion, so that the reader may neither incur weariness nor perhaps miss something necessary for understanding.

## X. On the Unified Significance of the Titles

It is clear that certain superscriptions of the Psalms are to be understood spiritually through a similar allusion. For if one does not consider the letter, it is strange, since one does not find in the Psalms the things contained in the titles. But if they are drawn toward a figurative understanding, they appear exceedingly appropriate. Such is the case where events are indicated—for example, “when he fled from the face of Absalom.” Elsewhere a place is indicated, as in “when he was in the desert of Idumaea.” Elsewhere a day, as in “on the first day of the Sabbath.” Elsewhere Hebrew names, as in “Jeduthun.” Elsewhere a comparison of events is made, namely, “when he changed his appearance before Abimelech.” Or a comparison with similar things, namely, “for the winepresses.”

Therefore, in the superscriptions of the titles, whether you happen to find “psalm,” “song,” “psalm-song,” “song-psalm,” “for the end,” or something belonging to the sixth combination that we mentioned; or whether you recognize one, two, three, or four of these inserted individually, draw them toward those virtues, because the recollection of these matters is subtly found to have been placed there as a likeness of hidden understanding.

For these hang before the entrances of the Psalms like sacred veils; and if you direct the gaze of your mind through them, as certain threads grow thin, you will easily behold their inner chambers. Who, indeed, thinks that the reasons for so many different names are idle, when it is impious to believe that the divine Scriptures contain anything superfluous? For it is written: “Amen, amen, I say to you, not one iota or one jot will pass from the law until all things are fulfilled” (Matt. 5:18).

## XI. What the Diapsalm Is

Among interpreters of the Psalms, a certain difference of opinion is known to have arisen concerning this term. Jerome, the most learned investigator of the Hebrew language, affirms that it is a continuation of the Holy Spirit, because *diapsalm* means “always.”

But blessed Augustine, the most subtle investigator of obscure matters, moving without stumbling among difficult questions, is known to have preferred this interpretation: that it should rather appear to be a division. Examining the quality of the term itself, he says that **σύμψαλμα** (*sympsalma*), as it is called in Greek, means a joined combination of voices, whereas **διάψαλμα** (*diapsalma*) teaches a broken continuation of speech, indicating that wherever it is found there is a change either of persons or of matters.

Therefore this term is rightly inserted where either the meaning or the person is shown to be divided. Accordingly, we too shall appropriately make divisions wherever a diapsalm may be found in the Psalms.

As for the remaining instances, we shall investigate them as opportunity permits, although the authority of this term may not be found there.

## XII. Whether the Text of the Psalms Is to Be Divided into Five Books, or Whether It Should Properly Be Called One Book

[Col. 1410B]

Blessed Jerome thought that the prophecy of the Psalms should be divided into five books, because in the text of this work one reads, at the fourth division, “Let it be, let it be.” Since this word intervenes, the work seems to disclose some division. Later generations agreed with him, I believe because they judged that they were consulting their own interests: what was cut into many parts was burdensome in its tedious length.

But Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, a most acute and profound investigator of divine matters, more appropriately judges that the Psalms ought to be called one book, because in Hebrew it is one volume, and especially because in the Acts of the Apostles it is written, “in the book of Psalms” (Acts 1:20).

Therefore it is rightly called one book, since it is supported by such authority.

## XIII. How Christ the Lord Is to Be Understood in the Psalms

The Psalms speak about the person of the Lord Jesus Christ in three ways, for the instruction of the faithful.

First, through what is known to belong to his humanity, as in the second Psalm: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” And in Psalm 20: “You granted him the desire of his heart, and you did not deprive him of the will of his lips.”

Second, through what shows him to be equal and coeternal with the Father, as in that same Psalm 2: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” And in Psalm 109: “With you is dominion on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

Third, through the members of the Church, whose leader and head is Christ himself, as in Psalm 21: “Far from my salvation are the words of my offenses.” And in Psalm 68: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you.” We ought to understand this statement as spoken on behalf of each of the faithful. For the rest, offenses are proved to be wholly alien to Christ. Hence Tichonius, in his *Books of Rules*, discussed this matter at greater length and with great care.

If we store this in our minds, we are disturbed by no confusion, because the greatest error arises when what is clearly said about one matter is inappropriately assigned elsewhere. For if he had spoken in only one way, who could have recognized his twofold substance, when even now, in so evident a distinction, some strive through sacrilegious intent to confuse the divine and human nature of the Lord Christ?

He also gives many admonitions according to the literal sense; he commands many things spiritually; and he appropriately changes persons suddenly, so that at one time Christ appears to speak as God, the incarnate Word and the man made head of the Church; at another time the Church herself; at another, a righteous man; at another, a penitent—so that he may touch upon and embrace everything necessary.

Everywhere the sacred utterance vibrates, full of heavenly realities, and through the manifold diversity of its virtues the merciful Redeemer reveals the mysteries of his kingdom, to bestow salvation upon the human race. We have said these things beforehand so that, when the reader comes to such passages, he may fearlessly hear what he recognizes himself already to have learned for his salvation.

Nevertheless, by the authority of the Fathers and by the firmest testimony of the truth itself, this must be held with unwavering faith: that one from the Trinity, or one person of the Trinity—God the Word—through spontaneous power and not through ministering necessity, became man from the Virgin Mary out of pity for mortals. He neither endured any change in his own nature nor, through the assumption of flesh, increased the Trinity; but, as someone has said: “He washed away our stains in blood, and also stretched out our wrinkles upon the cross.”

Although this is the unique safeguard of our hope, the blessedness of believers, and the great happiness of the righteous, heretics do not cease, through impious intent, to gnaw at what is known to have provided the human race with the cause of salvation.

## XIV. How the Exposition of the Psalms Is Arranged

First, with the Lord’s help, we must speak about the inscription of the titles. From these, as from full breasts, the milk of divine preaching flows forth.

Then each Psalm must be examined according to its own character, lest either a hidden change of subject or the variety of the speakers introduced into it confuse our understanding.

Third, I shall attempt to disclose the mystery of the Psalm, partly according to spiritual understanding, partly according to historical reading, and partly according to mystical meaning, examining the subtleties of the matters and, insofar as granted, the particular properties of the words.

Fourth, as the passage requires, I shall strive briefly to demonstrate its virtue, so that the intention of the ordered poem may, by divine gift, shine upon the eyes within.

By the virtue of the Psalm I mean the divine inspiration by which heavenly intention is opened to us; through Davidic speech it removes us from vices and persuades us to live rightly.

Fifth, when the matter requires it, we shall mention the order of the number of the Psalms, which has been sanctified by the honor of matters most worthy of reverence. We admit that it would have been difficult for us to do this for every single Psalm, since the authority of the Fathers has left the matter indeterminate and unresolved. Let the diligent investigator seek out the remaining reckonings for himself, since many things in the divine Scriptures will become clear with the passage of time that now appear hidden.

In the conclusions, we shall either encompass the whole Psalm in brief summary, or say something directed toward destroying heresies. For this is the true love of the Lord: to hate his adversaries with perfect hatred.

## XV. On the Eloquence of the Entire Divine Law

The eloquence of the divine law was not formed according to human modes of speech, nor does it proceed through confused and uncertain circumlocutions, so that it might either abandon past matters through forgetfulness, be disturbed by the confusion of present matters, or be deceived by the uncertain accidents of the future. Rather, speaking to the heart and not to bodily ears, judging all things with great truth and great firmness of foreknowledge, it stands established in the truth of its Author.

Thus it is said in the Gospel concerning the preaching of the Lord Christ: “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 7:29). He speaks without uncertainty to whom all things are present and to whom the outcomes of events are shown to be subject.

Eloquence is speech suitable and beautiful for each matter. This chaste, firm, truthful, and eternal preaching therefore shines with exceedingly pure eloquence. Its usefulness gleams; the magnificence of its virtue appears; the work of salvation delights, as it will also say in Psalm 118: “Your utterance will give me life”; and again: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths.” Truly it is light, because it always commands what gives life, forbids what is harmful, removes earthly things, and persuades us toward heavenly things.

For this reason the Teacher of the Gentiles also writes in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power.” The same apostle recalls in the Second Epistle to Timothy, saying: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproving, for instructing, and for correcting in the discipline that belongs to righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”

As the authority of Father Jerome testifies, among the Hebrews this work is composed either according to rhythm or according to metrical law, which, as they themselves say, is contained in *fastutiae*. For *fastutium* is a conception proceeding through cola and skillfully unfolded for expressing meaning.

If you diligently investigate its power, hear the Apostle speaking to the Hebrews: “For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

The sacred profundity of divine Scripture has such common and accessible speech that everyone admits it without hesitation. Yet it conceals the secret things of truth, so that within those very words the life-giving meaning must be sought with the greatest diligence. It is chiefly granted to be understood as divine from this fact: the uneducated are perceived to have been able to transmit the most subtle things, temporal people eternal things, only when filled with the divine Spirit.

Finally, how many miracles were continually performed until Scripture itself, spread throughout the world, filled the compass of the earth, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5)! This provides the greatest proof that the divine law has been received throughout all parts of the world.

It exercises its various kinds of speech in many ways: concise in definitions, adorned with figures, marked by the particular properties of words, made clear through the combinations of syllogisms, and shining with disciplines. It does not merely receive foreign ornament from these things; rather, it confers its own dignity upon them. For when these elements shine in the divine Scriptures, they are certain and entirely pure. But when they come into the opinions of human beings and the most empty questions, they are tossed about by the ambiguous waves of disputation, so that what is always most firmly true here is often rendered uncertain elsewhere.

So also in our own language, when it sings the Psalms, it is adorned with the nobility of truth. But when it turns to foolish stories and blasphemous words, it is excluded from the honor of uprightness, as the apostle James says: “With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the image and likeness of God” (Jas. 3:9).

The experts in worldly arts—who clearly existed much later than the beginnings of the divine books—transferred these things to the collections of arguments that the Greeks call *topica*, and to the arts of dialectic and rhetoric, so that it might be evident to all that what was first given to right minds for expressing truth was later judged by the Gentiles to be suited to human wisdom.

These things shine in sacred readings like the brightest stars and fittingly illuminate the meanings of matters with the most useful brevity. We shall briefly point them out in the most appropriate places, since the matters themselves will most suitably bring them into view, through which the intended meanings will shine more clearly.

For Father Augustine also declared in Book III of *On Christian Teaching*: “Let the learned know that our authors used all the modes of speech which grammarians call by the Greek name *tropes.” And shortly afterward he continues: “Those who know these tropes—that is, the modes of speech—recognize them in the sacred writings, and through their knowledge are helped somewhat toward understanding them.”

He also made the clearest mention of this matter in other books of his. In the books he called *On the Modes of Speech*, he proved that various figures of secular literature are found in the sacred writings. He also declared that there are other modes proper to divine utterances, which grammarians and rhetoricians have not touched at all.

Other very learned Fathers have said this among us as well—namely Jerome, Ambrose, and Hilary—so that we may appear not to be presumptuous inventors of this matter, but followers.

But someone may say: “The parts of syllogisms themselves, the names of figures, the terms of the disciplines, and other things of this kind are nowhere at all found in the Psalms.”

They are plainly found in the power of the meanings, not in the utterance of the words. Thus we contemplate wine in the vines, the harvest in the seed, leaves in the roots, fruits in the branches, and the trees themselves in their kernels. A delicious fish is also drawn from the deepest abyss, although before it is caught it is not seen by human eyes.

Therefore we rightly say that those things exist which we nevertheless perceive to be present in their power. For the Apostle forbids us to be led astray by the empty wisdom of the world (Eph. 5:6); yet he does not deny that these things exist in the divine writings.

Let us certainly approach the Psalms and ask the testimony of the matters themselves, which is greater than every argument.

This principal, virginal, and saving kind of speech often reports certain matters, and frequently explains things quite different from what is heard. It possesses a twofold simplicity and a guileless double speech, as Joseph did. Although he had recognized his brothers by their very appearance and native speech, he appeared to speak to them in such a way that he could not at all be recognized (Gen. 42:8). This was not undertaken for the purpose of deception, but was brought about for the advantage of a great benefit.

It employs Hebrew expressions, suggesting the deepest causes. It frequently places one thing in both evil and good, so that what appears to be common by name may be shown to differ in quality. It compares heavenly things with earthly things, so that what the incomprehensible greatness forbids us to understand may be perceived through familiar likenesses.

There is marvelous power in the sowing of words, so that things suddenly hidden and incomprehensible may be explained in two or three expressions. What could I say more briefly? Frequently even one syllable demonstrates the ineffable nature of the Lord, as in: “He Who Is sent me” (Exod. 3:14). Every word of this statement, carefully investigated, pours forth an abundance of meanings.

For just as a most fertile field produces fragrant herbs suited to our health, so divine reading, whenever it is examined word by word, always contains there a remedy for the wounded mind.

Many Fathers have spoken at greater length and more extensively about the modes of this eloquence; we have decided that their names should be mentioned in the introductory books. But that heavenly fountain, the more constantly it is known to be drawn from, the less it knows exhaustion.

And so that we may not linger longer in generalities, let us, with the Lord’s help, touch upon the particular features of the Psalter. For the matter itself is clearly recognized: after general matters have been set forth, it is then described according to some particular property.

## XVI. On the Particular Eloquence of the Psalter

First, the Psalms alone are called by this singular name. With the assistance of experts in this language, and by comparing them with their volume, we judged that they should be rendered in the verses proper to them, preserving the usage of those who sing the Psalms, lest an authority mingled into an assumed order cause confusion.

Next, no other work of divine authority is contained in 150 sections. Where else are so many titles written with such varied diversity? Here the votive name *Alleluia* begins in the superscriptions; here a recollection of history drawn from the Book of Kings, placed at the very threshold, is known to indicate the virtues of the Psalms; here only diapsalms are shown to have been inserted; here the Psalms hold the orders of numbers according to their virtues.

The book begins with the blessedness of Christ, passes through the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments, and concludes with sacred praises and holy jubilation, so that the Church rightly consoles herself with such a gift. Here she is known to be wounded by the afflictions of many calamities.

For she knows, by the Lord’s favor, how to triumph even when weighed down by her disasters. She progresses through persecutions, is always increased through afflictions, is watered by the blood of martyrs, is raised up more by sorrow, is enlarged by distress, is nourished by tears, is refreshed by fasts, and grows precisely from the point at which the world declines.

What will you not find in that book from which the human race ought sweetly to console itself? It is a treasure continually increasing in a pure heart, great consolation for those who mourn, the blessed hope of the righteous, and a useful refuge for those in danger. From it one always takes what is beneficial, while its fountain is preserved in unfailing continuity.

Blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, also says the following in the book that he sent to his dearest Marcellinus *On the Particular Character of the Psalter*, to use his own words:

“Whoever recites the words of the Psalter’s [Cassio’s, *of the Psalter*] Psalms sings them as his own words, and sings a Psalm as though he himself had written it. He does not take and read them as though someone else were speaking or as though they signified something about another person, but, as though he himself were speaking about himself, he utters words of this kind. And whatever is said, he seems to offer words to God as though he himself were acting accordingly and speaking from himself.”

It is also a particular property of the Psalter that through it one enters into the holiness of the divine law. Beginners do not begin with Genesis, nor with the Apostle; at the outset they do not approach the holy authority of the Gospel. Although the Psalter is the fourth book of divine authority, beginners who are beginning the sacred Scriptures appropriately make their first beginning in reading from it.

## XVII. Praise of the Church

O truly holy, O immaculate, O perfect mother Church, who, through the gift of divine grace, alone give life, alone sanctify, and through your instruction restore the human race, lost through its own sins. Nothing can be added to or taken away from your devout confession.

Throughout all the Psalms and all the songs, you insert proclamations of the Holy Trinity, so that praise and sweetest glory may always be returned to the one whose sacred words we speak.

You alone, in the likeness of that ark of Noah which clearly bore your image, sail steadily through the savage storms of this age and of the heretics, without injury to the course of faith and without danger from the flood. You do not yield to any errors, although you still remain amid the grave necessity of the perversities of this age.

Whatever is found outside your life-giving womb is certainly a deadly shipwreck. For while detestable Sabellius errs concerning the Father, mad Arius sins concerning the Son, sacrilegious Manes denies the Holy Spirit, other wicked men diminish the Old Testament, and some do not follow the grace of the New, you alone, through faithful devotion and with the Lord’s aid, embrace all things without stumbling.

You teach that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son. Proclaiming one God, the Holy Trinity, coeternal with itself and equally omnipotent, you confess that the Lord Christ, remaining in his divinity and in the flesh of the humanity he assumed, with the particular property of each nature preserved, is one person. You make the Old Testament testify to the New, recognizing that the New arose from the Old.

And, to embrace everything briefly, you do not know how to speak except of what ought to be believed. Although you are afflicted here by various distresses and shaken by the opposition of the deceitful enemy, nevertheless, gathered from the whole circle of the world and shining forth, you are carried toward the eternal kingdoms in the form of a most beautiful pyramid.

You are not improperly compared with this figure, because, raising a precious summit from all nations, you send the souls of the righteous, like a splendid light, toward the heavenly kingdoms. You are a rick full of heavenly grain; a blessed gathering of the holy from diverse peoples; a shining assembly of serene minds; an indissoluble structure built from living stones; the eternal happiness of all the blessed, brighter than the sun, whiter than snow, without spot and without wrinkle.

Concerning you it is written in the *Song of Songs*: “Who is this who comes forth like the dawn, rising, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?” And shortly afterward: “Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing, all bearing twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon” (Song 4:1–3)—mother and virgin, fruitful and intact, a parent and incorrupt, whose mouth exhales the fragrance of every virtue.

Concerning you the bridegroom says: “The fragrance of your mouth is like apples” (Song 7:8). And shortly afterward: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices. Your lips, O bride, drip with honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song 4:10–11).

You deserve, finally, to kiss Christ and to preserve that beauty, ever virgin. For it is said to you: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments” (Song 1:1–2), and the other things that that divine book embraces in mystical preaching.

Therefore, having, as I think, sufficiently prepared the hearers through a certain *isagoge*—which is an introduction to the work that follows, an index of heavenly mysteries, and a herald of sacred discourse—and having kindled them by divine generosity with heavenly desire, let us now, with Christ’s help, come to unfold what was promised.

[Col. 1416D]

Grant, O Lord, whose is everything that is beneficial, that we may deserve to be heard intelligently, willingly, and profitably. For we need your assistance in every way, so that we may be able, to some extent, through the speech granted to us, to expound the words of your majesty. Amen.

## Prolegomena, That Is, Matters to Be Said Beforehand

Before I taste the honey of the heavenly Psalter and, with the Lord’s favor, touch those glorious fields of his passion, certain things seem to me to be disclosed under divided headings concerning the text of the poem itself, so that we may teach readers more distinctly and may proceed through the very order without any impediment.

In the first part, the Lord’s bodily life is described.

[Col. 1417A]

In the second, the nature of his divinity is subtly indicated.

Third, it speaks of the peoples multiplied against him, who were striving to destroy him.

Fourth, the Prophet perseveres in the same admonitions, so that the Jews may cease thinking or doing evil, since they should know that they will be destroyed by divine powers.

In the fifth, the Lord Christ cries out to the Father that his prayer may be heard and, in his resurrection, may grant benefits to the world.

Sixth, throughout the whole Psalm the words are those of a penitent; six others of the same kind are joined to it, although they are described in the conclusion of Psalm 50.

In the seventh part, Christ humbly asks that the Father come to his aid, but he possesses confidence in the uprightness of his conduct, which pertains more to his divinity. Yet, according to the manner of the humanity he assumed, he asks that help be given to him, lest the devil seize his soul through wicked presumption and his glory, brought down into the dust, perish.

In the eighth, the drama that follows proceeds through gathered parables and figurative allusions, and everything is referred to the Lord Christ through allegorical likenesses. We shall point out these figures in the most suitable places with the greatest clarity, so that every ambiguity may be removed from the diligent reader.

Ninth: after the many proclamations of praise, which are assigned now to his divinity and now to his humanity, with persons and titles changed, comes *Alleluia*, which means: “Praise the Lord.”

[Col. 1417C]

Tenth: the Gradual Psalms follow, leading our spirit toward the Lord and Savior through pure and humble satisfaction.

Eleventh: with words varied, it again celebrates the praises of the Lord in hymnic exultation, at one time praying to the majesty of the Father, at another to that of the Son, and at another to that of the Holy Spirit, so that no one may doubt that the Holy Trinity, singularly omnipotent, wills to act in heaven and on earth.

Twelfth: seven Psalms are left at the end, which with hymnic exultations celebrate together, with devoted mind, the entire glory of the Holy Trinity.

Thus the text of the whole Psalter, divided into twelve parts in the number of the Apostles, concludes with wondrous praise, so that it too may do what we know Christ’s disciples did.

There is also another, more evident sacrament of the same matter: for the earth was cleansed of its sins when the flood prevailed for 150 days. In the same way, these Psalms, extended to that number, appropriately render the human race, polluted by its sins, absolved.

“Serve the Lord in fear.” This is a brief and plain admonition, by which we are urged to serve the Lord God not with slavish fear but with a loving fear. And lest the service of God perhaps be thought exceedingly harsh, he added:

“And rejoice in him,” because the fear of the Lord leads not to misery but to joy. And again, lest this rejoicing should become careless, he added: “with trembling.”

“Give heed to my words, O Lord; understand my cry” (Ps. 5:2). By saying, “Give heed to my words,” he signifies the psalmody of the mouth. He continues, “understand my cry,” so that he might open the affection of the heart. For this voice was not the rattling of the lips but the affection of the heart.

“Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength; we shall sing and psalm your powers.” To sing is to utter the Lord’s words with the mouth. To sing psalms, however, is constantly to fulfill the divine commandments through good works. These two things are required of us in every way: that we faithfully sing the Lord’s praises with our mouths and perform his commandments in our works.

“You who fear the Lord, praise him.” He says “you who fear the Lord” because human fear does not produce praise but reproach. The fear of God, however, because it is just and upright, produces praise, grants love, and kindles the ardor of charity, since no one is worthy to proclaim God except one who is known also to fear him. Therefore he said: “you who fear, praise.”

“With you is my praise in the great Church; I shall fulfill my vows in the presence of those who fear him.” Our praise ought to be with God—that is, concerning God—and this in the Catholic Church, so that our vows may be acceptable to God, since we offer them before those who fear him.

“That I may hear the voice of your praise and recount all your wonders.” Perhaps he desired to hear that voice of praise with which the angels of the Lord praise God, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3). Today the holy Church sings this in the celebration of the Mass. For whenever we sing this praise devoutly, we are undoubtedly joined to the voices of the angels.

“Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory.” By the beauty of the house he does not mean the beauty of the walls or the most precious furnishings of the services, but the quality of good actions, which consists in the jubilation of the Psalms, the holiness of prayers, and the deepest devotion of the Christian people.

“Sing psalms to the Lord, you his saints, and confess the memory of his holiness.” Those who are holy are commanded to sing psalms to the Lord, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9). The memory of his holiness must be confessed and praised; remembering the human race mercifully, it brings about what enables him to save us.

[Col. 1418D]

“Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous.” Let the unrighteous rejoice in the world. When the world ends, the rejoicing of the unrighteous ends. But let the righteous rejoice in the Lord, because, while the Lord remains, the rejoicing of the righteous will remain.

“Rejoice in the Lord”: it is fitting that we praise him who alone possesses nothing displeasing to us. “Praise is fitting for the upright” (Ps. 32:1). Those are upright who direct their hearts according to the will of God and praise God both in prosperity and in tribulation.

“Confess to the Lord on the lyre; sing psalms to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.” The lyre has wood below it, upon which the strings are placed; when touched, they resound. The psaltery, however, has the wood itself above.

By the lyre is understood earthly prosperity or adversity. Therefore, confess on the lyre: whether something earthly abounds for you, give thanks to the one who gave it; whether it is lacking or perhaps taken away through loss, likewise give thanks. For the one who gave has not been taken away from you, even if what he gave has been taken away; if he wishes, he is able to bestow more upon you.

By the psaltery are signified the commandments given to human beings from heaven. It is called a ten-stringed psaltery because there are ten words of the law; if we fulfill them, we sing perfectly to God on the psaltery.

“Confess to the Lord on the lyre,” and so forth. These are the righteous whom he previously said sing the Lord’s praise with devoted melody through holy actions.

As was already said in the preface, the lyre is the excessive hollowing of a wooden belly, which, sending the threads of its strings upward, speaks through the sweetest sounds when struck. It received this name because it is struck in rapid repetition.

Works that are extended from earthly things toward heavenly grace are rightly compared with it: when we feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and so forth. Although these things may appear bodily, they are nevertheless performed out of love for divinity.

We also play the lyre when, amid our sufferings or losses, we say confidently and joyfully: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

We have said that the psaltery is ten-stringed. In the reverse arrangement, it has the belly of the lyre above, from which the melodious strings descend toward the lower part. The commandments of the Decalogue are appropriately fitted to it, because according to the form of this instrument we receive the Lord’s commands coming from above.

And consider that it is the only musical instrument called “ten-stringed” on account of its excellence. For we do not remember reading this of the lyre or of other instruments of this kind.

The ten-stringed psaltery, as the ancients said, also indicates this sacrament to us, so that we may refer three commandments to God, who is Trinity:

First: “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exod. 20:3).
