Second: “You shall not make for yourself a graven image” (ibid., 4).

Third: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (ibid., 7).

To these he joins the commandment concerning the Sabbath.

The seven that follow, they said, pertain to love of one’s neighbor:

“Honor your father and your mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not speak false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not desire his wife” (Exod. 20:12–17).

Thus the complete power of the ten-stringed psaltery is shown to be perfect and worthy of honor.

We also sing on ten strings when we conduct ourselves commendably through the five bodily senses and the five spiritual senses. Yet these things of which we speak are not placed outside us, as they are in the discipline of music. The lyre is within us; the psaltery is within us. Indeed, we ourselves are the instruments when, by the Lord’s grace, we strive to imitate them through the quality of our actions.

This is also understood from that example where he says: “In me, O God, are vows which I shall render to you as praises” (Ps. 55:12). These and similar statements, as we have often said, are expressed through figurative allusions.

“Sing to him a new song; sing psalms to him well in jubilation.” Sing a new song: put off the old self. The new song does not belong to old people. Sing psalms to him well, in heart and voice, lest perhaps he be displeased with it. For God does not wish his ears to be offended.

The one who sings in jubilation embraces such great praise of God with the Savior in his heart that he cannot fulfill it with his voice. Yet no one can sing psalms well in that jubilation unless he has joined to it a zeal for good conduct.

I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth [Col. 1420B]. You must praise and bless God not only when you come to offer him praise, but at all times—that is, you must show yourself to be such that, even if your tongue is silent, your life praises God. Whether you are in prosperity or adversity, always praise God. When you have earthly prosperity, praise God, who gave it. When adversity comes, likewise praise God, by whose just judgment it happens that adversity befalls you. The one who is humble praises God at all times. What does it mean to be humble? It means not to wish to be praised in oneself. Whoever wishes to be praised in himself is proud; and whoever is proud cannot praise the Lord at all times.

To proclaim your righteousness well in the great Church; behold, I will not restrain my lips. He proclaims the righteousness of God well in the Catholic Church who lives well, and who, in praising and proclaiming God, does not become sluggish, but by his example urges others to praise God [Col. 1420C].

Sing psalms to our God, sing psalms; sing psalms to our King, sing psalms. To show this salutary work, he repeated “sing psalms” four times. To sing psalms is to sing praises to God through good actions; and, if this is properly performed, it is shown to be something we share even with the angels. “Sing psalms to our King”: he says this of Christ, not of another, for this praise is fitting for him.

For God is King of all the earth; sing psalms wisely. He truly is King of all the earth, to whom we must sing psalms wisely, so that we may sing psalms not only by singing but also by understanding. No one does anything wisely that he does not understand.

[Col. 1420D] Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and pay your vows to the Most High. Who sacrifices a sacrifice of praise to God, unless he has been separated from earthly vices [Edit. Basil: “who dies to the world, so that he may become a door for Christ”]? For the Lord is not pleased if a morally disgraceful person sings his praises. By a morally disgraceful person I mean one who has been made disgraceful through vices and sins, because the Lord must be sung to with heart, voice, and deed; whoever sings in this way praises God perfectly.

The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God. This is directed against those who, though unworthy, presumed to sing the praises of the Lord. “The sacrifice of praise will honor me”—not the kind sung by the wicked, but the kind that a pure mind is accustomed to offer. [Col. 1421A] For that sacrifice of praise honors the Lord which has been offered with purity of faith and uprightness of action. It follows: “And there is the way.” He calls the most blessed psalmody a way. But he explains where this way leads: “By which I shall show him the salvation of God.” It is a glorious path that leads to the Creator of heaven and earth. Yet this way that has been mentioned is walked not with feet but by holy minds, because, while one is delighted by the sweetness and pleasantness of song, the grace of compunction is generated in the heart through divine visitation. Hence another psalm says: “A sacrifice to God is a spirit troubled; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.” From this sacrifice, in which the spirit is humbled, streams of tears are accustomed to flow, because, when it is troubled according to God, it grants us the absolution [Col. 1421B] of sins. God does not despise this sacrifice; rather, he approves it, chooses it, and admits it into his presence.

My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and recite a psalm to the Lord. He says that he has his heart ready to give thanks to the Lord rather than to seek worldly honors and ambitions. He says that he will sing, that is, give thanks with his voice. To recite a psalm, however, is to praise the Lord through an action worthy of proclamation.

Thus I will recite a psalm to your name for ever and ever, that I may pay my vows day by day. Let us too pay our vows in this passing day, so that, with his assistance, we may deserve to sing the praises of the Lord in that eternity.

[Col. 1421C] Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; recite a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise. He exhorts every human being to psalmody, so that by such confession he may give thanks to the Lord’s name. He gives glory to his praise who celebrates the Lord’s proclamations with continual rejoicing.

Let all the earth adore you and sing psalms to you; let it recite a psalm to your name, O Most High. This is what we must truly offer to the Lord: that he be adored—that is, that God be believed in with the heart—to whom we are commanded to sing psalms, that is, to resound his mighty works with the sweetness of psalmody. To recite a psalm means to confess the Lord through good works.

Sing to God; recite a psalm to his name; prepare a way for him who rises above the setting place; the Lord is his name [Col. 1421D]. Rejoice in his presence. He sings to God who always contemplates him with a pure and faithful mind. He recites a psalm to his name who performs the works that he commanded. It follows: “Prepare a way for him,” that is, prepare your purified hearts, which the holy Lord may deign to enter. He added:

“Rejoice in his presence.” Not in the presence of human beings, where joy is fleeting, but in his presence, where purity of mind continually delights itself.

Princes went before, joined with those who sing psalms. He indicates a united multitude of those singing psalms, who resounded the Lord’s praises both with their voice and with good works.

[Col. 1422A] Telling of the praises of the Lord and his powers, and of his wonders, which he has done. To tell of the Lord’s deeds is to have praised him, for whenever his works are recounted, his glory is always increased.

Blessed is the people that knows jubilation. That people is blessed which sings God’s praises not only with its mouth but also understands them by the light of the mind. To understand means to take care to examine the holy Scriptures according to catholic principles.

On the ten-stringed psaltery, with a song upon the lyre. The ten-stringed psaltery signifies the ten commandments of the Law; we truly sing them when we fulfill them in action. He sings with the lyre who performs good works without the harshness of sadness.

Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout joyfully to God our Savior [Col. 1422B]. Like some herald of the judge, the cock that awakens the people of the Church, he invites those who pray to awaken from the sleep of this age and to sing praises to the Lord with joyful exultation. And because there is an exultation of this age that chiefly occupies human minds, he therefore admonished us that, when we come, we should rejoice and shout not for the age but for the Lord.

Let us anticipate his face in confession, and let us shout joyfully to him in psalms. To anticipate is to do something before the one believed to be coming can be seen. Therefore, before the Lord comes, let us confess to him—that is, let us render praises to the Lord with religious devotion. Let us also shout joyfully to him in psalms, that is, let us offer the gladness of the heart through the modulation of psalmody. In the work of praise and psalmody, both things must be joined together [Col. 1422C], so that the office of our tongue may be fulfilled with a corresponding joy.

Sing a new song to the Lord; sing to the Lord, all the earth. He sings a new song to the Lord who, having put off the old person and been happily renewed through the grace of baptism, praises the Lord. This is the song that consoles the purest mind; this is the melody that delights to the core when the soul truly sings, believing that by God’s grace it has been freed from sins.

Sing to the Lord and bless his name; proclaim his salvation from day to day. We are commanded to sing to the Lord and bless his name not merely in the course of a single day, but “from day to day,” that is, always, according to the custom of the holy Church.

[Col. 1422D] Sing a new song to the Lord, because he has done wonders. The prophet admonishes faithful Christians to rejoice in the exultation of the new song, since the coming of Christ the Lord has been confessed as wondrous. The new person ought to sing a new song, not the old one who, not yet laying aside Adam’s sins [Adae, Edit. Basil], persists in the transgression of the old person.

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing, rejoice, and sing psalms. “To shout joyfully” means to leap forth into the joy of the voice with great delight. To sing is for the mouth of a most serious Christian to resound with praises to the Lord. To rejoice is to declare the desires of the soul with great feeling [Col. 1423A]. To sing psalms, however, is to fulfill the Lord’s commandments through good works.

Sing psalms to the Lord on the lyre, on the lyre and with the voice of a psalm. He sings psalms to the Lord on the lyre who performs the commandments of divinity through bodily action. He added “with the voice of a psalm” so that God might be sung to not only in deed but also in voice.

Shout joyfully to the Lord, all the earth; serve the Lord in gladness. This is the perfect devotion of the righteous: to serve the Lord with gladness of mind, just as the Apostle also admonishes: “Always rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things. This is the will of God in Christ Jesus.” Although the Lord’s servants may appear to carry out their service through different offices—ecclesiastical orders, monasteries, assemblies of the faithful, hermits, solitaries, laypeople, and the devout [Col. 1423B]—all are properly directed to this: that the Lord be served with gladness, not in murmuring or bitterness of mind.

Praise his name, for the Lord is sweet. So that no one might think that he would become weary from praising, or grow tired through continual labor, he gave the reason why his name should be praised: namely, because the Lord is sweet, his mercy is eternal, and his truth endures for ever and ever.

I will sing psalms and understand in the blameless way. When will you come to me? He sings psalms to the Lord who strives to please him by his good deeds. This is the most pleasing virtue of harmony: when the voice is recognized to accord with one’s deeds. For if these two things disagree with one another in discordant variation, they cannot possibly produce a measured song of psalmody. What confounds itself through mutual contradiction does not reach the Lord’s ears. But if that disciplined psalmody is properly directed to the Lord, see what it accomplishes: it causes one to understand the blameless way, when the Lord may deign to come to him—the Lord whom he was eagerly awaiting.

Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion; bless the Lord, O my soul. Since all things are his work, everything ought to bless its creator. And just as no creature is commanded to be excluded from the Lord’s praises, so no place is left outside such a duty. When it says [Edit. Basil: “it is said”], “in every place,” it signifies the Church [Edit. Basil adds: “the Catholic Church”]. For she blesses the Lord everywhere [Col. 1423D], praises him everywhere, and celebrates his greatest thanks with hymn-like [Edit. Basil: hymnodic] exultation. Let us therefore bless the Lord together as one; let us celebrate his works with hymn-like exultation. For what sacrilege it is that, when every creature is commanded to bless the Lord, a human being should cease to praise God, who is known to have been created in his image and likeness.

Confess to the Lord and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. “Confess,” that is, praise him, and acquire for yourselves the grace of divinity through good deeds, because to praise the Lord means both to render him honor with the mouth and to carry out his commands through works. When he says, “Proclaim his works among the nations,” he admonishes the pastors of the Church to proclaim God’s mighty works without ceasing [Col. 1424A].

His praise remains for ever and ever. His praise is enclosed by no [Edit. Basil: “not by any”] limit. Therefore whoever desires to praise him in the eternal homeland must devote himself continually to the praises of God in the present age.

Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. The voice of the apostles commands all nations to praise the Lord in the holy Church. It is a common praise: the praise of all the faithful brought together as one, when the whole Church continually praises the Lord. This must always be done. But especially at the appointed times it must be done by every believer, so that he may be joined with the saints in their praises.

[Col. 1424B] Your ordinances were songs for me. When he says “songs,” he signifies that psalmody is to be performed with great delight, as the Apostle says: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to God.” Song always lightens labors and does not allow weariness to steal into the mind, which is caressed by the great sweetness of contemplation.

At midnight I rose to confess to you—that is, to praise you. He rightly rises to praise at such a time, because at midnight, as the Gospel says, the bridegroom came, lest he be found among the foolish virgins with the door shut.

Seven times a day I praised you. He signifies those seven occasions by which the whole Church consoles itself: matins, terce, sext, none, lucernary—that is, vespers—and nocturnal compline [Col. 1424C]. At these times, if the whole Church praises God, those who have been ordained for this purpose ought especially to do so.

Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants. That is: you who are servants of the Lord, praise him with willing submission. For if you praise well, you acquire grace; but if you neglect him, you will be condemned for neglected [service] owed to him.

I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard the words of my mouth; in the presence of the angels I will sing psalms to you. How strong and complete this confession is, is shown by the union of the whole heart. For when it says “with my whole heart,” no part occupied by the ambition of this age is left behind; rather, the whole and undivided heart is applied, as is fitting, to the praises of the Creator [Col. 1424D].

In the presence of the angels I will sing psalms to you. Here the power of psalmody is revealed: whoever sings psalms with a pure heart among human beings appears also to sing above with the angels.

I pour out my prayer in his presence. It says “in his presence” because divinity observes good prayers. And although our will cannot be seen by human beings, it is nevertheless certain that God attends to it.

Praise the Lord, O my soul. So that the will might not remain idle in earthly desires, and the mind’s attention be occupied, as usual, with foolish cares [Col. 1425A], the prophet gives himself the salutary counsel that his soul should praise the Lord. Hence he promises:

I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am. He says that he delights in the praises of the Lord, lest he be occupied by the enticements of the world that bring harm.

Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good. Let praise be pleasing to our God. Let us therefore praise him with whatever devotion we can, and here let us meditate on those blessed gifts. For what is happier than to practice now what you hope to be able to perform in future blessedness?

Let praise be pleasing to our God. Praise is pleasing to our God when voice and life come together in one fellowship. For what sort of thing is it if a psalm speaks of chastity, while the singer does not withdraw from obscenity? If it preaches humility, while its speaker swells with proud utterances [Col. 1425B]?

Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. What should be said of this psalm and of the other two that follow, in which every creature is summoned to praise God? At the end it says: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” If every creature is urged to praise God, how much more should the human being, who possesses understanding and surpasses all creatures, praise God, since he was made in the image of God? He ought to praise the one who made us and, when we were lost, redeemed us from the slavery of the devil and in his mercy granted us the heavenly kingdoms. Therefore the service of God must be undertaken in every way with the greatest zeal, so that we may reach the joys he has promised.

Cassiodorus says in the conclusion of Psalm XXIV:

[Col. 1425C] The twenty-four elders celebrate the Lord together with tireless voices and sweet melody, admonishing us to sing psalms with continual devotion in imitation of them.

The same author, in the conclusion of Psalm XXXII:

The blessed have their own music, which enters the hearing of the faithful soul; its sound does not cease, nor does its attention grow weary. Therefore abandon, lovers of spectacles, your deadly pleasures, and gather instead for these joys, for these mysteries, where lyre and organ stir up virtues, not the desires of depraved pleasure [ms. “will,” less suitably].

The same author, in the conclusion of Psalm XXXIII:

The sacred mysteries of this psalm have been completed, and the order of the Mass has been brought to its fulfillment in such a way that you might think it had been written in Christian times [Col. 1425D]. Here too the order of the hymns has run its course; here the devout people are commanded to approach communion; here those who are receiving the first rudiments of the faith are invited to come, so that all may praise God in concord.

The same author, on Psalm CXVII:

We read in the Apocalypse of John that a great multitude of saints sing “Alleluia” in heaven; the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders also adore the Lord and say it. The whole heavenly army celebrates together in the voice of a very great trumpet, with hymn-like exultation.

The same author, on Psalm CXXXIV:

After the most beautiful construction of the Gradual, which reaches that summit that makes people secure and happy for eternity, “Alleluia” is most fittingly placed, so that the holy Church may enjoy the Lord’s praises, for which she is known to have been prepared by such a gift. Therefore let us hasten to say “Alleluia” with sincere minds, so that by divine grace we may be joined to them [Edit. Basil: “to that holy people”].

The same author, in the conclusion of Psalm CXXXIV:

This is a wondrous psalm for instructing the most devout peoples. For after such great benefits we can offer nothing except that, as was said at the beginning, we proclaim our Lord with a threefold confession. Let us praise the Father, let us praise the Son, let us praise the Holy Spirit, the one and almighty God, so that, just as there is not a different substance in him, so there may be no diversity in that praise itself [Col. 1426B]. This is truly the praise that refreshes us; this is the nourishment by which the devout soul is fattened. It is both our reward and our work. Through it we are so refreshed that no pleasure seems comparable. Let us therefore proclaim him now, so that we may deserve to praise him eternally with the angels.

The same author, on Psalm CXLV:

Behold, once again heavenly authority resounds in our ears and strikes at the doors of the heart with “Alleluia,” lest we be occupied with empty and worthless thoughts, since a soldier of Christ ought not to have idle time. The tongue also has its fruits. Indeed, a most abundant harvest is gathered from it if it is moved to the praises of the Lord with a pure mind. It is a spiritual member when it serves its Creator [Col. 1426C]; it also commends the soul itself when it speaks the truth. Therefore let us fill the air with the sweetest sounds. For this salutary music not only delights the hearing of mortals but also pleases the angelic understanding.

The same author, on Psalm CXLVIII:

This part of the prayer is confined to a few syllables, but, when considered, it is always extended. For it sends forth the sweetest new meanings when the mind’s attention examines it. When it is spoken by the reader, it is a proclamation of praise; when it is answered by the people, it is a hymn. Thus one voice accomplishes so diverse a mystery, although nothing in it appears to have been changed. This psalm must be treated with subtlety, because through the brief mention of a few creatures the prophet urges all creatures [Col. 1426D] to sing the Lord’s praises: rational and intellectual creatures in themselves, and those lacking intellect or sense through those creatures that praise the Lord’s works with the wisest consideration.

The same author, in the final conclusion of the Psalms:

For what could you fail to find in this heavenly treasury of the divine Scriptures? Do you seek the origin of the world? Here it is explained how the world was fashioned. Prophecies [Edit. Basil: “prophets,” perhaps]? Who has spoken so much about the Lord’s incarnation? Do you desire the Gospel? It clearly sets forth the passion and resurrection of Christ the Lord in countless places. Do you want the Apostle? Listen to the teacher [Col. 1427A]; listen to him who shows mercy, who proclaims the future judgments for the sake of correction and frequently intercedes for sinners. And, not to prolong matters: whatever is done in heaven and on earth, in the sea or among the dead, if you read with the greatest care, you will recognize that everything has been appropriately placed in its proper locations. The magnificent discourse of Bishop Athanasius is a witness to this: examining the powers of the psalms with penetrating truth, he proves that everything contained within the compass of sacred Scripture is present there. He even makes the nature of God understood, if it is permissible, in two words. “I today”—something that no books or writings can successfully contain, as has been explained: what is briefly said is understood in part, while what is left unsaid is perceptible in some measure. For in the second psalm the Father says to the Son: “I have begotten you today.” [Col. 1427B] In these two words he subtly signifies something that seems capable of transcending human understanding.

It embraces the New and Old Testament with such completeness that you may truly understand a spiritual library to have been constructed in this book. For if paradise is considered desirable because the courses of four rivers are known to make it pleasant, how much happier is the soul that is watered by the springs of 150 psalms? Nor did divine power operate only within this number; many further and varied miracles lie open, whether partly understood or still entirely unknown.

Here begin the sayings of Saint Isidore concerning temples. (Ibid., *On the Offices*, book I, chapter 2.)

[Col. 1427C] Moses the lawgiver first built the tabernacle for the Lord; Solomon later established the temple in order to seek wisdom. After these, the faith of our own times consecrated throughout the world the courts of Christ.

The things celebrated in the ecclesiastical offices are found to have been established partly by the authority of the holy Scriptures, partly by apostolic tradition, and partly by the custom of the universal Church. Therefore, retracing their beginnings and the authorities from whom they arose, let us report them, as we said above.

(The chapter concerning the Church and the names of Christians is not present in the manuscript.)

## Concerning choirs

Moses first instituted choirs after the crossing of the Red Sea; with the two sexes arranged in distinct groups, he leading together with his sister, he thoroughly taught them to sing a triumphant song to God in choirs [Col. 1427D]. A choir derives its name from the image of a crown, and is so called for that reason. Hence the book of Ecclesiasticus writes of a priest standing before the altar, with a crown of brothers around him (Ecclus. 50:13). Properly speaking, a choir is a multitude of singers. Among the Jews it consists of no fewer than ten singers; among us, however, it consists of an indeterminate number, whether fewer or many, without any distinction.

## Concerning songs

Moses first introduced the song when, after Egypt had been struck by ten plagues and Pharaoh had been drowned, the Israelite people went out rejoicing by the unfamiliar paths of the sea toward the desert, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord gloriously,” and so forth (Exod. 15:2). Later Deborah, a woman of no small distinction in the book of Judges, is found to have carried out this ministry. Afterward, many men and women filled with the divine Spirit are said to have sung the mysteries of God. A song, however, is a human voice, whereas a psalm is what is sung to the psaltery.

## Concerning psalms

The Church reveals, in a great mystery, that after Moses the prophet David was the first to make use of psalms. From childhood he was specially chosen by God for this ministry and deserved to become the leader of singers and the treasury of psalms. For this reason the Church frequently uses his psaltery with the melody of sweet songs, [Col. 1428B] so that minds may more easily be bent toward compunction. The primitive Church sang psalms in such a way that the singer’s voice resonated with only a slight inflection, making him closer to one who recites than to one who sings. The custom of singing was established in the Church for the sake of the carnal, not the spiritual, so that those who are not moved to compunction by the words might be moved by the sweetness of the melody. Thus the most blessed Augustine, in book ten of his *Confessions*, approves the custom of singing in the Church, saying that “through the delight of the ears, the weaker mind may rise to an affection of piety.” For, he says, “our minds are moved more religiously and ardently toward an affection of piety by the holy words themselves when they are sung than when they are not sung.” For all our affections, according to the diversity or [Col. 1428C] novelty of sounds, are stirred more strongly by some hidden familiarity when the words are sung with a pleasing and skillful voice.

## Concerning hymns

It is clear that the same prophet David first composed and sang hymns, and afterward other prophets did so as well. Later, the three young men placed in the furnace, having summoned all creation, sang a hymn to the Creator of all things. Thus, in singing hymns and psalms, we have the example not only of the prophets but also of the Lord himself and the apostles, as well as useful instructions on this matter for moving the soul piously and inflaming its love of God. There are divine hymns, and there are also hymns composed by human ingenuity. Hilary, a Gallic bishop of Poitiers, distinguished for his eloquence, first flourished in the composition of hymns [Col. 1428D]. After him, Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a man of great glory in Christ and a most illustrious teacher in the Church, is known to have excelled more abundantly in this kind of composition. Hence hymns are called Ambrosian after his name, because they first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan in his time. The devotion of this observance was afterward maintained throughout the Churches of the West. Any songs that are sung in praise of God are called hymns.

## Concerning antiphons

The Greeks first composed antiphons, with two choirs singing alternately, like two seraphim and the two Testaments crying out to one another. Among the Latins, however, the most blessed Ambrose was the first to establish antiphons, imitating the example of the Greeks [Col. 1429A]. From then on their use became widespread throughout all the western regions.

## Concerning responsories

Responsories were discovered by the Italians long ago. They were given this name because, while one person sings, the choir responds in harmony. Formerly each person performed this alone; now sometimes one, sometimes two or three sing together, while the choir responds for the most part.

## Concerning praises [Edit. Paris: “concerning Alleluia”]

Lauds—that is, the singing of “Alleluia”—are ancient, according to the custom of the Hebrews. Its interpretation consists in two words: “the praise of God.” Concerning its mystery, John reports in the Apocalypse that, by revelation of the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of the heavenly army of angels, like the voice of mighty thunder and like the voice of many waters, saying “Alleluia” (Apoc. 19:6). From this no one ought to doubt that this mystery of praise, if celebrated with worthy faith and devotion, is joined to the angels.

“Alleluia,” like “amen,” is not translated from Hebrew into another language, not because it cannot at all be interpreted, but, as the teachers say, because its antiquity is preserved for the sake of more sacred authority.

In the regions of Africa, however, “Alleluia” is not sung at all times but only on Sundays and during the fifty days after the Lord’s resurrection, as a sign of the future resurrection and of joy [Col. 1429C]. Among us, in accordance with the ancient tradition of the Spanish Churches, “Alleluia” is sung at all times except on days of fasting or during Lent. For it is written: “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2). The fact that “Alleluia” is sung at the end after the completion of the psalms or the proclamation of the readings is done by the Church in hope of the future, signifying that after the proclamation of the kingdom of heaven—which is proclaimed to the world in this life through both Testaments—our activity will consist in nothing except the praise of God. For it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). Hence the Book of Psalms also concludes with praise, so that the same eternal praise may be shown after the end of the age [Col. 1429D].

(The chapters concerning the offertories, the Mass and prayers, the Nicene Creed, blessings upon the people, the sacrifice, and so forth, have been omitted.)

## Concerning the offices of the third, sixth, and ninth hours

Daniel and the three young men devoted the third, sixth, and ninth hours to supplications, namely so that, from daybreak until the time of prayer, the three extended hours might declare reverence for the Trinity to us; likewise, from the third hour to the sixth and from there to the ninth, the Trinity, invoked three times a day, might be worshiped through equal intervals of light bounded by fixed measurements. This also contributes to the proof of the venerable Trinity: the Holy Spirit descended to earth at the third hour, that is, in his proper place, [Col. 1430A] number, and time, to fill the grace that Christ had promised. At the sixth hour Christ suffered; at the ninth he extended the torments of the cross. Through such a sacrament, at the lawful times for prayer, the perfection of the Trinity is either praised in celebrations or obtained through prayers during the three-hour periods. And if the daytime celebration is counted through the number four until the vespertine office—that is, four times [Edit. Paris: “fourfold”]—this signifies that the world, divided in four ways, is saved in the Trinity. Indeed, even in the night, military watches and vigils are assigned in four divisions, determined by periods of three hours, so that in these nocturnal and worldly offices also the mystery of the Trinity may be revered.

## Concerning vespers

The vespertine office, the office at the end of the day, is the setting of the day’s alternating light; its solemn celebration comes from the Old Testament. In former times it was customary at this hour to offer sacrifices, burn them upon the altar, and burn spices and incense. The hymn-like [Edit. Paris: “hymnodic”] royal and priestly figure who performed this office bears witness to this, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2). In the New Testament also, at that time, while the apostles were dining, our Lord and Savior first handed on the mystery of his body and blood, so that the time itself might indicate the evening of the age. Therefore, in honor and remembrance of such great mysteries, it is fitting that at these times we should appear in the sight of God, resound in his worship, offer him the sacrifice of our prayers, and rejoice together in his praises [Col. 1430C]. Vespers is named from the star called Vesper, which rises as the sun departs. Concerning it the prophet says: “And you cause Vesper to go forth over the children of human beings” (Job 38:32).

## Concerning compline

Concerning the celebration of compline, we also find an example among the Fathers, with the prophet David saying: “If I ascend upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob” (Ps. 131:3). Who would not be astonished at such devotion of the soul in the love of God, that he forbade himself sleep—without which human bodies certainly fail—until the king and prophet found a place and temple to be built for the Lord in his breast [Col. 1430D]? This ought powerfully to admonish us that, if we ourselves wish to be the Lord’s place and his tabernacle, or desire to be regarded as a temple of the Holy Spirit, we should imitate the examples of the saints as far as we can, lest what is understood be said of us: “They slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75).

## Concerning vigils

The authority of vigils is ancient, and devotion to vigils was a familiar good among all the saints. The prophet Isaiah finally cries out to God, saying: “My spirit keeps vigil for you from the night, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth.” David likewise says: “At midnight I rose to confess to you, because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. 118). At this time the destroying angel passed through and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians. Therefore we too ought to keep vigil, lest we be mixed with the danger of the Egyptians. In the Gospel the Savior also asserted that he would come at these same hours. Hence he taught his hearers to keep watch, and, awakening them, said: “Blessed are those servants whom, when their lord comes, he finds watching. And if he finds them at the evening hour,” he says, “or at midnight, or at cockcrow, watching, they are blessed. Therefore you also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not know.”

For he taught vigils not only in words [Col. 1431B] but also confirmed them by example. The Gospel testifies that Jesus spent the night in the prayer of God (Luke 6). Paul and Silas are likewise remembered to have been praying in the public prison around midnight and, though bound, to have spoken a hymn while all listened. Suddenly an earthquake occurred, the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors opened of their own accord, and everyone’s chains were loosed. Therefore at these hours we ought to maintain frequent psalmody and prayer in the holy offices, and await our end—or, if it should come—more securely while engaged in such an activity.

There is, however, a certain kind of heretics who consider sacred vigils superfluous and unproductive in spiritual work. They say that divine ordinances are violated by those who do this, since God made the night for rest just as he made the day for labor. These heretics are called in Greek νυκτάζοντες (*nyktazontes*), that is, “sleepy ones” or “somnolent people” [Note: [Col. 1431D] *Nyctages Nystatae*. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book III, chapter 3].

## Concerning matins
## On the Antiquity and Authority of Matins

The same prophet David bears witness to the antiquity and authority of Matins, saying: “In the morning I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper” (Psalm 62). And elsewhere: “My eyes have anticipated you at dawn, that I might meditate on your words” (Psalm 118).

Cassian, however, says:

The office of the morning solemnity, instituted at a time still recent, was first established in the monastery at Bethlehem, where our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born of the Virgin for the redemption and salvation of the human race; and from that time the custom of celebrating it spread throughout the whole world. We pray at dawn for this reason: that Christ’s resurrection may be celebrated. For when the light of morning shone forth, the Lord and Savior rose from the underworld; then the light began to rise for the faithful, a light that had set for sinners when Christ died. Indeed, at that same time all are believed to receive the hope of the future resurrection, when the righteous, and all people, will rise from this temporal death as though from the sleep of slumber and awaken.

### Another rule of Saint Benedict: how the divine offices are to be performed during the day

[Note: From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 16.]

As the prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (same source). We shall fulfill this sacred number seven in the following manner: by performing the offices of our service at Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. For concerning these divine hours the Prophet said: “Seven times a day I have praised you.” Concerning the nocturnal vigils, the same Prophet says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Psalm 118). Therefore, at these times let us offer praises to our Creator for the judgments of his justice—that is, at Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline—and let us rise at night to give thanks to him.

## On the Discipline of Psalmody

[Note: Same source, chapter 19.]

We believe that the divine presence is everywhere, and that the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked in every place; yet we must believe this especially and without any doubt when we attend the divine office. Therefore, let us always remember what the Prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Psalm 2); and again: “Sing psalms wisely” (Psalm 46); and: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you” (Psalm 137). Let us therefore consider how we ought to be in the presence of the Divinity and of his angels; and let us stand for psalmody in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice.

## On Reverence in Prayer

If we wish to make some request of powerful human beings, we presume to do so only with humility and reverence; how much more, then, must we entreat the Lord God of all things with complete humility and devoted purity. Let us know that we are heard not through many words, but through purity of heart and compunction expressed in tears. Therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure, unless it is extended by the fervor of inspiration from divine grace. In an assembly, however, prayer should be shortened altogether, and when the prior gives the sign, all should rise together.

## Another rule: for what virtues each part of the entire course is sung in the Church of God

First, the nocturnal office is sung because of that virtue which God displayed when he killed all the firstborn of Egypt and destroyed all the idols, or when he liberated Paul and Silas from prison. The Evangelist says: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” (Matthew 25).

The cockcrow is sung for this reason: it recalls the time when Saint Peter denied Christ three times during the Passion and was afterward tested and confirmed in the faith.

Matins is so called because Christ rose in the morning, as one Evangelist said: “On the first day of the week they came to the tomb when the sun had already risen.” Another says: “On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene came while it was still dark.” A third says: “In the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first day of the week, because … [lacuna] … who commanded that throughout that whole hour they should praise him together upon the earth.” Then, at his resurrection, he liberated all the souls of the righteous who were in the underworld, because Christ rose in the morning.

Prime is sung for this reason: at that hour the plot was formed against the Son of God, concerning how they might destroy him.

[Col. 1433A] Terce is sung because at that hour the Jews judged the Lord, when they said: “Let Christ be crucified.” At the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles when they had been gathered together in one house. And the Lord said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.”

Sext is sung because at that hour the Lord ascended the cross. Then darkness was made until the ninth hour. At that time the Lord called Paul, when he was persecuting Christians, and said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.” At that time also the voice came to Cornelius, when the Lord said: “Cornelius, your prayer has been heard.”

None is sung because at that hour the Lord gave up his Spirit from the cross; and at the ninth hour the vessel descended to Saint Peter, in which were all things clean and unclean.

Vespers is sung because at that hour Christ supped with his disciples, when he fasted forty days and forty nights. Thus the old law ceased and the new law began.

The twelfth hour is sung because at that time the Lord went up Mount Olivet and prayed alone, and drops of blood fell from his forehead in his sweat. And they prefer the merit expressed in what is said to Adam: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread”; and for this reason he liberated us.

## Sayings of Bede, from a homily on the Gospel concerning Easter

At dawn, therefore, we bring spices to the Lord’s tomb when, mindful of the Passion and death that he endured for us, we show outwardly to our neighbors the works of goodness and inwardly burn in our hearts with the sweetness of pure compunction. This ought to happen at every hour, and especially when we enter the church to pray, and when we approach the altar to receive the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood.

For if the women sought the Lord’s dead body with such care, how much more fitting is it that we—who know that he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and is everywhere present by the power of his divine majesty—should stand before his presence with complete reverence and celebrate his mysteries [we must].

It is rightly said that they carried the spices they had prepared. To prepare beforehand the spices that we carry in the Lord’s service means to cleanse the heart, before the time of prayer, of useless thoughts, so that at the very time of praying we receive nothing filthy into the mind, think about none of the things that pass away, and know how to remember nothing except what we pray for and him himself. This accords with the example of the one who says: “My heart is ready; I will sing and recite a psalm to the Lord.”

For whoever enters the church to pray and, amid the words of supplication, neglects to drive from his mind the habit of useless thoughts is like someone seeking the Lord who has brought spices that were insufficiently prepared. We must believe, above all, that angelic spirits are present with us when they have been specially assigned to divine services—that is, when we enter the church and lend our ears to sacred readings, devote ourselves to psalmody, apply ourselves to prayer, or celebrate the solemnities of the Mass.

[Col. 1434A] Therefore the Apostle instructs women to have a veil over their heads in church, because of the angels. And the Prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you.” Nor may we doubt that, where the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood are celebrated, an assembly of the citizens above is present—those who guard with such diligent watchfulness the tomb in which that venerable body had been placed and from which it departed by rising again.

Therefore, my brothers, we must diligently strive that, when we enter the church either to render the duties of divine praise or to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, we may always remember the angelic presence and, with suitable fear and veneration, complete the heavenly office, following the example of the women devoted to God, who, when angels appeared at the tomb, are said to have been afraid and to have lowered their faces to the ground.

## Sayings of Bede, from a homily on the Canaanite woman

Meanwhile, it must be noted that this persistence in prayer deserves to be fruitful only if, whatever we ask with our mouth, we also meditate upon with our mind, and if the attention of our thoughts is not divided from the cry of our lips.

There are some who, when they enter the church, prolong their psalmody or prayer with many words, while directing their hearts elsewhere; they do not even remember what they are saying. They pray with their mouths, but by allowing their minds to wander outside, they deprive themselves of every fruit of prayer. They think that a prayer is heard by God which they themselves, the ones uttering it, do not hear. No one can fail to perceive that this happens through the prompting of the ancient enemy.

For he knows the benefit of prayer and envies human beings the grace of obtaining what they ask. He sends upon those who pray many kinds of frivolous thoughts, and sometimes even fantasies that are shameful and harmful, by which he obstructs prayer. Thus it sometimes happens that, prostrate in prayer, we endure such great waves of wandering thoughts.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must take care to overcome the devil’s recognized malice: by calming, as far as we can, our minds from such clouds as the enemy delights to scatter, and by continually asking the protection of our merciful defender, who is able to grant even unworthy petitioners the grace both to pray purely and to obtain their requests completely.

The purity of prayer is greatly aided if, in every place and at every time, we restrain ourselves from unlawful deeds; if we always discipline both our hearing and our tongue by abstaining from idle conversations; and if we become accustomed to walk in the law of the Lord and to search his testimonies with our whole heart.

Whatever we habitually do, say, or hear most often must necessarily return again and again to the mind, as to its accustomed and proper dwelling. Just as pigs habitually seek muddy wallows and doves clear streams, so unclean thoughts disturb an impure mind, while spiritual thoughts sanctify a chaste one.

Indeed, if we persevere in prayer and remain steadfast, following the example of the Canaanite woman, the grace of our Creator will be present. It corrects all our errors, sanctifies what is unclean, and calms what is turbulent. For he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from every iniquity, if we cry out to him with the diligent voice of the mind—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Augustine speaks on the praise of the Psalms

You will find all virtues in the Psalms, if you have deserved from God that he reveal the secrets of the Psalms to you. If you wish to do penance for your sins, confess your sins, and ask forgiveness for your offenses, then, as far as you are able—not by the speed of your words, but by thinking and searching with your mind—sing the seven penitential Psalms of David. Their beginnings are: “Lord, rebuke me not in your anger”; two begin, “Lord, hear”; also, “Blessed are they”; “Have mercy on me, O God, according to …”; and “Out of the depths.” You will quickly find the mercy of God illuminating your whole mind with spiritual joy and gladness and promising you great hope of pardon.

If you wish to pray, entrust your mind to the power of the Psalms whose beginnings are: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up”; “In you, O Lord, I have hoped”; “Incline, O Lord”; “O God, come to my assistance”; “O God, in your name”; “May God have mercy on us”; and “Hear, O Lord, my justice.” In no way could you explain your misery, tribulation, and the anguish of various temptations with your own tongue or by human understanding so perfectly, or implore his mercy so effectively, as through these Psalms and others like them.

If you wish to praise almighty God and give thanks to his majesty for all his benefits, by which from the beginning of the world he has shown mercy to the human race in the Old Testament through the patriarchs and prophets, and in the New through the incarnation of his eternal Son, sing those Psalms whose title is “Alleluia.”

These begin with “Give thanks,” or “Praise the Lord,” or “Praise God,” or also “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” You will offer almighty God a gift sweeter than every honey and honeycomb if you continually praise and magnify him with these Psalms.

If you are afflicted by various tribulations, bound on every side by human or spiritual temptations, and seem to yourself to have been abandoned by God—who often abandons the saints for a time in order to test them—and if the temptation seems greater than can be endured, sing inwardly, with your whole mind, those Psalms whose beginnings are: “O God, my God, look upon me”; “Hear, O God, my prayer when I am in tribulation”; and “Save me, O God.” Then the merciful Lord will immediately help you, and you will be able to endure the temptation you suffer.

If the present life has become wearisome to you and nothing below [supplied] delights your mind, contemplate the heavenly homeland and, with ardent desire and attentive mind, sing these Psalms: “As the deer longs”; “How lovely are your dwellings”; and “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn.” The merciful God will soon console your mind.

[Col. 1436B] If you understand that you have been abandoned by God amid tribulations, sing these Psalms with a contrite heart: “How long, O Lord”; “O God, we have heard with our ears”; “Have mercy on me, O Lord”; “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise my petition”; and “In you, O Lord, I have hoped.” Then God will immediately gladden you.

After receiving a period of rest and prosperity, sing these Psalms: “I will bless the Lord at all times”; “Bless the Lord, O my soul”; and “I will exalt you, my God and King.” At every time, whether of prosperity or adversity, always sing the hymn of the three youths, because no mortal can explain the power of this hymn, in which every creature is summoned to praise the Creator.

If you wish to exercise yourself with your whole heart in divine praises, sing the Psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” in which there is scarcely a verse that does not contain either the way of God, or the law, or God’s commandment, precepts, words, justifications, judgments, or sayings.

Remember how Saint Samuel the prophet also taught in the Old Testament, saying: “Prepare your hearts for the Lord, serve him alone, and he will deliver you from the hands of your enemies.”

See how he commands the hymn of the three youths to be sung and summons all creatures, at intervals, to praise God—not as you sing it, confusedly, making no distinction, but by rushing through it and failing to separate the words. This you must correct.
